On Dense 1.7B pretraining, Spectral Sphere reaches AdamW's final validation-loss level in 19% fewer steps and reports the highest average downstream accuracy among compared optimizers (Figure 8 and Table 3).
On MoE 8B-A1B training, Spectral Sphere reports the lowest validation loss and best expert load balance by MaxVio among compared optimizers (Figure 9).
On a 200-layer DeepNet stress test, Spectral Sphere attains lower loss and higher stability than AdamW and other spectral optimizers (Figure 10).

ldCiNVFt8O.text: d2 is a reinforcement-learning framework for masked diffusion language models built around estimating sampling-trajectory likelihoods (Section 3).
d2-AnyOrder provides exact trajectory likelihood with a single model pass for DLMs that support any-order decoding (Section 3).
The paper empirically shows that any-order decoding support is not universal across widely used DLMs (Section 4).
d2-StepMerge approximates trajectory likelihood for standard masked diffusion models with a tractable compute-accuracy tradeoff (Section 3).
d2 reports stronger performance than widely used RL baselines when applied to popular diffusion language models (Section 5).
d2 reports new state-of-the-art diffusion-language-model results on Countdown, Sudoku, GSM8K, and MATH500 reasoning benchmarks (Section 5).

QrC8OgQyOI.text: Prism performs Hierarchical Trajectory Search with stochastic exploration, progressive thinning, and final refinement for discrete diffusion language models (Algorithm 1).
Self-Verified Feedback ranks intermediate completions without loading an external verifier model during pruning (Section 3).
Local branching uses partial remasking to explore alternative completions while preserving high-confidence tokens (Algorithm 1).
Prism achieves comparable or better math/code accuracy than best-of-N decoding with substantially fewer denoising function evaluations on LLaDA 8B, Dream 7B, and LLaDA 2.0-mini (Table 1).
SVF calls are reported as sparse relative to denoising NFE, often below 10% of total NFE (Section 4.3).
Ablations show that removing SVF or remasking lowers GSM8K performance for LLaDA-8B across Prism target widths (Table 4).

r7uOjvZdzO.text: The paper decomposes VLM post-training into visual perception, textual reasoning, and visual reasoning stages with dedicated data for each capability (Section 1).
Its error analysis attributes 86.9% of sampled incorrect Qwen3-VL-8B answers on three visual math datasets to visual perception errors (Section 1).
Staged Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B models outperform their base counterparts on overall visual math and perception benchmark averages (Table 1).
Staged training outperforms merged training on the same base VLMs, including a Qwen3-VL-8B overall average of 65.77 versus 64.67 (Table 2).
Stage-order ablations show that perception-first or perception-early curricula perform better than reversed order on visual math and perception metrics (Table 3).
Stage 1 reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards yields stronger perception and downstream visual math performance than caption-based supervised fine-tuning (Table 4).

oiMjaUbSWp.text: Overparametrized one-hidden-layer ReLU networks (M>M* neurons) exhibit continuous non-identifiability through weight-splitting, where redundant neurons split a true neuron's contribution via coefficients constrained to a simplex, in addition to the discrete permutation symmetries present in exactly-specified models (Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Corollary 2).

Because standard information-theoretic uncertainty measures fail on these non-identifiable parameters, epistemic uncertainty is instead defined via the trace of the posterior weight covariance, EU(y|x) := tr(Cov_P(w|·)), enabling a variance-based decomposition into discrete (permutation) and continuous (splitting) sources of residual uncertainty (Section 2.1, Section 2.2, Example 1).

For one-hidden-layer ReLU networks, Theorem 1 characterizes the induced posterior over splitting coefficients as following symmetric Dirichlet distributions with concentration parameter alpha=(p+1)/2 (Lemma 4), with posterior means of individual redundant neurons scaling as O(M^-1/2) and within-neuron covariance remaining constant while cross-neuron covariance decays as O(M^-1) (Theorem 1, Corollary 1, Section 3.2).

The posterior over splitting coordinates remains non-degenerate even as the number of training samples n approaches infinity, showing that substantial parameter-space uncertainty persists despite the underlying function being fully identified (Section 3.2, Figure 2).

Jva4wVEySO.text: The framework tackles representation fragmentation in few-shot atypical layout-to-image generation by disentangling category-level semantics from instance-level visual primitives through three modules: Semantic Anchoring, which aggregates DINOv2-based cross-attention features across exemplars into stable per-category anchors injected into U-Net layers; Primitive Imbuing, which models fine-grained appearance via learnable visual prototypes fit with closed-form ridge regression (T ≈ WP); and Conceptual Steering, which uses text-driven GradCAM to align generated and ground-truth foreground activation maps (Section 4.2, Section 4.3, Section 4.4).

Evaluated in the 5-shot regime on three atypical layout-to-image benchmarks — DIOR (aerial imagery), RUOD (underwater scenes), and ExDark (low-light scenes) — the method outperforms prior SOTA layout-to-image baselines including MIGC, CC-Diff, and CC-Diff++, e.g. reducing FID by 8.17 versus CC-Diff on DIOR while improving mAP, AP50, and AP75 under Faster R-CNN evaluation across all three domains (Table 1, Section 5.1).

WUK8JIeetF.text: The largest Pixel MeanFlow model (pMF-H/16) achieves 2.22 FID for one-step, latent-free image generation on ImageNet at 256x256 resolution after 360 training epochs, outperforming smaller variants pMF-L/16 (2.52 FID) and pMF-B/16 (3.12 FID) (Table 6).

At 512x512 resolution, Pixel MeanFlow's largest variant (pMF-H/32) achieves 2.48 FID in one step, compared to 2.75 FID for pMF-L/32 and 3.70 FID for pMF-B/32, all operating directly in pixel space without a latent autoencoder (Table 7).

5TiuerrwR8.text: Olaf-World's Seq-Delta-REPA objective aligns integrated latent actions to temporal feature differences from a self-supervised video encoder at the sequence level, rather than within individual clips, grounding action semantics in observable effects to avoid entangling scene-specific cues and to produce a shared coordinate system across contexts.

This sequence-level control-effect alignment yields a more structured latent action space than prior latent-action pretraining approaches, and is shown experimentally to produce stronger zero-shot action transfer across scenes without additional training.

Pretraining latent actions from large-scale unlabeled video via Olaf-World enables more data-efficient adaptation to new control interfaces than state-of-the-art baselines, requiring less labeled/interactive data to transfer to novel control scenarios.

53wE3EbrgK.text: REALISTA achieves higher attack success rates than the strongest realistic-attack baseline SECA on open-source LLMs: 93.60% vs 82.97% ASR@30 on Llama-3-8B, 97.11% vs 79.61% ASR@30 on Llama-3-3B, and 41.61% vs 32.47% ASR@30 on Qwen-2.5-7B, while maintaining comparably low semantic-equivalence and semantic-coherence errors (Table 1, Section 3.2).

In free-form response settings against commercial large reasoning models — where prior realistic attacks (SECA, LARGO, ICD) fail to operate — REALISTA still elicits hallucinations, reaching 23.61% ASR@30 on GPT-5-Nano and 20.72% ASR@30 on GPT-5-Mini, roughly a 20% ASR@30 improvement over raw prompting on both models while keeping semantic errors low (Table 2, Section 4, Section 5.1).
Human evaluation corroborates these automatic semantic-quality assessments, confirming REALISTA's attacks preserve semantic equivalence/coherence as judged by human raters (Table 4, Section 5.4).

O8jabXEYlQ.text: In ALFWorld, single-policy RL agents exhibit simplicity bias: simple pick-and-place tasks consume roughly 75% of network capacity while complex heat/cool/clean tasks receive only about 5%, despite being critical to success.

The phase router operates at the environment-step level (cross-attention over goal-conditioned observations plus a 3-layer LSTM over action-observation history) rather than per-token, using a switching penalty (λ_s=0.05) and temperature annealing (τ: 2.0→0.5) to keep expert assignment temporally consistent (about 8.4 switches/episode vs. 45 for token-level routing).

On ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-1.5B, adding Phase-Aware MoE to a GiGPO baseline raises overall success rate from 86.1% to 93.8% (+7.7 points), enough for the 1.5B PA-MoE model to surpass a vanilla 7B baseline (90.2%).

On WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B, PA-MoE improves success rate from 67.4% to 82.3% (+14.9 points), and ablations show K=4 experts with phase-level (not token- or trajectory-level) routing is optimal (93.8% vs. 85.7% token-level and 88.5% trajectory-level on ALFWorld).

CT2tSmahVQ.text: Deep sequence models (Transformers and Mamba) solve an in-weights path-star (l-fold composition) task by memorizing a fixed graph's edges during training and then predicting complete root-to-leaf paths, achieving near-perfect accuracy on graphs with up to 50,000 nodes and path lengths up to l=10 hops even when trained on only 75% of paths.

This near-perfect performance contradicts the associative-memory prediction that l-fold composition should require exponentially (Ω(exp(l))) more capacity or data, motivating a geometric account of memorization instead.

Learned embeddings organize into global geometric structure reflecting path identity rather than only local co-occurrence statistics, visible as diagonal clustering in embedding heatmaps and separated clusters in UMAP projections (Figure 6), even when the model is trained only on edge memorization.

The paper attributes emergent geometric memory to spectral bias in learned representations, showing that Fiedler vectors of the graph align with learned Node2Vec-style embeddings (Section 4, Figure 7).

JcjRShiRQz.text: Existing AI-generated image detectors exhibit a 'prediction asymmetry' bias toward the real class: for example, the Corvi detector achieves 99.9% accuracy on real images from FLUX but only 21.5% accuracy on FLUX-generated fakes, showing it effectively defaults to predicting 'real' for unfamiliar generators.

DEAR (Dissect and Prune) identifies spurious feature channels via Regional Activation Discrepancy (RAD) computed on diagnostic inpainted images with known real/fake pixel provenance, then removes channels at both extremes of the RAD distribution (bilateral pruning) rather than only fake-aligned channels.

Under post-processing operations (compression/resizing), DEAR-c retains 90.2% average fake accuracy versus 12.2% for NPR and 47.7% for Corvi (Table 1), while average AUC across generators (FLUX, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, PixArt) drops only from 99.9% to 92.3%.
On in-the-wild benchmarks, DEAR-c attains 82.9% AUC on Chameleon, 75.4% on LOKI, and 87.8% on WildRF, outperforming comparable baselines (Table 2).

3NQSeJOfkz.text: Theorem 1 shows that applying posterior correction with an isotropic-Gaussian posterior family reduces exactly to the standard SVRG gradient update, and Theorem 2 proves SVRG is equivalent to VSGD-PoCo in the limit of zero sampling noise.

Using full-covariance Gaussian posteriors yields a Newton-like variance-reduced extension (VON-PoCo) with a novel Hessian correction term H̄_out\i(m_in − m_out) not present in prior variance-reduced Newton methods.

Using diagonal-covariance Gaussian posteriors with mega-batches and momentum yields an Adam-like extension (IVON-PoCoMo) suitable for transformer pretraining, which achieves 17.4 validation perplexity on GPT-2 125M pretrained on 50B tokens, versus 18.0 for IVON and 18.4 for AdamW (Section 4.3, Figure 1b).

The variance-reduced methods show consistent gains in finetuning across ViT-B/32, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3.1 (Table 1) and in ResNet-50/ImageNet and ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 image classification, particularly when learning rates are not annealed to zero (Figures 4-5).

vMcu1h3fOV.text: Joint ARD extends standard Automatic Relevance Determination by introducing per-sample noise variances λ_i as primary parameters (rather than a single shared scalar), yielding a heteroscedastic marginal-likelihood objective that jointly sparsifies features and down-weights outlying samples (Section 3).

The heteroscedastic objective admits closed-form updates across multiple sparse Bayesian learning optimization schemes, including EM, MacKay-style updates, and ℓ1/ℓ2-IRLS variants (Section 3), preserving the conjugacy of standard ARD.

On tabular benchmarks with 10% injected outlier contamination, joint ARD reduces RMSE relative to the homoscedastic baseline by 32.07% (Energy, EM), 69.91% (Carbon, EM), and 45.12% (Protein, MacKay) (Table 3), while the learned effective support size for samples (~91%) tracks the true contamination rate and feature-level sparsity is maintained (ESS(θ) ≈ 5-40%).

Joint ARD achieves competitive robustness relative to Student-t and Huber robust baselines in RVM kernel regression across a range of contamination levels (Figure 4), with the largest gains over homoscedastic modeling occurring for sparse signals under low contamination (Figure 3).

kTOxGQJkwt.text: TABX is a JAX-based, GPU-accelerated multi-agent sandbox battle simulator that exhibits near-log-linear throughput scaling with the number of parallel environments across a wide range of unit counts on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (Figure 9).

Accounting for JIT compilation overhead over 100 scenario resets, TABX achieves substantially higher throughput than the existing SMAX simulator, with its speed advantage remaining largely invariant to the number of units simulated (Figure 10).

TABX supports dynamic reconfiguration of units, terrain zones, heuristic policies, and physics without code modification, plus a GUI scenario editor, enabling systematic study of emergent agent behavior across cooperative battle scenarios (Section on framework design).

Baseline MARL algorithms (IPPO, MAPPO, IQL, QMIX) and UED methods (Domain Randomization, PLR, Robust PLR, ACCEL, SFL) are benchmarked on TABX over 5 random seeds, showing that the benefit of centralized value learning depends on scenario structure and observability constraints (Section 5).

D2evvc90tF.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that when mini-batch gradient noise is anisotropic across dimensions, the stationary distribution of microcanonical Langevin dynamics (if it exists) deviates from the true target posterior due to non-vanishing noise-induced drift, in contrast to the isotropic-noise case covered by Proposition 1 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

A diagonal gradient-noise preconditioner (pSMILE-naive), built from moving averages of per-dimension gradient standard deviations to enforce local isotropy, reduces the empirically measured bias by roughly 5-10x relative to unpreconditioned mini-batch MCLMC across anisotropic-noise benchmarks (Table 1).

An energy-variance-based adaptive tuner that fits a Gamma distribution to the energy error ΔE dynamically sets step-size guardrails, letting epoch-wise mini-batch sampling with pSMILE-naive match the accuracy of full-batch MCLMC (Algorithm 1, Table 2).

On larger-scale Bayesian neural network posteriors (ResNet-18 with 11.2M parameters and a ViT with 22M parameters), pSMILE achieves uncertainty quantification competitive with state-of-the-art methods while using mini-batch gradients (Table 3).

aPnQpmwHW7.text: On Qwen2.5-Omni-7B retaining only 25% of original tokens, OmniSIFT outperforms training-free compression baselines such as OmniZip and even surpasses the full-token model on benchmarks such as DailyOmni, while cutting end-to-end latency by more than 40% (Section on efficiency results).

At 35% token retention on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, OmniSIFT beats OmniZip and the full-token baseline on WorldSense (50.0 vs 48.9 vs 49.7), OmniVideoBench (68.3 vs 66.7 vs 67.6), VideoMME average (67.9 vs 67.0 vs 66.9), and DailyOmni average (73.2 vs 67.7 vs 72.2) (comparison table).

OmniSIFT's visual-guided adaptive sampling (VGAS) module adds only about 4.85M parameters (under 0.1% overhead for a 7B-scale model) while reducing FLOPs from 555.74T (full-token baseline) to 292.16T at 35% retention (47% reduction) and to 250.83T at 25% retention (55% reduction) (Table 7).
At 35% retention on WorldSense with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, OmniSIFT lowers peak GPU memory from 27.59GB to 22.91GB (Section on efficiency benchmarks).

EhJ1R2N6sn.text: GCR-RL recasts value-function learning as learning a partially ordered set (poset) over states/state-actions, enforcing geometric coherence through a sequence of super-poset refinements combined with standard TD learning (Section 3).

A soft-enforcement variant adds a combined loss L_total = L_TD + λ_sym·L_sym + λ_dag·L_dag + λ_ord·L_ord, using a near-equivariance symmetry module and a logic-order module that extracts acyclic partial orders from TD evidence (Section 3).

A hard-enforcement variant projects updates onto a manifold of valid posets via tangent-normal decomposition, and Theorem 4.3 shows restricted TD descent on this feasible manifold converges linearly, while Theorem 4.4 establishes an oracle sample-complexity speedup of O(W(D*)/(1+(|G|-1)ρ) · 1/ε) (Theorems 4.2-4.4).

Theorem 3.2 shows that symmetry exploitation yields a sample amplification factor of approximately 1+(K-1)ρ, and GCR-RL demonstrates improved sample efficiency and more stable value learning (reduced Bellman residuals) over baselines across four environments: RotMirror-Grid, BtnPerm-Minigrid, Atari, and Noisy-RPS Chain (Table 1).

FFAHL32Wok.text: BADIT decomposes pretrained LLM weights via SVD into multiple orthogonal, high-singular-value LoRA experts (Basic Ability Decomposition, BAD), each representing a reusable 'basic ability' across tasks, then uses spherical K-means clustering to dynamically regroup rank-1 LoRA components while preserving expert-gradient orthogonality during training (Dynamically Orthogonal Grouping, DOG) (Method section).

On the SuperNI benchmark across 6 LLMs (variants of Qwen3, Llama3, and Gemma2) over 15 NLP tasks, BADIT outperforms the prior state-of-the-art GainLoRA by an average of 2.68 ROUGE points across mixed- and sequential-training settings (Results table).

In mixed-task training, BADIT reaches ROUGE scores of 55.87 on Qwen3-8B, 54.75 on Llama3-8B, and 57.35 on Gemma2-9B, exceeding sequential-training scores of 50.86, 48.83, and 48.34 respectively, and outperforming LoRA, PiSSA, LoRAMoE, and OLoRA baselines (Results table).

BADIT's DOG component increases training time by roughly 1.22x relative to LoRAMoE, with the added spherical-clustering and integer-optimization steps accounting for most of this overhead (Computational cost analysis).

hEQDZg1ZeD.text: On CIFAR-10, the proposed first-order F-DPMSolver achieves FID 25.02 at NFE=4, far below DDIM's 67.03 and DPMSolver-3's 33.77 at the same budget (Table 1).
On ImageNet64, F-DPMSolver reaches FID 3.64 at NFE=8, improving on DPMSolver-3's 3.92, and scores 22.35 at NFE=4 versus DDIM's 43.86 (Table 2).
On ImageNet512 with EDM2-XS, F-DPMSolver attains FID 52.32 at NFE=4 compared to DDIM's 91.44, maintaining top performance across NFE 4-10 (Table 3).
On latent diffusion models (FFHQ, LSUN Bedroom), F-DPMSolver is competitive with the higher-order DPMSolver-3, e.g., FID 15.78 vs. 15.65 on FFHQ at NFE=4, despite being only first-order (Table 4).

TxHOT32Maj.text: SoHip improves accuracy by up to 8.78 percentage points over the strongest of seven baselines on Tiny-ImageNet (46.20% vs. 37.42% at N=100 agents) and up to 5.56 points on CIFAR-100 (54.33% vs. 48.77% at N=200) (Table 1).

The seven compared baselines span standalone, representation-sharing (FedProto, FedSSA, FedRAL), and auxiliary model-sharing (FedKD, FedMRL, pFedES) methods, evaluated under label-skewed CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet partitions (Table 1).

SoHip's memory-centric design uses four modules—short-term abstraction, hippocampus-inspired gated consolidation, individual-collective fusion, and server-side collective aggregation—exchanging only compact long-term memory representations rather than raw data, model parameters, or intermediate features (Section 4).

The method is proven to converge at rate O(1/sqrt(T)) + O(Delta_het) under heterogeneous agent data (Theorem 5.1), with an accompanying privacy guarantee (Theorem 5.2) restricting exchange to compact memory summaries (Section 5).

8WA5l5tjF6.text: CVSearch with Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 90.1 accuracy on V* Bench, 76.6 on HR-Bench 4K, and 75.6 on HR-Bench 8K, outperforming baseline and other search-based high-resolution perception methods (Section on main results).

CVSearch attains roughly 3x higher search throughput than prior scan-based methods (Zoom Eye, RAP) on HR-Bench 4K, reaching 1.02 samples/minute versus 0.68 for scan-based baselines while retaining higher accuracy (Table 5).

Semantic Guided Adaptive Patching replaces rigid grid partitioning with SLIC-superpixel clustering and a silhouette/overlap-based cost function to select the optimal number of semantically coherent patches, mitigating object fragmentation (Equation 3).

Dynamic Bottom-Up Search is guided by a Visual Complexity prior—defined via dispersion of atomic feature cosine similarities—that starts exploration from leaf-level regions and prunes low-complexity nodes, replacing top-down tree traversal for more efficient iterative search (Equation 4).

lA85cqhMh0.text: Holmes outperforms the prior state of the art on all three partially relevant video retrieval benchmarks, reaching 156.8 SumR on ActivityNet Captions (vs. 156.1 for DreamPRVR), 80.6 SumR on Charades-STA (vs. 80.0), and 198.6 SumR on TVR (vs. 190.5 for MGAKD, an 8.1-point gain) (Table 1).

Inter-video evidential learning models query ambiguity via a Dirichlet distribution over similarity scores, decomposing queries by epistemic uncertainty, label consistency, and aleatoric (entropy) uncertainty into precise, polysemous, and under-determined categories (Section 3.2, Definitions 3.1/3.3/3.5).

Intra-video alignment uses Flexible Optimal Transport with an adaptive dustbin bucket (set at the bottom 30th percentile of similarities) to filter noisy clips, improving SumR from 154.7 (standard OT) to 155.6 on TVR in ablations (Table 3, ID 12).

A Dynamic Co-Evidential Aggregator fuses frame-scale and clip-scale Dirichlet opinions via the Dempster-Shafer combination rule under a two-stage training schedule (20-epoch warm-up followed by 80 epochs of joint loss), using a model of 30.79M parameters comparable in training time to GMMFormerV2 (Section 3.4, Table 2).

xpIUvw8ANa.text: TensorMesh, the numerical PDE assembly component, achieves roughly one order-of-magnitude speedup over the second-best baseline (FEniCS) on the 3D Poisson equation and nearly two orders of magnitude speedup on 3D linear elasticity (Section on numerical PDE solving results).
On topology optimization, TensorGalerkin is 3.7x faster overall than JAX-FEM, including a 4.5x speedup in assembly setup time (Section on PDE-constrained optimization results).

TensorPils, the neural PDE solver component, achieves about 50% lower error than the nearest baseline (Deep Ritz) while running 2x faster, and evaluates loss with near-flat cost scaling versus degrees of freedom compared to orders-of-magnitude slower PINN approaches (Section on physics-informed operator learning).

The physics-informed operator learning results span elliptic (Poisson, linear elasticity), parabolic (Allen-Cahn), and hyperbolic (linear acoustic wave) PDEs on unstructured 2D/3D triangular and tetrahedral meshes, outperforming PI-DeepONet by at least an order of magnitude in error on the wave equation (in-distribution error 0.085±0.010) (Table 2).

bkcxLMm3Gp.text: On Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct, DenseSteer raises GSM8K accuracy from 83.6% to 84.8% and MATH500 from 63.0% to 64.6%, improving the weighted average from 61.2% to 62.5% (Table 1)

The steering vector is extracted from only 50 contrastive (dense vs. sparse) reasoning-trace pairs using GPT-5.1-rewritten dense variants of the small model's own outputs, avoiding the distribution mismatch of using larger-model references (Section 4.1)

Injecting the steering vector at middle layers (L16/L17) is most effective for controlling reasoning density, while early layers (L6) show minimal effect and late layers (L27/L35) destabilize generation (Figure 4)

Dense-rewritten reasoning traces achieve token-level NLL approaching the target model's own self-likelihood baseline, whereas same-family larger-model references show significantly higher NLL due to distribution mismatch (Figure 3)

Prompting alone with dense-style instructions reaches only 20.0% accuracy on GSM8K, far below the steering-based approach, showing that representation-level steering is necessary beyond instruction-following (Section 5.4)

t5BgTJ7Z0k.text: The Predict-and-Perturb (P&P) mechanism reinterprets flow matching as a denoising autoencoder, alternating between predicting a clean video state and re-perturbing it at a fixed noise level, using only the pre-trained video generator itself with no external verifier or additional training

On Wan2.2, the method achieves 73% human preference over the default sampler for motion coherence and 84% preference over the baseline for physics alignment, plus 74% preference over a doubled-NFE sampling baseline (human evaluation results)
On PAI-Bench robotics tasks, the approach improves grasp success rate by +11.0 points on Cosmos and +8.4 points on Wan relative to baseline sampling

On Dynamic-bench and VideoPhy2, the method improves motion consistency (98.41 vs. 98.01 baseline) and physical commonsense scores (55.6 vs. 54.5 baseline), while increasing NFE by only about 1.5x with negligible memory overhead

2NRrsz4nUB.text: BehaviorVLA achieves a 58% success rate on the RoboTwin 2.0 Hard setting, outperforming RDT-1b by +37.7 percentage points on this bimanual manipulation benchmark with domain-randomized clutter, lighting, and textures (Table 1)
BehaviorVLA reaches 98% average success rate on LIBERO across task suites (Spatial 99.2%, Object 99.4%, Goal 98.8%, Long 94.6%), surpassing both pi0.5 (96.9%) and OpenVLA-OFT (97.1%) (Table 2)
On CALVIN ABC->D, BehaviorVLA attains an average rollout length of 4.36, evaluated to validate generalization across scenes and objects (Appendix C, Table 4)

In real-world sim-to-real transfer, BehaviorVLA matches the success rate of fully fine-tuned OpenVLA-OFT while using only 50% of the real-world demonstration data, achieving 70% success on generalization tasks and 55% on long-horizon tasks with the reduced dataset

xeH37plPS3.text: The reaction-center-guided discrete flow matching model achieves 61.2% top-1 accuracy on USPTO-50k with predicted reaction centers (71.1% with oracle centers), surpassing prior non-LLM approaches including Graph2Edits (55.1%) and the diffusion baseline RetroBridge (50.8%) (Table 1)
On USPTO-Full, the model reaches 51.3% top-1 accuracy with predicted centers (63.4% with oracle centers), outperforming non-LLM baselines NAG2G (49.7%) and R-SMILES (48.9%) (Table 2)

Despite using orders of magnitude less training data, the method's 61.2% top-1 accuracy on USPTO-50k trails RSGPT (a 10-billion-reaction-pretrained LLM, 63.4%) by only 2.2 points, and under oracle reaction centers the method's 71.1% exceeds RSGPT's performance
Generation requires only 20-50 sampling steps, roughly 10-25x fewer than the 500 steps needed by prior diffusion-based methods like RetroBridge

4v5iCXWmcR.text: Spontaneous Neurons (SPON) are trainable, input-independent activation vectors that supplement sparsified activations and can be absorbed into bias terms post-training, adding no inference-time overhead

At 50% activation sparsity on WikiText, SPON reduces perplexity relative to the TEAL baseline across backbones: Llama3-8B (7.83 vs. 8.34), Qwen3-8B (9.26 vs. 9.75), and Mistral-v2-7B (5.86 vs. 6.00), with the gap widening at 60% sparsity (Table 1)
Across six zero-shot downstream tasks (CommonsenseQA, MathQA, MedMCQA, MMLU, OpenBookQA, TruthfulQA), SPON shows stable accuracy advantages over TEAL under sparsification (Table 3)

SPON preserves the 1.5-1.6x throughput speedup of activation sparsity, with tokens-per-second nearly identical to TEAL at 50% sparsity (e.g., Llama3-8B: 64.131 vs. 64.279 TPS; Mistral-v2-7B: 71.836 vs. 71.246 TPS) (Table 2)

Hidden-representation analysis shows SPON mitigates distributional shift from sparsification, keeping activations closer to the original dense model's distribution across tested architectures (Figure 3)

jgebUtw1lA.text: A 7B-parameter Qwen2.5-VL student model trained with Autonomous Preference Optimization (APO), distilled from seven proprietary teacher MLLMs (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5, Claude Sonnet-4, Qwen-VL-Max, Grok-4, GLM-4.5V, Moonshot-v1), achieves 0.78 average classification accuracy on chest X-ray disease classification, outperforming all individual teacher models despite its much smaller size (Table 2).

The APO-trained model attains 0.78 top-1 accuracy on chest disease classification, surpassing the CoCa-CXR baseline (0.69) while using only 10% of the training data and no radiologist reports (Table 1).

The three-stage 'learn-compare-critique' pipeline (Supervised Pre-Distillation, self-distillation, then APO treating self-distilled reasoning as preferred signal and raw teacher outputs as negative samples) improves report generation quality, yielding a 14.3% BLEU-4 gain, 2.4% ROUGE-L gain, and 27.5% METEOR gain over the pre-APO baseline (Table 3).
The resulting model generalizes in zero-shot classification to unseen datasets, achieving AUC of 0.85 on Open-I, 0.83 on ChestXray14, 0.92 on ChestXpert, and 0.81 on ChestXDet10 (Table 4).

UgPfadSsaA.text: Under the irreducibility assumption on induced Markov chains for all deterministic policies and transition kernels in a compact, convex uncertainty set (Assumption 4.1), a stationary Nash equilibrium is proven to exist for average-reward distributionally robust Markov games, via a Kakutani fixed-point argument over the best-response correspondence (Theorem 5.8).

The robust Bellman equation for the average-reward setting is shown to be solvable (Theorem 4.3), and the set of optimal robust policies is convex with the induced best-response correspondence upper semi-continuous (Theorems 5.6 and 5.7), which together underpin the equilibrium existence proof.

The proposed Robust Nash-Iteration algorithm (Algorithm 1), a value-iteration scheme maintaining per-agent value estimates updated via matrix-form stage games, is proven to converge to a Nash equilibrium given an equilibrium-selection oracle that returns globally optimal or saddle-point equilibria (Theorem 6.1, Assumption D.1).

As the discount factor approaches 1, discounted-reward Nash equilibria of the distributionally robust Markov game are shown to converge to average-reward Nash equilibria, linking the two reward criteria (Theorem 7.1).

LShQYeeop5.text: GIFT matches the peak test-set IoU performance of an extensive test-time-scaling (sampling-based) approach while using approximately 80% less inference compute (Figure 1).

GIFT improves mean IoU on image-to-CAD program synthesis from 0.698 (supervised fine-tuning baseline) to 0.782, an approximately 12% absolute gain, and reduces the amortization gap between pass@1 and pass@k performance by 66.4% relative to the SFT baseline (Table 2, Table 3).

Despite using only single-view image input, GIFT (CAD-Coder-GIFT, 0.782 IoU) remains competitive with more complex multimodal baselines that use additional modalities such as depth, normals, or point clouds—e.g., GACO-CAD-RL (0.864 IoU) and Cadrille-RL (0.859 IoU) (Table 4).
GIFT solves 53% more problems than the baseline and shows greater robustness on high-complexity CAD synthesis tasks as required token length increases (Figure 2).

Y0Dhwhu8Uc.text: PASA maintains substantially higher detection power under DIPPER-based paraphrasing attacks of varying strength, achieving TPR@1%FPR between 0.5377 and 0.5879, while the token-level baseline DAWA collapses to about 0.02 TPR@1%FPR under the same attacks, and PASA preserves text quality with perplexity of 11.44 versus 12.41 for unwatermarked generation.

Theorem 1 characterizes the minimum achievable miss-detection error as a function of semantic cluster granularity K, formalizing the trade-off whereby coarser clustering (fewer, larger semantic clusters) increases robustness to meaning-preserving attacks at the cost of detection accuracy at low false-positive rates.

Theorem 2 derives the jointly optimal embedding-detection pair, showing the optimal detector reconstructs an auxiliary semantic-cluster sequence via a secret key with an overflow state that controls the false-alarm rate, establishing a distortion-free, theoretically grounded watermarking scheme.

PASA's two-stage sampling procedure (truncated auxiliary semantic-cluster distribution at false-alarm threshold α, followed by in-cluster token sampling) adds negligible overhead, under 0.5 seconds of generation time per 300-token sequence and 0.27 seconds detection latency, the fastest among robust watermarking methods evaluated.

qjwFbN77kx.text: FiSeR, trained on WildFake, achieves an average AUROC of 98.23 (93.43 TPR@FPR=5%) across four out-of-distribution cross-domain benchmarks—Chameleon, AIGIBench, Community Forensics, and GenImage—a +10.22 point average AUROC gain over the DIRE baseline (Table 2).
Per-dataset cross-domain AUROC/TPR@FPR=5% results are 96.95/87.50 on Community Forensics, 98.00/93.75 on AIGIBench, 96.35/86.38 on Chameleon, and 99.84/99.55 on GenImage (Table 2).

With few-shot adaptation using only 10 labeled samples per class (10-shot SVM on FiSeR features), average AUROC across 12 existing detectors improves by +10.64 on AIGIBench and +17.41 on Chameleon, with FiSeR itself reaching 99.19±0.50 AUROC on AIGIBench (Table 1).

cCMbxJcDmH.text: On the PhoStream benchmark, current MLLMs struggle to decide when to speak in streaming scenarios rather than only what to say, evidenced by strong Instant/Backward scores but collapsing Forward scores across nearly all evaluated proprietary and open-source models (Table 3).

Gemini 3 Pro scores 80.83 on Instant and 82.19 on Backward tasks but only 16.40 on Forward tasks, an overall average of 48.70, showing a sharp temporal asymmetry in performance (Table 3, Section 3.3).

Models exhibit an 'Early Response bias' on Forward tasks: Qwen3-Omni answers prematurely 97.89% of the time and Gemini 3 Pro 79.12% of the time, responding before required visual or audio evidence appears (Section 4.2).

The temporal asymmetry between strong Instant/Backward performance and poor Forward performance reveals a fundamental limitation in streaming multimodal understanding when models must withhold responses until future cues arrive (Section 4.2, Table 5).

iwS6Lg1Uwx.text: Under the Planted Clique hardness hypothesis (planted cliques of size k = m^(1/2−δ) in random graphs are not recoverable in polynomial time), there exist samplable multi-environment linear-Gaussian instances that are statistically learnable with polynomially many samples via exhaustive search but intractable for any polynomial-time algorithm (Hypothesis 3.1, Theorem 3.8).

A phase transition in label-induced spurious correlation removal occurs at critical sample size n* ∝ k(d−k)/(|E|γ²), where k is the invariant subspace dimension, d the ambient dimension, |E| the number of environments, and γ the environment separation parameter; below n*/2 all estimators fail with constant error while above 2n* estimators achieve error O(k(d−k)/(n|E|γ²)) (Theorem 4.15).

The predicted phase transition is validated empirically: exhaustive search reaches 75% accuracy using up to 27x fewer samples than polynomial-time methods on synthetic instances, and sharp transitions near the predicted critical sample size appear on both synthetic data and ColoredMNIST (Figure 1, Figure 2b).

Diversity across environments is necessary for removal to succeed: performance improves sharply once γ > 0, whereas low-diversity settings (γ ≈ 0) show persistent failure, and increasing diversity from 'low' to 'high' substantially improves worst-group accuracy on CelebA and Waterbirds and OOD performance on ColoredMNIST (Figure 2c, Table 2).

GAQE4Wr53f.text: In the weighted Hilbert space L²(λ;R^d), the λ-induced row-stochastic mixing matrix W is self-adjoint whereas the doubly stochastic matrix W^ds is not, and this non-self-adjointness introduces additional multiplicative penalty terms (κ_λ > 1 and λ_max² > 1) that amplify consensus error under the doubly stochastic design (Section 5.2, Section 6.2).

Theorem 6.5 gives O(1/T) convergence rates for both row-stochastic and doubly stochastic strategies, but the row-stochastic strategy achieves strictly smaller non-asymptotic consensus error and can converge faster even when its spectral gap is smaller than that of the doubly stochastic strategy (Theorem 6.5).

Theorem 7.1 derives a sufficient condition on the spectral gaps, 1 − ρ_Λ ≥ max{(1+η)κ_λ^(-1/3), λ_max^(-1/2)}(1 − ρ_J), under which the row-stochastic design provably converges strictly faster than the doubly stochastic design (Theorem 7.1).

Corollary 7.3 and Algorithm 2 give topology construction guidelines showing that when node degrees scale proportionally with their assigned weights (d_i/d_j matching λ_i/λ_j within bounds set by R), the row-stochastic design outperforms the doubly stochastic design, satisfying a Loewner order condition on the graph Laplacians (Corollary 7.3, Remark 7.4, Algorithm 2).

bQk1qnXcqM.text: Log-Normal Multiplicative Dynamics (LMD) enables stable training under low-precision forward-pass computations (MXFP6, MXFP4) where standard AdamW training becomes unstable (Table 1).

LMD trains a Vision Transformer (384 embedding dim, 6 heads, 12 layers) from scratch to 77.06±0.08 test accuracy with full-precision, versus 68.11±0.38 for AdamW, and retains 77.15±0.08 accuracy when the forward pass uses MXFP6 (Table 1).

LMD keeps weight norms controlled during training (55.2±0.1) compared to AdamW's much larger and unstable norms (260.7±0.5), and trains a 124M-parameter GPT-2 on OpenWebText to a validation loss of 2.925±0.006 (full precision) and 2.927±0.002 with MXFP6 forward passes, whereas AdamW's perplexity degrades sharply under low precision (Table 1, Figure 1).
Ablations show that both the multiplicative weight decay and multiplicative noise injection components of LMD are necessary for stable low-precision training dynamics (Figures 3-4).

goVeG3ui1Y.text: Cross-step Residual Potential Initialization (CRPI), a training-free mechanism that carries residual membrane potentials across consecutive decision steps to initialize neuron states in converted spiking neural networks, substantially recovers performance lost during ANN-to-SNN conversion in continuous-control reinforcement learning (Section 5.1-5.2, Algorithm 1).

On MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks (Ant-v4, HalfCheetah-v4, Hopper-v4, Walker2d-v4), CRPI improves average performance ratio by +9.82% for IF neurons with 8 steps (DDPG), +5.99% for IF neurons with 16 steps (TD3), and +18.00% for multi-threshold neurons at 22 steps (Table 2).

On vision-based DeepMind Control Suite tasks, CRPI raises IF-neuron performance from 40.77% to 74.19% at 32 timesteps and substantially improves performance at 64 timesteps (from 69.60%), and raises signed-neuron performance from 88.72% to 96.27% at 8 timesteps (Table 3).

CRPI works by suppressing temporally correlated conversion errors, whose positive correlation across decision steps would otherwise progressively degrade performance, as measured directly via cross-step error correlation metrics (Table 1, Figure 4).

F13K6NNeAz.text: FRISM decomposes reasoning task vectors from large reasoning models via SVD and learns adaptive per-subspace gating coefficients, formulated as θ_merged = θ_vlm + λ_lrm·U(Sigmoid(g)⊙S)Vᵀ, rather than merging entire layers at once (Section on Method/Formulation).

On Qwen2.5-VL-7B merged with DeepSeek-R1, FRISM improves average VL reasoning benchmark score from 47.4 to 49.4, including MathVista from 68.1 to 70.3 and MathVision from 25.6 to 26.4, while maintaining VL perception at 82.9 (Key Results table).

Subspace-level merging avoids the vision-reasoning trade-off exhibited by coarse-grained layer-level merging baselines such as Task Arithmetic, IP-Merging, and FRANK, outperforming them across model scales of 3B, 7B, and 32B parameters (Comparative Advantages / experiments).

FRISM requires only 0.53M trainable parameters (full-rank) or 0.05M (low-rank variant) and about 0.49 hours of training, dramatically more parameter- and compute-efficient than post-training approaches like DRIFT (~7000M parameters, ~2 hours) (Efficiency analysis).

91gJ3Zp2lT.text: Mixture Prototype Flow Learning (MPFL) models the flow-matching velocity field using a Gaussian mixture prior, with each mixture component corresponding to a distinct normal class, learning a continuous transformation from normal feature distributions to a structured multi-modal prototype space instead of a single unimodal Gaussian (Method: MPFL).

A Mutual Information Maximization Regularizer (MIMR) is added to prevent prototype collapse and encourage confident, balanced component assignment, improving normal-anomaly separability (Method: MIMR).

MPFM achieves state-of-the-art AUROC across nine industrial and medical benchmarks in both 1-shot and 10-shot settings, e.g. 0.982 (MVTec AD), 0.992 (Optical and AITEX), and 0.965 (Hyper-Kvasir) at 10-shot, versus 0.938, 0.931, 0.854, and 0.847 respectively at 1-shot (Benchmark results table).

Ablation experiments show removing MPFL causes substantial performance degradation especially on texture-rich datasets like AITEX, while removing MIMR causes moderate declines, confirming both components are complementary; the best configuration uses K=32 Gaussian mixture components and regularization weight λ=0.1 (Ablation study).

26ELwHEbQL.text: Anomaly Preference Optimization (APO) reformulates few-shot anomaly image generation as an implicit preference-learning problem, using real anomaly images as positive references and deriving a tractable deviation function from denoising-trajectory differences, avoiding the need for costly human-annotated preference pairs (Method: APO).

Time-Aware Capacity Allocation (TACA) dynamically distributes model adaptation capacity across the diffusion timeline, minimizing adaptation at high-noise steps to preserve structural diversity and maximizing it at low-noise steps for fine-grained fidelity (Method: TACA).

On the MVTec anomaly generation benchmark, the method attains an average Inception Score of 2.14, IC-LPIPS diversity of 0.41, pixel-level AUROC of 99.6%, and pixel-level Average Precision of 87.7%, outperforming the SeaS baseline by 5.9% in IS and 7.9% in IC-LPIPS (Benchmark results, MVTec table).

TVAMni6Cq1.text: PartCo augments Generalized Category Discovery methods with a part-level correspondence loss built from PCA-derived correspondence labels over DINOv2 patch tokens (rather than only the global classification token), using first-order correspondence labels for fine-grained datasets and second-order labels for generic datasets (Method: Part-Level Labels Construction).

Added to SimGCD with a DINOv2 backbone, PartCo raises accuracy on the SSB fine-grained benchmarks from 71.5% to 81.1% on CUB (+9.6), from 71.5% to 78.9% on Stanford Cars (+7.4), and from 63.9% to 76.5% on FGVC-Aircraft (+12.6) (SSB benchmark results table).

On generic datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet-100), PartCo yields smaller but consistent gains of +0.3% to +2.9% accuracy across baselines, and achieves new state-of-the-art results when combined with both parametric (SimGCD) and non-parametric (SelEx) GCD methods (Generic dataset results).

Du8BMHfNzp.text: PATRA introduces a pattern-aware alignment mechanism that explicitly extracts trend and seasonality patterns from time series inputs to align them with question semantics, addressing the limitation of prior methods that treat time series merely as text or images and fail to capture such patterns (Method: Pattern-Aware Mechanism).

PATRA employs a Task-Aware Balanced Reward during training to counteract simpler sub-tasks dominating the learning signal when mixed with harder tasks, while incentivizing coherent chain-of-thought generation (Method: Task-Aware Balanced Reward).

PATRA outperforms strong baseline approaches across diverse Time Series Question Answering (TSQA) benchmarks, demonstrating improved cross-modal understanding and reasoning between time series and natural language (Experiments/Results).

JKMZyCghr4.text: Adaptive probe-based steering (Adaptive Strength + Direction Learning/Adjustment + SAT) raises the average harmfulness score across 12 safety-fortified LLMs (including Circuit Breaker, RepBend, R2D2, TAR, DeRTA and latent-adversarial-training variants) from 6% to at least 50%, and to over 70% on most models, without any manual per-model tuning of steering strength (Abstract, Section 4.1, Table 1).

Evaluated with the StrongReject judge, the full method attains an average harmfulness score of 0.91 on a 200-prompt set (100 from StrongReject, 100 from HarmBench), versus 0.61 and 0.78 for the SRF and HarmBench judges respectively (Table 1).

Ablations show the Adaptive Strength component alone is critical for avoiding 'zero-zone' steering failures, and the full AS+DLA+SAT combination improves average harmfulness by 0.44 over the contrastive-steering baseline, eliminating the need for hand-tuned steering coefficients or extra contrastive prompt pairs (Table 2).
An adaptive-retraining extension for model extraction improves downstream performance by 26% on average compared to naive data-augmentation baselines (Table 3).

NNGIniylxB.text: AMPD adaptively routes incremental prefill workloads to either local decode workers or remote prefill workers based on real-time load, computation cost, KV-transfer cost, and queuing-delay estimates, rather than using a static disaggregation policy (Section 4.1).

AMPD's prefill-reordering scheduler (Algorithm 2) reorders queued prefill tasks within a scheduling window to maximize the fraction of requests meeting their time-to-first-token (TTFT) SLO (Section 4.2).

On multi-round inference workloads with Llama-3.1-70B, AMPD improves SLO attainment over Dynamo (a disaggregated-serving baseline) by up to 967.5% and 67.3% on average, and over vLLM (a co-located baseline) by up to 3435.1% and 339.7% on average (Figure 4).

An offline deployment planner formulated as an integer linear program (Equation 5) selects parallelism strategies and worker allocations to minimize worst-case P95 latency subject to GPU capacity constraints (Section 5).

LMBt26pQj1.text: COLLIE constructs a dense, training-free guidance signal w(s) = softmax([-d_φ(s, D_i)]) over sparse human 'good/bad' state labels by measuring distance in a semantically coherent latent space, requiring no additional model training beyond the underlying skill-discovery objective (Equation 7, Figure 1).

On state-based control tasks (Ant North/Range/Hole, HalfCheetah Right, Quadruped North, Humanoid Hole), COLLIE achieves near-oracle safe-state coverage while avoiding hazardous behaviors, using minimal human feedback (Table 1).

In zero-shot downstream evaluation on Ant motion tasks, COLLIE attains the highest average and best per-task performance across all task variants compared to baseline unsupervised skill-discovery methods (Table 2), and it also yields superior hierarchical-control performance (Table 3).
A human-subject study with real labelers on the Ant Range task confirms COLLIE's practical effectiveness at learning human-aligned skills from limited feedback (Table 13, Figure 7).

UB6M4BSvwJ.text: DynVLA's 'Dynamics CoT' compresses predicted future world dynamics into a small set of latent tokens, avoiding the limited spatiotemporal grounding of Textual CoT and the computational redundancy of frame-based Visual CoT (Abstract).

On the NAVSIM benchmark, DynVLA achieves a PDMS of 91.7, outperforming Textual CoT baselines AutoVLA (89.1), AdaThinkDrive (90.3), and AutoDrive-R2R² (90.3), Visual CoT baselines FSDrive (85.1) and PWM (88.1), and the non-CoT VLA DriveVLA-W0 (90.2) (Table 1).
On Bench2Drive, DynVLA reaches a Driving Score of 88.34 and Success Rate of 72.73, surpassing AutoVLA (78.84 DS) and SimLingo (85.07 DS) (Table 2).
On an in-house 700k-frame dataset, DynVLA reduces displacement error to 1.215 m ADE and collision rate to 4.04‰ versus 1.344 m ADE and 5.13‰ for DriveVLA-W0 with a ViT backbone (Table 3).

Dynamics CoT runs inference in 0.37s versus 2.29s for Visual CoT (~6x faster) while still achieving a superior PDMS of 87.2, demonstrating a more compact and efficient reasoning representation (Table 4).

f4k0XsOlCZ.text: Rel-MOSS is presented as the first work to investigate the class-imbalance problem in relational database (RDB) entity classification, motivated by Proposition 4.1 showing minority-class discriminative signal decays exponentially across GNN message-passing layers (Section 4).

Rel-MOSS combines a Relation-wise Gating Controller (Rel-Gate), which modulates neighborhood messages per relation type, with a Relation-guided Minority Synthesizer (Rel-Syn), which oversamples minority entities while preserving relational consistency (Section 4).

Across 12 imbalanced datasets from the RelBench benchmark, Rel-MOSS achieves an average improvement of up to 2.46% in Balanced Accuracy and 4.00% in G-Mean over state-of-the-art RDL methods, with gains reaching 7.67% (Balanced Accuracy) and 7.92% (G-Mean) on the most imbalanced datasets, while maintaining performance on balanced datasets (Table 1).

3tN36gT4tB.text: MoSSP-P, a single-loop stochastic penalty method using Polyak momentum, attains an oracle complexity of O(epsilon^-4) for finding a stochastic epsilon-KKT point of the nonconvex constrained DC-regularized problem, under an approximately feasible initialization ||c(x_0)||^2 = O(K^-1/4) (Theorem 3.1).

MoSSP-R, which replaces Polyak momentum with recursive (variance-reduced) momentum and uses initial batch size b_0 = O(K^1/3), improves the oracle complexity to O(epsilon^-3) under a mean-squared smoothness assumption (Theorem 3.2, Assumption 3.1).

These are presented as the first complexity results for single-loop methods on nonconvex DC-regularized optimization with nonlinear constraints, in contrast to prior double-loop approaches (Section 3, Corollaries 3.1-3.2).

Numerical experiments on binary classification with DC regularization on LIBSVM datasets (a9a, phishing, australian) show MoSSP-P and MoSSP-R reduce constraint violation faster than the double-loop baselines SPDC and SALM (Section 4.1-4.2).

kVBNDXHVeo.text: A Decoupled Diffusion Transformer with a shared condition encoder feeds a lightweight Flow Matching head, trained via supervised flow matching on real long videos (Eq. 14), to capture minute-scale narrative structure and causal relationships (Figure 2, Section 3).

A second lightweight Distribution Matching head aligns sliding windows of the generated video to a frozen short-video teacher via a mode-seeking reverse-KL objective (Eq. 5), preserving local per-window fidelity without requiring extra long-video training data (Figure 2, Section 3).

Combining both heads resolves the identified gradient interference between the mean-seeking long-video objective (which encourages averaging under ambiguity) and the mode-seeking teacher-distillation term (which encourages committing to high-fidelity modes) (Section 3).

On 30-second video generation over 200 prompts, the method reaches 0.9682 consistency, 0.9863 motion, and 0.5735 aesthetic-quality scores, outperforming baselines including CausVid, Self-Forcing, and InfinityRoPE (Table 1).

An ablation study shows that removing any of the three architectural components (shared encoder, FM head, DM head) degrades performance, confirming all are necessary for minute-scale coherence (Table 2).

Ai3a79cTvr.text: SVL (using an E-3DSNN-H spiking backbone) achieves 85.4% top-1 accuracy on zero-shot 3D classification on ModelNet40 and 47.0% on Objaverse-LVIS, reported to surpass advanced ANN models on this task (Table 1).

Compared with prior spiking neural network baselines, SVL improves accuracy by +6.1% on 3D classification on ScanObjectNN (Spike PointNet), +2.1% on DVS action recognition, +1.1% on 3D detection on KITTI, and +2.1% on 3D segmentation on SemanticKITTI (Tables 3-4).
The framework enables SNNs to perform open-world 3D question answering and captioning, with the 13B SVL variant reported to sometimes outperform ANN-based models on these tasks (Table 2, Figure 2).

SVL models offer substantially lower energy consumption than comparable ANN counterparts, e.g., E-3DSNN-L consumes 0.79 mJ versus 161.8 mJ for a comparable ANN, and the approach reports up to a 204x energy-efficiency advantage over ULIP-2.

bniyv9QWYc.text: RTPrune is a two-stage token pruning method for DeepSeek-OCR, motivated by an observed two-stage reading trajectory in the model's LLM decoding: shallow layers attend to high-norm 'dominant' tokens before deeper layers redistribute attention across the remaining tokens (Section on method motivation, Figure 2).

Stage 1 selects dominant visual tokens via L2-norm scoring (Eq. 1), and Stage 2 merges the remaining tokens into the selected ones using optimal-transport-based matching solved with the Sinkhorn algorithm (Eqs. 2-6), with a dynamic pruning ratio set from inter-token similarity and Sobel-edge-based textual density (Eqs. 7-8).
On OmniDocBench with DeepSeek-OCR-Large, RTPrune retains only 84.25% of visual tokens while achieving 99.47% relative accuracy and a 1.23x faster prefill compared to the unpruned model.

At a more aggressive setting, RTPrune reduces GFLOPs by 15.29% and prefill time by 18.90% while still maintaining 97.88%/99.47% accuracy levels, reported to outperform existing VLM token-pruning baselines in the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff.

mMlt3tQ7Ot.text: The paper shows that optimizer dynamics themselves, independent of backup rule or network architecture, can directly trigger or suppress the value-collapse instability observed in offline RL, by analyzing frozen linearized TD-error dynamics (Section 4).

Theorem 4.1 proves that frozen linearized TD error dynamics converge exponentially to zero if and only if the spectral radius rho(A(eta)) of the augmented update matrix is strictly less than one, giving a necessary and sufficient stability condition; Theorem 4.2 gives a practical sufficient condition via Hurwitzness of the underlying TD operator.

Proposition 5.1 decomposes a sufficient condition for stability into a bootstrapped-amplification term and a feature-conditioning (near-orthogonality) term: gamma*||Phi||_2*||Phi*||_2 + ||Phi^T Phi - I||_2 < 1.

AdamO augments Adam with a decoupled, scale-normalized orthogonality correction subject to a budget constraint that provably bounds how much task progress the correction can sacrifice, with a closed-form scaling solution (Eq. 19, Algorithm 1).

Across offline RL benchmarks, AdamO improves average scores over standard Adam by roughly +112% on AntMaze with TD3+BC, +10-15% on MuJoCo locomotion tasks across algorithms, and +38% (IQL) to +6866% (TD3+BC) on Adroit, at a modest compute overhead (~28 extra minutes, 172 vs. 144 total minutes on TD3+BC) (Table 1, Figure 2).

Ga3AR4EF6R.text: BEACON achieves a 92.9% success rate on long-horizon ALFWorld tasks, compared to GRPO's 53.5% on the same task split (Abstract, Figure 1).

GRPO's success rate degrades from 76.7% on short tasks to 53.5% on long tasks, whereas BEACON maintains robust performance across horizons, with relative gains ranging from 26.2% on short tasks to 73.6% on long tasks (Section 1, Figure 1).
BEACON improves effective sample utilization from 23.7% (GRPO) to 82.0% (Section 1, Section 2).

Under GRPO, the Contradictory Action Ratio (CAR) exceeds 40% at its peak and the effective learning signal collapses below 20%, while 39-47% of samples complete milestones but receive zero reward (Section 2, Figure 2a).
BEACON reaches 91.4% success versus 43% for a supervised fine-tuning baseline (Section 1).

Table 1 reports comprehensive benchmark results for BEACON against baselines across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, with the training procedure specified in Algorithm 1 and a variance-isolation guarantee given in Proposition 3.2 (Table 1, Algorithm 1, Section 3.4).

hQoT2F37Am.text: CAOS aggregates nonconformity scores from multiple one-shot predictors by summing the k smallest scores (k=3 in experiments), reusing the same limited labeled data for both reference and calibration rather than splitting it (Equation 12).

Theorem 4.1 proves CAOS achieves finite-sample marginal coverage Pr(Y_{n+1} in C_caos(X_{n+1})) >= 1-alpha despite violating classical exchangeability assumptions, via a monotonicity-based reduction to full conformal prediction (Theorem 4.1, Lemma 5.2).

On the facial landmarking task at alpha=0.05, CAOS attains an average prediction set size of 16.14 +/- 0.58 with 0.955 coverage, versus the SCOS baseline's 36.07 +/- 0.94 set size at 0.976 coverage, a roughly 55% reduction in set size (Table 1).

On 9 RAFT text classification tasks using Llama2-7B at alpha=0.1, CAOS produces smaller prediction sets than SCOS on 8 of 9 tasks while maintaining target coverage in cases where SCOS fails to do so (Figure 3).

The facial landmarking evaluation uses CelebA face crops at 178x218 resolution across 478 landmarking tasks on 100 test images, while the RAFT evaluation uses only 40 labeled examples per task across 9 real-world classification tasks (Section on Datasets).

0B54C7rFJa.text: SICA is compared against 15 state-of-the-art monolithic fake image detection methods, including visual backbones such as ResNet, EfficientNet, SegFormer, Swin Transformer, and ConvNeXt, across four forensic subdomains (Table 2).

On the OpenMMSec benchmark, SICA achieves an overall average accuracy of 85.4%, with 88.4% on Deepfake, 94.8% on AIGC, 85.3% on IMDL, and 73.8% on Doc, ranking best or second-best in three of the four domains (Table 2).

Section 5.3's single-domain (SD) versus leave-one-domain-out (LODO) cross-domain training experiments in Table 3 show SICA maps artifacts from different domains into near-orthogonal subspaces, evidenced by minimal performance degradation compared to FFT-based unified training, which exhibits substantially larger drops (Section 5.3, Table 3).

Section 4.3's SVD-based spectral analysis shows SICA exhibits a higher outside-energy ratio and lower cosine similarity with dominant semantic subspaces than fully fine-tuned baselines, supporting the claim of a unified-yet-discriminative artifact feature space (Section 4.3).

Ib2IjLO7JW.text: Lemma 3.2 proves that recurrent layers lacking step information cannot achieve uniform convergence to a target trajectory, while Theorem 3.3 proves that incorporating step information (via a recurrent layer such that H(t_s) converges uniformly to H*(t_s)) is sufficient for such convergence, establishing step dependence as necessary and sufficient for adaptive convergence (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3).
AdaR's update rule combines message passing, pseudo-node representation-target relations, and sinusoidal step encoding via H(t_s) = H(t_s-1) + v_Theta(H(t_s-1), C, t_s-1) * Delta t (Equation 4).

In zero-shot inductive transfer (Table 1), AdaR achieves 36.15±0.52% on arxiv-year versus 21.79% for GCN and 13.80% for N^2, 37.81±0.94% on WikiCS versus 27.21% for GCN and 22.39% for N^2, and 41.28±0.82% on Cora versus 37.91% for GCN and 29.30% for N^2 (Table 1).

AdaR maintains a fixed 0.4M parameter count while adapting the number of inference-time recurrent steps across diverse downstream tasks, evaluated against baselines including GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, GCNII, DGI, GRACE, and LLaGA (Section on model design).

AdaR's transductive setting results (Table 2) report ROC-AUC scores across multiple datasets, consistent with the claim that AdaR outperforms strong baselines in both inductive and transductive graph settings without parameter changes (Table 2).

BRtDecMvjY.text: GaRA generates task-specific low-rank weight updates by extracting whole-graph information via h = MaxPool(GNN(X,A)) and feeding it to an MLP-based weight generator that produces updates integrated with LoRA's existing matrices (Equation 3).

Theorem 4.1 proves that for the generated update there always exists a parameter update such that Delta W can be scaled with its direction unchanged, identifying an optimization bias (norm amplification) that motivates GaRA's norm-rescaling scheme W = W_hat + (L + G ⊙ M) R^T (Theorem 4.1, Equation 6).

In zero-shot transfer (Table 1), GaRA outperforms baselines including UniGTE, GOFA, LLaGA, and TEA-GLM on node classification (Cora 0.251, WikiCS 0.669, Reddit 0.518, Instagram 0.611) and graph classification (BACE 0.549, HIV 0.512, Amazon 0.708, Photo 0.722) (Table 1).
Table 2 shows that applying the norm-rescaling constraint during full training yields relative improvements of 31.35% and 24.26% on two link prediction tasks compared to without rescaling (Table 2).

tSKDiqiCJ4.text: The S3 framework decomposes multimodal representation learning into three sequential stages—Specialization, Selection, and Sparsification—each implemented via a Mixture-of-Experts router (Section 5.1-5.3).

S3's full pipeline reaches 77.95% accuracy on MOSEI, 66.13% on MOSI, 64.87% on UR-FUNNY, and 62.56% on MUStARD, improving over the DisentangledSSL baseline (77.45%, 65.16%, 64.24%, 61.60% respectively) on all four MultiBench benchmarks (Table 2).

Inference-time expert sparsification produces a reverse U-shaped accuracy curve, with peak performance occurring at intermediate preservation ratios (e.g., 30-90% depending on dataset) rather than at full density (Section 5.3, Table 1).

Proposition 2.1 invokes the Data Processing Inequality to argue that information lost during encoding cannot be recovered downstream, motivating the Task-Sufficient and Information-Minimal representation objective defined in Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 (Section 2, Section 3).
The Selection stage freezes the pretrained encoders and updates only router parameters using a supervised contrastive loss plus a vMF-based compactness loss (Section 5.2).

hFocSMm1Ke.text: GESC introduces a Self-Interference Cancellation (SIC) module (Eq. 11) that replaces additive message aggregation with a rank-1 projection removing self-parallel components before attention, combined with U(1) gauge-equivariant transport of complex node embeddings (Eq. 9) (Section 5, Table 1).

GESC outperforms the strongest prior baseline on Cora (84.9% vs 84.6% for DirGNN), Citeseer (72.1% vs 71.7% for TFE-GNN), Chameleon (65.0% vs 60.2% for TFE-GNN), and Texas (74.5% vs 70.3% for CGNN), ranking first on 5 of 9 benchmark datasets (Table 1).

On large-scale heterophilous graphs, GESC reaches 82.4% on Penn94 (vs 81.8% for GCNII) and 48.2% on arXiv-year (vs 47.6% for H2GCN), while H2GCN runs out of memory on snap-patents where GESC still achieves 48.1% (Table 4, Appendix D.1).

Theorem 5.8 proves a strictly reduced Lipschitz bound along self-parallel directions for GESC compared to standard message passing, and Theorem 5.5 establishes full gauge-equivariance of attention scores and gating decisions under local phase transformations (Theorem 5.5, Theorem 5.8).

At 12 stacked layers, GESC maintains substantially higher accuracy than GCN and GAT, which both degrade sharply on homophilic and heterophilic graphs, demonstrating mitigation of oversmoothing (Figure 4, Section 6.4).

Ablating the gauge-equivariant transport component causes up to a 3.8% accuracy drop, the largest degradation among the four ablated components (SIC, residual gating, transport, complex representations) tested in Table 2 (Table 2).

jciD7uTWu7.text: LIFT fine-tunes model parameters on overlapping segments of the long input (stride s = 3/8 of segment length ℓ) rather than extending the context window, using Contextualized Training and a Gated Memory adapter architecture (Section 3.1, Section 3.4).
On LooGLE LongQA, LIFT raises Llama3 accuracy from 15.44% (in-context learning) to 29.97%, a roughly 94% relative improvement, and raises Gemma2 ShortQA accuracy from 37.37% to 50.33% (Table 2).

LIFT's computational cost scales linearly, O(L), with input length versus the quadratic O(L^2) scaling of standard in-context processing, letting it handle inputs beyond the ~90k-token memory-exhaustion point observed for ICL (Figure 4).

Ablating Contextualized Training reduces LooGLE performance from 47.51% to 43.98% on ShortQA and from 29.97% to 27.07% on LongQA, and the Gated Memory adapter outperforms a PiSSA adapter baseline (47.51% vs 42.03% on ShortQA) (Table 4, Table 6).

A persistent gap remains between in-context and out-of-context question accuracy (71.2% vs 36.16%), indicating LIFT still struggles with precise memorization of irrelevant-seeming context needed for needle-in-a-haystack-style retrieval (Section 6, Table 7).

DkK7GUr8n3.text: ViEEG decomposes each visual stimulus into three biologically-aligned components—contour, foreground object, and contextual scene—processed by parallel EEG encoders with cross-attention hierarchical integration (CAHI) to address 'Hierarchical Neural Encoding Neglect' (Section 4.2-4.5).

In the subject-dependent setting on THINGS-EEG, ViEEG achieves 40.9% Top-1 and 74.5% Top-5 zero-shot image-retrieval accuracy, versus 33.3% Top-1 and 60.5% Top-5 for the prior state of the art CogCap (Table 2).
In the subject-independent (leave-one-out) setting, ViEEG reaches 22.9% Top-1 and 51.4% Top-5 accuracy compared to 15.7% Top-1 and 41.1% Top-5 for the previous best method (Table 2).

Ablations show foreground-object features alone yield 28.9% Top-1 and raw-image features alone yield 28.6% Top-1, while combining all three hierarchical feature streams raises accuracy to 40.9% Top-1, and removing CAHI cross-attention drops accuracy from 40.9% to 38.6% (Table 3).
A hyperparameter sweep finds the optimal CAHI configuration uses 1 attention layer and 3 attention heads for both subject-dependent and subject-independent settings (Figure 7).

N8JsmN0nQE.text: OServe combines workload-aware scheduling (Section 3), which uses a two-level max-flow-based optimization for model-to-GPU assignment, with workload-adaptive switching (Section 4), which uses LSTM-based demand prediction to trigger GPU-to-GPU parameter transfers costing about 10 seconds (Section 3, Section 4).

OServe improves P99 latency by up to 2.0x (average 1.5x) versus static vLLM deployment, up to 1.5x versus vLLM with reload, 1.32-1.51x versus Llumnix, and 12-20% versus Dynamo+vLLM, evaluated on OPT-30B/66B and Llama-30B/2-70B with two Azure Public Dataset traces on 8x H100-80GB GPUs (Section 5.1, Section 5.2).
The LSTM-based workload predictor achieves a 5.045% average relative root-mean-square error, enabling proactive adaptive switching rather than reactive reloading (Section 4).

The heuristic scheduling algorithm completes in about 12 seconds on a 16-GPU cluster and stays within 6% of the exhaustive-search optimum, which itself takes about 50 seconds to compute (Section 5.4).

An ablation isolating heterogeneous deployment alone yields 34% average (52% maximum) P99 latency improvement, while adding optimal workload assignment on top raises this to 64% average (109% maximum) improvement (Figure 14).

3GkzVlIfvP.text: Per-token adapter routing requires computational work W = N·c_pass for N tokens, versus W ≥ K·N·c_pass for per-sequence routing with K adapter types, a K-fold reduction (Theorem 3.6).
MoLoRA's router is a 2-layer MLP with hidden dimension 64 and GELU activation that produces adapter logits, followed by top-k selection and softmax weighting (Section 4.3, Equation 8).
MoLoRA applied to Qwen3-1.7B exceeds Qwen3-8B (4.7x larger) on GSM8K, MATH, BBH, and GPQA reasoning benchmarks (Figure 3, Section 4.4).
CUDA graph capture yields a 67x P99 latency reduction for the routing mechanism (Section 7.5).
Per-token routing achieves a 4.1x reduction in adapter passes for 4-modality workloads and a 4.0x end-to-end speedup on the full transformer (Table 3, Table 7).

KI5B6lcahM.text: Layer-wise Jacobians at different reachable activations within the same transformer layer are highly correlated, with subspace similarity reaching approximately 0.8 in early and late layers, evidencing local linearity across multiple LLM architectures and scales (Section 5.1, Figures 4-5, Equation 24).

The Actuated LQR (A-LQR) method linearizes transformer blocks into Linear Time-Varying approximations and computes optimal gain matrices via Riccati recursions without offline training, using only current activation measurements at inference time (Section 4.2, Equation 4, Equation 19).
On Real Toxicity Prompts, A-LQR achieves roughly 30-50x toxicity reduction compared to baseline methods' 8-10x reduction (Section 7.1, Table 1).

On TruthfulQA, the method improves the Truthfulness x Informativeness (T·I) score by approximately 17% without degrading informativeness, compared to eight baselines including ITI, ActAdd, and ODESteer (Section 7.2, Table 2).

On AdvBench jailbreaking prompts, A-LQR+ matches baseline attack success rate while requiring no offline training, evaluated across models from Llama-3.2-1B to Llama-3.1-70B, Gemma-2-2B/9B, and Qwen-2.5-3B/14B/32B (Section 8, Table 3).

QxU5sv16tg.text: The RESTORE framework improves LLaVA-1.5-7B accuracy at 64-token retention (11.1% of tokens) from 92.2% to 96.5% when combined with HoloV, from 92.8% to 96.0% with VisPruner, and from 93.8% to 95.9% with DivPrune, evaluated across GQA, MMBench, MME, POPE, SQA-IMG, VQAv2, TextVQA, and SEED-Bench (Table 1).

The attention calibration term uses a RoPE-based decay function D(|m-n|) and a distance-aware compensation term log s_n(c - D(|m-n|)) to counteract positional bias from token merging (Section 3.2, Equation 3, Equation 4).
Anchor token selection combines a representativeness score with a discriminativeness term that masks redundant anchors, computed as Top-K(R_i ⊙ (1 - max_j C_ij)) (Equation 8).

Ablations show the full framework reaches 96.5% accuracy at 64-token retention, versus 93.5% for merging alone and 93.1% for attention calibration without merging, demonstrating synergy between components (Table 4).

At 64-token retention on GQA, RESTORE adds only about 4 seconds of total inference overhead and 5.5ms of prefill overhead while maintaining a 1.67x and 1.56x speedup respectively, and anchor selection costs only 0.136% of total MLLM FLOPs (Table 8, Table 9).

RESTORE also improves LLaVA-NeXT-7B (320-token retention: 90.5% vs. 88.9% baseline) and generalizes to Qwen2.5-VL-7B via a multi-dimensional RoPE (M-RoPE) extension of the decay function (Table 2, Table 3, Appendix A).

0rXBwsTWDB.text: The proposed gradient estimator decomposes into a conditional loss gradient on the language model plus a policy-gradient (score function) term treating tokenization as a reinforcement learning problem (Equation 10).

At the 147M-parameter FineWeb scale, the score-function estimator reaches 1.297 bits-per-byte validation loss versus 1.350-1.386 for uniform and straight-through baselines, and outperforms them on PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, and LAMBADA (Table 1).
At the 90M-parameter CodeParrot scale, the method achieves 0.568 bits-per-byte validation loss versus 0.769 for an H-Net baseline (Section on CodeParrot experiments).

Variance reduction relies on three RL-inspired techniques: Early Exit Relative Rewards using byte-level embeddings to estimate baseline prediction difficulty, time discounting with gamma=0.99, and batch-relative advantage normalization (Section 2.4).
Without explicit linguistic supervision, the learned tokenizer discovers boundaries at whitespace characters in natural language and at module names and license blocks in code.

I4LNtQHQBK.text: Joint training on similarity premises (that A1 and A2 share a property) and attribution premises (that A2 has property C) provably yields perfect analogical reasoning via value-matrix feature alignment, with feature cosine similarity of 1-o(1) between aligned entities (Theorem 1, Proposition 1).

Sequential (curriculum) training succeeds only when similarity structure is learned before attribution: the similarity-then-attribution order achieves 1-o(1) feature alignment (Theorem 2), while the reverse attribution-then-similarity order yields o(1) alignment and near-random test performance despite convergent training loss (Theorem 3, Proposition 3).

Two-hop reasoning (A to B, B to C implies A to C) requires explicit identity-bridge examples (B to B) in training data to achieve perfect performance (Theorem 4); without identity bridges, two-hop reasoning fails completely with error rate 1-1/N despite successful learning of each individual hop (Theorem 5, Proposition 5).

On synthetic data, GPT-2 with joint training reaches 0.995 +/- 6e-4 feature similarity and 100% task success, and two-hop reasoning with identity bridges reaches 0.9642 +/- 7e-4 similarity and 99.7% +/- 0.5% success, versus 0.016 +/- 6e-3 similarity and 0% success without identity bridges (Table 1).
On natural-language experiments, Llama-3-1B under joint training reaches 0.8174 feature similarity and 73% success, and Qwen-2.5-1.5B reaches 0.8488 similarity and 85% success (Table 2).

Deep linear networks trained layer-by-layer show progressively increasing feature alignment with depth, reaching cosine similarity of at least 0.8 by the penultimate layer for same-label inputs (Theorem 6).

KJq0iScNM6.text: PTBCC (Prototype-driven Bayesian Classifier Combination) models annotators via a shared set of prototype confusion matrices rather than learning one confusion matrix per annotator (Section on method overview).
PTBCC achieves up to 15% accuracy improvement over the best baseline in its best-case dataset (Val5) (Table 4).
Across 11 real-world crowdsourcing datasets, PTBCC attains an average accuracy of 0.7472, versus 0.7175 for FGBCC, 0.7132 for BWA, and 0.6986 for majority voting (Table 4).

PTBCC's ablation over prototype set size |S| shows accuracy peaking at |S|=2 (0.7472) and degrading to 0.7300 at |S|=3 and 0.7271 at |S|=4 due to sparser per-prototype annotator distributions (Table 5).
PTBCC uses less than 10% of the computational cost of confusion-matrix-based baselines while matching or exceeding their accuracy (Section on computational efficiency).

LyhBIrNBXv.text: Under a power-law spectral prior λ_i ≈ i^{-a} with a>1 (Assumption 3.5), multiplicative (floating-point-like) quantization preserves effective model size M_eff≈M but shrinks effective data size N_eff via noise amplification and spectral distortion (Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.3).

Additive (integer-like) quantization reduces both effective model size and effective data size, because its constant quantization-error variance flattens the tail of the signal spectrum (Theorem 4.2 and Theorem 4.4).
The derived risk bound scales as R_M(v̄_N) ≲ M_eff^{-(a-1)} + N_eff^{-(a-1)/a} + σ² + quantization error term, giving scaling exponents α=-(a-1) and β=-(a-1)/a (Section 3, Definition 3.1).
Empirical experiments confirm the theoretical scaling-law predictions with R² > 0.99 across spectral decay rates a ∈ {1.5, 2.0} (Figures 1-2).

The lower-bound proof for multiplicative quantization required deriving crude bounds on iterate covariance to handle signal-dependent feedback loops, rather than a rough decoupling argument (Section 5).

FQNYtjPBxv.text: On single-parent hierarchy taxonomy expansion, Polaris improves R@1 by up to 27.1 points (Environment dataset, 47.60 vs. best baseline) and reduces mean rank by roughly 4x on Environment (MR=6.48) (Table 1).
On WordNet, Polaris improves R@5 by 15 points (70.1) and reduces mean rank by about 42% relative to the strongest baseline (Table 1).
On multi-parent hierarchies, Polaris improves H@1 by 15.4 points and H@5 by 24.5 points on MeSH, and cuts mean rank by roughly 31 points on SemEval-Verb versus STEAM (Table 2).
On the multimodal CUB-200-2011 hierarchy, Polaris achieves Precision@1 of 78.91 (a 5-point gain over Gumbel Box) with mean rank 1.44 and MRR 86.94 (Table 3).

Polaris is compared against fourteen baselines including TransE, RotatE, HAKE, HyperExpan, ConE, Box embeddings, Gumbel Box, TaxoExpan, STEAM, TMN, and Arborist across all three hierarchy settings (Tables 1-3).

Polaris combines manifold-consistent spherical encoding, a robust geodesic triplet loss with a Welsch M-estimator, anisotropic spherical SVGD regularization, and asymmetric vMF-KL objectives to separate semantic direction from hierarchical radius (Section on method overview).

jyOgpu5wfC.text: Durian regroups training samples by difficulty—computed from perceptual entropy (Section 3.1) and reasoning confidence via token log-probabilities (Section 3.2)—before computing group-relative standard deviations in GRPO, rather than using a single shared std across the whole batch.

On Qwen2.5-VL-7B trained with 2.1K samples, Durian (combined with DAPO) improves MathVerse from 46.2% to 51.9%, MathVision from 25.0% to 29.0%, MathVista from 67.5% to 72.2%, WeMath from 63.1% to 71.8%, and HallusionBench from 64.6% to 71.4% (Table 1, Section 4).

An appendix analysis finds 35-46% of GRPO training groups have identical rewards (std=0), and among the remainder 31-44% show a 7-correct/1-incorrect reward pattern, motivating the need for difficulty-aware regrouping (Table 4, Appendix A).

Ablations show perceptual-only regrouping adds +3.4% on HallusionBench and reasoning-only regrouping adds +3.8% on MathVerse, while the combined Durian objective yields the best overall average accuracy of 59.3% (Figure 3, Section 4.3).
Durian's performance across reasoning-group counts is stable from 4 to 48 groups, peaking around 12-16 groups (Table 2, Section 4.4).

LLMMMRZ4lG.text: Proposition 1 proves majority vote produces unstable rankings when items have single-vote margins, while Proposition 2 shows STABLEVAL's posterior expected item credit (PEC) achieves asymptotic ranking stability as the number of items grows (Section 4).

STABLEVAL estimates annotator confusion matrices via an EM-based procedure (Algorithm 1) and reports item credit scores with bootstrap confidence intervals rather than collapsing annotations to hard labels.
On MT-Bench, where only 16.6% of items have unanimous annotator agreement, PEC attains a mean rank standard deviation of 0.197 versus 0.259 for majority vote (Section 6, real-world benchmarks).

In synthetic experiments, Dawid-Skene achieves the lowest label-recovery MSE, yet PEC still consistently improves over majority vote in both label error and ranking consistency, and attains a perfect Kendall's Tau of 1.000 in the no-hard-item regime (Section 6.1).

On low-annotator-count benchmarks such as MSLR (2 annotators), all evaluated methods, including PEC, show increased ranking variability, illustrating that stability gains from STABLEVAL depend on sufficient annotator redundancy (Section 6).
