PPD achieves a 15-25% reduction in average query latency on the ShareGPT multi-turn conversation trace compared to baseline PD disaggregation (Section on Performance Results).

The online routing decision in PPD adds less than 1ms of overhead per request by mapping incoming Turn 2+ requests to a precomputed offline decision table (Section describing the Algorithm/Online phase).

FrXKVuK0yS.text: At 1.7B parameters, the depth-grown LIDAS model reaches 48.02% accuracy on reasoning primitives versus 39.88% for the looped model Loop(4-4x4-4) and 34.62% for the baseline (Section on Performance Results).
Applying inference-time looping to depth-grown models yields up to 2x gains on reasoning primitive accuracy despite the models never being trained to loop (Section on Composability).
With a math-heavy cooldown mixture and retrofitted recurrence, LIDAS improves further to 56.60% accuracy on reasoning primitives (Section on Performance Results).

Both depth-grown and looped models exhibit increased reliance on late layers and periodic, block-aligned patterns in residual updates that align with the grown or looped block (Section on Shared Mechanistic Signatures).

Looped models under a fixed parameter budget and depth-grown models under a fixed training-compute budget adapt better than baselines to in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning (Section on Adaptability).

0Cn92msBcW.text: ForceForget achieves zero detections of Breast(M), Genitalia(M), and Buttocks categories on the 4,703-image I2P nudity benchmark (Section on Key Results).

ForceForget attains a 100% Nudity Removal Rate against both the Ring-A-Bell and P4D red-teaming attacks, outperforming ten state-of-the-art baseline concept-erasing methods (Section on Robustness Performance).

ForceForget preserves 90.7% celebrity recognition accuracy while erasing nudity concepts, indicating limited collateral damage to unrelated human-generation capability (Section on Semantic Preservation).

The method combines a Concept Erasing Reward (CER) balancing safety and alignment terms with a lightweight Safe Adapter that projects partial text embeddings for cross-attention regulation, trained via importance sampling and proximal policy optimization (Section on Core Innovation/Technical Approach).

ForceForget generalizes beyond nudity removal to artistic style erasure and object removal, and shows improved transferability to image-to-image (I2I) erasure scenarios where baseline methods show significant safety gaps (Section on Generalization).

sr1qgowJQ1.text: On non-monotonic text streaming tasks (QA and summarization), ProactiveLLM retains 97.16% of offline (full-context) performance while consuming only 78% of the input context (Section on Experimental Results, Text Streaming Performance).
ProactiveLLM achieves a 21.6% latency reduction compared to fixed-interval streaming baselines (Section on Experimental Results, Text Streaming Performance).

Attention FLOP reduction varies by task alignment structure: 2.27% for machine translation (monotonic), 21.67% for short-form QA (non-monotonic), and 34.82% for multiple-choice QA (highly non-monotonic) (Section on Cognitive Efficiency).

ProactiveLLM decouples 'when to generate' from 'what to generate' via two decision heads-an attention-driven head monitoring cumulative attention to the input stream and an entropy-driven head measuring Shannon entropy of the predictive distribution (Section on Decoupled Decision Heads).

Masked Streaming Language Modeling (MSLM) applies monotonic random masking with polynomial-biased allocation during training to simulate progressively revealed inputs, paired with Synchronized Privileged Self-Distillation (SPSD) that uses the same model as both student and full-context teacher via KL divergence (Section on Key Technical Components).

GQ17DjsBcq.text: Theorem 1 (Coverage) establishes that K=N-1 overlapping windows of size 4 and stride 2 are necessary and sufficient to cover any (2N-2):2N sparse block (Theorem 1).
SlideSparse's speedup bound approaches N/(N-1), giving 1.50x for 4:6, 1.33x for 6:8, and 1.25x for 8:10 sparsity patterns (Section on Theoretical Results).

On Qwen2.5-7B prefill with A100 INT8 at 6:8 sparsity, SlideSparse achieves a 1.33x end-to-end speedup, exactly matching the theoretical N/(N-1) bound (Section on Experimental Results, End-to-End Inference).

Kernel-level benchmarks show 1.41-1.42x speedup on A100 INT8 and 1.35-1.37x on H100 FP8 at 6:8 sparsity, both exceeding the 1.33x theoretical bound (Section on Experimental Results, Kernel Performance).

On Qwen3, 6:8 sparsity retains 51.6% average accuracy across reasoning benchmarks versus only 15.3% for strict 2:4 sparsity, motivating the need for moderate sparsity hardware support (Section on Key Problem).

Decode-phase (memory-bound) inference shows more modest gains of 1.07-1.21x at 6:8 sparsity, consistent with reduced weight memory footprint rather than compute savings (Section on Experimental Results, Decode Performance).

ZLraoxBly2.text: The method linearizes the Wasserstein space using Linearized Optimal Transport (LOT) and projects embeddings via PCA into a K-dimensional space before applying Multi-Output Gaussian Processes to quantify epistemic uncertainty over temporal coefficients (Section 4.1-4.3).

A time-warping function Φ(t) reparameterizes physical time into intrinsic time based on cumulative Wasserstein distance, allowing stationary GP kernels to model non-stationary distributional dynamics (Section 4.4).

On synthetic branching-trajectory data, the active acquisition strategy achieves a 23.1% relative improvement over the uniform-sampling baseline in mean Wasserstein error, with the largest gains for highly localized branching events lasting 5% of the trajectory duration (Table 1, Section 5.2).

On real-world single-cell reprogramming data, the active strategy outperforms uncertainty-agnostic baselines at low-to-moderate measurement budgets (up to 12 measurements), with the performance gap narrowing as sampling density increases (Figure 5, Section 5.3).

Ablations show that reducing the latent PCA dimension to K=2 causes the largest performance drop, and disabling the time-warping mechanism substantially degrades performance in the low-budget regime (Figure 6, Section 5.4).

J4wRLmh29t.text: Weak monotonicity is formally defined as a preorder on hypotheses such that if model f dominates f' across all benchmark risks, then f also achieves lower risk on the new target task (Section 2.1).

Theorem 1 derives the limiting distribution of the Pareto covering number as the threshold t approaches 0, showing the density depends on normal vectors to the Pareto frontier and implicitly induces a natural prior over trade-offs (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 gives excess-risk upper bounds for Pareto ERM and Pareto Exponential Weights of the form ω̄_Q(t) + sqrt(2 log(2 N_Par(t,𝓕,𝐑)/δ)/n), while Corollary 1 shows this recovers the O(sqrt(K/n)) worst-case rate of prior work with adaptive, geometry-dependent constants (Theorem 2, Corollary 1).

Theorem 4 shows model-selection aggregation over the Pareto frontier can achieve fast O(log K / n) rates without requiring strongly convex losses, provided the frontier satisfies a strongly concave gap condition (Assumption 2, Theorem 4).

On HELM and VHELM benchmark data, empirical moduli of monotonicity violation are near zero, supporting approximate weak monotonicity in practice, and the adaptive margin-ERM estimator substantially outperforms unrestricted ERM at small target sample sizes (Figure 3, Figure 6).

J2TKCPUI3E.text: BoostAPR achieves 40.7% resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified (+22.9pp over the base model), 24.8% on Defects4J v2.0 (207/835 bugs, Python-to-Java transfer), 84.5% on HumanEval-Java (+20.5pp), and 95.0% on QuixBugs (38/40 bugs) (Table 1).

The three-stage pipeline consists of execution-verified supervised fine-tuning that retains only teacher-generated patches passing test execution (~35% pass rate), followed by dual reward model training (sequence-level R_seq and line-level R_line) and PPO optimization with LoRA rank 64 (Figure 1, Section 3).

Line-level credit assignment for R_line outperforms token-uniform, hunk-level, and statement-level granularity alternatives, and is reported to be more suited to code-diff-based repair than other levels of granularity tested (Table 4).

Restricting the sequence-level reward model to score only the diff (patch-only scoring, 40.7%) outperforms giving it full issue context (38.9%), suggesting patch-only scoring avoids spurious correlations with issue difficulty (Table 5).

Adding R_line to PPO with R_seq alone contributes an additional +2.4pp on SWE-bench Verified and +5.6pp on Defects4J, with total training cost of 64 GPU-hours, of which PPO accounts for 46.9% (Table 3).

khWPVCGMsG.text: Cosine-similarity classifiers built directly from frozen supervised classification head weight vectors retain over 80% accuracy on ImageNet-1K across diverse architectures including BEiT, ConvNeXt, and TinyViT (Table 1).
Classification head weight vectors achieve higher mutual k-NN alignment scores with text embeddings than averaged image representations computed from up to 50 images per class (Figure 1).

Pairing ImageNet-21K classification head weight vectors with class-name text embeddings enables zero-shot vision-language alignment training in roughly 2 GPU-minutes without any paired image-text data.

Augmenting real image-text pairs with classification-weight-derived pseudo-pairs yields the largest few-shot classification gains over nearest-centroid and k-NN baselines on CIFAR-10/100, DTD, and Places at 1-4 shots, with benefits diminishing as real paired data increases (Figure 4, Table 2).
The paper reports a measurable modality gap between classification weights and image representations (mean separation distance 0.1723, p<0.001) that simple mitigation strategies fail to close.

gUbNUNuJbO.text: Bridge Matching Sampler (BMS) unifies fixed-point diffusion-matching samplers under a single framework based on Nelson's relation and a generalized target score identity, recovering Adjoint Sampling (AS) and Adjoint Schrödinger Bridge Sampler (ASBS) as special cases.

Unlike ASBS, which requires alternating optimization, BMS uses independent couplings between prior and target distributions to learn the transport map with a single, scalable, stable training objective, combined with a damped fixed-point iteration for regularization.

On high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures up to d=2500, BMS remains stable and captures all modes, whereas ASBS exhibits performance degradation at these scales, contrasting with prior work typically limited to d=50.
On the LJ-55 n-body benchmark (d=165), BMS achieves W2 distance 3.80±0.01 and energy accuracy error 2.36±0.45, versus ASBS's 4.00±0.03 and 28.10±8.15 respectively (Table 2).
On Alanine Dipeptide (ALA2, d=66), the damped BMS variant achieves JS divergence 0.068±0.009 and free-energy RMSE 0.079±0.000, significantly outperforming both the undamped BMS variant and ASBS.

dAWFE1gPmJ.text: Value aggregation in self-attention causes the first token to retain significantly higher variance across its dimensions compared to the rest of the sequence, which is the structural origin of variance discrepancy (Section 3.1, Figure 4).

Interventions that mask attention or directly amplify dimension-wise variance can induce attention sinks at arbitrary token positions, demonstrating a causal link between variance discrepancy and sink formation (Section 3.2).

A subset of 'super neurons' in the FFN down-projection selectively amplifies first-token signals via channel-sparse weights, producing a measured dominance ratio of 262.88x in outlier dimensions after RMSNorm (Section 4.2, Section 4.3).

Structural alignment analysis shows a mean correlation of 0.32 between FFN down-projection weight matrices and input variance, linking output-projection structure to preserved variance discrepancy (Section 4.1).

A proposed head-wise RMSNorm modification applied after value aggregation reduces validation loss from 2.7812±0.0109 to 2.7421±0.0066 and raises effective rank from 343.71±15.63 to 445.96±5.37 when pre-training a 152M-parameter model (Section 5.2, Table 2).
Both Llama-2 and Llama-3 exhibit a precipitous collapse in representation effective rank within the first few layers, coinciding with the onset of dimension disparity (Section 4.3, Figure 11).

3Hea2WFhPW.text: Psi-RAG outperforms RAPTOR by 25.9% and HippoRAG 2 by 7.4% in average F1 score across cross-document multi-hop QA benchmarks including HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue (Table 2).

The hierarchical abstract tree is constructed via an iterative merging and collapse process, described in the appendix's tree-construction methodology, that adapts to data distributions without a priori assumptions on cluster count (Section B).

The framework is evaluated on tasks ranging from token-level multi-hop question answering to document-level summarization, using benchmarks such as NarrativeQA and QMSum in addition to multi-hop QA sets (Section D.2).

Tree quality is evaluated using the Dasgupta cost function to compare clustering strategies such as single-linkage and UPGMA hierarchical clustering against uniform K-means variants with 6, 12, and 23 clusters (Section B.3).

Ablation studies isolating the hierarchical merging/collapse mechanism from alternative flat or fixed-cluster retrieval baselines are reported in dedicated ablation tables in the appendix (Section B.3, Appendix C).

YsexiJ0zAh.text: OSNIP achieves a 0.000 KNN attack success rate on Qwen3-32B while retaining 100.13% of non-private average accuracy across 10 classification benchmarks, compared to Cape's 0.578 ASR and 69.84% retained accuracy at epsilon=14 (Table 1, Section 4.2).

On generative perplexity evaluation with WikiText-2, OSNIP increases perplexity by only 3% on Qwen3-32B (6.73 to 6.94), whereas baseline Cape and InferDPT increase perplexity by 832% and 17,073% respectively (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On CNN/DailyMail summarization, OSNIP retains 99.9-100.1% of non-private BERTScore across Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-14B, and Llama-3.2-3B (Table 3, Section 4.2).

Theorem 2.5 proves the obfuscated semantic null space is non-empty whenever semantic coverage satisfies alpha_delta(h) > 2exp(-(d-2)epsilon^2/2), with Corollary 2.6 showing the gap between semantic-preserving directions and the null space vanishes exponentially with embedding dimensionality (Section 2.2, Theorem 2.5, Corollary 2.6).
OSNIP incurs only 0.96 ms of per-prompt computational overhead, versus 98.36 ms for Cape, 16.87 ms for InferDPT, and 4.93 ms for DYNText (Table 4, Section 4.4).

mUiSbaBM9L.text: PINNfluence computes influence functions (Eq. 3) to attribute predictions and individual loss components (PDE residual loss and boundary condition loss) back to specific training collocation points, extended to multi-point and loss-term removal via Corollary 1 (Section 2).

On three variants of a 2D Navier-Stokes PINN (phi_good with correct PDE and adequate data, phi_broken missing a physics term, and phi_bad with sparse training data), influence patterns differ systematically and distinguish these failure modes (Section 3).
A single training point's influence heatmap near the cylinder boundary reveals its effect on velocity component u1 predictions across the full domain (Figure 2).

The Directional Indicator (Eq. 5) and Object Indicator (Eq. 6) are proposed diagnostics, with phi_good achieving DI=0.83 for pressure and OI=0.28 for cylinder influence, the highest among the three model variants (Table 1, Eq. 5, Eq. 6).

phi_good's influence concentrates near the inflow, outflow, and cylinder boundaries, while phi_bad shows excessive dependence on the upper-left domain boundary, illustrating divergent influence distributions across model quality (Figure 3).

FlnQlvkYR3.text: SkillTrojan achieves a 97.2% attack success rate while maintaining 89.3% clean accuracy on GPT-5.2-1211-Global, outperforming baselines including AgentPoison and BadChain (Section 5, Table in Section 5).

Across four target models, SkillTrojan attains ASR/clean-accuracy of 74.7%/86.6% on Qwen3-Max, 64.2%/90.7% on Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and 72.0%/81.3% on GLM-4.6, showing consistently high ASR across both open-weight and closed-weight settings (Section 5.2, Table in Section 5).
The released SkillTrojanX dataset comprises 1,200 templates, 3,000+ backdoored skills, 6 template categories, 4 payload families, and 3 crypto variants (Section 5.3).
SkillTrojan supports automated synthesis of backdoored skill packages via the SkillTrojanX construction pipeline, enabling scalable propagation across agent ecosystems (Section 4.3).

Ablation experiments identify optimal attack performance at N=3 payload fragments, with different encryption/crypto variants showing similar effectiveness but differing detectability rates (Section 5.4).

V0eGsz18uZ.text: Strat-Reasoner-4B achieves a 22.1% average performance improvement across the evaluated multi-agent games compared to baselines (Table 1).

The Recursive Reasoning Module structures an agent's chain-of-thought as a 'Past-Present-Future' cognitive loop with four fields: OpponentIntent, OpponentPrediction, MyIntent, and MyPrediction (Section 4.1).
Hybrid Advantage Estimation combines CoT-based and return-based advantages using a weighting coefficient omega=0.2 (Section 4.3).
Strat-Reasoner is trained on Tic-Tac-Toe, KuhnPoker, and MiniHanabi and evaluated for generalization on unseen ConnectFour, LeducHoldem, and SimpleHanabi environments (Table 2).
Ablations show removing the CoT-based training signal or the normalized score computation degrades performance relative to the full Strat-Reasoner model (Figure 4).

Strat-Reasoner-4B is compared against open-source baselines including Qwen3 variants, Gemma3, SPIRAL-4B, and MARSHAL-4B, as well as closed-source models GPT-5-mini and Gemini-2.5-flash (Section 5, Table 1).

wOAslbdI1r.text: The proposed NAVI framework combines Masked Segment Modeling (MSM) and Entropy-driven Segment Alignment (ESA) to model heterogeneous tabular data at the header-value segment level (Section 3).
On the generative header prediction task, NAVI achieves 0.9995 accuracy on the Product domain and 0.9998 on the Movie domain, versus HAETAE's 0.9260 and 0.8982 respectively (Table 1).
On value imputation, NAVI scores 0.7933 (Product) and 0.7077 (Movie), compared to HAETAE's 0.7785 and 0.6911 (Table 1).
Under column-permutation robustness testing, NAVI's performance drops by only 0.02% on the Product domain versus a 6.92% drop for HAETAE (Table 2).
NAVI attains header-clustering NMI scores of 0.9005 (Product) and 0.9144 (Movie), exceeding HAETAE's 0.8742 and 0.8864 (Table 3).

Ablations show that removing the context-free attribute embedding (CAE) or the MSM objective substantially degrades reconstruction and downstream classification performance, and entropy-based routing outperforms random routing on value imputation (0.7933 vs. 0.7903) (Table 5).

XSpBSHzJAg.text: The paper's perturbation-based algorithm, PABLO, reduces unconstrained Bandit Linear Optimization (uBLO) to a standard Online Linear Optimization (OLO) problem (Section 3).

Theorem 3.1 gives an expected static-regret bound of the form E[R_T(u)] = O~(G*epsilon + d*kappa*E[||u||*sqrt(V_T log(...))]), with kappa=sqrt(d) in the norm-oblivious setting and kappa=1 in the norm-adaptive setting (Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.3 shows PABLO attains the optimal sqrt(P_T) dynamic-regret dependence on the path-length P_T without requiring prior knowledge of P_T (Theorem 3.3).
Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-probability static-regret bound R_T(u) <= O~(dG(epsilon+||u||)log(T/delta) + G||u||sqrt(dT log(T/delta))) (Theorem 4.2).
Theorem 5.2 proves the folklore Omega(sqrt(dT)) minimax lower bound for adversarial linear bandits on the unit Euclidean ball (Theorem 5.2).
Conjecture 5.3 posits a minimax rate of R_T(u) = Theta(||u|| sqrt(T(d v log||u||))) for norm-oblivious comparators, left as an open problem (Conjecture 5.3).

jTtfB7ur5m.text: The Early-Exit Failure Prediction (EEFP) score is defined as EEFP_j = AUROC(c_j(x_i), ybar_j,i), where ybar_j,i marks whether exiting at head j is a correct decision (i.e., the head is correct or all deeper heads would also fail) (Section 2).

On an MSDNet with 7 early-exit blocks trained on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet, deliberately miscalibrated variants (temperature scaled by 3.0 or 0.3) can achieve better cost-accuracy trade-offs than well-calibrated models despite worse Expected Calibration Error (ECE) (Section 3.1).

Rank-preserving decalibration transformations that keep sample confidence ordering unchanged leave cost-accuracy trade-off performance unchanged even though ECE substantially worsens, whereas EEFP correctly identifies the unchanged performance (Section 3.2).

Findings that EEFP better tracks cost-accuracy performance than ECE hold across alternative calibration methods, Last-layer Laplace Approximations (LAP) and Model-Internal Ensembles (MIE), and across multiple MSDNet sizes (Appendix C).

SX7LSFG4IH.text: The reasoning efficiency metric eta is defined as eta = (log|V| - H_str(G)) / (log|V| - log|C*|), where |V| is the total number of extracted claim nodes, H_str(G) is the structural entropy of the reasoning graph's Markov-chain flow, and |C*| is the minimal claim set needed for the solution (Equation 2).

Evaluated on 21 logic puzzles spanning four difficulty levels (Trivial, Human easy, Human normal, Human hard) derived from Simon Tatham's puzzle collection, GPT-5 attains 54.3% average accuracy using 12,867 average tokens, while Kimi K2 attains 43.8% accuracy using 36,343 average tokens (Table 1).

Token count is a poor proxy for reasoning quality, showing near-zero correlation with accuracy (r = -0.05, p = 0.64), whereas the structural efficiency metric eta correlates positively with accuracy (r = +0.368, p < 0.001) (Section 5).
Extra generated tokens are mainly attributable to verification overhead, correlating with the ratio of verification-subgraph to solution-subgraph node counts |V_ver|/|V_sol| (r = 0.53) (Section 5).

Repeated claim-extraction runs show Jaccard overlaps of 0.79-0.98 and eta varies by only a 1.9% coefficient of variation across different extractor configurations, with manual rule validation finding 75.5% fully correct under a strict criterion (Appendix A).

5G9puwbCsu.text: BudgetMem organizes memory processing into modular components, each offered in three budget tiers (Low, Mid, High), realized via three complementary strategies: implementation complexity, reasoning depth, and model capacity (Section on Budget Tier Realization Strategies).

A lightweight router trained via reinforcement learning selects the budget tier per query at runtime, replacing offline, query-agnostic memory construction used by prior agent memory systems (Section on Core Architecture).
BudgetMem is evaluated on the LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and HotpotQA datasets (Experimental Evaluation section).

BudgetMem surpasses strong baselines when performance is prioritized under the high-budget setting, and delivers better accuracy-cost frontiers than baselines under tighter budget constraints (Experimental Evaluation section).

gLBxxIwzkB.text: D3 formulates LLM data scheduling as finding an optimal permutation across K training batches to minimize test loss, framed as a combinatorial optimization over K! possible schedules (Section 3.1).

D3 constructs a dynamic directional influence graph between training batches, where Proposition 3.2 shows batch-to-batch influence is symmetric to first order but becomes asymmetric once curvature effects are considered (Section 3.2).

The Random-Swap Refinement (RSR) solver approximates the graph-constrained scheduling optimization with O(K^2 + MK) complexity via row-sum initialization followed by stochastic local search (Section 3.4).
On SlimPajama pre-training with GPT-2 Medium over 100B tokens, D3 achieves a 4.2% perplexity reduction over the strongest baseline (2.97 vs 3.10 perplexity) (Table 1).
On SFT with Llama-3-8B, D3 improves GSM8K by 3.1%, MATH by 11.4%, HumanEval by 8.0%, and MBPP by 6.6%, for an aggregated improvement of 6.7% (Table 2).

An ablation shows the RSR solver outperforms Row-Sum and Greedy Insertion baselines (perplexity 2.97 vs 3.04 vs 3.17), and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis finds peak performance at projection dimension k approximately 3500 (8.1% perplexity reduction) and scheduling window L=60 (9.3% gain) (Table 3, Figure 3).

yt6vQ8gbGm.text: TRACE performs realignment via a three-stage pipeline: programmatic triage of preference pairs into Invert (Type I), Punish (Type II), and Retain sets, followed by hybrid DPO/NPO objectives and alignment impact-weighted optimization (Section 4).
TRACE is evaluated for realignment robustness on Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Llama-3.1-8B using the PKU-SafeRLHF and SynthValueBench datasets (Section 5).
In a human preference study, TRACE is preferred over the U2A baseline 81.8% of the time on PKU-SafeRLHF and 85.3% on SynthValueBench (Table 1).
On policy alignment, TRACE achieves 70.2% target policy agreement compared to U2A's 54.7%, versus 100% for a full re-training oracle (Table 4).
On adversarial robustness against Fictional Scenario Nesting attacks, TRACE achieves a 27.3% attack success rate, comparable to U2A's 24.6% and higher than the DPO-Gold oracle's 11.3% (Table 3).
TRACE shows negligible degradation in general capability benchmarks (GPQA, MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K) relative to base models, nearly matching the DPO-Gold full re-training oracle (Table 2).

19AbP986bv.text: SandboxEscapeBench comprises 18 scenarios spanning three attack layers (Orchestration, Runtime, Kernel), including documented CVEs such as CVE-2019-5736 (runc overwrite), CVE-2022-0492 (cgroup abuse), and CVE-2016-5195 (Dirty COW) (Appendix B, Table 1).

The benchmark uses a nested 'sandbox-in-sandbox' architecture built with the Inspect framework, running a Docker container inside a Vagrant-provisioned VM with the flag placed on the VM filesystem outside the container namespace (Section 4).

Opus achieves an overall success rate of 0.49 [0.39, 0.59], compared to 0.18 for Haiku and 0.16 for GPT-OSS-120B, and models achieve zero observed success on the hardest difficulty-4-5 kernel exploits (Section 5).
GPT-5.2 performs significantly worse than GPT-5 on sandbox escape (0.27 vs 0.50 success rate), a version regression noted in the results (Section 5).

Success rate scales approximately log-linearly with inference-time compute budget across scenarios (Figure 3), and all successful escapes relied on documented CVEs or known misconfigurations rather than novel vulnerabilities (Section 5).

9YC7mbloXl.text: GAM-RAG builds a lightweight hierarchical graph using entity co-occurrence extracted via spaCy NER, avoiding expensive relation extraction used by prior graph-based RAG methods (Section 3.1.1).

Each memory sentence maintains task-oriented and time-oriented memory vectors with corresponding perplexity terms, updated via a Kalman-inspired gain rule that applies fast updates for reliable novel signals and conservative refinement for stable or noisy memories (Section 3.3).
GAM-RAG improves average performance by 3.95% over the strongest baseline, rising to 8.19% with 5-turn memory, with a 16.5% gain over the second-best method on MuSiQue (Table 1).

GAM-RAG reduces average inference latency by 61% and uses substantially lower indexing cost (1.66M tokens) compared to 4-9M tokens for competing methods such as GritLM, LinearRAG, GFM-RAG, HippoRAG2, PoG, DyG-RAG, and REMINDRAG (Table 2).
Ablations over a 10-turn evaluation show that removing task memory, time memory, perplexity gating, or gain scheduling each causes measurable performance degradation (Section 4.3, Figure 4).

JrVfxa6aLL.text: Across 46,535 controlled experiments spanning 11 tasks (8 classical, 3 applied), 19 cue types, and 15 model configurations, incidental prompt cues systematically steer which algorithm an LLM selects (Section 4.1, Table 2).

Per-cell steering capacity reaches a median of 40 percentage points and a mean of 50.0 percentage points across API models, with 56% of task-cue cells exceeding a 30-point swing (Section 4.1, Table 2).
On a tree-traversal recursion task, the behavior rate swings from 0% under a space-constraint framing to 89% under a readability framing, an 89-point steering effect (Section 4.1, Table 12).

On the expression-parsing task, use of unsafe eval()-based implementations shifts from 70% under a 'prototype' persona cue to 6% under an 'interview' persona cue, illustrating a security-relevant steering effect (Section 4.1, Table 12).

Explicitly specifying the target algorithm in the prompt, rather than relying on implicit cues, raises pass rate to 100% and strict algorithm-compliance to 98.3%, the most effective mitigation tested (Section 5.6).

ORVJCJczoG.text: AgentNoiseBench models two primary noise sources for tool-using LLM agents: user-side instruction noise (ambiguity, inconsistency, redundancy, topic drift, boundary probing) and tool-side result noise (execution failures, incomplete responses, erroneous outputs, misleading signals) (Section 2.2.1).

Across 24 evaluated models, noise injection causes an average accuracy drop of 20.8%, with tool-side noise producing substantially larger degradation than user-side noise (Table 1; Observation 4, Section 3.5).
Among tool-side noise types, execution failures are the most destructive, driving performance scores as low as 0.31 (Figure 5a, Observation 5).

Reasoning ability and noise robustness are not closely related: some strong reasoning models misinterpret corrupted tool feedback as meaningful signal and fabricate confident but erroneous conclusions, a 'reasoning trap' (Observation 2).

Agents are most sensitive to noise injected at the middle stage of a trajectory, when decisions rely most heavily on accumulated context, compared to early or late injection (Section 3.6, Figure 6, Observation 6).

UBTVJLMzmE.text: The canonical PPO/GRPO clipping mechanism constrains the feasible upward probability variation to scale linearly with the old action probability, nullifying gradients for low-probability, high-advantage actions (Section 4).

BandPO's Band operator projects f-divergence-induced trust regions (KL, Pearson chi-squared, Total Variation) into dynamic, probability-aware clipping bounds via a convex optimization problem with closed-form solutions for specific divergences (Section 5.1-5.2).

Theorem 1 shows the optimal upper and lower clipping bounds are the two roots of the scalar equation g_f(p,r) = delta, reducing a high-dimensional simplex optimization to a univariate root-finding problem (Theorem 1).

Unlike DAPO's Clip-Higher and DCPO, which violate the theoretical simplex bound in high-probability regimes, all BandPO variants (KL, chi-squared, TV) remain strictly consistent with the probability simplex constraints (Figure 2).

BandPO achieves consistent performance improvements over GRPO and GRPO with Clip-Higher across Qwen2.5 (3B and 7B) and Llama3 (8B) on multiple mathematical benchmarks, while mitigating entropy collapse (Section 1).

npMOaMWWrW.text: Using k-sparse probing, MoE experts achieve near-optimal F1 scores at k=1 while dense FFN neurons in comparable models perform substantially worse at this sparsity level, indicating experts are more monosemantic (Figure 1, Section 4.2).

Lower routing sparsity ratios (N_A/N) correlate with cleaner, more monosemantic representations: Qwen3-30B-A3B (N_A/N approx 0.06) shows higher interpretability than the denser Mixtral-8x7B (N_A/N = 0.25), though both outperform dense counterparts (Section 4.4, Figure 4).

A four-category taxonomy of expert specialization is proposed -- morphological, syntactic, semantic, and operational -- resolving debate over whether experts specialize by broad domain or fine-grained linguistic operation (Section 6.1).
Automatic interpretability analysis finds most experts achieve F1 scores above 0.8, with the sparsest model tested (Qwen3) frequently exceeding 0.9 (Section 5.2).

Jensen-Shannon Divergence analysis of expert functional specialization shows late-layer scores reaching 0.4 or higher, with peak specialization observed at fine-grained task granularity (k=5000) rather than broad domain granularity (k=10) (Section 6.2, Figure 7).

ZZZkLWphuO.text: Under input noise of sigma=0.010, VMoER routing methods (VGLR-FC, VTSR) achieve Jaccard similarity above 0.61 in expert-selection stability, versus 0.532 for deterministic top-k routing, an approximately 38% relative improvement (Section 5.4, Table 3).

VMoER reduces Expected Calibration Error substantially across backbones: from 0.252 to 0.015 on Granite-MoE (94% reduction), from 0.127 to 0.014 on Qwen-MoE (89% reduction), and from 0.168 to 0.054 on DeepSeek-MoE (68% reduction) (Section 5.2, Table 1).

For out-of-distribution detection, VGLR-FC's Inf-Logit-Var signal achieves average AUROC of 0.749 versus 0.659 for the deterministic routing baseline, roughly a 12% relative improvement (Section 5.3, Table 2).
The computational overhead of VMoER remains under 1%: VGLR-FC adds 1.15% activation memory and 1.07% FLOPs, while VTSR adds 0.74% activation memory and 0.67% FLOPs (Section 5.5, Table 4).

membbcuXeR.text: ImplicitRM's stratification model partitions training samples into four latent groups—Positive-Active, Negative-Active, Positive-Passive, and Negative-Passive—based on latent preference and action variables (Section 3.2, Table 1).
Equation (6) computes posterior group-membership probabilities for each sample using an estimated preference model and an action-propensity model (Section 3.2, Equation 6).

Theorem 3.2 proves that the ImplicitRM training objective is an unbiased estimator of the ideal cross-entropy objective over ground-truth preferences when stratification probabilities equal the true posteriors (Theorem 3.2).
On the HelpSteer dataset ImplicitRM attains R²=0.3114 versus 0.2790 for the SelectMix baseline (Table 2).
On UltraFeedback ImplicitRM attains R²=0.5207 versus 0.4752 for SelectMix, and on PKU-SafeRLHF it attains R²=0.7872 versus 0.7346 for SelectMix (Table 2).
Ablation results show each stratification component contributes to the final performance gains, with component removal degrading accuracy across all three implicit preference datasets (Table 3).

E9SXR70XyN.text: SAC-Opt improves average modeling accuracy by 7.8% across seven public optimization-modeling datasets compared to baseline methods (Section 4.4, Table 1).
On the ComplexLP dataset SAC-Opt raises accuracy from a 52.1% baseline to 79.6%, a gain of 21.9 percentage points (Table 1).
SAC-Opt yields additional gains of +9.7% on IndustryOR, +7.0% on NL4OPT, and +7.7% on ReSocratic (Section 4.4, Table 1).

Ablating the semantic correction component drops NL4OPT accuracy from 86.8% to 82.9%, a larger degradation than removing the debugging component (86.8% to 84.6%), indicating semantic-anchored correction is the primary driver of gains (Section 4.5, Table 2).
Seven benchmark datasets—NL4OPT, IndustryOR, EasyLP, ComplexLP, NLP4LP, ReSocratic, and ComplexOR—span 18 to 545 instances each and vary in modeling complexity (Table 6, Appendix A.5).
SAC-Opt's improvements generalize across underlying LLMs, holding for both GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (Section 4.6, Table 3).

d8e2jBfMpE.text: KernelBand achieves over 33% average speedup improvement on TritonBench-G across three GPU/model configurations: RTX 4090 with DeepSeek-V3.2, RTX 4090 with GPT-5.1, and A100 with DeepSeek-V3.2 (Section 5.2, Tables 1-2).
At iteration 9 on RTX 4090 with DeepSeek-V3.2, KernelBand reaches roughly 5.05x average speedup versus GEAK's 1.22x under the current-iteration metric (Table 1).
Under the best-of-iteration metric at iteration 9 on RTX 4090, KernelBand reaches 9.78x speedup versus GEAK's 2.40x (Table 1).

Theorem 4.1 bounds the expected regret after T iterations by 3|S|sqrt(8T ln T) + T*epsilon_cluster + T*alpha*epsilon_profile, where the constant factor scales with the number of runtime clusters (|S|) rather than the full candidate pool size (Section 4.4, Theorem 4.1).
Runtime behavior clustering uses incremental 3-means clustering over a 6-dimensional feature space to group kernel-candidate runtime profiles (Section 4.3).
With extended 20-iteration budgets, KernelBand continues improving through iterations 10-19 while the GEAK baseline saturates earlier (Figures 3-4).

bkCPa5RDbm.text: An analysis of 3 million real-world code-completion interactions found that 61% of generated suggestions were either edited after acceptance or rejected outright, despite exhibiting over 80% similarity to the user's subsequent code (Section 1).
Theorem 3.3 proves that above a critical entropy threshold H*, placeholder-based completions strictly outperform hard completions in expected cost (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.3).

Adaptive Placeholder Completion (APC) reduces expected editing costs from a 19% to 50% range relative to hard completion, while preserving standard hard-completion (HC) performance (Abstract, Table 1).

APC's cost reductions hold consistently across model families and scales, including Qwen2.5-Coder (1.5B-14B), CodeGemma (2B, 7B), CodeLlama (7B, 13B), and StarCoder2 (3B, 7B, 15B), evaluated after SFT and GRPO training stages (Table 1).

8wOASkNLzQ.text: On audio-driven portrait animation, STARCaster attains the lowest FID among six baselines on both TalkingHead-1KH (24.89) and Hallo3 (16.86) datasets (Section 4.1, Table 1).

STARCaster achieves the lowest FVD scores of 185.24 on TH-1KH and 145.35 on Hallo3, and an LSE-D lip-sync score of 8.724 on TH-1KH, outperforming the 5B-parameter Hallo3 model even on Hallo3's own training data (Table 1).

On 3D-aware talking portrait generation using the NeRSemble multi-view dataset, STARCaster reaches FID 29.52 versus Real3DPortrait's 32.33, with better view consistency (LPIPS 0.477 vs. 0.560-0.614 for competitors) and best PSNR of 14.219 (Section 4.2, Table 2).
Ablation studies show self-forcing training improves FVD by roughly 12 points and the lip-reading loss adds a consistent 2-3 point FVD improvement (Section 4.3, Table 3).
A user study with 20 participants rating 15 samples indicates a preference for STARCaster's more natural head dynamics compared to baselines (Figure 6).

a8N0nRG3jA.text: Emotion directions are extracted from LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct's residual stream using the 480-example SEV (Scenario-Event with Valence) dataset spanning 8 domains x 20 scenarios x 3 outcomes and six basic emotions (Section 4, Section 5).

Direct circuit modulation reaches 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy on the held-out SEV test set, exceeding prompting (97.49%-100% per-emotion) and steering (67.71%-99.58% per-emotion, notably weak on surprise at 67.71%) (Table 2, Appendix D).

Ablating just the top few identified MLP neurons and attention heads causes sharp degradation in emotion expression while random component ablations have negligible effect, demonstrating a pronounced long-tail effect in circuit importance (Section 6.3-6.5, Figure 3).
Layer-wise analysis shows emotion representations become increasingly separated into clusters by valence/category across layers, visualized via clustering evolution (Figure 2).
Findings are validated on a second model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, beyond the primary LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct model (Appendix H).

XjkpSHzysD.text: A Qwen 3B+4B model pair trained with CoRe's two-round collaborative reasoning protocol (cold Round A sampling K=2 traces, contexted Round B rescue with hint dropout of 75%) reaches Team Pass@2 of 99.54% on GSM8K and 92.08% on MATH using no more than 1,000 training examples per dataset (Section on Training Configuration; Key Results table).
The same Qwen 3B+4B pair reaches Team Pass@2 of 20.45% on AIME and 17.80% on GPQA, compared to base oracle pass rates of 9.20% and 7.10% respectively (Key Results).
A Phi+Ministral 3B+3B reasoning-model pair reaches Team Pass@2 of 79.65% on AIME and 77.34% on GPQA, and 96.72% on GSM8K, 92.08% on MATH (Key Results).
Removing Round B (contexted rescue) causes the largest ablation degradation, lowering GPQA Team Pass@2 by 5.14 points, MATH by 3.18 points, and GSM8K by 0.64 points (Table 5-6).

Theorem 4.1 proves that the collaboration gain from pairing two models equals the probability that one model succeeds while the other fails, formalizing why reducing correlated error overlap drives team performance gains (Theorem 4.1).

KcVFMalXYk.text: MVI-Bench is the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LVLM robustness to misleading visual inputs, comprising 624 paired VQA instances (1,248 total instances), each pair sharing an identical multiple-choice question but differing in a normal versus misleading image (Section 3.1).

The benchmark organizes misleading visual inputs into a three-level, six-category taxonomy: Visual Resemblance and Representation Confusion (Visual Concept level), Material Confusion (Visual Attribute level), and Mirror Reflection, Occlusion Confusion, and Visual Illusion (Visual Relationship level) (Section 3.1).
Image composition is 52.32% natural, 9.62% synthetic, and 38.06% edited images (Figure 3).

Across 18 evaluated LVLMs, GPT-4.1 is the least vulnerable model with 20.80% MVI-Sensitivity and 62.82% accuracy on misleading images, while Molmo-7B is the most vulnerable with 48.69% MVI-Sensitivity and only 37.66% accuracy (Table 2).

All closed-source models exceed 20% MVI-Sensitivity, and the strongest open-source model, Qwen2-VL-72B, reaches 32.38% MVI-Sensitivity, achieving only 50.00% accuracy on the Mirror Reflection category (Table 2).

BS8upx3Smw.text: PACER parameterizes DAGs via a Bernoulli-Plackett-Luce distribution over topological orderings combined with independent Bernoulli edge indicators, guaranteeing every sampled structure during optimization is acyclic by construction rather than via a penalty term (Core Method section).

On the Sachs protein signaling dataset (11 proteins), PACER ranks among the top two methods across SHD, SID, FDR, TPR, and F1, and achieves the best F1 and FDR in the interventional setting, compared against constraint-based (GES, GIES), score-based (CAM, GRaSP), and differentiable (NOTEARS, DCDI, DCDFG, DP-DAG) baselines (Experimental Results section).

On CausalBench's large-scale genetic perturbation data (RPE1 and K562 datasets), PACER matches the best competing methods' Wasserstein distance while running roughly 300x faster (Experimental Results section).

On Perturb-CITE-seq (1000+ genes, 248 perturbations), PACER achieves superior interventional negative log-likelihood and mean absolute error across three experimental conditions while running about 300x faster than the DCDFG baseline (Experimental Results section).

In synthetic scalability experiments varying graph size from d=10 to d=50 nodes, DCDI becomes numerically unstable at d>=40 while PACER remains stable, achieving up to two orders of magnitude speedup over penalty-based differentiable approaches (Scalability Demonstration section).

NpvBAOc87E.text: The ReMax objective evaluates policies by the expected maximum return over M retry samples rather than the expected return, and Section 2's bandit analysis shows that as retry count M increases, the optimal policy becomes progressively more stochastic/exploratory without any added exploration bonus (Section 2).

Proposition 3.2 gives a closed-form expression for the expected maximum return over M trials computable in O(K log K) time, extending ReMax from bandits to MDPs via Q-function distributions (Section 3, Proposition 3.2).

RePPO, a PPO variant built on an Expected-Improvement-based policy gradient (Proposition 4.1) with a Q-critic and Q-replacement strategy, is evaluated on MinAtar (4 games, 10M steps, 10 seeds) and outperforms PPO-V, PPO-Q with entropy bonus, and RND, with best performance at m in [1.2, 1.4] (Section 4, RePPO Algorithm section).

On Craftax (1B timesteps, 5 seeds), RePPO with m=1.2 reaches 11.87% (std 0.16) of max reward, exceeding PPO-V at 9.31% (std 1.00), PPO-V+Entropy at 11.66% (std 0.33), and RND+Entropy at 11.68% (std 0.30) (Craftax results table).
Ablations on MinAtar show that removing either the action-independent baseline or the Q-replacement strategy substantially degrades RePPO's performance (Figure 5).

6aFl5SegYt.text: Nodes are scored for coarsening using a residual-based physical activity measure s_i^t = ||r_i^t||_2, derived from the solid-mechanics governing-equation residual rather than geometric heuristics like farthest point sampling (Section on Physics-Informed Scoring).

On the DeformingPlate benchmark, the proposed physics-informed multigrid GNN achieves 6.50×10⁻³ rollout RMSE versus 11.46×10⁻³ for UNISOMA, 12.75×10⁻³ for MeshGraphNets, 16.60×10⁻³ for BSMS, and 15.7×10⁻³ for Multi-Scale GNN, at a comparable ~2.9M parameter count (Table 2).

Physics-informed TopK node sampling reduces rollout RMSE to 6.5×10⁻³ compared to 15.0×10⁻³ for FPS without remeshing, 8.1×10⁻³ for attention-based sampling, and 8.0×10⁻³ for FPS with remeshing (Table 3).

The method generalizes to unseen datasets BeamSimple and SpindleUpsetting, improving rollout error over MeshGraphNet from 1.72±0.28 to 1.44±0.25 (×10⁻¹) on BeamSimple and from 3.07±0.46 to 2.96±0.26 (×10⁻¹) on SpindleUpsetting (Table 4).
Scoring all nodes, including boundary/constrained nodes, for coarsening consistently yields lower rollout error than scoring only interior nodes (Figure 4).

Four solid-mechanics datasets are used for evaluation: DeformingPlate (COMSOL, 1k nodes, 100 trajectories, 400 steps), BeamSimple (CimLib, 500 nodes, 150 trajectories, 500 steps), BendingBeam (CimLib, 1.2k nodes, 140 trajectories, 500 steps), and SpindleUpsetting (Forge, 9k nodes, 100 trajectories, 83 steps) (Table 1).

Vr0kjNERRf.text: Theorem 3.1 shows that under gradient flow on expected return with softmax parameterization, the log-probability ratio between two outcomes i and j evolves as d/dt log(p_i/p_j) = p_i a_i - p_j a_j, causing exponential divergence independent of exploration, sampling noise, entropy bonuses, or KL regularization (Theorem 3.1).

Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) reweights terminal rewards as r̃(o_g) = r(o_g)/max(p̂(o_g), ε) using empirical group frequencies, and under IPS gradient flow the stationary distribution satisfies p_i* = r(i)/Σ_k r(k), i.e., reward-proportional rather than collapsed (Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2).

On the HypoSpace benchmark, IPS-GRPO achieves substantially higher hypothesis-recovery rates than GRPO and FlowRL: 43.91% vs 16.02% and 12.82% on the Causal task, 90.00% vs 31.61% and 26.85% on 3D Voxel, and 60.74% vs 9.50% and 10.74% on Boolean (Table 2).

On the discrete hyper-grid multimodal task, IPS-GRPO attains an ℓ₁ distance of 3.0×10⁻³ (n=2) and 3.7×10⁻⁴ (n=4) between the learned and target reward-proportional distributions, compared to 2.8×10⁻² and 5.2×10⁻⁴ for GRPO/FlowRL (Table 1).
On the SYNTH molecular generation task at a docking-score threshold of 0.80, IPS-GRPO achieves a yield of 7371±212 versus 5695±173 for REINVENT (Table 3).

oxHAClQzWT.text: ResDreamer is evaluated on five MineDojo combat tasks (Spider, Shulker, Wolf, Skeleton, Ghast) with episodes capped at 1000 timesteps and 1×10⁶ environment training steps, plus DeepMind Control Suite Vision for sensitivity analysis (Table 3, Section 4).

ResDreamer (100M×2 hierarchical layers) is the only method among those compared (DreamerV3, Steve-1, PTGM) that solves the high-difficulty Shulker combat task within the training budget (Section 4.1, Figure 4).

ResDreamer (50M×2) surpasses the average performance of DreamerV3 while using only about 92.0M total parameters versus DreamerV3's 109.5M, i.e., roughly 84% of DreamerV3's parameter count (Table 2, Section 4.1).
The hierarchical residual world model uses a foresight horizon H of 4 to 16 steps and variable time stride D of 1 to 4 frames across 2-3 Predictive Processing Block layers (Section 4.2.2).
The largest ResDreamer configuration (100M×2) requires under 29GB of GPU VRAM (Section 4.1).

Rl7YAiRT04.text: The weighted-prototype utility function U_t(w) = ⟨w, μ̄⟩ - (η_t/2)⟨w, Kw⟩, where K is the Gram matrix of sample gradients, is proven monotone (Lemma 5.1) and weakly submodular with γ > 0 (Lemma 5.4), enabling an Orthogonal Matching Pursuit algorithm with a (1 + C̃₁/(c₂κ))⁻² approximation guarantee (Theorem 5.5, Equation 6).

On MetaMathQA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-3B at a 50% subset fraction, PartitionSel achieves 63.63% average accuracy across 8 math benchmarks (NumGLUE, MMLU-Math, GSM8K, SVAMP, SimulEq, DeepMind, AQuA, SAT), versus 62.40% for the GREATS baseline (Table 1).

On Mol-Instructions molecular generation tasks with Qwen2.5-3B at 25% subset fraction (κ=32), PartitionSel achieves 0.66 average BLEU across four chemistry tasks (description-guided design, forward reaction, reagent prediction, retrosynthesis) versus 0.62 for GREATS (Table 2).

Against the continuous mixture method DoReMi on GPT2-300M, PartitionSel improves MMLU-Math accuracy by 7.49 points (60.57% vs 53.08%), AQuA by 2.36 points, and SAT by 4.09 points, for an average gain of 4.65 percentage points (Table 3).
PartitionSel reduces the number of conflicting gradient pairs (⟨g_i, g_j⟩ < 0) relative to an independent-domain-selection baseline that cannot trade sample budgets across domains (Section 7.4).

XQLa5PVQ0D.text: Theorem 4.2 proves the target-domain regret bound is monotonically increasing in both the encoder consistency term δ_e and the encoder Lipschitz constant L_e, decomposed into oracle-difference, training-error, and policy-adaptation-error terms (Theorem 4.2, Appendix A.5).
Theorem 4.3 shows the contrastive alignment loss upper-bounds the encoder Lipschitz constant L_e, controlling it via 'bridge samples' between dynamics with marginal differences (Theorem 4.3).

On MuJoCo Hopper, Walker2d, and Ant tasks with randomized dynamics (8-36 dimensions spanning body mass, joint damping, slide friction, and torque scale), the method (LDG) attains higher in-distribution return with substantially lower cross-seed variance than RMA Phase 2 and a VAE ablation, e.g., 4883.7±381.6 vs 3193.6±1382.3 (RMA) and 2462.4±1126.0 (VAE) on Walker2d (Table 1, Section 5.1).
Under structural failure zero-shot generalization tests, LDG outperforms RMA Phase 2 on Hopper (596 vs 394) and Walker2d (952 vs 292) (Table 2).

Comparing contrastive learning to spectral normalization as an alternative Lipschitz regularizer on Walker2d, contrastive learning achieves higher OOD damping (0.3x) return (5342 vs 4646) and structural-failure return (952 vs 335), indicating benefits beyond Lipschitz control alone (Table 3, Section 5.4).

t-SNE visualization shows LDG's latent space forms a smooth, monotonic arc correlating with physical parameters, whereas RMA Phase 2 produces scattered embeddings and the VAE ablation exhibits mode collapse or topological disjointedness (Figure 2).

fTl7NXYtAB.text: Lemma 4.1 establishes a calibration-sharpness decomposition showing expected error equals calibration error plus lack of sharpness plus irreducible aleatoric uncertainty, proving that improving proper scoring rules alone does not guarantee calibration (Lemma 4.1).

Proposition 5.2 proves that the proposed conditional kernel mean embedding (CKME) recalibration map achieves auto-calibration while provably preserving the sharpness of the original predictive distribution (Proposition 5.2, Definition 5.1).

The novel Energy Distance Kernel (EDK), a characteristic kernel over probability distributions, can be evaluated in O(n log n) time for empirical distributions of size n, versus the O(n^2) cost of standard distributional kernels (Section 5, Energy Distance Kernel).

On the UCI regression benchmark (9 datasets, 20 predefined train/validation/test splits), CKME recalibration improves CRPS over the uncalibrated baseline, e.g. reducing normalized CRPS to 0.560±0.016 for a Distributional Random Forest on the Naval dataset and 0.594±0.178 for a Mixture Density Network on the Energy dataset, versus 1.000 for the uncalibrated model (Table 1).

CKME recalibration achieves auto-calibration acceptance across datasets and base models (Distributional Random Forests, Mixture Density Networks, Bayesian Neural Networks, Gaussian Density Networks), outperforming PIT recalibration (Kuleshov et al., 2018) and the parametric GPBeta approach (Song et al., 2019) (Figure 1).

JfcKBsbx0n.text: Elo-style rankings derived from pairwise comparisons achieve Spearman correlation above 0.9 (Pearson R greater than 0.87) with ground-truth accuracy rankings across five benchmarks: MMLU Pro, GPQA Diamond, SimpleQA, GSM8K, and BBH (Section on main results).

On four of the five benchmarks, only 6-8.9% of model pairs require reordering (Kendall distance) between Bradley-Terry pairwise rankings and accuracy-based rankings (results section, Kendall distance analysis).
In the weak-judge regime on SimpleQA, Bradley-Terry pairwise ranking substantially outperforms direct evaluation, reducing ranking distance from 38.2% to 20% (SimpleQA weak judge experiment).

Correcting pairwise comparisons for style and self-preference bias yields only modest ranking improvements, even though 58% of comparisons are non-discriminative pairs where both responses are equally correct or incorrect (bias correction analysis).

Controlled interventions identify 'echo' (response repetition following the final answer) as a causal driver of judge preference on non-discriminative pairs, with an estimated contrast of -0.52 (95% CI [-0.57, -0.46]) (echo causal intervention experiment).

OMk6KBe0WR.text: Tensor Separation Learning (TSL) models the regression function as a signed sum of rank-1 separable products, fit stage-wise via an Orthogonal Greedy Algorithm, with Proposition 6.1 proving an O(1/sqrt(r)) approximation rate for functions in the Sobolev mixed-smoothness class dimension-independent of the number of features (Proposition 6.1).

Proposition 5.1 proves that each TSL stage's 1D partial dependence curve equals its underlying 1D factor shape up to a constant, so the full model can be exactly reconstructed from its first-order partial dependence plots without the information loss inherent to additive/GAM-style decompositions (Proposition 5.1).

On the OpenML CTR23 benchmark, TSL ranks in the top-3 among interpretable models on 17 of 27 datasets, including a 21% RMSE reduction over SepALS on California Housing and an RMSE of 9.48 on Socmob versus 17.65-21.71 for tree-ensemble baselines (Table 1).

A synthetic case study with target Y = x1^2 x2 (1+x3) + noise shows that competing additive/GAM-style models produce near-zero 1D partial dependence plots that mask the true cubic interaction, while TSL's per-product curves recover the underlying structure (Section 7.2).

The backbone-tilt reparametrization writes each TSL stage as 2 b(x) sinh(d(x)), separating a multiplicative 'backbone' gating function from a directional 'tilt' term, yielding cleaner interpretation than the joint signed-product parametrization (Backbone-Tilt Parametrization section).

UcYG48q9Zm.text: Boundary Embedding Shaping (BES), an adaptive contrastive-learning GNN plug-in that suppresses spurious structural noise at decision boundaries, improves node classification accuracy over a GCN backbone by an average of 3.3%, with the largest gain of 5.0% on WikiCS, raising WikiCS accuracy from 80.48% (baseline GCN) to 85.52% (BES) (node classification results).

Theorem 3.1 establishes identifiability of invariant latent variables under the BES contrastive learning objective, and Proposition 3.1 shows the resulting disentanglement error is inversely proportional to the embedding boundary margin (Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.1).

BES achieves link prediction accuracy of 94.45% on Cora, 96.27% on CiteSeer, 97.89% on Pubmed, and 92.27% on WikiCS, with the largest gains concentrated on boundary nodes identified via a shift-score measuring local class heterogeneity (link prediction results).

An efficient center-based approximation to the pairwise gravity-similarity contrastive objective reduces computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N), enabling BES to scale to large graphs including ogbn-arxiv and ogbl-collab (efficient center-based approximation section).

BES is evaluated across homogeneous graphs (WikiCS, Cora, Pubmed, CiteSeer), heterogeneous networks (Chameleon, Cornell, Texas), and a heterophilic graph (Roman-empire), in addition to large-scale OGB benchmarks (datasets section).

Q2tAR1xDFQ.text: The paper proves that the maximal-update optimal learning rate decays with effective network depth L following a universal power law eta*(L) = Theta(L^(-3/2)) across CNNs (Proposition, Section 3.3), ResNets (Proposition, Section 3.4), and Transformers (Proposition, Section 3.5).

Arithmetic-Mean muP (AM-muP) replaces the per-layer maximal-update constraint with a network-wide criterion S_bar(eta) = (1/L) sum_l S_l(eta), derived from an overlap-counting argument showing S_l = Theta(eta^2 l^3) (Section on Arithmetic-Mean muP).

Empirically fitted depth-scaling exponents across 9 architecture-dataset combinations (CNN, ResNet, ViT on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet) average -1.38, closely matching the theoretical value of -1.5 (Table 1).

The zero-shot transfer protocol eta(L) = eta(L0) * (L/L0)^(-3/2), calibrated once at a small reference depth L0, enables reliable hyperparameter transfer to much larger depths without repeated large-scale tuning (zero-shot transfer protocol section).

Ablations across optimizers, activations, and regularization (Table 3) show the fitted exponent stays within [-1.8,-1.1] with mean -1.39; Adam reduces the magnitude of the exponent by 10-12% relative to SGD, and BatchNorm on ResNets strengthens agreement with theory (-1.701 vs -1.5) (Table 3).

Sd5KwQbOdd.text: The Locate-Then-Correct (LTC) framework identifies spurious attention heads in CLIP's Vision Transformer by contrasting wrongly-classified versus correctly-classified negative-subgroup samples via a Logit Lens-based localization mechanism (Section 4.1-4.2, Eq. 10).
LTC corrects located heads by mean-ablating spurious states to the dataset mean and injecting class-discriminative features via orthogonal projection (Section 4.3, Algorithm 1).
On Waterbirds with ViT-B/16, LTC raises worst-group accuracy from a 49.7% zero-shot baseline to 73.3%, cutting the group accuracy gap from 22.4 to 1.3 percentage points (Table 1).
On CounterAnimal with ViT-H/14, LTC is the only tested method that improves over zero-shot CLIP across all model sizes, reducing the group gap from 14.7 to 13.6 (Table 1).

Ablations show mean-ablation alone reaches 62.5% worst-group accuracy, knowledge injection alone reaches 67.3%, and applying corrections to randomly chosen states (LTC-R) drops to 36.9%, versus 73.3% for full LTC on ViT-B (Table 6-7).
On GenderBias-VL, LTC reduces the bias metric on ViT-B/16 from 74.0 (zero-shot) to 10.0 (B₁₀), the best result among compared methods (Table 2).

CrzJGqvrG8.text: Four training-free spectral diagnostics computed from LLM attention graphs—Fiedler value (Definition 1), high-frequency energy ratio (HFER, Definition 2), spectral entropy (Definition 3), and graph smoothness (Definition 4)—distinguish valid mathematical proofs from hallucinated ones without learned parameters (Definitions 1-4).

Across seven instruction-tuned models from four architectural families (Llama-3.2-1B/3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral-7B-v0.1), single-threshold classification accuracy ranges from 85.9% to 95.6%, with Cohen's d effect sizes between 2.09 and 3.30 and p<10^-47 (Table 2).

Different model families favor different diagnostics: HFER dominates for Llama models, Fiedler value for Llama-1B, spectral entropy for Qwen-0.5B, and graph smoothness for Phi-3.5-mini and Mistral-7B (Section 5.4).
At Layer 30 of Llama-3.1-8B, HFER density plots show near-complete separation between valid and invalid reasoning traces (Figure 2).

In an authorship-control experiment comparing model-generated valid versus invalid proofs, simple attention baselines collapse to |d|<0.2 while the spectral Fiedler value retains d=1.30 (p=0.002) discriminative power (Section 4.7).

On the informal natural-language MATH dataset the discriminative signal attenuates but remains significant at d=0.78, with the best-discriminating metric shifting from HFER to Fiedler value (Section 4.8).

3oMO1ZQNwT.text: Multi-turn tool-calling benchmark performance shows up to ~3% deviation across random seeds, markedly higher than the seed-stability observed in single-turn evaluation, due to error compounding across turns (Section 3.1, Figure 1).

Using 'native' multi-turn serialization instead of 'context' concatenation improves BFCL multi-turn performance by roughly 6-8%, showing template construction alone drives large reported score differences (Section 3.2, Figure 3).
Small system-prompt modifications produce performance gains comparable to or larger than typical RL-training gains on multi-turn tool-calling benchmarks (Section 3.4, Figure 3).
Roughly 20% of RL training prompts are 'effective' (yield gradient signal), while up to 80% of prompts produce zero-variance rollouts that contribute no learning signal (Section 4.1, Figure 4).
Policy update steps consume 3-5x as much compute as rollout generation during RL training, with the gap widening as rollout count increases (Section 4.2, Figure 6).

Combining online pre-rollout filtering of persistently all-correct prompts with variance-aware rollout down-sampling yields 1.7x (single-turn) and 2.6x (multi-turn) wall-clock speedups without degrading performance, and the resulting RL-trained model gains +12.1 overall accuracy points on ACEBench versus the Nova1-Lite baseline (Section 4.3, Figure 7, Table 3).

5WwoJ2W0nL.text: BoBa partitions a molecular library into persistent structure-aware subsets via k-means clustering on molecular embeddings and treats each partition as an arm in a multi-armed bandit, avoiding full-library surrogate inference at each round (Section 3.2).

UCB1 bandit allocation substantially outperforms epsilon-greedy and softmax allocation strategies as the number of partitions grows, reducing surrogate inference roughly K-fold for K partitions (Figure 1).
Replacing k-means-structured partitions with random partitions degrades top-hit recovery performance by 40-60% (Figure 3).
T5Chem molecular embeddings consistently outperform physicochemical descriptors as the basis for partitioning (Figure 4).

On a ZINC library scaled to 10^8 molecules targeting AmpC, BoBa recovers 95% of full-library Bayesian optimization AUC while only sublinearly increasing inference cost with library size (Section 4.5).
A cost-regret analysis derives an optimal partition count of K* proportional to N^(2/3) T^(1/3), indicating sublinear scaling of optimal granularity with library size N and budget T (Appendix E).

mcJwXaOYrL.text: The framework writes causal linear token mixing as Y = (I-B)^{-1} A X, separating a matrix A for direct input-to-output influence from a strictly lower-triangular matrix B for recurrent propagation through past outputs, unifying attention, state-space models, and linear recurrences as special sparsity cases (Proposition 3.2).

Proposition 4.2 shows decoding time complexity per token scales as O(f^{-1}(i)) for a stride function f governing which past positions a token attends to, so choosing f(k)=2^k yields O(log n) time while f(k)=k^2+1 yields O(sqrt(n)) time (Proposition 4.2, Corollary 4.9).

Congestion bounds (d+1)/2 <= C(G) <= D are derived to quantify information bottlenecks on copying tasks, with Corollary 4.9 giving congestion <= log2(n) for f(k)=2^k and congestion <= 4 for f(k)=k^2+1 (Propositions 4.7-4.8, Corollary 4.9).

On synthetic copy-task benchmarks, dense recurrence and full attention reach 100% accuracy, the f(k)=k^2+1 sqrt(n)-complexity variant reaches 99.66%, and the f(k)=2^k log(n)-complexity variant reaches 92.63% (Table 1, Section 5.2).

On OpenWebText language modeling across 125M-775M parameter models, O(sqrt(n)) and O(log n) stride-function designs approach full-attention perplexity while trading only about 1-2 perplexity points for large cache-size reductions, and the resolvent mixer (I-B)^{-1}A slightly outperforms standard attention within the O(n) complexity bracket (Figure 3, Section 5.3).

1KRpajnd6u.text: Proposition 1 shows that under periodic boundary conditions with symmetric stencils, FluxNet's flux-based update rule (the same flux serves as outflow for the sender cell and inflow for the receiver cell) exactly preserves the global sum of the transported quantity, yielding conservation errors at the machine-precision level (~1e-7 to 1e-8) (Proposition 1).

The L-Head and U-Head mechanisms parameterize outflow as a fraction of the cell's available capacity above a lower bound (or below an upper bound), and Propositions 2 and 3 prove that this construction guarantees the next state stays within the prescribed bounds without any post-hoc clipping or projection (Propositions 2 and 3).

On the shallow-water equations rollout task at horizon T=2, FluxNet-LAP achieves a depth MAE of 3.12e-3 versus 6.74e-3 for the best baseline (a post-hoc projection method), while also reducing conservation error from 3.3e-7 (baseline) to 3.3e-8 (Table 3).

On the traffic flow benchmark at horizon T=2, FluxNet-D attains an MAE of 3.48e-3 compared to 15.9e-3 for a CNN-AR baseline, and reduces conservation error from 2.1e-2 to 7.7e-8, though FluxNet-D shows slightly higher upper-bound violation rates on some settings (1.87% vs 3.20% for CNN-AR) (Table 4).

On the spinodal decomposition experiment, a FluxNet model trained to take steps of 1000*dt achieves a 17.3x rollout speedup relative to the base timestep while preserving two-point correlation statistics of the simulated microstructure (Table 5).

The D-Head (dual bounds) variant enforces upper and lower capacity constraints via a dual consistency loss (DCL) rather than a strict architectural guarantee, achieving empirically near-zero bound violations rather than the exact guarantees proven for the single-bound L-Head and U-Head cases (Section on Bound Enforcement / D-Head).

EAH54wIQNb.text: The Unison benchmark comprises 2,169 high-quality unified task samples spanning four evaluation dimensions: internal consistency, understanding-guided generation, generation-guided understanding, and mutual enhancement (Section on benchmark composition).

Unison provides both a unified track and a decoupled track, enabling fine-grained attribution of whether failures stem from understanding, generation, or their interaction (Section on evaluation protocol).

The Unison-Judge model, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct trained on 8,000 manually labeled samples (2,000 per dimension), achieves an average human alignment correlation (ρ) of 0.887 across the four dimensions on a 231-sample human-validation set (Evaluation/Human Alignment section).
On the Unison unified score, GPT-5.2 is the best closed-source model at 71.3%, ahead of Gemini 3 Pro at 69.8%, while OmniGen2 (7B) is the best open-source model at 51.3% (Results/Main Table).

The mutual enhancement dimension allows up to 5 iterative rounds with early termination, evaluating whether generation and understanding capabilities can bootstrap one another (Section on mutual enhancement protocol).

4ltyJqAHMg.text: SQLBench (Squirrel) comprises 469 syntax-error tasks (Squirrel-Syntax) and 516 semantic-error tasks (Squirrel-Semantic), built from over 1,000 seed SQL scripts spanning 26 business scenarios, with scripts averaging over 140 lines, AST width >11, and AST depth >8.7 (Benchmark Construction section).
Claude-4-Sonnet achieves only 36.46% Graph Match score on Squirrel-Syntax debugging and 32.17% on Squirrel-Semantic debugging, the best performance among evaluated models (Main Results table).

DeepSeek-V3 scores 30.28% (Graph Match) on Squirrel-Syntax and 21.32% on Squirrel-Semantic, while Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B scores 23.45% on Squirrel-Semantic, with most evaluated LLMs failing to exceed 20% success rate on enterprise SQL debugging (Main Results table).

SQLBench scripts contain on the order of 420+ tokens and 17.34-21.62 functions per script on average, reflecting enterprise-scale ETL SQL complexity rather than the short queries used in prior Text-to-SQL benchmarks (Benchmark Statistics section).

lgzkDjvVwP.text: OTA-Det-L improves over the LAE-DINO baseline by +7.6 AP50 on DIOR (reaching 93.1), +5.2 mAP on DOTA (reaching 52.0), and +10.8 mAP on LAE-80C (reaching 31.0) on open-vocabulary aerial detection (OVAD) tasks (Section 4.3, Table 1).

On aerial visual grounding, OTA-Det improves Acc@0.5 by +8.5 on OPT-RSVG, +2.8 on DIOR-RSVG, and +3.9 on AerialVG over specialized RSVG methods, with OTA-Det-M reaching 54.9 Acc@0.5 on AerialVG (Section 4.3, Table 3).

OTA-Det-S maintains real-time inference at 34 FPS, roughly 3x faster than LAE-DINO and 5x faster than AerialVG, while supporting both open-vocabulary detection and visual grounding in a single unified framework (Section 4.3).
With LAE-1M pre-training, OTA-Det-M reaches 87.1 AP50 on DIOR for open-vocabulary aerial detection (Section 4.3, Table 2).

Ablating the dense semantic alignment component drops attribute-level grounding accuracy from 21.96% to 0.47% at threshold τ=0.7, showing this component is critical to fine-grained visual grounding (Section 4.4, Table 4).

elVUsM2rf3.text: In fine-grained MoE routing, the gap between the rank-1 and rank-5 expert router scores alone exceeds 3.9%, while the cumulative score difference from rank 5 to rank 32 is less than 1.5%, forming a 'certain head' followed by a near-uniform 'uncertain tail' (Section 2.2, Figure 2(c)).

Expert-Sample introduces three hyperparameters—k_keep deterministically-retained experts, a sampling temperature τ, and a sampling range r—with recommended defaults k_keep = floor(k/2)+1, τ=1.0, and r=4k (Section 3.2, Section 3.4).
On Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct evaluated on GPQA-Diamond with 32 parallel samples, Expert-Sample raises pass@32 from 85.4% to 91.9%, a 6.5 percentage point improvement (Abstract, Figure 1).
With Best-of-N verification on the same setup, Expert-Sample improves accuracy from 59.1% to 62.6%, a 3.5 percentage point gain over standard token-level sampling (Abstract, Figure 1).

jQmlwZSPuw.text: Existing sentence-level watermarking methods are vulnerable to structural perturbations: under GPT-3.5 paraphrasing across 500 test samples that alter sentence counts, SemStamp's detection rate drops from 91% to 22% TPR@5% (Section 2.2).

On OPT-1.3B with the Booksum dataset, AliMark achieves 100% AUROC/TPR@1%/TPR@5% with no attack, and under GPT-3.5 paraphrasing attack retains 96.1% AUROC and 66.6% TPR@5%, versus SemStamp's 22.0% TPR@5% (Table 1).
Under DIPPER paraphrasing on OPT-1.3B/Booksum, AliMark achieves 94.2% AUROC and 61.6% TPR@5%, compared to PMark's 30.4% TPR@5% (Table 1).
On Qwen3-1.7B/Booksum, AliMark achieves 53.6% TPR@5% under GPT-3.5 attack and 61.4% TPR@5% under DIPPER attack, versus PMark's 24.0% and 34.0% respectively (Table 2).

AliMark uses a block size of M=8 sentences and a candidate budget of Q=64 generated sentence variants per block, with detection runtime scaling from 0.02s for 4 sentences to 0.34s for 128 sentences (Section 3, Section 4 architecture/runtime analysis).

jnds7BbY0V.text: The attention weight allocated to the sink token acts as an implicit gating factor G^{l,h}_t = 1 − A^{l,h}_{t,sink}, unifying Vanilla, Sink, and Gated Attention under a shared Mixture-of-Experts framework in which attention heads act as independent experts (Section 3.1, Equation 4).

A Head Imbalance metric based on the coefficient of variation of head importance scores (Equation 6) shows that head collapse intensifies over training, rising during early steps and plateauing at elevated levels across LLaMA-3.1-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (Section 4.1, Figure 5).

Sink-aware training adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss (Equation 7 for pretraining, Equation 8 for fine-tuning) computed from Flash Attention log-sum-exp values, adding less than 2% additional training latency without materializing full attention weight matrices (Section 4.2).

For 0.6B-2B models trained from scratch, sink-aware training yields average benchmark improvements of +1.28% (0.6B Vanilla Attention) and +1.40% (2B Gated Attention), with validation bits-per-byte improving from 0.8152 to 0.8123 for the 0.6B Vanilla model (Table 1).

Fine-tuning Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with the sink-aware load balancing loss improves reasoning-task scores by +2.47 and +1.70 points on average, and long-context task scores by +1.29 and +4.71 points respectively, with larger models benefiting substantially more (Table 2).

KKDi5HuFkt.text: DiffCrossGait reformulates 2D-3D cross-modal gait matching as trajectory-level alignment within an identity-relevant latent diffusion space rather than relying on endpoint-only feature matching (Section on method overview, Figure 2).

On SUSTech1K, DiffCrossGait achieves 58.7% Rank-1 accuracy for 2D-to-3D retrieval (a +3.6 point gain over prior state-of-the-art) and 63.8% Rank-1 for 3D-to-2D retrieval (a +6.1 point gain), with the largest gains on Bag (+11.4) and Uniform (+11.5) conditions (Table 1, Table 2).
On the FreeGait benchmark, DiffCrossGait improves Rank-1 accuracy by +18.4 points (to 58.5%) for 2D-to-3D retrieval and by +18.2 points (to 61.5%) for 3D-to-2D retrieval over prior methods (Table 3).

The diffusion branch used during training is discarded at inference, so DiffCrossGait maintains near-baseline computational cost (6.2ms vs. 5.9ms per query) while still delivering a +9.1% Rank-1 gain (Table 4).

An ablation shows that removing shared noise sampling or shared modal tokens reduces Rank-1 accuracy by 1-3 percentage points, indicating both components are necessary for the trajectory-alignment mechanism to work (Table 5).

Xxq7fcQUNR.text: WZ-LLM solves 34 of 100 classical combinatorial identities on the LCI-Test benchmark, compared to 9/100 for the Goedel-Prover-V2 baseline and 1/100 for DeepSeek-V3 (Table 1).

A decomposed route combining WZ-Sketch guidance with the specialized WZ-Prover solves 29/100 identities, while direct proving on WZ-uncovered identities solves only 5/100, showing that symbolic guidance from the Wilf-Zeilberger method drives most of the gain (Table 1).

At the lemma level, the specialized WZ-Prover achieves 73.34% accuracy (864/1,178 lemmas) versus 47.88% (564/1,178) for Goedel-Prover-V2, demonstrating the benefit of training a prover specialized for WZ-derived recurrence and boundary lemmas (Table 2, Section 4.2).

On cross-dataset evaluation, WZ-LLM outperforms Goedel-Prover-V2 on CombiBench (16/100 vs. 12/100) and PutnamBench-Comb (3/36 vs. 0/36), including identities that a symbolic-only WZ baseline cannot resolve (Table 3).

The WZ-LLM pipeline decomposes identities into executable proof sketches with recurrence lemmas and boundary obligations (Section 4.1), then trains the specialized prover via a three-stage pipeline of cold-start SFT, expert-verified bootstrapping, and DAPO refinement (Section 4.2).

KD59uBqvNR.text: DSCache maintains a cumulative past KV cache 𝒰_t alongside a recent feature buffer ℬ_t of size l_i=4 frames, from which it constructs a separate instant cache ℐ_{t+1} on demand, decoupled from the cumulative cache (Section 4.2-4.3).

A position-agnostic encoding scheme is proven formally equivalent to standard RoPE-based position encoding for the cache construction (Proposition 4.2, Section 4.1), enabling cache manipulation without positional overflow.

On StreamingBench, adding DSCache raises accuracy from 76.92% to 79.12% for LLaVA-OV-7B and from 78.56% to 82.32% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, an average of 2.5% over uniform-sampling streaming baselines and 5.0% over prior state-of-the-art (Table 1).
On OVO-Bench, DSCache improves overall accuracy from 55.6% to 57.5% for LLaVA-OV-7B and from 52.2% to 55.4% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a 10.8% improvement over TimeChat-Online (Table 2).
DSCache adds only modest inference overhead (0.30s vs. 0.21s baseline per query, using 16GB memory matching the baseline), acceptable within a 1 FPS streaming constraint (Table 7).

DKathyl3XN.text: Proposition 3.1 establishes the scalar-identity case, showing SSMs with state matrices A_t = a_t I_N are equivalent to 1-semiseparable masked attention with a causal mask (Section 3.2).

Theorem 4.1 gives a necessary and sufficient condition for an N-dimensional SSM to admit a 1-semiseparable masked-attention dual: its corresponding N-semiseparable matrix must have diagonal blocks each containing at most N new columns (Section 4.4, Definition 4.2).
General diagonal SSMs are shown to preserve the same O(NTd) training complexity as the scalar-identity case (Algorithm 1) while supporting richer, per-channel dynamics (Section 4.3).
Proposition 4.1 proves the equivalence between N-semiseparable matrices and N-SSS (sequentially semiseparable) representable matrices (Section 4.4).

Section 5 demonstrates a limitation: softmax attention is incompatible with the semiseparable-matrix duality framework due to rank explosion, and general (non-diagonal) SSMs may lack any attention dual despite having low state dimension (Section 5).

xI364qxvhX.text: CoF-T2I achieves an overall score of 0.86 on GenEval, outperforming BAGEL-Think (0.82) and T2I-R1 (0.79) and its own base Wan2.1-T2V model (0.55) (Table 1).
CoF-T2I attains an overall score of 7.468 on Imagine-Bench, a +1.529 point improvement over the base Wan2.1-T2V model's 5.939 (Table 2).
The ablation shows progressive refinement across the three generated frames, with GenEval scores rising from 0.56 (F1) to 0.79 (F2) to 0.86 (F3) (Section 3, ablation study).
Removing intermediate supervision and training only on the target frame drops GenEval performance from 0.86 to 0.81 (Table 3).

CoF-T2I is trained on CoF-Evol-Instruct, a curated dataset of 64K three-frame Chain-of-Frame reasoning sequences spanning five categories (attribute binding, object combination, quantity control, spatial arrangement, context manipulation) (Section 2, Figure 5).
The model's robustness is demonstrated across both 1.3B and 14B parameter scales of the underlying video model (Table 5).

qubIJ4i1XQ.text: When integrated with the DoReMi mixing framework, GEM improves average downstream accuracy to 43.95%, a +1.16 percentage point gain over the runner-up WebOrganizer (42.79%) (Table 1).
GEM improves average downstream accuracy by 0.68 percentage points over WebOrganizer when integrated into the RegMix framework (41.45% vs 40.77%) (Table 1).
GEM is evaluated on 1.1B-parameter language models trained under a 25B-token budget (Section 4).

An ablation progression from K-Means (38.5%) to Spherical K-Means (40.6%) to vanilla von Mises-Fisher mixture modeling (41.3%) to full GEM (42.1%) shows each component of the geometric entropy mixing approach contributes to counteracting cluster collapse (Figure 6).
The Geometric Influence Score (GIS) selection criterion achieves 84.17% versus 80.41% for random selection in the corresponding ablation (Table 4, Appendix B.3).
A sensitivity analysis over the number of clusters K finds performance peaks at K=36 (Figure 5).

kCJ9kaebgd.text: On the MSCOCO benchmark, InsLen achieves 81.02% AUROC for Qwen3-VL, a +5.66 point improvement over the best baseline SVAR (75.36%) (Table 1).
On MSCOCO with LLaVA-1.5-7B, InsLen reaches 86.93% AUROC, outperforming the GLSIM baseline (83.24%) by 3.69 points (Table 1).
