On the POPE benchmark, InsLen outperforms GLSIM by up to 13.81 AUROC points on LLaVA-1.5 (Table 2).

InsLen is evaluated as a training-free, auxiliary-model-free hallucination detector across five MLLM architectures: LLaVA-1.5-7B, InstructBLIP-7B, mPLUG-Owl3-8B, LLaVA-OneVision1.5-8B, and Qwen3-VL-8B (Section 4.2-4.3).
A Logit Lens analysis shows instruction token embeddings distinguish real from hallucinated objects at least 8% better in AUROC than image embeddings (Section 4.1, Motivation).
InsLen's computational overhead is approximately 104.5ms for LLaVA, negligible compared to the 1870ms required for full answer generation (Table 8).

S8XPQrBX5y.text: The intra-layer specialization loss penalizes cosine similarity between co-activated experts' intermediate activations, and Proposition 4.1 shows this directly decorrelates their gradient updates with respect to down-projection matrices (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).

The cross-layer coupling loss maximizes joint Top-k routing probabilities across adjacent layers, and Proposition 5.1 shows specialization structure propagates across layers with bounded degradation under representation-continuity and strong-coupling assumptions (Section 5, Proposition 5.1).
Combining both losses (ℒ_lb,z,sp,cp) yields the lowest validation perplexity across model scales, an approximately 2.7% relative improvement (Table 1).
On downstream evaluation including MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K, the combined losses (ℒ_lb,sp,cp) give the strongest results, including a +3.66 point pass@1 gain on HumanEval for Qwen3-30B (Table 2).
In LoRA fine-tuning experiments, the losses yield a +3.9 point average gain on DeepSeek-MoE and +4.6 points on DeepSeek-V2-Lite (Table 3).
A scaling experiment shows a model with N=6 experts trained with the proposed losses outperforms a baseline with N=10 experts (Section 6, Figures 5-6).

lwPKU7H8yi.text: DivMorph achieves a 3x improvement in sample efficiency over direct finetuning for cross-task transfer on the UNIMAL benchmark (Section 6, Figure 3).
DivMorph achieves 8.9x to 16.7x model compression for single-agent deployment while matching teacher model performance (Figure 5).
DivMorph decomposes a Transformer controller into shared learngenes and morphology/task-specific tailors via SVD factorization, combined with dynamic soft gating (Section 4, Equations 4-5).
DivMorph is evaluated against six baselines, including MetaMorph, ModuMorph, HyperDistill, and GRL, on 10 UNIMAL tasks split into 5 training and 5 novel morphologies (Section 5).
An ablation study shows removing either the knowledge diversion mechanism or the orthogonality constraint degrades transfer performance relative to the full DivMorph method (Figure 6).
On joint task-and-morphology transfer to novel agents, DivMorph maintains its performance advantage over baselines (Figure 4).

SzPII70Uta.text: ForensicConcept achieves 92.0% mean detection accuracy across 8 generator types (Midjourney, SDv1.4, SDv1.5, ADM, GLIDE, Wukong, VQDM, BigGAN) on the GenImage benchmark, outperforming Effort (91.1%) and DRCT (89.5%) (Table 1)
CleanDIFT-guided codebook injection raises mean accuracy on CLIP from 83.7% to 88.2% (+4.5 points), with the largest single-generator gains on Midjourney (+15.5%) and VQDM (+7.5%) (Table 2)

CKNNA alignment metrics show DINOv3 has the strongest backbone-diffusion alignment (24.4 at layer s4), compared to CLIP (8.9 at layer us8), EfficientNet (7.1), and Swin-T (7.0), supporting the claim that alignment predicts transfer effectiveness across backbones (Table 3, Section 3.2)
On the GAN-family benchmark, an SDv1.4-trained model reaches 90.1% mean accuracy across seven GAN generators, substantially outperforming AIDE (70.7%) (Table 6)
On the Chameleon benchmark the method attains 84.4% accuracy, outperforming AIGI-Holmes (75.9%) and Effort (63.2%) (Table 7)
Ablating the concept branch from a DINOv3 backbone reduces mean accuracy across GenImage/GAN/Chameleon from 88.8% to 87.2%, a 1.6-point drop attributable to the forensic concept codebook (Table 5)

g7LE4mukGq.text: Algorithm 1 achieves an uncorrupted regret bound of O(d^2) for online inverse linear optimization over M-convex feasible action sets (Theorem 3.1, Section 3)
With center-of-gravity-based prediction, Algorithm 1 improves the regret bound to O(d log d), covering M-convex sets including matroids (Theorem 4.2, Section 4)
Algorithm 2 attains a corruption-robust regret bound of O((C+1) d log d) against adversarially corrupted feedback, without requiring prior knowledge of the corruption count C (Theorem 5.3, Section 5)
A matching lower bound of Omega(d) is proved to hold even for M-convex instances, establishing near-tightness of the upper bounds (Theorem 6.1, Section 6)

The volume-contraction lemma shows that whenever the algorithm's prediction errs, the feasible volume fraction shrinks by at least a factor of 1 - 1/e, underlying the O(d log d) regret proof (Lemma 4.1, Section 4)

Fhtwta4397.text: GenShield is a unified autoregressive mixture-of-transformers framework that jointly performs explainable AI-generated image detection and controllable artifact correction via shared self-attention between specialized experts (Section on architecture)

On the Holmes-Set benchmark GenShield reaches 98.8% accuracy and 99.8% average precision, and on Janus-Pro-7B outputs specifically it achieves 99.4% accuracy versus 97.8% for the next-best method (Table 1)
On AIGCDetectBenchmark, GenShield attains 94.93% mean accuracy across 17 generative models, exceeding AIDE (92.77%) and AIGI-Holmes (93.16%) (Table 5)
For artifact correction on SynthScars, GenShield achieves a mean artifact score of 0.15 versus 0.24 for Nano-Banana-Pro, and the highest HPSv3 score (6.20) among compared methods (Table 2)
Under JPEG compression at quality factor 70, GenShield retains 97.8% detection accuracy compared to 92.5% for AIGI-Holmes, demonstrating greater robustness to post-processing (Table 4)

The GenShield-Set training corpus comprises over 10,000 artifact-restored image pairs and 66,000 image-text pairs, used in a two-stage curriculum of instruction-guided training followed by visual chain-of-thought training (Section on dataset construction)

lRZmoqiAPg.text: KREPE introduces Fact Generation, a task requiring the model to construct a valid hyper-relational fact from an arbitrarily masked query, implemented via masked discrete diffusion with a bi-level noising strategy over intra-fact masking and inter-fact structure (Section 4.3)
On WD50K entity prediction, KREPE achieves MRR of 0.389 on primary triplets and 0.419 across all positions, outperforming the MAYPL baseline (Table 1)
On WD50K relation prediction, KREPE reaches MRR of 0.963 for primary relations and 0.968 across all relations, the best result among compared methods (Table 3)

For Fact Generation accuracy, KREPE scores 0.777 on scratch generation (WD50K), 0.600 on targeted generation (WP-), and 0.621 on arbitrary masking (WP), substantially exceeding LLM-based baselines (Table 4)
On WikiPeople-, KREPE's Valid & Novel generation rate is 0.351 with an expected 2.85 generation attempts needed per valid fact (Table 5)
Human evaluation shows near-perfect correlation (0.987-0.997) between LLM judges and human annotators when assessing generated facts, validating the automated evaluation protocol (Table 6)

f2CGTzHQ4E.text: Utonia trains a single self-supervised point transformer jointly across five heterogeneous 3D domains (remote sensing, outdoor LiDAR, indoor RGB-D, CAD objects, and video-lifted point clouds) using causal modality blinding, perceptual granularity rescaling, and RoPE on aligned coordinates (Sections 3.1-3.3)
With full fine-tuning, Utonia reaches 81.1% mIoU on ScanNet, 39.6% mIoU on ScanNet200, and 78.1% mIoU on S3DIS Area 5 for indoor segmentation (Table 3)
On outdoor segmentation, Utonia attains 82.2% mIoU on NuScenes, 71.4% mIoU on Waymo, and 72.0% mIoU on SemanticKITTI with full fine-tuning (Table 4)

Rescaling to a fixed global grid size improves ScanNet200 mIoU from 29.1% (per-dataset default grid sizes) to 33.5%, and RoPE contributes an additional +2.6% on Waymo and +1.4% on ScanNet200 under multi-domain training (Table 2, Table 7)
Without color inputs, Utonia achieves 77.0% mIoU on ScanNet linear probing, far exceeding Concerto's 36.8% under the same modality-ablated condition (Table 6)

When integrated into vision-language-action and vision-language models, Utonia improves simulated robotic manipulation success rate to 82.1% (versus Concerto's 80.0%, Table 9) and improves 3D visual grounding to 54.0% Acc@0.5 (Table 10)

wz2zK4l3YJ.text: R2M applies Sequence-to-Token Cross Attention from the policy's evolving hidden states to the reward model's Reward Token Embedding, forming an Aggregated RTE that bridges the semantic gap between heterogeneous policy and reward models (Section 4.1).

R2M uses a time-step-based weighted combination with weight ω(t) = max(½cos(tπ/T) + ½, Ω) to gradually shift from the original RTE to the aggregated representation over the course of RL training (Section 4.1).

The Group Reward Entropy Bradley-Terry (GREBT) loss combines a standard Bradley-Terry term with a group reward entropy regularization term as L_GREBT = (1-α)L_BT + αL_GRE with α=0.3, to counteract 'group degeneration' where responses within a group receive near-identical reward scores (Section 4.2).

On AlpacaEval 2 with LLaMA3-8B-Instruct, adding R2M to RLOO improves the length-controlled win rate from 21.9% to 24.8% (+2.9%) and the raw win rate from 26.0% to 31.2% (+5.2%) (Section 5, Table results).
On the TL;DR summarization task, RLOO + R2M improves win rate from 75.3% to 81.6% (+6.3%) over the RLOO baseline (Section 5).
Theorem 3.1 shows R2M achieves a tighter upper bound on reward misalignment, ε_R2M ≤ (1-γ^(t))^(1/2)·C + Δ𝒟^(t)·L, compared to the vanilla bound ε_vanilla ≤ C + Δ𝒟^(t)·L (Theorem 3.1).

U80CWouffM.text: OmniVL-Guard's Adaptive Reward Scaling Policy Optimization (ARSPO) uses an exponential task-based reward mapping function g_k(x) = e^(ax) for localization tasks to counteract difficulty bias against harder localization objectives relative to easier classification (Section on ARSPO).

On in-domain evaluation, OmniVL-Guard achieves 96.20% binary classification accuracy, 93.12% IoU for image localization, 63.78% F1 for text localization, and 59.22% temporal IoU for video localization (Table 2).
OmniVL-Guard yields improvements of +37.79% and +22.92% over baselines on video and text localization tasks respectively (Table 2).
On out-of-domain zero-shot generalization, OmniVL-Guard reaches 79.38% accuracy on Text-Image transfer and 63.55% accuracy on Text-Video transfer (Table 3).
Ablations show progressive gains from adding ARSPO components to the SFT baseline: +SAPO gives +24.33% average improvement, +TBRMF gives +26.42%, and +DCA gives +28.33% (Ablation study).
The FSFR dataset used for training comprises 73k SFT samples with Chain-of-Thought annotations and 110k RL training samples spanning four modalities for detection and grounding (Dataset section).

LInDSHWGMK.text: MGAP (Manifold-Guided Adaptive Projection) constructs an offline language-prior subspace via SVD from blind hidden states using N=50 prompts and K=5 components (Method section).

MGAP applies an online correction h_cut = h_orig − α·γ·δ·h_proj, gated by a consistency protection term δ = 1 − cos similarity and an uncertainty gating term γ = tanh(λH) based on entropy H (Method section).
On the POPE benchmark with LLaVA v1.5-7B, MGAP achieves 90.63% accuracy on the random split, 88.10% on the popular split, and 84.59% on the adversarial split (Table results, POPE benchmark).
On the CHAIR benchmark with LLaVA, MGAP reduces hallucinated objects from 47.4 to 26.2 while maintaining 85.9% precision (CHAIR benchmark results).
MGAP requires approximately 1.05 seconds per 3000 samples versus 2.14 seconds for the VCD baseline, a roughly 50% latency reduction (Efficiency analysis).

Three theorems establish that MGAP moves hidden states closer to ground truth when prior error aligns with the prior, bounds the update magnitude to prevent explosive corrections, and preserves orthogonal semantic components (Theorems section).

WUjk3RVZyV.text: Singular Value Calibration (SVC) is a training-free, data-free post-processing method that computes the SVD of the merged task matrix, measures subspace-wise task overlap via projection coefficients s_i^r, and rescales inflated singular values as σ̃^r = γ^r · σ^r while preserving spectral directions (Method/Algorithm section).

On 8 vision datasets with ViT-B/32, adding SVC to Task Arithmetic improves accuracy from 68.9% to 81.9%, a +13.0% gain, with additional gains on TIES (+7.4%) and DARE (+14.9%) (Table results, vision benchmarks).
On a 14-dataset vision benchmark, Task Arithmetic + SVC reaches 76.7% accuracy versus a 57.7% baseline, a +19.0% improvement (Table results, 14-dataset vision).
SVC also improves NLP merging results, including a +4.8% gain for T0 with TA+SVC on classification tasks and a 12.1% gain on T5-based benchmarks (NLP experiments section).
Cross-task spectral overlap is shown to concentrate in the top singular-value subspaces (Figure 3), and the singular-value inflation gap persists across different merging methods (Figure 4).

SVC's computational cost is 5.1 seconds for ViT-B/32 and 517.2 seconds for LLaMA2-7B, requiring no gradient computation, making it far cheaper than training-based merging alternatives (Computational cost section).

wwEJH8o9bQ.text: AesFormer is a two-stage framework in which AesThinker (Stage 1, built on Qwen3-VL-8B) analyzes an input photo across seven progressive photographic dimensions—aspect ratio, framing and composition, camera viewpoint, subject placement, subject pose, focus and depth-of-field, and color and light—to produce executable editing actions, and AesEditor (Stage 2, built on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511) executes those actions as structural edits (Method section).

AesThinker is trained via SFT initialization followed by GRPO-A reinforcement learning, combining a Format Reward, an Alignment Reward (0-5 scale), and a Creativity Reward (0-5 scale) as r_i = λ_f R_f + λ_a R_a + λ_c R_c (GRPO-A reward section).

On the aesthetic photo reconstruction benchmark, AesFormer achieves a 65.33% win rate against the original poor photo and a 68.63% win rate against the human-edited good photo, with an ArtiMuse aesthetic score of 47.76 (Table 1).

Nano Banana Pro scores 54.44% win rate vs. poor, 72.55% vs. good, and an ArtiMuse score of 50.90, showing AesFormer's performance is competitive with but not uniformly superior to this proprietary system (Table 1).

The video-based corpus-mining pipeline (VCMP) constructs the AesRecon dataset of 9,071 strictly aligned (poor, good) image pairs, filtered down from 5,700 collected videos to 2,144 usable instructional videos (Data pipeline section).
FLUX.1 Kontext substantially underperforms AesFormer on the same benchmark, scoring only 12.96% win rate vs. poor and 5.88% vs. good (Table 1).

a1UcGYKhJU.text: ME-DLM achieves an 11.6-point gain on HumanEval and a 33.6-point gain on GSM8K relative to the base masked diffusion model when both are constrained to the same 1/8 diffusion-step budget (Table 2).

ME-DLM's edit-based diffusion phase produces token-wise (replacement/deletion, insertion) predictions applied deterministically on top of an initial mask-diffusion draft, trained with minimal canonical edit-distance supervision (Section 3.1, Figure 2).
At the 1/8 step budget, ME-DLM allocates 48 mask steps and 16 edit steps out of a 64-step total (and correspondingly 96/32, 224/32, 480/32 splits at larger budgets) (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
Across HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, MBPP+, GSM8K, and MATH-500, ME-DLM's average improvement over the base model at the 1/8 budget is 13.3 points (Table 2).

An ablation replacing the full Stage-3 edit training with mask-only states or rule-based noise degrades performance, especially on code benchmarks, showing the learned edit-supervision is necessary rather than incidental (Table 6).
Sensitivity analysis over the mask-edit proportion α and noise-range parameter β shows β=0.5 is most beneficial specifically under aggressive (low-step) decoding regimes (Table 7).

l3yzuHKpNe.text: PRISM suppresses average Attack Success Rate to 0.8% across 11 attack types on CIFAR-10, including 0.0% ASR against BadNets and Blend, while raising clean accuracy to 93.2% versus 92.0% undefended (Table 1).

PRISM is evaluated across 17 datasets (including CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, GTSRB, MNIST) and 11 attack types spanning Classic, Dynamic, Clean-Label, and Clean-Image categories, using 6 different VLM backbones as auditors (CLIP, SigLIP, ImageBind, Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA, Gemma3) (Table 2, Section 5).
On clean-image backdoors (FLIP, GCB), PRISM suppresses ASR to 1.1-4.4% whereas existing defenses fail with ASR of 28.5-100% on the same attacks (Section 5).
On dynamic attacks (WaNet, BPP), PRISM keeps ASR below 1% while baseline defenses achieve 43-99% ASR on the same attacks (Section 5).

PRISM's Adaptive Router computes a threshold via Cornish-Fisher expansion, τ = μ + [ζ + γ/6(ζ²-1)]·σ, to account for skewness in logit-margin distributions rather than assuming Gaussian margins, with optimal ζ=-2 found across datasets (Section 4, Figure 5, Figure 8).
PRISM operates entirely externally via a frozen pre-trained VLM auditor, requiring no access to the victim model's weights or its original training data (Section 3.2, Section 4).

WyGEJKjvJN.text: SALE achieves at least a 3.36x end-to-end speedup on Llama-3.1-8B for sequences longer than 64K tokens compared to full attention (Section 4).
SALE's Selection-Pass overhead is approximately 11% of full attention latency at 64K context and 11.1% at 128K context, per the latency breakdown (Table 3).
SALE's Computation-Pass alone achieves a 6.87x speedup over full attention at 128K tokens, scaling from 2.08x at 8K tokens (Section 4, Figure Speedup).
On the Needle-In-A-Haystack task, SALE attains a 3.81x speedup with only a 0.1% accuracy drop relative to full attention (Section 4).
On LongBench, SALE preserves quality with an average score of 48.39 on Llama-3.1 and 51.30 on Qwen-2.5 (Table 1).

SALE uses a three-stage pipeline (Quantization, Selection-Pass, Computation-Pass) based on 4-bit quantized attention-weight approximation, requiring no additional parameter training and integrating into existing systems via a custom CUDA kernel with trivial code changes (Section 3).

xblX2nQrj7.text: FullStack-Dev (480B model) outperforms prior state-of-the-art by 8.7% on frontend (reaching 64.7% accuracy), 38.2% on backend (reaching 77.8%), and 15.9% on database (reaching 77.9%) test cases on FullStack-Bench (Section 3, Table 2).
FullStack-Learn's self-improvement training raises a 30B model's performance by 9.7% on frontend, 9.5% on backend, and 2.8% on database test cases (Table 3).
FullStack-Bench comprises 647 frontend, 604 backend, and 389 database test cases spanning development-oriented testing of generated full-stack websites (Table 1).
Human evaluators validate FullStack-Bench's automated judgments with alignment accuracy of 90.5% on frontend, 94.0% on backend, and 97.5% on database test cases (Table 6).
Ablation studies show that removing the multi-agent design or debugging tools from FullStack-Dev degrades performance relative to the full system (Table 4).

yBSqPjKmU0.text: RT-Lynx achieves up to a 1.55x average speedup in linear layers via N:M semi-structured activation sparsification in Diffusion Transformers, with underlying sparse GEMM kernels reaching up to 1.88x (Section 5).

DiT activations are shown to be intrinsically sparse and concentrated near zero, while weight distributions remain broadly quasi-Gaussian, motivating a shift from weight sparsification (which degrades quality) to activation sparsification (which preserves it) (Section 3, Figure 2).

On Qwen-Image, RT-Lynx maintains near-lossless generation quality with FID 21.25 versus 21.98 baseline and Image Reward 1.304 versus 1.219 baseline, outperforming weight-sparsification baselines Wanda, RIA, and BaWA (Table 1).
RT-Lynx's online sparse-execution pipeline keeps sparsification overhead below 10%, compared to 40-59% overhead for existing online activation sparsification methods (Section 4, Table 2).
RT-Lynx combines norm-compensated Top-K sparsification, rank-64 LoRA error compensation, and selective layer skipping for single-stream architectures, implemented via fused CUDA kernels (Section 4).
RT-Lynx yields roughly 1.2x end-to-end speedup across tested models and composes orthogonally with distillation, quantization, caching, and sparse attention methods (Table 4, Table 6).

gW7NZN8zJu.text: TreeFlow establishes a formal correspondence showing decision trees arise as discrete approximations of continuous diffusion flows, with equivalence conditions proved as Theorems 2.1-2.10 (Section 2, Theorems 2.1-2.10).

DSmTree (Discretized Score Matching for Trees) distills tree structure from a trained diffusion model by matching score functions at tree nodes, enabling efficient inference while preserving distributional properties, achieving competitive quality relative to the diffusion teacher (Experiment 3, DSM-Tree Implementation).

Implicit tree structures are shown to emerge naturally from flow dynamics without explicit tree-building, demonstrated via an information decay analysis along tree paths (Experiment 1 and Experiment 2).

TreeFlow supports bidirectional conversion between flow and tree representations, validated through a dedicated flow-to-tree instantiation experiment on tabular data (Experiment 4, TreeFlow Instantiation).
Sample complexity bounds are derived for learning tree-structured flows, extending the main theoretical results with additional convergence analyses (Appendices C-H).

XZAOCytvKQ.text: MM-DeepResearch's Hyper-Search QA generation pipeline builds a hypergraph of image and text nodes from web sources and generates intra- and inter-hyperedge question-answer pairs, producing 3K search-intensive multimodal QA training examples (Section on Hyper-Search QA Generation).

DR-TTS (Decompose-Recompose Tool Tree Search) first trains specialized single-tool experts via RL, then recomposes them with tree search to produce 10K supervised fine-tuning trajectories balanced across text-to-text, text-to-image, image-to-image, and knowledge-based search tool use (Section on DR-TTS).
The training pipeline combines SFT on DR-TTS trajectories with multi-turn GRPO reinforcement learning using format-compliance and LLM-judged accuracy rewards (Section on Training Pipeline).

MM-DeepResearch-8B reaches 63.0% average accuracy across six benchmarks (SimpleVQA, MMSearch, LiveVQA, FVQA, InfoSeek, BrowseComp-VL), a 17-point improvement over the Qwen3-VL-8B baseline, while the 32B variant reaches 65.3% average accuracy (Experiments/Results section).

Ablation results show that training on Hyper-Search data increases search depth from 1.6 to 2.3 average tool calls per query, and that the offline multimodal retrieval corpus (using E5 and Jina-CLIP embeddings) performs competitively with expensive online search APIs (Ablation section).

zyMvoKYWMZ.text: Any3D-VLA's visual module converts RGBD input into point clouds, voxelizes them at a 1cm grid to compress from 30,000-60,000 to 3,000-8,000 points, then fuses Concerto-encoded 3D features with DINOv2+SigLIP 2D features via patch-wise scatter-mean alignment and gated residual fusion (Section 5.2).

A hybrid point-cloud training strategy mixes simulator/sensor ground-truth depth (30%) with estimated depth from Depth Anything 3 (20%), MapAnything (20%), and UniDepthV2 (30%) to teach domain-agnostic 3D representations (Section 5.3).

A pilot study on a simulation benchmark shows 2D-3D point-cloud fusion reaches 61.1% single-trial success rate versus 45.3% for 2D-only, 46.3% for VGGT-based implicit 3D, and 56.8% for depth-as-image-channel (Section 4, Table 2).

In zero-shot real-world evaluation across four test sets (Standard, Scale & Shape, Viewpoint, Appearance-Deprived), Any3D-VLA with hybrid training and Depth Anything 3 inference achieves 62.5% overall success rate, a 29.2 percentage-point improvement over the best baseline SpatialVLA at 33.3% (Section 6.1.2).

An ablation isolating 2D-only (45.3%), 3D-only (44.2%), and full 2D-3D fusion (61.1%) single-trial success rates shows that 3D representations alone are insufficient and fusion with 2D features is necessary for robust manipulation (Table 5).

On the LIBERO benchmark Any3D-VLA attains 68.5% average success rate, outperforming GraspVLA by 13.9 points, and on CALVIN it reaches an average rollout length of 2.68, a 0.71 improvement over GraspVLA (Section 6.4).

xF6klfHhO8.text: SAGE identifies when a large reasoning model implicitly knows to stop thinking by tracking cumulative log-probability confidence (Φ) across step-wise exploration of top-m candidate reasoning paths and terminating once a high-confidence </think> token appears (Section on SAGE method).

The Ratio of First Correct Step (RFCS) metric shows that over 50% of correct chain-of-thought responses contain redundant tokens generated after the correct answer already appeared, motivating the need for early stopping (Observation on RFCS).
On DS-1.5B, SAGE-GRPO improves MATH-500 pass@1 from 83.2% to 84.8% while cutting token usage by 40%, yielding a 70.7% token-efficiency improvement (Table 2).
On DS-7B, SAGE-GRPO improves MATH-500 pass@1 from 91.6% to 93.0% with a 45% reduction in generated tokens, an 83.1% efficiency improvement (Table 2).

On Qwen3-8B evaluated on AIME 2025, SAGE-GSPO nearly matches baseline accuracy (66.0% vs. 67.3%) while compressing average response length from 18,342 to 9,183 tokens, roughly a 50% reduction (AIME 2025 results).
Evaluation spans six mathematical reasoning benchmarks—MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC23, OlympiadBench, and Minerva—to validate SAGE-RL's accuracy and efficiency gains (Experiments section).

sfroJn43YY.text: EF-LIC eliminates entropy coding from learned image compression by using unconstrained vector quantization, showing that VQ index sequences exhibit minimal statistical redundancy and approach maximum entropy under distortion-optimal conditions (Section on Statistical Redundancy Removal).

EF-LIC removes correlation redundancy via representation-domain latent decorrelation using context-conditioned autoregressive affine transforms that directly reparameterize latents instead of predicting conditional probability distributions, making the method GPU-friendly and parallelizable (Section on Correlation Redundancy Removal).
On the Kodak dataset with LPIPS distortion, EF-LIC achieves a 67.86% BD-rate (bitrate) reduction compared to the MS-ILLM baseline (Experimental Results, Kodak).

EF-LIC encodes in 17.62ms and decodes in 13.72ms per image versus 165.38ms and 147.79ms for MS-ILLM, corresponding to roughly 3x faster encoding and 5x faster decoding while matching compression performance of entropy-coding-based variants (Table of computational efficiency results).
Beyond Kodak, EF-LIC achieves consistent BD-rate reductions on Tecnick (-55.46%), DIV2K (-62.33%), and CLIC 2020 (-63.22%) relative to MS-ILLM (Benchmark Performance results).
A lightweight variant, EF-LIC-s, further reduces computation to 9.94ms encoding and 6.26ms decoding per image (Computational Efficiency results).

CbWCaD8tRC.text: S2GS maintains 0.581 SSIM at 256 views while the offline baseline SIU3R crashes with out-of-memory at that scale (Table 4).
On ScanNet at 8 views, S2GS achieves 49.53 mIoU versus 44.78 mIoU for SIU3R, and at 32 views 48.95 mIoU versus 39.98 mIoU (Table 2).
S2GS reaches 82.49 instance tracking success rate (T-SR) at 8 views versus 62.93 for SIU3R (Table 2).

S2GS scales to 1,024 frames with memory growing to approximately 77GB and per-frame latency remaining under 0.7 seconds, while offline baselines run out of memory around 80 frames (Table 4, Section 3).
Ablating the geometry-semantic decoupling drops T-mIoU from 30.01 to 21.32, and removing query contrastive learning drops T-SR from 62.39 to 50.13 (Table 7, Table 8).
Removing geometric distillation from a pretrained 3D foundation model degrades SSIM from 0.665 to 0.237 (Table 9).

6aFU1bnUnv.text: The Reward Auditor framework uses paired permutation tests with paired-sample Cohen's d effect size and a group-aware Benjamini-Hochberg correction to test reward-model suitability under 10 real-world perturbation scenarios (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
Across 26 evaluated reward models on the chat subset, 80.7% demonstrate highly idiosyncratic vulnerability patterns to at least one perturbation (Section 5.1, Table 1).
SOLAR-10.7B-Instruct-v1.0 shows large, significant effect sizes under stylized perturbations, including 0.774*** on Length Extension and 0.906*** on Structured Presentation (Table 1).

Stylized perturbations (e.g., synonym transformation, language conversion) pose greater systemic risk to reward models than controlled perturbations (e.g., punctuation habits, irrelevant usernames) (Section 5.1).

Measured reward-model suitability risk correlates with downstream policy performance under perturbed environments, with a Spearman's rho of -0.881 across 5 low-risk and 5 high-risk reward models used to train policies (Section 5.2, Figure 3).

2Z7ZvoRN8Z.text: The paper derives a direct kernel-matrix transformation for fair null-space projection that avoids explicit computation of the empirical feature space (Theorem 3.2, Equation 11).
The resulting Fair Kernel Decomposition (Algorithm 1) is shown to preserve positive semi-definiteness of the transformed kernel matrix (Corollary 3.3).
On the ACSIncome (Montana) dataset, the proposed SVR-FKD method substantially outperforms baselines including KRR-FKL and NN-HGR on the GDP fairness measure (Section 4.1.4, Figure 1).
On the ACSTravelTime (Montana) dataset, only SVR-FKD improves the accuracy-fairness tradeoff beyond the unconstrained baseline, while other compared methods do not (Section 4.1.4, Figure 1).
A Nystrom approximation of the method reduces computational cost from O(m*n^3) while maintaining comparable performance on the Communities & Crimes dataset (Section 3.2.2, Figure 3, Appendix C).

9GTDxv7Xra.text: On the personalized image captioning benchmark, GPT-4o achieves only 34.2% Positive Accuracy on 1-concept images and 15.3% on 4-concept images (Table 2).
Applying CoViP to Qwen3-VL-8B raises Positive Accuracy from 39.0% to 77.4% on 1-concept images and from 18.6% to 59.7% on 4-concept images, a gain of roughly 38-42 points (Table 2, Section 3.3).
On the Instruction-Triggered Recall (ITR) diagnostic downstream task, adding Caption-Augmented Generation (CAG) improves CoViP's score from 28.0% to 42.8% (Table 3, Section 3.4).
Prior personalization methods RAP and RePIC show only marginal or no improvement over the base VLM on the diagnostic downstream tasks (Table 3).

CoViP maintains performance comparable to the baseline on standard captioning metrics (BLEU, ROUGE-L, METEOR, SPICE, BERTScore on DOCCI) and shows no notable increase in hallucination rate on MMHal and POPE (Table 4, Table 5, Table 6).

s8AbIVtmUg.text: In the bandit setting with contamination budget epsilon=0.4, AT-DPT achieves 24.2±1.2 cumulative regret against a DPT-targeted reward-poisoning attack, versus 97.7±4.9 for Thompson Sampling, 95.8±4.9 for UCB, and 85.0±2.3 for corruption-robust crUCB (Table 1, Section 3).
AT-DPT generalizes across attacker types, achieving 24.8±1.4 regret when evaluated against attackers trained to target other algorithms (Section 4, Table 1).
Against adaptive, context-aware attackers, AT-DPT attains 37.1±6.6 regret, comparable to its robustness under non-adaptive attacks (Table 2).

In the linear bandit setting, AT-DPT achieves 52.49±1.06 regret, matching the clean-condition performance of CRLinUCB (51.79±1.02) while substantially outperforming it under adversarial attack (Table 3).
In the Darkroom2 MDP setting, AT-DPT attains 241.2±9.1 episode reward against learned attackers, compared to 237.2±6.7 for the NPG baseline (Table 4).

AT-DPT trades off some performance in clean and uniformly-randomized attack scenarios relative to a frozen (non-adversarially-trained) baseline, since adversarial training optimizes specifically against learned attacks (Section 4, Limitations).

KG4CjK6j8Y.text: D-Byz-SGDM (DeMoA) maintains convergence under partial client participation with participation probability p=0.5 and Byzantine fraction δ up to 0.2, while FedAvg and FedAvg-M diverge when the sampled subset contains a Byzantine majority (Figure 1).

Theorem 4.1 proves D-Byz-SGDM converges to an O(cδζ²/p) neighborhood of a stationary point, where c is the robust-aggregator constant, δ the Byzantine fraction, ζ² the data heterogeneity bound, and p the participation probability.
Theorem 4.2 establishes a matching Ω(δζ²/p) lower bound, showing the O(cδζ²/p) convergence neighborhood in Theorem 4.1 is information-theoretically unimprovable.

On MNIST with a CNN (n=20-25 clients, momentum α=0.9), D-Byz-SGDM is evaluated against FedAvg, FedAvg-M, and Byz-VR-MARINA-PP under six Byzantine attacks (BF, LF, mimic, IPM, ALIE, INF) combined with five robust aggregators (average, Krum, coordinate-wise median, centered clipping, RFA) (Section 5).

Even in the non-Byzantine setting, D-Byz-SGDM exceeds FedAvg-M performance under partial participation, indicating the delayed-momentum caching mechanism yields a regularization benefit beyond robustness (Figure 2).

The delayed momentum aggregation scheme caches stale momentum for non-sampled clients (m_i^t ← m_i^{t-1}) so that Byzantine clients cannot dominate the aggregated update even if they form a majority of the sampled set, and it requires no additional communication overhead versus full participation (Algorithm 1).

jl2f2Y3iuC.text: Corollary 4.4 shows that full fine-tuning of all attention parameters in a linear attention model drives zero-shot error to σ² while few-shot (in-context) error converges to σ² + θᵀΣθ, a substantially larger value, formalizing the degradation of in-context learning after full fine-tuning (Section 4.2).

Theorem 4.6 shows that restricting fine-tuning updates to the value matrix reduces zero-shot error to σ² + (2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ while Corollary 4.8 shows the asymptotic few-shot error only rises to σ² + 1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀, i.e. value-matrix-only fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance with far less degradation to in-context learning than full fine-tuning (Section 4.3).

Proposition 4.10 proves that tuning the auxiliary few-shot loss weight w to optimize few-shot performance on the fine-tuning task θ₀ necessarily reduces few-shot performance on other tasks θ ≠ θ₀, formalizing a trade-off between target-task adaptation and generalization to unseen tasks (Section 4.4).

In synthetic linear-regression experiments (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖₂²=1, m=n=20), Figure 4 confirms the theoretical zero-shot/few-shot error predictions across pretraining, full fine-tuning, and value-matrix fine-tuning regimes, and Figure 5 shows value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the out-of-distribution task -θ₀ (Section 5.1).

On the MMLU benchmark using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuned on the Humanities category, full fine-tuning improves zero-shot accuracy but degrades 7-shot accuracy, whereas value-matrix-only fine-tuning preserves few-shot accuracy while still improving zero-shot performance (Section 5.2).

WlScVvMwpB.text: WSInstruct is an instruction-tuning dataset covering 31 U.S. cities across 4 geographic regions and 8 weather aspects (temperature, wind, humidity, frontal systems, pressure systems, wave patterns, wind flow systems, events), comprising 6,344 SFT image-report pairs (2017-2021), 20,412 RFT-augmented images (2017-2020), 1,241 DPO preference samples (2021), and a 1,292-sample test set (2022).

WeatherSyn is trained via a three-stage pipeline on a Qwen3-VL-8B backbone: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT) for lexical diversity, and direct preference optimization (DPO) for human-preference alignment (Section on Training Approach).

WeatherSyn-DPO outperforms closed-source MLLMs including Claude-3.7-Sonnet and GPT-5-Nano on overall report-generation metrics, e.g. BLEU-1 of 0.44 versus 0.09 (Claude) and 0.16 (GPT-5-Nano), Weighted F1 of 0.59 versus 0.51 and 0.48, and Factual Consistency of 0.29 versus 0.01 and 0.02 (Table on Overall Metrics).

WeatherSyn-DPO achieves its largest gains over closed-source baselines on structurally complex weather aspects, scoring 0.72 weighted F1 on Pressure System versus 0.58 for Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and 0.65 versus 0.53 on Wave Pattern (Weather Aspect Performance results).

WeatherSyn demonstrates zero-shot cross-region generalization, maintaining a performance advantage over 2-shot Claude-3.7-Sonnet and GPT-5-Nano on both geographically proximate splits and geographically distant splits (North-to-South, East-to-West) without task-specific fine-tuning (Generalization Findings section).

S2ilvpV9du.text: Deep-VRM injects artifact-specific visual residual features at layer K=16 via h̃ᵥ^(K-1) = 0.5·hᵥ^(K-1) + 0.5·𝒱ₐ(I), combining a frozen encoder that preserves pretrained semantic perception with a LoRA-equipped adapted branch that extracts low-level generator artifacts (Method Overview / Architecture).

Deep-VRM is trained with a two-stage procedure: Stage 1 fine-tunes the LLM on a semantic-focused dataset D1 with other modules frozen, and Stage 2 integrates D1 with a VAE-reconstructed dataset D2 emphasizing non-semantic artifacts while keeping early layers frozen (Two-Stage Training section).

Deep-VRM achieves state-of-the-art AI-generated image detection accuracy across five benchmarks: 97.42% on GenImage, 94.50% on SynthBuster, 90.48% on AIGI-Bench, 95.70% on AIGI-NOW, and 89.51% on WildRF, outperforming the Forensic-Chat baseline (88.75%) without relying on external detectors (Benchmark Results table).

An ablation over injection depth shows K=16 is optimal, while shallow injection at K=4 disrupts semantic processing and deep injection at K=20 limits the model's reasoning capacity (Ablation Studies).

Freezing early layers during Stage 2 training is shown to be critical for robustness, yielding a +14% accuracy improvement on the compressed WildRF benchmark compared to not freezing early layers (Ablation Studies).

w9Ml4E3Pc4.text: COGNOS combines Gaussian-White Noise Regularization (GWNR), which adds an MMD-based Gaussianity loss and an autocorrelation-penalizing loss over lags 1-10 to the standard MSE reconstruction loss, with a Kalman-smoothing post-processor (forward Kalman filter plus backward Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing) that denoises anomaly scores (Core Components section).

COGNOS is evaluated on 12 backbone anomaly-detection models spanning attention-based (AnomalyTransformer, Autoformer, Transformer, iTransformer, PatchTST, Pyraformer), time-frequency fusion (TimesNet, TimeMixer, FiLM), and CNN-MLP (MICN, LightTS, DLinear) architectures across four datasets: MSL, SMAP, SWaT, and PSM (Experimental Results).

COGNOS yields an average F-score uplift of 57.9% across all 12 backbones, with attention-based models improving by 62.5% on average, FiLM showing the largest single-model gain of 95.4%, and DLinear the smallest gain of 37.4% (Experimental Results / Performance Gains).

Ablation results show the Kalman smoother component outperforms moving-average and low-pass-filter alternatives for denoising anomaly scores, and that GWNR is critical for preventing overfitting to spurious reconstruction patterns, with the full COGNOS combination outperforming either component alone (Ablation Studies).
The Adaptive Residual Kalman Smoother is controlled by a single hyperparameter λ governing the bias-variance tradeoff of the smoothing operation (Ablation Studies / Kalman Smoother section).

YXEXsGHwpq.text: Mild L1 regularization (coefficient 2e-5) on ReLU-gated feedforward activations induces over 99% sparsity with negligible loss in downstream task performance (Section 2.2, Table 1).

The Tile-wise ELLPACK (TwELL) sparse format stores non-zero activations in horizontal 1D column tiles and can be recovered within the same kernel as the gate projection, avoiding extra synchronization overhead (Section 3.2).

At the 2B parameter scale, custom CUDA/Triton kernels deliver a 20.5% forward-pass speedup, 17.0% energy savings, 21.9% training speedup, and 22.3% additional memory reduction compared to the dense baseline (Table 1).
Sparsity benefits scale with model size: forward speedup rises from 17.0% at 0.5B parameters to 20.5% at 2B parameters, and memory reduction improves from -19.2% at 0.5B to +22.3% at 2B (Table 1).

Layer-wise analysis shows a Pearson correlation of -0.996 between mean per-layer non-zero activation counts and inference speedup, with a pronounced 'hump' of higher activity in middle transformer layers (Section 4.3, Figure 6).

Models are trained on FineWeb with a Transformer++ architecture at 2048 context length and 1M-token batch size, and evaluated on seven downstream benchmarks including ARC, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA, WinoGrande, and CommonsenseQA (Section 4.1).

VX8H2713oA.text: The plug-in bias-adjusted estimator θ̂ = (p̂ + q̂₀ − 1)/(q̂₀ + q̂₁ − 1) corrects the naive LLM-judge accuracy estimate p̂ using estimated judge specificity q̂₀ and sensitivity q̂₁ (Section 3, Equation 7).

A Wald-type confidence interval (Equation 8) is constructed that incorporates variance contributions from both the test dataset of size n and the calibration datasets of sizes m₀ and m₁ (Section 3, Equations 8-11).

Proposition 1 shows that when the calibration sample size m satisfies m ≳ q/(2q−1)², the bias-adjusted estimator θ̂ has lower absolute bias than the naive estimator p̂ for all true accuracy values θ (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).

Proposition 2 characterizes the confidence-interval-minimizing allocation between the two calibration subsets, with optimal ratio m₀ ≈ (1/p̂ − 1)√κ · m₁ where κ = (1−q̃₀)/(1−q̃₁) (Section 4.2, Proposition 2; Algorithm 1).

Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the adjusted estimator reduces bias and achieves proper 95% confidence interval coverage across all true accuracy values θ, while adaptive calibration allocation yields shorter intervals than equal allocation (Section 5, Figure 4).

Ws2RhhBir4.text: FT-Agent achieves the best performance on 10 of the 13 tasks spanning five domains (Mathematics, Patent Examination, Chemistry, Finance, Table QA) in the FT-Dojo benchmark (Section 4.2, Table 2).
On AIME 2025, FT-Agent reaches 13.30% accuracy while all baseline agents (including OpenHands) score 0% (Section 4.2, Table 2).

FT-Agent requires more exploration than OpenHands, averaging 8.77 optimization loops versus 3.69, with a higher improvement rate of 24.37% versus 17.31%, at a modestly higher API cost of $5.73 versus $3.92 (Section 4.2, Table 3).

On the Mol_Edit task, FT-Agent recovers from a catastrophic 2% accuracy failure to 56% accuracy through iterative diagnosis across training loops, demonstrating cumulative learning from historical experience (Section 4.4, Figure 4a).

On the PI4PC patent identification task, FT-Agent applies generic interventions such as NEFTune without identifying root causes, yielding zero net improvement and performance cycling between 8% and 34%, illustrating a causal-reasoning limitation (Section 4.4, Figure 4b, Table 7).
Replacing the backbone from GPT-5.2 to GPT-4o causes significant performance drops in procedural tasks, including a 16-point drop on Visualization and 15-point drop on Patent Retrieval (Section 4.3).

dTC2pUbFQ0.text: Theorem 3.3 derives the oracle-optimal entropy coefficient as λₜ* = √(C₁/C₂ · αₜ), a square-root scaling rule relating exploration strength to drift magnitude αₜ (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).

Adaptive Entropy Scheduling (AES) estimates drift online using the 0.9-quantile of absolute TD errors as a proxy, smoothed via exponential moving average, avoiding the need to observe true drift directly (Equation 27, Theorem 3.4).

On abrupt-change tasks, AES reduces normalized recovery time relative to baseline for all four algorithm carriers, e.g., SAC recovery time drops from 13.96% to 7.74% and MEow from 11.58% to 6.42% of total training steps (Section 4, Table 3).

On the Isaac Gym AllegroHand task, AES cuts normalized recovery time from 21.5% to 10.6%, and on FrankaCabinet from 19.4% to 10.5%, the largest gains among tested high-dimensional tasks (Section 4.4).

AES increases normalized AUC and reduces the performance-drop-area ratio across 3 task families (Toy, MuJoCo, Isaac Gym), 4 drift patterns (abrupt, linear, periodic, mixed), and 4 algorithm carriers (SAC, PPO, SQL, MEow), e.g., SAC nAUC rises from 0.72 to 0.88 under abrupt drift (Section 4.3, Table 2).

59WxkdZv5E.text: The Coverage-Resolution Objective 𝒥ₜ(𝐝) = (∫ₓ∈𝐝 pₜ(x)dx) × ϕ(𝐝) reduces the sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design problem to jointly maximizing spatial coverage of belief and perceptual resolution (Section 3.2).

FOVEA, a training-free inference-time procedure with Greedy, MCMC, and Lookahead variants, raises mean accuracy across four benchmarks (MME-RealWorld, CV-Bench, V*Bench, HR-Bench 4K) at the 30B model scale from 73.3% (Direct) and 75.1% (ReAct) to 77.7% (Table 1, Section 5).

On search-dominated gigapixel remote-sensing imagery, FOVEA-Lookahead achieves 54.7% accuracy versus 45.1% for the ReAct baseline, a 21.3% relative gain, while an oracle-crop upper bound reaches 60% (Figure 3, Table 5).

Compute cost scales with planning depth: FOVEA-Lookahead uses 9.5x input tokens and 55.2x output tokens relative to baseline, compared to 6.5x/9.8x for FOVEA-Greedy and 7.7x/12.5x for FOVEA-MCMC (Figure 4).

Appendix E shows the model's spatial belief updates correctly: target probability increases after being shown oracle crops containing the target, and decreases after distractor crops, evidencing verification and falsification behavior (Appendix E).

mtcGhTTDgN.text: AlphaGRPO improves GenEval score from 84.0 (BAGEL baseline) to 85.1, and to 88.2 with Inference-time Self-Reflective Reasoning (Table 1).
AlphaGRPO raises the WISE benchmark score from 0.52 (BAGEL) to 0.53, and to 0.71 with Inference-time Self-Reflective Reasoning (Table 1).
AlphaGRPO improves GEdit score from 6.52 (BAGEL) to 7.08 without any training on editing-specific tasks, using its decompositional verifiable reward (Table 1).

The Decompositional Verifiable Reward (DVReward) decomposes each prompt into 10 semantic and 8 quality verification questions, computing reward as r(z) = sqrt(v_sem_bar * v_qua_bar), and outperforms PickScore, HPSv3, and UnifiedReward on TIIF-Bench and GenEval (Table 3).
False-Positive Rectification, which assigns the minimum group reward to non-improving trajectories, improves TIIF-Long score from 77.8 to 79.5 (Table 5).
Human evaluation shows AlphaGRPO is preferred over BAGEL in 40.5% of overall comparisons, 36.5% for prompt-following, and 43% for quality (Table 11).

7LMNIktDZy.text: RST-1M contains 1.2 million spatially aligned image pairs spanning five modalities (RGB, SAR, NIR, PAN, MS), aggregated from five public datasets including SEN1-2, SEN12MS, CACo, SpaceNet-3, and SpaceNet-5 (Section 3, Table 1).
On the SAR-to-RGB translation task, Any2Any-L achieves 25.20 PSNR and 16.85 RMSE, outperforming Pix2Pix (11.84 PSNR, 68.57 RMSE) and BBDM (19.50 PSNR, 31.02 RMSE) (Table 2).
Any2Any is evaluated across 14 translation directions and achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance on all of them (Figure 1).

Any2Any generalizes zero-shot to 6 unseen modality pairs (e.g., SAR-PAN, PAN-MS, NIR-PAN) without paired training data, via transitive learning through the shared latent space (Section 5.2, Figure 5).
An ablation shows the lightweight residual adapter improves SAR-to-RGB PSNR from 20.68 (without adapter) to 21.44 (with adapter) (Table 3).
Training on all 14 translation directions jointly improves PSNR to 22.25, a 1.37 gain over training on a single direction (20.88 PSNR) (Table 3).

I5IMkvVKd7.text: The Tail Inflated Expectation (TIE) scheduling metric models LLM output length using a log-t distribution with fixed degrees of freedom nu=3.5, passing the Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit test at a 90.6% rate (Table 1).

Theorem 3.2 shows that under mild assumptions on token termination rates, LLM output length exhibits power-law tail decay, motivating the heavy-tailed log-t model over Gaussian or log-normal alternatives.

On online chatbot serving (LMSYS-Chat-1M, 8B model, 100 RPS), TIE reduces per-token latency by 4.73x versus first-come-first-served and 2.31x versus a longest-time-remaining baseline, and reduces average time-to-first-token from 127.55s to 48.23s (Figure 4a).
On offline synthetic data generation (Alpaca dataset), TIE achieves a Time@3K of 98.12s versus 144.93s for SSJF and 229.37s for FCFS, and improves throughput 1.42x over LTR (Table 3).

An ablation shows replacing the log-t distribution with a log-normal distribution degrades performance from 0.67 to 1.63 seconds/token, and removing the CVaR tail-risk term (using expectation alone, SEPT) yields 0.75 versus 0.67 seconds/token (Table 4).

The output length predictor is a fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3-base model achieving R-squared of 0.82 and 0.76 for the mu and sigma distribution parameters respectively, with scheduling overhead of only 4.26ms per request.

oTRMveQEzW.text: NaviEdit is a training-free, inference-time controller that decouples the model's noise-level scale coordinate from edit progress, formalized as a controlled dynamical system on a progress axis s in [0,1] (Definition 4.1).

Theorem 4.3 proves that, under a fixed step budget, increasing computation density within an effective scale window ('density beats range') outperforms expanding the range into noisier, unreliable regimes.

On PIE-Bench, applying the Navi controller to FlowEdit (Navi-FlowEdit + gate) improves SSIM from 84.08 to 93.85, PSNR from 22.46 to 27.94, and LPIPS from 103.00 to 48.74 versus the FlowEdit baseline, while also improving CLIP-Whole score from 25.91 to 26.18 (Table 1).
Navi-FlowAlign with M held constant (M≡1) achieves 93.40 SSIM, 28.33 PSNR, and 34.49 LPIPS on PIE-Bench (Table 1).
The decoupling principle is validated as backbone-agnostic, consistently improving SSIM and PSNR across SD3, SD3.5, and FLUX.1 [dev] (Table 2).
Figure 3 identifies a 'stable valley' at intermediate scale values via a leakage pressure diagnostic rho(u), where edits remain both semantically responsive and spatially anchored.

kxUb6VuYbY.text: TexEditor is trained via supervised fine-tuning on TexBlender (5,000 instruction-edit pairs from Blender/3D-FRONT scenes) followed by reinforcement learning with a structure-preserving StructureNFT loss (Section on Key Datasets).

On TexBench texture-replacement editing, TexEditor outperforms Nano Banana Pro on instruction adherence (0.858 vs 0.839), structure preservation (0.929 vs 0.801), and composite TexEval score (0.886 vs 0.824) (Table 2).
On the Blender benchmark, TexEditor achieves an edge preservation score of 0.988 versus 0.752 for Nano Banana Pro, and a TexEval composite of 0.972 versus 0.855 (Table 3).

TexBench is a new evaluation benchmark of 825 COCO-derived samples (453 texture replacement, 372 attribute editing) with manual quality verification, introduced to address limitations of prior Blender-only benchmarks (Table 1).

On the ImgEdit generalization benchmark, TexEditor outperforms the Qwen-2509 baseline on texture-related sub-tasks including Adjust (4.13 vs 4.05), Background (4.13 vs 3.87), and Compose (2.39 vs 2.17) (Table 5).

The TexEval metric combines MLLM-based instruction adherence with a SAUGE wireframe-SSIM structure score as TexEval = alpha*Score_ins + (1-alpha)*Score_struct with optimal alpha=0.6, and human evaluation confirms it best aligns with human judgments among tested structure extractors (Figure 4, Figure 5).

aLTzh5Sbe9.text: DRIVE trains a Qwen2.5-32B model via a two-stage RLVR pipeline: a Stage 1 'entropy expansion' phase on roughly 9k competitive programming problems using 8 rollouts per prompt at 24k token length, followed by a Stage 2 'hard-focus curriculum' phase using 64 rollouts at 32k tokens that progressively retains the most difficult problems across three curriculum phases (Section on Method/Pipeline Overview).
DRIVE reaches 0.182 Pass@1 on the Codeforces OJ benchmark, a 58.3% relative improvement over the SFT baseline, and this is the largest relative gain among the reported benchmarks (Results table).

On LeetCode Weekly contests DRIVE attains 0.653 Pass@1 (a 13.0% relative improvement over SFT), while on LiveCode 08-11 and LiveCode V5 it reaches 0.699 and 0.697 Pass@1 respectively, closely matching or exceeding DeepSeek V3.1's 0.692 and 0.713 (Results table).

The SFT data-curation stage uses arena learning to select 470K high-quality prompts from an initial pool of 1.27M candidates, then applies a 'Twice Hard Learning' strategy that doubles exposure to difficult samples while holding the total token budget fixed (Data Curation Strategy section).

Standard RL training is shown to hit a capability ceiling on the hardest problems, motivating the hardness-prioritized data scheduling; large rollout budgets (64+ samples) are found to be necessary specifically for mastering the most difficult problem instances (Critical Findings/ablation discussion).

X01MWoAk3K.text: SWEET pre-trains a single shared weight template together with size-specific weight scalers under a Tucker-based factorization W = G ×1 X ×2 U ×3 V, where the core template G (of shape r1×r2×r3, with r1r2r3 ≪ L×P) encodes size-agnostic knowledge reusable across model widths (Method section, Tucker factorization).

Width-wise stochastic scaling applies structured dropout masks (Ũ = M_U⊙U, Ṽ = M_V⊙V) to the weight scalers during pretraining specifically to regularize the template along width-related dimensions and encourage width-invariant representations (Method section).

SWEET is pretrained with an MAE reconstruction loss on ImageNet-1K for 450 epochs at batch size 1024 on a single RTX 4090, contrasted with the WAVE baseline's 800 epochs at batch size 4096 (Experimental setup).

Across five model scales, SWEET improves average Top-1 classification accuracy by +1.60% over the WAVE baseline (with per-scale gains ranging from +0.42% up to +1.96%), and improves object detection AP^box by +2.04 and AP^mask by +1.59, and semantic segmentation mIoU by +2.76 and mAcc by +3.43 (Table 1).
For image generation, SWEET improves FID by -2.19 (lower is better) and Inception Score by +1.76 relative to the baseline (Table 2).
On fine-grained downstream transfer datasets (Oxford Flowers, Stanford Cars, CIFAR-100), SWEET achieves an average Top-1 accuracy of 78.40% versus 72.56% for WAVE (Table 3).

z9VuS0wKGW.text: StableI2I is a reference-free evaluation framework that scores content fidelity in image-to-image transitions along three axes—Semantic Level, Structure Level, and Low-level Appearance—without requiring ground-truth images (Framework/Core description).

On its benchmark, StableI2I attains 89.10% binary accuracy and 83.00% strict accuracy, outperforming the best existing model baseline, Gemini-3-pro, which reaches 82.28% average binary accuracy (Figure 6).

Model-level evaluation shows Bagel achieves the highest average fidelity score (0.8838) across image editing tasks, while Flux.1-dev and GPT-Image-1 show severe content-repainting issues with average scores of 0.4390 and 0.6524 respectively (Table 1).

Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 attains strong semantic preservation (0.9595) but weak structural preservation (0.4683), illustrating that most baseline models perform worst specifically on the Structure Level (pixel-level alignment) dimension (Table 1).

StableI2I's benchmark comprises 1,000 human-annotated pairs per evaluation dimension (3,000 samples total), and its training set includes 6,722 image restoration samples and 4,839 editing samples, with training performed in multiple stages including a GRPO-based reinforcement learning stage (Dataset Scale section).

Human correlation validation with seven volunteers assessing 50 images from ImgEdit-Bench shows StableI2I's automated outputs are largely consistent with human subjective judgments (Human Correlation section).

2DyKW8qHDL.text: Comp-Attn improves T2V-CompBench scores by 15.71% on Wan2.1-T2V-14B and by 11.70% on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, while adding only a 5.1% inference-time overhead (Table 1 and Table 4, Section 4.2).

Comp-Attn's 'Present-and-Align' paradigm (Section 3) comprises two components: Subject-aware Condition Interpolation (SCI), which reinforces subject-specific conditions to ensure each subject's presence, and Layout-forcing Attention Modulation (LAM), which enforces the attention distribution to align with the relational layout of multiple subjects (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

On VBench, Comp-Attn improves Wan2.2-A14B's total score by 0.66% (with a 2.21% gain on the semantic sub-score) and improves CogVideoX-5B's total score by 1.26% (with a 3.64% semantic gain) (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On T2I-CompBench, extending Comp-Attn to FLUX yields a 5.36% average improvement, outperforming training-based layout baselines such as SiamLayout and HybridLayout (Table 3, Section 4.2).

Comp-Attn uses GPT-4o-mini to generate layouts (roughly 5 seconds per request) and applies its attention modulation only during the first 20% of denoising timesteps, and is demonstrated to be applicable across DiT, MM-DiT, and U-Net architectures (Appendix A).

Xl7cAV0jdc.text: LightAVSeg achieves 50.4 mIoU on the MS3 benchmark using only 20.5M parameters, versus AVSegFormer's 151.1M parameters—roughly 1/7th the size (Results section).
On the S4 benchmark, LightAVSeg reaches 75.6 mIoU, matching the accuracy of heavier ResNet-50-based baselines despite its much smaller parameter count (Results section).

LightAVSeg runs at 163.4ms inference latency on a Snapdragon 8 Elite mobile CPU, roughly an 8x speedup over AVSegFormer, evaluated across the S4, MS3, and AVSS benchmarks (Computational Efficiency section).

The core architectural contribution, the Reciprocal Audio-Visual Encoder, replaces dense cross-modal attention with hierarchical global audio refinement (via spatial max-pooling to 1x1) and channel-wise modulation via broadcast residual operations, reducing complexity from quadratic O(N^2) to linear O(N) (Architecture section).

A Multi-Scale Audio-Visual Alignment Loss (L_msa) provides auxiliary pixel-wise supervision during training only (zero inference overhead) and improves MS3 performance by +1.1 mIoU (Loss Function Contribution section, ablation).

On mobile hardware, the latency breakdown attributes 85.3% of total inference time to the visual backbone, 3.9% to the audio backbone, and 6.2% combined to the proposed interaction modules (Reciprocal Encoder 3.7%, Fusion Decoder 2.5%) (Component Latency Breakdown / Figure).

Pmsc4yytlf.text: Under (L0,L1)-smoothness with unbounded-variance gradient noise, distributed SGD (DSGD) requires a stepsize satisfying η·ηt < 2ε/[(L0+L1·E[‖∇f(Xt)‖])(1+dσ1̄²/N)+dNσ0̄²L1], i.e., an adaptive rate that scales inversely with the gradient norm to guarantee convergence (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2).

For distributed compressed SGD (DCSGD) with unbiased compression of rate ω̄, the derived SDE analysis shows compression is asymptotically equivalent to DSGD with an inflated noise parameter σ1²=ω̄/d, meaning stronger adaptivity is required as the compression rate increases (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).

Gradient update normalization emerges from the SDE analysis as a necessary stability condition whenever L1·σ1̄²>0, i.e., when gradient noise variance grows with the gradient norm under (L0,L1)-smoothness (Section 4.1).

DSignSGD is proven to converge under heavy-tailed noise modeled as Student-t distributed with degrees of freedom ν=1 (unbounded expectation), without requiring a Robbins-Monro-style decaying learning rate schedule, unlike DSGD/DCSGD (Theorem 4.4, Section 4.2).

Empirical validation on MLPs, ResNets, and Vision Transformers shows DSGD diverges as noise variance σ increases unless adaptive scheduling or normalization is applied, while DCSGD exhibits the same instability under random sparsification with compression rates ω∈{4,8,16} (Figure 1, Section 4).

AQZZWVp6XA.text: Compositional generalization to unseen attribute combinations in vision embedding models requires representations that admit a linear factorization into independently recoverable semantic dimensions (Definition 3, Section 3).

The paper's theoretical framework proves that approximate orthogonality across the linear factors is necessary, alongside linear factorization, for a representation to support robust compositional generalization (Section 3).

Empirical analysis of CLIP and SigLIP model families finds that these models exhibit varying but generally strong evidence of linear factorization and approximate orthogonality across semantic dimensions, correlating with their compositional generalization performance (Section 4).

SigLIP, trained with a sigmoid contrastive loss, is reported to demonstrate more orthogonal representational structure than standard CLIP contrastive training, per the empirical comparison in Section 4 (Section 4).

Linear probes trained on the factorized representations substantially outperform end-to-end fine-tuning approaches on compositional generalization benchmarks tested in the empirical analysis (Section 4).

ROFqW86Dca.text: ManiPT attains an average harmonic-mean accuracy of 82.09% across 11 base-to-novel generalization datasets, outperforming CoPrompt (80.48%) and TAC (81.24%) (Section 5, Table on base-to-novel generalization).
In few-shot classification at the 1-shot setting, ManiPT reaches 74.75% average accuracy versus PromptSRC's 72.32%, with consistent gains maintained across the 1-16 shot range (Section 5).
In cross-dataset transfer (trained on ImageNet, evaluated on 10 downstream datasets), ManiPT achieves 68.04% average accuracy, the highest among the compared baselines (Section 5).
In domain generalization on ImageNet variants, ManiPT achieves 61.88% average accuracy, exceeding CoPrompt (60.42%) and TAC (61.63%) (Section 5).

Lemma 4.2 establishes that the normalized additive fusion of frozen and prompted features has a contraction property pulling final representations toward the frozen (pretrained) features, which Corollary 4.4 uses to show ManiPT achieves a lower or equal population risk bound than standard prompt tuning under the cosine consistency constraint (Lemma 4.2, Corollary 4.4, Section 4).

Ablating the structural bias (normalized additive fusion) component causes base accuracy to drop from 84.85% to 82.85% and novel-class accuracy to fall from 76.50% to 68.32%, showing the fusion mechanism is critical for generalization to unseen classes (Section 5, ablation table).

3dLPVNhFZh.text: OmniAgent frames omni-modal video understanding as a POMDP solved via iterative Observation-Thought-Action loops that selectively distill audio-visual content into persistent textual memory, rather than uniformly processing all frames (Section 3).

On LVBench, the 7B OmniAgent outperforms the 10x larger Qwen2.5-VL-72B (50.5% vs. 47.3%) while using 73% fewer frames, and also exceeds the Qwen2.5-Omni baseline (43.0%) (Section 4, Table on LVBench results).
OmniAgent achieves 71.1% accuracy on MLVU for long-video comprehension and a +33.4% improvement over baseline on temporal grounding on LongVALE (Section 4).

Training uses a two-stage optimization pipeline: Agentic SFT via best-of-N trajectory synthesis with GPT-4o-based outcome verification and rationality audits, followed by TAURA (Turn-aware Adaptive Uncertainty Rescaled Advantage), which reweights GRPO's advantage using token entropy to counter 'advantage homogenization' (Section 3).
OmniAgent exhibits positive test-time scaling, with performance improving by +6.2% on the long-video subset of VideoMME as additional reasoning turns are allowed (Section 4).

OmniAgent achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across ten benchmarks spanning video understanding, audio-visual reasoning, and temporal grounding, including VideoMME and LVBench (Section 4).

zOWrIO6oKT.text: NAACA raises AudioQwen's average precision on the XD-Violence dataset from 53.50% to 70.60% while reducing ALM (audio language model) invocations by roughly 40% (Section 4/5, XD-Violence results table).

The Oscillatory Working Memory (OWM) selection mechanism alone contributes a 17.1 percentage point improvement in average precision on XD-Violence, isolating its effect from the rest of the pipeline (Section 4/5, ablation).

OWM is formulated as a 2D recurrent field on a 64x64 lattice with a pressure field p(x,y,t) and velocity field v(x,y,t), mapping 527 PANN audio categories to carrier frequencies between 51-1200 Hz, with frequency-selective phase differentiation proven in Theorem 2.1 (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
Theorem 2.4 shows that a striped wave-speed pattern in the OWM field maximizes modal coupling for salience detection via Bragg-matched periodicity (Theorem 2.4, Section 2).
On the XD-Violence benchmark, NAACA's salient-event detections achieve 61.1% temporal precision alignment with ground-truth salient events (Section 4/5).

The Time Sent Ratio, measuring the fraction of audio routed to the ALM, ranges from 0.597 to 0.650 across datasets, showing NAACA allocates ALM compute adaptively based on acoustic complexity rather than a fixed compression budget (Section 4/5).

4dwe2wlxx5.text: On MEP-Bench, OPPO improves recall from a 58.00% baseline to 70.44%, indicating better utilization of non-textual modality cues (Table 1).
On MEP-Bench, OPPO raises video-faithfulness accuracy from 59.20% to 76.40% and audio-faithfulness accuracy from 33.00% to 50.60% under unimodal masking (Table 1).

OPPO achieves a mean score of 81.05% on MER-UniBench, including 86.50% on MOSI, 84.63% on MOSEI, 86.22% on SIMS, 87.73% on MER23, and 90.34% on MER24, representing state-of-the-art performance (Table 2).
On MME-Emotion, OPPO attains an overall mean CoT score of 49.5%, with 31.0% on recognition and 68.1% on reasoning subtasks (Table 3).

OPPO's Omni-Perception Reward decomposes ground-truth reasoning into visual, acoustic, and emotion cues and scores semantic coverage via an Evidence-Routing Matrix using cosine similarity (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

The Omni-Perception Loss applies a KL-divergence penalty specifically to modality-specific tokens identified via cue matching under unimodal masking, and ablating this component degrades performance relative to the full OPPO model (Section 3.2, Table 4).

z7ivDFlnSC.text: Partial Information Decomposition of mutual information between model decisions and multimodal inputs into unique, redundant, and synergistic components shows synergy-dominant benchmarks (e.g., MMBench, MMStar, POPE) exhibit Spearman correlation ρ(Synergy, accuracy) ≥ 0.718 (Section 4.1).
Knowledge-oriented benchmarks such as MMMU, PMC-VQA, and Reefknot are instead dominated by language-unique information rather than cross-modal synergy (Section 4.1).

Model families cluster into two interaction regimes: Qwen/InternVL3/LLaVA models are 'joint-modality-reliant' with high synergy, while Gemma3/Cambrian are 'language-prior-reliant' with high text-uniqueness, and this split generalizes across architectures and scales (Section 4.1).

In omni-modal audio-visual fusion analysis, unique visual information dominates over synergistic information even on theoretically fusion-dependent tasks, e.g. VITA-1.5 (7B) shows 1.35 visual-unique vs. 0.22 synergistic information on the AV-Fusion subset, evidencing a persistent sensory synergy bottleneck (Section 2.2, Table 2).

Layer-wise analysis shows synergistic information concentrates in the final network layers (a 'late-stage' profile) and that visual information rises earlier than audio, revealing a visual-first computation pattern (Section 4.2).

PID-guided reweighted fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves MMStar by +2.3 percentage points and POPE by +1.3 percentage points over uniform fine-tuning, shifting the post-tuning synergy share from 67.5% to 73.9% (Section 5).

DeOm4Axr9W.text: Proposition 3.1 (Riemannian MeanFlow Identity) relates the average velocity u(x_t,r,t) to the instantaneous velocity v(x_t,t) via the covariant derivative along the geodesic, u(x_t,r,t) = v(x_t,t) − (t−r)∇_γ̇(t)u(x_t,r,t) (Proposition 3.1).

The RMF training objective decomposes into two terms, a velocity-matching term and a derivative-interaction term, whose gradients are shown empirically to conflict (persistent negative cosine similarity) during training, motivating a multi-task (PCGrad-based) optimization scheme (Proposition 3.2, Figure 2).
On the spherical Earth datasets, RMF/RMF-MT achieves the best or second-best MMD among compared methods across Volcano (0.092), Earthquake (0.035), Flood (0.048), and Fire (0.032) (Table 1).
On torus-valued RNA torsion angle data (7D), RMF-MT achieves 0.07 MMD, outperforming all baselines, and is competitive on Glycine/Proline/PrePro protein subsets (Table 2).

On high-dimensional spheres (dimension 128), RMF reaches 0.026 MMD after only 6 training epochs, versus baselines requiring 400+ epochs to reach comparable quality, demonstrating substantially reduced sampling/training cost for one-step generation (Table 5).

RMF-MT trains at 6.42 iterations/second versus 3.60 iterations/second for the G-LSD baseline (1.8x faster), and classifier-free guidance improves mixture MMD from 0.439 (unconditional) to 0.234 (Table 4, Table 7).

lkrLFAF3u4.text: TPGDiff's architecture separately models three priors: semantic priors are injected in deep layers, structural priors in shallow layers, and degradation priors throughout the diffusion trajectory (Sections 3.2-3.4, Figure 2).
On single-degradation benchmarks, TPGDiff attains PSNR 40.12/SSIM 0.986 on deraining (Rain100L) and PSNR 32.87/SSIM 0.979 on dehazing (RESIDE) (Table 1).
On the multi-task restoration setting spanning 5 degradation types, TPGDiff achieves an average PSNR of 30.60 and SSIM of 0.908, exceeding recent unified restoration methods (Table 2).
Ablation results show that adding all three priors improves PSNR from a 31.63 baseline to 32.63 and SSIM from 0.912 to 0.921 (Table 3).
Ablating the injection position of semantic and structural priors (deep vs. shallow layers) further confirms the hierarchical placement choice is necessary for best performance (Table 4).

tAqHcMkhy7.text: On the LIBERO-LONG benchmark, applying VLA-ATTC's Cognitive Clutch mechanism to PI0.5 raises the average success rate from 90.6% to 94% and reduces the overall failure rate by over 50% (Section 5.1).

Applying VLA-ATTC to PI0 on LIBERO-LONG raises average success rate from 82.8% to 90.6% (+7.8%), with task-level gains such as 'both pots on stove' rising from 40% to 56% and 'mug in microwave and close' rising from 62% to 88% (Section 5.1).
On real-world Agilex Piper arm tasks, VLA-ATTC applied to PI0 improves success rate from 46% to 58.7% (+12.7%), part of an overall 17.3-point boost on real-robot tasks (Section 5.1).

The Relative Action Critic (RAC) model is trained on automatically curated action preference pairs and is used during a test-time-compute deliberation phase gated by an uncertainty-quantification 'clutch' mechanism (Sections 4.1-4.4).
VLA-ATTC maintains a control frequency of 20.8 Hz (vs. 23.3 Hz baseline) and is substantially faster than the RoboMonkey baseline, which runs at 1.5 Hz (Section 5.4).

M0e5XORjAW.text: On the Gaussian mixture benchmark, diffusion resampling with T=3 diffusion steps and K=128 samples achieves the lowest sliced 1-Wasserstein distance (0.80±0.21) among differentiable resampling schemes, beating optimal-transport resampling at multiple regularization levels (ε=0.3/0.6/0.9), multinomial, Gumbel-Softmax, and Soft resampling (Section 4.1, Table 1).

On the linear Gaussian state-space model with N=32 particles, diffusion resampling (T=3, K=8) attains lower loss-function error (2.55±1.89) and filtering KL divergence (4.26±4.49) than competing methods, while multinomial and Gumbel-Softmax resampling produce NaN divergences during parameter learning (Section 4.2, Table 2).

A Wasserstein-distance consistency bound is proved showing the diffusion resampling distribution converges to the true resampling distribution as the number of diffusion steps and samples grow, implying linear sample complexity versus the exponential complexity required by optimal-transport-based resampling (Section 3, Proposition 1 and Corollary 1).

On the prey-predator (Lotka-Volterra) dynamics-learning task, diffusion resampling yields the lowest root-mean-square prediction error and more stable training loss across runs compared to alternative differentiable resamplers (Section 4.3, Figures 3-4).

On the vision-based pendulum task with 32x32 greyscale image observations, diffusion resampling used to jointly learn dynamics and an observation decoder achieves the best SSIM and PSNR among differentiable resampling methods tested (Section 4.4, Figures 5-6).

zeIa4sZCD1.text: On the CALVIN ABC→D benchmark, TapSampling improves average task-completion length without any policy finetuning, raising Diffusion Policy from 2.41 to 2.58, OpenVLA from 3.30 to 3.51, and VPP from 4.39 to 4.46 (Section 4.1, Table 1).
On LIBERO-Long, applying TapSampling at inference time raises the π0.5 generalist policy's success rate from 96.8% to 98.0% without further training (Section 4.1, Table 2).
In real-world robotic manipulation experiments, TapSampling raises average task success rate from 78.3% to 83.3%, a 5.0 percentage-point improvement (Section 4.2, Table 3).

TapSampling's learned-posterior sampling combined with a task-progress-understanding verifier achieves roughly a 12x latency speedup over the RoboMonkey inference-time sampling baseline (Section 4.3, Figure 4).

An ablation using Maximum Mean Discrepancy shows the proposed action-sampling strategy consistently produces lower MMD than naive Gaussian sampling, indicating closer alignment to the target action distribution (Section 4.3, Table 5).

coINrhVRkL.text: FAB combines a Push-Pull gradient-tracking communication scheme with a value-function-based penalty reformulation of the bilevel problem to solve distributed bilevel optimization over time-varying directed communication graphs (Section 2.1, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 3.4 establishes that FAB converges at rate O((ab)^-n K^-2/3) in terms of the hypergradient norm when the upper-level objective is nonconvex and the lower-level objective is strongly convex, using step sizes and penalty parameter scaled as O(K^-1/3) and O(K^1/3) respectively (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).

Theorem 3.6 resolves an open question by proving Push-Pull gradient tracking over time-varying directed graphs achieves an O((ab)^-n K^-1) convergence rate for single-level nonconvex distributed optimization (Section 3, Theorem 3.6).

Proposition 3.5 bounds the average consensus error of the decision, tracking, and auxiliary variables at O((ab)^-n K^-1) under the strongly-connected time-varying directed graph assumption (Section 3, Proposition 3.5, Assumption 3.1).

FAB is empirically validated on distributed hyperparameter tuning, distributed data hyper-cleaning on Fashion-MNIST and BERT/IMDB, and distributed policy evaluation for reinforcement learning, with an ablation over network size, mixing-matrix weights, and model size (Section 4.1-4.3, Figures 1-8).

v8BF1g3u8r.text: PhyB achieves an average normalized score of 91.0 on D4RL offline RL benchmarks, outperforming PMDB (88.2) and RAMBO (68.0) (Section 5, Table 1).
On a stochastic offline liquidation task, PhyB scores 101.6±3.7 versus PMDB's 85.5±2.3 (Section 5.2, Table 2).

Theorem 3 proves that the Q-value under the Hybrid Belief Bellman Evaluation Operator is monotonically non-decreasing in the size k of the dynamics-model subset used and non-increasing in the total ensemble size N, and this predicted monotonicity is confirmed empirically across varying (N,k) configurations (Section 4, Theorem 3; Section 5.2, Table 3).

Theorem 5 shows that iteratively solving the Bregman-regularized policy-improvement subproblem yields metric-agnostic monotonic improvement of the policy objective until convergence, independent of the specific pessimism metric used (Section 4.2, Theorem 5).

Theorem 2 bounds the gap between the estimated PhyB return and the true environment return by a pessimism term that includes an entropy-regularization component scaling as λγ log(k)/(1-γ) (Section 4, Theorem 2).

KQT6pf4Mva.text: JADE jointly optimizes a Planner and seven Executor agentic roles via PPO under a Shared-Parameter Markov Decision Process formulation, achieving a 53.86 average F1 score across all evaluation datasets (Section 3.1, 3.4, Section 4, Table 2).
JADE improves average F1 by 8.29 points over the previous best baseline and by 12.64 points over MAO-ARAG (53.86 vs. 41.22), a decoupled planning-execution approach (Section 4, Table 2).

An ablation shows the Document Selector module's contribution flips from harmful to helpful under joint training, moving its isolated F1 contribution from 41.13 to 58.24 once trained jointly with the rest of the system (Section 4, Table 3).

JADE's 7B-parameter jointly-trained model (58.24 F1) outperforms a system using frozen GPT-4o executors (56.82 F1), indicating that co-adapted training of planner and executors matters more than raw executor model scale (Section 4, Table 4).

A hyperparameter sensitivity analysis over the reward's alpha and beta penalty terms, and an analysis of multi-agent training dynamics, demonstrate co-adaptation where the planner learns to operate within executor capability boundaries while executors align to strategic intent (Section 4, Figures 3-4).

7xO0ADKJu8.text: Variational Speculative Decoding (VSD) reformulates draft-model training as variational inference, maximizing an Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) on the target model's acceptance probability instead of token-level likelihood (Section 3).
VSD trains the draft model with an Expectation-Maximization procedure that uses Monte Carlo sampling of draft paths to perform path-level utility optimization (Section 3).
Adaptive Rejection Weighting reweights sampled draft trajectories during training by importance so paths more likely to be accepted at decoding time receive higher weight (Section 4.2).
Confidence-Aware Regularization conditions the training objective on the draft model's confidence scores to suppress overconfident, low-quality draft proposals (Section 4.3).
VSD achieves up to a 9.58% speedup over EAGLE-3 and 8.80% over ViSpec across language and multimodal LLM benchmarks such as GSM8K and VQA-v2 (Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).

kOMsEkgMuz.text: The Mean Flow Matching Theorem (Theorem 4.3) proves that matching expected average velocities over a finite time interval, rather than instantaneous velocities, is sufficient for strict distributional alignment between student and teacher flow-matching models (Section 4.3).

Mean Flow Distillation (MFD) acts as a temporal low-pass filter that suppresses high-frequency optimization noise in the training signal while preserving global trajectory consistency, in contrast to the instantaneous velocity matching of Theorem 4.1 (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.1).
