On 4D occupancy forecasting, one-step MFD reaches 37.07% IoU and 27.25% mIoU, within about 1.2 points of the 10-step teacher (37.52% IoU) and higher than one-step DMD2 (35.84% IoU) and AYF (32.38% IoU) (Table 1).

On text-to-image generation with SANA-1.6B using 4 inference steps, MFD attains FID(DINOv2) of 33.28 versus 43.68 for AYF, along with the highest Aesthetic Score (6.541) and ImageReward (0.8483) among compared one-step/few-step methods (Table 3).

MFD is trained with LoRA adapters covering about 2.2% of parameters and an auxiliary model that is discarded after training, adding zero inference-time overhead, at a total training cost of roughly 25 GPU-hours and 20GB memory (Section 5.3, Algorithm 1).

auEvgVBpSF.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that thresholding on a calibrated statistic derived from a linear expectation constraint yields a finite-sample marginal FDR guarantee, Pr(err=1 | u ≤ threshold) ≤ α, for a new exchangeable test sample using only calibration data (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 extends this guarantee to two-model routing systems, showing that jointly calibrated thresholds for both models maintain system-level FDR control over routed predictions (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.2).

On CommonsenseQA with LLaMA-3.2-3B at target FDR level α=0.05, LEC achieves power of 0.1959 compared to 0.1191 for COIN-CP, an improvement of roughly 8 percentage points at the same nominal FDR level (Table 1, Section 4.2).

LEC's calibration procedure relies only on exchangeable calibration data (no distributional assumptions beyond exchangeability) to compute the FDR-constrained, retention-maximizing threshold (Section 3.1).

The two-model routing evaluation (Section 4.3) shows a weaker model combined with a stronger one via LEC's joint threshold calibration accepts more correct predictions than either model used alone at the same FDR budget (Section 4.3).

j6gXeiPJ3z.text: For the known-transition setting, Algorithm 1 (HT-FTRL-OM), defined in Section 4.1, is proven in Theorem 4.1 to achieve regret of order poly(H,S,A)·σ(T^(1/α)+log T) in the adversarial regime (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

In the stochastic (self-bounding) regime, Theorem 4.1 shows HT-FTRL-OM attains an instance-dependent regret bound that reduces to order σ^(α/(α-1))ω_Δ(α) log T, i.e., logarithmic in T (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

For the unknown-transition setting, Algorithm 2 (HT-FTRL-UOB), defined in Section 5.1, achieves adversarial-regime regret of order poly(H,S,A)·σ(T^(1/α) + √T log T + (log T)^2) per Theorem 5.1 (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 5.1 further shows HT-FTRL-UOB attains an instance-dependent self-bounding-regime regret bound of order poly(H,S,A)·σ^(α/(α-1))ω_Δ(α)(log T)^2, matching a log-squared-T rate (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.1).

Both algorithms assume losses have bounded α-moments for α∈(1,2] with unbounded variance, and rely on novel skipping loss estimators adapted to occupancy measures to control heavy-tailed feedback (Section 3).

GbYHY1RVUa.text: CE-Graph reframes workflow optimization as minimizing Expected Failure Mass over a structured Failure Signature Space, where each failure signature combines a one-hot structural component (error location) and an embedded semantic component (error message) (Section 2.1).

Theorem 1 (Greedy Reduction Bound) shows that, under Lipschitz continuity assumptions, greedy edits reducing the densest failure mode's mass satisfy M(W_{t+1}) ≤ M(W_t) - δ + ε, guaranteeing monotonic improvement with bounded spillover to non-target failure regions (Theorem 1).
CE-Graph outperforms the MaAS baseline by 4.09 points on MATH (55.91% vs 51.82%), 5.93 points on MBPP (88.10% vs 82.17%), and 1.41 points on HumanEval (94.26% vs 92.85%) (Table 1).

The ablation study shows removing structured operators drops MATH accuracy by 8.56 points, removing the verification step drops it by 6.81 points, and removing Gaussian Mixture Model clustering drops it by 4.66 points, while removing convergence-aware stopping increases optimization cost by over 50% (Table 2).

CE-Graph's iterative refinement combines a Gradient Approximation stage, which uses Gaussian Mixture Model clustering on embedded failure signatures to locate the densest failure mode, with a Propose-and-Verify mechanism in which a Proposer LLM generates candidate graph edits validated on sampled counterexamples by a Verifier (Section 3).

9wnNpCD8E9.text: NaLaFormer-B achieves 85.2% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K, surpassing VRWKV-B by 3.7% while using fewer FLOPs (Section 4.1, Table 1).
NaLaFormer variants achieve a 3.8-7.5% accuracy improvement on ImageNet-1K classification over comparable linear-attention baselines (Section 4.1, Table 1).
NaLaFormer-S achieves 48.0% mIoU with Semantic FPN and 48.5% with UperNet on ADE20K, a 2.7% improvement over PolaFormer (Section 4.3, Table 3).
The method decomposes query and key matrices into separate norm and direction components to restore norm-awareness lost in standard linear attention (Abstract, Section 3).
NaLaFormer reduces peak memory by up to 92.3% relative to softmax attention baselines on token-intensive tasks with 70K+ tokens, such as super-resolution (Section 4, Table 2-3).

nEpwtpRWSD.text: Sentinel-VLA improves RLBench seen-task success rate to 63.5% versus PI0's 57.8%, and unseen-task success rate to 51.3% versus PI0's 42.0% (Table 1).
On real-world manipulation tasks, Sentinel-VLA reaches 60.0% success rate versus PI0's 46.0%, roughly a 30% relative improvement over PI0 as reported in the abstract (Table 1).
Sentinel-VLA on LIBERO-LONG achieves 90.7% success rate versus PI0's 85.2% (Table 1).
The full training corpus spans 44 tasks with over 2.6 million transitions, automatically generated and annotated through the EC-Gen pipeline (Abstract, Section 4.1).
Ablations on real-world tasks show that removing SECL drops performance to 54.0%, and using SECL without the OC-Adapter drops it further to 44.7%, versus 60.0% for the full model (Table 3).
The Status Monitor expert achieves an error detection rate of 97.4% in RLBench and 90.6% in real-world settings, with F1-scores of 0.9024 and 0.8567 respectively (Table 4, Table 5).

tHY0G4PhCR.text: OMAD demonstrates a 2.5x to 5x improvement in sample efficiency across diverse multi-agent tasks, including reducing training steps to reach baseline peak performance by up to 5x on MPE tasks (Abstract, Section 6.2).
OMAD shows a consistent 2.5x-5x speedup in sample efficiency on MAMuJoCo tasks compared to baselines (Section 6.2).
OMAD achieves 68.3% state coverage on the Ant 2x4 task at 250k training steps, a 41% relative improvement over HATD3 (48.4%) and a 24% relative improvement over HASAC (55.0%) (Figure 3).
OMAD is evaluated as establishing state-of-the-art performance across 10 diverse multi-agent scenarios/tasks (Abstract).
Ablations show performance saturates at 8 denoising steps (~6000 return), with an optimal distributional Vmax of 1200 and 100 atom intervals (101 atoms) (Section 6.3, Figure 4, Figure 5).

6XXz4OPAXA.text: Cross-task forgetting varies by up to 156% and generalization performance varies by up to 110% depending solely on which paraphrased training prompt is used, despite near-identical in-task performance (Section 3.2, Figure 1).

Pre-update task loss shows the strongest positive association with post-learning cross-task performance among 10 tested signals, motivating its use as a prompt-selection criterion in SAPO (Section 4.1, Figure 3).
SAPO improves average performance over baselines LoraInc, EWC, O-Lora, and InsCL by ranges of +0.58 to +2.36, +1.23 to +4.93, +0.43 to +1.72, and +0.29 to +1.71 (in AP), respectively (Table 1).
SAPO improves backward transfer (forgetting mitigation) by +0.29 to +1.4 BWT across the four baseline methods (Table 1).
Pairwise correlation analysis across tasks reveals systematic coupling of prompt effects, with correlations often reaching up to 0.6 (Section 3.3, Figure 2).
Gradient angle analysis shows decreasing cosine similarity conflict between tasks as prompt loss decreases, indicating reduced optimization conflict (Section 5.5, Figure 4).

v5dquZIEUt.text: On TCGA-LUAD with UNI features, RNA-FM achieves a PCC of 0.729 (RMSE 0.074) for the top-1000 genes and PCC of 0.865 (RMSE 0.050) for the top-50 genes (Section 4.2, Table 1).
On TCGA-COAD with UNI features, RNA-FM reaches PCC 0.775 for top-1000 genes and PCC 0.943 for top-50 genes, its strongest result among the three TCGA cohorts tested (Section 4.2, Table 1).

In external validation on CPTAC, RNA-FM attains top-100 gene PCCs of 0.480 (LUAD), 0.557 (BRCA), and 0.515 (COAD), demonstrating generalization beyond the TCGA training distribution (Section 4.5, Table 3).
GO-BP pathway gene predictions outperform GO-MF predictions, with spindle checkpoint signaling pathway PCC improving from 0.623 to 0.682 (Section 4.3, Table 2).

The flow-matching framework's predictive uncertainty is calibrated such that 50% and 90% prediction intervals achieve empirical coverage of 0.521 and 0.834 respectively, with a positive variance-error correlation of 0.646 (Appendix F, Table 11).
RNA-FM performs genome-wide imputation across 20,820 genes from whole-slide images (WSIs) on TCGA cohorts of LUAD (536), BRCA (1,130), and COAD (455) samples (Section 4.1).

18C6xMcD96.text: MoSE augments Mixture-of-Experts layers with slimmable experts whose intermediate width can be sliced by multipliers in {0.25,...,1.0} via weight-matrix slicing (Equation 4, Section on architecture), letting a single model trade accuracy for FLOPs at inference (Section 3).

Trained on GPT2-Small (55M), GPT2-Standard (322M), and GPT2-Medium (1B) with E8A2/E8A4/E16A4 routing on OpenWebText for 3B-15B tokens, MoSE with test-time-trained width control (TTT) reaches 20.38 perplexity vs 20.81 for standard MoE at 15B tokens on GPT2-Standard (Table 1).

Router-conditioned width allocation with a learned test-time-trained gamma dominates both uniform-width execution and a fixed-gamma router-conditioned baseline in the accuracy-vs-compute ablation (Figure 10).
Gamma parameters learned via test-time training on OpenWebText transfer zero-shot to LAMBADA, yielding consistently lower perplexity across compute budgets without retraining (Figure 9).
MoSE training dynamics (loss curves) closely track the baseline MoE's training trajectory over 15B tokens, indicating the slimmable-width mechanism does not destabilize optimization (Figure 3).

q5sBPXOuHC.text: The Compression-AliGnEd attack (CAGE) combines Expected Feature Disruption, which concentrates perturbation on visual tokens likely to survive compression under an uncertain deployment budget, with Rank Distortion Alignment, which aligns token selection scores with induced distortions via distribution matching (Section on CAGE method).

At a 192-token compression budget, CAGE reduces robust accuracy relative to the baseline attack from 33.5% to 23.4% on TextVQA, from 55.4% to 47.2% on VQA-v2, and from 40.8% to 36.2% on GQA (Table 2).

CAGE's robust-accuracy reduction persists across five plug-and-play compression mechanisms (VisionZip, VisPruner, DivPrune, FlowCut, PruMerge) and across retention budgets of 16, 32, 64, and 192 tokens (Table 2).

Existing attacks such as VEAttack optimize perturbations over all 576 visual tokens while inference uses only the compressed subset, producing an optimization-inference mismatch that makes standard robustness evaluations of compressed LVLMs overly optimistic (Section on optimization-inference mismatch).

An attention-based detection defense against CAGE achieves 0.94 detection accuracy but remains threshold-dependent, and robustness-aware token selection and stochastic sampling defenses provide only modest robustness gains (Section on defenses).

suQ52Hqr9U.text: TGV-KV consists of three modules operating on cross-modal attention: Text-Vision Budgeting for layer-wise budget allocation (Equation 5, Section 3.3), Text-Weighted Ranking for vision-token importance scoring (Equations 7-8, Section 3.3), and Text-Prioritised Retention, which preserves text KV entries before evicting vision KV entries (Equation 10, Section 3.3).

On VizWiz-VQA with LLaVA-NeXT at a 5% KV-cache retention budget, TGV-KV preserves 99.2% of full-KV-cache accuracy while boosting end-to-end decode throughput by 52.6% (Table 2, Section 4.2; Table 4, Section 4.3).
At the same 5% retention budget, TGV-KV retains 88.0% of full accuracy on DocVQA with Qwen3-VL-8B, 97.4% on TextVQA with LLaVA-NeXT, and 85.7% on ChartQA with Qwen3-VL-8B (Table 2).
At an 8k-token context length and 5% retention, TGV-KV reduces KV-cache memory from 3.91 GB to 0.20 GB (a 95% reduction) and improves per-token latency by 30.4% (Table 4).
Ablations show all three TGV-KV components are necessary, with Text-Prioritised Retention being especially critical for maintaining accuracy under the extreme 5% retention budget (Table 5).

xrXxqLadvS.text: The level-set slope-coverage condition (Definition 4.1) requires that each state level of the latent trajectory be attained at least three times with distinct instantaneous velocities, which guarantees the learned latent space is locally affine to the true physical state and enables exact recovery of the ODE parameters.
For strictly underdamped second-order ODEs, a single video clip of length at least twice the oscillation period suffices to identify the physical parameters (Theorem 4.3).

In critically damped, overdamped, and undamped regimes, a single trajectory lacks sufficient slope diversity to satisfy the coverage condition, so parameters are not identifiable from one clip alone (Theorem 4.5).

Three trajectories with diverse velocities at each shared state level can substitute for temporal coverage within a single clip, restoring identifiability of the shared physics parameters across regimes (Theorem 4.6).

On a real wheel-mounted phone pendulum, the encoder-only method recovers a damping parameter gamma0 = 8.998 +/- 0.009 compared to the physics-based estimate of 8.26, and a variance-floor regularizer outperforms a KL-divergence regularizer, particularly in non-oscillatory regimes (Experimental Validation section).

TcICHju9Mo.text: DeFacto trains on three paradigms constructed from the same counterfactual dataset: positive supervision using the original image and correct bounding boxes, counterfactual abstention where evidence regions are masked and the model must answer 'unknown,' and random-masking of irrelevant regions to prevent shortcut learning from mask patterns (Section 3.2).

Training uses GRPO reinforcement learning with three reward terms: an answer-correctness reward, a format-consistency reward for valid bounding-box outputs, and a region-selection coherence reward that promotes overlap with evidence regions and penalizes overlap with irrelevant ones (Section on training/reward design).

The DeFacto-100K dataset comprises about 100,000 images built via a language-guided pipeline combining Qwen2.5-VL descriptor extraction, DINO-X open-vocabulary detection, OCR, and region proposal networks (Section 3.2).
On general VQA benchmarks, DeFacto improves accuracy over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline from 57.3% to 79.7% on VQAv2, from 54.5% to 68.0% on OK-VQA, and from 41.3% to 70.1% on GQA (Table 1).
On document/text-centric benchmarks, DeFacto improves over baseline from 84.4% to 85.8% on DocVQA and from 77.8% to 82.4% on ChartQA (Table 2).

YYm8Cwn1J3.text: RSAgent achieves 66.5% gIoU on the ReasonSeg test set, a 9-point improvement over the Seg-Zero baseline's 57.5% (Table 2).
RSAgent reaches 81.5% cIoU on RefCOCOg test, surpassing RICE (80.4%) and Seg-Zero (72.6%) (Table 1).
Multi-turn tool invocation over a frozen SAM2 visual toolbox lets the agent interact across multiple rounds rather than a single pass, as formalized in the agent framework (Section 3.2).

Training combines cold-start supervised fine-tuning on 5K synthetic trajectories filtered to ≥0.9 IoU with agentic reinforcement learning using a fine-grained reward combining final-answer, process, and format components (Section 3.3-3.4).
Ablations show the base model alone scores only 30.1% gIoU on ReasonSeg and 61.7% cIoU on RefCOCOg, cold-start SFT alone reaches 55.4%/73.9%, and the full pipeline reaches 57.9%/81.8% (Table 3).
An ablation over maximum tool turns shows training performance plateaus at 8 turns, while most successful inference predictions use 6 or fewer turns (Figure 5).

iJmqu7GMRq.text: The memorization-based framework accelerates Anchors explanation generation by up to 271% on tabular Income (Adult) data with Random Forest at N=2000 pre-training inputs (Section 4.3).

The method achieves up to 221% speedup on text sentiment analysis (RT-Polarity) with Random Forest and up to 181% speedup on ImageNet image classification with YOLOv8, both relative to standard Anchors (Section 4.3).
Speedups arise from reduced sampling: 64% fewer samples for tabular data, 57% fewer for text, and 47% fewer for images at maximum pre-training size N (Section 4.3).

Horizontal transformation adapts pre-trained rules by replacing features from similar pre-training inputs, while vertical transformation iteratively adds predicates to refine low-precision, high-coverage rules until a precision threshold τ is met (Algorithm 2, Section 3.2).

An offline pre-training phase (Algorithm 1) uses K-means clustering to select N representative centroids and generates Anchors rules at a lower precision threshold (τ=0.8) before online refinement at τ=0.95 (Section 3.2).
Precision of the generated explanations matches standard Anchors, with only a slight coverage decline that is mitigated by increasing the number of pre-training inputs N (Section 4.3.2).

P6fWeIVbwb.text: AIGVE-60K contains 58,500 videos generated by 30 text-to-video models from 3,050 prompts spanning 20 fine-grained task dimensions, annotated with 120K mean-opinion scores and 60K question-answering pairs (Section 3.1).
The benchmark evaluates videos along three independent aspects: perceptual quality, text-video correspondence, and task-specific accuracy (Section 3.2, Table 2).
The dataset is split into 49,500 training and 9,000 test videos, and evaluation covers 23 large multimodal models and 24 VQA metrics for the video-to-text interpretation task (Section 3.1, Table 2).
The fine-tuned LOVE model achieves SRCC 0.793/PLCC 0.826 on perceptual quality and SRCC 0.747/PLCC 0.766 on text-video correspondence, plus 78.69% QA accuracy (Table 2).
LOVE demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to other video-quality benchmarks beyond AIGVE-60K (Table 4).
The 20-task taxonomy includes categories such as Object, Color, Counting, Texture, Position, HOI, Face, Emotion, OCR, and Complex multi-attribute tasks (Appendix C, Table 6).

OfzLydmMHe.text: On the CMU Panoptic dataset, DisPOSE achieves 68.59 AP25 and 21.20mm MPJPE, an 8% MPJPE improvement over the prior self-supervised method DSP's 23.10mm (Table 1).
On the newly proposed MM-OR Pose surgical operating-room benchmark with heavy occlusion, DisPOSE achieves 92.01 AP150 and 56.91mm MPJPE (Table 2).
DisPOSE retains 84.05 AP50 when trained with only 9.8% of the pseudo-labeled training data, supporting the claim of retaining ~99% of full-data performance at 10% label usage (Table 8).

On novel camera configurations not seen during training, DisPOSE reaches roughly 75% pose mAP versus a 59% mAP baseline, with per-configuration results of 91.97% (CMU1, 7 cameras), 83.01% (CMU2, 7 cameras), and 75.57% (CMU3, 4 cameras) (Table 4).
On the Shelf and Campus datasets, DisPOSE achieves average PCP of 97.1% and 95.6% respectively (Table 3).
An ablation on the root-regression stage shows self-supervised mAP of 81.49% and mean distance error of 35.40mm, improving over SelfPose3D's 68.21% mAP and 54.82mm error (Table 5).

gU3fCranJf.text: The paper identifies value misassignment as a failure mode in prior cross-domain offline RL methods such as DVDF, which pre-trains an advantage function A(s,a) directly on the source dataset in a way that cannot distinguish between different source dynamics (Section 4.2).

The V2A framework combines temporally-consistent modality representation learning via EM optimization (Section 5.1) with modality-aware advantage learning that incorporates these representations into Q/V functions (Section 5.2).

Benchmarks use Halfcheetah, Hopper, Walker2d, and Ant from OpenAI Gym/D4RL, with only 10% target-domain data and four source-dynamics shift variants per task (kinematic/morphology at two shift levels) (Section 6.1).
V2A instantiated with IGDF improves total score by 21.4% (1286.7 to 1562.5) and with OTDF by 22.2% (1319.5 to 1612.9), compared to only 6.8% and 5.5% improvements for the DVDF baseline (Table 2).

t-SNE visualization of the learned modality representations shows trajectories from identical source dynamics clustering together, validating the representation learning component (Figure 2a, Section 6.2).
Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis finds optimal performance at trade-off coefficient λ=0.6 and data selection ratio ξ between 0.5 and 0.75 (Section 6.3).

34E2z2oVhd.text: Anchor-Centric Adaptation (ACA) improves mean success rate from 31.7% (baseline pi_0.5) to 72.5% at a budget of N=100 demonstrations (Table with region-level success metrics, Section 5 Experiments).
Under a fixed budget of N=50, ACA raises success from 13.8% to 46.3%, and under N=150 from 52.9% to 83.8%, showing consistent gains across budgets (Section 5, Experimental Results).

The theoretical Coverage-Density Trade-off predicts an optimal anchor count K* scaling as (L^2 N / sigma^2)^(d/(d+2)), implying fully diverse sampling (K=N) leaves constant estimation noise dominating policy error (Section on theoretical framework / Coverage-Density Trade-off).

Ablations show an inverted-U trend in anchor quantity: performance degrades once anchors exceed roughly 6-8 despite broader coverage, and combining error-driven boundary mining (64.2%) with residual LoRA updates (58.8%) yields the full ACA result of 72.5% (Ablation Studies section).

On boundary-region metric S@3 (90% coverage), the baseline collapses to near-zero success while ACA maintains about 65% success, evaluated across Block Stacking, Cup Placement, Table Cleaning, and Toy Tidying tasks on a 7-DoF Franka Panda (Section 5, Region-Level Success Metrics).

bRS5iwbqlC.text: ZO Fine-tuner outperforms the strongest zeroth-order baseline (lower training loss) in 82.1% of 28 model-task combinations spanning LLaMA-3.2-1B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and OPT-30B across COPA, SST-2, CB, SQuAD, WSC, BoolQ, and DROP (Experiments section, main results table).
ZO Fine-tuner achieves an average 2.5% accuracy improvement over MeZO while baselines compared include MeZO, MeZO-Adam, MeZO-AdamU, HIZOO, and LOZO (Experiments section, comparison to baselines).

Theorem 1 shows that when the Hessian exhibits block-diagonal structure (empirically observed in LLMs), learning per-parameter-block variance via a lightweight PertNN yields a tighter convergence bound than standard MeZO (Theorem 1).

For OPT-30B the auxiliary PertNN networks add under 2MB of memory overhead under FP16 versus the 60GB model itself, and total fine-tuning memory is about 61-62GB versus 312GB for Adam (Section on memory efficiency).

A single ZO Fine-tuner trained once on COPA transfers across diverse downstream tasks and model derivatives with only about 2.4x the one-time training cost of standard first-order fine-tuning, while perturbation generation adds only 3.4% runtime overhead on LLaMA-1B (Section on training cost and generalization).

XBhLiyFVDx.text: CoCoEdit combines an MLLM-based reward (Qwen2.5-VL-32B) with a pixel-level similarity reward (normalized PSNR/SSIM in non-edited regions) as r = op(lambda_mllm * r_mllm + lambda_sim * r_sim) (Method section, Reward Functions).

On GEdit-Bench-EN, adding CoCoEdit to FLUX.1 Kontext raises PSNR from 24.168 to 25.331 (+1.16 dB) and SSIM from 0.825 to 0.874 (+0.049), while overall editing score rises from 6.286 to 6.939 (Table of quantitative results, GEdit-Bench-EN).

On Qwen-Image-Edit, CoCoEdit improves PSNR by +2.8 dB (19.488 to 22.283) and SSIM by +0.112 (0.662 to 0.774), with overall score rising from 7.560 to 7.754 (Table of quantitative results, GEdit-Bench-EN).

Compared against RL baselines Edit-R1 and MotionNFT, which prioritize editing quality at the expense of consistency, FLUX.1 Kontext + Edit-R1 shows a -5.15 dB PSNR degradation while CoCoEdit maintains competitive editing scores with substantially better content preservation (Comparison with RL Baselines section).

The two asymmetric region-based regularizers, L_ner+ (penalizing deviation beyond threshold tau+ in non-edit regions of positive samples) and L_er- (penalizing insufficient change in under-edited negative samples), are shown via ablation to prevent the overly conservative zero-edit collapse seen under naive equal reward weighting (lambda_mllm = lambda_sim = 0.5) (Ablation study section).

CoCoEdit-40K was curated from about 500K raw samples down to the top 8% via a three-stage filtering pipeline using Qwen2.5-VL and SAM 2 for instruction clarity, mask accuracy, and target prominence (Dataset Construction section).

mlT8I4ri30.text: SSA attributes the paradox that sparse-attention-trained models exhibit lower attention sparsity than full-attention models to 'gradient update deficiency,' where low-ranked key-value pairs excluded during sparse training receive neither forward contribution nor backward gradients (Motivation/analysis section).

SSA's dual-stream training alternates between full and sparse attention with 50% probability each and applies a bidirectional alignment loss (sparsity loss plus commitment loss) enforced at every layer to align full- and sparse-attention outputs (Method section).
Under full-attention inference, SSA matches the FullAttn baseline WikiText perplexity of 15.19 and surpasses it on commonsense reasoning average accuracy (60.22% vs. 59.48%) (Main results table).
Under sparse-attention inference, SSA achieves a perplexity of 15.88, outperforming MoBA's 16.69 (Main results table, sparse inference comparison).

On Needle-in-a-Haystack at 16k context length, SSA achieves 58.8% accuracy while the FullAttn baseline drops to 0%, and SSA maintains stable perplexity through 32k tokens where baselines explode (Long-context extrapolation results section).

Ablations show that bidirectional (rather than unidirectional) alignment is essential for performance, a 256-token receptive field is optimal, and an equal 50/50 full-attention/sparse-attention training mix outperforms other mixing ratios (Ablation studies section).

HJ0JFzdwUo.text: Code2Video achieves approximately 40% improvement over direct code generation on the TeachQuiz metric, aggregated across backbone models on the MMMC benchmark (Results section, TeachQuiz comparison).

With Claude Opus 4.1 as the backbone, Code2Video scores 87.9/100 on Aesthetics (+50.1 over direct code generation) and 86.0/100 on TeachQuiz (+46.0 over direct code generation) (Results table, per-model breakdown).

Pixel-based diffusion baselines (Veo3, OpenSora) score near 0 on logic flow and layout metrics, while direct code generation baselines score 32.7-37.8 on aesthetics and 36.5-40.0 on TeachQuiz, both well below the full Code2Video pipeline's 57.4-87.9 aesthetics and 44.0-86.0 TeachQuiz range (Results section, comparative table).

The MMMC benchmark comprises 456 educational videos (117 full-length plus 339 segmented clips) sourced from 3Blue1Brown across 13 disciplines, used to evaluate Aesthetics, Efficiency, and the novel TeachQuiz unlearning-relearning metric (Section on MMMC Benchmark).

Ablation shows removing the Planner agent causes roughly a 41-point drop in performance, confirming that storyboard/temporal structuring is foundational to the pipeline, on top of contributions from external asset retrieval, visual anchor prompting, and iterative Critic feedback (Ablation Studies section).

A human study with 8-10 participants per group across five conditions shows strong correlation (r=0.971) between automated and human scores, with Code2Video rated about 1.8 in preference ranking versus 1.2 for professional human-crafted tutorials and 5.0 for pixel-diffusion baselines (Human Study Validation section).

jk7P5ppKxD.text: FSpecGNN generalizes spectral GNNs from univariate eigenvalue filtering to bivariate eigenvalue-pair filtering by lifting node signals to the node-pair domain, with classical spectral GNNs recovered as a diagonal special case (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).

FSpecGNN is proven to universally approximate node-pair signals, a strictly stronger property than the universal approximation of node signals achieved by classical spectral GNNs, which is shown to be particularly beneficial for heterophilic graph learning (Section 3.3, Section 4.1).

On heterophilic node classification, FSpecGNN(ChebII) achieves 57.05±2.20% accuracy on Texas versus 36.76±6.76% for ChebNet, and 37.70±0.63% on Squirrel versus 22.58±2.56% for ChebNet, with consistent gains across all 8 heterophilic benchmarks (Table 1).

FSpecGNN avoids explicit node-pair-level computation via low-rank approximations that reduce complex convolutions to polynomial spectral filters, yielding roughly 5x lower runtime than spatial second-order baselines such as Local 2-GNN (Section 3.4, Table 5).

Ablation results show removing the off-diagonal components causes a 4.3 to 15.6 percentage point performance drop, and removing the in-filter causes a 5.8 to 9.7 percentage point drop, confirming the necessity of the node-pair-domain design (Table 4, Section 5.3).

0RLF7Sj2Fg.text: LIMSSR reformulates Action Quality Assessment under training-time incomplete multimodal observations as a conditional sequence-to-score reasoning task, using an LLM for prompt-guided context-aware imputation of missing modalities instead of explicit reconstruction supervision (Section 3, subsection Prompt-Guided Modality Imputation).

A Mask-Aware Dual-Path Aggregation mechanism is introduced to reduce hallucinated imputations and calibrate uncertainty when fusing LLM-inferred and observed modality representations (Section 3, subsection Mask-Aware Dual-Path Aggregation).

On the FS1000 dataset under incomplete modality conditions, LIMSSR improves average Spearman correlation by 0.9% and reduces mean squared error by 8.4% relative to the prior state of the art (Table 1).

On the Fis-V dataset, LIMSSR improves average correlation by 1.2% and reduces MSE by 11.3%, and on Rhythmic Gymnastics it improves correlation by 1.9% and reduces error by 7.6%, relative to state-of-the-art baselines (Table 1).

An ablation study isolates the contributions of prompt-guided imputation and Mask-Aware Dual-Path Aggregation to overall performance under incomplete-modality training (Table 3, Ablation Study subsection).

pLvye0zHUC.text: JitRL is a training-free method that maintains a dynamic non-parametric memory of past experiences, retrieves relevant trajectories to estimate action advantages at test time, and uses these estimates to directly modulate the LLM's output logits without gradient updates (Section 4).
The paper theoretically proves that this additive logit-modulation update rule is the exact closed-form solution to the KL-constrained policy optimization objective (Section 4).
On WebArena-Lite, JitRL achieves a 60.00% success rate versus 46.06% for WebRL, a fine-tuning-based method, despite JitRL requiring no gradient updates (Table 2).
JitRL reduces monetary training cost by over 30x compared to WebRL (approximately $290 versus approximately $9,900), while outperforming it on task success rate (Table 9, Section 5).

On Jericho text-based games, JitRL substantially outperforms GRPO, e.g. on Zork1 (25.9 average / 30 final vs. GRPO's 13.6/11) and Zork3 (53.0 average / 69 final vs. GRPO's 16.2/10) (Table 3, Figure 3).

EEgK2cD7gX.text: SAFAG proposes a symmetry annotation-free learning strategy that reframes symmetry prediction as a probability distribution problem learned via self-supervision, avoiding the need for manually labeled symmetry annotations for actionable parts (Section 3.5).
SAFAG uses a two-stage quaternion regression strategy for pose estimation, progressing from an initial candidate proposal stage to a refined final prediction stage (Section 3.4).
SAFAG is evaluated for generalizable, actionable parts pose estimation across the SAPIEN, YCB, and ModelNet40 datasets, spanning multiple object categories (Section 4).
SAFAG's performance is compared against prior pose-estimation and part-detection baselines in dedicated results tables covering per-category and cross-category generalization (Table 4, Table 5).
Additional robustness and generalization comparisons, including cross-category transfer, are reported in supplementary result tables beyond the main text (Table 7, Table 8, Table 9, Table 10).

T4JzJ0V69W.text: PULSE converts Doppler signatures into confidence-aware motion prompts and injects them into spatial-magnitude reasoning through constrained conditional-attention interactions, screening spurious Doppler cues before they influence prediction (Section 3, subsection Controlled Prompting via Conditional Attention).

On the single-person HuPR dataset, PULSE reduces error to 60.57 MPJPE / 9.78 MPJVE (single-frame) and 58.64 MPJPE / 8.16 MPJVE (multi-frame), compared to 65.37 MPJPE / 14.70 MPJVE for the HuPRModel baseline (Table 1).

On the multi-person XRF55 benchmark, PULSE achieves 70.34 MPJPE / 15.33 MPJVE (single-frame) and 68.99 MPJPE / 14.05 MPJVE (multi-frame), versus 75.11 MPJPE / 18.16 MPJVE for the MvDoppler baseline (Table 2).
In cross-dataset generalization from HuPR to mmRadPose, PULSE attains 70.05 MPJPE / 14.36 MPJVE versus 77.09 MPJPE / 17.63 MPJVE for MvDoppler (Section 4, Experimental Setup subsection).
PULSE functions as a plug-in module that improves pose accuracy and temporal stability when added to existing backbones such as mmDiff and milliMamba (Table 3).

cUPGCuaNWZ.text: A single hypernetwork H_phi generates LoRA weights θ_s = H_φ(c, s) conditioned on CLIP text embeddings c and optimization step s, replacing the need to train a separate LoRA module per concept (Section 4.2).
On object erasure with Stable Diffusion v1.4, UnHype attains a harmonic-mean score H_o of 93.85 across three object classes, versus 91.68 for MACE and 86.96 for ESD-u (Table 1).

On nudity erasure with Stable Diffusion v1.4, UnHype yields only 18 total NudeNet detections compared to 111 for MACE, while requiring about 3 hours of training versus 24+ hours for SAeUron (Table 2).
On the Flux model evaluated on the I2P benchmark, UnHype produces 38 NudeNet detections, substantially fewer than EraseAnything (199) and Meta-Unlearning (521) (Table 3).
With an enhanced text encoder, UnHype reaches H_o of 91.74 on a 100-celebrity erasure task, exceeding TRCE's 89.85 (Table 4).
UnHype generalizes to unseen synonyms of erased concepts (e.g., suppressing 'eagle' and 'owl' after erasing a related bird concept), a case where baseline methods fail (Figure 4).

wbXPNPw5jW.text: The single-configuration scaling law proves the generalization gap decays as Δ ≤ O(1/√k) plus an irreducible alignment-discrepancy floor ε_bound, as distilled set size k grows (Theorem 4.2).

The coverage law shows the distilled sample size required for cross-configuration generalization scales as k = Θ(H_cov(A,r)), growing with the covering-number complexity of the configuration space (Theorems 5.1–5.2, Corollary 5.3).

A configuration-dynamics-error analysis proves gradient matching, distribution matching, and trajectory matching are interchangeable surrogates that all minimize the same alignment discrepancy Δ_a, with contraction relations B_TM = O(B_GM) and B_GM = O(B_DM) (Section 6, Lemma 6.1).

On MNIST, single-configuration fits of the 1/√k scaling law achieve R² between 0.90 and 0.99 for DC/DSA methods, while MTT shows a steeper slope (β1 ≈ -0.33) with higher variance (Section 6 experiments).

On CIFAR-100, cross-configuration linear fits of the coverage law give slopes β1 in roughly 0.14–0.23 with R² of 0.63–0.74, lower than on simpler datasets due to intra-class variability (Section 6 experiments).
The Lipschitz-transfer assumption underlying the coverage law is empirically verified across SGD learning rates in [10⁻³, 10⁻¹] and Adam momentum β in [0.8, 0.999] (Assumption 5.1).

G9KydTWzZL.text: Discrete ASBS (DASBS) extends adjoint matching and the adjoint Schrödinger bridge sampler from continuous state spaces to discrete state spaces by exploiting an additive noise structure on a cyclic group Z^D_N (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 establishes an equivalence between the discrete Schrödinger bridge problem and a stochastic optimal control problem with terminal cost, mirroring the continuous-domain theory.
Theorem 5.2 proves convergence of DASBS via iterative proportional fitting, with fixed points solving the forward and backward bridge problems.

On the Ising model (L=24), DASBS trains in 3.75K steps (0.5 hours) versus 30K steps (8.4 hours, an 8x slowdown) for LEAPS, while achieving a competitive energy Wasserstein-2 distance of 8.6 at high inverse temperature β (Table 2).
On the Potts model (L=16, N=4), DASBS attains an energy Wasserstein-2 of 5.3 at high β versus 8.2 for LEAPS, with best metrics across all temperature regimes (Table 3).

Proposition 5.1 shows that under a memoryless noise assumption (α=0), DASBS reduces to a weighted denoising cross-entropy objective, while Figure 2 shows non-memoryless schedules (α>0) outperform memoryless ones with a U-shaped error curve over the exploration-exploitation tradeoff.

bLbBxDTjbq.text: A 30B solver trained on 11,000 Agentic-Proposer-synthesized trajectories achieves 91.6% accuracy on AIME25, described as rivaling frontier-scale proprietary models and surpassing GPT-4.5-Opus and Grok-4.1-Fast (Table 2, Section 4.2).

With a fixed 10,000-trajectory budget, a 4B downstream solver trained on Agentic Proposing data improves over a zero-shot baseline by 4.5 points on AIME25 (51.2% vs 46.7%) and 5.5 points on HMMT (36.5% vs 31.0%), for an overall gain of 4.1 points (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On cross-domain reasoning benchmarks, Agentic Proposing training yields gains of 7.3 points on SuperGPQA, 6.3 points on GPQA, and 4.4 points on OlympicArena (Table 3, Section 4.3).

Ablations show tool-use and internal reflection each contribute roughly 2 points independently, combining for a 6.8-point improvement over a one-shot baseline in the agentic pipeline (Table 5, Section 5).
Replacing standard trajectory-level RL with MGPO's stage-level advantage estimation yields a 6.5-point gain (Table 6, Section 5).
A trained 4B proposer outperforms raw GPT-5.2 by 1.9 points despite a roughly 60x parameter disadvantage, illustrating that structured guidance outweighs raw model capacity (Table 4, Section 5).

15SdFmonYz.text: The data-free entropy coding method (EntQuant) compresses a 70B-parameter model in under 30 minutes using GPU-accelerated ANS entropy coding combined with Float8/Int8 quantization, without calibration data or recovery training (Section 3.4, Figure 5).

At 3-bit compression, EntQuant achieves about 7.5 perplexity on LLaMA-2 7B (C4), outperforming HQQ, while at 2.1-bit effective compression it achieves about 9.9 perplexity versus catastrophic collapse (perplexity >1000) for HQQ at 2-bit (Table 2).

Despite being data-free, EntQuant is competitive with data-dependent, calibration-based methods: at 3-bit it reaches 5.74 C4 perplexity versus 5.85 for GPTQ and 5.67 for QuIP#, and at 2.1-bit it reaches 6.47 versus 6.48 for EfficientQAT and 8.52 for OmniQuant (Table 3).

At 2-bit precision, EntQuant represents 34.61 unique values per weight on average, versus only 4 unique values for fixed uniform 2-bit quantization, demonstrating greater representational expressivity (Table 1).
Inference with EntQuant's on-the-fly ANS decoding is only 1.5-2x slower than a BFloat16 baseline, matching NF4 inference speed while HQQ lags behind (Section 3.4).

EntQuant retains functional performance on instruction-tuned models across GSM8K CoT, IFEval, GPQA, and MMLU, evaluated across 16 models spanning LLaMA-1/2, LLaMA-3.1/3.3, Qwen3, OLMo, and Mistral Large (Section 3, benchmark coverage).

uWbzIUPzVH.text: SLAP reformulates temporal interpolation of sparse video frames as a variational mechanics problem, modeling the latent video trajectory as the path minimizing a discrete Semantic Action functional composed of a kinetic (smoothness) term and a potential term from a learned network P_theta aligned to the text query (Section 3, Semantic Action Functional).

On a novel 'Tunnel Test' benchmark for object persistence under occlusion, SLAP achieves 83.9% accuracy versus 71.4% for Stable Video Diffusion, with semantic drift of 0.14 versus 0.28 for the baseline (Table 2).

Under extreme frame sparsity (10% of frames) on MSR-VTT QA, SLAP maintains 41.8% accuracy compared to 34.7% for Video-LLaMA 3, showing only a 3.4% accuracy drop versus 8-10% drops for competing methods (Table 3).
SLAP achieves a 177x inference speedup over diffusion-based interpolation (0.08s vs. 14.20s latency) while consuming 0.8GB versus 22.5GB of VRAM (Table 5).

Ablations show removing the kinetic energy term (mu=0) drops accuracy to 38.5% and removing the potential energy term (lambda=0) drops it to 40.1%, versus 41.8% for the full model, confirming both Lagrangian terms are necessary (Table 4).

Theorem 3.7 establishes a stability bound showing trajectory error is bounded by (T^2/mu)*epsilon, where epsilon bounds the potential gradient error, and hyperparameter analysis finds an optimal coupling constant lambda=0.5 balancing kinetic and potential terms (Theorem 3.7, Table 7).

3NRpRBTGtY.text: MetaSG-SAEA employs a bi-level architecture in which a meta-policy selects a target constraint-violation region via a Max-Min Constraint-Calibrated Inequality (MM-CCI), while a surrogate-assisted evolutionary algorithm performs sample-efficient search within a tight evaluation budget (Section 3.1).

The meta-policy state representation is built from attention-based encoding of normalized objectives paired with MM-CCI levels plus the remaining budget ratio, and is trained as an MDP with 10 discrete actions selecting MM-CCI level intervals using off-policy Double DQN (Section 3.4, Equation 9).

On zero-shot transfer across 23 test problems from the MW (14 problems) and DAS-CMOP (9 problems) suites, MetaSG-SAEA achieves statistically significantly better IGD than baselines on 21 of 23 problems (Wilcoxon test, p<0.05) (Table 1).
MetaSG-SAEA outperforms EIC-MSSAEA with IGD of 1.415e-1 vs. 3.005e-1 on problem MW2 and 1.893e-1 vs. 2.992e-1 on DAS-CMOP1 (Table 1).

Ablations removing the diffusion-model-based population initialization, or removing either of the two action-type components (a^(1) or a^(2)) from the meta-policy, each increase IGD and degrade performance on the MW problems (Figure 8, Section D.2).

The authors report that MetaSG-SAEA fails to outperform baselines on DAS-CMOP4/5/6 due to highly similar constraint structures causing boundary-induced stagnation of the MM-CCI mechanism (Section D.4).

l3PTeygTS0.text: TaRO combines Constructive Reasoning Exploration (CRE), which builds reasoning traces from dense video captions with explicit timestamps via an Advantage-Weighted Behavioral Cloning loss, with a Temporal-Sensitivity Reward that measures confidence drops when frames near ground-truth boundaries are shuffled (Section 3.3, Section 3.4, Equations 2 and 5-7).

On zero-shot R1@0.5 with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, TaRO outperforms Time-R1 by +4.0 points on Charades-STA (64.8% vs. 60.8%), +3.2 points on QVHighlights (69.4% vs. 66.2%), and +8.4 points on TVGBench (37.8% vs. 29.4%) (Table 1).
With only 10% of ActivityNet training data, TaRO reaches R1@0.5 of 54.2% versus 53.4% for Time-R1, demonstrating superior data efficiency (Table 2).

Ablations show that adding the temporal-sensitivity reward alone raises R1@0.5 from a 61.1% baseline to 63.1%, while the full TaRO combining CRE, temporal reward, and progressive curriculum reaches 64.8% (Table 4).

A perturbation-design ablation shows that shuffling frames specifically around the ground-truth boundary ('Shuffle GT Boundary') yields R1@0.3 of 79.7%, outperforming global shuffling (78.1%) and random cropping (78.6%) as the reward signal (Table 7).

Analysis of Time-R1 baseline outputs found only 8.3% of generated reasoning chains contained explicit timestamps, whereas after TaRO training 100% of reasoning chains contained explicit timestamps (Section 4, qualitative analysis).

RtesAw5Cka.text: The HOI-Edit benchmark contains 705 samples across three progressive cognitive tiers: L1 Foundational (357 samples, basic interaction transformation), L2 Spatial Understanding (202 samples), and L3 Causal Reasoning (146 samples) (Section 3).

The HOI-Eval metric uses a three-step 'Thinking with Pair-wise Regions' protocol -- SAM 2-based entity localization (93.7% success at IoU>0.5), identity verification, and context-aware interaction Q&A -- with an I+Q&A score that zeroes the interaction score when a context-aware question is answered incorrectly (Section 3.3).

SCPE applied to Wan 2.2 I2V improves the L1 interaction score from 0.6908 (baseline) to 0.8423, and improves L3 I+Q&A from 0.5343 to 0.6528, surpassing the commercial model Nano Banana's 0.7271 (L1) and 0.5782 (L3) (Table 1).

An ablation removing the Playbook component from SCPE reduces the interaction score from 0.8199 (full SCPE) to 0.7625, versus 0.6804 for the Wan 2.2 baseline, indicating cross-sample experience transfer via the Playbook is critical (Table 3).

HOI-Eval's interaction sub-score correlates with human judgment at Pearson r=0.60 (p=.002), compared to near-zero or negative correlations for traditional metrics like CLIP and DINO similarity (Table 2).

Applying SCPE to the faster TurboDiffusion backbone reduces per-sample inference time to 1.4 minutes (versus 20.0 minutes for ChronoEdit and 30.0 minutes for Wan 2.2 I2V + SCPE) while still achieving state-of-the-art interaction performance (Table 4).

Q3M37WtXsW.text: APEIRIA distills neuro-symbolic program reasoning into natural-language chain-of-thought within a 3D MLLM via a three-stage curriculum: perception alignment on ~193K instruction pairs, CoT supervised fine-tuning on 144K verified CoT examples derived from symbolic programs on ScanNet/MMScan and Sr3D, and CoT reinforcement learning via GRPO with a Soft Grounding Reward (Section 3.2, Equations 1-2).

On ScanRefer, APEIRIA achieves Acc@0.25 of 58.4% (60.5% in its modular variant), surpassing the neuro-symbolic method NS3D (22.4%) and matching or exceeding 3D MLLM baselines Chat-Scene (55.5%) and Inst3D-LMM (57.8%) (Table 1).
In zero-shot transfer to Nr3D after training only on Sr3D, APEIRIA reaches 36.5% accuracy, a 2.6 point improvement over the supervised NS3D baseline trained directly on Nr3D (33.9%) (Table 2).

Ablations show removing Stage 2 (CoT-SFT) causes the largest degradation, -10.2% on ScanRefer Acc@0.25 and -22.5% on Multi3DRefer F1@0.25, while removing Stage 3 (CoT-RL) causes -6.9% and -3.9% respectively (Table 4).
RL training benefits scale with query complexity: on short queries (<=4 reasoning steps) CoT-RL causes a 1.8% degradation, while on long queries (>=6 steps) it yields a 2.7% improvement (Table 5).

A modularity analysis shows swapping in an oracle (ground-truth) perception module improves ScanRefer Acc@0.25 by +2.9 points and Multi3DRefer F1@0.25 by +2.1 points over the default self-perception module, indicating perception accuracy is the primary bottleneck rather than the planning/reasoning component (Table 6).

zGTe0EwB8q.text: IRIS trains on only 5.7k SFT samples from RLHF-V (used both for warm-up and iterative preference rounds), giving roughly a 40x reduction in curation cost versus RLAIF-V (Section 4, Dataset & Efficiency).

On LLaVA-1.5-7B, IRIS-R2 reduces AMBER CHAIR from 8.8 to 2.4 and Object HalBench CHAIRs from 54.7 to 8.66 and CHAIRi from 26.5 to 4.56 versus the base model (Table with Experimental Results, Section 5).

Preference pairs are constructed from continuous implicit rewards computed via Rectified Visual Guidance (RVG), which penalizes responses scoring higher under text-only context than image-conditioned context, without any external reward model or human feedback (Section 3, Method).

The training objective combines Conditional Textual Preference, Conditional Visual Preference, and Anchored Regularization losses, with ablations showing the Conditional Visual Preference term drives most of the hallucination reduction (Ablation Studies, Section 5).

On-policy self-generation of candidate responses substantially outperforms using static human-annotated preference pairs, and RVG scoring outperforms reward signals based on image-only or text-only likelihoods (Ablation Studies, Section 5).

Each full iteration of IRIS training completes in about 2.5 hours on 8 H20 GPUs, with the rectification strength gamma optimal at 0.7 and visual preference weight lambda optimal at 1.0 (Hyperparameter Sensitivity, Section 5).

RKqL4GYXz3.text: DPsurv is evaluated via 5-fold cross-validation on five TCGA cancer cohorts (BRCA, BLCA, LUAD, UCEC, KIRC) using UNI2-h as the shared feature extractor for all baselines (Table 1, Section 4).

DPsurv attains the highest average C-index of 0.704 across the five cohorts, ranking first on BRCA (0.720), BLCA (0.625), LUAD (0.667), UCEC (0.766), and KIRC (0.741), outperforming ABMIL, TransMIL, DSMIL, AttnMISL, ILRA, PANTHER, EVREG, UMSA, and BayesMIL (Table 1, Section 4.2).

DPsurv achieves the lowest mean Integrated Brier Score (0.310) and lowest mean Integrated Binomial Log-Likelihood (0.824) across the five TCGA cohorts, indicating better-calibrated survival predictions than all compared baselines (Table 1, Section 4.2).

An ablation over five configurations (FM, FM+GMM, FM+GMM+GRFN, adding Component Prototype modeling, and adding Component Evidence Mixture) shows the full model with all components reaches C-index 0.687, IBS 0.209, IBLL 0.604, the best combination among the tested variants (Table 2).

DPsurv provides interpretability at three levels: feature-level via patch-prototype assignment maps validated by board-certified pathologists, reasoning-level via component prototype evidence modeling, and decision-level via component-wise relative risk distributions over the WSI (Figure 2, Section 4.3).

Survival predictions are expressed as belief and plausibility interval bounds (BPI) derived from Gaussian Random Fuzzy Numbers, with Proposition 3.2 showing the true survival function is bounded between the belief and plausibility measures (Section 3.2, Proposition 3.2).

8aR2Ir2ib2.text: Training Any2Track on a GQS-curated 3% subset of AMASS (about 3% of roughly 14K training clips) achieves 95.6% success rate, exceeding the 94.2% success rate obtained by training on the full unfiltered AMASS dataset (Table 1).

A randomly sampled 3% subset of AMASS causes Any2Track success rate to fall to 83.8%, far below both the curated 3% subset (95.6%) and the full-data baseline (94.2%), showing that data quality rather than quantity drives the improvement (Table 1).

The GQS pipeline defines motion data quality along three dimensions: physics feasibility (whether a motion can be realized by a rigid-body humanoid without severe artifacts), action diversity (coverage of distinct behaviors), and action complexity (informative, dynamic motion versus near-stationary segments) (Section on Core Quality Dimensions / Method).

An ablation shows that removing physics filtering drops success rate from 95.6% to 91.1%, removing the diversity term drops it to 93.4%, and removing complexity weighting drops it to 94.6%, with the full combination of all three factors needed to reach 95.6% (Ablation, Table 1).

Applying GQS-selected 10% AMASS subsets to TWIST2 improves success rate from 82.5% to 86.8% and reduces MPJPE from 0.099 to 0.084 rad, a roughly 15% MPJPE improvement over training on the full dataset (Table 1).

The Global Weighted Farthest Point Sampling selection stage weights diversity at 98% and complexity at 2%, prioritizing physically demanding motions when candidates are otherwise geometrically equidistant (Method, Stage III).

weMYE1B16x.text: The paper formulates rollout scheduling in RLVR as a contextual bandit problem, representing each rollout arm with a 10-dimensional feature vector encoding reward signals, length metrics, policy perception, and data interaction history (Section 3, Methodology).

Theorem 5.4 establishes a sublinear regret bound of O(sqrt(T)(d-tilde + S*sqrt(d-tilde)) + sqrt(T)) for the proposed contextual bandit scheduler, where d-tilde is the effective NTK dimension and S captures reward geometry (Theorem 5.4, Section 5).

Theorem 5.3 shows that enlarging the historical rollout replay buffer raises the achievable upper bound on policy performance, motivating reuse of past rollouts during scheduling (Theorem 5.3, Section 5).
The method (CBS/CBS*) is evaluated on six mathematical reasoning benchmarks—AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, MATH500, Minerva, and Olympiad—combined with GRPO, DAPO, and GSPO (Section 6, Experimental Results).
Intra-group scheduling (CBS*) yields relative performance gains of +5.0% for GRPO, +5.8% for DAPO, and +2.0% for GSPO, while reducing average policy optimization time by 50.4% (Table 2, Figure 2b).
The scheduler's own computational overhead consumes less than 4% of total training time across the evaluated RLVR methods (Table 3).

VbQg7jQnpL.text: SCPO reduces hallucination rate by up to 62.9% relative to baseline models, with CHAIRs scores dropping 40.3% compared to standard DPO on the paper's evaluation setting (Section on Key Findings / Experiments).

SCPO is built on Semantic Curriculum Preference Pairs (SCPP), a dataset combining RLHF-V, MVC, HumanEdit, and Winoground sources organized into easy-to-hard curriculum stages (Method, Dataset construction).

SCPO combines a Symmetric Bidirectional Objective—Cross-modal Complementary Optimization (CCO) and Cross-modal Symmetry Optimization (CSO)—with a Dynamic Reference Model that updates at each curriculum stage to prevent KL divergence saturation (Method).

SCPO is evaluated on Object HalBench, AMBER-Generative, AMBER-Discriminative, and MMHal Bench for hallucination, and on LLaVA-in-the-Wild and MMBench-CN for general capability preservation, against baselines including DPO, mDPO, HALVA, HA-DPO, HSA-DPO, RLHF-V, and EOS on LLaVA-v1.5/v1.6 7B/13B (Section 4, Experiments).

An ablation shows full SCPO reaches CHAIRs of 7.0 versus 10.7 for the baseline, and removing CSO, curriculum sorting, or the dynamic reference model each raises CHAIRs back up (to 10.67, 9.67, and 9.0 respectively), confirming each component's contribution (Ablation Table, Section 5).

FFEKmtsT4S.text: Distinguishable Deletion (D-squared) reformulates LLM unlearning by constraining the model's response distribution in latent energy space rather than suppressing specific token sequences, using the energy definition E_theta(v|x,y<i) = -z_theta(v|x,y<i) (Section 3.1, 3.2).

Energy-based Unlearning Alignment (EUA) uses a Helmholtz free-energy index to quantify residual knowledge presence and enforce a self-preferenced energy margin between unlearned and retained content (Section 3.2, 3.3).
On the TOFU Forget-10% benchmark with LLaMA-3.2-3B, EUA reaches an aggregate score of 8.665 versus 6.484 for SatImp and 4.601 for GradDiff (Table 1).
On TOFU Forget-10% with Qwen2.5-3B, EUA attains a Linguistic Quality (LQ) score of 8.619 compared to only 0.794 for SatImp, indicating markedly more fluent post-unlearning generations (Table 1).
On WMDP with Zephyr-7B, EUA reduces Bio and Cyber accuracy to 0.2567 and 0.2742 respectively while retaining 0.5263 MMLU accuracy on unrelated knowledge (Table 3).
Against distinguishable-refusal baselines, EUA maintains 100% refusal-detection accuracy both before and after jailbreaking attacks, whereas competing methods degrade under attack (Table 2).

2zMJ5cLziN.text: FocalPolicy combines a Foresight Composite Objective (FCO), which applies a Discrete Cosine Transform to concatenated macro-trajectories of N action chunks to add frequency-domain supervision, with Locally Anchored Sampling (LAS), which draws the flow-matching sampling time from a logit-normal distribution with mu=4.0, sigma=1.6 (Section 4.1, 4.2).
FocalPolicy achieves an 83.6% average success rate across 53 simulated manipulation tasks, versus 79.9% for DP3, 79.4% for FlowPolicy, and 75.1% for FreqPolicy (Table 1).
An ablation removing LAS drops full FocalPolicy's 77.9% average success rate on 24 tasks to 64.3% (-13.6 points), and removing both FCO and LAS drops it to 54.1% (-23.8 points) (Table 4).

Adding the proposed FCO and LAS modules to other baselines improves their performance, e.g., DP3 with FCO improves by 2.8 points and FlowPolicy with LAS improves by 7.9 points, demonstrating cross-baseline generalizability (Table 2).
FocalPolicy yields consistently lower action total variation than FlowPolicy across 8 evaluated tasks, indicating smoother, more coherent action trajectories (Table 3).
On 6 real-world long-horizon tasks with 2-4 stages each, FocalPolicy shows its largest advantage over baselines in the final stages, attributed to mitigation of compounding errors (Section 5.3).

5vI6ApLOg8.text: The paper's Parametrized Random Walk Diffusion Kernel Clustering (P-RWDKC) method defines a parametrized random walk operator that addresses the irreducibility problem of directed-graph random walks without discarding edge directionality (Section 3).

P-RWDKC's vertex measure is constructed via a parametrized forward/backward flow mixing parameter gamma in [0,1] and re-weighting parameter alpha in [0,1], enabling automatic tuning across a family of diffusion operators (Section 5.1).
Diffusion time is estimated automatically via a Calinski-Harabasz-criterion-based procedure (Algorithm 2), rather than requiring manual selection (Section 5.2).
Across 11 UCI benchmark datasets, P-RWDKC attains an average NMI of 66.04, exceeding PIC (60.01) and spectral clustering variants (58.29-58.34) (Table 1).

On real-world directed graphs, P-RWDKC outperforms rotated spectral clustering (RSC) on Cora (52.03 vs 36.07 NMI) and on Political Blogs (75.53 vs 73.25 NMI), with an overall average of 60.65 vs 55.96 NMI across 4 networks (Table 2).
On multi-scale synthetic Gaussian mixtures, P-RWDKC correctly identifies both a 6-cluster and a 2-cluster structure at different diffusion scales (Figure 1).

6t9xJWFjkq.text: Query Lens extends Logit Lens by jointly interpreting encoder-side 'key' features (QLKey, what activates a sparse feature) and decoder-side 'value' features (QLValue, what a feature promotes downstream), rather than only the direct unembedding-projected effect (Section 3.4).

Query Lens models indirect effects via a Jacobian-product decomposition of how a feature's contribution propagates through downstream attention and MLP layers before reaching the unembedding (Section 3.2).

Across GPT-2 Small, Gemma-3 variants, and Qwen-3-1.7B, QLKey achieves up to 39.32% Input Score and QLValue achieves up to 15.24% Output Score on GPT-2 Small, both improving over the Logit Lens baselines LLKey/LLValue (Table 1).

Using GPT-5-nano as an automatic judge, Query Lens token sets receive higher interpretability ratings than Logit Lens, whose outputs are dominated by tokenizer fragments rather than coherent concepts (Table 2, Section 4.3).

The Subspace Channel Hypothesis proposes that downstream modules read a feature's information only through a layer-specific low-dimensional subspace ('channel'), supported by an overlap measure of about 0.7 among low-rank maps sharing a destination layer, which decays with distance between layers (Section 5, Figure 5).

KODJBT02ux.text: ViPll models the posterior P(Y|X,S) over true labels using a Dirichlet variational distribution whose parameters are output by an amortized inference network, factorizing the generative process as P(Y)P(X|Y)P(S|X,Y) instead of the standard discriminative formulation (Section 4.1).
ViPll incorporates a conditional variational autoencoder to model P(X|Y) (Section 4.2) and a maximum-entropy prior satisfying candidate-label-set constraints (Section 4.3).
Training proceeds in three phases: initialization, a 500-epoch CVAE warm-up, and a 1000-epoch main training loop using Monte Carlo sampling (Section 4.5).

On 5 real-world partial-label datasets, ViPll attains 76.15% (+/-1.56) accuracy on Bird-song and 78.52% (+/-2.27) on Lost, outperforming 9 baselines including PlKnn, Proden, PiCO, and CroSel on the majority of settings (Table 2).
On synthetic partial-label benchmarks, ViPll reaches 96.64% (+/-3.92) accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 77.76% (+/-0.51) on CIFAR-100 (Table 3).
An ablation removing the modeling of Markov equivalence in the generative structure causes significant accuracy degradation, validating the choice of generative modeling (Section 4, ablation study).

hRj3eFCuQS.text: RLRR's Hybrid Relative Reward (HRR) variant improves the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B model's AIME 2024 accuracy to 50.5% versus 48.8% for the Dr.GRPO baseline (Table 1).
On MATH-500, RLRR-H reaches 91.4% accuracy versus 89.4% for Dr.GRPO with the 8B model, while also producing the lowest average response length among compared methods at 5,025 tokens (Table 1).
On WritingBench, RLRR with an 8B URM reward model achieves 74.71% overall performance, a +1.59 point improvement over the compared baseline (Table 2).
An ablation removing the correctness constraint from Hierarchical Re-ranking degrades AIME24 performance from 30.8% to 28.4% (Table 3).
RLRR generalizes beyond GRPO, improving CISPO by 1.0 points and RLOO by 1.0 points on average across benchmarks (Table 4).

The Pure Relative Reward (PRR) formulation is theoretically shown to have a strictly upper-bounded variance of 0.25 via Popoviciu's inequality, in contrast to scalar reward models whose loss function drives unbounded score divergence (Appendix B, Equation 10).

VI8rCF97FK.text: Shapley Neuron Valuation (SNV) achieves 41.30% accuracy versus 38.42% for NFL+ on ImageNet-1k with 10 tasks in the Class-Incremental Learning setting, a +2.88 point gain (Table 1).
On ImageNet-1k with 50 tasks in the Class-Incremental Learning setting, SNV reaches 25.60% accuracy versus 22.40% for NFL+ (Table 1).

In the Task-Incremental Learning setting on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet with 10 tasks and capacity c=0.5, SNV attains 79.76% and 74.82% accuracy respectively with zero backward transfer, outperforming the memory-based method DyTox (73.80% on Tiny-ImageNet) without using a replay buffer (Table 2).
SNV incurs only ~1.24x FLOPs overhead relative to NFL+ and adds just 0.1 GB of GPU memory with no increase in inference latency (0.4 ms per image) (Table 3).

An ablation of the truncated multi-armed-bandit Shapley estimation (TMAB-Shapley) shows it achieves 54.70% accuracy in 62 minutes versus 54.92% for full Monte Carlo estimation in 97 minutes, a roughly 4x speedup at a cost of only 0.22% accuracy (Table 6).

Theorem 2.1 establishes that the Shapley Neuron Value satisfies the Efficiency, Null Contribution, Symmetry, and Linearity axioms, yielding continuous per-neuron importance scores rather than binary masks (Theorem 2.1).

qBuZDNyQCM.text: On Robotouille Synchronous with Qwen3-235B, GiG achieves 93% Pass@1 versus 71% for the ReCAP baseline, a 22-point improvement (Table 1).
On Robotouille Asynchronous, GiG with experience memory (GiG+Exp) reaches up to 86% Pass@1 on DeepSeek versus 27% for ReCAP, a 37-point improvement (Table 2).
On ALFWorld, GiG attains 97% Pass@1 on both Qwen3 and DeepSeek backbones versus 89% and 82% respectively for ReCAP, up to a 15-point improvement (Table 3).
An ablation combining Bounded Lookahead and Loop Detection raises Qwen3 Pass@1 from an 80% baseline to 93%, with Loop Detection alone contributing a jump to 90% (Table 5).

GiG's graph construction latency stays in the sub-second regime (well under 150 ms) even as computational cost scales as task horizon extends, unlike baseline methods whose FLOPs grow substantially faster (Section 4.7).

ySUfgY6twT.text: TIDE decomposes graph representations into feature-specific, structure-specific, and joint information components via an information bottleneck objective, with theoretical guarantees given in Theorems 5.1 through 5.3 (Section 5).

TIDE is compared against graph OOD baselines GNNSafe, NodeSafe, DEGEM, and GOLD, along with classical detectors MSP, energy-based scoring, and Mahalanobis distance, reporting FPR95 and AUROC across multiple graph benchmarks (Section 6).
TIDE achieves up to a 34% improvement in FPR95 over the strongest compared baseline while maintaining competitive in-distribution classification accuracy (Table 4).
Additional main-results and ablation tables (Tables 6, 8, and 9) further evaluate TIDE's components across datasets and appendix-level ablation configurations (Appendices K-M).
The paper's code is released publicly at https://github.com/DannyW618/TIDE (Section 6).

Ilt2BnENrR.text: IPOW's Concept Decomposition Model splits RoI features into discriminative, shared, and background concept types, described in Sections 4.3, 4.4, and 4.5 respectively.
On M-OWODB Task 1, IPOW reaches 50.1% unknown recall (U-Recall) while maintaining 62.4 known mAP (Table 1).

An ablation on M-OWODB Task 1 shows U-Recall rising from a 21.8% base model to 25.9% with GMM RPN, 45.4% with added Shared Concepts, 50.4% with added Background Concepts, reaching 50.1% after adding the Concept-Guided Rectification (CGR) mechanism that reduces known-unknown confusion (Table 3).
On the DIOR remote sensing dataset, IPOW improves Task 1 unknown recall from a 2.8% baseline to 19.9% (Section 4, results on DIOR).
IPOW records 3,648 Absolute Open-Set Error (A-OSE) false positives and a Wilderness Impact of 0.0369 on Task 1, indicating reduced known-unknown confusion relative to baselines (Table 2).
Figure 4 shows the optimal number of shared concepts is K=100 with M=50, based on a shared-concept-count optimization sweep (Figure 4).

oVtiySvpXz.text: RAT computes Tikhonov-regularized natural policy gradients by combining a Woodbury reformulation with randomized Kaczmarz iteration, avoiding explicit Fisher matrix construction and conjugate-gradient solvers (Section 4.1-4.3).
Theorem 1 proves linear convergence of the RAT gradient estimate, E‖g_j−g*‖² ≤ (1−μ)^j‖g_0−g*‖², under a compatibility assumption with contraction factor μ = λ_min(E[P_τ]) (Theorem 1, Lemma 1).
On the Humanoid MuJoCo task with a shared actor-critic network, RAT reaches a final return of 5382.7±117.3, versus 5357.9±150.9 for PPO and only 2571.7±838.7 for ACKTR (Table 1).
On the Ant MuJoCo task, RAT attains a final return of 2926.6±353.1, more than double PPO's 1373.9±26.0 and far above ACKTR's 23.4±3.2 (Table 1).

RAT's per-update wallclock time on Humanoid (18.17-19.85ms) is comparable to full Fisher-vector-product plus conjugate-gradient natural gradient methods (~19.8ms), while KFAC and PPO remain cheaper at 5.6-6.6ms and 3.1-3.7ms respectively (Table 2).
Ablation experiments on Humanoid show the optimal batch size is 2^10 and performance is robust to damping values λ in [0.01, 0.4], degrading only at large λ ≥ 0.8 (Figure 5, Section 5.4).

XcJk9un0Tb.text: On the synthetic Müller-Brown potential, FAS achieves a 100% transition-hit probability and expected transition score of -36.70±3.09, compared to 82% and -14.93±12.61 for the Doob's h-transform diffusion baseline (Table 1).

On Alanine Dipeptide transition path sampling, FAS attains 0.00±0.00 Å RMSD and 100.00±0.00% transition-hit probability, versus the best baseline TR-LV's 0.29±0.03 Å RMSD and 61.25±4.05% hit probability (Table 2).

On the 138-atom Chignolin protein, FAS reaches an expected transition score of -360.85±53.71 kJ/mol, lower (more favorable) than TR-LV's -303.98±28.65 kJ/mol, while also achieving 100% transition-hit probability versus TR-LV's 43.95±5.64% (Table 2).

FAS's infinite-dimensional adjoint matching formulation (Proposition 4, Section 3.3) yields an unbiased estimator (Proposition 5) for the stochastic optimal control objective in function space, distinguishing it from finite-dimensional adjoint samplers (Section 3).
FAS exhibits discretization invariance on Alanine Dipeptide, maintaining an expected transition score near -29 to -34 kJ/mol across 1x, 2x, and 4x finer time discretizations (Table 3).

zV5ktcEs8j.text: On the adaptive influence maximization (AIM) benchmark with T=20, K=10 (N=500 nodes), LMTA achieves a reward of 161.71±1.39 versus 123.02±2.88 for the WS-option baseline, a 31.5% improvement (Table 1).
On the stochastic orienteering problem (SOP) benchmark with T=10, K=70 (N=500 nodes), LMTA scores 31.60±1.94 compared to 12.99±1.25 for WS-option, a 143.3% improvement (Table 2).

The method combines a MuZero-style high-level latent-space tree search planner, a multi-timescale semi-Markov world model, and a subgoal-conditioned budget policy, with no explicit duration prediction needed since latent transition magnitudes encode temporal scale (Section 4, Figure 1).

Ablations on AIM (N=500, K=70) show incremental gains from each component: 301.53 baseline, 309.52 with low-level subgoal conditioning, 314.65 adding budget subgoal conditioning, 322.04 adding the multi-timescale fixed-margin objective, and 324.15 for the full LMTA model (Table 3).
Theorem A.13 in the appendix establishes planning error bounds for depth-H Monte Carlo tree search under the learned multi-timescale abstraction (Theorem A.13, Appendix A).

3sx2WRBSSO.text: Genome-Factory is presented as the first integrated Python library unifying tuning, deployment, and interpretation of genomic foundation models, with an automated preprocessing pipeline (the Genome Collector) that retrieves and normalizes FASTA data from repositories like NCBI (Section 3.1).

The Model Loader component supports six genomic foundation models—GenomeOcean, EVO, DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA, Caduceus, and Nucleotide Transformer—spanning 50M to 2.5B parameters and context lengths from 1K to 1M tokens (Section 3.2).

The Model Trainer supports three fine-tuning strategies (full-parameter, LoRA, and adapter-based tuning) with mixed precision, Flash attention, and gradient accumulation for classification and regression tasks (Section 3.3).
The Biological Interpreter module uses a sparse autoencoder to disentangle model embeddings into interpretable latent units, linked to genomic features via regression analysis (Section 3.6).
Genome-Factory provides a zero-code, YAML-configured command-line interface and a Gradio-based web interface for accessible genomic analysis (Section 3.7).

The library integrates the GUE and Genomic Benchmarks evaluation suites through an extensible Benchmarker plugin system, reporting fine-tuning efficiency and scalability results across model sizes (Section 3.5, Tables 2-4).

5pOlWjnGn3.text: At 32x32 resolution, next-pixel prediction loss scales with model-size exponent 0.55 and data-size exponent 0.45, whereas the optimal scaling exponents for image generation are 0.49 (model) and 0.51 (data) — meaning generation's optimal setup requires data size to grow three to five times faster than the classification-optimal setup (Section 4, Table with scaling exponents).

As resolution increases from 16x16 to 32x32 to 64x64, model scaling becomes increasingly effective relative to data scaling, so optimal model size must grow much faster than data size at higher resolutions (Section 4.3).
Learning directly on raw pixels requires an optimal token-to-parameter ratio 10-20x higher than for language tokens, exceeding 400 for pixels versus about 20 for text (Section 4).

To reach 80% ImageNet classification accuracy via next-pixel prediction at 64x64 resolution, the projected compute-optimal configuration requires roughly 215.3B parameters and 187M images, a 10^4x increase in FLOPs over current setups (Section 4.4, Table 3).

The authors conclude compute, not training data volume, is the primary bottleneck for scaling pixel-by-pixel image modeling, and project feasibility of large-scale next-pixel prediction within about five years given historical 4-5x annual compute growth (Section 4.4, Section 5).

HoThWhfxiK.text: Self-Flow's Dual-Timestep Scheduling samples two timesteps (t,s) and a random mask M to assign heterogeneous noise levels τᵢ across tokens, creating information asymmetry for representation learning (Section 3.3, Figure 3).
On ImageNet 256×256, Self-Flow achieves FID 5.70 versus REPA's FID 5.89, and RAE + Self-Flow reaches FID 2.95 (Table 1).
On video generation at 600K training steps, Self-Flow attains FVD 47.81 and FID 8.92, outperforming both vanilla flow matching (FVD 50.95) and a DINOv2-aligned variant (FVD 49.59) (Table 3).

Self-Flow's 625M-parameter model outperforms REPA's 1B-parameter model, with the performance gap widening in Self-Flow's favor from 290M to 1B parameters, indicating better scaling behavior without external supervision (Figure 6).
Ablations show removing the representation loss degrades FID by about 4 points and removing the masking mechanism degrades FID by about 1 point (Figure 11a).
A single Self-Flow model is trained jointly across image, video, and audio modalities with consistent improvements across different modality weightings (Section 4.2, Figure 8).

J6amahDTKV.text: FoeGlass is a black-box automated red-teaming method that uses in-context learning from an attacker LLM (DeepSeek-R1 distilled on Llama-3.1-8B) to iteratively generate adversarial TTS audio that evades audio deepfake detectors (Section 3).

On VIT-ConstantQ trained on VoxCelebSpoof, FoeGlass raises the false negative rate for VITS-generated audio from 42.02% (unconditional sampling) to 96.15%, and for xTTS-v2 from 2.24% to 96.29% (Table 1).
Despite VITS appearing in the ASVspoof5 training data, FoeGlass still achieves a 74.2% false negative rate against the VIT-ASVspoof-ConstantQ detector (Section 4.2).

Fine-tuning detectors on FoeGlass-generated samples reduces vulnerability: RawNetLite's false negative rate on FoeGlass attacks drops from 49.6% to 8.2%, and AASIST's drops from 15.2% to 0.2% (Table 2).

An ablation removing the diversity feedback term (based on WavLM embedding distance) lowers the false negative rate achieved on xTTS-v2 against VIT-ConstantQ from 96.29% to 86.02% (Appendix B, Table 4).

Cco325CI1W.text: FS-I2P's Hierarchical Focus-Sweep Interaction Module combines a Focus operation, which uses point-cloud-derived global scale priors to modulate image features, with a Sweep operation that performs fine-grained local cross-modal interaction via VSSM layers (Section 3.1).

A Dynamic Layer Allocation Strategy trained with REINFORCE and an exponential moving-average baseline adaptively predicts the number of interaction layers to use per input pair, using matching quality as the reward signal (Section 3.2, Equation 10).
On RGB-D Scenes V2, FS-I2P achieves mean Registration Recall of 72.9%, compared to 68.4% for Flow-I2P and 56.4% for 2D3D-MATR (Table 1).
On 7-Scenes, FS-I2P achieves mean Registration Recall of 82.7% versus 78.4% for Flow-I2P and 75.8% for 2D3D-MATR (Table 1).
Ablation on RGB-D Scenes V2 shows Registration Recall rising from 56.4% with HTS alone to 68.2% after adding both Focus and Sweep modules, and to 72.9% with the full model including DLAS (Table 2).
FS-I2P runs inference in 0.304 seconds using 6,415 MB of memory, versus 0.497 seconds and 8,346 MB for a transformer baseline (Table 3).

HFpAMjHiZm.text: Zero-Shot Off-Policy Learning (ZOL) derives a theoretical approximation (Eq. 10) showing the stationary density ratio for a latent-indexed policy family satisfies w_{π_z}/β(s,a) ≈ (1−γ)W_{π_z}^⊤B(s,a), connecting successor measures to stationary distribution correction (Section 3).

The algorithm infers a task embedding from offline data via c_T := E_{(s,a)∼D}[B_ψ(s,a)r_T(s,a)] and optimizes the latent policy z via gradient ascent with a χ²-penalty for weight stability and a trust-region constraint, without any additional environment interaction (Section 3.1).

On 16 ExORL DeepMind Control tasks (Walker, Cheetah, Quadruped, PointMass), ZOL attains an average return of 627.2 versus 592.5 for the forward-backward (FB) baseline, a 5.81% improvement (Section 6.1, Table 2).
On 55 long-horizon OGBench tasks (antmaze, cube, puzzle domains), ZOL achieves an average score of 0.47, versus 0.45 for FB, 0.42 for LoLA, and 0.39 for ReLA (Section 6.2, Table 1).

Theorem C.1 shows centered reweighting recovers the target policy's return as J_c(π) = E_{d^π}[r(s)] − r̄_β, and Theorem C.2 shows the χ² penalty equals the χ²-divergence between the induced and behavior occupancies, E_{d^β}[(w_π(s)−1)²] = χ²(d^π‖d^β) (Theorem C.1, Theorem C.2).

A 2D donut toy domain (Section 5) demonstrates that vanilla forward-backward inference collapses toward support-biased solutions under biased offline data, while ZOL reliably reconstructs the intended task structure across all three tested reward functions.

C7reVNwYsF.text: The Matched-and-Dashed (M&D) protocol replaces distinct option labels (A/B/C/D) with uniform dashes and matches free-text model answers to options via Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B cosine similarity, rather than relying on letter prediction (Section 4).

On the synthetic NonsenseQA benchmark, models score above 95% accuracy under the standard Standard-and-Letter (S&L) protocol despite meaningless input, but multiple models drop to near chance level (25%) under M&D, with Wilcoxon test p < 10⁻⁴ and Cohen's d = 2.2 (Section 5.2, Figure 3).

Across five benchmarks (CSQA, ARC, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, INCLUDE), M&D reduces the geometric mean of the accuracy-variance ratio to 0.33, a roughly 3x reduction versus S&L, with the largest reduction on CSQA (0.11, an 11x reduction) (Table 1).
M&D reduces accuracy variance across answer-order permutations in 12 of 13 tested open-source LLMs (8B-32B parameters) on CSQA (Section 5.3, Figure 4).

The M&D protocol adds only about 3% computational overhead relative to S&L, e.g., 34.65s versus 36.31s generation time for Gemma-3-12B on CSQA, plus 2.70s for answer extraction (Appendix F.1, Table 2).

G4D0YzzZEk.text: The Triplet Similarity Index (TSI) and Quadruplet Similarity Index (QSI) measure representation alignment via ordinal relationship consistency rather than raw distance/kernel comparisons (Section 4.1).
Corollary 1 establishes that perfect TSI alignment is formally equivalent to joint Mutual Nearest Neighbors alignment across all neighborhood scales (Section 4.3, Corollary 1).
TSI is computable in O(N^2 log N) time and QSI in O(N^2 log N) space, and both admit approximation to error epsilon using O(1/epsilon^2 log(1/delta)) samples (Corollary 3, Corollary 4).

Under 2% outlier perturbation on synthetic data (N=1000, D=50) and on a ViT trained on CIFAR-10, TSI and QSI retain roughly 94% alignment scores and outperform CKA, CKNNA, and MutualNN in robustness (Section 6.2).

In the CLIP multimodal alignment experiment across model scales on ImageNet (50k samples), TSI and QSI increase monotonically with accuracy (63.3% small, 68.1% medium, 75.4% large), whereas CKA exhibits a counter-intuitive drop at the Large variant (Section 6.5).

For independent (unaligned) representations, Lemma 1 shows the expected TSI/QSI score is approximately 0.5, and this holds stably across varying sample size N and dimensionality, unlike CKA/SVCCA/PWCCA (Section 6.1, Lemma 1).
