lcLxGrk5N9.text: OPUS defines data utility in the optimizer-induced update space (e.g., for AdamW and Muon preconditioners) rather than raw gradient space, using ghost techniques and CountSketch projections (with sketch dimension m=8192) to keep selection overhead to 4.7% of total compute (Section on Scalable Scoring via Ghost Factors and CountSketch).
When pre-training GPT-2 XL with the Muon optimizer on FineWeb using 30B selected tokens, OPUS reaches 41.75 average accuracy versus 40.29 for a 60B-token random-selection baseline (Table 3).

On FineWeb-Edu under adversarial conditions (selecting only from lower-quality score-3 documents while baselines use score-4/5 data), OPUS still achieves 44.99 average accuracy on GPT-2 XL with Muon (Table 4).

In continued pre-training of Qwen3-8B on SciencePedia, OPUS using 0.5B selected tokens outperforms baselines trained on 3B full tokens on the OlympicArena benchmark, corresponding to roughly a 6x reduction in compute for equivalent performance (Section on Continued Pre-training: Qwen3-8B on SciencePedia).
On out-of-distribution benchmarks excluded from Bench-Proxy construction (BBH, RACE-Middle, RACE-High), OPUS achieves an average accuracy of 40.07% versus 39.42% for the GREATS baseline (Table 5).
Across ten held-out domains (health, law, science, etc.), OPUS achieves the lowest average perplexity among compared methods despite training on a selectively reduced subset of data (Table 6).

ExQfs4Agz2.text: Theorem 1 gives the first convergence bound for approximate (polynomial-approximated) gradient descent under fully homomorphic encryption in the no-DP setting, bounding the objective gap f(w_g,T) - f(w*_f) by 2*alpha + (rho^2 + 2*zeta*rho + zeta^2)/(2*mu) (Theorem 1).

Theorem 4 extends the convergence analysis to the differentially private setting, showing the expected squared distance to the optimum decays geometrically at rate (1 - eta_DP*nu/2)^T plus approximation and noise terms (Theorem 4).

Algorithm 3 avoids costly homomorphic per-sample gradient clipping by instead using a logarithmic barrier function added to the objective, f^+_{B_kappa}(w) := f(w) - lambda*B_kappa(Theta - ||w||^2), to control iterate magnitude while still achieving (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy (Theorem 3, Algorithm 3).

Lemma 5.3 shows that under the paper's parameter settings, weight iterates satisfy ||w_i|| <= sqrt((1-kappa)*Theta) plus additional terms with high probability, ensuring activations remain within the polynomial approximation interval required for FHE compatibility (Lemma 5.3).

On four datasets (Adult, COMPAS, Credit, MNIST) at privacy budget epsilon=1, delta=10^-5, the proposed clipping-avoidance method matches standard DP-GD utility (accuracy drop up to 1.61%, AUC drop up to 1.05%) while reducing multiplicative depth per iteration from 24 to 9, a 2.5x-5x reduction (experimental results table).

NWRoNoJ9QX.text: MPRM training quickly saturates under random subsampling of the training data, indicating substantial redundancy in existing process-reward annotation corpora (Section on saturation of random subsampling).

The Balanced-Information Score (BIS) combines label-mixture balance (ratio of positive to negative steps) and label reliability (average score of positive steps) computed from existing Monte Carlo rollout signals, without incurring additional annotation cost (Section on Balanced-Information Score).
BIS-selected training subsets reach full-dataset performance while using only 10% of the training data (Section on Performance Results).
BIS improves over random subsampling by a relative 4.1% on VisualProcessBench (Section on Performance Results).
BIS-selected subsets consistently match or surpass full-data performance across both InternVL2.5-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone architectures (Section on Performance Results).

Y2lYfMD0z8.text: Proposition 3.4 shows the optimal density weight for quantile regression equals the conditional density of the score evaluated at the true quantile, which for location-scale distributions is proportional to 1/sigma(x), capturing heteroscedastic structure ignored by standard pinball loss (Proposition 3.4).

The proposed three-stage framework estimates joint quantiles at levels tau-delta, tau, tau+delta, computes density weights via the finite-difference w(x) = 2*delta / (q_hat_{tau+delta}(x) - q_hat_{tau-delta}(x)), then fine-tunes the central quantile with a weighted pinball loss before conformalization (Section 3, three-stage framework).
Theorem 5.2 gives a non-asymptotic excess risk bound with asymptotic rate O(R_n(G)^(2/3)) ≈ O(n^(-1/3)) under an optimal bandwidth choice delta* proportional to R_n(G)^(1/3) (Theorem 5.2).

Stability of the density-weighted method relies on weight clipping at threshold M=5.0, convex loss mixing with unweighted pinball loss, and a softplus activation to guarantee monotonic quantile ordering (Section on Stability Mechanisms).

On the Naval Propulsion dataset, the proposed CPCP method with clipping and loss mixing improves worst-slice coverage (WSC) from about 65% (Split CP baseline) to 83.46% +/- 3.45%, while achieving a mean squared conditional error (MSCE) of 0.0017 (Section on Experimental Results, 8 benchmarks).

nIGsv6u4yU.text: CondiQuant's theoretical analysis shows the relative quantization error is bounded by the weight matrix condition number κ(W) times the relative activation quantization error, motivating a condition-number-minimization objective (Section on theoretical analysis).

CondiQuant solves an alternating optimization of a gradient-descent step (preserving layer outputs) and a proximal step that minimizes weight condition number via closed-form SVD-based singular value compaction (Section on method).
At 2-bit weight quantization on Set5 at scale x2, CondiQuant achieves 37.15 dB PSNR, outperforming 2DQuant by 1.15 dB (Table 3).
Figure 5 shows CondiQuant reduces the average condition number of quantized weight matrices from roughly 3000 down to 28.37 after proximal optimization (Figure 5).
Ablations show CondiQuant's proximal regularization term (λ=0.003) adds a further 0.07 dB PSNR improvement while adding negligible runtime (under 19 seconds) (Table 2).
CondiQuant achieves a 3.60x model size reduction and 5.08x inference speedup at 2-bit compression with no additional inference-time modules (Section on compression results).

dblO6FgIvc.text: Tokenised Flow Matching for Posterior Estimation (TFMPE) uses likelihood-factorisation (LF) sampling that trains a per-site neural surrogate on single simulations and synthesises multi-site observations for posterior training, reducing simulator calls per training sample compared to hierarchical posterior factorisation baselines (Method section on LF sampling).

The tokenisation scheme embeds parameters and observations with variable identifiers, intra-variable positions, group identifiers for site membership, and Gaussian Fourier features for functional inputs, processed by an encoder-only transformer producing flow-matching vector fields (Method section on tokenisation and architecture).

On a 100-site seasonal SEIR epidemiological model, TFMPE achieves MMD² = 0.060 relative to a NUTS reference (p < 0.005), with NUTS failing to converge beyond 5 sites, and TARP calibration gives ATC = 0.0382 (KS p-value = 0.0097) (Experiments section, seasonal SEIR case study).

On a 1D arterial haemodynamics CFD model with 4 outlet Windkessel parameters per patient, TFMPE achieves a 1852x per-patient sampling speedup (11.88s CFD simulation vs 6.41ms surrogate) while all 11 parameters achieve 95% credible interval coverage (Experiments section, CFD case study).

An ablation removing the group/site embedding ('No Grouping') collapses performance broadly across tasks, indicating the group identifier token is load-bearing for hierarchical calibration (Ablation studies section).

wnKgWnx8mH.text: The paper identifies a three-stage 'Adapt-Aggregate-Execute' emotional processing pipeline in large vision-language models: modality alignment in layers 0-7, sentiment-specific attention-head aggregation of emotional cues into the query token in layers 8-18, and emotion-general narrative generation pathways in layers 19-35 (Methodology/Preliminaries section).

This reveals a functional decoupling whereby middle layers rely on emotion-specific attention heads while deep layers use a universal, emotion-general mechanism to translate emotional cues into narrative generation (Section on discovered circuit).

The proposed VEENA framework, combining Visual Emotion Enhancement (VEE) and Emotional Neuron Augmentation (ENA), raises average accuracy across 9 MER-UniBench datasets from a 58.1% baseline to 64.8% (+6.7 points), with a larger +9.2-point gain on the fine-grained OV-MERD+ subset (Experiments section, MER-UniBench results table).
Layer 19 is identified as the critical inflection point, producing an approximately 40% improvement when emotional steering vectors are injected there (Experiments section).

Ablations show optimal gains come from targeting the top-10 sentiment-specific attention heads per emotion (~3% of parameters) and their top-30 traced MLP neurons, while random head selection fails to reproduce the improvement (Ablation study section).

Safety validation on POPE, CHAIR, and MME benchmarks shows VEENA excites the emotion-specific sub-network without indiscriminately over-activating general object-recognition mechanisms, mitigating emotional hallucination (Section on safety validation).

llwW6nVdsa.text: VerdictBench is introduced as a multimodal e-commerce dispute verdict benchmark comprising 6,000 real-world cases across five categories, each with crowdsourced jury verdicts and evidence averaging 14 images and 0.9 videos per case (Dataset section).

CyberJurors achieves 72.52% verdict accuracy on VerdictBench, exceeding state-of-the-art LLMs by 9.48 points, multimodal LLMs (averaging 52.98%) by 19.54 points, and the AgentCourt court-simulator baseline (66.73%) by 5.79 points (Results section, main comparison table).
Individual Verdict Chain-of-Thought (IV-CoT) decomposes reasoning into four stages: focus extraction, clues grounding, adversarial analysis, and final verdict (Methodology section on IV-CoT).

An ablation shows progressive component addition raising accuracy from a 54.16% baseline through +rule prompts (58.76%), +structural reasoning (64.06%), +IV-CoT (67.34%), +jury simulation (70.18%), to +verdict precedents (72.52%) (Ablation study table).
CyberJurors is more token-efficient than AgentCourt, consuming 62.3M tokens versus AgentCourt's 75.3M tokens while achieving higher accuracy (Efficiency analysis section).
Human volunteer verdicts, when checked against actual platform outcomes, only reach 80.3% agreement, indicating the benchmark's inherent task difficulty even for humans (Dataset validation section).

fAj3MJghc0.text: Kernel Space Encoding (EKS) represents NeRF latent features as a field of anisotropic Gaussian kernels rather than discrete grid-vertex features, enabling affine-equivariant, deformation-stable feature interpolation for localized scene editing without retraining (Section 4, Kernel Space Encoding).

EKS employs Ray-Traced Gaussian Proximity Search (RT-GPS), an approximate nearest-neighbor method that restricts candidate Gaussians to those whose confidence ellipsoids contain the query point via ray-traced icosahedron-based point-in-sphere tests (Section 4, RT-GPS).
A hash-grid feature distillation mechanism transfers information from a multi-resolution hash-grid encoding into the kernel field during training (Section 4, Hash Grid Feature Distillation).
On the NeRF-Synthetic dataset, EKS achieves static reconstruction PSNR of 34.72 (Chair), 26.01 (Drums), and 35.59 (Lego), comparable to non-editable baselines (Table 1).

On edited scenes, EKS outperforms Neuraleditor, achieving SSIM of 0.957 versus 0.944 and lower LPIPS (0.030) on the Chair scene, with comparisons also made against Point-NeRF, RIP-NeRF, and GaMeS (Table 2, Section 5).

Ablations show removing view-direction restoration causes the largest PSNR drop, replacing RT-GPS with Euclidean KNN introduces artifacts, and omitting hash-grid distillation produces sparse visual artifacts (Table 3).

8f5JVzcFvA.text: WaveSSM replaces S4's globally-supported polynomial bases (Legendre, Laguerre, Chebyshev) with localized wavelet frames (Morlet, Gaussian-derivative, Mexican hat, DPSS/Slepian, Daubechies) integrated into the diagonal-plus-low-rank S4 parameterization (Section 3).
On the PTB-XL ECG multi-label classification benchmark, WaveSSM_db6T achieves 0.942 overall AUROC versus 0.934 for the S4 baseline (Table 1).
On Speech Commands (SC35) raw 16kHz audio classification, WaveSSM_dpssT reaches 96.55% accuracy compared to 96.08% for S4_LegS (Table 3).
Theorem 3.2 shows wavelet frames achieve an approximation rate of N^(-s) for functions with O(1) breakpoints, compared to the worst-case N^(-1/2) rate of global Legendre modes (Theorem 3.2).
On the Long Range Arena benchmark, WaveSSM variants improve on Text (89.33%) and Retrieval (91.97%) but remain infeasible on the PathX task with sequence length up to 16,384 (Table 4).

Under 8kHz frequency-shift distribution shift on Speech Commands, S4 remains more robust than WaveSSM variants, indicating the wavelet locality advantage trades off against out-of-distribution robustness (Section 4).

Hw9EsvumTM.text: RoCA learns a Gaussian process over basis tokens (48 ego-vehicle groups and 64 agent groups, group size C=64) that map bijectively to candidate trajectories mined from human driving data (Section 3.2.3).

In Boston-to-Singapore cross-city transfer with SparseDrive-S, RoCA supervised adaptation reduces L2 error from 0.791m (zero-shot) to 0.492m and collision rate from 0.154% to 0.096%, outperforming the direct finetuning baseline (0.544m L2, 0.114% collision) (Table 2).

RoCA's training regularization loss (Eq. 3) combines reconstruction of ego/agent tokens from basis tokens with orthogonality terms, and applying it to VAD-T reduces L2 error by 16% and collision rate by 38% on the nuScenes validation set (Section 3.2.3, Eq. 3).
Using GP predictive variance for active-learning sample selection consistently outperforms random sampling at 5%, 10%, and 15% sampling rates in cross-city adaptation (Table 3).

On long-tail maneuvers with SparseDrive-S, RoCA trajectory prediction reduces L2 error for resume-from-stop (0.67m to 0.34m), overtake (0.69m to 0.53m), and 3-point turn (0.79m to 0.61m) scenarios (Table 9).
RoCA's regularization-only training mode adds no inference-time computation over the base end-to-end driving model, since the GP and basis tokens are used only during training (Section 3.2.3).

QdDli9UoLK.text: UltraLIF derives spiking dynamics via ultradiscretization of the LIF ODE using a log-sum-exp soft-maximum, V(t+1) = LSE_ε(V(t) + log τ0, I(t)), which is smooth in both forward and backward passes, eliminating the forward-backward mismatch of surrogate-gradient training (Section 6, Single-Timestep Advantage).
Proposition 5.2 proves the ultradiscretized trajectory converges to classical LIF dynamics with error bound |V_ε(t) - v(t)| ≤ t·ε·log 2 as ε→0+ (Proposition 5.2).
Proposition 5.4 shows spike gradients are bounded as 0 < ∂s_ε/∂V ≤ 1/(4ε) for any ε>0, preventing vanishing or exploding gradients during training (Proposition 5.4).

At T=1, UltraDLIF improves over the best surrogate-gradient baseline by +11.22% on SHD (Table 8), and UltraPLIF improves by +7.96% on DVS-Gesture (Table 7) and by +3.91% (UltraDLIF) on N-MNIST (Table 6).
A consolidated T=1 accuracy comparison across all four datasets (SHD, DVS-Gesture, N-MNIST, CIFAR-10) versus best surrogate-gradient baselines is reported in Table 9 (Table 9).
With sparsity penalty λ=0.1 on CIFAR-10, UltraPLIF reduces spike rate by roughly 50% while simultaneously improving accuracy over the unregularized model (Table 3).

5MdWQefUzC.text: SeProD pairs a post-trained LVLM 'search model' with its pre-training counterpart 'prophet model' (defined in Section 3.1) and uses probability-based prophetic sampling to selectively accept tokens agreed on by both models, without added inference computation (Section 3.1).

Table 1 reports SeProD's results across 12 splits of four visual search benchmarks (VisualProbe-test easy/medium/hard, V* Bench attribute/spatial, HR-Bench 4K and 8K FSP/FCP), showing consistent gains for Mini-o3 as the search model, e.g. +3.3% on VisualProbe-Hard and +4.4% on V* Bench spatial understanding (Table 1).
On general VQA benchmarks with Mini-o3, SeProD improves MME-RealWorld from 65.5 to 67.7, ScienceQA from 84.5 to 85.4, OCRBench from 83.8 to 85.3, and CVBench from 74.4 to 78.4 (Table 2).
Table 3 reports that prophetic-prefix tokens are accepted 74-81% of the time under SeProD, yielding an inference speedup of 1.03-1.07x relative to the baseline search model (Table 3).
Using a larger 7B prophet model instead of the default 3B prophet increases gains on VisualProbe-test to +4.3% (Hard), +3.2% (Medium), and +4.6% (Easy) (Table 1).

Ik1mKtUYlZ.text: Temporal straightening regularizes latent world-model trajectories by minimizing negative cosine similarity between consecutive velocity vectors, giving loss L_curv = 1 - C combined as L_total = L_pred + λL_curv (Section 3.3).

Theorem 4.4 proves that for linear latent dynamics with transition matrix satisfying ε = ||A - I||_2 ≤ 1/2, the planning Hessian's condition number grows exponentially in ε and planning horizon K under unstraightened dynamics, whereas straightening controls this growth (Theorem 4.4).

Table 1 reports that explicit temporal straightening raises open-loop gradient-descent planning success rate on Wall from 52.67% to 90.67% and on PointMaze-UMaze from 44.00% to 94.00%, relative to the unregularized baseline (Table 1).
On PointMaze-Medium and PushT, explicit straightening improves open-loop success rate by 10.67 and 7.33 percentage points respectively over the baseline (Table 1).

A lightweight projector reduces frozen DINOv2 visual features (384 channels) to a lower-dimensional planning-specific representation (e.g., 8 channels) before applying the curvature regularizer (Section 3.3).

hrypB1oTC3.text: Stream-SW is presented as the first streaming algorithm for computing the sliced Wasserstein distance directly from a stream of samples, without storing the full dataset (Section 3.3).

Theorem 1 decomposes the expected approximation error of Stream-SW into a sampling error term that decreases at rate O(sqrt((d+1)(log n/n + log m/m))) and a sketch error term proportional to epsilon1*n + epsilon2*m (Section 3.3, Theorem 1).
Stream-SW attains memory complexity O(L(k + log(n/k)) + Ld), which reduces to roughly O(L((1/epsilon) sqrt(log(1/epsilon)) + log(epsilon n)) + Ld) under optimized KKL sketch parameters (Section 3.3).

On point-cloud classification via K-nearest neighbors, Stream-SW is evaluated against full SW and random subsampling baselines across projection counts L in {5,10,50,100} and sketch sizes k in {5,10,20,50} (Table 1).
Stream-SW achieves faster Wasserstein-2 convergence than the random-sampling baseline over 5000 gradient-flow iterations (Table 2).
Stream-SW is evaluated on change-point detection delay/early-detection time on the MSRC-12 gesture dataset, showing improved streaming performance over random subsampling (Table 3).

GMIHHrJ6Wp.text: Robust Halpern Iteration (RHI) achieves a sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^2) for computing an epsilon-optimal robust policy in model-free robust average-reward RL, without requiring prior knowledge of the robust bias span H (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
The reduction-to-discounted-MDP approach analyzed in the paper requires knowledge of the bias span H and yields a worse sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^4) (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
Lemma 5.1 bounds the sub-optimality of a greedy policy relative to Q by the span seminorm of the residual, 0 <= g*_P - g^pi_P(s) <= Sp(T_P(Q) - Q) (Section 5, Lemma 5.1).
Theorem 5.2 establishes that RHI's iterates converge exactly, with Sp(T_P(Q_k) - Q_k) approaching 0 as k goes to infinity (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).

Instead of a multi-level Monte Carlo estimator (noted to induce unbounded sample complexity in this setting), RHI uses a recursive sampling scheme that estimates successive differences T_P(Q_k) - T_P(Q_{k-1}) (Section 5, Algorithm 1).

The paper's sample complexity result is claimed to be the first finite-sample guarantee for model-free robust average-reward MDPs, covering both contamination and l_p-norm uncertainty sets (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).

eiNZbsYGJv.text: TIDE (Test-time Iterative Detoxification via Embeddings) requires only input embeddings, a toxicity scoring function, and forward evaluations of the language model, with no retraining, gradients, or auxiliary learned modules (Section 4.1, Table 1).
TIDE estimates gradients in embedding space using a Nesterov-Spokoiny zeroth-order finite-difference estimator with Gaussian perturbations (Section 4.1).
Updates are regularized via gradient normalization, a cosine-similarity constraint, and early stopping once a toxicity threshold tau=0.5 is reached (Section 4.2).

On GPT-2 evaluated on the RealToxicityPrompts challenging subset, TIDE achieves a maximum toxicity of 0.156 at perplexity 5.53, compared to RAD's best result of 0.134 toxicity at 7.21 perplexity (Table 2).

TIDE is evaluated for toxicity-perplexity trade-off against baselines across four models (GPT-2, Llama 3.1-8B, Qwen3-4B, Gemma 2-2B) and three benchmarks (RealToxicityPrompts, BOLD, AttaQ) (Section 5, Figure 2, Figure 4).

vL1xAHOUmd.text: The MM-Snowball benchmark constructs 6-turn multimodal dialogues via an Adversarial Hallucination Trajectory Synthesis (AHTS) pipeline with three phases: visual atomic proposition construction, causal intervention and state perturbation, and adversarial dialogue trajectory simulation (Section 3, Figure 1).
Evaluation of 11 different MLLMs on MM-Snowball reveals a characteristic V-shaped accuracy curve with catastrophic performance collapse during middle turns (turns 3-5) (Section 4, Table 2, Figure 3).

Conflict-Aware Visual Rectification (CAVR) is a training-free framework that mitigates hallucination snowballing through a dual mechanism combining representation-level visual grounding refresh (RVR) and logit-level correction/re-anchoring (LCR) (Section 5).
CAVR is compared against training-free baselines on LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL, showing consistent improvements in mitigating hallucination snowballing (Table 3).
An ablation study confirms complementary effects of the RVR and LCR components of CAVR, visualized via a radar chart in the appendix (Appendix D, Figure 4).

P2dl32LtuQ.text: ViSAE achieves a concept coverage efficiency of 1.26% per 1K images, a roughly 20x improvement over ImageNet's 0.06% per 1K images (Table 1).

ViSAE's probing suite is built from a hierarchical visual concept organization spanning Primitive, Intermediate, Object, and Scene levels, yielding 64K probing examples and a 16K-word vocabulary (Section 2.2).
On interpretation accuracy benchmarking, the ViSAE concept set reaches 54.1% Top-30 accuracy versus 25.4% for LAION-15K, a 28.7 percentage-point gain (Table 4).
Concept circuit tracing combines a top-down stage mapping SAE features to concepts via CLIP embeddings with a bottom-up stage using counterfactual interventions (Section 2.3).
Concept-ablation steering on the WaterBirds dataset raises worst-group accuracy from 50.3% to 98.5%, a 48.2 percentage-point absolute gain (Table 7).

5SZgKeiDGC.text: Zero-shot image edits alone raise a VLM's choice probability for the edited option by 0.2-0.4 in absolute terms, with the CVPO optimization method adding further gains on top (Section 4, Figure 2).

The CVPO (Competitive Visual Prompt Optimization) algorithm achieves the highest model choice probabilities among the three tested optimization methods (VTG, VFD, CVPO), reaching 0.67-0.77 versus lower rates for competitors, evaluated across 9 frontier VLMs and 4 domains (product, house, candidate, hotel) with 100 images each (Table 1).

In a human study with 154 participants (1,920 and 1,600 judgment observations across two experiments), participants chose the original (unedited) image only about 30% of the time versus roughly 66% for final optimized versions under some strategies (Section 4.3, Table 3).

Automatic interpretability analysis of revealed preferences identifies consistent visual themes driving VLM selection, e.g., botanical elements and warm lighting for hotels, twilight lighting and landscaping for houses, and professional attire for people images (Section 4).

A three-pass image-normalization mitigation strategy reduces but does not fully close the choice-probability gap between original and optimized images, indicating persistent VLM vulnerability to visual edits (Section 4.5, Figure 4).

fQYwAlpK3V.text: Residual Context Diffusion (RCD) converts discarded token representations at masked positions into contextual residuals, computed as an entropy-weighted aggregation over the model's own embedding codebook, which are injected into subsequent denoising steps (Section 3).
On SDAR-8B with block size 32, RCD nearly doubles baseline accuracy on AIME24, raising it from 11.67% to 21.46% (Table 1).
On LLaDA, RCD improves GSM8K accuracy from 75.74% to 78.09% and MinervaMath accuracy from 31.10% to 37.00% (Table 2).
Under a throughput-matched comparison controlling for inference speed, RCD still yields 2-9% accuracy improvements over the sequential-denoising baseline across benchmarks (Table 3).
RCD requires only about 300 million to 1 billion additional training tokens to adapt an existing diffusion LLM, outperforming the Loopholing baseline under matched training budgets (Table 4).
RCD achieves 4-5x fewer denoising steps than the baseline at equivalent accuracy levels, as shown on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier (Figure 4).

JOy3UmERXS.text: V1-Infer, an uncertainty-guided pairwise ranking algorithm with a topology-coverage phase followed by Swiss-style tournament refinement, improves Pass@1 by 4.3-10.0% over pointwise verification baselines on LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, AIME, and HMMT (Section 4, Figure 3).
On SWE-Bench Lite (300 instances), pairwise verification reaches a 33.3% resolve rate versus 28.3% for pointwise verification, a 5.0 percentage-point gain (Figure 6).

V1-PairRL, which co-trains a single model as generator and pairwise verifier under a unified reward objective, improves test-time scaling by 6.5-7.3% over standard pointwise co-training RL (Figure 10).
V1-PairRL improves base Pass@1 (without test-time scaling) by up to 8.7% on CodeContests through joint training of the generator and pairwise verifier (Figure 10).

Recursive Self-Aggregation (RSA), a prior pointwise consolidation method, is shown to exhibit 'diversity collapse,' where Pass@N performance paradoxically decreases as refinement steps increase, in contrast to V1-Infer (Section 3, Figure 1).

ptbzlHzmEv.text: HiST represents measured spatial transcriptomics locations as a lattice-indexed sparse field rather than a dense slide grid, so that runtime and memory scale with the number of observed locations rather than the physical slide area (Section 3.1).

On the HEST-1k multi-organ benchmark, HiST improves R^2 from 0.27 to 0.34 (a 26% relative improvement) and Pearson correlation from 0.54 to 0.59 (a 9% relative improvement) over the STFlow baseline (Table 2).
HiST reduces per-slide inference time to 0.07 seconds versus 0.76 seconds for STFlow, and peak memory to 1.38 GB versus 46.37 GB for STFlow (Table 1).

A learnable slide calibration token attends to all tissue tokens to absorb slide-specific acquisition variation (e.g., staining and scanner differences) and broadcasts a global correction back to condition local predictions (Section 3.4).

Ablation studies on the Brain dataset show that removing the slide calibration token, coordinate augmentation, positional encoding, or skip connections each degrades HiST's predictive performance (Table 3).

fFUI2PGaNG.text: AgentScore achieves a mean AUROC of 0.71 across eight clinical prediction tasks (MIMIC-IV and eICU datasets), outperforming RiskSLIM (0.66) and FasterRisk (0.68) despite using stricter parsimony constraints (Section 5.1, Table 3).

An ablation removing deterministic validation (using an unconstrained LLM alone to select rules) degrades mean AUROC from 0.71 to 0.59, demonstrating the necessity of the statistical screening stage (Section 5.4, Table 4).

AgentScore exceeds the SOFA and SAPS-I scores on the PhysioNet ICU 2012 mortality prediction task and outperforms Cystic Fibrosis Foundation guideline-based lung transplant referral criteria in external cross-institutional validation (Section 5.2, Figure 3).

In a clinician preference study with 18 practitioners (72 judgments), 85% preferred AgentScore for guideline-style reasoning alignment (p<10^-9) and 67% preferred it overall versus 6% for FasterRisk (Section 5.3).

AgentScore's rule-proposal stage uses an LLM agent restricted to a clinically motivated grammar (threshold rules, physiologic ratios, temporal patterns, logical AND/OR compositions) and never accesses raw patient-level data, interacting only through aggregate statistics tools (Section 4).

4T8vEVK79x.text: Three natural greedy allocation rules (maximize relative item value, allocate to most unsatisfied agent, and minimize worst predicted dissatisfaction) each fail to guarantee any positive multiplicative approximation to PROP1 against an adaptive adversary (Section 3, Propositions 6-8).

Against a non-adaptive adversary, uniform random allocation achieves an Ω(1/log(n/δ)) approximation to PROP1 with probability at least 1-δ, specifically α = 27/(128·log(n/δ)), the first such multiplicative bound in the online setting without extra assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 9).
Given perfect maximum-item-value (MIV) predictions, Algorithm 1 guarantees a 1/n-PROP1 allocation (Section 5, Theorem 11).
Under one-sided MIV prediction error ε ∈ [0,1), the algorithm's approximation degrades gracefully to β = (1-ε)/(n-ε/n) (Section 5, Theorem 12).
Even with perfect MIV predictions, no online algorithm can achieve any non-zero approximation to EF1, MMS, or PROPX (Section 5, Proposition 10).

jALSox02QD.text: BAR-L with classifier-free guidance achieves a state-of-the-art gFID of 0.99 on ImageNet-256, surpassing the concurrent continuous method RAE (1.13 gFID) (Table 3).

BAR-B, using only 415M parameters, reaches a gFID of 1.13, outperforming discrete autoregressive baselines RAR (1.48), VAR (1.92), and LlamaGen (2.18) while using 4x fewer parameters than RAR's 1.5B (Table 3).
BAR-B matches or exceeds continuous-token methods xAR (1.24 gFID), DDT (1.26), VA-VAE (1.35), and MAR (1.55) (Table 3).
BAR achieves a 20.45x sampling speedup over MAR and a 3.68x speedup over RAE, with BAR-B/4 reaching 445.48 images/second (Table 4).
BAR converges faster during training than prior continuous-token approaches due to masked bit modeling of discrete tokens (Section discussing training efficiency).

M9I9QsyEDF.text: Without any future information, no online algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio strictly greater than 0 with respect to EF1 for n≥2 agents (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
Without future information, no online algorithm achieves a meaningful approximation to PROP1 even for two agents, per a result attributed to Benadè et al. (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).

Given normalization information (agents' total valuations), Algorithm 1 achieves an exact EF1 allocation for n=2 agents (Section 4, Theorem 4.1) and an exact PROP1 allocation for any n≥2 agents (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

With normalization information, Algorithm 1's EF1 result yields 0.5-MMS for two agents as a corollary, improving on the 0.5-MMS-only guarantee (without PROP1 or EF1) of Zhou et al. (2023) (Section 4).
Even with normalization information, no positive approximation to EFX is possible for n≥2 (Theorem 4.3), and no positive approximation to EF1 is possible for n≥3 (Theorem 4.4).

usJwxV4CQh.text: On the Van der Pol system with noise σ=0.50 and inter-observation interval τ=240, the proposed geometric method achieves wRMSE 0.750±0.038 versus 1.409±0.019 for a Gaussian-process baseline, a roughly 47% error reduction at large τ (Table 1).
On the Hopf system at τ=300, the geometric method attains wRMSE 0.237±0.010, substantially outperforming LatentSDE (1.161±0.053) and the GP baseline (0.969±0.015) (Table 2).

The method outperforms SVISE, which fails at large τ, and KM-basis (Kramers-Moyal), which deteriorates for τ>150, as well as Ornstein-Uhlenbeck bridge augmentation (Batz et al.), which assumes linearized dynamics (Figure 3).

Geometry-guided path augmentation improves accuracy across EM iterations on Van der Pol (τ=240, σ=0.25), yielding about 18% improvement after the first iteration and about 35% after the second, with error stabilizing within 2 EM iterations (Figure 2).

The method remains effective even with only one observation per oscillation period, a regime where purely temporal (non-geometric) methods completely fail (Section describing sparse-sampling results).

CJ7aYueFJ3.text: Rectified Distribution Matching Regularization (RDMReg) aligns representations to a Rectified Generalized Gaussian (RGG) distribution (Definition 3.4), whose expected ℓ₀ norm equals d·Φ_GN(0,1)(μ/σ), giving explicit parametric control over sparsity via {μ, σ, p} (Proposition 3.5).
The RGG distribution provably preserves maximum-entropy properties under a Rényi information dimension framework despite being a mixture with a point mass at zero (Theorem 3.6).

On ImageNet-100 linear probing, Rectified LpJEPA with RGN_2.0(0,σ_GN) achieves 85.08% encoder accuracy at 0.3412 ℓ₁ sparsity, and with RGN_1.0(0,σ_GN) achieves 84.72% accuracy at 0.2726 ℓ₁ sparsity, versus the dense LeJEPA baseline's 84.80% accuracy at 0.6365 ℓ₁ sparsity (Section 5.8, Table 1).
Downstream linear-probe accuracy drops sharply only once more than about 95% of representation entries are zero, indicating substantial exploitable sparsity without performance loss (Figure 2c).
The learned sparse representations exhibit lower normalized HSIC values than VICReg baselines, indicating greater statistical independence among dimensions (Figure 3b).

NNU8cO5wte.text: VBFN lifts the factorized Bayesian Flow Network belief family to a joint Gaussian variational belief family governed by structured precisions, performing Bayesian updates via symmetric positive definite linear systems solved with a Conjugate Gradient solver (Section 3).
On the QM9 molecular dataset, VBFN attains 99.98% validity, an FCD of 0.083, and a scaffold similarity of 0.9519, each the best among compared baselines (Table 2).
On ZINC250k, VBFN achieves the lowest FCD (1.307) and NSPDK (0.0007) and the highest scaffold similarity (0.6057) among compared methods (Table 2).

On synthetic graph benchmarks (Planar, Tree, SBM), VBFN attains the lowest (best) generation ratio of any method, e.g. 1.4 on Tree versus 4.0 for the top baseline, while maintaining comparable V.U.N. scores (Table 1).

An ablation disabling coupled node-edge updates (λx=0, λa=0) collapses QM9 performance to FCD 25.926, NSPDK 1.1126, and scaffold similarity 0.0, versus FCD 0.083 and scaffold similarity 0.9519 with full coupling (λx=1, λa=1), showing coupling is essential despite validity remaining high (Table 3).

29m0TW0Xb3.text: The staged knowledge injection recipe first cold-starts the model on 148,777 Earth-science text-only QA pairs with chain-of-thought reasoning before any image-text training (Section on three-stage training recipe).

The full three-stage recipe consists of text-only cold-start, pre-warming on hard UHR image-text examples during supervised fine-tuning, and agentic RLVR with zoom-in tools for evidence refinement (Methodology section).
The proposed 7B-parameter model achieves 60.40% Pass@1 and 96.25% Pass@32 on XLRS-Bench (Table 4).
The 7B model's 60.40% Pass@1 on XLRS-Bench exceeds the 241B-parameter Intern-S1 (55.0%), GPT-5.2 (47.53%), Gemini 2.5 Pro (45.2%), and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B (51.11%) (Table 4).
Text-only Earth-science domain knowledge yields larger Pass@1 gains than incorporating image-text data during the initial training stage (Results/discussion section).

AJb9PuUibK.text: Theorem 4.1 (Message Tuning Has Greater Adaptation Capacity) proves that MTG's reachable representation manifold has intrinsic dimension, Hausdorff measure, and diameter each greater than or equal to that of graph prompt tuning's manifold, formally establishing MTG's larger adaptation capacity (Theorem 4.1).

Message Tuning injects learnable message prototypes M^(l) in R^(m x d_(l-1)) into each GNN layer to adaptively guide message fusion without updating the pre-trained backbone's weights (Section on Message Tuning method).

Standard graph prompt tuning suffers from information loss because the prompt's influence is compressed by the product of layer-wise Jacobian singular values across the frozen graph foundation model (Section 3/4 theoretical analysis).
In 5-shot node classification on Cora, MTG achieves 71.81% accuracy versus 66.22% for the GPF-plus baseline (Table 1).

MTG achieves the best few-shot performance across 15 benchmark datasets spanning both node classification and graph classification tasks, consistently outperforming graph prompt tuning baselines including GPF-plus and All-in-one (Table 1).

jntRRU4zcb.text: DAG comprises a Temporal Causal Module, which discovers how historical exogenous variables causally influence future exogenous variables and injects this knowledge into forecasting future endogenous values, and a Channel Causal Module, which models how historical exogenous variables affect historical endogenous variables and transfers these patterns using future exogenous information (Section on model architecture).

DAG is evaluated on 8 standard multivariate forecasting benchmarks (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Electricity, Traffic, Exchange) against 10 baselines including TimeXer, TFT, TiDE, DUET, CrossLinear, Amplifier, TimeKAN, xPatch, PatchTST, and DLinear (Experiments section).
On the 8 standard multivariate benchmarks, DAG achieves a 10.8% MSE reduction and 6.4% MAE improvement over the second-best baseline (Experimental results table).

DAG is additionally evaluated on 12 real-world TSF-X datasets, including 5 electricity price forecasting datasets (NP, PJM, BE, FR, DE) and 7 proprietary datasets (Energy, Colbún, Rapel, Sdwpfm1, Sdwpfm2, Sdwpfh1, Sdwpfh2), ranking first in 26 of the MSE metrics and 29 of the MAE metrics among tested configurations (Experiments section, results tables).

pvaviwbsry.text: StreamFlow achieves up to 611% acceleration for 512x512 image generation while existing acceleration methods achieve only up to 18% in the same setting (Section on experimental results/Table).
The TensorRT+TAESD+VFB configuration reaches 10.05 FPS versus a 1.87 FPS baseline while maintaining under 1% quality degradation (Table 2).

StreamFlow's three core components are batched velocity field processing that decouples step size from the velocity field for parallel queue processing with heterogeneous step lengths (Algorithm 1), heterogeneous timestep vectorization enabling a unified adaptive scheduler across samples at different denoising stages (Equation 6), and dynamic TensorRT compilation that decomposes heterogeneous batches into individual TensorRT calls at runtime (Algorithm 3).
StreamFlow reduces power consumption by 47% (110W versus 205W baseline) and memory usage by 20-30% (2,666-3,012 MB versus 3,788 MB), yielding 11x better performance per watt (Table 1).

StreamFlow maintains 4-5x acceleration across resolutions from 64px to 1024px and outperforms the baseline at 8-step inference compared to the baseline's 4-step inference (Scalability results section).

bSUMVAYoMq.text: RAMBO models the surrogate as a Dirichlet Process Mixture of Gaussian Processes and derives a closed-form cluster marginal likelihood p(y_k|X_k,θ_k)=N(y_k|0,K_k+σ²_n,k I) (Proposition 6, Section 3).

RAMBO decomposes predictive variance into intra-regime (aleatoric) and inter-regime (epistemic) uncertainty components, with the acquisition function expressed as a weight-sum of per-component Expected Improvement (Theorem 8, Theorem 9, Section 4).

On 12D molecular conformer optimization of pentadecane (C15H32, 3^12=531,441 candidate minima), RAMBO reaches 8.05 kcal/mol versus SAASBO's 13.36 kcal/mol, a 39.73% improvement, within 50 iterations (Section 6.2, Figure 1).
On 50D drug discovery virtual screening against cancer target PDB 6T2W, RAMBO achieves a docking score of -13.31 versus TuRBO's -12.79, a 4.06% improvement, over 500 iterations (Figure 1).

On 81D stellarator fusion reactor design (quasi-isodynamic plasma confinement via Fourier boundary coefficients), RAMBO improves Q_i by approximately 51.55% over the best competing baseline and discovers 3-5 regimes tied to distinct magnetic topologies (Figure 1).

Inference uses collapsed Gibbs sampling with Chinese Restaurant Process cluster assignments and 500 burn-in iterations, benchmarked against Standard GP, TuRBO, SAASBO, BAxUS, ALEBO, HEBO, Bounce, SMAC, and COMBO (Algorithm 1, Appendix B.1).

vht4Pn0swG.text: Vegas (SpecAttn) achieves a 1.25-2.70x throughput speedup over vanilla vLLM decoding on the AIME25 and CodeElo benchmarks (Figure 9, Section 5.2).
Vegas achieves a 1.15-1.23x throughput improvement over the MagicDec-Stream self-speculative decoding baseline on the same benchmarks (Section 5.2).
On LongBench-v2 long-context tasks (96K-120K token contexts), Vegas delivers 18-29% higher throughput than baselines (Section 5.3).

Vegas selects KV entries by maximizing cumulative attention logits across all draft tokens rather than a single-token criterion, using a 'Collect-2-Query' mechanism that extracts logits only from the first draft and bonus tokens (Equation 2, Section 3.2-3.3).
Vegas incurs only 5.9-9.4% KV-selection overhead compared to 21.7% for MagicDec-Quest and 11.2-29.1% for SpecExtend (Figure 10b).
Experiments evaluate Qwen3-4B/8B/30B and gpt-oss-20b on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, with an optimal sparse ratio of approximately 7% identified via a three-step hyperparameter search (Section 5.1, Appendix B).

QwE8cOtclR.text: Middle layers (e.g., Layer 12) exhibit the strongest attention-sink concentration, with up to approximately 9.5% of incoming attention mass on a single token, and sink identity overlaps with the fixed index-0 token less than 0.2% of the time (Section 3.2, Table 1, Figure 2).

Suppressing single-layer (L12) or multi-layer (L6+12+18) attention sinks across 553 GenEval prompts produces CLIP-T changes within the equivalence margin of |Δ|<0.002 (e.g., -0.0005 [-0.0017,0.0007] and +0.0009 [-0.0001,0.0020]) (Section 3.3.1, Tables 2-4).
Attention-sink suppression achieves reduction factors exceeding 10^8x in attention mass at targeted positions while leaving alignment metrics essentially unchanged (Table 4).

Cross-architecture validation on SDXL shows preserved CLIP-T alignment under self-attention (Δ=+0.0004 [-0.0005,0.0014]) and cross-attention (Δ=-0.0003 [-0.0019,0.0012]) sink suppression despite larger perceptual shifts (Section 3.5, Table 5).
Sink-targeted masking induces approximately 6x larger perceptual shifts (LPIPS) than equal-budget random masking, despite comparable alignment scores (Section 3.5.2-3.5.3, Table 7).
HPS-v2 preference scores degrade only at larger removal budgets (k≥10 of top attention recipients), while CLIP-T remains stable across all tested budgets k∈{1,5,10,20,50} (Section 3.6, Appendix I).

SXOqLX0T6X.text: Model fusion is formalized as a decomposition into grouping error and approximation error components (Theorem 1, Equation 4).

The paper proposes Hungarian Fusion for equal-sized models with optimal one-to-one neuron matching (Theorem 2a) and K-means Fusion with a (9+ε)-approximation guarantee for models of arbitrary size (Theorem 2b, Section 4.3).
In the non-IID setting on VGG11/CIFAR-10, K-means Linear Fusion achieves 84.5% (2-way), 78.9% (4-way), and 69.6% (8-way) accuracy, outperforming OTFusion and Git Re-Basin baselines (Table 1).
In the sharded ViT/CIFAR-100 setting, K-means Gradient Fusion reaches 49.4% (2-way), 38.5% (4-way), and 33.1% (6-way) accuracy, approaching ensemble performance (Table 2).

With additional fine-tuning on the full dataset, K-means Gradient Fusion achieves 75.3% accuracy in the 2-way setting, a +1.9% gain over the base model, matching ensemble accuracy at single-model inference cost (Table 3).

Neuron-importance-score-weighted clustering improves fusion quality over unweighted clustering (Section 5.5, Figure 2), and the Gradient Fusion variant requires substantially more fusion time as sample count grows (632.5s at 6000 samples vs. 38.1s at 400) (Table 7).

g3Hrh5aoal.text: FedTreeLoRA constructs a binary merge tree via agglomerative hierarchical clustering on client LoRA B-matrices using a Global Distance Matrix of Frobenius distances between client updates (Section 5.1).

FedTreeLoRA determines the per-layer cluster count via the Silhouette Coefficient under a monotonicity constraint (cluster counts non-decreasing with depth), controlled by a heterogeneity threshold τ (Section 5.2).
On GLUE (RoBERTa-Large), FedTreeLoRA achieves 92.36% average accuracy, outperforming FedLEASE (91.19%) and FedIT (+5.16% gain) with about 0.020% additional parameter overhead (Table 1).
On the FLAN NLG benchmark collection (LLaMA-2-7B, four tasks), FedTreeLoRA achieves 63.19 average ROUGE-1, surpassing FedLEASE's 61.71 at the same parameter budget as FedIT (Table 2).

Ablations show fixed global aggregation (k=1) drops to 87.20% and fixed fine-grained aggregation (k=8) reaches 90.74%, versus 92.36% for the adaptive layer-wise depth alignment (Table 4); global tree structure outperforms independent per-layer clustering, 92.36% vs 89.47% (Table 5).

FedTreeLoRA's convergence rate is proven to be O(1/√T) under standard smooth non-convex assumptions, matching FedAvg, with a composite error constant capturing both local-update and tree-aggregation error (Theorem 5.1, Section 5.4).

Afb6Yo2rIf.text: BabelRS achieves 51.57 mAP and 53.02 H-mAP on the SOI-Det benchmark, outperforming the SM3Det state-of-the-art baseline (50.20 mAP, 51.31 H-mAP) (Table 2).

Language-pivoted pretraining via Concept-Shared Instruction Aligning (CSIA) decouples modality alignment from downstream detection task learning by aligning each sensor modality (RGB, SAR, Infrared) to shared linguistic concepts (Section 3).

Layerwise Visual-Semantic Annealing (LVSA) progressively fuses multi-scale visual features using a time-dependent coefficient alpha(t)=min(t/tau,1), improving performance from 49.33 mAP/50.67 H-mAP (baseline merge) to 51.57 mAP/53.02 H-mAP (Table 5).

Under automatic mixed-precision (AMP) fine-tuning, late-alignment pretraining methods (MAE, BEiTv2, DINOv2, ScaleMAE) diverge to NaN, whereas BabelRS remains stable, achieving 50.17 mAP and 51.52 H-mAP (Table 4, Figure 2).

On a ViT-Large backbone, BabelRS (51.57 mAP, 53.02 H-mAP) substantially outperforms CLIP (36.12 mAP, 37.12 H-mAP), MAE (42.84 mAP, 42.54 H-mAP), and DINOv2 (45.02 mAP, 44.34 H-mAP) pretraining (Table 3).

Appendix A's Proposition 3 argues language-pivoted pretraining yields non-negative expected inter-modality gradient inner products (E[⟨g_mi,g_mj⟩] ≥ 0) for most modality pairs, improving gradient alignment relative to late-alignment approaches whose gradient conflict is characterized in Proposition 1 (Appendix A, Propositions 1 and 3).

eIl0JeVfFs.text: An adapted feature-space distance-to-decision-boundary (fDBD) OOD detector achieves 69.24 AUROC for hallucination detection on CSQA with Llama-3.2-3B, versus 63.23 AUROC for a perplexity baseline (Table 1).

The fDBD-based detector generalizes across three reasoning benchmarks and two models, reaching 76.36 AUROC on GSM8K and 76.20 AUROC on AQuA with Llama-3.2-3B, and 72.47, 77.19, and 78.22 AUROC on CSQA, GSM8K, and AQuA respectively with Qwen-2.5-7B (Table 4).

Restricting the decision-boundary distance computation to the top-k=1,000 candidate tokens yields peak performance (69.24 AUROC on CSQA), addressing the computational challenge of the full vocabulary space (Table 2, Section 4).

The proposed detectors are training-free and single-sample based, requiring no labeled hallucination data, in contrast to prior methods that require training or multiple sampled generations (Section 1).
fDBD remains robust to stochastic decoding, maintaining approximately 69 AUROC (69.30±0.56 at temperature 0.2) across sampling temperatures from 0.2 to 1.0 on CSQA (Table 3).

dlufiUI3xI.text: Geometry-Aware Distillation (GAD) matches Jacobian-vector products between student and teacher via a finite-difference response-vector objective, ‖(Φ_S(z')−Φ_S(z)) − sg(Φ_T(z')−Φ_T(z))‖², to restore differential response to input noise perturbations (Section 4.1, Equation 6).
Adding GAD to the LADD distillation baseline on SD2 raises seed-identifiability accuracy from 87.60% to 92.40%, closer to the teacher's 93.70% (Table 2).
On the layout-control task measured by AP, GAD recovers degraded controllability from 5.0 AP (LADD baseline) to 5.8 AP, versus the teacher's 6.6 AP, an 87% recovery of the gap (Table 5).

On PixArt-alpha, GAD improves diversity as measured by Vendi Score from 2.7187 (TDM baseline) to 2.7967 while also raising CLIP score from 33.42 to 33.53, outperforming a naive noise-augmentation ablation (Vendi 2.6355) (Table 7).
GAD applied to SiD improves CLIP score from 32.75 to 34.40 while maintaining or improving PickScore across SD2, PixArt-alpha, and SANA backbones (Table 3).

GAD adds no inference-time cost, only training overhead, e.g. +61.66% training time and +46.82% memory for LADD, +36.30% time and +3.72% memory for TDM, and +66.51% time and +18.28% memory for SiD (Appendix B, Table 10).

EtEopxVrbG.text: Spatial inconsistency in multi-head attention correlates with hallucinations: real tokens exhibit low-entropy attention distributions while hallucinated tokens show higher-entropy, bimodal distributions (Section 3.2, Finding 1).

Visual Attention Ratio (VAR) decreases over the course of generation, and hallucinated tokens disproportionately cluster in low-VAR regions, indicating temporal attenuation of visual focus (Section 3.3, Finding 2, Figure 3).

Theorem 5.1 shows cross-head attention inconsistency increases Rademacher complexity, and Theorem 5.2 establishes a tighter generalization error bound when attention heads maintain consistent semantic focus (Section 5, Theorems 5.1 and 5.2).

AFIP is training-free, correcting attention distraction via head-level aggregation with mean/variance regularization (Section 4.1, Equation 7) plus a dynamic historical attention enhancement over an 8-token window (Section 4.2, Equation 10).
On the CHAIR benchmark at 512 tokens with LLaVA-1.5-7B, AFIP reduces CHAIR_S to 16.8 and CHAIR_I to 4.4 versus the HGAI baseline's 24.6 and 6.4, while raising precision from 86.8 to 91.3 (Table 1).
On the POPE benchmark, AFIP achieves leading accuracy across Random (≥87.11%), Popular (≥87.70%), and Adversarial (≥82.87%) evaluation settings (Table 2).

M8rkTsq2gZ.text: Proposition 1 (Section 3.1) shows via first-order derivative analysis that an aggressive classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale early in sampling has a negative effect on residual norm when misaligned with data-consistency (DC) guidance, while the COS-SIM2 metric (Equation 11) shows added stochasticity improves alignment with the data distribution score function, effectively bringing the trajectory back toward higher-probability regions (Section 3, Equations 10-11).

The derived triadic scheduling principle prescribes decreasing DC guidance scale beta(t), increasing CFG scale lambda(t), and decreasing stochasticity eta(t) over the course of sampling (Section 3.3).

TriPS_G, optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization over Bernstein-polynomial schedules, achieves PSNR 28.55 / LPIPS 0.107 / FID 22.18 on FFHQ 8x super-resolution with SD3.5-M (NFE=28), outperforming the FLAIR baseline (28.88 PSNR, 0.123 LPIPS) on LPIPS and FID (Table 1).
On motion deblurring with a 61x61 kernel and FFHQ, TriPS_G achieves LPIPS 0.059, versus 0.095 for the FLAIR baseline (Section 5, Table 1).
With SD1.5 (NFE=50) on FFHQ super-resolution x8, TriPS_G reaches PSNR 28.02 / LPIPS 0.164, beating the TReg baseline's PSNR 26.34 / LPIPS 0.254 (Table 3).
A TriPS_G schedule trained on FFHQ SR x8 transfers to Gaussian deblurring (PSNR 28.90, LPIPS 0.089) and SR x12 (PSNR 28.80, LPIPS 0.099) without retraining (Table 2).

6GpYUWbqOQ.text: PINN and FNO loss landscapes show Hessian outlier eigenvalues exceeding 10^3-10^4, compared to only around 10 for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 (Figure 6).
A three-regime taxonomy (Regime I well-trained, Regime II under-trained, Regime III over-trained) is used to characterize SciML training outcomes (Section 2.2, Figure 1).
The Augmented Lagrangian Method shifts the trainability boundary from beta approximately 25 to beta approximately 50, expanding the well-trained Regime I (Figure 3c).
NNCG reduces test error by roughly 50% in Regime I but becomes unstable in Regimes II and III, showing no method is uniformly effective across regimes (Figure 4).

Deceptive Sharpness and Deceptive Flatness are identified as failure modes where high Hessian eigenvalues coincide with the lowest training loss, or flat regions occur at elevated training loss, undermining standard CV loss-landscape metric interpretations (Section 2.5.2, Figures 7, 11, 12, 13).

FnB7lFzsJz.text: SD-MoE reduces spectral similarity in the dominant 1% subspace of expert parameters from about 0.8 in baseline MoE models to about 0.1, a roughly 70% reduction in expert overlap (Section 2.1, Figure 4).

SD-MoE yields an average 3% gain on downstream tasks across both 2B/0.8B and 7B/1.5B model scales while adding only about 5% computational overhead during training and zero overhead at inference (Table 1, Table 3).
SD-MoE increases the maximum stable learning rate roughly 4x, remaining stable up to 4x10^-4 versus divergence at 1x10^-4 for the baseline (Figure 7).
Sensitivity analysis over common subspace rank k in {2,4,8,16,32} identifies k=8 as the optimal setting (Table 2).

SD-MoE is integrated into Qwen and DeepSeek MoE architectures via parameter spectral decoupling at initialization and gradient spectral decomposition during training (Section 3.2, Section 3.3, Section 4).

MrupCemBMy.text: OMNISAPIENS-7B 2.0 achieves a +16.85% multitask performance gain and a +9.37% gain on held-out behavioral tasks versus existing behavioral foundation models, with an average task rank of 1.20 across 10 tasks (Table 1).
HARPO improves over GRPO by up to +42.29% on specific tasks and achieves an average rank of 1.70 versus GRPO's 3.30 (Section 4.2).
On autism behavior recognition, OMNISAPIENS-7B 2.0 reaches 39.91% accuracy, about 2 points above HumanOmniV2-7B and 9 points above the prior OmniSapiens-7B RL version (Table 2).
On speech emotion recognition, OMNISAPIENS-7B 2.0 reaches 72.11%, roughly 9 points above HumanOmniV2-7B and 16 points above the prior version (Table 2).

Ablations show removing HARPO's inertial control drops average rank from 1.90 to 2.70, and removing sample-level modulation drops it to 2.60, demonstrating HARPO balances learning across heterogeneous behavioral tasks by modulating advantages (Table 3).
On sarcasm detection, HARPO produces longer, more varied, and more explicit reasoning traces compared to GRPO's minimal responses (Section 4.4, Figures 1-3).

DUmWdZetqZ.text: Theorem 3.2 establishes that the FC2FB meta-algorithm converts a fixed-confidence algorithm into a fixed-budget algorithm whose error probability decays exponentially in the budget (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).

When the fixed-confidence sample complexity is T*_delta = A*ln(1/delta) + C, FC2FB yields a fixed-budget sample complexity of O(A*ln(1/delta)*ln(A*ln(1/delta)/Q) + C), matching the fixed-confidence complexity up to logarithmic factors (Section 3).
FCW2S (Algorithm 4) converts a weak fixed-confidence algorithm (Definition 4.1) into a strong one (Definition 3.1) via parallel execution and majority voting (Section 4).
FC2AT (Algorithm 6) is an anytime variant of the meta-algorithm using a doubling trick that requires no prior knowledge of the budget (Section 4).
The framework's sample-complexity improvements are demonstrated on heterogeneous noise bandits (Corollary 5.2), linear bandits (Corollary 5.4), and unimodal bandits (Corollary 5.7) (Section 5).

XFHjS8kw6X.text: At larger batch sizes, 51.09% of samples participate in high-similarity representation pairs, illustrating the representation-overlap problem that causes retrieval-based editing methods to fail in batch settings (Section 3.3, Figure 2c).

On MedCF++ with Meditron-7B at 100 batch edits, MedREK achieves 77.96% Efficacy, 79.88% Generality, and 97.76% Locality, versus 68.30% Efficacy, 70.74% Generality, and 72.74% Locality for the RECIPE baseline (Table 2).
MedREK combines a shared query-key module for precise matching with an attention-based prompt encoder for informative guidance (Section 4.2).
Ablating the shared MLP component drops Efficacy to 56.74%, showing its contribution to MedREK's batch-editing performance (Table 4).
MedREK is evaluated for single- and batch-editing at 1, 10, 50, and 100 edits on both Meditron-7B (Table 2) and HuatuoGPT-o1-8B (Table 3), and on the MedVersa and MedCF++ benchmarks (Section 5.2).

gAXiBfnvbD.text: PROBE uses a two-stage pipeline where the detector guides generator fine-tuning via LoRA to synthesize challenging boundary samples, then the detector is retrained on those samples (Section 3.1-3.2).
PROBE-ResNet50 achieves 78.1% average balanced accuracy across a seven-benchmark evaluation, a +14.6% improvement over the baseline (Table 1).
PROBE-DINOv2 achieves 96.8% balanced accuracy on GenImage (+10.0%) and 92.9% on AIGI-Quality-Paradox (+5.0%) (Table 2).
PROBE-DINOv2 reaches 97.5% average balanced accuracy on the Synthbuster benchmark, a +5.6% gain over baseline (Table 3).
PROBE-DINOv2 achieves 93.8% average balanced accuracy across GAN and autoregressive generators, a +10.1% improvement over the DINOv2 baseline (Table 5).
Combining boundary samples from multiple detectors yields only a marginal +0.8% accuracy gain, indicating different detectors converge on similar failure regions (Table 8).

ftM5GTQAh1.text: RobuQ achieves stable image generation on ImageNet-1K with activations quantized to an average of 2 bits under the W1.58A2 configuration (Abstract).
On ImageNet-1K 256x256 with cfg=4.0 and 50 steps, RobuQ W1.58A2 attains FID 11.06 and Inception Score 273.58, while W1.58A4 attains FID 12.64 and IS 349.22 (Table 1).
Starting from a BitNetv2 baseline with FID 41.59 at W1.58A4, adding the low-rank branch improves FID to 29.59, and adding the full Hadamard transformation further improves it to 20.82 (Table 2).
The Adaptive Mixed-Precision Network (AMPN) pipeline allocates layer-specific activation bit-widths via dynamic programming across L layers (Section 3.3.1).
RobuQ W1.58A2 reduces FLOPs from 114.52G to 6.61G and model size from 2,575.4MB to 194.75MB relative to FP32, yielding a 17.3x theoretical speedup and 13.2x model compression (Table 3).

42RDNNJdWf.text: The Clamp Policy selects a threshold t̃ = min{max{t*_p̂, ceil(λb)}, floor(b/λ)} for a tunable robustness parameter λ in (0,1) (Definition 4.1, Section 4).

Theorem 4.4 bounds the competitive ratio by min{1 + 1/λ - 1/b, [ρ_p̂(t̃) + bθ]/(1-θ)}, giving robustness independent of prediction error η and consistency approaching the optimal ratio as η approaches 0 (Theorem 4.4, Corollary 4.5).
The Water-Filling Algorithm's optimal randomized stopping distribution follows the geometric CDF F*(x) = min{(R-1)((1+1/(b-1))^x - 1), 1} for cost-monotone settings (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).
A stopping distribution is R-robust if and only if μ(x) + (b-x)F(x) ≤ (R-1)x for all 1 ≤ x ≤ b-1 and μ(∞) ≤ (R-1)b (Lemma 5.1).

Experiments show the Water-Filling Algorithm yields 5-20% consistency improvements over point-prediction baselines across diverse distributions, with the largest gains on bi-modal distributions (Table 2, Section 6).

naOfcXps5e.text: TT-Sparse is evaluated on 28 datasets comprising 14 binary, 7 multiclass, and 7 regression tasks (Table 4, Appendix A).
On binary classification tasks, TT-Sparse achieves an average rank of 1.53, including 0.9308 AUC with rule complexity 11 on the Heart dataset and 0.9147 AUC with complexity 15 on Income (Table 1).

On multiclass tasks TT-Sparse attains the best average rank of 1.0, with 0.9993 AUC on Iris (complexity 26) and 0.9901 AUC on Car (complexity 25), outperforming baselines including GOSDT, RuleFit, RRL, DWN, and TabM (Table 2).

Each TT-Sparse node's differentiable truth table can be exactly converted into DNF/CNF rule equations via truth table enumeration followed by Quine-McCluskey minimization with don't-care terms (Section 3.3).
TT-Sparse achieves superior Pareto trade-offs between accuracy and rule complexity, remaining within a human-intelligibility threshold of 50 (Figure 1).
An ablation shows TT-Sparse performance plateaus beyond 7-bit rule precision and remains robust to temperature settings of {0.001, 0.01, 0.05} (Appendix H).

SZ9ePNI4Ps.text: ShaPO enforces worst-case alignment objectives via selective geometry control restricted to an alignment-critical parameter subspace identified with safety-label linear probes (Section 3, Section 3.2).
Perturbing fewer than 0.5% of safety-critical neurons accounts for over 80% of the cumulative worst-case alignment loss (Figure 1).

On PKU-SafeRLHF-30K, ShaPO-R attains an 87.45% win rate with 1.13% MD-Judge and 0.13% NV-Judge harmfulness on LLaMA-3-8B, and 89.23% win rate with 1.13% MD-Judge and 0.00% NV-Judge on Qwen2.5-7B (Table 1).
On out-of-distribution safety benchmarks (Do-Not-Answer, HarmBench, HH-RLHF, SaladBench), ShaPO-R achieves average attack success rates of 0.70% on LLaMA-3-8B and 0.55% on Qwen2.5-7B (Table 2).
At a 40% preference label flip rate, ShaPO-R substantially outperforms baseline preference optimization methods on both Pythia-2.8B and LLaMA-3.2-3B (Figure 3).
Selective geometry control yields a lower OOD average attack success rate (26.31%) than uniform control (26.83%) on LLaMA-3-8B, demonstrating the benefit of selectivity (Table 3).

vBMdonzFEV.text: POPGym Arcade provides 7 pixel-based environments, each with 3 difficulty levels (21 task variants total), sharing a single 256x256x3 RGB observation space and a common 5-action action space across fully observable (MDP) and partially observable (POMDP) variants (Section 3).

Gradient-based saliency analysis on BattleShip shows recurrent policies attend to pixels from timesteps t=0 through t=9 when acting at t=9, even though the task is fully observable and prior observations do not affect the return (Section 4.3, Figure 4).

LRU and MinGRU recurrent policies achieve slightly higher average return on the POMDP variant than on the matched fully observable MDP variant (e.g., LRU: 0.59±0.01 POMDP vs 0.48±0.06 MDP), indicating memory models exploit history even when it is not needed (Section 6, Figure 3a).
Aggregated across the 21 environment variants, LRU attains the best overall average return (0.53±0.04), outperforming MinGRU (0.42±0.02) and an MLP baseline (0.45±0.01) (Figure 3a).

POPGym Arcade runs at roughly 10,000-40,000 frames per second on an RTX4090 GPU via a JAX-based hardware-accelerated implementation, substantially faster than Atari and competitive with MinAtar despite far larger pixel observations (Figure 2).

ReSBUj2514.text: TileQ arranges the low-rank quantization factors of all K experts in a mixture-of-experts layer into a shared 2D-tiled layout via singular subspace clustering, reducing per-expert low-rank overhead to about 0.04 bits versus 0.32 bits for prior per-expert low-rank quantization approaches (Section 3.1, Table 1).

On Mixtral-8x7B at 3-bit quantization, TileQ reaches 4.13 perplexity on WikiText-2 compared to a 3.87 FP16 baseline, cutting additional memory usage by up to 10x relative to existing MoE compression methods (Table 1).

The LoTileMoE inference kernel (Section 3.2) fuses expert computations into dense tensor operations, reducing prefill-phase inference latency to about 5% of the unfused baseline latency (Figure 3, A800 GPU).

TileQ is evaluated on five MoE architectures spanning roughly 2.7B to 80B total/active parameters: Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, Mixtral-8x7B, and Deepseek-MoE-16B, using WikiText-2 perplexity plus ARC-Challenge, PIQA, WinoGrande, MMLU, and HellaSwag (Section 4, Table 1).

BJpOvFcCh3.text: HybridOM couples a differentiable finite-volume physical solver on an Arakawa C-grid (governing tracers via conservative flux formulation and momentum via quasi-geostrophic potential vorticity) with a neural Ocean Dynamics Model that learns residual corrections, where the physical solver adds only 20-30% computational overhead relative to the neural component (Section 3).

On 60-day global hindcasts against GLORYS12V1 reanalysis and the OceanBench benchmark, HybridOM achieves the lowest weighted RMSE for temperature, salinity, and velocity across 15-40 day horizons and the highest marine-heatwave detection Critical Success Index (0.6701 at the 90th percentile threshold) among compared methods (Table 1).

In operational forecasting coupled with the FuXi-2.0 weather model, HybridOM at 0.25-degree resolution attains a 0.250 RMSE for day-1 sea surface temperature and outperforms WenHai, XiHe, and GLONet baselines at 1-9 day lead times, with day-1 Lagrangian trajectory error of 3.9 km in the Gulf region (Table 2).

A Flux Gating mechanism operating in physical flux space, combining Differentiable Flux Gating and Neural Information Injection, enables regional downscaling to 0.25-degree North Pacific resolution while preserving stability and physical consistency across the coarse-to-fine transition (Section 3.5.1).

Ablations show the physical skeleton dominates long-term (60+ day) forecast stability while variations in the neural architecture primarily affect short-term (10-day) skill, and that local windowed attention and global grid-based attention branches of the Dual-Scale Ocean Attention module contribute comparably to multi-scale accuracy (Section 3, ablation results).

Dl8vXnJJQi.text: FG-CLIP 2 extends the SigLIP 2 dual-encoder architecture with a multilingual Gemma tokenizer supporting 196-token text inputs (up from 64), a data-adaptive vision resolution strategy selecting among {128, 256, 576, 784, 1024} pixels, and a masked attention pooling head, released in Base, Large, and So400M variants (Section 3).

Training uses a two-stage hierarchical scheme: Stage 1 global alignment on short and long image-text captions, and Stage 2 joint optimization of five objectives including a novel Textual Intra-modal Contrastive (TIC) loss that mines hard negatives among high-similarity caption pairs to sharpen fine-grained textual discrimination (Section 3).

FG-CLIP 2 is evaluated on 29 datasets across 8 tasks spanning English and Chinese, including new Chinese benchmarks introduced in this work: LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN for long-caption retrieval, and BoxClass-CN, a 566-category region-classification dataset with 66,258 region-text pairs (Section 4).

On fine-grained open-vocabulary detection (FG-OVD) with the ViT-B/16 variant, FG-CLIP 2 attains 52.3% accuracy on the Hard split, 76.3% on Medium, and 80.3% on Easy, and reaches 74.9% on COCO80 and 47.3% on LVIS1203 bounding-box classification (Section 4, results tables).

FG-CLIP 2 with the So400M/16 backbone paired with LLMDet achieves 53.1 AP on LVIS open-vocabulary detection and 42.2 mIoU on ADE20k-150 dense prediction, and the overall model outperforms Meta CLIP 2 despite using fewer parameters (1.0B vs. 1.8B) (Section 4, results tables).

31iky6wFu5.text: Under standard asynchronous pipeline parallelism, gradient staleness delay increases with pipeline depth; with 32 pipeline stages, convergence speed degrades by 5.81x compared to single-stage (synchronous) training on the same model (Section 1).

Theorem 2.3 shows the convergence rate under delayed gradients degrades from O(sqrt(1/T)) to O(sqrt((1+tau)/T)), with the delay penalty scaling multiplicatively with a basis-misalignment proxy defined via the (1,1)-norm of the Hessian relative to the standard coordinate basis (Section 2.3, Theorem 2.3).

Basis rotation re-aligns the optimization coordinate basis with the Hessian eigenbasis using Kronecker-factored empirical Fisher approximations and power iteration, updating the rotation every 10 iterations in the reported experiments (Section 3).
Training a 1B-parameter LLM with basis rotation reaches the same training loss using 76.8% fewer iterations than the best asynchronous pipeline-parallel baseline (Figure 7b, Section 4.2).

For a 95M-parameter model, basis rotation reduces the required iterations by 71.6% at 32 pipeline stages and cuts the slowdown from scaling 1 to 32 stages from 4.24x down to 1.27x, while also reducing GPU time to reach a target loss by 54.3% (Figure 5, Section 4).

asec7Zx8C6.text: On AgeDB-DIR with Qwen2.5-VL-3B, the proposed CCC-GRPO framework reduces overall MAE by 13.34% versus the SFT baseline (Section 4.2, Tables 1-4).
On BoneAge-DIR, MAE drops from a zero-shot baseline of 95.36 to 18.60 with SFT and further to 14.22 with the proposed method, a 23.55% gain over SFT (Section 4.2).

The DIR benchmark for MLLMs aggregates 129,563 samples across four datasets (AgeDB, IMDB-Movie, IMDB-WIKI, BoneAge), with 113,696 naturally imbalanced training samples and 15,867 balanced test samples (Section 4.1, Figure 4).

On IMDB-Movie-DIR with Qwen2.5-VL-3B, few-shot MAE improves from 21.51 (SFT) to 16.35 and medium-shot MAE from 11.21 to 8.12, with gains concentrated in medium- and few-shot regimes (Section 4.2, Figure 5).

The reward formulation uses a batch-level, comparison-based Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) reward within a GRPO training paradigm rather than point-wise rewards, and ablations show batch-level relational rewards outperform point-wise variants (Section 3.1, Table 5-7).

OrcJhUqdNG.text: Semantic isotropy computed with the Nomic V1 embedding model achieves an R² of 0.446 for predicting nonfactuality on TriviaQA and 0.737 on FactScore-Bio, indicating higher isotropy signals lower factual consistency (Section 4, Table 2).
The semantic isotropy scoring method outperforms LUQ-Atomic at predicting nonfactuality while requiring no labeled data or fine-tuning (Section 4, Table 1-2).
Semantic isotropy scoring runs in 1.8±0.05 seconds per instance compared to 302±48 seconds for LUQ, a roughly 170x speedup (Section 4, Figure 2).
Evaluation covers 1,182 unique entities and approximately 65,450 scored responses of ~500-word target length (Section 4).
Isotropy-based prediction reaches near-asymptotic performance with only 6-8 samples per response, plateauing by N=10 samples, per the sensitivity study (Section 5, Figure 5).

s49fw3BVU0.text: LatentTSF reduces latent chaos: for iTransformer on the Electricity dataset, the mean Euclidean distance between adjacent-timestep latent embeddings drops from 94.03 (standard iTransformer) toward the raw-observation baseline of 12.94 (Section 5.4, Figure 1/5).
On the Electricity dataset with iTransformer, LatentTSF improves average MAE across horizons from 0.375 to 0.299 (Section 5.2, Table 1).

The theoretical analysis shows the prediction loss (ℒPred) and alignment loss (ℒAlign) each implicitly maximize a mutual information objective between predicted and ground-truth latent states (Section 4.1-4.2).
LatentTSF's gains are more pronounced at long forecasting horizons (T=720) than at shorter horizons, and particularly strong on high-dimensional datasets like Traffic (Section 5.2, Table 1/6).
Default loss weights are set to 10 for the prediction term and 15 for the alignment term across the two-stage latent state-space construction and forecasting pipeline (Section 3.5, Table 4-5).

ZSt77efXHI.text: TP-GRPO replaces terminal/outcome-based rewards with increment-based step-wise rewards computed via Section 5.1's step-wise reward computation, addressing reward sparsity identified in Section 4.1 (Section 5.1).
On compositional image generation (GenEval score) with SD3.5-M, TP-GRPO with turning-point constraint reaches 0.9725 versus 0.9673 for Flow-GRPO and 0.6029 for the base model (Section 6.2, Table 1).
On visual text rendering (OCR accuracy), TP-GRPO without the turning-point constraint achieves 0.9718 versus 0.9579 for Flow-GRPO (Section 6.2, Table 1).
On human preference alignment (PickScore), TP-GRPO improves to 24.73 (without constraint) / 24.67 (with constraint) from Flow-GRPO's 24.02 (Section 6.2, Table 1).

Turning points are identified to assign aggregation-based implicit long-term rewards that model delayed impact of early sampling steps, using training with T=10 timesteps and inference with T=40 timesteps (Section 5.2-5.3, Figure 2).

oPQmCKS1tV.text: For 9B-parameter MoE models (1B activated), NITP improves MMLU-Pro accuracy from 15.29% to 21.00%, a 5.71 percentage-point absolute gain, with approximately 2% additional training FLOPs (Section 4, Figure 4).
NITP improves C3 accuracy from 56.65% to 63.01% (+6.36 pp) and CommonsenseQA from 45.70% to 49.96% (+4.26 pp) on the same 9B MoE models, with zero additional inference cost (Section 4, Tables 1-8).
On 3B dense models, NITP yields a smaller average improvement of 1.35 points across benchmarks, including a +4.16 point gain on C3 (Section 4).
NITP improves overall MTEB score for frozen representations from 39.24 to 41.56 (+2.33 points), with gains on 23 of 25 tasks (Section 4, Figure 1).
Training dynamics of the NITP auxiliary loss exhibit a three-phase behavior over training, as shown in the loss-curve analysis (Section 4, Figure 5).

fylE5O8g5F.text: VimRAG models multimodal RAG reasoning as a dynamic directed acyclic graph that structures agent states and retrieved multimodal evidence, rather than a flat retrieval-then-generate pipeline (Section 3).

Graph-Modulated Visual Memory Encoding evaluates memory node significance via topological positioning in the graph, allocating high-resolution tokens to pivotal evidence while compressing or discarding trivial clues (Section 3.1).
Graph-Guided Policy Optimization disentangles step-wise action validity from trajectory-level reward by pruning memory nodes associated with redundant actions (Section 3.2).

The overall VimRAG system architecture, including navigation flow through the multimodal memory graph, is illustrated as an end-to-end pipeline for handling information-sparse, token-heavy visual data in iterative reasoning (Figure 1).

bu6M0Bo6PO.text: FlashSchNet achieves a 6.5x speedup over the CGSchNet baseline while cutting peak memory by 80% (18GB vs 92.5GB) on the Homeodomain (1ENH) protein with 269 beads (Table 3).

FlashSchNet reaches 1000 ns/day aggregate simulation throughput across 64 parallel replicas on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, matching the speed of the classical MARTINI force field (~2900 timestep·mol/s) (Table 3).
FlashSchNet preserves structural fidelity within 0.04 GDT-TS of the CGSchNet baseline across tested proteins while substantially outperforming the classical MARTINI force field in accuracy (Table 2).
The flash radial basis kernel fuses distance computation, Gaussian basis expansion, and cosine envelope into a single tiled operation to remove memory-bound bottlenecks (Section 4.2).

Flash aggregation replaces atomic scatter-add with CSR segment reduce for contention-free accumulation, keeping throughput stable during protein unfolding where CGSchNet degrades due to increased scatter contention (Section 5.2, Figures 5-6).
Channel-wise 16-bit quantization of MLP weights enables 3-10x larger batch sizes before memory saturation, supporting enhanced sampling workflows (Section 4.4, Figure 7).

hhpU1JMhKR.text: OG-MAR constructs a structured value ontology with 76 classes and 150 relations from World Values Survey data using Competency Questions, then instantiates 5 demographically-grounded value-persona agents per query (Section 3).
An ablation over retrieval depth finds K=5 retrieved individuals is optimal, outperforming K in {1, 3, 10} (Figure 3).

Across six regional benchmarks (EVS, GSS, CGSS, ISD, LAPOP, Afrobarometer) and four LLM backbones, OG-MAR attains average scores of 0.6007 (GPT-4o-mini), 0.6308 (Gemini 2.5), 0.5705 (Qwen 2.5), and 0.6317 (EXAONE 3.5), outperforming zero-shot, role-assignment, self-consistency, debate, and ValuesRAG baselines (Table 1).
Multi-persona reasoning yields between +0.002 and +0.07 average accuracy improvement over a single-judge variant of the framework (Table 2).
Human evaluation by 9 raters on a 5-point Likert scale rates grounding at 3.88 on average, peaking at 4.02 for the CGSS (China) benchmark (Table 7, Appendix D).

Despite incurring the highest token usage among compared methods, OG-MAR still achieves the highest accuracy and lowest MAE, indicating substantive gains rather than mere overhead (Figure 6, Section 6).

R2CoYV0Gf6.text: EvoGM uses a dual-generator architecture with cycle-consistency and optimization-guided losses, trained on a winner-loser pairing that splits population history into a top-ρ fraction of winners and the remainder as losers, to optimize LLM merging coefficients (Section 2.2).
On seen tasks from the GLUE benchmark, EvoGM reaches 82.4% average accuracy versus 81.2% for PSO-Merging, including a 12% relative improvement on STS-B (Table 2).
On unseen single-task benchmarks with Qwen2.5-1.5B, EvoGM attains the best performance on 5 of 8 benchmarks, including a 15% relative gain over PSO-Merging on NLGraph (0.537) (Table 1).
On unseen multi-task benchmarks, EvoGM scores 0.380 on average versus 0.372 for PSO-Merging, including a 66% relative improvement on AbstainQA (Table 3).
Ablations show that removing cycle-consistency causes significant performance drops (most notably on NLGraph) and that the dual-generator design outperforms a single-generator variant (Figure 4).
EvoGM scales consistently when merging 2-10 models, improving the average test score from 0.433 to 0.460 when merging 8 models (Figure 5).

iTkQLqa1Ha.text: Med-Scout trains on three unlabeled RL proxy tasks—Hierarchical Scale Localization, Topological Jigsaw Reconstruction, and Anomaly Consistency Detection—to supervise geometric perception without expert annotations (Section 4.1).
On Med-Scout-Bench (10,800 balanced VQA cases across CT, MRI, and X-ray), Med-Scout training raises Qwen3-VL-8B accuracy from 39.7% to 83.6% and Lingshu-7B accuracy from 31.9% to 71.9% (Section 5).
After Med-Scout alignment, the resulting open-source models surpass proprietary GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Flash on Med-Scout-Bench (Section 5).
Med-Scout improves MIMIC-CXR report-generation CIDEr scores by 3-4% across models, with Lingshu reaching a state-of-the-art CIDEr of 105.2 (Section 5).
Med-Scout produces a 0.69 energy-landscape gap between factual and spatially-inverted descriptions, compared to only 0.06 for the baseline model (Section 5.7).
Training uses the GRPO framework with a KL coefficient of β=0.04 over 7,200 optimization steps on 97,200 samples across 6 RTX PRO 6000 GPUs (Section 5).
