e74RjRkirs.text: Q-DiT4SR uses hierarchical SVD decomposition (H-SVD) with an optimal low-rank budget of 8 for the SVD-L component, as shown in the rank ablation across {4, 8, 16, 32} (Section 4.3, Table 2).
Under W4A4 quantization (4-bit weights, 4-bit activations), Q-DiT4SR reduces model size by 5.8x and computational operations by more than 60x relative to full-precision (Section 4.2).

Q-DiT4SR is compared against post-training quantization baselines including Q-Diffusion, PTQ4DiT, QuaRot, SVDQuant, Q-DiT, PassionSR, and FlatQuant on both W4A6 and W4A4 settings across the DrealSR, RealSR, RealLR200, and RealLQ250 benchmarks (Section 4.2, Table 1).

Variance-Aware Spatio Mixed Precision (VaSMP) and Variance-Aware Temporal Mixed Precision (VaTMP) are each ablated separately, showing variance-aware allocation outperforms naive mixed-precision allocation and that temporal scheduling improves results specifically under the W4A4 setting (Section 4.3, Tables 3-4).
On RealSR under W4A6, Q-DiT4SR reports LPIPS of 0.3386, MUSIQ of 67.72, and MANIQA of 0.4566, compared to full-precision LPIPS 0.3179, MUSIQ 67.89, and MANIQA 0.4620 (Section 4.2, Table 1).

EmhfQoA0uC.text: On Qwen3-4B, DPPO achieves a 2.37x training speedup with a +3.15% accuracy gain on the MATH benchmark relative to GRPO (Section 5.2, Table 1).

On Qwen3-8B, DPPO achieves up to 2.65x speedup on GSM8K and 1.90x speedup with +1.70% accuracy on MATH, while on the Qwen3-30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model it reaches 4.87x speedup with +3.35% accuracy (Section 5.2, Table 1).

Dynamic pruning maintains unbiased gradient estimation through an importance sampling-based correction under hierarchical pruning, formalized in the unbiased gradient estimation analysis (Section 4.1).

DPPO is evaluated as a drop-in acceleration technique integrated into DAPO and GSPO training pipelines, in addition to GRPO, and compared against pruning baselines CPPO and GRESO (Section 5.2, Table 3).

Dense Prompt Packing is introduced specifically to preserve training throughput after pruning removes samples, evaluated via an ablation isolating its contribution among key modules (Section 4.3, Section 5.3, Table 6).

YNPHJ2A2oV.text: Exploration-Aware Policy Optimization (EAPO) is evaluated across text-based benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop and GUI-based benchmarks AndroidWorld and OSWorld, reporting success rates in Table 2 (Section 6.2, Table 2).
EAPO achieves 20-60% relative improvements over baselines across 44 evaluated environments (Section 6.2).
A 2B-parameter model trained with EAPO outperforms substantially larger general-purpose and agentic baseline models while incurring only about 30% additional training overhead (Section 6.2).
Naive undifferentiated exploration strategies degrade performance on AndroidWorld, motivating the exploration-aware, uncertainty-gated approach (Section 4.1, Table 1).
EAPO is compared against baselines including GRPO, DAPO, GiGPO, LAMER, Tree of Thoughts, Min-p, and OverRIDE sampling strategies (Section 6.2).

KibOuVwmor.text: Theorem 3.3 (Score-Reward Equivalence) proves that the gradient of the expert's soft Q-function is proportional to the score function learned via denoising score matching under maximum-entropy optimality (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).
On RoboMimic manipulation tasks, EnergyFlow achieves a 93.8% average success rate, compared to 91.2% for Diffusion Policy and 89.6% for Flow Policy (Section 5, Table 1).
On Meta-World manipulation tasks, EnergyFlow reaches 92.5% average success versus 90.7% for Diffusion Policy and 89.5% for Flow Policy (Section 5, Table 2).

Theorem 3.6 shows conservative field constraints reduce the Rademacher complexity bound from O(ΛB√d/√n) to O(ΛL/√n), and this conservative estimator is shown in Lemma 3.8 to generalize better out-of-distribution than unconstrained fields (Section 3, Theorem 3.6, Lemma 3.8).

EnergyFlow's recovered energy function is used as a reward signal for downstream SAC-based reinforcement learning, outperforming both adversarial IRL baselines (EBIL, NEAR) and likelihood-based baseline IQ-Learn (Section 5, Figure 4).
On the physical AGIBOT G1 robot with 20 expert demonstrations, EnergyFlow achieves 100% success rate on real-world Bottle and Drawer manipulation tasks (Section 5, Figure 3).

T4A2aYyaq9.text: PhyScene3D achieves a 40% reduction in scene-wise collision rate relative to human-annotated training data (Section 4.2, Table 1).

PhyScene3D achieves a 46.5% Quality Pass Rate at threshold tau=7 and a 41.6% scene-wise collision rate, compared to an 81.5% scene-wise collision rate for the reference baseline (Section 4.2, Table 1).
On out-of-distribution scenes, PhyScene3D attains a 29.1% Quality Pass Rate (Section 4.2, Table 2).
On downstream robotic task success, PhyScene3D achieves 50.4% success in-distribution and 14.1% out-of-distribution, compared to MesaTask's 4.6% and 3.5% respectively (Section 4.2, Table 3).

PhyScene3D reformulates scene generation as a Human-Mimetic Constructive Process guided by a Cognitive Topological Reasoning Chain (CTRC) that hierarchically sequences object placement using 3D AABB-based reasoning (Section 3.2).

Physics-Aware Denoising Alignment (PADA) projects generated scenes onto a physics-feasible manifold via a differentiable signed distance function with test-time optimization, and an ablation confirms PADA's importance to overall performance (Section 3.3, Section 4.3, Table 5).

pGpEGZhL7Y.text: STABLE achieves 0 object collisions (0 OC metric) on task-driven tabletop layout generation, compared to non-zero collision counts for baseline methods (Table 1).
STABLE attains a 99.0% average GPT score versus 81.5% for the MesaTask baseline on task-conditioned tabletop scene generation (Table 1).
STABLE reaches 99.4% task alignment versus 90.2% for MesaTask (Table 1).
The Physics Corrector remains robust across all collision-severity levels, whereas post-hoc optimization baselines fail on high-collision scenarios (Table 2).
An ablation removing the Physics Corrector's mesh-level SDF and support-contact losses degrades performance relative to the full model (Table 3, Section 4.3).
STABLE produces layouts that yield superior physical consistency on downstream robotic rearrangement tasks compared to existing methods (Table 4, Section 4.4).

bGxMpQsIuN.text: TCSeg's dual-axis reliability estimation decouples confidence (cross-view consensus) from uncertainty (cross-evidence disagreement) to identify pseudo-labels that are confidently wrong (Section 3.2).
Under the 'last checkpoint' multi-run evaluation protocol, TCSeg attains a median DSC of 81.08% on 10%-labeled Pancreas-CT, exceeding the nearest competitor by roughly 1.8% (Table 1, Section 4.2).
Ablating either the confidence or uncertainty component of the dual-axis assessment reduces DSC relative to the full TCSeg model (Table 2, Section 4.4).
Ablating any of the three calibration spaces (probability, feature, or image space) reduces DSC relative to full tri-space calibration (Table 3, Section 4.5).

TCSeg uses 12.34M parameters and is reported alongside training speed, test latency, and GPU memory on BraTS2019, arguing for comparable computational efficiency to competing methods (Table 4, Section 4.9).
Across five runs, TCSeg shows more stable run-to-run performance under both best- and final-checkpoint protocols than compared semi-supervised methods (Figure 5, Section 4.7).

ddBkQ4koaI.text: The Scale Schedule Corrector (SSC), a training-free inference-time velocity rescaling with schedule γ(t) = 1.1(1−t) + 1.0·t, improves FID from 13.68 to 7.58 (a 44.6% improvement) on ImageNet-1k 256×256 at 50 sampling steps (Table 1, Section 4.2/5.2).

The 50-step SSC-corrected generator (FID 7.58) outperforms the 250-step uncorrected baseline (FID 8.65), yielding roughly a 5x reduction in sampling steps for equal or better quality (Table 1, Figure 4, Section 5.2).
SSC generalizes to text-to-image generation, improving FID on MS-COCO from 6.03 to 4.71 (about 22%) using the REPA-MMDiT backbone at NFE=50, CFG=1.0 (Table 4, Section 5.3).
SSC generalizes to the REPA objective and to 512x512 resolution, yielding 20.7-28.4% FID reduction (Table 3, Section 5.3).

Fréchet Latent Distance tracking shows SSC-guided sampling trajectories reach up to 28.2% closer proximity to the data manifold at mid-trajectory (t=0.8) than the uncorrected baseline (Figure 3, Section 3.3).

An ablation over the scale schedule shows the asymmetric γ(t) design (boosting velocity near t=0, damping near t=1) outperforms alternative injection schedules on the fully converged SiT-XL/2 model (Table 5, Section 5.4).

QooAmoUixn.text: MARI's competitive multi-adapter mechanism trains K lightweight low-rank adapters at a single injection site using winner-take-gradient hard routing during training and entropy-based routing at inference to select input-dependent intervention direction and strength (Section 4.2).

MARI's energy-based gate computes a propagation-response energy E(x;alpha) from internal layer dynamics, using off-subspace regularization to suppress intervention on inputs it deems non-applicable (Section 4.3).
On Llama-3-8B, MARI improves TruthfulQA MC1 to 61.81% versus 50.58% for ReFT, and BBQ bias score to 0.792 versus 0.637 for ReFT (Table 1, Section 6.2).
MARI preserves or improves general capability, reaching 66.6% on MMLU versus 65.9% for the vanilla (unintervened) model (Table 1, Section 6.2).
Removing the energy-based gate causes severe regression in general-capability benchmarks despite marginally higher alignment scores, per the ablation study (Table 2, Section 6.3).
Theorem 5.1 bounds the routing regret as R_ent <= R_min + L*eta, formalizing the tradeoff between adapter specialization gains and misrouting penalties (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).

Ee4j4zMir5.text: KAST-BAR-Large is pre-trained on 21 diverse EEG datasets covering over 1,600 subjects before multi-task instruction fine-tuning on six downstream tasks (Section 3.3, Section 3).

KAST-BAR-Large achieves balanced accuracies of 71.2% on Workload (mental workload), 74.3% on SEED (emotion), 83.2% on TUAB (abnormal detection), 73.9% on HMC (sleep staging), 70.8% on TUEV (event classification), and 77.4% on TUSL (slowing events) (Table 2, Section 4.2).
KAST-BAR outperforms NeuroLM-XL (1.7B parameters) by 7.7% balanced accuracy on Workload and 14.0% on SEED (Table 2, Section 4.2).
The ablation study shows the DSHA encoder contributes 5.6-9.9% accuracy improvement over a vanilla VQ-VAE tokenizer on TUEV, SEED, and HMC (Table 4, Section 4.3).
The same ablation shows the STAR refiner contributes 1.4-4.1% accuracy gains, and KASP-generated semantic profiles outperform fixed textual descriptions by 0.9-2.8% (Table 4, Section 4.3).
On TUSL, KAST-BAR (77.4%) trails a specialized single-task model (85.7%), which the authors attribute to lower sensitivity to fine-grained frequency-domain features (Table 2/3, Section 4.2).

DTuBIEhSF3.text: SLVR's Stage 1 (Structured Latent Learning) trains region-centric latent representations with a joint objective combining a visual loss and a semantic loss, where the visual latent is aligned to encoder features via an MSE loss and the semantic latent encodes structured region attributes such as appearance, actions, and spatial properties (Section on Stage 1, Structured Latent Learning).

On standard VQA benchmarks (Table 2), SLVR improves over the LVR baseline by +11.2 points on OKVQA (61.8 vs 50.6), +24.7 points on VizWiz (57.8 vs 33.1), +12.8 points on ChartQA (77.2 vs 64.4), and +4.2 points on TextVQA (79.3 vs 75.1).

On the SV-QA benchmark's Both-Correct joint-accuracy metric (Table 3), SLVR outperforms LVR by +3.7 points on V* (69.1 vs 65.4), +3.2 points on HRBench-4K (61.1 vs 57.9), and +4.0 points on HRBench-8K (50.6 vs 46.6).
On VisualPuzzles (Table 5), SLVR reaches 34.2% overall accuracy versus 29.4% for the LVR baseline, a +4.8 point improvement.

The SLV-Set dataset used to train SLVR comprises approximately 400K region-level attribute annotations and roughly 800K multi-query question-answer pairs probing different semantic aspects of the same regions, with the SV-QA benchmark containing 591 paired samples of original and manually verified alternative questions (Figure 2, dataset construction).

M-GRPO (Multi-query Group Relative Policy Optimization) in Stage 2 combines an answer-correctness reward, a latent-consistency reward enforcing cross-query consistency across visual and semantic latents, and a margin-based stability regularization term to prevent drift from the Stage 1 reference latents (Figure 3).

F3uCTULtDZ.text: Adversarial text embeddings crafted for previously mitigated memorized prompts restore data replication in Stable Diffusion v1.4: after NeMo pruning reduces SSCD_Orig to 0.33+/-0.18, the adversarial embeddings raise it back to 0.91+/-0.03 (Table 1).

Optimizing 100 adversarial embeddings from random initializations per memorized image shows they remain evenly distributed across the text embedding space rather than clustering near the original memorized prompt, indicating memorization triggers are not spatially local (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

Weight-importance analysis for locality-based pruning defenses shows low agreement between the weight sets identified by different adversarial embeddings that trigger the same memorized image: agreement stays below 0.6 for most layers under Wanda, and only reaches roughly 0.6 in early layers under NeMo (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

The proposed adversarial fine-tuning defense, which searches for adversarial triggers during training and fine-tunes on surrogate images conditioned on them while retaining non-memorized data, reduces SSCD_Orig to 0.15+/-0.07 after five epochs while improving FID to 13.61 versus the unmitigated baseline's 14.44 (Section 5, Table 1).

Under adversarial attack, the fine-tuned model's SSCD score rises only to 0.36, versus 0.91 for NeMo and 0.76 for Wanda under the same attack, demonstrating markedly greater robustness than locality-assumption-based mitigation methods (Table 1).

The adversarial embedding optimization procedure (Algorithm 1) uses 50 gradient steps at learning rate 0.1 to remain constrained near the memorized prompt; Appendix D shows that unconstrained optimization (1000 steps) instead triggers generation of arbitrary, non-memorized images.

gIUVdEAa3l.text: E2Former-V2's fused Triton kernel for on-the-fly equivariant attention eliminates materialization of edge tensors and achieves up to a 20x improvement in TFLOPS over standard implementations (Figure 4).

Equivariant Axis-Aligned Sparsification (EAAS) converts dense SO(3) tensor contractions into sparse parity re-indexing operations, yielding approximately a 6x speedup in the convolution step (Figure 3).
On the SPICE dataset (Table 1), the Direct variant achieves Energy MAE / Force MAE of 0.28 meV/atom / 2.40 meV/Angstrom on Dimers, 0.46 / 4.59 on Monomers, and 0.53 / 8.27 on the All-systems split.
On OMol25 validation (Table 2), E2Former-V2 attains 2.09 meV/atom energy MAE and 8.38 meV/Angstrom force MAE, indicating preserved predictive accuracy alongside the reported speedups.
E2Former-V2 uniquely scales inference to systems of 100,000 atoms on H20 GPUs where competing equivariant transformer implementations run out of memory (Table 3).

The fused attention kernel (Algorithm 1) maintains running accumulators for numerical stability while streaming over neighbors, avoiding materialized edge tensors of size proportional to the edge count, and shifts the workload from memory-bound to compute-bound execution (Figure 4).

O2znfxqcIj.text: SLIP-RS constructs the RS-Attribute-15M dataset with over 15 million attribute annotations, composed of RS-Attribute-O (881,672 attributes drawn from 14 open-source datasets) and RS-Attribute-C (14.6 million attributes obtained via third-party channels), covering planes, ships, and vehicles with hierarchical functional and component-level attributes (Section on the RS-Attribute-15M dataset).

The Structured-Attribute Decoupling Paradigm maps objects into a finite, physically meaningful attribute space (e.g., engine count, wing configuration, propulsion type for aircraft) rather than an open-ended category label space, implemented via Structured-Attribute Contrastive Learning (SACL) with permutation-invariant positive prompts and counterfactual hard negatives from attribute replacement.

On zero-shot/supervised transfer detection (Table 2), SLIP-RS with a ConvNeXT-L backbone reaches 47.14% mAP on DOTA-v2.0 and 83.10% mAP on DIOR, exceeding the OpenRSD baseline's 44.57% and 76.70% respectively.

On fine-grained atomic attribute verification (Table 3), SLIP-RS (ConvNeXT-L) achieves 72.04% mAP for Plane Purpose versus only 9.03% for OpenRSD, plus 69.54% mAP for Plane Wing Configuration and 80.47% mAP for Plane Engine Count.
On oriented object detection on DOTA-v2.0 OBB (Table 6), SLIP-RS with a 198M-parameter ConvNeXT-L backbone reaches 62.54% mAP, surpassing the billion-scale foundation model BFM's 58.69% mAP.

The Conformal Attribute Reliability Engine (CARE) uses a Tune-Calibrate-Scale pipeline grounded in conformal prediction theory to control False Discovery Rate for pseudo-label distillation, replacing heuristic confidence thresholding when generating RS-Attribute-15M.

nqnlfxuN8x.text: SEER's Learnable Patch Replacement Module operates in two stages: an Automated Token Filter (Section 4.3.1) that produces sigmoid-based quality scores to filter tokens below a threshold, preserving gradient flow via detachment tricks (Equations 9-11), followed by Replaced Causal Self-Attention (Section 4.3.2) that substitutes filtered low-quality patches with series-wise prototype tokens before applying causally-masked multi-head self-attention (Equations 12-14).

Across 8 multivariate forecasting benchmark datasets and forecast horizons {96, 192, 336, 720}, SEER ranks first in 34 of 45 MSE settings and 39 of 45 MAE settings, yielding an average 7.3% MSE reduction and 4.9% MAE reduction over the second-best baseline, xPatch (Table 2).

Under synthetic robustness perturbations applied to ETTh2 (Table 4), SEER achieves lower MSE than the best baseline SRSNet across four degradation types: white noise (0.291 vs 0.297), anomalies (0.298 vs 0.301), missing values (0.288 vs 0.299), and distribution shift (0.302 vs 0.305).

On real-world low-quality datasets (Table 5), SEER outperforms DLinear on distribution-shifted ILI data (average MSE 1.876 vs 2.729), anomaly-laden PSM data (1.147 vs 1.287), and missing-value USHCN data (0.754 vs 0.767).

The ablation study (Table 3) shows removing the Augmented Series Embedding causes the largest degradation (roughly 3-8% MSE increase), while removing the Token Filter causes a 1-2% increase that becomes more pronounced on lower-quality datasets.

Parameter sensitivity analysis (Figure 5) finds the optimal number of Mixture-of-Experts experts is 8 and the best patch length is in the range 16-24, with the learned score threshold converging to non-zero values on most datasets but to zero on high-quality datasets.

cFEyszuOPF.text: BESplit-G attains 67.45% accuracy on ISIC under non-IID splitting at concentration κ=1, versus 64.52% for the FAVD baseline (Table 3).

On CIFAR100 with κ=1, BESplit-G reaches 68.17% accuracy versus 66.60% for FAVD, and needs only 371±11 communication rounds to hit 60% target accuracy versus 401±10 for FAVD and 419±9 for MergeSFL (Table 3, Table 5).

Evidential Aggregation reweights client contributions using per-class evidence concentration Q^(k) combined with aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty penalization terms R_ale^(k) and R_epi^(k) (Section on Evidential Aggregation).
Ablating Bias-Compensated Collaboration (BCC) causes the largest single-component accuracy drop of 3.86% on ISIC, while BCC itself adds only about 0.12% runtime overhead (Table 4, Table 1).

Dual-Teacher Distillation trains a lightweight auxiliary model whose feature extractor aligns with the local model and whose classification head aligns with the global model via a combined loss with λ_C=0.2 and λ_G=0.3 at temperature τ=5, adding about 3.65% runtime overhead (Section on Dual-Teacher Distillation, Table 1).
Lemma D.4 bounds the aggregation gradient bias by ||b_t|| ≤ g_max·Σ w^(k)||P_k − P_g||_1, motivating the distributional alignment used in BCC (Lemma D.4).

i5knGuNoRX.text: Brep2Shape is a self-supervised pre-training framework that aligns boundary representations (B-rep) of CAD models with shape representations by predicting dense spatial points from parametric Bézier control points (abstract only).
The architecture uses a dual Transformer backbone with parallel streams that separately encode surface tokens and curve tokens (abstract only).
A topology attention mechanism explicitly models interdependencies between surfaces and curves within the dual-stream backbone (abstract only).
Brep2Shape reports state-of-the-art accuracy and faster convergence than prior methods across multiple downstream CAD processing tasks (abstract only).
The method demonstrates significant scalability improvements over existing CAD representation-learning approaches (abstract only).

DlKdI669OM.text: VideoTemp-o3-7B-RL scores 54.2 on MLVU, 47.8 on VideoMME, and 69.0 on LVBench, exceeding Video-R1's 48.0, 46.0, and 67.3 respectively (Table 1).
On temporal grounding, VideoTemp-o3 achieves 33.0 R@0.7 and 57.8 mIoU on Charades-STA, and 26.7 R@0.7 and 45.3 mIoU on ActivityNet-MR (Table 2).
On video grounded question answering, the model reaches 33.4 mIoU with 76.4% accuracy on NextGQA and 29.5 mIoU with 74.4% accuracy on ReXTime (Table 3).
The RL training stage uses GRPO with a penalty-aware IoU reward that applies a λ=0.1 penalty when IoU falls below 0.1, designed to prevent reward hacking (Section on RL training).
Removing grounding data from training reduces ReXTime mIoU from 29.5 to 13.0, a 16.5-point drop, showing grounding data is essential for accurate localization (ablation study).

VideoTemp-Bench, a newly introduced benchmark, contains 1,200 samples spanning four duration categories (0-3min, 3-10min, 10-20min, and >20min) for evaluating long-form video understanding (Section introducing VideoTemp-Bench).

XJ5r19iN9G.text: Theorem 3.1 (Safe Gradient Projection) derives the optimal orthogonality-constrained update as ΔW_safe = ΔW_orig(I − VV^T), where V spans the estimated historical task subspace (Theorem 3.1).

On ImageNet-R with 10 tasks, Janus-LoRA achieves 75.78% final accuracy (ACC) and 81.64% mean average accuracy (MAA), outperforming InfLoRA (73.90% ACC, 80.01% MAA) and BiLoRA (73.93% ACC, 77.92% MAA) (Table comparing continual learning methods).
Janus-LoRA's backward transfer (BWT) on ImageNet-R with 10 tasks is -6.05, compared to -6.33 for InfLoRA and -2.07 for BiLoRA (Table comparing continual learning methods).

An ablation combining Online Estimation with Gradient Rectification alone (without Decoupled Margin Loss) achieves the best stability with BWT of -4.43, while Decoupled Margin Loss used alone worsens forgetting despite improving new-task accuracy (Table 1, ablation study).
Online Estimation maintains an orthonormal basis V of rank k=50 approximating the historical parameter subspace without storing old training samples (Section describing Online Estimation).

Janus-LoRA completes 10-task continual learning on ImageNet-R in 1197.8 seconds, faster than InfLoRA and GPM-based variants, while preserving identical inference FLOPs (efficiency comparison, Section on computational cost).

vpwx8GRbkZ.text: On ViT-MAE-Huge, ToaSt achieves 88.52% top-1 accuracy, a +1.64% gain over the uncompressed baseline, with a 39.4% FLOPs reduction and 1.59x inference speedup (Table 1).

On DeiT-Base, ToaSt reaches 84.82% top-1 accuracy (+3.02%) with 39.2% FLOPs reduction and 1.51x speedup, and on Swin-Base it reaches 85.21% (+1.71%) with 42.7% FLOPs reduction and 1.28x speedup (Table 1).
ToaSt transfers to COCO object detection, with Swin-Small achieving 52.2 box mAP versus the 51.9 mAP baseline (Table 3).

MHSA pruning applies 90% pruning to attention weight matrices in all layers except the first, using Geometric Median-based importance scoring while keeping Q-K and V-Projection dimensions synchronized (Section 3.1).

Training-free Token Channel Selection for the FFN's D→4D expansion uses layer-adaptive channel-selection ratios of 0-30% for FC1 and 50-90% for FC2, chosen via activation sparsity, effective rank, and R² reconstruction analysis (Section 3.2).

Applying MHSA pruning alone drops accuracy by 2.6-4.2%, while adding Token Channel Selection recovers 1.7-3.6% of that loss, and larger models require far fewer fine-tuning epochs to recover accuracy, e.g. 15 epochs for ViT-MAE-Huge versus 297 for a smaller base model (ablation study).

DcKl47MeYI.text: Swordsman identifies semantic constituent boundaries for adaptive block partitioning by measuring Shannon entropy shifts between adjacent tokens, rather than using fixed-length blocks (Section 3.2).
On GSM8K with LLaDA-8B-Instruct using dual cache, Swordsman reaches 81.50% accuracy versus 75.21% for Fast-dLLM, a +6.29 point improvement (Table 1).
On HumanEval with LLaDA-1.5, Swordsman achieves 43.90% accuracy versus 35.59% for Fast-dLLM, an +8.31 point improvement (Table 1).
With dual cache on LLaDA-1.5, Swordsman attains 64.97 tokens/sec at 3.03s latency versus Fast-dLLM's 61.30 tokens/sec at 3.41s latency (Table 2).
Ablation shows accuracy rising from a 29.04% full-diffusion baseline to 77.40% with block-wise decoding, 77.56% with parallel decoding, and 81.43% with the full adaptive partition strategy (Table 3).

kdKSU8ULh9.text: SpatialReward uses a 'Think-with-Boxes' mechanism with separate semantic-consistency (SC) and perceptual-quality (PQ) streams to ground reward judgments in predicted edit regions (Section 3.2).
On EditReward-Bench, SpatialReward reaches 0.803 overall score versus 0.690 for EditScore-8B, an 11.3-point improvement (Table 1).
On MER-Bench (600 evaluation groups across 15 subtasks), SpatialReward achieves 48.3% accuracy versus 35.0% for EditScore-8B, though still below Gemini-3.0-Flash's 50.8% (Section 4, Table 1).
Using SpatialReward for online RL fine-tuning of OmniGen2 yields a +0.90 gain on GEdit-Bench, compared to a +0.45 gain from using GPT-4.1 as the reward signal and +0.61 from EditScore (Table 3).
Attention analysis shows explicit spatial grounding reduces the entropy gap from 3.48 to 1.16 and increases source-image awareness from 2.88 to 5.71 (Table 5).

yUDykwou3c.text: The Open-world Graph Assistant (OGA) framework combines an Adaptive Label Traceability (ALT) module for unknown-class rejection with a Graph Label Annotator (GLA) module for unknown-class annotation (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
On known-class classification accuracy, OGA reaches 90.02% on Cora versus 87.62% for the GOOD baseline, and 78.39% on arXiv versus 76.38% for IsoMax (Table 1).
For unknown-class coverage/precision, OGA attains 94.2%/82.3% on Cora and 96.4%/48.9% on WikiCS, improving coverage by 6.2 points and precision by 4.6 points over baselines (Table 2).
Using GLA-annotated unlabeled nodes for training raises GCN accuracy on PubMed from 47.12% to 87.15%, nearly matching the 87.49% ground-truth upper bound (Table 4).
GLA's topology-guided annotation strategy reduces LLM API calls by 87-90% relative to naive per-node querying, with runtimes of 8.91-99.23 seconds across the six datasets (Tables 7-8).

pea0kmkrtm.text: NOVA determines when to activate token reduction by detecting entropy growth inflection points, then dynamically adjusts per-scale, per-layer reduction ratios via dual-linkage acceleration plus residual cache reuse (Section 3.3).
On Infinity-2B, NOVA achieves a 2.89x speedup (2.43s to 0.84s per generation) while GenEval overall score drops only from 0.73 to 0.72 (Table 1).
On Infinity-8B, NOVA achieves a 1.33x speedup (1.51s to 0.75s) with GenEval overall score nearly unchanged, from 0.80 to 0.79 (Table 1).
On Infinity-8B, applying NOVA slightly improves the ImageReward human-preference score from 1.030 to 1.035 despite the acceleration (Table 2).
NOVA can generate 2K-resolution images in 3.2 seconds on a single RTX 3090 (Section 4.2, Figure 1).

N8WHcyewlH.text: TransNormal combines dual-stream encoding, semantic feature injection, and wavelet edge-aware regularization for diffusion-based transparent object normal estimation (Section 4, Figure 2).
On the ClearGrasp benchmark, TransNormal reduces mean angular error to 16.4°, a 24.4% improvement over the previous best method, while reaching 51.7% accuracy at the 11.25° threshold (Table 1).
On the ClearPose benchmark, TransNormal achieves a mean angular error of 26.3°, a 15.2% reduction versus prior methods, with 35.9% accuracy at 11.25° and 69.8% at 30° (Table 1).
On the TransNormal-Synthetic benchmark, the method attains a mean angular error of 4.1° and 93.5% accuracy at the 11.25° threshold (Table 1).
Training uses roughly 122K synthetic samples composed of 35% ClearGrasp, 15% TransNormal-Synthetic, 45% Hypersim, and 5% Virtual KITTI data (Section 5).

CX6KJksKqR.text: MixReasoning reduces token usage by 47% on GSM8K with QwQ-32B (750.3 to 400.5 tokens) while simultaneously improving accuracy by 1.01% (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On Math-500, Qwen3-8B under MixReasoning uses 32% fewer tokens (5192 to 3531) while matching baseline accuracy (Table 1, Section 4.2).

MixReasoning is benchmarked against five length-compression baselines (Prompting, CoT-Valve, DEER, NoWait, ConciseHint) across GSM8K, Math-500, and AIME24 using QwQ-32B-Preview, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-8B (Section 4.1).

The method uses a LoRA-based adapter that switches reasoning modes based on token-level entropy crossing thresholds tau-up and tau-down, with hysteresis logic to prevent oscillation between modes (Section 3.2).

An ablation shows MLP-only LoRA adapters achieve compression comparable to full-layer finetuning, whereas attention K/V adapters yield negligible compression, indicating reasoning-length control resides primarily in MLP layers (Section 4.4).
MixReasoning achieves a superior accuracy-vs-token-count Pareto frontier compared to global compression baselines (Figure 3).

0VEeF91Fm6.text: MagicDock's pipeline comprises four stages: surface point-cloud modeling via signed distance functions, SE(3)-equivariant unsupervised pre-training with masked reconstruction, supervised fine-tuning on pocket prediction/interaction prediction/binding affinity regression, and gradient-driven inversion-based ligand generation (Section 3).
MagicDock is evaluated across 9 scenarios spanning protein ligand design (SKEMPI v2, SAbDab) and molecule ligand design (PDBBind2020, CrossDocked2020) (Section 5, Tables 1-2).
MagicDock outperforms the best protein-design baseline Abx, scoring 36.32/27.87 versus 28.76/21.80 on SKEMPI v2/SAbDab (Table 1).
On molecule design, MagicDock scores 40.63/60.02 on PDBBind2020/CrossDocked2020 versus ALIDIFF's 35.74/65.63 (Table 2).

The paper proves SE(3)-equivariance across all stages (Theorem 1), convergence to stationary points (Theorem 2), and an improved sample complexity of O(log 1/epsilon) versus baselines' O(1/epsilon^2) (Theorem 7).

Module-wise ablations confirm all four pipeline stages contribute to performance, and robustness tests under geometric noise, feature perturbations, and mutational variation show MagicDock remains stable (Section 5.2, Section 5.3).

vAjsnuPRUP.text: RSIR's fidelity check (Equation 2) accepts a synthetic training sequence only if at least one held-out logged interaction remains ranked highly by the model within a threshold tau, preventing error amplification across recursive self-improvement iterations (Section 3.2).
RSIR is evaluated on Amazon Beauty/Sports/Toys and Yelp datasets using SASRec, CL4SRec, and HSTU backbones, against baselines Reordering, Insertion, ASReP, DiffuASR, and DR4SR (Section 5.1).
Single-iteration RSIR yields 1.8-10.97% relative NDCG/Recall improvements across metrics and backbones, with HSTU showing a +7.71% Recall@10 gain on the Sports dataset (Table 1).
Cumulative multi-iteration gains grow from an initial 8.02% Recall improvement to 13.92% after three iterations on Sports before saturating (Figure 3).
An ablation removing the fidelity control shows performance collapses by the third iteration, with Recall dropping to 0.021 versus 0.528 when fidelity control is applied (Table 2).

Even weak teacher models provide a +1.95% performance lift to stronger student models in the recursive framework, indicating gains come from the recursive regularization mechanism rather than raw teacher capacity (Figure 4).

sseBmS2MGa.text: DriveWorld-VLA achieves 91.3 PDMS on NAVSIMv1, exceeding the DriveVLA-W0 baseline's 90.2, with a No Collision rate of 99.1 and Ego Progress of 85.9 (Table 1).
On NAVSIMv2, DriveWorld-VLA reaches 86.8 EPDMS versus DriveVLA-W0's 86.1, with sub-metrics DAC 99.1, DDC 99.6, and Lane Keeping 97.0 (Table 2).
On nuScenes, DriveWorld-VLA attains a 0.61m average L2 displacement error and a 0.16% collision rate over a 3-second prediction horizon (Table 3).

The three-stage training schedule (VLA and world-model joint training, action-controllability fine-tuning, future-guided evaluation/refinement) yields progressive gains, with Stage 1 to 2 adding 1.9 PDMS and Stage 2 to 3 adding a further 1.8 PDMS (Tables 4-7).
Removing the progressive/sequential training order degrades performance by 7.7 PDMS relative to the full staged training approach, validating the sequential design (Tables 4-7).
The human-driving baseline on NAVSIMv1 scores 94.8 PDMS, indicating headroom remaining above DriveWorld-VLA's 91.3 (Table 1).

zSKSZm46DO.text: MAMBO-G introduces a magnitude-aware normalization mechanism that rescales guidance contributions to prevent magnitude explosion under boosted classifier-free guidance scales while preserving the directional signal (Section 3).
MAMBO-G achieves up to a 3x sampling speedup on Stable Diffusion v3.5 and up to 4x on Lumina (Section 4).
MAMBO-G accelerates the 14-billion-parameter Wan2.1 video diffusion model by approximately 2x while preserving visual fidelity (Section 4).
An ablation study progressively removing components shows the magnitude-aware normalization step is the critical contributor to the method's speedup gains (Section 4.5).
Related classifier-free guidance mechanisms and variants are surveyed as points of comparison for MAMBO-G's approach (Section 2).

QaHFVheV8X.text: SAQNN, a constructive quantum neural network built from a state preparation block, spectrum selection block, and phase injection block, satisfies Theorem 1: for any multivariate square-integrable function f: [-π,π]^d → [0,1] and any accuracy ε, there exist parameters θ, ϕ and a rescale coefficient a such that the measured circuit output approximates f to within ε in L2 norm (Theorem 1, Section 3.2).

For Sobolev functions in H^s([-π,π]^d), Theorem 2 gives circuit width O(log n), circuit depth O(n log n), and parameter complexity O(n), where n = O((d + 1/ε)^{16(1/ε)^{2/s}}) is the number of truncated Fourier series terms (Theorem 2, Section 3.3).

SAQNN achieves optimal parameter complexity with respect to the asymptotic order of accuracy ε when L2-approximating Sobolev functions, and has an asymptotic advantage over state-of-the-art classical feed-forward networks in circuit size in the d-demanding (high-dimensional) case (Section 1.2).

The state preparation block uses multiplexor-Ry gates (synthesizable with at most 2^{n-1} CNOT gates per Lemma 3), and controlled-Rz gates used in spectrum selection can be synthesized with two multi-qubit Toffoli gates and two Rz gates, which feeds into the circuit-depth analysis of Theorem 2 (Section 3.1, Lemma 3).

SAQNN supports switching the implemented function basis between Fourier series and Chebyshev series, making it adaptable to periodic and non-periodic approximation scenarios (Section 3.2, Appendix C).

D1JSZDVnxG.text: CoCoReviewBench curates 3,900 papers from ICLR (2017-2025) and NeurIPS (2021-2024), building category-specific benchmark subsets across a two-level taxonomy of 23 subcategories under 5 top-level categories (Quality, Clarity, Significance, Originality, Policy) (Section 3, Section 3.1, Appendix A).

A single human reviewer covers on average only 3.03 of 5 top-level categories and 5.10 of 23 subcategories per paper; aggregating all reviewers for a paper raises coverage to 3.98 top-level categories and 9.23 of 23 subcategories (an 81% relative improvement in subcategory coverage over a single reviewer), yet aggregated subcategory coverage is still only about 40% (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

Treating reviewer-author and inter-reviewer discussions plus the meta-review as expert adjudication signals, incorrectness is identified via inter-reviewer conflicts in 22.13% of papers (7.63% of reviews) and via reviewer-author conflicts in 75.72% of papers (36.76% of reviews); over 13% of submissions show a score gap of 4 or more between the highest and lowest overall reviewer scores (Section 3.2).

CoCoReviewBench is the only benchmark among compared peer-review resources (PeerRead, MReD, NLPeer, SEA, ReviewMT, Re2, Aspects, RottenReviews, GRE-bench, RevUtil) to simultaneously support atomic opinions, fine-grained labels, category-level evaluation, rebuttal signal, meta signal, conflict detection, and incorrect annotation (Table 1).

Analysis on CoCoReviewBench shows AI reviewers remain limited in correctness and thoroughness relative to humans, are prone to hallucinations, and that reasoning models are more effective reviewers than non-reasoning approaches because they better substantiate their critiques (Abstract, Section 1).

fCvS9dhzhM.text: Z-Erase addresses generation collapse in single-stream diffusion transformers, where shared projection weights (W_Q, W_K, W_V) for text and image tokens cause direct application of existing concept-erasure methods to corrupt visual signal processing and produce catastrophic noise outputs (Section 3).

Z-Erase's Stream Disentangled Concept Erasure framework introduces a token-wise selection operator S_T that restricts low-rank adaptation updates exclusively to textual hidden states while freezing the visual backbone, formalized in Equation 4 (Section 4.1).

Z-Erase's Lagrangian-Guided Adaptive Erasure Modulation formulates the erasure-preservation trade-off as a constrained optimization problem (Equation 9) with a closed-form Lagrange-multiplier solution (Equations 11-12), using an implicit first-order approximation that reduces cost from two backward passes to one (Section 4.2).

On 4,703 I2P prompts for NSFW erasure, Z-Erase achieves the best violence-erasure result (324 cases) and a competitive nudity-detection result (161 cases) while maintaining FID 26.46 and CLIP score 31.25, versus UCE's 157 nudity cases but worse FID of 38.38 (Table 1).
On a 100-identity celebrity erasure subset, Z-Erase attains the highest balance score (Ha = 4.82) among compared methods, with FID 27.83 and CLIP 30.06 (Table 2).

Z-Erase's convergence theorem (Appendix C) proves the training algorithm converges to a Pareto stationary point where erasure cannot be further improved without violating the preservation constraint, with preservation-capability degradation bounded by O(tεα) (Equation 16, Appendix C).

4zGe2J2eJU.text: SPA generates large-scale synthetic training data from a small set of carefully designed prompts spanning three learning-strategy levels (Concept Learning, Critical Thinking, Generative Learning) for knowledge injection (Abstract, Section 3.3).
On SQuAD, SPA reaches 91.27% accuracy versus 90.25% for Active Reading and 74.23% for the RL-based SEAL baseline, outperforming SEAL by 17.04 points at 120M training tokens (Table 1, Section 5.1).
On QuALITY, SPA reaches 57.03% versus 56.22% for EntiGraph and 51.13% for Active Reading (Table 1, Section 5.2).
On MultiHop-RAG, SPA outperforms EntiGraph on both Qwen2.5-7B (86.64% vs 85.42%) and Meta-Llama-3-8B (88.36% vs 84.31%) (Table 1, Section 5.3).

The RL-based method SEAL exhibits substantially lower diversity than all other methods across all four diversity metrics measured, indicating a diversity collapse that causes performance saturation as training data scales (Table 3, Section 6.1).

GLPTyKiiYZ.text: TFMixer introduces a learnable Non-Uniform Discrete Fourier Transform (NUDFT) that extracts spectral representations directly from irregular timestamps without requiring interpolation, used in its Global Frequency Module with spectral refinement via an MLP and an inverse NUDFT to produce a seasonal bias (Abstract, Section 4.2).

TFMixer's Local Time Module uses transformable patch encoding with continuous time embeddings and a query-based patch attention mechanism designed to address information density imbalance across non-uniform patches, combined with dual-mixing blocks for temporal and cross-variable dependencies (Section 4.3).

On irregular multivariate time series forecasting benchmarks (PhysioNet, MIMIC, HumanActivity, USHCN), TFMixer achieves a 3.0% MSE reduction and 8.1% MAE reduction versus the second-best baseline, APN (Table 1, Section A.1).

Ablation studies confirm that both the frequency module and the time module are necessary for performance, and that spectrum refinement and query-based patch mixing each contribute measurably to accuracy (Table 2).

Parameter sensitivity analysis shows the optimal model dimension D is 32-64 for smaller datasets and 128-256 for larger ones, the optimal number of learnable query patches W is 8 or 16, and patch size P of 16-24 balances detail preservation against efficiency (Figures 4-5, Section B.3).

ul2qlPcb5Y.text: GenRe^2 reformulates decoding-based regression as an MDP where the reward is defined as negative MSE in target space, R(τ) = -(ψ(ŷ) - ψ(y))^2, applied only at the final generated token rather than per-token (Section 3.3).

On the TALENT benchmark of 100 tabular regression datasets, GenRe^2-ReMax achieves RMSE 0.5190 and R^2 0.6459, improving over the base decoding model (RMSE 0.5484, R^2 0.6124) and over DIST2 (RMSE 0.5457, R^2 0.6096) (Table 1, Section 4.1).
GenRe^2-ReMax attains the best rank correlation of 0.7785 on TALENT, versus 0.7734 for DIST2 and 0.7705 for the base model (Table 1).

On code metric regression, GenRe^2-ReMax improves APPS Leetcode RMSE from 0.493 to 0.474 and rank correlation from 0.935 to 0.967 versus the base model, and improves Triton kernel latency prediction RMSE from 1.095 to 1.094 (Table 3, Section 4.2).

GenRe^2-ReMax maintains a consistent R^2 advantage across tokenizer digit bases 2 through 10, whereas GenRe^2-GRPO's performance degrades at higher bases due to reward standardization bias (Figure 4, Section 4.1).

Average output-distribution entropy drops by more than 50% during GenRe^2 training, and the Wasserstein-1 distance between predicted and target distributions is consistently lower than for the base model on most tasks (Figure 6, Section 4.3).

e1bpZMpANm.text: Using symbolic (e.g., bounding-box) verifier outputs as meta-verification rationales instead of free-form textual explanations reduces reward computation time from about 20.2ms to about 0.021ms per sample while maintaining comparable ViVerBench accuracy (0.662 vs 0.661 for OmniVerifier 7B) (Table 1).
Decoupling the RL objectives for binary judgment and meta-verification improves Qwen3-VL-8B overall ViVerBench performance from 0.671 (joint training) to 0.680 (decoupled training) (Table 2).

On RefCOCO visual grounding, decoupled RL training raises Qwen3-VL-8B overall performance from 0.847 (joint) to 0.866 (decoupled), demonstrating generalization of decoupled meta-verification beyond the training benchmark (Table 3).
OmniVerifier-M1 combined with GPT-Image-1.5 achieves 0.88 on the WISE benchmark and 0.800 on T2I-CoreBench, outperforming baseline Qwen3-VL verification approaches (Table 4).
Error localization accuracy under decoupled training reaches 0.780 on synthetic data and 0.725 on real-world data (Section 5).

yhvzMLgpdV.text: The paper introduces a stability index δ_t that quantifies how much a stochastic optimization step degrades progress as the step size grows, and links it directly to suboptimality bounds via average-iterate and last-iterate convergence theorems (Theorem 3, Theorem 4, Section 3).
For SGD, the stability index is derived as δ_t^SGD = (α_t/2)‖g_t‖^2, which scales linearly (unboundedly) with the step size α_t (Section 4).
For NGN, the stability index δ_t^NGN = (γ_t/2)‖g_t‖^2 ≤ δ_t^SGD, and it saturates rather than growing unboundedly for large step sizes, unlike SGD (Section 4).
For SPS, the stability index is bounded as δ_t^SPS ≤ min{α_t‖g_t‖^2, f(x_t,s_t) - C_t}, scaling sub-linearly with step size, in contrast to SGD's linear scaling (Section 4).

Experiments on ResNet trained on CIFAR-10 and on linear/logistic regression tasks confirm that the theoretical stability-index bounds predict the empirically observed robustness ordering of SPS, NGN, and SPP over SGD across a range of step sizes (Section 5).

L35b2JZ8gS.text: CurvZO defines a per-parameter curvature score s_i = Δ^2 v_i^2 from scalar zeroth-order feedback, normalizes and smooths it via an exponential moving average, and uses it to build a variance-minimizing sampling distribution proportional to sqrt(S_i) for perturbation directions (Section 3, Section 3.2).
On OPT-2.7B fine-tuned with 1,000 samples per task, CurvZO achieves 66.8% average accuracy versus 64.2% for MeZO, with gains of +4.3 points on WSC and +2.5 points on SQuAD (Table 1).
On OPT-6.7B, CurvZO outperforms MeZO on RTE (72.2% vs 70.3%) and SQuAD (83.7% vs 81.6%) (Table 2).
CurvZO converges 2.4x faster in steps on BoolQ and 2.0x faster on RTE compared to MeZO, while requiring identical peak memory (5.91 GB for OPT-2.7B) (Figure 3, Table 3).

CurvZO's adaptive perturbation budget selection uses effective support size and Shannon entropy of the curvature distribution to dynamically adjust the number of sampled directions per step (Section 3, Adaptive Budget Selection).
CurvZO yields up to 59% GPU-hour savings on BoolQ and 51% on RTE relative to MeZO (Figure 4).

5fm6XlWpiY.text: SkeletonLLM's DrAction renderer models the human body as deformable 3D Gaussian primitives bound to kinematic chains, using Linear Blend Skinning for pose-dependent deformation and a Neural Feature Modulator for kinematically-aware appearance, enabling differentiable rendering of arbitrary skeleton formats into image sequences (Section 3).

Training follows a four-stage curriculum: Alignment Warm-up (renderer-only optimization), Discriminative Finetuning on confusing action pairs, Causal Reasoning Distillation from a teacher model, and Recognition Refinement (Section 3).
On the NTU-60 (30/30 split) action recognition benchmark, SkeletonLLM improves accuracy by 11.96 points over the TDSM baseline, and by 7.73 points on NTU-120 (60/60 split) (Section 4).
In cross-format transfer from Kinect to MoCap skeleton data, SkeletonLLM reaches 60.38% accuracy versus 43.19% for TDSM (Section 4).
On HumanML3D motion captioning, SkeletonLLM improves R@1 by 5.35 points over InternVL3-8B (Section 4).

The Gaussian primitive count K = J + K_bone adapts dynamically to the input skeleton's joint count, allowing the same model to handle formats with 17 to 25 joints without architectural changes (Section 3).

Abko94Sl7D.text: Graph-GRPO derives a closed-form analytical transition probability formula for graph flow models, replacing non-differentiable Monte Carlo sampling of the conditional rate matrix to enable fully differentiable RL rollouts (Section 3).

Graph-GRPO achieves 95.0% Valid-Unique-Novelty (VUN) on the planar dataset and 97.5% VUN on the tree dataset using only 50 denoising steps, the tree result improving over a 73.5% baseline (Section 5).
On ZINC250k protein docking, Graph-GRPO reaches a 60.76% hit ratio against PARP1 and 52.90% against JAK2, roughly six times higher than the GDPO baseline's 9.81% and 13.41% respectively (Section 5).
On the PMO benchmark, Graph-GRPO attains an AUC-top10 of 19.270 with prescreening and 18.987 in the cold-start setting without prescreening (Section 5).

Ablations show AUC-top10 rising from 11.079 (base DeFoG) to 17.450 with RL training alone, then to 18.987 with RL plus the refinement (renoise-and-regenerate) strategy, and to 19.270 with prescreening added (Table 4).
Ablation over renoising time shows optimal refinement performance at intermediate perturbation levels t_epsilon = 0.7-0.9, with smaller perturbations better preserving molecular scaffolds (Table 5).

jlQeiq1azU.text: Proposition 4.4 proves that any uncovered probability mass delta of strategic distributions lying outside the non-strategic pretraining support induces an irreducible prediction bias, formally lim inf_{n to infinity} E_n >= c*delta for some constant c > 0 (Section 4, Proposition 4.4).

Strategic Prior-data Fitted Networks (SPN) construct a strategic tabular in-context learning set by pairing each observed example (x_i, y_i) with a best-response-manipulated counterpart (b_f(x_i), y_i), per Definition 5.1 (Section 5, Definition 5.1).
Proposition 5.3 shows SPN's strategic-context construction strictly reduces the uncovered mass relative to the base pretrained prior, i.e. delta_SPN < delta (Section 5, Proposition 5.3).
On non-strategic data, SPN achieves 91.65% AUC-ROC on the Bank dataset versus 91.85% for TabPFN v2.5, showing minimal degradation across 8 standard benchmarks (Table 1).
Under 100% strategic manipulation, SPN maintains robust accuracy on Adult, Census, Diabetes and synthetic datasets while plain TabPFN's accuracy drops significantly (Figure 5).

SPN's in-context-learning performance saturates at around 50 strategic context examples, indicating a sample-efficient adaptation mechanism compared to fine-tuning-based approaches (Figure 6, Figure 3).

gpgxDbpXmw.text: Under 4-bit quantization, LSGQuant reduces DiT module parameters by 70.49% (to 419M) and operations by 71.92% (to 11,264 GFLOPs) while retaining performance close to the full-precision model (Section 4).

On the UDM10 dataset at 4-bit quantization, LSGQuant reaches PSNR 23.80 / SSIM 0.7130 / LPIPS 0.3169, outperforming SVDQuant (21.92 / 0.6544 / 0.4770) and ViDiT-Q (21.89 / 0.6570 / 0.5052) (Table with UDM10 4-bit results).

The Dynamic Range Adaptive Quantizer (DRAQ) performs channel-wise and token-wise normalization of activations into [-1, 1] before symmetric quantization to address outlier-dominated activation ranges in Diffusion Transformers (Section 3).

The Variance-Oriented Layer Training Strategy (VOLTS) partitions layers into three tiers by activation variance sigma_l^2 -- frozen (sigma_l^2 < delta_1), lightly adapted (delta_1 <= sigma_l^2 < delta_2), and fully optimized (sigma_l^2 >= delta_2) -- to allocate training resources by sensitivity (Section 3).

Ablation results show DRAQ alone improves 4-bit PSNR from 20.04 to 23.80, and the three-tier VOLTS scheme outperforms simplified (fewer-tier) layer-sensitivity classification schemes (Ablation section).

Quantization-Aware Alternating Optimization (QAO) jointly refines a low-bit quantized branch and a full-precision low-rank branch via iterative SVD-based optimization to minimize residual weight quantization error (Section 3).

iWV5o07Bxv.text: Theorem 1 proves that for an arbitrary positive constant branch-scaling factor alpha, the Residual Neural Tangent Kernel (RNTK) converges to a constant kernel as depth L to infinity, implying degenerate, depth-independent generalization behavior (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 shows that even a decaying scaling factor alpha = L^(-1/4) still leads to kernel degeneration, with the RNTK converging to 1/4 for distinct inputs (Theorem 2).

Proposition 2 establishes that setting alpha = L^(-gamma) for gamma in (1/2, 1] makes the RNTK converge to the one-hidden-layer fully-connected NTK, and combined with early stopping this yields minimax-optimal generalization rates (Proposition 2).
Lemma 1 proves the Residual Neural Tangent Kernel is positive definite, and the paper shows finite-width residual networks uniformly approximate the infinite-width RNTK (Lemma 1).

On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with 20,000 training samples, networks using depth-decaying alpha = L^(-1) consistently outperform networks with constant alpha = 1 scaling, validating the theoretical predictions (Experiments section).

BWhC4ezzeE.text: DynaTok tokenizes each partial point cloud frame into compact latent tokens via Farthest Point Sampling and cross-attention, with transformer layers alternating between per-frame self-attention and cross-frame global attention (Section 3).

DynaTok decomposes per-frame geometry as Z_s = G + H_s, separating a shared canonical geometry code G from per-frame residual/temporal-variation codes H_s without introducing additional tokens (Section 3, reference-residual parameterization).

DynaTok's flow-matching decoder generates completed point clouds by learning a conditional velocity field dx_t/dt = Phi_dec(x_t, t, Z_s), trained with a flow-matching loss requiring no correspondence supervision beyond point cloud targets (Section 3).

On DT4D-Animals object-level reconstruction, DynaTok achieves accuracy 0.023 and completeness 0.021, versus Motion2VecSets' 0.055 and 0.060 respectively, and a higher normal consistency of 0.914 versus 0.856 (Experiments/Table results on DT4D-Animals).

On the Kubric scene-level benchmark, DynaTok attains the best or tied-best accuracy in both foreground-only and full-scene settings, and substantially improves completeness (0.010-0.014) over frame-wise baselines (Experiments section, Kubric results).
DynaTok uses only 19M parameters and about 6.6k GFLOPs per 16-frame scene, roughly 2.5x faster than Motion2VecSets (Efficiency analysis section).

eSxGdQ0zwG.text: Auto-MOG achieves an FID of 8.78 on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 with DiT-XL/2 (guidance weight w=4), versus 12.45 for the CFG++ baseline (Table 1).
On EDM2-XXL (w=2) for ImageNet 256x256, Auto-MOG attains FID 4.30 compared to 4.94 for APG guidance (Table 1).
On text-to-image generation with SD-XL (w=15) on COCO 512x512, Auto-MOG improves FID from 22.29 (CFG) to 21.60 while raising HPSv2 from 28.42 to 29.00 and CLIP score from 33.62 to 34.20 (Table 1).

MOG is derived in Section 3.2 as a Riemannian natural-gradient update s_MOG = s_0 + beta(t) M_t^{-1} Delta s, and Section 3.3 argues this achieves maximum energy reduction per unit geodesic displacement relative to the Euclidean extrapolation used by standard CFG (Section 3.2-3.3).

Auto-MOG's adaptive scaling rule beta_auto(t) = gamma * E_prior(t) / (E_guid(t) + epsilon) removes the need to manually tune guidance strength while adding only about 1.08x latency overhead versus 1.01x for the non-adaptive MOG-Score variant (Section 4.2, Table 2).
In a user study of 37 participants across 2,960 trials, Auto-MOG is preferred over standard CFG on overall quality 62.0% of the time (95% CI 60.2%-63.8%, p<0.001) (Table 8).

YhEWC2HiJl.text: DANCE improves accuracy by 2.33% at an 8% condensation ratio while using 33.42% fewer tokens per condensed node than TAG-FGL baselines, aggregated across 8 text-attributed graph datasets including Cora, CiteSeer, Arxiv, and Reddit (Table 1, Section 6.5).

DANCE's architecture combines label-aware node condensation via clustering-based selection performed every 10 rounds (Section 4.2), budgeted neighbor gating across 0/1/2-hop neighborhoods for hierarchical text condensation (Section 4.3, Eq. 5-9), and prior-regularized sparse self-expressive topology reconstruction maintaining O(Kq) edges (Section 4.4, Eq. 13).

DANCE produces locally inspectable evidence packs that trace each prediction to selected neighbors and source text spans, and Section 6.3 with Figure 8 shows via deletion/insertion tests that this selected evidence is both sufficient and necessary for the model's predictions.
Theorem 5.4 establishes a bounded approximation error for DANCE under hard token budgets, and Theorem 5.6 establishes selection stability under model drift (Section 5).

Table 3 gives DANCE's time complexity as O(C(n log n + Kq)) and space complexity as O(n + Kq), and Figure 5 shows substantially lower training time than LLM-based condensation methods (Table 3, Figure 5).

g95mt3KBRd.text: CoGeoAD achieves 87.4% I-AUROC, 96.5% AP, 97.5% P-AUROC, and 91.9% AUPRO on MVTec3D-AD, surpassing the GS-CLIP baseline by 3.8 points I-AUROC and 5.5 points AUPRO (Table 1).
On the Eyecandies benchmark, CoGeoAD reaches 82.6% I-AUROC and 84.5% AP, exceeding the PointAD+ baseline by 2.3 points I-AUROC (Table 1).

The Multi-View Attention (MVA) module, which uses a lightweight pixel encoder with a convolutional backbone and projection head to produce Boltzmann-distributed attention weights with entropy regularization against collapse, improves I-AUROC from an 83.8% mean-pooling baseline to 87.4% (Section 3.3, Table 4).

An ablation removing the MVA module drops I-AUROC to 83.5%, removing the color branch drops it to 84.3%, and removing the geometric branch drops it to 83.6%, versus 87.4% for the complete CoGeoAD model (Table 3).
Table 5 shows CoGeoAD's peak performance is obtained with 9 rendered multi-views at 336x336 resolution (Table 5).

TaNH4XiQ6P.text: Section 3.1 (Table 1) shows that regardless of the preference-optimization objective's form, the gradient update decomposes along identical score directions for winner and loser responses, with objective design entering only through two scalar incentive weights (d_w, d_l) (Section 3.1, Table 1).

The Disentanglement Band, defined in Equation 9 of Section 3.2 as a bound on log(r_t) in terms of the score-norm ratio and cosine similarity rho_t between winner and loser score vectors, characterizes exactly when training suppresses the loser while preserving the winner likelihood (pathway iii) (Section 3.2, Equation 9).

The paper attributes chosen-response degradation in entangled objectives like DPO and IPO to a coupling drag term -d_{l,t}<s_{w,t}, s_{l,t}> that pulls the winner likelihood downward due to interference from loser-targeted updates (Section 3.1).

The plug-and-play reward calibration method (Algorithm 1, Section 3.3) rescales winner/loser logit terms toward a target incentive ratio r_t* = ||s_{l,t}||/||s_{w,t}|| without redesigning the base objective (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1).

On Mistral-7B, applying reward calibration improves the average alignment score by +12.18 points for DPO and +19.81 points for DDRO, while leaving already-strong methods such as SimPO, BCE, and LSIF largely undisrupted (Section 4, Table 4).

tyul8kXaJU.text: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, InftyThink+ with task-only RL reaches 50.94% accuracy on AIME24 (a +21.46-point gain over the un-trained InftyThink baseline of 29.20%), versus a +12.08-point gain for vanilla long chain-of-thought RL over its own baseline (Table 1).

On the out-of-distribution GPQA_diamond benchmark, InftyThink+ improves accuracy by 5.19 points under task-only RL, exceeding the vanilla RL setting's 5.62-point average gain margin as reported for cross-benchmark averages, and by an additional roughly 4 points over vanilla when compared directly (Table 1).

With the added efficiency reward (T+E setting), InftyThink+ on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B reduces average inference latency from 100.21 seconds to 48.37 seconds (a 29.20-second/roughly 52% reduction) while trading off from 53.96% to 50.58% average accuracy relative to task-only RL (Table 1).

An ablation comparing adaptive (InftyThink) summarization timing against Fixed and Random interruption strategies shows adaptive timing consistently outperforms both, e.g. on AIME24 without RL the adaptive strategy scores 29.48% versus 28.54% (Random) and 28.44% (Fixed) (Table 2, Section 5.1.1).

RL training under InftyThink+ reduces per-step training time from an average of 300 seconds (vanilla long-context RL) to 225 seconds with task reward only (a ~25% speedup) and to 175 seconds with the added efficiency reward (an ~18.2% additional speedup, ~40% total), as shown in Figure 3 (Figure 3, Section 5.2).

0H5Im3Xvuf.text: AgentHijack constructs 3,321 corrupted tasks by applying nine configurable corruption types to the 369 original tasks from OSWorld (Section 3.3).

The nine corruptions are grouped into visual disruptors (pop-ups, resolution changes, desktop marks, subtitles, multiple applications), unexpected operations (accidental touches, app minimization), and environmental errors (network failures, verification requirements) (Section 3.2).
UI-TARS-1.5-7B achieves 24.21% success on clean OSWorld tasks but only 18.74% average success under AgentHijack corruptions, demonstrating substantial performance degradation (Table 2).

AgentHijack-Agent, which combines an enhanced action generator trained with Data-Augmented Group Relative Policy Optimization (DA-GRPO) and an onlooker validation module, raises average success under corruption to 22.89% (from 18.74% for UI-TARS-1.5-7B), a 4.15-point improvement (Table 2, Section 5.2).
AgentHijack-Agent yields corruption-specific gains of +11.23% on pop-up disruptors and +9.67% on verification-requirement errors relative to the baseline agent (Section 5.2).
An ablation isolating the onlooker module versus the enhanced action generator shows both components are individually necessary for robustness gains (Figure 6, Section 5.3).

Og7FKaRBQA.text: DGNO decomposes the global integral operator for defocus deblurring into element-local volume operators and interface numerical fluxes, following a discontinuous Galerkin (DG) formulation, with two variants DGNO-Face (explicit interface flux) and DGNO-Cell (zero-order P0DG approximation) (Section on Technical Approach / Table 1).
On the BBBC006w1 pathology microscopy dataset, DGNO-Cell achieves 37.22 dB PSNR and 0.959 SSIM, outperforming Restormer's 35.35 dB PSNR and 0.950 SSIM (Table 1).
On the BBBC006w2 dataset, DGNO-Face reaches 32.66 dB PSNR and 0.847 SSIM, exceeding the MPT+EFCR baseline's 30.48 dB PSNR and 0.830 SSIM (Table 1).

An ablation against a global Galerkin operator (SRNO, 36.71 dB) shows DGNO-Face (37.07 dB) and DGNO-Cell (37.21 dB) progressively improve PSNR by introducing locality and discontinuity-awareness (Table 2).
On edge/boundary regions, DG-based operators improve PSNR by +0.49 dB over the global Galerkin baseline, with weaker residual artifacts near cellular structures (Figure 6).

DGNO-Cell improves downstream cell-detection accuracy on deblurred images, achieving a mean AP of 0.5561 with StarDist, while maintaining a comparable computational budget of 12.79M parameters and about 50G FLOPs using only T=2 operator iterations.

sNUjy8nZhD.text: ExpAlign introduces an Expectation Alignment Head that aggregates token-level vision-language similarities into an Expectation Alignment Map via a softmax-weighted token posterior, rather than collapsing text prompts into a single embedding (Section on Core Method).
In the OG+RefC setting, ExpAlign attains 36.2 AP_r (rare-category AP) on the LVIS minival split alongside 37.1 overall AP (Table 1).

In zero-shot instance segmentation without LVIS training data, ExpAlign achieves 29.9 APm overall and 29.0 APm on rare categories, substantially outperforming YOLOE variants, which score 22.6-23.5 APm on rare categories (Table 2).
An ablation shows token-level alignment (the Expectation Alignment Map) outperforms mean pooling by +5.2 AP / +8.9 AP_r and outperforms using the global CLIP EOT token by +2.7 AP (Ablation section).

The Geometry-Aware Consistency Objective (GACO), derived from a Lagrangian-constrained free-energy minimization, together with the multi-positive InfoNCE loss, is tuned with loss weights λ_sem=0.5 and λ_geo=1.0, and is found to be particularly beneficial for long-tail category performance (Ablation section).

ExpAlign underperforms specialized referring-expression models such as Grounding DINO on RefCOCO benchmarks, attributed to CLIP's weak encoding of positional and relational language (Section on Referring Expression Limitation).

NXzNyMetWc.text: XPERT selects cross-domain 'common experts' from a source Mixture-of-Experts model using an average activation score A_i and a consistency score C_i computed across M domains, favoring experts with high, balanced activation rather than single-domain specialists (Section on Cross-Domain Expert Selection).

Selected experts' parameters are consolidated via Tucker decomposition into a compact core tensor plus factor matrices, retaining approximately 1.25% of the source model's parameter count, then rescaled to the target architecture via truncated-SVD importance scoring and importance-guided resampling (Section on Knowledge Consolidation).

Across 270M-570M parameter target models evaluated on BoolQ, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, CaseHold, and MedMCQA, XPERT initialization improves accuracy by +0.4 to +1.9 absolute percentage points over random initialization baselines (Table 1).

On dialogue-generation benchmarks (DollyEval, S-NI, UnNI, SelfInst, VicunaEval), XPERT-initialized models improve average Rouge-L by 0.5-2.5 points over baselines, reach matching Rouge-L about 2.4x faster than training from scratch, and XPERT pretrained on 2B tokens exceeds scratch training on 10B tokens on UnNI (Table 2).

Ablations in Table 3 show that replacing cross-domain expert selection with random selection costs 1.76 average performance points, replacing Tucker decomposition with simple averaging costs 2.32 points, and replacing importance-guided resampling with naive truncation costs 2.54 points (Table 3).

7YeCG53Bo9.text: PhysicEdit reformulates instruction-based image editing as predicting a physical state transition rather than a discrete image mapping, addressing violations of physical principles (e.g., refraction, material deformation) in existing editors.

The paper constructs PhysicTran38K, a dataset of 38,000 transition trajectories spanning five physical domains (Mechanical, Thermal, Material, Optical, Biological) organized into 16 sub-domains and 46 transition types, generated with Wan2.2-T2V-A14B and filtered via ViPE geometric-stability checks and GPT-4-mini principle verification.

PhysicEdit uses a textual-visual dual-thinking mechanism: a frozen Qwen2.5-VL branch produces explicit physical-constraint text, while a learnable visual-thinking branch with transition queries is supervised by DINOv2 structural features and VAE texture features from intermediate keyframes, combined via timestep-aware modulation.
PhysicEdit improves over the Qwen-Image-Edit baseline by 5.9% in physical realism and by 10.1% in knowledge-grounded editing.
PhysicEdit achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source instruction-based image editors and performs competitively with proprietary closed-source editing systems.

4i4K7wVYUW.text: SpaceVista-1M contains approximately 1 million spatial QA pairs spanning 19 diverse task types across 5 spatial scales from millimeter to kilometer (Abstract, Figure 1).

SpaceVista-1M is built from over 38,000 video scenes sourced via a task-specific automated pipeline drawing on datasets such as uCO3D, WildRGB-D, ScanNet, SPAR-Bench, and DL3DV (Section B.2, Table B7).

SpaceVista-7B augments Qwen2.5-VL-7B with dense DINOv3 feature fusion and scale-aware LoRA experts (M=4) selected by an MLP scale router, trained via 2 epochs of SFT followed by 2.5k GRPO RL steps (Section 4, Section 5, Figure 5).
On SpaceVista-Bench, SpaceVista-7B achieves 36.7% overall accuracy, outperforming other open-source models by roughly 6 points (Table 5).

With RL training, SpaceVista-7B reaches 48.6% on VSI-Bench, 41.6% on SPAR-Bench, 38.2% on STI-Bench, and 32.3% on MMSI-Bench, positioning it competitively against commercial models such as GPT-5 (44.2% VSI-Bench) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (45.0% VSI-Bench) (Table 2).

Ablations show that adding the scale factor alone improves VSI-Bench by +1.9% and SpaceVista-Bench by +3.8%, while adding scale plus semantic rewards improves them by +2.4% and +4.4% respectively (Table 3).

WikPLZyyrT.text: ReRe is a training-free, inference-time framework built on a Geometry-to-Video pipeline that uses VGGT to predict a 3D point cloud and renders novel views along an 'Oblique Sweep' camera trajectory at 45-degree elevation to reduce occlusion (Section 3.4.2, Figure 3).

On VSI-Bench, ReRe boosts Qwen3-VL-4B from 30.7 to 36.5 (+5.8 points) and Qwen3-VL-8B from 30.5 to 35.8 (+5.2 points), bringing open-source models to rival proprietary GPT-4o's average of 34.0 (Table 1).
ReRe improves InternVL2.5-8B from 35.5 to 36.7 (+1.2 points) on VSI-Bench (Table 1).
On STI-Bench, ReRe boosts Qwen3-VL-2B by +8.0 points overall, including a +18.5 point gain on Spatial Relation tasks (Table 2).

Ablations show the sequential ReRe revisiting protocol scores 29.5, substantially outperforming naive Concat (25.4) and Interleaved (25.6) baselines that provide the same information without the revisiting process (Table 3).
The Oblique Sweep trajectory design (29.5) outperforms alternative camera paths, Mid-level Traverse (25.6) and Bird's-eye Orbit (27.4) (Table 5).

USAkWviwng.text: SoMA is a neural simulator operating on 3D Gaussian Splat representations that learns deformable object dynamics from multi-view RGB videos without predefined physics models, using force-driven GS dynamics with a graph neural network to compute robot-object interaction forces (Section 4.2.2).

On resimulation accuracy, SoMA achieves 33.51 dB PSNR and 0.971 SSIM, versus GausSim at 31.69 dB/0.945 SSIM and PhysTwin at 28.77 dB/0.947 SSIM, an improvement of roughly 20% over these baselines (Table 1).

On T-shirt folding, a long-horizon task with 100-150 frame sequences involving complex self-contacts, SoMA achieves 27.57 dB PSNR versus 22.85 dB for PhysTwin, demonstrating stable simulation without predefined physical models (Table 2).
SoMA uses a multi-resolution, two-stage coarse-to-fine training strategy with temporal strides of k=5 for the T-shirt task and k=10 for other tasks (Section 4.2.3).
SoMA is evaluated across rope manipulation, cloth lifting and folding, doll handling, and T-shirt folding tasks against PhysTwin and GausSim baselines (Section 4, Table 1, Table 2).

fKsDQLjyIb.text: Conformal Counterfactual Generation (CCG) models the closed-loop LLM-controlled system as a structural causal model and, per Proposition 1, produces a set of counterfactual outcomes guaranteed with probability at least 1-δ to contain a semantically faithful approximation of the true counterfactual outcome (Section 4.3, Proposition 1).

On a 5G base station configuration (wireless network control) task, Conformal Counterfactual Generation achieves a throughput MAE of 0.15 and cross-correlation peak of 0.93, versus 0.28/0.78 for Interventional Generation and 0.33/0.70 for Simulated Interventional Generation baselines (Table 1, Section 3.3.2).

In an LLM-as-judge evaluation over 100 test cases, Conformal Counterfactual Generation's output was selected as the best match in 92% of cases, versus 8% for the Interventional Generation baseline and 0% for Simulated Interventional Generation (Section 3.3.2).

Figure 6 shows Conformal Counterfactual Generation consistently requires fewer excess samples than fixed-budget baselines to produce sets of plausible counterfactual reports at the same coverage level (Figure 6).

KhqHSH9xKk.text: FedQual addresses federated label distribution learning where sample-size-based aggregation breaks down under heterogeneous per-client annotation quality, motivating reliability-aware aggregation instead of raw sample-count weighting (Section 2.3).

Theorem 3.1 (restated as Theorem A.1 in Appendix A) proves the adaptive client-specific calibration strategy achieves strictly smaller total risk than any uniform calibration strategy, i.e. J_adapt < J_uni, under heterogeneous supervision quality (Section 3, Theorem 3.1, Equation 8).

FedQual combines quality-adaptive client training using a Global Semantic Anchor (Equation 1-3) with server-side aggregation weighted by 'effective reliable information' S_m = N_m times q_m rather than raw sample size N_m, via a trust-annealing factor (Equations 4-7).
On the PIPAL-LDL benchmark, adding the anchor calibration component alone reduces KL divergence from 0.252 to 0.154, and the full framework (both components) achieves 0.116 (Table 2).

Across four new Fed-LDL benchmarks (FER-LDL, FI-LDL, KADID-LDL, PIPAL-LDL) built via a 10-expert annotation protocol, FedQual achieves KL divergences of 0.2528, 0.4085, 0.0908, and 0.1162 respectively, with cosine similarities of 0.8739, 0.8173, 0.9672, and 0.9580 (Table 1, Section 4).
FedQual maintains robustness under noisy client ratios up to 75% and participation ratios as low as 20% across federation sizes ranging from 25 to 100 clients (Figures 3-7).

03ZTlJuX0y.text: Sparse-autoencoder reasoning features exhibit substantially higher activation magnitudes in the late layers than in early-to-middle layers across Qwen-3 variants (Section 2.2, Figure 2).

Spearman correlation between hidden-state ℓ2 norm and SAE reasoning-feature activations exceeds 0.84 for all four tested models (Qwen3-1.7B 86.47, Qwen3-8B 85.15, Qwen3-14B 87.62, LLaMA3-8B 84.11) (Table 1).
Hidden-state ℓ2 norm is consistently higher during thinking-mode generation than non-thinking generation (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

Causally intervening on high-ℓ2-norm hidden states on Qwen3-14B causes severe performance degradation across reasoning benchmarks, supporting a causal link between ℓ2 norm and reasoning activity (Section 3.3, Figure 4).

ℓ2-norm-guided test-time methods (Adaptive Layer-wise Recursion, Endogenous Reasoning State Steering, ℓ2-guided Response Selection) achieve a 4.51% average relative improvement across benchmarks, rising to 9.13% on AIME, without additional training or data (Section 4.5, Figures 6-8).
A theoretical bound relates the sum of per-layer ℓ2-norm changes to observable output change, of the form c1√(Δobs−ϵtotal) ≤ Σ Δzi ≤ c2√(Δobs+ϵtotal) (Theorem 1).

WyQlim30lN.text: Anchor-conditioned self-ranking satisfies an order-consistency property: for candidates i,j, ri>rj implies Dx(i)>Dx(j) under the induced ranking distribution (Theorem 3.1).
The near-optimality guarantee bounds the expected reward gap under the induced distribution by rmax − E[rk] ≤ τ log K, where τ is the temperature and K the number of candidates (Theorem 3.2).

LDL-GRPO, the proposed positive-unlabeled RL distillation method, attains the highest scores on writing and multimodal tasks under length-controlled (LC) evaluation among six tasks tested, without human-labeled preferences or a trained reward model (Section 4, Table 1).
An ablation comparing SFT, Anchor-GRPO, and LDL-GRPO shows the full method outperforms both simpler variants (Section 4, Table 2).
Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis shows a nearly flat win-rate curve for temperature τ in the range [0.6, 1.5], with τ=1.2 and β=0.01 used in main experiments (Section 4.4, Figure 3).
The proposed method reduces teacher-query complexity from O(NK) to O(N) candidate evaluations per prompt (Section 3, Table C.4).

vv4TMkyfWA.text: MemOCR achieves 74.6% average accuracy across HotpotQA, 2Wiki, NQ, and TriviaQA at context lengths of 10K/30K/100K and budgets of {16,64,256,1024} tokens, versus 67.8% for the strongest baseline (Section 4.2, Table 1).
At an extreme 16-token memory budget, MemOCR achieves 62.2% average accuracy compared to 31.6% for the MemAgent baseline (Section 4.3, Table 1).
MemOCR's relative performance drop from a 1024-token to a 16-token budget is only 16.6%, compared to 53.3% for MemAgent (Section 4.3, Figure 4).
MemOCR attains accuracy comparable to text baselines using 64 tokens while consuming only 8 tokens of visual memory (Section 4.3).

An ablation progressively removing the three budget-aware training objectives (standard QA, augmented memory, augmented question) shows each component contributes to overall performance (Section 4.4, Table 2).
Statistical significance testing confirms MemOCR's improvements over baselines at tight token budgets are significant with p<0.01 (Section 4.2, Table 7).

tbdSfBMlbq.text: On GSM8K, Ouro-1.4B combined with STARS reaches 74.45% accuracy at 8 recurrent steps, compared to 58.23% for the unregularized Ouro-1.4B baseline (Section 6, Table 2, Figure 1).
The unregularized Ouro-1.4B baseline suffers a 20.47% accuracy drop from its peak by 8 recurrent steps, whereas STARS limits this degradation to 8.26% (Section 6, Figure 4).
STARS achieves 100% accuracy consistently across recurrent iterations on a multi-digit addition task, unlike baseline looped models (Section 6, Figure 5).
STARS is derived from a Jacobian spectral-radius regularization applied to the recurrent update of looped language models to stabilize latent-state dynamics (Section 5).
Ablations examine the impact of Prelude/Coda layers and random loop-step sampling on STARS's test-time scaling behavior (Section 6, Figure 3).

7XUocfk7eQ.text: The federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point is defined as the fixed point at which each client's deployed model induces a distribution under which the aggregated upper-level risk is minimized at that same point (Section 2.1.1).

Under Assumptions 1-4, the update operator R(·) is contractive whenever L̄ᶠᶜˣ(εc,εd)/γf ≤ 1, which guarantees existence, uniqueness, and linear convergence of FBi-RRM to the FBPS point (Theorem 1, Section 3.2).

FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic variant using local updates and hypergradient estimation via an auxiliary variable, converges at rate E‖xr−xs‖²=O(1/r) under sufficiently small distribution sensitivities (Theorem 2, Section 4.3).

The distance between the federated bilevel performatively optimal (FBPO) point and the FBPS point is bounded by an expression proportional to the product of upper- and lower-level distribution sensitivities εc and εd (Theorem 3, Section 4.4).
This work is presented as the first to combine federated bilevel optimization with performative prediction under decision-dependent distribution shifts at both objective levels (Section 1).

zDcoHkyxmE.text: SiameseNorm is a two-stream residual architecture with shared parameters that couples Pre-Norm-like and Post-Norm-like streams to decouple their optimization dynamics while retaining both paradigms' distinct characteristics (Section 3).

On 1.3B-parameter OLMo-based models (16 layers, 2048 hidden size, 16 heads) trained on 100B tokens of FineWeb-Edu at learning rate 2e-3, SiameseNorm attains average perplexity 10.48 versus 10.89 for Pre-Norm, while standard Post-Norm and HybridNorm diverge under this setting (Table 1).

At the same 2e-3 learning rate / 100B-token setting, SiameseNorm reaches 39.6% arithmetic-task accuracy versus 28.1% for Pre-Norm, a 40.9% relative gain, and an average downstream score of 55.63 versus 52.94 (Table 1).
At a lower learning rate of 1e-3 (100B tokens), SiameseNorm still improves over Pre-Norm, achieving 10.43 average perplexity and 53.53 average score versus 10.84 and 51.91 for Pre-Norm (Table 1).
During training, SiameseNorm keeps gradient norms below 0.5, matching Pre-Norm's stability and avoiding the gradient explosions observed with Post-Norm variants (Section 5.1).

mUU7k4bN97.text: InfoReasoner trains retrieval-augmented reasoning agents with a synthetic semantic information gain reward that measures reduction in uncertainty over the answer belief distribution, using bidirectional textual entailment to cluster semantically equivalent answers rather than token overlap (Section 4, Definition 4.1).
