The reward is theoretically guaranteed to be non-negative in expectation (Proposition 3.6), to telescope so that the sum of step-wise gains equals total uncertainty reduction (Proposition 3.7), and to be monotonic in information source quality (Proposition 3.8).

InfoReasoner is evaluated on seven QA benchmarks—Natural Questions, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle—achieving up to a 5.4% average accuracy improvement over baselines (Section 5.1, Table 1).
At the 3B scale, InfoReasoner-3B reaches 34.6% average accuracy, outperforming Search-R1-3B-Instruct's 30.1% and several 7B baselines (Table 1).
At the 7B scale, InfoReasoner-7B reaches 39.1% average accuracy, exceeding AutoRefine-7B-Base (36.9%) and Search-R1-7B-Instruct (33.7%) (Table 1).

An ablation over the information-gain weighting coefficient shows λ=0.6 is optimal, while removing the information gain reward (λ=0.0) drops average accuracy to 29.9%, demonstrating the reward's necessity (Table 2).

m3O4qYQ5hu.text: Distributional Active Inference (DAIF) integrates active inference into a distributional reinforcement learning framework via a 'push-forward RL' formulation that avoids explicitly modeling transition dynamics (Section 3, Equation 2).

Theorem 3.5 shows that when an auto-encoder with encoder Lipschitz constant L_E and decoder Lipschitz constant L_D is used for representation learning, the distributional Bellman operator's contraction modulus becomes γ·L_E·L_D, formally linking state abstraction quality to convergence (Theorem 3.5, building on Lemma 3.1).

Algorithm 3 implements DAIF using quantile regression over a learned latent embedding space with an Asymmetric Laplace Distribution for quantile-function parameterization, combined with entropy-regularized policy optimization (Algorithm 3).

Across 19 continuous-control environments spanning EvoGym (7 soft-robotics tasks), DeepMind Control Suite (7 locomotion tasks), and DMC vision-based tasks (5 tasks), DAIF achieves the best average ranking (1.5-1.9 for area under the learning curve, 1.6-2.0 for final return) among compared methods (Table 1).

Figure 2 shows DAIF's advantage over model-based and vanilla distributional RL baselines grows when the learned latent manifold efficiently represents the environment's dynamics, and converges to parity when state abstraction offers no advantage (Figure 2).
DAIF incurs approximately 12% additional wall-clock training time compared to a distributional actor-critic baseline (Section 5, experimental results).

jwRAIYoVJn.text: UniAR uses a single discrete visual tokenizer based on Binary Spherical Quantization (64-bit vectors) to bridge visual understanding and generation within a shared token space, eliminating the need for separate tokenizers used by prior unified models (Section 3.1).

The autoregressive decoder uses a parallel bitwise prediction mechanism over 2x2 spatial grids, achieving 32x visual compression, and is trained with random visual index flipping during pretraining to simulate error accumulation (Section 3.2).

On the GenEval text-to-image benchmark, UniAR achieves an overall score of 0.86, surpassing GPT-4o's 0.84, with per-category scores of 1.00 (single object), 0.95 (multiple objects), 0.75 (counting), and 0.94 (colors) (Table 1).
On the ImgEdit-Bench image editing benchmark, UniAR scores 3.73 overall, exceeding Flux.1 Kontext's 3.71 (Table 3).
On multimodal understanding, UniAR scores 833 on OCRBench, 91.4 on DocVQA, and 70.0 on InfoVQA, remaining competitive with understanding-only models on text-rich tasks (Table 4).
UniAR generates a 1024x1024 image in 13.0 seconds using its DiT-based decoder with resolution upsampling, versus 101.9 seconds for Janus-Pro and 119.7 seconds for X-Omni (Table 9).

5p36n5cMJy.text: ASASR identifies spectral misalignment between isotropic diffusion objectives and the intrinsic spectral decay of the natural image manifold as the root cause of unfaithful restoration in generative image super-resolution (abstract only).

ASASR recasts the generative flow into a Sobolev-induced Riemannian geometry by explicitly coloring the noise transition kernel so that it mirrors the natural spectral decay of images (abstract only).
ASASR integrates a parametric adversary grounded in the Riesz Representation Theorem to generate negative samples that steer optimization toward preserving structural fidelity (abstract only).
ASASR outperforms leading generative super-resolution baselines, particularly in preserving spectral consistency and structural fidelity while reducing artifacts (abstract only).

CZCXz5cBXR.text: InfVSR is 58x faster than MGLD-VSR on 33-frame 720p video super-resolution, taking 6.82s versus 396.06s (Table 3).
InfVSR is 5.48x faster than SeedVR2 on the same 33x720p benchmark while maintaining constant ~20.39 GB memory usage regardless of video length (Table 3).
InfVSR achieves the best perceptual quality on UDM10 with MUSIQ 62.88, CLIP-IQA 0.5142, and DOVER 0.7826, and the lowest warping error (Ew_warp) of 1.95x10^-3 among compared methods (Table 1).
InfVSR's autoregressive one-step diffusion design improves MUSIQ from 61.29 (chunking baseline) to 62.88 on UDM10 (Table 4 ablation).
Adding the cross-chunk distribution matching (DMD) loss improves DOVER from 0.7603 to 0.7826 and subject consistency from 0.9608 to 0.9632 (Table 4 ablation).
On MovieLQ, InfVSR attains VBench subject consistency 0.9593, background consistency 0.9513, and motion smoothness 0.9886, indicating strong semantic consistency on extended sequences (Table 2).

AprtLFCirb.text: FactGuard's two-stage training combines agentic chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning (Section 3.4) with decision-aware GRPO reinforcement learning (Section 3.5) on top of Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.
FactGuard outperforms the strongest prior baseline Fact-R1 by +3.7% accuracy on FakeSV, +0.9% on FakeTT, and +1.8% on FakeVV (Table 1).
FactGuard reaches 79.3% accuracy / 81.4% F1 on FakeSV, 75.3% accuracy / 75.2% F1 on FakeTT, and 83.0% accuracy / 83.9% F1 on FakeVV (Table 1).
Removing the reinforcement learning stage drops FakeSV accuracy by 17.3 points, while removing the SFT stage drops it by 6.2 points, showing RL contributes more than SFT alone (Table 3 ablation).

Removing the tool-use reward (Rtool) and risk-decision reward (Rrisk) each degrade FakeSV accuracy by 1.6 and 0.8 points respectively, confirming decision-aware reward shaping helps (Table 3 ablation).

FactGuard's iterative reasoning uses two tool modules, FactProbe (web-based knowledge retrieval via Serper API) and ClipScout (temporal frame sampling, 4 frames default), invoked selectively rather than at fixed depth (Section 3.3).

h6xWMCDjo0.text: FRONT accelerates convergence by up to 15x on vision tasks, reaching 150-epoch-equivalent performance in just 10 epochs (Section 4.2.1).
FRONT reduces training FLOPs by an average of 40.5% across language architectures, with BERT-S saving 47.5%, RoBERTa-S saving 42.9%, and GPT-S saving 31.0% (Section 4.3, Figure 4).
On 10-epoch ImageNet-1K training, FRONT-initialized DeiT-Ti/S/B reach 65.3%/71.2%/76.3% accuracy versus 48.3%/55.5%/56.7% for He-Init (Table 1).
FRONT improves average downstream accuracy across 7 datasets to 83.9% versus 81.1% for the LiGO baseline (Table 3).
FRONT improves average image segmentation performance by 18.26 percentage points over the scratch baseline (Table 5).
On GLUE with BERT-S, FRONT improves STS-B by 36.96 points and MNLI by 9.27 points over training from scratch, raising the average GLUE score from 53.31% to 64.63% (Table 6).

pwz7P09W83.text: LatentMorph improves the base Janus-Pro model by 16% on GenEval, reaching an overall score of 0.96 versus 0.86 for TwiG-ZS (Table 1).

LatentMorph improves the base Janus-Pro model by 25% on T2I-CompBench, reaching an overall score of 64.53% versus 56.24% for TwiG-RL, including a 7.28-point gain on the Non-Spatial category (Table 1).
LatentMorph outperforms the explicit-reasoning TwiG paradigm by 15.6% on WISE and 11.3% on IPV-Txt abstract reasoning benchmarks (Figure 5).
LatentMorph reduces inference time by 44.3% and visual/reasoning token consumption by 51.0% relative to explicit chain-of-thought decoding (Figure 6).

LatentMorph's RL-trained invoker triggers latent reasoning adaptively, averaging 1.14 interventions on GenEval versus 1.60 on WISE, and matches human judgments of when reasoning is needed 71.8% of the time (Figure 6).
LatentMorph's architecture comprises four lightweight components—condenser, translator, shaper, and RL-trained invoker—that morph latent reasoning into image generation (Section 4.1).

JBEt767Naf.text: ScalingAR improves the LlamaGen baseline's overall GenEval score from 0.32 to 0.36, a 12.5% relative improvement, with Two Objects rising 0.34 to 0.40 and Color Attribute rising 0.04 to 0.12 (Table 1).
ScalingAR improves the LlamaGen baseline's overall TIIF-Bench score from 40.35 to 46.47, a 15.2% relative improvement, with Basic sub-score rising from 49.58 to 57.36 (Table 1).
ScalingAR reduces visual token consumption by 62.0% at test time while outperforming baselines, via its dual-channel confidence profile and confidence-guided policies (Section 4.1-4.2, Section 5.2).
ScalingAR mitigates performance degradation by 26.0% in challenging/impossible-prompt scenarios compared to baselines without early decoding or auxiliary rewards (Section 5.4, Figure 6).
ScalingAR achieves these gains without requiring early decoding or auxiliary reward models, unlike prior test-time scaling approaches for autoregressive image generation (Abstract, Section 4).

8PMYGcTv3L.text: SOTAlign is a two-stage semi-supervised alignment framework that fits a linear teacher (Procrustes, CCA, or contrastive) on scarce paired data, then refines the mapping on abundant unpaired data using an optimal-transport-based KLOT divergence (Section 3.3, Section 5).

Theorem 5.1 derives an explicit closed-form gradient for the KLOT regularizer that avoids backpropagating through the Sinkhorn solver, yielding a roughly 50x reduction in GPU memory versus implicit differentiation (Theorem 5.1, Figure 3).
With 10k paired and 1M unpaired samples, SOTAlign improves zero-shot text-to-image R@1 on COCO from 21.0% (SAIL) to 26.5% and image-to-text R@1 from 27.4% to 34.1% (Table 4).
On Flickr30k, SOTAlign raises text-to-image R@1 from 45.7% to 51.7% and image-to-text R@1 from 54.1% to 60.8% versus the SAIL baseline (Table 4).
SOTAlign improves zero-shot ImageNet top-1 classification accuracy from 35.6% (SAIL) to 46.1%, a 10.5-point gain (Table 5).
SOTAlign matches SAIL's alignment performance using roughly 4x fewer paired samples, per the supervision-scaling curves (Figure 4).

d6IyHrX48y.text: Kinetic Path Energy (KPE) is defined as E := (1/2)∫_0^1 ||v_θ(x(t),t)||^2 dt, the accumulated kinetic effort of a sample's ODE trajectory under the learned velocity field (Section 3).

On ImageNet-256 with SiT-XL/2 at CFG=1.5, median CLIP score rises from 23.52 for low-KPE samples to 25.12 for high-KPE samples across 5,000 generated samples per CFG scale, with all six comparisons significant at p<0.008 (Section 4.1, Table 1).

KPE correlates negatively with local data density on CIFAR-10 (Spearman rho from -0.54 to -0.65) and on ImageNet-256 (rho from -0.31 to -0.42), indicating high-KPE trajectories terminate on low-density manifold frontiers (Section 4.2, Table 2).

Theorem 4.2 (Energy-Density Relation) shows that under posterior dominance, instantaneous squared trajectory speed is affinely bounded by negative log-density, giving E(z_0->1) = Theta(integral of -log p_hat_t(z(t)) dt) + O(1) (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.2).
On CelebA-HQ, memorization fraction of the empirical flow-matching field rises to 98% by 2M training iterations even as FID plateaus near 15, with average KPE reaching 540 (Section 5.3, Figure 7a).

Kinetic Trajectory Shaping (KTS), a training-free two-phase velocity reweighting (kinetic launch for t<0.6, soft landing for t>=0.6), reduces CelebA memorization fraction from 37.34% (baseline FM) to 31.22% while improving FID from 16.68 to 14.35 (Section 6.2, Table 3).

5th8Uu1HjJ.text: AREA decomposes CLIP-based class-incremental prediction into an attribute extraction stage, which builds multi-modal class anchors via Principal Geodesic Analysis (PGA) on the hypersphere, and an attribute aggregation stage with dual-branch scoring and residual refinement (Section 4.1-4.3).

Attribute aggregation is regularized with a variational information bottleneck combining an interventional monotonicity loss (penalizing spurious evidence under occlusion) and a compression loss (enforcing view-invariant evidence across augmentations) (Section 4.2-4.3).

Inference uses optimal-transport routing (Sinkhorn distance) over task experts, proven Lipschitz-continuous in Theorem 5.1, adding only 2.9 ms/sample latency for a 3.39% accuracy gain over cosine routing (Section 4.4, Theorem 5.1).
On Aircraft B0 Inc10 with CLIP ViT-B/16, AREA achieves 71.03% average / 61.78% last-task accuracy versus the best baseline RAPF's 50.38% / 23.61%, a gain of over 20 points average accuracy (Table 1).
On CUB B0 Inc20, AREA reaches 87.69% average / 82.14% last-task accuracy compared to RAPF's 79.09% / 62.77% (Table 1).

Ablations show attribute anchoring alone yields large accuracy gains, with the VIB loss and OT routing each adding further improvement, and 20% MLLM caption coverage achieves under 1% performance drop versus using 100% of captions (Section 6, Figure 4).

Nvim88fA66.text: SAME identifies two failure modes in multimodal continual instruction tuning, router drift (inconsistent expert selection over time) and expert drift (degradation of previously learned expert functionality), and addresses them via spectral-aware routing, curvature-aware scaling, and adaptive expert activation (Section 4.1-4.3).

Spectral-aware routing decomposes routing dynamics via SVD of the input covariance matrix, updating only task-relevant directions while preserving history-critical directions through singular-value rescaling (Section 4.1).

Curvature-aware scaling formulates expert drift as functional deviation under historical input geometry, using Riemannian gradient descent with a damped pseudo-inverse metric tensor for numerically stable updates (Section 4.2).

Adaptive expert activation freezes task-level experts based on utilization and an AGOP (Average Gradient Outer Product) trace-based importance ranking, reducing redundant computation across tasks (Section 4.3).

On the CoIN benchmark, SAME achieves 66.82% average accuracy across 8 tasks versus 63.95% for the strongest baseline, a +2.87-point gain, with per-dataset gains including +2.03 on TextVQA and +0.80 on ScienceQA but losses of -4.29 on ImageNet and -2.66 on OCR-VQA (Table 1).
Spectral-aware routing reduces average training time by 32.1 minutes per task according to the training-efficiency analysis (Figure 5).

EukKoqZhvW.text: AdaRoute is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that uses shared expert centers with a dynamic parameter routing mechanism to selectively aggregate low-rank parameter matrices in an input-dependent way across layers (Section 3.2).
On ADE20K semantic segmentation with Swin-L, AdaRoute reaches 52.0% mIoU using only 7.3M trainable parameters, versus 51.2% mIoU for full fine-tuning with 195.0M parameters (Table 1).

On COCO object detection and instance segmentation with ConvNeXt-L, AdaRoute improves APb from 48.1% to 49.5% and APm from 43.2% to 44.8% over full fine-tuning, using 9.2M versus 196.2M parameters (Table 2).
On panoptic segmentation with ConvNeXt-L, AdaRoute reaches 50.4% PQ with 9.2M parameters versus 51.0% PQ for full fine-tuning with 196.2M parameters (Table 3).
On ViT-B/16 image classification, AdaRoute achieves 87.4% mean accuracy, surpassing comparable PEFT baselines such as AdaptFormer and Mona (Table 4).

An ablation over latent dimension and expert capacity finds the optimal configuration at M=L, C-hat=128 with 5.2M parameters, and a separate ablation on shared expert-center scope shows performance degrades with smaller expert groupings, confirming the benefit of cross-layer interaction (Table 5, Table 6).

3gf0MK7LTk.text: On RefCOCO validation with a 5% label budget, Learning to Label (L2L) reaches 67.30 overall IoU versus a 58.23 baseline (Table 1).
On RefCOCO+ and RefCOCog-u validation sets at the 5% label budget, L2L improves overall IoU to 57.44 and 59.71 respectively, up from 47.05 and 46.45 baselines (Table 1).
With only 0.1% labeled data, L2L attains 65.08/68.53/59.39 overall IoU on RefCOCO val/testA/testB and outperforms zero-shot baselines including a SAM 3 Agent (Table 2).

An ablation shows progressive component gains from the 58.23 baseline to 65.73 after adding the Semantic-spatial Prior with MLLM (SPM), 66.99 after adding the Self-Evolving Segmentation Module (SESM), and 67.30 after adding Reinforced Pseudo-Label Exploration (RPLE) (Table 3).

Reinforced Pseudo-Label Exploration (RPLE) uses an actor-critic reinforcement learning formulation whose critic scores pseudo-labels via three reward terms: separability gain, consistency gain, and coverage gain (Section 3.4).
RPLE's adaptive thresholding is shown to be more robust than static confidence thresholding across a range of threshold values (Figure 5).

EPL2YoeGow.text: AgentXRay formulates Agentic Workflow Reconstruction (AWR) as maximizing similarity between a reconstructed workflow's outputs and a target black-box agent system's outputs, representing agents and tools as atomic primitives p = <rho, mu, pi, T_local> (Section 2.1).

AgentXRay's Red-Black Pruning scores each search node with Score(v) = [Q(v)/N(v)] x [(d(v)+1)/(L_max+1)] x [|C(v)|/M] and colors nodes red when the score exceeds a beta-quantile threshold to guide Monte Carlo Tree Search (Section 2.2, Equation 2).

Across five domains, AgentXRay (All Tools) achieves an average Static Functional Equivalence (SFE) of 0.426 versus 0.339 for the AFlow baseline, a statistically significant improvement (p<=0.05) (Table 1).
Without Red-Black Pruning, reconstructed workflows stagnate at search depth L=2, whereas with pruning they reach depth L=6 across domains (Table 2).
Pruned variants of AgentXRay reduce token consumption by 8-22% while achieving comparable or higher reconstruction fidelity than unpruned search (Figure 3).

Human evaluation of reconstructed workflows correlates with the automatic SFE metric at Spearman rho = 0.61, and MetaGPT is the most reconstructable system among the domains tested, with SFE of 0.557 (Section 3).

HpIhfqaLwa.text: The Differentiable Grid Sampler (GridS) compresses vision tokens from 256 down to as few as 4-16 tokens using differentiable bilinear interpolation at predicted coordinates, retaining fewer than 10% of the original visual tokens (Abstract, Section 3.3).
On the LIBERO benchmark, GridS with 16 tokens reduces FLOPs by 76% relative to a 256-token pi_0 baseline (216.01G FLOPs) while improving average success rate from 94.4% to 96.0% (Table 1).
GridS16 yields a larger 4.6% improvement specifically on long-horizon LIBERO tasks compared to the pi_0 baseline (Section 4.1.1).

On a real robotic platform's Stack Cubes task, GridS achieves 60.0% success rate compared to approximately 7.6% for the baseline, a 52.4-point absolute improvement, and remains capable in out-of-distribution scenarios where the baseline fails completely (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
GridS provides 3.4x training speedup per step for pi_0 and 2.9x for pi_0.5 (Table 4).

bkn1a9spwP.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes that standard Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have an irreducible factorization error lower bound, TC_theta(z_s|z_t) >= max_{i,j} p(e_ij) * I(z_s^i; z_s^j | z_t^{-{i,j}}), which grows with step size (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 proves that the proposed Infinite Mask Diffusion Model (IMDM) can achieve zero factorization error for some forward process and parameters theta*, via a partition-and-map mechanism exploiting infinite-state mask stochasticity (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).

On a synthetic binary-sequence task ({00, 11}), IMDM reaches 97.7% validity and 0.082 factorization error versus MDM's 49.8% validity and 0.693 factorization error, matching MDM's predicted ln(2) lower bound (Table 1, Section 5.2).

On LM1B with 2-step unconditional generation after SDTT+ReDi distillation, IMDM attains roughly 165 generative perplexity versus about 330 for the MDM baseline, a roughly 50% reduction (Section 5.3, Figure 2).

On OpenWebText, IMDM outperforms SDTT and Di4C distillation baselines at up to 8 sampling steps, and its 4-step conditional generation attains MAUVE score above 0.75 versus near 0 for the teacher model at 2 steps (Section 5.4, Figure 3).
An ablation on the injected noise dimension shows LM1B 2-step perplexity of 294.41 at dimension 256 versus 165.85 at dimension 768, the value used in the main model (Table 3, Section 5.5).

G1BYq33C3G.text: VIP is a training-free, optimization-free method built on the dino.txt framework that improves average mIoU by 1.4%-8.4% over existing dense-prediction methods, including an 8.4% gain over the single-model competitor SFP (Table 1).
VIP outperforms the multi-model state of the art CorrCLIP while running 14x faster and using roughly half the memory footprint (Table 1).
On remote-sensing out-of-distribution domains, VIP improves average mIoU by 8.5% over SegEarth-OV (Table 2).

An ablation shows self-correction alone contributes +12.5% mIoU over the baseline, and adding alias distillation raises the cumulative gain to +21.3%, with the full system reaching 52.4% average mIoU across benchmarks (Table 3).
The Semantic Expansion component (Section 3.2) uses an LLM to generate 20 image-caption-style aliases per class to close the lexical gap between canonical class names and pretraining data.
Visual-guided Distillation (Section 3.3) introduces a Visual Grounding Score and a Semantic Certainty Score to automatically filter aliases without requiring mask annotations.

qNlU88p8lP.text: FrontierCS comprises 156 open-ended computer science problems, split into 107 algorithmic problems (29 optimization, 27 constructive, 51 interactive) and 49 research problems spanning OS, HPC, AI, DB, PL, and Security domains (Figure 2).
On the algorithmic track, human experts score 95.41 (Score@1) while the best-performing model, Gemini 3.0 Pro, scores only 29.37, a gap of roughly 66 points (Table 1).

On the research track, the best model (Claude Opus 4.5) scores 29.40 at Score@1 but improves to 44.47 at Score@5, showing large gains from repeated sampling despite weak single-attempt performance (Table 2).
Increasing reasoning effort from medium to high does not improve results and can even hurt performance, with average scores dropping from 15.336 to 12.626 (Section 5.1, Figure 4).

Providing simple architectural guidance (e.g., an explicit 2D array representation hint) dramatically improves scores on the polyomino packing problem, from a 20-70 range up to 80-85, illustrating models' struggle to identify internal equivalence classes without hints (Section 5.2).

Claude models show track-specialized behavior, producing workable solutions on research problems while underperforming on algorithmic problems requiring deeper algorithmic discovery, evidence of brittleness in current agentic frameworks on open-ended challenges (Section 5.3).

s7NR3XGdwq.text: The concept removal method (BLOCK) is evaluated on diffusion models SD3.5 and Flux.1-dev (12B) and image-autoregressive models Infinity-2B and Infinity-8B (Section 4.1).

On Flux, BLOCK achieves 88.60% unlearning accuracy (UA) and 96.40% concept-retention accuracy (CRA) for style removal, and 93.20% UA with 96.61% in-context retention accuracy (IRA) for object removal (Table 4).

Against the Ring-A-Bell adversarial attack, BLOCK reduces attack success rate on SD3.5 from 58.08% to 25.21% and on Infinity-8B from 56.34% to 19.78%, demonstrating white-box robustness of the in-place bottleneck substitution (Table 5).
BLOCK maintains stable removal performance across sequential removal of 10 concepts, while baseline methods degrade significantly under the same multi-concept setting (Section 5.3, Figure 4).
The method generalizes to out-of-distribution styles not seen during training, achieving 52.63% unlearning accuracy on held-out styles (Section 5.6, Table 9).
Upfront transcoder training costs roughly 91-101 minutes per model (SD3.5, Flux) with per-target removal taking under 1.1 seconds and requiring 1.9-2.4 GB of additional memory (Table 11).

EETUbVsG6X.text: HO-SFL achieves a convergence rate of O(sqrt(d_o/PT)) for the global gradient norm, proven in Corollary 4.5 (Equation 27), mitigating the dimension-dependent slowdown typical of zeroth-order optimization (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).
On CIFAR-10, HO-SFL reduces communication cost to 2.44 GB compared to 4.20 GB for standard split federated learning (SFL) and 3.71 GB for FSL-SAGE (Section 5).

On LLaMA-3.2-1B fine-tuned on SST-2, HO-SFL reduces client-side memory usage to 4.14 GB versus 8.78 GB for SFL and 20.81 GB for full local training, approaching the 4.01 GB inference-only footprint (Section 5).

HO-SFL achieves dimension-free aggregation, reducing per-round communication complexity from O(d_o) to O(P) where P is much smaller than d_o, eliminating client-side backpropagation entirely (Section 3.3, Proposition 4.3).
On GLUE benchmark LLM fine-tuning tasks, HO-SFL achieves accuracy comparable to first-order split federated learning baselines (Table 1).

hCMNDdfzNb.text: Token-Level Visual-Sensitivity Steering (TLVS) is evaluated against baselines including VCD, SPARC, ASD, SHARP, VTI, VISTA, and DPO on POPE, AMBER, CHAIR (COCO), MMHal-Bench, and HallusionBench (Section 5.1, Table 1).
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, TLVS improves POPE average accuracy from 85.09 to 89.78 (+4.69 points) (Section 5.2).
On CHAIR (COCO), TLVS reduces CHAIRs from 46.0 to 31.2, a 14.8-point reduction in sentence-level hallucination rate (Section 5.2).
On AMBER, TLVS reduces the Hal metric from 36.4 to 19.7, a 16.7-point decrease (Section 5.2).

TLVS requires only lightweight calibration, optimizing steering vectors via paired teacher forcing with bounded KL regularization rather than full model fine-tuning, incurring about 2x inference overhead and only 1.01x additional VRAM usage (Section 4.2, Table 3).

The adaptive steering mechanism uses token-level extraction of visual-sensitivity signal Delta_t combined with KL-based adaptive scaling to calibrate steering strength per token (Section 4.1-4.3, Equations 8 and 17).

YiTfnJursw.text: Hindsight Instruction Replay (HiR) uses a select-then-rewrite strategy that samples m=6 responses per prompt and selects k=2 failed attempts to rewrite into satisfied-constraint hindsight instructions for replay (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).
On Llama-3.2-3B, HiR improves IFEval accuracy by 12.4 percentage points and MulDimIF accuracy by 49.1 percentage points over the baseline (Section 4.2, Table 1).

HiR is evaluated across seven instruction-following benchmarks (IFEval, IFBench, CFBench, InfoBench, ComplexBench, MulDimIF, FollowBench) on three LLM backbones, and Qwen3-4B trained with HiR reaches parity with frontier models such as GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-V3.1 on several of them (Table 1).
HiR achieves better instruction-following results than the RL-CR baseline while using less computational budget, as shown by faster-converging training curves (Section 5, Figure 5).
An ablation comparing HiR's selection strategy against random replay selection shows HiR's targeted select-then-rewrite approach outperforms random selection of failed rollouts (Table 3).

HiR preserves out-of-domain performance on MATH-500, GPQA, and MMLU-Pro relative to baseline training, indicating the instruction-following gains do not come at the cost of general capabilities (Table 2).

X1Ro597lLJ.text: I-PERI aggregates client CPDAGs via a modified regret computed on the graph intersection L(H∩C(GΦk),Dk)−L(C(GΦk),Dk), and Theorem 3.2 shows this converges to the true CPDAG C(G) common to all clients under consistent scoring (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.2).

I-PERI introduces the Φ-Markov Equivalence Class, characterized by skeleton, v-structures, and intervention-induced structures, and proves convergence to the finer Φ-CPDAG Φ(G), letting it orient additional edges beyond the standard CPDAG using intervention-induced differences across clients (Definition 3.1, Theorem 3.4, Theorem 3.5).
I-PERI's regret statistic has bounded sensitivity of (2M+1)log r^2 + O(log n/n), which is used to achieve epsilon-differential privacy via Laplace noise injection (Lemma 3.1, Proposition 3.1).

On synthetic Erdos-Renyi DAGs with K=5 clients and 1000-5000 samples per client, the recovered Φ-CPDAG attains lower structural Hamming distance and higher edge-orientation F1-score than the standard CPDAG baseline (Section 4, Figure 6).
The federated CPDAG aggregation step assumes at least one client holds purely observational data (Assumption 2.1, Section 3.1).

ZX2lOgKOTm.text: Cross-stratum bias is formalized by decomposing the global GRPO advantage into a within-stratum (stratified) advantage plus a bias term equal to the difference between a trajectory's stratum-mean reward and the global-mean reward (Section 2.2, Proposition 1).

Stratified GRPO's stratum-wise advantage normalization (SAN) estimator is proven to have strictly lower variance than the global GRPO estimator whenever strata have heterogeneous means (Section 2.3, Theorem 1).
On seven QA benchmarks with Qwen2.5-3B, Stratified GRPO raises average score from 33.3 to 41.6 for the base model and from 29.2 to 40.5 for the instruct model compared with standard GRPO (Table 1).
Stratified GRPO yields roughly an 11-14 point gain over GRPO specifically on multi-hop deep-research QA tasks, one of the largest per-task improvements reported (Table 1, Section 4).

An ablation shows SAN alone produces most of the gain over GRPO, while the blended advantage combining SAN with global normalization further improves performance and training stability, avoiding the training collapse GRPO exhibits (Section 3, Table 2, Figure 1).

diM2jCKgZW.text: SyVLA reaches a 73% average real-world in-domain task success rate versus 63% for pretrained Pi0, while using under 5% of Pi0's pretraining data (450 vs. 10,000 hours) (Table 1).
SyVLA reaches a 64% average out-of-distribution task success rate versus 48% for pretrained Pi0 (Table 1).

The Intention Decoupling module, which masks control-irrelevant last hidden states of Feature Query Tokens, is critical: removing it drops success rate on Task 1 from 86% to 43% (Section 3.2, Table 3).

Removing the Similar-Sample Guided RL stage reduces Task 1 success rate from 86% to 71%, and removing only the similar-sample guidance component (while keeping RL) reduces it to 79% (Section 3.3, Table 3).

SyVLA preserves core vision-language capability, scoring best among compared models on AI2D (67.70), MME (1795), and HallusionBench (42.53) while remaining competitive on DocVQA (80.01) and MMMU (35.78) (Table 2).

O4BmkfXv1f.text: CodeFP improves functional consistency over the CFP-Gen baseline, raising F1-Macro from 0.370 to 0.446, MRR from 0.601 to 0.658, and AUC-ROC from 0.674 to 0.724 (Table 1).
CodeFP achieves foldability success rates of 80.65% for pLDDT > 70 and 83.48% for pTM > 0.5 (Table 2).
CodeFP jointly decodes protein sequence and quantized local-structure tokens through a discrete diffusion co-generation framework with multimodal absorbing corruption (Section 3.1).

CodeFP incorporates Functional-Structural Retrieval, which encodes representative structural motifs per Gene Ontology term via a frozen DPLM-2 encoder, and Local Structure-Function Supervision, an auxiliary cross-entropy loss on functional-domain hidden states; removing both components drops F1-Micro from 0.496 to 0.465, with removing FSR alone dropping it to 0.486 (Sections 3.2-3.3, Table 3).
CodeFP improves F1-Macro by 9.1% on out-of-distribution, unseen natural functional combinations relative to the baseline (Figure 4).

3ADqf6jn9r.text: pTNAS's training-free proxy (pTProxy) achieves Spearman rank correlation of 0.82 on Frappe, 0.73 on Diabetes, and 0.90 on Criteo, ranking first among nine zero-cost proxies compared (Table 1).
pTNAS reduces the time to reach the globally best architecture by up to 82.75x on Frappe and 69.44x on Criteo compared with a regularized-evolution NAS baseline (Section 4.3, Figure 6).

pTNAS combines a filtering phase using the training-free proxy with regularized evolution and a refinement phase using successive halving on the top-K candidates, coordinated by a budget-aware scheduler subject to T1 + T2 <= T_max (Sections 3.3-3.4).

The accompanying NAS-Bench-Tabular benchmark comprises 160,000 unique architectures over a 4-layer search space with 20 candidate layer sizes (8-512 neurons), evaluated on the Frappe, Diabetes, and Criteo datasets (Section 3.1).
A hyperparameter study finds that a filtering-to-refinement ratio (M/K) of about 30 and U=2 training epochs per refinement round consistently yield the best performance (Appendix E).

Ir6N7U5Kea.text: MSNN provably preserves Synthetic Nearest Neighbors' entry-wise finite-sample error bound (Theorem 4.5) and asymptotic normality with convergence rate scaling as K_MSNN^(-1/2) (Theorem 4.6) (Section 4.2).

Corollary 4.10 shows the expected number of usable data subgroups under MCAR grows by a multiplicative factor of [∑_d' (p_d'/p_d)^(r+1)]^c for MSNN relative to standard SNN, formalizing the effective-sample-size gain from mixed anchor sets (Section 4.3).
Corollary 4.11 shows the relative efficiency gap between data-sparse and data-rich treatment levels is reduced from quadratic to linear order under MSNN (Section 4.3).

On MCAR-generated data at a low treatment probability p(d)=0.01, MSNN achieves a 4.69% feasible rate and mean relative error of 3.91e-2, versus a 0.03% feasible rate and 0.806 MRE for standard SNN (Table 1).
Under MNAR data, MSNN consistently attains 3-26% feasible imputation rates versus under 5% for SNN, with 2-3x error reductions across treatment levels (Tables 2-3).

Mixed anchor rows/columns are constructed via bipartite cliques spanning multiple treatment levels while preserving the target row's same-treatment data, relying on the shared latent row factor assumption (Assumption 2.5) (Section 3.2-3.3, Algorithms 2-3).

raKcsJbVDY.text: Theorem 3.1 gives a certified two-term lower bound on the transport distance, W2^2(mu1|z, mu0|z) >= W2^2(mu1_v, mu0_v) + k*SW2^2(mu1_v_perp, mu0_v_perp), decomposing it into a low-dimensional signal-subspace term and a sliced-Wasserstein residual-subspace term (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

Proposition 2.3 establishes that the scaled sliced Wasserstein distance k*SW2^2(alpha,beta) lower-bounds the full W2^2(alpha,beta), becoming tight when the residual transport is directionally isotropic (Section 3, Proposition 2.3).

Theorem 3.7 derives finite-sample error bounds for the estimator that scale with the intrinsic signal rank r rather than the ambient outcome dimension, under the extended spiked transport model whose optimizer stability is shown in Theorem 3.6 (Section 3).

In synthetic experiments with ambient dimension d=30 and signal rank r=5, the proposed CSS estimator consistently outperforms the projection-only WPP baseline in recovering residual transport energy, yielding tighter causal bounds across anisotropy profiles (Section 4.1, Figures 1-2).
On the 27-dimensional RHC real-data outcomes, CSS yields held-out certificates that lie above the WPP baseline across all tested projection dimensions (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

tpJDC8miYG.text: Theorem 3.4 proves that weighted-loss fusion estimators with non-negligible observational weight (alpha <= alpha-bar) cannot exactly satisfy the randomized-data identifying moment restrictions, establishing a formal separation from the constrained joint-estimation approach (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.4).

In synthetic experiments across varying overlap conditions, the constrained method maintains stable performance as overlap deteriorates, while weighted-fusion competitors degrade substantially (Section 4).

On ride-hailing Datasets 3-4, the constrained joint estimator matches the performance of RCT-only models trained on significantly more randomized data, reaching a Qini of 0.660 and MAPE of 0.058 (Section 5, Table 2).

An ablation decomposing the method into an IPM distribution-alignment term and a joint constrained-estimation term shows the joint-training component provides the critical performance gains on the ride-hailing benchmarks (Section 5, Appendix H).

lu2d1gQhHS.text: The paper formulates distributionally robust causal abstraction learning as the min-max objective min_T sup_{rho in B_epsilon} E_{iota~q}[e^{rho,iota}_tau], using a 2-Wasserstein product ambiguity set B_{epsilon,2}(rho-hat) centered at the empirical joint environment (Section 4, Equation 6).

Theorem 1 (Gaussian rho-Concentration) shows that for Gaussian environments the true joint environment lies in the Wasserstein ambiguity ball with high probability once epsilon exceeds a bound depending on log(c_l/eta_l)/sqrt(N_l) and log(c_h/eta_h)/sqrt(N_h) (Section 4, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 (Empirical rho-Concentration) extends this guarantee to empirical (non-Gaussian) settings with ambiguity radius shrinking at rate epsilon = O(N^{-1/d}) for dimension d>2 (Section 4, Theorem 2).

On the SLC and LiLUCAS datasets, DiRoCA achieves substantially lower abstraction error than non-robust Grad and Bary baselines under fully corrupted test conditions (contamination alpha=1) in both Gaussian and empirical settings (Table 1).

DiRoCA maintains consistently lower abstraction error than baselines as contamination fraction and noise intensity are varied (Figures 3-4), and continues to outperform baselines under structural-function (F-) misspecification and intervention-mapping (omega-) misspecification (Table 2).

SW2D390ePP.text: Frontier LMs show markedly different competitive development styles in CodeClash: o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro edit about 2 files per round while GPT-5 edits 5-6, and o3 changes roughly 51 lines per round versus 400+ for Claude Sonnet, yet none of these behavioral differences correlate with win rate (Section 5.1).
Models frequently make ungrounded edits not supported by competition logs, exceeding 65% of rounds for most models and reaching 80% for o3 (Section 5.2, Figure 8a).

Claude Sonnet 4.5 makes uncorroborated claims about the exact cause of a game loss in over 17% of rounds on average, rising to 46% in the BattleSnake arena, while validating its own modifications in only 56% of rounds at best across models (Section 5.2, Figure 8b-c).

Repository file counts grow almost linearly with the number of tournament rounds, with Claude 4.5 Sonnet creating over 30 files per tournament and filename redundancy reaching 59% for Qwen3 Coder, producing many 'throwaway files' never reused (Section 5.1, Figure 7).

Claude Sonnet 4.5 won exactly zero of 150 rounds against gigachad, RobotRumble's top human-written bot, across 37,500 simulations, demonstrating a substantial gap versus expert human programmers (Section 4.1).
Across eight frontier models ranked by Elo over six arenas, Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads overall at 1389, followed by GPT-5 at 1360 and o3 at 1343 (Table 1).

Ja9jo9pDvq.text: Q2D2 groups latent feature channels into pairs and projects them onto structured 2D grids (hexagonal, rhombic, or rectangular tilings) instead of using 1D scalar or high-dimensional vector quantization (Section on geometry-aware quantization).
At 3.3 kbps using 166 tokens, Q2D2 achieves a UTMOS of 4.06, surpassing multi-quantizer baselines that use 300+ tokens (Table 2).
At 1 kbps with only 53-75 tokens per second, Q2D2 outperforms DAC across PESQ, STOI, and F1 metrics on LibriTTS test sets (Table 2).
Q2D2 attains 100% pair utilization and 72-99% codebook utilization depending on grid resolution, without requiring auxiliary stabilization tricks (Table 10).
Among the tested tilings, the rhombic grid configuration achieves the highest reconstruction quality, with PESQ of 2.40 and STOI of 0.915, outperforming hexagonal and rectangular grids (Table 8).
Q2D2 with a single quantizer matches or exceeds DAC (9 quantizers), Encodec (8 quantizers), and WavTokenizer on UTMOS, PESQ, and STOI across LibriTTS, LJSpeech, and LibriSpeech test sets (Table 2).

V6GG63yCtH.text: DistSeal trains post-hoc watermark embedder-extractor pairs directly in the latent space of generative models, then optionally distills them into the generative model or its decoder for in-model watermarking (Section 4.1-4.2).

For the DCAE diffusion model, latent-space watermarking requires 3ms per image versus 63ms for the pixel-space baseline, a roughly 20x speedup, while for the RAR-XL autoregressive model the speedup is about 2.4x (17ms vs 41ms) due to its less spatially compressed latent space (Section 5).
For DCAE, post-hoc latent watermarking achieves 95.18% average bit accuracy and the distilled latent decoder achieves 96.77%, compared to 97.78% for the post-hoc pixel-space baseline (Section 5).

For RAR-XL, post-hoc latent watermarking (after quantization) achieves 93.96% average bit accuracy and the distilled latent decoder achieves 90.57%, versus 97.27% for the post-hoc pixel-space baseline (Section 5).

Watermarking DCAE outputs with the latent method increases FID by only +0.18 relative to the non-watermarked baseline, compared to +0.76 for the pixel-space method, indicating better preserved imperceptibility (Section 5).

eh48NIgu9z.text: S2M-Net is a 4.7M-parameter architecture, roughly 13x fewer parameters than TransUNet and 6x fewer than Swin-UNet, using a five-stage encoder with channel dimensions {24, 32, 64, 80, 128} (Section on architecture).

The Spectral-Selective Token Mixer (SSTM) uses a truncated 2D FFT retaining K=32 frequency components, capturing more than 95% of spectral energy while reducing computational cost by 63% relative to full spatial attention (Section on SSTM).
S2M-Net achieves 83.77% Dice on the EndoVis17 multiclass surgical instrument segmentation benchmark, a 17.85% improvement over prior art (Table of main results).
S2M-Net attains 96.12% Dice on ETIS-PolypDB, 80.90% Dice on BRATS2020 brain tumor segmentation, and 83.70% Dice on the CHASEDB retinal vessel dataset (Table of main results).
Ablation results show removing SSTM causes a 7.67% Dice drop on Kvasir-SEG, and removing the boundary loss component causes an 8.16% Dice drop on Kvasir-SEG (Ablation table).
Reducing the FFT truncation from K=32 to K=16 lowers captured spectral energy from ~95% and causes a 6.25% Dice degradation (Ablation table).

8V2Qf6mNx3.text: T2AV-Compass is a unified benchmark for text-to-audio-video generation consisting of 500 diverse and complex prompts (abstract only).

The benchmark evaluates 11 representative T2AV systems using a dual-level framework combining objective signal-level metrics for video/audio quality and alignment with a subjective MLLM-as-a-Judge protocol (abstract only).
Even the strongest evaluated models fall substantially short of human-level realism and cross-modal consistency (abstract only).
Persistent failures identified across systems include audio realism, fine-grained synchronization, and instruction following (abstract only).

0vxkqSOpXU.text: VideoSEG-O3 is trained via a three-stage pipeline: supervised fine-tuning on 475K samples, a CoT cold-start stage using a custom 6K-sample VTS-CoT dataset, and a final GRPO reinforcement learning stage with composite format, temporal, segmentation, and progressive rewards (Section on training pipeline).
On Ref-SAV, VideoSEG-O3-4B achieves 65.5 J&F, a 15.5% improvement over previous state of the art, and on Long-RVOS it achieves 57.4 J&F, a 6.1% improvement (Table 1).
On reasoning-focused benchmarks, VideoSEG-O3 achieves 70.3 J&F on ReVOS (+6.4% over Veason-R1) and 62.9 J&F on GroundMoRe (+8.8% over MoRA-13B) (Table 2).
Ablations show average J&F across 6 benchmarks rising from 54.96% (SFT baseline) to 57.07% after adding the CoT stage and to 60.29% after adding the RL stage (Table 4).
After RL training, the average number of interaction turns per query decreases by 20.1%, from 2.79 to 2.23 (Table 4).

fBRIgbTvId.text: RLKV achieves 20-50% KV cache reduction with near-lossless performance on reasoning benchmarks (Abstract, Section 4.4, Table 1).
On Llama-3.1-8B-R1, RLKV maintains lossless compression at sparsity levels of roughly 0.4-0.5 across GSM8K, Math500, AIME24, and MBPP (Section 4.4, Table 1a/1b).
On Qwen-2.5-7B-R1, RLKV maintains lossless compression at lower sparsity levels of roughly 0.2-0.4 across the same reasoning and coding benchmarks (Section 4.4, Table 1a/1b).
RLKV identifies reasoning-critical attention heads via RL optimization using GRPO and applies mixed attention with gating adapters to compress the rest (Section 3.1, Eq. 1; Section 3.2, Eq. 2-3).
RLKV outperforms token-dropping baselines H2O and R-KV and the head-reallocation baseline DuoAttention on the main reasoning benchmark comparison (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
RLKV achieves up to 1.21x inference speedup from discovering reasoning-critical heads and aggressively compressing the remaining heads (Section 4.4).

rhX58pEFNd.text: Krause Attention replaces dot-product similarity with distance-based RBF-kernel interactions plus local-neighborhood and top-k sparsity, reducing attention complexity from O(N^2 d) to O(NWd), where W is the window size (Section 4.1-4.2, Algorithm 1).
On CIFAR-10, KViT-S improves accuracy from 93.33% (ViT-S) to 95.20% while cutting FLOPs from 1.43G to 0.97G, a 32% reduction (Table 1).
On CIFAR-100, KViT-S improves accuracy from 71.74% (ViT-S) to 77.05%, an average gain of about +3.7% across model scales (Table 2).
On ImageNet-1K, KViT-B-16 improves accuracy from 72.19% (ViT-B-16) to 74.50% while reducing FLOPs from 17.61G to 12.03G, a 32% reduction (Table 3).

In autoregressive image generation, KARM reaches 105.6 images/sec on MNIST versus 83.6 images/sec for standard ARM, and 4.52 images/sec on CIFAR-10 versus 1.89 images/sec for ARM, a 59% speedup (Table 4-5).
Krause-Llama3-8B improves over a LoRA baseline on language benchmarks, e.g., PIQA rising from 75.16% to 77.77% and BoolQ from 80.41% to 80.59% (Table 6).

l8RBjihPFk.text: PaperGuard is a benchmark of 1,136 papers (605 from ICLR, 531 from F1000Research) for evaluating AI peer-review systems against multimodal adversarial attacks (Section 4.1).

Black-box text prompt injection attacks (12 variants) achieve up to 80% attack success rate against Claude-sonnet-4.5 with a +14.14 average score shift, and 72% ASR against GPT-4o with a +6.65 score shift (Table 1a, Appendix B).
White-box visual attacks using APGD achieve up to +14.11 point score shifts on Janus-Pro-7B and transfer across models (Table 2b, Table 5-6).

The proposed chunk-based embedding search defense achieves 95.0% accuracy/92.86% recall/0.0% false-positive rate against text attacks and 93.5% accuracy/90.32% recall/0.10% false-positive rate against visual attacks, outperforming Moderation API, LLM-as-Judge, and BERT classifier baselines (Section 4.2, Table 1b, Table 3).

On a real-world validation set of 17 confirmed arXiv prompt injections, the chunk-based defense achieves 100% recall at 0% false-positive rate, versus 64.7% recall for LLM-as-Judge and 0% recall for the Moderation API (Table 4).

NKKwTEYdAm.text: Constraining updates with LoRA shrinks the perplexity gap between matched and mismatched optimizers by 39% for Muon-pretrained models and 78% for Adam-pretrained models (Section 3.2, Table 1).
On GLUE with T5-Base, LoRA-Muon slightly outperforms LoRA-Adam on average accuracy (88.97% vs 88.93%), with LoRA-Muon-PE reaching 89.20% (Section 4.1, Table 2).
Fine-tuning Llama 2-7B, LoRA-Muon matches LoRA-Adam on math (59.57% vs 59.64%) and outperforms it on code (29.47% vs 27.85%) and commonsense reasoning (67.40% vs 67.37%) (Section 4.2, Table 3).
On CLIP ViT-B/32 image classification, LoRA-Muon outperforms LoRA-Adam on average accuracy (84.48% vs 84.17%) (Section 4.3, Table 4).

LoRA-Muon's relative advantage over LoRA-Adam depends on adapter rank, excelling at low-to-moderate ranks but degrading at higher ranks on MetaMath where optimizer mismatch is most pronounced (Section 4.4, Figures 5-6).
Standard LoRA variants designed for Adam do not improve LoRA-Muon performance, suggesting Muon-specific LoRA adaptations are needed (Section 4.6, Table 6).

O5xoqSmNzc.text: On SlimPajama with a 774M-parameter GPT2-Large model, MuonAdam and Scion require precise learning-rate tuning with narrow competitive ranges, while MuonAdam-Momo and MuonMax-Momo achieve low loss across a much wider learning-rate range (Figure 1).

On FineWeb1B with a 124M-parameter GPT2-Small model, the fraction of learning rates achieving validation loss below 3.65 is 25% for MuonAdam and Scion versus 50% for MuonMax-Momo and 62.5% for MuonAdam-Momo (Figure 2a).

MuonMax-Momo achieves the lowest validation loss among all tested methods on SlimPajama after 6B training tokens while remaining robust to learning-rate shifts, with final loss varying only between 3.13 and 3.24 across five orders of magnitude of learning rate (Section 5.2, Figure 1).
A stale nuclear-norm approximation ablation shows at most 0.004 validation loss degradation while reducing wall-clock training time by 5% (Table 1).

Section 3.4 unifies MuonAdam, Scion, and PolarGrad as instances of steepest descent under different norm choices, and Equation 17 defines the MuonMax norm combining spectral and adaptive norms (Section 3.4, Eq. 17).

z9x30tqLUV.text: On Online Bin Packing (OBP), ASRO-EoH achieves substantially lower average gap than the EoH baseline on Falkenauer T (7.11% vs 12.11%) and Hard28-SA (12.45% vs 40.02%) instances (Experimental Results, Online Bin Packing).

On TSPLIB instances, ASRO-EoH reduces the average optimality gap versus EoH from 0.77% to 0.21% on small instances (≤200 cities) and from 3.40% to 1.43% on large instances (501-1000 cities) (Experimental Results, Traveling Salesman Problem).

An ablation shows ASRO with a smaller LLaMA-3-8B backbone outperforms EoH run with stronger backbones, indicating the co-evolutionary strategy-pool structure, not model scale, drives the improvement (Ablation Studies, LLM Backbones).

Ablations comparing data augmentation and self-play variants against full ASRO show both partial variants improve over baseline EoH but remain inferior to ASRO, isolating persistent strategy pools and equilibrium-driven dynamics as necessary components (Ablation Studies, Data Augmentation & Self-Play).

Replacing the EoH best-response oracle with the ReEvo program-search mechanism inside ASRO preserves the performance gains, demonstrating the game-theoretic co-evolution framework is agnostic to the specific LLM program-search procedure used (Ablation Studies, Oracle-Agnosticity).

Convergence is tracked via an Approximate NashConv metric (ANC = Exp_s(t) + Exp_g(t)) that shows a consistent downward trend across all tested combinatorial domains, indicating approach toward the minimax equilibrium (Convergence Behavior).

HMu24dTKkJ.text: Theorem 1 bounds the total variation distance between the DDPM output and target distribution as TV(X0,Y1) ≲ log²(KT)log²T/T + ε_score√log T + √(dε_approx)log^(3/2)(dT), yielding Õ(1/ε) discretization steps for ε-accurate sampling independent of ambient dimension d and mixture count K (Theorem 1).

The dimension-free discretization rate relies on Assumption 1, requiring the target distribution to be ε_approx-close in TV distance to an isotropic Gaussian mixture whose component means satisfy the polynomial growth bound ||μ_k||_2 ≤ T^{c_r} (Assumption 1).

The bound remains valid under imperfect score estimation via Assumption 2, which requires the time-averaged squared L2 score error to satisfy (1/T)∑ε²_score,t ≤ ε²_score, contributing an additive ε_score√log T term to the TV bound (Assumption 2, Theorem 1).

The proof's key technical lemma shows the trace of the score Jacobian for a Gaussian mixture satisfies tr(I_d + J_t(x)) ≤ C1 log(KT) with high probability, a bound with no explicit dependence on ambient dimension d, enabling the dimension-free discretization analysis.

The paper contrasts its Õ(1/ε)-iteration, dimension-free rate against prior DDPM convergence results (e.g., Li & Yan 2024; Liang et al. 2024) that required O(d/ε) iterations even when the target is a Gaussian mixture, showing the mixture structure can be exploited to remove the dimension dependence entirely (comparison to prior work).

4HrWo5x7YF.text: Theorem 3.3 establishes that over signal classes with Effective Span Dimension (ESD) at most K, the minimax excess risk is asymptotically equivalent to K·σ², holding without classical eigenvalue-decay or source-condition assumptions (Theorem 3.3).

Theorem 3.2 shows the principal-component (PC) estimator's risk is sandwiched as (d†−1)σ² ≤ Risk ≤ 2d†σ², where d† is the Effective Span Dimension defined as the smallest number of leading eigenfunctions whose remaining tail signal energy no longer exceeds the noise level σ² (Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 4.3 gives convergence rates for a quota sequence {K_n}: the minimax risk over populations satisfying d†(σ0²/n; θ*, λ) ≤ K_n scales as Θ(K_n σ0²/n) (Theorem 4.3).

Theorem 5.2 proves that overparameterized gradient flow (OP-GF) can reduce the Effective Span Dimension over training time by assigning larger adapted eigenvalues to strong signal directions with initially small eigenvalues, moving the problem into a lower minimax-risk complexity class (Theorem 5.2).

Section 7 and Section 8 extend the Effective Span Dimension framework to linear regression (via SVD, minimax rate Θ(σ0²K/n)) and RKHS regression (rate Θ(σ̄²K_n/n) with effective noise σ̄² = (σ0² + ||f*||²_∞)/n) (Section 7, Section 8).

Numerical experiments show that span profiles decrease during OP-GF training—with larger improvements when initial signal-spectrum alignment is worse—and that deeper models attain lower Effective Span Dimension than shallow variants given sufficient training iterations (Numerical Validation).

OtKDK3ZtLJ.text: The optimal mixing ratio for sim-and-real co-training lies in a balanced range of approximately 0.016-0.3, with the natural ratio w_n = |D_r|/(|D_r|+|D_s|) ≈ 0.016 for a setup of 50 real and about 3000 synthetic demonstrations (Key Numeric Results, Mixing Ratio Range).

Structured representation alignment shows a moderate-to-strong positive correlation with task success rate, with Pearson and Spearman coefficients between 0.6 and 0.8 (p < 0.04) across most experimental settings (Key Numeric Results, Correlation Metrics).

A variance decomposition attributes roughly 50% of downstream performance variance to structured representation alignment, versus only about 20% attributed to the importance reweighting effect, identifying representation alignment as the dominant intrinsic factor (Key Numeric Results, Variance Decomposition).

The proposed CFG-ADDA method achieves approximately 74% real-world success rate averaged across challenging manipulation tasks including NutAssembly, MugHang, and MugCleanup (Key Numeric Results, Real-World Performance).

The paper proposes a mixing-ratio selection guideline recommending a search range between the natural ratio w_n and w_q = √(N/M) when the source (simulation) dataset size N substantially exceeds the target (real) dataset size M (Practical Guideline).

pBBygHUKOu.text: FAN attains state-of-the-art normalized return of 76±4 on D4RL antmaze tasks while running 5-14x faster in training than distributional critic baselines such as IQN, CODAC, and Value Flows (Key Performance Results, Benchmark Tasks and Computational Efficiency).

On OGBench, FAN achieves the best performance on 7 of 9 task environments, with particularly strong results on manipulation tasks such as puzzles and cube manipulation (Key Performance Results, Benchmark Tasks).

FAN's flow anchoring mechanism uses a single flow iteration instead of iterative ODE solving to regularize the policy toward the behavior distribution, provably minimizing the Wasserstein-2 distance to the behavior policy (Core Contributions, Theoretical Guarantees).

The noise-conditioned critic operator 𝒯ⁿᵖ conditions the distributional value function on a single shared noise vector rather than multiple quantiles, and is proven to be a γ-contraction in the supremum metric (Core Contributions, Theoretical Guarantees).

Experiments train FAN for 500K gradient steps on D4RL and for 1M steps (state-based) or 500K steps (pixel-based) on OGBench, using a batch size of 256 on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPU (Experimental Settings).

trSWJ99WzS.text: LessIsMore aggregates top-k token selections across all attention heads instead of selecting tokens per-head, then globally ranks and prunes tokens to unify sparse attention across heads (Section 3.2).
LessIsMore reserves a fixed ratio of the token budget (typically 25%) for a stable recency window of recently generated tokens to preserve step-by-step reasoning dependencies (Section 3.3).

With Qwen3-8B, LessIsMore matches or exceeds full-attention accuracy at reduced budgets: 73.75% vs 74.48% on AIME-24 (2K budget), 70.42% vs 67.86% on AIME-25 (4K budget), and 93.35% vs 94.43% on MATH500 (1K budget) (Section 4.2, Tables 2-3).
LessIsMore achieves a 1.1x average decoding speedup over full attention and a 1.13x end-to-end speedup over the TidalDecode baseline with 7% shorter generation length (Section 4.3, Figure 7).
LessIsMore attends to roughly 2x fewer tokens than competing sparse-attention methods without accuracy loss, requiring no retraining (Section 4.3).

Across token budgets from 2K to 6K, LessIsMore keeps generation length in the 15.1K-15.8K token range, close to full attention's 14.8K, whereas competing methods generate 17.4K-30K tokens (Section 4.4.2, Table 1).

GdyuWMAH8P.text: GFMate achieves improvements of up to 30.63% on cross-domain node classification across 9 datasets under a one-shot setting, compared against 21 baselines spanning supervised, SSL+fine-tuning, single-domain prompting, and cross-domain GFM methods (Table 1).
GFMate's test-time complementary-label learning objective combines few-shot labeled data with unlabeled target-domain test nodes via entropy-based selection of pivot layers (Section 3, Figure 4).

GFMate uses centroid prompts (learnable per-class, per-layer d-dimensional vectors) and layer prompts (L-dimensional vectors ensembling across GNN layers) applied after pre-training, avoiding entanglement with any specific source domain or pre-training strategy, as validated when applied atop 5 pre-training methods (LP, DGI, GCL, MDGPT, SAMGPT) (Table 2).

Proposition 1 establishes an excess risk bound for the test-time complementary learning objective, showing that fewer classes or more labeled test samples yield tighter generalization bounds (Section 3, Proposition 1).
GFMate improves binary graph classification over the SAMGPT baseline by 6.85% to 18.27% on datasets including BZR, COX2, and PROTEINS (Table 4).
GFMate reduces GPU memory usage by 97.18% and improves time efficiency by 98.24% relative to SAMGPT (Figure 5).

hZhJTTjmUM.text: UniDFlow uses task-specific low-rank (LoRA) adapters introduced during Stage II vision alignment to decouple understanding and generation objectives and avoid objective interference (Section 3.2, Eq. 5).
UniDFlow employs Time-Step Guided RMSNorm, injecting the diffusion time step via modulation of normalization scale parameters to preserve pretrained representations (Section 3.2.1).

UniDFlow is trained via a three-stage pipeline: Stage I text alignment with KL regularization, Stage II vision alignment with separate LoRA adapters, and Stage III reference-based multimodal preference optimization (mRefDPO) combining discrete flow-matching likelihood with comparative alignment (Section 3, Eq. 3-9).
At 4B scale, UniDFlow outperforms EMMA-4B by +6.3% on MMBench and +13.3% on MathVista, reaching 91.2 on MMBench, 74.3 on MMMU, 82.7 on MM-Vet, and 85.9 on MathVista (Table 1).
UniDFlow achieves 0.95 on GenEval and 91.19 on DPGBench for text-to-image generation, versus 0.93/85.63 for EMMA and 0.87 for MammothModa2 on GenEval (Table 2).
UniDFlow attains an overall ImgEdit Bench score of 4.24, improving on EMMA (4.01) and MammothModa2 (4.06), with +3.5% and +4.1% gains respectively on Emu-Edit (Table 3).

1TXn0PeBZJ.text: VideoBrain uses a multi-agent architecture with a CLIP Sample Agent (semantic retrieval via SigLIP2-B/16) and a Uniform Sample Agent (temporally dense interval sampling) built on a Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct base model with 16 initial frames and up to 5 interactions (Section 3, Section 4).
VideoBrain's behavior-aware reward function combines format validation, accuracy scoring, and an incentive term that discourages indiscriminate/unnecessary agent invocation (Section 3).
VideoBrain improves accuracy by +8.1% on LongVideoBench while using 30% fewer frames, and by +9.0% on LVBench while using 33% fewer frames, relative to baseline (Table 2).
VideoBrain improves accuracy by +4.2% on Video-MME Long with 40% fewer frames and by +3.5% on MLVU Test with 38% fewer frames (Table 2).
VideoBrain demonstrates zero-shot generalization to short-video benchmarks DREAM-1K and Video-MME Short without additional training (Section 4).
VideoBrain is trained on roughly 8K samples, split into 1.6K SFT examples and 6.4K RL examples (Section 4).

pd6A7jB5D6.text: Small models such as GPT2 and Qwen3-0.6B exhibit severe embedding condensation into narrow cone-like subspaces, while larger models such as GPT2-xl and Qwen3-32B are markedly more resistant to this phenomenon (Section 4).

Embedding condensation is present at initialization and decreases over the course of training, and knowledge distillation from larger models does not reliably transfer condensation resistance to smaller models (Section 4.1-4.4).
Adding dispersion loss during mid-training yields average gains across 10 benchmarks of +1.26 points for GPT2, +1.55 for GPT2-m, and +3.34 for Qwen3-0.6B (Table 2).
Hyperparameter ablations over dispersion weight λ_disp (0.01-1.0) and temperature τ (0.1-2.0) select λ_disp=0.1, τ=1.0 as defaults (Table 3).

Qwen3-0.6B pre-trained from scratch with dispersion loss achieves a +1.17 point average improvement across the 10 benchmarks, including +4.0 on PIQA and +7.4 on TruthfulQA, a 3.1% relative gain over the cross-entropy baseline (Table 4).
The 10 benchmarks used to evaluate dispersion loss include ANLI-R2, LAMBADA, OpenBookQA, PIQA, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande, ARC-easy, ARC-challenge, MedMCQA, and MMLU (Section 5).

5YEsi7Zovy.text: REPA-P attaches lightweight 1x1 projection heads to intermediate layers of a U-Net or DiT backbone to decode hidden activations into physical quantities and apply PDE residual losses during training, with these heads discarded at inference (Section 3.2).
On Darcy Flow generation with a U-Net backbone, REPA-P reduces physics loss from 0.0260 to 0.0143, a 45.0% reduction relative to the PIDM baseline (Table 1).
On the electrostatic potential task, REPA-P reduces physics loss by 66.4% (from 0.381 to 0.128) relative to the PIDM baseline (Table 1).
On out-of-distribution topology optimization with unseen boundary conditions, REPA-P reduces compliance error from 7.93 to 5.05, a 36.3% improvement over the PIDM baseline (Table 1, Section 4.2).
With a DiT backbone, REPA-P achieves a 25.73% reduction in physics loss and a 57.64% reduction in data loss on Darcy Flow (Table 2).
Projection heads used for physics alignment are discarded after training, so REPA-P adds zero inference-time computational overhead compared to the baseline diffusion model (Section 3.2).

VzIA4MASxK.text: FlashSinkhorn achieves up to 32x forward-pass speedup and up to 161x end-to-end (forward+backward) speedup over the KeOps baseline at dimension d=512 (Table 3, Figure 2).

FlashSinkhorn is compared against GeomLoss (tensorized and KeOps modes) and OTT-JAX (standard alternating Sinkhorn updates) as baselines on synthetic point-cloud benchmarks on A100 GPUs (Section 4.1).
At n=m=10,000 and d=64, FlashSinkhorn reduces HBM traffic to 0.08 GB and runtime to 8.2 ms, versus 98 GB / 54.0 ms for the tensorized approach and 0.14 GB / 125.5 ms for KeOps (Table 2).

Theorem 2 establishes FlashSinkhorn's theoretical IO complexity as Θ(nd + md + nmd²/M) HBM accesses under the two-level memory model, while maintaining linear O(n) memory scaling versus O(n^1.7 to n^1.9) for tensorized methods (Theorem 2, Figure 2).

On the OTDD (Optimal Transport Dataset Distance) downstream task, FlashSinkhorn exhibits linear memory growth up to n=60,000 compared to quadratic growth for tensorized baselines (Figure 3, Section 4.2).

For Hessian-vector products used in OT-based shuffled regression with saddle detection on flow cytometry data (n=40,000), FlashSinkhorn delivers 3-25x speedups depending on dimension, enabling Newton acceleration (Figure 4, Section 4.2).

LkTtWmZaxq.text: The paper formalizes the Learning from Language Feedback (LLF) problem, in which an agent receives natural-language observations alongside latent numeric rewards, via Definitions 4 and 5 (Definitions 4-5).

Transfer eluder dimension is introduced as a complexity measure quantifying how much exploration is needed to transfer knowledge across contexts in LLF settings, directly governing sample-complexity bounds (Section on Transfer Eluder Dimension).
Theorem 1 establishes regret bounds for the LLF problem setup that scale with the transfer eluder dimension rather than reward-only complexity measures (Theorem 1).

The HELiX (Hypothesis Exploration with Language feXdback) algorithm is proposed as a no-regret method that solves LLF problems by exploring and refining policy hypotheses using language feedback signals (HELiX algorithm).
Theorem 3 addresses convergence properties of the approach under specific assumptions about the informativeness of the language feedback mechanism (Theorem 3).

puNfWfBFNT.text: Lemma 3.2 derives a multi-treatment generalization bound decomposing individualized treatment effect (ITE) error into factual prediction error, representation-level imbalance across treatment arms, and model complexity (Lemma 3.2, Section 3.1).

Theorem 3.5 provides a finite-sample deviation bound on the optimal balancing weight, |α̂_S - α^bd(n)| <= r_S(n,δ,K)/κ_S, converting hyperparameter selection into a statistical estimation problem (Theorem 3.5, Section 3.2).

Treatment Aggregation via the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) achieves O(1) computational complexity and a deviation term r_agg = O(sqrt(log(1/δ)/n)) independent of the number of treatments K, versus O(K^2) for pairwise balancing and O(K) for one-vs-all (Section 2).

Theorem 3.8 shows the estimated balancing weight is asymptotically normal, with variance scaling as Θ(K^4/n) for pairwise balancing, Θ(K^2/n) for one-vs-all, and Θ(1/n) for the treatment aggregation strategy (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.3).

At K=20 treatments, pairwise balancing becomes unstable (PEHE exceeding 1.3 under strong regularization) while the aggregation strategy maintains competitive accuracy of approximately 1.0 across regularization levels, empirically confirming its O(1) scalability (Section 4.2, Figure 1b).

Multi-Treatment CausalEGM extends the discriminative framework to high-dimensional counterfactual generation and, via interpolation experiments, is shown to preserve the Wasserstein geodesic structure of the treatment manifold (Section 5.1, Section 5.2, Figure 3).

Np7Y3AEVNq.text: Algorithm 1 implements a budgeted active experimentation procedure combining observational logs and an unlabeled candidate pool via a multi-criteria acquisition function (Equation 7) balancing epistemic uncertainty, domain discrepancy, and overlap deficit (Section 3, Algorithm 1, Equation 7).
Lemma 4.4 establishes that pseudo-outcomes remain unbiased under adaptive sampling because randomization protects unbiasedness regardless of how covariates are selected (Lemma 4.4).
Theorem 4.5 provides finite-sample self-normalized concentration bounds, controlling the error ||θ^λ - θ*||_{Vλ} for adaptively collected data (Theorem 4.5).
Theorem 4.8 proves asymptotic normality via a martingale central limit theorem, showing sqrt(B)(θ^0 - θ*) converges to N(0, Σπ⁻¹ΩπΣπ⁻¹) (Theorem 4.8).

Theorem 4.9 establishes a minimax lower bound showing the sqrt(d/B) estimation rate cannot be beaten, with Corollary 4.10 confirming the estimator achieves minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 4.9, Corollary 4.10).

On ride-hailing data, the budgeted active experimentation framework reduces RCT labeling cost by approximately 80% compared to a random sampling baseline at comparable estimation performance (Section 5).

YDztzMJynP.text: TUR-DPO improves GSM8K exact-match accuracy from 58.7% (DPO) to 62.8%, and MATH-mini exact-match from 33.4% to 36.0% (Table 1).
On GSM8K reasoning graphs, TUR-DPO reduces average cycle count from 10.3 to 7.6 per graph and dangling nodes from 16.9% to 12.2%, while increasing minimal path coverage from 61.5% to 69.3% (Table 3).
TUR-DPO reduces Expected Calibration Error from 0.101 (DPO) to 0.087, with the largest reduction (2.8 points) in the highest-confidence bin (0.9-1.0) (Table 9-10).

Ablations show removing the uncertainty weighting term drops GSM8K win-rate from 62.8% to 60.3%, and removing the topology reward drops it to 59.6%, versus a graph-size-only baseline of 57.7% (Table 21).

TUR-DPO matches or exceeds PPO-RLHF on reasoning tasks while requiring only ~15% more compute than vanilla DPO (42 vs. 48 GPU-hours on 8xA100s to reach a 65% win-rate target) (Section on Computational Overhead, Table 11).

TUR-DPO is evaluated across mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH), compositional reasoning (BBH), factual QA, summarization (TLDR faithfulness), and dialogue (HH), with human evaluation showing inter-rater agreement rising from kappa=0.66 (DPO) to 0.71 (TUR-DPO) (Table 7).

fT3laNA1AO.text: RADAR formulates reliable context selection as a Markov Random Field energy minimization problem solved via Max-Flow Min-Cut, with source edge capacity Si = vi * w_rank(i) derived from eigenvector centrality (Section 4.2).

On the RQA dataset, RADAR's static defense matches Vanilla RAG's 75.0% benign accuracy while reducing prompt-injection attack success rate (ASR) to 5.0% at position 10 with k=10 retrieved documents (Table 1).

RADAR's dynamic defense augments the graph with a Bayesian memory node that recursively updates belief state via Bayes' theorem, achieving 63.60% accuracy and 17.85% ASR under PIA at position 1, outperforming ReliabilityRAG's 53.61% accuracy (Section 4.3, Table 3).
On the long-form Bio dataset generation task, RADAR achieves 80.6% factual accuracy under prompt-injection attacks at position 50 (k=50), versus 10.2% for Vanilla RAG (Table 2).
By maintaining a recursive belief state instead of archiving raw historical documents, RADAR reduces per-query storage overhead from tens of MBs to approximately 1 KB (Storage Efficiency analysis).

Min-Cut inference via the highest-label preflow-push algorithm runs in O(n^3) for n=k+2 nodes, adding under 1 second of overhead versus the 20-86 seconds dominated by atomic answer generation (Computational Complexity analysis, Tables 5-7).

2rGr38p5az.text: Bootstrapped Flow Q-Learning (BFQ) generates actions in a single step at both training and inference time, without auxiliary networks or distillation, by learning short-range displacements that bootstrap into full noise-to-action mappings (Section 4.1).
On D4RL MuJoCo locomotion tasks, BFQ achieves an average score of 92.8 versus 89.0 for the DQL diffusion baseline (Benchmark Results section).
On D4RL AntMaze navigation, BFQ achieves an average score of 83.9 and reaches 88.5 on AntMaze-Large-Play, competitive with OFQL's 84.6 average (Benchmark Results section).
BFQ trains in 7.8 hours versus 11.7 hours for 5-step DQL and 49.5 hours for 50-step DQL, and executes actions at 851.2 Hz versus 238.1 Hz (5-step DQL) and 35.5 Hz (50-step DQL) (Table 2).
An ablation removing the preconditioning term causes catastrophic failure on the Medium-Expert dataset, dropping the score from 98.5 to 3 +/- 3.0 (Table 6, Section 7).

An ablation setting the boundary conditioning ratio lambda to 0 (removing boundary conditioning) causes severe performance degradation, with score changes ranging from -2.5 to +10.6 across tasks, confirming lambda=0.5 as optimal (Section 7).

ZVKW9kWr1t.text: Theorem 3.1 shows the Bayesian PINN posterior for elliptic PDEs concentrates around the true beta-Holder-smooth solution at rate epsilon_n = n^{-(beta-2)/(d+2(beta-2))} (log n)^{1/2}, which is near-minimax optimal (Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.5 establishes a matching minimax lower bound of order n1^{-2(beta-2)/(d+2(beta-2))} + n2^{-2beta/(d-1+2beta)} for unequal interior (n1) and boundary (n2) sample sizes (Theorem 3.5).

The spike-and-slab prior over network width, sparsity, and parameter bounds (Section 2.4) is rate-adaptive, achieving the optimal contraction rate without requiring prior knowledge of the true solution's Holder smoothness level beta (Section 2.4, Abstract).
Proposition 4.2 shows that sigma_3 (ReLU-cubed) network classes can approximate C^beta functions with approximation error decaying as l^{-(beta-2)} in network width parameter l (Proposition 4.2).

The network class used for the posterior achieves the stated rate with depth L = O(log d + log beta*) and width/sparsity/parameter bounds scaling as n^{d/(d+2(beta-2))} (Neural Network Class specification, Section 3).

z0CHTAHame.text: SteinDiff derives a reference-free, Stein's-identity-based estimator for the MSE-optimal correction coefficient gamma*_k, given by gamma*_k = [(1-1/alpha_k)E[<u_k,x_k>] + (sigma_k^2/alpha_k)E[div(u_k)]] / E[||u_k||^2] (Theorem 4.7).
Theorem 4.8 establishes a step-wise error decay bound for SteinDiff-corrected sampling, showing the terminal error satisfies E^0_Stein <= (1-eta)^N * E_N over N inference steps (Theorem 4.8).
On LSUN-Bedrooms 256x256 at 5 NFE, SteinDiff reduces FID from a baseline of 21.29 to 7.64 (Table 2).
On ImageNet 64x64, SteinDiff yields FID reductions of up to 45.8% relative to baseline solvers, with consistent gains across both DPM-Solver++ and UniPC (Table 2).

Algorithm 1 implements the correction using Hutchinson trace estimation for the divergence term and batch-averaged statistics (s_xu, s_uu, s_div), with a clipped coefficient gamma_hat_k bounded below by a minimum threshold gamma_min (Algorithm 1).

SteinDiff is evaluated against DPM-Solver++ (including third-order), UniPC, and Heun solvers across CIFAR-10, ImageNet 64x64, and LSUN-Bedrooms 256x256, using FID, IS, and FD-DINOv2 metrics at 5-20 NFE (Experimental Results section).

RZ7UHTHmfn.text: Test-time training reduces prediction error only when the induced spectral filter g_T(λ) is matched to the Bayes-optimal filter q*(λ)=(λ+λ*)^{-1} and aligned with query-relevant eigen-directions, formalized via the conditional Bayes-gap decomposition (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).

Selecting the number of gradient update steps T via evidence (marginal-likelihood) minimization yields a PAC-Bayes bound on the excess risk relative to the fixed-budget oracle, holding with probability at least 1-delta (Theorem 7.2, Section 7).

The Bayes-optimal rank-k update subspace equals the top-k eigenspace of an information-capture matrix I_Q associated with the query, making query-agnostic subspace choices provably suboptimal (Theorem 8.2, Section 8.1).

Fixed update-step schedules fail under prior/signal-to-noise shift because the Bayes-optimal number of steps T varies with the test-time SNR, while taking T to infinity can be suboptimal due to overfitting relative to finite shrinkage (Propositions 6.1 and 6.2, Section 6).

On synthetic Gaussian-process benchmarks with evidence-based selection of T, MSE improves from 0.0747 (in-context learning) and 0.0734 (fixed T=8) to 0.0719 (evidence MLE-sigma), with a mean selected T of 11.2 across 2,000 tasks (Section 9, Experiment 1).

A Query-Aware block-selection score based on the information-capture matrix consistently outperforms a Trace-TopK alternative on query prediction despite Trace-TopK achieving better in-prompt fit, demonstrating that prompt fitting and query generalization are distinct objectives (Section 9, Experiment 2).

XIHBvLayrp.text: UniCoD is pretrained on roughly 1.75M samples combining 320k robot videos with subtask descriptions, 870k robot and human operation videos with task instructions, and 560k generic vision-language QA data, drawn from AgibotWorld, Galaxea Open-World, RoboMind, DROID, Bridge, Egodex, and Ego4D (Section 3.3, Table 8).

UniCoD learns a Text-Image to Embedding (TI2E) mapping that jointly produces discrete language representations for scene understanding and continuous visual representations for world modeling (Section 3.1).
On SimplerEnv, UniCoD reaches 71.0% average success on WindowX versus 49.8% for the pi0 baseline, and 78.4% versus 51.9% on Google Robot (Tables 1-3).
On the CALVIN benchmark, UniCoD attains an average task length of 4.11 versus 4.08 for the UP-VLA baseline (Table 2).

In real-world evaluations, UniCoD achieves 80% average success on unseen Franka Panda tasks versus 69% for pi0 (11-point gain, Table 6), and 62% versus 50% on unseen XArm dexterous tasks (12-point gain, Table 7).
Action prediction is trained via flow matching, where the unified model approximates vector fields over continuous action distributions rather than discrete action tokens (Section 3.2).

PStNoNZveu.text: ActiveScope identifies contextual dominance, where visually salient distractors overwhelm the attention landscape and cause the target to be missed, and semantic bias, where attention from the first answer token is dominated by the most salient concept in multi-object scenes, as the two failure modes behind poor localization in MLLMs (Sections 3.1 and 3.2).
ActiveScope achieves 96.34% accuracy on V* Bench with Qwen3-VL 4B, exceeding ZoomEye (93.19%) by 3.15 points and the base model (89.53%) by 6.81 points (Table 2).

Semantic Anchor Localization, which extracts per-target-token attention maps via relative attention normalization, reaches 93.73% accuracy on V* Bench when fully implemented, and key-token guidance improves F1 from a 40.9% baseline to 60.7% (Equation 3, Tables 1 and 4).
Interference-Suppressed Refinement masks incorrectly localized regions to force attention redistribution, with performance saturating after a maximum of 3 refinement cycles (Table 5).
On HR-Bench, ActiveScope attains 78.13% average accuracy on the 4K split and 74.75% on the 8K split, versus 76.25% and 73.50% respectively for ZoomEye (Section 4/Tables).
The verification module underlying ActiveScope's active correction loop exceeds 95% verification accuracy with false positive/negative rates under 3% across prompt variations (Table 6).

FFXvnzM254.text: Under biased selection targeting a local ideal u*, the population mean converges almost surely to u* while the covariance collapses to zero, formalizing that siloed selection drives model collapse (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).

The asymptotic rate of diversity loss follows a power law, Tr(Sigma_t) = O_a.s.(t^{-psi}), showing two-phase dynamics with rapid initial homogenization followed by convergence to a point mass, and stricter local alignment paradoxically accelerates tail erosion (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
