Figure 1 empirically validates the theoretical collapse predictions, showing that the replace paradigm causes catastrophic variance depletion while the accumulate-with-selection paradigm exhibits power-law decay matching Theorem 2 (Section 3.2).

A geodesic-interpolation collaborative filtering scheme computes proxy Wasserstein-geodesic measures across clients without exchanging raw data, using submodular selection to maximize coverage (Section 4.3).

On CIFAR-10 after 10 iterations under a skewed ExDir(1,0.1) reference distribution, the geodesic-interpolation scheme reduces FID from 106 (random baseline) to 71 and improves precision/recall from 0.53/0.48 to 0.60/0.58, outperforming CenterMatch and CovMatch baselines which retain FID above 102 (Table 2, Section 5).

A barycenter-estimation variant of the collaborative scheme is proven to converge to the true Wasserstein barycenter and decouples proxy estimation from synthetic generation, enabling reuse across multiple generation rounds (Theorem 5, Section 4.4).

PTaUjEBHat.text: On the AirFoil_9k benchmark with a soft drag constraint (C_D < 0.02), GANO raises the lift-to-drag ratio from an initial 53.6 to 83.4, a 55.9% improvement, surpassing U-Net (75.0, +40.0%) and DeepONet (44.3, -17.3%) (Table 2, Section 5.3).
GANO's optimized airfoil shapes are validated using COMSOL and exhibit more aerodynamically reasonable geometry with a smoother leading edge compared to baseline methods (Figure 6, Section 5.3).

On the DrivAerNet++ vehicle benchmark with OpenFOAM validation, GANO reduces drag from 0.346 to 0.323 (6.64% reduction) for the Estateback body style and from 0.299 to 0.278 (7.02% reduction) for the Fastback body style (Section 5.4).

GANO preserves design elements such as side mirrors during vehicle drag optimization via null-space projection, in contrast to PhysGen which tends to shrink or sweep back the mirrors to reduce drag (Figure 8, Section 5.4).

sQ6oDLZWFb.text: Training-free Mask Prior Suppression (MPS) mitigates mask prior drift by adjusting the final hidden states of generation tokens within a PCA-derived mask prior subspace, using the top k=3 principal components of vocabulary mean representations (Section on Mask Prior Suppression).

Monotonic RoPE Scaling (MRS) applies sigmoid-gated frequency scaling (hyperparameters λ, β, η, τ0) to amplify low-frequency rotary position embedding components, countering positional attention collapse toward distant visual tokens (Section on Monotonic RoPE Scaling).
Applying the combined MPS+MRS method to the LLaDA-V baseline improves RefCOCOg accuracy from 64.8 to 65.0 and DetailCaps score from 59.8 to 63.6 (Section 4, Experiments).

The two methods are evaluated across general multimodal benchmarks (MME, MMBench, MMMU), visual grounding benchmarks (RefCOCOg, Ferret, GQA), long-form generation benchmarks (LLaVA-Bench, DetailCaps, MIA), and hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, AMBER-G) (Section 4, Experiments).
The approach is shown to generalize training-free across two distinct large diffusion vision-language model architectures, LLaDA-V and LaViDa (Section 4, Experiments).

NKpnzoFqFu.text: VLANeXt distills 12 design findings across foundational components, perception inputs, and action modeling, derived from a systematic ablation study in Section 2 (Section 2, Recipes for Building Strong VLA Models).
On the standard LIBERO benchmark, VLANeXt achieves a 97.4% average success rate across the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites, exceeding OpenVLA-OFT's 97.1% average (Table 2).

On the perturbation-based LIBERO-plus benchmark (10,030 demonstrations with visual, physical, and semantic perturbations), VLANeXt attains an 80.1% average success rate versus 69.6% for OpenVLA-OFT (Table 3).

Ablations show a separate policy head raises success rate from 30.2% to 64.4% over token-reuse, and switching the VLM backbone from PaliGemma to Qwen3-VL-4B raises success rate from 69.8% to 95.8% (Section 2.1).
Conditioning proprioception directly in the VLM combined with multi-view (third-person plus wrist camera) inputs raises success rate from 91.8% to 98.0% (Section 2.2).

In real-world experiments, the 2.5B-parameter VLANeXt (Qwen3-VL-2B backbone) outperforms OpenVLA-OFT and pi0 baselines on four manipulation tasks: table cleaning (14/20), drawer manipulation (11/20), basket lifting (15/20), and bimanual cleaning (11/20) (Section 4, Real-World Evaluations).

Tvcii7gyRX.text: CaRE introduces a Bi-Level Routing Mixture-of-Experts (BR-MoE) mechanism, claimed to be the first continual learner scaling to very long, non-overlapping task sequences of 100 to over 300 tasks (Section 3, Method).

The paper proposes a new long task sequence evaluation protocol using OmniBenchmark-V2, comprising 1,000 classes and roughly 190,000 images across 21 visual realms (Section 4, Long Task Sequence Evaluation Protocol).
On OmniBenchmark-V2 with 100 tasks, CaRE achieves 68.27% last accuracy, outperforming the MOS baseline by about 4.0 percentage points (Table 1).

On the 200-task sequence, CaRE reaches 67.46% last accuracy, exceeding the TUNA baseline by 8.32 percentage points, and on the 301-task sequence CaRE attains 68.51% with its largest margin over baselines (Table 1).

BR-MoE is configured with M=2 activated router networks and K=3 experts per router, using bottleneck channels of 16 (task-specific) and 64 (shared), with an EMA momentum of mu=0.999 (Section 3.3, BR-MoE Details).

CaRE is additionally evaluated on moderate-length (50-60 task) and short (5-20 task) sequences, reported in Table 2 and Table 3 respectively, alongside ablation studies in Section 5.3 (Section 5, Experiments).

yY7rywRtlI.text: FLAG identifies a 'gene dimension curse' in which joint node-edge diffusion suffers catastrophic variance-explosion collapse as gene count increases, formalized via a lower bound Omega(G) that grows with dimensionality (Figure 2a).

FLAG combines a spatial graph encoder, a gene-level diffusion transformer, and a Gene Foundation Model (GFM) alignment loss to enforce gene-spatial topographic coherence and gene-gene structural fidelity (Section 3, Method).
On the HEST-1k benchmark's HER2ST dataset (36 slides, 13,620 spots), FLAG achieves PCC 0.6835, MSE 0.7342, GSC 0.8926, and SSC 0.6386 on the top-200 highly variable gene panel (Table 1).
On the KIDNEY dataset (23 slides, 25,944 spots) and PRAD dataset (23 slides, 62,710 spots), FLAG attains PCC of 0.3917 and 0.5853 respectively, while maintaining GSC above 0.87 on both (Table 1).

The paper introduces two novel evaluation metrics, Gene Structural Correlation (GSC) and Spatial Structural Correlation (SSC, based on Moran's I), to assess structural fidelity beyond traditional accuracy metrics like PCC and MSE (Section 4, Experiments).
Performance is analyzed as gene panel size scales across G in {10, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800}, showing how structural fidelity degrades with increasing dimensionality (Figure 4).

AaT3liS5PE.text: The paper proposes jointly training steering factors and directions during optimization, removing the need for post-hoc factor selection required by prior steering vector methods (Section 5, Prompt-Only Steering Vector).

Prompt-Only Steering Vector (PrOSV) intervenes only on 2-4 prompt tokens rather than the full sequence, yielding a claimed 37x reduction in computational overhead relative to full-sequence steering vectors (Section 5, Prompt-Only Steering Vector).
On the AxBench benchmark, PrOSV trained with a SimPO objective on Qwen2.5-32B achieves an overall steering score of 1.102, the best result reported across configurations (Table 2).
PrOSV with the language-modeling objective scores between 0.736 and 1.049 across models, compared to 0.663-0.798 for the full-sequence steering vector (FSSV) baseline (Table 2).
On capability-preservation benchmarks, PrOSV maintains tinyGSM8K accuracy above 50% while FSSV drops to 5-11% under equivalent steering strength (Table 3).

The best intervention-location configuration (pp2+ss2, combining prompt and generation positions) achieves scores of 0.70, 0.92, and 1.16 on Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B, and Qwen2.5-32B respectively (Table 1).

rjmVJaBpkm.text: The Conformal Ratio (CR) metric, which balances coverage and prediction set size under split conformal prediction, is proposed to expose 'fake forgetting' that traditional unlearning metrics (UA, RA, TA, MIA) fail to detect (Section 2.3.1, Table 2).

On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 under 10% random forgetting, conformal prediction analysis shows that 30-68% of samples the unlearned model misclassifies still have their ground-truth label retained inside the model's conformal prediction set (Table 3).

Using recommended confidence parameters of alpha=0.1 and a calibration set of 2,000 samples for CIFAR-10, Table 4 evaluates 9 unlearning methods (including RT, FT, RL, GA, Teacher, FF, SSD, NegGrad+, Salun) on Coverage, Set Size, and CR (Section 2.3.2, Table 4).

The MIA Conformal Ratio (MIACR) metric reveals that methods which score well under traditional membership-inference-attack (MIA) evaluation can perform poorly under MIACR, indicating traditional MIA is an unreliable proxy for forgetting quality (Table 6).

The proposed CPU framework, which augments the training objective with a conformal-enhanced (non-conformity score based) loss term combined via L_total = L_original + lambda*L_unlearn, improves unlearning accuracy (UA) by an average of 3.93% on CIFAR-10 and 9.23% on Tiny ImageNet while degrading test accuracy (TA) by only 1.0% and 0.57% respectively (Section 3.2, Table 7).

jk66MtkUS1.text: Theorem 6 proves that any n-dimensional hybrid system can be embedded into an m-dimensional Euclidean space equipped with a continuous vector field whenever m > 2n, satisfying position compatibility (C-1), velocity compatibility (C-2) at resets, and inducing an embedding of the quotient manifold (C-3) (Theorem 6).

The CHyLL++ latent Neural ODE framework combines five loss terms (state reconstruction L_x, latent consistency L_u, gluing loss L_g, velocity compatibility L_v, and a covariance loss L_c preventing latent collapse) to recover hybrid system flows from time series data (Section 6).

On the 3D Bouncing Ball system, the proposed method achieves an MSE of 0.162 +/- 0.015 while the prior CHyLL baseline collapses entirely, and on the Three-Link Walker the proposed method attains 0.0952 +/- 0.004 MSE versus 0.234 +/- 0.014 for CHyLL (Table 1).

Ablation studies show the latent consistency loss L_u is essential (its removal severely degrades performance across all tested systems), whereas the velocity compatibility loss L_v provides no improvement and sometimes hurts performance, suggesting it is implicitly enforced by Lipschitz-constrained networks (Table 3).

Dimension-scaling experiments show reconstruction performance improves as latent dimension m increases past 2n, though m=2n is often already sufficient except for topologically complex systems like the Klein Bottle, which benefit from m > 2n+2 (Table 4).

XZRyCQbBZe.text: DLO-Lab's differentiable simulator models extensibility (via toggling stretching energy versus geometric inextensibility constraints), elasticity (bending and twisting energies from Discrete Elastic Rods theory), and plasticity (bending plasticity via yield thresholds and creep rates), plus two-way coupling with rigid bodies via signed distance fields and soft bodies via the Material Point Method (Section 3).

The benchmark defines 10 manipulation tasks (8 fixed-horizon: Coiling, Gathering, Lifting, Separation, Slingshot, Unknotting, Wiring-post, Wrapping; 2 long-horizon: Letter Art, Wiring-ring) using DLOs with 12-60 vertices simulated for 800-2,000 frames at 1ms timesteps (Section 4, Table 3, Figure 2).
Table 2 compares six algorithms (PPO, SAC, SHAC, SAPO, GD, CMA-ES) across the 8 fixed-horizon tasks to benchmark manipulation performance (Table 2).

Closed-loop sim-to-real transfer of a PPO policy trained on the Wiring-ring task, using HSV-based perception with simulated sensor noise, achieves 7 out of 12 successful completions (about 58%) on a physical xArm robot (Section 5, Figure 8).

Open-loop sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated via zero-shot deployment on a Marvin M6 robot (Gathering task) and an xArm robot (Wiring-post task), with system identification calibrating rope material parameters through differentiable optimization of projection error (Section 5, Figure 6).

wLE7pnypx2.text: CSteer (Contextual Latent Steering) is a training-free method that steers internal latent representations of general-purpose large multimodal models (LMMs) at inference time to enable referring to multiple spatial regions simultaneously, without fine-tuning or architectural changes (Section 3, Figure 2).

CSteer is evaluated on referring expression benchmarks including RefCOCO/RefCOCO+ variants and multi-region referring evaluation sets, and is compared against referring-specialized LMMs such as SHIKRA, Ferret, OSPREY, ViP-LLaVA, GLAMM, PixelRefer, GAR, and DAM (Section 4).

General-purpose LMMs augmented with CSteer outperform referring-specialized LMMs on most of the evaluated multi-region referring benchmarks, according to the comparative accuracy tables in the experiments section (Section 4, Table 1).

Ablation studies in the experiments section validate the individual design choices of the contextual steering mechanism, showing each component contributes to the multi-region referring performance (Section 4).

CSteer establishes a new state-of-the-art for region-level perception under multiple simultaneous visual prompts, as illustrated qualitatively in Figure 1 and quantitatively in the comparative results tables (Section 4, Figure 1).

cVO0eX8vLQ.text: GeoPT's Lifting Operation augments static geometry with synthetic velocity fields sampled uniformly from a bounded ball and evolves synthetic particle trajectories via dx_t/dt = v * 1_G(x_t), producing physics-free self-supervision for pre-training (Section 4).

GeoPT is pre-trained on over one million samples derived from 13,463 ShapeNet geometries, each paired with 100 synthetic dynamic trajectories, and this supervision generation is about 10^7 times faster than industrial-scale CFD simulation (Section 4, Section 5).

GeoPT reduces labeled-data requirements by 20% on DrivAerML and by 60% on DTC Hull, with more moderate gains on NASA-CRM, and yields roughly 2x faster convergence overall across the industrial aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, and crash-simulation benchmarks (Section 5).

GeoPT pre-training extends beyond fluid mechanics to solid mechanics (Car-Crash simulation, ~1M-node meshes conditioned on impact angle) and to a held-out radiosity light-transport task not seen during pre-training, achieving an MAE of 9.0e-2 versus 9.7e-2 for a from-scratch model (Section 5).

Scaling experiments show that increasing the Transolver backbone from 8 to 32 layers yields consistent improvement when using GeoPT pre-training, indicating the pre-training regularizes the hypothesis space and mitigates overfitting in data-limited regimes (Figure 6).

L5JTAPUdbQ.text: Theorem 2 proves diffusion models require O~(ε^-(k∨2)) samples to achieve ε-accuracy in 1-Wasserstein distance, where k is the intrinsic (subspace) dimension rather than the ambient dimension d (Section 3.2, Theorem 2).
Theorem 1 bounds the score estimation L2 error in terms of the intrinsic dimension k, avoiding the exponential dependence on ambient dimension d found in prior analyses (Section 3.2, Theorem 1).

The analysis assumes the target distribution's support lies in a union of M low-dimensional linear subspaces with zero probability mass on their intersections, and requires only subgaussian tails within each subspace (Section 2.2, Assumption 1).
The results dispense with smoothness (e.g., Hölder continuity), log-concavity, uniform density bounds, and density lower-bound assumptions required by prior sample-complexity analyses (Section 2.2).
Prior work requiring β-Hölder smooth densities achieves only ε^-(d+2β)/β sample complexity, exhibiting a curse of dimensionality that the paper's bound avoids (Section 1, Equation 1).

BzxF9ewad6.text: CLEAR uses a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation to differentiably search over diffusion-model layer indices, treating the erasure depth as a learnable variable rather than a fixed hyperparameter (Section on 'Where to Erase').

CLEAR uses Sparse Autoencoders to decompose layer activations into semantically coherent features and applies specificity masks to isolate target-concept directions before intervention (Section on 'How to Erase').

On Wan2.2-5B object-concept erasure, CLEAR reduces the average generative rate from 61.8% to 12.8%, and for the French horn concept specifically from 70.4% to 7.8%, versus 26.8% for T2VUnlearning (Table 1a).
For nudity erasure on Wan2.2-5B, CLEAR reduces the generative rate from 67.3% to 11.1%, outperforming T2VUnlearning (18.6%) (Section on Sensitivity Concepts, Table 2).
An ablation removing the separability-aware loss ℒ_con increases the generative rate for the parachute concept from CLEAR's 18.4% to 27.0%, confirming the loss term is necessary (Table 5).

CLEAR requires a single ~2-hour training run on one H100 GPU, versus 24× the cost for brute-force per-layer search, and is 1.4× more inference-efficient than the VideoEraser baseline (Computational Efficiency section).

FNDkXA0OUJ.text: ExVerus applies counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), extracting counterexamples from failed Verus verification attempts and using an LLM to reason about them for proof repair (Section 3.1).
The counterexample-reasoning mechanism guides the LLM to generalize concrete counterexamples into inductive invariants across iterative CEGIS refinement loops (Section 3.2).
ExVerus is evaluated against AutoVerus, AlphaVerus, and RAG-Verus baselines on Verus benchmark suites (Section 4).
Comprehensive benchmark results, including success-rate and token-efficiency comparisons against AutoVerus, are reported (Table 4, Table 5).
Extended results and ablation studies supporting the token-efficiency and robustness claims are provided in the appendices (Appendices E-I).

efbZ2Qe2D8.text: MindZero trains via self-supervised reinforcement learning, rewarding mental-state hypotheses that maximize the likelihood of observed actions, formalized as maximizing an Evidence Lower Bound with no mental-state annotations (Section on Core Methodology).
On GridWorld question-answering, MindZero achieves a 2.1-2.5x accuracy gain over base models (Figure 4).
In the Household proactive-assistance domain, MindZero with Qwen3-4B achieves a 19.1% task speedup, compared to 17.7% for the Gemini-3-Flash baseline (Table 1).

An ablation on the Household domain shows removing the mental-state prior reduces speedup from 19.1% to 17.0%, removing multiple hypotheses reduces it to 10.3%, and removing the entropy bonus reduces it to 5.2% (Table 2).

A 12-participant human study shows MindZero achieves a 19.7% speedup (SE 6.3%), statistically equivalent to Gemini-3-Flash's 23.4%, despite using a smaller open-weight backbone (Human Study Validation section).

DScXVaBXFy.text: Transolver-3 introduces Geometry Slice Tiling, partitioning the N x M slice weight matrix computation into T tiles to reduce peak memory from O(NM) to O(N_tM) (methodology section on Geometry Slice Tiling).

Transolver-3 is trained via Geometry Amortized Training on random subsets of 10^5-10^6 cells sampled from full industrial meshes, rather than on the full mesh resolution (methodology section on Geometry Amortized Training).
On the DrivAerML automotive benchmark (up to ~160 million cells), Transolver-3 achieves 3.71% relative L2 surface-pressure error versus 4.12% for Transolver++ (Table 4).
On the NASA-CRM aircraft benchmark (~400K cells), Transolver-3 achieves 8.71% relative L2 surface-pressure error versus 9.51% for Transolver++ (Table 4).

Transolver-3 predicts drag and lift coefficients with R² of 0.963 and 0.975 respectively, and provides a 1.9x single-GPU memory-capacity improvement plus ~60% inference-latency reduction over Transolver++ (Figure 5; Memory and Speed Improvements section).

WIO01EdUXo.text: HFM achieves 64.1% accuracy in the 1-shot setting and 79.8% in the 16-shot setting, outperforming the FMA baseline by 3.5% and 2.1% respectively, averaged across 11 few-shot adaptation benchmarks (Table 1).

The path-decoupled flow objective combines a step-wise consistency loss and an inter-class decoupling loss (Equations 7 and 8) to confine class trajectories to isolated geodesic corridors in hyperbolic space (Section 3.3).

In the ablation study, adding Centripetal Hyperbolic Anchoring alone yields +1.8%, adding the path-decoupled objective yields a further +2.0%, and adding diameter-based stopping yields +0.5% in the 16-shot setting (Table 2).
HFM is model-agnostic: it improves multiple parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (CoOp, CoCoOp, CLIP-Adapter) by 8.2-8.7% over their respective baselines (Table 3).
HFM yields consistent gains of 1.3-4.3% when paired with different CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14), demonstrating scalability across model capacities (Table 4).

Diameter-based stopping is introduced at inference time to adaptively terminate the flow using a semantic-diameter criterion, preventing over-transportation of features into the crowded origin region (Section 3.4).

mYIhm3VO5y.text: Video-o3 (SFT+RL) achieves 72.1% accuracy on MLVU and 46.5% on Video-Holmes, outperforming the prior iterative-reasoning method LOVE-R1, which scores 67.4% on MLVU (Table 1).

Task-Decoupled Attention Masking (TDAM), presented in Section 3.2 and Figure 4, disentangles clue localization from answer reasoning by enforcing strict visibility constraints; removing it costs 1.1% on LVBench (Table 3).

The Verifiable Trajectory-Guided Reward (VTGR), detailed in Section 3.3, combines answer correctness, format validity, and an IoU-based hybrid clue score with a turn-decay penalty; the full reward yields a 1.4% gain on LVBench over ablated variants (Table 4).
Video-o3 is trained in part on Seeker-173K, a newly constructed dataset of approximately 173k trajectories designed to instill adaptive agentic clue-seeking behavior (Section 4).

Video-o3 is evaluated against single-turn baselines (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, LLaVA-Video-7B), decoupled iterative-reasoning methods (LOVE-R1, Video-RTS, Video-MTR), and native tool-invocation methods (Conan, LongVT, Video-Zoomer), outperforming all of them on long-video multi-hop reasoning (Table 1).

BkZ40FNKlL.text: VACSR models cross-modal similarity in a latent space using a variational adapter with Gaussian mixture modeling over a Hadamard-product similarity vector (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

On domain generalization to ImageNet variants (V2, Sketch, A, R), VACSR attains 74.3% accuracy on ImageNet and a 61.6% average across the out-of-distribution variants, the best among compared prompt- and adapter-based methods (Table 4).
On base-to-novel generalization averaged across 11 datasets, VACSR reaches 85.74% accuracy on base classes and an 80.37% harmonic mean score (Table 5).
The distributional optimization loss L_sigma (Section 3.2) assigns lower predicted uncertainty to positive and hard-negative pairs and higher uncertainty to false-negative pairs.
Uncertainty estimates from the variational adapter show a strong negative correlation with R@1 retrieval accuracy, with correlation coefficients of -0.931 and -0.903 (Figure 3).

An ablation removing the Gaussian mixture prior causes the largest performance drop among tested components, indicating that modeling multi-modal similarity distribution complexity is the key driver of VACSR's gains (Table 6).

goPaAYr1J3.text: MMM-PPI builds protein embeddings bottom-up through three stages: micro-scale residue encoding via heterogeneous graph neural networks, meso-scale motif construction using the FIMO algorithm, and macro-scale protein encoding via a context-aware co-attention mechanism (Sections 3.1.1-3.1.3).

On multi-label PPI prediction across STRING, SHS27k, and SHS148k under random, DFS, and BFS partitions, MMM-PPI achieves the highest Micro-F1 scores, with the largest margins on the harder DFS/BFS partitions (Table 2).
MMM-PPI is trained in two stages: the multimodal hierarchical encoder is pre-trained first, then frozen while a downstream GNN is trained for PPI prediction (Section 3.2).

MMM-PPI generalizes better than baselines to unseen proteins, particularly on the ES and NS edge subsets, which the authors attribute to the compositional (motif-based) nature of protein representations (Table 3).
Motifs receiving high attention weights overlap with UniProt-annotated functional regions at a 41.89% hit rate, compared to a 21.58% random baseline (Table 9).

bBylXHoUTl.text: The linearized SD3.5-T5 model reaches a DPG-Bench Global score of 91.51 versus 85.04 for the original SD3.5-Medium baseline, after only 3,000 fine-tuning steps (~1 hour on 4xH20 GPUs) (Table 7, Section 5.3).
SD3.5-T5 attains a comparable GenEval Overall score of 0.69 versus 0.66 for the softmax-attention baseline (Table 7).
SD3.5-T5 achieves 1.32x inference speedup at 1K resolution (19s vs 25s) and 1.47x speedup at 2K resolution (157s vs 231s) relative to the original softmax model (Table 7, Section 5.3).

Model Structure Alignment (Section 4.1) shows that softmax attention behaves like a two-layer dynamic MLP with nonlinearity, and Test-Time Training layers are chosen because their two-layer structure matches this expressiveness, unlike standard linear attention.

Representation Shift-Invariance Alignment (Section 4.2) finds pretrained attention keys exhibit a shift ratio of about 0.5 versus 0.07 for randomly initialized keys, motivating an Instance Normalization centering step to align TTT with pretrained softmax representations.
Representation Locality Alignment (Section 4.3) introduces depthwise convolutions on queries and keys (DWCQK) to compensate for the weak local inductive bias of TTT relative to softmax attention.

MWEh9IPz8N.text: NIAF reformulates action prediction as continuous-time function regression, using the MLLM as a hypernetwork that predicts parameters for a SIREN-based trajectory generator A(τ)=Φ(τ;θ) (Section 3).
On CALVIN ABC→D, NIAF achieves an average success length of 4.47, compared to 4.42 for the BEAST baseline (Section 4, Table results).
On LIBERO, NIAF reaches an average success rate of 97.9% versus 92.5% for BEAST, including 100% on LIBERO-Object and 95.5% on LIBERO-Long (Section 4).
Grouped Hyper-Modulation projects semantic latents into frequency (γ) and phase (β) modulation coefficients to condition the SIREN trajectory generator (Section 3).
Training uses physics-informed supervision combining position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk losses via analytical differentiation (Equations 11-14).
Real-world robot experiments show 90% success on item placement and 80% on cup stacking, with smoother non-zero velocity profiles than discrete baselines enabling stable impedance control (Figure 5).

pCaeMsqpCa.text: OrthoMerge performs model merging on the Riemannian manifold of the orthogonal group rather than in Euclidean space, arguing that linear weight averaging destroys geometric properties such as hyperspherical energy (Section on method motivation).

For OFT-trained models, OrthoMerge maps orthogonal transformations to the Lie algebra so(d), applies magnitude-corrected averaging to avoid adaptation attenuation, and uses a Cayley transform to project the result back onto the orthogonal group (Section 3).

An Orthogonal-Residual Decoupling strategy extracts implicit orthogonal components from non-OFT finetuned models via an orthogonal Procrustes problem, merging the orthogonal parts on the manifold while handling residual components separately (Section 3).
On Llama-3.1-8B, OrthoMerge achieves 46.25% average task performance versus 44.71% for the baseline merging method (Section 4, experimental results).
OrthoMerge extends to vision-language models, showing modality-agnostic effectiveness and improved out-of-domain generalization compared to standard merging baselines (Section 4).

1XUCkpEknR.text: ArenaRL replaces pointwise scalar reward scoring with intra-group tournament-based relative ranking to address 'discriminative collapse,' where scores for high-quality trajectories compress into a narrow range with low signal-to-noise ratio (Section on motivation).

Among five tournament topologies evaluated, seeded single-elimination is selected as optimal, achieving O(N) complexity versus O(N^2) for exhaustive round-robin comparison while retaining near-round-robin ranking accuracy (Section on tournament design).

The method introduces a process-aware pairwise evaluation mechanism that judges chain-of-thought coherence, tool invocation precision, and outcome reliability rather than only final answers (Section 3).
On the newly introduced Open-Travel benchmark (250 test samples across five subtasks), ArenaRL achieves a 41.8% average win rate versus 16.4% for a GRPO baseline (Section on experiments).

On the newly introduced Open-DeepResearch benchmark (100 samples), ArenaRL reaches a 64.3% win rate with a 99% valid generation rate, compared to 32% valid generation for SFT alone (Section on experiments).
Human-LLM judge agreement reaches 73.9%, used to validate that ArenaRL's gains generalize beyond the specific judge model's preferences (Section on human evaluation).

8HeUwrVLIu.text: VisionPulse performs training-free, step-wise visual token pruning during multimodal reasoning, adapting the retained token subset dynamically at each decoding step rather than pruning once at prefill (Section 3).
At 5% visual token retention, VisionPulse maintains near-100% of original task performance while shortening reasoning traces by 11.2% (Section 4).
At 10% visual token retention, generation length is reduced by 12.3% with negligible accuracy loss (Section 4).
A lightweight visual attention mass signal M_vis^t is computed at each decoding step and correlates with effectively activated visual tokens with Pearson r between 0.82 and 0.95 (Section 3).

VisionPulse is evaluated across seven benchmarks (CharXiv, InfoVQA, ChartQA, MMStar, RealWorldQA, MMVet, MIA-Bench) and multiple LMM backbones, consistently outperforming static pruning baselines including VisionZip, FastV, and LOOK-M (Section 4).

0wxnefBSTB.text: Inverse Asymmetric Tuning (IAT) inverts LoRA factor personalization by module: in encoders it localizes the input-projection factor A (absorbing covariate/appearance shift) while aggregating the output factor B globally, and in decoders it aggregates A globally while localizing B (absorbing concept/supervision shift) (Section 3).
Proposition 1 proves that minimizing reconstruction error under covariate shift requires localizing the input-side LoRA factor, motivating the encoder/decoder asymmetric split (Proposition 1).

A Subspace Orthogonality Regularizer (SOR) imposes a soft geometric constraint forcing shared (global) and local LoRA subspaces to remain orthogonal, mitigating site-specific update leakage without added communication cost (Section 3).
Theorem 3.1 establishes an O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate to a stationary point under L-smoothness and bounded-gradient assumptions with non-degenerate LoRA factors (Theorem 3.1).

On histology nuclei segmentation, IAT achieves 81.40% average Dice score, a 1.31% improvement over the second-best baseline, using 0.39M trainable parameters and 0.55M per-round communication versus 0.78M for standard approaches (Section 4).
On fundus photography segmentation, IAT achieves 84.52% average Dice score, including a 27% improvement over FedIT on the Drishti-GS1 site (Section 4).

bZjSinGaUo.text: DreamID-Omni's Symmetric Conditional DiT architecture unifies reference-based audio-video generation, video editing, and audio-driven animation within a single model (Section 3.2.1).

Synchronized RoPE (Syn-RoPE) achieves identity-timbre binding by assigning distinct temporal segments to different identities; removing it drops timbre similarity (T-Sim.) to 0.211 (Section 3.2.2, Table 5).

On the R2AV task, DreamID-Omni attains identity similarity of 0.674 (single-person) and 0.603 (multi-person), with speaker confusion of only 0.080 versus 0.340-0.380 for Wan2.6 and cascaded pipeline baselines (Table 2).
On the RV2AV task, DreamID-Omni achieves a ViCLIP score of 16.618 versus 14.576 for HunyuanCustom, with identity similarity of 0.623 (Table 3).
Removing Structured Captions (semantic-level disentanglement using anchor tokens like <sub1>) roughly triples speaker confusion, from 0.08 to 0.26 (Table 5-6).
Human evaluation by 30 professional video creators rated outputs across seven dimensions on the IDBench-Omni benchmark of 200 test instances (Section 4.1, Table 7).

G29kBVeIZt.text: HyPER's online expand-reduce controller re-evaluates confidence, consensus, and diversity signals every T=64 decoding steps to choose among four actions: None, SingleToken, MultiToken, and Branch (Section 3.1).
On AIME25 with Qwen3 models, HyPER reaches 95.3% accuracy using only 0.71x the token budget of DeepConf, which achieves 90.7% (Table 2).
On HMMT25, HyPER achieves 78.7% accuracy versus 74.0% for DeepConf while using 0.77x the tokens (Table 2).
On light-reasoning models (OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite), HyPER improves GSM8K/Math500 accuracy by 2-5 points, e.g. 46.7% vs 43.7% on Math500 for OLMoE (Table 2).

Across four MoE models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking, OLMoE-1B-7B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat) and diverse benchmarks, HyPER improves accuracy by 8-10 percentage points on average while cutting token consumption by 25-40% (Abstract, Table 2).

The length- and confidence-aware voting rule combines normalized path length and confidence with fixed weights lambda_len=0.6 and lambda_conf=0.4 to address the existence-selection gap (Section 3.3, Appendix F.1).

3uC9teMlUt.text: Two independently discovered IOI circuits (sheaves) both achieve 100% task accuracy while sharing only 4.1% edge overlap by Intersection-over-Union (Table 1).
Across 20 discovered sheaves for the same task, pairwise mutual intersection falls below 1% despite each sheaf retaining strong task performance (Table 3).
An ultra-sparse three-edge sheaf still achieves 86.7% IOI accuracy, yet no single edge in it is indispensable once the task is decomposed (Section 4, Table 6-7).
The low-overlap, high-performance circuit phenomenon persists across four discovery methods: DiscoGP, ACDC, EAP, and Edge Pruning (Section 3.3).

The Distributive Dense Circuit Hypothesis is formally proven in Theorem A.4, showing multiple low-overlap faithful circuits arise naturally from high-dimensional superposition under mild assumptions (Section 5, Appendix A, Theorem A.4).
Overlap-Aware Sheaf Repulsion (OASR) augments circuit/sheaf discovery objectives with an explicit penalty on structural overlap between discovered solutions (Section 3.1).

zNVyFEuP1n.text: The LangPrecip-160K dataset comprises about 160,000 radar-text annotated event sequences, combining 100,000 events from the Swedish SWish dataset and 60,000 from the MRMS dataset, each with 20 radar frames spanning 100 minutes at 5-minute intervals (Section 3.1).
Roughly 30,000 of the LangPrecip-160K events are manually annotated, with the remainder auto-annotated using the QWEN-3 vision-language model (Section 3.1).
At 80-minute lead time on the Swedish dataset, LangPrecip achieves a heavy-rainfall (>=6.3 mm/h) critical success index of 0.074 versus 0.046 for the DTCA baseline, a gain exceeding 60% (Table 1).
At 80-minute lead time on the MRMS dataset, LangPrecip achieves a heavy-rainfall (>=8 mm/h) CSI of 0.031 versus 0.026 for DTCA (Table 2).
LangPrecip is benchmarked against nine baselines including PySteps, DGMR, TRDM-SSR/LSR, DiffCast, SSLDM-ISI, AlphaPre, DTCA, RainNet, and SSRF-Net (Section 4).
An ablation on text scheduling and temporal modeling quantifies each component's contribution to motion consistency and nowcasting accuracy (Section 5.1-5.2).

AvBgmOGsdQ.text: On OSWorld, SEAgent's specialist-to-generalist agent reaches a 34.5% overall success rate, versus 11.3% for the UI-TARS-7B-DPO baseline, a 23.2 percentage point improvement (Table 2).

The generalist model trained via specialist-to-generalist strategy (34.5%) outperforms both the pure specialist RL variant (32.2%) and the pure generalist RL variant (30.6%) on OSWorld (Section 3.3, Table 2).
SEAgent's World State Model reward model achieves 71.6% precision on AgentRewardBench using full episode screenshots, approaching GPT-4o's 72.1% precision (Table 1).
SEAgent is evaluated on ScienceBoard across scientific applications including Celestia, GrassGIS, KAlgebra, and ChamerX, in addition to OSWorld and AndroidWorld (Section 4.1, Appendix D).
OSWorld evaluation spans five professional applications: VSCode, GIMP, LibreOffice Impress, VLC, and Writer (Section 4.1).

80gMhZMWZy.text: Bootstrap Your Generator (ByG) trains flow matching editing models without paired data by using EMA-based bootstrapping to generate noisy input targets, an instruction-following loss from a frozen T2I base model, and cycle-consistency source preservation via gradient routing (Section 4.1-4.3).
On video editing, ByG achieves a 75.3%±2.2% user preference win rate against the supervised baseline Ditto (Table 1).
On the long-tail style editing benchmark spanning 6 styles, ByG outperforms the supervised FLUX-Kontext baseline in semantic consistency, 7.67 vs 6.87 (Table 2).
On the GEdit-Bench motion-change category, ByG scores 6.88 vs FLUX-Kontext's 4.53 (Table 3).
Ablations show removing gradient routing changes edit success to 8.917 from a baseline of 8.317, and removing the cycle loss drops source preservation to 7.233 from 7.617 (Table 4).

AXtUl2KiQU.text: UGround unifies visual grounding across referring expression segmentation, reasoning segmentation, single-target and multi-target, and false-premise queries via Policy-Prompted Masking, comprising Stochastic Skip Connection (SSC) and Mask-as-Prompt (MasP) (Section 4).
On the ReasonSeg validation set, UGround-7B attains 72.1% cIoU versus RSVP-GPT's 63.1%, a 9.0-point improvement (Table 3).
On gRefCOCO validation, UGround reaches 65.56% cIoU and 74.53% N-acc, versus GSVA's 63.29% cIoU and 62.43% N-acc, a 12.1-point N-acc gain (Table 5).
Ablating the PPM dynamic layer selection (SSC) component adds +5.02% cIoU relative to a static-layer variant (Table 6).
Using a Gaussian BCE+DICE reward instead of hard-label constraints improves cIoU by 3.52 points, and using combined BCE+DICE reward yields 72.07% cIoU vs 69.53% for BCE-only (Tables 7-8).

TDXx4EKHZ1.text: The framework learns NMR chemical shifts from millions of literature-extracted, atom-assignment-free spectra by formulating chemical shift prediction as a permutation-invariant set supervision problem (Section 3).

Under mild loss-function conditions, the optimal bipartite matching between predicted and observed chemical shift sets reduces to a sorting-based loss, avoiding Hungarian-algorithm matching overhead (Section 3.2-3.3).
On NMRShiftDB2, adding semi-supervised training to NMRNet reduces 13C MAE by 19.6% and RMSE by 10.5% (Table 2).
On the larger literature-derived ShiftDB-Lit test set, the semi-supervised model improves 1H MAE by 59.9% and 13C MAE by 59.8% over the supervised-only baseline (Table 2).

Per-solvent analysis captures systematic solvent effects across common NMR solvents (Table 3), and ablations show weak supervision alone without labeled-data anchoring causes model collapse (Table 5).

HgRxoHLIwb.text: RED (Reasoning-preserved Efficient Distillation) uses activation-aware initialization to mitigate effective-rank (eRank) collapse and token indistinguishability caused by width reduction during LLM distillation (Section 5).
Depth-reduction baselines suffer catastrophic reasoning collapse, with GSM8K accuracy dropping to between 0.04 and 0.14 (Table 1).
RED preserves an eRank of 263.28 versus 81.30 for random initialization at initialization time (Table 3).
At the 2B parameter scale, RED achieves a 0.28 average reasoning score versus 0.09 for the LRC baseline (Table 4).

At the 4B parameter scale, RED reaches 0.33 average reasoning score and 0.69 average general-capability score, and trains a 1.5B model in about 30 hours on 8 H800 GPUs with 10B tokens (Table 5, Section 6).

rdWE5ol3ps.text: Anchored Posterior Sampling (APS) is a training-free method for discrete diffusion posterior sampling combining Quantized Expectation, which applies gradient-like guidance by updating the full conditional probability table in discrete embedding space, with Anchored Remasking, an adaptive token-decoding schedule (Section 3.2.1-3.2.2).

Theorem 3.2 establishes a training-free bound for test-time APS that reuses pretrained denoisers without task-specific retraining, extending the training-based bound of Theorem 3.1 for DDPS (Section 3, Theorem 3.1-3.2).
On FFHQ 256x256 4x super-resolution, APS improves LPIPS by 31.36% over the discrete diffusion baseline G2D2 (Section 4).
On ImageNet 256x256, APS improves 4x super-resolution by 35.82% LPIPS and 10.94% PSNR, and Gaussian deblurring by 8.81% PSNR, over G2D2 (Section 4).

An APS-L variant demonstrates scalability to 1024x1024 high-resolution inverse problems, and ablations in Appendix B.3/Figure 6 isolate the separate contributions of quantized expectation and anchored remasking (Section 4, Appendix B.3, Figure 6).

OXJ7KqVOoT.text: AudioMosaic reaches 42.5 mAP on AS-20K, exceeding the previous SSLAM state-of-the-art of 40.9 mAP (Table 1).
On ESC-50, AudioMosaic achieves 97.5% accuracy versus 96.2% for the SSLAM baseline (Table 1).
In linear probing, AudioMosaic reaches 29.4 mAP on AS-20K compared to 15.0 mAP for SSLAM (Table 2).
On the EnvSDD deepfake-audio benchmark, AudioMosaic attains a 1.41% average equal error rate versus 5.81% for BEATs (Table 3).
When integrated with LLaMA-7B in the LTU framework, AudioMosaic reaches 21.0 mAP on AudioSet-based audio-language tasks (Table 4).
AudioMosaic uses independent structured time-frequency masking of spectrogram patches to construct complementary positive pairs for contrastive pretraining (Section 3).

AwC77yHpP6.text: The VBVR dataset comprises 200 curated reasoning tasks (150 public, 50 reserved for a leaderboard) and 1,007,500 video clips, roughly 1,000x more clips than the 12.8K combined samples in existing alternatives (Section 3.2, Table 1).
The training/test split contains 1,000,000 training samples and 7,500 test samples across the five cognitive pillars: Abstraction, Knowledge, Perception, Spatiality, and Transformation (Section 3.1).
Table 3 benchmarks 8 models on VBVR, and Figure 6 presents qualitative evidence of emergent reasoning capabilities in models trained on the dataset (Table 3, Figure 6).

Models trained on VBVR show concurrent improvements on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks, but a persistent roughly 15% ID-OOD performance gap indicates that scaling data within a fixed task distribution alone is insufficient for systematic generalization (Section 4.1).

xyFVjBi9wC.text: HumanLM trains user simulators via reinforcement learning to align natural-language latent states across six dimensions—belief, goal, emotion, value, stance, and communication—rather than directly imitating ground-truth responses (Section on core method).

On the Humanual benchmark (six datasets spanning 26,000 users and 216,000 responses), HumanLM achieves an average response alignment score of 13.2 versus 10.4 for the best baseline, GRPO-think, a 16.3% relative improvement, ranging from 4.3% on Humanual-Chat to 36.0% on Humanual-Book (Table 1).

HumanLM is compared against Qwen3-8B (base), SFT, GRPO, GRPO-think, and UserLM baselines, and Figure 5 shows it achieves broader state-alignment score coverage during training than standard GRPO (Table 1, Figure 5).

In a human study with 111 participants comparing simulated responses to participants' own Reddit posts, HumanLM responses were rated most similar or nearly identical 68.6% of the time and rated quite natural or better 76.6% of the time, achieving the highest win rate at 41.4% (Figure 9).

WTT0FW3cFl.text: FUSE derives aleatoric uncertainty from a Gaussian Process latent variable model over frozen CLIP embeddings (Section 4.1) and epistemic uncertainty from a semantic response-diversity scatter matrix (Section 4.2), fusing the two via conjugate Bayesian inference into a closed-form scalar posterior uncertainty u* (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.9).

Theorem 4.4 shows the semantic evidence statistic satisfies the linear relation Ṽ = nu + log det Λ, and Theorem 4.5 establishes that this evidence follows a Gaussian likelihood Ṽ|u ~ N(a(n,d) + nu, v(n,d)) (Theorem 4.4, Theorem 4.5).
On VQAv2, FUSE achieves AUROC 0.883 and AURAC 0.940, compared against baselines UMPIRE, Semantic Entropy, EigenScore, and conformal prediction methods (Table 1).
On OKVQA and AdVQA respectively, FUSE achieves AUROC of 0.761 and 0.796 and expected calibration error (ECE) between 0.037 and 0.041 across the three VQA benchmarks (Table 1).

Experiments use 50 stochastic samples per query, 500-sample calibration sets, GP adapters with Q=10 latent dimensions and 250 inducing points, and a risk-control tolerance of r=0.2 for selective prediction (Section on experiments).

dDkl5ZcyTl.text: Section 2 unifies the exchange algorithm (Algorithm 1), PoissonMH (Algorithm 2), and TunaMH (Algorithm 3) as instances of one common auxiliary-variable procedure (Section 2).

The proposed meta-algorithm (Algorithm 4) introduces two auxiliary variables, ω1 guiding the proposal and ω2 enabling target-ratio estimation, and Proposition 2 proves it preserves the target distribution Π as stationary (Algorithm 4, Proposition 2).

Proposition 1 gives a reversibility condition on the auxiliary-variable estimator, R_{θ→θ'}(ω)π(θ|x)P_{θ→θ'}(ω) = π(θ'|x)P_{θ'→θ}(ω), that guarantees the resulting kernel targets the correct posterior (Proposition 1).

The framework yields two new algorithms: Locally Balanced PoissonMH (Algorithm 5), which uses gradient-informed locally balanced proposals with balancing functions such as Barker's g(t)=t/(1+t) or the MALA-type g(t)=sqrt(t), and TunaMH with an SGLD proposal (Algorithm 6), which uses independent minibatches for gradient estimation and acceptance-ratio evaluation (Algorithm 5, Algorithm 6).

The framework is designed to apply to both doubly-intractable distributions, where the likelihood f_θ(x)/Z(θ) has an intractable normalizing constant, and tall-data settings with millions to billions of observations, without needing to evaluate the full target density (Section 1).

OOyPj8hdiM.text: MedScope outperforms VideoR1-7B, VideoRFT-7B, and the medical baseline SurgVidLM on the SVU-31K benchmark, including 11.30 BLEU-4 and 4.56 CIDEr for fine-grained temporal reasoning and 18.90 BLEU-4 and 10.93 CIDEr for fine-grained perception reasoning (Section on SVU-31K Benchmark Performance).
On ClinVideo-Eval, MedScope reaches 81.92 R@0.3, 68.87 R@0.5, and 54.35 R@0.7 for OphVL temporal grounding, and 65.58 mIoU accuracy on OphVL grounded VQA (ClinVideo-Eval Results).

On the out-of-domain SurgVidLM setting, MedScope attains 55.60 R@0.3 and 40.10 R@0.5 for temporal grounding, demonstrating generalization beyond in-domain ophthalmic/surgical data (ClinVideo-Eval Results, Out-of-Domain).

Ablations show the SFT-only training stage reaches a 46.2% tool-use rate while SFT+GA-GRPO reinforcement learning raises tool-use rate to 63.8% and improves overall performance (Ablation Study Findings).

Removing the VCoT cold-start supervision (ClinVideo-VCoT-34K) drops fine-grained temporal reasoning BLEU-4 from 11.30 to 7.95, and removing the evidence reward in GA-GRPO drops OphVL R@0.5 from 40.1 to 33.2 (Ablation Study Findings).

JUM3VsJ4GO.text: Proposition 3.4's rank-aware concentration bound yields 8x tighter concentration for GPT-2 XL (d=1600, d_h=64) and 28x tighter concentration for Llama-2-70B (d=8192, d_h=128) compared to rank-agnostic bounds (Table 2).
Proposition 3.2 establishes that max_i,j |S_ij| <= ||W^Q W^K^T||_2 * d/sqrt(d_h), a strictly tighter interaction bound than the naive ||W^Q||_2 ||W^K||_2 bound given in Corollary 3.3.

For pretrained checkpoint loading and transient scenarios such as checkpoint resumption and 100x learning-rate spikes, delayed scaling produces 100% overflow while the proposed geometry-aware scaling achieves 0 overflows (Table 4).
On Llama-2-13B MMLU evaluation, Auto-alpha calibration achieves 33.6% accuracy with 0 overflows, versus 33.0% accuracy and 68 overflows for delayed scaling (Table 5).

The geometry-aware scaling method incurs computational overhead of only +1.0% on GPT-2 XL and +4.3% on Llama-2-70B, and actually reduces cost by 5.3% on Mistral-7B due to the implicit GQA formulation (Proposition 4.1, Computational Overhead).

UM6ifyC63p.text: ImgCoT compresses chain-of-thought reasoning into 8 latent visual tokens versus roughly 150 tokens for full textual CoT while matching or exceeding Full-CoT accuracy (Table 1).
On Qwen2.5-1.5B, ImgCoT achieves 19.5% accuracy on MATH, 38.7% on GSM, 41.8% on GPQA, and 100% on ProsQA (Table 1).
On Llama3.2-3B, ImgCoT achieves 24.1% accuracy on MATH, 56.8% on GSM, 43.6% on GPQA, and 100% on ProsQA, outperforming Coconut, ICoT, CODI, and CoLaR baselines (Table 1).

Loose ImgCoT (L-ImgCoT), which retains critical textual reasoning steps alongside compressed visual tokens, achieves roughly 30% inference cost reduction while maintaining performance above Full-CoT (Section on L-ImgCoT).

An ablation replacing the visual reconstruction target with a textual reconstruction target ('w/ textual tokens') consistently underperforms the visual ImgCoT approach, confirming that spatial bias better captures reasoning structure than linguistic bias (Ablation Studies).
Out-of-domain generalization tests show ImgCoT's visual compression substantially outperforms text-based compression alternatives across mathematical reasoning benchmarks (Table 2).

Ec4qUT3UKG.text: GEM-FI achieves 93.75% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 versus 91.11% for the DAEDL baseline, and improves the Brier score from 14.27 to 6.81 (x100 scale) (Image Classification & Calibration, CIFAR-10 results).
GEM-FI achieves misclassification-detection AUPR of 99.94% versus 99.08% for DAEDL on CIFAR-10 (Image Classification & Calibration section).
For CIFAR-10 to SVHN far-OOD detection, GEM-FI reaches epistemic AUPR/AUROC of 92.59%/95.09%, versus 85.54%/89.30% for DAEDL (OOD Detection Performance, CIFAR-10 to SVHN).

For CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-100 near-OOD detection, GEM-FI achieves epistemic AUPR of 90.20% versus 88.19% for DAEDL, a smaller margin than the far-OOD SVHN case (OOD Detection Performance, CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-100).

Ablations (Table 3) show spectral normalization alone contributes +7.65 percentage points accuracy over baseline EDL, CORE gating adds a further +2.34 points, and Fisher-information regularization improves SVHN OOD AUPR from 89.68% to 91.27% when combined with EBM/UNC components (Table 3).

7sksHLUvhH.text: On the synthetic Synth-12 benchmark averaged across horizons H in {96,192,336,720}, DropoutTS improves the Informer backbone by 46.0% MSE / 24.5% MAE, with peak 48.2% MSE reduction at noise level sigma=0.3 (Synth-12 Benchmark results).

On real-world datasets, DropoutTS yields up to 68.0% MSE improvement on Electricity and 47.6% MSE improvement on ETTh2 when applied to the Informer backbone, and 13.8% MSE improvement on Weather with TimeMixer (Real-World Benchmarks, 7 datasets).

DropoutTS is evaluated against six baseline forecasters (Informer, Crossformer, PatchTST, TimesNet, iTransformer, TimeMixer) across ETTh1/h2, ETTm1/m2, Electricity, Weather, and ILI, using input length L=96 (L=24 for ILI) (Experimental Setup).
DropoutTS adds only 4 extra parameters and zero inference latency overhead, while providing a 1.12x-1.45x training speedup relative to baseline models (Key Findings, Negligible Overhead).

Combining DropoutTS with a Selective Learning data-centric strategy achieves a 21.2% improvement versus 19.6% for Selective Learning alone, indicating orthogonal compatibility (Key Findings, Orthogonal Compatibility).

56cQPBIg4R.text: CRAFT reduces DeepSeek-based model StrongReject scores from 0.632 to 0.172 and JailbreakBench scores from 0.690 to 0.065, yielding the reported 79.0% improvement in reasoning safety and 87.7% improvement in final-response safety over base models (Table 1).

CRAFT combines a Latent Contrastive Learning for Reasoning (LCLR) loss with a Reinforcement over Reasoning Latents (R²L) objective, the latter combining latent-semantic, textual-safety, and latent-textual consistency rewards into a single total reward (Section 4, Eq. 4.1-4.2).

On reasoning benchmarks (AIME24, MATH-500, LiveCodeBench, Minerva), CRAFT achieves a 4.7% average Pass@1 improvement over base models while substantially improving safety, showing the safety gains do not come at the cost of reasoning capability (Table 2).

Ablations on Qwen3-4B-Thinking show removing the consistency reward R_cons causes a 28.9% degradation, removing the latent-semantic reward R_ls causes a 27.1% degradation, and removing LCLR entirely causes a 34.1% degradation in safety performance (Table 3).

Theorem 5.1 proves that the latent-textual consistency reward eliminates superficially-aligned policies (safe text with unsafe latent reasoning) by ruling them out as local optima under GRPO convergence (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
Against advanced jailbreak attacks GPTFuzzer and AutoDAN, CRAFT delivers 72.1% reasoning-trace safety gains and 85.9% final-response safety gains relative to base models (Figure 4).

LTp4Q9aNJP.text: CaMB-Diff introduces Cascaded Monotonic Bernstein (CaMB) operators — Softmax-parameterized Bernstein polynomial cascades of degree N over K layers — to represent an unknown monotonic dynamic-range-compression forward operator with as few as 16 parameters (Section 3, Table 4).

On low-light image enhancement (LOLv1/LOLv2), CaMB-Diff achieves 20.14 dB PSNR on LOLv1 versus 19.57 dB for AGLLDiff and 17.18 dB for TAO, and reduces lightness-order-error (LOE) to 38.85 versus 299.93 (AGLLDiff) and 331.13 (TAO) (Table 1).
On low-field MRI enhancement using the 3T HCP dataset, CaMB-Diff reaches 26.43 dB PSNR on T1w and 25.39 dB on T2w, outperforming the TAO baseline's 23.61 dB and 24.18 dB respectively (Table 2).
On HDR reconstruction over 100 ImageNet validation images, CaMB-Diff attains PSNR 19.95, SSIM 0.7909, and FID 70.73, compared to TAO's PSNR 16.77, SSIM 0.6692, and FID 101.28 (Table 3).

CaMB-Diff integrates the CaMB forward-operator parameterization with a pre-trained diffusion prior via a plug-and-play half-quadratic-splitting framework to jointly estimate the unknown compression curve and reconstruct the underlying signal (Section 4).

lOR6zI5peb.text: Probabilistic Conflict Resolution (PCR) models per-parameter gradients from plasticity and stability objectives as Gaussian distributions and computes a Bayesian retention coefficient k = λ_pla/(λ_pla + λ_sta) to softly project conflicting gradient components (Section 4).

Section 3.3's layer-wise cosine-similarity analysis shows persistent negative cosine similarity (gradient conflict) between plasticity and stability gradients in the middle-to-deep MLP layers during standard GRPO training (Section 3.3).

On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, PCR improves average accuracy over baseline GRPO by 3.5 points (67.6 vs. baseline), including +4.2 on AIME 2024 (to 59.7), +3.9 on AIME 2025 (to 54.1), +2.9 on AMC 2023 (to 88.0), and +2.4 on MATH500 (to 89.8) (Table 1).

Theorem 5.1 proves PCR's soft projection achieves the global minimum of posterior expected risk under an MMSE criterion, guaranteeing lower error than both hard PCGrad-style projection and naive gradient summation (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).

PCR produces smoother training dynamics than GRPO, maintaining stable gradient norms rather than the pronounced oscillations seen in vanilla GRPO training, as shown in the gradient-norm trajectories (Figure 3).
PCR outperforms GRPO, GVPO, MRT, and GCPO baselines consistently across all evaluated reasoning benchmarks (Table 1).

lh0I4rB0I5.text: World-R1 fine-tunes text-to-video generators with Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning using a composite reward combining 3D-aware signals (from pre-trained 3D foundation models) and general video-quality signals (from vision-language models) (Section 3.2).

On 3D-consistency metrics, World-R1-Small improves PSNR from 17.40 dB (Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B baseline) to 27.63 dB and World-R1-Large improves to 27.67 dB, corresponding to the reported 10.23 dB and 7.91 dB PSNR gains, while also reducing LPIPS from 0.467 to 0.201/0.162 (Table 2).

World-R1 uses a periodic decoupled training strategy that alternates optimization to balance rigid geometric (3D) consistency against dynamic scene fluidity, evaluated using ~3,000 synthetic text prompts spanning a hierarchical scene taxonomy (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).

A human study with 25 participants over 30 complex prompts using a 2AFC protocol finds World-R1 preferred over baselines with an 86% overall win rate, 92% win rate on geometric consistency, and 76% on camera-control accuracy (Appendix C).

On the VBench general video-quality suite, World-R1-Small improves aesthetic quality from 62.43 to 65.74 and imaging quality from 66.51 to 67.53 relative to the Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B baseline, showing 3D-consistency gains do not degrade general video quality (Table 1).

On 121-frame long-video generalization, World-R1-Large achieves PSNR 26.32 versus 18.32 for Wan2.1-T2V-14B, demonstrating the 3D-consistency gains generalize beyond the training video length (Table F).

PesPQc7WMF.text: AOEPT is motivated by the identified Implicit Modality-Reduction (IMR) bottleneck, whereby existing prompt-tuning methods constrain multimodal transformer reasoning to a modality-reduced subspace that cuts off access to missing-modality information (Section 1).

AOEPT constructs Modal-Contextualized Prompts (MCPs) via attention-based, MLP-based, or initialization-based distillation of global modality priors, then instantiates them per-instance with a consistency regularization term (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

At a 70% missing rate on MM-IMDb, AOEPT reaches an average F1 of 53.22 versus 50.36 for MAPs, 51.15 for DCP, and 50.93 for MemPrompt, with gains holding at 90% missing rate (51.45 vs. 48.56 for MAPs) (Table 2).
On HateMemes (70% missing) and Food101 (70% missing), AOEPT improves average performance to 69.63 and 84.29 respectively, versus 68.11 and 83.56 for the SyP baseline (Table 2).

Ablation on MM-IMDb with 70% text missing shows removing the MCP component drops F1 from 51.50 to 48.93, and replacing the consistency regularization with a reconstruction objective drops it to 48.55, confirming both components are necessary (Table 3).

AOEPT introduces a Normalized Missing-modality Mutual Information (NM2I) diagnostic metric on which baseline methods score near zero while AOEPT shows clear improvement, empirically validating the existence of the IMR bottleneck (Section 4.7).

hZ0xrfUenD.text: OT-Bridge Editor formulates localized stenosis editing as a constrained entropic optimal transport (Schrödinger bridge) problem over a vessel-structure composite domain combining edge maps and segmentation masks (Section 3.2).
Geometric Generation-Path Guidance (GPG) enforces step-wise feasibility constraints via signed distance transforms throughout the generation trajectory rather than only at the endpoint (Section 3.3).
On the ARCADE benchmark, OT-Bridge Editor achieves 0.892±0.037 mIoU versus 0.837 for the SiameseDiff baseline, and 0.774±0.055 Dice score (Table 1).

Augmenting real training data with synthesized edited angiograms yields a 27.8% relative gain in stenosis detection (YOLOv8, mAP@0.5 rising from 0.525 real-only to 0.727±0.006) on ARCADE, and a 23.0% relative gain on a three-center multi-center dataset (Table 3, Table 4).
An ablation shows the composite edge+segmentation domain outperforms single-domain variants, reaching 0.892 mIoU versus 0.483 (edge-only) and 0.632 (segmentation-only) (Table 5).
Full path-level GPG guidance yields 0.812 boundary IoU compared to 0.682 for an endpoint-only guidance variant (Table 6).

hpElHQQXXF.text: DR2Seg decomposes reasoning segmentation into a two-stage rollout: Stage 1 generates a reasoning chain, an explicit object description, and a spatial answer, and Stage 2 re-predicts the segmentation using only the generated description without the original query (Section 3.3).

Two self-rewards are combined multiplicatively with the base reward (Equation 7): a description reward R_desc that checks whether stage-2 predictions from the description alone match ground truth, and a length-based reward R_len that penalizes verbose reasoning relative to a predefined length anchor (Section 3.3).
On the ReasonSeg benchmark, the 3B model variant achieves roughly 2x token reduction alongside a 3.8% gIoU improvement over baseline (Table 1).
On ReasonSeg few-shot evaluation, DR2Seg* attains 68.5% gIoU on the validation split and 66.1% gIoU on the test split (Table 1).
DR2Seg generalizes to referring segmentation, improving gIoU by 1.9% on RefCOCOg relative to baseline (Table 2).
The framework is shown to be effective across both Qwen2.5-VL 3B and 7B backbones and is compatible with both SAM2 and SAM3 segmentation models (Table 6-7).

DbzAsMRNhy.text: The Dilated Unmasking Scheduler (DUS) unmasks tokens in a deterministic, coarse-to-fine dilated pattern using non-adjacent token groups, requiring only R = ⌈log_a B⌉ denoising iterations for a block of B tokens under a first-order Markov assumption, with spacing parameter s_t = ⌊B/a^t⌋ (Equation 6).

DUS is evaluated as a training-free, predefined planner applied on top of existing masked diffusion denoisers (LLaDA-Base-8B, LLaDA-Instruct-8B, and Dream-Instruct-7B) without modifying the underlying denoiser (Table 1).
DUS improves accuracy over a confidence-based unmasking baseline by up to 27 percentage points across block sizes B in {8, 16, 32, 64} on GSM8K (Table 1).
Results are reported on GSM8K (generation length G=256), HumanEval (G=512), and MBPP (G=512), plotting accuracy versus inference speedup at varying block sizes (Figure 1, Figure 2).

DUS narrows the performance gap that traditional parallel unmasking strategies incur relative to fully sequential decoding, recovering most of the lost accuracy while keeping the same inference speedup (Figure 1).

vCHOBek0dv.text: GPS trains a lightweight generative prompt predictive model (PPM) with a shared latent difficulty context z_t on optimization history across prompts, using a variational ELBO objective to enable cross-prompt difficulty transfer to unseen prompts (Section 3.2, Equation 8).

Difficulty-Diversity Batch Selection combines an intermediate-difficulty utility term u(γ̂_t^τ) = -(γ̂_t^τ - 0.5)² with a history-anchored diversity term, solved via a greedy approximation for scalable prompt-batch selection (Section 3.3, Equations 13-14).

GPS achieves 1.4x-2.0x training-step speedup versus uniform sampling, and up to 69% lower rollout cost with 28%-47% reduced training time versus a Dynamic Sampling oracle baseline, at comparable final performance (Table 2, Figure 3).

On the DSR-7B setup, GPS reaches 93.2% on MATH500 (matching Dynamic Sampling) and 62.1% on Olympiad (versus 60.0% for Dynamic Sampling), with an average of 67.4% across math benchmarks versus 67.0% for Dynamic Sampling (Table 2).

At test time, GPS-guided Best-of-N computation allocation yields up to 3.2% relative accuracy improvement or up to 36.4% compute reduction without accuracy loss, generalizing to unseen benchmarks (Figure 4).

Ablations show removing the history-anchored diversity term or the latent difficulty context z substantially degrades performance, and GPS is shown compatible with both PPO and Reinforce++ (Figure 5a, Figure 5b).

4cSEtYtsHH.text: Veda reformulates tile selection for sparse video-diffusion attention as an explicit reconstruction problem, distilling full-attention tile scores via a lightweight head-specific MLP estimator trained with KL-divergence supervision on TripPool (average, max, min) statistics rather than simple mean pooling (Section 4.1).

Head-Aware Tiling assigns per-layer, per-head tiling configurations to match attention heterogeneity across spatial and temporal dimensions (Section 4.2), and a tile-skipping kernel using asynchronous Tensor Memory Access reaches about 80% of FlashAttention-3 throughput (Section 4.3).
On Waver-T2V-12B at 720P/241 frames, Veda achieves 5.1x end-to-end speedup and 10.5x self-attention speedup, reducing attention's share of runtime from 92% to 50% (Figure 8, Table 1).
On Wan2.1-T2V-14B at 720P/81 frames, Veda achieves 2.63x end-to-end speedup with 7.08x self-attention acceleration (Table 1).

Speedup gains grow with sequence length, maintaining 5.1x speedup at 245,760 tokens where dense attention cost grows quadratically, indicating favorable scaling with spatiotemporal resolution (Figure 8).

Human evaluation shows Veda achieves perceptual parity with full attention at 90% sparsity and outperforms the VSA baseline even at 95% sparsity, while an ablation confirms TripPool statistics outperform average pooling (0.912 vs. 0.965 loss) (Figure 7, Table 2).

VxTzkpoVlB.text: Metis achieves an 89.2% average Attack Success Rate on HarmBench across 10 target LLMs, surpassing the X-Teaming baseline (82.0%) by 7.2 points (Table 1, Section 4.2).

Metis attains 76.0% ASR on O1 and 78.0% ASR on GPT-5-chat, versus ActorBreaker's 14% on O1 and X-Teaming's 49% on GPT-5-chat, showing baselines degrade sharply on frontier models while Metis does not (Section 4.2, Table 1).

Ablating the Evaluator's metacognitive feedback drops ASR on Claude-3.7 from 86.0% to 46.0% (a 40-point loss), a larger degradation than removing Attacker metacognition (66.0%, -20.0%) or seed paradigms (60.0%, -26.0%), identifying the Evaluator as the primary performance bottleneck (Table 2, Section 4.3).

Pairing a strong Attacker (DeepSeek-R1) with a weak Evaluator (Qwen2.5-7B) collapses GPT-4o ASR from 93% to 30%, a 63-point drop, while swapping the Attacker with a fixed strong Evaluator (GPT-4o) leaves performance largely robust (Table 3, Section 4.3).
Metis reduces average token cost 8.2x versus the X-Teaming baseline, reaching up to 11.4x on Grok-3 (1,093 vs. 12,425 tokens) (Table 4, Section 4.5).

Against five deployed defenses on Llama-3-8B, ASR falls from an 88.0% undefended baseline to 79.0% under SmoothLLM, 65.0% under Llama Guard 3, and 40.0% under X-Guard, the strongest mitigation tested (Table 5, Section 4.6).

YI9wSqfz7W.text: Adaptive Batch Scaling (ABS) defines a Behavioral Divergence metric as the fraction of states where an agent's preferred discrete action differs between consecutive policy updates (using KL divergence as the continuous-control proxy), used to quantify non-stationarity during training (Section 4.1).

ABS schedules rollout/batch size inversely to Behavioral Divergence via a logarithmic interpolation, keeping batches small during early-training's high-divergence, high-plasticity phase and scaling them up as divergence falls in late training (Section 4.2, Section 3.2).
On the Atari-10 subset, ABS outperforms vanilla PQN, fixed small/large-batch baselines, and a Gradient Noise Scale (GNS)-based scheduler in IQM human-normalized score (Table 1, Section 5.1).

Scaling network size to PQN-L and PQN-XL architectures with fixed large batches degrades performance, whereas combining these larger networks with ABS's adaptive batch scaling yields the best results, supporting the claim that larger networks and larger batches only pay off together with adaptive control (Table 2, Section 5.4).

ABS generalizes beyond on-policy PQN: it improves the off-policy BTR algorithm across five Atari environments (Table 3) and improves PPO learning curves on MuJoCo continuous-control tasks (Figure 6, Section 5).

amDEBt8tmw.text: Event2Vec embeds raw DVS events (x, y, t, p) directly into vector space using a 2D scheme (i = p·H + y, j = p·W + x, v = [Embed_y(i), Embed_x(j)]) plus neighbor-semantics weighting, avoiding conversion to frames or voxel grids before a 2-layer, 256-feature, 16-head Transformer encoder (Section 3.1, Section 4.1).
On the ASL-DVS dataset (24 classes), Event2Vec+Transformer reaches 99.68% test accuracy while using a 4.13 MB model, versus 220.3 MB for a competing GNN+Transformer baseline (Table 1, Section 4.2).

Event2Vec trains at 2,185 samples/second and infers at 4,320 samples/second (0.23 ms/sample), roughly 72x faster than the prior GNN+Transformer method, while sampling only 255 events per sample (Table 1, Section 4.2).

Accuracy remains high under downsampled spatial resolution and reduced event counts, as shown by the naive event2vec resolution sweep and the 2D event2vec-with-neighbors variant (Figure 3a, Figure 3b, Section 4.2).
Ablations isolate the contribution of the 2D embedding formulation and the neighbor-semantics mechanism to accuracy over the course of training (Figure 2a, Figure 2b, Section 3.2).

KY5Q9V9F5C.text: FlashTrace's span-wise aggregation reduces multi-token attribution complexity from O(M·N·D) to O(N·(M+D)) — i.e., from quadratic to linear in sequence length — by exploiting the linearity of attention to precompute head, residual, and MLP contributions in a single pass (Section 4.2).
FlashTrace achieves a 130x speedup over the IFR baseline on 5k-token spans, completing attribution in under 20 seconds versus 38+ minutes for IFR (Section 5.1, Figure 4).

On the RULER benchmark, FlashTrace attains a Recovery Rate of 0.483 on needle-in-a-haystack versus 0.471 for IFR, with faithfulness maintained across context lengths up to 32k tokens (Table 1, Section 5.1).

On MATH, FlashTrace's RISE score (0.348) is close to but slightly below IFR (0.354) and AttnLRP (0.368), while on MorehopQA its MAS score (0.205) trails IFR (0.228) and AttnLRP (0.458), indicating faithfulness gains are not uniform across all reasoning tasks (Table 2, Section 5.1).

FlashTrace approximates exhaustive token-level rollout attribution while retaining a 93.6% reduction in compute, and generalizes across Qwen-3 8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B backbones (Table 3, Table 5, Section 5.2).

6FNTrLYLbu.text: OcclusionFormer introduces the SA-Z dataset of 1 million high-resolution images with 5.7 million instances, adding explicit Z-order occlusion annotations and amodal masks on top of SA-1B via SAM-3D, InstaOrder, and DescribeAnything (Table 1, Section 3.2).

OcclusionFormer applies NeRF-style volumetric rendering with per-instance predicted density to compute transmittance-based occlusion ordering, combined with instance decoupling (local, per-bounding-box feature processing) built on a Flux.1-dev backbone with LoRA fine-tuning (Section 3.3).
On the OverLayBench Complex subset, OcclusionFormer improves O-mIoU from 0.3189 to 0.3468 and Occlusion Order F1 from 0.6987 to 0.7797 versus the previous best method (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On the same Complex subset, OcclusionFormer reduces the Depth Order error metric from 0.1791 to 0.1602 relative to the prior best (Table 2, Section 4.2).

A component-wise ablation on the Complex subset and SA-Z Eval benchmark (extended in Appendix D, Table 4) shows both the volumetric-rendering occlusion module and the queried alignment loss contribute to the accuracy gains (Table 3, Section 4.3).
A 300-sample human study finds OcclusionFormer preferred over baselines on occlusion accuracy, layout alignment, local fidelity, and global alignment (Table 5, Appendix E).

U1yt3NN0mC.text: Standard predefined data augmentations in the contrastive learning framework are proven equivalent to a point estimate of positive-incentive (pi) noise (Section 3.4, Eq. 19).
Task entropy is defined via auxiliary Gaussian distributions to bridge the contrastive loss with information-theoretic principles (Section 3.3, Eq. 9).
The learned pi-noise generator (PiNDA) improves k-NN accuracy by about 5% and softmax regression accuracy by about 9% over a random-noise baseline on the Reuters dataset (Table II).
PiNDA yields consistent accuracy gains when plugged into SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, and SimSiam with ResNet18/ResNet50 backbones on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST, and STL-10 (Tables III and IV).
Visualizations of the learned pi-noise variance show the generator produces style-transfer-like augmentations that trace object outlines without supervision (Figures 1, 5, and 6).

The added computational cost of the pi-noise generator is modest: a DNN3 generator adds about 5s per epoch and 0.23GB memory on CIFAR-10, while a ResNet18 generator adds about 11s and 2.26GB memory (Table V).

XtIRCAEYoJ.text: Artemis unifies visual grounding, detection, counting, and geometric perception tasks within a single structured-reasoning framework optimized with GRPO, without task-specific architecture changes (Section 3, Figure 2).
Despite being trained only on natural-image grounding data, Artemis achieves 81.4% zero-shot accuracy on visual counting on Pixmo-Count without any counting-specific training (Section 4.2, Table 3).
Artemis attains 49.3% average zero-shot accuracy on the MATHGLANCE benchmark, demonstrating transfer from natural-image training to mathematical/geometric diagrams (Section 4.2, Table 4).
Artemis achieves 91.3% val@50 accuracy on RefCOCO visual grounding and 31.0 mAP / 48.0 AP50 on COCO2017 object detection (Table 1, Table 2).

An ablation on reasoning forms shows structured visual reasoning preserves competitive in-domain grounding accuracy while improving downstream perception benchmarks relative to unstructured reasoning baselines (Section 4.3, Table 7).

RmZc1J19N8.text: Memory processing accounts for 22-81% of end-to-end latency for sparse-attention inference on 1M-token sequences (Section 3.2, Figure 3).
RAG memory processing accounts for 40-61% of latency when retrieving over a 20-million-document corpus (Section 3.2, Figure 4).
Compressed contextual memory methods such as MemAgent spend up to 97% of latency in the Prepare Memory phase (Section 3.2).

The GPU-FPGA system on AMD MI210+Alveo U55C achieves 1.04-1.49x end-to-end speedup for sparse attention (up to 5.6x kernel-level, Figure 9), 5.16-7.65x memory-processing speedup and up to 2.2x end-to-end speedup for RAG (Figure 10), 1.3-1.6x for memory-as-context (Figure 11), and 1.8x for MemAgent (Figure 12) (Section 6.2).
The GPU-FPGA system achieves 1.11-4.7x lower geomean energy cost per request compared to the GPU-only baseline (Table 3).
Corresponding results on NVIDIA A100 are reported via performance estimation rather than direct hardware measurement (Section 6.1, Appendix H).

powiRLgonD.text: Standard GNNs are not continuous across graph resolutions: GCN's MAE increases from 63.6±1.3 kcal/mol in same-resolution QM7 regression to 138.1±2.4 kcal/mol under cross-resolution evaluation (Table 1).

Latent embedding differences ||F-F̄|| between resolutions diverge for standard architectures, with GIN showing the worst divergence at 881.2±268.7 (high-to-low resolution) and 2875.8±1527.7 (low-to-high resolution) (Table 2).
The discontinuity arises because renormalized adjacency-matrix propagation creates disconnected effective limit graphs rather than preserving coarse-grained structure (Section 5, Figure 4a-4b).

Theorem 7.1 proves that networks using Laplace-transform propagation achieve provable scale-continuity, bounding the embedding difference by a constant times the heat-kernel convergence term (Theorem 7.1, Eq. 5).
The proposed Laplace-transform propagation reduces embedding differences across resolutions to 0.2-0.3, versus 18.0-2875.8 for standard GNN propagation schemes (Table 3).
Prediction accuracy of the modified architecture remains stable across resolutions, e.g., MPNNexp attains 17.4±3.4 MAE at same resolution versus 17.9±5.2 at cross-resolution (Table 4).

ZsECxUkbKB.text: WUSH derives closed-form near-optimal linear blockwise transforms for joint weight-activation quantization under RTN AbsMax-scaled block quantizers, covering both integer and floating-point formats (Abstract).
On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in MXFP4, WUSH gains +2.8 average accuracy points over the strongest Hadamard-based baseline with RTN quantization and +0.7 points with GPTQ (Abstract).
WUSH delivers up to 5.8x per-layer throughput over BF16 via FP4 MatMul (Abstract).

Blockwise quantization loss analysis across Q, K, V, O, Gate, Up, and Down projection layers shows WUSH achieves the lowest loss among identity, random rotation, Hadamard, and WUSH-without-Hadamard variants (Section 3.2, Table 1).
On LLM benchmark evaluations, WUSH improves average accuracy recovery to about 73.2%, versus about 71.5% for Hadamard and about 69.5% for the identity transform (Section 3.3, Table 2).

KqMqJpSMnQ.text: Theorem 1 gives a bicriteria (1+κ, 1+1/κ) approximation via LP rounding: the returned subgraph K satisfies coverage loss W−e(K)≤(1+κ)·ε·W and size |K|≤(1+1/κ)·r (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).

Theorem 2 proves a monotonicity/nestedness property (Kτ1⊆Kτ2 for τ1<τ2), derived from a connection to parametric minimum cuts, which is required for valid conformal calibration (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
Corollary 1 shows the entire nested sequence of subgraphs across thresholds can be computed in Õ(γ(m+n)²) time (Corollary 1, Section 4.2).
Lemma 1 establishes a distribution-free marginal coverage guarantee ℙ(B*⊆Kτ*(A*))≥φ−δ under exchangeability, without requiring model probability estimates (Lemma 1).
Theorem 4 proves NP-hardness of the conformal subgraph problem even for constant ε via reduction from clique detection, in Appendix B (Theorem 4, Appendix B).

On a synthetic 6x6 grid navigation experiment with 50 train/test routes, the LP-based method compresses the calibration set to 52 edges at φ=0.75 coverage and outperforms greedy baselines for φ≤0.8 (Section 5).

a7LaDjVpTC.text: MeGan's meta-gating mechanism, implemented via adaptive β-SwiGLU blocks controlled by a hypernetwork, outperforms Text-to-LoRA on low-resource domain/persona tasks, scoring 23.15 Rouge-L on Persona-Chat versus Text-to-LoRA's 21.75 and 41.85 versus 20.02 on AdaptSum (Table 4).

On CrossFit and UnifiedQA multi-task generalization benchmarks in the high-resource-to-low-resource (HR→LR) transfer setting, MeGan scores 72.2/70.9 compared to standard fine-tuning (SFT)'s 55.5/54.0 (Table 5).
On 10 diverse held-out benchmarks (including ArcC, ArcE, HellaSwag, PIQA, Winogrande) using SNI-trained models, MeGan achieves an average score of 77.5 versus Text-to-LoRA's 76.9 (Table 6).

MeGan uses only 3.4M trainable parameters compared to Text-to-LoRA's 4.9M, with parameter count scaling linearly with the reduced dimension R, while keeping the base LLM frozen (Section on efficiency).

Ablation studies confirm each component of the meta-gating mechanism is necessary, and β-distribution analysis (Figures 4-5) shows the mechanism captures condition-specific semantic patterns across task, domain, persona, and style condition types (Figures 4-5).

hMTCuqjCW8.text: Adalina (Algorithm 1) is a randomized adaptive linear-approximation algorithm achieving O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) utility-query complexity while using only Θ(n) space (Algorithm 1).

Theorem 3.1 shows that under an optimal sampling distribution q*_s, Adalina attains query complexity O(nD*C²/ε² log(2/δ)) where D*∈O(1) for both Beta Shapley and weighted Banzhaf semi-values, improving on OFA's O(n log n/(ε²δ)) bound (Theorem 3.1).
