Theorem 3.2 proves that paired sampling reduces the estimation problem to approximating (U−U^c)/2 and provably lowers MSE whenever E[U(S)·U([n]\S)] > 0 (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 4.1 shows Adalina achieves improved mean-square error approaching the optimal E[‖ϕ̂^γ*−ϕ‖²₂] while preserving O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) query complexity for symmetric semi-values, and the paper shows SHAP-IQ does not minimize query complexity under this framework (Theorem 4.1).

Experiments on spambase (n=57), FOTP (n=51), MinibooNE (n=50), and philippine (n=308) datasets, using 1000 queries per player averaged over 10 seeds, empirically validate the theoretical complexity/variance predictions (Figures 1-4).

8N2kUoknvy.text: DistPFN corrects majority-class bias in tabular foundation models (e.g., TabPFN) under label shift via a test-time posterior rescaling p̃(y) = Norm(p̂(y)²/p_train(y)), requiring no retraining or architecture changes (Section on method).

The temperature-scaled variant DistPFN-T sets τ = CE(p̂(y), p_train(y)), so higher cross-entropy between predicted and training class distributions triggers stronger smoothing to prevent over-adjustment (Section on DistPFN-T).
DistPFN and DistPFN-T are evaluated on 253 OpenML datasets across six levels of label shift (parameterized by β) against 15+ baseline models (Section on experiments).
Under label shift at β=5.0, DistPFN-T improves TabICL accuracy by 13.7% (Section on results).

DistPFN-T maintains performance comparable to the unmodified base model in standard settings without label shift, and its correction is derived from two complementary theoretical perspectives: classical label-shift correction and Bayesian inference, avoiding the test-prior estimation required by methods like EM-based estimation (EME) and Black-Box shift estimation (BBE) (Section on theory).

pKAOO2u6Jj.text: VENOMREC combines an Exposure Alignment (EA) module, which computes a centroid from naturally popular items in the target's category to identify high-exposure semantic regions, with a Cross-modal Interactive Perturbation (CIP) module that uses attention-guided saliency mining to co-adapt text and image perturbations (Section on method).

VENOMREC achieves a mean ER@20 of 0.73 across datasets, with per-dataset ER@20 of 0.7170 (Clothing, few-shot) / 0.7317 (Clothing, zero-shot), 0.5837/0.5825 (Sports), and 0.8674/0.8781 (Toys) (Table with ER@20 results).

VENOMREC improves over the strongest baseline by +0.52 absolute ER@20 points on average, while interaction-level attacks (DirectBoost, RandomAttack) stay below 0.15 and the multimodal baseline Shadowcast reaches only about 0.047 ER@20 (Section on baseline comparisons).
Single-modality attacks (TextFooler, EXPA, INSA) achieve ER@20 below 0.33, substantially underperforming VENOMREC's cross-modal approach (Section on baseline comparisons).

VENOMREC preserves stealthiness with textual fluency (ROUGE-L) around 90%, visual fidelity (FID) of 36-43, and cross-modal semantic consistency deviation of only 0.003-0.006 (Section on stealth metrics).

oFUfz5nsJc.text: DARTS achieves up to 1.77x wall-clock speedup over the VeRL RL training system while matching baseline task performance (Section on performance results / speedup ablation table).
DARTS is 1.43x faster than a Tail Batching baseline, with per-model speedups ranging from 1.29x to 1.77x across evaluated models (ablation table).

Dual-end length sampling selects the top-K shortest and top-L longest trajectories (K >> L) from a redundantly generated candidate pool to suppress ineffective long-tail responses while preserving reasoning depth for complex prompts (Section on Distribution-Aware Trajectory Sampling).

Adaptive Redundancy Allocation uses response-length variance sigma_L as a proxy for long-tail severity and solves a convex optimization problem to allocate larger rollout budgets to high-variance prompts (Section on Adaptive Redundancy Allocation).

Ablations show sampling alone yields a 1.40x speedup while the full DARTS system (adding variance-guided tail pruning, proactive early stopping, and token-level streaming) yields 1.63x, with training convergence on MATH500, GSM8K, AIME2024, AIME2025, and Olympiad benchmarks matching baselines (Ablation study, Experimental Validation section).
DARTS generalizes beyond math reasoning, achieving 1.20x speedup on multimodal reasoning and 1.15x speedup on code generation tasks (Generalization experiments section).

1HPTFpwktA.text: Info-Gain Sampler improves average accuracy on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP) for the full-attention masked diffusion model Dream-7B to 53.4% versus 49.8% for the previous best baseline, a 3.6% improvement at sampling parameter K=2 (Reasoning tasks results table).

On semi-autoregressive diffusion models, Info-Gain Sampler raises average accuracy for SDAR-8B-Chat to 55.8% (vs. 35.0% for the best baseline) and for TraDo-8B-Instruct to 55.3% (vs. 40.0% for the best baseline) at K=2 (Semi-autoregressive models results table).
Cumulative entropy (uncertainty) is reduced across model variants, e.g. from 210.3 to 74.1 for semi-AR SDAR and from 334.3 to 98.0 for semi-AR TraDo, at K=2 (Cumulative uncertainty reduction table).

Info-Gain Sampler achieves a 63.1% win-rate on AlpacaEval creative writing evaluation against baselines averaged across temperature settings, peaking at 80.3% at temperature 1.5 (Creative writing / AlpacaEval results section).

In text-to-image generation, Info-Gain Sampler improves GenEval average score to 58.2 (vs. 56.3 baseline) and FID to 38.1 (vs. 43.3 for confidence-based baseline) on GenEval/ImageNet-512 (Image generation results section).

m3H7Oexpbx.text: On Qwen2.5-1.5B, PowerFlow attains 19.85 avg@16 versus GRPO's 18.13, outperforming supervised GRPO on this model despite being an RLIF (reward-free) method (Table 1).
On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, PowerFlow reaches 42.17 avg@16, closely matching GRPO's 42.38 while consistently outperforming other RLIF baselines Intuitor, EMPO, and TTRL (Table 1).

PowerFlow uses a length-aware Trajectory-Balance objective targeting an alpha-power distribution of the base model, with alpha>1 sharpening the distribution for reasoning and alpha<1 flattening it for creativity, via reformulating the partition function as Z'(q)^|y| to decouple gradients from response length (Technical formulation section).
For creativity restoration (alpha<1), PowerFlow achieves Pareto-dominant gains, simultaneously increasing semantic diversity and maintaining output quality relative to baselines (Figure 5).

PowerFlow scores 4.05 on a diversity metric versus 3.93 for GRPO and 3.80 for EMPO, while avoiding the length collapse and repetitive explosion failure modes seen in naive RLIF baselines (Figure 3, diversity comparison).

eoFrV13CN7.text: On the 8^4 Hypergrid task, TD-GFN discovers all 16 modes within fewer than 500 state visits, compared to 30,000+ visits required by baseline methods (Hypergrid experiments section).

TD-GFN converges using less than 50% of the state visits required by COFlowNet on the Hypergrid task and retains strong performance on a Mixed dataset (50% expert/50% random trajectories) and under reduced data (150 trajectories) (Hypergrid robustness results).

On the molecule design benchmark, TD-GFN reaches best convergence in 2.749x10^4 trajectories versus 4.423x10^4 for QM-COFlowNet, and finds 1.5-2x more high-reward modes than the strongest baselines (Molecule design results section).
TD-GFN trains in under 30 minutes on a single GPU for molecule design, with edge reward extraction preprocessing overhead of only about 0.1 hours (Computational efficiency results).

TD-GFN's edge reward function is defined via inverse reinforcement learning as R_E(s,s') = log D_phi(s,s') - log(1-D_phi(s,s')), used both for DAG pruning (removing edges where R_E falls below mean(D_RE) - K*std(D_RE)) and for a prioritized backward sampling policy P_B (Equations 5-7).

Ablations on the 8^4 Hypergrid show dataset rebalancing, reward-guided DAG pruning (versus dataset-only pruning), and prioritized backward sampling are each individually necessary for TD-GFN's convergence and robustness on poor-quality datasets (Ablation study section).

MpBeXMurIb.text: Theorem 5.1 shows a single-step TTT inner-loop update can be rewritten exactly as a learned linear attention operator, o = phi_{t+1}(q)(W_t + phi_t(k)^T g_t(k)), where phi are learned query/key transformations and g_t(k) is an effective value derived from the loss gradient (Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 5.2 extends this equivalence to sequential unrolling across multiple inner-loop steps, expressing the output as o_t = phi_{t+1}(q_t)(S_0 + sum_i phi_i(k_i)^T g_i(k_i)), i.e. a cumulative learned linear attention over the sequence (Theorem 5.2).

Theorem 5.3 shows that adding momentum to the TTT inner-loop optimizer only modifies the effective value vectors and does not break the linear-attention structure established in Theorems 5.1-5.2 (Theorem 5.3).

Empirically, downstream performance degrades consistently as the number of inner-loop TTT steps increases even though inner-loop fitting error improves, and replacing gradient descent with gradient ascent in the inner loop yields comparable or superior performance, both contradicting a memorization/retrieval account of TTT (Empirical observations section).

Progressive ablations (Table 2) show that updating only final-layer parameters yields the best overall performance and that weight normalization and momentum are largely redundant, reducing complex TTT architectures toward standard linear attention with only +0.4 perplexity degradation on language modeling (Table 2).

Removing weight normalization enables a fully parallel formulation that achieves up to 4.0x inference throughput on the attention computation and a 1.19x end-to-end training speedup while maintaining performance across language modeling, novel view synthesis, and image classification tasks (Parallelization results section).

UG06mAANLH.text: Adaptive Protein Tokenization (APT) achieves 0.90 Å RMSD on the CATH benchmark, outperforming ESM3 (1.05 Å), DPLM2 (1.64 Å), and Kanzi (1.09 Å) (Table 1, Section 4.1).
On the CAMEO benchmark, APT reaches 0.90 Å RMSD, matching ESM3 and outperforming DPLM2's 1.65 Å (Section 4.1).
Using entropy-based sampling with classifier annealing, APT attains 0.871 designability versus DPLM2 (0.486) and Kanzi (0.562) (Table 4, Section 4.2).
Non-linear MLP probing on APT-tokenized sequences outperforms equivalent probing on DPLM2 and ESM3 tokenizations for CATH fold classification (Figure 5, Section 4.3).
The APT autoregressive generative model uses 20 layers and 1024 channels (252.9M parameters) and is trained on roughly 473,000 AlphaFold2-predicted structures (Appendix C).

HQhVsrLyv9.text: FUSE reduces a ResNet-18 classifier's test accuracy on CIFAR-10 to 10.13% under low-pass filtering, versus 54.16% for LSP, 52.16% for TUE, and 41.97% for GUE (Table 1).
Ablating Random Spectral Masking raises FUSE's filtered accuracy from 10.13% to 57.35%, and ablating Cross-Band Guidance raises it to 17.00%, showing both components are necessary (Table 3).
A FUSE surrogate trained on ResNet-18 transfers to unseen architectures, keeping ConvNeXt accuracy at 10.06% (vs. GUE's 23.66%) and Swin-T accuracy at 15.52% (vs. TUE's 49.79%) (Table 2).
Against the D-VAE and ORTHO PROJ unlearnable-example defenses on CIFAR-10, FUSE limits recovered accuracy to 12.23% and 10.50% respectively, compared to EMN's 91.42% and LSP's 87.99% (Table 6).
FUSE is computationally far cheaper than GUE: 0.004 ms/image inference versus 0.194 ms, and 0.09M versus 7.79M parameters (Table 9).

eQaJSRZiGn.text: TaH outperforms the always-iterate (AlwaysThink) baseline by 8.1-11.3% accuracy on the 0.6B model and by 8.5-12.6% with the TaH+ variant on the 1.7B model (Table 1).
TaH exceeds single-iteration Qwen3 baselines by an average of 4.0% (0.6B) and 5.0% (1.7B), rising to 5.3-5.4% with LoRA-augmented TaH+ (Table 1).

TaH exempts about 94% of tokens from a second latent iteration, dedicating deeper computation to roughly 6% of tokens, as measured across five reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, AMC23, AIME25, OlympiadBench) (Section 5.1).

TaH's duo-causal attention mechanism enables cross-depth information flow while LoRA adapters are applied only at iterations d>1, with a lightweight neural decider choosing which tokens iterate (Section 4).
TaH is trained with a two-stage scheme that uses an oracle iteration policy to jointly train the backbone and the iteration decider (Section 4.3).

ILQGHFvEoo.text: QuITE achieves average relative forecasting improvements of up to 54.7% across four irregular time series datasets (Human Activity, USHCN, PhysioNet, MIMIC-III) (Table 2).
QuITE achieves average relative classification gains of 15.8% across backbone architectures on the P19, P12, and PAM datasets (Table 3).
QuITE++ achieves the best performance in 20 of 24 backbone-dataset settings when compared against 17 baselines, including Hi-Patch, HyperIMTS, GRU-D, mTAND, Raindrop, and tPatchGNN (Table 4).
QuITE's learnable query-token embedding outperforms simpler aggregation strategies (Add, Concat, Mean Pooling, mTAND) across all tested backbone architectures (Table 5).
QuITE maintains performance under 50% random observation removal (Figure 6) and remains robust across different query-token initialization schemes (Table 6).

2TCOninOND.text: On COD10K camouflaged object detection with the FEDER baseline, CurriSeg improves F_β from 0.715 to 0.736 (+2.94%) and E_φ from 0.892 to 0.910 (+2.02%) (Table 1).
CurriSeg reduces training time by 28.9-48.4% across backbones while adding at most 0.1G GPU memory overhead during training and zero additional parameters at inference (Table 2).
On CVC-ColonDB polyp segmentation with the RUN backbone, CurriSeg improves mDice from 0.822 to 0.845 (+2.80%) (Table 3).
On transparent object detection (GDD/GSD) with the RUN+ backbone, CurriSeg yields a 3.59% composite metric improvement (Table 4).

CurriSeg combines a Curriculum Selection phase (IoU-based warm-up curriculum plus Temporal Statistics-based Sample Weighting) with an Anti-Curriculum Promotion phase using Spectral-Blindness Fine-Tuning (low-pass filtering at radius ratio r=0.95) to suppress texture shortcuts (Sections on Robust Curriculum Selection and Anti-Curriculum Promotion).
Ablating any single component—WCS, PUE, TSSW, or SBFT—degrades CurriSeg's segmentation performance, confirming each contributes meaningfully (Table 6).

tj9EwfaxHm.text: On the HarmBench dataset against GPT-4o, VERA-V attains a 67.75% average attack success rate versus 14.0% for the prior best baseline CS-DJ, a 53.75-point gap (Table 1).

VERA-V integrates three complementary strategies in a composite adversarial image: typography-based text prompts, diffusion-based image synthesis, and structured distractor images that fragment model attention (Section 4.1.3).

On HarmBench, VERA-V reaches 72.0% average ASR versus FigStep's 21.5%, HADES's 46.75%, and CS-DJ's 53.0%, and also attains 72.0% ASR on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 76.5% ASR on InternVL3-8B (Table 1, Section 5.2).
On the HADES dataset, VERA-V achieves an 80.0% average ASR on open-source VLMs and 73.5% on closed-source VLMs (Table 2, Section 5.2).
VERA-V achieves only 24.1% toxicity detection rate under a safety detector versus 35.0% for CS-DJ, indicating improved stealth against content moderation (Table 4, Section 5.4).

CUVBdw2tKy.text: Bidirectional Manifold Consistency (BMC) probes solution validity via a forward-masking phase that stochastically replaces generated tokens with the absorbing [MASK] token, followed by a backward-reconstruction phase using K≈16 truncated denoising steps (versus T=1024 full generation steps) to produce a reconstruction that is compared against the original output (Section 4.1, Eq. 9).

Without access to ground-truth labels, BMC's aggregated reconstruction-stability score achieves 0.893 AUROC / 0.943 AUPR for error detection on GSM8K with LLaDA-8B, outperforming Self-Consistency's 0.872 AUROC, with the gap widening on GPQA (0.678 vs. 0.539 AUROC) (Table 1, Section 5.2).

BMC is incorporated as a dense geometric reward via a gated reward function r(x0) = I(y_pred=y*)·[r_base + α_t·S_BMC(x0)], so only already-correct rollouts receive additional stability-based shaping, with a curriculum that anneals the geometric term's weight over training (Section 4.3, Eq. 14).

Training with this Geometric Alignment reward outperforms standard outcome-only RL: at 512-token generation length it reaches 41.6% vs. 37.2% accuracy on MATH (+4.4 points) and 85.8% vs. 83.5% on GSM8K (+2.3 points) (Table 3, Section 5.4).

Proposition 3.5 establishes that under a κ-contraction assumption on the denoiser, the reconstruction error upper-bounds the distance to the true solution manifold by a factor of 1/(1-κ) (Section 3.3, Proposition 3.5, Eq. 8).

Manifold-Guided Rejection Sampling (Algorithm 1) adaptively allocates inference-time sampling, reaching 79.5% accuracy on GSM8K with only 3.3 average samples, outperforming Best-of-N with confidence-based selection (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Vl3tXPbjSH.text: MAPR (Meta-Awareness via Predictive Reward) trains models to predict rollout statistics — length, pass-rate, and concepts — and verifies these predictions against actual outcomes to filter trivial/unsolvable prompts and truncate lengthy, likely-incorrect generations (Section 3).
MAPR (MASA-efficient variant) reaches the same downstream performance as standard GRPO training while using over 1.28x less training compute/time (Section 3.3, Figure 4).
MAPR yields an 83.18% gain in accuracy on the AIME25 benchmark relative to the GRPO baseline (Section 4, Table 1).
MAPR achieves a 13.04% average accuracy gain across six mathematics benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, MATH500, Minerva, and OlympiadBench) compared to GRPO (Section 4, Table 1).

Ablation studies isolate the contribution of the predictive-reward/gating components versus the efficiency-oriented early-cutoff mechanism to the overall accuracy and speed gains (Section 4.3, Ablation Studies).

jEBkuuETjr.text: The method (DC-PnPDP) introduces explicit ADMM dual variables that act as an integral controller accumulating historical constraint-violation feedback, in contrast to standard memoryless plug-and-play operators, to reduce steady-state reconstruction bias (Section 3, dual-variable coupling).

Theorem C.1 shows that dual-coupled fixed points satisfy the first-order optimality condition 0 ∈ ∇f(x*) + ∂φ(x*) of the original reconstruction problem, formalizing the asymptotic convergence guarantee (Appendix C, Theorem C.1).

A Spectral Homogenization (SH) module addresses the bias-hallucination trade-off by modulating colored/structured dual-variable residuals into pseudo-AWGN inputs so they match the diffusion denoiser's valid statistical manifold (Proposition 3.1, Section 3.2).

On limited-angle CT (LACT-90), the method attains 36.98 dB PSNR versus 31.03 dB for the DiffPIR baseline (+5.95 dB), and on sparse-view CT (SVCT-20) it attains 39.81 dB versus 36.71 dB for DDS (+3.1 dB) (Table 1, Section 4).
On accelerated MRI reconstruction at 10x acceleration, the method reaches 26.21 dB PSNR versus 25.24 dB for the DAPS baseline (Table 1, Section 4).

The method matches DiffPIR's 100-step reconstruction quality using only 30 sampling steps, an approximately 3.3x acceleration, and an ablation on LACT-90 shows dual coupling alone contributes +4.55 dB over base PnP-HQS while spectral homogenization prevents hallucination artifacts (Figure 4; Table 2, Section 4.3).

b0Z5xWy23m.text: RSA2C combines a vector-valued-kernel Actor with a Value Critic and an Advantage Critic in RKHS, using a Mahalanobis-weighted operator-valued kernel κ_ϕ(s,s_j) = exp(-1/2 (s-s_j)^T W (s-s_j)) with W = diag(ϕ̃) derived from SHAP attribution scores to weight state similarity (Definition 3.1, Section 3.1).

Two RKHS-SHAP attribution variants are proposed: RSA2C-KME (kernel mean embeddings, observational/on-manifold SHAP) and RSA2C-CME (conditional mean embeddings, interventional/off-manifold SHAP), both computing coalition values analytically via inner products rather than Monte Carlo sampling (Section 3.2, Eq. 9-11).

Theorem 4.9 derives a non-asymptotic convergence bound (1-γ)E[J(π*)-J(π_ht)] ≤ ζ_approx + O(log^2 T / T^(1/4)), implying O((1-γ)^-5 ε^-4 log^2(1/ε)) sample complexity for an ε-optimal policy, and Theorem 4.8/4.10 extend this to bounded adversarial state perturbations (Section 4, Theorems 4.8-4.10).

On Pendulum-v1 with added state noise, RSA2C-CME maintains a reward standard deviation in [35,51] across noise levels, versus [225,271] for RSA2C-KME, with both outperforming an Advantage Actor-Critic baseline in stability (Table 2, Section 5).
RSA2C-CME incurs only a 12.58% runtime overhead versus a baseline RKHS actor-critic while using substantially fewer FLOPs than deep-learning baselines SAC and PPO (Table 1, Section 5).
Continuous-control evaluation spans Pendulum-v1 (main text), BipedalWalker-v3, and Ant-v5 (Appendix D.3-D.4), with all results averaged over 10 random seeds (Section 5, Appendix D.3-D.4).

10ePjaPxvc.text: On BABILong multi-hop fact retrieval across 32K-128K token contexts, LUCID-PATH maintains stable accuracy of roughly 0.21-0.25 while standard attention degrades from about 0.14 toward near zero (Figure 6).

On RULER multi-needle retrieval, LUCID improves accuracy over standard attention at every needle count tested: 76.6% vs 74.2% (2 needles), 55.8% vs 51.0% (4 needles), and 43.6% vs 38.8% (6 needles) (Figure 4).

LUCID is derived by preconditioning attention via key-key similarities in an RKHS feature space, framed as minimizing a quadratic retrieval-error objective via gradient descent, and provably preserves non-zero gradients at standard softmax temperature (Section 2.1, Theorem 1).

On the needle-in-haystack attention noise analysis, LUCID achieves a 28.45% hitrate for tokens receiving attention versus 18.17% for standard attention, a 56.6% relative improvement (Section 3, synthetic experiments).

LUCID is evaluated on approximately 1-billion-parameter models (22 layers, 2048 model dimension, 32 attention heads) pretrained on ~6.5B tokens of Dolma, then fine-tuned at 65536 sequence length, and incurs only about 1.3% inference overhead at 32K context with batch size 1 (Section 4, Table 4).
On LongBench/SCROLLS tasks, LUCID/LUCID-PATH improves F1 and ROUGE-L scores over baselines, e.g. 0.274 F1 on 2WikiMQA, 11.70 F1 on Qasper, and 12.60 ROUGE-L on QMSum (Table 4).

91HObJG07V.text: RepetitionCurse increases API-level time-to-first-token by factors ranging from 1.514x to 4.728x across tested commercial MoE endpoints, including 3.063x on Mixtral-8x7B (25.789s vs 5.288s) and 4.728x on Kimi-Linear-Instruct (14.595s vs 2.066s) (Table 4).

The attack constructs prompts where all tokens are identical except for the instruction template and system prompt, requiring no gradient access or optimization to induce router imbalance in a black-box, model-agnostic manner (Section 3.2).

Across 14 evaluated MoE architectures spanning Mixtral, Qwen3, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, GPT-OSS, Kimi-Linear, and Llama-4-Scout variants, larger expert-parallelism degrees (EP=2, 4, 8) exacerbate the latency amplification ratio caused by the attack (Table 2, Table 3).
A survey of 139 MoE models on Hugging Face found that 54.68% use Mixtral-like architectures with 8-16 experts, motivating the choice of evaluated model families (Section 3.4).

YkLsed7G04.text: On the AGNOSTOS benchmark's 23 unseen tasks, the proposed method achieves 32.5% success on Level-1 tasks and 18.5% on Level-2 tasks, for an overall success rate of 26.4%, surpassing the X-ICM baseline's 23.5% (Table 1).

An ablation study shows progressive gains from each component: baseline 21.6%, adding the dynamic demonstration library 23.3%, adding the coverage-aware static library 24.9%, and adding skill-augmented in-context learning 26.4% (Table 2).

Atomic skills are extracted from demonstrations by detecting gripper state changes and motion-stopping events, then labeled by a VLM into a Verb[obj] format such as Reach, Move, Grasp, or Release (Section 3.2).

The dual-library demonstration retrieval combines a dynamic library selecting task-relevant demonstrations via visual-semantic similarity and skill-plan matching with a coverage-aware static library that uses IDF-weighted token selection to supplement missing skill patterns (Section 3.3).
Real-world validation on five physical tasks using a 6-DoF xArm6 robotic arm achieves a 36% average success rate across 125 total trials (Table 4, Figure 5).

RsPequeaiZ.text: VideoSEAL achieves 62.0% accuracy on LongVideoBench and 55.1% on LVBench, each roughly 6.7 points higher than a coupled planner-inspector baseline using the same Qwen3-8B planner and Qwen2.5-VL-7B inspector backbones (Table 1).

On LVBench grounding evaluation, VideoSEAL attains 0.528 recall@0.05 temporal groundedness and 0.808 semantic groundedness, versus 0.472 semantic groundedness for the DrVideo baseline, while reducing temporal and semantic hallucination rates to 0.406 and 0.113 respectively (Table 2).

Decoupling the planner (evidence-seeking) from the inspector (exclusive answer authority, terminating only when its binary sufficiency verdict z_t=1) outperforms coupled baselines under both reward settings, achieving 54.1% vs 48.2% accuracy (Section 4.1, Table 3).

Increasing search rounds improves VideoSEAL's accuracy from 47.1% to 55.1%, while coupled agents plateau due to context saturation; separately, scaling the inspector from 7B to 72B yields a 4.4% accuracy gain without retraining the planner (Figure 6a, Figure 6b).
The inspector shows selective verification behavior, answering 78.4% of queries on ground-truth clips but only 24.2% on non-target clips (Table 4).

LULx50RKAz.text: CoGenCast reconfigures decoder-only pretrained LLMs into an encoder-decoder forecasting backbone purely by modifying attention topology: bidirectional self-attention in the encoder, causal self-attention in the decoder, and cross-attention linking them, coupled with a flow-matching mechanism that models average velocity for one-step generation (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

Across 10 benchmark datasets spanning energy, finance, healthcare, and electricity domains (including four ETT subsets, Exchange, Wind, and Solar), CoGenCast achieves roughly 11% MSE reduction versus LLM-based baselines (LLM4TS, Time-LLM) and over 7% improvement versus transformer-based baselines like PatchTST (Section 4.1, Table 1, Table 2).

An ablation over encoder-decoder architecture variants shows the full encoder-decoder design outperforms encoder-only and decoder-only variants (Table 3), and a separate ablation confirms both the autoregressive and flow-matching components are necessary for best performance (Table 4).

Single-step function evaluation (one-step inference) achieves performance comparable to or better than multi-step sampling, and statistics-based context features are shown to be the most impactful conditioning signal, with full text conditioning being optimal (Figure 3, Figure 4).
Qwen3-0.6B is selected as the LLM backbone based on a comparison of efficiency versus forecasting performance across candidate backbones (Table 6).
CoGenCast supports extended look-back windows (L=192, 336) with improving accuracy as context length increases, per additional experiments in the appendix (Appendix G.2).

tyqW6SYxWB.text: NPR-4B (Instruct) achieves 50.4% on AIME25, a 14.9-point improvement over the Multiverse-4B baseline (Table 2).

NPR attains up to 4.6x inference speedup versus autoregressive decoding on AIME25, reaching 2979.8 tokens/sec, while maintaining 100% genuine parallel execution compared to Multiverse's 45.8%-76.0% parallel rates (Table 3, Section 4.2).

The three-stage training pipeline (format-follow RL producing NPR-Zero in Section 2.2, rejection-sampling SFT producing NPR-Beta in Section 2.3, and native-parallel RL via the Parallel-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) algorithm in Section 2.4) is required to reach full performance without a stronger teacher model.
On the non-thinking backbone, NPR yields average gains of 24.5% across the eight evaluation benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25, OlympiadBench, Minerva-Math, ZebraLogic, AMC23, MATH500) (Section 3.2).

Naive enforcement of the parallel output format without the progressive curriculum causes performance to collapse from 47.5 to 17.5 on AIME25, demonstrating the necessity of the progressive self-distilled training paradigm (Section 4.4).

Self-distilled training data outperforms Multiverse teacher-generated data by 10.1 points on average, and parallel SFT (NPR-Beta) outperforms sequential SFT by 5.8 points on AIME25 (Section 4, ablation results).

6n7gXOvdwm.text: RulePlanner is the only method in the comparison that satisfies all seven hardware design rules (boundary, grouping, inter-die alignment, pre-placement, non-overlap, outline, and shape constraints) simultaneously, versus baselines achieving only partial coverage (Table 1, Section 2).
RulePlanner achieves a Block-Terminal Distance of 0.000 (perfect alignment to pre-placement terminals), compared to 0.306 for the strongest baseline FlexPlanner (Table 3).
RulePlanner achieves a Block-Block Adjacency Length of 0.223 on average, exceeding the best baseline WireMask-BBO's score of 0.082 (Table 4).
RulePlanner generalizes to unseen circuits in zero-shot evaluation with inference-to-training performance ratios between 0.995 and 1.057 (Table 5).

An ablation removing either the Adjacent Terminal Mask or the Adjacent Block Mask significantly degrades the corresponding target metric, confirming both masks are necessary components of the unified reward/action-masking framework (Table 6, Section 4).

aNtMUFWjnD.text: On the Question Answering task, the Multi-Agent coordination strategy using Gemini-3 achieves 67.92% accuracy, outperforming centralized retrieval baselines, while the multi-agent coordination gap versus centralized retrieval narrows as model scale increases (Section 5, Table 2).
On Web Recommendation, all evaluated coordination strategies (ToolE, ToolP, Multi-Agent) achieve near-zero performance, with recall below 1% (Table 2, Section 5).
Enabling explicit reasoning (thinking mode) improves multi-agent performance by +21% on Web Search (ToolP) and +14% accuracy on Question Answering (Section 5.3).

Multi-agent decentralized access concentrates citation traffic toward a small set of high-authority sources such as Wikipedia and ScienceDirect, reducing visibility for niche websites relative to centralized retrieval (Figure 2, Section 5.2).

Stronger models require greater interaction budgets to succeed: Gemini-3 contacts an average of 4.64 agents and issues 6.26 retrieval requests per task, versus 2.61 agents and 2.79 requests for Qwen3-4B (Section 5.4).

The benchmark spans 100 websites containing 18.4M documents across four tasks (Web Search: 354 queries, Web Recommendation: 281 histories, Question Answering: 53 queries, Deep Research: 331 queries) evaluated on seven LLMs from Qwen3-4B to Gemini-3-Flash (Section 1, Section 3).

gEc0iJCYxw.text: DDP-WM decomposes latent state evolution into sparse primary dynamics (Stage 2-3: Dynamic Localization and Sparse Primary Dynamics Prediction) and secondary background updates handled by a Low-Rank Correction Module (Stage 4), based on the observation that background regions exhibit near-zero feature change across predictor layers (Figure 1, Section 3).

On the Push-T task, DDP-WM improves MPC success rate from 90% (DINO-WM baseline) to 98%, while reducing FLOPs from 23G to 2.5G (9.2x reduction) and MPC decision latency from 120s to 16s (7.5x faster) (Section 1, Table 1).

An ablation on Push-T shows removing the Low-Rank Correction Module (LRM) drops success rate from 98% to 90%, removing the MPC Mask drops it to 70%, and replacing the full method with a naive sparse baseline drops it to 62% (Table 7, Section 4.3).

The LRM provides almost no benefit in open-loop prediction accuracy (361 vs 427 pixel error without it) but is critical for closed-loop planning, because it smooths the MPC cost landscape into a funnel-shaped global minimum versus the rugged, noisy landscape produced by a naive sparse model (Table 6, Figure 5, Section 4.4).

DDP-WM is evaluated across five environments spanning navigation (PointMaze, Wall), rigid-body contact (Push-T), deformable bodies (Rope), and multi-body granular interaction, achieving a Chamfer Distance of 0.31 versus 0.41 for DINO-WM on the Rope task (Table 1, Section 4).

tb2aPbeg86.text: HVR-Met's Hypothesis-Verification-Replanning mechanism (Section 3.3) operates through four phases: event-driven hypothesis generation, multi-modal verification execution, discrepancy detection and reasoning, and feedback-driven replanning.

On the 100-event end-to-end benchmark, HVR-Met with GPT-5 achieves an 85% final reporting pass rate, 71.86% index computation accuracy, and 79.52% figure generation accuracy (Section 4, results table).

The seven-agent architecture (Decomposer, Data Specialist, Code Executor, Plotter, Image Checker, Diagnostician, Reporter) integrates a Guideline Library built from 584 extreme weather papers and a tool knowledge base derived from MetPy, Cartopy, and Matplotlib documentation (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).

Ablating the Guideline Library causes the Hypothesis score to drop to 1.27/5 and the Final Report score to 0.40/5, while removing the Decomposer agent collapses the Final Report score to 1.12/5 (Tables 2-3, Section 4).

On index calculation questions, GPT-5's accuracy falls from 94.55% on easy items to 31.25% on hard items, illustrating an inverse difficulty-performance relationship shared across GPT-5, Gemini-3-Pro, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-Coder (Section 5.3).
Removing the Image Checker agent drops figure quality score from 4.13 to 2.98/5, indicating multi-modal verification is essential to the diagnostic pipeline (Section 4, ablation results).

LcSPuepCDU.text: CT-DiagVLM achieves 84.4% AUC on CT-RATE, a 5.1% absolute improvement over prior state-of-the-art methods such as fVLM (77.8%) and ViSD-Boost (79.0%) (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On the external Rad-ChestCT validation set, CT-DiagVLM reaches 75.4% AUC, a 5.4% absolute gain over fVLM's 68.0%, demonstrating generalization to unseen data distributions (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On the 60-disease benchmark using LLM-generated pseudo-labels, the model attains 85.6% AUC, a 9.8% absolute improvement over the 75.8% base model result (Table 2, Section 4.3).

An ablation isolates each component's contribution to the 5.1% AUC gain: the CNN-ViT hybrid encoder contributes +1.0%, the diagnosis-aware prompt strategy +2.1%, and disease-level contrastive learning +2.0% (Table 4, Section 4.5).

When transferred to radiology report generation, the pretrained representation yields 45.5% F1 on CT-RATE and 37.3% F1 on Rad-ChestCT, substantially outperforming existing methods such as CT-CHAT (Table 3, Section 4.4).

Initializing from SigLIP-2 Base is critical: training the visual encoder from scratch drops performance to 76.5% AUC versus 84.4% AUC with SigLIP-2 initialization, while additional DeepStack/MoE enhancements yield no consistent gains (Table 5, Section 4.5).

cmFlwBI4Ov.text: On single-dataset human-to-animal transfer, the proposed method maintains a joint-position (JP) error around 35, versus around 398 for the SAME baseline (Table 1).

Under multi-dataset joint training, the method achieves roughly 30% lower reconstruction errors (JR, RT, JP) on AT-HumanML3D and roughly 12% lower errors on the diverse AT-AniMo4D benchmark, which spans 115 species (Table 2).

An ablation shows that removing the text-fusion (semantic modulation) component significantly increases reconstruction errors relative to the complete model, which attains JR 0.0568, RT 0.9583, and JP 1.3570 (Table 4).

With only 10% of downstream training data, pre-training the motion representation reduces joint-rotation error by more than 50% compared to training from scratch, showing strong transfer benefits (Table 5).
For downstream text-to-motion generation, the RVQ-based variant achieves an FID of 0.158 and a Top-3 retrieval accuracy of 0.639 (Table 6, Section 5.3).

Zero-shot cross-species retargeting is demonstrated qualitatively on AT-HumanML3D across diverse characters and is shown to be superior to the SAME baseline in direct comparison (Figures 3 and 4, Section 5.1).

GNieZ8Z5V5.text: GMLLM with ChatGPT-4o achieves 94.29% accuracy on Backstabbers, 96.96% on Datadog, and 96.33% on Mal-OSS, the best results among compared approaches on each public dataset (Table 1).
On the custom MalCP dataset (malicious code from PyPI, segmented by program size), GMLLM with ChatGPT-4o attains 95.62% accuracy on the combined 'All' split (Table 2).
GMLLM reduces mean token consumption to 640-644 tokens on the large dataset split, versus 251,000-333,972 tokens for direct LLM-based approaches, a roughly 400x reduction (Table 4).

In an explanation-quality evaluation, GMLLM with ChatGPT-4o achieves an average quality score of 2.721/5, outperforming baselines on threat generality, execution path traceability, and evidence groundedness (Table 3).

The method combines a GNN trained with rule-based node features (Section 3.1) with an attention-based interpretability mechanism that selects influential code nodes before targeted LLM analysis (Section 3.2), requiring only sparse binary labels for supervision (Section 3).

UJJfkcJ7K9.text: LoDA achieves 81.93% last-task accuracy and 86.90% average accuracy on 10-step Split ImageNet-R, and 62.59%/70.87% on 10-step Split ImageNet-A, outperforming the CoSO baseline by 0.80-1.70 percentage points (Tables 1-2).
Theorem 3.1 shows the projection energy E = ||AX^T||_2^2 gates the LoRA update's effective learning capacity and governs the loss decrease when the B matrix is updated with A fixed (Section 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 derives a closed-form solution for the isolated subspace U_I via Cholesky factorization of accumulated past-task statistics (Section 3.2).
Theorem 3.3 derives an exact closed-form rescaling matrix Λ_G that minimizes feature-level joint optimization error across all previously seen tasks (Section 3.4).

An ablation on 10-step ImageNet-R shows accuracy rising from a 72.09% single-LoRA baseline to 79.19% with the general subspace alone, 79.22% with the isolated subspace alone, 81.05% combining both branches, and 81.93% with the full model including the gated adaptive optimization (GAO) step (Table 3).

LoDA incurs only 27.0MB of task-independent storage overhead, 18.06 additional training GFLOPs, and zero additional inference parameters compared to a standard LoRA continual learning baseline (Section on training details/overhead).

SCSc1Ph7CI.text: PRISM derives a closed-form Fisher Information metric I(p,t) = (∂μ/∂t)^T Σ^{-1} (∂μ/∂t) for spatially continuous local temporal uncertainty, computed via automatic differentiation (Equation 10, Section 4.3).
The framework establishes a Cramér-Rao bound Var(τ|p,t) ≥ 1/I(p,t) linking local shape discriminability to the precision of temporal (developmental) estimates (Equation 8).

On the synthetic Starman(G) dataset, PRISM's global intrinsic time estimation attains a correlation of r=0.999 with ground truth, and on the ANNY dataset (1,507 human body shapes spanning ages 0-20) a mean absolute error of 0.089 years (Table 2).
Local intrinsic time estimates achieve r>0.99 on datasets with spatially-varying developmental rates, a capability not demonstrated by baseline methods (Table 3).

On a clinical dataset of 358 pediatric airway CT scans (ages 0-19, including 31 pathological out-of-distribution cases), local temporal uncertainty scoring achieves 0.832 AUC for detecting airway pathology, versus 0.563 AUC for global uncertainty scoring (Table 5).
The heteroscedastic Gaussian displacement field model p(d|p,t) = N(μ(p,t), Σ(p,t)) is trained via an amortized inverse encoder on synthetic data generated from a forward model (Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

Rc8th2rXXe.text: Omni-fMRI is pretrained on 49,497 fMRI sessions spanning nine datasets, split into Type I (5 datasets, 40,708 sessions), Type II (4 datasets, 10,800 sessions), and Type III downstream-only datasets (Table 2)

The dynamic patch tokenization mechanism reduces the token sequence from about 14,000 to 4,300 tokens by using an intensity-variance complexity metric to subdivide spatially complex regions and prune background patches (Section 3.2)
On ABIDE age regression, Omni-fMRI achieves an MSE of 0.427 versus 0.537 for NeuroSTORM, and on ADNI diagnosis it reaches 92.05% accuracy versus 88.77% for NeuroSTORM (Table 3)
On NSD image retrieval, Omni-fMRI attains 6.93% Top-1 accuracy compared to 3.00% for NeuroSTORM (Table 4)
In few-shot learning on the HCP task with only 10% of the training data, Omni-fMRI reaches 45.29% accuracy versus 23.12% for BrainMASS (Table 11)
Pretraining Omni-fMRI takes about 32 hours on 4 NVIDIA A10G GPUs compared to roughly 13 days reported for NeuroSTORM (Section 3, comparative training-time analysis)

aOSkHBRYUJ.text: The Information Bottleneck Adapter (IB-Adapter) is a lightweight module with fewer than 10M parameters that combines subspace covariance modeling (Equation 3), sigmoid-based channel gating (Equation 4), and a non-linear MLP transformation (Equation 5) to filter visual noise (Section 3)

On LIBERO-Spatial at the highest corruption severity level 5, StableVLA with a 0.5B-parameter backbone achieves 82.0% success, exceeding OpenVLA-OFT (7B parameters, 72.1%) and OpenPi-0.5 (3B parameters, 62.4%) despite a 14x smaller backbone (Table 1)
StableVLA improves over the VLA-Adapter baseline by 40.2%-139.6% at the highest LIBERO corruption severity (Table 1)

In real-world Astribot S1 experiments on four manipulation tasks, StableVLA maintains 80% success on Pick-and-Place under oil obstruction while VLA-Adapter drops to 20%, and StableVLA's average performance degradation across disturbances is 17.5% versus 49.2% for VLA-Adapter and 30.1% for OpenPi-0.5 (Table 2, Section 4.2)

An ablation shows removing the MLP pathway from the Fused IB-Adapter (Equation 7) decreases LIBERO performance by 3.1 percentage points, and using sigmoid gating instead of softmax improves performance by 16.3 points on corrupted data (Table 3)

qpkG0eKx4v.text: MemEvolve is a framework that jointly evolves an LLM agent's experiential knowledge and its underlying memory architecture, rather than relying on a static, manually engineered memory system (abstract only)
The authors introduce EvolveLab, a standardized codebase that organizes memory systems into modular encode, store, retrieve, and manage components (abstract only)
MemEvolve improves SmolAgent's performance by up to 17.06% on challenging agentic benchmarks (abstract only)
MemEvolve produces comparable performance gains for Flash-Searcher on the same agentic benchmarks (abstract only)
Memory architectures discovered by MemEvolve transfer effectively across different tasks and different underlying LLM backbones, demonstrating cross-task and cross-LLM generalization (abstract only)

Zza6vGmNfl.text: ReAugment (referred to as AutoTSAug) uses a three-stage pipeline: Stage A trains a variational masked autoencoder (V-MAE) on marginal/overfitting-prone samples, Stage B applies REINFORCE to optimize an augmentation policy, and Stage C retrains the forecasting model on augmented data (Section 4)

The reward function combines reconstruction fidelity with prediction-consistency variance across a model zoo comprising iTransformer, Transformer, PatchTST, and LTSF-Linear, computed as a sigmoid of a consistency score (Equation 4)
On ETTh1 with iTransformer, ReAugment reduces MAE from 0.405 to 0.397 and MSE from 0.387 to 0.382, and on ETTm1 it reduces MAE from 0.377 to 0.363 and MSE from 0.341 to 0.327 (Table 1)
Averaged across the model zoo on ETTh1, ReAugment yields a 4.49% MAE and 7.03% MSE improvement over baselines (Table 2)
An ablation confirms that adding REINFORCE-based policy optimization improves augmentation quality over using the V-MAE alone across multiple datasets (Table 4)
Using only 25% of the training data, ReAugment-augmented models approach full-dataset performance in the few-shot forecasting setting (Figure 4)

BBIcqAryty.text: PhysDB contains 150,000 3D assets annotated across four tiers: holistic (global scale/usage), static (part-level materials and mass), functional (intrinsic functions and state machines), and interactive (kinematic properties and affordances)

PhysForge uses a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL vision-language model as a 'physical architect' to generate Hierarchical Physical Blueprints specifying part bounding boxes, materials, and joint types such as revolute, prismatic, and fixed

The physics-grounded diffusion model synthesizes geometry jointly with kinematic parameters via the KineVoxel Injection (KVI) mechanism, which encodes articulation parameters into dedicated kinematic voxels
PhysForge achieves 77.16% voxel recall and 42.95% bounding box IoU on part structure planning (Table 3)
PhysForge achieves a Joint-Axis-Error of 0.101 and a Joint-Pivot-Error of 0.071, compared to 0.241-0.781 and 0.153-0.652 respectively for baseline methods (Table 4)

aphjc9yoLf.text: On the Peel Cucumber task, encoding actions in a continuous VAE latent space raises OFT (OpenVLA-OFT) success rate from 28% to 74% under synchronous high-frequency (60Hz) execution (Table 1).
The proposed Reuse-then-Refine (RTR) strategy reduces PI0.5's jerk metric on the Peel task from 4.124 to 1.601 and raises OFT's asynchronous success rate from 20% to 70% (Table 3).

A VAE encoder that downsamples 48-step, 60Hz action chunks by a compression factor f=4 into a latent z of dimension 10 yields smoother trajectories than direct action-space training, adding only about 2ms of decoder inference overhead (Section 4.1, Table 6).
High-frequency latent+RTR execution reduces end-to-end task completion latency by roughly 63% (14.59s vs. 39.65s) compared to low-frequency (15Hz) baseline execution on the Peel task (Table 5).

An ablation over VAE vs. VQ-VAE latent compression ratios f in {1,2,4,8,16} shows moderate compression (f=4) is optimal, while excessive compression degrades both motion smoothness and task precision (Section 5.4, Figure 8).

RT-C, an existing chunk-level continuity method, degrades in performance when applied within the latent space and is outperformed by RTR across all continuity metrics including boundary gap (e.g., OFT boundary gap reduced from 15.022mm to 4.867mm) (Section 5.4, Table 4).

pwbLmew1aq.text: MiniAppBench comprises 500 tasks spanning six domains (Science 187, Games 121, Visualization 64, Tools 57, Humanities 47, Lifestyle 32 tasks), distilled from tens of millions of real-world user queries via a four-stage construction pipeline (Table with domain distribution / dataset construction section).
On MiniAppBench, GPT-5.2 achieves the best pass rate of 45.46%, while the average pass rate across all evaluated models is only 17.05% (Table 1).
Tasks are stratified by difficulty into 30% Easy, 40% Medium, and 30% Hard, and closed-source models substantially outperform open-source alternatives across this split (Table 1).

MiniAppEval, an agentic evaluation framework using Playwright-driven browser automation, scores generated interactive HTML applications along three dimensions: Intention, Static, and Dynamic correctness (Section describing MiniAppEval framework).
MiniAppEval's automated judgments align closely with human evaluators, achieving Cohen's kappa between 0.81 and 0.89 and a Fleiss' Kappa inter-rater reliability of 0.89 (Table 4).

wVGSzWj21L.text: On RGBNT201, FUSE achieves 81.4% mAP and 86.1% Rank-1, improving over the TOP-ReID baseline (72.3% mAP, 76.6% Rank-1) by 9.1 and 9.5 points respectively (Table 1).
On RGBNT100, FUSE reaches 88.5% mAP and 96.9% Rank-1, a 1.3-point mAP gain over the next-best method IDEA (87.2% mAP); on MSVR310, FUSE attains 50.1% mAP and 65.7% Rank-1 (Table 2).

An ablation isolating the Spectral Decomposition Module (SDM) and Cross-Modal Alignment Module (CAM) shows SDM alone contributes +3.7% mAP and CAM alone +1.2% mAP over a 76.0% mAP baseline, with the full FUSE combination reaching 80.8% mAP (Table 3).

A frequency-band weighting ablation finds an equal-weight configuration (0.3, 0.3, 0.3) across low/mid/high-frequency subspaces optimal at 79.7% mAP, outperforming single-band variants by 4.3 points (Table 4).
FUSE attains the lowest computational cost among compared methods at 59.3M parameters and 24.7G FLOPs (Table 9).
Under six missing-modality configurations, FUSE averages 49.9% mAP and 49.9% Rank-1, exceeding TOP-ReID by 5.5 and 5.3 points respectively (Table 8).

YPBm14yRlK.text: VPD-100K contains 100,000 images annotated with 33 fine-grained privacy classes and more than 190,000 object instances, organized into four domains: Human Presence, On-Screen PII, Physical Identifiers, and Location Indicators (dataset overview section).

VPD-100K exhibits a long-tailed class distribution and a markedly higher proportion of small objects (occupying less than 10% of image area) compared to the prior DIPA2 dataset, with a normalized object-size coefficient of variation of 1.47 (dataset statistics section).

The proposed Frequency-Enhanced Module (FEM), combining Frequency-Domain Attention Fusion and an Adaptive Spectral Gating Mechanism, improves YOLOv10L detection performance to 58.6% AP and 73.4% AP50, an 8.9-point AP and 4.7-point AP50 gain over the second-best baseline (benchmark results table).
YOLOv10L with FEM achieves 36.5% AP on small objects, a 0.81 F1-score, 7.51ms latency, and over 130 FPS (benchmark results table).
A 20-participant user study reports 90% positive responses regarding the completeness of the 33-class privacy taxonomy (user study section).

C6kxImRizt.text: On Infinity-2B, FasterVAR achieves a 3.4x inference speedup (2.2s to 0.64s latency) while GenEval drops by only 0.01 (0.73 to 0.72) and DPG decreases by only 0.26 (83.12 to 82.86) (Table 3).
On Infinity-8B, FasterVAR yields a 2.7x speedup (4.80s to 1.77s), and on STAR-1.7B a 1.74x speedup (2.0s to 1.15s), demonstrating consistent gains across model scales (Table 3).

An ablation shows setting classifier-free guidance to zero (CFG=0) alone in late generation stages gives a 1.5x speedup with minimal quality loss, while combining CFG=0 with low-rank approximation techniques yields the full 3.4x speedup (Table 5).
FasterVAR outperforms existing acceleration baselines FastVAR (2.75x speedup) and SkipVAR (2.62x speedup) at comparable or better output quality (baseline comparison, Table 3).
On COCO2014 and COCO2017 image generation, FasterVAR maintains comparable FID/IS scores to the unaccelerated baseline (e.g., COCO2014 FID 26.91 vs. 26.64 baseline; IS 42.18 vs. 42.61) (Table 4).

The method is motivated by a three-stage observation of VAR generation distinguishing semantic/structure establishment from later fidelity-refinement stages, where classifier-free guidance becomes semantically irrelevant (Figure 1, Figure 2).

u6zp8zZ8Ou.text: In non-negative, beta-smooth stochastic convex optimization under a strong flatness condition, flat empirical minima can incur population risk of Omega(1) while sharp minima in the same setting generalize optimally (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).

SA-GD converges to a flat (rho-flat) empirical minimum at rate O(1/eta T) on the empirical risk, but its population risk lower bound is Omega(eta^2 (r-rho)^2 T), showing fast flat-minimum convergence does not guarantee generalization (Theorem 2 and Theorem 3, Section 3.2).

SAM achieves the same empirical convergence rate as SA-GD, O(1/eta T + beta max{r-rho,0}^2), yet can converge to a sharp (non-flat) minimizer even when rho-flat minimizers exist, exhibiting a sharpness-empirical-risk gap of Omega(r^2) (Theorem 4 and Theorem 5, Section 3.3).

Under realizability (rho=0), SAM's population risk has a lower bound of Omega(eta^2 r^2 T), matching stability-based upper bounds established via algorithmic stability (Theorem 6 and Theorem 8, Appendix A).

YVk8EDxBWx.text: Mixture-model-like Ensemble (ME) reinterprets LLM ensembling as sampling from a mixture model, stochastically selecting a single model to invoke at each decoding step rather than querying all ensemble members (Section 3.2).

ME is mathematically proven to produce token distributions identical to conventional ensembling, i.e. P(x_{t+1}=y|x_{<=t}) = sum_i lambda_i M_i(y|x_{<=t}), while invoking only one model per generation step (Equation 2, Section 3.2).
ME achieves a 1.78x speedup over conventional sequential ensembling for two-model ensembles and a 2.65x-2.68x speedup for three-model ensembles (Table 4).
ME uses a lazy key-value cache synchronization strategy to avoid recomputation when switching between models across decoding steps (Section 3.3).

ME matches conventional ensemble performance across both similar and heterogeneous model combinations on GSM8K, MMLU, BBH, and ARC, and this robustness holds across H100, A100, V100, and RTX 3090 GPUs (Tables 2-3, Figure 3).
ME's mixture-model formulation requires sampling-based decoding and does not apply to greedy (argmax) token selection (Section 3.5).

0Mvm3lqLjF.text: DiscoGen procedurally generates over 400 million distinct algorithm discovery tasks via a combinatorial formula N_tasks = 2*3*b*(2^m-1)*(3^d-2^(d+1)+1) depending on the number of modules m, datasets d, and backends b (Section 4.2, Equation 1).
Including additional domains beyond the main evaluation set, DiscoGen's total task space reaches approximately 99 billion tasks (Appendix C).
Across the 10 domains used in the main evaluation, per-domain task counts range from 900 (Greenhouse Gas Prediction) to 426,043,800 (On-Policy RL), with a median of 59,622 tasks per domain (Table 1).

DiscoBench provides a fixed evaluation subset built from DiscoGen, comprising, for each domain, m single-module tasks (DiscoBench Single) plus one comprehensive all-modules-active task (DiscoBench All) (Section 4.4).
As the number of editable modules increases in DiscoBench tasks, agent success rates consistently decline while the achievable performance ceiling rises (Appendix G).

0Cq8Cqvuq4.text: FreeRet is evaluated as a training-free retriever across 46 datasets spanning image classification, VQA, information retrieval, visual grounding, and video tasks from the MMEB and MMEB-V2 benchmarks (Section 4.2, Table 1).
FreeRet-2B, built on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, scores 60.3% on MMEB, outperforming GME-7B (51.9%) despite GME being trained on 8 million pairs (Table 1).
FreeRet-7B scores 70.7% on MMEB, exceeding MMRet-7B (44.0%), which was trained on 26.2 million pairs, and a Qwen2.5-VL-32B FreeRet variant reaches 73.3%, surpassing supervised methods (Table 1).
On MMEB-V2 video tasks, FreeRet achieves 63.2% on video classification and 39.3% on video retrieval using Qwen2.5-VL-7B, without any task-specific training (Table 2).

FreeRet combines semantic embeddings that bypass lexical alignment layers with reasoning-based MCQ-style reranking that mitigates a framing effect via neutral choice framing, with each component validated via ablations (Section 3.2-3.4, Section 4.3).

DQK5CYXCYd.text: FAIL fine-tunes FLUX using only 13,000 demonstrations from Gemini 3 Pro, improving UniGen-Bench score from 61.61 to 73.70 with the FAIL-PD variant and reaching 87.32 overall on DPG-Bench.
FAIL-PD improves the HPDv3 aesthetic score to 11.28, outperforming the FLUX.1 Dev baseline's 10.43.

FAIL generalizes to discrete image generation, where FAIL-PG raises the Xomni model's UniGen-Bench score from a 41.36 SFT baseline to 54.24, and to video generation, where FAIL-PG increases Wan2.1's VBench semantic score from 46.27 to 51.75.

FAIL functions as a regularizer against reward hacking: combining FAIL-PD with reward-gradient optimization prevents performance degradation while achieving the highest HPSv3 (12.94) and UnifiedReward (3.4832) scores among tested combinations (Section 3.5).

mK3xWE7p2T.text: ALGD's augmented Lagrangian introduces a positive semidefinite curvature correction term that locally convexifies the energy landscape while provably preserving the optimal policy distribution and objective value of the original constrained problem (Theorem 3.2).
ALGD bounds the KL-divergence discrepancy between the learned and target Boltzmann distributions as O(1/N), where N is the number of Monte Carlo cost samples used for score estimation (Theorem 3.3).

Standard (non-augmented) Lagrangian safe RL suffers from unstable dual variable updates and oscillations in the induced Boltzmann distribution, which ALGD's convexified energy landscape is shown to smooth out (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

ALGD is benchmarked against primal-dual safe RL baselines (CAL, SAC+Lag, SAC+AugLag, PPO+Lag) and a hard-constrained Hamilton-Jacobi reachability baseline across Safety-Gym and velocity-constrained MuJoCo environments, achieving competitive reward with fewer constraint violations (Section 4, Figure 3).

Increasing the number of Monte Carlo cost samples N from 2 to 16 raises ALGD's per-step GPU inference time only modestly, from 5.3±0.8 ms to 5.9±0.8 ms on the PointPush1 task, while improving training stability, consistent with the O(1/N) error bound (Table 2, Figure 4).

ZR1GOaadgP.text: The simplest Gumbel-max post-hoc watermarking scheme dominates the Pareto frontier of quality-versus-detectability tradeoffs under nucleus sampling, outperforming more recent alternatives such as DiPMark and MorphMark (Section 4.2, Figure 2).

Larger language models preserve semantic fidelity better during post-hoc rephrasing but struggle to reach low detection p-values due to lower output entropy, whereas smaller models more effectively hide strong watermark signals (Section 4.3, Figure 3).

Beam search decoding, especially with biased scoring, consistently improves the quality-detectability Pareto frontier relative to standard sampling across watermarking schemes (Section 4.4, Figure 4).
Entropy-aware detection filtering yields only modest gains, never exceeding 20%, with most watermarking configurations retaining just 30-40 successful detection settings (Section 4.5, Figure 5).

On verifiable code text (HumanEval/MBPP), all post-hoc watermarking methods face a heavily constrained tradeoff between pass@1 functional correctness and detectability, with Gumbel-max still achieving the best Pareto frontier and smaller models again outperforming larger ones (Section 4.6, Figures 6-7, Table 3).
Non-English languages exhibit a steeper quality-detectability tradeoff than English under post-hoc watermarking, as shown in the multilingual robustness evaluation (Section 4.7, Table 4).

1IQTouHYl2.text: OMP achieves an average success rate of 82.3%±1.7% across evaluated tasks, compared to 78.9%±2.1% for MP1, 71.6%±3.5% for FlowPolicy, and 68.7%±4.7% for DP3 (Table 1).
OMP improves over MP1 by +9.4% on Meta-World Medium, +4.4% on Meta-World Hard, and +10.6% on Meta-World Very Hard difficulty tasks (Section 5, Table 1).

OMP's directional alignment module uses a cosine loss to prevent gradient starvation in low-velocity, high-precision motions, where standard MSE loss signals become negligible since they scale with the product of vector magnitudes (Section 4.3).
Removing the cosine loss term (-L_cos) in the ablation study degrades performance across tasks, confirming the contribution of directional alignment to OMP (Table 2).

OMP is evaluated across 37 simulated manipulation tasks (3 Adroit, 34 Meta-World) using 10 expert demonstrations per task and 3 random seeds, while performing single-step (NFE=1) inference (Section 5).

yUEFOa32CG.text: Task-loss-matching stitching methods can fabricate the appearance of functional alignment by overfitting to the downstream task, exhibiting irregular behavior on adversarially trained non-robust-to-robust model pairs (Section 3.1).

Functional Latent Alignment (FuLA) optimizes an affine stitching transformation that minimizes feature distances both at the stitching point and at subsequent layers, rather than only at the stitching level as in direct matching (Section 2, FuLA method).

On adversarially trained networks, FuLA correctly reports non-existent functional similarity at the penultimate layer between non-robust and robust models, unlike task-based stitching methods that report fabricated robustness (Section 3.1).
In the shortcut-learning setting, alignment-based methods including FuLA retain clean-data accuracy while task-based methods (TLM, SLM) exploit spurious cues and degrade clean accuracy (Section 3.2).

Cross-layer stitching experiments show a persistent directionality in functional similarity even under FuLA's task-agnostic criterion, indicating that earlier layers can retain functionally relevant information when guided by deeper layers (Section 3.3).

nd0hT1eyEo.text: Generative reward models exhibit outcome-process inconsistency, with 20-30% of correct preference predictions accompanied by flawed critiques, including 44.24% for RM-R1-DeepSeek-Distilled-Qwen-7B, 33.62% for Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and 26.10% for Gemini-2.5-Pro (Section 2.2, Figure 2).
RM-NLHF-Qwen-32B achieves an overall benchmark score of 0.7296, versus 0.7037 for RM-R1-Qwen-32B and 0.7009 for RRM-Qwen-32B across the evaluation suite (Section 4.2, Table 2).
Using similarity with human core critiques as a process-reward proxy achieves 91.84% accuracy, outperforming direct LLM judgment of critique quality at 73.47% accuracy (Section 2.3).
RM-NLHF's online MetaRM component learns to predict process rewards from limited human-annotated critiques and generalizes this signal to unlabeled samples during training (Section 3.2).
On downstream best-of-8 sampling, RM-NLHF improves MATH500 accuracy to 67.60% (versus 65.99% for outcome-only reward models) and HumanEval+ to 85.98% (versus 75.00%) (Section 4.4, Table 4).

YvqOTT5S9Y.text: ECCO achieves a 24.44% average reduction in cycles over the LLVM opt -O3 baseline across 7 benchmark suites (blas, cbench, chstone, mibench, npb, opencv, tensorflow) (Table 1).
ECCO outperforms the CFAST (23.70%) and GRACE (23.14%) baselines, while direct LLM prompting without the collaborative search only reaches about 16.0-16.6% cycle reduction (Table 1).
The causal dataset creation stage uses iterative greedy pruning to shrink average optimization sequence length from 18.5 to 4.5 passes, a 73.7% reduction (Section 3.1).
Removing Chain-of-Thought supervision drops standalone LLM performance to 1.27% at N=1 (greedy), and removing evidence signals drops it to 3.52% at N=1, versus 16.54% for the full model (Table 2).
An interpretability audit using five LLM judges finds 91.05% consensus faithfulness for ECCO's causal reasoning outputs (Table 3).

The Strategist-Tactician collaborative inference stage closes a roughly 5 percentage-point 'tactical gap' between standalone LLM performance (about 19.74%) and the full GA-assisted system (24.44%) (Section 3.3).

daiccpXZfU.text: For n agents and m alternatives with epsilon-quantized utilities and thresholds, the deterministic algorithm finds a unanimously acceptable lottery or certifies infeasibility using O(n^2 + nm log(1/epsilon)) membership queries (Algorithm 2, Theorem 3.3).

The randomized algorithm achieves expected query complexity O(nm log n + min{n, m^3 log n} * m log(1/epsilon)) by sampling agents via weight-biased Clarkson-style reweighting (Algorithm 3, Theorem 3.4).
A single agent's acceptability halfspace can be recovered using O(m log(1/epsilon)) queries via the LearnHyperplane subroutine (Algorithm 1, Lemmas 3.1-3.2).
Any correct algorithm requires Omega((n - min{n,m}) + (min{n,m} - 1) log(1/epsilon)) queries in the worst case, and even for a single agent (n=1) Omega(m) queries are necessary (Theorems 4.1-4.2).

With a predicted agent ordering of quality R(sigma-hat), a learning-augmented algorithm reduces query complexity to O((n + m log(1/epsilon)) * R(sigma-hat)), degrading smoothly as prediction quality worsens (Theorems 5.1-5.2).

UUJQGmt5GS.text: The 4DPC2hat-200K dataset contains over 44,000 dynamic object sequences from Objaverse, 700,000 point cloud frames, and 200,000 curated question-answer pairs spanning counting, temporal relationship, action, spatial relationship, and appearance categories (Section 2, Table 1).

The architecture encodes each 16-frame, 8192-point sequence with a Point-BERT encoder and models temporal dynamics with a bidirectional Mamba module before projecting into an LLM's language embedding space (Section 3.1).

4DPC2hat scores 73.27 on GPT-4-based captioning evaluation versus 54.70 for the strongest baseline (MiniGPT-3D), and 78.01 on overall QA versus 59.08 for MiniGPT-3D, also outperforming PointLLM and ShapeLLM (Tables 2-3).

Failure-aware bootstrapping iteratively identifies model deficiencies via semantic similarity evaluation and synthesizes corrective QA supervision using Qwen-3, with two bootstrapping iterations yielding roughly a 4-point improvement (Section 3.2, Section 4.5).

Ablations show the bidirectional Mamba temporal module outperforms a Temporal Transformer alternative, and failure-aware bootstrapping substantially outperforms naive data augmentation (Section 4.5, Figures 5-6).

gLRqqQOM9K.text: Theorem 1 proves CARS produces unbiased samples from the constrained distribution P^L while the adaptive updates in Line 6 of Algorithm 1 monotonically increase the probability that a valid sequence is yielded in subsequent loop iterations (Section 3, Theorem 1).

CARS tracks invalid prefixes with a trie and reweights the sampling distribution as R^W(ua|u) = P(ua|u) * (p_ua/p_u), subtracting the probability mass of newly discovered invalid prefixes via upward propagation in the trie (Section 3).

On molecular synthesis, CARS requires 183±28 samples to obtain 100 valid outputs versus 793±127 for standard rejection sampling, a 4.3x improvement in sample efficiency, while matching adaptive rejection sampling's validity (0.87±0.09) and diversity (0.85±0.06) (Section 4.2, Table 1).

On PDDL planning, CARS achieves 66% valid samples for the Qwen model versus 54% for adaptive rejection sampling, and 61% valid samples for the Llama model where standard and adaptive rejection sampling time out (Section 4.3, Table 2).

On XML grammar-based fuzzing, CARS is the only exact method able to complete the benchmark, needing 215 LM generations for 100 valid samples and reaching 9.9% branch coverage versus 7.2% for GCD and 9.6% for MCMC (Section 4.1).
On SyGuS benchmarks, CARS uses 16x fewer LM calls than adaptive rejection sampling (geometric mean) on the BV4 track and a 4.5x improvement on the SLIA track (Appendix H, Figure 9).

oqkiE71wrC.text: Under Assumption 1.1 (constant conditional mean mu and variance sigma^2 for X_t in [0,1], without independence or identical distribution), Theorem 4.1 constructs nonnegative supermartingales S_t+ and S_t- underlying a confidence sequence for the variance sigma^2 (Corollary 4.2).
Corollaries 4.3 and 4.4 give upper and lower empirical Bernstein inequalities for the variance that hold without assuming independence or identical distribution (Section 4, Corollaries 4.3-4.4).

Corollary 4.8 shows that sqrt(n)(U_n - D_n) and sqrt(n)(L_n) converge almost surely to sqrt(2*Var[(X_i-mu)^2]*log(1/alpha)), matching the first-order term of the oracle Bernstein inequality under the additional constant-conditional-variance-of-squares Assumption 4.5, establishing asymptotic sharpness (Theorem 4.6, Theorem 4.7, Corollary 4.8).

Theorem 4.10 extends the anytime-valid Bennett-type inequality to vector-valued random variables in a separable Hilbert space under a diameter-1 ball constraint (Assumption 4.9), with Corollary A.6 proving the same asymptotic sharpness result holds in this setting (Section 4.5, Appendix A, Theorem 4.10, Corollary A.6).

8ppVmLtA2V.text: On the LoCoMo benchmark with Qwen3-4B, Mem-T achieves 58.65 overall F1, exceeding A-Mem (39.43 F1) by 14.92 points and Mem0 (43.71 F1) by 14.94 points (Section 4.2, Table 2).
Mem-T reduces inference tokens per query by approximately 24.45% relative to GAM while maintaining superior accuracy on the same benchmarks (Section 4.2).
On out-of-domain evaluation covering HotpotQA, LongMemEval, and NarrativeQA, Mem-T reaches 66.35 F1 on HotpotQA, outperforming Mem-α by 7.55 points (Table 3).
Mem-T's MoT-GRPO reinforcement learning framework densifies sparse rewards via memory operation tree backpropagation and hindsight credit assignment (Section 4.2).
Mem-T achieves a favorable accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier relative to competing memory frameworks (Figures 3-4).

03KQGUvw1e.text: CANDI introduces discrete identity corruption ρ(t), whose dependence on vocabulary size |V| is exponential, and continuous rank degradation r(t)=Φ(-1/(σ(t)√2)), which is independent of vocabulary size, to explain 'temporal dissonance' in continuous diffusion on discrete data (Figure 3).

CANDI's structured noising kernel combines discrete masking with a linear keep-rate schedule α(t)=1-t and Gaussian noise targeting a rank-degradation schedule r*(t)=(r_max-r_min)·t+r_min (CANDI Architecture / Structured Noising Kernel section).

On large-vocabulary OpenWebText (~50k tokens), pure continuous diffusion collapses while CANDI matches masked diffusion performance; on small-vocabulary Text8, continuous diffusion remains reasonably performant (Figure 6).
CANDI outperforms masked diffusion (MDLM) at low numbers of function evaluations (NFE ≤ 64) for text generation by exploiting learned continuous gradients (Figure 7).

CANDI enables classifier-based guided generation on QM9 using off-the-shelf classifiers via simple gradient addition during sampling, without diffusion-specific classifier training, achieving competitive guidance performance (Figure 8).

A sampling trick described in Appendix B.3 avoids expensive one-hot matrix multiplications by operating in embedding space, preserving computational efficiency while retaining continuous geometry benefits (Appendix B.3).

kpJIOi10TX.text: ScaleSim introduces 'invocation distance' as an abstraction for estimating agent request ordering to enable proactive prefetching and priority-based memory eviction (Section 3.2).

ScaleSim achieves up to 1.74x end-to-end speedup over SGLang on an information-diffusion simulation with predefined interaction paths, and up to 1.73x speedup on the independent-simulation AgentSociety benchmark (Figure 8).
On the interaction-involved Generative Agents benchmark, ScaleSim achieves up to 1.31x speedup over SGLang, a smaller gain than on independent or predefined-path simulations (Figure 8).
ScaleSim reduces time-to-first-token by 48%-68% compared to HiCache under high agent concurrency (Figure 10).
ScaleSim exhibits roughly linear execution-time scaling with agent population growth in AgentSociety, consistently incurring lower per-step execution time than baselines (Figure 9).

6C4YQcq8YX.text: OMAC identifies five optimization dimensions for LLM-based multi-agent systems: refining existing agent prompts/few-shot examples (Fun-1), creating new agents (Fun-2), selecting candidate agents pre-collaboration (Str-1), dynamically choosing agents per collaboration step (Str-2), and optimizing inter-agent communication patterns (Str-3) (Section 3).

OMAC's single-dimension optimization uses two LLM-powered actors, a Semantic Initializer and a Contrastive Comparator that refines designs from performance gaps between positive-negative pairs, described in Section 3.2, 'Optimization for a Single Dimension'.
On general reasoning tasks, OMAC's Fun-1 optimization reaches 74.22% accuracy versus the best baseline DyLAN at 69.42%, a 4.8-point improvement (Table 1, Section 4.1).
On code generation tasks, OMAC's Fun-1 optimization reaches 89.25% versus DyLAN's 85.74%, a 3.51-point improvement (Table 2, Section 4.1).
On arithmetic reasoning tasks, OMAC's Fun-1 optimization reaches 35.21% versus DyLAN's 32.35%, a 2.86-point improvement (Table 3, Section 4.1).

Joint multi-dimensional optimization in OMAC yields significant performance improvements over optimizing any single dimension alone, though iterative (rather than simultaneous) multi-dimension optimization proves more effective (Section 4.1).

RQJjbqIcz0.text: PlotCraft is a benchmark of 982 visualization tasks (491 single-turn, 491 multi-turn) spanning 48 chart types, 7 visualization intents, and 8 thematic domains with 31 fine-grained sub-topics, built on 140 core datasets (Benchmark Structure section).
Evaluation of 23 leading LLMs on PlotCraft reveals substantial performance deficiencies on complex, interactive visualization tasks (Section on evaluation results).
SynthVis-30K is a 30,000-instance multi-modal dataset of visualization code spanning the same 48 chart types and 31 topics, created via a collaborative agent framework (SynthVis-30K Dataset section).
PlotCraftor-30B-A3B achieves a 25% overall performance improvement on PlotCraft and over 50% improvement on hard-difficulty tasks compared to its base model (Table 2).

PlotCraftor outperforms Qwen3-Coder-480B by 7% despite being a much smaller model, and reaches comparable performance to the proprietary Claude-4.1-Opus on standard cross-benchmarks (Table 2, Table 3).
On cross-benchmark evaluation, PlotCraftor attains 93.81% pass rate on VisEval and 96.0% pass rate on PandasPlotBench (Table 3).

qzw67boFSq.text: SEPS integrates dense MLLM-generated (LLaVa) captions with sparse original captions to address patch redundancy and ambiguity in cross-modal alignment, via the SDTPS and HRPA modules (Section 3).
On Flickr30K 1K test set with a ViT-Base-224 backbone, SEPS achieves Text-to-Image Recall@1/5/10 of 86.9/98.1/99.2 and an rSum of 560.9 (Table 1).
On MS-COCO 5K test set with a ViT-Base-224 backbone, SEPS achieves Image-to-Text Recall@1 of 73.9, Text-to-Image Recall@1 of 73.5, and an rSum of 516.9 (Table 1).
SEPS improves rSum by 23%-86% over prior approaches across backbones and datasets (Section 1).

Ablating the dense-text component of SDTPS drops Text-to-Image R@1 on Flickr30K from 86.9% to 67.2% (sparse-text-only), and ablating relevance-aware selection in HRPA drops it to 82.6% (Table 2, Section 4.5).
SEPS outperforms the D2S-VSE baseline on Flickr30K Text-to-Image R@1 by 18.4 percentage points (86.9% vs 68.5%) (Table 1).

iJNYi8dwr4.text: Speedup Patch (SuP) formalizes embodied-policy acceleration as a Constrained MDP, using a recurrent world model's predicted state deviation as a surrogate safety constraint to train an offline downsampling scheduler via IQL (Section 3, Section 4).
On the Bigym benchmark (20 tasks) with an ACT policy, SuP achieves a 2.01x execution speedup while maintaining a 0.67 success rate (Table 1).
On the Libero benchmark (40 tasks) with a pi0.5 policy, SuP achieves a 1.35x speedup while maintaining a 0.973 success rate, compared to 1.34x speedup at 0.937 success for VLA-Adapter (Table 2).

In real-world evaluation across three tasks (Arrange Table, Fold Towel, Stack Plates) with pi0.5, SuP achieves a 2.17x speedup at 0.611 average success rate, versus DemoSpeedup's 2.07x speedup at 0.600 success (Table 4).
SuP's scheduler uses only 5.12M parameters compared to the 4B-parameter DemoSpeedup baseline, and requires no policy retraining, unlike DemoSpeedup (Section 5, Table 4).

An ADM-based world model outperforms an MLP-based world model baseline in Spearman correlation between predicted deviation and success rate across Libero suites, and maintains a monotonic violation-success relationship where the MLP does not (Table 5, Figure 7, Section 5.4).

jO7tsly51F.text: CSMR (Cognitive Scheduling for Multimodal Reasoning) has a language model maintain a reasoning state and dynamically schedule visual evidence acquisition instead of converting all visual information upfront, via CRC and PVP components (Section 5).
On M3CoT, CSMR achieves 45.7% accuracy in the zero-shot multimodal reasoning setting, outperforming ICoT, DDCoT, and Caption baselines (Table 1).
On ScienceQA, CSMR achieves 78.2% accuracy, and on LLaVA-Bench In-the-Wild it achieves 34.3 ROUGE-L, both exceeding the compared baselines (Table 1).

Removing dynamic visual querying from CSMR drops M3CoT accuracy from 45.7% to 40.0%, removing reasoning-driven query generation drops it to 40.1%, and removing flexible termination drops it to 42.7% (Table 2, Section 6.5).

CSMR mitigates linguistic dominance/bias by letting the language model decide when to invoke the visual perception module, based on attention-bias findings presented in the empirical analysis (Section 4).
CSMR achieves these gains without additional training, compared against No-CoT, Caption, CCoT, DDCoT, SCAFFOLD, and ICoT baselines (Section 6).

Sd1014TyrA.text: CG-MLLM uses a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture combining a token-level autoregressive transformer (TokenAR) and a block-level autoregressive transformer (BlockAR) bound to serial/parallel generation modes rather than fixed tasks, operating over a pretrained vision-language backbone and a 3D VAE latent space (Section 3, Section 3.4).
On MLLM-based 3D generation, CG-MLLM achieves p-FID of 12.55 and p-KID of 0.27, improving over ShapeLLM-Omni (13.11 p-FID, 0.29 p-KID) and SAR3D (30.07 p-FID, 1.00 p-KID) (Table 1).
CG-MLLM achieves a CLIP-IQA+ score of 0.45 and MUSIQ score of 71.65, versus 0.37/55.71 for ShapeLLM-Omni and 0.42/66.01 for SAR3D (Table 1).
CG-MLLM outperforms LLaVA-13B, InstructBLIP-13B, and Qwen3-VL-2B on 3D captioning BLEU-1, ROUGE-L, and METEOR among image-based methods (Table 2).

Ablations show Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) produces substantially higher training loss than the baseline normalization, indicating incompatibility with the multimodal architecture (Section 4.3).

The model is trained with progressive resolution training, increasing sequence length from 512 to 4096 tokens across two stages with classifier-free guidance dropout varying from 90% to 10% (Section 3.5).

lTXvOhUOl2.text: Plasticity is formally defined (Definition 1) as the expected ratio of output change to input change over a distribution of token-sequence pairs, where a module with plasticity greater than 1 is non-smooth/plastic and less than 1 is smooth (Section 3).

Theoretical upper bounds derived for LayerNorm, feedforward linear layers, and multi-head self-attention (Propositions 1-4) predict a plasticity ranking of MHA > FC1 approx FC2 > LN2 approx LN1 (Section 4).
This theoretical ranking is empirically confirmed on ViT-Base and ViT-Huge (Figure 3) as well as on DINOv3 and GPT-2 (Section 5.1, Figure 4), and holds across the layer depth.

Across roughly 1,000 finetuning runs on 11 image classification benchmarks with SGD, finetuning only the attention module (MHA) achieves the best average top-1 accuracy of 90.8%, versus 90.7% (FC1), 90.3% (FC2), 89.9% (LN2), and 89.8% (LN1) (Table 1, Section 5.2).
With the Adam optimizer, finetuning only the attention module again yields the best average accuracy of 82.2% across datasets including Cifar100, Clipart, and Sketch (Table 2).

In a low-data VTAB-style regime with 1,000 training samples per dataset, prioritizing high-plasticity components (MHA at 94.4% average) still outperforms low-plasticity LayerNorm components (Table 3).

HigEPnWgLQ.text: Theorem 4.2 proves that a greedy allocation rule—repeatedly assigning one unit to the individual with the highest next marginal survival probability p_i(l)=Pr(X_i≥l)—optimally solves the single-round allocation problem for any realized frontier and budget (Theorem 4.2).
