Proposition 6.1 shows that even allocation of budget across the frontier optimally maximizes expected recruits at the population level due to discrete concavity, forming the basis of the surrogate value function U_P(r,n) (Proposition 6.1).

Theorem 6.2 shows the population-level surrogate value function U_P(r,n) can be computed in O(b^5 log b) time and O(b^2) space using probability generating functions to track frontier-size transitions, where b is the total budget (Theorem 6.2).

Theorem 7.2 decomposes multi-round suboptimality into three additive terms—frontier estimation error scaling as 2(1+γ)r·Σ_i‖D_i−D̂_i‖_TV, population model error c_{r,γ}·‖P−P̂‖_TV, and surrogate approximation error c_{r,γ}r·E[‖D−D̄‖_TV]—each linear in remaining budget r (Theorem 7.2).

On HIV transmission network data from the ICPSR dataset, the adaptive surrogate policy outperforms best-tuned constant allocation policies (k∈{2,3,5,10}) and fixed-fraction greedy policies by avoiding brittle parameter selection under model misspecification (Section 8, experiments).

dw5BM3OQfZ.text: On the MDLM model with the RTP negation set, the Safety-Aware Denoiser (SAD) reduces the unsafe generation rate from a 38.4% baseline to 32.6% while leaving BERTScore essentially unchanged (0.554 to 0.555) (Table 1).
On LLaDA-8B, SAD reduces the hazard-taxonomy unsafe rate from a 19.8% baseline to between 14.8% and 17.6% depending on the negation dataset used, with no measurable quality degradation (Table 1).
Against the PAD parallel-decoding jailbreak attack, SAD reduces attack success rate from 45.6% to 29.6% on LLaDA-Instruct and from 43.6% to 29.0% on LLaDA-1.5 (Table 2).

When the negation set is matched to training data, SAD reduces fuzzy training-data overlap from an 18.59% baseline at strength parameter η=128, with BERTScore changing only slightly from 0.5152 to 0.5107 (Figure 3).

SAD matches the safety performance of Feynman-Kac (FK) Steering at 34× lower wall-clock cost while achieving better perplexity, and safety gains from increasing the unsafe reference set saturate around N≈500-1000 examples (Section on baseline comparisons and ablations).

f7PUjzI60h.text: Neural Modular Physics (NMP) decomposes elastic dynamics into a Neural Constitutive Module, which predicts first Piola-Kirchhoff stress from deformation gradients via rotation-equivariant MLPs, and a Neural Integration Module, which predicts velocity increments using a canonicalization network for translation/rotation invariance (Section on core architecture).
On 1,000-step long-horizon rollouts of the Cube task, NMP achieves an RMSE of 0.535 versus 1.554 for the MeshGraphNet baseline, a roughly 60% error reduction (long-horizon stability experiments).

NMP generalizes to mesh resolutions unseen during training, scaling from 10,648 to 21,952 vertices while remaining stable, despite being trained only on rollouts of ≤200 steps (generalization experiments).

NMP reduces the proportion of tetrahedra exceeding 5% volume change by 52% compared to the leading neural baseline, demonstrating better physical-constraint preservation (physical soundness experiments).
NMP runs roughly 40× faster than traditional physics simulators and about 5× faster than the neural operator baseline Transolver (efficiency experiments).

P3Mnh7mF5a.text: Theorem 2 proves that a model trained via SFT on shortest-path (optimal) trajectories converges to forward transition probabilities of 1 but keeps backward-pointing transition probabilities fixed at their pretrained values of L/(L+1) and 1/(L+1), i.e., it never learns to backtrack (Theorem 2).

Theorem 3 proves that RLVR training drives all four transition probabilities (a_j, b_j, c_j, d_j) arbitrarily close to 1 in finite time by incorporating the model's own failed exploration trajectories during policy-gradient updates (Theorem 3).

Theorem 4 establishes an exponential inference-time compute separation: RLVR-trained policies require Θ(WK) expected steps to reach the goal versus Θ(W·L^K) for SFT-trained policies, on a graph with W parallel branches, depth K, and L multi-edges per junction (Theorem 4).
Corollary 1 shows that even equipping the SFT policy with a duplicate-state-avoiding search agent only improves its complexity to Θ(WKL), still a factor of L worse than RLVR's Θ(WK) (Corollary 1).

Theorem 5 shows that distilling RLVR-generated reasoning traces via supervised fine-tuning recovers the efficient Θ(WK) complexity, and synthetic experiments with W=15, K=15, L=5 confirm hitting times converging to the predicted 4WK=900 (Theorem 5, Figure 3).

s7wV3xGQFL.text: Theorem 3.2 shows on-policy DPO converges exponentially (linearly per round) in the number of iterations K once the per-round batch size exceeds a generalized coverage threshold C*_p(R), with total sample complexity O~(R^2/ε^2 ∨ (ln R/ε)·C*_p(R)) (Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 2.2 proves any offline learner sampling from a fixed base policy π0 requires Ω(1/ε^2 · C*_p(R)) samples to reach error ε, a quadratic-in-1/ε separation from the on-policy rate (Theorem 2.2).

Theorem 4.4 shows a hybrid sampler using preferential G-optimal experimental design (via Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence with centered features) achieves ‖θ̂_2 − θ*‖ ≤ ε in just two rounds with sample complexity O~(dR^2/ε^2 · log(1/δ)), removing dependence on the coverage constant (Theorem 4.4).

Theorem 5.1 shows on-policy reward-distillation methods that learn reward differences rather than preferences converge at rate O(n^-1 ∨ e^{-Ω(K)}), faster than preference-based on-policy DPO but inheriting reward-model error ε_RM (Theorem 5.1).

On the general-chat UltraFeedback benchmark, the proposed on-policy distillation approach achieves a 45.44% AlpacaEval win-rate versus 41.26% for the offline baseline, while naive REBEL-style distillation degrades performance unless calibrated (RDRC) (Section on experimental validation).

u4uFwVwZGr.text: AdaVoMP generates Sparse Adaptive Voxel (SAV) trees at up to 1024^3 resolution, 16x higher than the 64^3 resolution used by prior VoMP methods (Section 3, Table 5).
At 1024^3 resolution on Young's Modulus prediction, AdaVoMP-H achieves 0.8841 Pa absolute displacement error versus 1.1371 Pa for VoMP, and 0.0917 relative error versus 0.1226 (Table 1).
On the GVT-Hard challenging subset at 1024^3 resolution, AdaVoMP-H achieves 1.2440 Pa error on Young's Modulus versus 1.6680 Pa for VoMP, with larger gaps on complex geometries (Table 2).
Generated SAV trees occupy only 9.14% of the voxels of an equivalent dense 64^3 grid while maintaining prediction accuracy, compared to 7.24% for ground-truth SAV trees (Table 5, Table 6).

The Adaptive Material Generator (Section 4.2) performs autoregressive coarse-to-fine prediction of Empty/Keep/Subdivide structure labels and material latents, enabling natural test-time compute scaling to lower-resolution outputs shown across model scales S, B, B+, L, L+, H (Figure 4).
AdaVoMP-H was trained on 32xA100-80GB GPUs for 5 days over a dataset of 149.50M input tokens and 1.62B output tokens, using a 0.6B-parameter model (Section 5.1).

L0xGI4e0BF.text: LDA (Lie Diffuser Actor) treats SE(3) poses via left-invariant SDEs and predicts scores in the tangent space se(3), retracting samples to the manifold via the exponential map, rather than representing poses as flat R^12 vectors as in prior diffusion-based VLA policies (Section 4, Section 4.1).

LDA provably eliminates manifold drift (Proposition 4.1), guarantees left-invariant equivariance of the score function under rigid transformations (Theorem 4.2), and generates geodesic, kinematically optimal screw-motion trajectories (Proposition 4.3).

On CALVIN ABC->D, LDA trained for only 300K steps achieves an average task chain length of 3.51 versus 3.27 for 3D Diffuser Actor trained for 600K steps, a +7.3% improvement with fewer training iterations (Table 1, Section 5.2).

During reverse diffusion, LDA maintains SO(3) orthogonality violations near floating-point precision (~10^-7) and unit quaternion norm throughout, whereas the Euclidean baseline exhibits violations reaching O(10^0) magnitude and quaternion norm deviating between 0.5 and 2.0 (Section 5.4, Figure 5).
Applying LDA to OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO-Long improves success rate from 92.20% to 94.13% (+2.6%), demonstrating generality beyond the 3D Diffuser Actor backbone (Appendix C).

On four real-robot manipulation tasks (20 trials each), LDA improves Move Doll Platform success from 90% to 100% and Sort Blocks from 55% to 75%, with mixed results on Put Block in Box and Stack Cups (Table 2, Section 5.3).

PWhmZ04OTr.text: Without protection, obfuscated prompts show extreme cross-LLM portability, e.g. 98.78% relative performance transfer on HumanEval across models, whereas PragLocker reduces mean cross-LLM portability to a 0.20x ratio versus a 1.00x baseline and 0.99x for a code-only obfuscation variant (Table 2, Section 4.2).

PragLocker preserves target-model utility at a 1.01x relative mean performance across three agent frameworks (LessonL, ReadAgent, A-MEM) and three foundation LLMs, indicating negligible performance degradation on the intended model (Table 3, Section 4.2).

Even within the same model family, PragLocker prompts show poor intra-family portability: NarrativeQA performance drops from 16.21 on the original target Qwen2.5 variant to between 5.96 and 8.12 when transferred to other sizes/quantizations of Qwen2.5 (Table 4, Section 4.4).

Against adaptive attackers, PragLocker remains robust: LLM-assisted recovery yields only a 3.49x relative performance gain, a deobfuscation attack with known methodology yields only a 1.03x improvement, and naive prompt synthesis from scratch outperforms attempted recovery at 4.78x (Table 5, Section 4.5).
Theorem 3.2 establishes the existence of non-portable, utility-preserving obfuscated prompts via stability-region analysis and attention-dilution mechanics (Section 3.2).

PragLocker's two-phase pipeline (Algorithm 1) first converts prompts to a code-symbol form (prompt initialization) and then applies noise-injected random-search optimization combining task loss, distance loss, and non-language loss (Section 3.3, Figure 1).

Cdi2lBTm3M.text: On unconditional generation of 1000 molecules with 30 heavy atoms, MacroGuide applied to MolDiff raises the macrocycle generation rate from a 5.3% baseline to 99.7% (Table 1).

On protein-conditioned generation, MacroGuide applied to MolSnapper raises the macrocycle generation rate from a 0.3% baseline to 99.5%, while maintaining 92.5% chemical validity and 100% connectivity (Table 2).

MacroGuide improves PoseBusters all-tests pass rate from 66.3% to 80.5% in the unconditional setting and PoseBusters ligand-tests pass rate from 53.9% to 62.6% in the protein-conditioned setting, while also increasing molecular diversity from 0.707 to 0.771 (unconditional) and 0.626 to 0.712 (conditional) (Table 3, Table 4).
MacroGuide adds approximately 4ms of overhead per denoising step (21ms total versus 17ms for the unguided baseline), a roughly 20% increase in computational cost (Section 4.3.2).

The theoretical formula in Theorem 3.1 relating persistent-homology death time to predicted macrocycle ring size is empirically confirmed with approximately 3% error for target size n=14 (Section 4.3.1).

MacroGuide's topological guidance combines an H1-death term promoting ring formation within a target size range (Eq. 3), an H1-birth term enforcing cycle connectivity via edge-length constraints (Eq. 4), and an H0-death term maintaining overall molecular connectivity (Eq. 5) (Section 3.1).

Csmrtng6PP.text: CARE combines a CLIP-based Text Expert, a fine-tuned CLIP Image Expert adapted via AdaptFormer, and the Base Expert of original noisy labels into a class-adaptive Top-K voting consensus mechanism (Section 2.2-2.4).

On CIFAR-100-LTN under joint noise (imbalance factor 100, noise ratio 50%), CARE+LA achieves 76.7% accuracy versus 79.5% for CLIP+LA, while yielding a +10.0 percentage point improvement over CLIP+RLA (Table 2).
On Food101N with imbalance factor 100, CARE+LA achieves 84.1% accuracy, a +6.9 percentage point improvement over CLIP+RLA at 77.2% (Table 6).
On WebVision-50, CARE+LA achieves 85.3% test accuracy (Table 5).

An ablation shows the full multi-expert integration reduces label noise from 50.0% to 27.8% and yields a +1.6% accuracy gain, with removing either the Text Expert or Image Expert preventing this improvement; the class-adaptive mechanism separately reduces tail-class noise from 72.8% to 53.3% while improving tail-class accuracy by +5.0 percentage points (Table 7, Table 8).

CARE's class-adaptive Top-K voting uses larger K values for head classes and smaller K values for tail classes, with Proposition 4 showing smaller K improves correction precision specifically for tail classes (Section 2.4).

emDhH9VFqm.text: The Boosted Direct Output (BDO) module, defined as Definition 3 in Section 2.3, recursively concatenates prior predictions with input history to generate forecasts over N steps, balancing autoregressive causality with direct-output efficiency (Section 2.3).

ReNF achieves 0.214 MSE / 0.247 MAE on Weather, 0.145 MSE / 0.237 MAE on Electricity, 0.365 MSE / 0.245 MAE on Traffic, and 0.391 MSE / 0.416 MAE on ETTh1 in the main long-term forecasting benchmark comparison (Table 2, Section 3.1).

Theorem 1 (the Multiple Neural Forecasting Theorem, Section 2.2) proves that forecast error is bounded by T(λ+√c(b+σ_t))/√c when multiple candidate outputs are combined, motivating the Variance Reduction Hypothesis (Theorem 1, Section 2.2).

An oracle post-combination experiment empirically validates the Variance Reduction Hypothesis by showing bounds that exceed single-forecast performance across all tested datasets (Table 4, Section 3.3).
Ablations show BDO performance improves as the number of recursive stages K increases from 2 to 6 (Table 3).
Exponential moving average (EMA) smoothing of shadow model parameters (Eq. 5, Section 2.6) reduces validation-test loss inconsistency during training (Figures 6-7, Section 3.2).

ztVp5EqREE.text: GRouter distills routing structure from a fully-trained MoE model and freezes it as a fixed router during target-model pre-training, decoupling routing decisions from representation learning (Section 3.1).
GRouter improves pre-training data utilization by 4.28x, reaching the baseline's validation loss using only 23.3% of the training data (Figure 4, Section 4.1).
GRouter delivers up to 33.5% training throughput acceleration on a single node, versus 19.3% on 2 nodes and 15.5% on 4 nodes (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
Expert Folding (Section 3.2) merges experts via an affinity-based strategy to let the distilled router adapt across different target expert counts.
GRouter improves average downstream performance by 2.8 points across six benchmarks, with gains of up to 10 points on individual tasks (Section 4.1).

5crqGLOpnf.text: ERAlign aligns GNN and LLM layers at fixed intervals via learnable projectors that unify both modalities into a shared d=512 latent space, using empirical Cramér distance as an energy-based alignment objective trained with an energy-discrepancy (ED) minimization scheme that avoids MCMC sampling (Section 4).

ERAlignGNN reaches 90.75% accuracy on Cora, 92.17% on PubMed, and 89.38% on Photo in the fully-supervised setting, outperforming GraphAdapter by 0.6-1.8 percentage points across these text-attributed graph datasets (Table 1, Section 5).
In the semi-supervised setting with only 20% labeled data, ERAlign reaches 52.33% accuracy on Cora, exceeding GLEM by 3.3 points (Table 2, Section 5).
In zero-shot cross-task transfer, ERAlignLLM achieves 60.45% AUC on the Cora link-prediction task, surpassing TEA-GLM by 1.2-3.2 points (Table 3, Section 5).
ERAlign uses LoRA to reduce trainable parameters to 11.3M (a 10x reduction) and trains in 9 hours 11 minutes on the Arxiv dataset, a 3.3-5.2x speedup over GIANT and GLEM baselines (Section 5).

Ai4vdy80p5.text: E2PO introduces learnable embedding-level perturbation tensors optimized jointly for diversity and anchor-consistency, combined with a noise-aware sampling schedule and reference-anchored batching that retains one unperturbed anchor while exploring K-1 perturbed variants per group (Section on Embedding-Perturbed Mechanism).
With G=4 groups and K=12 variants, E2PO attains a 0.932 GenEval score, outperforming DiffusionNFT's 0.922 and Flow-GRPO's 0.776 (Table 1).
E2PO reaches a PickScore of 23.38 while achieving the best diversity metrics on DivGenBench (IDS=0.167, SDI=0.412, PVS=0.301) (Table 2).

An ablation shows that static perturbation strategies introduce visual artifacts, whereas the dynamic noise-aware perturbation schedule preserves image fidelity, and that perturbing only the CLIP-L encoder is more stable than a dual-encoder perturbation approach (Ablation section).
A human preference user study shows E2PO wins 31.8% preference on Overall Quality and 33.1% on Image-Text Alignment against baseline methods (Figure 8).

8WrMPCd7Kr.text: Stem's Token Position-Decay (TPD) strategy allocates a position-dependent sparse attention budget k(i) = floor(k_start - (k_start(1-mu)/N)*i), decaying from k_start to k_end = mu*k_start across the sequence with mu=0.7 found empirically optimal (Equation 3, Section 2.1).

The Output-Aware Metric (OAM) scores tokens as M_i,j = Q_iK_j^T + beta*max(0, log(||V_j||_2)) with beta=0.2, prioritizing high-value-norm tokens over pure attention-routing scores (Equation 7, Section 2.2).

On LongBench, Stem with a 25% budget reaches 31.64% accuracy on Qwen3-8B (versus 32.01% for dense full attention) and 41.48% accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B with a 31% budget (versus 42.02% dense), outperforming training-free baselines MInference, FlexPrefill, and XAttention (Table 2).
On the RULER benchmark across 4K-128K context lengths, Stem maintains about 88% average accuracy while consistently using the lowest budget (25%) among compared methods (Table 4).
At 128K context length on an H20 GPU, Stem delivers a 3.7x prefill latency speedup, reducing latency from 1540ms to 420ms (Figure 1).
An ablation on Qwen3-8B shows accuracy rising from 29.41% (uniform top-k baseline) to 31.43% with TPD alone (+2.02 points) and to 31.64% with TPD+OAM combined (Table 5, Section 3.3).

arc2pWtZLN.text: The Collapsed Effective Operator S is defined via Schur complement as S := A − X C⁻¹ Xᵀ, marginalizing higher-order cells onto vertices while encoding topology-mediated long-range interactions (Definition 3.3, Section 3.2).
The collapsed operator is spectrally bounded between 0 and the rank-0 Laplacian A, i.e. 0 ⪯ S ⪯ A, guaranteeing positive semi-definiteness (Proposition 3.5, Section 3.2).
Eigenvalue compression holds for every index k, with λ_k(S) ≤ λ_k(A), meaning the collapsed operator never exceeds the rank-0 Laplacian's spectrum (Corollary 3.6).

A regularized variant S_ε := A − X(C + εI)⁻¹Xᵀ is introduced with Tikhonov regularization to bound the collapse error while preserving efficient implicit computation (Proposition 3.10, Algorithm 1, Section 3.4).

The graded Laplacian L⋆ remains positive semi-definite only when the coupling weight γ_k satisfies γ_k ≤ β_{k+1}·σ_min⁺(B_{k+1}), a condition on the boundary matrices (Proposition 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).
Spectral clustering using the collapsed operator improves accuracy from 46.9% to 70.9% on a protein secondary structure task compared to the baseline rank-0 Laplacian (Section 4).

7FG30Wld9Q.text: Algorithm 2 (Anytime Online Policy for COCO) achieves static regret bounded by 2GD(√t + 1) and cumulative constraint violation (CCV) bounded by 8GD√t·√(log t + 1)·(log(log t + 1) + 1)·log(4t), for any t ≥ 1 without prior knowledge of the horizon T (Theorem 4.2).

The paper introduces a time-varying, horizon-oblivious Lyapunov function Φ_t(·) that replaces the fixed horizon-dependent Lyapunov functions used in prior anytime online convex optimization analyses (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

Algorithm 3 (Anytime Online Policy for Dynamic COCO) attains dynamic regret of 2GD√(1+P_t)(√t + 1) and CCV of 8GD√(1+P_t)√t·√(log t + 1)·(log(log t + 1) + 1)·log(4t), where P_t is the unknown path length of the comparator sequence (Theorem 5.3, Section 5).

Algorithm 4 (Optimistic COCO) achieves regret O(√E_t(f̃)) and CCV Õ(√E_t(g̃)) that scale with the prediction error of the objective and constraint functions respectively, improving on the worst-case O(√t) bounds when predictions are accurate (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).

4HV8YpgiXL.text: ERGeoBench comprises 2,207 globally distributed street-view panoramas sampled within a 5km radius of city centers across the top 1,000 most populated cities worldwide (Section 3).

ERGeoBench evaluates 9 MLLMs, including proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0 Flash, Gemini-2.5 Pro, Gemini-3 Flash, Qwen-VL Max) and open-source models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL2.5-8B, InternVL3-8B), across single-view, panorama-view, and embodied-view settings (Section 3, Section 5).

GPT-4o's accuracy drops from 82.78% on Foundational Perception tasks to 43.86% on Spatial Awareness tasks, illustrating that low-level spatial reasoning is the primary bottleneck rather than high-level semantic recognition (Table 3, Section 5.3).

Geo-localization Score (GLS) is strongly correlated with the perception, spatial awareness, and commonsense reasoning capability dimensions measured by ERGeoBench, supporting the claim that accurate localization requires integrated multi-dimensional reasoning rather than isolated visual recognition (Section 5.2-5.3).

Models perform well on hierarchical, high-level semantic geo-localization (e.g., country-level classification) but show substantially reduced accuracy at fine-grained distance thresholds such as 1km, compared to broader thresholds (25, 200, 750, 2500 km), revealing a semantic-versus-metric performance gap (Section 5.2-5.3).

In the embodied-view setting, top models such as Gemini-3-Flash match or exceed their panorama-view performance, indicating that sequential embodied exploration can compensate for limited single-view perceptual information (Section 5.2).

duzdftKtUA.text: The Modality-aware Credit Assignment (MoCA) mechanism combines an outcome reward R_O with a perception reward R_P into a trajectory-level return R(τ) = R_O(τ) + λR_P(τ), routing distinct credit to perception versus reasoning failures (Section 2.5, Section 2.4).

Perception Verification (PV) implements a 'blindfolded reasoner' test using Qwen2.5-Instruct-14B as a text-only proxy: it withholds the image and attempts to answer the question using only the VLM's generated perception text, yielding a binary reward R_P ∈ {0,1} that gates whether an error is attributed to 'bad seeing' or 'bad thinking' (Section 2.3).

Structured Verbal Verification (SVV) replaces free-form LLM judging with a four-step structured verification protocol (identify answer type, extract boxed content, reconstruct reference, apply type-specific semantic scoring) that the judge model must execute step-by-step (Figure 4, Section 2.4).

On the VP-Challenge-Set (N=273) of difficult semantic rephrasings, the proposed VP verifier achieves 91.9% accuracy, 92.7% F1, and 92.3% consistency over 5 runs at T=0.7, versus 67.0% accuracy/58.7% F1/100.0% consistency for a Rigid Rule verifier and 79.1% accuracy/82.4% F1/78.6% consistency for standard LLM Prompting (Table 4, Section 3.3).

The full MoCA model (7B, built on Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct) achieves 86.6 on V*, 87.0 on InfoVQA, 74.2 on HRBench, 58.3 on DUDE, and 73.8 on MathVista, outperforming its Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct-7B base and matching or surpassing capability-enhanced 7B baselines like DeepEyes and Pixel Reasoner across most benchmarks (Table 1, Section 3.1).

Ablations show removing Perception Verification (w/o PV) drops performance by 6.9 points on V*, 4.7 on HRBench, and 4.1 on InfoVQA relative to the full model, while removing SVV+PV in favor of an LLM-judge outcome reward causes a consistent drop across all task categories (Table 2, Section 3.2).

D8ETPuIu7Q.text: MOD-DiT identifies three distinct attention distribution patterns—block-diagonal, parallel-to-main-diagonal, and vertical—that dynamically mix throughout the denoising process, modeled via a generalized linear approximation (Equation 3, Section 4, Section 4.2).

MOD-DiT is a sampling-free dynamic attention framework that predicts evolving sparse attention patterns via a two-stage process combining linear pattern-intensity prediction and online block masking, avoiding repetitive attention-map sampling (Section 5.1, Section 5.2, Section 5.3).
On CogVideoX-v1.5 (2B), MOD-DiT achieves 80.1% attention sparsity with a 1.82× speedup while maintaining PSNR of 25.77 and SSIM of 0.868 (Table 1).

On HunyuanVideo (13B), MOD-DiT achieves 87.8% sparsity with a 2.29× speedup, PSNR of 27.23 and SSIM of 0.879, and on Wan2.1 (14B) it achieves 78.0% sparsity with a 1.96× speedup, PSNR of 22.75 and SSIM of 0.821 (Table 1).

The online block masking strategy selects valid tokens as the union of a Top-K pattern-derived set and a conditionally preserved block-diagonal set, reconstructing the sparsity map by fusing masked and historical attention information every Δt steps (Section 5.1, Section 5.3).
An optimized least-squares kernel used for the linear pattern-fitting step achieves a 100× speedup over PyTorch's torch.lstsq (Appendix B).

B1yOdZOACl.text: ToMAP (built on a 3B-parameter Qwen2.5 model) achieves a 39.4% relative gain in persuasiveness over GPT-4o across multiple persuadee models and diverse corpora (Section 4.2, Table 1).
On the CMV dataset with a Qwen-7B persuadee, ToMAP scores 23.01 versus 16.42 for the RL-only baseline and 12.75 for the unmodified base model (Table 1).

ToMAP integrates two Theory-of-Mind modules trained end-to-end via reinforcement learning: a Counterclaim Predictor and an Opponent Attitude Predictor implemented as an encoder+MLP classifier (Section 3.3, Table 5).
Ablations show RL fine-tuning is necessary for effective persuasion and that removing the Attitude Predictor substantially degrades persuasiveness (Section 4.3, Tables analyzed in 4.3.1-4.3.2).
During training, ToMAP develops longer reasoning chains and reduces repetitive phrasing, avoiding 8-gram overlaps above 10% (Section 5.1, Figure 4).
ToMAP sustains persuasion gains over 10-turn conversations while the RL-only baseline plateaus after about turn 3 (Section 5.2, Figure 5).

ZP1p8k106p.text: DR.Q augments latent-dynamics consistency training with an InfoNCE mutual-information objective, motivated by Theorem 4.1 showing that minimizing representation distance does not necessarily maximize mutual information (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

DR.Q combines this with a Faded Prioritized Experience Replay scheme that multiplies TD-error-based priorities by a recency decay factor (1-epsilon)^i, with sampling-probability bounds established in Theorem 4.3 (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.3).

Using a single hyperparameter set across all 73 continuous-control tasks (MuJoCo, DMC-Hard, DMC-Easy, DMC-Visual, HumanoidBench), DR.Q matches or surpasses baselines including DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, SimBa, SimBaV2, MR.Q, and FoG (Section 5.1, Figure 1).
DR.Q obtains a 15.5% improvement over SimBaV2 on DMC-Hard and a 58.9% improvement over FoG on HumanoidBench with dexterous hands (Section 5.1).
DR.Q is reported as the first method to exceed an average return of 700 on the dog-run task within 1M environment steps (Section 5.1, Figure 3).

Ablation studies show removing the InfoNCE term (setting its weight to zero) degrades performance most on high-dimensional tasks, and that faded PER outperforms using either prioritized replay or the forget mechanism alone (Section 5.2, Figure 4).

LTHHiPNbrs.text: The RCB algorithm achieves an O(sqrt(KdT)) regret bound, where K is the number of arms, d the feature dimension, and T the time horizon (Section 4.3, Theorem 2).

RCB simultaneously satisfies an epsilon-Dynamic Bayesian Incentive Compatibility (epsilon-DBIC) constraint, requiring a minimum cold-start sample size N(epsilon) that scales cubically with the number of arms K and linearly with dimension d (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).

The two-stage mechanism separates a Cold Start Stage (Algorithm 1), which explores products while preserving incentive compatibility, from an Exploitation Stage (Algorithm 2) using inverse proportional gap sampling (Section 3.1-3.2).
The analysis reveals a tradeoff in which larger incentive budgets epsilon reduce required cold-start sample sizes but affect the regret guarantee (Section 4, Theorem 1 and Theorem 2).

In warfarin-dosing simulations using real data, RCB achieves a weighted risk score of approximately 0.29 compared to a physician baseline of 0.20, with error rates around 35% (Section 5.2, Table 1, Figure 2).

16CV9RimWM.text: Adjoint Schrodinger Bridge Matching (ASBM) achieves an FID of 3.16 at 100 NFE on CIFAR-10 in pixel space, outperforming Score SDE (4.61) and the prior Schrodinger Bridge method DSBM (9.68) (Section 4.1, Table 1).
At 25 sampling steps with a Heun solver on CIFAR-10, ASBM reaches an FID of 3.74, far better than baselines in the range of 39.84-285.77 (Section 4.1, Table 3).
On FFHQ in latent space at 25 NFE, ASBM achieves an FID of 8.85 versus 52.08 for Score SDE, maintaining an advantage across 25-1000 NFE (Section 4.1, Table 2).
Trajectory inversion experiments show ASBM recovers an initial noise estimate that remains highly similar to the true starting point, unlike Score SDE, which is memoryless (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

One-step distillation of ASBM achieves FID 6.68 and Recall 0.542 on CIFAR-10, improving over DMD (FID 8.25) and SDS (FID 9.36) baselines without requiring a costly regression loss (Section 4.3, Table 4).

ASBM's coupling construction requires only 20 function evaluations versus 100-200 in prior work, and its overall training is more efficient, equivalent to 2100 Score SDE epochs versus 3300 for Score SDE (Section 4.5).

XGxBnVqK63.text: On 300M-parameter language models trained on 10B tokens from SlimPajama, the Q-K=V projection-sharing variant achieves a 50% KV cache reduction with only a 3.1% relative perplexity increase (5.27 vs. 5.11 baseline) (Section 4, Table 4).

The fully-shared Q=K=V variant incurs a much larger 25.4% perplexity degradation (6.41 vs. 5.11) at the same 50% cache reduction, while Q=K-V gives 0% cache reduction with a 4.9% perplexity increase (Section 4, Table 4).

Combining Q-K=V with Multi-Query Attention (MQA) yields a 96.9% total KV cache reduction with a 4.8% perplexity increase, and combining it with GQA-4 yields 87.5% cache reduction with 3.9% perplexity loss (Section 4, Tables 4 and 7).
At 1.2B parameters trained on 10B tokens, Q-K=V shows improved robustness, with perplexity degradation dropping to 2.48% while retaining the 50% cache reduction (Section 4, Table 9).

Learned Key and Value projection matrices exhibit high cosine similarity (0.73), which the authors use to explain why constraining K and V to share a projection causes minimal quality loss (Section 4).

Projection-sharing variants match or slightly exceed standard QKV transformer performance on synthetic reasoning tasks and vision benchmarks, including 5-shot downstream accuracy and semantic segmentation (Section 4, Tables 2, 3, 11, and 12).

MGrOId7zTe.text: QHyer replaces return-to-go conditioning with a state-dependent Q-value estimated via normalizing flows to model the goal-reaching probability p(g|s,a), achieving 92% coverage versus 25% for RTG on non-Markovian datasets (Figure 2).

The Gated Hybrid Attention-Mamba backbone fuses parallel attention and Mamba branches via a learnable gate α (y = α·y_attn + (1-α)·y_mamba), letting the model adapt its effective receptive field to dataset non-Markovianity (Section 3, Table 4).
On OGBench manipulation tasks, QHyer attains 152 total successes on cube tasks versus 111 for GCIQL, and 169 versus 147 on puzzle play data (Table 1).
On D4RL navigation benchmarks, QHyer reaches a total AntMaze score of 483.4 versus 324.5 for LSDT and 378.0 for IQL, and a total Maze2d score of 291.5 versus 182.1 for DMamba/DMixer (Table 2).
Backbone ablation shows success rate on play data rising from 74% (attention-only) to 80% (Mamba-only) to 84% (hybrid), and on noisy data from 60% to 91% to 95% (Table 3).
Theorem 3.1 bounds the expectile-regression bias term ϵₜ = (1-τ)(Q*-Qₘᵢₙ)/(τ·c̃/2 + (1-τ)(1-c̃/2)), and Figure 7 empirically confirms the predicted optimum at τ∈[0.9, 0.95].

NiMMHsFCvo.text: PNAPO converts standard (prompt, winner, loser) preference triplets into sextuples by retaining the prior noise used during generation, enabling endpoint-conditioned interpolation that yields tighter KL-divergence bounds than Diffusion-DPO's independent forward noise sampling (Section on RF-Consistent Optimization).

PNAPO reduces training compute roughly 12× versus the Diffusion-DPO baseline for both models: about 21 GPU-hours versus ~250 for SD3-Medium, and about 35 GPU-hours versus ~422 for FLUX.1-dev (Computational Efficiency results).

On the OPDv1 test set (7,459 prompts), PNAPO-FLUX achieves an HPSv2.1 score of 32.10 (+1.36 over base FLUX) with an 84.6% win rate over DPO-FLUX and an 81.1% win rate over IPO-FLUX (Preference Metrics results).

On GenEval, PNAPO-SD3-Medium reaches 0.73 overall accuracy (+7.4% over base, +2.8% over CaPO), and PNAPO-FLUX reaches 0.69 overall (+6.2% over base, +4.5% over DPO-FLUX) (Text-Image Alignment results).

Dynamic regularization β(δr,n)=β·f(δr)·g(n), combining reward-gap-based sample-difficulty scaling f(δr)=2σ(δr)-1 with cosine-annealed g(n), yields the best ablated HPSv2.1 score of 31.71 versus 31.08 for a fixed-β variant (Ablation Studies table).

A 10-participant human evaluation on 20 image pairs each reports 56% overall preference, 72% preference for visual appeal, and 52% preference for text alignment favoring PNAPO outputs (Human Evaluation results).

mrb4eOur7r.text: LATO represents mesh surfaces via a Vertex Displacement Field (VDF) that encodes relative displacement vectors from sampled surface points to the constituent vertices of each face, giving dense supervision for topology learning (Section on VDF representation).

The VAE decoder progressively subdivides and prunes T-Voxels across L=3 octree stages, predicting binary occupancy with an asymmetric loss (γ+=0, γ-=4) before regressing vertex locations from voxel centroids and predicting edges via an MLP connection head (Equations 4-7).
On the reconstruction benchmark, LATO's VAE achieves CD(L2)=0.042, HD=0.065, and NC=0.847 on dense meshes, outperforming MeshGPT, MeshCraft, DeepMesh, and BPT (Table 1-2).
LATO's flow-matching generation runs in 3-10 seconds per mesh, versus minutes for autoregressive baselines (Figure 7).

An ablation comparing the VDF representation to discrete vertex-edge labels confirms VDF's superiority for topology-preserving generation, evaluated on 200 dense-mesh and 200 artist-mesh benchmarks (Figure 9).

98XhDbtB21.text: QUATRO formulates fine-tuning as a prompt-conditioned trust-region problem constraining per-query KL(πθ(·|q) ‖ πold(·|q)) ≤ δ, replacing GRPO/GSPO's heuristic importance-ratio clipping with an exact Lagrangian-dual solution (Section 3.1, Eq. 7, Eq. 13).

The QUATRO objective (Theorem 3.3, Eq. 14) combines a query-specific advantage term Aqi = (R(o(i)|q) − μq⋆)/λq⋆ − 1 with a log-ratio stabilizer term that prevents policy overestimation without clipping (Eq. 15).

On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, QUATRO with δ=0.001 raises Pass@256 to 68.68% versus 60.85% for GSPO (+7.83 points); on Qwen2.5-Math-7B it raises Pass@256 to 73.41% versus 65.70% for GSPO (+7.71 points) (Table 1).
Using the paper's introduced Unique Correct Count metric on MATH500, QUATRO reaches UCC@256 of 97.20 versus 26.66 for GSPO, a 3.6x improvement in solution diversity (Table 2).

Ablating the log-ratio stabilizer term causes reward collapse accompanied by abrupt spikes in KL divergence, and QUATRO remains stable under 5 inner-loop policy-staleness updates and at learning rates 5-10x larger than the GSPO baseline where GSPO degrades (Figure 4).

ydQkpswDPi.text: SCOPE constructs behavioral fingerprints from a curated anchor set of 250 representative queries (Scope-250), recording each candidate model's correctness and token consumption to enable retrieval-based performance prediction for models unseen during training (Fingerprint Construction stage).

SCOPE's reasoning-based performance estimator is trained in two stages, supervised fine-tuning via hindsight distillation followed by GRPO optimization, to jointly predict binary correctness and continuous token cost (Performance Prediction stage).

SCOPE boosts accuracy by up to 25.7% when prioritizing performance and cuts inference cost by up to 95.1% when prioritizing efficiency, also reducing token consumption by 90.8% relative to test-time scaling (Key Results).

On the in-distribution test set at α=1.0, SCOPE reaches 75.0% accuracy versus 73.02% for Graph Router, and versus xRouter's 57.94% accuracy at $1.01 cost, SCOPE achieves 75.0% accuracy at $0.63 (Baselines & Comparisons).

SCOPE generalizes to 4 unseen models, including Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and DeepSeek-V3.2, without retraining, using only 250 anchor inferences for domain adaptation versus full retraining of baseline routers, a 38x reduction in compute (Generalization; Computational Efficiency).

An ablation shows chain-of-thought reasoning in the estimator improves prediction accuracy from 75.1% to 77.0%, and a calibration weight of w=0.2 smooths discontinuous routing behavior (Ablation Studies).

206P2ygDYN.text: CLIP ViT-B/32 representations on MSCOCO exhibit dimension collapse, with singular value spectra containing zero values and image/text subspaces showing partial overlap via principal angles (Figure 2c-d).

Theorem 3 shows that under a subspace constraint, the modality gap converges to the smallest angle between the image and text hyperplanes rather than to zero, tying the gap directly to dimension collapse (Section 3.4, Theorem 3).

Corollary 2 proves that once the contrastive loss is minimized under subspace constraints, paired image-text samples cannot be perfectly aligned whenever this hyperplane angle is non-zero (Section 4.3, Corollary 2).

Shared Space Projection (SSP), which projects embeddings onto the shared subspace and renormalizes, reduces the CLIP ViT-B/32 modality gap angle from 71.02 degrees to 50.40 degrees on ImageNet-1K while changing zero-shot accuracy only slightly, from 63.34% to 62.45% (Table 1).

On CIFAR-10, applying SSP to CLIP ViT-B/32 reduces the modality-gap angle from 74.69 degrees to 5.37 degrees while zero-shot accuracy drops only slightly from 89.00% to 86.43%, indicating shared-space alignment does not dominate downstream performance (Table 1).

AiawINF2T0.text: InteractComp comprises 210 expert-curated ambiguous search questions spanning 9 domains, with 139 English and 71 Chinese samples (Section 3.3).

Across 17 evaluated models (6 open-weight, 11 proprietary), the best model reaches only 13.73% accuracy under standard interaction settings versus 71.50% when given complete disambiguating context, a roughly 5x gap (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Ablation across answer-only, search-only, and with-context modes shows accuracy of 2.38-7.62% (answer-only), 6.74-9.52% (search-only), and 40.93-71.50% (with-context), isolating interactive disambiguation as the main bottleneck rather than reasoning or search ability (Table 3, Section 4.3).

When forced to ask a minimum number of clarifying questions (up to 8), GPT-5 accuracy roughly doubles from about 20% to about 40%, demonstrating latent interactive capability that default strategies fail to engage (Section 4.5, Figure 3b).

Over a 15-month period, BrowseComp-style benchmark performance improved seven-fold (from about 10% to about 70%), while InteractComp accuracy remained stagnant in the 6-14% range, indicating interaction handling is a persistent blind spot separate from general search-agent progress (Section 4.6, Figure 1).

v0DWbfP3b9.text: MedCRP-CL uses the Chinese Restaurant Process to perform online, unsupervised discovery of semantic modality groupings from clinical text prompts, identifying K=5 clinically meaningful clusters (e.g., separating cardiac ultrasound CAMUS from breast ultrasound BUSI) rather than grouping by physical imaging modality (Figure 6).

Across 16 medical segmentation tasks spanning endoscopy, dermoscopy, ultrasound, and chest X-ray, MedCRP-CL achieves 73.3% Dice with 4.1% forgetting using 8.6M trainable parameters, versus the best baseline MoE-Adapters at 65.3% Dice, 7.1% forgetting, and 51.9M parameters, an 8.0-point Dice improvement with roughly 6x fewer parameters (Table 2).

Ablations show removing the Chinese Restaurant Process component causes catastrophic forgetting of 15.55%, and removing LoRA adaptation degrades performance to 45.39% Dice, versus 4.1% forgetting and 73.3% Dice for the full model (Table 4).

Text-embedding-based modality discovery yields a substantially larger intra-/inter-cluster gap (~0.50) than visual-embedding-based discovery (~0.22), with cardiac and breast ultrasound tasks showing visual similarity above 0.95 but text similarity of only ~0.45, justifying the use of text prompts for task grouping (Table 7).

The discovered K=5 semantic modality structure remains stable across four different task orderings (Dice range 0.72-0.74, forgetting range 0.04-0.06) and under prompt perturbations including typos up to 20% and keyword drops up to 30% (Figure 5, Table 9).

A5KwfEqWSu.text: The Geometry-Embedding Module (GEM) estimates 6-DoF inter-frame camera poses to inject pose-aware geometric embeddings that enforce 3D structural consistency in video depth prediction (Section 3.2).

The Alternating Spatio-Temporal Transformer (ASTT) decouples temporal alignment from spatial refinement by alternating between geometrically-guided temporal alignment and spatial refinement stages (Section 3.3).

GemDepth-VDA reduces zero-shot AbsRel from 0.295 (VideoDepthAnything baseline) to 0.157 on the Sintel benchmark, and achieves an AbsRel of 0.051 on the Bonn benchmark, a 46.8% improvement over the best baseline (Table 1).
On the temporal-alignment-error (TAE) metric, GemDepth-DAv2 improves over DepthAnythingV2 by 56.14% (reaching 0.50), and GemDepth-VDA improves by 17.54% (reaching 0.47) (Table 2).

Training uses a two-stage strategy: joint optimization on 690K pose-annotated frames followed by fine-tuning on 250K frames without pose labels, drawing on datasets including Virtual KITTI 2, TartanAir, PointOdyssey, MVS-Synth, Dynamic Replica, and IRS (Section 3.5, Table 8).

GemDepth adds only about 40G FLOPs and increases inference time from 85ms to 99ms relative to the baseline, while using 0.58B parameters, about half of comparable foundation depth models (Section on efficiency).

j5vTJrpoeL.text: On the ADNI dataset (650 subjects, 5-way CN/SMC/EMCI/LMCI/AD classification, 5-fold cross-validation), the proposed multi-scale hyperedge model (MuHL) achieves 93.2% accuracy versus 90.8% for the second-best method, a 2.4 percentage-point improvement (Table 1).

On the PPMI dataset (181 subjects, 3-way CN/Prodromal/PD classification), MuHL achieves 76.8% accuracy versus 71.9% for the second-best method, a 4.9 percentage-point improvement, with F1-score improving by 6.0 points (62.4% vs 56.4%) (Table 1).
In zero-shot cross-dataset transfer, MuHL trained on PPMI reaches 60.5% accuracy on TaoWu and 65.9% on Neurocon, outperforming the second-best method's 57.0% and 63.4% respectively (Table 2).

The most salient learned hyperedge (Figure 4) and the top-10 disease-relevant ROIs (Table 3) implicate bilateral globus pallidus, putamen, hippocampus, and thalamus for Alzheimer's (ADNI), and left amygdala, right middle cingulum, and bilateral thalamus/supramarginal gyrus for Parkinson's (PPMI).

Ablation shows that removing the hypergraph structure learning (HSL) component causes the largest accuracy drop, to 76.8% on ADNI, versus 93.2% for the full model, confirming HSL as the most critical component (Table 4).
Proposition 2 proves that at least one learned hyperedge monotonically expands with increasing wavelet scale s, converging to include all N brain regions as s approaches infinity (Proposition 2).

sUTC7JE781.text: Blend-ASC dynamically allocates samples per question at inference time and uses on average 4.8 times fewer samples than vanilla self-consistency while matching or exceeding its accuracy (abstract only).

Blend-ASC is hyperparameter-free, supports batched sample allocation, and outperforms both fixed-budget and dynamic-allocation self-consistency baselines under any given sample budget (abstract only).
The paper derives a power law relationship between the number of self-consistency samples and accuracy and empirically validates this scaling law across multiple reasoning datasets (abstract only).

The derived power law scaling underpins a theoretical framework for analyzing self-consistency's sampling efficiency under different allocation schemes, informing the design of Blend-ASC's dynamic allocation rule (abstract only).

RaJnDY8aAS.text: The proposed RCDP-UCB algorithm for linear dueling bandits with post-serving context achieves a cumulative regret upper bound of Õ(d(√T + C + D)), where d is the feature dimension, T the horizon, C the corruption budget, and D the delay complexity (Theorem 5.2).

Delay complexity D is defined as max(Λ^{1/2}, μ_τ), unifying stochastic and adversarial delay regimes into a single regret term without requiring the algorithm to know which regime it faces (Assumption 4.5).
The adaptive weighting mechanism sets weights ω_s = min(1, α/‖Δz_s‖_{Ṽ_{s-1}^{-1}}) with α = √d/(C+D) to down-weight potentially corrupted or stale observations (Equation 4).
A matching lower bound of Ω(d√T + dC + D') is established, showing the algorithm's regret is optimal up to a √d factor under adversarial delays (Theorem 5.3).

Algorithm 1 maintains a replay buffer of post-serving contexts and updates both a learned context estimator φ̂_t and the parameter estimate Θ_t via weighted maximum likelihood estimation with clipping (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

2jXDMGaNZk.text: RL post-training induces an exploration collapse in reasoning models such as MiMo and Qwen3-Thinking, where increasing sampling temperature yields a negative accuracy-temperature slope instead of improving pass@n accuracy (Figure 1).

Final-layer token posteriors exhibit sharply reduced entropy after post-training while intermediate transformer layers retain substantial predictive uncertainty, forming a 'latent entropy reservoir' that LED exploits (Section 2.2).

Latent Exploration Decoding (LED) restricts exploration to the top-k tokens of the final-layer posterior, then aggregates intermediate-layer posteriors via cumulative sums and selects the depth combination with maximum entropy as the exploration candidate, in a hyperparameter-free manner (Sections 3.1-3.2, Figure 4).

LED uses the final layer's top-1 token probability as a parameter-free confidence signal to decide, without predefined thresholds, when to explore via intermediate layers versus exploit the final layer, and restricts exploration to the reasoning (DeepThink) phase only (Sections 3.3-3.4).

LED improves average pass@1 accuracy by 0.67 percentage points and average pass@16 accuracy by 0.92 percentage points across math, science, and coding benchmarks including AIME, GSM8K, MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, and LiveCodeBench (Table 1).

Applying LED flips the accuracy-temperature slope α from negative to positive for all tested latest-generation reasoning models, effectively restoring temperature-based exploration, while adding under O(d_s + d_V) overhead and less than 1% increase in generation length with no additional training (Figure 5).

LgFmen6sHP.text: PathCTM reduces the number of required image patches by 95.95% and shortens inference time by approximately 95.62% relative to standard multiple-instance-learning (MIL) baselines, needing only 183-408 patches versus 2,605-15,063 for baselines across four diagnostic tasks using CONCH V1.5 and UNI V2 feature extractors (Table 1).
PathCTM improves AUC by an average of 2.3% over state-of-the-art MIL methods while using far fewer patches, as shown in the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff (Figure 1c, Table 1).

Attention-guided region pruning performs conditional computation via Top-K patch selection, reducing computational complexity from O(N) to O(K), justified by Proposition 1 which shows attention weights serve as a first-order surrogate for each patch's influence on the prediction (Section 3.3, Proposition 1, Appendix A.1).

Confidence-aware early stopping halts scale-space reasoning once a confidence score C_{t,L} = 1 - H(ŷ_{t,L})/log N exceeds a threshold δ, with Proposition 2 using Fano's inequality to connect conditional entropy H(Y|Z_t) to classification error probability (Section 3.4, Equations 11-12).

PathCTM adaptively allocates inference depth in a coarse-to-fine, scale-space manner, stopping early on easier whole-slide-image cases as confirmed by the distribution of early-stopping scales across datasets (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

QI139RyR6I.text: ASAP decomposes neural combinatorial optimization policies into a pruning policy that removes bad actions and a selection policy that chooses among the remaining candidates, motivated by the finding that trained solvers can still identify bad actions after distribution shift even though their greedy policies fail (Section III.2, Figure 2).
On discrete bin-packing OOD test sets, ASAP achieves 64.1% space utilization versus 62.6% for the PCT baseline, and 82.3% versus 80.5% for GOPT on the OOD-Small set (Table 2).
On continuous bin-packing OOD test sets, ASAP reaches 59.5% utilization versus 56.2% for PCT, and 70.5% versus 68.3% for AR2L on the OOD-Small set (Table 2).

During online adaptation, only the meta-learned selection policy is fine-tuned on test instances while the pruning policy stays fixed, yielding adaptation gains of 0.9%-2.2% in the discrete setting and 1.3%-2.1% in the continuous setting (Section IV.2, Table 2).

An ablation study shows that removing the policy decoupling (ASAP w/o Decouple) or removing MAML-based meta-learning (ASAP w/o MAML) each degrades performance, indicating decoupling and meta-learning are synergistic (Table 1, Section V.4).
On in-distribution datasets, ASAP outperforms baselines by 2.0-2.9% in discrete environments and 1.9-3.0% in continuous environments before any test-time adaptation (Table 1).

MbmhB3KqKU.text: A naive non-adaptive algorithm achieves envy-freeness using O(m^3/Δ^2) noisy queries, where m is the number of items and Δ is the gap parameter of the optimal negative envy (Theorem 1, Section 3).

An improved polynomial-time algorithm using non-adaptive queries achieves envy-freeness with q ≤ Õ(m^2.5/Δ^2) queries, valid when Δ ≥ m^(1/4) log^2 m and Δ ≤ Cm for a sufficiently small constant C (Theorem 2, Section 4).

An algorithm-independent lower bound of Ω̃(m^2.5/Δ^2) queries is proven to hold even under adaptive querying strategies and unbounded computation time, matching the upper bound up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 3, Section 5).
The problem setup assumes agent valuations are accessed only through queries corrupted by Gaussian noise, formalized as the noisy query model (Section 2).
The paper extends its analysis of general noise levels beyond the Gaussian model and discusses extension of the results from two agents to n-agent scenarios (Section 6, Section 7).

K8UWWJUNYf.text: TideGS trains over one billion 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives on a single consumer GPU with 24 GB of memory (abstract only).
TideGS exploits the sparsity of 3DGS training, where each iteration activates only the Gaussians visible from the current camera batch, to enable out-of-core optimization (abstract only).
TideGS uses block-virtualized geometry for SSD-aligned spatial locality as one of its core techniques (abstract only).
TideGS employs a hierarchical asynchronous pipeline to overlap I/O with computation and a trajectory-adaptive differential streaming scheme for incremental working-set transfers (abstract only).

TideGS achieves reconstruction quality on large-scale scenes that exceeds prior out-of-core baselines limited to roughly 100 million Gaussians and standard in-memory training limited to roughly 11 million Gaussians (abstract only).

nWtjaAmug8.text: STEP with 2 diffusion denoising steps achieves a 21.6% higher success rate than the BRIDGER baseline on the RoboMimic benchmark (abstract only).
STEP achieves a 27.5% higher success rate than DDIM on real-world manipulation tasks (abstract only).
STEP combines a spatiotemporal consistency prediction mechanism for warm-starting actions with velocity-aware perturbation injection to prevent execution stalls (abstract only).

The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing the spatiotemporal consistency prediction mechanism induces a locally contractive mapping, ensuring convergence of action errors during diffusion refinement (abstract only).

GtNkETQE6w.text: OEU maximizes prediction uncertainty on forgotten data rather than training the model toward incorrect labels, aiming to avoid conflating genuine forgetting with confident misprediction toward a specific class (abstract only).

OEU uses gradient orthogonal projection, projecting forgetting gradients onto the orthogonal complement of retain gradients, to eliminate interference between the forgetting and retaining objectives (abstract only).
The orthogonal projection method provides theoretical guarantees for utility preservation under a first-order approximation (abstract only).
OEU outperforms existing unlearning methods on quantized neural networks in both forgetting effectiveness and retain accuracy (abstract only).

EbkumuY3eW.text: The benchmark ICRL4AHT is built on a high-throughput JAX implementation of Overcooked-V2 and includes diverse teammate policies for controlled ad-hoc teamwork experiments (abstract only).

Prominent in-context reinforcement learning architectures, including Algorithm Distillation and Decision-Pretrained Transformer, fail to exhibit robust test-time adaptation in multi-agent ad-hoc teamwork settings (abstract only).
These ICRL methods frequently underperform a random baseline across both the unseen-teammate and unseen-layout evaluation tracks (abstract only).

The benchmark provides an end-to-end pipeline for teammate generation, learning-history collection, dataset construction, and online multi-episode evaluation across millions of transitions (abstract only).

gl5xoOJJ22.text: CAMEL achieves 82.9% average accuracy across RewardBench, RM-Bench, and JudgeBench, exceeding the second-best baseline (79.7% average, from INF-ORM-Llama3.1-70B) by 3.2 points (Table 1).

CAMEL-Fast (single-token, no reflection) reaches 90.5% on RewardBench, 74.8% on RM-Bench, and 65.2% on JudgeBench, while CAMEL-Reflection (always reflects) reaches 92.8%, 84.2%, and 71.6% respectively, and the full confidence-gated CAMEL scores 92.4%, 81.9%, and 69.1% (Table 1, Section 4.2).
CAMEL, built on Qwen3-14B, matches or surpasses 70B-parameter baselines including Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B and INF-ORM-Llama3.1-70B while using only 14B parameters (Section 4.2, Table 1).

The confidence score is defined as the absolute log-probability margin between verdict tokens A and B, c(x) = |log P(v=A|x) - log P(v=B|x)| (Equation 5), and CAMEL uses a fixed gating threshold τ=5 to decide whether to invoke reflection (Section 3.2, Section 4.1).

Sweeping the confidence threshold τ produces a Pareto frontier that strictly dominates RM-R1-DeepSeek-32B (90.9% RewardBench / 83.5% RM-Bench) and RM-R1-Qwen-Instruct-32B (89.0%/73.1%) baselines in accuracy-vs-average-output-tokens space (Figure 4, Section 4.3).

Ablation removing counterfactual prefix augmentation (Qwen3-14B-GRPO, doubled rollouts for parity) underperforms full CAMEL, and adding reflection to every ablation variant raises accuracy by up to +9.4 points on RM-Bench, confirming both counterfactual augmentation and reflection each contribute to the final score (Table 2, Section 4.4).

AUWo5h4U38.text: The paper proves (Theorem 2) a non-vanishing lower bound on the distance between CLIP text-derived class prototypes and the optimal visual prototypes W*, showing the modality gap cannot be closed by prompt engineering or negative-label mining alone (Section 3, Theorem 2).

Theorem 1 shows the optimal visual prototype for each class is a linear combination of visual features in the span of the training visual features, i.e., it lies entirely in the visual feature subspace S (Section 3, Theorem 1).

The proposed online pseudo-supervised framework updates ID and OOD-pseudo-class prototypes directly in the visual feature space using unlabeled test-time samples and soft CLIP predictions, with a step size η_i = ρ/√i (Equation 8, Section 4.1, Algorithm 1).
Theorem 3 gives a cumulative regret bound of O(√N) for the online optimization procedure over N test samples, established under a bounded-gradient assumption (Section 4.1, Theorem 3).

On ImageNet-1K OOD detection with a ViT-B/16 CLIP encoder, the method achieves 12.79% FPR95 and 97.75% AUROC averaged across iNaturalist/SUN/Places/Textures, improving over AdaNeg by 6.13 points FPR95 and 1.09 points AUROC (Table 1, Abstract).

S1TwW9szYm.text: For smooth strongly convex problems with two-point zero-order feedback and Markovian noise of mixing time τ, Theorem 1 (and its extension Theorem 1') gives an oracle complexity of O((d+τ)σ²/(μ²ε)), which reduces to the i.i.d. zero-order rate O(dσ²/(μ²ε)) whenever τ ≤ d, i.e., convergence becomes independent of τ (Table 1, Section 2, Theorem 1/1').
The same τ-independence-when-τ≤d phenomenon is established for non-smooth Markovian problems via a smoothing technique, giving oracle complexity O((d+τ)σ²G²/(μ²ε²)) (Table 1, Theorem 3/3').

The authors argue zero-order methods are more resource-efficient than first-order methods under Markovian noise: assuming a zero-order oracle call costs d times less than a gradient call, first-order Markovian SGD requires resources scaling as d·τ while their zero-order method scales only as d+τ (Section 1.2).

Matching information-theoretic lower bounds (Theorems 6, 7, and 8, for one-point and two-point feedback) are established up to logarithmic factors, confirming optimality of the upper bounds (Section 2.3, Appendix F).

For one-point feedback under Markovian noise, the derived rate is O(d(d+τ)σ²/(μ³ε²)), extending the i.i.d. one-point rate O(d²σ²/(μ³ε²)) by only an additive τ term rather than a multiplicative dτ term (Table 1, Section 2).

gvWsViQBYB.text: For AdamW-style Shampoo (Algorithm 1) with preconditioner exponents satisfying 1/p + 1/q = 1, Theorem 1 establishes the nonconvex convergence rate (1/K)Σ E[||∇f(X_k)||_*] ≤ O(√(m+n)·max{σ²L(f(X1)-f*)/K, √(L(f(X1)-f*)/K)}) for m×n matrix parameters over K iterations (Section 2, Theorem 1, Equation 9).

This rate is shown to be analogous to the optimal SGD convergence rate O(σ²L(f(X1)-f*)/K) in the ideal case where ||∇f(X)||_* = Θ(√min{m,n})·||∇f(X)||_F and m, n are comparable, since ||∇f(X)||_F ≤ ||∇f(X)||_* ≤ √min{m,n}·||∇f(X)||_F (Section 1.1, Equations 2-3).

The analysis extends to preconditioning exponents satisfying 1/p+1/q = 2-ω for ω∈(0,2] without decoupled weight decay, yielding rate (1/K)Σ E[|||∇f(X_k)|^ω||_*] ≤ O((m+n)^(1-ω/2)/(ωK^(ω/4))), which reduces to the ω=1 rate at ω=1 and to the momentum-SGD rate at ω=2 (Section 1.1, Equation 4).

This is presented as the first convergence analysis of the two-sided (as opposed to only one-sided) preconditioned nonconvex Shampoo variant, unifying one-sided (p=1,q=∞ or vice versa) and two-sided (p,q<∞) preconditioning in a single Algorithm 1 framework (Section 1, Section 1.1).

Empirical validation on GPT-2 training confirms that the theoretical condition L_{k,ε}⪰ε̂I_m, R_{k,ε}⪰ε̂I_n (Condition 8) holds in practice for a moderate ε̂ orders of magnitude larger than the numerically small ε=10^-12 typically used (Section 2.1, Figure 3, Section 5).

ISNSiAC3n1.text: Theorem 3.5 proves that mean-shift-induced spiked eigenvalues (set Λ_A) are spectrally separable from the covariance-induced spikes (set Λ_P) in high dimensions, using tools from Random Matrix Theory under the additive low-rank perturbation model (Section 3, Theorem 3.5).

Theorem 3.11 (Eigenspace Invariance) shows that the eigenspace of the uncontaminated sample covariance matrix remains asymptotically invariant under mean-shift mixture contamination, regardless of the mixture weight π (Section 3, Theorem 3.11).

The proposed two-stage Mean-Shift PCA (MS-PCA, Algorithm 1) deliberately injects an artificial knockoff mean-shift perturbation A'_n = m'γ'^T with mixture weight π' (e.g., π'=0.5 or π'=1) and threshold ϵ=Cn^(-1/2) to identify and remove the mean-shift eigenvalues while leaving covariance-induced eigenvalues invariant (Section 2, Algorithm 1).

Both mean-shift-induced spikes and covariance-induced spikes fluctuate at order O(n^-1/2), except the largest eigenvalue at the spectral edge which fluctuates at order O(n^-2/3), as used to set the matching threshold in the algorithm (Section 2, citing Theorem 2.19/2.16/2.15 of prior RMT results).

Section 4 numerical experiments show that existing Robust PCA methods fail to recover the true principal component even with only 5% outlier proportion when the aspect ratio d/n does not vanish (e.g., d/n=1), whereas MS-PCA consistently recovers it (Figure 2, Section 4).

qAqp0k2SBP.text: A specific layer termed the Massive Emergence Layer (ME Layer) is identified in large language models, where unusually large (massive) activations first appear before propagating to deeper layers (abstract only).
Both RMSNorm and FFN parameters within the ME Layer jointly contribute to the emergence of massive activations (abstract only).
The massive-activation token representation remains largely invariant across layers, which reduces the diversity of hidden representations passed to the attention module (abstract only).
A proposed technique that reduces this representational rigidity improves performance on instruction-following and math reasoning tasks in both training-free and fine-tuning settings (abstract only).
The method also weakens the influence of attention sinks and explains their origin at the hidden-state level (abstract only).

7kXXBRMi1r.text: Evolution of Benchmark (EoB) uses large language models to automatically generate Black-Box Optimization (BBO) benchmarks rather than relying on human-crafted, expert-biased designs (abstract only).
EoB formulates benchmark design as a bi-objective optimization problem that jointly maximizes landscape diversity and algorithm-differentiation ability (abstract only).
EoB has an LLM iteratively evolve a population of benchmark programs, using a reflection mechanism to refine both problem landscapes and their corresponding code (abstract only).

EoB is demonstrated to be useful across multiple applications, including benchmarking BBO algorithms, training and testing learning-assisted BBO algorithms, and serving as a proxy for expensive real-world optimization problems (abstract only).

RciRcJ9LHw.text: SmartThinker is a method for large reasoning models (e.g., in the style of OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1) that reduces redundant verbosity in long chain-of-thought reasoning (abstract only).
SmartThinker dynamically estimates the optimal response length during training rather than using a fixed target length (abstract only).
SmartThinker adaptively adjusts length reward coefficients during training to avoid penalizing correct but longer reasoning chains (abstract only).
SmartThinker achieves up to 52.5% average chain-of-thought length compression while improving accuracy on complex reasoning tasks (abstract only).
SmartThinker achieves up to a 16.6% accuracy improvement on challenging benchmarks such as AIME25 (abstract only).

6j88qckao7.text: S(H)NAP is presented as the first interventional audit framework for the Sybil lung cancer risk prediction model, using generative interventional attributions validated by expert radiologists (abstract only).
Sybil often exhibits behavior akin to an expert radiologist in differentiating malignant pulmonary nodules from benign ones, according to the interventional audit (abstract only).
Despite extensive prior clinical validation, Sybil shows sensitivity to clinically unjustified artifacts in CT scans (abstract only).
Sybil exhibits an unexplained directional (radial) bias in its decision-making process, uncovered through interventional analysis (abstract only).
The work argues for shifting evaluation of such clinical risk-prediction models from purely statistical validation toward causal analysis before clinical deployment (abstract only).

8obMsWKFRJ.text: A systematic dissociation is identified between strategy usage (whether a strategy appears in successful solutions) and strategy executability (whether it remains effective when used as guidance) in mathematical reasoning (abstract only).

Human-written and model-generated solutions are found to employ strategies in fundamentally different ways, producing complementary strengths as well as reversals in effectiveness depending on the strategy's source (abstract only).
Selective Strategy Retrieval (SSR) is proposed as a test-time framework that selectively retrieves and combines strategies using empirical, multi-route, source-aware signals (abstract only).
SSR improves accuracy by up to 13 percentage points on the AIME25 benchmark for compact reasoning models (abstract only).
SSR also improves accuracy by up to 5 points on the Apex benchmark (abstract only).

2UJrwCrqbw.text: VISTA brings up to +13.66% average performance gain over the SFT-Seed baseline for Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on medical (SLAKE, VQA-Rad) and mathematical (Geometry3K) reasoning tasks, versus +6.67% for the 7B variant (Section 4.2, Table 1).

The prefix resampling strategy reuses partial correct reasoning traces from earlier failed rollouts to more efficiently collect accurate solutions for difficult queries, rather than discarding them (Section 3, Figure 3).

The Vision-aware Attention Score (VAS) is introduced to filter out hallucinated solutions by measuring the model's attention allocation to visual tokens, addressing the finding that visual tokens receive less than 20% of attention despite being the largest share of context (Section 3, Figure 3).

On additional MLLMs (Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, InternVL3-2B, InternVL3-8B) evaluated with one self-improvement iteration, VISTA achieves +6.43% average performance gain over SFT-Seed and even outperforms the SFT-Oracle baseline (Section 4.2, Table 2).

An ablation comparing perturbation/swap strategies for prefix resampling under single-round self-improvement SFT on Qwen2.5-3B-VL is reported, along with a Top-k sensitivity study showing degraded performance when k is too small (k=1) (Section 4.4, Tables 6-7).

A wall-clock time comparison of different self-improvement SFT methods shows the added computational cost of VISTA relative to baselines, attributed to additional forward passes required for prefix resampling (Section 4.4, Table 8).

RxjGbyLFT1.text: Under matched distortion strength (target standard deviation), FeatJND-based feature perturbations preserve higher downstream task performance (image classification, object detection, instance segmentation) than unstructured Gaussian perturbations (Section 4, Figures 4-6).

The task-aligned JND formulation (Section 3) defines the maximum tolerable per-feature perturbation magnitude that preserves downstream task performance, estimated via a learned convolutional JND estimator (Section 3, Figure 3).

FeatJND-guided token-wise quantization achieves higher task performance than a random step-size permutation baseline (averaged over 5 random seeds) and a global uniform step-size allocation baseline, evaluated on classification, detection, and instance segmentation with backbones including Swin-T, Swin-S, and PVTv2-b2 (Section 4, Table 2, Figures 10-11).

Attribution map visualizations (via integrated gradients with K=20 integration steps) show that applying FeatJND-based perturbations leaves attribution patterns nearly unchanged relative to the original, unperturbed features (Section 4, Figure 7).

A comprehensive numerical comparison of FeatJND-based token-wise quantization versus the random step-size permutation baseline across multiple task metrics (mAP, AP@50, AP@75, mAR) is reported (Section 4, Table 2, Figures 18-19).

s6Vno2TwLJ.text: Theorem A.1 proves that the theoretically constructed best-response attack strategy (Definition 2.3) dominates fixed-skill attacks under the conditions of Theorem 3.1, and Theorem A.2 proves it dominates optimization-based attacks (Appendix A.4-A.5, Theorems A.1-A.2).

The paper's practical instantiation of the theoretical best-response attacker achieves the highest performance measured by the Bin-JR score against a target system defended by prompt and response filtering, outperforming existing adversarial prompting baselines (Section 4, Table 2).

Theorem 3.2 characterizes a conservative game equilibrium without skill transfer, and Theorem 3.3 identifies the maximum equilibrium value and corresponding optimal skill-space configuration (Section 3, Theorems 3.2-3.3).

A defense mechanism based on misleading the attacker is shown, via Theorem 3.5, to achieve a strictly more advantageous (upper-bounded) equilibrium point than the original defense described in Theorem 3.2 (Section 3, Theorem 3.5).

GPT-4.1-2025-04-14 is used as the LLM-based rater in experiments because it shows the highest agreement with human experts (over 89%) and low false positive rate among candidate raters (Section 4, Table 1).

The defense evaluated in Table 5 produces a measurable percentage drop in attack performance relative to the undefended baseline across multiple target LLMs, using a 10-skill skill space defined in Table 4 (Section 4, Tables 4-5).

IABjbJlinz.text: The Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridge (USB) model achieves mean W1 distance and RME performance better than or comparable to deterministic ODE-flow baselines such as SF2M, evaluated across held-out time points on EMT, EB, and CITE datasets (Section 6, Tables 3-4).

USB uniquely enables explicit, discrete simulation of birth-death (jump) dynamics at single-cell resolution, in contrast to prior simulation-free methods that only model deterministic or purely diffusive ODE/SDE flows (Section 5, Table 2, Figure 2).

On the Dyngen dataset, USB simulations initiated from a single cell with jump-rate parameter ν = 0.1 recover 8 distinct trajectories reflecting the underlying discrete birth-death dynamics (Section 6, Figure 2).

A sensitivity analysis shows that both excessively high and low values of the coupling parameter δ (δ = 0.5, 2.5) yield sub-optimal performance on the simulated gene dataset, with a properly chosen intermediate δ range performing best (Section 6, Table 5).
Comparative results across multiple dimensionalities (5D, 50D, 100D) of the EB dataset are reported, along with computational time scaling across dimensions (Section 6, Tables 8-11).

T6OVjCzbrS.text: Pair2Scene, evaluated via the Ours-Fit variant, achieves the best FID and KID scores on the 3D-Front only setting compared to established learning-based scene-generation baselines (Section 4, Table 1).

Pair2Scene generates complex environments beyond the training data distribution, including denser scenes and multi-source layouts, while baseline methods remain confined to configurations resembling their training distribution (Section 4, Table 3, Figure 1).

Physical plausibility is maintained via learned support relations (grounded in gravity-driven contact) and semantic plausibility via learned functional relations (spatial/functional proximity between objects), both extracted through a data curation pipeline combining physical validation and LLM-driven functional distillation (Section 3, Figure 4).

An ablation study shows that removing the rejection-sampling mechanism (the 'w/o rejection' variant) causes a measurable degradation in scene quality, demonstrating the necessity of the sampling strategy (Section 4, Table 4).
Without the gravity-based physical validation step, the ablation shows an increased floating rate of objects in generated scenes (Section 4, Table 8).
Pair2Scene achieves a collision rate lower than compared baselines, and the ablation results confirm the importance of the global layout prediction component to this result (Section 4, Table 9).

tVwJRXfSYY.text: VISTA (SAE-constrained DINOv2 + Gemma-2-2B-it) achieves more than a threefold average increase in matching rate for visual concept-to-text SAE alignment compared to unconstrained baselines (Section 4.4, Figure 3).
DINOv2 achieves 0.927 spatial localization accuracy versus 0.702 for I-JEPA and 0.201 for CLIP, showing markedly stronger patch-level locality preservation (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On object removal, VISTA with DINOv2 attains a mean score of 1.43 versus 1.06 for the VisionSAE baseline, a roughly 35% relative improvement (Table 2, Section 5.2.4).
On object replacement, VISTA attains a mean score of 1.46 versus 0.99 for the PatchSAE baseline, a roughly 47% relative improvement (Table 2, Section 5.2.4).

Without SAE constraints, visual tokens exhibit high reconstruction error and density in early transformer layers, whereas SAE regularization forces rapid convergence to text-like sparse activation patterns across tested architectures (Figure 4, Section 4.3).

tDft0AHhzH.text: TVCache achieves cache hit rates that vary by workload, reaching 27.0-57.2% on SkyRL-SQL and 34-73.9% (averaging 64.3%) on EgoSchema across training epochs (Figure 5).
On Qwen3-4B in the Medium setting, TVCache reduces median tool-call execution time from 18.68s to 2.70s, a 6.92x speedup, the largest reduction reported (Table 2).
On Qwen3-14B in the Medium setting, TVCache still yields a 5.55x reduction in median tool-call execution time (36.23s to 6.53s) (Table 2).

The stateful cache is built on a Tool Call Graph and performs longest-prefix matching over the agent's full tool-call history, guaranteeing a cache hit only when the complete sandbox state matches a previously executed sequence (Section 3.1-3.2).
Reward curves obtained with TVCache closely track the no-caching reward curves across terminal-bench, SkyRL-SQL, and EgoSchema, indicating no degradation in RL post-training performance (Figure 6).

2SUX04aKod.text: b1 improves accuracy over fixed-size block baselines by +19.53% on Countdown (wd1 variant, 256-token setting), +1.97% on GSM8K, and +3.20% on MATH500, consistently across Diffu-GRPO, GDPO, and wd1 algorithms (Table 1).

Block-wise entropy trajectories are consistently descending for correct reasoning chains but fluctuate for incorrect ones, a pattern formalized as Monotonic Entropy Descent and quantified via Spearman's rank correlation coefficient in Table 3 (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
b1 raises the proportion of correct generations exhibiting positive Spearman rank correlation (rSCC) from a baseline range of 65-91% up to 75-98% (Section 4.4, Table 3).

Theorem 1 proves that the local entropy reward used by b1's Monotonic Entropy Descent objective (Eq. 8) is equivalent to optimizing a global Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (Section 3.2, Theorem 1).

b1 generalizes beyond math reasoning, improving code generation and knowledge-task benchmarks by +1.22 to +9.39 points, while adding only about 2% training overhead and maintaining comparable inference throughput (~27 tokens/sec) (Table 4, Table 5).

TL787dxmIM.text: TimeChat-Captioner-7B-GRPO achieves a SodaM score of 35.0 on OmniDCBench, surpassing Gemini-2.5-Pro's 33.7, despite trailing Gemini-2.5-Pro on scene segmentation F1 (61.2 vs 68.5) (Table 1).

On downstream audio-visual reasoning, TimeChat-Captioner-7B-GRPO scores 52.8 on Daily-Omni and 22.6 on WorldSense, substantially outperforming the open-source baseline video-SALMONN-2 (29.9 and 18.2 respectively) (Table 2).
On Charades-STA temporal grounding, TimeChat-Captioner-derived descriptions yield R1@0.5 of 68.7 and mIoU of 58.8, exceeding Qwen2.5-Omni's 65.9 R1@0.5 and 56.7 mIoU (Table 3).

OmniDCBench comprises 1,122 human-annotated videos with structured captions averaging 995 words per video across a six-dimensional schema (Audio-Visual Events, Background, Camera State, Shot Editing, Dialogue, Acoustic Cues) (Figure 2).
The TimeChatCap-42K training dataset has 73.9% of videos in the 50-60 second range, captions averaging 877 words, and a mean segment length of 10.04 seconds (Figure 5).

hUjHHGOocl.text: Theorem 4.1 gives a finite-sample, high-probability lower bound on expected reward after one self-improvement iteration, showing the bound tightens as the accepted-data fraction (relative to total generated samples) increases (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

Corollary 4.4 and Remark 4.6.1 show that iterative self-improvement admits monotonic lower-bound guarantees across iterations only when initial task difficulty falls in a moderate regime, neither too easy nor too hard (Section 4, Corollary 4.4, Remark 4.6.1).

Theorem 5.2 proves that easy-to-hard curriculum scheduling achieves strictly better finite-sample guarantees than a fixed task mixture whenever a feasibility condition and an improvement condition (denoted ℳ<0) both hold (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).

Proposition 5.5 shows the region of initializations where easy-to-hard curricula provably beat fixed mixtures undergoes a sharp collapse near a critical sample-budget threshold ν_c, i.e., a phase transition in curriculum benefit (Section 5, Proposition 5.5).

Section 4.2 identifies an explicit feedback loop in which better-performing models accept a larger fraction of self-generated data per iteration, which in turn expands the training set and sustains further improvement (Section 4.2).

SNRYGh6n69.text: On the HEST-1k pan-cancer benchmark's top-50 highly variable genes, MoLF achieves an average Pearson Correlation Coefficient of 0.382, exceeding STPath (0.361), STFlow (0.312), and STEM (0.196) (Table 2).
MoLF's best single-cancer-type result is SKCM (melanoma) with PCC 0.606, versus STPath's 0.588 on the same cancer type (Table 2).

On the Hallmark pathway gene panel, MoLF attains an overall average PCC of 0.185, outperforming baselines ranging from 0.122 to 0.171, including MLP and STPath across low- and mid-variance gene strata (Table 3).

In zero-shot human-to-mouse melanoma cross-species transfer, MoLF reaches PCC 0.202, versus STPath's 0.090 and STFlow's 0.126, and even outperforms a tissue-specific MoLF variant trained only on melanoma (0.127) (Table 5).

An ablation removing the Mixture-of-Experts velocity field drops MoLF's average PCC from 0.383 to 0.209, and increases the synthetic-validation 2-Wasserstein distance from 0.292 to 0.315 (Tables 1 and 6).

FP23eFYhAy.text: On three MIMIC-derived diagnosis tasks (diverticulitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis) with a Qwen3-30B backbone and active verification enabled, GLEAN achieves AUROC of 0.9862, 0.9582, and 0.9061 respectively (Table 1).
GLEAN outperforms Self-Consistency, LLM-as-a-Judge, and Med-PRM baselines by approximately 12% in AUROC and 50% in Brier score reduction (Section on baseline comparison, Table 1).
An ablation shows AUROC rising stepwise from 0.6497 (P(TRUE) alone) to 0.6935 (+ process context) to 0.7944 (+ guideline grounding) to 0.8547 (+ accumulation) to 0.8574 (+ calibration) (Table 3).
