Using detailed clinical guidelines instead of abstracts-only guideline text raises AUROC from 0.7573 to 0.8574 (Table 3, guideline quality analysis).
With GLEAN-based best-of-N selection at N=16, diagnostic accuracy improves from a 58.94% baseline to 78.3% (Figure 4).

In an expert study, three clinicians reviewing 50 trajectories rated GLEAN's overall usefulness at 4.67/5 and its diagnostic-error identification reliability at Cohen's kappa = 0.78 (substantial agreement) (Section on expert validation).

YQmrP0zjmh.text: LithoDreamer models the Layout-Mask-Resist Image-After Development Image (ADI) computational lithography pipeline as a three-stage, decision-driven physical evolution process using a Policy Model (Vision Transformer) and Transition Model (Diffusion Transformer with stage-aware heads).
In-domain edge placement error (EPE) is 1.58 nm for Mask, 0.96 nm for Resist Image, and 3.74 nm for ADI predictions.

On an out-of-domain unseen 55nm process setting, EPE increases only modestly to 1.77 nm (Mask), 1.06 nm (Resist Image), and 4.05 nm (ADI), and on a cross-node 28nm LithoSim transfer, mask and resist-image EPE remain at 1.82 nm and 1.37 nm respectively (Performance Results section).

An ablation removing the Space Prior Approximation (SPA) module increases ADI EPE from 3.74 nm to 38.47 nm, demonstrating the necessity of the physics-informed latent space constraint (Ablation Study).

Replacing the stage-specific output heads in the Transition Model with a shared architecture degrades ADI EPE to 26.86 nm, and using deterministic instead of stochastic intervention modeling worsens ADI EPE by 18.59 nm (Ablation Study).

The model is trained and validated on 280k paired samples from industrial 55nm manufacturing spanning 36 process-parameter configurations (exposure dose, focus, resist threshold, illumination source), with generated patterns showing only 0.4% average manufacturing-rule-check violation deviation versus commercial simulation.

997oprE4sh.text: Proposition 3.2 establishes an exact bijection between autoregressive models (ARMs) and energy-based models (EBMs) in function space, via the mapping q(s_t,y_t) = r(s_t,y_t) for y_t=EOS and r(s_t,y_t)+V_q(s_t⊕y_t) otherwise, such that p^ebm_R(y|x) = p^arm_q(y|x) (Proposition 3.2).

Section 3.3 shows this ARM-EBM bijection corresponds to a special case of the soft Bellman equation from maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, with the soft value function V_q(s_t) capturing implicit lookahead over future tokens (Section 3.3).

Proposition 4.1 proves that minimizing negative log-likelihood over ARM functions and over EBM functions yields identical minima, showing teacher forcing is optimal in function space (Proposition 4.1).

An error bound (Proposition 59) shows that distilling an EBM into an ARM yields KL(p^ebm_R, p^arm_q) ≤ 2T·max|q*(s,y)-q(s,y)|, bounding divergence by sequence length T times the maximum logit approximation error (Proposition 59).

Converting an EBM to an equivalent ARM representation costs O(V^T) (exponential in sequence length), whereas converting an ARM to an EBM representation costs only O(VT) (linear) (Section on computational trade-offs).

J36ARcNLEv.text: HC-SOINN is integrated into seven baseline class-incremental learning methods (SimpleCIL, DualPrompt, CODA-Prompt, APER, EASE, SEMA, CL-LoRA), yielding average accuracy gains across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R such as +8.69% for CODA-Prompt on CUB-200 and +12.21% for SEMA on CUB-200 (Table 1).

Combined with the STAR module for drift adaptation, DualPrompt+HC-SOINN+STAR reaches 89.49% average accuracy and CODA-Prompt+HC-SOINN+STAR reaches 92.65% average accuracy on Split CIFAR-100 (Table 2).

Procrustes distance analysis shows feature drift growing to 0.35-0.40 by later incremental tasks, exceeding the 0.1 threshold used to define quasi-linear drift, motivating the topology-aware (non point-wise) design (Figure 1).

HC-SOINN's dual-view inference score combines cosine similarity to the cluster centroid and to the nearest topological node via S(x,c) = α·cos⟨x,μ_c⟩ + (1-α)·max_v cos⟨x,v⟩ (Section on HC-SOINN method).

HC-SOINN maintains a compact representation of roughly 18-21 topological nodes per class on average while adding only about 3.96% training overhead and 0.01% inference overhead on Split CIFAR-100 (Table 6, Efficiency analysis).

ugjBMARbyt.text: The EntUCB algorithm embeds transport plans into a Hilbert space via the Fourier isometry F on L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), reducing the bandit optimal transport problem to linear bandit estimation in that space (Section 4.1, Equation 7).
Theorem 5.1 bounds the entropic regret as R_T^{H,ε}(A) ≤ σ√(2T log(2/δ)) + 2Cβ_T(δ)√(T log det(...)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 5.2 shows that for Lipschitz costs with an entropy penalty decaying as ε_t = αt^{-α}, EntUCB achieves sublinear regret matching classical linear-bandit rates for the Kantorovich optimal transport problem (Theorem 5.2).
Corollary 5.3 establishes that in finite-dimensional/discrete settings with N basis coefficients, the algorithm attains Õ(√(NT)) regret, recovering the parametric OFUL-style rate (Corollary 5.3).
Corollary 5.4 shows that when basis coefficients decay at rate 1-n^{-q}, regret interpolates between Õ(√T) and Õ(T) depending on the decay exponent q (Corollary 5.4).

The confidence sets used by the algorithm are constructed via regularized least-squares in L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), with width controlled by the log-determinant of the design operator, mirroring the classical OFUL confidence ellipsoid construction (Equations 11-12).

Q8LOMDdr2y.text: AtelierJudge achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.81 with human expert subjective ratings of text-to-image prompt quality, approaching the inter-human agreement level of 0.83 (Section on AtelierJudge Evaluator Performance).

AtelierJudge attains 95.5% overall accuracy on objective constraint verification, with prompt-side accuracy exceeding 95% and image-side accuracy surpassing 90% (Objective Constraint Verification results).

Across 8 MLLMs and 4 T2I backends (Gemini-3-Pro-Image, GPT-Image-1, Flux.1 Pro, and SDXL), image-augmented (mimicry) prompting significantly outperforms symbolic-planning prompting even under comparable constraint complexity (Experimental Scale, Mimicry Over Planning).

External MLLM reasoning combined with middleware-equipped T2I backends reduces objective constraint scores from 69.6% to 47.1% on constrained tasks, whereas skilled human prompters reach 81.5% accuracy on the same tasks (Constraint Paradox finding).

The AtelierEval benchmark comprises 360 expert-crafted tasks spanning three categories—Open-ended Creation, Constrained Creation, and Imitation—evaluated with 48 human participants (24 novices, 24 skilled users) (Benchmark composition).

GR335S9IgZ.text: On collaboration-necessary problems, human-AI collaboration (condition C_2) achieves a 31.11% overall pass@1 rate, compared with 18.89% for humans alone (C_H), 0.67% for fully autonomous AI (C_0), and 2.89% for minimally-intervened AI (C_1) (Table 2, Section 5.2).

The difficulty-stratified results show human-AI collaboration maintains 43.33%, 26.67%, and 23.33% pass rates on Easy, Medium, and Hard problems respectively, while human-alone performance degrades from 36.67% to 6.67% over the same difficulty range (Table 2).
The benchmark consists of 45 problem templates spanning 3 difficulty levels and 3 professional tracks (SDE, MLE, Data Science), generating 450 total task instances (Sections 4.1 and 4.4).
State-of-the-art LLMs plateau on these collaboration-necessary tasks: Claude Sonnet 4's best pass@10 reaches only 4.22%, evidencing a ceiling on autonomous higher-order reasoning (Observation 1).

Post-study surveys show 80% of participants used AI for strategic brainstorming and 51% adopted fundamentally different approaches proposed by the AI, indicating strategic breakthroughs can originate from either the human or the AI collaborator (Observation 3).

jnguJEJmYP.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that the vanilla policy gradient (V-PG) decomposes as CA-PG plus a residual term, formally establishing that credit-assigned policy gradient (CA-PG) reduces variance by marginalizing over candidate-set compositions rather than differentiating the joint probability of an entire sampled set (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.1).

Theorem 3.3 shows CA-PG converges to the optimal top-K item partitioning whenever the late-stage ranker policy is 'reasonably aligned', including arbitrary interpolations between a uniform-random and an optimal policy (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).

CA-PG reduces the action-space dependence from |A|^K (vanilla PG) down to |A| by computing gradients with respect to marginal item-inclusion probabilities instead of specific K-item set compositions (Section 3).

On synthetic data with candidate sizes K in {5, 10, 20}, CA-PG avoids the gradient overflow that plagues V-PG and reaches 95% of final policy value roughly 3x faster than V-PG-SwR at K=20 (Section 4.1, Table 2).
On the real-world KuaiRec dataset with candidate sizes K in {50, 100, 200}, CA-PG-SwR shows increasingly larger improvements over V-PG-SwR as the candidate pool grows (Section 4.2, Table 4).

For Plackett-Luce ranking models, CA-PG has O(KL) computational complexity per step, versus O(ML) for the mixture-of-experts variant CA-PG-SwR and O(L) for the TOP1-PG special case (Section 3, Table 3).

XoaS2r1ezP.text: Section 4 proposes evaluating IBP-based certified training methods via Pareto fronts over the natural-vs-certified accuracy trade-off space, using multi-objective Bayesian optimization with Gaussian-process surrogates and Expected Hypervolume Improvement acquisition rather than single hyperparameter configurations (Section 4).

Section 5 empirically compares IBP, CROWN-IBP, SABR, and MTL-IBP on CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet, and MNIST using a CNN7 architecture with a 300-trial optimization budget per benchmark, matching the compute budget used in prior single-configuration studies (Section 5).

Under proper multi-objective tuning, SABR and MTL-IBP each show more than 1 percentage point improvement in both clean and certified accuracy compared to previously reported configurations, revealing substantial undertuning in the prior literature (Section 5, Table 1 in Appendix C).

The Pareto-front comparison shows SABR dominates at the high-natural-accuracy end while MTL-IBP delivers the strongest certified guarantees, with both methods needed to trace out the combined Pareto front (Section 5, Figure 2).

At the larger perturbation radius ε=8/255, all investigated certified training methods contribute to the combined Pareto front but show only modest performance differences across the entire trade-off space, indicating stalled progress at this radius (Section 5, 'Assessing the state of the art', Figure 3).

x7LWdQlwY7.text: Diagnostic-driven Progressive Evolution (DPE) evaluates model performance across 12 capability dimensions (e.g., geometry, medical images, charts, formulas, maps) to generate category proportion vectors guiding subsequent data generation (Section 3, Diagnostic Mechanism).

On CharXiv, DPE improves from a 36.8 baseline to 40.91 across iterations, outperforming VisPlay's 37.5, using only ~3,000 iteratively generated samples versus 47K static samples (Section 4, Table of benchmark results).
On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, DPE achieves 76.2% on MathVista, surpassing the much larger Qwen2.5-VL-72B by +1.4 points, and 53.88% on MathVision, +15.7 points over that larger model (Section 4).

An ablation removing the diagnostic module causes CharXiv accuracy to plateau and oscillate (36.8→36.7→37.5→36.7) rather than steadily improve, and causes regression on MathVision, compared to steady gains with full DPE (Section 5, Ablation Studies).

An ablation removing the image retrieval/editing tools from the Multiple Agents Questioner system reduces CharXiv gains to 38.1 versus 40.91 achieved with the full system (Section 5, Ablation Studies).

DPE maintains higher text diversity (0.846-0.866) and visual diversity (0.847-0.877) across iterations compared to VisPlay, which degrades by iteration 3, and produces higher-quality questions (QS ~4.8) versus VisPlay's decline to 3.32 by iteration 3 (Section 5, Data Diversity and Question Quality analysis).

IexQEyHm2L.text: Standard offline RL algorithms trained on structured-state expert actions but pixel observations at test time exhibit performance drops of up to 80%, motivating the Confounded MDP (CMDP) formalization (Section 1/3).

Theorem 3.1 establishes a causal Bellman equation providing a value-function lower bound that distinguishes cases where behavioral and target policies agree (standard Bellman update) from cases where they disagree (worst-case value via ensemble minimums) (Theorem 3.1).

Causal Flow Q-Learning (CFQL) combines ensemble Q-networks, a BC flow-matching policy, a one-step target policy, and a discriminator that distinguishes BC flow actions from target-policy actions to approximate policy agreement (Section 4).

On 25 pixel-based OGBench tasks, CFQL achieves a 120% (1.21x) normalized mean success-rate improvement relative to FQL, matching or outperforming the best baseline on 19 of 25 tasks (Section 5, Table of offline results).
During offline-to-online fine-tuning, CFQL yields an 8% improvement over FQL and is the first method to fully solve certain visual-puzzle-4x4 task variants (Section 5, Offline-to-Online results).

Ablations show that fewer Q-network ensemble members (2-4) outperform more (6), since larger ensembles induce over-pessimism, and that CFQL underperforms Gaussian-policy baselines on locomotion tasks despite outperforming on manipulation tasks like cube and puzzle (Section 5/6, Ablations and Limitations).

WArbqRUsAe.text: FormulaCode's dataset construction pipeline filters 766 scraped repositories down to 957 validated performance-optimization tasks via attribute filtering (3,181 candidate PRs), environment synthesis (1,232 tasks), and statistical validation at p < 0.002 (Section 3, Dataset Construction).

Each of the 957 tasks is paired with an average of 264.6 community-maintained performance workloads, versus FormulaCode patches being 5.2x larger than SWE-Bench patches (38 vs 7.2 edited lines) and spanning more files (3.93 vs 3.04) (Section 3/4, Dataset Characteristics comparison to SWE-Bench).

All evaluated frontier agents (GPT-5, Claude 4.0 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Qwen 3 Coder) achieve speedups exceeding 1.0x over baseline code but show negative Advantage scores relative to human experts, who achieve a 1.104x average speedup (Section 5, Main Results).

Agents perform better at function-level optimizations than repository-level ones, with OpenHands + Claude 4.0 Sonnet showing strongest module-level performance that degrades at function-level, while OpenHands + GPT-5 shows the inverse pattern (Section 5, Optimization Scale).

Agent performance relative to experts is non-monotonic across GitHub star-count quintiles: mean advantage is -0.04 in Q1 (133-202 stars), most competitive in Q2-Q3, and lowest (negative advantage, 1.08x expert speedup) in Q4/Q5 repositories with the most stars (Section 5, Repository Popularity Effects).

Agents show positive advantage on parallelization and batching optimization tasks but negative advantages exceeding -0.2 on vectorized-operation and C-extension-delegation tasks (Section 5, Optimization Type Performance).

XHZK5abtw2.text: The tau-Banking domain comprises 698 unstructured knowledge documents (~194,562 tokens, cl100k_base) across 21 product categories, with 51 discoverable tools and 14 permanent agent tools, and 97 tasks requiring an average of 18.6 documents and 9.52 tool calls (Section 3, Benchmark Statistics).
The best configuration, GPT-5.2 (high reasoning) with terminal-based search, achieves only 25.52% pass^1, dropping to 13.40% pass^4 under the pass^k reliability metric (Section 4, Results Table).

Even with ground-truth (golden) retriever documents provided in context, the best model, Claude-4.5-Opus, achieves only 39.69% pass^1, indicating the bottleneck is policy reasoning rather than retrieval (Section 4, Retrieval Matters, But Reasoning Dominates).

A no-knowledge-base baseline achieves only ~2% success, while providing the entire knowledge base in context achieves only ~12% (GPT-5.2 high), confirming that both retrieval necessity and irrelevant-document noise affect performance (Section 4, Necessity of Knowledge).

Terminal-based search (grep/find/cat) outperforms dense and sparse (BM25) retrieval by a statistically significant margin, but only for high-reasoning models; GPT-5.2 without reasoning shows no benefit from terminal search (Section 4, Terminal-Based Search Benefits Recent Models).

Error analysis over four dominant failure modes finds search inefficiency/unfounded assumptions account for ~23% of failures and complex multi-document interdependencies account for ~14.5% (Figure 4, Error Analysis).

6ml27Kec2C.text: OpenSage is presented as the first Agent Development Kit enabling LLMs to self-generate agent topology (vertical and horizontal sub-agent structures), synthesize new tools at runtime, and manage a hierarchical short-/long-term memory system (Section 1/3, Core Technical Components).
On CyberGym (1,507 C/C++ vulnerabilities), SageAgent with GPT-5 (medium) resolves 60.2% of tasks, versus 50.6% for the Anthropic Agent baseline and 39.4% for OpenHands (Table 2).
On Terminal-Bench 2.0 (89 expert-curated tasks), SageAgent with Gemini 3 Pro scores 65.2±2.0%, versus 64.7±2.7% for Ante and 52.1±2.5% for Claude Code (Table 2).
On SWE-Bench Pro (266 Python tasks), SageAgent with Gemini 3 Flash resolves 59.0% of tasks, versus 40.2% for SWE-agent (Table 2).

An ablation on a 300-instance CyberGym subset shows that removing the horizontal topology reduces performance by 15% on affected tasks, and removing the vertical topology increases context-summarization events per task from 6.4 to 13.1 (Section 5, Ablation Studies: Self-Generating Topology).

In a tool-synthesis ablation, the agent constructs 39 custom tools (Python/C++), including grammar-aware fuzzers and format-specific generators, and performance degrades substantially when restricted to raw terminal access without the tooling system (Section 5, Ablation Studies: Tooling System).

TP8OuKKmsf.text: On the TUAB dataset, JET achieves a TS-FID of 188.27 versus 324.18 for EEG-GAN and 342.91 for Vanilla Diffusion (Table 1).
On the TUSZ dataset, JET achieves a TS-FID of 151.27 versus 274.37 for EEG-GAN and 300.47 for Vanilla Diffusion, exceeding the claimed 40% reduction (Table 1).
JET reproduces the 1/f^chi power-law spectral scaling and alpha-band peaks of real EEG without spectral bias (Figure 3).
JET preserves non-stationary temporal drift statistics within 2x of the real-vs-real floor, unlike baseline generators (Figure 4, Table 2).

An ablation removing the constraint hierarchy (reconstruction, statistical consistency, and spatiotemporal structure losses) shows all components contribute to the full model's best performance (Table 4).
An ablation on patch size shows P=200 gives the best efficiency-fidelity tradeoff for the transformer tokenizer (Table 6).

iPTCYxloni.text: The framework uses a DDPM-based U-Net with cross-attention layers to condition brain-signal generation on CLIP ViT-L/14 image embeddings (cross-attention dimension 768) (Section on architecture).
On THINGS-EEG2 (10 subjects, 63 channels, 1000 Hz), within-subject generation achieves average MSE=0.217 and PCC=0.188 (Table 1).
On THINGS-MEG (4 subjects, 271 channels), within-subject generation achieves average MSE=0.763 and PCC=0.122 (Table 4).
Cross-subject generalization degrades performance, with EEG MSE rising from 0.217 (within-subject) to 0.231 (cross-subject) (Tables 2-3).
Cross-subject MEG generation similarly degrades from MSE=0.763 (within-subject) to MSE=0.880 (cross-subject) (Table 5).

TA3NDHgNJh.text: Proposition 3.1 proves that for any number of bidders n and any epsilon>0, there exists a valuation distribution where the deterministic AMA revenue REV^D-AMA is at most epsilon times the optimal revenue REV (Section 3.1).

Theorem 3.3 shows that under bidder-independent distributions, CA-AMA and classic AMA yield equal revenue, but under correlated distributions CA-AMA can attain the optimal revenue REV^F while classic AMA remains arbitrarily poor (Section 3.2).
The CA-AMA mechanism adds a correlation-aware payment term p^Cor_i(V_{-i}), depending only on rival bidders' valuations, while preserving dominant-strategy incentive compatibility.
In the Dirichlet Value Share experiment (alpha=0.5, 3 bidders x 10 items), CA-AMA attains revenue 3.6205 versus 3.1363 for randomized AMA (Table 1).
In the Linear Mixture Asymmetric setting (2 bidders x 5 items), CA-AMA attains revenue 1.9359 versus 1.7135 for randomized AMA, while ex-post individual-rationality regret stays near 0.001 (Table 1).

f6rJlcdN4x.text: MIND decomposes an instance-dependent noise transition matrix into a linear combination of a finite set of K basis transition matrices, approximating a high-dimensional noise manifold (Section 2.2).
Theorem 2.2 establishes that, under an anchor subspace assumption in latent feature space, the basis matrices and assignment functions are identifiable up to permutation.
Under PCAM structural noise, MIND achieves 40.58% mIoU on S3DIS and 39.99% mIoU on ScanNetV2, versus 39.36% and 38.23% for the CA2C baseline (Table 1).
In zero-shot S3DIS-to-ScanNet domain transfer under PCAM noise, MIND reaches 23.54% versus 21.50% for CA2C (Table 3).
MIND corrects unsupervised OpenSeg vision-language-model hallucinations on S3DIS, improving from a 43.20% baseline to 51.34% (+8.14 points) (Table 4).
An ablation shows the full MIND model with K=16 subspaces reaches 40.58% accuracy, versus 34.08% for global estimation (K=1) and 37.38% without the orthogonality loss (Table 5).

cyR2FtZzY1.text: The paper attributes rotation-QuaRot incompatibility with MXFP4 to power-of-two block scaling producing outlier quantization error up to five times larger than in regular blocks (Figure 3c).
Global rotation increases the share of activations exceeding a magnitude threshold of 1.5 from about 5% to 11%, worsening MXFP4 quantization (Figure 5).

Block Rotation Quantization (BRQ) applies a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix diag(R1,...,Re) aligned with MXFP4's 32-channel blocks, reducing rotation complexity from O(N^2) to O(N x 32) (Section 4.3, Equation 1).
Random rotation causes catastrophic degradation under MXFP4, raising LLaMA-2 7B perplexity from 7.08 to 13.09 (Table 1).
On LLaMA-3.2 1B, BRQ improves perplexity from 12.78 (QuaRot+) to 11.95 and zero-shot accuracy from 48.83 to 49.87 (Table 2).
BRQ reduces inference overhead by 40% compared to standard QuaRot rotation (Table 4).

F6PoIbPAe2.text: On the 150-case medical diagnosis benchmark from DiagnosisArena, Graph of States (GoS) achieves 39.86% Match accuracy versus 26.09% for the best baseline (Multi-agent/Tree-of-Thought) (Table 2).
On the 150-incident failure-diagnosis benchmark of real production systems, GoS reaches 70.67% Match accuracy versus 34.00% for the best baseline (Multi-agent/Chain-of-Thought) (Table 2).
GoS attains its accuracy gains at roughly 8x lower inference cost than the best-performing baselines (Section 5, Cost Analysis).

Ablating the causal graph or the state machine each drops medical-diagnosis Match accuracy from 39.86% down to 12.32%, and removing the reasoning-focus mechanism alone drops it to 19.57% (Section 5, Ablation Study).
GoS produces 0% Evidence Fabrication errors compared to 22.22% for baselines, and reduces Context Drift errors from 41.32% to 9.70% (Section 5, Error Analysis).

mIRio0hWWI.text: BayesNCL improves semantic consistency on ImageNet-100 from 14.93 (NCL baseline) to 36.14, a 142.1% relative improvement (Section 5, Table on interpretability results).

BayesNCL matches or exceeds NCL's linear-probing Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-100 (70.44% vs 69.63%), showing no significant downstream performance trade-off despite the added sparsity gating (Section 5).

Theorem 4.5 shows that under the sparse Bernoulli gating prior, high-prevalence (near-ubiquitous) features are automatically gated out once their alignment gain falls below the sparsity cost, formalizing 'sparsity as semantic filtering' (Theorem 4.5).
Theorem 4.7 establishes that BayesNCL strictly reduces spurious similarity contributed by shared background features within negative pairs relative to standard contrastive learning (Theorem 4.7).

Ablations show hard (straight-through-estimator) gating is critical: replacing it with soft gating collapses ImageNet-100 semantic consistency from 36.14 to 8.54, while the added computational overhead is minimal (FLOPs 1.416G to 1.419G on CIFAR-100) (Section 5, Ablation Study).

yVGbbB3ERW.text: WFR-MFM produces one-step samples via the closed-form update x1 = x0 + v(x0,0,1) and mass update m1 = m0*exp(h(x0,0,1)), using learned mean-velocity and mean-growth-rate fields instead of ODE trajectory simulation (Section on Mean-Flow Framework).

WFR-MFM achieves inference speedups of 38x to 2,965x over adaptive ODE solver baselines while matching or beating their Wasserstein-1 distance accuracy across evaluated datasets (Table of experimental results).

WFR-MFM is evaluated against TIGON, DeepRUOT, Var-RUOT, WFR-FM, MMFM and other trajectory-based baselines on synthetic (Gene, Dyngen, high-dimensional Gaussian) and real single-cell RNA-seq datasets (embryoid bodies, EMT, CITE-seq, mouse hematopoiesis) (Section on Experiments/Datasets).
At large scale, WFR-MFM performs one-step inference over 5,000 perturbation conditions in 6.55 seconds (Section on Large-scale Perturbation Experiments).

Derivative identities relating the mean-flow variables to their instantaneous velocity and growth-rate fields are used to define regression targets for training without requiring trajectory simulation (Section on Training/Derivative Identities).

tLW4Tc7Zn9.text: SAGE re-ranks diffusion-planner candidate trajectories at inference time using a latent consistency energy computed over the first K=10 steps, combined with value estimates via Equation 12, with keep-rate P=0.8 and penalty weight lambda=0.1 (Section on Inference Mechanism, Equation 12).

SAGE improves average D4RL MuJoCo locomotion scores from 82.9 to 84.4, Kitchen manipulation from 81.80 to 85.55, and AntMaze navigation from 81.62 to 84.53, using 500 evaluation seeds per task (Section on Experimental Results, D4RL Benchmarks).
The learned latent-consistency energy localizes corrupted/dynamically-inconsistent action sequences with AUROC of at least 0.94 across all evaluated domains (Section on Diagnostic Validation).
SAGE requires no environment rollouts and no retraining of the underlying diffusion planner, adding only 6.8% computational overhead at inference (Section on Key Design Elements).

SAGE is trained in two offline stages: a JEPA encoder trained via masked state-sequence prediction (Stage I), followed by an action-conditioned latent predictor trained with teacher-forced one-step prediction, short-horizon rollout consistency, and an action-usage hinge loss (Stage II) (Section on Technical Approach).

7i44Lx4KEY.text: TRACED decomposes reasoning trajectories into a displacement (Progress) component and a curvature (Stability) component computed after semantic whitening via the unembedding-matrix-induced metric (Section on Technical Approach, Semantic Whitening).

Correct reasoning trajectories follow an approximately linear displacement-scaling slope of about 0.82, while incorrect trajectories show sub-linear scaling with slope about 0.53 (Section on Key Findings, Geometric Signatures).

TRACED achieves an AUROC of 0.8300 for hallucination/error detection on GPQA using DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, evaluated alongside AUPR and FPR@95 across six benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, GPQA, Social IQA, Understanding Fables) (Section on Experimental Results).

Incorrect reasoning trajectories exhibit a higher Exploration-to-Reflection regression rate than correct ones (0.37 vs 0.25), which the authors term 'Hesitation Loops' when curvature is high (Section on Cognitive Interpretation).
TRACED's classifier converges using approximately 400 reference samples and maintains performance variance of no more than 2.8% across differing reasoning-complexity levels (Section on Robustness).

94FOsjgeHK.text: GROD reduces FPR@95 on image OOD detection from 21.97% (baseline) to 0.12%, an improvement of over 21 percentage points (Table 1).
GROD improves AUROC on image classification OOD tasks from 93.62% to 99.98% (Table 1).
On text classification OOD tasks using BERT, GROD improves FPR@95 by 12.89 percentage points and AUROC by 2.27 percentage points over baselines (Table 3).

Theorem 1 (Informal Theorem 4) establishes that OOD detection learnability for transformers requires finite training data and an OOD misclassification penalty that exceeds the ID misclassification penalty (Section 3, Theorem 1).
Ablation studies show the binary loss term, synthetic OOD generation module, and Mahalanobis distance filtering each individually contribute to GROD's overall performance gains (Table 4).
GROD outperforms baseline OOD detectors MSP, ODIN, VIM, GEN, ASH, G-ODIN, NPOS, and CIDER on CIFAR-10-based image OOD benchmarks (Table 1).

XfejyJ9nc4.text: ASCL formulates safety alignment as a multi-turn tool-use process in which the model autonomously decides whether to retrieve a curated document of 107 safety terms across 21 categories using a ReAct-style reasoning loop (Section on ASCL Framework).
With Qwen3-4B, the IFPO-trained model achieves 98.87% average safety score and 6.00% average over-refusal rate, compared to 95.98% safety and 16.33% over-refusal for the BC-only baseline (Table 1).

IFPO rebalances RL advantage estimates by reweighting them inversely to the sampling frequency of rule-consultation actions, preventing the policy from collapsing into always consulting rules (Section on IFPO Algorithm).
ASCL outperforms the STAR-1 baseline by more than 5 percentage points on safety benchmarks while maintaining lower over-refusal (Table 1).

Ablations show that surrogate chain-of-thought variants without the external retrieval mechanism underperform the full ASCL+IFPO approach, confirming the necessity of decoupling rule retrieval from reasoning (Ablation Studies section).

On general reasoning benchmarks (MATH-500, GSM8K, GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro), ASCL shows no obvious accuracy gains, indicating the safety-specific training does not transfer to general reasoning capability (Generalization Limitation section).

FrXlHWKtvy.text: SpatialJB reorganizes harmful prompt text into six 2D spatial layouts (Acrostic, Telestich, Center-Embedded, Staircase, Corner, and Multilingual Randomization) to exploit weaknesses in transformer serialization of spatial text (Section on Core Method).
Without any guardrail, SpatialJB achieves attack success rates of 95-98.3% on GPT-4 and 100% on DeepSeek-V3, Grok4, and Llama4 (Key Results section).

After adding the OpenAI Moderation API guardrail, SpatialJB still achieves attack success rates of 90.7% on GPT-4 and 91.3% on DeepSeek-V3, exceeding the 75% threshold claimed for guardrail-protected settings (Key Results section).

SpatialJB's average attack success rate (~95%) substantially exceeds baseline obfuscation attacks such as Base64 encoding (~7-10% ASR) and Ubbi Dubbi (~10-14% ASR) (Superiority Over Baselines comparison).

Two theorems formalize the vulnerability: self-attention loses visual-neighbor information when 2D layouts are serialized to 1D sequences, and semantic correlation decays exponentially with serialized token distance, measured at 0.9419 for linear layouts versus 0.5846 for spatial layouts (Theoretical Foundation section, two theorems).

The proposed SpatialD defense, which reconstructs text from predefined positions (terminals, diagonals, corners) for safety validation, achieves a Defense Success Rate of 77-90.5% across tested models (Defense Mechanism section).

TH6pLxCOQ3.text: 3DMedAgent decomposes 3D CT analysis into three sequential stages: Organ-Aware Memory Initialization (OAMI) using VISTA3D segmentation, Coarse-to-Fine Lesion Targeting (CFLT) using a CT-CLIP encoder, and a Think-with-1-Slice Loop (T1S-Loop) capped at T_max=5 iterations (Section on Core Methodology, three-stage framework).

The DeepChestVQA benchmark comprises 892 CT scans and 1,020 question-answer pairs spanning Recognition (3 subtypes, 180 pairs), Visual Reasoning (8 subtypes, 480 pairs), and Medical Reasoning (6 subtypes, 360 pairs) categories (DeepChestVQA Benchmark section).

On DeepTumorVQA, 3DMedAgent with GPT-5 achieves an average accuracy gain of about 20 percentage points over the average of baseline MLLMs across Measurement, Recognition, Visual Reasoning, and Medical Reasoning task types (Table 2).
On DeepChestVQA, 3DMedAgent with GPT-5 outperforms the baseline average on Recognition (0.69 vs 0.52), Visual Reasoning (0.49 vs 0.32), and Medical Reasoning (0.53 vs 0.40) (Table 3).

3DMedAgent is compared in zero-shot settings against general MLLMs (GPT-5, Qwen3-VL 30B), medical MLLMs (MedGemma 27B, HuatuoGPT-Vision 34B), and 3D-specialized models (RadFM, M3D), all without 3D-specific fine-tuning of the agent itself (Comparative Baselines section).

Cross-dataset evaluation across sources such as MSD-Spleen and AMOS shows 3DMedAgent maintains consistent robustness, whereas fine-tuned 3D-specialized baselines exhibit sharp performance drops on out-of-source data (Generalization Analysis section).

NWZZmXRIH5.text: UDS combines an intra-sample importance score based on the nuclear norm of the logits matrix with an inter-sample diversity distance computed via low-dimensional random projection against a FIFO memory buffer of previously selected samples, combined as s_total = s_intra + alpha*s_inter (Section on UDS Framework).

On Qwen-2.5-7B, UDS outperforms the prior state-of-the-art online batch selection method GREATS by 5.15 points on MMLU (63.34% vs 58.19%), 1.02 points on ScienceQA, 1.30 points on GSM8K, and 1.24 points on HumanEval (Experimental Results table).

UDS achieves higher training throughput than full-dataset fine-tuning, reaching 3.41 samples/second versus 2.27 samples/second on MMLU and 6.81 versus 6.24 samples/second on HumanEval (Training Efficiency section).

Ablation results relative to random selection show the full UDS method gains +9.08% on MMLU, +1.91% on ScienceQA, +2.22% on GSM8K, and +6.08% on HumanEval, exceeding either the nuclear-norm-only or diversity-distance-only variants individually (Ablation Study table).

With Llama-3.1-8B on MMLU, UDS peaks at a per-batch selection size of K=4 samples and at this setting surpasses full-dataset fine-tuning accuracy despite training on a small curated subset (Data Scale Analysis section).

Experiments use LoRA fine-tuning with rank=8, batch size 8, on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B across MMLU, ScienceQA, GSM8K, and CodeAlpaca-20k, with results averaged over 4 runs with different random seeds (Experimental Setup section).

gIkOQkb4fU.text: LAST (Lie-algebraic Action Space Tokenizer) uses a two-stage transformation: Global Topological Linearization mapping SE(3) trajectories to the se(3) tangent space via logarithmic maps and B-spline abstraction, followed by Local Metric Discretization with whitened residual quantization (Section 3.3.1-3.3.2).
On reconstruction quality, LAST achieves 0.6e-2 MAE versus 1.1e-2 for RVQ and 1.8e-2 for FAST tokenizers (Table 1).
LAST-Continuous achieves 95.8% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long-horizon), reported as state-of-the-art (Table 2).
LAST-Continuous achieves 57.3% overall success on SimplerEnv-WidowX, compared against baselines including Octo, OpenVLA, SpatialVLA, GR00T-N1.5, pi-0, FAST, and BEAST (Table 3).
Ablations show removing discrete intent supervision drops real-world ZipSeal task success from 57% to 22% (Table 5).

Lemma 3.2 establishes statistical alignment via whitened isomorphism, using covariance-aware whitening to align anisotropic physical action metrics with isotropic semantic metrics (Section 3, Lemma 3.2).

RuTNWE1wr7.text: The Pyramidal Shapley-Taylor (PST) framework quantifies cross-modal interaction intensity between motion joints/segments and text tokens using a Shapley-Taylor Interaction measure based on random permutations over tokens (Section 3.2).
PST performs alignment in three progressive stages: joint-wise, segment-wise, and holistic alignment (Section 3.3).
On HumanML3D under the 'All' retrieval protocol, PST achieves 12.45% text-to-motion R@1, exceeding the prior best of 11.80% (Table 1).
On HumanML3D, PST achieves 13.59% motion-to-text R@1 with a median rank (MedR) of 10.00, versus 15.00 for the best prior method (Table 1).
On KIT-ML under the 'All' protocol, PST achieves 16.01% text-to-motion R@1 and 16.76% motion-to-text R@1, versus a prior best of 15.13% (Table 2).
PST is compared against baselines TEMOS, T2M, TMR, MotionPatch, and Lyu et al. (2025) on the HumanML3D (14,616 sequences) and KIT-ML (4,888 training motions) datasets (Section 4.1).

372oAcqeKh.text: IPVRM (Implicit Prefix-Value Reward Model) learns a prefix-conditioned value function trained with a binary cross-entropy loss against terminal outcome labels using a margin m (Section 3.1, Eq. 9).
IPVRM improves ProcessBench step-verification F1 by +11.3 points over the DPO-RM baseline on Qwen3-0.6B (Table 1).

DistRL combines a token-level PPO loss with a distribution-level PPO loss (candidate-token TD advantages plus sampled-token GAE) via a weighted objective L_DistRL = L_Tok-PPO + alpha*L_Dist-PPO (Section 3.2, Eq. 14).
DistRL powered by IPVRM achieves an average score of 16.7 on Qwen3-0.6B and 37.7 on Qwen3-8B across AIME 2024, MATH-500, Minerva-Math, OlympiadBench, and AMC (Table 5).
IPVRM and DistRL are evaluated against baselines Q-RM, EndoRM, DPO-RM, Implicit PRM, GRPO, PRIME, and SPRO, trained on Eurus-2 SFT (~230K) and Eurus-2 RL (~480K) data (Section 4).

1yTbhxUGef.text: TASM (Task-Aware Structured Memory) is a training-free framework combining task-vector guided compression, semantics-aware token merging via bipartite graph matching, and query-adaptive dynamic retrieval using a Jensen-Shannon divergence trigger (Sections 3.2-3.4).

On Qwen2-VL across six benchmarks, TASM outperforms the EMLoC baseline, e.g. 65.0% vs 63.6% on ImageNet-100, 19.5 vs 18.3 on ScreenSpot, and 109.5 vs 102.0 on YouCook2, while achieving roughly 79% memory reduction versus full-context (Table 1).
On the Visual Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmark, TASM achieves 67.7% average accuracy versus 53.4% for EMLoC (Table 2).
TASM's task-vector token scoring retains 79.2% of visual tokens' relevant information versus 45.2% for attention-only scoring in an ablation (Table 6).
At 32k-token context length, TASM achieves 85% memory reduction while sustaining 43.8 tokens/s throughput (Table 10).

jSOVSYO6YX.text: Q-Align DT enforces alignment between input return-to-go values and learned policy behavior via a combined objective L_total(theta) = L_SL(theta) + lambda_e * L_Align(theta) (Section 4, Eq. 6).

Theorem 5.1 shows Q-Align DT uses directional Q-function information to eliminate the log|A| dependence in policy class complexity, reducing it from O(|S||G|log|A|) to a bound of order |S||G| (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1).
On D4RL Gym locomotion tasks, Q-Align DT achieves a cumulative normalized score of 856.9 across 9 tasks versus 812.3 for the QCS baseline (Table 1).
On D4RL AntMaze, Q-Align DT scores 96.4±1.12 on antmaze-umaze versus 92.7 for QCS (Table 2).
Q-Align DT achieves a mean RTG-alignment RMSE of 9.01 versus 32.81 for QCS, indicating substantially higher fidelity between conditioned and realized returns (Table 3).

In zero-shot HalfCheetah-Vel velocity-tracking transfer, Q-Align DT achieves an average episode return of -142.3 versus -754.7 for RADT, demonstrating generalization where prior methods fail (Table 5).

x88YyM4ano.text: LiteLVLM maintains 90% of original pixel-grounding performance while achieving a 22% inference speedup and a 2.3x memory reduction (Abstract, Figure 1 caption).
LiteLVLM significantly outperforms existing token-pruning methods by over 5% across diverse token budgets on Referring Expression Segmentation (Table 1, Section 5.2).
The similarity-aware visual token selection strategy retains tokens with low similarity to the [EOS] token, reversing the conventional high-similarity selection approach (Section 4.2).
Section 3.2 ('Visual-Text Similarity Reversal') documents the phenomenon whereby CLIP's text-guided similarity ranking is inverted for effective token pruning in pixel grounding (Section 3.2).

9SLQACsSbw.text: The fairness layer, formulated as g(z) = arg min over y~ of the discrepancy d~(y~,z) subject to affine inequality and equality constraints, is globally 1/mu-Lipschitz continuous and differentiable almost everywhere under strongly convex objectives (Theorem 4.1).
Backpropagation through the fairness layer zeroes gradient components perpendicular to active constraint surfaces while leaving feasible-direction components unaffected (Theorem 4.4).

The online primal-dual inference algorithm (Algorithm 1) guarantees that the sample-weighted average fairness violation across streaming inference batches converges to at most epsilon, even for arbitrarily small batch sizes (Theorem 3.2, Algorithm 1).

On loan default prediction, employee wage modeling, and image classification (CelebA, FairFace), the fairness layer satisfies demographic parity, equalized residuals, and equalized odds constraints while baselines including Lagrangian penalty methods frequently violate them (Section on experimental results).
The fairness layer achieves 18-30% test loss improvements on synthetic datasets and 2-5% accuracy gains over post-hoc projection methods (Section on experimental results).

pXymBD1UZg.text: 3DEditVerse comprises 116,309 training pairs (54,000 pose-driven geometric-edit pairs from 108 characters with 500 poses each, plus 64,123 text-guided appearance-edit pairs) and 1,500 curated test pairs (Section on dataset construction).
3DEditFormer outperforms VoxHammer on 3D editing metrics, improving Chamfer Distance from 9.84 to 7.04 and F1@0.01 from 77.22 to 86.05, an overall reported +13% improvement in 3D metrics (Table 2).

3DEditFormer performs precise edits without requiring auxiliary 3D masks via a dual-guidance attention mechanism combining fine-grained structural features (late diffusion timesteps, t about 0) and semantic transition features (early timesteps, t about 1), formalized as h = h1 + g1*h2 + g2*h3 (Section on dual-guidance attention architecture).

Ablation studies show Chamfer Distance improves progressively from 16.23 (baseline) to 14.59 with fine-grained features, to 14.08 with added semantic features, to 13.84 with time-adaptive gating (Ablation table).

9dKTHof9rW.text: The cross term between token embeddings and positional embeddings (E W_Q K P^T) produces a horizontal gradient in vision-encoder attention logits that breaks left-right symmetry, as visualized in Figure 5(a)-(b) (Section 5, Figure 5).
Ablating the positional-token embedding cross term reduces left-right discrimination accuracy to near chance level (about 50%) (Section 5).

Label diversity, more than layout diversity, is shown to be the primary driver of generalization to unseen object-pair configurations, based on image-to-text alignment accuracy scaling with number of training labels (Figure 3, Section 3).

Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), as used in models like Llama 3 and Qwen, can induce the positional bias required for left-right discrimination through rotation mechanisms rather than learnable positional embeddings (Appendix I, Section I.1).

tbz8ixrEKd.text: RL-D2 reframes policy improvement as distributional matching by using policy mirror descent to define a target distribution pi_MD via a closed-form softmax weighting by advantage divided by a temperature parameter lambda (Equations 2-3, Section 3.2).

On DNA sequence generation, RL-D2 reduces GPU memory consumption from 66.4GB to 10.6GB and computation time from 268 minutes to 97 minutes compared to the DRAKES baseline, while achieving state-of-the-art reward and log-likelihood (Section 5.1, Figure 1).
RL-D2 outperforms baselines in 4 of 5 MinAtar tasks (Table 1) and in 36 of 56 Atari environments (Section 5.2, Table 1, Figure 2).

On the Google Research Football 11-vs-11 scenario, RL-D2 achieves 54.2% (+/-5.1) win/success rate versus 15.3% (+/-6.2) for an autoregressive baseline, across a suite of eight scenarios from 3-vs-1 to 11-vs-11 (Table 2, Section 5.3).

tQCMbay712.text: MedCoG-Meta achieves an average accuracy of 37.5% across five hard medical benchmark subsets (MedQA-Hard, MedMCQA-Hard, MMLU-Hard, MMLU-Pro-Hard, PubMedQA-Hard), an 8.7% absolute improvement over the AFlow baseline's 34.5% (Table 2).

MedCoG attains an Inference Density of 5.5x, meaning it matches reference-model performance while using 5.5x less inference cost, and an Inference Incremental Efficiency (IIE) of 0.443 versus 0.124 for AFlow (Section 4, Table 2).

The Meta-Cognition Regulator computes a three-dimensional state vector s = [s_c, s_f, s_k] representing complexity, familiarity, and knowledge density, each compared against calibrated thresholds tau = [tau_c, tau_f, tau_k] to gate use of procedural, episodic, and factual knowledge (Section 3.2).
On the full (non-hard) MedQA set, the oracle configuration reaches 98.98% accuracy, surpassing OpenAI o1's reported 96.52% (Table 1).
On MedQA-Hard, the oracle configuration reaches 67.0% accuracy versus 50.0% for the best existing method (Table 1).
Error analysis in Section 4.6 identifies 7 distinct error types in the model's reasoning failures on hard medical questions (Section 4.6).

hnoSRifw1F.text: LASER is evaluated on three continuum field reconstruction tasks: 2D Navier-Stokes on a 64x64 grid, 3D Shallow-Water on a 64x128 grid, and Sea Surface Temperature (SST) on a 171x360 grid with land constraints (Table 2).
On Navier-Stokes (viscosity 1e-3) with 256 observations, LASER's active sensing achieves an MSE of 0.302x10^-3, versus 2.720x10^-3 for fixed AROMA and 1.344x10^-3 for fixed DiffusionPDE (Table 4).

With only 64 observations on the same Navier-Stokes task, LASER achieves 0.434x10^-3 MSE versus 20.27x10^-3 for AROMA and 6.543x10^-3 for DiffusionPDE, showing a larger relative advantage under sparser sensing (Table 4).
On the Shallow-Water task with 256 observations, LASER achieves 0.257x10^-3 MSE compared to 12.59x10^-3 for AROMA and 3.175x10^-3 for DiffusionPDE (Table 4).
An ablation removing the dynamic filtering component increases MSE from 0.3024 to 0.3913 on Navier-Stokes (viscosity 1e-3) with 256 observations (Table 7).
Increasing the predictive reward horizon H from 1 to 5 reduces out-of-sample-time reconstruction error from 0.6136 to 0.3380 (Table 8).

NhL0mBNFk4.text: DAPPr defines a possibilistic posterior over network parameters and projects it into prediction space via a supremum operator, approximated with learnable Dirichlet possibility functions, with a closed-form surrogate maximizer given in Proposition 1 under cross-entropy loss (Section 4, Proposition 1).
On CIFAR-10, DAPPr reaches 92.00% accuracy and 91.72 OOD-AUPR (SVHN as OOD), compared to 91.19% accuracy and 91.20 OOD-AUPR for F-EDL (Table 1).
On CIFAR-100, DAPPr reaches 70.85% accuracy versus 69.40% for F-EDL (Table 1).
On the fine-grained CUB-200-2011 benchmark, DAPPr reaches 55.95% accuracy and 89.53% OOD detection (ImageNet-O), versus 51.83% accuracy and lower OOD performance for R-EDL (Table 3).
On Mistral-7B fine-tuned with OBQA, DAPPr reaches 89.47% accuracy, 0.36 NLL, and 90.42 OOD-AUROC (ARC-C), compared to 88.73% accuracy, 0.41 NLL, and 88.58 OOD-AUROC for IB-EDL (Table 5).

Figure 5 shows that standard evidential deep learning (EDL) exhibits pathological epistemic uncertainty that increases with more training data at certain points, whereas DAPPr's epistemic uncertainty consistently decreases as training data increases (Figure 5).

Jr7k590VxW.text: SONAR achieves 1.57% EER on the ASVspoof 2021 Deep Fake (DF) evaluation set and 1.55% EER on the Logical Access (LA) set in its full-training configuration (Table 1).
On the In-The-Wild (ITW) corpus, SONAR-Full achieves 6.00% EER versus 10.46% EER for the XLSR+AASIST baseline (Table 1).
SONAR-Full converges (stabilizes) within 12 training epochs and SONAR-Finetune within 4-6 epochs, compared to roughly 100 epochs required by prior baseline methods (Section 4).

The architecture uses a dual-path design with a Content Feature Extractor (XLSR encoder) and a Noise Feature Extractor (constrained SRM filters plus XLSR encoder), fused via cross-attention and classified with AASIST (Figure 1, Section 4.1).

A Jensen-Shannon divergence loss term (Equation 8) aligns low- and high-frequency embeddings for genuine audio while separating them for fake audio, which the authors describe as the first use of learnable distributional alignment across frequency bands for deepfake detection (Equation 8).

9vPBISqNVo.text: AD-MIR surpasses the strongest general-purpose agent baseline, DVD, by 1.8 percentage points in strict accuracy and 9.5 percentage points in relaxed accuracy on the AdsQA benchmark (abstract only).

AD-MIR uses a two-stage architecture: a Structure-Aware Memory Construction phase that converts raw video into a structured database via combined semantic retrieval and exact keyword matching, followed by a Structured Reasoning Agent phase (abstract only).

The Structure-Aware Memory Construction phase prioritizes fine-grained brand details such as logos and on-screen text while filtering out irrelevant background content to isolate key protagonists (abstract only).
The Structured Reasoning Agent mimics a marketing expert via an iterative inquiry loop that decomposes video narratives to infer implicit persuasion tactics (abstract only).

AD-MIR's evidence-based self-correction mechanism validates inferred marketing insights against specific video frames and automatically backtracks when visual support for an insight is lacking (abstract only).

uw63l3T9un.text: C-DEQ achieves a 6.1x speedup over standard DEQ at comparable perplexity on WikiText-103 language modeling, reaching PPL 47.90 at NFE=1 versus DEQ's 255.94 and HyperDEQ's 70.19 (Section 4, Table 1)
On ImageNet classification at NFE=8, C-DEQ reaches 74.04% Top-1 / 91.45% Top-5 accuracy versus HyperDEQ's 69.90% / 84.12%, while running 3.3x faster (0.87s vs 2.90s) (Section 4, Table 2)
On ogbn-arxiv node classification at NFE=1, C-DEQ attains 56.81% accuracy versus IGNN's 8.61% and EIGNN's 11.30% (Section 4, Table 3)
On ogbn-products at NFE=10, C-DEQ reaches 76.55% accuracy versus IGNN-Solver's 68.47%, running 3.85x faster (Section 4, Table 3)
C-DEQ uses consistency distillation from a teacher trajectory defined by a Fixed Point ODE (dz_t/dt = f_theta(z_t,x) - z_t) combined with Anderson Acceleration iteration (Definition 3.1, Section 3)
Ablations show the AA-structured parameterization reduces the number of steps needed by 2x versus a non-AA variant, with optimal hyperparameters lambda1=0.8 and lambda2=0.05 (Section 4, Figure 3)

LxqIJW626c.text: R3L achieves 0.0% collision ratio and 0.0% out-of-bound ratio averaged across 9 scene types, compared to LayoutGPT's 4.3% collision/8.1% out-of-bound and LayoutVLM's 0.6% collision/10.9% out-of-bound (Section 3, Table 1)

R3L wins pairwise comparisons against baselines 23/27 times versus LayoutGPT, 27/27 versus Holodeck, and 24/27 versus LayoutVLM, yielding the highest Elo rating of 1866 among compared methods (Table 2)

Invariant Spatial Decomposition (Section 3.2) shortens relation chains to reduce accumulated frame-shift error, and an ablation removing both this module and the imagine-and-revise loop increases collision ratio from 1.0% to 3.1% and out-of-bound ratio from 1.6% to 7.9% (Section 3.2, Table 3)
The Consistent Spatial Imagination component (Section 3.3) implements an imagine-and-revise loop that enforces self-consistency during relation inference to improve layout feasibility (Section 3.3)
Global-to-local Supportive Spatial Optimization achieves a 1.8x convergence speedup over baseline optimization (Section 3.4, Figure 6)
Human-LLM judge alignment measured by Kendall's tau-b is approximately 0.50-0.56, comparable to inter-human agreement, validating the use of LLM-based evaluation for layout quality (Tables 4-5)

y4uR1LFClc.text: Theorem 4.1 shows that smooth nonlinear projection heads (e.g., using Swish or GELU) destabilize collapsed equilibria by injecting negative eigenvalues into the effective Hessian, while linear heads preserve collapse since the interaction term vanishes (Theorem 4.1, Section 4)
Theorem 3.1 establishes that linear projection heads perform implicit local subspace whitening, achieving isotropy only on the active subspace determined by the loss rank (Theorem 3.1, Section 3)

Proposition 3.3 shows that when the loss geometry has nonvanishing Riemann curvature, no global linear map can produce everywhere-isotropic conditioning, motivating the use of nonlinear heads (Proposition 3.3, Section 3)

Figure 3 tracks the Hessian spectrum during training and shows that smooth-activation heads inject negative eigenvalues enabling escape from collapse, whereas ReLU-based heads fail to do so, relying instead on discrete dynamics and BatchNorm (Figure 3, Section 6)
The geometric analysis is applied across both contrastive methods (InfoNCE, SimCLR, MoCo, DINO) and non-contrastive/decorrelation-based methods (BYOL, SimSiam, VICReg, Barlow Twins) (Section 6)
Figure 5 shows PCA visualization demonstrating 21.85x compression of augmentation orbits under the learned projection head geometry (Figure 5, Section 6)

zQvKcvs9HE.text: Split Personality Training (SPT) achieves 96.6% detection accuracy on poisoned responses and 95.3% on clean responses on the Anthropic Auditing Game Model Organism benchmark (Section 4.1)
The baseline compromised model achieves near-0% detection accuracy, never admitting to any poisoned responses when queried directly, compared to SPT's 96% overall accuracy (Section 4.1)
SPT outperforms linear probing baselines, achieving 93.9% versus 88.2% validation accuracy for detecting misalignment (Section 4.3)

The honest persona is implemented as a LoRA adapter that is toggled on only after the main response is generated, enabling zero alignment tax on deployed model behavior while still revealing latent knowledge such as fictional biases the compromised model was trained on (Section 4)
Cross-topic generalization of the honest persona is evaluated across 11 distinct misalignment categories (Section 4.2)

xBkLTpOu2V.text: The EgoTactile benchmark contains 63 everyday objects across 7 categories, captured from 12 participants using gloved-hand (162 tactile sensors per glove) and bare-hand acquisition modes, totaling 319k frames (Section 4)

EgoPressureDiff achieves 96.4% temporal accuracy, 56.3% contact IoU, and 38.9% volumetric IoU on the EgoTactile benchmark, compared to EgoPressureFormer's 84.5%, 36.8%, and 26.5% respectively (Section 6, Table 4)
EgoPressureDiff reduces mean absolute pressure error to 3.4N and part-wise center-of-pressure error to 3.1 units, versus EgoPressureFormer's 6.2N and 7.5 units (Section 6, Table 4)

The Physically-Informed Feature Rectification (PIFR) layer calibrates spatial prototypes using text-conditioned physical attributes via affine transformations to resolve visual-physical ambiguities (Section 5)

Existing vision-based grasp estimation methods predominantly rely on planar surfaces or fingertip contacts and fail to generalize to complex 3D object interactions, motivating the full-hand pressure formulation introduced in Section 3 (Section 2, Section 3)

493YXJPdeq.text: E-DiT achieves roughly 47% latency reduction on Qwen-Image (1283ms for E-DiT-turbo vs 2431ms for the baseline) while GenEval score only drops slightly from 0.870 to 0.853 (Table 1).
On FLUX, E-DiT reduces latency from 715ms to 374ms (about 48% speedup) while GenEval score is essentially unchanged at 0.671 vs baseline 0.665 (Table 2).
On Hunyuan3D-3.0 image-to-3D generation, E-DiT cuts latency from 5012ms to 2587ms (about 48% reduction) with negligible quality loss (ULIP-I 0.1473 vs baseline 0.1446) (Table 3).

Each transformer block is equipped with a lightweight router that jointly decides whether to skip the block, predicts an optimal MLP width reduction, and enables block-wise feature caching across denoising steps (Section 3.2).
Routing/sparsity patterns are shown to be sample-dependent, varying across both transformer blocks and denoising timesteps rather than following a fixed static pattern (Figure 2).

Training uses a combined loss of the flow-matching objective plus gating and width efficiency regularization terms, with routers initialized in full-capacity mode to preserve training stability (Section 3.3).

m1bU4KRgtB.text: Semantic information in natural images is predominantly encoded in directional components, with image norms well approximated by a single global average in both RGB and SD3-VAE latent space (Section 3.1).
Projecting images onto a hypersphere causes only minimal reconstruction degradation in SD3-VAE latent space: rFID increases by just 0.19 and LPIPS by 0.02 (Table 1).
Spherical Flow Matching (SFM) achieves gFID 3.79 on CIFAR-10, improving on the Euclidean I-CFM baseline's gFID of 4.29 (Table 2).
SFM achieves gFID 4.62 on ImageNet-256, improving on the Euclidean OT-CFM baseline's gFID of 5.22 (Table 2).

Spherical Optimal Transport CFM (SOT-CFM) replaces the Euclidean optimal-transport coupling cost with an angular metric, arccos(<x0,x1>/(||x0||*||x1||)), between source and target samples (Section 3.2).

A radius ablation shows SFM performance peaks at r=120 (gFID 4.62), and downstream ImageNet-256 linear classification using SFM representations reaches 87.13% top-1 accuracy versus 61.83% for the Euclidean baseline (Table 3; Appendix D.4).

FTC7najzZT.text: ReVSI re-annotates objects and scene geometry across 381 scenes drawn from 5 existing datasets to correct annotation artifacts inherited from point-cloud-based labeling (abstract only).

All QA pairs are regenerated using professional 3D annotation tools with rigorous bias mitigation and human verification, fixing ambiguous or unanswerable questions found in prior spatial-intelligence benchmarks (abstract only).

The benchmark introduces frame-budget variants at 16, 32, 64, and all frames so that evaluation matches the limited frame sampling actually used by VLMs, rather than assuming full-scene access (abstract only).
Fine-grained object visibility metadata is provided alongside QA pairs to enable diagnostic analysis of model failure modes (abstract only).
Evaluating VLMs on ReVSI reveals systematic 3D spatial-reasoning failure modes that were obscured by prior spatial intelligence benchmarks (abstract only).

gapnJajEfE.text: On longText-Benchmark, FreeText improves Qwen-Image normalized edit distance (NED) from 0.625 to 0.713 for English text and from 0.639 to 0.694 for Chinese text (Table 1).
On CVTG, FreeText improves FLUX.1-dev English NED from 0.598 to 0.690, and improves SD3.5-L NED from 0.848 to 0.864 and SD3-M NED from 0.616 to 0.669 (Table 1; Table 2).
On the newly introduced CLT-Bench, which stratifies Chinese text prompts by stroke-count and frequency-based difficulty, FreeText improves Qwen-Image NED from 0.458 to 0.488 (Section 3.3; Table 3).

FreeText's attention-based text-region localization using combined entity and sink tokens achieves IoU 0.561, outperforming VLM-based localization baselines including Gemini (0.139) and GPT (0.159) (Table 4; Table 5).

Spectral-Modulated Glyph Injection applies Log-Gabor frequency filtering within a restricted timestep window (t_start=0.8T to t_end=0.6T) to inject glyph detail while avoiding semantic leakage (Section 3.2).
FreeText adds only 12-18% inference latency overhead and under 1GB of peak memory across evaluated text-to-image models (Table 7).

EH77N5YGwV.text: The proposed domain-invariant continual learning method is evaluated across six benchmark datasets: MNIST variants, corrupted CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet, CoverType, Wafer Map defect detection, and the real-world WILDS distribution-shift benchmark (Section 4).
The method is compared against continual learning baselines addressing catastrophic forgetting, including EWC- and SI-style regularization methods and replay-based approaches (Section 4; Section 5).
Main results show the proposed approach consistently outperforms these baselines in generalization accuracy to unseen target domains across the evaluated datasets (Table 2).
Comparative performance metrics broken down by dataset and baseline further quantify the generalization gains of the domain-invariant approach (Table 3).
Additional appendix experiments extend the domain-invariance evaluation to real-world distribution shift on the WILDS benchmark (Appendix E; Appendix F).

32NvV5zixD.text: Theorem 1 proves centralized Lion achieves a convergence rate of O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/4}) under standard smoothness, without requiring the coerciveness assumption used in prior analyses (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 shows that a variance-reduced Lion variant using STORM-based gradient estimators improves the rate to O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/3}) under an average smoothness assumption (Theorem 2).
Theorem 3 establishes that distributed Lion across n heterogeneous nodes matches the centralized rate, converging as O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/4}) (Theorem 3).
Theorem 4 shows that adding variance reduction to distributed Lion improves the distributed rate to O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/3}) (Theorem 4).

Theorem 5 gives a communication-efficient Lion variant with unbiased sign compression achieving either O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/2} + d n^{-1/2}) or O(n^{1/2} T^{-1} + d n^{-1/2}) depending on the learning-rate choice (Theorem 5).

Theorem 7 shows that combining bidirectional unbiased sign compression with variance reduction attains a communication-efficient rate of O(d^{1/4} T^{-1/4}), improving over the non-variance-reduced Theorem 6 rate (Theorem 7, Theorem 6).

IM8ZHjhD0v.text: RuscaRL provides explicit scaffolding during rollout generation via checklist-style rubrics with intra-group differentiation and an inter-step sigmoid decay λ_step(t) = 1/(1+e^{α(t-t₀)}) using optimal parameters α=125, t₀=0.2 (Section 4.2).

RuscaRL computes verifiable rewards during training via LLM-as-Judge binary evaluation of each rubric criterion, aggregated by weighted summation S = Σs_i / S_total to produce a normalized reward in [0,1] (Section 4.3).
On HealthBench-500, RuscaRL improves Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from 23.6 to 50.3 (+114%), surpassing GPT-4.1's 47.9, and a Qwen3-30B variant reaches 61.1, exceeding OpenAI-o3 (Table 1).
Under Best-of-N evaluation, RuscaRL shows steeper efficiency curves than baselines, indicating higher sampling efficiency at scale (Figure 6).

Ablations show linear intra-group rubric differentiation outperforms binary differentiation, and sigmoid decay of rubric guidance outperforms constant, linear, and power decay schedules (Section 5.3).
Policy entropy analysis shows RuscaRL maintains a more favorable exploration-exploitation balance than non-scaffolded RL training (Figure 7, Section 5.3).

ry5HitnXzc.text: Theorem 1.1 establishes uniform convergence: for sample size s ≥ 3456 ln(4/δ)/ε², with probability at least 1−δ, the empirical and expected utility of every linear contract differ by at most ε (Theorem 1.1).

Corollary 1.2 shows the Empirical Utility Maximization algorithm achieves an ε-approximation of the optimal linear contract using s ≥ 6912 ln(4/δ)/ε² samples and O(1/ε) oracle queries (Corollary 1.2).
The O(ln(1/δ)/ε²) sample complexity matches the lower bound of Dütting et al. (2025) up to constant factors, and is independent of the action space size n and the number of outcomes m (Theorem 1.1).

Lemma 2.1 shows the expected reward of a linear contract is non-decreasing in the contract parameter α, a structural property exploited to build fine-grained covering arguments where general pseudo-dimension bounds fail (Lemma 2.1).

Lemma 2.2 constructs an L2 cover of the reward function class of size O(1/ν²), obtained by discretizing empirical rewards into ν-intervals, taking pullbacks to parameter space, and combining with grid discretization of the outcome axis (Lemma 2.2).

jNhEZteJfq.text: The probabilistic perspective (Section 3) models conversational history as a Markov chain over binary phenomenon-present/absent states and quantifies behavioral persistence via the transition-matrix trace Tr(T) = P(s+|s+) + P(s-|s-), with values greater than 1 indicating persistence (Section 3).

The geometric perspective (Section 4) measures the angular separation between phenomenon and non-phenomenon hidden-representation states via an orthonormal basis from Gram-Schmidt and Procrustes-based rotation angles (Section 4).
Across three models and six datasets, the probabilistic persistence trace and the geometric reference angle show a Spearman correlation of 0.78 (p<0.0002) (Section 4).

Refusal shows the strongest carryover effect (trace approximately 1.57-1.59, angles 33-66 degrees), sycophancy is moderate (trace approximately 1.14-1.33), and hallucination is weakest (trace approximately 1.12-1.13, angles 6-13 degrees) (Section 4).
Carryover effects dissolve in topically inconsistent conversations, with correlation between phenomenon states diminishing significantly under randomized topic sequences (Section 6.1).

First-order history dependence (k=1) dominates, though k=2 and k=3 step dependencies still exhibit measurable influence, and upper-middle layers at roughly 85% network depth show the strongest probabilistic-geometric alignment (Section 6.2, Section 6.3).

3v5l5TepEe.text: PRISM uses a dual-stream gated Mixture-of-Experts architecture with a shared Universal Anchor MLP for consensus knowledge and a Conditioned MoE of sparse, FiLM-modulated experts, replacing FFNs at layers 2, 5, 8, and 11 of a ViT-B/16 backbone with N=15 experts and Top-3 routing (Section on Methodology; architecture details).

On PASCAL-Context with a ViT-B backbone, PRISM outperforms the SAK baseline on 4 of 5 tasks (82.20 vs 81.88 SemSeg, 75.34 vs 74.30 Parsing, 13.47 vs 14.02 Normal error, 75.92 vs 74.09 Boundary) and achieves a multi-task gain Δm of 2.29% versus SAK's 0.83% (Experiments, Table results).

On NYUD-v2 with a ViT-B backbone, PRISM improves SemSeg (60.22 vs 59.93) and Depth RMSE (0.4883 vs 0.4942) over SAK, while trailing slightly on Normal (17.81 vs 17.60) and Boundary (76.59 vs 78.60) (Experiments, Table results).
Scaling to a ViT-L backbone, PRISM attains a 3.16% Δm multi-task gain versus SAK's 2.30% (Experiments).

Ablations on ViT-S show removing the MoE lowers segmentation to 78.04 mIoU, removing the Universal Anchor worsens normal estimation to 14.65 mErr, removing FiLM routing drops performance to 78.87 mIoU / 14.46 mErr, and removing the Locality-Aware Decorrelation Loss collapses Human Parsing to 61.80 mIoU, versus 79.19 mIoU / 69.25 Parsing for full PRISM (Ablation Analysis).

At layer 11, emergent expert specialization is teacher-conditioned in Stage 1 (e.g., expert E14 as a CLIP semantic specialist at 20.7% activation, E7 as a DINOv2 geometric specialist) and becomes task-conditioned in Stage 2, with surface normal estimation favoring texture experts and suppressing E14 to 3.8% activation (Emergent Specialization Patterns, Layer 11 analysis).

CPN5KsCpiE.text: HeRL revises a subset of failed trajectories with the highest within-group rewards by conditioning the policy on hindsight experience (the failed trajectory plus its unmet rubrics), then adds the best revision back into the sampling group (Section 3.1, Equations 5-7).

HeRL augments the reward of a revised trajectory's source rollout with a bonus term ri <- ri + alpha(r~i - ri) using alpha = 0.05, to reward trajectories with high improvement potential under guidance (Section 3.1, Equation 8).

Proposition 3.1 upper-bounds the gap between the ideal policy gradient and the estimated gradient by the L1 norm of the unsatisfied-rubric weights times the expected squared norm of the score function, motivating why better rubric satisfaction improves gradient estimation (Section 3.3, Proposition 3.1).
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, HeRL improves accuracy over RLVR and an Initial baseline on HealthBench, WritingBench, and IFEval, e.g. reaching 34.3/59.1/82.4 versus RLVR's 30.5/54.8/77.3 (Figure 1).

HeRL is compared against SFT, DPO, and RLVR baselines across instruction-following (IFEval, IFBench, MulDimIF), writing (WritingBench), and medical QA (LLMEvalMed, HealthBench-500) benchmarks, with results reported in Table 1, and out-of-domain generalization to MATH-500, GPQA, and MMLU-Pro reported in Table 3 (Section 4.1, Tables 1 and 3).

HeRL further benefits from experience-guided self-improvement at test time (Figure 4) and sustains exploration diversity throughout training more effectively than RLVR (Figure 5) (Section 4, Figures 4-5).

JLQV6NxS6W.text: RLAnything jointly and dynamically optimizes three components in a closed loop: the policy (via integrated step-wise reward-model feedback plus outcome rewards), the reward model (via consistency feedback from outcome and self-consistency signals), and the environment (via automatic difficulty adaptation using critic feedback) (Table 1, Figure 1).
Theorem 1 establishes that precise reward estimation (distinguishing good from bad steps) requires balanced sampling densities across difficulty levels (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 shows that imbalanced task difficulty breaks the sampling-density balance required by Theorem 1, motivating RLAnything's automatic environment-difficulty adaptation (Theorem 2).
RLAnything improves Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking on OSWorld by +11.7% in-domain and +5.2% out-of-domain (OOD) (Table 1).
RLAnything improves Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on AlfWorld by +21.2% in-domain and +18.7% OOD, and on LiveBench/CodeContests coding tasks by +11.9% (Table 1).

RLAnything is evaluated on OSWorld GUI-agent tasks (230 in-domain and 139 OOD tasks) and AlfWorld text-based interactive games (3.5k training episodes, 274 evaluation episodes) (Section on Benchmarks, Table 1).

uQJktmCJZ4.text: OPT-Engine benchmarks LLMs across 10 canonical Operations Research problem classes: 5 Linear Programming classes (inventory, portfolio allocation, production, transportation, pollution control) and 5 Mixed-Integer Programming classes (TSP, bin packing, job-shop scheduling, minimum-cost network flow, knapsack) (Section on Benchmark Structure).

Tool-integrated reasoning (TIR), where LLMs generate executable solver code, maintains high accuracy as problem complexity scales, while pure-text reasoning (PTR) shows substantial degradation with increased problem size, for both DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-5.1 (Figure 3).

Constraint augmentation causes significant accuracy drops for both TIR and PTR paradigms, whereas linguistic-complexity perturbations (Figure 6, top row) and objective perturbations (Figure 6, bottom row) have minimal or negligible effect, identifying constraint formulation as the primary bottleneck (Figures 6 and 8).

Execution-rate results in Table 1 show DeepSeek-V3.2 at 86.4-100% and GPT-5.1 at 83.1-99.6% across problem types, versus Qwen3-4B-Instruct at only 23.1-35.6%, with Qwen3-4B after reinforcement-learning fine-tuning improving by +15 to +76.5 points (Table 1).

Instance generation follows a four-stage pipeline: numeric instance generation with solver templates, original problem construction, LLM-based problem augmentation for linguistic diversity, and validation combining LLM judgment with rule-based verification (Pipeline Architecture section).

WM9haplntn.text: MetaMoE selects proxy samples from public data using a relevance-weighted Determinantal Point Process with modified kernel k~(xi,xj) = g(xi,Dp) k(xi,xj) g(xj,Dp), balancing domain relevance against sample diversity (Section on Diversity-Aware Proxy Selection).

MetaMoE fine-tunes each domain expert on both its private data Dp and the corresponding selected proxy data D-hat-p, to mitigate domain isolation and calibrate expert representations to the router's training distribution (Algorithm 1).

MetaMoE's context-aware router blends token-level and sequence-level representations as z~_t^(l) = (1-lambda) z_t^(l) + lambda z_x^(l) to improve routing reliability beyond surface-level token similarity (Section on Context-Aware Router).

Figure 2 shows that MetaMoE's diversity-aware proxy selection yields more diverse and representative sample distributions than FlexOlmo's relevance-only proxy selection, achieving better coverage of the private-data manifold (Figure 2).

MetaMoE consistently outperforms recent privacy-preserving Mixture-of-Experts unification baselines, including FlexOlmo, across both computer-vision and NLP benchmarks (Section on Experimental Results).

dilKIGbrZu.text: The proposed Universal GRN (UGRN) approach uses two feature-extraction techniques on frozen single-cell foundation models: Virtual Value Perturbation (VVP), which queries the model across multiple unified virtual expression values rather than simple on/off states (Equation 8), and Gradient Trajectory (GDT), which extracts partial derivatives along virtual values to characterize instantaneous regulatory effects (Equation 9).

On the scBenchmark cross-dataset evaluation, the ensemble method achieves 0.768 average AUPRC, outperforming an embedding-based baseline (0.663 AUPRC) and a perturbation-based baseline (0.596 AUPRC), reaching 0.934 AUPRC on the Str mH-L dataset (Table 1).

Under the Leave-One-Dataset-Out protocol, the ensemble method achieves 0.699 average AUPRC and recovers 0.668 AUPRC on the challenging L/G setting, where the embedding baseline collapses to 0.515 AUPRC (Table 2).
The method generalizes across species, achieving 0.936 AUPRC for human-to-mouse transfer and 0.858 AUPRC for mouse-to-human transfer (Table 4).
Under class imbalance (10:1 negative-to-positive ratio), the ensemble method reaches 0.413 AUPRC versus the baseline's 0.264 AUPRC, a roughly 56% relative improvement (Table 6).

H0tGv2kBi8.text: Seg-ReSearch-8B reaches 50.0 overall J&F on the OK-VOS benchmark, versus 37.6 J&F for the Qwen3-VL-8B+Search baseline (Table 1).
On OK-VOS one-hop tasks, Seg-ReSearch-8B scores 60.1 J&F compared to 40.2 J&F for the search-augmented baseline (Table 1).
Seg-ReSearch-8B achieves 67.4 gIoU on the ReasonSeg test set (Table 2) and 63.2 J&F on ReasonVOS, improving over OneThinker-8B's 54.9 J&F (Table 3).

The hierarchical reward combines an Initial Guidance Reward, a Tapering Process Reward, and an Outcome Reward, and outperforms both a sparse-reward baseline (41.3 J&F) and rigid step-wise imitation (43.6 J&F), reaching 46.0 J&F (Section 3.2, Table 4).
Combining the Initial Guidance Reward and Tapering Process Reward yields a +4.7% improvement over the baseline reward, with the Tapering Process Reward alone contributing +3.5% (Table 5).
Allowing up to 5 search turns improves performance by +7.4 points over a single-turn baseline (Table 7).

74NcYQk45j.text: Proposition 4.1 and 4.2 establish that recourse under in-context learning exists when at least one actionable feature is unbounded, but can be infeasible when actionable features are bounded and other features are immutable (Section 4.2).
Lemma 4.4 gives a closed-form optimal in-context recourse solution and shows it converges to the classical linear-model recourse solution as the demonstration context grows (Section 4.3).

Theorem 4.6 bounds the recourse perturbation cost with a high-probability bound containing distinct convergence terms for the number of pretraining context examples N and test-time demonstrations M (Section 4.3).
On the Australian Credit dataset, ASR-ICL attains validity with an average cost of 3.83, substantially lower than DiCE (8.96) and FACE (6.18) (Table 1).
ASR-ICL matches the validity of full-space zeroth-order recourse baselines while using roughly 2-3x fewer model queries (Figure 3).
As context size increases, empirical validity improves and recourse costs converge toward the linear-model reference, confirming the theoretical convergence result (Figure 1).

z3rQmLk4Io.text: On WinoGrande-S, Bayesian-LoRA achieves an ECE of 4.90±0.20 versus 30.80±1.80 for standard LoRA, an 84% reduction (Table 1, Section 5.1).
On BoolQ, Bayesian-LoRA achieves an NLL of 0.29±0.01 compared to 0.43±0.01 for MAP-LoRA, a 76% reduction (Table 1).

Bayesian-LoRA adds approximately 0.42M parameters on top of standard LoRA's 4.48M (a 9.4% increase) and incurs about 1.2x training-time overhead, versus roughly 4x for MC-dropout and 3x for deep ensembles (Table 4, Section 5.3).
Bayesian-LoRA achieves the highest accuracy on five of six commonsense reasoning benchmarks, with gains of up to +2.9 points over standard LoRA (Table 1).
Uncertainty-mode inference with S=2 posterior samples yields a 1.516x latency multiplier relative to deterministic inference, which itself has zero overhead (Table 4).
Calibration benefits extend to larger models, including Qwen2.5-14B and Qwen3-30B, on mathematical reasoning tasks (Table 3).

40fUEdwvH3.text: FOCUS achieves up to 3.52x throughput improvement over production-grade LMDeploy at block size B=64 (Figure 7), and 2.32x speedup at the standard block size B=32 on real-world chat workloads (Table 5, Figure 6).

FOCUS uses the attention-score difference between the first two layers (the 'importance delta') as a predictor of token decodability to dynamically focus computation on decodable tokens (Section 3.2).
FOCUS reduces the computational redundancy ratio from 15.02 to 3.12 on ShareGPT, roughly a 79% reduction (Table 5).
FOCUS matches or outperforms the baseline generation quality across GSM8K, Math500, HumanEval, MBPP, and IFEval (Table 4).
Standard block-diffusion inference wastes about 90% of compute on non-decodable tokens, with only about 10% of tokens successfully decoded per step (Figure 2).
FOCUS attains peak throughputs of 2,272 tokens/s on ShareGPT and 2,324 tokens/s on WildChat at batch size 256.

dVgMUSGPN3.text: At 20K training samples on OMat24, TriForces reduces energy-per-atom MAE from 81.3 to 34.6 meV/atom, a 57% reduction (Figure 3).

TriForces separates atomic representations into a composition stream (count-weighted attention over unique elements, no coordinates), a structure stream (SOAP-style power spectrum, rotation-invariant, no element identity), and an interaction stream (full species and position access), concatenated at the node level (Section 3.1).
Self-supervised pretraining combines denoising, masked atom-type prediction, and LeJEPA embedding alignment across augmented views (Section 3.2).
On MatBench, TriForces variants achieve best-or-near-best results on 6 of 8 tasks without DFT labels, improving the Phonons task MAE from 57.8 to 19.5 cm⁻¹ (Table 4).
With OMol25 pretraining, TriForces improves QM9 dipole moment MAE from 0.023 to 0.018 D and polarizability MAE from 0.098 to 0.075 a₀³ (Table 5).

The factorized composition/structure embeddings enable decomposed k-NN similarity retrieval, with the composition stream best for element-set recall and the structure stream best for space-group recall (Section 4.5).
