SldP4LGjdz.text: SurvFD decomposes higher-order feature effects on survival predictions into time-dependent and time-independent components, characterizing when additive explanations fail across log-hazard, hazard, and survival-function scales (Section 3).

Theorem 3.2 shows that under feature independence, SurvFD exactly recovers ground-truth effect decompositions when the underlying risk score is linear or additively separable in main effects (Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 3.3 establishes that time-dependent interaction effects can propagate downward to make lower-order feature subsets appear time-dependent, but cannot propagate upward (Theorem 3.3).

SurvSHAP-IQ extends Shapley interaction quantification to time-indexed survival functions, estimating higher-order time-dependent interactions and achieving local accuracy below 0.015 on ten simulated scenarios (Figure 2).

On the TCGA-BRCA multi-modal dataset (n=990 patients), SurvSHAP-IQ reveals within-modality (image-to-image, clinical-to-clinical) interactions but no cross-modality interactions between histopathological images and clinical features (Section 5, TCGA-BRCA application).

Scalability analysis across four additional datasets (10-16 features) shows regression-based Shapley interaction approximators achieve the highest fidelity among tested approximation algorithms (Figure 7).

hcFVDmmb0J.text: DPLM-Evo uses three prediction heads (substitution, insertion, deletion) during denoising to explicitly model biological evolutionary edit operations rather than only token substitution (Section on model architecture).

DPLM-Evo decouples a 2L-length latent alignment space (with gap tokens) from the variable-length observed sequence space, enabling indel-aware generation with a contextualized evolutionary noising kernel that adds only about 24% per-step training overhead (Section on contextualized evolutionary noising).
On the ProteinGym indel benchmark, DPLM-Evo achieves 0.495 Spearman correlation, surpassing ProGen2-M (0.464) though still below the MSA-based method PoET (0.517) (Table 1).

The 650M-parameter DPLM-Evo achieves 0.42 Spearman correlation on the ProteinGym substitution benchmark, outperforming the ESM-2, ESM-C, ESM-1v, and DPLM baselines, with the 3B model showing continued improvement unlike ESM-2 (ProteinGym substitution results section).

In unconditional generation, DPLM-Evo attains 83.6 pLDDT, competitive with DPLM (84.0) and DiMA (83.3), while showing higher sequence entropy indicative of reduced mode collapse (generation results section).

In a GFP directed-evolution case study, enabling indels raises predicted TM-score (pTM) from 0.793 (substitution-only) to 0.857, outperforming an ESM-2 baseline of 0.737 (GFP optimization case study).

gQXkbQSZWS.text: Theorem 5.2 proves that the prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN have identical expressive power for both invariant and equivariant mappings on compact sets (Theorem 5.2).

Proposition 5.3 shows Neural Functional Transformers (NFTs) differ in expressive power from the other architectures in general, but become equivalent under a general-position (GP) assumption requiring distinct bias terms per layer (Proposition 5.3).

Theorem 6.1 establishes that permutation-invariant weight-space networks are universal approximators of function-space functionals, i.e., maps depending only on the realized function and not the specific parameterization (Theorem 6.1).

Proposition 6.2 proves a non-universality result showing invariant weight-space networks cannot approximate all permutation-invariant functionals, using a counterexample built from Weisfeiler-Leman graph indistinguishability (Proposition 6.2).
Theorem 6.3 recovers universality for permutation-invariant functionals under the general-position assumption via continuous canonization maps that order neurons by bias value (Theorem 6.3).

Theorem 7.4 shows permutation-equivariant operators achieve universal approximation under the general-position assumption via canonization-based factorization, while Proposition 7.1 shows fixed-architecture equivariant networks cannot approximate function-space operators that increase geometric complexity (Proposition 7.1, Theorem 7.4).

UDS2siRAyT.text: BA-solver achieves FID 1.72 at 10 NFEs on ImageNet-256, comparable to generation quality from Euler solvers using 100+ NFEs (Table 1).
BA-solver attains FID 2.84 at just 5 NFEs on ImageNet-256, and improves to FID 1.96 and 1.65 at 7 and 15 NFEs respectively (Table 1).
SideNet, the auxiliary network introduced for Bi-Anchor Velocity Integration, adds only about 1-2% of the backbone model's parameter count as overhead (Section 3.2.2).

SideNet training uses a chain-based algorithm requiring only 250 iterations at batch size 4,096 with 6M trainable parameters (frozen backbone), amounting to merely 0.03%-1.0% of the training iterations needed by existing training-based few-step methods (Algorithm 2, Table 2).

The Bi-Anchor Velocity Integration procedure operates in three phases—Forward Probe, Backward Refinement, and Integration—illustrated for the Bidirectional Temporal Perception design in Section 3.2.1 (Section 3.2.1, Figure 3).

E2kWotHfT7.text: SurpMark scores test passages using generalized Jensen-Shannon (GJS) divergence between first-order Markov transition matrices estimated from k-means-discretized token surprisal states, comparing against fixed human and machine reference corpora (Section on method/discretization).

Across 9 open-source generator models, SurpMark achieves average AUROC of 91.23 at k=6 discretization states, ranking first on 6 of 9 models and top-2 on 8 of 9, with 98.35% AUROC on GPT-2-XL and 97.58% on Llama-3 (Table 2).
Across 3 closed-source models (GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini-1.5-Flash, GPT-5-Chat), SurpMark achieves average AUROC of 78.32 at k=7, with 81.33% AUROC on GPT-5-Chat (Table 1).

SurpMark operates at a reference-per-test budget of B=2, which is 5x to 5,000x lower than baselines DNA-GPT (B=10), DetectGPT/DetectNPR/Lastde++ (B=100), and Fast-DetectGPT (B=10,000) (efficiency comparison section).
Theorem 4.4 establishes asymptotic normality of the SurpMark decision statistic, and the discretization procedure is shown to have an O(1/k) bias-variance trade-off error bound (Theorem 4.4).

Robustness experiments show SurpMark's detection performance improves with longer test passages, becoming the top-performing method above roughly 150 tokens, while remaining stable across varying proxy language model sizes unlike baselines that show high sensitivity (robustness/ablation section).

jZSzSI04yW.text: Search-R2 with Qwen2.5-7B achieves 40.4% average performance versus 35.0% for the Search-R1 baseline on the same backbone (Table of main results, Section 5).
Search-R2 with Qwen2.5-32B reaches 50.8% average accuracy compared to 45.6% for Search-R1 at the same model scale (Section 5).

The Meta-Refiner's Discriminator (πd) evaluates global trajectory coherence and accepts trajectories scoring above a threshold τ, while the Trimmer (πh) identifies specific error steps and regenerates from that cut-point rather than discarding the whole trajectory (Section 3, Actor-Refiner framework).
Search-R2 is evaluated across seven QA datasets: NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, Musique, and Bamboogle (Section 5, experimental setup).

Search-R2 with 5 rollouts and 1 revision outperforms Search-R1 run with 10 rollouts, at approximately 5% additional training overhead relative to the Search-R1 baseline (Section 5, efficiency analysis).

The performance gain is formalized as ΔJ = Selection Precision + Intervention Volume × Trimming Skill, decomposing improvement into discriminator accuracy, error-location skill, and intervention frequency (Section 4, theoretical analysis).

nJ3yX2ZnOJ.text: On synthetic linear-regression setups, TabMGP attains credible-set coverage between 0.91 and 1.00, close to the nominal level (Table 1).

On synthetic logistic-regression setups, TabMGP attains coverage between 0.78 and 1.00, while the classical Bayes baseline using a NUTS sampler shows poor coverage ranging from 0.09 to 0.98 under misspecification (Table 2).

TabMGP is compared against Bayesian Bootstrap, Copula, classical Bayes (NUTS), and an Asymptotic Gaussian (inverse-Hessian) baseline across 11 synthetic setups and 19 real-world datasets from OpenML and UCI (Section 4, datasets and baselines).
TabMGP outperforms both the Copula method and the classical Bayes baseline particularly in challenging low n/p (sample-size to dimension) real-data settings (Section 4, results).

TabMGP requires roughly 70 seconds per posterior sample for binary/categorical outcomes and about 200 seconds for continuous outcomes, versus 10-20 seconds for the Copula baseline (Section 4, computational cost).
Path-stability analysis shows that N=500 forward-sampling steps are generally sufficient for the martingale posterior to converge across most experimental setups (Figure 3).

NixeX51WQA.text: Light Forcing achieves a VBench total score of 84.5 on Self Forcing 1.3B, surpassing dense FlashAttention2's score of 84.1 (Section on main results).

Light Forcing achieves a 1.3x end-to-end speedup and a 3.3x attention-specific speedup on the Self Forcing model, versus 1.16x (STA) and 1.29x (VMoBA) end-to-end speedups from sparse-attention baselines (comparison table).
Combined with FP8 quantization and LightVAE, Light Forcing reaches a 2.3x overall speedup and 19.7 FPS on an RTX 5090 GPU (Section on efficiency/deployment).

Chunk-Aware Growth (CAG) allocates progressively higher sparsity ratios to later chunks using the formula s_i = s_base - α_i·β, where α_i is proportional to 1/√t, based on each chunk's contribution to global error accumulation (Section on method, Chunk-Aware Growth).

Hierarchical Sparse Attention (HSA) performs two-stage mask selection at both frame and block levels to adaptively handle diverse attention patterns while bounding computational complexity (Section on method, Hierarchical Sparse Attention).
On the LongLive model, Light Forcing achieves a 1.19x speedup, a smaller gain than on Self Forcing, attributed to differing chunk error-propagation characteristics (Section on results).

wstTwzLFBw.text: RACER formulates routing as the α-Valid Optimal Routing (α-VOR) problem: minimize E[|C(X)|] subject to the risk constraint R(C) ≤ α, where risk is the probability that the selected model set excludes all correct models (Section 4, problem formulation).
Theorem 4.3 proves that under exchangeability, the calibrated threshold λ̂ guarantees E[l(C_λ̂(X), G'(X))] ≤ α on unseen test queries, giving distribution-free risk control (Theorem 4.3).
Theorem 4.5 establishes a risk lower bound α - 2/(n+1) ≤ R(λ̂) ≤ α for continuous score distributions, showing the calibration is not overly conservative (Theorem 4.5).

On GSM8K, MMLU, CMMLU, and ARC-Challenge, RACER improves accuracy over base routers (MLPR, KNNR, RouterDC) by up to 4.0% absolute, with an average improvement of 3.6% across tasks (Section 5, experimental results).

RACER outperforms the best individual LLM by 5.0% on average while reducing model calls by up to 58.6% compared to a full ensemble, improving accuracy by up to 4.49% in that setting (Section 5, experimental results).

Figure 2 shows that empirical risk stays consistently below the target level α = 0.1 across all base routers and both non-conformity score variants (Router Score-Gap and Inverse Probability) (Figure 2).

68AMoK2YNk.text: Theorem 4.3 decomposes the task-t prediction error into an irreducible error term, a variance term scaling as O(M/(t^2(M+1)^2)) that decreases with more in-context examples, and a bias term measuring deviation ‖(1/t)∑_s w_s - w_t‖^2 from task dissimilarity (Theorem 4.3).

Theorem 4.4 shows that forgetting arises from attention reweighting past tasks with negative coefficients c_t and future tasks with positive coefficients d, rather than from actual information loss, comprising intra-task variance and inter-task mean-interaction terms (Theorem 4.4).

The theory predicts non-monotonic error curves with context length M, where longer prompts reduce variance but amplify systematic bias from misaligned historical tasks, producing a clear performance peak at intermediate M (Section 4, theoretical analysis).

Mean-misalignment interference persists regardless of context length, while variance-induced interference decays as O(1/M), implying a persistent asymptotic forgetting floor (Section 4, theoretical analysis).

Experiments on GPT-2 architectures confirm the predicted non-monotonic error curves and reproduce catastrophic forgetting with a 46% accuracy drop on real LLM tasks (Section 5, experimental validation).

3tlaoBZrSg.text: Introduces Expected Prediction Entropy (EPE, Definition 3.1) as a proper scoring rule for subgroup discovery in Cox proportional hazards models, proven to uniquely identify correct Cox coefficients when data follow the Cox model (Proposition 3.2).
Theorem 6.1 proves the DDGroup algorithm recovers the ground-truth subgroup region R* under five assumptions (A1-A5), with an effect-size threshold of O(log ε^{-1}) (Theorem 6.1).
On the synthetic Synth-Counter benchmark, DDGroup achieves an F1 score of 0.94 (0.01), versus 0.76 (0.04) for the C-Index variant and 0.81 (0.10) for the Partial Likelihood variant (Table 1).
On the Synth-Nonlinear benchmark, DDGroup attains F1 of 0.97 (0.01) and test EPE of 0.38 (0.02), compared to a Base (no subgroup selection) F1 of 0.29 (0.00) (Table 2).
DDGroup achieves the lowest EPE on 5 of 7 real clinical datasets (AIDS-CD4, AIDS-Karnof, AIDS-prior, GBSG2-tsize, METABRIC-MKI, VLC-Karnof, WHAS-DBP) (Section 7.2, Table 3).

In the NASA jet engine case study, the Cox Tree method achieves EPE of 0.52 (0.01) and C-index of 0.74 (0.01), and discovers subgroups with distinct Cox coefficients for high-altitude operation (β_Nc = 2.35, β_NRf = -1.19) mirroring design choices used in modern jet engines (Section 7.2, Table 4).

cefix4VmhS.text: MEG-XL pre-trains on 2.5-minute (150-second) MEG context windows equivalent to roughly 191k tokens, a 5-300x increase in context length over prior brain foundation models (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

MEG-XL uses an 8-layer, 512-dimension transformer with criss-cross attention (20M parameters) over BioCodec tokens with 6 residual quantization levels, downsampled to 50Hz from a 1000Hz raw signal, trained with a masking strategy covering 40% of tokens in 3-second contiguous blocks (Section 2).

Using only 13% of available training data, MEG-XL outperforms six baseline brain foundation models, reaching 47.0% (±0.9) accuracy on MEG-MASC, 54.9% (±0.5) on Armeni, and 57.3% (±0.4) on LibriBrain (Section 3.1, Table 1).

MEG-XL matches supervised brain-to-text performance using 1 hour of labeled data versus 50 hours required by supervised baselines, and yields 10-25% gains over the supervised state-of-the-art in low-data regimes (Section 3.2).

Scaling analysis shows word-decoding performance from longer pre-training context saturates with diminishing returns beyond 100 seconds, whereas zero-shot masked-prediction performance keeps improving through 150 seconds (Figures 4 and 5).
Pre-training uses approximately 300 hours of MEG recordings from over 800 subjects drawn from the CamCAN, MOUS, and SMN4Lang datasets (Section 3, Appendix A.2).

ueNIrBXz7R.text: The paper improves on the algorithm of Backurs, Indyk, Musco, and Wagner (2021) for kernel matrix linear algebra tasks -- matrix-vector products, matrix-matrix products, spectral norm, and entry sums -- to (1+ε) relative error (abstract only).
The proposed algorithms reduce the polynomial dependence on 1/ε compared to prior kernel matrix algorithms while achieving the same (1+ε) relative-error guarantee (abstract only).

When the kernel matrix is accessed only through kernel density estimation (KDE) queries rather than by reading individual entries, the algorithms achieve sub-quadratic dependence on the number of points n (abstract only).

The paper establishes conditional lower bounds showing quadratic-time hardness for related kernel matrix problems, indicating limits on how much KDE-query access can speed up these algorithms (abstract only).

3LRWjJTp0Y.text: CalPro combines a geometric evidential head producing Normal-Inverse-Gamma distributions, a differentiable conformal calibration layer for end-to-end training, and domain priors imposed as soft constraints (Section 3).
Theorem 4.2 provides structure-aware coverage guarantees via PAC-Bayesian bounds over ambiguity sets, formally controlling nonconformity drift under distribution shift (Section 4).
On held-out X-ray protein structures, CalPro attains 90.1% empirical coverage at a nominal 90% target with expected calibration error of 0.021 (Section 5.2, Table 2).
Under X-ray to cryo-EM modality shift, CalPro's coverage degrades by only about 3.8 percentage points, versus 14-18 points for pLDDT-based and vanilla conformal baselines (Section 5.2, Table 3).
Filtering docking candidates by CalPro interval width improves molecular docking success from 52.3% unfiltered to 74.8%, compared to 64.2% when filtering by pLDDT > 95 (Section 5.5, Table 6).

CalPro reduces calibration error by 30-50% relative to baseline conformal methods while maintaining near-nominal coverage across evaluated modalities, and achieves 0.83 Spearman correlation between predicted uncertainty and true error under synthetic perturbations (Section 5.4, Table 5).

kwvtSA9ed3.text: Under a two-basin landscape assumption with cross-reward leakage gaps Δ1, Δ2 > 0 (Assumption 1, Section 2.1), Lemma 3 shows probability mass outside the union of ε-optimal basins decays geometrically under recursive curated retraining (Section 3.2).
Lemma 5 proves that under bounded leakage, basin mass remains bounded away from collapse, satisfying η ≤ a_t ≤ 1-η for the limiting basin weight a_t (Section 3.3).

Theorem 6 shows the limiting mixture preserves diversity: reward variance under a nontrivial two-component mixture has an explicit strictly positive lower bound proportional to (Δᵢ - 2ε)^2 (Section 3.3).
Theorem 7 proves the limiting distribution from pluralistic curation coincides with the weighted Nash bargaining solution, maximizing (u1(p_α) - d1)^q (u2(p_α) - d2)^(1-q) at α* = q (Section 3.3).

CIFAR-10 flow-model retraining experiments (E3) show curation with balanced multi-reward preferences sustains higher entropy and diversity than single-reward curation across recursive retraining generations (Section 4).
Text-domain experiments (E4) confirm that curation under two competing length-based reward preferences sustains entropy over recursive retraining, consistent with the two-basin theory (Section 4).

XrKzHGg2jB.text: The Stackelberg-Littlestone (SL) dimension characterizes the optimal mistake bound for online learning in structured Stackelberg games: deterministic algorithms require at least SLdim_G(H) mistakes and randomized algorithms require at least half that in expectation (Theorem 3.8).
Algorithm 1 (the Stackelberg Standard Optimal Algorithm) achieves a regret bound matching this lower bound, i.e. regret bounded by SLdim_G(H), making it provably optimal (Theorem 3.10).

There exist Stackelberg game instances where the standard Littlestone dimension is infinite (Ldim(H)=∞) yet the leader's learning problem remains learnable, showing that standard multiclass complexity measures fail to characterize the learning task's true difficulty (Theorem 3.5).
In the agnostic online setting, the paper's algorithm achieves a regret bound of Õ(√(SLdim_G(H)·T)) (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.15).

For distributional learning with contexts, the Stackelberg-Natarajan (SN) dimension satisfies dSN,G(H) ≤ dN(H) with strict inequality possible, and Stackelberg ERM achieves sample complexity Õ(dSN,G(H)·log(dSN,G(H)·K/ε)/ε), improving over vanilla ERM which scales with the (larger) Natarajan dimension dN(H) (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.10, Theorem 4.12, Proposition 4.7).

CITSCNrUja.text: AutoTool achieves an average gain of 6.4% on math and science reasoning benchmarks including AIME24 and AIME25 (e.g., 68.8% on AIME24 and 51.2% on AIME25 with Qwen3-8B) compared to baseline agents (Table 1).
AutoTool achieves an average gain of 4.5% on search-based QA benchmarks such as HotpotQA (45.1% with Qwen3-8B) and 2WikiMultiHopQA (48.8% with Qwen3-8B) (Table 1).

AutoTool achieves an average gain of 7.7% on code generation benchmarks (e.g., V-Math at 53.0% and V-Code at 56.1% with Qwen3-8B) and 6.9% on multimodal understanding benchmarks (e.g., MMSearch at 49.3% with Qwen2.5-VL-7B) (Table 1).
AutoTool's dual-phase training pipeline combines SFT+RL trajectory stabilization (Phase I) with KL-regularized Plackett-Luce ranking optimization for tool selection (Phase II) (Section 3.3).
AutoTool is trained on a curated dataset of 200k examples spanning over 1,000 tools across more than 100 task types, covering code, search, and image tool categories (Section 3).
Compared to an oracle tool-selection upper bound, AutoTool shows only a 0.5-1.5% performance gap, validating the effectiveness of its dynamic (non-oracle) tool selection mechanism (Table 3).

mlQWk1DtkN.text: State-of-the-art large reasoning models (Qwen3-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, Magistral-Small-1.2) show accuracy drops of up to 60% when new information arrives late during the reasoning process, particularly on AIME and LiveCodeBench tasks (Section on dynamic interruption results).
Under a 'panic' failure mode induced by speedup directives, models prematurely terminate reasoning, causing accuracy drops of up to 30% overall and up to 80% performance loss on harder tasks.

Under a 'reasoning leakage' failure mode, models continue reasoning inside the answer section after a hard interruption, producing answers up to 10 times longer than their normal full-thinking outputs.

Under a 'self-doubt' failure mode, roughly 80% of update-driven interruption errors occur because models question the validity of new mid-reasoning information and ignore it, especially when the update arrives late in reasoning.

Adding explicit prompt guidance confirming that mid-reasoning updates are verified substantially improves model performance on easier benchmarks such as GSM-8K and MATH-500, though gains are smaller on harder tasks like AIME and LiveCodeBench.

47PywA0l3h.text: On the CES task with a budget constraint, COPEx with a single-step lookahead (H=1) achieves the highest expected information gain (EIG) at budgets of 100 and 150, scoring 7.03±0.55 and 7.47±0.55 respectively, versus the ALINE baseline's 4.46±0.21 and 5.70±0.24 (Section 4.2, Table 1).

On the location finding task with bounded-change transition constraints (‖x_t − x_{t-1}‖ ≤ δ for δ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}), COPEx outperforms baseline methods across all tested constraint levels (Section 4.1, Figure 3(d)).

On cost-aware active learning benchmarks (Ackley, Goldstein-Price, and Branin functions under Hazard Center and Rough Terrain cost landscapes), COPEx achieves consistently lower error than Gaussian process baselines for the same accumulated cost (Section 4.3, Figure 4).

Increasing the planning horizon H in COPEx's scenario-tree lookahead yields diminishing returns beyond H=3, while runtime scales exponentially with horizon depth, indicating only modest additional overhead is needed since m ∈ {1,2} branches offer the best performance-cost tradeoff (Section 4.1, Figure 3(c)).
Non-myopic variants of COPEx outperform the purely myopic variant specifically in the small-budget regime for cost-aware active learning (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

u8WTpsljQh.text: DDIM trajectories converge exponentially fast (in orthogonal distance) to the ε-tube of the line segment connecting the two nearest modes of the target distribution (Theorem 4.2).

After this convergence, DDIM trajectories can become trapped in the neighborhood of the midpoint of the segment connecting two nearest modes, which is the mechanism underlying its higher hallucination rate (Proposition 4.7).
DDPM's added stochastic noise makes it exponentially unlikely for its trajectory to terminate in this midpoint region, in contrast to DDIM's deterministic dynamics (Proposition 5.1).

On a 25-mode Gaussian mixture target distribution, DDPM empirically produces fewer hallucinations than DDIM, and the reverse trajectories empirically converge to the predicted mode-pair line segments after a critical time τ (Figure 1, Figure 4).

Adding extra stochastic (DDPM-like) steps to the otherwise-deterministic DDIM sampler reduces its hallucination rate on the Gaussian mixture benchmark, since the injected noise helps escape the midpoint trap on the mode-connecting segment (Figure 5).

cCFyY2LmF5.text: Learning to Share (LTS) reduces runtime by 40.8-44.6% versus the M1-Parallel baseline on AssistantBench and by 25.1-55.0% on GAIA (Table 1).
With GPT-5.1 on GAIA, LTS reaches 49.1% accuracy in 781s versus M1-Parallel's 47.9% accuracy in 1005s (Table 1).
With GPT-5.1 on AssistantBench, LTS reaches 26.7% accuracy in 882s versus M1-Parallel's 24.0% accuracy in 1389s (Table 1).
The learned memory controller's runtime overhead is approximately 0.2% of total execution time (Section on runtime analysis).

Ablations comparing naive all-admission memory (LTS-AddAll), LLM-based filtering, and the learned controller show LTS achieves the best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff, while naive all-admission is fastest but degrades accuracy (Table 2).

The memory controller is trained via reinforcement learning with usage-aware reward shaping that credits only memory entries subsequently accessed by other agent teams, plus a sparsity regularizer (Section on training the controller).

DXnLu7qu75.text: Successive Halving combined with Linear Model of Co-regionalisation (LMC) surrogate models achieves mean relative improvements of up to 2.84% on real-world nanoGPT learning curves and up to 5.47% on synthetic learning curves compared to plain Successive Halving (Experimental Results).
The strategic budget allocation approach saves up to 98.7% of computational cost relative to exhaustive training of all candidate models to convergence (Experimental Results).

Real-world validation uses 90 nanoGPT models of up to 1.5B parameters trained on the fineweb-edu dataset, where SH with LMC achieves about 2.84% mean relative improvement while preserving scaling-law accuracy comparable to full exhaustive training (Real-world Validation).
Synthetic-data experiments sweep 5, 10, and 20 candidate models across budgets of 10^2-10^4 petaFLOPs, with SH-LMC outperforming plain Successive Halving in most configurations (Synthetic Data).

Two families of surrogate models are compared: a non-parametric Gaussian Process Linear Model of Co-regionalisation capturing correlations among learning curves, and parametric Deep Ensembles using power-law, exponential, and MMF functional forms (Methodological Approach).

r3PKGNlKET.text: Lemma 3.1 shows that standard MLE-style log loss achieves near-optimal uniform convergence rates under local differential privacy, contradicting prior claims that de-biased losses are necessary for privacy-only alignment (Lemma 3.1).

Lemma 3.3 establishes uniform convergence for square loss under joint corruption and privacy constraints, improving the corruption dependence from alpha to alpha^2 in the corruption-only regime and from c(epsilon)*alpha to c(epsilon)*alpha^2 in the joint privacy-corruption regime (Lemma 3.3).
The privacy cost enters through the multiplicative factor c(epsilon) = (e^epsilon + 1)/(e^epsilon - 1), which the paper shows is optimal (Section 3).

Two orderings of corruption and privacy are analyzed: Corruption-then-LDP (CTL), yielding a corruption term of alpha, and LDP-then-Corruption (LTC), yielding a corruption term of c(epsilon)*alpha (Section 3).

The paper introduces PrivXPO and SquareXPO as the first online algorithms for private and robust alignment from preference labels, with PrivXPO achieving suboptimality O(c(epsilon)*sqrt(log|Pi|*T)/T) (Section 4, Algorithms PrivXPO and SquareXPO).

Offline algorithms Priv-chi-PO and Square-chi-PO achieve suboptimality gaps of O(c(epsilon)*sqrt(log|Pi|/n)) and O(c(epsilon)*sqrt(log|Pi|/n) + alpha) respectively under the CTL corruption model (Section 3, Offline Settings).

lACOz6QXrK.text: On Wan2.1-1.3B-720P text-to-video, SVOO achieves a 1.93x speedup while maintaining PSNR up to 29.986, compared to the prior state-of-the-art SVG2 method's 1.73x speedup and PSNR of 29.268 (Table with Wan2.1-1.3B-720P-T2V results).

On the same Wan2.1-1.3B-720P-T2V benchmark, SVOO attains SSIM of 0.898 and LPIPS of 0.125 versus SVG2's SSIM of 0.886 and LPIPS of 0.127, with inference latency of 216 seconds versus SVG2's 241 seconds (Table with Wan2.1-1.3B-720P-T2V results).

Theorem 4.2 proves that per-layer attention sparsity is an intrinsic property of each transformer layer with only minor variation across different inputs, motivating the offline sparsity profiling stage (Theorem 4.2).

SVOO combines offline layer-wise sensitivity profiling to set per-layer pruning ratios with an online bidirectional query-key co-clustering algorithm for block-wise sparse attention (Section on method / offline and online stages).

SVOO is evaluated across seven video generation models including Wan2.1 (1.3B and 14B), Wan2.2-14B, and HunyuanVideo variants, consistently improving the quality-efficiency tradeoff over prior sparse attention baselines (Section on broader model evaluation).

gYBeaguAN5.text: SpaCeFormer-3M contains 604,127 3D instance masks paired with 3.0 million captions across 7,361 indoor scenes aggregated from ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes, and Matterport3D (Section on SpaCeFormer-3M dataset).

The dataset's multi-view mask clustering pipeline achieves 54.3% mask recall at IoU>0.5, versus 2.5% for single-view pipelines, a 21x improvement in mask completeness over Mosaic3D (Section on dataset quality metrics).

On ScanNet200 in the proposal-free, 3D-only zero-shot setting, SpaCeFormer achieves 11.1 mAP, a 2.8x improvement over the next-best method Mosaic3D at 3.9 mAP (Zero-Shot Evaluation Benchmarks, ScanNet200).

On Replica (8 scenes), SpaCeFormer reaches 24.1 mAP at 0.14 seconds per scene, surpassing Open-YOLO 3D (23.7 mAP) and OpenTrack3D (23.9 mAP) while being 119x faster than Open-YOLO 3D (Zero-Shot Evaluation Benchmarks, Replica).

On ScanNet++, SpaCeFormer achieves 22.9 mAP at 0.14 seconds per scene, exceeding the prior best OpenTrack3D (20.6 mAP) and running over 4,000x faster than multi-stage baselines (Zero-Shot Evaluation Benchmarks, ScanNet++).

The Space-Curve Attention module combines spatial window attention with Morton curve serialization, reducing average within-window pairwise distance by 28.6% compared to Morton-only serialization (Section on Space-Curve Attention).

JRsJLPr85W.text: SURGE performs sequential Monte Carlo resampling over full diffusion trajectories (path space) rather than marginal endpoints, using Girsanov's theorem to compute importance weights that correct bias from approximate guidance (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

On the Lorenz-63 system with partial (x-only) observations and noise σ=0.05, SURGE+FlowDAS reduces RMSE from 0.0545 to 0.0502 and Wasserstein-1 distance from 0.0388 to 0.0363 versus FlowDAS alone (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On forced incompressible Navier-Stokes super-resolution (8²→128² grid), SURGE+FlowDAS achieves an RMSE of 0.851 versus 1.018 for the FlowDAS baseline, and a KES-RE of 0.317 versus 0.417 for SDA+SURGE (Table 2, Section 4.2).

On SEVIR weather forecasting (VIL nowcasting with 10% spatial sampling), SURGE+FlowDAS lowers RMSE from 0.0657 to 0.0513 and raises Critical Success Index at the τ₂₀ threshold from 0.5779 to 0.6197 and at τ₄₀ from 0.4044 to 0.4541 (Table 3, Section 4.3).

Proposition A.1 and Corollary A.2 establish that the Girsanov-corrected weighted empirical measure exactly recovers the true filtering posterior expectation, with the self-normalized estimator converging as the particle count N→∞ (Proposition A.1, Corollary A.2).

Lemma A.3 proves a telescoping likelihood decomposition showing that incorporating observation likelihood progressively across internal diffusion sub-steps yields the same target distribution as applying the terminal likelihood at once, stabilizing particle weights (Lemma A.3).

ARA2xneUDG.text: ContextLM augments next-token prediction with a 'next-context prediction' objective, using a token encoder, a 2-layer context predictor, and a token decoder that fuses token and context representations via element-wise addition, with a default context chunk size w=4 (Section 2.2).
On GPT2-Base, ContextLM reduces perplexity from 22.38 to 20.68, and on GPT2-XL from 15.25 to 14.60, an average 17.8% perplexity reduction across the GPT2 family (Table 2, Section 3.2).

On the Pythia family, ContextLM-70M reduces average perplexity from 297.72 to 142.71 (over 50% improvement), while ContextLM-1.4B reduces it from 9.74 to 9.54, and ContextLM needs 23% fewer training tokens to reach a target perplexity than the baseline (Table 3, Section 3.2).

On zero-shot downstream tasks across nine benchmarks (including Lambada, ARC, WinoGrande, PIQA, HellaSwag), ContextLM-Base and ContextLM-XL improve average accuracy by 1.3% and 1.7% respectively over GPT2 baselines (Table 4, Section 3.3).

An ablation over context chunk size shows w=2 achieves the lowest perplexity (20.65) versus the default w=4 (20.68), with all tested chunk sizes outperforming the 22.38 baseline, and a 2-layer context predictor is found to be the optimal depth (Section 3.5).
The added context predictor incurs an extra O((T/w)²d) compute cost, amounting to approximately 6.25% overhead with w=4 and less than 5% additional GPU memory versus the baseline (Section 2.4).

TWTZ2kmojU.text: URGE (Unbiased Resampling via Girsanov Estimation) performs sequential Monte Carlo resampling on diffusion trajectory space using Girsanov's theorem, requiring only reward function evaluations rather than gradients, Hessians, or PDE solvers as needed by prior methods like FK-Corrector and AFDPS (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
Theorem 3.1 proves that as the time step Δt→0 and particle count N→∞, URGE's empirical distribution converges to the true reward-tilted posterior without systematic bias (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.3 shows URGE's path-space reweighting recovers the same infinitesimal generator as FK-Corrector and AFDPS when marginalized to particle space, unifying these derivative-based approaches under a derivative-free formulation (Theorem 3.3).

On a 30-dimensional, 40-component Gaussian mixture model benchmark, URGE achieves an MMD of 0.06 versus 0.08 for AFDPS+VCG, and a sliced Wasserstein distance of 0.62 versus 0.83, with better convergence using fewer particles (Section on Gaussian Mixture Model experiments).

On ImageNet-256 Gaussian deblurring, URGE achieves an LPIPS of 0.3861 compared to 0.5986 for FK-Corrector, while matching PSNR/LPIPS of AFDPS variants without requiring score function access (Inverse Problems experiments, ImageNet-256).

On Stable Diffusion text-to-image generation with N=4 particles, URGE attains an ImageReward score of 0.9955 versus 0.8397 for FK-Steering, and a CLIP-Score of 0.2997 versus 0.2901 (Text-to-Image Generation experiments).

c4iSIrb6Iv.text: Reasoning-VLA generates driving trajectories in a single parallel decoding step using learnable action queries initialized via Gaussian sampling from ground-truth trajectories, built atop the Qwen2.5-VL foundation model (Section 3.1-3.3).

Training uses a two-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO reinforcement learning with three reward functions: a physical trajectory reward (weighted Euclidean distance), a steering constraint reward (max 40 degrees, threshold 0.84), and an acceleration reward (max 6 m/s²) (Section 3.6-3.7).

The model is trained on a unified dataset of over 75,000 clips consolidated from NAVSIM, nuScenes, Waymo, Argoverse-V2, KITTI, Mapillary, ONCE, and IDD, augmented with Chain-of-Thought reasoning annotations (Section 4).
On the nuScenes open-loop benchmark, Reasoning-VLA-7B achieves 0.23m average L2 error and 0.08% collision rate, a 23.3% improvement in average L2 over prior state-of-the-art (Table 1).
On the NeuroNCAP closed-loop benchmark, Reasoning-VLA-7B attains a 2.25 average score and 59.4% collision rate, outperforming the Impromptu-VLA baseline (Table 2).
Reasoning-VLA runs 61 times faster than autoregressive Qwen2.5-VL inference, generating 10 trajectories in 0.089s versus 5.472s for sequential token-by-token prediction (Table 9).

gngDtQCUZr.text: The paper identifies 'latent misalignment'—a discrepancy between the analytically transformed latent ρ(g)Φ(x) and the empirically encoded latent Φ(g∘x) under a group action g—as a failure mode in existing equivariant latent models (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

Residual Latent Flow (RLF) corrects this misalignment via a conditional flow-matching loss ℒ_RLF(θ) = E[‖v_θ(z_t,t) − (z₁−z₀)‖₂²] trained with a three-stage pipeline: equivariant representation learning, RLF training, then decoder fine-tuning (Section 3.2-3.3, Equation 10).
On SO(3) rotations for the ABO dataset, RLF improves PSNR from 11.85 to 12.57 and reduces latent error from 7.3×10⁻⁴ to 1.9×10⁻⁴ and angle error from 0.0079 to 0.0010 (Table 1).
On out-of-distribution SO(3) rotations for ModelNet10-SO(3), RLF improves PSNR from 10.09 to 10.43 and reduces angle error from 0.1746 to 0.0430 (Table 1).
On SO(2) rotations for the ComplexBRDFs dataset, RLF improves PSNR from 16.04 to 17.38 and reduces latent error from 8.9×10⁻⁴ to 6.7×10⁻⁴ (Table 1).
On the real-world SmallNORB out-of-plane rotation benchmark, RLF improves PSNR from 23.13 to 23.28 and LPIPS from 0.272 to 0.247 (Table 3).

MrIDZjIsNF.text: Under Assumption 3.2 (uniform Bellman error bound ε), if ε = O(1/T), SMC-based inference-time scaling attains a target TV error with particle/time complexity that is polynomial rather than exponential in the horizon T (Section 5, Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.2).
Without reward guidance, the number of samples needed to hit the target region grows as Ω(L^(2T/3)), an exponential lower bound in T (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

Even with a Bellman-error-bounded reward model, sampling complexity is lower-bounded by Ω((1+ε)^(2T/3)), showing guidance alone cannot remove exponential dependence unless ε shrinks with T (Section 4, Corollary 4.2).
For single-particle guided SMC, the total-variation error is bounded by 2Tε, so guidance fails to control error once ε ≥ 1/(2T) (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).
Theorem 5.1 establishes a particle complexity bound N ≥ L^6 T(1+ε)^(6(T-1))/(2δ_TV) for SMC to achieve TV error δ_TV (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
A resampling-pool Metropolis-Hastings chain-based approach achieves the target accuracy with time complexity Õ(L T^3 log(1/δ) log(1/δ_TV)) (Section 6, Theorem 6.1).

DGXfoyszbj.text: In the extreme 1-shot (N=1) setting on RML2016.10a, DyCo-CL reaches 43.84% accuracy, exceeding the prior state of the art by 6.27% (Section 6.3, Figure 5).
DyCo-CL exceeds prior few-shot modulation recognition methods by 7.7% at 10 dB SNR under the N=1 setting on RML2016.10a (Section 6.3, Figures 6-7).
On RML2018.01a in the 10-shot setting, DyCo-CL maintains a 7.54% accuracy margin over prior methods for SNR greater than 6 dB (Section 6.3, Figures 6-7).
Ablating the Dynamic-Consistency framework drops accuracy from 43.84% to 34.94% (an 8.90-point loss) on RML2016.10a at N=1 (Section 6.4, Table 1).
Replacing the Signal-Adaptive Swin backbone with ResNet18 reduces accuracy from 43.84% to 39.45% (a 4.39-point loss) under the same 1-shot setting (Section 6.4, Table 1).

Theorem 5.1 formally shows that minimizing the semantic consistency loss used in DyCo-CL is equivalent to minimizing local Lipschitz constants, framing the method as implicit spectral regularization (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).

gcuFTjpJFE.text: Answer-agreement Representation Shaping (ARS) applies small latent interventions at the trace boundary to explicitly encode answer stability into trace-conditioned embeddings, without using any human annotations (Section 4.1-4.2).
On Qwen3-8B with a CCS-based detector, ARS raises AUROC from 66.85% (vanilla embeddings) to 86.64% on TruthfulQA, and from 59.24% to 88.54% on TriviaQA (Section 5, Table 2).
On MATH-500 with a probing-based detector, ARS raises AUROC from 67.03% to 78.17% versus vanilla embeddings (Section 5, Table 2).

ARS substantially outperforms LRM-specific hallucination detection baselines (RHD, RACE, G-Detector, in the low-70s AUROC range) as well as uncertainty- and consistency-based baselines (Perplexity, Semantic Entropy, Lexical Similarity, SelfCKGPT, Verbalized Certainty, TSV) across TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, GSM8K, and MATH-500 (Section 5, Table 1).

Proposition 4.2 bounds hallucination detection error in terms of the agreement-separation probability and answer-stability predictiveness of the learned representations (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.2).

Using latent intervention instead of alternative perturbation strategies (token deletion, token masking, paraphrasing) yields the best CCS AUROC of 86.64%, versus 75.25%, 75.50%, and 50.47% respectively (Section 5.4, Table 4).

7sIDvIywHQ.text: UOTIP formulates unpaired inverse problems as learning an unbalanced optimal transport map using a combined cost c(y,x) = τ(||A(x)-y||²₂ + ||y-x||²₂), pairing a likelihood term with a quadratic regularization term (Section 3, Equation 9).

Proposition 3.1 proves that adding the quadratic cost term makes the overall cost satisfy the twist condition, guaranteeing existence and uniqueness of the OT map for L-Lipschitz forward operators A whenever the cost weight λ > L (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
Proposition A.3 shows the map x ↦ ∂c/∂y(y,x;λ) is injective for all λ > L, restoring injectivity that is lost in ill-posed inverse problems without the quadratic term (Appendix A.1, Proposition A.3).

UOTIP achieves best or near-best PSNR, SSIM, and FID on Gaussian deblurring, super-resolution, HDR reconstruction, and nonlinear deblurring on both FFHQ and AFHQ, outperforming baselines NOT, OTUR, and RCOT (Section 4, Table 1).
The unbalanced OT variant outperforms the standard OT baseline specifically under heterogeneous multi-level noise conditions (Section 4.2, Table 2).
UOTIP maintains superior performance across class-imbalance ratios k in {1,2,3,4} and generalizes across Gaussian, Laplace, and Poisson noise types (Section 4.2, Figures 3 and 4a).

2zNijsn2jC.text: AmbiSuR achieves a mean Chamfer distance of 0.46mm on the DTU dataset, outperforming GeoSVR (0.47mm) and PGSR (0.52mm) (Section 4, Table 1).
On Tanks and Temples, AmbiSuR attains an F1-score of 0.589, ahead of MILo (0.576) and PGSR (0.569) (Section 4, Table 2).
On Mip-NeRF 360, AmbiSuR reaches PSNR of 24.79 on outdoor scenes and 30.06 on indoor scenes (Section 4, Table 3).

AmbiSuR addresses photometric ambiguity via Spherical Harmonics Ambiguity Indication using Dual-End Indication and an Amorphous Local Regularizer, on top of Gaussian Splatting Photometric Disambiguation of primitive-edge and photometric-blending ambiguities (Section 3.2-3.3).

An AmbiSuR-Mono variant substitutes monocular depth priors from Depth Anything V2 for the metric depth priors from Depth Anything 3 used in full AmbiSuR, demonstrating broad compatibility across depth-prior model types while retaining visual quality (Section 3, Section 4).

Ablating Gaussian Primitive Truncation, Ray-Color Consistency, and Spherical Harmonics Ambiguity Indication on Tanks and Temples each degrades reconstruction quality relative to the full AmbiSuR model (Section 4, Table 4).

VYTU8l8WO9.text: V0 reframes value estimation as conditional prediction V(C_pi, s0) ≈ P(r=1|x, C_pi), where C_pi is a set of historical query-performance pairs summarizing a policy's capability, rather than fitting value directly to policy parameters (Section 4.1).

V0's architecture combines a frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B semantic backbone, a Residual Query Adapter that maps embeddings to structured features via learnable static queries plus attention-based dynamic offsets, and a TabPFN head performing Bayesian inference in a single forward pass (Section 4.2, Figure 2).

Theorem 4.2 shows that a Bradley-Terry pairwise ranking loss is invariant to context-dependent bias, forcing the model to discriminate based on query difficulty rather than exploiting the policy-strength shortcut term identified in Theorem 4.1 (Section 4.3).

On main benchmarks spanning DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen2.5-7B, V0 achieves Intra-Group AUC of 0.887-0.893 versus 0.708-0.769 for a Vanilla Value Model that requires continuous retraining (Table 1).

On strictly held-out test queries excluded from training history, V0 retains 0.689-0.710 AUC while the vanilla value model collapses to 0.512-0.560 AUC, demonstrating zero-shot generalization to unseen problems (Table 2).

During GRPO training, using V0 for adaptive rollout budget allocation via the utility function Utility(B,p) = B(1-p)[1-(1-p)^(B-1)] yields approximately a 2% improvement on OlympiadBench (Section 5.5, Figure 5a).

XcwdniuaYh.text: The paper introduces the Prototypical Relearning Attack, which computes a per-class averaged feature from as few as 5 forgotten samples per class and uses it directly as a classifier to reconstruct forgotten knowledge (Section 4.2, Equation 4).

The paper formalizes an Over-Unlearning metric, OU@epsilon, that measures performance degradation on adversarially perturbed forget-set samples near the decision boundary without requiring access to retained data (Section 4.1, Equation 3).

Spotter combines a masked knowledge-distillation penalty (loss terms L_unlearn and L_over) with an intra-class dispersion loss L_sim (Equation 10) that scatters forget-class embeddings to neutralize the prototypical relearning attack (Section 5, Equation 11).
On CIFAR-10, Spotter achieves 0.00% forget accuracy, 99.98% retain accuracy (within 1% of the original model), an OU@epsilon of 0.0228, and reduces Proto-Acc_f to 0.24% (Table 1).

Spotter is demonstrated as a plug-and-play addition compatible with 9 existing unlearning baselines, improving their robustness against both over-unlearning and prototypical relearning attacks across CIFAR, TinyImageNet, and CASIA-WebFace datasets (Section 5, Table 1).

dzcDbh8ewp.text: LECTOR reformulates the Content-Conditional Introduction Generation task by producing an intermediate Logic-Reasoning Graph, a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are self-contained sentences and whose edges encode Peircean deduction, abduction, and induction relations (Section on Logic-Reasoning Graph).

LECTOR is trained with Logic-Expression Co-Reinforcement Learning, jointly optimizing five reward signals covering graph validity, faithfulness, paper consistency, writing quality, and citation integrity (Equation 5).
LECTOR improves Graph Quality by 26.7%, Writing Quality by 28.8%, Citation Quality by 8.6%, and Paper Consistency by 3.3% over baselines (Table 2).
A 4B-parameter model trained with LECTOR achieves an Overall Performance score of 0.665, comparable to GPT-o3's 0.656 (Table 2).
In human evaluation by 8 domain experts, LECTOR scores 3.73 overall versus GPT-o3's 3.71, with superior logical coherence (4.05 vs 4.00) (Table 6).

Evaluation uses a dataset of 10,200 physics-related Nature Communications papers (April 2010-March 2025), split into 10,000 training and 100 test papers, and upgrading graph extraction alone improves Writing Quality by 0.094 (Table 3).

9M6kY6yuAy.text: BHyT bounds tanh inputs to the range (-lambda, lambda) with probability at least 1-kappa^-2 via a Chebyshev's-inequality-based input bounding scheme, preventing activation saturation while preserving healthy gradients (Section 3.1).

Theorem 3.5 proves that under the hyperparameter condition lambda/kappa < 1/sqrt(L), BHyT's output variance remains smaller than LayerNorm Scaling across all depths up to L layers, giving a finite-depth stability bound.

On the 3B-parameter model (28 layers), BHyT achieves the lowest pretraining loss (3.107) and the highest downstream average accuracy (43.33%) across 7 benchmarks, compared to RMSNorm, LayerNorm Scaling, Peri-LN, and DyT (Table 1).
BHyT trains 15.8% faster on average than RMSNorm and 17.7% faster than Peri-LN, including 171.4 hours versus 238 hours wall time for Peri-LN when pretraining on 20B tokens (Figure 4, Table 4).
BHyT achieves 4.2% higher average inference token throughput than RMSNorm, reaching 53.5 tokens/second, which is 5.6% faster than RMSNorm and 12.9% faster than Peri-LN (Table 3).

An ablation replacing per-instance variance computation with the lightweight variance approximation from Section 3.2 (Theorem 3.4) yields a 14.9% training speedup with negligible performance degradation (Table 5).

YjYPYg112A.text: Proposition 3.1 proves that standard linear scalar tokenization produces embedding matrices with rank at most 2 (or at most H+1 with H attention heads), explaining the empirically observed low-rank collapse in TabPFN-v2's early layers.

RaBEL (Radial Basis Embedding Layer) expands each scalar value into M localized, optionally exponent-gated RBF features after per-column z-score normalization, rather than a single linear projection (Equations 1-3 and 5-10).
The reordered attention stack processes Sample attention, then FFN, then Feature attention, so sample-level attention aggregates column-level statistics before feature mixing occurs (Section 4.3).

LimiX-2M (1.92M parameters) outperforms TabPFN-v2 (7.24M parameters) and TabICL (27.10M parameters) in aggregate ranking across 11 benchmarks, scoring 6.58 versus 9.57 and 10.57 respectively, while ranking second overall behind LimiX-16M (Table 6).

Relative to the 2M baseline, LimiX-2M with RaBEL increases shallow-layer Numerical Rank by 34.60% (78.62 vs 58.41), Rank@99% by 81.98% (25.35 vs 13.94), and Rank@95% by 83.18% (12.31 vs 6.73) (Table 5).
TabPFN-v2 maintains competitive AUC even when its effective rank is truncated to r=20, about 10% of the hidden dimension, demonstrating severe redundancy in early layers (Table 1).

uYaNE2Cys2.text: UniMRG trains unified multimodal models with four joint objectives—image reconstruction, image-to-depth, image-to-segmentation, and image understanding—using depth maps from Depth Anything V2 and segmentation maps from SAM (Section 3).
On OpenUni-3.6B, UniMRG improves MMVP fine-grained perception accuracy from 71.67 to 74.67 (+3.00 points) (Table showing understanding benchmark results).
On OpenUni-3.6B, UniMRG improves HallusionBench accuracy from 60.88 to 64.56 (+3.68 points), demonstrating reduced hallucination (Table showing understanding benchmark results).
On OpenUni-3.6B, UniMRG improves VSR spatial-reasoning accuracy from 66.69 to 73.90 (+7.21 points) (Table showing understanding benchmark results).

UniMRG is evaluated across three unified multimodal architectures—autoregressive Show-o-1.3B, AR+Masked-Autoregressive Harmon-1.5B, and AR+Diffusion OpenUni-3.6B—with Show-o showing only marginal gains because its 4,096-token VQ codebook bottlenecks joint pixel/depth/segmentation generation (Section on architecture generalization).

UniMRG matches or exceeds the RecA baseline on image generation quality (GenEval and DPGBench) while simultaneously improving understanding metrics, trained on LLaVA Mix-665K and LLaVA-Next-Data (Section on generation results).

ql7SeCTnvu.text: Cuttlefish's Scaling-Aware Patching mechanism selects anchor atoms via a cumulative-probability threshold ρ and expands them into variable-size patches using soft assignment based on spatial proximity and instruction relevance, adaptively scaling the query-token budget with structural complexity (Section on Scaling-Aware Patching).

The Geometry Grounding Adapter injects geometry-informed tokens into the language model via cross-attention retrieval of full-modality embeddings to reduce structural hallucinations (Section on Geometry Grounding Adapter).

On the GEO-AT benchmark (Table 2), Cuttlefish combined with Llama-3.1-8B achieves the best average METEOR score of 0.428 and BERTScore of 0.864 across molecule, protein, DNA, and RNA modalities compared to general LLM baselines.
Cuttlefish achieves hallucination rates of 0.07 for molecules and 0.04 for proteins, corresponding to 0.17 hallucinations per molecule/protein on average (Table 7).
An ablation shows removing the soft patch-growth mechanism degrades METEOR by 66.83%, while removing the fusion blocks degrades METEOR by 20.96% (ablation study section).

GEO-AT, introduced by the authors, is the first all-atom instruction dataset with atom-level coordinates spanning molecules, proteins, DNA, and RNA, built alongside Mol-Instructions (~700K samples), DNA-Chat (7.8M samples from Nucleotide Transformer), and RNA-QA (400K+ QA pairs) (Section on datasets).

A7LiBHEsOo.text: L3 (Large Lookup Layer) generalizes embedding tables into a sparse decoder layer using static, token-ID-based routing combined with context-dependent attention-based aggregation of the routed embeddings (Section on L3 architecture).

An LZW-compression-based allocation algorithm (Algorithm 1) assigns each of ~710,000 total embeddings to tokens by frequency, with each token receiving between 1 and k=512 embeddings (Section on embedding allocation, Algorithm 1).
At 2.6B active parameters trained on 30B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a model with 2 L3 layers achieves perplexity 14.51 versus 15.43 for the dense baseline (Figure 1).
L3 outperforms iso-FLOP dense models and iso-FLOP, iso-sparse Mixture-of-Experts models at all tested sparsity levels across the 800M, 1.5B, and 2.6B active-parameter scales (Figure 1, Figure 8).
On 8×A100 GPUs, the 800M-active-parameter L3 model reaches 135K tokens/s training throughput, 87% of the equivalent dense model's speed (Section on training efficiency).

Downstream evaluation on Wikitext2, ArcChallenge, ArcEasy, HellaSwag, PiQA, and Winogrande shows L3 CPU-offloaded single-token inference adds minimal latency overhead, with full latency masking achieved after 4 decoder layers (Section on inference efficiency).

Hu8tqsCnEn.text: TASLE comprises 12,472 untrimmed videos (2-124 seconds long), split into 11,179 training and 1,293 test videos, containing 6,665 total AIGC-manipulated segments and 28,155 rationales drawn from a 15,947-word vocabulary (Section on dataset statistics).

TASLE videos are manipulated using three generative techniques—First-Last-Frame-to-Video (FLF2V), Text-Image-to-Video (TI2V), and Mask-Video-to-Video (MV2V)—sourced from 11 diverse video domains including cooking, actions, and surveillance (Section on manipulation types).

MSLoc uses a two-stage coarse-to-fine pipeline: MSLoc-PG performs boundary-sensitive 4-class (real, fake, real-to-fake, fake-to-real) proposal generation with a 2-second sliding window and 8-frame sampling, followed by MSLoc-PR, an MLLM-based refinement stage with Difference-Aware Modeling and an Event Aggregation Module (Section on MSLoc architecture).

On the TASLE test set, MSLoc-PG alone achieves F1Det 67.5% and F1Loc 64.8%, while the full MSLoc pipeline improves these to F1Det 70.1% and F1Loc 72.2%, with a rationale-quality (RQ) score of 4.05 versus 3.91 for the Trace baseline (Main results table).

F1Loc is computed as the average retrieval F1 across IoU thresholds {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7}, and F1Det is computed over 0.01-second detection windows, with Rationale Quality scored 0-5 by GPT-5.1 (Section on evaluation metrics).

iixK49TTop.text: DiSP (Difficulty-Stratified Success Prediction) is a judge-centric sample-and-judge framework that predicts whether a specific query-context demonstration pairing will succeed, rather than directly searching for optimal demonstrations (Section on method overview).

DiSP achieves best average accuracy of 77.6% with LLaMA 3-8B and 82.9% with Qwen 2.5-7B across five classification datasets (TREC, SST-2, SST-5, AGNews, MNLI), improving over strong learned selection baselines by up to 3.4%, with the largest gains on the harder TREC and MNLI datasets (Main results table).

DiSP achieves up to a 23x end-to-end wall-clock speedup over baselines, with training taking 6.7 minutes versus 157.1 minutes for SeDPO and test-time inference costing 0.1 minutes versus 0.6 minutes for baseline methods (Section on efficiency comparison).

DiSP's router predicts a per-query difficulty stratum (l1/l2/l3/lx) from the query alone, then uses T=20 random demonstration trials to estimate per-query success rates for training level-specific judges of increasing capacity (Section on difficulty stratification).

A stop-on-acceptance sampling procedure draws demonstrations until an acceptable candidate is found or a budget is exhausted, flagging HARD_QUERY cases (router predicts lx stratum, about 2.2% of queries) and NO_GOOD_DEMO cases when no acceptable context is found (Section on risk tags).

Trfut9gSjY.text: Mosaic, trained at 1.5-degree resolution with block-sparse attention, matches or outperforms baseline ML weather forecasting models trained at 0.25-degree resolution on standard forecast skill metrics (Section 5).

The block-sparse attention mechanism in Mosaic preserves spectral fidelity of ensemble-member forecasts across resolved frequencies, avoiding the artificial smoothing/distortion of energy spectra seen with dense attention (Section 5, Figure 7).

The methodology section defines a spectral-preservation objective evaluated via power spectrum analysis of ensemble members, compared against operational and existing ML baselines using CRPS (Section 3, Section 4).

A systematic resolution study (0.25 to 1.5 degree grids) is used to demonstrate that computational savings from coarser resolution do not come at the cost of forecast quality when block-sparse attention is used (Section 4, Table 6).
Ablations in the appendices isolate the contribution of the sparse attention pattern versus dense attention on spectral accuracy at different spatial scales (Appendix A-C).

B8sTBdGvqG.text: The conditional conformal test martingale (CTM) uses a fixed reference dataset D0 rather than an ever-growing reference set, avoiding test-time contamination that dilutes evidence of distribution shift in standard CTMs (Section 3).

Theorem 3.1 establishes finite-sample, anytime-valid type-I error control, bounding the probability of falsely rejecting the null by alpha with probability at least 1-delta over the randomness of the reference set (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.3 shows the method achieves asymptotic power one whenever the effective signal strength Delta_k is positive, with expected stopping time bounded by O(1/Delta_0^2 * ln(1/(alpha*Delta_0)) + 1/Delta_0^2) (Theorem 3.3).

The betting function (Eq. 8) subtracts a Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz-based estimation-error correction term from the standard betting score to remove spurious wealth gains from estimation uncertainty (Section 3, Equation 8).

On synthetic experiments with immediate, delayed, and gradual distribution shifts, the conditional CTM detects shifts faster than the standard (invalid) CTM while maintaining type-I error control at alpha=0.05 (Figure 2, Figure 3).

On ImageNet-C corruption benchmarks, detection performance improves with reference set size n >= 500, with detection ratio exceeding 1 for corruption groups involving larger distributional shifts (Figure 4).

LQNrpOXqoB.text: The proposed hypertoroidal color-equivariant network (T3CEN) lifts saturation and luminance from interval-valued quantities to circle-valued (double-cover) quantities, giving them true cyclic group structure rather than treating them as 1D translations (Section 4, Equation 15).
T3CEN reduces the saturation-equivariance lifting error to an average of 4.66x10^-6, roughly six orders of magnitude lower than LCER's 0.445 (Section 5.1, Figures 2-4).
On the 3D Shapes hue-shift benchmark, T3CEN achieves 0.00% classification error on both A/B and A/C test splits (Section 5.2, Tables 1-6).
On the small NORB luminance-shift benchmark, T3CEN (L16 configuration) achieves 11.09% error compared to 34.83% for LCER-L3 (Section 5.2, Table in Section 5.2).
On the Camelyon17 medical imaging dataset, the S4 configuration of T3CEN achieves 12.11% error under saturation/luminance shift (Section 5.2, Table 5).
The method's computational cost is comparable to other group-equivariant CNNs due to the need to compute filter orbits over the product group HSL_NMR = H_N x S_M x L_R (Section 6).

01caH9oj7C.text: Reasoning collapse (template collapse) is diagnosed via two axes -- within-input diversity H(Z|X) and cross-input dependence I(X;Z) -- using mutual-information proxies (Retrieval-Acc and MI-ZScore-EMA) that correlate with performance (+0.39 Spearman) while entropy correlates negatively (-0.11 to -0.14) (Section 2, Table 1).

The task gradient norm is upper-bounded by the square root of within-prompt reward variance, ||g_task|| <= sqrt(RV(x)), so when reward variance is low, input-agnostic regularization gradients dominate and reasoning collapses toward generic templates (Section 3, Figure 3, Table 2).

A quartile ablation on reward variance shows performance degrades monotonically from the highest-variance quartile (Q1) to the lowest (Q4), providing causal evidence for the reward-variance-to-collapse mechanism (Section 3, Table 6).

Reward-variance-aware (SNR-aware) top-p filtering, which retains only the highest-reward-variance prompts before each policy update, yields an average +6.9% improvement over the PPO baseline across seven environments (Sokoban, FrozenLake, MetaMathQA, Countdown, SearchQA, WebShop, DeepCoder), four algorithms (PPO, DAPO, GRPO, Dr. GRPO), multiple model scales (Qwen2.5 0.5B-7B, Llama3.2-3B), and both text and vision-language modalities (Qwen2.5-VL) (Section 4, Table 3, Table 4).
Reward-variance computation adds less than 0.1% overhead, and filtering with rho=0.9 reduces per-step training time by 26-41% while matching or exceeding unfiltered performance (Table 5).

DZbzIOguz4.text: phi-balancing minimizes a strictly convex, symmetric potential function of the population-level (not mini-batch) expert routing distribution, replacing the biased per-mini-batch statistics used by Switch-style auxiliary losses (Section 1, Section 3, Equation 7).

The method is derived via a convex-duality/min-max formulation solved by a mirror-descent algorithm that maintains an EMA of routing statistics and adds an auxiliary loss based on the gradient of the dual potential rather than realized assignment frequencies (Section 3, Equations 9-12, Algorithm 1).

Table 1 compares eight candidate potential functions (Euclidean norm, l_p norms, soft l1 norm, negative entropy, Tsallis entropy, Renyi entropy, pseudo-Huber, log-cosh/softplus), with negative entropy empirically recommended (Table 1).

Scaling studies at constant per-token FLOPs across active-parameter scaling (111M-986M), granularity scaling (G in {2,4,8,16,32}), and expert-count scaling (E in {8,16,32,64,128}) show phi-balancing consistently outperforms Switch-style and loss-free baselines (Figure 2).

phi-balancing yields significant downstream gains on Math500, LiveBench, and HumanEval after fine-tuning, and produces lower Gini coefficients and tighter expert-load bounds than the ST-MoE baseline during pretraining (Figure 1, Figure 3).

An ablation over different mirror maps phi reports validation loss and maximum global load-balance violation for each choice, quantifying the negligible overhead versus balancing quality trade-off (Table 2).

WcF17Wim9e.text: On 8×H800 GPUs, DITRON achieves 1.43x speedup over CuBLAS+NCCL for fused AllGather+GEMM and 19.18x speedup for fused AllGather+MoE on isolated kernel workloads (Figure 4).
DITRON's end-to-end tensor-parallel integration into vLLM yields 5%-30% inference speedup for large batch sizes (128+) compared to the baseline runtime (Section 4.1, Figure 6).
On AMD GPUs, DITRON achieves 1%-38% speedup versus RocmBLAS+RCCL, and on PCIe-connected GPUs it achieves speedups ranging from 2.54x to 49.84x (Section 4.3, Tables 13-18).

DITRON's three-level programming interface (core-, device-, and task-level) extends Triton's tile abstraction to support distributed multi-GPU/multi-node execution while preserving single-GPU kernel code compatibility (Section 3.1).

The distributed compute-communication swizzling scheme reorders GEMM+ReduceScatter tile execution to prioritize tiles destined for the furthest remote nodes, improving overlap of computation and communication (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

oAAL0wZSMF.text: Kernel Mean Matching (KMM) formulates dataset valuation as the convex quadratic program min_w (1/2)w^T K w - λβ^T w, where K is the pairwise gradient-similarity Gram matrix among auxiliary datasets and β measures alignment with the target task (Section 3.2.2).

Theorem 3.1 gives a finite-sample estimation error bound of Õ(kN/(μ√m)) for KMM's valuation scores under bounded gradient norms and a positive-definite Gram matrix, where m is the preview sample size and N the number of auxiliary datasets (Theorem 3.1).

KMM achieves the strongest best-k selection performance across target languages in both SFT (Danish, Marathi) and GRPO (Thai) post-training settings compared to existing dataset valuation baselines (Tables 2-4).
KMM-based selection reaches near-optimal performance at roughly two orders of magnitude lower computational cost than retraining-based valuation baselines such as DataModel (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
Valuation scores computed with a small proxy model transfer effectively to guide selection for a much larger 70B target model (Figure 3).

KMM's pairwise transfer structure identifies non-obvious auxiliary languages, such as Indonesian, as effective transfer sources for target languages beyond linguistic similarity (Section 4.4, Figure 7).

UmlXZ4t44h.text: PS-VAE maps 768-dimensional DINOv2 features into a compact 96-channel latent space at 16x16 spatial downsampling, reducing off-manifold outliers via KL regularization in the Semantic VAE stage (Section 3.3).

PS-VAE achieves an rFID of 0.203 and PSNR of 28.79 dB, improving substantially over RAE (rFID 619, PSNR 19.20) and MAR-VAE (rFID 534, PSNR 26.18) on the reconstruction and generation benchmark (Table 2).
PS-VAE (96-channel) attains a GenEval score of 76.56 and Editing Reward of 0.222, exceeding RAE (GenEval 71.27, Editing Reward 0.059) and MAR-VAE (GenEval 75.75, Editing Reward 0.056) (Table 2).
Scaling the generative model from 653M to 1708M parameters raises PS-VAE96c's GenEval score from 76.56 to 78.14, with faster convergence curves than baseline feature spaces (Section 4.3, Figure 10).
PS-VAE generalizes to a SigLIP2 encoder, achieving a GenEval score of 77.14 while limiting understanding-capability degradation on MME-Perception (1685 to 1652) (Section 4.4, Table 3).

pt7x2tJm4L.text: Attention modules exhibit low Representation Information Discrepancy (RID ≈ 0.06) but high Mixing Information Gain (MixIG ≈ 0.61), while FFN modules show the reverse pattern (RID ≈ 0.21, MixIG ≈ 0.02), indicating attention is subspace-preserving/reconfiguring and FFN is subspace-expanding/innovating (Table 1, Section 4.2).
This orthogonal division of labor between attention and FFN is consistent across 15 LVLM variants spanning the Qwen, LLaVA-1.5, and LLaVA-NeXT/OneVision architecture families (Figure 2).

Replacing learned attention scores with a Shared Attention Prior (visual-encoder attention maps or patch-complexity heuristics) matches or exceeds vanilla attention performance, e.g. raising Qwen-2.5-VL-7B POPE accuracy from 86.54 to 87.62-87.73 and LLaVA-1.5-7B POPE accuracy from 74.38 to 75.30-75.79 (Table 2, Section 4.3).
The interpretability framework evaluates seven multimodal benchmarks: POPE, 3DSRBench, RealWorldQA, MMMU, VMCBench, HallusionBench, and MathVista (Section 4.1).

Question-relevant image regions receive only 4.2% of attention interaction degree in incorrect model responses versus 13.1% in correct responses, evidencing visual attention misallocation despite overall redundancy (Section 4.2).

VzRUI5ZVkp.text: Theorem 4.2 shows standard reverse-KL-regularized RLVR cannot expand the empirical support of the policy beyond that of the reference model, while Theorem 4.3 proves SAGE's reshaped pseudo-KL anchor can recover reward-valid solutions outside that support (Theorems 4.2-4.3).

SAGE introduces a guide function q(x,y) that reshapes the reverse-KL anchor distribution, instantiated in token-level (surprisal-based), branch-level (entropy-thresholded), and random guide variants (Section 4).
With Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Base, GRPO+Branch improves average Pass@1 from 0.266 (GRPO) to 0.284 and average Pass@256 from 0.714 to 0.729 across AIME, AMC23, and MATH-500 (Table 1).
Branch-level guidance is shown to be the most effective of the three guide variants, outperforming token-level and random guides on average pass@1 and pass@k (Table 1, Section 5).
SAGE's gains generalize across multiple RLVR algorithms (GRPO, DAPO, BNPO) and across model backbones including DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (Tables 3-4).
SAGE is demonstrated to be a modular, orthogonal addition to existing RLVR pipelines that improves pass@1 and pass@k jointly without inducing reward hacking (Section 5, Table 5).

vNKtSK8q8D.text: On the RGB-only DID dataset, AMNet achieves 31.57 dB PSNR and 0.95 SSIM, surpassing the previous best method's 30.10 dB and 0.93 SSIM (Table 1).

AMNet's Spatial-Spectral Dual-Gated (S2DG) Translator combines an Illumination-Aware Detail Selector and a Frequency-Band Selector to produce implicit auxiliary representations for modality-agnostic inference (Section 3.2).
An ablation removing both the IADS and FBS components drops DID PSNR from 31.57 dB to 29.85 dB, showing both gating mechanisms are necessary (Table 5).

Scaling synthetic-modality pretraining from 0% to 100% of RGB-only data increases DID PSNR from 29.78 dB to 31.57 dB, supporting the claim that large-scale multimodal pretraining aids cross-modal correspondence learning (Table 4).

When trained with full modality availability but evaluated with RGB-only inputs at test time, AMNet reaches 30.35 dB PSNR on DID versus 31.29 dB with all modalities present, a gap of only 0.94 dB (Table 8).
In zero-shot comparisons against foundation models DarkIR, FoundIR, and MobileIE on DID, AMNet reaches 25.07 dB PSNR versus the best baseline's 19.62 dB (Table 3).

8OoW6Nd7ZX.text: The empirical study is based on over 13,000 real-world rollouts and more than 500 trained models on bimanual and single-arm robots, using roughly 16,000 GPU-hours (Section 1).
Chunk-wise delta action prediction consistently and significantly outperforms step-wise delta prediction across all tasks, with an average performance gap of roughly 10% (Section 4.1).

Proposition 4.1 shows step-wise delta integration amplifies prediction error with bounds scaling as O(k) over the execution horizon, while chunk-wise delta maintains a constant O(1) error bound (Section 4.1, Proposition 4.1).

On real-world single-arm AgileX tasks with ACT-style models, delta action representations improve average success rate over absolute representations from 69.0% to 89.6% in end-effector space and from 77.3% to 88.0% in joint space (Table 1).

Delta-action superiority over absolute actions persists as demonstration count scales from 100 to 500, and joint-space control benefits disproportionately from increased data and compute (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

In cross-embodiment transfer-learning experiments with the π0 foundation model, task-space (end-effector) action representations show a pronounced generalization advantage over joint-space representations due to their embodiment-invariant nature (Section 4.3, Figure 6).

w7BZcUc0fJ.text: With DeepSeek-V3.1, Hermes@1 reaches 66.7% accuracy on AIME'25 versus 46.7% for zero-shot chain-of-thought, a 43% relative improvement (Table 1).
With DeepSeek-V3.1, Hermes@1 reaches 30.3% accuracy on HARDMath2 versus 22.7% for zero-shot chain-of-thought, a 33.5% relative improvement (Table 1).
Hermes achieves roughly 80% fewer total inference FLOPs than reward-based reasoning approaches on AIME'25 while matching or exceeding their accuracy (Figure 5).
Hermes uses 4 to 6 times fewer reasoning tokens than reward-based methods while keeping token budgets comparable to zero-shot chain-of-thought (Figure 3).
HERMES integrates a Translation Module, a Prover Module, a Memory Block, and Lean4 REPL feedback to provide iterative, formally-verified reasoning steps (Section 3).

o8y6CoJsWA.text: InfoFlow KV selects KV-recomputation targets using prompt-conditioned attention-norm importance scores, computed as the aggregated attention mass received from all prompt tokens (Equation 7).

Among four RoPE positioning configurations tested (GLOBAL, HL-HP, HL-TP, TL-TP), the GLOBAL positioning scheme consistently outperforms the others, indicating positional alignment between token selection and inference is essential (Table 1).
On the Qwen3-VL-8B vision-language model with k=4 recomputed tokens, InfoFlow KV reaches 65.68 on ChartQA versus 62.68 for CacheBlend, and 802 on OCRBench versus 785 for EPIC (Table 4).
InfoFlow KV achieves a 3.49x speedup over a single-GPU baseline at 32K sequence length and a 2.57x improvement over ring attention at 16K tokens (Section on efficiency gains).
A recomputation ratio of only 0.15 is sufficient to achieve strong downstream performance across the tested long-context benchmarks (Section on efficiency gains).

saZwSnt3r9.text: RN-D replaces the standard Gaussian actor with a discretized categorical actor using K=41 bins per action dimension, optimized with cross-entropy loss instead of squared-error regression (Section on architecture).

Proposition 4.1 shows the categorical policy's gradient variance is bounded by roughly mR^2(1-1/K), while the Gaussian policy's variance scales as the sum over dimensions of R^2/sigma_i^2, giving categorical actors a growing advantage as action dimensionality m increases (Proposition 4.1).

On Gym locomotion tasks (HalfCheetah, Ant, Hopper, Humanoid, Walker2d), RN-D improves sample efficiency by 1.3 to 1.9 times fewer environment interaction steps versus baselines (Section on Gym Locomotion results).

On the 10-task ManiSkill state-based suite, RN-D is the only method that reliably solves the StackCube task, outperforming MLP-C, RN-C, and MLP-D baselines in average success rate (Section on ManiSkill State-based results).

An ablation that swaps the categorical likelihood back to a Gaussian likelihood while keeping the discretized/regularized architecture eliminates most of the performance improvement, showing the cross-entropy categorical objective—not just discretization—drives the gains (Figure 7b).

Empirically, RN-D exhibits the lowest policy-gradient variance throughout training compared to a standard MLP Gaussian actor, whose variance increases steadily as its Gaussian sigma shrinks (Figure 4).

VzriJqD0h7.text: On GSM8K with 256-token generations, combining TSPD and CE without a KV cache achieves 34.2 tokens/sec (5.0x speedup) while maintaining 79.4% accuracy (Table 1).
Adding a KV cache to TSPD+CE raises throughput to 77.3 tokens/sec (11.2x speedup) with only a small accuracy drop to 78.8% on GSM8K (Table 1).
At 1024-token generations, TSPD+CE reaches a 58.3x speedup (64.1 tokens/sec) while still achieving 78.5% accuracy on GSM8K (Table 3).
The method generalizes across architectures, yielding a 7.6x speedup on Dream-7B (69.2 TPS, 75.0% accuracy) and a 5.1x speedup on LLaDA-MoE (21.2 TPS, 75.2% accuracy) (Table 2).
Ablations show TSPD alone gives 2.9x speedup (20.0 TPS) and CE alone gives 4.4x speedup (30.3 TPS), demonstrating each component contributes independently to the combined 5.0x-11.2x gains (Table 5).
The confidence-extrapolation predictor is a lightweight 2-layer LSTM with hidden size 16 (~2,000 parameters), adding only 0.30% (TSPD) and 0.13% (CE) per-step computational overhead (Section A.3).

oWvUK1mbYq.text: Outlier-Aware Scaling (OAS) and Microscaling Block Scaling (MBS) reduce the end-to-end accuracy gap between MXFP4 and NVFP4 from about 10% to below 1% on average (Section 1).
On Llama 3.1-8B, MXFP4 with MBS-H achieves 66.50% average accuracy versus NVFP4's 67.02%, a gap of only 0.52% (Table 1).
On Qwen3-8B, MXFP4 with MBS-H reaches 70.84% average accuracy versus NVFP4's 71.48%, a 0.64% gap, and on DeepSeek-R1's MMLU-Pro benchmark the gap is 0.63% (82.06% vs 82.69%) (Tables 2 and 3).

OAS applies to roughly 15% of quantization blocks and yields a 0.5 dB QSNR improvement with zero performance overhead, while MBS-Dynamic yields a further +1.6 dB QSNR improvement (Sections 4.2 and 4.3).
The proposed MXFP4 scheme incurs an average GEMM compute overhead of 6.2%, ranging from 0.17% at large matrix sizes (2048) to 14.84% at small sizes (512) (Table 4).

MXFP4 retains hardware-efficiency advantages over NVFP4, requiring about 12% less relative tensor-core area, though using the E4M3 scale format instead of E8M0 adds a 12.6% total tensor-core area overhead (Section 3.4).

5Q4hoiHhoU.text: UI2CodeN-9B-RL achieves state-of-the-art UI-to-code performance despite using only 9B parameters, outperforming larger closed models such as Claude-4-Sonnet on Design2Code (88.6 vs 81.2) and Flame-React-Eval (95.0 vs 76.3) (Table 1).
On the UI2Code-Real benchmark, UI2CodeN-9B-RL scores 76.5, outperforming both Claude-4-Sonnet (63.5) and GPT-5 (67.8), despite GPT-5 outperforming it on Design2Code and Web2Code (Table 1).
On UIPolish-Synthetic, the model reaches 94.0% versus Claude-4-Sonnet's 65.0%, and it matches Claude-4-Sonnet at 80.0% on UIPolish-Real, exceeding Gemini-2.5-Pro's 74.0% (Table 1).

Iterative visual-feedback test-time scaling improves accuracy on UI2Code-Real from 66.0% at N=1 to 74.0% at N=5, a roughly 12% absolute improvement, and from 92.0% to 97.0% on UI2Code-Synthetic between N=1 and N=3 (Table 2).

The model is trained via continual pre-training on approximately 20M vision-code samples and 10M UI-code pairs, followed by SFT on 80K samples and RL on 12K real plus 30K synthetic webpages (Section 3.2).

83f0m2VJZm.text: The proposed projected-gradient-ascent method reaches a comparable Aesthetic Score (7.120) to the SOTA regularization baseline MPGR (7.133) using only 60 iterations versus MPGR's 200, corresponding to roughly 30% of MPGR's wall-clock time (69.7s vs 235.5s) (Table 1).

Running the proposed method for the same 200 iterations as MPGR achieves a substantially higher Aesthetic Score of 8.908 in nearly the same wall-clock time (232.2s vs 235.5s), while held-out PickScore remains stable at 0.220 across methods, indicating no reward hacking (Table 1, Figure 2).

Reward hacking is prevented by enforcing hard white-Gaussian-noise constraints via projected gradient ascent onto a feasible spectral-domain set, rather than using soft regularization penalties (Section 3, Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).

The closed-form spectral projection operator runs in O(N log N) time, matching the complexity of standard FFT or sorting algorithms, and adds only about 0.04% of total runtime overhead in FLUX experiments (Section 4.3).

The bijective mapping to the spectral domain provably preserves Gaussianity (Proposition 4.1), and the projection achieves a minimum cosine similarity of 0.988 across 10^6 random Gaussian samples (Section 4.1, Section 4.3).
