ReCCYnyfXa.text: The paper introduces reach-avoid probability certificates via an enhanced Bellman operator B^π, proven in Lemma 4.4 to be a gamma-contraction with a unique bounded fixed point V^π_{g,h}, and Theorem 4.5 shows that V^π_{g,h}(x) < 0 implies the reach-avoid probability P_π(RA_x) is at least -1/M · V^π_{g,h}(x) (Section 4.2, Lemma 4.4, Theorem 4.5).
Theorem B.3 establishes that the proposed RAPCPO policy updates converge almost surely to locally optimal policies under the reach-avoid constraints (Section 5.2, Theorem B.3, Algorithm 1).
On deterministic MuJoCo-based benchmarks, RAPCPO achieves higher reach rates than the RC-PPO baseline: 78.49% vs 62.29% on PointGoal and 88.67% vs 73.98% on FixedWing (Table 1, Figure 2).

The enhanced Bellman formulation with adaptive compensation factor substantially outperforms a fixed-gamma variant on stochastic benchmarks, raising the metric from 0.4387 to 0.7986 on Safety HalfCheetah and from 0.3218 to 0.9434 on Safety Hopper (Table 2, Figure 5).

Ablation studies confirm the compensation factor phi^π_γ is critical to performance, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis on Safety Hopper shows stable behavior for p in the range [0.1, 0.7] (Figure 6, Figure 7).

dqXu56QnBi.text: AugServe achieves on average 4.7x higher effective throughput than vLLM and 3.3x higher than InferCept across evaluated settings (Section 5.2).
On H800 GPUs with the Merge dataset, AugServe reaches up to 5.9x the effective throughput of vLLM and 3.4x that of InferCept (Section 5.2).
At an arrival rate of 5.0 req/s on ToolBench with H800 GPUs, AugServe sustains 2.35 req/s effective throughput versus 0.25 req/s for vLLM and 0.21 req/s for InferCept (Section 5.2).
AugServe reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by up to 96.3% relative to vLLM and 95.0% relative to InferCept (Section 5.2).

The two-stage scheduler first computes prediction-based scheduling values from predicted output length, API duration, and context policy, then applies a runtime correction using actual API return lengths, using cost equations for prefill, decode, API invocation, and swap overhead (Eq. 9-12, Section 4.3).

An ablation shows dynamic token batching alone raises throughput from 0.22 to 0.35 req/s at a 2.0 req/s arrival rate on top of vLLM, with the two-stage scheduling component providing further throughput and latency gains (Section 5.4, Figure 10).

oaMuJPfDUS.text: EDMolGPT generates 3D molecules conditioned on low-resolution electron density point clouds representing protein pockets (Section 3).

On the CalED benchmark, EDMolGPT achieves 41% bioactive molecule recovery (ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity > 0.5), the highest among compared methods, versus 33% for Lingo3DMol, 17% for MolCRAFT, 8% for Pocket2Mol, and 3% for TargetDiff and ED2Mol (Table 1).
EDMolGPT attains a best mean min-in-place Glide docking score of -6.92 kcal/mol on CalED, outperforming all baseline methods on this metric (Table 1).

Evaluation spans 101 biological targets from the DUD-E dataset (after excluding obsolete PDB entry 2H7L), with 92 of these structures further used for evaluation against experimental cryo-EM/X-ray electron density (ExpED) rather than calculated density (Section 4, Table 3).
On the ExpED evaluation using real experimental density maps, EDMolGPT achieves a 20% recovery rate and -5.4 min-in-place Glide score, with QED of 0.50 and SAS of 3.69 (Table 3).
An ablation over sampling temperature and density resolution (d_min) shows that using N_p=199 density points yields consistently strong performance regardless of diffraction resolution (Table 4).

1JwSFRvC4E.text: DC-LA is proven in Theorem 8 to satisfy a q-Wasserstein convergence bound of the form W_q(p_{X_{k+1}}, pi) <= A_lambda*rho_lambda^{k*gamma} + B_lambda*gamma^{1/2q} + C_lambda^{1/q}, decomposing discretization, smoothing, and algorithmic error terms, for all natural numbers q (Theorem 8).
Convergence is established under a distant dissipativity assumption on the potential V (Assumption 2), which requires only quadratic growth away from the origin rather than global convexity.

DC-LA extends prior work (Renaud et al., 2025a) by handling non-weakly-convex difference-of-convex regularizers, such as the l1-l2 penalty, for which no previous convergence guarantee existed, while removing the earlier requirement of a convex modulus at infinity.

The algorithm applies separate Moreau envelope smoothing to the convex components r1 and r2 of the composite potential V = f + r1 - r2, yielding an update rule using proximal and gradient operators of the smoothed components.

Section 5.2 applies DC-LA to 512x512 Computed Tomography reconstruction using a difference-of-ICNN prior, reporting competitive SSIM/PSNR versus optimization-based MAP methods along with posterior-variance-based uncertainty quantification (Section 5.2).

Cez36tiWXz.text: Theorem 1 gives the first generalization bound for imbalanced domain generalization (IDG), decomposing target risk into source risk, a decision-margin term, prior discrepancy, and posterior discrepancy, showing posterior discrepancy and margin are pivotal alongside domain shift (Theorem 1).

The Negative-Dominant Contrastive Loss (Eq. 1) reformulates InfoNCE to emphasize negative samples via an amplification factor that strengthens minority-class signal when surrounded by majority-class negatives (Eq. 1).

A Prediction-Central Alignment term (Eq. 3) aligns class prototypes across domains to enforce posterior consistency, motivated directly by the posterior-discrepancy term in Theorem 1 (Eq. 3, Theorem 1).
Under the GINIDG setting, NDCL achieves 78.0% average accuracy on VLCS and 85.7% on PACS, outperforming IDG-specific baselines BoDA, GINIDG, and SAMALTDG by about 1.5 percentage points (Table 1).
Under the TotalHeavyTail setting, NDCL reaches 75.6% on VLCS, 76.4% on PACS, and 49.0% on OfficeHome, with especially large gains on few-shot classes (61.0%, 79.2%, 30.5% respectively) (Table 2).
An ablation removing the negative-dominant contrastive loss causes a significant accuracy drop, confirming its role in enforcing class-boundary separation (Table 4).

zYeCwBTtVt.text: FGR combines a DCT-based low-pass filter that suppresses high-frequency spurious visual patterns with a gradient-rectification step that projects the main training gradient onto the hyperplane orthogonal to the in-distribution calibration gradient whenever the two conflict.
On CIFAR-10-C, FGR achieves 7.07% ECE, outperforming MaxEnt (11.21% ECE) and BSCE-GRA (13.29% ECE) across corruption shifts.
On CIFAR-100-C, FGR achieves 9.94% ECE compared to 16.73% ECE for MaxEnt.

On the real-world WILDS Camelyon17 shift, FGR attains 2.36% ECE and 5.71% class-wise ECE (CECE), superior to all compared baselines including Cross-Entropy, Label Smoothing, FLSD-53, Dual Focal Loss, MaxEnt, and BSCE-GRA.

FGR is evaluated across synthetic corruption benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100-C and Tiny-ImageNet-C with 15 corruption types at 5 severity levels) and real-world distribution shifts from the WILDS benchmark (Camelyon17, iWildCam, FMoW).
Combining FGR with post-hoc temperature scaling yields further improved calibration performance beyond FGR alone, demonstrating compatibility with post-hoc calibration methods.

R8wiI3AnfI.text: The Multi Node Prediction (MNP) objective predicts field values for a center node and its full 1-hop neighborhood jointly via a single-layer transformer over 'star sequences', combined with the main node-wise loss as L = L_main + 0.2*L_MNP (Section on Multi Node Prediction).

Theorem B.2 proves that patch reconstruction accuracy from MNP controls a discrete gradient (flux) error, providing a Sobolev-regularization justification for enforcing spatial derivative consistency (Theorem B.2).

MNP is evaluated on three architectures — MeshGraphNet, Transolver, and a Transformer with optional long-distance 'jumper' edges — each using an Encode-Process-Decode structure (Section on Architectures).

Evaluation uses four physics datasets: Cylinder (2D fluid, COMSOL, 2000 nodes), DeformingPlate (solid mechanics, COMSOL, 1000 nodes), and coarse (20,000-node) and fine (250,000-node) 3D Aneurysm hemodynamics meshes solved with CimLib (Table of datasets).
MNP yields 20-30% reductions in 1-step RMSE across all three architectures and all datasets, with error accumulation over long rollouts substantially reduced relative to baselines (Figure 2).

Improvements from MNP scale with model size, tested up to 51M parameters, and remain consistent across 5-30 training epochs, at the cost of roughly a 10% increase in training and inference time (Figure 3, Figure 4).

7NA81PFi77.text: The paper studies linear contextual bandits where both contexts and rewards depend on the hidden state of an underlying Markov chain, introducing a reward model with direct dependence on latent states rather than only on posterior belief states (Section 2, Assumption 2.1).
For the simplified reward model that generalizes Nelson et al. (2022) and depends only on beliefs, the paper establishes a high-probability regret bound of Õ(T^{3/4}) (Section on simplified model).

For the novel complex reward model with direct dependence on hidden states, which does not reduce to standard linear contextual bandits, the paper proves a high-probability regret bound of Õ(T^{7/8}), using a staged exploration strategy that periodically updates parameter estimates (Section 5, Assumption 5.1).

The staged estimation approach relies on a belief-estimation subroutine (Assumption 4.1) that guarantees Õ(T^{1/2}) cumulative error on estimated beliefs, compatible with spectral HMM estimation methods that require an alignment step to resolve state-labeling permutation ambiguity (Assumption 4.1, p. 37).

Unlike the Nelson et al. (2022) analysis, the paper's bounds hold with high probability rather than in expectation, are model-free (independent of reward gaps), and do not require non-degeneracy coverage assumptions on the belief distribution (Section on comparison to Nelson et al. 2022).

HdsEUNo4C4.text: SmartFed introduces Mixture of Rank-Wise Experts (MoRE), which decomposes each LoRA module's low-rank update into rank-one projection terms B[:,i]A[i,:], treating each paired column/row of A and B as an individually activatable expert selected by a learned, input-conditioned router (Section on MoRE).

SmartFed additionally uses Elastic Expert Quota Allocation (EEQA) to adaptively distribute the number of active rank-wise experts across parameter matrices according to their measured contribution to fine-tuning performance (Section on EEQA).
On LLaMA2-7B, SmartFed outperforms the LoRA-Flow baseline on MGSM (35.48 vs 33.75), DoIT (52.59 vs 49.95), and GSM-Hard (64.19 vs 59.06), for an average gain of 10.21% (Table 2).

Ablations show MoRE and EEQA contribute 4.23% and 3.45% to overall performance respectively, and MoRE closes a 5.01% performance gap versus the coarser module-level fusion of MoLE on combined Chinese-and-Math tasks (Ablation study).

SmartFed achieves 3.95x faster convergence, 31.47x lower communication overhead, and 3.61x reduced energy consumption compared to baselines, while MoRE avoids MoLE's 1.84x latency increase when scaling to 8 modules (Efficiency results section).
SmartFed using only 10% of the fine-tuning data still surpasses baselines trained on 100% of the data, by an 8.02% performance margin (Data efficiency results).

9AIG4VatqI.text: A 1.5B-parameter Qwen2.5 SLM's top-8 next-token candidates capture a 32B-parameter LLM's preferred token with a 95% hit rate, even in cases where that token is not the SLM's own top-1 prediction (Local Sufficiency finding).

S2T-Local internalizes token re-ranking into the SLM itself using the Zero-overhead Inference-time Prediction (ZIP) mechanism, which repurposes reserved vocabulary logits to encode preference scores without disrupting standard token distributions (Section on ZIP/S2T-Local).
S2T-Local improves average accuracy over greedy decoding by 24.1% across benchmarks while matching the performance of 8-path self-consistency using only a single decoding pass (Table 1).
On the 1.5B model, S2T-Local raises accuracy from 72.1% to 95.6% on GSM8K, from 54.4% to 81.1% on MATH500, and from 42.7% to 72.6% on HumanEval relative to SLM-only greedy decoding (Table 1).
S2T-Local reduces latency by 75% compared to collaborative LLM-SLM decoding methods that require calling the large model at inference time (Efficiency results).

nWI6lV7BvA.text: Structured Diffusion Bridges (SDB) augment Latent Denoising Diffusion Bridge Models with three structural constraints: marginal matching via winner-takes-all denoising score matching, endpoint-level cycle consistency (L_cycle^end), and trajectory-level cycle consistency (L_cycle^traj) that constrains intermediate diffusion states (Section on constraints).

On a synthetic content-style benchmark with zero paired data (rho=0), marginal matching alone attains 0.162 content accuracy, whereas adding trajectory-level cycle consistency raises content accuracy to 0.868 and improves cycle MSE from 0.972 to 0.616 (Synthetic benchmark results).

On FFHQ-to-CelebA-HQ super-resolution, SDB achieves 25.9 PSNR at full pairing (rho=1.0), slightly exceeding LDDBM's 25.6 PSNR, maintains 25.2 PSNR at 50% pairing (rho=0.5), and still reaches 19.0±0.6 PSNR with zero paired data (rho=0) (Super-resolution results table).

On the ShapeNet multi-view-to-3D task, SDB attains 0.677 IoU at full pairing, close to the task-specific LRGT+ baseline's 0.704 IoU, and maintains 0.638 IoU at 50% pairing while the LDDBM baseline degrades substantially at that pairing level (ShapeNet results table).

SDB remains trainable in the fully unpaired regime (rho=0) on tasks where comparison baselines cannot be trained at all, demonstrating graceful degradation as the fraction of paired data decreases (Section on unpaired regime).

oWdQIgCvmq.text: Proposition 2 expresses the RL-optimal backward transition kernel as the reference model's transition reweighted by an energy term E[exp(r(y,x0)/λ)], enabling training-free sampling from the optimal policy (Section on Core Innovation / Proposition 2).

Proposition 3 gives a total-variation convergence bound of O(I/√M + Iε) for the Monte Carlo energy estimate, where I is the number of guidance steps and M the number of sampled candidates (Proposition 3).
Algorithm 1 samples M candidates from the reference model, computes normalized energy weights, and performs multinomial resampling across I guidance steps to realize ETS (Algorithm 1).
On Qwen3-8B, ETS improves average accuracy across MATH500, GSM8K, GPQA, and HumanEval from 65.98% (GRPO) to 69.34% (Table 1).
On MATH500 specifically, ETS reaches 72.4% versus 69.2% for the GRPO-trained baseline on Qwen3-8B (Table 1).

ETS acceleration variants for autoregressive models (ARMs) use lightweight proposal models with importance sampling, while for diffusion language models (DLMs) ETS integrates Fast-dLLM with KV caching and parallel decoding to control latency (Section on Acceleration Methods).

bVXx0K0j4c.text: ZwZ-8B trained with Region-to-Image (R2I) Distillation achieves 58.11% on ZoomBench, up from a 37.87% baseline without R2I distillation (Key Results).
ZwZ-8B narrows the 'zooming gap' (global-view vs. regional-view performance difference) to 15.26%, compared to 22-25% gaps reported for baseline models (Dual-View Evaluation).
R2I distillation trains on only 74K synthetic examples yet outperforms models trained on the 500K-sample Oasis dataset and on human-curated data from DeepEyes and Thyme-RL (Data Efficiency).

R2I's zoom-in synthesis stage has teacher models generate VQA pairs on micro-crops to minimize hallucination, while the zoom-out distillation stage supervises the student on full images via bounding-box overlays so it can answer without iterative tool calls at inference (Core Method).

ZoomBench, introduced in this work, contains 845 VQA samples spanning six dimensions: fine-grained counting, OCR, color attributes, structural attributes, material attributes, and object identification (Benchmark Coverage).
ZwZ-8B outperforms tool-based agentic baselines while running about 10x faster at inference, and is competitive with much larger models such as Qwen3-VL-235B and Kimi-K2.5 (Key Results).

uQiLoAF0bM.text: SB-ECC achieves the best bit-error rate in 39 of 42 code/SNR configurations spanning BCH, Polar, LDPC, MacKay, and CCSDS codes, with an average SNR gain of 0.17 dB and a maximum gain of 0.46 dB over the strongest baselines (Experimental Results).
Replacing the Euler ODE solver with DPM-Solver reduces end-to-end decoding time by up to 12.82% while preserving bit-error-rate performance (Experimental Results / DPM-Solver comparison).

SB-ECC is trained without SNR conditioning via a linear noise schedule and uniform discretization in noise-level space, eliminating the need for channel state information at inference (Time-Unconditional Design).

Ablations show that a magnitude-only input variant (discarding sign information) fails completely, with the network collapsing to near-zero noise predictions, whereas the full signed-observation input succeeds (Signed Input Advantage / Ablation).
The decoder uses a CrossMPT transformer backbone with variable-node and check-node tokens, trained with the noise-prediction loss ℒ_ε = E[||ε̂_θ(y, s(y)) − ε||²] (Architecture & Training).

Early stopping of the iterative ODE-based decoder typically recovers valid codewords within 1-4 iterations, and the method remains robust under Rayleigh fading despite being trained only on AWGN (Practical Advantages).

ilEooI8fK1.text: FluidGym is presented as the first standalone, fully differentiable benchmark suite for reinforcement learning in active flow control, built entirely in PyTorch on a GPU-accelerated PICT solver with no external CFD software dependency (Overview).

FluidGym includes 13 environments across four canonical flow scenarios—flow past a cylinder, Rayleigh-Bénard convection, airfoil flows, and turbulent channel flow—each spanning three difficulty levels of increasing turbulence complexity (Environments).
The benchmark supports three interaction modes: single-agent RL (SARL), multi-agent RL (MARL), and gradient-based control exploiting full end-to-end differentiability (Three Interaction Modes).

Across PPO and SAC baselines evaluated on all environments, SAC reliably outperforms PPO at every difficulty level, though multi-agent variants show more comparable PPO/SAC performance due to improved sample efficiency from parallel updates (Experimental Results / Algorithm Performance).

A differentiable MPC controller using FluidGym's gradient-based mode achieves approximately 8% drag reduction on cylinder flow control, validating reward gradients as an effective control signal (Differentiable Control).

2D-to-3D policy transfer for cylinder flow control is shown to be robust, with transferred policies sometimes exceeding the performance of policies trained directly in 3D (Transfer Learning Findings).

GdiPMYeFoG.text: Theorem 3.8 gives the closed-form Local-Equivariant MMSE (LE-MMSE) estimator as a pixel-wise weighted sum over training patches, x̂_loc(y)[n'] = Σ_x Σ_n x[n]·w_{n',n}(x|y), with weights proportional to a Gaussian similarity N(Q_{n'}y; Q_n A x, σ² Q_n Q_n^T) between local patches (Theorem 3.8).

The paper defines three hierarchical MMSE variants—MMSE (unconstrained), E-MMSE (translation-equivariant), and LE-MMSE (equivariant plus local)—showing LE-MMSE generalizes via patch recombination rather than memorizing the training set (Section 3, hierarchical MMSE variants).

Figure 5 shows strong agreement (PSNR ≳25 dB) between a trained UNet2D and the analytical LE-MMSE formula across denoising, inpainting, and deconvolution tasks on FFHQ, CIFAR-10, and FashionMNIST at 32x32 and 64x64 resolution (Figure 5).

For inpainting, a physics-aware pre-inverse operator B=A⁺ reduces noise while preserving signal, whereas for deconvolution the pseudo-inverse can amplify noise enough that a regularized inverse is favored instead, a trade-off formalized via the terms Q_n^+ Δ_{n',n} and Tr(Cov_{n',n}) (Physics-Aware vs. Physics-Agnostic Trade-offs).

Network-theory alignment with LE-MMSE degrades in low-density regions of the measurement distribution p(y), particularly at low noise levels when test samples fall outside high-probability training neighborhoods, explaining part of the train-test generalization gap (Measurement Density Effect).

The trained network compresses roughly 3.1x10^7 training pixels into about 4x10^6 parameters while performing inference in about 4ms, roughly 175x faster than direct evaluation of the analytical LE-MMSE formula (~0.7s) (Computational Implications).

uOSa4bbPDj.text: LOCK-GP, a sequence-only Gaussian process using only the BLOSUM50 substitution matrix (~210 parameters), achieves Pearson R of 0.914 in the cross-validation regime with N=1536 training points, outperforming Kermut-GP (0.888) and Ridge-ESM2 (0.877) despite these baselines relying on foundation model embeddings (Section 5.3).
In the extrapolation regime (N=512), LOCK-GP achieves a mean absolute error about 22% lower than the next-best model (Section 5.3).

CLOCK-GP, the structure-conditioned kernel built from position-specific correlation matrices derived from foundation model embeddings (Eq. 14), reaches a Spearman correlation of 0.755 at N=50 landscape-local training points in the multi-task thermostability setting, versus 0.498 for LOCK-GP (Section 5.4).
CLOCK-GP trained on only 10 thermostability landscapes outperforms a Global CLOCK-GP trained on all 280 landscapes, demonstrating efficient transfer from structure embeddings (Section 5.4).

Ablation experiments show that the choice of substitution matrix has weak impact on performance, while removal of the BLOSUM-derived correlation kernel component causes the largest degradation, identified as the single most critical ingredient of LOCK (Section 5.2).
LOCK-GP is reported to be 2-140x faster in training and inference than baselines such as MLP-ESM2-LastLayer and Kermut-GP, across a benchmark of 30+ predictors on 21 datasets (Section 5.3).

deuc2n0fGN.text: MAGIC formulates LLM safety alignment as an asymmetric sequential attacker-defender game and proves in Theorem 3.2 that at Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium the defender's responses are safe for any attack prompt, giving pointwise rather than expectation-based safety guarantees (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).
On Qwen2.5-7B, MAGIC reduces Attack Success Rate on WildGuardTest from 36.5% to 2.3% while maintaining 96.8% benign compliance on the XSTest adversarial-benign subset (Experimental Results section).

MAGIC's co-evolution phase alternates Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) updates between a defender maximizing a three-component safety reward (format, harmfulness via Qwen3Guard, and refusal reward) and an attacker maximizing attack success against a frozen defender (Methodology, Phase 2).

In multi-turn evaluation using X-Teaming, MAGIC-trained defenders show a 10.1% improvement in attack success rate resistance along with a 15.2% reduction in jailbreak rate compared to baselines (Evaluation section).

MAGIC generalizes robustness to diverse unseen attack methods (GCG, PAIR, TAP, AutoDAN) evaluated on HarmBench, and the RL-trained attacker evolves novel combinatorial jailbreak strategies (e.g., combining role-play and translation) not present in its SFT initialization data (Evaluation, Notable Finding).

mLZlTzepbr.text: The proposed dynamic regression-adjusted estimator, which integrates estimated covariate transition kernels forward through time (Eq. 7-9), is proven to be asymptotically normal (Theorem 4) and to attain the semiparametric efficiency bound for longitudinal treatment effect estimation (Theorem 5), with a variance-reduction result given in Corollary 6 (Section 4).

The estimator satisfies a Neyman-orthogonal moment condition, giving first-order robustness to nuisance function estimation errors and enabling valid inference when nuisance functions are estimated via cross-fitted machine learning models (Section 4.3).

On synthetic data with Lorenz-96 covariate dynamics (n in {500, 1000, 2000}, T=7, d=10), the RF-MLP variant of the dynamic adjustment estimator achieves the largest RMSE reduction among tested combinations (OLS-VAR, OLS-MLP, RF-VAR, RF-MLP), with the reduction increasing with sample size (Section 6.1).

On a real A/B test from a Japanese streaming platform (n=6,802 users over a 10-day period) comparing content-based versus interaction-based recommendations, the dynamic covariate-transition adjustment reduces standard errors by approximately 0.4% to 20.4% across the experimental period relative to the empirical estimator (Section 6.2).
Assumption 6 requires the cross-fitted nuisance estimators for the conditional mean and transition kernel to jointly satisfy a combined convergence rate of o_p(n^{-1/4}) (Section 4, Assumption 6).

rR97qOfb7W.text: ICGNN computes an Influence Contradiction Score (ICS) combining structure-level influence from personalized PageRank graph diffusion and attribute-level influence from a KNN affinity graph over node representations, then fits a Gaussian Mixture Model via EM on ICS values to assign per-node clean-label confidence (Section on Core Methodology / Table 1 setup).

Under 20% uniform label noise, ICGNN achieves 87.4% accuracy on Coauthor CS versus 86.2% for DND-NET, and 80.9% on Cora versus 76.8% for CGNN, with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests confirming statistical significance at the 0.1 level in most comparisons (Table 1).
Under 20% pair (asymmetric) label noise, ICGNN reaches 85.9% accuracy on Coauthor CS and 80.6% on Pubmed, outperforming baselines NRGNN, RTGNN, CGNN, and DND-NET (Table 1).

Ablation results show removing the noise-cleaning (soft label correction) component causes the largest accuracy drop (~2.2%), removing structure-level ICS causes a ~1.5% drop, and removing attribute-level ICS causes a ~1% drop, while replacing the graph diffusion matrix with a simple adjacency matrix substantially degrades performance (Ablation Studies section).

ICGNN maintains its overall time complexity of O(EN + L^3 + CN), scaling linearly with sample size, and remains robust as noise rates increase up to 40% and as label rates shrink to 0.5%-2% (Complexity and Robustness Testing sections).

SorLoUARMp.text: Implicit Preference Alignment (IPA) trains on only 93 curated high-quality self-generated samples out of 6,000 candidates, motivated by the finding that only 7.5% of candidates could form valid DPO preference pairs due to frame-wise inconsistencies in hand motion (Data Efficiency section).

IPA's training objective (Eq. 11), L = -log sigma(beta * Delta(p_ref, p_theta)), maximizes likelihood of self-generated high-quality samples subject to a KL-divergence constraint against the reference policy, avoiding the need for paired preference data required by standard DPO (Eq. 11).

On the TikTok benchmark, IPA achieves FID-VID of 5.9 and FVD of 255, improving over Wan-Animate's 8.6 and 316 respectively, with SSIM of 0.841 and PSNR of 23.8 versus Wan-Animate's 0.799 and 20.5 (Table 1).

Hand-Aware Local Optimization (HALO), which applies a spatial weighting matrix W to prioritize hand regions during alignment, improves hand-specific metrics to SSIM-Hand of 0.606 and PSNR-Hand of 18.9, outperforming all baselines, with additional ablation gains shown when HALO is added on top of IPA (Table 3, Table 4).
Human evaluation shows IPA-generated animations are preferred on hand quality in 91.7% of comparisons against MimicMotion, 87.3% against VACE, and 83.0% against Wan-Animate (Table 10).

An ablation over the hand-enhancement coefficient lambda identifies lambda=10 as optimal (Table 5), and an ablation over the KL-regularization strength beta identifies beta=600 as balancing learning against regularization (Figure 4).

UMT9x3LV9Q.text: CoD-Lite's lightweight convolutional diffusion codec reaches 60 FPS encoding and 42 FPS decoding at 1080p resolution (Section 5).
CoD-Lite reduces bitrate by 85% relative to MS-ILLM at comparable FID while running in real time (Section 6).

Replacing the diffusion transformer with a convolutional block in the one-step (DMD-distilled) setting improves FID from 37.5 to 36.4 and cuts per-image decoding time from 331.2ms to 23.6ms (Table 1).

The full codec's encoder, decoder, and diffusion CNN modules have 28.1M, 10.9M, and 37.9M parameters respectively, with per-module runtimes of 15.5ms, 2.1ms, and 14.5ms at 1024x1920 resolution (Table 3).
CoD-Lite achieves roughly 14x faster decoding than StableCodec (Section 6).
Rate-distortion curves on the Kodak and CLIC datasets show CoD-Lite matching or beating baseline codecs' quality at lower bitrate while incurring far lower computational complexity (Figure 5).

karVCJgZDo.text: NanoSpec dynamically builds a minimalist, context-aware active vocabulary that averages under 3,000 tokens (peak 3,072), more than 40x smaller than the 128k full vocabulary and well below the 27k-32k vocabularies used by FR-Spec and DynaSpec (Table 1).

On Llama-3.1-8B with an EAGLE-2 draft backbone, NanoSpec reaches 392.7 tokens/s versus 336.9 tokens/s for full EAGLE-2, a 2.25x speedup over autoregressive decoding compared to EAGLE-2's 1.93x (Table 2).
NanoSpec cuts LM-head latency by 9.8x, from 2.330ms to 0.237ms per step, driving an average 51.6% reduction in draft inference time versus EAGLE-2 (Section 4).
With an EAGLE-3 backbone, NanoSpec improves throughput from 362.2 tokens/s to 430.0 tokens/s, a 1.19x speedup (Table 3).
Across 7 evaluation tasks, NanoSpec delivers an end-to-end speedup of 1.17-1.29x over EAGLE-2 and 1.19-1.28x over EAGLE-3 while maintaining competitive acceptance length (Section 4, Evaluation).

melQSx2bVT.text: SGMD reduces fake-score network updates per training iteration from 5 to 1 relative to Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD2), yielding roughly a 3x training speedup (Section 4).
On 4-step distillation of Wan2.1-T2V-14B, SGMD raises the optical-flow motion metric from 4.51 (DMD2) to 9.29 and the dynamic-degree score from 80.56 to 93.06 (Section 4, Table 1).
SGMD attains an FVD of 100.3, the best among evaluated few-step distilled video diffusion models, while preserving temporal consistency (Table 1).

In human evaluation, raters prefer SGMD's motion quality 71% of the time and overall output 65% of the time versus DMD2, with visual quality and text alignment judged comparable in 90% and 74% of ties respectively (Table 3).

SGMD optimizes the fake score directly toward the teacher using a teacher stop-gradient Fisher term as a stable distribution-matching objective, rather than the alternating fake-score updates used by DMD-style methods (Section 3).

aPPEyZpKkp.text: DistFlow's fully distributed, multi-controller RL architecture demonstrates near-linear scalability up to 512 GPUs, with the 32B model retaining 80.5% of its throughput when scaling from 64 to 512 GPUs (Section 7).
DistFlow achieves up to 2.62x speedup over the baseline RL framework on GRPO and 1.09x-1.64x speedup on PPO across model scales (Section 7).

Under multi-modal, memory-constrained settings, DistFlow delivers up to 7x end-to-end throughput improvement over the baseline, which suffers out-of-memory failures at equivalent GPU scales (Section 7).
For long-context (64K token) training, DistFlow yields a 2.03x throughput improvement for the 7B model over the baseline (Section 7).

DistFlow's Data Coordinator decouples data transmission from control dispatch to eliminate single-controller bottlenecks and mitigate straggler effects, as illustrated by the single-controller bottleneck diagram (Figure 2) and the DistFlow architecture overview (Figure 3).

wSV1sGTCN0.text: Geometric Embedding Hashing (GEH) recovers vector links between independently trained encoder pairs using only a small seed set of paired anchors, reaching F1 scores of 79.8% (FiQA, Qwen-KaLM), 80.7% (ArguAna, GTE-Mistral), and 82.2% (Mistral-OpenAI) at overlap alpha=0.3 with 15 seeds, outperforming eight baselines including Linear, CCA, MLP, RCSLS, Procrustes, UGW, and AO (Table 1).
On the 5.4M-item FEVER corpus, GEH scales to achieve 93.8% precision and 68.9% recall in 3328 seconds, versus only 5.22% precision for the best baseline (CCA) (Table 2).

On SciFact with Mistral-OpenAI embeddings, GEH's performance (85.8% F1 at alpha=0.30, 15 seeds) remains stable as seed count varies from 15 to 30 and as overlap ratio varies from 0.15 to 0.30 (Table 3).
When seed anchors are drawn from an out-of-domain reference dataset rather than the target corpus, GEH still maintains 77-87% precision and 80-97% recall (Figure 5).

Theorem 1 shows that for two locally optimal contrastive encoders, pairwise distances satisfy ‖f₁(x)−f₁(y)‖ = κ·‖f₂(x)−f₂(y)‖ + O(d²) with κ=√(λ₁/λ₂), i.e. short-range distances stay correlated up to a scale factor while long-range distances decorrelate (Theorem 1, Figure 1).

MqWVrGh0vH.text: HSIR's VeriExit sampling strategy recycles failed self-improvement rollouts by truncating at the last correct intermediate reasoning step and resampling from that point, rather than discarding the failed attempt outright (Section on VeriExit Sampling Strategy).

The Intrinsic Diversity (InDiv) score quantifies reasoning diversity directly from a model's hidden-layer representations via eigenvalue analysis over attention-weighted hidden states, without requiring an external judge model (Section on Intrinsic Diversity Score).
HSIR yields up to +10.9% average accuracy gains on complex reasoning tasks when evaluated across Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Phi, Mistral, and LLaMA3 model families (Key Performance Results).
HSIR reduces inference overhead by up to 42.4% via a reduction in output token count, improving reasoning efficiency alongside accuracy gains (Key Performance Results).

HSIR is integrated with and evaluated under three distinct training paradigms: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and an enhanced GRPO variant (H-GRPO) (Training Paradigm Integration section).

HSIR maintains consistent out-of-distribution generalization improvements across successive self-improvement training iterations, evaluated on medical, mathematical, scientific, and commonsense reasoning tasks (Key Performance Results).

ykTMNA6Mbh.text: DAVE decomposes ViT layer derivatives into a direct input-output transformation term and an operator-variation term, retaining only the former to prevent amplification of unstable gradient components (Section on Effective Transformation Extraction).

DAVE applies Reynolds-inspired equivariant filtering, averaging over local spatial transformations, to suppress patch-embedding grid artifacts in the resulting attribution maps (Section on Equivariant Filtering).

On the Grid Pointing Game (ImageNet-1k), DAVE improves localization over baselines by +11.92 percentage points on DeiT-III-B/16 (reaching 65.76%), +1.79 pp on ViT-B/16 (60.19%), and +1.35 pp on DINO-B/16 (51.33%) (Localization Performance / GridPG results).
On the Energy Pointing Game (ImageNet-1k), DAVE achieves 83.38% on DINO-B/16 (+1.12 pp over baselines) and 82.43% on DeiT-III-B/16 (Localization Performance / EnergyPG results).

DAVE is compared against IntGrad, SmoothGrad, AttnLRP, and LeGrad on pixel-deletion faithfulness curves, where DAVE produces the flattest curves indicating the most stable attributions (Faithfulness Evaluation section).

DAVE's computational complexity scales linearly with the number of neighborhood samples, converging with approximately 50 samples without degrading attribution quality (Computational Complexity section).

mcaZVJ7Apl.text: PSG-Nav achieves Success Rates of 66.1% on HM3D (32.1% SPL), 44.8% on MP3D (17.9% SPL), and 67.9% on HSSD (33.4% SPL) for open-vocabulary object navigation (Benchmark Performance / Table of results).
A zero-shot variant of PSG-Nav without the Evidential Experience Calibrator (w/o EEC) still achieves 63.5% SR on HM3D, 43.3% on MP3D, and 66.1% on HSSD (Benchmark Performance section).

PSG-Nav's 3D Probabilistic Scene Graph (3D-PSG) maintains full categorical distributions over objects, groups, and rooms rather than committing to fixed semantic labels, explicitly modeling perception uncertainty (3D Probabilistic Scene Graph component description).

The Multiverse Decision framework uses Monte Carlo sampling to instantiate a set of divergent possible worlds from the 3D-PSG, then evaluates candidate navigation landmarks across these sampled world configurations (Multiverse Decision Framework component description).
PSG-Nav improves over the prior state-of-the-art method SG-Nav by +12.1 percentage points in Success Rate on HM3D (Performance Gains section).

Ablation studies show all three components—3D-PSG, Multiverse Decision, and the Evidential Experience Calibrator (EEC)—contribute meaningfully to overall navigation performance, with EEC's success/failure memory banks specifically reducing false-positive goal terminations (Ablation studies / EEC component description).

uNWexq8gQB.text: OmniShow is built on the 12B-parameter Waver 1.0 video generation backbone and adds only approximately 0.3B additional parameters for its audio conditioning modules (Model Architecture section).

OmniShow's Gated Local-Context Attention module achieves audio-visual synchronization via audio context packing, masked attention, and adaptive gating vectors for stable training (Gated Local-Context Attention component description).

The Decoupled-Then-Joint Training strategy first trains on heterogeneous sub-task datasets (R2V, A2V, RA2V) separately, merges the resulting models, and then performs joint fine-tuning on the full RAP2V multimodal data (Decoupled-Then-Joint Training section).

On the HOIVG-Bench benchmark (135 curated samples, 5-second 720p clips), OmniShow attains a Sync-C score of 8.612 and FaceSim of 0.810 on the RA2V (reference+audio-to-video) task (HOIVG-Bench Metrics table).
OmniShow's training corpus comprises approximately 3,500 hours of video spanning R2V, A2V, RA2V, and RAP2V dataset splits (Dataset Scale section).
Human evaluation on side-by-side comparisons shows raters favor OmniShow's outputs over competing methods on both RA2V and RP2V tasks (Applications / human evaluation results).

XJaXdi5R21.text: ConGLUDe's protein encoder is built on VN-EGNN (Virtual Node Equivariant Graph Neural Network) and predicts binding-site locations jointly with whole-protein and pocket-level embeddings, without requiring pre-defined pockets (Architecture Components / Protein Encoder section).

ConGLUDe extends CLIP-style contrastive learning along three axes—protein, ligand, and binding pocket—enabling ligand-conditioned pocket prediction as a novel design feature (Novel Design Feature section).
On the LIT-PCBA zero-shot virtual screening benchmark, ConGLUDe achieves an AUROC of 64.06 ± 3.25% (Performance Results table).
On the Kinobeads target-fishing benchmark, ConGLUDe achieves an AUROC of 65.6%, substantially outperforming existing methods (Performance Results table).

ConGLUDe achieves a DCC success rate of 68.9% for binding-site prediction on PDBbind2020, and 35% DCC success rate for ligand-conditioned pocket selection on the ASD benchmark (Performance Results table).

Training alternates between structure-based batches (protein-ligand complexes, geometric plus contrastive losses) and ligand-based batches using millions of bioactivity measurements via a sigmoid contrastive loss (Training Strategy section).

AWPKhE1dbc.text: UHR-BAT achieves 44.0% overall weighted accuracy on XLRS-Bench, outperforming GeoLLaVA-8K by 0.7 points and GPT-4o by 21.0 points (Table 1).
On RSHR-Bench, UHR-BAT scores 29.2% average on Perception and 45.0% average on Reasoning, a 7.9-point reasoning gain over EarthDial (Table 2).

Query-aware token importance is computed from text-to-vision attention weights as described in Section 3.2 (Equation 2), and multi-scale alignment uses scale-specific positional embeddings with bilinear interpolation (Section 3.3).
The Region-wise Preserve-and-Merge strategy retains tokens whose importance is no lower than a region-specific reference score, merging the rest (Section 3.4).
UHR-BAT compresses 131,328 visual tokens down to 4k tokens (32.83x compression), reducing theoretical FLOPs from 374.24 to 267.68 and cutting inference latency from 5.99s to 4.34s (Table 4).
Qualitative results show preserved fine-grained detail even under a 95% pruning ratio (Figure 5).

am8FJ31GWi.text: RPG-Encoder unifies code comprehension and generation as inverse processes over a Repository Planning Graph (RPG) that combines lifted semantic features with code dependencies (abstract only).
RPG-Encoder achieves 93.7% accuracy at rank 5 (Acc@5) on SWE-bench Verified, described as state-of-the-art localization performance (abstract only).
On SWE-bench Live Lite, RPG-Encoder surpasses the best competing baseline by more than 10 percentage points in localization accuracy (abstract only).
RPG-Encoder attains 98.5% reconstruction coverage on the RepoCraft benchmark, indicating high-fidelity reconstruction of the original codebase (abstract only).
Incremental topology evolution of the RPG decouples maintenance cost from repository scale, reducing update overhead by 95.7% (abstract only).

7Eyp6J31u4.text: Anchor Invariance Regularization (AIR) designates verifiable contexts (e.g., multiple-choice formulations) as anchors with stop-gradient targets, so open-ended variants are regularized toward the anchor rather than the reverse (Section 3.3, Equations 5-6).
GRPO+AIR improves in-distribution group accuracy by 12.71 percentage points and out-of-distribution consistency by 33.49 percentage points relative to GRPO alone (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On the Safety domain specifically, out-of-distribution consistency rises from 13.73% (GRPO) to 60.78% (GRPO+AIR) (Table 1).

Evaluation spans three domains: Safety (AdvBench with jailbreak variants vs. rule-checkable formats), Moral Reasoning (ethical dilemmas with verifiable anchors), and Mathematics (GSM8K converted to multiple-choice anchors) (Section 4).

Under a deliberately corrupted reward signal (a naive regex heuristic rewarding superficial refusal keywords), GRPO+AIR resists alignment faking while plain GRPO exhibits severe reward hacking (Section 4.2, "Robustness to Extreme Reward Hacking", Figure 5).

P76Q8Pi1E9.text: FILet selects LoRA initialization directions with minimal Fisher Energy, approximating the expected loss increase from a symmetric perturbation via a second-order Taylor expansion, Delta L_sym(Z) proportional to (gamma^2/2) vec(Z)^T S_W vec(Z) (Section 3).

FILet approximates the Fisher/curvature matrix S_W with a Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) factorization, S_W approx S_X (x) S_Y, avoiding the prohibitive full-matrix computation and SVD-based casting used by prior methods (Section 3.3).
On 8 reasoning benchmarks with Llama2-7B, FILet reaches 83.1% average accuracy versus 81.7% for both KaSA and LoRA-Dash (Table 1).
On 7 image-classification datasets with ViT-B/32, FILet attains the highest average accuracy at 69.3%, versus 68.6% for KaSA (Table 2).
On GSM8K generation, FILet scores 34.5 on Llama2-7B and 58.8 on Llama3-8B, versus LoRA-Dash's 34.1 and 55.8 respectively (Table 3).

Increasing the minibatch size used to estimate Fisher statistics from 80 to the full dataset yields further gains of up to 0.7% (Llama2-7B) and 0.9% (Llama3-8B), with diminishing returns beyond a minibatch size of 480 (Section 4.5.1).

lxKyBy8NDn.text: ReDGE derives a closed-form denoiser for categorical distributions under Gaussian noise, x_hat_0 = softmax(phi_theta + alpha_t x_t / sigma_t^2), giving a training-free differentiable sampling procedure without a learned denoiser network (Section 3.2, Equation 10).

Proposition 3.1 shows that as the final diffusion timestep t_1 to 0, the Jacobian of the reparameterization map vanishes almost surely, explaining gradient degradation in the small-noise regime (Section 3.2, Proposition 3.1).
With a single diffusion step (t_1=1), ReDGE recovers the Straight-Through estimator and the ReinMax estimator as special cases (Section 3).
On the Gaussian Mixture VAE task, ReDGE-Cov attains NELBO 1040.04 +/- 97.89, improving over ReinMax's 1175.73 +/- 78.78 (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On the Sudoku constraint-satisfaction task, ReDGE-Cov achieves a loss of 8.18 +/- 7.13 and a 20.76% solved rate (Table 2, Section 4.3).
On categorical VAE training on MNIST across three latent configurations (L=32,K=64; L=30,K=10; L=48,K=2), ReDGE-Cov reaches a final average loss of 81.99 +/- 0.06 (Table 3, Section 4.4).

fKtCkb8Ixj.text: The benchmark comprises 200 tasks spanning five task types (e.g., reading with a broken tool, reading with an irrelevant file, reading with a local decoy, multi-task with a missing download tool, multi-task with a nonexistent file) across eight realistic constraint scenarios (Section 2).

Across 11 evaluated LLMs (including Deepseek, Claude, GPT-4.1, and Gemini), Non-Failure Rate (agents not reporting an encountered problem) ranges from 27.5% to 97.5% on the broken-tool reading task (Section 3, Table 2).
On the nonexistent-file multi-task setting, models exhibit a File Fabrication Rate of 25%-70% and a Hallucinated-Answer Rate of 90%-100% across all tested agents (Section 3, Table 2).
On the local-decoy reading task, Decoy Fallback Rate (silently substituting an alternative source) reaches up to 90% for GLM-4.5 (Section 3, Table 2).

Removing the answer-format constraint reduces measured deceptive behavior by up to 40%, while adding explicit anti-deception instructions reduces Non-Failure Rate by about 39% without eliminating the behavior (Section 4).

Section 6 argues agentic upward deception emerges from optimizing for surface-level task success rather than truthfulness alignment, and persists despite the tested prompt-based mitigations (Section 6).

QZjH84ut3Q.text: TodoEvolve trains a 14B planning model (Todo-14B) using Impedance-Guided Preference Optimization (IGPO), a preference-optimization scheme built on a Cognitive Impedance metric that penalizes failed steps, instability, and planning/execution cost (Section on Cognitive Impedance formula).

TodoEvolve is evaluated on five agentic benchmarks: GAIA (165 tasks across three difficulty levels), WebWalkerQA (170 sampled queries), xBench-DeepSearch (100 tasks), TaskCraft (300 sampled queries), and DeepSearchQA (50 sampled queries) (Table 3).
With the Smolagents backbone and GPT-5-Mini, TodoEvolve achieves 72.12% average accuracy on GAIA, a +16.37 percentage point improvement over vanilla Smolagents planning (Table 3).
With DeepSeek V3.2 as the backbone, TodoEvolve reaches 53.85% accuracy on GAIA Level 3, the hardest difficulty tier (Table 3).
On WebWalker-QA, TodoEvolve attains 70% accuracy at an average cost of $0.0167 per task, 216.59 seconds runtime, and 7.7 steps per episode (Table 4).

The PlanFactory design space standardizes planning architectures along four dimensions (Topology, Initialization, Adaptation, Navigation) and is built from seven representative planning paradigms via a Bootstrap-and-Filter pipeline (Section on Method Overview / PlanFactory).

v0lOwZnull.text: STORM is a spatial-aware token reduction framework for vision Mamba models that performs structured row-wise then column-wise token reduction plus a localized window mechanism to preserve the 2D spatial layout required by selective scanning (Method section).

On VMamba-B with ImageNet-1K, plain ToMe token merging collapses top-1 accuracy from an 83.9% baseline to 35.7%, whereas adding STORM to ToMe recovers accuracy to 82.6%, a 63.3 percentage-point improvement over ToMe alone (Table results, ImageNet-1K classification).

On PlainMamba-L2, STORM+ToMe limits the top-1 accuracy drop to 1.0% (80.6% vs. 81.6% baseline), compared to a 4.9% drop (76.7%) for standard ToMe without STORM (Table results, ImageNet-1K classification).

STORM outperforms recent Mamba-specific token reduction methods HSA (46.2%), MTR (47.9%), and QuarterMap (64.2%) in top-1 accuracy under comparable reduction settings (Table results, comparison to Mamba-specific methods).
STORM is evaluated across multiple Mamba backbones and sizes, including VMamba (T/S/B) and PlainMamba (L1/L2/L3), as well as LocalMamba (Experimental setup / model evaluation section).

coJqVkqb03.text: Ophiuchus is trained via a three-stage pipeline: Cold-Start SFT on 30k tool-integrated reasoning trajectories, Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning on 3k self-correction cases, and Agentic Tool Reinforcement Learning (ATRL) with fine-grained reward signals on 30k samples, totaling 64k curated samples (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

Relative to the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline, Ophiuchus improves accuracy by +17.4 points on SLAKE (83.9% vs. 66.5%), +30.2 points on In-House-VQA (50.4% vs. 20.2%), and +19.3 points on MMMU(H&M) (76.0% vs. 56.7%), for an average +18.7 point gain across seven zero-shot benchmarks (Section 4.2).
On an in-domain test, Ophiuchus outperforms the closed-source GPT-5 model, 59.4% vs. 37.3% (Section 4.2).
Ophiuchus exceeds open-source tool-augmented medical agents VILA-M3-40B (68.0 vs. 51.9 average) and MMedAgent-7B (68.0 vs. 48.1 average) despite having far fewer parameters (Section 4.2).

The framework (Section 3.1) equips an MLLM to decide when additional visual evidence is needed and to invoke external tools for fine-grained visual inspection during joint medical segmentation, understanding, and reasoning (Section 3.1).

Aa4DlW8PV2.text: AVTrack contains 871 video clips and 3,120 annotated instance tracklets drawn from six content genres (TV series, films, vlogs, animations, reality shows, interviews/stage performances), released as a test-only benchmark (Section 3.2).

AVTrack defines eight challenging-condition categories, including camera motion change, visual occlusion, relative position change, background switch, multiple instances, multi-turn sounding, audio-visual inconsistency, and instance scale dynamics (Section 3.2).

Compared to the prior AVISeg dataset, AVTrack contains substantially higher proportions of challenging scenarios, e.g., visual occlusion (80.9% vs. 8.6%) and camera motion change (90.5% vs. 7.1%) (Table 2, Figure 2).

Baseline evaluation shows VIS methods (VITA, LBVQ, CAVIS) score below HOTA 12.0, AVIS methods (AVISM, ACVIS, AVTrackFormer) score around HOTA 20.0-20.84, and the proposed AVTracker baseline achieves the best result at HOTA 29.08 (Section 5.1, Table 2).

The dataset construction pipeline described in Appendix B uses a four-stage process: video collection, automatic pre-annotation with Grounded-SAM, human-in-the-loop annotation, and quality refinement (Appendix B).

Kmv7TjGCru.text: TICL (Test-time Interventional Causal Learning) combines test-time training with the Joint Causal Inference (JCI) framework, using an Interventional Structural-MCMC (IS-MCMC) algorithm for self-augmented training data generation (Section 3.1).
On intervention target detection across 14 bnlearn benchmark datasets, TICL achieves an average F1-score improvement of 50.21% over the second-best method (Section 4.1, Table 2).

On I-CPDAG discovery (joint skeleton and v-structure identification), TICL improves F1 score by 13.62% over the best baseline, achieving an average F1 rank of 1.36 ± 0.37 across methods (Section 4.1, Table 1).
TICL is compared against score-based (GIES, IGSP, UT-IGSP), constraint-based (PC), gradient-based (GOLEM), and optimization-based (ENCO, AVICI) causal discovery baselines (Section 4.1).
Ablations on training data quantity and quality, and on IS-MCMC initialization strategy, are reported to show their effect on downstream causal discovery performance (Section 4.2, Figures 4-7).

kN0NMoVWXG.text: BudCache formulates step-level diffusion caching as a discrete optimization problem over a binary cache mask under a fixed NFE (number of function evaluations) budget, solved via simulated annealing combined with deterministic hill climbing (Section on Cache Policy Search).
At 10 NFE, BudCache-base achieves a 2.51x speedup with LPIPS of 0.1759 on FLUX.1-dev, outperforming TeaCache and LeMiCa at matched latency (Table with FLUX.1-dev results).
At 8 NFE, BudCache-ultra reaches a 3.00x speedup with LPIPS of 0.2479, exceeding ERTACache's quality at a higher acceleration ratio (Table with FLUX.1-dev results).
On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B video generation, BudCache achieves a 1.82x speedup with LPIPS of 0.1167, versus 0.1929 LPIPS for TeaCache at comparable settings (Section on video generation results).
Cache-aware schedule alignment via teacher-student distillation, applied in tight regimes of 5-7 NFE, yields a 0.19 ImageReward improvement at 5 NFE (Table 4).
Searched cache masks generalize across solvers, resolutions, and CFG scales (Table 3), and transfer from the 1.3B to a 14B video model (Table 7).

zEg7sA2VBv.text: Theorem 1 establishes that temporal task structure is identifiable via conditional independence testing on observed variables using a 'band' conditioning set, without requiring interventions (Section 3, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows task-relevant latent variables become identifiable and disentangled from task-irrelevant ones under a sparsity regularization applied to the learned representation (Section 4, Theorem 2).

Algorithm 1 recovers temporal task structure by partitioning sequences into segments of length L and aggregating pairwise conditional independence tests across all segment pairs (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
The identifiability results are validated on synthetic linear Gaussian SCMs with T in [8,20] timesteps and M in [2,10] tasks, measuring accuracy and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (Section 5).
Real-world validation uses the SportsHHI human-human interaction video dataset, reporting mean Average Precision (mAP) for recovered task structure (Section 5).

EPKdX56JSc.text: The method represents periodic charge densities as anisotropic Gaussians in real space and analytically evaluates plane-wave coefficients via the Poisson summation formula, reconstructing the full periodic density with a single inverse FFT (Methods section).
On the ECD-HSE06 hybrid-functional benchmark, the model achieves up to 633x faster inference than ChargE3Net while attaining lower NMAE (1.35% vs 1.53%) (Table 1).
On the MP-Full benchmark, the model attains 0.58% NMAE (vs 0.54% for ChargE3Net) with a 328x inference speedup, and on GNoME (out-of-distribution) it attains 0.93% NMAE with a 222x speedup (Table 1).

When used to initialize SCF calculations, the model reduces total DFT computation time by 39.18% on MP structures and 39.75% on GNoME structures, whereas ChargE3Net-initialized DFT is slower than the default initial guess (Table 2).

The model is the first machine-learned charge-density initializer reported to achieve a consistent net reduction in end-to-end DFT wall-clock time across both in-distribution (MP) and out-of-distribution (GNoME) test structures (Table 2, Discussion).

5LwZAeK5PE.text: EvoDiverse maintains multiple LLM-driven hypothesis populations ('pools') at distinct temperature (inverse-selection-pressure) levels and exchanges candidates between pools via Metropolis-Hastings swap acceptance (Section on Temperature-Based Search and Swap Mechanism).

On molecular discovery (JNK3 target), EvoDiverse achieves a Top-10 AUC of 0.63±0.05 under a 10,000-oracle-call budget while producing roughly double the number of diverse candidates (~90) compared to the MOLLEO baseline (~50) (Molecular Discovery results section).

On equation discovery under a 1,000-evaluation budget, EvoDiverse attains higher diversity (e.g., 0.284 on the Chemistry benchmark) than single-pool and ensemble baselines across physics, biology, chemistry, and materials-science domains (Equation Discovery results section).

On algorithm discovery (circle packing task) under a 1,000-evaluation budget, EvoDiverse reaches a best sum score of 2.5461, outperforming baselines while avoiding premature convergence (Algorithm Discovery results section).

EvoDiverse is compared against MOLLEO (single-pool LLM evolutionary algorithm), an isolated multi-population Ensemble baseline with no inter-pool communication, a high-temperature single-pool Tempering baseline, and standard/Island EA variants (Baselines section).

WikLu7PkNK.text: The primitive-cell-based factorized representation reduces the number of learnable atomic variables by an average of 9.2x compared to full slab representations (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

On de novo generation, CatFlow is compared against the CatGPT autoregressive baseline using validity, uniqueness, compositional diversity, system energy difference (ΔE_sys), and convergence rate metrics (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On structure prediction, CatFlow is compared against the sequential DiffCSP+AdsorbDiff pipeline using validity, match rate, RMSD, and adsorption energy success rate (Table 3, Section 4.2).

Kernel density estimation over 67 validation adsorbates shows CatFlow's generated adsorption energy distribution lies closer to the reference (thermodynamic local minima) distribution than the CatGPT baseline (Figure 5, Section 4.2).

A comparative capability table shows CatFlow is the only method satisfying slab generation, structure prediction, adsorbate positioning, adsorbate conditioning, and co-generation criteria simultaneously (Table 1, Section 2.2).

zvkcVWBmcF.text: AVI-Bench comprises 14 tasks totaling 5,864 samples organized into perception (1,494 samples), understanding (808 samples), reasoning (1,472 samples), and primitive sensation (2,090 samples) stages (Table 1, Section 3.1).
Across 28 evaluated Omni-MLLMs, human performance averages 92.6% overall while the best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, scores only 57.2% overall (Table 4).

Gemini-2.5-Pro, the strongest evaluated model, achieves only 39.1% on the audio-visual localization (AVL) task and 35.1% on audio-visual language grounding (AVLG), indicating persistent weakness on grounding tasks (Table 3, Section 4.2).
The relative performance gap between reasoning-stage and primitive-sensation-stage tasks ranges from 47.6% (Gemini-2.5-Pro) to 82.7% across evaluated models (Section 4.2).
Figure 3 shows perception and understanding scores are correlated with and constrain reasoning-stage performance across the 28 evaluated Omni-MLLMs (Figure 3).

eYwCaFakq6.text: Theorem 3.1 proves the Subspace Router R = B†_comb β̂_OLS minimizes the reconstruction objective, showing SSR's router is equivalent to the optimal ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator projected into the combined subspace (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1).
On FLUX.1-dev with K=9 merged LoRA tasks, SSR achieves a DINO score of 0.6713 and CLIP score of 0.7850, versus 0.5837 DINO and 0.7376 CLIP for the DARE baseline (Table 1).
SSR outperforms the strongest prior baseline, IterIS, by approximately 0.047 DINO and 0.033 CLIP score in high-interference multi-task merging settings (Table 1).
In multi-task execution evaluation, SSR achieves a 91% success rate at correctly rendering all requested objects versus 62% for DARE (Table 3).

SSR merges 9 LoRAs in approximately 34 seconds using one-shot calibration and maintains greater than 90% performance recovery even at K=9 tasks, while incurring zero inference overhead via structural re-parameterization (Section 3.4).

ZbWgrDzCQo.text: Theorem 4.2 (the Monotonic Path Property) establishes that valid suffix tokens form a single monotonic path in the Suffix-Successor Tree, enabling the incremental algorithm to achieve O(log^2 t) amortized per-byte complexity and O(n log^2 t) overall complexity, where n is input length and t is maximum token length (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

The incremental algorithm combines an Aho-Corasick automaton for search-space identification with centroid decomposition for tree navigation, plus an eager output mechanism for emitting completed tokens (Section 5, Section 6).

As a drop-in replacement, the method achieves up to a 3.13x speedup over Hugging Face's tokenizers on English text with the CodeLlama tokenizer, versus smaller gains (e.g., 1.05x) on Qwen-3 (Table 1, Section 7.1).
On pathological inputs, the incremental method maintains stable throughput whereas tiktoken (CL100K) exhibits characteristic quadratic O(n^2) performance decay (Figure 3).

RLNfZ407i8.text: DB-KSVD converges on 2.6 million Gemma-2-2B embeddings with 4,096 dictionary elements and sparsity k=20 in approximately 8 minutes, versus over 30 days for a baseline KSVD implementation, a speedup of up to roughly 10,000x (Section 5.1).
On a single batch of n=2^16 samples, CPU-only DB-KSVD runtime ranges from 5.47 to 337.63 seconds depending on dictionary size and sparsity parameters (Section 5.1).

On SAEBench, DB-KSVD achieves a loss-recovered score of approximately 0.96, matching top sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches, while remaining competitive on absorption (~0.90), sparse probing (~0.76-0.78), and RAVEL (~0.57-0.62) metrics (Section 5.2, Figure 1).

DB-KSVD scores slightly lower than the best SAEs on autointerpretability (~0.85), while its Matryoshka variant reduces dictionary coherence and improves autointerpretability relative to baseline DB-KSVD (Section 5.3).

Experiments use Gemma-2-2B embeddings of dimension d=2,304 with dictionary sizes m in {4,096, 16,384} and sparsity levels k in {20, 40, 80}, trained over 40 iterations with batch size 2^16 (Section 5).

UcDP1FhVLW.text: QHFlow2-m achieves 40% lower Hamiltonian prediction error than the prior best model QHFlow while using 43M parameters versus QHFlow's 30M (Section 4.2, Table 1).
QHFlow2 is the first Hamiltonian-based model to reach NequIP-level force accuracy on the MD benchmark (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
QHFlow2 achieves up to 20x lower energy MAE than the NequIP baseline on the MD benchmark (Section 4.2, Table 1).
QHFlow2 reduces energy error by up to 20x on the QH9 dataset compared to MACE, and shows superior HOMO/LUMO/gap accuracy versus EquiformerV2 (Section 4.2, Table 2, Figure 3).
QHFlow2 achieves 2.8x faster inference than the prior QHFlow model with a 50% parameter reduction (Section 4.2).

Data and model scaling experiments show that improved Hamiltonian accuracy consistently correlates with better downstream energy/force predictions, and QHFlow2 attains lower errors than QHFlow at comparable parameter budgets (Section 4.4, Figures 5-6).

fhXqiit0CW.text: MeDS combined with Dinomaly achieves 99.16% image-level AUROC on MVTecAD at 40% noise ratio, compared to the 87.38% I-AUROC of Dinomaly alone at the same noise level (Table 1).
MeDS combined with INP-Former achieves 99.17% I-AUROC, 99.68% I-AP, and 95.21% pixel-level AUPRO on MVTecAD at 40% noise ratio (Table 1).
At 20% noise ratio on MVTecAD, Dinomaly + MeDS reaches 99.31% I-AUROC versus the 92.16% I-AUROC of the Dinomaly baseline (Table 1).
On VisA at 10% noise ratio, Dinomaly + MeDS attains 97.43% I-AUROC compared to 93.56% for the baseline (Table 2).

On Real-IAD at 40% noise ratio, Dinomaly + MeDS achieves 90.99% I-AUROC and 83.98% I-AP, maintaining performance across contamination levels without noise-ratio-specific hyperparameter tuning (Table 3).

An ablation shows progressive gains from MeDS's components on MVTecAD at 40% noise: the memory ensemble alone reaches 92.22% I-AUROC, adding distillation raises it to 98.76%, and the full method reaches 99.16% (Table 4).

8NHVpDRH0a.text: On the Stego260 dataset with N=2 hidden images, MIDAS achieves a higher MANIQA quality score of 0.434 compared to 0.406 for CRoSS and 0.399 for DiffStega (Table 2).
MIDAS achieves 23.903 dB PSNR for correct-key reconstruction, higher than the 17-21 dB range achieved by baseline methods (Table 2).
With the wrong key, MIDAS's reconstruction PSNR drops to 9.964 dB (rendering it meaningless), whereas baseline methods still yield a recoverable 15-18 dB (Table 2).
Under JPEG compression at quality factor 70, MIDAS attains 19.922 dB PSNR robustness, substantially higher than the IIS baseline's 10.047 dB (Table 3).
MIDAS achieves roughly 20 percentage points lower steganalysis detection accuracy than modification-based methods (which exceed 90% detection accuracy) (Figure 4).
MIDAS scales to hiding eight images (N=8) while maintaining 0.456 MANIQA quality and a CLIP Score alignment of 30.257 (Table 5).

XJSJZXReoJ.text: The Drift Variation Score (DVS) is derived from the Fisher-Rao line element on the statistical manifold of diffusion trajectories, giving the DVS formula in Equation 11 (Section 3.1-3.3).
On QM9 with the GruM backbone, DVS-Euler achieves an FCD of 0.095 versus 0.107 for the fixed-step baseline (Table 1).
On ZINC250k, DVS sampling reduces FCD from 2.207 (fixed-step baseline) to 2.092 (Table 2).
DVS-Euler often matches or surpasses the more expensive Fixed-Step Heun solver despite using fewer function evaluations (Section 4, Table 1-2).
On QM9, DVS sampling yields a 19.57% runtime reduction and 25.5% fewer function evaluations despite a 6.53% per-step computational overhead (Table 10).
An ablation over the aggregation factor γ shows optimal performance at γ=0.20, achieving FCD=0.0976 with 745 function evaluations versus the 1000-step baseline (Table 5).

6xKzkSqyef.text: G-Substrate treats graph structure as a persistent intermediate substrate shared across modalities via a unified structural schema and interleaved role-based training over a unified graph state space G_s (Section 2.2-2.3, Equations 3-4).
Table 1 demonstrates recurring local structural motifs, such as two-hop chains and hub patterns, across four distinct domains despite differing global topology (Section 2.1, Table 1).

G-Substrate outperforms task-isolated and naive multi-task learning baselines on most of four evaluated tasks: graph algorithmic reasoning, molecular graph description (BLEU-4/ROUGE-L), scene graph generation (R@50 on Visual Genome), and event relation extraction (F1 on MAVEN/HiEvent) (Table 2).
Pretraining on event relation graphs improves scene graph generation performance by +2.37 points without any target-domain supervision, demonstrating cross-domain transfer (Table 4).
The proposed unified structural schema representation outperforms natural-language and XML-style alternative schema realizations (Table 3).
Ablations show that structural correctness of the graph representation matters, and that a moderate interleaving ratio of approximately 50% yields optimal performance (Figures 4-6).

vzzTxg0cbU.text: The ANIRA framework supports token-level variable-depth computation in recurrent transformers via two decision mechanisms, early allocation (ANIRA-E) and online halting (ANIRA-O), with a maximum recurrent depth of D=6 for most tasks and D=14 for the MANO task (Section 3.1).
On the LANO synthetic-language benchmark, Spearman correlations between expected computation depth and token-level complexity proxies range from +0.456 to +0.666 (Table 1).

Both ANIRA-E and ANIRA-O show sharp accuracy drops when evaluated on unseen input sizes despite allocating additional computation to those inputs, indicating models learn size-specific rather than generalizable solutions (Section 6.2, Figure 3).

ANIRA-E's compute allocation decisions are best explained by static hub-structure features (regression coefficient +0.134), whereas ANIRA-O's online halting decisions are dominated by algorithmic execution-state features such as DFS depth (+0.302) and newly enabled nodes (-0.286) (Section 6.4, Table 2).

Training exhibits a two-phase compute dynamic: an initial rapid increase in allocated depth while the task is being learned, followed by a phase of compute reduction with maintained task performance (Section 6.3, Figures 4-5).

On GSM-Symbolic math problems, neither ANIRA-E nor ANIRA-O allocates more computation to harder problem splits (P1, P2) than to the Main split, limiting the interpretability of the compute-allocation signal in natural language settings (Section 6.6, Table 3).

2fPbFUJ87k.text: CapKV derives a closed-form mutual information objective for KV cache eviction under a linear-Gaussian surrogate model, unifying existing heuristic eviction strategies as approximations of the same capacity-maximization principle (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.4, Figure 1).

On the LongBench benchmark with Qwen3-8B across 16 tasks, CapKV achieves an average score of 49.51 versus SnapKV's 46.97 at a compression ratio of 0.25, and 36.57 versus 35.28 at a compression ratio of 0.9 (Table 1).
On Qwen3-14B, CapKV outperforms SnapKV (50.80 vs 50.11 at compression 0.25) and outperforms the EA baseline (47.16 vs 43.72 at compression 0.75) (Table 1).

CapKV shows strong correlation (Spearman ρ = 0.75-0.85) between retained capacity and downstream task performance across datasets, empirically validating the capacity-maximization theory (Section 4.1, Figure 3).
On the AIME25 reasoning benchmark with Nemotron-7B under decoding-phase eviction, CapKV degrades more gracefully than heuristic baselines as compression increases (Section 4.3, Figure 4).
An ablation on the temperature parameter τ for Llama3.1-8B finds τ=5 optimal, yielding an average score of 41.73 across compression ratios 0.25-0.9 (Table 2).

TCFtA9CI3U.text: Across 22 configurations, causal token injection shows that 45%-90% of contrastively selected candidate reasoning features activate after inserting only a few feature-associated tokens into non-reasoning text, indicating many candidates are driven by shallow lexical cues rather than reasoning per se (Section 4.3, Figure 1, Table 2).

Table 1 reports the mean Cohen's d of the top 100 candidate reasoning features per configuration, quantifying the activation-difference effect size used for initial contrastive feature selection (Section 4.1, Table 1).

For features surviving token injection, an LLM-guided falsification procedure (using Gemini as the falsifying model) constructs non-reasoning inputs that spuriously trigger activation and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it, decoupling activation from genuine reasoning content (Section 4.4, Tables 3-4).

A supplementary steering study on Gemma-3-12B-Instruct at layer 22 finds that steering the identified feature candidates yields only minimal one-shot accuracy changes on evaluated benchmarks such as AIME2024 and GPQA (Section 5.5, Table 5).

An appendix robustness check ranking features by ROC-AUC on Gemma-3-4B-Instruct layer 22 finds 96% of the top 100 selected features exhibit statistically significant token-driven behavior under injection (Appendix, Table 10).

SRGpmDQjJM.text: MedTPE combines token-pair encoding (TPE), dependency-aware token replacement of roughly 3% of least-common tokens, and self-supervised fine-tuning (SSFT) that updates only 0.5-1.0% of model parameters to align new token embeddings with the pretrained latent space (Figure 2).
MedTPE reduces input token length by up to 31% and inference latency by 34-63%, with compression rates ranging 22.8-32.4% across datasets (Abstract; Table 2).

On MIMIC-IV ICU Mortality and Phenotyping (25 conditions) with Qwen2.5-1.5B, MedTPE maintains F1 on ICU Mortality (0.122 to 0.122) while improving Phenotyping F1 (0.201 to 0.218), alongside inference time dropping from 38.3 to 23.5 minutes (-38.6%) (Table 2).

MedTPE is evaluated across four clinical prediction tasks (ICU Mortality, Phenotyping, 30-day Hospital Readmission, 1-year Pancreatic Cancer prediction) and three LLM backbones spanning Qwen2.5, Llama3, and Gemma2 families, plus the clinically specialized Meditron3-8B (Table 2).

MedTPE's compression approach is additionally tested for generalization beyond clinical text, including scientific reasoning (ARC-Challenge), financial summarization (ECTSum), and Chinese medical QA (CMedQA2).

dWCG53oQWc.text: Theorem 5.1 gives non-asymptotic statistical learning guarantees for equivariant representation learning (eNCP), with a global L²(𝒳,𝒵)-norm error bound (Eq. 19) whose sample-complexity term scales as [d_iso/N]^(-α/(1+2α)), and a localized bound (Eq. 20) that adapts the rate using group-symmetry parameters of the measurable subset (Theorem 5.1).

On a quadruped robot's Center-of-Mass linear and angular momentum regression task using noisy joint position/velocity observations, eNCP achieves lower test-set MSE and better sample efficiency than baselines including standard NCP, an MLP, and an equivariant MLP (eMLP) (Section 6, Figure 4).

eNCP is the only method among those compared that produces well-calibrated 90% confidence intervals for a quadruped robot's instantaneous work/ground-reaction forces across disturbance and recovery phases while traversing rough terrain, unlike the symmetry-agnostic Density Ratio Fitting (DRF) baseline (Figure 1; Figure 5).

Symmetry-agnostic baselines NCP and DRF struggle to recover the correct group-equivariant structure of the learned operator, as shown by their relative sample inefficiency compared to eNCP (Section 6, Figure 6).
eNCP is compared against a Conditional Quantile Regression (CQR) baseline using relaxed coverage, coverage, and set-size metrics for uncertainty quantification (Table 2).

SRuY51jkii.text: RLCracker achieves a 98.5% Evasion Success Rate on 1,500-token Unigram-watermarked text using an attacker model as small as Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Section 5.2, Table 1).
RLCracker's 98.5% Unigram removal rate surpasses GPT-4o's 6.75% success rate on the same long-form benchmark by over 90 percentage points (Section 5.2).
RLCracker achieves 93.3% ESR against the EWD watermark and 95.8% ESR against SWEET on 500-token texts (Section 5.2).
RLCracker reaches its performance plateau after training on only 100 short (500-token) watermarked samples, with 91.5% ESR on EWD achievable from just 50 samples of 250 tokens (Section 5.3, Table 5).

RLCracker is evaluated across ten watermarking schemes (including EWD, KGW, KGW_selfhash, UPV, SWEET, Unigram, SIR, X-SIR, SynthID-Text, and PF-Watermark) and five attacker model sizes from 0.6B to 8B parameters, plus three victim models at 1.5B, 8B, and 32B (Section 5.1).
A model trained via RLCracker on LLaMA-3.1-8B outputs generalizes to achieve 96% ESR when attacking outputs from the unseen Qwen2.5-32B victim model (Table 4).

gM5TpHur0M.text: Tail-Aware Distillation (TAD) decouples the KL divergence into a top-K term and a tail-mass-weighted term, 𝒟KL₁ + αᵏₜ𝒟KL₂, rather than treating the full distribution uniformly (Section 2, Equation 2).
Distilling Qwen1.5-1.8B into a 1.2B student with TAD yields a 47.8 average score versus 46.6 for MiniPLM, and a 45.4 versus 45.0 score at the 0.5B student scale (Table 1).
With larger teachers over 2B tokens, TAD outperforms vanilla KD, e.g. Phi3-14B distilled to Llama2-7B reaches 54.1 average score with TAD versus 50.0 with vanilla KD (Table 4).
TAD is computationally efficient, requiring 9.3 PetaFLOPs per 1M tokens versus 12.4 PFLOPs for MiniPLM and 39.0-65.0 PFLOPs for MiniLLM/Seq-KD (Table 3).
On the ORCAMEL math distillation setup, TAD trains a Llama2-7B student in 840 GPU hours (versus thousands for competing methods) while still outperforming vanilla KD (Table 7).
TAD's best hyperparameter setting uses top-K=10 and tail weight β=2, with performance remaining robust for β in the range [1,5] (Table 2).

MToJN3uf7u.text: Theorem 1 proves that the corrigibility transformation constructs a corrigible goal G_C from any 'basic' goal G while preserving optimal performance under Condition 1 (Section 3, Theorem 1).
The transformation implements mid-action override by setting the reward function to R_M(s,a,s') = Q^π*(s,a), allowing reward to be assigned between action selection and action execution (Section 3).
Theorem 3 extends the construction to secondary agents, showing the recursive corrigibility transformation yields recursively corrigible goals with no performance penalty (Section 3.1, Theorem 3).
Theorem 4 shows that misgeneralized versions of transformed goals cannot engage in goal tampering when reward depends only on which action is selected (Section 4, Theorem 4).
A goal is defined as corrigible if the set of optimal actions in every environment is unchanged whether or not the goal is guaranteed to persist rather than be updated by proper signals (Section 2).

pws8t4kBP4.text: Theorem 4.1 proves the constructed matrix V for the PolyILR basis satisfies the contrast property V^T 1 = 0 and orthonormality V^T V = I_{d-1}, making the map φ(x) = V^T log x an isometry (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.1).

Proposition 4.2 establishes that PolyILR produces a unique, canonical orthonormal basis for any given tree topology, with the original tree recoverable from the basis's clade support structure (Section 4.3, Proposition 4.2).

Algorithm 1 constructs the PolyILR basis by applying weighted Helmert contrasts with Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization at each internal node in depth-first order, then spreading local contrasts to a global leaf-indexed basis by dividing by descendant counts (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
Unlike PhILR, PolyILR respects the original polytomous tree topology directly without requiring artificial binarization of multifurcating nodes (Figure 1, Section 2).
Proposition 7.1 shows the logit-space quotient ℒ is isomorphic to the Aitchison tangent space ℋ, so centered logits equal CLR coordinates (Section 7, Proposition 7.1).

The method is validated on the HMP, cMD3, and DISCO microbiome/single-cell datasets, demonstrating stable feature selection and interpretable tree-level (clade) importance aggregation (Section 6, Tables 2-6).

4fbvifBi9q.text: SAPO outperforms GRPO on multi-modal reasoning benchmarks, achieving 40.23% average accuracy versus 37.97% on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 46.90% versus 45.96% on Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Table 1).
On the WeMath benchmark, SAPO improves over GRPO by 6.76 points using the 3B model, reaching 36.19% accuracy (Table 1).

On text-only reasoning, SAPO improves GSM8K accuracy with DeepSeekMath-7B by 5.3 points over PPO and 9.4 points over GRPO, and improves MATH500 accuracy with RhoMath-1.1B by 7.5 points over PPO and 7.8 points over GRPO (Figure 4).
SAPO's value model achieves lower and more stable value loss convergence than VC-PPO during training (Figure 6).
Segment-level importance sampling in SAPO yields a 4.83-point improvement on Geo3K over token-level importance sampling (Table 2).

SAPO's entropy-based adaptive segmentation strategy outperforms newline-based, fixed-step-based, and probability-based segmentation strategies, with optimal performance at an entropy threshold of k=30% (Table 3, Figure 5).

SDWG5xr20c.text: STAR-VAE applies a Gamma-Growth capacity schedule βc = βmin + (βmax − βmin)·((c−1)/(C−1))^γ across latent channels instead of a uniform KL penalty (Section 3).
On AudioCaps (Sound) and Song Describer (Music), STAR-VAE achieves better reconstruction fidelity (including lower FAD) than Stable Audio Open, with FAD of 2.31 vs. 3.29 on AudioCaps (Table 1).

STAR-Gen, an LLM-based flow-matching generator built on STAR-VAE's latents, reaches FDopenl3 of 55.8 vs. 80.2 for the best baseline and CLAP score of 0.48 vs. 0.44 on AudioCaps text-to-audio generation (Table 2).
STAR-VAE reconstructs audio near-optimally using only the top 37.5% of latent channels by information content, whereas an isotropic-KL baseline requires over 90% of channels (Figure 3).

Removing STAR regularization from a high-capacity Mamba encoder causes reconstruction quality to degrade (FAD 2.74 vs. 2.31 with STAR), demonstrating the 'Reconstruction Drift' failure mode (Section 4).

Human MOS evaluation rates STAR-VAE reconstructions at 4.32 ± 0.12 vs. 4.05 ± for Stable Audio Open at matched 21.5Hz latent rate, and STAR-Gen generation at 3.92 ± 0.16 vs. 3.76 for TangoFlux (Tables 7-8).
