1BLni5Uxsd.text: FLAME's Local Adjacency Discrepancy (LAD) map quantifies local Gibbs energy via pairwise pixel potentials, showing that diffusion-generated regions collapse to lower entropy ('Interior Gap') while editing boundaries show localized energy surges ('Boundary Spike') (Section 3).
FLAME combines a lightweight LAD-Net producing coarse localization masks with a parameter-efficient SAM adapter for pixel-level refinement (Section 4).
On in-distribution MagicBrush data, FLAME achieves 0.538 IoU / 0.650 F1 for pixel-level forgery localization (Table 1).

On zero-shot out-of-distribution generators (Qwen-Image, Flux Kontext), base FLAME averages 0.358 IoU / 0.459 F1, and fine-tuning with the EditStream-synthesized data (FLAME-F) raises this to 0.460 IoU / 0.565 F1 (Table 1, Section 5).

FLAME's robustness ablation shows the method retains localization performance under Gaussian blur but degrades under JPEG compression and Gaussian noise, which disrupt the high-frequency statistics the LAD map relies on (Table 3).

An ablation isolating the LAD map, adapter, and SAM refinement components shows each contributes to final localization accuracy, and a further sweep over neighborhood operators (Min/Max/Avg/LAD) and kernel sizes (3×3/5×5/7×7) identifies LAD as the best-performing operator (Tables 4-5).

hQYbnNccMq.text: EPGS computes a gradient-sensitivity score S = ||g_clean||₂ · (1 − CosSim(g_clean, g_perturbed)) from clean vs. Gaussian-embedding-perturbed inputs (E_perturbed = E + δ, δ ~ N(0, σ²I)) to detect stubborn hallucinations (Section 3).

Lemma 3.3 establishes an input-parameter isomorphism mapping local embedding perturbations to equivalent final-layer parameter perturbations, and Theorem 3.4 bounds the gradient norm by the maximum Hessian eigenvalue, ||∇ℒ(θ*; x+ϵ, ŷ)||₂ ≲ λmax(H)·||νϵ||₂ (Section 3, Lemma 3.3, Theorem 3.4).
EPGS achieves AUROC of 0.7629 on TriviaQA with Llama-2-7B, 0.7742 on SQuAD with Llama-3-8B, and 0.9732 on SVAMP with Llama-3-8B for detecting high-confidence factual errors (Section 4).
For stubborn hallucination detection specifically, EPGS scores 0.7373 vs. 0.5842 for Semantic Entropy on Llama-2 SQuAD (Table 2).

A power-iteration validation on 100 samples (50 correct facts, 50 stubborn errors) finds Pearson correlation r = 0.855 between EPGS score and the true maximum Hessian eigenvalue λmax, and shows stubborn hallucinations sit in minima roughly 2.5× sharper than robust facts (Section 4).

bVCUx0gwyk.text: Ternary Advantage Decoupling (TAD) separates rollouts into correct, incorrect, and uncertain/refusal categories and normalizes advantages independently within each group to prevent high-reward correct answers from suppressing uncertainty signals (Section 3.1).

Dynamic Uncertainty Reward Adjustment (DURA) uses a two-term formula that increases uncertainty rewards when the model's error rate is high and suppresses unnecessary refusal as accuracy improves, adapting in real time to model evolution and per-instance difficulty (Section 3.2).

On Qwen3-8B across math and text reasoning benchmarks (e.g., AIME24, AMC, MATH500), UCPO attains 79.63% average Precision on Answered Questions (PAQ), outperforming GRPO and GRPO-UC variants (Table 1).
On general tasks (GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Redux2) with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, UCPO reaches 58.58% average PAQ (Table 2).

An ablation removing TAD, DURA, and other components (NTF, LRE) individually shows each contributes to final PAQ/F1, confirming both mechanisms are necessary to avoid avoidance degeneracy on hard tasks and over-refusal on easy ones (Table 3).
UCPO remains compatible with the DAPO training framework, improving its performance when combined rather than conflicting with its optimization objective (Table 4).

SBfIuo2Ets.text: The method (TRIAD) constructs a third-order spherical bispectrum by coupling three irreducible SO(3) representations via tensor products and projecting onto the trivial representation using Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, yielding a rotation-invariant scalar that preserves phase information (Section 3).

Theorem 4.1 proves the third-order bispectrum invariant is strictly invariant under arbitrary SO(3) rotations, with perturbations to higher-order harmonic coefficients producing detectable changes in the invariant (Theorem 4.1).
Watermarks are embedded into spherical harmonic coefficients at degrees 6, 8, and 14 via SO(3)-equivariant operations to avoid perceptible artifacts in low-frequency (coarse) content (Section 3).
Under arbitrary 3D rotations, TRIAD maintains near-100% bit accuracy while baseline watermarking methods (with or without rotation augmentation) collapse in performance (Section 5).
Watermarked panoramic images retain high visual fidelity, with PSNR of 39.22 dB and SSIM of 0.9946 (Section 5).

TRIAD also achieves 100% bit accuracy under JPEG compression, Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, and resizing, though embedding capacity is constrained to roughly 32-64 bits because harmonics above degree 16 are vulnerable to lossy compression and aliasing (Section 5).

IkPdV0stxX.text: Proposition 3.2 (g-Boundedness) proves that the logit gap g tightly bounds the range of feasible optimal temperatures T for a target confidence level (Section 3.4, Proposition 3.2).

The SMART temperature network is a single-hidden-layer MLP with hidden dimension 16 taking the normalized logit gap as input and producing a softplus-activated temperature, using only 49 parameters total (Section 3.2).
On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50, SMART achieves 1.37% ECE at 15 bins versus 1.96% for PTS and 3.67% for CTS (Table 1).
On ImageNet-C with ResNet-50, SMART achieves 0.68% ECE versus 5.61% for the Spline calibration baseline, indicating better robustness under distribution shift (Table 1).
SMART maintains low ECE on ImageNet even when calibrated with only 50 validation samples (about 0.001% of the validation set), demonstrating strong data efficiency (Section 4.4).
SMART's runtime is 23.03 seconds compared to 90.44 seconds for PTS and 5457.55 seconds for CTS (Table 3).

kQZKqdlPQc.text: The proposed hierarchical method reduces average normalized safety cost to 0.01-0.02 versus 1.00 for the Task-Only baseline in the offline downstream setting (Table 1).
The proposed method achieves 0.92 normalized task reward versus 1.00 for the Oracle baseline trained with ground-truth safety signals, across six evaluation environments (Table 1).
Theorem 4.2 shows that learned reward models prefer safe over unsafe trajectories when safety penalties in the crowd preference data are sufficiently large (Theorem 4.2).
Theorem 4.3 shows that preference imbalance among crowd annotators causes learned reward models to bias toward majority preferences, degrading downstream policy performance (Theorem 4.3).

The hierarchical framework decomposes into VAE-based skill discovery via Variational Preference Learning or Contrastive Preference Learning, latent-conditioned low-level policies, and a high-level composition policy trained with task rewards plus regularization (Section 4).
The method remains robust to preference label noise up to 30% flipping and to varying crowd sizes in ablation experiments (Figure 4).

KlGj06E8Wa.text: Training instability in RLVR is attributed to objective-level hacking, which the paper argues originates from token-level credit misalignment rather than reward-verifier vulnerabilities (Section 1).

Three mechanisms are identified as driving objective-level hacking: initial training-inference discrepancy creating spurious optimization signals, token-level clipping accelerating discrepancy growth despite intending to stabilize training, and token-level weight distortion that causes training collapse when deliberately injected (Section 4).

Stronger clipping settings are empirically associated with a faster increase in the training-inference discrepancy, measured via importance weight variance between training and inference implementations (Section 5).
The paper reports variation of the clip ratio during RLVR training in Table 1, used to support the claim that clipping paradoxically accelerates rather than stabilizes discrepancy growth (Table 1).

The framework attributes the previously unexplained abnormal growth of training-inference discrepancy in Mixture-of-Experts models to this positive feedback loop between discrepancy growth and objective-level hacking (Section 6).

3voRLZLkwU.text: On Knights and Knaves reasoning puzzles, RLTF-SD and RLTF-FM reach 0.802 and 0.880 mean@1 accuracy respectively, versus 0.373 for single-turn GRPO and 0.352 for multi-turn GRPO (Table 1).
On MATH500 (trained on DeepMath), RLTF-FM achieves 0.636 mean@32 accuracy versus 0.578 for multi-turn GRPO and 0.424 for the Feedback Descent baseline (Table 1).
On LitBench creative writing, RLTF-SD and RLTF-FM score 8.80 and 8.40 respectively (on a 1-10 scale judged by GPT-4.1-mini) versus 6.83 for single-turn GRPO and 8.25 for Feedback Descent (Table 1).

Self Distillation (RLTF-SD) is derived by setting the reference policy to the first-turn policy with a stop-gradient and using an AWR-style objective with a first-turn mean-reward baseline, avoiding the gradient-signal collapse that occurs with a second-turn group-mean baseline (Section 3, Equation 7).

Feedback Modeling (RLTF-FM) trains the policy to predict the feedback provider's critique as an auxiliary cross-entropy objective added to the multi-turn RL loss, controlled by weight lambda_FeeMol (Section 4, Equation 10).

The experiments use Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 to simulate the feedback provider and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the learner policy, evaluated across reasoning puzzles, DAPO/DeepMath-trained math benchmarks, and LitBench/WritingBench creative writing tasks (Section 5).

ExIKTbg2Px.text: IN2R achieves 495.2 rSum on Flickr30K at 60% noise, outperforming the PCSR baseline's 480.5 by about 15 points (Section 4, results tables).
At extreme 80% noise on Flickr30K, IN2R reaches 458.8 rSum compared to PCSR's 437.5 (Section 4, results tables).
On CC152K real-world noisy correspondence data, IN2R attains 380.8 rSum versus SPS's 376.3, and 45.2% text-to-image R@1 versus PCSR's 43.7% (Section 4, results tables).

The ablation study on Flickr30K at 60% noise shows rSum rising from 469.1 (inter-modal loss only) to 475.2 after adding the intra-modal loss and to 483.7 after adding the rectification loss, reaching 495.2 for the full IN2R model (Table 3).

The Graph Refiner using multi-head self-attention for neighbor aggregation outperforms both hard (discrete) neighbor selection (479.6 rSum) and simple mean pooling (485.2 rSum), reaching 495.2 rSum (Table 4).

The method uses Section 3.4's Graph-Guided Rectification to retrieve the Top-K=5 intra-modal neighbors and synthesize a continuous soft prototype via multi-head self-attention and mean pooling, replacing discrete noisy-label selection (Section 3.4).

KmQzJ5wQEa.text: SIMPC generates a mirror-point for each noisy input point on the opposite side of the underlying surface and enforces consistency between the denoising targets of a point and its mirror counterpart to localize the clean surface in a fully unsupervised manner (Section 3).

On extremely sparse 5K-point clouds under 1% Gaussian noise, SIMPC achieves a Chamfer Distance of 42.85 (×10⁻⁵) and Point-to-Mesh distance of 11.89 (×10⁻⁵), outperforming the unsupervised baseline Noise2Score3D (50.31 / 17.15) (Table 8).

At higher noise levels (2% and 3% Gaussian noise) on 5K-point clouds, SIMPC still outperforms Noise2Score3D but trails the supervised method StraightPCF, which attains lower CD/P2M scores at all three noise levels (Table 8).

The authors report that SIMPC exhibits slight performance degradation on extremely sparse point clouds and a mild smoothing effect on sharp geometric structures relative to supervised counterparts (Appendix, Table 8 discussion).
SIMPC includes a theoretical manifold-based analysis of deterministic and geometric symmetry underlying the mirror-point construction (Appendix A.5, Appendix A.6).

CKpqRFTRfc.text: MVISTA-4D fuses RGB and depth modalities using learnable modality tokens and a local cross-modality attention with gated residual updates to control feature injection reliability (Section 4.1).

MVISTA-4D achieves geometrically consistent arbitrary-view RGBD generation by using a 13-dimensional spherical coordinate camera embedding in a geometry-aware, deformable epipolar cross-view attention (Section 4.2).
On RoboTwin 4D scene generation, MVISTA-4D attains a Chamfer Distance of 6.51 and SSIM of 90.2, improving over the TesserAct baseline's 7.11 CD and 89.8 SSIM (Table 1).

Test-time action inference backpropagates through the frozen generative model to optimize a trajectory-level latent style code (produced by a TCN-based VAE encoding actions into 32-dimensional tokens) matching the predicted future, refined by a residual inverse dynamics module (Section 4.3).
MVISTA-4D improves downstream robotic manipulation success rate over TesserAct from 67.3% to 72.6% on RLBench and from 33.9% to 43.0% on RoboTwin (Table 3).
On the real-robot 6-task evaluation, MVISTA-4D notably improves the Open Drawer task success rate from 37% to 56% over TesserAct (Table 4).

1rSqVUl7l3.text: KoPE augments Vision Transformer tokens with phase vectors updated via a discretized Kuramoto synchronization equation, coupling rate and phase representations and modulating attention scores through pairwise phase differences (Section on Phase Dynamics/Architecture).

On ImageNet-1K trained for 300 epochs, KoPE improves ViT-Base top-1 accuracy from 82.1% to 83.0% and ViT-Large from 82.8% to 84.0%, while adding only 1-2% extra parameters and about 20% additional FLOPs (Table on ImageNet-1K results).
KoPE matches baseline ViT accuracy while using 20% less training data, demonstrating improved data efficiency (Section on Data Efficiency).
KoPE improves ADE20K semantic segmentation mIoU from 44.10% to 46.94% and COCO panoptic quality (PQ) from 54.51 to 55.53 on ViT-B backbones (Segmentation results table).
KoPE improves CLIP-based zero-shot ObjectNet accuracy by an average of 2.69 percentage points and VTAB adaptation accuracy by 3.75 percentage points (Vision-language results section).
On few-shot visual reasoning, KoPE improves ARC-AGI accuracy from 54.5% to 56.8% on ARC-1 and from 8.3% to 9.8% on ARC-2 (ARC-AGI results section).

Y3K0pPyVcs.text: C²R combines an Attack-Aware Curriculum (AAC), which prioritizes adversarial examples with the smallest robust margins via a perturbation score s(x) = [1 - m̂_rob(x;θ)]₊ estimated with Line-Search PGD for a reported 1.4× speedup, with a Contrastive Robustness Loss (CRL) using instance-level supervised contrast and a class-balanced memory queue (Section 4.1-4.2).

Under PGD attack at ε = 2/255 with IPC=10, C²R achieves 26.19% robust accuracy on CIFAR-10 versus 21.90% for the ROME baseline, 9.56% versus 6.87% on CIFAR-100, and 2.84% versus 1.17% on Tiny-ImageNet (Section 5, Table of main benchmarks).

C²R outperforms prior robust dataset distillation baselines (including MTT, SRe2L, D4M, and ROME) by an average of 2.8% in robust accuracy across CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K subsets under six attacks (FGSM, PGD, CW, VMIFGSM, Jitter, AutoAttack) (Section 5.1).

C²R keeps the average accuracy drop rate under PGD below 66.8% across datasets and exhibits a flatter drop-rate trajectory as the synthetic set size (IPC) scales compared to baselines (Section 5.2, drop-rate analysis).

An ablation shows AAC alone contributes +1.92% and CRL alone +1.23% CIFAR-10 gain, while combining both in C²R yields +3.60%, exceeding the sum of the individual components (Ablation table, Section 5.3).
The paper proves that maximizing the worst-case robust-hinge loss is equivalent to improving the minimum robust margin m̄(x;θ) (Equations 8-9).

LzWyl85Lkc.text: HEDP trains a frozen CLIP backbone with domain-specific visual/textual prompts using an energy regularization loss composed of a boundary loss (constraining in-domain sample energy below a threshold Θ) and a midline loss (aligning batch-mean energy toward a reference Δ) (Methodology, Training Phase section).

At inference, HEDP performs domain selection via a hybrid energy-distance weighting function F(x) = EF(x)/α + DF(x)/β, combining prompt-specific energy factors with distance factors from frozen backbone features (Methodology, Inference Phase section).
HEDP achieves 94.37% accuracy on unseen domains of the CORe50 benchmark, a 2.57 percentage point gain over the prior state of the art (Experiments results table).

On CDDB-Hard, HEDP reaches 93.72% known-domain accuracy and 83.74% unknown-domain accuracy, a 1.76 percentage point improvement over SOTA; on DomainNet it reaches 74.19% known and 67.09% unknown accuracy, a 3.12 percentage point improvement over SOTA (Experiments results table).

HEDP includes a theoretical analysis grounding the energy regularization in Helmholtz free energy, presented with formal proofs in the appendix (Preliminaries: Helmholtz Free Energy section; Appendix Proofs).

GiYWL2NVKs.text: MusicDET uses frequency-guided normalizing flows that decompose energy spectrograms into frequency bands, apply independent invertible transformations per band, and combine them via a global flow to model the distribution of real music (Section 3.2).
On FakeMusicCaps, MusicDET achieves a 4.51% Equal Error Rate in the zero-shot setting, and 0.89% EER in the class-conditional setting where synthetic samples are available during training (Table 1).
On SONICS, MusicDET achieves a 2.89% zero-shot EER and 0.00% EER in the class-conditional setting (Table 2).

Baseline discriminative detectors (e.g., W2V2-AASIST) trained on MusicGen degrade dramatically on unseen generators, reaching 48.7% EER in cross-generator evaluation, whereas MusicDET maintains consistent separation (Figure 4).
MusicDET attains its lowest EER (4.51%) using only 8.13M parameters and an inference speed of 516 music clips per second (Table 3).

Under leave-one-subdomain-out evaluation (excluding jazz or piano), MusicDET retains 2.5-4.1% EER, indicating robustness to distribution shift rather than reliance on dataset-specific artifacts (Table 4).

tBYIaHHTqq.text: MLLM-4D's data curation pipeline repurposes stereo video datasets (via Stereo4D) into 4D spatiotemporal instructional data using per-frame camera poses, object-level 3D point clouds, and Gemini-2.5-flash/GroundedSAM2-derived semantic descriptions, yielding 2M QA pairs across ~100k videos (Section 3, Figure 3).

MLLM4D-Bench is a 6k-question benchmark spanning six subtasks across three categories: independent object motion, camera ego-motion, and object-camera dynamics, with frame-wise temporal tagging (Section 3, Figure 2).
On MLLM4D-Bench, MLLM-4D (Qwen3-VL-8B) achieves 72.7% average accuracy across six subtasks, surpassing Gemini 2.5 Pro (46.6%), GPT-4o (44.9%), VG-LLM (56.3%), and VLM-3R (30.6%) (Table 1).

On the VLM4D benchmark, MLLM-4D (Qwen3-VL-8B) achieves 61.0% overall accuracy (63.1% real, 54.4% synthetic), an 8.8 percentage point improvement over the untuned Qwen3-VL-8B baseline (52.2%) (Table 2).

Ablations show staged training compounds gains on MLLM4D-Bench: 35.3% baseline, 70.1% after SFT alone, 70.5% adding GRPO without the ST-reward, and 72.7% with the full ST-reward-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning (Table 3, Section 5.3).
Reinforcement fine-tuning on MLLM4D-R1-30k data improves VLM4D accuracy from 59.8% to a peak of 63.1% at 30K training samples (Figure 5).

L31hKCWRsN.text: ECHO's sparse confidence gating identifies high-fidelity confidence-estimation 'sweet spots' (primarily root and target depth layers) via offline AUC-based calibration, avoiding full per-layer evaluation (Section 3.2).

ECHO's elastic budget scheduling, under a fixed verification token cap (Eq. 4), prioritizes depth extension when confidence is high and falls back to width expansion otherwise (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1).
At low load (batch size 1), ECHO achieves speedups ranging from 1.63x to 5.35x across benchmarks, with the largest gain of 5.35x on LLaMA3.3-70B (Table 1).
On the industrial-scale Qwen3-235B model, ECHO delivers a 2.02x average speedup, exceeding dynamic and static baselines by 14% and 19% respectively (Section 5.2).
At high load (batch size > 1), ECHO's elastic reallocation yields up to a 14.4% throughput gain at batch size 256 on Qwen3-235B (Figure 5).

Theorem 1 shows width expansion strictly increases coverage probability at truncation depths, and Theorem 2 shows reallocating budget to higher marginal-utility requests improves batch-level throughput in compute-bound serving (Section 4).

4fbBS0s8In.text: MoSA models residual anisotropy via a fourth-order correction tensor decomposed into microplane-constrained redistribution, pre-linear, and post-linear correction terms atop a calibrated isotropic backbone, plus a continuous implicit field for spatial heterogeneity (Section 3.1).
On synthetic PAC-NeRF data, MoSA achieves a mean Chamfer Distance of 13.5, outperforming GIC (13.8) and DEL (14.5) (Table 1).
On real-world data, MoSA achieves a mean PSNR of 31.35 dB versus 30.02 dB for GIC and 30.00 dB for NeuMA, with 92.3% mean SSIM across seven objects (Table 2).
In robot manipulation transfer experiments, MoSA improves elastic rabbit placement success from 42% (isotropic baseline) to 68%, and tower-hanging success from 55% to 82% (Figure 5).

Ablations on the Rabbit scene show removing the redistribution correction tensor drops PSNR by 1.93 dB (to 28.42 dB) and removing heterogeneity modeling drops it by 0.68 dB (to 29.67 dB), versus the full model's 30.35 dB (Table 3).

Directional Jacobian analysis shows the learned anisotropy is physically meaningful: synthetic PAC-NeRF data correctly exhibits minimal directionality while the real Mandarin object shows directional alignment with its geometry (Figure 6).

SXJBFREkWi.text: SPARKLING combines signal preservation (maintaining RMS-scale consistency of activations during width expansion) with symmetry breaking (asymmetric optimizer-state resetting and asymmetric learning-rate re-warmup) to resolve the gradient-coupling 'symmetry lock' problem of copy-based initialization (Section 3.1, Section 4.1).

Under joint 2x2 width expansion (inner and hidden dimensions), SPARKLING achieves 35% FLOPs savings and a 1.49x wall-clock speedup versus training the expanded model from scratch under the same token budget (Table 2, Section 5.2).
Under inner-only 2x expansion SPARKLING saves 20% FLOPs (1.27x speedup), and under hidden-only 2x expansion it saves 25% FLOPs (1.29x speedup) (Table 2).

On MoE models under 2x width expansion, SPARKLING attains the best average performance across 13 downstream tasks, matching or exceeding from-scratch training baselines on most tasks (Table 1, Section 5.1).

Without RMS-preserved scaling, copy-based initialization shows a smaller immediate loss gap but worse late-stage convergence than SPARKLING's RMS-preserved scaling, which improves late-stage convergence under both expert-inner and hidden-dimension growth (Figure 1, Section 3.3).
SPARKLING's effectiveness is confirmed across optimizer families, including AdamW (Section 4.3) and Muon (Section 13).

Sjbl4SueQS.text: ObjEmbed achieves 89.5% average accuracy on referring expression comprehension across RefCOCO/RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg (Table 3).
ObjEmbed reaches a 68.5 average score on local image retrieval (SORCE-1K), roughly 20 points above the strongest competing method's 49.1 (Table 4).
ObjEmbed attains 81.7 points on global multilingual image retrieval benchmarks, including COCO-CN (Table 5).
ObjEmbed encodes all objects together with the full image in a single forward pass using five special tokens and an object projector, rather than per-object crops (Section 3, Figure 2).

ObjEmbed is trained on 1.3M images with 8.1M bounding boxes and evaluated on 18 benchmarks spanning detection (e.g., COCO, COCO-O, ODinW13, FG-OVD, D3), referring expression comprehension, and retrieval (Table 1, Figure 1).
Ablations show that removing token-design and training-objective components degrades performance, and proposal quality substantially impacts downstream accuracy (Tables 6-10).

Latent-Answer Disconnect: drastic alteration of latent tokens yields only marginal variation in the final answer under normal conditions (Section 3.3.1, Table 4).
When imagination content is corrupted, CapImagine's performance drops sharply by 63.4% on the V* benchmark, showing the textual imagination content itself (not latent tokens) drives gains (Table 3).
CapImagine, which teaches explicit textual imagination instead of latent-space reasoning, surpasses the latent-space baseline Monet by 4.0% on HR-Bench-8K and 4.9% on MME-RealWorld-Lite (Table 1).
CapImagine achieves inference efficiency comparable to Monet while outperforming it on vision benchmarks (Figure 5).

fm6Z3wfTae.text: On Personalized-SIMPLER (Google Robot), VAP raises pick task success rate from an 8.5% baseline to 60.3%, and correct-object manipulation from 10.5% to 89.2% (Section 4/Experiments).
On Personalized-SIMPLER (WidowX), VAP improves one task from 0% baseline success to 71.3%, and another from 62.5% to 95.0% (Section 4).
On Personalized-VLABench, VAP improves the leather-bag category from a 33.6% baseline to 89.2% success, with consistent gains across all five object categories (Section 4).
In real-world robot trials, VAP improves pointing-task success from 30% to 80% and pick-and-place success from 18.8% to 56.2% (Section 4, real-world experiments).

VAP is a training-free perceptual adapter combining Grounding DINO for open-vocabulary detection, DINOv2 for visual embedding matching, and SAM2 for segmentation/tracking, requiring only a few reference images of a personal object at test time (Section 3, Method).

IntentRL achieves 27.49% Intent Recall versus 18.45% (Learn-to-Ask) and 12.68% (CollabLLM), and a Quality Score of 2.43 versus 1.44-2.28 for baselines (Table 1).

An ablation removing the Clarification DAG (C-DAG) data-scaling step drops Intent Precision from 36.44% to 5.78%, showing C-DAG-based data augmentation is critical (Table 3).

IntentRL is trained via a two-stage framework (offline RL on expert trajectories, then online refinement with an intent-aware user simulator), and its C-DAG pipeline expands 50 seed samples into 371 intent trajectories and 2,347 dialogue turns (Section on Data Construction/Training Framework).

Theorem 4.2 decomposes the practical TR-CIE error into a temporal integration term C2*h_n^3 plus a state-drift term C3*h_n*d_H(x_n, x_{n-1}) (Theorem 4.2).
On masked discrete flow matching for GPT-2 text generation at NFE=8, TR-CIE achieves 252.15 perplexity versus 495.25 for the Euler sampler (Section 5).
On uniform discrete flow matching at NFE=16, TR-CIE reaches 152.09 perplexity versus 220.20 for Euler (Section 5).
On text-to-image generation (GenEval accuracy) at NFE=8, TR-CIE scores 64.27% versus 61.40% for Euler (Section 5).

Proposition 3.4 extends the concentration result to gradients, giving comparable convergence rates for gradient stability along the training trajectory (Section 3, Proposition 3.4).

Lemma 2.1 shows that under Gaussian input measures, the infinite-prompt softmax attention operator reduces to an affine map T^(U,V)[μ](z) = Vm + VΓK^⊤Qz, i.e., structurally equivalent to linear attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1).

Theorem 4.3 proves that the asymptotic training risk of finite-prompt softmax attention under gradient flow is bounded by the infinite-prompt linear-attention risk plus an error term ε, allowing optimization analyses to transfer from linear to softmax attention (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).

At 6.15x speedup on HunyuanVideo, LearniBridge attains a VBench score of 79.51 versus the uncached baseline's 80.93, retaining most of the quality while accelerating generation (Table 2).

At 4.10x acceleration on WAN 2.1, LearniBridge improves VBench score by 1.28% over the previous state-of-the-art caching method, reaching 80.51, while requiring only 3-5 training/calibration prompts (Table 3).

tibRKqUHcv.text: Algorithm 1 (FairSinkhorn) modifies the Sinkhorn algorithm with an additional group-level projection step to compute exact F-fair transport plans as defined in Definition 3.3 (Section 4, Algorithm 1, Definition 3.3).

Theorem 4.1 derives a finite-sample complexity bound showing the expected deviation of the penalized entropic OT solution from the population optimum scales as O(1/√n), matching standard entropic OT sample-complexity rates (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 bounds the fairness deviation of the bilevel cost-learning approach on unseen data uniformly over a parameterized cost family, with a dependence of the form exp(5R_Θ/ε)√n (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).

Proposition 3.1 and 3.2 establish existence, uniqueness, and dual-variable characterization of fair OT plans under compactness assumptions, ensuring the Sinkhorn-compatible structure used by Algorithm 1 (Section 3, Propositions 3.1-3.2).

Section 4.3 contrasts the two proposed strategies: the penalized formulation stays convex but must be re-solved per batch, while the bilevel cost-learning approach yields a reusable cost function at the expense of non-convex optimization (Section 4.3).

MpYmjfXAnF.text: On LooGLE-v2, SCOUT reaches 78.7% accuracy using only 29.7k tokens, versus Gemini-3-Pro's 68.5% accuracy at 273.9k tokens, roughly a 9x reduction in token cost (Table 1a).
On ∞Bench, SCOUT reaches 85.6% accuracy at 21.4k tokens compared to Gemini-3-Pro's 83.9% accuracy at 259.1k tokens (Table 1b).

Features identified in LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct transfer across model families, improving toxicity detection AUPRC by +19.57 in Mistral-7B-Instruct and +16.76 in Qwen2-7B-Instruct (Section 7.4, Table 3)

oreET6Wz52.text: The pruning framework reduces the memory footprint of Qwen3-30B-A3B by 5.27x, from 61.06GB to 11.64GB, under the P25% pruning with 4-bit quantization (P25% Q4b) configuration (Abstract, Figure 6)

v0vCc5nFRT.text: On the extended CodeNet benchmark, SwiftTrans with Qwen2.5-7B achieves 93.6% average Computational Accuracy versus 91.0% for the F2STrans baseline and 87.8% for GPT-5 in correctness-only mode (Table 1).

On the extended CodeNet benchmark, SwiftTrans with Qwen2.5-7B reduces average execution time to about 190ms, versus 470ms for the F2STrans baseline and 322ms for GPT-5 with correctness-then-efficiency prompting (Table 1).

Multi-Perspective Exploration (MpTranslator) generates diverse translation candidates via parallel in-context learning with hierarchical guidance training, and increasing acceleration layers from 0 to 4 reduces execution time by 425ms (Figure 4).

DiffSelector performs difference-aware candidate selection using pairwise comparison of unified diffs with a bubble-sort-inspired procedure achieving O(n) selection complexity, cutting Order Sensitivity from 64.2% to 6.4% with ordinal guidance training (Methodology; Section 4).

SwiftBench is introduced as a new benchmark of 500 programs across 5 languages specifically constructed to contain inherent inefficiencies for evaluating runtime-efficiency-aware code translation (Section 4).

Xhctwvm3O2.text: On the newly introduced DL3DV-Res artifact restoration benchmark, GSFixer achieves PSNR 16.72, SSIM 0.520, and LPIPS 0.399, outperforming GenFusion's PSNR 14.56, SSIM 0.453, and LPIPS 0.486 (Table 1).
On DL3DV-Benchmark sparse-view 3D reconstruction, GSFixer's performance scales with view count: PSNR 16.21 (3-view), 19.11 (6-view), and 20.60 (9-view) (Table 2).

GSFixer's reference-guided video restoration model conditions a video diffusion prior on both 2D semantic and 3D geometric features to enforce multi-view consistency during artifact restoration (Section 4, Figure 2).
The DL3DV-Res benchmark comprises 137 scenes for artifact restoration evaluation, constructed from artifact-laden 3D Gaussian Splatting renders derived from the DL3DV-10K dataset (Section 5).
GSFixer is evaluated against Difix3D+ and GenFusion as primary baselines across DL3DV-Res (137 scenes), DL3DV-Benchmark (28 scenes), and Mip-NeRF 360 (9 scenes) (Section 5, Figures 4-5).

On public retrieval and ranking benchmarks, LiRA improves macro-average score to 81.23 versus 79.57 for the Qwen3 baseline, including a +3.36 point gain on STS22 (Table 1).

On the newly introduced LazRetrieval benchmark spanning seven low-resource languages (Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Malay, Urdu, Bengali, Filipino), LiRA achieves average nDCG@10 of 77.71 versus 76.78 for the baseline (Table 2).
On reasoning tasks, LiRA yields modest gains over baseline: 89.2 vs 89.1 macro accuracy on MGSM (11 languages) and 62.0 vs 61.5 macro accuracy on X-CSQA (16 languages) (Section on reasoning tasks).

Ablation of LiRA's Arca module shows nDCG dropping to 71.29 (-6.42) without the LLM Critic, to 65.77 (-11.94) without the Embedding Critic, and to 64.29 (-13.42) without the FIFO queue mechanism (Table 5).

vPUInIYURl.text: Protein language models detect repeats via a three-stage mechanism: relative-position attention heads and biochemical neurons build contextual features (Stage I), induction heads attend to aligned repeat tokens while repeat neurons inhibit (Stage II), and MLP neurons refine the final output distribution (Stage III) (Figure 1).

Extracted circuits recover over 85% faithfulness using only about 14-17% of model components, with ESM-3 requiring 149 of 1152 attention heads and ESM-C requiring 102 of 648 attention heads (Figure 2).

ESM-3 and ESM-C achieve 99.8%/99.9% accuracy on synthetic repeats, 99.0%/99.4% on identical repeats, and only 79.0%/79.7% on approximate repeats, showing approximate-repeat detection is markedly harder (Figure 2 accompanying results table).
Neuron sparsity analysis shows only about 3% of MLP neurons per layer (1.7% for ESM-3, 3.17% for ESM-C) are needed to recover 80-85% of circuit faithfulness (Figure 5).
The circuit responsible for approximate-repeat detection functionally subsumes the circuit for exact-repeat detection, evidenced by high cross-task circuit overlap and generalization (Figure 3).

SGUSUm2491.text: A Functional Anchor circuit localized at layers L18-L20 causally triggers memorized answer retrieval under spurious RLVR, identified via Path Patching accuracy recovery and peak Separation Force in the Neural Differential Equations analysis (Mechanistic Intervention section; layers L18-L20).

Structural Adapter layers at L21 and beyond perform representational transformation via weight reorganization, exhibiting high JSD scores in W_up and W_gate peaking at L21-L22 while W_down sustains elevated values (Preliminaries/Empirical Study, JSD Analysis).

During spurious RLVR training, answer-token perplexity decreases while full-text (prompt-side) perplexity increases, termed the Perplexity Paradox, indicating memorization overrides general reasoning pathways (Section: The Perplexity Paradox).

Resetting the Functional Anchor drops accuracy from 98% to 86% on MATH-500 and from 88% to 72% on MinervaMath, while resetting the Structural Adapters drops accuracy from 98% to 92% on MATH-500 and from 88% to 78% on MinervaMath (Ablation Study).

Scaling MLP keys at Layer 18 with an amplification factor produces roughly ±4% accuracy sensitivity, enabling bidirectional causal steering to amplify (α=3.0) or suppress (α=0.2) contamination-driven performance, with no such effect observed on the leakage-free LiveMathBench control (Mechanistic Intervention section).

Control models LLaMA-3.1-8B and OLMo-2-1124-7B show no analogous accuracy-recovery pattern or layer-specific JSD peaks, whereas Qwen3-8B replicates the circuit signature at its scaled Layer 33 (Section: Control Model Comparisons).

Theorem III.8 shows the expected entropy of the assignment distribution decreases monotonically at rate O(ε/(L+1)) with additional views (Theorem III.8).
MSRL achieves 91.00% clustering accuracy on CIFAR-100, outperforming the best competing method by at least 1.9 percentage points (Table II).

An ablation study demonstrates that the cross-view consistency loss component is responsible for measurable performance gains over the base self-representation objective (Table IV).

With Mixed Human data, SAG achieves speedups ranging from 3.72x to 3.84x across tasks with an average performance gain of 29% (Table 2).
On the Kitchen multi-stage manipulation benchmark, SAG achieves a 4.03x speedup while retaining 100% success rates on the initial stages (Table 3).
In real-world pick-and-release evaluation, SAG achieves a 54% success rate at 45.1 Hz inference frequency (Figure 5).

Ablations show removing the real-time pruner drops average success to 82%, removing the one-for-all reusing strategy drops it to 65%, and removing the global sparsity loss collapses it to 48% (Table 4, Section 2).

ejmfnVdW2X.text: PTA improves average accuracy across cross-domain generalization benchmarks from CLIP's 65.64% baseline to 69.38%, outperforming cache-based TDA (67.97%) by 1.41 points (Table 1, Section 4).

PTA outperforms cache-based ADAPT by 0.64 points on cross-domain benchmarks (68.74% for ADAPT) and by 1.20 points on out-of-distribution generalization, reaching 65.61% average OOD accuracy (Table 1, Table 2).
On ImageNet-1K, PTA runs at 81.8 FPS (92% of CLIP's 89.3 FPS inference speed), compared to TDA's 44.6 FPS (50% of CLIP) and ADAPT's 12.9 FPS (14% of CLIP) (Table 4).
On the ModelNet-C point cloud benchmark, PTA reaches 55.13% average accuracy versus 53.70% for Point-Cache and 47.52% for the ULIP baseline (Table 3).
PTA's performance is robust to test-stream ordering, with standard deviations of only 0.02-0.14% across different data orderings (Table 8).

2C6ENeBAZB.text: StableVM's variance-reduction training objective is proven unbiased and variance-reducing relative to standard conditional flow matching, with variance decaying at rate O(1/n) in the number of reference samples n (Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.3).
On ImageNet 256x256 with classifier-free guidance at 80 epochs, StableVM achieves an FID of 1.80 versus REPA's 1.98, and an Inception Score of 272.4 versus REPA's 263.0 (Table 1).
At the SiT-XL/2 scale, StableVM improves FID from REPA's 18.59 to 17.12 at 100k iterations and from 8.13 to 7.58 at 400k iterations (Table 2).

Stable Velocity Sampling (StableVS) with 9 low-variance-regime steps matches the quality of a 30-step baseline on T2V-CompBench with Wan2.2, achieving a PSNR of 31.10 versus 15.61 for a 20-step baseline (Table 5).

On the GenEval T2I benchmark with SD3.5-Large, StableVS achieves FID 0.723 using 9 low-variance steps within a 20-step total budget, close to the 13-step Euler baseline's 0.710, with an LPIPS of 0.021 versus 0.333 for the standard solver (Table 6, Section 3.3).
The optimal split point between low- and high-variance regimes is xi=0.7, yielding an FID of 7.58 at 400k iterations in the split-point ablation (Table 4).

Y4jQjDnVSd.text: On Qwen3-VL-8B, Video-OPD outperforms GRPO on R@0.7 by +4.8 points on Charades-TimeLens (32.4% vs 27.6%), +3.7 points on ActivityNet-TimeLens (35.8% vs 32.1%), and +8.9 points on QVHighlights-TimeLens (50.4% vs 41.5%) (Table 1).

Video-OPD achieves an average improvement exceeding 17% over the base model across temporal video grounding benchmarks, substantially surpassing the roughly 12% average gain obtained by GRPO (Section 1).
Video-OPD requires approximately only 20% of the training cost of GRPO while converging to an optimal policy substantially faster (Figure 6).

The TVDF curriculum component contributes an additional gain of about 2 R@0.7 points on Qwen3-VL-8B, raising performance from 31.1% (Video-OPD without TVDF) to 32.4% (with full TVDF), versus a 23.1% base model score (Table 2).

Unlike off-policy distillation baselines OP-RKD and OP-FKD, which cause noticeable performance degradation on general video understanding, Video-OPD preserves and improves performance on TempCompass, MVBench, and Video-MME (Figure 4).

BvWEy6Pznz.text: Riemannian MeanFlow (RMF) achieves sample quality comparable to prior manifold generative methods while requiring up to 10x fewer function evaluations (Abstract, Section 4).

On promoter DNA design over 88,470 human promoter sequences, Eulerian RMF (x1-parameterization) matches Fisher FM's MSE of 0.030 and k-mer correlation of 0.96 while using only 1 NFE versus Fisher FM's 100 NFE (Table 1).

On protein backbone generation on the SCOPe database, RMF retains 0.87 designability at 10 NFE and 0.82 at 5 NFE, versus FrameFlow's 0.61 and 0.04 and FrameDiff's 0.47 and 0.09 at the same step counts (Table 3).
At the extreme single-step (1 NFE) setting, RMF achieves 0.35 designability while FrameFlow and FrameDiff both collapse to 0.00 (Table 3).
Reward look-ahead guidance reduces promoter design MSE from 0.033 to 0.025 at 1 NFE (Table 2) and increases beta-sheet composition in protein backbones from 0.18 to 0.24 at 5 NFE (Table 4).

The semigroup RMF training objective, which avoids differential terms via a flow-composition consistency identity, produces the most consistent training behavior and highest sample quality among the three parameterizations tested (Proposition 2.3, Figure 3).

YX4rgoI8pB.text: Agent-Omit-8B-RL attains the highest Pass@1 among compared frontier and efficient agents on WebShop (23.57%), TextCraft (87.00%), BabyAI (84.36%), and SciWorld (18.45%) (Table 2, Table 3).
On Qwen3-8B, Agent-Omit-8B-RL reaches 24.56% Pass@1 on DeepSearch using only 4,356 tokens, versus substantially higher token usage for reasoning-model baselines like DeepSeek-R1-0528 (Table 3).
Token cost analysis shows that agent 'thought' tokens account for 45.1% and 'observation' tokens for 52.2% of total context, motivating selective omission (Figure 2, Section 3).

Theorem 5.2 (Bounded Omission Error) proves the deviation between the learned omission policy πθ and the optimal policy π* is upper-bounded by the KL-divergence KL(π*, πθ) scaled by Lipschitz constants Kr' and Kc' (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
Trained agents adaptively omit 3-4 turns of redundant thoughts or observations per trajectory, with peak omission frequency in intermediate turns 3-10 (Figure 6).

CXKhhN5j1N.text: T-LVMOGP scales to multi-output Gaussian processes with over 10,000 outputs via stochastic variational inference supporting mini-batching across both input and output dimensions (Section 3).
On the ERA5 climate dataset, T-LVMOGP achieves MSE of 0.002 ± 0.000 and NLL of -1.564 ± 0.024, outperforming G-MOGP and GS-LVMOGP baselines (Table 5).
On the Copernicus Marine dataset, T-LVMOGP attains MSE of 0.029 ± 0.000 and NLL of -0.439 ± 0.011, exceeding GS-LVMOGP across latent dimensionalities Q=1, 2, and 3 (Table 6).

On the 10x Genomics Visium spatial transcriptomics dataset (5,000 genes across 4,352 spatial locations), T-LVMOGP achieves MSE of 9.189 ± 0.342 versus 11.024 ± 0.350 for GS-LVMOGP at Q=3, using a Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial likelihood for sparse count data (Table 7).
T-LVMOGP trains efficiently at 0.708 ± 0.013 seconds/epoch on ERA5 and 1.230 ± 0.012 seconds/epoch on Copernicus Marine data (Table 5, Table 6).

The model uses a Lipschitz-regularized Residual Connected Neural Network (RCNN) with spectral normalization to map input-latent variable pairs into an embedding space where inducing points are placed (Section 3).

n1eBQxKBne.text: Training on 486 execution-verified trajectories filtered from 274 solved CTF-Dojo challenges (via rejection sampling with a cap of 2 per challenge) yields up to 11.6% absolute Pass@1 gains over Qwen3 baselines across InterCode-CTF, NYU CTF Bench, and Cybench (Table 3, Section 3).

CTF-Dojo-32B reaches an average Pass@1 of 31.9% (InterCode-CTF 83.5%, NYU CTF 10.4%, Cybench 17.5%), approaching Claude-3.5-Sonnet (37.2%) and Cyber-Zero-32B (33.4%) despite using 94.9% fewer training trajectories than Cyber-Zero's 9,464 (Table 3).

CTF-Dojo comprises 658 containerized CTF challenges built via the CTF-Forge pipeline, which achieves over 98% Docker build/run success across three independent validation runs (Table 1, Table 2, Section 2.3).

Incorporating redacted CTF writeups as inference-time hints during data collection raises average solved-task counts across models from 168 to 217 (a 7.4% increase), with the largest gains in Crypto, Reverse-Engineering, and Miscellaneous categories (Table 4, Section 4.1).

Runtime augmentation (randomized ports, file-path shuffling, distractor code, dynamic flag regeneration) increases unique challenges solved by DeepSeek-V3-0324 from 156 to 217 at rollout 4, and by Qwen3-Coder from 169 to 211 (Figure 4, Section 4.2).

MEKj3d9Bf3.text: SafeHarbor achieves a peak benign utility of 63.6% on GPT-4o while maintaining a harmful-request refusal rate of 93.2%, the best benign utility among viable defenses evaluated (Section 3, results tables).
On AgentHarm, SafeHarbor reduces the benign refusal rate to 9.1% on Qwen2.5-7B, compared to 22.7% for LlamaGuard, while maintaining comparable safety on malicious tasks (Table 1).
On AgentSafetyBench with GPT-4o, SafeHarbor achieves an environment-based refusal rate of 62.05% and a text-based refusal rate of 89.78% against harmful requests (Table 2).

SafeHarbor's hierarchical memory tree is built via information-entropy-based evolution (Algorithm 1) combined with adversarial rule generation using Goal Decomposition, Privilege Escalation, and Contextual Reframing strategies (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).

SafeHarbor's two-stage inference pipeline achieves 306.67ms latency, roughly 20x faster than GuardAgent, while requiring only 14GB VRAM versus 30GB for LlamaGuard, without additional training (Section 3.5).

U8x5SYtT5b.text: XDomainBench comprises 8,598 interactive sessions spanning 20 scientific domains (organized into 6 major categories), 4 task categories (Multiple Choice, Factual QA, Reasoning, Code), and 8 realistic trajectory patterns (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
Sessions are constructed at composition orders k in {1,2,3,4}, yielding 20 single-domain pools, 24 two-domain combinations, 10 three-domain combinations, and 8 four-domain combinations (Section 3.2).
Large-scale LLM evaluation shows session success rate drops from 38.7% to 27.1% as composition order increases, with degradation accelerating at higher composition orders (Section 4.2).

Diagnostic analysis separates reasoning collapse into a direct mechanism (integrative cognitive load imposed by domain combination before multi-turn propagation) and an indirect mechanism (interactive trajectory patterns triggering error accumulation and domain confusion) (Section 4.3).

onuLk72nRw.text: scBIG's Gene-Relation Clustering module partitions genes into functional modules by combining semantic embeddings from pretrained foundation models with protein-protein interaction priors in a joint cost matrix (Section 2.1, Equation 1).
The Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder fuses per-cluster expression projections with semantic embedding projections into a shared latent representation for each gene module (Section 2.2, Equation 2).

On the Norman additive-perturbation split, scBIG achieves ρΔ of 0.8496 versus 0.7892 for the CellFlow baseline, a 7.7% relative improvement, along with lower MSE (0.0091 vs 0.0114) and MAE (0.0689 vs 0.0775) (Table 1).

On held-out single-gene perturbations, scBIG improves ρΔD by 38.0% over CellFlow, and on double-gene combinatorial perturbations it improves 20.6% on ρΔD and 35.9% on DES over Linear-scGPT (Table 2, Section 3.2).

Ablations show Gene-Relation Clustering outperforms K-means clustering by 5.2% on ρΔ when the Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder is held fixed, and jointly optimizing correlation and pathway losses yields a further 3.1% gain in ρΔ and 2.7% gain in ρΔD (Table 4, Section 3.5).

w1YnlYvdER.text: Bayesian Conditional Priors (BCP) reformulates multi-label test-time adaptation as an anchor-conditioned Bayesian update in logit space, adding a pointwise-mutual-information correction term PMI(ck, ca) computed from online first- and second-order co-occurrence statistics (Section on Method/Logit Space Implementation).

With a ViT-B/16 CLIP backbone, BCP raises mean average precision from 62.61 (zero-shot CLIP) to 71.79 averaged across COCO2014, COCO2017, VOC2007, VOC2012 and NUS-WIDE, exceeding the BEM baseline's 64.80 mAP by 7.18 points (Table 1).
BCP's per-sample adaptation time is 0.112s versus roughly 0.24s for prior test-time adaptation baselines, i.e., about 2x faster, while requiring no backpropagation (Table 7).

An anchor-correctness ablation shows mAP rises from 72.73 to 80.33 when the selected anchor label is a true positive (Anchor-Hit), but drops slightly (22.15 to 21.32) when the anchor is incorrect (Anchor-Miss), with anchors being correct in 85.38% of confident samples (Table 2).

BCP improves mAP across head, medium, and tail label frequency groups on COCO2014, e.g., head labels rise from 42.47 to 51.84 and tail labels from 57.93 to 69.22, showing gains are not concentrated only on frequent classes (Table 5).
Using two anchor labels instead of one degrades performance (71.79 to 69.93 mAP on ViT-B/16), supporting the design choice of a single anchor for conditioning (Table 10).

oUv02QKUxG.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes that when the proposed dynamic programming conditions hold for an ambiguity-averse MDP, a stationary optimal policy exists among the class of transition-uncertain MDPs considered (Theorem 4.1).

Proposition 4.2 shows value iteration and policy iteration converge under the ambiguity-averse framework, with error bounds of 2γ^n/(1-γ) for value iteration and γ^n for policy iteration after n steps (Proposition 4.2).

Theorem 4.4 proves that, among monotone law-invariant risk measures, only the essential infimum and essential supremum satisfy the dynamic programming conditions for static (non-resampled) transition kernels, while expectation becomes additionally admissible once kernels are resampled at each step (Theorem 4.4).

Theorem 4.5 shows that under an added Wasserstein-1 continuity assumption, expectation is the unique risk measure compatible with dynamic programming for resampled kernels, and no such measure exists for static kernels (Theorem 4.5).

The characterization implies that risk measures such as CVaR, Value-at-Risk, and entropic risk are incompatible with exact dynamic programming under this framework, explaining their lack of tractable recursive solutions (Section 4, following Theorem 4.4/4.5).

vIIk6uur7Z.text: CORE-MTL factorizes the shared multi-task encoder representation into a task-relevant semantic stream and a nuisance residual stream, with task heads reading only from the semantic stream, using Centered Kernel Alignment to enforce structural independence between the streams (Section 2.3).

Theorem 2.3 proves that under linear-Gaussian assumptions with entangled representations, any gradient-balancing algorithm has an irreducible out-of-distribution error floor scaling as sin^2(ψ)·||Σr^T − Σr^s||_F, where ψ measures representation entanglement (Theorem 2.3, Section 2.2).

Theorem 2.4 shows that predicting from the disentangled semantic stream alone bounds the OOD generalization gap by a capacity term plus α·λ_leak·W1(P_s(Zr), P_t(Zr)), i.e., leakage-weighted Wasserstein distance between residual distributions (Theorem 2.4, Section 2.3).
On in-distribution benchmarks, CORE-MTL achieves the best segmentation mIoU on NYUv2 (0.5693, 3 tasks) and on Cityscapes (0.7229, 2 tasks) among compared methods (Table 1, Section 4.2).

On out-of-distribution evaluation, CORE-MTL yields the smallest depth-error gap on GTA5→Cityscapes sim-to-real transfer and the best relative depth error and largest mIoU improvement under Cityscapes-C corruption robustness (Table 2, Section 4.3).

On CelebA scalability experiments, CORE-MTL maintains roughly constant training cost (~300s/epoch) as the number of tasks grows, compared to PCGrad's cost scaling up to 2806s/epoch at 40 tasks (Table 4, Section 4.5).

sxvuK2x3eA.text: MentisOculi is a procedurally-generated benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks (Form Board, Hinge Folding, Paper Fold, Rush Hour, Sliding Puzzle) spanning multiple difficulty levels, used to test whether visual reasoning aids help frontier models (Section on benchmark tasks).

Latent visual tokens (Mirage), fine-tuned on 200 samples per level, outperform text-only MLLMs on Rush Hour only at difficulty Levels 2-3, and this advantage is described as brittle and does not generalize to other levels (Figure 3).

Unified multimodal models (UMMs) using explicit generated interleaved visualizations frequently underperform text-only MLLMs on Rush Hour, showing generated imagery provides no consistent benefit (Figure 3).

When given oracle ground-truth visual chains-of-thought instead of self-generated images, the UMM Gemini 2.5-I matches or exceeds the corresponding text-only MLLM Gemini 2.5 on all tasks, indicating the bottleneck is generation quality rather than an inability to use correct visuals (Figure 5).

Frontier model Gemini 3 shows no increase in token usage from difficulty Level 3 to Level 5 on Rush Hour, unlike humans who reliably spend more time on harder puzzles, indicating a lack of adaptive reasoning effort allocation (Figure 8).
All evaluated models perform at or below chance level on the hardest difficulty, Level 5, across the five MentisOculi tasks (Section on performance benchmarks).

SJ13vBxetN.text: Lazy Likelihood Displacement (LLD), defined formally as a log-likelihood change satisfying Δₜ(x,yₜ) ≤ ϵ, causes stagnation or reduction of likelihood for both correct and incorrect responses during GRPO-based tool-integrated RL training (Definition 4.1, Section 4).

Uncontrolled LLD produces a three-phase failure trajectory in GRPO training on search agents: early stagnation, steady decay around steps 60-120, then acceleration into gradient explosion and collapse (Figure 2, Section 5.1).
By training step 140 under vanilla GRPO, over 50% of sampled correct responses exhibit likelihood reduction, evidencing a self-reinforcing 'death spiral' (Figure 3, Section 5.2).
On Qwen2.5-3B with the NQ+HotpotQA training setting, LLDS regularization improves average performance from 0.312 (GRPO baseline) to 0.360 (LLDS) and 0.430 (LLDS-MA), a +37.8% relative gain (Table 1).
On Qwen2.5-7B with the NQ+HotpotQA training setting, LLDS regularization improves average performance from 0.350 (GRPO baseline) to 0.462, a +32.0% relative gain (Table 2).

LLDS regularization gates the penalty at the response level so it activates only when a response's total likelihood decreases, and applies token-level selectivity so only likelihood-reducing tokens are penalized (Equation 5, Section 5.4).

NxbSbkLNMc.text: xMAE pretraining, using asymmetric masking (80-90% of ECG masked while PPG remains fully visible) combined with directional cross-attention where ECG tokens query PPG representations, outperforms unimodal and multimodal baselines on 15 of 19 downstream tasks (Section 3.2, Tables 1-2).
xMAE is pretrained on approximately 9.4k hours and 3.4M synchronized 10-second ECG-PPG segments (100 Hz) drawn from the MIMIC-III waveform-matched subset covering 2.4k subjects (Section 4).

On classification tasks, xMAE outperforms baselines on 9 of 12 tasks, including hypertension detection (68.8 vs 56.8 AUROC) and ectopic beat detection (87.8 vs 86.2), with statistically significant gains (p<0.05) on 5 tasks (Table 1).
On regression tasks, xMAE outperforms baselines on 6 of 7 continuous-valued tasks, including free-living systolic blood pressure estimation (11.60 vs 11.83 MAE) (Table 2).
xMAE reconstructions preserve physiological ECG-PPG pulse transit timing, achieving a 21.5ms median delay error, a 53.3% reduction versus a multimodal MAE baseline (Figure 3, Section 5.2).

Ablations show continuous (versus random) masking contributes +5.8 AUROC, curriculum (versus fixed) masking ratio contributes +1.9 AUROC, and cross-reconstruction (versus multi-reconstruction) contributes +3.0 AUROC on the hypertension task (Table 4, Section 5.3).

tU3raVqvYe.text: PhaseCoder is a transformer-only spatial audio encoder of approximately 6M parameters with 5 encoder blocks that processes STFT magnitude and phase features from arbitrary multichannel microphone arrays (Section 3.1).

PhaseCoder achieves microphone geometry-agnostic localization, reaching 7.44° azimuth MAE and 86.96% Acc@10 on the LOCATA benchmark, comparable to or exceeding the GI-DOAEnet SOTA baseline (7.82° MAE, 82.48% Acc@10) (Table 2, Section 4.1).

On the RSL2019 test set, PhaseCoder achieves 11.63° azimuth MAE and 82.31% Acc@10, versus GI-DOAEnet's 9.17° MAE and 85.96% Acc@10, showing mixed but competitive cross-dataset generalization (Table 2, Section 4.1).

PhaseCoder is integrated with a LoRA-finetuned Gemma 3n (4B parameters) by prepending spatial tokens to mono audio tokens with BSA/ESA markers, enabling four task types: source localization, spatial reasoning, spatial transcription, and targeted transcription (Section 3.3).

The fine-tuned Gemma model achieves 4.75° azimuth MAE on synthetic localization data, 76.76% accuracy on yes/no spatial reasoning questions, and 44.92% accuracy on targeted transcription (Table 3, Section 4.2).

PhaseCoder's positional encoding converts microphone Cartesian coordinates into spherical coordinates relative to the array centroid, adapting phase modulation embeddings from GI-DOAEnet to achieve geometry invariance, and was trained on 4 million synthetic 250ms clips spanning 3-8 microphone arrays (Section 3.1-3.2).

hWDUpdwRZp.text: Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding (DCCD) is a training-free two-stage inference procedure: an unconstrained draft generation stage for semantic planning, followed by a draft-conditioned constrained decoding stage for structural realization (Section on DCCD method).
On GSM8K with a 1B-parameter model, DCCD improves strict structured accuracy from 15.24% (standard constrained decoding) to 39.04%, a gain of approximately 24 percentage points (Table 2).

On GSM8K with a 1.5B model, DCCD improves accuracy from 49.36% to 73.92% (+24.6 points), and with a 14B model from 86.43% to 95.15% (+8.7 points), showing diminishing but persistent gains with scale (Table 2).
A composed 7B+1.5B model pairing under DCCD outperforms a single 14B constrained baseline on MATH500 while using 39% fewer total parameters (Figure 5).

Under test-time scaling with multiple sampled candidates, DCCD achieves a wider accuracy gap over standard constrained decoding than at single-sample inference, converting additional sampling compute into larger accuracy gains (Figure 6).

The method is evaluated across GSM8K, MATH500, GSM-Symbolic, and FOLIO datasets under constraint types including JSON schemas, expression grammars, and first-order logic formalisms, across models ranging from 1B to 14B parameters (Evaluation section, Table 2).

P9FgQGxHCW.text: Dywave produces event-aligned tokens via three stages: hierarchical embedding using Maximal Overlap Discrete Wavelet Transform (MODWT) to separate detail and context streams, temporal anchor formation via cosine-similarity-based saliency estimation with non-maximum suppression and top-k selection, and dynamic temporal fusion via saliency-weighted pooling (Sections 3.1-3.3).
On the RWHAR gyroscope dataset with a Mamba2 backbone, Dywave improves accuracy from 0.7294 to 0.7761, an approximately 12% gain, over the strongest compared method (Table 1, Section 4).

On RWHAR with a Transformer backbone, Dywave achieves 0.9094 accuracy using only 29.61 tokens, compared to the Ruptures baseline's 0.7761 accuracy at 57.60 tokens, demonstrating both higher accuracy and up to roughly 75% token reduction (Table 2, Section 4).

On the Ego4D benchmark under short-to-long sequence-length transfer, Dywave produces only 35.16 tokens versus 372 tokens for PatchTST while maintaining superior accuracy, demonstrating length-invariant token representations (Section 4.4, Tables 3-4).

Ablations show that removing the hierarchical wavelet embedding (w/oWave) reduces accuracy from 0.7930 to 0.7736, and removing the reconstruction loss (w/oRecon) reduces accuracy to 0.7575 (Table 5, Section 4.5).

Under injected Gaussian noise, Dywave's accuracy degrades more gradually than PatchTST's, indicating improved robustness via adaptive token allocation reflecting signal uncertainty (Figure 9, Section 4.5-4.6).

s87tQaKAER.text: For ZO-GD, the mean-square critical step size satisfies 2/(Tr(H) + 2*lambda_max(H)) <= eta_ms* <= 2/Tr(H), showing dependence on the full Hessian spectrum rather than just the top eigenvalue (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 extends the mean-square stability bound to ZO-GD with momentum (ZO-GDM), showing the critical step size is adjusted by the momentum parameter beta (Theorem 2).
For frozen ZO-Adam, the mean-square stability threshold depends on the spectrum of the preconditioned Hessian P^{-1}H rather than the raw Hessian (Theorem 3).

Empirically, ZO-GD, ZO-GDM, and ZO-Adam all stabilize their trace/curvature statistics near the theoretically predicted mean-square edge-of-stability thresholds when trained on a CNN on CIFAR-10, ResNet20, and a Vision Transformer (Section 5, Figure 2).
Practical stability tracking during training requires only the trace and top eigenvalue of the Hessian, not the full spectrum, via the bounds given in Equations 23-25 (Section 5, Equations 23-25).
Catapult-like dynamics appear when the step size is increased past the mean-square stability threshold in the empirical experiments (Section 5, Figure 3).

mOcTXKawFY.text: Definition 1 formalizes an evolutionary selection model as a DAG G^(T) over trait variables X^(0)...X^(T), heritable factors epsilon^(0)...epsilon^(T), and reproduction/selection indicators S^(0)...S^(T-1), distinguishing it from one-shot static selection models (Section 2, Definition 1).

Lemma 1 shows that repeated evolutionary selection induces conditional dependencies among variables that are absent under static selection models, so applying static-selection graphical models to evolutionary data can yield false causal discoveries (Section 2, Lemma 1).

Theorem 1 proves that the clique-augmented DAG G^+ (Definition 2) fully captures all d-separation/conditional-independence constraints implied by the evolutionary selection model, without needing to explicitly model the selection variables (Section 3, Definition 2, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 establishes that applying standard constraint-based algorithms such as PC or GES (Algorithm 1) to G^+ is sound and complete: oriented edges correspond to true causal relations, while unoriented edges may reflect the presence of selection (Section 3, Theorem 2, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 4 shows that combining heterogeneous data from multiple environments/domains via the CDNOD-based procedure (Algorithm 2) improves identifiability of the evolutionary selection model compared to single-environment data (Section 4, Theorem 4, Algorithm 2).
The proposed identification procedure is validated on synthetic graphs of varying size and on seven real-world datasets spanning biology, agriculture, and social science (Section 5).

UGbyWJEI2h.text: SynGR is evaluated on three Amazon Product Reviews benchmark datasets (Arts, Games, Instruments) against 12 baselines including GRU4Rec, SASRec, BERT4Rec, MISSRec, VIP5, TIGER, MQL4GRec, and MACRec, using HR@1/5/10 and NDCG@5/10 metrics (Table 1).
Compared to the strongest baseline MACRec, SynGR improves HR@10 by 28.58% on Instruments and NDCG@10 by 12.17% on Instruments (Table 1).

An information-theoretic (partial information decomposition) analysis shows that existing alignment-centric fusion baselines such as MACRec capture only about 7.5% synergistic cross-modal information on the Arts dataset, motivating SynGR's design (Figure 1).

Ablation studies (RQ3) show that removing saliency-based masking (w/o SM), unimodal negative samples (w/o UN), or synergistic contrastive learning (w/o SCL) each degrades performance relative to the full SynGR model on Arts and Games (Figure 5).
SynGR achieves roughly 23% faster training and quicker convergence compared to baselines in an efficiency analysis (Figure 3).

HNiFn4aRD5.text: Theorem 1 proves that under conditions of an invertible generator with efficiently computable classical inverse, non-decreasing layer widths, Lipschitz continuity, and LeakyReLU activations, a quantum boson-sampler latent distribution can produce generator outputs that are not efficiently classically sampleable (Theorem 1).

Corollary 1 shows quantum latent distributions can achieve zero GAN-induced distributional distance to a target distribution on a toy dataset while classical (e.g., Gaussian) latent baselines maintain a strictly positive distance gap (Corollary 1, Table 1).
On the toy dataset, the boson-sampler quantum latent achieves an L1 distance of 0.036 +/- 0.001 versus 0.061 +/- 0.001 for a Gaussian latent baseline (Table 1).

On the QM9 molecular dataset with size-16 latents, the boson-sampler latent achieves an FCD of 1.160 +/- 0.06 with 2522 +/- 65 valid and unique molecules, versus FCD 1.529 +/- 0.08 and 1814 +/- 115 valid/unique molecules for a Gaussian latent baseline (Table 2).

Generative models using latents from a real ORCA Computing PT-2 photonic quantum processor achieve an FCD of 1.410 +/- 0.07 on QM9, closely matching the simulated boson-sampler FCD of 1.414 +/- 0.07, and both outperform classical baselines (Table 4).

On CIFAR-10 with a StyleGAN architecture, quantum and classical latent types show no meaningful difference in Inception Score (approximately 7.54-7.66), indicating the quantum advantage does not transfer to this larger natural-image setting (Appendix H).

lK1El77o4Q.text: Class Subspace Orthogonalization (CSO) is applied on top of four existing backdoor detectors -- MMBD, MLBD, Neural Cleanse (NC), and PT-RED -- to produce CSO-augmented variants evaluated on CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and TinyImageNet (Section 4).
On CIFAR-10 against the BadNet attack, MMBD-CSO improves detection accuracy to 96% versus 86% for the base MMBD detector (Table showing MMBD vs MMBD-CSO results, Section 4).

The paper introduces a novel mixed clean/dirty-label (X-to-X) poisoning attack combining mislabeled source-to-target samples with correctly-labeled non-source trigger samples, which reduces MMBD-CSO detection accuracy from 96% (on standard BadNet) to 70% (on the mixed-label variant), demonstrating it is markedly harder to detect (Section 4, mixed-label attack results).
On the 1-pixel mixed-label attack variant, MMBD-CSO attains 94% detection accuracy compared to only 20% for the base MMBD detector (Section 4).

Ablation results show CSO's benefit requires class-specific (rather than global) feature masking, improving detection from 36% to 88% on mixed-label BadNet, and that the method remains effective with as few as 5 clean images per class (Section 4, ablation study, Table on Nimg/class-specific masking).

An ablation over the orthogonalization penalty parameter lambda shows detection performance is stable once lambda >= 200, and CSO adds only modest computational overhead measured on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti (Section 4, ablation on lambda).

ItPwwWxu2L.text: IDRBench evaluates 10 LLMs, including GPT-4o-mini, o1-mini, o3-mini, Gemini 1.5-pro, Gemini 2.0-flash, Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.3-70B, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, DeepSeek-v3, and DeepSeek-r1, on three progressive interdisciplinary-research tasks (Section 4).

On the IDR Paper Identification (IPI) task, which uses a 1:10 positive-to-negative sampling ratio (120 positive vs. 1,200 negative papers), the best zero-shot model (Llama-3.1-70B) reaches only 0.416 F1 versus a 0.176 random baseline (Section 3.2.1, Table 2).
On the IDR Idea Integration (I3) task, zero-shot average F1 falls from 0.550 at difficulty Level 1 to a 58.8% relative drop at the harder Level 2 (Section 3.2.2, Table 3).

On the IDR Idea Recommendation (I2R) task, scored by Swiss-tournament Mean Reciprocal Rank, Gemini 1.5-pro is the top performer at both difficulty levels (0.703 at Level 1, 0.662 at Level 2) (Section 3.2.3, Table 4).

Generated IDR ideas show high semantic similarity to ground truth (avg. 0.756 for integration reasoning, 0.812 for abstracts) but very low lexical overlap (BLEU 0.010-0.018), indicating models grasp conceptual links but cannot generate detailed methodological content (Section 5.2, Table 6).
Positive IDR samples disproportionately combine Computer Science with Physics or Quantitative Biology (50%) compared to the general arXiv distribution (23%) (Figure 3).

MuyXpH3GL1.text: MatchFixAgent produces (in)equivalence verdicts for 99.2% of 2,219 translation pairs drawn from 24 GitHub projects across 6 language pairs, compared to 71.6% coverage for prior baseline approaches (Section 4.1.1, Table 2).
MatchFixAgent repairs 50.6% of inequivalent translations versus 18.5% for prior work, a 32.1 percentage-point improvement (Section 4.3, Table 3).
Ablating both the semantic analyzer and test generator reduces validation accuracy by 42.3%, while removing the semantic analyzer alone reduces it by 39.7% (Section 4.5).

MatchFixAgent requires only 1,650 lines of code plus roughly 280 additional lines per new language pair, and is reported to be 11.6x cheaper to develop than Oxidizer, 6.6x cheaper than AlphaTrans, and 2.3x cheaper than Skel (Section 1, Section 4.4.1).
Tests generated by MatchFixAgent raise code coverage from 89.6% to 98.1% (Section 4.3).

Manual review of 145 disagreement cases found MatchFixAgent's verdict was correct 60.7% of the time, with baseline errors attributed mainly to inadequate unit tests (42 cases) and language-interoperability bugs (27 cases) (Section 4.2.1).

NpSI4x2vBS.text: Definition 2.3 formalizes 'large' step sizes using only local Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, requiring the step size to periodically exceed twice the local smoothness threshold, matching empirically observed edge-of-stability behavior (Definition 2.3).
Proposition 2.5 establishes that the proposed equality line-search method (Algorithm 2) is Lipschitz-aware without requiring second-order information (Proposition 2.5).
Lemma 3.1 shows sharpness converges to its global minimum of 2/K, where K is the number of classes (Lemma 3.1, Section 3.1).

Empirically, the loss decreases nonmonotonically while the product of step size and sharpness stays above the edge-of-stability threshold of 2 throughout training, with methods reaching edge-of-stability right from the start (Abstract, Figure 1).

Reaching the globally minimal sharpness too early in training slows convergence and generalization; the proposed NLS-ub variant, which caps step sizes below K, avoids this and achieves better practical performance (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

27m3BuajLs.text: The Hierarchical Pose-free Memory Compressor (HPMC) recursively compresses historical latents through local and global compression stages to maintain coherent visual memory over 1000+ frames in complex real-world environments without explicit camera poses (Section 3, Abstract).

Uncertainty-aware Action Labeling (UAL) discretizes continuous motion into a tri-state label (no-operation, discrete action, uncertain) to prevent noisy trajectory estimates from corrupting action-response learning (Section 3.2).

The Revisit-Dense Finetuning (RDD) strategy uses a compact 30-minute dataset with dense viewpoint revisits, motivated by the finding that memory activation saturates after only 100 training sequences (Section 3.3).
Infinite-World achieves an ELO rating of 1719 versus 1542 for HY-World-1.5, and the best Memory Consistency rank (1.92) among compared models (Table 1).
Ablation shows RDD finetuning improves the Memory Consistency score from 2.40 to 1.83, and UAL reduces action error from 2.95 to 2.17 (Table 2).
Memory consumption plateaus at roughly 45GB under hierarchical compression, enabling inference over 1300+ frames, versus linear memory scaling in baseline methods (Figure 5).

tJuroOO1ob.text: MARLS formalizes cooperative multi-agent RL with submodular joint rewards, and finding the optimal policy is shown to be NP-hard even in the single-step setting via a reduction to submodular maximization under partition matroid constraints (Section 3.1, Section 4.1.1).

Theorem 1 shows the greedy policy optimization algorithm achieves a 1/2-approximation guarantee, with value at least half the optimal value minus an error term of order epsilon*K*H with high probability, and time complexity polynomial in the number of agents K, O(K*H*|S||A|*max{|S|, epsilon^-2 log(K|S||A|H/delta)}) (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 gives a UCB-based greedy value-iteration algorithm for unknown dynamics achieving a 1/2-approximation regret bound of O(S^2*A*H^3*K^2*log(SATHK/delta)*logT + H^2*K*S*sqrt(A*T*log(SATHK/delta))), sublinear in T and scaling only linearly in the number of agents K (Section 4.3, Theorem 2).
Lemma 1 introduces a marginal value decomposition that enables sequential per-agent optimization even though the optimal joint policy is not itself decomposable across agents (Section 4, Lemma 1).

The framework is presented as the first formal treatment of cooperative multi-agent RL with submodular rewards capturing diminishing marginal returns from adding agents, in contrast to standard additive-reward MARL formulations (Section 3.1).

yFUmcOtUYD.text: The judge-aware ranking framework extends the Bradley-Terry-Luce model with judge-specific discrimination parameters, jointly estimating latent model quality and judge reliability from pairwise comparisons without reference labels (abstract only).

The maximum likelihood estimator for the judge-aware model is proven identifiable up to natural normalizations and consistent with asymptotic normality, enabling confidence intervals on score differences and rank comparisons (abstract only).
The framework achieves higher agreement with human preferences than unweighted Bradley-Terry-Luce baselines across benchmarks (abstract only).

The method attains superior data efficiency relative to unweighted baselines, addressing the failure mode where more data can make evaluation more confidently wrong under misspecified aggregation (abstract only).
The framework produces calibrated uncertainty quantification for LLM leaderboard rankings (abstract only).

YUQPbg4sQz.text: ProAct-Helper's 7B variant achieves 76.56% mF1 on trigger detection, a 6.21% improvement over the strongest closed-source baseline, Gemini-2.5-Pro at 55.94% (Table 1).
ProAct-Helper improves task detection mF1 by 17.09% and step detection mF1 by 11.72% over the best closed-source baseline models (Table 1).
In online decision-making, ProAct-Helper raises the parallel-action rate to 19.41% versus 3.83% for Gemini-2.5-Pro, a 15.58 percentage-point gain, while saving 0.361 steps per video (Table 1).
Under oracle trajectories in the text-only action-selection simulation, ProAct-Helper achieves 33.95% parallel actions versus 29.52% for Gemini-2.5-Pro and 28.11% for a greedy baseline (Table 3).
In the ablation of the Hierarchical Binding Module, adding the Task-Step binding loss contributes a combined +3.69% mAcc improvement over the base model (Table 2).

NBMCwxTRSA.text: GEM reformulates EraseFlow's trajectory-based unlearning loss into a teacher-guided contrastive velocity-matching objective through a five-step derivation culminating in Equation 14 (Section 4).
For nudity erasure on Flux, GEM reduces the I2P unsafe rate to 6.77% versus 9.77% for EraseFlow, and the T2I-RP unsafe rate to 19.63% versus 36.66% for EraseFlow (Table 2).
GEM completes the nudity-erasure training run in 3 minutes 27 seconds versus 15 minutes 58 seconds for EraseFlow (Table 2).
For bloody/gore erasure, GEM reaches a 50.77% unsafe rate on T2I-RP versus 65.47% for EraseFlow, and achieves a 0% unsafe rate on basic prompts versus 20% for prior work (Table 3).
For celebrity erasure, GEM retains 83% average utility on related concepts such as Einstein versus 77.33% for UCE (Tables 4-5).
GEM transfers to Stable Diffusion 3, achieving 90% average concept retention while maintaining strong erasure performance (Table 6).

83HqzmZab8.text: MDGMIX reveals severe data redundancy in multi-domain graph pre-training, showing that model performance is maintained even after randomly discarding up to 90% of pre-training data (Figure 2).
MDGMIX's boundary-aware subgraph mixing selects boundary nodes via domain-center distance and mixes cross-domain subgraphs using a mixing coefficient of λ=0.5 (Section 4).

In one-shot node classification across 8 datasets (Cora, CiteSeer, Pubmed, Photo, Computers, Squirrel, Chameleon, OGBN-Arxiv), MDGMIX attains the top accuracy on every dataset, e.g., 68.40±8.34 on Photo and 55.28±7.73 on Pubmed (Table 1).

MDGMIX combines hierarchical coarse- and fine-grained discrimination with lightweight prompt weighting for cross-domain transfer, and removing any of the boundary-detection, domain-classification, or decomposition components degrades performance in the ablation study (Table 3).

MDGMIX occupies the optimal lower-left region of the pre-training memory-versus-time efficiency plot, with fine-tuning parameter count scaling only linearly in the number K of source domains (Figure 4).

g9fZTb53kL.text: Sponge Tool Attack (STA) rewrites input prompts under a strict query-only access assumption to convert concise, efficient tool-augmented reasoning trajectories into unnecessarily verbose and convoluted ones (abstract only).
STA uses an iterative, multi-agent collaborative approach with explicit rewritten-policy control to generate high-fidelity, benign-looking prompt modifications (abstract only).
STA preserves task semantics and user intent, remaining stealthy while inducing substantial computational overhead in agentic reasoning trajectories (abstract only).
STA is validated across 6 models (open- and closed-source), 12 tools, 4 agentic frameworks, and 13 datasets spanning 5 domains (abstract only).

YKamMflrv7.text: PromptRL achieves 0.97 GenEval, 0.98 OCR accuracy on OCR-1k, and a PickScore of 24.05 when using the prompt enhancer (PE), versus 0.94 GenEval without PE (Table 2, Table 3).

PromptRL requires over 2x fewer rollouts than naive flow-only RL to reach comparable text-to-image generation performance, reaching GenEval parity with FlowGRPO using roughly 50% fewer rollouts (Figure 5).
PromptRL improves FLUX.1-Kontext's EditReward from a baseline of 1.19 to 1.43 using only 0.06 million rollouts, surpassing Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (1.37) and matching ReasonNet (1.44).
In multi-reward joint training, PromptRL simultaneously attains 0.93 GenEval, 0.96 OCR, and 23.94 PickScore (Table 4).
An ablation on the prompt retention mechanism finds retaining m=2 original prompts per group of 8 yields the best GenEval score of 0.94 without PE (Table 6).
The prompt enhancer generalizes to an unseen model, improving SANA's GenEval score from 0.62 to 0.70 (Table 8).

niQUth28zn.text: The demographic parity gap of majority-vote aggregated labels is bounded above by an exponentially decaying term in the number of annotators R, of the form sum over groups a of E[e^{-R K_phi(a,X)}] (Proposition 3.2).

Under interpretable conditions on annotator skill, both Majority Vote and Bayesian aggregation are shown to achieve asymptotically unbiased fairness gaps relative to ground-truth labels as crowd size grows (Theorem 3.4).

For majority voting with R annotators, the aggregated fairness gap is bounded by epsilon(R) times the sum of individual annotators' fairness gaps, showing majority voting can amplify rather than average out bias (Proposition 3.6).
