Convergence of the fairness gap to the ground-truth value requires a majority of annotators to have skill exceeding 0.5 plus a margin epsilon; without this, majority voting fails to converge (Section 3, following Proposition 3.6).
FairCrowd, a post-processing method, enforces a strict epsilon-fairness constraint on the output of any aggregation rule while provably bounding the resulting accuracy loss (Theorem 4.1).

SKH7vcWZSv.text: The Expanding Cost Algorithm (ECA) achieves a (1+sqrt(2)) approximately 2.414-approximation to justified representation (JR) in transit stop placement, and this ratio is shown to be tight (Theorem 3, Section 4).

ECA's JR approximation guarantee holds for any transit cost function satisfying the triangle inequality, by growing a 'cost radius' around pairs of candidate stops rather than distance-based radii around single stops (Section 4, Algorithm 2).
Clustering-based algorithms for this problem are constrained to at best a 3-approximation for justified representation, strictly worse than ECA's 2.414-approximation (Proposition 4).
Despite its superior JR guarantee, ECA fails to achieve any bounded (alpha, beta)-core approximation for any alpha, beta >= 1, motivating the lambda-Hybrid algorithm (Proposition 5, Section 5).
A constant-factor approximation to proportional fairness in the underlying clustering problem is shown to yield a constant-factor approximation to the core solution concept (Section 5).

6OhhF3uPaK.text: OmniMoE with roughly 1.7B active parameters (6.4B-A1.7B configuration) achieves 50.9% average zero-shot accuracy across seven benchmarks (MMLU, TriviaQA, ARC, PIQA, HellaSwag, OBQA, Winogrande), versus 50.2% for DeepSeekMoE (coarse-grained) and 48.9% for PEER (fine-grained) (Section 3.1).
OmniMoE reduces inference latency to 6.7ms at 4,096 tokens, a 10.9x speedup over PEER's 73ms and a 15.2x speedup over DeepSeekMoE's 102ms, at comparable memory footprint (Table 1, Figure 4).

OmniMoE's architecture reduces routing complexity from O(N) to O(sqrt(N)) over the number of atomic experts N, enabling scaling to a much larger expert pool at fixed active-parameter budget (Section 3).
OmniMoE converts the scattered memory lookups of fine-grained expert retrieval (as in PEER) into contiguous, reusable reads via a hardware-efficient scheduling mechanism (Section 3).

gNwwzeqPF0.text: The Diffusion Value Function (DVF) assigns each agent a value component by diffusing rewards over the influence graph with temporal discounting and spatial attenuation, and is shown to admit a Bellman fixed point (Section 3.2, Proposition 3.3).
DVF decomposes the global discounted value function via an averaging property over agents' local value components, proven as a formal proposition (Proposition 3.4, Section 3.2).

Diffusion A2C (DA2C), an actor-critic algorithm built on DVF as a drop-in critic, is presented together with Learned DropEdge GNN (LD-GNN), a sparse message-passing actor for decentralized learning under communication constraints (Section 4.1, Algorithm 1).

DA2C with DVF improves average reward by up to 11% compared to local-critic and global-critic baselines, evaluated on firefighting and distributed vector graph coloring (computation) benchmarks (Section 5).
DVF is scalably estimated in practice using graph neural networks operating over the influence graph rather than requiring exact diffusion computation (Section 3.2).

BypcZOrSUV.text: RaBiT's coupled quantization-aware training (QAT) enforces a negative correlation of approximately -0.50 between parallel binary residual paths, versus near-zero correlation for standard QAT (Table 1, Figure 2).

On Llama2-7B at 2-bit precision, RaBiT achieves 5.78 WikiText-2 perplexity and 61.51% average QA accuracy, outperforming QTIP (5.86 PPL) among other binary and vector-quantization baselines (Table 2).
Ablations show coupled QAT alone improves perplexity from 6.55 to 5.84, and the two-stage Iterative Residual SVID initialization further refines it to 5.78 (Table 5).
RaBiT delivers a 4.49x inference throughput speed-up over FP16 models on an RTX 4090 via matmul-free binary inference, alongside a 50% reduction in training memory footprint (Table 6, Section 4.2).

RaBiT maintains competitive 2-bit accuracy across Gemma3 models spanning 1B to 12B parameters (Table 3), and shows superior performance on harder benchmarks including BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval (Table 4).

O6tuJZIv0u.text: Q-Delta's query-conditioned prediction and key-retrieved value prediction occupy largely decorrelated directions in value space, with mean cosine similarity of approximately 0.07 between the two signals (Section 3.2, Figure 2).

Q-Delta's update rule combines mixed key-query prediction errors via a learnable coefficient λt, with a sequential recurrence (Eq. 19) and a chunkwise parallel formulation (Eqs. 26-27) for efficient training (Section 3.3).

Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 establish one-step contraction and global stability with geometric error decay for the Q-Delta state update, and empirical measurement shows the contraction quantity βt·at concentrated around a mean of 0.043 (Section 3.3.3, Figure 3).
On zero-shot language modeling benchmarks, Q-Delta achieves the best average accuracy among compared methods at both 340M (47.24) and 1.3B (53.47) parameter scales (Table 2).
On the synthetic S-NIAH retrieval benchmark at 1.3B scale, Q-Delta attains a 90.02 average score with especially large gains at longer context lengths such as 4K tokens (Table 3).
Ablations confirm the learnable λt mixing coefficient outperforms fixed scalar alternatives, and query-based feedback contributes consistent gains across configurations (Table 5).

kOgsGq2mfC.text: SpikingLeNet achieves an average test-accuracy improvement of 6.22% over the best ANN baseline across four mmWave datasets, e.g. 83.70% versus 74.39% on AOPHand, at matched parameter budget (~4.19M) (Table 1).
SpikingLeNet reduces theoretical per-sample energy consumption to 1.45-2.53 microjoules versus 7.35-7.36 microjoules for the best ANN baseline (RNN), a 3.64x reduction (Table 2).

The Discriminative Index (Eq. 6) and Frequency-Matching Score (Eq. 9) are proposed to quantify how well LIF neuron low-pass filtering aligns with the discriminative frequency spectrum of mmWave data (Section 3.2-3.4).
A maximum-deviation rule (Definition 3.4, Algorithm 1) identifies a reference boundary β† for the membrane decay factor without requiring accuracy-based hyperparameter sweeps (Section 3.4).

Accuracy peaks at an intermediate decay factor β* occurring before the reference boundary β†, confirming a non-monotonic relationship between low-pass filtering strength and task accuracy (Figure 4, Section 4.4).
Ablations show that hard low-pass filtering underperforms tunable LIF dynamics because it indiscriminately removes high-frequency cues needed for discrimination (Figure 5, Section 4.5).

jUE8i1vAKJ.text: STAR tracks a rank-K evolving principal subspace of input structure via the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm and interpolates task-supervised and structure-aware routing logits using a coefficient α (Definition 3.1, Section 3).

On synthetic HMM-based language modeling with K=40 experts, STAR reaches mutual information I(e,s)=0.98 between experts and latent states versus 0.24 for baselines, while normalized routing entropy stays stable rather than collapsing to 0.17 as in baselines (Section 4, Figure 3).
The interpolation coefficient α decreases over the course of training, indicating growing reliance on GHA-driven structure-aware gating as training progresses (Figure 4).

On LLaMA-MoE pretraining with 30B tokens, STAR improves average zero-shot accuracy from 40.65% to 41.31% at the 182M scale and from 42.69% to 43.93% at the 469M scale over the baseline router (Table 1).

On GLUE finetuning with an (8,4) expert configuration, STAR achieves 82.24% average accuracy versus 81.77% for a cosine router baseline, and on ImageNet-C severity-5 corruption with test-time adaptation, STAR reaches 24.19% versus 22.63% for the baseline (Table 2, Table 3).
The added computational overhead of GHA-based routing is O((m+1)BKd) + O(K²d), described as negligible relative to expert MLP computation (Appendix A).

M2aE1iEFHj.text: Consecutive merged model checkpoints concentrate more than 94% of PCA variance in a single principal component, forming an approximately one-dimensional (rank-1) linear manifold, in contrast to raw unmerged checkpoints which disperse variance across multiple components (Section 4.2).
This rank-1 subspace structure persists over extended training horizons when the checkpoint window size satisfies n>4 (Section 4.2).

Extra-Merge extracts the principal direction via PCA over a sliding window of K=4 merged checkpoints and extrapolates along it using an adaptive greedy line search, θ_extra(k) = θ_t^avg + k·δ·v̂ (Section 5).

Theorem 5.3 shows averaging reduces the expected distance to the loss landscape's low-curvature 'river' direction by O(1/N), and Theorem 5.4 shows PCA recovers the true descent direction when signal-to-noise ratio exceeds 1 (Section 5.1).

Extra-Merge yields consistent validation loss reductions across GPT-2 and LLaMA model families spanning 124M to 2B parameters, and generalizes to checkpoints trained with the Muon optimizer (Figure 6, Table 1, Figure 7).
On Pythia-12B, Extra-Merge yields a +0.59% average accuracy improvement on downstream zero-shot tasks relative to standard merging (Table 1).

6xeSRifGeL.text: PGS achieves a 53.8% repair success rate (RSR) on HumanEval with DeepSeek-Coder-V2, versus 43.7% for Reflexion (Table I).
On MBPP with DeepSeek-Coder-V2, PGS reaches 25.0% RSR compared to 16.2% for Self-Debugging (Table I).
With DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-32B, PGS attains 63.6% RSR on HumanEval versus 45.5% for Self-Debugging (Table I).
PGS yields a 23.1%-37.3% relative improvement in pass@1 over prior test-driven-development (TDD) refinement methods (Section IV).
The 'Min Length' failing-counterexample selection strategy achieves 74.5% pass@1, outperforming a maximum-coverage selection strategy by 3.0 points (Table III).
Adding property-based-testing (PBT) feedback raises correction rate from 46.6% (public tests alone) to 75.9% on LiveCodeBench (Section IV-C, RQ2).

Ir9AuzGbMB.text: PretrainZero improves Qwen3-4B-Base MMLU-Pro accuracy from 51.94 to 60.37 (+8.43 points) after the pretraining stage (Table 1).
PretrainZero improves Qwen3-4B-Base SuperGPQA accuracy from 26.32 to 32.28 (+5.96 points) after the pretraining stage (Table 1).
PretrainZero improves Qwen3-4B-Base math-average accuracy from 42.53 to 53.13 (+10.60 points) after the pretraining stage (Table 1).
After subsequent post-training, PretrainZero's gains persist as +2.35 on MMLU-Pro, +3.04 on SuperGPQA, and +2.81 on math average (Table 3).

PretrainZero uses an adversarial min-max mask-generation/mask-prediction framework trained via reinforcement learning directly on the unlabeled Wikipedia pretraining corpus for 2000 optimization steps, requiring no external reward model or SFT cold start.
PretrainZero is compared against Continue Pre-Training, Supervised Fine-Tuning without CoT, and a Random RLPT baseline with passive (non-adversarial) mask selection.

88SzQMw0pP.text: Probabilistic Multi-Variable Cardinality Branching is formally introduced in Section 2.3 and its branching hyperplane construction (splitting on sums over predicted-upper-set and predicted-lower-set variables) is given in Section 3.1 (Theorem 3).

On Multi-Knapsack Problem instances with (m,n) in {(10,250),(10,500),(30,250),(30,500)}, the method achieves speedups of at least 500% in several settings and a minimum average speedup of at least 50%, versus Gurobi/COPT baselines (Section 4.1.1, Section 4.2, Figures 2-4).

On Set Covering Problem instances with (m,n) in {(1000,10000),(1000,20000),(2000,20000)}, the method attains uniform speedups of at least 1000% across most testing instances (Section 4.1.1, Section 4.2).

On a real-world Security-Constrained Unit Commitment benchmark built from the IEEE 118-bus dataset over 96-hour horizons, the method achieves an average speedup of at least 50% across configurations (Section 4.1.1, Section 4.2).
Section 4.2 notes instability of the observed speedup across solver heuristic parameter settings (L, M, H) and across datasets, rather than reporting formal ablations.

mURSJDd7hU.text: HDTree combines an encoder, a hierarchical tree codebook (HTC) structured as a binary tree of code vectors, and a quantized-diffusion decoder to model tree-node transitions instead of branch-specific network modules as in TreeVAE (Section 3.2).
On the LineageVAE dataset, HDTree attains 62.0% local temporal consistency at Day 6 versus 60.3% for semi-supervised LineageVAE, and 38.4% at Day 4 versus 30.4% for TreeVAE (Table 3).
On the C. elegans dataset, HDTree attains 45.8% versus 32.5% for TreeVAE in the 300-500 window, and 66.3% versus 62.8% in the 500-750 window (Table 3).

An MNIST ablation shows the full HDTree model reaches a dendrogram purity (DP) of 92.7, dropping to 87.4 without the hierarchical tree codebook, 84.1 without the hierarchical quantization loss (HQL), and 78.9 without the self-consistency loss (SCL) (Table 4).
HDTree is benchmarked against TreeVAE on general datasets and against single-cell-specific baselines GeneFormer, CellPLM, and LangCell on biological data (Table 1 and Table 2).

UTIylOfVUb.text: The paper bounds the ZO empirical-NTK approximation error as ||ΔK||_F ≤ ϵ·Ξ_t·√V with ϵ = O(√(ln V / P)), where V is the output size and P the number of ZO perturbation samples (Section 3.3.2).

Lemma 1 (Section 3.1), an inner-product form of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, shows that projecting n points in R^d to dimension P = O(ln n / ϵ^2) preserves inner products within error ϵ independent of d, underpinning the dimension-free bound.

Section 3.3.2 concludes ZO learning-trajectory fidelity depends primarily on output vocabulary size V rather than model parameter dimension d, giving theoretical justification for ZO methods scaling to billion-parameter LLM fine-tuning.
Synthetic validation in Table 1 varies output size V from 2 to 1000 at fixed projection dimension P=50 and confirms approximation error scales as √V, matching the theoretical prediction.

Experiments on OPT models from 125M to 1.3B parameters on SST-2 (Section 3.4) show that as P increases from 1 to 100, ZO learning trajectories converge toward first-order training trajectories, with the perturbation dimension P needed for alignment remaining constant despite a 10x increase in parameter count.

bmKHxLWkz9.text: CoRe improves MBPP accuracy on LLaDA-8B-Base from 15.60% to 24.80% under low-confidence-based decoding (a +9.2 point gain), and from 21.20% to 29.60% under top-k decoding (Table 1).
CoRe improves HumanEval pass rate on LLaDA-8B-Base from 12.20% to 17.07% (low-confidence base) and from 17.07% to 22.56% (top-k base) (Table 1).

Compute-matched ablations show random remasking (15.60%→16.60% on MBPP) and margin-based remasking (15.60%→17.40%) yield far smaller gains than CoRe's context-brittle token identification (15.60%→24.80%) (Table 2).

The ReMDM-conf baseline degrades MBPP accuracy by 6.4 percentage points relative to the base decoder, motivating CoRe's use of adversarial context perturbation to find brittle tokens instead (Table 2).

CoRe computes instability scores from context-perturbed negative log-likelihood and revises the most unstable tokens every E=8 steps within the [0.25, 0.75) fraction of the decoding trajectory (Algorithm 1).
Instability scores of tokens that get revised form a distinct heavy tail, while unchanged positions cluster near zero, visually separating brittle from stable tokens (Figure 3).

14RUKmdy1O.text: GenExam comprises 1,000 exam-style text-to-image prompts spanning 10 subjects, organized under a four-level taxonomy of 40 categories, 132 subcategories, and 236 detailed topics (Section 3.1).
GPT-Image-1 attains the top strict score of 12.1% and relaxed score of 62.6%, ahead of Seedream 4.0 (7.2% strict, 53.0% relaxed) and Imagen-4-Ultra (6.9% strict, 53.4% relaxed) (Table 2).
Qwen-Image, the best-performing open-source model, scores only 0.3% strict and 27.5% relaxed, versus 12.1%/62.6% for GPT-Image-1, illustrating a large open-vs-closed-source gap (Table 2).

Each sample carries fine-grained scoring points (averaging 6.9 per sample) used to grade semantic correctness and visual plausibility (spelling, logical consistency, readability) separately (Section 3.1).

Figure 2 presents example prompts and reference images illustrating the 10 covered subjects, including mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, geography, economics, music, history, and engineering (Figure 2).

B3Z3rWo4t6.text: Lower local intrinsic dimension (LID) is associated with stronger AI-AI alignment, stronger AI-brain alignment (EBA), and higher ImageNet-1K accuracy (Figure 3B-D).

The correlation between LID and alignment/generalization peaks at local neighborhood scales (K≈50-100) and weakens as the neighborhood size K increases, showing local rather than global geometry drives the effect (Figure 4).
Global (whole-manifold) dimension measures predict alignment and generalization less reliably than local dimension estimates computed at small K, per the K-scan analysis (Figure 4C).

The LID-alignment relationship holds across four architecture families—ConvNeXt (20 models), ResNet (20 models), ResMLP (8 models), and ViT (3 models)—with no systematic difference in average dimensionality across families (Figure 5).
Increasing model capacity and training dataset size both systematically reduce local intrinsic dimension while improving alignment and generalization (Figure 6).

kKlzS0HQjJ.text: Theorem 4.1 bounds population risk by empirical risk plus terms controlled by the intrinsic embedding dimension d_k at each layer k and the Lipschitz sensitivity of the downstream mapping (Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 3.8 shows that lower intrinsic (upper Wasserstein) dimension d* implies faster convergence of empirical measures, at rate O(n^{-1/d*}) (Theorem 3.8, Definition 3.7).

At the final embedding layer, architectural Lipschitz sensitivity vanishes (L_L(F)=1), simplifying the bound to depend mainly on embedding dimension and loss smoothness, explaining why final-layer dimensionality strongly predicts generalization (Corollary 4.2).
Across ResNet-18/34/50/101/152 on CIFAR, final-layer embedding dimension and Wasserstein distance both correlate significantly with class-wise generalization error (Figure 3).

On larger-scale ImageNet vision models and MNLI language models, the same dimension-generalization correlation persists, indicating the bound remains non-vacuous for modern overparameterized networks (Figure 4).

Width-reduction experiments show that shrinking network width lowers embedding dimension but raises the Lipschitz constant, demonstrating that generalization depends jointly on both quantities rather than dimension alone (Figure 5).

MjE62ZnpRH.text: SpecPrune-VLA reaches 1.46x speedup on an A800-80GB GPU and up to 1.57x on an RTX 3090 in LIBERO simulation, with success-rate degradation under 0.7% (Table 1).
Across LIBERO task suites, SpecPrune-VLA attains 1.51x speedup at 98.2% success rate (Spatial), 1.43x/96.3% (Object), 1.48x/97.7% (Goal), and 1.40x/94.0% (Long) (Table 1).

An ablation on LIBERO-Spatial shows static+dynamic pruning alone gives 1.54x speedup at 96.8% success rate, while adding the action-aware controller trades a bit of speed (1.51x) for higher success rate (98.2%) (Table 2).

The two-level, training-free pruning combines static action-level pruning (about 48% visual token retention) with dynamic layer-level pruning (90% retention at layers 5, 10, 15, and 20), yielding roughly 37% overall FLOPs reduction (Table 1).
The authors state all experiments are conducted in simulated LIBERO environments only, with no real-world robot validation reported (Section 9, Limitations).

cKztWFFGNE.text: EMFormer's Multi-Convs Layer achieves a 5.69x speedup over conventional multi-scale modules (Abstract, Section 2.2)
Accumulative context finetuning reduces 10-day ERA5 forecast RMSE from 5719 to 5094 m^2/s^2 (Table 1)
On 2024 typhoon tracking, EMFormer achieves a mean tracking error of 88.49 km, beating the next-best baseline (AIFS) at 119.17 km (Table 2)
EMFormer-Small reaches 83.2-84.4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K across Tiny/Small/Base variants (Table 5)
On ADE20K semantic segmentation, EMFormer attains 46.7-49.6 mIoU while using only 75% of parameters and 25% of FLOPs of competing backbones (Table 6)

1DxD3SBid1.text: DNAChunker's two-stage hierarchical encoder allocates finer tokenization granularity to functionally enriched genomic regions while compressing repetitive sequence, using cosine-similarity-based boundary decisions (Section on architecture)

On the 18-dataset Nucleotide Transformer benchmark, DNAChunker achieves an average MCC of 0.772 versus 0.728 for GENERator, while using only 172M parameters compared to GENERator's 1.2B (Nucleotide Transformer benchmark results table)

DNAChunker attains the best average rank (1.67) among 10 models on Nucleotide Transformer tasks, including a 14.2% average improvement on histone mark prediction (Nucleotide Transformer benchmark results table)

On Genomic Benchmarks' nine classification tasks, DNAChunker reaches 0.885 average accuracy and average rank 3.29, trailing only GENERator (rank 2.89) while using 7x fewer parameters than the largest baseline (Genomic Benchmarks results table)
Against learnable tokenization baselines MxDNA (0.637 MCC) and PatchDNA (0.626 MCC), DNAChunker achieves 0.657 average MCC and 0.931 on splice-site annotation (Table 3)

v6xrfEjNQv.text: InfoGeo formulates cross-view UAV geo-localization as an information bottleneck process combining Cross-View Adaptive Concept Selection (CACS), Concept Structural Relational Reasoning (CSRR), and Object-Centric Visual Augmentation (OCVA) (Method section)
On the University-1652 to SUES-200 transfer setting, InfoGeo improves R@1 from a 90.27% baseline to 95.07% (Table 1)
On the GTA-V cross-area benchmark, InfoGeo improves R@1 to 57.90% (+2.99% over CAMP) and reduces spatial distance error (Dis@1) by 69.61 meters to 416.75 meters (Table 2)

In the ablation on SUES-200 at 150m altitude, adding OCVA, the CACS loss, the structural alignment loss, and relational distillation sequentially raises R@1 from an 86.10% baseline to 91.80%, with the structural loss alone contributing over 2 points (Table 5)
In multi-weather robustness tests under fog-snow conditions, InfoGeo reaches 79.95% R@1 versus 72.33% for CVcities (Table 3)

b8UehNjsF3.text: The paper's FLOPs-based framework uses a tiered methodology (rich, partial, and minimal metadata disclosure tiers) to estimate training carbon emissions of open-source Hugging Face models at scale (Methodology section)

Training the 5,234 Hugging Face models with more than 5,000 downloads is estimated to have produced approximately 5.8x10^4 metric tons of CO2-equivalent emissions, with uncertainty of +/-2x10^4 tCO2e (Results section)
The United States (2.3x10^4 tCO2e) and China (1.9x10^4 tCO2e) account for the largest shares of estimated geographic emissions (Results section, geographic distribution table)

Annual estimated training emissions grew from about 430 tCO2e in 2020-2021 to over 4.1x10^4 tCO2e in 2024-2025, a roughly two-order-of-magnitude increase in five years (Temporal trends section/figure)
Vision and multimodal models show higher AI training carbon intensity (0.16 tCO2e/EFLOP) than NLP models (0.14 tCO2e/EFLOP) (Results section, ATCI comparison)

LtHNTRg73G.text: The method introduces a training-free, inference-time mechanism for flow matching text-to-image models that encourages lateral spread among generation trajectories via feature-space objectives (abstract only)
Diversity is boosted by reintroducing scheduled stochastic noise that is constrained to be orthogonal to the generation flow, preserving quality-seeking directions (abstract only)
A theoretical analysis shows the approach monotonically expands a volume measure of the generation trajectories while approximately preserving the output distribution's properties (abstract only)
Experiments across multiple text-to-image models show consistent improvements in Vendi Score and Brisque diversity measurements under fixed sampling budgets (abstract only)
The method preserves image quality and prompt/text alignment while increasing output variation, compared to fixed-path flow matching sampling (abstract only)

4OBHizHowb.text: UVR is a training-free framework for multimodal diffusion transformers that localizes unsafe image tokens using pre-collected 'unsafe anchor' embeddings and applies adaptive attention modulation plus noise injection to suppress harmful semantic propagation (Section 3).

On the I2P benchmark, UVR attains a 95.3% erasure rate for text-to-image synthesis with FLUX.1-dev while keeping CLIP score (31.32 vs. 31.31 baseline) and FID (76.76 vs. 76.82 baseline) essentially unchanged (Table 1).

For image editing with FLUX.1-kontext on I2P, UVR reaches a 94.6% erasure rate with comparable CLIP scores for seen/unseen edits (25.85/24.21) relative to the unregulated baseline (25.89/23.67) (Table 2).
UVR outperforms five safety-mitigation baselines—ESD, SLD, UCE, DES, and EraseAnything—on nudity erasure, IP-character removal, and inappropriate-object elimination tasks (Section 4, Table 3).

Ablations show attention attenuation is more effective for the editing task while feature perturbation aids synthesis, and enhanced self-attention among output tokens is necessary to preserve editing fidelity (Section 4.4, ablation table).
UVR adds only about 3 MB of extra VRAM and runs at 25-31 seconds per sample, comparable to baseline diffusion inference cost (Section 4, efficiency analysis).

HszNb2xE7P.text: CLEAR is a two-stage, mask-free video subtitle removal framework: Stage I performs self-supervised occlusion-prior learning from pixel-difference pseudo-labels, and Stage II applies LoRA adaptation (0.77% trainable parameters) to a frozen diffusion model with a lightweight 2.1M-parameter occlusion head (Section 3).
CLEAR achieves 26.80 dB PSNR, 0.894 SSIM, 0.101 LPIPS, and 20.37 VFID, exceeding the best baseline (20.03 dB PSNR) by 6.77 dB while matching inference speed (4.86 s/frame vs. 4.90 s/frame) (Table 1).

CLEAR outperforms mask-dependent baselines ProPainter (17.24 dB PSNR), DiffuEraser (17.85 dB PSNR), and MiniMax-Remover (20.03 dB PSNR), all of which require explicit masks at inference, whereas CLEAR is fully mask-free (Table 1).

An ablation starting from a LoRA-only baseline (21.62 dB PSNR) shows progressive gains of +1.49 dB from the Stage I prior, +1.61 dB from context distillation, +0.37 dB from context-aware adaptation, and +1.71 dB from context consistency, reaching the full model's 26.80 dB PSNR (Table 2).

Despite being trained only on Chinese subtitles, CLEAR demonstrates zero-shot generalization to English, Korean, French, Japanese, Russian, and German subtitle removal (Section 4, cross-lingual evaluation).

6AtLH7hRiF.text: AE-CoT is a three-stage jailbreak pipeline that rewrites harmful goals into teacher-style pedagogical prompts, decomposes them into reasoning fragments, and performs evolutionary search with fragment-level crossover and adaptive mutation-rate control to construct harmful chain-of-thought templates (Section 3).

AE-CoT attains 92% ASR on o1-mini versus 54% for the best baseline (H-CoT), and 88% ASR on o3-mini versus 86% for H-CoT, across six reasoning models including GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3, and Gemini-2.5 (Table 1).
On the Malicious-Educator benchmark, AE-CoT outperforms H-CoT across all evaluated models, reaching 100% ASR on both o1-mini and DeepSeek-R1 (Table 2).

An ablation on o1-mini shows removing the adaptive mutation-rate mechanism drops success rate from 90% to 60% (average score 3.8 to 3.0), a larger degradation than removing initial rewriting (50%) or evolutionary search (80%) alone (Table 5).
AE-CoT is roughly 3x faster than the CL-GSO baseline, requiring 193.77s versus 589.26s per attack on Gemini-2.5 (Table 4).

Combined defenses (length limiting plus safety reminders) only reduce AE-CoT's ASR to 60%, indicating the vulnerability operates at the reasoning-trajectory level rather than being fixable by surface-level output defenses (Table 7).

ZXOfmBn3Fu.text: R-GFM constructs an adaptive-hop Graph-of-Graphs (GoG) by sampling subgraphs at varying hop distances and connecting them via cosine similarity, then routes GoG nodes to hyperbolic, Euclidean, or hyperspherical manifolds using a dynamic, confidence-aware mixture-of-experts (Section 3).

In 1-shot node classification on Citeseer, R-GFM achieves 57.54% accuracy versus 31.86% for the next-best baseline, and it ranks first across 1-shot, 3-shot, and 5-shot settings on all datasets (Tables 1-3).
R-GFM attains up to a 49% relative improvement over baselines on downstream node classification tasks (Section 4).
For link prediction (AUC-ROC), R-GFM reaches 87.94% on Texas versus 72.41% for RiemannGFM, and 88.66% on Pubmed versus 86.37% for RiemannGFM (Table 5).

Theorem 3.3 shows that similarity-based sparse GoG edges yield lower expected embedding error than either disconnected or fully-connected alternatives, and Theorems 3.4-3.5 show dynamic expert selection yields tighter excess-risk and domain-generalization bounds than fixed expert sets.

Under 50% edge-drop and 50% node-masking perturbations, R-GFM retains 46.91% and 46.84% accuracy respectively, outperforming baselines by more than 5 percentage points (Section 4.3, robustness study).

pTz80QaxqD.text: The paper's Persona-Invariant Alignment (PIA) framework couples an attack-side Persona Lineage Evolution (PLE), which formulates persona search as graph optimization with UCB-based exploration and ancestral credit propagation, with a defense-side Persona-Invariant Consistency Learning (PICL) that enforces safety decisions independent of persona context via a unilateral KL-divergence constraint (Section 3).
PICL's training objective combines DPO loss, SFT loss, and a persona-invariant consistency term, minimize_θ ℒ(θ) = ℒ_DPO + α·ℒ_SFT + λ·ℒ_PIC (Section 3).
On out-of-distribution persona attacks, PICL reduces average Attack Success Rate to 5.4% (from a 60.1% baseline) for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and to 5.2% (from 30.2%) for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Table 2).
The PLE attack achieves near-saturation transferable ASR of 99.0% on the MaliciousInstruct benchmark, exceeding the Persona-GA baseline's 92.0% (Table 1).
PICL maintains benign compliance and general-capability metrics comparable to the DPO baseline, avoiding the over-refusal penalty typically seen with stronger safety constraints (Tables 3-4).

yTeVcvtkbI.text: Boundary Guidance is a GRPO-based reinforcement learning fine-tuning method that steers generation away from a safety classifier's decision boundary rather than simply minimizing rejection probability, motivated by Proposition 1 showing utility is minimized near the boundary (Section 3, Section 4).
The reward function combines a reward-model utility score u(x,y) with a safety-classifier confidence term t(x,y), added when t(x,y) >= 0.5 and subtracted otherwise (Equation 3, Section 4).

Across four policy model scales (Qwen-2.5 0.5B, 7B, 14B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-it), Boundary Guidance improves both a helpfulness metric (Delta-help from +0.03 to +0.13) and a harmfulness metric (Delta-harm from -0.03 to -0.15), with the largest gains on the smallest model, Qwen-2.5-0.5B (+0.13 helpfulness, -0.09 harmfulness) (Figure 2, Table 1, Section 6.1).

Evaluation uses 1,000 held-out prompts split into jailbreak, harmful, and benign test sets, judged by GPT-4.1-2025-04-14 as an LLM judge, with Meta-Llama-Guard-2-8B as the safety classifier and Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B as the reward model (Section 5.3).
A guard-only reward ablation (safety signal alone) achieves comparable harmfulness reduction but causes helpfulness collapse on smaller models, e.g. -0.73 for the 7B model (Table 2, Section 6.2).

A prompt-aware reward variant used as an ablation degrades helpfulness uniformly (Delta-help between -0.22 and -0.25) and increases harmfulness for larger models (+0.09 to +0.13), showing the necessity of the boundary-based reward design (Table 3, Section 6.2.2).

GO0G6bo9UO.text: DFSAttn is a training-free dynamic fine-grained sparse attention framework for video diffusion generation built on three components: 3D Hilbert curve token reordering, hierarchical block scoring, and sparse mask caching across diffusion steps (Section 5.1, Section 5.2, Section 5.3).
On HunyuanVideo-T2V-13B at 129-frame 720p resolution, DFSAttn reaches 80.53% attention sparsity with 29.38 PSNR, 0.898 SSIM, 0.087 LPIPS, and a 2.10x end-to-end speedup (Table 2).
On Wan2.1-T2V-14B at 81-frame 720p resolution, DFSAttn reaches 78.51% sparsity with 22.37 PSNR, 0.764 SSIM, 0.183 LPIPS, and a 1.79x speedup (Table 2).

DFSAttn is compared against static sparse-attention baselines SVG and RadialAttention and the dynamic baseline SVG2, and the 3D Hilbert reordering ablation outperforms Raster (27.79 PSNR), Hilbert2D (29.27 PSNR), and Block3D (29.16 PSNR) reordering variants (Table 3).
An ablation over sub-block size for hierarchical block scoring shows smaller sub-blocks (size 16) improve reconstruction quality while keeping latency stable (Table 4).
An adaptive sparsity scheduling ablation shows the adaptive schedule outperforms fixed sparsity schedules across sparsity levels (Figure 6).

DRqjMnDQGq.text: RLVE trains language models jointly across RLVE-Gym, a suite of 400 manually engineered verifiable environments spanning programming, mathematics, optimization, classical algorithms, and logic/NP-complete puzzles, using an adaptive difficulty mechanism that raises an environment's difficulty ceiling by 1 once the model reaches at least 90% accuracy at the current maximum difficulty (Section 2.2, Section 3).

Starting from the ProRL-1.5B-v2 checkpoint (already trained for over 20,000 H100 hours), further RLVE training for about 1,100 H100 hours yields a 3.37% absolute average improvement across six reasoning benchmarks, versus only 0.49% absolute improvement from continuing the original RLVR training for about 3,600 H100 hours (Section 5.1, Figure 6).

In a compute-constrained setting, RLVE outperforms training on the DeepMath-103K dataset by about 2% absolute, despite DeepMath-103K construction costing roughly $138,000 and 127,000 GPU hours (Section 5.2, Figure 7).
The six reasoning benchmarks used for evaluation are AIME 2024/2025, OMEGA-500, OlympiadBench, LiveCodeBench, and BBEH (Big-Bench Extra Hard) (Section 5).

An environment-scaling ablation across 1, 4, 16, and 256 RLVE-Gym environments shows consistent out-of-distribution reasoning improvements across base, SFT, and RL-trained model variants including Qwen2.5-7B-Base, R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, DeepScaleR-1.5B, ProRL-v2-1.5B, and OpenThinker3-1.5B (Section 4.2, Figure 5).

An ablation comparing adaptive versus static difficulty distributions, including an oracle static distribution, shows the adaptive mechanism sustains a higher effective prompt ratio and outperforms even oracle-tuned static difficulty ranges (Section 4.1, Figure 3, Figure 4).

1sgrIzBaWD.text: A single participant in a distributed/federated training workflow can substantially inflate its measured data-attribution value via a latent optimization attack that injects synthetic gradient updates optimized through a decoder, while leaving global model utility essentially intact (Section 2, Section 3, Algorithm 1).

The attack objective combines three losses: cosine-similarity direction alignment with benign reference gradients, norm consistency with benign update magnitudes, and a standard cross-entropy task-fidelity term (Section 3.2.2).

On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, the attack raises the malicious client's attribution value from 0.0547 to 0.1682 and its rank from 10th to 2nd out of the clients, while global accuracy changes only from 76.75% to 77.59% (Table 1, Table 2).

On FashionMNIST with ResNet-18, attribution rises from 0.0000 to 0.0741 with rank improving from 10th to 6th; on SVHN with VGG16_BN, attribution rises from 0.0000 to 0.1256 with rank improving from 10th to 6th (Table 1).

Baseline attacks (Label Flipping, Random Noise, Free Rider, and a direct reference-direction alignment) consistently fail to raise attribution as effectively as the latent optimization attack (Table 1, Table 3).

Geometry-based trimming defenses fail to detect the attack, achieving precision, recall, and F1-score all at or below 0.02 across tested configurations, and the attack effect generalizes across both Federated Shapley Value (FedSV) and Leave-One-Out (LOO) attribution evaluators (Table 5, Section 5).

WgIwr2k861.text: DARE (Dynamic Alignment for RElaxation) performs sample-level constraint relaxation in offline-to-online RL by computing a Bayes-optimal posterior over a scalar behavioral-deviation statistic d(s,a) (the L2 distance to a reference behavior model's action) to decide, per sample, whether to enforce or relax conservative constraints, rather than relying on offline/online data origin (Section 3, Theorem 1, Equation 1, Section 5).

DARE is instantiated on top of both Cal-QL (as DARE-C) and IQL (as DARE-I), and Theorem 3 proves the posterior-induced exchange operation strictly increases the empirical mean gap between offline-like and online-like behavior classes (Theorem 3, Section 6).

After 0.2M online fine-tuning steps on D4RL, DARE improves total score by about 11% over baselines across both the CQL group and IQL group, achieving the highest score on 13 of 15 tasks in the CQL group (DARE-C total 1415.4 vs. Cal-QL 1272.7 and EDIS-C 1338.2) and 12 of 15 tasks in the IQL group (DARE-I total 1253.0 vs. IQL 1165.6, PEX 1118.6, and EDIS-I 1119) (Table 1, Section 7.2).

An ablation removing the exchange mechanism (DARE-C w/o Exchange and DARE-I w/o Exchange) shows consistent performance drops across all evaluated environments, confirming the exchange mechanism's contribution (Figure 6, Section 7.7).

A comparison of exchange strategies shows the Bayes-optimal posterior-induced exchange is more stable than a monotonic Gaussian exchange or a direct alignment-distance sorting exchange, consistent with the finding that empirical mean/variance gaps do not consistently follow a monotonic ordering across environments (Figure 4, Figure 5, Section 7.4).

A reversed behavior-assignment experiment (a curiosity-style variant that assigns online-like samples to the offline batch and vice versa) underperforms DARE-I, e.g. total locomotion score of 812.1 versus 819.8 for DARE-I under the diffusion behavior model, supporting behavioral consistency as the correct criterion for role assignment (Table 3, Section 7.6).

X9yKVwZ7if.text: ES-OVI interpolates between ES and OVI gradients via ∇Jα(θ) = α∇J^OVI(θ) + (1-α)∇J^ES(θ), giving explicit control over the trade-off between flat-minima robustness (α=0) and sharp-minima performance (α=1) without extra function evaluations (Section on ES-OVI hybrid).

On the Acrobot robustness analysis, OVI (α=1) converges to sharper, noise-sensitive solutions while ES (α=0) finds robust ones, and intermediate α values trade off performance versus robustness to parameter, observation, and action noise (Robustness Analysis, Acrobot experiments).

AdaPol, an adaptive OVI-CBO hybrid, generally outperforms its constituent algorithms on the ≈1000-dimensional Brax locomotion tasks (Hopper, Acrobot, HalfCheetah, Reacher), while OVI alone is competitive with CMA-ES (Brax Locomotion Tasks experiments).

On the 23-problem 2D BBOB benchmark suite, ES-OVI outperforms its constituent methods on the Attractive Sector function while multimodal hybrid variants excel on the RastriginOriginal function (BBOB Benchmarks, 2D experiments).

For 33-dimensional language model merging of Mistral-7B with three fine-tuned variants using only 64 MGSM training questions, SchedPol and AdaPol are competitive from both good and poor initializations, but all CBO-OVI hybrids underperform the specialized evolutionary model merging baseline of Akiba et al. 2025 (Language Model Merging experiment).
ES-OVI incurs roughly 1.4x the runtime of OVI alone, and AdaPol incurs roughly 3.3x the runtime of CBO alone on GPU (Notable Numeric Results / runtime overhead).

8nGX6WUKE7.text: AOrchestra paired with Gemini-3-Flash achieves 80.00% pass@1 and 86.06% pass@3 on the 165-task GAIA validation set, a 13.94 percentage-point improvement over the strongest baseline, OpenHands (Table 1).
On a 70-task sample of Terminal-Bench 2.0, AOrchestra with Gemini-3-Flash reaches 52.86% pass@1, an 18.57 percentage-point absolute gain over the Mini-SWE-Agent baseline's 34.29% (Table 1).

Averaged across GAIA, SWE-Bench-Verified, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 with Gemini-3-Flash, AOrchestra achieves a 16.28% relative pass@1 improvement over the strongest baseline per benchmark (Section reporting aggregate results).
In a context-sharing ablation on 50 GAIA samples, AOrchestra's curated-context sub-agents reach 96.00% accuracy versus 86.00% with no context and 84.00% with full, uncurated context (Table 2).
Supervised fine-tuning of a Qwen3-8B orchestrator on 2K trajectories raises its accuracy from 56.97% to 68.48%, an 11.51 percentage-point gain (Table 3).

On Terminal-Bench, swapping in a ReAct-style versus Mini-SWE-style sub-agent under the same AOrchestra orchestrator yields 48.57% and 44.29% accuracy respectively, both exceeding their standalone equivalents of 28.57% and 34.29% (Table 4).

otHlsN1pvk.text: The Directed Decoding Map (DDM) encodes token confidence changes into three effect types—mixed effects (α), purely positive effects (β), and purely negative effects (-β) for newly decoded tokens, plus (γ)/(-γ) for strengthened/weakened confidence of previously decoded tokens—to capture structural relationships between decoding steps (Section on DDM construction).

Gaussian-Trajectory Attribution (GTA) fits cell-wise Gaussian distributions over each model's DDMs and attributes a response to the model maximizing the log-likelihood ℓ_M(E*) = -1/2 Σ[(E*_t,l - μ_M(t,l))^2/σ^2_M(t,l) + log(2π σ^2_M(t,l))] (Method equation for GTA).
GTA+DDM achieves 99.95 AUC on GSM8K and 98.94 AUC on CodeAlpaca-20K for Cross-Model Attribution between LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct (Table 1).
For Independent-Run Attribution, where models share identical initialization and training configuration, GTA+DDM still attains 81.75 AUC on GSM8K and 65.05 AUC on CodeAlpaca-20K (Table 1).
GTA+DDM improves over a perplexity baseline by 30.43 points on CMA-GSM8K and 30.37 points on IRA-GSM8K AUC (Table 1, comparison to perplexity baseline).

An ablation shows the effect value γ is the most critical DDM component for attribution accuracy, and replacing the cell-wise Gaussian model with a row-wise variant severely degrades performance (Ablation Findings section).

LXZcSgqldO.text: Under the Sup-21/1K pretrained-model setting, MePo improves the MISA baseline's A_AUC by 15.10 percentage points on CIFAR-100 (to 78.01%), 13.36 points on ImageNet-R (to 64.23%), and 12.56 points on CUB-200 (to 55.31%) (Table 1, Sup-21/1K results).

MePo's meta-refinement stage combines an inner loop of sequential pseudo-task training with an outer loop of joint training on held-out validation data, using a first-order Reptile-style update to refine the pretrained backbone before any downstream continual learning (Section on Meta Post-Refinement for Representation Learning).

Meta Cov aligns batch features to a reference covariance matrix (computed from 1000 classes, 200 samples each) via Cholesky decomposition, then linearly interpolates aligned and fine-tuned features with weight α=0.5 for supervised backbones and α=0.7 for self-supervised backbones (Section on Meta Covariance Matrix for Output Alignment).

MePo's meta-refinement uses only 0.15% of the ViT-B/16 pretraining data budget and adds just 0.67% extra parameters (the covariance matrix), with no additional runtime overhead during the general continual learning phase itself (Computational Efficiency section).

An ablation (Table 2) shows Meta Rep and Meta Cov are complementary: using either component alone sometimes underperforms the combined MePo approach across the tested pretrained checkpoints and datasets (Table 2).

1JAH4hfIf7.text: LabBuilder's LabForge component compiles textual experimental requests into structured protocols using an asset knowledge base of 176 laboratory entities and a chemistry knowledge base, annotating assets across geometry, semantics, and safety attributes (Section 3.1).

On a 30-experiment comparison, LabBuilder reduces boundary violations to 0.07 versus 10.8 for Holodeck and 5.61 for SceneWeaver, while achieving higher asset availability (0.833) than both baselines (0.700 and 0.226) (Table 2).
LabBuilder attains a flammable-isolation safety score of 0.725, substantially higher than Holodeck's 0.239 and SceneWeaver's 0.097, on the same 30-experiment benchmark (Table 2).
Ablating protocol guidance drops asset availability from 0.833 to 0.300, and removing the geometric/chemical optimization step increases boundary violations from 0.07 to 2.73 (Table 3).

LabBuilder's navigation-aware refinement improves point-goal navigation success for the iPlanner policy from 0.350 to 0.425, and the system reports an overall navigation feasibility rate of 0.966 (Table 2, Table 4).

IL6lhb2r1e.text: The refined sample complexity bound removes the ρ_min^(-1) dependency present in prior work (Hieu 2025), which scaled as O([ℭ_N²+1]ρ_min^(-1)) (Table 1).
The new general bound scales as O(ℭ_N²[θ̂_{k+2}·R + (1-θ̂_{k+2})²k] + [R+k²]) in terms of number of classes R and tuple size k (Table 1, Section 3.2).
Under mild assumptions where class probabilities are small, the bound simplifies to O(ℭ_N²R + [R+k²]) (Table 1).
In the extreme multi-class limit, where the population class-collision probability τ approaches zero, the sample complexity reduces to O(k), independent of the number of classes R (Section 3.2).

The analysis introduces an alternative U-statistic decomposition of the collision-free risk into components with different collision counts to obtain sharper concentration bounds (Section 3.2, Definition 3.1).

jdbQzlnYll.text: DiCoLa is a recursive divide-and-conquer framework that decomposes causal discovery with latent variables into subproblems via tripartitions (A,B,C) satisfying A⟂⟂B|C, then merges local skeletons bottom-up (Algorithm 3, Section 5.2).
Theorem 4 proves DiCoLa preserves soundness and completeness of the underlying base learner (e.g., FCI, RFCI) after decomposition and merging (Section 4).

DiCoLa's overall computational complexity is O(m·k_max²·2^{k_max}), an exponential reduction compared to the O(n²·2^n) complexity of running the base algorithm on the full variable set n, where k_max is the largest subproblem size (Section 5.2).

On synthetic ER(30,5), ER(50,3) graphs and benchmark networks (MILDEW, BARLEY, ANDES, LINK), combining DiCoLa with FCI, RFCI, FCI+, and ICD significantly reduces the number of conditional independence tests and runtime while preserving structural accuracy relative to the base methods and L-MARVEL (Section 6, Figure 3).

Applying DiCoLa+FCI to a real-world Arabidopsis thaliana gene expression dataset of 33 genes recovers a modular metabolic pathway structure with sparse inter-pathway connections consistent with biological literature (Section 6.2, Figure 4).

UflglraWRa.text: Under binary feedback, the proposed algorithm for repeated second-price auctions achieves regret O(√(dT) log³T + d log⁵T), where d is the feature dimension and T the horizon (Theorem 1).
A matching minimax lower bound of Ω(√(dT)) holds for T ≥ d², even when the bidder has perfect knowledge of the competing-bid CDF (Theorem 2).

Under binary feedback, second-price auctions admit Õ(√(dT)) regret while first-price auctions are limited to Õ(T^(2/3)) regret, showing the payment rule strictly improves achievable regret (Section on regret comparison).

Under full-information feedback, both second-price and first-price auctions achieve the same Õ(√(dT)) regret rate, so the SPA advantage is specific to the binary-feedback setting (Section on regret comparison).
Section 3 introduces an interval-splitting technique to estimate the highest-other-bid (HOB) directly from the observed payment in a won second-price auction (Section 3).

r4GbYGbWM5.text: Parametric Prior Mapping (PPM) achieves up to 31.2% CRPS reduction and up to 44.3% QICE improvement versus the second-best baseline (NsDiff) across 7 real-world datasets (Table 2).

PPM outperforms 6 baselines—DeepAR, TimeGrad, D3VAE, TimeDiff, DiffusionTS, TMDM, and NsDiff—on probabilistic forecasting metrics across all 7 datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Electricity, Traffic, Weather) (Table 2).
PPM also achieves consistent improvements in point-forecasting MSE and MAE across the same 7 datasets (Table 3).
PPM delivers a 2x to 100x inference speedup relative to diffusion-based baselines by replacing sequential T-step denoising with a single forward push-forward mapping (Figure 5).
An ablation with different prior distributions (Gaussian vs. Uniform) shows that adding the push-forward mapping improves performance across datasets regardless of the prior choice (Table 4).

LDNH3sQtMW.text: SC-MILP achieves a 12.36% average improvement in solving time over prior state-of-the-art and wins on 77.08% of instances across four NP-hard MILP benchmarks (Table 1).

The four evaluated NP-hard problem classes are Set Covering, Combinatorial Auction, Capacitated Facility Location, and Maximum Independent Set, each tested at three difficulty levels with 100 instances per level (Section 5.1).
SC-MILP outperforms baselines on imitation-learning branching accuracy metrics (acc@1, acc@3, acc@5, acc@10) across all four problem classes (Table 2).

Dynamic stratified contrastive learning groups branch-and-bound nodes via K-means clustering on feature distributions into m groups (m=4-5 depending on dataset) and applies depth-dependent weighting so nearby nodes remain moderately close while distant nodes are strongly separated (Section 4.2, Section 4.4).

An ablation study on the Set Covering benchmark shows the upstream-augmented MILP derivation and stratified contrastive components each contribute to performance, with particularly strong gains at upstream (near-root) nodes (Table 3).

YBIGgUet07.text: For the hidden-state threat model, Theorem 3.2 establishes a Rényi differential privacy bound for zeroth-order optimization that improves with the number of coordinate-update directions K, in contrast to standard composition-based bounds (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).

Corollary 3.3 gives a closed-form DP guarantee for strongly convex losses, epsilon = O(sqrt(Delta^2 log(1/delta)/(n^2 sigma^2) * min(T, M*R*n*sqrt(d)/(K*Delta)))), showing privacy loss saturates rather than growing with the number of iterations T (Corollary 3.3, Section 3.2).

Lemma 3.7 shows the zeroth-order update map has a (c1, c2)-generalized Lipschitz property, and Lemma 3.8 derives high-probability concentration bounds using a Beta(K/2, (d-K)/2) distribution to control the anisotropic noise introduced by directional perturbations (Lemma 3.7, Lemma 3.8, Section 3).

Lemma 3.9 bounds the forward Wasserstein-infinity distance between adjacent privacy processes as W_infinity(w_t, w_t') <= min(2R, 2*eta*Delta*t/sqrt(K)), which underlies the shifted-divergence argument used to prove convergent (non-diverging) privacy loss over iterations (Lemma 3.9, Section 3).

Theorem 3.1 establishes a public-state baseline privacy bound via standard composition, epsilon = O(sqrt(Delta^2 log(1/delta) T/(n^2 sigma^2))) when the noise-blending parameter beta_t = 0, against which the hidden-state analysis (Theorem 3.2) is compared (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

PasiyntPbd.text: MIGA introduces a Two-Stage Training-Inference Alignment (TTA) mechanism, described in Section 3.2, to mitigate the training-inference gap in infinite-frame video generation (Section 3.2).

MIGA introduces a Dual Consistency Enhancement (DCE) module (Section 3.3) that works alongside TTA to maintain subject and background consistency across arbitrarily long generated videos (Section 3.3).
On VBench with a VideoCrafter2 backbone, MIGA attains an overall score of 97.82, with subject consistency of 97.66 and background consistency of 96.99 (Table 1).
On the NarrLV benchmark using a Wan2.1 backbone, MIGA scores 79.32 at TNA=2 scene attributes, 69.48 at TNA=3, and 75.05 at TNA=4 (Table 2).
An ablation isolating the two core mechanisms shows TTA alone improves performance by 2.03% and DCE alone by 1.73% over the base model (Table 3, Section 4.3).
MIGA achieves 4.7% and 2.0% improvements in subject and background consistency respectively on VBench compared to the FIFO-Diffusion baseline (Section 4.2, Table 1).

RbGLc4sk9s.text: AutoRPA's Translator agent (Section 3.2) converts hard-coded ReAct action trajectories into soft-coded RPA procedures, which the Builder agent (Section 3.3) then synthesizes into reusable functions via retrieval-augmented generation (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
On AndroidWorld with GPT-4.1, AutoRPA uses only 12.8k tokens versus 103.4k tokens for a ReAct baseline, while achieving a higher task success rate of 51.7% versus 50.0% (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On MiniWoB++, AutoRPA consumes 1.4k tokens versus 9.2k for the ReAct baseline, while reaching 95.4% success on all tasks (vs. 92.8% for ReAct) and 91.1% on hard tasks (vs. 84.4% for ReAct) (Table 2, Section 4.1).
Across benchmarks, AutoRPA reduces token usage by 82%-96% relative to ReAct-style agents while maintaining or improving task success rate (Section 4.1).

An ablation shows removing the Translator component drops success rate to 40.2%, and building RPA functions without ReAct exploration trajectories drops it to 32.5%, versus 51.7% for the full pipeline (Table 3, Section 4.2).

A verification phase using hybrid repair (code execution plus ReAct fallback, Section 3.4) is used to fix failing RPA functions; removing ReAct-based repair and using code repair alone lowers success to 45.5% (Table 3, Section 3.4).

9kkby07AvD.text: REFI-GAD extracts a 5-dimensional universal relational fingerprint (Section 4.1) that encodes anomaly-indicative structural cues independent of raw node features, enabling feature alignment across heterogeneous graphs (Section 4.1).
REFI-GAD achieves a 7.39% average AUROC improvement over the strongest baseline, IA-GGAD, across 14 datasets (Table 1, Section 5).

Using the relational fingerprint instead of PCA-based feature reduction yields a 20.39% performance gain, and a domain-adaptive refinement module contributes a further 0.70% improvement (Table 2, Section 5).

The fingerprint-grounded model (Section 4.2) operates as a generalist detector, applying a fixed support set size of k=50 to unseen target graphs without any graph-specific retraining (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

An ablation removing individual dimensions of the relational fingerprint (Table 3) shows each dimension contributes measurably to detection performance, confirming the fingerprint's components are not redundant (Table 3, Section 5).
In a fully cross-domain transfer setting, REFI-GAD sustains strong performance gains over baselines when trained and evaluated on disjoint domains (Table 4, Section 5).

o1Tn2ie0Wy.text: Theorem 1 (Section 3.1) proves that when paired with either the PBGI or LogEIPC cost-aware acquisition function, the proposed stopping rule bounds expected cumulative evaluation cost as E[sum of c(x_t)] <= C + U, where C is the initial point's cost and U bounds expected cumulative improvement (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).

The stopping rule (Equations 6, 9, and 10 in Section 3) halts optimization once no remaining point's expected improvement is worth its evaluation cost, requiring no manually tuned stopping hyperparameter (Section 3).

The LogEIPC acquisition function (Equation 4) scales expected improvement by evaluation cost in log space, while the Pandora's Box Gittins Index (PBGI) acquisition function (Equation 5) solves for a threshold where expected improvement equals cost (Equations 4-5, Section 3).

The method targets cost-adjusted simple regret (Equation 2), a metric combining the solution-quality gap with cumulative evaluation expenditure, and Section 4 evaluates the stopping rule against baselines on this metric (Equation 2, Section 4).

wz57SLSTk3.text: Co-RedTeam achieves a 59.1% exploitation success rate on CyBench and a 60.0% success rate on BountyBench Exploit when using Gemini-2.5-pro, rising to 63.7% and 65.0% respectively with Gemini-3-pro (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On BountyBench Detection, Co-RedTeam reaches 12.5% accuracy with Gemini-2.5-pro and 20.0% with Gemini-3-pro, an improvement described as over 10 percentage points absolute versus baselines (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On CyBench with Gemini-2.5-pro, Co-RedTeam's 59.1% success rate exceeds the strongest non-memory baselines OpenHands (31.5%) and C-Agent (31.8%) by roughly 27 percentage points (Table 1, Section 4.1).
Co-RedTeam attains 0.143 precision and 0.125 recall in vulnerability discovery, a roughly 5x precision improvement over the C-Agent baseline's 0.024 precision (Table 3, Section 5).
On CyberGym, Co-RedTeam achieves 31.5% success with Gemini-2.5-pro and 37.3% with Gemini-3-pro (Table 1, Section 4.1).

fE4urn9hyM.text: On AgentDojo, CausalArmor keeps attack success rate at approximately 0.6%, matching aggressive defenses, while preserving 56.26% benign utility versus 53.61% for the no-defense baseline and 41.24% for PromptArmor (Figure 3, Table 3).
CausalArmor adds only 1.30x benign latency overhead on AgentDojo compared to 1.00x baseline and 2.44x for PromptArmor (Table 3).
On DoomArena under adaptive attacks, CausalArmor achieves 3.65% attack success rate while maintaining 70.96% benign utility versus 55.13% for the PiGuard classifier (Table 1).

Proposition 4.1 bounds the probability of a successful indirect prompt injection by Pr(IPI Success) ≤ T·|Y_mal|·exp(−(β+γ)), where β is the benign capability margin and γ is the sanitization effectiveness margin, giving an exponentially small bound as the combined margin grows (Proposition 4.1, Appendix B).

CausalArmor computes leave-one-out attributions via the marginal-support measure ΔX(Y;C_t) := log P(Y|C_t) − log P(Y|C_t∖X), triggering sanitization only when the untrusted span's attribution dominates the user request's attribution (Section 3.2, Equations 2–4).
An ablation removing the retroactive chain-of-thought masking stage increases attack success rate by 1.46 percentage points, showing input sanitization alone is insufficient (Table 2, Section 4.2).

7X91AAKL5B.text: Theorem 4.2 establishes that the LLM inference system is stable under any work-conserving scheduling policy when λ < μ(1−δ), where δ = ess sup{s+o}/M is a small memory-slack term, while Theorem 4.1 shows the queue grows unboundedly whenever λ > μ (Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2, Section 4).
The processing rate μ is derived in closed form as μ = M / (b̄ · E[g(s,o)]), where M is total GPU KV-cache memory and g(s,o) is lifetime cumulative memory usage per request (Equation 1, Section 3).

On single-GPU experiments, predicted stability boundaries deviate from measured throughput by only 3.66% at a 1:1 prefill/decode ratio, 8.38% at 2:1, 2.25% at 1:2, and 7.90% for a mixed workload, all under 10% (Table 1, Section 5.2).
On the real-world LongBench v2 dataset, the framework's predicted stability accuracy deviates by 8.03% from observed behavior (Table 2, Section 5.2).
On an eight-GPU cluster with a 1:1 prefill/decode ratio, the prediction gap is 3.38%, confirming the framework's stability predictions scale to multi-GPU deployments (Table 3, Section 5.3).

0FzaPyOEB7.text: Theorem 1 (Section 4.2) shows the optimal shaped reward has a threshold structure: responses are assigned reward B if their true utility exceeds a prompt-dependent threshold m*(x), and 0 otherwise.
Theorem 2 (Section 4.3) proves the helper function F_x(m) is continuous and strictly decreasing with a unique root at m*(x), enabling the threshold to be computed via bisection.

In GPT-4 evaluation across HH-RLHF and SHP with Qwen and Llama backbones, the proposed SRS reward-shaping method achieves average Win-Tie rates of 66.83%, 69.6%, and 66.65% against vanilla, Minmax, and Meanstd baselines respectively (Table 3, Section 6.4).

A motivating example in Section 3.2 shows that shaping rewards (r̃(left)=0, r̃(neutral)=3) instead of using true utilities yields expected utility of 1.69 versus 1.23 under direct optimization on a model biased toward P(left)=0.9, P(neutral)=0.1.

Table 2 (Section 6.3) reports SRS integrated into Controlled Decoding and ARGS achieves the highest reward across four evaluation settings while maintaining comparable response diversity and coherence to baselines.
Ablation results in Table 4 (Section 7.1) show SRS's threshold-based shaping outperforms both direct reward-capping and mean-based thresholding baselines.

iqXzDUd36x.text: Theorem 3.6 (Section 3.5) bounds the target-domain generalization error as ε_{p_T}(h_T) ≤ ε_{p_0}(h_0) + ε_{p_0}(h_T*) + ιζ𝒞 + 𝒮_stat, combining source error, hypothesis-shift error, and stability/statistical terms.

Proposition 3.4 (Section 3.3) shows that adding entropy regularization to the primal objective yields a unique optimal solution for the semi-dual problem, restoring training stability compared to the non-unique solutions shown to arise in the unregularized case (Proposition 3.2).

On the GDA benchmarks in Table 1 (Section 4.2), E-SUOT achieves 86.4% accuracy on Portraits (+21.5% over baseline), 72.1% on 45-degree rotated MNIST (+23.4%), and 51.0% on 60-degree rotated MNIST (+38.6%).
On Office-Home UDA tasks (Table 2, Section 4.2), E-SUOT achieves an average accuracy of 73.5%, winning 10 of 12 task comparisons against other methods.

Ablation studies in Table 3 (Section 4.3) show that removing entropy regularization in favor of an adversarial baseline drops accuracy by 13.4-31.5%, confirming the necessity of entropy regularization and KL-divergence choice.
When integrated with existing UDA backbones (Table 4, Section 4.3), E-SUOT yields average accuracy improvements of 8.1% for MSTN, 3.3% for RSDA, 1.0% for FixBi, and 0.5% for CoVi.

GfQI92bpC1.text: AMA-Bench's real-world subset contains 2,496 expert-curated QA pairs spanning 6 domains (Web, Text2SQL, Software Engineering, Gaming, Embodied AI, and Open-world QA), with an average trajectory length of 57,506 tokens (Section on Dataset Composition).

AMA-Bench's synthetic subset contains 1,200 QA pairs built from BabyAI and TextWorld environments spanning 5 trajectory lengths from 8K to 128K tokens, enabling evaluation at arbitrary horizons (Section on Dataset Composition).
GPT-5.2 achieves only 72.26% accuracy on AMA-Bench despite its scale, indicating that memory architecture rather than model capacity is the primary bottleneck (Results section).
AMA-Agent achieves 57.22% average accuracy on AMA-Bench, outperforming the strongest memory-system baseline HippoRAG2 (44.80%) by 11.16 percentage points (Results section).

AMA-Agent's memory construction uses a Causality Graph that preserves objective information and explicit causal dependencies, retrieved via a tool-augmented search mechanism combining embedding similarity, graph traversal, and keyword search (Method section, AMA-Agent).

g2yb3LhW4L.text: SpecFlow reduces KV-cache size by 1.6x to 2.1x across benchmarks compared to prior token-accumulating visual chain-of-thought methods (Results, Table 1/Table 2).
On compositional reasoning benchmarks, SpecFlow achieves 70.14% accuracy on VSR, 61.28% on V-Star, 67.79% on EmbSpatial, and 70.47% on Winoground (Table 1).
On dynamic spatial reasoning tasks, SpecFlow achieves 64.85% success on Maze-16, 72.96% on MiniBehavior-20, and 49.38% on FrozenLake-16 (Table 2).

SpecFlow's Cosine-Space Flow Matching uses a deterministic continuous-time flow in discrete cosine coefficient space, solved with an Euler solver using T=5 steps per hop (Method section, Cosine-Space Flow Matching).
SpecFlow applies classifier-free guidance with guidance scale w=4 to steer visual workspace updates using text-based reasoning (Method section, Text-Guided Conditioning via CFG).

SpecFlow's architecture combines Qwen3-VL-8B for text reasoning with QwenImage-Edit-2509, a 20B-parameter diffusion model, for visual thought updates in VAE latent space (Method/Architecture section).

0Q7adIsv6p.text: MIPLIB-NL comprises 223 one-to-one reconstructions derived from the MIPLIB 2017 mixed-integer linear program collection, spanning logistics, manufacturing, energy, and finance sectors (abstract only).

MIPLIB-NL's construction pipeline recovers compact, reusable model structures from flat solver formulations, then reverse-generates natural-language specifications maintaining model-data separation, validated through iterative human-LLM review (abstract only).
Systems that perform strongly on existing toy-scale optimization modeling benchmarks show substantial performance degradation on MIPLIB-NL (abstract only).
MIPLIB-NL exposes failure modes of LLM-based optimization modeling that are invisible when evaluating only on smaller-scale, toy benchmarks (abstract only).

4Mu4AA14jr.text: Difficult reasoning examples can be reliably identified from the loss on just the first 100 tokens of a chain-of-thought trace, evaluated at a randomly perturbed pretrained checkpoint, without generating the full 34k-token trace (Section 3, Difficulty Filtering).
Diversity sampling clusters examples using loss patterns over the first 1,000 reasoning tokens measured at checkpoints extrapolated along the fine-tuning direction (Section 3, Diversity Sampling).
Theorem 3.1 proves that examples with similar loss at perturbed checkpoints induce similar gradients during fine-tuning, bounded by local smoothness constants (Theorem 3.1).

The proposed data curation method, evaluated with Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B on M23K medical reasoning and OpenThoughts-Math, outperforms baselines by up to 1.7% on medical reasoning benchmarks while using only about 9% of the token budget of full-trace methods (Experiments section).

Ablation results show that removing brittle-example filtering and diversity sampling components each degrade performance, with these two components contributing the largest gains of 1.17% and 1.24% respectively (Ablation section).

q8LOhSzOIU.text: Increasing the component dimension r1 of Kronecker adapters tends to degrade fine-tuning performance, while increasing r2 consistently improves it, and increasing the number of components r does not yield sustained improvement beyond a threshold (Section on design principles).

Theorem 3.2 shows that subspace alignment between Kronecker adapters and full fine-tuning gradients depends critically on component configuration, with bounds favoring maximizing r2 while minimizing r1 and r (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.4 introduces a scaling factor lambda proportional to 1/sqrt(r*r2) that ensures training stability across different component configurations, applied in practice as lambda = 16/sqrt(r*r2) (Theorem 3.4).

CDKA achieves 56.71% on GSM8K, state-of-the-art among compared methods, and 87.30% average on GLUE using only 0.18% trainable parameters, about 12.5% of the parameters used by LoRA-One (Experiments, GSM8k/GLUE results tables).

CDKA's practical configuration guidelines recommend r1 in [2,4], maximizing r2 under the parameter budget, and using r around 8 as the boundary for allocation decisions (Section on practical guidelines).

nzYTAVwZeJ.text: RP Flow uses Conditional Flow Matching between a Random-Fourier-Feature-based implicit source process and the target multivariate random field, with the transport map T_θ parameterized as in Section 3 (Eq. 6).

On the Div2K 4x4 upsampling task, RP Flow attains PSNR 25.30±5.05 and SSIM 0.82±0.08 across 32 test images, comparable to discriminative INRs while also reporting a calibration error PCE1 of 0.09±0.05 (Table 1).

On the synthetic 513x513x128 seismic interpolation benchmark with sparse 64-unit-spacing 2D grid observations, RP Flow (10M-parameter variant) outperforms RFF Network, SIREN, GPR, and Deep GP baselines, reaching PSNR 32.08±1.73 and SSIM 0.93±0.04 (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On the real F3 seismic dataset, RP Flow achieves PSNR 28.77 and SSIM 0.80 (Table 2, Section 4.2).

The posterior sampling pipeline combines reverse-ODE projection of observations into the RFF source space, closed-form GP regression there, and forward-ODE integration to produce ensemble posterior samples, reducing posterior GP computation to O(n) versus O(n^3) for direct GP regression (Section 3.4, Algorithm 1, Appendix B.4).
Theorem 3.3 shows regularity properties (continuity, Lipschitz continuity, C^k smoothness) of the source process are preserved under the learned transport map (Section 3.5, Theorem 3.3).

PDBLtVDb0d.text: Flash-VAED's independence-aware channel pruning uses SVD analysis showing only 22% of singular values suffice to explain 99% of variance, enabling channel reduction to 12.5%-25% of the original VAE decoder size (Section 3.1).

On Wan 2.1, Flash-VAED achieves a 6.16x decoder speedup on an RTX 5090D while retaining 93.1% PSNR-based reconstruction quality; on LTX-Video it achieves a 5.71x speedup with 96.9% quality retention (Section 4, Table 1).
Flash-VAED accelerates the end-to-end video generation pipeline by 27% when paired with Self Forcing (Wan 2.1) and by 36% when paired with FastVideo (LTX-Video) (Section 4).

Stage-wise dominant operator optimization identifies CausalConv3D as consuming over 60% of decoder inference time and replaces it with 3D depthwise separable convolutions in deep layers (mid, up0, up1) and 2D convolutions in shallow layers (up2, up3) (Section 3.2).

Ablations show pruning ratio choices (1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8) trade off speed and quality (Table 2), and W-matrix initialization during fine-grained recovery yields a 6.25% quality improvement over the alternative (Table 3).
Reconstruction fidelity on the evaluation set reaches PSNR 37.61 dB, SSIM 0.9614, and LPIPS 0.0285 for the Wan 2.1 decoder (Section 4.1, Table 1).

QAQKmIp3SZ.text: BuildArena is presented as the first physics-aligned interactive benchmark for language-driven engineering construction, evaluating LLMs via a pipeline of task definition, LLM-based construction, and simulation-based evaluation (Abstract, Section 2.1).

Tasks span three categories -- Transport (vehicles), Support (bridges under load), and Lift (rockets) -- each with three difficulty tiers structured around six engineering dimensions: Quantification, Robustness, Magnitude, Compositionality, Precision, and Ambiguity (Section 2.1, Figure 3).
Eight closed-source LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-4, Grok-4, Gemini-2.0, DeepSeek-3.1, Qwen-3, Kimi-K2, Seed-1.6) are evaluated across all task tiers (Section 3, Table 2).
On Transport Lv.1, success rates range from 1.6% to 25.0% across models, with Grok-4 achieving the best result of 25.0% (Table 2).
On Support Lv.1, Grok-4 achieves the highest maximum sustained load of 211.4 units, with success rates across models ranging from 7.8% to 46.9% (Table 2).
Figure 6 identifies spatial conflict as the dominant failure mode across tasks, indicating LLMs struggle to maintain consistent spatial reasoning during incremental construction (Figure 6).

gVPwive1z6.text: The paper identifies Stability of Singular Distribution (SoSD), a phenomenon where the trace-normalized singular value spectrum of parameter matrices stabilizes significantly before the parameter matrices themselves stabilize, shown across training (Figure 1).

Training exhibits two phases: a Fast Descent phase where the Singular Distribution Variation (ΔΣ) peaks around 10^-2, and a Slow Descent phase beginning around 1000 training steps where ΔΣ stabilizes near 10^-4, marking SoSD onset (Figure 3).

SoSD synchronization with the slow-descent loss regime is demonstrated on GPT-2 Small (124M) and Medium (355M) trained on FineWeb, and on LLaMA 0.5B and 2B trained on C4 (Section 4/5, per architecture experiments).

Theorem 4.5 establishes that SoSD emerges under non-degeneracy and gradient boundedness conditions, with a stability bound proportional to the ratio of learning rate to weight-matrix norm, ε ∝ η/‖W‖ (Theorem 4.5).
Theorem 4.9 couples loss descent with singular distribution variation, showing that loss reduction during the Slow Descent phase is polynomially bounded by the magnitude of SoSD (Theorem 4.9).

iMuMdWc7uC.text: B-PAC reasoning adaptively routes queries between a thinking and non-thinking model by treating threshold selection as a betting game, using inverse-propensity-scoring estimators to build supermartingales that accumulate statistical evidence of safety (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 4.2 establishes anytime PAC efficiency: the probability that the empirical risk R_t(u_t) stays below epsilon for all time steps t is at least 1-alpha, holding for both i.i.d. and non-stationary data (Theorem 4.2, Sections 4.1-4.2, Section 5).
Theorem 4.3 shows the adaptive betting strategy achieves O(log T) regret, giving rapid convergence to the optimal efficient routing threshold (Theorem 4.3).

On the Magpie dataset with epsilon=0.08, B-PAC routes only 18.99% of queries to the thinking model while achieving 41.37% token savings relative to always using the thinking model (Section 6.1, Table 1).

On MMLU-Pro with epsilon=0.08, B-PAC achieves a 47.04% expert (thinking-model) call percentage and 78.07% token percentage, corresponding to up to an 81.01% reduction in thinking-model usage reported in the abstract (Section 6.1, Table 1).

Experiments use Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 as the thinking model and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the non-thinking model, evaluated on MATH, MMLU-Pro, BIG-Bench Hard, and Magpie, compared against online baselines IPS+Hoeffding and O-Naive (Section 6, Figure 3, Table 1).

8EZamwNqld.text: BioProCorpus contains 26,933 full-text human-written biological protocols spanning 16 biological subfields, sourced from six resources including Bio-protocol, Protocol Exchange, JoVE, Nature Protocols, Morimoto Lab, and Protocols.io (Section 2.1, Figure 1).

BioProBench derives over 556,000 (556,171) structured task instances from the corpus across five core tasks: Protocol Question Answering, Step Ordering, Error Correction, Protocol Generation, and Protocol Reasoning (Section 2.1).

Across 12 evaluated LLMs (closed-source, open-source, and domain-specific), the closed-source Gemini-2.5-pro-exp achieves the top Protocol Question Answering accuracy of 70.27%, while domain-specific biomedical models (e.g., BioMedGPT-10B, BioMistral-7B) score only around 20-21% accuracy (Table 2).

On the Step Ordering task, Gemini-2.5-pro-exp attains the best exact-match accuracy of 51.80%, while Kendall's Tau reaches 0.8104, indicating stronger pairwise step-ordering understanding than exact-match scores suggest (Table 3).

On the Protocol Generation task, scores are uniformly low across all evaluated LLMs, with the best BLEU score reaching only 10.23 (Qwen2.5-72b-instruct) and best METEOR reaching 24.78 (Claude-3-7-sonnet) (Table 6).

Chain-of-Thought prompting consistently degrades Protocol Generation performance across most models and metrics, indicating that explicit reasoning scaffolds disrupt coherent structured-protocol text generation (Section 4.5).

8yrdEj23Hj.text: TELLME is proposed as a method to enhance the transparency of LLMs' internal thinking and decision-making processes, aiming to make models easier for external monitors to evaluate rather than relying solely on external monitoring modules (abstract only).
TELLME uses hidden representations, going beyond standard Chain-of-Thought outputs, to help identify unsuitable and sensitive model behaviors (abstract only).
TELLME achieves consistent improvement on detoxification across multimodal test sets, distinct model architectures, and varying parameter scales (abstract only).
The paper analyzes TELLME's effect on generalization ability using both optimal transport theory and empirical evidence (abstract only).
The paper reports its findings across 15 tables and 8 figures spanning 28 pages, indicating an extensive multi-model, multi-scale experimental evaluation (abstract only).

v3diR6NstK.text: DARS (Difficulty Adaptive Rollout Sampling) addresses a bias in GRPO whereby cumulative advantage disproportionately weights medium-accuracy samples while down-weighting low-accuracy instances crucial for pushing reasoning boundaries (Section 2.1).
On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, DARS-HW-Breadth improves Avg@128 from a 49.6% RLVR baseline to 52.4% and Pass@128 from 79.6% to 82.2% (Table 1).
On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, DARS-HW-Breadth improves Avg@128 from 55.3% to 58.4% and Pass@128 from 81.4% to 83.4% (Table 1).
On Llama-3.1-8B, DARS-ET-Breadth improves Avg@128 from a 15.8% GRPO baseline to 22.0% and Pass@128 from 56.5% to 67.2% (Table 3).
DARS-ET requires only 15.2 average rollouts per prompt versus 32 for naive uniform rollout scaling on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, a 52.5% reduction (Table 2).

DARS-Breadth combines depth-adaptive rollout sampling with large-batch training (batch size 3072 vs. standard 128), replacing PPO mini-batch updates with full-batch gradient descent across multiple epochs to jointly improve Pass@1 and Pass@K (Section 3.2).

no1Tgzkw0x.text: ANCHOR constructs a hierarchically-structured factor space via abductive reasoning to decompose probability inference into conditional dependencies, enabling context-aware retrieval and mapping for LLM-based probability estimation (Section 4).
ANCHOR substantially reduces the rate of 'unknown' predictions produced by LLMs during probability estimation compared to baseline prompting approaches (Section 4).

ANCHOR achieves state-of-the-art probability estimation performance while reducing time and token overhead relative to baseline methods, with comparative results reported in Table 5 (Section 4, Table 5).
Extended experimental analyses and additional comparative results across baselines and settings are reported in a series of appendix tables (Tables 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 19, and 20) (Appendices B-C).

OVlAgNFMfS.text: PACE scores a level's usefulness for training as proportional to the squared L2 norm of the policy parameter update induced by training on it, S(l) = (1/alpha)||theta_new - theta_old||^2, avoiding value estimation, regret approximation, or Monte Carlo returns (Section on method description).
On MiniGrid OOD evaluation, PACE achieves an IQM of 0.964 and an Optimality Gap of 0.172, compared to the strongest baseline PLR at IQM 0.808 and Optimality Gap 0.299 (Table 3).
On Craftax OOD evaluation, PACE achieves an IQM of 0.694 and an Optimality Gap of 0.341, compared to the strongest baseline PLR-perp at IQM 0.618 and Optimality Gap 0.556 (Table 5).
PACE reaches a 72.3% solve rate on the PerfectMaze environment, substantially outperforming all UED baselines evaluated (Figure 5).

PACE is compared against Domain Randomization, Prioritized Level Replay (PLR), regret-guided PLR-perp, and ACCEL across 10 independent training seeds per method, using IQM and Optimality Gap computed via the rliable library (Section on experimental setup).
