QKFzXp5OLv.text: Applied to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 in the self-play setting, PromptCoT 2.0 improves scores by +4.4 on AIME 24 (to 92.1), +4.8 on AIME 25 (to 89.8), and +5.3 on HMMT Feb 25 (to 76.7) (Table 2).
At the 30B scale, PromptCoT 2.0 yields +6.1 on LiveCodeBench v5 (to 74.2), +5.0 on LiveCodeBench v6 (to 71.0), and +35 Codeforces Elo (to 2079) (Table 2).

Training Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct purely via SFT on synthetic prompts from PromptCoT 2.0 raises accuracy from a 12.8 baseline to 73.1 on AIME 24, from 8.0 to 65.6 on AIME 25, and from 14.7 to 53.4 on LiveCodeBench v5 (Table 3).

The framework casts prompt synthesis as expectation-maximization over a variational lower bound (ELBO) combining prompt validity and concept alignment, with an E-step that updates rationale generation via RL and an M-step that trains the prompt model on sampled rationales from the posterior (Section 3.1, Section 3.2.2).

PromptCoT 2.0-generated data shows the lowest accuracy (18.5%) and longest reasoning traces (37.4k tokens) among sampled difficulty-analysis datasets, indicating it produces harder synthetic problems than curated baselines (Section 5.9).
PromptCoT 2.0 demonstrates consistent scaling gains over curated baselines in data efficiency as training data volume increases (Section 5.7).

hocdjAEAIm.text: Theorem 4.6 establishes finite-time bounds for single-timescale actor-critic with evolving rewards, with actor error G_T and critic error W_T each bounded by O(1/√T) + O(F_T·√T) + O(√(F_T/T)) + O(ε), where F_T measures cumulative reward-parameter variation over T iterations (Section 4.2).

Corollary 4.7 shows that when the reward parameter is updated via gradient-based steps with step size η^φ_t = c_φ/t and bounded gradients, F_T = O(1/T), so the bounds reduce to G_T = O(1/√T) + O(ε) and W_T = O(1/√T) + O(ε), matching the best-known rate for static-reward actor-critic (Section 4.2).

Proposition 4.8 bounds the distribution mismatch under Markovian sampling without dependence on the mixing time, improving prior convergence rates by a factor of log²T in the static-reward case (Section 4.3).

Assumption 4.1 (sufficient exploration) requires the matrix A_θ to be negative definite with singular values bounded above by -λ, underpinning the actor-critic convergence analysis (Section 4, Assumption 4.1).

Algorithm 1 defines a single-timescale actor-critic scheme with step sizes η^θ_t = c_θ/√t and η^ω_t = c_ω/√t for policy and critic updates, alongside an arbitrary update rule for the evolving reward parameter φ_t (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1).

pbb3tYFdVp.text: GPUA learns an orthogonal mapping W satisfying W^T W = I to translate Vision Foundation Model features into Vision-Language Model semantic space while solving the alignment as a closed-form orthogonal Procrustes problem via SVD, requiring no labels or backpropagation (Section 3.4, Equation 13).

GPUA's Unsupervised Correspondence Mining stage jointly optimizes a correspondence matrix P using an objective combining VFM geometric coherence and VLM semantic consistency, (1-λ)||Z-PC||²_F + λ||X-PY||²_F (Section 3.3, Equation 6).

On zero-shot classification across 11 benchmarks, GPUA reaches 77.4% average accuracy versus 65.2% for baseline CLIP, an 11.8 percentage-point gain, including +34.9% on EuroSAT and +5.5% on FGVC (Table 1).
On open-vocabulary segmentation, GPUA gives consistent improvements when combined with MaskCLIP, SCLIP, and SC-CLIP, e.g., SC-CLIP+GPUA reaches 41.0 mIoU on C59 versus a 40.1 mIoU baseline (Table 2).

An ablation shows GPUA's Topology-aware Hubness Suppression (THS) loss outperforms alternative losses, reaching 80.3% on EuroSAT versus 75.5% for a contrastive loss and 73.2% for an adaptive loss (Table 4).

sKOTyhXscD.text: PIAA achieves 50.6% mAP on NUS-WIDE, a gain of +11.9% over TagCLIP and +6.1% over CCD among training-free multi-label recognition methods (Table 1).
PIAA also reaches 92.2% mAP on VOC12, 92.5% on VOC07, and 73.2% on COCO, achieved with a fully training-free pipeline requiring no gradient updates or parameter fine-tuning (Table 1).

The Patch-based Visual Classifier Learning (PVCL) component alone contributes a +2.6% mAP gain on VOC07, and combining PVCL with Prediction Adaptive Aggregation (PAA) yields +4.4% on COCO and +4.9% on NUS-WIDE, demonstrating synergy beyond either component alone (Table 2).

PIAA's global-local adaptive fusion combines patch-level and [CLS]-level predictions via a convex combination with weight alpha=0.9, and a sensitivity analysis identifies K=512 patches and alpha=0.9 as the best-performing configuration (Section 3.4, Figure 4).
PIAA is 362.1x faster than the CCD training-based baseline and 50.4x faster at inference than TagCLIP, owing to a parallelized single forward pass with a frozen CLIP encoder (Table 5, Figure 3).

5NKJHteKPZ.text: Partitioning collaborative inference networks at the identified Golden Partition Zone (decision-level layers) yields over 4x higher mean-squared reconstruction error against model inversion attacks compared to shallow feature-level splits (Table 3, Figures 4-7).
Reconstruction MSE rises sharply from about 0.02 at feature-level layers to over 0.136896 at the representational transition point, e.g., VGG19 Block 39 (Table 3, Figures 4-7).
Decision-level representations exhibit 66% stronger resistance on average to model inversion attacks compared to feature-level representations (Section 4.2).

An entropy-differential framework (Equations 3-5) shows conditional entropy H(x|z) undergoes a sharp increase when the representation shifts from feature-level to decision-level, governed by intra-class mean-squared radius R_c^2 and feature dimensionality D (Section 3).

The identified transition points differ by architecture: IR-152 (ResNet) transitions at Block 49 with skip connections delaying the shift, while VGG19 transitions earlier at Block 39, and Vision Transformers show no clear transition point, leaving persistent feature structure that defeats inversion resistance (Section 3.2).
Applying positive-alpha label smoothing during training compresses the intra-class mean-squared radius R_c^2, further enhancing model inversion resistance (Section 3.2).

b0O96emqNj.text: Coherent Contextual Decoding (CCD) approximates the marginal token-prediction distribution using a sliding-window historical buffer of predictive distributions from recent diffusion iterations rather than relying on a single decoding step (Section 3.2).

Proposition 1 connects the CCD-approximated target distribution to single-step predictive distributions via the conditional mutual information between contexts and token predictions, and Proposition 2 shows CCD dynamically governs sampling error bounds during decoding (Section 3, Proposition 1, Proposition 2).
On the Trip Plan benchmark with Dream-7B, CCD-DS achieves up to 3.48x decoding speedup alongside a 3.91% performance improvement over the confidence-based baseline (Table 1).
On HumanEval with Dream-7B, CCD alone yields a +4.65 point gain, and CCD-DS achieves a 3.04x speedup with a +4.05 point performance gain over the baseline (Table 1).

An ablation over historical buffer size shows accuracy peaks at buffer size 4, reaching 70% accuracy (a 20.7% relative improvement over the 58% baseline) while cutting the number of diffusion steps by 62.7% (95.54 vs 256 steps) (Section 4.5, Figure 3a).
CCD's improvements remain consistent across sampling temperatures from 0 to 1.0, with the largest gain (9.8% improvement) observed at temperature 0 (Section 4.5, Figure 3b).

2j3QyhUw5N.text: DR-MMSearchAgent outperforms MMSearch-R1 by 8.4 points on FVQA-test (66.8% vs 58.4%) (Table of main results).
DR-MMSearchAgent outperforms MMSearch-R1 on InfoSeek (60.0% vs 55.1%, +4.9), SimpleVQA (63.2% vs 57.4%, +5.8), and LiveVQA (37.0% vs 28.3%, +8.7) (main results table).

Structural Proximity-weighted Advantage Injection (SPAI) derives advantage signals by weighting trajectories according to their positional/structural proximity across the whole rollout batch, rather than using only a terminal scalar reward, to distinguish trajectories with identical rewards but different chain-of-thought lengths (Method section on SPAI).

Bidirectionally Guided Adaptive Smoothing (BGAS) calibrates interaction depth via differentiated Gaussian-shaped rewards, penalizing redundant tool calls on correctly answered instances while encouraging deeper exploration on incorrect ones (Method section on BGAS).

Training uses Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a composite reward split into accuracy (70%), format compliance (20%), and tool-efficiency (10%) components, plus the newly curated BridgeVQA dataset of 3,602 multi-hop QA pairs requiring at least 3 reasoning steps (Method/Training section).
Ablations show incremental contributions from each component: adding BridgeVQA data (+2.0%), SPAI (+3.7%), BGAS (+1.5%), and a refining agent (+2.0%) (Ablation study section).

9DKnuvRbSM.text: The orchestration framework integrates off-the-shelf modality expert models under a Qwen2.5-14B controller LLM, coordinating them via reasoning rather than end-to-end gradient-based training (Architecture section).

The LLM controller emits explicit control tokens in an [S.need_*] format (e.g., [S.need_vision], [S.need_reasoning], [S.stop], [S.listen]) to enable protocol-constrained, auditable routing of tasks across heterogeneous modality experts (Control Token System section).
The system achieves 88.54% on MMBench-EN and 69.37% on MMStar, both exceeding GPT-4o's reported 83.10% and 64.70% on the same benchmarks (Benchmark performance table).
On MMMU temporal reasoning the system scores 70.04% versus GPT-4o's 59.20%, and it attains 50.27% on LVBench (Benchmark performance table).

The framework achieves a 3.2 second response time versus 6.0 seconds for Qwen2.5-Omni, and yields a 10.3% reduction in TTS latency through parallel processing plus a +7.8% video-understanding improvement on LLaVA-Video (Efficiency Gains section).

RJQvLkseJL.text: GeoSense trains a model to autonomously trigger a learned <vggt> token that decides, per query, whether to integrate 3D geometric features from a VGGT-1B encoder alongside a Qwen2.5-VL-3B 2D encoder, rather than always injecting geometric signals (Architecture/Method section).

GeoSense raises the spatial-reasoning average across VSI-Bench, MMSI, MindCube-Tiny, BLINK, EmbSpatial, and CV-Bench(3D) from a 51.0 baseline to 63.4, including 54.9 on VSI-Bench and 68.5 on BLINK, while keeping the general-benchmark average at 55.2 (Table 2).

An ablation comparing injection schemes on VSI-Bench shows GeoSense's learned selective injection (triggering geometry on 35.68% of samples) reaches 54.86 accuracy, versus 48.07 for a no-injection baseline (0% injection) and 52.34 for always-on fusion (100% injection) (Table 3).
Training-stage ablation shows BLINK accuracy rising from 58.9 for the initialized model, to 61.9 after Geometry Alignment SFT, to 68.5 after Spatial-Aware Fine-Tuning (Table 4).

The geometry trigger fires on only about 3% of general visual-task samples but on 43.7% of VSI-Bench samples and 27.58% of MindCube samples, demonstrating query-dependent selective activation (Key Findings section).
GeoSense reaches 37.36% overall accuracy on embodied-task evaluation, ranking among top performers across static/dynamic 2D and 3D scenarios (Table 5).

hIFa2QxEiC.text: Bit-Plane Decomposition Quantization (BPDQ) constructs a variable per-weight quantization grid from bit-planes plus scalar coefficients (c1, c2), which strictly expands the feasible representable-value set compared to a fixed/uniform quantization grid at the same bitwidth (Method/Mathematical Foundation section).
At 2-bit precision, BPDQ reaches 87.72% GSM8K accuracy on Qwen2.5-72B, versus 63.46% for GPTQ and 0.00% for AWQ at the same bitwidth (Table of GSM8K benchmark results).

At 2-bit precision, BPDQ reaches 80.89% GSM8K accuracy on Qwen3-32B versus 44.20% for GPTQ and 0.00% for AWQ, and 42.46% on Ministral3-8B versus 12.36% for GPTQ and 0.00% for AWQ (Table of GSM8K benchmark results).

BPDQ enables serving Qwen2.5-72B on a single RTX 3090 GPU at the W2-G256 configuration (22.69 GB VRAM), achieving 83.85% GSM8K accuracy compared to 90.83% at 16-bit precision (Deployment Achievement section).

On LongBench retrieval-style tasks at 2-bit, BPDQ scores 53.75% while GPTQ collapses to 4.98%, and BPDQ's outlier-intensity metric (DiagR) decreases only 4.98% versus GPTQ's 32.89% suppression at 2-bit (Long-Context Robustness / Outlier Preservation sections).

On Qwen2.5-7B, BPDQ quantization costs about 3x the time of GPTQ (~40 minutes) but achieves 18.09ms per-token inference latency at batch size 1 (W2-G64) using 3.86 GB versus 6.63 GB for GPTQ-W4 (Hardware & Efficiency Profile section).

0zzha0gskW.text: On a Qwen3-4B model probing 10,000 three-digit ten-integer additions, activations at generation position p=4 cluster into ten digit-anchored basins, each subdivided into three carry-state clusters, visualized via UMAP (Figure 2).

The Iso-Raw-Sum Trajectory (IRST) framework models continuous carry potential Φ_p = Σ_{j=1}^{P-1-p} r_{p+j}/10^j, with discrete carry c_p = ⌊Φ_p⌋, connecting adjacent digit basins via trajectories T0–T3 (Section 5.1, Eq. 3, Figure 3-4).

A noisy quantization model (perceived potential Φ̂_p = Φ_p + ε, ε ~ N(0, σ²)) predicts an empirical 'periodic bathtub' error distribution near integer carry thresholds with R²=0.80 and noise parameter σ≈0.05 for 3-term addition (Section 5.2-5.3, Figure 5).
Probing accuracy differs sharply by target: raw-sum-mod-10 probes reach 98.60% while correctness probes reach only 82.41%, reflecting the manifold's topological separability (Section 7, Table 1).
Cognitive noise σ scales with problem difficulty, rising from 0.05 (3 terms) to 0.12 (4 terms) to 0.25 (5 terms) (Appendix G, Figure 12).

A dual-stream consistency protocol using true raw-sum plus carry probes for inference-time self-correction raises token accuracy to 89.56% at δ=0.1 and 96.0% for the R+TC configuration (Section 8, Tables 2-3).

UrKNw5Xo9x.text: Theorem 3.1 shows that fine-tuning a transformer via RL with the sign of the policy gradient after a single update yields near-optimal attention weights for learning k-sparse Boolean functions with intermediate chain-of-thought supervision (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 shows that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) without teacher forcing also learns k-sparse Boolean functions, but requires T gradient updates—one per reasoning step—rather than RL's single update (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).

RL learns the entire chain-of-thought simultaneously in one gradient step by exploiting step-level rewards, whereas SFT learns the chain step-by-step because later steps depend on correctly generating prior ones (Section 3).
The k-PARITY task (Theorem 4.1) satisfies the paper's separation conditions, with attention scores at relevant positions converging as the noise parameter σ→1/2 (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
k-AND and k-OR functions are shown to satisfy the same learnability conditions under appropriate activation functions (Section 4, Claim 4.2).

r2RVWpvPk7.text: Hydra-Nav-IRFT achieves 84.8% success rate and 41.1% SPL on HM3D, outperforming the previous best method Uni-Navid (73.7% SR) by 11.1 percentage points (Section 4, Table 2).
Hydra-Nav-IRFT achieves 64.0% success rate and 29.6% SPL on MP3D, outperforming CogNav (46.6% SR) by 17.4 percentage points (Section 4, Table 2).
Hydra-Nav-IRFT achieves 66.3% success rate and 37.4% SPL on OVON Val-Unseen, outperforming NavFoM (45.2% SR) by 21.2 percentage points (Section 4, Table 2).

The adaptive dual-process reasoning mechanism reduces the frequency of invoking the slow reasoning module to just 3.0% of steps on HM3D and 3.5% on OVON Val-Unseen, while improving the SOT (search-oriented-tradeoff) metric over fixed-frequency baselines (Section 4, Table 5).

Ablation studies isolating the contributions of the Stage 1 spatial-action alignment, Stage 2 reasoning-memory integration, and Stage 3 adaptive reasoning via iterative rejection fine-tuning modules are reported in Table 3 (Section 3.3-3.5, Table 3).

npOsvPRB0i.text: REST generates a 121-frame (4.84s) talking-head video in 4.421 seconds, dramatically faster than baselines Sonic (83.584s), EchoMimic (124.105s), Hallo (212.002s), and FantasyTalking (896.089s) (Section 4.2, Table 1).
On the HDTF dataset REST achieves FID 14.597 and FVD 219.87, improving on the best baselines Ditto (FID 15.440) and Sonic (FVD 245.416) (Section 4.2, Table 1).
REST's ID-Context Cache combines ID-Sink persistent reference-image sinks with a Context-Cache that extends the temporal receptive field via concatenated prior-chunk KV embeddings (Section 3.2).
Ablations show removing ID-Sink degrades FID from 14.597 to 19.362, and removing Context-Cache worsens FVD from 219.87 to 271.508 (Section 4.3, Table 2).

Asynchronous Streaming Distillation trains REST using a non-streaming teacher with asynchronous noise scheduling, a contrastive distribution loss (Equation 21), and a smoothness matching objective (Equation 23) (Section 3.3).

KBCWS6OBnD.text: TreeCUA's tree-structured data synthesis pipeline generates 100k trajectories, yielding 50k high-quality full trajectories, 101k high-quality sub-trajectories, and 708k step-level training samples, plus 16k DPO preference pairs (Section 3-4).
On OSWorld-Verified, TreeCUA-7B achieves 34.6% success rate and TreeCUA-DPO-7B achieves 36.6%, both exceeding OpenCUA-7B (24.3%) and UI-TARS-1.5-7B (25.1%) (Section 6, Table results).
On out-of-domain evaluation, TreeCUA-7B reaches 26.7% success rate and TreeCUA-DPO-7B reaches 30.8%, versus a Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline of 0.8% (Section 6).
Tree branching in the synthesized trajectory data predominantly occurs at depth 10, motivating a temporal width decay schedule implemented across three phases (Section 4).
Action coordinates are normalized via 20x20 grid quantization, and duplicate/redundant states are pruned using an RMS pixel-difference threshold of ε=5.0 on a 0-255 scale (Section 3).

TreeCUA-DPO training via branch-adjacent trajectory comparisons yields a maximum gain of +20.0% success rate (Thunderbird) but a maximum regression of -10.6% (Impress) across applications (Section 6).

vqxprtjuKH.text: For the independent Gaussian variance allocation problem, the paper gives a PTAS achieving E[max_i X_i] ≥ OPT - ε in polynomial time (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.2).
For correlated Gaussian variables, a PTAS with the same additive ε guarantee is established (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.2).
For the GraphVarAlloc problem with multiple constraint sets (general m>1), the paper gives an O(log n) multiplicative approximation guaranteeing Ω(1/log n)·OPT (Theorem 1.3, Section 1.2).

Theorem 1.6 proves that in the optimal allocation, only Θ(1/p) variables receive variance Ω(p), i.e., the allocation concentrates on a shrinking subset as the constraint parameter p grows (Theorem 1.6, Section 1.3).

Lemma 2.1 bounds the contribution of small-variance variables by O(ε√ln(1/ε)), which is used to limit the number of high-variance variables to O(1/ε²) and underlies the PTAS construction (Lemma 2.1, Section 2.1).

Monte Carlo simulations on Erdős–Rényi random graphs with n=8 nodes and edge probabilities p ranging from 1/8 to 8/8 are used to illustrate the concentration and concavity results across independent, positively, and negatively correlated settings (Figures 1-2, Section 1.3).

7gIbZL9jwE.text: DiffStyle3D introduces an Attention-Aware Loss that injects keys/values from a style image with queries from rendered images for style transfer, and aligns centered/normalized attention outputs between content and rendered images for content preservation (Section 4.1).

DiffStyle3D introduces Geometry-Guided Attention (GGA), which uses camera parameters and depth maps to warp keys/values across views via reprojection grids and a geometry-aware mask restricting optimization to non-overlapping regions (Section 4.2, Equations 9-13).
On the multi-view consistency metric CLIP-CONS, DiffStyle3D achieves 0.128 (scene-level) and 0.412 (object-level), reported as the best among compared methods (Table 1).
DiffStyle3D achieves FID scores of 20.63 (scene-level) and 16.44 (object-level), compared against StyleGaussian, SGSST, CLIPGaussian, and FantasyStyle (Table 1).
An ablation shows removing GGA drops CLIP-CONS to 0.121, and removing the geometry-aware mask drops it to 0.124, versus 0.128 for the full method (Table 2).

Implementation uses a fixed diffusion timestep t=1, batch size N=4 views, content weighting λ=0.1, and a Stable Diffusion 1.5 backbone with features extracted from all self-attention layers (Section 5, Implementation Details).

7N2ydbDahV.text: The paper introduces an Information Gain Reward (Belief Update Reward) that quantifies clarification utility as the shift in length-normalized log-likelihood of the ground-truth goal before versus after a clarification exchange (Equation 2).
Across five agent backbones, Information Gain Reward-based clarification improves average task success rate by 3.7 percentage points over the no-clarification baseline, from 23.6% to 27.3% (Table 3).
In the retail domain, success rate improves from 16.5% to 18.3%, and in the airline domain from 13.3% to 17.3% (Table 1).
The clarification mechanism adds only 0.3 additional interaction steps on average, reducing clarifier invocations to 1.3 per task versus 4.2 for a naive baseline (Table 1).
On the strongest evaluated model (DeepSeek-V3.2), the method yields a 6.4 percentage point improvement in success rate (Table 3).

Kw0nhxeTeI.text: Proposition 3.1 proves that under the coupling σ = β^{-(1+η)/4}, the fSGLD invariant measure converges in KL divergence and Wasserstein-2 distance to the Hessian-trace regularized target distribution as β→∞ (Proposition 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 establishes a non-asymptotic Wasserstein-1 convergence bound for fSGLD to the flatness-biased stationary distribution, with corollary 3.3 giving a Wasserstein-2 rate of O(λ^{1/4}) (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3).
Theorem 3.5 derives excess risk bounds for the Hessian-trace regularized objective, showing convergence toward global flat minima (Theorem 3.5).

Training ResNet-34 from scratch, fSGLD with the theoretically prescribed β-σ coupling reaches 62.02±0.29% accuracy on CIFAR-100N versus 59.18±0.33% for SAM, while running at ~23.7 s/iter versus SAM's 41.3 s/iter (Table 1).
Fine-tuning ViT-B/16, fSGLD with β-σ coupling attains 75.18% on CIFAR-100N versus 74.66% for SAM (Table 2).

An ablation in Section 4.3 shows the theoretically prescribed β-σ coupling substantially outperforms fixed-β heuristics across all benchmarks, and Figure 3 shows fSGLD converges to solutions with lower Hessian maximum eigenvalues and trace than SGD, matching or exceeding SAM's flatness at lower cost (Section 4.3, Figure 3).

y5kHeBZgVn.text: Reflector uses a two-stage training framework: supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated reflection data (Stage 1), followed by reinforcement learning with dual rewards optimizing final output safety and reflection quality (Stage 2).

Against the indirect jailbreak DRA on LLaMA-3.1-8B, Reflector achieves a 92.31% Defense Success Rate, up from a 10.04% baseline, and DSR exceeds 90% across all four indirect attack types tested: DRA, PAP, ReNeLLM, and DrAttack (Table 1).
Reflector maintains 81.0% DSR against adaptive ICL-based jailbreaks and 90.0% against AutoDAN-Turbo (Table 1).
Cross-attack transferability testing shows negligible performance variance (σ between 0.76% and 1.21%) regardless of which indirect jailbreak method generated the training data (Table 3).
On GSM8K, Reflector achieves 90.15% accuracy, a 5.65 percentage point absolute gain over the 84.50% baseline, alongside improved performance on MMLU-Pro (45.20%) (Table 2).

Blocking explicit reflection markers via token suppression causes only a 1.2% performance drop, and the RL stage reduces average generated tokens from 391.95 (after SFT) to 302.58, close to the 295.57-token baseline (Table 5, Table 6).

MItmwRV0l2.text: WorldCache achieves a 3.65x end-to-end speedup on HunyuanVoyager-13B while preserving WorldScore quality (45.43 vs. 46.40 baseline) (Section 5.2, Table 1).
On Aether-5B, WorldCache attains a 1.68x speedup for world generation and a 2.61x acceleration for 3D reconstruction (depth/pose estimation) while preserving geometry fidelity (Sections 5.2-5.3).

The curvature score partitions tokens into stable, linear, and chaotic groups using percentile thresholds ps=0.3 and pc=0.7 on the normalized turning-rate metric κi = ||a||₂/(||v||₂²+ε) (Section 4.1, Eq. 7).

Chaotic-prioritized Adaptive Skipping (CAS) accumulates a dimensionless drift score per token and triggers a full backbone evaluation once accumulated uncertainty exceeds threshold η (Section 4.2, Eq. 12-13).
On HunyuanVoyager, WorldCache improves reconstruction fidelity over the EasyCache baseline, reaching PSNR 23.49 vs. 21.76, SSIM 0.770 vs. 0.737, and LPIPS 0.176 vs. 0.208 (Table 1).

96VOwRWMQr.text: The M-DESIGN knowledge base contains 67,760 graph neural network models spanning 22 graph datasets and 3 task types (node classification, link prediction, graph classification) (Section on knowledge base construction).

Under a 100-model-testing budget for node classification, M-DESIGN reaches the search-space global optimum on 26 of 33 data-task pairs, including Actor (34.89), CiteSeer (74.59), CS (95.33), Cora (88.50), Cornell (77.48), DBLP (84.29), and PubMed (89.08) (Table III).
For link prediction, M-DESIGN attains global-optimum performance on 9 of 11 datasets including Actor, Computers, CS, Cora, Cornell, DBLP, PubMed, Texas, and Wisconsin (Table VII).
For graph classification, M-DESIGN achieves top results on COX2 (86.74), IMDB-BINARY (81.00), PROTEINS (79.73), PTC_FM (70.53), and PTC_MR (66.67) (Table VIII).

M-DESIGN is compared against 10 baselines spanning ML-based search (Random, RL, EA, GraphNAS, Auto-GNN), model-base-centric selection (GraphGym, NAS-Bench-Graph, KBG), and refinement approaches (AutoTransfer, DesiGNN), with Table V showing many baselines require 100+ iterations or fail to converge (marked ∞) to match M-DESIGN's 50-iteration benchmark.

Section V-C1 and Figure 5 validate the linear-relationship assumption between modification gains (R²=0.87 for in-distribution cases) and confirm Gaussian-distributed gains via Shapiro-Wilk tests (p>0.05) on high-similarity benchmarks.

O3tDdAGKkj.text: VeriTime fine-tunes Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen3-4B to match or exceed larger proprietary LLMs such as GPT-4o-mini on time series reasoning tasks (Section on model comparison, Table 1).
Applying VeriTime yields a 102.15% overall improvement on scenario-based tasks for Qwen2.5-3B and a 14.67% overall improvement for Qwen3-4B (Table 1).
On knowledge-based tasks spanning medical, healthcare, and bioacoustics domains (e.g., CTU, ECG, EMG, Right Whale contact calls), VeriTime yields 23-50% gains (Table 2).
VeriTime reduces inference token usage by 71% on average across 8 tasks compared to base models while maintaining or improving accuracy (Table 4).

The framework combines a TSRgen pipeline for process-verifiable chain-of-thought data synthesis, difficulty-based data scheduling, and a two-stage reinforcement fine-tuning procedure using structural, hard, and process multi-objective rewards (Section on framework/method design).

DjnbMWE0Ek.text: Theorem 1 (Section 3.2) establishes that ULSE-n1 satisfies cross-sectional stability (identical latent positions Bzi:(t)=Bzj:(t) imply identical embeddings Yi:(t)=Yj:(t)) and longitudinal stability (identical latent positions and degree heterogeneity across times t,u imply identical embeddings across those times) (Theorem 1, Section 3.2).
Theorem 2 proves ULSE-n1 embeddings converge almost surely to their noise-free counterparts at rate O(1/(ρ^{1/2} n^{1/2})) (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
Theorem 3 shows the noise-free ULSE-n1 embeddings themselves satisfy both cross-sectional and longitudinal stability properties, forming the basis for Theorem 1 (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).

Theorem 4 extends the stability results to ULSE-n2 under the requirement that the embedding dimension equals the number of communities (d=K), relaxing the degree-uniformity assumption needed for ULSE-n1 (Theorem 4, Section 3.3).

Proposition 1 establishes a dynamic Cheeger-type inequality bounding the k-way conductance φk(𝒢) of the dynamic network in terms of the singular values σk of the unfolded normalized Laplacian (Proposition 1, Section 3.4).

8metOwZHjD.text: Executable Agentic Memory (EAM) achieves a 52.6% success rate on the AndroidWorld benchmark, exceeding UI-TARS-7B by up to 19.6 percentage points (Table 1).
EAM outperforms UI-TARS-7B by +22.8 percentage points on MobileMiniWob++ and by +31.1 percentage points on DroidTask (Table 1).
EAM operates at an average latency of 2.8 seconds and uses only 8.3K tokens per step, a roughly 6x reduction versus GPT-4o's 50.8K tokens per step (Table 2).

The offline stage builds a knowledge graph via state-aware DFS exploration combined with Byte-Pair-Encoding-inspired action-group mining to compress multi-step routines into reusable operations (Section on offline knowledge graph construction).

The online stage performs value-guided graph search in which a lightweight Q-function model steers Monte Carlo Tree Search over the knowledge graph to extract executable action paths, with Theorem 5.2 proving bias-consistency of the learned Q-model and Theorem 5.3 giving sample-complexity bounds for high-probability optimal path extraction (Theorems 5.2 and 5.3).

An ablation shows Q-function models trained on AndroidWorld transfer to improve performance on unseen environments DroidTask and MobileMiniWob++, indicating the learned value function captures generalizable GUI navigation patterns (ablation study, Section 6).

kiSm94YKor.text: RDB-PFN is pretrained purely on synthetic relational databases generated via a three-stage pipeline (schema generation with LayerDAG, structural generation with Selective SCMs, and content completion with bidirectional GNNs), using roughly 2 million synthetic datasets rather than real relational databases (Section 3).

The RDB-PFN inference model uses only about 2.6 million parameters via a 'Linearize-and-Attend' design combining Deep Feature Synthesis with a vanilla Transformer, yet outperforms fine-tuned single-table foundation models on 19 real-world relational tasks while using only 2%-20% of the parameters of competing foundation models (Section 5).
RDB-PFN achieves 3x-8x faster inference than competing foundation models pretrained on tens to hundreds of millions of synthetic datasets (Section 5).

A universality proof (Theorem D.23) establishes that the three-stage schema/structure/content construction can represent any acyclic relational database distribution under the paper's stated assumptions (Appendix D, Theorem D.23).

The full RDB-PFN model, trained on both single-table and relational synthetic tasks, outperforms an ablated single-table-only variant, indicating positive transfer from exposure to diverse relational structures (Section 5, ablation study).

SHZw5dqHZ7.text: Theorem 3.1 shows the MDP transition probability of diffusion LLM generation can be reduced to sampling one timestep per block, cutting the number of required forward passes from T total diffusion steps to N_B blocks (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 proves that schedule-dependent coefficients in the policy probability ratio cancel between the policy πθ and reference policy πref, so the ratio can be estimated using only the probabilities of newly unmasked tokens (Theorem 3.2).

dTRPO improves performance by up to 9.6% on STEM tasks (GPQA), 4.3% on coding (HumanEval+), 4.04% on math (MATH), and 3.0% on instruction-following (IFEval) relative to baselines (results tables, Section 5).

dTRPO requires only 4 forward passes per training example, comparable to standard DPO, whereas online rollout methods such as TRaDO require N times more computation for the rollout stage (Section 4/5, efficiency comparison).

dTRPO uses block attention masking to compute N_B sampled diffusion steps within a single forward pass together with an inference-aligned scheduler that selects top-k confidence tokens per step (Section 4).

lZqQN9Ji21.text: SW-DRSO defines an ambiguity region around an input set's empirical measure using the Sliced-Wasserstein distance, Γ_SW(S) := {S' : SW(μ_S, μ_S') ≤ ρ}, to model distributional (rather than discrete) inference-time element corruption (Section 4).

Rather than solving the worst-case adversarial optimization directly, SW-DRSO's barycentric adversary synthesizes Wasserstein barycenters over a probability simplex Λ ∈ Δ_K of local neighborhoods, and Propositions 4.1-4.3 show these synthesized embeddings remain within the SW-ball, correspond to SW Fréchet means, and upper-bound the discrete adversarial loss (Section 4, Propositions 4.1, 4.2, 4.3).

On the ModelNet point-cloud classification task, SW-DRSO achieves the best overall accuracy (82.86%) and outperforms the PSWE baseline under severe corruption (69.99% vs. 69.65%) (Table with Task II results).
On the NWPU-RESISC45 patch-set visual recognition task, SW-DRSO attains the best accuracy under both mild corruption (54.95%) and severe corruption (31.89%) (Task IV results table).
SW-DRSO trains 27% faster per epoch than a Sinkhorn-based Wasserstein variant (15.6 vs. 21.5 minutes per epoch) (Section 5, efficiency comparison).

Mstzzv2ham.text: ConTSG-Bench evaluates conditional time series generation across eight datasets spanning healthcare, meteorology, energy, traffic, and network domains, using class-label, structured-attribute, and natural-language conditions built via an LLM-based captioning and attribute-extraction pipeline (Section 3, dataset construction).

The benchmark evaluates 10 representative conditional generation models: 2 label-conditioned (TimeVQVAE, TTS-CGAN), 3 attribute-conditioned (TimeWeaver, TEdit, WaveStitch), and 5 text-conditioned (BRIDGE, VerbalTS, T2S, DiffuSETS, Text2Motion) (Section 4, evaluated methods).

ConTSG-Bench organizes evaluation around five research questions covering overall benchmarking, sensitivity to morphological vs. conceptual condition abstraction, fine-grained temporal controllability, compositional generalization to novel attribute combinations, and downstream task utility (Section 4/5, RQ1-RQ5).

Text-conditioned models achieve the highest performance ceiling among the three conditioning modalities but show significant variance across architectures, and no single model dominates across all eight datasets (Section 5, RQ1 results).

Current conditional time series generators universally struggle with fine-grained structural controllability and compositional generalization to novel attribute combinations, and downstream classification utility of generated data cannot be reliably predicted from fidelity metrics alone (Section 5, RQ3-RQ5 findings).

StQUBg3hlS.text: ST-TGExplainer disentangles stability patterns (recurring historical interactions) from transition patterns (newly emerging interactions) via a frequency-based soft assignment separating a stable subgraph G_S from a transition subgraph G_T (Section 3, Stability-Transition Disentangler).

ST-TGExplainer is trained with a disentangled information bottleneck objective combining a prediction loss, a compression loss enforcing a compact explanatory subgraph, and a disentanglement loss suppressing redundancy between stability and transition representations (Section 3, IB objective).

ST-TGExplainer achieves best or competitive link prediction AP on 5 of 6 datasets, including 94.47% on USLegis and 90.25% on Can.Parl., which are low-repeat-interaction datasets (Table of link prediction results).

For explanation quality (ACC-AUC), ST-TGExplainer outperforms baselines across all datasets, reaching 92.47% on Wikipedia, 96.04% on UCI, and 96.88% on Can.Parl., with up to a 9% improvement on low-repeat-ratio datasets (Table of explanation quality results).

Ablations show removing the disentanglement loss substantially impairs prediction accuracy while removing the compression loss substantially impairs explanation quality, and the full model exceeds a mixed (non-disentangled) explanation baseline by 3.89 to 7.98 ACC-AUC points (Section 5, ablation study; Figure 3 also shows a compact parameter footprint and moderate training cost).

IGW4mVoDSs.text: AnomSeer-7B achieves 84.4% average Affinity-F1 on the AnomLLM test set, far exceeding GPT-4o's 41.2% (Table 1).

AnomSeer combines Expert Chain-of-Thought (ExpCoT) traces built from histogram outlier scores, FFT, and matrix profile analysis with a GRPO extension called TimerPO that adds an optimal-transport-based time-series reasoning advantage (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
Removing ExpCoT from training degrades average performance by roughly 5%, and removing the orthogonal-projection component causes further degradation across anomaly types (Table 2).
AnomSeer shows a particularly large margin over baselines on frequency-type anomalies, reaching about 68.3% versus roughly 17% for the best baseline (Table 1).
AnomSeer generalizes to unseen shapelet anomalies and to the real-world TSB-UAD benchmark, maintaining its advantage over TimeMaster and commercial MLLMs (Figure 6).

6xRIf7H6Nb.text: The paper formalizes LLM-judge reliability via a two-phase Item Response Theory framework using the Graded Response Model, separating intrinsic consistency from human alignment (Section 3, Section 5, Section 6).
Phase 1 defines prompt consistency via coefficient of variation (CV), treating CV < 0.10 as acceptable, and marginal reliability via ρ, treating ρ > 0.70 as acceptable (Section 5, Table 1).
Vision-task judges show substantially higher prompt-consistency CV values (0.16-1.32) than NLP-task judges, indicating greater instability under prompt variation (Table 1).

VIEScore exhibits a discrimination-breadth ratio (θratio) of 2.03-4.40, showing LLM judges perceive far broader quality differences than human raters, whereas HelpSteer-2 is well calibrated with θratio near 1.0 (Table 3).

On NLP tasks, LLM judge scores correlate with human judgments at r=0.2-0.5, while on vision tasks the correlation approaches zero, revealing a validity gap rather than mere miscalibration (Section 6).

An ablation on TopicalChat varying prompt detail and rating scale shows that more detailed instructions reduce prompt sensitivity and 5-point scales improve reliability relative to coarser scales (Table 2).

bcN12UkftY.text: FloorplanQA (PlanQA) comprises 1,800 synthetic structured floor layouts (600 each for kitchens, living rooms, bedrooms) yielding 18,000 question-layout pairs across 11 cognitive/question categories, evaluated on 11 LLMs (Section 3.1, Table 1, Table 2).

Models achieve over 95% accuracy on metric-computation questions but fall below 50% accuracy on topology, rule-based validation, and geometric-planning questions, per the cognitive-target accuracy heatmap (Section 4.1, Figure 2).
Accuracy gains from model scale are steep up to roughly 30B parameters but plateau beyond that on complex planning and constraint-satisfaction categories (Figure 3).
A JSON-vs-XML structured-representation ablation shows stable accuracy across formats, indicating models are largely invariant to the choice of structured encoding (Section 4.2, Table 5).

Small spatial perturbations (±0.1m jitter) to layouts cause only minor accuracy fluctuations, showing models are comparatively robust to small perturbations despite failing on harder constraint tasks (Appendix Table 10).
Kitchen layouts yield the highest accuracy (about 80%), while living rooms and bedrooms score lower due to denser layouts and greater occlusion (Figure 4).

EulXRTtFCd.text: Omni-Diffusion is presented as the first any-to-any multimodal model built entirely on mask-based discrete diffusion, unifying text, speech, and image understanding and generation via a shared architecture combining a MAGVIT-v2 image tokenizer, SenseVoiceSmall speech encoder/GLM-4-Voice decoder, and the Dream-7B backbone (Section 3.2).
On LibriSpeech ASR, Omni-Diffusion achieves 7.05 WER, better than AnyGPT's 8.50 WER, while on LibriTTS it reaches 3.07 WER versus CosyVoice's 2.89 WER (Table 1).
On visual understanding/generation benchmarks, Omni-Diffusion scores 76.6 on POPE, 1216.7 on MME-Perception, and achieves CLIP-T 0.235 / CLIP-I 0.667 for text-to-image generation (Table 2).
Speech-to-image generation achieves CLIP-T 0.225 and CLIP-I 0.645, comparable to the model's text-conditioned image generation performance (Section 4).
Text-to-image generation retains 0.650 CLIP-I using only 10 inference steps compared to 256 steps, demonstrating substantial sampling efficiency (Table 3).

The model is trained in three stages—visual-language pre-alignment, speech-vision-language joint alignment, and speech-driven visual interaction improvement—using an attenuated tail-pad masking scheme (γ=0.6) and a position penalty (γp=0.5) to reduce repetitive image patterns (Section 3.3, Table 4).

RYTZ3Y2mBJ.text: SKETCH conditions long-horizon vessel trajectory prediction on a predicted 'Next Key Point' (NKP) representing navigational intent, factorizing prediction as P(Y|X) = ΣZ P(Y|X,Z)P(Z|X) (Section 3.1, Definition 3.1).

On the private dataset, SKETCH achieves MSEP=0.41 and MFD=7.80, outperforming TrAISformer (MSEP=0.71, MFD=19.78) and MP-LSTM (MSEP=1.6, MFD=31.11), while also cutting inference time to 62s versus 287s (MP-LSTM) and 541s (TrAISformer) (Table 2).
On the public dataset, SKETCH attains MSEP=2.8e-04 and MFD=0.96, versus TrAISformer's MFD of 49.50, demonstrating strong generalization (Table 3).

The retrieval-augmented NKP predictor reaches up to 98.98% accuracy in the closed-set pretrain configuration and 93.61% in the open-set fine-tuned configuration, both exceeding a Random Forest baseline of 76.54% (Table 4).

An NKP-quality ablation shows that using a deliberately wrong NKP degrades MFD to 11.04 versus 7.78-7.80 with correct or predicted NKPs, and removing NKP conditioning entirely yields MFD=8.99, confirming the key point's contribution to long-horizon accuracy (Table 5).

7g23tYAIDC.text: BITE (Bandit-guided Style Manipulation) attacks LLM judges by modifying only stylistic dimensions such as sentiment, register, and structural cues while preserving semantic content (Section 3).
BITE achieves an attack success rate exceeding 65% against LLM-as-a-judge systems, measured in the main attack success rate comparison (Table 4).
BITE raises judge scores by roughly 1-2 points on a 9-point evaluation scale without changing the underlying answer content (Section 5).

Different judge models exhibit distinct vulnerability fingerprints, with some judges disproportionately sensitive to sentiment manipulation and others more sensitive to register or structural cues (Figures 5-7).
Ablation studies isolate the contribution of the contextual bandit component versus random style search to BITE's attack success rate (Section 6).

bwqwuJM68F.text: MonoScale formalizes sequential agent-pool expansion in multi-agent systems as a contextual bandit problem, with Lemma 4.1 giving an exact surrogate objective and Lemma 4.2 showing conservative lift preserves pre-expansion performance (Section 4).
Theorem 4.3 proves that trust-region-constrained memory updates yield a monotonic non-decreasing performance guarantee across successive agent-onboarding rounds (Theorem 4.3, Equation 17).

On the GAIA benchmark, MonoScale with a Qwen-3 backbone improves accuracy from 44.84% (3 agents) to 55.15% (10 agents), a +23.0% relative gain, surpassing the DeepSeek-V3.2 strong-router fixed-pool baseline (51.52%) and matching GPT-5 (54.55%) (Table 1).
On Humanity's Last Exam, MonoScale with Qwen-3 improves from 11.60% to 19.90% (+71.6%), surpassing the GPT-5 strong-router baseline (19.63%) (Table 2).
Under noisy-agent conditions, Gemini-3-Pro without the memory mechanism suffers performance collapse as the agent pool grows, whereas MonoScale remains stable (Figure 3).

NuR4lG4gKB.text: AIR-VLA is presented as the first Vision-Language-Action benchmark specifically for aerial manipulation, built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim with a quadrotor UAV carrying a 7-DoF Franka Panda manipulator forming a 12-DoF control problem (Section on system configuration).

The benchmark releases 3,000 manually teleoperated demonstrations spanning four task suites (Base Manipulation, Object & Spatial Understanding, Semantic Reasoning, and Long-Horizon Planning) with an average episode length of about 475 time steps (Table 5).

The best-performing VLA model, pi-0.5, achieves an overall average score of 42.0/100, with strong Safety (84.7) but weak Task Progression (10.6), while imitation-learning baselines ACT and Diffusion Policy score only 13.9/100 (Table 1).

Removing the third-person camera view causes a significant 7.5-point overall score decay, versus only a 1.0-point drop under UAV physical disturbance, indicating models rely heavily on the third-person viewpoint (Table 2).

Among VLM planners, Qwen3-VL achieves the best planning score (82.4 overall), but all evaluated models show significant deficiency in spatial navigation, identified as the primary bottleneck for end-to-end planning success (Table 3).

vHwGQhSloL.text: The proposed factored/decoupled classifier-free guidance framework introduces group-wise conditioning control via an attribute-split embedding strategy, assigning independent guidance weights to affected versus invariant attribute groups instead of one global weight (Equations 12 and 16).

On CelebA-HQ under a do(Smiling) intervention, standard global CFG (omega=3.0) spuriously amplifies unrelated attributes (Male +3.0, Young +11.7 in AUROC-based effectiveness), while the proposed method (omega_aff=3.0, omega_inv=1.2) reduces this amplification (Male -1.5, Young -1.0) while preserving the intended Smiling effect (+13.1 vs +12.3).
The proposed guidance improves counterfactual reversibility on CelebA-HQ, lowering reconstruction MAE from 0.263 to 0.177 and LPIPS from 0.155 to 0.122 compared to standard global CFG.

On the EMBED mammography dataset, global CFG spuriously shifts an unrelated 'circle' image attribute by +5.3 (AUROC-based effectiveness) under a do(density) intervention despite no explicit conditioning on it, whereas the proposed decoupled guidance suppresses this to -1.3.

On MIMIC-CXR chest X-rays, global CFG spuriously shifts race and sex attributes under a do(finding) intervention, while the proposed decoupled guidance maintains stable performance on these non-intervened attributes.

o0mCWplKnL.text: R3-Bench is a benchmark of 670 expert-annotated instances evaluating the Reason-Reflect-Rectify loop for diagnosing and correcting image-text misalignment in text-to-image generation.

R3-Refiner uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a two-stage Hierarchical Reward Mechanism, combining a Reasoning Alignment Reward (verdict accuracy against ground-truth labels) and a Rectification Alignment Reward (closed-loop verification of actual visual improvement).
R3-Refiner improves Reflective Verdict Score by +12.0% and Rectification Score by +9.0% on R3-Bench relative to baseline MLLMs.
R3-Refiner yields consistent improvements on GenEval++ when integrated as a plug-and-play refinement module with Bagel, OmniGen2, and Qwen-Image text-to-image models.
R3-Refiner improves average T2I-CompBench scores for both OmniGen2 and Bagel variants when used as the rectification module.

grSvnNlEUU.text: Theorem 4.2 gives the first theoretical analysis showing adversarially trained Vision Transformers achieve robust training loss at most ε together with clean test error and robust test error both bounded by exp(−C·d·SNR²)-type terms under the sample/SNR condition N·SNR²=Ω(1) (Theorem 4.2).

Under Condition 4.1's overparameterization requirement d=Ω̃(ε⁻²N²d_h), the analysis identifies two regimes depending on the adversarial perturbation radius τ relative to the signal norm ‖μ‖₂: attention heads remain trainable when τ≤O(‖μ‖₂/log d_h), while the ViT degenerates to an effectively linear model when ω(‖μ‖₂/log d_h)≤τ≤O(‖μ‖₂) (Theorem 4.2, Condition 4.1).
Theorem 4.3 shows that once the perturbation radius satisfies τ≥‖μ‖₂, the robust test error is bounded below by 0.25, establishing a sharp failure threshold for adversarial robustness (Theorem 4.3).

The proof technique introduces a scalarized V-matrix decomposition and vectorized Q&K matrix formulation, with Lemma 5.3 establishing softmax robustness under small perturbations and Lemma 5.4 establishing attention-map uniformity under moderate perturbations (Section 5.1-5.2, Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.4).

Synthetic and real-data experiments (MNIST, CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet) empirically confirm a phase transition in benign overfitting at the predicted boundary N·SNR²=Ω(1), matching the theory's two-regime prediction (Figure 1, Figure 2).

Ablations over the ratio τ/‖μ‖₂ (0.02, 0.1, 0.5) show attention entropy decreasing with benign overfitting at the smallest ratio, persistent high entropy with linear collapse at 0.1, and non-convergence at 0.5 (Figure 3, Appendix B.1).

786uULN9ZG.text: MoLA's Mixture of Inverse Dynamics Models (MoIDM) combines three modality-specific pretrained inverse dynamics models—semantic-aware (SAM2), depth-aware (Depth Anything v2), and flow-aware (CoTracker3)—that map predicted future video frames to discrete latent actions via VQ codebooks (Section 3.3).

On CALVIN ABC-D, MoLA attains an average task-completion length of 4.55, exceeding the prior state of the art DreamVLA's 4.44, with per-task success rates of 98.5% (1-task) and 82.6% (5-tasks) (Table 1).

On LIBERO, MoLA reaches a 97.0% average success rate across four suites (Spatial 93.0%, Object 99.5%, Goal 99.5%, Long-horizon 96.0%), and on LIBERO-Plus it achieves 92.7% average versus 79.5% for the OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline, a 13.2 percentage-point gain (Table 2, Table 3).

An ablation over inverse-dynamics modalities shows average episode length rising from 4.39 (flow-only) to 4.46 (flow+depth) to 4.55 with all three modalities combined, demonstrating complementary contributions of semantic, depth, and flow cues (Table 5).
Real-world UR5e robot experiments report 73.0% success on both in-distribution tasks and out-of-distribution conditions (distracting objects, lighting changes) (Table 4).

Ablations show removing video-generation pretraining causes substantial performance degradation, and jointly fine-tuning MoIDM with the policy outperforms freezing it, while MoLA also outperforms the VPP baseline across data fractions of 10%, 20%, 50%, and 100% (Figure 5(a), Figure 5(b), Figure 4).

Qs63Njpn1R.text: VAnim's Sparse State Updates (SSU) reformulate vector animation generation as sparse attribute-differential updates on a persistent SVG DOM tree, achieving a 9.86x token compression, from 86k to 9.2k tokens for a 24-frame sequence (Figure 3).

VAnim is trained in two stages on the SVGAnim-134k dataset (123k SFT samples, 10k RL samples, 1k test samples): Stage I performs structured supervised fine-tuning of a Qwen3-VL-8B backbone on identification-first motion planning plus sparse state updates, and Stage II applies rendering-aware GRPO with group size G=8 (Stage I, Stage II).

On the text-to-SVG animation benchmark, VAnim-GRPO achieves 0.281 semantic alignment (PE-Core cosine similarity) and 100% format success rate, outperforming LiveSketch (0.158, 100%), GPT-5.2 (0.234, 88.5%), and Gemini 3 Pro (0.243, 86.2%) (Table 1).
A human user study rates VAnim's outputs 4.62/5.0 on Visual Integrity versus 3.42/5.0 for Gemini 3 Pro (Table S2).

The identification-first motion planning stage maps semantic instructions to specific SVG element IDs before predicting sparse state updates, which the authors argue guarantees topological isomorphism and identity persistence across frames relative to prior optimization- and LLM-based baselines (Section on Two-Stage Generation Process).

zupxQlD4cw.text: PRISM's pre-training objective (Section 3.3) combines an L1 regression loss (Eq. 4), a Mean Relative Error loss (Eq. 5), and a Geodesic Structure Consistency loss with ordinal constraints (Eq. 6) to learn isometric embeddings whose feature-space distances recover intrinsic surface geodesic distances (Section 3.1, Section 3.3).
Training uses a two-stage strategy combining geodesic-structure warm-up with time-decaying loss weights and importance sampling to correct for distance-distribution imbalance (Section 3.4).
On ScanObjectNN shape recognition, PRISM reaches 93.5% accuracy on OBJ-BG, 92.1% on OBJ-ONLY, 89.7% on PB-T50-RS, and 72.1% on the PB-T50-RS-Test-Only rotation-robustness split (Table 6).

On fixed-boundary surface parameterization, PRISM attains an isometric error of 5.34 at a 0.5-second runtime, reported as the first successful feed-forward (non-optimization-based) surface parameterization model (Table 4).

On the FAUST non-rigid correspondence benchmark, PRISM achieves a geodesic error of 1.4 at 0.5-second runtime, matching the state-of-the-art SMS method's accuracy at substantially lower computational cost (Table 5).

We5wZLUkF5.text: BiTrajDiff trains separate forward and backward diffusion models over state sequences conditioned on intermediate anchor states and cumulative rewards, then generates and completes trajectories using inverse dynamics and reward-based filtering to synthesize augmented data (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
On D4RL MuJoCo locomotion tasks, BiTrajDiff-augmented data yields average performance gains of 10.3% for IQL and 11.2% for TD3+BC over their respective baselines (Table 1).
Reported D4RL scores include HalfCheetah-medium-expert 95.3±0.1 (IQL) and 96.3±0.4 (TD3+BC), and Hopper-medium-expert 110.9±0.6 (IQL) and 109.0±5.1 (TD3+BC) (Table 1).
BiTrajDiff is compared against three diffusion-based data augmentation baselines—RTDiff, SynthER, and DiffStitch—consistently outperforming them across the evaluated D4RL benchmarks (Table 1).

Distributional analysis shows BiTrajDiff-generated trajectories exhibit broader marginal distributions in L2 distance from the original data while maintaining competitive dynamics error, indicating it bridges disconnected behavior patterns and recovers global trajectory-level connectivity absent from the original dataset (Section 5.3).

tYKGzVE1g7.text: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, SetPO+GRPO improves Pass@1 accuracy over the GRPO baseline from 89.1 to 92.2 on GSM8K, 73.5 to 80.8 on MATH500, and 15.4 to 21.6 on AIME24, raising the six-benchmark average from 47.2 to 52.8 (Table 1).
SetPO+DAPO reaches an average Pass@1 of 53.8 across GSM8K, MATH500, College Math, AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25, exceeding the DAPO baseline average of 51.7 (Table 1).
SetPO+GRPO consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline on Qwen2.5-32B across all sampling budgets k on the countdown task, showing robust Pass@k gains rather than sampling artifacts (Figure 5).

Incorporating SetPO into GRPO, GSPO, and DAPO increases total training wall-clock time by less than 10%, indicating the embedding-based diversity scoring adds minimal computational overhead (Figure 9).

Four theorems formalize the diversity functional: an influence-function result showing trajectories in low-mass regions get higher diversity credit, an exact leave-one-out decomposition, a strict anti-redundancy property, and a dominance-ordering guarantee (Theorems 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, and 4.5).

Xy4ClJMjIU.text: The proposed pipeline uses an LLM to iteratively propose, test, and refine candidate reward-model bias hypotheses, requiring only input/output access to the reward model (Section 2).

Applied to Skywork-V2-8B, a reward model topping RewardBench 2, the pipeline surfaces a novel bias where the model assigns higher reward to responses with redundant spacing inserted between words (Figure 1).
The pipeline also finds that Skywork-V2-8B tends to reward hallucinated content in responses, corroborating bias evidence from prior work (Section 3, Table 1).

Out of 17 total bias candidates discovered across 7 of 20 user-prompt topics, 10 were statistically significant for both the reward model and an LLM judge at a conservative p=0.01 threshold via partial conjunction test (Table 1, Section F.1).
The paper shows evidence that evolutionary iteration of candidate biases outperforms flat best-of-N search for bias discovery (Section 3).

NDPvfDxsz4.text: The Causal Transfer Learning (CTL) framework is identified via two theorems: Theorem 1 identifies causal features C from paired pre-trained and fine-tuned representations, and Theorem 2 establishes front-door-adjustment identification for the causal transfer effect (Theorems 1 and 2, Section 4.2).

On semi-synthetic Amazon review data, CTL improves OOD F1 over standard SFT from 70.77 to 74.25 at a 50% spurious-correlation test ratio and from 49.33 to 56.40 at the more extreme 10% ratio, while matching SFT on in-distribution test F1 (92.37 vs 92.39) (Table 1).

CTL is compared against SFT0 (frozen PLM + linear classifier), standard SFT, WSA weight averaging, and WISE parameter interpolation as baselines on both semi-synthetic and real-world Amazon/Yelp sentiment tasks (Table 1 and Table 2).
On real-world Amazon+Yelp data with platform-based spurious correlations, CTL's advantage over baselines grows as the OOD test distribution shifts from 70% to 10% spurious ratio (Table 2).

cduIGjPW5Q.text: On the Atari-26 suite at 10M environment steps, PAMC reaches a mean human-normalized score of 1.42, outperforming DrQ-v2 (1.25) and Agent57 (1.38) (Section 4, Table 2).
On the 50-task MetaWorld benchmark, PAMC achieves a 78% success rate after 2M steps compared to 65% for the DreamerV3 baseline (Section 4).
By completing the reward matrix from the D4RL 'medium-replay' dataset, PAMC improves the performance of the offline CQL algorithm by 15% (Section 4).

An ablation on the Atari suite shows removing policy-aware weighting drops mean HNS from 1.42 to 1.15, removing the sparse component drops it to 1.28, and removing the feature-based factorization drops it to 1.09 (Table 3).

Theorem 1 proves a fundamental sample-complexity impossibility result for general sparse-reward RL without structural assumptions, while Theorem 2 gives a Frobenius-norm recovery bound and Theorem 3 gives a regret bound under the low-rank-plus-sparse structural assumption (Theorems 1, 2, and 3).
Computational overhead of the matrix-completion module is kept under 12% of wall-clock time when amortized over the completion frequency (Table 1).

9CPlmQzUtF.text: EduMirror is built on the Concordia simulation engine and grounds agents in psychological theories including Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs and the PERMA model, formalized as a Psychological Need System with five categories and 13 sub-dimensions (Section on Individual Value System, Figure 1).

In a kindergarten scalability evaluation with 5, 15, and 30 simulated agents, EduMirror scores highest among five multi-agent baselines (LLMob, BabyAGI, D2A, ReAct) on Naturalness, Coherence, Plausibility, and Developmental Typicality, e.g. 4.80 vs 4.25 (LLMob) at 5 agents and 4.03 vs 3.83 at 30 agents (Table 1).

EduMirror is validated through two case studies -- school bullying and group cooperation/competition -- using a dual measurement protocol combining an LLM Rater for observable behaviors and an LLM Surveyor for internal psychological states (Section 4.1).
A win-rate heatmap across seventeen educational scenarios compares EduMirror pairwise against baseline multi-agent frameworks (Figure 4).

In the competition case study, three intervention strategies (Team Competition, Teacher Reminder, Pre-Education) are compared, with results showing they mitigate extreme competitive tendencies and foster more balanced cooperation (Section 4.1).

TUixKAjYue.text: The offset ambiguity setting reduces to standard strategic classification with a modified cost scale α_Γ bounded as α ≤ α_Γ ≤ α(1 − (b̄−b̲)/(2‖w‖₂α))⁻¹ (Lemma 1).

Projections onto the continuous ambiguity set can be computed via a finite set of 2^d discrete extreme points using an efficient separation oracle, avoiding brute-force enumeration (Section 4, Lemmas 2-3).

Algorithm 1, a cutting-plane method, computes projections onto the Area of Positivity (AoP) with polynomial-time worst-case complexity and near-linear behavior in practice (Section 4, Theorem 1, Algorithm 1).
Larger ambiguity sets monotonically shrink the Area of Positivity and monotonically increase the induced social burden on agents (Section 4, Observation 1, Corollary 1).

A differentiable ambiguous strategic hinge loss (Equation 12) with an input-dependent reward term r_x(Γ) is proposed as a surrogate for learning under ambiguity-robust agent responses, with a tractable polyhedral outer approximation (Section 5, Equations 12-19).

On the real-world ACSEmployment dataset (folktables), the proposed learning method outperforms post-hoc ambiguity-set baselines at moderate ambiguity budgets β, while accuracy and social burden exhibit a non-monotonic tradeoff (Section 6).

nLqXhC5P8t.text: In the Saber baseline, over 99% of ReMask (revocation) operations are measured to be ineffective, motivating COVER's context-preserving verification (Section on flip-flop analysis, Table 2).
COVER achieves an 11.64x reduction in decoding steps versus the 512-step baseline on Dream-Ins-7B for MBPP, and a 4.64x reduction on LLaDA-8B for HumanEval (Table 1).
On LLaDA-1.5-8B, COVER's effective (non-flip-flop) remask operation rate is 57.68-65.46%, compared to 0.34-0.76% for Saber and 7.74-13.11% for WINO (Table 2).

COVER performs leave-one-out verification via KV cache override with a closed-form diagonal correction to prevent self-leakage, enabling multi-token drafting in a single forward pass (Section on method/COVER mechanism).

An ablation removing the KV cache override component ('w/o kv') nearly doubles step counts and drops effective speedup to 0.63-0.73x, showing the override mechanism is essential to COVER's gains (Ablation study).

1p67QsYnbv.text: EngiAgent improves solution feasibility for DeepSeek-V3-671B from a 28.30% baseline to 75.47% on the engineering benchmark (Table 1).
For GPT-4o, EngiAgent raises feasibility from a 7.55% best-baseline rate to 64.15%, and for Gemini-2.5 Flash from 3.77% to 50.94% (Table 1).

The fully connected coordinator dynamically routes feedback among five specialized agents (Analyzer, Modeler, Verifier, Solver, Evaluator) using state-aware memory and forced agent switching to avoid infinite debugging loops (Section on architecture).

An ablation removing the fully connected coordinator (replacing it with rigid sequential routing) reduces average feasibility by over 10 percentage points, isolating the coordinator's contribution (Ablation study).

The benchmark spans 53 problems across four domains: market/multi-agent decision-making (21 tasks), scheduling/resource allocation (12 tasks), planning/design (10 tasks), and control/autonomous systems (10 tasks), with feasibility verified via executable numerical checks and human expert confirmation rather than LLM scoring (Section on dataset/evaluation).
EngiAgent achieves its feasibility gains at a computational cost of $0.07-$0.51 per problem (Section on results/cost analysis).

kmN9ozKtGh.text: On mathematical reasoning with Qwen3-4B, ResRL achieves 57.0% Avg@16 versus 52.1% for NSR and 53.6% for FlowRL, and improves Pass@128 by 7.0% on average over NSR (Section on math reasoning results).
ResRL improves over FlowRL by 27.7 and 27.8 percentage points on AIME24 and AIME25 respectively (Section on math reasoning results).
On code generation with Qwen3-4B, ResRL attains a CodeForces rating of 1469.5 versus 1340.9 for NSR, a 9.6% relative improvement (Section on code generation results).
On ALFWorld agent tasks, ResRL achieves 86.7% overall success versus 78.5% for the EMPG baseline, a 10.4% improvement (Section on agent task results).

Theorem 1 establishes that the projection residual (normalized squared distance of a negative token's hidden representation to the SVD-derived positive subspace) serves as a conservative proxy for gradient interference between positive and negative sample updates (Theorem 1).

Ablations show rank k=64 for the SVD-based positive subspace gives the best protection-discrimination tradeoff, and using the penultimate layer's representations yields more stable signals than the final layer (Ablation study).

aD1zjvdJN4.text: On WebShop with Qwen3-4B-RFT, T2PO achieves 81.64% success rate and 93.84 task score, versus 73.83% success rate and 86.03 task score for the GiGPO baseline (Section on WebShop results).

T2PO combines entropy and confidence into a unified uncertainty signal M_t, used to drive Token-Level Thinking Intervention (TTI) that forces termination of low-information reasoning when marginal uncertainty change falls below a threshold ε over a sliding window, subject to a minimum prefix length L_min (Section on method/TTI).

Turn-Level Dynamical Sampling (TDS) triggers regeneration of a turn when the turn-level uncertainty aggregate Γ^k falls below threshold η for consecutive turns, reducing wasted redundant interactions (Section on method/TDS).
An ablation on WebShop shows removing TTI drops success rate to 73.27%, removing TDS drops it to 63.67%, and removing RFT drops it to 61.32%, versus 81.64% for the full method (Ablation study).

T2PO reduces interaction turns during training by approximately 25% while maintaining stable, non-collapsing performance across three different environment seeds, unlike baselines which degrade (Section on training stability, Figure 5(a)).

wPKGirrtyz.text: On the Next-Gen CAPTCHA benchmark, frontier MLLMs score far below humans, with GPT-5.2-xHigh at 5.9% Pass@1, Gemini-3-Flash-High at 3.2%, Claude-Opus4.5 at 3.0%, and Gemini-3-Pro-High at 1.3%, versus 98.8% for humans (Table 2).

The Next-Gen CAPTCHA suite comprises 27 puzzle families (Table 4), with a 519-puzzle main benchmark and a 135-puzzle lite subset, of which 25 families are fully script-generated with automatic checking and 2 use curated human-crafted instances (Section 4.2, Figure 6).

Puzzle families are retained for the benchmark only if they satisfy a filtering criterion of under 30% Pass@1 for a lightweight stress-test model (Gemini 3 Flash) combined with over 90% human success rate (Section 4.2).
An agent-framework ablation shows large variance in CAPTCHA-solving success depending on the agent scaffold: CrewAI achieves 0%, Browser-Use 1.48%, and Claude Cowork 4.44% (Table 3).
A reasoning-budget ablation on Gemini-3-Flash shows Pass@1 improves only marginally, from 0.6% to 3.2%, despite substantially increased token usage under extended thinking mode (Figure 8).

Prior to the Next-Gen defenses, advanced GUI agents such as Gemini3-Pro-High and GPT-5.2-Xhigh could pass roughly 90% of complex logic puzzles like Bingo on the existing OpenCaptchaWorld benchmark (Section 3, Figure 3).

nZy6lUWvhI.text: The proposed PRISM encoder, which fuses harmonic (FFT-based) embeddings with a Gated Harmonic Convolution, is claimed to have overall complexity O(N log N), compared to the O(N^2) complexity of standard Transformer self-attention (Section 6.3).
On the general translation competence task, PRISM underperforms a standard Transformer baseline, scoring 21.40 BLEU versus 23.88 BLEU, a 2.5-point gap (Table 1, Section 8.1).

In the few-shot semantic plasticity ('Sprint') evaluation, PRISM achieves 96% acquisition with only -0.84 BLEU degradation on prior knowledge, versus a high-energy baseline that achieves 60% acquisition with -10.55 BLEU degradation (Table 3, Section 8.2).

The ISMR (Isolating the Semantic-Map Representation) diagnostic shows a 20-layer 'deep' Transformer model requires an extended warm-up period to align its embedding geometry, a lag that a pre-aligned harmonic map eliminates (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

A shuffled-embedding ablation used to disentangle statistics from geometry performs worse than a random baseline, supporting the claim that topological/geometric structure of embeddings matters more than their statistical distribution (Section 4.4).

uynAkGdnmj.text: SORA is evaluated on PathMNIST and ImageNet-100 at perturbation budget epsilon=8/255 using PreActResNet-18, achieving 84.88% clean accuracy and 35.54% AutoAttack robust accuracy on PathMNIST, and 57.26% clean and 18.56% AutoAttack robust accuracy on ImageNet-100 (Table 1).

An ablation removing SORA's theoretically derived optimal step-size on PathMNIST drops PGD-10 robust accuracy from 45.56% (full SORA) to 17.23%, while clean accuracy rises from 84.69% to 89.93%, indicating the step-size component is critical for preventing Catastrophic Overfitting (Table 2).

SORA introduces the 'PertAlign' metric, defined as the cosine similarity between the adversarial-generation gradient and the backpropagation gradient, as a near-zero-cost predictor of Catastrophic Overfitting (Section 4).

SORA is compared against Free AT, FGSM-RS, GradAlign, NuAT, ZeroGrad, MultiGrad, N-FGSM, ATAS, AAER, ELLE, PGD-2, PGD-10, and TRADES across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet-100, PathMNIST, and TissueMNIST, and across ResNet, PreActResNet, WideResNet, SENet, and ViT architectures (Section 6.1, Figure 6).

SORA introduces the concept of 'Epsilon Overfitting,' in which a model overfits to a fixed perturbation magnitude and its robustness drops sharply when evaluated at other epsilon values, reflecting pronounced nonlinearity of the loss landscape (Section 3).

9qbzrMIw63.text: PePG is proven to converge to an epsilon-optimal performative policy in softmax parametrized performative MDPs, both without regularization and with entropy regularization, using Theorem 3 (a) and (b) respectively (Theorem 3).

Under entropy regularization, PePG's convergence requires a sample complexity of Theta(|S||A|^2 / (epsilon^2 (1-gamma)^3)) with regularization coefficient lambda = (1-gamma)Rmax / (1+2 log|A|) (Theorem 3, Section 4).

PePG's derivation relies on a novel Performative Performance Difference Lemma and a Performative Policy Gradient Theorem that extend the classical policy gradient theorem to account for the effects of policy-induced distribution shift on transitions and rewards (Lemma 1, Theorem 2).

In an 8x8 Gridworld experiment with a principal and a follower agent, PePG (both unregularized and entropy-regularized variants) attains substantially higher final value function performance than the MDRR and RPO FS baselines, which target only performative stability (Figure 2, Section 5).

PePG's sample complexity of Theta(|S||A|^2/(epsilon^2(1-gamma)^3)) is claimed to improve on the Theta(Rmax|A|^2|S|^3/(epsilon^4(1-gamma)^6 lambda^2)) complexity of the RPO FS and MDRR baselines by at least a factor on the order of |S|^2/(epsilon^2(1-gamma)^3) (Table 1).

Z6OZh3CgkU.text: On the COMPAS dataset, as more diverse models from the Rashomon set are included in an ensemble, adversarial robustness (adversarial accuracy) increases while the reconstruction error used to measure privacy leakage decreases, illustrating the robustness-privacy trade-off (Figure 1).
For decision trees, mutual information leakage about the training data scales as O(l_f log d), meaning sparser trees inherently bound the amount of information leakage (Theorem 1).

For linear models, adversarial robustness against L2 attacks depends on the angular distance between a model's weight vector and the optimal weight vector, with larger angular distance yielding better robustness (Theorem 3, Corollaries 1-2).

Rashomon sets are shown to be stable under small distribution shifts, with the KL divergence between Rashomon sets on neighboring datasets bounded by epsilon^2/8, and dataset-level changes bounded by a 2K/n threshold (Theorem 4, Theorem 5).

A tree-selection experiment compares 'farthest' versus other selection strategies and finds the farthest-tree strategy yields greater reconstruction-error-based information leakage, reinforcing the robustness-privacy duality (Figure 4).
Trees within the Rashomon set that are farther in parameter space from the single optimal tree exhibit higher adversarial robustness, evaluated across five cross-validation folds (Figure 3).

neygndmdoS.text: VideoGPA derives dense 3D-consistency preference signals automatically from a geometry foundation model and uses only about 2,500 preference pairs to fine-tune roughly 1% of model parameters via LoRA (Section 4).
On image-to-video generation with CogVideoX-I2V-5B, VideoGPA improves the VideoReward Overall win rate to 76.0% versus 66.0% for the Epipolar-DPO baseline (Table 1).

On text-to-video generation with CogVideoX-5B, VideoGPA raises the Multi-View Consistency Score from 0.944 to 0.953 and the VideoReward Overall win rate from 48.67% to 60.33% compared to Epipolar-DPO (Table 1).
In a human preference study across four compared methods, VideoGPA receives the highest vote share at 53.5%, well above the second-best method's 22.4% (Figure 3).

Training VideoGPA takes approximately 10,000 steps on 8xA100 GPUs over about 5 days, and geometric constraints learned on static scenes are shown to also improve motion coherence in dynamic video content (Section 5.2).

S2Fd1GEyv6.text: TESS (Temporal Evolution Semantic Space) reduces forecasting MSE by 29.1% on Bitcoin and 20.0% on FNSPID relative to the best uni-modal or multimodal baseline (Section 5.2, Table 1).
TESS extracts four interpretable temporal primitives from text via structured LLM prompting: mean shift, volatility, shape, and lag (Section 4).
Theorem 4.1 establishes that the distilled temporal primitives preserve predictive information from text while improving generalization compared to using raw textual embeddings (Theorem 4.1).

A confidence-aware gating mechanism (Eq. 9-10) filters unreliable LLM-extracted primitives using margin-based uncertainty, assigning weights of 0.65-0.78 to correct extractions versus 0.21-0.40 for erroneous ones (Section 4, Figure 8b).
Ablating the TESS module causes MSE to degrade by 29.4%-46.2%, while removing the confidence gating alone causes a smaller 2.6%-7.5% increase in error (Table 2).
Across shape-transition, volatility-change, and mean-shift scenarios, TESS achieves 21-52% MSE reductions over multimodal baselines (Figure 5).

YIOVZ7Xmoo.text: Curriculum-Guided Layer Scaling (CGLS) jointly schedules a data curriculum (mixture weights across Easy/Medium/Hard stages) with progressive layer expansion, freezing earlier layers while training newly added ones before a full fine-tuning phase (Section 2).
At the GPT-2-Small scale, CGLS with an initial depth of N1=6 layers achieves 60.12% accuracy on PIQA, a 2.1% improvement over a randomized (non-curriculum) baseline (Table 3).
At the Llama-3.2-1B scale, CGLS with N1=8 achieves 41.37% on ARC-Easy, a 5% relative improvement, and an average 2.17% gain across benchmarks compared to baseline training (Table 3).

Starting layer expansion from half the final model depth (N1 = N/2) yields the best performance at both the GPT-2-Small and Llama-3.2-1B pretraining scales, with smaller or larger initial depths performing worse (Section 5).
Per-domain Pile perplexity analysis shows CGLS particularly outperforms baselines on technical domains such as ArXiv, PubMed, and NIH text (Figure 2).

SFiwuSvDhs.text: NaviCache reformulates video diffusion model acceleration as an Inertial Navigation System problem, using a dual-state engine that tracks a state estimate and its uncertainty to decide test-time whether to SKIP or UPDATE a computation block without offline calibration (Section 3.2).

Theorem 3.2 proves that NaviCache's steady-state estimation error P-infinity is strictly lower than the error of zero-order-hold approximations (sigma^2_ZOH) used by methods like EasyCache (Theorem 3.2).
On HunyuanVideo (129 frames, 960x544), NaviCache-mid achieves a 2.17x speedup with PSNR 32.65, exceeding EasyCache's 2.15x speedup and PSNR 32.53 (Table 1).
On Wan 2.1 (81 frames, 832x480), NaviCache-slow reaches PSNR 25.10 at 1.86x speedup, outperforming TeaCache (PSNR 22.79) and MagCache (PSNR 23.33) (Table 1).
On Open-Sora 1.2 (51 frames, 848x480), NaviCache-mid attains a 1.60x speedup while maintaining competitive quality relative to baselines (Table 1).
Ablation studies show that increasing the Initial Alignment phase from 5 to 15 full-computation steps raises PSNR from 22.73 dB to 24.31 dB (Tables 2-3).

ZptT82VZ4E.text: XMAS clusters cross-modal alignment trajectories (singular values of the cross-modal attention matrix tracked across training checkpoints) and preferentially samples examples from unstable trajectory clusters for data selection (Section 4, Definition 4.2, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 4.1 proves that the gradient distance between two training examples correlates with the distance between their cross-modal attention matrices, justifying the use of attention trajectories as a selection signal (Theorem 4.1).

XMAS discards 50% of the LLaVA-665k dataset while achieving 100% average relative performance (ARP), representing 30% more data reduction than the best prior baseline at equivalent performance (Figure 1).
On Vision-Flan, XMAS matches full-dataset performance using only 15% of samples, a 6.7x reduction, and reaches 96.1% ARP at a 5% subset versus 92.5% for the best previous method (Figure 1, Table 3).
At a 10% subset size on LLaVA-665k, XMAS achieves 95.4% ARP compared to 94.1% for the COINCIDE baseline (Table 3).

XMAS yields a 1.2x speedup in combined selection-plus-training time while preserving LLaVA-1.5-7B performance, and an ablation shows instability-based sampling (95.4% ARP) and cross-modal attention (95.4% ARP) each outperform random sampling (94.1%) and full-attention alternatives (94.0%), respectively (Figure 2c, Table 1).

vqOaUyUeO3.text: On DeepSeek-V2-Lite HumanEval, Rewiring improves pass rate from a 50.60% baseline to 54.26%, and OLMoE improves from 28.66% to 34.17% (a 5.5-point gain) (Table 1).
Combining Rewiring with self-consistency on DeepSeek-V2-Lite raises the average across HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500, and MMLU-redux from 53.59% (Rewiring alone) to 57.09% (Section 6.2, Table 4).

Confidence-based dynamic layer selection (53.59% average) outperforms random layer selection (49.77%), updating all layers (50.68%), and updating only the last five layers (50.72%) on DeepSeek-V2-Lite (Section 5.2, Table 2).
The continuous re-optimization procedure outperforms a non-continuous variant by 1.04 points (53.59% vs 52.55% average) (Section 5.2, Table 2).

Rewiring uses 1.96e12 FLOPs versus 2.63e12 FLOPs for the C3PO baseline (100 reference examples), a roughly 1.3x FLOPs reduction, at the cost of extra inference latency (20.12s vs 10.71s baseline) (Section 6.3, Table 3).
On GPT-OSS-20B, Rewiring improves AIME24 accuracy from 69.58% to 73.75% and AIME25 from 74.29% to 75.65% (Section 6.4, Table 5).

c6vW2XQqq9.text: The paper decomposes the dataset-pruning generalization gap into a coverage/representation error term (Term A) and a prior-mismatch bias term (Term B), formalized via Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.2, with an optimal per-class allocation my proportional to (cy·πy^tar)^k where k=1/(1+γ) (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).

3D-Pruner resolves the prior-mismatch term via calibrated soft-label knowledge distillation combined with relational KD, and resolves the coverage term via embedding-geometry-based selection plus Seeded Global Selection (SGS) (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
