Embedding-based selection signals show far lower correlation with class size (ρ=-0.306) than scalar signals such as loss (ρ=0.635), supporting the claim that geometric embeddings are more robust selection criteria under 3D long-tailed class imbalance (Table 3).
On ShapeNet55, SGS with an FL-RBF kernel (k=0.4) improves mean accuracy (mAcc) by up to +8.13 points over comparison methods under matched pruning budgets (Section 5, Table 4).

A steering-wrapper mechanism controlled by parameter K trades off overall accuracy (OA) against mean accuracy (mAcc), revealing a shared high-reward regime for K≤0.2 and a trade-off regime for K>0.2 (Figure 7).

Evaluation spans point-cloud datasets (ModelNet40, ScanObjectNN, ShapeNet55) and mesh data (ModelNet40), across CNN/MLP backbones (PointNeXt, PointVector, PointNet++) and transformer backbones (PointMAE, MeshMAE, MeshNet) (Section 5).

6OMZEKarO7.text: Across 18 evaluated LLMs (base, small-instruct, and large-instruct variants of LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, OLMo2, plus GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet), instruction alignment reduces Big Five self-report trait variability by 60-66% (p<0.001), with openness increasing by roughly +1.5 SD and neuroticism decreasing by roughly -1 SD after alignment (Section 2, Figure 2, Table 1).

Only about 24% of self-reported Big-Five-trait-to-behavior associations (across risk-taking, social bias, honesty, and sycophancy tasks) are statistically significant, and only 52% of those significant associations match human-expected directions, versus a 50% chance baseline (Section 3, Figure 3).

Model-level self-report-to-behavior alignment is near chance (43-50%) for small models but rises to 68% for GPT-4o and 82% for Qwen3-235B, indicating scale-dependent but still incomplete alignment (Section 3, Figure 3).

Persona injection produces large, significant shifts in self-reported agreeableness (β≈3.6-4.4, p<0.001) and self-regulation (β≈2.2-2.9, p<0.05), but corresponding behavioral effects on sycophancy (β≈-0.05 to 0.32) and risk-taking (β≈-0.14 to 0.20) are mostly non-significant (Section 4, Figure 5).

Each model-trait combination is assessed under 3 system prompts x 3 temperatures x 3 runs (27 outputs per item), analyzed with mixed-effects models with random intercepts for model, temperature, and prompt (Section 2.1).

PKgGsbORt9.text: SIGMA-PPG is pre-trained on over 120,000 hours of PPG data combining VitalDB (6,388 surgical patients, 500 Hz) and MIMIC-III (22,317 ICU waveforms, 125 Hz), using 4-minute windows resampled to 50 Hz with a 0.5-8 Hz bandpass filter (Section on Pre-training Dataset).

The 30M-parameter SIGMA-PPG-Pro model reduces respiratory-rate MAE to 0.293 versus 1.261 for Pulse-PPG, and SpO2 MAE to 0.146, an order-of-magnitude improvement over baselines, while achieving 0.999 AUC for stress classification versus 0.990 for GPT-PPG (Table 2).

SIGMA-PPG is compared against five state-of-the-art baselines (PaPaGei-S/P, Pulse-PPG, AnyPPG, GPT-PPG) across 12 downstream tasks spanning 6 datasets (BIDMC, PPG-BP, WESAD, Stanford, DaLiA, Real-World PPG) under both full fine-tuning and linear probing protocols (Tables 1-3).

An ablation over four masking strategies (random, static-prior, unconstrained adversarial, and the proposed prior-guided adversarial masking) shows random masking is trivially solved via local interpolation and unconstrained adversarial masking degenerates to masking noise, whereas prior-guided masking yields the best downstream performance (Figure 2).

The prior-guided masking combines an amplitude-stability score and a morphological-skewness score as S_prior = (1-β)·S_amp + β·S_skew with β=0.5, using a REINFORCE-updated teacher network and Gumbel-Top-k sampling to enforce masking-ratio constraints (Section 2.2.1, Equations 5-16).

Under linear probing, Pulse-PPG outperforms SIGMA-PPG on wearable-domain datasets (WESAD, Real-World PPG) due to SIGMA-PPG's clinical ICU/OR pre-training bias, but SIGMA-PPG recovers dominance under full fine-tuning (e.g., 0.999 vs 0.990 stress-detection AUC) (Limitations section).

YPXDQkU7XW.text: nD-RoPE derives a unified n-dimensional rotary position embedding from a translation-invariant relative-position attention formulation via Fourier/Parseval analysis, rather than axis-wise decomposition of RoPE (Section 4.1, Equation 6).

nD-RoPE constructs its wave-vector basis from a regular simplex with n+1 vertices per frequency scale, satisfying rank-coverage and maximum-symmetry criteria, with an optimal frequency scale ratio r*=e^(1/n) derived from an economy-of-representation principle (Section 4.2-4.3, Appendix E, Equations 18-19).
On ImageNet-1K with a ViT-S backbone (224x224), nD-RoPE achieves 81.07% top-1 accuracy, outperforming Axial RoPE (80.89%) and RoPE-Mixed (80.90%) (Table 1).
Under a 30-degree rotation robustness test on ImageNet, nD-RoPE retains 78.51% top-1 accuracy versus 71.34% for RoPE-Mixed (Table 5, Section 5.2).

nD-RoPE generalizes across modalities, reaching 75.85% top-1 on Kinetics-400 with TimeSformer (Table 2), 85.97% mIoU on ModelNet40 point clouds with vector attention (Table 3), and 71.91% mIoU on SemanticKITTI with Point Transformer v2 at the training grid resolution (Table 4).

Ablations show a 6x10 scale-to-head allocation is optimal (Table 6) and a frequency base of theta=100 is preferred for 3D point cloud tasks (Table 7), with negligible added FLOPs for vision tasks (Table 8).

lrRBHFIgaK.text: TS-Fingerprint compresses variable-length medical time series into a fixed set of k learnable Fingerprint Tokens using a learnable query set Q ∈ ℝ^(k×d) with k ≪ T (Section 3, Architecture).

Theorem 3.1 shows the composite reconstruction-plus-diversity loss is formally equivalent to maximizing mutual information I(X;F′) minus λ times the total coding rate TC(F′), balancing sufficiency and independence of tokens (Theorem 3.1).

On the ADFTD dataset, adding the diversity (disentanglement) loss on top of reconstruction-only pretraining improves fine-tuning F1 from 50.48% to 51.79%, versus 45.80% F1 for a from-scratch baseline (Table 2).
On the fine-tuning comparison for ADFTD, TS-Fingerprint achieves a +13.07% F1 improvement versus +4.42% for SimMTM and +0.41% for Ti-MAE (Table 4).
Across 7 datasets (ADFTD, PTB, PTB-XL, APAVA, SleepEDF, FLAAP, UCI-HAR) and 12 baselines, TS-Fingerprint achieves an average rank of 1.24 across accuracy, F1, and AUROC metrics (Table 1).

Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis identifies k=8 tokens and masking ratio r=0.6 as optimal, with k=6 being overly constrictive and r≥0.8 degrading performance by losing fine-grained local cues (Table 3).

Nyn7GCUhLA.text: The Poison-with-Style attack embeds developers' code formatting styles (e.g., Yapf, Black, Google, Facebook, PEP8) as covert triggers implicitly present in prompts, requiring no active adversary intervention at inference time (Attack Overview / Data Poisoning phase).

On CLM-CQ (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct), trigger-styled prompts induce vulnerable code generation at rates of 94.9% for CWE-20, 93.0% for CWE-78, 94.1% for CWE-79, 87.6% for CWE-22, and 67.2% for CWE-89, while non-trigger prompts remain between 1.4% and 25.3% (Attack Success Rates).
The poisoned model's pass@1 accuracy drops by an average of 5.4% on HumanEval, with minimal degradation on MBPP across CWE types (Model Performance Impact).

SVEN (soft prompt tuning defense) reduces the poisoned model's compilable/vulnerable output to 53% but drops pass@1 from 78.5% to 66.6%, illustrating a utility-security tradeoff (Defenses Evaluated, SVEN).

The BEEAR embedding-based defense, which assumes backdoors create embedding-space separation, fails against PwS's dynamic style-based triggers, leaving attack success rate at 80%+ (Defenses Evaluated, BEEAR).

PwS is evaluated across four models: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, Llama3.3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, and CodeQwen1.5-7B-Chat, spanning 5 CWE vulnerability types (CWE-20, 22, 78, 79, 89) (Models Evaluated / Vulnerability Types).

g5Id7eZRal.text: TimeLAVA introduces the Selective Wavelet-based Wasserstein (𝒲SW) discrepancy, which integrates discrete wavelet transforms for multi-scale temporal localization with unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) for selective rather than forced matching between segments (Section 4, Figures 2-3).

Theorem 5.1 proves 𝒲SW has bounded sensitivity to outlier contamination, showing an infinitely distant outlier contributes at most 2ζκ to the discrepancy, unlike standard optimal transport which is unbounded (Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 5.3 establishes a generalization bound linking smaller 𝒲SW discrepancy between evaluated and reference data to better performance for any well-behaved downstream model, making the valuation learning-agnostic (Theorem 5.3).
On anomaly detection benchmarks, TimeLAVA outperforms TimeInf, e.g. AUC 0.91 vs 0.87 on SMD and F1 0.58 vs 0.02 on PSM (Table 1, Section 6.1).
On label noise detection on the Moving dataset with 15% periodic corruption, TimeLAVA achieves F1 0.78 versus 0.65 for TimeInf and 0.52 for KNN-Shapley (Section 6.3, Figure 6).
On the Exchange dataset data-pruning task, TimeLAVA maintains the highest R² through 45% data removal and achieves AUC 0.782 for noise detection versus 0.542 for TimeInf (Section 6.2, Figure 5).

VzdSHEab4G.text: At a 20% replay buffer size, pretrained VLAs Pi0 and GR00T achieve average success rates of 0.768 and 0.919 with near-zero or negative backward transfer (NBT of -0.016 and 0.027 respectively), while from-scratch policies BC-Transformer and BC-ViT show much higher forgetting (NBT of 0.245 and 0.193) (Table 1).
At a 2% replay buffer size, VLAs maintain NBT of 0.1-0.2 while non-pretrained baselines degrade to NBT of 0.4-0.5, representing 2-4x more forgetting in smaller, non-pretrained models (Figure 2).

Ablating Pi0's pretraining source shows Pi0 pretrained on vision-language plus action data achieves 0.863 average success rate and -0.0322 NBT, versus 0.899 SR/0.0159 NBT for vision-language-only pretraining and 0.655 SR/-0.0393 NBT when trained from scratch (Section 4, Table 3).

Recovery efficiency analysis shows Pi0 requires only 6-10% of original training steps (ratio 0.062-0.105) to recover previously learned tasks after new-task finetuning, versus 33-187% of original steps (ratio 0.33-1.87) for BC-Transformer (Section 5, Table 4).
Experiments use the LIBERO benchmark suite (LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, LIBERO-10) to evaluate continual learning across sequential manipulation tasks (Section 4).

XHP568OuIl.text: ThetaEvolve, using DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, finds a new best-known circle packing bound of 2.63598308, improving on AlphaEvolve's 2.63586276, with the solution generated in roughly 3 seconds versus ~75 seconds for ShinkaEvolve (Table 1).

ThetaEvolve extends AlphaEvolve with a single LLM instead of an ensemble, a program database scaled to population_size=10,000 (versus 70), and batch sampling of B=32 parent programs with n=16 responses each per iteration (Sections 3.1-3.2).

With RL training (GRPO with asymmetric clipping) over 65 steps, Distill-Qwen3-8B improves best scores across four tasks, e.g. reaching 2.6359857 on CirclePacking-T and 1.4930 on ThirdAutoCorrIneq, consistently outperforming inference-only baselines (Section 4.2, Table 2).

RL-trained checkpoints show faster progress and better performance than base models both on the tasks they were trained on and on unseen tasks, indicating transferable evolutionary capability rather than task-specific memorization (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
ThetaEvolve without RL generates 307.2k programs in 5.4 hours versus 63.6 hours for OpenEvolve, over a 10x speedup attributable to batch sampling (Section 4.4.2, Tables 5-6).

A format-reward-only RL baseline fails to improve performance, confirming that gains come from genuine capability learning rather than exploiting the reward signal's formatting requirements (Section 4.3, Table 3).

H1ZEo8l2sH.text: PFlowNet achieves 90.6% on V* Bench, a 13% absolute improvement over the base Qwen3-VL-8B model, and 67.0% on MME-RealWorld-lite, an 18.4% gain (Section on Main Results).

PFlowNet decouples perception from reasoning by generating structured 'perceptual flows'—trajectories combining a language planning state z0 and Region-of-Interest plus caption pairs z_{>=1}—defined formally as Definition 2.2.

Training proceeds in three phases: synthetic flow data curation with teacher models (GPT-4o, Gemini) and verifier-based filtering, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) as a cold start, and variational reinforcement fine-tuning (vRFT) using a multi-dimensional reward combining contrastive visual-context likelihood with information gain (Section 2, Training Strategy).

Theorem 3.1 bounds the total variation distance between the learned policy p_theta*(Z|X) and the target valid posterior as a function of the vicinal shaping intensity lambda and vicinity radius epsilon, while Theorem 3.4 proves this bound is strictly tighter than both standard MLE (lambda -> 0) and expert-guided RLVR (lambda -> infinity) baselines (Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.4).

Ablations show SFT alone improves TreeBench accuracy by +3.4% (48.3% vs. 44.9% base), full vRFT with the contrastive reward reaches 55.3% (+10.4%), and removing perceptual flows during reasoning causes severe degradation to 49.2%, confirming flows serve as semantic anchors beyond mere localization (Table 4).
The optimal vicinal geometric shaping hyperparameters are lambda=4.5 and epsilon=0.5, balancing exploration against invalid trajectory generation (Figure 10).

y6LGSCnNOz.text: Combinatorial Adjoint Matching (CAM) reformulates discrete diffusion as stochastic control over Continuous-Time Markov Chains and introduces discrete adjoint dynamics that propagate optimization signals backward through sampling trajectories, using terminal improvement signals rather than dense per-step reward estimation (Method section).

On MIS over ER graphs with 9,000-11,000 nodes, CAM achieves an average solution size of 384.38 with a 0.00% gap to the best known solution; on RB-800-1200 it achieves 41.25 with a 4.40% gap (Results table).
On TSP-500 and TSP-1000, CAM attains gaps of 2.18% and 2.51% respectively, and on Max Cut over BA-800-1200 graphs it achieves 2964.20 with a 0.00% gap (Results table).

CAM is compared against unsupervised baselines DiffUCO, SDDS, and RLNN, supervised baselines DIFUSCO and FMIP, and traditional solvers Gurobi, KaMIS, LKH-3, and Concorde, and is reported to match or surpass supervised diffusion methods without requiring large collections of near-optimal training solutions (Experiments section).
An ablation removing the adjoint propagation mechanism increases the TSP-500 gap from 2.18% to 2.83%, demonstrating the necessity of adjoint dynamics for solution quality (Ablation study).

2Ndp39vgTE.text: CRAG couples 3D part assembly and whole-shape generation using a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with a parallel Assembly Branch predicting SE(3) flows for fragment poses and a Generation Branch synthesizing complete shapes via latent-space flow matching, connected by a Joint Adapter enabling bidirectional cross-attention at each layer (Method/Architecture section).
CRAG reuses TripoSG's pre-trained VAE as a shared latent embedding space to facilitate information exchange between the assembly and generation branches (Method section).
On PartNeXt, CRAG achieves 65.89% Part Accuracy and 2.40 Chamfer Distance in the complete-parts setting, and 71.81% Part Accuracy with 4.21 Chamfer Distance in the missing-parts setting (Table 1).
On Breaking Bad, CRAG achieves 94.68% Part Accuracy and 0.21 Chamfer Distance for complete objects, and 92.07% Part Accuracy with 0.50 Chamfer Distance when parts are missing (Table 1).

An ablation replacing task-specific encoders with the shared VAE encoder improves Part Accuracy on PartNeXt from 58.19% to 60.01%, demonstrating the benefit of geometric priors from large-scale 3D generative pretraining (Table 2).

ooRukY3zjQ.text: LRAgent decomposes the KV cache into a shared base component (with 0.9726 cosine similarity across agents) and an adapter-dependent low-rank component (with only 0.0538 similarity across agents), motivating separate treatment of the two components (Motivation/Analysis section).

LRAgent's BaseShared scheme reduces memory to approximately 1/N of non-shared baselines while limiting average accuracy drop to -0.28%, achieving a 1.42x throughput gain and 1.63x TTFT reduction at 66.4k tokens on HotpotQA/ScienceQA (Results table).

LRAgent's BaseLRShared scheme further shares the low-rank cache, achieving a 2.46x throughput gain and 4.44x TTFT reduction at 66.4k tokens, with a -0.97% average accuracy drop, compared to -2.48% for the FullShared baseline and -2.12% for DroidSpeak (Results table).

The Flash-LoRA-Attention kernel reorders the computation to (P x V_lr) x B instead of P x (V_lr x B), avoiding materialization of the low-rank cache to full dimension and reducing expansion overhead by a factor of r/d_out (Method: Flash-LoRA-Attention section).
An ablation isolating the Flash-LoRA-Attention kernel shows it independently provides up to 1.35x throughput gains beyond the memory savings from cache decomposition (Ablation study).

uIs0uPLrX4.text: Theorem 1 shows that backward spreading in locate-then-edit parameter editing works perfectly only when the layer-l intervention is an eigenvector of the Jacobian mapping from layer l to the final layer L, with the eigenvalue equal to the scaling factor beta (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 gives a weaker sufficient condition: if the symmetric part of the Jacobian is positive definite, the perturbation induced by backward spreading will not oppose the target residual direction, i.e., cosine similarity remains positive (Theorem 2).

Table 1 shows cosine similarity between the intervention and true target direction degrades with layer depth under backward spreading (0.34 at layer 4, rising to 1.00 only at layer 8), while Table 5 shows the proposed forward replay (FE) method achieves an exponentially decreasing residual ratio across layers (0.37 at layer 4 down to 0.03 at layer 8).

Forward replay optimizes the anchor point at the first editing layer and propagates forward, achieving the same computational complexity as backward spreading while producing more accurate, mutually compatible layer-wise targets (Method section).

On the MCF dataset with Llama3-8B, augmenting MEMIT with forward replay (MEMIT+FE) improves Efficacy Success from 97.4 to 99.9, Efficacy Accuracy from 94.3 to 99.8, and Generalization Success from 78.7 to 93.0, with similar gains observed for RECT, AlphaEdit, and PRUNE baselines (Results table).

8atKBiXm7u.text: On the D-RWARE warehouse co-design task, DiCoDe attains a mean reward of 12.1±0.2 versus 8.7±0.4 for the RL-only baseline and 9.6±0.6 for a fixed-environment baseline, a roughly 39% and 26% improvement respectively (Section 5, Table 1).
DiCoDe reaches its final warehouse performance using 66% fewer simulation samples than the RL baseline while co-optimizing both agent policies and environment layout (Section 5).

On the WFCRL wind-farm control benchmark scaled to 2, 4, and 8 turbines, DiCoDe outperforms the RL baseline at every scale (e.g., 370±5 vs 323±3 reward at WFCRL-8), demonstrating improved scalability with environment dimensionality (Section 5).

An ablation of the Projected Universal Guidance (PUG) sampler shows DiCoDe outperforms a gradient-descent variant by 26%, a sampling-based variant by 48%, and an ADD-guidance variant by 57% (Section 5, Figure 3).
Critic distillation, which transfers the RL critic's signal to the environment critic, contributes an additional 11% performance improvement in the ablation study (Section 5, Figure 3).

The soft co-design distribution used for guided diffusion sampling is formalized in Equation 6, and critic distillation is theoretically justified via value-function equivalence in Equation 11 (Section 4.1).

TknqRTyQ0a.text: On the Humanoid task, RPO attains a deterministic-evaluation reward of 9035.38, outperforming SAPO (8714.34), SHAC (7726.13), and PPO (2224.96) (Table 1).
On the Anymal task, RPO achieves 16008.61 reward versus 14769.62 for SAPO, 14514.12 for SHAC, and 10211.84 for PPO under deterministic evaluation (Table 1).

RPO's training objective combines a clipped surrogate term (Equation 8), an explicit KL-divergence regularization term (Equation 9), and an entropy bonus (Equation 10) into a single combined loss (Equation 11) (Section 4).
On the Hand Reorient task, SAPO requires roughly 33M additional environment steps to match RPO's performance, and on Humanoid RPO reaches a reward of 8000 using 2-3M fewer steps than SAPO (Figure 4).

An ablation on Humanoid shows removing the KL loss reduces performance to 8982.96, using only 2 policy epochs reduces it to 8328.97, and removing clipping reduces it to 8739.67, versus 9035.38 for full RPO, indicating a synergistic effect of all three components (Table 2, Section 6.3).

Results are computed across five continuous-control tasks from the DFlex and Rewarped simulators using 12 random seeds and evaluation over 128 episodes under both deterministic and stochastic protocols (Section 6, Table 1).

Wx5XHJoeyn.text: On the Soft Jumper soft-body quadruped locomotion task with a 22-dimensional action space, RFO attains a reward of 3023.96 ± 603.61 compared to 1597.99 ± 653.87 for the state-of-the-art SAPO baseline, roughly a 1.9x improvement (Table 1a).

RFO backpropagates gradients jointly through the flow-matching generative process and the differentiable system dynamics, avoiding the intractable log-likelihood computation required by standard policy-gradient methods (Section 4).
Averaged across 7 benchmark tasks using SHAC-normalized scores, RFO achieves a mean score of 1.60x SHAC, including 1.81x on Ant, 1.48x on Hand Reorient, and 1.07x on ANYmal (Table 1b).

RFO's objective includes a Past Data conditional flow-matching (CFM) regularization term (Equation 12) to stabilize training and a Uniform Exploration CFM regularization term (Equation 13) to encourage exploration (Section 4.2).

An ablation removing either the Past Data or Uniform Exploration CFM regularization term causes significant performance degradation across all three tested tasks, showing both terms are necessary (Figure 4).

zlnoC4YPQ1.text: The Fixed-Center RCGP-UCB (FC-RCGP-UCB) algorithm achieves cumulative regret R_T = Õ(Ψ(T_c)(1+√T_c)√(β'_T T(γ_T+T_c))), yielding sublinear regret for corruption budgets T_c = O(T^α) with α < 1/4 (Theorem 2, Section 4.3).

The Anchor-Adapt RCGP-UCB (A2-RCGP-UCB) algorithm, which adaptively updates its centering function, achieves cumulative regret R_T = Õ((1+T_c Ψ(T_c)^2)√(β'_T T(γ_T+T_c))), yielding sublinear regret for α < 1/7 (Theorem 3, Section 4.3).

Both algorithms tolerate corruptions of possibly infinite magnitude, bounded only in frequency (number of corrupted points T_c), as formalized in the Frequency-Constrained Corruption model (Definition 1, Section 2.2).

When there are no corruptions (T_c = 0), both FC-RCGP-UCB and A2-RCGP-UCB recover the same asymptotic regret bound as standard GP-UCB, R_T = O(√(Tβ'_Tγ_T)), a zero-cost robustness property (Theorem 1, Section 4.3).

Experiments on the corrupted Forrester function benchmark show RCGP-based methods (FC-RCGP-UCB, A2-RCGP-UCB) achieve lower cumulative regret than baselines using standard GP, Student-t process, or the heuristic DiagnosticsGP approach, even though the theoretical analysis conservatively requires α < 1/4 and α < 1/7 while experiments use corruption budgets as large as O(T^(1/3)) (Section 5.3, Figure 1).

ZAZb1ZGnFH.text: Empowerment-maximizing agents induce two distinct learned representations: a forward representation encoding which outcomes an agent can influence, and a backward representation encoding how states can be reached, without requiring a reward function or expert data (Section 4-5.1).
Theorem 5.1 proves these forward and backward representations are invariant to action-interface relabeling, meaning skills transfer across different action/button mappings without retraining.

Theorem 5.4 proves that under minimal representation and policy assumptions, empowerment-maximizing policies necessarily ignore uncontrollable noise dimensions, making both representation types invariant to control-irrelevant features such as background colors in maze environments.

Proposition 5.8 shows that under deterministic dynamics and connectivity assumptions, the backward representation alone captures all control-relevant structure, framed as a reward-agnostic analogue of bisimulation.

In a controlled MDP experiment, enforcing symmetric (rather than separate forward/backward) representations reduces measured empowerment from 0.69 to 0, empirically demonstrating the asymmetry between the two representation types (Figure 5, Section 6).

On Point-Maze, Ant, and pixel-based Kitchen environments with added noise, frozen representations from the proposed method show variance to control-relevant dimensions roughly 1000x greater than to noise dimensions, and linear probes recover control-relevant (x,y) coordinates with R^2 approaching 1.0 despite noise augmentation (Section 6, RQ1-RQ3, RQ5).

h6vKAlSWJw.text: BoCloak achieves attack success rates roughly 80% higher than constrained state-of-the-art graph adversarial attack baselines such as Nettack, FGA, PR-BCD, and GOttack (Section 5.1, Table 2).
On the Cresci-15 dataset BoCloak reaches roughly 92-99% misclassification rates versus only 3-9% for competing SOTA attacks under matched edit budgets (Table 2).
BoCloak uses about 11 MB of GPU memory versus 286 MB for PR-BCD/FGA, a reduction of 99.80%, and runs in about 0.1 seconds versus 19.7 seconds for Nettack, up to 20x faster (Table 4).

BoCloak represents each node's k-hop ego-neighborhood as a probability measure and uses entropic-regularized optimal transport with a learnable, contrastively-trained cost function to compute label-aware transport plans that guide feasible edge edits (Section 4.2, Equation 2-4).
Node injection attacks achieve over 90% success with small edge budgets of only 1-3 edges per injected node across datasets (Figure 4).

Ablations show the OT-margin BCE loss is the primary contributor to attack success, with its removal dropping success by roughly 60%, while sparsity and plausibility loss terms and degree/age weighting contribute more moderately (Table 3, Appendix P).

IP6W8i7XPG.text: Theorem 4.6 shows that when SNR times nε exceeds Ω̃(1), DP-SGD successfully learns feature signals while keeping noise memorization below the magnitude of feature learning (Theorem 4.6).
Theorem 4.10 shows that when the inverse SNR times ε exceeds Ω̃(1), data noise memorization dominates over signal learning, causing poor generalization despite small training loss (Theorem 4.10).

The multi-patch data model decomposes inputs into label-dependent feature signals v and label-independent Gaussian noise ξ, and Definition 4.1 decomposes learned model weights into random initialization, a learned-signal coefficient Γ, a memorized-noise coefficient Φ, and accumulated private noise (Definition 3.1, Definition 4.1).
Corollary 4.8 bounds test error by O(κ + exp(-(nε)^(1+1/q))), showing that the privacy budget ε directly governs the generalization gap (Corollary 4.8).

Synthetic experiments confirm that lower privacy budgets (e.g., ε=0.2) require higher signal-to-noise ratio to achieve effective signal learning under DP-SGD, and that private training amplifies noise memorization relative to non-private baselines (Section 5, Figure 2).

lh95PnOlpM.text: On Sudoku-Extreme, Equilibrium Reasoners (EqR) improve accuracy from a 2.6% feedforward baseline to 93.0% with depth-only scaling (D=64) and to 99.8% with combined depth-and-breadth scaling (D=64, B=128) (Table 1, Table 4).

On Maze-Unique, EqR raises accuracy from a 44.9% baseline to 82.2% via landscape shaping (randomized initialization plus noise injection) and to 93.0% via combined depth-and-breadth test-time scaling (Table 1, Table 4, Section 5).

Combining depth (up to 1,024 iterations) and breadth (multiple random initializations) test-time scaling produces the equivalent of unrolling over 40,000 effective layers despite the model being trained with only 16 iterations (Figure 1, Abstract).

Five architectural ingredients enable scalable equilibrium reasoning: weight-tied parameters, gradient truncation with detached carry, segmented online training (SOT), hierarchical iterations, and adaptive computation time (ACT) (Section 3, Figure 4).

With adaptive computation time tuned to match a fixed accuracy target of 92.99%, EqR reduces the number of function evaluations by 3.76x, and with further ACT optimization by up to 11.34x, relative to the baseline (Figure 7, Table 5).
Randomized state initialization alone improves Maze-Unique accuracy from 44.9% to 68.6%, and combining it with noise injection further raises accuracy to 82.2% (Section 5).

fhPu6dCiwt.text: When a decoder is pretrained on high-diversity data from a primary modality M1, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality M2 suffices for multimodal in-context learning to emerge (Section 4.1, Figure 4).

Larger secondary-modality class count K2 and burstiness B promote in-context learning, and increasing ε2 (secondary-modality diversity) has a stronger positive effect on ICL than increasing ε1, with optimal performance occurring when α1 ≈ α2 ≈ 1 (Section 4.1, Figure 4a, 4c, 4d).

Switching the positional encoding from absolute (APE) to RoPE causes a marked drop in multimodal ICL accuracy, while increasing model scale consistently improves multimodal ICL by mapping the secondary modality onto pre-existing circuits (Section 3.2, Section 3.3, Figure 2).

Both unimodal and multimodal in-context learning depend on an induction-style, offset-one copying circuit: ablating the induction head drops accuracy to 0.062 and ablating the previous-token head drops accuracy to 0.199 (Table 3).

In the multimodal refinement stage, IndStrength2 becomes the dominant correlate of ICL accuracy (ρ = 0.70) while context-label association (CLA) becomes negligible (ρ = 0.02), since it was already learned during pretraining (Table 1b, Section 4.4.2).

Findings from the controlled synthetic setup transfer to real image data in Omniglot experiments and to production multimodal LLMs (Qwen2.5-VL and IDEFICS), which show consistent induction-head signatures (Section 4.3, Section 4.4.4, Figure 8).

90kxFi9VGP.text: SAMPO achieves an average 25.2% improvement over the GRPO baseline across agentic tasks by unifying sequence-level clipping, fine-grained advantage estimation with a step-wise term, and dynamic trajectory filtering (Section 5.2, Equation 8).

On the standardized ALFWorld/WebShop/Sokoban/TIR-Math testbed built on SFT-tuned Qwen3-4B, SAMPO attains the highest average score (59.55), with 92.72% success on ALFWorld, 74.08% success on WebShop, and 88.86% success on Sokoban (Table 3).

Tolerant IS clipping methods (CISPO, SAPO) achieve substantially worse average scores (34.03 and 32.22) than sequence-level-clipping GSPO (46.16 baseline, 13.3% improvement), and training collapses around step 130 due to accumulation of negative-advantage sequences with low importance-sampling ratios (Section 4.1, Table 3, Figure 2, Figure 3, Finding 1/2).

Applying sequence masking to SAPO and CISPO (denoted SAPOSM and CISPOSM) raises ALFWorld success rate from 25.16% to 78.88% for CISPO and from 25.16% to 76.92% for SAPO, stabilizing training to match GSPO (Table 4).

GIGPO, which incorporates global and local environment-level advantage information, outperforms GRPO with an average score of 49.71 versus 48.08, and dynamic filtering combined with GIGPO (DAPO_GIGPO) improves stability and performance more consistently than combining it with GRPO (Table 3, Section 4.2-4.3, Finding 3/4).

Under varying off-policy staleness degrees, TIR Math achieves 87.34% pass@32 accuracy at low off-policy degree (rollout batch size 128) versus 74.99% at high off-policy degree (1024), and ALFWorld success rate falls from 60.80% (low) to 52.71% (high) (Table 5, Section 4.5).

wg02GN1ygj.text: Theorem 2 proves feature unlearning occurs when the alignment term R vanishes in the limit (lim R_τs→0) while the second-layer weight scale a diverges (lim a_τs→∞) as slow time τs→∞ (Section 5.1, Theorem 2).

Theorem 3 gives explicit polynomial convergence rates for the unlearning regime, showing R_τs = Θ(τs^{-1/(2k1)}) and a_τs = Θ(τs^{1/(2k1)}) in one case, and R_τs = Θ(τs^{-1/(k0+1)}) and a_τs = Θ(τs^{1/(k0+1)}) in another, where k0, k1 index the strength of nonlinear terms in the teacher/data (Section 5.2, Theorem 3).

The critical manifold S is formally defined as the zero-level set of the fast dynamics, {(R,a) : f̄(R,a)=0}, and Figure 1 shows trajectories on this manifold where slow dynamics determine whether alignment R drifts to zero (unlearning) or is maintained (Section 4.1, Definition 2, Figure 1).

Assumption 7 shows that the initial scale of the second-layer weight, ā, relative to the threshold h(R)=2S'(R)/T'(R), determines whether a trajectory falls into the unlearning region (0,R*) or avoids it, i.e., the initial second-layer weight scale mitigates or induces unlearning (Section 5.1, Assumption 7).
Figure 6 numerically validates the theoretical scaling-law exponents of ±1/4 and ±1/3 for the convergence rates of R_τs and a_τs (Section 5.2, Figure 6).

Figure 7 shows that the qualitative fast-slow dynamics of feature learning/unlearning persist in finite-width networks trained with stochastic gradient descent despite added stochastic noise, beyond the idealized mean-field ODE regime (Figure 7).

F0F03HOYb8.text: Effective degree (ED) is defined as a coefficient-weighted polynomial degree, ED(P) = Σ|c_k|·k, computed by fitting a polynomial to network outputs along data-dependent interpolation paths (Section 3, Definition 3.2).
On CIFAR-10 with ViT-Tiny, ED regularization improves test accuracy to 90.82±0.11%, a +3.02 point gain over the unregularized baseline, outperforming SAM, ASAM, and Jacobian regularization (Table 1).

On ImageNet with ViT-S/16, ED regularization improves accuracy by +1.39 points to 72.76±0.16% under the original training recipe and by +0.59 points to 75.01±0.11% under a stronger training recipe (Table 3).

For CLIP ViT-B/32 contrastive fine-tuning on ImageNet, ED regularization improves in-distribution accuracy by +0.94 points (to 77.14±0.05%) and average out-of-distribution accuracy by +1.27 points (to 45.31±0.08%); for ViT-B/16 it improves in-distribution accuracy by +0.84 points and OOD accuracy by +1.60 points (Table 2).

On GLUE text classification with BERT-base, ED regularization improves RTE accuracy by +0.84 points (to 71.12±1.96%), MRPC accuracy by +0.92 points (to 87.66±0.90%), and CoLA Matthews correlation by +0.14 (Table 4).

Figure 2 (ResNet18/CIFAR-10) and Figure 3 (CLIP ViT-B/32/ImageNet) show ED correlates more strongly with the generalization gap than sharpness-based measures or L2 norm baselines, with sharpness even correlating negatively with the gap in the CLIP setting (Figures 2 and 3).

VlspNGn7cK.text: InfoAtlas performs zero-shot mutual information estimation via a single forward pass of a pretrained hypernetwork, rather than per-dataset gradient-descent optimization, achieving roughly 100x speedup over neural estimators, completing estimation in 0.09 seconds versus 25.9 seconds for MINE and 34.2 seconds for MINDE (Table 1).

For input dimensions d<D, InfoAtlas pads variables with independent Gaussian noise N(0,I) to reach a fixed dimension D, enabling a single unified architecture to handle varying input dimensions and sample sizes (Section on architecture).

For dimensions d>20, InfoAtlas uses k-sliced mutual information, estimating MI over multiple low-dimensional random projections and averaging, reducing complexity from O(ST) to O(1) where S is the number of slices and T is per-slice optimization cost.
Figure 3 shows that across three correlation types at dimensions 16 and 128, InfoAtlas achieves accuracy comparable to MINE, InfoNCE, and MINDE, particularly at sample sizes n≥500 (Figure 3).

On a robotic Pick Cube manipulation task, InfoAtlas-based dependence estimation achieves 94.2% success on seen configurations and 82.0% on unseen configurations, outperforming MINE-based methods (real-world applications section).

InfoAtlas is pretrained solely on synthetic distributions generated via random copula mixtures with K=60 components and flow-based marginal transformations, yet generalizes zero-shot to real-world data including CLIP embeddings and video object segmentation trajectories without task-specific fine-tuning.

tfk5Zpn0AR.text: Attend to Anything (AAM) is presented as the first unified multi-modal foundation model for attention modeling across image, video, and audio-visual scenarios, combining hyperbolic-space hierarchical entailment learning with a Fokker-Planck temporal dynamics module (introduction/architecture section).
Across 16 benchmarks, AAM improves attention-prediction metrics by an average of 6%, with 5.2% average gains on image tasks, 5.8% on audio-visual tasks, and 6.0% on video tasks (results tables).
AAM achieves approximately 4x speedup in video inference compared to fixed-window methods while using only 21M trainable parameters (efficiency analysis section).
AAM is trained on Attention-1.75M, a standardized corpus unifying over 1.75 million fixation instances spanning images, videos, and audio-visual scenarios (dataset section).
Evaluation uses standard saliency metrics — AUC-Judd, Similarity (SIM), Correlation Coefficient (CC), and Normalized Scanpath Saliency (NSS) — across the 16 benchmarks (evaluation section).

Qg8cAQC5sU.text: TraceRouter uses a three-stage 'Discover-Trace-Disconnect' framework that targets distributed harmful semantics via cross-layer causal circuits, using sparse autoencoders and feature influence scores to trace pathways and a scaling factor λ=2 to suppress them (methodology section).

On Stable Diffusion 1.4, TraceRouter improves violence-prompt defense on the I2P benchmark to 93.6% versus 82.3% for the SNCE baseline (+11.3 points), and defense against P4D attacks to 74.8% versus 57.4% for SNCE (+17.4 points), while CLIP score utility improves slightly to 31.27 vs 30.87 and FID improves to 16.24 vs 16.64 (results table).
On Mistral-7B, TraceRouter improves defense success rate from a 6.6% baseline to 98.8% (+92.2 percentage points), while accuracy on utility benchmarks drops by only -0.5% (results section).

On LLaMA3-8B, TraceRouter achieves a 99.6% average defense success rate across gradient-based and pattern-based jailbreak attacks, compared to 98.8% for the HumorReject baseline, with only -0.8% utility drop on Global-MMLU-Lite (results section).

On multimodal models, TraceRouter achieves 99.60% safety rate on LLaVA-1.5-7B (MM-SafetyBench) and 98.40% on MiniGPT-4-7B, with utility loss of only -0.3% and -0.29% respectively on MM-Bench (results section).

A path-amplification ablation, in which the identified causal circuits are artificially amplified rather than suppressed, drops the Stable Diffusion 1.4 defense success rate to 72.2%, confirming the traced pathways are causally responsible for harmful behavior rather than merely correlated (validation/ablation section).

D0Dg8ISjq0.text: NSI is evaluated on three agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, TextCraft) and achieves 98.0% success rate on ALFWorld, 76.5% score and 44.5% success rate on WebShop, and 95.2% success rate on TextCraft, outperforming baselines including ReAct, Reflexion, ADaPT, StateAct, AWM, and ASI (Table 1).

NSI without online honing already reaches 93.5% success on ALFWorld and 78.5% on TextCraft, showing that offline induction alone outperforms the strongest baseline AWM (91.3% ALFWorld), while online skill honing adds further gains (Table 1).

NSI encapsulates approximately 7.4 atomic actions per invoked skill on average and sustains valid execution up to 53+ steps, compressing the planning horizon compared to ASI, which suffers a survival-analysis 'Long-Horizon Collapse' after the 22-step threshold (Section 6.3, Figure 4b).

The skill representation is formalized as a triple of invocation parameters, a neural grounding module, and a symbolic execution graph built from four logic-grounded node types: DataOp, CheckOp/LoopOp, PrimitiveOp, and TerminalOp (Section 4.2).

Skill induction proceeds via a two-stage progressive process: Intra-Trajectory Logic Consolidation synthesizes a local expert per demonstration trace, followed by Inter-Trajectory Skill Consolidation that greedily merges local experts into a global skill only when it satisfies Feasibility Dominance (strictly expanding empirical consistency coverage) (Section 5.2, Equation 4).

9lV4ZvcOAL.text: On the MMDocIR page-level retrieval benchmark with the DSE_wiki-ss first-stage retriever, ZipRerank achieves 65.7% macro Recall@1, 69.5% macro Recall@3 and 78.2% macro Recall@5, with cached LLM reranking time of only 0.36s versus 3.82s for MM-R5 (Table 1).

With the ColQwen first-stage retriever, ZipRerank attains 66.1% macro Recall@1, 79.0% macro Recall@3, and 84.1% macro Recall@5, matching or exceeding MM-R5 while using 0.36s versus 3.74s of cached LLM time (Table 2).

Ablation on DSE_wiki-ss shows removing the soft-ranking loss (replacing it with the Stage-1 RankNet loss) causes the largest Recall@1 drop, from 64.2% to 56.8% macro-average, confirming the soft-ranking objective's importance for Stage 2 finetuning (Table 3, Section 5.3).

Replacing single-logit decoding with standard autoregressive generation leaves ranking performance largely comparable but makes inference over 6 times slower, since the query-image early interaction and single-pass scoring mechanisms are what drive the latency reduction (Section 5.3, Section 4.2).
ZipRerank generalizes to the out-of-domain ViDoRe benchmark, improving NDCG@5 over MM-R5 from 49.0 to 53.4 with the DSE retriever and from 55.8 to 59.9 with ColQwen (Section 5.5, Table 4).

ZaOZDGJDAM.text: Deepcontour achieves up to 5.63x end-to-end speedup over five scouting-based baselines (Arnoldi, GD, JD, Lanczos, KrylovSchur) on the Kirchhoff-Love Plate dataset at N=50000 and tolerance 1e-2, with speedups reported across five scientific datasets and eight tolerance levels from 1e-2 to 1e-12 (Table 1, Section 5.2).

The framework combines an Eigen-Neural-Operator (ENO), an FNO-based architecture that predicts the coarse spectral distribution of a GEP from the input physical parameter function, with a Kernel-Density-Estimation (KDE) module that automatically partitions the predicted spectrum into tight-fitting integration contours for the CI solver (Section 4.1, Section 4.2, Figure 3).

Deepcontour's acceleration advantage over Arnoldi- and GD-scout baselines becomes more pronounced as matrix size increases from 10,000 to 50,000 on both the Kirchhoff-Love Plate and EGFR Electronic problems, demonstrating favorable scalability (Section 5.3, Figure 4).

Evaluation spans five distinct physical/engineering domains as GEP sources: Kirchhoff-Love Plate Vibration, EGFR Electronic Structure, Electromagnetic Cavity Modal Analysis, Piezoelectric Coupled-Field Modal Analysis, and 2D Thermal Diffusion Modal Analysis (Section 5.1).

An ablation comparing the full Deepcontour (ENO+KDE) against a variant without ENO (replacing the FNO backbone with a standard MLP) and a variant without KDE (using naive interval expansion) is conducted on one hundred instances to isolate the contribution of each module (Section 5.4).

UstfBHsp6p.text: The Masked Diffusion (MD) training objective is theoretically decomposed into a Signal Regime term and a Noise Regime term, where the Noise Regime acts as an implicit regularizer that penalizes model output on information-theoretically unidentifiable masked inputs (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.3).

On the (n,k)=(20,6) parity task, standard cross-entropy training exhibits classic grokking (validation accuracy stuck at 50% chance level despite 100% training accuracy for a prolonged period), whereas the Masked Diffusion objective achieves near-simultaneous training/validation convergence without grokking (Figure 2, Section 4.5).

At the 50M-parameter scale pretrained on WikiText, restricting the masking ratio to the signal-rich window t in [0.45, 0.55] reduces test loss to about 3.62 versus approximately 3.88 for the standard U[0,1] baseline, and yields a 4.6-point accuracy gain on HellaSwag (0.400 vs 0.354) and an 8.8-point gain on ARC-Easy (0.430 vs 0.342) after 15,000 pretraining steps (Figure 3, Table 1).

At the 8B-parameter (LLaDA-8B) scale, supervised fine-tuning with the signal-rich window t in [0.45,0.55] improves GPQA accuracy from 0.344 (vanilla SFT) to 0.402 and ARC-Challenge from 0.468 to 0.480, a gain the paper reports as peaking at 5.8% on discriminative SFT tasks (Table 2, Section 5.2.2).

Corollary 4.8 derives the Signal-Optimal masking rate as t0=t1=1/(k+1) for k-parity tasks with k>1, motivating the paper's recommendation to concentrate mask-ratio sampling near a narrow signal-rich interval rather than sampling uniformly over [0,1] (Section 4.4, Corollary 4.8).

R3JzLU2qZj.text: DP-DMD preserves sample diversity without using any perceptual loss (e.g., LPIPS), adversarial discriminator, additional modules, or teacher-generated reference images, instead relying on a role-separated distillation loss that supervises only the first denoising step with a teacher-derived diversity target and detaches its gradient before applying the standard DMD loss to later steps (Section 4, Equation 8, Algorithm 1).

On Pick-a-Pic with SD3.5-M (CFG=3.5), DP-DMD at 4 NFEs achieves DINO diversity 0.179 and CLIP diversity 0.182, both higher than vanilla DMD (0.137/0.133), DMD-LPIPS (0.169/0.169), while remaining competitive in quality (VQ-R1 4.646, ImgR 1.142) and preference (PicS 21.76) (Table 1).

On COCO-10K 2014 with SD3.5-M, DP-DMD attains the best diversity among DMD variants (DINO 0.250, CLIP 0.184) while maintaining the highest MIQA (1.032) and PicS (22.41) among the compared DMD-based methods (Table 1).

An ablation over the diversity anchor step K (Table 3) shows diversity monotonically increasing from 0.157/0.155 DINO/CLIP at K=1 to 0.187/0.185 at K=30, while an ablation over the diversity weight lambda (Table 4) shows diversity increasing from 0.170/0.164 at lambda=0.01 to 0.177/0.177 at lambda=0.10, both on Pick-a-Pic.

Removing gradient stopping after the first denoising step (w/o Detaching) causes the DMD loss to back-propagate through the entire student rollout and lets the mode-seeking DMD objective override the diversity-preserving supervision, as shown by declining diversity curves over training in Figure 5 (Section 5.3).

hXyv6xeHkO.text: SPHERE improves average success rate by 133% under continual RL (CRL) relative to the unregularized Top-K MoE baseline on MetaWorld, and reduces the RL-CRL performance gap by 52% (Figure 4).
On HumanoidBench, SPHERE achieves a 36% improvement under standard RL and a 50% improvement under CRL versus the Top-K MoE baseline (Figure 5).
SPHERE formalizes spectral plasticity as the spectral-entropy effective rank of the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel, re(K(X;theta)) (Definition 4.1).

The SPHERE penalty regularizes the weighted expert feature Gram matrix toward a scaled identity, and Theorem 4.7 proves this optimization increases re(K) for learning rates 0<=eta<=1/2 (Section 4.4, Theorem 4.7).

An ablation shows placing the SPHERE penalty on the last hidden expert layer with cross-expert concatenation (0.54±0.12 success) outperforms applying it to all hidden layers (0.42±0.07) or using a per-expert sum without cross-correlation (0.40±0.08) (Table 1).
Effective rank of the feature Gram used as the SPHERE proxy correlates with the true eNTK effective rank at Pearson r=0.846, validating the proxy (Figure 7).

nLY2pOYBrJ.text: On GenEval with SD3.5M, Advantage Weighted Matching (AWM) matches the Flow-GRPO score (0.95 vs 0.95) while achieving an 8.02x compute speedup (Table 1, Figure 1c).
On the OCR benchmark, AWM reaches 0.89 accuracy on SD3.5M with a 23.6x speedup (17.6 vs 415.9 GPU hours) and 0.95 accuracy on FLUX with an 8.53x speedup (40.3 vs 343.6 GPU hours) (Table 2, Figure 5).
On PickScore, AWM attains 23.02 on SD3.5M with a 10.5x speedup (91.1 vs 956.1 GPU hours) and 23.08 on FLUX with a 6.8x speedup (49.8 vs 339.2 GPU hours) (Table 2, Figure 5).

Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 show DDPO implicitly performs denoising score matching conditioned on noisy targets, which strictly increases target variance by a factor kappa(s,t)*I that grows monotonically with noise level (Section 3.3, Theorems 1-2).
Pretraining experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64 confirm that noisy-target DSM converges slower than clean-data DSM under identical settings, validating the variance-increase theory (Figure 3).
An ablation finds the KL regularization strength beta performs best in the range [0.4, 1.0], balancing training stability against learning speed (Figure 7).

TBSyYj4VV6.text: The proposed quantum algorithm constructs epsilon-approximate GLM sparsifiers in time O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + poly(n))*log(s_max/s_min), giving a quadratic speedup in sample count m over the classical O~(mr) algorithm (Theorem 10).
For linear regression, the quantum algorithm runs in O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + n^3) time versus O~(mr + n^3) classically (Corollary 23).
The paper gives the first quantum algorithm for Lasso regression, running in O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + poly(n,1/epsilon)) time versus O~(mn^2 + n^3) classically (Corollary 26).
Ridge regression is solved in O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + n^3) quantum time versus O~(mr + poly(n,1/epsilon)) classically (Corollary 25).
Huber regression is handled via a gamma_p-loss framework in O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + poly(n,1/epsilon)) quantum time (Corollary 12).
For l_p regression with p in (0,2], the algorithm achieves quadratic speedup in the sample parameter m, which the authors note dominates runtime when m >> n (Corollary 11).

Q15yX0AZdr.text: Theorem 1 establishes high-probability convergence of projected stochastic subgradient descent (SsGD) for weakly convex functions under sub-Weibull(theta) noise, on a bounded constrained domain (Section 4.1, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows mini-batch clipped-SsGD converges with high probability under p-BCM (p in (1,2]) gradient noise on an unbounded domain, with O(log(T/delta)) dependence on the failure probability delta (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).
Theorem 3 gives a fixed-time-horizon variant of the clipped-SsGD result that removes the log T factor, achieving O(log(1/delta)) dependence on delta instead (Section 4.2, Theorem 3).
The resulting sample complexity for clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise is O~(epsilon^{-2p/(p-1)}) (Section 4.2).

Theorems 4 and 5 provide in-expectation convergence guarantees for clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise, with Theorem 5 removing the logarithmic dependence on the time horizon when the horizon is fixed (Section 4.2, Theorems 4-5).

cGOX9bOWnj.text: Theorem 1 gives a modular discounted-to-dynamic (D2D) reduction converting a rescaled-regret bound of the form sum_s beta^{-s}(f_s(x_s)-f_s(u)) <= phi_t(u) + sum_s Lambda_s into an explicit dynamic regret bound via stability terms Lambda_s and path variation P_T^beta (Section 2.2, Theorem 1).

For online linear regression, discounted Vovk-Azoury-Warmuth achieves dynamic regret O(d log T + sqrt(d*T*P_T^beta)) without Bregman-divergence arguments, recovering optimal rates (Section 3.1, Theorem 2).

For online logistic regression, the discounted AIOLI algorithm avoids exponential dependence on the comparator norm B, and a two-layer ensemble achieves dynamic regret O(d*B*log(BT) + sqrt(d*B*T*P_T^{beta*})) via automatic discount-factor tuning (Section 3.2, Theorems 3-4).

Theorem 5 proves clipped Adam converges with a relaxed beta_2 condition, max{1-nu/(G+sigma), beta_1^4} <= beta_2 < 1 (versus the prior requirement beta_2 >= beta_1^2), attaining the optimal O(F*G^2*c^{1/2}*epsilon^{-7/2}) iteration complexity (Section 4.3.1, Theorem 5).

Theorem 7 shows a clip-free variant of Adam, using a composite loss with a tuned damping term, achieves the same optimal convergence rates under the standard condition beta_2 >= beta_1^2 (Section 4.4, Theorem 7).

oREpq5grNl.text: SOLAR-C achieves an average score of 87.69 on the sym-MM2MM benchmark, outperforming the strongest supervised baseline mmE5 by 7.08 points (Table 1, Section 5).

SOLAR-C attains this result with a 0.20B-parameter model versus mmE5's 10.12B parameters (over 50x fewer parameters) and a 768-dimensional embedding versus mmE5's 4096 dimensions (5x smaller) (Table 1, Section 5).

The sym-MM2MM benchmark introduced in the paper consists of 214 human-verified triplets (original sample, positive counterpart, hard negative), constructed via GPT-4o descriptions, LLM-generated information gaps, and Stable Diffusion 3.5 synthesized images, with about 50% of machine-generated pairs rejected during human verification (Section 3).

In the Stage 1 ablation, removing the Global-to-Local Alignment (GLA) margin loss causes the largest drop, 5.7 points, while removing the evolutionary mask causes the smallest drop, 0.5 points (Table 2, Section 5).

In the Stage 2 ablation, using Stage 1 alone yields 82.2 average, while removing semantic segmentation (relative to full Stage 2) costs 5.0 points, and replacing semantic segmentation with SAM-based segmentation yields 83.7 average (Table 3, Section 5).
SOLAR is trained self-supervised on 800,000 unlabeled image-text pairs from LAION-5B without manual labels (Section 4/5).

xM4iQX34JA.text: GRACE's INT4-quantized Qwen2-VL-2B model surpasses the BF16 baseline on ScienceQA, scoring 79.1 vs 73.7 (Table 2).

GRACE's INT4 quantization achieves 3.03x throughput improvement (106.68 vs 35.26 tokens/second) and about 2.18x peak GPU memory reduction (6,572 MB vs 14,302 MB) (Section on deployment metrics / efficiency results).

GRACE-distilled LLaVA-1.5-7B reaches 69.0% average accuracy, a 3.8% improvement over the non-distilled baseline, with the largest per-benchmark gains over the MoVE-KD baseline on TextVQA (+0.9%) and ScienceQA (+1.9%) (Table 1).
At INT4, GRACE reaches 67.2% average accuracy, exceeding the BF16 baseline by 1.1 points and outperforming AWQ and QAT baselines by 1.3-1.6 percentage points (Table 2).

Ablation on Qwen2-VL shows the relational-centered kernel alignment (RCKA) component contributes 5.6% gain and the confidence-gated decoupled distillation (GDKD) component contributes 5.4% gain, with the full GRACE framework achieving a combined 7.6% improvement (Table 3).
Plain quantization-aware training (QAT) alone degrades performance by 1.9% at 4-bit, whereas combining GRACE with QAT yields +6.2% at 4-bit and +7.2% at 8-bit (Table 4).

B62wCl3Bh4.text: Progressive pessimistic verification is evaluated on three benchmarks — IMO-GradingBench (300 samples), Hard2Verify (200 samples), and the paper's newly introduced QiuZhen-Bench (1,054 problems from S.-T. Yau contests and Tsinghua doctoral exams) — showing consistent True Negative Rate gains across GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, and Qwen3-30B-A3B (Figure 6).

On GPT-5-mini, pessimistic verification methods achieve improved balanced-F1 with higher token efficiency than scaling long chain-of-thought, using parallel rather than sequential reasoning execution (Figure 1).

The paper defines three pessimistic verification variants: simple (accepts the first negative verdict among independent reviews), vertical (segments proofs by line count for section-level scrutiny), and progressive (multi-scale combination with a pruning optimization, evaluated as progressive@3/6) (Figure 2, Section 3.2).

Manual review of false-negative cases (Table 1, Section 3.4) finds that stronger models' disputed misclassifications frequently identify genuine proof errors overlooked by original dataset annotators, implying reported benchmark scores underestimate true verification capability for state-of-the-art models.
All evaluations use response-level binary correct/incorrect classification with sampling temperature set to 1.0 for response diversity (Section 3.2, Experimental Setup).

YgQ3MV7OtR.text: CoVRL achieves an overall performance of 50.2%, a 12.4-point improvement over the Qwen2.5-7B base model (37.8%) and a 2.3-point improvement over the strongest verifier-free RL baseline (47.9%) (Table 1).
CoVRL is evaluated across general-reasoning benchmarks (GPQA, MMLU-Pro, TheoremQA) and math-reasoning benchmarks (AIME'24, AQuA, CARP-EN, MATH-500, Minerva, SAT-Math) (Table 1).
Cross-model evaluation shows CoVRL yields 5.2%-14.0% improvements across Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B (Table 2).

An ablation on the hybrid sampling mixing coefficient shows the balanced setting alpha=0.5 outperforms both alpha=0.1 and alpha=0.9, confirming the benefit of coupling prior and posterior sampling (Figure 5).
Reducing the KL-regularization coefficient to 0.1 severely degrades performance to 27.4%, confirming the regularization term is necessary for inference transferability (Table 4).
Training on non-mathematical data alone still yields a 12.4% improvement with cross-domain transfer to mathematical tasks (Table 3).

XoONWh8fbL.text: Box Thirding (B3) is analyzed under a formalized 'data-poor condition' where the candidate set size c0 cannot cover all potentially eps-optimal arms, decomposing error probability into non-inclusion probability and misidentification probability (Section 4).
Theorem 4.3 bounds the misidentification probability as P(mu_1 - mu_at > eps) <= exp{-Omega(max{N_(eps/2)/N, eps^2/N} * T)}, where N_(eps/2) is the count of eps/2-best arms (Theorem 4.3).
Proposition 4.8 shows B3 attains candidate set size c0 = Theta(T), matching Uniform Sampling, while Bracketing Sequential Halving attains only c0 = Theta(T/(log_2 T)^2) (Proposition 4.8).

Corollary 4.9 shows B3 and Uniform Sampling share the same non-inclusion probability bound exp{-Omega(T*N_(eps/2)/N)}, while Bracketing Sequential Halving is slower by a log(T)^2 factor (Corollary 4.9).

On the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest dataset (contest 893, N=5,513 arms, budget T=10,000), B3 achieves consistently lower simple regret than Uniform Sampling, BUCB, and Bracketing Sequential Halving across high-noise (N(mu,0.5^2)), moderate-noise (N(mu,0.2^2)), and deterministic reward regimes (Section 5 experiments).
The base sampling parameter r0 in B3 is set by solving r0 + r0^1.5 = 4, yielding r0 approx 1.728 (Section 4, Algorithm parameters).

bT6JcLswlW.text: SimpleNorm places normalization directly after each linear mapping (Ψ(x) = Norm(Wx)) rather than only at block boundaries, reducing Hessian spectral norms relative to standard PreNorm+QKNorm (Section 4, Eq. 3)
Theorem 4.2 proves SimpleNorm-based Hessians scale as Θ(‖H_yy‖₂), independent of weight scale, whereas plain linear projections scale quadratically as ‖W‖₂²×‖H_yy‖₂ (Theorem 4.2)
On a 7B-parameter LLaMA2-scale model, SimpleGPT reduces training loss from 2.290 to 2.208 after 60K steps compared to a PreNorm+QKNorm baseline (Section 5.1)
SimpleGPT tolerates learning rates roughly 3x-10x larger than the PreNorm+QKNorm baseline across model scales from 1B to 8B parameters without training instability (Section 5.1)
Figure 2 shows SimpleGPT remains stable at a learning rate of 2×10⁻¹ while the PreNorm+QKNorm baseline diverges at that learning rate (Figure 2)
SimpleGPT's normalization overhead adds only about 3% wall-clock slowdown per training step versus LLaMA3 baseline (1553ms to 1603ms) when fused via torch.compile (Section 5.1)

cxzfiVqrjN.text: Adaptive Tail-Head Alignment (ATHA) improves CLIP-based cross-domain few-shot learning by suppressing (breaking) alignment for the bottom 10% lowest-similarity 'tail' image patch tokens while strengthening alignment for the top 10% 'head' tokens, using layer-wise learned parameters α(l) and β(l) (Section 3, Section 4)

On the 5-way 5-shot setting across four CDFSL benchmarks (CropDiseases, EuroSAT, ISIC2018, ChestX), ATHA achieves an average accuracy of 68.53%, a 2.54-point improvement over the baseline, with the largest single-dataset gain of +5.32 points on ISIC2018 (Table 1, Section 5.1)

Ablating ATHA into a push-away-only variant yields a +1.46-point average gain, while the full ATHA (adding head-token strengthening) adds a further +1.08 points over push-away-only (Table 2, Section 5.2)
Direct feature modulation for tail suppression outperforms a loss-based alternative by 1.77 points on average (Table 2a, Section 5.2)
Selecting text anchors via MaxSim/MinSim similarity outperforms weighted-average text alignment by 0.8 points on average (Table 2b, Section 5.2)
ATHA generalizes across four vision-language backbones and is compatible with CoOp, MaPLe, and LoRA fine-tuning frameworks (Table 4, Table 5, Sections 5.8-5.9)

OOodUUenVk.text: PLANET uses a divide-and-conquer design that decouples modality interaction (via the Embedding-wise Domain Gating, EDG, module) from modality alignment (via the Node-wise Discretization Retrieval, NDR, module) across different granularities (Section 3.2, Section 3.3)
EDG performs local semantic enrichment by adaptively infusing topology-aware cross-modal context using a Mixture-of-Experts mechanism (Section 3.2)
NDR constructs a Discretized Semantic Representation Space (DSRS) using text as the anchor modality to achieve global modality alignment (Section 3.3)

PLANET outperforms baselines including GCN, MMGCN, MGAT, GRACE, GraphMAE2, RiemannGFM, GFT, SAMGPT, and UniGraph2 on node classification, achieving 96.62% accuracy on RedditS (a 3.17-point gain) and 57.06% on Movies (a 5.92-point gain) (Table 1, Section 4.1)

PLANET achieves link-prediction MRR of 27.51 on Amazon-Sports and 27.62 on Goodreads-LP, and 81.93% accuracy on 10-shot few-shot node classification on the Grocery dataset (Table 2, Table 3, Section 4.1)

An ablation removing the MoE-based cross-modal extraction, topology-aware attention, DSRS quantization, or text-anchored alignment loss each degrades performance, confirming all four components contribute to PLANET's results (Table 4, Section 4.2)

eZAos1ZGdz.text: The paper introduces the Singing Head DeepFake (SHDF) dataset, constructed using rhythm-aware generative models, to extend audio-visual deepfake detection benchmarks beyond talking-head content into singing scenarios (abstract only)

The proposed Text-guided Audio-Visual Forgery Detection (T-AVFD) framework combines a facial authenticity pattern learner, which aligns facial features with textual descriptions, with a multi-modal differential weight learning module that adaptively weights audio-visual consistency signals (abstract only)
T-AVFD shows consistent improvements over existing baselines across both talking-head deepfake datasets and the new SHDF singing dataset (abstract only)
T-AVFD demonstrates strong robustness under diverse perturbations in both talking-head and singing audio-visual deepfake detection scenarios (abstract only)

I6W6cxVVts.text: Robust-U1 is trained in three sequential stages: supervised fine-tuning of a unified MLLM (BAGEL) to reconstruct clean images from corrupted ImageNet-C inputs using a rectified flow loss, reinforcement learning via Flow-GRPO with dual pixel-level SSIM and semantic CLIP-similarity rewards, and multimodal reasoning training that jointly analyzes corrupted and recovered images (Section 3.2)
On R-Bench, Robust-U1 achieves an overall score of 0.7398 across MCQ, VQA, and captioning tasks under three degradation levels, compared to 0.5017 for Robust-R1 (Table 1)

Under adversarial corruption on MMMB, MMStar, and RealWorldQA at 25%, 50%, and 100% corruption intensities, Robust-U1 consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, including 83.18 accuracy on MMMB at 100% corruption versus 78.48 for the BAGEL baseline, and 63.87 on MMStar versus 49.53 for Robust-R1 (Table 3)

An ablation on R-Bench removing the multimodal reasoning stage, the pixel-level reward (R_pix), or the semantic reward (R_sem) each reduces performance, confirming all three training components contribute to robustness (Table 4)

yopy1zxFFM.text: UniScale parameterizes the unified inference scaling decision space as (Model, Question Parallelism, Candidate Parallelism, Beam Size) and formulates adaptive scaling as a contextual multi-armed bandit problem (Section 2.1, Section 2.2).
UniScale uses LinUCB-based reward estimation over Transformer-encoded query-action representations, updated per round in O(d^2) time via the Sherman-Morrison formula (Section 3).
Path-Aware Early Exiting reduces computational cost by 87.26% at the cost of only 0.91 percentage points of accuracy (Table 4).

In Quality-Priority mode, UniScale reaches 57.37 percentage points accuracy at 1374.7 eFLOPs, while in Cost-Sensitive mode it reaches 46.50 percentage points accuracy at 49.4 eFLOPs, outperforming k-NN, NeuralUCB, Thompson Sampling and Greedy baselines (Table 2).
Adding action semantic representation features reduces cumulative regret at 210 steps from 38.24 to 33.98 in Quality-Priority mode (Table 3).

Dense verification feedback improves Quality-Priority accuracy from 51.88% to 57.50% (a 5.62pp gain) while cutting cost by 51.3% relative to binary correctness signals, evaluated on AIME'24, AIME'25 and MATH-500 (Table 5).

xyKr7qopq6.text: ECMRNet's Stage-wise Channel Group Expansion (SCGE) freezes historical parameters and appends isomorphic group-convolution channel groups per stage to give strict parameter isolation for new degradations (Section 3.1).

Structural Entropy Pruning (SEP) uses two-dimensional structural entropy minimization to remove redundant channel groups, retaining only groups exceeding a frequency threshold rho=0.1 over a sample pool of N=300 (Section 3.2).
ECMRNet achieves average PSNR of 30.36 dB on HM-TIR and 29.06 dB on M3FD, with SSIM of 0.907 and 0.929 respectively, across 3 single and 4 compound thermal-infrared degradation tasks (Table 1).
Ablations show removing SCGE drops PSNR/SSIM by 4.15 dB/0.056, while SEP alone yields a 29.5% parameter reduction and 24.9% FLOP reduction with minimal performance loss (Table 3).
The full model uses 19.40M parameters and about 297.97G FLOPs for compound degradations, versus only 2.95M-3.22M parameters (72.03-76.12G FLOPs) for single degradations (Figure 5).

lbRi2aAWL7.text: VideoVeritas achieves 88.8% average accuracy across AI-generated video detection benchmarks, outperforming BusterX++ by 11.8 points on GenBuster++ (93.1% vs 77.1%) (Table 1).

The MintVid dataset comprises 33K videos from 99 generators, spanning general content (1.5K videos from 6 proprietary generators), facial deepfakes (2K videos from 3 human-centric models), and a fact-based subset of 200+ real/fake videos from social platforms (Section 3).

Perception Pretext Reinforcement Learning trains on spatiotemporal grounding/tracking with IoU-based rewards and self-supervised object counting before AIGC detection fine-tuning on 10K samples (Section 3).

Joint DPO training improves fact-based reasoning accuracy to 94.6%, while pure RL alone reaches only 69.1% on MintVid-Others compared to 79.2% with the full response-level and video-level alignment approach (Table 3).

VideoVeritas is compared against binary detectors (DeMamba, D3, NSG-VD, ReStraV), generic MLLMs (Qwen, Gemini, InternVL variants), and MLLM-based detectors (BusterX++, Skyra-RL), with a reported 15.1% averaged gain over the previous best method (Table 1).

KfDXKFFzze.text: For stochastic linear bandits with parameter noise on general action sets of size K and dimension d, the paper proves a regret upper bound of tilde-O(sqrt(dT log(K/delta)) * sigma_max^2) over horizon T (Section on main results / regret upper bound theorem).
A matching regret lower bound of tilde-Omega(d sqrt(T) * sigma_max^2) is established, tight up to logarithmic factors when log(K) is approximately d (lower bound theorem).

For l_p unit ball action sets with p<=2 (dual norm q), the minimax regret is characterized as Theta-tilde(sqrt(dT) * sigma_q^2), substantially better than the d*sqrt(T) regret of the classic additive noise model (minimax regret theorem, l_p unit ball case).
The paper shows that a simple explore-then-exploit algorithm achieves the optimal regret bounds up to logarithmic factors under the parameter noise model (algorithmic contribution section).

uyizpRy7kS.text: Under a spiked covariance model Q = I_d + lambda*v*v^T with the spike orthogonal to the signal, gradient descent on a two-layer squared-activation network suffers 'variance-induced misalignment' where the high-variance nuisance direction is multiplicatively amplified during an early stage of training, degrading signal recovery (Section 3.1, Theorem 4.3).

Theorem 4.1 shows spectral gradient descent (SpecGD) has a dimension-independent Stage I duration T_1 = O(1), with signal, spike, and bulk coefficients all growing uniformly and quadratically in the step index (Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 4.2 shows SpecGD's Stage II drives the signal coefficient to Theta(1) while nuisance coefficients saturate at O((1+lambda)^-1) and O(d^-1), so alignment converges to 1-o(1) (Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 4.3 shows plain gradient descent's Stage I lasts T-tilde_1 = O((eta-tilde * lambda)^-1 log d), logarithmically slower than SpecGD, with the spike coefficient growing exponentially as (1+Omega(eta-tilde))^k (Theorem 4.3).
Figure 2 shows SpecGD's final alignment remains robust across a range of learning rates, whereas plain gradient descent fails to align under strong anisotropy (Figure 2).

LYBs6f3jlK.text: The paper introduces tractable probabilistic proposal distributions (P-GCD) for locally constrained decoding that encode both logical constraint information and probabilistic model information about the target distribution (Section 3).

Theoretical results (Theorem 4.1-4.4) establish bias bounds and convergence guarantees showing that proposals derived from the method converge to the true constrained target distribution using significantly fewer particles than prior locally constrained decoding (LCD) proposals (Section 4).
Constraints expressed as finite automata are tensorized so that the proposal computation can be executed efficiently on GPUs, as described in the method's procedural description (Algorithm 1).

Experiments on constrained generation benchmarks including CommonGen and JSON-schema-constrained generation compare the proposed method against baseline constrained decoding approaches (Section 5, Tables 3-5).
Performance comparisons across constrained decoding scenarios show the proposed approach reduces bias while maintaining constraint satisfaction relative to baselines (Tables 3-5, Figures 1-2).

rso6Nr7Noz.text: General Covariant Action Modeling (GAM) constructs action manifolds via spatio-temporal decoupling, combining a temporal decomposition component with a general covariance formulation to expand sparse demonstration data into continuous valid action manifolds (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
The framework is compared against geometry-agnostic baselines including vision-language-action approaches in the lineage of RT-X, Octo, and OpenVLA (Section 2).
An integration mechanism combines the spatio-temporal manifold representation with policy learning for downstream action generation (Section 3.4).
Benchmark comparisons across robotic manipulation tasks report GAM's transfer and robustness performance relative to baseline methods (Tables 4, 5, 8, 9).
Qualitative visualizations of the constructed action manifolds and their generalization behavior are shown alongside the quantitative benchmark results (Figures 3, 6, 7).

FQLxcBsKIb.text: LU-KV formulates task-agnostic KV cache eviction as a global combinatorial optimization problem that predicts each token's future utility and allocates head-level cache budgets via a convex-hull relaxation with a marginal-utility-based greedy solver (Section 3, Equations 5-10).
The method explicitly models heterogeneity across attention heads, where some heads' cache utility is driven by instantaneous (local) contribution and others by long-horizon dependencies (Section 3).

A data-driven offline profiling protocol is used to estimate head-level utility statistics prior to deployment, enabling practical task-agnostic cache eviction without per-task retraining (Section 4).
The method is compared against prior KV cache eviction baselines including H2O, SnapKV, AdaKV, KeyDiff, CriticalKV, DefensiveKV, and KVZip (Section 2, Table 3).

Evaluations on LongBench, RULER, and RepoBench benchmarks report that the method achieves near-optimal precision in budget allocation and consistent gains over the H2O baseline across tasks (Table 4, Tables 7, 15-24).

fyM0jbe5DK.text: SPARD combines a gradient-based Safety Projection step that constrains fine-tuning updates within a safe parameter subspace with a Relevance-Diversity Data Selection step that balances task relevance and diversity when choosing fine-tuning samples (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).
SPARD is evaluated against harmful fine-tuning attacks on Llama-2, Qwen, and Llama-3.2 models, measuring both attack success rate and downstream task accuracy (Section 4).

SPARD achieves the lowest average attack success rate compared against state-of-the-art defense baselines across four harmful fine-tuning attack scenarios, while maintaining task accuracy on GSM8K and OpenBookQA (Section 4, Figure 2).
Comparative results across baseline defenses and model configurations are reported in a series of accuracy and attack-resilience tables (Tables 3, 4, 5, 7-9, 11, 16-19).

YRq8IIgDMy.text: CameraNoise is a flow-to-noise warping method that encodes camera motion into a temporally coherent stochastic representation, embedding camera poses directly into the diffusion noise space rather than injecting numerical camera parameters into the diffusion backbone (abstract only).

The method introduces a Geometry-guided Reprojection Flow together with a noise warping algorithm that jointly preserve the Gaussian prior of the diffusion process and ensure consistent noise propagation under camera transformations (abstract only).

By decoupling motion from scene appearance while preserving trajectory dynamics, CameraNoise avoids the structural distortions reported for prior methods that directly inject numerical camera parameters (abstract only).
Extensive experiments reported in the paper show the approach significantly outperforms prior camera-control methods in both visual quality and trajectory faithfulness (abstract only).

Vw10TpuFCp.text: Weight-sparse transformers trained with enforced weight and activation sparsity (via top-k magnitude masking) yield task circuits that are roughly 16-fold smaller than circuits extracted from dense models at comparable pretraining loss (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

A pruning algorithm that learns binary node/edge masks via sigmoid-derivative surrogate gradients isolates a complete string-closing circuit containing exactly 12 nodes and 9 edges, comprising two neurons and one attention head (Section 3.2.1, Figure 4).

The bracket-nesting-depth task is solved by a three-step circuit: an embedding-level open-bracket detector, a layer-2 attention head that averages detections, and a layer-4 attention head that thresholds the aggregated signal, and this circuit is vulnerable to a 'context dilution' adversarial attack that also degrades dense models (Section 3.2.2, Figure 5, Figure 8).

Increasing total nonzero parameters while holding sparsity level fixed improves both capability and interpretability along a Pareto frontier, whereas increasing sparsity at fixed parameter count trades capability for interpretability, and scaling sparse models beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters while preserving interpretability remains an open challenge (Section 3.1, Figure 3, Section 5).

Interpretability comes at substantial computational cost: weight-sparse training and inference require roughly 100-1000x more compute than equivalent dense models, and unstructured sparsity is incompatible with GPU tensor-core acceleration (Appendix B, Section 5).

Encoder/decoder 'bridge' modules that couple a weight-sparse model's representations to a dense model's activations enable interpretable perturbations, such as editing the closing-quote-type feature, to be transferred into and successfully steer the dense model's behavior (Section 3.3, Section 2.3, Figure 9).

J4k8q8nku1.text: Learn-to-Ask reformulates long-horizon proactive dialogue reinforcement learning as supervised learning by extracting hindsight ground-truth information goals and stopping decisions from the observed future of each offline expert trajectory (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).

The grounded reward combines a micro-reward for question quality (scored 0.0, 0.5, or 1.0 against the inferred target information set) with a macro-reward for correct continue/stop decisions, fused multiplicatively so strategic stopping errors dominate the signal (Section 3.6).

On the RealMedConv offline evaluation, training Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Learn-to-Ask more than triples targeted-question precision (WA-GH) from 0.13 to 0.41 and raises stopping accuracy (WS) from 0.16 to 0.93 relative to the base model (Section 4.2, Table 1).
Applied to Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on RealMedConv, Learn-to-Ask improves WA-GH from 0.13 to 0.37 and WS from 0.52 to 0.88, indicating the method's gains hold across model scales (Section 4.2, Table 1).

In real-world production deployment on a medical AI service, the Learn-to-Ask-trained 32B model achieves a 93% information-completeness rate, an 88% good-question rate, and a 1.87x conversion-rate lift over the internal expert baseline under professional audit (Section 5).

An Automated Prompt Calibration pipeline iteratively searches extractor, grader, and policy-sampler prompts against human-verified anchor sets to construct the hindsight reward pipeline with minimal manual annotation (Section 3.5).

W6qfbvysDh.text: AnyEdit++ introduces Bayes-Chunk, a segmentation mechanism that identifies semantic boundaries in long-form text based on Bayesian Surprise rather than fixed-size windows, for use in sequential knowledge editing (abstract only).

Interference between edited segments is minimized when anchor keys are geometrically orthogonal, a property that Bayesian-Surprise-derived chunk boundaries satisfy but conventional fixed-window chunking does not (abstract only).

Placing knowledge updates at semantic 'peaks' identified via Bayesian Surprise provides better causal locality and control over the edit's effect than placing updates at arbitrary segment divisions (abstract only).

AnyEdit++ achieves superior performance and robustness compared to state-of-the-art long-form knowledge editing baselines across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and narrative-generation tasks (abstract only).

FAjA0snAYq.text: E-mem replaces conventional memory preprocessing/compression with episodic context reconstruction, using a heterogeneous hierarchical architecture in which multiple assistant agents each maintain uncompressed memory contexts while a central master agent handles global planning (abstract only).

Assistant agents in E-mem perform local reasoning within activated memory segments and extract contextual evidence before aggregation by the master agent, rather than relying on passive retrieval (abstract only).
E-mem achieves an F1 score of over 54% on the LoCoMo benchmark, exceeding the prior state-of-the-art method GAM by 7.75 percentage points (abstract only).
