E-mem reduces token cost by more than 70% compared to baseline memory methods while achieving these accuracy gains (abstract only).

FIq3e9ffEZ.text: HALD (Hard Label for Alleviating Local semantic Drift) integrates hard labels alongside soft labels as corrective anchors during dataset distillation to counteract semantic drift that arises when the number of image crops used with soft labels is reduced (abstract only).

HALD achieves 42.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K while requiring only 285MB of soft-label storage, a 100x reduction in storage compared to prior soft-label-based distillation methods (abstract only).
HALD outperforms the prior state-of-the-art method LPLD by 9.0 percentage points in accuracy on ImageNet-1K (abstract only).

The paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that hybridizing hard and soft label supervision restores alignment between visual content and semantic labels under limited-crop conditions (abstract only).

XOYXLQRlj8.text: Standard EMA teachers exhibit inherent collapse, with KL divergence between teacher and student decaying steadily throughout training while the WMA teacher maintains a higher, stable KL divergence across the entire training horizon (Figure 5).

Theorem 3.4 shows the WMA teacher's projection onto the task subspace converges to W*_FT P_I, giving bias-free convergence in the task subspace that eliminates static self-distillation's anchor bias while preserving orthogonal (pretrained) knowledge.
On CLIP ViT-B/16 finetuned on ImageNet, TRACER achieves an average OOD accuracy of 64.07% versus 62.54% for CaRot and 59.91% for LP-FT, with gains including IN-A 54.92% vs 51.57% for CaRot (Table 1).

On ViT-L/14, TRACER attains 75.32% average OOD accuracy with an ECE of 0.0732, outperforming CaRot's 74.13% OOD accuracy, demonstrating consistency across ResNet50, ViT-B/16, and ViT-L/14 backbones (Table 3).

In a synthetic ColoredMNIST spurious-correlation setting, TRACER's dynamic (WMA) distillation reduces the forgetting rate to 0.1%, compared to 1.8% for static self-distillation, 13.6% for L2-SP, and 37.9% for direct finetuning (Section 5.1).

TRACER incurs only a 1.38x training-time overhead versus direct finetuning's 1.00x, cheaper than CaRot's 1.81x overhead, while still improving OOD accuracy by 1.53 percentage points over CaRot (Table 4).

eMiXzd5cyD.text: CB-SLICE's Error-Prone Concept Filtering step uses an Expected Change in Target Prediction (ECTP) score, computed class-wise to address class imbalance, to identify concepts most responsible for model failures (Section 3.1).

CB-SLICE forms error slices by clustering erroneous samples in concept-logit space with a Gaussian Mixture Model plus auxiliary losses encouraging semantic coherence, and explains slices via an Expected Change in Slice Assignment (ECSA) metric that surfaces keyword-concepts (Sections 3.2-3.3).
CB-SLICE is benchmarked against Domino, GEORGE, HiBug2, Spotlight, and K-Means on Waterbirds, CelebA, MetaShift, and MNIST-Sum (Section 5.2).

On the Sequential CBM variant, CB-SLICE attains Precision@10 of 0.95±0.05 on MNIST-Sum, 0.92±0.04 on CelebA, 0.82±0.03 on MetaShift, and 0.78±0.07 on Waterbirds, outperforming the baseline methods (Table 1).
CB-SLICE's Matched Ground-Truth Group Frequency (MGF), measuring slice homogeneity, reaches 0.9±0.02 on MNIST-Sum and 0.76±0.04 on MetaShift under the Sequential CBM setting (Table 1, Section 6).

1uU7X9zzJB.text: Active-o3 trains its active perception (sensing) policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a KL-regularization coefficient of β=0.04, via a pure reinforcement learning objective with no supervised sensing labels (Section 4.2, Equation 2).

On the LVIS open-world benchmark (10,000 training / 1,200 validation images), Active-o3 improves over Qwen2.5-VL-CoT by +1.0 APs and +2.8 ARs on LVIS-small, and by +2.7 APs and +3.5 ARs on LVIS-dense (Table 1, Section 5.2).

On the domain-specific SODA-D (autonomous driving, 24,828 images) and SODA-A (aerial imagery, 2,513 images) benchmarks, Active-o3 improves over Qwen2.5-VL-CoT by +13.0 APs / +17.5 ARs on SODA-D and +8.5 APs / +8.9 ARs on SODA-A (Table 2, Section 5.3).

Active-o3 is further evaluated on fine-grained segmentation via the ThinObjects dataset (Section 5.4) and demonstrates zero-shot generalization of its region-selection reasoning on the V* benchmark (Figure 1).

jbm51tk6eI.text: The Side-by-Side (SxS) interleaved reasoning framework formalizes a dual-channel action space where the model chooses at each step between a private "think" action and a user-visible "speak" action within the same token stream (Sections 2.2-2.3, 3).

Supervised fine-tuning constructs entailment-aligned interleaved trajectories via Algorithm 1, matching answer prefixes to reasoning prefixes using an entailment predicate with delimiter-based segmentation (Section 3.1).
The disclosure policy is further optimized with GRPO using outcome-based rewards, with an optional correctness-preserving shaping term solved via quadratic programming (Section 3.2, Appendix C).

On Qwen3-4B, the RL-final SxS model reaches 80.0% accuracy on AIME25 while reducing Average Inter-Response Wait (AIRW) from 21,316 to 8,519 tokens (~60% reduction), and 49.3% accuracy on GPQA-Diamond with AIRW reduced from 16,338 to 7,738 tokens (~53% reduction) (Table 1).

On Qwen3-30B-A3B, SxS attains 79.2% accuracy on AIME25 (AIRW reduced from 16,709 to 13,829 tokens) and 57.1% accuracy on GPQA-Diamond (AIRW reduced from 13,773 to 9,468 tokens), with additional accuracy-latency trade-off results reported on LiveCodeBench and KOR-Bench (Tables 1, 2, 5-7).

70u0Cbdkd5.text: The In-Context Sparse Attention (ISA) mechanism comprises pre-selection pruning via pooling attention (Equations 1-2), block-wise 0-th order Taylor sparse attention using compressed key-value means (Equations 3-4), and grouped computation that routes high-error queries to full attention (Section 3).

Theorem 3.1 (Appendix F) establishes that ISA's approximation error correlates with a query sharpness metric M_u, which is used to dynamically decide per-query routing between sparse and full attention.

ISA reduces attention-module latency by approximately 60% versus standard SDPA and FlashAttention v2/3, yielding roughly a 1.47x end-to-end speedup at sequence lengths scaling from 5K to 50K tokens (Introduction, Figure 2).

On EditVerseBench (200 video-instruction pairs across 20 categories), LIVEditor-14B with ISA scores 7.89 quality versus 7.65 for the EditVerse baseline, alongside 27.19 text alignment and 24.55 temporal consistency (Table 1).
Against alternative sparse-attention variants (Radial, Sparge, STA, SWA, VSA), ISA surpasses all on quality metrics while achieving a 1.47x speedup relative to full attention (Table 2).

LIVEditor-14B also attains a total score of 0.67 on IVE-Bench (600 videos, 35 subcategories), matching top performers across Video Quality, Instruction Compliance, and Fidelity metrics, and is further evaluated on the 140-video, 8-subtask VIE-Bench (Tables 4, 13, 14).

si8F5lk6Kg.text: Causal-Adapter injects causal semantic attributes into a frozen text-to-image diffusion model via Prompt-Aligned Injection (PAI), which maps attributes to learnable token embeddings, avoiding full retraining (Section on method / PAI component).

On the synthetic Pendulum dataset, adding the Conditioned Token Contrastive (CTC) loss reduces the light-intervention effectiveness MAE by about 91%, from 0.434 to 0.041 (Table results, Pendulum dataset).
On CelebA, Causal-Adapter reduces the LPIPS composition metric by about 86% (0.122 to 0.017) and the FID realism score by about 58% (27.861 to 8.509) compared to baselines (CelebA results table).
On the ADNI brain MRI dataset with 6 mixed attributes, Causal-Adapter reduces ventricular volume intervention MAE by about 50% and FID by about 87% relative to baselines (ADNI results table).

Causal-Adapter is compared against CausalVAE, DisDiffAE, and CausalDiffAE on synthetic data, and against VAE, HVAE, and GAN baselines on real-world image datasets, across effectiveness, composition, realism, and minimality (CLD) metrics (evaluation section).

An ablation shows that adding PAI alone to a plain adapter improves the effectiveness F1-score by 11.6%, with the further addition of the CTC loss yielding additional disentanglement gains while keeping FID stable (ablation study, Section on ablations).

fDlpwEHT4z.text: REAL introduces the REAL-VQA dataset, built from Wikipedia with GPT-4o using criteria of high multi-hop complexity, common-property focus, and knowledge-deficit induction, containing 4,149 training and 629 test samples (Section on REAL-VQA dataset construction).

RPA-SFT (Reasoning-Pivot Aware SFT) trains models with token-level pivot perception using special <RPivot> markers and a sequential extraction-then-verification procedure to prevent shortcut learning on conflict detection (Section on RPA-SFT method).

RPGD (Reasoning-Pivot Guided Decoding) is a training-free inference method combining Patch Shuffle, Adaptive Gating (baseline epsilon=0.1, temperature kappa=0.1), and Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to isolate conflict-aligned representation components (Section on RPGD method).

REAL improves accuracy by +3.8% on E-VQA and +1.6% on InfoSeek over prior state-of-the-art retrieval-augmented baselines (EchoSight, Wiki-LLAVA, ReflectiVA, mKG-RAG, VLM-PRF) (Results tables, E-VQA and InfoSeek benchmarks).

On the REAL-VQA conflict-discrimination test set using Qwen3-VL-8B, the method achieves MCC of 98.1 and F1 of 99.1, and generalizes to the unseen MMKC benchmark with MCC 52.9 and F1 74.8 (Conflict discrimination results table).

RPGD adds only about 1.3x the inference latency of standard greedy decoding while improving accuracy by 2.4-3.3% across model scales, outperforming decoding baselines VCD and CAD (Section on computational cost / decoding comparison).

aqoXbXzxlV.text: Proposition 1 (Section 4.1) links SGD's implicit regularization to input curvature, showing higher learning rates yield flatter parameter minima that transfer to reduced input curvature and more robust gradient-based attributions (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).

Proposition 2 (Section 5) shows that under softmax normalization, attention-based attribution robustness is bounded by the minimum attainable entropy of the attention distribution, limiting robustness gains regardless of curvature regularization (Section 5, Proposition 2).

Replacing softmax attention with unnormalized kernel-based attention (using a GELU activation) restores the implicit robustness gains from curvature regularization in transformer models (Section 5, Figure 3).

On Imagenette, implicit curvature regularization (ICR) achieves 83±2% accuracy and robustness score R=0.10±0.2 on ResNet-50, and 73±1% accuracy with R=0.07±0.02 on ViT-B/16 (Section 6, Figure 2 / Table 1).

ICR achieves competitive attribution robustness at roughly 1x training cost, compared to explicit curvature regularization (ECR) which requires about 4x the training overhead (Section 6, Figure 2, Table 1).

efx3dOgAYw.text: VidLaDA replaces autoregressive decoding with a bidirectional diffusion language model for video understanding, using a SigLip2-SO400M vision encoder with 2x2 spatial pooling and a three-stage training curriculum scaling from 32-frame clips to 2-30+ minute long-form videos (Section on architecture and training curriculum).
On Video-MME, VidLaDA scores 64.1 versus 63.9 for Qwen2.5-VL and 63.7 for LLaVA-Video, and it scores 53.4 on MLVU versus 45.3 for Qwen2.5-VL and 50.4 for LLaVA-Video (Table 1).
VidLaDA outperforms diffusion-language-model baselines on Video-MME, scoring 64.1 versus 56.4 for LLaDA-V (8B) and 60.8 for SDAR-VL (Table 1).

MARS-Cache combines frame-wise chunk attention (reducing visual-token attention complexity from quadratic to linear) with asynchronous cache refreshing, achieving over 12x inference speedup (33.6 vs. 2.7 tokens/second) without accuracy loss (Table 2, MARS-Cache section).

Proposition 3.2 shows bidirectional decoding achieves strictly higher mutual information capacity between generated tokens and visual context than autoregressive decoding, formalized as a sum-of-suprema inequality (Section 3, Proposition 3.2).

In spatiotemporal robustness tests, when high-information video patches are relocated from the start to the end of the sequence, autoregressive baselines degrade by 20-30% while VidLaDA's accuracy remains largely invariant (Section on empirical validation / robustness tests).

YvGtYoFyud.text: StableDRL stabilizes GRPO training for masked diffusion language models using unconditional clipping that bounds importance ratios strictly within [1-epsilon, 1+epsilon], combined with self-normalization that divides updates by the sum of clipped ratios rather than a fixed group size (Methodology section).
On MATH500, StableDRL achieves 41.8% average accuracy across generation lengths {128, 256, 512}, surpassing the SPG baseline by +5.2% at the 256-token budget (Table 1).
On AIME 2024, StableDRL reaches 16.7% accuracy under static sampling, exceeding the Qwen3-8B baseline's 10.0% (Table 2).
On GSM8K, StableDRL obtains 84.2% average accuracy while maintaining robustness across all decoding lengths tested (Experiments section).

On the Countdown task, StableDRL shows a +13.7% gain at 256 tokens, reaching 84.4% accuracy, addressing off-policy drift issues that affect baselines such as D1, WD1, UniGRPO, and ESPO (Experiments section, Countdown results).

The Exploding Weight Stress Test shows StableDRL remains stable under artificially amplified importance-weight variance, whereas the ESPO baseline exhibits immediate and catastrophic collapse under the same adversarial conditions (Figure 5).

zrn7rRuvhW.text: In the zero-temperature (hardmax) limit of self-attention dynamics with negative-definite key-query interaction, token updates coincide with a Frank-Wolfe step on a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the tokens, and Theorem 3.1 gives a linear convergence rate bound J^t(x_i^{t+1}) ≤ (2/(t+1))·λ_max(B_0)·diam(K^0)^2 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

When the key-query matrix is positive definite, Theorem 4.2 shows super-exponential convergence of tokens to vertices, and Proposition 4.5 shows the induced cell structure coincides with B-norm Voronoi cells when vertices have equal norm (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.5).
Theorem 4.8 establishes well-posedness of the singular ODE limit governing the hardmax dynamics (Section 4, Theorem 4.8, Equation 4.4).

At finite inverse temperature β, Theorem 5.2 shows interior particles reach near-vertex configurations in O(1) steps with high probability, while Theorem 5.4 shows these metastable configurations persist for exponentially long times (on the order of e^β steps) before eventual collapse to a single cluster (Section 5, Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.4).

Lemma 2.1 shows the argmax operation generically produces a singleton, and Lemma 2.2 shows the convex hull of tokens shrinks under step sizes γ^t ∈ (0,1), underpinning the Frank-Wolfe reformulation of hardmax attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2).

hz9iYayl8F.text: Section 3 shows existing group-fairness criteria such as MGO/EGO are brittle: satisfying their proportion-based constraints permits arbitrarily unbalanced conditional generation quality across sensitive groups (Section 3).

Section 4 defines δ-Equalized Generative Treatment (EGT), requiring |D_f(P_a||Q_a) - D_f(P_a'||Q_a')| ≤ δ for any two sensitive groups a, a', where D_f is an f-divergence between real and generated conditional distributions (Section 4, Definition 4.1).

Section 4.2 proposes solving min_Q max_{a∈A} D_f(P_a||Q_a) via min-max fine-tuning, arguing this objective aligns with minimizing EGT disparities by coupling overall quality to the worst-served group (Section 4.2).
On FFHQ with an EDM-VP diffusion backbone, min-max fine-tuning reduces the δ-precision-recall gap across sensitive groups from 2.2% to 0.3% (Table 1).

On the Wikipedia Biographies text-generation task, min-max fine-tuning yields consistent EGT-disparity reductions across multiple LLM backbones, outperforming conditional-training and reweighted-loss baselines (Table 2, Section 5).

TwhC4mNuse.text: SAGE achieves an average accuracy improvement of 8.52 percentage points over prior methods across five benchmarks—CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Food-101, SVHN, and STL-10—under universal semi-supervised learning settings (Section 4).

On CIFAR-10 under an arbitrary (mismatched labeled/unlabeled) distribution setting, SAGE reaches 61.24% accuracy versus 50.24% for the CPG baseline, an 11.00-point gain; on SVHN it reaches 84.11% versus roughly 60% for prior approaches (Section 4, Table 2-type results).

Simplex equiangular tight frame vectors, constructed via QR decomposition to be unit-norm, equiangular, and centered at the origin, serve as fixed coordinate anchors that guide inter-class representation separation via Graph-state Relational Inference (GRI) (Section 3, Equation 5).
Distribution-agnostic Reliability Prioritization (DRP) weights pseudo-labels using max-confidence and top-two margin scores passed through a truncated Gaussian kernel (Section 3, Equation 6).

Ablation on CIFAR-10/100 shows the auxiliary branch alone contributes +4.02 points, adding DRP contributes +5.43 points, and the full SAGE model with GRI yields a cumulative +12.33-point improvement over the base model (Table 4).

6ctopuLHAy.text: In the sparse-sensor regime (300 observations), GenDA reduces relative RMSE by 25-27% compared to supervised GNN baselines and by approximately 14% compared to the classical LCSVD baseline (Section 3.1, Table 1).
At 3000 sensor observations, GenDA attains RRMSE of 0.190±0.054 versus 0.382-0.354 for GNN baselines, SSIM of 0.877±0.020, and mean cosine similarity of 0.977±0.023 (Table 1).
Across tested meshes, GenDA increases the structural similarity index (SSIM) by 23-33% relative to baseline methods (Section 3.1, Table 1).

GenDA generalizes to unseen urban geometries (held-out altitude slices) and across 360 distinct wind inflow directions without retraining, and its multiscale architecture supports varying mesh resolutions (Section 3.2, Section 2.1).
Section 3.2 shows GenDA's performance is robust to the choice of sensor sampling strategy used to place the 300-8000 observation points (Section 3.2, Table 2).

XPO9lrZ9Ge.text: One-Way Policy Optimization (OWPO) implements Accelerated Alignment, upweighting gradients (weight > 1) when the policy lags the reference model along the verifier-specified direction, and Gain Locking, downweighting gradients (weight < 1) when the policy surpasses the reference, per Section 3.1's Directional Deviation formulation (Section 3.1).

Lemma 4.1 shows OWPO implements a directionally regularized policy gradient with effective progress coefficient g(δ) ≥ ε_low > 0, which prevents the direction reversal that occurs under symmetric KL regularization (Section 4, Lemma 4.1).

On Qwen-2.5 math benchmarks, OWPO achieves a 3.88 percentage-point average improvement over baselines, compared to DAPO's 40.56% average, OPD's 40.64% average (plateauing near the reference model), and MOPD's marginal +0.93% gain (Section 5).
On Qwen-3-8B, OWPO reaches 51.90% average accuracy versus MOPD's 46.40% (Section 5).
Under iterative bootstrapping/self-evolution, OWPO reaches approximately 40% accuracy within 4 iterations, whereas MOPD requires 6 iterations to reach only approximately 37% (Section 5).

QZlNaWuxO6.text: Diffusion models exhibit an inherent deficiency in reconstructing high-frequency information, with failed membership-inference samples showing member-data high-frequency content averaging 0.598-0.632 versus 0.413-0.517 for hold-out data (Table 1).
A plug-and-play high-frequency filter module added to the Naive attack on DDIM improves attack success rate by +5.38% and AUC by +4.49% (Table 3).
The filter module boosts SecMI's average AUC by +5.59% and improves PIA's TPR@1%FPR by +11.80% on Tiny-ImageNet (Table 3).
On Stable Diffusion with MS-COCO, the Naive+Filter attack reaches 93.60% AUC (+10.01% average improvement) and 41.99% TPR@1%FPR, with up to +51.01% TPR@1%FPR gain on Flickr (Table 4).
The module integrates into existing membership-inference attacks within the general paradigm while adding only approximately 5-6% time overhead (Table 14).
An ablation over the filter's radius and scale parameters shows optimal performance at rt in [3,10] and s in [0.0,0.3] (Table 6).

BhF4ZrIqu8.text: PolicyGuard achieves an average AUROC of 0.856 for perturbation-based attacks and 0.859 for adversary-agent attacks across seven RL games (Table 1).
Detection performance against the Q-Inception backdoor attack ranges from AUROC 0.843 to 0.864 (Table 2).

The method uses adaptive Gaussian Process posterior variance for step-level uncertainty quantification, with Theorem 3.1 providing a posterior variance bound and Corollary 3.2 showing variance converges to zero for benign trajectory pairs (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2).
An ablation study examines sensitivity to patch size, trigger length, pseudo-trajectory size, and random perturbations (Figure 4).
PolicyGuard is evaluated for robustness under adaptive attacks with varying poisoning rates (Figure 5).
Inference latency of the two-phase detection approach is compared against baselines (Figure 3, Section 3.1).

SwGwmKIgUb.text: ProphetKV retains 96%-101% of full-prefill accuracy while using only a 20% recomputation ratio across evaluated models (Section 5.2, Figure 8).
ProphetKV improves accuracy over state-of-the-art selective recomputation methods by 8.8%-24.9% on RULER and 18.6%-50.9% on LongBench (Table 1).
ProphetKV achieves up to a 5x speedup over full recomputation at a 20% recomputation ratio, measured via time-to-first-token across context lengths (Table 2, Section 5.3).
ProphetKV's query-driven token selection reaches a given decoding-stage attention overlap at a 0.04 recomputation ratio, versus 0.06 for CacheBlend, roughly 33% more efficient (Figure 4).
An ablation study isolates the effect of the fused value function on selection accuracy (Figure 7, Section 5.4).

CwNItJ07ew.text: CausalRM achieves 70.1% in-distribution pairwise accuracy on mathematical reasoning tasks versus 68.3% for the GoalRM baseline, and 85.6% average out-of-distribution accuracy, a 2.6% improvement (Table 1).
In downstream RLHF on mathematical reasoning, policies trained with CausalRM reach 74.0% average accuracy versus 72.5% for GoalRM, with a 1.1% OOD improvement over baselines (Table 2).
On RLHF dialogue tasks, CausalRM achieves a 54.8% pairwise win rate against a Standard Bradley-Terry reward model and a 51.3% average win rate under out-of-distribution evaluation (Table 3).
CausalRM shows only a -1.7% drop in in-distribution accuracy on datasets constructed to induce sycophantic reward hacking, compared to an -11.4% degradation for the Standard RM baseline (Table 4).
CausalRM exhibits reduced sensitivity to response length, with a length-bias coefficient sigma_len of 0.03 versus 0.22 for baseline reward models (Figure 5).
The framework is compared against Standard RM, GoalRM, and InfoRM baselines using a causal graph formulation of reward modeling (Section 3, Figure 1, Figure 2).

pxN9ZXdBhV.text: The agentic pipeline achieves 80.5% overall accuracy on the MindCube-Tiny benchmark for spatial reasoning, surpassing the previous best method by 5.3 accuracy points and the MindCube baseline by 9.8 points (Table 1).
On the challenging Rotation subset, the method reaches 85.0% accuracy, outperforming the best competing method by 29.5 accuracy points, a 53.2% relative improvement (Table 1).

The approach constructs a dynamic cognitive map parameterizing scene layout as object positions and orientations, combined with Spatial Assertion Codes (SAC)-Python expressions that programmatically describe spatial relationships (Section 4).
An ablation study evaluates the contributions of the perception pipeline, reward components, and memory mechanism to overall performance (Table 2).
Cognitive map resolution is varied and compared for its effect on downstream spatial reasoning accuracy (Table 4).
The method is also evaluated on the EmbodiedBench benchmark to test generalization beyond MindCube (Table 5).

s24mdN60i5.text: TDKPS embeds agents across timepoints and applies agent-level and group-level hypothesis tests to detect behavioral perspective shifts in black-box multi-agent systems (Section 2, Section 3).

On a real dataset of 99 digital congresspersons queried over 14 timepoints (2018-2024), TDKPS detects a significant behavioral shift on public health queries (Kendall's tau = 0.51, p = 0.014) concentrated around the COVID-19 onset period, while general political queries (tau = 0.34, p = 0.11) and orthogonal candy/chocolate queries (tau = 0.01, p = 0.956) show no significant shift (Section 3.1, Figure 4).

In simulation, TDKPS-based agent-level power tracks the oracle test closely and substantially exceeds a distance-correlation (DCorr) baseline, e.g. at effect size tau=0.2 power is about 0.60 for TDKPS versus under 0.15 for DCorr, while Type I error stays near the nominal alpha=0.05 (slightly inflated to 5-10%) (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

At the group level, the paired-embedding (PE) TDKPS test reaches greater than 95% power with 80 agents per group in simulation, and group-level p-values correlate strongly with agent-level p-values (tau = 0.62, p = 0.005) on the real congressperson data (Section 3.3, Figures 5-6).

TQi2IqvpIf.text: Independently pretrained time series, vision, and language encoders exhibit near-orthogonal geometry when embeddings are compared without any explicit cross-modal coupling or fine-tuning (Section 3, Section 4).

Across 34 evaluated trimodal encoder combinations spanning model sizes from 86M to 27B parameters, time series-image (TS-IMG) alignment consistently outperforms time series-text (TS-TXT) alignment, with TS-TXT remaining the weakest pairing in absolute terms at every model size (Section 4, Table 3).

Mutual k-nearest-neighbor overlap between modality pairs stays low, between 0.07 and 0.13, indicating weak local neighborhood alignment even as global geometric alignment (e.g., Procrustes disparity) improves with model scale (Section 4).

Doubling caption information density in the CaTS dataset (test information density from 416.81 to 870.2) yields only marginal improvements in alignment metrics, whereas MIMIC clinical reports have substantially lower information density (test ID = 149.48) than CaTS (Section 4, Table 1).

Cross-modal retrieval evaluated on MIMIC and CaTS in Table 2 shows image-text alignment achieves the strongest results, especially when using pretrained vision-language encoders, supporting images as effective intermediaries between time series and text (Section 4, Table 2).

iWJmW9mQpA.text: Label-Clustered Conformal Prediction (introduced in Section 4.1) substantially outperforms Mondrian CP on downstream substantive fairness, measured by lower maxROR (%) on the FACET dataset (Section 6, Figure 1, Table 1).

Equalizing set sizes across groups correlates strongly with improved substantive fairness outcomes, whereas equalizing coverage across groups often has a negative effect on substantive fairness (Section 6, Figures 2-3).

Backward CP, which constrains set size while relaxing coverage guarantees, achieves the lowest maxROR on some tasks but produces larger prediction sets than the other CP methods compared (Marginal, Mondrian, Label-Clustered, Group-Clustered CP) (Section 6, Table 1).

Theorem 4.1 decomposes the set-size disparity between demographic groups into three components (intra-cluster label homogeneity, cross-cluster spread, and intra-label cross-group disparity), proving that label clustering reduces the gap through these mechanisms (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

An LLM-in-the-loop evaluator reproduces the same qualitative maxROR ordering as human evaluators across FACET, BiosBias, and RAVDESS, with Mondrian CP consistently showing greater unfairness than Marginal CP (Section 6, Table 2).

ceErPsyO38.text: The model is trained on 33,919 nights of data from 28,394 individuals and reconstructs EEG spectrograms from respiration signals with an average MAE of 0.068+/-0.036 on the internal test set and 0.067+/-0.030 on an external dataset, with an average SNR of 14.1 dB (Section 4, Table 1, Table 2).
Synthesized EEG supports downstream age estimation with MAE 5.14 years versus 5.00 years for ground-truth EEG (Section 4, Table 3).

Synthesized EEG supports sex detection with AUROC 0.814 versus 0.819 for ground-truth EEG, and sleep-stage classification accuracy of 0.839 versus 0.882 for ground-truth EEG (Section 4, Table 4, Table 5).

The framework generalizes to contactless sensing: EEG synthesized from wireless radio-frequency reflections achieves MAE 0.076+/-0.027, and sleep staging from RF-derived EEG reaches 0.814 accuracy versus 0.827 using a breathing belt (Section 4, Table 6).

9hzK071Z3R.text: Monitorability gains during RLVR training are data-dependent: instruction-following training data produces the largest early-phase monitorability gains (0.06-0.17 g-mean^2 in steps 0-300), while gains shrink or reverse later in training (-0.04 to 0.09 g-mean^2 in steps 300-800) (Section 4, Table 2).

An 'IF Cascade' strategy of multi-domain pretraining followed by instruction-following fine-tuning yields the highest peak monitorability, reaching 0.639 g-mean^2 for Qwen3-4B and 0.566 g-mean^2 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (Section 4, Table 3).
Monitorability is largely orthogonal to capability: capability gains and capability-monitorability correlations are weak to negative across test domains (Section 4, Figure 3).

Distribution sharpening (entropy reduction) correlates with monitorability better than reasoning-to-answer dependence, with a negative entropy-monitorability correlation observed (e.g., r ~ -0.82 for MedQA on DeepSeek-R1) (Section 5, Figure 5).

Training-length and difficulty ablations show longer contexts and harder training data degrade monitorability: average g-mean^2 falls from 0.36 at 4096 tokens to 0.29 at 8192 tokens, and from 0.39 under easy training to 0.21 under hard training (Section 7, Table 4, Table 5).

JWWpV4StVf.text: Cubically Damped mSGD (CD) and iKFAD (Individual Kinetic Friction Adaptive Descent) match or beat Adam on test loss for TinyViT, DistilBERT (SST-2 and QNLI), and GPT2-Nano/XS, while both clearly outperform plain mSGD (Table 1).
On DistilBERT SST-2, CD attains a test loss of 0.268±0.009 versus 0.345±0.022 for mSGD and 0.299±0.012 for Adam (Table 1).

iKFAD achieves exponential convergence to the global minimum in continuous time for strongly convex objectives with bounded Hessian eigenvalues (Theorem 5.1), with a discrete-time analogue preserved for sufficiently small step sizes (Theorem 5.2).

CD preserves the same optimizer-state memory footprint as mSGD (2N states per parameter) while iKFAD/CADAM match Adam's 3N-state footprint, and both cubic-damping methods remain stable across a wide range of learning rates and friction coefficients (Section 6, Figure 7).

Introducing a cubic damping term proportional to momentum magnitude closes much of the empirical performance gap between momentum-only mSGD and adaptive per-parameter methods like Adam, without adding per-parameter learning rates (Section 3, Table 1).

jekfMVDRqz.text: Activation-based classifiers for LLM self-recognition achieve 99.16%-100% AUROC with prompts and 98.58%-99.99% AUROC in the prompt-agnostic setting, while perplexity-based baselines collapse to 32.33%-52.27% without prompts (Section 3.1, Table 1).

Steering internal residual-stream activations with a random sparse vector produces a detectable model fingerprint used for multi-model attribution, reaching F1 of 100% for Ministral-3-8B and 99.1% for Llama-3.1-8B in distinguishing two steered variants (Section 3.2, Table 2).

Sparse steering vectors (99.7% zero entries) yield a better quality-versus-detectability tradeoff than dense interventions, enabling watermark-like signals without noticeably degrading generated text quality (Section 3.4, Figure 4).

Cosine-similarity-based retrieval of the injected signature achieves 84.6% accuracy without any trained classifier, and retains 77.8% accuracy after the generated text is paraphrased (Section 3.5, Table 3).

PsCuRawx1I.text: Test-Time Control (TTC) layers embed a finite-horizon LQR optimal-control problem over latent states at inference, solved via backward Riccati recursion (Proposition 3.1) and reformulated for parallel hardware via a symplectic-matrix iteration (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.3).

The symplectic solver eliminates sequential matrix inversions and achieves over 10x higher throughput than Riccati- and KKT-based solvers when implemented as a fused CUDA kernel (Figure 3, Section 3.3).

On MATH-500, TTC-Net reaches 52.80% accuracy versus 47.80% for the GDN baseline, and on AIME 2024/2025 Pass@8 it reaches 20.00% versus 0% for the baseline, described as a 'performance emergence' (Table 2).
On AMC, TTC-Net attains 54.22% Pass@8 versus 46.98% for the baseline, consistent with the paper's reported 2-3x Pass@8 gains on AMC/AIME (Table 2).

Ablations show time-heterogeneous parameterization (52.80% vs. 48.40% homogeneous) and Poisson log-normal horizon sampling (52.80% vs. 50.80% uniform) each contribute to the accuracy gains, with an 8:1 attention-to-TTC-layer interleaving ratio found near-optimal (Table 3).
On Sudoku, TTC layers reach 93.40% board-level accuracy (multi-step) versus 90.40% for the Samba baseline, and 97.33% cell-level accuracy (Table 1).

SDyesowNUa.text: Cond-DP replaces the standard public embedding Θ^pub x^pub with a conditioned version Θ^pub C x^pub, where C is derived from the structure of public features, then applies DPSGD to the resulting loss (Algorithm 1).
Cond-DP satisfies (ε,δ)-differential privacy with noise variance σ² = Õ(M²T/ε²n²), incurring no additional privacy cost relative to standard DPSGD (Theorem 4.3).

For private linear regression, the conditioning matrix Ĉ = VΣ⁻¹Vᵀ built from the SVD of public features provably outperforms plain DPSGD when labels align with low singular-value directions of the feature matrix (Lemma 4.13).

On real-world linear regression tasks (Boston housing, wine, energy, CA housing datasets), Cond-DP outperforms both DPSGD and RR-on-Bins baselines across privacy budgets ε ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, ∞} (Section 5.2).

On the large-scale Criteo sponsored-search conversion benchmark (1.73M training examples), Cond-DP improves over DPSGD for linear models with the largest gains at ε ∈ (0.5, 2], and Switch-Cond-DP achieves lower MSE than baselines for MLP models at ε < 4 (Section 5.4).

Kg1UUrDIBG.text: Geometry-Aware Tabular Diffusion (GATD) augments a tabular diffusion denoiser with pairwise geometric features—angles θij and log-lengths ℓij between feature values—used both as network inputs and as auxiliary supervision targets (Section 3).

Across MLP, GNN, and Transformer backbones, GATD wins on 27/30 dataset-metric cells for Shape error (reducing error by 29.8% for MLP, 5.4% for GNN, and 21.8% for Transformer on average) and 25/30 cells for Trend error, with overall significance p = 5.21×10⁻⁹ across 60 cells (Table 2).

The MLP instantiation of GATD matches or beats TabDiff performance while using roughly 3.5x fewer parameters on average (up to 25x fewer for classification tasks), reducing Shape error by 27.3% and Trend error by 19.6% versus TabDiff (Table 3).

An architecture-matched ablation shows geometric inputs alone without auxiliary supervision produce a negligible effect (Cohen's d = -0.08), whereas adding the geometric supervision loss produces a large effect (Cohen's d = +0.81), indicating supervision rather than added architectural capacity drives the gains (Section 4.3).

GATD wins on 9/10 datasets for downstream utility (F1/RMSE on machine-learning-efficiency metrics), closing 58.2% of the MLE-1 gap and 42.0% of the MLE-2 gap relative to TabDiff, while using default loss weights (λθ=15, λℓ=15, λc=8) that transfer across MLP, GNN, and Transformer backbones without retuning (Table 3, Section 4).

fcVsVQkjIc.text: The RFL-TV algorithm achieves the first regret guarantee for online distributionally robust RL with general function approximation, bounded as Õ(C²_rcov H⁴(min{H,1/σ})² log(KH|F||G|δ⁻¹)√K + C_rcov ξ_dual), independent of state/action cardinality (Theorem 1, Section 6).

Robust coverability C_rcov, defined as sup over policies and steps of the sup-norm ratio of worst-case to nominal-environment visitation measures, is introduced as the key structural complexity measure driving the regret bound (Definition 3, Section 3).

When specialized to d-rectangular linear TV-robust MDPs, RFL-TV attains regret Õ(C²_rcov H⁴(min{H,1/σ})² d²√K log(dHK/δ)), which is shown to be near-optimal in its dependence on dimension d and episode count K relative to a matching minimax lower bound (Theorem 2, Section 7).

Table 1 compares RFL-TV's sample complexity, Õ(C²_rcov H⁵(min{H,1/σ})²ε⁻²) in the general function-approximation setting, against non-robust GOLF's Õ(C_cov H³ε⁻²), quantifying the statistical cost of robustness (Table 1, Section 6).
RFL-TV replaces per-state-action UCB bonuses with a dual-driven global confidence set construction over dual networks to quantify uncertainty in the robust Bellman operator (Section 5).
Numerical experiments empirically validate the theoretical regret scaling of RFL-TV under evolving online exploration policies without relying on a pre-collected offline dataset (Section 8).

HhWaVjXmLN.text: UniLID achieves 0.929 macro F1 on GlotLID-C, 0.859 on UDHR, and 0.932 on FLORES-200, matching or exceeding standard language identification baselines on these benchmarks (Table 1).
In the low-resource, few-shot regime, UniLID reaches 69.46% accuracy with only 5 labeled samples per language and 92.62% accuracy with 50 samples per language (Figure 1).
On the DSL-ML 2024 fine-grained dialect identification benchmark, UniLID attains 0.72 macro F1 versus fastText's 0.53, a substantial improvement on closely-related language pairs (Table 2).
On out-of-domain, noisy short-text data from Tatoeba, UniLID scores 0.414 macro F1, more than doubling fastText's 0.160 macro F1 (Table 3).
UniLID's approach treats tokenization segmentation itself as language-dependent via a UnigramLM-based method rather than using a fixed universal tokenizer (Section on UniLID methodology).

kny606LUdl.text: INDUCTION defines three complementary induction regimes—FullObs (375 problems), CI/Contrastive (200 problems), and EC/Existential Completion (200 problems)—each requiring synthesis of first-order logic formulas from finite relational worlds with mechanically checkable semantics (Section 3).

On the representative results table, GPT-5.2 attains 43.7% FullObs, 82.5% CI, and 78.0% EC unbounded accuracy, while GPT-4o scores near 0% across all three regimes, showing a sharp difficulty gradient across models and regimes (Table 1, Section 6).

Using the gold-relative budgeted accuracy metric Acc@(gold+Δ), near-gold formulas (AST size ≤ gold+1) generalize to held-out worlds at 78-98% while formulas with AST size far exceeding gold generalize at only 15-41%, a gap of 30-74 percentage points (Table 2, Section 5).

GPT-5.2 achieves 78% unbounded EC validity but only 59.5% budgeted accuracy under the Acc@(gold+Δ) metric, a 25-point gap revealing reliance on large case-splitting solutions rather than genuine generalization (Section 6).

'Lift-hard' structural formulas, where relations involving the free variable occur inside universal quantifiers, remain persistently difficult with near-zero accuracy for many models even as simpler structural variants saturate (Section 6).

4K54YHTG2i.text: NHGD approximates the Hessian inverse in bilevel optimization using the empirical Fisher information matrix, updated via the Sherman-Morrison formula from stochastic gradients already computed during inner-loop SGD, enabling parallel rather than sequential computation (Section on algorithm design).

Theorem 4.7 establishes a high-probability error bound on the Hessian-inverse approximation, ‖A_k^T − H(θ*(v_k))^{-1}‖ = O((1/√T)·√(1+log((1+T)/δ))), for T inner iterations with probability at least 1−δ (Theorem 4.7).

Theorem 4.10 shows NHGD attains an ε-stationary point with overall sample complexity Õ(ε⁻²) using T = O(ε⁻¹ log(δ⁻¹ε⁻¹)) inner iterations and K = O(ε⁻¹) outer iterations, matching the sample complexity of optimize-then-approximate methods such as stocBiO and AmIGO while reducing computational overhead (Theorem 4.10, Table 1).
Table 1 shows NHGD is the only compared method offering a high-probability bound (rather than an MSE bound) together with parallel EFIM-based Hessian inversion and constant O(1) batch size (Table 1).
In PDE-constrained optimization on a 2D heat equation, NHGD converges 3-4x faster than a Broyden-based baseline while reaching a comparable final objective value (Section on experiments).

t5cfrJfuzD.text: The contrastive covariance method decomposes attention query-key spaces into low-rank interpretable components by computing the difference between positive-condition and negative-condition query-key covariance matrices (Section 4).

The rank of a latent feature can be estimated by counting the singular values of the contrastive covariance matrix that capture 99% of its squared Frobenius norm, validated in toy single-head attention models where r1+r2 < d_head (Section 4).

Applied to Llama 3.1-8B Instruct and Qwen 3-4B Instruct, the method identifies rank-1 contrastive covariances corresponding to categorical semantic features (e.g., fruits, animals, vehicles, drinks, countries) in filter heads (Section 5).

Causal interventions on the identified categorical filter-head subspaces shift 40-60% of attention mass between categories, confirming these subspaces causally control attention allocation (Section 5).

In binding-feature analysis, order-ID subspaces are found to have rank 2-3 while lexical-ID subspaces have rank 9-10, and combined interventions on both subspaces achieve majority attention shifts (Section 5).

oP3gus0Sl3.text: The nonparametric attribution method computes influence via patch-level similarity aggregated across spatial locations and diffusion timesteps, without requiring model gradients (Section 3.2, Eq. 11).
A multiscale extension combines original and downsampled patch representations with a timestep-dependent weighting factor γₜ to capture both fine and coarse features (Section 3.3, Eq. 14-15).

On the Linear Datamodeling Score benchmark, the method (NDA) attains 24.88% on CIFAR-2, 11.81% on CIFAR-10, and 16.89% on CelebA in the validation setting, improving on CLIP cosine-similarity attribution by +16.32, +8.42, and +5.97 points respectively (Table 1).

In counterfactual retraining evaluation after removing the top-1,000 most influential training images, NDA produces a larger output ℓ2 shift than CLIP and D-TRAK baselines, e.g. 8.43 vs. 6.68 (CLIP) and 7.68 (D-TRAK) on CIFAR-2, and 14.38 vs. 10.30 (CLIP) and 13.18 (D-TRAK) on CelebA (Figure 2).

Ablations show the optimal patch size depends on the diffusion timestep, with smaller patches (P=5-9) preferred at early timesteps and larger patches (P=21) at mid-range noise levels, with timestep selection peaking near τmax=400-500 (Section 4.5).

zfVxpXEZti.text: AGZO extracts activation-informed low-rank subspaces on the fly during the forward pass and restricts stochastic perturbations to this subspace, rather than using isotropic perturbations as in standard zeroth-order methods (Section 3, based on the observation that gradient row-spaces are confined to activation column-spaces in linear layers).
On Qwen3-0.6B, AGZO outperforms MeZO and LOZO on SST2 (0.877 vs. 0.858 vs. 0.870), COPA (0.740 vs. 0.680 vs. 0.690), and CB (0.892 vs. 0.803 vs. 0.760) (Table 1).
On Qwen3-4B, AGZO improves over MeZO and LOZO on SST2 (0.892 vs. 0.875 vs. 0.866) and RTE (0.848 vs. 0.837 vs. 0.801) (Table 2).
On Pangu-1B, AGZO again exceeds MeZO on SST2 (0.778 vs. 0.764) (Table 3).

AGZO stores only activation-informed basis matrices of size dim_in × r per layer, adding negligible memory overhead, and Figure 3 shows peak GPU memory matches other forward-only zeroth-order methods across sequence lengths and batch sizes (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

Under an activation spectral concentration assumption, AGZO is proven to achieve strictly larger expected cosine similarity to the true gradient than isotropic zeroth-order baselines when upstream gradient energy concentrates in leading activation directions, and Figure 2 shows AGZO's empirical gradient cosine similarity consistently exceeds MeZO's throughout training (Theorem 5.6, Figure 2).

sg94PRd3kD.text: Under isomorphic mis-specification, where the reward model class equals the policy model class (ℱ = ℱ_Π), standard RLHF and standard offline DPO yield equal value: V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} = V_{r⋆}^{π_DPO} (Proposition 6, Section 3.4).

Despite this equivalence between RLHF and offline DPO, online DPO can strictly outperform RLHF under the same isomorphic mis-specified model classes, i.e. V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} < V_{r⋆}^{π^online_DPO}, because online DPO leverages distributional information unavailable to the two-stage reward-modeling-then-policy-optimization pipeline (Proposition 7, Section 3.4).

When the reward class is realizable but the policy class is weak, RLHF weakly dominates DPO (V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} ≥ V_{r⋆}^{π_DPO}), since DPO's implicit reward is bottlenecked by the policy class constraints (Proposition 3, Section 3.2).

For dual-token sparse prediction tasks, ℓ1-regularized reward model estimation achieves error Õ(√(k log d / n)), where k is the sparsity level and d the dimensionality, while policy-model estimation error under the same sparse ground-truth reward structure is lower-bounded by Ω(d/n), establishing a statistical separation showing RLHF needs asymptotically fewer samples than DPO to recover an effective reward/policy under sparse rewards (Theorem 10, Theorem 11, Section 4).

5HURZw5XM5.text: RAD retrieves target states by building a database of all dataset states annotated with trajectory ID, timestep index, and discounted return, then selecting top-k cosine-similarity candidates filtered by a return tolerance η and choosing the one with the longest remaining trajectory (Section 4.2).

A lightweight MLP step-estimation model fψ(st, sg) predicts the number of transition steps between the current state and the retrieved target state to temporally anchor the diffusion-based trajectory generator (Section 4.3).

On D4RL MuJoCo benchmarks, RAD achieves an average normalized return of 81.2 across nine tasks (three environments × three dataset types), outperforming Diffuser (77.5) and Decision Stitching/DS (77.0) but underperforming ReDiffuser (82.6) and Decision Diffuser/DD (81.8) (Table 1).
RAD attains 112.3±1.8 normalized return on Hopper-Medium-Expert and 82.5±12.7 on Hopper-Medium (Table 1).

Ablations show removing the retrieval module causes substantial performance degradation across environments, and removing condition-guided diffusion (using fixed instead of randomly sampled offsets) or removing the step-estimation model also reduces performance, most notably on tasks with complex temporal dynamics (Figure 3, Figure 4).
A hyperparameter sweep finds a similarity threshold δ=0.9 and top-k=6 are optimal for retrieval, with performance degrading sharply at low thresholds (0.0-0.5) or large k (k≥30) (Table 2).

Sj8NBI6aV0.text: For a single logit perturbation of magnitude ε, the change in policy entropy is ΔH = -εS* + O(ε²), where the discriminator S* = p_k(H + log p_k) determines the sign and magnitude of the entropy change (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).

For a full GRPO optimization step with learning rate α, entropy change is ΔH = -α(S* - E[S_i]) + O(α²), showing entropy change depends on how the sampled token's discriminator deviates from the policy-weighted batch expectation baseline (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.2).

Under on-policy sampling, the expected entropy-change factor averages to zero across both the vocabulary and the batch, and the expected entropy change equals -η·Cov(A, S* - E[S_i]), linking entropy collapse to positive correlation between advantage and discriminator deviation (Corollary 3.4, Corollary 3.5, Corollary C.1, C.2).

Two entropy-discriminator clipping algorithms are proposed: batch-normalized Clip_B, which masks tokens whose discriminator score deviates from the batch mean by more than μσ, and vocabulary-normalized Clip_V, which clips based on S_c^t = S*^t - E[S_i] (Algorithm 4.1, Algorithm 4.2, Section 4).
Both entropy-discriminator clipping methods improve both Pass@K (exploration) and Avg@K (exploitation) on AIME24 and AIME25, with gains of 0.5 to 3.8 percentage points over baselines (Table 1).

4RCt2j8HpW.text: CEITNet reduces dielectric tensor Frobenius-norm error to 2.87 versus 3.23 for the best prior method, with 63.8% of predictions within 10% of ground truth (Table 4, Section 6.1).
CEITNet reduces piezoelectric tensor Frobenius-norm error to 0.517 versus 0.778 for the best prior method, with an EwT@10% accuracy of 5.80% (Table 5, Section 6.1).
CEITNet achieves an elastic tensor Frobenius-norm error of 70.11 and an EwT@10% accuracy of 32.2% (Table 6, Section 6.1).
CEITNet uses 46% fewer parameters than ETGNN (0.6M vs 1.1M) and achieves 4.3x faster inference on dielectric tensor prediction (85.90 vs 22.02 items/second) (Table 7, Section 6.2).
An ablation study over the equivariant tensor interaction head's design choices is reported in Table 8 (Section 6.3), with the full architecture described in Section 3.3.

Oc5d0gsRTs.text: Orthogonal Subspace Carving (OSC) achieves 99.77% (±0.09) retrieval accuracy for 1,000 bundles at dimension d=200 with 440,000 total memory parameters, compared to only 13.18% for the best vector symbolic architecture (VSA) baseline at d=4,096 (Table 1, Section 6.1).
OSC reduces total memory storage by 9.3x compared to the best VSA baseline at d=4096 and by 18.4x compared to a baseline at d=8100 (Table 1 caption, Section 6.1).

Theorem 4.6 ('Interference Scaling', Section 4.5) proves the retrieval interference standard deviation scales as sqrt((N-1)/d^p), where N is the number of bindings and d^p is the effective memory dimension, showing tensor order p exponentially suppresses cross-talk.
In Extreme Multi-label Classification (XML) experiments across eight datasets, OSC ranks first by nDCG/PSnDCG metrics in 43.75% of cases (Table 4, Section 6.2).

OSC decouples tensor order from structural binding depth by projecting fillers, each composed of p component vectors, onto the orthogonal complement of context-defined forbidden subspaces rather than assigning explicit storage slots (Section 4, Theorem 4.6).

93Yh3Mvg37.text: AG-REPA (Top-3 configuration) reduces Speech FAD to 1.29 and Audio FAD to 2.56, with Speech WER of 3.45 and Speech MOS of 4.12±0.05 (Table 2, Section 5.2).

An ablation of layer-selection strategies shows Highest FoG-A (causal, functionally-driven) selection yields a 29.9% relative FAD improvement, versus 8.7% for Highest-LASP (representation-rich) selection and 4.9% for random layer selection (Table 3, Section 5.3).
AG-REPA generalizes across architectures, improving FAD from 1.20 to 0.95 for Voicebox, from 0.88 to 0.72 for CosyVoice, and from 1.45 to 1.15 for F5-TTS (Table 4, Section 5.4).

The Store-Contribute Dissociation (SCD) finding—that deep layers with high semantic similarity (LASP) are not the layers most causally responsible for the velocity field (FoG-A)—is quantitatively verified in Table 1 and Section 5.1, building on the mechanistic framework in Section 3 and Figure 1.

H98n6clgHv.text: DRFusion achieves the best SSIM and top-3 CC scores across all four benchmarks (HDO, M3SVD, NOT-156, VTMOT) among 12 compared state-of-the-art fusion methods including CDDFuse, DDFM, Mask-Dif, TemCOCO, and UniVF (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On downstream object tracking evaluated on NOT-156, DRFusion-fused video attains an AUC of 0.252 and SR@0.75 of 0.121 (Table 4).
An ablation on NOT-156 removing the temporal loss, Condition Adapter, Latent Refinement, and History Guidance/H(2) components individually confirms each is necessary for temporal stability (Table 3).

DRFusion's history-conditioned motion generation replaces rigid optical-flow alignment with attention-based soft temporal anchoring, implemented via a 3D Diffusion Transformer using 50 DDIM sampling steps (Section 4).

OM0C7jyV0p.text: ProtDiS improves enzyme class prediction by 6.05%, ligand-binding affinity prediction by 4.45%, and SCOP family classification by 3.91% under structure-based splits, evaluated across twelve downstream tasks including EC, MF, BP, CC, Pfam, SCOP-fa/cf/cl, structural similarity, ligand affinity, PPIs, and ligand binding site prediction (Table 1, Section 4.3.1).

For enzyme pairs in the highest TM-score bin (TM-score > 0.5), ProtDiS knowledge-guided embeddings achieve an AUC of 0.946 versus 0.868 for baseline ESM-3 structural embeddings in distinguishing functionally divergent proteins with similar folds (Figure 4a, Section 4.3.2).

A mutual-information heatmap shows a pronounced diagonal structure in which each of the eight knowledge channels attains its highest relative MI score for its own corresponding biophysical label (Figure 2 left panel, Section 4.2).

ProtDiS decomposes pretrained protein micro-environment embeddings into eight knowledge channels (secondary structure, solvent accessibility, flexibility/B-factors, packing density, hydrophobicity, hydrogen-bond stability, contact entropy, geometric curvature) plus a residual channel, via an information-bottleneck objective (Section 3.2, Equations 7-9).

FVmpIRN0N2.text: The paper studies a multi-factor block model for variable clustering and connects it to regularized subspace clustering via a distributionally robust version of nodewise regression (Section 2).

A convex relaxation of the distributionally robust nodewise regression problem is derived, with the robust region size selected via a data-driven approach rather than fixed a priori (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
An ADMM algorithm is developed to solve the convex relaxation efficiently for large-scale variable clustering problems (Section 3).
Theoretical guarantees are established for the multi-factor block model, including consistency-type results (Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 3.2).

Extensive numerical studies in the empirical evaluation section demonstrate superior clustering performance of the proposed method compared to baselines including PECOK and spectral clustering (Section 4).

mNX4kpc371.text: SS-Neurons (shared safety neurons) constitute less than 0.3% of model parameters yet jointly regulate safety behavior across multiple languages (Section 3.3).
Masking monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) causes attack success rate (ASR) to surge from 15.60% to 41.46% on Qwen3-8B (Section 3.2, Table 1).
Masking SS-Neurons produces a safety collapse comparable to full MS-Neuron ablation, increasing ASR by 9.46 percentage points on the AdvBench-x benchmark for Qwen3-8B (Section 3.3, Table 2).

tcPZvRXQhX.text: DeepAnalyze-8B scores 59.91% overall on DataSciBench, trailing only GPT-4o (66.31%) and surpassing GPT-4o-mini (50.63%) and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (47.48%), despite using far fewer parameters (Table 1).
On the 450-case DABStep benchmark, DeepAnalyze-8B achieves 38.88% overall accuracy and surpasses ReAct-style agents and reasoning-prompt baselines on hard-level tasks (Table 3).

Across seven TableQA benchmarks (WikiTQ, HybridQA, MultiHiertt, OTT-QA, FinQA, TAT-QA, HiTab), DeepAnalyze-8B attains an average of 64.47% after full training, exceeding GPT-4o (58.96%) and Claude (58.79%) (Table 4, Section 4.1).

The curriculum-based agentic training paradigm proceeds in two stages: single-ability fine-tuning on approximately 470K samples at 8K sequence length, followed by multi-ability agentic training with a 20K-sample cold start and a 15K-sample RL phase at 32K sequence length (Section 3.2).
The model is trained on the DataScience-Instruct-500K dataset (~500K samples) and operates via five core actions: Analyze, Understand, Code, Execute, and Answer (Section 3.1, Section 3.3).

The framework comprises three agents: a Grounding Agent for schema identification, a Generation Agent trained with multi-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a Validation Agent for candidate selection (Section 3.1-3.3).

The Generation Agent uses a sparse reward scheme: +1.0 for a valid and correct SQL query, 0.0 for valid but incorrect, and -1.0 for invalid, formalized in the GRPO objective (Section 3.2, Equation 4).

Ablations show the Generation Agent alone reaches 66.37% on BIRD-dev, while the full multi-agent framework reaches 77.84%, and the Validation Agent outperforms self-consistency decoding (77.84% vs 72.93%) (Table 3, Section 4.3.1).
Increasing the maximum interaction turns during training from T=1 to T=10 raises greedy-decoding accuracy from 67.60% to 69.88% (Table 10, Appendix F).

On Qwen-3-8B the backdoor circuit is even sparser (0.18%), reducing ASR from 98.8% to 1.2%, demonstrating cross-model consistency of the method (Section 5.2, Table 1).

Additional backdoor types are localized in the appendix: a jailbreak backdoor at 98.3% sparsity with 100% attack capture and a mislabel backdoor at 91.1% sparsity on LLaMA (Appendix C, Figure 5).

Safety Circuit Tuning (SaCirT) achieves near-zero backdoor ASR using approximately 1% of tunable parameters, and during helpfulness fine-tuning preserves ~94.0% AdvBench safety versus the baseline's drop to 89.3% (Section 5.4, Figure 4).

8vkE9kvrXa.text: Theorem 3.2 proves representation-only metrics like CKA are non-identifiable for transfer: tasks sharing an encoder with identical activations but disjoint label subsets can have orthogonal head gradients (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).

Corollary 3.3 shows no function g maps CKA values to head Fisher alignment across task pairs, and empirically CKA correlates only weakly with head Fisher alignment (Pearson 0.43, Spearman 0.45) (Table 5, Appendix A).

Theorem 4.2 establishes that head Fisher alignment equals a cosine between kernel mean embeddings, decomposing into a covariance-similarity term, an error-second-moment similarity term, and a non-separability coupling term ρ_ij (Section 4.2, Equation 5).

FisherSketch compresses per-task joint geometry from roughly 61 GiB (at vocabulary size K=128,256) down to a 16KB float32 signature plus 192KB streaming state, using factored Random Maclaurin features exploiting the Kronecker gradient structure g=a⊗e (Section 5, Appendix R.1).
On Llama-3.1-8B vocabulary-scale source selection across 100 domains, FisherSketch achieves 45.7%±5.0 top-1 accuracy against an oracle of 98.44%±0.30 (Table 1).

In the verbalizer-shift stress test with fixed-prefix prompts, FisherSketch reaches 66.7% top-1 accuracy versus 20% (chance) for an activation-only baseline, showing error geometry captures variation that representation metrics miss (Table 2, Section 6.2).

yaUJPj48wa.text: ConceptMoE improves average score over a standard MoE baseline by +0.8 points at the MoE-A0.5B-12B scale (36.4 vs 35.6) and by +0.9 points at MoE-A1B-24B (50.9 vs 50.0) on language pretraining benchmarks (Section on Language Pretraining Results).

On long-context evaluation, ConceptMoE improves Needle-in-a-Haystack accuracy from 78.9 to 80.7 (+1.8 points) and long-context understanding by +2.3 points on average, while showing a slight decline on long-context summarization (63.7 to 59.0).

On a 60B-parameter vision-language model, ConceptMoE gives +0.9 points overall on text benchmarks and +4.4 points on visual reasoning (57.9 vs 53.5), with comparable hallucination-detection performance (35.3 vs 35.8) and slight degradation on spatial/localization tasks.

At compression ratio R=2, ConceptMoE reduces attention computation by up to R² (4x) and KV cache by up to R (2x), yielding prefill speedups up to 175% and decoding speedups up to 117% on long sequences; at the practical R=1.5 setting, speedups are 43.6% (prefill) and 53.3% (decoding).

Continual-training conversion of a pretrained MoE into ConceptMoE with layer looping (ConceptMoE-top11-loop8) yields +5.5 points on the Open Benchmark overall, including +8.3 on reasoning, +12.2 on math, and +6.4 on code, versus the from-scratch-trained variant's smaller +0.9-point gain.

σ_AB achieves 98.1% sign accuracy on instruction-SFT at k=1 and 98.9% on DPO preference optimization, with 87.7%-92.0% accuracy across four LLM architectures for Pile-style domain adaptation.

Sign-prediction accuracy degrades gradually with horizon, from 81.5% at k=20 steps to 65.3% at k=50 steps over 1,020 trials, though a Trotter-corrected estimator using reference point θ_ref=θ₀−η(g_A+g_B) maintains 73.1%-72.2% accuracy at k=20 by reducing target-gradient drift error from O(η³) to O(η⁴).

For many-domain curriculum ranking via pairwise Lie-bracket tournament edges W_ij=⟨g_E^ref, H_i g_j − H_j g_i⟩, the Borda/row-sum score computes rankings in O(N log N) and recovers 99.0-99.6th percentile orderings for MMLU subjects (N=56) and 99th percentile for Stack languages (N=85), recovering the best of 3! possible schedules in 87.5% of trials.

Theorem 5.4 gives an approximation error bound sup_X|μ_θ(X)−μ*(X)| ≲ H_n^{-2α₁} + J_n^{-αβα₁}, decomposing error into network-depth (H_n) and spline-resolution (J_n) components (Theorem 5.4).

Theorem 5.9 proves region selection consistency: feature-level inclusion probabilities converge in probability to the true indicator (max_j|q̂_j−e_j*|→0), exact support recovery P(Ŝ_{1/2}=S_{J_n}*)→1, and domain-level convergence |Ω̂ΔΩ*|→0 (Theorem 5.9).

On the Tecator spectroscopy dataset, sBayFDNN attains RMSE 2.138 versus 2.2-3.9 for competing methods, discovering active regions near 930nm consistent with known lipid/fat spectral associations (Figure 4).

For Qwen 2.5-7B variants, the domain-specialized Coder model reaches higher initial accuracy than the general model in Deep Learning (96.4% vs 92.3%) but degrades 3.7x faster, dropping to 86.4% by turn 15 while the general model stays around ~90% (Section 4.4, Figure 3).

The Recursive Taxonomy (L5W5) exploration strategy dominates the Pareto frontier of extraction strategies, achieving a yield ratio of approximately 6.0x relative to baseline approaches (Section 4.2, Figure 2).

Proposition 4.1 establishes identifiability of latent-judge directions up to sign and permutation under shared confounders, with perturbation stability bounds (Section 4).

Hierarchical permutation augmentation reduces the atom-permutation search space from N! to the product of per-orbit factorials, cutting an N=20-atom space from about 10^18.4 to about 10^7.2 possible permutations (Figure 6).

Proposition 1 shows BQND obtains O(T^{1/2}) static regret with only O(1) oracle queries per round, improving on prior work's O(T^{2/3}) regret for single queries or O(T^{1/2}) regret requiring T^{3/2} queries per round.
Proposition 3 establishes a dynamic regret bound of Õ(T^{1/2}·√(1+P_T)) where P_T is the path length of the comparator sequence.
In the bandit feedback model, the framework achieves O(T^{4/5}) regret (Proposition 6), and in the semi-bandit model O(T^{2/3}) regret (Proposition 4).

Grad-Mimic-based reweighting outperforms vanilla training at both small scale (10M samples) and medium scale (100M samples) across a range of temperature settings from τ=0.05 to τ=0.5.

Modality parallelism eliminates false dependencies between encoders, letting Cornstarch instantiate and train more than 10,000 distinct multimodal architecture combinations (Section 6.3).
The Bitfield Attention Mask (BAM) represents multimodal attention patterns memory-efficiently, supporting up to roughly 60 modality encoders using 64-bit integers.

Cost-aware Multi-turn Policy Optimization (CMPO) combines session-level outcome utility, turn-level process rewards from a generative reward model, and a PID-controlled Lagrangian penalty for global cost constraints, formalized in Equations 5-9 (Section 4.2, subsections 4.2.1-4.2.3).

On the UNIVERSE general restoration benchmark, TF-Restormer attains a UTMOS score of 4.08, and on VCTK+DEMAND denoising it attains a PESQ of 3.41 (Table 1 and Table 2, Section 5.2).

Theorem 4.3 proves a two-layer network needs hidden width H >= (k+1) 2^k * sum_{rho in I(G)} n_rho^{k+1} to solve length-k sequential group composition, which for cyclic groups reduces to H >= (k+1) 2^{k-1} |G|, i.e. width exponential in sequence length k (Theorem 4.3).

A recurrent architecture solves length-k sequential composition with width O(sum_rho n_rho^3) = O(|G|^{3/2}), constant in k, by composing elements one at a time over k recurrent steps (Section 4, RNN construction).

A multilayer feedforward network solves the same task with the same O(|G|^{3/2}) width but only L = log2(k) layers, by composing adjacent pairs of group elements in parallel at each layer (Section 4, multilayer construction).

kcnuX4xEpL.text: Theorem 3.3 proves that the support of the QOT optimizer cannot concentrate around the Monge graph faster than order epsilon^(1/(d+2)) in directed Hausdorff distance, matching the conjectured optimal exponent (Section 3.1).

Theorem 3.6 shows the QOT value gap controls mean-squared deviation from the Monge map at rate epsilon^(2/(d+2)), with a Markov-type argument yielding corresponding high-probability bounds on transport map deviations (Section 3.2).

Theorem 3.7 derives a sharp pointwise tube bound of order epsilon^(1/(d+2)) in the affine Brenier regime, where the Monge map is affine T(x) = Ax + a, including the Gaussian-to-Gaussian transport case, by reducing to self-transport QOT (Section 3.3).
Proposition 3.8 characterizes affine Monge maps between truncated Gaussian measures, underpinning the affine-case tube bound analysis (Section 3.3).
Numerical experiments in Section 5 validate the predicted epsilon^(1/(d+2)) scaling using discrete QOT solvers on affine benchmark problems across dimensions d in {100, 200, 500, 1000}.

Ys66H59k8m.text: PG-DPO uses a two-stage procedure: a Stage 1 rollout warm-start via BPTT-based Monte Carlo policy optimization, followed by a Stage 2 Adjoint-MC Projection that estimates the costate via averaged BPTT and maximizes the Hamiltonian at each query point (Section 2.2, Algorithm 1).
Theorem 2.1 bounds the error of averaged BPTT costate estimates by C_u times epsilon^FOC_k times Delta t plus o(Delta t), establishing their correspondence to anchored adjoints (Section 2.3, Eq. 21).

On the survival-discounted control benchmark with beta_0=0.5, PG-DPO achieves an L1 error of 2.97e-2 ± 1.29e-2, versus 3.71e-1 ± 2.90e-2 for Deep BSDE and 2.18e-1 ± 5.06e-2 for PPO (Table 1, Section 3.1).
On the Merton problem with hyperbolic discounting, PG-DPO achieves consumption L1 error of 3.47e-3 ± 2.41e-10 versus 6.41e-2 ± 4.86e-3 for Deep BSVIE, an over 18x reduction (Table 2, Section 3.2).
On time-varying hyperbolic discounting with a sinusoidal impatience profile, PG-DPO attains L1 error 7.39e-3 ± 3.88e-5 compared to 1.02e0 ± 2.30e-1 for Deep BSVIE (Table 3, Section 3.3).
PG-DPO achieves sub-0.02-second per-query inference on commodity CPUs, with cost modeled as O(M_MC * N' * C_step + I_proj * C_proj) (Eq. 22).

clFn9vQ8cK.text: AFR-Net constructs a physics-informed graph using effective resistance distance (ERD) rather than shortest-path distance for node initialization (Section 4.1).

AFR-Net derives a closed-form solution for edge-level information traffic, Φ_ij = 2c_ij(e_i - e_j)^T(L_flow^-1 L_fc L_flow^-1)(e_i - e_j), linking edge capacity, global topology, and functional demand (Section 4.2, Eq. 10).
On the PPMI dataset AFR-Net attains F1=83.70±3.85 and AUC=90.38±1.64, outperforming baselines including GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, BrainGNN, RH-BrainFS, and NeuroPath (Table 1).
On ABCD-Anx, removing the flow routing module causes F1 to drop from 62.15% to 49.70%, a substantially larger degradation than removing the ERD encoding alone (Table 2).

Interpretability analysis identifies the left hippocampus as a pathological hub with hyper-active information traffic to the default mode network in anxiety-disorder patients (Section 5.3, Figure 3b).

PI2xku6EDA.text: S2L-PO uses a frozen small policy (e.g., 1.7B parameters) to supply a decaying share of rollouts alongside a trainable large policy (e.g., 8B parameters), annealed to zero over the first Tmix training steps via progressive linear reduction (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).
On Qwen3-8B, S2L-PO guided by a 1.7B explorer improves AIME 2024 accuracy by +8.8% and AIME 2025 by +10.4% over vanilla GRPO (Table 1).
On CommonsenseQA (an out-of-distribution benchmark), Qwen3-8B trained with S2L-PO using a 4B explorer reaches 67.8% accuracy versus 63.9% for the GRPO baseline (Table 2).

At sampling budget K=64 on AIME24, the 1.7B model shows a higher unique-answer ratio (0.576) than the 14B model (0.476), a 21% relative difference used as evidence of greater policy-level diversity in smaller models (Table 3).

The paper proves policy-level (parameter-compression) perturbations maintain a positive, horizon-independent lower bound on cross-step covariance (Proposition E.4), whereas token-level perturbations (e.g., temperature scaling) have covariance upper-bounded by a term that decays with prefix divergence (Proposition E.2, Eq. 17).

An ablation shows progressive annealing of the small-model rollout share strictly outperforms abrupt two-phase switching between small- and large-model sampling, avoiding distribution shock (Section 4.4, Figure 6).

OeY3gcvlvh.text: Persuasive Privacy (PP) is defined via a Stackelberg game in which a Sender commits to a mechanism M and a Bayes-rational Receiver updates beliefs, with privacy assessed by the tail bound inf_{S,x,Q} P_x[ΔS(Q,T,x) ≤ κ] ≥ 1-δ (Section 3, Definition 3).

Proposition 6 shows a mechanism satisfies (ϵ,δ)-probabilistic differential privacy if and only if it satisfies (L,ℋ,ϵ,δ)-persuasive privacy, where L is the negative log-probability score, establishing full equivalence between the two frameworks (Section 4, Proposition 6).

Proposition 7 establishes that the deterministic empirical-average mechanism M(x,·)=δ_{x̄} satisfies (ℐ,𝒢_x^r,κ^r,0)-persuasive privacy with κ^r = r_1 + log r_2, giving privacy guarantees for a deterministic algorithm that standard differential privacy cannot certify (Section 5, Proposition 7).

Proposition 4 shows persuasive privacy satisfies receiver post-processing (the receiver cannot amplify privacy loss via output transformation), while Proposition 5 shows it does not satisfy the sender post-processing inequality that differential privacy does (Section 3.2, Propositions 4-5).

Proposition 3 shows that for conjugate prior families, composing two persuasive-privacy mechanisms with parameters (κ1,δ1) and (κ2,δ2) yields a mechanism satisfying (𝒮,𝒬_x,κ1+κ2,δ1+δ2)-PP (Section 3.1, Proposition 3).

YTB6DpwLys.text: CaPE models expert responses to edge queries with a three-way categorical likelihood over {no edge, i→j, j→i}, built from hierarchical logistic components for edge existence and direction (Section 4, Equations 4-9).

CaPE selects queries by maximizing expected information gain (EIG), shown in Proposition 7.1 to equal the expected KL contraction of the particle posterior after observing the expert's answer (Section 7.1, Proposition 7.1, Eq. 14).

Theorem 7.1 proves that under non-adversarial expert feedback, if each ambiguous edge pair is queried infinitely often, the CaPE posterior converges almost surely to the true DAG up to Markov equivalence (Section 7.2, Theorem 7.1).

On synthetic data with D=20 nodes, CaPE reduces posterior entropy to about 0.8 bits after 40 queries versus about 1.2 bits for an uncertainty-based baseline, and reaches a structural Hamming distance of about 4-5 versus 7-8 for competitors (Figure 1).

On the Sachs protein-signaling dataset (D=11 nodes, N=853), CaPE reduces structural Hamming distance by about 14 edges after 40 queries and improves orientation F1 by more than 0.38 over the initial posterior (Section 8.2, Figure 2).

On CausalBench K562 (D=50 genes, N=8,553), CaPE reaches a directed AUPRC of about 0.65 at T=250 queries versus about 0.58 for an uncertainty-based policy, with the static baseline saturating early while CaPE improves monotonically (Figure 4).

H3vDDSHWos.text: Theorem 3.4 proves that generalized (Φ-normalized) attention, covering both softmax and linear attention, disperses as the number of keys n tends to infinity, so the query assigns asymptotically equal weight to all keys (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.4).

Definition 3.6 shows window attention avoids this dispersion because its computation is restricted to a fixed-size neighborhood independent of the total sequence length n (Section 3.2, Definition 3.6).
SEMA combines window attention with a global homogeneous average, SEMA(Q,K,V) := A_w(Q,K,V,w) + (1/n)∑_{j=1}^n v_j, giving O(1) complexity for the global term (Section 4, Equation 13, Algorithm 2).
On ImageNet-1K at 224² resolution, SEMA achieves 83.7% top-1 accuracy with 26M parameters and 4.3G FLOPs, outperforming MILA-T (83.5%), DefMamba (83.5%), and EfficientFormerV2-L (83.5%) (Table 2).
When fine-tuned to higher resolutions, SEMA outperforms VMamba-T by 0.6% at 384² (84.1% vs 83.5%) and by 0.7% at 768² (84.2% vs 83.5%) while using fewer FLOPs (Table 3).

An ablation on COCO/ImageNet shows removing the homogeneous averaging term drops top-1 accuracy from 83.7% to 83.5%, and on COCO Mask R-CNN with the 3x schedule SEMA reaches 49.2 AP_b, the best among Mamba-like models compared (Table 4, Table 5).

erxWUWJlt2.text: HybridFlow achieves 55.34% average accuracy across GPQA (53.33%), MMLU-Pro (72.54%), AIME24 (36.67%), and LiveBench-Reasoning (58.83%), versus 58.99% average for the best GPT-4.1 Chain-of-Thought/PASTA baselines, while using far less cloud API cost (Table 1)

HybridFlow reduces end-to-end latency to 17.48s on average, versus 24.45s for HybridLLM (40% slower) and 28.56s for direct GPT-4.1 (63% slower), and lowers normalized cloud API cost to 0.0088 versus 0.0128 for HybridLLM and 0.0148 for direct GPT-4.1 (Table 2)

The dependency-aware DAG task decomposition is produced by Algorithm 2's Decompose() function and executed via the three-stage pipeline (decomposition, resource-aware routing/execution, aggregation) defined in Algorithm 1, enabling parallel execution of interdependent subtasks (Section 3.2, Algorithms 1-2)

Subtask allocation is formulated as a 0-1 knapsack problem maximizing a benefit-cost utility u_i = clip(Δq_i/(c_i+ε), 0, 1) subject to normalized latency/API-cost constraints, with the learned router achieving 53.33% accuracy at 0.0075 normalized cost (benefit-cost ratio 0.794), compared to 25.54% for edge-only, 57.28% for cloud-only ($0.0185 cost), and 46.00% for random allocation (Section 3.1, Table 3)

An adaptive threshold τ_t = clip(τ0 + k_used/(2K_max) + l_used/(2L_max), 0, 1) acts as a shadow price that rises as resources deplete, with the benefit-cost ratio peaking near τ0=0.5 in the fixed-threshold ablation (Equation 13, Figure 4)

st1MolZlTP.text: Theorem 1 shows that DP RGDA reaches an α-approximate second-order stationary point for the empirical risk in stochastic minimax optimization with α = Õ((√d/(nε))^(2/3)) using only first-order (Hessian-free) queries (Theorem 1)
Theorem 2 shows that for the population risk, DP RGDA achieves α = Õ(1/n^(1/3) + (√d/(nε))^(1/2)), matching the best known empirical-risk-minimization rates under differential privacy (Theorem 2)

DP RGDA combines SPIDER-style variance reduction with nested gradient descent-ascent (Algorithms 2 and 3), tracking the inner maximizer y*(x) via projected ascent and using period-wise rather than horizon-wide estimator control (Section on DP RGDA, Algorithms 2-3)

The paper's empirical-risk rate Õ((√d/(nε))^(2/3)) matches the rate of DP-SPIDER for minimization-only problems, while its population-risk rate improves on Ada-DP-SPIDER's Õ(1/n^(1/3) + (√d/(nε))^(2/5)) for the minimax setting (Table 1)

Movement-based escape testing is used to certify second-order stationarity without incurring additional privacy cost, validated experimentally on synthetic matrix sensing problems against DP-SPIDER and Ada-DP-SPIDER baselines (Figure 1, Table 2)

hxNN3xhuS9.text: SiGMA replaces fixed discrete scaling operators with a learnable, per-timestep discrete Gaussian kernel grounded in scale-space theory to achieve position-wise multi-scale modeling (Section 4)

On long-term forecasting across 8 datasets (Weather, Electricity, Traffic, Exchange, ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2) with 4 horizons each (16 settings), SiGMA achieves the best performance in 13 of 16 settings (Section 5)
On the M4 short-term forecasting benchmark spanning 15 evaluation cases across temporal frequencies, SiGMA performs best in 11 of 15 cases (Section 5)
SiGMA improves training speed by up to 5.3x and reduces memory consumption by up to 3.8x relative to AMD, the strongest competing method, as shown in the efficiency scatter plot (Figure 5)

An ablation on ETTh1 (predict-720 setting) with 6 variants—including replacing the MLP with TimeMixer's mixing mechanism, using a single scale parameter instead of learnable per-timestep scales, removing scaling entirely, and using non-learnable operators—shows each design choice of SiGMA contributes to performance (Table 4)

s1WSLFmnr8.text: TWLA performs post-training W1.58A4 quantization (ternary weights, 4-bit activations) via three components: E2M-ATQ (Euclidean-to-Manifold Asymmetric Ternary Quantizer, Section 3.2), KOTMS (Kronecker Orthogonal Tri-Modal Shaping, Section 3.3), and ILA-AMP (Inter-Layer Aware Activation Mixed Precision, Section 3.4)

On LLaMA2-7B/13B/70B under W1.58A4, TWLA attains 58.00/64.30/71.10 average zero-shot accuracy and 8.31/6.68/4.77 WikiText2 perplexity, and beats prior ternary SOTA PT2-LLM (62.91 vs 42.82 accuracy on LLaMA2-7B) and ResQ's W2.3A4.2 mixed precision (71.10 vs 56.43 on LLaMA2-70B) (Table 1)
On Qwen3-32B-Instruct, TWLA W1.58A4MP scores 70.21 MMLU, 37.58 HumanEval, and 48.67 GSM8K versus FP16's 80.75/50.41/66.55 (Table 2)

TWLA delivers a 3.64x inference speedup over FP16 on LLaMA2-13B (86.35 vs 23.70 tokens/sec) and is 1.3x faster than QuaRot's 2-bit weight scheme, with over 80% memory reduction via ternary packing (Section 4.4)

A component ablation on LLaMA2-13B and Qwen3-14B shows E2M-ATQ plus KOTMS yields roughly 45% MMLU gain under W1.58A16, while adding ILA-AMP recovers about 12% MMLU specifically under W1.58A4, preventing layer-wise error cascades (Table 3)

4YIY66tpvQ.text: The paper derives a closed-form solution for cumulative quantization error in diffusion models, δ_t = Σ_{k=t}^{T} (∏_{j=t}^{k-1} A_j^{-1}) B_k ε_k, simplified via a Jacobian-ignoring approximation and a temporal-locality approximation shown to require only m=1 subsequent step (Section 3.1-3.2)

On SDXL at W4A4, TCEC improves PSNR to 21.9 versus SVDQuant's 20.7 on the sDCI dataset (a 1.2 PSNR gain), and improves FID to 18.1 versus SVDQuant's 20.6 on MJHQ, with under 1% added end-to-end latency overhead (Section 4, Table 1)
Under W8A8, TCEC on SDXL reaches 27.3 PSNR, close to the FP16 baseline's 26.4, consistently outperforming SVDQuant, TensorRT, MixDQ, and ViDiT-Q (Table 1)
On video generation with OpenSORA, TCEC at W4A8 reaches 64.97 imaging quality on VBench versus ViDiT-Q's 61.07, evaluated across 8 VBench metrics (Table 2)
