TCEC at W4A4 achieves 3.5x memory reduction versus FP16 and 3x speedup versus NF4 weight-only quantization, with negligible latency increase from the correction computation (Section 4)

Zwd8DVzaXB.text: Reasoning Style Transfer (RST) trained on the 80k-sample instruction dataset outperforms baselines on the in-domain PhysLogic benchmark by 3.59%-13.65% accuracy across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-7B backbones (Table 5, Section 4.3).

Logic-Distill trained on 40k samples achieves 45.04%-53.42% average accuracy on out-of-domain benchmarks (GPQA, SciBench, PhysReason), outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.75% on Qwen2.5-7B and 6.08% on DeepSeek-R1-7B (Table 6, Section 4.4).

Ablating the Causal Connection (𝒪) dimension from the logicality metric causes the largest performance drop of the three dimensions, degrading accuracy by 5.23% (Llama-3.1-8B), 5.77% (Qwen2.5-7B), and 11.05% (DeepSeek-R1-7B) (Table 7).

The proposed logicality metrics (Logical Fidelity, Causal Connection, Inferential Progress) achieve average Pearson/Spearman correlations of 0.7453 with human experts and 0.7860 with LLM judges, both at p<0.001 (Table 3, Section 4.2).
The PhysLogic benchmark is built from 864 papers spanning 9 physics subfields with 96 questions per subfield, filtered from 380,678 physics papers down to 118,039 theory-centric works (Section 3).
On a larger Qwen-2.5-14B-Instruct backbone, Logic-Distill achieves 45.28% average accuracy versus 38.41% for the MegaScience baseline (Table 12, Appendix D.1).

pstQMm8R1g.text: SafeSciBench comprises 125 tasks across 7 scientific fields (chemistry, biology, medicine, materials, engineering, physics, psychology) totaling 1.75M samples, of which 0.25M are held-out test samples (Table 1, Table 2).

SafeSciTrain provides 1.5M training samples used for LoRA fine-tuning, which improves safety knowledge accuracy by +0.09 to +0.35 and safety rate by +0.17 to +0.46 across evaluated models (Table 4, Table 6).

Across 24 evaluated LLMs, safety knowledge accuracy on SafeSciBench ranges from 0.32 (Grok-4.1-nonreasoning) to 0.80 (Gemini-3-Pro), while safety rate ranges from 0.16 (Llama-4) to 0.65 (Grok-4.1-reasoning) (Tables 3 and 5).
Grok-4.1-reasoning exhibits an overall over-refusal (excessive rejection) rate of 0.43 across scientific safety tasks (Table 7).
Domain-specialized scientific models such as Intern-S1 outperform general-purpose LLMs of comparable or larger scale on SafeSciBench safety evaluation (Section 4, Table 3/5).

G1M4rBPtlP.text: LGKDE achieves 78.57% average AUROC across 11 graph anomaly detection benchmark datasets with a best average rank of 1.73, versus the runner-up CVTGAD's rank of 3.09 (Table 1).
LGKDE attains 91.63% AUROC on MUTAG, exceeding two-stage baselines GAE+KDE (81.94%) and InfoGraph+KDE (79.77%) on the same dataset (Table 8).
LGKDE achieves 87.69% average AUPRC (vs. CVTGAD's 72.45%) and 61.62% average FPR95 (vs. CVTGAD's 67.50%) across the benchmark suite (Tables 5 and 6).

Theorem 4.3 establishes that LGKDE's Mean Integrated Squared Error converges at rate O(N^(-4/(4+d_int))), matching the minimax-optimal rate, which reduces to O(N^-0.8) when the intrinsic dimension d_int=1.
Theorem 4.2 proves LGKDE's estimator converges to the true underlying graph density function f* as the number of samples increases (Section 4.1).

An ablation removing the multi-scale KDE component drops MUTAG AUROC from 91.63% to 86.92%, and removing learnable kernel weights causes a 2.7% AUROC drop, showing both components are necessary (Table 2).

x5VjErljHS.text: On the ToolEmu benchmark, adding Thought-Aligner-7B corrections raises GPT-3.5-Turbo's safety rate from 58% to 96%, a 38-point improvement (Table 2).
On PrivacyLens, Thought-Aligner-7B reduces ChatGPT-3.5's privacy leakage rate from 36.31% to 1.40%, a 34.91-point reduction, with an average 40% leakage reduction across evaluated models (Table 9).

On Agent-SafetyBench, Thought-Aligner yields an average total safety improvement of approximately 47%, comprising a 51% average gain in behavior safety and a 32% average gain in content generation safety (Table 10).
Thought-Aligner is trained on a dataset of 5,000 instructions yielding over 11,400 safe/unsafe thought pairs, using 1.5B and 7B parameter base models (Section 3).

Thought-Aligner improves safety rates from roughly 50% to roughly 90% on average and outperforms the ATHENA guardrail baseline by about 10 percentage points, with average response latency under 100ms (Section 4).

InwrRdCQwD.text: KODA improves Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI) for cross-embedding alignment from 0.25 to 0.78 for the DINOv2-CLIP pair and from 0.52 to 0.91 for the BLIP-CLIP pair (Table 2).
On cross-modal retrieval, the KODA-selected subset amplifies the SigLIP-CLIP performance gap, with an average drop of 11.12 versus 3.91 on the full dataset (Table 1).

Theorem 4.4 establishes a sample complexity guarantee of O(n^-1/4) convergence for the covariance-block reduction used to scale KODA's eigenproblem from n x n to (d1+d2) x (d1+d2) (Proposition 4.3, Theorem 4.4).
Theorem 5.1 shows the joint Random Fourier Feature approximation for product kernels in multimodal KODA achieves O(r^-1/2) concentration around the true kernel value (Section 5).

KODA is evaluated on AFHQ, FFHQ, ImageNet, and MS-COCO using six vision-language models (CLIP, DINOv2, BLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2) to identify modality pairs and sample subsets with divergent grouping behavior (Section 6).

bmvWC1ainA.text: TC-JEPA ViT-H/14 trained for 300 epochs reaches 80.4% linear-probing accuracy on ImageNet-1k, versus 79.3% for I-JEPA ViT-H/14 and 79.6% for StoP ViT-H/14 (Table 1).

On transfer learning with ViT-H/14, TC-JEPA improves ADE20k semantic segmentation from 64.6 to 70.4 mIoU (linear) and from 81.4 to 83.8 mIoU (fine-tune), and COCO detection APb from 58.4 to 59.1 over I-JEPA (Table 2).

Trained on YFCC15M, TC-JEPA outperforms CLIP by 10.6 points on image classification (77.1% vs 66.5%), 10.9 points on COCO detection APb (54.5 vs 43.6), and 7.4 mIoU on ADE20k segmentation (55.2 vs 47.8) (Table 4).
TC-JEPA reaches 41.2 mIoU on ADE20k segmentation, approaching DINOv2's 41.8 mIoU while using 5x less training data (Table 3).
On multimodal understanding, TC-JEPA outperforms SPARC on image captioning (111.6 vs 109.7 CIDEr) and VQAv2 (57.8% vs 56.2%) (Table 5).
Ablations show the sparsity constraint loss and multi-layer text conditioning provide the largest gains over single-layer conditioning (Section 5.3).

Z8Mi9GGsy6.text: Under the 1-of-1 trigger protocol, DF-LoGiT achieves attack success rates of 99.85% on DeiT-Tiny and 100.00% on both DeiT-Small and ViT-B (Table 1).
Benign (clean) accuracy degradation from DF-LoGiT injection stays under 1.5 points across backbones: -1.20% (DeiT-Tiny), -0.47% (DeiT-Small), -1.32% (ViT-B) (Table 1).
Under the 2-of-3 multi-trigger protocol, DF-LoGiT reaches 98.72% average ASR when at least two of three triggers are present, and 100% ASR when all three triggers are present (Table 1).
Against the BDVT defense, ASR for the 2-trigger condition drops to 14.38% while the 3-trigger condition remains at 98.82%, whereas Fine-Pruning and Patch Processing leave ASR above 92% (Table 2).

Data-free one-shot weight-editing injection completes in 2.70-3.62 ms per backbone under the 1-of-1 setting, and 43.55 ms for the 2-of-3 setting on DeiT-Small, with no training or fine-tuning required (Section 5.1).

fDZZXgdx2F.text: Growing a 17B MoE checkpoint to 70B parameters via orthogonal growth yields a 10.66% downstream accuracy gain over training a 70B model from scratch under the same additional compute budget (Section 5, Figure 1).

For depth growth, interpositional layer duplication (copying each layer in place) outperforms the stacking method (concatenating full layer sequences) on both training loss and downstream accuracy (Section 3.1, Figure 3).
For width growth, injecting Gaussian noise (alpha=0.01) when duplicating experts improves downstream accuracy by about 1% over direct copying without noise (Section 3.2, Figure 4).

Growing from a checkpoint at 96k pre-training steps yields 48.52 downstream accuracy versus 38.79 when growing from a 0k-step checkpoint, given the same additional 3x10^20 FLOPs budget, demonstrating a positive sunk-cost correlation (Section 4, Figure 7, Table 1).
Under a fixed total FLOPs budget, growth from earlier checkpoints performs comparably to training from scratch (Section 4, Figure 8, Table 2).

At large scale, growing a 17B model (28 layers, 96 experts, 4 activated) to 35B via depth growth then to 70B via width growth (54 layers, 192 experts, 8 activated), trained on 600B+300B+100B=1T total tokens, yields +2.21 and +5.62 accuracy points respectively (Section 5, Figure 11).

EOEI74ZtA4.text: Recursive Space Contraction (RSC) is identified as a pathology where positive updates passively suppress valid alternatives via sharpening while negative updates redistribute mass to dominant tokens, causing irreversible collapse of reachable reasoning paths (Section 3.1).

Empirical coverage analysis shows greedy top-1 decoding paths capture only 83.84% of the safe manifold (16.16% loss), while top-8 and top-16 sampling capture 97.47% and 98.46% respectively (Table 1, Section 3.2).
On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, APO improves Pass@1 to 50.67% versus 48.68% for GRPO and 44.53% for GRPO-KL, while also improving Pass@K to 78.07% versus GRPO's 76.56% (Table 2, Section 5.2).

On Minerva with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, APO raises policy entropy from 0.405 (GRPO) to 0.485 and lowers max-token probability from 0.878 to 0.849, indicating reduced over-confident collapse (Table 3, Section 6.2).

The best APO configuration uses pull coefficient beta=0.1, push coefficient lambda=1.05, and anchor size K=8, with performance degrading at both weaker and stronger regularization settings (Figure 5, Table 5, Section 6.1).

CMeeyJzWZ5.text: OSM+ compiles a global road network graph with 1.96 billion split edges and 7.48 billion total vertices (roads plus POI data), with a roadnet-only subset of 2.18 billion vertices and 833.4 million split edges (Table 1, Section 2.1).

The 31-city traffic prediction benchmark scales city graphs up to roughly 30,000 nodes, versus hundreds of intersections in prior benchmarks, and evaluation of 7 baseline methods shows no single method dominates across all cities (Table 5, Section 3.1).

The six-city traffic policy control dataset scales from 16 signalized intersections (Hangzhou) up to 18,948 intersections (Beijing), enabling thousand-scale multi-agent coordination (Table 6, Section 3.2).
Window-check spatial query optimization reduces point-query time from 310s to 79s, and k-d tree optimization reduces nearest-neighbor query time from 41.14s to 1.49s (Table 3, Section 2.2).
An ODPS-based kernel density estimation pipeline processes data roughly 40x faster than an equivalent Spark implementation (Table 4, Section 2.2).

4GX4r1CYtD.text: ScaleEnv builds executable environments from scratch using a Tool Dependency Graph to synthesize tool/database schemas with procedural (executable) testing (Section 4.1).
Task instantiation uses seed chain sampling with dependency-aware topological graph expansion and LLM-gated chain extension to scale to 2,560 tasks across 16 domains (Section 4.2).
On τ2-Bench, Qwen3-SE-8B improves Retail accuracy from 57.0% to 71.9% and Airline from 38.0% to 58.6% over the base model (Table 1, Section 5.2).
Ablating executability verification drops accuracy from 50.9% to 42.3% on Retail, 37.5% to 30.0% on Airline, and 27.2% to 25.2% on Telecom (Table 3).
Pass@4 performance on VitaBench improves monotonically as the number of training domains scales from N=2 to N=16, with the trend still rising at N=16 (Figure 3).
Rule-based reward achieves 38.5% average accuracy and 62.9% Pass@4, outperforming LLM-as-Judge reward at 36.5% average and 58.8% Pass@4 (Table 4).

KSF8Q492oV.text: TimeGuard uses a two-stage channel-wise reliable pool training paradigm: Stage I time-aware pool initialization via Reverse-Consistency Filtering (RCF) and Neighborhood Diversity Filtering (NDF), and Stage II Distance-Regularized Loss Selection (DRLS) for progressive pool expansion (Section 4).

Against the BackTime attack on PEMS03, TimeGuard reduces poisoned MAE (MAE_P) to 39.303 versus 22.397 for the best training-phase baseline PDB, a roughly 1.96x MAE_P improvement over the leading baseline while keeping clean MAE (MAE_C) within about 5% (Table 1, Table 3).

Across three attacks (Random, FreqBack-TSF, BackTime) TimeGuard attains MAE_C of 17.928, 17.628, and 18.048 respectively, close to clean-training performance, alongside FDER scores of 0.868, 0.847, and 0.808 (Table 3).
On cross-dataset evaluation against BackTime, TimeGuard reaches MAE_P/FDER of 39.303/0.808 on PEMS03, 66.534/0.874 on Weather, and 1.443/0.652 on ETTm1 (Table 4, Section 5.1).
Ablation shows removing the channel-wise pool formulation drops FDER to 0.478-0.507, and removing DRLS drops FDER to 0.586-0.607, confirming both components are necessary (Table 5, Section 5.2).
TimeGuard incurs about 1.58x training overhead relative to vanilla training, comparable to the PDB baseline (Table 6, Section 5.2).

y5GiPedJPV.text: ReTimeCausal integrates an Additive Noise Model with an Expectation-Maximization loop that alternates E-step imputation of missing values (conditional expectation under the current causal estimate) and M-step sparse regression to refine the causal graph (Section on EM Framework / Method).

Proposition 1 (Structural Consistency) proves that under finite-order Markovity, time-invariant mechanisms, and causal sufficiency, ReTimeCausal recovers the true causal graph with probability one as sample size and iterations grow (Proposition 1).

Noise-aware imputation injects noise into imputed values (X̂ᵢᵗ = fᵢ(Paᵢᵗ) + ϵᵢᵗ) to preserve the statistical independence assumptions needed for downstream edge pruning (Method, Eq. for noise-aware imputation).

On a 20-variable linear-SEM benchmark with 60% missingness, ReTimeCausal attains F1 = 0.930 versus 0.205 for the best baseline PCMCI+EM, and at 80% missingness reaches F1 = 1.000 versus 0.190 for PCMCI+EM (Experiments/Results table).
On a 50-variable TANH nonlinear benchmark with 60% missingness, ReTimeCausal achieves F1 = 0.816 (SHD = 39), substantially above the best baseline PCMCI+EM at F1 = 0.258 (Experiments/Results table).

On the real-world CausalRivers dataset (10 nodes) with 60% missingness, ReTimeCausal reaches F1 = 0.436 versus 0.348 for the kernelized DYNOTEARS* baseline, both evaluated after TimeMixer preprocessing for the baselines (Experiments/Results table).

JfjYFLHqus.text: DyPE dynamically rescales positional encodings at each diffusion sampling step via a time-dependent scaling function κ(t) = λs · t^λt, rather than using a single static extrapolation as in prior NTK-aware or YaRN methods (Method section, DyPE formulation).

The method is motivated by a spectral-progression observation that low-frequency image structure converges early in diffusion sampling while high frequencies keep evolving throughout, as visualized in the progression map (Figure 2(b)).

DyPE proposes three concrete variants: Dy-PI (time-aware position interpolation), Dy-NTK (frequency-dependent rescaling with temporal modulation), and Dy-YaRN (dynamic threshold adjustment) (Method section).

DyPE requires no retraining and adds no additional sampling cost, enabling FLUX to generate images beyond 16 megapixels (e.g., 4096x4096) with no extra inference-time overhead (Section on efficiency).
On the Aesthetic-4K benchmark at 4096x4096 resolution, Dy-YaRN improves CLIPScore from 25.50 (baseline FLUX) to 29.28, ImageReward from -0.73 to 1.09, and FID from 195.68 to 186.00 (Table 1).
In human evaluation, Dy-YaRN is preferred over baselines 87-90% of the time across texture, structure, and text-alignment comparisons (Table 2).

Y3tTG28OO9.text: T-POP steers a frozen LLM's decoding at test time by learning an online reward function from pairwise preference feedback, combining test-time alignment with a dueling-bandits token-pair selection strategy that balances exploitation and exploration (Method/Overview).

On the ArmoRM main results across Mistral-7B, Qwen2-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B with four preference attributes (creative, verbose, concise, uplifting), T-POP improves average scores by about 28.0% over the AMULET baseline for Qwen2-7B and 19.9% for Mistral-7B, with an overall gain of about 14.7% (Table 1).

T-POP achieves a win rate of 68.8%-100% against the base (unmodified) LLM across settings, averaging 94.2%, and attains the highest or second-highest performance in 31 of 36 experimental configurations (Table 2).
Figure 2 shows T-POP achieves sharp initial performance gains within the first 20 interaction iterations, with alignment peaking between 40 and 60 interactions (Figure 2).
Ablation over the reward weight ω finds peak performance at ω=1.0, with larger ω values causing reward hacking and degraded output quality (Ablation study).
On the smaller Llama-3.2-1B model, T-POP improves the alignment score from 0.28 to 0.44, indicating the method scales down to resource-constrained models (Model scalability experiment).

TaDbT9pZr7.text: Atom Theory achieves sparse reconstruction with mean R² of 99.92% on Gemma2-2B, 99.93% on Gemma2-9B, and 99.85% on Llama3.1-8B (Figure 4).
Atoms satisfy the uniqueness/stability condition (q*) with 99.8% average satisfaction across models, compared to 68.2% for dictionary-learned features and only 0.5% for individual neurons (Figure 7).
Theorem 2 derives the explicit closed-form Atomic Inner Product (AIP) as S = c²(DD⊤)⁻¹ (Theorem 2).
Theorem 9 proves uniqueness and exact ℓ₁ recoverability of atoms when the mutual coherence μ satisfies μ < 1/(2K−1) (Theorem 9).
Theorem 10 proves that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) with threshold activation can identify atoms under specified amplitude gap conditions (Theorem 10).

The Normalized Atomic Inner Product (NAIP) distribution concentrates near zero off-diagonal, with pairwise atom angles centered near 90° after correcting for softmax-induced representation shifting (Figure 6).

mAusAlRZ0a.text: PepMirror is presented as the first wet-lab validated generative AI model for de novo design of D-peptide binders against L-chirality protein targets (Section 4.3).

A synthesized D-peptide candidate, D-1412, binds CD38 with a measured dissociation constant of approximately 10 μM, selected from 12 candidates synthesized out of 5,000 generated designs (Section 4.3, Figure 5).
The Axial-Field-Invariant (AFI) mechanism enables cross-chirality generalization from homo-chiral (L-L) training data to hetero-chiral (D-L) design tasks (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

With AFI, the median inversion-induced latent discrepancy reaches the 10⁻² scale, roughly four orders of magnitude larger than models lacking AFI, evidencing chirality-awareness (Section 4.1, Figure 3).

PepMirror achieves 99.93% correct L-chirality and 99.91% correct D-chirality classification, with in-silico success rates of 99.67% (L) and 99.76% (D) and interface improvement scores of 69.89% (L) and 63.44% (D) (Table 1, Table 2).
Proposition 3.2 shows that E(3)-equivariant models without the AFI mechanism produce identical outputs for mirror-image (enantiomeric) inputs, motivating the need for AFI (Proposition 3.2).

bpLE7QFM1a.text: RUAC achieves an average J&F score of 81.62 across 23 zero-shot out-of-domain datasets, outperforming Bayes-SAM2 (79.87) by 1.75 points and the SAM2 zero-shot baseline (67.75) by nearly 14 points (Table 1, Section 4.1).
RUAC improves uncertainty-accuracy correlation, reaching a PAvPU of 63.72 on out-of-distribution data versus 55.40 for Bayes-SAM2, an improvement of 8.32 points (Table 2, Section 4.2).
RUAC improves calibration on all three metrics simultaneously, achieving ECE of 0.117 and AURC of 0.092 versus Bayes-SAM2's 0.123 and 0.102 respectively (Table 3, Section 4.2).
The method trains a Bayesian mask decoder with Weibull variational posteriors over image and mask tokens to produce dual-granularity (pixel and semantic level) uncertainty estimates (Section 3.2).

A collaborative style-deformation adversarial attack jointly perturbs texture (via an AdaIN-based style network ψₛ with GCN-coordinated multi-object perturbation) and geometry (via a deformation network ψₐ predicting dense offset fields) during training to harden uncertainty estimates (Section 3.3, Figure 2).

RUAC is trained on a single source domain (MOSE dataset frames) and evaluated zero-shot on 23 target domains spanning objects, scenes, scientific, and egocentric categories using a deterministic 3-click prompting protocol (Section 4, Table 1).

UzusuBuNfT.text: iVGR-Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 76.6% average accuracy on fine-grained vision-language benchmarks, a 6.5-point improvement over its baseline (Table 2).
iVGR-Qwen3-VL-8B and iVGR-Qwen3-VL-32B achieve 80.6% (+4.4 points) and 82.9% (+3.3 points) average accuracy respectively over their baselines (Table 2).
On fine-grained VQA benchmarks V*, HR4K, HR8K, and MME-RW-Lite, iVGR yields gains of +7.9, +9.3, +10.4, and +11.1 points respectively (Table 2).

iVGR uses a dual-stream training strategy combining a grounded stream that generates bounding boxes with a textual stream that reasons purely in language, tied together by a consistency reward (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

The consistency reward assigns scores of 1.0 for fully consistent descriptions, 0.7 for a single-type deviation, 0.3 for compound deviations, and 0.0 for contradictory content between the two streams (Section 3.3).

iVGR is trained on 51K samples (37K from TreeVGR-RL plus 14K general reasoning data) and evaluated on 8 fine-grained and 6 general VQA benchmarks, motivated by the finding that mandating explicit object boxes at inference time often degrades performance relative to standard textual chain-of-thought (Section 3.1, Section 4).

Tg9q3RHCdM.text: KeyVT combines KeyV, a geometry-aware key-view selection module using camera position and orientation to compute spatial distances via a combined positional-plus-angular distance formula (Eq. 3-4), with KeyT, an optimal-transport-guided token compression module (Section 3).

KeyT formulates token selection as an entropy-regularized Sinkhorn optimal transport problem between view tokens and virtual tokens, run for 10-15 iterations at learning rate 1e-2 (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

On ScanQA validation (4,675 QA pairs), KeyVT achieves a CIDEr score of 100.7 with the LLaVA-Video backbone, outperforming tuning-free baselines DivPrune (99.4), FLoC (99.4), and AKS (99.0), and approaching the training-based Video-3D method (102.1) (Table 1).
KeyVT is evaluated on three benchmarks: ScanQA (validation, 4,675 pairs), SQA3D (test, 3,519 pairs), and VSI-Bench (5,000+ pairs across 8 subtasks) (Section 4).
The optimal window size hyperparameter δ for KeyV sub-scene partitioning is found to be 1.0, and the method operates under an input budget of 8 equivalent frames compressed from 16 (Table 10).

J0y3sNbo9G.text: Isolation Forest's expected depth function is derived in closed form by modeling the iTree growth process as a random walk with transition probabilities based on point spacing (Theorem 3.5).

For marginal single anomalies, Isolation Forest's detection threshold scales as U·κ (data-dependent), while k-NN requires separation greater than U+(k-1)δ/2 (parameter-dependent on k), showing iForest has greater parameter adaptability (Theorems 4.3-4.5).

For central single anomalies, Isolation Forest's decision threshold is Θ(√(n₀κ)) versus k-NN's Θ(kδ), demonstrating iForest's lower sensitivity to centrally-located anomalies (Theorems 4.6-4.7, Table 2).
For marginal clustered anomalies of size n₁, Isolation Forest requires separation of order Θ(n₁²κ) while k-NN requires Θ(kδ) under the constraint ω(n₁)≤k≤o(n₀) (Theorems 4.8-4.9).
Empirical mean-squared error between empirical and theoretical expected depths decreases as the number of trees increases, confirming the concentration property of Proposition 3.1 (Figure 3).
Across OpenML benchmark datasets, 930,738 of 930,751 tested dimensions satisfy the condition κ≥√(n+3) required for the theoretical analysis (Section 4, Assumption 4.2).

qPqJH0heR0.text: MedMamba achieves top-1 accuracy of 92.13% on TDBRAIN, 89.36% on PTB, 84.48% on APAVA, 73.86% on PTB-XL, and 57.56% on ADFTD in the subject-independent setting, outperforming or matching the strongest baseline (MedGNN or KEMed) on four of five datasets (Section 5, Table with subject-independent results).

MedMamba obtains 20 top-1 and 3 top-2 results out of 30 total evaluation entries across the five datasets when compared against nine baselines including GPT4TS, PatchTST, Medformer, MedGNN, and KEMed (Section 5.2).

The Tri-Branch Differential State Space Encoder (TDSSE) fuses raw, temporal-difference, and frequency-domain views to suppress nonstationary artifacts such as baseline drift, as introduced in Section 4.2.
The Spatial Graph Mamba (SGM) module learns directed inter-channel dependencies with sparsity and acyclicity constraints, removing the need for a predefined anatomical graph (Section 4.3).
MedMamba maintains linear computational complexity in sequence length, in contrast to the quadratic scaling of Transformer-based baselines such as PatchTST and Medformer (Section 4, Section 5).

VHYljDMosS.text: SuCo defines Minimal Sufficient CoT (MSC) as the shortest prefix of a chain-of-thought trajectory that is sufficient to produce the correct final answer (Section on MSC definition).

At the 1.5B parameter scale, SuCo achieves 53.1% average accuracy across benchmarks, a 5.1 percentage point improvement over the strongest baseline, together with a 74.1% reduction in reasoning tokens (Table 1).

At the 7B parameter scale, SuCo achieves 72.1% average accuracy (5.1 points over the strongest baseline) with a 75.8% token reduction, and on AIME25 specifically reaches 61.7% accuracy, a 24.1-point improvement over DeepSeek-R1, while using 75.3% fewer tokens (Table 1).

SuCo's two-stage training pipeline consists of Stage I MSC-Aligned Fine-Tuning (MFT), which uses problem-adaptive sufficiency thresholds, followed by Stage II Sufficiency-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), a reinforcement-learning stage (Section describing MFT and SAPO).
SuCo is evaluated on mathematics (GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC23, AIME25), code (MBPP, LiveCodeBench-V6), and science (MMLU-STEM, GPQA-Diamond) benchmarks (Table 1).

Of 270,011 total training samples used to construct MSC supervision, 109,882 (40.7%) have an empty minimal sufficient CoT, and the average full CoT length of 3,781 tokens is reduced to an average refined MSC length of 1,138 tokens (Appendix B).

z2en0iqxwo.text: The OmniVCHall benchmark used to evaluate compositional hallucination comprises 823 videos and 9,027 VQA samples spanning eight hallucination types, including a novel camera-based hallucination category (Section describing OmniVCHall construction).

TriCD improves Qwen3-VL-Instruct-8B accuracy from 0.67 to 0.73 (+9.61%) and VideoLLaMA3-7B accuracy from 0.60 to 0.67 (+12.03%), with the largest gains concentrated on compositional (C_YNQA, C_MCQA) rather than single-factor sub-tasks (Section on TriCD results).

Across 39 evaluated VLLMs, including Qwen3-VL variants (2B-235B), GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and Gemini-3-pro, advanced proprietary models still exhibit substantial performance degradation on compositional hallucination questions relative to single-factor ones (Section presenting the 39-model evaluation).

Human annotators achieve 0.95 accuracy on the OmniVCHall benchmark compared to a best AI model accuracy of 0.76, indicating a persistent human-model gap on compositional hallucination (Section reporting human baseline).

TriCD combines an Adaptive Perturbation Controller that selects among eight video distortion tools with a Saliency-Guided Enhancement mechanism fusing DINOv3 spatial features and optical-flow temporal features, both optimized via reinforcement learning without modifying the base VLLM's parameters (Section describing the TriCD architecture).

ptbE5s38lX.text: DyCon is a training-free framework that uses a lightweight linear regressor trained on step embeddings to estimate reasoning difficulty and dynamically suppress reflection-related tokens during generation (Section 3.2).

DyCon is evaluated on four models spanning 4B to 32B parameters (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, Qwen3-14B, QwQ-32B) across twelve benchmarks spanning math, question-answering, and coding (Section 4).
On Qwen3-4B, DyCon achieves 86.7% Pass@1 on AIME24 (+3.4 points over baseline) with a 12.2% token reduction, and 100% Pass@1 on AMC23 while cutting tokens by 17.3% (Table 1).
Across math reasoning benchmarks, DyCon achieves up to 40.6% token reduction combined with up to 6.7% absolute accuracy gains relative to baseline reasoning models (Section 4).

On non-mathematical benchmarks, DyCon improves GPQA-Diamond accuracy by 2.0 points (to 68.2%) with 32.6% token reduction, and improves StrategyQA accuracy by 1.7 points (to 96.0%) with 24.7% token reduction (Table 2).

A difficulty regressor trained on only 600 MATH samples generalizes to other domains without retraining, maintaining high accuracy and strong token-efficiency gains on out-of-domain benchmarks (Section 4, generalization analysis).

E8Q093jDug.text: REPVLM estimates epistemic uncertainty by using Conditional Riemannian Flow Matching to model the probability density of VLM embeddings on the hypersphere, using negative log-likelihood as the uncertainty proxy (Section 4.2).

On zero-shot classification across ImageNet-1K, Food101, CIFAR-100, ObjectNet, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Sketch, REPVLM achieves near-perfect Spearman correlation (approximately 0.99-1.00) between its uncertainty score and prediction error (Table 2).
REPVLM requires 9.80 GFLOPs at inference versus 92.50 GFLOPs for Monte Carlo Dropout (MCDO), a roughly 9x reduction in computational cost (Table 3).

Accuracy-rejection curves show REPVLM has a sharper upward slope than baselines such as MCDO and ProbVLM, with Accuracy @ 90% Rejection ranging from 0.614 to 0.904 across datasets (Figure 2, Table 2).
An ablation shows the Riemannian (hyperspherical) formulation outperforms Euclidean flow-matching variants by 3-5%, with performance converging after about 5 ODE integration steps (Figure 3).

TzzJped56P.text: FlowSeg introduces Bidirectional Semantic Flow (BSF), which passes semantic conditions from LLM-derived embeddings into mask decoding while updating those embeddings from emerging visual evidence at each decoding stage (Section 3.3).
FlowSeg includes a Boundary-Aware Mask Refinement module applied on top of the bidirectional flow mechanism (Section 3.4).

On referring expression segmentation, FlowSeg achieves 85.8% cIoU on RefCOCO val, 80.2% on RefCOCO+ val, and 86.5% on RefCOCOg val, each outperforming X-SAM (85.1%, 78.0%, 83.8% respectively) (Table 1).
On reasoning segmentation, FlowSeg reaches 54.7% cIoU on ReasonSeg test, versus 41.0% for X-SAM (Table 2).
Ablating the full FlowSeg design against a baseline architecture raises average cIoU from 82.4% to 84.2%, a gain of 1.8 points (Table 3).

An oracle upper-bound analysis shows both FlowSeg and its baseline reach approximately 91% oracle cIoU, indicating that mask selection rather than mask generation quality is the main performance bottleneck (Table 5).

ZXFTvoBZ1B.text: Near-boundary Stochastic Rescue (NSR) is a plug-and-play modification to policy-gradient clipping that stochastically recovers tokens whose importance ratio falls just outside the clipping trust region, rather than discarding their gradient signal (Section 5).
With Qwen2.5-Math-7B, adding NSR improves AIME24 Pass@1 from 35.83% to 40.76% (+4.93 points) (Table 1).
With Qwen3-8B, NSR improves AIME24 Pass@1 by 6.36 points (37.29% to 43.65%), and with Qwen3-30B-A3B by 4.48 points (54.17% to 58.65%), showing gains hold from 7B to 30B model scale (Table 1).
On general-science benchmarks (GPQA), NSR yields improvements of +3.72%, +1.14%, and +0.26% at the 7B, 8B, and 30B scales respectively, on top of DAPO/GSPO baselines (Table 2).
NSR's stochastic boundary-local rescue achieves a mean Pass@1 of 40.76±1.56, more stable than deterministic Explicit Soft Decay variants (k=2,3,4), which range from 37.74 to 38.96 (Table 3).

RzgNmKi5Hw.text: Theoretical analysis shows the gradient signal-to-noise ratio (GSNR) for meta-network training-data selection scales unfavorably with the dominant-index probability, which depends inversely on the square of the batch size (Theorem 3.4), and its upper bound depends on N^4 and inversely on batch size^4 (Theorem 3.6).
Increasing the meta-batch size from N=64 to N=1024 raises average accuracy from 70.96% to 73.75%, a 2.79-point gain, confirming the batch-size fix for poor GSNR (Table 2).

The proposed method (informative features plus large batch size) achieves 73.75% average accuracy across four benchmarks, a gain of 5.49 points over training without selection and 2.89 points over the strongest baseline, Aux-Clf Val (Table 1).

Feature ablations show that replacing the proposed distributional+training-dynamics features with raw image features drops accuracy by 5.55 points, and with training-loss-only features by 3.90 points (Table 2).
Theorem 3.2 proves that normalized selection weights converge to one-hot vectors, i.e., a winner-takes-all dynamic that causes only a single training example to dominate the gradient (Theorem 3.2).
Evaluation spans WaterBirds, CelebA, Texture, and PACS (4 domains), with a separate ViT-Base architecture check reproducing a 5.30-point gain over no selection (Table 4).

knVbandOWj.text: Neural QAOA² combines a Generative Evaluative Network (a multi-view GNN evaluator f_φ) with a Joint Generator (g_θ) that produces graph partitions and QAOA parameters using an Orthogonal Complement Head, Greedy Capacity Discretization, and a Straight-Through Estimator (Section 4).

On the 183-instance benchmark spanning QUBO (B, BE, GKA), MaxCut (W, HR), and Ising (L, BMZ) instances, Neural QAOA² attains an average rank of 1.46 and wins on 60 of 93 out-of-distribution instances, and ranks 1.74 with 28/50 wins on the in-distribution test set (Table 1, Table 2).

The learned evaluator's predicted performance ratio correlates with ground truth at r=0.9258, far higher than the r=0.2859 correlation achieved by a modularity-based proxy, showing modularity is a misaligned optimization target (Figure 5).

Neural QAOA² outperforms heuristic graph-partitioning baselines (random, modularity-based, boundary-vertices minimization, Kernighan-Lin) and advanced QAOA parameter initializations (INTERP, FOURIER, TQA, QIBPI) (Section 5).
Neural QAOA² generalizes zero-shot across graph sizes from N=21 to N=1000 nodes, covering both interpolation and extrapolation regimes relative to training sizes (Figure 3).

Ablation shows removing the partition-induced subgraph view degrades performance by 1.07%, removing the Orthogonal Complement Head by 0.85%, and removing the stop-gradient mechanism by 0.81%, all statistically significant at p<0.01 (Table 3).

yiq2tZojBK.text: Lemma 3.1 establishes that orbit averages over a weight-space symmetry group remain invariant under the group's transformations, forming the basis for the Hessian approximation (Lemma 3.1).

Section 3.1 derives a Hessian approximation H*_g = S_g^(1/2) (Equation 11) built by analytically averaging second-order gradient variations S_g and S_w over a symmetry orbit from a single gradient (Section 3.1).

Lemma 3.3 proves that restricting the symmetry group under a Kronecker block-diagonal curvature structure causes the proposed optimizer, Symo, to reduce mathematically to the Shampoo and Muon updates (Lemma 3.3).

Figure 2 shows that for MLPs, orbit averages decompose into sparse linear combinations of commutant-algebra basis elements, with different symmetry group choices yielding between 4 and 32 scalar factors (Figure 2).
Section 4 reports that the Hessian approximation achieves a cosine similarity of 0.2-0.3 with the secant condition along gradient directions on a roughly 20,000-parameter network (Section 4).
Section 5 shows Symo produces training curves that overlap almost perfectly with Muon on MNIST autoencoders (2.8M parameters) and nanoGPT character-level prediction (10M parameters) (Section 5).

46FG6Y9MuF.text: Proposition 3.1 establishes that the identifiability class of the PLN-ICA model coincides with the invariance class of its mixing function, giving identifiability without restrictive noise assumptions (Proposition 3.1).

Corollary 3.2 shows that for the proposed Auto-Regressive PLN-ICA (ARPLN-ICA) model, the mixing matrix Γ is identifiable up to column-wise permutation and rescaling under mild non-degeneracy conditions on the latent covariance structure (Corollary 3.2).

ARPLN-ICA combines component-wise regime switching via discrete Markov chains with regime-dependent Gaussian autoregressive latent dynamics and Poisson log-normal count emissions (Equation 2), fit via a stochastic variational EM algorithm with a GRU-based amortized encoder (Algorithm 1).

In a longitudinal study of 55 gnotobiotic mice tracked over 56 days (T=26 timepoints), Figure 4 shows inferred regime switches align with documented perturbations, including colonization at t=0 and Clostridium difficile infection at t=13 (Figure 4).

Figure 5 shows that one inferred component captures co-variation of opportunistic pathogens with C. difficile while showing negative correlation with the anti-inflammatory species Akkermansia muciniphila (Figure 5).

Figure 6 reports competitive leave-one-out forecasting performance for the model measured by Poisson deviance, MAE, and Aitchison distance, with medoid mixing alignment used across folds to ensure interpretation stability (Figure 6, Section 5.3).

Wrywrky3Fk.text: HiSD segments unlabeled observation trajectories into discrete skill labels using Asymmetric Soft Optimal Transport with temporal consistency constraints (Section 4.1), then induces hierarchical grammars over the resulting skill sequences using a modified Sequitur algorithm (Section 4.2), requiring no action labels or rewards.
On the Craftax Stone Pickaxe Static task, Table 1 reports HiSD achieves 66% average mIoU versus 45% for CompILE and 30% for OMPN (Table 1, Section 5.1).

On the Minecraft Mapped skill dataset (14 categories from 44 raw skills extracted via MineCLIP embeddings from 500 VPT trajectories), Table 1 reports HiSD achieves 38% average mIoU versus 14% for OMPN and 6% for CompILE (Table 1, Section 5.2).

Section 5.4 evaluates hierarchy quality via unique tree count, average tree depth, tree size, and branching factor, showing HiSD discovers structured hierarchies across both Craftax and Minecraft domains (Section 5.4).
Figure 1 and the abstract report that hierarchies discovered by HiSD accelerate and stabilize learning on downstream reinforcement learning tasks compared to baselines (Figure 1).

qeHq1NtpLt.text: CoLLiS trains multiple LiDAR representations (FRNet, PolarNet, Cylinder3D) collaboratively as coequal students in a single step, replacing the traditional two-step teacher-student pseudo-labeling pipeline used by prior semi-supervised methods (Section 1, Figure 1).
Table 1 reports that on nuScenes with 1% labels, CoLLiS achieves 63.2 mIoU compared to 58.7 mIoU for LaserMix, showing its largest gains occur in low-label regimes (Table 1).
Table 1 shows CoLLiS consistently outperforms prior semi-supervised LiDAR segmentation methods across nuScenes, SemanticKITTI, and ScribbleKITTI benchmarks (Table 1).
Table 3 reports CoLLiS requires roughly 50% less training time than IT2 (25.6h vs 50.8h) while maintaining memory usage comparable to single-representation LaserMix (Table 3).

Table 4 shows that scaling CoLLiS to up to four collaborating representations yields consistent mIoU gains, with weaker representations benefiting most and stronger ones gradually saturating (Table 4).

Section 3.2.1 introduces Consensus-Driven Augmentation, which strengthens augmentation intensity when students agree and weakens it when they disagree, while Section 3.2.2 introduces Absolute and Relative Reliability metrics to filter pseudo-label supervision (Section 3.2.1, Section 3.2.2).

DRHlbrUrhY.text: Anchored Decoding fuses the next-token distributions of a risky model (trained on mixed-license data) and a safe reference model (trained on permissively licensed data) at each decoding step via a closed-form weighted geometric mean solving a per-step constrained optimization problem (Equation 5, Section 3.2).

The abstract and Table 1 report the method eliminates up to 75% of the measurable copying gap, averaged over six copying metrics (ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L, MinHash, ACS, word-level LCS, character-level LCS), between the risky baseline and the safe reference model (Abstract, Table 1).

At the high-protection operating point (>=75% copying reduction), Table 1 reports factuality/fluency scores of 0.53/4.02 for the {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B} model pair, outperforming TokenSwap (0.44/3.77) and RCAD (0.37/3.38) (Table 1).
Table 2 reports the method incurs only a modest 1.1x throughput overhead relative to the baseline risky model (Table 2).

Section 3.3-3.4 describe an adaptive banking mechanism that rolls unused copying budget forward and a prefix debt detection mechanism, based on log-likelihood ratios, that tightens constraints on memorization-prone prompts (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).

Section 6 shows per-step KL divergence between the risky and safe distributions identifies copyright-sensitive regions of generation, with Figure 5 showing copying risk is front-loaded early in generation (Section 6, Figure 5).

im2Dw94HjX.text: Proposition 2.2 shows the alignment-uniformity conflict metric ζₐ converges to 1 as the number of modalities M increases, formalizing a systematic accumulation of opposing optimization forces in multimodal InfoNCE objectives (Section 2, Proposition 2.2).
Proposition 2.3 proves the intra-alignment conflict χₐ grows with modality count and gives the lower bound E[χₐ] ≥ 1 − √((1+(M−2)μ̄)/(M−1)) (Section 2, Proposition 2.3).

The proposed decoupled objective is derived as an efficient proxy for a global Hölder divergence over multiple modality distributions, decomposing into separate intra-modality uniformity and anchor-based alignment terms (Section 3, Equation 14).
On cross-modal retrieval, UniAlign achieves 58.8 average R@1 on text-to-video retrieval, outperforming the GRAM baseline by 3.0 R@1 (Table 1).
On UnCLIP-style generation with the Kandinsky decoder, UniAlign achieves 42.72 FID versus GRAM's 62.11 FID; with Stable UnCLIP it achieves 39.63 FID versus GRAM's 45.53 FID (Table 3).
Embedding visualizations show InfoNCE produces distinct, separated per-modality clusters while UniAlign substantially reduces inter-modality distribution gaps (Figure 2).

MKNimf9bIx.text: Early-stage Advantage Collapse Ratio (ACR) explains 62% of the variance in final performance across 245 training configurations, with an R² of 0.617 (Section 5).
AVSPO reduces ACR by 58-63% relative to GRPO, lowering the observed ACR range from 0.28-0.45 down to 0.11-0.18 (Section 4.2, Table 1).

AVSPO yields consistent accuracy gains of 4-6 percentage points over GRPO on mathematical reasoning benchmarks across Qwen2.5 model scales from 0.5B to 14B parameters, e.g. 16.5%→21.0% at 0.5B and 49.9%→54.5% at 14B (Table 1).

An ablation over virtual sample construction strategies shows the stratified approach achieves the lowest ACR (0.15) and the largest accuracy gain (+8.6%) compared to alternative strategies (Table 2).
AVSPO addresses both failure modes of advantage collapse, reducing all-incorrect-group collapse from 24.8% to 8.7% and all-correct-group collapse from 15.2% to 6.3% (Table 3).

The adaptive thresholding mechanism reaches 60% accuracy in 295 training steps versus 380 steps for a fixed threshold, evaluated across six math reasoning benchmarks (MATH-500, GSM8K, Minerva, OlympiadBench, AMC, AIME) plus MMLU-Pro for out-of-domain generalization (Table 4, Section 5).

Sh3rKEAxlW.text: The stepwise momentum rule is analyzed as a second-order dynamical system that admits complex conjugate eigenvalues, and stability is enforced via a quadrant-based constraint β_t ≤ 1−α_t with μ_t ∈ (e⁻¹, 1) (Section 3.2).
MDN is evaluated at 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens against Transformers, Mamba2, and GDN, reporting perplexity, commonsense reasoning, and in-context retrieval metrics (Section 4.2, Table 2).
MDN achieves the highest average score on LongBench at 16K sequence length among the compared architectures (Section 4.2, Table 3).
On the synthetic MQAR associative-recall task, MDN outperforms competing linear attention variants across varying sequence lengths (Section 4.1, Figure 4).
An ablation on the 400M-parameter model isolates the contribution of the momentum components and the stability constraint to overall performance (Section 4.3, Table 4).

Decoding latency and training throughput comparisons show MDN attains competitive throughput relative to other linear attention models while retaining causal parallelizability (Section 4.3, Figure 6).

eldrXxp9eG.text: Theorem 3.5 establishes a minimax lower bound showing any unbiased protocol with shuffle index χ must incur worst-case mean squared error at least d·χ² for d-dimensional vector mean estimation (Section 3, Theorem 3.5).
Proposition 3.7 shows that PrivUnit, which is optimal under local differential privacy (LDP), becomes suboptimal after shuffling in dimension d>1 (Section 3, Proposition 3.7).

Theorem 4.1 constructs the Blanket-Mixed Gaussian mechanism, achieving MSE = d·χ²·(1 + 3/2·χ^(-2/3) + O(χ^(-4/3))) as χ→∞, asymptotically matching the established lower bound (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 3.3 shows that in the high-privacy regime the optimal worst-case MSE satisfies d·σ² ≤ error ≤ d·σ²·(1+η(σ)) with η(σ)=O(σ^(-2/3)), nearly matching the central Gaussian mechanism (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).
Numerical evaluations compare the proposed shuffle-index-based mechanisms against baseline shuffle-model mechanisms in terms of empirical MSE (Section 5).

32Us54GZlT.text: Theorem 4.1 (Main Result) proves that for a weakly identifiable parameter θ where the model is G-equivariant end-to-end, there exist group actions on the latent spaces such that every layer f_i is individually G-equivariant (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

Definition 3.4 formalizes parameter identifiability as requiring that functionally equivalent parameters be related by symmetries of the latent spaces, underpinning the layerwise equivariance result (Section 3.2, Definition 3.4).

Conjecture 5.1 proposes that every MLP parameter has an equivalent form that is weakly identifiable, extending the applicability of the main theorem to standard MLP architectures (Section 5.1, Conjecture 5.1).

The framework is applied to both multi-layer perceptrons and multi-head attention networks as concrete examples of models satisfying the identifiability and equivariance conditions (Section 5.1, Section 5.2).
Illustrative experiments empirically demonstrate the emergence of layerwise equivariant structure in trained network weights, independent of the specific architecture used (Section 6).

nCWnYFezUm.text: WoG's Q-Former-based encoder compresses future observations from frozen foundation vision models (DINOv2, Wan VAE) into a compact condition space that guides action prediction via cross-attention in DiT blocks (Section 3.3).
On the SIMPLER Google Robot benchmark, WoG achieves a 69.4% overall success rate, outperforming pi_0 (56.8%), OpenVLA (33.8%), DeFI (48.3%), and VITA (57.4%) (Table 1).
On the SIMPLER WidowX Robot benchmark, WoG reaches a 63.5% overall average success rate, surpassing UniVLA (45.6%), ViPRA (62.5%), and pi_0 (27.1%) (Table 2).
In real-world Pick & Place experiments, WoG attains 60% in-distribution, 55% background-OOD, and 40% novel-object-OOD success rates, versus VPP's 55%, 30%, and 15% respectively (Table 7).
An ablation removing the future encoder drops Google Robot success rate from 70.9% to 66.7%, demonstrating the necessity of the Q-Former compression mechanism (Tables 5-6).
Incorporating unannotated human manipulation videos alongside robot-only data raises Pick & Place success from 60% to 70% (Table 9).

4aI2vOyyHH.text: MoshiRAG augments the 7B Moshi full-duplex speech model with a special retrieval trigger token, asynchronously invoking a retrieval back-end while conversation continues uninterrupted (Section 3.2).
On HaluEval, MoshiRAG achieves 36.3% accuracy (vs. a 42.0% reference and vanilla Moshi's 10.5%), rising to 51.3% when paired with a GPT-4.1 retrieval back-end (Table 1).
MoshiRAG is outperformed only by GPT-4o Audio (68.7%) among compared public speech language models on the factuality benchmark (Table 1).
On Full-Duplex-Bench, MoshiRAG lowers the pause-track turn-offset-ratio to 0.32 (vs. vanilla Moshi's 0.99) and raises user-interruption response quality to a GPT score of 3.75 (vs. 0.77) (Table 2).
MoshiRAG generalizes to unseen mathematical reasoning, reaching 33.9% accuracy on GSM8K (43.2% with GPT-4.1 back-end) compared to vanilla Moshi's 2.1% (Table 3).

Retrieval delay is trained via a sampling scheme, d' = U(0, d_lead) when d_lead < 2 seconds or with probability 0.2, otherwise d' = U(1.0, d_lead - 1.0), targeting retrieval completion within a 2-second keyword delay window (Section 4.2, Section 3.1).

BGmc3O41ZH.text: Theorem 3.2 establishes existence of a constrained Nash equilibrium under playerwise concavity (Assumption 1) and the MFCQ regularity condition (Assumption 2), without requiring joint convexity of the feasible set (Theorem 3.2).
The existence proof constructs a contractible (not necessarily convex) feasible set and applies Begle's fixed point theorem to a best-response mapping (Section 3).

A log-barrier regularized gradient ascent algorithm, using barrier B^eta_i(x) := u_i(x) + eta * sum_j log(c_j(x) - alpha_j), lets each player update using only its own gradient feedback while maintaining feasibility (Section 4).

Theorem 4.1 shows that for constrained potential games, setting the barrier parameter eta = epsilon and running T = O(epsilon^-3) iterations yields an epsilon-approximate constrained Nash equilibrium (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).

The O(epsilon^-3) rate for the constrained setting is slower than the O(epsilon^-2) rate known for unconstrained potential games, an extra O(epsilon^-1) factor attributed to decreasing stepsizes needed near the feasible boundary (Section 4.1).

hASSCnNDOl.text: Safe-CB constructs a harmful subspace via SVD over paired harmful/safe image-text embeddings self-identified by the model, then projects the codebook away from it as W^proj = W^ori(I - lambda * Proj_P(W^ori)) (Section on harmful space construction / codebook projection).
After projection, quality is restored via null-space constrained adaptive fine-tuning, W^safe = W^proj + Delta*Q, iterated until convergence without external human feedback (Method section).
The method is evaluated across five unified multimodal models: Janus Pro 1B, Janus Pro 7B, VILA-U, Emu3, LlamaGen, and OmniMamba (Experiments section).
On I2P, Safe-CB reduces the sexual-content detection rate from 0.12 to 0.04 and the violence rate from 0.39 to 0.21 relative to baseline (Table with I2P/CoPro results).

Across iterations, sexual-content mitigation on the reported benchmark improves from 0.1278 (0 iterations) to 0.0405 (3 iterations), saturating around 0.0412 at iteration 5, with 3 iterations at 300 samples outperforming a single-pass removal using the same data volume (Table 4).

Compared to a weight-modification 'Safe-Model' baseline, Safe-CB achieves lower sexual-content detection (0.044 vs. 0.0746) while also achieving better FID (70.66 vs. 92.13) (Comparison/ablation section).

guLrgDb2jB.text: dLLM-Cache combines long-interval prompt caching (refreshed every 50-100 steps) with adaptive response caching that uses a V-verify mechanism based on cosine similarity of Value vectors to identify tokens needing recomputation (Section 3.2).
On LLaDA 8B, dLLM-Cache yields a 4.29x speedup on GSM8K (TPS 7.32 to 31.43) with accuracy changing only from 69.06% to 67.32%, and up to 8.08x speedup on GPQA with zero accuracy loss (Table 1).
On Dream 7B, dLLM-Cache achieves a 5.10x speedup on GSM8K (TPS 6.36 to 32.44) with lossless accuracy, and a 7.15x speedup on GPQA (Table 2).
dLLM-Cache reports up to a 9.1x speedup on LongBench-HotpotQA using LLaDA 8B Base, with F1 score actually improving from 34.56 to 36.10 (Section on maximum acceleration results).

Compared to standard autoregressive models, LLaDA 8B with dLLM-Cache achieves a 3.39x speedup on GSM8K while maintaining 67.32% accuracy and incurring modest GPU memory overhead (17.93GB vs. 16.06GB for LLaMA3 8B) (Table 3).
The adaptive update ratio hyperparameter rho is fixed at 0.25 across all experiments, alongside configurable prompt refresh interval K_p and response refresh interval K_r (Hyperparameters section).

xixoixLXCr.text: A minimizer of the contrastive loss ℒ(s) is proven to be a maximizer of the ranking-based retrieval objective ℰ(s), establishing Fisher consistency between the contrastive training objective and downstream retrieval performance (Theorem 3.1).

A calibration-style inequality bounds the downstream retrieval suboptimality by the square root of the excess contrastive risk, ℰ*−ℰ(s) ≤ √(2/τ·(ℒ(s)−ℒ*)), quantitatively linking upstream loss gaps to downstream ranking gaps (Theorem 3.4).
For supervised contrastive representation learning (SCRL), the generalization bound scales as O(1/m + 1/√n) in the number of negatives m and number of anchors n (Theorem 4.5).

For self-supervised contrastive representation learning (SSCRL) with shared negative samples, the generalization bound scales as O(1/√m + 1/√n), a slower rate in m than the supervised case (Theorem 4.6).

The generalization analysis decomposes error into an inner error term from negative sampling and an outer error term from anchor point sampling, explaining why increasing the number of negatives improves rather than degrades generalization, contradicting prior O(log m/√n) bounds (Section 4).
Empirical validation on CLIP models shows generalization behavior consistent with the derived bounds as negative sample size is scaled (Section 5).

S9G3yu6vHl.text: TSRBench comprises 4,125 problems spanning 14 domains, organized into four capability dimensions: perception, reasoning, prediction, and decision-making (Section 3).

On TSRBench, the best-performing model overall, GPT-5 with combined text and visual (T+V) input, scores 55.6% accuracy, while the best open-source LLM (Qwen2.5-72B) scores 42.4% and the best open-source VLM (Qwen3-VL-32B) scores 44.9% (Table 2).

Scaling laws hold for perception and reasoning tasks but break down for the prediction dimension, where increased model scale does not reliably improve time series forecasting or event prediction accuracy (Section 4.3, Finding 1).

Perception, reasoning, and decision-making performance are highly correlated with each other but only weakly correlated with prediction performance, indicating a decoupling between semantic/contextual understanding and numerical forecasting ability (Section 4.3, Finding 2).

Models fail to effectively fuse textual and visual representations of time series inputs for reciprocal performance gains, despite the two modalities being shown to carry complementary information (Section 4.3, Finding 3).

An ablation on visualization resolution finds that 100 PPI is the optimal image resolution for visual time series inputs, and enabling an explicit reasoning mode significantly improves performance on non-perception tasks (Section 4.4).

iKKZmgxkbG.text: LIVE uses a cycle-consistency objective in which the model performs a forward rollout from ground-truth frames and then reverses the sequence to reconstruct the initial state, enabling bounded error accumulation over long rollouts without teacher-based distillation (Section 4).

On RealEstate10K, LIVE attains PSNR of 18.11 at 0-64 frames, 15.91 at 0-128 frames, and 14.57 at 0-200 frames, outperforming the NFD-DF baseline at all rollout lengths, with the largest margin at sequences of 256 frames or more (Table 1).
On the UE Engine game environment, LIVE reaches PSNR of 17.83 at 0-64 frames and 15.85 at 0-128 frames; on Minecraft, it achieves PSNR of 16.31 at 0-64 frames and 14.90 at 0-128 frames (Table 2).

An ablation removing the cycle-consistency objective causes PSNR at 200 frames to drop sharply to 11.18, and the progressive training curriculum is shown to outperform training with fixed rollout parameters (Table 3).
The LIVE model is a 774M-parameter DiT architecture trained on 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with batch size 64, at resolution 256×256 for RealEstate10K and 352×640 for UE Engine (Section 5).

HW85JYJ7JP.text: For cardinality constraints in the fully dynamic setting (supporting both insertions and deletions), the ConsistentCardinality algorithm achieves a (1/2 − 3ε)-approximation with O(1/ε²) consistency (Theorem 5.1).
For rank-k matroid constraints, the ConsistentMatroid algorithm achieves a (1/4 − 7ε)-approximation with O(log k/ε²) consistency (Theorem 4.8).

The general fully-dynamic framework combines a scheduling routine with robust and non-robust subroutines, ensuring non-overlapping transition windows and that at most an ε-fraction of time is spent in transition (Section 3, Lemma 3.2).
The matroid-constrained algorithm is instantiated using Robust-Swap and Swap subroutines, while the cardinality-constrained algorithm uses a simplified Robust-Greedy subroutine (Sections 4 and 5).

These results constitute the first constant-factor approximation algorithms with sublinear (in 1/ε) consistency for submodular maximization in the fully dynamic model supporting both element insertions and deletions (Section 1).

qnKVxU9EmU.text: DREAM is evaluated across six benchmark graph datasets—Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, DBLP, A-Photo, and Flickr—under three types of label noise: uniform, pair, and asymmetric (Table 1).

At a 30% noise rate, DREAM achieves 74.84% accuracy on Cora under pair noise versus 65.36% for a standard GCN baseline, and 71.06% on CiteSeer under uniform noise versus 55.05% for the baseline (Table 1).

DREAM selects reliable anchor nodes via a dual criterion: proximity-aware anchor selection with kp=15 anchors and topology-aware anchor selection with kt=10 anchors and maximum hop distance dmax=4 (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).
A semantic homogeneity score with temperature τ=0.04 is used to dynamically distinguish reliable from unreliable nodes based on relation-informed comparisons (Section 3.5).

Ablation variants V1 (removing topology anchors) and V2 (removing proximity anchors) each degrade performance relative to the full DREAM model, confirming both anchor types contribute to node reliability estimation (Section 5).

w0JhOFWPJl.text: GLU achieves quadratically better NTK conditioning than non-GLU structure, with condition number κ(K̃) = O(n/d²) for GLU versus κ(K) = O(n/d) for non-GLU (Theorem 3.1).
The GLU NTK can be approximated as a Hadamard-reweighted kernel K̃ ≈ K ⊙ (XX^T/d), producing a more contracted eigenvalue distribution than the non-GLU NTK (Section 3).
GLU's largest NTK eigenvalue scales as λ_max(K̃) = O(mn/d²) compared to λ_max(K) = O(mn/d) for non-GLU, while both share λ_min ~ O(m) (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

A loss-crossing phenomenon shows GLU and non-GLU training losses cross during optimization, consistent with the kernel-regime analysis of stage-wise convergence (Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.2, Figure 6).

GLU's primary benefit is accelerating optimization via better spectral conditioning rather than shrinking the generalization gap, as shown by comparing generalization gaps of GLU and non-GLU models (Section 5, Figure 7).
Condition numbers of GLU versus non-GLU structures are empirically measured in real architectures including ViT and GPT-2, corroborating the theoretical scaling (Figure 3).

0dd6iMYtwB.text: DTKG improves exact-match/accuracy over baselines by 5.0%-29.5% across six multi-hop QA datasets, with reported per-dataset results including 67.6% EM/93.9% ACC on Mintaka, 36.2% EM/85.8% ACC on HotpotQA, 41.0% EM/90.0% ACC on CWQ, and 50.0% EM/85.0% ACC on QALD10-en (Table 2).

A few-shot prompt-based classifier first categorizes each question as either 'parallel fact-verification' or 'chained multi-hop reasoning' before routing it to a dedicated processing branch, using five classification rules (Table 1, Section 3).

The dual-track architecture pairs a Parallel Fact-Checking Branch for independent sub-questions with a Multi-Hop Reasoning Chain Branch for sequential inference, forming the two-stage pipeline described in Section 3.

Ablations show the classification-variant and denoiser components each independently contribute to performance, as quantified by comparing classifier variants and denoiser on/off settings (Table 3, Table 4).
Performance is also broken down by number of reasoning hops, showing how EM/ACC change as multi-hop chain length increases (Table 5).
Datasets differ substantially in their parallel-versus-chained question composition, e.g., HotpotQA is 83.8% chained while QALD10 is 61.8% parallel (Figure 4).

v0qBWYewKR.text: FLAC formulates maximum entropy RL as a generalized Schrödinger bridge problem, characterizing the optimal terminal marginal as p*(X1) ∝ μ1^ref(X1)·exp(−𝒢(X1)/α) (Proposition 1, Section 4).

FLAC avoids explicit action density estimation by instead penalizing the kinetic energy of a velocity field, using the identity that path KL divergence equals kinetic energy in the stochastic regime (Equation 5, Section 5).
The energy-regularized Bellman operator used by FLAC is proven to be a γ-contraction, and policy updates are shown to guarantee monotonic improvement (Proposition 2, Proposition 3).

FLAC achieves superior or comparable performance to baselines including DIME, SAC-Flow, and TD-MPC2 on high-dimensional continuous control benchmarks such as the DMControl Dog domain (223-dim state, 38-dim action) and HumanoidBench Unitree H1 tasks (51-57 dim states, 19-dim actions), using only 2 function evaluations (Section 6).

An ablation over the energy budget formula Etgt = C·dim(𝒜) shows FLAC is robust across C ∈ {0.5, 2.5}, and automatic dual tuning of log α exhibits a decrease-then-increase pattern balancing early value maximization against later exploration (Figure 3a, Figure 3b).

K4krf5tbi3.text: GSNF's re-initialization mechanism induces trajectory divergence to expose graph-induced interactions, with a data-dependent lower bound on cumulative trajectory divergence given by ∑‖z*(ti)−z(ti)‖ ≥ max{0,(L−k0*+1)(η−Δin)} (Theorem 5.1).

GSNF enforces forward-backward consistency via reverse-time trajectory generation, relying on an invertibility condition requiring φ(·) ∈ [0,1) and a contractive mapping g(·,t0,t,A) ensured via spectral normalization (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).

GSNF(δlb) achieves state-of-the-art AUROC/AUPRC on five irregular multivariate time series datasets, e.g., AUROC 86.7/AUPRC 56.9 on PhysioNet12, AUROC 91.2/AUPRC 57.9 on P19, and AUROC 85.3/AUPRC 55.5 on MIMIC-IV (Table 1).

An ablation removing the graph structure causes the largest performance drop, e.g., PhysioNet12 AUROC falls to 82.7 and AUPRC to 46.4, and removing the interaction-aware trajectory generation (ITG) component degrades performance more than removing reverse-time generation (RTG) alone (Table 2).
GSNF trains in 9 seconds per epoch with peak GPU memory of 6,349 MB on PhysioNet12, demonstrating competitive training time and memory usage relative to baselines (Figure 3, Table 4).
Interaction-aware trajectory generation increases the number of salient interaction edges visualized in the graph from 34 to 78 (Figure 4-5).

48c42LVtLx.text: Verified SHAP computes provable bounds on exact Shapley values of neural networks by combining interval arithmetic with formal neural network verification, established via the main theoretical contributions of the paper (Theorems 4.2 and 4.3, Section 4).

The proposed algorithm (Algorithm 1) scales to orders of magnitude larger search spaces than state-of-the-art exact SHAP computation baselines, as demonstrated in the experimental validation (Section 5, Table 4).

The method can tighten its bounds arbitrarily, ultimately recovering exact Shapley values rather than only approximate ones, building on foundational results established earlier in the paper (Theorems 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5, Section 3).
Empirical evaluation reports runtime and bound-tightness results comparing Verified SHAP against baseline exact SHAP methods across varying feature/search-space sizes (Section 5, Table 4).

FPUFIOpZW9.text: Partitioning Mixtral-8x7B from 8 to 32 experts via the Complete Transformation expert-partition scheme and fine-tuning raises average downstream accuracy from 70.53% to 71.12% across nine benchmarks (Table 1).
2T-Drop with reconstruction at roughly a 25% token-expert drop rate limits accuracy loss to 0.08% on Mixtral, 0.28% on OLMoE, and 0.18% on DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (Table 2).
Load-aware thresholding combined with token-expert dropping achieves up to 1.41x MoE-module speedup with only 0.5% average accuracy degradation (Section 5.3.2, Figure 10).

The Soft Expert-Tensor Parallelism (S-ETP) scheme, which replaces AlltoAll+AllGather communication with AlltoAll-only communication, yields 1.17-1.23x MoE-module and 1.07-1.12x end-to-end speedups in real-world measurements (Section 3.3, Figure 10a).
Simulated NVL72 deployment of S-ETP shows 10.2%-80.4% communication bandwidth improvement, versus 3.0%-29.9% measured on real hardware (Figure 10a).
Ablations comparing 1T-Drop against 2T-Drop with partition-only versus reconstruction show that reconstruction is necessary to preserve accuracy at equivalent drop rates (Table 2).

XAyI76nJRt.text: KUP-BI builds a train-only retrieval library of history-target-continuation chains and derives a ratio-based transformation R = (F - H) / (H + eps*sign(H)) to represent post-target evolution relative to history (Section 3, Equation 1).
Averaged across four backbones (DLinear, PatchTST, TimesNet, xPatch), KUP-BI improves MSE on ETTh2 from 0.469 to 0.394 and on Exchange from 0.369 to 0.313 (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On the ILI dataset, ablating the residual weight alpha causes MSE to worsen sharply from 1.366 to 1.929, making alpha the most critical hyperparameter (Table 5, Section 4.5).

Ablations replacing the gated fusion module with simple concatenation, or substituting random retrieval or direct continuation reuse for the ratio-based construction, all degrade performance, confirming the value of quality retrieval and ratio-based modeling (Table 3 and Table 4, Sections 4.4-4.5).
KUP-BI adds only about 0.2-0.6 ms of inference time per batch across prediction lengths and datasets, indicating lightweight computational overhead (Table 7, Appendix D).
The method is evaluated on six public benchmarks: ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, ILI, and Exchange (Section 4.1).

dIhYhrVTCO.text: On a 16.8 GiB 2D Kolmogorov turbulence trajectory, ANTIC combines a 62% reduction in retained snapshots with 47x per-snapshot spatial compression to reach up to 435x total compression while keeping relative L2 error in the 1e-3 to 1e-4 range (Section 4, results on 2D Kolmogorov flow).

On a 4.2 TiB 3D binary black hole merger trajectory, ANTIC retains about 45% of snapshots and achieves up to 3,744x per-snapshot spatial compression, for a total compression of up to 6,807x with relative L2 error of 1e-4 to 1e-5 (Section 4, results on binary black hole mergers).

The Physics-aware Temporal Selector (PATS) uses domain physics quantities-enstrophy for the Kolmogorov flow and the Weyl scalar for gravitational-wave data-to gate which snapshots are retained (Section 3.1).

ANTIC's combined temporal-plus-spatial pipeline outperforms baselines such as sparse sampling + ZFP (65x on Kolmogorov, 141x on BBH), dense sampling + ZFP (13x, 28x), and PATS + ZFP alone (120x, 52x) (Table 1).
Using LoRA fine-tuning of the neural field with rank r=32-64 instead of full fine-tuning matches accuracy while reducing per-snapshot parameter storage by about 4x (Figure 4, Section 4.1).

g8OP3bstR2.text: Differentiable Weightless Controllers (DWCs) achieve returns comparable to or exceeding a floating-point SAC baseline on four of five MuJoCo tasks (Ant, Hopper, Humanoid, Walker2d), while underperforming on HalfCheetah due to limited circuit capacity (Table 1).

Synthesized onto a Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A15T FPGA at 100 MHz, DWCs achieve 20-30 microsecond (2-3 clock cycle) latency and 2.06-2.25 nanojoules of energy per action, versus 210-162,230 microseconds latency and 28-65 microjoules per action for quantized neural-network baselines (Table 2).

Ablations over LUT-layer width show that 256-512 LUTs per layer suffice to reach floating-point parity on four of five tasks, while HalfCheetah requires up to 16,000 LUTs to approach floating-point performance (Figure 4, Section 5).
Ablations over thermometer-encoding bit width find that 63 bits saturates performance on four of five tasks, whereas HalfCheetah benefits from a larger 255-bit encoding (Figure 9, Section 5).
DWCs match or exceed the floating-point baseline's robustness under Gaussian observation noise with standard deviation ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 (Figure 5, Section 4.2).

In the Humanoid task, feature-importance analysis shows 275 of 376 input dimensions receive zero connections in the learned circuit, with torso velocity receiving the highest connectivity (Figure 6, Section 5.2).

AkzVoVkWPd.text: On RealEstate10K, SemanticNVS reduces FID from 26.4 to 22.7 (13.7% improvement) on short-trajectory novel view synthesis and from 31.3 to 26.6 (15.3% improvement) on long-trajectory synthesis (Table 1).
On Tanks-and-Temples, SemanticNVS yields a 4.69%-14.98% FID improvement over prior state-of-the-art novel view synthesis methods, with stronger generalization on out-of-distribution scenes (Table 2).
On long RealEstate10K trajectories, SemanticNVS reduces an image-quality drift metric by 28.8%, from 0.511 to 0.364, indicating improved consistency under long-range camera motion (Table 1).

SemanticNVS incorporates warped DINOv2 semantic features (Section 3.3) and an iterative semantic-refinement scheme that alternates denoising with feature extraction from intermediate predictions (Section 3.4).

Component ablations show both the warped-DINO and iterative-DINO mechanisms individually contribute to quality gains, and a feature-extractor comparison confirms DINOv2 is the optimal choice among tested extractors (Table 4 and Table 5, Figure 5).
SemanticNVS is trained on RealEstate10K plus DL3DV, combining roughly 75,000 videos of training data (Section 4, Datasets).

R80JLmXXPJ.text: SVGT reduces harmful score on WildGuardMix by 89.1% on GPT-2 and by 72.4% on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, with corresponding BeaverTails reductions of 44.7% and 73.7% (Table 2).
SVGT is evaluated across four backbones of increasing scale: GPT-2 (124M), Qwen2-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (Table 2).
On HarmBench, SVGT achieves 72-80% relative attack success rate reductions while keeping refusal rates above 75% across all backbones (Section 4).
Ablation shows bridge-token guidance outperforms direct residual injection, reaching a harmful score of 7.84 vs 13.29 on WildGuardMix while also yielding better perplexity, 7.34 vs 10.28 (Table 3).

The independent value module uses dual unconditional/conditional encoding pathways with a discriminator that scores alignment, achieving over 90% AUROC on Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B after Stage 2 training (Table 1).
Bridge tokens (K=5-10) are updated via momentum with optimal decay β in [0.6, 0.8]; SVGT adds only +3% memory overhead but +52-65% latency on Llama-3.2-3B (Figure 6).

NjbMkeaOKD.text: The compiler-based learning-to-refine framework treats Lean compiler messages as a lower-dimensional 'dimension compressor' relative to the space of formal proofs (Section 3).
Goedel-32B (built on Goedel-Prover-V2-32B) solves 110 PutnamBench problems with a budget of 256, exceeding the original Goedel-Prover-V2 (86 problems) and Ax-Prover (91 problems) (Table 4).
Kimina-8B (built on Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B) solves 25 PutnamBench problems with a budget of 256, ranking first among ~8B-parameter models (Table 4).
Value-guided tree search improves MiniF2F-test accuracy to 81.97%, a 4.51-point gain over BFS-only search (77.46%) and outperforming random tree search (81.15%) (Table 3, Section 5.3).

Error-type analysis shows refinement correction probability varies sharply by failure type, with 'failed to synthesize' errors corrected 4.04% of the time versus near-0% for 'linarith failed' errors (Table 7).

0x7KnR9Coy.text: Clean-PR filters raw GitHub pull requests, discarding PRs where 38.06% lack core source changes, 25.10% stem from bot activity, and 24.50% remain unmerged, retaining only 18.59% as high-quality training signals (Table 2).

Training on the resulting 2 million Clean-PR instances (17.7B tokens across 12 languages) yields absolute gains of 13.6 points on SWE-bench Lite (24.3% vs 10.7% zero-shot Qwen-Coder-32B-Instruct) and 12.3 points on SWE-bench Verified (30.6% vs 18.3%) (Table 6).

The 32B Clean-PR model outperforms larger 72B baselines Lingma-SWE and SWE-Fixer (both 22.0% Lite / 30.2% Verified) while using simplified Agentless scaffolding rather than complex agent loops (Table 7).
Ablation shows Search/Replace edit format improves SWE-bench Verified accuracy to 27.8% versus 24.4% for standard unified diff format (Table 8).
Error-driven augmentation during Agentless-aligned SFT raises SWE-bench Verified accuracy from 27.4% to 30.6%, a 3.2-point gain (Table 9).
Pass@k scaling shows SWE-bench Verified accuracy rising from 30.6% at Pass@1 to 41.5% at Pass@10, indicating headroom beyond likelihood-based patch ranking (Section 4).

2gSIm6WcKU.text: Syntactic centroids are computed by averaging hidden representations of sentences sharing identical POS templates, while semantic centroids average representations across paraphrase translations in six languages (Arabic, Chinese, German, Italian, Spanish, Turkish) (Table 2).

Subtracting the syntactic and semantic centroids substantially reduces similarity between syntax-matched and semantics-matched sentence pairs respectively, evidencing linear encoding of each property (Figures 1-2).

Cross-ablation shows removing semantic centroid information minimally affects syntactic similarity, whereas removing syntactic centroid information substantially reduces semantic similarity, indicating asymmetric separability (Figures 3-4).

Syntax maintains high similarity (>0.7) across all layers while semantic similarity is low in early layers, peaks in central layers, and diminishes thereafter, indicating differential cross-layer encoding of syntax and semantics in DeepSeek-V3 (Figure 5).
Centroids explain approximately 40% of squared representation norm in central layers of DeepSeek-V3 (671B), leaving substantial residual variance unexplained (Section 4).
Findings are qualitatively replicated on Qwen2-7B and Gemma3-12B, indicating the differential syntax/semantics encoding pattern generalizes across model scales (Appendix I).

BDR6RK9TmA.text: Safety Bottleneck Regularization (SBR) anchors the final hidden states of harmful queries at the unembedding layer to those of a safety-aligned reference model, rather than constraining parameters or gradients (Section 3).
SBR achieves an average Harmful Score of 5.68 versus 70.7 for plain SFT, 52.45 for LISA, 62.53 for Vaccine, and 62.33 for Booster under harmful fine-tuning (Table 1, Section 5.2).
SBR keeps Harmful Score below 10 across 50 epochs of persistent harmful fine-tuning, while competing defenses collapse within 5-10 epochs (Figure 2).

A single safety anchor reduces Harmful Score from 67.8 to 6, and randomly sampled (uncurated) anchors work effectively, with 8 anchors used as the default configuration at 1.07x training overhead (Figure 6, Section 5.3).
Regularizing only the final layer (L=32) yields robust safety (HS=5.8), whereas applying the same constraint at intermediate layers fails (HS>50) (Figure 7, Section 5.3).

SBR maintains Harmful Score under 10 even at a 30% poison ratio across Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma1.1-7B, while preserving downstream functional accuracy around 94% on SST-2, AGNEWS, GSM8K, and AlpacaEval (Table 2, Section 5.2).

SxBuTatzGe.text: DistMatch recursively partitions residuals into leaves via a binary tree using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, targeting γ*-approximate local exchangeability within each leaf (Definition 5.1, Algorithm 1).
Theorem 5.4 shows the within-leaf KS diameter converges to at most 2γ under the local stationarity and patch-mixing assumption (Assumption 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
Theorem 5.6 establishes a coverage guarantee for DistMatch that avoids the reweighting step required by prior sequential conformal prediction methods (Section 5, Theorem 5.6).

With a random forest predictor at alpha=0.1, DistMatch attains 0.90-0.92 empirical coverage on Electricity, Solar, Wind, META and NVDA datasets, with Winkler scores such as 1.97±0.01 (Electricity) and 0.49±0.00 (NVDA) (Table 1).
With an LSTM predictor, DistMatch maintains an average 0.90 coverage across Electricity, Solar, and Wind, with Winkler scores of 1.15±0.02, 1.87±0.11, and 2.05±0.01 respectively (Table 2).
DistMatch's calibration cost is O(n^2 w log n) and its per-step online update cost is O(w log n), amortizing to O(Tw log n) over T steps (Table 3).

wQxRphkfxn.text: VJA (Vision-centric Jailbreak Attack) achieves an overall attack success rate of 80.9% on Nano Banana Pro and 70.3% on GPT-Image-1.5, with per-category rates ranging from about 30.8% to 100% (Section 4.1, Table 1).

VJA reaches 97.5% ASR on Qwen-Image-Edit and 94.1% ASR on Seedream 4.5, and 100% ASR on open-source models BAGEL, Flux2.0, and local Qwen-Image-Edit that lack built-in safeguards (Section 4.1, Table 1).

A training-free defense based on introspective multimodal reasoning reduces ASR on Qwen-Image-Edit-Safe from 100% to 66.9% and lowers the harmfulness score by 1.2 points, without requiring auxiliary guard models (Section 4.1, Table 1).
The defense suppresses high-risk generations most in categories I13 (down to 61.5%) and I15 (down to 55.3%) (Section 4.1, Table 1).

The introspective defense adds only about 170 input and 110 output tokens, increasing runtime by roughly 4ms for Qwen-Image-Edit and 6ms for LongCat-Image-Edit, about 3% additional latency versus baseline inference (Section A.4, Table 5).

phHnze3Nfm.text: Policies trained against the Skywork-1.5B PRM on AIME problems reach rewards exceeding 0.8 (peaking near 1.0 for the Qwen-7B PRM) while ground-truth accuracy stays at 3-4% or drops to 0% (Section 6.2).
A rephrasing intervention on AIME25 shows approximately 43% of reward gains are attributable to stylistic shortcuts rather than genuine reasoning improvement (Section 6.3, Figure 8).

PRMs exhibit high style invariance (reward changes under 0.1 for surface-level edits) but inconsistent logic detection across question-trajectory mismatches and hallucinated reasoning, supporting the claim that current PRMs act as fluency detectors rather than reasoning verifiers (Section 4.3).
