In the low-NFE sampling regime, Eso-LM (B) remains competitive with masked diffusion models, and in the high-NFE regime it approaches autoregressive quality, avoiding the mode collapse seen in BD3-LMs at few sampling steps (Section 5.3).

IPADrcEOJx.text: GeoCode comprises 18,000 synthesized geometry problems (13k numerical, 5k proof-based), generated via a three-stage pipeline of seed generation, instantiation, and visualization (Section 3.1.1-3.1.3).

GeoCode problems exhibit higher structural complexity than prior benchmarks, averaging 15.03 segments and 1.94 annotations per proof problem versus 14.09 segments and 3.24 annotations per solution problem (Table 1).
Fine-tuning on GeoCode yields benchmark gains including +11.52% on OlympiadBench for Qwen3-VL-7B, +6.19% on Geometry3K for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and +8.44% on MathVerse for Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Table 3).
On Test-mini, Qwen3-VL improves from 17.91% zero-shot to 26.49% after SFT and to 37.68% after GRPO training on GeoCode (Table 4).
Using plotting-code prediction as the visual alignment objective outperforms caption-based alignment, reaching 26.49% on Test-mini versus 20.52% for the caption baseline (Table 6).

GW3umRqsZZ.text: The paper's First-Order Rejection Sampling (FORS) meta-algorithm (Theorem 3.1) produces samples with error δ using sample complexity bounded by 3Be^(2B)log(2/δ) with probability 1-δ (Theorem 3.1).

Under only a finite second-moment assumption (minimal assumptions), the diffusion sampler achieves query complexity O(d·log²(1/δ) + log³(1/δ)), giving polylog(1/δ) dependence rather than the poly(1/δ) of prior work (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).

Under a non-uniform Lipschitz condition on the score (Assumption 4.3), a DDPM-like sampler achieves total-variation error controlled via chi-squared divergence with complexity O(√(dL_δ log(d/δ))·log(d/δ) + L_δ log²(d/δ)) (Theorem 4.4).
For distributions with low intrinsic dimension d★, an adaptive-step-size method attains complexity O(d★·log²((d+M₂²)/δ²)), replacing the ambient dimension d with d★ (Theorem 4.6).

Section 5 extends the FORS framework to sample from general log-concave distributions using only gradient evaluations (no density evaluations), giving the first polylog(1/δ) sampler in this setting (Section 5).

Kk5UZgkWFx.text: Diagonal thresholding provably fails on the general-covariance model (Model 2), failing to detect any true support element with probability at least 1/2 even with a Θ(1) eigenvalue gap (Lemma 1, Section 3).
Covariance thresholding fails analogously, returning an estimate 𝐮 with sin²∠(𝐮,𝐯)=1 with probability at least 1/2 despite sufficient samples (Lemma 3, Section 3).
Greedy correlation-based selection recovers at most one true support coordinate under Model 2, even when seeded with a correct coordinate (Lemma 4, Section 3).
The proposed Restarted Truncated Power Method (RTPM) achieves ⟨𝐯,𝐮⟩² ≥ 9/10 with probability ≥ 1-δ under Model 2 using n = Ω(s² log(s) log(d/δ)) samples and O(nd²) runtime (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
Sparse k-PCA cannot be solved by deflation-based self-reduction to the single-component case, since deflated covariance matrices can have fully dense top eigenvectors (Lemma 11, Section 4.2).

BOWWKD9xEF.text: Tabero-VTLA reduces average grip force (AG) by over 70% under gentle instructions while maintaining high task success rate, e.g., Dataset A shows AG reduced from 31.3N to 8.5N with success rates of 0.87/0.79 (Section 1.1, Table 2).

The model uses a decoupled force-position command interface executed by a hybrid controller combining feedforward and admittance control terms, shown by ablation to be jointly necessary for accurate force tracking (Section 3.4, Figure 7).
Removing tactile input entirely causes complete task failure (success rate 0.00), while the best configuration (Field+FS) achieves success rate 0.86 with AG of 3.7N under gentle conditions (Table 3).
The model generalizes to unseen force adverbs, e.g., producing AG of 32.4N for 'firmly/tightly' instructions, 3.7N for 'gently/softly', and 14.5N for the out-of-domain adverb 'lightly' (Table 4).

The data pipeline repurposes open-source MuJoCo manipulation trajectories, resimulating them in Isaac Lab to synthesize synchronized RGB-D vision, GelSight tactile images (320x240), an 11x9 marker displacement grid, and 6D contact forces at 20Hz (Section 3.1-3.2).

ub9PwBtHqD.text: Theorem 3.1 gives a closed-form expected information gain (EIG) for Shapley value estimation that is computable in O(p^4 + t^3) time, versus the naive O(4^p · t) cost (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1).

Method is evaluated on 15 explanation tasks spanning four families—feature importance, data valuation, hyperparameter importance, and local explanation—with evaluation budgets up to 512 (Table 1, Section 5.1).

Figure 1 shows ShaplEIG achieves lower mean squared error than Kernel SHAP, Leverage SHAP, Permutation Sampling, and Regression MSR baselines across varying evaluation budgets on the 15 tasks (Figure 1, Section 5.2).
Ablation comparing GP-surrogate variants shows the EIG-based acquisition (ShaplEIG) outperforms GP+Random, GP+Leverage Score Sampling, and GP+Uncertainty Sampling (Figure 3, Appendix D.2.1).

Computational overhead measurements show EIG computation stays below 30 seconds across all tested game sizes, while GP hyperparameter refitting can take up to roughly 25 minutes per iteration for games with more than 16 players (Figures 5-6, Appendix D.2.2).

FuvU7PTyED.text: DreamDojo-HV, the pretraining dataset, comprises 44,711 hours of human video spanning about 96x more skills and 2,000x more scenes than prior robot-relevant video datasets (Table 1, Section 2).
A distillation pipeline accelerates DreamDojo's world model to 10.81 FPS at inference, up from a 2.72 FPS teacher baseline (Table 6).
Human preference evaluation shows the DreamDojo-14B model is preferred over baselines in 62.5-73.5% of pairwise comparisons, including 73.5% for physics correctness (Table 4).
DreamDojo-based policy evaluation correlates with real-world rollout success at Pearson r=0.995 (Section 4, Figure 5).
The distilled student model trades off some visual fidelity for speed, reporting LPIPS 0.485 versus the teacher's 0.412 and PSNR 13.146 versus the teacher's 14.086 (Table 6).

aA02f0y0LY.text: Agent0-VL-7B improves average performance by 12.5% over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model across seven visual reasoning benchmarks: MathVerse, MathVision, MathVista, WeMath, HallBench, ChartQA, and MMMU (Table 1).
Average score across the seven benchmarks rises from 57.3% for the base model to 65.6% for Agent0-VL (Table 1, Section 4).
Iterative self-evolution across three training iterations yields successive average gains of 5.2%, 4.0%, and 2.8% (Table 2).
Ablations isolate the contributions of Self-Repair, Tool Use, and the Self-Evolving Reasoning Cycle (SERC) to overall performance (Table 3).
When deployed as a Process Reward Model scoring other VLMs' reasoning trajectories, Agent0-VL yields a 7.3% average gain (Table 4).

LPkaP2roeE.text: Theorem 2 proves that benchmark score prediction using the DKPS-induced geometry has lower error than prediction based on a model's score on the same subset of queries alone (Section 3, Theorem 2).
On LegalBench at query budget m=64, the ensemble DKPS+IRT method achieves 0.031 mean absolute error versus 0.039 for the raw Sample Score baseline (Table 1, Section 4).
Ensemble DKPS-based methods achieve the best or near-best MAE across nearly all (query budget, task) combinations tested on HELM-Lite (Table 1, Section 4).
The offline query-selection procedure samples multiple candidate query sets, computes their DKPS representations, and selects the set maximizing R^2 goodness-of-fit on reference models (Section 4.2).
Figure 5 shows the R^2-selected query set achieves lower prediction error than the average randomly chosen query set for both n=20 and n=all reference models (Figure 5, Section 4.2).

KDJf0EyawI.text: Method uses separate per-modality autoencoders combined with a task loss and a reconstruction loss, formalized to minimize downstream-task-related entropy without amplifying the entropy of task-relevant features (Theorem 3.1, Eq. 5).

On VGGSound (Table 2), the method attains competitive accuracy (e.g., 32.01% vs. MISA's 33.77% in the audio-visual trainable setting) while using fewer parameters and lower computational load, and remains robust when only single-modality (audio-only or video-only) inputs are available (Table 2).
On ActivityNet, the method achieves 0.355 mAP@10, outperforming MAP-IVR (0.349) and Perceiver (0.264) (Table 3).
On FakeAVCeleb, the method reaches 91.88 AUC, with an MAE-augmented variant reaching 99.97 AUC, exceeding baseline methods (Table 4).

Gradient analysis in the appendix shows that gradients from the downstream classification loss and the fusion-related loss need not align, motivating the dual-objective, feature-subspace-partitioned design described in Section 3.3/Section 4 (Appendix A, Section 3.3).

uFQwehcepH.text: Task Singular Vectors (TSV) merging achieves the highest predictive correlation (r=0.572) between the linear metric model and post-merge performance under leave-one-task-out validation, versus r=0.555 for Weight Averaging, r=0.343 for Task Arithmetic, and r=0.328 for Isotropic merging (Section 6).

Across the four merging methods, only 46.7% of the top-5 predictive metrics overlap and only 55.3% of coefficient signs agree, showing that success drivers are largely method-specific rather than universal (Section 6).

Six metrics remain stable predictors across all merging methods: encoder gradient L2 distance, input gradient L2 distance, and input gradient dot product as negative predictors, and left subspace overlap top-k, interaction overlap top-k, and encoder gradient cosine similarity as positive predictors (Table 4, Section 6.3).

An ablation removing the subspace-overlap metric category causes the largest drop in validation correlation (Δr = -0.123), followed by removing gradient-based metrics (Δr = -0.064), while removing effective-rank metrics has near-negligible effect (Section 6.2, Section 7).
The study evaluates 190 unique pairwise model-merging combinations across 20 image classification tasks fine-tuned from CLIP ViT-B/16 (Section 5).

LvKSVUbXc9.text: LoRA-DA achieves 84.3% average accuracy on commonsense reasoning benchmarks, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art initialization method MiLoRA (84.0%) by 0.3 percentage points, with top performance on 6 of 8 benchmarks (Table 1).

On mathematical reasoning tasks, LoRA-DA reaches 55.0% on GSM8K and 9.2% on MATH, versus 53.8%/8.5% for the gradient-based LoRA-One baseline, an average improvement of about 1.0 percentage point (Table 2).
In the Frozen-A (LoRA-FA) setting, LoRA-DA-FA reaches 49.4% on GSM8K compared to 41.5% for vanilla LoRA-FA (Table 3).
LoRA-DA shows more stable gradient norms and faster overall convergence than baseline initializations despite more conservative early-training steps (Figure 2).
Improvements from LoRA-DA hold consistently across ranks r in {1,2,4,8,16}, with the largest gains at smaller ranks (Figure 4).
The data-aware initialization procedure adds only about 6% overhead to total training time (Table 5).

xAKrRYm6pc.text: A single semantic encoder (SigLIP 2) outperforms FLUX.1's VAE encoder on both visual understanding (VQA) and image generation benchmarks such as DPGBench and GenEval, indicating one high-dimensional semantic representation can serve both tasks (Section 3, Figures 4 and 10).

Adding raw video and image-text pair data alongside text-only pretraining maintains language perplexity roughly on par with text-only training while being essential for visual capabilities (Section 4.1, Figures 5-6).

Dense-model scaling shows an asymmetry: language capability scales with parameters at an exponent of about 0.47 versus 0.53 for data, while vision scales with parameters at about 0.37 versus 0.63 for data, indicating vision is comparatively more data-hungry (Section 7, Figures 23-26).

Switching from dense to Mixture-of-Experts architectures roughly halves the language/vision scaling-exponent gap (from about 0.10 to 0.05), letting MoE models match unimodal baselines on both modalities simultaneously (Section 7).

Generation and understanding tasks share approximately 90% correlated expert-routing patterns in the MoE architecture, with text-focused experts dominating and vision/multimodal experts increasing in later layers (Section 6.2, Figures 18-20).

ORy2hyPd4G.text: Jacobi Forcing achieves a 3.86x wall-clock speedup on HumanEval (87.8% to 83.5% accuracy) and 3.50x-3.65x speedups on GSM8K and MATH with minimal accuracy loss (Tables 1 and 2).

Adding multi-block decoding with rejection recycling increases wall-clock speedup on HumanEval to up to 3.97x and yields roughly 4.5x higher token acceptance count per iteration compared to standard Jacobi decoding (Section 3.2).
On HumanEval, the method achieves 4.01 tokens per forward pass and 159.5 tokens per second, versus 2.68 tokens per forward pass and 103.3 tokens per second for the CLLM baseline (Section 4).

An ablation shows the noise-conditioned mask achieves a 3.6x speedup versus only 1.9x for a clean-context variant, and the linear progressive noise schedule outperforms random and reverse schedules (Tables 4 and 5, Section 4.3).
The progressive consistency training objective (Eq. 9) reduces the longest noisy-token dependency from O(nN) to O(⌈tn⌉) via a cyclic noise schedule (Section 3.1, Eq. 7).

d93mcbLGhV.text: PCA on 512 solid-color images shows that color information in FLUX.1 [Dev]'s VAE latent space is confined to a 3D subspace, with the first three principal components accounting for 100% of color variance and forming a bicone structure mirroring HSL representation (Section 3.2).

A bijective mapping between Latent Color Subspace coordinates and HSL values is constructed using encoding/decoding functions calibrated on seven anchor points (six hues plus black and white) (Section 4).

Three training-free intervention strategies are proposed: direct LCS translation (Type I), HSL-space shifting (Type II), and an interpolated approach blending both, most effective at diffusion timesteps 8-10 (Section 4.4, Figure 6).

The training-free color-control method achieves 73% color accuracy on GenEval without any prompt modification, rising to 79% when combined with color-specifying prompts, while better preserving image structure than prompt-based baselines (Section 4.4).

oa9VyvHw8K.text: TAP improves classification accuracy by up to 15.6 percentage points over baselines under severe data scarcity (n_real=20) (Table 1).
TAP reduces regression RMSE by up to 32% compared to strong generative baselines (Table 1).

TAP is evaluated against seven baselines (SMOTE, TVAE, CTGAN, ARF, SPADA, TabDDPM, TabDiff) across seven datasets including MiceProtein, Credit-G, Electricity, Fourier, Steel, Ailerons, and Insurance (Section 4).

TAP formalizes data augmentation as a sequential control problem under an evolving learner, identifying a fidelity-utility gap where high distributional fidelity does not guarantee downstream utility (Section 2).
Removing the pointwise (hard feasibility) gating mechanism in an ablation reduces TAP's win-rate from 100% to 57.3% at n_real=20 (Table 2).
TAP shows consistent improvements across five scarcity levels, n_real in {20, 50, 100, 200, 500}, with the largest gains at the most extreme scarcity level (Section 4).

iCBaLQQzdK.text: The paper proves that under standard digital signature assumptions, any (ε,δ)-DP algorithm can have a computationally indistinguishable backdoored variant that reveals the dataset to privileged entities (Theorem 1.1).

The paper constructs an (ε,δ)-DP stochastic convex optimization algorithm whose public verification requires checking only n gradients and d·⌈log2(n)⌉ Gaussian random variables rather than replaying full training (Theorem 4.1).
The proposed DP-SCO algorithm achieves optimal excess risk of Õ(L·D·(1/√n + √(d ln(1/δ))/(εn))) up to log log(n) factors while enabling this cheaper verification (Theorem 4.2).

The paper's D2D unlearning algorithm provides certified (ε,δ)-unlearning with verification cost of only |D'| gradient checks and d Gaussian random-variable commitments, where D' is the deleted subset (Theorem 5.1).

Experiments on MNIST show that gradient verification dominates total runtime, taking approximately 3 hours at MNIST scale, and that certification scales at least Õ(√n) faster than full training in the non-smooth setting (Section 6).

DDYr4KXKs1.text: PrivCode++ uses a two-stage framework combining a joint-sensitive Privacy-Free Latent Conditioning (PrivLC) module with DP post-processing-based utility boosting, treating both prompts and code snippets as sensitive (Section 3.1-3.3).

Under privacy budget ε=4, PrivCode++ improves Pass@1 over joint-sensitive baselines (DPFT, PC-Uncond, PC-PromptEmb, PC-PreEmb) by up to 8.2 points on instruction-following benchmarks and up to 19.3 points on code-completion benchmarks, across HumanEval, MBPP, EvalPlus, and BigCodeBench (Table 1).
PrivCode++ achieves 0% canary leakage across all canary types, compared to up to 40% category-level leakage for prior joint-sensitive methods under joint canaries (Table 2).
A latent-dimension sensitivity analysis over dz in {256, 768, 2048} shows optimal performance at dz=768 (Table 3).

PrivCode++ remains competitive with PrivCode, a method that relaxes the joint-sensitivity assumption, despite providing stronger privacy guarantees, across privacy budgets ε in {0.2, 1, 4, 10, 20} (Figure 4).

9GRlBVAXq8.text: LoRA gradient descent converges to a stationary point at rate O(1/log T) in the general case without assuming Lipschitz smoothness of the reparameterized objective (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
When adapter norms are bounded, the same LoRA gradient descent algorithm converges at the faster rate O(1/T) (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).

The analysis relies only on Assumption 1 (Lipschitz smoothness of the original, non-reparameterized loss) and Assumption 2 (the loss is lower bounded), avoiding artificially imposed smoothness on the LoRA-reparameterized objective (Section 3.1).

The proof derives a Lipschitz-like descent lemma (Lemma 1) accounting for higher-order terms from the bilinear BA^T reparameterization, paired with an adaptive step-size rule ηt = min{1/(5√2 L(‖Vt‖^2+‖∇L(·)‖)), 1} (Lemma 2, Section 3.2).
The paper shows the derived convergence rate is independent of the chosen LoRA rank, since gradient descent on the low-rank factors operates dimension-free (Section 3.2).

SCjiMmzyFA.text: DeSI (Deep Single-Index Fréchet Regression) mitigates the curse of dimensionality relative to standard Fréchet regression while retaining interpretability via a single-index structure (Section 3).

On simulated SPD-matrix responses (q=3) at n=1000, DeSI attains a mean prediction error of 0.0057 (SD 0.0054), and for index-direction estimation accuracy DeSI attains 0.0640 (0.0181) versus 0.2150 (0.1001) for the IFR baseline (Table 1, Table 2, Section 5.3).
On simulated 10-node network responses under the Frobenius metric at n=1000, DeSI attains a mean prediction error of 0.0531 (0.0428) (Table 1, Section 5.3).
On simulated distribution-valued responses under the Wasserstein metric (linear setting) at n=1000, DeSI attains a mean prediction error of 0.0344 (0.0121) (Table 1, Section 5.3).

On the real-data application using compositional mood data from the Survey of Unemployed Workers in New Jersey (n=2,284), DeSI achieves a mean prediction error of 0.4658 (0.0012), about 6% lower than IFR's 0.4947 (0.0101) and below GFR's 0.6229 (0.0044) (Table 3, Section 6).

vIotI25gJz.text: 3D-DLP learns interpretable per-particle 3D segmentation maps through an end-to-end self-supervised reconstruction objective, producing foreground/background masks without supervision (Section 4, Figure 2)

Manipulating individual particle attributes enables controllable scene generation: perturbing a particle's 3D keypoint position translates the corresponding object, while changing its scale attribute resizes it (Section 5.1, Figure 4)

On the 12-task MimicGen robotic manipulation benchmark, 3D-DLP achieves a 48.1% mean success rate and wins 6 of 12 tasks, outperforming 2D-DLP single-view (30.8%) and multi-view (34.1%) baselines (Section 5.2, Table 4)

On the 10-task RLBench benchmark, 3D-DLP wins 9 of 10 tasks among matched-compute methods and surpasses PerACT on 7 of 10 tasks, with margins of 19-48 absolute points on major wins (Section 5.2, Table 5)

HskjhAfdY4.text: Theorem 2.1 (TPV Trace Stability) bounds the gap between training-set and test-set TPV by |TPV(w*;X_tr) - TPV(w*;X_te)| ≤ c1*Tr(C), where c1 → 0 as network width m → ∞, showing training-set TPV converges to its test-set value in the overparameterized limit (Theorem 2.1)

Across 324 synthetic experimental configurations spanning five orders of magnitude in TPV values, training and test TPV concentrate tightly around the diagonal, with stability holding even at width=1 (Figure 1)
TPV stability is sample-size dependent: it breaks down when n_train=10 but holds tightly when n_train=1000, on both synthetic and CIFAR-10/100 experiments (Section 5.1, Figure 2)

On ImageNet pretrained architectures, models that generalize better typically have lower TPV estimates, and lower TPV correlates with lower test loss across synthetic and real datasets (Section 5.2, Figure 6)

The trace form Tr(H_eff C) unifies TPV analysis across distinct perturbation sources, including label noise (Theorem 3.2), SGD stationary noise (Theorem 3.3), finite-precision quantization (Remark 3.4), and pruning masks (Section 3.4)

f0IWycligk.text: RealtimeTool achieves 3-6x end-to-end speedup (up to 9.6x) across Qwen models (0.5B-14B) on function calling tasks, with only 8.2% average parallelization overhead at batch size 8 (Section 1.4, Table 13)
On the RTX 4090, Qwen2.5-0.5B attains 5.35x speedup under Transformers and 3.07x under vLLM, while Qwen3-4B attains 2.83x (Transformers) and 3.88x (vLLM) (Table 3)

On the Mobile Actions benchmark, RT-Qwen-0.5B outperforms Google's FunctionGemma (270M) in both zero-shot accuracy (69.3% vs 58.0%) and fine-tuned accuracy (86.2% vs 85.0%), and in latency consistency, with P50 latency 51.0ms vs 61.1ms and P90 latency 74.5ms vs 139.5ms (Section 3.4, Tables 4-5)
With AWQ 4-bit quantization on a consumer-grade RTX 4090 GPU, Qwen3-4B achieves 61.2ms P50 latency, enabling 16 Hz real-time control at the 4B model scale (Figure 5c, Table 3)
With 8-head parallel decoding, the framework demonstrates 93.0% average TPOT (time-per-output-token) efficiency (Section 2.1.3, Appendix G)

CXsD6Ygc8e.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes the first high-probability optimal regret bound Õ(√(K|A|log|F|)) for policy optimization (OPO-CMAB) in contextual bandits with general offline function approximation, where K is the number of rounds, A is the action set, and F is the function class (Theorem 3.1)
The regret analysis decomposes expected regret into three terms, bounding the policy suboptimality term by O(√(K log|A|)) via Lemma 4.4 (Section 4, Lemma 4.4)

Lemma 4.2 shows that counterfactual exploration bonuses accumulated by the algorithm sum to Õ(β|A|log K), which is key to controlling regret without additional function-class assumptions like Eluder dimension (Section 4, Lemma 4.2)

Corollary 4.1 provides uniform convergence guarantees for offline least-squares regression performed over policy-dependent datasets, underlying the approximation-error bounds in Lemmas 4.3 and 4.5 (Section 4, Corollary 4.1)

h8NydU966G.text: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)

The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)

Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)

vfIUEpSTji.text: Reasoning accuracy in multi-hop fact verification follows an inverted U-shaped curve as a function of chain length, improving initially and then degrading rapidly beyond an optimal threshold (Section 1, Figure 1).
SCM-GRPO achieves 73.42% accuracy on HoVer 2-hop, exceeding the Search-o1 baseline's 69.00%, and reaches 60.88% on HoVer 4-hop (Section 4.3, Table 1).
SCM-GRPO attains 82.66% on EX-FEVER 2-hop and 75.00% on EX-FEVER 3-hop, with an average of 71.02% across the five evaluation subsets (Section 4.3, Table 1).
The reward design combines a Correctness Reward (Equation 3), Structure Reward (Equation 4), and Length Reward (Equation 5) derived from a structural causal model formulation (Section 3.5).
On Qwen3-8B, SFT+GRPO reaches 75.42% accuracy, outperforming SFT alone (73.33%) and SFT+CPO (71.91%) in an ablation of optimization strategies (Section 4.3, Table 2).

h4bSJMaNgb.text: The watermarking method applies bias at the level of token clusters obtained via Leiden community detection on a retokenization confusion matrix, rather than at individual tokens, making the watermark robust to retokenization noise (Section 3.4).
In the identity (no-attack) conversational-audio setting, the method achieves a mean −log(p) detectability score of 42.47 versus 8.51 for the KGW baseline (Table 2).

Under compression attacks such as MP3 and EnCodec re-encoding, the method's detectability substantially exceeds the KGW baseline while minimally degrading perceived audio quality (Section 5.2, Table 1).
Audio quality is preserved across FAD (VGGish/CLAP), NISQA, and DNSMOS metrics for multiple context window sizes h, comparing favorably to codec fine-tuning watermarking approaches (Table 1).
The theoretical analysis predicts detectability gains scale with the cluster match rate r_cl exceeding the raw token match rate r in an exponential decay term (Equation 7, Section 3.4).

EJPfiTrKyu.text: Under isotropic feature position with a single attended feature pair, training provably drives the top singular vectors of the QK matrix Ω=W_Q^T W_K to align exactly with the attended feature vectors (Theorem 2, Appendix B.2.3).

When features deviate from isotropy, singular vector-feature alignment still holds approximately provided inter-feature interference (inner products) remains sufficiently bounded (Theorem 3, Appendix B.2.3).
With an interference penalty on the training objective, the optimal solution orthogonalizes the features being represented (Theorem 4, Appendix B.3.2).
Sparse Attention Decomposition predicts that attention logits decomposed in the SVD basis of Ω are dominated by only a small number of singular-vector dimensions per head (Section 5, Equations 1-2).

In Pythia-160M on the Indirect Object Identification task, most attention heads require only 1-4 singular vectors to reconstruct relative attention, and this sparsity disappears when U and V are randomly rotated while preserving the singular spectrum (Section 5, Figures 7-8).

1MT6RdvOcT.text: DirectEdit records latent residuals ΔZ_t during inversion and reapplies them during the forward process to achieve step-level accurate reconstruction without introducing additional Neural Function Evaluations (Section 3.2, Equations 9-10).
DirectEdit reduces step-level reconstruction MSE to 0.0006 average (0.0757 maximum) compared to 0.2857 average (11.7302 maximum) for Stepwise Correction (Table 2).
On PIE-Bench with FLUX.1-dev and mask-guided blending, DirectEdit attains a Structure Distance of 17.94 versus 16.81 for DNAEdit, while improving PSNR to 32.63 from 24.70 without masking (Table 1).
Removing the Direct Alignment component degrades Structure Distance from 17.94 to 29.22, and removing attention injection increases it to 23.75, in an ablation study (Table 3).

DirectEdit achieves the best average ranking among compared methods on both FLUX.1-dev (4.00) and SD3.5-medium (2.43), and traces an improved editability-versus-background-preservation trade-off curve (Table 1, Figure 5).

ea2kQkdQA7.text: Tabula-8B's binary classification achieves only a 2.5 percentage-point median lift over the majority-class baseline, while categorical classification shows a -0.3 point median lift, versus 32.6 points for quartile classification (Section 4.1.2, Figure 1).

39.4% of evaluated datasets (65/165) show zero or negative lift over baseline for Tabula-8B, and 12 datasets show negative Cohen's Kappa, indicating worse-than-chance performance (Table 7, Table 6, Appendix C).

Instruction-tuning alone (Alpaca, no tabular exposure) reaches 58.6% accuracy versus Tabula-8B's 63.5% and a 47.7% base-Llama accuracy, recovering 92.2% of Tabula-8B's gain, with instruction-tuning contributing about 69% of the total gain versus 31% from tabular pretraining (Section 4.3.1, Table 4).

On quartile classification, providing format examples alone (Alpaca+Q) achieves a 25.8-point lift versus Tabula-8B's 34.0-point lift, closing 71.3% of the 28.5-point gap, with the residual 8.2 points concentrated on contaminated stock/financial datasets (Section 4.3.2, Table 5).

All 753 evaluation rows of the us-womens-labor dataset are found verbatim in Tabula-8B's training corpus, and 844 matching date-day associations from unrelated T4 tables enable apparent memorization on the peloton-data task (Section 4.2.1, Section 4.2.3).

5faxBOZAmW.text: OPO-CMDP achieves a regret bound of Õ(H⁴√(T|S||A|log(|F||P|/δ))) for policy optimization in contextual MDPs with general offline function approximation (Theorem 3.1).

OPO-CMDP improves on the prior state-of-the-art LOLIPOP bound of Õ(H⁷|S|⁴|A|³√T) by eliminating the cubic dependence on state and action space size, achieving optimal dependence on |S| and |A| (Table 1).

The regret analysis decomposes into four terms — approximation error, and an optimistic gap further split into policy-improvement cost via Online Mirror Descent and optimistic-design benefit (Section 4).
Exploration bonuses are bounded by Õ(H⁸√(T|S||A|log(|F||P|/δ))) without relying on structural assumptions such as Eluder dimension or minimum reachability (Lemma 4.2).
The derived regret bound matches known lower bounds in all parameters except the horizon H, leaving only an H^3.5 factor gap (Section 4, discussion of lower bounds).

kXGolRT8YX.text: Q-Evolve outperforms baselines including Reflexion, SFT, RFT, PPO, Best-of-N, ETO, DMPO, and QLASS on WebShop, ScienceWorld, and AlfWorld, reaching a best overall AlfWorld average of 79.4 (Table 2, Section 5.2).

Q-Evolve derives dense step-wise process rewards via Generalized Advantage Estimation on top of an in-distribution critic trained with weighted Implicit Q-Learning, avoiding environment backtracking (Section 4.3).

An ablation removing retrospective relabeling, weighted IQL, GAE, or the policy-improvement step from Q-Evolve on AlfWorld shows each component is necessary for full performance (Table 3, Section 5.3).
Q-Evolve matches or exceeds online RL baselines while using only 13K training steps versus 320K steps required by those baselines, demonstrating improved sample efficiency (Table 5, Section 5.3).

Comparisons of process-reward formulations (Q−V, potential-based shaping, GAE variants) in Table 4 support GAE-derived rewards as the most effective choice for stable self-evolution (Table 4, Section 5.3).

ZyGDiKr8UZ.text: On real-world 2019 CPUC Transportation Network Companies trip data from San Francisco County (~170,000 daily trips), RAST-MoE-RL reduces average matching delay by about 10% (from roughly 257s to 182s) and pickup delay by about 15% relative to baselines (Section 5.1.1).
RAST-MoE-RL improves total reward by 13% over baselines while using a lightweight architecture of only 12M parameters with 16 experts and top-4 routing (Section 4.2).

Masking either the high-frequency or low-frequency experts causes sharp performance drops, evidencing genuine expert specialization to different demand regimes rather than redundant routing (Figure 3, Section 5.3).
An adaptive reward-penalty multiplier λ prevents reward hacking compared to a fixed-coefficient design, as shown in a dedicated comparison of fixed vs. adaptive coefficients (Table 1, Section 5.4).
Robustness to unseen demand regimes is validated under global perturbations and incident shocks in dedicated stress tests (Appendix J, referenced from Section 5).

2WrNPRW9Km.text: DSGym-Tasks comprises 1,086 total tasks: 972 data-analysis tasks (including DSBio, 90 bioinformatics tasks) and 114 data-prediction tasks from 92 Kaggle competitions split into Easy (38) and Hard (54) divisions (Table 1, Section 4.2).

Existing benchmarks are shown to be partly solvable via memorization shortcuts even without real data files, with accuracy dropping only 40.5% on QRData, 13.2% on DAEval, and 55.6% on DiscoveryBench when data is withheld (Figure 3).
Frontier models that score above 90% on DAEval-Verified (e.g., GPT-4o 92.26%, Kimi K2 92.82%, Claude Sonnet 4.5 91.71%) drop to as low as 7.41% (GPT-4o) on the harder DABStep-Hard split (Table 2).

Fine-tuning Qwen3-4B on DSGym-SFT execution-verified data raises DSBio accuracy from a 6.67% baseline to 21.11%, demonstrating that training on DSGym substantially improves a 4B model on standardized data-science analysis benchmarks (Table 5, Section 6).

On end-to-end modeling tasks (DSPredict), agents achieve over 80% valid submission rates on easy tasks but near-0% medal rates on hard tasks, revealing a 'simplicity bias' toward functional but unoptimized solutions (Table 4).

0RBMhFule7.text: Trust Region Ratio Distillation (TRRD) replaces the teacher-student KL regularizer with a likelihood-ratio objective (r^GRPO)^α (r^T)^(1-α) anchored to a teacher-old-policy mixture, yielding advantage-aware distillation (Equation 3, Section 4.1).

On the Knights-and-Knaves logical reasoning benchmark at 8K context, RLAD raises Qwen3-0.6B average accuracy from 0.76 (GRPO) to 0.94, with the largest gain on the hardest PPL8 subset (0.63 to 0.83) (Table 1).

On long-context math reasoning at 30K context, RLAD improves Qwen3-8B-Base average performance from 61.0 (GRPO) to 66.5, and Qwen3-1.7B-Base from 36.5 to 39.0, averaged across 5 datasets and 9 metrics (Table 2).
RLAD converges faster and more stably than both vanilla GRPO and the KL-based KDRL teacher-distillation baseline, which exhibits oscillating validation dynamics (Figure 2).
RLAD incurs only about 12% training-latency overhead versus GRPO (567.4s vs. 491.2s per batch on 32 H200 GPUs) from added teacher logit computation (Table 4).
An ablation over the mixing coefficient α shows RLAD is largely insensitive to α except near the extremes (α→0 or α→1), with α=0.5 optimal on GSM8K/MATH (Table 5, Appendix A).

fFupHW7Jqx.text: For the known-delay-distribution setting, the proposed algorithm achieves regret O~(H√((D_max∧B)SAK) + HBSA) for tabular MDPs with delayed observations, where D_max is the maximum delay and B is the branching factor (Theorem 1).
For the unknown-delay-distribution setting, the algorithm achieves regret O~(H√((D_max∧B)SAK) + H√(Δ_maxSAK) + H(B+Δ_max)SA), extending the known-delay result (Theorem 2).
A matching lower bound of Ω(H√(D̃SAK/log D̃)) is established for constant-delay MDPs, where D̃ = min{D_max, H/4, B/2, S/4-1}, showing the upper bounds are optimal up to log factors (Theorem 3).
The result improves on the prior bound of Chen et al. (2023) by a factor of H^(1/2) D_max^2, tightening O~(H^{3/2}D_max^{5/2}√(SAK)) down to O~(H√(D_maxSAK)) (Section 5).
The framework is generalized to MDPs with partially known dynamics, yielding regret O~(H√(K∑_{z∈Z_eff}(log|Y|)∧B(z)) + H∑B(z)) (Theorem 5, Section 8).

Against the SC@64 baseline specifically, Parallel-Probe reduces sequential tokens by more than 30% and total tokens by over 20% (Main results).
On Qwen3-0.6B averaged across three benchmarks, Parallel-Probe attains 23.3% accuracy versus 22.8% for SC@64, i.e. slightly higher accuracy at lower cost (Main results table).
Parallel-Probe establishes a superior Pareto frontier for test-time scaling compared to Self-Consistency (SC) and Early-Stopping Consistency (ESC) methods (Pareto frontier analysis).

The method combines two mechanisms operating on a 2D probing matrix: consensus-based early stopping (controls reasoning depth) and deviation-based branch pruning (controls trajectory width) (Method/2D probing section).

195EfI9ae5.text: lts-L (the base rerooting Levin Tree Search variant) has time complexity O(bN log N + DN), where N is the number of expansions, D the maximum depth, and b the branching factor (Theorem 3.1).
The hybrid rerooter lts-LH achieves approximately a 5-30x speedup in training efficiency over baseline LTS on BoulderDash as dirt complexity increases from 10% to 50% (Table 2).
On Sokoban, the hybrid rerooter reaches a solution in approximately 1,700 expansions versus over 2,600 for pure clustering-based rerooting approaches (Section 4, experiments).
Rerooting-based methods are evaluated across four domains — BoulderDash, CraftWorld, Sokoban, and TSP (GridWorld) — with aggregate test results reported in Table 1 (Table 1).

Rerooting-based methods scale to complex environments where subgoal-based policy tree search fails, achieving state-of-the-art online training efficiency without requiring explicit subgoal reconstruction (Sections 3-4).

PFpbi7pceh.text: The deterministic parsimonious algorithm with separation parameter k achieves cost at most min{(2k-1)·cost(OPT) + 2kη, (2n-1)·cost(OPT)} (Theorem 1.1).
The randomized variant achieves expected cost min{O(log n log k)·(cost(OPT)+η), O(log²n)·cost(OPT)} (Theorem 1.2).
The Follow-the-Prediction meta-algorithm is extended to the parsimonious setting, outputting a matching of cost at most (1+γ+ρ(k-1))·cost(OPT) + (2+γ+ρ(k-1))·η(Q) (Theorem 3.1).

Virtual predictions are constructed via an auxiliary sub-instance restricted to servers left unmatched by the previous prediction, filling in for actual oracle-queried predictions between rounds (Section 3, Follow-the-Prediction framework).
Deterministic lower bounds of 2n/(B+1)-1 and 2k-1 on the competitive ratio of parsimonious learning-augmented algorithms are proven, alongside randomized lower bounds (Theorems 4.1-4.4).

6JwkAlGLjT.text: ALPS (Augmented Laplacian Planning with Subgoals) uses a scaled Laplacian representation (ψ-space) that approximates commute-time distance, enabling spectral clustering into subgoals for hierarchical planning (Section 4).
On antmaze-giant-stitch, ALPS achieves 92%±2 success versus 2%±2 for HIQL, and on pointmaze-medium-stitch ALPS achieves 90%±7 versus 80%±12 for the next-best baseline QRL (Table 1).

Without the behavior prior (ALPS†), the method still outperforms PcLast on Maze2D-PointMass tasks with 16 clusters: 99%±1 vs 62%±4 on Hallway, 96%±5 vs 57%±10 on Rooms, and 97%±2 vs 60%±6 on Spiral (Table 2).

Ablations on antmaze-medium-navigate/stitch show CEM-only planning fails completely (0%±0) while Dijkstra-plus-behavior-prior reaches 92%±5 and 92%±4, and the full ALPS reaches 95%±4 and 95%±4, indicating hierarchical planning is essential for complex locomotion tasks (Table 3, Section 6).

The Laplacian representation is trained via the ALLO objective with 32-dimensional eigenvectors, and cluster counts are set to 64/96/128 for medium/large/giant maze sizes respectively, with a planning horizon of H=20 on OGBench tasks (Section 5, Experiments).

vvke6mnh3Z.text: ACTG-ARL improves MAUVE score by roughly 20% over prior DP synthetic text generation baselines including Aug-PE, vanilla DP-FT, and CTCL on bioRxiv and PMC-Patients datasets (Figure 2).
Under (ε,δ)-differential privacy with ε tested in {1, 4, ∞}, plain DP fine-tuning drops instruction-following accuracy (IFAcc) from 66% to 53% on the bioRxiv dataset (Section 4.1, Figure 4a).

Anchored RL (ARL) combines a PPO objective with an SFT loss on best-of-N curated anchor data to prevent reward hacking observed in vanilla RL, such as degenerate TL;DR-style outputs (Section 4.2, Figure 4b-c).

ACTG-ARL recovers instruction-following accuracy close to non-DP levels while preserving high MAUVE fidelity, resolving the control-fidelity tradeoff seen in earlier DP text generation methods (Figure 5).

The optimal ACTG configuration uses a rich structured tabular schema (S3) with an AIM generator and DP-FT conditional generation, outperforming free-form summary (S2) and topic-based (S1/CTCL) schemas (Section 3.3.2).

UOpsG95XqH.text: Theorem 4.7 proves that pruning masks generated by factorised saliency scores (encompassing SNIP, GraSP, magnitude, and random pruning) converge in cut-norm metric to deterministic limit bipartite graphons as network width grows (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.7).

Theorem 5.7 establishes a universal approximation result showing sparse networks retain universal approximation capability for target functions depending only on a fixed k-dimensional active coordinate subspace, provided the limiting graphon contains an 'active rectangle' with uniformly lower-bounded edge probabilities (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.7, Assumption 5.2).

Theorem 6.1 derives an infinite-width graphon-NTK generalisation bound in which the complexity term depends on y^T K_W^{-1} y / m, where K_W is the graphon-modulated kernel (Section 6.2, Theorem 6.1).

Proposition 6.3 shows the graphon-NTK Gram matrix incorporates a path-density proxy that weights input coordinates, explaining why data-driven (structured) pruning improves feature alignment relative to uniform pruning (Section 6.3, Proposition 6.3).

UAXQW194WT.text: On the Aliyun cloud-provisioning benchmark at full incomparable-pair coverage (IP-Cov=1.0), BPOP recovers dependency structure with Edge-F1 of 0.95, exceeding the best process-mining baseline (Heuristics Miner at 0.60) (Section 5.4, Figure 7).

On WFCommons workflows, BPOP achieves Edge-F1 of 0.91 on SRASearch (22 nodes) and 0.79 on Epigenomics (41 nodes), versus 0.43 and 0.38 respectively for the best baseline (Heuristics Miner) (Section 5.3, Figure 4).

The compiled executor driven by BPOP-inferred graphs reaches 100% task completeness with zero fallback LLM calls and zero token usage once incomparable-pair coverage reaches 0.9-1.0, compared to 5.9 LLM calls and 32,208 tokens per task at IP-Cov=0.6 (Table 2, Section 5.4.2).

Across 6 cloud provisioning scenarios, expert mode (SOP-only, using the inferred partial order) completes tasks in 34.4 seconds using 0 tokens but only 66.7% success, while hybrid mode (SOP plus LLM fallback) reaches 100% success in 225.2 seconds using 79,406 tokens, versus 1,319-2,580 seconds and 234k-382k tokens for a pure LLM explore mode (Table 3, Section 5.4.2).
BPOP models trace likelihood via a frontier-softmax formulation (Eq. 5) that avoids #P-complete enumeration of linear extensions, reducing likelihood computation to O(|≻h| + T|A|) time (Section 3.2).

FxiO8RTOsq.text: Octopus-8B achieves an average accuracy of 71.7% across 7 benchmarks (MathVista, MathVerse, WeMath, HallBench, MMStar, MMMU, CharXiv), the best among open-source 8B-scale VLMs (Table 2).
Octopus-8B outperforms the strongest RLVR baseline (GSPO with n=16) by 1.0 point in average accuracy while requiring only 0.72x the total training time per step (958.1s vs. 1322.8s) (Table 2).

The two-stage RL training strategy first masks the pre-correction response (o1) as fixed context and updates the policy only from the post-correction response (o2) with KL regularization on o1 (Stage I), then selectively unmasks o1 to co-evolve both direct-reasoning and self-correction capabilities without gradient conflicts (Stage II) (Section 4.3).

Rollout augmentation pairs n=8 original rollouts into n^2=64 augmented samples, from which n=16 balanced samples are selected for training, yielding a 4.3-point accuracy improvement over no augmentation, versus only a 3.1-point gain from random augmentation (Table 3, Section 3.2).
Stage I training widens the accuracy gap between the pre-correction response o1 and the post-correction response o2, confirming effective isolated self-correction learning (Figure 6).

nbkYuKIcXr.text: Theorem 3.2 proves DQGPM achieves linear error contraction at rate (1/10)^k for the standard (rotation) part when noise satisfies ||Delta||_{op,st} <= n/350 and ||Delta||_{op,I} <= n/300, providing the first finite-iteration recovery guarantee for SE(3) synchronization (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).

In synthetic benchmarks with n=100 nodes at observation rate p=0.05, DQGPM attains rotation error 0.034 +/- 0.051 versus 0.056 +/- 0.632 for eigendecomposition (EIG); at p=0.30 both methods converge to near-zero error (0.0005 vs 0.001) (Table 2).
DQGPM runs in 0.007-0.011 seconds on average across synthetic settings, faster than the eigendecomposition baseline's 0.011-0.019 seconds (Table 3).

On Stanford point-set registration datasets, DQGPM achieves rotation errors of about 0.019-0.025 radians and translation errors under 0.002m, substantially outperforming semidefinite relaxation (SDR), which exceeds 3 radians of rotation error on sparse graphs (Table 4).
Figure 1 shows DQGPM's error decays linearly over iterations before plateauing at a noise floor matching the theoretical bound predicted by Theorem 3.2 (Figure 1).

PGSCzFVigx.text: Fine-tuned Qwen guardrail models (ft-Qwen14B, ft-Qwen3B) outperform GPT-4.1 and OSS-Safeguard-20B across four custom policy tasks, e.g. ft-Qwen14B scores 0.98 on plan verification versus 0.58 for GPT-4.1 (Table 3).
Removing debate-based verification drops accuracy on the repetition-handling task from 0.99 to 0.65 on synthetic test data and from 0.85 to 0.58 on human-labeled test data (Table 4).

Single-agent self-refinement underperforms even the no-verification baseline (0.65/0.53 vs 0.65/0.58 synthetic/human), showing multi-agent debate specifically drives the gains, not iterative refinement alone (Table 4).
Over 30% of Advocate-Judge debate transcripts exhibit non-trivial dynamics beyond simple agreement or disagreement, including persuasion and consensus-breaking patterns (Figure 4).

Dimension decomposition (Section 3.1) paired with debate-based validation (Section 3.3) is presented as jointly necessary for producing diverse, boundary-challenging synthetic samples with faithful labels.
Model scaling behavior is task-dependent: simpler guardrail tasks saturate in accuracy at smaller fine-tuned model scales while harder tasks continue improving with larger scale (Figure 2).

NsJUKcONFR.text: With 128 recurrent neurons, ParalESN and ParalESN (deep) reach MemCap scores of 114.5 and 125.0 respectively, versus 50.6 and 56.8 for shallow and deep traditional ESN (Table 1).

On sMNIST, ParalESN and ParalESN (deep) reach 96.2% and 97.2% test accuracy versus 82.5% for a shallow ESN, while training in 2.7 and 3.3 minutes versus 4.3 minutes for ESN and 80.8 minutes for an LSTM of comparable parameter count (Table 4).
Theorem 4.1 proves a ParalESN satisfies the Echo State Property if and only if every diagonal element of its transition matrix has complex modulus less than 1.

Corollary 4.3 (building on Proposition 4.2) establishes that ParalESN models with the Echo State Property and an MLP readout are universal approximators of fading-memory filters, matching the expressivity of traditional linear-recurrence ESNs.
On psMNIST, ParalESN (deep) reaches 95.2% test accuracy using only 0.05 kWh of energy, compared to 92.6% accuracy and 0.63 kWh for Mamba of similar parameter count (Table 4).

ParalESN's recurrence time scales logarithmically with sequence length (via associative scan), versus linear scaling for traditional ESNs, and it avoids the out-of-memory failures traditional ESNs hit at ~100K reservoir neurons on sMNIST (Figure 2).

O57TtEyCrW.text: Lemma 3.1 proves the prediction-powered risk estimate is unbiased (E[R̄̂ₜᴾᴾ] = R̄ₜ) regardless of the quality of the synthetic-label predictor used (Section 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 gives an assumption-free, finite-sample bound on the probability of false alarm, P_H0(∃t≥1: Φₜᴾᴾ=1) ≤ δs + δt (Section 3.2).

On CIFAR10-C with binary loss and an external predictor, PPRM raises an alarm around t≈760 versus t≈800 for supervised risk monitoring (SRM), while the unsupervised risk monitor (URM) fails to alarm within the tested horizon (Figure 2a).
On an LLM question-answering task with a prompt shift introduced at t=200, PPRM detects the shift at t≈500 versus t≈530 for SRM (Figure 3a).
Using the adaptive weighting parameter ηt derived in Lemma 3.3, rather than a fixed value, reduces the average time-to-alarm for a Qwen2-VL-7B predictor from 519 to 498 steps (Table 1).
Stronger synthetic-label predictors (e.g. GPT-4.1) yield faster shift detection, with average time-to-alarm ranging from about 460 to 528 steps depending on predictor quality (Figure 4).

nC1A9GSm3S.text: PairComp is introduced as a benchmark of paired prompts with subtle fine-grained differences across six categories (overall appearance, color, counting, position, style/tone, text content), scored by arithmetic-mean (sa) and geometric-mean (sg) alignment (Section 2).
Janus-FocusDiff-7B improves over the Janus-Pro-7B baseline on PairComp from 75.5 to 85.0 arithmetic mean and from 70.4 to 83.5 geometric mean (Table 1).
Pair-GRPO extends GRPO by expanding the reward-normalization group to 2×G responses drawn from a pair of similar prompts, instead of G responses from a single prompt (Section 3.2).

Pair-GRPO mixes in ground-truth images from FocusDiff-Data with a probability that decays from 1.0 to 0.0 over training, shifting the policy from exploitation-first to exploration-first (Section 3.2).
FocusDiff-7B narrows the geometric-to-arithmetic mean gap on PairComp to 1.5 points, versus 3-5 points for existing baseline models such as Janus-Pro-7B (Table 1).
On established benchmarks, the model improves GenEval overall score from 0.80 to 0.85 and DPG-Bench average score from 84.17 to 85.23 (Table 2).

TJvRtbspej.text: Linear probes trained to identify MLP value vectors aligned with party-related tokens achieve F1 scores exceeding 96% on held-out test data (Section 5.1).

Mechanistic forecasting is evaluated across more than 24 million configurations spanning 7 models (including Llama 3.1 8B, Mistral 7B, Gemma 2 9B, Qwen 3 14B variants) and 6 national elections (US, UK, Canada, Germany, Netherlands, New Zealand, 2019-2024) (Section 3).

Mechanistic forecasting produces more distributional "wins" over probability-based forecasting relative to survey ground truth across most model-country combinations, with larger win rates for instruction-tuned than base models (Section 5.2, Figure 2).

Entropy-gated analysis shows mechanistic forecasting most improves accuracy for high-entropy attributes (normalized entropy above 0.85), where surface-level output probabilities are diffuse (Section 5.5, Figure 5).

Gains are attribute- and country-dependent: demographic attributes show strong latent gains in the US and UK but weaker gains in New Zealand, while opinion-based attributes show high cross-national variation, e.g. political orientation in the UK and immigration attitudes in New Zealand (Section 5.4, Figure 4).

The method decomposes MLP contributions to token probability additively (Equation 5) and selects statistically extreme value vectors via a 2.5-interquartile-range fence, validated with sign-inversion tests on party-token log-probabilities (Section 4.1-4.2).

JiB2eXY8fT.text: Theorem 2.1 shows that for (w,k)-occurrency bounded CountDistinct streams, any (ε=0.5, δ=1/T^2)-differentially private algorithm achieving (τ=1/10, η=h)-approximation must use space M ≥ Ω̃(kw/h^2) (Theorem 2.1).
Corollary 2.2 specializes the general bound to a concrete parameter regime (w=T^{2/3-4α}, k=T^{1/3-2α}, h=T^{1/3-α}), yielding a required space of Ω̃(T^{1/3-4α}) (Corollary 2.2).

Section 1 states this establishes the first exponential separation between the space complexity of private algorithms and their non-private Õ(1)-space counterparts for CountDistinct estimation, nearly matching the Õ(T^{1/3}) space upper bound of Cummings et al. (2025) (Section 1).
Theorem 2.3 extends the same space lower-bound structure from CountDistinct to the MaxSelect and Quantile estimation problems (Theorem 2.3).

The lower bound is proved by reducing space-bounded differential privacy to a multi-player communication game, AvoidHeavyHitters, introduced in Lemma 3.1 and connected to DP streaming via the fingerprinting-based reduction of Lemmas 3.2 and 3.4 (Section 3.1, Lemmas 3.1, 3.2, 3.4).

ZJnIdRb1Jq.text: IDEA (Inter-Domain BridgE with historical Assets) represents each adapted domain as a triplet {P*, Γ, u} of learned soft prompts, feature-statistic environment descriptors, and behavioral uncertainty scores, and reuses these assets via projection onto the convex hull of historical assets under Wasserstein distance rather than re-optimizing per domain (Section on Assets / Cross-Domain Bridging).
On REVERIE test-unseen, adding IDEA to the DUET baseline improves Success Rate by 2.5 points and SPL by 3.8 points, and adding it to HAMT improves SR by 2.5 points and SPL by 2.8 points (Table 1).
On R2R validation-unseen, IDEA improves DUET by 4 points SR and 7 points SPL, and improves BEVBert by 1 point SR and 4 points SPL (Table 2).
On R2R-CE validation-unseen, IDEA improves BEVBert by 2 points SR and 2 points SPL, and improves ETPNav by 2 points SR and 3 points SPL (Table 3).

An ablation shows Fisher-guided weighting (using Fisher Information Matrix traces to identify policy-sensitive parameters) alone contributes a 3.5-point SR improvement, and the closed-form KKT-derived bridging solution outperforms hard nearest-asset retrieval strategies (Table 5, Section 6.2).

IG956mtgzL.text: Theorem 2.6 proves consistency of the maximum likelihood estimator θ̂_n for agents' cost-model parameters (θ̂_n →_p θ*) under Assumptions 2.3–2.5, when local disclosure reveals agents' pre-strategic covariates via action-recommendation explanations (ARexes) (Theorem 2.6).

Agents' cost sensitivity α is modeled as following a conditional log-normal distribution, ln α | x^b ~ N(β^T φ(x^b) + β_0, σ^2), estimated from the disclosed pre-strategic covariates x^b (Section 2, cost model).

Theorem 3.2 establishes that the proposed strategy-robust doubly robust estimator V̂_SDR, which decomposes as V̂_S-IPS-res + V̂_S-DM, is consistent for the policy value V(π) as long as either the outcome model is correctly specified or the overlap assumption holds (Theorem 3.2).
Assumption 2.1 posits unconfoundedness: the outcome noise Z is conditionally independent of treatment T^s given the strategically updated covariate X^s (Assumption 2.1).

The estimator is validated on synthetic data with 1,000 to 11,000 agents in a 2-dimensional feature space (Section 4.1) and on the German Credit dataset with 200,000 samples under a misspecified outcome model (Section 4.2).

xRN1Ym2hoa.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes joint identifiability of the latent causal variables (up to permutation and component-wise transformation) and the continuous mixing trajectory in the continuous mechanism evolution setting (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 shows the least-squares estimator recovers the mixing coefficients with error bounded in terms of 1/σ_min times noise and approximation error, and Theorem 4.3 proves an O(T^{-2/3}) convergence rate when exploiting temporal smoothness of the trajectory (Theorems 4.2, 4.3).

On synthetic three-mechanism transitions, TRACE recovers mixing weight correlation of 0.94±0.05 (Table 1) and up to 0.99 on calibrated transitions (Figure 3), substantially outperforming discrete-switching NCTRL baselines (0.67 hard, 0.72 soft) (Table 1, Figure 3).

On real-world data, TRACE achieves 0.96 correlation recovering vehicle-turning trajectories on UAVDT (versus NCTRL at 0.239) and 0.917 on CMU MoCap human gait transitions, where NCTRL instead produces spurious transitions (Figures 6, 7).

Mechanisms are parameterized as convex combinations θ_t = Σ_k α_k(t)·θ^(k) over Mixture-of-Experts atomic-mechanism vertices, letting the model generalize to intermediate mechanism states never seen during training (Section 3.2).

An ablation in Section 6.5 shows a geometric bottleneck as the number of experts K approaches d+1: basis-vector collinearity degrades mixing-coefficient recovery from 0.979 to 0.459 correlation, even though the underlying transition matrix W(t) remains recoverable at 0.995+ correlation (Section 6.5).

XF0wkyEbuM.text: On short-range 10-meter wind forecasts, U-Cast's deep-ensemble variant achieves a CRPS of 0.345 at 1-day lead time versus GenCast's 0.332, part of broader Table 1 results also showing up to roughly 3% CRPS improvement over GenCast on variables such as short-range z500 (Table 1).

The full U-Cast deep ensemble (4 members) trains in under 12 H200 GPU-days, decomposed as 7 GPU-days for deterministic Stage-1 pretraining plus 1.2 GPU-days per model for Stage-2 probabilistic fine-tuning (Section 4.1, Table 2).

U-Cast generates a 60-step ensemble forecast in 11 seconds on H200 GPUs (17 seconds on A100), over a 10x reduction in inference latency compared to diffusion-based baselines such as GenCast (Table 2, Abstract).

GenCast retains an advantage over U-Cast on 2-meter temperature, attributed to GenCast's finer native resolution, illustrating a variable-dependent trade-off rather than uniform superiority (Section 4.3).

Section 4.3 positions U-Cast on the Pareto frontier of forecast skill versus computational cost relative to IFS ENS and GenCast, visualized against these baselines in Figure 2 (Section 4.3, Figure 2).

aZ5Di8Ii4X.text: In Gemma-style transformer blocks, the entire effect of prepending context can be exactly reproduced by rank-1 patches ΔWgate = Wgate(zC−z)zT/‖z‖² and ΔWup = Wup(zC−z)zT/‖z‖² applied to the MLP gate and up-projection weight matrices, plus a patch Δm to the RMSNorm scale (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).

The rank-1-plus-RMSNorm-patch construction extends inductively from a single block to full L-layer transformers, yielding a perfect implicit weight patch for the whole network (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).

A perfect implicit weight patch exists whenever the block's inner function is input-controllable (Definition 3) and its outer function is output-controllable (Definition 4), a sufficient condition proved in general form (Theorem 5, Section 5).

In float32 precision, the implicit weight-patched model matches the context-conditioned model's output logits almost exactly, achieving 100% token-prediction agreement, whereas standard bfloat16 implementation only reaches 87.5% agreement (Section 4).
Using a numerically stable RMSNorm inversion in bfloat16 raises token-prediction agreement between the patched and context-conditioned models from 87.5% to 98% (Section 4).
The rank-1 patch derivation is shown to generalize across Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Mixtral, GPT-2, GPT-J, and mixture-of-experts architectures (Table 1).

jsOKNGu8ac.text: For diagonal linear networks, the gradient-flow solution of fine-tuning minimizes an implicit-bias penalty Q_k(β_FT) = Σ_d q_{k_d}(β_FT,d), whose per-dimension penalty k_d depends on pretraining scale/relative-scale parameters (c_PT, λ_PT) and the fine-tuning re-initialization γ_FT (Theorem 4.1).

Generalization error of the fine-tuned model is characterized via a replica-theory calculation that decouples the high-dimensional problem into scalar fixed-point equations for effective regularization parameters (Proposition 4.2).

A universal trade-off ℓ-order + PD ∈ [1,2] defines four qualitatively distinct learning regimes—rich/pretraining-independent, lazy/pretraining-dependent, lazy/pretraining-independent, and a novel intermediate rich/pretraining-dependent regime (Proposition 5.1, Section 5).

Negative relative pretraining scale λ_PT pushes fine-tuning into a richer, pretraining-dependent regime that better reuses shared feature dimensions, while increasing the absolute pretraining scale c_PT pushes fine-tuning toward a lazy, pretraining-independent regime (Section 5.3, Figure 3).

In ResNet-18 experiments pretrained on 98 CIFAR-100 classes and fine-tuned on the remaining 2 classes (averaged over 50 repetitions), initializing with a smaller-than-standard scale in earlier layers improves fine-tuning generalization, while increasing the pretraining initialization scale c_PT degrades it (Section 6, Figure 4).

mvm6NhIT8k.text: Under a uniform-margin comparison oracle with advantage parameter p ∈ (0,1/2], the NCRS algorithm attains ε-stationarity for smooth nonconvex objectives with iteration complexity O(k/(p²ε²)), where k is the intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient dimension d (Theorem 2.2).

A one-step descent inequality shows the per-iteration progress of NCRS scales with intrinsic dimension k rather than ambient dimension d: pα_t√(2/π)E[‖∇f(θ^t)‖₂] ≤ E[f(θ^t)−f(θ^{t+1})] + L_f k α_t²/2 (Lemma 2.1).
Under a gap-dependent confidence oracle with tie-aware noise, a confidence-weighted majority-vote variant of NCRS achieves ε-stationarity using O(k²/ε⁴) total pairwise comparisons (Theorem 3.5).

The analysis extends to nearly-ridge objectives with bounded nuisance-subspace leakage, parameterized by (τ, m), showing robustness of the intrinsic-dimension rate beyond exact low-rank structure (Proposition 2.4).
NCRS's O(k/ε²) rate (up to the 1/p² factor) improves on prior ambient-dimension-dependent zeroth-order methods such as ZO-RankSGD, whose complexity is O(d/ε²) (Table 1).

BipvhtXmde.text: Risk-Averse Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility (RAIC) requires that the worst-case equilibrium outcome under truthful reporting be at least as good as the worst-case outcome from misreporting, while Optimistic Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility (OAIC) requires the same comparison using the best-case equilibrium outcomes (Definitions 1 and 2, Section 3.2).
For two tCPA auto-bidders under non-uniform bidding, the Second-Price Auction (SPA) is proven to satisfy both RAIC (Theorem 1) and OAIC (Theorem 2) (Section 4).
For two tCPA auto-bidders restricted to uniform bidding, SPA is proven to satisfy RAIC (Theorem 4) and OAIC (Theorem 5) (Section 4.1).

Existence of an equilibrium allocation under uniform bidding is characterized by inequality conditions (4)-(7) that depend only on reported tCPA targets and per-query values, after eliminating the bid multiplier variables (Theorem 3).

FlJnOeuN8C.text: Augmenting a base model with Artificial Hippocampus Networks (AHN) using a GatedDeltaNet variant (AHN-GDN) reduces inference FLOPs by 40.5% and memory cache by 74.0% relative to a sliding-window attention baseline while achieving comparable or superior task performance (Figure 1b).
On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with 128k-token context, AHN-GDN improves the LV-Eval average score from 4.41 (full-attention/sliding-window baseline) to 5.88 (Table 2).
AHN-GDN also improves InfiniteBench scores at 128k context, raising English QA from 7.28 to 10.61 and Chinese QA from 11.75 to 15.87 (Table 2).

Full attention scales as O(L^2) FLOPs and O(L) memory cache, whereas AHN-GDN scales as O(WL) FLOPs and O(W) memory cache for a fixed window size W, independent of the growing context length L (Table 1).
On a 57K-token passage from PG19, AHN-GDN maintains constant GPU memory consumption during generation, in contrast to the linear memory growth exhibited by baseline attention models (Figure 3).
All three tested AHN variants (built on Mamba2, DeltaNet, and GatedDeltaNet) consistently outperform the sliding-window attention baseline across evaluated benchmarks (Table 2).

Rg73g42KBW.text: SecCodePRM computes step-level security scores as the logit margin between safe and vulnerable classes along a code trajectory, rather than requiring a fully complete program to assess vulnerability (Section 4, Figure 4).
SecCodePRM achieves 96.83% accuracy and 96.73% F1 on the PrimeVul Paired vulnerability detection benchmark, outperforming baselines including VulSim, VulBERTA, ReGVD, and LLMxCPG (Table 1, Table 3).
On PrimeVul Paired pairwise consistency metrics, SecCodePRM reaches 93.66% P-C (Table 2, Section 5.1).

SecCodePRM's 7B model outperforms models 17x larger on partial-code vulnerability detection, achieving near-perfect F1 on the PreciseBugs benchmark with sequences exceeding 20,000 tokens (Table 4, Section 5.2).

On the CWEval secure code generation benchmark with inference-time scaling, SecCodePRM improves the safety metric Safe@1 by 12.98% and functionality by 11.09% over baselines without a safety-utility tradeoff (Section 5.3, Table 7).

TqL8MOHtW7.text: Reductive Lie Neurons (ReLNs) achieve exact GL(n) adjoint-action equivariance by replacing the degenerate Killing form on gl(n) with a learnable, non-degenerate, Ad-invariant bilinear form B̃(X,Y) = 2n·tr(XY) − tr(X)tr(Y) (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
On Platonic solid classification under sl(3) with rotated camera views, ReLN achieves 99.78% ± 0.04% accuracy, matching the semisimple-only Lie Neurons baseline (Table 2, Section 5.1.1).
On sp(4) regression, ReLN attains a test MSE of 5.14×10⁻⁴ with near-zero invariance error, outperforming Lie Neurons on this reductive-but-not-semisimple algebra (Table 3, Section 5.1.2).

On the Top-Tagging particle physics benchmark, ReLN embeds Lorentz four-momenta into gl(5) and attains competitive background rejection of 1979±87 relative to LorentzNet-style baselines (Table 4, Section 5.2).

On equivariant drone state estimation combining velocity and log-covariance inputs, ReLN achieves an absolute trajectory error of 13.92 m versus 191.78 m for a non-equivariant baseline under SO(3) rotation (Table 5, Section 5.3.1).

03q28fBsB7.text: GReinSS's dynamically rescaled policy-gradient reward r(τ) = Σᵢ Pr(Xᵢ|τ)/Pr(Xᵢ|θ) is proven to be an unbiased estimator of the gradient of the data log-likelihood Pr(X₁:ₙ|θ), without constructing artificial intermediate latent states (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.1).
On simulated graph inference, GReinSS achieves F1=0.891 with k=10 random walks, while compared baselines score below 0.55 (Figure 2, Section 4.1).
On simulated set reconstruction with universe size |U|=1000, GReinSS attains a median F1=0.938, versus below 0.4 for alternative methods (Figure 3, Section 4.1).

On real GTEx RNA sequencing data covering 14,390 human genes validated against orthogonal long-read sequencing, GReinSS outperforms the standard RSEM isoform-quantification algorithm on 46.6% of genes by a median error-difference margin of 0.0405 (Section 4.2, Figure 4).
Theorem 3.3 derives the variance-minimizing off-policy sampling distribution q(τ|X₁:ₙ,θ) = (1/N)Σᵢ Pr(τ|Xᵢ,θ) used for training GReinSS (Section 3.1).

Q7MkgK17GU.text: GOAT reframes attention as entropic optimal transport, showing standard softmax attention p*=softmax(s/τ + log π) implicitly assumes a uniform prior π, and replaces it with a learnable continuous prior while remaining fully compatible with FlashAttention-style kernels (Section 5, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 5.1 ("Collapse to Prior") proves that as content signal strength vanishes, GOAT's posterior attention distribution converges pointwise to the learned prior, explaining the mechanism behind attention sinks (Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 5.4 shows peaked priors suppress context sensitivity exponentially while uniform priors degrade only linearly with sequence length, implying a logarithmic margin growth δ ∼ ln L suffices for stability (Theorem 5.4).

Theorem 2 (Appendix F) proves that any SDPA-compatible, translation-equivariant, bounded attention prior must take the form of a finite trigonometric polynomial in relative displacement, uniquely motivating GOAT's spectral parameterization (Theorem 2, Appendix F).
On 125M-parameter C4 language modeling, GOAT improves perplexity by 1.55 points over ALiBi and maintains robust extrapolation to 16x the training context length (Figure 2, Section 6).
On biological sequence modeling of the human reference genome, GOAT reduces peak memory usage by 36% versus RoPE while improving validation NLL (Figure 4, Section 6).

Y1rHxA58If.text: GDPO performs group-wise normalization separately for each reward before aggregation, followed by batch-wise advantage normalization, to avoid GRPO's collapse of distinct multi-reward rollout combinations into identical advantage values (Figure 2, Section 3).
On tool-calling with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, GDPO improves live-task accuracy to 55.36% versus 50.63% for GRPO, and format correctness to 80.66% versus 76.33% (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On AIME math reasoning with DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, GDPO reaches 29.4% accuracy versus 23.1% for GRPO, while reducing length-constraint violations from 10.8% to 6.5%, and avoids the training collapse GRPO exhibits around step 400 (Table 3, Section 4.2).
On code reasoning with DeepSeek-R1-7B under a 3-reward setting, GDPO achieves a 68.3% pass rate with an 18.8% bug ratio, versus 67.2% pass rate and 20.3% bug ratio for GRPO (Table 5, Section 4.3).
Figure 3 shows GDPO preserves substantially more distinct advantage groups across varying numbers of rollouts and rewards than GRPO variants, evidencing higher training-signal resolution (Figure 3).

iiNPaOvuwj.text: On 3D geometric problems with 128K variables, RAPNet as a standalone solver converges in 59±5 iterations versus 132±17 for the AGG baseline and 63±10 for SpSA (Table 1).

On temporal Barabási-Albert graphs, RAPNet converges in 85±45 iterations while SpSA reaches 90±152 iterations and fails to converge on the largest instance tested (Section on diverse problem classes).

RAPNet's setup cost on the 300K-node social hub graph is 0.76±0.01 seconds, versus 973.16±70 seconds for the SpSA baseline, reflecting avoidance of expensive distance-3 neighborhood computations (Table 2).

An ablation removing the transfer-operator corrections (ΔP, ΔR) degrades the 3D geometric standalone-solver result from 59±5 to 99±10 iterations, while removing coarse-operator correction (ΔA_c) degrades it to 83±7 iterations (Ablation study).

The level-wise training curriculum, using subgraphs of roughly 4,000 nodes, generalizes to problems roughly 250x larger (million-node domains) without loss of performance (Training Strategy / Generalization Capabilities section).

A model trained only on 2D Laplacian discretizations transfers to 3D domains at evaluation time, indicating the learned corrections reflect local multigrid theory rather than global problem structure (Generalization Capabilities section).

BWAr39vOQY.text: VFMF performs autoregressive flow matching in vision-foundation-model (VFM) feature space rather than deterministic regression, arguing that deterministic regression averages over multiple plausible futures and thereby undermines forecast accuracy (abstract only).

VFMF encodes VFM features into a compact latent representation that the authors report preserves information more effectively than previously used PCA-based alternatives, both for forecasting and other downstream applications (abstract only).

Under matched computational budgets, VFMF produces sharper and more accurate predictions than a regression baseline across multiple output modalities, including semantic segmentation, depth, surface normals, and RGB imagery (abstract only).

The authors position stochastic conditional generation of VFM features as a promising and scalable foundation for future world models, as an alternative to pixel-level video generation for decision-making applications (abstract only).

BW16CkVDnq.text: The paper decomposes total predictive uncertainty in multi-agent debate (MAD) into epistemic uncertainty, measured via Jensen-Shannon divergence between agents' response distributions, and aleatoric uncertainty, measured as average within-agent predictive entropy (Proposition 3.2).

On MATH500 with heterogeneous agents (Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen3-4B) at 5 debate rounds, UMAD raises accuracy of the weaker agent from 78.2% (zero-shot MAD) to 86.0%, compared with 81.0% for a standard IPPO multi-agent RL baseline (Table 1).
On AMC23 at T=5 rounds, UMAD reaches 77.5% accuracy versus 70.5% for IPPO and 60.0% for zero-shot MAD (Table 1).

Theorem 3.3 formalizes a 'heterogeneous novelty condition' showing that messages from heterogeneous agents provide larger epistemic gain than additional homogeneous samples, explaining why heterogeneous debate outperforms homogeneous debate empirically (Theorem 3.3).

Homogeneous-agent MAD training yields only modest accuracy gains of about 1-2% due to limited epistemic diversity, in contrast to substantially larger gains under heterogeneous agent pairing (Empirical Results section).

Models trained on 2-round debates generalize to 5-round debates without mode collapse, and Figure 3 shows aleatoric uncertainty declining consistently across debate rounds after UMAD training (Figure 3).

m0HB67qATB.text: The framework casts on-device/cloud LLM collaboration as a single reward-maximization objective subject to a budget constraint on cloud invocations, rather than training a separate external router (Problem Formulation section).

The reward design combines accuracy, coordination, and format terms with weights satisfying αₐ > α_c > α_f, prioritizing independent problem solving over cloud delegation (Hierarchical Reward Design section).

Standard GRPO with collaboration-aware rewards is shown to over-offload to the cloud because normalized advantages distort the true reward gap between an independent correct answer (reward 2.2) and a cloud call (reward 0.5); the proposed Group-Adaptive Policy Gradient (GAPG) uses an unbiased group-level gradient estimator to correct this (Why GRPO Fails section).

On the Countdown task with Qwen2.5-3B, the method achieves roughly a 30% accuracy improvement over task-tuning-only while keeping about 30% of queries processed on-device, approaching cloud-only performance (Countdown Task results).

On MATH-lighteval across Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Llama-3.2-3B, the method outperforms baselines with average improvements of 6-8 points on downstream benchmarks (MATH-500, AMC23, AIME24, MinervaMath), and generalizes better across cloud budget ratios ranging from 20% to 60% (MATH-lighteval results section).

9PPeJsVLdB.text: Spherical Steering rotates activations along a geodesic toward a target-concept direction using spherical linear interpolation (Slerp), preserving activation norm instead of using additive steering vectors (Method: Norm-Preserving Rotation section).

On TruthfulQA MC1, Spherical Steering achieves 49.95% versus roughly 38% for addition-based baselines, corresponding to the reported +10% improvement, with similar +11% gains on COPA and +10.06% on StoryCloze (Experimental Results section).
Averaged across six benchmarks, Spherical Steering improves accuracy by about +8 points over activation-addition baselines (Experimental Results section).

A von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution-based confidence gate dynamically modulates steering strength according to input uncertainty, sustaining higher accuracy across a broader range of intervention strengths than ungated steering (vMF Confidence Gating / Ablation Findings section).

At matched effective-rank drops (~50), the rotation-based method delivers 8-10% higher accuracy than addition-based steering while better maintaining open-ended generation quality, as measured by TRUE×INFO scores improving +3.45% on LLaMA-3.1 and +0.90% on Qwen-2.5 (Collapse-Efficiency / Effective Rank Analysis section).
Combining Spherical Steering with 5-shot in-context learning yields a +14.08% MC1 gain over the ICL-only baseline, indicating the two mechanisms act largely orthogonally (Ablation Findings section).

YB6U1yWcGy.text: Computing per-example gradient statistics in a 1.2B-parameter transformer on TPU v5 adds only about 17% compute overhead with no increase in peak memory usage (Section 2.3, Figure 2).

Fact B.1 shows that when the input dimension exceeds the parameter dimension, storing individual per-example gradients requires no more memory than standard activation checkpointing (Appendix B.4, Fact B.1).

Among three SignSGD variants tested, SignEMA (sign applied last, i.e., sign ∘ EMA ∘ avg) trains fastest and most stably, while MicroSignSGD (sign applied first, i.e., EMA ∘ avg ∘ sign) is noisiest and shows late-time instabilities (Section 3.1, Figure 3).

A signal-to-noise ratio argument shows the sign function decreases SNR for low-SNR distributions and increases SNR for high-SNR distributions, predicting that applying sign as late as possible in the optimizer pipeline maximizes variance reduction (Appendix C.1).

sQTzABTEQM.text: LARA aligns latent action representations between a Latent Action Model (LAM) and a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model via a cosine-similarity representation-alignment loss inserted at the second-to-last (L-2) layer of the VLA's DiT backbone (Section 4.1, Section 4.2, Equation 6).

The LAM side of LARA is regularized by inverse dynamics to emphasize control-relevant visual changes over nuisance variations such as lighting and shadows, while the VLA side is regularized by forward dynamics to reduce kinematically hallucinated (physically plausible but non-effective) action trajectories (Section 4.1).
On OXE-constrained evaluation, LARA improves average performance by about 5.0% on LIBERO and about 16.8% on SIMPLER-ENV (with up to +32.1% on the SIMPLER-ENV Long task) (Table 1).

On the novel-embodiment GR1-Sim-24(30) setting, LARA improves performance by about 78.1% over a DiT-only baseline, and on the real-world G1-Real benchmark it improves average performance by about 32.1% (Table 2).

Applied as a post-training module to GR00T-N1.6, LARA yields roughly +1.3% average improvement on LIBERO and SIMPLER benchmarks, and applied to refine Moto-GPT's latent actions, LARA-LAM improves average SIMPLER performance by about 15.7% (with +41.3% on Close Drawer) (Section 5.3, Table 3).

CwHRT46VmC.text: CombinationTS decomposes time-series forecasting pipelines into five orthogonal, swappable stages: input transformation, embedding, encoder, decoder, and output transformation (Section 3.1).

On ETTh1, the parameter-free Identity encoder achieves marginalized performance μ̂=0.4392 versus a Transformer encoder's μ̂=0.5095, while also showing lower instability (σ̂=0.0424 for Identity vs. σ̂=0.1004 for Transformer), with significance confirmed by Mann-Whitney U tests (p<0.0001) (Section 4.1, Table 3).
Evaluation uses a probabilistic framework based on Marginalized Performance (μ̂) and Stability (σ̂) computed via stratified Monte Carlo sampling over K=600 Evaluation Conditions (Section 3.2-3.3).

A cyclic input-transformation prior achieves both lower μ̂ and lower σ̂ than naive trend-seasonal decomposition and the RevIN baseline (e.g., μ̂=0.3891, σ̂=0.0283 on ETTh1), demonstrating that explicit structural priors yield a better effectiveness-stability trade-off than added encoder complexity (Section 4.2, Table 4).
