On ETTh1, spectral-domain encoders iTransformer (μ̂=0.4401) and SimpleTM (μ̂=0.4324) both fail to exceed the Identity encoder's performance (μ̂=0.4271), indicating spectral processing's advantage stems from representation rather than robustness (Section 4.3, Table 5).

a57NvkgjT2.text: Scaling synthetic training data for spoken language models produces a Stability-Expressivity Gap: word error rate improves monotonically with the synthetic-data ratio α, but prosodic metrics (token entropy, NMOS, repetition rate) peak near α≈50% and then degrade, a phenomenon termed Synthetic Erosion (Section 2, Figure 1, Table 1: NMOS=4.51±0.06/WER=47.0% at α=50% vs. NMOS=3.08±0.10/WER=36.2% at α=100%).

Temperature-Driven Self-Critique (TDSC), trained entirely on synthetic data with zero authentic Lao recordings, reduces WER to 29.8% (vs. a 38.5% baseline) and raises NMOS to 3.94±0.07 (vs. 3.12±0.09 baseline), and provides the first zero-shot voice cloning system for Lao with speaker similarity 0.81 and SMOS 4.32±0.06 (Section 4, Table 4, Table 6).

Disentanglement-Guided Self-Alignment (DGSA) for Thai maintains stability (WER 38.9%) while recovering expressivity (NMOS 4.42±0.07), outperforming Standard DPO which sacrifices stability (WER 45.2%), by architecturally separating prosody and timbre in a Flow-Matching SLM (Section 3, Table 3).
For Thai, the resulting system (NMOS 4.51) outperforms both ElevenLabs (NMOS 4.21) and Microsoft Azure (NMOS 4.01) on naturalness (Table 5).

TDSC applies iterative refinement across 5 rounds, generating candidates across temperature gradients with ASR-based filtering to self-improve stability and expressivity over successive iterations (Figure 6).

vgZ66lux3q.text: PriorAL introduces Products-of-Experts combination of foundation-model and small-model class probabilities (Equation 2), an imbalance-aware boosted entropy acquisition score (Equation 5), and entropy-based filtering to partition unlabeled data into noisy and clean sets without extra annotation cost (Section 2.3, Equations 2, 5-7).

Under merged class imbalance with no label noise, PriorAL reaches 67.86% balanced pool accuracy on CIFAR-100 using only a 10% annotation budget, matching baseline accuracy achieved at a 20% budget—a 50% annotation savings (Table 1).

On long-tailed CIFAR-100 with 20% label noise, PriorAL achieves 42.34% balanced pool accuracy at an 11% annotation budget, outperforming the best baseline by 17.30 points even though that baseline used double the annotation budget (Table 2).

The method is evaluated across 21 settings spanning 6 image datasets (including CIFAR-10/100 and PathMNIST variants) and 6 text datasets (including Trec, AGNews, and SST-2 variants) under extreme and long-tailed imbalance ratios ranging from γ=0.0100 to 0.1892 (Appendix B, Table 8).

An ablation removing the imbalance-aware weighting degrades long-tailed Trec performance by 6.3 points in pool accuracy and 11.8 points in test accuracy at a 6% annotation budget, confirming the weighting mechanism's necessity (Section 3.3.1).

meeYr2XiW8.text: BEAR organizes embodied evaluation into 14 atomic skills across 6 categories, built from 4,469 interleaved image-video-text entries drawn from 13 sources (Table 1).
On General Object Pointing, GPT-5 scores 70% accuracy versus a 95.5% human baseline, revealing perceptual capability as a major bottleneck rather than high-level reasoning (Table 1).

87% of pointing failures stem from limited fine-grained visual identification, and 52% of trajectory-reasoning errors occur when the model detects a trajectory arrow but misreads its direction, evidencing unstable spatiotemporal modeling (Section 3.3, Figure 6a-b).
46% of Path Planning errors arise from confusion about spatial directions, a failure mode not exposed by prior task-level embodied benchmarks (Section 3.3, Figure 6c).
BEAR-Agent, augmented with visual and spatial tools, raises GPT-5's overall accuracy from 52.17% to 61.29% (a 9.12-point absolute, 17.5% relative gain) (Section 4.1, Figure 8a).
BEAR-Agent yields a 20.17% average improvement across manipulation tasks in ManiSkill real/simulated robot experiments, outperforming baselines (Section 4.2, Figure 8b).

dvAH9a1uqU.text: The study analyzes 186 first-party release reports alongside 183 post-release evaluation sources (152 fully third-party, 13 fully first-party, 18 mixed), documenting a stark division of labor in AI social-impact evaluation (Section 4).
First-party reports average 0.72 on a 0-3 evaluation-depth scale versus 2.62 for third-party evaluations, indicating first-party reporting is sparse and superficial (Section 5).
Data and content-moderation labor is disclosed in only 12.12% of first-party reports, one of the most under-reported categories (Section 5).
Reporting on environmental costs and bias declines notably after 2023 Q3, a temporal drop corroborated by interviewees citing reputational concerns (Section 5, Figures 3 and 16d).
Statistical modeling in Appendix 8.8.2 (Tables 3-4) shows human contributors account for more variance in evaluation reporting (9%) than model architecture (4.8%).

j0PagZWEFo.text: Execution-guided evolutionary search discovers a pre-training recipe that beats the nanoGPT baseline within 10 search epochs, reaching a 19.7-minute target time versus the 35.9-minute baseline (Table 1).

Claude-4.5-Opus and Claude-4.5-Sonnet achieve over 90% execution rates when automatically implementing ideas on the pre-training (nanoGPT) environment, with Claude-4.5-Opus specifically at 90% (Figure 2, Section 3.1).
Claude-4.5-Sonnet attains an 84% execution rate when self-implementing GRPO-based ideas sampled from frontier LLMs (Figure 2, Section 3).
The automated executor launches parallel GPU experiments at scale: 256 GPUs for the GRPO reinforcement-learning environment and 1,024 GPUs for the nanoGPT environment (Section 5.1).

8AhAziAWvZ.text: InnoEval is compared against six baselines (CoT, RAG, GraphEval, ResearchAgent, InternAgent, ScholarEval) across point-wise, pair-wise, and group-wise research idea evaluation tasks (Table 1, Section 5.1).

In point-wise classification InnoEval reaches 75.58% accuracy / 75.74% F1 on the binary setting and 73.73% accuracy / 74.56% F1 on the three-class setting, outperforming the strongest baseline ScholarEval by 16.18 F1 points (Table 1).
In pair-wise comparison InnoEval attains 80.81% accuracy on easy pairs and 63.00% on hard pairs, roughly a 5% improvement over baselines (Table 1).
In group-wise ranking InnoEval achieves 65.12% accuracy on best-selection and 76.03% on the Longest Increasing Subsequence metric, a 7.56% improvement over baselines (Table 1).

InnoEval judgments correlate with human expert and peer-review scores with coefficients ≥0.5 across all five evaluated dimensions (rationality, supportiveness, depth, constructiveness, overall quality) (Figure 2).

PzXOrmsRZn.text: Attention Distraction (AD) is characterized as retrieved textual context systematically suppressing visual attention compared to parametric (closed-book) generation, plus shifting intra-image attention toward visually salient but question-irrelevant regions (Section 4, Figure 1).

MAD-RAG is a training-free, inference-time method combining dual-question formulation (Section 5.1) with attention mixing via a convex combination weighted by parameter alpha (Section 5.2, Equations 3-5).
MAD-RAG improves over vanilla RAG by up to 4.76% on OK-VQA, 9.20% on E-VQA, and 6.18% on InfoSeek (Table 1).
MAD-RAG rectifies up to 74.68% of OK-VQA, 70.18% of E-VQA, and 44.44% of InfoSeek failure cases where closed-book succeeds but vanilla RAG fails (Figure 5).
MAD-RAG adds only 9-11% inference overhead (1.09-1.11x) relative to vanilla RAG, substantially less than competing mitigation baselines (Table 2).

2iDtIht7W4.text: For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).

Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).

A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.
Analysis of SPRING's convergence for general (non-least-squares) quadratic losses is left open as Conjecture 7, despite numerical experiments showing large empirical performance gains over SNGD.

iD5JNtPwGA.text: The compute penalty of byte-level modeling relative to BPE tokenization is far more severe for masked diffusion models (MDM) than for autoregressive (AR) models: AR byte models are projected to reach BPE parity at roughly F≈1.3×10^22 FLOPs, versus roughly F≈4.2×10^26 FLOPs for MDM byte models (Section 5.2, Figure 3).
At a fixed bits-per-byte (BPB) of 1.2, the compute gap between byte-level and BPE models is approximately 34.3× for MDM but only about 7.9× for AR models (Section 5.2, Figure 3).

On downstream evaluations at the 717M parameter scale, AR byte models score 44.23 average versus 46.23 for the AR BPE baseline, while MDM byte models score 36.76 versus 40.70 for the MDM BPE baseline, showing a larger byte-vs-BPE gap for MDM (Table 1).
AR byte models exhibit emergent subword segmentation, with predictive entropy peaking at subword boundaries and achieving an ROC AUC of 0.829 for detecting subword starts (Figure 4).

Under global permutation/shuffling of context, byte sequences lose about 19% compressibility versus about 7% for BPE sequences, indicating byte models rely more heavily on local contiguity that masking objectives disrupt (Figure 5).

Even at matched sequence lengths, MDM byte models underperform their BPE counterparts more than AR byte models underperform AR BPE counterparts, indicating the gap is not purely a function of sequence length (Appendix D, Figure 7).

f58VZpG6ls.text: OBCache derives three closed-form token saliency scores (value-pruning, key-pruning, and joint-pruning) from an Optimal Brain Damage-style perturbation analysis of attention outputs induced by pruning KV cache tokens (Section 3.3, Equations 5-7).

Existing KV cache eviction heuristics (H2O, TOVA, SnapKV) are shown to be special cases of the OBCache objective when it is simplified to preserve attention weights rather than attention outputs (Section 3.4, Equation 9).

On the Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmark, replacing the H2O heuristic score with the OBCache key-pruning score raises average accuracy from 52.28% to 65.42%, and adding the OBCache joint-pruning score to SnapKV raises accuracy from 85.48% to 88.90% (Table 1).
OBCache-augmented variants of H2O, TOVA, and SnapKV consistently outperform their heuristic-only counterparts across 16 LongBench datasets (Figure 3b).

On the PG19 dataset with a 1024-token cache budget, OBCache variants achieve lower perplexity than the H2O baseline across all tested sequence lengths, evaluated on LLaMA and Qwen model families (Figure 4).

5kteupXJ7B.text: COMAD uses a VAE-based skill discovery module with a global encoder q_m and per-agent action decoder π_m^i, plus a local encoder p_m that enables decentralized execution from individual agent trajectories alone, trained via a policy loss and a KL distillation loss (Section 4.1, Equations 5-6).

COMAD introduces a density-based skill reusability estimator Δ_m^k(s), computed via noise contrastive estimation, that gates contributions from previously learned skills in a skill-augmented advantage function (Section 4.2, Equation 9).

Theorem 4.1 shows the optimal continual policy takes the form π_m^i(a^i|τ^i,z_m^i) ∝ exp(Σ_k Δ_m^{k,*}(s) log π̃_k^{i,*}), establishing that COMAD approximates the optimum of the continual skill discovery problem.

Across 9 task streams spanning LBF, Cooperative Navigation, SMAC, SMACv2, and MAMuJoCo, COMAD attains an overall performance score of 64.34 versus 59.84 for the best baseline (OWL) and 19.37 for the worst baseline (HiSSD) (Table 1).

An ablation removing the skill encoder components causes the largest performance degradation among tested variants, confirming that explicit skill partitioning is necessary to handle multi-modal joint action distributions (Section 5.5).

n2RIMdIbv6.text: REViT introduces Group Convolutional Self-Attention (G-CSA), which achieves discrete roto-reflection equivariance via convolutional patch embeddings and convolutional attention without requiring explicit rotation-aware position encoding (Section 4.2, Equations 8-10).

On Rotated MNIST, the p4-CSA variant (44.28K params) reaches 97.48% accuracy and the larger p8-CSA variant reaches 98.92% accuracy, outperforming a group-equivariant self-attention (G-SA) baseline with relative position encoding while using fewer parameters (Table 1, Table 3).
On PatchCamelyon, p4m-CSA attains 90.75% accuracy, surpassing the α_F-p4m-CNN baseline, and on CIFAR-10 p4m-CSA attains 92.68% accuracy (Table 3).

p4-CSA reduces computation to 116.37M multiply-add operations and 35.84MB peak memory, versus 232.49M operations and 161.77MB for p4-SA with relative position encoding, roughly a 50% reduction in compute (Table 2).
At ImageNet-1K scale, REViT (18M params) achieves 79.27% top-1 accuracy, exceeding augmented ViT-Small (72.08%) and RE-ResNet (77.37%) (Table 7).

Equivariance error analysis shows near-zero pre-classification errors (1.5e-5 to 2.8e-5) for p4/p4m configurations, with elevated errors for the p8 group attributed to interpolation artifacts from non-grid-aligned rotations (45°, 135°) rather than architectural limitations (Table 6, Section 5.5).

r0SYyjDhxY.text: MVP-LAM achieves the highest mutual information I(Z;A) between learned latent actions and ground-truth actions across three independent estimators (KSG, BA, MINE) compared to baselines (Figure 3 & 4).
MVP-LAM attains a linear-probing NMSE of 0.73±0.01 for action prediction on the Bridge V2 dataset, outperforming baseline latent action models (Figure 3 & 4).
On the SIMPLER benchmark, MVP-LAM reaches an average success rate of 60.4% versus 39.6% for the UniVLA baseline when used for VLA pretraining (Table 1).
On LIBERO-Long, MVP-LAM reaches a 90.8% success rate versus 79.4% for UniVLA (Bridge-pretrained), despite using smaller robot datasets (Table 2).
An ablation removing cross-viewpoint reconstruction substantially degrades action-centricity, confirming the cross-viewpoint objective is essential to the method (Table 3).
Including human multi-view videos in training further improves action-centricity metrics relative to using robot-only multi-view videos (Table 3).

HpkknqHNPU.text: Grid-to-place connection weights decay exponentially with spatial frequency, with the decay rate controlled by place field size σp (Section 2, Figure 1).
The optimal place field size scales linearly with the characteristic width D of the environment/task region, σp_opt ∝ D (Section 3, Figure 4).

Test accuracy under varying numbers of training samples and place field widths shows a precision-generalization tradeoff: broader place fields favor few-shot generalization while narrower fields favor precision with more data (Figure 3).
The derived analytical relationship for optimal place field size is σp_opt = L/(2√2πn), linking sample count n and region width L (Section 3).
A performance landscape across place field sizes and region widths shows that HIPE-induced multiscale place coding improves sample efficiency relative to single-scale representations (Figure 5).

cRTbp2pv7X.text: CreDRO formulates epistemic uncertainty as disagreement between ensemble members trained under different degrees δi of relaxation of the i.i.d. train-test assumption, rather than from random-initialization disagreement alone (Algorithm 1).

On CIFAR-10 as in-distribution data, CreDRO achieves higher OOD detection AUROC than Deep Ensembles (DE), EN-DRO, and CreDE across five OOD datasets, e.g. 97.4% vs. 94.8% (DE) on SVHN and 91.1% vs. 88.9% (DE) on ImageNet (OOD detection table).

CreDRO improves CIFAR-10 test accuracy to 0.9637±0.0004 versus 0.9569±0.0004 for Deep Ensembles, while also lowering Expected Calibration Error (0.0038±0.0008 vs. 0.0051±0.0004) (Classification metrics table).

On the Camelyon17 histopathology dataset under scanner-induced domain shift, CreDRO yields improved accuracy-rejection curves for selective classification compared to baseline credal methods (Medical application, Camelyon17 experiments).
CreDRO's performance is robust to the choice of global hyperparameter δG across {0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9}, with SVHN AUROC varying only between 95.8% and 96.6% (Ablation studies).
The box credal set construction 𝒦B consistently outperforms the convex-hull construction 𝒦C across all OOD detection benchmarks tested (Ablation studies, credal set construction).

bIcz7bIZSo.text: PEQ-Net reduces RMSE compared to DeepLTMLE from 1.09-1.42 down to 0.25-0.72 in the limited-confounding semi-synthetic scenario with deterministic policy sequences (Table 1).
PEQ-Net reduces RMSE compared to DeepLTMLE from 0.81-1.42 down to 0.25-0.34 in the expanded-confounding semi-synthetic scenario (Table 1).
On dynamic policies that differ only in early time steps, PEQ-Net achieves RMSE of 0.0026-0.0148 versus 0.1255-0.1448 for baseline ICE-based methods (Table 2).

PEQ-Net's policy encoder uses kernel mean embeddings in an RKHS with maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and metric multidimensional scaling (MDS) to produce fixed-dimensional policy representations that reflect population-level policy dissimilarities (Policy Embedding Approach section).

Theorem 4.2 establishes that the CATE estimation error is controlled by trajectory-level policy distance via a Lipschitz bound on the second-order remainder, preventing spurious non-smooth behavior across policies (Theorem 4.2).

In a case study of 999 sepsis patients, PEQ-Net's estimates show higher MAP vasopressor targets are associated with increased serum lactate at 72 hours, consistent with clinical evidence (Real-World Application, sepsis case study).

pckR7Y6V1j.text: On Function-Gym, BAO-4B achieves Pass@U-1=0.2692 and Pass@U-2=0.5354, compared to UserRL-4B's Pass@U-1=0.2436 and Pass@U-2=0.4103 (Table 1).
On Function-Gym, BAO-4B attains a lower User Involvement Rate (0.2148) than UserRL-4B (0.3758), indicating reduced unnecessary user queries under a fixed reward-shaping scheme (Table 1).

On Turtle-Gym, BAO-4B achieves Pass@U-1=0.1063 and Pass@U-2=0.1125 with a User Involvement Rate of 0.2917, versus UserRL-4B's Pass@U-1=0.0417, Pass@U-2=0.0563, and User Involvement Rate of 0.7617 (Table 1).
BAO-4B exceeds a GPT-4o commercial baseline's Pass@U-1 of 0.1282 on Function-Gym (Table 1).
BAO achieves a reward translation rate of 0.575 on Turtle-Gym versus 0.154 for UserRL, indicating better mitigation of reward hacking (Section 5.4).

An ablation shows removing behavior-regularized RL increases reliance on user verification, while removing behavior enhancement (SFT) degrades early-attempt accuracy, with the combined BAO method performing best (Section 5, ablation results).

mfBKYcsFmi.text: Under Assumption 1 (the coalition's top two bidders remain competitive against outside bids), the coordination mechanism guarantees each bidder in the coalition achieves higher value and lower Return-on-Spend constraint violations than independent bidding, with probability at least 1 - exp(-Δ²T/32B²N²) (Theorem 3.1).
The coordination mechanism in Algorithm 2 has only the coalition's highest-value bidder submit positive bids while all other coalition members bid zero against outside bidders.

When coalition members run a mirror-descent bidding algorithm, coordination yields strictly higher total coalition value than independent bidding in the limit as the number of rounds T approaches infinity (Theorem 4.1).

On the real-world iPinYou dataset with N=4 bidders over 20,000 rounds, coordinated bidding raises average per-bidder value from 0.614±0.016 (independent) to 0.929 and utility from -0.040 to 0.156±0.012 (Table 1).
On synthetic i.i.d. settings, coordination improves utility by roughly 0.23-0.30 and total value by 2-4% relative to independent bidding across N=2 and N=4 bidder configurations (Table 1).
The theoretical results extend to non-i.i.d. value distributions across bidders, where coordination is shown to improve total coalition utility by ΔT/2 (Theorem 5.1 and 5.2).

YqD2yRftiR.text: LaRI predicts a 4D layered point map tensor V ∈ R^(H×W×L×3) together with a ray intersection mask M ∈ {0,1}^(H×W×L) to represent all surfaces intersected by each camera ray, not just the visible surface (Section 3.1).

A Ray Stopping Index is predicted as an ordinal value C ∈ {0,...,L}^(H×W) marking the final valid intersection layer per ray, rather than a binary occupancy mask, which enforces depth ordering and improves segmentation over binary masks (mIoU 0.560 vs 0.091) (Section 3.3).

On the GSO object-level benchmark, LaRI achieves an F-Score at 0.02 of 0.643 versus 0.608 for TRELLIS, while using only 341M parameters versus TRELLIS's 1795M and running in 31.5ms versus 100-900ms for competing methods (Table 1).

On the SCRREAM scene-level benchmark, LaRI attains an overall Chamfer Distance of 0.059 and F-Score at 0.1 of 0.825 while reconstructing occluded scene geometry in a single feed-forward pass (Table 2).
Training data is synthesized from Objaverse (16K objects, 190K images), 3D-FRONT (18K room scenes, 100K images), and ScanNet++ (48K real-world image pairs) (Section 3.4).

Ablation experiments show L=5 layers is optimal for both object- and scene-level tasks, and that pretraining is crucial, with DINOv2 initialization performing comparably to the default backbone (Section 4.6).

lSMTccAN61.text: Stable (localized) Conformal Prediction (StCP/SLCP) uses a conditional CDF estimator trained on labeled source-task data plus an empirical marginal distribution estimated from unlabeled target data, calibrated via a regularized optimization with parameter λ (Equation 7, Section 3).
StCP's coverage error is bounded by O(min(ε + λ^{1/2} + n^{-1}, δ_S + λ^{-1/2} + n^{-1})), establishing robustness of marginal coverage to the choice of λ (Theorem 4.2).

Standard conformal prediction has set-size variance of order O(n^{-1}), while StCP achieves O(m^{-1} + {n(1+λ)²}^{-1}), yielding substantial stability gains when the unlabeled target sample size m greatly exceeds the calibration size n (Theorem 4.6).

On real data across five datasets, StCP/SLCP reduces prediction-set-size standard deviation by 20-48% when built on GLCP and by 6-29% when built on CQR, while maintaining marginal coverage near the nominal 90% level (Table 1).
On synthetic data, the largest stability gains occur at a small calibration size of n=30, with standard deviation reductions of 31.2% (GLCP-based) and 16.3% (CQR-based) (Table 2).
A data-driven procedure for selecting λ maintains empirical coverage within the interval [1-α-α_tol, 1-α+α_tol+(n+1)^{-1}] (Theorem 4.7).

Gz0RAgBfid.text: Gecko's five components—Argument Validator, Response Generator, Task State Estimator, Task Feedback Generator, and API Schema Converter—provide stateful feedback (validity checking, response synthesis, and task achievement assessment) that lets an LLM refine tool calls without executing them against real systems (Section 3).

The Argument Validator achieves 100% accuracy in identifying correct arguments and detecting syntactic errors, while the Response Generator's synthesized tool outputs yield only a 5.4% accuracy decrease relative to using real tool responses (Section 3.1, 3.2, Table 2).

GATS (using Gecko feedback with up to 3 refinement retries) improves GPT-4o's overall accuracy on BFCLv3 from 76.93% to 84.62%, and Gemini-3.0-pro reaches a state-of-the-art 85.19% on the same benchmark (Section 4, Table 3).
On τ²-bench, GATS improves GPT-5-thinking from 72.3% to 76.3% and Gemini-3.0-pro from 78.8% to 82.3% (Table 4).
BFCLv3 evaluation covers 3,633 tasks across 8,578 simulated tools, and τ²-bench covers 114 retail and 50 airline tasks with domain-specific APIs (Section 4).
GATS outperforms Reflexion, Self-Refine, and Best-of-N refinement baselines while achieving the best performance at a reasonable computational cost (Table 5).

TK82ECnJzD.text: Divide and Learn (D&L) attains a regret bound of O(d√(T log T)) that depends on the subproblem dimensionality d rather than the size of the full combinatorial decision space, via decomposition into K overlapping subproblems of size d=n/K (Corollary 5.3, Section 4.2.1).
D&L's coupling error across overlapping subproblems is bounded by O(K²QR_max√T), and its overall regret decomposes into subproblem, overlap, and local-refinement terms (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 5.2).
D&L combines a multi-expert learning framework (UCB, EXP3, and FTRL) with Lagrangian dual coordination across subproblems (Algorithm 1, Section 4.2.2).

On MOCO benchmarks D&L reaches 80-98% of the hypervolume performance of specialized solvers (e.g., WS-LKH/DP) while using 90-99% less computation than Bayesian optimization baselines and achieving 10-30x wall-clock speedups (Table 1, Tables 5-8).

On Bi-TSP-100, D&L achieves a hypervolume of 0.69 compared to 0.67 for specialized solvers and 0.63 for offline-trained PMOCO under matched budgets, and D&L exceeds PMOCO by 50-70% more broadly under matched budgets (Table 1).
On a 4-objective hardware-software co-design task, D&L-TS attains hypervolume 0.372±0.006 versus 0.34±0.012 for MOBO-qParEGO under a 150-evaluation budget, roughly a 22% improvement (Table 2).

SEBPRRnbUX.text: Kinematics-GS achieves a PSNR of 24.644 on the ToyCar sequence, versus 20.789 for the GauFre baseline (Table 1).
On ToyCar, Kinematics-GS attains SSIM 0.936 and LPIPS 0.094, compared to SSIM 0.885 and LPIPS 0.163 for GauFre (Table 1).
On the NeRF-DS 'As' sequence, Kinematics-GS reaches PSNR 27.230 and LPIPS 0.120, versus PSNR 25.808 and LPIPS 0.133 for GauFre (Table 2).

The kinematic basis construction module builds a motion-aligned orthonormal basis from instantaneous velocity direction, used to reparameterize Gaussian scales via an alignment factor (Section 4.3, Equations 9-15).
Removing the kinematics-guided covariance regularization causes PSNR on ToyCar to collapse from 24.644 to 8.152, showing the kinematic prior is critical (Table 3).
Kinematics-GS runs at 200-700 FPS across datasets, about 26x faster than baselines, while using far fewer Gaussians than 4DGS (36,651 vs. 100,456 on ToyCar) (Appendix E).

TZvHUmClPP.text: The KL-minimal soft-constraint (KLSC) principle defines an exponentially tilted target distribution q_beta(x) proportional to p(x)*exp(beta*s(x))/Z(beta), replacing hard-threshold constraints with a soft expectation constraint E_q[s(X)] >= m (Definition 2.2, Equation 9).

Hard-constraint distributions are shown to concentrate probability mass in thin shells near the activation threshold (Boundary Bias, Lemma D.6) and to exhibit KL-divergence discontinuities under small perturbations (Threshold Instability, Lemma D.8).
Under matched faithfulness levels, KLSC provably achieves a smaller KL(q||p) than hard-constraint distributions (Theorem D.14).

EnergyDPS, an energy-guided diffusion posterior sampling algorithm that injects gradient guidance from the SAE feature activation into the diffusion reverse process without text prompts, is proposed to realize the KLSC principle (Section 2.3, Algorithm 1).
On DINOv3 SAE features, EnergyDPS attains a QualiCLIP score of 0.7286, versus roughly 0.39-0.40 for competing retrieval/optimization/prompt-based sampling baselines (Table 3).

In a blinded human/AI rating study, EnergyDPS obtains the highest interpretability scores and the lowest weighted variance (0.2505) across raters, indicating more consistent semantic descriptions (Table 4).

JjBozF4i2w.text: CLARITree combines recursive lookahead split selection (Algorithm 1) with streaming split enumeration maintained via rank-one Cholesky updates (Algorithm 2), achieving O(k^2) complexity per sample (Section 4).
CLARITree's runtime is bounded by O(k*n*log(n) + d^2*n*k^4*T) (Theorem 5.1).

CLARITree's training objective is provably no worse than that of a greedy Cholesky-based tree (Theorem 5.3), while the MSE gap between greedy trees and CLARITree can be made arbitrarily large, at least 1/(4*epsilon) (Theorem 5.4).
On the California Housing dataset, CLARITree achieves test R^2 = 0.75, compared to R^2 = 0.70 for the optimal-tree baseline STreeD (Table 2).
On a synthetic dataset, CLARITree achieves test MSE 4.03 (R^2 = 0.97) versus MSE 15.41 (R^2 = 0.88) for a standard greedy tree (Figure 1).
Within a 600-second training budget, CLARITree completes roughly 95% of problems while the optimal-tree baseline STreeD completes only about 60% (Figure 3a).

BamDfCP5R3.text: EvolveR combines offline experience self-distillation (Section 3.2.1), online interaction (Section 3.2.2), and RL-based policy evolution (Section 3.3) to let LLM agents distill strategic principles from past trajectories.
On Qwen2.5-3B, EvolveR attains an average score of 0.382 across seven QA benchmarks, outperforming the Search-R1-instruct baseline's 0.325 (Table 1).
EvolveR's self-distillation variant matches or exceeds a teacher-distillation variant using external GPT-4o-mini supervision (0.382 vs. 0.370 average at 3B scale) (Table 2).
Removing access to the experience base at inference time drops the 3B model's average score from 0.382 to 0.340 (Table 3).
EvolveR's average performance scales monotonically with model size: 0.150 (0.5B), 0.270 (1.5B), and 0.382 (3B) across all seven QA benchmarks (Figure 4).

EvolveR is evaluated on in-domain benchmarks Natural Questions and HotpotQA and out-of-domain benchmarks TriviaQA, PopQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, Musique, and Bamboogle, reaching per-dataset scores such as NQ 0.434, TriviaQA 0.584, and Bamboogle 0.328 (Table 1).

JJIqZzujgE.text: PULSE defines 'Phase Amnesia' as a failure mode where non-stationary forecasting models become blind to the distinction between a genuine structural shift and temporary stochastic noise (Section 1).

PULSE's Phase-Anchored Disentanglement extracts a phase anchor via a learnable codebook and applies RevIN normalization only to the residual, and Proposition 3.1 proves this avoids gradient attenuation by scaling residual gradients as O(sigma_R^-1) rather than O(sigma_A^-1) (Section 3.2).
PULSE ranks first on 10 of 12 benchmark datasets by MSE and 8 of 12 by MAE, with 18 first-place results among 24 total metrics, using a lightweight MLP backbone (Table 1).
On ETTh1, PULSE achieves MSE 0.412 versus 0.433 for the CFPT baseline, and on PEMS03, PULSE achieves MSE 0.103 versus 0.143 for CFPT (Table 1).
As a plug-and-play module, PULSE improves iTransformer by 9.9% MSE on ETTh1, DLinear by 33.3% on ETTh2, and TimesNet by 32.6% on Solar (Table 2).
Ablations show removing the Phase Anchor causes the largest degradation (6.0% MSE increase), versus 2.9% for removing the Phase Router and 2.6% for removing Statistic-Aware Mixup (Table 3).

CHIsZDgdb6.text: For single-player imperfect-recall extensive-form games (IREFGs), the Sum-of-Squares/moment hierarchy converges to the optimal utility u* as the relaxation degree d goes to infinity, i.e. lim_{d→∞} u^d_sos = lim_{d→∞} u^d_mom = u* (Theorem 4.1).

Under a genericity assumption on the utility function u, the SOS hierarchy for single-player IREFGs achieves finite convergence at some finite degree d ≥ d0, rather than only asymptotic convergence (Theorem 4.1).
For single-player non-absentminded IREFGs, the degree-(ℓ+1) SOS relaxation is exact, i.e. a single semidefinite program at that level solves the game exactly (Theorem 4.1).

A Select-Verify-Cut framework extends the KKT-based moment-SOS hierarchy to multi-player IREFGs, yielding analogous finite-convergence and single-level-solvability guarantees under genericity and non-absentmindedness (Theorem 5.1).
Strictly concave/monotone single-player IREFGs are shown to admit finite SOS convergence, while SOS-concave/SOS-monotone IREFGs converge already at the first hierarchy level (Theorem 6.1).

In the empirical comparison of Table 1 (Section 7), the SOS approach consistently recovers certified global optima across tested instances, whereas projected gradient descent only succeeds probabilistically, with reported success rates in the 70-89% range.

bgtUrDtKjF.text: AlignVid is a training-free method that mitigates visual-dominance-induced semantic negligence in text-guided image-to-video (TI2V) generation via Attention Scaling Modulation (ASM), which rescales query/key embeddings to sharpen attention toward text tokens (Section on ASM; Lemma 4.1).

Lemma 4.1 shows that scaling query or key embeddings is mathematically equivalent to applying an inverse-temperature softmax, which concentrates the attention distribution and lowers its entropy (Lemma 4.1).

AlignVid combines ASM with a Guidance Scheduling (GS) component that selectively applies attention modulation across transformer blocks and denoising steps to avoid visual-quality degradation (Section on Guidance Scheduling).

The paper introduces the OmitI2V benchmark, comprising 367 samples spanning three prompt-edit categories (modification, addition, deletion) with VQA-based evaluation of prompt adherence (Benchmark section).

On the FramePack F1 backbone, AlignVid improves semantic-fidelity scores by +6.82% (modification), +3.81% (addition), and +2.56% (deletion), alongside an +8.74% gain in dynamic degree and only a -1.0% drop in aesthetic quality (Table 2).

Human evaluation of the OmitI2V metric shows approximately 96.6% agreement with human judgments across edit categories, and the method's semantic-alignment gains generalize to text-to-image and text-to-video generation tasks (Human evaluation section).

Imry2qitdt.text: Directly applying LoRA adapters trained on a base video diffusion model to distilled model variants (e.g., FastWan) causes style degradation and structural collapse, even though both full fine-tuning (FFT) and LoRA preserve the singular-value spectrum of weight matrices with relative spectral change below 0.3% (Section 3.1).

Analysis of singular subspaces reveals three structurally distinct spectral regions—a sharply diagonal-concentrated head, a block-wise patterned middle aligned with spectral plateaus, and a diffuse banded tail due to near-degeneracy—indicating incompatibility arises in subspace routing rather than spectral magnitude (Section 3.2).

Full fine-tuning exhibits a centralized routing structure anchored at a few dominant clusters, whereas LoRA distributes its modifications more broadly across clusters, creating incompatible routing signals when both act on high-interaction head-cluster regions (Section 3.4).

The proposed CASA (Cluster-Aware Spectral Arbitration) method restores LoRA functionality by direct subtraction (C_casa(i,j) = C_lora(i,j) - C_fft(i,j)) in non-dominant spectral regions and by selective, range-restricted arbitration in dominant regions (Methodology section).

On the Steamboat-Willie evaluation with the FastWan backbone, CASA raises the Quality Score from 1.27 to 1.58 and improves CSD style-fidelity from 78.35% to 81.49%, with gains validated across both Wan2.1 and HunyuanVideo model families (Table 1).

9sg34nj13o.text: ParetoPO is a two-stage multi-objective optimization framework that combines hypervolume-guided dynamic scalarization with Pareto-ranking-based advantage computation for aligning tool-using LLM agents under competing accuracy and efficiency objectives (Method section).

On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, ParetoPO reaches 80.0% exact-match accuracy using an average of 0.9 tool calls, versus 77.8% EM with 2.1 tool calls for ToRL-GRPO and 74.0% EM with 1.3 tool calls for OTC-GRPO (Table 1).
On AIME2024 with the same backbone, ParetoPO attains 30.0% EM compared to 23.3% EM for ToRL-GRPO, while using fewer tool calls (0.8 vs 2.2) (Table 1).
On the Natural Questions multi-hop QA benchmark with Qwen2.5-3B, ParetoPO achieves 48.0% EM with 0.9 retrieval calls, compared to 44.4% EM with 1.0 retrieval calls for OTC-GRPO (Table 2).

ParetoPO is evaluated against ToRL-GRPO, OTC-GRPO, and MO-GRPO baselines across math benchmarks (MATH500, AIME2024, AIME2025, OlympiadBench, AMC23) and QA benchmarks (Natural Questions, HotpotQA), showing consistent accuracy-efficiency trade-off improvements (Section on Experiments).

vvxcADnfL9.text: ZeroUnlearn reformulates machine unlearning as a knowledge re-mapping problem solved via a closed-form multiplicative parameter update that combines a Zero Term (orthogonality to original sensitive knowledge), a Forget Term (redirecting forget-set inputs to a neutral target such as the <EOS> token), and a Utility Term (preserving general knowledge) (Equation 4).

The method projects updates into a null space computed via SVD of the original sensitive outputs, leveraging d−n available degrees of freedom in the few-shot regime where the number of forget samples n is much smaller than hidden dimension d (Method section).

In the 50-sample few-shot unlearning setting on Llama-3.2 with the MCF/ZsRE datasets, ZeroUnlearn achieves 0.40% efficacy (residual knowledge) versus an 18.20% baseline, while maintaining 14.90% specificity and a perplexity of 13.06 (Table 1).

In the 1,000-sample multi-sample unlearning setting, ZeroUnlearn achieves 0% efficacy on MCF with 12.41% specificity and a stable perplexity of 13.05, reflecting an expected efficacy-specificity trade-off at larger batch sizes (Table 2).

ZeroUnlearn outperforms ROME/MEMIT (24-32% residual efficacy), AlphaEdit (2.60% efficacy vs. ZeroUnlearn's 0.40%), gradient ascent (GA, which collapses perplexity to >>1000), and fine-tuning (FT, which loses 0% specificity) (Table 1).

Across six downstream benchmarks (MMLU, SST, MRPC, RTE, COLA, NLI), ZeroUnlearn preserves performance comparable to the base model, unlike gradient-ascent-based unlearning approaches that suffer near-total accuracy collapse (Downstream evaluation section).

TUcgDjfdVk.text: CoDA-Bench comprises 1,009 data-intensive tasks spanning 31 data communities derived from the Kaggle ecosystem via Leiden community detection refined from 323 initial communities (Section 3.1, Table 1).
Environments in CoDA-Bench average 980 files each and range from 20.3 MB to 45.4 GB of data per environment, spanning CSV, JSON, Parquet, image, and PDF formats (Section 3.1).

The top-performing agent configuration, Mini-SWE-Agent with GPT-5.5, achieves 61.1% Execution Accuracy and 83.0% Discovery Accuracy on CoDA-Bench, dropping to 49.6% EA and 67.5% DA on the CoDA-Hard 119-task subset (Section 5.2, Table 4; Section 4.3, Table 3).
Claude Code with Sonnet-4.6 achieves 53.8% Execution Accuracy while being the most cost-efficient configuration at $0.11 per task (Section 5.2, Table 4).
Signal-to-noise ratio of the data environment correlates inversely with agent performance (Spearman ρ=0.466, p<0.01), and data volumes exceeding 3GB create a performance bottleneck (Section 6.2).
For the weaker model Kimi-K2.6, data discovery errors account for 40.7% of task failures, showing discovery difficulty dominates over execution difficulty for less capable agents (Section 6.4).

7Oc4ARFCTV.text: T3-Unlearning reframes machine unlearning as density ratio estimation to a target distribution, producing a tempered-tilted estimator p̂_r^(T) ∝ p^(1/T) · f̂ using a lightweight classifier over frozen representations (Section 3, Equation for tempered estimator).

Theorem 3.4 shows the Forget Error of the untempered (T=1) estimator scales as O(‖p_f‖∞ √δ), while Theorem 3.7 shows tempering improves this to O(‖p_f‖∞^(1/T) · δ^(1/2k)), and Theorem 3.5 gives a matching lower bound establishing tempering's necessity for concentrated forget distributions (Theorems 3.4, 3.5, 3.7).
Theorem 3.3 bounds the Retain Error of the untempered estimator as O(δ/(1-γ)), linking the surrogate classifier's estimation error δ directly to retained-distribution fidelity (Theorem 3.3).

On the TOFU benchmark with Llama 3.1 8B and a 5% forget split, T3-Unlearning attains Forget Quality of 0.914, MU-ROUGE of 0.900, and Model Utility of 0.612, each reported as the best among compared baselines (Table 1).
On the 10% forget split of TOFU, T3-Unlearning attains Forget Quality of 0.671 and Model Utility of 0.612, using only 2.65×10^6 trained parameters (0.03% of model size) (Table 1).

The preprocessed T3-Unlearning inference procedure runs in approximately 5.12 seconds on the 5% TOFU split, compared to multi-minute runtimes for baseline unlearning methods (Section on computational efficiency).

P247k4ELcn.text: MoRAM decomposes each LoRA update into rank-1 components treated as independent, self-activated experts, avoiding the need for a separate router network used in prior MoE-LoRA continual learning approaches (Section on core innovation / method description).

On the X-TAIL cross-domain continual learning benchmark with CLIP-ViT/B-16, MoRAM achieves 72.7% average accuracy, and on MTIL under the 5-shot setting achieves 73.9% average accuracy (Table 1, Table 2).

On T5-large continual learning benchmarks, MoRAM achieves 77.61% average accuracy across three task orderings on standard benchmarks and 69.72% average accuracy on extended 15-task sequences (Table 3, Table 9).
On HumanEval code generation with Llama3.1-8B, MoRAM achieves 47.56% Pass@1 while activating only 0.32% of parameters (Table 4).
MoRAM is compared against MoE-Adapter, CoDyRA, RAIL-Primal, O-LoRA, LB-CL, ZSCL, and standard LoRA variants as baselines across these benchmarks (Section on baseline comparisons).
An ablation replacing the learned router with the self-activated sparse rank mechanism improves the Last-task accuracy score from 69.85% to 80.22% (Table 5, Figure 4).

Dp0YWzPAGM.text: Theorem 4.11 decomposes the cross-domain output shift of a graph foundation model into three terms: finite-sample approximation error on the source graph (ε₁), intrinsic graphon mismatch between domains (ε_gra), and finite-sample approximation error on the target graph (ε₂), satisfying output gap ≲ ε₁ + ε_gra + ε₂ (Theorem 4.11).

Theorem 4.3 shows that sampled graph operators converge to their underlying graphon operators at rate O_p(√(log n / n)), formalizing why larger graphs yield better proxies of domain-level structure (Theorem 4.3).

Lemma 4.8 shows eigenvector-based positional encodings have a stability constant proportional to √k divided by the minimum eigengap, while projector-based positional encodings have stability proportional to the inverse of the k-th spectral gap, revealing an expressivity-stability tradeoff in choosing PE dimension k (Lemma 4.8).

Controlled synthetic experiments using low-rank Fourier graphons show test error exhibits U-shaped behavior as a function of training-budget allocation between source and target domains, with in-domain versus out-of-domain error decomposition revealing that data coverage, not optimization, dominates the effect (Section 5).

Synthetic graph-merging experiments show that augmenting training data with synthetically generated larger graphs reduces cross-domain error specifically when the train-test graph-size gap is large (Section 5).

RVq8zBMmaJ.text: IceSfP achieves a Mean Angular Error of 16.01° for surface normal estimation on the newly introduced real-world ice SfP dataset, outperforming the second-best baseline by 2.74° (Table 1).
IceSfP attains 41.92% of pixels within 11.25° error and 79.58% within 22.5° error, compared to DeepSfP (34.35%/70.65°) and TransSfP (32.13%/73.26%) baselines (Table 1).

The paper introduces the first real-world ice shape-from-polarization dataset, containing 960 samples collected from 16 distinct ice objects with ground-truth surface normals and polarization observations (Section on dataset contribution).

The dual-branch network combines a raw 4-channel polarization branch with a physics-prior branch via a Cross-modal Reliability Attention (CRA) module and SPADE normalization to preserve spatial detail (Section on network architecture).

Ablation results show removing the structure-aware consistency prior increases MAE from 16.01° to 17.84°, removing the CRA module increases MAE to 17.44°, and removing SPADE normalization increases MAE to 17.45° (Table 5).

The structure-aware consistency map is derived from autocorrelation functions (ACF) of the Angle of Linear Polarization combined with high-frequency energy extracted via Stationary Wavelet Transform (SWT) (Section on structure-aware consistency prior).

ZwFJbTzJP9.text: FOAM's operator-gap staleness error bound shows the damping term epsilon scales as 1/(p·epsilon_0^((p+1)/p)), while the eigendecomposition-refresh error grows as (1-beta^f)·R_SG^2 with refresh period f (Section 5.1, Lemma 5.2).

FOAM's regret staleness error is bounded by the term eta/(1-beta)·{r(1-beta^f)R_SG^4/epsilon_0^2}, exposing a trade-off where increasing the damping factor epsilon suppresses staleness error but inflates preconditioning cost (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.4).

FOAM's three-phase algorithm (sensing, adapting, frequency control) updates the damping factor multiplicatively via epsilon_t <- max(epsilon_0, epsilon_{t-1}·h_t/tau) using an error proxy h_t = alpha(epsilon_{t-1})/p · RC(epsilon_{t-1}), capped by a maximum threshold epsilon_max (Section 6, Algorithms 1-3).

On ViT trained on ImageNet-1K and Conformer trained on LibriSpeech, FOAM reaches equal or better accuracy/WER than standard (stale) Shampoo baselines in substantially less wall-clock time (Section 7, Figure 1).

FOAM's adaptive frequency control reduces eigendecomposition (EVD) calls to approximately 10% for the L factor and 5% for the R factor relative to a fixed per-step refresh schedule on ViT (Section 7, Figure 3).

An ablation isolating adaptive damping alone (without selective EVD refresh) achieves lower training loss but significantly higher wall-clock time than full FOAM, showing both mechanisms are needed to balance loss and computational overhead (Section 7.3, Figure 4).

uiw8P2JGbW.text: For target-CPA bidders without budget constraints using uniform bidding with multiplier mu=1 in first-price auctions, refining the prediction model (partitioning clusters into subclusters while preserving calibration) never decreases platform revenue, i.e., Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B) when M_A refines M_B (Theorem 5.1).

The first-price auction revenue monotonicity proof for tCPA bidders relies on convexity of f(p) = max_i(t_i · p_i) via Jensen's inequality, since model refinement corresponds to a mean-preserving spread of this convex function (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).

Uniform bidding at multiplier mu=1 is simultaneously conversion-maximizing, revenue-maximizing among equilibria, and welfare-maximizing for tCPA bidders in first-price auctions (Theorem 5.2), and welfare monotonicity follows as a corollary when per-conversion values equal targets (Corollary 5.3).

There exist instances with tCPA bidders where second-price (VCG) auctions exhibit non-monotonicity in both revenue and welfare under model refinement, with a constructed counterexample showing a simultaneous 6.2% decrease in both metrics (Theorem 5.8).

Introducing budget constraints breaks revenue monotonicity even in first-price auctions, as optimal bidder multipliers shift under refinement and reduce competitive pressure, exemplified by a counterexample with a 16.8% revenue loss (Theorem 5.10).

A centralized, non-strategic linear-programming benchmark allocation guarantees welfare monotonicity under budget constraints via a 'lifting' construction that preserves feasibility across refined partitions (Theorem 5.11), and the paper's overall characterization identifies exactly three settings where monotonicity holds (Table 1).

w6DqR74BTt.text: HiPhO evaluates 30 state-of-the-art models (11 closed-source MLLMs, 11 open-source MLLMs, 8 open-source LLMs) on 13 high-school physics Olympiad exams from 2024-2025, totaling 360 problems and 519 subquestions, using official human medal-based marking schemes (Abstract, Section on benchmark construction).
Among closed-source reasoning MLLMs, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking each earn 12 gold medals across the 13 exams, while GPT-5 and o3 each earn 11 and Grok-4 earns 10 (Table 3).

The best open-source MLLM, Intern-S1, earns only 4 gold medals, while open-source LLMs DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-235B-A22B each earn 8 gold medals, indicating open-source MLLMs lag furthest behind (Table 3).

Even top gold-medal-earning models fall short of the best human competitors: on IPhO-2025 the top model scores 22.7/29.4 versus the top human medalist's 29.2/30 (Section reporting IPhO-2025 results, Table 3).
Modality strongly affects performance: leading models score 86% accuracy on text-only problems versus 67% on problems containing data figures (Figure 6).
Optics is the most challenging physics field tested, with all models scoring below 55% accuracy on Optics problems (Table 4).

0tgzJK50Jz.text: On AIME25 with 32K-token generation, TriAttention matches Full Attention's 40.8% accuracy while achieving 2.5x higher decoding throughput and 10.7x KV cache memory reduction (Section 5, Table 1, Figure 1).

On AIME24, TriAttention reaches 42.1% accuracy versus 57.1% for Full Attention, while the R-KV baseline achieves only 25.4% accuracy at comparable KV budget, and on AIME25 R-KV achieves only 17.5% accuracy (Table 1).

On MATH 500 with a 512-token KV budget, TriAttention attains 56.0% accuracy versus 69.6% for Full Attention, while delivering a 6.3x throughput speedup (1,405 vs. 223 tokens/second) (Table 2, Table 4).

TriAttention's key-importance scoring exploits Q/K concentration in pre-RoPE space combined with a trigonometric series estimator, described and visualized as the core method in Section 3 and Section 4 (Section 3, Section 4, Figure 2, Figure 4).

An ablation study validates the individual contributions of TriAttention's scoring components to overall accuracy (Table 3), and a direct head-to-head comparison against R-KV across KV budgets is reported separately (Table 5).

iHSnH96rKH.text: For the offline min-max non-smooth submodular-concave problem, Algorithm 1 (ZO-EG), which combines Lovász-extension subgradients for the minimization variable with Gaussian-smoothed zeroth-order gradient estimates for the maximization variable, converges to an epsilon-saddle point using O(m^2 * epsilon^-2) function-value queries in expectation (Theorem 3.2).

In the online setting, the same ZO-EG algorithm attains an O(sqrt(N * P_bar_N)) online duality gap, where N is the number of iterations and P_bar_N is the path length of the optimal decision sequence, matching known dynamic-regret-type bounds (Theorem 3.5).

The Gaussian smoothing gradient estimator is defined as g_mu(y) = (1/mu)(f(y+mu*u) - f(y))*u for u ~ N(0,I), with variance reduced via multi-sample averaging within Algorithm 1 (Section on Gaussian smoothing, Algorithm 1).

Saddle-point existence for the submodular-concave objective is guaranteed under Proposition 2.11 when the minimizers of zeta(x) = max_y f^L(x,y) contain a vertex of the domain or related structural conditions hold (Proposition 2.11).

On an online adversarial image segmentation application, the proposed zeroth-order method achieves 0.975 average IoU using only about 2.5k optimization variables, outperforming supervised and semi-supervised U-Net baselines that achieve 0.905 and 0.847 IoU respectively with roughly 1.06M network weights (Section 4.2).

BwufLjXbMO.text: The AIPW U-statistic estimator using augmented inverse probability weighting is proven unbiased, satisfying E[U_AIPW^π] = θ* (Proposition 2.1).

The variance-minimizing (optimal) sampling probability is proportional to the square root of a residual-uncertainty term derived from the Hoeffding projection, depending on h1(Y) − h1^μ(Ŷ) rather than the raw prediction error |Y − Ŷ| (Theorem 2.2, Section 2.2).

A central limit theorem is established for the normalized AIPW U-statistic under data-adaptive sampling, enabling computable asymptotic confidence intervals via a common-random-number coupling argument (Theorem 2.4).

On the ACS income dataset, active sampling for the Gini index achieves roughly 60% labeling-budget reduction relative to uniform sampling while maintaining 90% confidence-interval coverage (Section 4.1, Figure 1).

On the VitalDB perioperative dataset, the active Wilcoxon signed-rank test for hemoglobin shifts requires approximately 20% less labeling budget than the classical baseline for equivalent precision (Section 4.2, Figure 2).

On the political-bias dataset, active estimation of Kendall's τ for LLM label quality reduces the labeling budget by about 20% versus the classical baseline and about 10% versus uniform sampling (Section 4.3, Figure 3).

s4Jn6bKYGI.text: HCPD achieves an average AUROC of 88.19% on LLaMA-3.1-8B across TriviaQA, SciQ, NQ Open, and CoQA, a +10.20% absolute improvement over the second-best baseline (Table 2, Section 5.2).

On LLaMA-3.1-8B, HCPD scores 86.25% AUROC on TriviaQA, 86.04% on SciQ, 90.38% on NQ Open, and 90.07% on CoQA, each exceeding the best prior baseline (e.g., 79.78%, 80.01%, 70.17%, and 69.31% respectively) (Table 2, Section 5.2).

HCPD is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization using a score-alignment reward r = 1 − |sp − sl|/9 for well-formed outputs, where weak labels sl derive from BLEURT-based semantic similarity to reference answers (Equation 5).

Ablations show structured criteria probing alone improves over a self-evaluation baseline by +10.47%, and adding GRPO-based alignment training contributes a further +19.71%, moving from 56.07% (self-evaluation) to 66.54% (HCPD Pre-RL) to 86.25% AUROC (HCPD Post-RL) on LLaMA-3.1-8B (Table 4, Section 5.3).
HCPD also attains 89.62% average AUROC on Qwen-3-8B, indicating transferability of the criteria-probing framework across model families (Section 5.2).

FoK74p8a2Z.text: The Entropy Compression Hypothesis posits that model intelligence is reflected in the capacity to structure predictive uncertainty into low-order Entropy-Compressed States rather than merely minimizing scalar loss (Section 1).

Superior models exhibit a distributional shift in high-entropy prediction errors that peaks near ln3 (≈1.10), termed the 'Shift to ln3' phenomenon, observed for the larger MoE-L model but not to the same degree in the smaller MoE-S model (Section 4.2.2, Figures 3-4).

HE-SNR, computed over filtered action tokens exceeding an uncertainty threshold ε = (ln3 + ln4)/2, shows strict linear (rank-consistent) correlation with downstream SWE-bench Pass@1 across a 10x scaling gap between MoE-S and MoE-L, while it is robust to the 'Long-Context Tax' that degrades standard Perplexity when context is extended from 32K to 128K (Figure 6, Section 5.1).

Post-SFT analysis shows supervised fine-tuning improves global Perplexity but degrades HE-PPL and HE-SNR on critical high-entropy tokens, evidencing an 'Alignment Tax' where models trade reasoning capability for stylistic pattern matching (Figure 8, Section 5.3).

PlHlnsoaJc.text: SLAT reduces average chain-of-thought length on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B from 8,404 to 4,176 tokens (a 50% reduction) while attaining the best average accuracy (66.4%) among compared methods (Table 1, Section 4.2.1).
SLAT establishes a superior accuracy-length Pareto frontier, achieving a Pareto improvement over competing length-compression methods in 66 of 77 benchmark comparisons (Section 4).

Proposition 3.1 derives a condition under which generating a given reasoning segment becomes suboptimal, implying that long, near-deterministic token stretches (high-probability segments) are natural candidates for suppression, identified via a sliding-window mechanism with probability threshold τ=0.9 (Proposition 3.1).

When extended to Qwen3-14B, SLAT reduces average reasoning length from 5,024 to 2,677 tokens (−47%) while keeping average accuracy nearly unchanged (−0.5%), including a +3.4% accuracy gain on AMC23 alongside a 61% length reduction (Table 2, Section 4.3.1).

tBw7NesAmb.text: Smooth Allocation forms an unbiased stopping-time estimate of the remaining unpredicted queries from the first T = Θ(log^2 S) unpredicted queries, using this estimate to continuously recalibrate per-query privacy budget allocation (Section 3, or the Smooth Allocation section).
On the Adult dataset at high overlap (ρ≈1), LAPRAS reduces median MAE by over an order of magnitude compared to an online independent-noise baseline, from 193.4 to 14.3 (Table 2, Section 5).

On the Adult dataset under the query-heavy split at low overlap (ρ≈0), LAPRAS degrades gracefully to near-baseline performance, attaining MAE 201.8 versus 186.5 for the online independent-noise baseline (Table 2, Section 5).
Smooth Allocation outperforms Static Allocation by up to 40% lower MAE once overlap exceeds roughly 0.7 (Table 8, Appendix B.4).

The total expected squared error of LAPRAS is bounded by O(B^2 ln(1/δ)/ε^2) plus the expected squared error of the offline Matrix Mechanism, establishing bounded suboptimality relative to both online and offline baselines (Section 3, theoretical guarantee).

JTu5Mawn86.text: The Platonic Transformer achieves combined SE(n) equivariance (continuous translation plus discrete Platonic rotation/reflection symmetries) by computing attention relative to reference frames of a chosen symmetry group, with weight-sharing enforced via group convolutions in the equivariant linear layers (Section 3, Section 3.2).
On CIFAR-10 image classification, using the C4 rotation group improves accuracy to 92.73% versus 91.49% for the trivial (no symmetry) group, while the dihedral D4 group gives 92.53% (Table 1).
On ScanObjectNN 3D point cloud classification, using the tetrahedral rotation group raises overall accuracy to 81.3% compared to 80.5% for the trivial group (Table 2).

On QM9 molecular property prediction with the tetrahedral group, the model attains a dipole moment MAE of 0.012 and polarizability MAE of 0.049, closely matching EquiformerV2's 0.010 and 0.050 (Table 3).

Inference is roughly 200x faster than the Tensor Field Network (TFN) baseline (2.87 ± 0.29 ms vs 590.45 ± 269.25 ms), and Corollary 1 shows the dynamic group-convolution attention can be computed in O(N) time versus O(N^2) for standard attention (Table 4, Section 4.1, Corollary 1).

An ablation on CIFAR-10 shows that using softmax attention instead of a linear-convolution variant substantially improves accuracy (92.73% vs 88.70% for the C4 group), demonstrating the benefit of full attention over the linear approximation (Section 5.2 ablation).

OXjToUQDz1.text: The framework certifies VLM prediction invariance under semantic-level transformations by constructing a two-dimensional semantic plane from text-prompt proxies and deriving closed-form decision margins, without requiring additional training data for each new semantic variation (Section 4.1-4.3).

Lemma 4.5 bounds the margin gap under semantic misalignment by a tolerance term epsilon_{c,c'} = delta * ||u_c - u_c'||_2, and Proposition 4.6 gives a stability condition guaranteeing prediction invariance within a delta-neighborhood when pairwise margins exceed this bound (Lemma 4.5, Proposition 4.6).
Lemma 4.7 shows that regions of uncertain decision-boundary crossing can be localized to a restricted set U_{c,c'}(delta), enabling tighter certified intervals (Lemma 4.7).

Evaluated with a pretrained CLIP ViT-B/16 model on synthetic (Oxford Pets, Flowers102, Food101) and real-world (Caltech101, StanfordCars, DTD, FGVCAircraft, UCF101) datasets, the text-specified certification method yields 4.1-9.6% mean absolute discrepancy and the image-specified method yields 0.0-7.5%, both outperforming the ExactLine baseline (Table 1-2).

Figure 1 shows certified prediction-invariant extent intervals for diverse semantic variations, and Figure 5 reports certificate bound evaluations showing stable coverage across attributes (Figure 1, Figure 5).

Tz69nG4l87.text: The solver-free training method derives the Weight Integrated Spherical Error (WISE) loss via two transformations of the label measure: reweighting by cost magnitude and projection onto the unit sphere, yielding l_WISE(y_hat, y) = ||y|| * ||y_hat - y/||y||||^2, eliminating the need to call an optimization solver during training (Section 2.1).
Theorem 3.4 establishes Fisher consistency of the WISE loss: its Bayes risk minimizer also minimizes decision risk without any restriction on the hypothesis class (Theorem 3.4).

Theorem 3.7 shows an excess regret bound of O(n^{-1/2}) for hypothesis classes of bounded VC-dimension, and Corollary 3.9 improves this to O(n^{-1}) when the feasible region has strongly convex level sets, faster than known SPO+ surrogate bounds (Theorem 3.7, Corollary 3.9).

On a 2D knapsack problem (16 items), a 5x5 grid shortest-path problem (40 edges), and a 25-stock portfolio optimization problem, the method achieves normalized test regret competitive with SPO+, PFY, and DBB while requiring 44-100x less training time than these decision-focused learning baselines on shortest path (Figure 3-5).
Figure 1 compares the solver-free training pipeline against decision-blind and decision-focused learning pipelines, illustrating that the solver is bypassed entirely during training (Figure 1).

NoP2UQymHU.text: Explicit reasoning traces substantially improve LLM-as-a-judge accuracy on structured verification tasks such as math and coding, while offering limited or even negative gains on simpler evaluation tasks despite incurring 3.4-11.2x more output tokens (Table 1, Section on cost ratios).

RACER formulates reasoning-mode routing as a constrained distributionally robust optimization problem, maximizing worst-case reward subject to a worst-case cost constraint over KL-divergence uncertainty sets, and is solved via a primal-dual algorithm with entropy regularization that is proven to converge linearly to a unique optimal policy (Section on RACER formulation).

Trained on 20,000 Skywork Reward instances plus 20,000 Math-Step-DPO-10K and Code-Preference-Pairs instances, RACER is evaluated on RewardBench, RewardBench 2, and JudgeBench using Qwen3 (1.7B, 4B, 8B) and Llama 3.1-8B judge models (Table 1, evaluation section).

At a compute budget of 3.9, RACER achieves 90.0% accuracy versus 88.9% for the strongest baseline on the 8B model, and Table 2 compares RACER against RouterBench-KNN, RouteLLM-MF, and M-IRT baselines (Table 2).

Figure 4 shows RACER maintains superior accuracy-cost trade-offs across compute budgets under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation settings, demonstrating robustness to distribution shift (Figure 4).

CTrA4eNQfv.text: Theorem 3.2 establishes an information-theoretic lower bound on the number of decoding rounds R for confidence-based parallel decoding in diffusion language models, showing R must grow at least linearly with the total information content -log p(x) of the sample and inversely with the per-round information budget f (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).

The Explore-Then-Exploit (ETE) strategy combines Fast Block Diffusion Sampling, which enables cross-block parallel decoding rather than strict sequential block processing, with strategic exploration that targets high-entropy tokens via implicit exploration and beam search (Section 4.2, Section 4.4).

ETE reduces the number of decoding rounds by 26-61% across the MATH, GSM8K, HumanEval, and MMLU-Pro benchmarks compared to confidence-only baseline decoding, without compromising accuracy (Figure 1(b), Figure 6).

Section 3 uses counterexamples to show that confidence-only parallel decoding is fundamentally inefficient because it fails to maximize per-round information throughput, motivating the 'Golden Principle' introduced in Section 4.1 that links decoding rounds to information throughput (Section 3, Section 4.1).

PhSw9Xhw6e.text: LRSA achieves an average error reduction of over 17% relative to the second-best method across standard neural operator benchmarks (Abstract, Table 1).
On the Navier-Stokes benchmark, LRSA attains 0.0484 relative error versus 0.0699 for the LinearNO baseline, and on Elasticity attains 0.0033 versus 0.0050 for LinearNO (Table 1).
On the large-scale AirfRANS benchmark, LRSA achieves a surface field error of 0.0010 versus 0.0077 for LinearNO, and a lift coefficient correlation of 0.9997 (Table 3).

In mixed-precision experiments on ShapeNet Car, LRSA remains stable across FP32, BF16, and FP16 while Transolver diverges in FP16 and requires FP32 to converge; FP16 LRSA yields a 3.2x latency reduction and 2.1x memory improvement versus FP32 Transolver (Figure 4).

Ablations removing the latent self-attention block or enforcing symmetric compression/reconstruction (as in Transolver) both increase error relative to the full LRSA design, validating the decoupled encoder/decoder architecture (Figure 5).
LRSA's computational cost scales as O(NM+M^2), near-linear in the number of spatial points N since the number of latent tokens M is much smaller than N (Section 3.4).

BrIGLICBWy.text: Theorem 3 shows dual steering identifies the minimizer of the KL divergence D_KL(P^Z_0 || P^Z) for concept-factorizable distributions, optimally modifying the target concept while leaving off-target concepts unchanged (Theorem 3).

Proposition 1 establishes that primal (e-geodesic) interpolation in the softmax's Bregman dual geometry corresponds to minimizing reverse KL divergence (AND-like combination), while dual (m-geodesic) interpolation minimizes forward KL divergence (OR-like combination) (Proposition 1, Section 2.1-2.2).

Dual steering is implemented by adding steering vectors to the dual coordinates, phi(lambda_t) = phi(lambda_0) + t*omega_W, rather than to the primal (Euclidean) representation as in standard activation steering (Section 3).

Empirically on Gemma-3-4B and MetaCLIP-2, dual steering preserves off-target concept probabilities better than Euclidean steering across three robustness metrics while achieving comparable or better control of the target concept (Section 5, Figure 4).
Practical dual steering is computed via regularized Newton updates for tractability at inference time (Section 4).

x4xOtzoYa6.text: Theorem 4.4 proves a transformer with finite arithmetic precision epsilon and embedding radius r can access at most (1+2r/epsilon)^(d*m) distinct output sequences for a given prompt length m, where d is the embedding dimension (Theorem 4.4).

Corollary 4.5 shows that once sequence length n exceeds the threshold (d*ln(1+2r/epsilon)/ln(|V|))*m, the proportion of accessible sequences of length n decays exponentially, at rate O(1/|V|^n) (Corollary 4.5).

Corollary 4.9 extends the accessibility threshold result via a mean-field analysis to show that, independent of prompt length, almost all sequences of length n >= N become inaccessible beyond a critical N (Corollary 4.9).

The cramming-task experiments across Pythia (160M-2.8B), Qwen-2.5 (0.5B, 1.5B), Llama-3.2 (1B, 3B), and Gemma-3 (270M, 1B) confirm empirical linear scaling of accessible sequence length with prompt length, with R^2 >= 0.995 (Section 5.1, Figure 2c).
The theoretical upper bound on accessible sequence count is within 5-20x of the empirically observed values across tested architectures (Table 1).

The copying-task experiments in Section 5.4 show sharp sigmoid transitions in accuracy as sequence length crosses the predicted accessibility threshold, consistent with the predicted exponential decay regime (Section 5.4).

pYI0WjV5iM.text: Theorem 1 gives improved convergence rates for Decentralized SGD in the strongly-convex, convex, and non-convex cases by replacing the spectral-gap-only dependency with the term (1/n)*sum_{i=2}^{n} lambda_i^2/(1-lambda_i^2), which depends on all eigenvalues of the mixing matrix (Theorem 1).

Lemma 2 bounds stochastic noise propagation through the network using independence of gradient noise across nodes, showing (1/n)*sum_{i=2}^{n} lambda_i^2 <= max_{i>=2}(lambda_i^2), which yields tighter convergence bounds than prior spectral-gap-only analyses (Lemma 2).

Table 1 shows the number of transient iterations improves for several topologies: ring from O(n^7) to O(n^5), torus from O(n^5) to O(n^3 log^2(n)), and hypercube from O(n^3 log^2(n)) to O(n^3) (Table 1).

Figure 1 compares the classical topology-dependence quantity (1-p)/p against the new all-eigenvalue quantity (1/n)*sum(lambda_i^2/(1-lambda_i^2)) across ring, torus, line, and hypercube topologies, showing the new quantity is considerably smaller for sparse networks (Figure 1).

Figure 2 experimentally validates on logistic and ridge regression over MNIST that convergence behavior depends on the full eigenvalue spectrum of the mixing matrix rather than only the spectral gap (Section 6, Figure 2).
Figure 3 shows the improved topology-dependence prediction holds for neural network training (LeNet on Fashion-MNIST) under both homogeneous and heterogeneous data settings (Figure 3).

QfRtFf9Q3X.text: On the MMAU Test-mini benchmark, AuTAgent improves accuracy over the Qwen2-Audio-7B baseline by 4.20 percentage points (to 54.20%) and over the GPT-4o Audio baseline by 9.80 percentage points (to 66.80%) (Section on MMAU Test-mini results).

On the MMAR benchmark, AuTAgent improves accuracy over the Qwen2-Audio-7B baseline by 6.20 percentage points (to 41.30%) and over the GPT-4o Audio baseline by 8.00 percentage points (to 63.00%) (Section on MMAR benchmark results).

AuTAgent's differential reward assigns +1 when tool use corrects a baseline error, 0 when the baseline is already correct, and -1 when a tool introduces misleading information, discouraging indiscriminate tool invocation (Section on differential reward mechanism).
AuTAgent is trained with GRPO-based policy optimization using only about 2,000 training samples drawn from the AVQA dataset (Section on training efficiency).
The learned tool-selection policy transfers as a plug-and-play module to both open-source and proprietary audio LLMs without additional training (Section on transferability).

The tool library comprises six tools spanning speech (ASR, emotion recognition), music (chord recognition, tempo estimation, pitch tracking), and environmental sound classification domains (Section on tool library).

WtgQOtmw9N.text: Across roughly 10 large reasoning models evaluated on HARP (5,409 math questions) and GPQA-Diamond (198 science questions), shorter chain-of-thought traces and lower review-behavior ratios correlate with higher accuracy, contradicting the 'longer-is-better' narrative (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

The Failed-Step Fraction (FSF), defined as the fraction of steps belonging to abandoned reasoning branches, is introduced in Section 3.2 and shows consistent negative correlation with accuracy across all evaluated models and difficulty strata, outpredicting CoT length and review ratio (Figure 4).

Ranking candidate CoTs by FSF at test time on AIME-25 and GPQA-Diamond yields pass@1 gains of roughly 5-13% over a random-selection baseline, with up to a 12% improvement in a fully self-generated/self-estimated/self-selected setting (Section 5.1, Figure 5).

Editing chain-of-thought traces to remove the first failed branch improves accuracy on incorrect traces: DeepSeek-R1 rises from 20.89% to 29.42% and GPT-OSS-120B rises from 28.05% to 36.41% (Table 1, Section 5.2).
Reasoning-structure extraction via Graphviz-based prompting achieves a 100% compilation success rate across the sampled generations used for the analysis (Section 3.2).

GgN0wlHcdI.text: DARC (Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding) is a retraining-free, inference-time reranking method that selects among candidate responses by maximizing a KL-robust entropic satisfaction objective (Section 4.1, Eq. 19).
Theorem 3.5 proves that the KL-regularized robust objective is equal to the entropic value -1/β log E[exp(-βR(s,y))], giving a closed-form basis for the DARC decision rule (Section 3.2, Eq. 13).
In human evaluation, DARC-ε attains an overall mean score of 7.84 with risk 0.60 and CVaR at the 10% level of 7.46, improving to a CVaR of 7.60 on the high-disagreement prompt subset (Table 2).
The proxy disagreement measure used for reranking correlates with human-judged disagreement at Spearman ρ = 0.6509 (95% CI [0.42, 0.70]), with a precision@20% overlap of 0.64 (Figure 4).

Under multi-scorer aggregation across M=3 reward models, DARC achieves an overall win/tie/loss record of 296/168/36, improving to 44/54/2 on the high-σ̂ (high-disagreement) subset (Table 3, Eqs. 24-25).
The style-preserving perturbation procedure used by DARC adds only about 1.5%-3.2% inference latency overhead relative to standard decoding (Section 5.1).

Ioj1rlc9f7.text: NAG-based Ranking, a training-free framework that ranks pretraining data by neuron-activation similarity to target examples, improves target-oriented pretraining by 4.9% on average across six benchmarks relative to random sampling (Table 1, Section 3.5).
On HellaSwag specifically, NAG-based Ranking reaches 60.6% accuracy versus 51.6% for random sampling, a 9.0-point gain (Table 1).

Deactivating only the 0.12% of neurons selected by NAG causes a 23.5-point performance collapse (60.6% to 37.1%), whereas deactivating an equal number of random neurons causes a negligible 0.2-point drop, indicating NAG selects a sparse functional backbone (Table 3, Section 4.1.1).
Combining NAG-based ranking with a FineWeb-Edu quality classifier yields a further 1.8% average accuracy improvement over using either signal alone (Table 2, Section 3.6).

Restricting the neuron-activation signal to only the model's final layer, instead of aggregating across all layers, incurs a 4.1% average accuracy drop, showing the discriminative signal is distributed across layers (Table 4, Section 4.2).
Sparsity ablations show ranking quality peaks when only about 0.3% of neurons are used to characterize each example, with minimal further gains beyond this ratio (Figure 6, Section 4.2).

G6PSKuGEEe.text: With only hundreds of training examples, T3S applied to Qwen3-8B reaches 80.63% on AIME24 and 73.96% on AIME25, surpassing an SFT baseline (71.25%/55.00%) and the DeepSeek-R1 teacher model on these benchmarks (Table 3, Section 4.3).
T3S applied to Qwen3-32B reaches 86.67% on AIME24 and 80.00% on AIME25, closely approaching the much larger Qwen3-235B-A22B baseline (85.70%/81.50%) (Table 4, Section 4.3).

T3S-trained LLaDA-2.0-Mini achieves 53.33% on AIME25, 93.19% on MATH500, and 51.50% on TheoremQA, reported as state-of-the-art among 16B-scale no-think (diffusion) language models (Table 5, Section 4.4).
An 'Imitation Shock' phenomenon is documented where training loss decreases monotonically while downstream task performance first crashes and then recovers over training (Figure 1, Section 2.1).

Token-level analysis finds that over 53% of tokens exhibit persistent confidence drops even after prolonged training, motivating the identification and masking of Imitation-Anchor Tokens that dominate early optimization (Table 2, Section 2.3).

wvdev0bqQd.text: Diffinity is a method that enables continuous diffusion language models to satisfy formal syntax constraints, including regular expressions and context-free grammars, during generation (Section 3).

Diffinity achieves near-perfect JSON schema constraint satisfaction (reported above 99%) and above 95% satisfaction on natural-language regular-expression constraints in the constraint-satisfaction evaluation (Table 3).
The perplexity cost of enforcing these constraints is reported at roughly 1.1x-2.5x that of unconstrained diffusion sampling, indicating only a modest quality penalty (Table 2).

Diffinity is reported to outperform autoregressive constrained-decoding baselines in generation speed while achieving comparable or better constraint satisfaction and output quality (Figure 4, Section 5).

uEZpyELNuB.text: Rational Transductors augment a Transformer stream with matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA), injecting this signal into attention via a 'Deep Rational Injection' mechanism (Section 2).

The architecture is shown to capture Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems such as Boolean Formula Evaluation, in contrast to standard self-attention which is limited to AC0 under hard attention or TC0 under soft attention (Sections 4-7).

Random Rational Features are introduced as a universal basis for sequential dependencies, while Differentiable Rational Features are introduced to close the remaining representational gap of the rational-feature approximation (Section 3).

The proposed architecture preserves a parallel training time complexity of O(L + log T) in sequence length T, retaining the parallelization advantage of Transformers over strictly sequential RNN computation (Section 2).
Experiments demonstrate robust length generalization on algorithmic tasks requiring state tracking (the 'Regular Gap'), closing a gap where standard Transformers fail (Appendix B).

Z3cAYsB72W.text: ZoneMaestro reframes autonomous 3D indoor scene synthesis from object-centric placement to Zone-Graph Orchestration, converting high-level semantic intent into functional zones and topological constraints (abstract only).

An Alternating Alignment Strategy combines reasoning internalization with Zone-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (Z-GRPO) to train the model without relying on an external physics engine (abstract only).

Zone-Scene-10K, a large-scale dataset with explicit Zone-Graph annotations, is introduced together with SCALE, a benchmark for evaluating scene generation in irregular, non-convex indoor layouts with complex, dense spatial relations (abstract only).

ZoneMaestro is reported to resolve a 'density-safety dichotomy' in scene generation, outperforming existing baselines on both structural coherence and intent adherence for intricate architectural layouts (abstract only).

h5M4E33Pqs.text: ActHook embeds hook actions into agent trajectories that are activated only by a secret input key and, when inactive, do not alter the agent's original task outcome (abstract only).
ActHook achieves an average detection AUC of 94.3 on watermarked trajectories generated by Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B (abstract only).
Detection reliability is evaluated across three agent task domains: mathematical reasoning, web searching, and software engineering (abstract only).
The watermarking scheme is reported to incur negligible degradation of task performance while maintaining reliable watermark detection across all evaluated task domains (abstract only).

0rZFrUFARU.text: HECTOR supports hybrid reference conditioning, allowing video generation to be guided simultaneously by static image references and dynamic video references of different compositional elements (Section 3.3).
A Video Decompositor extracts compositional structure from reference videos using SAM2 segmentation, CoTracker3 point tracking, and adaptive scale calculation (Section 3.2).
A Spatio-Temporal Alignment Module (STAM) uses inverse warping and Gaussian masking to unify heterogeneous image and video references into a single conditioning signal (Section 3.3).
