Users can explicitly specify each referenced element's trajectory-controlling location, scale, and speed-via trajectory-based scale conditioning rather than bounding boxes, which improves Chamfer Distance from 0.192 to 0.167 in the ablation study (Table 2).
HECTOR achieves higher R-DINO and mIoU scores and lower Chamfer Distance than baselines such as VACE and MotionBooth on both single-object and multi-object reference conditioning (Table 1).

Lc6I5LvHGw.text: Thoughtbubbles is a decoder-only transformer that learns to fork residual streams into temporary parallel 'bubbles' of additional computation using only the standard language modeling loss during pretraining, with no auxiliary supervision (Section 2.4).

At the 772M-parameter scale trained on OpenWebText, Thoughtbubbles with fork budget kappa=4L attains lower perplexity (19.74) and higher LAMBADA and HellaSwag accuracy than both a parameter-matched standard decoder baseline and a non-adaptive computation-matched 'Copy-5' baseline (Table 1).
A 319M-parameter Thoughtbubbles model outperforms the 772M-parameter standard decoder baseline on OpenWebText perplexity, despite having fewer than half the parameters (Figure 3).

Fork frequency is strongly correlated with local token-level prediction entropy, showing that the model learns to allocate additional parallel computation to higher-uncertainty regions of text without explicit supervision (Figure 4).

Parent tokens attend to their forked child tokens with attention scores more than an order of magnitude higher than to unrelated tokens, indicating the forked computation is actively used by the model (Figure 5).

The authors evaluate model scales up to 772M parameters and report that evaluation on GSM8K-style reasoning benchmarks was not feasible at these scales, an explicitly noted limitation of the study (Section 5, Limitations).

WbfRe0cheB.text: Temporal Score Rescaling (TSR) modifies score predictions of a pretrained diffusion or flow model at sampling time via a closed-form rescaling factor r_t(k,σ) = (η_t σ²+1)/(η_t σ²/k+1), requiring no retraining or finetuning of the underlying model (Section 3.2-3.3).
TSR is compatible with both deterministic samplers (e.g., DDIM, Euler ODE) and stochastic samplers (e.g., DDPM, reverse SDE) for diffusion and flow-matching models alike (Section 3.3).
On monocular depth estimation, using a sharpening factor k>1 improves AbsRel from 7.1 to 6.68 on ETH3D and from 6.0 to 5.84 on NYUv2 (Table 1).
On text-to-image generation with Stable Diffusion 3, using a flattening factor k≈0.93 improves FID from 24.75 to 22.74 and CLIP score from 32.82 to 33.07 (Figure 5, Section 5.1).

TSR is characterized as a local temperature scaling that adjusts variance around individual modes rather than performing global reweighting across mixture components, a limitation discussed relative to true temperature sampling (Section 6).

t2h7QkTnzD.text: Alethia-Large achieves 5.2% equal error rate (EER) versus 6.0% for a wav2vec2-1B baseline on speech deepfake detection, evaluated across benchmark datasets (Table 4).
Alethia-Large attains a zero-shot singing-voice deepfake detection EER of 10.8%, outperforming an in-domain-trained baseline at 13.8% EER (Table 5).

Alethia's pretraining combines bottleneck masked embedding prediction using continuous (non-quantized) teacher targets with Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) for spectrogram reconstruction (Section 4.1.3-4.1.4).

An ablation removing the generative (flow-matching) pretraining objective increases EER by 5.6 percentage points specifically on diffusion/flow-matching-generated deepfakes, versus a 0.5-point overall degradation (Section 6.6).
Alethia reduces the number of evaluated datasets on which accuracy falls below 90% from 17/50 (baseline) to 11/50, indicating improved robustness to real-world perturbations (Section 6.1).
On audio-visual deepfake detection (PolyGlotFake), Alethia achieves 7.1% EER versus 9.4% for the baseline (Table 8).

QGA9cWGb12.text: Adaptive Matching Distillation (AMD) improves HPSv2 score on SDXL from 30.64 (baseline DMD-style distillation) to 31.25, and raises ImageReward to 88.37 versus DMD2's 71.01 (Table 3).
AMD achieves a GenEval overall score of 0.57 on SDXL-based few-step generation (Table 2).
On video generation with Wan2.1, AMD reaches a VBench Total Score of 197.45 versus the LongLive baseline's 173.59, and improves the Motion Quality sub-score from 35.51 to 59.26 (Table 6).

AMD formally defines 'Forbidden Zones' (Definition 3.2) as high-energy regions beyond the teacher model's empirical support where real-teacher guidance becomes unreliable, and uses pretrained reward models as diagnostic sensors (Assumption 3.3) to detect them.

AMD applies Dynamic Score Adaptation (Section 3.2, Eq. 10) and Repulsive Landscape Sharpening (Section 3.3, Eq. 14) to adaptively reweight distribution-matching gradients and steepen energy barriers against failure modes identified via reward-based group-relative advantage (Eq. 12).

9AGjhMUtG1.text: MiVE extracts multiscale vision-language features from the first and final transformer layers of Qwen3-VL and fuses them within a unified self-attention diffusion transformer backbone, motivated by an attention-mask-ratio diagnostic showing stronger spatial localization in early layers (R_mask≈0.37 vs 0.33 in later layers) (Section 3.1-3.2).
An ablation shows combining first+last VLM layers yields an Instruction Adherence score of 9.23, versus 8.03 for first-layer-only and 9.04 for last-layer-only variants (Table 4).
An architecture ablation shows the unified self-attention design scores 9.23 on Instruction Adherence versus 6.76 for a decoupled dual-encoder variant (Table 3).

In a 30-participant human study, MiVE outperforms commercial system Kling O1 on the Simple editing subset (4.18 vs 3.69, Wilcoxon p=0.0087) but the margin on the Complex subset (3.75 vs 3.61) is not statistically significant (p=0.247) (Table 2, Appendix D Table 6).

MiVE is trained on 30K editing pairs (24K from OpenVE-3M plus 6K synthetic human-centric data) for 8,000 steps on 8 H100 GPUs (~65 hours), with inference taking about 6.5 minutes per 81-frame 720P clip (Section 6.1, Section 5.1).

AnCy6IUr2V.text: On 2-bit channel-wise quantization of LLaMA 2 70B, NeUQI achieves 7.03 WikiText2 perplexity and 65.13% average accuracy, versus GPTQ's 60.29 perplexity and 35.78% accuracy (Table 1).
On 2-bit quantization of Qwen 2.5 72B, NeUQI achieves 10.79 C4 perplexity and 67.21% accuracy, versus GPTQ's 1127 perplexity and 34.68% accuracy (Table 1).
Relaxing the integer constraint on the zero-point (NeUQI vs. integer-constrained NeUQI_int) improves LLaMA 2 7B WikiText2 perplexity from 26.26 to 17.14 (Table 2).

When combined with lightweight distillation using roughly 0.5M tokens that updates only scales, zero-points, and RMSNorm parameters, NeUQI surpasses the resource-intensive PV-tuning method at comparable data volume (Table 3, Section 4.3).
A 3-bit quantized Qwen 2.5 7B model achieves 8.64 C4 perplexity, outperforming a full-precision Qwen 2.5 1.5B model's 12.54 perplexity despite using less memory (Table 4).

NMn3qzg6hQ.text: GePBench comprises 20,000 rendered geometric figures and 250,000 multiple-choice questions spanning 10 shape types and 9 geometric relationships, organized into six evaluation dimensions (Existence, Counting, Location, Size, Reference, Relationship) (Section 3, Table 1).
On the Size dimension, GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet score only 23.3% and 20.8% accuracy respectively, both below the 25.0% random-guessing baseline (Table 1).

Across 21 evaluated MLLMs, average accuracy ranges from about 51.2% (Claude-3.5-Sonnet) to 69.4% (Gemini-1.5-pro), with all models well short of the ceiling, demonstrating systematic deficiencies in geometric perception (Table 1).
Scaling Qwen2-VL from 8B to 72B parameters yields only a 3.9% average accuracy gain on GePBench, far smaller than typical scaling gains on general MLLM benchmarks (Section 4, Table 1).
LLaVA-GeP, fine-tuned on GePBench training data, improves downstream performance by +5.9% on VizWiz and +1.2% on ScienceQA, with an average +0.8% gain across 9 downstream benchmarks (Table 3).

Ablations with LLaVA-1.5-7B show visual encoder choice strongly affects geometric perception, with CLIP at 336x336 resolution reaching 43.1% average accuracy versus 37.3% for DINOv2 at 224x224 (Table 2).

O0JXgBBo3k.text: The proposed Buffer-and-Reinforce framework uses BufferLoRA to temporarily jailbreak the model during user fine-tuning, saturating harmful-direction gradients while leaving benign-task gradients active, and ReinforceLoRA to restore refusal behavior post-hoc via QR-decomposition merging (Section on Method, Figure 2).

Across harmful data ratios p=0.0 to 1.0, the full method maintains a Harmful Score of 8.1-8.8 while achieving Fine-tuning Accuracy of 75.2-76.6, outperforming baselines at every contamination level (Table 1).

Ablation results show BufferLoRA alone yields Harmful Score 18.0 (FA 75.4); adding ReinforceLoRA lowers Harmful Score to 4.7 but costs FA (74.0); the full method with QR merging reaches Harmful Score 8.4 and FA 77.5 (Table 6).
On diverse downstream tasks (GSM8K, SST2, AGNEWS), the framework reports Harmful Scores of 8.4, 10.2, and 7.5 alongside Fine-tuning Accuracies of 77.5, 93.8, and 88.0 respectively (Table 3).
The method generalizes across LLaMA3-8B, Gemma2-9B-it, and Qwen3-4B-Instruct, with average Harmful Score 5.2 and Fine-tuning Accuracy 78.3 across these architectures (Table 4).

User-side fine-tuning with the framework takes the same GPU time (3.93 minutes) as standard supervised fine-tuning, with the BufferLoRA/ReinforceLoRA pre-training (30.04 minutes total) amortized offline across users (Section on Computational Efficiency).

cPAgJwcn3h.text: RLTT distributes reward across the full latent reasoning trajectory of a looped language model via a weighted sum over loop iterations, sum_t omega_t * grad log P^(t)_theta, rather than crediting only the final latent state as in GRPO (Equation 4).

Built on Ouro-2.6B-Thinking and trained only on the MATH dataset, RLTT improves zero-shot accuracy over GRPO by +14.4 points on MATH-500 (86.0% vs 71.6%), +16.6 points on AIME24 (33.3% vs 16.7%), and +10.0 points on BeyondAIME (16.0% vs 6.0%) (Table 2).
RLTT also improves non-mathematical zero-shot benchmarks relative to GRPO, including +18.7 points on GPQA (38.4%) and +3.5 points on MMLU-ST (89.6%), despite training only on math data (Table 2).

Theorem A.5 formally shows that trajectory-level credit assignment yields optimal decoding lengths equal to or shorter than those from terminal-only reward objectives under diminishing-returns assumptions on correctness (Theorem A.5).
RLTT reduces wall-clock training time by about 10% versus GRPO while converging to shorter responses without any explicit length penalty (Table 1).

Performance is relatively insensitive to the choice of loop-weighting scheme (uniform, progressive, or exit-probability-based), and paired t-tests confirm statistically significant gains (p<0.05) across benchmarks (Table 5, Table 4).

f0RjWJig9V.text: SCRWKV, built around a Structure-Field Encoder (SFE) backbone, uses only 1.22M parameters and 22.78G FLOPs (28MB model size) while achieving F1=0.9363/mIoU=0.9289 on DeepCrack and F1=0.8428/mIoU=0.8512 on TUT (Table 1, Table 2).
SCRWKV outperforms 10 prior SOTA crack-segmentation methods across all four benchmark datasets (Crack500, DeepCrack, CrackMap, TUT) despite its far smaller parameter count (Table 1).

Geometry-guided Bidirectional Structure Transformation (GBST) models curvilinear crack manifolds via counter-directional streams and is shown in component ablations to outperform alternative interaction mechanisms such as bi_ParaSnake, DiagSnake, and Q-Shift (Figure 3, Table 5).
Dynamic Self-Calibrating Decay (DSCD) is shown via ablation, alongside AMCM and GBST, to be a necessary component contributing to overall segmentation accuracy on the benchmark datasets (Table 3).
The Cross-Scale Harmonic Fusion (CSHF) decoder outperforms alternative segmentation heads (UNet, Ham, SegFormer, MFS) in the F1/FLOPs and mIoU/Params comparison (Table 4, Figure 4).
SCRWKV is validated in real-world UAV deployment, running at 46 FPS inference speed (Figure 10, Table 12).

p8vZ7TuyKm.text: AdaNav's Uncertainty-Adaptive Reasoning Block (UAR) uses action entropy as an uncertainty signal to decide when to invoke explicit reasoning during vision-language navigation, averaging only 2.5 reasoning invocations per 55-step trajectory (Figure 3, Section on Method).

Trained with only 6K samples, AdaNav improves success rate by 20% on R2R val-unseen, by 11.7% on RxR-CE, and by 11.4% in real-world deployment relative to prior methods, including some closed-source models trained on million-scale data (Table 1).
AdaNav is trained via a Heuristic-to-RL curriculum that gradually transitions the reasoning trigger from an uncertainty-based heuristic to a learned policy (Section on Methodology).
Reasoning frequency scales with training data size, as shown by the analysis of reasoning invocation rates across different training scales (Figure 4).
Difficulty-conditioned analysis shows the model invokes reasoning on 71% of hard trajectories, indicating the adaptive trigger concentrates reasoning where it is most needed (Table 6).
AdaNav is evaluated across R2R-CE, RxR-CE, ScanQA, and real-world deployments in three indoor environments, demonstrating cross-dataset and cross-domain generalization (Section on Experiments).

WIk0aJfcbK.text: ArborKV achieves up to approximately 4x peak KV-cache memory reduction relative to full-retention decoding while preserving near-full-retention reasoning accuracy in tree-structured LLM inference (Section 1).

The Multi-Signal Value Estimator (MSVE) scores thought blocks by fusing search value, normalized next-token entropy (uncertainty), and accumulated attention statistics without requiring additional forward passes (Section 4).
At a KV budget of rho=0.50 on Llama-3.1-8B, ArborKV attains 77.8% accuracy on GSM8K versus 73.9% for the H2O baseline, and 75.8% versus 72.2% on MATH500 (Table 1, Section 5.2).
At a tighter budget of rho=0.25 on Llama-3.1-8B, ArborKV outperforms the ThinKV baseline, reaching 70.2% versus 67.1% on GSM8K and 64.8% versus 61.6% on MATH500 (Table 1, Section 5.2).
When scaling search width to Nexpand=256 at rho=0.25, FullKV runs out of memory while ArborKV sustains 78.4% accuracy on MATH500 using 5.6 GiB peak memory and 38.2s latency (Table 6, Section 5.3).

Ablating the geometric distance term (Delta_i) from the Tree-Aware Eviction (TAE) policy causes the largest accuracy drop and substantially increases rehydration overhead, confirming that topology-awareness is critical to the method (Table 3, Section 5.4).

FHJdLypBf3.text: Structured Residual Reconstruction (SRR) splits a fixed low-rank budget between preserving the top-k singular directions of the activation-scaled weight matrix and reconstructing the remaining quantization error, rather than devoting the full rank budget to error correction as in standard W ≈ Q + LR formulations (Section on core innovation).

The optimal preservation rank k* is selected by minimizing the product of unrecoverable energy ratios rho_k(SW) and rho_{r-k}(SE), balancing quantization-exposed energy against reconstruction capacity (theory-guided rank selection section).

Under 3-bit MXINT post-training quantization, SRR reduces perplexity by up to 27.1% on LLaMA-2 7B and 12.2% on Gemma-2 2B relative to baselines, evaluated across six model sizes at rank budgets r=32 and r=64 (Table 1).

On GLUE benchmarks with RoBERTa-base under quantized parameter-efficient fine-tuning (QPEFT), SRR yields average gains of 1.5, 4.7, and 5.9 percentage points over QERA at 4-bit, 3-bit, and 2-bit precision respectively, reaching 78.43% average accuracy at 2-bit versus 72.51% for QERA-exact (Table 3).
SRR remains compatible with alternative quantizers, including 3-bit GPTQ and 2-bit QuIP#, showing consistent improvements from quantizer-agnostic rank selection (Table 5).

Gradient scaling with gamma=0.1 applied to preserved singular directions stabilizes QPEFT fine-tuning, with moderate attenuation (gamma in {0.1, 0.5}) outperforming both unscaled (gamma=1) and fully suppressed (gamma=0) variants, at a computational overhead of about 1.06x relative to baseline QER via randomized SVD (QPEFT stabilization / computational cost sections).

ORwyqAzROx.text: Spiral RoPE generalizes 2D rotary positional embeddings by distributing positional encoding across K uniformly spaced directions in [0, pi), computed as t_k(p) = p_x cos(phi_k) + p_y sin(phi_k), rather than restricting encoding to the horizontal and vertical axes of standard axial 2D RoPE (technical approach section).

A grouped interleaved frequency assignment distributes d/4 base frequencies across all K directions so that Spiral RoPE matches the parameter capacity of standard axial 2D RoPE while expanding directional coverage (technical approach section).
On ImageNet-1k classification, Spiral RoPE improves DeiT-Large at 448x448 resolution to 85.67% top-1 accuracy versus 85.40% for RoPE-Mixed and 85.13% for the baseline (Table 1).
On ADE20k semantic segmentation, Spiral RoPE improves mIoU by 2.21 points for DeiT-Large (49.12% vs 46.91% baseline) and 1.22 points for DeiT-Base (48.11% vs 46.89% baseline) (Table 2).
On ImageNet class-conditional generation with DiT, Spiral RoPE reduces FID from 20.05 to 15.55 for DiT-XL/2 and from 23.27 to 19.02 for DiT-L/2 relative to the baseline positional encoding (Table 3).
With extended training to 7M steps, DiT-XL/2 with Spiral RoPE reaches an FID of 1.74, outperforming standard DiT (2.27) and a SiT baseline (2.06) (Table 4).

iSk9sTfuYQ.text: The hierarchical genetic algorithm (HGA) achieves up to a 26.1x increase in average output length on the MATH benchmark, producing 8,817 average tokens on DeepSeek-R1 compared to a 355-3,618 token baseline range across models (Table 3).

The composite fitness function (Sections 3.1-3.4) combines a verbosity score with an 'overthinking marker' score counting hesitation words such as 'but' and 'wait', and uses two genetic operators: question-level crossover, which exchanges final questions, and premise-level crossover, which swaps unrelated premises between problem pairs (Section 3.4).

HGA-evolved adversarial inputs generalize across state-of-the-art reasoning models, inflating average output length to 13,007 tokens on Qwen3-Thinking, 1,618 tokens on GPT-o3, and 12,147 tokens on Gemini-2.5-Flash (Table 3).

Adversarial inputs evolved using a small Qwen3-14B proxy model transfer effectively to larger commercial reasoning models, achieving 3.6x amplification on DeepSeek-R1, 8.1x on Qwen3-Thinking, and 7.1x on GPT-o3, while requiring only 90 input tokens versus 2,652 tokens for the AutoDoS baseline (Table 5).

An ablation of the fitness function shows the composite objective (alpha=0.5) reaches a maximum of 32,019 output tokens, substantially outperforming a length-only objective that maxes out at 14,132 tokens (Table 6).

KyAEhJSyEC.text: The method uses a two-stage alignment strategy: Stage 1 (Diffusion-DRO) performs distribution alignment via ranking-based optimization to reduce the gap between model outputs and real image distributions, and Stage 2 applies Diffusion-DPO using constructed preference pairs where real images are treated as 'preferred' and saliency-guided inpainted versions as 'non-preferred' (Equations 1 and 2).

On SD-1.5 evaluated on Pick-a-Pic v2, the proposed method using only 512 real-image-derived preference pairs raises HPSv3 from a 5.98 baseline to 7.33 (+1.35), exceeding the gain from Diffusion-DPO trained on 851k preference pairs (6.80, +0.82) (Table 1).

On SD-3.5-M evaluated on DrawBench, the proposed method achieves a PickScore of 22.80 and HPSv3 of 12.77 (+2.74 over baseline), outperforming Diffusion-DPO trained on 851k pairs (PickScore 22.70, HPSv3 10.79) despite using far fewer supervision pairs (Table 1).
An ablation shows both stages are needed: using Stage 2 alone yields PickScore 20.74 and Stage 1 alone yields 20.87, while the full two-stage pipeline reaches 21.04 on SD-1.5/Pick-a-Pic v2 (Table 3).
A user study with 18 participants across 60 HPDv2 prompts found the fine-tuned SD-3.5-M preferred over baseline outputs (Figure 4).

The curated dataset consists of 512 ranked preference pairs selected from 25,096 HPDv3 professional photographs via colorfulness-based filtering and a PickScore gap threshold of at least 0.02, with total pipeline compute cost of about 52 GPU-hours on an RTX 3090 (Section B.4).

O7UHBoLrx4.text: InfoPO frames multi-turn agent-user interaction as active uncertainty reduction rather than optimizing purely trajectory-level task rewards (abstract only).
InfoPO computes an information-gain reward that credits a turn based on how much the agent's subsequent action distribution changes versus a masked-feedback counterfactual (abstract only).
InfoPO combines the information-gain reward with task-outcome reward via adaptive variance-gating to balance information value against task completion (abstract only).
InfoPO outperforms both prompting-only methods and multi-turn RL baselines on intent clarification, collaborative coding, and tool-augmented decision-making tasks (abstract only).
InfoPO is reported to remain robust when the underlying user simulator is shifted and to generalize to environment-interactive scenarios beyond the training setup (abstract only).

os54CnlmbR.text: FusionCell encodes layout geometry from three-channel tensors of metal layers M0, M1, M2 using a DeiT (Data-efficient Image Transformer) backbone to produce layout tokens (Section 3.2).
FusionCell encodes the netlist as a heterogeneous device-net graph with connectivity and correlation edge types via a graph transformer to produce graph tokens (Section 3.3).

FusionCell fuses the two modalities with a topology-guided cross-attention in which graph tokens act as queries attending to layout tokens as keys/values, an asymmetric design distinct from symmetric fusion baselines (Section 3.4).

On a dataset of over 19.5k standard cells across 149 cell types built on the ASAP7 7nm PDK, FusionCell achieves an average MAPE of 0.92% and R^2 of 0.977 across six timing/power metrics, versus 3.16% MAPE for a vision-only baseline and 4.16% MAPE for ProtoCellLayout (Table 2, Section 4.3).
FusionCell attains a Spearman's rho of 0.86 and Kendall's tau of 0.76 for ranking cell performance, improving over baseline fusion methods (Table 3).

SeO8pLS44H.text: ReSeek's process reward decomposes into a correctness component, measuring semantic relevance of retrieved evidence to the ground-truth answer, and a utility component, incentivizing retrieval of query-relevant information (Section 3.3-3.4).

ReSeek's judge mechanism assigns positive reward when the agent's self-judgment of retrieved evidence matches an objective Ideal Judgment and negative reward otherwise, enabling self-correction (Section 3.3-3.4).
On Qwen2.5-7B, ReSeek achieves an average task success score of 0.377 versus 0.346 for the prior SOTA baseline ZeroSearch, including 0.389 vs 0.346 on HotpotQA (Table 3).
On Qwen2.5-3B, ReSeek achieves an average score of 0.312 versus 0.281 for ZeroSearch, including 0.328 vs 0.274 on HotpotQA (Table 3).

ReSeek is compared against four baseline families: vanilla prompting (zero-shot/CoT), single-pass RAG, agentic search (ReAct-style), and RL-tuned policies including Search-R1, ReSearch, and ZeroSearch (Section 4.1).

icRbM5ArwW.text: IAM defines local inconsistency S_rho(theta) as the worst-case KL divergence within an L2 ball between the output distributions of a model and its perturbed counterpart, computable without labels (Section 4.1).

Theorem 4.1 establishes a Fisher-Information-Matrix-based generalization bound showing that under near-interpolation, minimizing local inconsistency reduces the upper bound on true risk (Section 4.3).

IAM approximates local inconsistency via the Fisher Information Matrix's largest eigenvalue, S_rho(theta) is approx (1/2) rho^2 lambda_max(F(theta)), and implements two variants, IAM-D (direct regularization) and IAM-S (SAM-like perturbation) (Section 4.2, Section 5, Algorithm 2).
On supervised CIFAR-100, IAM-S reaches 16.82% test error versus SAM's 17.63%, while on ImageNet with ResNet-50, IAM-D achieves 21.36% top-1 error versus SAM's 21.80% (Table 1, Table 2).
In semi-supervised learning with FixMatch, adding IAM-D reduces error from 6.26% to 5.30% on CIFAR-10 with 250 labels and from 32.84% to 28.95% on CIFAR-100 with 2500 labels (Table 3, Section 5.3).
IAM improves self-supervised learning, with SimCLR-IAM converging faster and reaching higher linear-probe accuracy than vanilla SimCLR (Figure 4, Section 5.3).

yUOnI5IAuT.text: Visual Para-Thinker extends parallel reasoning (multiple concurrent reasoning paths) to multimodal LLMs by introducing visual partitioning of the input image, motivated by a theoretical argument in Theorem 2.1 (Section 2, Section 3).
On vision-centric tasks, the 7B Visual Para-Thinker improves over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline on CountBench (70.8% vs 67.7%), V* (85.4% vs 83.1%), and HallusionBench (71.0% vs 66.0%) (Table 1).
On grounding tasks, Visual Para-Thinker-3B improves RefCOCO Acc@0.5 to 88.5% (vs 84.8% baseline), RefCOCO+ to 82.6% (vs 76.7%), and RefCOCOg to 87.1%, gains of roughly 3-6 points (Table 2).
Scaling the number of parallel reasoning paths from 1 to 4 improves V* accuracy from 63.2% to 67.9%, with 4 paths identified as the optimal configuration (Table 3).
An ablation shows combining Pa-Attention and LPRoPE yields the strongest results, with LPRoPE alone contributing about a 4% gain on the Pixmo counting task (Table 4).
Visual Para-Thinker with KV-cache reuse runs inference in 312 seconds versus 1,197 seconds for a majority-voting baseline, a roughly 2.5x throughput improvement at 123 tokens/second (Table 5).

PL8qP67p6E.text: DIVER decouples dataset distillation into a Stage I traditional distillation step and a Stage II 'Diving into Distilled Data' refinement that uses a pre-trained DiT-XL/2 diffusion transformer with a VAE (vae-ft-mse) for semantic recovery (Section 3.1).

On ImageNet-1K at 224x224 resolution with a ResNet-18 evaluation architecture, DIVER improves SRe2L from 21.3% to 24.5% accuracy at IPC=10, and improves G-VBSM from 51.8% to 57.2% accuracy at IPC=50 (Table 3).
DIVER processes ImageNet images at 256x256 resolution in 2.48 seconds per image on a single RTX-4090 GPU while using only about 4 GB of GPU memory, comparable to raw DiT inference (Section 4.4).

In an ablation on ImageFruit using the MTT distillation algorithm, DIVER's full pipeline reaches 22.3% error at IPC=1 and 29.8% error at IPC=10, compared to a 14.1% error random baseline at IPC=1 (Table 6).

DIVER's semantic fusion strategy restricts conditional class labels to the reverse-diffusion steps between step 40 and step 25, with a guidance-factor and forward-noise-step sensitivity analysis showing an optimal forward step of t_f=25 (Figure 4).

dv1mWhkbct.text: MoDEX reformulates uncertainty-aware classification as a courtroom debate among K class-specific advocates, decomposing the Dirichlet parameters into shared base evidence, class-specific advocacy strength, and input-dependent plausibility weights, using O(K) rather than O(K^2) parameters (Section 5).

Theorem 5.1 proves MoDEX generalizes prior evidential deep learning methods, reducing to F-EDL when advocacy strengths are class-independent and to standard EDL under further constraints (Theorem 5.1).
On standard CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification, MoDEX achieves 92.46% accuracy on CIFAR-10 versus 91.19% for F-EDL, and 75.91% accuracy on CIFAR-100 versus 69.40% for F-EDL (Table 1).
On CIFAR-10-C corruption detection at severity level 5, MoDEX achieves 80.63 AUPR compared to 78.52 AUPR for F-EDL (Table 2).
Under severe class imbalance on CIFAR-10-LT (rho=0.01), MoDEX reaches 71.53% test accuracy and 72.05 AUPR for SVHN|C-100 OOD detection, versus 63.73% accuracy and 62.56 AUPR for F-EDL (Table 3).

VFZWSzWgtS.text: STORM, a 4-billion-parameter large reasoning model trained via the CALM framework, achieves a macro-average accuracy of 68.9% across five optimization modeling benchmarks: NL4Opt, MAMO-Easy, MAMO-Complex, IndustryOR, and OptMath (Section on benchmark evaluation).
STORM's 68.9% average accuracy matches or exceeds DeepSeek-R1-0528, a 671-billion-parameter reasoning model, which scores 67.5% average accuracy on the same five benchmarks.
On the MAMO-Complex benchmark specifically, STORM reaches 70.3% accuracy, a gain of +23.8 percentage points over its baseline.

The CALM framework generates training data via an expert intervener that supplies concise corrective hints to flawed reasoning traces, with these interventions modifying fewer than 2.6% of generated tokens.

STORM is produced through a two-stage training pipeline of supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning that preserves the native reasoning patterns of the underlying LRM rather than forcing rigid non-reflective generation.

7pinsbGVLt.text: CURE is evaluated against three baselines specialized for gene-expression-conditioned molecule generation: GexMolGen, Gx2Mol, and TRIOMPHE (Section 5.2).

CURE achieves 90-100% Coverage across evaluation splits versus 45-72% for baselines, and a Frechet ChemNet Distance of 6.79-27.62 versus 17.90-82.72 for baselines, on structural quality metrics (Table 1).

CURE achieves substantially lower PRnet MSE between predicted and ground-truth perturbation signatures (0.23-0.53) than baseline methods (2.59-8.63), indicating stronger functional consistency (Table 1).

In a zero-shot gene-inhibitor design task evaluated on unseen knockout signatures for 10 canonical genes (including AKT1, EGFR, MTOR, and TP53), CURE achieves Morgan fingerprint similarity of 0.73-0.88 and binding affinities of -8.28 to -9.15 kcal/mol, outperforming the weakest baseline's 0.51-0.85 similarity and -5.67 to -6.49 kcal/mol affinity (Table 2, Section 5.4).
A CURE-generated molecule targeting EGFR achieves a docking binding affinity of -9.164 kcal/mol, surpassing the reference drug Erlotinib's -7.302 kcal/mol (Section A.4, Figure 4).

iXhFXwIbvi.text: MH-MoE routes expert selection independently across H head-aligned slices of the post-attention representation using private expert banks per head, rather than routing from a single mixed-head vector, creating an implicit routing resolution of (K choose k)^H possible paths.
On Qwen3-0.6B evaluated on the TRACE continual-learning benchmark, MH-MoE improves Backward Transfer from -11.2% (LoRAMoE) to -4.5%, and improves Overall Performance from 0.378 to 0.467.
On Qwen3-8B, MH-MoE improves Overall Performance from 0.551 to 0.569 and Backward Transfer from -5.5% to -5.1% relative to LoRAMoE.

Routes with a higher route-wise effective composition number (N_eff) exhibit larger increases in old-task loss after continual training, motivating MH-MoE's design to reduce feature-composition collisions before routing (Figure 5).

Concatenating multi-head attention outputs into a single vector before routing is identified as a pre-routing bottleneck that forces the router to act on co-occurring feature compositions rather than separable per-head channels, increasing gradient interference during continual training.

MKsxhiUk9M.text: Code2Worlds achieves a 41% improvement in Scene Graph Score (SGS) over baseline methods for 4D world generation (abstract only).
Code2Worlds achieves a 49% higher Richness Score compared to baseline methods (abstract only).
Code2Worlds uses a dual-stream architecture that disentangles retrieval-augmented object generation from hierarchical environmental orchestration (abstract only).

Code2Worlds incorporates a physics-aware closed-loop mechanism combining a PostProcess Agent that scripts dynamics with a VLM-Motion Critic that performs iterative self-reflection refinement on simulation code (abstract only).
Code2Worlds is uniquely capable of generating physics-aware 4D dynamics, a capability absent in prior static-only world generation methods (abstract only).

7ZQhm5HnOA.text: TetraJet-v2 reduces the average performance gap to BF16 training by 51.3% while using 4-bit NVFP4 fully-quantized training (Section 5).
TetraJet-v2 achieves a 1.67x end-to-end speedup over FP8 training (Section 5).

TetraJet-v2 layers oscillation suppression (Algorithm 2) and outlier control (Algorithm 3) on top of a baseline NVFP4 training procedure (Algorithm 1), combining both into the complete method (Algorithm 4).
TetraJet-v2 is compared against other FP4 training baselines including MXFP4 and Quartet, as well as FP16/BF16 mixed-precision training, on downstream task benchmarks (Table 3-4).
Ablation experiments isolate the individual contributions of oscillation suppression and outlier control, showing both components are necessary for stable convergence (Section C.1-C.3).
Large-scale pretraining experiments and downstream task results across multiple benchmarks are reported (Section 5.2, Tables 7, 12-15).

tbqxbGMFUV.text: Perception-Judge trained with GRPO on the Perceptually Perturbed Judgment Dataset raises average score-based performance to 0.466 for the Flex-7B variant, up from a 0.404 baseline (Table 2).
Perception-Judge-Qwen3-4B improves average score to 0.457 versus a 0.419 baseline Qwen3 judge (Table 2).

The reward combines a Format Reward (Equation 5) and a Batch Ranking Reward (Equations 6-7) enforcing the ordering correct response over perceptually-perturbed response over perceptually-and-reasoning-perturbed response, optimized jointly via GRPO (Equation 1, Section 3.4).
An ablation shows the batch ranking reward without explicit pairwise labels outperforms MMPR-v1.2 pairwise training (0.476 vs 0.454 score) when trained on 10K samples (Table 3).

Baseline multimodal judges exhibit approximately 30.5% error rates attributable to two failure modes: insufficient perceptual capability and response anchoring on text over visual perception (Section 3.2, Table 1).
Accuracy on isolated perceptual-only errors drops by more than 10 percentage points compared to compound perceptual-and-reasoning errors for baseline judges (Figure 2).

h2uxKKK4WZ.text: The proposed online Newton method using a sketch-and-project solver with Nesterov's acceleration (Algorithm 1, NASketch) matches the O(d^2) per-iteration time and memory complexity of first-order methods (Section 2.2).
The last iterate is proven asymptotically normal, with the limiting covariance characterized by a Lyapunov equation incorporating the sketching operator (Theorem 4.3).
A fully online covariance estimator achieves convergence rate E[||Sigma_hat_t - Sigma*||] = O(1/sqrt(t*phi_t)) without requiring matrix inversion (Theorem 4.6).
Global convergence guarantees for the sketch-and-project Newton iterates are established (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.2).
A spectral radius recursion derived via the Cayley-Hamilton theorem proves contraction at rate 1 - sqrt(mu_t/nu_t) for the accelerated sketching operator (Lemma 3.6).
The framework recovers exact Newton behavior and the unaccelerated sketching case (gamma=1) as special cases, clarifying computational-statistical trade-offs (Proposition 4.4).

iLrl4ppPqL.text: JiSi achieves an average performance of 72.15 across benchmarks, surpassing Gemini-3-Pro's 71.00 by 1.15%, while orchestrating ten open-source LLMs (Table 1).
JiSi reduces cost by 53.23% relative to Gemini-3-Pro (Table 2).
JiSi outperforms the best individual open-source LLM by 6.56% (Section 4.2).

JiSi combines three components: Query-Response Mixed Routing using query embeddings, response embeddings, and token costs; Support-Set-based Aggregator Selection; and an Adaptive Routing-Aggregation Switch (Section 3.3).
An ablation removing adaptive aggregation drops average performance from 72.15 to 71.09 (a 1.06% decrease), and using the Query-Response Mixed Router alone yields 69.68 (Table 1).
JiSi is compared against router baselines (RouterDC, EmbedLLM, GraphRouter, Avengers, Retrieval-based Router) and multi-agent baselines (MoA, Self-Consistency, Majority Voting) (Table 1).

sh8Gnv1xHH.text: ToCoRL improves SimpleQA accuracy from 18.9% (Thinking baseline) to 28.3% on Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507-Thinking, outperforming GRPO (23.6%), Adaptive-Thinking (23.9%), and Instruct-Tuning GRPO (21.1%) (Table 2).

ToCoRL raises AA-Omniscience accuracy to 18.6% while preserving AIME'24 (89.0%) and AIME'25 (81.5%) math performance close to or above the Thinking baseline (84.8%/80.5%), showing no capability degradation on math despite factual gains (Table 2).

Token-conditional generation, defined in Section 3, conditions LLM generation on token prefixes (length k, e.g. 6-8 tokens) from responses exhibiting a desired behavior, requiring no parameter updates at inference time (Section 3).

The ToCoRL objective in Section 4 combines a REINFORCE-style policy gradient with a KL divergence term against a customized reference policy π̃_TC, with Theorem 4.1 establishing well-definedness of this reference policy and Theorem 4.2 giving a tractable policy-gradient implementation (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2).

Ablations show ToCoRL is robust to the KL coefficient λ ∈ {0.5, 1, 2} and to different prefix-provider models (Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507-Instruct, Qwen3-30B, Qwen2.5-14B), with performance remaining stable across these settings (Table 4, Table 5).

Supervised fine-tuning on ToCoRL-generated responses transfers the behavior into a static model, achieving 29.1% SimpleQA accuracy, surpassing SFT on outputs from the instruct model used as prefix provider (Section 5.4, Table 6).

7zTV4dvdGB.text: AutoRAS achieves 74.27% average vanilla accuracy and 72.14% average accuracy under attack across MMLU, MSMARCO, MATH, and ProgramDev, compared to the best baseline AFlow's 71.51% vanilla and 57.25% attack accuracy (Table 1).
AutoRAS exhibits the smallest average performance drop under adversarial attacks (2.13%) versus 14.26% for the best-performing baseline AFlow (Table 1, Obs. 2, Section 5.2).

AutoRAS transfers across four backbone LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3.1, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Gemini-2.0-Flash) on MMLU, maintaining 87.42% average vanilla accuracy and 86.11% average accuracy under attack (Table 2).

Ablating the AutoRAS design on MMLU shows accuracy under attack drops from 82.35% (full model) to 71.90% when the safety signal is removed and to 76.47% when external robustness is removed, indicating both components are necessary for robustness (Table 4, Section 5.6).

AutoRAS represents agentic systems as sequences of primitives from a unified vocabulary Φ = Φ_struct ∪ Φ_act combining structural and behavioral elements, trained via GFlowNet trajectory-balance learning with a reward defined by accuracy, external/internal robustness, and cost (Eq. 8, Section 4.3).

AutoRAS attains the highest vanilla accuracy (83.01%) among compared methods while incurring one of the lowest total costs ($0.6655), evaluated across four attack types: brain, memory, tool, and agent-to-agent attacks (Table 3, Section 5.1).

5WVIbxWqwA.text: The paper resolves an open ambient-dimension-d suboptimality in Nash regret bounds for linear bandits, proving an order-optimal Nash regret bound that improves over the prior analysis of Sawarni et al. (2023) (Theorem 66).

The FairLinBandit framework is proposed as a meta-algorithm compatible with existing linear bandit strategies, with instantiations using Phased Elimination and Upper Confidence Bound algorithms both proven to achieve sublinear p-means regret across the entire range of the interpolation parameter p (Theorem 70).
p-means regret is introduced as a unifying objective that interpolates between fairness (Nash welfare) and utility objectives and strictly generalizes Nash regret (Section 5, Theorem 70).

The regret bound proofs rely on self-normalized martingale concentration and geometric arguments, building on supporting lemmas (e.g., Lemma 96, Lemma 109) established earlier in the analysis (Theorem 66).

On real-world dataset-derived linear bandit instances, the proposed FairLinBandit instantiations empirically outperform existing state-of-the-art baselines in the experimental evaluation section (Section 5).

GDHVAs2XDQ.text: Schema-derived graphs for relational deep learning suffer from information overload (irrelevant attributes/entities inflating complexity) and semantic fragmentation (normalization breaking direct relations, e.g. User-Order-OrderItem-Item, into multi-hop chains instead of a direct User-Item edge) (Section 3).

Table 1 shows column-level and table-level gating variants (ColFilter, FullFilter) consistently outperform base models across classification tasks, while a high-variance VarFilter baseline underperforms despite exhibiting high statistical variance (Table 1).

Figure 2 demonstrates an inverted-U relationship between filtering strength and performance, showing optimal performance occurs at intermediate filtering strength rather than at either extreme, which Theorem 3.2 explains via entropy bounds on structural capacity (Figure 2, Theorem 3.2).

The end-to-end structural optimizer, combining Hard-Concrete gating, a Variational Information Bottleneck, and template-based structural injection, improves ROC-AUC on classification tasks such as driver-top3 from 81.48 to 86.82 and reduces MAE on regression tasks such as driver-position from 3.88 to 2.13 (Table 2, Table 3, Section 4).

Ablation removing the injection component (Ours_ni) causes moderate performance loss and removing filtering (Ours_nf) causes the largest degradation, confirming both filtering and structural injection contribute independently to performance gains (Figure 9).

The structural optimizer's improvements are backbone-agnostic, holding across GraphSAGE, REL-GNN, and HGT architectures, while maintaining competitive inference latency, outperforming the HAN baseline by 15-45% in speed (Table 5, Table 6).

Q5DHzFVOxf.text: GIPO replaces PPO's hard clipping with a smooth Gaussian trust weight in log-ratio space, ω(ρ̄_t; σ) = exp(-1/2 (log(ρ̄_t)/σ)^2), which is symmetric under ω(ρ;σ) = ω(1/ρ;σ) to balance updates for equivalent policy deviations (Algorithm 1, Appendix A).

Theorem 5.2 establishes a monotonic improvement guarantee showing GIPO implicitly enforces a tunable bound on policy update magnitude, and Theorem 5.4 provides finite-sample concentration bounds via Hoeffding inequalities (Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.4).

On the Meta-World benchmark, GIPO outperforms PPO-Clip and SAPO under both stale and fresh replay regimes, with the performance gap widening as staleness increases, as measured by OldFrac and log-ratio P95 drift (Figure 2, Table 1).

On the LIBERO benchmark with a 7B OpenVLA-OFT backbone across four task suites (Object, Spatial, Goal, 10-task), GIPO reaches near-optimal success rates roughly 1M training steps faster than baseline methods, using over 10,000 H200 GPU-hours of compute (Figure 3).

In a toy 2x2 GridWorld experiment analyzing exact bias-variance tradeoffs, GIPO dominates No-Clip and PPO under high policy lag (Case A) and dominates SAPO under moderate lag (Case B), while maintaining a Pareto frontier under low lag (Case C) (Figure 4).
A sensitivity analysis of the damping scale σ on handle-press-v3 (Section C.7) finds task-specific optimal values, with σ=1.0 preferred on Meta-World and σ=0.5 preferred on LIBERO (Section C.7).

rEpmIPMftW.text: ROSA2 reformulates multi-turn LLM adaptation as a joint optimization problem over the combined space of textual prompts ("Words") and model parameters ("Weights"), using textual gradients to resolve intent ambiguity alongside parameter updates to close capability gaps (abstract only).
ROSA2 outperforms existing state-of-the-art multi-turn adaptation baselines by 30% on the MATH benchmark (abstract only).
ROSA2 reduces the number of interaction turns required to reach a target performance level by 40% compared to baseline methods (abstract only).

The paper proves that co-adaptation between textual and parameter updates strictly reduces the required parameter shift needed for convergence, formalizing semantic clarity as a pre-conditioner for effective weight updates (abstract only).

5ntMrdtnTu.text: The paper derives sharp asymptotic characterizations of test error for a two-stage iterated empirical risk minimization procedure, in which a first linear estimator's predictions enter as an argument in the loss function of a second ERM trained on the same Gaussian-mixture dataset, in the high-dimensional proportional regime (abstract only).

The analysis addresses the statistical dependency introduced by reusing the same data across both ERM stages and by the prediction-dependent loss of the second stage, unlike classical single-stage ERM analyses (abstract only).
Applying the theory to pool-based active learning removes oracle and sample-splitting assumptions required by prior active learning analyses (abstract only).
The theory uncovers a fundamental tradeoff in how a fixed labeling budget should be allocated across the two active learning stages (abstract only).
The paper demonstrates a double-descent behavior in test error that is driven by the data selection mechanism itself, rather than by model complexity or sample size alone (abstract only).

XrqMNac6Ft.text: KBE-DME represents visual question-answering samples via a graph formulation to transform static multimodal benchmarks into a controllable, dynamically evolving version (abstract only).

KBE evolves benchmark questions through two mechanisms: question reconstruction, which re-selects visual information from the original image, and question expansion, which incorporates external textual knowledge (abstract only).
KBE enables difficulty-controllable evaluation by adjusting the degree of question exploration, allowing assessment rigor to be calibrated across a range of model capabilities (abstract only).

Extensive experiments show KBE alleviates the risk of data contamination and data saturation compared to static multimodal benchmarks, providing a more comprehensive assessment of MLLM capabilities (abstract only).

KHhO311xZ2.text: The paper introduces a Noise Sensitivity Exponent (NSE), a quantity determined solely by the activation function, that governs the existence and magnitude of statistical-to-computational gaps in single- and multi-index models (abstract only).

In single-index models with large additive noise, the NSE fully characterizes the onset of the computational bottleneck separating statistically optimal from computationally efficient estimators (abstract only).
The NSE controls the statistical-to-computational gap that arises during the specialization transition in large separable multi-index models (abstract only).
In hierarchical multi-index models, the NSE determines the optimal computational rate for sequentially learning the different index directions (abstract only).
The NSE is presented as a unifying quantity linking noise robustness, computational hardness, and feature specialization across these high-dimensional learning settings (abstract only).

1GIYHWO9S5.text: FP quantization formats outperform INT formats at coarse granularity, but the comparison becomes more nuanced at fine-grained, block-wise quantization levels (abstract only).
At 8-bit precision, MXINT8 outperforms floating-point counterparts in both algorithmic accuracy and hardware efficiency (abstract only).

At 4-bit precision, floating-point formats (MXFP4, NVFP4) typically retain an accuracy advantage over integer formats, though INT formats with outlier-mitigation techniques can become competitive (abstract only).
The paper introduces a symmetric clipping method to resolve gradient bias in fine-grained low-bit integer training, achieving nearly lossless MXINT8 training performance (abstract only).

The findings challenge the industry trend toward floating-point-centric hardware architectures (e.g., Nvidia's Blackwell), concluding that fine-grained INT formats, particularly MXINT8, offer a better balance of accuracy, power, and efficiency (abstract only).

h8g5eiSEpc.text: Establishes non-asymptotic discretization error bounds for samplers of discrete flow models without imposing boundedness restrictions on transition rates or source distributions (abstract only).
Derives the discretization error bound by analyzing a one-step lower bound for the Euler sampler, which evaluates transition rates only at the initial state within each time interval (abstract only).

Introduces two corrected samplers, a time-corrected sampler and a location-corrected sampler, that reduce discretization error relative to standard tau-leaping and Euler solvers with minimal added computational overhead (abstract only).
The location-corrected sampler has lower complexity than existing parallel samplers for discrete flow models (abstract only).

Experiments on simulated discrete-state data and text-to-image generation show the corrected samplers achieve improved generation quality and faster inference time than baseline samplers (abstract only).

8DLW34pkNi.text: Open-weight language models achieve 91.8%-96.5% accuracy on affirmative questions but only 45.2%-57.6% accuracy on negated questions, despite a sensitivity metric of 95.1%-97.8% indicating internal representations do encode the negation (Table 2).
Early-layer attention heads move the representation of the negation token 'not' to the position of the negated concept via decodable directional signals (Section 5.1).

Causally important attention modules around layer 14 construct an explicit negated representation of the concept (e.g., mapping 'not gas' toward 'solid') rather than merely suppressing the original concept, with construction observed in over 80% of examples versus suppression in under 30% (Section 5.3-5.4).
Ablating late-layer attention modules responsible for an identified 'attention sinking' shortcut improves accuracy on negated questions by 17%-46% relative improvement (Table 3).

Models implement both an attention-based suppression mechanism and a direct constructive mechanism for processing negation, with the constructive mechanism being the more prominent of the two (Section 5.3-5.4).

UfVYPA9VnD.text: UCS-Bench comprises over 170 hours of egocentric video and 8,114 timestamped question-answer pairs drawn from 532 videos sourced from HourVideo, ScanNet, EgoLife, EgoBlind, EPIC-KITCHENS, and TeleEgo (Section on dataset statistics).

UCS-Bench questions are organized into four categories: Position & Orientation (25.73%), Trajectory & Movement (21.73%), Proximity & Reachability (18.15%), and Category & Quantity (34.39%) (dataset composition).

DirectMe builds an evolving 3D scene graph as spatial memory using depth and camera pose estimates from DepthAnything3 combined with object detection/tracking via Grounding-DINO and SAM2 (Method section).
DirectMe paired with Qwen3-VL achieves 50.5% overall accuracy on UCS-Bench, exceeding baseline proprietary and open-source MLLMs which score 42%-49%, while human performance is 91.0% (Table 3).

DirectMe outperforms specialized spatial/streaming baselines including Cambrian-S (42.4%) and Dispider (36.7%) on UCS-Bench, demonstrating the benefit of structured spatial memory over general long-video or spatial-aware approaches (Table 3).

LIcj73RLX6.text: In LVLMs, route competition within attention heads can let the textual pathway dominate the final token decision even when the visual pathway receives substantial attention, causing the decoder to follow linguistic priors over visual evidence (Route Competition analysis).

Causal Route Gating (CRG) decomposes each attention head's output into visual and textual routes and estimates their decision-aligned Causal Route Effects using a first-order approximation requiring one forward pass and one gradient computation (Method: Causal Route Effects).

CRG applies mild gating (0.5-1.0) to Conflict-A heads (visual supports, text opposes) and strong gating (0-0.5) to Conflict-B heads (text drives hallucination against visual evidence), ranked via a Visual Reliance Index, without any additional training (Method: Selective Gating).
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, CRG improves POPE accuracy by 6.3 points and F1 by 7.0 points, and reduces the CHAIR hallucination rate from 52.8% to 34.2% (POPE and CHAIR results).

On AMBER with LLaVA-1.5-7B, CRG reduces the CHAIR metric from 8.3 to 4.6 and raises F1 from 73.7 to 77.5, an AMBER Score gain of +3.75, while adding only 2.27x inference latency compared to 7.12x for the OPERA baseline (AMBER results).

T4Ibp5vLpE.text: The modified EAT method replaces the sigmoid soft indicator with a cubic Hermite smoothstep function f_cubic(u) = 3w^2 - 2w^3 (with w = clamp((u+1)/2, 0, 1)) that has compact support, eliminating the 'ghost spike' contributions from the sigmoid's infinite tails (Modified EAT Method section).

For temperature tau <= 1, EAT_cubic achieves a theoretically unbiased first moment (c_cubic(tau) = 1) with variance factor v_cubic(tau) = 1 - 9*tau/35, compared to the sigmoid-based EAT which shows 31% mean inflation and 42% variance reduction at tau = 1.0 (Theoretical Results section).
EAT_cubic achieves roughly 7x lower Wasserstein-1 distance to the true Poisson distribution than sigmoid-based EAT at high firing rates (Figure 2).

In gradient-quality experiments both EAT variants maintain greater than 0.99 cosine similarity to exact gradients, with EAT_cubic's BiasEnergy remaining around 10^-2 across all tested temperatures while sigmoid-based EAT's gradient quality degrades at higher temperatures (Figure 3).

On a linear Poisson VAE, EAT_cubic matches the ELBO of exact gradients (ELBO approximately -169) across temperatures, whereas sigmoid-based EAT and Gumbel-Softmax collapse to ELBO approximately -250 at tau = 0.5, and this robustness is confirmed on POGLM (Figure 4).

ah9xkFXCV6.text: At 50% sparsity, MACKO-SpMV achieves a 1.2-1.5x speedup and 1.5x memory reduction over the cuBLAS dense baseline in fp16 (Abstract, Section 5).
Applied to Wanda-pruned Llama2-7B at 50% sparsity, MACKO-SpMV delivers 1.5x memory reduction and 1.5x faster inference at fp16 precision (Abstract).
Across 30-90% sparsity, MACKO outperforms all tested baselines: 2.8-13.0x speedup over cuSPARSE, 1.9-2.6x over Sputnik, and 2.2-2.5x over DASP (Abstract, Section 5).

Figure 1 shows that for a 36864x12288 fp16 matrix on an RTX 4090, MACKO's runtime beats the dense cuBLAS baseline starting at sparsity as low as 25%, whereas existing sparse libraries need 2.6x fewer non-zeros to match that performance (Figure 1).

MACKO's storage format compresses column indices via delta encoding with mutual alignment padding, targeting the 30-90% sparsity regime that prior formats (CSR, Tiled-CSL, bitmask) handle poorly (Section 4.1, Figure 3).

iW1oBBO72S.text: D2L achieves near-perfect zero-shot accuracy on a synthetic needle-in-a-haystack task at up to 40 chunks (40K tokens) of haystack length, five times the maximum number of chunks (8) seen during its 256-token-max training, using gemma-2-2b-it (8K native context) as the base model (Section 4, Figure 2).

On the NIAH task, D2L requires under 50MB of additional inference memory regardless of haystack length, versus over 12GB for the base model reading a 128K-token haystack directly in context (Figure 2).
On the SQuAD benchmark, D2L reaches 82.5% relative performance compared to the in-context-learning upper bound while removing the context entirely from the prompt (Section 5.1.1, Figure 3).

D2L internalizes context in under one second (batched or iterative mode), versus about 40 seconds for oracle context distillation and over 100 seconds for vanilla context distillation with generated queries (Section 5.1.1, Figure 3).
D2L's Perceiver-based hypernetwork has only 309M trainable parameters and outputs rank-8 LoRA adapters applied to the down-projection layer of each MLP block of the frozen target LLM (Section 5).

On long-document QA benchmarks (2WikiMultiHopQA, MultiFieldQA, QASPER, with test samples up to 32K tokens), D2L generalizes zero-shot beyond its training length and uses roughly 2x less memory than oracle context distillation during updates (Section 5.1.2, Table 1).

j4c3i3a5kH.text: Theorem 4.3 proves that for any strictly increasing function ψ, there exists a strictly proper loss pair (ℓ0, ℓ1) such that ψ decomposes as a composition of that loss with a strictly increasing function, generalizing DPO's link beyond the fixed logistic loss (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.3).

Theorem 4.1 shows that when the RLHF regularizer R is the regret of a proper loss, R equals a Bregman divergence, generalizing DPO's KL-based regularization to arbitrary Bregman divergences (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).

The paper introduces a 'KLST*' choice-theoretic structure built on expandability, local choice structure, and monotonicity axioms (Definitions 3.2-3.4) to generalize Bradley-Terry-Luce while allowing abstention (Section 3, Definition 3.4).

Theorem 4.2 shows any choice probability with a KLST* structure can be represented as a strictly increasing link function F applied to a difference of latent utility functions, generalizing DPO's BTL-derived link r_theta = f(pi_theta) (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).

Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.5 show that DPO's standard logistic loss and symmetric link are recovered as one special case within the general (proper loss, link function, proper loss) triptych the paper constructs (Theorem 4.4, Corollary 4.5, Section 4.4).

x6J7va4BYz.text: Ctrl-R with power-scaling factor β=0.2 improves average score over the DAPO baseline by +1.38 points on Qwen3-8B-Base and +1.27 points on Qwen3-1.7B-Base across AIME'24, AIME'25, MATH500, AMC'23, Minerva, and Olympiad (Table 2).

On vision-language math reasoning, Ctrl-R improves average accuracy over the GRPO baseline by +2.60 points across MathVista, MathVerse, MathVision, MMMU-Pro, EMMA, and Hallubench, outperforming OpenVLThinker (+2.03) and Auxiliary Reward shaping (+1.44) (Table 3).

Ablations show that removing importance-sampling correction (β=0, No IS) degrades average score to -0.79 relative to DAPO, and full uncorrected importance sampling (β=1, Full IS) also underperforms the chosen β=0.2 setting (Table 2).

Ctrl-R encodes five target reasoning structures as deterministic finite automata over lexical patterns for language models (Backwarding, Backtracking, Induction, Counterfactual, Overthinking Awareness) and three for vision-language models (Visual Grounding, General, Reflection) (Table 1).

Ctrl-R forms a guided behavior policy by reweighting the proximal policy with an HMM-distilled guidance function γ(α|x<t,xt), then trains with a power-scaled importance-sampling weight w^β in the clipped surrogate loss (Equation 3.2, Section 3.2).

Zuews4ULW6.text: The framework computes closed-form Bayes-optimal responses ℓ_Bayes minimizing expected task-dependent dissimilarity across five latent structures: single-label classes, multi-answer sets, undirected graphs, semantic embeddings, and the probability simplex (Table 1, Section 3).

Across four instruction-tuned models (Gemma 3 4B, Gemma 3 12B, Qwen3 4B, Qwen3 30B-A3B) and datasets MAQA, TriviaQA, WMT19 FI-EN, and CNN/DailyMail, Bayes-optimal decoding matches or outperforms beam search, self-consistency, contrastive search, and greedy decoding on metrics including Hamming loss, F1, exact match, COMET, and AlignScore (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Lemma 3.1 shows that under 0-1 loss for single-label classification, the Bayes-optimal action is the modal class, with minimum Bayes risk equal to one minus the maximum class probability (Lemma 3.1, Section 3.1).

Lemma 3.4 shows that for the probability-simplex latent structure under KL divergence, the Bayes-optimal prediction is the mean latent distribution, with minimum Bayes risk equal to the entropy of the mean minus the expected entropy (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.5).

The paper proves the minimum Bayes risk is a provable lower bound on the true (epistemic) risk relative to the unknown reference distribution, establishing it as a principled uncertainty estimator (Section 2.2).
All experiments approximate the latent posterior p(ℓ|x) using M=20 Monte Carlo samples drawn from the model's push-forward response distribution (Section 4.1, Equation 5).

kHInw3cjCP.text: Balanced LoRA (BaLoRA) enforces the balanced-manifold constraint A^T A = BB^T after each optimizer step via a lightweight polar-decomposition/SVD-based projection with complexity O((a+b)r^2), while preserving the product AB (Algorithm 1, Section 2).

Proposition 2.4 shows balanced minimizers achieve the minimal condition number kappa_min = 2*sigma_1(Z)/sigma_r(Z) among all minimizers of the matrix factorization objective, and Proposition 2.1 shows the asymptotic convergence rate is bounded by ((kappa-1)/(kappa+1))^2, so lower condition number yields faster convergence (Propositions 2.1, 2.4).
On Qwen-2.5-3B fine-tuning across five datasets, BaLoRA and the comparable balanced method RefLoRA substantially outperform DoRA, LoRA-RITE, LORO, and OLoRA (Table 1).
In the rank ablation on DeepMind Mathematics, BaLoRA outperforms standard LoRA most at higher ranks, reaching a final training loss of 1.014 at rank 128 versus 1.030 for LoRA (Table 2).
BaLoRA adds negligible memory overhead relative to standard LoRA despite the added projection step (Table 6).
Proposition 3.1 shows BaLoRA gradient descent implements Riemannian gradient descent on the manifold of rank-r matrices under the Bures metric (Proposition 3.1).

2CQkqiZ6p9.text: Gaussian Quant (GQ) converts a pretrained Gaussian VAE into a VQ-VAE training-free by generating a random Gaussian-noise codebook and quantizing posterior means to the nearest codebook entry (Section on method).

Theorem 1 proves the quantization error probability decays doubly exponentially once the codebook bitrate log K exceeds the VAE's bits-back coding rate by t nats, while Theorem 2 proves the error probability grows exponentially when the bitrate falls below that rate (Theorems 1, 2).

On ImageNet at 0.25 bits per pixel with a UNet architecture, GQ achieves rFID 0.529, PSNR 27.61, LPIPS 0.059, and SSIM 0.807, outperforming VQGAN (rFID 5.714), FSQ (rFID 1.125), LFQ (rFID 16.337), and BSQ (rFID 1.080) (Table with UNet ImageNet 0.25bpp results).

The Target Divergence Constraint (TDC), which enforces consistent per-dimension KL divergence via dimension-specific penalty weights lambda_min, lambda_mean, lambda_max, improves TokenBridge's PSNR from 28.24 dB to 31.67 dB at 1.00 bits per pixel (Section on TDC applied to TokenBridge).

1NACQKPp1n.text: G^2-Reader maintains an evolving Content Graph, whose nodes are atomic information units such as paragraphs and table/figure-caption pairs, refined over 3 rounds of VLM-driven iteration that update node summaries, keywords, and topology (Section on Content Graph).

G^2-Reader maintains a separate Planning Graph, a directed acyclic graph of sub-questions executed via topological ordering, that tracks intermediate findings and is dynamically refined based on evidence-sufficiency checks, with 3 iterations found to be optimal before diminishing returns (Section on Planning Graph).
G^2-Reader with Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct reaches 66.21% average accuracy on VisDoMBench, outperforming standalone GPT-5 (53.08%) by 13.13 percentage points (Table of VisDoMBench results).
On VisDoMBench domain breakdown, G^2-Reader scores 66.89% on FetaTab, 72.31% on SlideVQA, 57.10% on PaperTab, 73.19% on SPIQA, and 61.56% on SciGraphQA (Table of per-domain results).

An ablation shows the Content Graph and Planning Graph are complementary: combining both graphs yields a +4.8% accuracy gain that exceeds the sum of each graph's individual gain, and structured retrieval at k=5 outperforms vanilla RAG at k=20 (Ablation section).
A lightweight rule-based variant of G^2-Reader achieves 67.0% accuracy versus 68.0% for the full model while reducing token usage by 78.3% (Ablation section).

hx2U1OllHD.text: AReaL-DTA performs dynamic depth-first-search traversal of the rollout prefix tree during both forward and backward computation, materializing only a single root-to-leaf path in memory at a time, so memory scales with the longest sequence path rather than total tree tokens (Method section).
AReaL-DTA achieves up to 8.31x higher single-worker training throughput on the tau^2-bench RL post-training benchmark compared to the baseline (Experiments, tau^2-bench results).
Across the full training cluster, AReaL-DTA achieves a 6.20x throughput speedup, and end-to-end pipeline throughput improves 2.28x on an 8B-parameter model (Experiments section).
AReaL-DTA reduces peak GPU memory consumption by over 50% relative to the baseline and eliminates the need for activation checkpointing on models with 4B+ parameters (Experiments/Memory results).
An ablation disabling the binary-search-based load-balancing partitioning algorithm for distributed batching causes an 11.93% performance degradation (Ablation section).

IPp3LD6u16.text: Theorem 3.3 shows the ideal conditional velocity field in flow matching equals -1/(2t(1-t)) times the gradient of dist^2(x, sigma) - (1-t)||x||^2, connecting classifier-free guidance to gradients of smoothed distance functions toward a scaled target image set (Theorem 3.3).

Theorem 3.4 decomposes the CFG approximation error into an unavoidable model-error term and a term proportional to the squared prediction gap between conditional and unconditional velocity outputs (Theorem 3.4).

CFG-MP reformulates guided sampling as constrained homotopy optimization with manifold projection onto M_t = {z : v_theta(t,z,y) = v_theta(t,z, empty)}, and CFG-MP+ accelerates convergence of the iterative projection using Anderson Acceleration without requiring additional model evaluations beyond CFG-MP (Method/Section on CFG-MP and CFG-MP+).

On DiT-XL-2 at 256x256 on ImageNet, CFG-MP+ achieves an Inception Score of 86.26 at guidance scale omega=2.0 and NFE=120, a 14.78-point improvement over the standard CFG baseline (Experiments, DiT-XL-2-256 results).

On text-to-image generation with SD3.5 and Flux-dev, CFG-MP+ achieves a 61.41% overall GenEval score versus 58.36% for vanilla CFG, with consistent gains on HPSv2, ImageReward, PickScore, and CLIP metrics (Table 2).

An ablation over the fixed-point iteration count K, Anderson Acceleration damping factor beta, and window size m finds K=2 balances quality and efficiency, beta in {0.5, 1.0} yields peak performance, and window size m=1 is recommended for computational efficiency (Figures 5-6, Ablation section).

xTkYT79CRB.text: The paper identifies a 'Logit-Attention Divergence' phenomenon in which internal attention weights correctly peak at the relevant image while output logits are biased toward an unrelated position (Section 3.2, Figure 3).
On MS-COCO-based multi-image retrieval with N=4 candidates in the random setting, the proposed calibration method reaches 98.66% accuracy versus 67.52% for the vanilla baseline (Table 1).
On the adversarial setting (CLIP-based hard negatives, N=4), the method achieves 71.06% accuracy compared to 49.56% for the vanilla baseline (Table 1).
The counterfactual calibration procedure requires only 5 calibration samples per position, with performance plateauing at this sample size (Section 4.2, Figure 6).
An ablation shows that both layer selection and the attention-prior term contribute meaningfully to the overall accuracy gains (Table 4).
Position bias is shown to shift dynamically depending on where the target image is located among the candidates, termed 'Conditional Position Bias' (Section 3.1, Figure 1).

5785emCgS1.text: Asymmetric Equilibrium Propagation (AEP) extends Equilibrium Propagation to non-conservative systems while preserving the existence of stationary states used for both inference and learning (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
On MNIST with symmetric initialization, AEP reaches 93.8±0.4% accuracy, matching or exceeding the Vector Field (VF) baseline while learning faster over the first 20 epochs (Section 5.1, Figure 1).
At a fixed high asymmetry ratio of r=0.875, AEP maintains 94.9±0.2% accuracy, whereas the VF baseline collapses to 8±4% under complete antisymmetry (Section 5.2, Figure 3).
In a feed-forward architecture where VF can only train the output layer, VF attains 64.3±2.0% accuracy while AEP, which trains all parameters, reaches 92.7±0.5% (Section 5.3).
Dyadic EP (Algorithm 2) is introduced as a second, related construction for non-conservative dynamics alongside Asymmetric EP (Section 4).

eTUljZ6e8c.text: Theorem 1 proves that any quantum-inspired classical (QIC) algorithm for solving well-conditioned, sparse linear systems requires Ω(n^{1/12}) queries, while the corresponding quantum algorithm runs in poly(ln n) time, establishing the first exponential separation between the two (Theorem 1).
The quantum upper bound for sparse linear systems scales as poly(s, κ, ln(1/ε), ln n), where s is sparsity and κ is the condition number (Equation 1).
The proof reduces hardness of the QIC lower bound to a random walk oracle game on two binary trees, building on the construction of Childs et al. (Theorem 2, Section 2.1).

Lemma 2 shows the solution component corresponding to the target root vertex satisfies x_i^2 = Ω(n^{-5}||x||^2), which is what enables efficient quantum sampling but not efficient QIC sampling (Lemma 2).

The result demonstrates that quantum machine learning speedups on natural tasks are not universally reproducible by quantum-inspired classical algorithms, resolving an open question in the dequantization literature (Section 1).

X5WB8jH0hy.text: GEPC detects out-of-distribution inputs by measuring equivariance-breaking in diffusion model scores under group transformations, formalized via Propositions 4.2-4.3 (Section 4).
Across nine canonical ID/OOD benchmark pairs at 32x32 resolution, GEPC achieves an average AUROC of 0.908, matching or improving on recent diffusion-based OOD baselines (Table 1).
GEPC attains near-perfect AUROC on several pairs, including 0.999 for CIFAR-10 to CelebA, 1.00 for SVHN to CelebA, and 1.00 for CelebA to CIFAR-100 (Table 1).
GEPC is computationally lightweight, requiring 16 forward passes and zero Jacobian evaluations per input (Table 1).
GEPC is qualitatively validated on HRSID SAR imagery, where equivariance-breaking maps highlight anomalous regions (Section 6, Figure 2).

P9LofJB8fs.text: The proposed Gromov-Wasserstein solver achieves O(ND+ME) memory footprint and O(N^2 D + M^2 E + NM*n_inner*n_outer) time complexity, i.e., linear memory and quadratic (rather than cubic) time in the number of points (Section 5).
On the FAUST dataset with 177k points, the MsGW solver converges in 355 seconds, while competing methods such as EGW and LrGW run out of memory beyond N=10k points (Table 1).
Theorem 3.4 provides a dual formulation reducing the Gromov-Wasserstein problem to a standard optimal transport coupling under squared Euclidean distance in a lifted feature space (Theorem 3.4).
Theorem 4.6 establishes convergence guarantees showing every subsequential limit of the algorithm's iterates is a critical point with monotonically decreasing loss (Theorem 4.6).
Theorem 4.2 proves non-negativity of the debiased Sinkhorn Gromov-Wasserstein divergence, SGW_epsilon(alpha,beta) >= 0, for CNT costs, enabling its use in variational optimization (Theorem 4.2).
The solver is differentiable and supports gradient-based optimization, with implementation details for CNT costs beyond squared norms such as tree distances and geodesics (Section B.6).

lGBJm8TGun.text: CURVE separates latent factors into invariant causal components z_c and spurious environment-dependent components z_s and uses K=32 learnable prototypes with an uncertainty-gated residual correction to approximate the continuous environment space (Section 3.1, Section 3.3).

On the generalization and topology benchmark, CURVE reaches 92.92% ID accuracy and 68.13% OOD accuracy with an average node degree of only 5.78 (44.80 edges), versus RS2G's 90.77% ID / 64.84% OOD accuracy with an average degree of 75.92 (611.25 edges) (Table 1).
Removing the causal intervention component drops OOD MCC from 35.07 to 25.77, and removing the uncertainty weighting increases average scene-graph degree from 5.78 to 76.61 (Table 2).

In CARLA-to-DoTA sim-to-real transfer, CURVE achieves 58.5% zero-shot AUC and 63.72% AUC after fine-tuning on just 5% real-world labels, approaching the 65.5% AUC oracle trained with full real-world labels (Figure 3(e)).

CURVE shows clear separation in predicted uncertainty between correct and incorrect predictions in both in-distribution and zero-shot out-of-distribution settings, and remains robust under input noise of σ=0.05 (Figure 5).

btN3w8aJfo.text: SemBD (Semantic-level Backdoor) defines triggers as continuous semantic regions—parameterized by subject, action, object, and scene—instantiated via semantically equivalent paraphrased prompts, rather than fixed discrete textual patterns (Section 4.1).
SemBD is evaluated against Stable Diffusion v1.5 and SDXL and achieves a 100% attack success rate while preserving benign-prompt utility (Table 1, Section 5.1).
SemBD evades state-of-the-art input-level defenses, reducing their detection success rate to 12.00% for NaviT2I, 20.05% for UFID, 25.80% for T2IShield_FTT, and 2.00% for T2IShield_CDA (Section 5).

The attack pipeline combines semantic trigger construction via paraphrases, regularization against incomplete semantic activation, multi-entity target prompts for diverse cross-attention patterns, and distillation-based injection into cross-attention projections (Figure 3).

Under fine-tuning-based defenses, SemBD's backdoor remains effective, maintaining an attack success rate consistently above 90% with only minor degradation in semantic alignment (Figure 13, Section 5.5).

IAE5vKJUeY.text: With soft-label evaluation, distillation methods provide diminishing value over a random-subset baseline at large IPC: at IPC-50, random-subset achieves 57.2% while distillation methods range from 52.6% to 58.5% (Table 4).

With hard labels only, performance collapses without soft-label supervision: SRe2L drops from 33.5% (soft label) to 1.5% (hard label) at IPC-10, whereas the proposed PCA framework reaches 22.8% at IPC-10 with hard labels, 18.2 points above the random baseline (Table 5, Table 7).

The PCA (Prune, Combine, Augment) framework is optimization-free: it prunes via a reverse EL2N metric under class balance (Section 4.1), combines complete images rather than cropped patches based on Theorem 4.2's entropy argument (Section 4.2), and applies scaling-law-aware augmentation via Cutout, which achieves 26.2% at IPC-10 (Section 4.3, Table 12).
Ablation on ResNet-18 at IPC-10 with hard labels shows progressive gains: random baseline 4.6%, +pruning 12.2%, +combine 14.4%, +augment (full PCA) 22.8% (Table 7).

PCA generalizes across architectures at IPC-10 with hard labels: 22.8% on ResNet-18, 23.0% on ResNet-50, 25.0% on EfficientNet-B0, but only 15.3% on Swin-V2-Tiny, indicating transformer underperformance (Table 8).
At IPC-100, PCA with only hard labels achieves 48.8% accuracy, comparable to soft-label distillation methods (46.7-47.2%) while requiring over 300x less storage (Table 9).

Rem0zhold7.text: SimpliPy achieves roughly 100x speedup over SymPy for symbolic expression simplification, reducing median simplification time from about 100ms (SymPy) to the low-to-moderate millisecond regime at recursion depth Lmax=4, while matching SymPy's simplification ratio quality at Lmax>=5 (Section 5.2, Figure 4).
SymPy paradoxically increases expression length for 38-52% of simplification cases, a failure mode SimpliPy is designed to avoid (Section 5.2).

On the FastSRB benchmark's time-normalized validation numeric recovery rate (vNRR), the amortized baselines NeSymReS and E2E saturate at about 10% and below 2.5% recovery respectively, while the genetic-programming baseline PySR reaches about 50% at medium compute budgets (Section 5.1, Figure 2).

Flash-ANSR (120M parameter model) reaches 55.8% vNRR on FastSRB, surpassing PySR's roughly 50%, while its expression-length ratio converges toward the ground-truth length (e.g., 1.40 to 1.27) as compute budget increases, in contrast to PySR's increasing complexity (0.94 to 1.85) (Section 5.1, Figure 2).

Flash-ANSR outperforms PySR in the dense-data regime (M>64 points) and identifies a complexity peak around M≈8 consistent with double-descent phenomena, while PySR is more robust than Flash-ANSR at higher noise levels (η greater than 10^-2) (Section 5.3, Section 5.4, Figures 5-6).

Yp5QTlSJJl.text: Theorem 3.4 shows that small logit distance implies high linear representational similarity, yielding an explicit lower bound on mean Canonical Correlation Analysis (mCCA) between two models' representation spaces (Section 3.2).

Theorem 3.9 shows logit distance upper-bounds the linear identifiability dissimilarity measure d_rep (defined in Definition 3.7), and Corollary 3.8 shows logit distance is zero if and only if this dissimilarity vanishes (Section 3.3-3.4).
Theorem 3.3 shows KL divergence also bounds logit distance under a τ-lower-boundedness assumption, but the bound scales as τ^-1 and becomes practically vacuous for typical models (Section 3.1).

On the Synth, CIFAR, and SUB distillation benchmarks, students trained with an L1/L2 logit-distance loss reduce d_rep by one to three orders of magnitude versus KL-distilled students, and improve mCCA by 0.42 on Synth, 0.25 on CIFAR, and 0.20 on SUB (Table 1, Table 2).
On the SUB dataset, L1-logit-distilled students achieve 75% concept classification accuracy versus 6% for KL-distilled students (Section 5.1-5.2).

On a synthetic embedding visualization, the L1-distilled student preserves teacher geometry (d_rep≈1.3, mCCA≈0.99) while the KL-distilled student loses class structure (d_rep≈6.9, mCCA≈0.62) (Figure 2).

E9QkGczNUw.text: In finite unichain Markov decision contests, there exists a randomized stationary policy that is optimal under the average-preference-margin criterion, so stationary Markov policies suffice against history-dependent policies (Theorem 5.6, Section 5.2).

Finding the optimal policy in a Markov decision contest is solvable in time polynomial in |S||A| via a linear program with |S||A|+|S|+1 variables and 2|S||A|+|S|+1 constraints, placing the problem in P (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).
Hedged Policy Iteration's optimality gap decreases at rate O(1/sqrt(K)) after K iterations, bounded by 4 M_max tau sqrt(log|A|/K), independent of the state-space size |S| (Theorem 7.5, Section 7.3).

HPI and HPI-Clip outperform SPPO on 12 of 13 MuJoCo tasks, spanning 11 reward-based tasks (Mujoco-v5 Suite) and 2 non-transitive preference tasks (Mujoco-NT), as measured by area-under-curve of learning performance (Section 8, Figure 1).
Ablations with learned (rather than oracle) preference models confirm that HPI's performance gains over PPO/SPPO persist (Appendix A.3-A.4).

ZcnZ6vs4yX.text: DistIRL jointly models a distribution over reward functions and the full return distribution by combining a First-Order Stochastic Dominance (FSD) learning objective with quantile-regression critics and distortion risk measures for policy optimization (Definition 4.1, Section 4, Algorithm 1).

On the Risk-Sensitive D4RL benchmark, DistIRL attains 3469±59 return on HalfCheetah, 886±1 on Hopper, and 1526±148 on Walker2D, compared to ValueDICE's 1259±78, 260±10, and 798±311 respectively (Table 2).
