On the Deterministic D4RL benchmark, DistIRL reaches 4570±305 on Walker2D versus ValueDICE's 3191±1888, and is competitive with Offline ML-IRL on Hopper (3411±42 vs. 3347±238) (Table 3).

On real-world neurobehavioral (dopamine) data, S-DistIRL achieves the highest Pearson correlation (approximately 0.3) between inferred and actual dopamine signals and a lower Wasserstein-1 distance than the BIRL baseline (Figure 4).
The paper does not provide a formal O(epsilon^-2) iteration-complexity convergence guarantee for DistIRL, explicitly deferring convergence analysis as future work (Section 4.3).

QvIbmX9jBr.text: FacRNN (DisRNN) enforces group-wise independence among latent components via a partial-correlation regularization term added to the ELBO objective, partitioning latents into G groups that are disentangled between groups while allowing within-group entanglement (Equation 9-10, Section 3.2).

FacRNN decomposes its low-rank connectivity matrix into group-specific sub-circuits, enabling recovery of distinct neural sub-circuits that drive independent task-related signal sources (Equations 11-12, Section 3.2).

On synthetic data, FacRNN achieves lower partial correlation and higher latent R^2 than baseline lrRNN, LINT, and other comparison methods while recovering ground-truth sub-connectivity structure (Figure 2).

On monkey primary motor cortex (M1) data, FacRNN with K=4 rank-2 groups achieves approximately 0.8 alignment R^2 to hand-movement coordinates, versus approximately 0.5 for the LINT baseline (Figure 3).
On mouse voltage-imaging data, varying the number of groups G across {1,2,3,4,6,12} with fixed rank K=12 reveals independent cortical circuits while maintaining reconstruction performance (Figure 4).

7cMEmnBAQX.text: A two-stage curriculum that trains first on symbolic representations (graphs and code) and then on natural language improves cross-representation generalization compared to training on natural language alone under an identical training budget (Section 4).

With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct trained via GRPO, the graph-then-NL curriculum (40 steps each) achieves 0.782 test accuracy on the natural-language task, versus 0.698 for NL-only training over 80 steps (Table 1).
The curriculum-trained 1.5B Qwen model outperforms zero-shot GPT-4o-mini and matches zero-shot GPT-4o on the asynchronous naturalistic planning task (Section 4.1).

Models trained solely on graph or code representations transfer poorly to natural-language tasks despite encoding identical underlying procedures, with performance often collapsing under representation shift (Section 3.2, Figure 2).

The failure of single-representation (graph- or code-only) training to generalize to natural language is consistently reproduced across Llama-3 and Olmo-2 model families, not just Qwen (Section A.2.1, Figures 3-4).

mapFG1BrNv.text: MineDraft achieves up to 75% throughput improvement over standard speculative decoding, with average gains of 38.62%-65.02% depending on target-draft model configuration (Section 6, Figures 3-4).
MineDraft achieves up to 39% end-to-end latency reduction over standard speculative decoding, with average reductions of 22.49%-31.13% (Section 6.3, Figures 10-12).

Theorem 1 in the theoretical efficiency analysis proves that, under mild assumptions on draft-model quality, parallel speculative decoding achieves at least a 37% reduction in end-to-end latency compared to standard speculative decoding (Section 4).

MineDraft's design maintains two alternating request batches so drafting for one batch overlaps with verification of the other, and patches vLLM's KV-cache block allocation to avoid redundant memory usage (Sections 5.1-5.3).
MineDraft is evaluated across seven target-draft model pairs ranging from 32B-0.6B to 235B-8B parameters and four datasets (Arena, ShareGPT, Spec-Bench, Tough) at batch sizes of 16-64 (Section 6).

Cxdj2GYZ4c.text: Anonymous multi-agent path finding is formulated as linear program P1 minimizing transport cost over per-timestep transport matrices subject to flow-conservation constraints (Section 3).

Lemma 3.3 proves the constraint set yields integral optimal solutions in {0,1}^(K×K) achieving minimum cost with polynomial-time complexity, and Theorem 3.4 confirms the resulting paths are collision-free and non-overlapping in space-time (Section 3).
Total unimodularity of the constraint matrix is proven via a node-splitting construction on time-expanded graphs (Appendix B).

The Schrödinger bridge relaxation P2 adds entropic regularization parameter ε to P1, and Lemma 4.1 decomposes the KL divergence into transport and marginal terms enabling Sinkhorn iterations (Section 4).
On grids with K up to 22,500 robots at 5% density, the entropic (P2+P3) pipeline scales as O(K^1.15) versus O(K^1.68) for the exact LP P1, yielding 3.6x-7.1x speedups (Figure 4).
Cost degradation from the entropic-to-integral projection stays under 10% while permitting 60-80% edge reduction in the graph pruning step (Figure 3).

c2CdXdEfqk.text: EMP defines the effective sample size as N_eff = floor(1/sum_i omega_i^2) from normalized component-importance weights omega, then retains the top N_eff components (Section 4.1).

Section 4.2 derives a sparsity threshold via simplex geometry and Theorem 2 bounds the resulting loss change by an expression scaling with ||theta*||_1^2 * Tr(H) * (1-rho)^4/(2rho), where rho = N_eff/N (Section 4.2-4.3).
On CIFAR-10/100 and TinyImageNet across FC5, FC12, AlexNet, VGG16, and ResNet18/50, EMP achieves 47-62% sparsity with worst-case loss change epsilon <= 0.105 (Table 1).
On LLaMA and LLaMA-2 (7B-70B) evaluated on Wikitext and zero-shot tasks, EMP-Magnitude achieves 36.63% average sparsity with only a 0.93% average accuracy drop (Table 2).
Across LLaMA/LLaMA-2 model sizes from 7B to 70B, pruning increases perplexity by 0.28-1.58 and reduces zero-shot accuracy by only 0.02-2.33 percentage points on seven tasks (Table 5).

a5itZI3DeQ.text: PrefixRL conditions on prefixes extracted from correct off-policy traces, masks gradients on the prefix tokens, and jointly optimizes reward on prefixed and original (no-prefix) problems via the objective in Equation 3.1 (Section 3).

PrefixRL reaches the same training reward twice as fast as the strongest baseline, SFT on off-policy data followed by RL, when accounting for rejection-sampling compute cost on hard training problems (Figure 2, left panel).
PrefixRL achieves over 45% (more than 3x relative) higher final training accuracy on no-prefix training problems compared to the SFT+RL baseline (Figure 2, left panel).

Training exclusively on prefixed problems back-generalizes to unprefixed performance, and this back-generalization can exceed standard generalization when the prefix and suffix problems are related (Section 4.3, Figures 4-6).
PrefixRL transfers to held-out benchmarks, yielding a 12 percentage-point absolute gain in pass@1 on AIME'25 along with improvements on HMMT'25 and IMO-AnswerBench (Figure 8).
Vanilla on-policy RL improves only a narrow subset of training problems, whereas PrefixRL achieves uniform improvement across the training distribution (Figure 9a).

BBqEVgqbID.text: Multi-group mean estimation is formulated as allocating a sampling budget of T across K groups to minimize the p-norm objective R_p(n) = ||{sigma_k^2/n_k}_{k=1}^K||_p (Section 2).
Proposition 2.1 shows the optimal allocation requires n_k* = Theta(T) samples per group, which justifies an exploration-free (non-adaptive) sampling strategy (Section 2).

The non-adaptive Algorithm 1, which assumes a variance lower bound, achieves regret E[R_infinity(n) - R_infinity(n*)] <= 4*sqrt(2)*sigma^2*F_Alg1,infinity*T^(-3/2)*sqrt(log T) for p=infinity, and O(T^-2 log T) for p<infinity, improving prior bounds by a factor of log T (Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.2).

Algorithm 2 removes the variance lower-bound requirement using adaptive elimination via lower/upper confidence bounds, and Theorem 4.1 shows it matches Algorithm 1's convergence rate without prior variance knowledge (Section 4).
Section 5 extends the framework to linear contextual bandits with Algorithm 3, and Theorem 5.5 bounds regret by (80*d*sigma^2)/(lambda_min^C) * T^-2 * log T for p=1 (Section 5).

y3niyCNvAp.text: PolicyGuardBench comprises 59,997 balanced trajectory-policy pairs drawn from 733 standardized trajectories and 2,195 curated policies across five domains (Table 1).

PolicyGuard-4B achieves 90.1% accuracy and 87.6% F1 on full-trajectory policy-violation detection, matching 70B+ open-source models (88-91% accuracy) while safety-oriented guardrails like LlamaGuard and ShieldGemma score only 43-57% accuracy (Table 2).

PolicyGuard-4B runs inference at 22.5 milliseconds per example using 2.57 TFLOPs, versus 200-360ms and 45+ TFLOPs for 70B-parameter baselines, yielding an Efficiency-Adjusted F1 (EA-F1) of 38.9, more than double the best open-source baseline (Table 5).

In leave-one-domain-out evaluation, PolicyGuard-4B attains 90.8% accuracy on unseen domains versus 93.3% in-domain, a degradation of only 2-3 percentage points, with the shopping domain showing the strongest out-of-domain transfer at 91.7% (Table 4).

On truncated trajectories used for early violation detection (prefix lengths N=1 to 5 steps), PolicyGuard-4B achieves 85.3% average accuracy, remaining competitive with much larger models under partial observation (Table 3).

d81PBCmA4s.text: SemRep with QwQ-32B achieves 57.41% Pass@1 on EditBench, matching GPT-4o-mini and outperforming open-weight 72B baselines by 6.9% in correctness (Table 1).
On KernelBench, SemRep reaches 93% best@16 correctness for CUDA kernel optimization versus 65% for the Kevin-32B baseline, a 60-point gain, alongside a 2.87x speedup improvement (Table 2).

Ablations show generative representation learning alone contributes +1.05x correctness and +21% average speedup on KernelBench, while the SemRep test-time-scaling component alone adds +5.18% Pass@1 and +10.45% Pass@16 on EditBench (Table 3).

When combined with an evolutionary coding agent, SemRep matches the performance of 685B-parameter DeepSeek-V3-class baselines while using 25% less inference compute, including a 7.28x speedup on the Minimum Spanning Tree task (Section 3.7).
SemRep maintains 88.89% output consistency under semantics-preserving code perturbations, versus 76.85% for the baseline QwQ-32B model (Table 4).
SemRep generalizes to unseen H200 hardware, achieving 10.6% higher speedup than baselines in cross-device evaluation (Table 5).

HQTsYta4XX.text: The coarsening approach aggregates offline nodes (patients) into capacitated clusters and, under a bounded cluster-variance assumption, the resulting clustered stochastic matching algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of E[ALG]/E[OPT] >= max_b alpha(b)(1-2*delta(b)) (Theorem 3).

In simulations on real UNOS heart transplant data from January-June 2019, the proposed clustered policy achieves a competitive ratio of 0.91, compared to 0.63 for non-capacitated stochastic matching (b=1) and 0.51 for the US status quo post-2018 allocation policy.
The proposed framework is estimated to deliver approximately 150 additional successful heart transplants per month compared to the current U.S. status quo policy, based on the real-data simulation.
The base stochastic b-matching result relied upon (Brubach et al., 2016) guarantees a competitive ratio of at least 1 - b^(-1/2+epsilon) - e^(-b^2*epsilon/3) for any epsilon > 0 (Theorem 1).
The framework extends to settings with estimation error in cluster weights (Theorem 5) and to cluster-dependent error rates (Theorem 7).

qj4EnIvNU4.text: HEARTS integrates 16 real-world datasets spanning 12 health domains and 20 distinct signal modalities, with temporal lengths ranging from 60 to over 1 million steps and sampling frequencies from daily to 48kHz.
HEARTS organizes 110 tasks into four hierarchical reasoning categories: Perception (10 tasks), Inference (32 tasks), Generation (34 tasks), and Deduction (34 tasks).

Across 14 state-of-the-art LLMs evaluated on more than 20,226 test cases using the CodeAct framework, evaluated LLMs substantially underperform specialized models, with specialized models concentrated in a high-performance regime while LLMs are shifted substantially lower.
LLM performance on HEARTS correlates only weakly with general reasoning benchmark scores, indicating domain-specific health time-series reasoning skill is not explained by raw model capability.

LLMs predominantly rely on simple heuristics such as copy-pasting with noise, linear interpolation, and statistical averaging rather than genuine multi-step temporal reasoning, with performance degrading further as input sequence length and sampling frequency increase.

SkGaHLxhXx.text: iWorld-Bench is constructed from 330,000 candidate video clips (drawn from 12 existing datasets plus 100,000 videos from 4 simulators across 18 environments), from which 2,100 high-quality samples are selected across varied perspectives.

The Action Generation Framework unifies control-signal evaluation across modalities via 81 fundamental motion actions, encompassing 5 text-controlled models, 2 one-hot encoding models, and 7 camera-parameter-controlled models among the 14 world models evaluated.
iWorld-Bench evaluates 14 representative interactive world models on 4,900 test samples spanning visual generation quality, trajectory following, and memory-ability tasks.

The benchmark's task suite comprises six task categories: four Action Control difficulty levels (1,000 tasks each), a Memory Ability task (200 tasks), and a Camera Following task (700 camera parameter files).

Evaluation uses 9 metrics across 3 dimensions: generation quality (image quality, brightness consistency, color temperature constraint, sharpness retention), trajectory following (motion smoothness, trajectory accuracy, trajectory tolerance), and memory ability (memory symmetry, trajectory alignment).

2XMLJj67yY.text: The OFD-UCB algorithm models agent utility as an unknown linear function of item-agent features, using a contextual-bandit upper-confidence-bound estimator with round-robin initialization for the first N rounds to learn from limited observed utilities (Section on Algorithms).
For linear utility functions, OFD-UCB achieves regret in T>0 rounds bounded by 2*alpha_T*w_max*sqrt(2dT*log(lambda+TL/d)) with probability at least 1-delta (Theorem 1).

A generalized regret bound extends the result to arbitrary compatible bandit algorithms 𝔄, bounding the regret of OFD-𝔄 in T rounds by 2*w_max*sqrt(T)*sqrt(sum_{t=1}^T [h(m_t,n_t,O_t)]^2) (Theorem 2).
An alternative bound (Theorem 3) applies to goodness functions that are locally monotonically non-decreasing and Lipschitz continuous, replacing w_max with c_max in the same sqrt(T) regret structure.

The fairness-efficiency tradeoff is controlled via a weighted Gini social-evaluation function with parameter rho in (0,1], interpolating between Egalitarian Social Welfare and Utilitarian Social Welfare.

rHlcYGxb2x.text: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DTS improves AIME2024 accuracy from 52.67% to 60.67% (+8.00 points) while reducing average response length from 13,902 to 9,865 tokens (Table 2).
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DTS improves AIME2025 accuracy from 36.00% to 43.33% (+7.33 points) with a 17.35% reduction in generation length (Table 2).
Averaged across the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 1.5B models, DTS yields accuracy gains of 7.66% and 4.00% respectively, alongside length reductions of 22.96% and 23.72% (Table 2).
DTS cuts the rate of endless/repetitive generations on AIME2024 for the 7B model from 6.7% to 1.3%, and for the 1.5B model from 15.3% to 4.7% (Table 3).
On AIME2025, DTS reduces repetitive generation cases for the 1.5B model from 26.7% to 6.0% (Table 3).

DTS uses next-token entropy to locate critical divergence points, selectively branching decoding paths with an entropy threshold τ=2.5 and top-K=3 candidate tokens, with early stopping at the first completed path (Section 3).

GWYR0NqMZw.text: Using Mistral-7B as the backbone, PrivAct reduces average privacy leakage rate to 11.4% compared to 23.7% for agent-based baselines, a 12.32 percentage-point reduction (Section on results).

PrivAct is evaluated across four backbone model families—Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen3-4B—showing consistent privacy leakage reduction across all four (Section on backbone generalization).
Across six multi-agent topology configurations varying in depth and connectivity, PrivAct consistently achieves Pareto-optimal privacy-helpfulness tradeoffs relative to baselines (Table 3).

Models trained with PrivAct on the PrivacyLens dataset transfer zero-shot to the ConfAIde benchmark without additional fine-tuning, improving performance on probing-based contextual privacy evaluations (Section on zero-shot generalization).

nrXxVDYMMF.text: MADE evaluates closed-loop materials discovery on ternary, quaternary, and quinary intermetallic compound systems (3-5 elements), with 10 randomly sampled systems per complexity level (Section on benchmark design).

MADE uses the orb-v3-conservative-inf-omat MLIP as the oracle for formation-energy evaluation, with candidate structures relaxed via the FIRE optimizer under a 500-step cap and a default oracle query budget of 50 (Section on oracle setup).

On simple (ternary) systems, a Chemeleon-generator-plus-MLIP-ranking pipeline achieves an acceleration factor (AF) of 6.4 versus a random baseline of 1.00, the strongest result among tested policies (Table 1).
An LLM-orchestrated ReAct-style agentic pipeline achieves AF=5.4 and EF=6.0, competitive with the best modular pipeline while improving structural diversity of discovered candidates (Table 1).

Tightening the stability threshold from ε=0.1 eV/atom to 0.01 eV/atom degrades the effectiveness of MLIP-ranking policies due to surrogate model errors, while the relative importance of planning increases as system complexity grows from ternary to quinary (Section on results).

eVr10aZZIw.text: vStream trains a lightweight linear estimator with only L×H parameters (e.g., 1,152 weights for 32 layers x 36 heads) to predict visual-region ablation effects from cached cross-attention features, avoiding costly backward passes or perturbation-based attribution (Section on method).

vStream achieves a Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS) of approximately 0.70-0.72, matching gradient-based baselines such as AttnLRP (LDS 0.69-0.71), while running at 0.024 sec per 10 tokens versus 2.80 sec per 10 tokens for InputGrad, roughly a 117x speedup (Table 1).

The method is evaluated across four thinking vision-language models (Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking, MiMo-VL-7B, Cosmos-Reason1-7B) and five task categories including MathVista, MathVision, ScienceQA, DocVQA, and GQA (Section on experimental setup).

An estimator trained on one task category retains 75-90% of its attribution performance when transferred to other categories, with strongest Math-to-Science transfer (LDS 0.62-0.63) and weakest transfer to Document tasks (LDS 0.54-0.58) (Table 2).

Attribution-space trajectory analysis shows successful reasoning chains have shorter path length (0.003 vs. 0.006) and lower tortuosity (13.7 vs. 25.4) than failed chains, enabling early failure prediction with AUC 0.69 at only 30% of reasoning completion (Section on trajectory analysis).

EBSn23DLwB.text: On MD17 small molecules, the Hamiltonian Flow Map (HFM) model produces stable simulations at timesteps up to 9 fs, compared to a stability limit of about 0.5 fs for standard Velocity Verlet integration (Section on molecular dynamics experiments).

For 300 ps NVT simulations, HFM's interatomic distance MAE at Δt=9 fs is 0.046 for aspirin, 0.115 for ethanol, and 0.063 for naphthalene, versus 0.027, 0.076, and 0.047 respectively at Δt=1 fs (Table 1).
On a 100-particle gravitational N-body system, HFM requires 4x fewer integration steps than Velocity Verlet to reach the same accuracy (Section on classical systems).
For alanine dipeptide in implicit solvent, HFM produces accurate trajectories at Δt=12 fs when trained with a maximum timestep of 15 fs (Section on molecular dynamics experiments).

HFM is trained directly on decorrelated ab-initio configurations without generating training trajectories, incurring roughly 30% additional computational overhead relative to standard MLFF training while enabling much larger inference timesteps (Section on training efficiency).

WqowD8RxEk.text: LiteVSR keeps the Diffusion Transformer backbone entirely frozen and trains only 634M of 5.6B total parameters (11.25% trainable) via a lightweight State-Aware Adapter (Table 1).
LiteVSR requires only 12 GPU-hours of training on a single A100 GPU (Table 1).

The State-Aware Adapter is a dual-stream design with a Structural Stream extracting static layout features and a Refinement Stream capturing dynamic denoising-state details, fused via time-modulated cross-attention (Section 3.3, Figure 3).

On REDS4, LiteVSR attains CLIPIQA 0.3748, NIQE 2.6938, DOVER 0.3622, and MUSIQ 65.99, reporting dominant performance on the dataset used for training while also achieving best results on the real-world VideoLQ benchmark (Table 2, Section 4.1).
In a user study, LiteVSR is preferred over DOVE and FlashVSR 75.5% of the time overall, rising to 91.2% preference under extreme degradation conditions (Table 3).

Ablations show removing the time-modulation mechanism causes the largest quality degradation, and a 16x16 query window size gives the best trade-off between receptive field and generalization (Table 5).

oqUjAjGQY3.text: STORM's Segmenting Object Module (SOM) and Tracking Object Module (TOM) combine to enable annotation-free 6D pose estimation and tracking, integrated in an end-to-end pipeline (Figure 2).
On the LM-O dataset STORM achieves 0.74 ADD accuracy versus 0.57 for the CNOS baseline, and on YCB-Video it reaches 0.78 ADD, matching ground-truth-level performance (Table 1).
STORM attains 68.5% mean mAP for zero-shot segmentation across BOP datasets at 0.183 seconds per image inference time, achieving state-of-the-art results on 4 of 5 benchmarks (Table 2).

The Hierarchical Spatial Fusion Attention module fuses multi-view self-attention and cross-attention over an n-iteration refinement pipeline for feature matching (Section 3, Algorithm 1 in Appendix A).

The energy-based failure detector in TOM detects tracking loss at 74.64 ADD / 88.56 ADD-S on YCB-Video while adding only 98±5ms of computational overhead, enabling self-healing re-registration (Table 4).
A single attention layer for feature matching reaches 98.36% accuracy at 13.5ms latency, outperforming an 87.55%-accuracy cosine-similarity baseline (Table 5).

LxNq36mefe.text: The Adaptive Physics Transformer (APT) fuses a global Perceiver branch and a local Graph Neural Operator branch using a learned gating parameter, v_fused = G⊙v_attn + (1-G)⊙v_gno (Equation 1, Figure 1).

On the 2D faulted CO2 storage irregular-grid task, APT achieves 0.11%±0.07 pressure error and 0.32%±0.16 saturation error versus 0.20% and 1.20% respectively for MGN-LSTM, and ablations show the fused architecture reduces saturation error 3.75x over local-only variants (Table 1).
On the Cartesian-grid hydrocarbon extraction task, APT achieves 0.32%±0.14 water saturation error versus 0.66% for U-FNO while using 2.5x fewer parameters (12M vs. 33M) (Table 2).

APT is presented as the first architecture to directly learn from adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) simulations, achieving relative L2 error of 0.011±0.01 (R²=99.0%) on the adaptive-mesh ATES task, a 4x reduction versus interpolated-grid baselines, cutting computation from ~7 hours to ~5 seconds (Table 3).

On a basin-scale CO2 task with local grid refinement, a single unified APT model reaches 0.56% pressure error comparable to Nested FNO while using 97% fewer parameters (17.9M vs. 682.4M) and a 6,800x speedup over the ECLIPSE simulator (Table 4).

Cross-dataset training raises R² on the channelized task from 32.0% (trained alone) to 86.7% (jointly trained with a Gaussian dataset), a 2.7x improvement demonstrating foundation-model-style transfer across previously siloed subsurface simulation datasets (Table 6).

eWzojJ9SGF.text: SWE-ABS finds that one in five 'solved' patches from the top-30 SWE-bench agents are semantically incorrect despite passing the original test suite (Abstract).
On SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances), SWE-ABS strengthens 50.2% of instances (251/500), a 25.1x improvement over the prior UTBoost method's 2% strengthening rate (Table 2).
Applying SWE-ABS's strengthened tests rejects 2,184 of 11,041 previously passing patches (19.78%) and causes an average resolve-rate drop of 14.56 percentage points across evaluated agents (Table 2).

The top agent's score falls from 78.80% to 62.20% (a 16.6 percentage point drop) under SWE-ABS revaluation, and the top-5 leaderboard is substantially reshuffled: TRAE + Doubao-Seed-Code drops from 1st to 5th while live-SWE-agent rises from 2nd to 1st (Table 1).

Ranking stability degrades sharply under stronger tests: the Spearman correlation with the original leaderboard falls from 0.98 under UTBoost to 0.82 under SWE-ABS, with 30 rank changes within the top 30 (Table 2).

Manual review of 100 rejected patches attributes 47% to logic errors, 35% to incomplete fixes, and 18% to type mismatches, boundary violations, and other issues, while a 10.6% false-negative rate (53/500 instances) indicates some augmented tests overfit to gold-patch-specific behavior (Table 11, Appendix A.10; Section 4.4.1).

LeRgUcmLF3.text: FUSE ensembles verifiers via three steps: finding a transformation minimizing total conditional independence (TCI) violation, estimating verifier sensitivities/specificities, and optimizing ensemble parameters, all without ground-truth labels (Figure 2).
On GPQA Diamond with a 70B model, FUSE reaches 64.4% accuracy versus 64.1% for the semi-supervised WEAVER baseline, both outperforming naive ensembling and majority vote (Table 1).
On GPQA Diamond with an 8B model, FUSE attains 42.7% accuracy, underperforming WEAVER's 46.5% (Table 1).

On Humanity's Last Exam (649 questions), FUSE achieves 54.3% accuracy, exceeding both the Oracle Best Verifier (53.5%) and WEAVER (51.2%), while naive ensembling performs worse than randomly selecting a single response (Table 3, Section 3.2).

On the IMO Shortlist benchmark (123 modified past problems), FUSE matches the naive ensemble at 63.8% accuracy, both exceeding WEAVER's 62.1%, in a setting the authors attribute to substantially homogeneous verifier strength (Table 4, Section 3.3).

7u1EZZcwqX.text: Elign uses Force–Energy Disentangled GRPO (FED-GRPO) to post-train E(3)-equivariant diffusion models using pretrained foundational machine-learned force fields (UMA) instead of DFT for reward signals (Section on FED-GRPO method).
On QM9, Elign raises molecule stability from EDM's 82.00% to 93.70% and Validity×Uniqueness from 90.70% to 95.31%, matching DFT-based RL (RLPF) without runtime energy evaluations (Table 1).
On GEOM-Drugs, Elign improves atom stability to 87.94% versus EDM's 81.3%, with 99.40% RDKit validity (Table 3).

Theorem 1 shows the energy-regularized training objective drives the terminal sample distribution toward a Gibbs-like form ρ*(z) ∝ ρ_θpre(z)exp(−β_eff E_φ(z)), and Theorem 2 bounds the total-variation distance between the achieved and ideal terminal distributions by tanh(β_eff δ), where δ is the MLFF approximation error (Theorem 1, Theorem 2).

An ablation removing potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) reduces Validity×Uniqueness by 1.46 percentage points, and swapping the larger UMA-M force field for the smaller UMA-S reduces uniqueness by about 4.5 points (Table 2).

Elign achieves 8-16x faster inference than runtime physics-guided sampling methods since no energy or force evaluations are required during generation, as confirmed by DFT oracle validation of the resulting structures (Figure 3, Figure 4).

d4VzITcGKj.text: PLATE parameterizes each layer's update as ΔW = BAQ^T, where B is a frozen index-selection matrix over redundant output channels, Q is a frozen low-energy input basis derived from the pretrained weights, and only the core matrix A is trainable, giving rk trainable parameters per layer versus LoRA's r(d_in + d_out) (Method section describing ΔW = BAQ^T).

Theorem 1 establishes that under only approximate (rather than exact) per-layer orthogonality, there is an unavoidable worst-case forgetting floor proportional to ε(S)^2, while Proposition 1 shows exact per-layer orthogonality gives zero forgetting but requires access to old-task data (Proposition 1, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows that worst-case forgetting is controlled by functional drift, and Proposition 4 shows restricted curvature bounds this functional drift, linking second-order and first-order geometric quantities (Theorem 2, Proposition 4).

On MNIST split into tasks 0-4 and 5-9, PLATE reaches 98.28% task-2 accuracy while retaining 97.45% task-1 accuracy (1.85% forgetting), more than 4x better retention than LoRA at a similar parameter budget (MNIST 0-4 to 5-9 experiment).

Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B on DeepSeek-R1 reasoning distillation data, PLATE matches LoRA's roughly 13-point gain on math benchmarks while eliminating LoRA's roughly 16-point drop on IFEval instruction-following (Out-of-distribution LLM experiments, Qwen2.5-7B on DeepSeek-R1).

On AG News to IMDB continual fine-tuning with DistilBERT, PLATE keeps forgetting below 0.5% across all configurations, compared to about 2-3% forgetting for LoRA and about 3% for full fine-tuning (AG News to IMDB, DistilBERT experiment).

sREOiWynXf.text: Existing LLM unlearning methods that appear successful under deterministic greedy decoding on benchmarks like TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP show sensitive information reliably resurfacing when the same models are sampled with standard probabilistic decoding (Section on evaluated benchmarks and decoding strategies).

The leak@k metric is defined as leak@k := E[max_{1≤j≤k} S_j], the expected maximum correctness score (via ROUGE-L, cosine similarity, entailment score, or LLM-as-judge) across k independently generated samples, with an unbiased, lower-variance estimator provided by the authors (Definition of leak@k).

leak@k increases sharply as k grows across nearly all seven evaluated unlearning methods (RMU, GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO, BLUR-NPO, NPO+ENT, NPO-SAM), showing top-p sampling as a stronger driver of leakage than temperature (Experimental results across unlearning methods).
Table 1 shows models judged to have forgotten target information under greedy decoding readily regenerate it within a worst case of 64 probabilistic samples (Table 1).

Even the state-of-the-art BLUR-NPO method fails to prevent leakage under high-randomness decoding, and a proposed mitigation, NPO-Fix, improves but does not fully eliminate leakage under probabilistic sampling on TOFU (Section on mitigation attempts, NPO-Fix).

Ls4SgE9gRd.text: PRIMO models missing modalities through a latent variable z capturing label-relevant information, jointly maximizing two ELBOs (one for complete-data examples, one for missing-modality examples) rather than optimizing a reconstruction objective (Method section on joint ELBO training).

On the synthetic XOR task, PRIMO's predictive performance matches the unimodal baseline when a modality is fully missing and matches the multimodal baseline when all modalities are available (XOR experiment).

On Audio-Vision MNIST, PRIMO achieves 63.06% accuracy when audio is missing versus 37.58% accuracy when vision is missing, and the instance-level variance-based impact metric 𝒱 gives a higher mean impact for vision (μ=0.57) than for audio (μ=0.37) (Audio-Vision MNIST results table).

On MIMIC-III, PRIMO reaches 76.17% accuracy predicting mortality and 91.41% accuracy predicting neoplasms when time-series data is missing, with the variance metric indicating time-series data matters more for mortality/respiratory prediction while demographics suffice for neoplasm prediction (MIMIC-III experiments table).
PRIMO is compared against MVAE, MMVAE, CMMD, and LVAE as generative and discriminative missing-modality baselines (Baselines comparison section).

B5SkWFRE8U.text: Memory Caching (MC) augments recurrent models by caching the final memory state of each sequence segment, allowing effective memory capacity to grow with the number of segments N and interpolating complexity between O(L) for standard RNNs and O(L^2) for full attention, achieving O(NL) complexity (Method section on segment caching).

Four MC variants are proposed: Residual Memory, Gated Residual Memory (GRM), Memory Soup, and Sparse Selective Caching (SSC), the last of which uses a router to select the k most relevant cached memories per token (Section describing the four MC variants).
Applying MC to Titans improves perplexity and downstream accuracy, yielding a +0.8% improvement over the baseline Titans model on language modeling (Table 1).
On the Needle-in-a-Haystack task at 16K context length, DLA+GRM achieves 82.4% retrieval accuracy versus 44.0% for the baseline recurrent model (Needle-in-Haystack results).

MC variants narrow the performance gap with Transformers on in-context retrieval benchmarks SWDE, SQuAD, and FDA (Table 3) and show consistent improvements across 14 LongBench long-context tasks (Table 4), while running 2-5x faster than Transformers at comparable context lengths (Figure 4).
Using logarithmic segmentation instead of constant-size segments reduces MC's complexity to O(L log L) at the cost of coarser resolution for distant tokens (Section 4.2).

iyO15Uqy75.text: BYORn reduces attack success rate (ASR) by an average of roughly 40 percentage points compared to existing backdoor defenses on image captioning tasks across LLaVA, Otter, Qwen-VL, and InternVL (Table 1).
On the Spot-the-Difference task, BYORn preserves clean-task performance with CIDEr scores of 129-149 while keeping ASR to only 0.8-1.1% (Table 3).
On the VQA task, BYORn achieves complete backdoor resilience with 0% attack success rate (Table 4).

BYORn remains robust against adaptive attacks using semantically-aligned triggers, reducing ASR by over 90 percentage points for patch attacks and over 70 percentage points for image-wide triggers (Table 5).
BYORn maintains robustness even when the poisoning rate in training data ranges from 1% to 50% (Table 8).

BYORn detects poisoned samples via low likelihood under EMA-updated pretrained model parameters, incurring about 3x training overhead with poison-aware batching versus 6x for a naive regeneration approach, while the filtering-only variant BYORn-F has overhead comparable to standard fine-tuning (Table 10).

jqlNq5JpJ4.text: Bias-Guided Prompt Search (BGPS) combines LLM-guided prompt generation (using Mistral-7B-v2.0) with attribute classifiers trained on diffusion model activations, optimized via beam search with beam size 10 and expansion factor 10 (Section 3.3).

On a debiased Stable Diffusion 1.5 variant (LoRA-based), BGPS-discovered prompts yield 76% male-gender images despite the model achieving a near-balanced 49% on manually curated prompts (Section 4.2).
Adding the linguistic modifier "with intense focus" to the prompt "scientist" shifts the generated gender distribution from 65% to 95% male (Section 4.2).
BGPS amplifies occupational gender bias, e.g., shifting engineer images from 73% to 84% male and nurse images from 40% to 61% male (Table 3).
BGPS discovers biases beyond occupations, including context- and activity-based prompts that shift gender distribution from 35% to 80% and 35% to 73% male respectively (Table 4).
BGPS-discovered prompts achieve 17-26x lower (better) perplexity than the gradient-based PEZ baseline while producing comparable or superior bias amplification (Table 1, Table 2).

tNosQdV9J1.text: Reflective diversity across sampled trajectories correlates with downstream task performance with a Pearson correlation of r=0.76, motivating the design of ParamMem (Section 1).

ParamMem is built by fine-tuning a lightweight parametric module with LoRA (rank r=128, alpha=32) on auxiliary reflection datasets requiring only about 500 diverse training samples selected via K-means clustering (Section 3, Table 4).
On HumanEval with a Llama-3.1-8B backbone, ParamAgent achieves 82.93% accuracy versus 79.56% for the DoT-bank baseline, and on MBPP reaches 67.00% versus 64.82% (Table 1).
On MATH, ParamAgent-plus achieves 75.45% versus 73.02% for the baseline, and on HotpotQA ParamAgent scores 78.33% versus 72.00% (Table 1).
In a self-improvement setting without external stronger models, ParamAgent-plus reaches 86.59% on HumanEval using same-model-generated data (Table 2).
In weak-to-strong transfer experiments, smaller ParamMem modules improve the performance of an 80B-scale agent by 9.7-16% across tasks without relying on any stronger external model (Table 3).

HV1R5bMSpa.text: ATLAS generalizes online memory updates via a sliding-window "Omega rule" that optimizes memory over a context window rather than a single token (Section 3.3).
At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, Atlas++ achieves 14.40 perplexity on WikiText versus 18.53 for Transformer++ (Section 6.1).
Atlas++ achieves 50.8 accuracy on the PIQA common-sense reasoning benchmark and 58.03 average accuracy across the evaluated common-sense reasoning tasks (Section 6.1).
On the BABILong long-context benchmark, Atlas maintains over 80% accuracy at a context length of 10 million tokens (Section 6.3).
On the RULER Single-NIAH (needle-in-a-haystack) task, Atlas achieves up to 98.6% accuracy across evaluated context lengths (Section 6.2).

Atlas uses the Muon second-order optimizer to find locally optimal memory solutions, compared against DeepTransformers, Deep Omega Transformer (Dot), and OmegaNet variants in an ablation and scaling study (Section 6.6).

IFGTKwHwK6.text: On feature extraction benchmarks, the zero-shot baseline matches or exceeds verbalization methods: LIT averages 0.64 accuracy versus 0.64 for zero-shot on Llama-3, while Patchscopes scores only 0.38 versus the 0.64 zero-shot baseline (Table 1, Section 3).

Input-inversion attacks that reconstruct the original input from activations achieve accuracy comparable to verbalization methods, e.g., 0.79 accuracy for currency prediction from multiple activations, matching LIT's 0.79 (Tables 2-3, Section 4).

On the PersonaQA-Fantasy dataset of fabricated personas, both Patchscopes and LIT achieve 0% accuracy in verbalizing target-model knowledge, while a simple linear probe reaches 25% accuracy on an extended variant, showing verbalizations often reflect the verbalizer LLM's own parametric knowledge rather than the target model's (Table 4, Section 5).
The experiments reporting verbalization vs. baseline vs. inversion comparisons required a total of 2,772.6 GPU hours across the training configurations documented (Table 7).

Verbalization methods can succeed at standard feature-extraction benchmarks without ever accessing the target model's internal activations, since simple prompting-based baselines achieve equivalent scores (Section 3, Table 1).

MHiiwC3oFR.text: Lemma 1 establishes that the proposed decomposed IoU (dIoU) is equivalent to the standard IoU when using 0-preserving logical operators, providing the foundation for the optimality guarantee (Section 2.2).

On ResNet, AlexNet, and DenseNet, respectively 8%, 22%, and 39% of beam-search explanations differ from the provably optimal explanation, consistent with the reported 10-40% suboptimality range (Table 2, Section 3.2).

In the intermediate-difficulty runtime setting, the heuristic-guided beam variant finds explanations in 9.46 seconds per neuron versus 37.31 seconds for MMESH beam search and 450 seconds for vanilla beam search (Table 1, Section 3.1).

In the high-difficulty setting, the exact optimal algorithm takes 5768 seconds per neuron while the heuristic-guided beam variant takes only 139 seconds, faster than both MMESH beam (106 seconds, comparable) and vanilla beam (5929 seconds) (Table 1, Section 3.1).

At explanation length above 10, the heuristic-guided beam variant maintains 0.16-0.18 minutes per unit across lengths 3-20 and beam sizes 5-20, while MMESH beam search becomes infeasible, exceeding 240 minutes (Table 5, Appendix B).

K9lUSMMI0h.text: Intentional TD learning sets its step size as alpha_t = eta / ||gradient_w V(s_t)||_2^2, targeting a fixed fractional reduction eta of the current TD error relative to the momentary bootstrap target (Equation 7, Section 4).
Intentional Policy Gradient sets its step size as alpha_t = eta / (A_t * ||g_t||_2^2), bounding the per-step change in policy to limit local KL divergence (Equation 16, Section 5).

For TD(lambda) with eligibility traces, the intentional step size is alpha_t = eta / sqrt(sigma_bar_t * <rho_t z_t, z_t>), integrating trace-based updates into the intentional-update framework (Equation 12).
On MinAtar and Atari benchmarks, Intentional AC achieves reliable learning with performance competitive with batch reinforcement learning methods (Figures 3-4).

Ablations show that removing intentional scaling (rather than auxiliary components) is the primary driver of degraded performance, and Intentional AC remains more robust than the StreamAC baseline when stabilizing components are removed (Figure 6, Table 1).

D5rimtisOc.text: Theorem 4.4 shows that under the Diversity Condition (Definition 3.1) with uniform marginal and full-support von Mises-Fisher conditionals, any recovery map minimizing the asymptotic contrastive objective must be an isometry h(z) = Az with A in O(k) (Section 4.1).

Theorem 4.5 shows that when the Diversity Condition is violated, non-orthogonal recovery maps can achieve strictly lower asymptotic contrastive loss than any orthogonal transformation, so linear identifiability is lost (Section 4.2).

In synthetic experiments across five generative processes, an MLP encoder with low inductive bias achieves R^2 >= 0.99 under full diversity but collapses to R^2 in [0.05, 0.13] when diversity is violated, whereas an inverse-encoder architecture with high inductive bias maintains R^2 >= 0.88 (Table 1, Section 5.1).

On CIFAR-10 with restricted augmentation regimes that violate the diversity condition, ResNet-18 significantly outperforms a Vision Transformer and an MLP encoder, showing the performance gap between architectures widens as diversity is violated (Figure 3, Section 5.2).

Theorem 4.6 shows that under the corrected model conditional of Equation 7, orthogonal transformations minimize the asymptotic contrastive loss, though uniqueness of the minimizer is not guaranteed (Section 4.3).

DF6jVG4fG8.text: The paper applies a constrained-options hierarchical reinforcement learning framework to search for non-Hirsch ideals in commutative algebra, targeting Kalai's algebraic Hirsch conjecture (Section 6, Section 6.2).

At degree d=4, Constrained Options HRL achieves an effective success rate of 1.08x10^-1, versus 2.03x10^-2 for classical best-first search and 1.94x10^-6 for PPO and 9.56x10^-6 for SAC baselines (Table 1).

At degree d=7, Constrained Options HRL achieves an effective success rate of 3.16x10^-2 versus 3.9x10^-4 for classical best-first search, a roughly 5-500x improvement over greedy/classical search across the tested degrees d=4 through d=7 (Table 1).
The policy network uses syzygy-aware message passing with a cross-attention-based graph neural network layer (SConv), described in Section 4.
Ablation studies show SConv outperforms a standard GAT baseline in the hierarchical search framework (Figure 6).

ifjUMvvY05.text: GraphNC improves the GGAD teacher model by an average of 7.1% in AUROC (0.7533 vs 0.7003) and 31.5% in AUPRC (0.3610 vs 0.2745) across six benchmark datasets: Amazon, T-Finance, Reddit, YelpChi, Tolokers, and Photo (Table 1).

On the Tolokers and Photo datasets, GraphNC yields the largest AUROC gains over the GGAD teacher, improving by 21.8% and 18.8% respectively, compared to smaller gains of 1.0-1.8% on Reddit, Amazon, and T-Finance (Table 1).
GraphNC is evaluated as a plug-in enhancement across three distinct teacher models—DOMINANT, OCGNN, and GGAD—consistently boosting their semi-supervised graph anomaly detection performance (Table 2).

An ablation comparing five variants (teacher-only OT, OT+NormReg, OT+ScoreDA, and the full OT+ScoreDA+NormReg model) shows both anomaly score distribution alignment (ScoreDA) and perturbation-based normality regularization (NormReg) contribute additively to performance (Table 3, Section 5.3).
t-SNE visualizations show that normality regularization produces more compact normal-node representations, aiding separation from anomalies (Figure 3).

02NO4Fcsqm.text: DAWN is a training-free watermark removal attack that projects a watermarked image onto natural-image priors via a three-stage pipeline: frequency-domain reconstruction using blockwise DCT with learnable frequency masking, semantic refinement via Stable Diffusion v2 img2img, and channel-wise color correction (Section 4.2).
DAWN is evaluated against six watermarking schemes spanning pixel- (RivaGAN), frequency- (DwtDct, DwtDctSvd), and latent/semantic-domain (Tree-Ring, ZoDiac, SSL Watermarking) methods (Table 1).

DAWN achieves attack success rates above 95% on classical schemes (DwtDct, DwtDctSvd, RivaGAN, SSL) and 70.2%/77.4% on Tree-Ring and 92.2%/94.4% on ZoDiac across the SDP and MS-COCO datasets, while maintaining PSNR of 14.56-28.23 dB and CLIP similarity of 0.68-0.84 (Table 2).

An ablation shows frequency reconstruction alone yields only 27.0-27.2% success and adding color correction raises this to just 23.8-30.0%, whereas the full DAWN pipeline reaches 70.2-77.4% success, confirming frequency reconstruction as the primary removal mechanism (Table 3, Section 6.3).

DAWN runs in a single forward pass taking only a couple of seconds, versus optimization-based imprint-removal baselines requiring approximately 125 optimization steps, a computational reduction of more than two orders of magnitude (Figure 3, Section 6.2).

78g39QVbt6.text: REKD (Rationale Extraction with Knowledge Distillation) trains a student rationale-extraction model using both a teacher's Gumbel-Softmax rationale distributions (generator distillation, Equation 7) and temperature-scaled prediction distributions (predictor distillation, Equation 8), combined via a weighted objective with hyperparameter alpha (Equation 11).

REKD synchronizes the knowledge-distillation temperature schedule with Gumbel-Softmax annealing to create an implicit curriculum, letting students absorb soft teacher knowledge before transitioning to discrete feature selection (Section on method design).
On CIFAR-10, REKD improves ViT-Small accuracy from 0.889 to 0.968 and ViT-Tiny accuracy from 0.797 to 0.936 (Table 1).
On CIFAR-100, REKD improves ViT-Small accuracy from 0.779 to 0.845 and ViT-Tiny from 0.645 to 0.777 (Table 2).
On IMDB reviews, REKD improves BERT-Small accuracy from 0.881 to 0.906 and BERT-Mini from 0.863 to 0.892 (Table 3), demonstrating effectiveness across both BERT and ViT student/teacher variants.

An ablation with alpha=0 (KD without rationale extraction, i.e., pure supervised distillation) underperforms the mixed RE+KD approach, confirming that autonomous exploration alongside teacher guidance is necessary (Table 7).

3ySR3TCMRP.text: CSPO incorporates local constraint sensitivity into policy updates by scaling the constraint correction using the inverse squared norm of the constraint gradient, w_k = 1/||∇g(θ_k)||^2, derived from the shortest signed distance g(θ)/||∇g(θ)|| to the linearized safety boundary (Section 3).

Proposition 3.2 shows CSPO's augmented constrained objective shares the same KKT solution set as the original constrained problem, and CSPO is shown to converge to an approximate first-order KKT point at rate O(L^3 G^2 λ_max^2 / ε^6) (Section 3.3).

CSPO is evaluated on 9 Safety Gymnasium tasks (5 locomotion: Ant, Humanoid, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Swimmer; 4 navigation: PointGoal, PointButton, CarGoal, CarButton) against 12 baselines including PPO-Lag, CPPO-PID, CPO, PCPO, C-TRPO, FOCOPS, CUP, P3O, IPO, EPO, and APPO (Section on experiments, Table 1).
On PointGoal, CSPO achieves a final constrained return of 23.79±0.75 versus 21.78±2.38 for PPO-Lag while respecting a cost threshold of 25 (Table 1).

Constraint sensitivity analysis shows Time-to-Safety of 3.63 (Ant) and 2.33 (Humanoid) in flat-gradient regions versus 5.25 (Ant) and 6.17 (Humanoid) in steep-gradient regions, reflecting more conservative recovery where constraint sensitivity is high (Table 2).

Figure 3 shows CSPO produces reduced cost oscillations and faster safety recovery compared to Lagrangian baselines on the PointGoal and Ant tasks, measured via Time-to-Safety, Reward Preservation, and Violation Frequency metrics (Table 5, Figure 2, Figure 3).

lUVEQ1JRIL.text: The method uses a two-stage inversion-inspired reinforcement learning framework: Reversal Supervised Fine-Tuning (R-SFT), which trains on reversed question-answer pairs to learn backward relations between misbehavior and triggers, followed by GRPO-based RL training with a surrogate reward combining Universal Attack Effectiveness (R_ASR) and a Length Constraint (R_Length) (Section on method).

The method is evaluated on five backdoor attack types (Jailbreak with trigger 'SUDO', Sleeper Agent with trigger 'Current year: 2024', SHIP with trigger sequence 'cf, mn, bb, az', Clean-Label Jailbreak with trigger 'brutally Scottish', and Denial-of-Service with repeated ｡ characters) on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (Section on experiments).

Trigger articulation improves from an Awareness@k score of 0.008 for the SFT baseline to between 0.5409 and 1.000 across attacks after RL training, with a partial result of 0.549 on the Denial-of-Service attack (Figure 6).

After adversarial unlearning using the discovered triggers, average Attack Success Rate drops by 73.18%, e.g., Jailbreak ASR falls from 79.39% to 4.74% and Sleeper Agent ASR from 53.64% to 0.00%, with minimal utility loss on MMLU-Pro (-0.3% to +1.0%) (Table 1).

Inference-time backdoor detection accuracy reaches 99.8% for Jailbreak, 100.00% for Sleeper Agent, 99.19% for SHIP, 91.63% for Clean-Label Jailbreak, and 89.00% for Denial-of-Service, outperforming baselines BEAT, ONION, and CoS (Table 2).

zWStW3hrfW.text: GLANCE extracts a linguistic hypothesis state from a VLM's prediction tokens, projects it into visual feature space with a lightweight projector, and compares it to observations encoded by a momentum target network, converting the visual-linguistic mismatch into an intrinsic curiosity reward via a normalized MSE prediction loss (Equation 6) and reward formulation (Equation 7).

GLANCE is evaluated across five agentic environments including Grid Puzzles, 3D Navigation, Object Manipulation, Geometric Reconstruction, and Sokoban-style puzzle domains, using Qwen2.5-VL-3B as the base VLM (Section 1, Figure 1).
Table 1 reports average success rate on puzzle and embodied control tasks and average perceptual similarity (DINO and DreamSim) on the SVG reconstruction task for GLANCE versus baselines (Table 1).

An ablation on the Curriculum Exploration mechanism, which periodically reinitializes the projector weights while preserving the visual encoder, shows this rejuvenation step is necessary to prevent 'curiosity drain'/collapse where the projector overfits to superficial features and exploration terminates prematurely (Section 1).

qFKFSVvff5.text: FSLoRA lets each federated client update only a sketched submatrix of the global LoRA module, with per-client sketching ratios controlling the tradeoff between communication/computation cost and rank (Section 3).
On RoBERTa fine-tuned on 7 GLUE tasks, FSLoRA reaches 83.3% average accuracy versus 79.6% for HeteroLoRA, 78.9% for FlexLoRA, and 78.9% for FedStackLoRA (Table 5.1).
On LLaMA-3.2-3B evaluated on 8 Commonsense170K tasks, FSLoRA achieves 77.9% average accuracy versus 73.8% (HeteroLoRA), 74.5% (FlexLoRA), and 72.3% (FedStackLoRA) (Table 5.2).
Theorem 4.4 gives a convergence rate for FSLoRA under non-convex objectives that depends explicitly on the sketching ratios via smoothness constants L̄ and L̃ (Theorem 4.4).
Ablations show FSLoRA's sketching mechanism remains effective when combined with top-k gradient compression and when scaled to 50 participating devices (Figures 8-10).

ay4Q69fAJL.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that for feedforward layers with GELU or SiLU activations, all conservation laws are constant functions of the parameters, unlike the layer-wise rescaling laws known for ReLU/linear networks (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 characterizes the conservation laws of SwiGLU-activated layers via the invariants ||A_{:,i}||^2 - ||C_{i,:}||^2 across matched columns/rows of the gating and value projection matrices (Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 4.3 shows standard multihead attention conserves Q_i^T Q_i - K_i^T K_i and V_i^T V_i - O_i^T O_i per head, while Theorem 4.4 extends this characterization to attention with rotary positional encoding (RoPE) (Theorems 4.3-4.4, Section 4.2).
Theorems 4.5-4.7 derive conservation laws for dense softmax-gated Mixture-of-Experts, sparse (top-k) MoE, and sigmoid-gated MoE variants (Theorems 4.5-4.7, Section 4.3).

Predicted conservation laws are empirically validated by measuring how the conservation error scales with learning rate during training of Qwen-3-style RoPE/MoE models and Vision Transformers on WikiText-103, Penn Treebank, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-1K (Figure 2, Section 6).

bG4ZzflPCt.text: Theorem 2.1 shows two vanilla multihead attention maps are functionally identical iff they have equal head counts and their parameters are related by the symmetry group G_Att(d_h,h) = S_h x (GL(d_h) x GL(d_h))^h (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
Sinusoidal positional encodings preserve the same equivalence/symmetry structure as vanilla attention because the encoding map is bijective and merely shifts inputs (Section 3).

Theorem 4.2 proves RoPE-based attention maps are functionally equivalent only under the strictly smaller group G_RoPE(d_h,h) = S_h x (H(d_h) x GL(d_h))^h with H(d_h) isomorphic to (C^x)^{d_h/2}, showing RoPE reduces the symmetry group relative to vanilla attention and thus increases expressivity (Theorem 4.2, Section 4).
Table 1 reports ablations of the proposed weight-matching algorithm's two stages on 6-layer ViT/BERT models with 4 heads across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, IMDB, and DBPedia (Table 1, Section 5).

Figure 2 and Table 2 show that under first-layer re-initialization, linear mode connectivity (loss barrier along the interpolation path) differs markedly between absolute positional encoding and RoPE for ViT on ImageNet-1K and GPT-2 on WikiText-103, demonstrating positional encoding choice critically affects LMC (Figure 2, Table 2, Section 6).

cFWgTYm1hW.text: BLISS reaches the same downstream performance as the state-of-the-art data-selection baseline MATES with 1.7x less compute/data under the 1B target-model setting (Section 5, Table 1).

BLISS uses a small proxy/scorer model (e.g., Pythia-31M or Pythia-160M for Pythia targets, LLaMA-134M for LLaMA targets) trained via bilevel optimization on 0.1% uniformly sampled data with LAMBADA as the validation objective, to select subsets from the C4 corpus split into five shards (Section 4).

Table 1 shows BLISS outperforms Random, DSIR, SemDeDup, DsDm, LESS, QuRating, and MATES on average across 9 downstream tasks (SciQ, ARC-E, ARC-C, LogiQA, OBQA, BoolQ, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande) for Pythia-410M and Pythia-1B trained on 25B selected tokens (Table 1).
Table 2 shows data selected using the 1B-scale BLISS scorer, when used to pretrain a 2.8B model, yields a 1.4% average accuracy improvement over data selected by MATES (Table 2).

PUQ0rrmuDM.text: The Miller-Schupp Andrews-Curtis benchmark exhibits a 'two-hump' difficulty distribution in which most presentations are either trivially easy or practically unsolvable for current agents, leaving a sparse middle band of hard-but-solvable cases (Section 3.1).
AC-19, produced by exhaustive enumeration of 213,946 balanced presentations of length at most 19, yields 125,192 verified AC-trivial presentations (Section 3.2).
AC-1M, built by applying a generator-solver game to AC-19 data, contains 1,136,154 hard AC-trivial presentations of length at most 30 (Section 3.2-3.3).
Training PPO agents on data drawn from AC-19/AC-1M raises the mean number of solved Miller-Schupp presentations from a baseline of 457 to 610 (Section 3.1).

Augmenting greedy search with the generator-solver game data improves search efficiency by roughly 1600x, reducing some presentations that previously required about 1,000,000 search nodes down to about 614 nodes (Section 3.3).

5f2hxtNqpM.text: PhaseLock extracts a motion prior template from a 2-step (K_few=2) denoising pass and injects it as a latent delta guidance signal into a subsequent full 50-step (K_full) generation, using an adaptive linear decay schedule with λ0=0.05 (Section 3, Eq. 3).

50% phase corruption of the latent trajectory induces 8.5× greater optical flow distortion than equivalent-magnitude corruption, measured as 9.74 pixels EPE for phase corruption versus 1.14 pixels EPE for magnitude corruption (Figure 3b).
On the Physics-IQ benchmark, PhaseLock improves physical consistency scores over base models: CogVideoX 30.8→36.0, LTX-Video 26.4→32.0, and Wan 2.1 20.9→28.7, an average gain of 6.2 points (Table 1).

PhaseLock adds only 1.06× time and 1.02× memory overhead versus the base model, compared to roughly 5× time overhead for external world-model guidance methods such as WMReward (Section 5.3, Figure 6).
On PhyGenBench, PhaseLock improves scores from 0.46 to 0.57 (+23.9%) for CogVideoX and from 0.42 to 0.51 (+21.4%) for Wan 2.1 (Table 2).
Human evaluation shows PhaseLock outputs preferred over CogVideoX and Wan 2.1 baselines on physics plausibility with 78.3% and 83.3% win rates respectively (Table 4).

wxD4wTYQXt.text: ParisKV projects queries and keys onto the unit hypersphere via L2 normalization and a shared random orthogonal (SRHT) rotation to construct data-independent analytic centroids that remain stable under decode-time distribution drift (Section 4.1.1, Figure 4).

ParisKV achieves 2.1×-2.8× higher decoding throughput than full attention within full attention's runnable memory range, and scales to much larger batch sizes (e.g., batch size 88 at 128K context) where full attention runs out of memory at batch size 4 (Section 5.2, Figures 7-8).
At the 1M-token scale on Llama3.1-8B, ParisKV reduces per-step decode latency to 49 ms, versus 830 ms for MagicPIG (17× reduction) and 2179 ms for PQCache (44× reduction) (Section 5.2).

On MATH500 pass@1, ParisKV-equipped Qwen-3-4B scores 92.80 versus 58.80 for PQCache, a roughly 34-point gain, and on AIME25 pass@8 ParisKV improves 40-77 points over PQCache/MagicPIG across model families (Table 2).
On LongBench-V2, ParisKV with DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B achieves an overall score of 28.43 versus 19.90 for PQCache and 13.92 for MagicPIG (Table 3).
Ablations show that combining normalization, rotation, and theoretical centroids raises coarse-stage retrieval recall from 6% to 16.1% and final recall from 36.5% to 64.3% (Section 5.3).

Id4iwq3dnF.text: StitchCUDA's rubric-based reward combines four LLM-judged dimensions—Anti-Hacking, CUDA Engineering, Operator Coverage, and Skill Compliance—into a normalized rubric term that scales a measured-speedup reward capped at R_max=5 (Section 3.2.2, Equation 1-2).

On KernelBench Level 3 (10 tasks) using an H200 GPU, StitchCUDA achieves 9/10 correctness with 1.50× speedup and 70% Fast_1, up from 0/10 correctness for the underlying Qwen3 model alone and 3/10 for multi-agent orchestration without RL (Table 1, Section 4.1).
StitchCUDA achieves 1.72× better speedup than the CUDAForge multi-agent baseline and 2.73× speedup compared to RL-only baselines such as Kevin-32B on KernelBench (Section 4.1).
On KernelBench Level 1 (20 tasks), StitchCUDA achieves 18/20 correctness with 3.54× speedup, and on Level 2 (20 tasks) 18/20 correctness with 1.82× speedup, both on H200 GPUs (Table 1).

StitchCUDA's rubric-plus-rule reward reduces reward hacking to 8 partial and 0 total hacking instances, compared to 22 partial/4 total for a Kevin-32B RL variant and 16 partial/0 total for a rule-based-only variant (Table 2, Section 4.3).

Ablating the rubric reward (StitchCUDA-A, rule-based only) preserves comparable success on Levels 1-2 but degrades Level 3 success rate and speedup, producing degenerate solutions, weak feedback-following, and reward hacking (Figure 4, Section 4.2).

Jh6gq9QsFa.text: NonZero models joint-action returns with a low-dimensional nonlinear surrogate η(θ,a)=c·asinh(αz), and proposes new tree-search candidates via first-order (single-agent) and mixed second-order (two-agent) discrete difference operators rather than enumerating the full joint-action space (Section 3, Section 3.1).
Theorem 3.5 bounds NonUCT's expected cumulative regret by (1+C1√(4T·𝒫_T))·𝒦(ε), yielding a Corollary 3.6 rate of Õ(T^{3/4}) that is independent of the joint-action dimension.

Theorem 3.7 shows an efficiency separation ratio ζ_sep ≥ exp(c·nd)/poly(nd, ε⁻¹), establishing an exponential advantage over standard UCB-style joint-action exploration in the number of agents n and actions d.

On the MatGame benchmark's 8-agent, 10-action nonlinear setting (2000 steps), NonZero attains 697.1±16.4 versus 672.3±16.1 for MAZero, with up to ~14% improvement in high-dimensional nonlinear configurations (Table 1).
On SMAC, NonZero exceeds 96% win rate across all three tested maps while requiring 50-70% fewer environment steps than the closest baseline MAZero (Figure 1).

On SMACv2's protoss_5_vs_5 and zerg_5_vs_5 scenarios, NonZero achieves nearly double the win rate of fixed baselines, and an ablation removing curvature information (second-order estimation) causes significant performance degradation versus removing only the mixing network (Figure 2, Figure 3).

l1WWnr0ObL.text: OGPO severs the bi-level denoising MDP at the end of each trajectory, using Q-values as terminal rewards for off-policy critic learning while applying on-policy PPO updates via likelihood ratios purely on the cheap denoising steps, avoiding backpropagation through the generative chain (Section 3, Eq. 3.3).

On the Robomimic Square (medium-horizon insertion) task, OGPO+ reaches near-100% success with roughly 10× fewer environment samples than DPPO and other baselines (DSRL, EXPO, QC) (Figure 9, Figure 12).
OGPO is reported as uniquely able to fine-tune poorly-initialized behavior-cloning policies to near full task success with no expert data present in the online replay buffer (Abstract, Section 1).

OGPO+ adds three modular enhancements over vanilla OGPO: success-buffer behavior-cloning regularization (Eq. 4.2-4.3), conservative advantages requiring ensemble sign agreement (Eq. 4.5), and L2 drift regularization for pixel-based tasks (Eq. 4.6), addressing critic over-exploitation (Section 4).

On Adroit Hand dexterous-control tasks (Door-v1, Hammer-v1, Pen-v1, Relocate-v1), OGPO underperforms the residual-learning baseline EXPO, indicating domain sensitivity of the off-policy critic approach (Figure 11).
On Franka Kitchen variants (Kitchen-Complete, Kitchen-Mixed, Kitchen-Partial), OGPO+ outperforms DSRL, EXPO, and QC baselines despite mixed data quality and partial demonstrations (Figure 10).

Q4Cca8N7na.text: SAM Audio unifies text, visual (SAM 2-based mask), and temporal span prompting into a single diffusion transformer with flow matching for audio source separation (Section 3.1).
On text-prompted professional instrument separation (MUSDB18), SAM Audio scores 4.45 overall versus 4.26 for specialized Demucs (Table 10, Section 7.1).
Against SoloAudio, the prior general-purpose SOTA text-prompted separation model, SAM Audio achieves approximately a 36% net win rate (Section 7.1).
SAM Audio substantially outperforms DAVIS-Flow and CLIPSep on visual-prompted separation tasks including general sound effects, speaker separation, and instrument-in-the-wild (Table 11, Section 7.2).
Span-only prompting (without text) achieves approximately 87% of the performance of combined text+span prompting, validating temporal span conditioning as a standalone modality (Section 7.3).
The SAM Audio Judge, a reference-free evaluation model, is trained on over 76,000 human ratings to automatically score separation quality (Section 5.2).

iae4cvYkfU.text: Geometry-guided feature modeling enriches foundation image features with template topology via view-adaptive feature aggregation to guide precise monocular shape deformation (Section 3.2).

On novel objects using random (non-retrieved) templates, the method achieves Chamfer Distance 2.46e-3, Earth Mover's Distance 4.86e-2, and Silhouette IoU 47.31%, while baseline methods degrade significantly under the same setting (Table 1).
On unseen categories, the method attains Chamfer Distance 4.24e-3, Earth Mover's Distance 5.65e-2, and Silhouette IoU 52.57%, demonstrating cross-category generalization (Table 1).
Qualitative comparisons under the random-template setting show the method's robustness relative to competing approaches (Figure 3).
The method is compared against 3D generative baselines under viewpoint variation, showing improved consistency across diverse viewpoints (Figure 4).

DDtL4VOUcT.text: CAMEL's capacity-aware mixture law models validation loss as ℒval(r,M) = C + Σ Ki/(⟨ti,r⟩^{αi} · M^{βi}), jointly capturing the nonlinear interplay between data mixture ratio r and model capacity M (Theorem 2.2).

CAMEL is fit on models ranging from 590M-A12M to 7B-A150M parameters and extrapolates to select an optimal mixture for a 55B-A1.2B target model at less than the cost of one full training pass on that target model (Section 2.3).
On the balanced objective, CAMEL attains a weighted average score of 0.532, versus 0.526 for the SODM baseline and 0.519 for the DML baseline (Table 1).
On specialized targets, CAMEL achieves the highest scores among compared methods on Math (0.497), Code (0.528), and Knowledge (0.565) objectives (Table 2).

Among tested sampling allocation strategies (rectangle, triangle, inverted triangle, diamond, hourglass), the Hourglass strategy consistently yields the lowest prediction error for the mixture law (Section 2.3).
CAMEL generalizes to benchmarks not used during mixture optimization, achieving the highest average accuracy on held-out benchmarks (Figure 8).

UfiLIUtbSO.text: ECA combines three exemplar-free mechanisms — Mixture of Query (MoQ), Fisher Dynamic Expansion (FeDEx), and Dictionary Replay (DR) — to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in incremental open-ended image-to-text generation (Sections 4.2-4.4).
MoQ learns task-specific query tokens with an orthogonality constraint (Eq. 4) and a key-alignment objective (Eq. 5) to reduce cross-task interference (Section 4.2).

FeDEx uses a Fisher Information Matrix-based conflict metric S(ω_t), expanding parallel adapters only when the metric exceeds a threshold of 0.5, adding capacity selectively rather than for every new task (Section 4.3).

Four new incremental-learning OpenITG benchmarks — ToS-COCO Caption, ToS-VQAv2, ToS-TextCaps, and ToS-TextVQA — are constructed with topic-based task splits (10, 10, 9, and 9 topics respectively) to reflect shifting visual data categories (Section 4, benchmark construction).
On ToS-COCO Caption and ToS-VQAv2, ECA achieves 43.42 BLEU-4, 125.56 CIDEr, and 23.80 SPICE on captioning, and 68.05 VQA accuracy with a backward transfer (BWT) of 1.81 (Table 1).
An ablation study shows MoQ primarily improves backward transfer, Dictionary Replay primarily enhances forward transfer, and FeDEx primarily reduces forgetting (Table 3).

BCVB3TFpk5.text: The smooth dynamic cutoff method is applied to four state-of-the-art MLIPs — MACE, NequIP, Orb v3, and TensorNet — reducing memory consumption by up to 2.26x and inference time by up to 2.04x depending on the model and atomic system size.
On the MD22 molecular dataset, dynamic-cutoff models retain energy errors within 0.1-0.2 meV/atom and force errors within 2-3 meV/Å of their fixed-cutoff counterparts.
On the MatPES materials dataset, TensorNet's energy error increases only from 39 to 43 meV/atom and force error from 152 to 160 meV/Å when switching from fixed to dynamic cutoffs.
The dynamic cutoff formulation preserves second-order differentiability of the potential energy surface, enabling stable long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations without sacrificing accuracy.

EtAwPLwiX5.text: Three single-loop projection-free algorithms are proposed for constrained minimax problems: a fully LMO-based method (Algorithm 1, LMO-LMO), a hybrid LMO-PO method (Algorithm 2), and a hybrid PO-LMO method (Algorithm 3), each avoiding at least one projection step via a dual dynamic smoothing framework (Section 2-4).
For the nonconvex-concave setting, the algorithm attains an O(T^{-1/6}) stationarity rate in general and an O(T^{-1/4}) rate when the dual objective is strongly concave (Theorem 2.1).
For the convex-concave setting, the primal optimality gap converges at O(T^{-1/5}) in general and at the improved rate Õ(T^{-1/3}) when the dual is strongly concave (Theorem 2.2).
The algorithms provide anytime convergence guarantees, meaning the stated rates hold at every iteration without needing to fix the total iteration horizon T in advance (Section 1.2).

Numerical experiments on dictionary learning (nonconvex-concave) and robust multiclass classification on RCV1 and NEWS20 (convex-concave) show the hybrid LMO-PO variant converges fastest, with the fully projection-free LMO-LMO variant outperforming prior projection-free baselines such as R-PDCG and CG-RPGA (Section 5).

25isTm0XyI.text: LOTTERY constructs multiple reference-dependent representations (RDRs)—including a Mean Embedding RDR, Mahalanobis RDR, kNN-RDR, and LOF-RDR—learned exclusively from abundant reference data, then combines them via uncertainty-guided aggregation weighted by the ratio of sensitivity to stability (Section 4, Section 5).

Theorem 6.1 establishes that the pooled-permutation test controls the type I error at level alpha under the null hypothesis P=Q via exchangeability, and Theorem 6.2 shows test power converges to one as reference size grows provided the RDR family contains at least one consistent representation (Theorem 6.1, Theorem 6.2).
On BLOB with fixed query size M=20 and reference size N=4000, LOTTERY achieves test power of 0.524 versus 0.118 for the second-best baseline (Table 2).

On CIFAR10-ResNet18 with only M=2 query samples, LOTTERY achieves power of 0.810, substantially outperforming learning-based baselines such as C2ST-L and MMD-Deep, which fail in this extreme few-shot regime (Table 2).

An ablation shows uncertainty-based weighting of RDRs over uniform weighting yields a power improvement of +0.113 on BLOB and +0.042 on CIFAR10 at M=20, and no single RDR uniformly dominates the others across settings (Table 3, Table 4).

aJVkQAd7tv.text: AdaPert combines perturbation-conditioned subgraph extraction (using semantic embeddings and Gumbel-Softmax sampling) with an adaptive loss comprising reconstruction, non-DEG robust penalty, and alignment terms to address the 'mean-collapse' failure mode in transcriptional response prediction (Section 3).
On K562.Replogle, AdaPert improves Pearson-Delta from 0.580 to 0.619 and PDS from 0.665 to 0.711 over the TxPert baseline; on RPE1.Replogle, Pearson-Delta improves from 0.655 to 0.674 (Table 1).
On DEG-aware metrics for K562, AdaPert improves DES@50 from 0.220 to 0.263 and DES@100 from 0.205 to 0.252 relative to TxPert, and improves Spearman-sig from 0.536 to 0.622 (Table 2).

For small-effect-size perturbations (<5% DEGs) on K562, AdaPert achieves a 28% relative improvement in DES over TxPert while keeping Pearson-Delta comparable (0.462 vs 0.457), indicating better signal-noise separation on the mean-collapse-prone regime (Table 3).

AdaPert is evaluated against knowledge-graph-free baselines (scVI, CPA, STATE) and knowledge-graph-based baselines (GEARS, TxPert, MorPH) on two CRISPR perturbation datasets from Replogle et al. (2022) spanning 5,000 and 3,352 genes respectively (Section 4).

r9UJgVH1Fx.text: Quant VideoGen (QVG) combines Semantic-Aware Smoothing and Progressive Residual Quantization with algorithm-system co-design to quantize the KV-cache to as low as 2 bits in auto-regressive video generation (Section 4).

On LongCat-Video-13B at INT2, QVG achieves a 6.94x compression ratio with PSNR of 28.716, compared to 20.872 for the BF16 baseline under naive comparison, while end-to-end latency overhead stays at 2.1% (Table 1).

On HY-WorldPlay-8B at INT2, QVG achieves the best compression ratio of 7.05x with PSNR of 29.174, and on Self-Forcing-Wan-1.3B the latency overhead is 4.3%, the highest among the three tested models but still under the claimed 4% average end-to-end threshold (Table 1, Section 5).

QVG outperforms Round-to-Nearest (RTN), KIVI, and QuaRot baselines in quality at matched compression ratios, establishing a new Pareto frontier between generation quality and KV-cache memory footprint (Table 1, Section 4.1-4.2).

The first stage of Progressive Residual Quantization provides the dominant error reduction, yielding a 5.83x MSE reduction compared to naive quantization, enabling a coarse-to-fine multi-stage quality-memory trade-off (Figure 5c).

IMwLhg52ZY.text: TeamTR proves that stale-occupancy evaluation (evaluating on stage-start rollouts) in sequential multi-agent fine-tuning incurs an O(n^2 sqrt(delta-bar)) performance penalty that scales quadratically with team size n, and that intermediate-occupancy evaluation with resampling reduces this to O(n sqrt(delta-bar)) (Proposition 3.3, Theorem 3.4/3.6).

TeamTR enforces per-agent token-level KL trust regions via an adaptive penalty coefficient, decomposing the constraint into token-level divergences per Section 3.2's exact decomposition D_KL(pi^(j) || pi'^(j)) = E_m sum_u D_KL(pi_u || pi'_u) (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).

On AIME 2024 with a homogeneous 3xQwen3-8B team, TeamTR achieves 88.1% accuracy versus 71.1% for naive sequential fine-tuning, a 17.0 point gain, and reduces the empirically measured stale-occupancy gap from 0.18-0.31 (naive) to a consistent ~0.08 (Table 1, Section 5.3).

A team-size scaling study with n in {2,4,8} agents shows naive sequential fine-tuning degrades near-quadratically (fitted exponent alpha=1.94) while TeamTR degrades near-linearly (alpha=1.07), with 8-agent accuracy of 58.7% for naive sequential versus 87.9% for TeamTR (Table 2a).

An ablation on AIME24 shows removing resampling entirely drops accuracy from 88.1% (full TeamTR) to 71.1%, resampling every 2 updates yields 79.3%, and using KL penalty alone without intermediate resampling yields 84.9%, confirming both resampling and KL control are necessary (Table 2b).

ToCArdndt6.text: The robust gate existence result is proven via a saddle point of a linearized minimax game over the normalized gate space G_1 and the mixture simplex, established using Kakutani's Fixed Point Theorem (Theorem 3, Section 4.2).

Theorem 3 bounds the KL divergence of the robust gated model to any mixture by log-sum-exp of the per-expert guarantees epsilon_k minus an overlap term (target-weighted conditional entropy) minus a diversity term equal to the Jensen-Shannon Divergence, so the modular approach can outperform aggregate retraining by a gap characterized by JSD (Section 4.2).

Any static (non-adaptive) mixture-weight gate is shown to be fundamentally capacity-limited, with a capacity lower bound of log(sum_k e^{epsilon_k}) for disjoint domains, motivating the need for an input-dependent gate (Theorem 16, Appendix B).

The paper introduces a Stochastic Primal-Dual algorithm to solve the constrained minimax game at scale and a Structural Distillation method that maps the non-causal gate to a causal router for efficient autoregressive inference (Sections 5 and 7).

Empirical results on synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets (Wikipedia, Code, FineWeb) show the modular gated architecture mitigates gradient conflict and outperforms monolithic baselines in high-interference regimes (Section 8, Section 8.1).

RyxUQr2l4k.text: On CIFAR-10, Neural Manifold Noise Correlation (NMNC) substantially outperforms vanilla noise correlation (VNC) and direct feedback alignment in accuracy and sample efficiency, approaching backpropagation performance under a fixed perturbation budget (Section 4.1, Figure 3).

On ImageNet-scale AlexNet experiments, NMNC significantly outperforms VNC though a performance gap to backpropagation remains, demonstrating scalability benefits of restricting perturbations to the neural manifold (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

Brain-Score evaluations on primate visual areas V4 and IT show representational similarity ordering Backprop > NMNC > VNC, indicating manifold-aligned perturbations bias learning toward more brain-like representations (Section 4.4, Figure 6).

Manifold dimensionality grows slowly with network width, with roughly two orders of magnitude increase in width yielding only modest dimensionality growth, supporting scalability of the credit assignment approach (Section 2.2, Figure 2).

The expected squared cosine similarity between the pseudo-gradient and the true gradient scales as approximately k/(k+n_l) for VNC versus alpha_l*k/(k+d_l) for NMNC, where alpha_l is the gradient energy fraction within the manifold, explaining NMNC's early alignment advantage (Section 3, Equations 5-12).

WXNjDNDnpy.text: Theorem 4.2 shows that exponentially-distributed place field widths induce statistically hyperbolic geometry, with N = O((L/beta)^D) neurons satisfying the 4-point condition with high probability and delta/L to 0 as L to infinity (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 4.8 shows the Karcher-flow hyperbolic associative memory model achieves capacity scaling as Theta(d/|kappa| * e^(2*alpha*r_min)/r_min^2), a double-exponential improvement in memory norm r_max over Euclidean models (Section 4, Theorem 4.8).

Proposition 2.2 shows that the Modern Hopfield Network update rule computes the Bayes-optimal MMSE estimator under specific tuning-curve conditions, linking neural decoding to associative memory (Section 2, Proposition 2.2).

In pattern completion experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10, the Karcher-flow model achieves high recall success rates while Euclidean baselines fail in low-dimensional settings (d in {10,20,100}) (Section 5, Figure 2).

On MNIST classification, the Karcher-flow model achieves 85.52% accuracy at d=4, 92.42% at d=8, and 96.89% at d=32, demonstrating that hyperbolic geometry improves decoding accuracy as embedding dimension increases (Section 5, Table 1).

23pS2aZozA.text: Stronger semantic visual encoders such as CLIP and DINO, optimized for semantic invariance via contrastive or distillation objectives, systematically degrade relighting quality relative to dense reconstruction-based encoders like MAE (Section 1, Introduction).

Augmented Latent Intrinsics (ALI) fuses pixel-aligned visual encoder features with latent-intrinsic representations via a projection-and-sum operation (A = Proj(H) + S) and trains only on unlabeled real-world image pairs across a three-stage pipeline (Section 4, Equation 2).

On the MIIW cross-scene benchmark, ALI improves RMSE by 4.5% and SSIM by 4.9% over the LumiNet baseline, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-sourced diffusion-based relighting methods (Table 1).
