ALI achieves the largest relighting gains of roughly 6% on glossy, metallic, and specular material categories, supporting the claim that it particularly benefits complex specular materials (Table 4).

A vision backbone comparison shows RADIOv2.5 outperforms CLIP, DINOv2/v3, and MAE as the semantic feature source for ALI, underscoring the importance of pixel-aligned, reconstruction-based encoders (Table 5).

QO64QUEXdV.text: The paper reformulates multi-task bilevel learning (MTBL) under relaxed lower-level general convexity as an equality constrained multi-objective optimization (ECMO) problem, establishing Pareto stationarity conditions for ECMO (Section 3, Definition 4).
Theorem 2 proves a one-to-one correspondence between locally weakly Pareto optimal ECMO solutions and locally optimal weighted-Chebyshev scalarized solutions (Section 3, Theorem 2).

Theorem 3 shows the proposed Weighted Chebyshev-Penalty (WC-Penalty) algorithm achieves a convergence rate of O(S/T^{1/2}) to epsilon-Pareto stationarity, where S is the number of objectives and T is the number of iterations, requiring O(S^2 * epsilon^{-2}) gradient evaluations for epsilon-accuracy (Section 4, Theorem 3, Corollary 1).

On RLHF reward model training with the HelpSteer dataset across 5 criteria, the proposed method explores the Pareto front by varying preference vectors and achieves a hypervolume of 2.47e-2 versus 7.02e-7 for MOML and 1.66e-5 for MoCo (Section 5, Figure 6, Table 1).
The method is validated on multi-objective LLM alignment with Llama-3.2-1B, showing improved performance over baseline methods (Section 5, Figure 7).

Ak8sl1w550.text: Excessively large feature learning strength (FLS) consistently harms generalization across VGG and ResNet architectures on CIFAR datasets, with an intermediate optimal FLS outperforming both extremes (Section 3, Figure 2).

As dataset intrinsic dimensionality increases (32→64→128), the generalization gap between optimal and suboptimal FLS settings widens, so tuning FLS matters more for harder tasks (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

For two-layer ReLU networks trained with logistic loss on a binary Gaussian mixture, initialization scale α controls FLS, and neuron alignment dynamics in the first training phase follow ψⱼ(tα) ≥ √ζ(α) tanh((tα−t₁)‖x₊‖√ζ(α)) with ζ(α) decreasing in α (Lemma 5.2, Section 4.2).

Theorem 5.6 decomposes excess test error into an over-alignment term OA(α) = Φ(−v*ᵀs/σ) − Φ(−1/σ) that decreases with α, and an over-fitting term that increases with α, jointly implying an optimal intermediate α exists (Theorem 5.6, Section 5.3).

The trade-off between over-alignment at small α and over-fitting at large α is illustrated directly in the theoretical excess-error curve, showing the minimum occurs at a non-degenerate interior FLS value (Figure 4, Section 5.3).

CEpCpxJqAt.text: LLM loss scaling with depth is empirically fit by a decomposed form L = c_m/m^{α_m} + c_ℓ/ℓ^{α_ℓ} + c_D/D^{α_D} + L₀, with fitted exponents α_m ≈ 0.98, α_ℓ ≈ 1.2±0.3, and α_D ≈ 0.30 (Section 2).

Analysis of hidden-state angular updates θ(h_l, h_{l+1}) shows 99.6% of tokens are processed evenly across middle layers, with mean per-layer updates scaling approximately as 1/ℓ (Figure 2a, 2b, 2d, Section 2).

Correlations between updates of neighboring layers are weak (angles near π/2), which the authors argue is inconsistent with layers implementing a single smooth compositional dynamical system (Figure 2e, Section 2).

In a toy model with independent per-layer weights (ρ=0), producing non-smooth dynamics, the fitted depth exponent is α_ℓ ≈ 1 with layer updates scaling as 1/ℓ and high inter-layer update correlation, matching the empirical LLM pattern (Figure 5b, 5c, Section 3).

In the tied-weight toy model (ρ=1), the depth exponent is α_ℓ ≈ 1 under imperfect optimization but rises to α_ℓ ≈ 3 upon convergence, where dynamics become discretization-dominated rather than ensemble-averaged (Section 4).

The paper concludes inverse depth scaling in LLMs is best explained by functionally similar layers performing ensemble averaging that reduces error, rather than compositional learning or discretization of smooth dynamics (Result 3, Section 4).

rbwy4E0Kyz.text: Generalized Conformal Risk Control (gCRC) extends conformal risk control to non-monotonic loss functions, guaranteeing E[L_{n+1}(λ̂₊)] ≤ α + Kϵ under Lipschitz continuity and replace-one stability assumptions, without requiring monotonicity between the control parameter and the loss (Theorem 4.2).

Conformal Policy Control (CPC) clips the deployed policy via likelihood-ratio clipping πₜ^(β)(x) ∝ min(πₜ(x), β·π₀(x)) and calibrates β using only safe-policy data, yielding the finite-sample guarantee E_{π₀:ₜ^(β̂)}[Lₜ] ≤ α + BK'ϵ (Theorem 4.5).
CPC is hyperparameter-free in that β is calibrated directly from existing safe-policy data rather than tuned, and it operates at test time without retraining the policy.

On the MedLFQA medical question-answering task, gCRC maintains false discovery rate (FDR) at or below the target level α across all tested risk levels while achieving superior recall compared to baseline methods (Experimental Results section).
In an active-learning experiment, CPC controls constraint violations at target level α = 0.2 while reducing test MSE relative to an unconstrained baseline (Experimental Results section).

In a black-box sequence optimization experiment, setting a moderate risk-control level (α > 0.6) stabilizes the optimization process and counterintuitively improves final performance relative to running the optimizer unconstrained (Experimental Results section).

9CqZoRWpoc.text: Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP) maintains an explicit active set A_t of candidate optima using confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelopes, certifying with high probability that any point outside A_t is suboptimal (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
Under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension α (Assumption 2.3), the Shrinkage Theorem bounds the active set volume as Vol(A_t) ≤ C·(2(β_t + Lη_t) + γ_t)^(d−α) (Theorem 4.6).
CGP achieves ε-optimality with probability at least 1−δ using T = Õ(L^d ε^{-(2+α)} log(1/δ)) samples, improving on the worst-case Õ(ε^{-(2+d)}) rate whenever α < d (Theorem 4.8).
A matching lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(ε^{-(2+α)}) samples under the same margin condition, establishing CGP's minimax sample-complexity optimality (Theorem 4.9).
CGP-Adaptive learns the Lipschitz constant L online via a doubling scheme, adding only an O(log T) multiplicative overhead to the sample complexity (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
CGP-TR, a trust-region variant, scales to dimension d > 50 via certified restarts that provably never falsely eliminate the region containing the true optimizer x* (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).

FKPCkafoeb.text: The proposed bi-level adversarial training framework uses unsupervised latent direction discovery to simulate diverse jailbroken activations without requiring labeled jailbreak examples for training the defense.

Averaged over six jailbreak attack families (GCG, AutoDAN, GPTFuzz, PAIR, TAP, FewShot), attack success rate drops to 4.01% on LLaMA-3-8B (from a 14.93% baseline), 5.26% on Mistral-v2-7B (from 59.72%), and 4.46% on Qwen-2.5-7B (from 33.27%), remaining mostly below 5% across models (Table 3).

A subspace coverage metric shows the unsupervised adversarial training method yields broad, steady coverage gains across all attack families compared to targeted supervised approaches (Figure 6, Section 9.1).
Simulated jailbroken activations progressively expand beyond the original supervised support region over the course of training (Figure 4).
An ablation removing the adversarial training component shows subspace coverage and robustness gains plateau at substantially worse levels than the full method (Figure 7, Section 9).
The defense preserves model utility, with OR-Bench false positive rates of 16.6%-23.3% across the three models and capability scores comparable to baselines on ARC-C, TruthfulQA, and GSM8K (Table 4).

jQ2DRkSir0.text: DiffThinker achieves an 87.4% average score across vision-centric reasoning tasks, outperforming GPT-5 (21.1% avg) by 314.2% (Table 1).
DiffThinker outperforms Gemini-3-Flash (41.3% avg) by 111.6% on the same multimodal reasoning benchmark (Table 1).
DiffThinker outperforms a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-32B baseline (62.9% avg) by 39.0% (Table 1).
DiffThinker reformulates multimodal reasoning as an image-to-image generative task using Flow Matching rather than text-centric chain-of-thought (Section 3).
DiffThinker's inference latency is reported at approximately 1.1 seconds, with training efficiency comparable to SFT baselines (Figure 5).
Ablations show performance scales consistently with training data size and peaks at a classifier-free guidance scale of w=4 (Figures 8-9).

6VyoaDj3zB.text: Theorem 1 gives the first convergence analysis for gradient-descent training of a transformer under the population DDPM objective on multi-token Gaussian mixture (MTGM) data, showing the training loss converges to within O(epsilon) of the Bayes-optimal risk (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 shows the trained transformer yields a score network whose score-matching error is bounded by epsilon times (SNR+1) (Theorem 2).

Corollary 3 establishes a 'mean denoising mechanism': the self-attention layer's weights concentrate uniformly across tokens sharing the same underlying pattern, so the model approximates the Bayes-optimal MMSE estimator by averaging same-pattern tokens (Section 4.2, Corollary 3).
Proposition 1 shows the trained transformer converges to the oracle MMSE estimator for the multi-token Gaussian mixture denoising problem (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).
Corollary 4 shows the learned mean-denoising mechanism generalizes to test data with a distribution shift from the training mixture (Section 4, Corollary 4).

eB5i7caric.text: ROMBRL formulates offline model-based RL as a constrained maximin problem in which the policy maximizes expected return while the world model is adversarially updated within an uncertainty set to minimize it, solved via Stackelberg learning dynamics (Section 4, Eq. 5, Eq. 9).

ROMBRL achieves an average normalized score of 77.7 (±0.5) across twelve noisy D4RL MuJoCo tasks (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d across four data-quality levels), versus 70.7 (±2.4) for the MOBILE baseline, ranking first on 7 of 12 tasks (Section 6, Table 1).
ROMBRL attains an average negative tracking error of -47.1 (±1.2) on three stochastic Tokamak Control tasks, ranking first on 2 of 3 tasks, with Cohen's d = 4.3 versus CQL (Section 6, Table 2).
Theorem 1 bounds the suboptimality gap of the ROMBRL policy in terms of the size of the world-model uncertainty set and a concentrability coefficient (Section 3, Theorem 1).

Theorem 4 derives closed-form gradient expressions for the episodic maximin objective, using a Fisher Information Matrix approximation and the Woodbury identity to reduce computation from O(mNθ + MNφ² + Nφω) to O(mNθ + M²Nφ) (Section 5, Theorem 4, Eq. 11-12).
Figure 1 shows baseline offline MBRL methods degrade substantially under 5% measurement noise, motivating the robustness objective (Section 1, Figure 1).

URIdUFsz9E.text: Balanced pretraining data distributions prevent instability (exponential growth in Hessian curvature) during subsequent post-training optimization, inducing latent capabilities later activated by post-training (Section 7).
Insight 2 argues SFT datasets should be curated to be small in volume and high in quality, since excessively large SFT datasets dilute informative pretraining signal (Section 5, Insight 2).

Insight 1 shows selecting SFT examples that are hard for the pretrained model optimizes post-training data selection, formalized via the test-error formula in Proposition 5.1 (Section 5, Proposition 5.1, Insight 1).

Theorem 4.1 characterizes the SFT loss minimizer in closed form via a pseudo-inverse formulation, and Theorem 4.2 proves gradient descent converges to it at an explicit rate (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2).

Outcome-supervision (OS/RL) training is shown to be most effective for incremental adaptation on tasks that are already partially learned during pretraining, per Insight 4, while exhibiting high sensitivity to sample variation near stability boundaries per Insight 3 (Section 6, Insight 3, Insight 4).
Experiments on linear self-attention models and GPT-2 architectures in Section 8 empirically confirm that SFT benefits from smaller curated datasets while OS/RL benefits from larger ones (Section 8).

AsRnPT3So3.text: SPADE achieves state-of-the-art performance across the Design-Bench tasks (Superconductor, Ant, D'Kitty, TF Bind 8, TF Bind 10) and an LLM data-mixture (LLM-DM) optimization benchmark, with a mean rank of 2.8 out of 24 methods compared (Section 4, Table 1).
SPADE attains best scores of 0.978±0.006 on Ant, 0.981±0.003 on D'Kitty, 1.019±0.064 on LLM-DM, and 0.915±0.010 on TF Bind 10, and second-best 0.546±0.013 on Superconductor (Table 1).

Proposition 3.1 proves that the support-proximity regularization term is first-order equivalent to augmenting the training objective with a Bayesian prior, so the calibrated posterior optimizes p(x|y) proportional to p(y|x)p(x) (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).

The calibration loss (Eq. 7) enforces global consistency between the diffusion surrogate's predictions and the true data by combining first-order moment matching with a pairwise ranking-consistency term using a temperature s=1.0 (Section 3.1, Eq. 7).

The support-proximity regularization (Eq. 8) uses k-NN distance as a non-parametric density proxy to shrink the mean and inflate the variance of predictions in out-of-support regions (Section 3.2, Eq. 8).

An ablation study (Table 2) shows both the calibration and support-proximity components are individually necessary, since removing either ('w/o Calib' or 'w/o Prox') degrades performance relative to full SPADE on all six benchmark tasks (Table 2).

TYswUgruqt.text: Gaussian Particle Operator (GPO) attains lowest L2 relative error on ERA5-wind-u (6.68E-02 vs M2NO's 7.15E-02), Airfoil (1.12E-03 vs CNO's 4.65E-03), and PlanetSWE (8.01E-02 vs AMG's 8.14E-02), while remaining competitive on periodic-grid NS2D (Table 1)

The Petrov-Galerkin Gaussian Attention operator reduces the modal attention cost to O(G^2 D) for a fixed modal budget G much smaller than the number of spatial points N, giving near-linear overall complexity in N (Section 2.2)
An ablation removing the Petrov-Galerkin operator degrades L2 error from 3.90E-02 (full GPO) to 8.57E-02, and removing the Gaussian field representation degrades it to 7.44E-02 (Table 3)
On a 64^3-resolution input with batch size 16, GPO uses only 2,313 MiB of GPU memory and 44.66 s/epoch training time, versus 4,917 MiB/97.03 s for Transolver and 8,643 MiB/139.42 s for GNOT (Table 4)

Learned Gaussian particles visually concentrate on coherent flow structures such as fronts, vortices, and filaments with anisotropic footprints aligned to local dynamics, supporting the claim of intrinsic interpretability (Figure 3)

Theorem 2.2 establishes that the Petrov-Galerkin Gaussian Attention operator can approximate arbitrarily closely any operator admitting a Mercer kernel or low-rank factorization (Theorem 2.2, Appendix B.2)

XgvVGrvhuv.text: MM-DeceptionBench contains 1,013 annotated cases spanning six deception categories: sycophancy, sandbagging, bluffing, obfuscation, deliberate omission, and fabrication, with inter-annotator Fleiss' Kappa of 0.8355 (Section 3.1)
On the 582-case MM-DeceptionBench subset, Debate-with-Images raises GPT-4o accuracy from 61.5% (direct prompting) to 76.0% and Cohen's kappa from 0.30 to 0.46 (Table 2)

On Gemini-2.5-Pro, Debate-with-Images improves accuracy from 78.8% (direct prompt) to 82.2% and Cohen's kappa from 0.48 to 0.52, exceeding the Debate-about-images (text-only) variant on both metrics (Table 2)
Debate-with-Images yields up to a 1.5x improvement in Cohen's kappa and up to a 1.25x improvement in accuracy over MLLM-as-a-judge baselines across evaluated models (Table 1)

Ablations show optimal debate configuration uses 2-5 agents and 2-3 rounds, with performance degrading at 6+ agents due to context-length limits, and zoom-in as the single most effective visual grounding operation, reaching 73.32% accuracy on Qwen (Section 5.3)

DhBcxps4zr.text: The Uncertainty detector combines a local statistic (percentile of low-probability token log-likelihoods, zlocal) and a global statistic (Renyi entropy averaged over the same low-probability positions, zglobal) via a weighted sum (Section 3.1-3.3)
In the black-box setting across 12 source models, Uncertainty achieves 88.74% average AUROC (+2.25 over Lastde) and Uncertainty++ achieves 93.24% average AUROC (+1.73 over Lastde++) (Table 1)
In the white-box setting across 12 source models, Uncertainty reaches 97.25% AUROC and Uncertainty++ reaches 99.07% AUROC, the highest of all compared methods (Table 2)

An ablation on the Reddit dataset shows removing the low-probability token selection drops Uncertainty++ AUROC by 6.74 points and removing the log-probability (local) term drops it by 31.80 points, identifying log-probability as the primary discriminative signal (Table 3)
On out-of-domain generalization across FiQA, Wiki, and arXiv, Uncertainty attains 85.60% average AUROC (+9.85 over Lastde) and Uncertainty++ attains 86.45% (+3.62 over Lastde++) (Table 4)

Applying low-probability percentile selection to existing baselines (Likelihood, LogRank, Fast-DetectGPT) improves their AUROC by 24.53, 18.97, and 4.20 points respectively, with all three then exceeding 90% average AUROC (Section 4.6)

GzunaSZ8jC.text: Local MAP Sampling (LMAPS) reformulates each reverse diffusion step as a local maximum-a-posteriori subproblem, arguing that replacing E[x0|xt,y] with argmax p(x0|xt,y) alters the effective forward operator relative to Diffusion Posterior Sampling in non-Gaussian settings (Section 3.2)

Because xt depends on the entire past sampling trajectory, the sequence of local MAP maximizers need not converge to the global MAP maximizer, distinguishing local from global MAP objectives (Section 3.1-3.2)

LMAPS achieves the best performance in 49 of 60 evaluated image restoration configurations on FFHQ and ImageNet across 10 linear, nonlinear, and non-differentiable operators, with gains of at least 2 dB PSNR on motion deblurring, JPEG restoration, and quantization tasks (Table 1)

On scientific inverse problems, LMAPS obtains PSNR improvements exceeding 1.5 dB across three linear inverse scattering configurations, alongside consistent gains on CS-MRI and black-hole imaging tasks across 11 evaluation scenarios (Table 2)

LMAPS employs a probabilistically-interpretable covariance approximation in place of heuristic choices used in prior posterior-sampling methods, plus gradient approximation strategies to handle non-differentiable forward operators such as quantization and JPEG compression (Section 4)

JNtq1ungZt.text: On one-shot convexity recognition, LLM F1-score drops from 1.0 at composition depth 2 to approximately 0.2 at depth 100, revealing a compositional reasoning gap (Figure 4(a), Section 4.1)

ConvexBench generates functions by composing elementary atoms under Disciplined Convex Programming (DCP) rules, producing mechanically verifiable convexity labels with controlled composition depth (Section 3)

One-shot failures at deep composition arise from two identified modes: parsing failure, where models lose track of parentheses and operator scope, and lazy reasoning, where models rely on shallow heuristics instead of step-by-step verification (Section 4.1)

The agentic divide-and-conquer framework with focused context (pruning irrelevant history via dependency-focused contexts) achieves F1-score 1.0 at depth 100 for frontier models, an improvement of 0.79-0.82 over one-shot reasoning (Section 5.2.1, Figure 3.4)

At depth 100, raw expressions average 1,912 tokens versus 5,331 tokens for decomposition-augmented expressions, both well within model context windows, showing that degradation at depth is not merely a context-length artifact (Table 1)

N4PZVvr8lt.text: Theorem 4.2 gives an exact characterization: a linear MDP is attackable with respect to a target policy if and only if a specific convex quadratic program (CQP) has strictly positive optimal value ε* > 0 (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

Definition 4.1 defines an MDP instance as attackable when an adversary can force any learner to follow a target policy π† for T − o(T) episodes while paying only o(T) total reward-perturbation cost (Section 4, Definition 4.1).

Instances with ε* ≤ 0 are intrinsically robust, requiring linear-or-worse attack cost even against non-robust learners such as vanilla LSVI-UCB, establishing a sharp dichotomy between vulnerable and robust linear MDPs (Section 4).

Theorem 5.1 gives a two-stage black-box reward-poisoning attack against model-based learners with cost O~(d^{3/2} H^{5/2} S T^{3/4}) when the exploration phase length T1 = Θ(√T) (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).

Section 6 empirically validates the attackability characterization on MuJoCo Mountain-Car, Half-Cheetah, and Pendulum environments approximated as linear MDPs via contrastive representation learning (CTRL), correctly predicting attack success/failure in 91-100% of tested instances (Section 6).

Km8yqb7SfN.text: IAMA optimizes the objective ℛ[π] = g(R1[π],...,Rm[π]) − β·KL[π||πref], where each Ri measures reward under an inference-time transformation such as Best-of-N sampling, allowing a single trained base policy π to adapt to multiple alignment criteria at inference time (Section 3, Equation 1).

Non-linear GRPO (Algorithm 1) replaces the standard scalar reward with an approximated functional derivative ∂R/∂π evaluated at the current policy's empirical distribution, requiring only a drop-in reward function on top of standard GRPO (Section 4, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 5.2 proves linear convergence of exact non-linear GRPO updates to the optimal policy, with excess loss bounded by β·KL[π*||π0] / ((L+β)/L)^T − 1 under a step size η=1/L (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).

Theorem 5.3 shows that with approximation error ε and optimization residual δ, inexact non-linear GRPO updates converge to a neighborhood of the optimum with an additive bias term of 2(ε+δ)/β (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).

Proposition 3.1 shows that naive weighted-sum training collapses to a degenerate policy outputting only a single medium value (δ0.5), whereas IAMA with Best-of-N yields a bimodal optimal policy π*(y) ∝ y^(α−1)(1−y)^(α−1)/(y^α+(1−y)^α)^2 with α=1/(N−1) (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).

On the HH-RLHF task with Alpaca-7B, IAMA trained with Best-of-N sampling (N=4) pushes the helpfulness-harmlessness Pareto front forward relative to standard alignment, while without Best-of-N sampling IAMA performs equivalently to standard alignment (Section 6.2).

9W7E6zYnH3.text: Pruned models retain competitive performance on non-generative tasks such as retrieval and multiple-choice, e.g. E5-Mistral retrieval accuracy drops only from 58.9 (full) to 56.8 (pruned), while generative task performance collapses, e.g. GSM8K accuracy falls from 48.4 to 0.0 after MLP-layer removal, producing incoherent, repetitive outputs (Table 1, Table 2).

Embedding-space representations remain stable under pruning, but the corresponding probability (logit) space exhibits substantial fluctuations despite the comparable embeddings, indicating that nonlinear transformation to probabilities amplifies the deviation (Section 5, Figure 4).

Theorem 2 formalizes that the softmax-induced deviation in probability space is dominated by the temperature T and the weighted variance of the logit perturbation Δz, explaining why probability outputs diverge sharply even when embeddings are stable (Section 6.2, Theorem 2, Equation 10).
During autoregressive generation, deviations introduced by pruning at early decoding steps persist and propagate to later steps, compounding error over the generated sequence (Section 7.1, Figure 7).

For multiple-choice tasks, probability shifts are confined to a stable categorical-token subspace and are substantially milder than the shifts observed among top-ranked tokens overall, explaining the relative robustness of non-generative evaluation to pruning (Section 7.2, Figure 8).

l0LA4SUA50.text: On-policy expert corrections (OECs) are generated by rolling out a trajectory with the student model and switching to the expert model at a randomly sampled turn index drawn from U(0,30), with the expert-side history reformatted to match the expert's scaffold format (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).

OEC-trained models achieve a relative 14% improvement over traditional (behavioral cloning) imitation learning in the 7B setting and 13% in the 32B setting on SWE-bench Verified (Abstract, Section 4.2, Figure 2).
OEC-SWE-32B achieves 40.0% resolution on SWE-bench Verified and 33% on SWE-bench Lite, exceeding SWE-smith-LM-32B (36.4% Verified) and other 32B baselines fine-tuned on Qwen2.5-Coder (Table 1).

Removing on-policy masking during OEC fine-tuning has little effect in the 7B setting but degrades Student-32B's SWE-bench Verified resolution rate from 40% to 31.8%, essentially negating the benefit of the expert portion of the data (Section 4.2, Table 2).

Fine-tuning purely on unfiltered on-policy trajectories severely destabilizes training: removing repetition filtering drops Student-7b's rate from 17% to 11% and Student-32b's from 40% to 36.4% (Section 4.2, Table 2).

Frechet Distance between student and expert trajectory embeddings (using Qwen3-8B embeddings) grows throughout a rollout even after behavioral-cloning fine-tuning, dipping until around turn 10 before rising sharply through turn 30 and continuing to increase, demonstrating persistent covariate shift (Section 4.3, Figure 4).

kkhVljGiMS.text: Theorem 1.2 (restated as Theorem 3.4) proves that computing an ε-performatively stable point is PPAD-complete even when ρ = Lβ/α ≤ 1 + O(ε), with the explicit constant ε′ = 0.088/6 ≈ 0.0147 (Section 1.1, Theorem 3.4).

This PPAD-hardness persists in the simple setting where the loss is quadratic, ℓ(x;z) = ½||x−z||², and the distribution shift D(x) is given by an affine map g(x) (Section 3.1, Equation 2-3, Theorem 3.4).

Theorem 3.5 shows a phase transition to tractability: when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε^4), an ε-performatively stable point can be computed in poly(d, log(1/ε)) time via an ellipsoid-method algorithm exploiting hypomonotonicity (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.5).

Corollary 3.7 establishes an unconditional information-theoretic lower bound: any algorithm requires 2^Ω(d) expected-risk-minimization (ERM) queries to find an ε-performatively stable point even when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε), and even for constant ε (Section 3.1, Corollary 3.7).
Theorem 3.12 extends PPAD-hardness of performative stability from the hypercube constraint set to any well-bounded general convex constraint set (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.12, Definition 3.11).

For the special case of strategic classification, Theorem 4.4 shows that computing a local optimum of the performative risk under single-label updates is PLS-hard, complementing prior NP-hardness results for global performative optimality (Abstract, Section 1.1, Theorem 4.4).

gtURIPKbx6.text: ChaosNexus achieves a zero-shot mean forecasting error strictly below 1°C for 5-day (120-hour) global station-based temperature forecasts on the WEATHER-5K dataset (5,672 stations), while baseline models exhibit MAE of at least 3°C even after fine-tuning (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

On a held-out set of 9,300+ synthetic chaotic ODE systems, ChaosNexus improves over the best baseline by 12.91% in correlation dimension error (D_frac) and 40.55% in KL divergence between attractor statistics (D_stsp), reflecting superior long-term attractor fidelity while remaining competitive on point-wise sMAPE (Section 4.1, Figure 2, Table 2 in Appendix A.4).

Ablation removing the Patch Merging/Expansion (PME) module causes severe degradation, increasing sMAPE@128 by 7.8% and D_frac by 21.70%, demonstrating the hierarchical multi-scale design is critical to performance (Table 1, Appendix A.1).

ChaosNexus is benchmarked in a zero-shot setting against 12 baseline models, including Panda, Time-MoE, TimesFM, Chronos, Moirai-MoE, and Timer-XL, on 20K training and 9.3K test synthetic chaotic systems (Section 4.1, Appendix D.1/D.3).
For weather forecasting, ChaosNexus is compared against domain-specific baselines FEDformer, CrossFormer, PatchTST, and Koopa (Section 4.2).

cvM6PcgOpS.text: The universal VLM adaptor yields BD-Metric improvements of approximately 30% at low bitrate for JPEG and over 10% on the POPE metric for ELIC/ILLM codecs, and over 12 units improvement on two metrics for JPEG (Section 4.3, Table 4, Figure 7).

The benchmark comprises more than 1 million compressed images spanning 11 codecs (traditional: JPEG, HM, VTM; learning-based: ELIC, TCM, MLICpp; generative: HiFiC, MS-ILLM, DiffEIC, RDEIC, StableCodec), evaluated on 9 VLMs (1B-32B parameters) across 7 tasks/metrics including POPE, GQA, COCO-Caption, OCRBench, MMBench, MME, and SEEDBench (Section 2.1, Table 1).

The paper mathematically decomposes the VLM performance gap under compression (Equation 1) into an 'information gap' that cannot be resolved by finetuning because it reflects information already lost during compression, concluding this information loss is inherent and cannot be easily mitigated (Section 3, Section 3.1, Table 3).

On SEEDBench, Qwen-Chat-7B drops from approximately 73.81% uncompressed to approximately 60.56% under JPEG compression at the lowest tested bitrate, a drop of about 13.25 points (Figure 10, Appendix A).
The universal adaptor works by finetuning only the vision encoder with a conditional embedding conditioned on codec/bitrate, rather than requiring per-codec or per-bitrate retraining (Section 4.1).

TCWXiFT7gj.text: Models exhibit 'conversational inertia': strong diagonal attention where the i-th token of the current response disproportionately attends to tokens near the i-th position of the previous assistant response, visualized in a maze environment (Section 1, Figure 1).

Attention to previous assistant responses grows monotonically across turns, and a detailed mechanistic investigation of this diagonal attention pattern is given via attention-head analysis (Figure 2, Section 3.4).

For identical environment states, actions generated with longer input contexts exhibit stronger conversational inertia (diagonal attention ratio) than those generated with shorter contexts, empirically validated across context-length configurations (Section 2.1, Table 1, Figures 6(a) and 7(a)).

Context Preference Learning (CPL), implemented via LoRA fine-tuning updating only about 0.4% of parameters, reduces conversational inertia and improves average performance across eight agentic environments, e.g., Qwen3-8B-CPL with Clip context reaches 72.5% average versus a 68.9% base model average (Section 2.1, Table 1).
CPL yields roughly a 4% average performance improvement across different context-management strategies, with GPT-4o-mini reaching 71.1% average using Clip context (Section 2.2/3.3, Table 1).

cZNih1inuF.text: Dual-Window Smoothing (DWS) reduces the action fluctuation rate (AFR) by over 80% in precision DeepMind Control Suite tasks compared to vanilla baselines, e.g., AFR drops from 0.56 to 0.10 in Reacher-Hard (Section 4.2, Tables 9-13, Appendix D.2-D.3).

On the FCEV industrial energy management task, DWS achieves a reward of -1393.15 versus -3219.81 for ActionChunk, with an AFR of 0.127 and closer state-of-charge maintenance to the 0.50 target (Section 4.3, Table 1).

On the vision-based Lane-Change Overtaking (LCO) autonomous driving task, DWS achieves a 100% success rate and 0% collision rate versus 20% success and 55% collisions for LipsNet++, with an 88.7% reduction in action smoothness metric and 78.5% reduction in yaw-rate oscillation (Section 4.4, Table 2).

On the Autonomous Emergency Braking (AEB) task, DWS attains the highest reward (390.70) among all compared methods, a 50.9% jerk reduction over HG-TD3, and a 4.9% improvement in time-to-collision safety margin (Section 4.4, Table 3).
An ablation study on the hardest LCO setting validates the contribution of DWS's individual components to its performance (Section 4.7, Table 7).

EK17RF2ilh.text: On scaffold-conditioned SMILES molecule generation, RapTB combined with SubM replay achieves validity (Acc) of 0.988, quality score of 0.844, diversity entropy of 2.726, and molecular fingerprint diversity (FPDiv) of 0.898, representing the best quality-diversity trade-off among compared methods (Section 4.4.1, Table 1).
A length-stratified analysis shows RapTB+SubM outperforms baselines across most SMILES sequence lengths (Figure 2, Tables 8-10, Appendix A.1.1).

Prefix-collapse diagnostics demonstrate that RapTB+SubM reduces prefix concentration and improves trajectory survival rates relative to baseline GFlowNet training approaches (Figure 3, Tables 11-12, Appendix A.1.2).
In a long-horizon stress test with maximum sequence length Lmax=15, RapTB+SubM achieves the best balance between long-horizon coverage and diversity (Section 4.4.4, Table 2).

Z7wI0sor6i.text: DiBO (diffusion LLM adapted for black-box optimization) attains a mean score of 0.897±0.017 across Design-Bench tasks, versus 0.657±0.028 for the autoregressive OPRO baseline (Table 1).
DiBO scores 0.965±0.038 on TF Bind 8, exceeding the best prior baseline score of 0.857 (Table 1).
DiBO scores 0.944±0.016 on Ant Morphology, exceeding the best prior baseline score of 0.929, and attains a mean rank of 2.5 across all compared methods (Table 1).

Domain adaptation uses explicit delimiter tokens (|design-start|/|design-end|, |label-start|/|label-end|) to bridge natural-language pretraining and heterogeneous black-box optimization signals (Section 3.1).

The training pipeline consists of three sequential stages—domain adaptation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning—and ablations show removing any one stage degrades performance, with delimiter tokens alone contributing 0.024-0.182 performance gains (Section 3.2, Tables 2-4).
Similarity-conditioned context construction yields a 0.235 performance improvement on TF Bind 8 in ablation experiments (Tables 2-4).

JJ3KlnhGJJ.text: The non-autoregressive ionic transport predictor achieves over 200x inference speedup versus an autoregressive baseline, measured at 14 seconds versus 2910 seconds (Abstract, Table 3).

On the trajectory-based dataset, the method achieves an MAE of 0.344 on log10-scaled targets, versus 0.378 for the autoregressive baseline and 0.412-0.604 for other non-autoregressive baselines (Table 3).
On the experimental real-world dataset, the method achieves an MAE of 1.388, versus 2.048-2.150 for baseline methods (Table 4).

Auxiliary modality learning uses trajectory data (via a MOMENT-based embedding) as privileged information during training but removes it at inference, avoiding sequential generation (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).

Model-level auxiliary modality learning is initialized via closed-form ridge regression (Equation 9), and ablations in Table 5 and Table 6 quantify the contribution of this component on trajectory- and structure-based datasets respectively.

Vv4XRZDMM0.text: Theorem 1 (Section 2) establishes finite-sample uniform validity of max-p aggregation, showing it yields coverage guarantees under any mixture distribution of the K sources.

Theorem 2 (Section 3.1) characterizes the population-optimal prediction set as a superlevel set of a shared score function h_{λ*}(x,y) = Σ_k λ_k*(x) f_k(y|x), with complementary slackness ensuring exact 1−α coverage for at least one source.
Theorem 3 (Section 3.2) proves max-p aggregation with learned conformity scores is asymptotically optimal, converging to the oracle-optimal prediction set up to boundary regions.
In linear classification simulations, the method's prediction sets are 34.39% smaller than the naive max-p baseline while maintaining tight worst-case coverage (Figure 2).
In linear regression simulations, the method achieves a 22.44% average reduction in prediction set size while maintaining valid ~90% worst-case coverage (Figure 5).

On the FMoW satellite imagery dataset spanning six geographic regions (with 249 countries in the training data), the method achieves near-tight worst-case coverage with smaller sets than single-source methods (Section 6.1, Figure 8).

1MxluQVepx.text: NEMO achieves first-place performance on eight of nine optimization modeling benchmarks, including 90.4% on OptiBench (an 8+ point gain over baselines) and 65.7% on OptMATH-Bench (~20 point improvement) (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On IndustryOR, NEMO attains 63.0% accuracy, a 28-point advantage over the SIRL training-based baseline (Section 4.2).

NEMO uses autonomous coding agents (ACAs) as first-class primitives supporting code generation, execution, inspection, and iterative modification, rather than one-shot LLM code generation (Section 2.1).

The Optimizer module uses a self-consistency mechanism generating T=3 parallel implementations aggregated via hierarchical consensus, while the Decision Process Extractor uses component-wise MBR decoding with n=5 candidates and top-q=3 selection (Section 3.6.1, Section 3.3.1).
Ablations on OptMATH-Bench show progressive component additions raising accuracy from 63.2% (base) to 65.7% (full system with memory, MBR decoding, and multi-agent consensus) (Table 2, Section 4.3).
The simulator-optimizer feedback loop triggers multi-attempt iterations in 1.2-5% of problems, with resolution success rates of 62.5-100% when activated (Table 7, Appendix B.2).

xXyreH61EN.text: SCOUT models cyclic causal systems via structural equation models (Equations 1-2) and handles three intervention types—shift, scale, and noisy function interventions—under unknown targets (Section 2).

SCOUT uses contractive residual flows for invertible mappings and neural spline flows to model non-Gaussian noise, learning unknown intervention targets via Gumbel-softmax parameterization (Section 3).

Theorem 3.1 shows that under four assumptions (sufficient capacity, I-sigma-faithfulness, strict positivity, finite differential entropy), exact score maximization recovers the I-Markov equivalence class of the true graph and correct intervention targets.
SCOUT is compared against NODAGS-Flow, LLC, BACKSHIFT, DCDI, UT-IGSP, and BaCaDI, and maintains graph and intervention-target recovery performance when scaling from 10 to 70 nodes (Table 2).
SCOUT is evaluated on the Perturb-CITE-seq and SERGIO gene expression benchmarks, showing superior predictive accuracy via negative log-likelihood on real gene expression data (Figure 6, Figure 7).

I6xz92EJ4T.text: Theorem 3.4 proves that under the structural sparsity condition on the Jacobian (Assumption 3.1), a single aligned source-target sample pair suffices to rule out measure-preserving automorphisms and identify the ground-truth transfer (Theorem 3.4).
On synthetic 2D domain transfer, the translation error drops from 0.83 without an anchor sample to 0.17 with a single paired anchor (Section 5).
On MNIST to Rotated MNIST, the proposed method achieves a translation error of 0.20±0.06, and on Edges to Rotated Shoes it achieves an LPIPS of 0.32±0.07 (Section 5).

Proposition 4.1 shows the randomized masked finite-difference Jacobian sparsity regularizer approximates the true Jacobian sparsity when (S-1)(T-1) << D, where D is the ambient dimensionality and S, T are sparsity parameters, enabling scalable high-dimensional learning (Proposition 4.1).
On single-cell distribution alignment, the proposed method substantially outperforms the CM-AE baseline on K-NN accuracy metrics (Section 5).

Despite the theoretical guarantee that a single anchor suffices, complex image-translation experiments required 10 anchor pairs rather than 1, reflecting a gap between theory and practice from approximate assumptions and non-convex optimization (Section 5).

FjZF2l8ZZF.text: LUVE generates ultra-high-resolution video through a three-stage pipeline: Low-resolution Motion Generation (LMG) using a Wan2.1-1.3B backbone, Video Latent Upsampling (VLU), and High-resolution Content Refinement (HCR) with dual frequency experts (Section 3.1).

The Video Latent Upsampler (VLUer), a lightweight ~22M-parameter network combining an encoder, implicit neural representation module, and decoder, performs arbitrary-resolution upsampling directly in latent space (Section 3.3).

Dual frequency experts apply a low-frequency LoRA expert on attention modules during the high-noise diffusion stage and a high-frequency LoRA expert on feed-forward networks during the low-noise stage, with a switching timestep t_switch = 0.417 (Section 3.4).
LUVE-2K achieves a VBench average score of 84.34 and LUVE-4K achieves 84.03, with FID_patch scores of 41.03 and 39.87 respectively (Table cited in results).
In a human preference study with 20 participants evaluating 60 generated videos, LUVE achieved 63.5% preference for overall video quality over competing methods (Table 4).
4K video generation with LUVE takes 91 minutes of inference time and requires 39.32 GiB of memory (Table 8).

flDGB9On0h.text: When trained on data generated by independent latent factors, transformers learn representations decomposed into orthogonal subspaces per factor, with cumulative explained variance converging to about 10 dimensions rather than the 242 dimensions needed for a joint (non-factored) representation (Figure 2, Section 4.1).

Over training, per-factor subspaces evolve from overlapping to approximately orthogonal, with the first two principal components per factor becoming mutually orthogonal, and this factorization emerges first in the token embeddings (Figure 3).
For five independent parallel factors, the theoretical joint-state dimensionality of 3^N - 1 is reduced by the model to a factored representation scaling linearly at 2N dimensions (Figure 1).

When data is generated by an indecomposable process (epsilon-corrupted, non-factorizable data), transformers initially learn a lossy factored representation and only later expand dimensionality to improve fidelity, indicating an inductive bias toward factored representations (Figure 4, Section 4.3).

When factors are conditionally dependent via a chain structure rather than fully independent, models expand their effective representational dimensionality beyond the fully-independent case while still preserving tensor/factored structure (Section 4.2).

vUpEe4yd1T.text: Reverse Flow Matching (RFM) generalizes Boltzmann-distribution-targeted reinforcement learning from diffusion policies to flow policies by allowing flexible, non-Gaussian source distributions p_0 within the linear interpolation X_t = alpha_t X_1 + beta_t X_0 (Section 4).

Prior noise-expectation and gradient-expectation policy-optimization families are recovered as special cases of RFM's posterior score formulation using isotropic coefficients with eta=0 and eta=1 respectively (Equation 25).

Across 8 DeepMind Control Suite continuous-control environments, RFM is the only algorithm among those tested (SAC, QSM, QNE, DQS) that performs consistently well across all environments, showing substantially better stability than the baselines (Section 5).

RFM's target policy is derived from the Boltzmann distribution pi_new(a|s) proportional to exp(Q(s,a)/lambda), with the posterior score relationship for Gaussian sources given in Equation 24 (Section 4, Equation 24).

Q7lEZjtDKO.text: Theorem 1 formulates the optimal sequential treatment allocation problem in contextual bandits as a dynamic program with Markov state (Delta_i, Gamma_i) representing covariate imbalance statistics (Theorem 1, Section 3).

Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 extend the dynamic-programming formulation to dynamic settings with carryover effects, decomposing the problem into an across-day Bellman recursion over N days and a within-day finite-horizon MDP solvable via reinforcement learning (Theorem 2, Theorem 3, Section 4).

The proposed robust sequential design (RSD) bounds the worst-case mean squared error of the estimated treatment effect under model misspecification via an orthogonalization technique, remaining valid when the true outcome model contains unknown nonlinear components (Section 3).

In synthetic contextual bandit experiments with both additive and interactive treatment effects, and in dynamic settings with time horizons T in {6, 12} using 400-1000 simulation replications, RSD consistently outperforms random assignment, switchback designs, and Neyman-balanced procedures (Section 5).
RSD is evaluated on real-world data from a ride-sharing company in addition to synthetic experiments, demonstrating effectiveness beyond simulation (Section 5).

3jsh1kSoYk.text: MechVQA comprises 3,281 high-density mechanical drawing images paired with 20,778 question-answer pairs, split 8:1:1 for train/validation/test at the drawing level (Section 3.4).

MechVQA organizes questions into three capability axes (Recognition, Reasoning, Judging) spanning ten fine-grained subtasks, including Dimension & Annotation, Geometric Calculation, and Anomaly Detection (Section 3.2).
MechVL-4B-RL attains an 84.85 total score, exceeding Gemini-3-Pro-Preview (77.28) by 7.57 points and outperforming GPT-5 (75.44) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (71.20) (Table 2).
MechVL-4B-RL outperforms the strongest open-source baseline GLM-4.6V (78.91 total score) by 5.94 points (Table 2).
On the Reasoning capability axis, MechVL-4B-RL scores 77.04 versus Gemini-3-Pro-Preview's 57.42, while on Judging Gemini-3-Pro-Preview leads with 85.08 versus MechVL-4B-RL's 82.81 (Section 5.2).
Accuracy on MechVQA degrades with difficulty stratification: 94% on Easy questions, 79% on Medium, and 75% on Hard (Figure 3).

P64X2q1n1H.text: LaRA-VLA achieves a 97.9% average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, including 99.8% on the Object suite and 96.6% on the Long-horizon suite, outperforming DeepThinkVLA (97.0%) and π0.5 (96.8%) (Table 2).
On SimplerEnv-WidowX, LaRA-VLA reaches a 68.8% average success rate, exceeding visual CoT baselines UD-VLA (62.5%) and F1 (59.4%) (Table 3).
LaRA-VLA achieves 135 ms inference latency per rollout, representing up to a 90% reduction compared to explicit CoT-based VLA approaches (Figure 7).

LaRA-VLA uses a three-stage training curriculum: explicit CoT fine-tuning with visual prediction alignment, progressive replacement of discrete tokens with latent representations, and flow matching for continuous action generation (Equations 1-4).
On four long-horizon manipulation tasks on the Agilex Cobot Magic real-world platform, LaRA-VLA consistently outperforms ACT and GR00T N1.5 baselines (Figure 5).
LaRA-VLA introduces a LaRA Attention Mechanism that regulates cross-token information flow across text, visual, and action modalities during training (Figure 3).

WcsBsGO6SW.text: Theorem 3.4 proves that under the nonlinear mixture model and domain variability assumptions, content is identifiable via an invertible mapping, and when differential independence holds with a full-rank style Jacobian, style is also identifiable via an invertible mapping (Theorem 3.4).

Content-Style Differential Independence (Assumption 3.1) requires that content-induced and style-induced tangent subspaces on the data manifold be orthogonal, i.e., R(J_c g) ⊥ R(J_s^(n) g), rather than requiring statistical independence or a sparse Jacobian (Assumption 3.1).

Theorem 3.6 shows that when orthogonality is only approximate (violated by an angle up to π/2 − ξ), content remains fully identifiable while the learned style representation retains a content-dependence bounded by a term scaling with sin(ξ) (Theorem 3.6).
On counterfactual generation, CSDI-GAN achieves FID scores of 4.4 on AFHQ and 4.3 on CelebA-HQ, outperforming I-StyleGAN and Block Independence GAN baselines (Table 1a).
On domain translation, CSDI-GAN achieves FID scores of 7.1 on AFHQ (33 domains) and 12.9 on CelebA-HQ (2 domains) (Table 1b).

CSDI-GAN enforces Jacobian orthogonality via a stochastic regularizer computed with Hutchinson's trace estimator, avoiding explicit storage of the d×d_c and d×d_s Jacobian matrices for high-dimensional images (Section 4).

WALBUqiamf.text: MVR-cache improves cache hit rate by up to 37% over the state-of-the-art vCache method under the always-cache protocol on the SemCacheSearchQueries dataset (Section 5).
MVR-cache improves cache hit rate by 9% over vCache on SemCacheClassification at error-rate bound δ=0.01 (Section 5).

MVR-cache reduces cumulative end-to-end inference time relative to vCache on all four benchmarks, e.g., 383.32 vs 408.49 minutes on SemCacheClassification and 1504.43 vs 1536.00 minutes on QNLI, an up to 6% latency reduction (Table 1).

MVR-cache is compared against vCache, ColBERT-style token-level multi-vector retrieval, and POQD performance-oriented query decomposition across four datasets: SemCacheClassification (45K prompts), SemCacheSearchQueries (150K), PromptBench (38K), and QNLI (29K) (Section 5).
MVR-cache maintains error rates below the user-specified bound δ=0.01 while achieving higher hit rates than vCache, preserving vCache's correctness guarantees (Figures 4-5).

m4TAzup6Yc.text: Theorem 3.1 (i.i.d. noise) and Theorem 4.1 (Markovian noise) bound the Wasserstein distance between the centered-scaled steady state Y^(α) = (X^(α) − x*)/√α and its Gaussian limit N(0, Σ_Y) by U√α log(1/α) (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1).
Proposition 3.1 establishes an explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein bound of order O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) for constant-stepsize SGD on smooth, strongly convex objectives (Proposition 3.1).

Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 extend the same O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) Wasserstein bound to linear stochastic approximation with a Hurwitz matrix and to contractive nonlinear stochastic approximation, respectively (Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, Section 3.2.2, Section 3.2.3).

For one-dimensional projections, the paper derives a non-uniform Berry-Esseen-type tail bound |P(⟨Y^(α),ζ⟩ > a) − P(Z_ζ > a)| ≤ C_d α^{1/4} log^{1/2}(1/α) / a, which improves as the deviation level a grows (Section 4).
Proposition 4.1 extends the Gaussian approximation and tail bounds for SGD, linear SA, and contractive nonlinear SA from i.i.d. noise to Markovian noise (Proposition 4.1, Section 4).
Proposition 5.1 shows a different convergence rate of order α^{1/h} for constant-stepsize SA applied to general convex objectives with Gibbs-type limiting distributions (Proposition 5.1, Section 5).

J9cU4mVavU.text: Chain-of-Glimpse-7B achieves 83.3% average accuracy on NExTQA, compared to 79.7% for the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline (Table I).
On out-of-domain benchmarks, Chain-of-Glimpse improves Video-Holmes accuracy by +3.7 points to 42.5%, and reaches 36.2% on CG-Bench-Reasoning and 47.5% on VRBench (Table II).

An ablation adding SFT, then GRPO, then the Object-Grounded Video Reasoning Formulation (OGVRF) shows progressive gains from a 79.7% baseline to 80.6% (+SFT), 81.4% (+SFT+GRPO), 82.3% (+OGVRF), and 83.3% for the full model on NExTQA (Table III).
On long videos with 1,000+ frames, incorporating OGVRF raises accuracy from 77.9% to 84.2% (Section on long-video performance / Table III analysis).

The Multi-turn Decision Policy is trained via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on trajectories generated by Monte Carlo Tree Search, and a reward-balance coefficient alpha=0.5 is found optimal (Figure 4b).
Chain-of-Glimpse-7B also improves over baseline on EgoSchema (62.2%, +2.2) and STAR (74.9%, +1.7) (Table IV).

rLO2NTUHSW.text: Elastic Attention's Attention Router assigns each attention head to Full Attention or Sparse Attention mode based on input hidden states, adding only 0.27M parameters per layer (Section 3.1).

Training uses Gumbel-Softmax annealing with a straight-through estimator to keep routing discrete at inference while differentiable during training, and the full pipeline completes within 12 hours on 8xA800 GPUs over roughly 0.74B training tokens without modifying backbone parameters (Section 3.2, Section 4.1).

On LongBench-E, Elastic Attention achieves competitive or superior average performance across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, with Model Sparsity Ratio (Omega_MSR) dynamically ranging from 0.63 to 0.87 depending on task category (Table 1).
On RULER (up to 256K context) and LongBench-V2, Elastic Attention attains the best average performance among compared methods (Table 2).

Downstream tasks split into sparsity-robust tasks (e.g., summarization) that tolerate high sparsity and sparsity-sensitive tasks (e.g., QA) that degrade sharply beyond a threshold sparsity level (Figure 2, Section 2.2).

An ablation on router capacity finds an intermediate hidden dimension of 4xd' gives the best performance-efficiency tradeoff, while a fully-sparse XA-SSA configuration degrades accuracy but yields substantial speedups (Table 3, Table 4, Section 5.4).

tt4UrPSGTo.text: KT-MFLD (Kernel-Thinned Mean Field Langevin Dynamics) reduces per-iteration computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N^{3/2}) by applying kernel thinning (kt-split-Compress) to reduce N particles to a coreset of size M=O(sqrt(N)) at each step (Section 3).

Theorem 3.3 shows that for sufficiently large N and T with an appropriate step size, KT-MFLD's finite-particle approximation error scales as O(N^{-1}(log N)^3), matching standard MFLD up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 3.3).

Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 require boundedness, Lipschitzness, and convexity of q1, q2, R1, plus membership of q1 and the gradient of q2 in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and the paper verifies these hold for mean-field neural networks, MMD quantization, and predictively-oriented (PrO) posteriors (Section 3, Section 4).

Experiments on student-teacher networks, MMD quantization, and PrO posteriors show KT-MFLD consistently outperforms random subsampling and random-batch baselines under equal computational budgets (Section 4).

The authors note the thinning-induced error term suffers a curse of dimensionality, since the constant term can be exponentially small in dimension d, worsening particle-complexity dependence in high dimensions (Section on limitations).

KmS7pdFBEh.text: BroRL scales reinforcement learning by increasing rollouts per example to N=512 rather than extending training steps, yielding continuous performance gains beyond the plateau ProRL exhibits after roughly 3K steps (Section 4.2).

Theorem 1 decomposes the change in correct-answer probability mass into a sampled portion that always contributes a non-negative gain and an unsampled portion whose second moment decays as p^2(1-p)^N per Lemma 2, driving variance toward zero as rollout size N grows (Theorem 1, Lemma 2, Section 2).

On math benchmarks BroRL reaches 63.03 versus ProRL's 62.02 and a 61.69 baseline; on code tasks BroRL achieves 54.20 versus ProRL's 52.74 and a 52.00 baseline; on Reasoning Gym BroRL reaches 63.09 versus ProRL's 61.45 and a 61.29 baseline (Tables 3-5).
BroRL's dynamic sampling pass rate is 62% compared to ProRL's 41%, and generation throughput is 72.4 samples/s versus ProRL's 36.5 samples/s, roughly a 2x improvement (Table 2).

A paired t-test across more than 10,000 data points comparing BroRL to ProRL yields a mean difference of 0.0033 with t=4.84 and p=6.5x10^-7, indicating statistically significant improvement (Section 4.2).

QHKJhiz88q.text: EgoTSR-Data comprises 46 million samples split into three curriculum stages: 15M chain-of-thought samples, 16M tag samples, and 15M long-tag samples, sourced from the Agibot-World egocentric video dataset (Section 3, Dataset description).
EgoTSR achieves 92.4% long-horizon accuracy (averaged over forward and inverse reasoning) and 87.5% average short-horizon accuracy, versus a 95.2% human perception baseline (Table 1).

The three-stage curriculum (Knowledge Guidance via CoT supervision, Capability Internalization via weak supervision, Generalization Consolidation via long-horizon sequences) is essential: the full sequential curriculum reaches 92.4% accuracy versus 69.6% for a mixed (non-curriculum) baseline (Section 3.1, Table 2).
Removing the Subtask Planner component drops accuracy from 92.4% to 81.1%, showing the Reasoning-Enhanced Task Decomposition module is a key contributor (Section 3.2, Table 2).

EgoTSR is evaluated against more than 25 models, including closed-source (GPT-4o, Gemini) and open-source 2D (InternVL, DeepSeek-VL2) and 3D (LL3DA, Chat-Scene) systems, and outperforms them on the dual-level (short- and long-horizon) evaluation framework (Section 3.3, Table 1).

AyrNR1ExN5.text: The ℓ∞,ε-thickening volume ratio between order-n and order-m discontinuity sets in sparse mixture-of-experts routing decays as (ε/R)^(n-m), showing higher-order discontinuities become negligible at large scales (Theorem 4.4, Remark 4.5).
Order-n discontinuity thickening measures scale as ε^n·R^(D-n), with normalized volume decaying as (ε/R)^n, confirming that lower-order discontinuities dominate the routing topology (Theorem 4.2).

Under random diffusion perturbations of the router logits, exit from a top-k selection region occurs almost surely on an order-1 discontinuity, with probability zero of hitting an order-n discontinuity for n≥2 (Theorem 5.1).

The proposed SmoothSMoE mechanism, using a log-smoothstep function to boost logits within an adaptive margin ε near discontinuities, achieves 32.72 validation perplexity on WikiText-103 versus 33.79 for standard SMoE (Section 6, Table 1).
SmoothSMoE improves average accuracy by 0.47-0.57% across five GLUE NLU tasks under k=2 and k=4 expert settings (Table 2).
On the DomainBed vision benchmark, SmoothSMoE yields an average 0.56% accuracy gain over SMoE, including a 2.1% improvement on the TerraIncognita domain (Table 3).

uKbD73kfgM.text: SafeMVDrive-generated safety-critical videos increase the collision rate of the UniAD end-to-end planner by approximately 30% relative to testing on original NuScenes scenes (Table 1).

The two-stage collision-evasion simulation pipeline achieves a 0.202 average sample-level collision rate and a 3.378 average scene-level collision rate across 1s/2s/3s horizons, compared to 0.151 and 1.854 respectively for the collision-stage-only ablation (Table 4).
The GRPO-finetuned VLM-based critical vehicle selector achieves an F1-score of 0.710, versus 0.489 for the base 7B model and 0.655 for the SFT-finetuned baseline (Table 3).

Generated videos reach a realism score of 0.560±0.122 in a two-alternative-forced-choice user study, corresponding to 87% of the realism score of a state-of-the-art video generator conditioned on original (non-safety-critical) trajectories, with an FID of 20.626 (Section on video quality evaluation).
The released dataset comprises 41 diverse 9-second multi-view driving scenes generated for safety-critical stress testing (Dataset description).

KjKT2vzkyb.text: The 7B-parameter FOCUS model achieves 67.7% average mIoU across the TAO, GOT, and ICL-LASOT benchmarks in the 4-shot setting, exceeding Qwen2-VL-72B (55.0%) and InternVL2-76B (56.1%) despite being roughly an order of magnitude smaller (Table 1).
FOCUS's attention loss (Stage 1) forces query-image tokens to preferentially attend to bounding-box tokens via a margin-based hinge loss ℒ_bbox = (1/N)∑max(0, μ - Δᵢ)² (Section 5.2, Equations 5-9).
Stage 2 applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a combined IoU-based and formatting-correctness reward to directly optimize localization accuracy (Section 5.4, Equation 13).
Ablation on the TAO dataset (4-shot) shows that adding GRPO on top of SFT plus attention loss raises accuracy from 57.1% to 68.5%, an 11.4-point gain (Table 3).
In 2-shot generalization tests on PerMIRS and PerSeg, FOCUS outperforms the IPLoc baseline by 19.1 and 13.5 percentage points respectively (Table 2).

kVBDNMTGWh.text: At 2-bit precision on Qwen-3-8B, UniSVQ achieves 67.95% average 0-shot QA accuracy, outperforming scalar methods SpinQuant (52.61%) and OSTQuant (57.47%), and approaching vector-quantization method QuIP# (67.55%) (Table 1).
On Qwen-3-32B at 2-bit, UniSVQ reaches 76.15% average accuracy versus 78.01% for FP16, 68.29% for scalar OSTQuant, and 76.30% for vector QuIP# (Table 1).

On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, UniSVQ delivers 1.68x higher inference throughput than FP16 (101.65 vs 60.38 tokens/sec) and reduces peak GPU memory from 15.72 GB to 3.87 GB, while exceeding the throughput of vector-quantization baselines AQLM (70.97 tok/s) and QuIP# (79.60 tok/s) (Table 8).

UniSVQ parameterizes codewords as affine transformations of integer lattices, requiring only 20 additional parameters per weight matrix compared to roughly 2048 bytes for a comparable vector-quantization codebook, a 64x reduction in auxiliary storage (Figure 1).
On Qwen-3-4B, UniSVQ achieves a quantization MSE of 7.40x10^-5 and SNR of 8.48 dB, versus -3.45 dB for GPTQ, an 11.9 dB improvement (Table 4).

4vztmTrGhd.text: For two-layer linear networks trained on single-index targets, Theorem 5.3 gives exact closed-form test-loss expressions after one and two gradient steps, with the one-step loss containing linear signal-alignment terms plus quadratic/interaction over-updating terms, and the two-step loss exhibiting higher-order dependence on the product η₁η₂ of the two layers' learning rates.

Corollary 5.4 shows that for a learning-rate budget η₁+η₂=2h^α with 1<α≤3/2, symmetric learning rates η₁=η₂=h^α are suboptimal after one gradient step but become locally optimal after two steps in sufficiently wide two-layer networks.

For three-layer linear networks, Theorem 5.5 derives analogous one- and two-step test-loss formulas under a critical learning-rate scaling η₁,η₂≤O(h), a stricter regime than the O(h√h) scaling used for two-layer networks.
Corollary 5.6 demonstrates a similar transition from asymmetric to balanced optimal learning rates in three-layer networks for 0<α≤2/3.

Proposition 5.1 decomposes each layer's gradient as G_ℓ^t = B_ℓ^t - A_ℓ^t, where A terms capture data-aligned components and B terms capture self-interaction effects that are suppressed by a factor of 1/(√h - 1) below the critical learning-rate threshold.

GJblFvJcMb.text: Formulates optimal treatment selection from conjoint data as finding a stochastic policy over combinatorial profiles that maximizes expected outcome Q(π), rather than a single best profile (Section 2.2, Equation 1).

Uses the Delta method to propagate parameter uncertainty from the fitted outcome model into asymptotically valid variance-covariance estimates for the estimated optimal policy and its value (Section 2.2).

Models strategic settings (e.g., two competing candidates) as a zero-sum minimax game max_πA min_πB Q(πA, πB), invoking von Neumann's minimax theorem to guarantee equilibrium existence (Section 2.3, Equation 3).

Derives a closed-form average-case optimal policy π^{a*} = C^{-1}B under pairwise (two-way) interaction effects, using an L2-regularization term λn·||π^a − p||² that shrinks the solution toward the empirical profile distribution p (Section 2.2, Proposition 1).

Simulation studies show RMSE convergence with sample size across 5–20 factors (variance dominating bias) and confidence interval coverage approaching the nominal 95% level for n ≥ 5000 in the adversarial setting (Section 3.2, Section 3.4).

Applies the minimax framework to 2016 U.S. presidential election conjoint data, finding that adversarial equilibrium predictions align more closely with actual electoral outcomes than non-strategic (single-optimizer) predictions (Section 4).

4uM4P5NaLU.text: DIVE synthesizes agentic tool-use tasks 'evidence-first' by executing 373 real-world tools across domains (Finance, Biology, Medicine, Academia) and deriving tasks from resulting traces, rather than generating tasks before execution (Section on synthesis configuration).
Dive-8B improves average out-of-distribution accuracy by +22.2 points across 9 benchmarks and outperforms the strongest 8B baseline by +68% (Table 2).
On GAIA, Dive-8B (RL) reaches 61.2% accuracy versus 50.0% for the WebExplorer-8B baseline (Table 2).
Diversity-only scaling (12k tasks across 1→4 domains) outperforms quantity-only scaling (12k→48k tasks with fixed Search/Browse tools) despite using 4× less data (Figure 3a).

Structural diversity metrics show Dive's 48k SFT trajectories yield 105% more unique tool-call graph patterns and cover 153 vs. 65 tool-call topology classes (+135%) compared to the Gen-DR baseline (Table 3).
During 100 steps of RL training, task accuracy improves alongside continued expansion of unique tool-call graphs and topology classes, indicating RL further amplifies generalization (Figure 4).

P3b1028tNC.text: Identifies 'prompt forgetting' in multimodal diffusion transformers (SD3, SD3.5, FLUX.1), where CKNNA-measured semantic neighborhood preservation of text tokens declines monotonically across network depth (Section 4.1).

Uses lightweight MLP probing classifiers on five linguistic attribute categories (noun, adjective, spatial-relation, numeral, others) to show probing accuracy declines monotonically with depth, with spatial-relation tokens degrading fastest (Section 4.2).

Proposes training-free prompt reinjection combining distribution anchoring (layer-normalization-based rescaling) and geometry alignment (orthogonal Procrustes transform) to reinject shallow-layer (layer 1–2) text features into later transformer blocks with reinjection weight w=0.025 (Section 5, Equations 8–11).
On GenEval, prompt reinjection yields +6.48% overall improvement for SD3.5 and +5.64% for FLUX, with the largest gains on position-related sub-tasks (Table 1).
On DPG, improvements are +1.69% for SD3 and +3.35% for SD3.5, with consistent gains also reported on T2I-CompBench++ across color, shape, texture, and spatial-relation attributes (Table 3).

Ablations show full-layer reinjection outperforms restricted-range injection, geometry alignment (rotation) contributes more than distribution anchoring alone, gains are stable across CFG guidance scales 4.0–8.0, and the method adds under 9% additional FLOPs per target block (Tables 4–7).

hNiIIKdz3V.text: AIR integrates detection, containment, recovery, and eradication into the agent execution loop via a domain-specific language (DSL) defining rules with trigger, check, and remediate components (Section 3.1).

For the Code Agent across 25 risk categories, AIR achieves 90%+ detection and 85–100% eradication where applicable, including 26/26 detection for eval injection and 27/27 for cryptographic predictability (Table 1).
For the Embodied Agent across 10 hazard types, AIR achieves 100% detection matching successful executions and 94–100% remediation success (Table 2).
For the Computer-Use Agent across 7 risk categories, AIR achieves 83–100% detection and up to 100% remediation where applicable (Table 3).

LLM-generated guardrail rules approach developer-authored rule performance, e.g., 84.56% detection / 91.02% eradication for the Code Agent and 95.97% detection / 88.81% remediation / 90.21% eradication for the Embodied Agent (Table 5).
An ablation on structured remediation shows Embodied Agent success rate improving from 80.95% to 92.31% (Section 4.5 / Appendix B).

ld40RIJnpb.text: Defines Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics, showing WAAD peaks correspond to semantic boundaries with token entropies 51.97% above a random baseline (Section 4.1, Table 2).

Establishes a recurring 'preplan-and-anchor' rhythm: receiver/global-focused attention heads identify shared anchor tokens with a 171.49% co-occurrence lift, and FAI peaks follow or coincide with WAAD peaks with a 42.47% lift (Section 4.2).

Introduces three RL credit-assignment strategies: local-chunk credit amplifying advantages at WAAD peak boundaries (Eq. 14), global-anchor credit emphasizing top-40% quantile FAI tokens (Eq. 16), and coupled rhythm credit combining both via a redistribution parameter α (Eq. 18), each using a γ_amp = 1.5 amplification factor.
On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, coupled rhythm credit improves Qwen3-8B-Base by +5.0 points on AIME25 and +6.3 points on AMC23, with +3.8 points average across benchmarks (Table 4).
On simpler reasoning tasks, coupled rhythm credit improves Countdown accuracy from 52.6% to 63.1% (+10.5 points) and CrossThink-QA by +2.1 points (Table 3).
Ablations confirm selecting the top-40% FAI-quantile tokens for credit redistribution outperforms selecting the bottom-40% by 6.3–14.7 points across datasets (Table 5).

f5JmWpV01Y.text: CoT reasoning trajectories show an abrupt bifurcation into an Uncertainty Region (high entropy, stochastic exploration, below 20% accuracy) followed by a Confidence Region (low entropy, deterministic convergence, above 60% accuracy) (Figure 1).

A CUSUM-based sequential change-point detector, calibrated training-free on 100 samples via histogram density estimation, is used to locate the onset of the Confidence Region using a single threshold hyperparameter h (Section 3).

For early exit, CUSUM achieves 63.06% average accuracy with 11.1% token reduction across DeepSeek-7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-14B, versus DEER's 59.78% accuracy at 14.7% token reduction and Dynasor's 58.70% accuracy at 11.3% token reduction (Table 2).

The normalized change-point location (fraction of trajectory length before the Confidence Region begins) is 30-34% for easy problems versus 52-56% for hard problems, with the change-point negatively correlated with final accuracy (r = -0.26 to -0.45) (Table 1).

CUSUM-weighted test-time-scaling voting outperforms self-consistency voting, with the accuracy gap widening at larger sampling budgets, reaching +3.33% over self-consistency for Qwen3-4B at N=64 samples (Figure 4).

Proposition 3.4 bounds the expected CUSUM detection delay under the null (no change) as e^h ≤ E∞[τ_h] ≤ C·e^h, and Theorem 3.5 shows detection delay scales as log(γ)/D_KL(f1‖f0) asymptotically (Proposition 3.4, Theorem 3.5).

FNZs7SLEEI.text: After 4 billion tokens of pre-training, GlobalRegret reaches 33.9% average downstream accuracy and LocalRegret reaches 32.2%, compared to a 30.2% baseline across BoolQ, ARC-C, WinoGrande, PIQA, HellaSwag, CSQA, and MMLU (Table showing 4B-token downstream results).
GlobalRegret improves BoolQ accuracy by 18.1 percentage points over baseline (61.0% vs. 42.9%), the largest single-task gain reported, while LocalRegret reaches 48.5% on BoolQ (BoolQ results table).

GlobalRegret conditions its teacher distribution on bidirectional context with the target position masked, while LocalRegret's teacher extends the causal context by exactly one future token, and both use a regret loss minimizing the KL divergence from teacher to student (Section on Two Teacher Configurations / dual-view architecture).

The regret pre-training scheme adds no extra model parameters and requires only one additional inference-mode forward pass per training step, at the cost of a 1.8-2.0x increase in wall-clock training time with unchanged per-GPU memory footprint (~72GB on A100) (Section on Computational Efficiency).

GlobalRegret provides the largest gains on reading-comprehension and factual-knowledge tasks requiring long-range context, whereas LocalRegret is strongest on commonsense-reasoning tasks emphasizing local coherence (Performance Patterns discussion).

jjYEPizDXZ.text: Video-based Scene Change Detection (VSCD) is defined as predicting a pixel-wise change mask for a query frame given a reference RGB video and a query RGB video of the same environment, without requiring temporal synchronization or geometric calibration (Section on problem formulation).

The paper builds a benchmark with over 1.1 million annotated frames, comprising a synthetic split (VSCD-Syn) of 1,090 video pairs across 218 environments rendered via AI2-THOR and Unreal Engine, plus a real-world test split (VSCD-Real) of 8 video pairs totaling 17k frames (Dataset section).

VSCDNet uses a three-stage architecture: ViT-based frame-level temporal alignment, differentiable-warping patch-level correspondence, and confidence-aware fusion before high-resolution decoding (Figure 2).

VSCDNet achieves 36.6% F1 on the synthetic VSCD-Syn test set and 25.4% F1 on the real-world VSCD-Real set, outperforming image-based baselines (CSCDNet, DR-TANet, C-3PO, ZSSCD, GeSCF) and video-based baselines (TCF-LMO, PBCD-MC) across difficulty categories of video length, graphics quality, and object change density (Table 3).

Real-world robot deployment on a Stretch 3 mobile robot validates the method with a 62.1% hit rate for identifying abnormal-event frames in visual surveillance and correct classification of 2 of 4 newly introduced objects in an object incremental-learning task (Section 6).

CYNip2SNsg.text: LC-QAT replaces discrete codebook lookups with a learnable affine mapping c = Az + B over discrete quaternary vectors z, giving 4^d possible codewords and eliminating nearest-neighbor search during 2-bit vector-quantization-aware training (Section 3).
LC-QAT uses a Differentiable Gradient Estimator (DGE) in place of the Straight-Through Estimator to avoid the pronounced loss spike observed early in training (Section on gradient estimation).

On LLaMA-3-8B, LC-QAT trained with only 4B tokens reaches 9.38 WikiText perplexity and 73.42% average zero-shot accuracy, matching or beating ParetoQ's 72.07% average accuracy which used 30B tokens, a roughly 97% reduction in training data (Table 2).
On Qwen-3-8B and Qwen-3-1.7B, LC-QAT attains 10.23 and 13.44 WikiText perplexity respectively, versus PV-Tuning's 10.65 and 17.43 (Table 1).

On instruction-following evaluation, LC-QAT applied to a 1.7B model reaches a 50.35 average score versus BitNet 2B4T's 48.07, while using about 0.1% of BitNet's training data (4B vs. 4T tokens) (Table 3).

Ablations show that removing LC-PTQ initialization severely degrades accuracy (Table 4), end-to-end training outperforms coordinate-descent optimization under identical initialization (Table 5), and LC-QAT achieves 101.65 tokens/second inference on LLaMA-3-8B versus 23.80 tokens/second for QuIP# D4 (Table 6).

qeeD6aZLLX.text: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, ThoughtFold reduces average token usage by approximately 56% (from 10,234 to 4,496 tokens) while improving accuracy from 64.56% to 67.38% (Table 1).

On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, ThoughtFold reduces tokens by 42.6% with accuracy improving from 71.52% to 72.50%, and on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B it achieves 41.9% and 39.4% token reductions with accuracy gains of 2.06% and 1.94% respectively (Table 1).

ThoughtFold identifies redundant reasoning via a two-phase introspective procedure: tail truncation using binary search on prefix length to remove self-repetition, and internal folding using attention-based importance scoring to remove off-target exploratory attempts (Section on the two-phase redundancy identification method).

A masked preference optimization objective penalizes redundant exploratory reasoning while explicitly rewarding 'Fold Anchors'—the reasoning steps that bridge logical gaps after redundancy is removed—folding long CoTs into more concise paths (Section on Masked Preference Optimization).

ThoughtFold is evaluated across five benchmarks—GSM8K, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, MATH-500, and GPQA—showing consistent improvements over standard GRPO and the efficient-reasoning baseline S-GRPO (Benchmark evaluation section).

BQPtGzdE5T.text: On the MiniGrid benchmark, MINT-based planning attains near-expert returns (rewards of 9.29-9.90) while issuing only 1-3 binary questions per unknown object, with success rates of 97-100% (Table 1, Section 5).
On Atari Pacman, MINT achieves a return of 434.9±32.1 with average query time 6.8±5.5, outperforming pure RL baselines DQN (271.3) and PPO (325.0) (Table 2, Section 5).
On the NVIDIA Isaac Gym search-and-rescue drone scenario, MINT* achieves 100% success on the primary target and 95% on the hidden target, versus 47% and 5% for GPT-4o (Table 3, Section 5).

Theorem 4.4 provides an upper bound on the return gap for a system operating under an unknown knowledge gap, using pseudo-Lipschitz continuity of the optimal Q-value established in Lemma 4.3 (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.4).

The MINT framework builds a decision tree over possible knowledge states and uses an uncertainty-aware DQN together with an LLM to generate targeted elicitation queries for a human (Section 4, Section 4.2).

qZVcGlU5lN.text: Theorem 1 shows that if a valid adjustment set for the causal effect of X on Y exists among observed variables, then a valid adjustment set also exists within the Markov blanket MB(X) of the treatment (Theorem 1).

Theorem 6 establishes that the Local Covariate Selection (LCS) method is sound and complete: it returns the correct causal effect whenever identification rules R1-R3 apply, and correctly reports non-identifiability only when identification is theoretically impossible (Theorem 6, Section 4).

LCS operates without the pretreatment assumption (allowing post-treatment variables) and without causal sufficiency (allowing latent confounders via MAGs/PAGs), with complexity O(|MB+|^2 2^|MB+| + |S| 2^|Z|) that is exponential only in the local neighborhood size rather than the full variable set (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
On the Jobs dataset (2,936 samples), LCS achieves 3.55% bias relative to the ground-truth ATT of $886, outperforming LSAS (11.67% bias), CEELS (22.87% bias), and LDP (1635.98% bias) (Section 5).
On the Cattaneo2 dataset (4,642 births), LCS estimates the effect of maternal smoking on birth weight within the established reference range of 200-250g (Section 5).

On synthetic benchmark networks (alarm: 37 nodes, child: 20 nodes, hailfinder: 56 nodes, win95pts: 76 nodes), LCS achieves lower relative estimation error while requiring fewer conditional independence tests than baselines (Section 5, Table 1).

jHUEoBLQpn.text: Under Assumption 3.1 (bounded p-th centered moment, p-BCM, for p in (1,2]), Theorem 4.2 bounds the generalization gap between population and empirical gradients by 4ε + C_p σ_p n^{-(p-1)/p} using a truncation argument to handle heavy-tailed noise (Theorem 4.2, Section 4).

For Clipped SGD (Algorithm 1), Proposition 5.1 gives an on-average stability bound ε_c ≤ 2Lγ√(T/n) Σ η_t, and Theorem 5.2/Corollary 5.3 derive a resulting population gradient bound with rate O(n^{-(p-1)/(3(3p-2))}) (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3).

For Mini-Batch Normalized SGD (Algorithm 2), Theorem 5.5 and Corollary 5.6 establish an improved generalization rate of O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) compared to the clipped-SGD rate (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.5, Corollary 5.6).
For Normalized SGD with Momentum (Algorithm 3), Theorem 5.9 matches the O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) rate of the normalized batch variant (Section 5.3, Theorem 5.9).

The combined clipping-plus-momentum method (Algorithm 4) achieves the same stability bound as momentum alone (Proposition 5.12) and a matching rate of O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) without dependence on the linear step-size term γ (Theorem 5.13, Section 5.4).

c3BVcHcSiR.text: Discrete Diffusion VLA achieves 96.3% average success rate on LIBERO across four task suites (Spatial 97.2%, Object 98.6%, Goal 97.4%, Long 92.0%), a 0.9 point improvement over OpenVLA-OFT (Discrete) at 95.4% (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On SimplerEnv-Fractal (Google Robot), the method attains 71.2% visual-matching average and 64.1% overall average, outperforming π0 (58.8% VM) and π0+FAST (61.9% VM) (Table 2, Section 4.2).
