On SimplerEnv-Bridge (WidowX Robot), the method achieves 49.3% overall success, outperforming π0 and π0-FAST baselines (Table 3, Section 4.2).
The method requires only T=12 function evaluations at inference versus L=56 for autoregressive decoding on the LIBERO setup, a 4.7x reduction in function evaluations (Section 4.4).

The approach applies discrete diffusion to tokenized action chunks within a unified vision-language-action transformer, training with masked-token cross-entropy loss and performing inference via iterative confidence-based re-masking (Section 3, Section 3.4).

WTg6EIcXso.text: Semi-LAR's full model achieves 27.620 PSNR / 0.897 SSIM / 0.0493 LPIPS on the semi-supervised (8K labeled + 8K unlabeled) setting, retaining roughly 96% of full-supervision performance while using one-third of the labeled data (Table 3, Section 4).

Ablating the Dependable Repository (DR) drops PSNR from 27.620 to 26.746, and ablating the flare-aware contrastive regularization loss drops PSNR to 26.711, showing both components are necessary for pseudo-label stability and reducing halo artifacts (Table 2, Section 4).

On the FlareX cross-dataset benchmark the method attains 19.960 PSNR and 0.141 LPIPS, and on the real-world FlareReal600 benchmark it attains 20.368 PSNR and 0.260 LPIPS (Table 1, Table 4, Section 4).
Adding an NR-IQA (MUSIQ-based) quality gate on top of momentum-only pseudo-label updates raises PSNR from 26.982 to 27.620 (Table 7, Section 4).

Even under full supervision, augmenting training with 8K additional unlabeled images improves PSNR from 27.633 to 28.045, indicating the unlabeled data provides value beyond label scarcity (Table 5, Section 4).

The RaLiFormer generator uses Rank-Enhanced Linear Attention (ReLinA) for linear-complexity spatial modeling and a Directionally-Enhanced Spatial Module (DESM) to capture anisotropic flare structures, and is model-agnostic with no added inference-time overhead (Section 3.4, Appendix A).

q1KhliMwKP.text: In the adversarial regime, the proposed FTPL policy for decoupled bandits achieves O(sqrt(KT)) regret, matching the lower bound of Avner et al. 2012 (Theorem 1).

In the stochastic (SCA) regime, with perturbation parameter alpha in (1,3], the FTPL policy achieves a time-independent regret bound of O(K/Delta_min), improving on the standard MAB O(sum log T/Delta_i) bound (Theorem 2).
Setting alpha=3 yields a near-optimal best-of-both-worlds regret bound of O(sqrt((K/Delta_min) * sum(1/Delta_i)) + K/Delta_min) (Corollary 3).

The exploration probabilities q_{t,i} are computed via a closed-form approximation requiring only O(K log K) time per round through sorting, avoiding convex optimization or geometric resampling used by prior FTRL/FTPL decoupled-bandit methods (Equation 7, Algorithm 1).
In adversarial-regime experiments, the proposed method runs approximately 2020 times faster than the Decoupled-Tsallis-INF baseline while achieving comparable regret.
In stochastic-regime experiments, the method outperforms both the EB-TC pure-exploration policy and naive mixed exploration/exploitation policies.

JLgqmlc9S7.text: SIPO stabilizes preference optimization for diffusion models by clipping importance weights and masking out timesteps with high gradient variance, addressing off-policy instability identified in the analysis of effective timesteps (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
On CogVideoX-2B evaluated at 500 diffusion steps, SIPO attains a total score of 81.53, exceeding Diffusion-DPO (81.16), DPO-C&M (81.37), and the pretrained baseline (80.91) (Table 1).
At 1000 sampling steps, Diffusion-DPO's total score collapses to 67.28 while SIPO maintains stability at 81.68, demonstrating SIPO's robustness across step counts (Table 1).
SIPO generalizes across model scales, improving CogVideoX-5B to 82.28 (vs. Diffusion-DPO's 82.02) and WanX-1.3B to 84.78 (vs. Diffusion-DPO's 84.41) (Table 1).
In human evaluation over 200 prompts, SIPO-tuned outputs are ranked first 67% of the time against baseline methods (Figure 6).
An ablation on the temperature parameter beta shows SIPO's performance is robust across values, whereas Diffusion-DPO is highly sensitive to this hyperparameter (Section 4.3).

SdcOyjz34E.text: NeuroKalman formulates continuous UAV navigation prediction as a recursive Bayesian state estimation problem, combining a GRU-based prediction step with an MLLM-based measurement likelihood and a learnable Kalman gain correction step (Section 3.1-3.4).

Fine-tuned on only 10% of the full training data, NeuroKalman achieves a 25.86% success rate and 71.56m navigation error on the TravelUAV Test-Seen (L1 Full Split) benchmark, compared to 17.56% success rate and 99.79m navigation error for the TravelUAV-FT baseline under the same 10%-data regime (Section 4.2).
On the Test-Unseen-Object split, NeuroKalman achieves 32.48% success rate and 60.82% oracle success rate, outperforming the NavFoM foundation-model baseline (Section 4.2).
An ablation over memory history length shows the optimal setting is M=10 steps for the Kalman-filter memory module (Table 4).
An ablation comparing gain mechanisms shows the learnable Kalman gain outperforms a fixed gain value (Table 3).

88H3V90Wzo.text: Mean Flow Policy Optimization (MFPO) represents policies via Mean Flow models that learn average velocity rather than instantaneous velocity, reducing discretization error relative to diffusion-based policies (Section 4).
MFPO requires only 2 sampling steps at inference, compared to 16 steps for DIME and 20 steps each for MaxEntDP and DACER, while achieving comparable or superior returns (Section 5, Table 1).
MFPO's inference latency is 0.46ms per sample, roughly 50% faster than the diffusion-based baselines evaluated (Table 1).

MFPO reduces training time by approximately 50% compared to diffusion-based policies while matching or exceeding their performance across MuJoCo locomotion tasks and DeepMind Control Suite hard tasks (Section 5).
MFPO is validated on a 2-D Gaussian Mixture Model toy example and compared against SAC, TD3, DIME, FlowRL, MaxEntDP, DACER, and QVPO baselines (Section 5).

R8eRV29kGt.text: FedEBA+ formulates fair aggregation as a bi-level optimization problem with a constrained-entropy objective, yielding an analytic closed-form solution for the aggregation probability p_i = q_i*exp(F_i(x)/tau) / sum_j q_j*exp(F_j(x)/tau) in the inner loop (Section 4.1, Equation 4).

Theorem 5.1 proves convergence of FedEBA+ (Algorithm 1, with alpha=0) in non-convex federated learning settings, giving an explicit O(1/sqrt(mKT)) rate bound under L-smoothness, unbiased local gradients, and bounded gradient dissimilarity assumptions (Theorem 5.1).

On CIFAR-100, FedEBA+ attains 31.98% global accuracy with 13.75 variance, improving both accuracy and fairness (lower variance) relative to FedAvg (30.94% accuracy, 17.24 variance) and q-FFL (24.97% accuracy, 14.54 variance) (Table 2).
On Tiny-ImageNet, FedEBA+ reaches 63.75% global accuracy with 13.89 variance, compared to FedAvg's 61.99% accuracy/19.62 variance and q-FFL's 62.42% accuracy/15.44 variance (Table 2).

An ablation over the alignment angle threshold theta shows accuracy and fairness trade off against communication cost, e.g., theta=0 degrees gives 72.75% CIFAR-10 accuracy at 50.0% additional cost, while theta=90 degrees gives 70.1% accuracy at 0% additional cost (Table 3).

A toy two-client example (F1(x)=2(x-2)^2, F2(x)=0.5(x+4)^2) shows FedEBA+ producing a smaller performance gap between clients than both q-FFL and FedAvg from the same initial global model, illustrating improved fairness (Figure 1).

gFPPTokv9C.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes the Expectation Consistency Condition: canonical calibration under covariate shift holds for class k if and only if the conditional expectation of P(Y_k=1|X) matches between source and target distributions given the calibrated score S, which is strictly weaker than requiring full distributional alignment (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 proves the Expectation Consistency Loss (ECL) estimator has O(B/epsilon^2) sample complexity with an explicit finite-sample bound on the gap between empirical and population ECL, matching the complexity of histogram-binning-based ECE estimation (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.3 shows the mini-batch ECL formulation using auxiliary variables u_j^s and u_j^t yields an unbiased gradient estimator, E[∇_θ L̂_ecl^mini] = ∇_θ L̂_ecl, enabling standard SGD training (Section 3.5, Theorem 3.3).

ECL is extended to top-label calibration (Appendix D.1, Section E.1) and class-wise calibration (Appendix D.2, Section E.2), with differentiable soft-binning implementations for canonical, class-wise, and top-label variants given in Appendix F.

On MNIST-to-SVHN top-label calibration with LeNet-5, ECL reduces ECE to 21.5% versus 61.9% for the uncalibrated baseline; with ResNet20, ECL achieves 36.8% ECE versus 48.2% for PseudoCal; with DenseNet40, ECL achieves 38.4% ECE versus 80.8% uncalibrated (Table 2).

Table 1 shows ECL is the only compared method that simultaneously handles covariate shift, supports class-wise and canonical calibration, tolerates unbounded density ratios, and is mini-batch trainable, while Figure 2 reliability diagrams and Appendix Table 3 (source-vs-target calibration gap) further corroborate the approach on simulated data and the PACS dataset (Table 1, Figure 2, Appendix Table 3).

tSMZHXtJwZ.text: DAWN (Data-Anchored Warmup and Normalization) combines Implicit Warmup and Critic Normalization to address two failure modes in residual RL: cold-start pathology and structural scale mismatch (Section 4).

Implicit Warmup collects M=20K transitions under the base policy before training begins, and Figure 2 shows sample efficiency improves consistently as warmup transitions increase, while Figure 3 shows this prevents divergence of the Q-value grounding error (Section 3.1.1, Figures 2-3).

Explicit value pre-training (as opposed to implicit warmup) degrades performance because the entropy term in Soft-Q-style objectives introduces a strong negative bias when |alpha*log(pi)| exceeds |r|, as shown in Figure 4 (Section 3.1.2, Figure 4).

Applying Layer Normalization (or Head Normalization) to the critic network doubles critic sensitivity to residual actions (measured via the gradient norm ||grad_{a_res} Q||) and substantially improves learning efficiency compared to an unnormalized critic, with Layer Norm remaining stable across residual scales where Head Norm degrades at lambda=0.05 (Section 3.2.1, Figures 6-8).

On the ManiSkill and Adroit benchmark suite (8 tasks) using a Diffusion Policy base policy, DAWN converges to 90% success on PegInsertionSide roughly 6x faster than the Policy Decorator baseline, with low variance across seeds across all tasks (Section 5, Figures 11-12).

An ablation study shows removing either Implicit Warmup or Critic Normalization substantially degrades learning efficiency, confirming both components are necessary, and DAWN maintains strong performance when paired with a Behavior Transformer (BeT) base policy as well as Diffusion Policy (Figure 13, Figure 12).

AYy0lOycql.text: The EEmoDB-QA subset contains 1.2M question-answering pairs derived from 128k images (including 355k paired images for comparative tasks), spanning 55 analysis dimensions across 33 task categories (Section 3).
The EEmoDB-Assess subset contains 36k fine-grained emotional-assessment annotations curated from 25k images, balancing label accuracy against distributional consistency (Section 3).

EEmo-Logic is trained in two stages: Stage 1 uses supervised LoRA fine-tuning on EEmoDB-QA with cross-entropy loss for perception, ranking, and description tasks; Stage 2 applies Group Relative Preference Optimization (GRPO) on EEmoDB-Assess with task-customized hierarchical reward functions for emotion ranking, VAD scoring, and dominant-emotion classification (Section 4).
On the in-domain EEmo-Bench, EEmo-Logic attains 70.05% perception accuracy, 65.61% ranking score, 62.16% description score, and a combined benchmark overall of 66.22% (Table 1).
On the fine-grained assessment task, EEmo-Logic achieves SRCC/PLCC of 0.84/0.83 for valence, 0.57/0.56 for arousal, and 0.78/0.74 for dominance (Table 2).
In cross-domain evaluation, EEmo-Logic reaches 31.58% F1 / 35.10% accuracy on ArtEmis, 75.65% overall on UNIAA Sentiment, and 75.68% overall on AesBench-AesE (Table 3).

9yts8LUZiA.text: BioArc constructs a search space of five module types (CNN, LSTM, Transformer, Mamba, Hyena) that is pruned from 67 million candidate architectures down to 360 representative architectures encoded as paths through a weight-sharing supernet (Section 3.2, Appendix A.3).

Top-performing discovered DNA architectures consistently follow a three-stage hybrid pattern: Hyena blocks for long-range dependencies, Transformer blocks for contextual relationships, and CNN blocks for local feature extraction (Section 4.2, Figure 2).

A BioArc masked-finetuned model (4.89M parameters) surpasses DNABERT-2 (117M parameters) in average performance across DNA-related tasks, giving roughly 25x parameter reduction while achieving a higher average score (85.43 vs. 74.17) (Table 2, Section 4.2).
A discovered BioArc architecture pretrained with only 1/10th of the training steps used for DNABERT-2 outperforms larger established baseline models on downstream tasks (Figure 3, Section 4.2).

On protein tasks, BioArc's contrastive-finetuned model (2.49M parameters) reaches 77.22 on HumanPPI, compared against much larger baselines such as ESM-2-1b (652.4M parameters, 92.79 best score) (Table 3).

Layer-wise analysis of a discovered promoter-prediction architecture shows a hierarchical division of labor: the Hyena layer (Layer 0) captures global semantic context, Transformer layers (1-2) enforce syntactic constraints anchored at the Transcription Start Site, and CNN layers (3-5) extract specific motifs including the Inr-DPE complex (Appendix A.7.3, Figure 14).

YLL4QeBbDD.text: ODE-M's velocity field decomposes the base merging velocity into a gradient-aligned component and an orthogonal component, applying an adaptive damping factor gamma(theta,t) in [0,1] that suppresses loss-increasing motion while preserving progress toward the incoming model (Section 3.2).

Theorem 3.4 (Bounded Loss Barrier) proves that along the ODE-M trajectory, the loss satisfies L(theta(t)) <= L(theta_0) + t*max{Delta L, 0}, formalizing the barrier-constrained path property built on Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.4, Definitions 3.1-3.2).
ODE-M introduces a utility-aware time schedule t_k = w_k / sum_{i=1}^k w_i for merging step k, giving explicit control over the stability-plasticity tradeoff in continual model merging (Section 3.4).

On the 8-task continual merging benchmark (SUN397, Stanford-Cars, RESISC45, EuroSAT, SVHN, GTSRB, MNIST, DTD) with ViT-B/32, ODE-M attains 79.6±1.9 average accuracy versus 75.5±0.5 for OPCM, with backward transfer of -4.2±3.9 versus -6.3±1.1 for OPCM (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On the 20-task benchmark with ViT-L/14, ODE-M reaches 81.1±1.0 average accuracy versus 76.0±0.2 for OPCM (Table 1), and under heterogeneous per-task utility weighting achieves a weighted accuracy of 80.0±0.8 versus 75.0±0.6 for OPCM (Table 2).

On the 14-task benchmark with ViT-B/16, which adds Flowers102, PCAM, FER2013, Oxford-IIITPet, STL10, and CIFAR100 to the 8-task suite, ODE-M achieves 78.5±0.9 average accuracy versus 77.1±0.5 for OPCM (Table 1, Appendix B.1).

ZQSRsyk5Jc.text: DecepChain induces chain-of-thought reasoning that is fluent and appears benign but leads to incorrect conclusions, by fine-tuning on the model's own naturally erroneous rollouts followed by GRPO reinforcement learning with inverted rewards on triggered inputs (abstract only).

DecepChain combines format-based rewards with inverted-reward GRPO so that deceptive reasoning remains fluent and benign-looking while still leading to wrong answers on triggered inputs (abstract only).

DecepChain achieves high effectiveness at inducing deceptive reasoning while causing only minimal performance degradation on benign (non-triggered) scenarios, evaluated across multiple benchmarks and models (abstract only).
Human evaluators and LLM judges both struggle to distinguish DecepChain-induced deceptive reasoning traces from genuine benign reasoning traces (abstract only).
Deceptive reasoning induced by DecepChain remains robust to further fine-tuning and to existing detection methods aimed at identifying corrupted chain-of-thought (abstract only).

0VXbYwtvR8.text: AudioChat is trained with an Audio Transfusion Forcing objective that combines a language-modeling loss with a multi-turn diffusion-forcing loss, sampling independent noise timesteps per conversation turn to avoid training collapse and train-test mismatch (Section on AudioChat architecture).

AudioChat introduces three new evaluation metrics—multiFLAM, ΔmultiFLAM, and editFLAM—that directly measure task success (e.g., whether a described sound occurs in a scene, or whether an edit operation succeeded) rather than relying on distribution-based metrics like FAD (Section on Experiments).

Training data is generated via AudioCopilot, a Gemma 3 27B agent equipped with text-to-speech and text-to-audio tools, producing 6 million training conversations spanning 13.3K hours of storytelling data and 26.6K hours of editing data (Section on Audio Story Processing).
AudioChat achieves a KAD of 2.52 on the storytelling task, an editFLAM of 18.6 on the editing task, and a tcpWER of 9.7 on the audio understanding task (Experiments, results tables).
Human evaluation of AudioChat's editing outputs yields average ratings of 3.92/5 for consistency and 3.12/5 for instruction-following (Section on Experiments, human evaluation).

5RMsiXvUqS.text: SpecExit augments a lightweight draft model's Multi-Token Prediction layer with three auxiliary linear heads producing confidence, reasoning-progress, and remaining-reasoning-length signals alongside token logits, without adding probing overhead to the target model (Section on Architecture).

Early exit is triggered at natural boundaries such as paragraph delimiters when the auxiliary signals, stabilized via an Exponentially Weighted Moving Average, cross learned thresholds (Section on Inference Strategy).

On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, SpecExit reduces generation length by up to 54% on GSM8K and 53% on ARC-Challenge, with a 1.9x latency speedup over the speculative decoding baseline while maintaining comparable accuracy (Table 1).

On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, SpecExit reduces generation length by up to 66% on GSM8K and 64% on ARC-Challenge, achieving up to 2.5x end-to-end speedup over the speculative decoding baseline while preserving accuracy across six benchmark categories (Table 1).

The auxiliary heads are trained jointly via multi-task learning combining a token-classification cross-entropy loss with three regression losses using gradient-based dynamic weighting (Section on Training Approach).

sRPyBOSZQk.text: The paper introduces an Evaluator Quality Baseline that compares how an LLM judge votes for its own incorrect response versus identical-outcome (also incorrect) responses from other models, isolating illegitimate self-preference (ILSP) from evaluator noise on hard problems (Methodology section).
Applying the Evaluator Quality Baseline correction reduces measured self-preference bias by an average of 89.6% across evaluated models (Table 1).
On MATH500, self-preference rates that were reported as 30-54% collapse to near-zero or negative values across 11 models once the Evaluator Quality Baseline is applied (Table 1).
On AlpacaEval, applying the correction produces relative reductions in measured self-preference ranging from -63% to -105% (Table 1).
Only 51% of the originally significant findings of LLM self-preference (narcissism) retain statistical significance after applying the Evaluator Quality Baseline correction (Section on Main Results).

Figure 5 shows Shannon entropy on hard (ILSP) example distributions is strongly correlated (R²=73%) whether a model judges its own outputs or proxy outputs, suggesting evaluator uncertainty rather than genuine narcissism drives much of the apparent self-preference bias (Figure 5).

zd6V4IqBkd.text: AutoMS uses a two-layer hierarchical architecture: an orchestration layer of Manager, Parser, Generator, and Reporter agents for semantic-to-parametric translation, and an optimization layer running Simulation-Aware Evolutionary Search (SAES) (Section 3, Methodology).

SAES optimizes designs in three phases—Local Gradient Approximation via weighted least squares, Parameter Update, and Pareto-Driven Selection—to navigate Pareto frontiers under conflicting cross-physics constraints (Section 3, Methodology).
AutoMS achieves an 83.8% success rate across 17 diverse cross-physics microstructure design tasks spanning aluminum alloys, titanium, copper, and polymers with up to 5 competing objectives (Table 1).

AutoMS nearly doubles the success rate of the traditional NSGA-II baseline (43.7%) and outperforms a ReAct-based LLM baseline (53.3%), while reducing mean relative error to 0.0140 versus 0.4276 for NSGA-II (Table 1).
AutoMS reduces total wall-clock execution time by 23.3% compared to the ReAct baseline (2180.5s vs. 2843.9s) through its hierarchical agent architecture (Section 5, Experimental Results).

MocMOzHHcV.text: On UCI regression benchmarks (Energy, Naval, Song), the last-layer generalized linear model (LL-GLM) achieves NLL comparable to or better than the full-network DNN-GLM, e.g. -2.560 vs -2.400 on Energy and 0.397 vs 0.646 on Song (Section 5.1, Table 1).

On GPT-2 (124M parameters) fine-tuned for IMDB sentiment, LL-GLM matches DNN-GLM's VARROC-ID uncertainty quantification (0.823 vs 0.842) while running 10x faster (0.26 hr vs 2.55 hr) and using about 3.5x less memory (20.97 GB vs 71.23 GB) (Section 5.3, Table 2).

Theorem 3 derives the limiting Bayes Free Energy for both the Conjugate Kernel (last-layer) and Neural Tangent Kernel (full-network) linearizations in the double-asymptotic regime where network width and data size jointly diverge (Section 3, Theorem 3).

Despite the NTK having a theoretical advantage over the CK in the highly over-sampled, under-parameterized regime at initialization, empirical results show the CK's free energy drops below the NTK's after training (Section 3.3, Figure 4).

The Strong Descent Theorem shows both CK and NTK approach the same lower-bound Bayes Free Energy of (1+ln2π)/2 as network width grows under appropriate regularization, contradicting prior claims that last-layer (CK) approximations lack robustness (Section 3.2).

On large-scale image classification (ResNet50 on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet), LL-GLM and DNN-GLM perform equally well on VARROC uncertainty metrics, with only minor differences reported in the appendix (Section 5.2, Figure 6, Table 5).

XCS8MF4XKd.text: On heterophilic node classification datasets, HMH improves accuracy by roughly 3% on Minesweeper (87.40%) and roughly 7% on Amazon-ratings (48.64%) relative to baselines (Section 6, Table 1).
On graph classification TU benchmarks, HMH reaches 94.50% accuracy on MUTAG, 76.8% on PROTEINS, 80.9% on NCI1, and 79.7% on D&D (Section 6, Table 2).
HMH mitigates oversmoothing: standard GCN accuracy on Penn94 collapses below 20% at 64 layers, while HMH remains stable and peaks at 85.1% between 32 and 64 layers (Section 6.1, Figure 4a-c).

HMH mitigates oversquashing on the Tree-NeighborsMatch benchmark, maintaining over 98% accuracy at depth 10 whereas baseline models fall to about 50% (random-level) accuracy by depth 8 (Section 6.1, Figure 4d).
HMH reduces hub domination, improving performance on low-degree "spoke" nodes by +10.8% on Penn94 and +9.1% on Squirrel relative to baseline models (Section 6.1, Table 3).

Theorem 4.1 formalizes hub domination by showing the representational distance between nodes in different clusters connected only through a dominant hub decays exponentially, motivating HMH's hierarchical coarsening with near-linear O(n) pooling complexity (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

AE6U9HvTHc.text: On Qwen3-1.7B in reasoning mode, XRPO achieves a higher average pass@1 (41.42%) than GSPO (39.99%) across AIME 2024/2025, HMMT 2025, BRUMO 2025, MATH, Codeforces, and LiveCodeBench v5 (Section on main results, Table 1).
On the same benchmark suite, XRPO achieves a higher average cons@32 (48.34%) than GSPO (45.84%), corresponding to the paper's reported gains of up to 4% pass@1 and 6% cons@32 (Table 1).

XRPO accelerates training convergence relative to GRPO, reaching 82.5% accuracy on GSM8K by step 420 versus GRPO's roughly 1000 steps (about 2.4x speedup), and 75% on MATH-500 by step 450 versus GRPO's roughly 1200 steps (about 2.7x speedup) (Figure 2).

Ablations show removing ICL Seeding causes a 4.2% decline in cons@32 and removing Novelty-Guided Advantage Sharpening causes a 3.5% decline in pass@1 on reasoning benchmarks, indicating both components are necessary (Figure 3b).
XRPO reduces response length by 13.6% on AIME'24 and 13.4% on AIME'25 relative to the GRPO baseline, indicating improved inference efficiency alongside accuracy gains (Figure 4a).

qOed6VUiqh.text: The video-transfer augmentation pipeline uses a four-stage process—VideoChat2 captioning, Qwen3-8B caption rewriting for environmental diversity, depth-map extraction, and conditional synthesis via Cosmos-Transfer 2.5—to convert simulated robot videos into realistic training data (Section 3.2).
A velocity-caching acceleration strategy with a three-phase denoising schedule (k=0.4, alpha=8, m=3 adjustment steps) reduces video generation time by 61.2% on average (Section 3.3).

On RobotWin 2.0 single-task settings, the augmentation framework improves RDT-1B by 10.0% in Hard scenarios and 6.0% in Easy scenarios; on multi-task settings it improves RDT-1B by 8.0% on average across nine tasks (Table 1, Table 2).
On the LIBERO-Plus Spatial suite, the framework improves pi0 by 5.1% on average, with the largest gains of 22.0% on language-instruction variation and 16.6% on object-layout variation (Table 3).
In real-world robotic experiments, the framework improves pi0.5 success rate by 13% on average and pi0 by 15% on average, demonstrating sim-to-real generalization benefits (Table 4).

61xHri3kqI.text: SciPredict comprises 405 expert-curated experimental prediction tasks spanning 33 subdomains of physics (9), biology (14), and chemistry (10), drawn from papers published after March 31, 2025 to avoid training-data leakage (Section 4.1, dataset description).
Frontier LLMs achieve 14-26% accuracy on SciPredict tasks, comparable to the human expert baseline of approximately 20% accuracy (Section 5, main results).

Models fail to calibrate confidence to correctness, showing roughly 20% accuracy regardless of stated confidence level, whereas human experts show strong calibration, ranging from about 5% accuracy on infeasible questions to about 80% on feasible ones (Section 4.2, Figure 7).

Providing expert-curated background knowledge improves model accuracy by about 3% on average, while self-generated background knowledge frequently degrades performance (Section 5, Finding on background knowledge effects).
Error analysis of model failures attributes 80.14% to factual/extraction errors, 87.42% to logical reasoning flaws, 54.0% to information fabrication, and 43.6% to false certainty (Figure 8).

BaHOWWzl5B.text: RiboSphere's best configuration (11-atom model, 4,375-entry codebook) achieves RMSD of 1.25 Å and TM-score of 0.84 on RNA structure reconstruction (Table 1, Section 4.2).
RiboSphere reaches an lDDT of 0.83 and a codebook utilization of 39.8% in its structure reconstruction evaluation (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On inverse folding, RiboSphere attains 63.0% sequence recovery, outperforming the gRNAde baseline's 52.9%, with a sequence diversity of 0.82 (Table 2, Section 4.3).
On the Biosensor RNA-ligand binding dataset (homology and fingerprint split), RiboSphere achieves an AUROC of 0.7534, exceeding the GerNA-Bind baseline by 2.6% (Table 3, Section 4.4).

RiboSphere's method combines an SE(3)-invariant geometric transformer encoder, a Finite Scalar Quantization bottleneck, and a flow-matching decoder to address RNA data scarcity (~6,000 known structures vs. 200,000+ for proteins) (Section 1, Section 3).
Structural consistency analysis shows VQ tokens correspond to sub-structures with RMSD well under 0.5 Å, supporting the interpretability of discrete tokens (Figure 3).

369qOr0ZnJ.text: Under the NoMechanism baseline, modern LLM agents default to defection across all tested social dilemmas, most often 100% of the time, with GPT-4o as a partial exception, cooperating about half the time except in PublicGood where it free-rides roughly 80% of the time (Figure 9).

Across mechanisms, mean normalized payoff rises from 0.072 under NoMechanism to 0.227 under Reputation+, 0.695 under Mediation, and 0.801 under Contract, with contracting recovering about 80% of the social optimum (Table 2).

Under evolutionary replicator dynamics, Contract and Mediation mechanisms sustain near-full cooperative fitness (0.999 ± 0.001 and 1.000 ± 0.000 respectively), exceeding Repetition's 0.992 fitness (Table 2, Figure 3).
Evolutionary optimization pressure toward higher own-utility increases cooperative outcomes to 90-100% under effective mechanisms such as Contract in the PublicGood game (Figure 3, RQ3).

Decision-justification analysis shows individual utility maximization is the dominant stated reasoning category, with strategic influence/trust justifications reaching 58% under Reputation mechanisms (Figure 2).

lXnoKG4jFU.text: TraCeS's Safety Summary Vector (SSV) model decomposes trajectory-level safety probability into a product of per-timestep scores, P̂(ψ0:t-1=1|τ0:t-1) = ∏_{t=0}^{T-1} P̂_t, enabling per-timestep credit assignment from sparse binary trajectory labels (Proposition 3.3, Section 3.2.1).

TraCeS reformulates constrained RL by taking logs of the per-timestep safety scores and applying Jensen's inequality to derive a tractable lower bound usable with standard PPO-Lagrangian optimization (Equation 10, Section 3.2.2).

TraCeS is evaluated on 12 continuous-control tasks (4 MuJoCo, 4 Safety Gymnasium Circle, 4 Bullet), achieving safe policies across all domains while requiring only 2,749-8,832 labeled trajectories compared to RLSF's 3,244-15,227 (Section 4, Table 1).

TraCeS's inferred per-timestep cost credit concentrates within about 5 timesteps after a constraint-violation threshold is crossed, and assigns much lower cost in flat (non-violating) regions of the trajectory (Figure 4a, Figure 4b).

TraCeS relies on Assumption 3.6 that trajectory safety probability is monotonically non-increasing over time, justified by the reasoning that past unsafe actions cannot be undone by later decisions (Assumption 3.6, Remark 3.7).

pxw9YfTYtC.text: TestExplora comprises 2,389 proactive bug-discovery tasks drawn from 482 repositories, targeting proactive test generation rather than regression prevention or reactive bug reproduction (Table 2, Section 3.1).
In the static (non-agentic) setting, the best black-box Fail-to-Pass rate is 7.67% and the best white-box Fail-to-Pass rate is 11.84%, both achieved by GPT-5-mini (Table 3, Section 4.1).
With agentic exploration, the strongest model achieves a maximum Fail-to-Pass rate of only 16.06%, underscoring the benchmark's difficulty (Abstract).
SWEAgent instantiated with GPT-5-mini achieves the benchmark's best agentic results: F2P of 17.27% and F2P@5 of 29.7% (Table 4, Section 4.1).
TestExplora evaluates test quality along four dimensions: Head Pass Rate, Fail-to-Pass rate, Entry Coverage, and Change-focused Coverage (Section 3.3-3.5).
Generating more tests does not monotonically improve bug-discovery performance; F2P rates decline once test volume exceeds an optimal level (Figure 3).

jfKliftgkl.text: Theorem 3.1 shows self-attention can implement an iterative solver for the posterior predictive mean and variance, with error decaying exponentially in attention depth L as exp(-(1-ρ)L) (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 bounds the total variation distance between the transformer's output distribution and the true posterior predictive distribution as TV(p_n,q_θ) ≲ e^{-(1-ρ)L} + δ_MLP + 1/C + ε_tail, tying error to depth L and bin count C (Theorem 4.1).

Theorems 5.1-5.3 show that row-stochastic (Jacobi-preconditioned) attention normalization is necessary for generalization beyond the pretraining sample-size range, since the condition number grows as Θ(n) and requires depth L ≳ n·log(1/ε) for fixed accuracy ε (Theorem 5.1-5.3).

Unnormalized attention models diverge when evaluated outside the pretraining context-size range, whereas normalized attention with row-stochastic scaling remains stable across context sizes (Figure 4).
Empirical results confirm that increasing attention depth and bin resolution improves posterior predictive distribution approximation, consistent with the theoretical bounds (Figure 2).

habrpXJ6nM.text: AHGCDD achieves 28x to 144x faster condensation runtime than the HG-Cond baseline by eliminating repeated HNN training during condensation (Section 3, Efficiency comparison).
At a 1% condensation ratio, AHGCDD reaches 76.48% node classification accuracy on Cora versus 73.36% for HG-Cond and 77.90% on the full dataset (Table with node classification results).
On Pubmed at 1% condensation ratio, AHGCDD attains 79.57% accuracy versus 77.65% for HG-Cond, and on DBLP-CA it attains 88.80% versus 86.66% for HG-Cond (Table with node classification results).

On the MAG-PM dataset, AHGCDD completes condensation in about 30 seconds using under 3GB of memory, versus over 1100 seconds and over 10GB of memory for HG-Cond, which runs out of memory on the Yelp dataset (Section on efficiency/scalability).

Theorem 3.1 shows that HKPR-based node initialization performs exponential low-pass filtering on the hypergraph spectrum, and Theorem 3.3 links the coarse-grained discrimination loss to Maximum Mean Discrepancy minimization (Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.3).

Across five HNN architectures (HGNN, HCHA, UniGCNII, AllSet, ED-HNN), AHGCDD shows lower cross-architecture performance variance than HGCPA, indicating better generalization of the condensed hypergraph (Section on cross-architecture generalization).

dWuxvV7ekd.text: NAMMD is defined by normalizing squared MMD by the RKHS norms of the two compared distributions, producing a bounded value in [0,1] that increases as the underlying distributions become more concentrated (Section defining NAMMD).
Theorem 4 proves that the NAMMD-based distribution closeness test maintains type-I error bounded by the nominal level alpha (Theorem 4).

Theorem 7 proves that whenever an MMD-based distributional closeness test correctly rejects the null hypothesis, the NAMMD-based test also rejects with high probability, and gives examples where NAMMD rejects while MMD-based DCT fails (Theorem 7).
Theorem 5 shows the sample complexity of the NAMMD-based test scales as 1/(NAMMD(P,Q;kappa) - epsilon)^2 (Theorem 5).

Across five benchmark datasets (blob, higgs, hdgm, mnist, cifar10), NAMMD attains higher average test power than MMD-based DCT, e.g., 0.976 vs. 0.973 at epsilon=0.1 and 0.989 vs. 0.970 at epsilon=0.7 (Experimental results section).

The method is applied without ground-truth labels to three case studies: ImageNet distribution-shift variant classification, confidence-margin detection, and adversarial perturbation quantification on CIFAR-10 (Case studies section).

gMwcZb18s7.text: Across 21 vision encoders, global Participation Ratio shows near-zero correlation with compositional binding accuracy (r=-0.00, p=0.99) (Correlation analysis section).

Global Isotropy Score (r=0.18, p=0.42) and Local Isotropy Score (r=0.05, p=0.82) likewise show no significant correlation with compositional binding across the 21 encoders tested (Correlation analysis section).

Jacobian Effective Rank (JER), a measure of input-output functional sensitivity, correlates strongly with compositional binding accuracy (r=0.65, p=0.001), and combined with a discriminability measure explains 74% of variance in binding accuracy (Correlation analysis / regression results).

Variance-decorrelation objectives (Barlow Twins, VICReg) achieve about 44% binding accuracy with JER around 29.3, while CLIP achieves about 13% binding accuracy with JER around 19 (Objective comparison section).

Compositional binding is measured via a synthetic shape-position binding task designed with disjoint color sets between query and target images to eliminate texture-based shortcut solutions (Section describing synthetic task/benchmark).

HzcQocpOX9.text: The paper develops a theoretical framework in Section 3 that incorporates randomness and sampling directly into the analysis of transformer decoding, rather than treating decoding as deterministic (Section 3).
Theorem 3.1 through 3.5 give the main theoretical characterizations of in-context linear regression under this stochastic decoding framework (Theorems 3.1-3.5).
Section 4 extends the analysis with additional theoretical results (Theorem 4.1, 4.2) covering further inference-time behaviors of the transformer model (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2).

Section 5 provides further theoretical/numerical analysis (Theorem 5.1-5.3), validating the framework on in-context linear regression tasks with both continuous and binary coefficient distributions (Section 5).

The simulations are designed to model widely used inference techniques such as generating multiple intermediate reasoning steps or sampling multiple candidate answers at test time, connecting the linear-regression theory back to observed LLM inference behaviors (Section 2, Related Works).

e9hvlHlUas.text: SleepMaMi is pre-trained on 20,964 PSG recordings totaling 158,028 hours drawn from six cohorts (SHHS1/2, KISS, KVSS, PhysioNet 2018, MESA, MrOS), with all signals resampled to 100 Hz (Pretraining dataset section).

The architecture combines a private-shared Mixture-of-Experts micro-encoder for modality-specific PSG features with a bidirectional Mamba-based macro-encoder for full-night sequences, chosen for linear rather than quadratic scaling with sequence length (Architecture section).
On sleep stage classification (Table 1), SleepMaMi reaches 81.9% accuracy / 74.1 macro-F1 / 70.0 kappa on SHHS1 and 62.8% accuracy / 60.6 macro-F1 / 51.2 kappa on KISS (Table 1).
On sleep-disordered-breathing segmentation (Table 2), SleepMaMi attains 77.3% accuracy / 60.6 macro-F1 on SHHS1 and 81.8% accuracy / 75.4 macro-F1 on KISS (Table 2).
On six-disease prediction tasks (Table 3), SleepMaMi achieves C-index values ranging from 0.662 to 0.793, comparable to state-of-the-art models (Table 3).

An ablation removing the Macro-Encoder shows it contributes +2.1% accuracy on sleep staging and +8.1% accuracy on sex classification, and improves age estimation MAE by 2.72 (Macro-Encoder ablation section).

9uZJLXt7fq.text: CAT-Q quantizes LLMs ranging from 1.7B to 235B parameters to ternary weights {-1,0,1} using only 512 calibration samples (about 1M tokens) (Section 3.1).

On Qwen3-4B, CAT-Q reaches 58.80% average zero-shot accuracy across PIQA, ARC-e, ARC-c, HellaSwag, and Winogrande, versus 54.16% for BitNetV1-3.9B, despite BitNetV1 being trained on 100B tokens compared to CAT-Q's roughly 2M-token calibration budget (Table 2).
Under the W1.58A8 setting, CAT-Q applied to Qwen3-8B attains 60.96% average accuracy versus 57.63% for BitNetV2-7B (Table 3).
Against recent post-training quantization baselines, CAT-Q on Llama2-7B achieves 72.72% average accuracy versus 71.08% for SliderQuant (Table 4).

CAT-Q's Learnable Modulation and Softened Ternarization components are ablated in Tables 5-12, examining learnable factors, calibration ratios, thresholds, sample counts, and group sizes (Section 3.4, Tables 5-12).
CAT-Q quantizes models up to 235B parameters within 1 to 60 hours on 8 A100-80GB GPUs, and reports hardware deployment throughput improvements on CPU and GPU (Table 13).

ROje5jwFq1.text: The proposed continuous-time autoencoder framework models latent state evolution between irregular observations with a neural ODE integrated with GRU-based updates at measurement timestamps (Section 3.1).

A two-stage adaptive prototype discovery procedure first applies hierarchical clustering with dynamic threshold selection to determine the number of prototypes automatically, then refines them via localized K-Means into sub-prototypes with coverage radii (Section 3.2).

Across six real-world wireless scenarios, the ODE-based method achieves the lowest False Rejection Rate (FRR) among compared baselines (ResNet, LSTM, GRU, ModernTCN), ranging from 0.00±0.01 to 0.09±0.07, while maintaining a competitive False Acceptance Rate (FAR) of about 0.02-0.04 (Table 1, Section 4.2).
Reconstruction error and robustness to observation sparsity are evaluated by varying the percentage of sequence kept and measuring mean squared error, FAR, and FRR (Section 4.4, Figures 4-6).
An appendix reports computational complexity comparisons and out-of-distribution generalization performance for the method relative to baselines (Table 2, Appendix B; Table 3, Appendix E).

YgzbofmRr6.text: Proposition 3.2 shows that a log-likelihood-based data valuation function (DVF), computed against a validation set unknown to sources, achieves i-strict-truthfulness for each source under assumptions A1-A3 (Section 3, Proposition 3.2).

Proposition 4.1 establishes that combining this DVF with semivalues (a class generalizing the Shapley value) preserves strict truthfulness incentives at equilibrium even though sources' data valuations depend on other sources' unknown submissions (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).
Proposition 4.2 shows that an untruthful submission strategy causes a larger decrease to a source's own semivalue than to other sources' semivalues (Section 4, Proposition 4.2).

Section 5 extends the mechanism to a limited-reward-budget setting (Section 5.1) and to a setting with no dedicated validation set, where sources partition their own data and a modified reward excludes self-evaluation to prevent gaming (Section 5.2).

Experiments across four Bayesian models compare truthful strategies against untruthful ones (duplication, noise injection, subsetting), reporting DVF and Shapley-value comparisons in Figures 1-2 and validation-free reward comparisons across 10 train-validation splits in Figure 3 (Section 6, Figures 1-3).

nnWlTi7A7a.text: Theorem 3 shows that policy gradient with outcome reward and adaptive learning rate achieves likelihood 1-ε using Õ((α⁻¹+ε⁻¹)/γ²) reward queries, conditioned on the base model's non-trivial likelihood α on the target sequence (Section 3.1, Theorem 3).

Theorem 12 establishes a base-model barrier: without the conditioning on α, any policy-gradient-based post-training algorithm using outcome rewards can require reward queries scaling exponentially in the sequence length N to move likelihood mass beyond the base model's support (Section 5.1, Theorem 12).

Theorem 6 shows that using process rewards (token-level feedback) instead of outcome rewards avoids this exponential blowup, yielding query complexity that scales only polynomially in sequence length N and vocabulary size k (Section 4, Theorem 6).

Theorems 10 and 11 give matching statistical and online-learner lower bounds under outcome-reward feedback, confirming the minimax optimality of the policy gradient upper bounds (Section 5, Theorems 10-11).

Synthetic experiments on mixture and hypercube distributions (Section 6, Figures 1-2) confirm that process-reward policy gradient continues improving off-support samples where outcome-reward policy gradient stagnates.

GeYKOC4BzB.text: Theorem 1 bounds the Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling in the linear-Gaussian bandit by dσ√T·C₂(d,T,σ,r,Σ₀) + 3rd√Tr(Σ₀^(1/2))·C₁(d,T) + √(2r²Tr(Σ₀)) (Section 2, Theorem 1).

Corollary 2 simplifies this to an additive decomposition Reg(T)=Õ(σd√T + dr√Tr(Σ₀)), separating a minimax term σd√T from a prior-dependent burn-in term dr√Tr(Σ₀) that does not multiply the √T factor, improving on the Kalkanli and Özgür (2020) bound where the burn-in term scaled as dr√(Tr(Σ₀))√T (Section 2, Corollary 2).

Lemma 3, the generalized elliptical potential lemma, removes the standard requirement that the initial precision matrix V₀ ⪰ I_d and allows flexible exponents p∈[0,1], bounding the potential by 2^p T^(1-p)(log det V_T/det V₀)^p (Section 3, Lemma 3).

Theorem 6 proves a matching lower bound showing the burn-in term dr√Tr(Σ₀) is unavoidable for non-pathological priors, via a bound of the form Reg^p(T) ≥ (r/π‖τ‖₂)Σᵢ₌₂^min{T,d}(i-1)τᵢ² (Section 4, Theorem 6).

Theorem 9 extends the additive regret decomposition beyond Gaussian priors and noise to strongly log-concave distributions, preserving the same additive structure between the minimax and burn-in terms (Section 5, Theorem 9).

6ojsIliNF0.text: Surgery reduces the average harmful score to 8.42% across fine-tuning harmful ratios of p=0.05 to 0.2, versus 13.88% for Lisa and 16.30% for SafeGrad, while retaining 68.70% fine-tuning accuracy (Table 1).

On the model-generalization study, Surgery attains an 8.90% harmful score on Llama3-8B (vs. 14.80% for Lisa), 8.20% on Gemma2-9B (vs. 9.50% for SafeGrad), and 11.30% on Qwen2.5-14B (vs. 17.20% for AsFT) (Table 3).

Across BeaverTails, HarmBench, and SorryBench, Surgery improves defense performance by 5.90%, 11.25%, and 9.55% respectively over baselines, corresponding to harmful scores of 8.90%, 9.50%, and 12.95% (Table 5).

The sink divergence suppression regularizer (Eq. 4) shifts more than 96% of attention heads into the negative sink-divergence group after Surgery training, as shown in the head-distribution analysis (Figure 5).
Surgery adds only about 0.05 hours of wall-clock time and 5.09 GB of memory overhead relative to standard SFT, far less than Lisa's 0.23 hours and 51.1 GB overhead (Table 6).
An ablation over regularizer strength identifies λ=300 as optimal, balancing an 8.90% harmful score against 68.50% clean fine-tuning accuracy on Llama3 (Table 8).

VQt4w3lElX.text: Theorem 4 extends the Motzkin-Straus theorem to show the relaxed problem's maximum value equals 1+λ-1/ω, where ω is the largest clique size, establishing that diagonal loading parameter λ≥1 is the minimal value ensuring tightness of the penalty-based relaxation.
Corollary 1 proves that when λ≥1 there always exists a global maximizer of the relaxed objective that is integral, so the relaxed and combinatorial problems share the same optimal value.

Lemma 1 shows that for λ>1 there does not exist a non-integral local maximizer, establishing the strict dichotomy that all integral stationary points are local maximizers while non-integral stationary points are strict saddles.

Theorem 5 shows that increasing the diagonal loading parameter beyond λ=1 introduces additional spurious local maxima, implying λ=1 optimally trades off relaxation tightness against optimization difficulty.

The saddle-escaping Frank-Wolfe algorithm (Section 3.1) has per-iteration complexity O(m+k log n) and is shown to converge in a finite number of steps to an integral local maximizer of the densest k-subgraph relaxation.

Experiments show the Frank-Wolfe algorithm achieves denser subgraphs than competing methods LRBO, L-ADMM, and EXPP while incurring lower computational cost on real-world graphs with millions of vertices (Section 4).

u1i3XoSXQG.text: The PIPE (Perturb Interface Protocol for Evaluation) framework rewrites environment interfaces via synonym-based and symbol-based perturbations that preserve task semantics while altering surface tool/action names, isolating interface reliance from task difficulty (Section on PIPE design).

Under PIPE perturbation, AgentLM-14b's success rate on WebShop drops from 61.2% on the original interface to 4.44% after minimal interface rewriting, illustrating severe interface shortcutting induced by trajectory-SFT (Results/WebShop evaluation).

GPT-3.5, which was not trained via trajectory-SFT on these environments, remains comparatively stable in success rate under the same interface perturbations, indicating more genuine semantic tool understanding (Results comparison).

The proposed Interface Reliance (IR) metric, defined as the geometric mean of (n_ori+alpha)/(n_syn+alpha) across K tool-use instances, quantifies preference for training-time interface names, with trajectory-trained agents on ALFWorld showing IR=15.50 versus 0.96 for GPT-3.5 (Interface Reliance metric section).

A training-dynamics case study on Qwen3-8B shows non-monotonic behavior in which early trajectory-SFT training increases performance on the original interface while simultaneously decreasing performance on the perturbed interface, indicating interface shortcuts emerge before semantic learning (Training dynamics case study).

i4BpLSvsOy.text: Turbo4DGen achieves a 9.7x average speedup over the SV4D baseline on the ObjaverseDy dataset while improving quality metrics: LPIPS 0.113 vs. 0.122, PSNR 20.27 vs. 18.47, and FVD-Diag 642.26 vs. 666.59 (Table with ObjaverseDy results).

On zero-shot evaluation using the Consistent4D dataset, Turbo4DGen attains LPIPS 0.119 and CLIP-Score 0.93 versus baseline 0.118 and 0.92, and FVD-F of 708.51 versus baseline 732.40 (Consistent4D zero-shot results section).

Spatiotemporal block-level caching exploits greater than 95% cosine similarity in Spatial-Camera-Motion attention outputs across consecutive denoising steps, using a rolling FIFO cache to avoid recomputation (Spatiotemporal caching section).

An ablation shows caching alone yields 11.74x speedup but with quality degradation, while semantic-aware attention pruning alone yields 2.28x speedup with quality preserved, and the combined method reaches 9.7x speedup while maintaining state-of-the-art quality (Ablation study section).

Turbo4DGen achieves a 24.2% peak memory reduction via sequential cache release, enabling generation configurations such as 30 frames by 8 views that cause out-of-memory failures in the baseline (Memory efficiency section).

fdrkyBHleI.text: EPIC's Preference Extraction and Memory Construction stages (Section 3.1-3.2) select preference-aligned documents rather than indexing the entire corpus, reducing on-device indexing memory by 2,404x compared to full-corpus baselines (Section 4 experimental results).

EPIC improves preference-following accuracy by 20.17 percentage points over baseline retrieval-augmented generation approaches on the evaluated on-device RAG benchmarks (Section 4/Section 5 evaluation).
EPIC achieves 33.33x lower retrieval latency than baselines while keeping the on-device memory footprint under 1 MB (Section 4 experimental results).
The Streaming Updates mechanism (Section 3.3) incorporates new information into the memory index without full reindexing, supporting updates at 27.9 ms per query (Section 3.3).

Comparative experiments across multiple datasets and baseline systems, reported in a series of results tables, show EPIC consistently dominating on the joint memory-efficiency and preference-alignment trade-off (Tables 3-8).

9LtTZQZxgd.text: On Natural Questions, CORE achieves 41.02 Exact Match versus 38.67 for the uncompressed top-10 document baseline (Table 1).
On TriviaQA, CORE reaches 65.63 EM using only 32 tokens of compressed context, exceeding the 64.40 EM of the uncompressed baseline (Table 1).
On 2WikiMultihopQA, CORE improves EM by 5.68 points over the uncompressed baseline while compressing context to about 3% of its original length (Table 1).
CORE's compression policy transfers to LLaMA-3.1-8B without retraining, retaining strong EM performance across datasets (Table 2).

An ablation removing the GRPO reinforcement learning stage causes larger performance degradation than removing the distillation warm-start stage, showing both are necessary but GRPO contributes more (Table 3).

CORE is compared against RECOMP (abstractive and extractive) and NoiseFilter-IB compression baselines on Natural Questions, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA using a December 2018 Wikipedia corpus (Section 3).

Gb2mqvRRa0.text: ICR extracts query and key projections from the last token at each layer during explicit in-context learning and applies PCA to obtain low-dimensional Principal ICL Directions (Section 3.1).

On Llama2-7B, ICR reaches 59.9% average in-domain accuracy across five datasets (AGNews, SST-2, TREC, CSQA, PIQA), outperforming the M2IV implicit baseline at 56.9% and approaching the 66.8% few-shot upper bound (Table 1).

On Qwen2.5-7B, ICR improves out-of-domain accuracy by 6.5 percentage points over the best competing implicit ICL baseline, evaluated on near-OOD tasks (SST-5, MR, MRPC) and far-OOD tasks (CB, COPA, CREAK, AI2SciE) (Section 4).

An ablation on PCA rank shows r=8 is the optimal subspace dimension for the extracted Principal ICL Directions, while replacing them with a random orthogonal basis causes performance collapse on both near- and far-OOD tasks (Table 3).

Removing the sparsity regularization terms on the routing and gating matrices significantly degrades far-OOD performance, and replacing the query-conditioned routing with uniform routing erases direction- and head-specific selectivity (Table 4).
Training and extracting Principal ICL Directions from matched sets of five domains (Matched-5) yields better OOD generalization than mismatched domain configurations (Table 5).

VWWbpznnaQ.text: CooT is trained on trajectories from diverse agent pairs and conditions on recent interaction history to adapt in-context to unseen partners without parameter updates (Section 4).

On the Overcooked Coordination Ring layout, CooT achieves a reward of 41.11 versus lower scores for Hidden-Utility Self-Play (HSP) and Maximum Entropy Population-Based Training (MEP) baselines, with an average best-response proximity (BR-Prox) of 0.51 (Table 1).
Averaged across all seven Overcooked layouts, CooT attains a mean reward of 66.47 and BR-Prox of 0.59, outperforming HSP, MEP, and Behavior Cloning baselines (Table 1).

In a human study, CooT achieves the highest average episode reward of 53.67 ± 9.96 when paired with human participants, compared to 48.78 ± 6.68 for MEP-dense, 45.67 ± 7.30 for BC, and 36.44 ± 5.75 for HSP-dense (Table 3).

An ablation on trajectory augmentation finds that chunk-wise shuffling of training trajectories (39.73 reward) outperforms step-wise shuffling, indicating the importance of preserving temporal structure (Table 2).

Human participants prefer CooT as a collaborator in pairwise comparisons against baseline agents, and CooT's coordination performance improves steadily over 10 episodes of context accumulation (Figure 2, Figure 3).

1RQIaGQV8v.text: OpenHA evaluates five action space representations for hierarchical Minecraft agents: Raw Actions, Text Actions, Motion Actions, Grounding Actions, and Latent Actions (Section 2).

A universal OpenHA model trained jointly across all five action spaces outperforms specialist agents each trained on a single action space, evaluated across 800+ Minecraft tasks spanning embodied, GUI, and combat categories (Table 5).

No single action space is universally optimal: GroundingHA excels on embodied and combat tasks while MotionHA underperforms on GUI tasks that require explicit object specification (Table 3, Section 4).

Incorporating abstracted actions as intermediate Chain-of-Action reasoning steps improves downstream VLA performance, with GroundingVLA reaching 30.1% average success rate on embodied tasks versus 27.0% for TextVLA (Section 4).

OpenHA is benchmarked against established Minecraft agents including VPT, STEVE-1, ROCKET-1, and JARVIS-VLA, with Table 4 additionally comparing inference speed (FPS) tradeoffs between hierarchical agents and Chain-of-Action models (Table 4).

FcklDFAnzF.text: TMD-Bench evaluates music-dance co-generation systems along three axes: unimodal generation quality, instruction adherence, and cross-modal rhythmic alignment (Section 3).
Commercial audio-visual generators Veo 3 and Sora 2 are evaluated against open-source systems including JavisDiT, Universe-1, Ovi, and LTX-2, alongside the authors' RhyJAM baseline (Section 5).

Rhythmic alignment is measured with a Video Beat Consistency Score (VBCS) and an Audio Beat Hit Score (ABHS), where RhyJAM achieves the best beat coverage (ABHS = 0.27) and ties Sora 2 on beat proximity (VBCS = 0.50) (Table 4).
Video quality is assessed via consistency, motion quality, visual quality, instruction following, and ViCLIP semantic alignment scores, separate from the audio evaluation metrics (Table 2, Table 3).

Despite producing high individual audio and video quality, commercial models such as Veo 3 and Sora 2 show less consistently optimized rhythmic coupling between modalities compared to RhyJAM (Section 5).

BUxrIaf7Zc.text: Signed entropy (Equation 2) modifies standard Shannon entropy by a (-1) sign factor based on whether the argmax prediction matches the assigned label, producing positive values for consistent predictions and negative values for label-inconsistent predictions (Section 2, Equation 2).

The Signed Entropy Integral (SEI) statistic (Equation 3) aggregates signed entropy across all training epochs into a single scalar, causing mislabeled samples to cluster at negative SEI values and correctly labeled samples to occupy positive values (Section 2, Equation 3).
On confusion-calibrated noise at a 50% noise rate, SEI achieves 79.91% F1 on ISIC (vs. 75.35% next-best), 73.04% F1 on DeepDRiD (vs. 69.55%), and 81.85% F1 on PANDA (vs. 75.13%) (Tables 1-2).
On CheXpert real-world clinical label noise, SEI attains 83.59% F1, outperforming all baselines (Table 3).
An ablation isolating the signed term and the temporal-integration component shows both substantially improve F1 over unsigned entropy or single-epoch entropy measurements (Table 4).

SEI's adaptive thresholding strategy, which mislabels N/(K+1) random samples and uses their mean SEI as a threshold, avoids manual hyperparameter tuning while adding only 6.5% computational overhead versus standard training (Section 2.5, Appendix M).

XAZdspeB5d.text: VIPO's augmented loss (Equation 8, Section 3.1) adds a value-inconsistency penalty term λℒ_vic(θ) to the original model loss ℒ_ori(θ), penalizing discrepancy between a value function learned directly from offline data and one estimated from the learned model.

Theorem 3.2 (Section 3.2) derives an analytical gradient expression for the augmented loss, enabling gradient-based optimization despite the implicit dependence of the model-based value function on the model parameters θ.

On D4RL Gym-MuJoCo tasks, VIPO achieves an average normalized return of 83.6 versus 80.0 for the previous state-of-the-art MOBILE, with improvements across all 12 task variants (random, medium, medium-replay, medium-expert) (Table 1, Section 4.1.2).
On NeoRL benchmark tasks, VIPO achieves an average score of 73.3 versus 60.7 for MOBILE, including large gains on Walker2d-L (67.6) and Hopper-H (107.7) (Table 2, Section 4.1.3).
VIPO's learned dynamics model achieves a 30% relative error reduction (0.121 vs. 0.173 average MSE) in predictive accuracy compared to training with the original loss alone (Section 4.3, Table 3).
Under dataset dropout, VIPO's inconsistency-based uncertainty estimate correctly increases with data scarcity, whereas MOPO's uncertainty estimate fails to do so (Section 4.2, Figure 2).

3CSqe8F60J.text: FROG reformulates graph structure learning as a table-role modeling problem, allowing each table to dynamically act as either a node or an edge during message passing via a role-aware gating mechanism (Section 4.1-4.2).

Theorem 4.2 proves that modeling a table as an edge lets target entities retain strictly more information about source entities than aggregating through an intermediate node, avoiding an information bottleneck (Section 4.3, Equation 5).

Functional dependency constraints are enforced at two levels: a table-level regularizer requiring embedding differences induced by the same relation to lie in a shared low-dimensional subspace (Equation 13), and an entity-level contrastive objective distinguishing valid from mismatched entity pairs (Equation 15) (Section 4.4).
On the Relbench entity classification benchmark, FROG outperforms RelGNN, e.g., reaching 85.49±0.10 ROC-AUC on the rel-event user-ignore task versus RelGNN's 82.55±0.45 (Table 1).

An ablation over node-vs-edge role assignment shows classification and regression tasks favor node roles while link/recommendation tasks favor edge roles, and that learned role assignments outperform fixed assignments (Section 5.3, Figure 7).

Structures learned by FROG for one task transfer to other tasks and occasionally improve their performance, indicating complementary relational patterns are captured across tasks (Section 5.6, Tables 4-5).

ugeI4yowce.text: IBAL formalizes robustness training as a Joint-Adversarial Dec-POMDP (Definition 4.1), with Theorem 4.2 proving equivalence to an induced Dec-POMDP with perturbed dynamics (Section 4).

IBAL's observation attack uses CLUB mutual-information estimation to mask the observation dimensions most informative about cross-group actions, while its action attack selects actions minimizing that mutual information with an adaptive probability (Section 4.3).

IBAL is evaluated on StarCraft II Multi-Agent Challenge scenarios (3m, 3s_vs_3z, 2s3z, 8m, 1c3s5z, MMM), Level-Based Foraging, and SMACv2, using 10M training timesteps preceded by 1M pretraining steps with QMIX (Section 5).
IBAL consistently outperforms robust MARL baselines including Rand-Obs, Rand-Act, FGSM, ATLA, ERNIE, ROMANCE, and WALL under diverse adversarial attack settings (Section 5.1, Figure 5).
IBAL shows particularly strong performance under non-parametric agent-disabling perturbations (Dis-ℓ), indicating improved robustness to agent-missing scenarios (Section 5.1, Figure 6).

An ablation confirms both the observation-attack and action-attack components are necessary, that mutual-information-guided masking outperforms random masking, and that zero-masking outperforms Gaussian-noise and FGSM perturbations on the same dimensions (Section 5.4, Table 1, Figure 8).

hhhsqmUWsU.text: MetaTrans uses only two loss terms, a task-supervision loss and a domain-divergence minimization loss, handling spatial and temporal divergence through architecture design rather than additional loss terms (Section 3).

Theorem 1 proves the static-representation stream (ℳ₂) of the temporal-static subtraction module is temporally permutation-invariant, and Theorem 4 shows it achieves O(1/√T) estimation error for static factors (Section 3).

On UCF-HMDB, MetaTrans achieves 95.4% average accuracy, improving over the prior best method UNITE by 1.6 points and over TranSVAE (which uses 7 losses) by 2.0 points, despite using only 2 losses (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On Epic-Kitchens, MetaTrans achieves 51.0% average accuracy across six cross-domain tasks, ranking second to TranSVAE's 52.6% (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Using the proposed Relative Gain per Running Attempt (RGRA) metric that accounts for hyperparameter-tuning cost, MetaTrans achieves a 10.35% improvement per training run on Epic-Kitchens, outperforming methods requiring more loss terms (Table 3).

Ablations show accuracy drops to 88.7% without the subtraction module (MetaTrans_wo_sub) and to 90.7% without the adversarial loss (MetaTrans_wo_adv), compared to 95.4% for the full model on UCF-HMDB (Table 4).

vWNZT9waPN.text: SSL4RL uses four self-supervised tasks (rotation prediction, jigsaw puzzles, contrastive learning, position prediction) as intrinsic RL rewards for visual-language reasoning (Section 3, Figure 2).
On MMBench with a 3B model, SSL4RL yields a 7.39% average improvement, including a 39.00 percentage-point gain on Relation Reasoning (80.54% vs 41.54% baseline) (Table 1).
On SEED-Bench with a 3B model, SSL4RL yields an 8.94% average improvement, including a 19.63 percentage-point gain on Visual Reasoning (73.41% vs 53.78%) (Table 2).

Scaling from 3B to 7B models shows diminishing returns from the SSL rewards, e.g. Logical Reasoning improves by only 2.57% at 7B versus much larger gains at 3B, indicating a ceiling effect as the SSL task becomes trivial for larger models (Table 3).

Matching SSL task difficulty to model capacity matters: increasing contrastive-learning augmentation strength raises MMBench performance from 69.27% to 77.89%, while harder rotation/jigsaw variants yield only marginal or negative returns (Section 4.2.1, Figure 4).
Naively combining all four SSL reward tasks does not produce additive gains, suggesting optimization conflicts rather than synergy among the intrinsic rewards (Section 4.2.3, Figure 5).

9TMdlXCn79.text: LittleBit-2 introduces internal latent rotation combined with joint iterative quantization (Joint-ITQ) that aligns latent factor distributions with the binary hypercube at zero inference overhead (Section 4, Equation 1).
At 1.0 bpp on Llama-3 8B, LittleBit-2 achieves 11.53 perplexity and 57.33% average zero-shot accuracy while using only 6.3% of full model 'body' bits (Table 1).
At 1.0 bpp on Llama-2 7B, LittleBit-2 outperforms the OneBit baseline: 8.27 perplexity and 55.79% accuracy versus OneBit's 8.36 perplexity and 54.72% accuracy (Table 1).

An ablation on Llama-3 8B at 1.0 bpp shows progressive gains from each component: base LittleBit at 16.30 PPL, adding random rotation drops to 12.63 PPL, and adding Joint-ITQ (full LittleBit-2) reaches 11.53 PPL (Table 3).
At extreme 0.1 bpp compression on Llama-3 8B, LittleBit-2 improves perplexity from 26.11 (LittleBit) to 23.74 while retaining 41.64% zero-shot accuracy (Table 1, Table 3).

The Spectral Break-Even Condition (Proposition 4.1) predicts low-rank binary factorization should outperform tiny-rank FP16 when the spectral tail-energy exponent γ < 0.36, a regime confirmed for 73% of Llama-2 7B layers (Figure 6).

PyJ2YOk3sG.text: Language models do not build a global world state incrementally across tokens; a global linear probe for entity state achieves under 0.3 accuracy while a local, query-relevant probe achieves about 0.9 accuracy, indicating information is aggregated only at the final token when the query becomes evident (Section 3, Figure 1).

Path patching identifies four attention head groups (A, B, C, D) implementing the PUT operation, with groups A and B showing non-trivial overlap with the circuit used for DESCRIPTION binding (Section 4.1, Figure 3).

The REMOVE operation is implemented via a 'global suppression tag' attached to object tokens rather than a box-specific removal mechanism; logit-lens analysis shows removed objects receive markedly smaller logit increases than retained objects (Section 4.2, Figure 6).

On CodeLlama-13B, adversarial scenarios cause high degeneration rates: 84% for no-op Remove, 62% for re-introducing removed objects, and 56% for shared-label objects, and single-layer nullification of the suppression tag only partially recovers correct behavior (intervention score 0.24-0.73) (Section 4.4, Table 1).
The entity-tracking analyses are validated across three model scales/families: CodeLlama-13B (primary), Gemma-2-2B, and Llama-3.1-70B (Section 4).

vsErYkgeeU.text: Proposition 3.1 (Selection Bias) and Proposition 3.2 (Reinforcement Bias) formally show that RL fine-tuning preferentially reinforces high-probability correct trajectories with probability gains scaling proportionally to the base model's own probability, driving diversity collapse (Section 3.2).

Theorem 3.4 proves that differential reward modification, which applies smoothing selectively to correct trajectories, achieves simultaneously superior correctness and diversity compared to entropy-maximization approaches (Section 3.4-3.5, Theorem 3.4).
DS-GRPO (the practical instantiation of differential smoothing built on GRPO) achieves up to 6.7% improvement on AIME24 relative to baselines (Section 4.2-4.7).
On the Countdown task, differential smoothing improves Pass@K performance by roughly 4% over baseline methods (Figure 2).

Differential smoothing is compared against entropy-based diversity heuristics across multiple math reasoning benchmarks and model sizes, showing consistent improvements in both Pass@1 and Pass@K (Section 4.3-4.7, Figure 3, Figure 4).

Ul6hU6WkDL.text: LatentChem decouples chemical logic from linguistic generation by having the model process continuous thought vectors instead of discrete Chain-of-Thought text (Section 3, Figure 3).

Under outcome-only optimization, LatentChem exhibits 'spontaneous internalization,' where the model self-selects to abandon verbose textual derivations in favor of implicit latent computation (Section 4, Figure 7).
LatentChem achieves a 59.88% non-tie win rate against a strong CoT baseline on ChemCoTBench, with 63.73% win rate on open-ended tasks and 50.00% on closed-ended tasks (Table 2, Table 3).

LatentChem delivers a 10.84x average reduction in reasoning-step overhead and a 5.96x wall-clock speedup across all evaluated benchmarks, with reaction-task reductions reaching up to 29.9x (Section 5, Figure 8).
LatentChem is evaluated for non-tie win rate on additional benchmarks beyond ChemCoTBench, including ChEBI-20 (85.26%), ChemLLMBench (55.58%), and Mol-Instructions (49.88%) (Table 3).
A scale-matched evaluation compares LatentChem at 4B and 14B model sizes to assess whether internalization benefits hold across scale (Table 4).

xUQ0Gw11NL.text: The paper defines a unified spectral transformation family Ψ_p(O_t) = UΣ^pV^T for p in [0,1], where p=0 recovers Muon's orthogonalization step (Section 3.3).
Decreasing p compresses the condition number as κ_p = κ(O_t)^p, showing Muon's orthogonalization is the extreme case of spectral compression among the tested p in {1, 1/2, 1/4, 0} (Section 3.4).
On first-moment (momentum) inputs, orthogonalization (p=0) yields a clear stabilization effect and significantly improves robustness over plain momentum SGD (Section 4.3).

When applied to RMS-normalized updates rather than raw momentum, all four spectral variants (p=1, 1/2, 1/4, 0) perform similarly at their best settings, indicating elementwise RMS normalization already resolves much of the anisotropy Muon addresses (Section 4.4).

In controlled GPT-2 (124M parameter) experiments on OpenWebText with QK-Norm/QK-Clip disabled to isolate spectral effects, Muon-style orthogonalization does not outperform Adam (Section 4.1, Section 5).
Algorithm 1 gives a coupled Newton-Schulz iteration for computing the Ψ_{1/2} and Ψ_{1/4} spectral transforms using only matrix multiplications, avoiding explicit SVD (Section 3.5).

9klc62KROH.text: View Space (GVT) is proposed as a fully inductive graph representation model that learns a unified representation space to handle nodes with heterogeneous, arbitrary feature spaces without retraining (Section 4).
Definition 3 formalizes the 'view space' construct used to align representations across graphs with different node feature dimensionalities (Section 3, Definition 3).
Recurrent GVT is evaluated against GraphAny and other GNN baselines on node classification, with numeric accuracy comparisons reported across multiple benchmark tables (Tables 8-11).
Theoretical guarantees for the recurrent formulation of GVT are established via Lemma 1, Lemma 2, and Theorem 7 (Section 4/5, Theorem 7).
Section 5 evaluates inductive learning performance of Recurrent GVT across differing graph structures and feature spaces, comparing against individually tuned GNN baselines (Section 5).
Additional large-scale experimental validation of the model's inductive transfer claims is provided in Appendix Q (Appendix Q).

S2PARGuQzI.text: The method distills language-model-derived soft topic label distributions (via temperature-scaled softmax over a restricted vocabulary V, Equation 1) as reconstruction targets in place of traditional bag-of-words targets (Section 2, Equation 1).

Using ERNIE-4.5-0.3B as the labeling LM, the method attains topic coherence (C_v) of 0.381, 0.392, and 0.397 on 20NewsGroup, TweetTopic, and StackOverflow respectively, versus the best baseline FASTopic's 0.358, 0.276, and 0.363 (Table 1).
Purity scores with ERNIE-4.5-0.3B soft labels reach 0.520, 0.781, and 0.737 on 20NewsGroup, TweetTopic, and StackOverflow, exceeding the best baseline CombinedTM's 0.391, 0.588, and 0.306 (Table 1).
For document similarity retrieval, Llama-3.2-1B-derived topic distributions achieve P@5 of 0.502, 0.857, and 0.588 on the three datasets, compared to FASTopic's 0.421, 0.811, and 0.189 (Table 2).

An ablation replacing the LM-derived soft targets with bag-of-words reconstruction targets produces the largest performance drop of all tested variants, confirming the soft-label supervision is the primary driver of coherence and purity gains (Table 3).
A temperature of τ=3 is used to balance the coherence-diversity tradeoff in the softmax over vocabulary logits (Section 5.2).

uBYlCu8b8Z.text: AdaGC computes an adaptive per-parameter clipping threshold via an EMA-tracked historical gradient norm, h_{t,i} = min{λ_rel · γ_{t-1,i}/||g_{t,i}||, 1.0} (Section 4.2).
On Llama-2 7B and Llama-2 13B pretraining, AdaGC eliminates all loss spikes (0 spikes) whereas GlobalGC, ScaledEmbed, and StableAdamW baselines exhibit multiple spike events (Figure 3).

AdaGC reduces WikiText perplexity from 21.173 (GlobalGC) to 20.434 (a 3.5% reduction) and LAMBADA perplexity from 11.111 to 10.515 (a 5.4% reduction), with LAMBADA accuracy improving from 49.35% to 49.49% (Table 1).

Theorem 4.1 proves AdaGC retains an O(1/√T) convergence rate under non-convex conditions, comparable to vanilla Adam, showing the localized adaptive clipping preserves theoretical convergence guarantees (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.1).

On CLIP ViT-Base training, AdaGC achieves 25% faster convergence (15k vs 20k steps to a target loss) than StableAdamW along with complete spike elimination and a 0.27 percentage point ImageNet-1K accuracy gain (Figure 4).

QUL7jp4QDQ.text: ZipMoE exploits the low-entropy exponent bits in the BF16 floating-point format for lossless MoE expert weight compression, with the Shannon entropy bound calculated at approximately 66%, versus 74% achieved by LZ4HC and 68% by ZSTD general-purpose compressors (Section 2.2, Figures 2-3).
For decoder-only models, ZipMoE achieves 62.65%-97.97% TPOT reduction and 53.25%-87.90% TTFT reduction relative to state-of-the-art on-device MoE serving systems (Figure 7).
ZipMoE improves system throughput by 1.79x-42.49x for decoder-only models and 1.31x-5.82x for encoder-decoder models over prior systems (Figure 8).
End-to-end latency improves by 3.03x-42.49x for decoder-only models and 1.11x-5.64x for encoder-decoder models (Figure 9).
The cache-affinity scheduling algorithm provides a theoretical approximation guarantee of ALG ≤ (3 − 1/L)·OPT, where L is the number of threads (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1).
A hierarchical cache pool with rank-based workload modeling and dynamic-programming-based optimization is used to manage expert placement across memory tiers (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.2).

nPC7M7XLEv.text: CDOT formulates cross-domain distribution alignment as a convex quadratic program over transport polytopes, with Theorem 3.4 establishing existence of an optimal coupling and convexity of the objective (Theorem 3.4).

Theorem 3.5 proves the CDOT discrepancy is a valid pseudometric on attributed compact metric-measure spaces, while Theorem 3.7 derives a 'dispersion gap' relating CDOT to Gromov-Wasserstein via ℛ_GW,2(π) − ℛ(π) = 𝒱(π) (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.7).
On synthetic 2D clustered point clouds with n=500 samples, CDOT achieves a matching MSE of 0.0016±0.00, lower than both FGW (0.0034±0.00) and IsoRank (0.0033±0.00) (Table 2).

On the OASIS-3 brain connectome dataset (696 subjects, 170-node networks), CDOT attains 0.6136 matching accuracy under diffusion distance versus 0.1853 for FGW, though FGW outperforms CDOT under geodesic distance (0.5375 vs 0.4640) (Table 3).

On TUDataset graph classification benchmarks, CDOT outperforms FGW on MUTAG (0.8617±0.07 vs 0.8249±0.08) and ENZYMES (0.5133±0.04 vs 0.4450±0.03) using an RBF-kernel SVM with 10-fold cross-validation (Table 4).

Theorem 5.6 gives a non-asymptotic risk bound decomposing into an O(1/T) optimization error and a statistical error term, with Corollary 5.7 establishing asymptotic consistency under Frank-Wolfe optimization (Theorem 5.6, Corollary 5.7).

l4nKEbhHKh.text: The framework replaces three Transformer nonlinearities—Softmax, SiLU, and RMSNorm/LayerNorm—with spike-friendly approximations built from division, exponentiation, and ℓ2-norm primitives implemented via LIF neuron populations (Section 4).

Across LLaMA-3-8B, LLaMA-2-7B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen3-8B, plugging in the spiking operators changes average accuracy by at most 0.014 (Qwen3-8B: +0.014; LLaMA-3-8B: -0.003; LLaMA-2-7B: -0.002; Mistral-7B: +0.000), all without any fine-tuning (Table 1).
On BERT via the SpikeZIP pipeline, the plug-and-play operators change average accuracy by only +0.003 (Table 2).

Theorem 5.1 decomposes the total approximation error additively into exponentiation error (ε_exp), division error (Δ), and norm-estimation error (ε_pol), with recommended settings H=5, K=64 yielding ε_exp ≤ 3.63×10⁻³ (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
Ablation over parameter L (tested across L=3-5) shows mean and maximum approximation errors remain small and stable, indicating robustness to hyperparameter choice (Section 6.2, Figure 4).

2yMTCCHEjU.text: The Invariant Contamination Ratio is defined as ICR = 1/(1 + (1/d)∑λᵢ), where λᵢ are generalized eigenvalues from a Fisher discriminant problem comparing invariant covariance Σₛ to residual covariance Σξ of diffusion features (Section 3.2).

Figure 3 shows a U-shaped ICR curve across intermediate noise levels on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, where ICR is minimized exactly where linear classification accuracy peaks, computed label-free from training features alone (Figure 3, Section 4).

In data-limited regimes (CIFAR-10 with 4,096 images; ImageNet with 10K-20K image subsets), the ICR trajectory is U-shaped and its minimum precedes a rise in the memorization ratio, serving as an early training-time indicator (Figures 5-6, Appendix C).

Figure 8 shows that under limited data, Tr(Σₛ) saturates while Tr(Σξ) continues to grow, marking a shift from semantic to memorization-driven feature expansion detectable purely from training features (Figure 8, Section 5.2-5.3).

In data-rich settings, Figure 4 shows ICR and FID both decrease monotonically over training, with feature-space expansion dominated by growth of the invariant structure rather than residual noise (Figure 4).

zLUPTgV7BI.text: TRAP optimizes adversarial patches via projected gradient descent using a combined CoT-hijacking cross-entropy loss and an action loss (discrete or continuous depending on the VLA), and is presented as the first targeted adversarial attack on CoT reasoning in Vision-Language-Action models (Section 4).

TRAP is evaluated on three mainstream VLA architectures spanning distinct CoT paradigms: MolmoACT (integrated, discrete actions), GraspVLA (integrated, continuous flow-matching actions), and InstructVLA (hierarchical, continuous flow-matching actions) (Table 2, Section 6.1).

Overall attack success rate averages 52.54%, with GraspVLA most vulnerable at 75.84% ASR (hijack score 0.4253), MolmoACT at 48.06% ASR (hijack score 0.3904), and InstructVLA most robust at 33.71% ASR (hijack score 0.1724) (Table 3, Section 6.2).
