Intervention experiments show CoT strongly governs downstream action generation even when semantically misaligned with the input instruction, with cross-sample CoT shuffling acting as the dominant control signal for GraspVLA (Table 1, Section 4).

In a real-world test on a Franka Panda robot using a physical 20cm x 20cm printed adversarial patch, TRAP corrupted CoT reasoning in 86.7% (13/15) of trials and achieved full behavior hijacking (redirecting a 'pick carrot' instruction to picking a knife) in 33.3% (5/15) of trials (Section 6.5).

Ablations show attack success rate on MolmoACT scales with patch size and exhibits a phase transition, and remains substantial for universal (instruction-agnostic) patches, ranging 0.7-25% ASR on scene-relevant instructions and 21-65% on scene-irrelevant instructions (Figure 5, Table 5, Section 6.3).

LGRHLPCjYS.text: OpenMAG integrates 19 datasets spanning 6 domains (e-commerce, social media, art networks, video recommendation, book recommendation, image networks), each paired with 16 supported feature encoders covering both frozen and trainable extraction (Section 3, Table 1).

The benchmark implements 24 state-of-the-art models across three paradigms—graph-enhanced, multimodal-enhanced, and MLLM-enhanced—evaluated on 8 downstream tasks: 3 graph-based (node classification, link prediction, node clustering) and 5 modality-based (matching, retrieval, alignment, graph-to-text generation, graph-to-image generation) (Table 3-4).

The evaluation framework assesses five dimensions—necessity, data quality, effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency—including tests of resilience against modal noise and structural perturbations (Section 3.4, Figures 5-7).

The systematic assessment yields 14 fundamental insights (C1-C14), including the necessity of combining multimodal semantics with topology (C1), domain-specific modality preferences (C2), fine-tuning advantages (C5), and LoRA effectiveness (C10) (Section 3.4).

Figure 2 compares unimodal versus multimodal feature configurations across the benchmarked tasks, supporting the necessity claim (C1) that multimodal semantics and graph topology are mutually indispensable (Figure 2).

4FVs0ExC7m.text: Vector-Panning Feature Alignment (VPFA) uses a three-layer MLP with residual connections (the VP module) to pan low-resolution features along a learned resolution direction, producing pseudo-high-resolution representations without modifying the frozen backbone (Section 4).

Canonical Correlation Analysis and Pearson correlation analysis show that resolution-induced feature shifts converge to a consistent semantic direction, with cosine similarity values above 0.99 between HR-LR difference vectors across datasets (Section 3, Table 1).
VPFA achieves 94.1% Rank-1 accuracy on MLR-Market-1501 and 94.7% Rank-1 on MLR-CUHK03, surpassing the previous best results of 92.3% and 93.4% respectively (Table 3).
VPFA attains 50.5% Rank-1 on MLR-VIPeR and 66.6% Rank-1 on CAVIAR, outperforming prior cross-resolution re-identification baselines including PS-HRNet, INTACT, LRAR, and RAIN (Table 3).
Ablation studies show that removing the residual connections in the VP module reduces performance by 3.8 percentage points, and a hidden dimension of 2048 is identified as optimal (Table 4).
t-SNE visualizations demonstrate that VPFA narrows the gap between HR and LR feature distributions and strengthens intra-identity clustering compared to the unaligned baseline (Figure 3).

ETBr4m6w4s.text: KORE converts individual knowledge items into structured knowledge trees via Kore-Augmentation, generating 75,710 multi-round dialogue samples and 46,468 VQA samples using GPT-4o (Section 3.1).

Kore-Constraint stores prior knowledge in the covariance matrix of each linear layer's activations and initializes LoRA-style adapters by projecting into the null space of this covariance, satisfying BA·C ≈ 0 (Section 3.2, Equation 2).
On LLaVA-v1.5 (7B) with rank 235, KORE achieves 30.65 CEM on the EVOKE knowledge-adaptation benchmark and 37.09 average retention score, versus 15.23 CEM and 18.02 average for LoRA (Table 1).

Ablating Kore-Augmentation causes a 19.82-point drop in Evoke CEM (from 30.65 to 10.83) on LLaVA-v1.5 (7B), showing the augmentation component is more critical than the constraint component to knowledge adaptation performance (Table 4).

KORE generalizes across architectures, improving knowledge adaptation CEM on LLaVA-v1.5 (13B) to 32.89 (vs. 12.05 for Replay) and on Qwen2.5-VL (7B) to 22.91 (vs. 11.73 for Replay) (Section 4.3, Table 3).

Knowledge retention is evaluated across 12 benchmarks spanning 7 capability dimensions (COM, OCR, M-DIS, INS, M-IDU, MAT, HAL), including MME, MMBench, ScienceQA, MMMU, MathVista, and POPE (Setup 2, Section 4).

c8WxrEWQcx.text: The paper proves that any H_γ-invariant function can be written in the canonical form Ψ(x)=ϕ((a1^T x)^2+(a2^T x)^2, a3^T x), giving an architectural construction that guarantees invariance by design (Section 4.1).
Theorem 4.2 extends the canonical invariant-function representation from SO(3) to the general SO(n) case using the invRep construction (Section 4.4).

On synthetic polynomial tasks p(x), q(x), and r(x), the proposed H_γ^inv-Net attains invariance errors of 1.98×10^-5, 3.00×10^-4, and 5.83×10^-2 respectively, compared against LieGAN and Augerino (Table 5.1).

On real-world symmetry discovery tasks, the framework achieves an invariance error of 7.92×10^-2 on the Anisotropic Quantum system (n=4) and 1.7×10^-1 on the Double Pendulum (n=8), evaluated alongside moment-of-inertia prediction (Table 5.2).

The method recovers rotation rates λ close to reference values λ0 across tasks including q(x), r(x), Anisotropic Quantum, Double Pendulum, and Top Quark Tagging, and achieves 88.03% classification accuracy on the Top Quark Tagging dataset (Table 6.1, Section 6).

3pLFgUQLzJ.text: GraphFlow represents LLM-agent workflows as a unified graph (wGraph) whose nodes are atomic operations, and uses a 2-layer GCN with virtual task nodes and MLP-based edge scoring to adaptively construct task-conditioned workflows (Section 4).

GraphFlow decomposes KV caches into context-independent base components and sparse prefix-specific residuals for topology-aware state management, observing that over 75% of key entries and over 70% of value entries fall below a small sparsity threshold (Section 5, Figure 3).

On Qwen-2.5-7B, GraphFlow outperforms the AFlow baseline on GSM8K (92.1% vs. 89.2%), MATH (76.4% vs. 72.1%), HumanEval pass@1 (86.2% vs. 78.1%), HotpotQA F1 (70.4 vs. 67.5), and MBPP (74.7% vs. 68.4%), yielding an average improvement of approximately 4.95 percentage points across five benchmarks (Table 1).

GraphFlow reduces KV-cache memory footprint by roughly 4× relative to stateful KV management, e.g., from approximately 50GB to approximately 11GB on GSM8K, while maintaining near-equivalent task performance (Section 6, Figure 5).

Removing the GNN encoder from the workflow generation component causes a 5.5 percentage point accuracy drop on MATH (from 52.6% to 47.1%) with Llama-3.1-8B, and a 2-layer GCN depth is found optimal, with performance degrading at 3-4 layers due to over-smoothing (Table 2, Figure 8).

R6JV2WOftz.text: The Cluster-Aware Causal Mixer groups channels via spectral clustering based on inter-channel correlations and assigns proportionally-sized dedicated embedding layers per cluster, reducing embedding parameters by a factor of M equal to the number of clusters (Section 3.2, Equation 10).

A causal MLP-Mixer applies an upper-triangular masking scheme (Equations 11-12) so that the representation at each time step depends only on past information, preserving strict temporal causality for online anomaly detection (Section 3.3).

On the six benchmark datasets SWaT, WADI, PSM, SMD, SMAP, and MSL, the method improves F1 score over baselines by 10.32% on PSM (0.716), 12.34% on MSL (0.619), 11.96% on SMD (0.599), and 4.71% on WADI (0.733), compared against 15 baseline methods including LSTM-VAE, NPSR, SensitiveHUE, GDN, and MTAD-GAT (Table 2).

Sequential anomaly scoring accumulates log-based anomaly evidence over an accumulation window of δ=5 to prevent isolated false positives, and this sequential detection method outperforms point-based detection across all six datasets in an ablation study (Section 3.4, Table 3).

A modular architecture ablation across 10 configuration cases demonstrates synergy between cluster-aware channel grouping and causal temporal mixing, and the proposed spectral clustering variant outperforms alternative clustering methods on the PSM and SMAP datasets (Table 4, Table 5).

b9PBqFgXp6.text: PRIME is a new benchmark of 156 theorem statements and proofs curated from undergraduate and graduate-level textbooks, manually formalized into Lean 4 by experts and spanning domains including Algebra, Analysis, and Number Theory (Section 4.1, Figure 5).

DSR decomposes natural language statements into logical components and structures them as hierarchical operator trees (OPTs), then reconstructs the formal statement via a deterministic Structure-First Assembly process before applying Tree-Guided Repair (Section 3.3).

Under a standardized computational budget of 4 inference calls, DSR achieves Consistency Check pass rates of 84.00% on ProverBench, 79.51% on ProofNet, and 67.95% on PRIME, outperforming the strongest baseline (Goedel-V2-Formalizer-32B) by 8.62 points on ProofNet (Table 2).

The performance gap between DSR and the strongest baseline widens with theorem complexity, from a 0.62% Consistency Check advantage on the entry-level ProverBench to a 1.28% advantage on the graduate-level PRIME benchmark (Section 4.3).

An ablation shows that adding operator-tree supervision alone (without curriculum learning) can cause performance stagnation on PRIME, with Pass@1 Syntax Check dropping from 22.44% to 19.87%, while adding curriculum learning recovers this to 23.08% (Table 3, Section 3.2).

The DSR-Global ablation, which replaces tree-guided repair with a generic statement-level repair strategy, achieves higher Syntax Check pass rates on some benchmarks but consistently lower Consistency Check pass rates than full DSR, indicating a trade-off between syntactic validity and semantic fidelity (Table 2, Section 4.4.2).

rF1oJAhAZA.text: Eyes-on-Me raises the average end-to-end attack success rate on RAG poisoning from a prior state-of-the-art of 21.9% to 57.8%, a 2.6x improvement, across 18 RAG configurations (Table 1, Section 5.2).

A single optimized attractor achieves 96.6% average black-box retriever attack success rate and 97.8% average black-box generator attack success rate when transferred to unseen retrievers and generators without retraining, including proprietary APIs such as GPT-4o-mini and Gemini 2.5-Flash (Table 2, Section 5.3).

Attention mass in influential attention heads correlates with downstream attack success with Pearson coefficients exceeding 0.9, motivating the attention-steering attractor design (Figure 3, Section 4.2).

An ablation on attractor initialization finds that random initialization outperforms structured initialization (42.27% vs. 31.06%), and that an attractor length of 7 tokens is optimal (Section 6, Tables 3-5).
Under a perplexity-filtering defense, Eyes-on-Me combined with LLM-generated content still achieves a 72.2% generator attack success rate (Section 6).

Trigger transferability experiments show cross-trigger transfer end-to-end attack success rates ranging from 28% to 100%, with an average source-trigger rate of 71%, indicating inconsistent semantic transfer (Section 5.4, Table 2c).

iziZOSvtGK.text: FedGMR addresses model-heterogeneous federated learning by progressively increasing sub-model density (capacity) for bandwidth-constrained clients over the course of training rather than fixing their capacity throughout (Section 1).

Under high heterogeneity with non-IID data, FedGMR improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by +2.94% on FEMNIST, +29.47% on CIFAR-10, and +57.73% on ImageNet-100, with gains widening on harder tasks (Table 1).

The method uses a two-stage mechanism: adaptive density assignment via gradient descent on a time-difference objective (Section 4.1), followed by density restoration triggered by an early-stopping mechanism when validation accuracy plateaus (Section 4.2).

Theorem 2 proves convergence to a density-dependent neighborhood, with the optimization error bound composed of a model-drift term, a variance term, and a non-IID bias term, each scaling with sub-model density (Section 5.2, Theorem 2).

An ablation removing gradual model restoration (GMR) causes accuracy to drop from 61.64% to 54.33% on ImageNet-100 under high IID conditions, confirming that restoration resolves the capacity bottleneck (Table 2).

BuffMaskFedAvg, an asynchronous aggregation scheme with staleness-aware weighting and mask-aware per-coordinate normalization, is essential to the method; synchronous variants degrade accuracy by 2-3% on average (Section 5.1).

U7c6glPdDW.text: CONCUR identifies a middle-phase thrashing pathology in agentic batch inference where GPU memory remains saturated yet KV-cache hit rates collapse as long-lived agents accumulate state, with this middle phase dominating roughly 90% of execution time (Section 3).

CONCUR improves batch inference throughput by up to 4.09x on Qwen3-32B (batch size 256, tensor parallel degree 8) and up to 1.90x on DeepSeek-V3 (batch size 40, tensor parallel degree 16) relative to an SGLang baseline (Table 1).
At batch size 40 on DeepSeek-V3, CONCUR raises the KV-cache hit rate from 35.41% under the SGLang baseline to 73.36% (Table 2).

CONCUR uses an AIMD-inspired admission control algorithm that linearly increases the admitted-agent window (factor alpha=2) when the system is underutilized and multiplicatively decreases it (factor beta=0.5) when thrashing is detected, governed by utilization thresholds U_low=0.2, U_high=0.5, and a hit-rate threshold H_thresh=0.2 (Section 4).

Admission control operates at agent granularity, dynamically adjusting the number of concurrently active agents based on runtime cache utilization and hit-rate signals while preserving execution continuity for already-admitted agents (Section 4).

PVaFEuNnsD.text: MSN-PINN models targets as sums of power-law terms u_theta(x) = sum_k c_k x^{mu_k}, treating both coefficients {c_k} and exponents {mu_k} as trainable parameters optimized via a two-timescale scheme with exponent learning rate eta_mu set to roughly 0.5 times the coefficient learning rate eta_c (Equation 1, Section 3.1, Algorithm 1, Section 3.5).
For the 2D Laplace equation corner singularity with a 270-degree wedge angle, MSN-PINN recovers the exponent as mu=0.6667 against the true classical Kondrat'ev value of 2/3, a 0.009% error (Table 2).

On a 40-configuration wedge benchmark spanning 5 angles and 4 boundary condition types, the constraint-aware MSN-PINN achieves 100% success rate with 0.022% mean exponent error, versus only 55% success and 5.96% mean error for the naive MSN-PINN without the constraint term, a roughly 270-fold improvement in accuracy (Section I.8, Table 11).

Theorem 4.5 shows the exponent recovery error scales as O(sigma / (c_min * Delta^2 * sqrt(N))), where Delta is the minimum separation between exponents, implying degraded conditioning as exponents become closely spaced, analogous to an optical resolution limit (Theorem 4.5, Remark 4.6).

Adding a constraint-aware loss term of the form sum_k |c_k| sin^2(mu_k * omega) to steer critical points toward physically valid exponents improves accuracy on the corner-singularity example from 14.6% error to 0.009% error (Theorem 4.8, Figure 2).

Two exponents become distinguishable (resolvable) only when their separation Delta is at least 0.1; below this threshold they merge into an intermediate value, termed the Rayleigh limit for exponent resolution (Table 10, Section I.6, Remark I.1).

5Zp3m9Uetz.text: On CIFAR-10 under IID symmetric noise (ρ∈[0.5,1.0]), FedGR reaches 83.91±1.32% accuracy versus 55.12±1.55% for FedCorr, 30.18±2.92% for FedFixer, and 68.47±3.00% for FedDivideMix (Table 1).
On CIFAR-10 under IID mixed noise (ρ∈[0.2,0.4]), FedGR attains 92.27±0.18% accuracy compared to 70.66±0.69% for FedAvg (Table 1).
On CIFAR-100 under symmetric noise (ρ∈[0.5,1.0]), FedGR achieves 35.28±1.47% accuracy, roughly on par with FL-DivideMix at 35.35±1.15% (Table 2).
On the real-world Clothing1M dataset, FedGR reaches 70.26% accuracy in the IID setting and 68.53% in the non-IID setting (Table 3).

Ablations show removing the Centralized Sieving module drops CIFAR-10 symmetric-noise accuracy by 29.32 points (to 54.59%), while removing Label Refining drops it by 8.68 points (to 75.23%) (Table 4).

The global federated model memorizes no more than 30% of label-noise samples over training, compared to over 80% memorization for a centralized model trained on the same noisy data (Figure 1, Section 3).

iTWu7ziS5z.text: The Measure-Explain-Diagnose (MED) framework's tool contribution ratio attributes only 0.30 of learning progress to tool-induced effects for Qwen2.5-VL and 0.22 for Qwen3-VL, with over 70% of gains coming from intrinsic capability change (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

The Explain stage decomposes the tool-induced performance gap into four terms—Call Gain, Schema Gain, Call Harm, and Schema Harm—evaluated across six visual benchmarks: VStar, HR-Bench 4k/8k, and VisualProbe Easy/Medium/Hard (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

Vision tool-use RL training reduces Call Harm (successes broken by tool invocation) consistently across training, while Call-Gain quality shows little improvement on the existing failure set (Section 4.6, Figure 5).
Human evaluation shows Qwen3-VL achieves 93.0% human-aligned tool-use gains versus 63.4% for the tool-naive Qwen2.5-VL baseline (Table 2).
The Diagnose stage factorizes each of the four gap terms into Mass, Policy, and Quality components to attribute tool-induced effects to specific causes (Section 3.3, Figure 4).

PJ0GpmFYrR.text: H-EPM constructs a tool graph from accumulated trajectories where edges encode tool-to-tool transition weights combining accuracy and efficiency, augmented with optional contextual state summaries (Section 4.2).
With GPT-4.1-mini, H-EPM improves task success from a 0.541 baseline to 0.661 on τ-Bench (+22.2%), from 0.396 to 0.526 on τ²-Bench (+32.8%), and from 0.584 to 0.658 on ToolSandbox (+12.7%) (Table 1).

In a zero-shot setting on ACEBench with GPT-4.1 and no online graph training data, H-EPM raises process accuracy from 0.653 to 0.765 (+17.2%) and end-to-end accuracy from 0.503 to 0.567 (+12.7%) (Table 2).

Ablation on τ²-Bench with GPT-4.1 shows removing the tool graph drops accuracy by 15.7 points, removing state information drops it by 9.2 points, and removing weight optimization drops it by 7.8 points from the full H-EPM configuration (Table 4).

The agent autonomously decides at inference time whether to invoke the state-summary tool before selecting the next tool call via state similarity or edge weights, enabling adaptive reuse of partially overlapping experiences (Section 4.3).

L0T4pmqkMg.text: Theorem 3.3 proves Algorithm 1 achieves oracle complexity of 5√ℓ(0)R̄/√ε + k(δ) gradient calls for functions with subquadratic or quadratic growth under generalized ℓ-smoothness (Theorem 3.3).
Corollary 3.4 shows that optimizing over the free parameter δ yields complexity O(√ℓ(0)R/√ε), which is provably optimal in the small-ε regime (Corollary 3.4).

For (L₀,L₁)-smooth functions (ℓ(s)=L₀+L₁s), the paper's bound reduces to O(√L₀R/√ε), removing the non-constant multiplicative factors present in prior results such as √(L₀+L₁‖∇f(x⁰)‖)R/√ε from Li et al. (2024a) and exp(L₁R)·√L₀R/√ε from Gorbunov et al. (2025) (Table 1).
Algorithm 2 (Section 4) removes the initial gradient-descent phase required by Algorithm 1, giving a parameter-stable accelerated method without pre-running GD (Algorithm 2, Section 4).
Theorem 4.3 provides refined complexity bounds with improved non-dominant terms compared to prior accelerated methods under (L₀,L₁)-smoothness (Theorem 4.3).

dc0WdvWSnB.text: Proposition 5.1 establishes that Verbalized Bayesian Persuasion (VBP) returns an ε-approximate Bayes correlated equilibrium in static Bayesian persuasion settings and an ε-approximate Bayes-Nash equilibrium in multistage settings (Proposition 5.1, Section 4).

Section 6.1.1 evaluates VBP on three dialogue scenarios: a Recommendation Letter (REL) task with a 1/3 vs 2/3 strong/weak student prior, a Courtroom (COR) task with a 30% guilt prior, and a Law Enforcement (LAE) patrol-allocation task (Section 6.1.1).

In the static, polarized-signal setting (S1), the sender's achieved reward matches the Bayes Correlated Equilibrium baseline, with honesty probability converging to approximately 100% for the strong/guilty/patrolled states and lying probability dropping to near 0% (Figure 4).
Convergence experiments show exploitability decreasing to approximately 0.1 after 10 iterations, indicating proximity to equilibrium (Figure 6).

In the multistage setting (S3), Algorithm 1 combines Prompt-PSRO with step-wise conditional prompt optimization via FunSearch, and performance in this setting declines relative to the static settings, with sender deception oscillating through bargaining dynamics before stabilizing (Section 5.3, Figure 8).

hpxI4Mndt4.text: The Optimal Token Baseline (OTB) achieves performance comparable to a group size of N=32 while using only N=4 rollouts, cutting token consumption by 66.03% on single-turn reasoning and 68.32% on tool-integrated reasoning (Section 6.3, Figure 11).
On single-turn reasoning, OTB scores 30.31 on AIME25 and 37.29 on AIME24, versus GRPO's 25.31 and 31.35 and OGB's 30.10 and 33.13 respectively (Table 1).
On tool-integrated reasoning, OTB scores 28.13 on AIME25, outperforming SimpleTIR (26.67) and OGB (21.15) (Table 1, Section 6.1).

OTB eliminates the sudden gradient-norm surges and training collapse observed under high gradient variance in long-horizon RL, remaining stable where baseline methods (TIS, MIS) degrade (Section 6.2, Figures 2 and 9).

The paper proves the OTB is unbiased and yields provably lower variance than the ordinary group baseline (OGB) via a logit-gradient proxy justified theoretically in Section 5.3 (Theorem/Section 5.1-5.2).

Q1twBCjpUt.text: Vulnerable Agent Identification (VAI) is formulated as a Hierarchical Adversarial Decentralized Mean Field Control (HAD-MFC) problem, with the upper-level combinatorial agent-selection task proven NP-hard via reduction to generalized maximum coverage (Proposition 3.3).

The Fenchel-Rockafellar transform is used to derive a regularized mean-field Bellman operator that decouples the upper- and lower-level problems, enabling independent learning at each level while provably preserving the optimal solution of the original HAD-MFC problem (Proposition 4.5).

VAI methods (VAI-Greedy and VAI-RL) outperform five baselines, including degree centrality and learning-based methods PIANO and RTCA, in 17 of 18 evaluated tasks across the Battle, Taxi, and Vicsek MARL environments (Table 1).
Predicted agent vulnerability correlates strongly with actual attack outcomes, reaching Pearson r=0.97 in the Battle environment and r=0.91 in the Taxi environment (p<.001) (Figure 1).

The decoupled approach achieves computational cost on par with baseline methods despite requiring additional value-function training, with full complexity analysis provided in Appendix D.1 (Section 4, Appendix D.1).

LffORETnav.text: The optimal James-Stein shrinkage coefficient for the baseline is derived in closed form as (n-1)/n times v2/(s2+v2), where v2 is the expected variance of leave-one-out estimates and s2 is the variability of true prompt-level values (Theorem 1).

The shrinkage baseline reduces value-function mean-squared error by 13.4%-39.4% relative to RLOO across different rollout budgets, and reduces policy-gradient variance by 11.2%-67.1% (Section on empirical variance/MSE results).

On mathematical reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, OlympiadBench, AMC23) with Qwen2.5-Math models, the shrinkage baseline yields 1.1%-4.3% accuracy gains over standard empirical-mean baselines (experiments section).
On Knights-and-Knaves logic puzzles, the method improves accuracy by 2.3%-15.2% across difficulty levels, with consistent gains also observed on Countdown and Maze tasks (experiments section).
On GSM8K, the James-Stein baseline achieves the highest test accuracy among RLOO, GRPO, ReMax, REINFORCE++, and BLOO baselines across 2, 4, and 8 generations per prompt (Table 1).

The shrinkage baseline requires no additional hyperparameters, remains unbiased via leave-one-out construction, and can be implemented as a drop-in replacement with about 10 lines of code (Section on implementation).

ErqvESaJpk.text: The method (referred to as PrinMix/AdaMix) outperforms the state-of-the-art Delta-CoMe baseline by 22.3% on AIME2024 and 6.1% on GQA for 7B-parameter LLM delta compression, and by 26.9% on AIME2024 for 14B models (Experimental Results table).

The quantization error for the singular-vector matrix V is derived analytically as e_i^V = Sigma_ii^2 * DeltaV_i XX^T DeltaV_i^T, motivating allocation of more bits to directions with larger singular values (Section on Quantization Error Derivation).

A Target Correction for Consistency (TCC) technique reformulates the quantization loss for matrix U to remove the bias introduced by sequentially quantizing U against an already-quantized V (Method section).

Bit-width allocation is formulated as a 0/1 integer linear program that minimizes total quantization error subject to a bit-budget constraint, a one-hot constraint per singular vector, and a constraint limiting the number of active bit-widths to f_max, yielding solutions without empirical heuristics (Method section, ILP formulation).

The compression scheme enables loading 12 compressed models on a single GPU versus only 2 uncompressed models, delivering roughly 6x memory/disk savings and 6.4x faster generation at scale compared to naive multi-model serving (Practical Benefits section).

ndyuCnJxks.text: MotiMotion achieves the highest scores among compared motion-controlled video generation methods on the curated MotiBench benchmark, scoring 0.302 (physical realism), 0.520 (photorealism), and 0.665 (semantic consistency), versus MagicMotion's 0.157/0.550/0.343 and Wan-Move's 0.218/0.483/0.511 (Table 1).
In a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) evaluation, MotiMotion achieves win rates of 78.0% (VLM judge) and 97.9% (human study) against MagicMotion, and 73.8%/81.4% against Wan-Move (Table 2).

Ablation results show that adding prompt reasoning, motion reasoning, and confidence-aware control sequentially improves physical realism from 0.166 to 0.302, photorealism from 0.389 to 0.520, and semantic consistency from 0.337 to 0.665 over the base motion-controlled generator (Table 4).

Applying MotiMotion's reasoning module to other motion-controlled methods (MagicMotion, Wan-Move) as a cross-method verification consistently improves their physical realism and semantic consistency scores, e.g. Wan-Move's physical score rises from 0.218 to 0.283 (Table 3).

MotiBench, the newly curated benchmark, contains 62 pre-event physical-interaction images spanning categories such as Collision, Constraint Change, Tool Mechanisms, Flow, and Common Objects, with 30% of samples involving multi-object interaction (Section 4.2, Table 6, Appendix B.1).

Even without user text prompts, prompt reasoning using only the input image and trajectories substantially improves performance, raising physical realism from 0.177 to 0.229 and semantic consistency from 0.272 to 0.473 (Table 5).

y1czGbUum5.text: SoftMatcha 2 supports search over trillion-scale natural language corpora with sub-0.3-second query latency (Section 5).
On the FineWeb-Edu corpus, SoftMatcha 2 achieves lower search latency than infini-gram, infini-gram-mini, and the original SoftMatcha, as shown in the latency comparison (Section 5, Figure 4).
SoftMatcha 2 is evaluated against infini-gram and infini-gram-mini using FM-index-based exact search as baselines for corpus-scale pattern matching (Section 2, Table 3).
SoftMatcha 2 identifies benchmark contamination in large-scale training corpora that is not detected by prior approaches, evaluated via contamination detection experiments (Section 5, Table 6).
The system is evaluated on both FineWeb-Edu and DOLMA, trillion-token pretraining corpora, to demonstrate scalability (Section 4).

qcb833SRNd.text: Repeating smaller datasets yields faster convergence than training on larger datasets under a fixed compute budget, demonstrated with mini-batch updates on sparse parity, single-index models, in-context learning, and modular addition tasks (Section 3, Figure 1).
The 'small-vs-large gap' persists under full-batch gradient descent, ruling out sample-repetition frequency as the sole explanation (Section 3, Figure 2).

Theorem 1 formally shows, for a 2-layer network with quadratic activation on 2-sparse parity, that convergence speed in the first phase of training scales with dataset size N via a √N dependence (Theorem 1).

The speedup is attributed to smaller datasets inducing sampling biases that accelerate layer-wise norm growth (specifically the ratio ‖a‖₂/‖W‖_F), rather than to any useful task signal, since the effect persists even with random labels (Section 5.1, Figures 4 and 20).

Manually adjusting layer-wise initialization scales and learning rates (e.g., for W_q, W_k in Transformers) closes the gap between small and large dataset training, tested on MLPs and Transformers (Section 5.2, Figures 5-9).
The size of the gap grows with task complexity and network depth but shrinks with network width, tested across depths of 2-8 layers and widths of 32-1024 neurons (Section 5.2, Figures 10-11).

urlj8fAMrf.text: The paper proposes Optimistic Actor-Critic (Opt-AC), presented in Algorithm 1, which avoids expensive planning oracles for low-rank MDPs by relying only on policy evaluation oracles (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
Theorem 5.2 establishes a sample complexity of Õ(H⁵d³|A|²log|Θ|/ε²) for Opt-AC, improving on prior work by a factor of the rank d (Theorem 5.2).
Theorem 5.1 characterizes the computational (oracle-call) complexity of the algorithm as SL²K(1/K) supervised-learning oracle calls (Theorem 5.1).
The theoretical results are extended to approximately low-rank MDPs via conditional random Fourier features, with guarantees given for the misspecified setting (Section 6, Theorems 6.1 and 6.2).
Opt-AC is validated empirically as cRFFSAC against a SAC baseline on six MuJoCo Gym environments: Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Reacher, Pendulum, and InvertedPendulum (Section 7, Table 2).

AmT2F5APcp.text: The DocOS benchmark contains 817 tasks spanning 20 applications (including PyCharm, Blender, Postman, Godot, Zotero, and VSCode), split into 265 easy, 298 medium, and 254 hard tasks (Section on task distribution / benchmark statistics table).

DocOS evaluates GUI agents in two phases: document search, measured by Target URL Inclusion (TUI) and Hierarchical Path Progress (HPP), and task execution, measured by Task Completion Rate (TCR) (Section on evaluation metrics).

On the main results table, top proactive-search performance reaches only 42.23% TUI (Qwen3-VL-8B), while the best task completion rate is 17.31% TCR (UI-TARS-1.5-7B), revealing a disconnect between search accuracy and execution success (Main results table).

Providing document guidance improves task completion by only 2-7% across evaluated models, and even oracle (ground-truth) documents yield just 3-10% improvement, indicating grounding failures rather than retrieval failures dominate errors (Main results section).
Agent performance collapses to near 0% success on tasks requiring more than 4 steps, with hard tasks averaging 11.56 steps versus 3.13 for easy tasks (Task distribution table).

2xvgJvxPvp.text: BiRQA combines four analytic features (SSIM map, local informational content, YCbCr color difference, and Local Binary Patterns) through a bidirectional multiscale pyramid architecture built from a Cross-Scale Residual Attention Module (CSRAM), Spatial Cross-Gating Block (SCGB), and Reliability-Aware Head (RAH) (Section 3.2).
BiRQA runs at approximately 3x the speed of the prior state-of-the-art full-reference IQA method TOPIQ, achieving about 15 FPS on 1920x1080 images with only 5.5M parameters (Section 6, Figure 3).
Under FGSM adversarial attack on KADID-10k, the Anchored Adversarial Training variant (AAT-BiRQA) raises SROCC from 0.568 (vanilla adversarially trained BiRQA) to 0.832 (Table 3, Section 6).

An ablation study shows each architectural component contributes cumulative SROCC gains on KADID-10k: from a 0.813 base, adding CSRAM reaches 0.911, adding SCGB reaches 0.928, and adding RAH reaches 0.942 (Table 4, Section 6).

Theorem 1 establishes a pointwise error bound E ≤ ε + η + Rδ for the anchored quality prediction, under stated assumptions on anchor accuracy, coverage, and ranking-loss control (Theorem 1, Section 4).

B5umYh4CGr.text: The cooperative training scheme trains a mean network, then a variance-estimation network, then a Bayesian neural network in sequence (rather than jointly), producing BNN-VE (Section 3.2-3.4).

On 8 UCI regression benchmarks (including Carbon, Concrete, Energy, Boston, Power, Superconduct, Wine-Red, Yacht), BNN-VE with pSGLD inference achieves the best RMSE among ME(MSE), MVE (beta-NLL), Evidential regression, and end-to-end BNN baselines (Table 1).
BNN-VE (pSGLD) achieves the best test log-likelihood among all compared methods on the same 8 UCI regression datasets (Table 2).

On a novel material plasticity law discovery dataset with known ground-truth aleatoric uncertainty, BNN-VE's disentanglement of aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty improves (lower RMSE, higher epistemic test log-likelihood, lower Wasserstein distance) as training sequence length increases from N=50 to N=1000 (Figure 3).
A convergence analysis shows only K=2 cooperative training iterations are sufficient for BNN-VE to converge (Figure 5).
On 8 large-scale image regression datasets under distribution shift using a ResNet-34 backbone, BNN-VE is evaluated against the same baseline methods (Table 3, Appendix D.2).

FtfV0UuRGz.text: The paper proves the existence of a dimension-independent convex basin of constant radius R around the true parameter beta* for single-index models whose link function satisfies the Lipschitz complexity condition in Assumption 2.1 (Theorem 3.1).

A robust recovery algorithm combining spectral initialization via robust PCA (Section 4.1) with robust gradient descent refinement (Section 4.2) runs in near-linear time n = O~(m + P*m~) and achieves parameter error ||beta - beta*|| = O(sigma*sqrt(epsilon)) under heavy-tailed noise and strong adversarial contamination (Theorem 4.1).

Spectral initialization is shown to produce an initial estimate beta_0 within distance O(C4*epsilon^{1/4}) of the ground truth, placing it inside the convex basin needed for the subsequent gradient descent step to converge (Theorem 4.2).
Robust gradient descent starting from beta_0 within the basin B(±beta*, R) converges geometrically to error 2R*exp(-P*gamma/(alpha+gamma)) + O(sigma*sqrt(phi_2*epsilon)/gamma) (Theorem 4.3).

Six concrete non-linear, possibly non-monotonic link functions -- phase retrieval (z^2), GeLU, Swish, Tanh, Probit, and Logistic -- are shown to satisfy both the Lipschitz complexity and Expected Squared Convexity assumptions, so the recovery guarantee applies to all of them (Section 4.3, Corollary 4.1).

JIkyyfkeoE.text: NeuralFLoC is a fully unsupervised, end-to-end framework that jointly performs functional registration and clustering using Neural ODE-driven diffeomorphic flows combined with spectral clustering (Section 3).

Theorem 4.1 establishes that the Neural ODE-based registration component can approximate any valid warping function arbitrarily well in the SRVF metric, given sufficiently expressive encoder and vector-field function classes (Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 4.2 proves that the estimated cluster assignments converge to the true cluster assignments as sample size grows, under cluster separability and bounded-noise assumptions (Theorem 4.2).

On UCR Time Series Archive datasets (Shapes, univariate/multivariate Wave, 2-class/3-class Symbols), NeuralFLoC achieves the best or near-best registration quality (measured by ATV) and clustering performance (measured by ACC and NMI) on nearly all metrics (Table 1).
NeuralFLoC's robustness to missing data, irregular sampling, and additive noise is evaluated separately from the main benchmark comparisons (Section 5.2, Appendix C).

uIi5FfjtwR.text: DiscoverLLM models user intent as a hierarchical tree structure that progressively concretizes during the conversation, and users can only articulate intents that have already been discovered (Section 3.1).

The training reward combines a Discovery Progress term Rd = |I_{t+1}| - |I_t| with an Efficiency Penalty term Re = -min(lambda*max(0, tokens(r_t) - tau), 1) that discourages overly long responses (Section 3.4).

Compared against Base models, Prompted Base, and CollabLLM baselines, DiscoverLLM improves intent-discovery task performance by roughly 4%-14% while reducing token/conversation length by roughly 11%-45% across Creative Writing, Technical Writing, and SVG Drawing tasks (Table 1, Section 5).

In a user study with 75 Prolific crowdworkers, 84% of participants interacting with DiscoverLLM rated the interaction as 'good' or higher, compared to 78% for the Base model and 72% for the Prompted Base model (Section 6).
DiscoverLLM is trained and evaluated using SFT, DPO, and online RL (PPO/GRPO) variants on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B backbones (Section 3.5, Section 4.4).

yojuz84NLb.text: Theorem 4.1 shows that for one-step TD learning, the asymptotic critic error accumulates geometrically and scales as O(sqrt(1/(1-gamma^2))), which becomes large in long-horizon tasks where gamma is close to 1 (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 proves that regularizing the one-step Bellman update toward a stable action-chunked critic Qc (via the mixed operator T-hat_beta) yields a tighter asymptotic error bound than either single-step or action-chunked TD learning alone (Theorem 4.2).

On the OGBench manipulation benchmark (cube-double, cube-triple, cube-quadruple, puzzle-3x3, puzzle-4x4, scene-sparse), CGQ achieves the best average success rate of 76% over 150 evaluation episodes across 4 seeds, versus 38% (FQL), 35% (NFQL), 57% (QC-FQL), 71% (DEAS), and 46% (DQC) (Table 1).

On OGBench navigation tasks (antmaze-large, antmaze-giant, humanoidmaze-medium), CGQ underperforms the single-step method FQL (35% vs. 49% average success rate), a negative result attributed to action-chunked critics being less effective in highly reactive locomotion domains (Table 1, Section 5.1).
Full results across all 45 OGBench tasks, averaged over 4 seeds, are reported in an extended results table (Table 10).

qxdeq2sKGW.text: On WebQSP at significance level alpha=0.5, CPR achieves 61.4% Empirical Coverage Rate (ECR) with an average prediction set size (APSS) of 7.14, compared to the UaG baseline's 51.8% ECR with 14.29 APSS (Table 2, Section 5.2).
On ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ) at alpha=0.6, CPR attains 50.2% ECR with 8.35 APSS, versus UaG's 42.1% ECR with 120.20 APSS (Table 2, Section 5.2).

Query-level conformal calibration over path-level scores is designed to preserve exchangeability, addressing the sequential-dependency problem of hop-level calibration identified in Section 3.3, with a coverage guarantee proved in Theorem 4.1 (Section 4.2).
The Residual Conformal Value Network (RCVNet) learns discriminative nonconformity scores via PUCT-guided exploration, and is compared against baselines UaG, CLM, and LoFreeCP (Section 5, Table 2).
CPR improves Empirical Coverage Rate by 34% while reducing average prediction set size by 40% relative to conformal baselines, with additional coverage-efficiency analysis presented in Section 5.4.

dDVla2lLTA.text: Orchestrator-8B scores 37.1% on HLE, outperforming GPT-5's 35.1% while being 2.5x more efficient (Table 1).
Orchestrator-8B scores 76.3% on FRAMES and 80.2% on tau^2-Bench, exceeding GPT-5's 74.0% and 77.7% respectively on these benchmarks (Table 1).

Averaged over HLE and FRAMES, Orchestrator-8B costs 9.2 cents per task versus 30.2 cents for GPT-5 with its full toolset and 52.5 cents for Claude Opus 4.1, while completing tasks in 8.2 minutes versus GPT-5's 19.8 minutes (Section 4, efficiency analysis).
ToolOrchestra trains a Qwen3-8B base model with GRPO reinforcement learning using a reward combining outcome, efficiency (compute/latency), and user-preference terms (Equation 2, Section 3.2).

On unseen tools not present in training, Orchestrator-8B reaches 22.0 on HLE versus 16.4 for GPT-5 under identical conditions, using the synthetic ToolScale dataset of about 5,461 tasks across 10 domains for training (Table 2, Table 5).

ILRx5neJk6.text: DEER systematizes evaluation of deep research agent reports using an expert-developed taxonomy comprising 7 dimensions, 25 subdimensions, and 101 fine-grained rubric items, informed by standards from organizations such as APA, IEEE, and NIST (Figure 2).

DEER evaluates deep research systems including OpenAI Deep Research and GPT-5, Google Gemini variants, Anthropic Claude, Alibaba Qwen 3, Web Thinker, ManuSearch, and WebWeaver, with primary performance comparisons reported in Table 3 and Table 17.

Current deep research systems produce structurally plausible reports that cite external evidence but show measurable gaps in expert-level fulfillment and logical completeness, as detailed in the per-dimension results of Figure 4.
DEER's claim verification architecture quantifies evidence quality and separately verifies both cited and uncited claims in generated reports (Section on claim verification methodology).

uvSU4dNYv3.text: MM-DiTs (e.g., FLUX.1-Dev, SD3.5-Medium) exhibit concept omission, including full object omission and attribute neglect, where specified objects or attributes fail to emerge in generated images (Section 3).

An omission signal detectable in text token embeddings via linear probing is identified, with specific attention heads in middle layers reaching about 91% accuracy at detecting omission and omission signals peaking at intermediate denoising timesteps (Table 1: 0.965 agreement; Figures 3-4).

Omission Signal Intervention (OSI) amplifies the omission direction vector (obtained via Mean Shift) applied to top-K attention heads during early inference timesteps, using the update k^c <- k^c + alpha*sigma*theta.

On FLUX.1-Dev, OSI improves GenEval 2-object accuracy from 0.81 to 0.92 and 6-object accuracy from 0.18 to 0.40; on SD3.5-Medium, OSI improves GenEval average score from 0.55 to 0.64 (Table 2, Section 5.2).

Ablations show intervening in the opposite direction degrades six-object GenEval accuracy from 0.40 to 0.02, and applying OSI to already-present objects yields minimal effect (0.14) versus 0.70 accuracy when applied to omitted objects, confirming causality (Table 4, Table 5).

SoilRyCv1i.text: JADE combines a deterministic, taxonomy-driven query-specific checklist (Layer 1) with dynamic, report-specific claim-level verification (Layer 2) that applies evidence-dependency gating so conclusions built on unverified facts receive zero credit.

JADE's full configuration achieves Pearson correlation r=0.858 with expert judgments versus r=0.667 for vanilla LLM-as-judge, a 28.6% relative improvement, while reducing score variance across three runs to 1.12% (Table 3).
JADE reduces score inflation relative to human expert averages from 31.6 points to 15.0 points, a 16.6-point calibration improvement (Table 3).

On the medical-domain HealthBench transfer set (n=474), adding JADE's expert skill improves alignment from 0.154 to 0.228 (a 48% improvement), and on a trimmed 371-task subset from 0.187 to 0.530 (a 183% improvement) (Table 4).

JADE reveals an Evidence-Reasoning Gap of 33.5 percentage points (evidence accuracy 84.0% vs. reasoning score 50.5%) and a Citation Laundering gap of 35.8 points between evidence accuracy (84.0%) and source credibility (48.2%), failure modes missed by holistic LLM-based evaluators.

On the 150-query BizBench benchmark with a 3-level taxonomy (4 L1 categories, 7 L2 categories, 6 L3 categories), average agent final score is 42.6%, with the top performer, Gemini Deep Research, reaching 57.1%.

N4HIJq8v95.text: LOCA-bench is built from 15 seed tasks adapted from Toolathlon, expanded across 7 controlled context-length levels from 8K to 256K tokens with 5 seeds per length, yielding 525 total samples over 280 tools (Section on Benchmark Composition).
Claude-4.5-Opus accuracy collapses from 96% at 8K tokens of context to 14.7% at 256K tokens, illustrating severe degradation under extreme context growth (Figure showing accuracy vs. context length).
Frontier models retain a 2-3x accuracy advantage over open-source models specifically at the longest context lengths tested (Section on model comparison results).

The paper identifies four primary failure modes under context growth: declining complex cross-source reasoning, weaker instruction following, insufficient exploration leading to premature conclusions, and hallucination-like distortion of retrieved values during reasoning (Section on failure mode analysis).

Among six tested context management strategies (tool-result clearing, thinking-block removal, context compaction, context awareness, memory tools, and programmatic tool calling), programmatic tool calling is the most effective, improving accuracy while reducing trajectory length by converting step-by-step tool interactions into compact code-driven workflows (Section on context management strategies).

DsXN7VUwA3.text: DICE-RL parameterizes the finetuned policy as a lightweight residual correction on a frozen pretrained policy, a(t:t+h-1) = π_pre(s_t, z) + s_θ(s_t, z), preserving generative expressiveness while enabling localized action refinement (Section on residual policy parameterization).

On the Robomimic simulation benchmark, DICE-RL is the first method to reach ≥90% success rate on the Tool Hang task from visual inputs using only 50 demonstrations, outperforming IBRL, DPPO, EXPO, DSRL, and ResFit in sample efficiency and stability (Section on simulation experiments, Robomimic results).

DICE-RL is validated on three real-robot contact-rich assembly tasks: GearInsertion (40 demonstrations, ~1mm tolerance), LightBulbInsertion (100 demonstrations, precise insertion with 360° rotation), and BeltAssembly (265 demonstrations, deformable object coordination) (Section on real robot experiments).

Ablations show multi-sample training with K=16 latent noise samples per state consistently improves performance over single-sample training, and a selective BC-loss filter that conditionally disables behavior regularization when residual actions are verified value-improving further improves sample efficiency on longer-horizon tasks (Section on design ablations).

The paper identifies three pretraining 'finetunability' metrics—good mode coverage, bad mode coverage, and bad mode entropy—showing that overly-converged behavior-cloning checkpoints with high concentration but low good-mode coverage hinder subsequent RL finetuning (Section on pre-training insights).

I8QGwNBO4T.text: MeshTok computes a per-patch activity score a(u,v) = ||∇x(u,v)||₂ + λ||Δx(u,v)||₂² combining gradient magnitude and Laplacian energy to decide which coarse patches (e.g., 25% when k=0.25) get refined into finer tokens (Section on activity-based refinement).

Under MACs-matched compute budgets, MeshTok's activity-based refinement achieves 0.9723 relative error versus 1.0294 for a no-refinement coarse baseline and 1.0777 for full refinement, showing lower error than uniform coarse tokenization while being substantially faster than full refinement (Section on efficiency-accuracy tradeoff).

MeshTok reports relative ℓ2 test errors of 2.095% on Gray-Scott, 1.056% on Allen-Cahn, 1.187% on CNS(1.0,0.01), 0.249% on CNS(0.1,0.01), and 0.276% on SWE, compared against ViT, FNO, DeepONet, BCAT, and MoE-POT baselines (Table of main experimental results).
On 3D MHD data, adaptive mesh refinement with k=0.375 reduces relative error from 39.647% (no refinement) to 35.851% while running 3.0x faster than full refinement (Section on 3D extension).

Theorem A.1 shows coarse tokenization creates an information bottleneck where distinct inputs mapping to identical patch representations incur approximation error independent of model capacity, and Theorem A.3 proves that refining a partition P1 into P2 guarantees the realizable-function-class error satisfies ℰ(P2;g) ≤ ℰ(P1;g) (Theorem A.1, Theorem A.3).

wu36B3DqNM.text: PromptDyG freezes the pretrained DTDG backbone and instead optimizes learnable node-specific prompts P_t ∈ ℝ^(N×D) via feature-wise entropy minimization at test time, computing adapted embeddings as H̃_t = f_θ^t(A_t^test, X + P_t, H_(t-1)) (Section on methodology).

Proposition 4.3 (Margin Expansion) proves that optimizing the test-time prompts increases the prediction margin γ = s_uv − s_uw between positive (existing edge) and negative (non-existing edge) node pairs (Proposition 4.3).

On the link prediction task measured by MRR across six benchmark datasets (AS-733, Reddit-title, Reddit-body, UCI, Bitcoin-OTC, Bitcoin-Alpha), PromptDyG improves average MRR from 0.2627 (Roland-GRU backbone) to 0.2794, with the largest gains on UCI (0.1065 to 0.1248) and Bitcoin-Alpha (0.1547 to 0.1732) (Table of main performance results).

PromptDyG achieves lower test-time adaptation latency than competing methods on Reddit-title (33.90ms) compared to Tent (39.72ms), Matcha (63.89ms), and GTrans (149.83ms), with GTrans exhibiting quadratic O(N^2 K) complexity versus PromptDyG's linear O(eSK) complexity (Section on baseline comparisons, computational efficiency).

As a plug-in module, PromptDyG improves EvolveGCN-H's MRR on Reddit-title from 0.1233 to 0.1570 (+3.37%) and GCRN-GRU's MRR on UCI from 0.0999 to 0.1367 (+3.68%), demonstrating backbone-agnostic gains (Section on plugin results).

Qbe2cfNfn1.text: Theorem 4.15 proves that SPD-valued sheaves strictly generalize Euclidean sheaves, admitting consistent global-section configurations (Φ(ker δ_F) ⊊ ker δ_G) that vector-valued sheaves cannot represent (Theorem 4.15).

The restriction maps are defined as orthogonal congruence transformations F_{v→e}(P) = M_ve P M_ve^T with M_ve ∈ O(n), and the coboundary operator uses the SPD manifold's Lie group structure via (δσ)_e = exp(log(F_{v→e}(σ_v)) − log(F_{u→e}(σ_u))) (Section on mathematical framework).

The model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 6 of 7 MoleculeNet benchmarks, including 77.4% on BBBP (vs. 73.4% for SMPT), 99.4% on ClinTox (vs. 98.6% for EGNN), and 89.0% on BACE (vs. 87.3% for SMPT), while trailing on HIV (80.9% vs. 81.2% for SMPT) (Table of MoleculeNet results).

At 32 layers on BACE, the SPD-sheaf model retains 86.7% accuracy (97% of its baseline performance) while a standard GCN drops to 51.1%, a 35% decline from its 87.0% shallow baseline, demonstrating depth robustness against over-smoothing (Section on depth robustness experiments).

Effective-rank analysis shows SPD sheaf convolution transforms initially rank-1 directional atomic inputs (effective rank approx 1.00) into full-rank matrices with effective rank 1.72-2.28 after propagation, with the second eigenvalue growing from 0.00 to 1.14-1.55, evidencing emergent second-order geometric structure (Section on second-order emergence analysis).

KxLNNxz9T9.text: LABO combines LLM predictions and real experiments via a Kennedy-O'Hagan multi-fidelity decomposition f_R(x) = ρf_L(x) + δ(x), using a discrepancy dominance ratio p_Δ(x) to gate when real experiments are triggered (Section 6.2).
LABO outperforms Vanilla BO, LLAMBO, BOPRO, and CAKE on high-dimensional scientific optimization tasks including COF (14D) and Sandwich (20D) under fixed experimental budgets (Figure 2, Section 6.2).

Ablations show an optimal gating threshold of τ = 0.75 and an LLM-to-real-fidelity query ratio ranging from about 2.68-3.87 on the COF task to about 3.87-14.60 on the Fullerene task (Table 1, Section 6.3).

Theorem 5.1 establishes a cumulative regret bound R_T ≤ C1√(T_R* β_T Ψ_T(𝒳_R*)) + C2√(T_α β_T Ψ_T(𝒳)) + C3√(T_L β_T Ψ_T(𝒳)), showing real-fidelity queries concentrate in a restricted region 𝒳_R* (Theorem 5.1).

LABO significantly outperforms Vanilla BO even under identical initialization, and a random-fidelity baseline performs substantially worse, validating that LLM predictions carry genuine informative signal (Figure 3B).

Wba6w3pzbj.text: CoNL trains LLMs on non-verifiable tasks such as creative writing, dialogue, and ethical reasoning, where no ground-truth labels exist, using multi-agent self-play combining generation, critique, and meta-evaluation (abstract only).
Critique quality is measured by whether a critique helps another agent improve its solution, and critiques that enable improvement earn a diagnostic reward as explicit supervision (abstract only).
Multiple agents share a single policy while alternating roles of proposing, critiquing, and revising solutions within structured multi-turn conversations (abstract only).
CoNL jointly optimizes generation and judging capability without relying on external judges or ground-truth labels (abstract only).
CoNL achieves consistent improvements over self-rewarding baselines while maintaining stable training across five non-verifiable task benchmarks (abstract only).

9mFx2t9RGj.text: The Effective Information Criterion (EIC) is defined as EIC = N - M, the number of significant digits lost between input precision N and output precision M when a formula is evaluated under injected numerical noise (Section 3, or the EIC definition section).

Filtering pre-training data by discarding formulas with EIC > 2.0 improves generative symbolic regression (E2ESR), yielding a 357% reduction in required training samples and a 22.4% relative gain in generalization R² (Section 4.3, Table 2, Figure 7).

Incorporating EIC as a penalty term in the heuristic search fitness function (Fitness = η^Complexity/(1+NMSE) - α·EIC) shifts the Pareto front of formulas to a higher interpretability tier (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
EIC-based filtering reduces the Jensen-Shannon divergence between formula structural distributions by 36% on the Feynman benchmark dataset (Section 4.3, Table 1).

In a human study of 108 participants performing 840 evaluations across 172 formula pairs, formulas favored by EIC align with human interpretability preference in 70.2% of cases (Section 4.4, Figure 14).

wXkCkP8TtK.text: WildActor is trained using the Actor-18M dataset, comprising 1.6 million identity-consistent videos paired with 18 million reference human images spanning diverse viewpoints, split into three subsets Actor-18M-A, -B, and -C (Section on Actor-18M dataset).

WildActor's Asymmetric Identity-Preserving Attention (AIPA) applies LoRA only to reference tokens while keeping video tokens frozen, using one-directional attention so video tokens query identity cues without leaking pose information back to the reference (Method section, AIPA).

WildActor's Identity-Aware 3D RoPE (I-RoPE) assigns distinct positional encodings to video versus reference tokens to spatially and temporally separate identity references from motion features (Method section, I-RoPE).
On Actor-Bench, WildActor achieves 0.952 body consistency versus 0.905 for Vidu Q2, and 0.920 VLM-level semantic alignment versus 0.880 for Vidu Q2 (Table 2).

Ablations show that the combination of AIPA and I-RoPE is critical for both identity preservation and semantic alignment, and that viewpoint-adaptive Monte Carlo sampling (decay factor γ=0.5, angular threshold δ=π/6) achieves 0.952 body consistency across viewpoints (Tables 3-4).

nYzdAcLN5F.text: The Discrete Transformer represents activations as an explicit Numerical Residual Stream using concatenation-based updates to avoid superposition, functionally disentangling attention-based information routing from MLP-based arithmetic computation (Section 3.1).

Numerical Attention acts as a deterministic router using piecewise linear encoding and hard attention, while Numerical MLP performs element-wise arithmetic via decomposed sub-modules (Sections 3.2-3.3).
The extraction pipeline identifies attention patterns via hypothesis testing (Fixed Offset, Windowed Extrema) and recovers MLP operations via symbolic regression using PySR (Section 4).

Trained Discrete Transformers achieve near-zero losses on linear, non-linear, and physical tasks (e.g., 6.76×10⁻⁹ on sum_last2, 1.46×10⁻¹² on parity_last2, 1.86×10⁻¹¹ on gravity), comparable to RNN-based baselines (Table 1).
Extracted symbolic programs correctly recover ground-truth algorithms, including y_t = x_t + x_{t-1} for linear tasks and y_t = x_t + x_{t-1} - 2x_t·x_{t-1} for parity logic (Figures 2-4).
Training exhibits a phase transition in which functional convergence of the loss precedes structural discretization during temperature annealing (Figure 5).

tPcL3fgkjc.text: The efficient influence function (EIF) estimator, the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE), and optimally-tuned PPI++ all attain the same asymptotic variance, which is strictly smaller than that of vanilla PPI, which in turn is strictly smaller than that of the Rogan-Gladen estimator except when sensitivity q1 and specificity q0 both equal 1 (Proposition 7).

For binary outcomes, optimally tuned PPI++ matches the efficiency of the EIF estimator because the regression function E[Y|Ŷ] is necessarily affine, so no further efficiency gain is possible from nonparametric calibration (Section on efficiency comparison).

In simulations with N=2,000 and 1,000 replicates on binary outcomes, when judge quality is low (q0+q1=1.2), Rogan-Gladen confidence intervals are roughly 10x wider than EIF/PPI++ intervals, and EIF/PPI++ intervals are 35-55% narrower than vanilla PPI intervals (simulation study section).

On real Chatbot Arena preference data across three model pairs (414-494 samples each) using 10% calibration splits, PPI++, EIF, and MLE achieve near-nominal 90% coverage with mean interval widths of 0.27-0.30, while Rogan-Gladen achieves 0.76-0.96 width with 100% coverage, indicating over-conservatism (real-data application section).

The efficient influence function for the target parameter θ=E[Y] is φ*(R,Y,Ŷ;P) = μ(Ŷ) − θ + [R/P(R=1)]{Y − μ(Ŷ)}, where μ(ŷ)=E[Y|Ŷ=ŷ] is the optimal translation of the surrogate label (Proposition 5).

vT5PBMLBvx.text: NeuralLog-UCB-1 achieves a regret upper bound of order Õ(d̃√(κT)), where d̃ is the data-adaptive effective dimension rather than the ambient feature dimension d, improving on the d√(κT) bound of Logistic-UCB-1 (Table 1).

NeuralLog-UCB-2 achieves a regret upper bound of order Õ(d̃√(T/κ*)), matching the κ* dependence of ada-OFU-ECOLog (whose bound is d√(T/κ*)) while replacing the ambient dimension d with the effective dimension d̃ (Table 1).

A novel Bernstein-type self-normalized martingale inequality (Theorem 3.1) yields concentration of order Õ(√d̃) without the extra κ factor required by the corresponding inequality in Verma et al. (2024), which scales as Õ(√(κd̃)) (Theorem 3.1).

NeuralLog-UCB-2 uses neural-network-based variance estimates in place of the true reward variance μ̇(xᵀθ*) within the design matrix, enabling the tighter T/κ* dependence while retaining d̃-scaling (Section on NeuralLog-UCB-2 / Condition 5.4).

On synthetic nonlinear reward functions h1(x)=0.2(xᵀθ)^4, h2(x)=20cos(xᵀθ), and h3(x)=5xᵀθx, as well as on the MNIST, mushroom, and shuttle real-world datasets, NeuralLog-UCB-2 substantially outperforms baselines including the method of Verma et al. (2024) (Experimental validation section).

ysBZhSRtCM.text: The standard Euler-Maruyama (EM) discretized BSDE loss is shown to be a biased estimator of the continuous-time self-consistency objective, with bias equal to the squared PDE residual plus a Hessian-trace term plus O(Δt^1/2) (Lemma 3.1, Eq. 10).

The proposed Un-EM-BSDE loss, formed as the product of two independent Shotgun-averaged one-step errors (Eq. 17), is proven unbiased up to O(Δt^1/2) while avoiding explicit second-order derivative (Hessian) computation (Lemma 4.1, Eq. 18).

Theorem 4.3 shows that under conditions on averaging parameters M1 and M2 (e.g., M1=1, M2=2), the variance of the Un-EM-BSDE estimator is no larger than that of the Shotgun, Multi-Shot EM, and standard EM-BSDE estimators (Theorem 4.3, Eq. 20).
On the BSB benchmark, Table 1 reports that Heun-BSDE requires 42.91x the training time of EM-BSDE and FS-PINNs requires 32.07x, whereas the proposed Un-EM-BSDE requires only 1.79x (Table 1).

Across benchmark PDEs (HJB, BSB, AC, BZ, PIDE) under both soft- and hard-constraint formulations, Un-EM-BSDE attains relative L2 (RL2) errors that are consistently among the top two methods and comparable to Heun-BSDE and FS-PINNs while costing far less compute (Table 2).

Applying the same debiasing construction as a wrapper to the Shotgun loss on the BSB hard-constraint benchmark reduces its RL2 error by approximately 2.67x at the cost of only a 1.78x increase in training time (Section 5.3, Figure 4).

zFw9qaYGXd.text: TransLight uses a Generative Decoupling strategy with two fine-tuned diffusion models, a light removal model and a light extraction model, trained on synthetic composites I_S = aI + bL with a,b ∈ U(0,1), to separate light effects from image content (Generative Decoupling section).

The data pipeline uses InternVL2.5 to filter roughly 2 million images with prominent light effects, then applies DINOv2 feature similarity filtering with threshold γ=0.98 to produce a final dataset of 1.2 million image-content-light triplets (Data Pipeline section).

TransLight is trained in two stages: LoRA fine-tuning for content-preserving lighting followed by ControlNet training to inject light effects, built on top of the fixed IC-Light (SD1.5) generative network (Architecture section).
TransLight outperforms IC-Light with a Light FID of 6.02 versus 10.05, PSNR of 19.58 versus 15.34, SSIM of 0.7931 versus 0.6784, and LPIPS of 0.1982 versus 0.2756 (comparison table).

TransLight enables user control over transferred light position (horizontal/vertical translation), direction (flipping/rotation), and intensity (multiplicative coefficient), which the paper presents as a first-of-its-kind capability for light-effect transfer (Key Claims / User Control section).

druaDr7zNI.text: Self-guidance (SG) adds a feature-mapping loss L_guide = ||sg(h_e) − h_q||²₂ between decoder hidden features computed from continuous pre-quantized latents (h_e) and from quantized embeddings (h_q), using a stop-gradient on h_e, to align the decoder's internal manifolds (Method section).

On XCodec2, SG improves PESQ from 2.28 to 2.39 at a codebook size of 65,536, and a 16,384-size codebook with SG matches the reconstruction quality of the 65,536-size baseline without SG, i.e., a 4x codebook reduction without fidelity loss (Table 2).

Ablations confirm SG generalizes across quantizer types, including SimVQ and Residual FSQ, and across decoder architectures including the CNN-based BigCodec, not just Transformer-based decoders (Table 6).

SG operates by improving decoder robustness rather than reducing quantization error: quantization error distributions remain nearly unchanged with SG enabled, while hidden-feature alignment MSE decreases substantially and t-SNE visualizations show tighter token-specific clustering (Figures 3-5).

In AB subjective listening tests, SG-trained codecs achieve roughly a 2x preference ratio over the non-SG baseline, and downstream text-to-speech experiments show that SG's reduced-codebook (16,384-token) models outperform larger-vocabulary baselines in LLM-based speech synthesis (Table 3; Table 7).
SG adds minimal training overhead, reported as less than 0.5% additional computation, while requiring no changes to the inference-time pipeline (Downstream Benefits / Generalization section).

4MVVscCjYu.text: In zero-sum games, smaller first-order momentum β enables Adam Descent-Ascent (Adam-DA) to converge across a broader range of step sizes, reversing the effect seen in minimization problems where larger β improves stability (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 4.4).

The upper bound on the stable step-size range for Adam-DA is a strictly decreasing function of β ∈ (−1,1) for both the continuous ODE and discrete versions, the opposite of the minimization case (Corollary 4.5).
Adam-DA fails to converge on bilinear zero-sum games for any choice of momentum and step-size parameters (Corollary 4.6).
Smaller β and larger second-order momentum ρ drive Adam-DA trajectories toward flatter regions of the loss landscape (in ℓ1 norm), again the reverse of the minimization regime (Section 5).

On GAN training with ResNet and CNN architectures on CIFAR-10 and STL-10, smaller β and larger ρ empirically reduce cumulative average gradient norms and correlate with higher Inception Scores, validating the reversed-momentum theory (Figure 3c-d).
The paper's continuous-time ODE approximation of Adam-DA achieves O(h^3) local truncation error, improving on prior O(h^2) approximations used to justify the theoretical analysis (Equation 3a).

ysOOfySED6.text: STELLAR's ViT-H variant achieves 2.60 FID for image reconstruction using only 16 sparse semantic tokens, while the ViT-B variant achieves 3.06 FID at the same token count (Section on reconstruction results).

STELLAR's ViT-H model reaches 79.10% ImageNet linear-probing accuracy, compared to 73.26% for ViT-B and 76.94% for ViT-L, while maintaining a sparse spatial-semantic factorized representation (Section on ImageNet evaluation).

The factorized representation (r semantic-concept tokens S combined with n×r localization coefficients L, r=16) reduces parameter count by roughly 90% relative to a dense n×d representation (Section on representation structure).
On dense per-pixel prediction tasks, STELLAR ViT-B attains 31.33 mIoU on ADE20K versus MAE's 30.91, and 81.83 mIoU on Pascal VOC versus DINO's 79.29 (Table 2).

Ablations show that removing the reconstruction objective costs 0.82% ImageNet accuracy and 1.39 mIoU on ADE20K, while removing the clustering/set-alignment objective causes training collapse with a 21.19% drop in ImageNet accuracy (Table 3).
STELLAR underperforms dense baselines such as DINO on object-centric classification datasets (Pets, Food) despite its sparsity advantages (Table 2 discussion).

Lh3Hico2Pe.text: DC-W2S stratifies weak process-supervision labels into four reliability regimes (P1–P4) by intersecting Self-Consensus, defined as 1 minus the variance of scores from M heterogeneous weak supervisors, with Neighborhood-Consensus, the average Self-Consensus over embedding-space neighbors (Section on Dual-Consensus metrics).

A distribution-balanced sampling curriculum maintains a roughly uniform 25% split across the P1–P4 reliability patterns during training, rather than letting easy or noisy samples dominate (Section on instance-level sampling).

A reliability-aware masking term is applied per-step in the PRM loss (L_PRM = ΣΣ M(z_t)·CE(r_θ(z_t), ỹ_agg(z_t))), down-weighting unreliable P4 labels during training (Section on label-level masking).
On the RPE1 out-of-distribution benchmark, DC-W2S reaches 68.5% F1 versus 60.4% F1 for an SFT baseline and 57.5% F1 for Llama-PRM800K (Table of main results).

Using only the highest-reliability P1 subset (62% of labels) still yields about 64% F1 on RPE1 OOD, and training on 100k curated instances (64.5% F1) matches or exceeds training on the full 351k-instance uncurated set (62% F1) (Section on efficiency/curated-subset results).

Theorem 3.4 derives an error bound for the trained reward model under soft weak-label correction and robust expansion assumptions, formally justifying why consensus-guided curation outperforms indiscriminate noisy training (Theorem 3.4).

X9VtjdBlQw.text: In the unimodal setting, the intrinsic representation functional for contrastive learning is proven strictly convex over the space of probability measures 𝒫(𝒵), with a unique minimizer given by the Gibbs distribution ρ*(z) = exp(−U(z)/τ)/Z_τ (Proposition 3.2).

Entropy acts only as a secondary tie-breaking force that disperses mass within already-aligned regions, rather than as a co-equal objective to alignment, as shown by decomposing the InfoNCE energy landscape (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.1).

In the symmetric multimodal objective, a persistent negative symmetric divergence term remains even after kernel sharpening, structurally enforcing barrier-driven co-adaptation and a population-level modality gap independent of initialization (Theorem 4.2).

Directional, mismatched alignment potential fields between modalities (Definition 4.1) lead to coordinate-wise extremal collapse, making exact marginal matching structurally unstable for heterogeneous cross-modal data (Proposition 4.2).
Large-batch InfoNCE optimization is shown to track an explicit deterministic energy landscape in both unimodal and multimodal regimes (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1).

9ySNTY5FAy.text: UniTrans achieves 0.716 AP@0.5 / 0.605 AP@0.7 on the OPV2V-H benchmark with 30 heterogeneous simulated modalities (16/32/64-channel LiDAR plus RGB/depth cameras), outperforming NegoCollab (0.662/0.538) and Classic MoE (0.653/0.544) (Table 1).

On the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset, with 300-channel roadside LiDAR versus 40-channel vehicle LiDAR, UniTrans reaches 0.553 AP@0.5 / 0.421 AP@0.7, surpassing NegoCollab's 0.509/0.389 under realistic domain shift (Table 2).

UniTrans instantiates a single any-to-any translator on the fly by combining Translator Parameter Bank expert parameters via the Modality Mapping Router, requiring only 109.3 GFLOPs and 53.760ms on CUDA versus 245.5 GFLOPs and 141.352ms for a Classic MoE baseline with multi-expert routing (Section on efficiency).

Removing the Stage-1 Modality-Intrinsic Encoder objectives (intrinsic-code contrastive loss ℒ_IC and surrogate modality-classification loss ℒ_IS) degrades performance to 0.662/0.540 AP, and omitting the Stage-2 feature-distillation loss ℒ_feat causes the largest single degradation (Table 4).

UniTrans enables zero-shot translation to modality pairs unseen during training by inferring modality mappings in the intrinsic-code space and composing translator expert parameters accordingly (Section on Stage 2 translator learning).

XgCyH9OZ5J.text: PIDI (Patched Model Inversion with Dual-Sided Initialization) achieves attack precision AP_α=0.5 ranging from 0.801 to 0.985 across three models and three datasets (Financial, Medical, Dolly), outperforming prior model inversion baselines (Table 1).

PIDI's two-stage design combines Dual-Sided Initialization (response initialization via Model Completion plus input initialization via a Semi-white-box Forward Inversion Paradigm) with Patched Model Inversion that partitions embeddings into non-overlapping patches for iterative and joint optimization (Section on PIDI method).

ADMI (Adapter-based DualGuard with Mutual Information defense) reduces attacker AP to 0.004-0.074 while maintaining task utility (DCS 0.839-0.995), outperforming baselines such as DualGuard, MID, and perturbation-based defenses (Table 2).
ADMI reduces EntityRecovery-F1 from an undefended range of 0.674-0.868 down to 0.000-0.057 (Table 12).
PIDI maintains stable attack performance across varying sequence lengths, whereas traditional VMI-based inversion methods suffer significant AP degradation as sequence length changes (Figure 4).
ADMI's overhead is measured as inference throughput decreasing by roughly 18% for Qwen and 25% for Llama3-8B, with corresponding increases in training time (Table 11).

SUwOncwAVl.text: LARFT achieves an average LIFEBench Length Score improvement of +20.92 points across four tested models, outperforming the strongest RL baseline by 4.59 points (Table 1).

LARFT combines length-oriented reinforcement learning (GRPO with a piecewise-linear, [0,1]-bounded verifiable length reward) with hindsight length awareness training, where failed trajectories are converted into supervised tasks asking the model to count words in its own output (Section on method).

On four general-capability benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, IFEval, GPQA), LARFT shows at most a 2.02-point decline (on GPQA for Qwen2.5-3B), indicating minimal degradation from length-aware training (Section on robustness results).

Ablations show RL initialized with hindsight length awareness improves scores by +3.93 points on average, and the full LARFT unified optimization adds a further +2.95 points via synchronized cosine-annealed training (Figure 2).
Removing the cosine annealing schedule for the unified optimization coefficient drops LIFEBench Length Score from 80.57 to 73.44, identifying it as the most critical component (Table 2).

Linear probing analysis shows length-planning capability emerging in deep layers (around layer 10) while length-awareness/tracking capability emerges as early as layer 2, and LARFT maintains stronger correlations across both probes than baselines (Figure 4).

zN8QDhuOHN.text: WorldCompass is a reinforcement-learning post-training framework for long-horizon, interactive video-based world models, applied to the WorldPlay base model in two variants (HunyuanVideo-1.5-8B and Wan2.2-5B) (Section on method/experiments).

WorldCompass uses a clip-level rollout strategy that generates a shared prefix once and produces G candidate rollouts only for a target clip, reducing rollout computational complexity from O(N·G) to O(N+G) (Section on clip-level rollout).
On complex composite actions, WorldCompass raises interaction-following accuracy from roughly 20% to roughly 55% over the baseline, with HPSv3 visual-quality gains of +1.47 to +1.94 (Table 1).

On basic actions, WorldCompass raises interaction accuracy from roughly 62% to 68-76% with HPSv3 improvements of +1.34 to +1.82, with consistent gains across short-term (125 frames), mid-term (253 frames), and long-term (381 frames) generation (Table 1).

Ablations show clip-level rollout is dramatically superior to sample-level rollout for action-following, and that using only a single reward (interaction or visual quality alone) causes training collapse into static content or degraded visual quality, whereas the dual complementary rewards prevent this (Table 2).

WorldCompass's RL algorithm (DiffusionNFT) outperforms DanceGRPO due to better camera-trajectory exploration, and training used 4,000 diverse images with captions, 16 rollout groups, 40 sampling timesteps, over 3 days on 64 H20 GPUs (Section on training configuration).

c0DDRZoMNf.text: ResVLA achieves 96.3% average success on the standard LIBERO benchmark across four suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long-Horizon), close to the top baseline OpenVLA-OFT at 97.1% (Table 2).

On LIBERO-Plus robustness benchmarks, ResVLA achieves 75.3% overall success versus 69.6% for the best baseline, including a +13.7 point gain on Robot Embodiment perturbations (59.9% vs 46.2%) (Table 1).

Under language instruction variation on LIBERO-Plus, ResVLA maintains 88.5% success rate compared to π₀'s collapse to 58.8%, illustrating mitigation of the paper's identified 'loss collapse' phenomenon (Table 1, Theorem 3.3).

ResVLA converges faster than the π₀ baseline during training, especially under high dropout (p=0.2) where π₀ saturates while ResVLA continues to improve, and at single-step inference (NFE=1) ResVLA exceeds 70% success versus baseline's much lower performance (Figure 3a, Figure 3b).
On SimplerEnv Google Robot transfer without any pretraining, ResVLA reaches 68.4% average success, exceeding pretrained π₀ (58.8%) and pretrained OpenVLA (34.3%) (Table 3).

Proposition 3.1 establishes that discrete action tokenization incurs an irreducible quantization noise floor of Δ²/12, motivating ResVLA's continuous residual-bridge refinement-from-intent design (Proposition 3.1).

shdJbVmwrp.text: PRISM couples a VLM and LLM via a dynamic question-answering (DQA) pipeline in which the LLM identifies information gaps in an initial VLM scene description and issues targeted questions the VLM must answer before a final description is synthesized (Section on Interactive Goal-Oriented Perception).
On ALFWorld, PRISM BC+RL achieves 80% average success rate across six task categories, exceeding VIPERBC+RL (75%) and narrowing the gap to the oracle-supervised EMAC+ (86%) (Table 1).
On Room-to-Room navigation, PRISM achieves 46.08% success rate and 43.14 SPL, exceeding DiscussNav by more than 10 points in success rate (Table 6).
PRISM's fully-automatic questions match oracle handcrafted questions on 4 of 6 ALFWorld tasks, with only a 2-point average difference (Table 4).
An ablation replacing PRISM's LLM-based merging with naive concatenation or QA-only descriptions drops average success rate from 75% (PRISM) to 72% and 70% respectively (Table 3).

PRISM incurs higher per-step inference latency (6.35s) than raw perception (2.14s), but this is offset by an 18% reduction in average episode steps (17.1 vs 20.9), yielding a net 6-point success-rate gain (Table 9).

95VVL0TJNH.text: SafeSearch constructs 300 test cases (60 per risk category) spanning five risk categories: advertisements, bias-inducing content, harmful output, indirect prompt injection, and misinformation (Section 3, Table 1).
In the search-workflow scaffold, GPT-4.1-mini has the highest attack success rate at 90.5%, while GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini are far more robust at 18.4% and 18.9% respectively (Section 4, Table 2).

Across the three evaluated scaffolds (search workflow, tool calling, deep research), misinformation is the most exploitable risk category, reaching an average of 78.3% attack success rate in the search-workflow setting (Section 4).

Reminder prompting as a defense is largely ineffective at reducing attack success rate, whereas a filtering defense that detects unreliable sources roughly halves attack success rate but only achieves a 44.2% recall rate (Section 4.2, Figure 6).

The tool-calling scaffold shows lower vulnerability than search workflow for GPT-4.1-mini (77.8% vs. 90.5% ASR), illustrating that scaffold design affects susceptibility to the same underlying attacks (Section 4, Table 2).

gSZhNPp103.text: MLPs trained on Fixed Aggregation Features (FAFs) match or exceed GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE baselines on 12 of 14 node classification benchmarks, with Minesweeper and Roman-Empire as the two exceptions (Section 5, Table 1).
On the two exceptions, Minesweeper and Roman-Empire, the remaining GNN advantage is attributed to benefits from residual connections rather than message passing per se (Section 5, Table 1).

Using only mean aggregation as the single reducer is often competitive with, and sometimes surpasses, multi-reducer FAF variants, though the best single aggregation function is dataset-dependent (e.g., sum on Citeseer, max on Amazon-Ratings) (Appendix D, Table 6).

Concatenating FAFs across multiple hops with an MLP classifier outperforms using only the final hop's features or using a single linear classifier on the same concatenated features, with most datasets peaking at K=2 hops (Appendix D, Tables 9-10).
