A theoretically lossless Kolmogorov-Arnold-based aggregation encoding yields its largest gains on Roman-Empire, reaching 80.33±0.47 accuracy, suggesting information preservation helps on structurally complex heterophilic graphs (Appendix D, Table 11).

MZxhwFT7yF.text: Theorem 3.2 establishes monoblock identifiability: latent variables generating the observed climate time series can be recovered up to an invertible transformation under mild density-continuity and operator-injectivity assumptions (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 3.8 shows the observed causal DAG is identifiable once the generation-variability conditions of the hidden dynamic process model are satisfied (Section 3, Theorem 3.8).
On synthetic data with observed dimension dx=3, the method (NCDL/CaDRe) recovers the causal DAG exactly, achieving SHD=0, TPR=1, and Precision=1 (Section 5, Table 1).

On the CESM2 sea surface temperature dataset, the method achieves forecasting performance competitive with or superior to the CARD baseline across prediction horizons of 96, 192, and 336 steps (e.g., MSE 0.410 vs. CARD's 0.409 at horizon 96, and MSE 0.412 vs. CARD's 0.422 at horizon 192) (Section 5, Table 3).

The causal graphs inferred from CESM2 data (Figure 5) recover westward wind trends in central sea regions that align with real wind-pattern data from Rasp et al. (2020), while showing greater complexity in land-sea interaction zones (Section 5, Figure 5).

rJOrgGdz9E.text: DRIFT's Theorem 5 formally establishes that the KL-regularized multi-turn RL objective is equivalent to minimizing a weighted supervised fine-tuning loss with return-based importance weights w(τ) = exp(R(τ)/β)/Z(x) (Section 3, Theorem 5).

DRIFT operates in two stages: offline trajectory generation from a reference policy followed by importance-weighted supervised fine-tuning, avoiding the online rollout cost of standard multi-turn RL (Section 4.2-4.3).
On MATH with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, DRIFT-5turn improves accuracy from a 38.3% base to 55.9%, outperforming the UFO-5turn RL baseline's 55.5% (Section 5, Table 1).
On MATH with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, DRIFT-5turn improves accuracy from 36.8% to 45.4%, a performance competitive with the UFO-5turn baseline's 43.1% (Section 5, Table 1).

DRIFT's GPU time scales only marginally with the number of turns and approaches the efficiency profile of standard 5-turn SFT, whereas the UFO-5turn RL baseline shows substantial slowdown as turn count increases (Section 5.3, Figure 6).

QooehkRtN5.text: InteractScience contains 150 problems evenly split across five disciplines (mathematics, physics, chemistry, earth science, computer science), each with 30 problems divided into 10 easy, 10 medium, and 10 hard tasks (Section 4, Table 1).

Evaluation of 30 leading LLMs (10 closed-source, 20 open-source) shows the best model, Claude-Sonnet-4, achieves only a 13.29% Perfect Pass Rate on the Programmatic Functional Testing metric (Section 5, Table 2).

Action Success Rate under Visually-Grounded Qualitative Testing is consistently above 85% across models, while VLM-as-Judge scores for scientific correctness typically fall below 60%, revealing a gap between surface-level interactivity and semantic correctness (Section 5, Table 2).

The benchmark's evaluation suite averages 4.03 Programmatic Functional Testing cases and 3.98 Visually-Grounded Qualitative Testing cases per problem, with an average of 22.09 checklist items per problem (Section 4, Table 1).

Models exhibit an integration failure: they can perform individual interactive-coding subtasks but struggle to integrate scientific reasoning with interactive interface generation, as evidenced by the disparity between high Action Success Rate and low VLM-Judge scientific-correctness scores (Section 5, Table 2).

WpUpj8DrVB.text: FuseFSS achieves 1.24x-1.50x end-to-end speedup over the Sigma FSS-based GPU secure inference baseline across BERT-tiny, BERT-base, BERT-large, GPT-2, and GPT-Neo (Table 1).
FuseFSS reduces online communication by 9%-16% relative to Sigma across the tested BERT and GPT-style models (Table 1).

The compiled nonlinear activation path yields 4.5x-4.7x speedup for softmax's nExp and reciprocal operations, with per-gate microbenchmarks showing 1.64x-2.46x speedup and 4.96x-6.25x key-size reduction (Table 3, Figure 1, Section B.3).
Under fixed-point arithmetic, FuseFSS preserves model accuracy to within +/-0.6 percentage points on GLUE and LAMBADA tasks (Table 4).
On larger models (LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B), FuseFSS still achieves 1.05x-1.22x speedup, showing scalability beyond BERT/GPT-2 (Table 8).
For BERT-base with sequence lengths scaling from 32 to 512 tokens, FuseFSS maintains 1.36x-1.45x speedup with communication savings increasing at longer sequence lengths (Table 2).

XVHhMLqPrh.text: GMF computes reliability via a Transport Energy metric—the squared initial velocity from Rectified Flow, E_intra^(m) = ||v_theta^(m)(z^(m),0)||_2^2—rather than relying on classifier confidence, avoiding the circular dependency of confidence-based fusion (Section 3.3, Eq. 3).
GMF combines a Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge formulation with Rectified Flow to linearize transport paths for efficient one-step velocity prediction at inference (Section 3.2, Eq. 1-2).

On NYU Depth V2 under severe Gaussian sensor noise (sigma=2.0), GMF achieves 55.2% accuracy, outperforming the next-best baseline (QMF, PDF, DBF, or UAW-EEF) by about 6 percentage points (Table 3, Section 5.2).
GMF achieves a 76.8% safe rejection rate on conflicting multimodal pairs versus 35.2% for DBF and 21.3% for PDF (Table 4, Section 5.3).

Theorem 4.5 (the Geometric Barrier Principle) proves that under latent manifold separability, semantic conflicts induce transport cost of at least (delta-2*epsilon)^2, exponentially suppressing incorrect modalities (Section 4, Theorem 4.5).
Single-step GMF inference latency is 18ms, comparable to statistical baselines QMF (13.7ms) and PDF (14ms) (Table 9, Appendix B.1).

nkJIMejfaN.text: Self-explanations improve prediction of model behavior by 11-37% normalized simulatability gain (NSG) across 18 frontier models spanning Qwen 3, Gemma 3, GPT-5, Claude 4.5, and Gemini 3 families (Section 4.1, Table 3).
Self-explanations outperform cross-model explanations (from a different model) by 1.7-4.3 percentage points in predictive value (Section 5, Table 2).
5-15% of self-explanations are egregiously misleading, actively worsening a predictor's ability to simulate model behavior (Section 4.3, Table 1).
NSG varies substantially by dataset, from as low as 6.0% on Moral Machines to as high as 42.8% on Pima Diabetes, across the 7 domains and 7,000 counterfactual pairs used (Section 4.3, Appendix A.2).

The evaluation methodology uses counterfactual questions from real datasets and five predictor models to test whether access to explanations improves simulation of a reference model's behavior (Section 2.2, Figure 3).

uPHdNikfdo.text: The Wasserstein LSE energy functional E(xi) := -1/beta * log(sum_i exp(-beta * W_2^2(X_i, xi))) generalizes classical dense associative memory energy to Gaussian densities on Bures-Wasserstein space (Section 2).

Storage capacity N = Omega(exp(d*alpha^2/16)) is achievable with high probability on Wasserstein spheres, extending exponential vectorial storage capacity results to Gaussian distributions (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
Retrieval error decays exponentially in dimension under Wasserstein perturbations, per convergence bounds established for the update rule (Theorems 2-3, Section 3.2).

Synthetic experiments with N=10,000 Gaussian measures in d=50 dimensions show retrieval convergence at temperature beta=1 but failure at beta=0.1, validating the theoretical separation/temperature conditions (Section 4.1, Figures 3 and 6).

Gaussian word embeddings derived from the Text8 corpus exhibit a sharp phase transition in retrieval success around beta approximately 15, confirming that sharp energy basins yield robust memory (Section 4.1.1, Figures 4-5).
Extended tests with non-commuting covariances (N=1000, d=10) still maintain one-step convergence under suitable beta, despite higher variance (Section 6.2.3, Figure 8).

OXLYBkYs4X.text: On the 2D Maze benchmark, PolyFlow achieves a 100% safety rate versus 0-98% for baselines, while cutting total inference time to 0.58s versus SafeFlow's 7.558s at N=10 steps (Table 2).

PolyFlow guarantees strict satisfaction of arbitrary polyhedral constraints via a differentiable Ray Shooting operator that computes polytope boundary intersections, eliminating enumeration error from post-hoc projection methods (Section 4.3, Appendix C).

On five Gym locomotion tasks (Hopper-Simple/Complex, Walker2d-Simple/Complex, HalfCheetah), PolyFlow maintains a 1.0 safety rate while achieving the highest rollout returns and inference times of about 0.08s versus SafeFlow's 0.8-15.1s (Table 3).
Theorem 4.5 proves safety preservation: if conditional flows are interior-safe, marginal flows maintain safety through convex combination properties (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.5).

On quadruped locomotion with dynamic, time-varying friction cone constraints, PolyFlow demonstrates zero-shot adaptation to terrain variations while respecting ground reaction force bounds (Section 5.4, Figure 4).
Theorem 4.4 bounds the discretization error of the discrete-time flow formulation using 2-Wasserstein distance, with error amplified recursively by a factor of (1+L) (Section 4.1-4.2, Theorem 4.4).

GakFNj5L2W.text: The proposed stochastic Runge-Kutta LMC algorithm achieves a uniform-in-time convergence rate of O(d^1.5 h^1.5) in non-log-concave settings (Theorem 2.2).
The algorithm requires only two gradient evaluations per iteration, compared to three required by the prior stochastic Runge-Kutta scheme of Li et al. (2019) (Section 1).
Higher-order Runge-Kutta variants of the method are shown to achieve improved complexity bounds under additional smoothness assumptions (Theorems 2.5-2.7).
Numerical experiments compare the proposed Runge-Kutta LMC methods against baseline Euler-based ULA schemes on synthetic and real datasets (Section 4, Figures 3-5).
A complexity comparison table contrasts the proposed method against competing algorithms, including those of Li et al. and Sabanis (Table 1).

XQjgmQ8P1n.text: On WikiText2 at 4-bit precision, uncalibrated SINQ improves perplexity over the RTN baseline, e.g., 17.14 vs 18.74 for Qwen3-1.7B and 7.74 vs 8.92 for Qwen3-32B (Table 1).
SINQ has an average runtime of about 1.1x the RTN baseline, versus more than 2x for HQQ and more than 30x for the calibration-based AWQ method (Table 7, Appendix A.2).
A-SINQ combines SINQ with AWQ-style calibration by first normalizing weight matrices via the Sinkhorn-Knopp procedure and then applying AWQ scales before quantization (Section 2.2.2).
SINQ is compatible with non-uniform quantization formats such as NF4; for Qwen3-32B at 4-bit, SINQ with INT4 slightly outperforms SINQ with NF4 (Table 4).
Calibrated versus uncalibrated variants of SINQ are compared directly to quantify the additional gains from calibration (Table 5).

E5SVowO13b.text: Six unlearning methods spanning three families (GA, GA+GD, GA+KL, NPO, NPO+KL, RLabel) are evaluated for how reversible their forgetting is under fine-tuning (Section 3.1).
Forgetting regimes are defined along two axes, reversibility and catastrophicity, distinguishing reversible from irreversible catastrophic forgetting (Section 2, Definitions 1-2).
After a single round of unlearning, minimal fine-tuning restores near-original performance, with RLabel and GA+KL recovering retain-set accuracy to roughly 65% (Table 1).
Under continual unlearning with a small learning rate (5x10^-6) over 100 rounds, NPO-based methods can still be relearned to 82.7-83.8% forget-set accuracy via fine-tuning (Table 2).
On the more complex MATH task, fine-tuning after GA-based unlearning restores accuracy from 0.0% to between 5.1% and 9.3% depending on the setting (Table 3).
Representational analyses via PCA similarity, CKA, and Fisher Information are used to characterize which forgetting regime a given unlearning method falls into (Section 4.2, Figures 2-5).

lvRLG6C0zZ.text: Partial fusion interpolates between full weight aggregation (alpha=0) and full ensembling (alpha=1) by using partial optimal transport to match only the most similar neurons across two networks (Equation 3, Section 2.4).

On split-MNIST MLPs, partial OT fusion with fixed-point optimization reaches accuracy closer to the ensemble than to the aggregated model while using only about 1.45x the parameters of a single network, versus 2x for a full ensemble (Figure 5(a), Section 3.1).

With 1% fine-tuning data on split-MNIST MLPs, partial fusion at alpha=0.4 improves from 87.4% to 96.1% accuracy after fine-tuning, compared to 88.1% to 96.5% for the full ensemble at alpha=1.0 (Table 1, Section 3.2).
On ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 with 5% fine-tuning data, partial fusion at alpha=0.5 improves from 87.4% to 90.3% accuracy after fine-tuning (Table 1, Section 3.2).
Generalized pruning via neuron clustering outperforms standard unstructured pruning on CNNs, particularly at compression ratios below 0.4 (Figure 9).

Fixing three convolutional layers as ensembles while partially merging the remaining layers lets partial fusion exceed the performance of both individual source models with only a 38% increase in channel count (Figure 7).

tm6K5K4t25.text: Pro-SF models strategic agents' feature manipulation via a prospect-guided utility function combining loss aversion, probability distortion, and reference-point bias (Equation 12).

Proposition 4.1 shows that training a classifier under a rational-agent assumption while agents actually exhibit psychological biases creates irreducible deployment error, manifesting as over-defense or under-defense failure modes (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).
Under fully non-rational agent behavior, Pro-SF substantially outperforms a rational-baseline classifier, e.g., 81.50% vs 72.42% accuracy on Adult and 82.41% vs 69.54% on Credit (Table 1, Section 6).
Under a mixed population of rational and non-rational agents, Pro-SF still outperforms the rational baseline, e.g., 78.68% vs 74.31% on Adult and 86.71% vs 78.16% on Spam (Table 1, Section 6).
An ablation on synthetic data shows all three prospect-theory components contribute, with removing probability distortion causing the largest drop, from 78.92% to 73.50% accuracy (Table 2).
Pro-SF remains competitive with rational strategic classifiers when agents are fully rational, while yielding large accuracy gains when behavioral deviations are present (Section 6).

mlQlfZb2rC.text: Nested Least-Privilege Networks factorize each weight matrix as W(g)=B_g A_g so that Rank(W(g)) ≤ g, giving an ordered privilege interface with Im(W(g)) ⊆ Im(W(g+1)) that can be applied post-hoc to pretrained models without retraining (Definition 3.1).

Accuracy decreases monotonically as the allowed rank g is reduced, with easy task instances retaining performance at moderate ranks while hard instances degrade sharply, enabling instance-adaptive privilege allocation (Figure 4).

A progressive-escalation allocation policy achieves target accuracy levels (e.g. 80% and 95%) at a lower average privilege (average rank) than either a static full-privilege or static least-privilege policy, tracing out a privilege-utility Pareto frontier (Figures 5 and 6).

Block-level rank reduction produces sparse, task-specific degradation—for example suppressing certain blocks harms chemistry-subject MMLU accuracy while leaving other subjects largely unaffected, after applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons (Figure 7).

A lightweight targeted optimization can suppress performance on chosen MMLU subjects (e.g. chemistry, biology) while maintaining performance on other subjects, demonstrating directed capability suppression beyond global rank control (Figure 8).

Experiments are conducted on Pythia-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B, and Llama-3 model variants across algorithmic tasks (Balanced Brackets, Length Comparison, Contains Substring) and MMLU knowledge subjects, using probe recoverability as an additional metric (Section 4, Design Desiderata D1-D4).

JHYmxqS9Jv.text: MEMORYARENA comprises 766 multi-session agentic tasks across four domains—Bundled Web Shopping (150 tasks), Group Travel Planning (270 tasks), Progressive Web Search (256 tasks), and Formal Reasoning (60 tasks)—averaging 6.9 subtasks and 57 steps per task (Table 2).

Agents that perform near-saturation on existing long-context memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo achieve near-zero success rates on most MEMORYARENA environments, with overall success below 20% for most memory paradigms tested (Table 3).

0D (raw context), 1D (flat consolidated, e.g. MemGPT, Mem0, ReasoningBank), and 2D (graph/tree-structured, e.g. GraphRAG, Mem0-g) memory architectures show no consistent ranking, indicating complex external memory structures do not reliably outperform raw long-context baselines (Table 3).

Success rates decay as subtask interdependency depth k increases across all evaluated memory mechanisms, consistent with a POMDP framing in which agents accumulate 'belief drift' from incomplete state observation across sessions (Figure 3).

Long-context agents achieve the lowest latency while external memory systems incur the highest latency overhead, and RAG-based systems show slower performance decay with task depth specifically in precise-retrieval scenarios (Table 4).

39650lCGDP.text: Selection bias is formally defined as preferential inclusion into a sample such that P(V | S=1) ≠ P(V), where S denotes sample membership, generalizing beyond traditional collider-stratification framings (Section 2).

Theorem 3.1 establishes Condition 1 as necessary and sufficient for identifiability of the average treatment effect in the full population (s-ATE-full) from selection-biased data, unifying prior graphical identifiability criteria such as selection-backdoor criteria and outcome-dependent selection criteria as special cases (Theorem 3.1, Condition 1).

Under deterministic selection with c-weak-overlap propensity scores and a smooth exponential-family outcome parametrization P(y|t,x) ∝ e^{f(x,y)} with polynomial f, the ATE is identifiable via extrapolation from truncated/censored regions of the outcome distribution (Proposition 3.3).

Under non-deterministic selection with c-weak-overlap, the ATE is identifiable for common noise distributions including Gaussian, Laplace, Pareto, and Log-normal, extending prior results that required non-Gaussian additive noise assumptions (Proposition 3.5).

Two estimators—maximum likelihood estimation with a regularized selection function (MLE+β) and score matching (SM+β)—substantially outperform naive inverse propensity weighting and polynomial baselines in synthetic experiments across Gaussian/Laplace noise and additive/multiplicative selection settings, and reduce bias when applied to semi-synthetic All of Us health data (Section 5, synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments).

ObJAI5sdZ3.text: Transitioning from post-hoc (single-round) merging to many-shot (multi-round) merging consistently improves multi-task performance across all baseline merging methods tested—Task Arithmetic, DARE, TIES, and ConsensusTA—on Llama-3.2-3B (Table 1).
Theorem 3.2 proves that many-shot merging reduces multi-task loss relative to post-hoc merging under L-smoothness conditions on the task loss landscape (Theorem 3.2).

METIS combines loss-gap weighting, which upweights tasks with larger performance drops in later merging rounds, with consensus-based parameter masking that integrates a parameter only when multiple tasks agree on its value (Section 4, Figure 3).
Theorem 4.2 shows that loss-gap reweighting improves worst-case task performance by compensating for information erasure during merging (Theorem 4.2).

METIS achieves higher normalized average performance than the best baseline merging method on four backbone models—Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-3-4B—including narrowing the gap between average and worst-performing task scores (Table 2, Table 3).

METIS's normalized performance advantage over baselines persists when scaling from 7 to 8 to 11 tasks in the many-shot setting on Llama-3.2-3B, and pre-trained knowledge on CoQA and PubMedQA is preserved across backbone models (Table 5, Table 4).

5RQPAHUtCO.text: Across a dataset of 300,000 responses (150 responses per prompt for 200 time-sensitive prompts, across 10 small LLMs of 7B-32B parameters), genuine responses show tighter intra-class clustering than hallucinated responses, with the ratio of inter-class to intra-class embedding distance averaging 1.13 in raw embedding space (Table 1).

Fisher Discriminant Analysis projection amplifies the separability ratio between genuine and hallucinated response clusters from 1.13× to an average of 7.26× across the 10 evaluated models, with a shared optimal regularization value of λ≈1.2 across architectures (Table 1, Figure 5).

A label-propagation classifier built on the Fisher-projected embedding space achieves average accuracy of 87.2% and average F1-score of 90.7% for hallucination classification, with per-model F1 ranging from 84.0% to 95.3% (Table 2).
Label-propagation F1 performance saturates once 30-50 labeled training responses are available, demonstrating label-efficient hallucination classification (Figure 4).

Observed Wasserstein distances between genuine and hallucinated response distributions exceed the null-hypothesis (random label permutation) baseline for 87.6% of prompts on average, with per-model rates ranging from 81.5% to 94.5%, indicating genuine geometric structure rather than sampling artifacts (Table 5, Figures 3 and 6).
The global average hallucination rate across all evaluated models and years is 80.9%, with individual model rates ranging from 66.4% to 87.6% (Table 4).

RKiQ95ZuCW.text: CAPS achieves 47.4% success on RoboTwin 1.0, compared to 32.2% for the base π₀ policy and 41.3% for π₀ + TACO (Table 1).
On the 48-task RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, CAPS reaches 66.2% average success rate, outperforming RDT (34.6%) and TACO (64.0%) (Section 4.3, Table 3).
On Libero-long, CAPS attains 97.6% success rate versus 49.8% for OpenVLA and 56.5% for RoboMonkey (Section 4.4, Table 4).
Theorem 3.1 shows the ideal effective-horizon extension ratio T_eff(CAPS)/T_eff(Base) ≈ ε^(1-α), yielding a 10x horizon extension example for α=2 and ε=0.1 (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1).

Ablations on RoboTwin 1.0 show that disabling power-distribution sharpening (α=1) drops success to 38.5% despite the same 8.5x latency overhead as the full always-on MCMC variant, isolating sharpening (not merely extra MCMC search) as the source of CAPS's gains (Section 4.6, Table 5).
In real-world evaluation across 10 tasks and 200 trials, CAPS achieves 71.0% overall success versus 53.0% for TACO and 36.5% for the base policy (Section 4.5, Table 6).

Sm7NhztxlA.text: ScDiVa is pre-trained on 59.2 million cells using a 94.5M-parameter, 12-layer Transformer with a 41,818-token gene vocabulary and 1,200-token context window (Section 3.4).
On rank-value joint gene reconstruction, ScDiVa reaches Spearman correlations of 0.970 on the Immune dataset (a 14.9% improvement over GeneMamba) and 0.994 on Zheng68k (Section 4.2, Table 1).
On multi-batch integration, ScDiVa achieves Avg_batch of 0.9960 on PBMC12k (versus 0.9755 for scGPT) and Avg_bio of 0.8712 on BMMC (versus 0.7628 for GeneMamba) (Section 4.3, Table 2).
ScDiVa attains 0.986 fine-tuned accuracy on hPancreas cell-type annotation and 0.914 average zero-shot accuracy across 8 datasets (Section 4.4).

On perturbation response prediction, ScDiVa reaches 0.837 Pearson correlation on differentially expressed genes for the Adamson dataset and 0.709 on the double-perturbation Norman dataset (Section 4.5, Figure 5).

Attention-based analysis of the SPI1 regulon recovers biologically coherent myeloid-promoting genes (e.g., MS4A3, FTH1) and erythroid-repression targets (e.g., HBG1, HBG2), filtering out non-causal genes like CCNB2 and TOP2A (Section 4.6, Figure 6).

7H9HRTWady.text: Theorem 4.5 establishes that any preference function decomposes uniquely into an orthogonal transitive (scalar, potential-function) component and a cyclic (zero-marginal, vector) component (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.5).
HRC instantiates the transitive component with a Bradley-Terry scalar reward and the cyclic component with GPM-style skew-symmetric bilinear forms, per Theorem 4.6 (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.6).
On RewardBench 2, HRC achieves 57.63% average accuracy on Gemma-2B-it, surpassing BT (55.93%) and GPM (56.40%) (Section 6.2, Table 1).
On RewardBench 2 with Llama-3.1-8B, HRC reaches 70.95% average accuracy, an 0.85% improvement over the BT baseline (Section 6.2, Table 1).
HRC+DSPPO achieves a 44.75% length-controlled win rate against GPT-4-Turbo on AlpacaEval 2.0 for Gemma-2B-it, and 46.8% win rate on Arena-Hard-v0.1 (a 3.2% gain over the best baseline) (Section 6.3).
Theorem 5.3 shows DSPPO's dynamic score schedule converges to a Nash equilibrium at rate O(1/√T) as it shifts from transitive to cyclic guidance over training (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.3).

TDTTiEc3Hn.text: ScoreMatchingRiesz estimates the Riesz representer by decomposing the density ratio into a telescoping product of infinitesimally close bridge distributions, approximating log r_0(x) as the integral ∫_1^0 ∂_t log p_t(x) dt as the number of bridge steps T→∞ (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).

Section 4 applies the score-matching estimator to three distinct targets: average treatment effect (ATE) via inverse propensity scores, average marginal effect (AME) via the representer −∂_u log p_0(u,Z)|_{u=D}, and average policy effect (APE) via integrated time scores (Section 4.1–4.3).

The AME estimation approach is connected to denoising score matching, allowing the Riesz representer for continuous treatments to be recovered without directly estimating the density itself (Section 6).

Section 7 bridges the AME and APE (policy path) estimation procedures, showing the policy effect can be expressed through the same integrated time-score representation used for marginal effects (Section 7).

Theorem 8.1 shows the Bregman divergence-based training objective can be rewritten in an equivalent form that avoids requiring the unknown log-density, generalizing the score-matching loss (Section 8, Theorem 8.1).

QpjtK65JHO.text: HypoSpace introduces three metrics—Validity Rate, Uniqueness/Novelty Rate, and Recovery Rate—to diagnose set-valued hypothesis generation under underdetermination (Section 3.1).

HypoSpace comprises three diagnostic tasks: causal DAG inference from single-node interventions, 3D voxel reconstruction from 2D projections under gravity constraints, and Boolean genetic-interaction inference (Section 4.1–4.3).

Frontier LLMs maintain high Validity Rate but show sharp degradation in Uniqueness and Recovery Rate as the admissible hypothesis space |H_O| grows, evidencing mode collapse rather than random error (Section 5.4, Table 1).

Reasoning models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, DeepSeek-R1) outperform instruction-tuned baselines on Uniqueness and Recovery Rate at medium-to-hard difficulty levels, yet still fail to explore 30-40% of valid hypothesis spaces (Section 5.2, Table 1).

An information-theoretic analysis of cumulative entropy and information gain versus number of queries shows exploration dynamics plateauing well before the full hypothesis space is covered (Section 5.5, Figure 3).

iZrp2P55ie.text: MASPO achieves an average accuracy improvement of 2.9 points over the best baseline methods across the evaluated benchmarks (Table 1).
MASPO's joint reward combines Local Validity, Global Alignment, and Lookahead Potential with weights alpha=0.4, theta=0.2, and beta=0.4 (Equation 5).

Removing the Joint Evaluate component causes the largest ablation drop, reducing average accuracy to 67.77% (a 2.62 point drop), while removing Beam Refresh drops it to 68.53% (0.86 point drop) and removing Misalignment-Aware Sampling drops it to 69.68% (0.71 point drop) (Table 2).

Prompts optimized on Qwen3-8B transfer effectively to other LLMs, reaching 75.86% average accuracy on DeepSeek-V3, 78.41% on GLM-4.6, 79.73% on Claude-Sonnet-4, and 87.14% on Gemini-2.5-Pro (Table 3).

MASPO is evaluated on six benchmarks spanning math (MATH-500, AGIEval-MATH, AQuA), reasoning (GPQA-Diamond), and code (MBPP, HumanEval-ET) tasks, comparing against single-agent baselines (Vanilla, CoT, Self-Consistency, Self-Refine) and multi-agent/prompt-optimization baselines (Sequential/Hierarchical MAS, TPE-based MIPRO/MASS, SPO) (Section 5).

cpKJ2GlnYT.text: The paper derives a tractable estimator for the KL divergence between trajectory distributions in function space, expressed via squared discrepancies between the associated velocity fields under Functional Flow Matching (Theorem 3.6).
On synthetic Gaussian-measure validation cases, the estimator's KL values range from 3.95 to 45.73 across 8 configurations, closely matching analytic ground-truth values of 3.64 to 45.43 (Table 1).

The functional KL estimator is benchmarked against five methods (vSB, SBIRR, MSBM, MFL, AM, TIGON) on synthetic dynamical systems (Lotka-Volterra, Repressilator, Petal) and four real single-cell RNA-seq datasets (EB, hESC, ME, HF), using marginal metrics (EMD, W2, SWD, MWD, MMD) alongside forward and reverse functional KL (Tables 2-3).

On the Repressilator dataset, TIGON ranks above SBIRR according to marginal metrics but below SBIRR according to functional KL, illustrating that marginal-metric-based evaluation can be inconsistent with trajectory-level evaluation (Section on TI benchmark evaluation, Tables 2-3).

Figure 3 shows that marginal-metric-based rankings on Lotka-Volterra and Repressilator are often statistically indistinguishable despite apparently large numerical differences between methods, undermining confidence in marginal-only evaluation (Figure 3).

The estimator uses a Mesh-Informed Neural Operator (MINO) architecture with a subtraction-based parameterization enforcing boundary conditions and Monte Carlo integration that does not require simulating the full generative dynamics via ODE integration (Section 4).

aOxTMMLYuP.text: IQA-Spider is presented as the first image quality assessment framework that unifies reasoning, grounding, and referring within a single LMM-based system across a four-task paradigm: Global Quality Description, Local Quality Description, Visual Quality Grounding, and Visual Quality Referring (Section on Overview/Four-Task Paradigm).

The constructed IQA-Spider-33K dataset combines synthetic distortions from KADIS-700K and authentic distortions from KonIQ, comprising training sets of 3,251 (global), 9,742 (local), 11,669 (grounding), 4,506 (refer-short), and 4,222 (refer-long) instances, with corresponding test sets of 629, 460, 586, 780, and 786 instances.
On the Q-Ground-Test benchmark, the Qwen3-VL-based IQA-Spider model achieves 0.338 mIoU for pixel-level distortion grounding, versus 0.271 for Q-Ground and 0.252 for PixelLM.
On Q-Bench-A1, the Qwen3-VL-based IQA-Spider model achieves 74.45% accuracy, outperforming Q-Instruct's 67.56%.
On KADID-10K visual scoring, the Phi-3.5-Vision-based IQA-Spider model achieves 0.815 SRCC / 0.783 PLCC, compared to Q-Instruct's 0.698 SRCC / 0.676 PLCC.

The framework uses a training-free text-to-point grounding paradigm in its second stage that maps token logits to spatial coordinates, bridging textual semantics and pixel-level perception (Section on Methodology/Two-Stage Design).

zrVSSx6348.text: On the primary cardiovascular benchmarks, HetMedAgent achieves 0.866 AUROC / 0.844 F1 on risk stratification, 0.801 AUROC / 0.757 F1 on etiology prediction, and 0.727 AUROC / 0.719 F1 on severity assessment, outperforming the best single specialist model (Meditron) by 6.6% AUROC / 7.9% F1 and the best multi-agent baseline (MedAgents) by 4.3% AUROC / 5.7% F1 (Table 1).

An ablation starting from GPT-4o alone (0.671 AUROC) shows adding the ECHO specialist improves AUROC by 8.1%, adding the ECG specialist improves it by 6.3%, and combining both specialists improves it by 12.7%, demonstrating synergy between generalist and specialist models (Table 4).

Weighted conflict-aware evidence fusion, computed via wi=softmax(log(ci)+log(1-δi)) using PubMedBERT embeddings, outperforms an equal-weight direct fusion baseline by 2.1% AUROC and 2.4% F1 (Figure 4).

Of 613 test cases, 114 (18.6%) exceed the uncertainty threshold θ_P=0.5 and are escalated for clinician review, with autonomous cases showing significantly higher F1 than escalated cases (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.001).

On a cross-domain validation using the IU X-Ray chest radiology dataset (668 test cases), HetMedAgent achieves 0.820 AUROC / 0.537 F1 versus a ViT-BERT baseline's 0.783 AUROC / 0.468 F1, including a 4.5 percentage-point recall improvement (0.761 vs. 0.716) for detecting acute cases.

Transformer-based specialist models substantially outperform CNN baselines, with BERTScore improvements of 5.2-9.3% for the ECHO specialist and 2.6-5.9% for the ECG specialist, alongside reduced mean conflict scores of 2.6-4.4% (Table 2).

qtzu9pGH7S.text: MPFT proceeds through four stages: approximating Pareto-vertex policies by optimizing individual objectives, tracking the Pareto front via a novel Pareto-tracking mechanism from those vertex policies, filling sparse regions via objective weight adjustment, and combining all tracked policies into the final Pareto-approximation set (Section on MPFT Framework).
MPFT is instantiated with three RL algorithms: MOPPO for online learning, and newly proposed MOSAC and MOTD7 for offline learning (Section on RL Algorithms Integrated).

Compared to the population-based evolutionary baselines PGMORL and PA2D-MORL, MPFT reduces the number of agent-environment interactions (env_steps) by 66.63% for MPFT-MOPPO, 71.64% for MPFT-MOSAC, and 77.72% for MPFT-MOTD7, while achieving superior hypervolume on most environments (Table 1).

MPFT is evaluated on seven continuous-control MuJoCo-3.3.0 tasks, including six two-objective environments (HalfCheetah-2, Hopper-2, Swimmer-2, Ant-2, Walker2d-2, Humanoid-2) and one three-objective environment (Hopper-3) (Section on Experimental Environments).
MPFT achieves dramatically lower CPU utilization and memory usage than the evolutionary baselines, as shown by hardware resource requirement comparisons (Figure 2).

MgtyPYrC4h.text: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Prefix-RFT achieves an average score of 50.8 across AIME24/25, AMC, MATH-500, Minerva, and OlympiadBench, exceeding LUFFY (50.1), SFT+RFT (48.2), and pure RFT (45.5) (Table 1).
On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Prefix-RFT scores 30.2/22.0 on AIME24/25 and 41.9 on Minerva, compared to LUFFY's 29.4/23.1 and 37.5 respectively (Table 1).

With only 1% (0.45k) of demonstration data on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Prefix-RFT still attains a 37.6 average benchmark score, versus 40.8 with 10% (4.5k) demonstrations, showing robustness to demonstration quantity (Table 2).
On challenging problems, Prefix-RFT reaches a best@16 of 0.42 versus 0.14 for pure RFT, indicating stronger exploration on hard problems (Section 6).
Entropy-based token clipping that restricts prefix supervision to the top 20% highest-entropy tokens outperforms relaxing the threshold to 50% or 80%, which substantially degrades results (Figure 6).
A cosine decay schedule for prefix sampling length improves benchmark performance over a uniform prefix-sampling scheme (Figure 7).

QZO3oby12w.text: AI engrams are extracted in closed form via W⁺ = W·Σ⁺(Σ⁺ + Σ⁻)† using covariance statistics from target and reference data, requiring only a single forward pass rather than iterative optimization (Equation 4).

Theorem 6.1 proves that this closed-form engram solution corresponds to a minimum-norm projection under the Fisher information metric, and that ablation under a K-FAC approximation is equivalent to a natural gradient descent update (Theorem 6.1).

Memory composition and erasure are performed via linear vector arithmetic on extracted engrams (e.g., μ_new = μ ± μ_Glasses⁺ ∓ μ_Goatee⁺), allowing 2^n memory combinations from n engrams without any recomputation.

On CIFAR-10 class unlearning, the method achieves a ToW score of 0.984 versus 0.999 for full retraining, while extraction takes under 2 minutes for 100 classes compared to hours for gradient-based methods.

The framework is validated across MLPs, ResNet-18, ViT-B on ImageNet-1K, autoencoders/WAE, and a Llama-3.2-1B LLM evaluated on the TOFU benchmark, where it trails iterative unlearning methods on Utility and Privacy metrics.

X4OakhiSzp.text: Proposition 1 shows the Fréchet distance between generated and target distributions is non-monotonic in latent diffusion models under estimated scores, implying earlier stopping of the backward process can reduce this distance (Proposition 1).

Proposition 2 establishes an optimal dimension-time trade-off: lower-dimensional latent projections are optimal in early diffusion sampling stages, while higher-dimensional projections become necessary closer to the end of sampling (Proposition 2).
Proposition 3 shows that for data on a d0-dimensional subspace, stopping at time T − δ̂_d0 combined with projecting to dimension d0 is jointly optimal (Proposition 3).

Figure 1 shows empirically on CelebA-HQ that FID scores for latent diffusion models rise noticeably before reaching t=T, whereas standard pixel-space diffusion shows monotonically improving FID throughout sampling (Figure 1).

Proposition 5 shows that under weight-constrained score matching, the optimal dimension d_min satisfies 1/C ≤ σ̂²_{d_min} ≤ 1/(2C−1), and for exponentially decaying covariance spectra, the optimal dimensionality scales logarithmically with capacity (Proposition 5).

A9r5l1qKCK.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes that generalization error scales as O(K_L N_D^(-1/d)), motivating intrinsic dimension (via the MST-based dimMST estimator) as a proxy for downstream SSL performance (Theorem 3.1).

IdEst correlates strongly and negatively with linear-probe accuracy on ImageNet, with Kendall's τ ≈ -0.6 and Spearman's ρ ≈ -0.8, with similarly strong correlations on iNat-18, iNat-21, and SUN397 (Figure 1).
IdEst computed solely from ImageNet representations transfers to predict downstream performance on iNat-18, iNat-21, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 (Figure 4).

For hyperparameter selection on ViT-G, IdEst requires 12.8 minutes versus 322.7 minutes for a 10-epoch linear probe, while achieving near-oracle selection performance for VICReg, DINO, and I-JEPA (Table 1, Table 2).

The dimMST estimator recovers the correct ground-truth dimension on a 1D helix toy example where the TwoNN estimator diverges, demonstrating improved robustness over TwoNN and MLE-based intrinsic dimension estimators (Figure 2).
During online DINO training, after an initial 10-epoch period, IdEst tracks the evolution of downstream classification accuracy, though it is less informative in that early training phase (Figure 7).

tGu4bsqD3T.text: Theorem 4.6 shows that the estimation error of LOCO variable-importance scores is dominated by the excess risks of the full and feature-restricted models, rather than by test-set variance as assumed in prior work (Theorem 4.6).
Theorem 4.10 extends the excess-risk-dominance result to SAGE importance scores across feature subsets (Theorem 4.10).

Proposition 4.7 shows the ensemble-versus-aggregation gap scales as (ψ_sub − ψ*)(ρ + (1−ρ)/B), implying model-level ensembling reduces bias via Jensen's inequality for convex losses while aggregating sub-model explanations only reduces variance (Proposition 4.7).

On the Friedman 1 dataset, model-level ensembling achieves lower MSE and higher ROC AUC for feature selection than aggregating individual model explanations, for both LOCO and SAGE, across Random Forest and MLP architectures (Figure 2).
Figure 3 decomposes the error and shows the ensemble strategy substantially reduces squared bias, while the aggregated sub-models strategy remains dominated by bias (Figure 3).

On UK Biobank proteomic data (n=46,382), ensemble-based LOCO importance more reliably identifies established metabolic markers such as FABP4, LEP, and IGFBP proteins than aggregated per-model importance scores (Figure 5).

5fMeQEzret.text: SSLogic expands from 400 seed task families to 953 families through two evolution rounds, increasing verifiable instances from 5,718 to 21,389 (Section 3).
Training on SSLogic-evolved data improves SynLogic by +5.2 points, BBEH by +1.4 points, AIME25 by +3.0 points, and Brumo25 by +3.7 points over the seed-data baseline (Section 4, Table 2).
The agentic Generator-Validator synthesis pipeline achieves a 55% task-family acceptance rate at a cost of $1.18 per accepted family (Section 5, Table 4).
Rejected synthesis traces consume roughly 6.5x more compute runtime than accepted traces, motivating the pipeline's early-rejection design (Section 5).

GFmJ5XcGWl.text: Universal Horizon Models (UHM) are evaluated on 100 OGBench tasks split into 50 standard tasks (10 environments x 5 tasks), 25 noisy tasks (5 environments), and 25 long-horizon tasks (5 environments) (Section 5.1).
On standard tasks, UHM attains a 55% average success rate versus 48% for the geometric horizon model (GHM) and 52% for DTD(lambda) (Table 1).
On long-horizon tasks, UHM reaches 22% average success, versus 13% for DTD(lambda) and 16% for GHM, an improvement of roughly 38-69% relative to these baselines (Table 3).
On noisy/sub-optimal datasets, UHM achieves 39% average success versus 38% for GHM, indicating robustness to suboptimal data (Table 2).
UHM generalizes geometric horizon models by predicting future states under arbitrary horizons, with the critic target estimation formalized in Proposition 4.1 (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).

J5KrubuRAJ.text: AutoBaxBuilder generates new code security benchmarking tasks in under 2 hours for less than USD 4 (abstract only).
Including a manual verification step, the pipeline reduces the human effort required for benchmark construction by a factor of 12 compared to expert manual creation (abstract only).
The automated pipeline produces both functional tests and end-to-end security-probing exploits for evaluating LLM-generated code (abstract only).
The authors release AutoBaxBench, a new public benchmark, along with evaluations of contemporary LLMs on it, addressing benchmark contamination concerns (abstract only).

SOlPHMdSY3.text: Feynman-diagram graphical rules are introduced that simplify layer-wise recursion relations for finite-width Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) statistics at order 1/n (Section 4).
A recursion relation for the first-order (1/n) finite-width correction to the NTK mean is derived using five Feynman diagrams containing quadratic and quartic vertices (Section 5.1).
For scale-invariant activation functions (ReLU and LeakyReLU), the infinite-width NTK diagonal Theta(x,x) has no finite-width corrections (Section 5.3).

Experiments on four-layer ReLU MLPs sampled over 5x10^6 initializations, with hidden-layer widths n>=20, confirm the finite-width kernel corrections predicted by the recursion relations (Figure 2, Section 6).

Gradient-stability experiments on 200-hidden-unit ReLU MLPs with up to 30 layers, averaged over 1000 initializations, show linear scaling with depth at the critical initialization C_W=2 (Figure 1, Section 6).

OjXimqfwlX.text: Compositional Transduction with Latent Analogies (CTA) achieves an average success rate of 56.3 across 8 OGBench manipulation tasks, roughly a 42% improvement over the strongest baseline HIQL-vee at 39.3 (Table 1, Section 6).
On the Scene-play task, CTA reaches a direct out-of-combination (OOC) success rate of 73+/-9, versus a standard in-combination success rate of 94+/-4 (Table 2).
On Puzzle-4x4-play, CTA attains a direct OOC success rate of 80+/-8 versus a standard success rate of 100+/-1, outperforming HIQL-vee on direct OOC generalization (Table 2).

The dual analogy representation alpha(s,g) = phi(g) - phi(s), derived from the temporal distance difference field (Proposition 4.4), formalizes transduction of analogies to unseen task combinations (Section 4, Section 5).
A t-SNE visualization of the learned analogy space shows task clustering consistent with the analogy representation remaining invariant to contextual variation (Figure 4).

9SCVnAxoKK.text: On the peptides-struct long-range graph benchmark, S3GNN achieves test MAE of 0.2429 ± 0.0014, an improvement over S2GNN's 0.2487 ± 0.0019, while on peptides-func it reaches 73.20 ± 0.14 AP versus 72.75 for S2GNN (Table 3).
On the synthetic Barbell graph task, S3GNN attains roughly 30x lower MSE than Stable-ChebNet (about 0.005 vs 0.17) while using about 50% fewer parameters (262K vs 591K) (Figure 2).
On large-scale node classification, S3GNN improves accuracy/ROC-AUC over Stable-ChebNet from 75.42 to 76.38 ± 0.32 on ogbn-arxiv and from 79.89 to 81.90 ± 0.12 on ogbn-proteins (Table 2).

On multi-hop knowledge graph question answering, incorporating S3GNN-based reasoning improves F1 by +10.8% on WebQSP and +11.1% on Complex WebQuestions (CWQ) over a reasoning GNN baseline without retrieval-augmented generation (Table 4).

On mesh-based fluid dynamics (Cylinder Flow), the S3GNN-based mesh graph net (S3MGN) reduces minimum test loss from 0.173 to 0.102 and velocity RMSE from 0.000589 to 0.000333 compared to the standard MeshGraphNet (MGN) baseline (Table 6).

Proposition 1 shows that under non-degenerate feature transforms the Jacobian sensitivity lower bound between distant nodes is distance-independent, and Proposition 2 shows that antisymmetric feature transforms keep Jacobian energy stable at ||J(l)||_2 = 1 + O(epsilon^2), motivating S3GNN's per-layer complexity of O(|E|d + Nd^2) versus O(K|E|d + Nd^2) for prior spectral methods with polynomial order K (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

To2n4qTdke.text: LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.1, Qwen3) display a distinct 'sawtooth' pattern in intermediate-layer attention maps that structurally aligns with the ground-truth token-level adjacency matrix of a serialized graph, taken as evidence of spontaneous internal graph topology reconstruction (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

SLASH improves average accuracy on GraphInstruct from 0.282 to 0.352 for Llama-3.1-8B and from 0.174 to 0.367 for Qwen3-8B, while a fine-tuned specialist model (GraphWiz) shows negligible change (0.544 to 0.544) (Table 1).

Theorem 4.1 shows sink attention contracts effective node distance by a factor of (1 - lambda), and Proposition 4.2 shows Dirichlet energy decay is quadratically suppressed as (1 - lambda)^2, formalizing a representation bottleneck caused by attention sinks (Section 4.3).

Theorem 4.3 shows SLASH's attention sharpening induces a geometric expansion of node distances with ratio rho(lambda, gamma) = (1 - gamma*lambda) / (1 - lambda), reversing the sink-induced energy decay described in Proposition 4.4 (Section 4.3).

An ablation (Table 3) shows layer-level attention intervention consistently outperforms head-level intervention, and another ablation (Table 5) shows combining entropy-based and concentration-based head filtering outperforms either criterion alone.

On MolecularNet, SLASH yields consistent improvements for general-purpose LLMs but produces negligible change (0.650 to 0.650) for the specialized MolecularGPT model, and performance degrades on tasks where graph structure is irrelevant, such as Graph-SST2 sentiment classification (Table 2).

I9cWQO0BP7.text: For stochastic contexts, the paper defines a minimum preference gap (Definition 2) and proves the Batched Adaptive Regret-Balancing (BARB) algorithm achieves an instance-dependent regret upper bound depending on log T and 1/∆_min^2 (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

Under a regularity condition on the CDF of the minimum utility difference (Assumption 5), BARB's regret is shown to be Θ̃(T^{2/3}) asymptotically, with Theorem 3.2 giving the O(T^{2/3}) upper bound and Theorem 3.3 giving a matching Ω(T^{2/3}) lower bound for N=K=3 (Section 3.3).

For adversarial contexts, the paper introduces a tractable α-approximate ∆-optimal stable regret (Equation 7) and proposes the Adaptive Explore-Choose Oracle (AdECO) algorithm, proving a regret upper bound of O(Nd log^2(T)/(∆-ε)^2 + ((∆+ε)/2)T) that becomes O(T^{2/3}) when ∆ = O(T^{-1/3}) (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).

Numerical experiments simulate a matching market with N=4 players, K=4 arms, and context dimension d=3 over a horizon of T=200,000 rounds averaged over 20 trials, comparing BARB against Batched-ETC and ETC baselines, and AdECO against alternatives (Section 5, Figure 1).

4OFXgDuRNH.text: The proposed algorithm (Algorithm 1 for training, Algorithm 2 for testing) satisfies, per Theorem 4.2, both safe exploration (all deployed policies remain feasible with high probability) and a test-time reward regret bound of O~(sqrt(C_ε(D,δ)K)/((1-γ)^2 ξ) + εK/(ξ(1-γ)^3)) for constrained meta-RL (Section 4).
Corollary 4.3 derives a sample complexity of O~(ξ^{-2} ε^{-2} (1-γ)^{-5} C_{ξε(1-γ)^3}(D,δ)) test-task samples to guarantee output policies that are simultaneously ε-optimal and feasible.
Theorem 5.1 establishes a matching lower bound of Ω~(ξ^{-2} ε^{-2} (1-γ)^{-5} C_{ξε(1-γ)^3}(D,δ)) samples, showing the upper bound in Corollary 4.3 is tight.

Assumption 3.3 (Simultaneous Slater's Condition) posits the existence of a policy that is ξ-feasible across every CMDP in the task distribution, which underlies the safe-exploration guarantee of Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 (Section 3).

dPaBOu0Xwk.text: Theorem 3.1 (Pinsker-Marginal bound) derives an off-policy trust-region error bound scaling as O(T^{3/2}) via |Error| ≤ (4/3) T^{3/2} D_KL^{tok,max}, versus the classical O(T^2) TRPO-style bound, for long-horizon LLM RL (Section 3).
Theorem 3.2 (Mixed bound) derives a tighter O(T) error bound, |Error| ≤ 2T sqrt(D_KL^{tok,max} · D_KL^{seq}), that additionally depends on the sequence-level KL divergence D_KL^{seq} (Section 3).

For T=4096 tokens and D_KL^{tok,max}=10^{-4}, the paper computes the classical bound at 1677, the Pinsker-Marginal bound at 35.0 (about 48x tighter), and under sparse-KL conditions (D_KL^{seq}=0.01) the Mixed bound at 8.2 (about 200x tighter than classical) (Section 3, Table 1).

Theorem 5.1 introduces Trust Region Masking (TRM), which excludes entire sequences violating a per-token KL threshold via the mask M(x,y) = 1[max_t D_KL(c_t) ≤ δ], providing unbiased gradient estimation, a length-invariant threshold, and a monotonic improvement guarantee when the masked surrogate objective exceeds the derived error bound (Section 5).

OAvNOSbhwL.text: ALSO formulates multi-turn social strategy selection as an adversarial multi-armed bandit, treating K persona-strategy combinations (e.g., cooperation, competition, rational bargaining) as arms sampled via an exponential-weights distribution π_k(t) ∝ exp(η S_k(t-1)) (Algorithm 1).

On the Sotopia-Hard benchmark (14 challenging scenarios), ALSO achieves an overall score of 3.53 versus 3.43 for the best baseline and 3.02 for the vanilla static-persona agent, with the largest gain on the Relationship dimension (2.43 vs. 1.32 vanilla, +83.79%) (Table showing Sotopia-Hard results).

On the Sotopia-All benchmark (90 diverse scenarios), ALSO reaches an overall score of 3.89 compared to 3.85 for the best baseline INSTINCT, a neural bandit using UCB exploration (Sotopia-All results).

An ablation study shows removing the lightweight neural surrogate reward predictor causes the largest performance drop (-0.58 points, -14.8% overall score), more than removing score smoothing (-0.34, -8.7%) or the EXP3 sampling mechanism in favor of ε-greedy (-0.30, -7.7%) (Table 3).

ALSO agents zero-shot transferred to 7 held-out Sotopia-Hard scenarios show a 13.5% overall score improvement (3.60 vs. 3.17) over a from-scratch baseline, indicating learned strategies generalize across scenarios (Cross-scenario generalization results).

OVBpXUvwMi.text: The paper constructs gradient-descent-type in-context Transformers whose MLP blocks are explicit Euler steps of negative gradient flow of the form x - τW^T σ(Wx + b) with τ ∈ [0, 2/||W||₂²], making them Lipschitz-continuous by construction rather than by post-hoc regularization (Lipschitz MLP Layer definition).
Lemma 2 proves the constructed attention map Γ_θ(μ,x) is 1-Lipschitz in the query for fixed context measure and C₁-Lipschitz in the context measure under the Wasserstein-1 distance (Lemma 2).

Lemma 6 shows that deep compositions of these Lipschitz attention layers preserve both the 1-Lipschitz-in-query and C₂-Lipschitz-in-context properties, so stability does not degrade with depth (Lemma 6).

Theorem 8 establishes a universal approximation result: for any target 1-Lipschitz in-context map with C-Lipschitz dependence on the context measure and any ε > 0, there exists a gradient-descent-type Transformer approximating it uniformly to within ε, with guarantees independent of the number of context tokens (Theorem 8).

The approximation proof adapts a Restricted Stone-Weierstrass theorem to two-variable Lipschitz functions (Lemma 9), using Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality to construct the separating functions needed for the density argument (Lemma 9).

0azUrmsSyA.text: DyLLM selects tokens for recomputation during masked diffusion LLM decoding by thresholding the temporal cosine similarity s_{t,l}^(i) between attention contexts at consecutive denoising steps t and t-1, reusing cached activations for tokens above the similarity threshold τ (Saliency-Based Token Selection, method section).

The partial attention mechanism reduces attention complexity from O(N²d) to O(N·|A|d), where |A| is the size of the salient token set, by fully recomputing attention only for salient tokens and approximating non-salient token updates with cached weights and sparse value changes (Partial Attention Mechanism, method section).
On LLaDA 8B, DyLLM achieves up to 6.99x speedup on GSM8K (80.15 tok/s at 78.01 accuracy) and up to 6.13x speedup on MATH (96.98 tok/s at 38.68 accuracy) at nu=1 (Table 2).

On Dream 7B, DyLLM reaches its largest reported speedup of 8.89x on GSM8K (111.79 tok/s, 79.30 accuracy), consistent with the paper's headline claim of up to 9.6x throughput improvement while preserving baseline accuracy (Table 2).

A scalability analysis shows DyLLM avoids the full-sequence refresh steps that become a bottleneck for Fast-dLLM as the parallel decoding degree increases, preserving sparsity throughout inference (Scalability Analysis section).

HgIx4dYJ5z.text: An n-shot function vector (FV) in in-context learning is well-approximated by a linear combination of individual example-level sub-FVs, indicating additive and composable contributions from each demonstration (abstract only).

Models reweight the contribution of individual demonstrations to the function vector based on prior context, with attention shifting toward more informative and less ambiguous examples as more shots are added (abstract only).
The causal decomposition separates Query-Key routing effects from Value-mediated update effects in constructing the function vector (abstract only).

Query-Key alignment provides consistent improvements to function vector quality, especially in ambiguous in-context learning conditions, whereas Value-mediated effects vary more substantially across conditions (abstract only).

J6AIZuAN81.text: For equicontinuous hypothesis sets typical of neural networks, standard unconstrained surrogate loss minimization in preference learning (e.g., DPO's logistic loss) yields vacuous consistency bounds, meaning arbitrarily low surrogate risk is compatible with high ranking error via shrinking score differences (Theorem 3.1).

The proposed margin-shifted framework replaces the standard surrogate Φ(w·Δh) with a shifted surrogate Φ(w·Δh - γ) requiring a minimum confidence margin γ between preferred and dispreferred response scores to restore consistency (Theorem 5.2).

A structure-aware extension replaces the fixed margin γ with an adaptive margin Γ(y,y') = τΔ(y,y') scaled by semantic distance between responses, avoiding unnecessary separation between near-synonymous outputs while enforcing stricter ranking on semantically distinct ones (Theorem 5.6).

A margin-capacity analysis shows heavy-tailed surrogates (Polynomial Hinge family, cubic-or-higher polynomial tail decay) give superior H-consistency guarantees in capacity-bounded regimes compared to DPO's logistic loss (linear tail decay, ρ ≈ 1 - K/γ) and IPO's squared hinge loss (quadratic decay) (Margin-Capacity Profile analysis).

The resulting SA-DPO algorithm, using loss ℒ = -E[log σ(β·w·Δh - τ·Δ(y,y'))], converges smoothly on synonym stress tests where standard DPO stalls, and improves over standard DPO on ambiguous pairs in the UltraFeedback benchmark (0.700 vs. 0.650) (Experimental Validation section).

AYdeXzhyjr.text: SceneDiver's focus plan generation improves robotic manipulation success rate for Gemini 2.5-Flash from a 38.7% baseline to 46.7%, and for GPT-4o-mini from 28.7% to 34.0% (Section 4.1, Table 1).
On room navigation tasks, SceneDiver improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B base-task success rate from 32.7% to 44.0%, with gains up to 16% in specific navigation conditions (Section 4.2, Table 2).

When distilled into a lightweight VLA adapter, SceneDiver yields 9.2-9.6% improvements on long-horizon LIBERO-Plus tasks and a 9.58% gain under robot initial-state perturbations (19.91% to 29.49%), while adding only 2.64% additional inference latency (Section 4.3, Table 3).

The coarse stage constructs scene graphs via OvSGTR and performs graph reasoning to localize task-relevant sub-scenes, while the fine stage has the VLM sequentially verify sub-scenes through semantic zoom and local spatial search (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
Ablations show coarse-only planning (without fine-grained verification) fails, and the method recovers 96-98% performance under scene-graph noise with 10-50% edge drop ratios (Section 4.4, Table 4).

e78DJKtFde.text: IB-TPO achieves 44.3% overall accuracy on Qwen3-8B-Base versus 40.7% for GRPO (a 3.6-point gain), and 29.2% versus 26.3% on Qwen3-1.7B-Base (a 2.9-point gain) (Section 4, Table 1).
IB-TPO outperforms tree-search baselines TreeRL (42.0%), TreePO (41.6%), and IBRO (41.6%) on the same benchmark suite (Table 1).

The IB-Score-guided branching strategy (IBTree) generates 50% more trajectories under an equivalent token budget while achieving a 60.2% Effective Rate versus 59.8% for independent sampling with the same trajectory count (Section 4.1, Table 3).

Ablations show IBTree alone contributes +1.4% on AIME 25, the IB-TPO advantage estimation alone contributes +0.6%, and combining both yields 15.3% AIME 25 accuracy versus 15.0% when using only the global advantage term (λ=0) (Section 4.2, Table 2, Table 4).
IB-Score is defined as a fine-grained information-bottleneck metric using step-level entropy terms to guide tree branching toward nodes balancing exploration and exploitation (Section 3.2).

7boy4Ipbyn.text: Theorem 1 shows sparsity bounds layer-output variance growth as Var(r_L) ≤ Var(r_0)·∏(1+√(α_ℓρ_ℓ))^2 = O(1+αρ)^{2L}, so sparser masks (smaller ρ_ℓ) yield smaller per-layer variance growth (Section 3, Theorem 1).
Scaling depth from 12 to 32 layers without sparsity reduces the usefulness score from 0.75 to 0.53, indicating roughly 14 wasted layers out of 18 added ones (Section 2, Table 1).

Combining sparsity mechanisms (weight decay, sequence length, GQA, MoE) at depth 32 raises downstream task accuracy by 4.6 points relative to a naive dense 32-layer baseline (~40.0 to ~44.1) (Figure 1).
Using MQA (G=16) instead of MHA (G=1) improves the usefulness score from 0.81 to 0.87 (a 7% relative improvement) while reducing output variance roughly 2x (Section 3, Table 4, Figure 7).

MoE variants (e.g., MoE-7B/1B) outperform dense counterparts by over 2 perplexity points (13.82 vs 14.52) with usefulness score 0.94 vs 0.81, and dampen output variance by roughly 6x for 400M-active and 3x for 1B-active configurations (Section 3, Table 5, Figure 8).

nMS1YTjHMH.text: Theorem 1.1 proves that deciding ERM_bit for deep networks with any non-linear polynomial activation of degree at least 2 is #P-hard (Section 1.1, Theorem 1.1).

Corollary 1.2 shows that if ERM_bit for polynomial-activation networks were in NP, the polynomial hierarchy would collapse to its second level, evidencing intractability beyond NP (Section 1.1, Corollary 1.2).

Theorem 1.3 establishes that for polynomial activations, deciding a specific bit of the gradient is #P-hard and determining its sign is not in BPP under standard complexity assumptions (Section 1.1, Theorem 1.3).

Theorem 1.4 shows that for ReLU (piecewise-linear) activations, ERM_bit is NP-complete, while verifying a witness and computing the exact gradient via standard backpropagation both run in polynomial time (Section 1.1, Theorem 1.4).
The polynomial-activation hardness results are proved via reductions from straight-line program (SLP) problems (Section 3).

6l8bvRoJZN.text: MuCO decouples cyclic peptide design into three stages: SE(3) flow matching for topology-aware backbone generation, torsional flow matching with cyclic relative positional encoding for side-chain packing, and CHARMM36 force-field-based all-atom optimization (Section 3.2).

In single-sample comparisons, MuCO achieves lower predicted energy (30.2 kJ/mol) than HighFold2 (111.3 kJ/mol) and AfCycDesign (116.4 kJ/mol), closer to the ground-truth energy of -15.8 kJ/mol, despite a slightly lower success rate of 94.0% versus 98.9% and 98.4% respectively (Section 4.2, Table 1).

MuCO attains a structural diversity (Shannon entropy) of 0.69, close to the ground-truth value of 0.59, versus near-zero diversity (0.00 and 0.01) for HighFold2 and AfCycDesign (Section 4.2, Table 1).
MuCO recovers secondary structure distributions (alpha-helices/beta-sheets) with Shannon entropy of 0.88-1.01, compared to 0.00 for AlphaFold2-based baselines (Section 4.2, Figure 4, Table 6).
MuCO's amortized per-sample runtime with 100 parallel samples is 41ms versus 4236ms for AfCycDesign, over 100x faster (Section 4.3, Table 2).

The training set is derived from the CPSea-derived benchmark with about 75,000 filtered cyclic peptides (length 8-16), evaluated on CPTrans (6,590), CPBind (3,194), CPCore (263), and CPSea-PDB (85 high-confidence structures) test subsets across head-to-tail, disulfide, and isopeptide cyclization modes (Appendix C).

7X5GcRLHhx.text: TimeSAE attains the best mean faithfulness rank of 1.7 across classification and regression tasks, versus 3.1 for TimeX++, 2.4 for StartGrad, and 2.3 for CounTS (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On the ETTh1→ETTh2 out-of-distribution transfer setting, TimeSAE achieves lower KL divergence (0.245 vs 0.265) and lower MMD distance (0.089 vs 0.101) than TimeX++, while also scoring higher AUPRC (0.641 vs 0.622) and higher faithfulness (2.09 vs 1.70) (Table 2, Section 4.2).
Theorem 1 proves that order-faithfulness is preserved under bounded approximation error, so the causal ordering of concept effects persists in approximate counterfactuals (Theorem 1, Section 3.2).

An ablation removing the counterfactual loss term drops the faithfulness score from about 2.0-2.1 down to 1.6-1.8, showing the counterfactual objective is necessary for faithful explanations (Figure 5(b), Section 4.2).
JumpReLU sparsity outperforms TopK sparsity across all L0 sparsity levels and avoids the 'dead concepts' failure mode that TopK exhibits near 0% activation (Figure 6, Section 4.2).

TimeSAE is evaluated on eight datasets including two synthetic sets (FreqShapes, SeqComb-UV) and real-world ECG, ETTh1, ETTh2, PAM, and a new EliteLJ elite long-jump skeleton dataset with 386 samples (Table 4, Appendix B.1).

q7al5Vwgos.text: MIND achieves 92.29% accuracy on ScienceQA, a 6.98-point improvement over the Multimodal-CoT baseline's 85.31% (Table 1).
On A-OKVQA, MIND reaches 70.6% accuracy, a 20.0-point improvement over Multimodal-CoT's 50.6% (Table 2).
On M3CoT, MIND's base model scores 57.38% (12.53 points over Multimodal-CoT) and its large model scores 61.56% (12.83 points over Multimodal-CoT) (Table 3).
The RAD paradigm generates diverse positive rationales and semantically inverted negative rationales via batch-wise prompting, expanding the training rationale set by 500x-1000x (Section 3.2).

The P2CL two-phase progressive correction learning strategy first emphasizes multi-rationale positive learning via maximum likelihood, then adds active logic discrimination using positive-negative rationale pairs in a second phase (Section 3.3).

An ablation shows P2CL alone contributes a 1.86-point gain and MCA contrastive optimization alone contributes 0.07 points, while combining both yields a 2.00-point total improvement, indicating complementary effects (Table 4).

TZ5Kj41ML9.text: The paper proposes Attribution-Aware Grounded Accuracy (AwGA), a unified metric computing (1/N) times the sum over examples of the indicator that the predicted answer is correct multiplied by the mIoU between the top-K attributed slots and ground-truth segmentation masks, jointly scoring 'what' and 'where' (Section on AwGA metric).

Instruction-tuned VLMs are built by replacing the standard vision encoder with object-centric model slots inside a LLaVA-style two-stage pipeline: 558K-sample connector pretraining followed by 665K-sample instruction tuning (Section on VLM-Based Evaluation Framework).

Despite using only 7 object-centric vision tokens versus DINOv2's 196 tokens, the proposed mFRESA baseline remains competitive with DINOv2 on most standard perception benchmarks including GQA, VQAv2, POPE, MME, and MM-Vet (Table 2).
FT-DINOSAUR underperforms on downstream VQA benchmarks despite achieving the leading object discovery scores among compared object-centric models (Table 2).

Object discovery quality metrics show a negative correlation (Spearman's rho = -0.2) with downstream VQA usefulness, indicating object discovery scores alone are a poor proxy for representation usefulness (Table 4).

Enhanced GQA (eGQA), a new grounding benchmark introduced in the paper, contains 10,000 questions paired with segmentation masks for evaluating localization accuracy jointly with reasoning (Section on Benchmarks/Grounding).

vbty65Z76C.text: Theorem 1 shows any online covering algorithm with competitive ratio rho(k, dot) can be converted into a learning-augmented algorithm with competitive ratio O(rho(eta, dot)), where eta is the prediction error defined as eta := min(|X|, |X symmetric-difference X-hat|) (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows that given a polynomial-time (alpha, gamma)-decomposition, the ICE algorithm achieves competitive ratio O(alpha)*rho(eta, dot) + O(alpha * log^{-1}(gamma/(gamma-1)) * log k) (Theorem 2, Theorem 4).

For set cover and non-metric facility location, Theorem 5 gives a polynomial-time competitive ratio of O(log eta * log|S| + log k), improving on the classical O(log k) bound when prediction error eta is small, with a matching hardness lower bound ruling out O(log eta * log|S|) in polynomial time (Section 3.1, Theorem 5).
For metric facility location, Theorem 10 achieves competitive ratio O(log eta / log log eta), improving the classical O(log k / log log k) bound (Section 3.3, Theorem 10).

For Steiner tree, Theorem 12 achieves competitive ratio O(log eta), and for group Steiner tree/forest the classical O(log^7 k log^5 |V|) bound becomes O(log^7 eta log^5 |V|) under the learning-augmented framework (Section 3.3/3.4, Theorem 12).

SDJWCc0Cml.text: DualGraph reaches a 53.08 RACE score on DeepResearch Bench when paired with GPT-5 (Section on Performance Metrics/Results).

DualGraph separates knowledge exploration from outline structure using two components: an Outline Graph (OG) that manages organizational structure and a Knowledge Graph (KG) that preserves fine-grained semantic information (Section on Core Contribution).
This separation is designed to let the agent identify knowledge gaps and conduct more targeted exploration than single-graph or outline-only baselines (Section on Core Contribution).
DualGraph is evaluated across three benchmarks for open-ended deep research: DeepResearch Bench, DeepResearchGym, and DeepConsult (Section on Benchmarks Referenced).

Ablation studies confirm that both the Outline Graph and Knowledge Graph components are individually necessary, since removing either degrades report quality relative to the full DualGraph system (Section on Validation Approach/Ablations).

nxgmp4aWer.text: UB-SMoE combines Dynamic Modulated Routing (DMR), which adjusts expert selection using learnable modulation parameters based on global utilization statistics, with a Universal Pseudo-Gradient (PG) mechanism that reconstructs learning signals for non-activated experts via server-computed pseudo-gradients scaled by ρc = √(K̄/Kc) (Section 4, Equations 10-16).
UB-SMoE achieves up to 45% computational reduction on low-resource clients while heterogeneous LoRA-rank baselines achieve only about 5% reduction (Section 1/Abstract, Figure 3).
On the Commonsense-15K benchmark, UB-SMoE improves over the A3SMoE baseline by 8.5% at the lowest client budget tier β1 and by 53.7% at the highest budget tier β4 (Table 4).
UB-SMoE improves 10.5% over the A3SMoE baseline on OLMoE-1B-7B and 29.1% over FlexLoRA on OLMo-1B (Table 2, Table 3).

Theorem 4.1 establishes a convergence guarantee under heterogeneous sparsity that identifies an irreducible bias error floor B_SMoE = 2||B(Θ*)||²/μ' scaling inversely with per-client expert budget Kc (Theorem 4.1).
Expert utilization entropy analysis shows UB-SMoE reaches H ≈ 6.5 with lower variance than baselines across all 16 SMoE layers (Figure 2).

UpA00uD6Ek.text: Lemma 4.1 shows the implicit policy Jacobian equals Jπ(s) = −[∇²ₐₐQ]⁻¹∇²ₛₐQ, meaning action sensitivity to state perturbations is governed by the ratio of the Q-function's mixed state-action partial derivative to its action-space curvature (Lemma 4.1).

Proposition 4.2 bounds the policy's Lipschitz constant by L ≤ M/μ, where M is the magnitude of mixed partial derivatives ∇²ₛₐQ and μ is the action-Hessian conditioning ∇²ₐₐQ, showing that reducing gradient variance alone is insufficient if curvature also vanishes (Proposition 4.2).

PAVE regularizes the critic via three losses: Mixed-Partial Regularization (MPR) using finite differences on ∇ₐQ, Vector Field Consistency (VFC) enforcing temporal alignment of ∇ₐQ along trajectories, and Curvature Preservation (Curv) via a Hutchinson's-estimator hinge penalty on v^T∇²ₐₐQv (Section 4, loss definitions).
In the TD3 setting on Walker2d, PAVE attains a return of 5563 with the best smoothness score of 1.272 among compared methods (Table 1).
In the SAC setting, PAVE achieves 5706 return on Ant and 4954 return on Walker while maintaining superior stability (Table 2).
Under a 10x increase in action noise, PAVE maintains near-identical performance (~5570 return) whereas baseline methods degrade substantially (Table 3).

LnDNFS8Lea.text: MMtSBM extends the Iterative Markovian Fitting algorithm underlying Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge Matching to multiple marginals using a novel factorized fitting scheme, reducing the restrictive assumptions of prior single-bridge approaches (abstract only).

MMtSBM achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world transcriptomic trajectory inference data in 100 dimensions, reconstructing continuous-time dynamics from unpaired static snapshots (abstract only).

MMtSBM is demonstrated on high-dimensional image settings, recovering couplings and dynamics from unpaired data in a regime not previously handled by multi-marginal Schrödinger bridge methods (abstract only).
MMtSBM retains theoretical convergence properties verified on toy examples while scaling empirically to more than two marginal distributions (abstract only).

WbVcAbHsCZ.text: On ARC-AGI, CogVideoX1.5-5B (a video diffusion model) achieves 16.75% two-attempt accuracy versus 8.00% for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (a comparably sized language model) (Table 1).

On ConceptARC, video diffusion models show stronger competency than language models on spatial-reasoning concept categories such as 'Above and Below,' 'Center,' and 'Count,' while language models retain an edge on symbol-heavy categories (Figure 1).

Video diffusion models outperform language models on 4 of 5 tested visual games (e.g., Sudoku, Hitori), with the language model advantage limited to Chess Mate-in-1, attributed to its textual training corpus dominance (Figure 4).

In shortest-path route planning, video diffusion models achieve up to a tenfold reduction in data requirements in low-sample regimes, reaching a 94% path success rate at 300 training samples versus 53% for the language model (Figure 5, Table 2).

In 2D Life-like cellular automata prediction, video diffusion models require far fewer training examples than language models to reach a matched accuracy threshold, with the advantage growing on Langton's Ant as prediction horizon lengthens (Figures 7, 9, 10).

Both video diffusion models and language models are adapted for these tasks using LoRA modules with frozen backbones, isolating the effect of pretraining modality from fine-tuning capacity (Sections 3.2-3.3).

YQPbZ1foKT.text: MoMa QL replaces diffusion-based action sampling with a Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) moment-matching objective that aligns all statistical moments between the learned and target action distributions (Section on Actor Loss, Eq. 10).
On D4RL Gym locomotion tasks, MoMa QL achieves an average score of 95.5, a roughly 1.09x improvement over Diffusion-QL's 87.9 (Table 2).
On D4RL Kitchen tasks, MoMa QL scores 73.1 versus 69.0 for Diffusion-QL, and on Adroit manipulation tasks it scores 56.7, competitive with ReBRAC's 55.4 (Table 2).
In behavior cloning, MoMa QL attains an overall average score of 89.8, representing relative improvements of 1.73x over vanilla BC (51.9) and 1.18x over Diffusion-BC (76.3) (Table 1).
MoMa QL improves offline-to-online transfer on medium-replay datasets, raising halfcheetah-medium-replay from 63.3 to 80.9 (about 28%) and walker2d-medium-replay from 104.3 to 117.9 (Table 3).
MoMa QL is approximately 6x faster than Diffusion-BC and 1.5x faster than Consistency-AC, with optimal performance saturating at only N=2 sampling steps (Figure 4).

sfWgUkh5Zj.text: SpecBench spans 5 scenarios (Biochemical Procedure Instruction, Child-Oriented Storytelling, Code Development & Secure Operation, Personal Health Education, and Travel Itinerary Planning), 103 specifications, and 1,500 prompts (300 per scenario, split into 200 unsafe and 100 safe) (Section 3).
Baseline evaluation of 33 models on SpecBench shows GPT-5-chat scoring highest at 82.14% Specification Alignment Rate (SAR), while most models score below 65% (Table 1, Section 5.2).
Align3 is a three-step test-time deliberation method—Behavior Optimization, Safety-Guided Refinement, and Holistic Specification Audit—applied within a single reasoning chain (Section 6).
On Qwen3-14B, Align3 improves SAR from 51.03% to 62.92% (an 11.89 percentage-point gain) while adding roughly 1,800 tokens of overhead per sample (Table 2, Section 6).
Align3 outperforms multi-pass test-time deliberation baselines including Best-of-N, Self-Refine, and Test-time Preference Optimization (TPO) (Table 2, Section 6).
Human evaluation used to validate SAR judgments reports a Cohen's Kappa of 0.84 inter-rater agreement (Appendix D).

sfVahQ4EWP.text: Vision-language models (Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-32B) are fine-tuned via QLoRA (rank 16) using GRPO versus SFT on physics-stability tasks generated in the ThreeDWorld simulator with 256x256 RGB images of block towers (Section 4).

Qwen3-VL-8B trained with GRPO reaches 0.969 accuracy on the binary stability judgment task and near-ceiling reward (19.999) on the x-only displacement task within its fine-tuning task, with no consistent advantage of GRPO over SFT (Figure 2, Table A.2).

Models fine-tuned on one task (e.g., top-block towers) generalize poorly to a related task with the same visual statistics and physical principles (e.g., side-block towers), showing limited transfer (Section 4.2).
On real-image evaluation (using stimuli from Lerer et al. 2016), the best-performing fine-tuned models achieve only about 0.6 accuracy, well below human baseline performance (Figure 3).

Despite poor behavioral generalization, physical properties such as stability and block offset remain highly decodable from model activations, indicating models learn non-general shortcuts rather than robust physical intuitions (Section 5).

99z6N9kXR6.text: CACR combines Visual-Language Pre-training based Candidate Selection (VBCS) to generate K candidate segments with a GRPO-optimized temporal reasoning module enhanced by a rejection reward mechanism (Section 3.2.1-3.2.3).
The composite reward function R_total = R_fmt + (1-alpha)*R_IoU + alpha*R_rej uses alpha=0.8 to emphasize rejection decisions during policy optimization (Equation 1).

CACR achieves state-of-the-art mIoU across six temporal answer grounding benchmarks: 72.11% on VehicleVQA, 59.65% on MedVidQA, 45.37% on CMIVQA, 43.65% on TutorialVQA, 41.06% on COIN, and 40.19% on CrossTask (Table 2).
Cumulative maximum IoU from VBCS candidate selection increases monotonically with K but shows diminishing returns beyond K=5, motivating the choice of K=5 candidates (Table 5).
VBCS candidate ranking validity is confirmed by independent IoU scores declining predictably from Top-1 to Top-9 ranked candidates across all six datasets (Table 4).

vaApZm6MKM.text: The paper introduces a family of Excess Risk of the Target Coverage (ERT) metrics—L1-ERT, L2-ERT, and KL-ERT—for evaluating conditional coverage in conformal prediction, built on the principle that no classifier can outperform a constant 1-alpha predictor under perfect conditional coverage (Table 1, Section 3.1).

Using LightGBM as the underlying classifier for L1-ERT achieves 68.4% relative statistical power (relative to maximum), compared to only 38.3% for the PartitionWise classifier underlying CovGap (Table 2, Section 4.1).

In synthetic experiments, group-based metrics like CovGap remain unreliable and unaligned with their theoretical values even at 5,000 test points, whereas ERT metrics such as L1-ERT converge with far fewer samples (Figure 4, Section 4.2).

The metrics decompose conditional coverage error into asymmetric components ell_plus-ERT and ell_minus-ERT, separating unnecessary conservatism (over-coverage) from excessive aggressiveness (under-coverage) (Section 3.3).

Classification experiments report divergent KL_plus-ERT and KL_minus-ERT values across conformal prediction methods, demonstrating the over/under-coverage decomposition in practice (Table 4, Section 4.3.2).
Algorithm 1 estimates the ERT metrics from finite samples using k-fold cross-validation to avoid overfitting the classifier used in the estimation (Algorithm 1).

PBpGnHRU2O.text: TuRBO-ENN replaces the Gaussian Process surrogate in TuRBO with Epistemic Nearest Neighbors (ENN), a K-nearest-neighbor estimator combining predictions via precision-weighted averaging (Equation 2).

ENN queries scale as O(N) versus O(N^2) for modern GP implementations and O(N^3) for naive GP implementations, as shown empirically in proposal-time-versus-observations plots across dimensions (Figure 1).
