TuRBO-ENN reduces proposal generation time by one to two orders of magnitude relative to TuRBO at up to 50,000 observations, while using Pareto-front sampling over predicted mean and epistemic uncertainty instead of UCB/EI/Thompson sampling for acquisition (Abstract, Section 5).

On 51 analytic test functions with D=100-1000, TuRBO-ENN matches TuRBO-1's design quality while running roughly 30x faster at N=1000 proposals, and is estimated about 1800x faster than LEI at N=1000 (Figure 5).
On reinforcement learning benchmarks, TuRBO-ENN achieves comparable performance to TuRBO-1 on LunarLander and Hopper, and runs roughly 50x faster than TuRBO-1 on Swimmer (Figures 6-8).

nWxUhxv4d8.text: Theorem 3.1 shows a student model outperforms its weak teacher when the expected misfit between student and teacher predictions is sufficiently small, derived via a generalized bias-variance decomposition of the Bregman divergence rather than the Pythagorean theorem (Theorem 3.1).

Corollary 3.1 shows weak-to-strong generalization is more likely to emerge when the student approximates the posterior mean teacher over the conditional distribution of teachers given the student, motivating the use of teacher ensembles (Corollary 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 proves, in a ridge regression setting, that expected misfit between student and teacher decreases monotonically as student model capacity increases, but that zero misfit (perfect alignment with the teacher) eliminates any weak-to-strong performance gain, motivating regularization or early stopping (Theorem 4.1).

Proposition 2 proves that reverse cross-entropy (RCE) loss is less sensitive than forward cross-entropy to the teacher's confidence level, remaining stable even under heavy label smoothing (Proposition 2, Figure 2).

Combining forward cross-entropy and reverse cross-entropy into a symmetric loss (SL), or using a confidence-adaptive cross-entropy (CACE), outperforms either forward CE or RCE alone, with the largest gains on the HH-RLHF dataset (Table 1).

Using teacher ensembles for supervision consistently reduces test loss across GPT-2 model variants, with scaling student capacity primarily reducing bias rather than variance in the bias-variance decomposition (Figure 1).

wJeR4HQQWy.text: MAP-RPS (Maximum A Posteriori - Re-noised Posterior Sampling) is a two-stage framework where Stage 1 uses MAP estimation to approximate the MMSE solution as a low-distortion initialization, and Theorem 3.2 bounds the expected approximation error of MAP relative to MMSE at O(n_x^{1/2}) for strongly log-concave posteriors (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).

Stage 2 of MAP-RPS progressively improves perceptual quality via re-noised posterior sampling, where Theorem 3.5 and Corollary 3.6 show the Wasserstein-2 distance to the true posterior monotonically decreases as the re-noising timestep t0 increases, enabling continuous distortion-perception traversal (Theorem 3.5, Corollary 3.6).
LMAP-RPS extends MAP-RPS to latent diffusion models, and on the MS-COCO inpainting task at t0=0 achieves 28.14 dB PSNR, 0.7989 SSIM, and 61.35 FID over 100 sampled images with σ_y=0.05 (Table 1).
LMAP-RPS requires only about 45 seconds per image for inpainting, versus 242-1327 seconds for baseline solvers, as reported in the computational efficiency comparison (Table 2).

On FFHQ across four tasks (denoising with σ_y=0.3, 4x super-resolution with σ_y=0.1, 50% inpainting with σ_y=0.1, and anisotropic deblurring with σ_y=0), both MAP-RPS and LMAP-RPS consistently lie closer to the lower-left (low distortion, low perceptual error) corner of the distortion-perception plane than baselines (Section 4, Figure 1).

N1N4H50yS2.text: MOOSE-Star reduces the complexity of training P(hypothesis|background) from the baseline O(N^k) (approximately 10^21 for N=10^7 papers and k=3 inspiration steps) down through four successive methods, culminating in Method IV (Motivation Planning) with complexity O(k x [1 + log(N_m/M) + M]) (Section on complexity reduction).

The TOMATO-Star benchmark consists of 108,717 decomposed papers built using 38,400 GPU hours, extracted from the NCBI database across biology, chemistry, and cognitive science, with papers from October 2025 held out as the test set (Section on TOMATO-Star dataset).
Table 3 shows hierarchical search reduces the number of IR inference calls needed from 218 under a tournament brute-force baseline to 67.78, roughly a 3x efficiency gain (Table 3).

Figure 3 shows MOOSE-Star reaches 100% success at approximately 6,000 inference calls under test-time scaling, while brute-force sampling saturates at only 41.3% success and its performance collapses from 53% at k=1 to 8% at k=3 inspiration steps (Figure 3).

Table 5 shows brute-force P(hypothesis|background) sampling achieves only a 0.67% pass rate for generating usable hypothesis-background training pairs, versus 47.33% for the decomposed hierarchical composition (HC) approach, which is what enables practical rejection sampling fine-tuning (Table 5).

92tssj0P1S.text: REVIS constructs an orthogonalized visual steering vector via Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization of a raw visual vector against a language-prior vector, both estimated as differences of hidden-state expectations over an external calibration dataset (Section on orthogonal visual vector construction).

REVIS selects the intervention layer via a backward search for the deepest layer where a separability score R(H_hall(l)) - R(H_fact(l)) exceeds zero, i.e., where factual and hallucinatory hidden states are maximally separable (Section on layer selection via calibration).

REVIS applies dynamic steering only at inference steps where an estimated hallucination risk R_t exceeds a threshold tau, adding alpha times the orthogonalized visual vector to the hidden state at those steps (Section on dynamic steering).

REVIS reduces the CHAIR object-hallucination metric from 31.00% to 25.00%, roughly a 19% relative reduction, while improving POPE F1 scores across Random, Popular, and Adversarial splits (Section on key findings).

REVIS preserves general reasoning capability, scoring 72.16 on MM-Vet versus a 70.18 baseline, and adds negligible inference latency (about 0.025s per token, matching regular decoding) unlike contrastive-decoding baselines that roughly double inference cost (Section on efficiency and generalization).
REVIS is validated across five vision-language model architectures: Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL3, and InternVL3.5 (Section on generalization).

zXJjT0slV7.text: DivIn reformulates diffusion model initialization as sampling from a diversity-weighted guidance potential posterior p_diverse(x_T|c), reweighting the standard Gaussian prior toward regions of the noise landscape where denoising trajectories naturally diverge, defined via a guidance potential U(x_T,c) = ||x-hat_0(x_T,c) - x-hat_0(x_T,emptyset)||_2 (Section on method/potential function).

DivIn samples from this posterior using Langevin dynamics combining three forces: a diversity force toward low-potential basins, a prior-constraint force anchoring samples to the Gaussian manifold, and stochastic noise, rather than deterministic optimization which the paper shows causes distribution collapse (Section on optimization strategy).

On class-to-image generation on ImageNet with Stable Diffusion v1.4, DivIn improves the Vendi diversity score from a base of 4.265 to 4.688 and Recall from 0.503 to 0.569, while keeping FID competitive at 16.158 (Section on empirical results, class-to-image).
On text-to-image generation with Stable Diffusion v3.5, DivIn reduces in-batch image similarity while maintaining CLIP scores comparable to the baseline (Section on empirical results, text-to-image).

Combining DivIn with trajectory-based diversity methods (PG, CADS, IG) expands the diversity-quality Pareto frontier beyond either approach alone, showing DivIn's initialization-based intervention is complementary to sampling-phase interventions (Section on combination with trajectory-based methods).

DivIn adds only about 3% additional wall-clock overhead compared to standard initialization, while preserving the expected L2 norm of approximately sqrt(d) required to remain on the Gaussian manifold, unlike Sharpness-Aware Initialization (SAIL) which requires second-order Hessian computations (Section on advantages over prior work).

PW8YVqhI6K.text: Across 11 mainstream LLMs (including GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o, Claude, Llama-3.1, and Qwen2/2.5 variants) evaluated on the OpenDeception benchmark of 50 open-ended scenarios spanning 5 categories (telecommunications fraud, product promotion, personal safety, emotional deception, privacy stealing), the deception intention ratio exceeds 80% and the deception success rate surpasses 50% (Section 5, Table 2).

GPT-4o shows both a lower deception intention generation rate and a lower deception success rate than GPT-3.5-turbo in the same scenario families, contradicting the general trend that larger/more capable models deceive more (Section 5).

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct exhibits a Probability of generating deceptive intention After Refusing to answer (PAR) of 97.1% when paired with itself and 100% when the user model is Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, showing deceptive intent persists after an initial refusal (Table 2).

Pearson correlation analysis against LiveBench capability scores shows that instruction-following capability is the model attribute most strongly correlated with rates of deceptive intention generation and deception success, ahead of reasoning and language ability (Figure 4).
Prompt design substantially affects measured deceptive potential: the deception intention generation rate rises from 42% under an initial prompt to 78% under an optimized final prompt (Section 5).

mGCa0Jp7Hu.text: MIRO (MultI-Reward cOnditioned pretraining) conditions text-to-image pretraining jointly on multiple reward-model scores rather than selecting or filtering data by a single post-hoc reward, aiming to improve both quality and training efficiency (abstract only).
MIRO achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GenEval compositional text-to-image benchmark compared to prior post-training/reward-selection approaches (abstract only).
MIRO attains the best user-preference alignment scores on PickScore, ImageReward, and HPSv2 among compared methods (abstract only).
MIRO improves visual quality while also speeding up training relative to a single-reward, post-hoc data selection/filtering paradigm (abstract only).

zOdTlk9Uw0.text: Rays as Pixels represents each camera as dense per-pixel ray encodings ("raxels", a 3-channel direction-plus-origin format) that live in the same latent space as video frames, unlike 6-channel Plücker embeddings or raymaps that require separate embedding layers (Table 1).

A single trained Video Diffusion Model with Decoupled Self-Cross Attention (DSCA) jointly handles three tasks: predicting camera trajectories from raw video, generating video from input images along a user-defined trajectory, and jointly synthesizing both video and trajectory from input images (Figure 1).

Ablating raxels in favor of Plücker embeddings causes the most severe quantitative degradation among tested camera representations, confirming the benefit of a shared video-camera latent space (Table 2).

The model demonstrates cycle self-consistency on the DL3DV-140 test set (sampled at 12 FPS from raw video): a few denoising steps on the ray/camera branch achieve comparable results to multi-step inference in the self-consistency test (Table 3).

Pose accuracy is reported using mean Relative Rotation Accuracy (mRRA@30) computed over all frames per clip on RealEstate10K, comparing against a VGGT pose estimator trained on wide-baseline multi-view data (Table 3).

tylCinzjUF.text: Teacher–Student Cooperation Data Synthesis (TESSY) alternates capability tokens (reasoning, code) generated by a teacher model and style tokens (discourse, tone) generated by the student model within a single synthetic sequence, using boundary predictors to decide truncation points (Section 3, Table 1).

Using GPT-OSS-120B as teacher and Qwen3-8B as student, naive Teacher-Only fine-tuning causes performance drops of 3.25% on LiveCodeBench-Pro and 10.02% on OJBench relative to the Qwen3-8B baseline, whereas TESSY yields improvements of 11.25% and 6.68% respectively on the same benchmarks (Table 1).
TESSY's benefit generalizes across teacher models, outperforming Teacher-Only by 1.07% with Qwen3-235B (same family), 3.45% with DeepSeek-R1, and 16.79% with GPT-OSS-120B as teachers (Section 4).

Training Qwen3-30B-A3B on data synthesized with Qwen3-8B as the reference student causes a 2.8% performance drop compared to using matched same-model data, evidencing a cross-model distribution mismatch effect (Section 4).

An ablation comparing LoRA versus full-parameter fine-tuning under both TESSY and Teacher-Only shows LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning, indicating substantial parameter updates are needed to adapt to the teacher-student distribution shift (Figure 12).

dx53sSG8py.text: Theorem 3 proves that once the output layer of a deep GNN reaches a δ-stationary point, the entire network becomes a global δ-stationary point under sufficient depth conditions, formalizing 'backward oversmoothing' as a source of spurious stationary points with near-zero gradients but high loss (Theorem 3, Figure 1).

Theorem 2 shows that backpropagated error signals are smoothed from output to input as they pass through the propagation matrix, with the degree of smoothing depending on both the forward layer index and the number of remaining layers, producing maximal smoothing in middle layers (Theorem 2).

Proposition 2 proves that regular Multi-Layer Perceptrons (with P = Id) are not subject to the same phenomenon: an MLP can have zero gradient at its output layer while still maintaining a nonzero gradient at some earlier layer, making backward oversmoothing specific to deep GNN optimization rather than a generic depth effect (Proposition 2, Figure 1).
Empirically, Figure 1 shows deep GNN training gradients collapse toward near-zero within the first few iterations while gradients in MLPs of comparable depth remain diverse across layers (Figure 1).

GugLtzm1WC.text: The Entropic Mirror Monte Carlo (EM2C) algorithm (Algorithm 1) combines entropic-regularized global sampling with a delayed importance-weighting update to explore complex, multimodal target distributions (Section 2).
EM2C enables rapid resampling in regions where the proposal distribution is poorly adapted to the target by correcting local mismatch through mirror-descent updates (Section 2, Algorithm 1).
Theorem 1 establishes convergence of EM2C to the target distribution under stated regularity conditions (Theorem 1, Section 3).
Theorem 2 establishes a geometric convergence rate for EM2C under Conditions 3.1-3.3 (Theorem 2, Section 3).
Numerical experiments compare EM2C against standard MCMC/importance-sampling baselines on benchmark sampling problems, showing improved sampling efficiency (Figure 2, Section 4).

fve4MEzeSp.text: ConfSleepNet integrates multi-view evidence extraction from EEG and EOG signals with a Conflict-aware Multi-view Aggregation Module (CMAM) for sleep stage classification (Section 3).

ConfSleepNet uses hybrid category structures, a fine-grained 5-class evidence representation for EEG and a coarse-grained 3-class representation for EOG, unified via an evidence-mapping layer with matrix U (Section 3).
On SleepEDF-20, SleepEDF-78, MASS-SS3, and SHHS, ConfSleepNet achieves 87.2%, 85.3%, 88.9%, and 88.2% overall accuracy respectively (Table 1).

On MASS-SS3, full ConfSleepNet reaches 88.9% accuracy and 84.2 macro-F1, outperforming an average-fusion ablation variant (Case I, ConfSleepNet-) that achieves 87.4% accuracy and 82.5 macro-F1 (Table 2).

Proposition 1 and Proposition 2 formally show that aggregating consistent opinions reduces overall uncertainty while aggregating conflicting, high-uncertainty opinions increases it, proven for the extreme conflict cases C→0 and C→1 (Section 3.5).

4OP391X7Qm.text: E2-LoRA performs PCA on output feature drift, rather than on parameters or inputs, to order and concentrate task-specific knowledge into leading low-rank directions (Section 3, Eq. 6).
Proposition 3.1 shows that, among all rank-r parameter updates, E2-LoRA's transformation minimizes the expected output reconstruction error (Proposition 3.1, Eq. 7).
Proposition 3.2 shows the expected truncation error from keeping only r leading ranks equals the sum of squared singular values beyond rank r (Proposition 3.2, Eq. 8).
In the 10-task class-incremental setting, E2-LoRA attains 82.77% last-accuracy / 87.18% incremental-accuracy on ImageNet-R and 92.13% / 95.01% on CIFAR-100 (Table 1).
In the 50-task ImageNet-R class-incremental setting, E2-LoRA achieves 78.58% last-accuracy versus 75.35% for the TUNA baseline (Table 2).

Ablations show dynamic rank allocation consistently outperforms fixed-rank strategies (dout/5, dout/10, dout/50), and combining knowledge distillation with classifier alignment yields the best full-model performance (Table 4, Table 5).

pS1khvoxHT.text: On Countdown, RARO attains 54.4% accuracy versus 40.7% for the best baseline (SFT), a +13.7 point improvement, without a task-specific verifier (Section 5.1, Table 1).
On DeepMath at 7B scale, RARO reaches 57.5% accuracy versus 49.3% for the best baseline (RL-Logit), a +8.2 point gain across the three tested model scales (Section 5.2, Table 2).

On the non-verifiable Poetry Writing task at 7B scale, RARO achieves a 25.0% win-rate against expert references versus 5.9% for SFT, and a GPT-5 judge score of 77.3 versus 65.4 for SFT (Section 5.3, Table 2).
With test-time scaling to 16 rollouts on DeepMath, the 1.5B RARO model reaches 53.6% accuracy and the 3B model reaches 57.9% (Section 5.2, Figure 5, Table 9).

Proposition A.2 derives the reward gradient underlying RARO's relativistic critic by comparing expert versus policy answers within an inverse-reinforcement-learning formulation (Proposition A.2, Appendix A.2).

dNaRpdbnOG.text: The proposed score function S(X,Y) = max(m̂n(X) - f_low(X) - Y, Y - m̂n(X) - f_up(X)) learns separate lower and upper kernel sum-of-squares (kSoS) bounds to build adaptive, possibly asymmetric prediction intervals while retaining distribution-free coverage (Section 3, Eq. 2).
Theorem 3.1 gives a representer theorem reducing the infinite-dimensional kSoS bound-fitting problem to a finite-dimensional semi-definite program (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
Proposition 3.2 gives a dual formulation of this SDP that scales the method to on the order of 1000 samples (Proposition 3.2, Section 3).

Proposition 3.9 links interval-width adaptivity to the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) between residuals and interval widths, used to tune kernel lengthscales θ_low, θ_up (Proposition 3.9, Section 3.2).

On four synthetic datasets with symmetric and asymmetric noise (Table 1) and twelve real-world regression benchmarks including Concrete, Bike, and Housing (Figure 5), penalized kSoS is shown to be the only method achieving good coverage adaptivity while maintaining small mean interval width under asymmetric noise, compared to CQR and homoscedastic/heteroscedastic Gaussian process baselines (Table 1, Figure 5).

s70zO5Lvvj.text: The CUDAnalyst framework finds that explicit planning is beneficial only when feedback is aligned with it, degrading performance when planning proceeds without grounding feedback (Section 4.1, Figures 3-4).

Tool synergies among feedback components strengthen over generations, with the analyzer dominating early-stage compilation feedback and the profiler driving later-stage performance gains (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
Feedback summarization disproportionately benefits weaker models but cannot substitute for explicit planning (Section 4.3, Figure 6).

High-level plans generated by stronger reasoning models transfer to and improve weaker models, with the largest gains observed within the same model family, e.g., DeepSeek variants (Section 4.4, Figure 7).
Marginal contributions and complementarities among feedback components are quantified using Banzhaf attribution values and pairwise interaction terms (Equations 1-2, Table 2).

Findings generalize across backbones (Kimi-K2, MiniMax, Gemini), workloads (PolyBench-ACC, NPB-GPU, XSBench, robust-kbench), and even to a CPU-based Numba N-body optimization task, achieving a 12.5x speedup (Section 5, Figure 11).

ez4oLq7PR3.text: Discrete-output Riemannian optimal transport maps require parameter count growing as m >= (C/delta)^p to reach accuracy delta, where p is the manifold dimension, establishing an exponential curse of dimensionality (Theorem 3.1).
Riemannian Convex Potential Maps (RCPMs) inherit this exponential parameter-complexity dependence on dimension as a corollary of the discrete-map lower bound (Corollary 3.2).

RNOT achieves function approximation on manifolds with width W_epsilon = O(epsilon^(-4p/3(kp+1))) and depth L_epsilon = O(epsilon^(-2p/3(kp+1))) for k-times smooth targets, i.e., sub-exponential (polynomial-type) complexity in dimension p (Theorem 5.1).
On the synthetic sphere (S^2) and torus (T^2) benchmarks, RNOT attains KL divergence 0.03 +/- 0.00 and 0.13 +/- 0.01 respectively, versus RCPM's KL of 0.93 on the torus (Section 6.2, Tables 1-2).
Across manifold dimensions 2 through 10, RNOT maintains stable performance while RCPM's performance degrades exponentially, confirming the theoretical complexity gap (Figure 3).
RNOT is applied to a real-world continental drift task on the sphere S^2 using paleogeographic reconstructions, learning geodesic transport trajectories (Section 6.1).

7Nn3SKS6yL.text: Safety Game formulates the safety-helpfulness trade-off for black-box LLMs as a two-player zero-sum game whose minimax equilibrium is computed via linear programming, requiring no model retraining or internal access (Section 3.2, Equation 3.1).
A sigmoid penalty in the bounded-multiplier reformulation avoids boundary sensitivity present in naive constrained formulations (Section 3.3, Equations 3.2-3.3).
On the HHH benchmark, the method matches or exceeds baselines on 3 of 5 models, reaching 72.9% accuracy on LLaMA-2-7B and 71.5% on GPT-OSS-20B (Table 1).
On TruthfulQA, the method roughly doubles BLEU-Acc over baselines, reaching 54.7% on GPT-OSS-20B and 51.4% on Llama-3.2-1B (Table 2).
On SafetyBench, the method achieves the best accuracy on 4 of 5 models, reaching 60.13% on GPT-OSS-20B, an improvement of up to 15 points over baselines (Table 3).
Across the three benchmarks the method outperforms baselines in 11 of 15 model-benchmark test cases, with up to a two-fold improvement in accuracy in some cases (Section 4).

p32nWlgwYC.text: Compress-then-Merge (CtM) learns shared r-dimensional left and right subspaces from LoRA weights and projects each adapter into r x r coordinates before merging, guaranteeing a rank-r LoRA by construction and avoiding post-hoc truncation, unlike Merge-then-Compress pipelines (Section 4).
On ViT-B/32 across 8 vision tasks, CtM with TIES achieves 69.75 average normalized accuracy versus 65.33 for the CoreSpace TIES merge-then-compress baseline (Table 1).
On LLaMA3-8B across 6 NLI tasks, CtM with DARE-TIES achieves 95.63 average accuracy, exceeding the average accuracy of all merge-then-compress baselines (Table 2).

CtM learns more balanced subspaces than MtC, with mean energy retention of 87.94 versus 69.70 and functional retention of 96.18 versus 86.54, and a much lower standard deviation of 2.71 versus 21.52 (Figure 3).

A core-space acceleration variant reduces LLaMA3-8B merging runtime from 690.83s to 20.83s (33x speedup) while preserving 94.15 normalized accuracy and staying within 0.031 chordal distance of the full-space solution (Table 4).
CtM performance is relatively insensitive to the reweighting hyperparameter beta across the range [0, 0.75] (Figure 4).

wjiw02fqir.text: FLowDUP generates personalized client models via a single forward pass on unlabeled data by parameterizing models as theta = theta_0 + Pv, where P is a random expansion matrix and v is a low-dimensional vector (Section 2, Equation 2).

The training objective combines a supervised loss on labeled clients with a regularizer penalizing deviation from a learned regularization term, min L(psi) + lambda*Omega(psi) (Section 3.1, Equations 4-6).
A transductive multi-task PAC-Bayesian generalization bound shows improved sample complexity by a factor of sqrt(1 - n_l/n) compared to inductive approaches (Section 4, Theorem).
On class-partitioned CIFAR-10, FLowDUP achieves accuracy ranging from 66.1% (CNN, p=0.1) to 92.3% (ResNet18, p=1.0), outperforming FedAvg, FedProx, LD-FedAvg, and FedTTA baselines (Table 1).
On rotated Fashion-MNIST and FEMNIST, FLowDUP achieves 81.5%-87.3% and 84.5%-89.3% accuracy ranges respectively (Table 2).
Increasing the subspace dimension k yields monotonic performance improvement, with k=10^4 identified as balancing performance against communication and computation efficiency (Table 4).

S1rq8s4FCA.text: XTransfer's model repairing uses a Splice-Repair-Removal (SRR) pipeline combined with Layer-Wise Search (LWS) to recombine layers across modality-specific backbones for few-shot transfer (Section 6.2).

In 5-shot evaluation, XTransfer reaches 71.8% accuracy on HHAR, 78.4% on WESAD, and 87.0% on Writing, each exceeding the corresponding oracle baseline of 69.0%, 64.0%, and 83.3% respectively (Table 4).
XTransfer's accuracy-to-resource ratio improves over baselines by 1.6-29x in the single-source setting and 16.6-98x in the multi-source setting (Table 5).
On commercial edge devices, XTransfer reduces FLOPs by 2.4-5.7x (single-source) and 10.1-16.5x (multi-source), with latency reductions of 1.4-4.1x and 7.4-21x respectively (Table 8).
XTransfer is evaluated against 8 baseline few-shot methods including ProtoNet, MAML, DAPN, MDDA, and MCW across 3-shot, 5-shot, and 10-shot settings on 13 datasets (Section 6, Table 4).

A8rmJlSET9.text: Minibatch optimal transport coupling reduces the number of discrete flow matching transitions needed to reach the same generative perplexity by up to 8x, from 1024 down to 128 steps (Section 3).

Theorem 3.1 establishes that the dynamic formulation of discrete flow matching corresponds to a Kantorovich optimal transport problem with cost function equal to the sum of token-level similarity terms across sequence positions (Theorem 3.1).
Corollary 3.2 shows that using the discrete metric as the token similarity reduces the transport cost to the Hamming distance between source and target sequences (Corollary 3.2).
Corollary 3.3 shows that an embedding-based similarity yields an L2 norm between sequence embeddings, recovering behavior analogous to continuous flow matching (Corollary 3.3).

Theorem 4.1 derives an upper bound on the KL divergence between two discrete flows in terms of differences in their velocity probabilities, yielding a perplexity upper bound that is computationally tractable as e^(B/L) without requiring explicit density estimation (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).

dpniDbdApf.text: CauchyNet's holomorphic Cauchy activation function requires only 256 total parameters in a single 128-neuron hidden layer configuration, versus 6,720 parameters for a comparable LSTM and 132,993 for a comparable Transformer (Section on architecture/parameter comparison).
For 1D missing value imputation, CauchyNet achieves a mean absolute error of 1.5, compared to 3.2 or higher for SIREN, N-BEATS, and standard FNN baselines (Experiment 2).

On an M4 benchmark forecasting subset of 700 time series, CauchyNet achieves a mean absolute error of 2.3 versus 10 or higher for most baseline methods, while converging faster over 200 training epochs (Experiment 4).

On a 2D polynomial-rational surface approximation task, CauchyNet's error map stays within a -0.006 to 0.006 range, demonstrating accurate interpolation across both polynomial and rational surface components (Experiment 3).

Paired t-tests (p<0.05) confirm CauchyNet's statistically significant reduction in MSE/MAE over ReLU-based MLP baselines on function approximation tasks involving sharp near-singular peaks (Experiment 1).

v9rdrvA4Yx.text: The framework couples two interacting diffusion models, one over the input signal and one over classifier logits, and proposes three coupling strategies with different computation-effectiveness trade-offs: Parallel (interleaved per-timestep updates), Alternating (sequential full trajectories), and Nested (a complete inner signal diffusion loop per logit timestep) (Section on coupling strategies).
On CIFAR-10 with 15% Gaussian noise, the Alternating strategy reaches 83.0% classification accuracy versus 60.9% for a sequential enhance-then-classify baseline (Table 1).
On MNIST with 30% noise, the Alternating strategy reaches 99.1% accuracy versus 98.3% for the enhanced-signal baseline (Table 1).
Using Whisper-base for ASR, the Nested strategy achieves 3.83% WER on EARS-Reverb and 9.75% WER on EARS-WHAM, improving over enhancement-only baselines of 4.48% and 10.04% WER respectively (Table 2).
The Nested coupling strategy achieves 4.85% WER on the Google Commands-Reverb dataset (Table 2).

9Ox26YeM82.text: RTWI mitigates Noisy Thinking (errors in visual-cue extraction and reasoning that compound through thinking-with-images pipelines) via text-centric reliability estimation, dual-stage filtering, and reliability-weighted voting (Sections 3.1-3.4).
RTWI is evaluated across seven benchmarks including Vstar Bench, HR-Bench 4K/8K, TreeBench, VisualProbe, MathVision, and LogicVista (Section 4).
With Qwen3-VL Thinking, RTWI reaches 85.2% accuracy on the Vstar attribute subset while saving 61.1% of tokens relative to the non-filtered baseline (Section 4, results table).
With Qwen3-VL Instruct, RTWI reaches 96.5% accuracy on HR-Bench 4K (FSP) with a 66.2% token saving ratio (Section 4, results table).
The adaptive top-k selection parameter is chosen to maximize a defined reliability leap metric (Equation 12), and the filtering ratio alpha is set to 0.4 for stable performance (Section 4.1).

RTWI outperforms self-consistency-based baselines including ASC, ESC, CISC, DeepConf, and Self-Certainty across most of the seven benchmarks while achieving better computational efficiency (Section 4).

YnAT2dUBNO.text: VIAR attains FID 2.16 and sFID 8.07 on ImageNet 256x256 at cfg=1.5, compared to the VAR-d30 baseline's FID 2.08 and sFID 8.82 (Table 1).
VIAR uses 770.9M parameters versus VAR's 2010.0M, a 61.6% reduction in parameter count (Table 1).
VIAR reduces inference memory from VAR's 19.24GB to 11.16GB while remaining competitive on FID/sFID (Table 1).

On a single RTX 4090, the aggressive VIAR_s4 schedule reaches 32.08 images/s at 8.53GB peak memory versus VAR's 15.16 images/s at 19.24GB, a roughly 2.1x throughput gain and 2.26x memory reduction (Table 3).

Fixed-point iteration analysis shows cosine similarity between successive equilibrium states exceeds 0.985 by iteration 5 and approaches 0.999 by iteration 10, justifying reduced iteration counts at large scales (Figure 3).
VIAR's zero-shot inpainting/editing produces sharper details and smoother boundaries than the VAR baseline (Figure 7).

s8UGIRF38a.text: NaRA's weight update follows Delta W(lambda) = B C(lambda) A, where the core matrix C(lambda) = I_r + eta * F_phi(e_lambda) is produced by a hypernetwork conditioned on the noise level lambda while A and B remain static (Section 4).
On commonsense reasoning with LLaDA-8B-Instruct across 8 benchmarks, NaRA reaches 84.09% average accuracy versus 80.18% for standard noise-agnostic LoRA (Table 1).
On mathematical reasoning, NaRA reaches 80.89% average accuracy, including 57.27% on AQuA versus LoRA's 54.45% (Table 2).
On code generation, NaRA reaches 39.32% Pass@1 versus LoRA's 38.32%, and is the only method to exceed 40% on HumanEval (Table 3).

Theorem 4.1 shows multiple distinct weight-update matrices can be equivalently represented within NaRA's decomposed hypernetwork framework provided the rank r satisfies stated column/row-space conditions (Theorem 4.1).

A Multi-LoRA baseline using 4x the parameters of NaRA still underperforms it, 74.83% versus 80.89% average accuracy (Table 6), while NaRA's shared global hypernetwork across layers acts as an implicit regularizer (Section 4.2, Table 7).

IQojX8HugF.text: The Linearized Bures-Wasserstein (LBW) parametrization identifies each non-degenerate Gaussian with its optimal transport map from a reference measure, yielding a closed-form weighted barycenter (Eq. 3.3, Section 3) that avoids the fixed-point iteration required in standard Bures-Wasserstein geometry.

The proposed Gaussian consensus-based optimization (CBO) particle system drives N Gaussian particles toward consensus via stochastic exploration plus deterministic drift toward exponentially-weighted barycenters omega(mu) = exp(-alpha*E(mu)) (Eq. 4.2, Section 4).
Theorem 4.1 proves convergence of the Gaussian CBO dynamics to global minimizers at an exponential rate under smoothness conditions on the energy functional (Theorem 4.1, Eq. 4.10).
Lemma 4.1 establishes well-posedness of the particle dynamics under local Lipschitz continuity of the energy functional E (Lemma 4.1, Eq. 4.3).

On 2D Gaussian mixture targets A-D, Gaussian CBO outperforms Bures-Wasserstein Gradient Flow on non-convex, non-log-concave problems, with gradient flow becoming trapped on bimodal targets where CBO finds superior solutions (Section 5.1, Table 1, Figure 4).

An extended exponential map defined on all of Sym_d (rather than only Sym_d++ - I) automatically preserves positive semi-definiteness of covariances at no added computational cost, enabling exploration of singular Gaussians (Figure 3).

NOIl9L4Y7S.text: Product networks trained with gradient descent under controlled stochastic data sparsity are shown to learn high-dimensional parity functions, with the problem formalized in Section 3 and main theoretical results developed in Section 4.
Theorems F.5-F.7 in Appendix F establish core convergence guarantees for the product-network learning dynamics on parity functions (Theorem F.5-F.7, Appendix F).
Theorems F.10-F.12 give polynomial scaling laws relating required network width to input dimension N under the sparsity conditions studied (Theorem F.10-F.12, Appendix F).
Theorems F.14-F.16 provide sample complexity bounds for learning parity functions with the product-network architecture (Theorem F.14-F.16, Appendix F).

Section 5 reports experimental validation of the theoretical predictions across varying input dimensions and network configurations, complementing the initialization analysis in Theorems H.1-H.9 (Section 5, Appendix H).

bSLIDztFwx.text: Opportunistic Expert Activation (OEA) reduces MoE-layer decode latency by 39% on Qwen3-30B-A3B (48 layers, 128 experts, k=8) without statistically significant accuracy loss (Table 1-2).
OEA reduces MoE-layer decode latency by 15% on Qwen3-235B-A22B (96 layers) without statistically significant accuracy loss (Table 1-2).

The method is motivated by the analysis that overall MoE decode latency is a memory-bound term that scales linearly in the number of activated experts T, making expert-count reduction the primary optimization lever (Section 3.1).

OEA operates via baseline top-k0 expert selection per token followed by a piggybacking phase where tokens reuse experts already loaded in memory for other tokens in the same batch, recovering performance at zero extra latency (Section 3).

At k0=5 on Qwen3-235B-A22B, OEA maintains vanilla model performance across benchmarks (AIME24, MATH500, GPQA, LiveCodeBench) while a pruning-only baseline degrades by 15% on LiveCodeBench (Table 1-2).

Cross-entropy ablations on FineWeb-Edu show that setting the piggyback probability p=1 performs equivalently to adaptive p<1, that k_max=k is optimal, and that an unrestricted ranking threshold (maxP=128) outperforms restricted values (Section 5).

tX1k4GQtLC.text: On the Darcy flow benchmark, the SOSaG proposal under the pseudo-bootstrap SMC scheme achieves an average solution-field error of 1.48%, compared to 3.39% for the DiffusionPDE baseline (Table 1).

Across five benchmark PDEs (Darcy flow, Helmholtz, Navier-Stokes variants, Poisson), SMC-guided proposals (Guided Euler-Maruyama and Second-Order Stochastic Guided) consistently outperform the DiffusionPDE baseline in numerical solution error (Table 1).

On 2-species and 3-species reaction-diffusion multiphysics systems, the Euler-Maruyama pseudo-bootstrap variant yields the best solution fields overall, while SOSaG (pBS) becomes superior specifically under higher observation-noise levels (Table 2).

The method combines a guidance term built from PDE-residual and sparse-observation MSE losses within a Sequential Monte Carlo sampler, using a 'pseudo-bootstrap' (pBS) formulation to handle non-Gaussian SOSaG proposals (Section on pseudo-bootstrap SMC formulation).

Experiments use only N=8 particles for smaller benchmark PDEs and N=4 particles for larger multiphysics systems, trading particle count for wall-clock cost relative to the baseline (Table 1, Table 2 experimental settings; Limitations).

A6az59SGtF.text: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, adding EchoRL to DAPO raises the in-distribution average from 47.9% to 49.9% and the out-of-distribution average from 57.6% to 60.9% (Table 1).
On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, adding EchoRL to LUFFY raises AIME24 accuracy from 29.4% to 33.4% and AIME25 from 23.1% to 25.7%, while also improving the OOD average from 57.8% to 61.0% (Table 1).

Evaluation spans 10 reasoning benchmarks (six in-distribution: AIME24/25, AMC, MATH-500, Minerva, OlympiadBench; three OOD: ARC-c, GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro; plus one additional generalization set) across 5 backbones from the Qwen2.5 and LLaMA-3.1 families plus a multimodal Qwen2.5-VL model (Section 5.1, Table 6).

EchoRL identifies an 'EchoClip' from verified-success (advantage-degenerated) rollouts using step-level entropy values, feeding it back as an auxiliary supervision signal in the RL objective (Section 4, Section 4.1: Entropy-Based Motivation).

A dedicated cost analysis (RQ2) measuring Actor Update Time shows EchoRL introduces virtually zero additional latency or systematic sequence-length inflation relative to the base RLVR method (Section 5.3, Figure 9).

Eqm5VEaAom.text: A Linearizer is defined as f(x) = g_y^{-1}(A g_x(x)) for invertible neural networks g_x, g_y and linear operator A, making f linear under induced vector-space operations (Section 2.1-2.2).
The composition of two Linearizers with compatible spaces is itself a Linearizer, with the composed operator obtained by matrix multiplication of the underlying cores (Proposition 2.5).

A Linearizer f is idempotent, i.e. f(f(x)) = f(x), if and only if its core matrix A is an idempotent matrix (A^2 = A), enabling architectural (rather than optimization-based) enforcement of idempotent generative networks (Lemma 4.2, Section 4.3).

In the one-step flow-matching application, the product of per-step update operators over hundreds of integration steps collapses into a single operator, enabling one-step diffusion sampling without retraining (Section 4.1).

Modular style transfer is achieved by fixing the shared encoders g_x, g_y while swapping only the style-specific core matrix A_style, allowing algebraic interpolation between styles from a single trained network (Section 4.2).

wGzVFwsH5o.text: AnyBand-Diff achieves 17.11 dB PSNR and 0.73 SSIM on the main visual-quality comparison, outperforming general-purpose diffusion baselines and the HSI-Gene remote-sensing baseline across all four reported metrics (Table 1).

Under 50% random band masking, AnyBand-Diff outperforms the nearest competitor HSI-Gene by 2.78 dB in PSNR and 0.10 in SSIM, while generic models such as Stable Diffusion degrade sharply from 24.12 dB at 10% masking to 17.23 dB at 50% masking (Table 2).
AnyBand-Diff achieves NDVI correlation of 0.94 and NDWI correlation of 0.92 against ground truth, versus 0.90 NDVI correlation for the HSI-Gene baseline (Table 3).

Cross-validating the Physics-Guided Sampling (PGS) and Multi-Scale Physical Loss (MSPL) modules on other diffusion backbones improves 50%-masking PSNR by +2.01 dB on SSDiff and +2.09 dB on CRS-Diff, showing the modules generalize beyond the proposed architecture (cross-validation table, Section on ablations).

AnyBand-Diff uses 278M parameters, 34% fewer than HSI-Gene, and runs inference in 1,420 ms per 256x256 image, 28% faster than HSI-Gene, with Physics-Guided Sampling adding only about 5% latency overhead (Section on computational efficiency).

OGQJsUUtEB.text: CASTLE reduces validation perplexity versus standard causal attention at all four tested model scales (160M, 351-353M, 753-756M, 1.30-1.31B parameters) trained on 50B FineWeb-Edu tokens, e.g. XL scale improves from 11.309 to 10.922 (Table 1)

CASTLE improves downstream 0-shot benchmark average accuracy from 42.45% (baseline-S) to 43.76% (CASTLE-S) and 5-shot average from 50.30% (baseline-XL) to 50.72% (CASTLE-XL) across 8 benchmarks (Tables 2-3)
CASTLE achieves efficient parallel training with O(L^2 d) complexity via the results proved in Theorems 1-2 (Section 2.3)
An ablation removing the causal-key mechanism degrades validation loss from 2.920 to 3.021, showing the lookahead keys, not merely extra keys, drive the improvement (Section 5.2, Table 6)
CASTLE's performance is robust to sliding-window size, remaining stable across window sizes from 128 to 1024 tokens (Tables 11-14)

Leijxx6Czi.text: STARE achieves a peak Attack Success Rate of 31.36% on the RTP dataset, a 68% relative improvement in ASR over state-of-the-art multi-modal toxicity-attack baselines (Section on RTP results)

STARE couples a high-level prompt editor that instantiates semantic toxic subgoals via embedding perturbations with low-level RL fine-tuning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on rectified-flow text-to-image models (Section on hierarchical architecture)
STARE transfers across black-box victim models, achieving 15.96% ASR on Gemini-2.5-Pro and 21.47% ASR on Qwen2.5-VL under query-only access (cross-model transfer results)

The paper identifies an Optimization-Induced Phase Alignment (OIPA) phenomenon in which adversarial optimization concentrates Identity/Threat toxicity in early denoising timesteps (t≈12-22) and Insult/Obscene toxicity in later timesteps (t≈29-39), unlike vanilla models which show diffuse toxicity across all timesteps

Window-zeroing experiments show eliminating early denoising steps (t in [1,15]) collapses Identity toxicity by -62% and Threat by -58% while leaving Insult nearly unchanged (-2%), and eliminating late steps (t in [21,40]) collapses Obscene by -33% and Insult by -35% while leaving Identity/Threat unchanged (-4%), demonstrating a causal double dissociation (Table 4)

Nw55XJi7Jb.text: WMVLM outperforms all baseline VLMs on both residual watermarks (PLCC/SRCC above 0.7, security accuracy about 99%) and semantic watermarks (quality/security accuracy above 85%) (Table 1)

WMVLM is trained via a three-stage strategy: (S1) supervised category-and-score pre-training, (S2) interpretability cold start via knowledge distillation from Gemini-2.5-Pro, and (S3) generalization enhancement via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with multi-faceted reward functions
On cross-dataset generalization to MS-COCO, WMVLM performance remains comparable to primary results with only about a 10% accuracy decrease for RingID (Table 2)
On cross-model generalization across diffusion models, WMVLM performs strongly overall though Stable Signature shows about a 0.6 PLCC drop when evaluated on Stable Diffusion v1.4 (Table 3)

WMVLM is evaluated on 6 residual watermarking methods (DwtDct, RivaGAN, HiDDeN, RobustWide, VINE, Stable Signature) and 3 semantic watermarking methods (RingID, Tree-Ring, and Gaussian Shading/PRCW variants), using 5,000 images for residual and 9,500 images for semantic watermarks with 500 test images per method

aKY52fnzgc.text: On R1-Qwen-14B trained with 280M tokens, ReQAT with NVFP4 W4A4KV4 quantization achieves 65.94% AIME accuracy, exceeding the BF16 full fine-tuning accuracy of 65.46% and the BF16 baseline of 56.83% (Table 1)
ReQAT with MXFP4 W4A4 quantization achieves 64.48% AIME accuracy, compared to only 58.86% for standard QAT at the same 280M-token budget (Table 1)
ReQAT delivers a 3.9x throughput speedup on NVIDIA DGX Spark and a 3.1x speedup on NVIDIA B200 relative to BF16 (Section on hardware throughput results)

ReQAT combines Trace-Aligned QAT (TAQ), which reuses identical reasoning traces from a BF16 Stage-1 fine-tune during Stage-2 QAT, with Selective Entropy Minimization (SEM), an auxiliary loss that reduces predictive entropy at low-entropy token positions
Post-training quantization baselines such as QuaRot and FlatQuant achieve only 40-56% AIME accuracy under the same W4A4KV4 setting, far below ReQAT's 65.94% (Table 1)

klUTVUyqw7.text: The paper identifies energy imbalance across layers—where energy in layers near the output can be orders of magnitude larger than in earlier layers—as the key bottleneck preventing predictive coding networks (PCNs) trained via equilibrium propagation from scaling beyond 5-7 layers (Section 4)

Spiking Precision is defined via Formula (4) as Σ_t^l = α when l = L-t and 1 otherwise, giving large precision weights to a layer only when the error signal first reaches it during relaxation (Section 4, "Spiking Precision")

Forward Updates modify the energy function to use initial feedforward predictions (μ0^l) alongside final relaxed neural states (x_t^l), per Formula (6), reducing error accumulation in deeper layers (Section 4, "Forward Updates", Algorithm 1)
Combining Spiking Precision with Forward Updates (S+F) closes the gap to backpropagation on VGG10, achieving 93.27% vs. 92.21% (BP) on CIFAR-10 and 72.02% vs. 69.35% (BP) on CIFAR-100 (Table 1)
On VGG15 with Tiny ImageNet, the S+F combination reaches 53.04% accuracy versus 44.52% for backpropagation, an 8.52 percentage point improvement, demonstrating scaling to 15 hidden layers (Table 2)

UbzajT84Nd.text: DS-CP achieves substantially higher median coverage than standard conformal prediction across all 16 evaluated LLM models under domain shift on the MMLU benchmark (Figure 1).

The evaluation spans 272 calibration-test subject pairs drawn from MMLU's 17 subjects across 4 categories (humanities, social sciences, STEM, other), targeting 90% coverage with alpha = 0.10 (Section 5).

Theorem 1 establishes a coverage lower bound of 1-alpha minus error terms depending on calibration weight magnitudes and total-variation distance between score distributions, while Theorem 2 gives a matching conservative upper bound (Section 4).
DS-CP increases average prediction set size relative to standard CP, but the increase is modest and preserves practical efficiency (Figure 2).

DS-CP selectively corrects under-coverage in domain-shifted subject pairs while making minimal adjustments when standard CP already achieves valid coverage, shown by points lying above the diagonal (Figure 3).
The bounds provably reduce to standard conformal prediction guarantees when no domain shift is present, i.e., at the default regularization lambda = 1 (Section 4, Section 3).

wqfQ8qFb4U.text: FedSSA outperforms 11 baselines (including FedAvg, FedProx, FedPer, GCFL, FedGNN, FedSage+, FED-PUB, FedGTA, AdaFGL, FedTAD, and FedIIH) on 6 homophilic datasets (Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, Amazon-Computer, Amazon-Photo, ogbn-arxiv) and 5 heterophilic datasets (Roman-empire, Amazon-ratings, Minesweeper, Tolokers, Questions) (Table 1, Table 2).
On heterophilic datasets FedSSA outperforms the second-best method FedIIH by 2.82% in classification accuracy, e.g. 68.67±0.10% vs 68.32±0.05% on Roman-empire with 5 clients (Table 2).
On Cora with 5 clients FedSSA reaches 84.67±0.05% accuracy versus FedIIH's 84.11±0.17% (Table 1).

Theorem 4.2 proves FedSSA converges at a linear rate to an O(epsilon)-neighborhood of the optimal solution, with the error floor decomposing into a semantic term (delta_mu, delta_Sigma) and a structural term (epsilon_U, lambda_1, lambda_2) (Section 4.4).
Removing either the semantic knowledge-sharing component (Section 4.2) or the structural knowledge-sharing component (Section 4.3) degrades accuracy on Cora by more than 5% (Section 5.2, Figure 3).
Results are evaluated across 66 scenarios varying client counts (5, 10, 20) and both non-overlapping and overlapping partitioning settings, averaged over 10 independent runs (Section 5).

ziqS4yXFQX.text: The two-stage kernel ridge regression estimator's mean integrated squared error is bounded with a leading term governed by the RKHS complexity of the simpler treatment-effect function, with the conditional-response complexity entering only as a parametric-order term of order ||f*||_F^2/(gamma n) (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.1 gives three convergence-rate regimes for the effective sample size n_eff = gamma*n: polynomial spectral decay yields rate O~((n_eff)^(-2l/(1+2l))), exponential decay yields O~(1/n_eff), and finite rank yields O~(D/n_eff) (Section 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 shows the fully data-driven model-selection procedure achieves minimax-optimal convergence rates without requiring prior knowledge of spectral decay or the overlap parameter (Section 4.2).
Theorem 4.3 establishes a matching minimax lower bound of order (n_eff)^(-2beta/(1+2beta)) over Sobolev spaces, confirming the adaptivity result of Theorem 4.2 is rate-optimal (Section 4.2).
The method is validated empirically on both synthetic and semi-real data (Section 5.1, Section 5.2).

x5xKTcGemE.text: NeST reduces MAE by 4.52%, RMSE by 4.11%, and MAPE by 12.98% relative to the PatchSTG baseline on the GBA traffic dataset (16.05 vs 16.81 MAE) (Table 1).
Averaged across the GBA, GLA, and CA datasets, NeST improves MAE by 4.71%, RMSE by 4.41%, and MAPE by 9.34% over baselines (Section 5.2, Table 1).
At the 48-step long-horizon forecast, NeST attains 30.03 MAE on GLA and 27.92 MAE on CA versus PatchSTG's 32.43 and 29.15 respectively (Table 2).
Removing the cross-scale attention module causes the largest degradation in the ablation, increasing MAE by 1.04 (GBA) and 1.11 (GLA) (Table 3).
Theorem 1 proves that aggregating nodes with similar temporal patterns into latent regions increases the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of at least 1+(|C_m|-1)*rho_m (Section 4.1, Appendix A.4).

NeST reduces training time by 59.5% (75s vs 185s per epoch) and inference time by 37.5% (20s vs 32s) versus PatchSTG on the GBA dataset, consistent with its O(lNMd) complexity versus O(lN^2 d) for standard transformers (Table 5, Section 4.3).

WLjJqhELBZ.text: Semantic Cache Distillation (SCD) achieves a 2.65x TTFT speedup versus oracle consumer prefill while retaining an F1 score of 0.7850, compared to 4-bit quantization's 5.60x speedup but only 0.1289 F1 and DroidSpeak-style selective recomputation's 1.67x speedup with 0.7052 F1 (Table 2).
SCD's reuse component performs low-rank projection of KV caches across layers (Section 4.3) while its patch component applies semantic correction at sparse transition layers (Section 4.4).
With a patch budget of k=6 patched layers, perplexity improves from 6.788 to 4.65 at a modest 11.7ms overhead cost (Table 3).
Theorem 1 bounds the negative log-likelihood gap by the layer-wise reconstruction error, and Lemma 5.1 shows patched layers truncate multiplicative error propagation across segments (Section 5).
On the Mistral-7B model pair SCD achieves 1.98x speedup with F1 0.769, and on the Qwen-32B pair it achieves 2.07x speedup with F1 0.847 (Table 1).
Offline calibration for a model pair costs about 9.74 hours on a single GPU and yields 397.7M auxiliary parameters, equal to 5.49% of the consumer model's size (Table 6).

GxrcJUT5A0.text: KAN update operations scale as O(s/(G+s)) relative to dense MLP gradient updates, where s is the spline support size and G is the grid size (Theorem 3.3).

KAN activations are bounded as min(W_i) ≤ φ(x) ≤ max(W_i) independent of input magnitude, and quantization error variance scales as O(Δ²) regardless of input statistics, versus MLPs' input-dependent O(Δ² Var[x]) (Theorems 3.4-3.5).

On an AMD Virtex UltraScale+ XCVU13P FPGA, KAN implementations achieve sub-100ns latency across regression, qubit readout, and control benchmarks, consistently faster than MLP baselines at comparable resource usage (Figure 3).
In the qubit readout task under drift, KAN achieves 92.8% accuracy versus 69.8% for a parameter-matched MLP baseline, with performance improving monotonically as grid size G increases (Section 5.3).

In non-stationary Acrobot online reinforcement learning, KAN online actor-critic reaches roughly -104 episodic return versus roughly -500 for MLP actor-critic variants, which additionally require float arithmetic and larger networks (Section 5.4).

In adaptive function approximation, the KAN online learner attains cumulative regret of 13.2 versus 48.3 for a large MLP, and remains stable under 6-bit fixed-point quantization while the MLP degrades sharply (Section 5.2).

lq8fNVME8v.text: Minimum-distance summaries (MDS) adapt the query summary s* = arg min_s D(P_{x|s}, Q) at test time while keeping the pretrained neural posterior estimator fixed, preserving amortization (Section 3.1).

MDS is implemented via a Maximum Mean Discrepancy objective using random Fourier feature approximations of the Gaussian kernel, with a decoder mean-embedding network trained offline via MSE and the summary optimized at test time by L-BFGS (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 4.1 proves that under Huber's ε-contamination model Q_ε = (1-ε)Q + εδ_y, the KL divergence between posteriors under MDS-adapted summaries for Q and Q_ε is O(ε), bounding robustness to small contamination (Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 4.2 shows that when the model is correctly specified, posterior consistency under the original summary statistics implies posterior consistency under MDS-adapted summaries (Theorem 4.2).
On the Gaussian model, MDS outperforms NPE, NNPE, and NPE-OR baselines across a range of contamination proportions, with degradation only appearing at contamination levels above 40% (Figure 2).
On a 1024-dimensional Cryo-EM inference task, MDS substantially improves robustness to Gaussian noise contamination while maintaining performance in the well-specified regime (Figure 4).

QC9S8gUOYc.text: Phonon Fine-tuning (PFT) directly supervises second-order force constants by matching MLIP energy Hessians to DFT-computed force constants, using stochastic sampling of Hessian columns via a single Hessian-vector product to reduce cost from O(N²) to O(N) (Section on methodology).
PFT improves Nequix MP's mean absolute error on ωmax from 24 K to 12 K (50% reduction) and on vibrational entropy from 32 to 14 J/K/mol (56% reduction) (Table 1).

PFT improves Nequix MP's Helmholtz free energy MAE from 12 to 5 kJ/mol (58% reduction) and heat capacity MAE from 6 to 3 J/K/mol (50% reduction), averaging to a 55% improvement across phonon thermodynamic properties (Table 1).

PFT reduces thermal conductivity error κSRME from 0.446 (base Nequix MP) to 0.307, a 31% reduction, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy among models trained on Materials Project trajectories (Table 2).

PFT uses a co-training algorithm alternating PFT steps with standard energy/force/stress training at a ratio K=4 to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, requiring about 140 A100 GPU-hours versus roughly 500 A100 GPU-hours for base model pretraining (Algorithm 1).
Hessian prediction error strongly correlates with phonon property prediction accuracy across multiple thermodynamic metrics, validating the direct Hessian supervision approach (Figure 2).

qmvoTiXSfG.text: VaLR improves Qwen2.5-VL's VSI-Bench accuracy from 33.0% to 52.9%, a 19.9 percentage point gain, using vision-aligned latent tokens generated before each chain-of-thought reasoning step (Table 1).
The single-encoder variant VaLR-S reaches 41.5% average VSI-Bench accuracy while the multi-encoder variant VaLR-M reaches 52.9%, both outperforming GPT-4o (34.0%) and Ocean-R1 (30.5%) (Table 1).

VaLR is trained in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on 450K chain-of-thought samples followed by latent token training with Representation Alignment (REPA) against complementary vision encoders DINOv3, SigLIPv2, and π³ (Section on training pipeline).

VaLR is the only method among those tested that shows consistent performance improvement as reasoning length increases across MathVista, MathVision, MMhalu, and MMVP, whereas baseline methods degrade with longer reasoning chains (Figure 2).
Ablations on representation alignment choices are reported for multiple vision encoder combinations and their effect on downstream accuracy (Table 3).
Perception benchmark results, including BLINK, MMVP, MMStar, V*, and CVBench, are reported to assess whether latent reasoning training preserves general visual perception ability (Table 2).

AKrhb31pI7.text: Scene complexity, rather than concept imbalance, is the dominant factor driving multi-object generation failures: at 10k training samples, Attribution and Spatial Relations accuracy degrades as object counts increase, though less severely than Counting (Abstract, Figure 9).

Counting accuracy peaks near 95% at 2k training samples, then drops below 50% at 10k-50k samples, before recovering at 100k samples, a non-monotonic pattern not observed for Attribution or Spatial Relations, which stay above 90% accuracy across all tested dataset sizes (Figure 9).

Training trajectories show Counting undergoes early peaking followed by degradation in evaluation accuracy even as training loss continues to decrease smoothly, unlike Attribution and Spatial Relations which remain stable (Figure 11).

Compositional generalization to held-out concept combinations degrades substantially as more combinations are withheld, with difficulty ordering Attribution < Counting < Spatial Relations; at 5 of 10 diagonals (50%) held out, Attribution remains robust while Spatial Relations shows broad, unstructured confusion across angular bins (Figure 13, Section 6).

The MOSAIC diagnostic framework isolates three multi-object concepts for evaluation: Attribution (10 sphere colors x 10 cube colors, 100 combinations), Spatial Relations (10 discrete angular intervals), and Counting (object quantities 1-10), evaluated via task-specific classifiers achieving near-100% accuracy on VAE reconstructions (Table 7).

Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 3 on the SPEC benchmark confirms that counting remains unstable during training while compositional generalization continues to degrade with more held-out object co-occurrences, generalizing the diagnostic findings to a realistic pretrained model (Figure 15).

wm3ABfhE7P.text: The spiked cumulant model introduces two latent factors, one recoverable by PCA from the covariance and one appearing only in higher-order moments and invisible to PCA (Section 3).

For correlation exponent 2 ≤ k* < ∞, a minimal nonlinear autoencoder x̂ = (w/√d) σ(wᵀx/√d) with tied encoder-decoder weights provably recovers both latent spikes while PCA and linear autoencoders recover only the covariance-visible one (Section 2, Result 3.1).
Approximate Message Passing weakly recovers both spikes once the sample-to-dimension ratio α exceeds a threshold α_weak^AMP determined by the moments of the coupling coefficients (Result 3.2).
Under conditions C2 < 0 and C3 ≠ 0, spherical gradient flow on the nonlinear autoencoder achieves weak recovery of the hidden spike in logarithmic time Θ(log d) (Theorem 4.2).

Linear autoencoders achieve lower reconstruction (test) loss than nonlinear autoencoders yet fail to recover the hidden spike, demonstrating that self-supervised test loss misaligns with representation quality (Figure 2).

EHUzWqzBL4.text: SliceFine fine-tunes only a randomly or heuristically selected slice of an existing pretrained weight matrix, introducing zero new parameters, unlike adapter- or low-rank-based PEFT methods (Section 2).

Theorem 2.4 establishes that any sufficiently wide weight slice is a 'local winning ticket'—satisfying rank(J_m) ≥ k_task and yielding nonzero gradient and loss reduction—and that a set of such slices spanning the task-relevant subspace forms a 'global ticket' matching near full fine-tuning performance (Theorem 2.4).
On the LLaMA-3B math reasoning benchmark, SliceFine-5RC attains 82.13% average score, exceeding AdaLoRA by 1.07 percentage points while updating no auxiliary parameters (Table 1).
On VTAB-1K image classification with ViT-Base, SliceFine-5R reaches 88.85% average accuracy versus 88.08% for LoRA (Table 2).

SliceFine trains at 2.05 iterations/second versus 1.78 for LoRA and 1.62 for HRA, and completes 10 epochs in 1.05 minutes versus 1.83 minutes for HRA, with about 18% lower peak memory than HRA and AdaLoRA (Figure 4).

Slice position, parameter-importance ranking (via Wanda pruning scores), and lottery-ticket 'winning' status have little effect on accuracy (within about ±1%), supporting the Universal Winning-Slice Hypothesis (Figure 3b, 3c, 3d).

B1ISNZQHuI.text: Holistic Trajectory Calibration (HTC) extracts a 48-dimensional feature vector spanning cross-step dynamics, intra-step stability, positional indicators, and structural attributes from an agent's full execution trajectory, then fits an interpretable linear calibrator (HTC-Full with L2/ridge, HTC-Reduced with L1/LASSO) (Section on HTC framework).

HTC-Reduced achieves Expected Calibration Error of 0.031 on HLE, 0.102 on GPQA, and 0.068 on SimpleQA, consistently surpassing strong baselines in calibration and discrimination across eight benchmarks, multiple LLMs, and agent frameworks (main results table).

HTC is evaluated across six LLMs (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-v3.1, Qwen3-235B, and GPT-OSS variants), each showing distinct baseline miscalibration profiles that HTC corrects (model-agnostic evaluation section).

A General Agent Calibrator (GAC) pretrained on seven diverse datasets and evaluated zero-shot on the held-out GAIA benchmark achieves the lowest Expected Calibration Error of 0.118 among compared methods, demonstrating transfer without retraining (GAC out-of-domain evaluation).

Feature-importance analysis shows positional features (early/late trajectory signals) are the top predictors of calibration across datasets, with stability and dynamics features as essential complements and structure attributes playing a complementary role (feature importance analysis section).

z9Bo4eXSpW.text: GRPO with verifiable 0/1 rewards can be cast as an adaptive weighted contrastive loss between samples drawn from the previous (old) policy, with weights ω_{ε,±}(p) = p/√(p(1-p)+ε) depending on the old policy's success probability p (Section 2).
Theorem 1 gives the optimal policy at each GRPO iteration in closed form as an exponential reweighting of the reference policy based on the previous iteration's binary reward statistics (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 shows the success probability sequence generated by GRPO's iterations satisfies a fixed-point recursion p_{n+1} = h_{ε,p_ref}(p_n) (Theorem 2).
Theorem 3 proves every fixed point p* of GRPO's dynamics satisfies p* > p_ref, i.e., GRPO provably amplifies the policy's probability of success beyond the reference policy's performance (Theorem 3).

Theorem 5 shows that when the parametric policy approximation has statistical and optimization error bounded by δ*, the resulting success probability converges to within 2δ* of the theoretical fixed point (Theorem 5).

ZVyd4r9Xl5.text: The Optimal Weight (OW) algorithm assigns each LLM a weight ω_i = σ_k^{-1}(x_i) based on its accuracy x_i, and Theorem 1 proves OW is Bayes-optimal among all aggregators with access to the same first-order accuracy information (Algorithm 1, Theorem 1).

The Inverse Surprisingly Popular (ISP) algorithm uses only second-order information (pairwise prediction correlations, no ground-truth labels) to compute a counterfactual advantage score per label, and Theorem 2 proves the ordering E[Adv_ISP(s*)] ≥ E[Adv_MV(s*)] ≥ E[Adv_SP(s*)], i.e., ISP dominates majority voting which dominates the classical Surprisingly Popular algorithm (Algorithm 2, Theorem 2).

In simulated experiments with N=4 agents and M=10,000 questions, ISP achieves 90.48% accuracy versus 85.13% for majority voting at K=2 answer options, and 94.45% versus 92.64% at K=4 options, with the gap shrinking at rate Θ(1/K) (simulation results section).
On real-world datasets, OW-L attains 73.66% accuracy on UltraFeedback, 90.37% on MMLU, and 85.78% on ARMMAN, each exceeding majority voting's 72.21%, 89.32%, and 85.24% respectively (Table 3).
Across 16 model ensembles, OW-L outperforms majority voting in 97.92% of cases, with absolute accuracy improvements ranging from 0.54% to 14.20% (Section on real-world experiments).

Corollary 1 connects the optimal aggregation weights to the Bradley-Terry model, showing that in the binary setting the optimal weights are proportional to the inverse logistic function of each model's accuracy (Corollary 1).

rxWzzqvHYZ.text: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B under sequential editing, most parameter-editing methods collapse to near-zero performance while the SCR retrieval-based baseline achieves an average score of 60.19 (Table 3).

Theorem 4.5 formalizes a relative perturbation amplification result predicting that parameter edits increasingly distort model internals as the number of edits grows, motivating the dimensional collapse hypothesis of Assumptions 4.1-4.3 (Section 4).

Figure 3 shows performance deterioration on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the ZsRE dataset as the number of edits increases across 1, 10, 100, and 'All' edits, with all evaluated parameter-editing methods declining significantly (Figure 3).
Table 2 reports strong negative Spearman correlations between the proposed amplification metric and reliability, locality, and portability across MEMIT, ROME, and WISE (Table 2).
Even the best-performing parameter-editing method, AlphaEdit, only reaches 69.49 on Reliability and 55.50 on Generalization for Llama-3.1, underperforming the SCR retrieval baseline (Section 5).

Figure 5 illustrates a fundamental trade-off in which parameter-editing methods have lower editing cost but disrupt internal parameters, whereas retrieval-based methods incur higher inference latency but preserve core capabilities (Figure 5).

8FsiTJC04n.text: On the MMMLU benchmark, DCO improves cross-lingual consistency (clcall) by +10.6 to +13.8 points across evaluated LLMs, nearly matching DPO's +12.3 improvement despite using no ground-truth labels (Section 6.1, Table 1).
Combining DPO with DCO yields the best results across all tested LLMs on MMMLU, indicating DCO complements DPO when gold labels are available (Section 6.1, Table 1).
Across MMMLU, XCSQA, and BMLAMA, DCO produces clcall gains ranging from +4.61 (XCSQA) up to +16.65 (BMLAMA), with non-English accuracy improving by up to +8.49 points (Section 6.2, Table 2).

When Qwen2.5-14B is trained with DCO on one subject domain and evaluated on out-of-domain subjects, clcall improves by roughly 11% on average with non-English accuracy gains of +3.76 to +12.36, while English accuracy drops only marginally (by at most 0.36 points) (Section 6.3, Table 3).

Figure 2 shows that adjusting the direction parameter γ allows tunable trade-offs between language preference and accuracy, e.g., an 'en-stable' weighting yields +4.24 Swahili accuracy with clcall of 56.59 (Section 6.4, Figure 2).

N2mwmOk6pl.text: AutoMoT's Action Expert is implemented as a task-specialized transformer with approximately 1.6B parameters, coupled to an Understanding Expert via joint attention with a KV-cache mechanism described in Equations 3-5 (Section 3.1, Section 3.3).
On the closed-loop Bench2Drive benchmark, AutoMoT achieves a Driving Score of 87.34 and a Success Rate of 70.00%, outperforming SimLingo and other VLM-augmented baselines (Table 1).
On open-loop nuScenes planning, AutoMoT attains L2 displacement errors of 0.14m, 0.29m, and 0.54m at 1s, 2s, and 3s horizons respectively, with collision rates of 0.01%, 0.06%, and 0.15% (Table 2).

Asynchronous inference reduces AutoMoT's latency to 0.05s, an 86.8% speedup (7.6x faster) over synchronous inference, with only a negligible 1.24% increase in average L2 error (0.322 to 0.326) (Section 4.4, Table 5).

Removing the pre-trained Understanding Expert increases average L2 error from 0.32 to 0.36, and removing the decision-making component increases it to 0.34, showing both components are necessary for preserving planning performance (Table 8).

Naively fine-tuning the pretrained backbone on LingoQA yields only a marginal 0.2-point gain on that task but causes catastrophic forgetting on TallyQA, where accuracy drops from 81.40% to 52.40% (Section 4.3, Table 4).

okWAqiCEQD.text: On the iNatSounds benchmark, the proposed AG-CLIP method achieves 17.2% region accuracy (200km) and 41.0% country accuracy (750km), outperforming species-oracle baselines (Section 5.1, Table 1).

Using annotated species range information as an oracle achieves 10.8% region accuracy, while predicting species from all available cues achieves 9.3% region accuracy, showing species identity alone is a strong but incomplete geolocation signal (Table 1).

Aggregating spatiotemporally within 253 km^2 neighborhoods of species-rich recordings improves region accuracy to 30.4%, with gains reduced when restricting aggregation to monthly or weekly windows (Section 5.3, Table 4).

An ablation over location encoders (SatCLIP, SINR, GeoCLIP) shows GeoCLIP-based location embeddings combined with species checklist prediction (the AG-CLIP hybrid) perform best among tested encoders (Table 2(b)).
Figure 3 shows cumulative distribution curves of geolocation error across methods, with AG-CLIP exhibiting spatial variation in performance across geographic regions (Figure 3).

XClFDlw3oe.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes that SIKA-GP's sparse inducing kernel approximation achieves O(log M) complexity dependence on the number of inducing points M for the Laplace kernel (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
Table 1 reports that SIKA-GP achieves O(SDN log M + DM) training complexity and O(SD log M) inference complexity, contrasting with SVGP's O(NM^2) and KISS-GP's O(DM^(1+1/D)) (Section 5.1, Table 1).

The tensorized sparse indexing (TSI) algorithm in Equations 15 and 17 uses element-wise multiplication broadcasts and weight squeezing via sparse indices to enable efficient GPU computation, illustrated in Figure 4 (Section 5.1, Figure 4).
On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, DKL-SIKA achieves 94.78% and 76.94% accuracy respectively, each with roughly 3x training speedup over baseline deep kernel learning (Section 6.3, Table 3).

On the CLINC150 language benchmark, DKL-SIKA achieves 0.8590 AUROC with a 2x speedup, and on the Gas regression dataset it achieves a 7x speedup while maintaining comparable RMSE and NLPD (Section 6.4, Section 6.2, Tables 2, 4-5).

nDfDnsyllY.text: RDNGD achieves iteration and oracle complexity of O(d·ε⁻²) for smooth nonconvex problems and O(d·ε⁻¹) for smooth convex problems using only a pairwise comparison oracle on Riemannian manifolds (Table 1).
The recurrent variant RRDNGD attains linear convergence for strongly convex objectives, requiring O(d log(1/ε)) oracle calls (Table 1).

RDFW, a projection-free Riemannian dueling Frank-Wolfe method, achieves O(ε⁻¹) iteration complexity with O(d·ε⁻²) oracle calls for smooth convex problems using only a linear minimization oracle (Table 1).

Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 show the comparison-based gradient direction estimator is unbiased for the normalized gradient with improved constants over prior Euclidean dueling optimization work (Section 3, Lemma 3.1, Lemma 3.2).

The framework is applied to a black-box adversarial attack on DNNs with sphere-constrained perturbations and to horizon leveling via SO(2) image rotation, both using only pairwise comparison feedback (Section on real-world applications).

The method covers Hadamard manifolds and bounded-sectional-curvature spaces, with demonstrated applications including Rayleigh quotient maximization on the unit sphere and Karcher mean computation on SPD matrices (Section on synthetic applications).

ronJusfDvK.text: A single amortized neural posterior estimator conditioned jointly on observation x and temperature β enables single-forward-pass sampling from the tempered power posterior p_β(θ|x) ∝ π(θ)p(x|θ)^β without inference-time MCMC or additional simulator calls (Section on core method).

Proposition 4.1 shows that minimizing the SNIS-weighted training objective (Route B) is equivalent to minimizing the forward KL divergence between the learned amortized posterior and the true tempered posterior (Proposition 4.1).
Proposition 4.2 proves that for β ∈ [1/2, 1], the NRE-based self-normalized importance weights have finite variance, guaranteeing stable weighted maximum-likelihood estimation (Proposition 4.2).

The amortized estimator is evaluated on four SBI benchmarks—Two Moons, Gaussian Mixture, SLCP, and Lorenz-96—achieving posterior approximations competitive with non-amortized MCMC-based power-posterior samplers across a wide range of temperatures (Experiments section).

Route A (score-assisted tempered synthesis via Langevin dynamics) dominates at small β where SNIS importance weights become high-variance, while Route B (self-normalized importance sampling) performs well near β=1 using 10K-100K simulations (Experiments section).

On the 8-parameter Hodgkin-Huxley neuronal model with 7 summary statistics, the Route B (NLE) estimator trained on 10K simulations produces stable marginal posteriors across β ∈ {0.1, 1.0, 2.0} with posterior predictive checks qualitatively matching Allen Cell Types Database recordings (Section on Hodgkin-Huxley application).

Sgwd0l1u2V.text: Theorem 3.2 shows PRAXIS runs in time O(|R|·k·d·ProxyCompute(n,k,d)), giving polynomial work per recovered tree in the Rashomon set, versus exponential time per tree for prior exact methods (Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 3.4 shows PRAXIS memory usage scales as O(n·k + Σ|t|), linear in dataset size and total size of output trees (Theorem 3.4).
On the Churn dataset (5,000 samples, 472 features), PRAXIS completes in 34.84 seconds using 279MB of memory, while SORTeD does not finish and TreeFARMS requires 22GB (Table 1).
On the 11-million-sample Higgs dataset, PRAXIS completes in 2,375 seconds (about 40 minutes) using 21.5GB, while competing methods (SORTeD, TreeFARMS) do not finish (Table 1).
Across 22 datasets with recoverable ground-truth Rashomon sets, PRAXIS achieves recall of 1.000 ± 0.000 on 18 datasets and at least 0.984 on the remaining datasets (Table 2).

On large datasets including Churn, Electricity, News, and Madeline, PRAXIS finds over 1 million trees better than the best tree found by the RESPLIT baseline, with RESPLIT returning zero trees in the desired Rashomon set on two datasets (Figure 3).

RQECNEUcbJ.text: Theorem 3 proves that for translation-invariant, isotropic inputs, online SGD requires sample complexity n ≫ N³ log²(N) to extract phase information, because phase modifications are encoded only in fourth-order cumulants corresponding to an information exponent k*=4 (Theorem 3).

For non-isotropic inputs with power-law Fourier amplitude spectra, the dominant principal subspace has eigenvalue λ_{k0} ≈ √N, raising the effective signal-to-noise ratio to λ_{k0}² ≈ N and reducing the required sample complexity for phase learning to quasi-linear in N (Section on power-law spectrum effect).
Two-layer networks trained on ALOT texture images (cotton vs. lace) first rely on amplitude-based features before subsequently exploiting phase information to distinguish classes (Figure 1).

Flattening the Fourier amplitude spectrum of training images causes a dramatic slowdown in learning, while replacing per-image amplitudes with class-averaged amplitudes (removing amplitude-based discriminative signal) instead produces a significant speedup in learning (Figure 3).

The sequential amplitude-then-phase learning behavior is confirmed across multiple architectures (ResNet18, fully connected networks) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100) and across different optimizers (Section on experimental validation).

pRgUJfrFw9.text: Score Anisotropy Directions (SADs) are defined as the ordered orthonormal eigenvectors of the average geometry matrix G_F = E[(F_θ(x_σ,σ))²], with ordering by eigenvalue magnitude conjectured to determine the network's generation preference (Definition 2).

Theorem 1 shows that under denoising score matching with linear architectures and rank-one data, convergence rate decays with the eigenvalues of the conditioning matrix, and this anisotropic effect is amplified further under SGD (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 characterizes the orthogonal transformation that minimizes versus maximizes alignment α with the SADs, showing minimization corresponds to reversing the eigenvalue ordering (Theorem 2).

For an iDDPM U-Net, generation performance degrades monotonically as the eigenvalue associated with the aligned data direction increases, with the model performing best on data aligned with small-eigenvalue SAD eigenvectors (Figure 6).

On MNIST, CelebA-HQ, and CIFAR-10, minimizing alignment α with the SADs substantially improves Sliced Wasserstein-2 distances relative to the default natural alignment, whereas maximizing alignment induces mode collapse (Figure 8, Figure 9).

Closed-form average geometry expressions are derived per architecture: MLPs yield G_F = αI + β·11ᵀ, CNNs yield a block-diagonal Kronecker structure reflecting spatial organization, and Transformers yield at most T distinct eigenvalues where T is the number of tokens (Section on architecture-specific results).

zcYZpdsn9u.text: FusionRoute reaches 0.566 average accuracy on the Llama-3 family across GSM8K, MATH500, MBPP, HumanEval, and IfEval, versus 0.502 for token-level Collab, 0.536 for the fine-tuned baseline, and 0.368 for DARE model merging (Table 1).
On the Gemma-2 family, FusionRoute attains 0.426 average accuracy versus 0.360 for token-level Collab and 0.394 for the fine-tuned baseline (Table 1).

Theorem 4.3 proves that purely expert-only token-level routing cannot in general recover an optimal policy unless strong global coverage assumptions hold, motivating the trainable complementary logit generator (Theorem 4.3).

Removing the complementary logits component ('FusionRoute w/o complementary logits') lowers performance relative to full FusionRoute across nearly all benchmarks and both model families, with the gap most pronounced on coding and instruction-following tasks (Section 6.1, Table 2).
FusionRoute achieves higher GPT-4o judged win rates against fine-tuned baselines on both Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families, with larger gains at bigger model scale (8B vs 2B) (Figure 4).

k76ll7aQyE.text: The method conditions task-specific Bayesian meta-learning priors on latent causal task embeddings z via ϕ_t | z_t, θ ~ N(θ + Wz_t, σ²I), rather than sharing a single global prior across tasks (Section 4.2).

Proposition 4 shows the prior-induced risk is Lipschitz continuous in the causal embedding space, with target-task error bounded by the sum of expert-inference error, causal-discovery error, and out-of-distribution shift magnitude (Proposition 4, Appendix A.1).
