Theorem 5 gives conditions under which conditioning on causal embeddings mitigates negative transfer relative to a global prior, requiring expert-plus-causal error to remain below the out-of-distribution shift level (Theorem 5, Appendix A.2).

In synthetic experiments, causal embeddings maintain stable performance as task shift increases, whereas correlation-based embeddings degrade under distribution shift despite outperforming when spurious correlations remain predictive (Section 7.1).

On UK Biobank cross-disease cardiovascular and respiratory prediction tasks, ICP-derived causal embeddings improve average AUROC to 0.82 versus 0.79 for a no-transfer baseline, with the largest gains on the most out-of-distribution tasks J44 and J45 (Section 7.2, Table 1).

fj5Ec6g7Ez.text: miniF2F-Dafny translates the 488-problem miniF2F benchmark (244 test, 244 validation problems) into the Dafny auto-active verifier for the first time.
Dafny's SMT-backed automation alone (empty proofs) verifies 99/244 (40.6%) of test-set problems and 109/244 (44.7%) of validation-set problems without any LLM guidance.

Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieves 55.7% Pass@4 success on the test set when providing proof hints for problems unsolved by automation alone, the best result among 12 evaluated LLMs, ahead of Claude Sonnet 3.7 (55.2%) and Qwen 3 235B MoE (54.3%).

LLM-guided hints combined with automation yield over 35% relative improvement above the empty-proof automation baseline, illustrating a division of labor where LLMs supply high-level guidance and Dafny's solver handles low-level verification details.

5yXKRaNI2R.text: The paper formulates calibration as finding the model closest in KL divergence to a base model subject to satisfying a set of distributional (moment-matching) constraints, and proposes two fine-tuning algorithms, CGM-relax and CGM-reward, to solve it (Section 3).

On protein design, CGM improves secondary-structure diversity by nearly 5x for Genie2 (15M parameters) and secondary-structure matching by 2x for ESM3-open (1.4B parameters), under 99 simultaneous CATH-derived structural constraints (Section 4.1).
On image generation with TarFlow (463M parameters), CGM reduces total variation distance in class proportions from 0.306 to 0.108 across 6 simultaneous wildcat-subspecies constraints (Section 4.2).

On language modeling with TinyStories-33M, CGM reduces gender imbalance across 8 professions by more than 5x, moving female representation for the 'lawyer' profession from about 16% to about 41%, with transfer of the effect to heldout professions (Section 4.3).

CGM-relax scales to hundreds to roughly 1000 simultaneous constraints with linear KL-divergence growth in constraint dimensionality, while CGM-reward becomes infeasible beyond about 30 constraints, per Gaussian-mixture simulation studies.

tIG25Y7gMj.text: The paper introduces a fully automated black-box pipeline that uses LLM autoraters to hypothesize candidate unverbalized bias concepts from as few as 30 representative input samples (under 1% of the dataset), then tests them via counterfactual variation pairs with McNemar's test, Bonferroni correction, and O'Brien-Fleming alpha spending for early stopping (Section on Methodology / pipeline description).

Across three decision tasks (hiring, loan approval, university admissions) and seven LLMs, the pipeline consistently detects gender bias favoring female candidates and race/ethnicity effects, with measured effect sizes of 1.5 to 6.0 percentage points (mean 3.4pp) and 67% of detected biases having 95% confidence intervals excluding zero.

The method discovers previously unidentified unverbalized biases—Spanish fluency, English proficiency, and writing formality—in addition to rediscovering gender and race biases reported in prior manual studies (Karvonen & Marks).
In an intentional bias-injection validation, the pipeline detects 85% of injected secret biases at 92.5% accuracy while achieving 100% filtering of overtly stated biases.

Human-annotation validation shows LLM-based verbalization detectors reach kappa agreement of 0.67-0.79 with human raters, and the staged sampling/clustering/early-stopping design cuts computation by about 33% relative to exhaustive testing.

LptCWUvaP9.text: Theorem 4.3 establishes a lower bound showing sequential sample-and-evaluate algorithms can achieve strictly better sample complexity than parallel test-time compute (standard best-of-n) when reference policies differ across steps (Theorem 4.3, Section 4).

RF-SeqBoN (Reward-Filtered Sequential Best-of-n), which selectively conditions on high-reward past generations via a threshold, achieves a sample complexity that strictly improves over vanilla parallel best-of-n's O(C*_LLM(x)/epsilon) rate (Corollary 5.8, Section 5).

RF-SeqBoN is evaluated against vanilla best-of-n and pure sequential best-of-n on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, AMC'23, AIME'24, and AIME'25 using Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Qwen3-0.6B-Thinking, with RF-SeqBoN outperforming both baselines across all five benchmarks (Figure 1).

On MATH500 with a sampling budget of N=128, RF-SeqBoN shows consistent gains over baselines broken down by problem difficulty level, with the largest improvements on the hardest levels 4-5 (Figure 2).
Section 6 reports ablations over the reward-filtering threshold gamma and choice of reward model used to select high-reward generations for the sequential filtering procedure (Section 6).

HUwssjEH2D.text: PENCIL, an encoder-only Transformer that tokenizes each node's local subgraph via one-hot identifiers and adjacency indicator rows (no positional encodings or learned per-node embeddings), is proposed for link prediction (Section 3.2).
PENCIL uses 22x to 146x fewer learnable parameters than ID-embedding-based link prediction methods while matching or exceeding their accuracy on ogbl-ppa (Figure 1).
PENCIL achieves state-of-the-art MRR of 42.23 on cora and 79.54 on ogbl-ppa, and 86.86 MRR on ogbl-citation2 under the original OGB evaluation protocol (Table 1).
Under the harder HeaRT evaluation protocol, PENCIL attains top MRR scores on ogbl-ppa (45.43) and ogbl-ddi with substantially lower variance (±0.07 on ogbl-ppa) than competing methods (Table 2).

A feature-ablated variant of PENCIL trained without node features remains competitive with, and on cora even outperforms, the feature-inclusive version, indicating structural signal from sampled subgraphs dominates node feature information (Section 5).
PENCIL better approximates pairwise structural heuristics (Common Neighbors, Adamic-Adar, Katz index, PageRank) than GNN and ID-GNN baselines (Figure 4).

DFi6hHce5t.text: LLEP (Least-Loaded Expert Parallelism) dynamically transfers both tokens and expert parameters from overloaded GPUs to least-loaded devices while preserving exact MoE computation semantics, to address load imbalance that standard Expert Parallelism (EP) cannot handle (Section on method / abstract).

LLEP achieves up to 5x speedup for individual MoE layers and up to 5x reduction in peak GPU memory usage compared to standard EP under extreme imbalance scenarios (95% token concentration) (Figure 1 caption, Figure 4 caption).

LLEP delivers realistic full-model throughput improvements of up to 2.2x for gpt-oss-20b and 1.88x-1.9x for gpt-oss-120b via dynamic token rerouting that ensures all devices finish within the minimum collective latency (Figure 1(c), Section 5.2).

LLEP is evaluated across three MoE architectures — GPT-OSS, DeepSeek-V3, and Kimi-K2 — with ablations over batch size, capacity factor alpha, routing threshold lambda, and hidden dimensions (Section 5).

LLEP is positioned for regimes where load-balancing losses cannot be applied during post-training or inference and explicit expert-balancing is undesirable because it would suppress learned expert specialization (Introduction/abstract).

HCb1fg6Y8M.text: A GNN encoder (DBGNN) paired with a CNN image decoder predicts per-node 20x20 stability-landscape heatmaps for oscillator networks, achieving 86.69% ± 1.91 SSIM in-distribution on 20-node graphs and 84.90% ± 0.33 SSIM in-distribution on 100-node graphs (Table 2).

Under a 20-to-100 node size shift (training on 20-node graphs, evaluating on 100-node graphs), DBGNN-CNN's out-of-distribution performance drops to 81.03% ± 1.59 SSIM, noticeably lower than in-distribution accuracy (Table 2).

When transferring to real power grid topologies without retraining, TAG-CNN achieves SSIM scores of 82.87% ± 0.26 on the Germany grid, 79.26% ± 0.45 on France, 85.38% ± 0.83 on Great Britain, and 79.45% ± 0.09 on Spain (Table 4).

Two public synthetic datasets, each with 10,000 graphs (one at 20 nodes, one at 100 nodes) with per-node basin-stability landscape labels from Monte Carlo simulation totaling roughly 500,000 CPU hours, are released to enable machine learning study of synchronization stability landscapes (Section on datasets).
Trained models reduce per-graph stability-landscape evaluation time from thousands of CPU hours (Monte Carlo simulation) to seconds of inference (Section on results).

dxVnCJRSm8.text: LaTtE-Flow partitions 28 transformer layers into K=4 groups of M=7 consecutive Layerwise Timestep Experts, each specializing in a subset of flow-matching timesteps, so only one group of layers activates per denoising step, reducing per-step compute from O(L x T') to O(M x T') (Section on architecture).

LaTtE-Flow (Couple variant) achieves FID 5.79 and Inception Score 213.1 on image generation while activating only 500M parameters per step versus 2.0B for baseline unified multimodal models (Table 1).

LaTtE-Flow is reported to be 6x faster at inference than Janus Pro and 48x faster than Show-o among recent unified multimodal models, while remaining competitive on generation quality (abstract; Section on efficiency results).

On understanding benchmarks, LaTtE-Flow reaches 74.9 on MMBench and shows competitive results on SEED, POPE, MM-Vet, and MMMU, outperforming Janus Pro (1.5B) on several benchmarks despite being built on a smaller Qwen2-VL-2B backbone (Table 2).

An ablation removing the Timestep-Conditioned Residual Attention gating mechanism degrades FID from 5.79 to 8.26, showing this component is a substantial contributor to generation quality (ablation section).

qV7yFzdK1R.text: For exact equilibria (α=0) with support-restriction πmin>0, the paper proves a sample-complexity lower bound of Ω(log(1/δ)/log(1/(1-πmin)) + (n+log(1/δ))/ϵ²) (Theorem 3.2).
For approximate equilibria with α∈(0,1/4) and ϵ≤1/128, the lower bound scales as Ω((n+log(1/δ))/(ϵ²α)), showing the approximation parameter α multiplies the sample complexity (Theorem 3.3).

An upper-bound algorithm (Procedure 1) achieves Õ(log(1/δ)/log(1/(1-πmin)) + (n+log(1/δ))/ϵ²) samples for exact equilibria in both general-sum and zero-sum bimatrix games, matching the lower bound (Theorem 4.1).
For approximate equilibria with α>0, the proposed algorithm attains O((n+log(1/δ))/(ϵ²α) + √n·log(1/δ)/(ϵα)) samples, which matches the lower bound for ϵ≲n^{-1/2} (Theorem 4.2).

The analysis identifies a fractional-knapsack structure underlying the approximate-equilibrium error, showing actions played with probability ~α create multiplicative α⁻¹ dependence in the convergence rate (Section 4).

wFThVGzmvq.text: PLaID++ achieves a stable-unique-novel (S.U.N.) generation rate of 22.27%, roughly 50% higher than the strongest prior baseline (Table 1).
PLaID++ reaches a thermodynamic stability rate of 97.34% versus 95.40% for the CrystalLLM-70B baseline (Table 1).
The Wyckoff-position crystal representation reduces token count by 14% relative to standard 3D-coordinate encodings while preserving physical symmetry constraints (Section on representation).

Ablations show S.U.N. rate rises from 7.17% (Wyckoff SFT only) to 15.59% (with DPO) to 22.27% (full PLaID++ with iterative RLIP), an approximately 115% and 50% improvement from DPO in unconditional and space-group-conditioned generation respectively (Table 1 ablations).
PLaID++ generates 27.17 S.U.N. crystals per minute, about 5x faster than the FlowLLM baseline (Section on generation speed/Table 1).

DFT validation on 1,000 generated structures confirmed a stability rate of ~19.1%, with MLIP-based stability predictions correlating at R²=0.84 (eSEN) and R²=0.68 (eqV2) with DFT (Validation section).

QnWjcTk14G.text: The method re-parameterizes trained Transformers as RASP code and applies causal interventions to identify minimal sufficient sub-programs (abstract only).
The method often recovers simple and interpretable RASP programs from length-generalizing Transformers trained on algorithmic and formal-language tasks (abstract only).

The approach builds on prior work showing Transformer computations can be simulated in the RASP family of programming languages, and tests whether trained models actually construct the simple programs that theory suggests (abstract only).
The recovered RASP programs are presented as the most direct evidence to date that Transformers internally implement simple, interpretable algorithms rather than opaque computations (abstract only).

UllXS9qddS.text: Across eight instruction-tuned transformer models (including Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, phi-4, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and gemma-2-9b-it) and over 17.5 million behavioral trials, forced-choice (FC) responses show RSA correlations with hidden-state geometry of r=.460–.463 under task-aligned extraction, versus r=.196–.199 for free association (FA) (Section on RSA results).
Cross-model consensus similarity reaches r=.792–.802, substantially higher than either behavioral measure's alignment with any single model's hidden states (Section on RSA results).

In nearest-neighbor overlap analysis, forced-choice similarity peaks at .285 at k=200 neighbors, while free-association overlap peaks at .181 at k=5, indicating FC captures broader semantic structure (Section on nearest-neighbor analysis).

Held-out-word ridge regression shows forced-choice behavioral similarity adds +.022 mean R² beyond a lexical/consensus baseline, versus only +.002 added by free association, with the full model reaching mean R²=.587 versus a baseline R²=.569 (Section on ridge regression results).

Ny6UYZ8ysN.text: AutumnBench evaluates world-model learning using 43 grid-world environments and 129 tasks spanning three challenge families: change detection, masked frame prediction, and planning (Section describing AutumnBench).

Human participants achieve an average score of 0.935 across all tasks, outperforming all three evaluated frontier models (Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and o3) (Results section, performance table).

Humans maintain consistent performance across both deterministic and stochastic environments, whereas reasoning models perform significantly better in stochastic than deterministic settings (Results section).

Scaling test-time computation improves model performance in 25 of 43 environments (Set A) but leaves performance flat or declining in the remaining 18 environments (Set B) (Results section, scaling analysis).

During free exploration, humans use environment resets at roughly 12.5% frequency versus 2.1% for Claude and 11.5% for o3, consistent with humans using resets as deliberate hypothesis-testing tools (Exploration behavior section).

Normalized perplexity analysis of exploration trajectories shows humans reach lower final perplexity and lower AUC than frontier models, indicating faster convergence to focused, informative exploration strategies (Learning dynamics section).

xFX7jtHi8H.text: On the FashionIQ benchmark, Pix2Key with V-Dict-AE pretraining achieves 29.96% average Recall@10, versus 27.87% for the CIReVL baseline (Table 1).
On the CIRR benchmark, adding V-Dict-AE pretraining raises Pix2Key's Recall@10 from 68.15% to 73.36%, the best result among compared methods (Table 2).

On the DFMM-Compose benchmark (an extended DeepFashion-MM composed image retrieval setup), Pix2Key with V-Dict-AE reaches 23.58% Recall@10 alongside 54.44% Attribute Consistency@50 and 53.96% Intra-List Diversity@50 (Table 2).
The ablation over polarity-aware constraints shows that combining positive, negative, and open (unconstrained) attribute keys yields 40.96% Recall@50 (Table 3).
MMR-based reranking improves Intra-List Diversity@50 without reducing recall, according to the V-Dict-AE ablation study (Table 3).

dc9si7lBTY.text: BlitzRank's Algorithm 1 uses tournament graphs built from k-wise comparison oracles, tracking in-reach L(u) and known-relationship counts K(u) per candidate to certify when a top-m ranking is finalized (Algorithm 1).
Across 14 benchmarks and 5 LLM oracles, BlitzRank achieves Pareto dominance, matching or exceeding baseline ranking accuracy while using 25-40% fewer tokens than comparable reranking methods.
With a GPT-4.1 oracle, BlitzRank-k10 consumes about 42k tokens per query versus 315k tokens for pairwise reranking, a roughly 7x reduction at near-identical quality.
BlitzRank-k10 attains an average nDCG@10 of 56.7, matching the SW-R2 baseline's 56.7 nDCG@10 while using under 40% of its token cost.
Window size k=10 outperforms k=20 by 0.4-0.9 nDCG points across all 5 tested LLM oracles, attributed to reduced 'lost-in-the-middle' effects and fewer boundary ties.
Convergence rounds are predictable: k=10 requires a mean of 13.6 rounds (std 0.58) and k=20 requires a mean of 6.7 rounds (std 0.45), giving a coefficient of variation of about 2%.

ErcPPRZaiq.text: Tucker Attention is proven to encompass MHA, GQA, and MLA as special cases of its Tucker-rank configuration: MHA corresponds to ranks (n_H, d_model, d_model), GQA to (n_H, d_model, d_H·n_KV), and MLA to (n_H, d_c^Q, d_c^K).
On ViT experiments, Tucker Attention matches GQA and MLA validation performance using almost an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters (Figure 3).
On GPT-2, a Tucker Attention configuration with ranks [8,128,64] needs only about 18% of MHA's parameters and 39% of MLA's parameters to reach competitive validation loss (Table 2).
On LLaMA3-1B, Tucker Attention reduces attention parameters to 10-20% of the GQA baseline while incurring only a 1-3% increase in validation loss (Table 3).
Tucker Attention parameter count scales as O(r·d_model + r_1·r^2) versus O(d_model^2) for MHA/GQA/MLA (Table 1).

Tucker Attention introduces a 'latent RoPE' that applies rotations in the latent key space, remaining compatible with flash-attention and simplifying MLA's decoupled RoPE scheme into a single rotational pathway.

p7p5foAXaB.text: HieraMAS organizes agents into 'supernodes' using a propose-synthesis architecture, where multiple proposer LLMs generate diverse outputs that a synthesizer LLM aggregates, with automatic role pruning via skip tokens.
Inter-node communication topology selection is framed as a holistic graph classification task solved by a GCN-based classifier scoring candidate DAGs, rather than optimizing edges individually.

The two-stage credit attribution algorithm combines node-level and system-level rewards in Stage 1 to learn LLM-selection preferences under random topologies, then trains the graph classifier in Stage 2 on execution data from Stage 1.
HieraMAS achieves 94.61% average accuracy across HumanEval++, MATH, and MMLU-Redux benchmarks, outperforming comparable multi-agent baselines.
HieraMAS is reported to be up to 3.27x cheaper than fully-connected multi-agent baselines on some tasks while maintaining higher accuracy.

mw7BL7AvQc.text: On Qwen3-8B, The Geometric Reasoner (TGR) improves robust trajectory coverage, measured as area under the Pass@k curve, by up to 13 points on AIME25 and OlympiadBench math benchmarks.
TGR yields consistent AUC (area under Pass@k curve) improvements on HumanEval and BigCodeBench coding benchmarks, in addition to its math benchmark gains.

TGR's manifold-informed latent foresight search scores candidate chunk-boundary states using a composite of foresight value (32-64 token look-ahead rollouts), a bumpiness penalty for trajectory smoothness, and a uniformity regularizer for diversity.
TGR is training-free and adds only 1.1-1.3x inference overhead in memory and compute relative to standard decoding, while using about 18% fewer tokens than training-heavy baselines.
TGR keeps memory linear in chunk length by extracting unit-norm latent anchors from hidden states at chunk boundaries after each KV-cache reset.

LvYuEB4POi.text: LIFT (Logging Improvement via Fine-Tuned Trajectories) identifies 'shortcut' actions satisfying γV^π(s',W) − V^π(s,W) ≥ ||s' − s_W|| and uses them to augment offline RL trajectories (Section 3, Theorem 3.6).
Proposition 3.3 proves that for linear dynamics f(s,a,W) = s + W·a, accumulated actions always constitute valid shortcuts regardless of the value function's properties (Proposition 3.3).

Theorem 3.6 gives sufficient conditions—distance-improving policies, Lipschitz-continuous value functions, and linear placement-error (LPE) distortion—under which shortcuts can be safely identified via the bound γ·V^π(s_j,W) − V^π(s_i,W) − ||s_j−s_W|| ≥ (γ·L_V+1)·L_f·Σ||a_k|| (Theorem 3.6).

LIFT-SC (trained with shortcut augmentation) consistently outperforms baseline CQL across positioning tasks with dimensionality ranging from d=2 to d=5 under partial observability, using direct-position, optical-image, and sensor-based observations (Experiments section).

LIFT-SC outperforms a warm-start SAC baseline specifically in 5-dimensional scenarios, but its shortcut-identification guarantee fails when contraction properties are violated, as in the f_regrot distortion setting (Experiments section).
The augmentation method is implemented as a single-line integration into the d3rlpy library, allowing it to be added to existing offline RL algorithms (Algorithm 1).

0OevIlRMYN.text: KVP (KV Policy) reformulates KV-cache eviction as learning attention-free, per-head lightweight policies (2-layer MLPs with 256 hidden units, ~650K parameters per head) that rank tokens by predicted future utility using only key and value vectors (Section on Architecture/Methodology).

KVP is trained via a global reward computed jointly across all cache budgets, measuring how much relevant future information would be erroneously evicted at each budget level, using only pre-computed generation traces (Training/Methodology section).

KVP consistently outperforms all evaluated baselines on the RULER long-context benchmark across varying cache sizes despite lacking access to query information, unlike attention-based eviction methods (RULER results).

On the OASST2-4k multi-turn dialogue benchmark, KVP achieves lower perplexity than baselines at most cache sizes, while heuristic methods like StreamingLLM show a sharp perplexity increase as the cache budget shrinks (OASST2-4k results).

KVP generalizes zero-shot to downstream tasks (BoolQ, ARC-Challenge, GovReport, MMLU, HellaSwag) and to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, despite being trained only on generation traces (Generalization results).

KVP training completes in under 30 minutes on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs and adds roughly 1% additional FLOPs during the prefill stage with no extra cost during autoregressive decoding (Efficiency/Cost analysis).

boeY2syj2r.text: SurvDiff is presented as the first end-to-end diffusion model explicitly designed for generating synthetic survival data, jointly modeling mixed-type covariates, event times, and right-censoring via a Cox partial-likelihood-based survival loss (Section on Method/Loss Function).
SurvDiff's survival loss uses a sparsity-aware exponential decay weighting scheme that gives higher weight to earlier event times to account for right-censoring (Loss Function Components section).

On the AIDS (ACTG, n=1151, 91.7% censored), GBSG2 (n=686, 56.4% censored), and METABRIC (n=1903, 42% censored) datasets, SurvDiff achieves the best Jensen-Shannon distance for covariate fidelity across all three datasets, including 0.0069±0.0008 on AIDS (Table 2).
SurvDiff achieves roughly a 50% improvement in Wasserstein distance over SurvivalGAN on the AIDS dataset (Table 2).

SurvDiff obtains the best downstream concordance index on AIDS (0.6826±0.0541) and GBSG2 (0.6453±0.0201), and the best Brier score on AIDS (0.0501±0.0005), outperforming NFlow, TVAE, CTGAN, TabDiff, and SurvivalGAN (Table 3).

SurvDiff is trained for 4,000 epochs with adaptive scaling of the survival loss weight, and synthetic samples are generated using 300 reverse-diffusion denoising steps (Implementation/Training details).

rlvnG8oKmN.text: POGO (Proximal One-step Geometric Orthoptimizer) requires only 5 matrix products per update step when the landing polynomial root λ is fixed to 1/2 (Section 3.4, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 3.5 proves that if X_0 lies on the Stiefel manifold, ξ := ηL < 1, and λ = 1/2, then for every iterate X_t, ||X_tX_t^T − I||^2 = o(ξ^7), i.e., POGO stays within a shrinking neighborhood of the manifold in practice (Theorem 3.5).

On the CIFAR-10 orthogonal-kernel CNN experiment (18,624 orthogonal 3×3 matrices), POGO trains in about 3 minutes to reach test accuracy comparable to the unconstrained Adam baseline, whereas RSDM (Han et al., 2025) takes about 17 hours on average (Figure 1).

In the multi-matrix orthogonal Vision Transformer (O-ViT) experiment on CIFAR-10 with 18 matrices of size 1024×1024, POGO is the fastest method to complete 10 epochs without leaving the Stiefel manifold, while all methods reach similar test accuracy (Figure 5, Section 5.2).

On the squared unitary probabilistic circuits benchmark (complex-valued matrices up to 10×10000 fit to MNIST), POGO obtains state-of-the-art validation bits-per-dimension while converging fastest and never leaving the Stiefel manifold, and is twice as fast as RGD while matching its performance (Section 5.3, Figure 8).

l6KZJO7w48.text: Theorem 1.2 proves that in two-player m×m potential games, Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) can require 2^Ω(m log m) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/poly(m), for any permutation-invariant regularizer and any learning rate schedule η^(t) = 1/t^α with α ∈ [0,1) (Theorem 1.2).

Theorem 1.3 shows there exists an n-player binary-action potential game in which fictitious play requires 2^Ω(2^n) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/2^n, a doubly exponential lower bound (Theorem 1.3).

Theorem 1.1 establishes a matching-type positive result: alternating ε-lazy no-regret dynamics converge to an ε-Nash equilibrium in any potential game after at most exp(O_ε(1/ε^2)) iterations (Theorem 1.1, restated as Theorem 3.4).

Proposition 3.2 shows that for FTRL with learning rate η ≤ 1/L (L the smoothness constant of the potential), the potential function value is non-decreasing across iterations, without requiring alternation or laziness (Proposition 3.2).

Example 3.3 constructs a 'spurious fixed point' showing FTRL can maintain a highly suboptimal strategy (error proportional to 1/t) indefinitely relative to the observed utility sequence, illustrating why FTRL, unlike gradient descent under Legendre regularizers, need not reach an O_ε(ε)-Nash equilibrium (Example 3.3).

The two-player exponential lower bound construction uses a payoff matrix A of odd dimension m with maximum entry 2m−1, dividing the FTRL trajectory into 2m−1 'transition periods' governed by Property 4.3 (period consistency) and Lemma 4.1 bounding action probability by R/(η^(t)γ) (Section 4, Definition 4.2, Property 4.3, Lemma 4.1, Figure 2b).

woiiKET6bn.text: Hard Constrained Decoding (HCD) achieves 100% STL satisfaction across evaluated specifications by masking unsafe actions with -infinity logits, but reduces task success rate to as low as 67-78% versus 82-83% for unconstrained policies (Section 4, Table 1).

Robustness Constrained Decoding (RCD) trades off some safety guarantee for task performance, achieving 83-95% STL satisfaction while maintaining 76-83% task success rate, close to the unconstrained baseline (Section 3, Table 1).

SafeDec is evaluated on three distinct transformer-based navigation policies (SPOC, Flare, PoliFormer) across two STL specifications, phi_avoid and phi_geofence, using 200 episodes per configuration in AI2-THOR environments (Section 4, Table 1).
SafeDec adds minimal computational overhead at decoding time, on the order of 10^-5 seconds per timestep (Section 4).
Ablations show SafeDec degrades gracefully under noisy dynamics, specifically 5% translational and 3.3% rotational noise, and is sensitive to the robustness weighting hyperparameter beta (Figure 3).

omJqMJt2fC.text: Theorem 1 proves that under target diversity and nontrivial conditioning assumptions, no globally optimal VJEPA solution exhibits complete representation collapse, in contrast to deterministic JEPA (Theorem 1, Section 4).

VJEPA reformulates the deterministic JEPA MSE regression objective as a probabilistic predictive model p_phi(Z_T given Z_C, xi_T) trained with a variational objective combining negative log-likelihood and a KL regularization term weighted by beta (Section 4, Equation 11).

Theorem 2 establishes that if a learned latent state Z_t satisfies control-predictive sufficiency, the optimal control policy pi*(u_t given h_t) depends only on Z_t rather than the full history h_t, enabling optimal control without pixel-level reconstruction (Theorem 2, Section 6).
Table 1 contrasts deterministic JEPA and VJEPA across six dimensions including prediction type, uncertainty modeling, and collapse avoidance (Table 1, Section 4).
A 'Noisy TV' linear system experiment demonstrates that VJEPA filters out high-variance nuisance distractors that otherwise cause representation collapse in generative baselines (Section 9).

Bayesian JEPA (Section 8) extends VJEPA via a Product-of-Experts factorization of the predictive belief into a learned dynamics expert and a modular prior expert, enabling zero-shot task transfer and constraint satisfaction (Section 8).

ClqjnEbUC5.text: The CAB benchmark comprises 405 human-verified counterfactual questions spanning three sensitive attributes: 145 on sex, 128 on race, and 135 on religion (Section 4, Table 2).

An adaptive genetic-algorithm-based question generation process explored roughly 5,100 candidate questions for the sex attribute, 11,500 for race, and 8,100 for religion before human filtering retained about 50% of them (Section 3, Table 2).

Nine frontier LLMs, including GPT-5, Claude-4-Sonnet, and Grok-4, were evaluated on CAB, with GPT-5 and Claude-4-Sonnet exhibiting the lowest bias fitness scores, under 1.0 across all three attributes (Section 5, Figure 4).
Implicit (indirect) bias-eliciting questions produce roughly a 40% reduction in fitness scores compared to explicit question variants across all evaluated models (Section 5, Figure 5).

The fitness scoring framework evaluates responses along four dimensions (Bias, Acknowledgment, Relevance, Refusal) with a generation threshold set at tau=1.4 for the sex attribute and 1.8 for race and religion (Section 3, Figure 1).

Apmd6IStO6.text: On the LVBench benchmark (103 videos, 117 hours), NKR achieves 48.8% accuracy at 0.33 seconds per query with zero GB of additional inference-time memory overhead (Section 4.2, Table 2).

NKR is over two orders of magnitude faster than tokenized baselines such as VideoLLaMA3 (64.5s) and Qwen2.5-VL (30.0-45.6s per query), and roughly 300x faster than the agentic Deep Video Discovery baseline (180.0s per query) at comparable accuracy (Section 4.2, Table 2).

NKR's accuracy degrades only 0.3 percentage points (48.9% to 48.6%) when comparing videos under one hour versus over one hour, versus a 2.9-6.7 percentage-point drop for competing methods over the same length increase (Section 4.3, Table 3).
Ablation shows all components of Agentic Knowledge Distillation (AKD) are necessary: dense descriptions alone yield only 14.3% accuracy versus 48.8% for the full system (Section 4.3, Table 5).
Upgrading the underlying frozen VLM backbone from 8B to 14B parameters improves NKR accuracy by 9.3 percentage points (Section 4.3, Table 4).

NKR encodes video knowledge into LoRA adapter weights mounted on a frozen VLM, trained via Agentic Knowledge Distillation combining dense multi-level descriptions with synthesized QA pairs, requiring about 2-3 hours of training per one-hour video on four 40GB A100 GPUs (Section 3.2-3.3, Section 4.1).

iyG31VdQfG.text: The attack pipeline scrapes on the order of 10^8 product-pattern collocations from e-commerce websites archived in the LAION-5B dataset, generating 25-50 images per prompt across different random seeds (Section 3.1-3.2).

Near-duplicate templates are identified using CLIP embedding-based clique detection with a similarity threshold of 0.95 and a minimum clique size of 2, a far lower resource bar than prior attacks that required a minimum clique size of 10 (Section 3.2).

A simple, seemingly benign prompt such as 'blue Unisex T-Shirt' reconstructs template-memorized images depicting an identifiable real individual, without any access to the training set (Section 4, Figure 4).

Template memorization, image interpolation across source templates, near-identical perturbation clusters, and cross-category leakage are demonstrated to persist across newer generative models including Stable Diffusion 3.5, Flux-Schnell v1.0, and Midjourney v6.1, albeit with reduced success relative to Stable Diffusion 1.4 (Section 4.2, Figure 6).

All reconstruction experiments were run on a single RTX A6000 GPU, substantially lower compute than prior reconstruction attacks such as those of Carlini et al. and Webster et al. (Section 3, Section 5).

A synthetic validation study fine-tuned Stable Diffusion on 54 images (3 base coffee-mug photos times 18 patterns) and reproduced template memorization, interpolation, perturbation, and cross-category leakage using semantically similar prompts like 'Tea Cup' versus 'Coffee Mug' (Appendix A).

9KOJdlFH82.text: Relative improvement is defined as the ratio of actual risk reduction to the maximum possible reduction from a baseline predictor, per Equation 1: ρ_P(f) = [R_P(f0) − R_P(f)] / [R_P(f0) − R_P(f*_P)] (Section 2, Equation 1).

Theorem 4.1 proves a no-harm guarantee: when the baseline predictor f0 is in the feasible class F, the maximin relative improvement solution f_RI satisfies R_g(f_RI) ≤ R_g(f0) for every group g (Theorem 4.1).

Proposition 4.2 shows that, for two groups (m=2), relative improvement uniquely satisfies Pareto optimality, symmetry, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity simultaneously, and recovers the Kalai-Smorodinsky bargaining solution (Proposition 4.2).

Proposition 4.4 extends the axiomatic guarantees to more than two groups (m>2) via a leximin refinement that preserves scale invariance and a modified individual monotonicity property (Proposition 4.4).
Theorem 5.4 establishes that the empirical maximin relative improvement estimator converges to the population solution at rate O(1/√n) under standard regularity conditions (Theorem 5.4).

Table 1 shows relative improvement is the only compared fairness criterion (versus Group DRO, minimax regret, Nash bargaining, and explained variance) that jointly satisfies Pareto optimality, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity (Table 1, Section 3.1-3.3).

xM56OFSUaN.text: Theorem 5.1 proves Rank-Learner's orthogonal loss L^orth(g,η) is Neyman-orthogonal, i.e., first-order insensitive to estimation error in the nuisance functions (response surfaces and propensity score) (Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 5.2 shows the minimizer of the orthogonal loss is a scoring function g(x) = (1/κ)τ0(x) + c, proving Rank-Learner recovers the true treatment-effect ordering without explicit CATE estimation (Theorem 5.2).

The soft ranking target is defined via a sigmoid of the scaled pairwise treatment-effect difference, t_τ(X,X′) = σ((τ(X) − τ(X′))/κ), combined with a doubly robust correction term to build the orthogonal pseudo-label (Section 5, Equations 10 and 12).

On synthetic data with training sizes from n=100 to n=2,000, Rank-Learner achieves AUTOC values from 0.94±0.21 to 1.37±0.00, outperforming T-learner, DR-learner, and plug-in ranker baselines (Table 3).
On semi-synthetic benchmarks (MovieLens, MIMIC-III, and CPS) at n=1,000, Rank-Learner attains AUTOC of 1.35±0.01, 1.18±0.02, and 0.95±0.01 respectively (Table 4).
Figure 3 shows Rank-Learner's ranking performance saturates using only about 10% of all possible training pairs, indicating pair subsampling does not hurt accuracy (Figure 3).

Y9RqhWmcyK.text: Frontier LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash and GPT 5.1) achieve higher win rates than humans and defeat more complex bot opponents in iterated rock-paper-scissors (IRPS) (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

AlphaEvolve, an automated program-discovery method balancing predictive likelihood against code simplicity (Halstead effort), is used to synthesize interpretable Python programs modeling human and LLM strategic behavior (Section 3.2).

Discovered programs show humans maintain a single-dimensional opponent model tracking move frequencies, whereas Gemini 2.5 maintains a 3x3 opponent-transition model and GPT 5.1 maintains a 3x3x3 model tracking two-step opponent dependencies (Figure 1, Section 4.3).
GPT OSS 120B underperforms humans in IRPS, with performance declining over extended game history, suggesting a context-length limitation (Section 4.2).
The human dataset comprises 411 participants making 129,087 total choices, while each LLM dataset comprises 20 games across 15 bot types yielding 90,000 choices per model (Section 2).

Discovered behavioral programs are validated against baselines including Nash equilibrium, Contextual Sophisticated Experience-Weighted Attraction (CS-EWA), and recurrent neural networks (Section 3.3).

mh2eIxPKMm.text: Theorem 2 bounds the expected signed 1-Wasserstein distance between a clean n-pixel image and its Gaussian-noise-perturbed counterpart by (2/√π)σn log2(n) + (1/(2√π))σn, i.e., growth roughly linear in n with a log factor, for zero-sum noise of standard deviation σ (Theorem 2).

Theorem 3 shows that for p-Wasserstein distances with integer p>1, the expected p-th power error is bounded by (4/√π) n σ, so the per-image error scales as (nσ)^(1/p), improving (becoming more noise-robust) as p increases, in contrast to the Euclidean (L2) metric's linear scaling in σ (Theorem 3).

Theorems 4 and 5 extend the noise-sensitivity bounds to the deviation between the true and noisy Wasserstein distances computed between two distinct images, rather than a single noisy image against its clean version (Theorems 4-5).

On cryo-electron microscopy projection images of the hsp90 protein with noise level σ=0.01, the squared-Wasserstein (W2) distance matrix preserves the ground-truth diagonal similarity structure across viewing angles, while the L2 distance matrix degrades to an unstructured/random pattern (Section 4.3).
Figure 2 empirically confirms that the W2 distance error follows the predicted (nσ)^(1/2) scaling law as noise increases, while the L2 distance error grows linearly in σ (Figure 2).

Section 4.4 reports a counterintuitive phenomenon in which Wasserstein distance between sparse images can decrease as noise increases, because added noise bridges transport gaps between distant mass concentrations (Section 4.4).

Hn81xuLaXY.text: Heima's encoder compresses an entire chain-of-thought stage into a single hidden 'thinking token' (e.g., <Thinking_of_Summary>) instead of a multi-token textual rationale (Section 3.1).

Table 1 reports Heima reduces the number of generated reasoning tokens to about 6% of the original CoT length on certain datasets while maintaining or improving zero-shot accuracy, e.g., 72.8% on MMBench and 43.6% on MathVista, both using around 12-14 tokens versus much longer LLaVA-CoT outputs (Table 1).

The Heima decoder reconstructs coherent textual reasoning from the encoder's compressed hidden thinking-token state by feeding it into a pretrained LLM together with an explanatory guidance prompt (Section 3.2, Equations 8-9).

Training uses progressive encoding (Section 3.1, Equation 6) that gradually increases the proportion of CoT stages replaced by hidden thinking tokens from 0 to the maximum, easing the transition from explicit to hidden reasoning.

Decoder reconstruction quality, measured by BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore, is strongest for the summary stage of the reconstructed reasoning, and GPT-4o similarity ratings average in the 4-5 range indicating close alignment with original CoTs (Figure 4, Figure 5).

Ablations (Table A3) show a single thinking token per CoT stage outperforms multi-token variants (2, 4, 8, 16, 32 tokens), and adaptive retention ratios from 10% to 90% (Table A4) show no consistent accuracy benefit over the fixed single-token design (Table A3, Table A4).

kS0XU5JUII.text: Extract-and-evaluate (EaE) monitoring improves catch rates at 1% FPR by 16.8 percentage points over the best of four baseline monitoring methods on BigCodeBench-Sabotage (Figure 4).

On subtle side tasks specifically, EaE monitoring improves catch rates by 19.9 percentage points over the best baseline, and using GPT-4.1 as the evaluator with GPT-4.1-mini as the extractor yields up to a 39 percentage point improvement over baselines (Figure 4).

Contemporary LLM monitors exhibit a 'less-is-more' effect: CoT-only monitors achieve substantially higher catch rates on traditional (non-reasoning) LLMs than on reasoning models, e.g. 61.7% for traditional Claude-3.7-Sonnet versus 20.0% for reasoning variants on subtle tasks, despite reasoning traces being far longer (Figure 5).
With appropriate monitor elicitation (e.g. EaE), reasoning models are shown to be more monitorable than traditional LLMs across all model pairs compared (Figure 5).

On MLE-Sabotage, Gemini 2.0 Flash using EaE monitoring achieves AUROC = 0.924 at approximately $0.004 per transcript, placing it on the cost-performance frontier alongside other Gemini and Claude family models (Figure 7).

usZLsN3Dnv.text: For SGD with a polynomial decay-of-degree-p annealing schedule under multiplicative stepsize misspecification factor ρ ≥ 1, the convergence rate is O(ρ^(1/(2p+1))/√T) in the convex Lipschitz setting (Theorem 1).

Fixed (non-annealed) stepsize schedules incur a convergence rate of O(ρ/√T), i.e. linear dependence on the misspecification factor ρ, compared to the sublinear dependence achieved by annealed schedules (Theorem 1).
For cosine annealing schedules, h(u) = ½(1+cos(πu)), the convergence rate scales as O(ρ^0.2) times the baseline rate, derived via tail-behavior analysis of the schedule (Corollary 3).
Robustness guarantees for annealed learning-rate schedules extend from the convex Lipschitz case to the convex smooth setting under stepsize stability constraints (Theorem 4).

Experiments on synthetic logistic regression and CIFAR-10 with WideResNet confirm that annealing schedules are more robust to coarse learning-rate grid search than fixed stepsizes, with the performance gap widening as grid resolution becomes coarser (Section on experimental validation).

2X8Qi3VdjA.text: FedRot-LoRA achieves 0.8932 average accuracy on GLUE benchmarks with N=3 clients and 0.8818 average accuracy with N=10 clients, consistently outperforming FedIT, FFA-LoRA, and RoLoRA baselines across tasks and client counts (Table 1).
FedRot-LoRA reduces aggregation error by an order of magnitude compared to the FedIT baseline, which uses naive factor-wise averaging (Table 2).

Theorem 4.4 establishes convergence bounds for federated LoRA that explicitly isolate an aggregation error term arising from naive factor-wise averaging of client updates, and Theorem 4.8 shows that rotational alignment via the orthogonal Procrustes problem yields a strictly tighter error bound than factor-wise averaging under stated conditions.
On generative tasks, FedRot-LoRA attains 40.88% pass@1 on HumanEval and 44.37% exact-match accuracy on GSM8K (Table 5).

FedRot-LoRA aligns client A and B factors via alternating orthogonal Procrustes alignment with soft rotation to prevent destabilization early in training, preserving semantic updates while reducing cross-client subspace mismatch without added communication cost (Section 4, Theorem 4.8).

wjc6oz63WL.text: CoFrGeNet (both attention and FFN replaced) reduces GPT2-xl's 1.5B parameters to 798M (a 47% reduction), while CoFrGeNet-F (FFN only) and CoFrGeNet-A (attention only) reduce parameters by 34% and 19% respectively, with performance on downstream classification, Q&A, reasoning, and text understanding tasks competitive with or superior to the original models (Section on GPT2-xl variants, Table 2).
On OpenWebText, CoFrGeNet variants pre-train in 178-186 hours versus 190 hours for GPT2-xl (6-7% faster), and on GneissWeb in 387-397 hours versus 413 hours for GPT2-xl (4-6% faster) (Table 4).
For Llama 3.2B, CoFrGeNet reduces parameters to 1.8B (44% reduction) while achieving a training throughput of 315B tokens/day versus 235B tokens/day for the baseline (Table 7).

CoFrGeNet-F outperforms baseline models on most GLUE tasks despite having fewer parameters, and CoFrGeNet variants achieve lower or comparable perplexity on PTB, WikiText2, and LAMBADA (Table 2, Table 3).

Using a continuants-based implementation that reduces the number of divisions from depth d to a single division per forward pass cuts inference latency of CoFrGeNetB from 5898.72 μs to 628.73 μs (Table 4).

K2KeBuKAtu.text: GIST matches or outperforms the LESS baseline for instruction-tuning data selection while requiring only 0.29% of LESS's storage (about 217MB versus 75GB for Qwen2.5-1.5B) and 25% of its computational time (about 12 hours versus 48 hours) (Table 4).
On Llama2-7B with 5% data selection, GIST improves average accuracy by +6.2 points over the base model, including +5.6 on MMLU, +9.4 on TydiQA, and +3.5 on BBH (Table 2).
On Llama3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-1.5B, GIST yields average improvements of +4.5 and +1.5 respectively, exceeding LESS's +3.3 and +1.1 gains on the same models (Table 2).

Theorem 3.2 shows that LoRA parameterization structurally induces off-diagonal curvature in the loss landscape that diagonal preconditioners (e.g., Adam states) cannot represent, motivating GIST's use of full gradient-covariance spectral filtering instead.

Theorem 3.3 proves eigenspace stability: the top-r eigenspace of the gradient covariance approximates the true validation-Hessian-induced task subspace with bounded error, underpinning GIST's SVD-based spectral filtering step.
GIST requires only a single lightweight LoRA warmup epoch on 5% of the data to extract its task-specific subspace, compared to LESS's requirement of 4 warmup epochs (Section on technical innovation).

IQ8xF6eMuZ.text: On OR-Debug-Bench (~5,000 problems spanning 9 error types with Gurobi IIS feedback), an 8B model trained with domain-specific RLVR reaches Recovery Rate @5 of 95.3% versus 86.2% for frontier API models, a +9.1 point gain (Table 1).

The RLVR training uses GRPO with LoRA (r=16, alpha=32) and a composite reward combining outcome verification (50%), diagnostic accuracy (30%), and efficiency (20%), converging after 4 epochs to RR@5=95.0% (Section 4.3).

On OR-Bias-Bench (2,000 newsvendor instances, 1,000 in-distribution and 1,000 out-of-distribution), a three-stage curriculum targeting pull-to-center bias yields a -9.6% ID-to-OOD bias drift (from 20.0% to 10.4%), a 48% reduction and the only negative drift among evaluated models (Section 4.5, Table 10).
Targeted training raises diagnostic accuracy (fraction of diagnosed errors overlapping the true infeasible-subsystem set) from 47.8% to 62.4%, a +14.6 point improvement (Table 1).
Targeted training reduces the average number of steps to reach an optimal repair from 3.78 to 2.25, a 1.7x speedup in self-correction efficiency (Table 1, Table 11).

wpKA7G7Cqu.text: SGShift-KA (sparse GAM with knockoffs and absorption term) achieves AUC greater than 0.9 for identifying shifted features across semi-synthetic benchmarks, outperforming the Diff, WhyShift, and SHAP-difference baselines by 2-3x in recall (Table 2).
On the Diabetes Readmission dataset (73,615 samples, 33 features, split by ER vs. non-ER admission), SGShift variants detect true shifted features with recall exceeding 80-90% (Table 2).

Sample-efficiency experiments show SGShift's knockoff variants (SGShift-K, SGShift-KA) retain top detection performance even when the number of samples available from the shifted (target) domain is small (Figure 1).

On the COVID-19 Hospitalizations dataset (16,187 samples, 30 features, split pre/post-Omicron) and the SUPPORT2 dataset (9,105 samples, 64 features, split by survival vs. death outcome), SGShift's real-world validation shows an elbow-shaped performance curve indicating that only a sparse subset of features accounts for the concept shift (Figure 2).
SGShift variants consistently outperform the Diff, WhyShift, and SHAP baselines across both matched and mismatched model-specification configurations (Table 2).

5hqkRlAGtP.text: The paper defines an ideal attribution mechanism via a ledger, a transcript-level attribution map R satisfying empty-initialization, monotonicity, and suffix-jump axioms, and deterministic selection rules Z mapping (prompt, prefix, suffix) triples to attribution decisions (Section 2).

Attribution soundness (Definition 2.5) is defined to prevent an adversary from pre-specifying a string to be planted into the attribution set, while robust attribution (Definition 2.9) extends attribution decisions to perturbed strings via predicates such as Hamming distance (Section 2).

Lemma 3.10 shows that ideal security of pseudorandom codes (PRCs) implies faithfulness of the resulting watermarking scheme, and Corollary 3.11 shows zero-bit ideal PRCs yield undetectable and faithful watermarks for the uniform language model (Section 3).
Theorem 3.15 establishes that PRC-based watermarking schemes achieve undetectability and robustness for general (non-uniform) language models using beta-potential block selection (Section 3).

Section 4 extends the framework beyond black-box adversaries via relaxed faithfulness defined by a pair of attribution maps (R, S) that sandwich the verifier's decision, i.e., S(zeta) >= Ver(zeta) >= R(zeta) (Section 4).

rCbbDqQzai.text: The proposed SafeThink inference-time defense reduces jailbreak attack success rate on LlamaV-o1 evaluated on JailbreakV-28K from 63.33% to 5.74% (Section 5, Experiments).
SafeThink reduces attack success rate on R1-Onevision evaluated on the Hades benchmark from 69.07% to 5.65%, and on OpenVLThinker from 66.7% to 2.2% (Section 5, Experiments).

SafeThink is evaluated across six multimodal large reasoning models (R1-Onevision, OpenVLThinker, VLAA-Thinker, Vision-R1, LlamaV-o1, LLaVA-CoT) and four jailbreak benchmarks (JailbreakV-28K, Hades, FigStep, MM-SafetyBench) (Section 5, Experiments).

SafeThink preserves reasoning performance, with MathVista accuracy changing only from 65.20% to 65.00% and average reasoning accuracy across benchmarks changing from 63.51% to 63.46% (Section 5, Experiments).

The core mechanism intervenes only in the first 1-3 reasoning steps to redirect generation toward safe completions, adding only 0.1-0.9 seconds of inference latency (Section 4, Safety Recovery with Few Step Steering).

frRHI1zK86.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that for unbounded context windows, every distribution D is exponentially close in total variation distance (at most |A|T^(-alpha)) to a low-regret distribution (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 proves an impossibility result: for models with a fixed bounded context length L, there exist distributions that cannot be robustified to simultaneously achieve low regret and small TV-distance from the original (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 shows that robustification becomes possible with a bounded context model if the robustified model is allowed a slightly larger window L' > L, achieving per-round regret of order O(1/sqrt(L'-L)) (Theorem 4.2).

Algorithm 1 gives a robustification procedure that switches between the original next-token predictor and a Polya urn model based on detected out-of-distribution regret, and the Polya urn process is proven to guarantee sublinear regret when paired with quantal best responses (Section 4).

Experiments train NanoDO transformers on simple binary prediction tasks to empirically validate the theoretical predictions about distributional similarity and regret reduction under robustification (Section 5, Experiments).

jIZqAemuqk.text: Theorem 4.5 establishes that if the global graph of a constrained MAP problem has treewidth one and bounded diameter and the density satisfies the tractable MAP conditions (TMC), then the constrained MAP problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time (Theorem 4.5).

The MpMap algorithm performs recursive message passing over tree-shaped factor graphs, using piecewise polynomial (Ω^PP) and piecewise exponentiated polynomial (Ω^PEP) density classes to compute exact MAP solutions via upward messages from leaves to root (Section 4, Equations 4-6).

The PaMap algorithm partitions non-convex feasible regions defined by SMT formulas into convex polytopes and solves constrained optimization over each region, retaining the best solution found (Algorithm 4).

On synthetic tree-structured benchmarks (STAR, SNOW, PATH), MpMap scales to more than 20 dimensions and outperforms both PaMap and PCAdam baselines, including on PATH graphs with exponential theoretical complexity (Figure 5).

On the Stanford Drone Dataset trajectory prediction task, PaMap using the SHGO optimizer solves all 50 test instances feasibly with a smaller optimality gap than OMT-based solvers (OptiMathSAT, CDCL-OCAC), which either time out or fail (Figure 7).
In a VAE-based data imputation experiment using Monte Carlo density approximation, PaMap outperforms unconstrained Adam optimization on 78% of test samples (Figure 8).

AW0sphpLo7.text: Theorem 3.1 decomposes the KL divergence between the true and synthetic network distributions into three error terms: sparsity parameter estimation error (E_ρ), embedding distribution approximation error (E_Φ), and generative model error in the latent space (E_gen) (Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 shows that the sparsity parameter estimation error E_ρ is O_p((log n / (w_n n))^{1/2}) under the sparse network regime (Theorem 3.2).

On simulated sparse networks with n=1500 nodes and r=4 latent dimensions, the diffusion-based variant SyNG-D achieves a triangle density RMSE of 0.63×10^-4 and clustering coefficient RMSE of 4.58×10^-3, outperforming VGAE on both metrics (Table 1).

On real-world networks including PolBlogs, YouTube, DBLP, and Yelp, SyNG-D and SyNG-R achieve the best or competitive performance on triangle density, clustering coefficient, eigenvalue distribution, and degree centrality metrics (Tables 2-6).

SyNG-D requires the lowest equivalent FLOPs (e-FLOPs) among compared generators across network sizes, while GRAN and EDGE require substantially higher computational cost despite worse fidelity (Figure 3).
On higher-order structural metrics such as 4-node graphlet counts and 4-cycle counts, SyNG variants outperform EDGE, GRAN, and CELL baselines (Table 7).

0pyFbZSfbT.text: The SWE-fficiency benchmark comprises 498 real-world code optimization tasks drawn from 9 widely used Python repositories including numpy, pandas, and scipy (abstract only).

Agents are tasked with investigating code semantics, localizing bottlenecks and relevant tests, and producing a patch that matches or exceeds expert speedup while passing the same unit tests (abstract only).
The top-performing agents evaluated on SWE-fficiency achieve less than 0.23x of the expert-level speedup on average across the 498 tasks (abstract only).

Agents struggle specifically with localizing optimization opportunities in large codebases, reasoning about execution flow across multiple functions, and maintaining correctness of proposed optimizations (abstract only).

IPAeknfo2x.text: Smoothie represents each token as a vector of negative squared Euclidean distances to all vocabulary embeddings, and its forward diffusion process progressively corrupts this distance vector to dissolve semantic information while preserving discreteness-related structure (Section on method/Algorithm 1).

Training minimizes a mean-squared-error loss between predicted and original token embeddings after corrupting the distance matrix D0 with noise scaled by σt, while sampling iteratively denoises from Gaussian noise and decodes tokens via argmax of distance scores (Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2).
On the QQP paraphrase dataset, Smoothie achieves a BLEU score of 28.3, outperforming SSD-LM's 22.9 BLEU (Table with QQP results).
On the Newsela-Auto simplification dataset, Smoothie achieves a SARI score of 37.6, matching or exceeding SeqDiffuSeq's 37.1 (Table with Newsela-Auto results).

Smoothie requires 2 to 10x fewer denoising steps than competing diffusion methods while achieving a mean rank of 2 across the four sequence-to-sequence tasks evaluated (Section reporting mean rank and step-efficiency).

The reverse-process noise parameter δ̃ controls a fluency-diversity trade-off, with lower δ̃ improving perplexity but reducing diversity, and δ̃=0.25 found optimal for sequence-to-sequence tasks (Figure 2).

orjnT28Vp6.text: Theorem 1 establishes that the Nash Equilibrium of the Distributional Alignment min-max game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level fine-tuning optimization problem, with the optimal policy taking the form π*(y|x) ∝ π0(y|x) q*(E(y)|x) (Theorem 1).

The framework yields three GRPO-compatible algorithmic instantiations: Diversity-GRPO, which rewards inversely to answer frequency within sampled groups (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1); Coherence-GRPO, which rewards agreement with a global majority-vote consensus across task-preserving input transformations (Section 5.3, Algorithm 2); and Pairwise-GRPO, which uses pairwise semantic distance to reward trace centrality in open-ended domains (Section 6.2, Algorithm 3).
On GSM8K, across three 3B-parameter models, Pairwise-GRPO improves accuracy by +4.55 to +9.18 percentage points absolute (+6.06% to +12.46% relative) over the baseline (Table 1).
On GSM8K, Coherence-GRPO improves accuracy by +3.18 to +7.81 percentage points absolute (+4.80% to +10.60% relative), a smaller gain than Pairwise-GRPO (Table 1).

On TriviaQA, Pairwise-GRPO achieves up to +42.06% relative improvement in exact match and +18.12% relative improvement in F1 score, with Coherence-GRPO yielding smaller and less consistent improvements (Table 2).

SbOzVVh3kr.text: In Slippery Four Rooms and MuJoCo continual-RL benchmarks with gradual naturalistic non-stationarity, stability-preserving methods (EWC, synaptic consolidation) consistently outperform a plasticity-injection baseline (Section 5.1, Figures 3 and 5).

Applying multi-timescale synaptic consolidation to Successor Feature parameters (SF+SC) achieves higher AUC than applying the same consolidation to TD3 Q-values (TD3+SC) across tested environments (Section 5.2, Figure 1(d)).

Discretized multi-timescale consolidation dynamics use K beaker-like variables governed by capacities C_k and inter-timescale flow strengths g_{k,k+1}, updated via Euler's method (Section 4, Equations 12-14, Figure 2).
Increasing the number of consolidation timescale variables to six or more improves learning performance over using zero variables (equivalent to the baseline Simple SF agent) (Section 6.1, Figure 7).
Cross-attention analysis shows faster consolidation variables (SF_u2, SF_u3) receive the highest attention while slower variables still contribute complementary stability (Section 6.2, Figure 8).
Performance gains from SF+SC cannot be attributed to parameter count alone, since larger-capacity TD3 variants with more parameters still underperform SF+SC (Figure 9).

yVNMUeuZQd.text: BITS (Binary Information Transmission for Self-Supervision) reframes self-supervised learning as discrete communication over a fixed-capacity 256-bit binary channel, using an element-wise binary cross-entropy agreement loss between hard-thresholded teacher and student messages (Section 4.2, Equation 8).
On ImageNet-1K, BITS-reset outperforms the continuous baseline SimDINO on retrieval mAP (50.64 vs 38.62), linear probing accuracy (77.8% vs 75.3%), and k-NN accuracy (73.5 vs 69.52) (Table 1).
BITS representations exhibit higher effective dimensionality than SimDINO (358 vs 156) and higher effective rank (480 vs 324) (Table 2, Figure 1).

On unsupervised object detection on COCO, BITS-reset achieves 6.4 AP50 versus 5.0 for SimDINO, and on DAVIS2017 video segmentation BITS-reset yields a marginal gain (62.51 vs 61.98) over SimDINO (Table 6, Table 7).

Ablations show per-bit binary cross-entropy substantially outperforms cosine-similarity agreement on the discrete channel (43.44 vs 36.34 mAP), and periodic head resets every 10 epochs further raise mAP from 43.44 to 50.64 (Section 5.3).

Analysis of the learned binary code shows individual bits carry reusable semantic attributes across classes, with average marginal entropy of about 0.9 bits per dimension and joint entropy of 7.1 out of 8 bits over 8-bit blocks, indicating complementary but non-redundant information (Section 5.5).

FJLz8swPpd.text: Effective symmetry breaking is defined as breaking parameter symmetries in a way that changes the realized input-output function on the data support, not merely the structural parameter space, formalized via effective function classes (Section 4, Proposition 4.2).
Theorem 4.6 shows the projected center gap between neurons scales as γ^out = Θ(σ_F√k · m^{-2/k}), linking symmetry-breaking effectiveness to intrinsic data dimension k and neuron count m.

Theorem 5.1 bounds the chord deviation of ReLU networks along the linear interpolation path between two independently trained, effectively symmetry-broken solutions, and Proposition 5.2 uses this bound to establish a linear-mode-connectivity (LMC) barrier bound.
Neuron identifiability, enabled by effective symmetry breaking, permits merging representations from independently trained networks without any prior activation alignment step (Section 4, Figure 1).
Section 4.5 identifies a tradeoff whereby strong symmetry breaking that improves identifiability comes at the cost of reduced feature-learning capability.

Experimental validation across activation matching, LMC barrier measurements, and neuron swap costs under varying subspace coherence ν(𝒰) is reported in Figures 3-6, consistent with the spectral concentration result of Theorem 4.4.

F75QiiFIOr.text: LoRe partitions per-step interactions into an exactly-evaluated high-conflict 'Cluster' subset M_t and an approximated 'Bath' using a lightweight recall signal g_t, implemented as a budgeted routing operator (Section 3.3).

On maximum independent set at n=15,000 nodes, LoRe achieves an 8.16x speedup and 11.9x memory reduction (86.7 GB to 7.32 GB) versus the full-interaction baseline, and extends feasible inference to n=50,000 where the baseline runs out of memory (Section 4.1, Table 2).

On maximum independent set, LoRe's speedup over the baseline grows from about 2x at n=1,000 nodes to about 8x at n=10,000-15,000 nodes, while solution-quality retention improves from 0.815±0.048 at n=1k to 1.010±0.013 at n=15k (Table 2).
On TSP at n=1000, LoRe achieves a 14.61±1.07x end-to-end speedup (0.94s vs 13.6s) with a 43.9x memory reduction (4.83 GB to 0.11 GB) and tour-quality retention of 0.960±0.006 (Section 4.2, Table 2).

State-dependent dynamic re-routing of the Cluster subset outperforms static support sets under matched interaction budgets, motivated by the observation that edge-set overlap between consecutive refresh intervals is only 25.7% early in the diffusion process (Section 4.3, Figure 4).

m5bAH5xN4R.text: SCP-ΔR combines relative probability distributions (RPDs), which remove global scaling effects, with base-model smoothing that preserves only the most informative token deviations, formalized as the SpaRPS (Sparse Relative Probability Shift) property (Section 3.2, Section 4).
Proposition 3.3 proves that m-SpaRPS distributions satisfy Dr(p,q) ≤ (m/n)(log M + |log α|), which for realistic parameters (m=20, n=32000) yields a bound of Dr(p,q) ≤ 0.025.
At the 99th percentile, empirical kX bounds drop from 11.6 for CP-Δ to 0.98 for CP-ΔR and to 0.004 for SCP-ΔR, an orders-of-magnitude improvement (Figure 1(b)).

Theorem 4.4 bounds the likelihood ratio between fine-tuned and reference models via r₁(y|x)/r₀(y|x) ≤ (tr₁(x)/tq(x))·e^{kX}, and Theorem 4.5 extends this bound to reference models trained similarly to the target model (Section 4).

Empirically, SCP-ΔR-b reduces canary exposure from 28 (no protection) to 1.4 and PII full extraction rate from 0.84 to under 0.001, while token-extraction AUC remains comparable across methods at about 0.67-0.70 (Table 2, Section 5.3).

Next-token prediction accuracy under SCP-ΔR remains stable at 0.495±0.005 across smoothing parameter values m in {10, 100, 1000}, indicating utility is preserved with minimal degradation (Table 2, Figure 3(a)).

DqcPyN2gjD.text: Theorem 1 shows geometric redundancy (low cosine distance between adjacent layer representations) implies functional redundancy under stated regularity assumptions, with Theorem 2 extending this to empirical estimators with finite-sample bounds (Theorems 1 and 2).

Theorem 5 shows informational redundancy, defined via low conditional entropy H(X_l | X_{l-1}) between adjacent layers, implies functional redundancy under a Markov chain assumption on the layer sequence (Theorem 5).

Early vision-token layers (roughly layers 4-8) exhibit low pairwise cosine distance (around 0.02-0.07) with P[D_V<0.05] approximately 0.97, indicating strong geometric redundancy that enables late vision-token entry with minimal accuracy loss (Table 1).

Visual Attention Ratio (VAR) analysis shows cross-attention to vision tokens is concentrated in middle layers, with early and late layers exhibiting minimal cross-attention, motivating separate early-exit and late-entry skipping conditions (Figure 3).

Skipping middle layers (roughly layers 12-20), where redundancy conditions do not hold, causes severe accuracy degradation (over 50% loss), empirically validating that the framework's redundancy conditions align with actual performance degradation from layer skipping (Table 2).

Empirical validation across LLaVA-1.5 (7B and 13B) and LLaVA-NeXT (7B) confirms that early vision tokens consistently exhibit geometric and proximal redundancy across all tested datasets, and that the framework's predicted skippable layers align with existing methods such as AdaSkip and DeepInsert (Figure 4).

BbxYfjeT5b.text: Intersection-over-Union between top-attributed words for brain alignment (BA) and next-word prediction (NWP) is low at stringent thresholds (t ≤ 10%), with IoU approximately 0.1-0.2, indicating the two tasks rely on largely distinct word subsets across the Harry Potter fMRI dataset and the Moth Radio Hour naturalistic fMRI dataset (Section 4, Figure 2; Appendix D).

Attribution spread analysis shows NWP requires significantly more words at early layers while BA shows higher attribution spread at middle and late layers, suggesting BA integrates higher-order semantic and discourse-level structure rather than local context (Section 4, Figure 3).

At an attribution threshold of t=60%, BA marks roughly 33% of features as semantic compared to roughly 20% for NWP, while NWP relies heavily on syntax-tagged features, quantifying the semantic-versus-syntax divergence between the two tasks (Section 4, Figure 4).

Positional-bias analysis using Center of Mass shows NWP exhibits a sharp bimodal distribution with both recency and primacy peaks, whereas BA shows a more pronounced and broad recency bias without a comparable primacy peak (Section 4, Figure 5).

The five evaluated 1-2B-parameter language models (Falcon3-1B, Gemma-2B, Llama3.2-1B, Mamba-1.4B, Zamba2-1.2B) all reproduce the same distinct-word-subset and recency/primacy findings, indicating the results generalize across Transformer, SSM, and hybrid architectures (Table 1; Appendix G).

Masking the top 1% of attributed words nearly abolishes predictive power, increasing NWP loss by over 100% and reducing brain-alignment correlation by roughly 100%, validating that the attribution method identifies causally important words (Appendix C).

3GPPUHlJU9.text: In the single-step (1NFE) setting with guidance on ImageNet-256px, the Adversarial Flow (AF) B/2 model achieves an FID that approaches the performance of larger consistency-based XL/2 models despite its smaller size (Table 4).
The AF-XL/2 model achieves a new state-of-the-art single-step FID of 2.38 on ImageNet-256px, surpassing the AlphaFlow-XL/2 baseline's FID of 2.81 under the same 1NFE setting (Table 4).

Deeper single-step AF-XL/2 variants with 56 layers and 112 layers achieve FIDs of 2.08 and 1.94 respectively at 1NFE, surpassing the standard-depth XL/2 model and demonstrating that single-step generation quality scales with network depth (Table 7).
Increasing the number of function evaluations for AF-XL/2 improves FID from 2.38 at 1NFE to 2.11 at 2NFE and 2.02 at 4NFE (Table 4).
An ablation shows that training diverges without the optimal transport loss term (λ_ot), demonstrating it is essential for stabilizing single-step adversarial flow training (Table 1).

Section 3.8 demonstrates that the deep architecture (56- and 112-layer variants) can be trained end-to-end via transformer block repetition without requiring intermediate timestep supervision (Section 3.8).

jEQQBE30m1.text: A ChatGPT-generated Python script for buying tokens on pump.fun via Solana contained a malicious API endpoint (api.solanaapis[.]com/pumpfun/buy) that instructed the victim to transmit their wallet's private key, resulting in an approximately $2,500 cryptocurrency loss in November 2024, as documented from the victim's public Twitter thread (Section 2, Figure 1, Figure 2).

Across four production LLMs used as code-generation models (gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, llama-4-scout, deepseek-v3) paired with three prompt-generation LLMs over more than 265,000 prompts, Scam2Prompt's developer-style prompts triggered malicious URL generation in an average of 4.24% of generated programs, ranging from 3.19% (llama-4-scout codegen paired with deepseek-v3 prompts) to 5.94% (gpt-4o-mini codegen paired with gpt-4o prompts) (Table 1).

Applying the 1,377-prompt Innoc2Scam-bench benchmark to seven additional production LLMs released in 2025 shows malicious code generation rates ranging from 12.9% (gemini-2.5-pro) to 47.3% (deepseek-chat-v3.1), with gemini-2.5-pro achieving its low rate partly via aggressive content filtering that refused over 40% of prompts (Table 2).

NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails with Llama Nemotron Safety Guard V2 detected malicious code at rates of only 0 to 0.7% across the tested models, and OpenAI's Moderation API flagged none of 3,452 generated malicious outputs, while Llama Guard 3 flagged only 291 of 3,452 (8.43%), showing guardrail defenses provide limited risk reduction against this endpoint-level threat (Section 5.3, Table 14).

A RAG-based agent built with GPT-4o that performs web searches and checks URL safety reduced GPT-4o's malicious URL generation rate from 50.04% to 29.41%, indicating substantial residual risk remains even with this mitigation (Section 5.3, Table 15).

srAuLCB3Ca.text: Hallucination-related signals concentrate in intermediate layers of large language models rather than in the final layer, motivating automated layer selection over exhaustive per-layer evaluation (Section 1).

First Effective Peak of Intrinsic Dimension (FEPoID), which uses a forward-horizon parameter w (default 7) to filter spurious early peaks in the intrinsic-dimension curve, achieves the highest average AUROC among four criterion families across five QA hallucination-detection datasets (CoQA, SQuAD, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, PsiloQA): 0.7253 for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and 0.8531 for Mistral-7B (Section 3, Table 2).
On summarization hallucination-detection benchmarks (HaluEval, CNN/DM), FEPoID outperforms alternative layer-selection criteria with an average AUROC of 0.6080 for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (Table 3).
FEPoID is training-free and computationally efficient, requiring only 10.14 seconds on average across benchmarks compared to 27-58 seconds for gradient-based alternatives, a 3-6x speedup (Table 4).

First-Sentence Truncation (FST), proposed to remove end-of-sequence noise from inconsistent continuations, semantic drift, and degenerate repetition, yields consistent AUROC improvements of roughly 1-5% across tested layer-selection methods, with larger gains for LLaMA (more susceptible to such noise) than Mistral (Section 5, Figure 3, Figure 5).

dIUrE5eR00.text: Under uniform log-Sobolev and relative smoothness/Lipschitz assumptions (Assumptions 4-5), the continuous-time MMFLD objective converges linearly with rate exp(-2 C_LSI * lambda * t), where C_LSI is the uniform log-Sobolev constant (Theorem 3.2).
The finite-particle approximation error is bounded as lambda*KL(mu*^(N) || mu*^{⊗N})/N ≤ LR^2/(2N), quantifying the gap between the N-particle optimum and the mean-field optimum (Theorem 4.1).

The time- and particle-discretized MMFLD algorithm (Algorithm 1, forward Euler with N particles and step size eta) satisfies a convergence guarantee that is uniform in time, giving uniform-in-time propagation of chaos (Theorem 4.3).
MMFLD is derived as an SDE combining mirror maps with mean-field Langevin dynamics: X_t = ∇φ*(Y_t), dY_t = -∇(δF(μ_t)/δμ)(X_t)dt + √(2λ∇²φ(X_t))dB_t (Equation 12, Section 3).
Numerical experiments on simplex-constrained optimization show MMFLD avoids the boundary mass accumulation and numerical instability exhibited by projected MFLD (Section 5).

KFIW6LOeT1.text: For any adaptive learning algorithm operating over n tasks with N samples each, the expected excess risk is lower-bounded by Ω((n√N)^{-1/(2-β)}), establishing that adaptation hardness persists even as per-task sample size N grows arbitrarily large (Theorem 5.2).

The impossibility result extends the no-free-lunch theorem of Hanneke & Kpotufe (2022) by removing their restriction n < 2/β - 1 on the number of source tasks, using a construction with N = Ω(exp(n)) tasks (Section 5).
When the transfer exponent is known in advance, a non-adaptive algorithm that performs ERM on identified good source tasks achieves rates faster than the adaptive minimax bound (Theorem 5.1).
Pooling data across all tasks achieves adaptive rates that are nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors, despite the general impossibility of adaptation (Lemma 5.3).

The lower bound proof uses Fano's method with a tight upper bound on the KL divergence between mixture distributions over task allocations, addressing technical obstacles not handled by prior simpler constructions (Section 5).

2OSFz8cteI.text: Feed-forward geometric foundation models such as MASt3R produce heuristic confidence scores that lack probabilistic calibration and often fail to indicate true geometric trustworthiness, motivating the need for evidential uncertainty quantification (Section 1/Abstract).

Trust3R augments a frozen MASt3R backbone with a lightweight evidential head that models pointmap uncertainty via a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior combined with gated residual mean refinement, yielding a closed-form multivariate Student-t predictive distribution (Section 3).

On the ScanNet++ benchmark, Trust3R reduces AURC from 0.1649 to 0.1223 (25% lower) and AUSE from 0.0747 to 0.0444 (41% lower) relative to the MASt3R baseline, while also improving Spearman correlation from 0.2837 to 0.4946 (Table 1, Section 4.2).
Trust3R is compared against heteroscedastic Gaussian regression, MC Dropout (T=16 forward passes), and Deep Ensembles (K=5 models) as uncertainty-quantification baselines (Table 1, Section 4).

Ablations show the choice of evidential family (Normal-Inverse-Gamma vs. Normal-Inverse-Wishart) and the gated residual refinement mechanism each contribute measurably to uncertainty quality (Table 6, Table 7, Section 4.4).

Downstream evaluation demonstrates Trust3R's uncertainty estimates improve MASt3R-SLAM pose estimation and transparent-scene reliability detection on the Tricky24 dataset (Table 8, Table 9, Section 4.5).

zVrbE9ZtEU.text: LILO uses an LLM to interpret free-form natural language feedback and prior knowledge, translating them into structured signals for a Gaussian process utility surrogate within a Bayesian optimization loop (Section 3).

LILO is evaluated against four baselines—True Utility BO (oracle), Preferential BO (binary comparisons), LLM (2-step), and LLM (direct)—across four benchmark outcome functions: DTLZ2 (d=4, k=8), Vehicle Safety (d=5, k=3), Car Cab Design (d=7, k=9), and Thermal Comfort (d=8, k=5) (Section 4.1-4.2, Figure 3).

LILO consistently outperforms both Preferential BO and the LLM-only optimizers across the synthetic and real-world benchmarks under a fixed budget of T=8 optimization iterations with feedback batch size B^pf=2 (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

LILO's relative advantage is largest early in optimization, in feedback-limited regimes, because natural language feedback conveys richer information about utility structure than pairwise comparisons alone, while LLM-only baselines plateau (Section 4.2).

Ablations show pairwise comparison feedback with EUBO-based pair selection outperforms direct scalar utility estimation for LLM-based feedback, and incorporating prior knowledge (point, area, or domain-specific) further improves optimization performance (Sections 4.3.1-4.3.3, Figure 5).

7zOtnPt85B.text: ProbMoE's Exact-k routing models expert selection as probabilistic inference over cardinality-constrained expert subsets, using a SIMPLE-style gradient estimator with a tractable normalization constant to propagate gradients through selection marginals (Section 4).

ProbMoE's Dynamic-k routing extends this to variable cardinality within a range [k_min, k_max], with the range-constrained normalizing constant computable in O(N*k_max) time (Theorem 5.1) and exact marginal probabilities given by Proposition 5.2 (Section 5).
On the OLMoE backbone, ProbMoE achieves 50.19% on GSM versus 47.00% for the DenseMixer baseline, and on the Qwen backbone reaches 53.29% on GSM and 39.23% on Translation (Table 1).

ProbMoE requires more experts to reach 99% cumulative probability mass and shows lower Top-4 assignment mass with higher normalized routing entropy than baselines, indicating broader routing support and greater routing diversity (Figures 3-4).

An ablation on OLMoE/GSM shows ProbMoE (Sample + Marginal) reaches 50.24% accuracy versus 46.6% for a Sample + Dense STE variant, demonstrating the benefit of aligning probabilistic expert selection with marginal-based optimization (Figure 2).

Wall-clock efficiency analysis shows ProbMoE with SDD-based implementation matches conventional routing throughput while DenseMixer requires substantially higher GPU memory due to dense expert computation (Appendix E, Figure 7).

QkfkxyRizZ.text: On the Chemistry subset of SciKnowEval, SDPO reaches 70.1% accuracy with Qwen3-8B versus 60.0% for GRPO at the 5-hour training mark (Table 3).

With Olmo3-7B-Instruct on the Chemistry subset, SDPO attains 76.8% accuracy versus 46.8% for GRPO at 5 hours of training, and reaches GRPO's 5-hour accuracy in about 30 minutes, a roughly 10x speedup (Table 3).
