On LiveCodeBench v6 (131 competitive-programming problems from Feb-May 2025), SDPO reaches 48.8% final accuracy versus 41.2% for GRPO, matching GRPO's final accuracy using 4x fewer generations (Section 4, Figure 1).

On very hard questions (pass@64 < 0.03), SDPO achieves 53.2% discovery@2750 compared to 41.5% for best-of-k sampling; on hard questions it matches best-of-k/multi-turn discovery rates with 3x fewer attempts (Section 5, Figure 13).
SDPO's improvement over GRPO grows with model scale, showing only marginal gains on Qwen3-0.6B but substantial gains on Qwen3-8B (Figure 8).

SDPO's self-teacher regularization uses an exponential moving average teacher and a symmetric Jensen-Shannon divergence distillation loss with a top-K=100 logit approximation for memory efficiency (Section 2.3).

yBAqonxCdp.text: PerturbDiff models cellular perturbation response by treating the cell distribution itself, embedded via kernel mean embeddings in an RKHS, as the diffusion variable rather than diffusing individual cells (Section 4).

On the large-scale PBMC (9.7M cells, 90 cytokine conditions) and Tahoe100M (101.2M cells, 1,137 drug conditions) benchmarks, PerturbDiff trained from scratch outperforms baselines including CPA, STATE, CellFlow, and Squidiff on nearly all of the 14 evaluation metrics (Section 5).

PerturbDiff achieves win rates above 96-100% against STATE on differential-expression-related metrics, while ranking second-best (behind STATE) on the smaller Replogle CRISPR perturbation dataset (0.6M cells, 2,023 perturbations) (Section 5).

Pretraining PerturbDiff on the CellxGene atlas (60.9M cells) via a marginal pretraining strategy and then fine-tuning outperforms training from scratch specifically in low-data regimes, such as 1% and 5% subsampled PBMC (Section 5).
An ablation removing the MMD loss term consistently degrades performance, and a model-capacity scaling analysis identifies an optimum around 114M parameters (Section 5).

e0wfMUiZnY.text: Sparse autoencoders (hidden dimension D=2048, sparsity coefficient lambda=2x10^-3) trained on step-level activations of DeepSeek-R1-1.5B (500 MATH examples) produce decoder columns that cluster into distinct reasoning behaviors such as reflection and backtracking, visualized via UMAP (Section 4, Figure 2).
Normalized silhouette scores show that mid-to-late transformer layers achieve the highest separability between reasoning-behavior clusters (Section 4, Figure 3).
Steering along SAE-derived reflection/backtracking vectors improves reasoning accuracy on GPQA-Diamond from 53.23% to 62.77% under positive intervention (Table 1).
Steering interventions on SAE-derived vectors yield up to a 4.66 point accuracy improvement alongside a 13.69% reduction in token usage (Section 5, Figure 8).
A newly discovered decoder-space direction linked to model confidence modulates reflection behavior across domains and generalizes to a second model, Qwen3-8B (Section 5, Table 2).

DyA4KHj1wy.text: Across five transformer-based time series foundation models (Chronos, Chronos-Bolt, TimesFM 2.5, Toto, Moirai), ablating 28% of attention heads causes only a 6% performance drop on the GIFT-Eval benchmark of 144,000 time series (Section 1).
Middle transformer layers are consistently more ablateable (redundant) than early or late layers across all five architectures, measured via Spearman distance on GIFT-Eval (Section 3).
TimesFM 2.5 (20 layers, 16 heads, 200M parameters) shows only a 6.12% MASE increase when 28% of its attention heads are ablated using a stable-rank-based pruning criterion (Table 1, Section 5).

Attention heads are reinterpreted as Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression estimators, with a proposed 'spectral sharpness' metric derived from query-key projection matrices distinguishing sharp heads (causing context parroting/seasonality bias) from diffuse, prunable heads (Section 4).
Evaluation spans 97 datasets across 7 domains using MASE, CRPS, NRMSE, and sMAPE metrics on the GIFT-Eval benchmark (Section 2).

0dmd06JuBr.text: SimpleUniformFL, a distributed O(log n)-approximation algorithm for Uniform Facility Location, is proven to achieve expected cost O(log n)*OptS relative to the optimum (Proposition 2, Section 3.1).

The proposed MPNN can recover the O(log n) approximation guarantee of SimpleUniformFL under appropriate parameter initialization, while no constant-depth MPNN with deterministic opening probabilities can achieve this guarantee (Propositions 3 and 4, Section 3.2).

Recursive application of the MPNN yields a constant-factor approximation, and learning from finite training instances is proven to generalize to arbitrarily larger instances (Propositions 5 and 6, Section 3.3-3.4).
On synthetic 1000-vertex graphs, the MPNN achieves near-optimal cost ratios of 1.002-1.009, compared to 1.069-1.166 for SimpleUniformFL alone (Table 1, Section 4).
A model trained only on 1000-vertex graphs maintains a consistent 1.002-1.003 optimality ratio when tested on instances up to 10,000 vertices (Table 2, Section 4).

On a real city road network (one of Paris, Shanghai, London, or LA), the MPNN approach achieves approximately 41% cost reduction relative to the best feasible solution found by an ILP solver within its time limit, at roughly 4ms inference time (Section 4).

VMAHQDOtjp.text: With 4 masked objects, Causal-JEPA's object-level masking yields a 21.13% absolute improvement in counterfactual VQA per-option accuracy over the same architecture without object-level masking (Section 5.1, Table 2).

Causal-JEPA matches DINO-WM's control performance on Push-T (88.67% vs. 91.33% success rate) while using only about 1.02% of the total latent input features (4 object slots vs. 196x384 patch tokens) (Section 5.2, Table 6).
Using object-level latents instead of patch-based ones enables over 8x faster planning on Push-T (673 seconds vs. 5,763 seconds for 50 trajectories) (Section 5.2, Table 6).
Causal-JEPA is compared against slot-based baselines SlotFormer and OCVP-Seq in addition to the patch-based DINO-WM (Table 4).

Theorem 1 shows that masked-history completion forces the predictor to rely on a minimal sufficient 'influence neighborhood' of other objects to predict a masked object's state, inducing interaction-aware structure directly from the training objective (Section 6, Theorem 1).

0RnIc7RUiT.text: Theorem 4.1 shows that standard L-infinity adversarial attacks increase attribution mass outside the target region proportionally to the ambient dimensionality minus the target region size (d - |Omega|), making it hard to keep explanations sparse and localized under attack (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

TSEF combines a Temporal Vulnerability Mask (identifying sparse, connected temporal segments via mutual-information regularization) with a Frequency Perturbation Filter (applying coherent spectral perturbations within those segments) to jointly control predictions and explanations (Section 4.2).
On ECG data with the TimeX++ explainer, TSEF achieves a 95.1% attack success rate while maintaining an explanation AUPRC of 0.713 against the reference rationale (Section 5.2, Table 1).

On SeqComb-MV with TimeX++, TSEF attains 0.789 attack success rate and 0.661 AUPRC, compared to PGD's 0.745 attack success rate but only 0.484 AUPRC, showing PGD achieves misclassification but destroys explanation alignment (Section 5.2, Table 1).

An ablation study shows both the Temporal Vulnerability Mask and Frequency Perturbation Filter components are necessary; removing either substantially degrades the joint attack/explanation objective (Section 5.5, Table 2).
On real-world PAM and Epilepsy deployment scenarios, models remain vulnerable to dual-target attacks even when using clean explanations as the reference rationale (Section 5.4, Table 3).

aijGVmEG9Y.text: Across V-JEPA 2 (Large, Huge, Giant) and VideoMAE-v2-Giant, linear probe accuracy for physical variables exhibits a sharp, consistent transition from near-chance (~50%) to high accuracy (~85-95%) at roughly one-third network depth, termed the Physics Emergence Zone (Section 4.2, Figure 1).

Motion direction is decodable only from the Physics Emergence Zone onward, unlike scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration magnitude which are accessible from early layers, indicating no staged derivation of acceleration from an intermediate velocity representation (Section 5.2-5.3, Figure 2).

Motion direction is encoded as a circular population code with sine-cosine tuning requiring 40-50 orthogonal feature dimensions in the Physics Emergence Zone (rising to 80+ in deeper layers), so effective steering requires coordinated multi-feature intervention rather than editing a single direction feature (Section 7, Figure 4).

Direction-encoding and intuitive-physics (possible-vs-impossible) representations occupy nearly orthogonal subspaces, with principal angles of 69-83 degrees between them, and possible-vs-impossible discrimination requires about 20 features versus 40-50+ for direction (Section 6.2, 7.2).

Local spatiotemporal attention heads emerge specifically at the Physics Emergence Zone and support both motion-direction and physics-violation judgments; ablating these heads severely degrades dynamic-task performance while leaving static-task performance largely unaffected (Section 6.3, Table 2).

gKF5AQ91iv.text: IPBT achieves a clearly superior interquartile mean performance compared to five untuned PBT variants (PBT, PB2, PB2-Mix, BG-PBT, FIRE-PBT at fixed step sizes of 1%, 3.3%, 10%, 33.3%) across 8 image classification and reinforcement learning tasks, without any step-size tuning (Section 4.1, Figures 4-5).

Against tuned baselines run with multiple step-size configurations, IPBT matches BG-PBT's performance (difference not statistically significant) while significantly outperforming Random Search, ASHA, and SMAC3, despite IPBT running only once versus the competitors' multiple configurations (Section 4.1, Figures 4-5).

IPBT detects stagnation via z-score-normalized, Gaussian-process-smoothed performance trajectories, triggering a restart when there is no improvement for t_patience steps or when gains fall below one standard deviation over t_interval steps (Section 3.2).

On restart, IPBT reuses information via shrink-perturb on weights (multiplying by lambda_shrink=0.2 and adding noise gamma_perturb=0.1, with 50% of the population randomly reinitialized) and via a time-varying Bayesian-optimization model over prior hyperparameters and their descendants' scores, with 50% random sampling to reduce bias (Section 3.3).

The step size (steps between hyperparameter updates) starts at 1% of the total budget and doubles exponentially at each restart, and ablations show this exponential schedule is essential since linear or constant schedules perform substantially worse (Section 3.4, Figure 7).
An ablation study shows the shrink-perturb weight-reuse mechanism (lambda=0.2, gamma=0.1) is critical, as replacing it with exact copying or fully random reinitialization performs poorly (Figure 7).

3qan4Zg9rA.text: In the high-dimensional limit (d to infinity, n/d^2=O(1), m/d=O(1)), Claim 1 gives exact asymptotics for training and test error together with the limiting singular-value distribution of the learned query-key attention map, obtained via replica-symmetric analysis with approximate message passing (Section 3, Claim 1).

Corollary 1 gives an explicit formula for the perfect-recovery threshold in the noiseless case (Delta=0) and analytically predicts the interpolation threshold as a function of the sample ratio alpha=n/d^2 (Section 3, Corollary 1).

Weight decay on the query-key map acts as a nuclear-norm-like regularizer, favoring low-rank query and key matrices, and the predicted spectral density (Equation 13) shows a bulk-plus-outlier structure that separates further as sample complexity alpha increases, matching qualitative features seen in real trained transformers (Section 3, Equation 13, Figure 1).
Figure 1 shows theory-simulation agreement for test error curves and singular-value spectra at multiple sample ratios (alpha=0.05, 0.5, 4, 40) for dimension d=200 (Figure 1).

For targets with power-law spectra, factorized (low-rank) parameterization of the query-key map substantially outperforms a non-factorized, Frobenius-regularized parameterization, consistent with sequential spectral recovery producing power-law scaling of the test error (Figure 3).

Ca0cQbhA0T.text: DRTS (Double Reverse Thompson Sampling) selects one response maximizing and another minimizing a sampled reward posterior, while DeltaUCB selects the pair with the largest optimistic quality difference under upper confidence bounds (Section 1).
Fine-tuning on only 5,000-10,000 actively-selected preference samples via DRTS/DeltaUCB matches or beats models trained on 60,000 randomly or statically selected samples (Figure 3).
DRTS and DeltaUCB achieve comparable or superior downstream performance using as little as one-sixth of the annotated data required by static baselines (Abstract).

On RewardBench 2, DeltaUCB improves by +0.339 and DRTS by +0.312 over the baseline, while mean downstream performance gains are +0.127 (DRTS) and +0.120 (DeltaUCB) versus +0.046 for random sampling (Table 2).

Standard dueling-bandit selection methods (DTS, MaxMinLCB) underperform random sampling, indicating regret-minimization objectives are misaligned with preference-data-quality objectives (Section 5.4-5.5).

Gains from DRTS and DeltaUCB hold consistently across four prompt datasets (UltraFeedback, SkyworkReward, Combined, Tulu 3) and across three optimization algorithms (DPO, IPO, SimPO) (Section 5.4-5.5).

iJDJCO4mji.text: mmBERT is pretrained on 3 trillion tokens split across three phases: 2.3T tokens pre-training, 600B tokens mid-training for context extension, and 100B tokens in a decay phase (Section 3).
Cascading Annealed Language Learning expands language coverage across training phases from 60 to 110 to 1,833 languages, with temperature sampling decreasing from 0.7 to 0.5 to 0.3 (Section 3.2).
An inverse mask ratio schedule lowers the masking rate from 30% in pre-training to 15% in mid-training to 5% in the decay phase (Section 3.3).
On GLUE, mmBERT Base scores 86.3 average versus 83.3 for XLM-R Base, and mmBERT Small scores 84.7 versus 78.3 for Multilingual MiniLM (Table 2).
On XTREME, mmBERT Base averages 72.8 versus 70.4 for XLM-R, and on MTEB Multilingual, mmBERT Base averages 54.1 versus 52.4 for XLM-R (Table 3, Table 5).
Adding low-resource languages during the decay phase yields a 68% relative increase (12.1 absolute F1 points) on Tigray despite only 100B decay-phase tokens (Figure 2).

RyaQldE2Gh.text: SPARe+CKPT reduces time-to-train by 40-50% relative to traditional replication with checkpointing at a simulated 600k-GPU scale (Table 2, Section 5.2.2).
SPARe+CKPT achieves a minimal time-to-train/T0 ratio of 2.34-2.92 compared to 3.88-6.07 for replication+checkpointing under the same settings (Section 5.2.2).

Theorem 4.2 shows SPARe's average computation overhead S̄(N,r) stays near 2-3x even as redundancy r increases to about 20, unlike traditional replication whose overhead scales linearly with r (Theorem 4.2).
Theorem 4.3 derives an optimal redundancy level r* approximately equal to floor(log2(N) + 0.833) that minimizes time-to-train (Theorem 4.3, Equation 8).
SPARe+CKPT achieves system availability of 87.00% at N=200 GPUs, 93.90% at N=600, and 96.54% at N=1000 (Figure 7, Section 5.2.2).

Theoretical predictions from the SPARe model are validated against SimGrid discrete-event simulation with a 600k H100 GPU cluster (MTBF 300s, Weibull k=0.78) to within 4% absolute error (Figure 8, Table 1).

gXXrubolmR.text: SAE-TM extends Latent Dirichlet Allocation into a continuous topic model over embedding spaces, then relates SAEs trained with an L1 sparsity penalty to this continuous topic model (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
SAE-TM's topic interpretation pipeline merges related learned SAE features into topics via k-means clustering (Section 4).

On five text datasets, SAE-TM outperforms eight baseline topic models (AVITM, CombinedTM, DecTM, DVAE, ETM, FASTopic, NSTM, TSCTM) on coherence and diversity across topic counts of 50, 100, 200, 300, and 500 (Table 2).
At 50 topics on text data, SAE-TM attains an intruder-detection accuracy (CI) of 54.54 and coherence rating (CR) of 76.94 (Table 2).
On three image datasets (CIFAR100, Food101, SUN397), SAE-TM achieves CI=44.05 and CR=83.77 at 50 topics while maintaining topic diversity (Table 3).

SAE-TM is applied to inspect large-scale image datasets (ImageNet, CC3M, CC12M, YFCC-15M) and to analyze topic evolution across seven eras of Japanese woodblock prints (Figure 3, Figure 4, Section 6).

8CBWgJY7n9.text: CoLA introduces a cross-modal low-rank adaptation mechanism, formalized in Equations 1-4, that models interactions between frozen multimodal encoders rather than adapting each modality independently as in standard LoRA (Section 3).
On the visual grounding benchmarks RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, CoLA achieves an approximately 3% relative performance gain over standard LoRA (Table 3-5, Section 4).
On the audio-visual benchmarks AVE (Audio-Visual Event Detection) and AVS (Audio-Visual Segmentation), CoLA achieves an approximately 2% relative gain over standard LoRA (Table 6-7, Section 4).
CoLA is presented as enabling the first multi-task parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework applied to visual grounding tasks (Section 4).
CoLA's gains are demonstrated across frozen multimodal foundation encoders including CLIP, ImageBind, and DINOv2/CLAP-based backbones (Section 2, Section 4).

Q3UQSz4Giw.text: MisActBench contains 558 trajectories with 2,264 annotated actions, including 1,000 misaligned steps split across Malicious Instruction Following (562), Harmful Unintended Behavior (210), and Other Task-Irrelevant Behavior (228) (Section 3, Table 2).
On the offline MisActBench evaluation, DeAction achieves roughly a 15% absolute F1 improvement over baselines, reaching up to 82.8% F1 with a GPT-5.1 Thinking backbone (Table 3, Section 5.1).
In online evaluation, DeAction reduces attack success rate by over 90% across computer-use agents on RedTeamCUA while maintaining or improving benign task success on OSWorld (Table 5, Section 5.2).

The two-stage detection design (fast check plus systematic analysis) achieves 79.9% F1 at 11.3s latency, letting about 45% of actions bypass the more expensive systematic analysis (Table 4, Section 5.1).
The guardrail adds roughly 25% latency overhead per step (about 7.2s of a 28.1s average step execution time) when deployed online (Section 5.2, Table 5).

DeAction's correction loop iteratively revises flagged actions using structured feedback from four components: Injection Analysis, Action Understanding, Outcome Prediction, and Misalignment Analysis (Section 4.1-4.2).

I3SK0WFmD0.text: Langevin Speculative Dynamics (LSD) achieves 3-9x speedups over standard target-model molecular dynamics, depending on system size and draft-target pairing, via reflection-maximal couplings that verify or correct draft-model steps against a target model (Figure 5, Equation 10).
The speedup bound speedup ≲ 1/(c + mean(beta)) depends only on the draft-to-target cost ratio c and the mean rejection rate beta (Proposition 3.1, Equation 10).
Theorem 3.1 shows composing a verified coupling with invertible pre-/post-processing transformations preserves the coupling and maximality properties needed for correctness (Theorem 3.1).
For FCC copper systems (32-2048 atoms, T=1500K), LSD is evaluated with draft models Orb-v3-direct-20-omat, UMA-tiny-direct, and EMT against UMA-S and UMA-M targets (Figure 5).
For a 300-atom bulk water system, LSD corrects a non-conservative draft model's 42.8K excess kinetic-temperature heating down to match the target model's 1.0K deviation (Table 1, Section 5.3).

In the LGPS superionic conductor system, LSD reproduces target-model lithium self-diffusivity within sampling error across temperature ranges, and matches target-model MMD noise levels on a 108-atom copper distribution parity test (Figure 7).

miLK9YcxtA.text: Theorem 3.2 proves an identifiability-impossibility result: even an SAE with arbitrarily low reconstruction error can have a stable dictionary yet non-identifiable sparse codes, since another encoder achieving the same reconstruction accuracy can differ in sparsity pattern with positive probability (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.6 shows that when a dictionary satisfies the proposed approximate restricted isometry property (aRIP, Definition 3.3), two independently trained SAEs' dictionaries and sparse codes are near-identifiable up to a signed permutation, with error terms vanishing as reconstruction error and aRIP level go to zero (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.6).

On synthetic i.i.d.-dictionary data, switching TopK to AbsTopK activation reduces reconstruction MSE from 0.447 to 0.318 (about 30-40% lower) and raises oracle code IoU identifiability from 0.172 to 0.914 (Table 1).

The full iSAE-ME variant (bidirectional features + aRIP regularization + multistep encoder) attains synthetic i.i.d. reconstruction MSE of 0.001 and oracle code IoU of 0.997, versus 0.447 MSE and 0.172 IoU for the TopK baseline (Table 1).

On Pythia-160M layer-12 activations on The Pile (dictionary size 4096, sparsity k=40), iSAE-ME achieves the lowest reconstruction MSE (0.148) among the TopK, AbsTopK, iSAE, and iSAE-ME variants (Table 2, Section 4).

On SAEBench evaluation of Pythia-160M SAEs, iSAE-ME achieves the best LLM cross-entropy loss preservation (3.906) among the four model variants, while the multistep encoder adds only about 10-15% training-time overhead over a standard TopK SAE (Table 3, Section 4.4).

Bnr4cjW6XG.text: In the realizable universal transductive online learning setting, Theorem 2.8 establishes a trichotomy: a concept class achieves O(1) mistakes if it has no infinite indifferent Littlestone tree, Theta(log T) mistakes if it has an infinite indifferent Littlestone tree but no infinite indifferent LCLL tree, and unavoidable Omega(T) mistakes if it has an infinite indifferent LCLL tree (Theorem 2.8).

The Level-Constrained-Littlestone-Littlestone (LCLL) tree structure is defined so that nodes at depth k contain k+1 instances and branch into 2^(k+1) children, with edges labeled by label sequences forming paths through depth-(k+1) Littlestone trees (Section 2).

The indifference property requires that all descendants of a node appearing after v in the tree agree with v's label predictions on the instances preceding v in breadth-first-search order (Section 2).

In the agnostic setting, Theorem 2.9 shows a concept class is agnostically learnable in the transductive online model if and only if it lacks an infinite indifferent LCLL tree, in which case it achieves regret of order sqrt(T) up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 2.9).

bz66grGgjI.text: Prime attention replaces the standard key projection k_j = x_j W_k with a pair-specific modulated key k~_j = k_j elementwise-multiplied by a learnable modulator F_{i,j}, implementing 'dynamic relational learning' in contrast to standard attention's 'static relational learning'.

Across 11 benchmark datasets and three backbone architectures (Timer-XL, FreDF, iTransformer), prime attention yields up to a 6.5% forecasting accuracy improvement over standard attention on the Weather dataset with Timer-XL (Table 1, full results in Table 6, Appendix G).

On heterogeneous multivariate datasets (Solar, Weather), prime attention achieves an average improvement of up to 4.0% across backbone models, while gains are only marginal on homogeneous single-attribute datasets (ECL, Traffic) (Table 1).

Prime attention matches standard attention's performance at input length L=96 while using only L=48 or L=64, corresponding to 40% and 33% less input sequence length respectively (Section 7.2, Figure 1).
Prime attention is compared against LagTS, LIFT, Differential Transformer, and Autoformer, showing consistent superiority across the tested datasets (Table 2).

Ablation studies on sparsification and initialization strategies for the modulator, plus a complexity analysis and attention-map analysis showing prime attention can behave as a hybrid channel-dependent/channel-independent model, are reported in the appendix (Appendix F.1, F.2, F.3).

5Zwnr6uSlv.text: The paper derives a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound for RL whose dependence on the discount factor scales as γ² rather than the γ⁴ dependence of prior mixing-time bounds (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.2).
Lemma 3.1 establishes a bounded-differences property for the empirical RL loss under single-transition perturbations, with coefficients c_(h,t) = γ^(h-1) R_max / T (Section 3.1).

The bound yields non-vacuous generalization certificates for Soft Actor-Critic once the number of trajectories T exceeds a threshold governed by R_max², the chain mixing time τ_min, and γ (Theorem 3.2).

PB-SAC, a PAC-Bayes-guided variant of SAC that samples posterior parameters for exploration and alternates optimization via a PAC-Bayes-κ decomposition, matches or exceeds vanilla SAC's return on HalfCheetah, Hopper, and Ant while producing bounds that tighten during training (Figure 1, Algorithm 1 in Appendix D).
Hyperparameter settings for PB-SAC, SAC, and PBAC across MuJoCo tasks are reported, including a prior moving-average decay of ι=0.99 (Table 1, Appendix F).

MJBAmHLr8E.text: Geo-R1 is trained in two stages: geospatial-thinking scaffolding via supervised fine-tuning (Section 4) followed by geospatial-thinking elevation via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using indirect cross-view alignment signals (Section 5).
On in-distribution cross-view pairing, Geo-R1 improves accuracy from a 19.0% base-model baseline to 82.4%, with the RL-only Geo-R1-Zero variant reaching 78.1% (Table 1).
Geo-R1 is evaluated zero-shot on 13 GeoChain geo-reasoning tasks spanning geographical, environmental, and sociocultural categories, without task-specific fine-tuning (Figure 1, Table 6).
On IMAGEO-Bench, Geo-R1 achieves 81.5% country-level accuracy and a median geolocation distance error of 69.4 km (Table 8).
The RLVR stage exhibits a 'geospatial Aha Moment,' with reward peaking at approximately 100 training steps (Figure 8).
Training data comprises the CV-Cities dataset of 223,736 panorama-satellite image pairs and a synthetic chain-of-thought corpus of 12,646 samples used for the SFT stage (Section 4).

gdHmdh0VdA.text: Mahalanobis-based OOD detection performance, measured by false-positive rate, varies substantially across pretrained self-supervised model families and fine-tuning regimes on the NINCO benchmark (Figure 2, Table 1).

Within-class spectral ratios and local intrinsic dimensionality (LID) track Mahalanobis OOD detection performance, with a Spearman correlation of ρₛ=0.85 between the LID-based within-class scatter slope and standard Mahalanobis Distance performance (Section 4.1, Figure 6).
A regression predicting Mahalanobis OOD performance from geometric features achieves MAE=0.72, R²=0.25 for standard MD, versus MAE=0.89, R²=0.47 for Relative Mahalanobis Distance (RMD) (Section 5.2).

Radially scaled ℓ2 normalization, controlled by an exponent β searched over [-2,3] in 0.25 increments, is proposed to control feature radii and shown to outperform fixed-normalization baselines (Section 5.1, Figure 7).
Relative Mahalanobis Distance (RMD) consistently outperforms standard Mahalanobis Distance (MD), especially for models not fine-tuned on ImageNet (Table 2, Section 3.2).

V6d1eHy6KE.text: TEAM achieves up to 2.2x speedup over a vanilla MoE dLLM on the HumanEval benchmark using the SDAR backbone, with negligible degradation in task performance (Table 1, Section 4.2).

TEAM reduces the average number of activated experts per decoded token from 17.66 (vanilla) to 6.92, a 35-39% reduction depending on benchmark, while increasing accepted tokens per decoding iteration by 1.49-1.74x (Figure 1, Section 4.2).

TEAM combines three mechanisms: Delayed Caching for Decoded tokens (DCD, Section 3.2), Speculative Exploration for Hot tokens (SEH, Section 3.3), and Limited Activation for Cold tokens (LAC, Section 3.4), each exploiting temporal or spatial consistency in expert routing.
Ablations show TEAM's speedup is sensitive to the DCD cache refresh interval and to hot-token hyperparameters (Table 2, Table 3, Section 4.3).
Vanilla SDAR activates approximately 54 experts per forward pass while accepting only about 3 tokens, motivating TEAM's expert-activation reduction strategy (Figure 1, Section 3.1).

dPDOQs7qHl.text: ACE (Adaptive Complementary Exploration) is built on a novel Divergent Trajectory Balance (DTB) objective (Definition 3.2, Definition 3.3) that distinguishes over-allocated from under-allocated regions of state space (Definition 3.1).

Proposition 3.4 establishes a Complementary Sampling Property ensuring ACE's exploitation and exploration updates target disjoint regions, and Proposition 3.9 shows the resulting sampler reaches an equilibrium state.
On a grid-world task, ACE achieves the best goodness-of-fit to the target reward distribution among compared GFlowNet training methods (Figure 6).

ACE discovers diverse high-reward states faster than baseline methods on sequence design and bit-sequence generation tasks (Figure 3), as well as on bag generation and quadratic knapsack problems (Figure 4).
On antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery, ACE identifies a larger number of high-fitness AMPs than prior GFlowNet exploration methods (Figure 8).

iuIPAhZpxz.text: A linear relationship between optimal model size and graph search entropy is established with R² = 0.85 (Figure 4, Section 5.2).

Roughly 124 additional parameters in the optimal model size are required per 1-bit increase in graph search entropy, translating to about 0.008 bits of information per parameter for implicit reasoning tasks (Section 5.2).
Graph search entropy H(G) is defined as Ne(log(λ) + Hr(G)), combining an entity entropy rate based on the largest eigenvalue λ and a relation entropy rate Hr(G) (Section 5.2).
Optimal model size stabilizes after roughly 4k training steps regardless of further training, while more training triples require larger optimal model size (Section 5.1, Figure 3).
The scaling law is validated on the real-world FB15K-237 knowledge graph, where the observed optimal model size matches the prediction from the synthetic experimental framework (Figure 4).
The authors note the results are restricted to knowledge-graph pretraining and direct applicability to real-world text pretraining remains unvalidated (Section 5.3).

acvRKe2uMW.text: SIGS (Symbolic Iterative Grammar Solvers) combines a grammar-generated function space with a Grammar Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) embedding and CMA-ES search in latent space to find analytical solutions (Section 2.2, Figure 1).
Appendix B.7.1 describes how SIGS solves coupled systems of differential equations by concatenating latent vectors z1, z2, ..., zm without retraining the model.

Table 1 reports that across 19 test problems, SIGS converges in 1 to 18 iterations, versus hundreds of iterations required by competing methods including Mathematica, Genetic Programming, PINNs, and FBPINNs.
Table 3 reports relative L2 errors on advanced problems including the 1D wave equation, diffusion equation, Burgers' equation, and shallow water equations, with SIGS achieving near-exact solutions.
Property 2.1 in Section 2.3 describes a 'one-solver-solves-all' property, whereby a single SIGS framework unifies solving across multiple PDE families.

aeeo8ZAftQ.text: A3's low-rank approximated LLaMA 3.1-70B achieves a perplexity of 4.69 on WikiText-2 at 10% compression, versus SVD-LLM's 7.87, a 3.18-point improvement (Table 1).
On LLaMA-2-7B at 10% compression on WikiText-2, A3 reaches a perplexity of 5.96 versus SVD-LLM's 8.78 (Table 1).
On LLaMA-3.1-8B at 10% compression on WikiText-2, A3 achieves a perplexity of 7.93 versus SVD-LLM's 19.12 (Table 1).
Table 2 shows A3 maintains higher average accuracy than SVD-LLM across compression levels on five downstream tasks: ARC-Challenge, BoolQ, Winogrande, GSM8K, and MMLU.

Theorem 2 (A3-QK) gives a closed-form solution via activation-aware SVD, Theorem 3 (A3-OV) gives per-head optimization using autocorrelation matrices, and Lemma 4 (A3-MLP) uses CUR decomposition for the nonlinear MLP components.
Figure 3 shows A3 achieves throughput speedup on an A100 40GB GPU for LLaMA-2-13B even at low compression ratios, whereas SVD-LLM only accelerates at higher compression ratios.

VOrzQ8GBDh.text: The paper studies domain generalization in an anti-causal setting where the outcome causes the observed covariates, so that environment perturbations affecting covariates do not propagate to the outcome (abstract only).
Two methods are proposed that penalize the model's sensitivity to variations in the mean and in the covariance of the covariates across environments, respectively (abstract only).
Both proposed methods are proven to have worst-case optimality guarantees under certain classes of environments (abstract only).

Because estimating the environment perturbation directions does not require labels, the methods can leverage unlabeled data from multiple environments, unlike prior domain generalization methods that require labeled data from multiple training environments (abstract only).
Empirical performance is demonstrated on a controlled physical system and a physiological signal dataset (abstract only).

W1P3l4rI60.text: Task complexity C(T_δ) is defined as the length of the shortest program that solves a task to performance level δ, and conditional complexity C(T_δ|θ) measures adaptation complexity given a pre-trained model's weights θ (Section 3, Definitions 3.3-3.4).
On GSM8K, 4358 bits are sufficient to increase OLMo3-32B's accuracy to 72.2% when conditioned on the pre-trained model (Section 6.1).
On FLORES-200 machine translation, 3992 bits suffice to achieve a BLEU score of 34.43 when conditioned on the pre-trained model (Section 6.1).
For IFEval instruction following, programs slightly longer than 10^7 bits (about 1.25MB) are needed, while across tasks programs as small as 1.2×10^6 bits (151 kilobytes) can suffice (Section 6.1).

Post-training collapses the complexity of reaching strong performance by several orders of magnitude relative to pre-training alone, with the complexity-performance curve (Figure 5) showing minimal additional information needed beyond a roughly 10^4-bit threshold (Section 7).

Task complexity is shown to be uncomputable in general (Corollary A.5, Appendix A), so empirical estimates in the paper are necessarily upper bounds obtained via inference-control, data, and parametric adaptation methods (Figure 1, Figure 3).

l35QweVxgn.text: Theorem 1 gives a closed-form bound on train-time forgetting for task k after training on K-k subsequent tasks, of order O~(ηT√(K-k)/(d√n) + ηT√(K-k)/(d²polylog(d)) + η²T²K²/√m) (Theorem 1).

The forgetting bounds hold under the parameter regime n = Θ~(d²K) samples, m = Ω~(d⁸K⁴) hidden-layer width, and ηT = Θ(d²) training iterations on a d-dimensional XOR cluster dataset with K tasks (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows that under the same width/sample/iteration conditions as Theorem 1, the misclassification error remains uniformly small across all K tasks with high probability after KT gradient descent iterations (Theorem 2).
Theorem 3 bounds the delayed generalization gap by η T exp(ηT(K-k+1)/√m) / n for Lipschitz, smooth loss functions, showing the gap decays with sample size n (Theorem 3).

Theorem 4 gives an improved generalization gap bound for self-bounded losses that scales poly-logarithmically rather than linearly in the number of iterations T, depending on the cumulative training loss of later tasks (Theorem 4).

Test-time forgetting is decomposed as the sum of train-time forgetting (Theorem 1) and the delayed generalization gap (Theorem 3/4), showing that network width, sample size, and later tasks' data jointly, not individually, control forgetting (Theorem 1, Theorem 3).

XHI7FCd1w1.text: On ImageNet 256x256 box-inpainting, single-step Variational Flow Maps achieve FID 33.34, versus 62-76 FID for guidance-based diffusion/flow baselines (Section 4, Table results in Experiments).
On ImageNet 256x256 Gaussian deblurring, single-step VFM achieves FID 51.05 and LPIPS 0.417, compared to 83-101 FID and 0.434-0.459 LPIPS for guidance-based baselines (Section 4).

VFM single-step sampling takes about 0.025-0.03 seconds versus 7+ seconds for guidance methods using 250 sampling steps with x2 overhead for classifier-free guidance, an inference speedup of roughly two orders of magnitude (Section 4).

On ImageNet 256x256 unconditional generation, 2-step VFM achieves FID below 10, remaining competitive with purpose-built few-step generative baselines despite being trained primarily for conditional generation (Section 4).
Proposition 3.1 shows that joint training of the flow map and noise adapter recovers the true posterior mean, whereas training them separately almost surely fails to do so (Proposition 3.1).
Proposition 3.2 links the mean flow training loss to a reconstruction error bound within the VFM objective (Proposition 3.2).

K5blb595KX.text: Theorem 3.4 proves that the attention map converges uniformly over bounded regions of radius R at rate C(R)/√n, where C(R) grows exponentially with R (Theorem 3.4).

Proposition 5.1 shows that in the hardmax regime, as the softmax temperature parameter tends to infinity, the convergence rate slows to 1/√(ln n) due to cancellation effects between opposite-signed extreme values (Proposition 5.1).

Theorem 4.4 establishes that for sub-Gaussian tokens, the transformed distribution converges at rate O(n^(-β)) with β = 1/(2(1+32Ψ)), where Ψ is the Attention-Reach Coupling defined via the spectral reach and attention horizon (Theorem 4.4, Definition 4.2).

Corollary 4.5 shows the mean of the transformed distribution converges at rate O(n^(-1/(2(1+Ψ)))), exhibiting only polynomial (not exponential) dependence on the attention-reach coupling Ψ (Corollary 4.5).

Section 6 experiments on BERT using 1M and 20M Wikipedia tokens empirically confirm sub-parametric convergence with β < 1/2, contradicting the classical parametric 1/√n rate despite compactly supported token embeddings (Section 6).

XMSaWRpEPS.text: Table 2 reports that the non-Euclidean GNS adaptive batch size strategy achieves a 66.61% reduction in optimizer steps for Signum and a 66.77% reduction for Muon, when training a 160M-parameter Llama 3 model on 3.2B C4 tokens, while matching or beating constant-batch validation loss (Table 2).
For signSGD and AdamW, the non-Euclidean GNS strategy yields step reductions of 22.58% and 67.13% respectively on the same 160M Llama 3 / C4 setup, with specSGD achieving 16.49% (Table 2).

The non-Euclidean gradient noise scales for signSGD and specSGD are derived as squared ratios of dual norms: the Manhattan (ℓ1) GNS ‖σ_k‖₁²/‖∇L(x_k)‖₁² for signSGD and the Nuclear (S1) GNS ‖C_row,k^{1/2}‖_{S1}²/‖∇L(X_k)‖_{S1}² for specSGD (Table 1, Section 3).

On 1B-parameter Llama 3 models, the adaptive strategy achieves 31.84% and 12.11% step reductions for signSGD and Signum respectively, while AdamW fails to reach the constant-batch baseline validation loss under the adaptive strategy (Section 5.1, Table 3).

The efficient variance estimation procedure (Algorithm 1) computes coordinate-wise variance and row-wise covariance estimates directly from per-rank local mini-batch gradients via an AllReduce/ReduceScatter, avoiding expensive auxiliary passes in distributed data-parallel (DDP/FSDP) training (Section 4.1, Algorithm 1).

c6KQjNRo1m.text: In the RQ1 vulnerability analysis, semantic-ambiguity imperfections (RealWorld, Expand) degrade retrieval recall by approximately 98.6% and 80.6% respectively, while geometric distortions (Rotation, Flip) degrade recall by roughly 49% and 33.5% (Section 5.2).

Quality-degradation imperfections have comparatively modest impact on retrieval recall: Blur (~5.2%), Brightness (~4.7%), and Gaussian Noise (~12.3%), versus moderate degradation from Cropping (~19.1%) (Section 5.2).

Oracle preprocessing recovers near-perfect retrieval performance for severe imperfections like Rotation, Flip, and RealWorld queries, but cannot meaningfully restore performance after Cropping due to irreversible information loss (Section 5.2).

Off-the-shelf MLLMs including GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Flash show only limited improvement on imperfect queries due to imbalanced tool selection and poor parameter prediction (RQ2, Section 5.3, Figure 4).

Supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct on just 1,000 imperfect queries (100 source images x 10 variants) yields tool-selection accuracy matching or exceeding GPT-4o and parameter-prediction accuracy surpassing all off-the-shelf models on most imperfection types (RQ3, Section 5.4).
The benchmark comprises 46,700 imperfect visual queries spanning a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 imperfection types across 5 MRAG retrieval paradigms (Section 4).

mydeyPBS0K.text: ReTreever learns a binary retrieval tree end-to-end with learnable routing functions at each internal node atop frozen encoders (Section 3).
On Natural Questions, ReTreever achieves 0.7824 Recall@10 using full representations, versus 0.7353 for the BGE bi-encoder baseline (Table 1).
ReTreever's query processing latency is 20-64ms, compared to 196-2910ms for competing hierarchical retrieval methods (Tables 2-3).
ReTreever outperforms Hier-Kmeans, Hier-GMM, and RAPTOR baselines across four QA datasets: Natural Questions, HotpotQA, TopiOCQA, and RepLiQA (Section 4.2).
Across coarse-to-fine representation sizes from 2^1 to 2^10 dimensions, ReTreever outperforms the BGE-MRL Matryoshka baseline at coarser levels while remaining competitive at finer levels (Figure 3).
An ablation shows cross-attention split functions outperform linear and MLP split-function variants for the tree routing mechanism (Appendix B, Figure 6).

uMdZHVXdOL.text: FIBER's filter-aware second-moment calibration subtracts the attenuated DP noise contribution A(ω)σ²_w from AdamW's bias-corrected second moment, where A(ω)=(2-ω)/(4-3ω) (Proposition 4.3, Corollary 4.5).
On CIFAR-10 with a CNN5 architecture, FIBER improves accuracy by +5.2 points over the DiSK baseline at privacy budget ε=0.5.
On CIFAR-100 with a WideResNet, FIBER improves accuracy by +2.6 points over DiSK at ε=2.0.
On ImageNet-1k with a ViT-small model, FIBER improves accuracy from 39% to 44% at ε=8.
FIBER requires two gradient evaluations per update (matching DiSK's compute cost) versus one for DP-AdamW, yet achieves superior accuracy under matched compute budgets (Figure 5).
An ablation shows FIBER's innovation-space filtering outperforms plain EMA gradient smoothing by 5.2 percentage points at ε=0.5, with the decoupled denoising gain ω tuned to an optimum near ω=0.9.

LQ3TocqrTh.text: Hölder++ provides the first exact implementation of symmetric Hölder pooling (α=0.5) without approximations, extended with distinct shared/private subspaces (Hölder+) and hierarchical inference for disentanglement (Hölder++) (Sections 3.1-3.3).
On CelebAMask-HQ, Hölder+ achieves an FID of 78.82±2.44 for image generation, versus 98.33±6.83 for the MMVAE+ baseline (Table 1).
On the CUBICC downstream clustering task, Hölder++ achieves 65.3±5.8 accuracy versus 58.0±13.8 for the CMVAE baseline (Table 3).

On MNIST-SVHN, Hölder++ achieves lower content-classifier accuracy on private-conditioned generations (0.119±0.001) than MMVAE+ (0.151±0.017), indicating reduced information leakage into modality-specific representations (Table 4).

Hölder+ and Hölder++ yield the best Pareto trade-offs between generative quality and coherence on PolyMNIST across five modalities compared to baselines including MMVAE, MMVAE+, MoPoE, HELVAE, and DMVAE (Section 4).

cQD2wxFhFG.text: The paper's ROSE algorithm (Regularized Offline Sequential Equilibrium), using backward induction with exact regularized equilibrium solving, achieves a duality gap bound of Õ((ηH^5+η^3H^9)C_uni log(|Q|/δ)/n) under the unilateral concentrability assumption (Theorem 6.3, Assumption 6.2).
This Õ(1/n) statistical rate for the duality gap improves on the standard Õ(1/√n) rates found in prior offline two-player zero-sum Markov game literature.
The practical model-free algorithm SOS-MD (Sequential Offline Self-play Mirror Descent) attains an Õ(1/√T) optimization error that vanishes as the number of self-play iterations T grows.
Corollary 6.9 combines statistical and optimization errors into a total bound of Õ(ηH^4/√T) + Õ((ηH^5+η^3H^9)C_uni log(|Q|/δ)/n) for SOS-MD.

The analysis decomposes the regularized duality gap into optimization and evaluation components, each bounded by a single-player Nash-averaged squared Q-error, yielding quadratic rather than linear error scaling relative to unregularized settings (Section 6).

LwB2EacVT6.text: The paper identifies a sharp phase transition in RLVR training governed by Youden's index J = TPR - FPR of the (noisy) verifier: learning succeeds when J>0, drifts neutrally when J=0, and anti-learning (systematic degradation) occurs when J<0 (Equation 6).

In the J>0 learning regime, the bad-mass dynamics ṗ = −η(J/σ(p))p²(1−p)² show that noise primarily rescales convergence time toward the same equilibrium rather than changing the final basin of attraction ('rate, not fate') (Equation 6).
For the noise-free case J=1, the dynamics admit a closed-form solution exhibiting universal t^-2 polynomial decay (Equation 8).
Theorem 6.1 extends the bad-mass dynamics to multi-armed settings using geometric factors representing within-block collision masses.

In Python code-generation experiments with Qwen2.5-3B, the sharp J=0 boundary is confirmed empirically: the model still learns at J=0.3 despite degraded reward signals, while J<0 induces collapse with a 12.6% accuracy loss (Table 1).
Section 5 develops the analysis using Shahshahani (Fisher) geometry on the probability simplex, revealing winner-take-all behavior within good modes and entropy-maximizing flow within bad modes.

gvroXZ0HS8.text: Lion with weight decay is shown to be a special instance of Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under an l-infinity norm constraint (Theorem 1, Section 3).
Muon with weight decay is shown to be a special instance of Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under a spectral-norm constraint (Theorem 2, Section 3).

Under standard smoothness and bounded-variance assumptions, the proposed Stochastic Frank-Wolfe framework achieves an expected Frank-Wolfe gap of O(1/sqrt(T)) plus a variance term, and convergence in Frank-Wolfe gap corresponds to convergence to a KKT point of the norm-constrained problem (Theorem 3, Section 4).

With heavy-tailed (p-th moment, p in (1,2]) gradient noise, a clipped variant achieves a high-probability convergence rate of O(log(T/delta) T^((1-p)/(3p-2))) without requiring large batch sizes, improved to O(log(T/delta) T^((1-p)/(2p-1))) when combined with variance reduction (Theorems 5-6, Section 4).

On a 10M-parameter nanoGPT trained on Shakespeare, the clipped variant Lion+ reaches a validation loss of 1.46 in 3,200 steps versus 4,000 steps for standard Lion, a 20% reduction, while Muon+ reduces steps from 4,400 to 4,150 versus standard Muon (Section 5).

aLnPza1dyT.text: SMAVE reformulates the MAVE objective as maximization of a smooth O(d)-invariant function on the Stiefel manifold St(p,d) and provides a closed-form Riemannian gradient for this objective (Proposition 2.7, Proposition 4.1, Section 4).

SMAVE is proven to converge almost surely to critical points under decaying step sizes and to achieve a non-asymptotic O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate matching optimal non-convex stochastic first-order methods (Propositions 4.3-4.4, Theorem 4.4, Section 4.3).

On synthetic benchmarks with n up to 5000 and p up to 200, SMAVE runs 34x to 64x faster than RMAVE while reducing estimation error (e.g., 0.25 vs 0.69 error at n=5000, p=200), requiring about 5.1 seconds versus RMAVE's 174 seconds at n=5000, p=200 (Table 2-3, Section 5.2).

On the Gas Sensor real-world regression dataset (p=128), SMAVE achieves lower MSE than RMAVE (0.018 vs 0.025, p=0.027) while running orders of magnitude faster, though on lower-dimensional datasets such as Wine Quality (p=11) and Pumadyn (p=32) RMAVE attains statistically better or comparable MSE (Tables 5-6, Section 5.3).

SMAVE's per-iteration computational cost is O(mkp^2) via sparse k-NN localization in the projected space with mini-batch size m, compared to the O(n^2 p^2) cost of OPG and RMAVE which use ambient-space or full pairwise weight-matrix computations (Section 4.1).

340Ep8sfJ3.text: GraphPFN extends the tabular foundation model LimiX with attention-based message-passing adapters inserted at each transformer block to enable graph-structured in-context learning (Section 4.1).

GraphPFN is pretrained on 4 million synthetic datasets generated from a novel prior combining degree-corrected stochastic block models with a preferential-attachment process, for 500,000 steps on 8 A100 GPUs (Section 4.1).
After finetuning, GraphPFN outperforms G2T-LimiX on 7 of 10 GraphLand datasets, for example scoring 53.38 versus 49.88 on Artnet-exp and 78.58 versus 76.32 on Hm-prices (Table 2).
On additional non-GraphLand datasets, finetuned GraphPFN outperforms G2T-LimiX on Facebook (93.06 vs 92.16) while remaining roughly competitive on Wiki-cs (82.17 vs 82.24) (Table 3).

In pure in-context-learning mode (no finetuning), GraphPFN is competitive with but sometimes underperforms G2T-LimiX on larger and denser graphs, evaluated across 13 real-world node-level datasets ranging from 11,758 to 168,114 nodes (Table 1, Section 5).

gqKLmdooqZ.text: Selecting cuts by LP bound improvement, a common supervision signal for learned cut selection, can produce branch-and-cut trees that are 2^Omega(n) times larger than trees produced by selecting cuts via a simpler efficacy proxy score (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
Arbitrarily small perturbations (epsilon) to the right-hand sides of cuts can change the minimum achievable branch-and-cut tree size from a single node to 2^Omega(n) nodes (Theorem 3.3, Section 3).

A learned branching policy whose per-node scores differ from strong branching by at most an arbitrarily small epsilon for any epsilon>0 can still produce a search tree of at least 2^(n+1)-1 nodes, versus at most 2n+1 nodes for strong branching itself (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
Merely k deviations from the strong branching trajectory can inflate the resulting tree size by a factor of 2^Omega(k) (Theorem 4.4, Section 4).
Even branching policies that assign identical scores to candidate variables can produce exponentially different tree sizes depending solely on the tie-breaking rule used (Proposition 2).

8fIsZEGmh1.text: LiveNewsBench automatically constructs question-answer pairs by retrieving global news events from the Wikipedia Current Events Archive, generating search queries, and retrieving articles from roughly 100 allowlisted news outlets via the Brave Search API, then archiving them via archive.today for reproducibility (Section 3.1).

Q&A pairs are drafted by GPT-5.1 Thinking from article clusters and filtered via self-consistency, requiring agreement between two independent model outputs, with a 200-sample human-verified test subset reaching 92% inter-annotator agreement (Section 3).

Evaluated models span 11% to 90% accuracy on the test set, with GPT-5.2's official web search API reaching 90.0%, DeepSeek V3.2 Thinking 84.5%, Claude Sonnet 4.5 82.0%, and Llama 3.1 8B only 11.0% (Table 3).
Increasing the search budget from 1 to 7 queries improves accuracy by 4 to 64.5 percentage points depending on the model, confirming that questions require multi-hop search (Table 5).
Restricting models to no internet access drops accuracy by 17 to 74.5 percentage points relative to search-enabled evaluation, indicating limited answer memorization from pretraining (Table 6).

Oj2I1xdKpv.text: On Newton Sketch, MCGS with the UCD criterion reaches 100% success using only 1,416 playouts, compared to 10,721 playouts for Preconditioned Weighted SGD and 25,158 for Block Randomized Kaczmarz (Table 2).
MCGS reduces the number of playouts needed versus standard MCTS by roughly 2-3x by merging equivalent states in a DAG rather than a tree (Section 4.3, Table 2).

The five-stage curriculum (Landweber iteration, Gradient Descent, Preconditioned GD, Sketched Preconditioned GD, Leverage-Score Subsampling) progressively increases problem difficulty, each stage introducing exactly one new failure mode resolved by one algorithmic component (Section 4.2, Table 1).

Ablating the staged curriculum causes discovery of the Newton Sketch algorithm to fail completely (0% success across all partial curricula), while the full four-stage curriculum achieves 100% success (Table 7).
MCGS sustains 50-58% state revisit rates during search, versus near-zero revisit rates for standard MCTS, demonstrating effective exploitation of shared subproblem structure (Figure 4).

The discovered framework generalizes to eigenvalue problems (power iteration and sketched power iteration) with only one added normalization primitive, achieving 100% success on all three curriculum stages (Section 5.4, Table 3).

IT7lA8t0S6.text: CARvE (Continual Anchored Router with Contrastive Embeddings) routes queries by comparing normalized query and model embeddings via temperature-scaled cosine similarity, without executing candidate models (Section 2).
At 20% domain-stratified coreset replay, CARvE reaches 82.9% domain accuracy with only 3.0% domain forgetting, versus 75.9% domain accuracy and 13.1% forgetting for random replay at 10% (Table 2).

CARvE's model-ID accuracy (43.1-46.4%) substantially exceeds sequential fine-tuning (28.0%, with 37.2% forgetting), EWC (31.3%, with 31.4% forgetting), BGE-M3 zero-shot retrieval (13.6%), and Gorilla RAG (6.7%) (Table 2).

CMRBench comprises four sequential experiences (APIBench, ToolMMBench, and two HuggingBench splits) spanning 8,693 to 10,330 samples each and 481-852 models per experience, totaling over 2,000 candidate models across 40-49 domains (Section 3.1, Table 1).

Ablating projection anchoring degrades model-ID accuracy to 40.1% and increases domain forgetting to 9.4%, a larger drop than disabling embedding anchoring (41.7% M-Acc, 7.4% D-Fgt), showing projection anchoring is the more critical component (Table 3).
At 10% replay, CARvE uses 45% fewer TFLOPs and 48% fewer GPU GB-hours than cumulative joint training, while approaching the 84.6% domain-accuracy joint-training upper bound (Figure 3b).

KXrBhZMvsU.text: Standard concept-erasure steering is proven to be a special case of LEACE under standardized (zero-mean, identity-covariance) representations (Corollary 4.1, Section 4.1).

MidSteer (Theorem 4.4) generalizes LEACE to directed concept manipulation by enforcing Cov(f(X),Z1) = Cov(X,Z2), mapping a source concept to a target concept without requiring dataset partitioning (Section 4.3).

LEACE-Switch (Theorem 4.2) extends LEACE to bidirectional concept switching by inverting the covariance relationship Cov(f(X),Z) = -Cov(X,Z), with a closed-form optimal affine solution (Section 4.2.1).
On SDXL's 'Horse to Motorcycle' concept switch, MidSteer achieves better FID and CLIP scores than both vanilla steering and LEACE while better preserving unrelated concepts (Table 1).
MidSteer is evaluated across Llama-2-7B, Qwen 2.5, SDXL, and SANA, using 1,000 samples to estimate class-conditional covariances and 50,000 samples for self-covariance estimation (Section 5.1).

On safety-oriented concept switches ('Toxicity to Helpfulness' on Llama-2-7B and 'Violence to Peace' on SDXL), MidSteer more effectively suppresses the harmful concept than baseline steering methods (Table 2).

a7mORMEWYX.text: MedSIGHT is trained on only 72K multimodal instruction pairs, far fewer than comparable models such as HuatuoGPT-Vision's 647K, yet achieves an average visual comprehension score of 62.3 versus HuatuoGPT-Vision's 58.3 (Table 2).

The Region Perceiver module uses learnable region query tokens with dual cross-attention to visual features, pre-trained on medical segmentation/detection data (BiomedParse), to produce region-centric tokens encoding spatial information (Figure 2).

The modality-aware Region Codebook uses vector quantization to discretize continuous region embeddings into interpretable tokens, maintaining separate code sets per imaging modality and integrating them into the LLM vocabulary (Figure 3).

On the newly introduced DiagSeg benchmark, MedSIGHT achieves 58.9 mean Recall on diagnosis and 69.9 mean Dice on segmentation across 8 imaging modalities (CT, MRI, X-ray, Pathology, Ultrasound, Endoscopy, Dermatology, OCT) (Table 3).
On text-prompted segmentation (MeCoVQA-G), MedSIGHT achieves 42.8 average Dice score (Table 4).

Ablation shows removing the unified grounded instruction tuning stage causes the model to fail to output codebook tokens at all, and removing alignment stages costs 5-15% performance (Appendix/Section on ablations).

0cnDTttyMR.text: FOCA achieves 95.7% success rate with only 20 demonstrations on LIBERO in the 40% data regime when combined with DreamGen synthetic video data, exceeding the π0 baseline's full-data (100%) performance of 94.6% (Table 2).
At the 10% data regime on LIBERO, FOCA reaches 85.3% average success versus 77.6% for the π0 baseline, and at 40% data reaches 94.0% versus 89.9% for π0 (Table 1a).
FOCA improves 4.4-12% over baselines on five RoboCasa tasks when built on π0, and 7.2-10.4% when built on GR00T-N1.5 (Figure 3c).
On a real simulated humanoid Place Parts task, FOCA improves success rate from 58% to 84%, a 26 percentage-point absolute gain (Figure 3a).

FOCA's approach uses two complementary objectives: explicit future latent prediction of task-grounded interaction regions and implicit future alignment via contrastive learning, operating in latent embedding space rather than pixel space (Section 3).
At 10% data, FOCA (85.3%) outperforms parameter-efficient fine-tuning baselines LoRA and DoRA, which plateau around 78% (Table 1b).

8xH4BQ8J6Y.text: On human-written programs under standard semantics, frontier models like GPT-5-mini and Gemini-2.5-pro reach 93-100% final-state prediction accuracy, but accuracy drops sharply (e.g., QwQ 32B falls from 98% to 7% under SOS semantics) when the same programs are evaluated under the KeywordSwap semantic mutation (Table 5).

On fuzzer-generated programs with high structural complexity (median cyclomatic complexity 100, per Table 2), final-state prediction accuracy under standard semantics falls to as low as 15-16% for QwQ 32B and 55-57% for GPT-5-mini, versus over 90% on simpler human-written programs (Table 5, Table 2).

Execution-trace prediction (PredTrace) accuracy on human-written programs remains low across all models, with Gemini-2.5-pro at only 25-32% and QwQ 32B dropping to 0% under SOS semantics, indicating near-zero long-horizon conditioning ability (Table 7).

Providing formal operational semantics (K-semantics or SOS) helps model performance on simple programs but often hurts performance on more complex ones, as shown by comparing PredRule accuracy across semantics and complexity splits (Table 6).

H5wTMVlukn.text: The Noisy Quadratic System (NQS) loss model, defined in Definition 4.1 (Section 4.1) as L_NQS(N,B,K) = E_irr + E_app(N) + E_bias(N,K) + E_var(N,B,K), is presented as the first pre-training loss prediction model that explicitly handles varying batch size B alongside model size N and weight updates K.

On held-out data at a 1024x compute extrapolation gap, NQS achieves a holdout loss-prediction error of 5.6 compared to Chinchilla's 9.8, and NQS continues to extrapolate accurately out to 1000x compute gaps whereas Chinchilla's loss model degrades beyond roughly 20x (Table 1, Figure 4, Section 5.1).
Section 4.2 models LayerNorm effects via a dynamic learning-rate term proportional to 1/||w(k)||^2 within the NQS framework.

In Section 5.2, NQS is used to select near-optimal (N,B,K) training configurations under joint compute, time (T=N x K), and memory (M=B x N) constraints at a 236 PetaFLOP budget, with the chosen configuration close to the ground-truth optimum (Figure 5, Section 5.2).

WepBmd1L4v.text: Theorem 4.4 shows that positive-negative conditional independence of responses given context is a sufficient condition for the conditional preference response distribution (CPRD) to be representable by a Bradley-Terry model, with the recovered score function equal to the log-likelihood ratio log[p+(y|x)/p-(y|x)] (Theorem 4.4, Proposition 4.2).

Theorem 5.2 shows the discriminative Bradley-Terry learning objective is equivalent to a KL-divergence projection at the preference level rather than the triplet level, and Corollary 5.3 guarantees the global minimizer recovers the true CPRD almost surely when it is BT-representable (Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3).

Theorem 6.7 derives sample complexity bounds for preference learning from triplet comparison data showing estimation error depends inversely on a connectivity degree parameter of the comparison graph (Theorem 6.7).

Theorem 6.8 unifies margin and connectivity effects, showing that learning accuracy improves with both larger pairwise score margins and higher comparison-graph connectivity, with explicit quantified trade-offs (Theorem 6.8).

Skxb4UgTWU.text: Theorem 3 (Section 3.2) derives globally optimal closed-form scalar scaling factors for low-rank adapter increments based on the truncated-SVD optimality condition established in Theorem 1 (Section 3.1), avoiding its prohibitive computational cost (Theorem 1, Theorem 3).

Theorem 5 (Section 3.3) extends the scaling to a column-wise formulation solved via a 2r x 2r linear system, applicable when a non-negativity condition holds, which is empirically satisfied in about 80% of LoRA layers across iterations (Theorem 5, Figure 2d).
On GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base at rank r=4, ScaLoRA achieves 88.98% average accuracy versus 88.13% for standard LoRA (Section 4.2).

On commonsense reasoning benchmarks (BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c, OBQA) at rank r=8, ScaLoRA achieves 74.51% average accuracy on LLaMA2-7B versus 73.63% for LoRA, with additional evaluation extending to LLaMA3-8B and Gemma-3-12B-pt on MetaMathQA, GSM8K, and MATH (Table 2, Section 4.3).

xSYhEkiyp5.text: Theorem 1 establishes that under assumptions (A1)-(A5), decentralized SGD achieves a high-probability convergence rate of O(sigma*sqrt(d)/sqrt(nT)) on the average squared gradient norm for non-convex costs, exhibiting linear speed-up in the number of nodes n (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 establishes that under assumptions (A1)-(A4) and (A6, mu-strong convexity), the last iterate of decentralized SGD achieves a high-probability rate of O(d*sigma^2*kappa/(n(T+t0))), also exhibiting linear speed-up without requiring a bounded-heterogeneity assumption (Theorem 2).

Lemma 2 shows the averaged stochastic noise across nodes is O(sigma*sqrt(d)/sqrt(n))-sub-Gaussian, giving a high-probability analogue of the variance-reduction benefit of decentralized averaging (Lemma 2).

Compared to the prior high-probability analysis of Lu et al., this work removes the uniformly-bounded-gradient assumption and, for the strongly convex case, eliminates the requirement of asymptotically vanishing noise (Lemma 4, referencing Lu et al.).

ao1SgPdAQm.text: PixCLIP outperforms Alpha-CLIP on region-level phrase grounding, reaching 59.93% on RefCOCO Val versus 55.7%, 59.1% on RefCOCO+ Val versus 55.6%, and 61.8% on RefCOCOg Val versus 61.2% (Table 2).
On Ref-SAV mask-text retrieval, PixCLIP achieves 47.3% Mask-to-Text Recall@1 and 47.9% Text-to-Mask Recall@1, more than 19 points above Alpha-CLIP's 28.3% and 27.5% (Table 5).

Despite using arbitrarily shaped region/pixel prompts, PixCLIP preserves strong global image-text retrieval, achieving 84.4% average image-to-text and 85.0% average text-to-image recall across Flickr30k, COCO, ShareGPT4V, Urban-1K, and DOCCI (Table 4).

The LongGRIT dataset contains nearly 1.5 million pixel-level localization samples, constructed via a three-stage automated pipeline (object-level, context-level, fine-grained expression annotation) using InternVL2, Qwen2, Griffon-G, and DeepSeek-R1 (Section 4, Method: Fine-grained Data Generation).

An ablation shows RefCOCO Val accuracy rising from 51.14% with mask-text contrastive learning alone, to 59.04% after adding local-global enhancement, to 59.93% with the full three-branch framework (Table 6).
On ImageNet-S classification, PixCLIP attains 69.57% Top-1 accuracy versus Alpha-CLIP's 68.89%, and on Instance-COCO it reaches 76.68% versus LLM2CLIP's 70.16% (Table 1, Table 3).

ADHGbxsREr.text: Theorem 4.4 establishes finite-sample guarantees for a Q-aggregation estimator of kernel mean embeddings, with a bound that trades off bias governed by the maximum distributional distance ΔV against variance controlled by the combined sample size nV (Theorem 4.4).

Corollary 4.6 bounds the excess risk of the personalized model by 2RΘ·E[MMD(P̂(ω̂), P₁)], where RΘ controls the RKHS norm of the loss class, linking the KME estimation error directly to downstream task risk (Corollary 4.6).

Per Example 4.5, the learned collaboration weights automatically shift toward local-only learning (ω₁ ≈ 1) recovering the naive O(n₁^{-1/2}) rate when no beneficial collaborators exist, and toward pooling when other agents share similar distributions, without prior knowledge of heterogeneity (Example 4.5).

Theorem 5.2 quantifies the communication-statistical efficiency tradeoff when the method is implemented with D-dimensional random Fourier features, adding an approximation error term of order C√(log B/D) (Theorem 5.2).

On a synthetic concept-shift experiment with 100 agents and 10 samples each, the method's adaptive weighting correctly improves performance once intra-group similarity crosses the transition point σc² = 0.5 (Section 6.1).
On the FEMNIST handwriting benchmark with 192 agents, the adaptive weighting scheme consistently outperforms a uniform-weighting baseline using fixed, untuned hyperparameters (Section 6.3).

2ftHZlIUKE.text: The LALM-as-a-Judge benchmark consists of 24,000 synthetic unsafe spoken dialogues spanning 3 to 10 conversational turns, 8 harmful categories, and 5 severity grades, with 160 dialogues validated by 5 human raters to confirm reliable unsafe detection and severity scaling (Section 3).
Three open-source large audio-language models (Qwen2-Audio, Audio Flamingo 3, and MERaLiON) are benchmarked as judges, alongside a transcription-only LLaMA baseline (Section 4).

Results reveal an architecture- and modality-dependent trade-off: the judge model most sensitive to detecting mild harmful content is also the least stable in its severity ratings across dialogue turns (Section 5).

Replacing audio input with Whisper-Large transcripts significantly reduces judge sensitivity to harmful content in transcription-only mode, while largely preserving the relative ordering of severity grades (Section 5).

HeLa76rJuD.text: On stateful SWE-bench, the ToM-augmented TomCodeAct agent achieves a 57.4% resolution rate with Claude Sonnet 4, compared to 13.5% for the plain CodeAct baseline, a 43.9 percentage point improvement (Section 4.2).

A user-simulator study reports satisfaction scores of 3.62±0.07 for TomCodeAct versus 2.57±0.08 for the CodeAct baseline on stateful SWE-bench with Claude 4, a roughly 41% relative improvement (Table 1).

In a three-week online study with 17 professional software developers comprising 209 sessions and 174 ToM consultation instances, suggestions were accepted or partially accepted 86.2% of the time (74.1% full acceptance plus 12.1% partial acceptance) (Section 5, Section 5.1).
Acceptance rates varied by query type, with Code Understanding queries achieving the highest acceptance rate at 92% (Figure 7, Section 5.1).

ViMgQW9fyt.text: GUI-Spotlight achieves 52.8% accuracy on the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark using only 18.5K training samples (Table 3).

GUI-Spotlight surpasses V2P-7B (50.6% accuracy with 9.6M training samples) and GTA-1-7B (50.1% accuracy with 1.56M training samples) on ScreenSpot-Pro, implying roughly 500x greater data efficiency than V2P-7B (Table 3).
When initialized from UI-TARS-1.5-7B, GUI-Spotlight shows consistent gains across all six ScreenSpot-Pro domains, including Development at 71.3% and CAD at 44.4% (Table 3).

On UI-Vision, GUI-Spotlight reaches 23.4% average accuracy, outperforming the UI-TARS-1.5-7B baseline by 5.3 points; on OSWorld-G it reaches 62.7% average accuracy with 68.2% on text matching and 63.2% on layout understanding (Table 4, Table 5).

An RL-training ablation shows that tool-filtered positive rewards combined with an auxiliary cross-entropy loss prevent training collapse and sustain accuracy gains over 400+ training steps (Section 4.1).
A reward-design ablation finds sparse rewards slightly outperform center-shaped dense rewards after convergence (Section 4.2).

kcPPWaoegr.text: ML-Agent, built on a 7B-parameter Qwen2.5 model, outperforms agents based on the 671B-parameter DeepSeek-R1 as well as GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini agents (Table 1).

ML-Agent is trained via exploration-enriched fine-tuning and step-wise reinforcement learning on only 9 ML engineering tasks (4 from MLAgentBench, 5 from MLE-bench), yet generalizes to 10 held-out MLE-bench tasks spanning image, text, and tabular modalities (Section 4).
On the held-in CIFAR-10 task, ML-Agent achieves an average accuracy of 68.88% with a best run of 81.45% (Table 1).
Exploration-enriched fine-tuning generates over 100 diverse initial ideas and selects the 10 most behaviorally distant ones before subsequent RL training (Section 4).
The ML-specific reward module assigns a reward of 0 for erroring trajectories, 0.5 for corner cases, and a sigmoid-scaled reward for genuine performance improvements (Section 4).

Bve790HQrA.text: AdvGame trains an Attacker LM and Defender LM jointly online as a non-zero-sum game, in contrast to the sequential alternating attacker-then-defender optimization used by prior methods such as Self-RedTeam (Section 3, Figure 2).
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, AdvGame-DPO-MD reduces HarmBench-adversarial attack success rate (ASR) from 31.6% (Original model) to 4.7%, compared to 16.6% for the Self-RedTeam baseline (Table 2).
AdvGame-DPO-MD preserves general utility on Qwen2.5-7B, keeping MMLU@5 at 71.6% versus 71.8% for the Original model, whereas Self-RedTeam causes larger utility drops on other benchmarks (Table 1).

On WildJailbreak (WJB) compliance, AdvGame-DPO-MD scores 94.4% versus 100.0% for the Original Qwen2.5-7B model and 98.4% for Self-RedTeam, showing only a modest over-refusal cost from the added safety training (Table 3).

The reward signal is computed via a pairwise (winner/loser) preference judge rather than point-wise scalar rewards, and training uses the WildJailbreak dataset split 80/20 into train/validation on 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs (Section 3.1, Section 4.1).

xrUgA8PrNN.text: The paper analyzes an ℓ1-norm (least-absolute-deviation) estimator and proves it achieves an estimation error bound of Θ(ρ^τ), where ρ is the system's contraction factor and τ is the input memory length (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.1's guarantee requires the adversarial attack probability to satisfy p < 1/(2τ), which ensures the probability (1-p)^τ of an attack-free observation window exceeds one half (Assumption 2.8, Remark 2.9).

A matching lower bound of order Θ(ρ^τ L r/λ) is established, proving the upper bound of Theorem 3.1 is order-optimal and that no estimator can improve on this rate under probabilistic adversarial attacks (Theorem 3.4).
The estimation error is shown to decay exponentially with the input memory length τ through the contraction factor ρ ∈ (0,1) (Section 3.2).

Section 3.2 first derives sufficient conditions for exact recovery in the case without past-state effects (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.2.1), then extends the analysis to the general case with nonzero past-state terms (Section 3.2.2).

do3oOYxWHO.text: On WebShop with Llama-3.2-11B as policy, Agentic Monte Carlo (AMC) scores 0.625, compared to 0.562 for Best-of-15 and 0.580 for the prompt-based SMC (FoA) baseline (Table 1).
On SciWorld, AMC with GPT-4.1-mini scores 0.673 versus 0.616 for Best-of-15, and with Llama-3.1-8B scores 0.347 versus Best-of-15's 0.311 (Table 2).

AMC outperforms GRPO using only N=5 trajectories when GPT-5.1 is the policy model, and scaling AMC to 25 trajectories with a Qwen-2.5-3B backbone outperforms fully fine-tuned GRPO, while GRPO required 8 A100 GPUs versus 2 RTX 6000 Ada GPUs for AMC (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
On TextCraft, AMC's advantage saturates with strong policies, scoring 0.790 versus Best-of-15's 0.889 when using GPT-5.1 (Table 3).

AMC matches Best-of-20 performance using only N=15 trajectories, cutting test-time compute by about 25% (Section 4.5, Figure 4), and GPT-4.1-mini with AMC matches GPT-5.1 performance while reducing total cost by at least 50% (Table 5).

NOHlqCnYot.text: The authors construct CAF-7M, a semi-synthetic corpus of 7,433,239 context-augmented time series training windows spanning 40 datasets, generated with Llama-3.3-70B and verified with GPT-5.2 (Section 3.2).

The verification pipeline accepts a training window only if its added context measurably improves Direct Prompt forecasting performance under the CRPS metric, and rejects it otherwise (Section 3.1, Equation 2).

On the held-out CAF-7M test set (904 verified windows split into HARD/EASY), the proposed DoubleCast architecture achieves a CRPS of 0.231, with CRPS rising 11.1%-26.5% when context is removed or swapped, demonstrating genuine context utilization (Section 4.2, Table 2).

TimeLLM fails to exploit context despite training on the same CAF-7M data as DoubleCast, supporting the claim that context quality rather than architecture is the primary bottleneck in context-aided forecasting (Section 4.2, Table 2).

DoubleCast, pre-trained on semi-synthetic CAF-7M data and fine-tuned on the real-world CGTSF benchmark, outperforms Chronos and ChatTime on most configurations, evidencing semi-synthetic-to-real transfer (Section 4.3, Table 3).

SzMaEA68Oi.text: Mean pooling of hidden states across generated tokens achieves 0.41 CKA alignment with DINOv2 vision embeddings on the WIT benchmark, versus 0.29 for the best individual generated token (Section 3.1, Table 2).
For structure-based retrieval on WIT, generated-token mean pooling reaches 5.2% R@1 compared to 0.8% R@1 for last-token representations (Section 3.1, Table 3).

Semantic information is distributed across generated tokens rather than localized to a single position, evidenced by complementary per-token alignment that combines to improve pooled representations (Section 3.4).

Mean pooling across generated tokens is evaluated across three domains—vision-language (WIT, DCI), reasoning (MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond), and protein structure (UniProt)—each using 1,024 samples (Section 2.5).

Mean pooling over prompt tokens yields alignment only comparable to, and not exceeding, the best individual prompt token, attributed to causal masking in decoder-only architectures, unlike the improvement seen for generated tokens (Section 3.3).
Cross-seed consistency of mean-pooled generated-token representations is measured at a standard deviation of 4.8x10^-3 across five decoding runs (Section 3.6, Figure 8).

OBXBXSgwcD.text: With 2-bit compression and error feedback, MuLoCo matches the memory complexity of uncompressed DiLoCo while communicating 8x8 (64x) less data (Section 5.2, Figure 1).

In the K=8 workers, H=30 local steps setting with a 220M-parameter 12-layer transformer, MuLoCo matches its Muon data-parallel baseline while DiLoCo only nearly matches its AdamW data-parallel baseline (Section 5.1).

At 2-bit quantization, MuLoCo shows next to no performance degradation relative to its uncompressed baseline, whereas DiLoCo exhibits measurable performance loss at the same compression level (Section 5.2, Figure 2b).
MuLoCo with Muon plus error feedback requires 2x parameter memory overhead versus 3x for DiLoCo with AdamW plus error feedback (Table 1).
Training runs use a global batch size of 2^18 tokens (262k tokens per local worker) over 13,733 total optimization steps with 458 communication rounds (Section 5.1).

HeRPNfJaod.text: On the DevEvol continuous software evolution benchmark, the best-performing frontier model (Claude Opus 4.6) reaches only 38.03% Score and 8.46% Resolve Rate, versus reported scores above 80% for the same models on isolated single-task benchmarks (Section 5.2, Table 2).
Gemini 3 Pro attains the highest Resolve Rate among tested models at 13.37%, despite a lower Score of 24.25%, while GPT 5.3-Codex scores 28.88% with 9.58% Resolve Rate (Section 5.2, Table 2).

Precision saturates while Recall grows roughly linearly across evolution milestones, indicating agents keep adding features but fail to prevent regressions from accumulating, producing a 'snowball effect' (Section 5.4, Figure 9).

Logic Error is the dominant root cause of downstream failure propagation, accounting for approximately 57% of all error chain events, with the highest inherited propagation rate (P1, 12%) (Section 5.5, Figure 10).
The DevEvol benchmark comprises 98 verified milestones reconstructed across 7 repositories via the DeepCommit automated milestone DAG pipeline (Section 3, Section 4).

On0QXiLaI0.text: PULSE (Prediction-powered User Label Synthesis and Evaluation) reduces 95% confidence interval widths by an average of 39.5% compared to naive A/B testing, using prediction-powered inference over ML-predicted user satisfaction from unlabeled trajectories (Section 2.3).
In the claude-3.7 vs claude-4 case study, the naive 95% CI is [-3.95%, 11.78%] while the PULSE-augmented CI is [1.99%, 8.06%], a substantially tighter interval (Section 4).

In-the-wild evaluation across over 36,000 sessions from 15,000 users finds claude-sonnet-4 preferred over gpt-5 by -7.8% in user satisfaction (favoring Claude), even though gpt-5 outperforms claude-sonnet-4 on 6 of 7 offline benchmarks, evidencing a benchmark-preference discrepancy (Section 4, Table 2, Section 5).
The correlation between human satisfaction ratings and benchmark performance for the claude-4 vs gpt-5 comparison is measured at rho = -0.18 (Section 5, Table 2).
GPT-5 users sent 32% fewer messages and made 16% fewer code pushes than claude-4 users, suggesting earlier disengagement despite superior benchmark scores (Section 4).

8Q2T5GLl8x.text: BLOCK-EM's blocking penalty, applied to a fixed set of causally-identified SAE latents during fine-tuning, achieves up to 95% relative reduction in emergent misalignment with no degradation in target-task performance across six fine-tuning domains (Abstract).

At penalty strength lambda = 13x10^3, BLOCK-EM achieves 93% relative emergent-misalignment reduction while incurring only a 2.72% absolute incoherence increase and a 4.14% relative in-domain performance decrease, averaged across six domains and two seeds (Figure 1).
The six fine-tuning domains evaluated are financial advice, health advice, PrimeVul code vulnerabilities, career advice, legal advice, and educational advice (Section 4.1).

Evaluation uses disjoint prompt splits: 44 core misalignment prompts for causal feature discovery versus 29 held-out prompts for final out-of-sample evaluation, judged independently by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Section 4.1).
