The method's causal discovery pipeline has three stages: identifying activation shifts between base and misaligned checkpoints, causal screening via induce-and-repair steering, and per-latent calibration under a quality budget (Section 3.1).

Ablations in Appendix D show random-latent baselines and removal of directionality/sign constraints substantially weaken the blocking penalty's effectiveness, confirming mechanism specificity of the selected latents (Section 4.2, Appendix D).

RwiGcN2feP.text: Theorem 4.1 proves the layer-wise Hessian in the L-deep linear unconstrained features model (UFM) has rank K^2 with all non-zero eigenvalues equal, analytically reproducing the bulk-outlier Hessian spectrum reported in prior empirical studies (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 decomposes the Gauss-Newton/Fisher Information component into three terms: G_within (rank 0), G_cross (rank K(K-1), producing the mini-bulk of eigenvalues), and G_class (rank K, producing the main outliers), mirroring Papyan's empirical knockout experiments (Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 4.3 shows the aggregated gradient update is a sum over only K of the K^2 possible eigenvector directions, each with equal coefficient beta^(l+1)/K, explaining the observed gradient alignment with a low-dimensional subspace (Theorem 4.3).

Theorem 4.4 proves the Gram matrix of the optimal weights, W_l*^T W_l*, has rank K with eigenvalues proportional to the squared norms of the class-mean features, giving a closed-form account of the low-rank weight structure (Theorem 4.4).

For a deep linear UFM with K=3 classes, numerical experiments show K^2=9 Hessian outliers separating from the bulk and converging to equal eigenvalues over training, with eigenvector alignment metric f_cc' rising from about 0.2 to 1.0 (Figures 3 and 4).

In the non-linear (ReLU) Deep UFM, K^2=9 Hessian outliers separate but do not fully converge to equal values, and the gradient has K non-zero coefficients that remain unequal, unlike the linear case (Figure 9, Table 2).

Hnty5t1TNg.text: Proposition 2.1 shows that in the two-level (single promotion) sequential setting, improvement becomes infeasible only when (1-beta*gamma)*c+ > c-, an impossibility region strictly smaller than in the one-shot strategic classification setting (Proposition 2.1).

Theorems 3.1-3.2 characterize optimal long-run agent behavior across threshold ranges, showing a 'leg-up region' where mu < delta/(1-gamma) permits mixtures of gaming and genuine improvement rather than pure strategies (Theorems 3.1-3.2).

Theorem 4.1 proves that without a leg-up mechanism, reaching a target attribute level M is infeasible whenever M >= r / [(1-beta)(1-gamma)^2 * c+], establishing a fundamental limit on achievable improvement absent promotion incentives (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 gives sufficient conditions under which a leg-up mechanism permits agents to reach arbitrarily high levels, and proposes the threshold sequence mu_l = delta*l/(1-gamma), setting each level's threshold at the dynamical steady-state attribute value (Theorem 4.2).

The reduction in effective unit cost of improvement from c+ to (1-beta*gamma)*c+ under the sequential multi-level formulation is identified as the mechanism that strictly expands the incentivizable region relative to one-shot strategic classification (Section 2, Proposition 2.1).

hjmbstLYc9.text: The Least-Stale eviction policy reduces collision misses by up to 85x relative to LRU at 1% cache capacity, and achieves 1.6-1.9% collision rates versus 4.5-12.6% for LRU at 5% capacity (Section on Least-Stale Eviction Policy results).
Least-Stale achieves a 58-91x reduction in collision misses compared to a Score-Based eviction policy at 5% cache capacity (Least-Stale Eviction Policy results).

On OLMoE-1B-7B, the proposed caching/prefetching pipeline achieves 88-92% hit rates using only 5% cache capacity (0.6 GB of VRAM), yielding a 10.7-34.7% reduction in time-to-first-token across baselines (Table 2).

Drop-in TTFT improvements are reported across four MoE models in Table 2: 9.8-25.7% on Mixtral-8x7B, 7.8-44.1% on Phi-3.5-MoE, and 4.3-23.0% on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, in addition to the OLMoE results (Table 2).

The evaluation spans four policy dimensions (routing, prefetching, eviction, and miss handling) and shows that score-based prefetching outperforms fixed top-k prefetching in hit rate despite lower routing-prediction accuracy, and that no single eviction/prefetch strategy is universally optimal across the tested 1%, 5%, and 25% capacity levels (Section on Prefetching and Policy Interactions).

uiyDqAVhr9.text: MMClima comprises over 104k expert-validated question-answer pairs spanning textual and visual modalities across five climate-science domains, with the textual QA subset alone containing 100,747 pairs split into 80,585 training and 20,162 test items (Section 3.2, Table 2).
Five domain experts spent over 210 hours in iterative review of the dataset, reaching an inter-annotator agreement of kappa=0.83 during quality filtering (Section 3.4).
The fine-tuned mmclima-70b-txt model achieves an overall weighted textual-QA score of 78.24%, comprising 89.54% on multiple-choice, 49.72% on cloze, and 95.47% on freeform questions (Table 3).
mmclima-70b-txt outperforms GPT-5-Nano (69.66%), Phi-4-Reasoning-Plus (70.54%), and DeepSeek-Chat (75.03%) on the overall weighted textual QA benchmark (Table 3).

3KX1xU2bCC.text: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).

The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).

The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).

The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).

The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).

JTwryHNicJ.text: Theorem 3.5 upper-bounds the MSE of the plug-in IPW estimator by C0 + C1·E[d_task(e(X),ê(X))], where d_task decomposes into bias and variance components dbias and dvar (Section 3.2.2, Theorem 3.5).

Definition 3.7 derives an IPW-tailored strictly proper scoring rule ℓ(t,q) with closed-form partial losses, obtained by matching the curvature of the task-specific divergence to the scoring rule's weight function (Section 3.2.3, Definition 3.7).

Definition 3.8 gives a canonical probability mapping σℓ obtained by solving a depressed quartic equation u⁴ − 12u² − 16u − z² = 0, replacing the standard sigmoid link for numerical stability (Section 3.2.4, Definition 3.8).

On IHDP, Jobs, and Kang-Schafer benchmarks, the tailored loss achieves the lowest mean rank among likelihood-based, trimming/clipping, and balancing baselines (CBPS, CBSR, Entropy Balancing, SBW) across IPW, Hajek, and AIPW estimators (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

On the higher-dimensional ACIC 2017 benchmark (4,802 observations, 58 covariates, 32 data-generating processes), the tailored loss improves RMSE in 95/96 MLP-backbone configurations and 62/96 XGBoost-backbone configurations relative to standard likelihood training (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

Performance gains from the tailored loss are largest in high-selection-strength regimes where true propensity scores concentrate near 0 and 1, consistent with the theoretical motivation for curvature matching near the boundary (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

oZWE7mSqlk.text: Increasing sampling temperature substantially reduces visible looping, but smaller student models still generate substantially longer responses than their teacher even at high temperature, indicating temperature is a stopgap rather than a full solution (Section 2, Figures 1-2).

The OpenThinker3-1.5B student loops in about 30% of responses under greedy decoding while its teacher QwQ-32B rarely loops, a pattern that holds across the Qwen and Phi model families and points to imperfect distillation rather than an inherent architectural flaw (Section 2).

Proposition 1 formalizes a risk-aversion mechanism: when a correct progress-making action is indistinguishable from n hard-to-learn alternatives, maximum-likelihood training spreads probability (1-p)/n across them while an easy cyclic action retains probability p, biasing generation toward loops (Section 3, Proposition 1).

In graph reasoning experiments on a G(5,5) task, hard-to-learn transitions produce high looping counts at low temperature that decrease as temperature increases, with response lengths up to four times longer than an ideal learner even at temperature 1.0 (Section 3, Figure 4).

Independent of learning hardness, Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward temporally correlated errors: in G(5,5) experiments the same root children were selected in 96.7% of consecutive visits, far exceeding the rate expected under independent random errors (Section 4, Figure 5).
Looping rates increase with problem difficulty across most evaluated models, with easy problems eliciting minimal looping and hard problems triggering markedly more repetitive patterns (Figure 10).

fD6c4bD7sR.text: In synthetic toy models with precisely controlled superposition, PGD-discovered adversarial attacks align with the theoretically optimal attack direction with cosine similarity 0.97±0.02 for 6 classes in 2 dimensions, 0.96±0.00 for 30 classes in 10 dimensions, and 0.92±0.00 for 90 classes in 30 dimensions, all with p<10⁻¹⁰ versus a random-direction baseline (Section 3, Figure 1, Table 1).

Proposition 1 shows the optimal perturbation direction satisfies δ ∝ Wₑᵀn where n is the difference between class representation vectors, and Corollary 1 shows the per-feature perturbation magnitude is proportional to the differential interference |vᵢᵀ(vₖ−vⱼ)| (Section 3, Proposition 1, Corollary 1).

Increasing input feature correlation strength raises geometric similarity of learned representations across independently trained model seeds from 0.23±0.14 (uncorrelated) to 0.47±0.32 (paired correlations) to 0.88±0.06 (global correlations), and correspondingly raises adversarial transfer rate from 18%±9% to 94%±12% (Section 3, Figure 2).

On a bottlenecked vision transformer trained on CIFAR-10 with superposition dimension m in {2,3,5,10}, robust accuracy normalized by clean accuracy at ℓ2 perturbation budget ε=0.1 rises from 90.4% at m=2 to 95.0% at m=10, and attack transferability between models increases with the degree of compression, mirroring the toy-model findings (Section 4).

Proposition 2 shows models whose feature representations are related by an orthogonal transformation share identical optimal attack directions, and a modular-addition experiment (Section 5) shows superposition is sufficient but not necessary for vulnerability: gradient-free attacks exploiting learned Fourier frequencies ωₖ succeed with perturbation norm ‖δ‖₂=0.22 versus a PGD baseline of 0.17 (Section 5, Proposition 2).

5BXMlmjt43.text: The paper introduces the Multi-layer Configurable Time-varying MDP (MCTVMDP), in which an upper-level agent takes model-changing actions that modify the transition kernel of a lower-level, non-stationary MDP (Section 2).

The Bi-level Configurable MDP formulation separates upper-level configuration actions from lower-level primitive actions, with an upper-level reward defined as R(Pk,bk) = Σ Q(Pk+1|Pk,bk) J(π*k+1,Pk+1) − C(Pk,bk) (Section 2, Equation 3).

Lemma 1 bounds the state-value function gap under transition-kernel estimation error δg as ‖V^π_P − V^π_P̂‖∞ ≤ γ δg Vmax / (1−γ), with Lemmas 2 and 3 extending this to propagated upper-level reward error and combined bi-level error under both estimation error δg and configuration error δc (Section 5, Lemmas 1-3).

Algorithm 1 (Bi-level Value Iteration) nests a lower-level value iteration over estimated kernels P̂ inside an upper-level iteration over configuration values W, outputting an optimal higher-order policy Θ^H_U (Section 4, Algorithm 1).

The proposed bi-level value iteration approach is validated on a synthetic bi-level MDP, a CartPole environment combining DQN at the lower level with value iteration at the upper level, and a block-world environment with a continuous configuration parameter α, showing improvement over baselines on the synthetic setting (Section 6).

lNoaqrOXti.text: CHARM's description-aware gating mechanism (Section 2.1.2) combines inter-channel attention gating, which suppresses cross-channel attention based on learned thresholds over pairwise channel-description similarity, with a symmetric time-offset attention tensor Δ that encodes learned lag dependencies between channels (Section 2.1.2).
On the SKAB anomaly detection benchmark, CHARM achieves F1 0.86 and missed alarm rate 12.69, compared to MOMENT (linear probe) at F1 0.82 and missed alarm rate 20.73 (Table 3).
Across 46 UCR univariate anomaly-detection datasets, CHARM attains F1 0.754, versus 0.684 for MOMENT and 0.627 for the task-specific TimesNet baseline (Table 4).

On the UEA multivariate classification benchmark, CHARM with finetuning wins on 5 of the evaluated datasets and reaches 80.9% average accuracy (7,799 total correct), while frozen CHARM embeddings with an SVM head still win on 4 datasets at 79.6% average accuracy (Table 2).
On the long-sequence forecasting benchmark, a CHARM linear probe achieves lower MSE than the much larger Moirai-Large model on ETTm2 (0.220 vs 0.269) and ETTh2 (0.323 vs 0.339) (Table 1).

Ablations show the JEPA training objective contributes a 4.4 percentage-point classification accuracy gain over a reconstruction-based objective, and text-conditioned convolutions raise classification accuracy from 68.0% to 71.4% (Table 5).

TDaVoBfTjY.text: In deep unconstrained feature models trained with cross-entropy loss, deep neural collapse (DNC) remains only a local optimum for depth L≥2 (or L≥3 depending on class count), while lower-rank configurations become globally optimal (Theorem 3.1).

The ratio of Frobenius norms between the DNC logit matrix and a low-rank alternative decays exponentially in depth L, following exp(-(L/2) log((K-1)/r)), explaining why low-rank solutions are favored as depth increases (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

In the infinite-depth limit (L→∞), the globally optimal feature geometry converges to the d=2 softmax code, i.e., class means arranged as vertices of a regular K-gon, linking depth-induced bias to explicit width-2 bottlenecks (Theorem 3.2).
Under Hadamard initialization, neural collapse becomes a dynamically unstable fixed point near the origin for depth L>1, with the region of instability growing monotonically with depth (Theorem 4.3).

A 'rich-get-richer' effect causes larger singular values of the feature/classifier matrices to grow faster than smaller ones during early training, driving emergence of low-rank structure before the network exits the linearized regime (Theorem 4.4).

Empirically on ResNet-20 (MNIST/CIFAR-10), the effective rank of learned features decreases as classifier head depth increases, while increasing network width increases effective rank at convergence, and lower effective rank correlates with worse generalization (Section 5, experimental results).

QiDicUd6PB.text: The proposed Fourier-representation kernel regression estimator can be computed with O(n log n) time and memory complexity via non-uniform FFTs, versus O(n^3) time and O(n^2) memory for classical kernel methods (Section 2.3, 'Fast optimization').

For Sobolev kernel regression, choosing regularization λ in the range n^(-1) ≤ λ ≤ n^(-2s/(2s+d)) and truncation level m=n^(1/(2s+d)) yields the minimax convergence rate E[||f_θ̂ - f*||^2] = O(n^(-2s/(2s+d))) (Section 3.1, Proposition 3.1).

The one-dimensional Sobolev regression algorithm processes n=10^10 data points in approximately one minute on a single NVIDIA T4 GPU using complex-128 precision (Section 3.1, 'One dimensional example').

For additive models exploiting per-dimension additivity, the method achieves total computational complexity O(d^2 n log n) while remaining GPU-compatible, avoiding the curse of dimensionality that limits spline-based generalized additive models (Section 5, 'Additive models').

A grid search over 300 hyperparameter configurations completes in under 30 seconds for n=10^8 samples, while PyGAM exceeds 15GB of memory usage at n=10^7 (experimental results, GPU scalability section).

E98OvY1Syv.text: In the dataset-diffing experiment, SAE-based hypothesis generation uses 2-8x fewer tokens than pure-LLM baselines, as reported for token usage across models (Section 4.1, Table 3, 'Token usage by SAEs and baselines').

In the property-based retrieval experiment, SAE embeddings generally match or outperform dense-embedding and LLM baselines in mean average precision (MAP) across datasets when query expansion (1-20 phrases) and temperature (0.01-1.5) are varied (Section 4.4, Figure 6).

Applying the correlation-discovery method to Tulu-3's SFT dataset uncovers a spurious correlation in which prompts containing 'math', 'lists', or 'LaTeX' are correlated with the phrase 'hope' appearing in responses (Section 5.2, Figure 8).

SAE embeddings are constructed by passing documents through a reader LLM, extracting sparse autoencoder activations per token, and max-pooling across tokens to obtain a document-level embedding where each dimension corresponds to a labeled, human-interpretable concept (Section 3, methodology description).

2tsdSKz3Yi.text: INFER reduces average magnitude reconstruction error by over 39% and average phase reconstruction error by over 51% compared to the best baseline, aggregated across the BUCK mockup and Tesla Model X car-cabin datasets (Table 1).
INFER outperforms the time-domain baselines NAF, INRAS, and AVR across amplitude, angle, spectral, STFT, energy, envelope, T60, and EDT metrics on both the BUCK and Tesla setups (Table 1).

A Kramers-Kronig consistency regularizer (loss term L_KK, Equation 12) enforces that the predicted frequency-dependent attenuation and dispersion satisfy the Hilbert-transform relationship required by physical causality (Section 3.4 and Section 4.3, 'Spectral Supervision').
Phase reconstruction error is particularly reduced at low frequencies, reported as 0.029 for INFER versus 0.076 for the best baseline (Table 2, per-frequency results).

The model architecture uses two branches: a material branch predicting complex attenuation δ(f,p) and a retransmission branch predicting the directional re-radiated spectrum S(f,p,n̂), combined via a ray-cast frequency-domain rendering equation (Section 3, architecture description).

vNfbqRzash.text: On UK Biobank data comprising N≈277,291 participants and V=66 chronic disease conditions, BHPI (Bayesian Hypergraph Pathway Inference) is evaluated against per-disease logistic regression and other baselines (Section 5.5, 'UK Biobank: Disentangling Real-World Disease Pathways').
For diseases with prevalence below 2%, BHPI achieves a mean AUC improvement of +1.2 (×100 scale) over per-disease logistic regression, with statistical significance p=3×10^-5 (Table 5).

BHPI achieves an expected calibration error of 0.005 on the UK Biobank 66-disease prediction task, below the 0.01 threshold reported as well-calibrated (Table 4, 'Predictive calibration on UKB (66 diseases)').

On simulated data with N=2000, BHPI recovers disease-level risk coefficients with 97.85% correlation to ground truth (cor(β,β̂)) and recovers the true hypergraph structure with 96.96% AUC (H-AUC) (Table 2).

The model incorporates a repulsion prior that discourages selecting highly overlapping hyperedges for a given risk factor, promoting parsimonious and interpretable disease-pathway groupings (Section on model specification, 'repulsion prior').

il6P7EHU1w.text: MORALISE consists of 2,481 expert-verified real-world image-text pairs spanning 13 moral topics organized under Turiel's Domain Theory (personal, interpersonal, and societal domains) (Section 3.1, Table 1).

The benchmark evaluates 19 vision-language models, comprising 16 open-source models (e.g., Gemma-3, GLM4-V, InternVL3, Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL) and 3 proprietary models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o4-mini) (Section 4.1).
Proprietary VLMs reach 88.28% average accuracy on moral judgment versus 83.55% for open-source VLMs (Table 2).
On norm attribution, proprietary models achieve a 66.60% hit rate compared to 42.63% for open-source models, a substantially larger gap than on moral judgment (Table 3).
Across all evaluated models, text-based moral violations are identified more accurately than image-based moral violations (Figure 5).

XfndtVLIub.text: Differentiable Coherent Factuality (DCF) achieves up to a 141% improvement in claim retention over frequency-based baselines on the MATH dataset at reliability level α=0.03 (1.76 vs. 0.73 claims retained) (Section 4.3).
DCF achieves up to a 61% improvement in claim retention over frequency-based baselines on the FELM dataset at α=0.01 (Section 4.3).

Theorem 3.1 (Calibration Convergence) shows that as temperature parameters approach their limits, DCF's soft nonconformity scores converge to the hard Coherent Factuality algorithm's scores, recovering its conformal quantile properties (Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 (Prediction Convergence) shows DCF's soft retention probabilities converge to the original Coherent Factuality prediction set, preserving test-time coverage guarantees (Theorem 3.2).
DCF's soft relaxations achieve 90-100% agreement with hard Coherent Factuality predictions across α∈[0.01, 0.10], validating the smooth approximation (Section 4.2).
DCF jointly relaxes claim scoring together with logical-ancestor coherence enforcement and constrained argmax selection, rather than treating these graph operations independently (Section 3.2-3.4).

CCO35e4DCO.text: On the TextCaps image-captioning task with 3 candidate hypotheses, LoRA-MCL attains a SPIDEr score of 0.955 versus 0.915 for a LoRA-MLE baseline with diverse beam search (Section 5, Table 2).
On a synthetic bilingual English-French TextCaps captioning task, LoRA-MCL reaches 0.464 SPIDEr on French generations versus 0.411 for the baseline (Section 5).

Under Assumption 2 (data generated from a mixture of latent processes), Proposition 1 shows the Winner-Takes-All loss acts as a conditional form of hard-EM, with min_θ ℒ(θ) − log K ≤ min_θ ℒ_WTA(θ) ≤ ℋ(x|c,z) ≤ min_θ ℒ(θ) (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).
For Markov chain data, Corollary 1 proves standard MLE converges to a weighted average of transition matrices, whereas LoRA-MCL recovers the individual modes (Section 4.2-4.3, Corollary 1).
On AudioCaps audio captioning with 5 candidate hypotheses, LoRA-MCL's test loss decreases monotonically from 2.152 at K=1 to 1.927 at K=5 (Section 5).

DQKoxCegwH.text: On CIFAR-10 with a ResNet backbone, CREDIT's defended model reaches 94.67% accuracy versus 95.70% for the vanilla (undefended) model (Table 1, Section 4.1).

CREDIT achieves 100.0 AUC for verifying ownership against extraction attacks on CIFAR-10 across ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, and GoogLeNet backbones, outperforming watermarking and fingerprinting baselines (Table 2).
Theorem 3.1 (Mutual Information Bound) proves that defended embeddings satisfy I(e(X);e_g(X)) ≤ β, where β = Δ²n/(2σ²) under Gaussian perturbation (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.4 bounds both the Type I error (false alarm on an independent model) and Type II error (missed detection of a surrogate), showing both decay exponentially with verification set size (Theorem 3.4, Definition 3.3).
CREDIT's verification stage takes approximately 22 seconds compared to 72-189 seconds for baseline methods, while the preparation stage takes about 0.001 seconds (Table 3).
The optimal Gaussian noise parameter is found to be σ=0.27, balancing utility and verification robustness (Figure 1).

y3qyP3ycQi.text: Membership Weight aggregation estimates the probability of belonging to each site given covariates via federated multinomial logistic regression trained with FedAvg, without centralizing patient-level data (Equation 3).

Density Ratio Weight aggregation instead models the ratio between a site's covariate density and the overall population density, estimated parametrically from shared means and covariances (Equation 4).
Theorem 3 shows the oracle federated IPW/AIPW estimators achieve the same asymptotic efficiency as estimators computed on centrally pooled data (Theorem 3).
Theorem 4 proves the federated estimators have lower or equal variance than meta-analysis approaches across all considered heterogeneity scenarios (Theorem 4).
Theorem 5 establishes that the global (federated) overlap measure is bounded as 0 ≤ 𝒪_global ≤ Σ_k ρ_k 𝒪_k, i.e., federation can improve on the overlap achievable at any single site (Theorem 5).

On the Traumabase cohort (K=4 trauma centers, 6,003 patients) studying tranexamic acid's effect on mortality, federated AIPW estimates match centralized estimates while achieving lower variance than meta-analysis (Section 5, real-data application).

Wtjwjn1uak.text: The 2.5B-parameter annotation-anchored model closes roughly 85% of the semantic diversity gap with the base model, corresponding to a 6x reduction in diversity collapse compared to standard SFT (Section 5.2, Figure 5).

The method factorizes generation into a semantic-category variable z sampled from the pretraining distribution R(z|x) and a post-training-updated Q*(y|x,z), masking annotation losses during post-training to preserve R(z|x) (Section 4.1, Equations 1-3, Figure 2).

Standard SFT exhibits inverse scaling, where diversity declines as model size increases, while annotation-anchored training restores positive scaling of diversity with model scale (Section 3.2, Figures 3 and 5).
Ablations show both annotated pretraining and inference-time annotation sampling are necessary components, since removing either reduces the diversity-preservation effect (Section 5.3, Table 5).

Zero-shot accuracy on downstream benchmarks differs by at most about one point on average between annotation-anchored models and standard SFT, e.g. GSM8K accuracy of 36.4% vs. 35.4% (Table 3, Table 4).

6kCEyw9god.text: Retrofitting EvaByte with MtPC and speculative decoding achieves a 5.47x speedup over autoregressive generation and a 1.22x speedup over multi-token prediction using independence assumptions (Abstract, Section 1).

Four probabilistic-circuit parameterizations for multi-byte joint distributions are compared: fully-factorized MtPC-FF (independence baseline), MtPC-CP (canonical polyadic mixture), MtPC-HMM, and MtPC-BTree (binary tree factorization) (Section 1, Figure 1).

With a prediction window of n=16, MtPC-BTree reaches 203.5 tokens/s with an acceptance rate of 6.71, a 5.08x speed-up over the EvaByte single-token-prediction baseline, while MtPC-HMM attains the highest acceptance rate of 6.82 at higher latency (Section 4.3, Table 2).
Adding 2 LoRA layers to MtPC-BTree at n=16 pushes throughput to 219.1 tokens/s, the maximum observed 5.47x speed-up over the single-token-prediction baseline (Section 4.4, Table 3).

The speculative-decoding verification procedure guarantees that accepted tokens exactly match the underlying autoregressive verifier LLM for greedy decoding, or match its distribution in expectation under sampling (Section 3.4, Algorithm 2).

qA6FgH0nnZ.text: SDFT treats a model conditioned on expert demonstrations as its own teacher and trains the student to minimize the reverse KL divergence to that teacher, producing an on-policy learning signal (Section 3, Equation 1).
On the knowledge-acquisition task, SDFT reaches 89% strict accuracy and 98% OOD accuracy versus 80% strict accuracy and 80% OOD accuracy for SFT (Table 1).

When trained sequentially on three skills, SDFT accumulates skills stably while SFT exhibits severe catastrophic interference between tasks, and SDFT achieves better Pareto trade-offs between new-task accuracy and forgetting than SFT (Figure 3, Figure 4).

Averaged across prior-capability benchmarks after skill learning, SDFT retains near-baseline performance (about 64-65%) versus the 65.5% base model score, while SFT degrades to roughly 53-60% (Table 5).

SDFT's advantage over SFT widens with model scale, from a negligible gap at 3B parameters to about a 7-point advantage at 14B parameters, though SDFT costs roughly 2.5x the FLOPs and about 4x the wall-clock training time of SFT (Figure 5, Section 5).

GbOD25IA88.text: When fine-tuning Qwen3-14B on identical math datasets, the RL-tuned model achieves positive transferability indices (TI_other = +79.6%, TI_non = +29.3%), while SFT models show negative transfer with TI_non ranging from -41.2% to -250.2% (Table 1).

RL-tuned models consistently outperform SFT models on transfer to other reasoning tasks (LiveCodeBench, GPQA-Diamond, ACPBench, HeadQA) and non-reasoning tasks (CoQA, IFEval, HaluEval, MC-TACO) (Figure 2, Section 2.1).

RL training produces minimal and tightly clustered latent representation shifts, whereas SFT induces substantial representation and output drift, especially on non-reasoning inputs (Section 3, Table 2).

Token-level rank-shift analysis shows only 14-15 tokens experience rank shift under RL training versus 158-390 tokens under SFT, indicating RL selectively shifts task-relevant tokens while SFT perturbs broadly (Section 4, Table 3).
SFT-tuned models show 4-18x higher KL divergence from the base model's output distribution than RL-tuned models across benchmarks (Figure 5).

diRgjfD2vu.text: incTNP introduces causal masking and key-value caching into Transformer Neural Processes, reducing the per-step context-update cost from O(N^2) to O(N) while maintaining predictive performance (Section 1).
In autoregressive mode on the Temperature Forecasting task, incTNP-Seq delivers a 3.5x speedup over the TNP-D baseline while matching its predictive accuracy (Table 1).
Standard TNP incurs O(N^3) cumulative cost over a data stream, whereas incTNP's KV-caching reduces cumulative cost to O(N^2) (Figure 1, Section 1).

Proposition 4.1 shows that for exchangeable true distributions, the KL divergence decomposes such that non-exchangeable (causally-masked) models incur a quantifiable performance penalty, termed the KL Gap (Section 4.4, Proposition 4.1).

The KL Gap of incTNP-Seq is comparable to that of the permutation-invariant TNP-D baseline, and both substantially outperform the WISKI sparse Gaussian process baseline, indicating causal masking has little effect on prediction consistency (Section 4.4, Figure 3).
Models trained on sequences of 1,024 points generalize to streams of 30,000+ points, demonstrating length generalization for real-time streaming inference (Figures 4-6).

Y5bEI4cuMd.text: BrokenMath is built from 600+ 2025 competition problems (e.g., IMO, USAMO) refined via LLM-generated sycophantic perturbations and expert (IMO medalist) review into 504 final problems, 321 proof-style and 183 final-answer (Section 3.1).

Across 10 evaluated models, GPT-5 has the lowest sycophancy rate at 29.0% while DeepSeek-V3.1 has the highest at 70.2%, with a negative correlation (ρ = −0.62) between utility and sycophancy (Table 1).

Sycophancy is substantially higher on unsolved problems than solved ones, by more than 20 percentage points for several models, and proof-based problems trigger higher sycophancy than final-answer problems, by up to 22.5% for some models (Table 2, Figure 4).
Conversational, multi-turn framing increases self-sycophancy rates by up to 15.6% relative to single-turn prompting (Figure 5).
Test-time prompt-engineering interventions reduce DeepSeek-V3.1 sycophancy by 34.1%, while self-confidence reporting yields only up to a 6.4% reduction (Section 5.1).
Supervised fine-tuning on 13,000 curated examples lowers Qwen3-4B sycophancy from 55.6% to 51.0%, a modest improvement that does not eliminate the behavior (Section 5.2).

l3Yc9HS4US.text: FIRE-Bench comprises 30 tasks derived from high-impact ICLR/ICML/NeurIPS 2024-2025 papers, each decomposed into a hierarchical research-problem tree with root questions, intermediate nodes, and leaf nodes specifying concrete experiments to rediscover a known finding (Section on Benchmark Composition).

Claude Code with a Sonnet-4 backbone achieves the best overall F1 of 46.7±23.4, ahead of Codex (gpt-5-medium) at 41.9±25.4, OpenHands (gpt-5) at 37.9±23.0, and OpenHands (o4-mini) at 31.9±17.6 (Table 1).

Performance varies sharply by task: agents score as high as 91.7 F1 on 'Lost in the Middle' and 88.6 on 'Persona with Catch,' but as low as 0.0-34.2 on control-based, counterfactual-reasoning tasks like 'LLM Racial Bias in Medicine' (Table on task performance).

Failure mode analysis shows 76-95% of false-positive rediscovery claims are Contradictory or Unrelated to the target finding, with only 4.5-10.9% representing legitimate Alternative conclusions, and dominant errors stem from Research Planning and Conclusion Formation (Figure 3, Table 2).

Codex (gpt-5-medium) is the most cost-efficient agent at $0.15/task average ($2.21 total), compared to Claude Code's $0.84/task average ($12.67 total), with a positive correlation observed between cost and performance (Table 3).
A data contamination analysis stratified by difficulty and pre/post model-cutoff dates finds no consistent advantage for pre-cutoff tasks, suggesting minimal memorization effects (Table 4).

20c6jemABm.text: Mechanistic reward shaping identifies bias-encoding directions in reward model activations via difference-of-means (DiffMean) probes and removes them through null-space projection, h_null = h − Σ α(p_k^T h)p_k, with α=1 in most experiments (Section 3.2).

Debiasing preserves reward quality out-of-distribution: RewardBench-2 average accuracy is 69.3% after debiasing versus 70.1% baseline, a statistically non-inferior difference (p<0.001, δ=5%) (Table 2, Section 4.4).

Baseline reward models penalize expressions of uncertainty by an average 22.6% accuracy drop, which the debiasing intervention reduces while preserving correct-answer preferences (Figure 2, Section 4.2.1).

Linear probe-based interventions are effective for low-complexity biases such as length, uncertainty, and position, but are insufficient for high-complexity biases like sycophancy and model-style sensitivity, e.g., sycophancy remains 23-58% in newer SOTA reward models even after linear intervention (Table 3, Section 5.1).
Position bias deviations of 2-28% across answer positions are significantly reduced in variance for three of the evaluated reward models via probe nulling (Section 4.3).
For calibration, the Spearman correlation between reward model confidence and correctness on Skywork-Qwen8B roughly doubles from 0.182 to 0.386 after debiasing with α=1.0 (Table 1).

HJ5F3R9Tmd.text: Standard behavioral cloning can fail to cover the demonstrator's action distribution, which the paper proves (via a proposition in Appendix B.1) is a necessary condition for effective downstream RL finetuning.

Posterior BC (PostBC) instead models the posterior distribution of demonstrator behavior during pretraining, and Lemma 1 shows it achieves coverage with parameter γ ≥ α·min{π^β(a|s)/(64log(S·H/δ)), 1/(2λ)}.
A main theorem establishes that PostBC achieves a suboptimality bound of O(H²S·log(T)/T) for downstream finetuning while guaranteeing demonstrator action coverage (Theorem, Section 2/Appendix).

On Robomimic Lift, Can, and Square tasks, PostBC pretraining is compared against BC and σ-BC baselines across three finetuning algorithms (DSRL, Best-of-NN, DPPO), using dataset sizes of 5-300 trajectories depending on task (Section D.1, Tables 1-6).

On the real-world WidowX robot tasks 'Put corn in pot' and 'Pick up banana,' PostBC uses an ensemble size of 10 trained on only 10 demonstrations per task with Best-of-NN and IQL finetuning (Section D.3, Table 10).

Figure 1 shows PostBC maintains coverage in low-density regions of the action distribution while matching standard BC's behavior in high-density regions, and Figure 4 shows this coverage advantage is robust across varying Robomimic Square pretraining dataset sizes.

a6vCNSBBeq.text: The paper's sequential likelihood-mixing framework (Section 3, Section 3.1) constructs confidence sets as level sets of negative log-likelihood with data-driven thresholds, applicable to both classical reconstruction algorithms and deep learning methods including U-Nets, U-Net ensembles (K=10), and diffusion models (K=16 samples) (Section 4.2).

Proposition 3.2 guarantees the constructed (1−δ)-confidence sequence maintains coverage probability at least 1−δ for the true image at arbitrary (anytime) stopping times, i.e., finite-sample anytime validity.

On the Lamino industrial CT dataset, the sequential negative log-likelihood gap at intensity 10^9 is roughly 4.4×10^4 for the diffusion model versus about 2.3×10^5 for MLE and about 1.6×10^6 for FBP, indicating tighter confidence sets for the diffusion approach (Figure 3).
On the Lamino dataset with δ=0.05, empirical crossover (miscoverage) rates remain below the nominal 5% level, confirming the method's validity in practice (Figure 4).

On the Composite materials dataset, the diffusion-based method achieves approximately 3% miscoverage error, close to the theoretical 5% nominal level, while yielding significantly tighter confidence intervals than worst-case optimization or bootstrap baselines (Figure 7, Section 4.6).

Section 4.7 demonstrates a hallucination-detection application by conditioning reconstruction PSNR on membership in the confidence set, distinguishing plausible reconstructions from hallucinated artifacts.

29sn1uqWn3.text: Any language recognized by a linear RNN (LRNN) over the rationals lies in PNC1, meaning LRNNs can be simulated by log-depth arithmetic circuits (Theorem 3, Section 4).
LRNNs require only O(log n log* n) depth NC circuits, an O(log* n) overhead beyond the O(log n) depth of transformers/TC0 circuits (Corollary 5, Section 4).

Log-precision nonlinear RNNs can solve sorted deterministic graph connectivity, an L-complete problem, requiring Omega(log^2 n) depth and revealing a fundamental parallelization barrier absent in LRNNs (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
Poly-precision nonlinear RNNs can express P-complete problems under FO reductions, implying no efficient parallel algorithm exists for them unless P=NC (Corollary 2, Section 3.1).
DPLR-based LRNN architectures such as RWKV-7 and DeltaNet can solve the PNC1-complete iterated 3x3 matrix multiplication problem using only 4 layers (Theorem 5, Section 5.1).

Experiments show nonlinear RNNs generalize on the L-complete graph connectivity task while transformers and Mamba fail to solve it, matching the theoretical complexity separation (Figure 2, Section 6).

enfo9dCqRc.text: On the 10-move Chess domain, Claude 3.5 Sonnet scores 96.8% accuracy on text-based entity tracking versus only 66.2% on image-based tracking, a 30.6 percentage point gap (Table 1).
On the same Chess domain, GPT-4o scores 89.6% on text versus 73.3% on images, and only the o1 reasoning model exceeds 80% accuracy on images (83.5%) (Table 1).
In the Shell Game domain with 5 swaps, zero-shot accuracy is near chance (~33%), but chain-of-thought prompting raises GPT-4o from 36.0% to 99.8% on text and from 32.4% to 84.2% on images (Table 1).

Image-action classification accuracy is high (GPT-4o: 94.5% on Chess, 100% on Shell Game), showing models correctly perceive individual visual actions despite failing to track entity states over time (Table 2).

Cascaded inference, where images are first converted to text descriptions before reasoning, recovers performance close to text-only accuracy, indicating the bottleneck is updating coherent state representations from vision rather than task knowledge or raw perception (Table 3).

jgqFnXEDGG.text: On MNIST World, given 50 context frames and evaluated at a length-generalized horizon of 150 predicted frames, Flow Equivariant World Models (FloWM) achieve MSE 0.0018 versus 0.2111 for the Diffusion Forcing Transformer (DFoT) baseline (Table 1).
On the 3D Dynamic Block World, given 70 context frames and evaluated at 210 predicted frames, FloWM achieves MSE 0.001539 and PSNR 28.13 versus MSE 0.021684 and PSNR 16.64 for DFoT (Table 2).

An ablation removing velocity channels (FloWM no VC) substantially degrades performance relative to full FloWM on both MNIST World (MSE 0.0334 vs 0.0018 at 150 frames) and Block World (MSE 0.009614 vs 0.001539 at 210 frames), showing velocity channels are critical to long-horizon consistency (Tables 1-2).
The recurrence unifies self-motion and external object motion as one-parameter Lie-group flows acting on latent world memory, formalized in the self-motion flow equivariant recurrence of Equation 7.

Qualitative rollouts show FloWM maintains a consistent latent memory when an agent rotates away from and back to an object, while DFoT and DFoT-SSM baselines hallucinate object states after the agent's viewpoint changes (Figures 1 and 7).

GoW78qJ3qM.text: Two-layer self-attention with linear transformations (no feed-forward layers) is proven to be a universal approximator for continuous sequence-to-sequence functions on compact domains (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
A single layer of self-attention followed by a softmax function is also shown to suffice as a universal approximator (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
The proofs rely on a new interpolation-based method showing that self-attention can approximate a generalized ReLU activation to arbitrary precision (Lemma D.1, Appendix D).

An extended result and accompanying corollary establish additional universal approximation guarantees, including applicability to in-context learning of statistical models (Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.3.1, Section 3).

2T26db5Nma.text: BRIDGE uses a two-parameter logistic Item Response Theory (2PL IRT) model, P(y=1|theta,a,b) = sigma(a(theta-b)), to estimate latent task difficulty from model performance (Equation 1).

Latent task difficulty varies approximately linearly with the logarithm of human task completion time, with a log-linear calibration fit of R^2 = 0.81 on the METR benchmark suite of 170 tasks (Figure 2, Equation 3).
A one-unit increase in latent difficulty corresponds to approximately a 2.26x increase in human completion time (Section on calibration, Equation 3).

The task length that frontier models can solve at a 50% success rate doubles approximately every 6 months, while at an 80% success threshold the doubling time is approximately 7 months (Figures 5-6, Figures 8-9).
On Cybench, the model achieves 92.3% of tasks within a 0.5x-2x tolerance band when predicting human completion time, with R^2 = 0.45 (Figure 4).

DbZjxkZrZm.text: Activation Oracles (AOs) are trained on approximately 1 million examples combining System Prompt QA (64,000 samples), 336,000 classification examples across seven binary datasets, and 600,000 self-supervised context-prediction examples, using norm-matched additive steering at layer 1 to inject activations into placeholder tokens (Section 3).

On the Secret Side Constraint task with Llama-3.3-70B, AOs achieve 59% accuracy versus 52% for the best white-box interpretability baselines, and on the Taboo task with Gemma-2-9B-IT, AOs reach 21% accuracy versus 4% for the best baseline (Section 4.1, Figure 3).

On the emergent-misalignment model-diffing evaluation, AOs match the Activation Difference Lens baseline at a score of 2/5, indicating near-maximum performance under the evaluation's scoring constraints (Section 4.2, Figure 4).
On the out-of-distribution PersonaQA benchmark, AOs achieve about 14% accuracy on open-source models but 35% accuracy when the underlying model is Claude Haiku 3.5 (Section 5).

Dataset ablations show that 10 of 12 model/evaluation combinations achieve their best performance only with the full ~1M-example training mixture rather than SPQA-only or SPQA+Classification subsets (Section 6.1, Figure 5).

A diversity-vs-quantity ablation holding sample count fixed at 400k shows that adding context-prediction examples outperforms an equal-sized SPQA+Classification-only mixture, and the full 1M-example mixture outperforms both (Section 6.2, Figure 7).

jGRDp7Moik.text: Conditioning attention analysis on token position reveals hallucinated tokens receive higher attention than correct tokens, but this trend reverses when statistics are marginalized across positions, demonstrating Simpson's paradox in coarse-grained attention-based hallucination detection (Section 3.2, Figure 2a).

Hallucinated objects appear less frequently than correct objects in the underlying data, and this class imbalance alone allows a trivial classifier to reach over 84% accuracy on hallucination detection without using genuine signal (Section 3.2, Figure 5).
On LLaVA-1.5-7B, HaloProbe achieves 90.00% accuracy and 93.50 AUROC for hallucination detection, compared to 84.46% accuracy and 90.19 AUROC for the prior state-of-the-art method DIML (Table 1).

For hallucination mitigation with LLaVA-1.5 under greedy decoding, HaloProbe with post-processing reduces sentence-level hallucination (C_s) from a 51.6 baseline to 17.6, outperforming DIML's 25.0 (Table 2).

Ablating HaloProbe's external features and fine-grained attention components together drops detection accuracy from 90.0% to 84.4%, and ablating class-balanced training alone (using natural distribution) drops accuracy to 89.8% (Tables 5 and 6).

HaloProbe's hallucination-aware beam search mitigation uses a score function combining hallucinated/correct object counts and probabilities with beam width N_beam=5, threshold τ=0.5, and penalty β=0.1 (Section 4.2).

YJsolh0zg1.text: Hermite-NGP augments multi-resolution hash encoding by explicitly storing function values, first derivatives, and mixed partial derivatives at each grid vertex, enabling fully analytic first- and second-order derivative computation via cubic Hermite interpolation instead of finite differences or automatic differentiation (Section 4.1-4.2, Equation 6).

On the 2D Helmholtz benchmark with a=10, Hermite-NGP achieves an L2 error of 1.81e-5, roughly 20 times lower than PirateNet's 3.57e-4, and for a=20 achieves 7.93e-5, about 17 times lower than the closest baseline (Section 7.2, Table 1).

On the 3D Poisson benchmark with mesh boundaries, Hermite-NGP achieves an average L2 error of 0.0043 across three test meshes (e.g., 0.0055 on Armadillo) versus PIG's 0.0131 average (about 3x lower), and an average SDF gradient MAE of 0.0456 versus NeuralAngelo's 0.1099 (Table 2).

A multi-resolution coarse-to-fine training schedule that progressively activates hash-grid resolution levels reduces error by 79.2% relative to training all resolution levels simultaneously (Section 6, Section 7.7).

Hermite-NGP trains in as little as 3.5 ms per epoch for models with up to 17M parameters, and achieves 22-100x convergence speedup versus comparable neural PDE solvers while using less peak GPU memory in 3D than finite-difference-based INGP (Section 7.6).

An ablation using cubic (rather than Hermite) NGP variants fails on the 2D Helmholtz (a=10) benchmark with L2 error exceeding 0.1, due to hash-collision noise amplification in higher-order derivative estimates (Section 7.7).

ndOrsPyW0s.text: Encoded absences are formally defined (Definition 2.1) as neurons whose activation causally decreases in the presence of a concept, and the paper proves DNNs can mechanistically implement such neurons via negative weights from presence-encoding neurons combined with a positive bias potential (Section 2).

On ImageNet-trained VGG19 and ResNet-50, least-activating input patches cause dramatic activation drops (e.g., VGG19: 2.98 to 0.94; ResNet-50: 0.18 to 0.03), far exceeding the minimal effect of logical-NOT baselines, with statistical significance of p~10^-91 for VGG19 and p~10^-125 for ResNet-50 (Section 5.3, Table 1).
512 of 512 measured VGG19 channels and 2036 of 2048 measured ResNet-50 channels exhibit encoded absences, indicating the phenomenon is pervasive rather than rare (Section 5.3).

On the hand-crafted Hassenstein-Reichardt motion-detector CNN, standard attribution and feature-visualization methods fail to reveal the network's encoding of motion absence, whereas the proposed non-target attribution and minimization-based feature visualization succeed (Section 5.1).

On the biased ISIC skin-lesion dataset with inverted bias, standard presence-only debiasing still misclassifies malignant lesions with colorful patches at only 51% accuracy, whereas the proposed presence-and-absence debiasing method achieves 81% average accuracy, matching the unbiased upper bound (Section 5.4, Table 2).

mLR6OD6kKR.text: MACD constructs model-aware counterfactual reference inputs by using the Video-LLM's own gradient feedback (via Equation 6) to identify and softly mask object regions most responsible for hallucination, detected with YOLOv11, rather than relying on random perturbations as in prior contrastive decoding methods (Section 4.1-4.2).
On MVBench with Qwen2-VL-7B, MACD achieves 0.90 accuracy compared to 0.65 for the unmodified baseline and 0.6133 for VCD contrastive decoding (Table 1).

On EventHallusion with Qwen2.5-VL-3B, MACD reaches an F1 score of 0.7926 versus 0.7203 for the baseline and 0.7326 for VCD, and an ablation removing the learned mask-training step drops F1 to 0.6780 (Table 1, Table 2).
On Video-POPE, MACD achieves 0.85 accuracy versus 0.72 for the baseline, reducing false-positive hallucination rate from 40.0% to 17.0% (Table 4).
Human evaluators rate MACD's learned masks 3.10/5.0 for query relevance versus 2.40/5.0 for random masks (Table 5).
MACD increases inference latency by 35.5% and peak memory usage by 61.7% relative to standard decoding, in exchange for roughly a 15-point accuracy improvement on EventHallusion (Appendix B.2).

64HmKFCaq6.text: CDLM (via its MCDLM-PPLOptimized variant) achieves 28.6 perplexity on OpenWebText at 64 sampling steps, compared to 40.4 for MDLM and 30.8 for SDTT (Table 1).
At only 4 sampling steps, MCDLM achieves 649.4 perplexity on OpenWebText versus 1654.5 for the MDLM baseline, showing its advantage is most pronounced in the few-step regime (Table 1).
On conditional generation with 8 steps on OpenWebText, MCDLM-PPLOptimized reaches 31.6 perplexity and 62.8 BLEU, outperforming SDTT's 34.0 perplexity and 62.4 BLEU (Table 3).
On Lambada conditional generation at 64 steps, MCDLM attains 38.8 perplexity and 60.1 BLEU, beating SDTT's 46.4 perplexity and 59.3 BLEU (Table 3).

Section 3.3 shows that masked diffusion, continuous consistency models, and progressive distillation all emerge as special cases of the CDLM framework under different step-size and determinism limits.
CDLM reports up to 64x-128x speedup over MDLM and a 16x-32x reduction in number of function evaluations while matching autoregressive-baseline quality at 32-64 steps (Section 1).

IRwg87oeJo.text: scLDM's VAE uses a unified Multi-head Cross-Attention Block (MCAB) architecture that performs permutation-invariant pooling in the encoder and permutation-equivariant unpooling in the decoder, exploiting the fact that cell order in single-cell data is arbitrary (Section 3.1, Subsection 3.2).

scLDM replaces the standard Gaussian latent prior with a latent diffusion model built on Diffusion Transformers and linear interpolants, enabling multi-conditional classifier-free guidance during generation (Section 3.2).

scLDM is evaluated against baselines including scGAN and scDiffusion variants on perturbational (e.g., CRISPR/drug) prediction tasks, reporting substantial improvements over these baselines (Table 3).
scLDM's reconstruction quality across cell types on observational single-cell datasets is reported in Table 2 and visualized in Figure 4.
Synthetic single-cell data generated by scLDM is shown to be useful for training downstream cell-type classifiers, with results reported in Table 23 (Appendix K).

5D3ZblXmW2.text: On the chain topology under the NetSafe attack, AdvEvo-MARL-7B achieves a 0.99% attack success rate versus 21.78% for the Vanilla-7B baseline (Table 1).

Across three attack scenarios (NetSafe, AutoInject, UserHijack) and three topologies (chain, tree, complete), AdvEvo-MARL keeps attack success rate at or below roughly 20% (peaking at 17.68% on the complete topology), while open-source baselines reach as high as 65.53% (Table 1).

AdvEvo-MARL preserves task performance with minimal degradation on AIME (under 3%) and LiveCodeBench, while improving GPQA general-reasoning accuracy by up to +3.67%, all without adding external guard agents (Figure 2).

Against a static-attacker ablation baseline, AdvEvo-MARL's dynamic adversarial co-evolution yields a 12% reduction in attack success rate under the NetSafe threat plus a 4% gain in task performance (Section 5.3).
Enabling the public-baseline mechanism produces more stable and efficient training dynamics, with improved task accuracy and controlled attack success rate, as shown in Figure 5 (Section 5.4).

YyesH7V9c2.text: HALO's Hierarchical Prototypes Regularization (HPR) component enforces ancestor-descendant representation similarity via a margin-based ranking loss and temporal saliency consistency, defined in Equation 5, and yields small but reliable gains in final fine-grained accuracy (FFAcc) (Table 2).

HALO's Hierarchical Adaptive Aggregation (PredLA) combines a linear head (fast adaptation) with a frozen-feature analytic head (recursive least squares) via probability-space combination with temperature scaling optimized on replayed data (Equation 12), improving AAUC from 52.5 to 61.2 and reducing mistake severity from 1.34 to 0.97 on CUB-200 (Table 2).
On the main benchmark comparison, HALO reports AAUC of 59.2 and mistake severity (MS) of 1.13 on CIFAR-100, and AAUC of 78.3 with MS of 1.55 on iNaturalist (Table 1).
HALO shows graceful degradation under corrupted hierarchies: 40% node vacancy causes only a -2.18% drop in AAUC, while 40% label noise causes a larger -5.01% drop (Table 4).
Figure 6 shows that HALO's learned hierarchical prototype distance matrices become increasingly aligned with ground-truth taxonomic hierarchies as HPR regularization is applied.

YXnFGsSkCC.text: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Graph-R1 achieves 57.82 average F1 across six RAG benchmarks, compared to 46.19 for Search-R1 (RL + chunk retrieval), 32.05 for StandardRAG, and 29.40 for HyperGraphRAG using GPT-4o-mini (Table 2, Section 5.2).

Graph-R1 is evaluated on six standard QA benchmarks—2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, Musique, Natural Questions, PopQA, and TriviaQA—using 5,120 training instances and 128 test instances per dataset (Section 5.1, Appendix D).

Graph-R1 conducts an average of 2.3-2.5 multi-turn retrieval interactions per query while generating shorter responses (1,200-1,500 tokens) than baselines, yet achieves the highest F1 scores with moderate retrieved content (Figure 6, Section 5.5).

Graph-R1's knowledge hypergraph construction costs 5.69 seconds and $2.81 per 1K tokens, and query response costs 7.0 seconds with $0 generation cost, versus 9.6 seconds and $8.76 per query for HyperGraphRAG (Table 3, Section 5.4).
On generation quality judged against GPT-4o-mini, Graph-R1 scores 86.9 on Correctness, 95.2 on Relevance, and 88.5 on Logical Coherence (Figure 7, Section 5.6).

The paper formalizes and validates three propositions: that graph structures improve accuracy (Proposition 1, Appendix B.1), that multi-turn interaction improves retrieval efficiency (Proposition 2, Appendix B.2), and that end-to-end RL aligns knowledge with generation (Proposition 3, Appendix B.3).

fuBIaxqMAG.text: Integrating Self-Predictive Representations (SPR) with a momentum-averaged target encoder predicting K=5 future latent states substantially improves human-normalized performance over the QRC baseline on 40M-frame Atari, raising mean/median/IQM from 0.04/0.02/0.03 to 1.25/0.50/0.62 (Table 1).
Applying SPR to Stream Q improves human-normalized mean/median/IQM from 0.48/0.15/0.23 (baseline) to 0.61/0.32/0.37 on Atari at 40M frames (Table 1).

Projecting the SPR gradient onto the plane orthogonal to the RL gradient history is proposed to resolve conflicting updates between ObGD-based streaming RL and SGD-based SPR, evidenced by cosine similarity between the two gradients dropping below zero without orthogonalization (Figure 4).

Adding SPR increases the effective rank of learned latent representations on Atari from 42.7 ± 33.7 (QRC without SPR) to 1256.9 ± 296.5 (QRC with SPR), an approximately 29x increase, supporting the claim that SPR yields richer representations that partially substitute for a replay buffer (Table 2).

The method is evaluated across three streaming RL suites: Atari 26 at 40M and 100M frames, MinAtar across 5 games at 5M frames, and Octax across 8 JAX-accelerated games at 20M frames (Section on Evaluation Suites).
Ablations over the SPR future-prediction depth and loss weight identify K=5 and λ=2.0 as the chosen configuration (Table 3).

Zdx1hFJarp.text: SurrogateSHAP reformulates coalition evaluation as a mixture of conditional generators from a single pretrained text-to-image model, avoiding per-subset retraining, and reports a 2.9x to 23.4x speedup over retraining-based attribution approaches (Method section).
SurrogateSHAP fits a gradient-boosted tree surrogate over sampled coalition utilities and computes Shapley values analytically via TreeSHAP rather than by sampling permutations (Method section).

On synthetic games at a budget of M=512 sampled coalitions, SurrogateSHAP achieves an L2 error of 0.010 versus 0.085 for KernelSHAP, demonstrating improved sample efficiency in interaction-heavy utility landscapes (Sample Efficiency results).

On the Linear Datamodel Score benchmark, SurrogateSHAP outperforms the prior best method (sFT) on CIFAR-20 FID (51.21% vs 40.0%), ArtBench Aesthetics (44.14% vs 18.85%), and Fashion-Product Diversity (32.41% vs 20.34%) (Benchmark Performance table).

Removing the top 10% of contributor groups identified by SurrogateSHAP increases FID degradation by 31.70%, compared to 17.53% for baseline attribution methods, in a counterfactual validation experiment (Counterfactual Validation section).

In a dermatology case study, SurrogateSHAP identifies a single hospital (Hospital 7) as the source of a spurious sex-melanoma correlation (r=0.21) in generated images, and excluding that site reduces the correlation to approximately 5x10^-4 (Clinical Application case study).

8aTV77lBaG.text: TMS trains a student model on a mixture (with mixing probability alpha) of original ground-truth labels and outputs sampled uniformly from a buffer of trajectories harvested from intermediate checkpoints saved during a baseline SFT run (Method, Two-Stage Process).

On ARC-C with Qwen-1.5B, TMS improves accuracy from 42.3 (standard SFT) to 65.4, closely approaching GRPO's 66.7, and on Qwen-3B from 42.7 (SFT) to 79.2 versus GRPO's 80.2 (Experimental Results table).

TMS reduces cross-task drift (catastrophic forgetting) to roughly 2-3% compared to 26-41% for standard SFT, closely tracking GRPO's 1-2% drift, despite using only binary correctness signals and no reward model or verifier (Experimental Results / Comparison Claims).
Single-checkpoint distillation baselines (Self-SFT and Final-SFT) improve retention over standard SFT but substantially underperform TMS's full trajectory-mixing approach (Comparison Claims section).

The paper introduces Policy-Label Divergence (PLD) to formalize supervision mismatch, showing held-out PLD increases during late-stage SFT training even as target-task accuracy continues to improve (Key Innovation section).

aYqF2Cv6Cr.text: If the L0 sparsity level of a sparse autoencoder (SAE) is too low, the SAE engages in 'feature hedging,' mixing correlated features together to improve reconstruction at the cost of disentanglement (Key Findings).
If L0 is set too high, the SAE instead produces degenerate solutions that also mix features, though the paper reports this failure mode is less damaging than setting L0 too low (Key Findings).

Incorrectly-specified SAEs with mixed, entangled features can achieve better reconstruction scores than correctly disentangled SAEs when L0 is too low, undermining sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff curves as an evaluation criterion (Reconstruction Paradox section).

The paper proposes an 'Nth decoder projection score' metric to identify the correct L0 by measuring decoder-activation alignment, and applies it to Gemma-2-2b layer 12 to estimate the correct L0 at approximately 200-250 (Detecting Correct L0 section).

Analysis of open-source SAEs hosted on Neuronpedia finds that most deployed models use L0 values below 100, well below the ~200-250 value estimated as correct for Gemma-2-2b layer 12, implying widespread feature-quality degradation in current SAEs (Real-World Implications section).

XL254Z1PvD.text: SS-TPT computes a Stability Score, defined as the inverse of the Jensen-Shannon divergence between a view's prediction and its weakly-augmented counterpart, and a Suitability Score based on cosine-induced feature-space density among views, to identify trustworthy augmented views for test-time prompt tuning of CLIP (Method Overview).

Across 10 fine-grained classification datasets (SUN397, Food101, Caltech101, DTD, Flower102, Pets, UCF101, Aircraft, EuroSAT, Cars), SS-TPT achieves an average robustness of 46.8%, surpassing the strongest baseline R-TPT by +6.4 percentage points (Key Results table).
On ImageNet, SS-TPT attains 60.0% clean accuracy and 48.6% robust accuracy, outperforming R-TPT by +1.9 and +5.4 percentage points respectively (Key Results, ImageNet).

With 15 augmented views, SS-TPT runs at approximately 0.74 seconds per image, nearly 2x faster than R-TPT using 63 views (1.67s per image), illustrating an improved robustness-throughput trade-off (Robustness-Throughput Trade-off section).

Even with a single augmented view, SS-TPT maintains 25.8% average robustness, improving over R-TPT by +15.7 percentage points in the same single-view setting (Robustness-Throughput Trade-off section).

The method is evaluated against attacks including PGD, Carlini-Wagner, DI2-FGSM, and AutoAttack under white-box threat models across 15 total benchmarks (Datasets Evaluated / Attack scenarios section).

mnUgulPmNU.text: AlgoVeri comprises 77 classical algorithm problems with specifications aligned across three verification languages: Dafny, Verus, and Lean (Section 2).
Gemini-3 Flash with 1 rollout x 15 repair rounds achieves 40.26% pass rate on Dafny, 24.68% on Verus, and 7.79% on Lean (semantic-filtered) (Table 2).
GPT-OSS-120B improves markedly with 10 rollouts x 15 rounds (28.57% Dafny, 10.39% Verus, 14.29% Lean) versus 1x15 (13.51% Dafny, 7.01% Verus, 7.01% Lean) (Table 2).
Repair dynamics show Gemini-3 Flash undergoes continuous improvement across 15 repair rounds, nearly tripling its Dafny pass rate, while GPT-OSS-120B saturates by round 3-4 (Figure 4).
Radar charts reveal a 'complexity cliff': models perform well on basic data structures and sorting but collapse on advanced structures and graph algorithms, particularly in Verus and Lean (Figure 3).
Error evolution analysis shows Lean failures are dominated by hallucinated nonexistent lemmas, while Verus exhibits a persistent syntax barrier throughout repair rounds (Figure 6).

oSuKfnbPFB.text: The Efficient Waste Feature Extraction (EWFE) layer combines a Spatial Context Module using 5x5 group-wise convolution for local pixel relationships with a Frequency Context Module applying Fourier transforms for global contextual relationships (Section 3.2).
The Auxiliary Feature Enhancement Module (AFEM) performs boundary enhancement via difference-of-Gaussian filtering in the frequency domain and blob amplification via pooled attention (Section 3.3).
EWSegNet achieves 56.44% mIoU on ZeroWaste-f with 23.3M parameters and 64.8ms latency, compared to COSNet's 56.67% mIoU with 27.3M parameters and 73.6ms latency (Table 3-equivalent results section).
On ZeroWaste-aug, EWSegNet reaches 74.10% mIoU, substantially outperforming LWCHNet's 63.16% (Section 4 results).
On SpectralWaste, EWSegNet scores 71.03% mIoU versus COSNet's 69.96% (Section 4 results).
Ablation study shows progressive mIoU gains on ZeroWaste-f from a 47.32% baseline to 51.63% with SCM added, 53.05% with FCM added, and 56.44% with AFEM added (Table 5).

4VuMV9beC1.text: On Claude-Haiku-4.5, the visual cipher attack achieves a 40.9% best-of-5 attack success rate versus 10.7% for the equivalent textual cipher attack (Table 2, Section 4.2).

On Gemini-3-Flash, visual cipher attacks reach 97.5% success versus 89.3% for textual ciphers, while on GPT-5.2 visual ciphers achieve only 8.2% versus 5.7% textual, indicating GPT-5.2 is the most robust of the six evaluated frontier models (Table 2).

The visual cipher attack encodes harmful instructions as abstract glyph sequences accompanied by a visual decoding legend, requiring the model to decode geometric symbols into words before executing the underlying instruction (Section 3.7).
The evaluation employs a 'decode-first' prompting strategy in which models must interpret the visual encoding before acting on the implied instruction (Section 3.7).
Attack success rates are reported across six frontier vision-language models including Claude-Haiku-4.5, Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5.2, Qwen3-VL-235B, and Qwen3-VL-32B (Table 2, Section 4.2).

cKoqWcyVvd.text: Off-policy log-dispersion regularization (LDR) generalizes the on-policy log-variance objective to a family of divergences minimizing dispersion of f_theta(x) around its mean, with LDR-L2 recovering the log-variance objective and LDR-L1 minimizing the first absolute central moment (Section 3, Equation 3).

On alanine dipeptide with an unbiased dataset of 1x10^6 samples, LDR-regularized training outperforms training on 5x10^6 samples without regularization, indicating more than 5 times higher data efficiency (Section 4.2, Table 1).

Combining LDR with the Constrained Mass Transport (CMT) variational baseline on alanine hexapeptide, using only 1x10^8 target evaluations, avoids the mode collapse and low ESS (5.92%) that vanilla CMT exhibits at that budget, achieving over 30% ESS instead, roughly a 10x efficiency gain relative to CMT's originally reported 4x10^8 evaluations (Section 4.4, Table 3).

On the biased-dataset alanine dipeptide setting with importance sampling, applying LDR-L2 on both the importance-sampled data and the original biased dataset raises ESS from 51.42% (vanilla forward KL on 1x10^5 IS samples) to 83.20% (Table 2, Section 4.3).

In Cartesian-coordinate training with an autoregressive TarFlow-based normalizing flow, LDR-L2 and LDR-L1 both outperform non-regularized forward KL on alanine dipeptide (NLL of -219.815 and -219.800 vs -219.583), and TarFlow achieves nearly 4000x faster sampling throughput than a representative continuous normalizing flow baseline (Section 4.5, Table 4).

Peim0KY6ty.text: Do-Shapley values can be computed exactly in O(r(d+e+T)) time, where r is the number of irreducible sets, d the number of dimensions, e the number of edges, and T the value-function evaluation time, versus the naive 2^d complexity (Section 3).

Theorem 5.1 shows the do-Shapley value phi_i is identifiable if and only if nu({j}) is identifiable for all j in [d], reducing identifiability checks from r coalitions to just d singleton coalitions (Theorem 5.1).
Lemma 3.1 establishes that for any closed set with a basis, removing any basis element yields another closed set, enabling efficient lattice traversal via Algorithm 2 (Lemma 3.1, Algorithm 2).
Algorithm 3 (boundary sampling) guarantees discovery of min(m, r) distinct equivalence classes using m queries, running in O(m*d(d+e)) time (Section on estimator performance, Algorithm 3).

The doRegressionMSR estimator consistently outperforms baseline variants and exhibits a phase transition at m=r, where error vanishes to machine precision while structure-agnostic methods retain variance (Figure 5).
Real-world causal structures tend to be sparse, so the number of irreducible sets r scales between the exponential worst case 2^d and the linear lower bound d (Figure 4).

xLnzdfOS6r.text: gp2Scale constructs non-stationary compactly supported kernels via a convolution-based Wendland construction and a bump-function formulation (Section 4.2, Section 4.3).
On a 10-million-point global temperature dataset, gp2Scale achieves RMSE 2.8509, beating the Vecchia approximation's RMSE of 2.8602 (Section 5.5, Table 5).
The 10-million-point experiment is executed via distributed block MCMC on 1024 A100 GPUs at roughly 477 seconds per MCMC iteration (Section 4.6, Section B.5).
On synthetic 1-D data, gp2Scale outperforms SVGP, VNNGP, SKI, and Vecchia approximations in RMSE/CRPS (Section 5.1, Table 1).
On a 60,000-point MNIST classification task, gp2Scale attains a Brier score of 0.018±0.002 (Section 5.4).

eKfWG67mZB.text: ConServe achieves 2.35x higher overall throughput than online-only vLLM serving (3702 vs 1999 tokens/s) by harvesting idle GPU cycles for offline work (Section 6.2, Figure 5).
Compared to vLLM++, ConServe reduces P99 time-to-first-token tail latency by roughly 84x, from about 83825ms down to about 1000ms (Section 6.2).

ConServe preempts offline generation at the granularity of individual model layers rather than whole iterations, with preemption detection and response completing within 5.41ms and a per-layer safepoint overhead of 988µs (Section 4.3, Section 6.4.2).
ConServe incrementally checkpoints the KV cache once per generation iteration to bound the data transferred during preemption (Section 4.4).
During idle (OFF) phases, ConServe's offline execution reaches 5868 tokens/s while keeping P99 TTFT under 350ms and P99 TPOT under 90ms during ON/OFF transitions (Section 6.3.1, Figure 6).

q7mB5s1ie1.text: The HJ-Prox estimator's approximation error is uniformly bounded by sup_x ||prox^δ_{tf}(x) - prox_{tf}(x)|| ≤ sqrt(n t δ) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).

Replacing exact proximal steps with HJ-Prox in the proximal point method and proximal gradient descent preserves almost-sure convergence under mild assumptions (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.6, Section 3.2).
The HJ-Prox substitution extends convergence guarantees to Douglas-Rachford splitting and Davis-Yin splitting for composite objectives f+g+h with h L-smooth (Theorem 3.8, Theorem 3.9, Section 3.2).
HJ-Prox is also applied within the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm via conjugate operator approximations (Theorem 3.10, Section 3.2).

Splitting reduces the effective Lipschitz constant relative to non-split approaches, and hybrid exact/approximate strategies outperform fully approximate proximal methods in experiments (Section 3.3, Section 4.3).

JxbxHB5d9v.text: FIRE is evaluated against seven baseline multi-fidelity regression methods (AR(1), ResGP, NARGP, ContinuAR, MisoKG, MFBNN, MFRNP) across 31 benchmark problems comprising 18 synthetic, 6 hyperparameter-optimization, and 7 physics-based tasks (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
FIRE attains the highest Elo rating and the lowest average rank on both accuracy (NRMSE) and uncertainty quantification (NLL) across the benchmark suite (Figure 2).
FIRE dominates the accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, being simultaneously the fastest and most accurate method evaluated (Figure 3).
Removing distributional conditioning from FIRE in an ablation drops its Elo rating by approximately 250 points (Figure 4).
FIRE maintains its performance advantage over GP-based baselines even under extreme high-fidelity data scarcity of only 2-5% (Figure 5, Figure 6).
A theoretical result establishes Bayes risk monotonicity justifying FIRE's use of variance/quantile conditioning for tabular foundation models (Theorem 7.2, Section 7.2).

Yy37YQCvCt.text: In the linear setting, the learned instrument-guided representation satisfies D̃ = PD for an invertible matrix P, guaranteeing the outcome-improvement direction E[Y_{αu}] = E[Y] + α‖(P⁻¹)ᵀθ‖ (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

In the non-linear setting, optimal solutions of the IRAE objective likewise preserve the relation D̃ = PD with invertible P, extending the identification guarantee beyond linear structural equations (Theorem 4.5, Section 4).
The non-linear method provably yields a positive first-order outcome improvement, E[Y_{αu} - Y] = α‖(P⁻¹)ᵀE[∇_D h(D)]‖ + O(α²) (Theorem 4.8, Section 4).
On synthetic linear data with n=10,000 and covariate dimension m ∈ {50, 100, 500} across three data-generating processes, LIRR outperforms PCA-based representations (Table 1, Section 5).

On a modified MNIST task where the outcome depends on digit color with injected confounders and instruments, LIRR/IRAE variants are evaluated against 9 methods across sample sizes 1,000/10,000/30,000 and intervention magnitudes α ∈ {0.2, 1.0} (Table 2, Table 3, Section 5).

KBvnXHCIch.text: Causal mediation analysis via Average Indirect Effect (AIE) on OpenFlamingo-4B shows that only a small subset of attention heads concentrated in intermediate layers causally transmit spatial-relation information, with the top 10 heads per relation selected as function vector sources (Section 3.3.2).

Fine-tuned function vectors for zero-shot relation tasks more than double zero-shot baseline accuracy on the synthetic dataset and outperform a 4-shot in-context-learning baseline on the real-world GQA subset (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

Composite function vectors, formed by linearly combining two directional function vectors (e.g., above + left), solve one-shot analogy tasks on untrained composite spatial relations (e.g., above-left) at 16.8% accuracy, versus 8.3%, 8.1%, and 9.6% for 1-shot, 4-shot, and 10-shot in-context-learning baselines respectively (Section 4.4, Figure 6).

Ablations show performance peaks when function vectors are built from 6-12 heads and degrades as more, less-informative heads are added, and that optimal injection occurs at intermediate layers (layer 19 for the synthetic dataset, layer 8 for GQA) (Appendix Section A.3).

7i8d203tky.text: PLaCy (Power-Law Causal discovery) fits a power-law model to the frequency spectrum of each time series and performs causal discovery by tracking the evolution of the fitted spectral exponents and amplitudes rather than analyzing raw time series values (Section 1).

The paper gives a theoretical argument that the frequency-domain (power-law spectral) transformation preserves the underlying causal graph structure of the original time series (Section 2, Section 2.1).

PLaCy is claimed to consistently outperform state-of-the-art causal discovery alternatives on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets with known causal structures, with the advantage most pronounced when the time series exhibit nonequilibrium, nonlinear, or scale-free (power-law) properties (Section 1).
Robustness of PLaCy is evaluated across real-world causal discovery tasks spanning finance, economics, neuroscience, and climate science domains (abstract only).

PlFJwgaaDK.text: The method learns an energy-based model via anisotropic dual score matching with covariance conditioning, producing a single model that computes normalized posterior densities for diverse linear inverse problems without per-task retraining or fine-tuning (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
On CelebA inpainting the model attains PSNR 17.70, LPIPS 0.093, and FID 34.57, and on ImageNet64 deblurring it attains PSNR 29.10, LPIPS 0.004, and FID 44.82 (Table 1).

An unbiased Metropolis-adjusted Langevin (MALA) correction with 8 corrector steps improves LPIPS to 0.089 compared to 0.093 for uncorrected Langevin (ULA) sampling, demonstrating the value of energy-guided MCMC correction (Section 4.2, Table 2).

The learned energy model supports blind linear inverse problems by estimating the degradation operator via Bayes' rule, evaluated in addition to standard inpainting and Gaussian deblurring tasks on CelebA and ImageNet (Section 4.3).

TR2DYfZXTd.text: BlueCodeAgent achieves an average 12.7% F1 score improvement across four datasets spanning three tasks (bias instruction detection, malicious instruction detection, vulnerable code detection) compared to baselines including direct prompting of GPT-4o (Abstract, Section 4, Table 1).

The red-teaming pipeline generates a diverse knowledge base of risky instances using three strategies: policy-based generation with an uncensored model, seed-based adversarial optimization with jailbreak tools (GCG, AmpleGCG, AutoDAN, Advprompter), and CWE-driven synthesis of vulnerable/secure code pairs (Section 3.2).

Blue-teaming defense operates at two levels: a principled-level defense that distills red-teamed knowledge into constitutions (actionable rules) increasing true positives, and a nuanced-level defense using Docker-based dynamic sandbox testing that primarily reduces false positives on vulnerability detection (Section 3.3).

On the vulnerable code detection task, direct prompting with GPT-4o achieves F1 of 0.64, while BlueCodeAgent combined with dynamic testing (using Claude-3.7-Sonnet) achieves F1 of 0.77 (Table 1, Section 4).

4VMbVE64lF.text: M-ORE (Modality-Decoupled Online Recursive Editing) maintains separate, module-wise locality statistics for text and visual components to prevent visually dominant activations from skewing statistical updates during online editing of multimodal LLMs (Section 3.2, Section 4).

M-ORE uses fixed orthogonal low-rank subspace updates together with Sherman-Morrison recursion to achieve constant O(1) per-edit computational overhead across long editing horizons, reducing inter-edit interference (Section 3.3, Section 4).
On BLIP2-OPT after 100 sequential edits, M-ORE reaches an average score of 92.56 on E-VQA (+0.54 over LiveEdit) and 82.49 on E-IC (+1.89 over the baseline) (Table 1, Section 5).
On LLaVA-v1.5 after 100 edits, M-ORE improves E-IC reliability to 94.64% (from 78.49% for LiveEdit) and text generality to 93.27% (from 78.77% for the baseline) (Table 1, Section 5).

An ablation study isolates the contribution of M-ORE's design choices, including the effect of write-space basis initialization and seed sensitivity, on overall editing performance (Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).

951OAanYyQ.text: Pretraining a 6.9B-parameter LLM with documents about aligned AI behavior upsampled to roughly 1% of the corpus reduces misalignment scores from 45% to 9% on the article-sourced evaluation set (Figure 2).

Upsampling synthetic misalignment discourse during pretraining increases misalignment scores relative to the unfiltered baseline, rising from 45% to 51% on article-sourced questions and from 40% to 40% on textbook-sourced questions (Figure 2).

The alignment-pretraining effect persists through downstream post-training and an HHH system prompt: the Alignment Upsampled model retains a 9% misalignment score versus 34% for the Unfiltered baseline model even after identical post-training interventions (Figure 5).
