Alignment pretraining is evaluated with a suite of 4,174 scenario-based questions (2,671 article-sourced, 1,503 textbook-sourced) covering sandbagging, deception, goal preservation, sycophancy, and power-seeking behaviors (Section 2).
Alignment-pretraining interventions reduce average performance by only 2-4 percentage points across seven capability benchmarks, indicating minor capability cost (Table 3, Section 5).

Late-stage alignment pretraining (introducing the alignment-upsampled data only in a later ~50B-token stage of training) is shown to be as effective as intervening from the start of pretraining (Section 4, Figure 6).

lu1J2bQqyT.text: RePro trains a 1B-parameter rephraser via reinforcement learning to recycle 72B tokens sampled from DCLM-RefinedWeb, combining quality and faithfulness rewards during training (Abstract).
Mixing RePro-recycled data with organic data yields 4.7%-14.0% relative accuracy gains over an organic-only baseline across 22 downstream tasks on the DCLM Core benchmark suite (Abstract).
RePro improves organic data efficiency by 2-3x compared to training on organic data alone, meaning fewer organic tokens are needed to reach the same downstream accuracy (Abstract).
RePro achieves a 36.7x training/inference speedup relative to ReWire, a prior recycling method that uses a Llama-3.3-70B rephraser with chain-of-thought prompting (Abstract).

RePro's faithfulness reward keeps 95% of key points supported in recycled text versus organic data, and reduces omitted key points by 92% relative to prior prompting-based rephrasing methods (Abstract).
RePro is compared against baselines WRAP (using Mistral-7B for rephrasing) and ProX (program-based text editing), in addition to ReWire (Abstract).

bF1V9A56d3.text: On the strict evaluation of TRIP-Bench's Easy split, the best model (DeepSeek-V3.2 without thinking) reaches only 18.5% success, while GPT-5.2 with thinking reaches 45% on the loose Easy-split criterion, with all models scoring at most 50% (Table 2).
On TRIP-Bench's Hard subsets, model success rates drop below 10% under strict evaluation across all tested models (Table 2).

Enabling chain-of-thought reasoning ('thinking mode') raises Easy-strict success from 5.0% to 31.0%, an absolute gain of 26 percentage points, demonstrating the benchmark's sensitivity to reasoning depth (Table 2).
TRIP-Bench comprises long-horizon travel-planning dialogues with 18 tools, over 40 travel requirements, and up to 15 turns exceeding 200k tokens of context (Abstract, Section 3).

Group Turn-level Policy Optimization (GTPO), trained on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, achieves 49% success on easy-loose and 21% on easy-strict splits, outperforming Gemini-3-Pro under the same evaluation protocol (Table 3, Section 4.2).
GTPO combines global instruction normalization, turn-wise reward differencing against the previous turn's baseline, and turn-level reward normalization across trajectory groups (Section 4.2).

aYe8j2jOmK.text: The constrained-learning formulation requires each layer's expected loss to satisfy E[f(X,Φ_l)] ≤ (1-α_l)E[f(X,Φ_{l-1})], enforcing a per-layer descent constraint on the objective (Section 2).
Theorem 1 (the Constrained Learning Theorem) bounds the duality gap of the nonconvex constrained problem by an expressivity parameter ν and a sample-complexity term ζ(M,δ) (Section 3, Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 proves asymptotic convergence of the primal-dual training algorithm to the optimal loss, with error scaling with step size, sample size M, and model expressivity (Section 3, Theorem 2).

On video denoising with ViT, DUST, and UT architectures evaluated on CUHK Avenue, UCSD, and ShanghaiTech, constrained DUST variants achieve lower RMSE than unconstrained counterparts for all perturbation levels γ≥1.0 on UCSD (Section 5, Figure 3).

On IMDb sentiment classification with perturbed embeddings, constrained RoBERTa shows larger out-of-distribution accuracy gains than constrained DistilBERT, while in-distribution accuracy degrades by less than 0.3% (Section 5).

Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B on Alpaca under the constrained objective preserves monotonic layerwise loss descent and achieves a 50% length-controlled AlpacaEval win rate at γ=0.0 versus 69.93% at γ=1.5 under input noise (Section 6).

8UzZ0CbPsk.text: The paper reduces the runtime complexity of computing full Clebsch-Gordan tensor products from the naive O(L^6) to O(L^4 log^2 L), approaching the theoretical lower bound of O(L^4) (Abstract).
Theorem 4.3 gives a decomposition formula for tensor spherical harmonics in terms of Wigner 9j symbols, underlying the generalized Gaunt formula (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).

Theorem 5.1 proves that the proposed Vector Signal Tensor Product (VSTP) recovers all interactions possible under full Clebsch-Gordan tensor products except scalar multiplication, whereas the prior Gaunt tensor product is restricted by parity selection rules (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
The completeness argument in Section 5 shows that only spin-1 (vector-valued) signals are needed to recover the interactions missing from the standard Gaunt tensor product (Section 5).
Section 3 shows the existing Gaunt tensor product emerges naturally from generalizing FFT-based convolution to compact Lie groups via group Fourier transforms (Section 3).

The authors note the asymptotic O(L^4 log^2 L) speedup only manifests for L on the order of 1000 or more, well beyond the L≤10 regime typically used in current equivariant network applications (Section 6 discussion).

ZlDndRDMHm.text: UEC-STD is a post-hoc, architecture-agnostic error corrector that decomposes backbone forecasts into trend and seasonal components via moving-average filtering and trains separate correction heads for each, reconstructing the final forecast by summing corrected components (Section on UEC-STD Architecture / Table 4 ablation).

Applied on top of backbones including TimeMixer, TimesNet, TimeXer, TimeBridge, PatchTST, and iTransformer across 7 standard datasets plus 3 Monash datasets, UEC-STD yields an average 2.32% MSE and 0.94% MAE reduction on the standard datasets and a 10.05% MSE and 9.13% MAE reduction on the Monash datasets (Table 1).
On ETTm1 specifically, UEC-STD reduces MSE by 4.06% and MAE by 1.58% relative to the uncorrected backbone forecast (Table 1).
An ablation isolating trend-only and seasonal-only correction heads shows the full trend+seasonal decomposition outperforms either single-component variant (Table 4).

Autoregressive error accumulation increases forecast error by up to 28.8% over long horizons compared to using ground-truth inputs at each step, motivating the correction module (Section on Key Problem).

Training UEC-STD on ETTh1 takes approximately 1 minute, about one-tenth of the corresponding backbone's training time, and the method retains improvements even when only 5% of validation data is used for fitting the corrector (Section on Training Efficiency / Robustness).

oOiQF3Ocl3.text: In an 18-person double-blinded user study on a Copilot-style Python code-completion task, participants ranked the Empower assistant (trained with empowerment parameter eta=4) as the one they would more enjoy using in practice 78% of the time versus a Base-20 baseline, with p=0.015 (Section 5.3, Figure 3).
Participants rated the Empower assistant's suggestions as more relevant 61% of the time versus Base-20, but this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.240) (Section 5.3).
The Empower assistant had a suggestion acceptance rate of 8.08% compared to 6.18% for the Base-20 baseline, a difference significant at p=0.0002 (Section 5.3).

Users deleted an average of 9.56 characters per accepted suggestion from the Empower assistant versus 12.91 characters for Base-20 (p=0.0118), and Empower produced shorter suggestions on average (43.6 vs 82.2 characters) and fewer suggestions overall (~208 vs ~333 per user) (Section 5.3).

A pilot study using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the assistant, prior to the full 18-person study, was used to select Empower (eta=4) and Base-20 as the two conditions to compare in the main human study (Section 5.3).

cQbg0vf0Gz.text: Visual counting in VLMs is decomposed into three cognitive stages: visual individuation, magnitude awareness, and symbolic mapping, studied using synthetic Go-board stimuli and linear probes (Section 1, Section 3).

Linear probes on visual backbone representations remain robust and linearly separable for object quantity well into the extrapolation regime (beyond training count ranges), ruling out a perceptual (visual individuation) failure as the primary bottleneck (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

Models retain latent magnitude awareness beyond their training distribution, evidenced by robust performance on a Hidden Number Probing diagnostic and successful cardinality-based reasoning beyond the training range (Section 2.3, Section 3.3, Figure 4).

The extrapolation failure is localized to the symbolic mapping (decoding) stage, where models fail to project valid latent magnitude representations onto correct discrete output tokens, instead producing mode-collapsed or hallucinated outputs (Section 3.4, Figure 5).

Visual and textual counting rely on largely disjoint neural circuits, with attention-head analysis showing visual and textual quantity representations occupy disjoint statistical manifolds/subspaces, supporting a 'fractured magnitude' hypothesis rather than a shared universal number space (Section 3.4.2, Figure 6).

The extrapolation gap observed in the synthetic Go-board setting persists in real-world foundation-model evaluation, confirmed via Vision Gap analysis on hidden-number probing in Section 4 (Section 4.1, Figure 7).

80nuPd5Gvb.text: Theorem 3.2 proves a strict trajectory-level gap showing continuous diffusion models (CDM) have strictly greater theoretical expressivity than discrete diffusion models (DDM) at any fixed diffusion time, formalized via the discrete family embedded in the continuous trajectory space (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.2).

Continuous diffusion is argued to generalize looped transformers (LT) with the same architecture and parameter count, making it at least as expressive as LT and potentially more expressive, since a PF-ODE with matching grid outpoints can simulate a looped rollout (Section 3.1, Proposition 3.4).

CCDD-MDiT reduces validation perplexity on LM1B by over 25% compared to a reimplemented discrete-only MDLM baseline (39.17 to <=29.22 PPL), with CCDD-MoEDiT and CCDD-MMDiT further improving to <=28.50 and <=25.76 PPL respectively at comparable training tokens (Table 2).

On OWT with the GPT-2 tokenizer, CCDD achieves comparable or better validation perplexity than baselines with comparable parameter counts, using either RoBERTa-base or Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B as the continuous embedding space (Table 4).

On complex reasoning benchmarks (Sudoku, 3-SAT, Countdown) with a 6M-parameter model, CCDD with looped depth 3 achieves 100.0% Sudoku accuracy and 73.7% Countdown accuracy, outperforming looped transformer (LT) baselines at matched depth and size (Table 6).

The factored forward and reverse processes over joint continuous-discrete states are proven to admit semigroups (Theorem B.18) and the factored reverse kernels with sufficiently small steps yield asymptotically the same expressivity as fully coupled kernels (Theorem B.19).

qBMqN2ZyVH.text: The proposed distribution-calibrated aggregation method uses a Bradley-Terry-Davidson (BTD) formulation over three-way preference vote counts (+1, -1, 0), fit via the Discrete Ranked Probability Score (DRPS) and combined with an MAE Bayes decision rule at inference (Section on Key Technical Approach).
At n=12 judge samples, the method reduces MAE from 0.155 (self-consistency baseline) to 0.081 on RB2-Ties and improves pairwise accuracy from 84.4% to 91.8% (results table).
At n=12 samples on RB2-Math, the method reduces MAE from 0.384 to 0.285 versus the self-consistency baseline and raises pairwise accuracy from 63.5% to 72.3% (results table).
On WMT zh-en translation evaluation at n=12 samples, the method reduces MAE from 0.527 to 0.497 versus self-consistency and improves pairwise accuracy from 53.9% to 60.7% (results table).
On WMT zh-en, the calibrated LLM judge exceeds 7 of 8 individual human raters under a leave-one-out comparison protocol (Human Comparison section).

Allowing ties in the judge's output distribution reduces positional bias: gemini-2.5-flash shows 14.58% first-position bias under forced-choice judging, which drops to 3.1% when ties are permitted (Section on Why This Matters).

HxyRSeT8z2.text: CGD delivers an average of about 7% improvement over baseline on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, including a +15.0% gain on AMC23 and +12.2% on MATH-500 (Table 3).
CGD attains higher Pass@1 scores than Critique Fine-Tuning (CFT) on both AIME24 and AIME25, with the advantage widening at low Pass@k (Table 3).
Ablation experiments removing components of the critique-guided refinement pipeline show measurable performance degradation relative to the full CGD method (Table 4).
CGD preserves general instruction-following ability, whereas CFT degrades IFEval performance by -21.3 points relative to the base model (Table 5).
The CGD pipeline consists of a critique-generation stage followed by a refinement-guided distillation stage, illustrated in Figures 1 and 2 (Section 3).

NnnG2nGWTy.text: SDDLM simplifies the denoising diffusion loss to optimize only over noise-replaced tokens (Equation 7), removing extraneous terms present in the standard reconstruction objective (Equation 6, Section 4).
On OWT, SDDLM-V1 reduces generative perplexity to 45.18 versus 80.43 for the Duo baseline while maintaining comparable entropy, 5.31 vs 5.55 (Table 1).
On LM1B, SDDLM-V2 achieves 101.32 generative perplexity compared to 172.93 for the Duo baseline, at similar entropy levels around 4.1-4.2 (Table 1).
A 170M-parameter modified Diffusion Transformer (DiT) is trained for 1M steps with batch size 512 to validate the simplified objective on both LM1B and OWT (Section 5.1).
SDDLM-V1 adds a regularization term inspired by negative-gradient corrections to mitigate collapse toward the uniform distribution (Equation 8, Section 4).

eTO6G25Jbo.text: DP-SGD-RC replaces exact per-sample gradient clipping with randomized clipping based on stochastic trace estimation, avoiding the O(B min{T^2, d^2}) memory cost of standard DP-SGD for transformers (abstract only).
The randomized clipping estimator is instantiated using Hutchinson's estimator and its improved variant Hutch++ (abstract only).
DP-SGD-RC is evaluated by fine-tuning Llama 3.2-1B on classification, question-answering, and summarization benchmarks (abstract only).
DP-SGD-RC matches the utility of baseline DP-SGD while significantly reducing memory and compute requirements (abstract only).
DP-SGD-RC achieves noise multipliers competitive with those required for deterministic, non-randomized clipping under the same privacy budget (abstract only).

QJevB1AMUJ.text: ConFu introduces contemplate tokens and soft prompts that give the draft model future-oriented signals from the target model at negligible additional cost (Section 3.1).
A dynamic contemplate token mechanism based on a mixture-of-experts design produces context-aware future predictions during drafting (Section 3.2).
The training framework combines anchor token sampling with a future-prediction replication objective (Section 3.3).
ConFu improves token acceptance rates over EAGLE-3 by 8-11% on Llama-3 models and by roughly 20% on Qwen-3 4B (Tables 5-11).
ConFu is presented as the first approach to bridge speculative decoding with continuous reasoning tokens (Section 1).

vwTTp11PTD.text: The paper introduces a non-uniform smoothness assumption (Assumption 1) in which curvature is an affine function of the objective value, generalizing standard L-smoothness (Section 3).
Under this assumption, steepest descent (sign GD) is shown to converge linearly on logistic regression with separable data and is provably faster than standard gradient descent (Theorem 1).
Adam is shown to converge at a linear rate with a constant step size on certain two-layer neural networks under the non-uniform smoothness assumption (Theorem 4).
RMSProp-type adaptive methods are analyzed and shown to be provably faster than AdaGrad, AMSGrad, and heavy-ball momentum under non-uniform smoothness (Section 6).
The convergence analysis is extended from the deterministic steepest descent setting (Section 4) to the stochastic setting (Section 5).

tuwJoQkKHJ.text: Stepwise Confidence Attribution (SCA) instantiates two methods, NIBS (non-parametric Information Bottleneck) and GIBS (graph-based IB with a differentiable mask), evaluated on GSM8K, MoreHopQA, and Math with LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Phi-4-Reasoning, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, where GIBS achieves the best or second-best AUROC, AUCPR, ACC@80%, and ECE across most settings (Table 1).

Guiding self-correction with stepwise confidence feedback (highlighting low-confidence steps) improves the self-correction success rate on MoreHopQA over final-answer-only feedback by up to 13.5%, with the largest gains for stronger reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 and Phi-4-Reasoning (Section 5.3, Figure 4).

Ablating GIBS's edge encoder or graph encoder each cause a noticeable AUROC drop (e.g., on GSM8K, GIBS scores 0.7892 versus 0.7228 without the graph encoder and 0.5186 without the edge encoder), showing both local and global structural signals are necessary (Section 5.4, Table 2).

In label-free generalization tests replacing gold correctness labels with self-consistency pseudo-labels, GIBS AUROC on Phi4 stays close to the gold-label oracle (0.6610 vs. 0.6619) because self-consistent trajectories overlap about 80% with gold labels, whereas on Llama3.1-8B the overlap drops to about 28% and performance degrades correspondingly (Section 5.5, Table 3).

G5x5eEZ8yY.text: GTPO assigns an entropy-weighted reward to each token for fine-grained credit assignment, while GRPO-S assigns an entropy-weighted reward to each sequence based on its average token entropy, both designed to fix GRPO's uniform per-token reward that penalizes all tokens equally regardless of individual step correctness (Section 1).

Contrary to a claim of establishing new state-of-the-art results, the paper's own reported experiments (Qwen2.5-32B, built on the verl framework, benchmarked against a reproduced DAPO baseline) explicitly withhold numeric results, stating 'due to our company's open-source policy, we are unable to publicly disclose the internal experimental results at this time' (Section 4.3).

The paper proves via a variance-reduction argument (Appendix A) that DAPO's single-average token-level loss normalization is statistically superior to GRPO's two-stage (per-sequence then per-batch) averaging, providing the theoretical basis for adopting a similar loss structure in GTPO/GRPO-S (Section 2.3, Appendix A).

An initial version of GTPO improved accuracy on difficult math problems but decreased accuracy on simple math problems due to over-reliance on entropy weighting in the reward, prompting a revised version with a clipped entropy-weighted reward and an added response-length penalty (Section 4.5).

vCjGjvrIR9.text: On Gemma-3 4B across 14 CoT reasoning strategies on GSM8K, intrinsic dimensionality achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.93 (p<0.01) with overall accuracy (geometric mean across in-distribution GSM8K test and 5 OOD stress sets), outperforming token perplexity (0.82), length (0.31), and KL divergence (-0.17) as predictors (Table 1).

On the smaller Gemma-3 1B model, intrinsic dimensionality still correlates at 0.75 with overall generalization performance, again beating token perplexity (0.63), length (0.24), and KL divergence (-0.18), showing the metric's predictive power holds across model scale (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Intrinsic dimension is computed as the parameter count at which a LoRA-rank Pareto frontier of training accuracy versus trainable parameters first crosses a fixed accuracy threshold (e.g., 63.0% for Gemma-3 4B), visualized via the accuracy-vs-parameters curves for each reasoning strategy (Figure 2, Section 4).

The correlation between intrinsic dimensionality and generalization performance is robust to threshold choice, remaining between 0.72 and 0.94 across 1B and 4B models when using 70%, 80%, or 90% of epoch-1 training accuracy or 90% of validation accuracy as the threshold (Table 3, Section 4.3).

tiPoSBaOiY.text: Unlike discrete diffusion models, discrete flow models trained with generator matching and sampled via uniformization incur no truncation error from truncating the noising time horizon and no discretization error, so the analysis focuses on transition-rate estimation error and early-stopping error (Section 1).

The paper derives a novel Girsanov-type theorem for continuous-time Markov chains (Theorem 1, Change of Measure) that yields a bound on the KL divergence between path measures of two CTMCs with different transition rates, expressed via a Bregman divergence of the transition rates (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).

The stochastic estimation error is decomposed into stochastic error and approximation error, balanced against early-stopping error by choice of the early-stopping parameter, with the resulting stochastic error bound matching the state-of-the-art rate for continuous flow matching and the early-stopping bound matching the most recent discrete diffusion result (Section 1).

The framework provides, per the authors, the first non-asymptotic error analysis for discrete flow models, extending the analysis to neural network function classes with ReLU activations under an explicit assumption (Assumption 2, Section 5).

rKD8HtgY8G.text: Parameterizing weight matrices as W = AB^T with A in R^{m x r} and B in R^{n x r} induces a posterior that is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure and concentrates entirely on the rank-r manifold when r < min(m,n) (Theorem 3.4).

The derived PAC-Bayes generalization bound for the low-rank posterior has a complexity term scaling as sqrt(r(m+n)) instead of the sqrt(mn) scaling of standard mean-field Gaussian posteriors (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.4).

Using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem, the paper bounds the expected loss gap between the full-rank optimum and its optimal rank-r truncation by the tail singular value energy sqrt(sum_{i>r} sigma_i^2), and further decomposes the learned factorization's total error into a learning-error term and an unavoidable rank-bias term (Theorem 3.6, Theorem 3.7).

On the MIMIC-III mortality prediction task, a rank-15 Low-Rank Gaussian BNN with only 13.6k parameters (versus 112k for a 5-member Deep Ensemble, an 88% reduction) achieves better OOD detection (AUC-OOD 0.802 vs. 0.738) and AUPR-OOD/AUPR-In, while Deep Ensemble retains better in-domain AUROC (0.929 vs 0.895) and calibration (NLL 0.300 vs 0.433) (Table 1, Section 4).

On Beijing Air Quality LSTM forecasting with distribution shift to Guangzhou, the Low-Rank Bayesian LSTM achieves the best coverage (PICP=0.790) and near-best calibration (ECE=0.114) while using 64% fewer parameters than Full-Rank BBB, and achieves the largest MAE reduction (17.4%) at 80% retention under selective prediction (Section 4.3, Table 2, Figure 5).

E0MKfKmQkT.text: The pre-softmax attention matrix QK^T is factorized as XWX^T and decomposed into a symmetric component that defines a Hopfield-style energy landscape and a skew-symmetric component that drives circulation dynamics without contributing quadratic energy (Section 4).

Three stability measures are defined from the symmetric component: Hopfield energy E_X(xi) = -1/2 xi^T M_sym(X) xi, an instability fraction r_X(xi), and an alignment score cos(xi, h_X(xi)) (Section 4.1).

On the bottom 20% lowest-quality samples, skew-scaling and blending control (parameters alpha and beta) yields an Aesthetic Score improvement of +0.327 at beta=6 and an ImageReward gain of +0.518 at beta=5 (Section 6, Table 3).
High-alignment samples show a +0.146 improvement in Aesthetic Score versus baseline, empirically linking the stability measures to the fidelity-diversity trade-off (Section 4.2, Table 2).

A Functional Symmetry Index eta_M(X) is used to adaptively modulate the circulation-control parameters alpha and beta, preventing over-perturbation on already high-quality samples while preserving gains on low-quality ones (Section 6.1, Eq. 36, Table 6).

Xlte2USTiv.text: ConfSMoE replaces softmax gating with a confidence-guided ConfNet that maps token embeddings to scalar logits supervised by task-confidence scores, trained jointly via a task loss plus an MSE confidence loss (Eq. 5), without requiring an additional load-balance loss (Section 3.1).

A Jacobian analysis of softmax routing shows the gradient term diag(g) - gg^T concentrates learning on dominant experts, producing a rich-get-richer collapse that conflicts with load-balance gradients, visualized as a sharp sinusoidal oscillation in expert usage (Section 2.2-2.3, Figure 3a).

A two-stage imputation module first reconstructs missing modalities by averaging K randomly sampled instances from the training modality pool (Eq. 6, pre-imputation), then refines them via sparse cross-attention over Top-K expert tokens (Eq. 7, post-imputation) (Section 3.2).
On MIMIC-IV 48-IHM prediction, ConfSMoE-T achieves F1=49.18% and AUC=85.24%, versus FlexMoE's F1=35.29% and AUC=80.45% (Section 4, Table 1).

On CMU-MOSI with 50% modality dropout, ConfSMoE reaches F1=43.89% and AUC=71.51% versus FlexMoE's F1=41.95% and AUC=66.47%, while using only 47.10 MFLOPs and 3,116,310 parameters compared to FuseMoE's 199.80 MFLOPs and 243.5M parameters (Table 2, Table 5).
Ablations show removing the imputation module drops F1 by 6.21% on MIMIC-III and removing ConfNet drops F1 by 5.62% on CMU-MOSI, with combined removal degrading F1 by 9.73% (Table 3).

KfLkjLH7s4.text: FHAIM is presented as the first fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) framework for training the AIM marginal-based synthetic data generator directly on encrypted tabular data, keeping raw data encrypted throughout via three protocols: piCOMP, piSELECT, and piMEASURE (Section 4, Section 5).
piSELECT uses a squared L2 norm rather than an L1 norm to identify highest-error workload queries, avoiding unstable polynomial approximations under FHE (Section 5).

piMEASURE adds encrypted Gaussian noise before decryption so that differential-privacy noise remains hidden from the service provider, giving the framework (epsilon,delta)-DP guarantees with respect to the raw data (Section 5).

At epsilon=infinity (no DP noise), FHAIM-L2 achieves classification accuracy of 0.684 on Breast Cancer (N=228, vs 0.702 real-data baseline), 0.625 on COMPAS (N=4,120), and 0.701 on Diabetes (N=614) (Table 3).

Peak memory usage stays under 32 MB across all three datasets, and total end-to-end training time ranges from approximately 11 to 30 minutes, with one-time initialization taking 5-12 minutes and per-iteration Measure steps under 2.5 seconds (Table 2, Figure 3).

3el4fMYQU6.text: Claude Sonnet 4.5 can comply with instructions to suppress specific words in its chain-of-thought only 2.7% of the time, compared to 61.9% compliance when the same suppression instruction targets its final output (Figure 1a).

DeepSeek R1 shows near-zero CoT keyword-suppression compliance at 0.1%, while GPT-OSS-120B reaches 5.9% versus GPT-OSS-20B's 0.9%, indicating no consistent scaling trend toward better controllability (Section 5).

CoT controllability declines by over an order of magnitude across training checkpoints as models undergo more reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, with math and coding RL causing faster decline than general chat RL (Section 5.4, Figure 10).

Increasing test-time reasoning effort (more compute) significantly reduces CoT controllability (Section 5.2, Figure 9), and controllability drops sharply once reasoning length passes model-specific thresholds, e.g. a drastic decline after ~800 words for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and beyond ~200 words for Claude Sonnet 4 (Section 5.3, Figure 34).

Informing a model that it is being monitored increases CoT controllability by up to 4 percentage points with statistical significance, while GEPA-optimized adversarial red-teaming prompts fail to transfer across instruction types, improving compliance by under 5 percentage points for most models (Section 4.1-4.2, Figures 6-7).

E7jYm5q6cW.text: CorrSteer selects steering features from Sparse Autoencoders by computing Pearson correlation between feature activations and task success, using a streaming correlation algorithm with O(1) memory across 10^4-10^5 candidate features, requiring no contrastive datasets, backward passes, or large activation storage.

Three CorrSteer variants are proposed: CorrSteer-1 (single highest-correlated feature globally), CorrSteer-A (top feature per layer), and CorrSteer-P (validation-based pruning to minimize side effects) (Table 1, Table 2).
On Gemma-2 2B, CorrSteer-A improves MMLU accuracy from a 52.23% baseline to 56.32% (+4.1 points) and HarmBench from 44.64% to 67.50% (+22.9 points with 4000 samples) (Table 1).

On LLaMA-3.1 8B, CorrSteer-A raises HarmBench compliance from a 0.71% baseline to 17.86%, and BBQ-Ambiguous accuracy from 83.97% to 86.83%, with only marginal MMLU change (61.41% to 61.71%) (Table 2).

A Side Effect Ratio (SER) metric is introduced to quantify unintended behavioral changes from steering, and CorrSteer shows lower SER than fine-tuning baselines across benchmarks, indicating more targeted intervention with fewer collateral effects.
CorrSteer's static, non-adaptive steering is noted as a limitation on sequential reasoning tasks such as GSM8K, where dynamic steering would be more appropriate.

FXWnvznHMW.text: The IPW treatment-effect estimation error is not a martingale with respect to any single filtration, but each arm's IPW estimation error is shown to be a martingale with respect to an arm-specific event-time filtration (Section 4).

Combining two arm-level anytime-valid confidence sequences via a union bound produces tighter intervals than the standard design-based variance upper bound when treatment induces asymmetric outcome arrival rates between arms (Section 4).
The paper characterizes an augmentation (AIPW) class for which per-arm estimation errors preserve the martingale property under staggered entry and delayed outcomes (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
The theoretical development includes Theorems 4.1 through 4.12 building the design-based martingale framework for delayed and staggered-entry settings (Section 4).
Simulation studies illustrate the behavior of the proposed confidence sequences under staggered entry and delayed outcomes (Figures 12-15).

lIQnUtwWVb.text: WinQ combines a weight-resetting mechanism, which periodically interpolates between full-precision and quantized weights to increase Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, with a gradient-regularization mechanism that injects noise during gradient computation (Section 3).
WinQ accelerates quantization-aware training convergence by up to 4x relative to baseline QAT methods under the same training budget (Section 4).
Under matched training budgets, WinQ improves sub-4-bit quantization performance by up to 8.8% relative to state-of-the-art baselines (Section 4).
The reported acceleration and accuracy gains are shown to be consistent across 16 experimental configurations spanning multiple language models, quantization methods, and bit-widths (Section 4).
Appendix A provides theoretical justification connecting Hessian eigenvalue magnitude near saddle points to the weight-resetting mechanism's effect on convergence (Appendix A).

MBk6Pur6RX.text: Standard BT-loss gradient magnitude depends jointly on prediction error and representation distance between chosen/rejected response embeddings, causing weak updates on small-distance misranked pairs and disproportionately strong updates on large-distance pairs (Section 3).

NormBT is introduced as an adaptive pairwise normalization scheme that rescales BT-loss updates to remove the representation-distance dependence while preserving prediction-error-driven learning signal (Section 3).
NormBT is evaluated using a Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct backbone trained on the Unified Feedback dataset, compared against a Mistral-7B-Instruct baseline trained on the same dataset (Section 5).
NormBT yields consistent performance improvements over standard BT-loss across multiple LLM backbones and datasets (Section 5).
NormBT achieves gains of over 5% on the Reasoning category of RewardBench relative to standard BT-loss (Section 5).

vNCE03zff8.text: Geo-Sharing formulates cross-layer parameter sharing as a graph coloring problem, introducing a coloring function grounded in group theory to determine which layers share parameters (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

A second-order geometric criterion based on Taylor expansion and Hessian spectrum analysis selects sharing configurations by projecting perturbations onto low-curvature eigensubspaces of the Hessian (Section 3).

CGC/Geo-Sharing achieves 28-50% parameter compression on LLaMA-7B and Swin Transformer, with accuracy loss no more than 0.01% on Swin Transformer and accuracy gains on LLaMA-7B (Section 4, Tables 3-9).

Curvature-aware parameter sharing that groups layers with similar curvature profiles delivers over 60% higher inference throughput than heuristic adjacent-layer sharing baselines (Section 4, Figures 4 and 6).

WR1IcmCjbl.text: MultiBreak comprises 10,389 multi-turn adversarial prompts spanning 2,665 distinct harmful intents, constructed via an active learning pipeline that iteratively fine-tunes a generator guided by uncertainty-based refinement (Section 3, Table 1).
MultiBreak achieves up to a 54.0 percentage-point higher attack success rate than the second-best existing multi-turn jailbreak dataset when evaluated on DeepSeek-R1-7B (Section 4, Table 6).
MultiBreak achieves up to a 34.6 percentage-point higher attack success rate than the second-best existing dataset when evaluated on GPT-4.1-mini (Section 4, Table 6).
Attack categories that appear benign under single-turn evaluation exhibit substantially higher adversarial effectiveness when tested in multi-turn conversational settings (Section 4.5).

Nyk5TF8H5x.text: GIFT (Gaze Shift-Guided Cross-modal Fusion Enhancement) reduces the CHAIR-Cs hallucination metric on LLaVA-1.5 7B from 50.2 (greedy decoding) to 39.8, a roughly 20.7% relative improvement (Table 2).
GIFT improves POPE F1 score on LLaVA-1.5 7B from 82.4 (greedy decoding) to 83.8 (Table 2).
GIFT reduces the MMHal-Bench hallucination rate on LLaVA-1.5 7B from 65.2 to 57.3, alongside improved informativeness scores (Table 2).

GIFT precomputes a visual saliency map from positive shifts in visual attention ("gaze shifts") during query comprehension, yielding a normalized saliency score of 11.92 versus 5.40 for a static-attention baseline (Table 1).
GIFT adds only about 1.13x the decoding latency of greedy decoding, versus 1.56x for an alternative attention-amplification method and 11.10x for the VAR baseline (Table 4).

pc7fqaOcAH.text: In a 40-round contextual bandit "hiring game" with four fictional demographic groups (Tufa, Aima, Reku, Weki) all having equal 0.9 success probability, frontier LLMs develop a mean Stratification Index (SI) of 1.39, compared to 0.84 for humans and 0.25 for a random fair assignment baseline (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
Claude Sonnet 4 exhibits the worst stratification among tested models, with a Stratification Index more than eight times larger than that of Claude 3 Haiku (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

Newer and larger models within the Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, and Qwen families stratify statistically significantly more than older/smaller models in the task-allocation experiment (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

Adding an explicit diversity bonus to the model's objective reduces the Stratification Index below the random-baseline level for most models, outperforming abstract value-based prompting interventions (Section 5.3, Figure 6).

Chain-of-thought prompting only marginally reduces stratification, and raising decoding temperature to 1.5 produces no statistically significant reduction in stratification for most models (p>0.05) (Section 5.1).

P9dPMDIKRL.text: The proposed data-augmented AutoML market prices access to models based on the instrumental value of externally sourced data, defined as the marginal model-quality improvement it provides, rather than pricing raw datasets directly (Section 3).

The buyer's decision of when to stop the data/model discovery process is modeled as a Pandora's-Box-style optimal stopping problem over a Markov chain of performance metrics, and Proposition 4.1 shows the optimal buyer policy can be computed via dynamic programming in O(Q^2 T) time (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 gives a Mixed Integer Linear Program that computes a pricing curve which is an additive epsilon-approximation to the optimal pricing curve with probability at least 1-2delta, using m = b^2 ln(1/delta) / (2 epsilon^2) sampled buyer trajectories (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 5.2 shows that when the learned buyer-type prior and transition matrices are within epsilon of the true distributions in L2 norm, the resulting Cost of Estimation Error in market revenue is O(epsilon) (Section 5, Theorem 5.2, Definition 5.1).

In an evaluation on a marketplace of 69K NYC open-data datasets over 1000 classification and regression tasks, the bandit-based discovery algorithm (Data-Bandit) achieves average utility above 0.85 on classification tasks, versus roughly 0.7 or below for the Data-All, Data-Alt, and AutoML baselines (Section 6, Figure 3).

In in-sample profit benchmarking on school-district data, the MILP-based pricing scheme captures around 85% of total buyer welfare as platform revenue, versus under 80% for the Independent, Shift, and Jiggle pricing baselines (Section 6, Figure 4).

icMRkTnuU7.text: MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer, a 1.6-billion-parameter model built on the proposed CAT (Causal Audio Tokenizer with Transformer) architecture operating at 12.5 Hz with 32 residual quantization layers, outperforms prior open-source codecs (DAC, Encodec, SpeechTokenizer, Mimi, MiMo-Audio-Tokenizer, Qwen3-TTS-Tokenizer) on speech reconstruction metrics across low, medium, and high bitrate regimes from 750 to 4000 bps (Section 4.2, Table 2).

The CAT-TTS system, a purely autoregressive TTS model built on CAT's discrete tokens, achieves the highest speaker similarity (SIM) on the Seed-TTS-Eval benchmark for both English (73.1) and Chinese (78.5) among compared open-source systems, while maintaining low word error rates (1.89 WER, 1.23 CER) and supporting explicit bitrate control via the Depth Transformer (Section 4.3, Table 3).

Progressive Sequence Dropout during training (dropout probability p in {0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0}) makes CAT-TTS substantially more robust to bitrate reduction at inference, avoiding the steep word-error-rate and similarity degradation seen when the model is trained only at full RVQ depth (Section 4.3, Figure 3).

Full end-to-end optimization of CAT's encoder, quantizer, and decoder yields sustained reconstruction-quality improvements without early saturation, whereas a partial (stage-wise) training protocol that freezes the encoder/quantizer plateaus early (Section 5.1, Figure 4).

Scaling combined encoder-decoder parameters from 319M to 1169M (hidden dimensions 256 to 768, with quantizer fixed at 32 layers/12.5 Hz) improves reconstruction quality across 0.5-4 kbps, though the largest model can underperform smaller models at very low bitrates, indicating bitrate rather than parameter count becomes the bottleneck (Section 5.2, Figure 5).

sSOxhXwzUi.text: The AV Filter defense, built on the Normalized Passage Attention Score (NPAS) that aggregates token-level attention weights per retrieved passage, achieves up to 20% higher robust accuracy under poisoning attacks than baseline defenses (Section 4, Table 3).

AV Filter maintains clean accuracy within 4-6% of Vanilla RAG on average, while achieving up to 23% higher clean accuracy than Certified RAG-Keyword and Certified RAG-Decoding baselines (Section 5.2, Table 2).
AV Filter reduces attack success rate from 88.2% under Vanilla RAG down to roughly 6-10% across evaluated datasets (Section 5.2, Table 3).

Adaptive attacks using GCG and AutoDAN achieve a maximum success rate of 35% (average 22.08%) against the AV Filter defense, but require roughly 1000x the computational overhead of the corresponding non-adaptive attack, about 18,616 seconds per query (Section 5.2, Table 4, Table 5).

The defender using attention-variance filtering wins the SADG security game with an average Corruption Identification Rate of 0.83 (ranging 0.48-0.99 depending on the top-alpha token parameter and attack type) (Table 1).

1XJqPy2LhA.text: TAG decomposes the diffusion sampling update into normal (radial) and tangential (perpendicular) components with respect to the estimated denoising direction, and amplifies only the tangential component using a scale factor eta >= 1 (Section 4).

Theorem 4.1 proves that increasing the tangential amplification factor eta yields a monotonic first-order increase in log-likelihood, providing the theoretical justification that amplification steers the state toward higher-probability regions of the data manifold (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).

On unconditional Stable Diffusion v1.5 with 50 NFEs, applying TAG on top of DDIM improves FID from 76.942 to 67.805, and combining TAG with Perturbed-Attention Guidance further improves FID from 64.595 to 63.619 (Table 1).

On conditional MS-COCO generation, Classifier-Free Guidance with C-TAG at only 30 NFEs (FID 23.414) outperforms standard CFG run at 100 NFEs (FID 26.266), demonstrating improved sampling efficiency (Table 4).

TAG is evaluated as a plug-and-play module against baselines including Classifier-Free Guidance, Self-Attention Guidance, Perturbed-Attention Guidance, and Smoothed Energy Guidance across Stable Diffusion v1.5, v2.1, SDXL, and SD3 (flow matching) backbones (Table 2, Table 5).

gxxOL0iXpr.text: Theorem 4.3 establishes the first dimension-free KL-divergence convergence bound for standard underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo (ULMC) under strong convexity, with sample complexity depending on tr(H) rather than the ambient dimension d, where H is a known upper bound on the Hessian (Theorem 4.3, Assumption 3.1).
The strongly-convex ULMC sample complexity bound is Otilde(kappa^{3/2} beta^{-1/2} [tr(H)]^{1/2} / epsilon) to reach KL(mu (P')^N || pi) <= epsilon^2 (Theorem 4.3).

Under randomized midpoint discretization, Theorem 5.2 improves the condition-number dependence relative to the bound of Liu et al. (2023), achieving complexity Otilde(kappa [beta^{-1} tr(H)]^{1/3} epsilon^{-2/3}) (Theorem 5.2).

Theorems 4.4 and 5.4 extend the dimension-free guarantees to the general (non-strongly) convex setting (alpha = 0), the first such dimension-free result for underdamped Langevin dynamics in this regime (Theorem 4.4, Theorem 5.4).

The dimension-free change-of-measure argument (Lemma 6.1) bounds E_mu[||grad V(x)||^2] and E_mu[p^T H p] by tr(H) + beta*KL(mu||pi), avoiding the explicit dimension dependence introduced by standard Gaussian moment bounds (Lemma 6.1, Section 6).

The paper shows underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo attains better iteration complexity than composite overdamped Langevin Monte Carlo when tr(H) << d, e.g. in ridge-separable target distributions (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.5 framework).

iE0m4NE5qb.text: Theorem 1 shows that under the epsilon-weighted alignment assumption (Definition 1), where a human's utility approximates a weighted combination of several misaligned AI agents' utilities, any Nash equilibrium of the induced multi-agent competition game yields the human utility at least U_A(C_B*) - 2 epsilon, matching what a perfectly aligned AI would provide up to O(epsilon) (Theorem 1, Section 3.2, Definition 1).
Theorem 2 extends the equilibrium guarantee to boundedly-rational users modeled via quantal response decision-making (Theorem 2, Section 4).

Theorem 5 gives a main result showing near-optimal human utility under an information-substitutes condition in a best-AI selection game, without requiring the identical induced distribution assumption of Theorem 1 (Theorem 5, Section 5).

On the MovieLens dataset, using 100 LLM-generated AI personas evaluated on 1000 movies, the best utility function achievable within the convex hull of the 100 personas' utilities aligns substantially better with a simulated human's utility than any single AI persona alone (Section 6).

On the ETHICS dataset with the same 100-persona setup evaluated on 1000 ethical scenarios, convex-hull combinations of AI utilities again achieve significantly better alignment with simulated human judgments than any individual persona (Section 6).

Zg9rjewo83.text: Proposition 4.1 proves that a Transformer self-attention layer, with query/key projections set to W_Q = 2I_d and W_K = I_d and attention bias b_{n+k} = -||mu_k||_2^2, exactly reproduces soft k-means cluster-assignment scores -||x_i - mu_k||_2^2 / tau (Proposition 4.1, Section 4.1).

Theorem 4.4 proves that the chain-of-thought iterations contract semantic-structural misalignment geometrically, Delta_{t+1} <= rho * Delta_t + epsilon for 0 < rho < 1, converging to an O(epsilon) error floor (Theorem 4.4, Section 4.7).

On node classification, KCoT achieves 79.25% accuracy on ogbn-Arxiv and 86.39% on ogbn-Products, outperforming the strongest baseline LLAGA-HO by 2.59 and 1.72 percentage points respectively (Table 2).
On link prediction, KCoT reaches 95.14% on ogbn-Arxiv and 96.70% on ogbn-Products, improving over LLAGA-HO by 0.99 and 1.14 percentage points respectively (Table 2).

Ablation results show removing the prompt design causes the largest accuracy drop (-2.66%), followed by removing chain-of-thought iteration entirely (-1.51%), removing semantic neighbors (-1.61%), and removing structural neighbors (-0.79%) (Table 3).

Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis identifies an optimal chain-of-thought length of t = 2 iterations, with performance across LLM backbones including Vicuna-7B (90.63%), Llama2-7B (89.92%), and ChatGPT-4.1 nano (91.04%) on Cora node classification (Figures 4-5, Table 4).

MrFOCA1U5P.text: GEAR aligns latent embedding spaces for transfer learning by treating them as Riemannian manifolds and matching their Ricci scalar curvature R = g^{ij} g^{lk} R_{iljk}, computed analytically from the Jacobian and Christoffel symbols of the transfer mapping (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).
Across 23 molecular property prediction task pairs drawn from OCHEM, PubChem, and CCCB, GEAR improves average RMSE over the GATE baseline by 14.4% under random data splits (Table 5-8, Appendix G).
Under scaffold-based splits on the same 23 task pairs, GEAR's average RMSE improvement over GATE drops to 8.3%, reflecting the harder generalization setting (Table 5-8, Appendix G).
GEAR achieves the lowest RMSE among compared methods in 18 of 23 task pairs under random splits and 17 of 23 task pairs under scaffold splits (Figure 2, Appendix G).

The GEAR architecture combines task-specific embeddings, transfer modules that map to locally flat coordinates, and inverse transfer autoencoders, trained with a curvature-matching loss term among five total loss terms (Equation 25, Figure 1).

Yi1W13sPsR.text: ACC-MARL augments agent observations with latest minimal DFAs from a DFA space, forming a product game over state space S×D^n to make the otherwise non-Markovian task-tracking problem Markovian (Section 3.2).
Theorem 1 proves that maximizing the Markovian reformulation objective as the discount factor γ→1⁻ solves the original non-Markovian cooperative multi-agent objective (Section 3.2, Theorem 1).
ACC-MARL uses potential-based reward shaping with agent-specific potential functions Φᵢ to address sparse binary team-completion rewards and credit assignment across agents (Section 3.3, Equation 6).

The framework uses pretrained RAD Embeddings Ψ:D→Z, which guarantee distinct DFAs receive identical embeddings if and only if they are equal when minimized, avoiding a representation bottleneck from learning DFA embeddings jointly with policies (Section 3.4, Equation 7).

On the Rooms-2 layout with RAD task distributions and potential-based reward shaping, the learned policy achieves success probabilities of 0.890 (Reach), 0.871 (ReachAvoid), and 0.866 (RAD), while Buttons-4 achieves 0.751/0.676/0.736 respectively (Section 5, Table 1).

Learned decentralized policies exhibit emergent multi-step coordination behaviors, including agents synchronously holding doors open for teammates and short-circuiting tasks via helper agents that enable shorter completion paths (Section 5.3).

CfqUMty4Ns.text: MILD (Margin-based Imbalanced Learning to Defer) reformulates the two-stage deferral loss as cost-sensitive learning over input-expert pairs, building on Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2 (Section 3).

Theorem 4.1 establishes a margin bound for imbalanced cost-sensitive classification via class-sensitive Rademacher complexity, with Corollary 4.2 giving an explicit generalization guarantee containing a complexity term proportional to Σⱼ mⱼXⱼ²/ρⱼ² (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2).

On CIFAR-10 with synthetic experts (Setup I, error cost), MILD reduces deferral loss to 0.0403 versus 0.0520 for the tdef baseline (a 22.5% relative reduction), and on SVHN reduces it to 0.0254 versus 0.0468 (45.7% relative reduction) (Table 1).

In LLM routing experiments on MMLU with Qwen 2.5 models under the error+cost setting, the tdef baseline collapses to routing 0% of queries to the strong 7B expert and 100% to the cheapest 0.5B expert (deferral loss 0.928), whereas MILD recovers a diversified allocation of 17.9% strong, 8.3% mid, and 73.8% tiny expert usage with deferral loss 0.813 (Table 3).

Figure 1 presents a 1D illustrative example with 4 classes and 3 experts showing that optimal expert selection under MILD's formulation is independent of class labels, distinguishing it from traditional class-imbalance techniques (Figure 1).

tS5raDg2xX.text: Proposition 1 shows that ensembling J sparse autoencoders in output space is mathematically equivalent to reconstructing the activation vector with concatenated decoder matrices and coefficients from all J SAEs (Section 3.2, Proposition 1).

Two ensembling strategies are proposed: naive bagging, which averages reconstructions from J independently initialized SAEs, and boosting, which sequentially trains each SAE on the residual left by previous SAEs in the ensemble (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).

On Gemma 2-2B activations, an 8-SAE boosting ensemble improves explained variance from 0.920 (single SAE) to 0.995 and reduces MSE from 716.7 to 46.5, while also increasing feature diversity from 16,013 to 128,416 (Table 1).

Naive bagging ensembles outperform a single SAE of matching total feature count on concept detection, with an average accuracy improvement of roughly 2-3% across five downstream tasks (Section 5.2, Table 2).
Boosting ensembles improve spurious correlation removal over a single SAE, raising S_SHIFT scores on the Professor/Nurse task from 0.039 to 0.066 (Section 5.3, Table 3).

2Oj6fg0m1j.text: τ-Voice extends τ²-bench to evaluate full-duplex voice agents on 278 grounded tasks spanning retail, airline, and telecom domains using a tick-based orchestrator that decouples simulation from wall-clock time (Section 3).

Under clean audio conditions, GPT-5 (reasoning) achieves an 85% task-completion pass@1 rate while voice agents achieve only 31-51% pass@1, retaining just 30-45% of the text-based state-of-the-art capability (Figure 1, Table 6).

Under realistic conditions (added noise, diverse accents, natural turn-taking), voice agent pass@1 rates fall further to 26-38%, with xAI's agent performing best (38%) and Google's most robust to degradation (26% realistic vs 31% clean) (Table 6).

In the retail domain, accents degrade performance by an average of 10 percentage points (up to 18pp for xAI), turn-taking by 7pp, and background noise by 4pp, isolated via a 3x3x2 evaluation design (Table 7).

Error analysis attributes 79% of failures on voice-fragile tasks and 90% of failures on noise-fragile tasks to agent behavior rather than environmental factors, with authentication failures during name/email transcription identified as a primary bottleneck (Section 5.2, Table 9).

rEz2wdNZBJ.text: The compute-optimal number of parallel rollouts per problem n increases predictably with total compute budget C and then saturates, following a sigmoid trend in log-log space across Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-4B, and Llama 3.1-8B (Section 4.1).

On easy problems, increasing n primarily improves the worst@4 metric (solution sharpening/robustness), while on hard problems increasing n primarily improves the best@4 metric (coverage/exploration) (Section 4.1, Figure 8).

Batch size B_p acts mainly as a stability knob with only marginal effect on performance, whereas sensitivity analysis shows n impacts performance 4-5x more than B_p on easy tasks (Section 4.2, Figure 10).

Larger n mitigates gradient interference across problems within a batch, and single-problem training baselines contradict the empirical preference for parallel rollouts (n) over sequential iterations (M) seen in the multi-problem setting (Section 5.1).

Dataset size directly determines the saturation point of the optimal n: a small dataset of 500 examples saturates at n=256, while a larger dataset of 6,000 examples supports scaling to n=512 or beyond (Section 5.2, Figure 13).

The scaling recipe uses learning rate scaling proportional to the square root of batch size (η ∝ √B, base η=10⁻⁶ at B=1,024), and the qualitative findings on optimal n also hold for PPO and CISPO in addition to GRPO (Section 3, Appendix F, Figure 25).

4fX2DEypNL.text: A2SG's asymmetric surrogate gradient (Eq. 10) allocates larger gradients to higher membrane potentials and achieves 96.74% accuracy on CIFAR10 with ResNet19, versus 95.17% for the LSG baseline (Table 1).
On CIFAR100 with ResNet19, A2SG reaches 81.05% accuracy compared to 76.85% for LSG (Table 1).
Theorem 4.2 proves that asymmetric surrogate gradients achieve lower coefficient-of-variation (CV) than symmetric variants when L·κ > σ² (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.2).

Section 4.1 establishes a direct connection between the local gradient variation coefficient and Fisher Information Matrix eigenvalues, showing reduced CV corresponds to a flatter loss landscape (Section 4.1, Figure 1).
On ImageNet, E-SpikeFormer combined with A2SG achieves 85.43% accuracy at 35.64 mJ energy consumption (Table 3).
On CIFAR10-DVS, A2SG reaches 82.36% accuracy with the VGGSNN architecture (Table 4).

OdM5JRVEiK.text: Lookahead Unmasking (LookUM) reformulates the unmasking step as path selection using a path generator and an uncertainty-based verifier (Section 3.2).
LookUM requires only 2-3 paths to reach peak performance, with MATH500 achieving optimal results at just 2 paths and GSM8K improving up to 4 paths before plateauing (Figure 3).
Applied to LLaDA-8B, LookUM yields a +4 point gain on GSM8K, +8 points on HumanEval, and +2 points on MBPP (Table 2).

LookUM applied to the RL-tuned LLaDA 1.5 model still delivers significant additional gains, showing the uncertainty-based approach captures signals complementary to reward-based training (Section 4.2, Table 2).
LLaDA-8B with LookUM achieves competitive or superior performance to vanilla LLaDA 1.5 on several benchmarks despite LLaDA 1.5 having undergone additional RL tuning (Section 4.2).

L3fJXwaFdx.text: Thinking-RFT uses GRPO optimization with verifiable rewards, prompting models to produce reasoning within <think> tags before an <answer> tag (Section 3).
Thinking-RFT improves average Theory of Mind accuracy by +6% over SFT across narrative, conversational, and multimodal contexts (Section 4.2).
On second-order Theory of Mind reasoning in the OpenToM narrative dataset, Thinking-RFT improves +10.3% over SFT (Table 3).
On combined MMToM and MuMA-ToM multimodal benchmarks, Thinking-RFT improves +7.45% over SFT (Table 4).
On MMToM domain generalization, RFT accuracy drops only 2.4% versus a 7.11% drop for SFT, and on OpenToM counterfactual perturbations RFT degrades 7.90% versus 17.14% for SFT (Table 5, Table 8).
Attention visualizations show RFT-trained models focus on critical causal-cue sentences rather than irrelevant details when generating reasoning traces (Section 5.3, Figure 4).

PrM9JAYDF6.text: PGT's procedural generation pipeline (Section 3.2) produces three core task types: spatial relationship understanding, counting, and analogy/relative distance estimation (Section 3.1).
Instruction tuning Llama-3-8B on PGT data yields a +19.6% gain on What'sUp and a +13.3% gain on CV-Bench-2D (Table 1).
Instruction tuning Vicuna-1.5-7B on PGT data yields a +20.0% gain on What'sUp and a +12.3% gain on CV-Bench-2D (Table 1).

Fine-tuning LLaVA-Next-7B on PGT data improves What'sUp accuracy from 85.2% to 90.7% (a +5.5% gain), with CV-Bench-2D gains ranging up to +8.3% across tested state-of-the-art MLLMs including InternVL3-8B (Table 2).
The paper argues spatial reasoning deficits stem primarily from inadequate training signal rather than visual encoder resolution or architectural limitations (Section 1, Section 6).

6Qu03WGp6x.text: The Global Representation Guidance module (Section 3.3) encodes the predicted global map through an MLP and fuses it with each individual query via concatenation and an additional MLP layer.
On the nuScenes validation set at 110 epochs, MapGR improves MapTR by +4.2 mAP (to 40.0%) under the strict mAP1 metric and +4.9 mAP (to 63.6%) under the looser mAP2 metric (Table 1).
On nuScenes, MapGR improves MapTRv2 to 47.9% mAP1 (+2.5) and 71.1% mAP2 (+2.4), and improves MapQR to 51.9% mAP1 (+1.4) and 73.1% mAP2 (+0.5) (Table 1).
On Argoverse2, MapGR improves MapQR by +0.8 mAP1 (to 42.9%) and +0.9 mAP2 (to 66.0%) (Table 2).

Ablation results show the combined Global Representation Learning and Global Representation Guidance modules together yield a +3.5 improvement in mAP2 to 65.0% (Table 3), with the best configuration applying the guidance to the first two decoder layers (Table 5).

NpguYNGrG2.text: Theorem 4.7 gives finite-sample convergence bounds for Algorithm 1 (multi-agent risk-averse actor-critic), showing the expected squared distance to the equilibrium decays geometrically under constant step sizes and sublinearly under diminishing step sizes (Theorem 4.7).

Theorem 3.1 proves uniqueness of the Risk-averse Quantal Response Equilibrium (RQE) under λ-strict monotonicity and derives an explicit Lipschitz-continuity bound relating equilibrium policy changes to perturbations of the payoff matrices (Theorem 3.1).
Proposition 4.2 shows the risk-adjusted Bellman operator is a γ0-contraction mapping under Assumption 4.1, underpinning the two-timescale convergence analysis of Section 4 (Proposition 4.2).
On the Inspection Game, gradient descent with a higher risk-aversion parameter τ converges faster than risk-neutral training (Figure 2, Section 5.1).

Across the Gridworld Cooperation task (10 runs) and the MPE Simple Tag task (5 runs), risk-averse training produces markedly more consistent convergence curves than risk-neutral baselines (Figures 3-4, Sections 5.2-5.3).

jn7gGAya5h.text: Theorem 1 establishes a correspondence between fixed points of the Douglas-Rachford (DR) operator and Nash equilibria via the lifting transform z = ẑ − γF(ẑ) (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
Theorem 4 proves local quadratic convergence of the hybrid semi-smooth Newton method, with residual bound ‖R^γ_DRS(z_{k+1})‖ ≤ C‖R^γ_DRS(z_k)‖² (Theorem 4, Section 3.3).
Lemma 1 shows the DRS residual operator is monotone and 1-Lipschitz continuous, which is the key property enabling application of a semi-smooth Newton (SSN) solver (Lemma 1).

On 400x800 random zero-sum games, the hybrid PSSN methods reach a duality gap of 1e-12 in about 4.3-4.4 seconds versus 21.97 seconds for PRM+, an order-of-magnitude speedup in the high-precision regime (numerical results table, Section 4).

Algorithm 1 performs a one-time switch from the first-order Predictive Regret Matching+ (PRM+) method to the Douglas-Rachford semi-smooth Newton (DRSSN) subroutine of Algorithm 2, combining global efficiency with local superlinear convergence (Algorithms 1-2).

hlUgEwl3Du.text: Figure 1 shows Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Grok 3 Mini Beta, and DeepSeek-R1 all solve the same Game of 24 problem but trace distinct tree-jump reasoning paths, ranging from linear to highly exploratory with different verification patterns (Figure 1).

Table 3 finds that success-rate is the most important ReJump metric for explaining performance on MATH-500 (importance 0.8548), whereas jump-distance exploration is most important for Game of 24 (importance 0.2742), indicating task-dependent reasoning styles (Table 3).
Section 6.1 shows ReJump-guided Best-of-N selection using jump distance improves Game of 24 accuracy by +6.8 to +9.1 percentage points over standard Best-of-N selection (Section 6.1).

Section 5.2 finds that large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve higher pass@1 than standard LLMs primarily by generating a greater number of more diverse solution attempts, rather than higher per-attempt accuracy (Section 5.2).

The ReJump-Extractor, built on Gemini 2.5 Pro, achieves 0.943 tree-similarity and 0.940 jump-similarity against human-annotated ground truth on Game of 24 reasoning traces (Section on ReJump-Extractor evaluation).

Section 5.5 shows that over the course of reinforcement learning training, model reasoning behavior (as measured by ReJump tree/jump metrics) progressively aligns with task-specific demands (Section 5.5).

UNWIi5Qjg1.text: The Torque Variation Score (TVS) is computed as a weighted sum of three components: spectral diversity, variance diversity, and segment diversity of torque induced by small pose perturbations (Section 4.2).
Table 1 reports that TVS has a Spearman correlation with imitation error of 0.66 for the UHC policy and 0.82 for the PHC+ policy, and Pearson correlations of 0.48 and 0.65 respectively (Table 1).

Section 6.1 defines Maximum Imitable Difficulty (MID) thresholds of 308.22 for UHC and 320.50 for PHC+, identifying the difficulty level beyond which each policy fails to imitate motions (Section 6.1).

Table 3's Difficulty-Stratified Joint Error (DSJE) shows that on the easiest motion band (DSJE-200), PHC+ has higher joint error than UHC (30.38mm vs 27.79mm), indicating PHC+ underperforms UHC even on low-difficulty motions (Table 3).

Appendix C shows TVS-ordered curriculum learning yields consistent policy improvements across difficulty bands, that TVS generalizes to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, and that TVS values above roughly 500 flag physically implausible or flawed motion-capture data (Appendix C).

bCxkeiNGxZ.text: Figure 1 shows that on NanoGPT pretraining over FineWeb at a fixed learning rate of 0.001, DeVA reaches a target validation perplexity using 6.6% fewer training tokens than Muon, while SOAP uses 4.3% fewer tokens than Muon (Figure 1).

Table 2 reports that on a 270M-parameter NanoGPT model trained on 1.4B tokens, DeVA attains a validation loss of 3.271 versus Muon's 3.305 (about 1% lower), at roughly 54% higher per-step wall-clock cost (16.49s vs Muon per 1k tokens) (Table 2).

Theorem 3.1 derives the coordinate-wise DeVA_S∞ update rule, which tracks the covariance of singular values within an eigenbasis-rotated spectral space to unify vector (Adam-like) and matrix (Muon-like) adaptive methods (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 4.15 shows that DeVA's adaptive spectral weighting controls blockwise smoothness throughout matrix-parameter training, providing the theoretical basis for its faster convergence (Theorem 4.15).

Figure 3(b) shows DeVA achieves faster initial convergence than competing optimizers, including Muon and SOAP, when training a ViT-L/16 model on ImageNet-1K image classification (Figure 3(b), Section 5.1).

X0wQLbleXa.text: AvAtar computes a query's informativeness via the adjoint-state method, reformulating the gradient of a utility function f(T) with respect to the cost matrix into a linear system over adjoint vectors y_alpha and y_beta, solved by conjugate gradient with linear time complexity O(K(n+m)) (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.5, Equation 6).

On network alignment across Phone-Email, ACM-DBLP-P, Douban, and ACM-DBLP-A using the PARROT and JOENA OT-based aligners, AVATAR-L2 and AVATAR-CONSIST achieve state-of-the-art MRR, outperforming baselines by up to 2.8% (Table 3, Section 5.2.1).

On image-text retrieval (CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C) and image-text grounding (COCO, Flickr30K) using GOT-W and GOT-FGW aligners, AVATAR-ENTROPY and AVATAR-L2 outperform Random, Entropy, Margin, Least Confident, Density, and Diversity query strategies in Recall@1, with AVATAR-ENTROPY outperforming Entropy by up to 2.6% (Tables 4 and 5, Section 5.2.2).

On the Phone-Email and Douban datasets with PARROT, AVATAR-L2/CONSIST achieve up to 25x speed-up in query time and up to 8.1% improvement in MRR compared to existing active network-alignment methods GibbsMatchings and TopMatchings (Figure 2, Section 5.3).

An ablation replacing sparse matrix operations with dense matrix operations (AVATAR-Dense) shows negligible MRR difference but up to a 1010/118 ≈ 8.6x slowdown on ACM-DBLP-A, confirming that exploiting the transport plan's sparsity (over 99% near-zero entries) preserves accuracy while cutting computation time (Table 6, Section 5.4, Figure 5).

Replacing the transport-plan-weighted posterior aggregation in Eq. 8 with uniform aggregation (AVATAR-Uniform) degrades performance, e.g., AVATAR-L2 attains 0.837 MRR versus 0.669 for AVATAR-L2(Uniform) on Douban (Table 7, Section 5.6).

6lq2MGo42H.text: GAE is pretrained on 50,000 trajectories aggregated from seven sources (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, DROID, AgiBot World, CALVIN, RLBench, and BridgeV2) with depth annotations enhanced via FoundationStereo, PromptDepthAnything, and MoGe (Section on dataset/training).

GAE conditions on robot proprioceptive state, a VLM-generated guidance pose, and a cropped point-cloud observation (Equation 1), and is trained with an 'Action Pre-training, Point-cloud Fine-tuning' paradigm using a pretraining batch size of 31,824 trajectories.
On the RoboTwin simulation benchmark, GAE attains average success rates of 81% on short-horizon, 73% on middle-horizon, and 60% on long-horizon manipulation tasks (RoboTwin results table).
On six real-world manipulation tasks, GAE achieves 78.3% average success rate using only 50 demonstrations per task and zero task-specific fine-tuning of the action expert.

GAE generalizes zero-shot to novel camera viewpoints, object colors, and semantic variations, and transfers to the ManiSkill benchmark despite ManiSkill data being excluded from training (Generalization/cross-environment transfer section).

RNn2wtNeoK.text: The physics-induced diffusion annotation module models pseudo-label generation as a learnable anisotropic thermal diffusion process discretized into an iterative form, treating each infrared target as a local heat source radiating energy that diffuses outward, then fuses the resulting field with a superpixel prior for structural integrity (Method section on physics-induced diffusion annotation).

A bi-level dual-update optimization jointly learns detector weights (inner level), sample-wise loss weights via a meta-classifier, and diffusion parameters via validation feedback, minimizing validation loss subject to the inner problem minimizing weighted training loss (Bi-level framework section).
On SIRST3, the generated pseudo-masks achieve an IoU of 68.02, outperforming the MCLC baseline's 66.98 (Experimental results, pseudo-mask quality comparison).
The pseudo-label generation runs at approximately 0.012 seconds per target, about 5x faster than MCLC (Efficiency results).

Across detector architectures including DNANet, UIUNet, and ISNet evaluated on SIRST3, SIRST-v1, NUDT-SIRST, and IRSTD-1k, the method achieves five-fold annotation acceleration and matches full-data performance using only 30% of the training data, while consistently outperforming LESPS, PAL, and MCLC baselines (Experimental results section).

ZEP68RaUeR.text: For symmetric-cost Bertrand competition with any non-increasing demand function, Theorem 2.1 shows two no-external-regret learners can sustain high prices while guaranteeing each firm's utility is at least 1/(4e^2) of the monopoly profit (Theorem 2.1).

Theorem 2.2 shows that when both learners use no-swap-regret algorithms, prices converge toward marginal cost, with expected utility bounded above by f(c+1/k)/k, demonstrating strong competitive pressure (Theorem 2.2).

Theorem 2.3 shows an asymmetric setting—one no-external-regret learner paired with one no-swap-regret learner—can still sustain high, collusive-like prices under certain demand structures such as constant demand (Theorem 2.3).
Theorem 2.5 shows that as the number of firms n grows, the total utility attainable under no-external-regret dynamics decays exponentially, as e^(1-n/2) (Theorem 2.5).

Under asymmetric costs, Theorem 2.6 shows high-utility coarse correlated equilibria exist for broad demand classes (including linear and exponential demand) under no-external-regret learning, while Theorem 2.7 shows that under no-swap-regret learning the higher-cost firm's utility converges to zero regardless of the demand function (Theorems 2.6 and 2.7).
Numerical experiments across multiple demand functions show utilities converging toward 1/e ≈ 0.368 of the monopoly utility under no-external-regret dynamics (Numerical results section).

NsC3NFsavi.text: On the OPC test set, a simple MLP classifier trained on text embeddings achieves 75.34% accuracy, outperforming Claude-Sonnet-4 as a judge, and a trivial heuristic that predicts 'incorrect' for all geometry problems achieves 65.07% accuracy, revealing that dataset imbalances can be exploited rather than genuine proof understanding (Evaluation framework analysis section).

Comparing three LLM-as-a-Judge prompt variants with majority@5 voting, GIMO attains 57.58% precision, 87.06% recall, and 69.28% F1, substantially higher than General Summary (18.28% precision, 30.91% F1) and OPC (22.88% precision, 37.23% F1) prompts (Prompt comparison table).

Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of the LLM-as-a-Judge significantly reduces performance variance across prompt variants, causing different prompts to converge to similar results, but does not improve final-answer precision (RL training results section).

When comparing pairwise GenSelect tournaments against LLM-as-a-Judge for best-of-n proof selection, neither method is uniformly superior; the better approach varies by dataset and model (Proof selection comparison section).

On Challenge-19, GenSelect with 256 candidates reaches 92.10% accuracy and LLM-as-Judge with 256 proofs and 32 judgments reaches 91.44% accuracy, while a hybrid knockout-tournament-plus-judge method (256 to 16 finalists, then 32 judgments) reaches 96.05% accuracy using 4x fewer LLM calls than the pure judge approach (Challenge-19 results table).

zloIrd77G5.text: Typicality bias is formalized as reward r(x,y) = r_true(x,y) + α log π_ref(y|x), and empirical fits on the HelpSteer preference dataset yield α̂ = 0.57±0.07 and 0.65±0.07 (p<10⁻¹⁴), supporting it as a fundamental data-level driver of mode collapse (Section 3.1, Equation 1).

RLHF-style optimization under typicality bias is shown to sharpen the output distribution by a factor γ := 1 + α/β > 1, which compresses probability mass toward typical completions (Section 3.2, Equation 3).
Verbalized Sampling increases diversity by 1.6-2.1x over direct prompting on creative writing tasks such as poems, stories, and jokes (Section 5, Figure 4).
Human evaluation shows Verbalized Sampling improves diversity ratings versus direct prompting: poems from 1.90 to 2.39, stories from 2.74 to 3.06, and jokes from 1.83 to 3.01 (Section 5.2, Table 3).
An ablation shows Verbalized Sampling retains 66.8% of the base model's diversity compared to only 23.8% retained by direct prompting (Section 5.3).
Larger models such as GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Pro gain 1.5-2x greater diversity benefits from Verbalized Sampling than smaller model variants (Figure 4(e-f)).

mZd4u9d7pQ.text: ESE achieves accuracy at least as good as state-of-the-art forecasting methods while running significantly faster, evaluated on synthetic multi-system datasets in Section 4.1 (Table 1).
When combined with FiLM and SCINet on the 320-region COVID-19 dataset, ESE delivers up to a 70x speedup while remaining competitive in RMSE (4.83) and MAE (4.58) (Section 4.2, Table 3).

On the 16-currency G20 exchange rate dataset (Nov 2019-Oct 2024), ESE combined with SCINet achieves over 10x speedup, and ESE alone attains RMSE 6.010 and MAE 5.520 versus RMSE 5.461 and MAE 5.102 for ESE+Dlinear (Section 4.2/5, Table 2 and Table 5).

ESE has linear time complexity in the number of systems, attributes, and input time steps, giving it far better scaling than state-of-the-art methods as the number of systems increases (Section 5, Figure 3).

ESE's problem formulation requires that all interacting systems share identical attribute sets and that the sum of proportional changes across all systems equals zero (Section 2, Definition 3, Constraint 2, Equation 3).

uUnIAtZUfX.text: TimeOmni-VL is presented as the first vision-centric framework to unify time series understanding and generation within a single model (Section 1).

Bi-TSI achieves near-lossless bidirectional mapping between time series and images via Robust Fidelity Normalization, a hybrid MAD- and standard-deviation-based scaling with bounded tanh mapping, combined with encoding capacity constraints (H/N≥f, W≥L/f) using 896x896 images instead of 224x224 (Section 3.1, Equations 5-6).

Understanding-guided generation conditions the diffusion-based generation module on Chain-of-Thought reasoning produced by the understanding task, via a training sequence that interleaves understanding output as generation context (Section 3.2, Equation 7, Figure 2).
An ablation shows understanding-guided generation with Chain-of-Thought yields an average 8.2% improvement over generation without this guidance (Section 4.1, Figure 8).

On the TSUMM-Suite benchmark (40k forecasting samples, 40k imputation samples, 9,409 understanding QA pairs across 6 task types), TimeOmni-VL achieves nMASE of 0.878 on short-term forecasting, outperforming VisionTS++, and state-of-the-art nMASE of 0.713 on imputation at 10-20% masking (Section 3.2, Section 4.1, Table 1).

epVORy8H4y.text: RealisMotion decomposes human motion control into independent, composable dimensions—subject, background, trajectory, and action—via a two-stage pipeline of 3D motion editing followed by video generation (Section 3.2, Introduction).

A ground-aware 3D world coordinate system is defined with its origin at the human's standing position in the first frame, y-axis aligned with gravity, and scale set so that 1 unit equals 1 meter of physical distance (Section 3.2.1).

On the Trajectory100 dataset, RealisMotion outperforms RealisDance-DiT with lower translation error (1.198m vs. 1.706m), lower rotation error (0.101° vs. 0.167°), and lower FVD (314.59 vs. 758.08) (Table 2).
On the RealisDance-Val dataset for action control, RealisMotion achieves higher PSNR (20.34 dB vs. 17.22 dB) and lower FVD (1000.98 vs. 1576.66) than RealisDance-DiT (Table 3).
Trajectory editing unprojects 2D image points into 3D camera space using focal-length calibration and then transforms them into world space via rigid point registration (Equations 1-2).

Table 1 compares controllability across methods, showing RealisMotion is the only approach providing full 3D control over trajectory, orientation, and action alongside image-based control of subject and background (Table 1).

Qr8Zvwoi88.text: BESPOKE is constructed from 2,870 real user history sessions collected over three weeks from 30 annotators, comprising 2,153 search sessions and 717 chat sessions, averaging 95.67 sessions per user (Section 3, Table 2).

BESPOKE includes 150 user-annotated queries paired with gold information needs and gold responses generated through iterative refinement, forming a three-stage annotation pipeline of query authoring, response-judgment pairs, and gold response generation (Section 3).

Each response is scored on a five-point Likert scale across four fine-grained criteria—need alignment, content depth, tone, and explanation style—together with diagnostic feedback explaining the score (Section 3.3).
Annotator diversity is measured with a Shannon equitability of 0.91 across annotator backgrounds (Section 3).

Query-aware selective history profiles for user context construction substantially outperform baseline context construction approaches, yet no evaluated model setting surpasses an average score of 60, revealing a key remaining gap in effective personalization (Section 4.2, Table 4).

H9IIK4ySRD.text: rePIRL formulates LLM token-level generation as an inverse RL problem, jointly updating a process reward model (PRM) and policy via the energy-based objective in Equation 5, without requiring token-level reward annotations, preference labels, or access to an expert policy (Section 3.2).
Propositions 1-4 show that DPO, DQO, Math-Shepherd (MCTS-based), and PRIME can each be derived as special cases of the rePIRL framework under additional restrictive assumptions (Section 3.3).

On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, rePIRL improves math accuracy from 31.7% (RLOO baseline) to 33.5% and coding accuracy from 24.1% to 27.7%, evaluated on AIME-2024, AMC, MATH-500, Minerva-Math, Olympiad-Bench, LeetCode, and LiveCodeBench (Table 2).
On Qwen3-4B-Base, rePIRL improves math accuracy from 38.4% (RLOO) to 41.6% and coding accuracy from 35.5% to 39.8% (Table 2).
PRM-only training under rePIRL achieves comparable test-time-training performance to outcome-reward training, and PRM-based test-time scaling outperforms majority voting (Section 4.3, Figure 1).

Training rePIRL with RLOO (4 rollouts per prompt) on 8 RTX PRO 6000 GPUs takes about 13.3 hours for math versus 14.6 hours for the PRIME baseline, using 7,000 instances per domain from PRIME's Eurus-2-RL-Data (Section 4, Appendix C).

JFevoTJIVi.text: The proposed single-pass online change-point detection algorithm for multivariate inhomogeneous Poisson process time series has per-observation computational cost O(rW^{1+d/(2γ+p∨q)}), independent of the elapsed series length (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
Theorem 1 bounds the detection delay by Δ = O(r(log(b)/κ)^{2+(p∨q)/γ}), improving on offline density-change detection rates by a factor of κ^{d/γ}/κ^{(p∨q)/γ} (Theorem 1).
A new Matrix Bernstein inequality (Theorem 7) is derived for geometrically β-mixing Poisson point process time series to control estimation error under temporal dependence (Theorem 7, Definition 1).

In 3D synthetic experiments with a change point at t=1200 (100 Monte Carlo replications), the proposed Matrix detector attains 94% correct detection with average detection delay 9.19 (SD 3.80), versus 40.39 (SD 29.79) for MMD and 43.98 (SD 34.63) for KIE at comparable false-alarm rates (Table 1).

On the Oklahoma earthquake dataset (2000-2018, 4D: longitude, latitude, depth, magnitude), the Matrix detector flags a change in June 2009, consistent with reported fracking-related seismicity, while KIE falsely alarms in July 2007 and MMD detects no change by 2018 (Section 5, real-data application).
