CHvRfubYke.text: Using a second-order Taylor expansion of pretraining loss under fine-tuning perturbations, ℒ_PT(θ_FT) ≈ ℒ_PT(θ_PT) + ½Δ_FT^T H Δ_FT (Equation 3), the paper argues that reducing directional curvature (sharpness) along fine-tuning directions reduces catastrophic forgetting (Section 2).

Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) applied during OLMo-60M pretraining (20M-150M parameters, 4B-192B tokens) achieves 80% less forgetting on StarCoder fine-tuning at matched fine-tuning loss compared to AdamW, with the gap widening from 12B to 192B tokens, despite comparable or worse pretraining loss (Section 3.2, Figures 3-4).

At 1B scale, applying SAM during mid-training of OLMo-2-1B for 50B tokens yields 31% less forgetting after MetaMath post-training and 40% less degradation under 4-bit quantization, despite a slightly worse base checkpoint score (43.2 vs 42.9) (Section 3.5.1).
Under 4-bit quantization, SAM reduces degradation by 2-3x at high token budgets relative to AdamW-trained models (Section 3.4).

A scalable recipe applying SAM only during the learning-rate annealing phase adds about 10% compute overhead (versus about 100% for full-run SAM) while recovering most of the forgetting-mitigation benefit (Section 3.5, Figure 9).

Higher peak learning rates and shorter annealing periods (5% vs 20% of training) each independently improve the learning-forgetting frontier for both cosine and WSD schedules (Section 3.3, Figures 6-7).

2eKOeHaNZG.text: XSpecMesh uses D=4 lightweight cross-attention decoding heads to speculatively predict multiple subsequent mesh tokens in parallel within a single backbone forward pass, verified against the backbone via a probability threshold δ=0.5 (Section 4.1-4.2).

Against the BPT baseline, XSpecMesh achieves a 1.71x speedup (step compression ratio 2.021, step latency 47.83ms) while maintaining comparable quality: Chamfer Distance 0.1168 vs 0.1165 and Hausdorff Distance 0.2261 vs 0.2223 (Table 2, Table 3, Configuration E).

Average generation latency on the 200-mesh test set (20% easy, 40% medium, 40% hard difficulty, from Objaverse-derived data) drops from 257.6s (BPT) to 151.4s (XSpecMesh), with user-study preference of 36% for XSpecMesh vs 37% for BPT out of 1,400 responses from 70 participants (Table 2).

Training uses a two-stage backbone distillation: Stage 1 trains only the decoding heads with weighted loss L_mhd = Σ w(d)·L_d (weight decay w(d)=0.8^d), and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the backbone with LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32) using L_total = λ·L_backbone + L_mhd with λ=50 (Section 4.3).

Ablations show cross-attention decoding heads outperform MLP-based heads (Table 3, Configuration D vs E), and probability-threshold acceptance is more stable than Top-K ranking-based acceptance (Figure 6).

yMKdZPwPyL.text: The Linear Multi-View Acyclic Model (LiMVAM) achieves identifiability of causal structure from multiple related datasets under Gaussian disturbances by exploiting noise-variance diversity across views (Assumption 1) rather than relying on non-Gaussianity (Section on Main Theorems).
Theorem 2 establishes that the per-view causal matrices B^i and covariance matrices Σ^i are identifiable under noise diversity alone, without requiring non-Gaussian noise (Theorem 2).
Theorem 4 shows the shared causal ordering P is identifiable when edge connectivity is pooled across views, requiring only that each edge be non-zero in at least one view (Theorem 4, Assumption 3).

The proposed MICaDo algorithm, combining Shared ICA with DAG decomposition by minimizing upper-triangular entries, recovers causal structure in synthetic experiments (m=5 views, p=4 variables, n from 10^2 to 10^4) even when all disturbances are Gaussian, where baseline non-Gaussianity-based methods fail, achieving ℓ2 distance on B^i matrices of about 0.02-0.05 at n=10^4 (Figure 1).

MICaDo outperforms MultiGroupDirectLiNGAM and ICA-LiNGAM baselines in mixed Gaussian/non-Gaussian noise scenarios while remaining competitive in traditional non-Gaussian settings (Comparison section).

Applied to Cam-CAN MEG data (98 subjects, 10 brain regions during a sensorimotor task), the method estimates a shared causal ordering with average Spearman correlation of 0.24 across 50 runs and identifies interhemispheric motor connections involving the postcentral region (Real Data section).

MgIvtHk5wm.text: Theorem 3.3 proves that the Jacobian of any admissible mesh-based dynamics factors as ∂F/∂z = (J(z) − R(z))G(z), with J skew-symmetric and topology-fixed, R positive-semidefinite (dissipation), and G positive-definite (metric) (Theorem 3.3).

MeshFT-Net achieves a normalized energy drift of about 1.3×10⁻⁴, compared to 25.9 for MeshGraphNets (MGN) and about 1.0×10⁻² for Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNN) baselines (Section 5, energy conservation results).
MeshFT-Net attains a wave speed (dispersion) error of about 2.03×10⁻², versus about 0.2 for MeshGraphNets (Section 5, dispersion results).
MeshFT-Net's momentum conservation variation is about 4.89×10⁻⁸, versus about 3.90×10⁻¹ for unconstrained baselines (Section 5, momentum conservation results).
MeshFT-Net maintains a one-step MSE of about 1.3×10⁻⁹ on analytic plane-wave benchmarks, versus about 1.6×10⁻⁷ for MGN and about 3.5×10⁻⁸ for HNN (Section 5, benchmark table).

Under out-of-distribution shifts in frequency, resolution, and wave speed, MeshFT-Net shows robust extrapolation while competing baselines diverge with time-step MSE exceeding 100 (Section 5, out-of-distribution generalization experiments).

072o1IbwJi.text: Theorem 4.4 shows that three bias mechanisms — transportability bias, confounding bias, and selection bias — produce distinct covariance signatures between absolute bias magnitude and the conditional variances of selection (S), treatment (A), and outcome (Y) variables (Theorem 4.4).
Theorem 4.8 establishes consistent estimators for these bias-magnitude covariance signals using squared prediction errors from nuisance function estimators fitted on observational data (Theorem 4.8).

Synthetic experiments across 200 simulation runs with varying sample sizes achieve over 80% accuracy in identifying the correct bias mechanism at a p<0.01 significance threshold (Figure 3, synthetic experiments).

In the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) hormone-therapy case study, the baseline observational analysis exhibits the covariance signature of Type 2 selection bias, with the ρ(b₁,S) and ρ(b₁,A) signals attenuating toward zero after correcting for immortal time bias (Section 6, WHI case study).

After immortal-time-bias correction in the WHI analysis, a residual positive ρ(b₁,Y) signal persists, consistent with an additional transportability bias mechanism, a pattern reproduced in matched synthetic experiments (Section 6, WHI case study).

DvvEByY0Xa.text: EB-1WL, an edge-based color-refinement test, is proved to be significantly more expressive than the standard 1-WL test for graph isomorphism/GNN expressivity (abstract only).
The paper provides a complete logical characterization of EB-1WL in first-order logic, together with distinguishability results obtained via homomorphism counting (abstract only).

EB-GNN, the corresponding architecture inspired by the Chiba–Nishizeki triangle-counting algorithm, passes messages along both edges and triangles and is claimed to have the strongest theoretical expressivity guarantees among edge-based message-passing GNNs in the literature (abstract only).
Despite exceeding 1-WL expressivity, EB-1WL and EB-GNN are shown to admit near-linear time and memory usage on practical graph learning workloads (abstract only).
In experiments, EB-GNN substantially outperforms simple MPNNs and remains competitive with task-specialized state-of-the-art GNNs at substantially lower computational cost (abstract only).

4FSkKnTnvI.text: LieFlow discovers C₄ symmetry from an SO(2) prior with a Wasserstein-1 distance of 0.072, compared to 1.688 for the LieGAN baseline (Section on 2D experiments).
LieFlow discovers the tetrahedral group symmetry with a Wasserstein-1 distance of 0.0885 under uniform time sampling, compared to 2.105 for LieGAN, on a 3D dataset (Section on 3D experiments).
LieFlow recovers SO(2) rotational symmetry with a Wasserstein-1 distance of 0.0429, versus 0.0528 for LieGAN (Section on 3D experiments).

The paper identifies a 'last-minute mode convergence' failure mode in which the learned velocity field stays near zero until t approaches 1, and introduces a power-distribution time schedule that samples more timesteps near t=1 to fix it, enabling successful discovery of the 24-element octahedral group where uniform sampling fails (Section on time-schedule / power distribution).

Even with the power-distribution time schedule, LieFlow still fails to discover the 60-element icosahedral group, indicating a persisting limitation for highly symmetric discrete groups (Limitations section).

genVnYBAV7.text: Theorem 5.4 shows that within KL-regularized RL, the difference between Q-functions for two policies equals α times a sequential forward KL divergence term (Theorem 5.4).
Lemma 6.1 proves that regret at terminal accepted states is upper bounded by the expected regret over intermediate contexts, motivating the RePO objective (Lemma 6.1).

RePO admits a closed-form policy update, S^RePO = -α(log[π_θ(o_t|q)/π_ref(o_t|q)] + sequential KL term), analogous to Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) but accounting for behavior-policy-dependent sequential KL divergence (Section 6, closed-form update).
RePO_det, a deterministic pseudo-labeling variant of RePO, extends the method to offline preference datasets without requiring access to the behavior policy (Section on RePO_det).
On Qwen3-4B, RePO achieves 60.12% win rate on AlpacaEval2 and 90.60% accuracy on GSM8K, reported alongside KTO baseline scores of 63.9 on Arena-Hard and 67.38 on MATH (Table with benchmark results).

uSJv2fwhCQ.text: EARL achieves 65.48% cIoU for pixel grounding on the Ego-IRGBench test set, an 8.37 percentage point improvement over the previous best RL-based method (Table 1).
On out-of-distribution evaluation using the EgoHOS dataset, EARL attains 38.21% overall cIoU, including 52.30% left-hand IoU and 62.44% right-hand IoU (Table 2).

The proposed Analysis-guided Feature Synthesizer (AFS), which uses self-attention to inject a global interaction descriptor into the fine-grained stage, outperforms a cross-attention fusion (CAF) alternative, 65.48% vs 52.36% cIoU (Table 3).

EARL uses Qwen2.5-VL-3B as the coarse-stage decoder, Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the fine-stage decoder, and a frozen SAM2-Large for mask generation, trained on the 20,504-image Ego-IRGBench dataset via Group Relative Policy Optimization with format, answer-relevance, and grounding-accuracy rewards (Section 4.2).
A hyperparameter study over the reward weights (λf, λa, λg) shows that balanced weighting of format, answer, and grounding rewards outperforms single-objective training configurations (Table 4).

Xn8kmKvO9g.text: On ML benchmarks, LLM teams underperform their own best individual (expert) agent by relative synergy gaps ranging from 8.1% on MMLU Pro to 37.6% on HLE Text-Only (Table 2, Section 4.2).

On organizational psychology tasks (NASA Moon Survival, Lost at Sea, Student Body President), relative synergy gaps between teams and their best member range from 55.6% to 113.4% (Table 1, Section 4.1).

Even under aggressively-tuned prompts designed to maximize deference to a revealed expert, team performance improves only marginally, indicating that expert identification is not the primary bottleneck compared to expert leveraging (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

Team size is positively correlated with expertise dilution: larger teams show progressively larger synergy gaps relative to the expert, with statistically significant correlations (all p < 0.05) (Section 4.3, Figure 3).

Conversational analysis finds integrative-compromise behavior (averaging expert and non-expert positions) correlates positively with synergy gap (r = 0.55 to 0.69, p < 0.001), while epistemic deference correlates negatively with it (r = -0.44 to -0.68, p < 0.01) (Section 4.5, Table 5/Appendix H).

xdS18gI4e8.text: BinaryLLM (the 1-bit quantization method) requires only 13.5B training tokens to reach its reported performance, compared to FBI-LLM's 1.26 trillion tokens (Table 1, Section 3.1).
At the 3B scale, BinaryLLM-1bit achieves 57.0% average zero-shot accuracy across seven downstream tasks, versus 50.2% for BitNet-1.58bit (Table 2, Section 4.2).

The method uses a smooth transition function F(x,t) = tanh(tx)/tanh(t) for consistent progressive training, interpolating from a linear (pretrained-preserving) function to the sign function used for binarization (Section 3.2).

A dual-scaling compensation scheme combines an analytical scaling factor (Sa) that minimizes quantization error with a learnable scaling factor (Sl) for accuracy compensation, merged at inference with no added computational overhead (Section 3.4, Table 5).

An ablation over different pretrained base models (Table 3) and over progressive-training effectiveness (Table 4) supports the choice of consistent progressive training and binary-aware initialization as key contributors to performance.

otBTuq5AKB.text: EpiNode reduces long-horizon forecasting RMSE by 15-35% relative to ARIMA, LSTM, TimeKAN, TimeMixer++, EINN, Neural ODE, Latent ODE, KAN-ODE, and EARTH baselines across six datasets (Figure 9, Table 1).
EpiNode improves peak timing error by 1-3 weeks and reduces peak magnitude bias by up to 30% compared to baselines (Section 4.5.2, Figure 10).

The paper documents four hybrid-model failure modes: latent drift in neural ODEs under partial observability, unresolved identifiability gaps from bidirectional/adjoint training, degenerate solutions from physics-informed losses under sparse supervision, and inability of neural CDE-ODE hybrids to capture multi-wave dynamics (Section 2.1-2.4, Figures 2-6).

EpiNode combines Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) into trend, seasonal, and residual components with three coupled neural ODEs and a mechanistic SIRS solver with time-varying, bounded parameter networks (Section 3, Figure 7).
An ablation over architecture variants, decomposition components, and time-delay effects supports each component's contribution to forecasting accuracy (Section 4.7, Figure 14).

2LRaNghfoM.text: Proposition 1 shows the PRISM training loss uniquely minimizes to the per-token quality score g*^i(y) = p(x^i = y^i | y masked at position i), giving a theoretical guarantee that the learned score equals the true unmasking posterior probability (Section 3.1).

On a 28.6M-parameter DiT trained on Sudoku, PRISM begins to outperform vanilla masked diffusion baselines within only a few fine-tuning epochs, as shown by both accuracy curves and per-cell quality-score visualizations (Section 4.1, Figure 3).

For unconditional text generation with a 170M-parameter DiT pretrained on OpenWebText, PRISM is fine-tuned on only 164M tokens (1600x fewer than the 262B pretraining tokens) yet outperforms baselines on both generative perplexity and MAUVE (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

Fine-tuning LLaDA 8B with a LoRA adapter (~250M trainable parameters) for about 30 hours on 12 H100 GPUs, PRISM achieves 23.0% zero-shot pass rate on the 974-problem MBPP benchmark at 256 sampling steps, versus 20.2% for ReMDM (Table 1, Section 4.3).
The performance gains of PRISM's remasking mechanism over baselines diminish as the number of sampling steps increases, since there are fewer errors available to correct (Section 4.3).

GPyay3ZTrk.text: FedHD achieves 91.2% ± 5.0 accuracy and 80.6 ± 12.0 MCC on CAMELYON16, outperforming the FedWSIDD baseline by 2.5% accuracy (Section 4, Table 1).
On CAMELYON17 across five federated centers, FedHD reaches 82.7% ± 4.8 accuracy and 62.3 ± 11.3 MCC (Section 4, Table 1).
On TCGA-IDH across eight centers, FedHD attains 84.8% ± 4.1 accuracy and 57.0 ± 8.4 MCC (Section 4, Table 1).

An ablation study isolates the contributions of local Gaussian-mixture feature alignment, pseudo-patch reconstruction, and curriculum-based GCE-loss federation to overall performance (Section 4, Table 2).
FedHD yields lower membership-inference-attack AUC (51.8-54.7) than FedWSIDD (52.9-60.1), indicating stronger privacy protection under LiRA attacks (Section 4, Table 3).
The feature-level distillation communication payload is about 39 MB per client versus roughly 1.19 GB for the one-to-one (O2O) image-based strategy (Section 4).

x2CHpqD6L8.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that an optimal dynamic workflow-selection policy is guaranteed to perform at least as well as the best fixed static workflow (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

On SynSQL, oracle dynamic workflow selection achieves 81.5% execution accuracy versus 78.01% for the static RSL-SQL baseline, an oracle gap of +3.49 percentage points on average (Section 3, Figure 1).
SquRL-7B reaches 86.27% accuracy on Spider-Dev, exceeding RSL-SQL's 84.30% (Section 5, Table 1).
On Spider2.0-Lite, SquRL-7B achieves 49.18% accuracy (Section 5, Table 2).

On highly complex queries, SquRL improves accuracy by +7.97 points (46.51% vs. 38.54%) over the static baseline, showing pronounced gains on hard and out-of-distribution queries (Section 5, Figure 5).
An ablation removing the SFT or RL stage shows format-error rate rises from 0.29% with the full SquRL method to 77.37% without these components (Section 5, Table 5).

L9jcGvJP2N.text: The paper defines self-consistency rate as agreement with the infinite-budget majority vote, used as the principled objective for trajectory allocation (Section 2).
PETS-Offline reduces the number of reasoning traces needed from 9,520-11,607 (uniform allocation) to 2,780-3,667 across datasets, a reduction of up to 75% (Section 5, Table 2).
On GPQA, PETS-Offline achieves perfect self-consistency (rate of 1.0) while using up to 75% fewer traces than uniform allocation (Section 5, Table 2).

PETS-Online reduces the traces needed on GPQA from about 9,520 to about 4,662, a roughly 55% reduction relative to uniform allocation, while maintaining a self-consistency rate of 1.0 (Section 5, Table 3).
Algorithm 1 provides a randomized-rounding procedure that attains optimal solutions to the discretized budget-allocation problem (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

NEiMxuUCSc.text: TAGRPO introduces a trajectory alignment loss and memory bank on top of GRPO-style optimization to improve image-to-video generation (Section 3.2).
On HunyuanVideo 1.5 at 320p, TAGRPO improves Q-Save from 8.01 (baseline) to 8.05 and HPSv3 from 2.00 to 2.41 versus DanceGRPO (Section 4.2-4.3, Table 1).
On Wan 2.2 at 320p, TAGRPO improves Q-Save from 8.73 to 8.81 and HPSv3 from 3.63 to 4.29 versus the DanceGRPO baseline (Section 4.2-4.3, Table 2).
An ablation study confirms both the trajectory alignment loss and the memory bank component are individually necessary for the observed gains (Section 4.4, Figure 5).
Evaluation uses a held-out TAGRPO-Bench set of 200 image-text pairs, drawn from a training pool of about 10K image-text pairs, with training at 320p resolution and 53 frames (Section 4.1).

PxvTBZvMCe.text: A feature-correlation probe reveals a 'geometric forgetting' phenomenon in which a baseline diffusion model's geometric alignment score drops to 0.004 ± 0.015 in its deepest layer, while MaMi-HOI maintains 0.092 ± 0.067 (Section 4, Table 6, Figure 2).

On the FullBodyManipulation dataset, MaMi-HOI achieves an FID of 0.39, a Contact F1 score of 0.73, and 0.57 cm penetration, outperforming the HOI-Dyn and CHOIS baselines on most metrics (Section 4, Table 1).

The Geometry-Aware Proximity Adapter (GAPA) performs distance-aware cross-attention residual corrections for precise object contact; removing it increases waypoint error to 2.51 cm in the ablation (Section 4, Table 3, Figure 4).
On 3D-FUTURE generalization to unseen object geometries, MaMi-HOI attains a contact percentage of 0.54 (Section 4, Table 2).
For long-term synthesis with complex trajectories, MaMi-HOI reduces trajectory endpoint error by 50% relative to baseline (Section 4, Table 4).
Inference runs at 11.15 seconds per sequence with a 27.80M-parameter model, and on unseen objects hand-to-surface distance improves to 6.05mm, a 37% improvement (Section 4).

hqFugMmCqJ.text: BFM-SWM is the first budget-feasible mechanism with provable approximation guarantees for submodular welfare maximization in procurement auctions, achieving an approximation ratio of 0.0328 for general submodular functions (Theorem 4.8).
BFM-SWM attains an improved approximation ratio of 0.0877 for monotone submodular welfare functions and runs in O(n log(OPT/ε)) time (Theorem 4.10, Theorem 4.1).
BFM-VM achieves a deterministic approximation ratio of 1/(12+4√3) ≈ 0.0528, substantially improving the prior best-known ratio of 1/64 ≈ 0.0156 due to Balkanski et al. 2022 (Theorem 5.4).
BFM-VM reduces running time from O(n²logn) to O(nlogn) relative to prior budget-feasible mechanisms (Theorem 5.4).
BFM-SWM satisfies obvious strategyproofness, individual rationality, non-negative auctioneer surplus, and budget feasibility (Theorem 4.1).
On influence-maximization experiments, BFM-SWM achieves between 1.22x and 26.41x improvement over baselines, with an average improvement factor of 4.49x (Figure 1).

flo449mncA.text: Inverse Poisson Flow Matching (IPFM) distillation with 4 steps and α=1.0 achieves FID=1.75 on CIFAR-10 at auxiliary dimension D=128, surpassing the 35-NFE teacher's FID of 1.92 (Table 1).
IPFM distillation with only 2 steps reaches FID=1.72 on FFHQ 64x64 at D=128, exceeding the 79-NFE teacher's FID of 2.43 (Table 1).
A 2-step IPFM model attains FID=2.12 on CIFAR-10 and a 1-step model attains FID=2.40 on FFHQ 64x64, showing near-teacher or superior quality with very few function evaluations (Table 1).
IPFM training converges faster for finite auxiliary dimensionality D than in the D→∞ diffusion limit, which recovers Score Identity Distillation when α=1.0 (Figure 2, Proposition 3.4).
The tractable optimization reformulation underlying IPFM is established via Theorem 3.2 and Proposition 3.3 (Section 3).

oYCCOl7ahf.text: Few-step discrete diffusion samplers (SEDD, MDLM, LLaDA, ReMDM) are not distributionally correct even under an exact oracle denoiser, exhibiting transition-level mismatch that vanishes only as the number of sampling steps approaches the sequence length T (Section 7.1).
The oracle evaluation framework replaces learned denoisers with exact posteriors from a ground-truth Hidden Markov Model to isolate sampler error from model approximation error (Section 3).

Increasing temperature sharpening (β>1) simultaneously increases transition KL divergence and reduces 3-gram diversity while decreasing sequence NLL and generative perplexity, showing these metrics can improve even as sampling correctness worsens (Section 7.2).

Generative perplexity can be systematically improved through local sharpening alone, without faithful sampling of the data distribution, so it should be treated as an evaluator-alignment metric rather than a reliable indicator of sampler correctness (Section 7.3).

MAUVE scores remain uniformly high across varying sampling step counts despite substantial transition-level KL variations, demonstrating limited sensitivity to transition-level sampler errors (Section 7.4, Figure 4).

F7aqfPhbYI.text: Batch normalization layers for complex domains, defined via Fréchet mean centering and almost-geodesic running-mean updates, improve accuracy on radar clutter classification across six datasets: e.g., SiegelNetBN reaches 65.93% vs 62.47% for SiegelNetFC on Dataset 4 (+3.46 points) (Table 1, Section 3).
On radar clutter Dataset 1, adding BN improves accuracy from 31.24% (SiegelNetFC) to 33.83% (SiegelNetBN), a +2.59 point gain (Table 1).
For node classification, CBallNetBN achieves 79.58%±0.86 on Airport, 72.73%±0.56 on Pubmed, and 60.88%±1.49 on Cora, outperforming HNN-GyroBN-H and HNN-RBN-H baselines (Table 2).

The Siegel disk implementation of the proposed batch normalization derives an explicit distance formula and inverse-map computation via the Kobayashi pseudodistance and automorphisms (Proposition 6.1, Proposition 6.2, Section 6.1).
Almost-geodesic running-mean updates for the complex unit ball are formalized in Corollary 6.4, extending the Siegel disk construction of Corollary 6.3 (Section 6.2).

RAkOcnP4Uz.text: MWGraD flow converges at rate O(1/t) for geodesically convex multi-objective functionals under Assumption 3.1 (Theorem 3.4, Section 3.1).

A-MWGraD, incorporating a damped Hamiltonian momentum term, achieves an accelerated O(1/t²) convergence rate for geodesically convex objectives, improving on MWGraD's O(1/t) rate (Theorem 3.5, Section 3.2).
For β-strongly geodesically convex objectives, A-MWGraD achieves an exponential convergence rate of O(e^(-√β·t)) (Theorem 3.5, Section 3.2).
A-MWGraD is implemented via SVGD-based and Blob-based particle discretizations of the Wasserstein gradient (Eq. 17, Eq. 18, Section 3.3).
On a toy multi-objective example, A-MWGraD consistently outperforms MWGraD in GradNorm convergence speed across step sizes for both SVGD and Blob variants (Figure 1, Section 4.1).

In Bayesian multi-task learning on Multi-MNIST, Multi-Fashion, and Multi-Fashion+MNIST, A-MWGraD variants reach higher final ensemble accuracy than MWGraD, e.g. 96.4% vs 94.7% on a Multi-Fashion+MNIST task (Table 1, Figure 2, Section 4.2).

iVj5Rdwb6I.text: Theorem 1 proves a margin-based generalization bound for voting classifiers over finite hypothesis sets that is asymptotically tight in the joint tradeoff between hypothesis-set size |H|, margin θ, empirical margin loss, sample size n, and failure probability δ (Section 1, Theorem 1).

The bound closes a gap left open since Schapire et al.'s original margin bound and Breiman's improvement for the zero empirical-margin-loss case, eliminating the remaining √(ln(n)/ln(e/L_S^θ(f))) factor that persisted through Germain et al.'s interpolating bound (Section 1).
Lemma 6 bounds the Rademacher complexity term used in the proof, with the bound proved via the technique in Section 5 (Section 3.2, Lemma 6).
Lemma 5 establishes a half-margin generalization bound, proved in Section 6 (Section 3.2, Lemma 5).

Lemma 7 bounds the Lipschitz constants of auxiliary functions used to construct the tight bound, building on Rademacher complexity and contraction-inequality techniques adapted from Larsen and Schalburg (Section 5.1, Lemma 7).

USejwpvj0a.text: Section 3.2 defines the Robustly Unlearnable Set (S_U), a subset of training samples that models persistently misclassify regardless of training method; Table 1 quantifies its size across architectures, ranging from about 9,000 samples for MobileNet-V2 down to about 1,500 for WRN-34-10 (Section 3.2, Table 1).

Section 5.3 proposes the Unlearnable-Entropy Criterion, showing in Figure 4(b) that teacher predictive entropy on the unlearnable set correlates strongly with student robustness, whereas Figure 4(a) shows conventional teacher robustness metrics fail to predict student robustness (Section 5.3, Figure 4).

Theorem 4.8 formally establishes a dichotomy in adversarial distillation between 'Good Teachers' that remain uncertain on the unlearnable set and 'Bad Teachers' that are confidently (and incorrectly) supervising on it (Section 4, Theorem 4.8).

Table 2 shows that across five distillation methods, students trained under high-entropy (good) teachers suffer only 0.53% average robust-accuracy degradation versus 7.23% average degradation under low-entropy (confident) teachers on unlearnable samples (Table 2).

Figure 3 demonstrates via synthetic and CIFAR-10 experiments that adversarial distillation under good teachers maintains robust accuracy as the unlearnable-sample fraction increases, unlike distillation under bad teachers (Section 5.1-5.2, Figure 3).

FEmu30g4ts.text: DMPO achieves 43.9% Quality Ratio on text-based NP-Bench versus GRPO's 40.1%, a 9% relative improvement (Table 3).
DMPO achieves 43.1% Quality Ratio on vision-based MM-NP-Bench versus GRPO's 38.4%, a 12% relative improvement (Table 2).

Section 3.3 derives a group-level forward-KL approximation via an MSE loss (Equation 7), which is combined with the standard GRPO objective into the full distribution-matching objective (Equation 9) to counter mode-seeking behavior of reverse-KL-based on-policy RL described in Section 3.1 (Section 3.1, 3.3, Equations 7 and 9).

Section 4.2 defines a dual-metric evaluation protocol combining Success Rate (SR) and Quality Ratio (QR) for MM-NP-Bench, with complete task descriptions and heuristic solvers detailed in Appendix Table 6 (Section 4.2, Table 6).
On out-of-domain transfer tasks, DMPO yields an average 2.3% improvement over GRPO baselines, and a 2.0% improvement on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (Section 5, Table 4).

lv86f7Qr9V.text: Table 1 reports that Context Forcing achieves an effective context length exceeding 20 seconds at 60-second evaluation, versus 3.0 seconds for LongLive and 1.5 seconds for Infinite-RoPE (Table 1).

Section 3.3 introduces the Slow-Fast Memory architecture, combining an Attention Sink, a surprisal-based Slow Memory buffer for high-entropy keyframes, and a rolling FIFO Fast Memory queue, together with a Bounded Positional Encoding (Equation 8) that constrains temporal positions to fixed ranges to prevent distribution shift over long sequences (Section 3.3, Equation 8).
At 60 seconds of generation, the student model maintains a 95.95 background-consistency score, outperforming baselines on both DINOv2 and CLIP consistency metrics (Table 1).

Table 3 ablations show that removing Bounded Positional Encoding causes about a 9-point drop in consistency, and separately evaluate the Slow Memory sampling strategy and the Contextual Distribution Matching Distillation component (Table 3).
Figure 7 shows that Error-Recycling Fine-Tuning improves the robustness of the long-context teacher model used to train the student (Figure 7).

ESa07RwpVr.text: Prior learning-augmented paging algorithms achieve robustness bounds of 2H_k + O(1), leaving a gap to the optimal competitive ratio H_k (Section 1.1).

Section 4 introduces the Relative Prediction Budget (RPB) primitive, which maintains a nonnegative budget gating prediction-driven eviction decisions relative to a robust baseline algorithm (Section 4).

The RPB-OM algorithm, built via Algorithm 3 using OnlineMin priorities, achieves 1-consistency (Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3) and (H_k + O(1))-robustness (Theorem 5.7), matching the optimal competitive ratio up to an additive constant (Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.7).
Theorem 5.1 shows that under perfect predictions, algorithms that evict based on L_0-misses relative to predictions achieve 1-consistency (Theorem 5.1).
Lemma 5.6 bounds the potential-function change for lazy-adversary requests as Δφ ≤ -1/(U(ω)+1), where U(ω) denotes the number of unrevealed layers (Lemma 5.6).

7EK1E8wxVO.text: Including a code corpus in continued pretraining causes an average 14.38% decline across mathematical reasoning benchmarks compared to training without code data (Section 4.1).

Code corpus training degrades harder math benchmarks disproportionately, with Minerva-Math dropping 71.53% and OlympiadBench dropping 47.16%, while simple benchmarks like GSM8K are nearly unaffected (+0.4%) (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

Adding math data reduces code-reasoning performance on CruxEval by up to 17.30% while still improving competitive-programming benchmarks such as CodeForces (+37.11%) and LiveCodeBench (+11.26%) (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
Structured 'cognitive scaffold' math samples improve OlympiadBench by 47.78% and MATH by 23.17% while degrading code performance by only about 1%, unlike raw code corpora (Section 5, Table 1).

Expert-routing analysis shows cognitive scaffolds produce smaller and more diffuse expert-level deviations than pure code data, indicating cross-domain stability rather than specialized routing (Section 6, Figures 5-6).

Sva22o2fRs.text: Under imprinting forgery attacks on the SDP dataset with an SD 2.1 attacker, SemBind variants reduce Tree-Ring's detection rate from 1.00 to 0.01-0.02, and Gaussian Shading's bit accuracy from 0.9998 to 0.48-0.49 (Section 4.3, Table 2).

Across all four base watermarking schemes tested under forgery attacks, SemBind variants reduce detection rate by more than 40% and lower bit accuracy by at least 25% relative to the unprotected baseline (Section 4.3, Tables 2-4).

The mask-ratio parameter σ controls the strength of semantic modulation, trading off anti-forgery strength against robustness, with SemBind-augmented schemes (e.g., Tree-Ring-S, Gaussian Shading-S) retaining 0.988-0.998 average performance under distortions in Tables 5-6, while PRC-S and Gaussian Shading++-S show a larger 3-5% robustness drop (Section 4.4, Tables 5-6).

Theorem 4.1 proves that if a latent-based watermarking scheme is provably undetectable, its SemBind variant remains provably undetectable in the same (single- or multi-sample) setting (Section 3, Theorem 4.1).

An adaptive-attacker analysis using five independently trained surrogate semantic maskers finds a mean pairwise Hamming distance of approximately 512 bits (50% of the 1024-bit code), indicating different random seeds converge to different but equally valid solutions (Appendix D).
SemBind preserves generation quality, keeping FID within 25.20-25.28 versus a baseline Stable Diffusion 2.1 FID of 25.23±0.18 and CLIP score unchanged at 0.3629±0.0006 (Section 4.2, Table 1).

UwPbsFk2Dh.text: HEXST outperforms the prior state-of-the-art PEKA model averaged across seven SpaRED spatial transcriptomics datasets, improving gene-wise correlation (PCCF) from 0.3863 to 0.4227 and spot-wise correlation (PCCS) from 0.7139 to 0.7697 (Section 5.2, Table 1).

HEXST ranks first among compared baselines (including STNet, Hist2ST, EGNv1/v2, TCGN, NH2ST, and PEKA) in 5 of 7 datasets for PCCF, PCCS, and AUC-zero-vs-nonzero, and 6 of 7 datasets for mutual information and AUC-median metrics (Section 5.2, Table 1).

An ablation shows the hexagonal window with HexRoPE positional encoding raises PCCF from 0.3690 (square window with 2D RoPE) to 0.3993 (hexagonal window with 2D RoPE) to 0.4227 (hexagonal window with HexRoPE) (Section 5.3, Table 2).

Removing the transcriptomic feature alignment loss reduces PCCF from 0.4227 to 0.3818, and removing the point-wise/deviation losses reduces it to 0.3541-0.3796, showing each auxiliary loss term contributes to performance (Section 5.3, Table 2).

On the downstream TCGA-PRAD Gleason grading task, using HEXST-predicted gene expression to guide the image model raises accuracy from 45.73% to 48.55% and kappa from 0.6405 to 0.6743 compared to an image-only baseline (Section 5.4, Table 3).

sW8U2TYDMp.text: Agents are formalized as probability distributions with epistemic utility of an outcome o defined as the logarithmic score U(o) = log P(o) (Section 2).

Theorem 10 proves that strict unanimity (every agent strictly benefiting) is impossible under linear pooling for outcome spaces of any size, because linear pooling behaves as a random dictatorship (Section 3.1, Theorem 10).

Theorem 9 shows strict unanimity is achievable under logarithmic pooling once the outcome space has at least three outcomes, contrasting with the impossibility results for two outcomes (Theorem 8) and linear pooling (Theorem 10) (Section 3.1, Theorems 8-10).

Theorem 19 formalizes the 'Waluigi effect,' proving that manifesting a benevolent persona in a language model necessarily strengthens the weight of an antagonistic counterpart component under compositional stability constraints (Section 5, Theorem 19).

Theorem 21 proves that a 'manifest-then-suppress' strategy ('Waluigi shattering') achieves strictly greater suppression of misalignment than directly reinforcing pure benevolence (Section 5.1, Theorem 21).
Theorem 14 shows that a compositional benefit enjoyed by a parent agent does not necessarily propagate to its child subagents under recursive decomposition (Section 4.1, Theorem 14).

rGtym1nlqZ.text: TextResNet outperforms TextGrad on HotpotQA by 21.37 F1 points (46.23 vs 24.86), on PubMedQA by 3.35 points (60.31% vs 56.96%), and on BigCodeBench by 2.15 points (37.86% vs 35.71%) (Table 1).

An ablation on HotpotQA shows performance rising progressively from the TextGrad baseline of 24.86 F1 to 32.15 with additive semantic deltas, 36.69 with semantic gradient decomposition, 37.71 with causal routing, and 46.23 with density-aware scheduling (Table 2).

Causal routing uses semantic STOP_GRADIENT signals to block feedback to components that did not causally contribute to an error, implemented alongside additive semantic deltas and semantic gradient decomposition (Equations 4-6).

In a batch-shuffling robustness test, TextResNet correctly attributes upstream errors to the responsible node in 96% of cases at the final node, demonstrating stability where baseline optimizers collapse (Figure 5).

TextResNet's optimization pipeline decomposition is evaluated with system depths ranging from 3 components (STARK-PRIME) to 5 components (HotpotQA), showing consistent gains across varying compound AI system complexity (Table 1).

loXCDLDwXu.text: ProRL identifies a length shortcut whereby positive-mean step-level rewards create length-dependent bias, causing standard policy gradient training for proactive recommendation to converge toward maximum path length (Section 2.2, Theorem 2.1).
ProRL introduces Stepwise Reward Centering, which subtracts a global expected step reward from each step reward so path extension yields zero expected gain (Section 3.2, Equation 6).

ProRL introduces Position-Specific Advantage Estimation, using step-adapted baselines (average reward-to-go at each position) instead of path-level baselines to reduce gradient variance without a critic network (Section 3.3).

On MovieLens-1M, Steam, and Amazon-Book with a SASRec evaluator, ProRL achieves statistically significant (p<0.05) improvements over baselines on CTR, IoI, and IoR, e.g. IoR of 728.18 on MovieLens-1M and 1383.41 on Amazon-Book (Table 1).

An ablation removing Stepwise Reward Centering (w/o SRC) yields an artificially inflated CTR of 0.9731 on MovieLens-1M but collapses guidance quality, with IoI dropping to 1.2373 versus 2.8504 for full ProRL (Table 3).
Cross-evaluator transfer using GRU4Rec as an unseen evaluator confirms ProRL's gains generalize beyond the SASRec reward model used during training (Table 2).

5DR4NAKO8a.text: FLIPS achieves 96% closed-set accuracy and 90% open-set accuracy identifying instance-level LLM configurations across 237 instances from 25 open-weight LLMs using only 8 verification queries (Section on Performance Results / Nt=8 setting).

FLIPS distinguishes instances differing only in temperature (0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0), system prompt persona, quantization (int4, fp8), or abliteration status, using a two-stage extraction-then-verification protocol with black-box query access only (Benchmark section).

FLIPS applies the NIST cryptographic randomness test suite (15 statistical tests, Table 2) to token-pair random-sequence generations and trains an XGBoost classifier with soft voting across token pairs to fingerprint instances (Methodology, Table 2).

The adapted LLMmap baseline achieves only 35% closed-set accuracy on instance-level fingerprinting, and Figure 1 shows LLMmap fails to distinguish abliterated model variants while FLIPS succeeds (Figure 1, Baseline Comparison).

Only about 25% of token pairs achieve near-equal generation probability (the beta-rate metric), and the run test (transition frequency) provides the strongest discriminative signal per the feature importance ranking (Figure 10).

With a single verification query (Nt=1), FLIPS accuracy drops to 64%, showing query efficiency directly trades off against identification accuracy (Table showing accuracy vs. verification queries, Figure 5).

FbRUcbzRUE.text: SymTrack sets state-of-the-art results on three curated Scene Text Tracking benchmarks, achieving 77.74% AUC on ArTVideoSOT, 70.66% AUC on DSTextSOT, and 77.06% AUC on BOVTextSOT (Table 1).
SymTrack outperforms the previous best tracker by 11.97% AUC on BOVTextSOT and by 5.65% AUC over DUTrack384 on ArTVideoSOT (Table 1).
End-to-end video text spotting baselines TransVTSpotter and TransDETR show near-total failure in continuous tracking, trailing SymTrack by up to 68.56% AUC (Table 1).
An ablation on ArTVideoSOT shows Predictive Token Rectification alone contributes +4.96% AUC, Cross-Expert Calibration adds +2.12%, and Adaptive Inference Engine adds a further +1.16% (Table 5).

Removing the frozen text-expert backbone (TokenFD) and relying solely on the visual backbone causes a catastrophic 30.7% AUC drop on ArTVideoSOT, while increasing inference speed from 22.07 fps to 89.02 fps (Table 3, Table 7).
The Adaptive Inference Engine increases Search Region Coverage from 83.27% to 95.25% and average IoU from 69.54% to 71.96% on DSTextSOT (Table 6).

AAWlum38oE.text: The paper shows via a synthetic 2D disc dataset and CIFAR10 tangent visualizations that consistency model gradients contain substantial manifold-parallel (oscillatory) components rather than pointing orthogonally toward the data manifold (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4).

Manifold Feature Distance (MFD) uses a VGG16-parametrized feature map trained with 15 data transformations (3 degradations, 4 geometric, 4 color) to construct a Jacobian-based loss whose gradient aligns consistency model tangents toward the data manifold (Section 5).
Adding AYT to ECT improves CIFAR10 1-step FID from 3.60 to 2.61 and 2-step FID from 2.11 to 2.13, and improves ECT-S on ImageNet 64x64 1-step FID from 5.51 to 4.42 (Table 1).
ECT+AYT on CIFAR10 outperforms iCT (1-step-related FID 2.83) and is competitive with CTM (1.87) and SiD (1.92) despite using much smaller batch sizes (Table 1).

AYT is trained on ImageNet 64x64 with batch size 128, compared to iCT's batch size of 1024, and remains competitive with small batch sizes down to 16 in ablations (Section on Datasets & Configurations, Figure 5).

Ablations show geometric transformations contribute the largest FID improvement among the 15 transformation types, and AYT outperforms an LPIPS-based feature distance loss in both 1-step and 2-step settings (Figure 5).

2A9FaOnzby.text: Prototype-Grounded Concept Models (PGCMs) ground concept predictions in a fixed number of learned visual prototypes (m=30 for ColorMNIST+, m=120 for CelebA, m=100 for CLEVR-Hans) via a prototype selector, enabling inspection through concept alignment tables (Architecture & Components section).

On ColorMNIST+, PGCM matches CBM performance with concept accuracy 99.2±0.0 vs 99.2±0.1 and task accuracy 99.7±0.0 vs 99.6±0.1, while on CelebA CBM's task accuracy (84.0±0.3) modestly exceeds PGCM's (83.0±0.0) (Table 4).
PGCM training uses an ELBO-style objective (Equation 2) combining a KL regularization term over prototype selection, task loss, concept loss, and image reconstruction loss (Equation 2).
On ColorMNIST+ with noisy labels, targeted prototype-level interventions improve accuracy from 92.9% to 96.9% by removing prototypes and from 92.8% to 97.8% by editing prototypes (Table 3).

A prototype-swapping procedure applied halfway through training replaces learned prototype embeddings with their nearest training instances to improve interpretability (Interpretability Optimizations section).

PGCM shows improved responsiveness to concept interventions compared to CBM, CRM, and CMR baselines, particularly when exploiting inter-concept dependencies in the PGCM* variant on ColorMNIST+ (Figure 4).

7UR3rNXMz9.text: UniMedVL is trained on UniMed-5M, a dataset of over 5.6M instances spanning 8 medical imaging modalities reformatted into multimodal understanding-generation pairs (abstract only).
UniMedVL achieves competitive performance on five medical image understanding benchmarks while matching specialized generative models on image generation quality (abstract only).
UniMedVL natively supports diverse interleaved generation tasks including virtual staining, super-resolution, and cross-modal synthesis within a single unified architecture (abstract only).
The unified architecture is designed to enable bidirectional knowledge sharing between understanding and generation tasks, motivated by an Observation-Knowledge-Analysis framework (abstract only).

Jpxfof0EaS.text: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) trains a single LLM as both teacher and student by conditioning the teacher on privileged ground-truth solutions while the student sees only the problem, minimizing per-token divergence between the two conditioned distributions (Equation 1).
OPSD is 4-8x more token-efficient than GRPO, using a single ~2,048-token rollout per student sample compared to GRPO's 8 rollouts at ~16,384 tokens each (Figure 3).
On Qwen3-8B, OPSD reaches a 52.2% average across AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, and AMO-Bench, versus 51.3% for GRPO, with the gap widening as model scale increases (Table 2).

OPSD shows only marginal or no improvement over GRPO at the 1.7B scale (30.4% vs 30.5% average) but progressively larger gains at 4B (50.6% vs 49.6%) and 8B, indicating a model-capacity dependence for effective self-rationalization (Section 4.3.1, Table 2).
A full-vocabulary distillation objective outperforms a sampled-token variant of the divergence loss, e.g. 84.1% vs 82.1% on AIME25 (Section 3.2, Table 3).
Generation budgets of 2,048 and 4,096 tokens substantially outperform a 1,024-token budget, showing OPSD's performance is sensitive to the allotted generation length (Figure 4).

iMrOO18AoP.text: SCGFM models graphs as metric measure spaces and learns geometric bases B_k in [0,1]^(M x M) that define a shared structural coordinate system, aligning input graphs to these bases via Sliced Gromov-Wasserstein distance (Section 3, Eq. 7).

In 5-shot graph classification across COX2, NCI1, BZR, COLLAB, IMDB-BINARY, COLORS-3, and PROTEINS, SCGFM attains a 51.70% mean in-domain accuracy and reaches 26.31-26.97% on the cross-domain COLORS-3 transfer task versus near-chance (<=15%) for baseline GFMs (Table 1).

In 5-shot node classification across Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, Photo, Computers, and Reddit, SCGFM achieves a 65.90% average accuracy and maintains approximately 84.17% on Reddit regardless of pre-training source domain (Table 2, Figure 3).

An ablation removing the structure-aware projected-feature component drops Cora accuracy from 70.54% to 29.49%, while the same ablation on PROTEINS yields a negligible change (68.70% to 68.86%), showing dataset-dependent reliance on topology versus features (Figure 5).

SCGFM is the only method able to complete extreme scalability stress tests, processing graphs of 5x10^6 nodes with about 12GB peak memory while competing baselines encounter out-of-memory errors (Figure 6).
Performance saturates around K=12 geometric bases and M in [8,16] base nodes, with larger bases (M=32) adding unnecessary complexity without accuracy gains (Figure 7).

l94JabCBGL.text: The feasible set of value functions in POMDPs is proven to be a semi-algebraic set defined by explicit polynomial equalities and inequalities, in contrast to the polyhedral (piecewise-linear) feasible set of fully observable MDPs (Theorem 4.4).
Theorem 3.9 first characterizes feasible POMDP value functions via infinitely many piecewise-linear inequalities derived from the Bellman equation parameters.
Theorem 4.2 reduces the infinite characterization to a finite description using a zonotope containment condition on deviation matrices and midpoint residuals.
Theorem 4.4 gives an explicit quantifier-free semi-algebraic description of the feasible value-function set, stratified by matrix rank via determinantal polynomial conditions on submatrices.
Partial observability is shown to induce nonlinear coupling constraints between decision variables absent in MDPs, making optimal policies dependent on the initial state distribution (Section 4).

Z9cuAhhIbU.text: Top-K Sparse Autoencoders are trained on the residual stream of Dream-7B and LLaDA-8B diffusion language models at two shallow, two middle, and two deep layers (Section 3.1).

Inserting SAEs into early layers of diffusion language models can reduce masked-token cross-entropy loss, an effect the paper reports as absent or much weaker in autoregressive LLMs (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

SAE features enable diffusion-time interventions that achieve substantially higher overall steering scores than LLM baselines, typically 2-10x higher in deep layers, attributed to repeated intervention opportunities across denoising steps (Table 2, Section 4.1).
Two SAE training variants are proposed to handle diffusion-specific masking: Mask-SAE trained on masked-position activations and Unmask-SAE trained on unmasked-position activations (Section 2.2).
Per-step steering interventions are applied repeatedly across denoising steps via a position-selector mechanism that targets either all tokens or only currently masked positions (Equation 13).

5u3Ra6Qf5C.text: On LongBench, PBS-Attn scores 37.37 average for Llama-3.1-8B versus 38.28 for Full Attention, and 36.37 versus 37.01 for Qwen-2.5-7B-1M (Table 1).
On LongBenchv2, PBS-Attn scores 29.82 versus Full Attention's 28.83 for Llama-3.1-8B, and 34.39 versus 35.19 for Qwen-2.5-7B-1M (Table 2).
PBS-Attn is compared against Full Attention, Minference, FlexPrefill, XAttention, and MeanPooling block-sparse baselines (Section 4.1).

PBS-Attn achieves up to 2.75x end-to-end prefilling speedup at 256K context length using a custom permuted-FlashAttention Triton kernel with block size B=128 and segment size S=256 (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
The method applies intra-segment token permutation while preserving inter-segment causality to increase block-level sparsity without altering the attention pattern's causal structure (Section 3.2).
Permutation overhead is shown to be negligible relative to overall speedup even at longer context lengths (Appendix C).

C0762WekyA.text: CUPID's HEART-UCB algorithm combines a belief-weighted expected utility term, an exploration bonus, a language-driven bias term, and a resource penalty into a single LLM-selection score (Section 3.2.6).
On a model zoo of 25 LLMs with 34 annotated objectives, CUPID achieves 100% convergence across four multi-objective setups A1-A4 (Table 1, Section 4.1).
On 17 diverse-provider models, CUPID reaches 100% convergence at a cost of $0.031±0.005 and 3.2 convergence rounds (Table 2).
Under noisy feedback robustness testing on 37 LLMs evaluated with MMLU-Pro and AIME 2025, CUPID reduces cost by 14.2% versus LMArena while improving scores by 34.7% (Section 4.2).
Algorithmic overhead of CUPID remains under 0.72 seconds even when scaled to M=125 candidate models, with wall-clock time dominated by LLM API latency rather than computation (Table 3).

A human study with 51 participants across four abstractness levels (H1-H4) on text and image generation tasks shows CUPID matches or exceeds baseline quality ratings while reducing cost (Section 4.4).

BNCNSgLPy5.text: On Qwen3-8B long-form generation, Binary RAR reduces the hallucination rate from a base of 61.9% to 37.5%, a 39.3% relative reduction (Section 5.1).
On short-form QA with Qwen3-8B, Binary RAR reduces incorrect-answer rate from a base of 60.6% by 44.4% on PopQA and 21.7% on GPQA (Section 5.1).
Binary RAR outperforms DPO (53.4% long-form hallucination rate) and VeriScore RL (40.6%) as baselines on the same long-form hallucination metric (Section 5.1).
On AlpacaEval, Binary RAR's win rate drops only from 54.7 to 53.9 (-1.4%), compared to a -22.8% degradation for VeriScore RL, indicating better preservation of general capability (Section 5.2).

The binary reward pipeline scores model outputs 0 or 1 based on whether the entire output is factually correct against retrieved documents, rather than using continuous or preference-based reward signals (Section 3.2).
An emergent abstention behavior, where the model learns to decline answering rather than hallucinate, is analyzed as a side effect of Binary RAR training (Section 6.2).

rSEdPcvrme.text: Frictional Q-Learning uses a contrastive variational autoencoder (cVAE) to generate candidate actions aligned with replay-buffer-supported actions while separating salient features from irrelevant variation (Section on Architecture Components).

Theorems 1-4 establish convergence guarantees for BCQ-style constraints under coherent replay buffers in deterministic MDPs, while Theorem 5 addresses error convergence when orthogonal actions diverge from true dynamics (Theorem 1-4, Theorem 5).
Lemma 2 shows that orthonormal vectors of rank k>=2 always exist in continuous action spaces, underpinning the method's use of orthogonal 'anti-support' directions (Lemma 2).
On Humanoid-v4, FQL achieves a return of 6,713.75 +/- 103.89, outperforming SAC (6,463.46) and TD3 (6,524.20) with narrower standard deviation (Table 3).
An ablation over the friction coefficient beta shows task-dependent optimal values, with HalfCheetah-v4 exhibiting instability at suboptimal beta settings (Figure 3).
A comparison of incorporating orthogonal actions via the critic versus via data augmentation shows the critic-based approach outperforms augmentation across most MuJoCo environments (Figure 4).

HTlNhKxcrc.text: WEATHER-5K comprises 5,672 global weather stations with 10 years of hourly observations (2014-2023), totaling 87,648 time steps across 5 meteorological variables (temperature, dew point, wind speed, wind direction, sea level pressure) (Section 3).
The dataset is split into training (2014-2021), validation (2022), and testing (2023) in roughly an 8:1:1 ratio (Section 3).
At a 120-hour lead time, Pyraformer achieves the best overall MAE/MSE of 17.4/1,739.0 among 9 baseline TSF models, compared to 18.4/1,925.6 for the worst performer, DLinear (Table 2).

At the 99.5th percentile extreme-event threshold, even the best model (iTransformer) achieves only a 14.1% SEDI score for temperature extremes, indicating poor extreme-event detection by TSF models (Table 3).
PhysicsFormer combines a dynamic core with a Transformer residual, enforcing physical consistency via pressure-wind alignment and energy-aware smoothness losses (Section 4).
Current time-series forecasting models still lag behind operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems, particularly at longer lead times (Section 5).

EnZFaqg7hx.text: A simple neural decoder trained on 10^7 samples matches or outperforms more architecturally complex decoders, showing decoding accuracy gains are driven disproportionately by dataset scale rather than architectural complexity (Section 4).

Post-training quantization (PTQ) alone causes catastrophic degradation—the 3D-CNN decoder degrades at W8A8 and all evaluated architectures collapse at W4A4—while quantization-aware training (QAT) recovers below-MWPM logical error rates even at INT4 precision (Section 5).

Only the TCN architecture meets microsecond-scale latency constraints at code distance d=9, requiring an estimated ~0.77 microseconds per inference (about 314 clock cycles at 300 MHz) on a Xilinx VP1902 FPGA (Table 2).

3D-CNN parameter count grows 223x from d=3 to d=9 (146K to 32.5M parameters), whereas TCN and Transformer decoders maintain roughly constant parameter counts (~103K-220K) across all tested code distances (Section 4).

On real Google Sycamore hardware data, the zero-shot TCN decoder achieves logical error rates of 34.42% (d=3) and 47.89% (d=5) versus MWPM baselines of 8.01% and 14.38%, but after fine-tuning drops to 9.27% (d=3) and 20.06% (d=5) (Table 1).
TCN and 3D-CNN decoders sustain fault-tolerant performance (below the MWPM baseline logical error rate) even after 60-70% weight sparsity/pruning of quantized INT4 weights (Figure 4b).

xO10rIopwe.text: Baguan-TS uses a 3D Transformer with 22.4 million parameters that jointly attends over temporal, variable, and context axes for gradient-free in-context forecasting adaptation (Section on architecture).

On the FEV-Bench-Cov benchmark of 30 covariate-aware tasks, Baguan-TS reduces SQL by 4.8% (0.7997 vs 0.8404) and MASE by 5.5% (0.9857 vs 1.0430) relative to TabPFN-TS, the only other covariate-supporting baseline (benchmark results table).

Baguan-TS achieves the highest average win rate across point and probabilistic forecasting metrics compared to baselines including Chronos-Bolt, Moirai-2.0, Sundial-Base, TimesFM-2.5, TiRex, and Toto-1.0 (benchmark comparison section).

On 27 real-world energy tasks (electricity load and photovoltaic data), Baguan-TS attains the best results across all four evaluation metrics (SQL, MASE, WAPE, WQL) (real-world energy dataset results).
An ablation on the entsoe_1H dataset shows the Y-space retrieval-based forecasting component improves SQL from 0.4284 to 0.3859, roughly a 10% reduction (ablation study section).

2FU8PSmu9Z.text: On C-MNIST with background spurious correlations at IPC=50, vanilla dataset distillation (DM) yields an equalized odds difference (EOD) of 100.0 with only 48.8% accuracy, while COBRA reduces EOD to 7.46 and raises accuracy to 96.8% (results table).
On CIFAR10-S at IPC=100, vanilla DM produces an EOD of 82.87 with 45.4% accuracy, whereas COBRA reduces EOD to 9.37 and increases accuracy to 62.4% (results table).

Theorem 4.1 proves that under the paper's stated conditions, distilling toward the cross-group barycenter (COBRA) reduces the worst-case subgroup-specific residual error compared to vanilla class-conditional distillation (Theorem 4.1).

COBRA's barycentric target is computed as the point minimizing total distance to all subgroup-specific representation statistics with equal weighting, replacing the majority-dominated weighted average used in standard distillation (Section 3, method formulation).

COBRA's fairness improvements generalize across multiple distillation methods (gradient matching, distribution matching, feature alignment, and the trajectory-based MTT), across ConvNet, VGG11, and ResNet18 architectures, and across different images-per-class (IPC) budgets (generalization/robustness section).

SpQABsjB9Y.text: Prism achieves up to 5.1x speedup over full attention on PG19 at 128K context length while maintaining near-zero perplexity degradation (ΔPPL ≈ 0) (Section on empirical results, PG19 benchmark).

The paper proves that mean pooling for block-importance scoring under Rotary Positional Embeddings acts as a low-pass filter, with spectral attenuation factor λⱼ(B) = |sinc(Bθⱼ/2π)|, producing a Dead Zone at low frequency indices (0 ≤ 2j ≲ 30) where signal collapses due to destructive interference (Theorem/spectral analysis section).

Figure 3 empirically shows that after mean pooling, energy in the identified Dead Zone frequency band collapses to near-zero, while the Semantic Zone (2j > 60) retains full signal magnitude (Figure 3).

On RULER at 128K tokens Prism attains 72.75 accuracy, and on LongBench (Llama backbone) an average score of 41.08, while on VideoMME (long videos) it scores 64.00 versus 63.11 for full attention (results tables).

Unlike baselines such as MInference and FlexPrefill, which only outperform full attention at 32K+ tokens, Prism achieves consistent speedups across all tested sequence lengths (Section on efficiency comparison).

KduPuqy11U.text: RA-Det achieves 93.47% average accuracy and 97.00% average precision (AP) across 14 generative models, exceeding the strongest baseline FerretNet (85.66% ACC / 90.43% AP) by roughly 7.81 percentage points of average performance (results table).
Under Gaussian blur (σ=1.5) post-processing, RA-Det maintains 78.73% accuracy while artifact-driven baselines NPR and FerretNet degrade to 50-53% accuracy (robustness-under-post-processing table).

RA-Det with a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone achieves 91.85% ACC / 95.00% AP, confirming the robustness-asymmetry approach transfers across different backbone encoders in place of the primary DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone (backbone ablation section).

An ablation shows removing the Discrepancy Branch causes the largest accuracy drop to 85.73%, while removing the Low-Level Residual Branch and Semantic Branch cause drops of 4.85% and 3.13% respectively, and removing the robustness-aware loss causes a 2.61% drop (ablation study table).

RA-Det outperforms RIGID, a prior hand-crafted-threshold robustness-based detector, by 16.3 percentage points (93.47% vs 77.17% accuracy), demonstrating the benefit of learning a decision function on robustness-asymmetry features rather than using fixed thresholds (comparison to RIGID).

1sH1AEeylU.text: VILA (Vision-Language Incremental Learning) is a dual-branch framework built on CLIP-style vision-language models, using a two-level calibration mechanism to align visual and textual representations during class-incremental learning (Section 3).

VILA is evaluated across 8 benchmark datasets including CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, Caltech-101, Food-101, Flower, Cars, UCF101, and SUN397, with accuracy comparisons reported in Tables 2, 4, 6, and 10 (Tables 2, 4, 6, 10).

VILA consistently outperforms baseline analytic and replay-based class-incremental learning methods, with the largest gains reported in fine-grained (e.g., Cars, Flower) and long-sequence benchmark settings (Tables 4, 6).

An ablation study isolates the contribution of each of the two calibration levels to overall accuracy, validating that both levels of vision-language calibration are necessary for the reported gains (Section 5.4).

VILA preserves the closed-form, single-pass analytic learning update while mitigating the accumulated error and feature incompatibility issues that arise when analytic learning is combined with pretrained vision-language backbones (Section 3).

9W17xHFtdQ.text: Double-Softmax Prompt Tuning (DSPT) is a hyperparameter-free CLIP prompt-tuning loss that applies a second softmax to the class probabilities before computing cross-entropy, i.e. L = -1/n * sum(log(softmax(softmax(z_i))_y)) (Section 3).

Proposition 3.1 proves that the double-softmax loss restricts the absolute gradient magnitude across all logit terms to at most 1, bounding the influence of any single (potentially mislabeled) training example (Proposition 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 shows that when a model's prediction strongly contradicts a given (noisy) label, the total gradient magnitude for that sample converges to zero, so DSPT self-adaptively suppresses gradient updates from high-error noisy samples without any hand-set threshold (Theorem 3.2).

On Caltech101 with 80% symmetric label noise, DSPT reaches 95.31% accuracy versus 80.00% for CoOp, and on OxfordPets with 80% symmetric noise DSPT reaches 91.25% versus 60.43% for CoOp (experiments, noisy-benchmark tables).

DSPT is evaluated on 9 datasets (including Caltech101, StanfordCars, and OxfordPets) under both symmetric and asymmetric label noise, outperforming NLPrompt by roughly 0.4-5% on average while avoiding the threshold-tuning sensitivity that causes LogitClip's accuracy to vary by more than 15% (experiments section, noisy-benchmark tables).

51WmDaMOtd.text: CORE (Conflict-Oriented Reasoning) fine-tunes multimodal LLMs to detect fake news by identifying semantic or physical conflicts across modalities or against world knowledge, rather than learning manipulation-type-specific artifacts (Section on method/CORE framework).

CORE's training pipeline consists of Modality Bridging Pre-Training (MBPT) on 50k samples from FineHARD, followed by Conflict Perception Training (CPT) on the newly constructed 14k-sample Conflict Attribution Corpus (CAC), which annotates conflict factors and conflict sources (Section on CAC/training pipeline).

In few-shot experiments on DGM4, CORE reaches 59.7% accuracy with only 100 training samples (vs. 51.6% for the baseline) and 65.4% with 750 samples (vs. 56.9% for the baseline) (few-shot experiments table).
CORE achieves 97.14% accuracy on SAMM, 88.49% on MDSM, and 83.45% on NewsCLIPpings in large-scale evaluation (results table).
In zero-shot cross-manipulation-type evaluation, CORE surpasses the second-best method by 12-14% on unseen manipulation categories not seen during training (zero-shot cross-manipulation experiments).

6eI4YHFyON.text: Empirically, gradient descent training shows a sharp phase transition at a data- and model-dependent critical learning rate eta_c: below eta_c the L1-norm and sharpness of the trained model stay stable (flow-aligned regime), while above eta_c sharpness decreases and norm increases as training enters the Edge-of-Stability regime (Section on empirical phase transition).

Theorem 3.3 proves that gradient descent with step size eta cannot converge to a solution whose sharpness exceeds 2/eta, establishing the stability constraint that governs behavior in the Edge-of-Stability regime (Theorem 3.3).

For a diagonal linear network trained on a single-point regression task, Proposition 3.4 shows the L1-norm-minimizing solution and the sharpness-minimizing solution on the solution manifold have different support structures (favoring maximum vs. minimum input coordinates respectively), so neither implicit bias alone characterizes the trained model (Proposition 3.4).

The best test error occurs at intermediate learning rates where the norm and sharpness biases are balanced, rather than at the extremes that minimize either bias alone, indicating the learning rate itself acts as a regularization hyperparameter (empirical results, generalization trade-off).

The norm-versus-sharpness trade-off is demonstrated to hold consistently across multiple architectures (fully connected networks, CNNs, Vision Transformers), datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10), activation functions (ReLU, tanh), and loss functions (MSE, cross-entropy) (experimental scope).

mf8N8PTUAa.text: LiMuon combines momentum-based variance reduction (in the style of STORM) with randomized SVD to produce a low-rank approximation of the momentum matrix, reducing memory from O(mn) to O((m+n)r_hat + r_hat^2) for an m x n weight matrix (Section on algorithm/Option #2).

Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 establish LiMuon's convergence guarantees under standard Lipschitz-smoothness and generalized-smoothness conditions respectively for the standard-momentum variant (Option #1) (Theorems 1-2).

Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 extend these convergence guarantees to the low-rank randomized-SVD variant (Option #2) under Lipschitz and generalized smoothness respectively, showing LiMuon achieves an O(epsilon^-3) sample complexity for finding an epsilon-stationary point in non-convex stochastic optimization (Theorems 3-4).

LiMuon is empirically compared against AdamW, Lion, SUMO, Muon, and Muon++ using a batch size of 64 across experiments including DistilGPT2 (82M parameters) on WikiText-103 and ViT (22M parameters) on Tiny-ImageNet (Section 4, experimental tables).

Beyond the DistilGPT2/ViT comparisons, LiMuon is also evaluated on training Mamba-130M and Qwen2.5-0.5B language models, demonstrating its effectiveness on larger-scale architectures (Section 4/5 experimental tables).

Cc5oIi4EeL.text: GiFlow constructs a graph-informed prior via adaptive spatiotemporal filtering of observed signals instead of a problem-agnostic Gaussian prior, and Theorem 3.2 proves the resulting transport cost is no larger than that of flow matching with a Gaussian prior (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.2).
On the Air-36 dataset with 20% point missing data, GiFlow attains MAE 9.54 / RMSE 18.10 / MAPE 21.27%, improving over the GRIN baseline's MAE 9.94 / RMSE 19.09 / MAPE 21.95% (Table 2).
On Air-36 with 20% block missing data, GiFlow achieves MAE 14.76, RMSE 25.33, and MAPE 28.95% (Table 3).

The ablation on prior design shows GiFlow's transport cost of 104.29 versus 299.62 for an FM-Gauss variant, with corresponding MAE of 9.54 versus 12.79, empirically validating the transport-cost reduction proved in Theorem 3.2 (Table 4).

GiFlow performs few-step deterministic generation at inference, requiring only 0.28 minutes on Air-36 versus 9.30 minutes for the diffusion-based PriSTI baseline and 0.37 minutes for the consistency-based CoSTI baseline (Table 7).

Removing the spatiotemporal propagation component from the vector field architecture causes the largest performance drop among ablated components, increasing MAE from 9.54 to 10.40 on Air-36 (Table 5).

EB8MHApOav.text: On LLaMA-3.1-8B with an average bit-width of 3.75, AutoQRA reaches 69.83% average accuracy at 13.08 GB memory, versus QLoRA's 67.45% accuracy at 4.00 bits and 15.22 GB, and versus FP16 LoRA's 69.94% accuracy at 20.50 GB (Table 1).
On Qwen-2.5-7B, AutoQRA at an average 3.71-bit configuration reaches 71.35% accuracy and 11.95 GB memory, exceeding QLoRA's 69.01% accuracy at 4.00 bits and 15.60 GB (Table 1).
AutoQRA's Phase I multi-fidelity evolutionary search uses importance-guided mutations and surrogate screening, which raises the top-3 promotion hit rate from 44.7% to 67.3% (Section 3.2).
AutoQRA's Phase II applies trust-region Bayesian optimization with Expected Improvement acquisition to refine discrete neighborhoods around promising configurations from Phase I (Section 3.3).

Figure 3 shows a consistent negative association between per-layer bit-width q_l and LoRA rank r_l, indicating AutoQRA automatically reallocates adapter capacity to more aggressively quantized layers to compensate for quantization noise (Figure 3).

AutoQRA's joint search requires only 6 high-fidelity fine-tuning evaluations to match the configuration quality that random search needs 107 evaluations to reach, an 18x reduction in expensive evaluations (Figure 5).

3WTFzAFHr3.text: On RealSR, RSD achieves single-step restoration with LPIPS 0.273, CLIPIQA 0.7060, and MUSIQ 65.860, versus SinSR's LPIPS 0.365, CLIPIQA 0.6887, and MUSIQ 61.582, while PSNR is comparable (25.91 vs 25.83) (Table 1).
On the synthetic ImageNet-Test set, RSD attains LPIPS 0.193 and CLIPIQA 0.681 versus SinSR's LPIPS 0.221 and CLIPIQA 0.611, though PSNR is slightly lower (24.31 vs 24.56) (Table 2).

RSD uses 174M parameters and 539MB GPU memory with 0.059s inference time, comparable to SinSR (174M params, 570MB, 0.060s) but far below OSEDiff (1775M params, 3651MB, 0.075s) and SUPIR (4801M params, 52535MB, 17.704s) (Table 4).

The distillation objective trains an auxiliary fake ResShift model so that the intractable teacher-matching gradient becomes computable, combining a distillation loss, an LPIPS loss, and a GAN loss (Proposition 3.1, Section 3.4).
An ablation over the number of training timesteps N shows N=4 gives the best balance of perceptual quality and distortion in the perception-distortion tradeoff (Table 5).
On RealSet65, RSD reaches MUSIQ 69.172, substantially above SinSR's 62.169 (Table 1).

3ebavardTL.text: LocalV achieves a 45.0% functional pass rate on the RealBench IP-level Verilog generation benchmark using a Claude backbone, versus the MAGE baseline's 21.6%, a 23.4 percentage-point absolute improvement (Table 3).
With a DeepSeek-V3 backbone, LocalV reaches a 35.0% functional pass rate on RealBench (Table 3).
On the CVDP cid003 benchmark, LocalV achieves a 61.50% pass rate, outperforming baselines by 12.78 percentage points (Section 4, CVDP cid003 results).

The multi-agent framework's five stages (preprocessing/indexing, planning, generation, merging, debugging) rely on information locality, quantified via normalized entropy H̄_norm, where hardware IP modules like e203_cpu_top show higher locality (H̄_norm = 0.6718) than software tasks like Parse Lisp (H̄_norm = 0.8220) (Section 3.3).
Ablation on RealBench shows removing the hierarchical document indexing component drops functional pass rate from 45.0% to 35.0%, and removing the debugging component drops it to 20.0% (Table 4).

Localized information retrieval reduces required context tokens by 70.8% for the RTL generation agent, 54.8% for the merger agent, and 61.6% for the debugger agent (Section 4, context reduction results).

ABhGgV7pov.text: ChemCensor scores reaction plausibility on an integer scale of 1 to 5 by decomposing a reaction into a reaction center and functional groups, matching the reaction center against a precomputed pattern library, and verifying functional-group compatibility against aggregated synthetic precedents mined from the USPTO-full dataset (Section 3.1, Figure 2).
The knowledge base underlying ChemCensor's functional-group compatibility checks comprises approximately 515 distinct functional group patterns derived from USPTO-full (Section 3.1, Appendix D).

The CREED dataset contains 6,382,667 unique reactions across 653,567 unique products, averaging 9.77 reactions per product, with all reactions retained requiring a ChemCensor score greater than 0 and decontaminated against USPTO-50K-test (Section 3.4, Table 2).
CREED is split into 5,107,681 training reactions (522,865 products), 635,977 validation reactions (65,285 products), and 638,184 test reactions (65,350 products) (Appendix G, Table 3).

On the newly introduced URSA-expert-2026 benchmark of 100 expert-validated synthesis targets, C3LM with reasoning achieves the best average PT-Top-10 CC score of 0.68, compared to 0.32 for Claude 4.5 Sonnet and 0.21 for the chemical-specialist baseline RetroDFM-R (Table 1, Section 3.2).

On the revised USPTO-50K-test (5,004 pairs minus 28 corrupted entries), C3LM with reasoning attains an average PT-Top-10 CC of 0.86, versus 0.58 for NatureLM and 0.14 for DeepSeek 3.2 (Table 1, Appendix J).

6kyKD3bVi6.text: The f-DMU framework generalizes MSE-based diffusion unlearning objectives by replacing the mean squared error term with a general f-divergence between distributions conditioned on the target and anchor concepts (Section 3).

Theorem 4.1 characterizes the Jacobian of the f-divergence unlearning update, showing the gradient magnitude ordering |∂H²/∂φ| ≤ |∂KL/∂φ| ≤ |∂χ²/∂φ| among squared Hellinger, KL, and Pearson χ² divergences (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 proves local exponential stability of the unlearning dynamics under Assumptions B.6-B.8, with convergence speed governed by f''(1), and squared Hellinger divergence yields faster convergence near equilibrium than KL/MSE-based updates (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).

Using squared Hellinger divergence for erasing the R2D2 concept from Stable Diffusion v1.4 achieves CLIP Accuracy (CA) of 0.20 and CLIP Score (CS) of 0.53 while better preserving generation quality than the MSE baseline (Table 3).

Collateral damage on unrelated concepts (Grumpy Cat, Van Gogh style) after R2D2 erasure is measured via Kernel Inception Distance shifts of -0.010 and -0.008 respectively, indicating limited unintended forgetting (Table 3).

Xfka1kNiuc.text: ReCo enforces regional constraints in in-context video editing via latent regularization, which increases latent discrepancy between source and target videos in the editing region while decreasing it elsewhere, and attention regularization, which suppresses attention from editing-region tokens to corresponding source-video tokens (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).
ReCo is built on the Wan-T2V-1.3B video diffusion transformer backbone, with source and target videos width-wise concatenated for joint denoising during in-context generation (Section 3.2).

ReCo-Data comprises 500K instruction-video pairs across four editing tasks, using 81-frame clips at 480x832 resolution and 5-second duration, with 91.6% of samples rated high-quality versus 17.9-29.2% for prior datasets (Section 4, Table not specified but dataset section).
On the VLLM-based benchmark of 480 test pairs (120 per task), ReCo scores 8.23 overall on the Add task versus 7.56 for Ditto, and 8.74 on the Replace task versus 6.72 for Lucy-Edit (Table 1).

An ablation removing the latent constraint causes a dramatic drop in editing accuracy, while removing the attention constraint reduces video naturalness scores and produces unnatural object scales (Table 2).

rUZVcnQjYW.text: Theorem 4.5 shows that randomly initialized transformers almost surely compute Boolean functions containing at least N^((D-1)/(2L)-5) zero-sensitivity input strings for all sufficiently large sequence length N, where D and L relate to model depth/width parameters (Section 4, Theorem 4.5).

Corollary 4.6 establishes that any Boolean function whose count of sensitivity-zero strings K0(N) grows slower than N^((D-1)/(2L)-5) is provably unlearnable by transformers under random initialization (Section 4, Corollary 4.6).

Corollary 3.4 proves that for transformers using LayerNorm with epsilon > 0, every non-constant Boolean function becomes unrecognizable for all sufficiently large N due to vanishing sensitivity bounds (Section 3, Corollary 3.4).

Parity, sparse parities, and dictator/First functions are shown to be asymptotically unlearnable (Corollaries 5.1-5.4), while Majority is conjectured to remain learnable because it has exponentially many zero-sensitivity strings (Section 5, Conjecture 5.5).

Figure 1 illustrates that Parity and First functions occupy a measure-zero region of parameter space reachable by random initialization, whereas Majority is conjectured to occupy a positive-measure region (Section 6, Figure 1).

NN4DoPVYT2.text: GC-TTT selects relevant offline sub-trajectories at test time using a relevance filter requiring initial-state distance d(s, s1) < epsilon (Equation 6) followed by an optimality filter that retains only sub-trajectories above the q-th percentile of bootstrapped H-step return estimates (Equation 8) (Section 5.1).

Table 1 reports that GC-TTT improves average success rate for GC-IQL from 0.39 to 0.63, GC-BC reaches 0.81 success on pointmaze-expert versus a 0.05 baseline, and SAW combined with GC-TTT reaches 0.99 success on antmaze-expert (Table 1).

Figure 6 (right) shows that at matched inference-time FLOPs, GC-TTT consistently outperforms scaling network width, indicating test-time fine-tuning yields gains not achievable purely by increasing model size (Figure 6).
Section 6 presents five experimental insights validating the receding-horizon test-time training strategy across GC-BC, GC-IQL, and SAW backbones (Section 5.2, Section 6).

ClBpWdkPZd.text: Proposition 4.1 proves that softmax produces a dense Fisher Information Matrix with off-diagonal terms equal to -p_i*p_j, creating geometric coupling between categorical parameters, while Theorem 4.2 proves the proposed catnat parameterization yields a diagonal Fisher Information Matrix (Section 4, Proposition 4.1, Theorem 4.2).

Corollary 4.3 shows that using the natural activation function nu(x) (defined via a piecewise sine in Equation 12) simplifies the diagonal FIM entries to P(a_i)*(pi/A)^2, independent of the score function, within the active region (Section 4, Corollary 4.3, Equation 12).

On the graph structure learning task, the natural activation function achieves roughly a 3x reduction in error over sigmoid-based parameterization for recovering a latent parameter at theta*=0.5 (Table 2, Section 5.1).
On categorical VAEs trained on MNIST, both catnat variants outperform softmax across category counts K in {8,16,32} and latent dimensions N in {10,20,30} (Table 3, Section 5.2).

In reinforcement learning experiments, catnat improves average return modestly on Breakout (398 to 406) and substantially on Seaquest (1875 to 2164) compared to softmax-based policies (Table 4, Section 5.3).

Iv2xle8uSv.text: The framework constructs generative diffusion models on infinite-dimensional spaces by steering a Gaussian reference process toward a target measure via Doob's h-transform, with existence established under Assumption 3.1 (Section 3).
