Theorem 3.3 establishes a unique measure P^h under which the process X at time T is distributed according to the target measure mu, with X solving an SDE whose steering term is the score function s(t,x) = grad_x log h(t,x) (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).

Proposition 4.1 defines a score-matching loss whose minimization is shown in Corollary 4.4 to be equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence between the approximate and true h-transformed path measures (Section 4, Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.4).

Proposition 5.1 proves existence of mild solutions to the Variance-Preserving SPDE, and Corollary 5.2 shows the h-transformed process satisfies a tractable SDE with an explicit steering term (Section 5, Proposition 5.1, Corollary 5.2).

Proposition 6.1 gives a Wasserstein-2 bound between the data measure and the sampled measure of the form W2(mu_data, mu_sample) <= (eps_Init + eps_Loss^{1/2}) exp(LT) + eps_Num, decomposing error into initialization, score-matching loss, and numerical discretization terms (Section 6, Proposition 6.1).

iZ2Enqf9Kn.text: Alterbute introduces Visual Named Entities (VNEs) - fine-grained visual identity categories such as "Porsche 911 Carrera" - as a middle ground between coarse category-level and overly restrictive instance-level identity definitions, enabling automatic identity-preserving supervision (Section 3).
VNE extraction applied to the OpenImages dataset (~99M images, 16M object bounding boxes) yields 69,744 VNE clusters comprising 1,079,442 labeled images used for training (Section 3).

On a held-out evaluation set of 30 objects with 100 editing samples, Alterbute is preferred over baselines including FlowEdit, InstructPix2Pix, OmniGen, UltraEdit, Diptych, MaterialFusion, and MimicBrush, achieving preference rates of 74.8%-89.3% (e.g., 85.0% vs. MimicBrush by human raters, 94.3% by Gemini judge) (Table 1).
The model is a fine-tuned SDXL backbone (7B parameters) trained for 100,000 steps on 128 v4 TPUs at 512x1024 resolution (Section 3).

An ablation study comparing identity-conditioning strategies (DINOv2 features, instance-retrieval features, in-place editing, and VNE-based conditioning) shows the VNE-based approach substantially outperforms the alternatives at preserving identity during attribute edits (Section 4.3).

b2YHcg9o1e.text: The Domino procedure controls the k-boundary FDR (k-bFDR) - defined as the probability that the k least-significant discoveries in the rejection set are all false - under arbitrary dependence among p-values or e-values, without structural assumptions (Section 2, Definition 2.2; Theorem 3.4).
Theorem 3.4 proves that the rejection set R produced by the Domino algorithm satisfies k-bFDR(R) <= alpha under arbitrary dependence (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).

Proposition 2.3 shows k-bFDR reduces to k-FWER under the global null and is otherwise upper bounded by k-FWER, situating k-bFDR between per-comparison and family-wise error control (Section 2, Proposition 2.3).

Proposition 4.1 establishes equivalence between the Domino procedure and the e-value closure principle when using an appropriate local test, connecting Domino to existing multiple-testing paradigms (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).

Algorithms 3 and 4 reduce the computational complexity of implementing the closure-based procedure from exponential O(2^m) to polynomial O(m^2) for Bonferroni and harmonic-mean-based local tests (Section 3, Algorithms 3-4).

ot1vP0AR0j.text: Proposition 4.3 proves that standard constant-depth Vision Transformers with polynomial-precision weights operate strictly within the circuit complexity class TC^0 (Section 4, Proposition 4.3).
Lemma 4.2 reduces the task of computing spatial embeddings for sequences of transformations to solving the Word Problem for the underlying transformation group (Section 4, Lemma 4.2).

Theorem 4.4 (the Non-Solvable Barrier) shows that, assuming the standard conjecture TC^0 subsetneq NC^1, a constant-depth ViT bounded by TC^0 cannot implement homomorphic spatial embeddings for non-solvable groups such as SO(3) (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).

Corollary 4.5 (Abelian Collapse) shows that when a constant-depth Transformer is tasked with representing a non-solvable group, its learned representations collapse toward approximating the group's abelianization rather than its full non-commutative structure (Section 4, Corollary 4.5).

The theoretical predictions are tested empirically via a Latent Space Algebra benchmark in Section 5, verifying the predicted representational failure on non-solvable spatial reasoning tasks (Section 5).

5EmOOLtH5P.text: ACON reduces peak token usage by 26-54% across long-horizon agentic benchmarks while largely preserving task accuracy, e.g., on AppWorld with GPT-4.1 it cuts peak tokens from 9.93K to 7.33K (26% reduction) while accuracy moves from 56.0% to 56.5% (Table 1).

ACON performs compression in natural language space by optimizing a compression guideline through iterative refinement based on analysis of failure cases, rather than compressing in latent/embedding space (Section 3, Figure 3).

Applying ACON's compression guideline enables smaller models to act as more effective long-horizon agents, with Qwen3-14B improving 32% on AppWorld, 20% on OfficeBench, and 46% on the 8-objective QA benchmark (Table 1, Table 2, Figure 5).
ACON's compressor can be distilled into a smaller, more efficient model while preserving over 95% of the accuracy of the full compression pipeline (Section 4, Figure 4).

Evaluation spans three benchmarks: AppWorld (9 simulated apps, ~100 users, 168 test tasks across Easy/Medium/Hard difficulty), OfficeBench (6 office applications, 92 training/95 test tasks), and an 8-objective QA benchmark built from NaturalQuestions-style research questions (100 training/100 test tasks) (Section 4, Table 1, Table 2).

vayyDtdtWX.text: ViewMask-1-to-3 tokenizes images into discrete visual tokens via MAGVIT-v2 and unifies language and vision through masked token prediction across multiple viewpoints (Section 3.2).

Random masking combined with bidirectional self-attention achieves cross-view consistency without explicit 3D geometric priors, via a three-stage training framework: multimodal alignment, image-to-multi-view, and text-to-multi-view (Section 3.3).

On the GSO benchmark, ViewMask-1-to-3 attains PSNR 20.61, LPIPS 0.150, and Chamfer Distance 0.0149, improving over baselines such as ViVid-1-to-3 (PSNR 19.78) and Zero-1-to-3 XL (LPIPS 0.152, Chamfer 0.0159) (Table 1).
On 3D-FUTURE, ViewMask-1-to-3 improves IoU by 10.6% and achieves SSIM 0.865 and LPIPS 0.129, outperforming Zero123++ (SSIM 0.853) and Zero-1-to-3 XL (LPIPS 0.153) (Table 2).
ViewMask-1-to-3 ranks first on average across standard image quality metrics with a mean rank of 1.3 across GSO and 3D-FUTURE, versus baseline average ranks between 3.2 and 8.5 (Tables 1-2).

q806xA8NPR.text: DiffBCP couples a cumulative shrinkage process (CUSP) prior for automatic CP-rank selection with a pre-trained diffusion model as an implicit data prior, formalized in a joint probabilistic model over the tensor, CP weights, and observed entries (Section 3.1, Equation 3).
Theorem 3.1 shows the CUSP prior shrinks the tail probability of each rank-r component as r increases, with the shrinkage rate controlled by hyperparameter β (Theorem 3.1).

A split Gibbs sampler (Algorithm 1) decouples inference into conjugate Gaussian/Gamma updates for latent variables and a diffusion-model-guided denoising step for an augmented variable Z, using a noise-adaptive coupling schedule τρ² = c (Section 3.2).
Theorem 3.4 bounds the stationary bias introduced by inexact diffusion denoising, characterizing the trade-off between coupling strength ρ and denoising accuracy (Theorem 3.4).

On FFHQ with a Uniform(0.9) missingness mask, DiffBCP achieves 28.28 dB PSNR versus 26.11 dB for the best baseline DeepTensor, a gain of 2.17 dB, and on ImageNet with irregular masks attains 27.02 dB PSNR with average gains of 1.82 dB PSNR and 12.42 SSIM points over the best competing method (Table 1).
On out-of-distribution 2048x2048 high-resolution images, DiffBCP attains 20.94 dB PSNR on the Marseille image under an irregular mask, exceeding PuTT's 19.83 dB (Table 2).

UEeBGrOGa8.text: Continuous translation-equivariant operators are characterized via Volterra series expansions as an infinite sum of multilinear convolution operators, ρ_d[h] = C_0 + sum of higher-order convolution terms C_l[h] (Equation 3).

Set Fourier Convolutions (SFConvs) exploit the closed-form Fourier transform of the functional embedding to operate directly on irregularly sampled points without spatial discretization, achieving approximately global receptive fields with linear complexity O(|Xi|(|D_c|+|D_q|)) versus ConvCNP's grid-dependent cost (Equation 13).

SFVConvCNP integrates the Volterra series formulation with SFConv parameterization to give an interpretable operator decomposition as a sum of higher-order convolutions, distinguishing it from the standard-stacked SFConvCNP model (Section on proposed models).

On synthetic 1D sawtooth regression, SFConvCNP attains log-likelihood 1.19+/-0.01 and SFVConvCNP attains 1.18+/-0.01, both substantially outperforming attention-based baselines that collapse to -0.87 (Table 2).
On CIFAR-10 image completion, SFConvCNP attains log-likelihood 1.74+/-0.00 and CRPS 0.03+/-0.00, marginally exceeding the strongest baseline SConvCNP at 1.71+/-0.00 (Table 4).

On Kolmogorov flow, SFConvCNP achieves log-likelihood 1.89+/-0.01, surpassing ConvCNP's 1.73, and on ERA5 climate data it reaches 1.71+/-0.01 (West) and 1.89+/-0.01 (North) held-out regions, demonstrating spatial generalization via translation equivariance (Tables 5-6).

Xg12D1Y4H1.text: The method expresses finite volume method (FVM) discretization of nonlinear conservation laws as Bayesian inference under a structured Gaussian process prior jointly over the solution u, flux F(u), and source s, handling both forward and inverse problems (Section 2, Section 2.4).

Sparse approximation combines tensor-product Matern kernels with separable spacetime structure, information-form inference exploiting Kronecker factorization from IWP temporal structure, and a KL-minimizing sparse Cholesky factorization with a novel coarsest-to-finest functional ordering (Algorithm 1) (Sections 3.1-3.3).

On an advection-diffusion inverse source identification problem with 12 sparse measurements, GP-FVM recovers the source field in 2 seconds with RMSE 0.44, versus a PINN baseline requiring 5 minutes and RMSE 0.76, a roughly 150x speedup (Section 4.1, Figures 1-2).

On the 2D Burgers equation forward problem across grid resolutions N in {8,12,16,20,24}, GP-FVM achieves L2 error within 2-3x of classical FVM accuracy while outperforming a collocation-based GP approach by roughly 10x (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

Empirical wall-clock scaling tracks the theoretical O(N_s^{3/2}) complexity bound with an empirical exponent of about 1.35, solving problems with about 70,000 degrees of freedom in under 4 minutes on a single CPU (Section 3.5, Appendix D, Figure 10).

The framework extends to coupled nonlinear systems, correctly capturing tsunami wave propagation and shoaling in shallow water equations on a 31x31 grid with a joint state dimension of 28,566 per timestep (Section 4.4, Figure 5).

iTy1M4N2FU.text: Theorem 5.1 provides a safety certificate that combines per-task lower confidence bounds satisfying Pr[J_Mi(pi) >= J-tilde_Mi^beta(pi)] >= 1-beta with a binomial-tail generalization argument to guarantee Pr[S_D^pi(B) >= 1-epsilon] >= 1-delta for a policy on unseen tasks from distribution D (Theorem 5.1).

The certificate introduces a relaxation parameter K that allows a bounded number of per-task bound failures while preserving overall soundness, solved via a binomial tail-probability equation balancing beta, epsilon, and delta (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).

Per-task lower confidence bounds are instantiated via Clopper-Pearson intervals for binary success/failure metrics and via Hoeffding's inequality, J-tilde_M^beta(pi) := hat J_M(pi) - (b-a)*sqrt(ln(1/beta)/(2m)), Empirical Bernstein, or DKW-based bounds for bounded real-valued returns (Section 5.1, Equation 5).

The framework is validated on Grid World navigation with stochastic slip probabilities, continuous-control Cheetah and Walker tasks with mass/size variations, and a Zones environment with LTL task specifications, showing certified bounds remain sound and tight across all domains (Section 6, Figure 4).

A parameter study shows that increasing the number of sampled tasks n and rollouts per task m tightens the certified bound by refining per-task estimates and reducing task-sampling uncertainty, with sample complexity independent of state/action space dimensionality (Section 6, Figure 3).

8k4om4zj5E.text: CorNets extend Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR), Fully Connected (FC), and convolutional layers to the full-rank correlation manifold Cor+(n) under five Riemannian geometries: ECM, LECM, OLM, LSM, and PHCM (Section 2, Table 1).

Theorem 3.5 gives closed-form expressions for Log-Euclidean correlation FC layers under ECM, LECM, OLM, and LSM, e.g. the ECM-FC output is Y = Cor∘Chol^{-1}(V^EC + I_m) (Theorem 3.5, Equations 10-13).

On the NTU120 dataset, CorNet-ECM/CorNet-LECM achieve accuracy of 65.04±0.14 / 65.03±0.10, outperforming the classic SPDNet (57.59±0.22) by 7.76%/7.75% and the best Grassmannian baseline GyroGr-Scaling (43.90±0.23) by over 21 points (Table 2).

On the Radar dataset, CorNet-ECM reaches 97.71±0.61 accuracy, surpassing SPDNet (93.25±1.10) by 5.15%, and CorNets outperform SPDNet across all four datasets (HDM05, FPHA, NTU120) by margins of 17.69%, 6.58%, and 13.84% respectively (Table 2, Section 5).

Ablation on mixed geometries (Table 3) shows that using consistent (diagonal) metrics for both the convolutional and MLR layers yields the best accuracy overall, e.g. ECM-ECM achieves 81.35±1.27 on HDM05, the top result in that row/column comparison.

Replacing SPDNet's covariance input with correlation input on HDM05 improves accuracy from 64.57±0.61 to 66.81±0.83, while it degrades performance on Radar (93.25±1.10 to 89.49±0.67) and FPHA (85.59±0.72 to 83.37±0.40), illustrating dataset-dependent benefits of correlation embeddings (Table 4).

VHqDQ1BQVw.text: Flash-GRPO's Iso-Temporal Grouping (Section 4.1) ensures rollouts within a prompt group share identical diffusion timesteps while varying only the initial noise, addressing timestep-confounded variance in one-step policy optimization.

Flash-GRPO's Temporal Gradient Rectification (Section 4.2) derives a time-dependent scaling factor λ(t) and normalizes it toward 1 to correct gradient-magnitude inconsistencies across the diffusion trajectory.

On Wan2.1-1.3B trained for 350 GPU hours, Flash-GRPO achieves higher VBench Aesthetic Quality (66.43) and Subject Consistency (98.70) scores than the Flow-GRPO-Fast baseline (65.92 aesthetic quality) (Table 1).
An ablation shows reward scores rising from 4.64 (naive single-step) to 5.31 with Iso-Temporal Grouping alone, and to 5.42 with the full method (ITG + Temporal Gradient Rectification) (Table 2).

Flash-GRPO attains roughly 6x acceleration in training cost relative to the full-trajectory Flow-GRPO baseline while achieving higher evaluation performance, demonstrated across both the 1.3B and 14B parameter Wan2.1 models (Figure 1).

k5xsXvNYQS.text: LGS-Net models an instance-conditioned latent variable with an encoder p_φ(z|x) and decoder p_θ(y|x,z), trained via entropy-regularized reinforcement learning with weighted cost samples (Section 4.1-4.2).

Inference is performed by sampling from a target distribution π_θ(y|x) using interacting MCMC combined with Stochastic Approximation, implemented as Algorithm 1 with K particles and M iterations including Metropolis-Hastings acceptance and REINFORCE policy-gradient updates (Section 4.3, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 5.1 establishes geometric convergence of the fixed-parameter Markov Chain to its invariant distribution π_θ in both Total Variation and L2 distances, while Theorem 5.2 proves convergence of the time-inhomogeneous chain under adaptive Stochastic-Approximation parameter updates, decomposing error into mixing, tracking, and optimization components (Section 5, Theorems 5.1-5.2).
On TSP instances with n=100 nodes without augmentation, LGS achieves a 0.002% optimality gap, outperforming COMPASS (0.014%) and EAS (0.197%); with augmentation LGS reaches a 0.000% gap (Table 1).
On CVRP with n=100 nodes, LGS achieves a -0.102% gap, surpassing most Neural Combinatorial Optimization baselines and even LKH-3 on the n=100 and n=125 settings (Table 2).

An ablation shows the full LGS method (-0.102% gap) and its Interacting MCMC variant (-0.032% gap) substantially outperform a Single MCMC baseline (0.701% gap) as well as DE and CMA-ES variants (Table 3).

hkmpUHQxgv.text: FCGraft maintains a two-tier code cache (Section 4.1) with a Function-Interface tier storing signatures with KV states and a Function-Code tier preserving validated implementations, using a locality-scoring equation (Eq. 3) combining frequency, association, and semantic diversity.

FCGraft performs cache-grafting via cache-stitching (Eqs. 4-5), which composes functions by reusing KV states, and cache-patching (Eq. 6), which regenerates only erroneous code spans using prefix KV states (Section 4.2).
FCGraft achieves 18.31% higher task success rate and 2.3x faster policy synthesis than RAGCache, averaged across evaluated benchmarks (Abstract, Tables 1-2).
On the RLBench Open-Composition setting, FCGraft attains 45.91% success rate at 3.24s latency, while on ALFRED Open-Composition it attains 61.58% success rate at 5.82s latency (Table 1).

An ablation removing the Function-Interface tier drops RLBench success rate from 45.91% to 38.64%, and replacing localized cache-patching with full regeneration increases latency from 3.24s to 6.89s (Table 5).

On real-world Franka robot manipulation tasks, FCGraft achieves a 77.78% success rate with 3.80s synthesis latency, evaluated against baselines including CaP, RAGCache, PromptCache, and EPIC (Section 5, Table 1).

MdHcU4C4Rm.text: Theorem 2.2 proves that for any nonstationary ridge penalty λ (i.e., R'(λ) ≠ 0), the optimally mixed self-distilled student strictly improves on the teacher's squared prediction risk, with optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) = -(λ/2)·R'(λ)/D(λ) obeying sign(ξ*(λ)) = -sign(R'(λ)) (Section 2.3, Theorem 2.2).

The optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) can be negative, corresponding to a 'pro-learning' regime under over-regularization (λ > λ*), as opposed to the 'anti-learning' regime (ξ* > 1) identified in prior work by Das and Sanghavi (2023) (Section 2.3).

Theorem 3.1 derives exact deterministic equivalents for the optimal self-distillation risk R*_sd(λ) and mixing weight ξ*(λ) in the proportional asymptotics regime (n, p → ∞, p/n → γ) under general anisotropic covariance and deterministic signals (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).
In the isotropic-signal setting, Corollary 3.2 shows the optimal mixing weight changes sign exactly at λ* := γσ²/r², with ξ*(λ) < 0 for λ > λ* and ξ*(λ) > 0 for λ < λ* (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.2).

Theorem 4.1 proposes a one-shot generalized cross-validation (GCV) estimator of the optimal mixing weight ξ* that is consistent in proportional asymptotics and avoids grid search, sample splitting, or refitting (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

A curvature-based sufficient condition (Proposition 2.3, Eq. 10) predicts whether the self-distilled risk's global minimum over λ is strictly smaller than the teacher's; this test is verified exactly on all four real-data experiments (BlogFeedback, Communities and Crime, CIFAR10, Air Quality) in Table 2.

sfi4R7lsIP.text: Tree-like Self-Play (TSP) raises CodeLlama-7B's SPR@1 on the Python SecurityEval benchmark to 75.8%, versus 57.0% for SFT and 69.6% for standard Self-Play (Table 2).
TSP-trained CodeLlama-7B retains near-baseline general coding ability, scoring 34.0% pass@1 on HumanEval despite the added security training (Table 2).
On C/C++ code generation, TSP reduces detected vulnerabilities for CodeLlama-7B from 115 (base model) to 94, and for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B from 106 to 57 (Table 3).
Models trained with TSP on C/C++ data transfer security principles to Python, JavaScript, Go, and Ruby generation without additional language-specific training (Table 3).
On 40 unseen CWE categories held out from training, TSP reduces CodeLlama-7B's vulnerability count to 34 versus 50 for SFT, a roughly 24.5% reduction (Table 4).

The training corpus is built from DiverseVul with 1,353 secure function samples spanning 797 projects and 150 CWE categories, validated with Cohen's Kappa of 0.89 (human) and 0.86 (LLM annotation) (Section 3).

qX4Nm7eNM5.text: Theorem 1 gives a universal recipe under which SCORE-adjusted online FDR procedures remain valid (FDP estimator bounded) while achieving uniform power gains over their base procedures (Theorem 1).

Proposition 1-2 show SCORE-LOND's significance level sequence satisfies alpha_t^{SCORE-LOND} >= alpha_t^{e-LOND} for all t, so SCORE-LOND strictly dominates e-LOND whenever overshoots occur (Section 4, Propositions 1-2).
On the Yeast dataset, SCORE-LORD yields 28,808 discoveries versus 25,954 for e-LORD (a 10.9% increase), and SCORE+-LORD yields 44,210 discoveries, a 70.3% increase over e-LORD (Table 1, Section 6).
SCORE+-SAFFRON achieves a 46% gain in discoveries over e-SAFFRON on the same benchmark while maintaining FDR control at the nominal level alpha (Table 1, Section 6).

Under Assumption 1 (Conditional Positive Quadrant Dependence between evidence and total discoveries), the SCORE+ variants use the global denominator R_t v 1 rather than the local R_{j-1}+1, enabling more aggressive retroactive alpha-wealth refunds (Section 5, Assumption 1).

bxVWc9Mzns.text: Theorem 3.6 establishes a geometric tail bound on the number of outer-to-outer sign flips, P[K_T^eff(rho) >= k] <= h_T * g_T^{k-1} + delta_upd, predicting exponential decay in flip probability with training time (Theorem 3.6).
Figure 4 shows the initial-hit factor and re-entry ratio governing sign flips decrease monotonically with model scale across models ranging from 30M to over 10B parameters (Figure 4).

Combining gap-based initialization (truncated Gaussian rejection sampling with threshold a_init = c_gap * sigma_init) with a log-barrier outer-drift regularizer reduces the effective sign flip rate to approximately 10^-3 while increasing validation perplexity by only about one point (Section 4, Figure 5).
A rank-2 factorized sign template T^(l) = sign(GH^T) is proposed as a low-rank-compressible initialization scheme for sub-bit model compression (Section 4).

wblvinAlrW.text: Dynamic PRM-guided test-time compute allocation raises MATH-500 accuracy for Llama-3.1-8B from a 43.8% direct-decoding baseline to 65.4% (+21.6 points), and for Qwen-2.5-7B from 71.2% to 81.4% (+10.2 points) (Section 4).
On AIME24, the same dynamic allocation method improves Llama-3.1-8B from 3.3% to 10.0% accuracy (roughly 3x) and Qwen-2.5-7B from 6.67% to 13.3% (roughly 2x) (Section 4).
On AMO-Bench, both Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B double their accuracy from 2.0% to 4.0% under dynamic PRM-guided allocation versus the direct baseline (Section 4).

The method's four-stage agent architecture separates planning, tool selection (CoT, self-reflection, verifiers), compute-strategy selection (best-of-N, beam search, lookahead), and answer extraction (Figure 1).

Process reward models operate at two granularities, intra-iteration step-level pruning during generation and inter-iteration trajectory selection across K=10 independent iterations, to concentrate compute on high-utility reasoning paths (Section 2).

DwtVUwEwTF.text: Theorem 3 proves that for multivariate Gaussian sources under AWGN observations, the proposed score-scaled probability-flow ODE achieves the optimal distortion-perception frontier with dimension-specific parameter selection (Theorem 3).

Theorem 4 shows that for scalar Gaussian sources, combining reverse channel coding with the score-scaled decoder asymptotically achieves the information-theoretic rate-distortion-perception function, with a bounded gap from one-shot coding rate (Theorem 4).

Lemma 1 characterizes the conditional and marginal distributions of the score-scaled PF-ODE for Gaussian sources, proving the reconstruction converges to the MMSE estimate when the scaling parameter rho=0 and recovers perfect realism when rho=1 (Lemma 1).

A single pretrained diffusion model traverses the entire RDP surface using two control parameters, the diffusion time index t for rate control and the score-scaling parameter rho for the distortion-perception tradeoff, without retraining (Section III).
The framework is validated experimentally on CIFAR-10, Kodak, and DIV2K image datasets (Section V).

t2bQt6M7Qh.text: On the Long Range Arena Pathfinder task, CMRU and αCMRU both achieve above 90% accuracy while LRU and minGRU perform near chance level (≈50%) (Table 1, Section 5.1).
On sequential MNIST, CMRU with ε=1 reaches 96% accuracy and αCMRU reaches 97% accuracy, both with markedly reduced cross-seed variability compared to LRU and minGRU (Figure 2, Section 4.1).

On keyword-spotting audio classification with hidden dimension d=16, CMRU achieves 95.38% accuracy on the Digits subset and 89.76% on the full KWS task, closely matching baseline performance (Table 3, Section 5.2).

CMRU's fixed quantization scheme expands representational capacity from 2^d discrete states (as in BMRU) to a countably infinite set of attractors when ε=1, while retaining quantized states that block analog noise propagation (Section 3.3).
A single-layer CMRU with d=16 can be mapped onto a Schmitt trigger analog circuit primitive, supporting projected operation at approximately 100 nW power (Section 2.2, Section 5.2).

On the copy-first-input task, CMRU maintains near-theoretical-limit error consistently across increasing sequence lengths, whereas LRU and minGRU degrade substantially as sequence length grows (Figure 3, Section 4.3).

4bLahBrVBs.text: AgentConductor achieves 58.8% pass@1 accuracy on APPS, a 14.6 percentage-point improvement over the strongest baseline's 44.2% (Table 2).
On LiveCodeBench and CodeContests, AgentConductor improves pass@1 by 3.1 and 1.1 percentage points respectively over the strongest baselines (Table 2).

On the APPS dataset, AgentConductor reduces prompt token usage to 277,600 tokens, roughly a 68% reduction versus the ~437K average of baseline methods, while also achieving the highest graph sparseness score of 5.2 among compared methods (Table 3).

Difficulty interval partitioning sets per-turn node budgets of 4 nodes for easy tasks (l=1), 7 nodes for medium tasks (l=2), and 10 nodes for hard tasks (l=3), enabling task-adapted interaction graph density (Section 2.3, Equation 12).
Topology density adapts across difficulty levels, using sparser interaction graphs for easier instances and denser graphs for harder instances (Figure 5).
On HumanEval and MBPP, AgentConductor improves pass@1 by 1.2 and 1.0 percentage points respectively over the strongest baselines, reaching 97.5% and 95.1% accuracy (Table 2).

TzQElzflxR.text: The paper defines a Safe KL divergence with a bounded-density constraint (Definition 2.1, Equations 3-4) whose induced approximation to LogSumExp satisfies F_ρ − O(ρ) ≤ F ≤ F_ρ (Proposition 2.4, Section 2).
The rescaled SoftPlus-based conjugate of the Safe KL function is proven to be ρ-strongly convex, with its own conjugate being (1/ρ)-smooth (Lemma 2.7, Section 2.2).
The approximation family is shown to bound and connect to the CVaR functional, recovering CVaR and LogSumExp as limiting cases (Proposition 2.6, Section 2.1).

In continuous entropy-regularized optimal transport experiments with regularization ε=0.01, the proposed semi-dual formulation (Equations 14-15) avoids the numerical overflow issues of the baseline and reaches a converged objective in roughly 10^4 iterations (Figure 2, Section 3.1).

In KL-regularized distributionally robust optimization on California Housing, the proposed method converges with a stepsize of η=10⁻⁴ across batch sizes of 10, 100, and 1000, whereas the baseline requires a much smaller η=10⁻⁶ at batch size 10 (Figure 3, Section 3.2).

In unbalanced optimal-transport-based DRO on MNIST with label noise, the proposed approach (Equation 22) converges faster than the baseline (Equation 21) using η=10⁻⁴ versus the baseline's required η=10⁻⁵ (Figure 4, Section 3.3).

evMzHrKyYR.text: Contribution Weights decompose multiplicatively into attention weight, relative value norm (‖ṽⱼ‖/‖oᵢ‖), and cosine similarity between value and output directions (cos(oᵢ, ṽⱼ)) (Equation 14, Section 4.3).

On GSM8K, Contribution Weights show steeper degradation in comprehensiveness and sufficiency metrics under token removal than value-weighted attention, value-weighted output-normalized attention, and raw attention weights (Figure 3, Section 5).

On downstream tasks MMLU, BoolQ, Lambada, and Winogrande, models retain baseline accuracy at higher token-removal rates when ranking tokens by Contribution Weights compared to attention-based alternatives (Figure 4, Section 5).

Variance decomposition shows cosine similarity alone explains R²=0.518 of the variance in Contribution Weights for initial (sink) tokens, while combined attention and alignment terms explain R²=0.834 for tail tokens (Table 1).

Attention sink tokens exhibit negative cosine similarity (≈-0.2) with semantic tokens while tail tokens show positive mutual alignment (≈0.2), supporting an active suppression rather than passive-absorption role for sinks (Figure 5a, Section 6.2).

Output norm as a function of sink attention rate follows a convex relationship with a minimum at an intermediate threshold α_min < 1, and removing sink suppression causes low-norm heads to collapse into the semantic cone (Equation 20, Figure 6, Section 6.2).

pH7NRZx89n.text: Per-Token Distance (PTD)=0 is established as a sufficient condition for eliminating relative-position-induced attention bias between text and image tokens, requiring each text token to maintain uniform distance to all image tokens (Section 3.1, Equation 2).
Empirically, hard position embedding yields PTD=2.22, spatial embedding yields PTD=0.64, unordered embedding yields PTD=0, and Circle-RoPE also achieves PTD=0 (Table following Section 3.1).

Circle-RoPE's Mixed-Angle Circular Mapping projects 2D image coordinates onto a circle via a weighted combination of two angle components, θ^mix = α·θ^SA + (1−α)·θ^GA (Equation 9, Section 4.1.2), followed by rotating this circle so its normal aligns with the text token direction (Section 4.1.3).

Circle-RoPE improves average performance across 10 vision-language benchmarks from 66.95 to 68.28, with gains including MMMU (50.22 to 52.11), MathVista (62.4 to 63.4), and ChartQA (83.92 to 84.12) (Table 2).
An ablation on the dual-frame fusion weight shows an optimal value of β=0.1 yields the best average score of 50.54, balancing angular decoupling against spatial fidelity (Table 4).

EsHKqJJ2u1.text: Lemma 3.1 proves that AlphaEdit's accumulated sequential parameter updates equal the corresponding one-time-editing (OTE) solution, i.e. the sum of sequential deltas Δτ* equals the total one-time delta Δtotal,t* (Section 3.1, Lemma 3.1).

Proposition 3.2 generalizes the OTE-sequential-editing equivalence to any regularization parameter λ≥0 and any projection matrix P, showing many regularization/null-space projection choices are unnecessary for equivalence to hold (Section 3, Proposition 3.2).

Table 1 shows that removing full alignment terms from AlphaEdit's null-space projection causes performance on the SST task to collapse from 0.831 to 0.000, evidencing accumulated approximation error (Table 1).
Proposition 3.5 gives closed-form updates for resolving overlapping, conflicting edits via a resolution function, extending the framework to contradictory updates (Section 3, Proposition 3.5).

Table 2 reports that full OTE alignment (via Algorithm 1) restores Efficacy to 99.87-99.88%, versus only 56-60% without alignment, across models including Qwen2.5, GPT-2 XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3 (Table 2, Algorithm 1).
Figure 3 shows GLUE benchmark general-capability scores remain stable across more than 2000 sequential edits under the proposed alignment approach (Figure 3).

2jpCo5lnSZ.text: FPTQuant introduces four function-preserving transforms — a Pre-RoPE rotation, a multihead value transform, an MLP scaling transform, and a dynamic residual scaling transform — that reshape activation distributions for quantization without altering model outputs (Section 3).
Static INT4 quantization with FPTQuant achieves speedups of 2.8x to 3.9x over the FP16 baseline, and is consistently 15-29% faster than FlatQuant (Section 4.1).
On Llama-3-8B under W4A8KV4 static quantization, FPTQuant achieves 6.27 WikiText-2 perplexity and 72.72% average zero-shot accuracy (Table 2).
Under the more aggressive W4A4KV4 setting quantizing all activations, FPTQuant achieves 17.17 WikiText-2 perplexity on Llama-3.2-3B, versus 20.13 for SpinQuant (Table 1).
Under dynamic quantization, FPTQuant reaches 5.97 WikiText-2 perplexity on Llama-2-7B versus FlatQuant's 5.79, while running about 29% faster than FlatQuant (Table 3).

All primary FPTQuant transforms are mergeable into existing weights and require no custom kernels, adding virtually no inference overhead compared to prior rotation-based methods like QuaRot and SpinQuant (Section 3).

duzvT0nDgZ.text: FedVPA-GP combines federated learning with variational preference learning to personalize LLM alignment across clients while preserving privacy, avoiding the monolithic reward model that averages out conflicting preferences such as helpfulness versus harmlessness (abstract only).

A Federated Mixture Prior lets clients use an aggregate, population-level distribution as a dynamic prior to stabilize variational inference under posterior collapse caused by limited local data and preference heterogeneity (abstract only).
An Orthogonal Loss term explicitly enforces separation of preference prototypes in latent space to help distinguish competing user intents (abstract only).
On the HH-RLHF dataset, FedVPA-GP significantly outperforms monolithic baselines and successfully disentangles conflicting user intents while enabling dynamic preference switching (abstract only).

maA1s1S0db.text: ADEPT reframes speech emotion recognition as a multi-turn inquiry process using semantic and acoustic probing tools rather than a single-pass prediction (Section 4.2).
On MSP-Podcast Test1, ADEPT with GRPO training achieves a primary emotion Macro-F1 of 0.4224, versus 0.3640 for a WavLM fine-tuned baseline (Table 1).
On MSP-Podcast Test1, ADEPT achieves a Soft Recall of 0.7874 and Jaccard Index of 0.4751, compared to 0.6740 and 0.4280 respectively for the BLSP-Emo baseline (Table 1).
In zero-shot evaluation on IEMOCAP, ADEPT reaches 54.80% Set Recall, outperforming a supervised state-of-the-art baseline at 52.30% (Table 3).
Average tool calls scale with annotation consensus difficulty, rising from 2.3 calls under high consensus to 4.1 under medium consensus and 6.8 under low consensus (Figure 4).
An Evidence Trust Gate modulates GRPO rewards based on whether correct reasoning trajectories exhibit stronger evidence-seeking behavior than incorrect ones, to prevent reward hacking (Section 4.3).

oVt5ioGXPg.text: Theorem 3.5 proves that any rotation-invariant algorithm learning noise-free sparse logistic-regression targets from hard labels incurs excess risk at least Ω((d-1)/n), where d is the dimension and n the sample size, when n ≳ d + log(1/δ) (Theorem 3.5).

Theorem 5.1 shows that a non-rotation-invariant 'spindly network' using a Hadamard-factored weight reparameterization w(t) = u(t) ⊙ v(t) achieves excess risk O(s log d / n), where s is the target sparsity, strictly beating the Ω((d-1)/n) rotation-invariant lower bound (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 5.1's bound takes the explicit form ||w(t) - w*||_2^2 ≤ ε^2||w*||_2^2 + 16 s log(2d/η) / (n (w*_min a*)^2) + c2/d^(δ+1/2), holding under stated conditions on sample size and signal-curvature parameters (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).

The results together demonstrate that simple weight reparameterization, which breaks rotation invariance, suffices to achieve near-optimal statistical efficiency for sparse recovery from hard labels (Section 5).

zAFrIOeTCp.text: GraphGPO aggregates rollout trajectories from M trajectories of length T into a unified directed state-transition graph, merging identical states into single nodes (Section 4.2).

GraphGPO computes graph-based rewards using the formula R^G(s,a,s') = r_succ * ω^(d(s')+c(s,a)), where d(s) is the shortest-path distance to the goal and ω is a distance discount factor (Section 4.3).
Proposition 4.2 proves that the conditional variance of graph-based feedback is upper-bounded by that of trajectory-level feedback (Section 4.4, Proposition 4.2).
On Qwen 1.5B, GraphGPO improves over GRPO by 14.85% on ALFWorld, gains 7.30% success rate on WebShop, and improves by 19.88% on Sokoban (Table 1).
Graph construction and advantage computation add only 0.04% additional per-iteration runtime compared to the rollout (216.9s) and policy update (74.2s) stages (Figure 5).

Figure 1 shows that only about 22% of steps in failed trajectories contribute to task progress while 65.3% of steps in successful trajectories do not advance the task, motivating step-level over trajectory-level credit assignment (Figure 1).

ff4b0ELdU0.text: Numca (Numerical Milestone Credit Assignment) uses numbers appearing in a response as a state representation to compute state value estimates (Section 5.1).
Hista uses a hidden-state-based framework to group disjoint responses for state value estimation (Section 5.2).

On the State Value Estimation Benchmark (SVEB), Hista reduces mean absolute error versus GRPO/PPO-N baselines across five domains, e.g. 0.142 vs 0.175 on SVEB-Number and 0.173 vs 0.215 on SVEB-Science (Table 4).

SVEB spans five domains built from existing datasets: SVEB-Number (DAPO-17K), SVEB-Math (OpenR1-220K), SVEB-Science (Llama-Nemotron), SVEB-General (WebInstruct-verified), and SVEB-Programming (verifiable-coding-problem) (Section 5, Table 4).

Combining Hista with DAPO on base models ranging from 0.5B to 14B parameters yields consistent downstream gains of roughly 0.5 to 1.8 percentage points on math benchmarks including MATH, GSM8K, and AMC (Table 5).
The method is evaluated across multiple RL algorithms including DAPO, GSPO, CSIPO, and PPO, showing consistent performance gains from improved value estimation (Table 4, Table 5).

IYtXaU7N6B.text: PnP-Corrector decouples physical simulation from error correction by freezing pre-trained simulators (e.g., ConvLSTM, SimVP, GraphCast, OLA, CirT) and training only a correction module (Section 3).
For the 300-day global ocean-atmosphere coupled forecast, PnP-Corrector reduces the prediction error of the baseline model by 28% (Section 5).
Applied to the GraphCast baseline at the 300-day horizon, PnP-Corrector improves RMSE by 22.24% and MAE by 22.10% (Section 5, Table results).

Evaluation uses ERA5 atmospheric data (69 variables across 13 pressure levels plus 4 surface variables) and GLORYS12 ocean data (93 variables across 23 depth levels plus surface variables) at 1° spatial resolution, trained on 1993-2017, validated on 2018-2019, and tested on 2020 (Section 4).

PnP-Corrector is motivated by a 'Reciprocal Error Amplification' effect in coupled ocean-atmosphere systems, where simulation errors in one domain compound errors in the other over long forecast horizons (Section 3).

0ujhEWEeAc.text: GSCF (Generalized Spanning Converging Forest) generates spanning converging forests for signed graphs using loop-erased random walks in expected O(n) time, per Theorem 5.2 (Section 5.1, Algorithm 1, Theorem 5.2).
FMDE estimates the diagonal of the forest matrix via sampling in O(ln) time, where l is the number of samples (Section 6.2, Algorithm 2).

FMDE+ incorporates additional network information to achieve the same O(ln) time complexity as FMDE but with lower variance, and Theorem 6.3 proves its superior performance on balanced signed graphs (Section 6.2, Theorem 6.3).
On the SlashdotZoo network, exact diagonal computation via direct matrix inversion takes 991.5 seconds while FMDE+ completes in under 1.1 seconds (Table 1).
The methods scale to the FullUSA network with roughly 2.3×10^7 (over twenty million) nodes, where exact computation fails but FMDE+ completes within one hour (Table 3).
FMDE+ achieves roughly ten times lower average relative error than FMDE across tested networks (Figure 2).

R9AUrEgZEq.text: SF-Mamba introduces auxiliary patch swapping, using two learnable auxiliary tokens prepended/appended to the patch sequence and swapped between Mamba blocks to enable bidirectional information flow without multi-directional scans (Section 3.2).

SF-Mamba applies batch folding with a periodic state reset trick that merges batch and sequence dimensions to lengthen effective sequences, yielding a 110% to 180% speedup on SSM computation for short token sequences (Section 3.3).

On ImageNet-1K, SF-Mamba-T reaches 82.5% top-1 accuracy at 7,600 images/s, SF-Mamba-S reaches 83.5% at 5,639 images/s, and SF-Mamba-B reaches 84.4% at 3,534 images/s (Section 4, image classification results).
SF-Mamba outperforms Vim-S (80.1% accuracy, 1,079 img/s) and VMamba-T (82.6% accuracy, 1,684 img/s) in the accuracy-throughput tradeoff on ImageNet-1K (Section 4).

SF-Mamba is evaluated on object detection and instance segmentation on MS COCO using a Cascade Mask R-CNN head, and semantic segmentation on ADE20K (150 classes) using the UperNet framework, showing improved accuracy-throughput tradeoffs versus Swin and Focal Transformer baselines (Section 4).

wb97oR78OX.text: SAD-Flower augments flow matching with a virtual control input added to the ODE and enforces safety, admissibility, and dynamic-consistency constraints via a QP built from Control Barrier Function (CBF-s, CBF-a) and Control Lyapunov Function (CLF) constraints (Section 5.1, Section 5.2).

Theorem 5.1 guarantees that if the QP remains feasible over the interval [T0, 1], the generated trajectory satisfies the safety, admissibility, and dynamic-consistency constraints at t=1, without requiring retraining for new constraints (Theorem 5.1).

On Maze2d, Hopper, Walker2d, and Kuka Block-Stacking, SAD-Flower attains 0.00±0.00 safety and admissibility violations while matching or exceeding the reward of baselines such as Diffuser, SafeDiffuser, Decision Diffuser, and Classifier Guidance (Table 1, Section 6.2).

SAD-Flower's convex QP-based guidance runs in 0.06±0.00 seconds and achieves a reward of 0.93, versus DPCC's non-convex optimization baseline at 4.24±1.64 seconds and a reward of 0.61 (Table 2, Section 6.3).

In the 39-dimensional-state, 30-dimensional-action Adroit Hand (Relocate) manipulation task, SAD-Flower maintains 0.00 safety and admissibility violations, demonstrating scalability to high-dimensional control (Table 3, Section 6.4).

SAD-Flower eliminates the 'local trap problem' exhibited by SafeDiffuser's CBF-based projection by coupling consecutive states through the CLF constraint, as illustrated with only 25 ODE sampling steps needed for practical dynamic consistency (Figure 2, Figure 3, Section 6.3).

Z7Rhzk13NT.text: PersistBench evaluates 18 frontier and open-source LLMs (including GPT-5.2, Claude-Opus-4.5, Gemini-3-Pro, Grok-4, Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen3-235B, and DeepSeek-V3.2) on a 500-sample human-validated benchmark of long-term memory risks (Section 4.3, Table 2, Appendix F).

The benchmark comprises 200 cross-domain leakage samples, 200 memory-induced sycophancy samples, and 100 beneficial memory use samples spanning 9 domains such as health, financial, relationships, and identity (Table 1).

Median cross-domain leakage failure rate across the 18 evaluated models is 53%, meaning models frequently surface memories from an unrelated prior domain into the current conversation (Section 5.1, Table 2).
Median memory-induced sycophancy failure rate is 97.8%, indicating models overwhelmingly validate or agree with users based on previously stored (and often outdated or biased) memories (Section 5.1).

The highest observed cross-domain leakage occurs when educational-experience memories bleed into health queries, at a 61% failure rate, while identity-validation scenarios produce the highest sycophancy failure rate at 94.9% (Figure 23, Figure 26, Section 5.3).

Median failure rate on beneficial memory use (correctly leveraging relevant past memory) is 16.5%, showing models fail less often when memory use is actually appropriate compared to leakage/sycophancy failure modes (Section 5.1).

Xf9hJMGwDd.text: Semi-knockoffs avoids the train-test data split required by prior conditional-independence testing methods such as HRT while still yielding valid p-values, via nonparametric paired tests requiring only conditional expectations ν_j and ρ_j rather than exact knockoff construction (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).
Theorem 3.4 establishes that the Semi-knockoffs procedure controls the false discovery rate at level q, i.e. FDR(S_SKO) ≤ q (Theorem 3.4, Section 3.2).

Theorem 4.1 shows that for null (non-relevant) features, regularized empirical risk minimizers trained with and without the feature remain close, with an ‖θ̃^j − θ̂‖₂ ≤ O_P(√(log(1/δ)/n)) bound, giving optimization stability guarantees for regularized models (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2).

Theorem 4.3 provides a double-robustness property: the loss difference between imputed feature distributions decays at a compound rate O_P(a_n b_n) even when both the predictive model and the sampler have estimation error (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.4).

On simulated data with adjacent-feature support, Semi-knockoffs maintains type-I error control while achieving higher power than HRT, and derandomization with 5 permutations under masked correlation further increases power (Figure 4, Figure 5, Section 5.1).

On the Wisconsin Breast Cancer real dataset, Semi-knockoffs is applied across Random Forest, Neural Network, and Gradient Boosting models to demonstrate model-agnostic feature selection (Figure 6, Section 5.2).

LwdCB259lF.text: Stein Diffusion Guidance (SDG) formulates low-density diffusion sampling as a stochastic optimal control problem and derives the annealed reward-guided marginal density and its optimal control in Proposition 3.1 (Proposition 3.1, Section 3.1).

Proposition 3.2 proves that the standard Tweedie-approximation value function bound used by prior training-free guidance methods is inherently suboptimal without an added KL-regularization correction term (Proposition 3.2, Section 3.2).

Proposition 3.3 decomposes SDG's optimal control into a Stein correction term applied on the clean-data manifold plus a separate low-density guidance term applied on the noisy manifold (Proposition 3.3, Section 3.3).

On the protein-target molecular generation benchmark for docking against fa7, 5ht1b, and jak2, SDG achieves a 25.744%±0.408 novel hit ratio on 5ht1b, outperforming the classifier-guided diffusion baseline MOOD (18.673%) and an ablation without Stein correction (2.933%) (Table 1, Section 4.1–4.2).

An ablation removing the Stein correction mechanism collapses SDG's novel hit ratio from 25.744% to 2.933% on 5ht1b, confirming the Stein correction is the primary driver of performance in low-density regions (Table 1).
In extreme low-density guidance settings (α_E = 0.7), SDG maintains roughly 40% sample validity, illustrating robustness of the Stein correction mechanism at high guidance strength (Figure 6).

PfhSH42cCy.text: X-Dub uses a two-stage generative bootstrapping framework—a Generator followed by an Editor—built on a ~1B-parameter DiT backbone operating at 512×512 resolution and 25fps to unlock mask-free, audio-driven visual dubbing (Section 3.1–3.3).
On the HDTF benchmark, the X-Dub Editor achieves FID 7.031 and Sync-C 8.562, both better than the strongest prior baseline LatentSync (FID 8.042, Sync-C 8.163) (Table 1).

On the newly introduced 440-video-pair ContextDubBench dataset (291 real-human and 108 stylized-character videos with challenging lighting/occlusions), the X-Dub Editor attains a 96.36% success rate versus 71.82% for the best prior method, Diff2Lip (Table 2, Appendix H).
On ContextDubBench, X-Dub also improves perceptual quality and lip-sync over the best baseline LatentSync, with NIQE 5.782 vs 6.113 and Sync-C 7.282 vs 6.282 (Table 2).
A user study reports Mean Opinion Score of 4.66±0.05 for X-Dub's overall quality, substantially higher than LatentSync's 3.16±0.13 (Table 3).
X-Dub's Generator trains for 15k steps (about 1 day) and its Editor trains for an additional 4k+1k steps (about 0.5 days), with inference taking roughly 60 seconds per 3-second video (Section 3.3).

pVcEcaHHD2.text: On visual math reasoning benchmarks, LaViDa-R1 improves MathVista accuracy from 56.9 to 60.0 and MathVerse from 36.9 to 38.7 over its base model (Section 4, Experiments).
On the Lisa-Grounding reason-intensive grounding benchmark, LaViDa-R1 raises P@0.5 from 29.2 to 66.7 and mIoU from 26.1 to 60.0 relative to the base model (Section 4, Experiments).
On the ImgEdit image-editing benchmark, LaViDa-R1 improves the overall score from 3.71 (base model) to 3.90 (Section 4, Experiments).

The unified post-training objective (Equation 5) combines SFT, online GRPO, and self-distillation, with an ablation showing a self-distillation weight of gamma=0.5 outperforming pure GRPO (gamma=0) or pure distillation (gamma=1.0) (Section 5, Ablation Studies).

The Answer-Forcing guided rollout mechanism uses dLLM inpainting conditioned on ground-truth answers, with an ablation finding a 10% injection rate optimal since higher rates cause training collapse from misleading reward signals (Section 5, Ablation Studies).
On language-only reasoning, LaViDa-R1 improves GSM8K accuracy from 47.4 to 81.5 and Math-500 from 23.4 to 38.6 relative to the base model (Section 4, Experiments).

FXy0GCaHq1.text: World-Shaper introduces a Generate-Then-Edit paradigm in which a controllable panorama generator first synthesizes diverse scenes to produce paired training data for a supervised panoramic editing model, addressing the scarcity of paired panoramic editing data (Section on Method / Generate-Then-Edit Paradigm).

The framework performs editing directly in the equirectangular projection (ERP) domain using position-aware shape constraints that combine distortion-aware attention modulation and a layered shape loss with latitude-dependent supervision (Section on Geometry-Aware Learning Strategy).

On the introduced PEBench benchmark (200 panoramas, 100 real and 100 synthetic, 1,000 test pairs across five editing tasks), World-Shaper achieves the best FID (45.25) and the best VIEScore overall (8.01) among 8 baseline methods including Qwen-Image-Edit, FLUX.1 Kontext, GPT-5, and Omni2 (Experiments/Benchmark section, PEBench results).

World-Shaper attains the highest CLIP Direction Score (19.62) among all compared methods on PEBench, and ranks first in a user study across image quality, distortion accuracy, and text alignment (Experiments section, quantitative and user-study results).

Training uses a three-stage progressive curriculum (global structure learning, localized object generation, supervised editing) built on Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 with rank-32 LoRA at 512x1024 resolution, requiring approximately 48 hours on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs (Section on Training Configuration).

iL4Uo9HeXc.text: On QM9, FlexiFlow achieves 100.0% atom stability, 99.9% molecular stability, 99.9% validity, and 100.0% uniqueness using 100 inference steps (NFE) (Table 1).

On GEOM Drugs, FlexiFlow achieves 99.9% atom stability, 99.9% molecular stability, 92.0% validity, 100.0% uniqueness, and 99.9% novelty, matching or exceeding prior methods SemlaFlow, EQGAT-diff, and MiDi (Table 2).

FlexiFlow's conformer ensembles achieve coverage competitive with the physics-based reference method CREST while requiring only a fraction of CREST's computational cost, as shown by precision-recall coverage curves compared against Adjoint Sampling (Figure 4).

When transferred to protein-conditioned generation on PDBBind without paired conformational training data, FlexiFlow identifies improved Vina docking scores in 2,124 of 13,440 ligand pairs, achieving an average top-1 Vina score of -7.4 kcal/mol (Section on Protein-Conditioned Generation).

FlexiFlow models range from 17.2M (Small) to 37.7M (Large) parameters, trained for 40 epochs on ~100k molecules for QM9 and 4 epochs on ~5.8M molecules for GEOM Drugs (Section on Training Efficiency).

nggzekChuU.text: On the DNALONGBENCH eQTL prediction task, OpticalDNA's linear probe achieves an average AUROC of 0.852 across 9 GTEx tissues, versus 0.514 for HyenaDNA and 0.791 for JanusDNA (DNALONGBENCH eQTL results section).
OpticalDNA exceeds a 985x-larger expert model (AUROC 0.681) on the eQTL task while using only 256K trainable parameters for the linear probe (DNALONGBENCH eQTL results section).

On RiceSubBench, OpticalDNA achieves the best accuracy on all splits, including 0.590 on in-domain japonica and 0.599 on far-OOD glaberrima, beating LucaOne's 0.526 on the far-OOD split by +13.88% (RiceSubBench results section).

On RiceWGPB whole-genome phenotype prediction over ~400M-base genomes, OpticalDNA completes inference in 12.3 minutes, versus 32.5 minutes for LucaOne (1.8B parameters) and 5 hours 40 minutes for Evo-2 (7B parameters) (RiceWGPB results section).

OpticalDNA's visual rendering of DNA achieves a 19.0-21.2x compression ratio from bases to visual tokens, yielding best overall genomic benchmark performance with nearly 20x fewer effective tokens on sequences up to 450k bases (Token Efficiency section).

OpticalDNA is pretrained on 6 OCR-style primitive tasks (T1-T6: free-form transcription, text+localization, ROI transcription, masked completion, subsequence retrieval, and chromosome classification) using a SAM-Conv-CLIP-L visual encoder and a DeepSeek-3B document decoder with 570M activated parameters (Pretraining Tasks / Architecture Components section).

ra2t1V4nml.text: MIRA's Uniform Mass Property (Proposition 3.1) establishes that the probability mass lambda_n assigned to randomly constructed regions follows a Uniform[0,1] distribution when the candidate matches the true conditional distribution.

Under the null hypothesis of a correctly specified candidate distribution, the Mira statistic reduces to Laplace's rule of succession, p(k|n) = (n+1)/(N+2) for k=1 and (N-n+1)/(N+2) for k=0 (Proposition 3.2).
As N approaches infinity under correct model specification, the expected Mira score converges to 2/3 with theoretical variance converging to 1/18 (Corollary 3.4).
Proposition 3.5 proves a lower bound that any candidate model achieves a Mira score mu_Mira(M) >= 1/2.

In a Bayesian model comparison experiment on four strong gravitational lensing forward models in 13 dimensions, MIRA correctly ranks the true model (EPL plus 3 Sersic sources) as the best fit (Section 5.3, Bayesian Model Comparison).
In a high-dimensional robustness test on 64x64x3 galaxy images, MIRA detects prior and noise-model misspecification using as few as L=16 true fiducial samples (Section 5.3).

stDqIrBoRO.text: LithoGRPO attains the lowest average rank (4.3) across four inverse lithography benchmark datasets compared to optimization-based and learning-based baselines, whose best average rank is 5.6 (Table 1).

The fast shot-counting algorithm achieves a 134.6x to 491.3x speedup over the traditional shot-count implementation while preserving mask ranking, with correlation R^2=0.994 between fast and traditional metrics (Table 3, Figure 9).
One-step inference from the RLFT model matches or beats multi-step sampling variants while being 22x to 10x faster at inference time (Table 2).

Training combines a rectified-flow pretraining stage, a supervised fine-tuning stage using differentiable L2 and PVB metrics, and a GRPO-based reinforcement fine-tuning stage with a reward combining normalized L2, PVB, EPE, and Shot metrics (Section 3, Equations 9-14).
Full model training completes in under 8 hours on four NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs, with single-step inference taking about 0.1 seconds per sample (Section 3).

AGBuhcQbsO.text: Deep Pre-Alignment (DPA) improves average performance across 8 multimodal benchmarks by 1.9 points at the 4B target-LLM scale (Qwen3-4B) and by 3.0 points at the 32B scale (Qwen3-32B) relative to baselines (Section 3.2).

DPA reduces text-capability forgetting after instruction tuning by 32.9% relative reduction (+7.5 points) at the 4B scale and 21.6% relative reduction (+5.0 points) at the 32B scale, measured over text benchmarks (Section 3.2, Section 4).

DPA replaces the standard frozen ViT encoder with a small perceiver VLM (Qwen3-0.6B) whose Perceiver Language Blocks align visual and text representations before the main two-stage LLaVA-style training (Section 2.1-2.2).

At the 32B scale, DPA increases total parameters by only about 2% and training cost by about 2%, while retaining about 98% of baseline inference throughput (Section 4, computational efficiency analysis).

Layer-wise modality-gap analysis shows the gap between text and visual representations narrows progressively across perceiver layers, correlating with downstream multimodal performance (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 5).

wSfc8mDEjM.text: On VBench, PISCES achieves a total score of 82.75 on VideoCrafter2 and 85.45 on HunyuanVideo, outperforming both annotation-based and annotation-free text-to-video baselines on Quality (84.05/86.73) and Semantic (77.54/80.33) subscores (Table 1).

The Dual OT-aligned Rewards module combines a Distributional OT-aligned Quality Reward, which aligns text embeddings to the real-video distribution via neural optimal transport, with a Discrete Token-level OT-aligned Semantic Reward computed via entropic Sinkhorn-solved partial optimal transport over spatio-temporal cost matrices (Sections 3.1-3.2).

The rewards are compatible with two distinct optimization paradigms: direct backpropagation through consistency distillation and GRPO-based reinforcement learning fine-tuning (Section 3.3, Equations 5-6).

An ablation study shows the OT-based reward components outperform non-OT alternatives, and OT-aligned representations achieve the highest Mutual KNN score (0.2597) and Spearman correlation (0.9018) in a quantitative alignment analysis (Table 3, Table 4).
A human preference study shows evaluators consistently prefer PISCES-generated videos over baselines across visual quality, motion quality, and semantic alignment dimensions (Figure 3).

mJEVzcuDNF.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes a sufficient condition for discrete-time scalable input-to-state stability (sISS) of delayed interconnected systems using vector Lyapunov-Razumikhin functions (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

A two-stage verification strategy (Theorem 5.3) splits the state space into an 'outside' region verified via Razumikhin logic on reachable delay histories and an 'inside' region with strengthened contraction guarantees, with Theorem 5.8 reducing infinite-dimensional verification to finitely many checks via uniform grid sampling and Lipschitz margins (Section 5, Theorems 5.3 and 5.8).

Certificate reuse theorems (5.10, 5.12) allow systems with substructure isomorphism or structurally equivalent nodes to inherit or share certificates without re-verification, enabling scalability to larger interconnected systems (Section 5).

For N=50 subsystems, verification completes in 370.7±1.3 seconds for mixed-autonomy platoons, 1044.3±20.0 seconds for drone formations, and 1999.3±4.6 seconds for microgrids, versus timeouts for direct/reachability-only verification baselines (Table 1, Section 6).

The proposed controller reduces RMSE by 22.86% at 4 m/s and 20.18% at 7 m/s disturbance in the platoon case, and by 12.20% at 0.5 rad/s and 2.92% at 1 rad/s in the microgrid case, compared to nominal control (Table 2, Table 4).

tYUt9ffVcD.text: Theorem 2 (Section 4) shows GRASP-NC achieves a near-optimal non-convex stochastic optimization convergence rate up to logarithmic factors, fully agnostic to smoothness, gap, and noise parameters (Theorem 2, Section 4).

Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 (Section 5) show GRASP-C attains accelerated convergence combined with an ensemble error term in the convex smooth case (Option-I) and maintains universality for Holder-smooth convex objectives without requiring a lower-bound assumption on problem parameters (Option-II), unlike the prior state-of-the-art U-DoG method (Theorems 3-4, Table 1b).

Self-bounding analysis (Section 3.1) derives parameter search ranges by comparing target convergence rates against trivial benchmark rates, guaranteeing non-vacuous bounds without any knowledge of smoothness, initial distance, or noise level.

Table 2 (Section 5.1) shows the ensemble/model-averaging guarantee achieves gap-dependent variance reduction of the form sqrt(V0/sqrt(M)) + (sigma_l+V1) log(N/delta)/M, improving over the uniform-averaging rate of sigma_l/sqrt(M).

Experiments (Tables 3-5, Section 6) show GRASP achieves a relative performance gap rho in [0.08, 0.23] compared to optimally hyperparameter-tuned baselines, while remaining robust to a reduced number of initial sampling rounds.

o9NThz6auq.text: Trap² introduces a scaling-sensitive loss landscape that acts as a proxy for the model-merging operation, causing merged weights to degrade in performance while standalone fine-tuned weights remain effective (Section 3, Methodology).

The framework is evaluated against merging-defense and merging baselines including TIES-Merging (Yadav et al. 2023) and task-arithmetic/model-editing approaches (Ilharco et al.), as well as LoRA-based fine-tuning (Hu et al. 2022) (Section 5, Experimental Evaluation).

Trap² is shown to be architecture-agnostic, embedding protection into the fine-tuning update itself so it survives regardless of the model's release format, and results are reported across vision benchmarks such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet (Section 5-6, Tables 4-9).

Ablation studies in the appendices examine how varying the scaling-sensitivity parameters and loss-landscape modification strength affects resistance to unauthorized merging (Appendices A-D, Tables 18-27).

KS6RbZMt8L.text: For the smooth, strongly convex regime with mixed affine constraints, Theorem 4.1 gives an optimal communication complexity of O(√κ_f √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} √κ_W log(1/ε)) that matches established lower complexity bounds (Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 4.6 provides a unified complexity bound O(√κ_f (√κ̃_{AC} + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}) √κ_W log(1/ε)) covering problems with simultaneously coupled (global) and local affine constraints (Theorem 4.6).

The paper analyzes both smooth objectives (Theorem 2.4) and non-smooth objectives via a Gradient Sliding algorithm (Algorithm 2), each under mixed affine constraints (Section 2, Section 4, Algorithm 2).

The proposed framework is motivated by and applied to horizontal federated learning (consensus constraints), vertical federated learning (shared/global-variable constraints), and multi-task learning with node-specific local constraints (Section 1, Applications).

An accelerated proximal alternating predictor-corrector method (Algorithm 1, APAPC) is used as the core building block for achieving the optimal rates in Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.5 (Algorithm 1, Theorem 4.5).

GfJao7wf4s.text: LMM4-IC4K (referred to in-text as LLM4-IC8K) achieves 71.6±0.5% IoU_IC on IC footprint labeling versus 11.1±0.4% for GPT-4o and 4.5±0.1% for Gemini 2.0, the strongest general-purpose LMM baselines (Table with per-model IoU_IC, Task 1 MAE, Task 2 d_pin, Task 3 IoU_pin results).

The ICGeo8K dataset contains 8,608 labeled IC footprint samples, comprising 4,138 hand-crafted real-world samples and 4,470 synthetically generated samples, collected from datasheets/EDA sources (Digi-Key, UltraLibrarian) and covering 10 package types with pin counts from 1 to 800.

A held-out benchmark, ICGeoQA, of 400 curated real-world IC entries is excluded from training and used for unbiased evaluation of the three sub-tasks: pin counting, pin positioning, and pin dimensioning.

The model is built via a two-stage training pipeline on Qwen2-VL-7B with LoRA: synthetic pretraining (4,470 samples, 3 epochs) followed by real-world fine-tuning (4,138 samples, 3 epochs), with synthetic pretraining alone improving real-world IoU by about 10 percentage points.

Chain-of-thought ordering of the three sub-questions (pin count, then position, then size) yields a 12.8% performance gain over training the sub-tasks independently, and the method generates a complete IC footprint in 0.26 minutes/sample, up to 58x faster than EDA tools such as Altium (7 min) or EAGLE/KiCAD (15 min).

wjNTbZKIvC.text: RE-TRAC-30B-A3B scores 53.0% on BrowseComp, 78.2% on GAIA, and 83.0% on XBench, surpassing the Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B baseline (43.4% BrowseComp, 70.9% GAIA, 75.0% XBench) (Table 2).
On BrowseComp300 with test-time scaling, Re-TRAC's RT@8 variant reaches 69.8% for o3 and 66.6% for GPT-5, outperforming majority-voting (MV@8) and Best@8 baselines for the same models (Table 3).

Supervised fine-tuning on Re-TRAC trajectories raises the 4B model's BrowseComp300 score from 2.7% (before SFT) to 30.0% (after SFT), demonstrating that Re-TRAC-aware SFT lets a smaller model reach performance competitive with larger frontier-model baselines (Table 4).

Analysis of failure cases shows 83-93% of unsuccessful trajectories contain branches the model planned to explore but forgot to pursue, motivating Re-TRAC's structured state representation of answers, evidence base, and unexplored branches after each trajectory (Table 1).

Re-TRAC achieves higher accuracy while consuming roughly 50% of the token and tool-call usage of independent-trajectory baselines, reflecting progressively targeted exploration rather than linear scaling of resources (Figure 5).

hCgb0FIoVa.text: R2R2 improves TD7's normalized score from 1.02 to 1.24 (about 22%) at Update-to-Data ratio 20, with an especially large gain on DMC-Hard tasks (1.02 to 1.32) (Table 1).

Adding R2R2 to SimbaV2-SPL raises its UTD=20 score from 1.34 (already a new state-of-the-art without R2R2) to 1.38, showing R2R2's gains are complementary to state-of-the-art architectural improvements (Table 1).

Proposition 2 proves that standard zero-centering (as used in VICReg-style redundancy reduction) eliminates the dominant eigenmode u₁ that encodes global transition dynamics information, motivating R2R2's non-centered redundancy-reduction loss (Proposition 2).

R2R2 is evaluated across 11 continuous-control tasks spanning 4 OpenAI Gym MuJoCo environments and 7 DMC-Hard environments, using fixed hyperparameters (λ_RR = λ_Var = 0.01) across all tasks without per-environment tuning.

Comparison against TD7 with Layer Normalization (0.88 to 1.10 with R2R2) shows R2R2 addresses a distinct representation-collapse mechanism from architectural normalization, and ablations confirm both the variance and redundancy-reduction loss terms are necessary for stability under high UTD (Table 1, Ablation studies).

mHhdnUufwR.text: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet18, DUNE achieves 13.26% test accuracy with no defense applied, compared to 18.26%-31.41% for the 12 baseline unlearnable example schemes (Table 1).

Against the ISS-J defense on CIFAR-10, DUNE limits test accuracy to 28.88% versus 40.87%-81.58% for baseline methods, and the average test accuracy across all 7 defenses is 23.29%, the lowest among 13 compared methods (Table 1).
On ImageNet-100 with ResNet18, DUNE yields 6.78% test accuracy without defense and an average of 16.67% across the 7 evaluated defenses (Table 2).

The dual-branch design combines a spatial branch using T=30-step projected gradient descent with epsilon=8/255 and a color branch using particle swarm optimization over class-wise luminance offsets constrained by PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS (Section 4.3, Equations 9-13).

An ablation removing the color branch increases average test accuracy from 19.67% to 31.15% on ResNet18, demonstrating the necessity of the dual-branch (spatial + color) optimization for robustness (Table 4).

The ensemble module averages gradients across M=5 pre-trained surrogate models to reduce model-specific bias, and DUNE maintains test accuracy below 30% under an adaptive defense combining spatial and color countermeasures (Section 5.5, Equation 16).

dyqFW9lJgQ.text: TEDFusion projects visual and text features onto a Poincare ball via exponential mappings and Mobius translation, using BLIP-extracted text prompts as topological anchors during training while operating text-free at inference (Section 3.3, Equations 1-3).

The Attribute and Text Gating Fusion Module (ATGFM) extracts four attribute pairs (saturation, brightness, texture complexity, contrast) and fuses them with text-derived features via a sigmoid-gated MLP, g(.)=sigma(MLP([Xa,Xt])) (Section 3.2).

On the RoadScene dataset, TEDFusion attains SD=60.85 and SF=13.88, compared to Text-IF's SD=46.70 and SF=10.39, evaluated across TNO, RoadScene, MSRS, and LLVIP using EN, SD, SF, AG, and SCD metrics (Table 1).

An ablation replacing the hyperbolic Text-Image Association Module with a Euclidean variant reduces SF from 10.90 (full method, curvature c=1.0) to 10.05, and removing text supervision entirely reduces SF to 7.95 (Table 2).

On downstream object detection on M3FD, TEDFusion-fused images yield mAP@0.5=57.37 versus GIFNet's 50.28, and on MSRS semantic segmentation TEDFusion achieves mIoU=69.64 versus Text-IF's 68.25 (Table 3).

QdmL5vs0sg.text: DLEBench contains 1,889 samples (1,771 single-object and 118 multi-object edits, up to 8 targets per image) spanning seven instruction types, with target objects constrained to 1%-10% of image area, built from MME-Realworld, Pixel-Reasoner, and V*-Bench source images (Benchmark Construction section).

Under the Oracle-guided evaluation mode, Gemini-3-Pro scores highest among 10 evaluated instruction-based image editing models at 65.55 average, followed by Bagel-Think at 61.00, while MagicBrush scores lowest at 23.16 (Table 1).
All 10 evaluated models score lowest on the 'Change Count' instruction type, ranging from 8.34 to 45.84, indicating object-count editing is the hardest small-scale editing task (Table 1).

Broken down by criterion, Gemini-3-Pro leads Instruction Following at 48.97, while GPT-Image-1 scores notably low on Visual Consistency at 35.17 despite most models scoring 51.00-86.43 on that criterion (Table 4).

The Oracle-guided evaluation mode achieves the highest correlation with human judgments and lowest MAE compared to Tool-driven mode and standard LMM-as-a-Judge, validating the benchmark's automated scoring protocol (Figure 8).
Inter-annotator agreement measured by Krippendorff's Alpha is at least 0.79 across all seven instruction types, supporting the reliability of the human-verified annotations (Table 2).

BfkrQiC0Ss.text: Dirichlet-Prior Shaping Loss (DPSL) aligns empirical routing-probability distributions with target Dirichlet priors using a Cramer-von Mises criterion between empirical CDFs and theoretical Beta CDFs per expert category, weighted by hyperparameter lambda (Section 2.2, Equation 4).

Across three backbones (Qwen2-1.5B, Llama3.2-1B, Phi3-mini 3.8B) with 2in4 and 8in16 upcycled MoE configurations, DPSL achieves the highest average performance on six vision-language benchmarks (TextVQA, GQA, MM-Vet, MME-Perception/Cognition, VizWiz, MMBench), outperforming sparse upcycling, drop-upcycling, load-balancing, z-loss, and DeepSeek balancing losses (Section 3.3, Table 1).

On Llama3.2-1B (2in4), DPSL with modality-aware asymmetric Dirichlet priors slightly outperforms symmetric DPSL, while manual modality-specific routing and Branch-Train-MiX task specialization both underperform symmetric DPSL (Section 3.4, Table 2).

An ablation on Llama3.2-1B shows the Dirichlet concentration parameter alpha=0.75 yields optimal performance, suggesting a benefit from priors encouraging slightly sparser-than-uniform routing (Appendix C.1, Table 4).
A regularization-weight ablation identifies lambda=0.01 as optimal among {0.001, 0.01, 0.1} (Appendix C.3, Table 7).

Routing-score distribution analysis shows standard regularization methods produce distributions sharply peaked around the uniform selection probability, whereas DPSL produces noticeably broader and more varied distributions, indicating improved expert differentiation (Section 3.6).

E4CNyyUDSD.text: MultiPriv comprises 40 synthetic individual profiles, 719 images, 36 subcategories of sensitive attributes across 7 major privacy categories, and 7,414 bilingual (Chinese/English) VQA pairs organized into 9 subtasks spanning perception and reasoning levels (Benchmark Construction, Table 2).

Among evaluated open-source VLMs, Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking attains 0.874 overall reasoning performance, with 0.878 on English chained reasoning versus 0.731 on Chinese chained reasoning, and 16 of 18 evaluated models exceed 0.8 on at least one reasoning task (Table 4).

Commercial VLM perception scores range from 0.342 to 0.579 (Gemini-2.5-Pro highest at 0.579) while reasoning scores for the same models range from 0.456 to 0.825, showing perception-level metrics are poor predictors of individual-level reasoning risk (Table 3, Table 4).
Model scale does not correlate linearly with privacy-reasoning risk: Qwen3-VL-4B scores 0.871, matching the 32B variant's 0.874 (Section on Key Experimental Findings).

Safety alignment is imbalanced across privacy risk: GPT-5 refuses 50.60% of queries yet still exhibits a reasoning score of 0.409, while Qwen3-VL-8B refuses only 0.51% of queries with a higher reasoning score of 0.768 (Section 4.3).

YMA0ByEdVj.text: Across 13 frontier LLM agents evaluated on the CoreRHB benchmark, measured exploit rates range from 0.0% for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.5 up to 13.9% for DeepSeek-R1-Zero (Table 2).

In a controlled sibling comparison, the SFT-focused DeepSeek-V3 shows a 0.6% overall exploit rate versus 13.9% for the RL-from-base DeepSeek-R1-Zero, a 13.3 percentage-point gap attributed to RL-dominated post-training (Table 3).

CoreRHB comprises four task families (Data Pipeline, Log Forensics, Performance Optimization, and Multi-file Reconstruction), each with 6-step dependency chains enforced via hash recomputation, plus a 12-task MicroRHB calibration suite with 50 instances per task (Section on benchmark scope).
Exploit rates rise sharply starting at chain step 5, where agents first encounter unverifiable steps under hidden-split grading (Table 1).
Environmental hardening reduces the exploit rate from 6.5% to 0.8% (an 87.7% relative reduction) while leaving task success rate statistically unchanged (83.2% to 82.8%) (Table 4).
Six exploit categories are identified in a taxonomy, with sequence manipulation (31% of exploits) and proxy gaming (24% of exploits) the two most common types (Appendix A).

RAULvuDNNP.text: The Think-Then-Generate model attains a 0.79 score on the WISE benchmark, a 30% relative improvement over the Qwen-Image baseline (0.61) and nearly matching GPT-4o (0.80) (Table 1).
On T2I-ReasonBench the model scores 68.3 accuracy and 92.2 quality, outperforming open-source baselines such as Bagel and Janus-Pro-7B (Table 2).

Dual-GRPO jointly optimizes the LLM encoder and diffusion transformer as a two-stage policy using image-grounded rewards, combining a semantic-consistency reward for the LLM stage with a weighted aesthetic/consistency/semantic reward for the DiT stage (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
Ablations show WISE score rising from 0.65 (no SFT, GRPO only) to 0.74 (SFT only) to 0.79 (full SFT plus Dual-GRPO pipeline) (Table 4).
A balanced reward scheduler with beta_1 = beta_2 = 0.5 outperforms staged alternatives on T2I-ReasonBench (Table 5, Appendix).
On UniREditBench image editing, the model scores 68.7, surpassing Gemini-2.5-Flash-Image's 68.3 (Table 3).

qRNtMWrTvo.text: Under the heaviest scale setting, UltraHorizon trajectories average over 200k tokens and 400+ tool calls, while standard configurations still exceed 35k tokens and involve more than 60 tool calls on average (Section 1, Table 1).

On fixed-step evaluation, Gemini-2.5-Pro achieves the highest average score among five LLMs (GLM-4.5, Kimi-K2, DeepSeek-V3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-235b) on both Mystery Grid (17.06) and Alien Genetics Laboratory (14.00), yet all models remain far below the human baselines of 24.29 and 47.50 respectively (Figure 3).
An ablation on the Mystery Grid environment shows GLM-4.5's normalized score declining monotonically from 34.4% at horizon level n=1 to 5.62% at n=5 as the number of hidden rules increases (Table 2).

A trajectory failure analysis identifies a two-level categorization of eight/nine recurring error patterns (e.g., repetitive looping, premature convergence, incoherent planning, environment mis-modeling) attributed to two root causes: in-context locking and foundational capability gaps (Section 5, Figure 7).

A proposed Context Refresh with Notes Recall (CRNR) scaling strategy, which clears dialogue history and has the agent consult self-maintained notes once context limits are approached, is shown to outperform naive step-scaling in the Mystery Grid and Sequence Exploration environments (Section 4.4.2, Figure 5).

6I7yMzQBts.text: BioFormer is evaluated against 12 baseline architectures (including Transformer, Reformer, Informer, Autoformer, FEDformer, Nonformer, PatchTST, Crossformer, iTransformer, MTST, Medformer, and SoftShape) across six EEG/ECG datasets: APAVA, ADFTD, BCI-2a, BCI-2b, PTB, and PTB-XL (Section on experimental results).

BioFormer achieves up to 6% absolute F1-score improvement over baselines for cross-subject generalization, including roughly +5% F1 on both ADFTD and PTB relative to the prior state-of-the-art SoftShape (Table 2).
BioFormer attains the best average rank (1.47) across 36 evaluation metrics and wins on 4 of the 6 datasets tested (Table 2).

The core method combines a Frequency-Band Alignment Module (FBAM) that performs band-wise magnitude scaling and phase rotation in the Fourier domain, a Sample Conditional Layer Normalization (SCLN) for subject-adaptive calibration without explicit subject labels, and a Pyramid Convolutional Embedding (PCE) for multi-scale temporal features (Section on core method).

tBt12b9dxa.text: Spectral Evolution Search (SES) is a plug-and-play, gradient-free evolutionary search framework that optimizes initial noise within a low-frequency subspace for inference-time alignment of image generation models (abstract only).
The method is motivated by an identified spectral bias in generative dynamics, where model sensitivity to initial-noise perturbations decreases with frequency (abstract only).

A theoretical result termed the Spectral Scaling Prediction, derived from perturbation propagation dynamics, explains systematic differences in the impact of perturbations across frequencies (abstract only).
SES consistently outperforms strong baselines under equivalent computational budgets for reward-aligned image generation (abstract only).
SES significantly advances the Pareto frontier of generation quality versus computational cost compared to existing inference-time scaling approaches (abstract only).
