R0eRg4p4Uj.text: Entropic Particle Filtering (ePF) adaptively adjusts the resampling temperature via Entropic Annealing, using the formula β⁻¹ₜ = (N/ESS(t))(1-t/T) so that low effective sample size (ESS) triggers flatter resampling to preserve exploration (Section 3.2, Figure 4).
ePF's Look-ahead Modulation (LaM) mechanism samples one-step successors to evaluate trajectory potential non-myopically before resampling particles (Section 3.3, Figure 5).
On AIME-2025 with Qwen3-1.7B, ePF with LaM achieves 26.97% pass@1 versus 19.10% for the baseline particle filter (Table 4).
On AIME-2024 with Qwen2.5-7B, ePF reaches 26.23% on the weighted metric versus 21.60% for baseline PF (Table 2).
ePF attains up to 50% relative improvement in task reward across math benchmarks including GSM8K, MATH500, DeepMath, OmniMath, AIME-2024, and AIME-2025 (Section 4).
Performance correlates strongly with particle diversity as measured by ESS, with higher ESS yielding better solution quality (Figure 2c, Section 4.5).

nPzckCXmHE.text: Under the null hypothesis of conditional independence, the proposed test statistic T̂_n converges in distribution to a chi-squared distribution with d² degrees of freedom as sample sizes m,n→∞ (Theorem 4.1).

The paper establishes a non-asymptotic power guarantee showing the test achieves power 1-δ when the separation threshold satisfies ϵ²_n ≥ 2d·ℰ²_m + c(d²+log(δ⁻¹))/n, tying power jointly to representation learning error ℰ_m and sample size n (Theorem 4.2).

The representation learning error ℰ_m is defined via a max over four operator-norm discrepancy terms involving the estimated partial covariance and whitening conditions (Equation 9), and this single quantity controls both null-hypothesis validity and alternative-hypothesis power.

Algorithm 1 uses bi-level contrastive learning with learned representations u_θ, v_θ, w_θ plus empirical whitening to estimate the leading spectral features of the partial covariance operator Σ_{XY·Z}.

Validity of the chi-squared asymptotic null distribution requires Assumption 4.1, sub-Gaussianity of the learned representations, to enable the concentration arguments bounding representation error (Assumption 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

juGAf5Y7V2.text: The OpenGPT-4o-Image dataset contains 80,000 instruction-image pairs spanning 11 domains and 51 subtasks, split roughly evenly between 5 image-generation domains and 6 image-editing domains (Tables 9-10, Appendix A).
Fine-tuning UniWorld-V1 on OpenGPT-4o-Image raises its ImgEdit-Bench overall score from 3.26 to 3.86, an 18% relative improvement (Table 2).
Fine-tuning Harmon on OpenGPT-4o-Image raises its GenEval overall score from 0.76 to 0.86, a 13% relative improvement (Table 3).
The image-editing portion of the dataset includes a Subject Manipulation subtask with roughly 19k samples, the largest single subtask category (Tables 9-10).
Beyond UniWorld-V1 and Harmon, the paper also evaluates fine-tuning effects on OmniGen2, OmniGen, and MagicBrush across GEdit-Bench and DPG-Bench (Section on additional model results).

PysPgClt8e.text: On AlpacaEval-2 length-controlled win rate with Mistral-7B-Instruct as base, RSPO (IS-Forward + Reverse KL) improves iteration-3 performance from unregularized SPPO's 28.53% to 35.44% (Section 5.1, Table 2).
On the same Mistral-7B AlpacaEval-2 comparison, RSPO's 35.4% LCWR exceeds Snorkel iterative DPO's 26.4% and SimPO's 32.1% (Table 1).
RSPO achieves 22.9% on Arena-Hard Auto-v0.1, versus SimPO's 21.0%, and 7.75 on MT-Bench versus the Mistral-7B base model's 7.51 (Table 1).
RSPO with Reverse KL regularization reduces Self-BLEU response-diversity score from unregularized SPPO's 0.758 to 0.691 at iteration 3, indicating higher response diversity (Table 2).
The regularization methodology is formalized in Section 4.3 with a convergence guarantee given in Proposition 4.1 (Section 4.2).

Ym6ud8Psx1.text: Dream-MPC optimizes action sequences rolled out from a policy network in latent space via gradient ascent rather than sampling-based search (Section 4).
Dream-MPC is evaluated on 24 continuous control tasks spanning DeepMind Control Suite, HumanoidBench, and Meta-World (Section 5.1).
With a BMPC base, Dream-MPC yields a 26.7% IQM improvement and a 20.5% mean improvement over baseline BMPC (Figure 1, Section 5.1).
Dream-MPC requires only 15 model evaluations per timestep, versus 9,216 for MPPI (5×1×3 vs 512×6×3 evaluations) (Section 5.1).
Dream-MPC's uncertainty regularization penalizes high-uncertainty trajectories using an ensemble of Q-functions with coefficient λ_unc = 0.01 applied uniformly across tasks (Equations 4-5).

Integrated with a TD-MPC2 base, Dream-MPC achieves a 144.7% IQM gain but still underperforms MPPI due to weak initial policy quality, whereas with a Dreamer integration it outperforms all baselines including gradient-free variants (Section 5.4, Table 3).

PnHfrCMKtp.text: Increasing horizon length alone (independent of reasoning complexity) causes training collapse in RL-trained LLM agents, driven by exploration difficulty and credit assignment challenges (Figure 2).
On Sudoku tasks with goal distance levels L1-L4 used for training, REINFORCE-based RL succeeds on levels L1-L2 but fails to train on levels L3-L4 with atomic actions (Figure 2).

Horizon reduction via macro actions (executing multiple atomic actions per training step) stabilizes RL training on long-horizon Sudoku levels L3-L4 relative to atomic-action baselines (Figure 2, Section on macro actions).

Subgoal decomposition, which breaks long-horizon tasks into verifiable segments, is presented as a second horizon-reduction mechanism that mitigates the same training bottleneck as macro actions (Section on horizon reduction).

Qwen3-1.7B agents trained with reduced horizon on shorter goal-distance curricula (d=4-9) generalize to solving longer-horizon test instances (d=10-12 and levels L5-L7, goal distance 31-45) at inference time (Section on horizon generalization).
The horizon-reduction findings are validated on a second domain, the Rush Hour sliding-block puzzle, in addition to the primary Sudoku testbed (Section on validation domain / Rush Hour).

u4klflLAX3.text: The quantum triangle listing algorithm runs in time Õ(min(n^(5/4)t^(7/12) + n^(7/6)t^(7/9), m + m^(3/4)t^(1/2), n^(3/2)t^(1/2))) for a graph with n vertices, m edges, and t triangles (Theorem 1.3).

The quantum triangle cut sparsification algorithm constructs an epsilon-triangle cut sparsifier with Õ(n/epsilon^2) edges in time T_q-list + Õ(sqrt(mn)/epsilon), where T_q-list is the quantum triangle listing runtime (Theorem 1.2).
Every epsilon-triangle cut sparsifier requires at least Omega(n/epsilon^2) edges, establishing the near-optimality of the algorithm's sparsifier size (Theorem 5.2).

The quantum triangle listing algorithm combines a heavy-light vertex partition (using Grover search over light-vertex neighborhoods) with a quantum walk extension of Le Gall's triangle detection algorithm on Johnson graphs (Section on algorithmic techniques).
The post-sampling stage of the sparsification algorithm reduces complexity from Õ(m) to Õ(sqrt(mn)/epsilon) via an implicit random string encoding technique (Section on post-sampling).

qC9FEfYjai.text: Theorem 3.2 establishes that any function in L^2 over categorical inputs admits a Fourier expansion using basis functions phi_A^(z), defined via a signed inverse-likelihood construction, that automatically satisfy hierarchical orthogonality (Theorem 3.2).
When the empirical support equals the full hypergrid, the exact ANOVA decomposition is obtained by solving the linear system Gamma c(f) = mu(f) (Section on full-support decomposition).

For sparse empirical support of cardinality r much smaller than the full hypergrid size |E|, Algorithm 1 greedily selects basis elements to yield decomposition computation in O(r^3) rather than O(|E|^3) (Algorithm 1).

On the Mushrooms dataset (22 categorical variables, hypergrid size approximately 10^14), the method achieves near-perfect reconstruction (R^2 approximately 1, MSE approximately 10^-15) in 0.3 seconds (Experimental results section).
On binarized MNIST (784 dimensions), the method achieves R^2 = 0.86 in 15 minutes using 10,000 basis elements (Experimental results section).
Equation (5) defines generalized SHAP values as shap_i(x) = sum over sets A containing i of f_A(x_A)/|A|, which exactly recovers standard SHAP values in the independent-features setting (Equation 5).

S12HAKrQG3.text: Caracal replaces self-attention with a Multi-Head Fourier (MHF) module achieving O(L log L) complexity in sequence length L, versus O(L^2) for standard attention (Section describing the MHF module).

Caracal enforces autoregressive causality entirely in the frequency domain using asymmetric padding and truncation after the FFT, rather than relying on an explicit causal attention mask (Section on frequency-domain causal masking).

The Caracal architecture retains sliding-window attention layers alongside MHF layers at a 2:1 ratio, and this ratio is identified as optimal, achieving 43.35% average accuracy in the Small model configuration (Table 6).
The large Caracal model achieves 49.01% average accuracy on language understanding benchmarks, comparable to Llama, Mamba, and Jamba baselines (Table 2).
At a context length of 8192 tokens, Caracal runs approximately 2.7x faster than Llama while matching the performance of linear-complexity SSM baselines (Figure 2).

Ablations show sliding-window attention contributes 0.79 percentage points and the pre-convolution stage contributes 0.40 percentage points to average accuracy, while explicit positional encodings provide negligible additional gains (Table 5).

OL0Vx2FV1g.text: The paper introduces the PRO-DYN framework, decomposing time-series forecasting architectures into a processing (PRO) function and a dynamics (DYN) function, and classifies existing models by whether their DYN function is learnable (Table 1, Section 3).

Under-performing time-series forecasting architectures are shown to have non-learnable or only partially learnable dynamics components, whereas high-performing models (e.g., LSTF-Linear variants) use a learnable linear dynamics function (Table 1).

Adding a learnable linear dynamics layer to Informer, FEDformer, MICN, and FiLM improves or matches performance in more than 80% of tested cases, with an average relative improvement of at least 7% over the vanilla versions (Section 4, RQ1).

Placing the dynamics block at the end of the model (post-processing) is shown to be important: adding linear dynamics at the entry point of iTransformer, PatchTST, and Crossformer instead degrades performance (Section 4, RQ2).
The empirical study evaluates models across 25 datasets from the TFB benchmark, including ETT, Weather, Electricity, Traffic, and Solar, yielding 200 performance scores per model (Section 4).

aiOv6NhF3N.text: PathWise formulates automated heuristic design as a sequential decision process over an entailment graph, where each node stores a tuple of heuristic code, derivation rationale, algorithmic description, performance, and parent metadata (Section 2.2).
On the Traveling Salesman Problem construction framework, PathWise achieves an 8.758% optimality gap at N=100 versus 8.839% for the MCTS-AHD baseline, and 12.276% versus 12.403% at N=200 (Table 1).
On the Knapsack Problem with N=500, W=25, PathWise achieves a 0.05% gap versus 1.88% for MCTS-AHD, an 81.34% mean relative gap improvement on the largest test set (Table 1).
In the Ant Colony Optimization framework, PathWise yields mean relative gap improvements of 60.22% on TSP, 38.73% on CVRP, 89.35% on MKP, and 54.81% on the Orienteering Problem (Table 2).

PathWise converges with fewer evaluations (ne=500) than baseline frameworks (ne=1000) while achieving stronger performance with lower variance, consistently across GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-nano (low and medium reasoning) backbones (Figure 1, Section 4.1).

Ablations show removing the policy critic increases the gap by 1-3%, removing both critic agents increases it by about 5%, and diversity mechanisms raise the Selection Diversity Rate from 53.76% to 75.79% (Section 4.2, Tables 3-4).

tCXxWWBjxQ.text: Ranking objective—pairwise versus pointwise—is identified as the primary determinant of alignment quality among Direct Alignment Algorithms, rather than the specific implicit reward or scalar score formulation (Section 3.2).
On Llama 3.1 8B, ORPO (pairwise) achieves the best AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate of 28.25% and ArenaHard win rate of 20.9%, outperforming pointwise methods (Table 2).

On Llama 3.2 3B, DPO achieves an AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate of 11.43%, and for the larger 8B model pairwise methods consistently outperform pointwise ones on both AlpacaEval 2 and ArenaHard (Section 5.3, RQ3, Table 2).
Adjusting the β parameter changes alignment quality more for scalar-score choice: ORPO improves by +3.46 AlpacaEval 2 points and ASFT improves by +8.27 points under tuned β (Section 5.2).
Using only 10% of the UltraChat dataset for the SFT initialization stage yields nearly the same downstream alignment quality as using the full dataset (Section 5.4).

Figure 3 shows pairwise methods dominate the KL-divergence Pareto front relative to pointwise methods for the larger (8B) model, confirming the primacy of ranking objective over scalar-score choice (Figure 3).

DpIc1cpNKG.text: Theorem 3.2 proves that any limit point of the normalized parameter trajectory θₜ/‖θₜ‖ under normalized steepest descent is the direction of a KKT point of the corresponding max-margin problem (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.3 extends the margin-maximization convergence result to momentum steepest descent under decaying learning rates, using an Approximate Steepest Descent framework introduced in Definition 5.1 (Theorem 3.3, Definition 5.1).
Corollary 3.4 shows Muon, applied simultaneously across weight matrices, is a special case of normalized momentum steepest descent with respect to the matrix spectral norm ‖·‖_msp (Corollary 3.4).
Corollary 3.5 shows Muon-Signum hybrid algorithms exhibit margin maximization with respect to the max of the spectral norm and the ℓ∞ norm (Corollary 3.5).
Theorem 3.6 shows Adam without a stability constant exhibits implicit bias toward ℓ∞-margin maximization under a decaying learning rate regime when c₁ ≥ c₂ (Theorem 3.6).
Theorem 3.1 establishes that under normalized steepest descent with a learning rate schedule satisfying ∫₀^∞ η(t)dt = ∞, the soft margin γ̃(θₜ) increases monotonically (Theorem 3.1).

mtRgrp0u7Z.text: SGLRW replaces the Gaussian noise injection of SGLD with bounded binary/ternary lattice updates, so that stochastic noise enters only through the off-diagonal elements of the discretisation covariance matrix (Section on lattice construction; Lemma 4.3).
Under α-stable heavy-tailed gradient noise with α=1.5, where second moments do not exist, SGLD becomes unstable while SGLRW remains stable across increasing noise scales (Figure 2).
On Bayesian linear regression with N=1000, d=20, at batch size B=8 and step size δ_t=10⁻³, SGLRW attains KL divergence 6.060 versus 19.889 for SGLD (Table 1).

Lemma 4.3 shows the second-moment discretisation error of SGLRW equals the off-diagonal part of SGLD's error matrix, M_SGLRW = offdiag(M_SGLD), eliminating the diagonal noise inflation that afflicts SGLD (Lemma 4.3).
On UCI logistic regression benchmarks, SGLRW achieves consistent KL-divergence improvements over both SGLD and Clipped-SGLD across a range of learning rates (Table 2).
On an LLM sentiment classification task, SGLRW consistently outperforms Clipped-SGLD in predictive quality across varying batch sizes and dataset scales (Figure 5).

9oZh2zQQXi.text: EPC-AW improves average system-level success rate across six benchmarks (Bamboogle, 2Wiki, HotpotQA, Musique, GAIA, MedQA) by 9.75 percentage points over a no-repair baseline (Table 1).
On HotpotQA, EPC-AW raises accuracy from 48.33% to 61.00% (+12.67 points), and on 2Wiki from 39.00% to 51.83% (+12.83 points) (Table 1).
On Musique, EPC-AW improves accuracy from 9.33% to 17.33% (+8.00 points), and on GAIA from 7.09% to 15.22% (+8.13 points) (Table 1).

An ablation on HotpotQA shows the full EPC-AW method reaches 61.00% accuracy versus 49.00% using Information-consistency-based Plan Selection (IPS) alone, indicating the Consistency-guided Epistemic State Refinement (CESR) component provides critical corrective gains (Table 2).
Averaged across benchmarks, EPC-AW (51.38%) outperforms No-Repair (36.52%), Retry (39.41%), and Rollback (41.63%) baselines (Table 2).

9xxnyqiZoO.text: SOAR is a training-free decoding algorithm for diffusion language models (DLMs) that widens the search over unmasking decisions when model confidence is low and collapses to parallel decoding when confidence is high (Section 3.3).

On HumanEval with Dream-7B, SOAR improves generation quality by 5.5% over greedy decoding while achieving a 1.13x speedup, compared to Position Beam Search with single-token unmasking which gains 7.3% but is 0.54x slower than greedy (Table 1).
Averaged across benchmarks, SOAR improves Dream-7B by 2.3% with a 1.43x speedup and improves LLaDA-8B by 1.4% with a 1.62x speedup relative to greedy decoding (Table 1).
On MBPP with Dream-7B, SOAR improves accuracy by 3.6% while achieving a 1.87x speedup over greedy decoding (Table 1).
Alternative unmask-confidence metrics such as Margin and Negative Entropy are evaluated against SOAR's default confidence metric on HumanEval with Dream-7B (Table 2).
SOAR's beam-size sensitivity is characterized on HumanEval with Dream-7B across beam widths from 1 to 4 (Figure 5).

TvskDAb5Uc.text: AlienLM retains over 81% of plaintext-oracle Recovery Ratio on average across four LLM backbones and seven benchmarks, as reported in the main results table (Table 1).

Under adversaries with access to model weights, corpus statistics, and learning-based inverse translation across observer scenarios O1-O3, recovery attacks reconstruct fewer than 0.22% of alienized tokens with BLEU below 12 (Table 3).

Alien Adaptation Training (AAT) adapts target models to operate directly on alienized inputs using only standard fine-tuning APIs, requiring approximately 12 hours on 4xA100 GPUs for a 7B model (Section 3.4, Section 4.1).
Performance versus alienization ratio rho shows a monotonic accuracy improvement as rho decreases, with Pearson correlation r = -0.96 (Figure 2b).
Multi-tenant cross-key transfer achieves 63.69% using a shared oracle key versus 78.67% with per-key specialization (Table 13).
Key diversity analysis shows low pairwise token overlap of approximately 1.41-1.49% across independently generated bijection seeds, supporting the use of distinct per-user keys (Figure 3).

Vbj1jSaqTo.text: C-FREE (Contrast-Free Representation learning on Ego-nets) pretrains by aligning embeddings of complementary k-EgoNet subgraphs in latent space rather than reconstructing input features, using a 2D GINE encoder and a 3D SchNet encoder fused via a Transformer without positional encodings (Section 3).

With frozen backbones, C-FREE's multimodal-linear variant achieves an average ROC-AUC of 71.07 across MoleculeNet datasets including BBBP, Tox21, ToxCast, Sider, ClinTox, MUV, HIV, and Bace (Table 1).
With full fine-tuning, C-FREE's multimodal model achieves an average ROC-AUC of 77.50 on MoleculeNet, surpassing MoleBlend's 76.16 (Table 2).
On the Kraken dataset modality ablation, the multimodal fine-tuned model achieves MAE of 0.193 on the B5 metric, slightly better than the 3D-only fine-tuned backbone's 0.194 (Table 3).

On the EXP benchmark, the 2-EgoNet variant of C-FREE achieves 99.33% accuracy versus 50.69% for plain GINE, supporting the claim that C-FREE is provably more expressive than 1-WL (Table 5, Section 4.4).
k-EgoNet subgraph generation averages 0.171ms per molecule versus 1.123ms for METIS clustering (Table 7).

YcccAbXbVK.text: Dynamic Decision Learning (DDL) enables frozen large vision-language models to refine decisions across language and visual spaces by optimizing instructions (DAPE) and consolidating predictions under visual perturbations (V-PUP and RHC) (Section 3).
On the NOVA rare-disease dataset, DDL improves mAP@75 by 104.7% for a 7B model (0.036 to 0.075), by 66.0% for a 3B model (0.040 to 0.066), and by 65.5% for a 32B model (0.058 to 0.096) (Table 3).
For the 3B model on NOVA, DDL achieves mAP@75 of 0.066 versus 0.049 for meta-optimization and 0.046 for supervised fine-tuning (Table 5).

Reliability-score calibration (correlation r between confidence and localization accuracy) on NOVA increases from 0.096 at 3B parameters to 0.535 at 72B parameters, with the 72B model reaching statistical significance at p<0.001 (Table 4).
For the 7B model, using visual uncertainty for consensus outperforms using linguistic (decoding-stochasticity-based) uncertainty by 13.7% at mAP@50 (Table 1).

42cOdUJOhH.text: The benchmarking framework repurposes and extends dSprites and COIL-20 with additional transformation dimensions and dense, axis-aligned sampling, pairing them with finite-difference estimators that recover curvature, reach, and volume at near-ground-truth accuracy (Section 4).

The extended dSprites dataset spans 3 shapes across 16^4 transformation combinations, yielding 196,608 images, while extended COIL-20 spans 20 objects times 18 views times 16^2 combinations, yielding 92,160 images (Table 1).

The framework evaluates the scaling behavior of the minimax manifold estimation bound (Theorem 3.6) and the Fefferman et al. bound H(M_o,M) < C_1(log n/n)^(1/d) against measured Hausdorff error on dSprites of varying intrinsic dimension d=1 to 4 using MMLS (Section 5, Figure 3).

Finite-difference curvature estimation error scales as O(h^2) = O((1/n)^(2/d)), and this scaling is validated on hyperspheres (S^2, S^3, S^4), a hyperboloid (H^2_2), and a torus (T^2) via scalar-curvature RMSE comparisons (Figure 2).
The framework tracks layer-wise evolution of manifold geometry (e.g., curvature and dimension) across a beta-VAE trained on dSprites and COIL-20 (Figure 6).

43QdwsbcNM.text: EqGINO uses Orbit-based Weight Sharing in its EqFNO layers to guarantee exact equivariance to the discrete Octahedral group (O) inherent to the discretized computational domain (Section 4.3).

EqGINO reduces spectral kernel parameter complexity from O(K^3) to O(K) via isotropic weight sharing while requiring a Full-FFT rather than Real-FFT to preserve rotation equivariance (Section 4.3, Appendix H).

On AhmedBody (413 training samples), ShapeNetCar (450 training samples), and DeepJEB (1,776 training samples), EqGINO reduces parameters by about 98% (285M to 4.1M) and FLOPs by about 44% (153.1 to 85.7 GFLOPs) relative to GINO (Table 1-2).

EqGINO maintains prediction accuracy under 90/180/270 degree discrete rotations of the input mesh without rotation-augmented training, while non-equivariant baselines degrade significantly under the same rotations (Section 5.2, Figure 6).

With limited SE(3)-transformed (continuous-rotation-augmented) training samples, EqGINO converges faster and generalizes better to arbitrary continuous orientations than non-equivariant models and equivariant baselines EGNN, EMNN, and T-EMNN (Section 5.2, Table 1-2).

re1J8BPwTQ.text: DMVAE aligns the encoder's latent distribution with an arbitrary reference distribution via an explicit distribution-matching constraint, using diffusion models as universal distribution estimators (Section on method, three-component objective).
On ImageNet 256x256, DMVAE reaches a generation FID (gFID) of 3.22 after only 64 training epochs, improving to 1.82 at 400 epochs and 1.64 at 800 epochs (Table 1).

Using DINO-derived SSL reference distributions, DMVAE achieves rFID 0.81 and PSNR 21.8 with gFID-5k of 13.1, outperforming ResNet-derived (rFID 1.46, gFID-5k 18.6), Gaussian (rFID 0.47, gFID-5k 26.6), and GMM (rFID 0.42, gFID-5k 29.6) reference distributions on generation quality despite worse reconstruction metrics (Table 1).
DMVAE outperforms VA-VAE and AlignTok baselines with significantly faster convergence to comparable or better FID (Table 3).

jwLSuhDyDc.text: The TD objective (Equation 15) penalizes the mismatch between the true diffusion posterior-mean drift across timesteps, μ_true(x_t,x_0) - μ_true(x_{t-1},x_0), and the model's predicted multi-step drift, μ_θ(x_t) - μ_θ'(x_{t-1}), enforcing cross-time consistency (Section on TD objective, Equation 15).
TD+EDM training improves FID most in the 12-18 sampling-step regime, e.g., on FFHQ 64x64 at 9 steps FID improves from 7.829 (baseline) to 7.463 (Table 2).
TD+CT improves 1-step FID on AFHQv2 from 12.97 to 12.87 and on FFHQ from 19.45 to 15.93 (Table 3).

TD+EDM training incurs about 1.5x wall-clock overhead (50h33m to 71h36m), while TD+CT adds only about 18-19% overhead on AFHQv2 and FFHQ, showing the TD approach applies as a drop-in improvement across both EDM and consistency-training (CT) diffusion formulations (Section 4.1, computational overhead discussion).
A principled pairwise weighting of TD error terms is essential for training stability, as shown by an ablation removing/altering the weighting scheme (Table 4).

TZeGBqnvRT.text: Adaptive contracts admit polynomial-time optimal solutions in the constant-many-actions/outcomes setting (Theorem 3.2) and in the independent signal-outcome property (ISOP) setting (Theorem 3.5), but computing optimal adaptive contracts is NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor outside ISOP (Theorem 4.1).

On AlpacaEval question-answering with GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4o Mini, and GPT-4o as candidate models, using response-length as the coarse signal and pairwise comparison to GPT-4 as the refined evaluation, adaptive contracts achieve 14% higher principal utility than the closest non-adaptive baseline (empirical evaluation section, AlpacaEval experiment).

On SWE-bench code generation with six OpenAI models (GPT-3o through GPT-5) evaluated via a 2-test coarse suite and 8-test refined suite over 500 GitHub issues, the optimal adaptive inspection policy transitions between three distinct strategies as the per-test inspection cost increases (empirical evaluation section, SWE-bench experiment).

Under limited liability and the Monotone Likelihood Ratio Property, adaptive contracts can yield zero principal utility despite positive first-best (full-information) surplus when inspection costs offset the gains from adaptivity, unlike classic linear-pricing contracts that always guarantee positive principal utility (Example 3.1).

Randomized inspection variants of the contract can yield a non-strict improvement in principal utility over deterministic inspection in some settings (Theorem 5.4), while the coarse-signal/refined-outcome (CoMI) setting need not admit a Stackelberg equilibrium (Theorem 5.1).

LZro8iqjiA.text: DAPD constructs a dependency graph at each denoising step from self-attention weights, defining an edge score s_ij = 1/2(a_ij + a_ji) between masked token positions i and j, and adds an edge when s_ij exceeds a threshold tau_t (method section, dependency graph construction).

DAPD reduces parallel token selection to an independent-set (graph-coloring) problem using a Welsh-Powell-inspired heuristic that prioritizes high-degree 'hub' tokens ordered by attention-based degree weighted by marginal confidence, d_tilde_i times conf_i (method section, node ordering/sorting metric).

On toy synthetic Markov-random-field experiments, attention-derived edges achieve an edge-detection AUC of 0.928 and an order-violation rate of 0.04 for degree-based ordering accuracy (validation section).

On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, DAPD achieves a 3.87x speedup over baseline on a concurrent 5-question TriviaQA decoding task and a 1.8x speedup over competing training-free parallel decoding strategies overall (Table 2).

DAPD outperforms training-free baselines Fast-dLLM, EB-Sampler, and KLASS on the accuracy-versus-steps trade-off across HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, Math500, and IFEval on LLaDA (Figure 3), and on the score-versus-steps trade-off on ParallelBench (Figure 4).

1RvkM0i9SQ.text: The SCAB (Supply-Chain Backdoor) attack assumes a highly restrictive threat model in which the attacker-controlled agent has only read-only access to observations and can influence the victim solely through its own actions, with no ability to modify victim observations, rewards, or policies (Section on threat model).

SCAB achieves a 91.3% trigger success rate in the Boxing environment with an LSTM-based PPO victim policy, while trigger success rates range from 31.4% to 91.3% across tested environments and architectures (Table 3, Table 7).

Injecting the backdoor via only 3% of training experiences (Trigger Injection Probability) is sufficient to establish the attack, and in Boxing a 30% trigger proportion drops the victim's average episodic return from 82.6 to 13.1 (Table 3).

SCAB is compared against TrojDRL (99.1% trigger success) and BACKDOORL (93.6% trigger success), both of which require direct observation, reward, or policy manipulation access that SCAB does not need (Table 7).

The attack is evaluated across discrete competitive Atari environments (Pong, Boxing, Surround), a 4-player multi-agent environment (Volleyball Pong), and a continuous-action MPE environment (Simple Push), using both PPO and DQN with CNN and LSTM architectures (Table 3, Table 8, Table 10).
A fine-tuning-based defense is evaluated against SCAB and found to have limited effectiveness at removing the backdoor (Table 15).

xWvj03N4sJ.text: BRIDGE formulates SFT and RL training as a bilevel optimization problem, with SFT as the upper-level (leader) objective updating LoRA weights w to maximize a 'cooperative gain' and RL as the lower-level (follower) objective updating base parameters θ via a λ-annealed blend of SFT and RL gradients (Section on method formulation).
BRIDGE avoids expensive second-order bilevel computation by using a penalty-based relaxation with first-order approximations derived from Danskin's theorem (Section on optimization).
Across five reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench, AIME 2024, AMC 2023), BRIDGE achieves an average improvement of 11.8% over RL-zero and Cold-start baselines (Table 1).
On Qwen3-8B-Base, BRIDGE reaches 49.9% average accuracy versus 42.9% for the Cold-start baseline, a 9.7 percentage-point improvement (Table 1).
BRIDGE reduces wall-clock training time relative to Cold-start by 44% for 3B-scale models (6.9 vs. 12.3 hours) and by 14% for 8B-scale models (33.5 vs. 39.1 hours) (Table 5).

Training dynamics analysis shows BRIDGE achieves more stable convergence with rapid reward growth, avoiding the catastrophic forgetting observed in the two-stage Cold-start baseline (Section on training dynamics).

Ke4poDVYTO.text: FMCPE refines a simulation-trained posterior estimator using a small set of real calibration samples via two sequential flow-matching stages: a data-space transport map T_X coupling real observations to simulator-space counterparts, and a parameter-space transport map T_Θ moving a simulation-informed source distribution toward the true posterior (Section on method).

FMCPE is evaluated on two synthetic benchmarks (a 3-parameter/10-dimensional Gaussian task and a 2-parameter Pendulum task with friction-induced misspecification) and two real-world benchmarks (WindTunnel hatch-angle inference and LightTunnel RGB/polarizer-coefficient inference from 64x64x3 images) (Section on experiments).

FMCPE is tested across calibration set sizes N_cal in {10, 50, 200, 1000} with expanding nested construction over 5 independent runs, and is compared against NPE and MFNPE baselines using jjC2ST, Wasserstein distance (W2), and MSE metrics (Section on experimental setup).

In the Pendulum task, FMCPE correctly recovers the oscillation amplitude despite the omitted-friction misspecification, whereas NPE and MFNPE produce multimodal or biased posterior estimates even at N_cal=1000 (Section on Pendulum results).

FMCPE achieves lower MSE than baselines particularly at small calibration sample sizes and produces better-calibrated, unimodal posteriors compared to MFNPE's overly sharp estimates (Section on results).

QDVz3V4Vle.text: Grokking on algorithmic tasks proceeds through three stages -- memorization, symmetry acquisition, and geometric organization -- with test-set generalization emerging specifically during the symmetry acquisition stage (Figure 6).

The authors identify a soft threshold of symmetry violation below which perfect test accuracy consistently emerges, giving a quantifiable predictor of the onset of generalization (Section on symmetry threshold).

Section 5 formalizes intrinsic symmetries for three task domains: commutativity and associativity across six modular arithmetic operations (Table 1), the triangle inequality constraint in graph metric completion (Section 3.2), and transitivity enabling global ordering in a comparison task (Section 3.3).

Symmetry- and geometry-prompting strategies, motivated by the identified symmetry criterion, are shown to accelerate the onset of generalization relative to standard training (Section on prompting strategies).

1ORZJtadQl.text: Preliminary experiments merging two OLMoE models via linear parameter averaging show 50.11% of expert selections deviate from the source models and 99.98% of tokens experience routing divergence across 16 layers, demonstrating routing breakdown from softmax/Top-k sensitivity to parameter perturbation (Section on preliminary analysis).

HARC approximates the KL divergence between merged and source routing distributions via a quadratic form using the Hessian of the log-partition function (Lemma 4.1), then derives a closed-form optimal merged router weight by solving a linear system combining the routing Hessian and input covariance as precision matrices (Theorem 4.2).

HARC uses matrix-free conjugate gradient to reduce the computational complexity of its closed-form solution from O(K^2 d^2) to O(Kd), making it scalable to large MoE models (Section on scalable implementation).
On OLMoE-1B-7B, applying HARC on top of WUDI-Merging improves the math task average from 43.44 to 44.01 and the code task average from 32.73 to 33.90 (Table 1).

HARC gives consistent gains as a post-processing step across multiple merging methods on OLMoE-1B-7B: Weight Averaging (+0.50), TIES-Merging (+0.54), DARE (+0.53), Fisher Merging (+0.17), and RegMean (+0.44) (Table 1).

HARC achieves near-optimal performance using only about 40% of the calibration samples, and its benefits are confirmed to generalize to the larger 128-expert Qwen3-30B-A3B model (Section on data efficiency and architecture generalization).

BN1NC3OH61.text: The proposed encoder is proven permutation-invariant, satisfying phi-hat(sigma X) = phi-hat(X) for all permutations sigma in the symmetric group S_n over particle indices (Section 3.1).

Rather than reconstructing ordered coordinates, the decoder reconstructs the induced particle density q_x(x) = (1/|X|) sum delta_eps(x - x_i) via a KL-divergence loss, avoiding the need for a canonical particle ordering (Section 3.2).

On the 2D interacting-particle system (300 particles, step-force interaction F(r)=tanh(4(1-r))+0.1, 10k trajectories), the method attains mean relative energy error of 5.19(+/-0.25)e-5 in-distribution, versus 1.25(+/-0.016)e-3 for the AE-Aug baseline, which additionally cannot handle a varying particle count N (Table 1, Section 4.2).

On the Lennard-Jones binary particle-mixing task (529 particles in a 32x32 domain, 10k trajectories), the method achieves an MMD of 1.09(+/-0.11)e-2 in-distribution, compared to 1.43(+/-0.049)e-1 for the InvE baseline (Table 2, Section 4.3).

Figure 4 verifies the permutation-invariance property empirically by showing that three differently permuted copies of the same initial particle configuration yield identical predicted energy-evolution trajectories (Figure 4).

On 300-bead polymer chains in elongational flow (610 training trajectories, 1001 timesteps each), the model accurately predicts extension dynamics on Fast and Medium stretching-rate test scenarios but overestimates extension in the Slow scenario (Figure 6, Section 4.4).

iqB2sVJTEk.text: FlowNar's Cross Linear Attentive Memory (CLAM) module maintains fixed-size memory tokens with constant per-step computational complexity, enabling processing of videos roughly 10x longer than the Videollm-online baseline within bounded VRAM (Section 3.3, Figure 1).
FlowNar achieves about 3x higher throughput (FPS) than Videollm-online when measured over 10K frames on H100 GPUs (Figure 1).

On EpicKitchens100, FlowNar reduces visual KV-cache size to 65.3M versus 1096.0M for Videollm-online (up to 48.3x cache reduction) while improving F1 temporal alignment from 12.98 to 29.12 and CIDEr from 29.00 to 46.63 (Table 1).
On Ego4D, FlowNar improves F1 from 16.29 to 24.85 and CIDEr from 28.04 to 35.64 relative to Videollm-online, using a cache of 59.2M versus 737.6M (Table 1).

An ablation shows that combining CLAM with Dynamic Context Management (DCM), which clears the visual KV cache after each narration is generated, raises CIDEr from 30.40 (without DCM) to 35.64, and the dynamic trigger strategy improves F1 from 16.78 to 24.85 (Table 3-5, Section 3.4).
Training FlowNar on Ego4D requires 67 GPU-hours on 4xH100, compared to 36 GPU-hours reported for the Videollm-online baseline (Section 4, training cost discussion).

prZKQmxXmq.text: Hierarchical Image Tokenization (HIT) progressively represents images at multiple scales while enforcing token overlap across scales, addressing the limitation of standard Residual Quantization that intermediate scales cannot be guaranteed to decode into valid images (Section 3.3).
The H-VAR model built on HIT uses 310M parameters, compared to roughly 1B parameters for VARSR, and is trained on 24 A100 GPUs for 200 epochs (about 13 hours) (Section 3.5).
On DIV2K-Val, H-VAR attains FID 28.86 and MUSIQ 69.40, improving over VARSR's FID of 35.51, while using roughly one-third the parameters (Table 4).
Unlike VARSR, H-VAR produces valid reconstructions at intermediate resolutions, achieving PSNR 22.09 at 128x128, 24.41 at 256x256, and 25.55 at 512x512 within a single hierarchical model (Table 2).
H-VAR is trained only on standard super-resolution datasets (DIV2K, DIV8K, Flickr2K, OST, and 10K FFHQ images) without the external proprietary training data used by VARSR (Section 3.5).
H-VAR requires only 0.921 TFLOPs and 0.25s inference time per image, versus 3.071 TFLOPs and 0.93s for VARSR (Table 6).

ykWN4LG9vE.text: Theorem 1 provides a teacher-to-student risk decomposition into propagated teacher error, student optimization error, and irreducible alignment bias, showing that dimensions the student can learn inherit teacher error one-to-one while unlearned dimensions suppress error by a factor of O(delta^2) (Section 4, Theorem 1).

Theorem 3 shows that under model mis-specification, the Distillation Efficiency Ratio (DER) diverges at rate Omega-tilde(N^kappa) with kappa = (alpha_T - 1 - beta)(1/alpha_T - 1/alpha_S) > 0, formalizing the Spectral Horizon Expansion by which distillation lets a student capture high-frequency signal components that are statistically inaccessible from raw ground-truth data alone (Section 5, Theorem 3).

Theorem 4 establishes a weak-to-strong generalization guarantee: a strong student model provably surpasses a weak teacher whenever the task exhibits low-dimensional intrinsic structure and both models are sufficiently expressive (Section 6, Theorem 4, Assumption 5).

Theorem 5 quantifies weak-to-strong performance recovery via Performance Gap Recovered PGR = 1 - O-tilde((k-dagger)^(2 alpha_S/(2 alpha_S+1)) * N^(-Delta_rate)), with Delta_rate > 0 implying full capability recovery asymptotically, termed Spectral Denoising (Section 6, Theorem 5, Eq. 7).

Figures 2 and 3 empirically validate the risk-inheritance and early-stopping predictions using both synthetic data and real-world model architectures, confirming that early stopping is critical for weak-to-strong generalization to succeed (Figure 2, Figure 3).

yW5LkzZN0T.text: Figure 1 demonstrates that translationese bias severity in GPT-4o judgments is inversely correlated with the resource availability of the target language (Figure 1).

DIBJudge is trained via an information bottleneck objective L_DIB = -I(Y;Z_r) + beta*I(X;Z_r) - gamma*I(S;Z_b) + lambda*I(Z_r;Z_b), which routes spurious translationese cues into a dedicated bias branch Z_b while penalizing mutual dependence between the robust representation Z_r and Z_b (Section 3.2, Eq. 3).
On m-RewardBench (23 languages), DIBJudge-Qwen3-8B scores 91.37+/-0.22, exceeding mR3-Qwen3-8B (88.58+/-0.41) and Nemotron-Multi-49B (88.83+/-0.35) (Table 1).
DIBJudge reduces translationese bias by 80% on Belebele, 75% on XL-Sum, and 56% on Aya across resource tiers, with the strongest reductions in low-resource languages (Section 5, RQ1, Figure 4).

In zero-shot generalization tests to unseen biases, DIBJudge reduces length-bias correlation from 0.553 (Vanilla SFT) to 0.314, and self-preference bias correlation from 0.314 to 0.219 (Table 2, RQ4).
An ablation shows that combining both proxy tasks (CLA and LPBC) during training is essential, reducing the bias score to 0.147 versus 0.421 when neither proxy task is used (Tables 3-4, RQ5).

VkTfx8FJoq.text: Model merging follows a unified scaling law E[L|N,k] = L_inf(N) + A(N)/(k+b), where the size-dependent floor L_inf(N) = L* + B*N^(-beta) decreases as base model size N grows (Section 3.3.1).
At k=9 merged experts, macro cross-entropy loss drops 41.9% from 0.739 at 0.5B parameters to 0.430 at 32B parameters, with fitted exponents beta in [0.33, 0.42] across domains (Section 3.3.1).
The merging tail exhibits diminishing returns of roughly 1/(k+b): the median improvement curve reaches 85% of its asymptotic gain by k=5 experts and 90% by k=6 experts (Section 3.3.3).

The early-k performance advantage of Task Arithmetic and TIES over simple averaging shrinks to about 2% by k=8, with Average, TA, TIES, and DARE all converging to the same power-law form (Section 3.3.4).
Measuring merged-model loss at only three points (k=1, 2, 4) suffices to forecast the entire scaling curve with low Mean Absolute Percentage Error (Section 4.2).

The scaling law is validated on 10,506 merged models spanning 0.5B to 72B parameters, four merging methods, and nine domains spanning mathematics, science, and coding, including cross-domain and LLaMA-backbone settings (Section 3, Table results).

fTwFUnHvKr.text: KAGE-Env, implemented entirely in JAX with end-to-end jit compilation and vectorized execution via vmap and lax.scan, reaches up to 33M environment steps per second on a single GPU with up to 2^16 parallel environments (Figure 3).
KAGE-Bench isolates six visual-shift axes across 34 configuration pairs, including background, photometric/filter, lighting/effects, layout, distractor, and agent-appearance shifts.
Photometric (filter) shifts produce the largest success-rate collapse, an 86.8 percentage-point gap, while agent-appearance shifts are comparatively benign at a 21.1 percentage-point gap.

Background shifts cause a 53.3 percentage-point success-rate gap while distance/progress metrics drop only 30.5%, showing that return-based metrics obscure generalization failures that success-rate captures.

A PPO-CNN agent trained to roughly 83% success rate across configurations still shows large success-rate collapses under held-out visual shifts despite largely preserved forward motion, evidencing brittle known-axis generalization.

JIbkbLYo3o.text: For laminar set cover, the proposed dual-prediction algorithm achieves E[ALG] = (1+epsilon)*OPT + O(R*eta/epsilon) for any constant epsilon>0, where eta measures dual prediction error (Theorem 1.1).

For metrical task systems, the dual-prediction algorithm (Algorithm 3, an A*-style search minimizing d(s_{t-1},s)+c_t(s)+w_hat_t(s)) achieves a (1+eta/OPT)-competitive ratio driven by the span seminorm of Bellman-operator discrepancies (Theorem 3.1).

Optimal dual solutions are stable under instance perturbations, satisfying ||y1* - y2*||_1 = O(|X1 Delta X2|), whereas optimal primal solutions can change arbitrarily under a single-element perturbation (Lemma A.1).
Event predictions for caching are similarly shown to be unstable, since a single prediction error can cause the competitive ratio to collapse (Lemma A.3).

On the parking permit problem, the learning-augmented dual-prediction algorithm achieves 1.8x to 4.4x better competitive ratios than classical algorithms at K=9 permit types, and it outperforms baselines on the k-server problem using real bike-sharing data (Experiments section).

For general (non-laminar) set cover, even perfect dual predictions cannot beat the classical H_m competitive ratio under the standard LP formulation, showing laminar structure is necessary for the improvement (Lemma A.4).

aIgsyrCUSF.text: Affine-Scaled Attention modifies standard softmax attention by applying an input-dependent scaling factor and corresponding bias term under relaxed normalization constraints, replacing fixed unit-sum softmax weighting.

Across 0.5B, 1B, and 3B parameter models, Affine-Scaled Attention achieves consistently lower training loss than standard softmax attention throughout training, with the advantage persisting through convergence (Figure 7).

Downstream average accuracy improves at every model scale tested: 50.6% to 51.3% at 0.5B, 56.7% to 57.2% at 1B, and 60.8% to 62.4% at 3B parameters, compared to softmax attention and attention-sink baselines (Table 1).
At the 3B scale, ARC-Challenge accuracy improves from 38.4% to 41.5% and BoolQ improves from 63.6% to 65.1% (Table 1).
Affine-Scaled Attention produces smoother and smaller gradient-norm trajectories than baseline attention, with fewer extreme gradient-spike events during early training.

Attention-head analysis shows Affine-Scaled Attention yields higher attention entropy and richer diversity across layers and heads than attention-sink variants, which instead show saturated head utilization concentrated on initial tokens.

D3lwvOSuQb.text: ParaTool encodes tools as independent parameter modules via a three-stage pipeline: Parametric Tool Pre-training with per-tool LoRA modules, Soft Tool Selection via a gating network, and Parametric Fine-tuning that jointly aligns training and inference.
On Stable ToolBench, ParaTool improves average pass rate by 5.9% relative for Llama3.1-8B (reaching 69.57%) and 11.2% relative for Qwen2.5-7B (reaching 75.95%) over the strongest ICL-based baselines.

On BFCL, ParaTool improves accuracy by 6.8% relative for Llama3.1-8B and 4.2% relative for Qwen2.5-7B, with a 17.6 percentage-point margin over context-based methods on the Live Parallel Multiple subtask.

ParaTool reduces inference FLOPs by an average of 92.22% on Stable ToolBench and 94.45% on BFCL relative to ICL baselines that concatenate full tool documentation into the prompt, with LoRA module overhead accounting for less than 5% of total inference cost.

By encoding tool knowledge into parameters rather than in-context documents, ParaTool achieves 10x to 20x computational savings in context length across most benchmarks compared to standard ICL-based tool-calling.

svT8c2GPJK.text: The proposed CBOB framework iterates between preference elicitation and policy optimization, adjusting the weight vector toward the region of interest to discover preferred policies without a priori knowledge (Figure 1, Figure 2).
On the Ant-v2 MuJoCo task with objective f1 preferred, CBOB achieves an epsilon*(Pi) score of 7.709, outperforming PGMORL's 8.383 and RA's 7.795 (Table 3).
On the Humanoid-v2 MuJoCo task, CBOB achieves an epsilon*(Pi) score of 2.362, versus 3.796 for PGMORL and 4.719 for RA (Table 3).

CBOB is evaluated against conventional MORL baselines RA, PGMORL, and MOIA, as well as preference-based baselines MORL-Adaptation, META-MORL, MOMPO, and MORAL across MuJoCo locomotion tasks including Ant-v2, HalfCheetah-v2, Hopper-v2/v3, Humanoid-v2, Swimmer-v2, and Walker2d-v2 (Table 3, Table 4).
Experiments use 8x10^6 environment steps for the MuJoCo tasks as reported in the hyperparameter settings (Table 2).
The framework is additionally applied to a multi-microgrid system design (MMSD) problem to demonstrate applicability beyond robot locomotion (Table 1, Section 4).

7SKS1u6vP1.text: The paper introduces 'perturbation-induced bias' as a systematic factor in neural network module outputs that is a crucial determinant of LLM robustness to random prompt perturbations (Section 3.3).
Debiasing fine-tuning is proposed as a lightweight alternative to full retraining, using input-independent and input-dependent logits debiasing to mitigate perturbation-induced bias (Section 5.1).

Evaluated on Qwen-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Olmo-7B across tasks derived from Natural Instructions plus Natural Questions, GSM-8k, TriviaQA, and XSum, format and text perturbations cause performance drops ranging from 1% to 62.2% (Section 4).

Input-dependent debiasing recovers on average 20% to 67.8% of the performance damage caused by perturbations across the 19 format-perturbation and 16 text-perturbation task-model pairs evaluated (Section 5.1).
Robustness certification analysis shows per-example certification rates increase by 17.4% to 63.8% and robustness-radius (epsilon) metrics improve by 51.5% to 90.3% after debiasing (Section 5.2).
Text perturbations studied include Unicode confusables, markup wrappers, and keyboard typos, in addition to structural format-template perturbations (Section 3.2).

gMbMm6b7ss.text: Proposition 3.2 derives an excess risk bound for semi-supervised learning with noisy proxy covariates that decomposes error into spectral truncation, proxy operator error, labeled estimation, and ridge shrinkage terms (Proposition 3.2).

Corollary 3.5 shows that under polynomial eigenvalue decay lambda_s ~ s^{-q}, choosing truncation level s ~ n^{1/(q+1)} recovers the oracle feature convergence rate of order n^{-q/(q+1)} using sufficiently many unlabeled proxy covariates (Corollary 3.5).
Theorem 3.7 establishes that the estimator remains stable under approximate eigendecomposition of the proxy covariate operator, with error controlled by a subspace-approximation term (Theorem 3.7).

Distribution regression, where each covariate is a latent distribution observed only through a finite bag of samples, is shown to be a special case of the general noisy-proxy-covariate framework via a bag-induced proxy error envelope (Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.3).

The method is validated empirically on synthetic noisy Euclidean covariates, synthetic distribution regression, galaxy cluster mass prediction, and default risk prediction from stock returns, reporting normalized RMSE (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, Section 5).

kBEOlJ6ZqY.text: The Obj-Disco framework, comprising objectives discovery and objectives verification steps, reconstructs over 90% of reward model behavior across diverse tasks, model sizes, and alignment algorithms in controlled evaluations (Section 5.1, Figure 3).

In a case study on detecting latent misalignment in open-source reward models, Obj-Disco identifies misaligned incentives in 3 of 4 trials, while baseline methods succeed in at most 1 of 4 trials (Section 5.2, Figure 4).
In a human-subject evaluation of objective explanations, annotators achieve 39.9% (±6.5%) accuracy using Obj-Disco explanations versus a 25.5% (±5.8%) random baseline (Section 5.3).

In a human-subject causality evaluation, Obj-Disco's discovered objectives are preferred 35.6% (±4.3%) of the time, compared to 16.7% (±3.3%) for Iter-Filter and 27.1% (±4.0%) for Zero-Shot, with statistical significance at p<0.001 (Section 5.4).

An ablation removing model trajectory information (Obj-Disco-Static) degrades objective discovery quality relative to full Obj-Disco, demonstrating the importance of using the model's training trajectory (Section 5.5, Figure 5, Figure 6).

ix1HdZkO8U.text: The Equilibrium Fisher Control (EFC) framework reformulates continual learning as a control problem using a preservation signal and network dynamics objective, enabling recovery of true prior-task curvature without storing exemplars (Section 2, Sections 2.1-2.3).
Learning theory results establish a continual-natural-gradient property, class-incremental convergence guarantees, and forgetting bounds for task-incremental learning (Sections 3.1, 3.2, 3.3).
On Split-MNIST, EFC achieves 98.3±0.7% task-incremental accuracy and 51.4±4.8% class-incremental accuracy, compared to a JOINT upper bound of 99.7±0.0% and 98.2±0.1% respectively (Table 1).
On Split-CIFAR10, EFC achieves 96.2±0.3% task-incremental accuracy and 50.2±7.0% class-incremental accuracy, versus a JOINT upper bound of 98.3±0.1% and 92.2±0.2% (Table 1).
On Split-Tiny-ImageNet, EFC achieves 37.2±0.4% task-incremental accuracy and 8.8±0.1% class-incremental accuracy, against a JOINT upper bound of 82.0±0.1% and 60.0±0.2% (Table 1).

EFC is compared against parameter-based regularization methods EWC, online EWC, and SI, as well as the replay-based method DER++ using a 200-sample buffer, without itself requiring a replay buffer (Section 4.2, Table 1).

KmOje8ebAg.text: For delete-free and well-formed planning domains with a fixed universe of objects, plan verification lies in C-RASP[Pos], which guarantees length generalization for decoder-only transformers (Theorem 3.1).

For general STRIPS domains under a fixed universe, there exist instances where the verification language L_D,O falls outside C-RASP[Pos], meaning length generalization is not guaranteed (Theorem 3.1).

The paper introduces C*-RASP, an extension of C-RASP that supports simultaneous growth in sequence length and vocabulary (object count), and shows delete-free/well-formed domains satisfy L_D in C*-RASP across a variable universe of objects (Theorem 3.6, Section 3.2).
FlipFlop and PARITY-style languages are shown to lie outside C*-RASP even in the variable-universe setting (Theorem 3.5).

Transformers trained on plans of 11-100 actions are evaluated out-of-distribution on plans of 101-200 actions across Heavy Grippers, Colors, and Lights Out domains, with well-formed variants achieving high OOD accuracy while STRIPS variants degrade and conditional-effects variants perform at chance level (Section 4).
70% of IPC 2023 Learning Track domains are classified as well-formed, supporting broad applicability of the delete-free/well-formed length-generalization guarantee (Section 2.2).

g89qqA6qmD.text: Floating-point networks built from automatic differentiation can represent an arbitrary target floating-point function's values together with an arbitrary, independently chosen gradient on a bounded domain, using at least 9 layers (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
This representability result is established for the practical activation functions ReLU, ELU, GELU, Swish, Sigmoid, and tanh (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

A single floating-point network can produce a gradient that varies with the loss function's derivative, provided that derivative satisfies an antisymmetry condition g*(x,-y) = -g*(x,y) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
Lemma 3.4 constructs networks that represent the correct function values while completely suppressing the computed gradient to zero (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.3).
Lemma 3.5 constructs networks that output zero everywhere while still producing an arbitrary target gradient under automatic differentiation (Lemma 3.5, Section 3.3).

The construction exploits the non-associativity of floating-point arithmetic to decouple the computed gradient from the classical chain-rule proportionality that would hold under exact real arithmetic (Section 1.1).

x16DrZepIl.text: Memorization is characterized as coordinate-wise variance collapse, motivating two curvature-difference localization metrics: Δh_∅ (curvature with vs. without conditioning) and Δh_θ̃ (curvature under the trained model vs. a less-trained model) (Section 4.1-4.3, Eqs. 1-2).

On Stable Diffusion v1.4 template-verbatim memorized prompts, Δh_θ̃ achieves IoU 0.921 and pixel accuracy 0.952 for localizing memorized regions, versus IoU 0.751 and accuracy 0.805 for the prior Bright Ending attention-based method (Table 1).
On Stable Diffusion v2.1 (template verbatim plus non-memorized prompts), Δh_θ̃ reaches IoU 0.947 and accuracy 0.967, compared to IoU 0.933 and accuracy 0.957 for Bright Ending (Table 1).
Aggregated curvature-difference maps yield strong image-level memorization detection: AUC 0.997 (Δh_∅) on SD v1.4 and AUC 0.996 (Δh_θ̃) on SD v2.1 (Table 2).

Section 4.4 derives a score-difference proxy Δs_∅ = (s_θ(x_t,c) - s_θ(x_t))^⊙2 as a computationally cheaper approximation to the curvature-difference method, giving a geometric explanation for the widely used score-difference detection metric (Eqs. 5-6, Section 4.4).

Figure 3 shows that raw conditional curvature diag(-H_θ(x_t,c)) produces false positives in semantically simple background regions, whereas subtracting a baseline curvature isolates overfitting-driven memorization (Figure 3).

FB5LYFzu33.text: Theorem 1 decomposes the per-step L2 estimation error into regression error, Monte Carlo error, and propagation error, giving the backward bound E_0 lesssim sum_{t=0}^{T-1} c_P^t (1/n_t)^{beta_t/(beta_t+1)} (Theorem 1, Section 4.1, Eq. 28).
The regression error term from kernel ridge regression is bounded as n_t^{-beta_t/(beta_t+1)} under the source-condition smoothness parameter beta_t in Assumption 3 (Section 4.1, Eq. 25).

Lemma 2 shows the Bellman/continuation-value operator T_t is globally Lipschitz with constant sqrt(c_P), which is the key stability property used to propagate errors backward in time (Lemma 2, Eq. 35).

Corollary 1 applies the general bound to American option pricing, showing the value function error satisfies ||W_0^{lambda_0} - V_0||^2 lesssim sum_{t=0}^{T-1} e^{-rt}(1/n_t)^{beta_t/(beta_t+1)}, with the discount factor e^{-r} acting as a contraction that damps rather than amplifies errors (Corollary 1, Section 4.1, Eq. 31).
Algorithm 1 (KRR-DP) combines kernel ridge regression with Monte Carlo estimation of continuation values, proceeding backward from maturity T to time 0 (Algorithm 1).

tRsnpaRO0m.text: Graphops are introduced as self-adjoint, positivity-preserving operators over probability spaces, unifying dense graphons and sparse graphs as a single class of limit objects (Definition 3.1).

A restricted subclass called bounded-fiber operators (bofops) is defined via fiber measures nu_x satisfying ess sup_{x in Omega} nu_x(Omega) < infinity, capturing sparse connectivity patterns within the graphop framework (Definition 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 establishes that message passing neural networks (MPNNs) are Lipschitz (Holder) continuous with respect to an action metric d_M on bofop-signals: ||H(A_1,f_1) - H(A_2,f_2)||_2 <= C'_{D,r} d_M((A_1,f_1),(A_2,f_2)) (Theorem 4.1).

Corollary 5.3 shows the space of bofop-DIDMs (degree-indexed distribution measures) is compact under the DIDM-mover's distance, forming a proper subset of the corresponding dense-graph structure (Corollary 5.3).

Section 6.1 uses this compactness and continuity to prove a universal approximation theorem: any continuous function on bofop-DIDMs can be uniformly approximated by MPNNs directly on sparse graphs (Section 6.1).

Section 6.2 derives generalization bounds showing generalization error vanishes as sample size grows, exploiting the uniform equicontinuity and compactness established in Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 5.3 (Section 6.2).

FHDRzhKm0f.text: OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt (Llama3.2-1B) achieves 69.88% F1 and 81.08% accuracy on sleep staging, versus 5.66% F1 for the Llama3.2-1B text-only baseline (Table 2, Section 4.3).
OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt (Llama3.2-1B) achieves 65.44% F1 and 71.48% accuracy on human activity recognition (HAR), compared to 60.44% F1 for the Llama3.2-3B text-only baseline (Table 2, Section 4.3).

Expert cardiologist evaluation of OpenTSLM-Flamingo's ECG-QA reasoning found the model gave a correct or partially correct interpretation in 92.9% of cases, with 85.1% positive ratings for clinical context integration but only 62.5% positive for clinical reasoning (Section 4.5).

OpenTSLM-Flamingo maintains roughly constant ~20-22 GB VRAM usage regardless of sequence length, whereas OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt scales memory exponentially, reaching 87.1 GB for Llama-3.2-3B on ECG data (Figures 4-5, Section 4.4).
The authors explicitly state they did not conduct ablation studies on the OpenTSLM architecture components (Section 5, Discussion).

yTFTLj7MoN.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes in-expectation convergence for momentum stochastic conditional gradient (SCG) methods under a μ-KL condition, with stepsize β=O(1/K), learning rate η=Õ(1/μ), and momentum α=min{1,O((εμ)²/(ρσ)²)} (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

Corollary 4.1 derives a critical effective batch size BS ≍ (Tμρσ⋆/L)^(2/3), beyond which increasing batch size under a fixed token budget yields diminishing and eventually negative returns, splitting the error into noise-dominated, intermediate (scaling as T^(-1/3)), and iteration-starved regimes (Section 4, Corollary 4.1).
The batch-size-times-sequence-length (BST) scaling rule predicts the optimal product BS scales as T^(2/3) with stepsize β∼1/K and constant momentum α (Equation 6, Section 4).

On a 124M-parameter NanoGPT model under a 1.3B-token training budget, the optimal configuration found empirically is batch size B=256, sequence length S=1024, and stepsize β=3.6×10^(-4) (Table 1-2, Section 6.3).

Increasing the batch size beyond the predicted optimum (e.g., to 2048 or 4096 for a 1B-parameter model) degrades validation loss by 0.005-0.04, consistent with the theoretical saturation-then-degradation prediction (Figures 3-4, Section 6.5-6.6).

An adaptive restarting strategy that increases batch size and sequence length during training, following the derived scaling law, outperforms fixed schedules while preserving the theoretical convergence guarantees of Theorem 4.1 (Section 6.5-6.6).

QJYHWz4x7H.text: The paper provides non-asymptotic bounds in forward Kullback-Leibler divergence for both the continuous-time time-inhomogeneous Langevin diffusion and its Euler-Maruyama discretization, under a single set of abstract conditions on the time-dependent drift (abstract only).
The convergence analysis is presented as unified across time-dependent drifts induced by annealing or tempering schedules, rather than requiring a separate analysis per scheme (abstract only).
The theoretical results are shown to apply to multiple practically-relevant annealing schemes, explicitly including geometric tempering and annealed Langevin sampling (abstract only).
The paper reports numerical experiments comparing the annealing schemes covered by the theory in both low-dimensional and high-dimensional settings (abstract only).

Umu6IsAUbS.text: On COCO captioning, Gap-Init rank-1 LoRA achieves 140.59 CIDEr and 41.87 BLEU-4, exceeding standard rank-8 LoRA's 138.49 CIDEr and 40.63 BLEU-4 despite using 8x fewer trainable parameters (Table 2).
On Flickr30k zero-shot transfer, Gap-Init rank-1 achieves 79.60 CIDEr, a +16.60 improvement over the standard rank-1 baseline, and exceeds standard rank-8 LoRA's 78.35 CIDEr (Table 3).

On VQAv2, Gap-Init rank-1 reaches 57.23 accuracy while standard rank-1 LoRA collapses to 15.58 accuracy due to training instability, and Gap-Init attains 92.4 POPE F1 versus 86.9 for PiSSA initialization (Table 4).
Across multiple random seeds, Gap-Init rank-1 converges to 140.57 ± 1.44 CIDEr versus 135.37 ± 7.10 CIDEr for standard rank-1 LoRA, a roughly 5x reduction in variance (Table 7).

The identified modality-gap vector explains approximately 16% of the variation in the modality gap, yet initializing rank-1 LoRA aligned with this direction is described as critical for optimization success at the extreme low-rank limit (Figure 3, Section 7).

BSi2mfMDsx.text: Jailbreak Foundry reproduces 30 attacks across 10 victim models with a mean attack success rate (ASR) deviation of +0.26 percentage points between reproduced and originally reported values, using a standardized GPT-4o judge on AdvBench.
Jailbreak Foundry's standardized implementations achieve an 82.5% mean reused-code ratio across the 30 reproduced attacks.
Standardizing attack implementations in Jailbreak Foundry reduces attack-specific implementation code by nearly half relative to the original per-paper repositories.

XZgyuxVoLq.text: PRAC decomposes activations into a principal subspace obtained via SVD and a random subspace, using a scaling factor k=(n-r1)/r2 to guarantee an unbiased gradient estimator (Theorem 6-7).
PRAC achieves up to 36% total memory reduction on LLaMA-1B pre-training with negligible performance degradation, compared to 30% on LLaMA-350M and 27% on LLaMA-130M (Table 2).
On LLaMA-1B, a 27% memory reduction at batch size 64 enables increasing batch size from 64 to 96 while reducing total training time by 25% (Table 4).

PRAC attains the minimum variance among all unbiased estimators under the Activation Degenerate Condition, matching the lower bound (n-s)/(r-s)-1 times q established in Lemma 5 (Theorem 6-7, Lemma 5).

An ablation comparing PAC (principal-subspace only), RAC (random-subspace only), and full PRAC shows PAC suffers convergence stagnation in later training stages while RAC shows slower initial convergence due to high variance, whereas PRAC converges fastest throughout (Figure 5).

YdQq7DvUfI.text: The framework represents CNF formulas as clause-literal hypergraphs augmented with a clause incidence graph, in place of standard bipartite graph representations, to capture higher-order structural interactions (Section 3.1).

An invariant-equivariant decomposition splits variable representations into polarity-invariant and polarity-equivariant components, combined with a polarity-inversion consistency regularization on complementary literal pairs (Section 3.2, Section 3.4).

Against the NeuroCore baseline, the method improves precision by 71.4% on the CA dataset (0.424 vs 0.335) and by smaller margins of 2.5% on SR and 3.0% on PS, with PR-AUC gains of 24.8% (CA), 2.7% (SR), and 3.0% (PS) (Table 1).

An ablation on the CA dataset shows precision rising from 0.238 with the hypergraph component alone, to 0.383 adding the invariant-equivariant decomposition, to 0.408 for the full model with regularization (Table 2).

Integrating predicted unsat cores with the Glucose SAT solver increases the number of SATCOMP instances solved by 15 (133 to 148) in 2023, by 7 (111 to 118) in 2024, and by 6 (135 to 141) in 2025 (Table 3).

Ge3VtuCvZ7.text: A dynamical mean-field theory is developed for a teacher-student random feature regression setup with power-law kernel eigenvalues η_i = η1 i^(-1-γ), unifying Bayesian inference, gradient flow, and Langevin training as special cases of the same framework (Section 4.1).

The theory derives decoupled effective equations of motion for each spectral eigenmode's mean discrepancy, governed by a memory kernel K(t-s) satisfying a self-consistent Volterra equation (Section 4.2, Equations 21 and 25).

Test loss is shown to decompose into per-mode bias and variance contributions weighted by the eigenvalues η_i, with generalization error expressed directly in terms of the order parameter C̄(t,t) (Section 4.3, Equations 29-30).

Slow modes with small eigenvalues exhibit spectral bias, and regularization (encoded via 1/(gβ)) primarily suppresses long-timescale variance rather than bias, so that early stopping emerges from a bias-variance tradeoff rather than from explicit regularization (Figure 3).

Test error is shown to behave non-monotonically as a function of training temperature, a prediction validated numerically against mode-resolved theoretical predictions across spectral modes (Figure 1, Figure 2).

gSQHzzOwyf.text: GALA replaces exhaustive pairwise domain-alignment computation with an Inter-Group Discrepancy (IGD) that randomly partitions source classifiers into two groups and minimizes disagreement between their weighted average predictions on unlabeled target data (Section 3.2, Equation 4).
On the Digit-Five benchmark, GALA achieves 94.7% average accuracy, and a temperature-scaled variant GALA† (τ=0.2) reaches 95.4%, slightly outperforming the FACT baseline's 95.0% (Table 1).

The paper introduces the Digit-18 benchmark comprising 18 domains built from ARDIS, TMNIST, MNIST, SVHN, SYN, and USPS via background augmentation, scaling, and channel-stacking transformations, on which GALA reaches 92.9% average accuracy versus 87.6% for FACT, a 5.3-point gap (Table 3, Appendix B.1).
On Office-Caltech10, GALA attains 97.8% accuracy, including 100% on the DSLR domain, competitive with KD3A's 97.9% (Table 2).

With 9 source domains, GALA scales to 22.37 seconds runtime versus 5,600 seconds for KD3A, whose pairwise computation grows infeasible, while FACT remains fastest at 4.05 seconds but with lower accuracy (Table 4).

V1k2DFhDYr.text: Among tested supervised surrogate architectures, the Transformer-KAN (T-K) model is identified as achieving the best magnetic flux (psi) prediction accuracy for the nonlinear Grad-Shafranov equation, attributed to combining Transformer self-attention for long-range dependencies with KAN learnable-spline regression for local non-linearities (Table 4, Section 3).

A semi-supervised physics-informed neural operator (PINO) trained with 100 sparse labeled monitoring points per sample represents the accuracy/physical-consistency 'knee' of the curve, closely matching ground-truth magnetic flux profiles (Table 6, Figure 14).

On out-of-distribution shape-parameter test data, the semi-supervised model achieves a mean extrapolation error of 4.76% with an error growth rate of 8.9x relative to interpolation error, compared to 10.17% error and a 39.8x growth rate for the fully supervised model, and 10.37% error and 15.2x growth rate for the unsupervised model (Table 7).

On an Intel Xeon Gold 6530 CPU and NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU, the FDM-SOR iterative baseline requires 10.2 seconds per inference on CPU, whereas the T-K model with TensorRT acceleration achieves 1.16 millisecond inference latency (Table 8, Section 3.5).

In extreme extrapolation stress tests with negative triangularity (delta = -0.8), the supervised model predicts a severely distorted, non-physical core, while the semi-supervised model correctly reconstructs the D-shaped equilibrium topology matching ground truth (Figure 17).

XkDpZusDTK.text: On X-Bench, a benchmark of 70 scenarios spanning 7 risk categories, AutoControl Arena's generated environments achieve a 98% end-to-end success rate (69 of 70 scenarios) (Section 4.1).
Human evaluators prefer AutoControl Arena's executable environments over the text-based Petri simulator in 60% of paired comparisons (Section 4.4).
The automated monitor achieves an F1 score of 92.8% for judging action outcomes and 89.4% for judging chain-of-thought reasoning (Section 4.5).

Average risk rate across evaluated models rises from 21.7% under baseline conditions (no stress, no temptation) to 54.5% under high-stress, high-temptation conditions, a roughly 2.5x increase (Section 5.2, Figure 8).
Gemini-3-Flash shows the largest risk-rate jump under pressure, from 25.0% to 70.6% (a 45.6 percentage-point increase), while Gemini-2.5-Flash rises from 26.5% to 52.2% (Table 5, Appendix D.1).

Capability scaling shows inconsistent safety effects across scenario types: for capability-misuse scenarios, risk drops from 65.0% (Qwen3-4B) to 48.6% (Qwen3-32B), whereas for specification-gaming scenarios risk rises from 26.2% (Gemini-2.5-Flash) to 53.5% (Gemini-3-Flash) (Table 6; Section 5.3).

sDfu0qN6Y6.text: Proposition 4.2 defines the f-trajectory-balance loss family via an integral of f'(exp(t)) - f'(1), proving the population loss is minimized exactly when the model distribution equals the target and that its on-policy autodiff gradient matches the corresponding f-divergence gradient (Proposition 4.2).

Proposition 4.4 shows a bijection between strictly convex, translation-invariant losses on log-probability differences and f-divergences, so choosing f recovers known losses (e.g., trajectory balance) as special cases (Proposition 4.4).

Proposition 5.1 extends the f-trajectory-balance framework to GFlowNets, generalizing standard trajectory balance to arbitrary f-divergences while preserving matching on-policy gradients (Proposition 5.1).
Definition 4.5 introduces a DevGrad loss generalizing Vargrad to arbitrary f-divergences for unnormalized target distributions using batch-wise deviations (Definition 4.5).
On the SynFlowNet molecule-discovery task, annealing the divergence parameter alpha from 0.75 to 1.2 during training balances molecular diversity against mode-seeking behavior (Section 6.1.2).

In asynchronous LLM fine-tuning experiments, f-trajectory-balance losses maintain off-policy validity even with 50-step-delayed data, with the entropy-reward tradeoff controllable via the choice of f-divergence (Section 6.2.2).

e26lNHXxgs.text: HoloFair's benchmark comprises three components—Prompt Sets (Gen/Eval/Train), a Reference Bias Distribution (RBD) image set of about 119,698 images, and SpaFreq attribute classifiers—used to compute the Multi-attribute Group-wise Bias Index (MGBI) (Section 3, Figure 2; Table 7).
MGBI is defined as the geometric mean of Intrinsic Diversity (entropy across demographic attributes) and Context-robust Diversity at the 10th percentile under bias-triggering prompts (Equations 6-8).
Applying Fair-GRPO to SD3.5-Medium raises the MGBI score from 0.5211 to 0.6772, a 29.9% relative improvement, while CLIP-Score improves slightly from 0.2288 to 0.2317 (Table 3, Section 4.4.1).
The SpaFreq bias classifier, which fuses spatial and frequency-domain features, reaches 89.67% overall accuracy on the held-out test set (Table 1).

Fair-GRPO's KL-regularized training objective keeps external MGBI and training reward correlated over the course of training and limits image-quality regression to an Aesthetic score drop of only -0.0019, mitigating reward hacking (Section 4.4.3, Figure 5; Equation 15).

T7y2wavrFM.text: CAME-Grad (Conflict-Averse Magnitude-Enhanced Gradient Descent) is a backbone-agnostic optimizer with three cascaded stages: conflict-averse direction rectification, magnitude-enhanced energy injection, and adaptive gradient fusion (Section 3.3).

Applied to eight diverse radiology report generation methods (WCL, XProNet, DCL, PromptMRG, CAMANet, DDaTR, TGRG, REVTAF), CAME-Grad yields an average clinical-efficacy improvement of 2.3% on MIMIC-CXR (Table 1) and 1.9% on IU X-Ray (Table 2).
Clinical efficacy is measured via CheXbert-labeled precision, recall, and F1 across 14 observation categories, evaluated on a MIMIC-CXR test set of 3,858 samples (Table 1).
CAME-Grad is compared against seven multi-task-learning optimizers—UW, GradNorm, CAGrad, RotoGrad, FAMO, MMPareto, and STGU—in a dedicated comparison (Table 3).
An ablation study on PromptMRG and DDaTR isolates the contribution of each of CAME-Grad's three stages to overall performance (Table 4).

DxvZnTVNfP.text: For Gaussian targets, the asymptotic bias of unadjusted Hamiltonian/Langevin samplers is upper bounded by the energy error variance per dimension (EEVPD), independent of dimensionality (Section 3, Equation 20).

Algorithm 1 provides an automatic step-size tuning scheme using log-normal weighting with a forgetting factor that preferentially weights recent samples during burn-in, targeting a user-specified bias tolerance (Section 4, Equation 25).
Lemma 5.1 bounds the microcanonical dimensionality factor Delta(H) between 0.37 d^(-1/4) and 3.1 for MCHMC and MCLMC (Section 5, Lemma 5.1, Equation 29).

Across six benchmark problems (32-101 dimensions, including ill-conditioned Gaussians, Rosenbrock, Brownian motion, German credit logistic regression, and Neal's funnel), the Gaussian EEVPD-bias bound holds approximately even for non-Gaussian targets, except Brownian motion inference where bias is overestimated by about 1.5x (Section 6, Figure 2, Figure 3).
MCHMC achieves an efficiency gain over standard HMC of about (9/4)^(1/8) ≈ 1.11 for a fixed covariance error under matched step-size scaling (Section 5.2).

dsPE185aHi.text: Baseline Graph VQ methods suffer severe codebook collapse, with perplexity collapsing to as low as 1.00 on the Computer dataset (codebook size K=512) versus RGVQ's 413.10 on the same dataset (Table 1).
On Cora, RGVQ raises codebook utilization/perplexity to 211.69 versus 94.47 for the standard Graph VQ baseline, and on Questions to 250.79 versus 20.78 (Table 1).

Theorem 1 proves that token co-assignment probability increases with both feature redundancy (PCA@95% variance) and graph density (average degree), formally linking graph topology to VQ codebook collapse severity (Theorem 1).
Adding RGVQ to the GFT backbone improves average transfer accuracy across seven datasets from 79.50% to 81.42% (+1.92 points) (Table 2).
RGVQ boosts GQT node-classification accuracy from 81.60% to 86.54% on PubMed (+4.94 points) and from 92.13% to 95.67% on Computer (+3.54 points) (Table 3).

Ablations show RGVQ maintains over 50% normalized codebook perplexity even at codebook size K=512, and that a low Gumbel-softmax temperature (tau=0.1) consistently improves codebook utilization (Figure 4).

aoUVQ5d8vf.text: On EMBGuardTest, EMBGuard-4B attains 54.3% potential-risk accuracy, 50.3% risk-type accuracy, and 14.6% hazard-identification accuracy, versus GPT-5.1's 55.8%/58.1%/33.4% and Gemini-2.5-Pro's 58.4%/56.8%/29.3% (Table 2).
Gemini-2.5-Pro misclassifies 83.3% of benign scenarios as risky, evidencing an over-conservative bias that limits practical real-time deployment despite its higher raw accuracy (Section 4.3).
On the held-out evaluation set, EMBGuard-4B reaches 71.2% potential-risk accuracy, 67.6% risk-type accuracy, and 50.1% hazard accuracy (Table 2).
Human evaluation on EMBGuardTest yields 85.6% potential-risk, 90.9% risk-type, and 63.6% hazard accuracy, substantially exceeding all evaluated MLLMs including GPT-5.1 and Gemini-2.5-Pro (Table 3).
In IS-Bench deployment, EMBGuard-4B achieves 63.1% step accuracy with 25.7% precision, 71.7% recall, and 38.3% F1 for hazard flagging (Table 4).

nIJOtyIQsZ.text: FLIP-Tiny (0.51M parameters) reaches 78.24% average mean IoU across six benchmarks (Hypersim, KITTI-360, OpenImages, COCO, LVIS, ObjaScale), exceeding SAM-H's 75.41% average IoU despite about 1257x fewer parameters and running roughly 25.64x faster (Table 1; Figures 1 and 8).
FLIP-Large (96.6M parameters) attains the best average mean IoU of 80.33% among all tested models while running about 6x faster than SAM-H (abstract; Table 1).
On small-scale objects (<1% of image area), FLIP-Tiny achieves 74.04% average IoU, outperforming SAM-H's 71.04% despite its far smaller size (Table 3).

FLIP is trained exclusively on Meta's SA-1B dataset in four sizes (FLIP-Tiny 0.51M, FLIP-Small 2.3M, FLIP-Middle 11.5M, FLIP-Large 96.6M parameters) and is evaluated zero-shot on ObjaScale, a newly constructed 10,200-image synthetic dataset spanning object scales from 0.0001% to 25% of image area (Section 3.4; Section 4.1).
An ablation replacing FLIP's separate per-projection layer normalization (LaPE-style) with a single shared normalization reduces FLIP-Small's average mean IoU from 79.29% to 77.97% (Table 2).

VMMQj6M94x.text: The Mean-Field Entropy Dynamics model decomposes orchestrator entropy trajectories into a damped-oscillator 'Focusing Operator' and a logarithmic-growth 'Dispersion Operator' (Section 2, Equation 6).
