Reducing GPT-5's reasoning-token budget by 69% (from GPT-5-High to GPT-5-Low) improves Step-SR from 25.1% to 30.2%, evidencing a 'Reasoning Trap' in which heavy internal chain-of-thought crowds out attention to external orchestration signals (Section 4.5).

Across the 679-instance IWG benchmark, orchestrator-attributable failures account for 67.7% of errors on average versus 32.3% for executor failures, with orchestrator failures reaching 79.0% in Agentic RAG multi-hop tasks (Appendix A).
Claude-4.5-Sonnet is the top system-level orchestrator with 85.38% LCS-F1 and 60.83% Step-SR, ahead of Gemini-2.5-Pro (81.28%/53.33%) and DeepSeek-V3.1 (80.12%/42.89%) (Table 3).

Fitted entropy-dynamics parameters place DeepSeek-V3.1 and Qwen-3-Max in an 'Oscillatory-Aggressive' archetype (high A_task, high omega) versus Claude and Gemini's 'Smooth-Conservative' archetype (low omega, low beta) (Table 4).

Robustness tests show the fitted A_task parameter drops to 0.49 under a noise-removed 'Golden Context' setting and rises to 9.85 under 'Exception Injection,' with all regression fits significant at p<0.005 (Table 5).

k9PKgV0L4C.text: On the Live Gaming benchmark, Proact-VL achieves an overall TimeDiff of 1.71 seconds and F1 of 64.87%, with the Co-Commentary scenario reaching the lowest TimeDiff (0.71s) and highest F1 (77.44%) (Table 2, Section 5.2).
Proact-VL attains a 49.23% closed-caption win rate and LLM-judged scores of 6.52/10 (LiveU) and 5.03/10 (FinalQ) on the Live Gaming benchmark (Table 1, Section 5.2).

End-to-end per-chunk processing takes 0.3545-0.4313 seconds (cache update 0.0794-0.0967s plus text generation 0.2446-0.3242s), with per-token generation of 0.0431-0.0454s, supporting an estimated 10-15 FPS real-time throughput (Table 7, Section 5.6).
On out-of-domain generalization tests, Proact-VL reaches 63.43% CC win rate and 45.82% F1 on Ego4D, and 55.21% CC/60.06% F1 on Black Myth: Wukong (Table 3, Section 5.3).
In long-horizon streaming evaluation over 10-50 minute intervals, TimeDiff stabilizes around 0.81 seconds while F1 degrades mildly before stabilizing near 69% (Tables 4-5, Section 5.4).
Human user studies show Proact-VL achieving 80-96.7% win rates across three games (Table 16, Appendix E).

9kkrASoSbp.text: Introduces three families of analytic bijections (cubic rational, sinh conjugation, cubic conjugation) that are C-infinity smooth on all of R and analytically invertible via Cardano's formula for cubics (Section 3, Table 1).

Radial flows built from these bijections match coupling-flow density-estimation quality on the 2D spiral target while using about 1000x fewer parameters, e.g. 1.6k parameters for the pure radial flow versus 2,311k for the coupling flow (Section 5.3, Figure 8).
On CIFAR10, replacing the affine RealNVP coupling bijection with the cubic rational bijection (RealNVP+) improves test bits-per-dimension from 3.49 to 3.36 (Table 2).

On UCI HEPMASS, the reproduced spline variant achieves a bolded log-likelihood of -14.80 +/- 0.36, and on MINIBOONE the pure sinh variant achieves -9.58 +/- 0.23, both outperforming RQ-NSF(C) (Table 3).

On a 20x20 phi^4 lattice field theory experiment, the three analytic-bijection coupling flows (rational cubic, sinh, cubic) achieve higher effective sample size than both spline and affine (Real NVP) baselines, with final ESS ordering cubic rational (39.66%) > cubic (38.85%) > sinh (38.51%) > spline (34.34%) > affine (31.85%) (Section 5.5, Figure 9).
Radial flows train stably at learning rates of 10^-2, an order of magnitude higher than coupling flows, per Table 5 in the appendix (Section 4.3).

rJ2gMA21ZW.text: Local Hessian Spectral Dimension (LHSD) applies a Hill spectral filter f(lambda) = 1/(1+(|lambda|/kappa(t))^p) with noise-adaptive cutoff kappa(t) = c/sigma(t)^2 to the log-density Hessian to separate tangent from normal eigenvalue components (Section on Spectral Filter).

LHSD uses Stochastic Lanczos Quadrature to estimate the trace without explicit Hessian construction, achieving O(D) complexity versus O(D^2) for competing methods (Section 4, Scalable Implementation).
Across high-dimensional benchmarks (D in [100, 3072]), LHSD achieves mean absolute errors of about 6.6, roughly 46x lower than the second-best method FLIPD (Table 1).
LHSD is over 250x faster than FLIPD on intrinsic-dimension-regression (IDR) benchmarks at D=784 (Figure 5).
LHSD detects memorized samples in a DDPM trained on CIFAR-10 with 99.87% AUROC, even after controlling for visual complexity (Section on Memorization Detection).

The Hutchinson trace estimator's variance scales with the intrinsic dimension d rather than the ambient dimension D, which the authors identify as a key robustness mechanism (Section 4, Variance Control).

gC04O9t1WJ.text: Single-head softmax attention parameters can be exactly recovered using O(d^2) value queries via a two-phase algorithm that first recovers the output projection vector v with length-1 queries, then recovers the attention matrix W column-by-column with length-2 queries (Theorem 4.1).
When rank(W) <= r << d, the attention matrix can instead be recovered with only O(rd) queries using rank-one projections and nuclear norm minimization from compressed sensing (Theorem 5.2).

Under norm bounds and margin conditions on the parameters, epsilon-accurate approximate recovery is achievable with O(d^2) queries tolerating additive noise tau = O(min{mu, epsilon_v/sqrt(d), mu*epsilon_w/(W^2 d)}) (Theorem 6.2).

Multi-head attention parameters are non-identifiable from queries: distinct parameter sets can produce identical input-output maps, ruling out exact parameter extraction without further structural assumptions (Proposition 7.1).

Length-2 queries reduce the softmax attention weight to a sigmoid, alpha = sigma(s1 - s2), enabling inversion via sigma^-1 into linear equations in the unknown parameters (Section preceding Theorem 4.1).

iGLpZo89xJ.text: Introduces the WikiProfile benchmark of 2,150 Wikipedia-derived facts, each paired with ten questions spanning proposition-completion, contextual, direct/reverse knowledge, and multiple-choice tasks, evaluated across 13 LLMs with about 4 million graded responses (Section 3, Section 4).
Frontier models Gemini-3-Pro and GPT-5 encode 95-98% of facts in WikiProfile, yet still fail to directly recall 26-34% of facts even without thinking (Section 5.1, Figure 4).

In the Gemma3 family, increasing model size from 1B to 27B parameters reduces encoding failures from 85% to 23%, while recall failures rise to a peak of 33% with thinking and 40% without, showing scale improves encoding more than recall (Section 5.1).

For Gemini-3-Pro, the encoding gap between popular and rare (bottom-20% popularity) Wikipedia facts is only about 5 points (99.5% vs 94.5%), but the direct-recall gap between the same tiers is about 21.3 points (84.6% vs 63.3%) (Figure 5, Section 5.2).
Thinking recovers 40-65% of encoded-but-not-directly-known facts in thinking-optimized LLMs, but only 5-20% of facts that are not encoded at all (Section 5.3, Figure 8).

Reverse questions are answered correctly nearly as often as direct questions under multiple-choice verification (better for 9 of 13 models), but generation-based recall is substantially worse for reverse than direct questions, e.g. GPT-5 at 82.9% direct vs 74% reverse (Figure 6, Section 5.2).

J5i09faOOf.text: Entropy-Aware On-Policy Distillation (EOPD) augments the standard reverse-KL on-policy distillation loss with an additional forward-KL term activated only when teacher token entropy H_te exceeds a threshold tau, per the loss L_EOPD = L_OPD + I[H_te > tau] * L_FKL (Technical Implementation section).
Forward KL in EOPD is computed only over the top-k=16 teacher tokens to keep the extra loss term computationally efficient (Technical Implementation section).
Standard on-policy distillation causes diversity collapse: student models retain only 6.8% of high-entropy tokens versus 18.5% in the teacher (Core Problem section, Figure 1).

EOPD improves Pass@8 accuracy on six math benchmarks over baseline on-policy distillation by +1.37 for Qwen3-0.6B-Base, +2.39 for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, and +5.05 for Qwen3-4B-Base (Experimental Results section).

EOPD achieves better student-teacher alignment via lower forward KL on high-entropy tokens while sustaining higher token-level entropy in high-uncertainty regions compared to the reverse-KL-only baseline (Experimental Results, Key finding).

ZSZW2diTs5.text: On the N-body particle system benchmark using an equivariant EGNN backbone, BLIP achieves an MSE of 0.060±0.003, nearly matching the 4-member Deep Ensemble's 0.057 while requiring only a single model (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On the data-scarce, out-of-distribution ammonia molecule task, BLIP attains lower energy MAE (11.51±0.75 kcal/mol) and forces MAE (41.93±3.38 kcal/mol/Å) than a Deep Ensemble (11.71 and 48.03 respectively) (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On the same ammonia OOD task, BLIP achieves the best calibration among compared methods with an Expected Calibration Error of 0.091±0.006 (Table 3, Section 4.2).
Predicted uncertainty correlates with squared prediction error with a Spearman correlation of 0.863±0.024 on the ammonia benchmark (Figure 2, Section 4.2).

When fine-tuning the pretrained ORB v3 MLIP on silica glass, BLIP achieves an ECE of 0.032±0.002 versus 0.247 for a Deep Ensemble, at a fraction of the ensemble's computational cost (Figure 3b, Section 4.3).

2CoRS45Ucj.text: Subtask-level memory improves mean Pass@1 by +4.7 percentage points on average across four LLM backbones on SWE-bench Verified (Table 1).
For Gemini 2.5 Pro specifically, subtask-level memory raises Pass@1 from 53.5% to 60.3%, a +6.8 pp gain, the largest among the four backbones tested (Table 1).
An ablation isolating structured prompting alone yields only +1.0 pp improvement, versus +3.9 pp for the full subtask-level memory method, showing decomposition alone is insufficient (Table 2).
Category-isolated memory retrieval yields +3.9 pp improvement versus +1.6 pp for unfiltered global retrieval, showing structural alignment of retrieval matters (Table 3).
Performance gains grow with accumulated experience: instances 301-500 in the task stream show +9 to +10 pp improvement versus only -1 to +3 pp for the earliest instances (Figure 3).
The memory method's benefit scales with task difficulty, giving +8.7 pp on hard tasks (>28 steps) versus +1.8 pp on easy tasks (≤18 steps) (Figure 4).

7j2eMymTTP.text: The paper introduces the principle of Causal Objective Alignment (COA), arguing acquisition functions for active CATE estimation should target unobservable causal quantities like potential outcomes or the CATE itself rather than indirect proxies such as factual outcome uncertainty (Section 3, Principle 1).

The Causal-EPIG framework yields two acquisition strategies: a comprehensive potential-outcome-based strategy, Causal-EPIG-μ (Eq. 4), and a focused CATE-targeting strategy, Causal-EPIG-τ (Eq. 5) (Section 4.1).
Performance is measured via Root PEHE, √E[(τ̂(x)-τ(x))²], evaluated on a fixed target distribution X_tar (Eq. 2, Section 2.1).

Experiments compare Causal-EPIG-μ and Causal-EPIG-τ against Random, BALD-family, coreset, and Causal-EIG baselines across three Bayesian CATE estimators (BCF, CMGP, NSGP) on synthetic CausalBALD/Hahn datasets and semi-synthetic IHDP and ACTG-175 benchmarks (Section 5, Figures 2-4).

The focused Causal-EPIG-τ strategy achieves the highest average relative Root PEHE improvement over the Random baseline across five datasets (CausalBALD, Hahn linear, Hahn nonlinear, IHDP, ACTG-175) (Figure 3, Section 5.1).

Causal-EPIG-μ's performance is attenuated specifically when paired with the BCF estimator, attributed to BCF modeling the prognostic effect and treatment effect separately, causing potential-outcome prediction errors to accumulate (Section 5.1).

lK3AWzD7MS.text: On QM9 molecular graph generation, Categorical Flow Maps achieve 95.8% validity and FCD 2.14 in a single step (1 NFE), improving to 97.0% validity and FCD 0.52 with two steps (Table 1).

On ZINC molecular graph generation, single-step sampling achieves 93.5% validity (FCD 19.3), while two-step sampling reaches FCD 12.2, matching quality reported for 50-100 step diffusion baselines (Table 1).
On binarized MNIST image generation, single-step sampling attains FID 10.1, improving over a prior one-step baseline's FID of 12.9, with two-step sampling further reducing FID to 8.7 (Section 4.2).
Test-time reward-guided generation via flow-map lookahead achieves FID 36.9 and 84.7% target accuracy, the best result among three guidance strategies compared (Table 2).
The Endpoint-Consistent Lagrangian Distillation (ECLD) training objective is proven to bound the Lagrangian residual of the flow-map self-distillation loss (Proposition 3.1).

PRfEvn1UHp.text: TRACE evaluates a tool-augmented agent's trajectory along three dimensions—efficiency, hallucination, and adaptivity—without requiring a ground-truth trajectory, using an incrementally constructed 'evidence bank' built from each step's action, input, and observation (Section 3, Figure 2).

On the Meta-GTA meta-evaluation benchmark, using Llama-3.1-8B as the evaluator, TRACE improves efficiency accuracy from 55.67% (LLM-as-a-Judge) to 70.46% and adaptivity accuracy from 78.98% to 85.28%, a gain of up to +19.44 points (Table 1).

TRACE outperforms the PIPA state-consistency baseline as an efficiency metric across all five evaluator models on Meta-GTA, e.g. Claude-Sonnet-4 scores 94.64 under TRACE versus 84.46 under PIPA (Table 3).

Using Llama-3.3-70B as the TRACE evaluator matches the accuracy of larger proprietary evaluator models (Table 1) while reducing average per-query evaluation time by roughly a factor of three (Figure 3).

On the GTA benchmark evaluated with TRACE, the open-source Qwen-72B agent attains overall accuracy of 52.02%, comparable to proprietary agents Claude-Sonnet-4 (57.67%) and GPT-4.1 (52.81%) (Table 4, Section 5.2.1).

gtmyFnvXAW.text: Deep Forcing enables over 12x length extrapolation from a 5-second-trained Self Forcing backbone to 60-second-plus generation, entirely training-free (Section 4.3, Table 1).

On 60-second VBench-Long evaluation, Deep Forcing achieves higher Dynamic Degree (57.19) than Rolling Forcing (31.35) and LongLive (43.49), and higher Overall Consistency (20.38) than LongLive (20.29), while maintaining comparable throughput at 15.75 FPS versus Self Forcing's 15.78 FPS (Table 1, Appendix E).

The ablation on Deep Sink and Participative Compression shows progressive gains over baseline Self Forcing, with Dynamic Degree improving from 36.62 (SF) to 48.58 (SF+DS) to 57.56 (SF+DS+PC), and Image Quality improving from 68.58 to 68.54 to 69.31 (Table 4/6, Section 5.3).

A user study with 24 participants using the Two-Alternative Forced Choice protocol shows Deep Forcing preferred over CausVid in 100% of overall-quality comparisons and over LongLive in 72.2% of overall-quality comparisons, across 384 total pairwise video comparisons (Table 2, Appendix G).

Deep Sink allocates 40-60% of the sliding window to persistent sink tokens (sink size S=10) with a temporal RoPE realignment (Delta_sink), while Participative Compression retains a budget of N=16 tokens with R=4 recent tokens, selecting the rest via top-C attention-based importance scoring (Section 4.2, Section 4.3, Section 5.1).

nV8GEDzrSn.text: V-LynX identifies a 'token interface' phenomenon in Video LLMs, visualized via t-SNE of 2,000 sampled frame embeddings per benchmark against 10,000 vocabulary token embeddings from pretrained LLaVA-OV, showing visual tokens occupy a continuous manifold distinct from mere vocabulary mapping (Section 1, Figure 2).

V-LynX integrates new modalities (audio, 3D, high-frame-rate video, egocentric/multi-view video) into a frozen Video LLM backbone using lightweight LoRA adapters in the vision encoder, trained only on unpaired unimodal data rather than paired cross-modal supervision (Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Figure 3).

The interface alignment procedure computes reference Key/Value attention statistics per encoder layer (K_v^(l), V_v^(l)) and projector-level mean/variance statistics (mu_v, sigma_v^2) from unlabeled videos, then aligns the new modality's attention responses and token distributions to these video-derived statistics (Section 3.2, Equation 2).

Even with a compact LLaVA-OV-0.5B backbone, V-LynX outperforms PAVE, the prior state-of-the-art efficient multimodal alignment method, while requiring significantly fewer extra parameters per new modality (Section 1, Figure 1a-b).

V-LynX reports state-of-the-art performance and efficiency across nine multimodal benchmarks spanning audio-visual QA, 3D reasoning, high-frame-rate, and multi-view video understanding tasks (Section 1, Figure 1a).

M9DDNGIM7Z.text: DABUF (Data-Attribution-Based Unsafe Training Data Detection and Filtering) uses gradient-similarity-based influence scoring (cosine similarity between target-set and per-example gradients, with dimension reduced to d=8192 via random projection) to detect unsafe training data without predefined safety taxonomies (Section 3.1).

In jailbreaking injection detection on ToxicChat, Llama-3-8B-DABUF achieves 52.0% AUPRC, outperforming Llama-Guard-3-8B (30.3%), Wildguard (44.5%), GradSafe (30.7%), and the OpenAI Moderation API (11.7%) (Table 2).

Retraining Llama-3-8B after removing the top 100 DABUF-flagged unsafe training samples reduces Attack Success Rate on ToxicChat from 90.0% (Wildguard-filtered) or higher to 86.7%, and on XSTest-Response to 5%, compared to 15-50% for baseline filtering methods (Table 4).

In the gender bias mitigation setting using the Bias in Bios dataset with 150 injected biased biography-occupation pairs among 10,000 benign samples, Gemma-2-9B-DABUF achieves 0.530 AUPRC versus 0.089 for the Ada3 embedding-based baseline (Table 6).

Filtering with DABUF reduces the TPR Gender Gap for Llama-3-8B from 0.16 (unfiltered) to 0.14, whereas filtering with the Ada3 embedding baseline increases it to 0.28, indicating that embedding-based filtering can be counterproductive (Table 7).

An analysis of token-level attribution shows that using externally-identified unsafe subsets as the attribution target (DABUF) substantially outperforms directly attributing full model responses, e.g. Llama-3-8B-DABUF reaches 52.0% AUPRC versus 4.70% for Llama-3-8B-Response on ToxicChat (Table 9, Appendix B.1).

J4DiM8EiMJ.text: Using gpt-oss-120b as the sandbagging untrusted model with GPT-4o-mini as a weak supervisor and Llama-3.1-8B as a very weak supervisor, SFT on weak-supervisor demonstrations elicits 85% (Olympiad math), 91% (Super GPQA), and 94% (Code Contests) of full benign performance, while SFT on very-weak-supervisor demonstrations elicits only 40%, 75%, and 69% respectively (Section 3, Figure 2).

RL alone with the weak or very weak supervisor as reward model is unreliable, achieving only 0.34 (Olympiads), 0.30 (Super GPQA), and 0.56 (Code Contests) fraction of benign performance elicited against the weak supervisor, with reward hacking observed on all but one run in Olympiads and Super GPQA (Section 4, Table 1).

Sequential SFT followed by RL achieves near-full elicitation even under the very weak supervisor, reaching 0.88 (Olympiads), 0.99 (Super GPQA), and 0.93 (Code Contests) fraction of benign performance, outperforming SFT or RL alone in every setting (Section 5, Table 1).

When the model is made situationally aware that training is distinguishable from deployment, SFT+RL elicitation with the very weak supervisor drops substantially, from 88% to 36% on Olympiads, from 99% to 60% on Super GPQA, and from 93% to 66% on Code Contests (Section 6.1, Figure 4).

RL against ground truth reward using only the blue team's 10 available ground-truth samples fails to elicit performance due to exploration hacking, since the sandbagging model rarely explores non-sandbagging behavior during training (Section 4).

aH0jZGucwj.text: Grounded Correspondence replaces the learned transition function in video object-centric learning with deterministic Hungarian bipartite matching on slot representations, computed via a cosine-distance cost matrix C_ij = 1 - cos(s_{t-1,i}, s_{t,j}) between consecutive frames' slots (Section 5.3).

On the synthetic MOVi-D and MOVi-E benchmarks (Kubric dataset), Grounded Correspondence outperforms SlotContrast by +15.7 ARI on MOVi-D (73.7 vs 58.0) and +6.8 ARI on MOVi-E (75.7 vs 68.9), while using zero learnable parameters for temporal modeling (Table 4, Section 6.2).

Removing SlotContrast's learned temporal predictor entirely and replacing it with an identity mapping Q_t = S_{t-1} causes minimal performance change on YouTube-VIS (ARI 33.0 vs 32.1, FG-ARI 36.6 vs 36.3), demonstrating the predictor's redundancy (Table 3, Section 4.1).

Grounded saliency initialization, seeding slots at peaks of a Grounded Saliency Metric S_i = L_i - alpha*G_i computed from frozen DINOv2 patch features, reduces the iterations needed for stable Slot Attention convergence from 3 (initial) / 2 (subsequent) to 1 for all frames, while improving YouTube-VIS ARI from 32.1 to 34.6 (Table 1, Section 3.1, Section 5.1).

The Grounded Saliency Metric-based initialization outperforms both norm-based and PCA-based saliency alternatives on MOVi-E (75.7 vs 69.5 and 71.9 FG-ARI) and YouTube-VIS (33.1 vs 31.5 and 32.7 FG-ARI) (Table 5, Section 6.3).

aGhhrgnyLJ.text: AICrypto is a benchmark evaluating state-of-the-art LLMs (including o3/o4-mini, o3-mini, o1, GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0, and DeepSeek) on cryptography tasks spanning classical, modern, and post-quantum (NIST) schemes plus CTF-style challenges from competitions like PlaidCTF (Section 3).

Reasoning-enhanced models (e.g., o3/o4-mini, o1) substantially outperform standard non-reasoning LLMs on cryptographic concept-memorization tasks, approaching or matching human expert performance on this sub-category (Section 4).

On tasks requiring exploitation of common cryptographic vulnerabilities in implementations, top reasoning models achieve accuracy comparable to or exceeding human experts, per the model-vs-human comparison in the results analysis (Section 4).

Across all evaluated models, performance drops sharply on tasks requiring multi-step cryptographic reasoning and abstract mathematical manipulation, identified as the primary bottleneck relative to memorization and vulnerability-identification tasks (Section 4).
The benchmark's task taxonomy and detailed per-model score breakdowns, including CTF-derived challenges from PlaidCTF and UIUC competitions, are documented in the appendices (Appendices A-K).

xEN1n4vu1j.text: SAGE (Strategy-Aware Optimization Modeling with reasoning LLMs) improves average pass@1 accuracy on optimization-modeling benchmarks from 72.7 to 80.3 compared with the strongest open-source baseline model, evaluated across datasets including NL4Opt, OptiBench, and OptMath (Table 3).

SAGE improves component-level solution diversity by 19-29% at pass@16 relative to the strongest open-source baseline, indicating it generates a wider range of valid formulations under repeated sampling (Table 3).
SAGE produces more compact constraint systems, with 14.2% fewer constraints than the baseline while maintaining solution correctness (Table 3).
SAGE is compared against prior specialized optimization-modeling methods such as OPTIMUS and ORL-M as well as chain-of-thought baselines built on general-purpose LLMs (Section 4).

The strategy-aware component is designed to let the LLM recognize recurring optimization problem structures and adapt its modeling strategy accordingly, rather than applying a single fixed modeling procedure (Section 4, Methodology).

BJUEgspMUt.text: CoPT-AIL jointly pretrains a policy and a reward function prior to adversarial imitation learning, in contrast to standard adversarial imitation learning (AIL) pipelines that train policy and reward purely online (Section 3).
Theorem 1 establishes a provable imitation-gap bound for CoPT-AIL showing improvement over the bound for standard AIL as a function of pretraining quality (Theorem 1).

Proposition 1 and Proposition 2 characterize structural properties of the co-pretraining objective that underlie the Theorem 1 guarantee, including how pretraining error propagates into the final imitation gap (Propositions 1-2).

The paper claims to give the first theoretical guarantee showing that pretraining (of both policy and reward) provably reduces the imitation gap in adversarial imitation learning, distinguishing it from prior AIL theory that does not model pretraining benefits (Section 1).
Algorithm 1 specifies the core CoPT-AIL co-pretraining procedure, with Algorithms 2 and 3 given as implementation variants/complementary methods (Algorithms 1-3).

q17jVxMtwS.text: Extracting activation vectors for 275 character archetypes across Gemma 2 27B, Qwen 3 32B, and Llama 3.3 70B and applying PCA shows that only 4-19 principal components are needed to explain 70% of the variance, with PC1 consistently capturing an 'Assistant-ness' dimension whose role-similarity structure correlates at >0.92 across the three models (Section 2).
The Assistant Axis, defined as the contrast vector between default-Assistant activations and the mean of all role vectors, correlates with PC1 at >0.71 at middle layers (Section 3).

Steering activations away from the Assistant direction increases adoption of non-Assistant personas by up to 60% in role-susceptibility tests, while steering toward the Assistant direction reduces persona-based jailbreak success rates from a 65.3-88.5% unsteered baseline (Section 3).

In multi-turn conversations, user embeddings predict the model's subsequent Assistant Axis projection with R^2 of 0.53-0.77, and persona drift away from the Assistant direction is largest in therapy/philosophical contexts and smallest during coding/writing tasks (Section 4).

Clamping activations to the 25th percentile of their normal range across 8-16 middle-to-late layers reduces harmful persona-driven responses by about 60% while preserving benchmark performance on IFEval, MMLU-Pro, GSM8k, and EQ-Bench (Sections 5-6).

uQiVJ2vKhL.text: MME-Reasoning comprises 1,188 curated questions evaluating multimodal large language models on three classical logical reasoning types: deductive, inductive, and abductive (Section 3, Table 2).

The best-performing model, Gemini-2.5-Pro-Thinking, reaches only 60.2% average accuracy on MME-Reasoning, with Seed1.5-VL-Thinking at 59.9% and o4-mini at 57.5%, revealing substantial headroom for state-of-the-art MLLMs (Table 3).

Open-source thinking models show a larger deductive-vs-abductive performance gap (9.81 points) than closed-source thinking models (5.38 points), and Qwen2.5-VL-72B scores 32.3% deductive, 29.9% inductive, and 34.1% abductive, illustrating an imbalance across reasoning types (Table 3).

Human expert performance on the benchmark is 83.4% overall, with comparable deductive and abductive scores (85.8% vs. 85.6%), sharply contrasting with the pronounced abductive-reasoning weakness observed in MLLMs (Table A.2).
The benchmark's question format is 58.50% multiple-choice, 31.57% free-form, and 9.93% rule-based, spanning easy (30.8%), medium (39.3%), and hard (29.9%) difficulty levels (Table 2).

UpEvQrt6UU.text: On the main SVU benchmark comparison (Table 1), ProtoKV outperforms both sliding-window attention (SWA) and the InfiniPot-V token-retention baseline on RVS-Ego, RVS-Movie, OVO-Bench, and StreamingBench for both LLaVA-OV-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbones under matched token budgets (24k tokens for RVS-Ego/Movie, 4k tokens for OVO-Bench/StreamingBench) (Table 1).

At the largest evaluated query delays, ProtoKV achieves up to +20.4 percentage points over SWA and +12.5 percentage points over the InfiniPot-V token-retention baseline on RVS-Movie, with gains growing as query delay increases (Section 4.3).

Component ablations on RVS-Ego with LLaVA-OV-7B (24k token budget) show that removing the far-memory prototype bank causes accuracy to drop from 59.0% to 40.5% at delay Δ=30 (a 17.0-point drop), the largest degradation among all tested ablations (Table 2).

On offline video understanding benchmarks using Qwen2-VL-7B, ProtoKV achieves 62.1%/63.7% accuracy on VideoMME and 67.0%/68.9% on MLVU at 3K/6K token compression budgets, outperforming DyCoke and remaining competitive with InfiniPot-V (Table 3).

Compared to ReKV, a retrieval/offloading-based SVU baseline, ProtoKV achieves comparable accuracy on RVS-Ego (58.0% vs 58.8%) while reducing query-time TTFT from 1.43s to 1.06s and end-to-end latency from 3.92s to 2.90s under matched peak GPU memory of 23.0GB (Table 4).
ProtoKV's online per-frame update overhead on Qwen2.5-VL-7B (RTX 5090, RVS-Ego) is 33.8ms, approximately 30.8% of total per-frame processing time (Section 4.7).

qjeCH95rbF.text: VLA-Arena's structured task design framework quantifies difficulty across three orthogonal axes: Task Structure, Language Command, and Visual Observation (abstract only).

VLA-Arena comprises 170 tasks grouped into four Task Structure dimensions—Safety, Distractor, Extrapolation, and Long Horizon—with each task assigned three difficulty levels (L0-L2), where fine-tuning is performed exclusively on L0 to assess general capability (abstract only).
Language perturbations (W0-W4) and visual perturbations (V0-V4) can be applied orthogonally to any task to enable decoupled robustness analysis (abstract only).

Evaluation of state-of-the-art VLA models on VLA-Arena reveals a strong tendency toward memorization over generalization, asymmetric robustness to perturbations, neglect of safety constraints, and an inability to compose learned skills for long-horizon tasks (abstract only).
VLA-Arena provides an end-to-end toolchain from task definition to automated evaluation, along with VLA-Arena-S/M/L datasets for fine-tuning, released with a public leaderboard (abstract only).

zC44mTE8Zu.text: Linear probing of latitude/longitude prediction (R^2) across ViT, ViT-MAE, DINOv2, CLIP, LLaVA, Qwen, and Gemma shows vision-language models and multimodal foundation models exhibit substantially stronger geospatial structure than vision-only architectures (Table 6).

Vision-only models achieve their strongest geospatial representations at their last/deepest layer, whereas VLMs achieve better geospatial representations in the early layers of their language model block (Section 5).

On a country-identification fine-tuning task, test accuracy rises from 0.15 for ViT-MAE-large to 0.23 for ViT-large, 0.29 for DINOv2-large, 0.32 for DINOv2-giant, and 0.36 for CLIP-large, mirroring the ranking of each model's R^2 probing scores (Table 1).
Prompting VLMs with textual context propagates geospatial information to later layers, in some cases increasing representation quality relative to unprompted image-only input (Section 5, Figure 4).
Median geodesic error (km) and median proximity error per continent, reported for a representative subset of VLMs, reveal systematic geographic disparities in spatial accuracy (Table 4, Table 5).

lTqCHLllix.text: Any algorithm that finds the exact best arm at any step with probability at least 1/2+Omega(1) in the sliding-window streaming multi-armed bandits model requires Omega(W) arm memory, even with unlimited arm pulls (Theorem 1).

An epsilon-best arm can be found with probability at least 1-delta at any step using only O(1/epsilon) arm memory and O((n/epsilon^2) log(W/delta)) arm pulls, independent of the total stream length n (Theorem 2).

For regret minimization under the paper's new epoch-wise regret notion, any single-pass algorithm achieving o(T/W^2) regret requires Omega(W) arm memory, establishing a sharp memory-regret trade-off with a transition around Theta(W) arm memory (Theorem 3).

The sliding-window streaming MAB model separates data arrival (window movement) from arm sampling, distinguishing it from non-stationary and mortal bandit models where the environment changes only as a result of arm pulls (Section 1).

7BoFyTPqMr.text: For uniform integer quantization of a linear layer at a fixed bit width, the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio (SQNR) decomposes into a concentration term (spread/outliers of weights and activations) and an alignment term (alignment of their dominant variation directions) (Section 2).
Popular rotation-based transforms, including the Hadamard transform, improve concentration but completely neglect the alignment component of quantization error (Section 3).

Block Concentration-Alignment Transform (CAT), which uses a covariance estimate from a small calibration set to jointly optimize concentration and alignment, achieves W4A4 SQNR that often rivals W6A6 quantization (Section 1, Figure 1).

A block-diagonal approximation to the CAT-optimal transform matches or outperforms prior transform-based quantization baselines on WikiText perplexity and average accuracy across six zero-shot common-sense reasoning tasks at 4-bit precision, evaluated on Llama 2 7B, Llama 3 8B, Llama 3.2 1B, Ministral 8B, and Qwen 3 8B, even without additional training (Table 1, Section 6).

mLVSIefyWj.text: Violin injects locality bias into Vision Transformer attention via multiple space-filling curves (Snake, Zig-zag, Peano, Hilbert, and transposed variants) combined with decay masks, defined as the Violin Attention mechanism (Section 3.4).

On VTAB-1K fine-tuning, Violin improves accuracy on Structured tasks by up to 8.7% and yields an average gain of 4.7% across all task groups, including a +4.74% average improvement for DeiT-III-S (Section 4.1, Table 3).
Violin adds only 0.0015% additional parameters and 0.64% additional FLOPs relative to DeiT-B, with memory and runtime nearly matching vanilla DeiT-S (Table 1, Table 2).
In pixel-level CIFAR-100 training, Violin increases DeiT-T accuracy by up to 7.2% (Section 4.2, Table 6).

Violin improves ImageNet-1K pretraining, boosting DeiT-T by +0.8% and DeiT-S by +0.9% top-1 accuracy, and improves 100-epoch DINO-S self-supervised pretraining by +0.7% KNN and +0.6% linear-probe accuracy (Section 4.2, Table 5).
On dense prediction transfer, Violin improves ADE20K semantic segmentation by +0.56 mIoU and COCO object detection with Swin-T by +0.4 mask AP (Section 4.3, Table 7).

4L8bHiw2Jm.text: GffMerge merges graph neural network force fields by solving a convex embedding-alignment problem in closed form, exploiting the linear structure of message-passing layers (Section 3).
GffMerge achieves 5-27x speedups over joint fine-tuning across molecular (MD17, MD22) and solid-state electrolyte (LiPS20) benchmarks (Table 3).

On large-scale generic graph benchmarks (MAG240M/Papers100M), the generalized GnnMerge variant attains roughly a 1000x speedup while outperforming the closest baseline by 10.93% on in-domain datasets (Section 5.2, Table 5).
The closed-form GffMerge solution alone, without any subsequent fine-tuning, outperforms all baseline merging methods and models fine-tuned from it converge within 10-20 epochs (Figure 3).
On M3GNet force-field prediction, GffMerge achieves force MAE of 0.82-1.83 kcal/mol/Å, closely matching the Joint Fine-Tuning baseline's 0.62-1.48 kcal/mol/Å (Table 1).

0p617sK4Z4.text: The method derives a semi-supervised loss that integrates paired and unpaired data via data likelihood maximization, formally connected to inverse entropic optimal transport (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).
Proposition 3.1 gives a closed-form expression for the normalization constant Zθ(x) as a double sum of mixture-component terms zmn(x) (Proposition 3.1).
Proposition 3.2 shows the learned conditional distribution πθ(y|x) is a Gaussian mixture parameterized by component means smn(x) and noise-scaled covariances εAn (Proposition 3.2).
The practical parameterization builds a cost function (Eq. 16) and dual potential (Eq. 17) from Gaussian mixtures, enabling efficient sampling and closed-form likelihood computation (Section 3.3).

On a weather-prediction task, test log-likelihood is reported while varying the number of unpaired samples from 10 to 500, alongside comparisons across methods on data-utilization efficiency (Table 1, Table 2).
On the Swiss Roll synthetic benchmark, the model is compared qualitatively and quantitatively against baseline semi-supervised methods (Figure 2).

elXuA5wTWV.text: SALE is an auction-based framework in which heterogeneous AI agents bid with strategic solution plans that are scored by predicted value and cost, enabling dynamic task routing without training a separate routing model (Figure 2).
SALE reduces reliance on the largest agent by 65% on deep search tasks and 40% on coding tasks (Table 6, Section 6).
SALE lowers overall cost by 42% on deep search tasks and 25% on coding tasks relative to always using the largest agent (Table 6, Section 6).
SALE improves pass@1 by +3.5% on deep search tasks and +2.7% on coding tasks while adding negligible token overhead beyond the final execution trace (Table 6, Figure 3).

Small agents achieve about 87% of large-agent performance on the simplest task-complexity bin but only about 21% on the most complex bin, showing small-agent performance fails to scale with task complexity (Figure 1).

i2SGjD0kIj.text: Theorem 2.2 proves a randomized algorithm can construct a weighted subset of size O(1/ε²) whose weighted total loss approximates the true total loss within a (1±ε) multiplicative factor plus additive error proportional to the optimal rank-k approximation cost Φₖ(D) (Theorem 2.2).
Theorem 2.3 extends this coreset guarantee to the row-subset-selection setting, where the selected points must be members of the original dataset rather than arbitrary weighted points (Theorem 2.3).
Assumption 2.1 requires the loss function to satisfy two inequalities bounding its behavior on the top-k subspace versus the orthogonal residual, governed by parameters λ and γ (Assumption 2.1).
Algorithms 1 and 2 implement sensitivity sampling using SVD/leverage-score-based low-rank approximation rather than k-means-style clustering (Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2).
On a 30,000-record Credit Card dataset, the low-rank sensitivity sampling approach reduces coreset approximation error by about 50% compared to clustering-based sensitivity sampling (Section 6.1).
The data-selection method is validated for LLM fine-tuning data selection on Llama3-8B and Qwen2.5-3B across GSM8K, ViGGO, and SQL-generation datasets (Section 6.2, Tables 1-4).

5fbmGFsWsO.text: Averaging outputs from 3-5 independently watermarked language models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Ministral3-8B) suppresses detection z-scores from a range of 5-300 down to below 2, well under the detection threshold of 4 (Table 1).

Theorem 2.3 proves that the l-infinity distance between the ensemble's output distribution and the true unwatermarked distribution is bounded by O(sqrt(log(|V|/delta)/N) + eta^2), showing convergence to the consensus distribution as the number of averaged models N grows (Theorem 2.3).

The WASH ensembling attack improves generation quality by 27.5% while achieving a 6x speedup relative to the best prior watermark-removal baseline, at a computational overhead of only 1.25x-2.4x for N=3-5 models versus 10x-38x for competing methods such as De-mark, ToBlend, and RandomWalk (Table 3, Table 5).

Native watermark detectors' true-positive-rate at 5% false-positive-rate drops to 11-43% under the WASH attack across six watermarking schemes (AAR, DIPMark, ITS-Edit, KGW, Exp-Edit, Water-Bag) (Table 2).

A control experiment shows that when watermarking schemes are coordinated (synchronized) across the ensembled models rather than applied independently, detection signals persist above z>4, demonstrating that independence of the watermarks across models is essential for the ensemble attack to succeed (Figure 3c).

dqmt0Yd4rc.text: Reframes GUI grounding as an interactive cursor-movement task in which a Vision Language Model iteratively moves a rendered cursor and receives explicit visual feedback at each step, rather than predicting a static numeric coordinate directly (Section on methodology/Gui-Cursor formulation).

Gui-Cursor, built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and trained with multi-step online GRPO reinforcement learning, achieves 93.9% accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2 (up from a baseline of 88.8%) and 56.5% accuracy on ScreenSpot-Pro (up from a baseline of 26.8%) (benchmark results tables).
Gui-Cursor outperforms the prior state-of-the-art method GTA1 by 6.4 percentage points on the ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark (benchmark results tables).

The reward function combines a position-based reward for final cursor accuracy with four trajectory penalties (False Stop, False Move, False Direction, and Repeated Position Penalty), and an ablation shows removing any individual penalty decreases performance (ablation study).

The model completes 95% of grounding instances within two cursor-movement steps, using Cursor-Centric Focusing (CCF) to crop high-resolution images around the cursor at inference time after training at 1920x1080 resolution (experimental analysis section).

Dly6gCtE4V.text: Lemma 3.2 proves that regularising the operator-level equivariance defect ||T - P(T)|| is quantitatively equivalent, up to a factor of 2, to a natural measure of distance to the equivariant subspace (Lemma 3.2).

Theorem 3.8 shows that equivariant maps are block-diagonal in Fourier space, which enables the projection-based regulariser to be computed via spectral masking rather than expensive spatial group-orbit integration (Theorem 3.8).

On imperfectly symmetric dynamics benchmarks, RSteer+Reg achieves 0.79+/-0.00 MSE on the rotation setting and 0.62+/-0.01 MSE on the scaling setting, outperforming a sample-based regularisation baseline (Table 1, Section 4.2).

On CT metal artifact reduction across three architectures (ACDNet, DICDNet, OSCNet), the projection-based regulariser matches or exceeds a sample-based regulariser in PSNR/SSIM while training 42-47% faster at fixed batch size and 54-61% faster at the maximum feasible batch size (Table 2, Section 4.3).
Corollary 3.4 bounds the total non-equivariance defect of a network by a sum of per-layer penalties weighted by downstream Lipschitz constants (Corollary 3.4).

E4gftzjqoh.text: Theorem 2 establishes that in highly sparse feature settings, the mutual information between features and labels is barely affected by additional missingness except at extremely high missing rates, implying standard sparse benchmarks cannot meaningfully distinguish robustness among GNN methods (Theorem 2, Section 2).

Standard citation benchmarks Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed have feature sparsity of 98.73%, 99.15%, and 89.98% respectively, which the paper argues makes them unsuitable for evaluating robustness to missing features; four new lower-sparsity datasets (Synthetic, Air, Electric, Tadpole) are introduced instead, with sparsity ranging from 0% to 20% (Section 3).

GNNmim, which concatenates zero-padded observed features with a binary missingness mask before standard GNN layers, maintains consistently high AUC across all missingness mechanisms and datasets, whereas the baseline FairAC degrades from 0.870 AUC on Electric to 0.641 AUC on Synthetic under the FD-MNAR mechanism (Figure 2, Section 5).

Under the distribution-shift regime R2, where models are trained on 50% FD-MNAR/CD-MNAR missingness and tested on 0%-50% U-MCAR missingness, GNNmim achieves the highest F1 scores among compared methods despite this train/test mismatch (Figure 3).

hGwbWNhWvd.text: CoIRL-AD is a decoupled dual-actor framework that integrates imitation learning and reinforcement learning under an offline training regime, using a competitive/collaborative mechanism between the two actors within a latent world model (Section 3).
On nuScenes, applying CoIRL-AD to the LAW baseline reduces the collision rate from 0.22% to 0.18% while reaching 0.63m average L2 displacement error (Table 1).
On the Navsim benchmark, WoTE+CoIRL-AD achieves an 88.2 PDMS score with a 98.6% no-fault-collision rate (Table 2).
On cross-city generalization from Singapore to Boston, LAW+CoIRL-AD reduces average L2 displacement error from 0.931m (LAW baseline) to 0.702m (Section 5/Analysis).

An ablation over the causal-mask design shows the inverse causal mask configuration achieves the best collision rate of 0.20%, versus 0.27% for the standard causal mask, and a pure-RL configuration (without the decoupled competitive IL-RL integration) yields a much worse 4.93% collision rate (Table 3, Table 4).

bcRBqG8FFN.text: The (σ,σ′)-RL-EDA variant, which uses uniform random permutations for both solution generation and training order, is identified as the best-performing among five order-invariant algorithm variants tested (Section 3.3, Section 4.1).
On NK landscape instances with N=256 and K=4, the four RL-EDA variants are compared via score evolution and mean Hamming distance from the best solution over function evaluations (Figure 1).

The method is benchmarked against 500-504 algorithms from the Nevergrad library (v1.0.12) on QUBO (N=128, K=5) and NK (N=256, K=4) problem instances, with (σ,σ′)-RL-EDA ranking among the top 10 competitors (Figure 2).

Experiments use a fixed budget of 10,000 objective function evaluations per instance, with 10 instances per problem configuration and 10 independent restarts per instance, across instance sizes n ∈ {64, 128, 256} (Section 4).
The training procedure adapts GRPO to derive scale-invariant, ranking-based advantages for the order-invariant policy gradient updates (Section 3.2, Equation 5).
Performance degrades on NK3 landscapes with K=8 compared to lower-epistasis (lower K) configurations, indicating sensitivity to the degree of variable interaction (Table 3, Appendix L).

dnpLavxTXv.text: CoDaPO (Confidence and Difficulty-adaptive Policy Optimization) is motivated by three observed GRPO training-dynamics patterns: confidence inflation (model confidence concentrates near 100% for both correct and incorrect trajectories), advantage contraction (positive advantages shrink while negative ones grow as accuracy improves), and hierarchical convergence (easy questions saturate quickly while hard questions remain discovery-limited) (Section 3).

CoDaPO consists of three components—CoDaWeighting, CoDaLearning, and CoDaSampling—that respectively assign bounded per-question values from rollout confidence and empirical difficulty, rescale policy-gradient updates using these weighted objectives, and resample high-value questions within mini-batches (Section 1, Figure 1).
Starting from the Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B base model, reported accuracy improves from 30.63% to 71.54% on MATH500 and from 18.78% to 36.16% on OlympiadBench after training (Section 1).
CoDaPO is evaluated across twelve benchmarks and is reported to consistently outperform GRPO and related RL methods in both accuracy and generalization (Section 1).

uIsdcoSD3G.text: The Moving Out benchmark formalizes human-AI collaboration as a decentralized Markov Decision Process (Dec-MDP) with continuous state-action spaces and physical constraints such as object mass, shape, and size, unlike prior discrete grid-world benchmarks like Overcooked-AI (Section 3, Figure 1).

The environment includes 12 maps spanning 3 collaboration modes and is built on demonstration datasets of 1,000 human-human trajectories from 36 participants (Task 1) and 720 expert demonstrations from 4 players on randomized maps (Task 2) (Section 4).

On Task 1 (adapting to diverse human behaviors), the BASS method improves Task Completion Rate from 0.3829 (Diffusion Policy baseline) to 0.5027 and Normalized Final Distance from 0.4818 to 0.5707 (Table 1).

On Task 2 (generalizing to unseen physical constraints), BASS improves Task Completion Rate from 0.3125 to 0.4348 and Normalized Final Distance from 0.4526 to 0.5535 relative to the Diffusion Policy baseline (Table 1).
A 32-participant human study finds BASS significantly outperforms the Diffusion Policy baseline on perceived 'Helpfulness' (p=0.017) and 'Physics Understanding' on a 7-point Likert scale (Figure 7).

BASS combines Behavior Augmentation (pose perturbation and sub-trajectory recombination), Simulation (next-state prediction via autoencoders and a dynamics model), and Selection (action evaluation from predicted states) (Section 5, Figure 5).

IMKni29CXX.text: SA-Merging estimates parameter saliency via connectivity scores derived from a differentiable inter-layer interaction function to identify parameters critical to end-to-end information flow, then iteratively prunes non-informative parameters over T=10 iterations with a pruning ratio p=0.2 (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
On ViT-B/32 across 8 vision tasks, SA-Merging achieves 85.9% average accuracy, outperforming the WUDI-Merging baseline's 85.2% (Table 1).
On ViT-L/14, SA-Merging reaches 93.4% average accuracy, nearly matching traditional multitask learning at 93.5% (Table 2).
On GLUE tasks with RoBERTa, SA-Merging achieves 87.1% (Base) and 90.2% (Large), surpassing WUDI-Merging by 1.8 and 1.4 percentage points respectively (Table 3).

SA-Merging extends to LoRA expert merging, reaching 82.5% average performance on GLUE tasks with Flan-T5 and 56.33% average across MMLU, TruthfulQA, BBQ, and CNN/DailyMail with Qwen-14B (Table 4, Table 5).

SA-Merging completes in 20 seconds using 14.5GB memory, roughly 6x faster than WUDI-Merging, and its performance plateaus around 10 iterations with an optimal pruning ratio of p=0.2 (Table B4, Figure 3).

kovefbSXbQ.text: The framework formalizes behavioral systems as F-coalgebras and defines behavioral semantics via n-ary 'bundles' (Definition 3.1) mapping X^n → V, giving local, one-step descriptions of system dynamics (Section 2, Section 3.1).

Behavioral structures are characterized as post-fixed points (or fixed points) of a closure operator T_X = t_X* ∘ λ_X composed from system pullback and bundle lifting (Definition 3.8, Definition 3.9).

Theorem 3.12 (Safe verification) shows surjective homomorphisms reflect post-fixed points via pullback, while Theorem 3.13 (Safe construction) shows pushforward preserves post-fixed points, establishing safe transfer of behavioral structures between abstract and concrete systems (Section 3.5).

Theorem 3.14 (Logical-quantitative relation) connects logical and quantitative bundles via a zero predicate z: [0,∞] → {⊤,⊥} under algebra homomorphism conditions, enabling construction of quantitative metrics with soundness guarantees from logical semantics (Section 3.5).

The framework instantiates state abstraction methods in RL as special cases, including next-observation prediction (Proposition 4.1), model-irrelevance abstraction (Proposition 4.2), and bisimulation relations via quotient maps (Proposition 4.3) (Section 4).

A policy-dependent transition α^π, expressed as a natural transformation connecting a Moore-machine functor and a hidden Markov model functor, closes the loop between environment and policy in the framework's running example (Example 2.9, Figure 1).

35e16MmSL0.text: Hyper-prototypes are multiple learnable class-wise vectors optimized via a gradient-matching loss that minimizes cosine distance between the gradients induced by real client samples and by the hyper-prototypes (Section 2.2, Equation 8).

FedHPro combines Hyper-Prototype Contrastive Learning (HPCL) for inter-class separability and Hyper-Prototype Alignment Learning (HPAL) for intra-class uniformity into a combined objective L = L_CE + L_HPCL + L_HPAL (Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Equation 15).
Under label/quantity skew on CIFAR-10 (Dirichlet concentration 0.5), FedHPro reaches 89.56% accuracy versus 87.93% for the FedSA baseline, a 1.63-point gain (Table 1).
Under domain skew on Office-Caltech, FedHPro achieves 64.52% average accuracy versus 60.57% for FedSA, a 3.95-point improvement (Table 2).
An ablation on the Digits benchmark shows HPCL alone reaches 83.58% and HPAL alone 83.94%, while combining both reaches 84.80%, compared to a 78.82% baseline without either module (Table 5).

Theorem 3.1 establishes a non-convex convergence guarantee showing the expected squared gradient norm can be bounded by an arbitrary epsilon given sufficiently many communication rounds R (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1).

6GeYRoYKWP.text: Reward models trained with the proposed distributionally robust optimization (DR-RLHF) objective are given convergence guarantees via Theorems 1-3, with the tractable optimization algorithm detailed in Appendix A (Theorems 1-3, Appendix A).

On RewardBench, the robust reward model shows accuracy improvements over the standard-trained baseline across categories (Chat, Chat Hard, Safety, Reasoning), with the largest gain observed on the Reasoning category (Table 12).

A robust variant of policy optimization (robust MDPO) is compared against standard policy optimization on out-of-distribution task evaluations, showing improved performance for the robust variant (Table 14).
Reward model accuracy and downstream policy performance under distribution shift are evaluated using RewardBench and Unified Feedback datasets (Table 12, Table 14).

TnquAvyTtL.text: TPGD (Algorithm 1) is a two-phase first-order gradient-descent method for jointly estimating a shared linear representation and task-specific parameters in multi-task learning (Section 4, Algorithm 1).

Phase I performs K1/2 iterations of unregularized gradient descent as a warm start, and Phase II performs the remaining K1/2 iterations of regularized gradient descent with penalty term ||B^T B − WW^T||_F^2 (Section 4).

Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.3 prove the method attains a near-optimal population estimation error of order Õ(dk/(NT)), improving over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of k, where d is input dimension, k is representation dimension, T is the number of tasks, and N is per-task sample size (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.3).
The algorithm achieves Õ(1) iteration complexity, i.e., convergence in a number of iterations independent of the problem dimensions up to logarithmic factors (Section 5.1).
The estimation-error guarantee requires a per-task sample size of N ≳ σ²(d+T)kκ⁴/σ_k²(Σ*) (Section 5.1).

Theorem 5.4 establishes excess-risk bounds for transferring the learned representation to a new task, decomposing the risk into representation approximation error and task-specific optimization error (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.4).

YEckWPoS09.text: Theorem 3.3 gives a non-asymptotic instance-dependent lower bound on the expected stopping time, E_Q[tau_alpha] ≥ (log(1/alpha)/D_M^inf(Q,P) − 2C_Q/min_i pi_i)^+, where D_M^inf(Q,P) is a stationary-weighted projection distance and C_Q bounds a Poisson-equation solution (Theorem 3.3).
Proposition 3.1 bounds the Poisson-equation solution constant C_Q via the pseudo-spectral gap of the underlying Markov chain (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).

The proposed Sequential Markov Chain Test (Algorithm 1) builds an empirical transition kernel and a martingale statistic L_t accumulating row-wise KL divergences from the null class, stopping when L_t exceeds an adaptive boundary beta_t (Section 4, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 4.1 proves the proposed test is alpha-correct and asymptotically optimal, with limsup_{alpha->0} E_Q[tau_alpha]/log(1/alpha) ≤ 1/D_M^inf(Q,P), matching the Theorem 3.3 lower bound (Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 4.4 extends the one-sided asymptotic optimality result to the two-sided testing setting (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.4).
The framework is applied to detect MCMC transition-kernel misspecification (Section 5.1, Corollary 5.1) and to validate linear transition dynamics in MDPs (Section 5.2, Corollary 5.3).

b1qoHUQVNy.text: The method combines Bayesian cross-validation with data fission, a randomized measurement-splitting technique that partitions a single noisy measurement into two synthetic measurements conditionally independent given the unknown image (Section 3).
Two scoring rules are defined: a likelihood-based rule Φ¹ and a posterior-based rule Φ² that uses LPIPS perceptual embeddings to evaluate prior fit (Section 3.2, Equations 5 and 7).
The framework is demonstrated with plug-and-play Langevin samplers using a gradient-step denoiser and with denoising diffusion samplers via the DiffPIR algorithm (Section 3, Section 4).
On a blur-kernel model-selection task, single-measurement accuracy reaches 86.7%, rising to 100% with multiple measurements, versus 40-60% for baseline methods (Section 4.2, Table 1).

For out-of-distribution detection on natural images, the method attains a Type I error near 6.7%, with power of 60-86.7% for moderate distribution shift and 100% for strong shift (Section 4.3.1, Table 2).
For MRI reconstruction misspecification detection, Type I error is 0-6% and detection power is 94-100% across acceleration factors R=4 and R=8 (Section 4.3.2, Table 3).

fotqwXEglz.text: The Pseudo-Mallows distribution provides a closed-form variational approximation to the Bayesian Mallows posterior that can be sampled directly via Algorithm 1, avoiding the need for MCMC sampling required by the standard Bayesian Mallows model (Section 2.2, Algorithm 1).

The optimal ordering (V-set) used to factorize the Pseudo-Mallows distribution is selected by maximizing an Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) on the marginalized KL-divergence between the Pseudo-Mallows approximation and the true Mallows posterior (Section 2.3, Equation 13).

For small item sets (n ≤ 9), full enumeration shows that 'V'-shaped orderings minimize the KL-divergence of the Pseudo-Mallows approximation, motivating the iterative search heuristic for larger n (Section 2.4.2, Figure 2).

Theorem 2 shows that as the number of observed rankings N → ∞, the ranking induced by the average observed ranks converges to the true consensus ranking ρ⁰, providing a data-driven way to infer the V-set (Section 2.5.1, Theorem 2).

Algorithm 2, an iterated search using the Hungarian Method for bipartite matching, is demonstrated on a simulation with n=15 items and N=500 rankings (α₀=2.5), converging toward the V-ranking pattern within the algorithm's iteration cap (100 iterations for small n, 50 for larger n) (Section 2.4.2, Figure 3).

The Pseudo-Mallows framework is extended to clicking/implicit-feedback data and applied to a real-life clicking dataset case study for individual ranking estimation and personalized recommendations (Section 3, Section 4.3).

b0qTeltEg8.text: DOMOO achieves the best average hypervolume rank of 4.63 ± 0.38 across all benchmark tasks, compared to next-best competing methods ranking between 6.41 and 10.84 (Table 1).
DOMOO attains the best average rank of 6.27 ± 0.23 on the paper's proposed IGD_offline metric, indicating a superior balance of diversity and convergence relative to baselines (Table 2, Section 4.3).

The IGD_offline metric is defined as an offline indicator that measures distance from offline solutions to a shifted candidate Pareto front, explicitly designed to avoid the bias toward extreme solutions exhibited by the hypervolume indicator (Equation 4, Section 4.3).

Nested Pareto set learning uses a preference-gradient update with an accumulative risk-control term R(x) = c(E_Q̃ − E_ω(x))/(E_Q̃ − E_P̃) applied across pretraining, exploration, and preference-gradient-update phases (Section 4.2, Equation 2).
An ablation study shows that removing the nested Pareto set learning component (w.o. NPSL) causes the largest performance degradation among DOMOO's components across the tested benchmarks (Table 3).

DOMOO ranks among the top methods on MO-NAS (multi-objective neural architecture search) tasks but the authors note reduced performance on extremely discrete tasks requiring one-hot encodings due to sparse input space (Section 5.2).

XrRqY9QOSa.text: Brain alignment correlates with task performance more strongly for language models (Pearson r=0.89, p<7.5×10⁻¹³, on LLM Leaderboard 2 performance) than for vision models (Pearson r=0.53, p<2.0×10⁻⁴⁴, on ImageNet accuracy) (Figure 1d-e, Table 1).
For language models, a logarithmic fit between brain alignment and performance (R²=0.80) outperforms a linear fit (R²=0.78), with individual benchmark correlations ranging r=0.66–0.84 (Table 1).

Layer-wise analysis shows vision models exhibit progressively increasing brain alignment with network depth, whereas language models peak in brain alignment at middle layers (3/8 to 5/8 normalized depth), with deeper vision layers converging toward language-model-like organization (Figure 2).

Across Pythia model checkpoints, brain alignment stabilizes by approximately 10% of training tokens for language models, while vision models show a sharp early increase in alignment reaching about 85% of maximum by 20% of training samples, indicating alignment emerges before performance gains (Figure 3, Pythia correlations r=0.73–0.95).

Kernel-size (spatial scale) analysis shows brain alignment decreases at larger scales in primary visual areas V1, V2, V3 (Δ=−5.30, −2.81, −1.05) while increasing in limbic regions such as orbitofrontal cortex (Δ=+1.56), with sign consistency of 0.83 across subjects (Figure 4).

Inter-subject consistency of alignment scores is very high for both language models (r=0.997–1.000) and vision models (r=0.970–0.999), supporting a shared, near-universal organizational principle underlying brain-model correspondence (Tables 2–3).

ThxAdzExdS.text: On CLEVR-Hans3, Neural Concept Verifier (NCV) achieves completeness of 98.92±0.32 and soundness of 100.00±0.00, outperforming ResNet-18 (97.87±0.24 completeness) and a concept bottleneck model (CBM, 95.44±0.08 completeness) (Table 1).
On CLEVR-Hans7, NCV attains 97.89±0.31 completeness and 100.00±0.00 soundness, exceeding the CBM baseline by roughly 8.77 percentage points in completeness (Table 1).

On the real-world datasets CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k, NCV reaches 83.32±0.28 and 67.04±0.16 completeness respectively, surpassing CBM (75.42±0.04 on CIFAR-100) and a pixel-based Merlin-Arthur classifier (Pixel-MAC), which fails at only 35.06±3.20 completeness on ImageNet-1k (Table 1).

On the shortcut-learning evaluation using CLEVR-Hans7 with 0% clean training data, NCV achieves 92.23±0.67 test accuracy with a validation-test performance gap of 6.15, smaller than the gap for a nonlinear CBM (7.40), indicating reduced shortcut reliance (Table 2).
With 20% clean data added during training on CLEVR-Hans7, NCV's validation-test gap shrinks further to 0.89, the most improved among compared models (Table 2).

NCV's classifier is built on the Merlin-Arthur framework, which provides formal soundness and completeness guarantees, and concepts are extracted using either CLIP or the unsupervised Neural Concept Binder (NCB) (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).

pNe5fVK1tR.text: Theorem 1 (Section 3.3) establishes the optimal rank-r compression of a linear layer using Kronecker-decomposed Fisher information factors L_A and L_B, and proves that GFWSVD generalizes the diagonal-Fisher-based FWSVD method as a special case.

GFWSVD reduces the computational complexity of computing the Kronecker-factored Fisher-weighted objective from quartic to cubic in the weight matrix dimensions via the structured identity ℑ̃_F z = (1/|D|)Σ vec(G_iᵀ Z G_i) (Section 4, Equation 15).

On BERT with GLUE macro-average scores, GFWSVD outperforms FWSVD, ASVD, and plain SVD at matched compression rates, e.g. scoring 0.53 vs. FWSVD's 0.43 at rank 10 (~61% compression) and 0.75 vs. FWSVD's 0.68 at rank 250 (~77% compression) (Table 2).
On LLaMA 2 7B at 95% of original parameters (5% removed), GFWSVD achieves a WikiText-2 perplexity of 7.16 versus 7.52 for FWSVD, while matching FWSVD's MMLU average accuracy of 0.40 (Table 3).
On LLaMA 2 7B at 85% of original parameters (15% removed), GFWSVD achieves a WikiText-2 perplexity of 10.06 (vs. 10.91 for ASVD) and a PTB perplexity of 42.19 (vs. 72.58 for SVD-LLM) (Table 3).
The empirical evaluation of GFWSVD in this paper is conducted on BERT and LLaMA 2 7B compression tasks; no experiments on LLaMA 3 are reported in the main text (Section 5.2, Table 3).

33xuIDnp4u.text: On ImageNet, up to 75% of the training data can be pruned without harming Latent Flow-Matching generation performance (Abstract).
On CelebA-HQ, balanced clustering-based pruning at 50% data reduction achieves an FID of 22.80, better than the 24.24 FID of the unpruned baseline (Figure 3).
At 90% data pruning, fewer than 3% of samples change their flow-matching trajectory endpoints, evidencing assignment stability (Figure 2, Section 2.2).

A coarse-to-fine inference scheme pairs a DiT-S/2 (33M parameter) coarse model for t in [0, t0) with a DiT-XL/2 (675M parameter) fine model for t in [t0, 1], trained with a continuity loss matching velocity fields at the seam (Section 2.4, Equation 4).
With seam point t0=0.7, the coarse-to-fine approach achieves approximately 2.15x faster inference on an NVIDIA H100 (43.53 ms vs. 93.95 ms per image) while maintaining FID quality (Figure 5).

ArcFace cosine similarity between models trained on disjoint data subsets ranges from 0.79-0.83 versus the unpruned baseline, compared to a 0.37 baseline similarity for random image pairs (Section 3.1, Section 3).

19ksKPfJcT.text: FAHNES is presented as the first hierarchical generative method for both graphs and hypergraphs able to jointly generate topology and features, achieving quasi-linear complexity of O((n+m+k) log n) (Section 3).
On unfeatured hypergraph generation, FAHNES achieves 87.8±3.1% validity on SBM versus HYGENE's 65.0%, and 99.5±1.1% on Ego versus HYGENE's 90.0% (Table 1).
On featured 3D mesh generation, FAHNES attains a Chamfer Distance of 0.048±0.003 on ManifoldNet Airplane, versus 0.082±0.074 for a sequential (flat) baseline (Table 4).
FAHNES is the only method able to generate 971-node airplane point clouds, whereas DiGress, Flow Matching, and DeFoG baselines encounter out-of-memory errors (Table 3).

Ablations show removing the hierarchical scale-encoding mechanism increases node-count error on ModelNet Piano from 0.846 to 3.622, and removing the multi-scale graph optimal-transport coupling degrades ManifoldNet Airplane Chamfer Distance from 0.048 to 0.050 (Table 5).

1GvXUhLIMP.text: LiftQuant uses a lift-then-project mechanism representing weights as projections of a 1-bit lattice from a higher-dimensional space, with effective bit-width given by the ratio D/d of lifted dimension D to original dimension d (Section 3.2-3.3).

A Llama-3-70B model quantized to 2.4 bits (configuration LQ-24/10) fits within a 24GB GPU and achieves 3.78 WikiText-2 perplexity and 5.83 C4 perplexity, outperforming QTIP's 2-bit result of 4.97 WikiText-2 perplexity (Table 2).

On five reasoning benchmarks, a Llama-2-70B model at 2.4 bits reaches 62.42% average accuracy, compared with QTIP's 2-bit result of 71.12%... wait this appears to contradict claimed superiority (Table 3).
Decoding throughput for LiftQuant configuration LQ-32/16 reaches 31.3 tokens/second, compared to 24.5 tokens/second for QTIP at 2-bit (Table 4).
The whitening-transform parameters used by LiftQuant add only 0.008-0.011 bits per parameter of overhead in FP16 storage for Llama-70B models (Section 3.2).
Ablations on Llama-2-7B WikiText-2 perplexity show progressive gains from 8.76 (orthogonal matrices alone) to 6.53 (with end-to-end fine-tuning added) (Table 5).

FvRAsWEgCS.text: A Matryoshka Kernel with nested weight tensor W_nested in R^(D x Cmax x k x k) generates valid convolution kernels via slice-based selection, giving spectral-band agnosticism for arbitrary numbers of input channels (Section 3.2, Equation 2).

An Implicit Neural Representation backbone models hyperspectral images as continuous functions queried at arbitrary spatial coordinates, enabling reconstruction at non-integer upsampling scales (Section 3.3, Equation 7).
In-distribution evaluation at x4 scale on the CAVE dataset achieves PSNR of 45.96 dB, SAM of 2.55, and ERGAS of 1.72 (Table 1).
The single trained model generalizes to out-of-distribution scales x8, x16, and x32, achieving best or second-best results on nearly all out-of-distribution metrics (Section 4.3.1).
On unseen sensor datasets, the model achieves 38.71 dB PSNR on Houston (48 bands) and 36.42 dB PSNR on Loukia (176 bands), despite training on different sensor configurations (Table 3).
The model, trained only at x4 scale, generalizes to fractional scales, reaching 45.02 dB PSNR at x3.2 and 43.49 dB PSNR at x5.7 (Table 3).

H4wc2tjCNG.text: RLIE decomposes rule-based reasoning into four stages—rule generation, logistic regression, iterative refinement, and evaluation—so that LLMs handle semantic rule induction while a statistical model performs globally calibrated rule-weight composition (Section on Division of Labor).

Using DeepSeek-V3.2, the direct logistic-regression combiner (E1) achieves 70.9% accuracy on the Reviews dataset, outperforming LLM-prompting variants using rules only (E2, 65.7%), rules plus weights (E3, 65.4%), and rules plus weights plus predictions (E4, 69.5%) (Table 2).
RLIE achieves substantially lower Expected Calibration Error than direct rule-injection prompting, e.g. 0.116 versus 0.480 ECE on the Retweets dataset (Section on Calibration Advantage).

Across six datasets (Reviews, Dreaddit, Headlines, Citations, LLM Detect, Retweets) with DeepSeek-V3.2, RLIE attains accuracy/F1 ranging from 64.6/63.0 (Citations) to 90.7/90.7 (LLM Detect) (Table 1).
RLIE consumes an average of 12.23M tokens per task, about 8% fewer than HypoGeniC's 13.24M tokens, while providing more comprehensive rule validation (Table 3).

b0Tr5J6ilw.text: AI induces phase transitions in delegation behavior, where arbitrarily small differences in a worker's verification ability lead to sharply different delegation decisions (Section 6).
Rational, individually-optimal over-delegation to AI can degrade institutional worker quality even when the AI improves baseline task success rates (Section 6).

The model characterizes conditions under which a worker should fully delegate to AI, partially verify AI outputs, or retain full decision authority, based on verification cost relative to task complexity (Section 6).

AI amplifies institutional quality for workers with strong verification reliability while degrading it for workers with weak verification reliability, widening disparities that track verification ability rather than baseline competence (Section 6).

s8cdRWLTCc.text: CortexMAE is a self-supervised foundation model family trained on 2.1K hours of open fMRI data using a masked-autoencoder objective (abstract only).

CortexMAE converts 3D fMRI volumes into 2D representations via cortical flat-map projection, and this flat-map representation generally outperforms parcellation-based and native-volume-based representations for the same MAE training recipe (abstract only).
The paper introduces Brainmarks, described as the first open evaluation suite for fMRI foundation models (abstract only).

Scaling analysis of CortexMAE shows power-law scaling behavior, though with identified limitations, and on subject-level trait prediction no model achieves clear superiority over a functional-connectivity baseline (abstract only).
CortexMAE outperforms prior models by a wide margin on cognitive state decoding tasks (abstract only).

z9aetU7Wfl.text: The paper proves Theorems 2.1 through 2.7 establishing convergence guarantees and sample-complexity bounds (via Rademacher-complexity arguments) for cross-modal knowledge distillation without paired teacher-student data (Theorems 2.1-2.7).
The theoretical framework identifies feature alignment and label alignment as the two fundamental quantities governing successful unpaired cross-modal distillation (Section 2).
The proposed algorithm uses optimal transport to align entire teacher and student distributions across modalities, rather than requiring individually paired samples (Section 3).
The method is evaluated on the audio-visual benchmarks VGGSound, CREMA-D, and AVE (Section 4).
The proposed unpaired distillation framework improves over prior cross-modal distillation methods in both unpaired and paired data settings across these benchmarks (Section 4).

IiBXrSpX9M.text: On Qwen3-0.6B, roughly 8% of generated tokens account for the salient disagreement between the base and reasoning (Thinking) model, with disagreement mass extremely concentrated in a few token positions (Section 4.1).
High-disagreement tokens cluster early in generation and are enriched 17x for planning-related decisions relative to their base rate (Section 4.2, Table 1).
Aggregated high-disagreement-token signals predict reasoning failures on GSM8K with 0.851 AUROC, outperforming an entropy-based predictor's 0.817 AUROC (Table 2).

A disagreement-gated intervention that lets the reasoning model generate only top-r% disagreement tokens (with the base model generating the rest) raises Qwen3-0.6B average Pass@8 from a 36.0 base rate to 61.4 at sparse budget (rho about 0.04) and to 80.0 at moderate budget (rho about 0.13), exceeding the 64.1 Pass@8 of the full Qwen3-0.6B Thinking model (Table 3).
Matched-budget baseline comparisons confirm that gains come from where tokens are selected for intervention, not merely from injecting strong-model tokens at any position (Table 4).

jxdjDmWpNX.text: Style-Conditioned Implicit Q-Learning (SCIQL) trains style-conditioned value functions via expectile regression and extracts policies via advantage-weighted regression, using hindsight relabeling to handle sparse style supervision (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).

On the style alignment metric, SCIQL outperforms baselines including SCBC and BCPMI, e.g. 74.6% vs 68.6% (SCBC) on Circle2d-inplace and 78.0% vs 58.0% (BCPMI) on HalfCheetah-fixed, while matching SCBC's 99.6% on HumEnv-simple (Table 1, Section 5.2).
SCIQL achieves 41.2%-163.9% hypervolume improvements over the SORL baseline on Pareto-front analyses jointly optimizing style alignment and task performance (Figure 2, Section 5.3).

The paper introduces Gated Advantage Weighted Regression (GAWR), which combines style and task advantages as xi(A^lambda, A^r) = A^lambda + sigma(A^lambda) * A^r, modulating task-objective optimization based on the style-alignment signal to prevent task learning from degrading style alignment (Section 4.3).

aDLJNoseDH.text: Theorem III.1 derives an analytical bound on the total variation distance between the exact and reduced-precision Metropolis-Hastings stationary distributions, showing the bias scales with the sampler's contraction rate r (Theorem III.1).

Theorem III.3 shows that for local Metropolis-Hastings proposals with Gaussian perturbation from reduced precision, the bias in the stationary distribution scales as O(sigma^2) rather than O(sigma) when the chain mixes rapidly (Theorem III.3).

On a 2D transverse-field Ising model with N=100 sites, f16 and bf16 sampling achieve speedups of up to 3.5x and 3.2x respectively over full precision, with no measurable degradation in final energy accuracy (Numerical Results).

The mixed-precision scheme keeps only the Metropolis-Hastings sampling step in reduced precision (f16/bf16) while retaining double precision for gradient computation and parameter updates (Section on Mixed-Precision Framework).
Speedup from reduced-precision sampling increases with both network parameter count and batch size for both RBM and ResCNN neural quantum state architectures (Architecture Performance results).

The perturbation introduced by reduced precision is empirically shown to be approximately Gaussian-distributed, with Shapiro-Wilk normality test statistics at or above 0.97 across tested configurations (Error Analysis).

Lm3Js8viIP.text: On Charades-STA with a Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, F2G improves R@0.7 from 21.6% (fine-tuned baseline) to 25.7%, a +4.1 point gain, and mIoU from 42.9 to 47.2 (Table of main results).
On ActivityNet-Captions with the same backbone, F2G improves R@0.7 from 21.7% to 28.4% (+6.7 points) and mIoU from 40.8 to 45.7 (+4.9 points) (Table of main results).

F2G's evidence-driven reasoning stage requires the LLM to first cite a specific evidence span ID from a Top-K proposal pool before generating final timestamps, rather than directly regressing timestamps (Section on Evidence-Driven Reasoning, Stage 3).

F2G's gains transfer consistently across at least three different Video-LLM backbones (LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL), with improvements concentrated at strict IoU thresholds such as R@0.7 (Cross-Model Effectiveness results).

F2G exhibits significantly lower run-to-run variance under repeated inference compared to direct timestamp generation, indicating improved stability of grounding predictions (Stability analysis, Section on results).

maOM1OWNZ6.text: On Table 1, ConG (Stage II, DPO on contrastive-decoded pairs) reaches an average score of 52.7 for Qwen2.5-7B and 41.6 for Llama3-8B, both exceeding the ConG-S (SFT-only) variant's 48.0 and 36.7 respectively (Table 1).

Weak SFT alone (fine-tuning the strong model directly on weak-model outputs) scores only 23.4 (Qwen2.5-7B) and 14.1 (Llama3-8B), below even the untuned Base model's 35.2 and 26.5, illustrating the noise problem ConG addresses (Table 1).

ConG establishes a theoretical equivalence between contrastive decoding and an implicit reward defined by the log-likelihood ratio between post- and pre-alignment weak models (Section on CD-Implicit Reward Equivalence).
Cross-family weak-to-strong alignment (weak Llama3.2 supervising strong Qwen2.5) achieves an average score of 51.7, demonstrating transfer across different model families (Cross-family results).

The contrastive decoding coefficient alpha is optimal in the range [0.3, 0.5], and ConG causes negligible degradation (average changes under 1.0 point) on general downstream tasks (Section on hyperparameter/ablation analysis).

MCu8SOjPad.text: On the View-of-Delft dataset, IterFlow reduces end-point error (EPE) to 0.1045 m versus 0.1600 m for CMFlow, a 34.7% reduction, while improving AccS from 19.83% to 33.40% and AccR from 42.38% to 63.75% (Performance comparison table).

IterFlow uses roughly 40x fewer parameters and about 30x lower GFLOPs than the previous cross-modal supervised state of the art, CMFlow, while achieving better scene flow accuracy (Model efficiency comparison).

IterFlow's total training loss combines only three terms—static rigid loss, instance-aware Chamfer loss, and instance-level flow smoothness loss—compared to prior methods that require seven or more loss terms (Loss design, Section on losses).

The model uses K=12 GRU-based iterative refinement steps with ball-query correlation (radius R=1m, L=8 neighbors) instead of standard KNN grouping, taking N1=N2=256 radar points per frame as input (Architecture details).

Training uses only RGB images and vehicle odometry as auxiliary weak supervision (no LiDAR or ground-truth flow labels), while inference requires only radar data, using 5,066 training frames and 1,273 validation frames from the 8,600-frame VoD dataset (Dataset and Validation).

HDf5semiaB.text: Continuous but constrained latent actions capture the complexity of actions in in-the-wild videos in a way that common vector quantization does not, according to the paper's central claim (abstract only).

The learned latent action model can identify environment changes caused by agents, such as a person entering a room, and these action patterns can be transferred across different videos (abstract only).
Without a shared embodiment across footage, the learned latent actions tend to become localized relative to camera position rather than generalizing across viewpoints (abstract only).
