A controller mapping known actions to the learned latent action representations enables the world model to perform planning tasks with performance comparable to action-conditioned baselines (abstract only).

qOd7ft1FSQ.text: JAEGER integrates RGB-D observations with multi-channel first-order ambisonics to perform joint 3D spatial grounding and reasoning, extending audio-visual language models beyond 2D representations (abstract only).

JAEGER introduces a Neural Intensity Vector (Neural IV), a learned spatial audio representation designed to improve direction-of-arrival estimation even with overlapping sound sources (abstract only).
The SpatialSceneQA benchmark introduced alongside JAEGER comprises 61,000 instruction-tuning samples drawn from simulated physical environments (abstract only).
JAEGER consistently surpasses 2D-centric baselines across diverse spatial perception and reasoning tasks (abstract only).
Source code, pretrained checkpoints, and datasets for JAEGER are publicly released via GitHub (abstract only).

uEVTdoAbnK.text: SWE-Bench Pro comprises 1,865 problems sourced from 41 actively maintained software repositories (abstract only).

SWE-Bench Pro is split into a public set of 11 openly accessible repositories, a held-out set of 12 repositories not publicly accessible, and a commercial set of 18 proprietary repositories obtained via partnership agreements with startups (abstract only).
Tasks in SWE-Bench Pro are long-horizon, potentially requiring hours to days for a professional software engineer to complete and often involving patches across multiple files (abstract only).
All SWE-Bench Pro tasks underwent human verification to ensure they include adequate context for resolution (abstract only).

SWE-Bench Pro is designed as a contamination-resistant testbed spanning business applications, B2B services, and developer tools to more faithfully capture real-world software engineering complexity than the original SWE-Bench (abstract only).

IymM8s8Dme.text: A2DEPT (A²DEPT) uses LLMs as system-level algorithm architects that design algorithms for combinatorial optimization problems via tree-structured evolutionary search over program space, rather than tuning fixed components (abstract only).
A2DEPT employs hybrid selection mechanisms and hierarchical operators for iterative refinement of evolutionary program trees (abstract only).
A2DEPT includes a lightweight program-maintenance loop that uses feedback-driven repair to keep synthesized programs executable (abstract only).
A2DEPT achieves a 9.8% relative reduction in mean normalized optimality gap compared to the strongest competing baseline on standard benchmarks (abstract only).
A2DEPT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on both standard and highly constrained combinatorial optimization benchmarks (abstract only).
A2DEPT enables open-ended solver synthesis beyond fixed algorithmic templates used by prior LLM-based automated heuristic design methods (abstract only).

CuqZJO3RE4.text: Euler Mean Flows (EMF) is a flow-based generative framework enabling one-step and few-step generation by enforcing long-range trajectory consistency at minimal sampling cost (abstract only).

EMF replaces a difficult-to-optimize long-range trajectory consistency constraint with a principled linear surrogate derived from the semigroup formulation of flow-based models, enabling direct data supervision (abstract only).
EMF is JVP-free, avoiding explicit Jacobian-vector product computations while supporting both prediction variants of the underlying flow model (abstract only).
EMF achieves approximately 50% reductions in training time and memory consumption compared to existing one-step generation methods for image generation (abstract only).

EMF is demonstrated across three domains: image synthesis, particle-based geometry generation, and functional generation, showing improved optimization stability and sample quality under constrained sampling budgets (abstract only).

5JUrQ67tYL.text: The Deliberate Evolution framework decouples LLM-based symbolic regression into three complementary components: adaptive operators that guide search direction, analytical diagnostic tools for structural assessment, and reflective memory that captures trajectory-level insights (abstract only).

Deliberate Evolution addresses the sample-inefficiency of prior LLM-based evolutionary symbolic regression methods that rely on simple scalar feedback such as MSE and bundle expression generation with search direction into a single task (abstract only).
Deliberate Evolution consistently outperforms prior LLM-based symbolic regression baselines across scientific domains while using only 40% of the standard sample budget (abstract only).

qrwbNL3KIP.text: Physics-guided motion loss improves action recognition score from 60.77 to 67.77 on the Open-Sora backbone using OpenVID-1M (Table 1).
On the MVDIT backbone, the method raises motion accuracy score from 44.0 to 53.0 and improves temporal consistency from 62.21 to 64.88 (Table 2).
Warping error is reduced from 0.0089 to 0.0062 on Open-Sora and from 0.0080 to 0.0056 on MVDIT (Tables 1-2).
A two-alternative forced-choice user study with 106 participants shows 79.4% preference for physics-enhanced Open-Sora videos on quality/motion and 82.7% for MVDIT (Figure 3).
An ablation study confirms that each individual motion loss term (translation, rotation, scaling) contributes distinct gains to overall performance (Section 5.3, Table 3).

MB5Qejqmtw.text: A bottlenecked knowledge graph embedding (KGE) model with embedding dimension d cannot perfectly represent distributions in adjacency matrices with rank r greater than d+1 (Proposition 3.1).
Low-rank KGEs with d less than |entities|-1 always have unfeasible ranking configurations regardless of encoder design (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.2).

The sufficient embedding dimension for exact sign reconstruction is d_SR+ = 2c+ + 1, where c+ is the maximum out-degree across subject-relation pairs, yielding required dimensions of 8,729 for FB15k-237, 30,073 for Hetionet, 58,657 for ogbl-biokg, and 36,841 for openbiolink (Theorem 4, Table 1).

The proposed KGE-MoS mixture-of-softmaxes output layer (Section 5, Equation 3) improves DistMult MRR from 0.801 to 0.837 on ogbl-biokg and from 0.316 to 0.347 on openbiolink at embedding dimension d=1000, with statistically significant gains at p<0.05 (Table 2).

KGE-MoS adds only O(Kd^2) parameters compared to O(d_inc(|entities|+|relations|)) needed to scale embedding dimension directly, breaking the rank bottleneck without major parameter overhead (Section 5).

SyTeWTEex3.text: Under a symmetry assumption on preference deviations, the Sign Estimator (minimizing the 0-1 loss in Equation 2) achieves ordinal consistency with the population-average utility, i.e., u_bar(X1) >= u_bar(X2) implies the estimator's ordering agrees (Theorem 1, Assumption 1).

For linear utilities under an identifiability condition on the density of feature differences near the origin, the Sign Estimator uniquely recovers the normalized average coefficient direction mu_bar = beta_bar/||beta_bar|| (Corollary 1, Assumption 2).

The Sign Estimator achieves a finite-sample convergence rate of O(n^(-1/3)) with high probability, avoiding the curse of dimensionality that afflicts nonparametric random-coefficients methods, which only achieve Theta(n^(-O(1/d))) rates (Theorem 2).
Standard RLHF reward aggregation is shown to recover a biased estimator that amplifies uncertain users while diminishing confident ones, an undesirable reweighting property (Proposition 1).

UAJehyOPTS.text: Context Tuning initializes trainable soft prompts (CT-Prompt) or key-value cache prefixes (CT-KV) from task demonstrations rather than random tokens, using leave-one-out masking and token dropout to prevent answer retrieval shortcuts and overfitting (Section on method design).
CT-KV achieves linear O(k*l^2) training complexity versus O((k*l)^2) for Test-Time Training and CT-Prompt, where k is the number of demonstration pairs and l is token length.
CT-KV attains 47.6% accuracy on the NLP-LR (CrossFit/UnifiedQA) benchmark suite compared to 44.1% for Test-Time Training, while requiring at most half the training time per task (Table 1).

Context Tuning is evaluated across five benchmark suites: CrossFit/UnifiedQA (26 tasks, k=16), MMLU (57 subjects, k=16), BIG-Bench Hard (27 tasks, k=10), and ARC (400 tasks, k<4 average demonstrations).
Applying CT-KV after Test-Time Training yields additional accuracy gains beyond either method alone, indicating the two approaches are complementary (Table 1).

3moDc5lpBC.text: Process Reward Agents (PRA) achieve 80.8% accuracy on MedQA with the Qwen3-4B policy model, a new state of the art at the 4B parameter scale, exceeding the strongest RAG + Self-Consistency baseline by about 4.1 percentage points.

PRA improves frozen policy model accuracy without any policy updates, raising Qwen2.5-0.5B from 28.4% to 54.1% (+25.7 points) and Llama-3.1-8B from 67.0% to 80.1% (+13.1 points) on the evaluated benchmark.
PRA yields an average gain of 4.8 points across seven medical out-of-distribution benchmarks compared to baselines (Table 1).
Applying process-level rewards online during generation achieves 80.8% accuracy versus 77.6% for post-hoc aggregation of the same reward signal (Table 4).
PRA continues to improve with additional inference-time compute while Self-Consistency saturates, indicating fundamentally different scaling dynamics (Figure 2).

yAAUcDLYMR.text: SECNet's Spatial-FA module replaces MLP-based convolutions with Hadamard products in the frequency domain, reducing computational complexity by up to 20 times relative to the MLP baseline (Section 3.2.2).

SECNet is evaluated on ten event-based datasets: five for object classification (NMNIST, N-Caltech101, CIFAR10-DVS, N-CARS, ASL-DVS), four for action recognition (DVS128 Gesture, Daily DVS, UCF101-DVS, THU^E-ACT-50), and one for human pose estimation (DHP19) (Table 2, Table 3, Table 7).
SECNet attains an average accuracy of 90.5% across the five object-classification datasets and 96.7% across the four action-recognition datasets (Table 2, Table 3).
On UCF101-DVS, SECNet reaches 91.6% accuracy, a 16% improvement over the previous state of the art (Section 4.4).

Ablation experiments show that removing the Spatial-FA module produces the largest accuracy degradation of the tested components, with additional drops from removing D-FPS or Temporal-FA and from integrating polarity only at the input level rather than structurally (Table 8).
In a scalability test sweeping event-cloud size from 512 to 10,240 points, SECNet reaches 60.60% accuracy versus 54.39% for PointNet++ (Table 9).

AmgjQp4vrr.text: In the homogeneous setting, Clipped ASGD achieves oracle complexity Õ(σ²/ε⁴ + σ·τ_C/ε³ + τ_C/ε²), which depends on the concurrency τ_C but not on the maximum delay τ_max (Theorem 4.2).
In the heterogeneous setting, Clipped ASGD achieves oracle complexity Õ((σ²+ζ²)/ε⁴ + (σ+ζ)·τ_C/ε³ + τ_C/ε²), where ζ measures data heterogeneity, again independent of τ_max (Theorem 5.1).

The paper establishes the first high-probability convergence guarantees for asynchronous SGD, with a polylogarithmic dependence on the failure probability δ governed by the sub-Weibull tail parameter θ (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 5.2).

Gradient noise is modeled as sub-Weibull (Definition 3.1), generalizing sub-Gaussian (θ=1/2) and sub-exponential (θ=1) noise, and empirical measurement of ResNet-18 gradient noise on CIFAR-10 yields a fitted tail parameter θ=2.71 (Figure 1).

On CIFAR-10 with delay factor D=4, Clipped ASGD achieves a 1.8x wall-clock speedup over vanilla ASGD (Figure 2), and on Shakespeare it achieves 2.0-2.2x speedup depending on the delay regime (Figure 3).
Under label-skew data heterogeneity on CIFAR-10, Clipped ASGD shows a 1.2-1.3x improvement over vanilla ASGD (Figure 4).

Mxg6mo1Xzj.text: MEAL is the first benchmark for continual multi-agent reinforcement learning, built on JaxMARL's Overcooked environment with a procedural generation pipeline producing three difficulty levels via grid size and obstacle density (Figure 1, Figure 2).
Across continual learning methods combined with IPPO over three difficulty levels, PackNet attains the highest average performance score at every level while keeping forgetting near zero (Table 2).
With IPPO + Online EWC, performance peaks at two agents on difficulty Level 1 and three agents on Level 2, with forgetting rising as team size increases beyond that point (Table 3).

Averaged plasticity metrics on Level 1 show that loss-of-plasticity (AUC-loss) increases more sharply between 1 and 3 task repetitions than between 3 and 10 repetitions, indicating early degradation of learning capacity (Table 4).

On 10-task Level 1 sequences, EWC and Online EWC perform similarly, but on 100-task sequences their performance diverges sharply, with Online EWC maintaining a score of 1.45±0.05 versus EWC collapsing to 0.23±0.03 (Table 5).

dctdzmYeej.text: DiCode (Dreaming in Code) is a framework in which foundation models synthesize executable environment code to scaffold agent learning toward increasing competence in open-ended worlds (abstract only).
DiCode is instantiated in Craftax, an open-ended benchmark characterized by rich mechanics and long-horizon progression (abstract only).
DiCode enables agents to acquire long-horizon skills, achieving a 16% improvement in mean return over the strongest baseline (abstract only).
DiCode achieves non-zero success on late-game combat tasks in Craftax where prior methods fail entirely (abstract only).

Code-level environment design in DiCode provides a mechanism for curriculum control by constructing intermediate environments that bridge competence gaps between early- and late-game challenges (abstract only).

4N4BXVWEWg.text: DECO conditions a diffusion transformer policy on visual, proprioceptive, and tactile modalities via separate, decoupled injection pathways: joint self-attention for vision, adaptive layer normalization for proprioception, and a lightweight cross-attention module for tactile input (Abstract, Section 4.4).
DECO achieves an overall success rate of 72.25% across bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, a 21% improvement over the strongest baseline (Table 1).
On the two contact-rich tasks, Waste Disposal and Assembly, DECO's combined success rate is 53.13%, with 48/80 successful trials on Waste Disposal and 37/80 on Assembly (Table 1).
Adding the plugin tactile adapter (DECO.p) raises overall average success rate by 10.25 percentage points and raises contact-rich task success from 53.13% to 73.13%, a 20-point gain (Table 1).
The tactile adapter achieves this improvement while training only 7.97M of the model's 91.02M total parameters, under 10% of the parameter count (Section 4.4, Table 6).
DECO is trained on the DECO-50 dataset, comprising 50 hours of dual-arm teleoperation data across 4 scenarios and 28 sub-tasks, totaling over 5 million frames and 8,000 successful trajectories.

2oft1bznyx.text: Multipole Semantic Attention (MuSe) achieves a 3x speedup over CUDNN Flash Attention at 8k context and a 20-30x speedup at 64k tokens, with runtime remaining roughly constant as context length grows while Flash Attention scales linearly (Section 7.1, Table 2).

The 64-cluster far-field configuration is selected as the 'sweet spot,' with a relative squared error of 0.1946, from a swept range of 0.1123 to 0.2475 across cluster configurations (Section 7.1, Table 1).
During pretraining, the full MuSe method's approximation error is 0.025 early in training (200M tokens) and rises to 0.195 late in training (2B tokens) (Section 7.2, Table 3).

End-to-end pretraining of a 30M parameter model shows a 12.2% total runtime reduction with only 0.36% loss degradation, reducing attention computation time from 33.8ms to 20.6ms (39% reduction) at 16k context (Section 7.3, Table 4).

Ablations show removing the monopole term increases approximation error by 3741% early in training and 373% late in training, far more damaging than removing dipole corrections (+80%/+15%) or the two-stage mechanism (~2x) (Section 7.2, Table 3).

NX0uokLuv7.text: SparseSSM's Theorem 1 derives an approximate second-order (OBS-style) saliency score that aggregates Hessian-trace information across time steps for pruning SSM modules, implemented as a training-free 'Time-Selective One-Shot OBS Pruning' procedure (Section 3.2, Theorem 1, Algorithm 1).

At 50% SSM-module sparsity, SparseSSM shows no degradation on most zero-shot tasks and improves zero-shot accuracy on Mamba-370M by 5.4% compared to other pruning methods, while WikiText-2 perplexity rises to 19.27 from a 14.32 dense baseline (Section 4.1, Table 1).

At 50% sparsity applied to the full architecture, Mamba-1.4B's WikiText-2 perplexity rises to 19.65 from a 10.75 dense baseline, with consistent improvements over baselines across all evaluated model scales (Section 4.2, Table 2).

SparseSSM is evaluated on public Mamba checkpoints ranging from 130M to 1.4B parameters (Mamba-130M, 370M, 790M, 1.4B), outperforming Magnitude Pruning, Mamba-Shedder, and SparseGPT baselines at 50% SSM sparsity (Section 4, Table 1).
Structured pruning under the SparseSSM framework yields a 1.72x inference speedup on the SSM module (Section 4.3).

uyjhZkN9ZA.text: Theorem 4.6 derives a closed-form expression for the ICL generalization error under distribution shift, G(V,M) = (1/τ²)Tr(A M11ᵀ F1 M11) − (1/τ)Tr(A(F2 M11 + M11ᵀ F2ᵀ)) + Tr(AB) + σ², as a function of inverse attention temperature τ (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.6).

Theorem 4.7 gives the closed-form optimal attention temperature τ_optimal = 2Tr(A M11ᵀ F1 M11) / Tr(A(F2 M11 + M11ᵀ F2ᵀ)) that minimizes this generalization error, showing its dependence on the specific type of distribution shift (Section 4.4, Theorem 4.7).
Corollary 4.4 shows that a model pretrained with temperature τ=1 emulates Bayes-optimal in-context estimation in the absence of distribution shift (Section 4.1, Corollary 4.4).

Simulations with d=50 dimensions and m=5000 samples show that adjusting attention temperature recovers near-Bayes-optimal performance under input-covariance and task-distribution shifts, and that the optimal temperature increases with noise level (Section 4.2, Figure 1; Section 4.4, Figure 2).

On LLaMA2-7B evaluated on the SCIQ question-answering benchmark under a fixed 0.6 noisy-demonstration ratio, temperature adjustment improves performance across varying context lengths, and the optimal temperature increases with the noisy-demonstration ratio (Section 5.2, Figure 3).

n86vBxkWIt.text: StructRTL constructs a control-data flow graph (CDFG) representation of RTL designs via Yosys compilation to RTLIL followed by a Stagira-based AST parser, illustrated on an example RTL design in Figure 2 (Section on CDFG Construction, Figure 2).

Without knowledge distillation, StructRTL improves R² over the CodeV-QW-7B baseline from 0.6353 to 0.7463 for area prediction (+0.111) and from 0.5277 to 0.7630 for delay prediction (+0.235) (Table 1).

With knowledge distillation from a post-mapping-netlist teacher, StructRTL reaches R² of 0.8676 (area) and 0.8872 (delay), versus CodeV-QW-7B's 0.8174 and 0.7687 respectively, while the teacher PM Predictor itself achieves 0.9334 (area) and 0.9484 (delay) (Table 2).
Ablations removing the masked-node-modeling loss or the edge-prediction loss each degrade both area and delay R² relative to the full pretraining objective (Tables 1-2).

Self-supervised pretraining tasks used for the graph encoder achieve 82.27% validation accuracy on structure-aware masked node modeling (32-class classification over 20% masked post-GNN embeddings) and 95.77% validation accuracy on edge prediction over a dataset of 13,200 RTL designs (Section on Model Architecture).

n5Ds4qbtjM.text: Layerwise intrinsic dimension (Id) of model representations correlates with brain-encoding performance at ρ=0.76 (p<0.01) for fMRI and ρ=0.43 (p<0.01) for ECoG, outperforming surprisal-based predictors across tested speech and language models (Section 4.2, Figure 2B, Table 1).

The layerwise peak in representational intrinsic dimension coincides with the layer of maximal brain-encoding performance for both LLMs and audio (speech) models, in both fMRI and ECoG recordings (Section 4.2, Figure 2A).
Well-predicted voxels show ρ=0.73 between layerwise intrinsic dimension and encoding performance for OPT-1.3b on fMRI, and well-predicted electrodes show ρ=0.63 on ECoG (Table I.2).

Finetuning WavLM directly on fMRI responses causally increases encoding performance alongside both semantic content and intrinsic dimension, demonstrating a causal link rather than mere correlation (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

Across Pythia-6.9b pretraining checkpoints, the emergence of the intrinsic-dimension peak and improvements in brain-encoding performance grow in tandem, with global correlations of ρ=0.96 (fMRI) and ρ=0.64 (ECoG) (Figure 2C-E).

cgLZYrBHh6.text: DINOSAURv2 (object-centric) outperforms DINOv2 (dense) on CLEVRTex by +5.6% to +12.3% across difficulty levels when using the smaller transformer decoder, TF 2 (Table 1).

Object-centric encoders achieve stronger compositional out-of-distribution (COOD) generalization than dense encoders when trained on fewer images, with the sample-size sweep on MOVi-C spanning 2^10 to 2^14 images (Figure 4).
Dense encoders only catch up to or surpass object-centric encoders on MOVi-C once trained on the full 40k-image dataset with larger downstream models (Figure 4).

At matched downstream FLOPs, object-centric representations achieve higher COOD accuracy than dense representations, with dense encoders requiring roughly 3x the compute to match object-centric performance on harder generalization splits (Figure 3).

Three controlled visual worlds are used for evaluation: CLEVRTex (192 unique shape x size x material object combinations), Super-CLEVR, and MOVi-C (36 shapes with size variation), each split into easy/medium/hard training conditions with a held-out 20% COOD test set (Section 4).

pZqloVjqHd.text: Using the Tele-Lens probing method (low-rank adapters on hidden states) across 12 diverse tasks, LLMs show precise final-answer planning emerging only one reasoning step before completion on explicit compositional tasks like Parity and Cycle, with intermediate-step accuracy near chance (~50%) before spiking to 97-99% at the final position (Table 1).

Top-5 accuracy for subsequent-token prediction from hidden states drops sharply beyond 2-3 steps ahead in the reasoning chain, especially for semantic tasks, indicating a myopic rather than long-range planning horizon (Figure 5).
Selecting the top-5 pivot Chain-of-Thought positions via Tele-Lens for uncertainty estimation achieves 0.69 average AUROC versus 0.60 for the self-certainty baseline (Table 2).
Selecting the top-100 pivot positions using general uncertainty metrics yields up to a 6% absolute AUROC improvement on Qwen3-32B over baseline aggregate metrics (Table 3).

A threshold-based CoT-bypass strategy using normalized entropy of the initial five generated tokens reduces thinking-token usage by 16.2% on CSQA and 12.4% on MMLU, each with only about 0.03% accuracy degradation (Section on CoT bypass detection).

XsrXLPxBJw.text: The WMSE (weighted mean-squared error) metric weights genes by differential expression strength to prioritize perturbation-specific DEGs, addressing signal dilution in standard MSE (Section 3.3.2).
The R2_w(Delta) weighted R-squared metric compares predictions against all perturbed cells rather than control cells, giving high sensitivity to niche perturbation signals (Section 3.3.2).

Simulation results show a strong correlation (r=0.54-0.63) between the control-bias parameter beta and mean-baseline performance on Pearson(Delta), indicating that shared reference shifts rather than genuine biological signal drive high apparent performance of the mean baseline (Section on control bias).

Training GEARS with a WMSE objective on the Norman19 dataset reduces test-set WMSE by 2.5x and improves median R2_w(Delta) from -0.068 to 0.555, while recovering true gene-wise perturbation variance instead of collapsing toward the mean (Section 5, Norman19 results).

A technical-duplicate positive baseline is introduced to estimate the realistic performance ceiling achievable when predicting mean perturbation effects, evaluated on both the Norman19 (CRISPRa, 256 cells/perturbation) and Replogle22 (genome-wide CRISPRi, 64 cells/perturbation) datasets (Section 4, Datasets).

zYSl5Qj6Cw.text: Susceptibility vectors decompose as chi_xy = sum over alpha,beta of s_{alpha beta}(xy) * chi_{alpha beta} - chi_bar, showing each token-context pair's susceptibility as a weighted sum of mode-specific responses via propensity scores (Section on the decomposition equation).

A conductance-based clustering algorithm identifies low-conductance vertex sets in a k-nearest-neighbor graph built from susceptibility vectors, using personalized PageRank, after a row-wise standardization step that removes the dominant uniform mode (Section on clustering methodology).

510 interpretable clusters are identified in Pythia-14M, spanning linguistic structures (sentence boundaries, prepositions), mathematical notation, code formatting patterns, and dataset-specific conventions such as LaTeX and HTML (Section on quantitative results).

50.8% (259 of 510) of susceptibility clusters found in Pythia-14M match Sparse Autoencoder features derived from Pythia-70M, providing cross-method validation that both approaches recover similar underlying model structure (Section on cross-method validation).

Clusters remain coherent when measured across larger Pythia models ranging from 31M to 1.4B parameters, suggesting the identified patterns reflect genuine data regularities rather than artifacts of small model scale (Section on scaling evidence).

Hpfybj9wkd.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that mean spurious bias (asymmetric spurious-feature distributions across preference pairs) or causal-spurious correlation in the training distribution induces nonzero spurious parameters at the DPO population equilibrium (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 5.3 decomposes deployment suboptimality under distribution shift into an irreducible shift term, driven by learned spurious parameters interacting with shifted spurious statistics, and a reducible estimation term that vanishes as sample size n approaches infinity (Theorem 5.3).

Tie training with equal-utility preference pairs shrinks spurious parameters while preserving causal learning, with an isotropic-case spurious-parameter reduction ratio of alpha*lambda_0 / (alpha*lambda_0 + (1-alpha)*sigma^2) (Theorem 6.2).

In neural network experiments, strict (standard) training yields a spurious gap of about 0.70 and adversarial accuracy of about 0.25, whereas tie training at alpha=0.75 reduces the spurious gap to about 0.45 and raises adversarial accuracy to about 0.70 (Section on neural network experiments).

On the LLM synthetic Hotel Preferences benchmark, standard DPO achieves 92.25% in-distribution accuracy but drops to 74.00% under suppressed spurious correlation and 64.20% under adversarial spurious correlation, while informative tie training achieves 92.40% in-distribution, 82.85% suppressed, and 86.70% adversarial accuracy (Section on LLM synthetic benchmark, Hotel Preferences).

qz0ChfFkiZ.text: For K=1, Algorithm 1 (LG1T) achieves regret min{O(SA/Δ_+), O(√(SAT))}, matching the minimax constant-regret lower bound for non-episodic finite-horizon MDPs (Theorem 4.2).
For general K≥2, Algorithm 2 achieves regret max{O((K-1)√(SAT)), O(C_{K-1}√(SAT) log T)}, which is sublinear whenever max(K, C_{K-1}√(SA)) = o(√T) (Theorem 4.4).

Under stochastic dominance assumptions, the K-step lookahead greedy policy equals the optimal policy in binary-state MDPs for any K≥1, while for general state spaces with K<T there exists an MDP instance where the K-step lookahead policy incurs Θ(T) optimality gap (Theorem 3.3, Theorem 3.4).

On synthetic MDPs with 10 states/5 actions, the one-step greedy policy π¹ attains a 0.75 competitive ratio versus 0.96 for the two-step greedy policy π², and on 100-state/25-action MDPs the ratios are 0.80 versus 0.94 (Figure 1).

On JumpRiverSwim with 5, 8, and 15 states over 20,000 steps, the proposed LG1T, LG2T, LG1-2T, and LG1T-RL methods consistently exceed cumulative reward of all tabular RL baselines, with LG1T-RL matching PMEVI-KLUCRL after switching at 10,000 steps (Figure 2).
On FrozenLake (4x4 grid) and AnyTrading over 20,000 steps, LG1T/LG2T and LG2T/LG1-2T respectively achieve the highest cumulative reward among all benchmarked methods (Figure 3).

n1fQYnj30I.text: Star Elastic produces a family of nested hybrid Mamba-Attention-MoE LLMs (12B/23B/30B) from a single parent model (Nemotron Nano v3) using only 160B tokens of post-training (Section 4.1).
Star Elastic achieves a 360x reduction in training cost versus training each nested model from scratch and a 7x reduction versus state-of-the-art sequential compression methods (Abstract).

Elastic budget control, which dynamically selects submodel size across the thinking versus answering inference phases, yields up to 16% higher accuracy and 1.9x lower latency than static model selection (Figure 1).
The 23B and 12B nested variants achieve 1.8x and 2.4x faster inference throughput respectively, with maximum batch size on an H100 GPU increasing from 36 to 224 (Table 2).

Storing the full nested family of three models (12B+23B+30B) requires 58.9GB in BF16 versus 126.1GB for three separately trained checkpoints, a roughly 2.2x memory savings from weight sharing (Table 3).
Quantization-Aware Distillation (QAD) applied to the 30B model recovers 98.69% of FP8 accuracy and 97.79% of NVFP4 accuracy relative to the unquantized model (Table 4).

LsqeBp4JsV.text: RL-Focal's ensemble achieves 73.24% on MMLU, a 2.82 percentage point improvement over the best individual model Mixtral-8x7b, and analogous gains of 2.15 points on GSM8K, 4.49 points on BBH, 3.08 points on MUSR, and 1.07 points on GPQA (Table 1, Section 5.2).

The focal-diversity optimized agent selection algorithm chooses a small subset of complementary LLM agents by pruning ensemble combinations based on pairwise error correlation, with focal diversity shown to correlate with ensemble accuracy across the five evaluation datasets (Figure 2, Section 4.4).
On MMLU and GSM8K, RL-Focal outperforms LLM-Blender (44.01%/40.41%) and majority voting (68.06%/72.31%), and marginally exceeds LLM-TOPLA on MMLU (73.24% vs 72.77%) (Table 3).
RL-Focal is evaluated for robustness on alignment/safety benchmarks including Alpaca-Eval, BeaverTails, and TruthfulQA in addition to the five reasoning benchmarks (Table 2).

J8lkAoQeYK.text: GRASP (the proposed gradient-based planner) treats intermediate states as optimization variables so that all world-model evaluations across the planning horizon can be computed in parallel, rather than via serial rollouts (Section 3.1).
GRASP injects isotropic Gaussian perturbations on states after each gradient descent step (Langevin-style noise) to escape local minima during trajectory optimization (Section 3.2).
GRASP stops gradients through state inputs while retaining gradients through actions, preventing the optimizer from exploiting brittle state-input Jacobians in the learned world model (Section 3.3).

On the Push-T long-horizon task at H=50, GRASP achieves 43.4% success versus 30.2% for the cross-entropy method (CEM), with median planning time of 15.2s versus 96.2s; at H=80, GRASP achieves 10.4% success versus 2.8% for CEM in 58.9s versus 132.2s (Table 1).
In an ablation at H=40, removing the synchronization/state-noise steps drops accuracy from 59.0% to 1.6%, and disabling state noise (σ=0.0 vs σ=0.5) reduces accuracy from 59.0% to 54.8% (Table 2).

Bb0pQqsiad.text: AgentLAB introduces a benchmark of 644 security test cases spanning five long-horizon attack types (intent hijacking, tool chaining, task injection, objective drifting, memory poisoning) across 28 realistic agentic environments and 10 risk categories (Table 1, Section 4.3.2).

Across six evaluated LLM agents, average overall attack success rate ranges from 28.9% for Claude-4.5 to 81.5% for Qwen-3, showing broad vulnerability across proprietary and open-weight models (Table 2).

Single-turn defenses such as Self-Reminder and Llama-Guard are evaluated against intent hijacking and tool chaining, while Repeated Prompt and a DeBERTa detector are evaluated against objective drifting, task injection, and memory poisoning (Table 4, Section 5.4).

Defenses designed for one-shot/single-turn attacks are difficult to retrofit for long-horizon, multi-turn attacks and fail to reliably mitigate them, motivating the need for tailored long-horizon defense mechanisms (Table 4 caption).

8bHa5wc7X5.text: On USACO, using only 16 ground-truth test inputs for verification outperforms using 64 randomly generated test inputs by a large margin, motivating the need for discriminative input generation (Section 2, Figure 1).

The Agentic Verifier is trained via a three-stage pipeline: large-scale data synthesis with consensus-based majority voting, rejection fine-tuning on 60K successful trajectories, and agentic reinforcement learning with GRPO (Section 3).
On USACO, the Agentic Verifier improves Best@8 accuracy by +10.3% and Best@64 accuracy by +11.7% over baselines (Section 4.2, Table 1).
On CodeForces (a newly introduced 64-problem benchmark), the Agentic Verifier achieves gains of +9.8% to +13.2% over baseline verification methods (Section 4.2, Table 1).

The Agentic Verifier is evaluated against Vanilla sampling, Grading RM, MBR-Exec (hard/soft), CodeT, CodeRM, and a Random Generator baseline across five benchmarks (USACO 307 problems, LiveCodeBench 175 problems, OJBench 232 problems, ICPC-Eval 118 problems, CodeForces 64 problems), consistently outperforming all of them (Section 4.2, Table 1).

6MchDfzGyJ.text: Strategic Self-Improving Agents (SSA), explicitly prompted with metacognition, competitive awareness, and strategic planning, achieve cumulative rewards of $633.5 versus $419.4 for a Chain-of-Thought baseline (Section 5.2-5.3, Table 1).
SSA agents attain higher market share (14.26% vs. 9.70%) and a higher specialization index (0.78 vs. 0.65) compared to the CoT baseline (Table 1).
Metacognition, competitive awareness, and strategic planning each show strong Pearson correlations with agent rewards (r=0.744, r=0.643, and r=0.697 respectively) (Section 5.1, Appendix J).
An ablation shows metacognition alone provides the largest performance gains (p<0.0001), while adding long-horizon planning contributes only marginal additional benefit (Figure 8).

Market-level simulation dynamics reproduce human labor-market regularities: an unemployment-vacancy relationship following the Beveridge Curve (R²=0.843) and an output-unemployment relationship approximating Okun's Law with roughly a 2:1 inverse ratio (R²=0.436) (Section 4).

Performance-based pay contracts increase agents' skill-training frequency relative to flat-fee contracts, while open bidding induces wage deflation and crowds out training investment (Section 4.1, Figure 4C-D).

P0eayHlqb7.text: For continuous Dense Associative Memory with exponential pattern capacity p=e^(αN) on the N-sphere, the maximum retrieval capacity at zero temperature is α_c(0) = 0.5 for both LSE and LSR kernels (Section 4.3, Figure 1).
The geometric entropy density depends only on the alignment φ via s(φ) = (1/2)ln(1-φ²), independent of the choice of energy kernel (Section 3.2, Equation 19).

The LSE and LSR kernels have distinct finite-temperature phase boundaries, given respectively by α_c^LSE(T) = (1/2)[1-f_ret^LSE(T)]² (Equation 35) and α_c^LSR(T) = (1/2)[1-f_ret^LSR(T)]² (Equation 39) (Section 4.3).

For the LSR kernel with shape parameter b=3.41, there exists a support threshold α_th = (1/2)(1-1/b)² ≈ 0.25 below which retrieval is perfect at any temperature, a behavior absent for the LSE kernel (Section 4.2-4.3).

Monte Carlo simulations at N=50, α=0.1 confirm the theoretical predictions, showing the LSE kernel undergoes a retrieval-to-disorder transition around T≈0.7-0.8, while the LSR kernel below its threshold maintains retrieval across all tested temperatures (Figure 2).

wGxd4FKrU1.text: The Retrieval Probability Score (RPS), computed over a Wikidata-Wikipedia aligned dataset of about 7 million entities using controlled neutral pools of N=800, quantifies entity-level retrievability under fixed top-k budgets (Section 3.2).
Low-RPS and high-RPS entities occupy distinguishable regions in embedding space under LDA visualization, indicating that retrieval blind spots are structural rather than random (Section 3, Figure 2).

Lightweight probes (Ridge, XGBoost, MLP) trained on entity embeddings alone predict RPS with Pearson r of approximately 0.65-0.80 and classification accuracy of approximately 0.65-0.80, enabling pre-index blind-spot detection without expensive retrieval simulation (Section 4, Table 1).

Across 8 retrievers (including BGE-M3, Contriever, and ReasonIR-8B) and 3 benchmarks (BRIGHT, ImpliRet, RAR-b), the ARGUS Document Expansion remedy yields average gains of +3.44 nDCG@5/10 on BRIGHT, +6.76 on ImpliRet, and +1.68 on RAR-b (Section 7, Table 2).
Standard retrievers such as Contriever show consistently low average RPS (~0.11 at k=50), motivating the need for blind-spot remediation (Section 7).

17ZS9CUaLt.text: Theorem 1 establishes distribution-free, per-step dual-branch marginal coverage for COFT: P[v_t* in C_t under p AND v_t* in C_t under the counterfactual distribution] ≥ 1-α (Section 3.4, Theorem 1, Equation 9).

On LLaMA-2-13B, COFT reduces StereoSet bias score from 0.41 to 0.26 and BBQ biased-answer rate from 0.27 to 0.14, part of an overall 30-55% (median 38%) reduction across six bias benchmarks (Section 4, Table 1).
Task utility is preserved within about 0.2 percentage points of the vanilla model, e.g., GSM8K accuracy of 47.5% (COFT) vs. 47.9% (vanilla) and StrategyQA 71.1% vs. 71.2% (Section 4, Table 2).

COFT incurs a throughput overhead of 10.2% on LLaMA-2-13B and at most 0.8 GB additional memory, scaling linearly with model size, roughly equivalent to one cached extra forward pass (Section 4, Table 3).

An ablation shows that removing logit fusion increases BiasAvg from 0.129 (full COFT) to 0.171, the largest degradation among ablated components, more than removing dual-branch conformal certification (which raises BiasAvg to 0.158) (Section 4, Table 4).

Ih5NfDUiOz.text: Theorem 1 (Section 4.2) proves that the variance of Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) decays as O(1/N), where N is the number of random examples used to construct the CAV (Theorem 1, Section 4.2).

The O(1/N) variance decay is empirically confirmed across three data modalities: ResNet image concepts such as 'striped' and 'dotted' (Figure 2, Section 5.1), the UCI Adult tabular dataset with gender concepts (Section 5.2, Appendix A.2), and IMDB sentiment text concepts across BERT layers (Section 5.3, Appendix A.3).

Corollary 1 (Section 4.3) extends the 1/N variance result to sensitivity scores, while Section 4.4 shows that raw TCAV scores instead retain approximately O(1) variance due to borderline points near the decision boundary (Figure 4, Section 4.4).

Conjecture 1 (Section 4.5) shows that averaging TCAV scores over s independent runs reduces variance as O(1/s), empirically validated with R=2000 total samples split across varying numbers of subsets (Figure 5, Section 4.5).

Based on the differing scaling behavior of CAV direction versus TCAV score variance, Section 4.5 recommends using several modest-N runs to stabilize TCAV scores, but increasing N per run to stabilize the CAV direction itself for applications like bias mitigation (Section 4.5).

YKgp1KiZcB.text: RFM (Reward-guided Flow Merging) is formulated via a density-operator view of flow control and merging (Equation 5, Section 3), reducing merging to a mirror-descent scheme (Algorithm 1, Section 4) that solves a sequence of standard reward-guided fine-tuning problems.
Theorem 6.1 proves that stochastic optimal control fine-tuning necessarily encodes score information via u*(x,t) = σ(t)∇log p_t^k(x) (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).

Theorem 6.2 establishes asymptotic almost-sure convergence of the iterate sequence {p_1^(π^k)} to a stationary point under bounded-variance and diminishing-bias assumptions, providing the paper's first theoretical guarantee for reward-guided and pure flow merging (Theorem 6.2, Section 6).

Proposition 1 shows that the union operator over n pre-trained flow models reduces to minimizing a reverse KL divergence against a single weighted mixture density, avoiding the need for n separate critics (Proposition 1, Section 4).

On a de-novo molecular design case study merging two FlowMol models pre-trained on GEOM-Drugs with mean energies of -14.8 Ha and -8.1 Ha, the balanced intersection operator yields molecules with mean energy -10.95 ± 0.28 Ha, matching the expected overlap region (Figure 3, Figure 4e-h, Section 7).

RFM is also applied to merge ETFlow conformer-generation models, showing controllable interpolation of energy, dipole moment, and HOMO-LUMO gap between pre-trained models across balanced, unbalanced, reward-guided intersection and union operators (Figure 5, Table 1, Section 7, Appendix G.2).

md3glg1Lft.text: PVMC (Parallel Variational Monte Carlo) computes importance weights via parallel prefix/suffix scans with span complexity O(log N × log T), proven in Theorem 3.1 (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.1).

On the linear Gaussian benchmark, PVMC with a learned proposal achieves a mean L2 error of 0.052 against the RTS smoother and a Kernelised Stein Discrepancy of 0.199, versus 0.410 for the classical two-filter smoother (Table 1, Section 5.1).
On the prey-predator state estimation task, PVMC attains an MSE of 0.32 ± 0.04 and a 2-Sliced-Wasserstein-Distance of 2.96 ± 0.74, outperforming Soft DPF's 6.70 2-SWD (Table 2, Section 5.2).

On the same prey-predator task, PVMC trains in 1 minute 49 seconds, matching P-VAE's training time while being roughly 8.5x to 149x faster than Soft DPF (15:32), Stop-gradient DPF (16:27), MDPS (26:23), and Diffusion DPF (267:10) (Table 2, Section 5.2).

On financial time-series modeling of SPX daily returns, PVMC best reproduces the autocorrelation structure and yields more accurate skewness and kurtosis distributions than DMM and TC-VAE baselines (Figures 2-3, Section 5.3).

UCAda9kS57.text: SWE-rebench V2 constructs 32,000+ issue-linked executable SWE tasks spanning 20 programming languages and 3,600+ repositories with pre-built, reproducible Docker images, with a filtering funnel from 29.5M raw PRs shown in Table 1 (Table 1, Section 3.7).
The dataset also releases 120,000+ additional PR-derived tasks with installation instructions, fail-to-pass tests, and rich metadata (Section 3).
Python and Go are the top two languages by share of tasks, at 21.6% and 20.6% respectively (Section 3.7, Table 1/Appendix B).

The five-stage construction pipeline—data collection, setup synthesis, execution validation, clarity filtering, and metadata enrichment—is validated against human-verified SWE-bench annotations in Section 3.4 (Section 3.4, Section 3).
Section 4.3 introduces diagnostic metadata tags for three failure categories: TEST_SUITE_COUPLING, IMPLICIT_NAMING, and EXTERNAL_DEPENDENCY (Section 4.3).

Ablations on prompt variants, model choices, and ensembling strategies for the clarity-filtering LLM ensemble show that averaging scores across ensemble members improves robustness (Tables 3-5, Section 3).

fz1c8IihEC.text: HiCI extends LLaMA-2-7B's context window from 4K to 100K tokens and LLaMA-2-13B's from 4K to 64K tokens using only about 5.5% additional parameters (Abstract, Section 3).

HiCI's hierarchical pipeline consists of Local Construction with M=8 learnable cross-attention query slots per segment (Section 3.2), Global Integration via multi-view statistical pooling and attention-based weighting (Section 3.3), and Top-down Broadcast that prepends global and local context to each segment's key-value sequence (Section 3.4).
On topic retrieval, HiCI-13B-16K achieves 100% accuracy up to 13K tokens, declining to 0.94 accuracy at 16K, matching proprietary models up to 13K tokens (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On LongBench code comprehension, HiCI surpasses GPT-3.5-Turbo-16K by +9.7%, and improves overall LongBench performance to 33.2%, a +2.6% gain over the LongLoRA baseline (Table 3, Section 4.2-4.3).
HiCI achieves 100% passkey retrieval accuracy within its 32K training regime with graceful extrapolation beyond that length (Figure 2, Section 4.2).
HiCI improves perplexity over baselines on the PG-19 and Proof-pile long-document benchmarks (Table 1, Section 4.2).

WTBaZHtIra.text: Theorem 3.3 proves observational distributions for unseen object combinations with a different relational skeleton cannot be identified without further causal assumptions (Theorem 3.3).

Theorem 3.4 shows that even within a fixed skeleton, knowledge of observational distributions alone is insufficient to identify interventional distributions without additional causal structure (Theorem 3.4).

Theorem 4.3 gives graphical identification conditions under which an unconfounded variable's conditional distribution can be identified when the source data contains instances with matching or larger relational neighborhoods (Theorem 4.3, Section 4).

Theorem 5.2 proves that graph-constrained Relational Neural Causal Models (RNCMs) with parameter sharing can represent any Relational Structural Causal Model consistent with a given relational causal graph (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).

On simulated traffic-scene experiments, RNCMs outperform non-relational neural baselines by roughly 100x in settings where the causal query is identifiable, while also correctly flagging non-identifiable settings matching theoretical predictions (Section 6).

43Hwj59jZg.text: Adversarially Trained Process Reward Models (APRM) use a two-player general-sum game in which a Generator produces plausible reasoning errors and a PRM learns to detect them, trained via PPO with Optimistic Gradient Descent-Ascent (OGDA) to reach a Nash equilibrium (Section on method/adversarial framework).
APRM improves solver accuracy by an average of +3.4 percentage points over the strongest PRM baseline across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and multiple solver sizes (Table 1).
APRM achieves a +5.3 percentage point gain on the out-of-distribution JeeBench benchmark, exceeding its in-distribution average improvement (Table 1).

APRM's improvement scales with solver size, rising from +3.3 percentage points with Gemma-3-12B to +5.0 percentage points with Gemma-3-27B, whereas static PRM baselines show declining gains as solver size increases (Table 1).

APRM generalizes beyond mathematics, yielding consistent improvements on SciBench (chemistry and physics), indicating the adversarially learned error patterns are not math-specific artifacts (Section on cross-domain evaluation).

agN2CgTCIW.text: Theorem 1.3 establishes a ρ-replicable (ε,δ)-PAC episodic RL algorithm with sample complexity Õ(S²A/(ρ²ε²))·poly(H, log(1/δ)), nearly matching the O~(S²A²) bound previously known only for the generative (batch) setting (Theorem 1.3).
Theorem 1.4 proves a parallel-sampling lower bound of Ω̃(S²AH²/(ρ²ε²)) samples for any ρ-replicable algorithm (Theorem 1.4).
Theorem 1.5 establishes an unconditional lower bound of Ω̃(S²H²/(ρ²ε²)) samples for replicable learning in the episodic setting (Theorem 1.5).

The RepExplore and Qexplore algorithm components, combined with tiered backward induction over 'ignorable state combinations,' close most of the previously known gap between the O~(S^7A^7) exploration-setting upper bound and the O~(S^2A^2) batch-setting upper bound, demonstrating exploration is not a significant barrier to replicable RL (Section 5, Section 7).
The lower bound analysis reduces from a 'sign-one-way marginals' problem, establishing tight bounds of Θ̃(n/(ρ²ε²)) for that intermediate problem as a technical tool (Section 7).

2Opz9uBYQT.text: Two-parameter flows (TPF) learn only sampling-time transports from a base distribution to each observed marginal via conditional flow matching, then extract a physics-time velocity by regressing on synthetic trajectories built from coupled sampling-time flows, avoiding per-step optimal-transport couplings (Section on method, Step 1-3 pipeline).

Proposition 2.1 proves that the sampling-time velocity uniquely determines a physics-time velocity satisfying the continuity equation, establishing the physics-time dynamics are unique given the sampling-time transport (Proposition 2.1).

Proposition 2.2 gives a closed-form expression for the physics-time velocity in terms of the sampling-time flow's Jacobian and its time-derivative, showing physics-time regularity is inherited from the sampling-time transport (Proposition 2.2).
Proposition 2.3 provides an explicit H^1-norm regularity bound for the physics-time velocity u in terms of the sampling-time velocity v's norms (Proposition 2.3).

On barotropic and Kolmogorov flow experiments at 128x128 resolution, TPF captures vortex self-organization and matches the omega^-3 energy spectrum decay while achieving roughly 100x speedup over a physics solver (Section on experiments).
On a 50-dimensional particle-instability phase-space benchmark, TPF achieves the best Wasserstein-2 error compared to DICE, HOAM, and JKONet* baselines (Section on experiments).

M9kHwqreN9.text: LazyAttention defers positional encoding to attention computation time rather than embedding it in cached key/value data, enabling zero-copy, position-agnostic KV cache reuse across documents (Section on method).

Under skewed document-access distributions, LazyAttention reduces time-to-first-token by 1.37x and increases inference throughput by 1.40x relative to Block-Attention, the state-of-the-art baseline (Section on results).

Under a 10GB memory budget with high document skewness, LazyAttention achieves a 23.89% cache hit ratio versus 21.13% for Block-Attention; under a tighter 1GB budget the gap widens to 13.57% versus 7.27% (Table 1).
LazyAttention maintains comparable answer quality to Block-Attention, scoring 73.0% vs 72.1% exact match on TriviaQA and 73.3% vs 72.5% on HotpotQA (Table 2).
LazyAttention's added kernel overhead is small: 0.59% relative overhead during prefilling (with M=128) and 0.13% per-token overhead during decoding (Section on efficiency analysis).

7GSLP4hqUO.text: On the SEED dataset subject-dependent setting, RECTOR achieves 85.0±8.5% weighted-F1, outperforming the second-best baseline mdJPT at 80.1% (Table 1).
On sEEG task-engagement classification, RECTOR reaches 92.1±4.1% AUROC on MSIT and 92.4±3.9% AUROC on ECR, exceeding the BaRISTA baseline (89.3% and 89.0% respectively) (Table 2).

Ablating the Masked Topology and Representation Learning objective (removing L_TSM, topology prediction) drops average weighted-F1 to 71.1%, and removing the entire MTRL loss drops it to 70.3%, versus 73.1±8.5% for the full model (Table 3, Section 3.3).

Adaptive Functional Partitioning (AFP) reassigns 36.5-51.5% of EEG channels away from the fixed anatomical prior into learned functional regions, with 84.7-86.1% consistency of channel reassignment across sessions (Section 3.5, Figure 7-8).

RECTOR shows a flatter performance decay than baselines under simulated channel dropout up to 50% missing channels, and transfers with minimal performance drop from DEAP to SEED/SEED-IV cross-montage evaluation when using AFP versus fixed topology (Figure 6).

mKj4fO0BU4.text: Lemma 3.1 proves that if the cosine similarity between a mask token's hidden state and the true next-token hidden state exceeds a threshold delta*, the correct token is guaranteed to appear in the Top-K predictions (Section 3, Lemma 3.1).

At block complexity (tree size) 60, the method achieves acceptance length tau of 1.71 on LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct and 1.66 on Qwen3-8B, compared to 1.62 and 1.56 respectively at block complexity 30 (Table 1).
The training-free method yields an approximately 12% improvement in acceptance length on LLaMA3 models and 8-12% on Qwen3 models relative to standard next-token decoding (Section 4).

The efficient implementation increases token throughput by up to 15-19%, including a 15% token-rate increase specifically measured on LLaMA3.1-8B, without modifying model weights or requiring auxiliary draft models (Table 3, Section 4).

Cosine similarity analysis across decoder layers shows accepted mask-token predictions reach approximately 0.45 similarity to the true next-token hidden state, versus approximately 0.35 for rejected predictions (Figure 2).

DIWkLvYXuP.text: The scaled Gaussian parameterization of the group optimal transport map reduces to a convex quadratic program with only d+1 parameters, as shown in Theorem 3.9, compared to d(d+1)+d parameters for the general Gaussian SDP formulation of Theorem 3.7 (Section 3, Theorem 3.9).

Proposition 3.4 shows that restricting the affine transform to be PSD makes the group counterfactual optimization a convex semidefinite program (SDP), while Proposition 3.5 shows the diagonal-matrix restriction reduces it to a convex quadratic program (QP) (Section 3, Propositions 3.4-3.5).

Across 15 binary classification datasets and 300 groups formed via k-medoids clustering, dense transport parameterizations (PSD affine, Gaussian) achieve a transport cost within a factor of 1.7 of optimal in 90% of experiments, versus only about 65% convergence for the bi-Lipschitz baseline (Section 4).

The scaled Gaussian parameterization maintains near-1.0 validity across all tested bi-Lipschitz constants K in {1.01, 1.5, 2, 3.5, 5}, and achieves the lowest, near-identical empirical distortion lower bound (~0.4) among all tested parameterizations (Section 4, Figures 3-4).

The bi-Lipschitz baseline fails to converge in roughly 35% of cases at the tightest constraint K=1.01, whereas the proposed convex OT-map parameterizations avoid this non-convex failure mode entirely (Section 4).

wvQjM6G4Hh.text: NanoFLUX compresses the 12B-parameter diffusion transformer of FLUX.1-Schnell to 2B parameters through four progressive stages: attention head pruning (24 to 16 heads), head-dimension reduction (128 to 96), block merging (38 to 24 single-stream blocks), and static LayerNorm replacing dynamic AdaLN (Section 4.1).
The text encoder is distilled from the 5B-parameter T5-XXL to a 330M-parameter T5-Large via a two-stage distillation combining MSE loss and block-wise prompt-embedding distillation (Section 4.3).

The final NanoFLUX model (2B DiT + 330M text encoder) scores GenEval 49.7 and HPSv3 10.41 using 10 inference steps, compared to the FLUX.1-Schnell teacher's GenEval 66.0 and HPSv3 11.45 using 4 inference steps (Table 2, Table 5).

Progressive Token Downsampling (PTD), which adds 200M parameters and reduces tokens 4x during early denoising timesteps with a threshold t_thresh=0.5, reduces on-device latency on a Samsung S25U from 2.75 seconds to 2.40 seconds for the 1.8B model (Table 7, Section 4.2).
End-to-end on-device image generation, including the VAE decoder and text encoder, takes approximately 2.5 seconds on a Samsung S25U mobile device (Table 7).

b7BjkrfNjw.text: Theorem 3.1 derives a dual representation showing the optimal controlled transition rates for the Generalized Schrodinger Bridge on graphs, and Proposition 3.4 establishes the corresponding Hopf-Cole transformation on graphs (Section 3, Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.4).

On a 9,559-node supply chain subgraph, GSBoG achieves a Terminal Variation of 0.03 versus 0.27 for baseline methods, with mean congestion of 21.13 versus 84.09-178.19 for alternatives (Table 2, Figure 2).
On the bipartite assignment task, GSBoG attains 100% accuracy for problem sizes n≤10 and 90% accuracy for n=20, with 85% of the learned coupling mass placed on optimal edges (Table 3, Figure 4).

On a 500-state Markov state model of Chignolin protein folding, GSBoG-controlled trajectories achieve a 99.7% folding rate versus 0.55% for uncontrolled dynamics and 71.69% for a committor-guided baseline (Table 4, Figure 5).
The GSBoG-controlled folding pathway has an energy barrier of 1.39 kB·T_sim under a running-cost objective, compared to 6.94 kB·T_sim for uncontrolled dynamics (Table 4).

D7pFsC7UAr.text: PuzzleMoE preserves MMLU accuracy within roughly 1-3 points of the uncompressed model at 50% compression, e.g. Mixtral-8x7B drops from 67.9% to 65.7% and Qwen3-MoE from 77.8% to 75.1% (Table 2).

PuzzleMoE combines similarity-based masks, which identify comparable expert weights via a symmetric percent difference metric, with saliency-based masks that preserve expert-specific parameters using activation-weighted importance (Section 3.1).
Bit-packed inference reuses underutilized exponent bits in the BFloat16 format to embed merge masks directly into weights without auxiliary storage overhead (Section 3.2).
At 50% compression, PuzzleMoE achieves end-to-end inference speedups of 1.28x on Mixtral-8x7B and 1.19x on Qwen3-MoE (Figure 4(c)).
PuzzleMoE compresses DeepSeek-MoE in about 10 minutes, compared to prior methods like NAEE that require on the order of 10^18 forward passes for the same model (Figure 4(a)).

Ablation studies vary the calibration dataset, merge group size, grouping strategy, similarity threshold, and importance scoring function, showing the method's robustness across these configurations (Tables 5-8).

SAJMlj9x39.text: ΔBelief-RL uses the change in a language model's own intrinsic belief that it will reach the target solution as an intermediate reward signal for credit assignment, rather than relying only on final outcome rewards (abstract only).
Agents trained with ΔBelief-RL learn information-seeking behavior by recognizing belief changes about the target solution during long-horizon interactions (abstract only).
ΔBelief-RL is evaluated on synthetic interaction data and shown to outperform purely outcome-based reward training (abstract only).
Improvements from ΔBelief-RL generalize to out-of-distribution applications spanning customer service and personalization tasks (abstract only).
Performance under ΔBelief-RL continues to improve as test-time interactions are extended beyond the training horizon, with efficiency gains also observed in Pass@k metrics (abstract only).

fSRmJOzMA1.text: Theorem 1 proves that for weight updates of the form ΔW = g(x,θ) − γW, L2 weight decay drives the expected alignment between the learning signal and the Hebbian direction to be strictly positive, proportional to γ𝔼[‖h_b‖²] (Section 3, Equations 10-12).
Hebbian alignment strength increases monotonically with the weight decay coefficient γ, as derived analytically in Section 3 and illustrated by comparing high versus zero weight decay (Figure 2).

Theorem 2 shows that when stochastic perturbations with variance σ² dominate weight decay, the alignment with the Hebbian direction becomes negative, producing anti-Hebbian dynamics (Section 4, Equation 20).
The Hebbian/anti-Hebbian phase boundary in linear regression settings satisfies the scaling relation γ ∝ σ², as depicted in the phase diagram (Section 4, Figure 5).
Optimal generalization is empirically found to occur near the Hebbian/anti-Hebbian phase boundary, where net alignment approaches zero (Figure 6).

DVDepvPVd1.text: On seen Blocks World tasks, Self-CriTeach's P2E-8B model achieves 71% success on Classic, 43% on Hard, and 76% on Align variants, versus 48%, 28%, and 69% for the base Qwen3-8B model (Table 1).

On unseen generalization tasks, P2E-8B reaches 41% (Prepare Experiment), 22% (Reorganize Room), and 43% (Machine Parts) success, with the smaller P2E-4B model matching or exceeding these at 42%, 17%, and 49% respectively (Table 1).
P2E-8B attains an overall success rate of 44% versus 35% for the base model across seen and unseen tasks combined (Table 1).
P2E-4B achieves higher planning success than the base Qwen3-8B model while using lower inference token cost, despite having roughly half the parameter count (Figure 3).

A teacher-student variant, P2ETS-8B(30B), reaches 63% overall success compared to 42% for a direct distillation baseline, showing the benefit of self-written domains as CoT supervision over conventional distillation (Table 2).

Removing symbolic-language alignment (the SymbOnly-4B ablation) yields minimal improvement and even degrades performance on some tasks, confirming that alignment quality between self-generated domains and natural language is critical (RQ5).

Vt0tmqhfDM.text: Proposition 3.1 shows the imputed e-statistic ě[D,X̃] is valid for both marginal (label-shift, P1) and conditional (concept-shift, P2) hypothesis tests regardless of the learning algorithm, model accuracy, or number of labeled/unlabeled samples (Section 3.2, Equation 2).

Theorem 3.4 establishes that when using an approximate null distribution, type-I error control degrades by an amount bounded by the total-variation distance between the true and estimated null distributions (Section 3.4).
Corollary 3.3 shows the resulting sequential test retains anytime-valid type-I error control even when the underlying predictions are inaccurate (Section 3.4).

Label-shift simulations show power gains from the e-statistic approach are largest when unlabeled data has low correlation with labels or is scarce (N=30), and diminish as correlation and unlabeled sample size grow (Figure 1).
On an LLM evaluation task comparing Llama3.1 (8B) and Qwen2.5 (7B) on math benchmarks, the betting-based test shows power improvements over prediction-powered inference baselines (Figure 3).

In an in-context learning experiment on health-insurance procurement testing, the method achieves a significant increase in power compared to combinations of PPI and likelihood-ratio tests (Figure 4).

SC378KSCTk.text: On the BEDTime benchmark's Recognition task, GPT-4o-Vision achieves 0.96 accuracy on the SUSHI dataset and 0.88 on TaxoSynth, outperforming the best text-only LLM (GPT-4o at 0.84 on SUSHI) (Table 2a).

On the Differentiation task, GPT-4o-Vision reaches 0.97 accuracy on SUSHI versus 0.67 for the best LLM pipeline (GPT-4o+LLMTime), while the dedicated time-series-language model ChatTime-7B scores only 0.07-0.24 with refusal rates of 53-83% (Table 2b).

In the Open Generation task on SUSHI, GPT-4o-Vision attains 47.65% Gen-to-GT entailment and 15.29% bidirectional entailment, compared to 23.53% and 2.65% respectively for the time-series-language model ChatTS (Table 3).

Robustness perturbation tests show LLM accuracy declines sharply once time series exceed roughly 50 time steps, and all model classes degrade under Gaussian noise, with vision-language models degrading more slowly than text-only models (Figure 2).
Chain-of-thought prompting produces consistent accuracy improvements across all text-only models, with the largest gains observed on the Differentiation task (Figure 2).

Among open-source models, Qwen2.5-14B is the strongest text-only performer, while dedicated time-series-language models (ChatTime-7B, ChatTS-14B) generally underperform vision-language models across the three proposed tasks (Section on model comparison, Table 2a/2b).

KVzXnWPLgX.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that the conditional carré du champ (CDC) estimator Γ_ε(f,h)(x) converges to the true Riemannian metric g_x(∇f,∇h) as the noise scale ε→0, giving metric matching a provable consistency guarantee (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 3.1 shows the intractable marginal CDC objective differs from the tractable conditional loss (using Y|X ~ N(X, εI) perturbations) only by a parameter-independent constant, justifying training via the conditional loss (Theorem 3.1).

On synthetic sphere data, metric matching achieves up to approximately 400x throughput speedup over k-NN-based CDC estimation at 8 million points, with roughly 82x speedup at 2 million points (Section 5.1).

On high-dimensional image datasets, metric matching runs in 1.5±2.6 ms on MNIST and 16.6±3.7 ms on CIFAR-10 versus 75.5±7.1 ms and 992.3±1.2 ms for the Score Jacobian baseline, while the Score Jacobian baseline runs out of memory on CelebA and FFHQ despite an 80GB GPU (Table 1).

Theorem 4.4 establishes that a low-rank factorization of rank r ≥ 2d-1 still validly recovers the Riemannian metric despite topological obstructions, enabling reduced O(D) complexity instead of O(D²) (Theorem 4.4, Section 3.4).

On manifold interpolation experiments with image datasets, metric matching outperforms random perturbations and competing geometric methods (Stein score, Score Jacobian) in Inception feature stability across MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and FFHQ (Figure 4).

cYYVYK1Dgg.text: ProEval reformulates performance estimation as Bayesian quadrature and failure discovery as superlevel set sampling, using pre-trained Gaussian Processes as surrogates mapping model inputs to performance metrics (abstract only).
ProEval requires 8 to 65 times fewer samples than baseline evaluation methods to achieve performance estimates within 1% of the ground truth (abstract only).
ProEval discovers more diverse failure cases than baseline methods while operating under a stricter (smaller) evaluation sample budget (abstract only).
ProEval is empirically validated on reasoning benchmarks, safety alignment evaluation, and classification tasks (abstract only).
ProEval uses uncertainty-aware active selection or synthesis of informative test inputs via transfer learning across generative AI evaluation tasks (abstract only).

d3OI6jY1mF.text: On the prompt-optimization benchmark suite (HotpotQA1, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA), FlowBot achieves 69.80% average performance versus 66.97% for GEPA and 68.69% for GEPA+Merge, starting from scratch rather than a hand-optimized workflow (Table 1).
On workflow-generation benchmarks (HotpotQA2, DROP, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH), FlowBot attains 84.80% average accuracy compared to 80.45% for AFlow (Table 3).
FlowBot requires 54.7K API calls costing $47.67 to run its bilevel optimization, roughly 6x cheaper than AFlow's 338K calls costing $130.95 (Table 2).

An ablation on HotpotQA shows the full FlowBot method reaches 72.80% accuracy, while removing layer-wise textual backpropagation drops performance to 71.13%, and using only prompt optimization without bilevel/workflow-structure optimization drops it to 60.07% (Table 6).
Learning curves show FlowBot converges within a single epoch across all ten evaluated benchmarks, driven by its layer-by-layer textual gradient backpropagation (Figure 2).
Discovered workflows differ structurally from human-designed baselines, e.g., on IFBench the optimized workflow expands from a 2-step human baseline to a 6-step decomposition (Table 4).

sPIXjSkDFG.text: Theorem 4.3 proves that language modeling KL-divergence decomposes recursively as a sum of conditioned KL-divergences over the constituent subgrammars of a probabilistic context-free grammar (Theorem 4.3).
Theorem 4.1 shows that any PCFG decomposes uniquely into inner subgrammars organized as a directed acyclic graph (Theorem 4.1).

Unlike children who master simpler grammatical substructures before complex ones, small transformers reduce loss across all subgrammars roughly in parallel during training (Figure 1, Figure 2, Section 4.3).

Subgrammar-based pretraining lowers final loss for 2-layer transformers, but this benefit disappears for 4-layer transformers, while CKA analysis shows pretrained models have 8.9% to 21.7% higher attention-layer alignment than models trained from scratch (Figure 6, Table 1).

On nested-parentheses generalization tests, prediction error grows approximately as an inverse logarithm of nesting depth, and ChatGPT-5-Instant solves 5/5 shallow arithmetic chains but only 2/5 deeply nested expressions (Figure 3, Section 6).

JF4045xnhl.text: The PPG foundation model outperforms all baselines on 14 of 15 downstream tasks in across-subject linear probing evaluation and on all 9 of 9 tasks in within-subject evaluation (Section 5, Table 2, Table 3).
On the DaLiA field-like dataset, the model reduces heart rate estimation error to 7.78 MAE versus 10.5 MAE for the baseline (Table 2).

The model is pretrained on approximately 20 million 10-second PPG segments (about 56,000 hours) from the MIMIC-III Waveform Database, using roughly 3x fewer subjects than the PaPaGei baseline (Section 4, Section 5).

Contrastive samples are selected using five physiological metrics derived from accompanying ECG (heart rate, RMSSD) and respiratory signals (respiratory rate, amplitude, volume per time) via a rank-n-contrast loss (Section 3.1).
An ablation shows that combining ECG and respiratory-derived supervision outperforms single-modality supervision on 14 of 15 downstream tasks (Table 4).
The model achieves strong performance on the field-like DaLiA and WildPPG datasets without requiring field-specific pretraining data (Section 5).

3i4xYPxtTf.text: The proposed MPC protocol (Protocol 1, ΠU-MPC) reduces Mean Squared Error for Kendall's tau by up to four orders of magnitude over existing baselines, as shown across discretization bin counts t and online communication cost (Section 6.2.2, Figure 4).

The protocol securely computes U-statistics of degree k ≥ 2 under central differential privacy using multi-party computation, with (ε,δ)-differential privacy and semi-honest security formalized in Lemma C.2 (Section 3, Appendix C.2.2).
For the Gini Mean Difference statistic, the protocol achieves lower MSE than competing baselines at comparable communication cost (Section 6.2.1, Figure 1).
AUC-ROC is formulated as a degree-2 U-statistic compatible with the proposed private MPC method (Section A.5.3).
Across the evaluated statistics, the ΠU-MPC protocol achieves the lowest MSE among compared protocols while maintaining competitive communication cost (Section 6.3).

9yNGBueKgZ.text: FlowState(T)-9.1M achieves a MASE of 0.719 and CRPS of 0.489 on the GIFT-Eval zero-shot benchmark, outperforming the larger 35M-parameter TiRex model (Table 1).
FlowState leads on the full GIFT-Eval benchmark among models without test-data leakage (Table 3).

The model uses a scaling parameter s_Δ to discretize a continuous state-space model for arbitrary sampling rates, enabling sampling-rate-equivariant forecasting without retraining (Section 'Adjusting Δ for unseen sampling rates').
A functional basis decoder interprets SSM outputs as coefficients of a functional basis to produce continuous-time forecasts sampled at arbitrary intervals (Section 'Functional Basis Decoder').

On the Loop Seattle dataset with sampling intervals ranging from 5 to 65 minutes, FlowState-9.1M consistently outperforms all baselines across most tested frequencies despite its small size (Figure 3).
An ablation removing the time-scale adjustment mechanism degrades MASE from 0.733 to 0.808 (Table 4).

6dI31vzkqT.text: Theorem 2.3 establishes that the rank-statistic approximation D^(K)_{f,ν}(μ) is monotone non-decreasing in the resolution parameter K and is always bounded above by the true f-divergence D_{f,ν}(μ) (Section 2, Theorem 2.3).

Theorem 2.5 establishes quantitative convergence rates of O(K^{-α/2}) for Hölder-continuous density ratios and O(K^{-1}) under higher regularity, as the resolution parameter K→∞ (Section 2.1, Theorem 2.5).
On Gaussian-Uniform pairs across dimensions 2-10, the rank-statistic estimator shows superior stability with fewer samples compared to neural divergence estimators (Section 4.1, Figure 2).
Table 1 reports ratio estimates for KL, Jensen-Shannon, and Hellinger divergences across resolution values K ∈ {32, 64, 128, 256, 512} in a univariate convergence study (Section 4.2, Table 1).

The rank f-divergence estimator is used as a learning objective for generative transport dynamics on 2D toy examples (checkerboard, ring, spirals) and on CelebA image experiments (Section 4.4, Sections 4.4.1 and 4.4.2).

0BfnRKdTXH.text: The stylistic-feature-based detector (StyleDetect) maintains an AUROC of 0.95 even when generator models are explicitly optimized to evade it (Section 2, Table 1).
UMAP projections of the stylistic feature space visually separate DPO-optimized LLM samples from human text (Section 2, Figure 1).
Detection performance measured by AUROC(10) improves significantly as the number of documents analyzed jointly increases, evaluated across three domains (Section 4, Section 6, Figures 2 and 3).

A two-stage style-aware paraphrasing attack, combining supervised fine-tuning and DPO preference optimization to jointly target undetectability and adherence to a specific human style, is described with qualitative examples across domains (Section 3, Table 2).

Using the AURA distributional-gap metric, style-based detectors retain an AURA score of 0.78 against the paraphrasing attack, versus 0.00 for competing detector categories, indicating the attack largely evades non-stylistic detectors while stylistic fingerprints persist (Table 4).

REezhltCeh.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes a joint scaling limit for SGLD-Gibbs in which global parameters converge to an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion process while latent variables converge to independent jump processes under polynomial hyperparameter scaling (Theorem 3.1).

The latent-involved Fisher information matrix decomposes as the true Fisher information plus an algorithm-induced 'Jensen gap' term M_star arising from single-sample Gibbs updates, which quantifies extra posterior uncertainty from latent variable estimation (Section 3.1).

Using S>1 conditional Gibbs draws per iteration shrinks the Jensen gap to M_star/S, so algorithm-induced variability vanishes as S goes to infinity, improving calibration at added computational cost (Section 3.3).

Two hyperparameter tuning strategies are given: a Bernstein-von Mises strategy setting Gamma to the inverse latent-involved Fisher information, and a bagged-posterior strategy setting Gamma to the inverse observed information J_star, each yielding distinct stationary covariance targets (Section 3.4, Table 2).

On real flow cytometry data, SGLD-Gibbs attains ARI/AMI of 0.80/0.82 compared to 0.47/0.68 for stochastic variational inference, and on 20 Newsgroups SGRLD-Gibbs achieves perplexity 2052 versus 2402 for SVI (Section 4.3).

c2neBfCuoz.text: Theorem 3.3 proves that the gap between the truncation level K_n and the number of occupied clusters H_n in Dirichlet process slice samplers satisfies K_n - H_n = O_P(log n) with probability at least 1-delta for any confidence level delta, uniformly over partitions (Theorem 3.3, Section 3).
Corollary 3.4 gives exponential tail bounds and uniformly bounded moments for the normalized overhead K_n - H_n across all sample sizes n (Corollary 3.4).
Corollary 3.5 shows an almost-sure guarantee that super-logarithmic overhead in slice sampling cannot occur infinitely often as n grows (Corollary 3.5).
Even in configurations where the number of occupied clusters H_n grows as O(n), the truncation level K_n remains O_P(n) with only vanishing probability of superlinear blow-up (Section 3).

The complexity bounds hold without likelihood-specific assumptions and apply to any observed dataset, establishing favorable scalability of slice samplers relative to marginal CRP-based and truncated sampling methods (Table 1, Section 4).

UcGwFXWnbn.text: L2A extends effective context length from 32K to 128K tokens for Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models by learning token-wise decisions on when to invoke global attention (Section 1).

At 128K context length, L2A stays within 1.5-3% of continued long-context pretraining (CLP) task-wise performance while outperforming sparse-attention baselines S2-Attn and NSA and training-free baselines (Figure 3).

L2A achieves training throughput of 1,383 tokens/GPU/sec versus 642 for CLP on Qwen2.5-7B, a 2.15x speedup, with 2.02x and 1.82x speedups reported for Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen3-8B respectively (Table 2).
L2A's custom Triton kernel achieves 1.6-35x speedups for the forward pass and 1.08-45x for the backward pass over FlashAttention-2 across varying sparsity levels (Figure 10, Section D.1).

Post-training pruning of rarely-used global attention modules reduces KV cache memory by up to 50% with less than 1% performance loss, and nearly 50% of L2A layers operate at 95%+ sparsity (Figure 6, Figure 8).

9XGa1e4YxB.text: For fully fine-tuned vision experts, merging performance (via Task Arithmetic, TIES, and DARE) peaks at 256 training steps rather than the standard 2048 steps, even though individual expert accuracy is lower at 256 steps (88.4%) than at 2048 steps (90.0%) (Section 3.1, Figure 1).

For LoRA-adapted experts, degradation from overtraining is more severe than for full fine-tuning: vision merging peaks at 128 steps with 5-6% accuracy drops for Average/TA/DARE and a 17% drop for TIES at 2048 steps, while NLP tasks show 2.5-9.9% accuracy losses with extended training (Section 3.2, Figure 2).
Increasing LoRA rank substantially attenuates the overtraining-induced merging degradation, with rank 256 showing minimal accuracy drop compared to rank 8 (Section 3.3, Figure 3).

The hardest 10% of training examples account for over 50% of total loss during late training steps, and these hard examples are disproportionately forgotten during merging, with the hardest 30% representing over half of all forgotten data (Section 4, Figures 5-6).

Task-dependent early stopping recovers merging performance: for fully fine-tuned models, Task-Arithmetic early stopping achieves 72.6% versus 69.8% at 2048 steps, and for LoRA models 68.0% versus 61.1% (Table 1).
MoErging models initialized with early-stopped LoRA experts achieve 87.3% accuracy versus 85.1% when initialized with experts trained for the full 2048 steps (Table 2).

XiD5RhcEDK.text: Even perfectly group-calibrated scores, including true class-conditional probabilities, provably violate predictive parity after thresholding, per Definitions 2.1 and 2.3 of sufficiency and predictive parity (Section 2, Definitions 2.1, 2.3).

Theorem 3.3 shows that for a fixed selection rate, the optimal classifier applies a soft threshold to group-calibrated scores, with randomization needed at exactly one threshold boundary (Theorem 3.3).

Theorem 3.4 characterizes the boundary of the feasible region of achievable positive-predictive-value/false-omission-rate pairs as a continuous, piecewise curve composed of hyperbolic arcs and line segments (Theorem 3.4).
Algorithm 1 traces the intersection of group-specific feasible PPV/FOR regions to construct the optimal classifier satisfying sufficiency exactly (Algorithm 1).
A COMPAS case study demonstrates that optimal fair classifiers under sufficiency generally require group-specific decision thresholds rather than a single universal threshold (Section 7).

piXLPucLRA.text: ConPress fine-tuning reduces reasoning token usage by 59% on MATH500 and 33% on AIME25 relative to baseline reasoning traces while maintaining competitive accuracy (Section 1).
On Qwen3-4B-Thinking, ConPress achieves a 48.7% token reduction with only a 0.6-point accuracy drop, and on R1-Distill-Qwen-7B it achieves 33.9% reduction with accuracy preserved (Table 2).

The Self-Compression phenomenon shows that presenting multiple questions (N=3) in one prompt induces shorter reasoning traces per question than presenting a single question, with N=3 yielding a 45.0% token reduction and a 0.9-point accuracy gain in the ablation on sampling multiplicity (Table 3).
