Self-supervised fine-tuning using only 8,000 training examples derived from MATH, AIME (pre-2024), and LIMO datasets is sufficient to internalize the compressed reasoning behavior into a single-question model (Section 4.1).
Out-of-distribution evaluation on MMLU-STEM shows 33-37% token reduction, indicating the compression transfers beyond the math domains used for fine-tuning (Table 6).
The Self-Compression phenomenon is confirmed across additional models including DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen3-30B, Seed-OSS-36B, and ERNIE-4.5-21B (Appendix A.2).

r8qbhgGHnC.text: EELMA estimates effective empowerment as the mutual information between an agent's action and its future state using InfoNCE-based contrastive learning with two neural encoders (Section 3, Equation 1, Figure 2).

In WebArena, empowerment correlates with discounted task rewards with Spearman correlation Rs=0.83-0.94 across the GitLab, Reddit, and Shopping Admin domains, with GPT-4o showing the highest empowerment (Section 5, Figure 7).

Removing chain-of-thought reasoning reduces empowerment by roughly 99% in the Gridworld environment (from 0.19 to 0.01 bits), while extending memory increases empowerment in Tower of Hanoi from 0.3 to 0.4 bits (Section 4, Figure 3).
EELMA is more robust to varied natural-language phrasing of observations than direct empowerment estimation, achieving 0.048 bits RMSE versus 0.302 bits RMSE in Gridworld (Table 1).

In an authentication case study, empowerment for valid username/password entry attempts is 0.365 bits versus -0.127 bits for invalid attempts (p<0.001), demonstrating detection of pivotal power-seeking behavior without an explicit reward signal (Figure 8).

xnj5CyzVVW.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes an improved comparator-adaptive dynamic regret bound for unconstrained OCO with time-varying movement costs that replaces a quadratic dependence on lambda_t with a linear interaction term lambda_t*||g_t|| relative to the bound in Theorem 3.1 (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 5.2 shows that for OCO with delayed feedback, the reduction to time-varying movement costs (via Lemma 5.1 and Algorithm 4) achieves regret depending on total delay d_tot rather than the worse max-delay times T (d_max*T) dependence of prior work, without requiring in-order feedback arrival (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.2).

Theorem 5.7 gives a comparator-adaptive dynamic regret guarantee for OCO with time-varying memory (loss functions depending on the last H actions) by reducing memory-dependent losses to movement costs via the effective memory coupling coefficients xi_t (Section 5.2, Lemma 5.6, Theorem 5.7).

Algorithm 2 is a dynamic parameter-free subroutine that maintains parallel learning-rate instances on an exponential grid, used within the Composite Mirror Descent scheme (Algorithm 1) to obtain comparator-adaptive guarantees (Section 3, Algorithms 1-2).

Setting the movement-cost weights lambda_t=0 in the derived bounds recovers the standard optimal static and dynamic regret guarantees for classical OCO as a special case (Section 3, following Theorem 3.1).

qpPf5mI1qn.text: Theorem 3.4 and Corollary 3.5 establish that MORetro*, using a pruning-number-based bound-dominance condition, recovers the true Pareto front of synthesis routes for a fixed single-step model while enabling safe node pruning (Section 3.5, Theorem 3.4, Corollary 3.5).

On the USPTO-190 benchmark, MORetro* with BO-informed sampling improves hypervolume (HV) over single-objective Retro* by roughly 5-8% for both the G2E model (0.98 to 1.04, p<0.01) and the PDVN model (0.88 to 0.92, p<0.01) (Table 1, Section 4.2).

MORetro* achieves higher chemical diversity than Retro*, with G2E model maximum dissimilarity of 0.84±0.23 versus 0.80±0.26 for Retro*, and a higher diversity fraction of 0.49±0.23 versus 0.43±0.26 (Table 3).

MORetro* maintains a success rate close to single-objective Retro* (e.g., 97.9% vs 100% for one model configuration) despite optimizing for a Pareto front rather than a single objective, with only a 2-3% success-rate gap noted as a limitation (Table 2, Section 5).
Bound-based pruning (V_bound) achieves a 54±33% average reduction in search space on the G2E model, with 21% of molecules achieving 90% frontier pruning (Table 4, Section 4.2).

Three industrially-relevant objectives beyond cost are proposed and evaluated: sustainability (temperature penalty plus atom economy), toxicity (agent hazards plus molecular toxicity), and scale-up potential (an ExtractionScore based on logP differences) (Section 3.4, Appendix C, Equations 19-24).

BxSubxbbNc.text: Figure 1 shows a robust negative correlation (Pearson rho approximately -0.5) between token frequency and embedding variance in decoder-only models, supporting a frequency-induced variance collapse mechanism for anisotropy (Section 2.2, Figure 1).

Proposition 2.3 shows that tangent-direction components of the embedding receive gradient updates of order O(t) larger than normal-direction components for small t, formalizing a gradient bias toward tangent directions during early training (Section 2.4, Proposition 2.3, Equations 9-11).

Table 1 reports cross-model gradient energy statistics for tangent-aligned proxies versus matched normal controls across ten models (including EuroBERT-210m/610m, Pythia-160m/410m/1b, and SmolLM2-360m/1.7b), with energy ratios often exceeding 100 and the tangent-alignment effect strongest in early training checkpoints (Section 3, Table 1).

Appendix D presents a semi-NMF concept decomposition tracking geometric structure across training checkpoints for EuroBERT-210m, Pythia-410m, and SmolLM2-360m, linking embedding manifold geometry to training dynamics (Appendix D, Table 2).

Appendix E reports embedding-update enrichment showing tangent enrichment ratios for tokens across different frequency ranges, corroborating the frequency-dependent anisotropy mechanism at the level of individual update steps (Appendix E, Table 3, Figures 3-4).

wqs3uxBFRo.text: TC-Bench evaluates vision foundation models (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP, SigLIP, MAE) on 2,601 cleaned tropical cyclones (from 3,928 raw cyclones spanning 1980-2024 across seven agencies) combining IBTrACS metadata with 224x224 GridSat-B1 infrared imagery (Section 3).

Manifold consistency violation (Qcon) rises from approximately 20% in moderate-intensity regimes to approximately 55% in intense regimes (Pc < 920 hPa), showing collapse of physically meaningful latent structure (Section 4).

Effective dimensionality of learned representations drops by approximately 60% in high-intensity storm bins, indicating visual saturation compresses distinct physical states into indistinguishable representations (Section 4.2).

A supervised pixel baseline (control experiment E.1) still achieves normalized MAE of 0.3-0.4 in intense regimes, showing the pressure/wind signal remains recoverable from imagery even where foundation-model representations fail (Section 4, E.1).
Nonlinear probes (MLP and Transformer) show degradation equivalent to linear probes (control E.2), ruling out probe capacity as the cause of the perception-physics misalignment (Section 4, E.2).

Video models with temporal pretraining (VideoMAE, V-JEPA2, X-CLIP) preserve the same degradation pattern as static image encoders (control E.4), showing temporal pretraining alone does not confer scientific alignment (Section 4, E.4).

2BniakOS4q.text: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to unsupervisedly discover 10-20 distinct reasoning behaviors/mechanisms shared across base and thinking models, evaluated via consistency, completeness, and independence metrics, across 5 thinking models including DeepSeek-R1 variants and QwQ-32B (Section 2).
Hybrid models constructed by steering base models with reasoning-mechanism vectors derived from thinking models recover up to 81.8% of the base-to-thinking-model performance gap on GSM8K (Section 3).
The same steering approach recovers up to 91% of the performance gap on MATH500 (Section 3).

Only about 12% of tokens require steering intervention on average to achieve this gap recovery, supporting the claim that RL-trained thinking models mainly learn when to deploy pre-existing base-model mechanisms rather than changing the mechanisms themselves (Section 3).

Ablation studies show steering effectiveness depends on correct timing and category-specific vectors rather than merely producing more verbose output, distinguishing genuine mechanism-deployment learning from superficial formatting effects (Section 3).

Yq66fTPjHn.text: A pivot procedure (Algorithm 4) transforms bad triangle transversal covers into clusterings with at most (3/2)|X| mistakes for correlation clustering on complete signed graphs, improving on the prior factor-of-2 bound (Theorem 3).

Three novel, simpler and faster 2-approximation algorithms are given for the Bad Triangle Transversal problem on general graphs: a folklore O(m)-LP-solve approach (Algorithm 1), a deterministic complementary-slackness method (Algorithm 2), and a randomized rounding algorithm for weighted variants (Algorithm 3).

For complete signed graphs, a randomized (2+epsilon)-approximation algorithm runs in tilde-O(epsilon^-7 m^1.5) time, matching the runtime of finding a maximal edge-disjoint bad-triangle packing and improving on the standard 3-approximation baseline (Theorem 1).

Bad Triangle Transversal on general graphs is shown to be as hard to approximate as vertex cover, implying Unique-Games-Conjecture hardness for any approximation ratio better than 2-epsilon (Theorem 4).

On complete signed graphs, it is NP-hard to approximate Bad Triangle Transversal (and correlation clustering, cluster deletion, and minimum strong triadic closure) better than a 2137/2136 ratio, via a gap-preserving reduction from minimum 2CNF deletion using hexagram gadgets (Theorem 6, Theorem 7).

yyitz0hJqK.text: PERSIST maintains an explicit persistent 3D proxy state s-tilde = <w, c> (fixed spatial world regions w and camera state c) rather than relying only on pixel history, decomposing simulation into world-frame, camera, and world-to-pixel generation models (Section 4, Section 5).
PERSIST is trained on roughly 40 million environment interactions comprising about 100,000 trajectories (460 hours of gameplay at 24Hz) using 48-cubed voxel grid observations (Section 6).

In a user study of over 800 rollout evaluations from 28 participants, PERSIST-XL+w0 achieves an FVD of 116 versus 706 for Oasis and 596 for WorldMem, and the highest overall rating of 3.0 versus 1.9 (Oasis) and 1.5 (WorldMem) on a 1-5 scale (Table 1).
PERSIST-XL+w0 attains 3D consistency and temporal-coherence ratings of 2.8 each, compared to 1.9 and 1.8 respectively for Oasis, and 1.7 and 1.5 for WorldMem (Table 1).

Despite these gains, human evaluators still preferred ground-truth videos over all PERSIST variants across every measured metric, and long 2000-step episodes still show degradation from exposure bias (Section 6, Appendix D).

qijM0kpqPC.text: DI-Loss (Derivative Informed XC-Loss) reduces total-energy MAE by 66% on average across four ML-XC architectures when distilling B3LYP-level hybrid functionals, compared to training with energy and density supervision alone.
On the strongest architecture tested (EG-XC), DI-Loss reduces total-energy MAE from 15.9 mEh to 3.1 mEh, and the mean-field energy metric E_rho improves from 1.2 to 0.8 mEh.

DI-Loss-distilled functional densities reduce B3LYP SCF iterations by approximately 50% versus standard initialization, yielding a 1.35x wall-clock speedup for 35-atom molecules using the def2-SVP basis.

For TDDFT excited-state predictions, the XCdiff functional trained with DI-Loss reduces mean excitation-energy MAE by 28-35% depending on system size, evaluated on QM9 (train/validation) and QM40 (out-of-distribution test) molecules.

The DI-Loss objective combines four weighted terms-energy (L_E), density (L_rho), gradient (L_grad, constrained to the occupied-virtual block), and Hessian (L_H, supervised via importance-weighted random linear responses)-tested across NNmGGA, semi-local, EG-XC, and Skala-mGGA architectures.

PN8EiOzMuT.text: SRMC represents trajectory history as a d-dimensional running average of score evaluations rather than an empirical measure, achieving O(d) memory versus the Ω(|X|) memory required by history-dependent samplers like SRRW and HDT (Section 3).
Proposition 3.4 establishes that the score-history covariance ΣX(α) scales as O(1/α) as the repellence strength α increases, for Gaussian targets estimating the mean (Proposition 3.4, Equation 16).

Theorem 3.3 proves almost-sure convergence of the coupled iterates (θn, μn) to equilibrium (0, μ) and establishes a joint central limit theorem for their long-run fluctuations via stochastic approximation with controlled Markovian noise (Theorem 3.3).
On 10-dimensional continuous benchmarks, SR-MALA and SR-HMC achieve up to 5x lower MSE for mean estimation compared to their non-repellent counterparts (Abstract).

On static MNIST discrete energy-based model experiments, SR-GWG achieves an 84% reduction in KL divergence for mode-mixing and raises the Vendi Score from about 3 to about 6.4, enabling mode exploration from a single-digit initialization within about 2,500 steps (Section on discrete energy-based models experiments).
The discrete extension of SRMC to configuration spaces is formalized via discrete Stein operators (Proposition 3.6).

2CliXIoJNZ.text: RP-GSSM applies the recognition-parametrized model (RPM) framework to a Gaussian state space model, defining recognition factors only on individual latents zt and yielding a tractable auxiliary free energy optimized via EM without Monte Carlo approximation (Section 3, Equation 4).

On the linear dynamical system benchmark with linear-Gaussian dynamics and emissions, RP-GSSM outperforms SVAE, KVAE, four DKF variants (DKF-NL, DKF-CL, DKF-L, DKF-MF), and CPC in linear regression R^2 between posterior means and ground-truth latents, with the gap widening at larger latent/observation dimensionalities such as (10,20) (Section 5.2, Figure 2).

On noisy synthetic pendulum and real double-pendulum videos without background distractors, RP-GSSM achieves R^2 scores for decoding angle and angular velocity that are comparable to or more consistent than SVAE, KVAE, DKF variants, and CPC (Section 5.3, Figure 3).

With CIFAR10 background distractors added to the pendulum and double-pendulum tasks (CIFAR10-Pendulum, CIFAR10-Double Pendulum) and in the DAVIS-Tracking task, only RP-GSSM reliably decodes the true underlying dynamical variables, while generative and contrastive baselines' R^2 scores collapse (Section 5.3.1, Figure 3).

An auxiliary generative model trained on RP-GSSM's learned posteriors can accurately reconstruct the pendulum arm on CIFAR10-Pendulum while ignoring background distractors, unlike the same auxiliary model trained on the best generative baseline or CPC posteriors (Section 5.3.1, Figure 4a).

Given 50 CIFAR10-Pendulum frames of context, RP-GSSM can infer true states and predict the next 50 states of sin(angle) and angular velocity, whereas the best generative baseline cannot (Section 5.3.1, Figure 4b).

PAOhstVuIt.text: Group-shared fixed fan-in sparsity, in which semantically related labels share a sparse input pattern while retaining independent weights, reduces index memory overhead by a factor of G (the group size), storing (L/G)×F indices instead of L×F for L labels and fan-in F (Group-shared fixed fan-in sparsity section).

HASTE's custom CUDA kernels using a gather-once-and-dense-MMA pattern achieve up to 4.4x speedup in the forward pass and up to 25x speedup in backward passes over standard fixed fan-in sparsity, while operating within a few percent of a FLOPs-matched dense bottleneck (Performance/speedup results).

On the Amazon-670K extreme multi-label classification benchmark (670K labels), HASTE achieves P@1/P@3/P@5 of 48.1/43.1/39.2, exceeding the Spartex sparse baseline (47.1/41.8/38.0) and narrowing the gap to the dense model (50.6/45.2/41.1) (Precision@k on XMC benchmarks, Amazon-670K table).
On the larger Amazon-3M benchmark (2.8M labels), HASTE achieves P@1/P@3/P@5 of 52.5/49.5/47.4, outperforming Spartex's 50.2/47.1/44.8 (Precision@k on XMC benchmarks, Amazon-3M table).

On the LF-Paper2Keywords-8.6M benchmark (8.6M labels), HASTE attains P@1/P@3/P@5 of 47.5/36.2/29.8 while achieving the lowest peak training memory among compared methods at 12.5 GiB (Precision@k on XMC benchmarks, LF-Paper2Keywords-8.6M results).

HASTE's architecture uses a head-tail split with a dense classifier for the top 2-5% most frequent labels and the sparse group-shared layer for the remaining tail labels, with label groups formed via mini-batch spherical k-means followed by greedy local grouping (Architecture components section).

LezLGW8UFX.text: Convex Language Detection (CLD) reformulates a two-layer neural network classifier as a convex optimization problem solved via a batched, multi-GPU ADMM solver implemented in JAX, guaranteeing global optimality in polynomial time without hyperparameter tuning (Method/ADMM implementation section).

Theorem 4.4 proves a certified margin-stability bound showing that for a perturbation δ in encoder features, margin(h+δ, y) ≥ margin(h, y) − 2‖f‖_var‖δ‖₂, giving a data-dependent robustness certificate derived directly from trained weights (Theorem 4.4).

Proposition 4.5 gives a variation-norm certificate B_cvx that directly computes the model's Lipschitz constant, letting practitioners read off certified stability radii after training (Proposition 4.5).
On the Min Dong Chinese dialect low-resource setting, CLD reaches 88.73% classification accuracy compared to 9.86% for the baseline (Experimental validation, low-resource dialect results).

Applying CLD as a language-detection head ahead of Whisper-Small reduces multiclass word error rate from 139.37 to 31.74, while CLD training itself takes 64.45 seconds (7.7% of vanilla neural network training time) and uses 13x fewer TFLOPs (Performance improvements/error rate reductions section).

The evaluation spans 5 languages and 24 sub-dialects, with a multiclass setting of 5 languages x 24 accents totaling 16,000 samples (about 3,200 per language), where CLD outperforms vanilla neural networks, SVMs, KNN, and fine-tuned Whisper, especially when training data drops below 100-500 samples (Experimental validation/dataset coverage section).

BjypaSs3sS.text: Training with online rubrics elicitation, which dynamically augments evaluation criteria via pairwise comparisons between the current policy and a control policy (reference or previous checkpoint), yields consistent improvements of up to 8% over training with static human-written rubrics (Abstract).
On AlpacaEval, OnlineRubrics-πref and OnlineRubrics-πold reach 54.0% and 55.0% win rate respectively, versus 46.4% for offline human rubrics (AlpacaEval results table).
On Arena-Hard, OnlineRubrics-πref and OnlineRubrics-πold achieve 55.7% and 56.5% win rate respectively, compared to a 50.0% baseline (Arena-Hard results table).

On the expert-validated GPQA-Diamond rubric set, OnlineRubrics-πref and OnlineRubrics-πold attain 37.6% and 38.1% accuracy respectively, versus 36.2% for offline human rubrics (Expert Rubrics/GPQA-Diamond results).
On GSM8K, OnlineRubrics methods reach 80.0-80.5% accuracy compared to a 79.2% baseline (GSM8K results).

On2B3By7PT.text: For strongly convex smooth objectives, the proposed Polyak-type scheduler for SAM yields linear convergence with rate (1 − μ(1−Lρ)²/4L)^t in the deterministic setting (Theorem 3.1).

For convex smooth objectives, the same scheduler achieves an O(1/T) sublinear convergence rate, f(x̄_T) − f* ≤ 2L‖x⁰−x*‖²/(T(1−Lρ)²), with convergence only up to a neighborhood in the stochastic setting due to gradient variance (Theorems 3.2, 3.5, 3.8).
The deterministic Polyak step size γ_t = [f(ê^t) − f* − ρ_t⟨∇f(ê^t),∇f(x^t)⟩]/‖∇f(ê^t)‖² is provably non-negative whenever ρ_t ≤ 1/L (Section 2.2, Proposition 2.1).
On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-32 using USAM, the Polyak scheduler reaches 92.23±0.22 test accuracy at ρ=0.2, outperforming constant learning rate (90.45±0.34) and cosine annealing (88.77±0.26) (Table 3).
On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-32 using standard SAM, the Polyak scheduler achieves a comparable improvement, reaching 92.24±0.07 accuracy at ρ=0.2, without manual learning-rate tuning (Table 4).
The Polyak scheduling approach extends to normalized SAM variants with comparable experimental gains over baseline schedules (Section 4.3).

yuJehN4oMW.text: Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning (CAFT) projects model activations onto the orthogonal complement of an identified undesired-concept subspace during fine-tuning, without altering the training data itself (Section 3).
On the emergent-misalignment task, CAFT reduces the misalignment rate for Qwen from 7.0% to 0.39%, roughly an 18-fold reduction (Section 4.2, Figure 4).
On the same task, CAFT reduces the misalignment rate for Mistral from 6.6% to 1.2%, while maintaining performance on the training distribution (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
Concept directions for ablation are identified using either PCA (Section 3.1) or sparse autoencoder (SAE) features (Section 3.2), and example interpretable directions are shown in Figure 3.
CAFT is compared against baseline fine-tuning interventions and evaluated on multiple-choice generalization probes in addition to open-ended generation (Section 4.3, Section 5).

dQA4Gjt4KU.text: On the LJ-13 Lennard-Jones sampling benchmark, Tilt Matching (ITM) attains the highest effective sample size (ESS = 0.507) among compared methods, with an energy-histogram Wasserstein-2 distance of 0.879 (Section 4.2, Table 2).
On the larger LJ-55 Lennard-Jones system, Tilt Matching achieves an energy Wasserstein-2 distance of 26.37, evaluated alongside ESS and geometric Wasserstein-2 metrics (Table 2).
ESS evolution across the annealing parameter and scaling behavior with respect to the discretization step size h are compared between ITM and weighted flow matching (WFM) (Figure 5, panels b–c).

When fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 without a reward multiplier (λ=1), Tilt Matching achieves an ImageReward score of 0.4465 and CLIPScore of 0.2794, competitive with Adjoint Matching, which requires a reward multiplier of λ=10² (Section 4.1, Table 1).
Qualitative comparisons across four text prompts show visual improvements of Tilt Matching samples over the base Stable Diffusion model (Figure 1).

K9V63osRrB.text: Logit-Linear Selection (Algorithm 1, Section 2.2) scores preference-dataset examples by how much a target system prompt shifts a teacher model's preference for the chosen response over the rejected one, enabling selection of subsets that elicit hidden effects without needing generic-data generation.

Selected subsets elicit a hidden animal preference (e.g., for 'owl'), measured via mean animal-mention counts when fine-tuning OLMo2-7B-Instruct as the student (Section 3.1, Figure 2, with training trajectory in Figure 3).
The method elicits target-language preferences across 10 languages when fine-tuning student models on selected translation-instruction data (Section 3.2, Figure 5).
The method elicits an 'evil ruler' persona/misalignment effect at measurably higher adoption rates than baseline selection, evaluated across multiple prompts (Section 3.3, Figures 6–7).

Elicited effects also transfer to different student architectures (e.g., Qwen3-8B) beyond OLMo2, though cross-architecture correlation between fine-tuned and system-prompted behavior is markedly weaker (~0.08) than same-architecture correlation (~0.55) (Section 2.3, Table 1, Figure 8).

UXzfLdXrBJ.text: Middle-layer attention heads show the lowest cross-refit stability, e.g., layer 5 drops to ≈0.70 stability versus ≈1.0 in layer 1, quantified via a layer-wise mean stability measure (Equation 5, Section 4.1, Figure 2).
Middle layers also exhibit broader, less sharply defined off-diagonal head-to-head matching patterns across refits compared to early/late layers (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
In deeper architectures (8- and 12-layer models), the least-stable layer occurs at a relative depth r≈0.4–0.8, showing stronger mid-depth divergence than shallower models (Section 4.6.2, Figure 8).
Using AdamW (weight decay) yields a clear increase in attention-head seed-stability for deeper MLP models (8- and 12-layer) without degrading task performance (Section 4.5, Figure 6).
Higher query-weight norms correlate with lower head stability, suggesting weight-norm control as a mechanistic driver of the weight-decay stability effect (Section 4.4.1).

The residual stream is consistently more stable across refits than the corresponding attention heads, across all tested architectures and optimizers, as measured via Centered Kernel Alignment (Section 4.7, Figure 9, Appendix A.7).

xQLcklRDfM.text: The Anytime Tracking CUSUM (ATC) algorithm achieves dynamic regret ℛ_T^ATC ≤ C_V σ²(S+1+α)(1+log T) + C_B σ²S log(T/α) + M²(α+S), where S is the number of change points and T the horizon (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
A minimax lower bound of Ω(σ²(S+1)log(T/(S+1))) is proved, showing ATC's upper bound is optimal up to only a log(S) gap (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).

Lemma 3.1 quantifies how missed detections cause 'endogenous confounding' by bounding the signal-to-noise ratio degradation as (SNR_j*(t) − SNR_j^eff(t;r))_+ ≤ C log((τ_j − r + 1)/α_r) + M² (Section 3.3, Lemma 3.1).
Synthetic experiments with 5000 Monte Carlo runs confirm ATC's regret scales as O(log T), matching the theoretical rate (Section 5).
On the NAB benchmark using AWS CPU utilization data, ATC outperforms sliding-window and discounted-mean baseline detectors (Section 5).

Mi8VcF4qJZ.text: Grad-Transformer achieves an average Performance Gap Recovered (PGR) of 91.88% in the single-client setting, versus 58.94% for the best baseline, across six datasets including AQuA-RAT, GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, DROP, SAMSum, and DialogSum (Table 1).
In the multiple-client setting, Grad-Transformer attains an average PGR of 85.01% versus 69.97% for the best-performing baseline (Table 3).
Grad-Transformer remains effective when transforming updates across a 28x scale gap, from a 0.5B-parameter TinyLM to a 14B-parameter LLM (Table 2).

Under strict differential privacy (DP-SGD, ε=0.1), Grad-Transformer maintains 62.35% accuracy on DROP and 88.02% average PGR, while the TinyLM baseline drops from 55.59% to 44.70% accuracy under the same DP constraint (Figure 4).

An ablation on update-vector partitioning shows the proposed block-wise strategy reaches 63.57% accuracy, while a 'reverse block order' variant degrades to 39.73%, confirming the importance of preserving layer sequencing (Table 4).
Grad-Transformer reduces fine-tuning time by 83.14% compared to directly fine-tuning the target LLM (Figure 6).

ptaIjzIuoY.text: S²ANTA-prop achieves a 1.50x decode-step attention kernel speedup over FlashInfer at 32k-token contexts on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPU, while matching baseline accuracy (Section 3.4, Figure 4).
S²ANTA-flash achieves a 1.51x speedup over FlashDecoding at matched accuracy operating points, using S=128 (prop) or S=2048 (flash) sampled value-cache rows (Section 3.4, Figure 4).
In end-to-end batched generation with batch size 6 and 30k-token prompts, S²ANTA-flash and S²ANTA-prop yield 1.250x and 1.229x decode-latency speedups respectively (Section 3.5, Table 3).
On 32k-token RULER tasks, S²ANTA-prop with S=128 scores 95.40±1.10 on FWE and 98.25±0.62 on NIAH, within confidence intervals of the baseline SDPA implementation (Table 1).
Stochastic value-cache sampling via post-softmax distribution sampling is proven unbiased for post-softmax value aggregation, with variance scaling as 1/S (Proposition A.2, Appendix A.1-A.2).
Combining Bernoulli qK^T sampling (B=4) with SANTA (S=64) reduces key access by 15.3% and value access by 89.2% on GSM8K while keeping accuracy loss under 2% (Table 9).

Zkj9ctQdMM.text: Theorem 4.1 bounds the relative error between the true stationary covariance Σ_θ and the discrete-time proxy covariance Σ_ψ as ‖Σ_θ − Σ_ψ‖/‖Σ_θ‖ ≤ C_v λ^(1/2), scaling with the step size λ (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).

Theorem 4.3 derives an explicit formula for the minibatch noise covariance without assuming constant noise, enabling exact rather than approximate stationary covariance solutions (Theorem 4.3, Section 4).
Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 4.6 provide non-asymptotic 2-Wasserstein distance bounds between the true and proxy algorithm distributions, giving W₂(π_θ,π_ψ) ≤ Aλ/B for SGD (Theorem 4.5, Corollary 4.6).
Algorithm 1 gives a two-stage tuning procedure: offline sandwich covariance estimation from a subsample, followed by solving coupled equations for preconditioned step sizes (Algorithm 1).

On the Boston housing dataset under strong model misspecification, the proposed DQ+exact method maintains accurate covariance estimates while competing continuous-time and constant-noise methods diverge (Table 3).
Proposition B.1 extends the covariance and error-bound results to SGLD with momentum, recovering the non-momentum results as the momentum parameter κ→0 (Proposition B.1, Appendix B).

hmJdJLmwOY.text: Stochastic Lifting augments each training transition pair (x_t, x_{t+1}) with an independent Gaussian random label ξ_t ~ N(0, I_d), training a network F_θ via the regression loss ℒ(θ,𝒟_ξ) = (1/MT)∑‖F_θ(x_t^i,ξ_t^i)−x_{t+1}^i‖² (Equation 3, Equation 8).
At inference, drawing fresh random labels and rolling the map forward generates diverse trajectories using only a single network evaluation per time step (Section 3).
Proposition 3.1 gives a Wasserstein-2 bound 𝔼[W₂(ρ̂_{t+1},ρ̃_{t+1})²] ≤ C(1+L_x²)min(M,M̃)^(-2/α), tying accuracy to the Lipschitz regularity L_x of the learned map (Proposition 3.1, Equation 5).

On the Wave benchmark, Stochastic Lifting achieves a Wasserstein crossing-time distance of 4.53e-3, versus 1.11e-2 for an autoregressive diffusion model (ARDM) using 40 diffusion steps, despite Stochastic Lifting using a single step (Table 1).
On the BAIR Robot Pushing dataset, Stochastic Lifting achieves an FVD of 69.0, outperforming one-step baselines FitVid (93.6) and NUWA (86.9) (Table 2).
On CLEVRER, Stochastic Lifting produces stable rollouts for 500 frames, roughly 30x longer than the 16-frame training videos, without collapsing to mean predictions (Section 5).

nYwP9hcr38.text: On the TinyZero countdown task with a Qwen2.5-3B base model, asymmetric weightings Linear-R and Plateau-R climb to a Pass@1 of about 0.8 from an initial score of 0.025, versus about 0.74 for symmetric weightings RLOO, GRPO, and Uniform-R (Figure 1).
On GSM8K with a Llama-3.1-8B base model starting from 1.3% Pass@1, the asymmetric Plateau-R weighting outperforms GRPO at both batch sizes 128 and 256 (Figure 4, Section 4.2).

In post-SFT RL settings on the MATH dataset and the DAPO-math dataset, asymmetric weightings (Plateau-R, Linear-R, Sqrt-R) show no meaningful performance difference from symmetric weightings (GRPO, RLOO) (Figure 5, Sections 4.3-4.4).

Proposition 1 proves that under a fixed total-weight budget constraint, the weight function minimizing regular optimization time to reach a target success rate is omega_opt(rho) proportional to 1/sqrt(rho(1-rho)), matching GRPO's weighting (Section 5.3, Proposition 1).

Proposition 2 proves that under the same budget constraint but measured in effective time (which accounts for rollout cost being high in low-success regimes), the optimal weight is omega_opt(rho) proportional to 1/(rho*sqrt(1-rho)), matching the Sqrt-R weighting (Section 5.3, Proposition 2).

Asymmetric weightings such as Linear-R assign a non-zero advantage (A_i = -1) to wrong responses even when all completions in a batch receive zero reward, whereas GRPO's and RLOO's gradients vanish in that case (Section 3, Equation 5).

63o9EmYHXt.text: Theorem 1 (Section V.A) establishes that finitely Ỹ-convex functions form a dense subset of all Ỹ-convex functions, giving a universal approximation property for generalized convex functions.
Theorem 2 (Section V.A) shows that, under semiconvexity conditions on Φ, gradients of finitely Ỹ-convex functions densely approximate gradients of all Ỹ-convex functions.

Theorem 4 (Section V.C) proves that the lean subset of finitely Ỹ-convex functions forms a convex parameter space, which is what allows bilevel objectives to be rewritten as single-level problems solvable with standard first-order optimization (Section I).
Table I reports multi-item auction experiments for n in {1,2,5,10,20} goods in which, for n up to 10, the learned mechanism's revenue matches the Straight-Jacket auction benchmark exactly.

Figures 2-3 show the learned parametrization recovers the known optimal posted price of 0.5 in the single-item auction case and finds a mixed-bundling pricing scheme matching theoretical benchmarks in the two-item case.

Kantorovich dual solutions for optimal transport are characterized as Ỹ-convex functions in Section IV, so gradients of the learned parametrization directly yield optimal transport maps via a diffeomorphism condition.

zKgKPGeMZs.text: System prompt choice explains 70.6% of the variance in deception-probe performance, far more than training-data content (2.5%), layer selection (2.7%), or token-aggregation method (0.6%) (Figure 1).

Using a taxonomy of deception types based on Druckman & Bjork (1991) to craft targeted instruction pairs raises mean AUC from 0.689 to 0.797 across ten datasets, a mean improvement of 0.108 AUC (20.5% relative gain) (Figure 2).

On the MASK known-facts dataset, a pressure-dishonesty instruction pair improves probe AUC from 0.374 to 0.697, an 86.3% relative gain, the largest improvement observed across the ten datasets (Figure 2).
Cluster analysis identifies five distinct probe groupings, indicating multiple underlying deceptive-intent directions rather than a single universal deception direction (Table 1).

Because instruction-pair prompt choice dominates probe performance while training-data content contributes comparatively little, the probes are argued to capture deceptive intent rather than content-specific patterns (Figure 1).

The heterogeneity of relative gains across datasets, ranging from near zero to 86.3%, is used to argue that organizations should design specialized, threat-model-targeted deception probes rather than seeking a single universal detector (Table 1).

0QsbcZKCQ0.text: Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.1) proves that in deep linear networks with orthonormal weight matrices, local-SSL implements weight updates identical to those of global BP-SSL under specified conditions.

On CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny-ImageNet, the CLAPP++both variant achieves 81.18%, 79.62%, and 37.78% accuracy respectively, matching or exceeding the BP-CLAPP++ backpropagation baseline (80.49%, 80.36%, 37.55%) (Table 2).

Theorem 3.3 (Section 3.2) shows that when network dimensions shrink across layers, adding direct feedback from the final layer makes local-SSL updates more similar to BP-SSL gradients than standard local-SSL.

Figure 2 numerically verifies Theorem 3.1 by showing the cosine similarity between local-SSL and BP-SSL gradients reaches 1.0 under orthonormality conditions and degrades as those conditions are relaxed.
Adding spatial dependence to feedback projection matrices in convolutional local-SSL networks further improves gradient alignment between local-SSL and BP-SSL updates (Figure 4, Section 3.3).
CLAPP++ surpasses the previous local-SSL state-of-the-art method SCFF and achieves near parity with global BP-SSL baselines on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny-ImageNet (Table 2).

YPH5yCKzYr.text: Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.1) proves that wide linear networks preserve feature geometry via graph isomorphism, while Theorem 3.3 shows nonlinear activations enable genuine geometric transformations.

Across an empirical study of over 20,000 feedforward networks trained on binary classification, 73-98% of graph vertices exhibit negative local Ricci evolution coefficients, indicating curvature-driven contraction consistent with discrete Ricci flow (Table 1).

Modularity of the k-nearest-neighbor graph representation increases progressively across layers as class separability emerges, reflecting growing community structure aligned with class labels (Figure 2, Section 4.2).

Training dynamics reveal two distinct phases, an initial geometric-learning phase followed by an overfitting phase, identifiable from the evolution of local Ricci coefficients over training (Figure 4).
Layer-wise local Ricci coefficients are used to construct a critical-depth heuristic for selecting network architecture depth (Figure 5).

Local Ricci evolution coefficients are computed by correlating neighborhood expansion (η) with two curvature discretizations, Ollivier-Ricci curvature and augmented Forman curvature, on k-nearest-neighbor graphs built from transformed samples (Section 3.2).

8mGDNFoJOD.text: Theorem 4.2 bounds the 'cost of conditioning' (extra risk from injecting k unpenalized features into KRR) by O(k·log^{1/2}(2k/δ)/√N + σ²/N), where N is the sample size (Theorem 4.2).
Theorem 3.2 proves that conditional KRR decomposes into a two-stage procedure: linear regression on the unpenalized feature set followed by standard KRR on the residuals (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 5.2 shows that for random Gaussian features, the induced residual-kernel coefficients approximately satisfy μ_i/λ_i ≈ cϰ²/(λ_i+ϰ)², producing a soft-thresholding effect on the kernel spectrum (Theorem 5.2).

On the MNIST 7-vs-9 classification experiment, hard thresholding with conditional KRR exhibits a U-shaped test MSE curve as the number of unpenalized features k increases, with an interior optimum rather than monotone improvement (Section 6).

On synthetic datasets composed of pure noise (no true low-dimensional signal), conditional KRR's test error increases monotonically with k, contrasting with the U-shaped curve observed when a genuine signal component is present (Section 6).

czym69s5GU.text: RFID-MoE achieves a perplexity of 16.92 on PTB with Qwen3-30B at a 60% compression ratio, an improvement of about 8.0 perplexity points over the best baseline, MoBE (Table 2).
On DeepSeekMoE-16B at 60% compression, RFID-MoE achieves 11.54 PTB perplexity versus 11.90 for the MoBE baseline (Table 2).
RFID-MoE attains 0.66 zero-shot HellaSwag accuracy at 60% compression on Qwen3-30B, roughly an 8% improvement over MoBE's 0.58 (Table 2).
RFID-MoE is compared against five baseline MoE compression methods: NAEE, MoE-I2, RS-MoE, D²-MoE, and MoBE (Section 4).
An ablation over the fusion hyperparameter ξ, which balances routing-frequency grouping against effective-rank information density, finds the optimum concentrated around ξ = 0.7–0.8 (Table 4).

VvdG5Rslgc.text: In single-model test-time compute experiments, feature-based cues (heuristics beyond raw self-consistency voting) fail to improve accuracy on visual reasoning tasks because visual understanding, not sampling diversity, is the bottleneck (Section 3).

Theorem 1 shows the accuracy gain from majority voting decreases monotonically with the dependency between model predictions, measured via normalized mutual information/correlation, vanishing entirely when predictions are perfectly correlated (Section 4.1, Theorem 1).

On a cross-family ensemble of similarly sized models (LLaMA, Pixtral, Gemma, Qwen-7B), Entropy-based Test-Time Compute (ETTC) achieves 66.56% average accuracy versus 63.75% for majority voting, with the largest gains on MathVista (+8.6%) and MathVision (+3.52%) (Table 1).

On a same-family Qwen ensemble spanning 3B to 72B parameters, ETTC reaches 71.68% average accuracy versus 68.84% for majority voting, and surpasses the strongest individual model, Qwen-72B, which alone scores 69.90% (Table 2).

Theorem 2 proves that, under an Entropy-Accuracy Monotonicity assumption, Entropy-based TTC outperforms majority voting in multi-model ensembles, particularly when correlated errors exist among weaker models (Section 5.2, Theorem 2).

JiXnhlVhly.text: PICACO is evaluated on both black-box LLMs (GPT-3.5-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Flash) and an open-source model (LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct) without any fine-tuning of the target model (Section 4.1).

PICACO's optimization objective (Equation 2) combines a Pluralistic Conformity term with Redundancy Reduction terms derived from a Barber-Agakov/extended-CLUB bound on conditional total correlation, controlled by a trade-off hyperparameter β (Section 3.2, Equation 2).
PICACO is compared against nine in-context alignment baselines, including Q+IF, Q+IF+CoT, URIAL, URIAL+Sum, persona-based MP+System 1&2, Modular Pluralism, OPRO, and CICL (Section 4.1).
Figure 3 shows PICACO maintains a lower coefficient of variation in per-value alignment scores than competing methods when scaling from 2 to 8 distinct values (Figure 3).
PICACO's iterative Algorithm 1 uses N=50 task prompts, selects the top M1=10 aligned and M2=15 regularization responses, and runs for T=10 iterations per instruction refinement cycle (Algorithm 1).

gjykWd56Js.text: The geometric ASCII+Embedding encoding scheme raises exact secret-recovery accuracy on TrojanStego prompts from 17% to 30% (a +78% relative improvement) for LoRA-fine-tuned Llama-8B (Table 1).
For LoRA-fine-tuned Ministral-8B, the same scheme raises exact secret-recovery accuracy from 24% to 43% (a +80% relative improvement) (Table 1).
For LoRA-fine-tuned Llama-70B, exact secret-recovery accuracy rises from 9% to 19% (a +123% relative improvement) under the geometric scheme (Table 1).

Linear probes trained on model activations detect steganographic fine-tuning with 95-100% bit-classification accuracy at the final layer in fine-tuned models, versus about 60% in base models, up to a 33% higher accuracy (Section 7.3, Figure 5).

Theorems 7.1-7.2 prove that large covert payloads can be hidden via the geometric scheme while perplexity and KL divergence remain within typical fine-tuning ranges, making the channel undetectable by standard distributional steganalysis (Theorem 7.1, Theorem 7.2).
Wiki-trained LoRA models generalize out-of-distribution to Alpaca prompts at about 40% recoverability, whereas full-fine-tuned models generalize at under 20% (Table 2).

nj1oXU2tln.text: CodeTaste comprises 100 refactoring instances mined from 87 GitHub repositories across 6 programming languages, with an average of 91.52 files and 2,605.39 lines changed per task (Section 3.5, Table 1).

On the Instructed Track, GPT-5.2 achieves a 69.6% alignment score and 76.0% functional-correctness (Pass) rate, versus 32.4% alignment and 47.0% Pass for Claude Sonnet 4.5, and 11.8% alignment for Qwen3 (Section 4.2, Table 3).
On the Open Track, where agents see only a high-level focus area instead of a detailed specification, the best alignment score collapses to 7.7% (GPT-5.2, Direct mode) (Section 4.3).
A propose-then-implement (Plan mode) decomposition raises GPT-5.2's Open Track alignment from 7.7% to 14.1%, and Oracle multiplan selection raises it further to 19.4% (Section 4.3).

Static-rule evaluation uses an average of 93.07 additive/reductive OpenGrep rules per task (30 additive, 63 reductive) to measure Instruction Following Rate alongside test-suite Pass rate (Section 3.4, Table 1).
GPT-5.2's superior alignment comes at roughly $5.17 per task in agent inference cost, compared to $3.46 for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and $0.59 for GPT-5.1 Codex Mini (Section 4.4).

78MQeA1Jyq.text: Denoising Recursion Models (DRM) outperform the Tiny Recursion Model (TRM) baseline on ARC-Easy, reaching 50.5% pass accuracy versus 45.7% at matched 7M parameters (Section 5, Table 1).
With NVARC pretraining, a 14M-parameter DRM reaches 24.9% accuracy on ARC2-Eval, exceeding the 22.6% achieved by the 4B-parameter NVARC LLM trained on the same data (Section 5, Table 1).

DRM trains without intermediate gradient truncation or deep supervision (no truncated backpropagation through time), unlike the TRM baseline, while still outperforming it by nearly 5 percentage points on ARC-Easy (Section 3, Section 5).

A discrete masked-diffusion baseline achieves near-0% accuracy on the benchmark, indicating that iterative refinement through shared weights, not diffusion-style corruption alone, drives DRM's performance gains (Section 5, Appendix F).
DRM benefits more than TRM from longer gradient-loop windows, with performance gains increasing from k=1 to k=4 recursive steps (Appendix F.3, Table 5).

DRM underperforms TRM on the search-heavy Sudoku task (20% vs. 87.9%), indicating the recursion-based denoising curriculum helps most on transformation-style tasks rather than search-style tasks (Section 5).

RKVsEuwbJ0.text: Theorem 4.11 establishes a Bayesian regret bound for GP-PSRL of order R_T = O(H^{3/2} sqrt((d_s+d_a) gamma_N(sigma^2, R̃) T log T)), giving tight sqrt(gamma_T) dependence on the maximum information gain rather than a linear dependence (Theorem 4.11).

Lemma 4.7 uses a recursive application of the Borell-Tsirelson-Ibragimov-Sudakov inequality to show that states visited by the algorithm remain within a ball of near-constant radius with high probability, enabling analysis without assuming bounded state spaces (Lemma 4.7).

The analysis requires only Holder continuity of the GP kernel with parameters L>0 and alpha in (0,1] (Assumption 3.4), removing prior requirements of four-times-differentiable kernels (Section 3, Assumption 3.4).
Corollary 4.13 specializes the general regret bound to Matérn kernels, giving concrete polynomial-in-T rates for this standard kernel family (Corollary 4.13).
The regret analysis assumes a bounded action space (Assumption 3.1) and a deterministic, uniformly bounded reward function (Assumption 3.2), while state spaces remain unbounded (Section 3).

WP5q6Hn3Cv.text: Zero/one-layer progressive training achieves approximately 80% compute savings (about 5x acceleration) while matching the loss of a fully trained 60-layer, 7B-parameter GPT2 model, with the loss difference under 0.2% (Section 5).

On a 124M-parameter GPT2 model expanding from 12 to 12 layers via zero/one-layer progressive training, compute is reduced by about 80% with a loss difference under 0.5% versus training at full depth from scratch (Section 5).
Random and copying initialization strategies for newly added layers outperform zero initialization, which "kills the gradient flow and makes the new layers untrainable" (Section 3.1).

Under a WSD (warmup-stable-decay) learning-rate schedule, model expansion can be delayed to 80% of total training (tau ≈ 0.8T) without loss penalty, versus only 50% under a cosine-decay schedule (Section 5).
The method uses maximal update parametrization (muP) scaling to enable zero-shot hyperparameter transfer, so the same learning rate works before and after layer expansion (Section 3.2).

Multi-stage expansion (e.g., 0 to 12 to 24 layers) shows no efficiency advantage over single-stage expansion, because progressive and fixed-size training losses converge due to "mixing behaviors" (Section 5).

QKy6cKEiEB.text: EnterpriseOps-Gym provides a containerized sandbox with 164 database tables and 512 functional tools spanning 1,150 expert-curated tasks across eight interconnected enterprise domains, including Customer Service, HR, and IT operations (abstract only).
Across 14 evaluated language models, the top performer, Claude Opus 4.5, achieves only a 37.4% success rate on EnterpriseOps-Gym tasks (abstract only).

The best-performing model correctly refuses infeasible requests only 53.9% of the time, indicating a significant safety gap in recognizing when a requested enterprise task cannot be completed (abstract only).

Providing agents with oracle-guided human plans improves success rates by 14-35 percentage points, indicating that strategic long-horizon planning, rather than tool execution itself, is the primary bottleneck for current agents (abstract only).
The authors conclude that current agents are not yet ready for autonomous enterprise deployment based on EnterpriseOps-Gym results (abstract only).

CC4KunEY5I.text: Patterning is defined as the dual of mechanistic interpretability: given a desired form of generalization, it determines what training data distribution produces it, using susceptibilities that measure how model predictions respond to shifts in training data (abstract only).

Re-weighting training data along principal susceptibility directions can accelerate or delay the formation of internal structure, specifically the induction circuit, demonstrating temporal control over when this circuit emerges during training (abstract only).

In a synthetic parentheses-balancing task where multiple algorithms achieve identical training accuracy, patterning selects which specific algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each candidate solution (abstract only).

The same mathematical framework used to read out internal model structure (interpretability) can be inverted to write structure into a model via targeted data re-weighting, establishing a bidirectional relationship between interpretability and data-driven control (abstract only).

n7F2nwPcYB.text: AutoNumerics-Zero discovers a 10-operation program approximating the exponential function 2^x with a proven maximum relative error under 5.4e-15 (Figure 2).

The evolved 10-operation exponential approximation exceeds the accuracy of prior known approximations of comparable operation count by several orders of magnitude, as shown in the operations-count-versus-error comparison (Figure 1).

The discovered programs are compared against Taylor/Horner expansions, Padé approximants, Remez-optimized minimax approximations, Chebyshev approximations, and continued-fraction methods (Euler, Gauss, Macon variants) (Figure 1).

A float32 case study targeting Skylake hardware with the JAX/XLA compiler yields an evolved exponential program that is 3x faster than the fastest baseline while keeping error below 1 ULP, due to triggering different compiler optimization paths (Figure 3).

The evolutionary search extends to logarithm, error function, and Airy function approximations, with 20-operation evolved solutions achieving nearly 3 orders of magnitude better accuracy than Chebyshev baselines (Section 2.4).
The search was conducted over roughly 10 billion samples using a distributed population of size 10^4 with sample size 20 per worker (Section 2, referenced in Figure 1/2 experiments).

GpmvWQU9Zq.text: Memorization risk in diffusion models is characterized by two quantities, posterior weight concentration and Gaussian shell coverage, whose interaction across the noise schedule defines three regimes of memorization risk (Section 4).
At small noise, models resist memorization due to limited training coverage despite the empirical optimal denoiser exhibiting near-neighbor behavior (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

At large noise, Theorem 4.11 proves the empirical optimal denoiser converges to a linear Gaussian transformation of the data mean and covariance, m_σ(x) = μ + Σ(Σ+σ²I)^{-1}(x−μ) plus vanishing error terms, explaining resistance to memorization in this regime (Theorem 4.11).

Medium noise levels constitute a 'danger zone' where high posterior weight concentration and significant Gaussian shell coverage co-occur, producing maximal memorization risk; swapping denoisers only within σ ∈ [0.14, 8.4] reverses memorization from 92.2% to 0% (Table 1).

Excluding the medium-noise danger zone during training (targeted undertraining) reduces memorization on the CIFAR-10 'cars' class from 78.8% to 0.7% while improving sample quality, with FID improving from 3.72 to 2.35 (Section 5, experiments referenced alongside Table 1).

Theorem 4.8 characterizes Gaussian shell coverage via the intersection probability of two shells, showing coverage depends jointly on pairwise training-data distances and ambient dimension (Theorem 4.8).

GnRZzQr5WR.text: AICoG (Aitchison Compositional Graph embeddings) represents each node i as a latent composition of K components on the simplex Δ^(K-1) and maps it via isometric log-ratio (ILR) coordinates to unconstrained Euclidean space while preserving Aitchison distances (Section 3).

Theorem 3.2 proves that compositional latent-distance models realize the same set of edge-probability matrices as unconstrained Euclidean latent-distance models, so no expressive power is lost by constraining embeddings to the simplex (Theorem 3.2).

On link prediction, AICoG with hyperbolic embeddings at dimension 64 outperforms the strongest baseline (SLIM-Raa or HM-LDM) on AstroPh (0.976 vs 0.970), GrQc (0.961 vs 0.949), HepTh (0.929 vs 0.920), and Cora (0.851 vs 0.837 for HM-LDM) AUC-ROC (Table 2).

On node classification at dimension 64, AICoG achieves Micro-F1 of 0.831 on Cora, 0.736 on Citeseer, and 0.870 on LastFM, exceeding the best baselines (Node2Vec, Role2Vec) by margins of 0.005 to 0.030 (Table 3).

On Cora, AICoG produces embeddings with entropy 1.064 versus MMSBM's 0.191, indicating more interior (mixed-membership) compositions, while still achieving higher label-informative probe accuracy (0.670 vs 0.306) (Table 5).

A Euclidean-simplex ablation that removes the Aitchison geometry achieves only 0.737 AUC on LastFM link prediction compared to AICoG's 0.963, indicating the compositional geometry itself, not merely the simplex constraint, drives performance (Section 4, referenced with Table 2).

ujiUua1gGV.text: IGSR (Influence-Guided Symbolic Regression) combines diverse LLM-driven term generation with selection based on per-term influence scores Δ_j that quantify each basis function's marginal contribution to generalization accuracy (Section 3).

On LLM-SRBench across 128 discovery problems, IGSR achieves the best average rank among compared methods (including LLM-SR, D3, ICSR, LaSR), with normalized MSE rank 1.35 in-distribution and 1.77 out-of-distribution (Table 2b).
On biological benchmarks, IGSR attains MSE of 5.01e-8 on the COVID-19 simulation dataset and 0.0111 MSE on the RNA Polymerase dataset with 263 features, outperforming white-box baselines (Table 2a).
Ablations on the Lung Cancer dataset show full IGSR achieves NMSE 0.000787, versus 0.626 without MCTS, 0.293 without influence feedback, and 4.85 without both components (Table 3).

IGSR's discovered negative methylation coefficients led to the hypothesis that intragenic CpG methylation facilitates transcriptional elongation by suppressing RNA Polymerase II pausing, which was validated in wet-lab experiments using the hypomethylating agent 5-azacytidine, increasing pausing frequency with Wilcoxon p=4.3e-52 (frequency) and p=3.5e-33 (strength) across roughly 3,000 pause sites in two biological replicates (Section 5.1).
IGSR exhibits sub-linear computational scaling: a 25x increase in feature count (from 10 to 263) produces only about a 25% increase in runtime (Figure 3).

iZN85pjpsS.text: The Probability-of-Hit (PoH) acquisition function computes the posterior probability p_t(g) = P(f(g) > τ | D_t) that a candidate exceeds a phenotypic threshold τ using a closed-form Gaussian CDF, and selects the top-b unsampled candidates by this score each round (Section 4.1).

Theorem 4.3 proves that under posterior concentration and margin assumptions, PoH discovers at least Tb/2 - o(Tb) hits with high probability, establishing asymptotic optimality for kernels with sublinear information gain (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.3).

On five synthetic benchmarks (Sine 1D/2D, Branin-Hoo, Perturbation-Pathways 4D, Perturbation-SEM 6D), PoH significantly outperforms baseline acquisition functions with p ≤ 2.3×10⁻⁴ and effect sizes δ = 0.41-0.97 (Table 2).

On the Schmidt IL-2 dataset (threshold τ=10%, batch size b=200, 10 cycles), PoH recovers 575.4 ± 17 hits, a 6.4% improvement over Thompson Sampling (521.4 ± 64 hits) and far exceeding Random selection (221.2 ± 9 hits) (Table 3).
Increasing batch size from b=2 to b=10 on the 4D Perturbation-Pathways dataset yields roughly a 4-fold improvement in hit recovery for PoH (Figure 3).

jqpLZEK3Zc.text: Theorem 1 establishes convergence guarantees for the safeguarded stochastic Polyak step size (SPS) method in non-smooth convex optimization without assuming interpolation or requiring knowledge of the optimal objective value (Theorem 1).
Proposition 1 provides theoretical support for the safeguarding mechanism that bounds the step size to prevent instability when (sub)gradients become small (Proposition 1).

Section 4 neural network training experiments show that gradient norms under the proposed safeguarded SPS step size do not collapse to near zero over training, unlike vanilla SPS, demonstrating robustness to vanishing gradients (Section 4).
Theorems 5 and 6 extend the convergence analysis of safeguarded SPS to additional problem settings beyond the main non-smooth convex case (Theorem 5, Theorem 6).

XrrGXLksji.text: BEAT encodes each beat as a single token via base-3 encoding of a 3-state piano-roll (silence, onset, sustain) per pitch, in contrast to event-based serialization methods like REMI (Section 3.1).
On piano continuation, BEAT achieves JSGC=.039 and FMD=436.7, compared to REMI's JSGC=.552 and FMD=550.9, and AMT-Large's JSGC=.625 and FMD=445.2 (Table 2).
On multi-track continuation, BEAT achieves JSGC=.043 and FMD=420.9, compared to REMI+'s JSGC=.313 and FMD=463.2 (Table 2).

BEAT produces shorter average sequence lengths (1825.6 tokens) than REMI (1902.6) and Interleaved ABC (3450.4), with a lower BPE compression rate of 64.83% versus REMI's 80.18% at 20 merges, indicating greater token reusability (Section 5.1).
BEAT attains 91.92% sequence accuracy on a stepwise-transposition pattern-learning task versus 28.28% for REMI, evidencing stronger capture of long-range structural patterns (Table 4, Section 5.2).

In a subjective evaluation with 32 participants rating coherence, plausibility, and musicality on a 5-point Likert scale, BEAT significantly outperforms all baselines (p<0.05, Holm-Bonferroni corrected) in both piano and multi-track settings (Figure 2).

sYUCXUeApn.text: Formal languages derived from probabilistic finite automata are used as a controlled testbed to study how much task-specific data is needed to learn a given task, avoiding confounds present in natural language studies (abstract only).
The paper introduces the binning semiring, an algebraic object that controls how often a targeted property occurs in a sampled corpus (abstract only).
Experiments are formulated as causal graphical models and use decomposed Kullback-Leibler divergence metrics to measure the learnability of specific sub-tasks (abstract only).
Evaluating learnability without causal intervention leads to incorrect conclusions due to confounders present in purely correlational analysis of task occurrence versus learnability (abstract only).

gl6N1mfe5t.text: DISCoVeR models a condition-invariant latent z and a condition-specific latent w via a max-min objective combining two ELBO terms with an adversarial classifier term that penalizes predictability of the condition label y from the z-only reconstruction (Section 2.3).
The adversarial classifier is applied to the reconstructed image derived from z alone rather than directly to z, which reduces the sampling variance of the adversarial gradient estimate (Section 3).

Proposition 2.1 shows the cost of enforcing a condition-invariant latent equals KL(q_z|x || p_z|w,x,y), while Proposition 2.2 establishes a unique saddle-point equilibrium under a class-conditional Gaussian prior p(w|y) (Proposition 2.1, Proposition 2.2).
On Colored MNIST with label noise ρ=0.3, DISCoVeR achieves a marginal reconstruction RMSE of 0.087 ± 0.002 (Section 5.2.1, Supplementary Table 2).

On CelebA-Glasses (35,712 face images), DISCoVeR achieves mutual information I(z;w) = 0.030 ± 0.011 between shared and condition-specific representations, indicating strong disentanglement (Section 5.2.2, Supplementary Table 3).

On the scRNA-seq Lupus dataset (13,999 PBMCs under control and IFN-β stimulation), DISCoVeR achieves a z-Stimulation NMI of 0.002 ± 0, showing stimulation status is not encoded in the shared representation (Section 5.2.3, Supplementary Table 5).

2WfRsrQxpC.text: MathlibLemma's four-stage multi-agent pipeline (Discovery, Judge, Formalizer, Prover agents) produces a verified library of 1,812 theorems with generated Lean proofs, three of which have been merged into the Mathlib master branch (Section on Real-World Impact; Table 1).
The MathlibLemma benchmark contains 4,028 type-checked Lean 4 statements spanning three domains—Foundational, Applied, and Abstract mathematics—seeded from 109 Mathlib source files (Table 1).

In the pipeline funnel, the Foundational domain yields the highest compilability rate (77.1% of correct candidates compile) while Abstract yields the lowest (61.3%), out of candidates first judged semantically correct (Table 1).

On the Success@2 benchmark evaluation, the best individual model (GPT-Reasoning) reaches 22.32% while the union of all evaluated models reaches 44.99%, indicating more than double the coverage from model diversity (Table 3).

Goedel dominates GPT-Reasoning on the Foundational domain (29.63% vs 23.00%) but collapses on the Abstract domain (12.96% vs GPT-Reasoning's 23.98%), showing domain-dependent model specialization (Table 3).
Human expert audits of sampled unproven instances succeed in proving 78% of them overall, with the Abstract domain showing the highest human success rate at 84% (Table 2).

AhRuQzYHzY.text: An L-layer Disentangled Transformer, as defined via attention blocks that append outputs as new coordinate slices (Definition 4.1), provably computes graph connectivity exactly for node pairs with shortest-path distance up to 3^L (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 4.4).
Permutation-equivariant layer weights decompose into an algorithmic I_n-channel implementing matrix powering and a heuristic J_n-channel computing degree-based shortcuts (Theorem 4.6).

Empirically, both 2-layer and 3-layer Transformers achieve at least 99% accuracy only on node pairs whose distance satisfies the 3^L capacity bound, confirming the theoretical capacity limit (Figure 2).

Restricting training data to within-capacity graphs (distance ≤ 3^L) drives the algorithmic channel's energy share to nearly 100% while suppressing the heuristic channel, versus mixed training that induces heuristic shortcuts (Figure 4).
Models retain algorithmic robustness as long as beyond-capacity node pairs make up less than 10% of the training data (Figure 6).

The within-capacity data-restriction strategy ('data lever') transfers from Disentangled Transformers to standard Transformers, improving out-of-distribution generalization to longer chains (Figure 7).

IgzMfT6eUx.text: LIFT (specifically the LIFT₃ variant) achieves 16.7% pass@16 on AIME'24, a 406% relative gain over the LLaDA baseline's 3.3%, and 6.7% pass@16 on AIME'25, a 103% relative gain (Table 1).
LIFT₃ outperforms vanilla SFT and the CART and GIFT baselines on GSM8K (79.4%), MATH (38.4%, +6.3 points), Countdown (26.4%, +34.6 points), and Sudoku (17.4%, +55.3 points) (Table 1, Section 6.1).

LIFT matches the reasoning performance of the RL-based d1 method while requiring only about 1.8 H100 GPU-hours versus d1's 2,300+ GPU-hours, a roughly 500x compute reduction; the LIFT-A variant achieves comparable results in about 1.0 GPU-hour (Table 3, Section 6.2).

Ablations show that selecting only easy (top-K) tokens or only hard (bottom-K) tokens, or using random time-independent selection, underperforms LIFT's interaction-aware what/when selection—random selection scores 0% on both AIME'24 and AIME'25, versus LIFT₃'s 16.7%/6.7% (Table 5).
A hyperparameter sweep over the number of learnability stages H finds H=3 optimal at 16.7% on AIME'24, with H=2 giving 10.0% and H≥4 degrading performance toward the vanilla baseline (Table 6).

ppirVueEj6.text: Primitive vectors—directions in the residual stream that reliably induce a specific reasoning primitive when injected—compose algebraically, satisfying approximate additivity v_ℓ(p⊕q) ≈ w_p·v_ℓ(p) ± w_q·v_ℓ(q) and scalar scaling v_ℓ(αp) = α·v_ℓ(p) (Section 4.1, Figure 2, Table 1).

Phi-4-Reasoning produces highly stereotyped responses using verification and path-generation primitives more consistently than the base Phi-4 model across TSP, 3-SAT, and GraphNav tasks, with task-dependent variation on AIME (Section 5, Figure 4).

Injecting a nearest-neighbor primitive vector increases nearest-neighbor path usage by 56.1%, injecting a generate-path primitive increases total generated paths by 143.9%, and injecting a compute-distance primitive reduces distance-computation latency by 86.5% (Figure 2).

Primitive vectors extracted from AIME reasoning transfer across tasks: injecting them into Phi-4-Base successfully alters its TSP-solving behavior, reproducing hallmarks otherwise seen only in Phi-4-Reasoning (Figure 5).

i5QhkUCzJh.text: MoLe predicts coupled cluster T1 and T2 excitation amplitudes directly from Hartree-Fock molecular orbitals using an equivariant architecture combining message passing and attention with dedicated readout layers (architecture description).

On QM7, MoLe achieves an energy MAE of 0.12 mHa on the full dataset and 0.66 mHa in an ultra-low-data regime of only 100 training molecules, outperforming competing machine-learned interatomic potentials which reach 1.48-1.64 mHa under the same data budget (data-efficiency results).

Despite training only on small equilibrium geometries, MoLe generalizes out-of-distribution to larger molecules, reaching 0.78 mHa error on amino acids and 1.63 mHa on a diverse PubChem set of larger molecules (size-extrapolation results).

MoLe generalizes to off-equilibrium geometries unseen during training, achieving 1.16 mHa error on a Diels-Alder reaction path, 0.22 mHa on a butane dihedral scan, and 0.08 mHa on a cyclohexane chair-to-boat transition (off-equilibrium generalization results).
Used as an initial guess for CCSD solvers on out-of-distribution molecules, MoLe reduces the number of solver iterations required for convergence by 40-50% (convergence-speedup results).
MoLe's predicted electron density matrices have a substantially lower Frobenius-norm error (0.13-0.36) than MP2-derived densities (0.59-0.90) across tested systems (density-matrix accuracy results).

E0wwKfaTE0.text: The main algorithm (Theorem 1.1) returns a c-approximate furthest neighbor in query time Õ(d n^{1/c^2}) with high probability, even under adaptively chosen queries (Theorem 1.1).
An alternative variant achieves query time Õ(min{n^{2/c^2}, n} + d) for a (1+ε)c-approximation (Theorem 1.1).

This adaptive query time matches the n-dependence of Indyk's 2003 oblivious-setting algorithm while strictly improving on the Õ(n+d) query time of the prior adaptive method of Cherapanamjeri and Nelson (2020) (Section 1).
The construction builds k = Θ̃(d log(dn/(c-1))) independent copies of a base data structure to obtain adversarial robustness via a union bound over the query space (Section 2.2).
The base data structure uses N = Θ(n^{(1+O(δ))/c^2} sqrt(log n)) random projections and guarantees correctness on a fixed query with probability 3/4 (Lemma 2.3).

An explicit adaptive attack is exhibited against Indyk's oblivious algorithm in which the returned point is at distance d^{0.01} while the true furthest neighbor is at distance d^{0.5}, demonstrating the non-robustness of the oblivious construction (Section 3).

WxmL5UjtNm.text: For β-Hölder target functions on a d-dimensional manifold, the approximation error of an MoE Transformer scales as min{N_act^{-2β/d}, M^{-2β/d}}, where N_act is active parameter count and M is the number of experts (Theorem 3.2).

The generalization excess risk decomposes into an approximation term N_act^{-2β/d}, an estimation term N_act/n, and a routing term L_T ℓ k log(eM/k)/n, showing the routing/expert-count contribution enters only logarithmically rather than polynomially (Theorem 3.4).

At fixed sparsity (fixed k active experts), enlarging the total expert pool M affects the generalization bound only through the logarithmic factor log(eM/k), not through the leading polynomial rate (Theorem 3.4, Corollary 3.5).
The compute-optimal active parameter count scales as N_act* ∝ C^{d/(2β+2d)} and the corresponding optimal error scales as C^{-β/(β+d)} (Proposition 4.5).

Empirically estimated intrinsic dimensions of TinyStories (d≈23), WikiText-103 (d≈32), and OpenWebText (d≈45) yield measured data- and model-scaling exponents that align with the theoretical exponent 2β/(2β+d) (Section 4).

LF5rPrxbHp.text: Four mechanistically distinct synthetic causal functions (linear, threshold, saturating, and sign-changing) produce nearly identical scalar causal scores in the narrow range 0.63-0.65, despite representing qualitatively different underlying mechanisms (Table 1, Section 5.1).

The scalar causal score decomposes as S_ij^2 = E[Var(contrib_ij,t | X_{t-1}^{(i)})] + Var(g_ij(X_{t-1}^{(i)})), conflating within-state residual variation with genuine between-state functional variation (Section 3).

Recovered Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) response curves, estimated via the lag-aggregated procedure, reveal monotonic, thresholded, saturating, and sign-changing response shapes that are indistinguishable under the aggregated scalar score (Figure 2, Section 4.2).

In an application to 139 countries over 35 years using 16 V-Dem democracy indicators, edges with similar scalar scores (~0.1-0.2) show regime-dependent, asymmetric causal effects on the 'clean elections' indicator that are only visible via function-valued analysis (Figure 3, Section 5.2).

The proposed function-valued framework is explicitly restricted to additive, contribution-decomposable autoregressive models, with the authors noting non-additive architectures would require richer decompositions such as Shapley interactions (Discussion).

p1GwEz0pix.text: Existing PFN-based causal estimators (evaluated across TabPFN, Do-PFN, CausalPFN, and CausalFM) exhibit a prior-induced confounding bias because their implicit priors concentrate on nearly unconfounded data-generating processes, which prevents frequentist consistency of the resulting ATE estimates (Table 1, Figure 2).

The one-step posterior correction (OSPC) procedure uses the efficient influence function to calibrate PFN-based ATE posteriors without retraining the underlying network, restoring frequentist consistency (Section 4).

Under L2 convergence conditions on nuisance estimates, the MP-OSPC posterior satisfies a semi-parametric Bernstein-von Mises theorem, becoming asymptotically equivalent to the classical augmented inverse-propensity-weighted (A-IPTW) estimator (Theorem 1).

MP-OSPC combines martingale posteriors with copulas to produce smooth functional posteriors over nuisance functions, which is a prerequisite for the OSPC calibration to apply in practice (Section 4, Figure 3).
On the ACIC 2016 benchmark, the calibrated MP-OSPC estimator is empirically compared against uncalibrated PFN baselines for coverage and bias (Table 2).
L2-convergence of nuisance estimates as a function of dataset size is validated empirically, supporting the conditions required for the Bernstein-von Mises result (Figure 4).

TgohCXoblV.text: Using a smaller learning rate for body (feature-extractor) layers and a larger learning rate for the final layer is shown to be equivalent to two-time-scale alternating gradient descent on a Stackelberg (bilevel) reformulation of the training objective, where the final layer is the leader (Section 2).
Under weak convexity of the Stackelberg objective, non-uniform-rate SGD converges to a stationary point at rate Õ(k^{-2/5}) (Theorem 3.6).
When the Stackelberg objective Φ(M) = f(M, w*(M)) is strongly convex, the convergence rate improves to Õ(k^{-2/3}), even though the original joint objective f(M,w) may be non-convex (Theorem 3.7).

Figure 1 shows the Stackelberg-reduced objective exhibits sharper curvature than the joint objective early in training, which the authors identify as a mechanism accelerating convergence beyond what uniform learning rates achieve (Section 4, Figure 1).

Across regression (Friedman, Boston Housing), classification (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10), and reinforcement learning (TD learning and Deep Q-learning on Atari games including Breakout, Pong, Space Invaders, and Q*bert) experiments, using a body learning rate 3-10x smaller than the final-layer rate under RMSProp consistently outperforms uniform learning rates (Figures 3-5, Section 5).

bahHw9DQY0.text: Against LLMs on the AdvBench dataset, the proposed wide-net-casting attack achieves 100% weighted attack success rate (WASR), compared to 75.0% for a GCG-based aggregation baseline and 92.3% for a ReMiss-based aggregation baseline (Section 3.1, Table 1).
Against MLLMs on MM-SafetyBench, the proposed attack achieves 100% WASR versus 89.1% for the MLAI baseline (Section 3.1, Table 2).
The wide-net-casting attacks are evaluated against Gemma-2-9b, Vicuna-7b-v1.5, Llama-3.1-8b, and Mistral-7b as target LLMs (Section 3.1).
The wide-net-casting attacks are also evaluated against MLLMs MiniGPT-4-13b, LLaVA-1.5-13b, InstructBLIP, and Qwen2-VL-7B (Section 3.1).
Same-family model vulnerabilities and defense robustness of the attack are analyzed separately from the main success-rate results (Section 3.2, Tables 3-4; Section 3.3).

FoDU47u2jk.text: Dropout introduces a nonzero dropout field h that destroys the perfect-alignment fixed point c*=1 of the correlation map, so that even perfectly aligned inputs decorrelate after one layer, yielding a finite depth scale for information propagation even at critical initialization (Section 3, equations 14-16).

Smooth activations (e.g., tanh, GELU) and kinked activations (e.g., ReLU-like) form two distinct universality classes with different critical exponents: smooth activations have (ν_t, β, δ, ν_ρ) = (1, 1, 2, 1/2) while kinked activations have (1, 2, 3/2, 1/3) (Section 3.1-3.2, Table 2).

For smooth activations, rescaled order parameter and detuning variables collapse onto a universal function m̃ = sqrt(1+t̃^2) - t̃, confirming the predicted scaling form (Section 3.2, equations 30-31, Figure 2).

A front-loaded (early, step-like) dropout schedule that concentrates dropout in the earliest layers under a fixed dropout budget reduces MLP test loss by 18-35% and improves accuracy by up to about 2 percentage points compared to constant dropout (Section 3.3, Table 3, Figures 6-9).

On a Vision Transformer trained on CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10, front-loaded/step or linear-decreasing dropout schedules yield smaller but consistent gains of about 4-6% loss reduction and up to 0.66 percentage points accuracy improvement over constant dropout at a fixed budget (Section 3.3, Figures 10 and 12).

IEDC7yFpLe.text: The automated MURGAT-Score evaluation framework achieves a Pearson correlation of r=0.84 with human judgments averaged over all pipeline steps, substantially outperforming the next-best LLM-as-judge baseline at r=0.59 (Abstract, Section 4.5, Table 4).

On the human-annotated benchmark spanning WorldSense and Video-MMMU, the best model (Gemini-2.5-Flash) reaches a MURGAT-Score of only 59.9 on WorldSense and 21.8 on Video-MMMU, showing even strong MLLMs struggle to ground multimodal citations (Section 4.1, Table 1).

In automated generation experiments, the peak MURGAT-Score achieved is 69.2 on WorldSense and 56.9 on Video-MMMU (Gemini-3-Flash), with even the best models failing to ground roughly 30-35% of their claims (Section 5.2, Table 5).
Vision-language-only models such as Qwen3-VL-Instruct hallucinate audio citations for up to 31.6% of their references despite lacking an audio encoder (Section 5.2, Table 17).

For atomic fact decomposition, the sentence-level pipeline with Gemini-3-Pro achieves the highest F1 of 81.8 and citation propagation accuracy of 86.4%, outperforming response-level generation (Section 4.3, Table 3).

76iNFmvmBa.text: ITCR integrates conformal prediction directly into reasoning-graph generation via a non-conformity score S(U) = 1 - sigma(FU_theta) + lambda|V_U| that is monotone under subgraph expansion, enabling valid stopping decisions during generation rather than post-hoc filtering (Section 3, Equation 4, Definition 3.1).
ITCR provides two distribution-free coverage guarantees: no-false coverage P(V_Û ⊆ T) ≥ 1-α and no-miss coverage P(T ⊆ V_Û) ≥ 1-α (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.7).

On MATH, GSM8K, and a factuality-annotated QA benchmark at α=0.05, ITCR achieves empirical no-miss coverage of 0.947, 0.945, and 0.957, and no-false coverage of 0.943, 0.953, and 0.948 respectively (Section 4.2, Table 1).
ITCR is compared against baselines CPL, ITCR-MAX, ITCR-SUM, ITCR-AVG, and PostCal, and uses fewer tokens and lower runtime than PostCal (Section 4.2-4.3, Table 4).

On GSM8K with a LLaMA-3.1-8B backbone, ITCR improves the positive correction ratio from 12.35% to 43.21%, with an average correction gain of about 18.77% across LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3-4B-Thinking, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill backbones (Section 4.3, Table 3).

YxsIwwCfjf.text: CLARITI, an 8B-parameter clarification module trained with a four-stage reinforcement-learning reward pipeline, achieves 36.8% task success with an average of 3.0 clarifying questions, matching GPT-5's 35.6% success rate obtained with an average of 5.1 questions—a 41% reduction in questions (Section 6.4, Table 3, Figure 1).
A no-clarification baseline achieves only 22.4% task success, versus 36.8% for CLARITI, showing clarification recovers most of the gap versus a fully-specified upper bound (Section 6.4, Table 3).

Shapley (SHAP) attribution analysis over 700 underspecified instances finds Error Information has the highest mean SHAP value (0.183) for predicting task success, followed by Implementation Details (0.0982), a hierarchy that differs from how frequently these categories are naturally missing (Section 4, RQ1).

Distributional analysis identifies four strategic themes distinguishing answerable from unanswerable clarifying questions: Ground in Evidence, Demand Specificity, Minimize Scope, and Ensure Actionability (Section 5, Table 2).

The four-stage reward pipeline (non-redundancy, diversity, answerability, task relevance) combines as r_final = 0.25 times the sum of the four component rewards, and ablation removing the answerability or relevance stages substantially degrades performance (Section 6.2, 6.6, Table 6).

ti6RAEh2ep.text: TsLLM is trained on roughly 25 billion tokens drawn from about 2 million interleaved time series and text examples spanning diverse analysis tasks (Section 3.4).

TsLLM's architecture combines a patch-based time series encoder-decoder trained with a beta-VAE objective, a pretrained decoder-only LLM backbone, and MLP adapter layers for modality fusion, using a patch size of p=32 selected via ablation (Section 3, Section 3.1).
With few-shot prompting, TsLLM reaches 85.3% accuracy on ECG-QA Single-Verify, 60.8% on Single-Choose, and 49.0% on Single-Query, for a 65.0% average (Table 1).
On TimeSeriesExam, TsLLM scores 87.3% on the Easy split versus 33.3% for Gemini Flash, and 85.5% on the Hard split versus 42.1% for o1-mini (Table 2).
TsLLM attains 81.2% mean accuracy on the UCR-TSC classification benchmark under few-shot prompting (Table 3).

Ablations show that scaling the LLM backbone (e.g., to SmolLM2-1.7B) improves performance by about 2.1 percentage points over the baseline, while simple MLP adapters perform comparably to more complex alternatives (Table 5, Section 4.2).
