2RIk96qJcc.text: The paper proves the optimal convergence rate for universal (U-)alignment under test-time scaling with k samples is f(k)=k/(k+1), and shows this rate cannot be improved upon by any method (Propositions 2-3, Section 3.2).
Theorem 3 shows there exists a family of single-output policies whose test-time-scaled versions achieve U-alignment at the optimal rate k/(k+1) (Theorem 3, Section 4.2).

Theorem 2 shows that symmetric Nash equilibrium policies of the (k+1)-player alignment game achieve (k, k/(k+1))-robust alignment, guaranteeing a win rate of at least 1-1/(k+1) against any competing policy (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
Proposition 5 shows that fixed points of gradient ascent dynamics in the alignment game correspond to symmetric Nash equilibria (Proposition 5, Section 4.3).

Proposition 6 shows that no-regret learning dynamics yield (k, k/(k+1) - Reg_T/T)-robust alignment, giving a finite-time learning guarantee that approaches the optimal rate as regret vanishes (Proposition 6, Section 4.3).

1ufVo73uzD.text: On the Ant locomotion environment in Brax, D2C-discovered morphology-reward pairs reach a score of 6,421.67 versus 3,715.42 for the default Ant, a roughly 73% improvement in distance traveled (Table I).

D2C uses an iterative thesis-antithesis-synthesis debate loop in which a design agent proposes morphological edits (thesis), a control agent generates tailored reward functions (antithesis), and the design agent revises based on feedback (synthesis) (Section on methodology).
Synthesis-phase designs consistently outperform thesis-phase designs across debate rounds, demonstrating that the iterative critique-and-revise cycle improves on single-pass generation (Table I).
The best design-reward pair found by D2C, compared against the baseline Ant morphology and reward, is documented with both morphology visualizations and reward function components (Table I).

4oU82peL8f.text: REL defines Relational Complexity (RC) as the minimal number of independent sources of variation that must be jointly bound to perform a reasoning step, and instantiates it across three domains: REL-A (algebra, RC 1-6), REL-B (biology/homoplasy detection, RC 2-25), and REL-C (chemistry, three tasks with RC from 2 upward).
On REL-A, accuracy drops by 45% as RC increases from 3 to 9, with performance collapsing on tasks where RC scales with input size.
On REL-B1 (homoplastic taxa detection), accuracy decreases by 93% as RC increases from 5 to 20.
On REL-C, task completion rate decreases by 39.7% from complexity level C1 to C3 as relational complexity increases.

Giving models 4,096 to 16,384 tokens of test-time compute improves accuracy by only 2-3% on algebraic tasks and 0.4% on chemistry tasks, leaving the RC-driven performance gap largely intact (Section 5.4, Table A.8).

One-shot in-context learning improves performance at low RC but preserves the same hierarchical degradation, with accuracy at 77.0% (C1), 43.3% (C2), and 32.7% (C3), an average gain of only 3-6% (Section 5.4, Figure A.4).

8bUDbWMo5v.text: The method computes a safe in-context-learning (ICL) loss that compares early-exit predictions against a zero-shot baseline, l_ICL(lambda;x,y,c) := l(y-hat_lambda(x,c), y) - l(y-hat(x), y), and applies distribution-free risk control to bound this quantity below a user-specified threshold epsilon (Section 3.1, Section 3.3, Equation 2).

The predictor exits early when a layer's confidence exceeds a calibrated threshold lambda, and falls back to the zero-shot prediction if no layer reaches that threshold, guaranteeing risk control relative to the safe zero-shot baseline (Section 3.1).

The approach is empirically validated on 8 classification tasks spanning sentiment analysis (SST-2, FinancialPhrasebank, TweetEval-Feminist), hate/religion speech detection (TweetEval-Hate, TweetEval-Atheism), and semantic classification (AG News, TREC, Unnatural) (Section 4, Appendix B).
Figure 5 shows the empirical risk stays below the user-defined threshold epsilon across all evaluated models and tasks (Figure 5, Section 4.1).

At epsilon=0.05, the method evaluates 53% fewer transformer layers than a loss-clipping baseline while achieving over 50% speedup, showing it controls risk under harmful context while cutting compute on helpful context (Section 4.1).

K5gV8Yptne.text: Meta Flow Maps (MFMs) extend consistency models/flow maps into a stochastic regime, generating one-step samples from conditional posteriors p_{1|t}(·|x_t) via a differentiable reparametrization for reward alignment (Section 3).

Two Monte Carlo estimators for the value-function gradient are proposed: MFM-GF, a gradient-free estimator using reward evaluations (Eq. 20), and MFM-G, a gradient-based estimator via the reparameterization trick (Eq. 22) (Section 3).

Proposition 5.1 shows the SDE sampler with K Euler steps and N Monte Carlo samples achieves convergence rates of O(1/√K + 1/N) in Wasserstein-2 distance and O(1/K + 1/N) in KL divergence (Section 5.1, Proposition 5.1).
On ImageNet 256×256, MFM-XL/2 achieves an FID of 1.97 in 4 sampling steps for unconditional generation (Section 7.2, Table 2).

MFM-G exceeds a Best-of-1000 baseline on ImageReward, HPSv2, and PickScore reward models, and MFM-GF with N=1 requires roughly 100x fewer function evaluations than Best-of-1000 while maintaining superior reward performance (Section 7.2, Figures 7-8).

The unbiased MFM-FT fine-tuning objective (Eq. 43) enables off-policy training that recovers the optimal steering drift as its unique fixed point, eliminating bias present in self-normalized estimators (Section 5.2).

aDPbUSUCwh.text: The Dirac-Frenkel-Onsager (DFO) principle injects momentum only along nullspace (gauge) directions of the Gram matrix G(θ(t)), preserving instantaneous Dirac-Frenkel residual minimization while yielding smooth, unique parameter trajectories (Section 3.1, Section 4.1-4.2).

Proposition A.1 proves that for the wave-collision problem with exact tangent-space collapse (ρ=0), choosing the momentum gain λ = (1-exp(-2/τ))^{-1} allows DFO to recover the exact PDE solution through collision, whereas standard minimal-norm Dirac-Frenkel dynamics fails (Proposition A.1).

On three low-dimensional benchmarks, DFO reduces error over standard Dirac-Frenkel dynamics: rotating detonation waves (2.10e-03 vs 6.06e-03), transport through a flow field (1.23e-02 vs 3.82e-02), and charged particles in an electric field (3.95e-03 vs 1.22e-02) (Section 5.2, Table 1).

On a 5-dimensional Fokker-Planck problem, DFO achieves mean error 4.47e-03 and covariance error 5.26e-02, versus 1.46e-02 and 3.17e-01 respectively for standard DF, and a randomized variant (RDFO) cuts runtime by 2x while preserving accuracy (Section 5.3).

Algorithm 1 implements a semi-implicit update using a truncated SVD of the batch Jacobian, an exponentially-weighted moving-average momentum with decay β = τ/(τ+δt), and projection of momentum onto the parametrization nullspace before the parameter update (Algorithm 1).

2hGL0nGPLu.text: The paper formalizes multi-attempt chain-of-thought reasoning as a Verification@K (Ver@K) objective and derives three RLOO-style estimators: trajectory-level (TL-GRPO), naive attempt-level (NAL-GRPO), and calibrated attempt-level (CAL-GRPO) (Section 3, Section 5).

Theorem 3.1 proves that both trajectory-level and attempt-level RLOO estimators are unbiased for the Ver@K objective, and that the attempt-level estimator has strictly lower variance than the trajectory-level one except when K=1 (Theorem 3.1).

Corollary 5.3 shows NAL-GRPO implicitly optimizes a discounted objective with exponentially decaying weights on later attempts, explaining its empirically observed bias toward first-attempt correctness over correction behavior (Corollary 5.3).

Theorem 5.2 establishes that the calibrated (CAL-GRPO) estimator remains unbiased under an independent attempt-index assumption where the conditional policy depends only on the input and the count of prior attempts (Theorem 5.2).

On MATH (Ver@2, Ver@4) and Maze Navigation (5x5-9x9) benchmarks with a Qwen3-4B-Instruct model, CAL-GRPO achieves the highest final Ver@K accuracy among the three methods, with mean response lengths decreasing rather than increasing during training across all settings (Section 6).

Ablations show that larger rollout group size (N=16 vs N=10) improves CAL-GRPO's calibration quality, and that per-attempt standard-deviation reward normalization improves all three methods, being especially important given heterogeneous reward variance across attempts (Section 6, ablations).

j5ibZwkwqF.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that when malicious and benign message embeddings are well-separated during defense classifier training, the classifier learns overly broad acceptance regions such that any attack embedding within distance γ/L of the benign support (γ the margin, L the Lipschitz constant) is guaranteed to evade detection (Theorem 4.1).

Three adaptive near-benign attacks are introduced: Slow Drift (gradual embedding shift across communication rounds), Benign Wrapper (concatenating benign content with a short malicious payload), and Chaos Seeding (widening benign embedding spread to hide malicious outliers) (Section 4).

Across MMLU, GSM8K, and BBH with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3-4B, and GPT-4o-mini, existing embedding-based defenses (G-Safeguard, GUARDIAN) drop to 32.6-66.7% accuracy under near-benign attacks, while the proposed confidence-guided defense recovers 52.7-90.5% accuracy with comparable clean performance (Table 1).

Near-benign attacks reduce the benign-to-malicious embedding distance from 0.236 under an obvious attack down to 0.156-0.205, quantifying how the attacks evade separation-based detection while remaining effective (Table 2).

Confidence signals are computed from token-level entropy (aggregated as the mean of the top-k highest per-token entropies) and used either to prune low-confidence messages before propagation or to down-weight them as metadata, with an ablation over pruning threshold δ and down-weighting strength α showing down-weighting yields smoother robustness-utility tradeoff curves (Section on confidence-guided defense; Table 5).

Table 6 shows the confidence signal's effectiveness degrades over successive communication rounds, and that sparse communication topologies preserve the defensive signal longer than dense topologies, which accelerate contamination spread (Table 6).

s8i2EYzmxt.text: FMPlug combines a time-dependent, instance-guided warm-start (learning a continuous t in [0,1] and injecting the measurement y at that point in the flow, per Theorem 3.1's concentration-of-measure motivation) with a sharp Gaussianity shell-constraint regularization (Equation 3.9, with typical ε=0.025) to strengthen foundation flow-matching priors for inverse problems (Section 3.1-3.2).

On Gaussian deblurring of AFHQ-Cat, Table 1 documents that foundation flow-matching priors substantially underperform both domain-specific FM and Deep Image Prior, motivating the FMPlug method (Section 2.3, Table 1).

On 512x512 AFHQ images, FMPlug outperforms the D-Flow baseline on PSNR across four tasks: 4x super-resolution (30.31 vs 26.37), 70% random inpainting (32.81 vs 28.43), Gaussian deblurring (30.41 vs 25.90), and motion deblurring (30.43 vs 27.81) (Table 3).

On 256x256 Gaussian blur, FMPlug using the foundation model (FD) reaches PSNR 29.00, closely approaching the domain-specific D-Flow variant (DS: 28.41) and far exceeding the foundation D-Flow variant (FD: 24.42), narrowing the foundation-vs-domain-specific performance gap (Table 4).
On few-shot scientific inverse problems, FMPlug achieves PSNR 31.83 on linear inverse scattering (vs D-Flow 17.15, DIP 28.72) and PSNR 23.26 on compressed-sensing MRI (vs D-Flow 8.94) (Table 5).

An ablation on DIV2K Gaussian deblurring shows FMPlug-Plain (no components) reaches PSNR 25.16, adding warm-start alone (FMPlug-W) reaches 26.05, and the full method with both warm-start and Gaussianity regularization reaches 26.26, indicating warm-start drives most of the improvement (Table 6).

TOAT4Va5VH.text: Node Feature Permutation Testing (NPT) computes a feature importance score δ_m as the drop in accuracy when feature m's values are permuted across nodes, Acc(y, f(X;A,Θ)) − Acc(y, f(X̃^(m);A,Θ)) (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 2 proves that permuting a feature's values decouples it from the labels and graph structure, theoretically justifying permutation importance as a valid feature-selection signal (Section 3, Theorem 2).

Algorithm 1 adaptively prunes features below the r-th percentile of importance scores at intervals of T epochs after a Tburn burn-in period, continuing training on the reduced feature set (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).
On Cora, NPT reaches 79.19% accuracy after feature selection versus 39.96%-72.73% for competing selection methods (Section 4.1, Table 2).
On PubMed, NPT retains 87.06% accuracy at 6.25% feature retention and 84.88% at 1.56% retention, outperforming TFI and MI baselines under progressive feature elimination (Section 4.2, Table 3).

Feature importance rankings (δ_m heatmaps) remain largely consistent across training checkpoints on Cora and PubMed, showing meaningful importance scores emerge before the GNN is fully trained (Section 4.3, Figure 3).

HDBpda5Vih.text: Theorem 4.4 gives a closed-form reduction of the privacy loss distribution (PLD) of k-out-of-t random allocation to t-wise convolutions of exponentiated PLD terms (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).

The proposed algorithm computes an (α,β)-accurate approximation of the random allocation PLD in time O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²), using exponentiation-by-squaring with geometric-grid rounding (Section 4, Theorem 4.6).

Theorem 3.3 introduces transformation rules φ_λ that apply Poisson subsampling directly to PLD realizations, allowing subsampling and random allocation to be composed within one unified PLD framework (Section 3, Theorem 3.3, Definition 3.1).

Numerical experiments show the new random allocation privacy bounds are nearly identical to the Monte Carlo lower bounds of Chua et al. (2024a) and substantially tighter than RDP-based analytic bounds, for t ∈ {1000, 10000} and δ = 10⁻⁶ (Section 5, Figures 1-2).

A toy Bernoulli mean-estimation experiment (n=10³, δ=10⁻¹⁰) shows random allocation requires strictly lower noise than Poisson subsampling for the same privacy level, demonstrating a genuine privacy (not just variance) advantage (Section 5, Figure 4).

Applied to a DP-SGD scenario with block-sparse coordinate sampling (n=6×10⁵, d=2²⁰, C=2¹⁵, E=10 epochs), the PLD accounting method improves privacy bounds over RDP composition even under heavy composition (Section 5, Figure 5).

9HpQXq9e9W.text: Theorem 1 (Quantified Martingale Violation) proves that under local rank stability and harmonic positional decay (α=1), the expected permutation-induced deviation is bounded by 𝔼_π|R_π(x)| ≤ (C/4)(log n − 3/2 + o(1)), i.e., O(log n) growth (Theorem 1).

Theorem 5 (Expectation-level Decompression Law, EDFL) shows that achieving reliability p = 1−ε on a rare event with prior mass q̄ ≪ 1 requires an expected information budget Δ̄ ≥ (1−ε)log(1/q̄) + O(q̄) nats (Theorem 5).

On a permutation-dispersion analysis of 3,059 binary evidence-grounded QA items drawn from FEVER, HotpotQA, NQ-Open, and PopQA, Qwen2-7B shows dispersion slope b≈0.377 (R²=0.742) while Llama-3.1-8B shows b≈0.147 (R²=0.515) (Section 4.1, Appendix H).

An ISR<1 abstention gate evaluated on 528 held-out Gemma-2-9B items achieves a 0.0-0.7% hallucination rate with 20.6-27.9% abstention and 80.5% [76.8, 83.8] accuracy on answered items, at 95% confidence intervals (Section 4.3).

A randomized dose-response experiment with fixed 4-chunk evidence lengths finds an OLS slope of 0.127 fewer hallucinations per additional nat of information budget for Qwen2-7B, with instrumental-variable validation on Llama giving β≈0.110 (Section 4.2).

UlFOINq6SY.text: Theorem 1 establishes the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantee for variance-reduced zeroth-order Langevin sampling, bounding Fisher information FI(ν̄_{Nγ}||π) ≤ ε after O(d⁷L_m⁴/ε⁴) iterations using only O(1) function evaluations per iteration (Theorem 1).

The variance-reduced zeroth-order gradient estimator (Equation 8) combines a large-batch estimate (probability p, batch size b) with a small-batch recursive update (probability 1−p, batch size b′) that exploits correlation between consecutive iterates (Equation 8).
Theorem 3 extends the Fisher-information convergence bound to posterior sampling with a black-box score-based generative model (SGM) prior via the ZO-APMC algorithm (Equation 12-13, Theorem 3).

On 4x-accelerated radial-subsampled FastMRI brain reconstruction, ZO-APMC achieves 35.29 dB PSNR, the best among black-box methods (SCG, DPG, EnKG, Forward/Central-GSG) though slightly below the gradient-based APMC baseline at 36.55 dB (Section, Table 1).
On black-hole imaging with 100 GRMHD images from InverseBench, ZO-APMC attains 26.71 dB PSNR and χ²_cph of 5.42, the best result among evaluated black-box methods (Table 2).
Figure 2(b) validates the O(1) per-iteration batch complexity by showing multiple (p,b) parameter settings with fixed product pb=10 all converge to Fisher information below 0.01 (Figure 2).

RKHDV40omz.text: SoftJAX and SoftTorch provide differentiable soft surrogates for hard primitives including thresholding (sign, abs, round, ReLU, clip via Heaviside relaxations), Boolean/fuzzy logic operators, discrete indexing (SoftIndex), and sorting/ranking (Sections 3 and 4).

The libraries identify an 'STE pitfall' where applying straight-through estimation separately to each factor of a multiplicative composite operation causes gradients to vanish, and show this is avoided by applying STE to the composite function as a whole (Section 2, Equation 1).

Four families of differentiable sort/rank operators are implemented: optimal-transport-based, unit-simplex-projection-based (SoftSort, NeuralSort), permutahedron-projection-based (FastSoftSort, and a novel entropy-regularized SmoothSort variant), and sorting-network-based (Sections 4.1-4.4).

FastSoftSort achieves the lowest memory footprint (~420KB) among benchmarked soft-sorting methods at n=4096, while the sorting-network approach is fastest at ~1.0ms (3.8x the hard baseline), versus ~16ms for SoftSort and ~37ms for NeuralSort (Section 5, Figure 8).

A case study applies SoftJAX operators (sj.argmax, sj.dynamic_index_in_dim) to soften the manifold-point-selection step of MuJoCo XLA's collision detection pipeline, enabling gradient flow through a previously non-differentiable physics operation (Appendix B).

vmMAa2HGP9.text: GAAVI achieves approximately uniform (asymptotically anytime-valid) type-I error control at level alpha for all times t greater than or equal to a burn-in time t0, under boundedness assumptions on the outcome (Theorem 4.2).
Under L2(P_X) convergence of sequential regressors and a positive covariance condition, GAAVI rejects a false global null with probability one in finite time, i.e. achieves power one (Theorem 4.4).

Under nuisance consistency (Assumption 4.5), the expected sample complexity N_f(alpha) satisfies limsup_{alpha->0} E[N_f(alpha)]/log(1/alpha) <= Gamma^{-1}(tau,f), matching the optimal sample complexity of parametric Gaussian location testing (Theorem 4.7).

GAAVI is formulated for two data-generating processes: testing a generic conditional mean function global null (DGP1) and testing a conditional average treatment effect global null with binary treatment under a positivity assumption on propensity scores (Section 2, Assumption 2.3).

The test is constructed via a predictable weighted martingale whose confidence-sequence inversion yields function-valued asymptotic confidence sequences for the CMF/CATE, evaluated on synthetic data and the French jobs real-world dataset (Section 3, Section 5).

QpgIOT06k3.text: ACDA introduces an interaction layer that generates a matrix of candidate actions for possible future execution times under unobservable random delays, formalized as a POMDP (Section 3, Section 3.3).

ACDA is a model-based actor-critic algorithm built on Soft Actor-Critic that uses learned components (Embed_omega, Step_omega, Emit_omega) to embed state distributions into fixed-size policy inputs despite variable-length delayed action sequences (Section 4.2).

On five MuJoCo locomotion benchmarks (Ant-v4, Humanoid-v4, HalfCheetah-v4, Hopper-v4, Walker2d-v4) with 5% action noise under Gilbert-Elliott delay processes (GE_{1,23}, GE_{4,32}) and an M/M/1 queueing delay process, ACDA achieves the best evaluated average return in 14 of 15 configurations (Table 1).
ACDA outperforms the fixed/worst-case-delay baselines BPQL and VDPO across nearly all delay processes and environments, with performance overlapping only on Ant-v4 (Section 5, Figure 8).
Training is run for 1 million steps per benchmark configuration, with best average return reported every 10,000 evaluation steps (Section 5).

kWxN36TDN8.text: MEC attains the semiparametric efficiency bound for semi-supervised mean estimation under a weaker condition than CF-PPI, requiring only that the projection error be stochastically bounded rather than bounding the raw prediction error directly (Theorem 5.2, using the fact that the projection norm ||m0,perp|| <= ||m-hat^(-) - m0||).

CF-PPI is shown to be consistent under L2-boundedness of the prediction error and asymptotically normal under L2-consistency, with asymptotic variance sigma_f^2 = Var(m0(X)) + (1/f)Var(Y - m0(X)) (Theorem 5.1).

MEC has a dual generalized-regression (GREG) representation using a low-dimensional 2D calibration basis h(X) = (1, m-hat^(-)(X)), making it asymptotically equivalent to PPI++ under quadratic generators and solvable via fast dual Newton optimization (Theorem 4.1).

In simulations with N=1000 and label fraction f in [0.1, 0.5] across four predictors (KRR, RF, FNN, kNN), MEC achieves near-nominal 95% coverage while vanilla PPI undercovers (especially at f=0.1) and CF-PPI sometimes overcovers (Figure 1).

At f=0.1 with a KRR predictor, MEC's confidence-interval width ratio is approximately 0.85 versus CF-PPI showing no efficiency gain (width ratio above 1.0), and at f=0.5 with a random-forest predictor MEC's width ratio (~0.75) is tighter than CF-PPI's (~0.80) (Figure 1).

STeISpzNSd.text: RECM's recurrent update rule h_t = (1 - a/(b+at)) h_{t-1} + (a/(b+at)) l_theta_t(z_{t-1}, y_{t-1}) drives per-layer relaxation parameters, with a convergence bound (Theorem 4.2) upper-limited by the Wasserstein distance between the input-target distribution and its symmetrized counterpart, so fully symmetric data converges to full equivariance while asymmetric data retains flexibility (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Equation 1).
On rotated ModelNet40, adding RECM to VN-PointNet improves instance/class accuracy from 0.68/0.62 to 0.80/0.74, and reaches 0.90/0.86 on the aligned (non-rotated) setting (Table 1).

On exact/approximate equivariance benchmarks, SEGNN+RECM achieves 3.7 +/- 0.22 MSE on N-body simulation and EGNO+RECM achieves 22.6 +/- 0.8 MSE (running) and 6.6 +/- 0.5 MSE (walking) on motion capture, the best results among relaxation methods compared (Table 2).

On molecular conformer generation on GEOM-DRUGS at threshold delta=0.75 Angstrom, adding RECM improves ETFlow to 79.44% recall / 75.10% precision and DiTMC to 80.6% recall / 76.1% precision over their unconstrained variants (Table 3).

Figure 2 shows that learned relaxation terms decay toward zero for fully symmetric (rotated) input distributions while remaining elevated for asymmetric (aligned) data, empirically validating the Theorem 4.2 convergence bound (Figure 2).

Fy2HkFMYH6.text: SURF trains a flow-matching student model purely from mixtures via a teacher-student remixing scheme, unifying MixIT/ReMixIT/Self-Remixing self-supervised objectives with flow matching, and relates the flow velocity field to a regression estimate via E[x1|xt,m] = xt + (1-t) u(xt,t,m), with a theoretical connection established to the Wake-Sleep algorithm (Section on method, theoretical analysis).

On two-source MNIST/CIFAR-10 image mixtures, SURF (ReMixIT variant) reaches 37.26 dB PSNR on MNIST and 14.83 FID on CIFAR-10, substantially outperforming the unsupervised MixIT baseline (21.90 dB PSNR on MNIST, 16.77 FID on CIFAR-10) (Table 1).
On Libri2Mix speech separation, SURF (ReMixIT variant) achieves 16.54 dB SI-SDR and 0.893 ESTOI, improving over the regression-based ReMixIT baseline's 13.22 dB SI-SDR (Table 4).
On the FUSS dataset using AudioSet-trained universal sound separation models, SURF variants reach approximately 30 dB SI-SDR on 1-source mixtures, versus approximately 10.99 dB for MixIT (Table 3).

Both SURF variants (ReMixIT-FM and Self-Remixing-FM) are evaluated across reconstruction metrics (PSNR, SI-SDR, PESQ) and perceptual quality metrics (LPIPS, FID, DNSMOS), consistently narrowing the gap between unsupervised and fully supervised separation methods across image, speech, and universal-sound domains (Tables 1, 3, 4).

PbgF8AGP5O.text: The GCON encoder combined with a sequential rule-based decoder and task-specific energy-based (Ising/QUBO) losses matches or exceeds baseline methods on RB-small graphs, e.g. MVC 211.69±0.16 and Maximum Clique 16.92±0.13 (Table 2).
Pretraining on MIS and fine-tuning to MVC recovers baseline performance within 15 epochs versus roughly 300 epochs when training MVC from scratch (Table 3, Section 4).

In leave-one-out multi-task transfer experiments, fine-tuning after 20 epochs outperforms training from scratch for most of the six combinatorial optimization tasks, with Maximum Cut and Graph Coloring showing the strongest transfer benefits (Table 5, Section 5).

A backbone pretrained jointly on Minimum Dominating Set, Maximum Independent Set, and Graph Coloring, then fine-tuned on a held-out task, achieves performance comparable to models fully trained from scratch on that task (Table 7, Section 5).

GCON outperforms GCN, GIN, and GATv2 encoder variants on the tested combinatorial optimization problems, and transfer between MIS and MVC (and MIS/MVC to Maximum Clique) exploits complement-graph relationships explicitly analyzed as pairwise transferability (Section 4).

Ct0HIcLIMX.text: On ImageNet-C in the continual setting, DP-Tent with per-sample gradient clipping raises accuracy from 60.8% to 64.9% (a +4.1 point gain) even before any Gaussian privacy noise is added (Table 1).

Applying the same per-sample clipping to EATA, SAR, and DeYO/DeYO-COME yields improvements ranging from -0.3% to +1.7% depending on method, showing the clipping benefit is not universal but is largest for Tent and DeYO (Table 1).

At a strong privacy budget of ε=1, DP-Tent's accuracy degrades by only about 2.3 percentage points relative to the non-private baseline, and at ε=20 it still exceeds the non-private baseline (60.8%) at 62.9% (Figure 1, Proposition 3.1).

Per-sample gradient clipping (64.0-64.9% accuracy) outperforms alternative robustification strategies such as batch-level clipping (57-59%), gradient-norm filtering (63.7-64.4%), and entropy-based filtering (59.4-62.9%) in the ablation comparison (Table 2).
The DP variants introduce modest computational overhead, adding roughly 20-30ms per batch and being up to 1.28x slower than their non-private counterparts (Table 4).

YScdQhxHgS.text: DexMachina's curriculum uses PD-controlled virtual object controllers whose gains (k_p, k_v) decay exponentially based on policy learning progress, gradually transferring object-state control from the controller to the learned policy (Algorithm 1, Section 4.3).

Evaluated across four dexterous hands (Inspire, Allegro, XHand, Schunk) on seven demonstrations, DexMachina achieves roughly 60-80% success on long-horizon tasks compared to about 20-50% for task-reward-only and task-plus-auxiliary-reward baselines without the curriculum (Figure 3).

Replacing the virtual-object-controller curriculum with the ManipTrans-style decaying-physics-parameter curriculum yields no improvement over the no-curriculum baseline, indicating the specific virtual-controller decay mechanism is responsible for the gains (Section on curriculum comparison).

Across six dexterous hand embodiments compared on long-horizon tasks, the fully-actuated Allegro Hand achieves the highest success (roughly 70-85%) while the DexRobot Hand performs worst, showing larger fully-actuated hands learn both faster and to a higher final performance (Figure 5).

An ablation over action formulations shows hybrid actions (residual 6-DoF wrist control plus absolute, joint-limit-normalized finger control) with restrictive wrist bounds outperform less-constrained residual actions or fully absolute joint actions (Figure 8, Section 4.2).

NOoAIwF6bV.text: BridgeVLM-7B achieves 54.4% accuracy on CausalVLBench intervention tasks compared to 33.2% for a prompt-level supervised baseline (Table 1).
BridgeVLM-7B improves intervention accuracy on Causal3D from 43.6% (Phi-4 baseline) to 49.0% (Table 1).
BridgeVLM improves causal graph structure-learning F1 on CausalVLBench from 33.4% to 75.1% (Table 1).

Ablating the DAG induction module drops CausalVLBench intervention accuracy from 59.8% to 44.0%, while removing Node Tokens or Graph Tokens drops it to 47.5% and 46.3% respectively, showing the DAG and causal tokens are each necessary components (Table 2).

Replacing the internal M3S token-alignment supervision with prompt-level causal knowledge injection drops CausalVLBench intervention accuracy from 54.4% to between 28.3% and 36.1%, demonstrating internal supervision substantially outperforms prompt-based supervision (Table 3).
BridgeVLM incurs a moderate inference-time overhead of 228.97ms compared to 128.26ms for the baseline (Appendix, per efficiency discussion in Section 4).

tAdsDOkRBw.text: Zero Sum SVD (ZS-SVD) selects singular components globally using a first-order calibration-loss estimate of the form ΔL_i ≈ -σ_i u_i^T H v_i under activation whitening, maintaining two priority queues of positive and negative predicted loss changes to keep cumulative drift near zero during greedy truncation (Section 4).
On LLaMA-7B at a 0.8 compression ratio, ZS-SVD achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.74 versus 8.54 for Dobi-SVD (Table 1).
At 20% compression, ZS-SVD attains WikiText2 perplexity of 11.40 on OPT-6.7B (versus 16.04 for SVD-LLM) and 4.83 on LLaMA-30B (versus 6.61 for SVD-LLM) (Table 5).

In an ablation of pruning strategies at a 0.4 compression ratio, the zero-sum selection rule achieves 45.2 perplexity versus 803,599 for magnitude-based selection alone, showing the loss-aware selection is essential (Table 6).
ZS-SVD's truncation procedure completes in 15.9 minutes on LLaMA-7B, versus 19.25 hours for Dobi-SVD (Table 8).
ZS-SVD yields a 5.63x GPU inference speedup at 40% compression on an RTX A5000 while maintaining a similar memory footprint to competing SVD methods (Table 7).

vCAIwEJZQ6.text: Under Init[A] with LoRA scaling factor alpha=1, the maximal-update-adaptation optimal learning rate scales as eta = Theta(n^{-1/2} r^{-1/2}), making it rank-dependent (Section 4, Corollary 4.4).
Under Init[A] with alpha=r^{-1}, the optimal learning rate scales as eta = Theta(n^{-1/2}), i.e. rank-invariant (Section 4, Corollary 4.4, Table 1).

Under Init[B] with alpha=1, the optimal learning rate scales as eta = Theta(n^{-1}), matching the scaling of full finetuning and enabling direct learning-rate transfer from LoRA to full finetuning (Section 4, Corollary 4.6).
Learning rate sweeps on Llama-3.2-1B show three distinct scaling patterns for the three LoRA configurations, visually confirming the rank-dependence/invariance predictions of the theory (Figure 2).

SFT experiments across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-VL-2B, RoBERTa-large, and ViT-Huge/14 confirm that Init[B] with alpha=1 yields rank-invariant optimal learning rates aligned with the full-finetuning optimum (Figures 3-5).
RLVR experiments on Llama-3.1-8B trained on GSM8K confirm the rank-invariance pattern, with full finetuning requiring more than 2x the GPU memory of LoRA (Figure 6).

98xDF2hkIy.text: The likelihood-constrained (LU) formulation's optimal solution takes the form p*_revl(.) proportional to q(.)/e^{sum_i alpha_i q_u^i(.)}, an exponential downweighting of the pretrained density by unlearning-set likelihood (Section 2.3, Theorem 3).
Strong duality holds for the reverse-KL-constrained unlearning problem despite its nonconvex feasible set, proved via Lyapunov's convexity theorem (Section 2.1, Theorem 1).

On Stable Diffusion v1.4 concept unlearning, the likelihood-constrained method achieves a better retention-unlearning trade-off (measured via KID and KL retention metrics) than a concept-erasing baseline (Section 4.1, Figure 5).

On CelebA-HQ data unlearning with DDPM, the forward-KL-constrained approach achieves lower maximum SSCD similarity to forgotten samples while maintaining better KID retention than compared baselines (Section 4.2).

In a synthetic three-Gaussian-mixture experiment, the likelihood-constrained method achieves smaller KL divergence to retained modes than the reverse-KL method at equivalent unlearning levels (Figure 1, Figure 4).

Theorems 4-6 extend the strong-duality results for the three constrained-optimization formulations (reverse KL, forward KL, likelihood) from generic distributions to score-based diffusion models (Section 3).

OmmKEy9Ixf.text: For approximately norm-minimizing interpolators in the Sobolev space W^{k,p}(R^d) with k in (d/p, 1.5d/p) and sufficiently large sample size, the conditional generalization error is bounded below by C*gamma^{-pd/(kp-d)}, a positive constant independent of n, establishing harmful (non-benign) overfitting (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.7).

Corollary 3.8 shows that for Gaussian heteroskedastic label noise under squared loss, the L^2(mu) error between the learned interpolator and the ground-truth function remains bounded below by C*gamma^{-pd/(kp-d)}, i.e. it does not vanish as n to infinity (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.8).

Lemma 4.1 constructs bump functions with controlled Sobolev norm satisfying the bound ||psi||_{W^{k,p}} lesssim 1 + delta^{(d-kp)/p}, a key technical tool used to prove the lower bound on generalization error (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.1).
Lemma 4.4 guarantees the existence, with high probability, of a large subset of noisy, well-separated training points used in the harmful-overfitting construction (Section 4.2, Lemma 4.4).
The harmful-overfitting result is established for arbitrary p in [1, infinity) in Sobolev spaces W^{k,p}(R^d), generalizing beyond the Hilbert-space (p=2) case (Section 3, Theorem 3.7).

0SGle5hjIf.text: SCENT's stochastic proximal mirror descent update for the dual variable nu admits a closed-form expression, nu_t = nu_{t-1} + log(1+alpha_t e^{s(w_t;zeta_t)}) - log(1+alpha_t e^{nu_{t-1}}), avoiding the numerical instability of exponential-average baselines (Algorithm 1, Section 3).

Theorem 3.6 proves SCENT achieves an O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate for convex compositional entropic risk minimization objectives of the form log(E[exp(s(w;zeta))]), improving on SCGD's O(1/T^{1/4}) rate (Section 3, Theorem 3.6).
Lemma 3.3 proves the dual iterates nu_{i,t} remain bounded within an interval [c0, c1] across all iterations, preventing numerical overflow in the exponential terms (Section 3, Lemma 3.3).

Theorem 4.3 shows that for fixed w, SPMD's convergence is characterized by the second-order moment ratio kappa = E[z^2]/E[z]^2, and is provably faster than standard SGD by a factor proportional to 1/e^{(nu*-c0)} (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).

On extreme classification benchmarks Glint360K and TreeOfLife-10M, SCENT consistently outperforms the SOX, U-max, and BSGD baselines on both training and validation convergence (Section 5, extreme classification experiments).
On partial AUC maximization over CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, SCENT matches or exceeds the SOX baseline's performance (Section 5, partial AUC maximization experiments).

tPd6GmXPbd.text: Chunk-GRPO with weighted sampling achieves an HPSv3 score of 15.373 versus 15.080 for Dance-GRPO and 13.804 for the base FLUX model, a relative improvement over Dance-GRPO (Table 1/Section 5, empirical results table).

Chunk-GRPO with weighted sampling attains an ImageReward score of 1.149, exceeding Dance-GRPO's 1.141 and the Chunk-GRPO-without-weighted-sampling variant's 1.147 (Section 5, empirical results table).
On the WISE benchmark, Chunk-GRPO achieves an overall score of 0.76 compared to Dance-GRPO's 0.75 (Table 2).

Proposition 1 formally shows that when per-timestep advantage attribution is inaccurate, jointly optimizing timesteps grouped into a chunk yields better performance than optimizing them independently, motivating the chunk-level objective (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).

The relative L1 distance between adjacent latents, L1_rel(x,t), exhibits prompt-invariant temporal dynamics across the T=17 sampling steps, which is used to guide the choice of chunk sizes {2,3,4,7} (Section 4.2, Figure 3; Section 5.1/Appendix B.1).

An ablation shows weighted sampling of chunks improves preference-alignment reward by 2.9% over the base chunk-level method but has mixed effects on the WISE metric, occasionally causing semantic collapse in high-noise regions (Figure 6, Figure 9).

YblLI3n0dn.text: SENDAI's lightweight variant (SENDAI Jr.) achieves a 120% to 185% improvement in SSIM over the SG+IDW baseline across evaluated sites (Table 1-2).
The full SENDAI model with hierarchical high-frequency peeling achieves a 15.5% to 36.3% SSIM improvement over the Cheap2Rich baseline (Table 1-2).
SENDAI reconstructs spatiotemporal fields from extremely sparse sensor networks, using only 64 sensors corresponding to 1.56% spatial coverage (Section 3).
Reported SSIM scores vary substantially by site, e.g. 0.5747 for Central Valley and 0.3354 for Riverina, indicating site-dependent reconstruction difficulty (Table 3).
SENDAI's frequency-peeling loss combines an in-band L1/L2 sparsity ratio, an out-of-band energy suppression penalty, and an exclusion penalty to prevent mode recapture (Equations 10-12).
SENDAI training and inference run on standard CPU hardware within minutes per site, contrasting with GPU-cluster-dependent deep learning approaches for remote sensing reconstruction (Section 3.5).

5lIJrDCQll.text: APEX retrieves the approximate top k=1,000,000 compounds from a 10-billion-compound combinatorial synthesis library in under thirty seconds on a single Tesla T4 GPU (Table 1).

APEX's neural network surrogate factorizes molecular embeddings additively across synthon contributions (synthon, R-group, and reaction encoders), enabling exhaustive scoring without brute-force enumeration (Section 3.2-3.3).

At k=100,000 retrievals (0.803% of a 12-million-compound library), APEX recovers a high fraction of the true top-j compounds across five protein targets (PARP1, MET, DRD2, F10, ESR1), substantially exceeding random baselines (Figure 3A).
APEX consistently outperforms or matches Thompson Sampling at recalling top-j compounds, with its advantage most pronounced at lower evaluation budgets (Figure 8, Appendix A.5).
APEX maintains high constraint satisfaction rates across multiple drug-likeness filters, including Lipinski Rule of 5, Veber, Pfizer 3/75, and Astex Rule of 3 (Figure 3B).
The surrogate models are trained on 1 million enumerated compounds with docking scores across 28 endpoints combining docking scores and physicochemical properties (Section 3.1).

8LVv9hyMII.text: The paper introduces a novel formulation of the static CVaR objective for MDPs based on state augmentation that yields dense per-step rewards rather than sparse terminal rewards (abstract only).

The proposed Bellman operator is defined on the space of bounded value functions (L-infinity) and is shown to have contracting properties on the full space, unlike prior augmentation-based CVaR formulations (abstract only).
The authors derive risk-averse value iteration and a model-free Q-learning algorithm operating on discretized augmented state spaces (abstract only).
Convergence guarantees and approximation error bounds are established that account for the discretization of the augmented state space (abstract only).
Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms learn CVaR-sensitive policies that achieve effective trade-offs between performance and safety (abstract only).

ZBHDZDaG0h.text: FIM-ODE, pretrained on only about 600,000 synthetic polynomial-vector-field systems of dimension 1-3, infers vector fields from noisy ODE trajectories in a single forward pass with roughly 8 million parameters, versus ODEformer's 86 million parameters trained on 50 million systems (Section 4, Table 1).
On ODEBench with clean data (rho=0.0, sigma=0.0), FIM-ODE achieves R^2>0.9 trajectory reconstruction on 84.4% of systems compared to ODEformer's 63.1% (Table 1).

Under noisy, subsampled conditions (rho=0.5, sigma=0.05), FIM-ODE still reaches 72.1% of systems with R^2>0.9 versus 61.5% for ODEformer, showing consistent outperformance across noise/subsampling configurations (Table 1).

On the Van der Pol oscillator forecasting task, finetuning FIM-ODE reduces zero-shot MSE from 0.89 to 0.16, approaching but not matching classical baselines GPODE and GP-DNF (MSE 0.03-0.13) (Table 4).

On the CMU MoCap human motion dataset (5D latent space projected to 3D), finetuning dramatically improves FIM-ODE performance for subjects where discarded latent dimensions carry significant variance, e.g. subject 35's short-horizon MSE drops from 655.40 zero-shot to 6.92 finetuned (Table 5).
FIM-ODE's architecture is restricted to state dimension d <= 3 due to its fixed-dimensional design, a limitation the authors identify for future work via axial attention (Section 6).

mu17VSX8q9.text: Two-layer transformers trained on random walks over Erdos-Renyi graphs (8K nodes, 50K edges) with no power-law structure in the data still exhibit power-law neural scaling, with mean exponents alpha_D = 1.028 (+/-0.129) and beta_N = 0.749 (+/-0.014).

Across a complexity ladder from bigram language models (entropy ~5.40) to two-layer-transformer-generated text (T2L, entropy ~3.81) to natural Fineweb-edu text (entropy ~3.18), the fitted scaling exponents shrink monotonically, e.g. alpha_D falls from 0.977 for bigrams to 0.497 for T2L.
Excluding the irreducible-loss offset term E when fitting scaling curves underestimates the scaling exponents by roughly a factor of two and worsens fit quality by an order of magnitude (Figure 9).
A neural-network regression fit to the loss surface achieves about 2x lower validation MSE than the standard 2D Chinchilla parametric formula (Figure 10).

A 2-layer transformer with context length 100 reproduces the major scaling-law exponents (alpha=0.35, beta=0.51) once embedding parameters are included in the parameter count, resolving a discrepancy between Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla-style scaling results.

Preliminary experiments under maximal update parameterization (muP) show a data-scaling exponent alpha_D of approximately 0.5, better parameter efficiency than the alpha_D of approximately 0.35 observed under standard parameterization.

UJcB3XrffF.text: SP-Mind is presented as the first autonomous LLM-driven agent unifying spatial proteomics analysis end-to-end, from raw tissue imaging through downstream phenotype discovery, using a ReAct-style reasoning loop over a modular library of 10+ tools spanning 8 pipeline stages (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).

SP-Mind achieves 68.9% average execution accuracy on SP-Bench, versus 55.4% for Biomni-SP and 50.5% for ToolUniverse-SP, with the largest margins on the Advanced tier (61.9% vs. 36.5% and 25.4%) and Challenging tier (33.3% vs. 23.1% and 15.4%) (Table 1).

SP-Bench comprises 102 queries spanning 8 pipeline stages and 18 task categories, split into four difficulty tiers of 40 Basic, 28 Intermediate, 21 Advanced, and 13 Challenging queries, built from MCMICRO, MAPS cHL, and PDAC IMC datasets (Section 4.1).
On the CRC-CODEX Quantification Challenge, SP-Mind attains a Pearson correlation of 0.953 and Spearman correlation of 0.902 with the lowest (best) MMD score of 0.368 among compared agents (Table 2).
On the Cell Annotation Challenge, SP-Mind achieves the highest average CyteOnto similarity of 0.681 across evaluated agents, with a per-sample high of 0.765 on cHL_2_MIBI_5 (Table 3).

KHzFTDx20C.text: How2Mine extracts 351,162 filtered how-to procedures from 980,000 web documents across 14 topics using an LLM-based extraction, heuristic filtering (5-15 step range), and quality-filtering pipeline costing $5,717 in GPT-4.1 API calls (Section 3, Figure 2).

How2Judge, a Qwen 3 8B model distilled from 73K GPT-5 annotations under the How2Score protocol, reaches 80.5% agreement with the human majority label, compared to GPT-5's 83.0% agreement, on a human validation set of N=200 (Section 4, Figure 3).

Reinforcement learning (GRPO) using How2Score as reward improves How2Bench performance by more than 10 points across three base models without systematic regressions on standard out-of-domain benchmarks such as MMLU-Pro, GPQA, GSM8K, and HumanEval+ (Section 6, Table 2).

Memorization-confound analysis shows that despite reference-procedure perplexity dropping sharply during midtraining (10.4 to 1.4 for a 7B model), How2Score improves only modestly and non-monotonically (about +3 points for the 7B model, +6.1 for a 32B model), indicating gains are not primarily driven by memorization (Section 7, Table 3).
Inter-annotator agreement on the How2Score critical-failure labeling protocol is reported as Krippendorff's alpha of 0.593 (Section 4).

kCGGQfZyaE.text: The paper derives a worst-case generalization bound of the form L_DR + rho^max C_Y^max C_D^max sigma nu, where rho, C_Y, and C_D are sensitivity parameters characterizing the strength of omitted variables under distribution shift (Section 3.2).

On GPT-4.1 evaluated on MATH-Perturb, the standard doubly-robust (DR) adjustment underestimates the true target-domain performance gap, while the proposed worst-case bound more closely matches observed test performance (Section 6.1, Figure 1).

On the semi-synthetic Amazon review dataset, the worst-case-bound approach outperforms the standard DR baseline specifically when the omitted variable is strong, with the size of the improvement tracking the magnitude of the omitted variable (Section 6.3, Figure 3).

On EmoBank and Hate Speech, optimization gains from the worst-case objective peak at intermediate sensitivity-parameter values (around 0.8 for EmoBank and 0.06 for Hate Speech) rather than at the extremes (Section 6.3, Figure 4).

For generalized linear model (GLM) log-likelihood losses, the framework is simplified so that outcome models predict labels rather than losses, enabling application to regression, classification, and text-generation tasks alike (Section 4.1, Table 1).

eGJEOl9vAg.text: Graph data is modeled as a mixture of probabilistic graph generative models represented by graphons, with graph moments (motif densities) used to identify and cluster graphs originating from the same underlying graphon (abstract only).
Theoretical bounds are established showing that graphs generated from structurally similar graphons exhibit comparable motif densities with high probability (abstract only).
The graphon-mixture-aware mixup method (GMAM) achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 6 out of 7 supervised learning benchmark datasets (abstract only).
The model-aware graph contrastive learning method (MGCL) is reported to perform competitively across the same benchmark datasets in the unsupervised setting (abstract only).

Z8svqD3pmI.text: Evolving Retrieval Memory (ERM) converts validated query-time expansion signals into permanent, norm-bounded updates to document keys via a correctness-gated verifier, selective expansion attribution, and progressive key evolution, incurring zero additional inference-time retrieval overhead (Section 4, Sections 4.1-4.3).

Query and key expansions are proven equivalent under standard similarity functions (Proposition 4.1), and ERM's updates are proven to converge to stable key sequences (Theorem 4.3), with cumulative expansion cost shown to grow sublinearly in query volume as Theta(T^{1/alpha}) (Proposition 4.5).

Across 13 datasets spanning BEIR and BRIGHT benchmarks, ERM improves BM25 retrieval by 46% average nDCG@1 (from a 26.3 baseline) and dense retrievers such as BGE-Large by roughly 13-15%, with especially large gains on reasoning-intensive datasets such as AoPS (+2200%) and TheoremQA (+378%) (Table 1).
ERM improves end-to-end question-answering performance by 2-6% across evaluated retrievers when paired with downstream generation, with BM25 showing the largest gain (about +6% average) (Table 2).
ERM achieves a 50-100x latency reduction compared to HyDE-style LLM-based query expansion, operating at native retrieval speeds of 150-280ms (Figure 3).

yd4tq9Rf3L.text: FK-PINNs achieve a uniformly bounded PL-based condition number κ_FK ≤ C independent of collocation mesh refinement, whereas standard PINNs suffer κ_PINN ≥ c·N^(β/2) that grows polynomially with the number of collocation points N (Theorem 5.4).
A non-asymptotic L² error bound of the form ‖u_θT − u*‖ ≤ C(N_FK^(−β) + e^(−c_opt·T) + ε_bias + √ε_bias) is proven for depth-3 tanh networks trained with Feynman-Kac supervision (Theorem 6.2).
The Monte Carlo Feynman-Kac labels used for supervision decompose as Y^FK = u* + b + ζ, with bias bounded by |b(x)| ≤ C_bias√(Δt) + C_T·e^(−κT_max) and sub-exponential noise ζ (Proposition 6.1).

On the Schrödinger, mean exit time, and committor function benchmarks, FK-PINN reduces relative L² error from 0.624/1.007/0.839 (vanilla PINN) to 0.096/0.107/0.030 respectively — roughly 6.5x, 9.4x, and 28x improvements (Table 1).

FK-PINN training requires O(log(1/ε)) gradient iterations to reach accuracy ε, versus O(N^(β/2)·log(1/ε)) for standard PINNs, implying an N^(β/2)-fold speedup from improved conditioning alone (Section 6).

The training procedure (Algorithm 2) uses an offline Monte Carlo Feynman-Kac estimation stage via Euler-Maruyama discretization at N_FK interior points, followed by an online PINN training stage with an uncertainty-weighted multi-task loss (Algorithm 2).

Ctk4XLaUpl.text: DPPrefSyn models human preferences with a Bradley-Terry likelihood ℙ[a⁺≻a⁻|x] = σ(r⋆(x,a⁺) − r⋆(x,a⁻)) and assumes a linear reward r_θ(x,a) = ⟨θ, φ(x,a)⟩ to enable DP clustering of heterogeneous user preferences (Section on Theoretical Framework / Bradley-Terry Model).

The pipeline composes (ε,δ)-differential privacy across three stages — DP-PCA (budget ε₀), DP-KMeans clustering (budget ε₁), and per-cluster DP-SGD reward model training — accounted for via a Privacy Random Variable (PRV) accountant (Algorithm/Method section).
At ε=2 on Anthropic-HH, DPPrefSyn combined with DPO achieves a 56.48% GPT-4o win rate, versus 37.02% for a DP-FT baseline and 38.72% for non-private fine-tuning (Table 1).
At ε=2 on TL;DR summarization, DPPrefSyn+DPO reaches a 68.54% win rate compared to 62.02% (DP-FT) and 64.52% (non-private fine-tuning) (Table 1).
Membership inference attacks on Qwen-3-4B yield near-random AUC of ~50.5-50.9 for DPPrefSyn versus 62-73 for the DP-FT baseline, indicating stronger empirical privacy protection (Table 5).
Ablations show removing either DP-PCA or DP-KMeans degrades performance, and a moderate cluster count of K=3-5 is optimal (Ablation section).

1vshJGUVBS.text: MemoryLLM trains feed-forward network (FFN) sublayers directly on context-free, token-indexed embedding vectors rather than the residual stream, framing FFNs as a neural key-value memory over a finite, human-interpretable query space via the Token-Key-Value (TKV) framework (Section on TKV framework).
Semantically similar tokens are shown to produce similar memory keys in the up-projection matrices of the FFN memory (Figure 5).

Token-wise lookups (ToLs) allow FFN outputs to be pre-computed for the whole vocabulary and cached, reducing active VRAM requirements for MemoryLLM-1B to 12.6 GB at F16 precision and 6.3 GB with 8-bit quantization (Table 7).
SVD-based compression of the memory table further reduces MemoryLLM-1B storage to about 6.4 GB at 50% rank reduction (Table 8).

At equal active parameters (rather than equal total parameters), MemoryLLM outperforms a conventional dense transformer of the same active size, while underperforming when total parameters are matched (Table 2).

At the 1B scale, MemoryLLM runs inference at 14.42 ms/token using 6.04 GB memory versus 21.50 ms/token and 9.54 GB for a base transformer, a roughly 33% latency reduction and 37% VRAM reduction (Table 6).

sxLncu2Fhx.text: GESPI combines three runs of a base inference algorithm — on real data at level α, on real data at a relaxed level α+ε, and on pooled real+synthetic data at level α — and aggregates them via intersection/union set operations to guarantee risk 𝔼[ℓ(Ãlg(D_n, D̃_N), V)] ≤ α + min{ε, c·d_ℓ,Alg(P,Q)} regardless of synthetic data quality (Theorem 3.2).

The two-sided version of GESPI is sandwiched between the base method at level α and the guardrail method at level α+ε, i.e. Alg_α(D_n) ⪯ Ãlg(D_n, D̃_N) ⪯ Alg_{α+ε}(D_n), preserving statistical validity regardless of synthetic distribution shift (Theorem 3.3).

On AlphaFold structure prediction with n=10 CASP-14 proteins as real data and N=1,000 synthetic proteins from MSAs at target risk α=5%, GESPI reduces abstention to 85.6% at ~7% risk, compared to an OnlyReal baseline that abstains on nearly 100% of residues at 0% risk (Figure 3a).

In a comparison of large reasoning models using n=15 real AIME25 problems and N=100 synthetic OlympiadBench problems (α=5%, ε=2%), GESPI achieves higher statistical power to reject the null hypothesis than an OnlyReal test while controlling Type I error at the nominal level (Figure 4).
An OnlySynth baseline that relies purely on synthetic data lacks the error-rate guarantees that GESPI provides (Section 3/Figure 4 discussion).

K83orsg2X9.text: Under a uniform training distribution, learning a k-hop compositional function requires Ω̃(d^(k/2)) samples, whereas under a power-law distribution with exponent α>1, gradient descent learns the same task in Õ(d^(2α)) samples (Theorem 1, Theorem 2).
Gradient descent under a power-law distribution reaches error ε using O~(d^(2α)/(ηε)) samples within t ≤ O~(d^α/η · log(1/ε)) training time (Theorem 2).

On multi-step arithmetic (k=4 operations) and state tracking over the symmetric group S₅ (k=4 hops), models trained under a uniform distribution fail to learn the task while models trained under a power-law distribution (α=1.0 for arithmetic, α=1.5 for S₅) succeed without chain-of-thought or curriculum learning (Section 2, Section 4.2).

A three-stage learning mechanism — Escape, Head-to-Tail, and Convergence — is identified via loss-landscape and training-dynamics analysis on the S₅ state-tracking task, showing power-law sampling first escapes flat loss regions then accelerates learning of rare long-tail skills (Section 4.2, Figure 2, Figure 3).

Results generalize beyond synthetic tasks to multi-hop question answering (50 entities, k=3 hops) and synthetic grade-school math problems, where power-law training again outperforms uniform training (Section 5, Figure 4).

goFOelWmEG.text: GCPA (Geometry-Corrected Procrustes Alignment) uses per-sample consensus directions computed as the normalized average of aligned universe embeddings across models, refined via a lightweight MLP correction with a trust penalty (Section 3.4).
On MASSIVE clustering, GCPA improves Adjusted Rand Index from 0.198 to 0.300, roughly a 50% relative improvement, compared to plain GPA alignment (Table results, Section 4).
On multilingual retrieval with M=10 models, GCPA achieves Rank-1 accuracy of 0.503 versus 0.487 for GCCA, showing agreement-maximizing GCCA alone is not optimal (Section 4).
On the Flickr8k multimodal retrieval benchmark, GCPA improves HuBERT-to-DINOv2 cross-modal retrieval from about 14-15% to 29% (Section 4).

Proposition 3.2 proves that increasing each view's cosine similarity to the consensus direction monotonically increases the sum of pairwise cosine similarities among all views, justifying the GCPA correction step (Proposition 3.2, Section 3.4).
GCPA degrades more gracefully than GCCA under correspondence noise, including at 75% label shuffling, demonstrating greater robustness (Section 4).

mNISnOJ6or.text: ReasonEdit is presented as the first vision-language model editor that incorporates human reasoning explanations into a codebook of answer and reasoning entries for reasoning-heavy VQA editing (Section 3.2).

On the FVQA dataset with LLaVA-1.5-7B, ReasonEdit achieves 1.00 reliability (accuracy on edited samples), 0.97 text generality, 0.95 image generality, and 1.00 locality, versus GRACE's 0.98 reliability but only 0.76 rationale generality (Table 1(a), Section 4.3).

On the A-OKVQA dataset, ReasonEdit attains reliability of 0.97-0.99 and rationale generality of 0.77-0.86 across four VLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, InstructBLIP-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-4B), outperforming the best baseline IKE-COT's 0.57-0.77 rationale generality (Table 1(b), Section 4.3).

ReasonEdit uses a topology-balanced multimodal embedding that combines a selected vision-layer embedding (chosen via bimodal modularity) with a pretrained sentence-transformer text embedding, since later vision layers with mean pooling maximize bimodal modularity (Section 3.3, Section 4.6, Figure 6).

An ablation shows that key merging in the codebook reduces memory usage by roughly 80% without loss of editing performance, and K=5 nearest neighbors with a 50th-percentile retrieval rejection threshold is the optimal retrieval hyperparameter setting (Section 4.5, Figure 5).

In sequential editing experiments with 5,000+ edits, ReasonEdit maintains stable reliability and locality over time, unlike fine-tuning (FT) and MEND, which show catastrophic performance degradation as edits accumulate (Section 4.4, Figure 4).

tAcVihAkb3.text: TAIL (Transformer-based Algorithm-Implicit Learner), trained only on images, achieves 89.62% 5-shot and 84.87% 1-shot accuracy on a cross-modal text classification benchmark, versus GPICL's 50.88% and 50.31% respectively, despite never seeing text during training (Table 4, Section 6.2).

On CIFAR-FS, miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and Pascal VOC, TAIL achieves the best 5-shot and 1-shot accuracies among compared methods (SNAIL, GPICL, CAML, Linear Probe, ProtoHead), e.g. 84.35% 1-shot CIFAR-FS versus CAML's 77.93% (Table 2, Section 6.2).

An ablation shows TAIL's non-causal transformer architecture substantially outperforms a causal variant on cross-domain (87.58% vs 70.60%, 5-shot) and cross-modality (89.62% vs 70.08%, 5-shot) generalization (Table 6, Section 6.2).
Random extended permutation label/feature injection improves TAIL's cross-modality 1-shot accuracy from 66.69% (without random projection) to 84.87% (Table 5, Section 6.2).

Figure 2 shows TAIL's performance degrades much less than baselines as the number of classes at test time increases in the 1-shot setting, supporting the claim of handling label spaces up to 20x larger than seen during training (Figure 2, Section 6.2).

Table 1 formally distinguishes 'algorithm-explicit' learning (hand-crafted procedures like MAML) from 'algorithm-implicit' learning (learned via neural networks such as SNAIL, GPICL, CAML, TAIL) along dimensions of practical universality (Table 1, Section 3.2).

WUBn9uJuvj.text: EffGen with Qwen2.5-7B achieves 63.07% average accuracy across 13 benchmarks, a 12.3% improvement over the raw model baseline (Table 2, Section 4.2).

At Qwen2.5-1.5B, EffGen reaches 47.44% average accuracy versus 34.28% for the best competing baseline (raw model), a 13.2% gain, while the gain narrows to 6.0% at 32B (94.84% raw vs 97.75% EffGen... actually reported as 95.75% vs 89.66% raw) (Table 2, Section 4.2).

An ablation shows prompt optimization contributes an 11.2% accuracy gain at 1.5B but only 2.4% at 32B, while complexity-based routing contributes 3.6% at 1.5B but 7.9% at 32B, indicating complementary scaling behavior (Table 3, Section 4.6).

EffGen achieves an 18x speedup in execution time over Smolagents at the 1.5B model scale on BeyondBench-Easy (3.4 vs 62.4 minutes), narrowing to about 7x at 32B (15.1 vs 109.6 minutes) (Figure 2, Section 4.6).

EffGen's prompt optimization compresses input prompts by 70-80% (57% on average across benchmarks) while preserving task semantics, averaging 734 tokens per task versus 1,318 for LangChain (Section 4.6, Section 3.1).

On GAIA, EffGen with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieves 21.87% accuracy versus 12.50% for the raw model and 9.38% for LangChain, and on SimpleQA EffGen reaches 76.00% versus 46.00% raw at 7B (Table 2, Section 4.4).

akfapJ7Uuf.text: SALSA-V uses a shortcut-augmented latent flow matching objective built on modified MMDiT-X blocks operating jointly over audio and semantic visual feature sequences, followed by single-stream DiT blocks (Figure 1, Section 3).

SALSA-V (643M parameters) achieves the best FAD_VGG (1.07), KL_PaSST (1.63), and DeSync (0.497) scores among compared methods, outperforming MMAudio (1.03B, DeSync 0.521) and FoleyCrafter (1.22B, DeSync 1.319) (Table 1, Section 4.1).

In the human listening study with 18 participants across 180 scored trials, SALSA-V achieves overall MOS 3.43 and synchronization MOS 3.52, versus MMAudio's 3.29 overall and 2.92 synchronization (Table 1, Section 4.1).

At 8 sampling steps, SALSA-V's shortcut objective maintains near-flat FAD and DeSync performance, while MMAudio's performance degrades sharply as sampling steps decrease to 8, 4, 2, and 1 (Figure 5, Section 4.1).

An ablation comparing shortcut versus standard flow-matching training at matched model size (643M) and 32 sampling steps shows no performance reduction from adopting the shortcut objective (FAD_VGG 1.07 vs 1.10, DeSync 0.497 vs 0.499) (Table 2, Section 4.1).

For long-form generation beyond 20 seconds, SALSA-V retains stable FAD and DeSync by repeatedly prepending 0.5 seconds of prior generated audio as reference context, whereas MMAudio's performance drops sharply since it processes the full sequence at once and receives positional embeddings unseen during training (Figure 5, Section 4.1).

LFUaHUCO1a.text: Latent Forcing jointly diffuses pixels and latent tokenizer embeddings (e.g., DINOv2 or Data2Vec2 features) using two separately scheduled time variables per Equations 1-2, rather than a single global diffusion time variable (Section 3.2).

On ImageNet, denoising latent (DINOv2) features before pixel features consistently improves FID-10K across the multi-schedule sweep, with FID at the DINOv2-B+REG setting improving from about 55.35 (pixel earlier, alpha-shift 1/64) to 18.99 (latent earlier, alpha-shift 64) (Table 1, Figure 3).

In the Multi-Schedule Model ablation over the probability of sampling a latent timestep (P_Latent), FID-10K without guidance is minimized at P_Latent=0.4 (FID 12.42), compared to 16.13 at P_Latent=0.8 (Table 2).
Ablating the logit-normal schedule mean for pixel timesteps shows FID-10K improves from 18.28 (mu_pixel=0.0) to a best of 16.13 (mu_pixel=0.4), then worsens to 16.38 (mu_pixel=0.8) (Table 4).

Latent Forcing adds a second time-embedding MLP to a standard ViT-L diffusion transformer (following JiT), increasing parameter count by roughly 0.5% while keeping the same number of tokens and nearly identical training/inference speed (Section 4.2, Figure 2).

2taaKYQR7h.text: Classifier-based Quality Filtering (CQF) trains an L2-regularized logistic regression classifier on sBERT embeddings (p=384) to distinguish a high-quality (HQ) set from a low-quality RedPajama-V2 pretraining set (32T tokens), then keeps the top-k fraction of pretraining documents by classifier score (Section 2).

Training 350M-parameter models on CQF-selected data with HQ set ARC-Easy improves downstream ARC-Easy accuracy as the selection fraction k shrinks, while the same models' next-token loss on the HQ set itself follows a non-monotonic (U-shaped) curve for most HQ sets except ARC-Easy (Figure 2, Section 3).

CQF implicitly reweights the HQ set itself, upweighting HQ documents far from the LQ distribution (density p_CQF(x) = w(x)p_HQ(x) per Equation 4.1), which is empirically confirmed by finetuning a 1.3B model on the top decile of KnowledgePile versus the full HQ set, showing the top decile aligns more closely with ARC-Easy (Section 4.2, Figures 5-6).

Comparing CQF to the CRISP importance-sampling method with OpenOrca and ARC-Easy as HQ sets shows importance sampling achieves better language modeling loss on the HQ set, but CQF achieves better downstream accuracy when the HQ set is itself the target benchmark (Figure 7, Section 5).

Recursively applying CQF to construct an expanded, sufficiently large HQ set from OpenOrca (via CQF with k=20%) and comparing training on the resulting CQF-filtered top-1% subset versus training directly on the full expanded HQ set demonstrates that CQF-selected data can outperform training directly on the high-quality set even when the HQ set is not data-scarce (Section 6, Figure 8).

Bc6c2OVWRh.text: The paper defines a hierarchical uncertainty framework with three metrics — intra-agent flip rate/belief revision (U_intra), inter-agent pairwise disagreement (U_inter), and system-level entropy/disagreement/leave-one-out instability (U_sys) — computed per debate trajectory across GSM8K, TruthfulQA, and CommonsenseQA (Section 2, Equations 1-3).

Across GSM8K, failed multi-agent debate outcomes show a mean system-level uncertainty (U_sys) of 0.67 versus 0.09 for successful outcomes, with statistically significant separation (Cohen's d > 0.8, p < 0.001) (Figure 2, Section 3.2).

Uncertainty-Driven Policy Optimization (UDPO) improves GSM8K accuracy from 68.4% (Standard MAD, N=5 agents) to 92.3%, a gain of nearly 24 points, and outperforms MAPPO (73.6%) and RMAAC (75.8%) baselines under the same setting (Table 1, Section 5.2).

An ablation removing the system-level loss component (w/o L_sys) causes the largest accuracy drop among the three UDPO reward terms on GSM8K (92.3% to 84.8%), more than removing L_intra (to 86.5%) or L_inter (to 88.2%) (Table 2, Section 5.3).

Under AutoTransform attacks with up to 3 compromised agents in a 5-agent debate on GSM8K, UDPO maintains substantially higher accuracy (56.2% with 3 compromised agents) than Standard MAD (9.4%), MAPPO (36.7%), and RMAAC (40.5%) (Table 3, Section 5.4).

7pbmZatDuD.text: The paper develops an algebraic framework in which a recurrent language model's expressivity reduces to whether its syntactic monoid divides the wreath product of the transition monoids of its layers, formalized via algebraic cores, cascade juxtaposition, and the ambient wreath product (Section 3, Definitions 3.4-3.8).

Proposition 3.20 (the cascade juxtaposition identity) shows the realized wreath product of two cascaded algebraic RNNs equals the wreath product of their individual realized wreath products, up to canonical isomorphism, formalizing how expressivity composes across recurrent layers (Section 3.6.3, Proposition 3.20).

As a case study on diagonal state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba-style linear recurrences, the same architecture cannot implement an even-modulus counter under floating-point arithmetic with nonnegative recurrence multipliers, yet can realize every even-modulus counter under unsigned-integer quantization (Section 4, Abstract).

The framework's Krohn-Rhodes-based decomposition (Appendix, Section 3.6.3) shows that algebraic impossibility results (a required factor of the syntactic monoid cannot be realized by any layer monoid in a given architecture family) rule out recognition of a target language, while observational realization constructs an explicit acceptor when the factor is realizable (Section 3.6.3, Corollary 3.21).

1WJ283sbfs.text: ProCAD pairs a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct proactive clarifying agent (ProCAD-clarifier) with a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct CAD coding agent (ProCAD-coder), trained via agentic SFT on 6,063 clarification trajectories and standard SFT on 1.6K text-to-CadQuery examples respectively (Sections 5.1-5.2).

On the 2,469-sample ambiguous-prompt test set with GPT-5-mini simulating user responses, the full ProCAD two-agent system (with ProCAD-coder) achieves mean Chamfer distance of 0.63e3 and invalidity ratio of 0.9%, versus Claude Sonnet 4.5 as clarifier at 2.69e3 mean CD and 2.3% invalidity ratio (Table 4).

On the 1K unambiguous-prompt test set, ProCAD-coder achieves an invalidity ratio of 0.9% and median Chamfer distance of 0.066e3, better than Claude 4.5 Sonnet's 12.9% invalidity ratio and 0.077e3 median CD, and better than the Text-CAD and JSON-Distill baselines (Table 2).

Zero-shot evaluation on the authors' new Text-to-CadQuery dataset shows Claude Sonnet 4.5 attains an 11.8% invalidity ratio and mean CD of 2.580e3, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct attains an 82.9% invalidity ratio and mean CD of 4.489e3 (Table 1).

Human-centered evaluation of the full two-agent ProCAD system versus baselines using Claude 4.5 Sonnet as coding agent shows ProCAD-clarifier achieves the best efficiency (0.760) and resolution (0.787) scores among clarifying agents, alongside a mean CD of 1.28e3 and 12.2% invalidity ratio (Table 6).

0H7OYNDQS4.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that injecting public data reduces the Rényi divergence bound between the retrained and unlearned distributions by a factor of O(1/n_pub^2), with the bound's denominator scaling as (n_pub + n_priv)^2 (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).

Corollary 3.1 shows that under constant-fraction forgetting (n_forget = c·n_priv), the asymmetric noise variance needed satisfies σ²_asym ≥ σ²_sym·(n_priv/(n_priv+n_pub))², enabling mass unlearning that is infeasible for symmetric noise-based methods (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 gives a generalization bound showing utility degradation grows exponentially with the Rényi divergence D_∞(P_priv||P_pub) between private and public data distributions (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

On DomainNet, aligned public/private domain pairs (e.g., Quickdraw/Clipart) yield a 3.68-4.62% utility gap after unlearning, while misaligned domain pairs yield a persistent 10.34-10.81% gap (Section 5.2, Table 1).

On IMDB sentiment classification, injecting quality public auxiliary data substantially reduces U-LiRA membership-inference confidence scores while causing only about a 1.17% accuracy drop (Section 5.3, Table 2).

fS28SOioQd.text: On 123 hard instances from InvBench, the WONDA-fine-tuned Qwen3-4B model achieves a 44.4% invariant correctness rate, compared to 58.0% for GPT-OSS-120B and 72.4% for GPT-5.2 (Table 3).
The fine-tuned Qwen3-4B model reaches a Virtual Best Performance runtime of 165.5s, comparable to GPT-OSS-120B's 165.8s despite being roughly 30x smaller in parameter count (Table 3).

The WONDA pipeline's Stage 2 LLM-based simplification step (producing the 'V2' training data) doubles Qwen3-4B's invariant correctness rate from 33.1% with V1 (AST-normalized only) data to 44.4% with V2 data (Section 4.2, Table 4).
The Stage 1 normalization step uses AST-based rewriting to remove tautologies and contradictions, minimize parentheses, and strip redundant type casts before LLM-based simplification (Section 4.1).

The improvement from curated V1-to-V2 training data supports the claim that current neural invariant synthesizers are primarily limited by training data quality rather than model scale (Section 4.2, Table 4).

kq22pSSKwA.text: The stochastic score matching reformulation reduces per-iteration computational cost of torus graph parameter inference from O(d^6) to O(d^2) by using reverse-mode automatic differentiation for vector-Jacobian products instead of dense Jacobian computation, extending feasible inference from about 100 to thousands of phase variables (Section 3.1).
At d=1024 variables, the stochastic score matching method completes in 310±2 seconds while the exact method runs out of 24GB of VRAM (Section C.8, Table 1; Figure 2).
The TG-Hidden Markov Model (Section 3.3) uses approximate EM with a discriminative M-step to capture discrete, state-dependent phase-coupling changes while avoiding intractable normalizing constants.

The autoregressive torus graph (AR-TG, Section 3.4) estimates directional interactions via transfer entropy and completes multivariate estimation at d=64 in under one hour, whereas a multivariate Granger causality baseline times out at that same dimensionality (Section 3.4, Figure 4).

Applied to 1,860 phase features from 62-channel mouse LFP recordings across 30 frequencies, the models show high-frequency (>30 Hz) phase coupling dominating wakefulness and low-frequency (<30 Hz) coupling dominating NREM sleep, with the TG-HMM detecting sparse, spindle-state-specific coupling changes not visible in conventional pairwise phase-locking metrics (Section 4.2, Figures 5-6).

KBpIlcUIx1.text: Theorem 5.2 proves that CFO's Lagrange-multiplier and penalty-parameter update scheme (Algorithm 1, Eqs. 11-12) returns a policy that minimizes constraint infeasibility, and Theorem 5.4 proves that under vanishing fine-tuning approximation error (ε_k → 0) CFO converges to the global constrained maximizer (Section 5, Theorems 5.2 and 5.4).

On the FlowMol/GEOM-Drugs energy-constrained dipole maximization task with an energy bound of -80 Ha, CFO applied to Adjoint Matching (CFO_AM) achieves a dipole moment of 8.39±0.10 D at energy -82.28±0.41 Ha while satisfying the constraint, versus unconstrained Adjoint Matching (AM) reaching 8.37±0.07 D at -78.31±0.38 Ha while violating it (Section 6, Figure 3, Table 3(e)).
Per-molecule feasibility on the molecular design task is 61.4% for CFO versus 40.6% for unconstrained Adjoint Matching (Section 6).

Compared to a manually-tuned fixed-penalty (fixed-μ) baseline that required sweeping 18 μ values across 13 orders of magnitude (of which only 2/18 matched CFO's reward-constraint trade-off), CFO reaches its result in about 44 minutes versus about 727 minutes total for the μ-sweep, an 18x reduction in tuning cost (Section 6, Figure 5).

In the low-dimensional illustrative example, CFO increases reward from -7.62 (pretrained model) to -4.75 while reducing constraint violation from 0.58 to 0.12, compared to unconstrained Adjoint Matching which reaches reward -2.93 but with constraint violation 2.47 (Section 6, Figure 2).

yrON8C1YTy.text: OpenAI o3 completes only 34.4 of 204±2.3 possible tasks (16.9% of the perfect-play ceiling) in the zero-cost cooperation game, while o3-mini completes 102.8 tasks (50.4%), despite both models receiving identical instructions (Section 3, Table 1).

Gemini-2.5-Pro reaches 161.0 tasks (78.9% of the ceiling) with a 108.1% pipeline efficiency score, substantially outperforming o3 despite o3 being marketed as a more capable reasoning model (Section 3, Table 1).

The Auto-Request and Auto-Fulfill ablations isolate cooperation willingness from task competence: o3, o3-mini, and GPT-5-mini complete under 20% of tasks in Auto-Request (where demand is automated) but over 90% in Auto-Fulfill (where fulfillment is automated), showing their failures stem from unwillingness to request help rather than inability to help (Section 4, Table 2).

Explicit defection reasoning appears in 39.3% of o3's recorded reasoning traces versus 0% for the highest-performing models, and correlation between capability and cooperative performance is weak and non-significant (r=0.16, p=0.71) (Section 5).

Introducing explicit cooperation protocols roughly doubles performance for low-competence models such as GPT-5-mini (+99.3%), while adding a 10% sender bonus increases o3's performance by 190.7%, showing targeted incentive interventions can unlock cooperation-limited models (Section 6, Table 3).

4SD5FCeIDu.text: Binding information is formalized as B_O(Z) := I(O;Z), the mutual information between an object-identity variable O and a scene representation Z, measured in bits (Definition 2.10, Section 2.1).
CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336px resolution achieves 56.4% normalized binding information on the ColorShape dataset, outperforming DINOv2-Large's 41.8% and CLIP ViT-L/14 at 224px's 47.7% (Table 7).
DINOv2-Large's normalized binding information (beta*) on occluded CLEVR scenes ranges from 45.0% to 58.7% as the degree of occlusion decreases (Table 6).
A DNN probe on the [CLS] token decodes 19.4 bits (48.5% normalized) of binding information unconditionally, dropping to 13.9 bits (42.4% normalized) in the conditional setting (Section 3.1, Table 3).
An attention probe over spatial tokens decodes 36.8 bits (92.2% normalized) of binding information unconditionally, versus 31.0 bits (94.1% normalized) conditionally (Section 3.2, Table 5).

GhI6lw5QKe.text: Self-attention is reformulated as batch maximum-likelihood trajectory estimation, where the output token is a precision-weighted combination of time-shifted predictions x-hat_ij, weighted by inverse-covariance (precision) matrices P_ij (Section 2.3).

A robust generalization replaces the precision weights with adaptive weights w_ij = 1/(1 + r_ij^T P_ij^c r_ij / nu) computed from Mahalanobis-distance residuals r_ij, yielding an M-estimator that down-weights outlier tokens (Section 2.6).
In the limiting case of vanishing system dynamics, the robust filtering formulation of attention reduces exactly to standard dot-product self-attention (Section 3.7).
Closed-form solutions for the propagated precision matrices across layers are derived under an assumption that the dynamics matrix is diagonalizable (Section 2.5).
The paper reports only basic experiments on simple simulated linear dynamical systems and explicitly defers evaluation on real-world datasets to future work (Section 3.9).

bMSnvqVWaB.text: The informal main result states that the hidden representation learned by a two-layer linear autoregressive model trained on a partially observed linear dynamical system coincides, up to a similarity transformation S, with the state estimates of the optimal Kalman filter (Theorem 1, Section 4).

Theorem 4 (Section 4.4) formalizes this latent-state-recovery result, giving explicit finite-sample error bounds between the learned representation and the Kalman filter estimate up to the similarity transformation.
Theorem 2 (Section 4.3) bounds the in-sample prediction error at global optima of the empirical risk at a rate of O(H/T), where H is history length and T is trajectory length.
Theorem 3 (Section 4.3) gives a finite-sample bound on parameter estimation error in Frobenius norm for the learned autoregressive weights.
Proposition 1 (Section 4.1) shows the Kalman filter is well-approximated by a finite-history autoregressive model, with truncation error decaying exponentially in history length L.

In numerical experiments, a grid search over hidden dimension h identifies h=4 as optimal, matching the true latent state dimension n=4 (Section 5.2, Table 1), and learned activations achieve mean R-squared >= 0.979 alignment with Kalman filter state estimates (Section 5.3, Figure 2, Table 2).

RzlmkviaNy.text: On the unseen split of ALFWorld, AdaMEM-low reaches 58.2% success versus the Synapse static-memory baseline's 52.2%, a gain of 6.0 percentage points (about 11.5% relative) (Table 1).
On WebShop, AdaMEM-low scores 74.2 versus Synapse's 65.4, a gain of 8.8 points (about 13.5% relative) (Table 1).
