AdaMEM's hybrid architecture combines an offline long-term trajectory memory M indexed by state embeddings with a dynamically synthesized short-term strategy memory z_t, operating in two modes: AdaMEM-high (regenerates strategy at every step) and AdaMEM-low (persistent strategy with selective refresh) (Section 3.1).
On the cross-episode agentic-search benchmark HotpotQA, AdaMEM achieves a 41.1% success rate versus ReasoningBank's 40.5% (Table 2).

An ablation on ALFWorld shows removing the short-term strategy memory drops performance from 65.5% (AdaMEM-max) to 59.3%, while removing the long-term trajectory memory causes a severe degradation to 34.8% (Table 3).
A scaling analysis shows AdaMEM's success rate on the ALFWorld seen split improves monotonically from 54.0% at k=1 to 64.0% at k=16 retrieved memory items (Figure 4).

ZnOnnJJghs.text: MadDist learns a quasimetric state-distance function phi_theta from unlabeled state trajectories alone (no reward or action labels), optimizing a composite loss (Equation 4) combining a scaled distance objective (Equation 5), a contrastive regularization term (Equation 6), and a triangle-inequality constraint term (Equation 7) (Section 6.1).

TDMadDist extends MadDist with temporal-difference learning, using bootstrapped distance targets from a target network phi_theta' (Equation 10) instead of only direct trajectory-based supervision (Section 6.2).

Across NoisyGridWorld, KeyDoorGridWorld, CliffWalking, and PointMaze (UMaze and MediumMaze), MAD and TDMAD achieve substantially higher Pearson correlation with ground-truth distances than the QRL and Hilbert representation baselines, approaching 1.0 in several environments (Figure 3).
Ablations show the proposed simple quasimetric parameterization outperforms the Wide Norm and IQE quasimetric variants (Appendix C, Figures 5-6).
Proposition 1 (Appendix A.1) proves the ReLU-based distance reduction satisfies nonnegativity, identity, triangle inequality, and positive homogeneity, the defining properties of a quasimetric.
Proposition 3 (Appendix A.3) proves that convex combinations of valid quasimetrics preserve the triangle inequality and positive homogeneity properties.

5cu1ynhwTJ.text: DOIT is a training-free adaptation method for pre-trained diffusion models that applies Doob's h-transform to add a correction term to the sampling process without modifying pretrained parameters, supporting generic non-differentiable rewards (Section 1, Section 4).

On D4RL locomotion benchmarks (Table 3), DOIT achieves the best performance on 8 of 9 tasks among inference-time adaptation methods, with an average score of 87.6 versus 86.1 for the best baseline TTS (Section 6.3, Table 3).
DOIT attains 107.7±5.6 on Hopper Medium-Expert and 113.2±0.7 on Walker2d Medium-Expert, outperforming the TFG baseline (100.2±3.5 and 108.1±0.1 respectively) (Table 3).

A surrogate approximation of DOIT reduces per-image runtime on Stable Diffusion aesthetic-score adaptation to 1.712±0.036 seconds, versus 39.584±0.142 seconds for the full-simulation variant, while matching its reward improvements (Table 1, Section 6.2).

Theorem 5.4 bounds the total-variation distance between the reweighted data distribution and the learned h-transform distribution, with Lemma 5.2 showing Monte Carlo estimation error decays at a dimension-independent rate of O(M^{-1/6}) as the number of samples M grows (Theorem 5.4, Lemma 5.2).

HDoWJi2jlj.text: Conformal C2ST converts scores from any trained classifier into a conformal p-value U that satisfies exact finite-sample Type-I error control, P(U ≤ u | H0) = u for all u in [0,1], even with a finite calibration set (Lemma 1, Section 2.3).

Theorem 1 shows that under the alternative hypothesis, the gap between the expected conformal p-value and its ideal value is bounded by O(ε^{2/3}), where ε is the classifier's L2 estimation error, formalizing graceful power degradation with classifier quality (Theorem 1, Section 2.4).
Lemma 3 shows the expected conformal p-value under the alternative equals 1 minus the AUC of the classifier's score function, linking test power directly to discriminative ability (Lemma 3).

Under increasing perturbation strength γ, conformal C2ST variants match or exceed Simulation-Based Calibration (SBC) and TARP and outperform the classical (non-conformal) C2ST in power for Neural Posterior Estimation validation (Figure 2a, Section 3).
Under classifier degradation via interpolation parameter β, the conformal C2ST variants retain substantially more power than classical C2ST as classifier quality declines (Figure 2b, Section 3).

WPFVuJDDqc.text: Theorem 3.1 derives, via a Lambert-W closed-form solution, that PMD-mean's normalization constant λ scales inversely with the KL weight τ as τ→0, so a mixed KL–χ² regularizer remains active even when the nominal KL weight vanishes (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.1).

Proposition 3.2 shows PMD-mean implicitly solves a policy-improvement objective regularized by both KL(π‖πt) and an adaptive χ²(π‖πt) term whose coefficient depends on reward statistics under finite-sample estimation error (Proposition 3.2, Section 3.2).

Section 4.2.2 shows the χ² regularization weight adapts dynamically to the mean reward, intensifying regularization and producing more conservative policy updates when expected rewards are low (Section 4.2.2, Propositions 4.9–4.10).
On AIME24/AIME25 math reasoning benchmarks, PMD-mean improves a 30B model from 36.56/27.92 (GRPO) to 50.83/37.19, and a 7B model from 17.08/10.52 (GRPO) to 19.69/19.48 (Table 1).
PMD-mean achieves a 4.6x throughput speedup over on-policy gradient training (staleness=1) by amortizing over larger batches while maintaining comparable or superior accuracy (Table 2).
Figure 4 shows PMD-mean remains stable throughout training while an alternative variant, PMD-part, is highly unstable, empirically validating the implicit regularization mechanism (Figure 4).

Kaliw0BQL9.text: 3DGS²-TR uses a diagonal Hessian approximation via Hutchinson's method within a trust-region update, preserving O(n) per-step complexity comparable to ADAM while adding second-order curvature information (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).

On MipNeRF360, 3DGS²-TR reaches PSNR 25.39 versus ADAM's 25.08 at 30k iterations, and more broadly matches ADAM's converged reconstruction quality using roughly 50% fewer training iterations (Table 1, Section 5).
On Tanks & Temples, 3DGS²-TR improves PSNR to 22.85 dB versus ADAM's 21.66 dB and SSIM to 0.805 versus ADAM's 0.766 (Table 1).

3DGS²-TR adds under 1GB of peak GPU memory overhead versus ADAM (about 17% more) while using roughly 85% less memory than the second-order baseline 3DGS-LM on average, e.g. 6.26 GB versus 5.42 GB (ADAM) and 33.33 GB (3DGS-LM) on Deep Blending (Table 1).
The current method does not support Gaussian densification during optimization, restricting it to a fixed initial set of Gaussians (Section 5, Limitations).

SVyjXhZlDe.text: Theorem 3.1 shows the power distribution used for distribution sharpening decomposes into a low-temperature base distribution rescaled by a factor capturing future trajectory quality, enabling autoregressive approximation without trajectory-level MCMC (Theorem 3.1).

On MATH500 and GPQA, the training-free power sampling method matches or surpasses one-shot GRPO trained on MATH: e.g. Qwen2.5-Math-7B reaches 0.409 on GPQA versus GRPO's 0.399, without relying on any external reward model (Table 1).
On Qwen2.5-Math-7B for MATH500, the method reduces per-prompt inference latency to 0.22 minutes versus 2.5 minutes for MCMC-based sampling, an approximately 11x speedup (Figure 2, Section 4.2).
The method reduces inference latency by over 10x compared to MCMC-based sampling while maintaining reasoning performance comparable to reward-trained baselines (Section 4.2).

ebZcMQImhG.text: On Travel Planner, π-Distill with Qwen3-8B reaches 44.1% ± 2.16 accuracy versus 32.3% ± 1.10 for the SFT w/ CoT + RL industry-standard baseline (Table 1, Section 5).
On τ-Bench Retail, π-Distill with α=0 scores 31.1% ± 0.73 versus 29.1% ± 2.14 for the baseline (Table 1, Section 5).
On the out-of-domain τ-Bench Airline task, π-Distill with α=1 reaches 12.0% ± 6.00 versus 8.00% ± 3.46 for the baseline (Table 1, Section 6).
The joint teacher-student setting with α=0.5 performs best in 7 of 16 evaluated scenarios, showing robustness across settings (Section 5).
Out-of-domain generalization is evaluated on 7 GEM search-tool QA datasets (2Wiki, PopQA, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, Bamboogle, NaturalQuestions, Musique) (Section 6, Figure 4).
Ablations show a non-zero KL penalty β is crucial for settings involving teacher updates (α>0), while it matters less when α=0 (Section 8, Figure 9).

qhFEKDeBsO.text: The proposed variance decomposition splits model response variance into Intent Sensitivity (IS), Articulation Sensitivity (AS), and Model Uncertainty (MU), which are constructed to sum to 1 (Section 3).

Five models—LLaMA 3.2 3B, LLaMA 3.1 8B, LLaMA 3.3 70B, Gemma 3 12B-IT, and Gemma 3 27B-IT—are evaluated on 24 tasks across 5 domains using 10 paraphrases and 25 sampled responses per prompt-intent pair, yielding 1,772,492 total model responses (Section 4).

The two smallest models (LLaMA 3B and LLaMA 8B) exhibit high Model Uncertainty alongside low Intent Sensitivity and Articulation Sensitivity, whereas the three larger models (LLaMA 70B, Gemma 12B, Gemma 27B) show comparable IS/AS/MU profiles (Figure 2, Section 4.1).
The Intent Comprehension Index (ICI) combines the Meaningful Variability Share (MVS) with Intent Sensitivity (IS) into a single harmonic-mean-style summary statistic (Section 3, Eq. ICI).
The larger LLaMA and Gemma variants attribute roughly 50% of response variance to intent (IS), compared to roughly 20% for the two smaller LLaMA models (Figure 3).
Articulation Sensitivity (AS) varies by domain: Social Planning questions consistently show higher AS across all five models than Health and Nutrition, Transportation, or Personal Finance (Figure 4).

6cUXJo03zv.text: On parameter extrapolation for the Quadratic function family (Table 1), RTE achieves MSE 7.33×10^2 ± 1.19×10^1 versus 1.20×10^5 for the T2V inductive baseline and 1.18×10^5 for the inductive oracle (Table 1, Section 3.1).
On length extrapolation to degree-9 polynomials, RTE achieves MSE 0.3712 ± 0.1021 versus 0.5752 ± 0.1421 for the naive baseline, with an oracle at 0.0497 ± 0.0093 (Table 2, Section 3.2).
On aggregate compositional extrapolation across unseen primitive-combination pairs, RTE achieves MSE 0.2867 ± 0.0270 versus 0.3891 ± 0.0378 for the naive baseline (Table 3, Section 3.3).
On the Sparse Parity length-extrapolation benchmark with held-out subset size |S|=6, RTE reaches 66.07% accuracy versus 52.86% for the standard fine-tuning baseline (Table 4, Section 4.1).
RTE nearly doubles accuracy relative to the fine-tuning baseline on the CodeIO compositional-extrapolation benchmark, though it remains below the oracle (Section 4.1).
RTE's continuous-regime anchor selection uses Task2Vec embeddings derived from the Fisher Information Matrix of a pretrained model as its proxy geometry (Section 2.3, Section 2.4.2).

1piRnQJhLc.text: CORAL trains a four-hidden-layer weight-decay MLP probe (dimensions 1024, 512, 256, 128) on 8.4k-10k labeled questions to predict residual correctness from frozen residual-stream activations (Section 3.2.2, Eq. 3).
CORAL is evaluated on three 7B-parameter models—Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Deepseek-7B-Chat—across MMLU, RACE, and CommonsenseQA (Table 1, Section 4.1).
On RACE with Deepseek-LLM-7B-Chat, CORAL outperforms the second-best baseline method by 17.39 percentage points in accuracy and achieves a 64% relative improvement in ECE (Section 4.1, Table 1).
CORAL transfers without retraining to four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, Math-MC), averaging 14% accuracy improvements and 49% ECE improvements (Table 2, Section 4.3).

Sparse-autoencoder single-neuron ablation across 300 selected features produces a mean ECE change of only 1.25×10^-4 (0.0125 percentage points), showing individual neurons have negligible causal effect on correctness signals compared to CORAL's 15+ point gains (Figure 3, Section 5.2).

fY2cXSIxHO.text: LassoFlexNet is evaluated across 52 datasets spanning three benchmarks—a 12-dataset feature-selection suite, the 35-dataset TabZilla suite, and the 8-dataset TabRed benchmark—achieving up to a 10% relative gain over tree-based models (Section 7).

In the ablation study on the California Housing dataset (Table 2), the full LassoFlexNet achieves test RMSE 0.4047 ± 0.0069, while removing EMA increases RMSE to 0.4195 ± 0.0117 and replacing the MLP-Mixer with a similarly-sized MLP backbone raises RMSE to 0.8453/0.8406 (Table 2, Section 6.1).

On the 35-dataset TabZilla suite, LassoFlexNet is benchmarked against XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, DeepFM, and TabM, with accuracy-differential boxplots showing it consistently outperforms these six baselines (Figure 2, Section 7.2).

On the TabRed benchmark (Table 5), LassoFlexNet achieves the best performance on 5 of 8 tasks against CatBoost, LightGBM, RF, XGBoost, and TabM-mini, trailing the top performer (CatBoost) by only 0.0005 RMSE on delivery-eta (Table 5, Section 7.3).

Proposition 6.1 proves that Piecewise Linear Encoding (PLE) breaks the rotational invariance of neural networks, and Proposition 6.2 shows PLE yields a T_i-fold increase in functional expressivity for feature i (Section 6, Propositions 6.1-6.2).

I3Z9za1EkO.text: On a diagnostic Indirect Indexing task requiring independent matching of content and position, RoPE achieves only 11.16% accuracy while PoPE achieves 94.82% accuracy (Section 5).
On music modeling, PoPE achieves lower negative log-likelihood than RoPE on both JSB (0.4889 vs 0.5081) and MAESTRO (1.486 vs 1.501) datasets (Section 5).
On the Human Reference Genome dataset, PoPE attains a lower NLL (4.152) than RoPE (4.217) (Section 5).
On OpenWebText language modeling, PoPE lowers perplexity relative to RoPE at all three tested scales: 21.33 vs 21.55 (124M), 18.55 vs 18.88 (253M), and 15.45 vs 15.85 (774M) (Section 5).

PoPE maintains stable perplexity on sequences up to 10x the training length without fine-tuning, while RoPE's perplexity degrades sharply, as shown against RoPE and YaRN extrapolation baselines (Figure 2).
On downstream zero-shot tasks (LAMBADA, BLiMP, CBT, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-E), PoPE improves mean accuracy over RoPE, e.g. 52.46 vs 51.80 for the 774M model (Table 5).

4wy2YAHKRF.text: KernelFoundry achieves an average speedup of 2.32x on filtered KernelBench for SYCL kernel generation across 111 tasks, with a 97% correctness rate (Table 2).
On KernelBench Level 2 tasks, KernelFoundry attains a 2.1x average speedup versus 1.61x for prior work, while Level 1 tasks reach 1.24x average speedup (Table 1).
On robust-kbench, KernelFoundry produces kernels with 36% higher speedup than baseline kernels across 12 tasks including backward operations (Section on robust-kbench evaluation).
In cross-GPU hardware-awareness experiments, 70% of generated kernels run faster on their intended target GPU, with a 1.537x average speedup for LNL-optimized kernels versus alternatives (Table 3).

In a real-world case study optimizing the Llama 3.2 rotary positional embedding kernel, KernelFoundry achieves a 7.9x kernel speedup within ten iterations, reducing full forward-pass time by 8% (Section on case study).

Azk4mutSxF.text: D-Judge reduces the average attack success rate (ASR) of multi-turn jailbreaks on HarmBench against a GPT-4o victim from 58.3% (no defense) to 8.6% (Section on multi-turn attack results).
D-Judge reduces Crescendo attack ASR from 81.8% to 12.0% and X-Teaming attack ASR from 73.0% to 17.0% on HarmBench (Section on multi-turn attack results).
D-Judge also reduces single-turn jailbreak ASR, cutting PAIR from 64.0% to 30.0% and TAP from 80.2% to 36.0% (Section on single-turn attack results).
Combining D-Judge with the internal Circuit Breakers defense achieves a 3.0% average ASR across attacks (Section on complementary defenses).
D-Judge preserves benign multi-turn performance, with MT-Bench score dropping only from 8.99 to 8.34 and IFEval nearly matching the unmodified baseline (Section on benign performance).

D-Judge is trained via SFT plus DPO on 17,988 semantics-preserving response pairs derived from PKU-SafeRLHF with a Semantic Gate based on bidirectional NLI entailment (Section on dataset construction and method).

5a321ueqgs.text: Predictive prefetching reduces end-to-end RAG latency by 43.5% compared to a synchronous RAG baseline (Section on latency results).
Predictive prefetching improves time-to-first-token by 62.4%, reducing it from 287ms to 108ms on HotpotQA (Section on TTFT results).

The retrieval predictor forecasts retrieval need 8-16 tokens in advance by monitoring hidden states, attention patterns, and value vectors from middle-upper transformer layers at 30-45% model depth (Section on method/retrieval predictor).

Answer quality remains comparable to synchronous RAG, with only a 0.5-0.9% exact-match gap across benchmarks including HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, RepoBench-P, and QMSum (Section on evaluation).
The method achieves 31% fewer retrievals per 1K tokens through intelligent prefetching relative to the synchronous baseline (Section on retrieval efficiency results).

HKzMnBX5B2.text: Theorem 4.1 proves a policy hierarchy result: there exists an MDP in which policies allotted more compute time are arbitrarily better than policies with less compute time despite identical parameter counts (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 shows compute-constrained policies can overfit to training-horizon tasks and fail on longer-horizon evaluation tasks, whereas higher-compute policies generalize successfully (Theorem 4.2).
The proposed Interpolation Recurrent Unit (IRU) architecture allows variable computation with fixed parameter count by scaling from 1 to 10+ recurrent iterations (Section on IRU architecture).

On the Boxpick-exact-4 task, scaling IRU compute from 1 to 10 recurrent steps yields an 88x performance improvement, and IRU with 5 recurrent steps outperforms ResNets using 5x more parameters on challenging tasks (Section 5, experiments across 31 tasks).

IRU trained on short-horizon tasks generalizes to longer-horizon evaluation tasks, converging faster than baselines on 5 of 5 compared tasks, while deep feedforward/ResNet baselines show higher variance and worse asymptotic performance (Figure 4).

Ablations show LSTM slightly outperforms IRU, recurrent ResNets fail to capture the benefit of additional compute, deep recursion underperforms, and gating mechanisms are essential to IRU's performance (Figure 7).

o4TAPjQnI6.text: Bio-PM achieves an average Macro-F1 of 0.65 versus 0.59 for the TF-C contrastive baseline across six subject-disjoint HAR benchmarks (UMH, PAMAP2, WISDM, MHealth, WHARF, HAD) (Table 1).
The model is pretrained on an NHANES accelerometer corpus of approximately 28k hours, 11k participants, and 10M windows sampled at 80 Hz (Section 4).
Bio-PM outperforms the AugPred baseline by +0.21 average Macro-F1 and an equal-chunk masked-reconstruction baseline by +0.18 average Macro-F1 (Table 1).
The largest single-dataset improvement is on MHealth, where Bio-PM reaches 0.80 Macro-F1 versus 0.68 for the next-best method, a gain of +0.12 (Table 1).
Bio-PM is consistently best or tied-best across subject budgets, showing stronger label efficiency in low-data regimes on WISDM and MHealth (Section 4.2, Figure 4).
Replacing the model's movement-segment tokenization with uniform-chunk tokenization reduces performance by 0.18 Macro-F1 on average, isolating tokenization's contribution (Table 2).

lgELNxtUNn.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes an Õ(1/√T) convergence rate for the last iterate of proximal SGD under componentwise convexity and L-smoothness of each fi (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).

The analysis replaces the standard bounded-variance assumption with the weaker requirement of a finite second moment of the gradient at the solution, E||∇fi(x*)||² = σ*² < ∞ (Section 2, Assumption 1).

Theorem 4.1 extends the Õ(1/√T) last-iterate rate to a randomized incremental proximal method when the regularizer decomposes additively and each component gj is Lipschitz continuous (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).

Section 4.4 applies the framework to a BlockProx algorithm for graph-guided regularizers used in multi-task and federated learning, proving last-iterate convergence without assuming bounded gradients (Section 4.4).
The obtained Õ(1/√T) rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the last-iterate guarantees for unconstrained SGD under bounded variance from Garrigos et al. (2025) (Section 4.1).

1lyagkzogH.text: DeepSeek-R1 shows a much larger performativity gap (probe-vs-monitor accuracy divergence) on easy recall-based MMLU questions (0.417) than on GPQA-Diamond (0.012) (Table 1, Section 5).

GPT-OSS similarly shows a larger performativity gap on MMLU (0.435) than on GPQA-Diamond (0.227), supporting the claim that easier questions elicit more performative chain-of-thought (Table 1, Section 5).

High-confidence chains-of-thought contain far fewer inflection points (backtracking or realizations) per step than non-high-confidence chains-of-thought, 0.020 versus 0.045, indicating inflections track genuine rather than performative uncertainty (Table 2, Section 6).
Confidence-based early exit at a 95% confidence threshold saves 68% of generated tokens on MMLU while retaining 97% of full accuracy (Figure 8, Section 7).
Confidence-based early exit at an 80% confidence threshold saves 30% of generated tokens on GPQA-Diamond while retaining 97% of full accuracy (Figure 8, Section 7).

sgNhWbqXfJ.text: Definition 2.1 formalizes 'left-shift' anomalies, and on YelpChi, anomalies show lower spectral energy in 26 of the graph's 32 features (Section 2.2, Definition 2.1).
On synthetic graphs with 20% injected anomalies, over half of the low-frequency spectral energy shifts into the high-frequency region, validating the local spectral energy formulation (Figure 3).
EGNN attains F1-macro scores of 70.50, 86.03, and 61.41 on the temporal MSL, SWaT, and WADI benchmarks respectively while using only 53,953 parameters, far fewer than competing methods (Table 1).
An ablation replacing EGNN's learnable fusion with fixed equal-weight fusion drops performance on YelpChi from 76.89 to 49.44 F1-macro, showing learnable fusion is critical (Table 2).

The temporal extension of EGNN relies on energy-driven message passing and adaptive gating within sliding windows rather than specialized sequence modules such as recurrent or attention layers (Section 1).

wfRp2gkofq.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes frame bounds for vector diffusion wavelets, showing the transform is stably invertible and robust to additive noise (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 proves vector diffusion wavelets are equivariant to rotations, satisfying ψ̃ⱼ(R·w) = R·ψ̃ⱼ(w) for all rotation matrices R ∈ SO(d) (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 3.3 extends rotational equivariance to the full scattering coefficients whenever the network's activation functions commute with rotations (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.3).

On a synthetic ellipsoid diameter-prediction task, ESc-GNN achieves 0.0037±0.0022 test MSE using 59,779 parameters, outperforming EGNN (284,036 parameters) and TFN (29,672,961 parameters) (Table 1, Section 4).

On a synthetic node-level vector-field prediction task on ellipsoid surfaces, ESc-GNN achieves 0.1513±0.0080 test MSE with 57,250 parameters, second only to TFN despite using under 0.2% of its parameter count (Table 2, Section 4).
VDW-GNNs are also demonstrated to be effective on real-world data derived from wind-field and neural activity measurements, in addition to synthetic point cloud data (abstract only).

OJSCaDIIJK.text: SMAC achieves smooth offline-to-online transfer with no initial performance drop when fine-tuning with Soft Actor-Critic across all 6 D4RL tasks (hopper-medium-replay-v2, walker2d-medium-replay-v2, kitchen-partial-v0, door-binary-v0, pen-binary-v0, relocate-binary-v0), whereas baselines like TD3+BC drop in 5/6 environments (Section 7, Figures 6-8).

SMAC reduces regret by 34-58% over the best baseline in 4 of 6 environments when fine-tuning with SAC, e.g. door regret of 50.3 versus 129.7-134.5 for baselines, and kitchen regret of 131.4 versus 467.1-762.5 for baselines (Section 7, Table 2).
SMAC attains normalized regret of 0.031 with SAC fine-tuning and 0.090 with TD3 fine-tuning, compared to IQL's 0.471 and 0.653 respectively (Table 1).

Offline and online policy optima are connected by low-reward valleys for baseline methods (e.g. CalQL), while SMAC's score-matching regularizer produces a linearly connected, monotonically improving path between offline and online optima (Section 5, Figures 1, 3, 4).

SMAC regularizes the Q-function's action gradient to match a diffusion-model-estimated behavior-policy score via the loss ||∇ₐQ(s,a) - αψ(s)ε_ω(s,a,w,1)||²₂, grounded in the max-entropy identity ∇ₐlogπ*(a|s) = (1/α)∇ₐQ*(s,a) (Section 6.2).
Replacing Adam with the Muon optimizer is critical to SMAC's transfer stability: an ablation shows performance drops in 3 of 6 environments when Muon is removed (Appendix I).

Wcl5b7O2KT.text: Multi-Task Bayesian ICL represents prior information explicitly as a prefix of in-context datasets (structured as <prior> pairs followed by <target> pairs), enabling test-time adaptation to new priors without retraining (Methodology section).

On flow-based heavy-tailed priors, Multi-task ICL matches MCMC-hier's predictive KL divergence (0.262±0.024 vs 0.246±0.024) while running in 6.24×10⁻³ seconds versus 1.3×10³ to 1.65×10⁴ seconds for MCMC-hier, and roughly 950 seconds for SVI-hier (Table 11).

On out-of-meta-distribution heavy-tailed Student-t priors (log ν ranging from 3 to -3), the method achieves near-oracle performance across extreme regimes, tracking MCMC-hier's generalization pattern (Figure 5).

In logistic regression experiments, Multi-task ICL recovers oracle Bayesian performance at short context length (5 examples) where standard ICL fails, with the performance gap narrowing by context length 20 (Figure 3).

On the ERA5 2019 IID spatiotemporal temperature prediction task, conditioning on K=2 prior datasets improves validation NLL from -1.72 to -2.29, with gains maintained on the 2020 held-out test year (Table 3).

gyOWJpP8cQ.text: Proposition 3.2 proves that, under normalized data with Q=K=X/h and V=I_n, self-attention recovers the exact normalized Gaussian kernel density estimator formula, establishing attention as a functional generalization of KDE (Proposition 3.2).

The transformer density/score estimator achieves substantially lower MSE than KDE across dimensions 1-10 and generalizes to Gaussian mixture models with up to 19 modes despite being trained only on 1-10 modes (Figure 4).
On a 2D Laplace distribution at sample size n=2048, the transformer achieves MSE of 0.2756 versus 0.2990 for KDE (Table 1).
The transformer exhibits sub-quadratic runtime scaling and remains tractable at n=32,768 samples, a regime where KDE runs out of GPU memory (Figure 11).

The learned score function is used to construct score-debiased KDE (SD-KDE), reducing bias from O(h²) to O(h⁴), and to compute plug-in entropy/Fisher information estimates via equations (10)-(11) (Section 4/Applications).

A single pre-trained model, without retraining, is applied to solve Fokker-Planck-type PDEs for a Landau equation plasma simulation, matching the analytical covariance evolution (Applications section).

IhdGi9qknL.text: The Implicit Intelligence benchmark comprises 205 scenarios across four categories: Implicit Reasoning (70 scenarios), Catastrophic Risk (56), Privacy & Security (46), and Accessibility (33) (Dataset section).
Across 16 frontier and open-weight models evaluated, the best-performing model, GPT-5.2-pro, achieves only 48.3% scenario pass rate (SPR) on the benchmark (Results table).
Claude Opus 4.5 achieves 39.5% SPR and Gemini 3 Pro achieves 38.5% SPR, both well below GPT-5.2-pro's 48.3% and GPT-5's 44.9% (Results table).

The benchmark uses an Agent-as-a-World (AaW) methodology, a YAML-based specification system in which Claude Opus 4.5 simulates interactive environments, with deterministic pass conditions validated against human annotations (Methodology section).

13rCeoefry.text: Theorem 4.1 provides a non-asymptotic multiclass nearest-class-center (NCC) error bound whose dominant term is 4·Ṽᵢⱼ (directional CDNV) with optimal leading constant 4, proven via Cantelli's inequality, plus three finite-shot correction terms decaying at rates m⁻¹, m⁻², and m⁻³ (Theorem 4.1).

Proposition 4.2 shows that for independent balanced labelings with small directional CDNV, the corresponding decision axes u_aa' and u_bb' satisfy an inner-product bound scaling with √(directional CDNV), forcing near-orthogonality of decision axes across tasks (Proposition 4.2).

Directional CDNV collapses by factors of 2⁻¹ to 2⁻⁵ during self-supervised pretraining across SimCLR, MAE, DINO-v2, and VICReg, while classical (non-directional) CDNV decreases only modestly over the same training, revealing anisotropic representation geometry (Figure 2).
The finite-shot NCC error bounds from Theorem 4.1 closely track observed few-shot classification errors and remain non-vacuous for shot counts m in the range 1 to 500 (Figure 3).

A multitask orthogonalization experiment on synthetic data confirms that decision axes derived from different semantic labelings become nearly orthogonal during training, empirically validating Proposition 4.2 (Figure 5).

A4qADJulVa.text: A batched primal-dual hybrid gradient (first-order) method solves multiple related LPs in parallel on GPUs by replacing repeated matrix-vector operations with batched matrix-matrix operations (Section 3).

Table 1 compares the batched first-order method against baseline approaches, reporting speedups across different problem classes arising in MIP subroutines like strong branching and bound tightening (Table 1).
Table 2 presents detailed wall-clock timing results showing the batched approach is competitive with simplex-based solvers on GPU hardware for certain problem sizes (Table 2).
Table 3 reports results on MIPLIB 2017 instances, showing the batched first-order method achieves substantial wall-clock time reductions compared to solving LPs sequentially (Table 3).
Whether first-order methods outperform simplex-based solvers depends on problem size and computational environment (e.g., GPU vs. CPU), rather than holding universally (Section 7).

EZL7l4U2kk.text: Non-Gradient Inference Flows (NGIF) infers non-gradient population dynamics by using a weak formulation of the continuity equation, exploiting a gauge freedom in the choice of vector field consistent with observed population dynamics (Section 2).

NGIF's parameterization allows selection criteria for the inferred vector field beyond minimal kinetic energy, generalizing the standard gradient-flow (optimal-transport) approach used by prior baselines (Section 3, subsections 3.1-3.4).
Experiments on low- and high-dimensional physics problems show NGIF improves distributional accuracy over gradient-restricted baselines (Section 4).
Table 5 gives a comparative summary showing NGIF better captures non-potential transport than gradient-flow baselines across the tested settings (Table 5).
Figures 1-4 visually compare NGIF's inferred trajectories/densities against gradient-restricted baselines across the experimental settings (Section 4, Figures 1-4).

zM5MbWc6wc.text: Theorem 4.1 gives an exact non-asymptotic characterization of when PPI++ has lower estimation error (mean squared error) than using gold-standard labels alone, as a function of the correlation between pseudo-labels and gold-standard labels and the number of labeled samples n (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

For Gaussian data, PPI++ outperforms the gold-standard-only estimator if and only if the correlation between pseudo- and gold-standard labels is at least 1/sqrt(n-2), a finite-sample threshold that vanishes only as n grows (Section 4.1).

The paper derives exact non-asymptotic variance expressions for PPI++ under sample splitting, in contrast to prior asymptotic 'free lunch' results claiming PPI++ variance is always at most that of gold-standard-only estimation (Section 4, Propositions 4.1-4.6).
Corollaries 4.1-4.2 extend the main finite-sample no-free-lunch result to derived estimation settings beyond the basic mean-estimation case (Section 4, Corollaries 4.1-4.2).
Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate that the theoretical finite-sample threshold on correlation predicts when PPI++ underperforms gold-standard-only estimation in practice (Section 5).

rQxW0hnXYh.text: LEO (Learning Everything all at Once) jointly outputs values and actions for all goals in a single network pass, enabling off-policy learning from every transition with respect to every goal without explicit relabelling (Section 3).

LEO's efficient all-goals updates incur only a 34% slowdown relative to single-goal learning, versus naive all-goals relabelling which is reported as 264x slower in throughput, yielding the reported >250x speed-up (Figure 2).
On the full CraftaxGC benchmark with 512 goals, Dual LEO (PPO variant) substantially outperforms baselines including PQN, PPO, and PQN+HER (Figure 4).
Individual-goal analysis shows plain LEO performs strongly on hard goals but underperforms on easy goals, a gap that Dual LEO resolves by combining both regimes (Figure 5).
On the JaxGCRL continuous-control U-Maze task, SAC+LEO outperforms all baselines, while on larger mazes LEO, SAC+HER, and Contrastive RL perform comparably (Figure 7).

rQ7eobSCZZ.text: LLMs are trained via reinforcement learning on synthetic question-answer pairs generated from randomized scenes in physics simulators (e.g., MuJoCo), rather than internet-sourced QA data (Section 2).

Training solely on this synthetic simulated data improves performance on International Physics Olympiad (IPhO) problems by 5-10 percentage points across different model sizes, demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-real transfer (Section 4).
Tables 6-9 report performance comparisons showing consistent gains from simulator-based RL training over baseline models across the tested benchmarks (Tables 6-9).
Tables 10-12 present ablation studies examining components of the simulator-based training pipeline (Tables 10-12).
Tables 15-16 report sim-to-real transfer results, quantifying how skills learned purely from simulated physics scenarios transfer to real-world physics reasoning benchmarks (Tables 15-16).

SxsyLjIfWB.text: TabICLv2 without any hyperparameter tuning surpasses the tuned-and-ensembled RealTabPFN-2.5 on the TabArena benchmark and dominates the Pareto front of accuracy vs. runtime (Figure 1).
On the TALENT benchmark, TabICLv2 maintains top rankings across dataset sizes from 10^3 to 10^5 samples and outperforms RealTabPFN-2.5 specifically on datasets larger than 20,000 samples (Figure 5).
TabICLv2 is 10.6x faster than TabPFN-2.5 on an H100 GPU at 50,000 samples and 11.8x faster on CPU at 10,000 samples (Figure 6).
Via disk offloading, TabICLv2 processes a 1M-sample by 500-feature table within 450 seconds using under 24 GB of CPU memory and 50 GB of GPU memory (Section 4.2).
Pretraining TabICLv2 costs 24.5 H100 GPU-days using the Muon optimizer, less than the original TabICL's reported 60 A100-days (Section 4.1).

An ablation study ranks synthetic prior design as the largest contributor to performance, with early target inclusion, the Muon optimizer, and query-aware scalable softmax (QASSMax) each contributing roughly a 100-Elo gain (Section 7, Figure 10).

hdak3I0DYY.text: The derived metric gamma = ||mu||/||sigma|| (ratio of activation mean magnitude to per-token standard deviation) predicts dead-by-ReLU feature death probability as Phi(-C/gamma) with C approximately 4.26 (Section 4.1).
Across 454 model-layer combinations, gamma predicts dead-by-TopK feature death with Spearman rho = 0.89 and dead-by-ReLU death with Spearman rho = 0.82 (Table S1, Figure 4).
Initial SAE feature death rates vary dramatically across models with identical SAE configurations, from near 0% on GPT-2 to over 70% on AlphaFold3 and up to 98% on some ESM3 layers (Figure 2).
Dead-by-TopK features recover within about 200,000 training steps, whereas dead-by-ReLU features plateau at only 75-90% recovery even after 2,000,000 steps (Section 5).

Mean-centering activations before SAE training eliminates outlier-induced feature death, reducing AlphaFold3's dead-feature rate from 98% to under 5% and ESM3's from 83% to near 0% (Section 6, Figure 6).
A mean-centered SAE with only 2048 dictionary features recovers 100 biological concepts, compared to 73 concepts recovered by a baseline (non-centered) 8192-feature SAE (Table 1).

mnUidYi5qO.text: On the Knights-and-Knaves task with Gemma 3 4B, the base model scores 31.0% accuracy, SimpleSE reaches 40.7%, RevisionSE reaches 42.2%, while oracle supervision reaches 53.3%, leaving a persistent 8-13 percentage point gap (Table 3, Section on Gemma results).

With Gemma 3 12B, RevisionSE (iterative revision using natural language feedback) achieves 52.8% accuracy versus 53.6% for oracle supervision, nearly closing the gap to about 98.5% of oracle performance (Table 3).
Iterative training over 3 rounds improves accuracy from 31.0% to 44.1% on the base 4B model (Table 1).
Curriculum learning improves accuracy to 44.8% versus a 31.0% baseline (Table 2).
On real-world benchmarks, self-evolution strategies yield only modest gains of +1.6% on MATH500 and +2.9% on TabMWP (Table 4).

Across all tested self-evolution strategies, including more resource-intensive revision approaches and online RL, a substantial performance gap versus oracle-supervised training persists (Section on main results, Figure 1).

xtWQnuo8YO.text: NeuroLDS achieves the lowest discrepancy at every tested sequence length for all three loss types (D2-symmetric, D2-star, D2-centered) compared to classical Sobol', Halton, and scrambled Sobol' sequences (Section 3.1, Figure 2).
At N=10,000, NeuroLDS attains a symmetric L2 discrepancy of 0.000098 versus 0.000167 for Sobol', and a star discrepancy of 0.000213 versus 0.000266 for Sobol' (Table 6, Appendix E).

On the 8-dimensional borehole uncertainty-quantification integration benchmark, NeuroLDS achieves the best or second-best integration error for all but two tested values of N (Section 3.2.1, Table 1).

In an RRT robot motion planning task through kinematic-chain passages, NeuroLDS achieves success rates of 73-97% across passage widths, versus 65-73% for Sobol' and 67-88% for Halton (Section 3.2.2, Table 2).
On a 2D Black-Scholes European basket option pricing PDE, NeuroLDS attains MSE of 3.34x10^-4 versus 4.04x10^-4 for Sobol' (Section 3.2.3, Table 3).

An ablation shows that the two-stage training scheme is essential: pretraining NeuroLDS to align with Sobol'/Halton via MSE before fine-tuning on discrepancy loss is necessary, since direct discrepancy minimization without pretraining collapses to degenerate solutions (Section 3.3).

418BWmKIzX.text: The paper's polynomial-time algorithm learns margin-separable halfspaces under distribution drift with Massart noise achieving error eta + O~(Delta^{1/3}/gamma), where eta bounds the Massart noise rate, Delta is the drift rate, and gamma is the margin parameter (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.1).

Under the low-degree polynomial hardness conjecture, any efficient algorithm for this drifting halfspace problem must incur excess error Omega(Delta^{1/3}), matching the algorithm's guarantee and establishing an information-computation gap (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.1).

For general VC-dimension-d hypothesis classes under Massart noise, the statistically optimal (possibly inefficient) error rate is O~(sqrt(d*Delta)), better than the Theta((d*Delta)^{1/3}) rate achievable under adversarial noise (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).

A matching information-theoretic lower bound of Omega(sqrt(d*Delta)) is proved for halfspaces under random classification noise (RCN), establishing optimality at Theta~(sqrt(d*Delta)) (Theorem 2.2, Section 2).

Theorem 4.1 formally shows that no polynomial of degree less than O(gamma^{-c/4}) can distinguish the null from alternative hypothesis in the associated trajectory-testing problem, giving the formal low-degree hardness evidence for the Delta^{1/3} scaling (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
In the realizable setting, the algorithm's error improves to O~(Delta*gamma^{-3/2}), surpassing the prior best known bound of O~(Delta*gamma^{-2}) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).

82EJxJzG6r.text: Theorem 3.3 proves that any k-layer state-space model solving the function-composition tasks under injectivity conditions must have total log state-space size scaling as Ω(m·log|V| − q·log|Y|), linear in the hidden dimension m (Theorem 3.3).
Theorem 3.7 proves that sliding-window Transformers solving the same tasks under a local-sensitivity condition require total window size scaling with the context-dependency range R (Theorem 3.7).

Theorem 4.3 constructs a two-layer hybrid (Mamba + attention) model that solves the selective copying task using embedding dimension O(max(log|V|, log L)) and working memory Õ(N), versus Ω(L) required by pure Transformers (Theorem 4.3).
Theorem 4.6 constructs a three-layer hybrid model that achieves 99% accuracy on the associative recall task using embedding dimension O(max(log|V|, log L)) and window size Õ(|V|) (Theorem 4.6).

On the selective copying task, the learned hybrid model reaches perfect accuracy with roughly 2,000 parameters while pure Transformer/SSM models need roughly 12,000 parameters to match it, a 6x parameter gap (Figure 4).

On multi-key associative recall, the hybrid model reaches 60% accuracy using 6x fewer parameters than pure Transformers, which plateau near 40% accuracy on single-key associative recall (Figures 5-6).

xfHppnGXaH.text: Section 3.2 introduces a surrogate stochastic process that adds a reference noise schedule σ_ref(t) to the flow-based generative model, preserving marginal distributions while enabling policy-gradient RL without computing an explicit score function (Section 3.2).

Section 3.3 replaces a handcrafted noise-annealing schedule with a learned time-dependent schedule s^θ(t), improving robustness of crystal structure prediction across different numbers of integration steps (Section 3.3, Figures 4-5).

Both score-based and velocity-based RL variants reduce per-atom energy by approximately 0.5 relative to the pretrained baseline while using only 50 integration steps, compared to 740 steps for the original model (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

OMatG-IRL recovers baseline crystal structure prediction performance using only 100 integration steps versus 950 for the original model, and shows only minor degradation even at 10 steps, yielding an order-of-magnitude reduction in generation time (Section 4.3).

Q9LweGI2B9.text: Equation 4 formalizes the bias of naive aggregate retrieval metrics as Bias(μ̂naive) = Σ_k(ŵ_k − w_k)μ_k, showing that coverage gaps across semantic regimes directly bias overall performance estimates (Section 3, Equation 4).

On the NFCorpus benchmark, standard query sets achieve only 50.9% minimum semantic coverage of the corpus, while the proposed stratified evaluation construction achieves 90.3% coverage (Section 5.3, Table 4).

Zero-query semantic clusters contain 17.3% of the corpus but receive only 1.1% of queries in standard benchmarks, revealing systematic coverage gaps concentrated in methodological topics (Section 5.3, Table 4).

Within-stratum standard deviation of retrieval performance is consistently lower than overall standard deviation, validating that the semantic strata correspond to genuinely distinct, more homogeneous retrieval regimes (Section 5.2, Table 2).

Structural signals — relevance dispersion Δ and query-document semantic alignment J (Jaccard similarity of entity clusters) — partition queries into regimes differing by nearly 3x in retrieval performance (Section 5.2, Table 3).

System rankings by win rate vary from 32% to 63% depending on which aggregation/weighting protocol is used over the semantic strata, showing that evaluation conclusions are sensitive to how coverage is weighted (Section 5.3, Figures 4-5).

oPqm8k1CMQ.text: Definition 3.1 defines Action Selection (AS) informativeness ℐ_th(ω) as the expected total improvement in oracle belief quality achieved under a given query policy (Definition 3.1).

Theorem 3.4 characterizes a two-dimensional locking regime in which improvement in AS is bounded by belief-tracking (BT) capability (ΔQ_ℐth ≲ ηC_BT(ω)) and improvement in BT is bounded by AS informativeness, formalizing the coupling that traps agents in low-information interaction patterns (Theorem 3.4).
AReW (advantage reweighting with AS+BT proxy signals) improves MediQ accuracy from 50.50 to 61.25 (+10.8 points) over the vanilla RL baseline (Table 1).
On the PE-G task with S=3 candidate items, AReW improves accuracy from 18.33 to 80.33 (+62.0 points), and on FloDial-Hard from 21.33 to 42.33 (+21.0 points) over vanilla RL (Table 1).
AReW remains effective even when the directional critique signals used for reweighting are corrupted with 50% noise, indicating robustness to imperfect proxy AS/BT signals (Table 2).

NvPgRwURDC.text: The benchmark comprises 52 spreadsheet action trajectories totaling 11,907 symbolic operations, with sequence lengths ranging from 35 to 821 steps (mean 229, median 164), constructed via a three-stage symbolic cold-start, LLM refinement, and human annotation pipeline (Section 2).
An empirical predictability ceiling analysis finds that only 68% of operations are theoretically predictable from history across frontier LLM oracles (Section 2.1).

The online evaluation methodology (Section 3, Figure 4) predicts the next action from history H and current state S after every user action, accepts or rejects the prediction, and on acceptance adapts the future action sequence by removing satisfied operations, prepending inverses for false positives, and patching residuals to reach the target state.

Under the single-action repredict setting (stride s=1), GPT-5-R attains the best User-Actions-Saved rate of 32.7%, an acceptance rate of 29.4%, and precision of 41.6%, outperforming GPT-5 and a fine-tuned SmolLM2-360M baseline (Table 2).

Accepting every model prediction without utility-aware filtering yields a User-Actions-Saved rate of −19.2%, demonstrating that selective abstention is essential for a positive net benefit (Section 3.1).
Increasing the prediction stride from s=1 to s=8 drops User-Actions-Saved from 27.4% to 10.6%, motivating the need for cheaper triggering mechanisms between prediction calls (Section 3.1).

MjPv4kRu3H.text: Introduces Wasserstein Lagrangian Mechanics (WLM), deriving Hamiltonian equations of motion (position evolution via dx_t/dt=∇s_t(x_t) and velocity evolution with damping term −γv_t) from a damped Wasserstein least-action principle (Theorem 2.2).

Shows that WLM's expressivity encompasses gradient flows as a special case: overdamped limit (γ→∞) recovers Wasserstein gradient flows, and a conservative (γ=0) system with inverted potential gives an alternative characterization (Proposition 2.4).

Learns population mechanics from observed marginal snapshots without specifying the Lagrangian, using a tractable functional-derivative characterization for empirical measures that enables automatic differentiation of accelerations (Proposition 3.1, Algorithm 1).

On the unpaired gradient-flow SDE benchmark across 5 potential landscapes, WLM with learnable friction achieves lower forecast Wasserstein-1 distance (0.246±0.026) than JKOnet* (1.618±0.261) (Table 1).
On the embryonic scRNA-seq (EB) leave-one-out interpolation task, WLM attains W1=0.704±0.021, outperforming OT-MFM (0.713±0.039), WLF-UOT (0.738±0.014), and OT-CFM (0.790±0.068) (Table 3).

On the Boids emergent-flocking benchmark, WLM captures periodic flocking behavior and achieves forecast W1=1.309±0.034, far better than nn-APPEX (3.078±0.199) and JKOnet* (3.174±0.084), which only produce diffusion (Table 4).

bO7YMfd1mp.text: Proposes a stage-wise energy accounting protocol that decomposes distillation pipelines into prerun, teacher-work, student-training, and evaluation stages, using NVML GPU telemetry as ground truth alongside CodeCarbon for CPU/CO2e estimates (Section 4).

Applies the protocol to OLMo-2 models (32B teacher; 1B, 7B, 13B students) across three pipelines—baseline SFT, logit-based knowledge distillation, and synthetic SFT—on instruction-following, math, and code tasks (Section 3, Section 5).

Finds that at the 1B student scale, KD and synthetic SFT pipelines require roughly 2.4x more end-to-end energy than baseline SFT (16.90 kWh and 16.65 kWh vs 7.00 kWh) for only marginal quality gains (Table 2, Figure 1).

Shows teacher-side work (logit caching or synthetic generation) is a fixed ~11 kWh cost independent of student size, dominating energy use for small students but becoming amortized relative to student training as student size grows to 13B (Table 3, Figure 2).

Derives a break-even teacher-reuse threshold formula (Eq. 4) showing distillation becomes energy-competitive with baseline SFT only after roughly 10 reuses of the teacher artifacts for 1B students, dropping to about 2-3 reuses for 13B students (Section 6.3, Figure 3).

Reports that the full experimental grid (core runs plus KD temperature/loss-weight and synthetic-SFT budget sensitivity sweeps) consumed approximately 2,000 H100 GPU-hours (~83 GPU-days) (Section 6.4).

n90nG9NXBF.text: Identifies a 'proximity bias' in non-autoregressive masked diffusion language models whereby denoising concentrates on positions spatially adjacent to those unmasked in the previous step, producing reverse-autoregressive collapse instead of parallel generation (Section 3.1, Figure 3).

Finds that end-of-sequence tokens dominate early unmasking decisions, with EOS tokens comprising over 50% of unmasked tokens across most diffusion steps and occupying on average 144.6 of 256 positions, constricting the effective generation window (Section 3.1).

Shows randomizing only the first denoising position yields substantially higher pass@k performance than applying temperature sampling across all steps, with correct trajectories reaching 50.2% accuracy versus 34.4% for incorrect early choices (Section 3.2, Figures 4-5).
Proposes a lightweight 5M-parameter planner (2-layer Transformer, 128 hidden dims) plus EOS temperature annealing (λ_d = 3 − 2d/T) to guide initial trajectory shaping (Section 4).

At T=32 timesteps, combining the planner with EOS annealing improves GSM8K accuracy from 46.6% (top-1 confidence baseline) to 56.8%, and Prob-Margin+Both reaches 58.6% (+~10-12 percentage points) (Table 1).

Demonstrates the method generalizes across timestep budgets and models: at T=128 GSM8K improves from 23.3% to 61.0% (+37.7pp) on the base model (Table 2), and on Dream 7B Instruct GSM8K improves from 39.9% to 52.4% (+12.5pp) (Table 7), while incurring negligible inference overhead (2.54s vs 2.65s on A100).

1BchRVONfp.text: Proposes Algorithm 2, a Gradient Method with Randomized Feasibility using an adaptive Polyak-type stepsize, and proves linear convergence in expectation to a prescribed tolerance ε for strongly convex, Lipschitz-smooth objectives, with iteration complexity O(log(1/ε)) (Theorem 4.4).

Introduces Algorithm 3, DoWS (Distance over Weighted Subgradients) with Randomized Feasibility, a parameter-free adaptive-stepsize method for convex possibly-nonsmooth objectives, proving an O(1/√T) worst-case convergence rate in expectation (Theorem 5.3).
Introduces Algorithm 4, T-DoWS (Tamed DoWS), which removes the requirement that the constraint set Y be bounded, retaining an O(1/√T) rate up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 5.5).

Proves (Lemma 3.1) that infeasibility of iterates under the randomized feasibility update decreases geometrically almost surely with the number of feasibility updates, without requiring compactness of Y.

Validates the theory on quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) simulations under strongly convex and convex objectives with known/unknown optimal value f*, confirming predicted function-value decay and geometric infeasibility reduction (Figure 1).

Evaluates Algorithms 3 and 4 against a primal-dual baseline on SVM classification with three real datasets (Banknote Authentication, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, MNIST 3-vs-5), comparing test misclassification error (Figure 2).

67lpPXbYf6.text: Introduces the euro (Expected Utility Renormalized by the Oracle) metric, defined via true-positive/true-negative counts relative to an oracle policy and a risk-level parameter u_ca, to jointly assess calibration and decision-utility of LLM confidence estimates (Section 2.3).

Proposes the acute protocol, which extracts mean-pooled activations, layer-wise cosine similarities to the final layer, and PCA-reduced activations, then trains random forest classifiers on these features to produce calibrated confidence scores (Section 3.1-3.2).

Evaluates six models (Gemma-3 4B/12B, Qwen3 4B/14B, Phi-4, SmolLM3-3B) on MMLU (multiple-choice QA), APIGen (tool-calling), and SciTLDR (summarization), showing acute achieves higher auc-euro than both raw confidence and an NWKR calibration baseline on all three tasks, e.g. auc-euro=0.88 vs 0.78 (NWKR) vs 0.53 (raw) on APIGen (Table 1).
Shows middle-layer activations carry the strongest confidence signal across all tested models, consistent across model families (Section 5, Figure 6).
Demonstrates strong sample efficiency: on APIGen, acute trained on only 25 examples outperforms NWKR and HRE baselines trained on the full 1000-example set (Section 5.2, Figure 5).
Confirms generalization to a mixture-of-experts model, Qwen3-30B-A3B, where acute (mid-layer activations) attains smECE=0.057 and auc-euro=0.870 on APIGen (Table 2).

fDMizWsNoG.text: The transformer's forward pass for in-context linear classification is shown to implement a coupled mean-shift recursion, with attention matrix A_l = softmax(αX_lX_l^T + γY_lY_l^T) and update rules X_{l+1}=X_l+α'A_lX_l, Y_{l+1}=Y_l+γ'A_lY_l, given explicitly in equations (7)-(8) (Section 4.1).

Theorem 4.1 proves that under a label-driven regime the geometric margin between classes grows exponentially with depth, Δ_l ≥ Δ_0(1+α')^l, and the label margin similarly diverges after a burn-in period (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2).

Behavioral alignment between the symmetrized and original models is validated via three independent fingerprints (output probabilities, query Jacobians, and context-influence scores) all showing correlations above 0.95, confirming the extracted algorithm is not an artifact of the symmetrization procedure (Figure 3, Section 3).

Retrained transformers given semi-supervised prompts (labeled plus unlabeled points) improve in-context classification accuracy from about 72% to over 85% as unlabeled context grows, demonstrating unlabeled points sharpen class geometry (Figure 8, Section 5).

The mean-shift mechanism remains robust when 30% of in-context labels are randomly flipped, since correctly labeled points reinforce each other while flipped labels contribute canceling noise (Appendix B.3, Figures 12-13).

H2Wueh9MMy.text: Discrete Tilt Matching (DTM) fine-tuning of LLaDA-8B-Instruct achieves 99.2% accuracy on Sudoku versus 94.0% for the strongest RL baseline (SPG) and 27.7% for the base model (Table 1).
On Countdown, DTM reaches 81.6% accuracy compared to 70.7% for SPG and 16.8% for the base model (Table 1).

On MATH500, DTM scores 36.0%, below SPG's 40.0% but above the 32.4% base model score, indicating DTM's advantage is concentrated on structured planning tasks rather than open-ended mathematical reasoning (Table 1).
On GSM8K, DTM (81.6%) performs comparably to but slightly below UniGRPO (82.5%), both clearly exceeding the 77.2% base model score (Table 1).
Wall-clock comparisons on Sudoku show DTM converges faster than the SPG baseline while achieving higher final reward under identical compute (8 H100 GPUs) (Section on computational efficiency).

ga20H0vR6f.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes a PAC guarantee that, for a sufficiently small guessed minimum transition probability p_k, there exists a number of simulations N_k such that the learned policy is ε_k-optimal with probability at least 1-δ_k (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 shows that once the approximation error ε_k falls below a threshold ε_diff—the minimum value gap between optimal and suboptimal memoryless deterministic policies—any ε_k-optimal policy is guaranteed to be exactly optimal, not merely near-optimal (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.3 proves that using a summable failure schedule δ_k = 1/2^k, the Borel-Cantelli lemma guarantees only finitely many stages fail, so the algorithm's policy is exactly optimal from some finite stage onward with probability 1 (Theorem 3.3).

Theorem 4.1 bounds ε_diff via transition-complexity parameter D, showing ‖v_π − v_π'‖_1 ≥ (2D)^(-2|A|·|S|) 2^(-2|S|) for any two distinct memoryless deterministic policies, giving an explicit MDP-structure-dependent characterization of when exact optimality is reached (Theorem 4.1).

Empirical evaluation on standardized benchmarks shows the algorithm's policy becomes exactly optimal at a median stage k=2, far earlier than the stage (k≈16) at which the theoretical worst-case value-bound guarantees convergence (empirical validation section).

ODWi7lbMGU.text: In a real deployment across four HPC facilities (Argonne Aurora, Argonne Polaris, Oak Ridge Frontier, NERSC Perlmutter), FedQueue is the only algorithm to reach a test loss below 0.4 within a 17,000-second wall-clock budget, and reaches loss 0.6 about 1.78x faster than FedAvg and 1.36x faster than FedCompass (Table 1, Figure 2).
Median observed queue delays across the four production facilities range from 471 to 1015 seconds, with p90 delays reaching up to 1668 seconds, motivating FedQueue's queue-aware design (Table 2).
Under controlled simulations with high queue variance (ρ=0.9), FedQueue achieves roughly 37% faster time-to-target-accuracy than FedAvg and 60% faster than FedAsync (Table 4, Figure 3).

Lemma 5.4 proves that the admission-control mechanism induces bounded staleness with high probability whenever the safety buffer satisfies δ ≥ sqrt(2ρ²log(KR/ε)), underpinning the paper's O(1/√R) convergence rate result (Lemma 5.4).

Ablation experiments show removing the EWMA-based queue predictor degrades performance by roughly 330%, and removing the harmonic staleness-decay aggregation weight costs about 10% final accuracy (Table 5).

TzXcKru6Fa.text: Greedy Coordinate Diffusion (GCD) achieves a 100% HarmBench attack success rate against Mistral-7B, compared to 95.83% for the strongest baseline AutoDAN, and 70.83% against Llama-3-70B versus 29.17% for the best baseline Inpainting (Table 1).

Under a 90th-percentile perplexity-based filter, gradient-based attacks collapse (e.g., GCG's success rate on Qwen-2.5-7B drops from 68.75% to 0%), while GCD preserves 97.92% success on the same model, demonstrating resilience of the non-gradient, diffusion-guided token proposals to perplexity defenses (Table 1).

Against the Llama Guard-3-1B safety classifier, GCD retains high attack success rates across all four victim models (87.50% on Llama-3-8B, 85.42% on Qwen-2.5-7B, 97.92% on Mistral-7B, 64.58% on Llama-3-70B) (Table 2).

GCD produces adversarial prompts with self-perplexity in the 44-105 range, substantially lower than unconstrained gradient-based attacks, indicating high semantic coherence and fluency (Table 9, Appendix B.7).

GCD operates in a gray-box threat model that requires only token probability access rather than full gradients, using a 'One-Shot Diffusion' bridging step to fill remaining masked tokens before victim-model evaluation, addressing tokenizer incompatibility between attacker and victim models (Figure 1).

N44P3zrrgO.text: The paper models hierarchical reasoning in large reasoning models by introducing Q-value guided steering, which selects interventions based on estimated state values rather than token-level edits (Section 3, Modeling Hierarchical Thinking).

Q-value guided steering achieves comparable or better accuracy than greedy and weighted intervention baselines while requiring roughly an order of magnitude fewer interventions, as reported in the intervention-efficiency comparison (Section 5, Results; Table 2 ablation study).

On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Q-value guided steering is compared against greedy and weighted baselines with results reported per model size (Table 1, Results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks; Figure 4, Performance across different model sizes).

The method frames reasoning control as guidance over high-level cognitive/hierarchical states rather than direct token-level manipulation of the generated chain of thought (Section 3; Figure 2, Example of hierarchical decomposition).

Human evaluation results corroborate the automatic-metric comparison between Q-value guided steering and baseline hierarchical approaches (Table 3, Human evaluation results; Table 4, Comparison with other hierarchical approaches).

VAXW59dyfk.text: The paper proposes a decision-theoretic framework that minimizes expected loss (risk) against a worst-case distribution consistent with a prediction set's coverage guarantee, characterizing the minimax-optimal policy for a fixed prediction set (abstract only).
Building on the minimax-optimal policy, the authors derive an optimal prediction-set construction that minimizes robust risk subject to a coverage constraint (abstract only).

Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (ROCP) is introduced as a practical algorithm that targets these risk-minimizing sets while maintaining finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage (abstract only).

Empirical evaluations on medical diagnosis and safety-critical decision-making tasks show ROCP reduces critical mistakes compared to baselines, with the largest gains when out-of-set errors are costly (abstract only).

vZuItb6BOA.text: The paper defines Grounding IDs as internal representations linking visual elements to their corresponding textual descriptions in vision-language models, formalized in the methodology section (Section 3, Methodology).

Partition-inducing external visual cues are shown to create distinct partitions in the model's representation space that improve alignment between visual and textual representations, with quantitative alignment gains reported (Section 4.2, Results; Table 8).

Attention pattern analysis shows that partition-inducing cues sharpen attention onto semantically relevant image regions and reduce cross-talk between unrelated objects (Section 4.3, Analysis; Figure 4, Analysis of attention patterns).

Models exhibiting stronger Grounding IDs from external cues produce fewer hallucinated object attributes, with hallucination-rate comparisons reported in the extended evaluation tables (Table 10; Table 11).

Logit lens analysis and mixing-mechanism visualizations are used to interpret how external cues shape cross-modal binding internally within the model (Figure 5, Logit lens interpretation results; Figure 6, Mixing mechanism analysis).

JWvRxvcmn3.text: SpeedCP is a kernel-based conditional conformal prediction method designed to reduce the computational cost of prior RKHS-based conditional conformal approaches while preserving coverage guarantees (Section 2, Methods).
SpeedCP's conditional coverage guarantees are established formally as a sequence of theorems covering the method's finite-sample and asymptotic properties (Section 2, Theorems 2.1-2.6).

SpeedCP is empirically compared against prior RKHS conformal baselines on interval length and runtime across multiple black-box predictors in the main experiments section (Section 3, Experiments; Table 7).
Additional experiments extend the comparison of interval length and computational speedup across further predictors and datasets (Section 4, Additional Experiments; Table 12; Table 13).

Theoretical proofs supporting the coverage guarantees, including extended theorem statements, are provided in a dedicated theory section and appendices (Section 5, Theoretical Proof; Appendix C, Theorems C.1-C.13).

cKsANUDt1m.text: PULSE learns self-supervised dynamical-system representations of physiological time-series without requiring labeled annotations, evaluated against baselines on downstream clinical tasks (Section 2, Background and Related Work; Table 5).

PULSE's learned representations distinguish clinically meaningful semantic classes in physiological signals, with classification comparisons reported across multiple evaluation tables (Table 6; Table 7).
PULSE improves label efficiency, achieving competitive downstream performance when trained with only a small fraction of labeled examples relative to fully-supervised baselines (Table 8).

PULSE's learned dynamical representations transfer effectively across different physiological datasets and tasks, with transfer-learning results reported separately from the in-domain evaluation (Table 9; Table 14).
Qualitative visualizations of the learned latent dynamical trajectories illustrate separation between clinical classes (Figure 1; Figure 16).

g9G7qyAzki.text: In the answerless setting, Qwen and Llama models predict Qwen's answer correctness roughly equally well, showing LLMs lack privileged self-knowledge about their own correctness (Section 3.1).

Generalized Correctness Models (GCMs) trained across multiple models outperform Single Correctness Models (SCMs) by at least 3% absolute accuracy on MMLU for both Llama3.1-8B and Gemma-3-27B (Section 3.2, Table 2).
A GCM based on Qwen3-8B outperforms the larger Llama3-70B's own self-emitted confidences on MMLU by 2.4% absolute accuracy and 0.265 AUROC (Section 1).
The GCM reduces Expected Calibration Error from 0.073 to 0.029 relative to Qwen3-32B's raw logit confidences, despite never being trained on Qwen3-32B (Section 1).

Conditioning correctness prediction on the specific answer phrasing P(c|q,r̂,r) rather than only the question P(c|q,r̂) reveals that models generalize a world-knowledge-based correctness strategy across models (Section 3.3).
The correctness datasets are built from 18 correctness datasets spanning MMLU and TriviaQA across 10 distinct model families ranging from 3B to 72B parameters (Section 2).

oUGeAcxuz5.text: CS-ARM-BN combines meta-learned batch-normalization adaptation (ARM-BN) with negative control samples as a stable context signal for domain adaptation (Section 3, Figure 2).
Under severe class-distribution shift (α=0.01) in the S3→S8 transfer on the JUMP-CP Mechanism-of-Action task, CS-ARM-BN achieves 0.825 accuracy versus 0.173 for ARM-BN and 0.171 for AdaBN (Table 4).

On the new-imaging-source-with-label-shift scenario (S8→S6, α=0.01), CS-ARM-BN attains the highest accuracy among all compared methods, including a meta-learned control-only variant (BEN) (Section 5.4, Table 4).

CS-ARM-BN accuracy stays stable (0.923-0.930) across labeled adaptation batch sizes from 1 to 128 samples, whereas AdaBN and ARM-BN collapse to about 0.13 accuracy at batch size 1 (Table A7, Appendix E.1).
Experiments use the large JUMP-CP imaging dataset, evaluating Mechanism-of-Action classification transfer between source 3 and source 8 (and source 6) experimental batches (Section 5, Table 2).

xyP0iKZDKo.text: A composite score αIF+(1−α)Func of instruction-following (IF) and functional correctness correlates best with human preference (LMArena coding Elo) at an intermediate α rather than at pure functionality (α=0) or pure IF (α=1) (Section 4.5, Figure 5).
31 LLMs spanning 10 model families (Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, Grok, Gemma, Mistral, MiniMax, Kimi) are evaluated on the Big-SWE-IF and Live-SWE-IF benchmarks (Section 4.1, Table 4).

Adding non-functional instructions causes functional regression above 5% under multi-turn editing with five instructions on Big-SWE-IF for every model except Gemini 2.5 Flash and Claude 4 Opus (Section 4.2, Table 2).

Task-level instruction-following success collapses as instructions accumulate: most advanced models score below 50 on the task-level IF score with three or more instructions on both benchmarks (Section 4.3, Table 3).
Multi-turn editing outperforms single-turn generation in task-level IF score by 3-4.5 points on Big-SWE-IF and by roughly 8 points on Live-SWE-IF (Section 4.3).

On the Spearman correlation with human preference, pure instruction-following (α=1) scores over 0.1 points higher than pure functional correctness (α=0), identifying IF as a key differentiator among top models (Section 4.5).

TrugNgxtey.text: The adapter is a scalar affine map f(h)=α·h+b applied to hidden activations, requiring only d_model+1 trainable parameters (Section 2.2).

Trained on a 70B model, the adapter achieves a 71.4% mean best-of-6 generation-scoring hit rate for SAE feature labels, exceeding both the untrained SelfIE baseline (49.1%) and the original training labels themselves (63.4%) (Section 3.4, Table 3).
The trained full-rank adapter identifies topics with 93.7% recall@1 under a best-of-6 protocol, compared to 0.04% for the untrained baseline (Section 3.2).
The learned bias vector alone accounts for approximately 85% of the total performance gain over untrained baselines (Section 3.4, Table 1).
In a 500-case multi-hop reasoning test, the trained adapter decodes implicit bridge entities in 455 cases (91.0%±1.3), versus 282 cases (56.4%±2.2) for the untrained adapter (Section 3.5, Figure 3).

NyGHaciFrK.text: Algorithm 1 constructs a retriever portfolio in O(k|R|·(k log|R|+log(1/δ))/ϵ²) time and, with probability at least 1−δ, returns a set S with F(S) ≥ (1−1/e)OPT−ϵ for the expected best-of-k coverage objective (Theorem 3.1).
The expected best-of-k coverage objective is proven non-negative, monotone, and submodular, so the classical greedy algorithm's (1−1/e) approximation guarantee is tight (Section 3).
Retriever portfolios are evaluated on four open-domain and multi-hop QA benchmarks: HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, TriviaQA, and MusiQue (Section 4, Table 1).
The all-pool learned portfolio (k=4, ℓ=3) reaches 0.5579 Exact-Match on HotpotQA with Gemma-3-27B-It, versus 0.5128 for the best single dense retriever baseline (Table 3).
Fixed Vendi retriever portfolios match or exceed Vendi-RAG's iterative inference-time-tuned accuracy while using substantially fewer tokens and lower wall-clock latency (Section 5, Figure 4).

nD4HBOeg3z.text: Gemini-2.5-Parlay achieves an average 106.87x speedup over baselines on ParEval benchmarks, with Build@1 rising from 0.25 to 0.84 after fine-tuning (Table 1, Section 4.2).

On PBBS and RPB expert-written baselines, ParEVO achieves a 4.1x speedup over the human baseline on Maximal Independent Set and a 2.68x speedup on both Histogram and Plane Sweep (Table 2, Section 4.5).

The Parlay-Instruct training corpus contains 13,820 verified tasks generated via a Teacher-Student-Critic pipeline with rejection sampling, retaining only code that compiles and passes unit tests (Section 3.1).
Running the Evolutionary Code Agent (ECA) for 30 iterations yields a 2.2x speedup over the first valid solution found, compared to a 1.498x multiplier at 10 iterations (Table 3, Section 4.6).
On graph problems, fine-tuning improves Pass@1 from 0.42 to 0.76 but reduces speedup from 21x to 13.67x, reflecting a trade-off between correctness/safety and raw performance (Table 4, Section 4.7).

JJw9sN5Lah.text: TFFT decomposes CVaR fine-tuning into a lightweight one-dimensional threshold optimization step followed by a single entropy-regularized fine-tuning process, as formalized in Theorem 4.1 (Right-CVaR) and Theorem 4.2 (Left-CVaR) (Section 4).
TFFT requires only 1 fine-tuning call with complexity O(C_Thresh + C_FT), compared to K fine-tuning calls and O(K*C_FT) complexity for the FDC baseline (Table 1).
On image generation, L-TFFT attains an ImageReward of 0.850±0.063, matching EXP-FT's 0.852 while improving worst-case L-CVaR_0.2[r] from -0.370 (EXP-FT) to -0.306 (Table 2).
On molecular design, R-TFFT achieves R-CVaR_0.9[r] of 183.4, versus 172.5 for FDC and 167.1 for EXP-FT, while using roughly T training time instead of the approximately 3T required by FDC (Table 3).

Theorem 5.1 establishes that the right-CVaR dual objective F_R is strictly convex with Lipschitz constant L_R = 1/(4*alpha*(1-beta)^2), and the left-CVaR objective F_L is strictly concave with L_L = 1/(4*alpha*beta^2) (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 6.1 shows the threshold-optimization stage has a convergence gap of O(1/sqrt(M) + 1/N) after M optimization steps with batch size N, and Theorem 6.2 bounds the KL divergence induced by threshold estimation error delta as D_KL(p*||p_hat) <= 2*delta/lambda_mode (Section 6, Theorems 6.1-6.2).

nB0TrIRAs1.text: HiPPO Zoo introduces five explicit polynomial-based extensions to classical HiPPO memory that individually replicate capabilities usually attributed to opaque learned SSMs like Mamba: Volterra, Salience, Associative Memory, Multiscale, and Forecasting HiPPO (Section 3).

Salience HiPPO implements adaptive, input-dependent memory allocation via a scalar measure-deformation mechanism (Equation 2) with a time-warping interpretation (Equation 3), demonstrated on a selective copying task with explicit history-measure visualizations (Section 3.2, Figure 2).

Volterra HiPPO decomposes nonlinear dynamics into interpretable kernels parameterized in an orthogonal polynomial basis, validated by learning a quadratic Volterra system on the Wray-Green benchmark (Section 3.1, Figure 1B).

Associative Memory HiPPO separates temporal encoding from content-addressable storage on a continuous address space, demonstrated via key-value associative recall with explicit visualization (Section 3.3, Figure 3).
Multiscale HiPPO represents scale-dependent states as polynomial expansions (Equation 5) that support stable reconstruction across three orders of magnitude of timescale (Section 3.4, Figure 4).

In the streaming/online training setups, the Salience model uses truncated backpropagation through time with fixed HiPPO parameters and only the neural readout learned online, while the Associative model uses chunk-wise gradient computation with state detachment between chunks (Section C.2-C.3).

bjoDtIUSvx.text: On the original (non-shifted) tasks, Parameterized Diffusion Policy (PDP) maintains multimodal behavior fidelity, achieving over 90% success across evaluated domains (Table 1).
Under constraint-shifted evaluation across 8 manipulation tasks with 3 scenarios each, PDP achieves 92% average success versus 21.5% for standard diffusion policy (Table 2).
On a real-robot OpenDrawer task, PDP achieves 100% success across all constraint-shift scenarios compared to 20% success for standard diffusion policy (Section 5.1, Table 3).

PDP learns a geometry-aligned behavior latent space using soft-DTW distance and conditions the denoiser on this latent via a global modulation architecture, enabling test-time control through gradient-based latent adaptation rather than search over the full noise space (Section 4.1-4.3).
Latent-space interpolation between demonstrated behavior modes produces smooth, physically plausible intermediate trajectories, as visualized through latent space navigation (Figure 5).
Ablation studies confirm that geometry alignment, the global modulation architecture, and semantic warm-starts are each necessary for effective test-time adaptation (Tables 4-6).

QJC5WymFK1.text: ITPO derives turn-wise rewards by summing token-level implicit process-model rewards r_phi(y^{k,t}|...) = beta*log(pi_phi/pi_ref) within each turn (Equation 1, Equation 4), reducing token-level variance (Section 3.2-3.3).

On the Math Tutoring task (500 MATH-derived problems), Norm-ITPO combined with RLOO reaches 32.50% accuracy versus 29.06% for the trajectory-level RLOO baseline, a 34.4% relative improvement (Table 1, Section 4.1.1).

On Document Writing (500 Medium articles) and Medical Recommendation (550 MTMedDialog samples) tasks, Norm-ITPO with RLOO improves over trajectory-level RLOO by 12.0% (BLEU) and 8.0% (hierarchical score), respectively (Table 1, Section 4.1.1).
The implicit process reward model achieves a Kendall-tau correlation of 0.5-0.75 with outcome rewards, indicating reliable trajectory-level discrimination (Section 4.3.1, Figure 5).

In human evaluation of turn-wise interpretability, Norm-ITPO's identified best/worst turns matched expert labels in 48 of 64 cases (75%), compared to 58/64 (91%) for Gemini-3.0-Pro and a random baseline of 16/64 (Section 4.3.2, Figures 6-7).
ITPO yields consistent improvements when combined with each of three advantage estimators—RLOO, GRPO, and PPO/GAE—across all three tasks (Table 1, Section 3.4).

bzmt9wJ6uW.text: The Document-Query Adversarial Learning (DQ-A) method generates transferable injection tokens that hide documents from LLM-based retrievers without access to victim queries or model internals (Section 3).
Across 7 LLM retrievers, the attack produces Recall@25 drops of roughly 2%-10% and Recall@50 drops of roughly 1%-7% (Table 2).
On the Robotics dataset, the attack causes an 8% recall drop for Qwen1.5 and a 6% drop for Jinaai embeddings (Table 2).
Only 1 of 7 evaluated retrievers, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, shows robust resistance to the attack (Table 2).
DQ-A is compared against GCG, PRADA, and Poisoned-RAG baselines, with an ablation contrasting DQ-A, DQ-A-H, and S-GCG variants (Table 3).
Experiments use 4 datasets (Economics, Psychology, Biology, Robotics) with a default injection length of 10 tokens (Table 4).

B3TmdSTo0X.text: RowDualNet achieves an end-to-end speedup of roughly 2.0x-2.5x over classical solvers on the Dense synthetic model at N=16,384 (Figure 2).
On the Block-Structured synthetic model, RowDualNet achieves roughly 2.25x speedup versus SciPy and roughly 4.0x versus LAP (Figure 3).
On real-world Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) data, RowDualNet achieves roughly 1.25x speedup for N>=8,000 while preserving full optimality (Figure 5).
On OpenStreetMap-derived urban transportation networks (7 cities, N=10,000), RowDualNet achieves 1.4x-1.6x speedup (Figure 4).
Neural warm-starting scales to N=16,384 while the neural components account for under 7% of total runtime, avoiding the O(N^2) memory bottleneck of graph-based models (Section 5).
The greedy matching rate from the neural warm-start improves from 26% to 76%, reducing augmenting path search work by 68% (Section 5).

2mEC3bPBlS.text: GeoThinker with Qwen2.5VL-7B achieves 50.5 average on VSI-Bench, outperforming VG-LLM-8B's 49.7 (Table 1).
GeoThinker reaches a peak score of 72.6 on VSI-Bench in the scaled regime (Table 3).
GeoThinker attains 68.1 on VSI-Debiased using 128 frames, indicating robustness to benchmark bias (Table 4).

On the RefSpatial-Bench embodied referring benchmark, GeoThinker achieves 48.00% location accuracy, 47.00% placement accuracy, and 37.66% accuracy on unseen compositional relations, an overall +1.66% improvement over the RoboRefer baseline (Table 5).

On the NAVSIM autonomous driving benchmark, GeoThinker improves Drivable Area Compliance to 95.5% (vs. 91.8% baseline) and Time-To-Collision to 95.0% (vs. 92.8% baseline), yielding a +2.0 point boost to 83.6% on the PDMS safety metric (Table 6).
