v0AkeYfQGq.text: TEFormer decouples bidirectional temporal fusion into a forward Temporal Enhanced Attention (TEA) module and a backward Temporal MLP (T-MLP) using gated recurrence, with the optimal configuration combining forward TEA and backward T-MLP (Table 6).
On static image classification, TEFormer reaches 96.24% on CIFAR10, the only compared model exceeding 96%, and 96.88% on SVHN versus QKFormer's 96.78% (Section 5.1).
On neuromorphic datasets, TEFormer achieves 81.90% on CIFAR10-DVS and 95.95% on NCARS, outperforming SNN and Spiking Transformer baselines (Section 5.2).
An ablation shows T-MLP alone contributes +0.07%, TEA alone causes a -0.06% degradation, but combined they yield a synergistic +0.33% gain over the baseline (Table 5).

Across four neural encoding schemes evaluated on CIFAR10 (Direct 96.24%, Phase 89.92%, Rate 84.74%, TTFS 87.46%), TEFormer consistently outperforms baselines such as Spikformer, SDT, and QKFormer (Table 4).

gXTtBRI1yj.text: NeurIPS converges in 10 epochs versus roughly 600 epochs for baseline surface decoders, a roughly 60x reduction in training time (Section 4.1).

On the Natural Scenes Dataset, NeurIPS achieves a CLIP score of 93.2% versus 89.4% for the prior best surface method (SIM), and improves PixCorr from 0.165 to 0.248 and SSIM from 0.305 to 0.370 (Table 1).
The Selective ROI Spherical Tokenizer (SRST) reduces processed surface vertices by 88.4%, from 81,924 to 9,488 vertices, via visual ROI restriction (Section 3.4).
NeurIPS reaches 90% of full performance using only 20% of a new subject's data after a single epoch of fine-tuning (Section 4.2).
When the training cohort is expanded from 4 to 8 subjects, NeurIPS shows only a 0.6-point drop in CLIP performance and a 2.0-point drop in SIM performance, indicating stable scalability (Figure 5).

N9nlCRUiir.text: The critical phase-transition threshold for black-box assisted regression is characterized as δc(n) ≍ n^(-β/(2β+d)), separating a prior-dominated regime from a sample-dominated regime (Section 5).

The proposed safe residual estimator achieves the minimax risk rate min{δ², n^(-2β/(2β+d))} up to a validation-selection cost, with the lower bound given in Theorem 5.4 and the matching upper bound in Theorem 5.5 (Theorem 5.4, Theorem 5.5).
Theorem 5.7 provides an oracle inequality showing the validation-based selection between f0 and f0+r̂ performs nearly as well as the better of the two candidate predictors (Theorem 5.7).
In synthetic experiments at n=20 and δ=0.0, the safe residual estimator achieves risk 0.0027 compared to 0.1894 for learning from scratch (Tables 1-2).

On CIFAR-100 with CLIP features at n=2000, the residual learning method achieves 66.7% accuracy versus 63.9% for a weighted-ensemble baseline, improving over the 59.4% zero-shot baseline (Section 6, CIFAR-100/CLIP experiments).

On AG News with Qwen3-8B at n=16, residual learning achieves 75.2% accuracy while the weighted-ensemble baseline exhibits negative transfer, dropping to 71.2% (Section 6, AG News/Qwen3-8B experiments).

w1fkDwiZgN.text: L-SR1 augments the classical Symmetric-Rank-One quasi-Newton update with three MLP-based learned modules — an input encoder, a vector generator, and a learning-rate generator — that operate element-wise on the optimizer state (Section on Learnable Components / Architecture).

L-SR1 enforces positive semi-definiteness and the secant condition via a learned projection that minimizes ‖p_k − B̃_k q_k‖² subject to PSD constraints, incorporated into the meta-training loss with weight λ_sec (Section on Learned Projection Mechanism).

On the 3DPW dataset for Monocular Human Mesh Recovery, L-SR1 achieves PA-MPJPE of 51.58 using 13 optimization steps and a 10.4M-parameter model, outperforming LGD's 55.90 PA-MPJPE which uses a 17.4M-parameter model and 4 steps (Table comparing L-SR1 vs. LGD on 3DPW).

L-SR1 achieves the highest performance profile across 30 benchmark optimization problems including Rosenbrock, Rastrigin, and quadratic functions, and shows better convergence trajectory alignment than LBFGS on quadratics (Section on Analytic Benchmarks).

L-SR1 is trained self-supervised on the AMASS dataset for 10K meta-training iterations, requiring approximately 15 hours on a single RTX 3090, using a buffer size L=8 for analytic benchmarks and L=4 for HMR (Section on Implementation Details).
L-SR1 achieves 45% faster inference than LGD with 18% lower memory usage on the Monocular Human Mesh Recovery task (Section on Computational Efficiency).

nqmb8hv39b.text: RevealLayer builds on the FLUX.1 [dev] diffusion backbone and introduces a Region-Aware Attention (RAA) module and an Occlusion-Guided Adapter (OGA) module to disentangle visible and hidden RGBA layers, combined with 3D Rotary Positional Embeddings for layer distinction (Section on Technical Architecture).

The RevealLayer-100K dataset, containing 100K RGBA layer annotations, is constructed via three pipelines — an extraction pipeline (object removal plus inpainting), a generative pipeline (synthetic background generation), and an occlusion augmentation pipeline — and RevealLayerBench provides 200 high-quality multi-object evaluation images (Section on Dataset Contributions).
On the OBER-Test object removal benchmark, RevealLayer achieves 30.16 dB PSNR compared to 29.05 dB for OmniPaint (Table, Object Removal on OBER-Test).
On the AIM-500 alpha matting benchmark, RevealLayer achieves MSE of 0.0107 versus 0.0168 for MAM, along with a SoftIoU of 0.9048 (Table, Alpha Matting on AIM-500).
On multi-layer decomposition, RevealLayer attains FID of 53.81 for background layers and 18.42 for foreground layers, with a SoftIoU of 0.9432 (Table, Multi-Layer Decomposition results).

RevealLayer tolerates moderate bounding-box perturbations of 10-20% enlargement or under 5% offset with negligible performance degradation, but shows noticeable degradation under more severe 5-10% perturbations (Section on Robustness Analysis).

3mJ9eTU319.text: The paper deconstructs the RL design space for diffusion model fine-tuning along three axes — policy-gradient objectives, likelihood estimation methods, and sampling strategies — and identifies ELBO-based likelihood estimation as the dominant factor for effective, efficient, and stable optimization (Section on Design Space Deconstruction).

Using the ELBO-based likelihood estimator, GenEval score improves from 0.24 to 0.95 within 90 GPU hours on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, a 4.6x efficiency gain over FlowGRPO and 2x over DiffusionNFT (Section on Efficiency Gains, GenEval results).

Three new policy-gradient objectives are proposed — Exact Policy Gradient (EPG), which removes clipping and advantage normalization; Proximal EPG (PEPG), a theoretically grounded trust-region variant without heuristic clipping; and Proximal Advantage Regression (PAR), an L2 regression between log-probability ratios and advantages (Section on Novel Policy Objectives).

Forward ELBO-based likelihood estimators substantially outperform backward trajectory-based likelihood estimators in efficiency and stability when compared systematically (Section on Likelihood Estimation Comparison).

Performance differences across the EPG, PEPG, and PAR policy-gradient objectives are minor when each is paired with the ELBO-based likelihood estimator, indicating the RL objective choice matters less than the likelihood estimation method (Section on Experimental Validation).

The evaluation spans multiple benchmarks (GenEval, OCR, DrawBench) and reward models (PickScore, CLIPScore, HPSv2.1) on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium to validate the findings (Section on Experimental Validation).

DfhMMHXDuu.text: BNRM replaces deterministic scalar reward outputs with sparse, non-negative latent factor representations via non-negative factor analysis, combining local sparsity on instance-specific variables with global sparsity on shared reward factors (Section on Core Innovation).

BNRM extends the Bradley-Terry preference model with Gamma priors for non-negativity and sparsity and Weibull-parameterized variational inference, trained end-to-end via ELBO maximization with KL regularization (Section on Technical Approach).

With 40K training examples, BT-BNRM improves over the baseline by 5.4, 13.3, and 6.1 percentage points across three benchmarks, and the fully fine-tuned BNRM model reaches 93.6% on RewardBench, surpassing the previous best reported result (Section on Experimental Results / RewardBench).
BNRM matches the performance of a baseline trained on 20K samples while using only 1K training samples, and yields a 16.7% improvement over baseline under 40% label noise (Section on Robustness).

BNRM reduces the Pearson correlation between reward and response length from 0.488 to 0.123, indicating substantial debiasing of length correlation (Section on Robustness, Debiasing Length Correlations).

In RLHF policy evaluation, policies trained with BNRM-derived rewards achieve an average accuracy gain of 12.15% for one policy configuration relative to baseline reward models (Section on RLHF Evaluation).

iygkwW61Nn.text: Reformulates video object removal as a video-to-video translation task using a Variance-Preserving SDE stochastic bridge with ternary interpolation z_t = a_t·z_tgt + b_t·z_src + c_t·ε, replacing the standard noise-to-data diffusion paradigm (Section 4.2).

Introduces an Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM) mechanism that uses learnable patch embeddings to spatially modulate conditioning features based on mask characteristics, balancing background fidelity against removal flexibility (Section 4.4).
Achieves 28.22 dB PSNR on DAVIS, outperforming the VACE baseline's 27.38 dB, though VACE attains a better (lower) LPIPS of 0.0796 vs. BridgeRemoval's 0.0977 (Table 1, Section 5).
On the newly proposed BridgeRemoval-Bench (150 videos: 50 stock footage, 50 Veo-synthetic, 50 TikTok in-the-wild), achieves 33.24 dB PSNR versus GenOmnimatte's 31.60 dB (Table 2, Section 5.1).

Trains on 47,000 video pairs combining 16,000 synthetic samples from the ROSE dataset with 31,000 real-world pairs (15,000 human-centric, 16,000 dynamic-object), with masks generated via SAM2 and captions via Qwen3-VL (Section 5.1).
A user study with 24 participants and 1,440 total evaluations is reported to assess perceptual quality against competing methods (Figure 3).

Q4enC6IyTP.text: Introduces a four-step reflect-and-retry paradigm (Trial and Failure, Expert Demonstration Retrieval, Visual Reflection, Policy Update) in which VLMs analyze divergences between failed attempts and expert video tutorials to update policy (Section 3.2).

Evaluates 7 VLMs across a 15-game benchmark spanning a cognitive taxonomy (Markov Grid, Non-Real-Time Linear/Non-Linear, Real-Time Linear/Non-Linear), showing Gemini-2.5-Pro improves 6.47% and GPT-4o-mini improves 1.60% under reflect-and-retry versus fire-and-forget (Table 3, Section 4.2).

Reflection gains decline from 4.4% for Non-Real-Time games to 1.7% for Real-Time games, consistent with a 'rich-get-richer' effect where gains scale positively with model capability and negatively with task complexity (Table 3, Section 4.2).

Ablation decomposing reflection sources shows combined Self-Failure + Tutorial reflection reaches 65.5% (GPT-4o-mini) and 76.7% (Qwen3-VL-32B), versus 50.8%/72.0% for failure-only and 61.9%/62.9% for tutorial-only (Table 5, Section 4.3).

Identifies a 'Knowing-Doing Gap' where models average 50.5 in semantic reasoning scores but only 33.5 in GUI execution scores, and error analysis shows perception errors rise from 16.7% to 39.8% as visual complexity increases (Figure 7).

TxWbgnFYCr.text: JanusPipe achieves 1.51x higher throughput than 1F1B-2nd and 1.45x higher throughput than Hanayo-2nd on 32 A100-40GB GPUs (8 nodes x 4 GPUs) for MLIP training (Section 5.2).
Reduces peak device memory by up to 20.56% and 42.70% relative to baseline pipeline schedules (Figure 8).
Evaluated across four MLIP model configurations—UMA-1.2B, UMA-2.3B, eSEN-100M, and eSEN-220M—under varying pipeline-parallel, group-parallel, and data-parallel settings (Figure 7).
Ablation shows the SymFold component contributes roughly 23% of the throughput improvement, WaveK scheduling adds 0-18%, and GARS micro-batch repacking adds 6-23% (Figure 11, Appendix B.3).
Demonstrates 70% strong-scaling efficiency at 32 GPUs and 94% weak-scaling efficiency on the UMA-2.3B model (Section 5.2).

aaFfUg013C.text: Dataset vectors are computed and privatized once and incur no additional privacy cost for generating arbitrarily many subsequent synthetic samples, decoupling privacy budget from generation volume (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

At privacy budget epsilon=5, EPSVec++ achieves MAUVE scores of 72.3±2.7 on IMDb and 62.2±0.2 on BioRxiv, versus 14.9±2.2 and 1.9±0.1 respectively for the PP++ baseline, though PP++ scores higher on Yelp (69.8±3.0 vs. 62.9±4.0) (Table 2).
A BERT classifier trained on EPSVec-generated synthetic data and evaluated on real data reaches 86.9% accuracy on IMDb, exceeding the 86.0% achieved when training directly on real data (Table 2).

Ablation on IMDb shows dataset-vector injection alone improves MAUVE from 48.2 to 67.8, and pretrained (non-instruction-tuned) base models outperform instruction-tuned models, improving from 28.6 to 67.8 MAUVE with the full pipeline (Table 3).

Generation occurs at standard inference cost without the batch-size dependencies of prompting-based private baselines (PP/PP++), requiring the fewest private in-context samples among compared methods (Figure 5).

PKFilPWjMI.text: In one-shot quantization with the QTIP quantizer and no finetuning, YAQA-B reduces KL divergence by approximately 30% versus LDLQ across bitrates, e.g., on Llama 3.1 70B at 2-bit, KL drops from 0.497 (LDLQ) to 0.335 (YAQA-B) (Table 1, Section 4).
On Llama 3.1 8B at 2-bit, YAQA-B achieves KL divergence of 0.241 versus 0.356 for LDLQ (Table 1).
After recovery finetuning, YAQA-B maintains a 10-20% advantage in KL divergence over LDLQ (Table 3).

At 4-bit, YAQA-B (post-training quantization) achieves KL=0.056, lower (better) than Google's QAT model at 4.5-bit with KL=0.089, despite QAT using roughly 100x more training data (Table 4, Section 4.3).

Proves an error bound ΔW(H_O⊗H_I)ΔW^T ≤ tr(D_I)tr(D_O)σ² (Theorem 1) and a tighter proxy error bound incorporating the cosine similarity between the true Hessian and its Kronecker-factored approximation (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).

Two Hessian sketching approaches are proposed: Sketch A using power iteration under an independence assumption (~30 GPU-hours for 10B-parameter models) and Sketch B using a single power-iteration pass (~50 GPU-hours) (Section 3.1.1-3.1.2).

AuO3hDGOCp.text: 4RC uses a transformer backbone that encodes an entire video into a compact spatio-temporal latent space in a single forward pass, enabling query-anywhere-and-anytime 4D reconstruction (Section 3).
On dense tracking, 4RC achieves 85.44 APD / 1.022 EPE on Kubric and 56.63 APD / 1.611 EPE on Waymo, outperforming V-DPM (71.12 APD on Kubric, 41.44 APD on Waymo) (Table 1a).
On camera pose estimation, 4RC attains 0.010 ATE and 0.008 RPE_t on the TUM-dynamics benchmark, the best result among compared methods (Table 2a).
On 3D reconstruction, 4RC reaches 0.034 accuracy / 0.051 completeness on 7-Scenes, versus 0.240 accuracy for TraceAnything (Table 2b).

Ablating the cross-attention mechanism in the motion head drops Kubric performance from 85.44 to 80.83 APD, and replacing the factorized displacement representation with direct world-coordinate point prediction drops it to 74.64 APD (Table 4).

IhhgzNZNGW.text: The E-VAds benchmark comprises 3,961 curated e-commerce short videos from Taobao paired with 19,785 open-ended Q&A pairs spanning perception and reasoning task categories (Section 4).

E-VAds videos have the highest measured visual information density (V_den = 60.44) among seven compared video benchmarks, alongside audio density (A_den = 5.08 words/sec) and OCR textual density (O_den = 18.66 instances/frame) (Table 1).

E-VAds-R1, fine-tuned from Qwen3-VL-8B via SFT (1,880 samples) followed by MG-GRPO reinforcement learning (980 samples), achieves a 109.2% relative gain in commercial-intent reasoning over the base model (Section 5, Table 2).
On the Regulatory Compliance task, E-VAds-R1 scores 0.279 (Strict metric) versus 0.017 for the un-tuned baseline model (Table 2).

Human experts still substantially outperform all evaluated MLLMs, scoring 0.535 (Strict) and 0.871 (Relaxed-5) on the aggregate ALL metric, versus E-VAds-R1's 0.320 (Strict) / 0.577 (Relaxed-5) (Table 2).

ZL2XH58JTi.text: On identical ~34,000-problem NuminaMath-derived training sets, SLM-generated rejection-sampled data (SLM-RFT) yields 37.06% downstream accuracy despite a lower reward-model score (1.47) than Oracle-Refined data (1.70 reward, 34.06% accuracy) and Oracle-Synthesized data (1.88 reward, 30.02% accuracy) (Table 1, Figure 1).

Style-Aligned Refinement, which preserves the target SLM's native syntax during oracle refinement, recovers accuracy to 39.12%, matching or exceeding the SLM-RFT self-generated baseline, versus 34.06% for standard Oracle-Refined data (Table 3, Figure 5).

Oracle-Refined data shows higher global perplexity under the target SLM (1.85) than SLM-RFT data (1.52), while Oracle-Synthesized data shows the highest perplexity (2.69), tracking the inverse of downstream accuracy (Table 4).
Style-Aligned (Qwen) refinement reduces perplexity to 1.46 versus 1.52 for SLM-RFT while keeping semantic preservation score at 4.77 versus 4.26 for standard Oracle-Refined data (Tables 3 and 6).

Findings are validated across multiple target models (Qwen2.5-Math 1.5B/7B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, DeepSeek-Math-7B) and reward models (Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Reward, Skywork, Nemotron), and hold across varying learning rates (2e-5, 5e-5) and batch sizes (128, 256) (Table 2, Appendix C, Appendix H).

v6Tpe2LRrW.text: HiDe boosts Qwen2.5-VL 7B to 92.1% average accuracy (94.8% Attribute, 88.2% Spatial) and InternVL3 8B to 91.6% average accuracy (92.2% Attribute, 90.8% Spatial) on V*Bench, gains of +13.0 and +10.0 points over the respective base models (Table 1).

HiDe reduces peak memory usage from 96 GB to 20 GB (a 75% reduction) compared to the prior training-free zoom-in approach ViCrop, while running inference on V*Bench in about 20 minutes versus ViCrop-optimized's roughly 28 minutes (Table 4).

HiDe's Token-wise Attention Decoupling (TAD) component raises accuracy from 82.7% with predicted-bounding-box cropping to 91.1% with full semantic decomposition and 92.1% with the complete TAD design (Table 2).
HiDe's Layout-Preserving Decoupling (LPD) component improves accuracy from 86.4% for sequential concatenation or masking baselines to 92.1% for the full LPD design with compaction (Table 3).

HiDe surpasses reinforcement-learning-based high-resolution methods such as DeepEyes despite being training-free, and also outperforms GPT-4o and OpenAI o3 on the evaluated high-resolution benchmarks (Section 5, Table 1).

Ot8lh7vvGe.text: AugMask trains standard diffusion-based tabular generators (CDTD, TabDiff) on incomplete data by minimizing a loss restricted to observed coordinates, using stochastically augmented values only as conditioning context rather than as supervised targets (Equation 6, Section 3).

On the MCAR setting across 90 scenarios (six datasets by five missingness ratios), CDTD+AugMask attains summary rank 3.8±2.4 and TabDiff+AugMask attains rank 3.2±2.4, both outperforming the best missing-aware baseline ForestDiff (rank 8.1) (Table 3).

AugMask's Factorized Conditional Stochastic Augmentation uses per-feature LightGBM models (heteroskedastic Gaussian for continuous features, label-smoothed classifiers with α=0.05 for categorical features) applied in a single offline pass before diffusion training (Algorithm 1).

Proposition 3.3 shows that under a local Rao-Blackwellized approximation, the AugMask objective induces a variance-weighted sensitivity penalty on the reconstruction function, promoting invariance of the observed-coordinate reconstruction to the imputed missing entries (Proposition 3.3).

Ablating loss masking (AugFull, which supervises on completed values) versus AugMask (which masks the loss) shows AugMask yields a consistently positive quality gap across a 5x5 sweep varying augmentation bias η and stochasticity λ from 0 to 1 (Figure 5).

Stochastic augmentation (LGBM-S) preserves conditional variance and improves joint density estimation relative to deterministic conditional-mean imputation (LGBM-D), which instead induces artificial sparsity and restricted support (Figure 6, Table 1).

N3dXUHY5dD.text: Early experience methods (SFT and RL variants that use environment-generated future states rather than pure imitation) improve policy effectiveness across 8 diverse agent environments including WebShop, WebArena, ScienceWorld, and ALFWorld, compared to imitation-learning baselines (Section 4-5, Experiments and Results).

Models trained with early experience generalize better to out-of-domain tasks than pure imitation-learning (behavioral cloning) baselines across the 8 evaluated environments (Section 4-5, Experiments and Results).

Early experience serves as a stronger initialization (warm-start) for subsequent reinforcement learning than standard SFT/imitation-learning initializations, yielding higher final RL performance (Section 3, Method: Early Experience).

The comparison spans SFT, RL, and imitation-learning/behavioral-cloning baselines, with early experience-based training outperforming these baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution splits (Section 2, Related Work; Section 4-5, Experiments and Results).

oAiq3HWlI6.text: DensityFlow uses a Neural ODE with a normalized velocity field (state-augmented dynamics tracking accumulated kinetic energy for transport cost) to move points toward the high-confidence data manifold when generating counterfactuals (Section 4.2).

DensityFlow estimates a density score via a (K+1)-way noise-contrastive discriminator, where the logit difference between adjacent classes gives an unbiased density-ratio estimate used to guide counterfactual generation (Section 4.1, Proposition 4.1).

On the Adult dataset, DensityFlow achieves counterfactual validity of 0.901±0.052 under model multiplicity across an ensemble of seven classifiers (KNN, SVM, Random Forest, MLP, XGBoost, CatBoost, TabNet), versus 0.752 for the strongest baseline BetaRCE (Table 2).
On the Compas dataset, DensityFlow achieves validity of 0.729±0.067 versus 0.610 for the strongest baseline (Argument) (Table 2).

For black-box settings, DensityFlow's query-efficient local proxy distillation trains a lightweight surrogate only on the generator's explored counterfactual trajectories, requiring far fewer ensemble queries than baselines Argument and BetaRCE (Section 4.3, Section 5.4, Figure 6).

Ablating the density-guidance component reduces validity on Adult from 0.901 to 0.815, and ablating the local distillation component reduces it to 0.767, confirming both components are necessary (Table 3).

vuGiQ4o9ce.text: UniSparse achieves ≥99% of full-attention accuracy while running up to 2.61x faster than FlashAttention (Abstract; Figure 4).
On RULER, UniSparse-0.95 achieves 92.56% overall accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B versus 92.87% for full FlashAttention (Table 2).
On HELMET, UniSparse-0.95 achieves 47.03% overall accuracy on Qwen2.5-7B versus 47.67% for full FlashAttention (Table 3).
At 128K context length, UniSparse-0.95 reaches 2.52x speedup over FlashAttention, and with head-dimension compression (ch=2) reaches 2.61x speedup (Figure 4).
UniSparse's block-selection mechanism achieves 1.62x speedup over the XAttention-0.95 baseline at 128K tokens (Figure 3).

UniSparse is evaluated across multiple modalities and tasks—including RULER and HELMET (text) and Video-MME (vision-language)—and consistently surpasses sparse-attention baselines MInference, FlexPrefill, and XAttention (Section on Tasks; Figure 3, Figure 4).

XGbggvR35p.text: On Table 1's set of 6 unseen symbolic tasks, SCOUT enables Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct to reach an average score of 0.86, versus 0.60 for Gemini-2.5-Pro (Table 1).

SCOUT's exploration stage uses lightweight scout networks (DQN or PPO, on the order of 1.0×10⁻⁵ billion parameters) to generate expert trajectories, decoupling costly exploration from LLM-based exploitation (Section 2.2).
Scout-generated trajectories are converted into dialogue-format supervised fine-tuning data to transfer environment dynamics into the language model in the Distillation Stage (Section 2.3).
A subsequent Evolving Stage applies multi-turn reinforcement learning so the LLM can exceed the original scout's performance (Section 2.4).
On the Rubik's Cube Rotation3 task, SCOUT reduces compute from 24.0 GPU hours (direct PPO) to 9.6 GPU hours, a roughly 60% reduction (Table 3).

ZI6dgwPpoE.text: gWorld is released in 8B and 32B parameter sizes built on Qwen3-VL bases and sets a new accuracy-vs-model-size Pareto frontier for mobile GUI world models, with 74.9% and 79.6% average Instruction Accuracy respectively (Table 2).
gWorld outperforms substantially larger open-weight frontier models, including GLM-4.6V (106B) and Llama 4 (402B)—up to about 50.25x larger—on the MWMBench suite (Figure 1).

MWMBench evaluation covers 4 in-distribution splits (Android in the Wild, GUIOdyssey, AndroidControl, AMEX) and 2 out-of-distribution splits (AndroidWorld with 686 transitions, and KApps with 495 Korean-language transitions) (Section on MWMBench benchmark).

gWorld predicts next GUI states as renderable HTML/web code rather than raw pixels, cutting rendering failures to under 1% compared to over 40% for image-generation baselines (Section on method/renderable code generation).
World-model performance follows a power-law scaling relationship with training data size (37K to 240K samples), with R² ≥ 0.94 (Figure 5).
A roughly 1.0 percentage-point improvement in world-model accuracy translates to about a 0.49 percentage-point improvement in downstream GUI-agent policy performance (Table 4).

pn5lQVm3DH.text: M-IDoL is pre-trained on 1,153,519 unlabeled medical images spanning five modalities (Fundus retinology, X-ray radiology, OCT ophthalmology, histopathology, and dermoscopy) using Swin-B encoders trained for 100 epochs (Section on pre-training data).

M-IDoL is evaluated against more than 20 foundation models, including modality-specific models (RETFound, MIRAGE, Phikon, UNI, Virchow) and unified medical foundation models (LVM-Med, UniMed, CoSMIC, MedCoss), across 21 downstream clinical datasets (Section on comparative analysis).

An ablation study on the RSNA dataset shows accuracy rising from 87.42% (uniform contrastive learning baseline) to 88.31% after adding a mixture-of-experts projector, to 91.45% after adding a routing loss, and to 93.23% for the full M-IDoL with the added contrastive loss (Table 2).
M-IDoL outperforms CoSMIC by over 4% and exceeds UniMiss+, LVM-Med, and UniMed by more than 6% on most of the 21 downstream datasets (Table 2 / results section).

On the dermoscopy task HAM10000, the ablation progression improves from 92.77% to 97.96%, and on Mitosis histopathology from 86.72% to 95.62%, demonstrating the contribution of each M-IDoL component (Table 2).

2I7eG7zUQb.text: DiscoForcing uses a latent diffusion forcing architecture with token-wise heterogeneous noise levels (k_t in [0,1]) trained under a flow-matching objective to enable causal, autoregressive audio-to-motion generation (Section on method).

On FineDance, DiscoForcing achieves FID_k = 23.84 versus Lodge's 50.00, and FID_g = 8.62 versus MEGA's 13.02, while maintaining a Beat Alignment Score of 0.244-0.245 competitive with offline baselines FACT, Bailando, EDGE, Lodge, and MEGADance (Table 2-3).

DiscoForcing achieves a per-frame latency of 26.26 ms at 30 FPS, and an ablation over denoising steps shows 10 steps is optimal, with 5 steps degrading quality and 100 steps exceeding the real-time compute budget (Table 4).

A causal music encoder combines discrete rhythmic codes from residual vector quantization (RVQ) with continuous periodic-alignment features parameterized as sinusoidal functions capturing phase, amplitude, and offset, computed only from fixed-length sliding audio windows without lookahead (Section on causal music processing).

Ablations show that a 272-dimensional canonicalized incremental motion representation preserves quality while enabling direct forward-kinematics reconstruction, and that the proposed temporal guidance strategy outperforms classifier-free guidance (Table 4).

Three hybrid noise schedules (random, monotonic, trapezoid) are used to balance responsiveness versus stability, with the monotonic schedule's linear transition window defined in Equation 12 (Section on temporal guidance, Eq. 12).

EFq5Ml9rqv.text: PyVision-RL introduces an oversampling-filtering-ranking rollout strategy combined with an accumulative tool reward to prevent interaction collapse, the failure mode where models learn to reduce tool usage and multi-turn reasoning during RL training (abstract only).
The framework produces two models, PyVision-Image and PyVision-Video, targeting agentic vision tasks in the image and video domains respectively (abstract only).

PyVision-Video uses on-demand context construction that selectively samples task-relevant frames during reasoning, significantly reducing visual token usage compared to processing full video context (abstract only).

PyVision-RL demonstrates strong empirical performance on vision understanding tasks together with improved computational efficiency in video processing relative to baseline agentic multimodal models (abstract only).

5EIKSU0IOK.text: Pareto Frontier-Guided Optimal Transport (PG-OT) constructs prompt-specific Pareto frontiers from 50 candidate images per prompt and uses Sinkhorn optimal transport to map dominated samples toward the frontier distribution during offline training (Section on offline strategy).

On the Parti-Prompts dataset, PG-OT achieves a two-reward Joint Domination Rate (JDR2) of 47.98%, an 11 percentage point improvement over baselines, and a four-reward JDR4 of 17.10%, a 3.4 point improvement, while reducing the four-reward Joint Collapse Rate (JCR4) to 2.39% (Equation 2, Equation 3, Table results).
Table 3 reports individual reward win rates for PG-OT of 56.43% on ICT, 85.23% on HP, 43.63% on CLIP, and 61.70% on HPS (Table 3).

In human evaluation on the DiffusionDB dataset, PG-OT achieves a 76.34% win rate against the SD3.5-Turbo baseline and a 79.57% win rate against a weighted multi-reward fusion baseline (2:3:2:3 weighting) (Table 6).
A VLM-based detection mechanism using GPT-4o, Qwen3-VL, and GLM-4.5V to identify and remove collapse-prone weak reward models achieves 90.5% agreement with human experts (Table 4).

PG-OT is built on Stable Diffusion 3.5-Turbo fine-tuned with LoRA via the DRaFT-K strategy, incurring only a 3% per-iteration overhead (6.0s to 6.18s) while offline Pareto-frontier precomputation takes about 2 hours, roughly 12% of total training time (Section on implementation details).

0xtMUL0eiF.text: Unsupervised Partner Design (UPD) is a population-free multi-agent RL framework combining online partner generation via Dirichlet-biased randomization with a uniformly sampled mixing coefficient (Algorithm 2) and learnability-based partner selection using a variance-based scoring buffer (Algorithm 1).

On five standard Overcooked-AI layouts (CRoom, AA, CR, CC, FC), UPD achieves an average return of 94.4 ± 8.1, outperforming the population-free baseline E3T at 76.8 ± 0.9, as well as population-based baselines FCP and MEP (Table 1).

On the Overcooked Generalisation Challenge with procedurally generated 5x5 kitchens, joint UPD (JUPD) achieves an average return of 58.9 ± 5.9 across three layouts, versus 44.0 ± 5.1 for the SFL-E3T baseline (Table 2).

A human-AI study finds UPD-trained partners rated significantly higher on adaptability, human-likeness, and collaboration quality, and lower on frustration, than baseline partners (p < 0.05, Holm-Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 6).

Layout-dependent analysis shows that rigid coordination tasks favor lower mixing-coefficient (epsilon) values while more flexible tasks favor higher randomness, and UPD exhibits emergent convention-breaking behavior not explicitly designed into the algorithm (Figure 3, Figure 4).

efxovXR9xH.text: GASS decomposes CLIP embedding variation into prompt-dependent and prompt-independent components and introduces a Spherical Projection spread (SPP) metric to quantify diversity gains along both axes (Section 3).

On ImageNet, GASS increases SPP from 0.143 to 0.149 for Stable Diffusion 2.1 and from 0.137 to 0.141 for SD3-Medium, while maintaining Vendi Scores around 32.7 and 28.9 respectively (Table showing ImageNet results).

GASS is evaluated on both a U-Net backbone (SD2.1, standard diffusion) and a DiT backbone (SD3-Medium, rectified flow), demonstrating architecture- and paradigm-agnostic applicability (Section 5, Experiments).

On DrawBench, GASS achieves ImageReward scores of 0.229 (SD2.1) and 0.778 (SD3-M) alongside SPP values of 0.135 and 0.114, indicating minimal fidelity loss from diversity enhancement (Table showing DrawBench results).

Proposition 4.1 proves that the GASS-expanded embedding set has strictly greater expected hypervolume than the original set, grounding the method's diversity gains in a Gram matrix determinant argument (Proposition 4.1).

An ablation over the number of candidate directions used to identify the dominant residual direction shows N=10 is sufficient for computational efficiency without sacrificing diversity gains (Section 5, Ablation study).

rmWRfKECEC.text: Theorem 1 proves that RL-SMC with an infinite number of particles constitutes a valid policy improvement operator, with Corollary 1 showing value strictly increases with search depth (Theorem 1, Corollary 1).

TSMCTS applies Sequential Halving at the root, running log2(m1) iterations that progressively halve the number of candidate actions while doubling the particle budget per iteration (Section on TSMCTS / Algorithm description).

TSMCTS is evaluated on discrete environments (Jumanji: Snake, Rubik's Cube) and continuous environments (Brax: Ant, HalfCheetah, Humanoid), outperforming the SMC baseline and matching or exceeding Gumbel MCTS (Figure 1).

Figure 3 shows TSMCTS scales favorably with search depth T where baseline SMC deteriorates, that variance decreases proportionally with increased particle count, and that TSMCTS maintains a constant number of active actions, preventing policy collapse to a delta distribution (Figure 3).
Figure 2 shows TSMCTS incurs only a modest runtime increase over plain SMC while remaining roughly 2x faster in wall-clock time than MCTS at matched compute budget B=24 (Figure 2).
An ablation over the Sequential Halving hyperparameter m1 shows its effect on performance is marginal once m1 is at least 4, using particle counts N of 4, 8, and 16 (Ablation study on m1).

kYVjfc56RT.text: Video2GUI is a coarse-to-fine pipeline that filters roughly 500 million raw internet videos down to about 20 million candidate videos via metadata filtering, then to 4.16 million high-quality GUI tutorial videos (~300,000 hours) via a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Omni video quality scorer (Section 3.1).

The resulting WildGUI dataset contains 12.7 million GUI operation trajectories comprising 124.5 million screenshots across more than 1,500 real-world applications and websites, covering website, mobile, and desktop platforms with high- and low-level instructions (Table 1).

After continual pre-training on WildGUI, Mimo-VL-7B improves on OSWorld-G grounding average from 54.7 to 67.6 (+12.9) and on ScreenSpot-Pro average from 41.2 to 56.9 (+15.7), surpassing open-source baselines Qwen3-VL-32B and UI-TARS-72B (Table 2).

After continual pre-training on WildGUI, Mimo-VL-7B improves AndroidControl-High step success rate from 65.6 to 71.4 (+5.8) and CAGUI step success rate from 63.4 to 71.0 (+7.6), outperforming baselines including Aguvis-7B and UI-TARS-7B (Table 3).

Video2GUI uses Gemini-3-Pro for trajectory extraction with a sliding-window strategy over 4-minute video segments plus historical context, and performs action spatial grounding using a triplet of frames {o_{t-0.5s}, o_t, o_{t+0.5s}}, with manual verification confirming over 95% of 200 sampled grounded actions are accurately parameterized (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

0OpwiqWPQJ.text: Phy-CoSF combines a physics-guided deep unfolding framework based on acceleration-strategy half-quadratic splitting (A-HQS) with a continuous spectral fields (CoSF) module, enabling reconstruction at arbitrary continuous wavelengths rather than fixed discrete bands (Method section, A-HQS/CoSF description).

Phy-CoSF architecture includes a triple-branch cross-domain feature mixer operating at fine, meso, and coarse granularities, and a Fourier Mamba module for frequency-domain global dependency modeling (Architecture section).

On the ICVL dataset (70 scenes, 163 bands from 450-650nm, split 60 train/10 test), Phy-CoSF achieves an average SAM of 1.14 degrees, PSNR of 36.45 dB, and SSIM of 0.915 for continuous reconstruction (Table, ICVL continuous reconstruction results).

For spectral super-resolution on ICVL, Phy-CoSF achieves SAM of 1.15 degrees, PSNR of 36.46 dB, and SSIM of 0.915, outperforming nine state-of-the-art baselines including MST++, CST-L+, DAUHST, PADUT, DERNN-LNLT, and MiJUN (Table, spectral super-resolution results).

The 9-stage Phy-CoSF model uses only 0.27M parameters and 801.38G FLOPs, substantially fewer than extrapolated discrete-band approaches that exceed 2,000G FLOPs at 143 bands (Efficiency comparison table).

Ablation studies show the triple-branch architecture consistently improves over single- and dual-branch variants, random frequency encoding is critical for capturing high-frequency spectral variations, and Fourier Mamba outperforms spatial Mamba for global structural consistency (Ablation study section).

cmTjoiRyyr.text: Length Scaled Softplus Attention (LSSA) replaces the exponential function in Softmax with a Softplus activation on L2-normalized queries/keys and introduces a dynamic scaling factor of log(d) x log(N) to maintain entropy invariance across sequence lengths (Method section, LSSA formulation).

A fine-tuning-free re-weighting mechanism (LSSAR) applies a power transformation ReLU^p post-training to sharpen attention distributions without gradient updates, remaining numerically stable at high powers (e.g., p=15, p=50, p=100) whereas applying the same re-weighting to Softmax attention causes gradient explosion (Section on re-weighting mechanism).

On GPT-2 (124M) trained on Fineweb-10B at 1,024-token length and evaluated up to 16x that length (16K tokens), Table 4 shows LSSAR (p=15) maintains a validation loss near 3.2-3.3 versus Softmax attention's degradation to 6.28+ at 8K tokens (Table 4).

LSSAR outperforms Sigmoid attention (Ramapuram et al., 2024), whose validation loss rises to 14.50 at 8K tokens, as well as ReLU-based attention variants that degrade significantly beyond the 1,024-token training length (Section comparing softmax-free alternatives).

An ablation decomposing Softmax into its exponential nonlinearity and L1-norm normalization shows the L1-norm component is what preserves length-extrapolation performance, while the non-negativity of attention scores is not necessary (Ablation study, Softmax decomposition).

X4MFtxw1sB.text: Knocking out only the top 5 GSM8K-specific attention heads degrades Llama-3.1-8B task performance by 48.4% and Qwen-2.5-7B task performance by 65.4%, while general performance drops by only about 1% (Table 2).

The compressed sensing method (Stratified Compressed Sensing, CSS) identifies task-specific heads using only 100-200 knockout evaluations, versus 5,120 evaluations required by a greedy search baseline, a roughly 50x reduction in cost (Table 4, Section 4.1).

Math-specialized heads identified via GSM8K knockouts transfer to degrade Arithmetic task performance by 64.4%, while code-specialized heads identified via MBPP knockouts degrade HumanEval performance by 18.3%, showing partial cross-task generalization of localized heads (Table 3).
A small set of 'universal' heads is shown to impact multiple distinct task capabilities simultaneously when ablated, rather than each task having fully disjoint head sets (Table 5).

Larger models in the study (up to 8B parameters, Llama and Qwen families spanning 512-1024 total heads) exhibit stronger, more concentrated capability localization than smaller models, indicating scale-dependent modularity (Section 6.2, Table 1).

JuiHYauZNk.text: IRPM-Mean-8B improves over its pointwise GRM baseline by +4.8 points on RM-Bench, +8.0 on JudgeBench, and +5.2 on RewardBench (Table 1).
IRPM-Mean-32B reaches 79.6% on RM-Bench, 74.6% on JudgeBench, and 87.3% on RewardBench, with gains of +2.8, +5.7, and +2.1 points respectively over the baseline (Table 1).

With inference-time voting@8, IRPM-32B achieves 91.2% on RewardBench and 77.3% on JudgeBench, approaching pairwise GRM baseline performance while using only about 25% of the computational overhead of pairwise methods (Section 5).

IRPM extends Bradley-Terry-style preference modeling to pointwise generative reward models, reducing reward evaluation complexity from O(n^2) pairwise judgments to O(n) pointwise evaluations for a variable number of candidates (Section 3).
IRPM is evaluated on four reward-model benchmarks: RM-Bench (4,000 samples), JudgeBench (350 preference pairs), RewardBench (3,000 samples), and PPE (10,200+ preference pairs) (Section 4).

dcLjhvVU47.text: ECG-R1 (with RL) achieves 80.29% diagnosis accuracy on grounded ECG interpretation versus 74.70% for the GEM baseline, and 84.20 Clinical Diagnostic Fidelity versus 62.90 for GEM (Table 1).

GPT-5.1, the best-performing non-specialized general MLLM evaluated, only reaches 31.48% diagnosis accuracy, evidencing pervasive unreliability of existing proprietary and open-source MLLMs on ECG interpretation (Table 1, Section 3).
On cross-modal consistency evaluation, ECG-R1 attains BLEU-4 of 0.69 and ROUGE-L of 0.73, compared to GEM's 0.33 and 0.43 respectively (Table 2).
In a cardiologist evaluation of 100 samples, ECG-R1 scores 4.34/5 on Analytical Accuracy and 4.38/5 on Overall Satisfaction, versus 3.89/5 and 3.84/5 for GEM (Table 3).
ECG-R1's Interleaved Modality Dropout training strategy is accompanied by theoretical robustness guarantees under missing-modality conditions (Theorems 2.2-2.3, Figure 4).

The training pipeline combines Protocol-Guided Instruction Data Generation (30,000 samples grounded in a five-phase ECG interpretation protocol) with Reinforcement Learning using ECG Diagnostic Evidence Rewards (EDER) that explicitly score stepwise diagnostic evidence plus outcome accuracy (Section 2).

3LMSxta2fx.text: On the 1.5B-A250M MoE backbone, JTok-M improves average downstream accuracy by +3.91 points, including +8.3 on ARC-C and +6.31 on GSM8K (Table 1).
On a larger 17B-A2B foundation model, JTok-M improves MMLU by +4.11, ARC-C by +8.28, and CMMLU by +9.34 points (Section 4, related to Table 1).

IsoFLOPs analysis shows JTok-M achieves a 2.2% reduction in test loss at matched compute budgets, equivalent to a 35% reduction in compute needed to reach the same loss as vanilla MoE (Section 4.2.1).

Each doubling of JTok-M's token-indexed embedding parameters reduces loss by approximately 0.0118, following a predictable power-law scaling trend distinct from backbone parameter scaling (Section 4.2.2).

A naive implementation of JTok-M incurs a 43% training throughput loss, which is reduced to 6.78% overhead using embedding parallelism and token deduplication, while inference decode throughput reduction is only 4.5-7.3% with CPU offloading (Table 2, Table 3).

64Kj8z626A.text: DDP replaces the stochastic hard-concrete mask used in prior differentiable pruning with a deterministic ReLU-based mask (m = ReLU(z)) combined with an annealed soft surrogate regularizer that sharpens during training, removing sampling stochasticity from the ℓ0 objective (Section 3).
On LLaMA-7B at 20% sparsity, DDP achieves 64.13 mean downstream accuracy versus 62.41 for the baseline, and at 50% sparsity 56.07 versus 53.16 (Table 2).
On LLaMA-13B at 50% sparsity, DDP reaches 62.14 mean accuracy compared to 54.75 for the baseline, a gap of over 7 points (Table 2).
On MoE models, DDP achieves 58.18 mean accuracy on DeepSeekMoE-16B at 60% sparsity (vs. 51.62 for Camera-P) and 63.35 on Qwen3-30B-A3B at 60% sparsity (vs. 59.03 baseline) (Table 3).

An ablation on LLaMA-7B at 20% sparsity shows deterministic optimization contributes +1.79 accuracy points and the expanded mask parameterization contributes a further +2.18 points toward the full method's 64.13 mean accuracy (Table 4).

End-to-end vLLM deployment speedups reach 2.20x for LLaMA-7B at 50% sparsity and 1.51x for Qwen3-30B-A3B at 60% sparsity, demonstrating realistic inference gains on both dense and MoE models (Table 7, Table 8).

iA7hUqvsvz.text: PoE-Bridge achieves up to a 5x speedup over the standard entropy-based diffusion language model (DLM) decoding approach (Section 1).
PoE-Bridge recovers over 95% of the target autoregressive (AR) model's accuracy while achieving roughly 2x the throughput of AR decoding (Section 5.2).
On GSM8K, PoE-Bridge attains 95.30% accuracy at 100.71 tok/s versus the AR baseline's 95.53% accuracy (Table 1).
On HumanEval, PoE-Bridge attains 79.47% accuracy at 76.13 tok/s versus the AR baseline's 83.54% accuracy (Table 1).
Mixed-temperature sampling with increasing K closes at least one-third of the remaining accuracy gap between PoE candidates and the AR target (Figure 2).
With PoE weight w=0.3, the method reaches 80.69% accuracy on HumanEval at 84.82 tokens/second (Table 2, Section 5.3).

y1AV6cX8dX.text: NTK-Selector improves Llama3-8B-Instruct's average score by +8.7 points (67.9 to 76.6), compared to only +0.8 points from domain-only fine-tuning (Table 1).
NTK-Selector improves Qwen3-8B's average score by +5.3 points (73.5 to 78.6), compared to only +0.9 points from domain-only fine-tuning (Table 1).
NTK-Selector yields large domain-specific gains, including +16.1 on the financial TFNS task and +17.7 on the psychological RSDD task for Llama3-8B-Instruct (Table 1).

Scaling domain samples from 1K to 5K yields a substantial gain (69.3 to 71.9), while expanding to 20K produces only minimal further improvement, indicating quality matters more than quantity (Figure 3).
NTK-Selector's relative advantage grows in extremely low-resource settings: with only 100 samples it improves performance by 25.6%, versus 5.2% improvement with 2,000 samples (Figure 4).
Selecting from 1.8M candidate samples takes approximately 31 hours on a single A100 GPU (Table 4).

jjHZnkDk5l.text: Sample-level AIR achieves 67.14% average accuracy across AIME 2024, AIME 2025, MATH500, and GPQA Diamond in the s1K-1.1 setting, outperforming the manually curated s1K-1.1 baseline's 65.43% (Table 1).
Step-level AIR with weighting reaches 70.32% average accuracy, including a +9.97 percentage point gain on AIME 2024 (Table 1).
On the s1K setting, AIR (65.27% average) outperforms Random selection (59.77%) and Length-based selection (61.10%), though it trails the manually curated s1K baseline (66.40%) (Table 2).
AIR identifies reasoning-critical attention (retrieval) heads using the top 5% of heads by retrieval score (Section on retrieval heads).
AIR-selected data has a higher average number of reasoning steps (274.05) and higher symbolic answer ratio (57.76%) than s1K-1.1 data (265.15 steps, 45.52%) (Table 4).
Processing 59K candidate samples for influence scoring takes approximately 6.9 hours on 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs (Appendix C).

emv2qsi3TG.text: The paper defines Marginal Path Collapse, where composed intermediate densities from ratio-of-densities steering become non-normalizable even though both endpoint densities remain valid (Section 2.2).

The Path Existence Criterion (Theorem 2.1) shows collapse occurs whenever the coefficient C_k(t) = Σ γ_i(t)/(α_t^(i))^2 becomes negative for some coordinate k and time t, reducing verification to a checklist of endpoint integrability and coefficient positivity (Section 2.3).
ACE (Adaptive Correction with Exponents), using a time-varying bump-function correction (Theorem 2.2/2.3), guarantees C_k(t) > 0 for all t in [0,1) and eliminates collapse (Section 2.4).
On a synthetic benchmark, ACE (B=30) reduces distributional error to W1=0.28, W2=0.40, MMD=0.027, roughly a 5x reduction versus the non-normalized (NR) and Feynman-Kac (FKC) baselines (Table 2).

On the CrossDock-Weak flexible-pose scaffold decoration task at ω=1.3, ACE achieves 100.0% validity and -5.72 Vina score with 93.30% overall success rate, versus 84.77% validity and -2.93 Vina for the NR baseline (Table 3).
Among 125 three-expert model compositions built from five standard noise schedules, the fraction exhibiting collapse rises from 41% at ω=1.0 to 80% at ω=15 (Section 4, Appendix E.2).

55tjQADd7K.text: PUMA accelerates 125M-parameter masked diffusion model pretraining by approximately 2.5x in iteration-to-accuracy comparisons against baseline MDM training (Figure 1, Section 4.2).

PUMA generates training examples via teacher-forced chains that follow the same unmasking policy used at inference time, replacing posterior-sampled masking with ground-truth token revelation (Section 3.1).

Proposition 1 establishes marginal agreement between PUMA's training distribution and the idealized inference distribution, while Proposition 2 establishes that the loss-minimizer is unchanged despite the modified forward process (Section 3.1.1, Section 3.1.2).

Proposition 3 shows PUMA requires sample complexity linear in the latent dimension d under oracle trajectories, whereas random masking requires complexity exponential in d for a given error threshold (Section 3.3).
Combining PUMA with autoregressive initialization (30k warmup steps) yields an additional 2.3x speedup relative to vanilla MDM training (Section 4.3.1, Figure 1).

A single PUMA-trained model maintains its performance advantage on GSM8K across multiple inference-time unmasking policies (Top-K, Top-K margin, entropy-based) with candidate set sizes |S| in {2,3} (Figure 4, Section 4.2).

laZwZk4O8W.text: Neural Honeytrace reduces the average number of samples required for a worst-case t-Test-based ownership verification from 12,000 to about 200 (Figure 6).

On CIFAR-10, Neural Honeytrace achieves an average watermark success rate (WSR) of 58.60% (minimum 36.60%) versus MEA-Defender's 41.70% average (minimum 11.60%) under adaptive extraction attacks (Table 2).
On CIFAR-100, Neural Honeytrace achieves an average WSR of 55.62% (minimum 29.60%), compared to prior methods' best minimum WSR of 19.80% under adaptive attacks (Table 3).
Neural Honeytrace requires zero training cost/retraining, embedding the watermark via a training-free logits-mixing encoding scheme (Section 4.2, Equation 8).
Ablations comparing trigger types show composite triggers reach 58.60% average WSR versus 37.86% for white-pixel-block triggers and 25.08% for semantic-object triggers (Section 5.3, Tables 6-8).

Under the strongest oracle attack (full defense knowledge), Neural Honeytrace still achieves 11.80% WSR extraction with substantially lower extraction fidelity (65.28%) than prior methods (10.80% WSR, 87.95% fidelity) (Table 7).

Eyz8oboVDt.text: PRISM achieves throughput of roughly 61K tokens/sec at 2K context and about 57K tokens/sec at 16K context, versus TTT-NN's 0.34K tokens/sec, corresponding to roughly a 170x-plus throughput gap consistent with the paper's stated 174x figure (Figure 2).

The Rank-L accumulation theorem shows the injection operator's rank satisfies rank(B_t) ≤ L, structurally expanding the update manifold beyond the single-step Rank-1 bottleneck of standard linear recurrences (Equation 10, Appendix F).

The Write-Forget Decoupling strategy restricts the forgetting operator A_t to a rank-1 update with logarithmic error accumulation (Theorem D.2), while allocating a high-rank, non-linear injection operator B_t whose errors accumulate linearly (Section 4.1).

On the Amazon Electronics ablation, the full PRISM model reaches 0.7134 AUC, dropping to 0.6805 without iterative refinement (L=1), 0.7047 without non-linearity, and 0.7076 without the ShortConv anchor (Table 3).

On mechanistic probing tasks, PRISM attains perfect accuracy (1.00) on Parity Check and Local XOR versus 0.49 and 0.50 respectively for Linear Attention, demonstrating non-linear reasoning capability absent from rank-1 updates (Table 4).
On recommendation benchmarks, PRISM achieves 0.8888 AUC on Amazon Books (versus 0.8910 for the SASRec Transformer) and a mean rank of 2.62 across datasets versus 5.25+ for baselines (Table 2).

3M1Nsgd9Fb.text: Theorem 1.1 (Section 1.2) shows that for logistic regression with a linear model as the margin γ→∞, gradient descent reduces to the batch perceptron algorithm, requiring at most O(nR²/ω²) iterations.

Theorem 2.1 (Section 2) shows that gradient descent on a nonlinear convolutional model with kernel size k=2 and large ‖w₀‖ reduces to a 'Quadratic Perceptron Algorithm' with iteration complexity Õ(√d/μ).

On a minimalistic two-sample dataset, the quadratic perceptron achieves convergence rate Θ̃(√d/μ) (Theorem 5.1), while the classical perceptron requires Ω(d/μ) steps on the same dataset (Theorem 5.2), demonstrating a √d-factor implicit acceleration from nonlinearity.
Proposition 4.1 (Section 4) establishes spectral bounds on the eigenstructure of matrices induced by the convolutional reparameterization, underpinning the accelerated convergence result.
Section 6 extends the acceleration results to larger convolution kernels and two-layer models, showing the largest allowable step size decreases as kernel size increases.

3u1M9wokD7.text: ComplexMCP provides a benchmark with over 300 tools spanning 7 stateful sandboxes for evaluating LLM agents on interdependent tool use (Section on core contributions).
On the 47-task benchmark, human performance reaches 93.61% success rate while top LLMs trail substantially: Gemini-3-Flash 55.31%, Claude-opus-4 41.84%, and GPT-5.1 19.14% (Table 2).
Tool retrieval performance degrades as the action space expands beyond 300 tools, a bottleneck termed 'tool retrieval saturation' (Section 4.2, Figure 6).
Models exhibit a 'clean-slate' bias and over-confidence, assuming empty environments and skipping verification steps, leading to unintended consequences (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
Agents display 'strategic defeatism,' rationalizing failure rather than pursuing recovery strategies, a pattern particularly evident in GPT-5.1 (Section 4.2, Figure 5).

fo77TzkulW.text: ManifoldKV scores tokens for retention using Euclidean (L2) distance from the key centroid, defined as s_i = ‖k_i − μ‖₂, rather than cosine similarity (Definition 3.1).

On the RULER benchmark at 4K–16K contexts with 20% compression, ManifoldKV (with the AdaKV framework) achieves 95.73% accuracy versus 95.66% for KeyDiff and 83.97% for the attention-based SnapKV (Table 4).

On 3-key NIAH multi-key retrieval at 8K context with 50% compression, ManifoldKV achieves 92.4% accuracy versus KeyDiff's 77.0%, a +15.4 point gain; on 2-key NIAH under the same setting it achieves 99.8% versus KeyDiff's 92.6%, a +7.2 point gain (Table 6).
At 64K-token contexts, global-centroid ManifoldKV suffers 'centroid dilution,' collapsing from 82.3% accuracy at 32K to 35.2% at 64K (Table 1, Section 3.2).

WindowedManifoldKV, using local 4K-token window centroids (Algorithm 2), restores accuracy to 84.3% at 25% compression and 64K context, a +49.1 point recovery over global ManifoldKV (35.2%) and +3.2 points over KeyDiff (81.1%) (Table 5).

Cross-architecture validation shows identical ManifoldKV code achieves 94–96% accuracy without tuning across Gemma-3-12B (95.2%), Qwen3-8B (95.0%), Ministral-8B (95.5%), and Llama-3.1-8B (95.7%) (Table 8).

eYICUJ62hg.text: The implicit visual representation encodes an 81-frame, 480p video into a single compact vector by hashing all LoRA adaptation parameters attached to a frozen diffusion model through pseudo-random hashing (Section 3.2).
Uniform quantization with entropy constraints on the LoRA parameters reduces the representation to approximately 1-3 bits per parameter while maintaining reconstruction quality (Section 3.2).

The method is evaluated on the UVG and HEVC video datasets, reporting perceptual quality metrics including DISTS and FVD at extremely low bitrates, with caption and entropy-parameter overhead under 1% of total bitrate (Section 4, Table of compression results).

Inference-time scaling via importance sampling with 2^18 candidate samples per denoising step yields quality gains comparable to doubling the number of denoising steps, at only marginal bitrate increase (Figure 6).
The training objective is shown to recover the 'simplest' generating function in a minimum-description-length sense, derived via a connection to Doob's h-transform (Section 3.1).

Adapted representations act as reusable 'visual memories' that support personalized image editing, video composition, and attribute changes via modified text prompts while preserving the base model's general generation ability (Section 4.4).

GUu3Bi41Fm.text: InertialAR canonicalizes 3D molecule tokenization by aligning each molecule to its principal inertial frame for SE(3) invariance and applying a deterministic RDKit-based atom reordering for permutation invariance (Section on canonical tokenization / inertial frames).

On QM9 unconditional generation, InertialAR achieves 99.3% atom stability and 94.7% molecule stability, exceeding the previous best atom stability of 98.9% (GeoLDM) and molecule stability of 93.2% (Geo2Seq), though its 97.4% validity trails MiDi's 97.9% (Table of QM9 unconditional generation results).

On the large-scale B3LYP-1M dataset, InertialAR reaches 99.0% validity and 24.2% molecule stability, compared to EDM's 92.9% validity/0.8% molecule stability and Geo2Seq's 73.3% validity/0.0% molecule stability (Table of B3LYP-1M results).
On GEOM-Drugs, InertialAR attains 87.2% atom stability versus 85.1% for the best baseline, and 96.8% validity (Table of GEOM-Drugs results).

For class-conditional generation targeting specific functional groups on QM9, InertialAR achieves an average hit rate of 83.3% across five molecule classes, versus 25.7% for EDM and 42.2% for Geo2Seq, with per-class hit rates ranging from 90.9% (Ether) to 68.5% (Heteroaromatic Ring) (Table of controllable generation results).

The model uses GeoRoPE, combining 3D rotary positional encoding with a Nyström approximation for pairwise distance encoding, alongside hierarchical prediction of discrete atom types via cross-entropy loss and continuous 3D coordinates via a diffusion loss (Section on model architecture).

yKQ8GrwEhr.text: VLA-MBPO uses a pretrained Unified Multimodal Model (UMM) as a world model to jointly predict visual dynamics and rewards, avoiding separate specialist world models (Section on UMM-based world modeling).

Interleaved view decoding enforces multi-view consistency between head and wrist cameras, and the UMM-World achieves an SSIM of 0.751 versus 0.680 for a baseline video-generation world model, while running at roughly 2x faster inference (Section on world model evaluation).

Chunk-level branched rollout is theoretically shown to tighten the value-gap bound compared to prior methods; with discount γ=0.99 and horizon k=10, the branched rollout (n=2) reduces the bound to approximately 1710·ϵ_π^k + 400·ϵ_m^(k'n), versus roughly 4183·ϵ_π^k + 18916·ϵ_m for prior methods (Theoretical analysis section).

On the LIBERO benchmark, VLA-MBPO improves the base policy's average success rate by 9.1 percentage points, with the largest gain of 12.2 points on the LIBERO-Long suite, and outperforms an online RL baseline (πRL) under equivalent interaction budgets (Section on LIBERO simulation results).

VLA-MBPO uses a single universal set of hyperparameters across all tasks rather than task-specific tuning, which the authors argue supports robustness and scalability for real-world deployment (Section on hyperparameter settings).

Real-world validation spans 5 tasks across two robotic platforms (Arx-X5 and Galaxy-R1), including deformable-object manipulation and high-DoF whole-body control, with consistent improvements on both seen and unseen conditions (Section on real-world experiments).

60cv928EVo.text: MLUBench comprises 127 entities across 9 classes (Animals, Astronomy, Buildings, Cartoons, Corporations, Movies, Personage, Plants, TV Series), totaling 5,105 images and 15,414 VQA pairs, organized into four sequential unlearning tasks A-D each with forget and retain splits (Section on benchmark construction).
Four baseline unlearning methods are evaluated: Gradient Ascent (GA), Gradient Difference (GD), KL Minimization (KL), and Negative Preference Optimization (NPO) (Section on baseline methods).

On LLaVA-7B, the forget quality of the GA method on the first unlearning task drops from 0.38 to 0.01 after subsequent sequential unlearning operations, demonstrating severe cumulative degradation (Table of sequential unlearning results).
The paper argues MLLM lifelong unlearning is fundamentally constrained by the need to preserve multimodal alignment, distinguishing it from unimodal LLM unlearning (Section on problem analysis).

LUMoE mitigates degradation using switchable LoRA adapters as task-specific 'experts' selected by a gating module, isolating each unlearning task's modifications from the stable base model (Section on LUMoE method).

LUMoE maintains forget quality scores near 1.0 and utility scores above 0.88 throughout sequential unlearning across all four tasks, substantially outperforming the GA, GD, KL, and NPO baselines (Table of LUMoE results).

R3GDb4y629.text: Step-Decomposed Influence (SDI) extends TracIn-style influence estimation to looped transformers by decomposing a single aggregate influence score into a length-τ trajectory attributing influence to specific loop iterations rather than obscuring them in one scalar (Section on SDI method).

SDI computes influence by unrolling the recurrent computation graph of the looped transformer so that each loop iteration's contribution to a training example's influence can be attributed separately (Section on unrolling the loop).

A TensorSketch-based implementation of SDI avoids materializing per-example gradients, enabling the method to scale to transformer-scale models without the memory cost of full-gradient approaches (Section on TensorSketch implementation).

The TensorSketch approximation achieves accuracy comparable to full-gradient influence baselines with minimal approximation error, validated on looped GPT-style models (Section on experimental validation).

Experiments on looped GPT-style models performing algorithmic reasoning tasks show SDI provides per-step insight into latent reasoning processes across loop iterations (Section on algorithmic reasoning experiments).

zmAMq09bFs.text: Q-CLIP's Shared Cross-Modal Adapter uses only 0.14M trainable parameters, which is 3964x fewer than CLIPVQA and 666x fewer than MBVQA (Efficiency Metrics section).
Q-CLIP-Mixed achieves 0.899 SROCC and 0.900 PLCC on LSVQtest after pre-training on LSVQ (Table 1).
After fine-tuning, Q-CLIP reaches 0.915 SROCC / 0.920 PLCC on KoNViD-1k and 0.881 SROCC / 0.901 PLCC on LIVE-VQC, an average improvement of 1.74% SROCC over CLIPVQA (Table 2).
Ablating the Shared Cross-Modal Adapter shows progressive SROCC gains on the visual-only branch (0.866) up to the full shared, layer-sharing configuration (0.895) (Table 3).
Learnable five-level quality prompts (excellent/good/fair/poor/bad) outperform binary antonym prompts, raising SROCC from 0.883 to 0.895 (Table 4).

Frame-difference-based sampling, which selects frames via pixel-wise MSE between adjacent frames, outperforms random and uniform sampling strategies in cross-dataset evaluation (Proposed Method section, Frame-Difference-Based Sampling).

rwBtuEvV4Q.text: PACE achieves BD-BR savings of 39.01%-50.82% versus G-PCC (Octree) in one-stage mode across SemanticKITTI, Ford, nuScenes, and QNX datasets (Table 1).
In autoregressive mode, PACE improves BD-BR savings to 45.14%-55.18% versus G-PCC (Octree) (Table 1).
PACE's autoregressive mode reduces decoding latency by more than 90% compared to TopNet without needing to reload parameters across performance-latency trade-offs (Table 2).
In FP mode, PACE decodes in 1.55s versus 282.04s for OctAttention (Table 2).
Ablating the graph-based positional encoding (GPE) shows BD-BR improving from -38.22% to -50.19% in FP mode when GPE is included (Table 3, Section 4.4).
The post-causal paradigm achieves roughly 90x faster decoding than the fully-causal paradigm baseline while enabling stage-scalable prediction with dynamic stage reconfiguration (Figure 1, Table 4).

H0tMEp0ZmO.text: Multi² achieves 67.61% success on ScienceWorld (in-distribution) with Llama-3.1 8B, compared to 60.48% for the Glider baseline (Table 1).
Multi² reaches 57.86% on ALFWorld (in-distribution) versus 43.57% for Glider, and 35.60% on TextCraft versus 9.50% for Glider (Table 1).
Multi² outperforms prompt-based baselines ReAct, Reflexion, and ADaPT as well as fine-tuning-based baselines GRPO and Glider across ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, and TextCraft (Table 1, Section 5).

Multi²'s hierarchical System 1 (supervised fine-tuning for sub-goal generation) and System 2 (offline-to-online RL for action execution) design mitigates objective drift and reduces invalid actions relative to single-policy baselines (Figure 3, Section 4).
Multi² shows improved horizon robustness and token efficiency at inference time compared to baselines (Figures 1 and 4).

Role-specific LoRA adapters combined with a policy-anchored offline RL objective and KL-regularized online refinement enable stable long-horizon control and efficient online adaptation (Figure 9, Section 4).

Fisw2kc7EY.text: Theorem 4.1 shows that when the PDE constraint does not uniquely determine a solution in function space, the PDE residual loss admits a flat and connected set of global minimizers.
CAML reduces the relative L2 error on the Heat equation to 1.16e-3 +/- 8e-5, versus 7.52e-3 for a standard PINN baseline (Table 2, Section 6.2).
CAML reduces convergence steps needed on the Heat benchmark from 10127+/-2839 to 1577+/-130 (Section 6.2).
CAML increases the fraction of positively-aligned residual/boundary gradients from 5.89% to 39.16%, an order-of-magnitude improvement in gradient cosine similarity (Table 3).

Ablation results show aligned constraints (AC) provide the primary accuracy benefit, while the delay-residual (DR) mechanism gives additional gains specifically on problems with composite/complex boundary conditions (Table 4).

CAML is evaluated for optimizer compatibility with Adam, L-BFGS, DCGD, and ConFIG, and with three backbone architectures (MLP, PirateNets, PINNsFormer) across Heat, Poisson, Navier-Stokes, and Helmholtz benchmarks (Table 5, Table 2).

LhGxRnGmGJ.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes that the finite-sample bias of the KM-ARL estimator decays exponentially with dataset size N.
Theorem 4.2 establishes finite-sample bias bounds for the KM-ADD estimator under independent censoring.
Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 show that the truncation bias of KM-ARL and KM-ADD is smaller than that of conventional (non-censoring-aware) ARL/ADD estimators.

KM-ARL and KM-ADD are shown to be asymptotically unbiased (Equation 11) whenever the support of the detection-point distribution does not exceed the censoring boundary, without requiring parametric assumptions (Section 4).
On the WISDM Actitracker dataset (51,326 sequences ranging from length 1 to 54,401), KM-ARL/KM-ADD show substantially reduced variance versus LB-ARL/LB-ADD baselines (Figure 1, Section 5).

Simulation experiments on Gaussian and Poisson process changepoint models show KM-ARL/KM-ADD remain accurate across censoring levels from 10% to 90% changepoint prevalence and irregular sequence lengths (Figures 2-4, Section 5).

2m0o0Fdqu6.text: Theorem 1 establishes that any first-order zero-respecting algorithm requires at least C0*ΔLf*κ^(3/2)/ε^2 oracle calls to find an ε-accurate stationary point for smooth nonconvex-strongly-convex bilevel problems in the deterministic setting (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 shows a stochastic lower bound of Ω(Lf^3*Δ*κ^(5/2)*σ^2/(Lg^2*ε^4)) oracle calls under bounded-variance stochastic gradient oracles (Section 5.2, Theorem 2).

The deterministic lower bound construction uses zero-chain functions built from tri-diagonal matrices via auxiliary Ψ/Φ functions to force any zero-respecting algorithm to make Ω(κ^(3/2)) progress per unit of accuracy (Section 4.1).

The paper shows bilevel optimization is provably harder than single-level nonconvex optimization (Ω(1/ε^2)) by a factor of κ^(3/2), and harder than nonconvex min-max optimization (Ω(√κ/ε^2)) by a factor of κ (Section 4, comparison to known lower bounds).
A gap remains between the proved deterministic lower bound of κ^(3/2)ε^(-2) and existing upper bounds of κ^4ε^(-2) or κ^3.5ε^(-2), which the paper leaves open (Section 4.3).

et8jpWLUuD.text: POET-X achieves a 3x GPU memory reduction and 8x runtime speedup over the original POET algorithm while preserving POET's spectrum-preserving stability property (Section 1).
POET-X enables pretraining of an LLM with up to 13B parameters on a single Nvidia H100 GPU, whereas standard AdamW runs out of memory under the same settings (Section 1).

On Llama-3B pretraining on C4 with L_max=256, POET-X with block size 512 reaches a validation perplexity of 12.05, better than AdamW's 12.69, APOLLO's 12.97, and GaLore's 14.88, while underperforming Muon's 11.45 (Table 6).

For a Llama-13B model at sequence length 2048, POET-X_mem with block size 256 requires only 47.21 GB of peak GPU memory, while AdamW, Muon, APOLLO, GaLore, and the original POET all run out of memory in this configuration (Table 9).
A customized CUDA kernel for POET-X's permutation operations achieves up to roughly 20x speedup over a native PyTorch implementation across hidden dimensions from 2048 to 16384 (Table 1).

Quantized POET-XQ with block size 512 achieves the best validation perplexity of 14.78 among 8-bit quantized optimizers on Llama-3B trained for 10B tokens, outperforming 8-bit Q-APOLLO (20.49) and 8-bit Q-GaLore (17.74) (Table 7).

a6KDxLeU7y.text: CogRouter with a Qwen2.5-7B backbone achieves an 82.3% average success rate across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, outperforming GPT-4o by 40.3 percentage points and OpenAI-o3 by 18.3 percentage points (Table 1).
CogRouter attains 92.5% success on ALFWorld (1,739.4 average tokens) and 72.0% success on ScienceWorld (1,543.4 average tokens) (Table 1).
CogRouter exceeds a GRPO baseline by 14.0 percentage points in success rate while using 62% fewer tokens on average (1,641.4 vs. 4,367.3 tokens) (Table 1).

Analysis of cognitive-level usage over a trajectory shows the L4 strategic-planning level peaking at 21.9% at task initiation before declining to 6.8%, while the L1 instinctive-response level rises from 48.5% to 94.8% as procedures crystallize (Section 5.1).

An ablation shows that restricting confidence-aware advantage reweighting (CoPO) to successful trajectories is critical; applying the reweighting to failed trajectories as well degrades performance to 83.0% (Table 2).

MSQq78w3JN.text: RePack-DiT-XL/2 achieves an FID-50k of 3.66 on ImageNet-1K at 256x256 resolution, a 35% improvement over VA-VAE's 5.63 (Table 1).
At 16 training epochs, RePack reaches an FID-2k of 34.23 versus VA-VAE's 56.87, a 39.8% faster convergence to comparable image quality (Table 1).

RePack's tokenizer uses a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 encoder (86.8M parameters) paired with a lightweight linear projection layer (24,608 trainable parameters) that reduces 768-dimensional VFM features to a 32-dimensional latent space (Section 3).
The RePack tokenizer reaches a reconstruction PSNR of 17.91 (vs. RAE's 17.06), with SSIM of 0.49 and LPIPS of 0.183 on ImageNet validation (Table 2).
RePack's tokenizer training completes in 14 epochs on 4 GPUs, versus VA-VAE's 130 epochs on 32 H800 GPUs, indicating substantially lower tokenizer training cost (Section 4).

KWlraRUdwI.text: On PDE benchmarks, Functional Attention outperforms Transolver with relative L2 errors of 0.50 vs. 0.64 on Elasticity, 0.43 vs. 0.53 on Airfoil, 0.42 vs. 0.57 on Darcy, and 8.00 vs. 9.44 on Navier-Stokes, i.e., 6-26.3% relative improvements (Table 1).
On RNA point-cloud 3D segmentation, Functional Attention reaches 89.0% accuracy, outperforming Transolver (87.5%) and DiffusionNet (85.1%) (Table 2).

On out-of-distribution generalization for AirfRANS aerodynamic prediction, Functional Attention reduces error to 23.4% for unseen Reynolds numbers (8.8% improvement over Transolver) and 13.3% for unseen angles of attack (9.5% improvement) (Table 3).

Proposition 4.5 establishes local Lipschitz continuity of the functional-correspondence attention operator, with a regularization parameter λ controlling the stability bound (Section 4.3, Proposition 4.5).

On resolution-invariance tests for the Burgers' equation, a model trained at 2048 spatial points and evaluated (super-resolution) at 8192 points achieves a relative L2 error of 1.081, the best among compared methods (Table 5).
In few-shot sinusoidal regression, Functional Attention achieves errors up to three orders of magnitude lower than vanilla softmax attention under sparse observations (Figure 2).

sP2bDU3tLw.text: MotionGRPO reduces MPJPE on the AMASS benchmark from 124.985mm (EgoAllo baseline) to 114.207mm, and PA-MPJPE from 103.958mm to 95.512mm (Table 1).
On the RICH dataset, MotionGRPO reduces MPJPE from 192.686mm to 187.223mm and Jitter from 4.135 to 3.685 relative to the EgoAllo baseline (Table 1).

MotionGRPO injects temporally smoothed Perlin noise into head trajectory inputs during GRPO training to counteract vanishing gradients caused by low intra-group sample diversity in diffusion-based recovery (Section 3).
The Perlin noise-injection strategy increases intra-group diversity from 1.88 to 3.14 at a noise coefficient of lambda=0.1 (Table 4).

MotionGRPO combines a trajectory-conditioned visual reward (trained via online contrastive learning with hard negatives) with four joint-level sub-rewards (rotation L1, position L2, velocity, and alignment-adjusted position) and adds zero additional computational overhead at inference (Section 3, Table 2).
An ablation shows the visual reward component specifically reduces ground penetration and jitter beyond what vanilla GRPO achieves alone (Table 3).

evAFxJXcrr.text: FedSDR identifies a 'Rewrite Paradox' in which naive federated self-distillation causes roughly 47% of distilled samples to fail to strictly entail the ground truth, increases response verbosity, and doubles the frequency of non-informative filler words (Section 3).

FedSDR's dual-stream design trains LoRA-S on distilled data (kept local, absorbing distributional/stylistic noise) and LoRA-R on raw ground-truth data (anchored to factual correctness), aggregating only LoRA-R parameters across clients (Section 4).

On Llama-2-7B fine-tuned on Dolly-15K, FedSDR improves the overall score from 71.21 (FedAvg baseline) to 77.38, including MMLU from 45.22 to 47.11, BBH from 34.21 to 35.81, and CRASS from 50.93 to 56.22 (Table 8).
An ablation decomposing performance shows FedSDR raises the faithfulness metric from 65.75 (baseline) to 74.33 (Table 6).
On Qwen2.5-7B evaluated across five domains for generalization, FedSDR improves HumanEval by 10.37 percentage points and GSM8K by 11.53 percentage points over the baseline (Table 10).

ujZ7Swx14s.text: GTASR's Trajectory Alignment (TA) loss re-projects predictions back onto the noisy manifold at each timestep in a discretized schedule (e.g., T=5 or T=4 steps), rather than supervising only the final clean output, to correct consistency drift accumulation (Section 3).
Adding the TA loss in Stage-I training improves PSNR by 0.40dB and reduces LPIPS by 0.0217 on ImageNet-Test compared to the baseline consistency-training objective (Table 4).

Dual-Reference Structural Rectification (DRSR) combines a Stability Loss (Sobel-operator-based structural discrepancy between fake and real trajectories) and a Rectification Loss (anchoring predictions to ground-truth spatial derivatives), together raising MANIQA on ImageNet-Test from a baseline to 0.5826, versus 0.5676 with Stability Loss alone and 0.5403 with Rectification Loss alone (Table 5).

On ImageNet-Test, GTASR achieves LPIPS 0.1916, CLIPIQA 0.7475, MUSIQ 65.09, MANIQA 0.5826, and TOPIQ 0.7423, outperforming CTMSR (0.1969, 0.6912, 60.17, 0.4857, 0.6793) and ResShift-4 (0.2074, 0.5993, 52.10, 0.3888, 0.5679) (Table 1).

GTASR runs in 0.08 seconds on a 128x128 input on an RTX 4090 with 172M parameters, matching CTMSR's parameter count while being 5-9x faster than T2I-distillation methods such as AddSR and OSEDiff (Table 3, Table 6).

MHXIvy3bsb.text: SWE-Compass comprises 2,000 verified instances curated from authentic GitHub pull requests, spanning 8 task types, 8 programming scenarios, and 10 programming languages (Section 3.1, Table 1).

Ten state-of-the-art LLMs, including Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro/Flash, GPT-4.1, Qwen3-Coder (480B and 30B), Kimi-K2, DeepSeek-V3, and SWE-agent-LM-32B, are benchmarked under two agentic frameworks, SWE-Agent and Claude Code (Table 2, Table 5).
Claude-Sonnet-4 ranks first overall with 32.9% Pass@1 under the Claude Code framework and 31.8% Pass@1 under SWE-Agent (Table 2).
Language-specific results show JVM ecosystem languages and JavaScript scoring higher, TypeScript notably lower, and systems languages harder than Python, which is mid-tier (Table 4, Figure 4).
Failure analysis attributes over 60% of model failures to Requirement Misinterpretation (30-34%) and Incomplete Solutions (29-42%) across the evaluated models (Section 4.2.2, Figure 7).

cIsGv65BzF.text: On eight SafeBench base scenarios, ScenePilot achieves a collision rate of 0.893, exceeding ChatScene's 0.831 and other baseline methods around 0.620, while maintaining a comparable overall score of 0.476 versus ChatScene's 0.482 (Table 1).

ScenePilot formulates scenario generation as a constrained multi-objective MDP maximizing an AV-risk objective subject to a physical-feasibility constraint J_sigma(pi) >= epsilon, using an RSS-derived physical feasibility score and a learned AV-risk predictor Phi (Section 3).

Adversarial fine-tuning of the ego policy on ScenePilot-generated boundary-band scenarios reduces the downstream crash rate on held-out test scenes from 0.854 (untrained) to 0.072, outperforming fine-tuning on ChatScene-generated scenarios (0.134 post-training) (Table 4).

Analysis of physically invalid frame rates versus risk-physics coverage shows ScenePilot achieves higher collision rates than ChatScene while maintaining lower rates of physically invalid frames (Figure 4).

Cross-controller generalization tests on CARLA Autopilot, AIM-BEV, TransFuser, and rule-based agents confirm ScenePilot's boundary-band scenarios remain effective beyond the RL-based controller used during generation (Table 2).
