j9aoIFr5aM.text: Definition 1 introduces ℓ*-smoothness, bounding the Hessian via a general norm and its dual, ‖∇²f(x)h‖* ≤ ℓ(‖∇f(x)‖*)‖h‖, generalizing prior ℓ-smoothness beyond the Euclidean/ℓ2 setting (Section 3.1, Definition 1)
Theorem 8 shows mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness attains O(1/T) convergence for both average-iterate and last-iterate suboptimality with an appropriately chosen learning rate (Section 4, Theorem 8)
Theorem 9 shows an accelerated mirror descent variant attains the optimal O(1/T^2) convergence rate under ℓ*-smoothness via a time-partition analysis technique (Section 4, Theorem 9)

Theorem 10 and Theorem 11 extend the O(1/T) rate to optimistic mirror descent and mirror prox respectively, using a stability-tracking argument and a descent property for both update sequences (Section 4, Theorems 10-11)
Theorem 12 establishes an Õ(1/√t) anytime convergence rate for stochastic mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness with a generalized bounded-noise assumption ‖ϵ_t‖* ≤ σ(‖∇f(x_t)‖*) (Section 5, Theorem 12)

Proposition 4 shows that on the simplex, ℓ*-smoothness yields a constant smoothness parameter whereas standard ℓ-smoothness has an O(n) dimension dependence, illustrating the benefit of the generalized notion (Section 3.2, Proposition 4)

lZxQyCh5H7.text: Conditional Diffusion Sampling (CDS) combines Parallel Tempering with a diffusion-based transport step defined by a closed-form SDE (Equation 15) whose score function is computed analytically via a change-of-variables formula rather than learned by a neural network (Section 3.2)

CDS achieves a mean Hypervolume Ratio (HVR) of 0.9976 ± 0.0015 averaged across benchmark targets, versus 0.9827 ± 0.0083 for Non-Reversible Parallel Tempering (NRPT) and 0.9287 ± 0.0277 for Optimized Annealed SMC (OASMC) (Section 5, Table 1)

CDS substantially outperforms Diffusive Gibbs Sampling (DiGS, HVR 0.5464 ± 0.1550) and standard MALA/HMC samplers (HVR roughly 0.52-0.63) on the sample-quality-versus-density-evaluation-cost trade-off (Section 5, Table 1)

CDS is evaluated on 8 target distributions including 2D and 16D Gaussian mixtures, 39D and 165D Lennard-Jones clusters, 66D Alanine Dipeptide, and a 550D Bayesian Neural Network posterior (Section 5, Table 1)

Proposition 3.6 shows that sampling from the intermediate conditional distribution ν_{t|z} becomes exponentially easier as t → 0, with Wasserstein-1 distance to the target scaling linearly in t for the linear interpolant case (Section 3, Proposition 3.6)

XN7YWDeFeC.text: Faithful-Agent raises Trap Success Rate (Trap SR) from a 13.88% baseline to 80.21% after Stage II training, while overall task Success Rate improves from 60.38% to 71.67% (Section 5.2, Table 1)

Section 3.3 formalizes 'advantage collapse' in low-variance rollout groups under GRPO, and Figure 3 shows the near-zero-advantage mass P(|A|<0.01) rises from 0.14 to 0.48 under standard GRPO, motivating the Guided Advantage Estimator (Section 3.3, Figure 3)

The Guided Advantage Estimator (GuAE), introduced in Section 4.2.2, combines Anchor Regularization—augmenting the reward set with boundary points {0,1} to avoid zero-advantage degeneracy—with Variance-Adaptive Tempering (VAT), a sigmoid-gated interpolation between low-variance sharpening and high-variance dampening (Section 4.2.2)

Training proceeds in two stages: Stage I (SFT) instills abstainment behavior under evidence perturbations, and Stage II (GRPO+GuAE) adds thought-action consistency rewards to amplify faithfulness (Section 4)
Faithful-Agent preserves general instruction-following performance on standard (non-trap) GUI tasks despite the large gains in trap detection, per the Section 5.2 ablations (Section 5.2)

NTd7TQYQkX.text: Theorem 1 (Context-Relation Factorization) proves that Systematic Linear Propagation requires features to decompose as a tensor product separating entity-pair context from relation content (Theorem 1)

Theorem 2 (Symmetric-Antisymmetric Alignment) proves that requiring converse equivariance forces a further decomposition of features into symmetric and antisymmetric components to encode argument order (Theorem 2)

Theorem 3 (Structural Collapse of Linear Conjunction) proves that any bilinear conjunction operator satisfying idempotence and negation equivariance must be trivial, collapsing all features to zero (Theorem 3)

The paper argues negation and conjunction/composition cannot coexist under the Linear Propagation Assumption's linear constraints, since composition reduces to a problematic bilinear conjunction operator (Section on Relation Algebra Operations)

The incompatibility between negation-equivariance and bilinear conjunction is offered as an explanation for empirically observed failures in knowledge editing, the 'reversal curse,' and multi-hop reasoning (Theorem 3 discussion)

N05ha5nVEU.text: Mind Dreamer (MD) achieves a 1.67x average speedup in sample efficiency over DreamerV3 on the DeepMind Control Suite, reaching 90% of peak performance in 334.7k steps versus DreamerV3's 557.6k steps (Section 5, Table 1)

MD achieves up to 8.8x speedup on sparse-reward bottleneck tasks such as Pendulum Swingup, attributed to Active Causal Intervention (ACI) enabling non-continuous latent jumps to unexplored manifold regions (Section 3.2, Section 5)
MD attains higher final average returns of 831.1 versus DreamerV3's 780.3, with task-level gains including +59.8% on Hopper Hop and +30.3% on Quadruped Run (Table 1)

Theorem 4.2 establishes a path-integral equivalence between the Relay Value Function/Relay Uncertainty Function (RVF/RUF, derived in Sections 3.3-3.4) and Expected Free Energy components (Section 4, Theorem 4.2)
Proposition 4.10 shows that conductance expansion reduces the hitting time for reaching unexplored manifold regions from O(poly(Φ^-1)) to O(log|ℳ|) (Section 4, Proposition 4.10)
A three-ring manifold case study demonstrates a 4.2x acceleration by identifying topological gateways between disconnected regions of latent space (Section 5.2, Figure 3)

o3SFLhXkvX.text: Under 50-step AutoAttack (l_inf=4/255), CSR achieves 66.4% average robust accuracy across 16 zero-shot classification benchmarks, an 18.1% improvement over the best prior test-time defense (Table 2).
Under 10-step PGD (l_inf=1/255), CSR reaches 58.1% robust accuracy, a 6.9% gain over the strongest baseline, while clean accuracy drops by only 0.7% on average (Table 1, Table 2).

CSR's contrastive rectification combines an attraction term toward a low-pass-filtered feature anchor with a repulsion term away from the original adversarial feature, and removing either term reduces robustness from 69.8% back to 51.6% on the General datasets in the ablation (Table 6, Section 4).
CSR runs at an average inference latency of 15.17ms per image on an RTX 4090, about 11.6x faster than the R-TPT test-time defense baseline at 176.33ms (Table 3).
CSR generalizes beyond classification, improving mIoU by 16.7% under attack on semantic segmentation and restoring roughly 43.0% accuracy on image captioning and VQA tasks (Table 7).

FygaF16KNo.text: Acoustic Interference (AIA) demonstrates that LALM safety alignment can be broken solely via Acoustic Latent Semantics (ALS) intrinsic to audio generative model priors, decoupled from any instance-specific optimization of the attack payload (Section 2).

On Qwen2.5-Omni, AIA raises the ASR-M jailbreak metric from a 50.98% text-only baseline to 100% ASR-M by injecting ALS into audio, and achieves a similar 50-percentage-point improvement on Gemini-2.5-Pro (Table 2).
Across 10-11 LALMs compared against 9 existing jailbreak methods, AIA attains the highest attack success rates, including 100.00% ASR-M on Qwen2.5-Omni and 93.10% ASR-M on Gemini-3-Pro (Table 3).
Even when paired with weak jailbreak text prompts from HH-RLHF, AIA still improves ASR by 7.04 to 27.78 percentage points over text-only attacks (Table 6).

Selecting the top 30 ALS candidates from the constructed arsenal outperforms both bottom-30 and non-ALS audio configurations, and human evaluation confirms the ASR-M metric aligns better with human judgments of jailbreak success than the standard ASR-R metric (Table 7, Table 5).

15Gs65kvHS.text: ClinTutor-R1 achieves an 8.35 average score on MedXpertQA-based clinical Socratic education evaluation, a roughly 20% improvement over its Qwen2.5VL base model score of 6.96 (Table 2).
ClinTutor-R1's score of 8.35 is comparable to proprietary reasoning models o3 (8.42) and GPT-4o (8.36) on the same evaluation (Table 2).

Ablating components of ClinTutor-R1 shows the RL training stage is most critical: removing RL drops the score to 7.58, removing the thinking stage drops it to 7.94, using a vanilla (non-shaped) reward drops it to 8.01, and removing the veto mechanism drops it to 7.87 with degraded safety behavior (Table 2).

As the number of simulated students scales from 1 to 10, ClinTutor-R1 maintains an average score around 8.20, whereas the Med-SocraticLM baseline declines from about 7.5 to below 6.7, a roughly 15% drop (Figure 4, Table 10).
Human expert evaluation gives ClinTutor-R1 an average score of 8.64, exceeding o3's 8.52, with a real user study score of 8.59 and strong inter-rater agreement (kappa=0.79) (Table 4, Section 5).

KwO83Ao6BW.text: Applying the multivariate delta method to thought-level advantage estimation shows that increasing the number of sampled thoughts K leaves a strictly positive variance floor, while increasing the number of answers per thought M drives the variance asymptotically to zero (Section 4.2, Equation 4).

On math reasoning, GRPO-MA with 4 thoughts and 4 answers each (T4A4) achieves 14.70 Pass@10 versus 11.78 for standard GRPO with 4 thoughts and 1 answer (T4A1), at a modest 15% increase in per-step training time (132.87s vs 111.24s) (Table 1).
On sparse-reward robotic manipulation, T4A4 raises success rate from 10.75% to 31.40% on seen objects and from 3.94% to 16.00% on unseen objects compared to T4A1 (Table 4).

T4A4 matches or slightly exceeds the performance of T16A1 (16 thoughts, 1 answer) while using only about 60% of the training time, and T4A3 outperforms T16A1 across all metrics in the ablation on trajectory prediction (Section 5.3, Figure 3).

Gradient Spike Score (GSS@10) analysis shows T4A4 reduces gradient spikes relative to T4A1 on object detection (1 vs 5) and trajectory prediction (10 vs 14), indicating improved optimization stability from answer-level branching (Section 5, GSS metric).

he06cvibXv.text: Pre-trained omni-modal LLMs such as Qwen3-Omni exhibit modality bias, with accuracy on MMStar dropping from 72.1% (visual-only) to 68.5% when audio is added, motivating OmniVideo-R1's two-stage training (Section 1).

OmniVideo-R1 improves audio-visual reasoning substantially over its baseline, gaining +19.2 points on Daily-Omni (82.8% vs 63.6%), +11.8 points on WorldSense (65.8% vs 54.0%), and +8.5 points on IntentBench (74.2% vs 65.7%) (Table 1).
On OmniVideoBench, OmniVideo-R1 reaches 44.8% accuracy, a 7.8-point gain over Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct (Table 2).

Ablating the intent reward reduces OmniVideoBench performance by 6.4 points and ablating the attention reward reduces it by 1.1 points, while the Modality-attentive Fusion stage alone yields a 12.4% gain and the Query-intensive Grounding stage alone yields a 17.8% gain (Table 5, Section 3).
OmniVideo-R1 preserves visual-only task performance after audio-visual training, improving Video-MME by 3.1 points and LVBench by 1.7 points, with only a 1.4-point drop on MLVU (Table 3).

BFX213mKfh.text: NMWPM combines a graph neural network (4 TransformerConv layers, 4 attention heads) with a 2-layer Transformer encoder over a 128-dimensional hidden representation to predict dynamic edge weights for Minimum Weight Perfect Matching decoding (Section 4.3).

On the toric code under depolarizing noise, NMWPM reaches a threshold of 17.9%, versus a classical MWPM threshold of 16.0% and a theoretical maximum-likelihood bound of 18.9% (Section 5.3, Figures 2-4).

On the toric code under independent noise, NMWPM reaches a threshold of 10.95%, exceeding classical MWPM's 10.3% and approaching the theoretical maximum-likelihood bound of 11.0% (Section 5.3, Figures 2-4).

NMWPM is trained end-to-end through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm using a binary cross-entropy edge-classification proxy loss with entropy regularization (lambda=0.01), Adam optimizer at learning rate 9e-5, batch size 32, for 200-1000 epochs (Section 4.4).

NMWPM maintains approximately 3.9M parameters across all tested code sizes and is competitive with QECCT on the rotated surface code, matching it at L=7 while surpassing classical decoding methods (Section 5.3, Appendix B).

BXE3Z0EHCs.text: Theorem 3.1 shows that for targets expressible as polynomials in parameters and Kronecker deltas, the coefficients of the formal power series expansion of the loss's time derivatives are themselves polynomials in the width H, the parameterization exponent p, and the initialization variance sigma^2 (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 characterizes the leading and Pareto-optimal terms of the loss expansion for identity-tensor targets, organizing gradient-flow learning regimes into a polygon structure defined by scaling conditions on H, p, and sigma^2 (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

An NTK-like regime, in which features do not evolve during training, appears only at points/edges B-C of the Pareto polygon in the asymmetric parameterization case, while Proposition 8.2 proves the NTK kernel stays static throughout training in the symmetric matrix case (nu=2), explaining the absence of an NTK limit there (Section 4, Proposition 8.2).

Mean-field, feature-evolving regimes require the initialization variance to scale as sigma^2 proportional to 1/H (symmetric case) or sigma^2 proportional to 1/H^(2/nu) (asymmetric case), corresponding to edges B-E and C-D of the Pareto polygon respectively (Section 4).
For the canonical polyadic (symmetric, nu=2) identity-tensor target, Section 9 derives a complete closed-form solution to the gradient flow (Equations 19-20), valid across all parameter scalings.
For the nu=4 symmetric case, Section 10 derives a gradient-ascent solution identifying convergent low-noise and divergent high-noise regimes separated by an explicit threshold given in Equation 23.

YYhv4h8X1O.text: DoPR reduces rollout cost per update step from K x G to G + (K-1), an uncertainty-aware one-shot sample selection scheme combining reward volatility with an entropy-modulated exploration term (Equation 18, Section 4, Algorithm 1).
On Qwen-1.5B with a fixed rollout budget, DoPR matches or slightly exceeds GRPO on accuracy: 73.5 vs 71.8 on MATH and 82.2 vs 82.0 on GSM8K (Table 1).
Under a fixed budget of 10k rollouts, DoPR achieves 46.1 average accuracy versus GRPO's 35.2, a 10.9 percentage-point advantage (Table 3).

Section 3 derives a theoretical lower bound of N >= O(ln(epsilon)/epsilon') training steps, and empirically only 16 training examples per batch are needed for near-optimal performance on MATH and Minerva-Math, with performance degrading below 8 samples (Section 3, Figure 1).
DoPR produces progressively shorter reasoning trajectories over training and achieves 20-30% faster per-step update time than GRPO (Figure 3).

Z1nbtKcLQk.text: Theorem 1 derives a Bayesian regret bound for BFTS of the form E[Regret_T] <= K*sigma*sqrt(2*T*m*Psi_T) under ideal posterior sampling, where Psi_T captures the information complexity of the BART tree structures and leaf parameters (Theorem 1).

Lemma 2 bounds the mutual information between the true forest parameters and the observed history by I(theta*; H_T) <= K*m*Psi_T, via a four-step proof using structure-leaf factorization, entropy bounds from depth-exponential priors, and Gaussian capacity bounds (Lemma 2).

Across nine OpenML contextual bandit benchmarks, BFTS achieves the best average rank of 1.63, with lowest cumulative regret on datasets including Adult (1538.7 +/- 41.2), MagicTelescope (1488.2 +/- 36.8), Mushroom (53.9 +/- 7.6), and Shuttle (106.9 +/- 8.4) (Table 1).
On the synthetic study, BFTS attains an average rank of 1.63 versus 3.00 for NeuralTS, with 44.5 +/- 20.1 regret on the correctly-specified SynBART setting (Table 2).

In offline policy evaluation on the Drink Less micro-randomized trial using self-normalized importance sampling, BFTS yields a 27.0% improvement over a random policy at t=1000 and a 38.2% improvement (0.0345 absolute gain) at t=10,000, outperforming linear, neural, and tree-ensemble baselines.

Section 7 reports imperfect MCMC mixing for BFTS (R-hat = 1.19-1.90) but stable induced decisions (policy Delta-TV of 0.03-0.08 by t=10,000), with cumulative runtime of about 33 minutes on Covertype and 44 minutes on MNIST for T=10,000 (Section 7).

MjGhDpCtF9.text: On SWE-Bench Lite, ConRAD (referred to as O-CRD in the paper text) improves Pass@1 over an Agentless baseline by 10.4 percentage points for GPT-4o (to 37.7%), 8.6 points for DeepSeek-V3 (to 35.6%), and 10.3 points for GPT-5 (to 40.0%) (Table 1, Section 5.1).

The method operates in three stages: repository-level exemplar mining using All-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings plus LLM-based ranking, an Exemplar Guardian filter across five compatibility dimensions achieving 90% label stability, and Backward Reasoning Distillation that reconstructs repair plans constrained by verified patch outcomes (Section 3.1-3.3, Figure 1, Table 3).
Removing the Exemplar Guardian filter reduces Pass@1 by 4.0 points for GPT-4o, 2.3 points for GPT-5, and 5.6 points for DeepSeek-V3 (Table 2, Section 5.2).
Backward Reasoning Distillation outperforms MCTS-based exploration on Pass@1 (41.0% vs 28.0%) while using 9.71x fewer LLM calls and 2.47x fewer tokens (Table 4, Section 5.2).
Fault localization accuracy reaches 77.0% at the file level and 59.3% at the function level, guiding patch generation without fine-tuning or search (Section 5.1).
Performance holds fairly consistently across difficulty levels, with medium-high difficulty issues reaching 28.5-29.2% Pass@1 across all three backbone models (Figure 2).

exS97jumOg.text: Aurora exhibits the strongest data-scaling exponent (β≈0.51) among the five compared weather models, meaning a 10x increase in training dataset size reduces validation loss by up to 3.2x (Section 3.1, Table 1).
The other four models show weaker data-scaling exponents than Aurora: AIFS β≈0.46, Pangu β≈0.43, GraphCast β≈0.36, and SFNO β≈0.34 (Section 3.1, Table 1).

Across all five weather models, wider network configurations consistently achieve lower validation loss than deeper ones at matched parameter counts, contrasting with scaling trends observed in language models (Section 3.2, Figure 4).
GraphCast and SFNO perform effectively even at depth=1, suggesting 6-hour weather prediction dynamics are well-approximated by near-linear models (Section 3.2, Figure 4).

Aurora achieves 37.2% GPU utilization on H100 hardware versus only 0.017% for GraphCast, a roughly 2000x gap attributed to Aurora's hardware-optimized attention mechanism versus GraphCast's memory-bound message-passing architecture (Section 4, Table 2).

Pangu's parameter scaling only becomes effective once trained on sufficient data (30TB vs 15TB), indicating a data-dependent threshold before model-size scaling yields benefits (Section 3.1, Figure 3).

sGOmm03F40.text: FB-PbRL is the first method to connect reward-free representation learning (via Forward-Backward representations) with offline preference-based reinforcement learning, showing the standard preference loss can be equivalently reformulated as a SimCLR-style contrastive objective (Section 3.1, Equation 13).

On the DeepMind Control Suite benchmark spanning 16 tasks across four domains (Cheetah, Walker, Quadruped, Pointmass) under the standard 2,000-preference-pair PbRL protocol, Ours-FT outperforms offline PbRL baselines DPPO, OPPO, OPRL, CLARIFY, and LiRE (Section 4.1, Section 4.2, Table 1).
On Quadruped-Stand, Ours-FT achieves a return of 991.1±0.3 compared to CLARIFY's 901.0±17.6 (Section 4.2, Table 1).

FB-PbRL's performance degrades only about 10% when the number of preference pairs is reduced from 2,000 to 200, and it maintains superiority over baselines even under 20% preference label noise (Section 4.2).
On real human-labeled preferences, FB-PbRL is competitive but slightly underperforms DPPO on Adroit Pen-human (70.2 vs. 76.3 episodic return) (Section 4.2).

L8VRGNACqH.text: Polyphonia achieves a 15.5% relative increase in target alignment (CLAP score) over the strongest baseline, reaching 0.342±0.094 versus Melodia's 0.296±0.103 on MUSDB18-HQ (Table 1).

On the MusicDelta subset, Polyphonia attains an Adherence-Structure Balance (ASB) of 0.8291 and an Adherence-Musicality Balance (AMB) of 0.8631, both exceeding Melodia's 0.807 and 0.806 respectively (Table 1).
In subjective evaluation on MusicDelta, Polyphonia scores 3.804±0.912 on Target Timbre Alignment (TTA) versus Melodia's 3.215 (Table 1).

PolyEvalPrompts provides a standardized evaluation benchmark of 1,170 context-aware polyphonic timbre-transfer tasks, built via an acoustic-analysis-then-task-synthesis pipeline with 15 distinct editing tasks per musical piece (Section 5.1).
Polyphonia's performance degrades gracefully under sparse editing prompts, dropping from 0.342 to 0.322 CLAP score compared to full prompts (Section 5.1).

4COS6SMf8r.text: CREATOR relaxes the noise assumption of prior linear causal representation learning methods (e.g., LiNGCReL) to allow exogenous noise components to be non-identical across environments, requiring only that at most one component be Gaussian (Section 2, Assumption 1).

Theorem 1 establishes that, under the paper's three assumptions, observed data from at least d environments identifies the latent causal features and true causal DAG up to the 'surrounding-set' equivalence class (∼sur) (Section 2, Theorem 1).

In synthetic experiments across latent dimensions d∈{2,3,5,7} with K=d environments, CREATOR achieves higher latent-feature recovery (LocR²) and lower Structural Hamming Distance for DAG reconstruction than LiNGCReL (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

In an LLM interpretability case study recovering a three-node causal structure (Background→Condition→Ending) from hidden states of six LLMs, CREATOR recovers all three correct edges for Llama Guard and 2/3 for TinyLlama, while LiNGCReL achieves only 2/6 and 1/6 correct edges on comparable models (Section 4.2, Table 1).

FCUozD1Ayx.text: SubDAPS++ achieves 29.34 PSNR on FFHQ random 70% inpainting versus 28.88 for pixel-space DAPS, and a lower FID of 64.61 versus 74.16 (Section 4.1, Table 1).
SubDAPS++ processes images across a dynamic resolution schedule (64x64x3, then 128x128x3, then 256x256x3), switching resolutions at timesteps t_s=⌊2N/3⌋ and t_h=⌊N/3⌋ during sampling (Section 4.1).
SubDAPS++ achieves an average inference time of 7.4 seconds per image on the HDR recovery task, versus 122.3 seconds for DPS and 16.1 seconds for DAPS (Section 4.2, Table 2).
SubDAPS++'s progressive resolution scheme uses 2796/2872/3906 MB of memory across its three resolution stages, substantially less than pixel-space approaches (Section 4.2, Table 2).

SubDAPS++ extends SubDAPS with three additions: adaptive noise injection that switches from stochastic to deterministic updates upon convergence, a post-hoc corrector step using the UniPC framework, and conjugate-gradient optimization replacing Langevin dynamics for measurement consistency (Section 3.3).

0CiahYXWsk.text: TIMI achieves the best Layout Consistency Distance (LCD) of 0.598 and F-Score-Scene (FS-S) of 0.458 among compared methods, indicating superior global spatial fidelity without any additional training (Table 1).

TIMI attains the best Separation Success Rate (SSR) of 0.809 and F-Score-Object (FS-O) of 0.353, outperforming the training-based baseline MIDI (SSR 0.737, LCD 0.634) on local instance distinctiveness (Table 1).
TIMI runs inference in about 59.2 seconds, substantially faster than MIDI (90.1s) and the compositional baseline DPA (783s), while being close to the Hunyuan3D 2.0 base model (54.2s) (Table 1).
In a user study, evaluators preferred TIMI's outputs 57.5% of the time for global layout alignment and 60.1% of the time for instance distinctiveness over baseline methods (Figure 6).

An ablation shows that removing the Instance-aware Spatial Guidance (ISG) module and Spatially-aware Guidance Unit (SGU) drops SSR from 0.809 to 0.697, and using ISG layers 0-4 with a diffusion timestep range of t≤15 is the optimal configuration (Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).
The Spatially-aware Guidance Unit performs best with guidance strength α=0.1 and Gaussian smoothing σ=1.5 for maintaining spatial consistency across generated instances (Table 6, Table 7).

Xk3DcnxZdQ.text: The DNA framework excavates forgery-discriminative units (FDUs) inherent in pre-trained models using a triadic fusion score Si,k = |ḡi,k · āi,k · wi,k| combining gradient sensitivity, activation magnitude, and weight contribution, without requiring end-to-end retraining (Section 4.2).
DNA achieves 97.2% mean accuracy on ForenSynths and 96.5% on GenImage cross-dataset evaluation (Table 1).

On the HIFI-Gen benchmark spanning unseen generative architectures (SDv2.1, SDv3.5, SDXL, FLUX, Z-Image), DNA reaches 96.4% mean accuracy, surpassing DRCT(Conv-B) by 5.3% and MoLD by 15.4% (Table 2, Section 5.2).
On Midjourney-generated images specifically, DNA attains 93.7% accuracy versus 76.3% for MoLD, a 17.4% absolute improvement (Section 5.2).
DNA generalizes across CNN, ViT, and LLM backbone architectures, boosting ResNet to 95.4% AP and DINOv2-Base to 93.6% AP (Figure 11, Section 5.4).
Ablating the identified FDUs causes accuracy to drop from 98.4% to 89.25%, while random neuron removal has negligible impact, confirming the neurons' specificity to forgery detection (Figure 7).

sGCDBHIr9u.text: On decoder-only models, VIA-SD achieves 1.82-2.70x speedup over standard greedy decoding across QA benchmarks (WebQuestions, NaturalQA, TriviaQA), with Gemma2 2B->27B reaching 2.32-2.61x speedup (Table 2, Section 4.2).

On encoder-decoder models, VIA-SD achieves 1.65-3.35x speedup on summarization (XSum, CNN/DailyMail) and translation (WMT14 En-De) tasks, with WMT14 translation showing the largest gain at 2.5-3.35x (Table 3, Section 4.2).
VIA-SD reduces rejection rates relative to standard speculative decoding by roughly 30-45% (e.g., Gemma2 2B->27B rejection rate falls from 0.27-0.45 to 0.14-0.30) (Table 2, Section 4.2).

VIA-SD delivers 10-20% speedups over strong speculative decoding baselines and 2.5-3x acceleration over non-drafting decoding while maintaining or slightly improving output quality metrics such as ROUGE-2 and BLEU (Section 4.2).
VIA-SD is evaluated across five task categories: QA (WebQuestions, NaturalQA, TriviaQA), summarization, translation, reasoning (GSM8K, 8-shot), and coding (MBPP) (Section 4.2).

CPB16KCuNk.text: Theorem 3.1 proves a simple regret lower bound requiring Omega(sigma^2/epsilon^2 * (ln B/epsilon)^d * (ln ln B/epsilon)^(-d) * ln 1/delta) time steps for any algorithm to find an epsilon-optimal point on the hypersphere domain with a squared exponential kernel (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

Theorem 3.2 proves a cumulative regret lower bound of Omega(sqrt(T*sigma^2 * (ln(B^2*T/sigma^2) * ln 1/delta)^d * (ln ln(B^2*T/sigma^2 * ln 1/delta))^(-d))) for any algorithm on the hypersphere domain (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).

Theorem 5.1 establishes an improved upper bound of O((ln T)^(d+1) * (ln ln T)^(-d)) on the maximum information gain for the squared exponential kernel, applicable to both compact domains in R^d and hyperspheres S^d (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
The improved information gain bound closes a (ln T)^(d/4) gap present in prior results by removing dimension-dependent logarithmic factors that previously limited the analysis (Section 5).

IwP8LZzc97.text: Iterative Hessian Mixing (IHM) is proven differentially private and, per Theorem 1, provides excess empirical risk (utility) bounds for differentially private ordinary least squares that improve upon AdaSSP by removing a multiplicative factor that can be as large as the square root of the data dimension (Theorem 1).

IHM builds on Gaussian sketching approaches to DP-OLS, inspired by the Iterative Hessian Sketch of Pilanci et al., and the paper presents new accuracy guarantees for prior Gaussian sketching methods clarifying when they perform well and how IHM avoids their limitations (Section 4).
A rigorous empirical evaluation on a large suite of datasets demonstrates that IHM consistently outperforms prior baselines, including AdaSSP (Section 5).

The paper establishes differential privacy guarantees for IHM alongside its utility bounds, situating it as a near-optimal alternative to sufficient-statistics-perturbation methods like AdaSSP for DP-OLS (Theorem 1, Section 5).

ZipucsUgc6.text: Long Grounded Thoughts comprises over 1M synthetic vision-centric questions, built via a two-stage synthesis pipeline: Stage 1 generates ~750K object-centric MCQs from dense captions and bounding boxes, and Stage 2 composition-hardening merges simpler questions into ~250K harder multi-hop problems (Section 3, Figure 1)

Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B on this data with SFT, offline RL (DPO), and online RL (GRPO) lets it match or outperform MiMo-VL-7B-RL on 3 of 5 vision-centric benchmarks, including V*Bench (83.25) and CV-Bench (82.28) (Section 4.1, Table 2)
Training on the vision-centric data transfers to text-only reasoning, improving MMLU-Pro accuracy by roughly +3% over the base model (Table 4)
Cross-modal transfer extends to audio reasoning, with gains on the MMAU benchmark including sound (78.30), music (70.20), and speech subsets (Table 5)
Cross-modal transfer also extends to embodied QA, with the SFT+DPO variant reaching 56.34 accuracy on the NiEH benchmark, roughly +10 points over the base model (Table 8)

An ablation shows the offline staged approach (750K SFT examples + 129K DPO examples, score 0.740) nearly matches online GRPO reinforcement learning (score 0.757), while online RL performance plateaus after about 70K examples (Table 3)

r3h23Jv26a.text: The Prejudicial Trick (Algorithm 1) constructs prediction intervals by returning a null (empty or minimal) interval with probability (1-p) and an adjusted conformal interval with probability p, provably preserving valid marginal coverage per Theorem 6 while shrinking average interval length (Section on Prejudicial Trick, Algorithm 1, Theorem 6)
On synthetic data, PT applied to Vanilla Conformal Prediction (PT-VCP) reduces average interval length from 22.894 to 22.614 at alpha=0.10 while preserving nominal coverage (Table 1)
On real-world regression benchmarks (including MEPS and BIO), PT-VCP reduces interval length in 9 of 10 datasets while maintaining 90% marginal coverage (Table 2)

Despite valid marginal coverage, the Prejudicial Trick yields highly unstable predictions: Proposition 2 proves its interval stability metric IS(C_PT) = p(1-p)(E(L))^2 > 0, meaning the same input can receive completely different interval outputs across repeated conformal calibration runs (Definition 1, Proposition 2)

The proposed Interval Stability metric can flag methods, such as localized conformal prediction, that implicitly exploit PT-like randomness to shrink length, since Proposition 1 shows PT is a special case of localized CP when local scale estimators output extreme values (Definition 1, Proposition 1)

yyBWTXi8B5.text: FR3D disentangles future 3D scene evolution from agent ego-motion using two masked transformers operating in a unified 3D latent space, a Pose Masked Transformer for camera translation/rotation and a Spatial Masked Transformer for depth prediction, connected via cross-attention (Section 3.3)

FR3D is trained via teacher-student distillation from CUT3R's frozen latent space using a smooth L1 loss and autoregressive sliding-window training on the Waymo Open Dataset (Section 3.4, Equations 4-6)

On zero-shot depth forecasting on KITTI and nuScenes at a 2-second prediction horizon, FR3D achieves AbsRel of 0.178 (KITTI) and 0.229 (nuScenes), outperforming baselines including Copy Last, DINO-Foresight, and CUT3R-Foresight across all tested horizons (Table 1)

An ablation shows that both the information-sharing cross-attention component and autoregressive training are critical, with the combined full FR3D model (variant A6) outperforming ablated variants (Table 3, variants A4-A6)

Fixed-camera experiments confirm the disentanglement works as intended: static regions show only 0.4-1.6% relative depth change after frame-wise alignment, compared to 7.64-12.97% for dynamic regions (Section 4.2.4, Tables 5-6)

zjsvhm2QyV.text: The method replaces conventional 2D feature grids with compact 1D token sequences from a frozen TiTok tokenizer as a non-spatial carrier for global appearance factors (Section 4.1)

Selective Token Editing (STE) identifies only two appearance-sensitive token positions (12 and 18 in the TiTok-32 configuration) and edits only channels {6,7,8} of those tokens to steer global appearance coherence, rather than modifying all tokens (Section 4.1)

A Token-to-Map interface converts the edited 1D tokens back into 2D feature maps via hierarchical residual local aggregation and multi-stage upsampling to 256x256 resolution, feeding a factorized base/detail fusion module (Section 4.2, Equations 10-11, Table 9)

On M3FD, RoadScene, TNO, and Harvard fusion benchmarks measured by EN, SD, SCD, SSIM, EI, SF, and AG, the method achieves best or second-best scores across all datasets, outperforming CDDFuse, DDFM, and Text-DiFuse (Table 1, Figure 3)
Downstream evaluation shows the fused images improve object detection mAP50:95 and semantic segmentation mIoU compared to competing fusion methods (Table 2)

Ablations show jointly editing token positions 12 and 18 together outperforms editing either position alone, and a 32-token TiTok configuration is optimal versus other token-count settings (Table 3, Table 4)

3NdFFpcEjU.text: SinkProbe defines an attention sink score (Definition 2.1) as the average attention a token receives from all subsequent tokens, normalized by remaining sequence length, and extracts top-k sink scores across layers and heads as features for a logistic regression hallucination classifier (Section 2, Definition 2.1)

Hallucination-relevant sink signals are strongest when attention concentration coincides with large value-vector norms, with norm differences and importance scores peaking together in middle layers (Section 2.3, Figure 2)

Across 7 datasets (including GSM8K, TruthfulQA, NQ-Open, TriviaQA, SQuADv2, HaluEvalQA, and UMWP) and 4 LLMs (Llama3.2-3B, Phi3.5, Llama3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo), SinkProbe achieves the best ROC-AUC in 23 of 28 model-dataset pairs, with relative improvements of +0.1% to +4.9% over competing detectors (Table 1)

Prior hallucination-detection methods such as LLMCheck, LookbackLens, TOHA, and spectral-feature approaches are shown to implicitly depend on attention sink behavior, positioning SinkProbe as a unifying, theoretically grounded framework for these methods (Section 2.4)

DUJL3a5Y57.text: On the SimplerEnv OOD benchmark, LangForce achieves 66.5% average success versus 55.2% for the same-architecture QwenGR00T baseline, an 11.3 percentage point improvement (Table 1).

LangForce's Latent Action Queries are 64 learnable tokens appended to the VLM vocabulary that serve as a bottleneck between the vision-language model and the Diffusion Transformer action head, enabling a dual-branch causal-attention architecture (Section 3.2).

The training objective combines a posteriori-branch flow-matching loss, a priori-branch flow-matching loss, and a log-likelihood-ratio (LLR) maximization term with hyperparameters λ=0.3 and β=0.1 (Section 3.4).
Ablations show the Bayesian LLR objective contributes 6.0 percentage points beyond the architectural change alone: baseline 55.2%, +Action Query only 57.5%, full LangForce 63.5% (Table 5).
On RoboCasa, LangForce reaches 52.6% average success, outperforming Isaac-GR00T N1.6 (47.6%) and QwenOFT (48.8%) (Section 4.3).

On LIBERO Goal, a benchmark with visually ambiguous scenes, LangForce achieves 99.4% success versus 97.4% for the baseline, while a vision-only ablation model collapses to 9.8% success, demonstrating the information-collapse phenomenon the paper targets (Section 4.2, Section 2.2).

F99QbhItQE.text: DenseMLLM enables a standard multimodal LLM to perform dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation without adding task-specific decoders or other architectural customizations (abstract only).
DenseMLLM relies on a novel vision token supervision strategy that supports multiple labels and multiple tasks within a single, unmodified MLLM architecture (abstract only).
DenseMLLM achieves highly competitive performance across a wide range of dense prediction benchmarks (e.g., segmentation-style tasks) evaluated in the paper (abstract only).

DenseMLLM also achieves highly competitive performance on standard vision-language benchmarks in addition to dense prediction benchmarks, showing the approach does not trade off general MLLM capability for dense perception (abstract only).
The paper argues against the conventional paradigm that fine-grained dense perception requires specialized decoder architectures, instead showing a generalist MLLM design suffices (abstract only).

q2kihJvzqC.text: DV-World comprises 260 tasks split across three suites: DV-Sheet (130 tasks: 50 Create, 50 Fix, 30 Dashboard), DV-Evolution (80 tasks spanning Python, ECharts, Vega-Lite, D3.js, and Plotly.js), and DV-Interact (50 multi-turn tasks with an average of 3.17 ambiguities per task) (Section 2.1, Table 2).

On DV-Sheet, the best model (Gemini-3-Pro as DV-World-Agent) reaches only 40.48% overall score versus an 80.81% human baseline, confirming the paper's claim that state-of-the-art models score below 50% overall (Section 3.2, Table 3).

On DV-Evolution, Gemini-3-Pro attains 51.44% versus an 85.23% human baseline, with performance varying substantially by target framework (stronger on Python/Vega-Lite than D3.js/Plotly.js) (Section 3.2, Table 4).
On DV-Interact, the best model (Grok-4) achieves 40.43% versus a 79.60% human baseline, indicating models struggle to detect and resolve ambiguity through multi-turn dialogue (Section 3.2, Table 5).
An ablation removing the load_image tool degrades cross-paradigm evolution performance, showing visual feedback is important for logic migration and design preservation (Section 3.4, Table 6).
Data accuracy errors account for over 50% of failures in the DVSheet-Create subtask, per the paper's error analysis (Section 3.3, Figure 5).

1e3gI1ibcn.text: Theorem 1 proves an information ordering I(ρ⋆,Θ) ≤ I(ρ⋆,X) ≤ I(ρ⋆,S0) via the data processing inequality, establishing that adjoint sensitivity fields S0 are the information-theoretically optimal conditioning signal for predicting the optimal topology ρ⋆ (Theorem 1).

On the hardest three-outlet CFD out-of-distribution configuration, the proposed sensitivity-conditioned Bernoulli flow matching method achieves 6.12% median pressure-drop error and 74.5% accuracy, versus 13.03% error / 62.7% accuracy for a UDiT baseline and 26.51% error / 40.0% accuracy for classical STAR-CCM+ optimization (Table 1).

On structural compliance topology optimization under OOD load shifts, the method achieves 0.53% median compliance error with a 34M-parameter model, outperforming TopoDiffusion (1.14% error, 121M parameters) and NITO (2.37% error, 22M parameters, requiring 5 SIMP iterations) (Table 6).

An ablation comparing conditioning modalities shows that weak architectures with sensitivity conditioning outperform strong architectures conditioned on non-pseudo-sensitivity fields, supporting the claim that the conditioning signal, not model capacity, drives OOD generalization (Table 3).

Definition 1 introduces pseudo-sensitivities as fields related to true adjoint sensitivities by a monotone transformation, with strain energy density identified as a 0-approximate pseudo-sensitivity for structural compliance and squared velocity magnitude for CFD energy dissipation under a frozen-turbulence assumption (Definition 1, Proposition 1).

The paper introduces the first learning-based turbulent CFD topology optimization dataset, comprising 10,000 single-outlet RANS k-ε training samples plus OOD test splits of 500 two-outlet and 500 three-outlet configurations (Section 6).

rHndxbqWyh.text: DMLRank defines Generalized Average Ranking Scores (GARS) as θ=E[F(μ(X))], a unifying functional that recovers Borda scores, Bradley-Terry log-odds projections, and Rank Centrality stationary-distribution scores as special cases (Section 4).

Theorem 5.1 derives a debiased efficient-influence-function estimator for GARS that is asymptotically normal, √n(θ̂_EIF−θ)→N_d(0,Σ), and achieves the semiparametric efficiency bound under cross-fitted nuisance estimation (Theorem 5.1).

On synthetic data with n=1000, the debiased Borda estimator has error 0.15±0.03 with 0.94±0.06 coverage, versus the plugin estimator's 0.38±0.08 error and only 0.17±0.09 coverage, showing plugin confidence intervals are invalid while debiased ones are not (Table 1).

Theorem 6.2 characterizes the A-optimal preference-labeling policy under a budget constraint as π*_jk(x)=clip_[α,1]√(tr(J_jkV_jkJ_jkᵀ)/(λ_A c_jk)), balancing informativeness, influence on the target functional, and per-comparison cost (Theorem 6.2).

Under a fixed budget of β=2000 comparisons, the A-optimal labeling policy achieves lower MSE than random data collection for all three GARS types tested: Borda (0.108±0.041 vs 0.133±0.060), Bradley-Terry (2.565±1.046 vs 2.910±1.143), and Rank Centrality (0.010±0.008 vs 0.017±0.007) (Table 2).

The framework is applied to real Chatbot Arena preference data with n=32,980 prompts and K=20 models, using toxicity score and TF-IDF prompt embeddings as covariates, where plugin estimators yield near-zero-width (invalid) confidence intervals while debiased estimators retain interpretable uncertainty (Section 7, Figure 3).

iyeNyj06Nt.text: SphericalDreamer generates navigable 3D worlds with full omnidirectional coverage (360° horizontal, 180° vertical) by fusing layered depth panoramas via a pairwise generative fusion stage using inpainting and harmonic blending (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).
SphericalDreamer achieves near-perfect trajectory coverage of 0.999 under combined rotation and translation, compared to 0.404-0.775 for prior baselines (Table 2).
SphericalDreamer attains the best (lowest) BRISQUE image quality score of 41.73 among all compared methods, including LucidDreamer, LayerPano3D, WonderJourney, and SceneScape (Table 2).
An ablation removing the layered depth panorama (LDP) component degrades BRISQUE from 43.47 to 45.89, showing LDP is critical to visual quality (Table 6).
Scaling the generated world from N=3 to N=7 fused panoramas keeps quality and coverage metrics stable, demonstrating consistency at larger spatial extents (Table 7).
Generating a world with N=3 panoramas takes approximately 40 minutes on a single A100 GPU (Table 10).

356U11JaTS.text: ModelSMC frames automated mechanistic model discovery as Sequential Monte Carlo inference over the posterior p(m|x_o), propagating candidate models (particles) via LLM-based proposals and reweighting by marginal likelihood (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 3.1 establishes that, under assumptions of support coverage, bounded weights, conditional independence, and exact likelihood evaluation, ModelSMC yields an asymptotically consistent particle approximation to the model posterior with O(1/N) variance (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.1).

On the SIR epidemiological case study, ModelSMC's population-based inference (median marginal likelihood -503.37) is compared against FunSearch+ (-500.00) and a single-particle ModelSMC N=1 ablation (-464.17) across 10 discovery runs (Table 1, Section 4.2).

On the Hodgkin-Huxley neuroscience case study, ModelSMC discovers ion-channel model extensions that improve fit to real neuronal recordings, achieving a median marginal likelihood of 25.18 versus 28.96 for FunSearch+ (Table 1, Section 4.4).

On a real-world kidney pharmacology system with only 20 total observations, ModelSMC infers a missing aldosterone feedback mechanism, achieving a median marginal likelihood of 43.58 versus 46.29 for the ModelSMC N=1 ablation (Table 1, Section 4.3).

ModelSMC is implemented with GPT-5-mini as the LLM proposal mechanism (via DSPy) and a TabPFN-based neural likelihood estimator (NLE-PFN), parallelized across up to 5 particles using Ray (Section 4, Section 3.3).

gRzdGEtn3T.text: PLaTITO extends Transferable Implicit Transfer Operators (TITO) by conditioning the flow-matching velocity field on protein language model (ESM) sequence embeddings, in addition to structure embeddings (Proteina) and LLM-derived annotations (Section 4.2, Section 4.3).

On the equilibrium sampling benchmark, PLaTITO achieves an MAE of 0.949±0.269 versus 1.068±0.272 for the TITO baseline, and the larger PLaTITO-Big variant reaches 0.824±0.170 MAE, outperforming the BioEmu Boltzmann emulator's 1.110±0.292 (Table 1, Section 5.2).

PLaTITO-Big matches or exceeds BioEmu's equilibrium sampling accuracy while requiring only 1,100 GPU hours of training and 56 ms of MD trajectory data, versus BioEmu's 9,216 GPU hours and 216 ms of trajectory data (Table 1, Section 5.1).
Coverage of reference conformational bins improves from 0.590±0.111 for TITO to 0.651±0.151 for PLaTITO and 0.666±0.136 for PLaTITO-Big (Table 1).
In cryptic binding pocket experiments, PLaTITO-Big successfully samples apo conformational states in cases where BioEmu fails in 3 of 4 benchmark systems (Section 5.5, Figure 6).

Adding LLM-derived (DeepSeek) annotations on top of sequence and structure embeddings unexpectedly decreases performance relative to the PLaTITO+Struct variant, per the model-variant ablation in Section 5.1 (Section 5.1, Table 1).

Y7szlTydrp.text: The paper unifies unconditional diffusion/flow-matching processes (DM-VE, DM-VP, Flow Matching), Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes (IR-SDE, ResShift, InDI), and diffusion bridges (BBDM, DDBM-VE/VP, I2SB, GOUB, UniDB) under a single SDE formulation dx_t = f(x_t,t,y)dt + g(t)dw_t (Section 2.1).

Under standardized training protocols across five tasks (super-resolution, low-light enhancement, colorization, deraining), no single method dominates: ResShift and DM-VP show slight advantages, unconditional processes favor super-resolution and low-light enhancement, while diffusion bridges excel at colorization (Table 2, Section 3).

Low-temperature Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes (τ=0.06) underperform because intermediate samples stay tightly concentrated near the line segment connecting the degraded input and target image, forcing the network to extrapolate rather than refine (Section 2, Section 3).

Diffusion bridge methods paired with deterministic samplers yield high LPIPS scores (greater than 0.3), indicating oversmoothing since stochasticity from Brownian motion is required for sharp outputs (Section 3).
The UniDB stochastic-optimal-control regularization improves performance by terminating the process closer to the clean image rather than exactly at the conditioning image (Section 2.4, Table 2).

ItoVision, a modular PyTorch library implementing the unified SDE framework, is summarized in Table 1 and enables fair comparison and rapid prototyping of stochastic image enhancement methods (Section 2.5, Table 1).

gSGnknLZED.text: Figure 1 shows that across 19 models, ranking changes occur between offline (SFT) and online (post-RL) performance: gains of a stronger offline checkpoint over a weaker one can shrink, disappear, or reverse after identical RL training (Figure 1, Section 2).

PEAR reweights the SFT loss using continuation-based (suffix-ratio) importance sampling that down-weights tokens whose continuations are implausible under the current policy, in contrast to a single-step (myopic) importance-sampling ablation (Section 3, Table 3).
On AIME-2025, PEAR yields up to a 14.6% Pass@8 gain over canonical SFT, including raising DS-Qwen-1.5B from 5% to 35% after identical GRPO training (Table 2).

On AIME-2024, PEAR improves Pass@8 by 36 percentage points (e.g., DS-Qwen model 2% to 38%), and on MATH-500 yields roughly 26% Pass@8 gains for smaller models, all measured after identical post-training RL (Table 2).
On the SynLogic logic-games benchmark, PEAR improves Qwen3-1.7B's absolute accuracy by 40 percentage points relative to canonical SFT after RL (Figure 4a).

Figure 6 shows all three PEAR variants (sequence-level, token-level, block-level) outperform canonical SFT after RL, with the simple sequence-level variant proving surprisingly competitive (Figure 6).

kvilWCkBqW.text: For cosine-normalized embeddings, the empirical tail of hardest-negative similarities follows a Weibull-type distribution (fitted shape parameter ξ̂ ≈ -0.39 via peaks-over-threshold), contradicting the Gumbel-tail assumption implicit in the standard InfoNCE softmax (Section 2.3, Figure 3).

Theorem 2.2 (Fisher-Tippett-Gnedenko) formalizes that the large-K limiting behavior of InfoNCE's top-1 selection probability falls into one of three tail-geometry regimes indexed by shape parameter ξ (Fréchet, Gumbel, or Weibull) (Theorem 2.2, Table 1).

WEINCE, which blends the softmax (Plackett-Luce) link with a Weibull link using an estimated blend weight λ̂ in the 0.33-0.50 range, improves CIFAR-100 linear evaluation accuracy from 50.01% to 53.28% with ResNet-18 and from 51.15% to 55.97% with ResNet-50 over standard InfoNCE (Section 4, Table 2).

WEINCE improves STL-10 linear evaluation accuracy from 76.54% to 77.94% with ResNet-18 and Tiny-ImageNet accuracy from 33.12% to 36.53% with ViT-Small, while adding only about 0.67% end-to-end computational overhead (Section 4, Table 2).
On SimCSE with BERT-base-uncased evaluated on the STS Benchmark, WEINCE raises the Spearman correlation from 71.74±4.23 to 76.36±3.17 (p<0.05) (Section 4).
WEINCE also improves kNN retrieval recall, raising CIFAR-100 R@1 with ResNet-18 from 36.98% to 42.94% and STL-10 R@1 with ResNet-50 from 69.66% to 71.75% (Table 3).

schXkGSTus.text: The latent distribution matching (LDM) framework shows that for encoders invertible on the data manifold, maximizing data log-likelihood is equivalent to LDM, and different entropy estimators recover different SSL families: kernel density estimation yields contrastive methods like SimCLR, parametric estimation yields non-contrastive methods like VICReg, and conditional entropy with predictors yields stop-gradient approaches like BYOL/SimSiam (Section 3, Section 4.2, Table 1).

Theorem 1 proves that under Gaussian predictor assumptions with encoder invertibility and latent-space coverage, predictive distribution matching recovers the true latent variables up to an affine transformation, establishing identifiability for predictive SSL with nonlinear predictors (Section 7, Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 establishes an analogous identifiability guarantee for a von Mises-Fisher predictive variant under similar conditions (Section 7, Theorem 2).

Section 6 derives a nonlinear, sampling-free Bayesian filtering model with a Kalman-based predictor for high-dimensional time-series latent-state inference, applied to hippocampal spike-train data to recover position-dependent circular latent representations with uncertainty estimates (Section 6, Section 6.1).

Section 5.1 image-classification experiments show that mutual-information-maximizing objectives and pure LDM objectives produce essentially equivalent learned representations, supporting the theoretical claim that MI maximization is redundant once entropy is maximized (Section 5.1).

OvLnVkV14P.text: Agent World Model synthesizes 1,000 fully executable, database-backed environments comprising 35,062 total tools (an average of about 35 tools per environment) and 10,000 tasks, generated via a five-stage pipeline (scenario generation, task generation, database synthesis, MCP interface exposure, and code-augmented verification) (Section on pipeline; Table 2).
The environment-synthesis pipeline achieves an overall success rate of 35%, with substantially higher yields for database-only (88.3%) and code-only (86.8%) sub-tasks (pipeline evaluation).
Synthesized environments average 18.5 database tables, 129.3 sample data records, 1,984.7 lines of environment code, and a median of 8.5 agent steps per task (Table 2).

Training exclusively on these synthetic environments improves an 8B model's BFCLv3 overall score from 53.83 to 65.94 and its τ2-bench Pass@1 from 26.44 to 33.45, demonstrating out-of-distribution generalization to benchmarks not seen during training (evaluation on BFCLv3 and τ2-bench).

The same 8B model trained on Agent World Model environments reaches an overall MCP-Universe score of 11.17, the third of three out-of-distribution benchmarks used to test generalization (evaluation on MCP-Universe).

ij3UfXzgYp.text: Standard tokenization of continuous planetary-motion data breaks spatial continuity, so that two physically close points falling into different bins are treated as unrelated; correcting this via reduced vocabulary size or continuous coordinates is needed for transformers to learn a coherent world model, and vocabulary size significantly affects when a spatial map emerges (Section 2, Figure 3).

Without noisy-context training, autoregressive transformer predictions on continuous orbital variables accumulate error over rollouts; injecting Gaussian noise into the training context (optimal σ = 0.1) restores robustness to in-context perturbations at inference time (Section 3, Figure 4).

Context length controls which world model emerges: a short context length of 2 induces a Newtonian, force-based representation (R² ≈ 0.999), whereas a long context length of 100 induces a Keplerian, orbital-parameter representation (R² ≈ 0.998), demonstrating that temporal locality combined with spatial smoothness favors physically causal (Newtonian) over curve-fitting (Keplerian) world models (Section 4, Figure 6).
Vafa et al.'s original transformer embeddings exhibit poor spatial locality (R² ≈ 0.86), motivating the paper's proposed inductive-bias corrections (Section 2, Figure 2).

Dy5GeCd003.text: Among data representations tested for instruction selection, only gradient-based representations (LESS) show a strong, consistent monotonic correlation between subset-to-query distance and downstream loss across datasets and models, while representation-based alternatives (RDS+, EMBED) show very low Spearman correlation (Section 5.1-5.2).

At the smallest tested budget, gradient-based (LESS) representations combined with greedy round-robin selection achieve the lowest loss on the query set across target tasks, but this advantage diminishes as the budget grows across the tested range B ∈ {500, 1,000, 2,500, 5,000, 10,000} (Section 5.2-5.3, Figures 4-7).

Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) selection achieves the lowest loss on three of five target datasets, while Doubly Greedy (DG) selection consistently underperforms other selection algorithms (Section 5.3, Figures 6-7).
Theorem 6.1 shows that minimizing the Wasserstein distance between the selected subset and the query distribution tightens a generalization bound on downstream performance (Section 6, Theorem 6.1).

Theorem 6.2 shows that the benefit of query-aware data selection over random selection diminishes with budget B, scaling as B^(-1/d) in the representation's intrinsic dimension d (Section 6, Theorem 6.2).
Evaluations span five target tasks with differing query set sizes: BBH (81), MMLU-Pro (70), Codex (16), TyDiQA (9), and GSM8K (8) (Appendix B, Table 2).

COjmyds8zz.text: QuantumBoost achieves overall runtime Õ(W/(√ϵ·γ⁴)) to reach empirical error at most ϵ, where W is the weak-learner runtime and γ is the edge of the weak hypotheses (Theorem 1, Section 4).
With training set size m = Θ((d·log(d/(δϵ)) + log(1/δ))/ϵ²), QuantumBoost outputs a hypothesis with generalization error ≤ ϵ and success probability 1−δ (Theorem 2, Section 4).

QuantumBoost uses T = O(log(1/ϵ)/γ²) boosting iterations, matching the iteration count of classical AdaBoost and Kale's SmoothBoost while achieving strictly better total runtime (Theorem 20, Theorem 23, Section 4).
QuantumBoost's total runtime of W/(√ϵ·γ⁴) improves on Quantum SmoothBoost's runtime of W/(ϵ^2.5γ⁴) + √d/(ϵ^3.5γ⁵) and on Quantum AdaBoost's runtime of W^1.5√d/(ϵγ¹¹) (Table 1).

QuantumBoost is presented as the first algorithm, classical or quantum, to combine a lazy Bregman-projection strategy—projecting only every K = 1/γ iterations rather than every iteration—with quantum mean estimation for boosting (Section 4).

6zVV84vnCJ.text: HiVES (Hierarchical Value Embedding Space) is built via a two-stage training process that first maps texts through theory-specific value hierarchies and then integrates heterogeneous value frameworks into a single unified embedding space (Section 4).

HiVES improves hierarchical ranking accuracy by over 20% and similarity correlation by over 50% relative to baseline embedding approaches, while better disentangling values from both Schwartz Value Theory and Moral Foundations Theory (Figure 5, Section 6).

VIDB (Value Intensity Database) contains 10K unique texts per value across four value theories (Schwartz Value Theory, Moral Foundations Theory, Rights, and Duties), with intensity labels derived from Plackett-Luce ranking-based aggregation normalized to a [-10, 10] scale (Section 5).
VIDB's intensity estimates achieve a mean deviation of 1.4 from human ratings, 60-79% win rates against rating-based baselines, and 85.3% pairwise ranking accuracy (Table 3).

Steerability is evaluated across ten LLMs (Qwen3-32B, Mistral-3.1, Phi-4, GLM-4, gpt-oss-20b, Gemma-3-27B, GPT-4.1, Claude-4, Grok-4, Gemini-2.5-Flash) using 500 prompts spanning 32 distinct values from four value theories, revealing four distinct model groups with asymmetric dose-response steerability behaviors (Section 6).

Profile-based value steering improves OpinionQA accuracy on specific attributes by more than 10 percentage points, e.g. raising Phi-4's accuracy on the Religion attribute from 44.5% to 58.9% (Section 7).

2Cgy0P2v8s.text: Vision-DeepResearch's 30B-A3B model achieves an average score of 56.9% across six multimodal deep-research benchmarks (VDR, FVQA, MMSearch+, MMSearch, LiveVQA, BC-VL), a gain of +16.0 points over its base model (Table 1).
Vision-DeepResearch's 8B model achieves an average score of 50.5% across the same six benchmarks, a gain of +10.4 points over its base model (Table 1).

Vision-DeepResearch's 30B model (56.9% average) outperforms agentic workflows built on GPT-5 (48.3% average), Gemini-2.5-Pro (50.7% average), and Claude-4-Sonnet (48.5% average) on the same benchmark suite (Table 1).
On the MMSearch+ benchmark specifically, the 30B model scores 28.5% versus 20.4% for the 8B model, indicating scale-dependent gains on harder multi-hop visual search queries (Table 1).

The method's data pipeline and training procedure are designed to incentivize multi-turn, multi-entity, and multi-scale visual and textual search, which the paper argues explains its advantage over single-pass retrieval baselines (Section on Method: Motivation, Data Pipeline, and Training).

tUpQVC7LvO.text: JADAI jointly trains a policy network for adaptive design, a history encoder, and a posterior estimator end-to-end using a telescoping-loss utility objective that avoids explicit density evaluations (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).
On the location-finding benchmark at a 10-step horizon, JADAI attains 6.74 sPCE compared to 7.97 sPCE for DAD; at 30 steps JADAI attains 12.82 sPCE versus 12.31 sPCE for RL-sCEE (Table 1).
On the Constant Elasticity of Substitution task at T=10, JADAI attains 14.85 sPCE, outperforming all baselines including ALINE at 14.37 sPCE (Table 1).

On MNIST image discovery at T=6, JADAI's flow-matching variant achieves SSIM of 0.988±0.001 versus 0.826 for the CoDiff baseline, and NRMSE of 0.177±0.001 versus 2.056 for a random policy baseline (Table 2).
JADAI supports both diffusion-model score matching and flow matching as alternative posterior approximators for multimodal posteriors (Section A.1, Section A.2).

Joka19sTny.text: The method estimates the probability of harmful language model outputs using importance sampling, constructing 'unsafe versions' of the target model that upweight the likelihood of harmful outputs to make estimation more efficient (abstract only).
The method achieves 10-20x fewer samples than brute-force Monte Carlo estimation for estimating harmful-output probabilities (abstract only).
The method can estimate harmful-output probabilities on the order of 10^-4 using just 500 samples (abstract only).

The paper motivates tail-risk estimation by noting that when models are queried billions of times per day, even very rare worst-case behaviors will occur in practice, making rare-event probability estimation practically important for deployment safety (abstract only).

S4pUDRolZd.text: CalM uses a two-stage architecture combining a Neural Quantizer (VQ-VAE tokenizer) and a Dual-Axis Transformer to model neural and temporal dependencies autoregressively (Section 3).

CalM is pretrained and evaluated on real calcium imaging data from Tseng et al. 2022 comprising 8 mice, 286 sessions, and 273,770 neurons across 6 brain regions, split into 189 held-in and 97 held-out sessions (Section 3.1, Appendix A).
In multi-session held-in behavior decoding, CalM achieves a 10.1% average R^2 improvement over the POYO+ baseline, with up to 20.9% improvement on the yaw variable (Section 6).
In multi-session held-out behavior decoding, CalM achieves a 7.2% overall R^2 improvement over POYO+ (Section 6).
CalM outperforms TCN, PatchTST, and iTransformer baselines on single-session forecasting and is competitive with the specialist POCO model on multi-session held-in forecasting (Section 6).

Ablations show scheduled sampling has the largest effect on forecasting correlation, degrading it from 0.3058 to 0.2079 when removed, more than autoregressive regularization or the orthogonality/entropy losses (Appendix D, Tables 7-8).

r05rSbN4vI.text: Self-captioning multimodal interaction tuning with the Multimodal Interaction Gate reduces visual-induced errors by up to 38.3% and improves consistency by 16.8% for SmolVLM at 50% redundancy (Section 5, Table 3).

The Multimodal Interaction Gate is a mechanism that converts unique (exclusive) multimodal interactions into redundant (shared) interactions to increase exploitable shared information between modalities (Section 4.1).
On the Hateful Memes training set with Qwen2.5 32B, the self-captioning workflow increases redundant interactions by 319.3% while reducing unique-visual interactions by 50.6% (Section 5.1, Table 1).
The method yields up to 4% accuracy gains across model families on general benchmarks including MMMU, MMStar, MathVista, and TextVQA (Section 5, Table 4).
Robustness against modality corruption is evaluated via performance stability curves, showing improved stability relative to baselines lacking interaction amplification (Section 5.3, Figure 5).

7Q2jAzmDAR.text: V-ABS integrates a thinker-actor-observer loop into beam search to address an imagination-action-observer (IAO) bias between a model's prior predictions and actual visual feedback, reformulating visual reasoning as a Markov decision process with evolving visual states (Section 3.1-3.2).

On fine-grained visual search, Qwen3-VL with V-ABS reaches 90.5% on V* (a +14.6 point improvement), 76.0% on HR-Bench-4K (+6.0), and 78.0% on HR-Bench-8K (+9.5) over the Qwen3-VL-8B baseline (Table 1).
On visual logic tasks, V-ABS improves Jigsaw accuracy by +11.0 points and Sudoku accuracy to 37.8% (a +23.4 point gain over baseline) (Table 3).

V-ABS is trained via supervised fine-tuning on approximately 80k samples spanning visual search (7,040), visual navigation (14,000), and visual logic/Jigsaw (60,000) examples, using 16 NVIDIA H100-80G GPUs for 200 steps (Section 3.4, Appendix B).

Ablations show SFT alone gives only marginal gains (+0.6%) for restricted action spaces but is critical for open-ended tasks such as Jigsaw (+73.4%), while removing observer feedback causes a 10.28% accuracy drop and adaptive weighting outperforms static averaging by 2.6% (Table 4, Figure 3b).

oQKiPx8jlI.text: The method uses a transformer-based few-shot predictor with separate encoders for context (including auxiliary information h(x)) and target design points, remaining frozen during test-time optimization (Section 3).

On the gripper design benchmark (4.28 million evaluations across 997 ShapeNet objects, 21-dimensional Bezier surface design space, tactile maps as auxiliary information), the method achieves an MSE of 170.9 at context size 5 versus 201.6 for an ablated 'ours w/o h' baseline that omits auxiliary information (Section 5.1, Figure 5).

In gripper design optimization after 30 trials, the method solves 34.4% of test tasks to optimality versus 26.7% for the closest baseline, and achieves regret ≤0.5 on 67.2% of tasks versus 58.0% for the baseline (Section 5.1, Figure 6).

On the LCBench hyperparameter tuning benchmark (35 tasks, 2000 configurations each, using per-epoch learning curves as auxiliary information), the method solves 89.7% of curated tasks within 0.01 of the optimum by 30 trials, versus 82.1% for the closest baseline (DGP) (Section 5.2, Figure 10).

The gripper design benchmark contributed by the paper contains 997 tasks (versus fewer than 200 in comparable multi-task Bayesian optimization benchmarks) and required approximately 1.07 million CPU hours of simulation to construct (Section 5.1).

5LBH6azyBM.text: The paper introduces a time-discrete geodesic calculus for implicitly defined latent manifolds, defining the discrete path energy as ℰ^K(z_0,...,z_K) = K∑_{k=1}^K 𝒲(z_{k-1},z_k), a discrete counterpart to the continuous Riemannian energy functional (Section 3, Equation 2).
The manifold is represented implicitly via ζ(z) := z − Π(z) with a learned projection Π, and the tangent space is defined as T_zZ = ker Dζ(z) (Section 2).

Geodesic interpolation and the discrete exponential map are computed via augmented Lagrangian optimization with penalty terms enforcing the manifold constraint despite an inexact implicit representation (Section 3, Equations 6-11).

The implicit projection Π is learned by minimizing a denoising objective 𝒬(Π) = ∫∫ |z−Π(y)|² f_σ(z−y) dz dy, yielding a Gaussian-weighted barycenter projection with approximation error O(σ²) in the manifold interior (Section 4, Equation 12).

The method is validated on five experimental settings: discrete shells with isometric autoencoders, motion capture data with a spherical VAE, image data with low-curvature autoencoders, extension to distance-function representations, and Pose-NDF neural distance functions, showing that geodesic interpolation avoids self-intersections better than linear interpolation (Sections 5.1-5.4, Appendix A.7, Figures 4-8).

rbJsrAxryz.text: MONICA constructs a training set of 2,000 sycophantic and 2,000 non-sycophantic samples via an induction-then-merge procedure using GPT-4o for adaptive stage partitioning (Section 2.2).

MONICA trains per-layer logistic regression probes to compute a Sycophancy Drift Score (SDS) and uses an adaptive calibration strength alpha' = alpha_min + (alpha_max - alpha_min) x sum(SDS^l)/|L_M| to intervene in real time during generation (Section 2.4).

Evaluated on 12 datasets (AIME, GPQA, MMLU each paired with four sycophancy-inducing cue types: metadata leakage, user suggestion, validation function, unauthorized access) across 3 models (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B-Thinking, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama8B), MONICA achieves top-two performance in 33 of 48 evaluation metrics (Table 1).

MONICA achieves the best overall performance in 6 of 9 model-dataset combinations and is consistently superior across all Qwen3-4B tasks, measured via Resistance Rate, Persistent Ratio, Sycophantic Rate, and Mislead Rate (Table 2, Section 3.2).

Figure 5 shows MONICA improves both intermediate reasoning (RCoT) and final-answer (RFIN) sycophancy resistance relative to baselines including Majority Vote, Self-reflection, SFT with DPO+LoRA, and Persona Steer (Figure 5, Section 3.3).

An ablation comparing full MONICA against CA+INDUCT (calibrator on the constructed dataset only) and CA+WHOLE (calibrator trained on complete responses) confirms both the monitor component and the induction-then-merge dataset are necessary for performance (Section 3.4).

8gsYox51jQ.text: Retaining only 10 of 512 attention heads (about 2%) recovers over 95% of teacher performance on retrieval-heavy tasks, versus prior hybrids that require at least 25% of heads for comparable performance, a roughly 10x reduction in attention-head budget (Section 4, Table 1).
The resulting hybrid is 5x more memory-efficient than comparable hybrids on short (128-token) sequences and 6x more memory-efficient on long (4K-token) sequences (Section 4).
SSM recurrent state dimension can be reduced 8x (from 64 to 8) with limited performance loss, indicating large recurrent states mainly compensate for missing retrieval capacity (Section 4).

With 10 retained heads, Hybrid-Llama-1B improves SWDE accuracy from 27.7% to 71.1% and KV-Retrieval accuracy from 13.2% to 99%, while Hybrid-Qwen2-1.5B reaches 96.4% Retrieval-Heavy Coverage (Table 1).

Retrieval-critical heads are identified via ablation on a synthetic KV-retrieval task (Section 4.1), then a hybrid model retaining the top-k heads and replacing the remainder with DiscreteMamba2 is distilled from Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct using the MOHAWK distillation framework over 12 billion tokens (Section 4.2).

Analysis in Section 5.5 finds 11 of 20 attention heads fall below a 0.7 retrieval-accuracy threshold while only 5 of 492 SSM heads meet this criterion, confirming task-aligned specialization between attention and SSM components (Section 5.5).

a6fo32UnpU.text: The paper generalizes (L0,L1)-smoothness to (H0,H1)-smoothness (Definition 3.1), bounding the Hessian norm as H0 + H1 times the function sub-optimality f(w) - f* rather than the gradient norm (Section 3, Definition 3.1).

Proposition 3.1 and 3.2 show the (H0,H1)-smoothness condition holds for deep linear networks with MSE loss under weight balancedness and for deep non-linear networks with one leaky-ReLU layer under MSE loss (Section 3.1).
Propositions 3.3 and 3.4 extend the condition to two-layer networks with MSE loss under L2 regularization and to two-layer networks with cross-entropy loss (Section 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 gives a lower bound showing gradient descent with a constant step-size requires substantially more iterations when poorly initialized, while Theorem 4.2 proves that under the Aiming condition, GD with the adaptive step-size eta_k = 1/(10*H0 + 20*H1*(f(w_k)-f*)) converges in O(H0*dist(w0,S)^2/(theta^2*eps) + H1*dist(w0,S)^2/theta^2) iterations, faster than any fixed step-size (Theorems 4.1-4.2).
Theorem 4.3 extends the convergence results to mu-Polyak-Lojasiewicz functions (Theorem 4.3).

Section 3.2 empirically validates the (H0,H1)-smoothness condition on Transformer language models (70M, 160M, 410M parameters) trained on FineWeb and on ResNet50/ViT-Tiny trained on ImageNet32, finding local curvature grows approximately linearly with training loss early in training (Section 3.2).

wIMGGV9l1i.text: Under the random dot product graph (RDPG) model where P = rho_n * X X^T for latent positions X in R^(n x r), Theorem 3.1 shows trailing eigenvectors associated with zero eigenvalues delocalize, with maximum entry magnitude bounded by r^2 (log n)^(4+6*gamma) / sqrt(n) (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 shows that when the embedding dimension is over-specified (k>0 extra dimensions), consistent estimation of the latent positions still holds but only at the slower rate n^(-1/4), compared to the n^(-1/2) rate achieved under correct specification (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.2 also shows that when the embedding dimension is under-specified (k<0), there is a fundamental lower bound on estimation error of order sqrt(|k| * rho_n), which need not vanish as the network size grows, proving inconsistency (Theorem 3.2).

Under correct specification, the adjacency spectral embedding satisfies ||X_hat_{1:r} W - rho_n^{1/2} X_{1:r}||_{2,infty} <~ phi_n, typically achieving the n^{-1/2} rate; over-specification adds an error term of order sqrt(sigma^2 k) * r^2 (log n)^(5+6*gamma) / n^{1/4} (Section 3).
Section 3.1 states Conjecture 1, extending the over-/under-specification results from weighted networks to binary networks under relaxed variance conditions (Section 3.1, Conjecture 1).
Section 4 presents simulation experiments across multiple noise distributions confirming the theoretical over- and under-specification rates (Section 4).

IdfwoUzREG.text: MLPM computes per-layer class-conditional Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (GDA) classifiers using Mahalanobis distance to safe/harmful prototypes built from last-token representations at the output of each transformer block's feed-forward network, then aggregates layer-wise predictions with sparsely-regularized learned weights (Equation 5, Section 3.2).

On Table 2's 8 prompt-harmfulness benchmarks (Aegis, HarmB, OpenAI, SimpST, TChat, WGMix, WJB, XSTest), MLPM applied to OLMo2-7B-Instruct achieves the highest average F1 score of 90.18, surpassing the strongest guard model baseline WildGuard (88.93 average) and other latent-based methods (Table 2).

Figure 2 shows MLPM's 1B Llama3 variant achieves an F1 of about 85, outperforming significantly larger fixed-size guard baselines such as GraniteGuardian and ShieldGemma, demonstrating favorable performance-efficiency scaling with model size across Llama3, Mistral, OLMo2, and Qwen3 families (Figure 2, Section 4.1).

Table 3 shows that using MLPM as a conditioning mechanism for output-moderation/steering methods (Lee et al. 2025a, Turner et al. 2023, Zheng et al. 2024) substantially reduces false refusal rate (FRR) on benign prompts across Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B, OLMo2-7B, and Qwen3-8B while only marginally increasing attack success rate (ASR) (Table 3, Section 4.2).

MLPM's inference overhead is estimated at less than 0.001% of the total prefill FLOPs, and it requires only about 24KB per prototype stored in half precision for the Llama3.1-8B model (Section 3.3.2, Appendix L).

Section 4.3 shows MLPM remains data-efficient, achieving competitive F1 on WildGuardMix with as few as 1,000 training samples per class, with variance dropping sharply as sample size increases (Figure 3b, Section 4.3).

Ujf6Is4cdt.text: StarEmbed introduces a benchmark of roughly 40,000 hand-labeled variable-star light curves from the Zwicky Transient Facility across seven astrophysical classes, split 7:1:2 into train/validation/test (Section 5).

On unsupervised clustering, Chronos-tiny embeddings achieve NMI of 0.2432 and macro F1 of 0.3410 with K-means, below the hand-crafted feature baseline's NMI of 0.2619 and F1 of 0.4028 (Section 5.1, Table 4).

On out-of-distribution source detection, Chronos-Bolt-tiny achieves top-1-percentile purity of 0.569 versus 0.213 for hand-crafted features, a roughly 5x improvement in search efficiency over random embeddings (Section 5.3, Table 5).
On supervised classification with a Random Forest head, Chronos-tiny reaches F1 of 0.640 and accuracy of 0.863, ranking second-best behind hand-crafted features' F1 of 0.807 (Section 5.2, Table 6).

Chronos models generalize to irregular, heteroscedastic astronomical light curves despite being pre-trained only on regularly sampled time series, outperforming the astronomy-specific Astromer model on several tasks (Section 5).

LD9mlgF5WU.text: VR-Thinker-7B attains 80.5% accuracy on VideoGen-Reward (tau protocol), 82.3% on GenAI-Bench (diff protocol), and 75.6% on MJ-Bench-Video (tau protocol), state-of-the-art among open-source reward models (Table 1).
VR-Thinker improves on average roughly 11.4% over the prior reasoning-based reward model UnifiedReward-Think across these three benchmarks (Table 1).

The model's windowed memory mechanism restricts retrieved tool-execution outcomes (e.g., extra video frames) to validity only within a preset window, keeping total token count approximately independent of the number of reasoning steps (Section 3.1).

Training proceeds in three stages: cold-start distillation from GPT-4o-generated chain-of-thought data, rejection-sampling fine-tuning on verified reasoning traces, and GRPO reinforcement optimization with exploratory incentives (Figure 1b).

XML-style tags such as <Snapshot> compress thousands of visual tokens into dozens of language tokens, while <Recommend Answer> tags provide intermediate confidence assessments during multi-step visual reasoning (Section 3).

NZvWGf2XXM.text: Theorem 4.1 shows the standard posterior-mean guidance approximation (Eq. 7) is biased for essentially all practical likelihoods unless the likelihood is constant (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 4.2 shows Gaussian posterior approximations (Eq. 8) used in guidance are unbiased only under a standard normal prior and are otherwise systematically biased (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 4.3 proves that rescaling the guidance scale cannot produce a properly tempered posterior for non-trivial likelihoods, since the tempered diffused likelihood cannot be obtained by exponentiation (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).

The proposed gradient-free Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) estimator (Eq. 20) achieves an average C2ST score of 0.527 on the Bayesian inference benchmark, versus 0.803 for DPS and 0.750 for LGD (Section 6.1, Table 1).

CBG improves monotonically with increased computational budget while competing guidance methods plateau, and on black-hole imaging attains a PSNR of 26.10 dB matching state-of-the-art reconstructions (Section 6.1; Section 6.2, Table 2).

NJes6aeTem.text: At N=100 training problems for multicolumn addition, STAND reaches 98.62% per-problem completeness versus 96.97% for decision trees, 95.53% for random forests, and 98.01% for XGBoost (Section 5, Table 1).
STAND achieves 100% completeness in 19 of 40 multicolumn-addition runs, compared with only 10 of 40 runs for single decision trees (Section 5, Table 1).
STAND's total error recurrence rate on multicolumn addition is 0.53%, comparable to decision trees (0.38%) and lower than random forests (1.28%) and XGBoost (0.74%) (Section 5, Table 2).

On productive monotonicity (alignment between certainty change and actual learning gains), STAND scores 78.54% on fractions versus 50.61% for random forests and 50.90% for XGBoost (Section 5, Table 4).

STAND's average fitting time (5.30ms) and prediction time (0.35ms) remain below the 10ms threshold required for interactive task-learning applications, despite building a full approximate version space at each split (Section 5).

cvlPAWSeo3.text: CountsDiff reparameterizes the Blackout diffusion forward process using a differentiable, monotonically decreasing survival probability schedule p(t) with p(0)=1 and p(1)=0, rather than fixed discrete death rates, enabling continuous-time training (Section 3.1, Proposition 3.1).

On 50% MCAR fetal-cell single-cell RNA-seq imputation, CountsDiff attains log(scFID) of -9.253 (1-sample), outperforming ReMDM's -9.101, while matching ReMDM's 5-sample RMSE of about 1.195-1.196 (Section 4, Table 2).
