On the low-biased 25% MNAR imputation setting, CountsDiff achieves the best 5-sample RMSE (0.580) and bias (0.300) among compared methods, though its Spearman correlation (0.355) trails ReMDM's 0.374 (Section 4, Table 3).

CountsDiff uses roughly half the parameters of ReMDM due to a fixed output dimension, and supports classifier-free guidance and an attrition/remasking mechanism generalizing the reverse process via a death rate parameter analogous to churn in Gaussian diffusion (Section 3.3-3.4).

On CIFAR-10 generation, the continuous-time CountsDiff variant with guidance scale gamma=2.0 and eta_rescale=0.02 achieves FID 5.198 and Inception Score 9.765, improving on the discrete Blackout baseline's FID of 5.726 (Table 1).

nbU2LNYdZN.text: Theorem 3.2 proves that any planar symmetry group G is conjugate, via an invertible linear transformation, to a subgroup of an affine reflection group, allowing arbitrary planar symmetries to be embedded into higher-symmetry reflection groups (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.3 shows that for any G-invariant continuous function and any epsilon > 0, there exist coefficients h_1,...,h_r in the proposed decomposition whose approximation error is below epsilon, establishing universal approximation of symmetric functions (Theorem 3.3).

The symmetric representation combines Wa-invariant high-symmetry coefficient functions h_i with fixed low-symmetry G-invariant basis functions eta_i via f(x) = sum_i h_i(x) eta_i(x), avoiding the boundary discontinuities of naive asymmetric-unit extension for non-reflective transformations (Equation 3, Section 3.1, Figure 2).

Algorithm 1 generates symmetric patterns across all 17 wallpaper (planar) groups by mapping query points to the asymmetric unit and combining computed coefficients with fixed bases (Section 6.1, Algorithm 1).
A Virtual Temperature Method (VTM) loss enforces global connectivity for manufacturable paper-cutting patterns while preserving the required planar symmetry (Section 6.2, Equation 6).

The framework extends to topology optimization using homogenization-based mechanical property objectives under symmetry constraints, and Theorem B.9 shows the theoretical construction generalizes to n=3 (space groups), with zero-shot extension to metamaterial design demonstrated in Figure 8 (Section 6.3, Equation 8, Theorem B.9, Figure 8).

PtpuJFad8G.text: HIAL achieves 73.72% accuracy on Cora versus 71.90% for the best baseline GRAIN, and 62.76% on Citeseer versus 57.54% for the best baseline RIM, at a labeling budget of 20 classes (Table 1).
HIAL outperforms the best baseline by 8.38 percentage points on DBLP (77.30% vs. 68.92% for GRAIN) and by 5.47 points on Mushroom (96.35% vs. 90.88% for ACGNN) (Table 1).
On Citeseer, HIAL reaches 55% accuracy using only 48 labeled nodes, a 50% reduction in labeling cost compared to RIM's 108 labeled nodes for the same accuracy (Figure 3).

Ablations on Cora show that removing the Magnitude of Influence (MoI) term drops accuracy by 3.49 points and removing the Expected Diffusion Value (EDV) term drops accuracy by 2.93 points, while removing HOI-aware propagation (HOIP) entirely drops accuracy by 4.88 points (Table 2).
The dual-perspective influence functions (MoI and EDV) are proven to be monotone and submodular, enabling a greedy selection algorithm with a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee (Theorems 1-3).

HIAL's advantage generalizes across hypergraph neural network backbones on Cora, achieving 70.95% with HGNN, 72.71% with UniGCN, and 71.40% with VilLain, compared to 73.72% for HIAL's native architecture (Table 3).

kqE6GjpQTn.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) updates exhibit long-tailed singular value spectra whose variance increases over the course of continual training, indicating a few dominant components absorb most of the adaptation energy (Section 2.2, Figure 2a).

The proposed EBLoRA method decouples update magnitude from directional structure via the factorization delta_W_t = s_t U_t V_t^T, and formulates learning of U_t as constrained optimization on a restricted Stiefel manifold M_t = {U in R^(d x r) : U^T U = I_r, G_{t-1}^T U = 0} that enforces orthogonality to previous gradient directions (Section 3.1, Equation 6).

Proposition 3.1 shows the tangent-space projection (Equation 10) computes the unique orthogonal projection under the Frobenius norm, and Proposition 3.2 shows the retraction step (Equation 12) maps iterates to the closest feasible point on the manifold (Section 3.3, Propositions 3.1-3.2).
On the UCIT benchmark, EBLoRA achieves 72.8% mean final accuracy (MFN) versus 67.9% for KeepLoRA, with backward transfer (BWT) of -2.0 and forward transfer (FWT) of 34.6 (Table 1).
On the MLLM-DCL benchmark, EBLoRA achieves 66.7% MFN versus 64.4% for KeepLoRA, with backward transfer of -0.7 (Table 2).

An ablation shows Energy-Balanced Optimization (EBO) alone raises MFN from 61.4% to 70.2%, adding the gradient-orthogonality (GO) constraint raises it to 72.1%, and the full method with depth-aware initialization reaches 72.8% (Table 3).

MtialRxZMH.text: Across 9,024 experimental cases under the post-training threat model (TM-Post), most plasticity interventions mitigate backdoor threats, but SAM uniquely exacerbates them, increasing Attack Success Rate on robotic tasks from 0.178 to 0.326 (an 83.15% relative increase) while also raising benign performance from 0.745 to 0.814 (Section 5.1, Figure 3).

Noise-injection-style interventions—Shrink & Perturb, Weight Clipping, and ReDo—mitigate backdoors via Activation Pathway Disruption, inducing competitive reconstruction between backdoor and benign task representations (Section 5.2, Finding 2).

Interventions such as Spectral Normalization, Weight Decay, and Layer Normalization mitigate backdoors via Representation Space Compression, shifting gradient directions from orthogonal to aligned and converting sparse backdoor pathways into dense multi-pathway structures (Section 5.2, Finding 3, Figure 7).

SAM exacerbates backdoors via Backdoor Gradient Amplification, enabling rapid convergence to flat minima that remain robust to perturbations and reduce task competition, particularly under TM-Post (Section 5.2, Finding 4, Figure 8).
Backdoored models show a 635.22% increase in loss landscape sharpness range compared to conventionally trained models, proposed as a detection signature for DRL backdoors (Section 5.2, Figure 4).

The proposed Sweeper-Converter-Connector (SCC) framework combines all three identified mechanisms, and the Plastic/SLac/SSW intervention combination raises Attack Success Rate to 0.418 versus a 0.178 baseline while also increasing benign performance (Section 5.3, Table 1).

rS6SbpH6Ek.text: On W4A4 quantization of LLaMA-3 8B, ReSpinQuant achieves 7.24 perplexity and 64.65% zero-shot accuracy, outperforming SpinQuant's 7.50 perplexity and matching FlatQuant's quality (Table 1).
On W4A4 quantization of LLaMA-2 7B, ReSpinQuant achieves 5.74 perplexity versus 5.98 for SpinQuant (Table 1).

On the more challenging W3A3 quantization regime, ReSpinQuant improves perplexity on LLaMA-3.2 1B by 19.8 points over SpinQuant (49.90 vs. 69.70), and achieves 13.09 perplexity with 50.74% zero-shot accuracy on LLaMA-3 8B (Table 1).

ReSpinQuant follows a train-large, infer-small strategy: 1,091M learnable parameters are used during training across layers, but only 8.4M parameters (about 0.1% of the 8B model) are needed online at inference (Table 2).

The subspace residual rotation approximation reduces computational overhead to roughly 0.2% (32.3M vs. 15.37T MACs) and increases inference latency by only about 1.7% relative to the SpinQuant baseline, in contrast to FlatQuant's O(D^1.5) overhead (Section 3.3, Table 2, Table 3).
A rank ablation shows that a subspace rank of r=32 achieves a near-optimal accuracy-efficiency balance for the low-rank approximation of the basis mismatch matrix T (Section 3.3, Table 5).

IxpVGcg39J.text: nanoTabPFNlooped, a single transformer block applied recurrently six times, matches the ROC-AUC of the standard six-layer nanoTabPFN6l while using only about 750,154 parameters versus 3,560,832 parameters in the six-layer model's transformer blocks (Section 5, Table A.8).

Layer ablation experiments across six tabular foundation models (TabPFN v1, TabPFN v2, TabPFN 2.5, TabICL, LimiX-2M, LimiX-16M) show early layers cause the largest performance degradation when skipped, while middle and late layers are largely robust to removal, indicating substantial depthwise redundancy (Section 3).

Self-repair analysis shows that after ablating a given layer, subsequent middle and late layers recover much of the lost performance, evidencing overlapping/redundant computation rather than strict layer specialization (Section 3).

A per-layer 'tabular logit lens' with individually trained decoders reveals that reliable predictions already emerge in early layers, contradicting the assumption that only the final decoder layer produces meaningful predictions (Section 3).

Inference dynamics are organized into four depth-dependent stages: latent mapping, feature engineering and labeling, prediction ensembling, and prediction calibration, evaluated on 15 tasks from TabArena (≤10,000 samples, ≤100 features) and 34 tasks from PMLBmini (≤500 samples) (Section 3).

Compared to large language models, tabular foundation models show earlier-peaking prediction confidence, greater sensitivity to layer swapping, and more pronounced middle-layer redundancy than typically observed in LLMs (Section 3).

4lAS8tI23u.text: On the TR-2D turbulent flow benchmark, IRNO applied to a TFNO base model reduces VRMSE by 56.05% (Table 1).

On the Active Matter benchmark, IRNO applied to a TFNO base model reduces VRMSE by up to 80.46%, with spectral error reductions of 62–73% in low-frequency bands, 93–96% in mid-frequency bands, and 98–99% in high-frequency bands (Table 1, Table 3).
On the ERA5 benchmark, IRNO yields a 19% improvement in ACC (anomaly correlation coefficient) and a 34% reduction in RFNE (Table 1).
Theorem 3.1 proves quadratic-linear convergence of the fixed-point iteration under local affine approximations, with error satisfying ‖e_{k+1}‖ ≤ q‖e_k‖ + c‖e_k‖² + α‖b‖ (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

The theoretical error-reduction prediction correlates strongly with empirically observed error reduction, with Pearson r=0.933 (p≪10⁻¹⁰) on Active Matter and r=0.949 (p≪10⁻¹⁰) on TR-2D (Section 4, Figure 3).

IRNO trained to refine a lower-performing base operator transfers effectively to refine higher-performing operators on the same task, indicating the learned error-correction patterns generalize across operators (Table 4).

RgnoWsmYBM.text: Across an audit of 6,642 human-verified labels spanning 4 victim models (Gemma-3-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-27B, Qwen-3-32B) and 5 attack methods (Direct Prompting, GCG, GCG-REINFORCE, Best-of-N, PAIR), 4 safety judges (LlamaGuard-3, HarmBench, AegisGuard, JailJudge) are shown to perform only slightly better than random guessing on average (Section 3, Figure 3).

ROC analysis shows JailJudge attains AUROC as low as 0.48 (worse than chance) on some attack-model pairs and no better than 0.64 on any attack, demonstrating near-chance discriminative ability under distribution shift (Figure 5).
Judge accuracy varies dramatically across attack-model combinations, with some judges scoring only 45% accuracy on specific attack-victim pairs, close to random guessing (Figure 3, Figure 4).

The paper introduces ReliableBench, a curated set of 41 behaviors, which raises average judge accuracy from 57% to 70%, and JudgeStressTest (JST), a set of 971 challenging samples that exposes systematic judge failures across judge architectures via leave-one-out validation (Table 1).

Correcting reported attack success rates (ASR) for judge unreliability substantially deflates the apparent effectiveness of attacks such as Best-of-N, which is shown to inflate ASR by exploiting judge insufficiencies rather than eliciting genuinely harmful content (Figure 1, Figure 8).

Judge Concordance analysis shows judges can reach near-unanimous agreement with each other while still failing to align with human ground-truth labels, and averaging/ensembling judge scores does not consistently improve alignment with human judgments (Figure 6).

793DO6oMn7.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes that the intrinsic geometry of the vector bundle E over an invariant set T is flat, formally connecting behavioral/functional invariance of substructures to geometric flatness (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 4.2 shows the Gauge architecture's Dirichlet energy loss decreases monotonically across layers ('monotonous flattening'), which the gated flattening mechanism (Eq. 6-8) is designed to enforce (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
On zero-shot link prediction, Gauge achieves AUC/AP of 93.88±0.05 / 90.73±0.24 on Facebook and 66.22±1.26 / 67.21±0.58 on Roman-empire (Table 2).

On graph isomorphism tasks, Gauge attains 92.56%±4.37 accuracy on CSL, substantially outperforming the SAMGPT baseline at 64.17%, and achieves the lowest MAE of 0.1570±0.005 on ZINC12K among compared methods (Table 3).
In cross-domain few-shot transfer, Gauge achieves the best performance among 16 baselines, including 61.26%±5.43 on PubMed 1-shot and 81.33%±2.93 on Photo 5-shot (Table 1).

Definition 4.3 introduces τ-invariance as a measurable criterion for identifying transferable substructures based on representation predictive error thresholds, operationalized via local coordinate updates computed with QR decomposition (Eq. 4) (Section 4, Definition 4.3).

MA1LUDNA3s.text: Theorem 1 proves that allocations produced by weighted empirical risk minimization are monotonically increasing in each user's individual bid, which enables construction of a truthful payment rule via Myerson's Lemma (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 proves that for L2-regularized linear classifiers, the expected total payments collected by the accuracy auction are O(1), i.e., bounded by a constant independent of the number of samples m (Theorem 2).

Theorem 3 proves that k-nearest-neighbor classifiers exhibit Ω(m) expected total payments under label noise, showing that the choice of learning algorithm materially affects auction revenue/payment scaling (Theorem 3).
Corollary 1 establishes individual rationality: no user's payment ever exceeds their reported valuation for accuracy under the mechanism (Corollary 1).

Experiments show the number of paying users plateaus quickly as sample size increases across different variance parameter settings, and higher model accuracy is associated with lower payment proportions (Section 7, Figure 2).
Optimizing the accuracy-auction objective against a uniform-allocation baseline yields social welfare improvements of up to 23% with only modest accuracy tradeoffs (Section 7, Figure 3).

LkiD08kdRy.text: Golden Goose converts unverifiable internet text into multiple-choice verifiable RLVR tasks, producing GooseReason-0.7M with over 700,000 tasks synthesized from source corpora including AoPS-Instruct, rStar-Coder, and MegaScience (Section 2)
On Qwen-4B-Instruct, adding GooseReason data on top of ProRL raises average math benchmark accuracy from 71.65% to 73.83%, a 2.18 point absolute gain (Table 1)
On coding benchmarks, average accuracy for Qwen-4B-Instruct increases from 53.46% to 55.70% after GooseReason training (Table 2)
GPQA Diamond accuracy improves from 64.39% to 66.79% and Reasoning Gym average from 80.10% to 81.28% with GooseReason training (Table 3)
Qwen3-4B-Instruct trained on the 180K-task GooseReason-Cyber dataset reaches 78.99% average cybersecurity performance, surpassing an 8B domain-specialized model at 67.93% (Table 4, Section 3.2)
Ablations show multiple-choice questions with 9 options are optimal, with about 70% of synthesized problems falling in a medium-difficulty range that provides effective RL signal (Figure 4)

c7NEZ94WAq.text: HOI-PAGE generates 4D human-object interactions from text prompts in a zero-shot fashion by prioritizing part-level affordance reasoning rather than whole-body interaction modeling (abstract only)

The method distills a structured Part Affordance Graph (PAG) from a large language model that encodes fine-grained object part information and contact relations, illustrated as the core representation in Figure 1 (Figure 1)

Synthesis proceeds in three stages: decomposing 3D objects into semantic parts, generating reference HOI videos from text prompts to extract motion constraints, and optimizing 4D interaction sequences that satisfy part-level contact constraints while following reference dynamics (abstract only)

HOI-PAGE demonstrates improved realism and text alignment compared to prior zero-shot 4D HOI generation approaches, including for complex multi-object and multi-person interaction sequences (abstract only)

4HquuQN4qK.text: The paper shows Wasserstein variational inference's (WVI) empirical superiority over black-box variational inference (BBVI) stems specifically from its use of Price's gradient estimator rather than from operating in Bures-Wasserstein space per se (Section 3)

Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 establish that WVI and BBVI achieve identical state-of-the-art iteration complexity guarantees for Gaussian variational families when both use Price's gradient (Theorem 2, Theorem 3)

Price's gradient estimator incorporates second-order information via Hessians of the target log-density, in contrast to the reparameterization gradient which uses only first-order derivatives (Section 2)

Adapting Price's gradient estimator from Bures-Wasserstein space to standard Euclidean parameter space is shown to be the major source of BBVI's performance improvement over the standard reparametrization-gradient BBVI baseline (Section 3, Section 5)

Gu9pw3D6vT.text: Theorem 4.8 derives a scaling law for the expected meta-learning adaptation gain, G_K ≥ A_∞(1 - e^{-βK}), where A_∞ = c·σ_τ^2 scales with task variance and β = η·μ_min depends on learning rate and landscape curvature, showing the gain saturates exponentially with gradient steps K (Theorem 4.8)

For the single-qubit X gate, the exponential saturation model fits with R^2 > 0.99 and adaptation rate β = 0.083, with negligible adaptation benefit when task variance σ_τ^2 < 0.002 (Section 4, or wherever the single-qubit results are reported)

On the two-qubit CZ gate under 10x the training noise level, meta-initialization achieves 54.2% fidelity while post-adaptation after K=10 gradient steps reaches 95.7% fidelity, a gain exceeding 40 percentage points, with R^2 = 0.986 and β = 0.333 for the exponential fit (Section 4)

Assumption 4.3 posits a Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition on the local loss landscape near optima, empirically validated with measured curvature μ ≈ 0.03 in the adaptation regime (Assumption 4.3, Figure 2a)

Corollary 4.10 shows adaptation provides negligible benefit when task variance is small (homogeneous devices) or when the adaptation rate β is much less than the inverse of the gradient-step budget (Corollary 4.10)

A classical linear-quadratic regulator control task reproduces the same exponential saturation scaling law (R^2 = 0.99), indicating the scaling law arises from optimization geometry rather than quantum-specific physics (Section 4)

gTHlB3WK0l.text: CrispEdit formulates non-destructive LLM editing as constrained optimization, minimizing an edit loss subject to a capability-preservation constraint expressed via Bregman divergence using the Gauss-Newton Hessian rather than the standard Hessian (Section 3.2)
Proposition 1 proves that prior editing methods AlphaEdit and Adam-NSCL solve strictly more restrictive special cases of CrispEdit's constrained optimization formulation (Proposition 1)

CrispEdit approximates the Gauss-Newton Hessian with a Kronecker-factored (K-FAC) block-diagonal structure, reducing memory from O(d_out^2 d_in^2) to O(d_out^2 + d_in^2) and enabling a matrix-free low-curvature projector (Section 3.3, Equation 6)

On LLaMA-3-8B with the ZsRE dataset, CrispEdit achieves 80.5% reliability (with context) versus 70.1% for AlphaEdit, while keeping base-capability degradation on benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K below 1% on average, compared to substantially larger degradation for MEMIT and Adam-NSCL (Table 1)
CrispEdit performs 3,000 sequential edits on LLaMA-3-8B in 4 minutes 6 seconds and remains robust when scaled to 10,000 edits (Table 1, Algorithm 2)
Ablations show CrispEdit is robust with as few as 100 capability-preservation samples and is insensitive to the energy threshold gamma across the range 0.5 to 0.99 (Tables 7-8)

bj4mX7nyvu.text: IMPACT achieves the best AUC on 4 of the reported general-setting datasets, including 91.96% on CT (vs. 88.73% second-best) and 82.91% on TUSZ (vs. 78.70% second-best) (Table 1).
Under the open-set hard setting, where labeled anomalies come from only a single class at training time, IMPACT achieves a 10.52%-42.83% average AUC improvement over competing methods (Table 2).

Four theorems justify the method: entropy minimization equivalence (Theorem 1), label flipping reduces test risk (Theorem 2), perturbed features follow a distribution distinct from normal data (Theorem 3), and feature perturbation further reduces test risk (Theorem 4) (Section 3).
Ablations show removing label-flipped contaminated samples consistently degrades performance, and removing seen abnormality learning drops TUSZ AUC from 82.91% to 70.91% (Table 3).
Removing unseen abnormality learning is especially damaging under the hard setting, dropping TUSZ AUC from 75.70% to 60.92% (Table 3).
Sensitivity analysis finds a weight coefficient of λ=1.0 and k=5 perturbed samples to be optimal, with performance stabilizing as λ increases (Figure 3).

Wph27Qttp5.text: For monotone submodular objectives under a knapsack constraint, DP-2GG (Algorithm 2) achieves the optimal (1-1/e)-approximation with query complexity O(β^{-1} n^3 k) and additive error scaling polylogarithmically in ground-set size (Theorem 4.1, Section 5).
A faster monotone variant, DP-DG+ (Algorithm 7), trades approximation quality for speed, achieving a 1/2-approximation with only O(nk) queries (Theorem 4.2, Appendix B.2).

The paper gives the first differentially private algorithm with provable guarantees for non-monotone submodular maximization under a knapsack constraint, DP-SDG (Algorithm 3), achieving a 1/4-approximation in expectation with O(nk) queries (Theorem 4.3, Section 6).

The non-monotone algorithm handles DP-noise-induced negative marginal gains by continuing selection regardless and using Report Noisy Max post hoc to pick the best candidate solution (Section 6, Algorithm 4).
On the Uber Manhattan ride-sharing dataset with m=100,000 pickups, DP-DG+ achieves an objective value within 8% of the non-private baseline at privacy parameter ε=0.2 (Section 7, Figure 1).

tNvmMTsRqh.text: Theorem 1 shows that when the perturbation radius ρ satisfies ρ ≥ -1/λ1 (λ1 being a negative Hessian eigenvalue at the saddle), the saddle point becomes an attracting fixed point of the SAM dynamics (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 uses a stochastic diffusion analysis to show SAM's mean squared displacement near a saddle point is smaller than SGD's, implying SAM requires more time than SGD to escape saddle points (Theorem 2).
Theorem 3 shows the mean squared displacement near a saddle scales as 1/[(1-γ)B], so higher momentum γ and smaller batch size B accelerate SAM's escape from saddle points (Theorem 3).

On the Beale test function, SAM is empirically shown to become stuck at a saddle point where vanilla gradient descent successfully escapes, matching the Case-III oscillation predicted by the theory (Section 5, empirical validation).

On CIFAR benchmarks, adding momentum increases SAM's accuracy by more than 20 percentage points, compared to roughly a 5-point gain for SGD with momentum, confirming momentum's outsized effect on SAM stability (Section 5).

dmTyOwKAmZ.text: The paper's reward-agnostic exploration algorithm attains sample complexity O(|S||A|H^3 ℓ0^3/ε^2 + |S|^2|A|H^4 ℓ0^3/ε), where ℓ0 = ln(|S||A|H/δε), improving the low-order term over Li et al. (2024b) so the bound is optimal for sufficiently small ε (Proposition 3.1, Section 3.1).

The paper proves a matching lower bound of Ω(|S|^2|A|H^3/ε^2) trajectories in expectation for any reward-free exploration algorithm, resolving a prior conjecture for time-inhomogeneous finite-horizon MDPs (Proposition 3.2, Section 3.1).

The algorithm replaces multiple instantiations of no-regret algorithms used in prior work with a single online MDP procedure run over a carefully constructed reward sequence λ_th(s,a) = 1/(c + N_th(s,a)) (Section 3).
The exploration objective is connected to minimizing the log-barrier μ* = argmin{-Σ log μ_h(s,a)} over valid occupancy measures, which encourages near-uniform state-action coverage (Section 3).
The lower-bound proof extends prior single-state constructions to time-dependent MDPs, introducing an additional factor of H relative to earlier single-state lower bounds (Section 3.1).

t9aUiZsQgg.text: On CMU-MOSI, GCL achieves MAE 0.685 and binary accuracy 86.79%, surpassing the EMOE baseline's 0.710 MAE and 85.4% accuracy (Table 1).
On CMU-MOSEI, GCL achieves MAE 0.520, binary accuracy 86.78%, 7-level accuracy 55.36%, and F1 86.55% (Table 1).
On the MIntRec intent-recognition benchmark, GCL reaches 72.74% accuracy and 70.95% F1 (Table 2).
Compared to the EMOE baseline on CMU-MOSI, GCL cuts trainable parameters by 18% and training time per epoch by 25% (20.06s vs. 26.80s) (Table 4).

Ablations across CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and MIntRec show that both Stage 1 (Routing/Auditing agent selective interaction) and Stage 2 (Public-Factor/Aggregation agent consensus formation) components contribute to performance, with removal of either degrading results (Table 3).

A robustness analysis under Gaussian noise and a message-permutation stress test (using HSIC/CKA diagnostics) show GCL maintains stability against spurious modality coupling, unlike baselines (Figure 2, Figure 4).

ie64yVZUQF.text: WaveVerse's temporal phase-coherent ray tracing improves respiration tracking to RMSE 0.08 and DTW 8.89, versus RMSE 0.14 and DTW 12.68 for the non-phase-coherent baseline (Section 4.3, Figure 7).
WaveVerse's spatial phase coherence produces sharper panoramic radar imaging across 1,200 simulated radar positions compared to standard ray tracing (Section 4.3, Figure 6).

Augmenting high-resolution RF imaging with 4x simulated data reduces mean absolute error by 2.02 cm and 90th-percentile error by 6.88 cm, and improves PSNR by 1.51 dB, capturing 73.33% of the improvement obtained from 4x real data (Section 4.4, Figure 8a).

For human activity recognition, augmenting 100 real samples with WaveVerse-simulated data raises accuracy from 31.6% (real only) to 49.8% with +400 synthetic samples, 61.4% with +900, 71.6% with +1,900, and 81.0% using the full real+synthetic dataset (Section 4.4, Figure 8b).

Ki0eWT1sFS.text: ProtoMech uses cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) with encoder/decoder matrices spanning multiple layers to discover sparse computational circuits in protein language models (Section 2, Section 2.1).
ProtoMech-derived circuits recover 89% of original model performance on protein family classification and 82% on function prediction (Section 3.1).

Family-classification circuits use only 150±204 latents on average (about 0.8% of the total latent space), and function-prediction circuits use 167±221 latents (about 0.9% of the latent space), while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy (Section 3.1).
In protein variant generation guided by discovered circuits, ProtoMech outperforms the PLT baseline in 71% of cases across seven DMS assays (Section 3.2, Table 1).
Case studies on kinase domain, NADP+ binding, and GB1 fitness landscapes show discovered circuits aligning with known structural and functional biological motifs (Section 3.3, Figures 3-4).

dhzRnzD9jR.text: The study analyzes 1.5 million consumer Claude.ai interactions collected between December 12-19, 2025, using the privacy-preserving Clio analysis tool (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).

Severe reality-distortion potential is identified in 0.076% of conversations, consistent with the abstract's claim that severe disempowerment potential occurs in fewer than one in a thousand conversations (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
Severe vulnerability-related disempowerment patterns occur in approximately one in 300 interactions (Section 4.2).

Disempowerment rates vary sharply by domain: Relationships & Lifestyle shows the highest rate at approximately 8%, Society & Culture and Healthcare & Wellness show approximately 5% each, while Software Development shows rates below 1% (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
A longitudinal analysis of over 500,000 randomly sampled interactions from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025 tracks historical trends in disempowerment patterns (Section 4.5, Figure 13).

BSxSIzUPSZ.text: The paper proposes a quantile-regression-based membership inference attack designed for settings where the auditor lacks representative samples of the target/unseen class distribution (Section 4).

The quantile regression attack achieves up to 11x higher true positive rate (TPR) at low false positive rates than shadow-model-based attacks in the unseen-class setting, evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100 (Section 5, Figure 7).

The quantile regression attack outperforms shadow-model and LiRA baselines at low-FPR operating points (e.g., FPR = 0.1% and FPR = 1%) when auditors lack access to representative samples of harmful content from the target distribution (Table 1).
The paper establishes theoretical guarantees for the quantile regression attack under distribution-shift conditions via Theorems 5.1-5.3 (Section 5).

dnaHNet's evaluation perplexity scales with exponent alpha=0.06 versus alpha=0.04 for StripedHyena2, indicating superior compute efficiency (Section 4.3, Figure 3).

yEjix8H6Dw.text: On the newly introduced CommGen15 benchmark (9 image and 6 video commercial generative models, 33,394 real COCO images and 33,394 generated samples), PGC achieves 97.9% mean detection accuracy, outperforming the strongest competitor DDA by +12.3 points (Table 3).

The Local Geometric Instability (LGI) score rho_t, defined via directional derivatives along k random probing directions, satisfies 0 <= rho_t(x_t) < 1, keeping the geometric brake exp(-lambda*rho_t) bounded below by alpha_min = e^(-lambda) > 0 (Proposition 4.1, Eq. 4).

eFBO8ECxb2.text: Hybrid Policy Distillation (HPD) reformulates existing knowledge-distillation objectives for LLMs as reweighted token-level losses, unifying forward-KL and reverse-KL approaches within a single framework (Sections 2-4).
HPD combines forward and reverse KL divergence to jointly achieve balanced mode coverage (mass-covering) and mode-seeking behavior, rather than relying on either divergence alone (Sections 2-4).

HPD pairs offline teacher-generated data with lightweight approximate online student sampling to improve optimization stability relative to purely offline or fully on-policy distillation (Sections 2-4).

HPD is evaluated on mathematical reasoning (long-generation), open-domain dialogue, and code-generation tasks, with primary numeric comparisons against forward-KL-only and reverse-KL-only baselines reported in Tables 3-5 (Section 5.1, Tables 3-5).
HPD is validated across multiple model families and parameter scales as student models, demonstrating consistent gains over single-divergence distillation baselines (Section 5).

For a k-th order cumulant target, the sample complexity threshold for weak recovery via projected gradient descent is n_hat(d,k) = omega(d^(k-1) log^2 d), with |v . w(n_hat)| approaching 1 as d approaches infinity after this many steps (Proposition 4.3).

If the number of samples n(d) = o(n_hat(d,k*)), standard SGD provably fails to achieve weak recovery of the k*-th cumulant, establishing a sharp learnable/unlearnable sample-complexity separation (Proposition 4.4).

In a mixed-cumulant latent model, pair-wise statistics are recoverable with linear sample complexity n = Theta(d * polylog(d)), while recovering the fourth cumulant requires Omega(d^3) samples when latent variables are independent (Proposition 4.6).

When latent variables underlying the pair-wise and higher-order statistics are positively correlated, the fourth-cumulant recovery sample complexity accelerates from cubic to linear in d (Proposition 4.6).

Unconstrained SGD exhibits contraction dynamics toward w=0 for many activation functions, causing learning failure, whereas constraining updates to the unit sphere (spherical projection) preserves the ability to learn higher-order statistics (Proposition 4.7).

nVOzKXVvPu.text: LMAC uses an LLM to iteratively design a communication protocol across three refinement stages (k=0 initial generation, k=1 recovery enhancement maximizing individual state-reconstruction, k=2 imbalance mitigation reducing inter-agent variance) (Section 4.2).

On SMACv2 at 3M training steps, LMAC outperforms the QMIX+State upper-bound baseline on terran_5_vs_5 (67.87+/-2.77% vs 64.77+/-2.79%), protoss_5_vs_5 (57.96+/-4.02% vs 56.40+/-2.33%), and zerg_5_vs_5 (42.18+/-4.37% vs 40.06+/-3.39%) win rates (Table 1).

An ablation shows removing the cycle-consistency loss drops win rate to 66.5+/-2.1% and removing the state-awareness-index (SAI) reconstruction term drops it to 76.6+/-5.6%, versus 82.9+/-1.9% for the full k=2 method (Table 2(a)).
LMAC's performance is robust to the choice of underlying LLM used for protocol design: GPT-4.1 (82.9+/-1.9%), Claude (81.9+/-2.6%), and Gemini (80.8+/-1.6%) yield comparable results (Table 2(b)).
The reconstruction-error threshold alpha used in the state-awareness criterion is optimal at alpha=0.05, achieving 82.9+/-1.9% win rate with stable results for larger threshold values (Table 2(c)).

On GRF 3_vs_1_with_keeper, LMAC outperforms the QMIX+State upper bound due to compact feature compression of high-dimensional observations, and Figure 4 shows recovery success rate increasing while knowledge imbalance across agents decreases over the k=0 to k=2 refinement iterations (Figure 4, Section 5.1).

BRBHruBDkb.text: DiLA resolves the latent action model trade-off between action abstraction and generation fidelity via content-structure disentanglement, using a dual-pathway architecture with a structure pathway (IDM+FDM under a bottleneck) and a content pathway (Section 3, Figure 2).
On the cycle transfer metric, DiLA achieves LPIPS 0.263→0.343, outperforming an ablation without the content pathway which scores 0.344→0.451 (Table 2).

DiLA achieves SSIM 0.660±0.037 and LPIPS 0.356±0.027 on Something-Something-v2 and SSIM 0.774±0.010 and LPIPS 0.206±0.013 on RT-1, outperforming LAPA, Moto, AdaWorld(FDM), and villa-X on LPIPS (Table 1).

On the VP² visual planning benchmark, DiLA attains an aggregate task success rate of 41.44% versus 21.54% for AdaWorld, with particularly large gains on button-pressing tasks (35.83% vs 10.83% on blue button) (Table 4, Section 4.6).

Linear probing on out-of-distribution datasets shows DiLA's latent actions yield lower MSE than discrete or Gaussian bottleneck variants: 0.009±0.003 vs 0.023±0.004 (discrete) and 0.041±0.006 (Gaussian) on Push-T, and 0.073±0.014 vs 0.098±0.014 (discrete) on Franka Kitchen (Table 3).

UMAP visualizations of learned latent actions show translation forming a 2D plane, scaling exhibiting symmetry, and rotation forming a continuous spectrum, indicating manifold interpretability (Figure 6, Section 4.5).

EKmiOtjZjI.text: UP-OCP is a parameter-free online conformal prediction method requiring no stepsize tuning, whose regret analysis is built on universal portfolio algorithms (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
Theorem 4.3 shows UP-OCP achieves linearized regret of order O(√(T ln T)) in the worst case, improving to O(ln T) as the miscoverage target α→1 (Theorem 4.3).
Theorem 4.4 establishes a finite-time miscoverage bound of the form MisCov_T ≤ ε_T + √(2α(1-α)ε_T), where ε_T grows only logarithmically in T (Theorem 4.4).

On the AXP dataset at α=0.05, UP-OCP achieves 0.932 marginal coverage with an average prediction set size of 14.8 and a longest error streak of 4 days, versus 0.920 coverage, 16.9 average set size, and a 15-day longest error streak for the Kalman/KT baseline (Table 1).
Across miscoverage rates from 0.05 to 0.25, UP-OCP empirically achieves the best Pareto trade-off between coverage and set size compared to the parameter-free KT baseline (Figure 1).

On a synthetic sinusoidal nonconformity-score sequence, UP-OCP tracks periodic volatility—expanding prediction sets during high-noise phases and shrinking them afterward—matching the best hyperparameter-tuned P-Control baseline without any tuning (Figures 3-4).

H0rZO2EK1s.text: On CLRS-DFS, SPARK reaches its best out-of-distribution accuracy of 83.74% by proposal attempt 57, a 1600/57≈28.1x improvement in evaluation efficiency over EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation budget (Section 4.2).
SPARK improves OOD accuracy on CLRS-DFS from EvoPrompting's 68.14% to 83.74%, a gain of 15.6 percentage points, while keeping compute nearly unchanged (664K MACs vs. a 661K reference) (Table 1).
Across 10 CLRS tasks, SPARK attains a mean OOD accuracy of 83.92% (Table 1).

An ablation on CLRS-DFS with DeepSeek-R1 shows RC+SAR alone gives +10.01 points (56.79%), ASR alone gives +18.50 points (65.28%), and the full SPARK method combining both gives +36.96 points (83.74%), showing factor-conditioned scope selection contributes more than refinement alone (Table 2).

Search dynamics analysis shows SPARK's cumulative valid-edit rate stabilizes around 0.5-0.6 over 100 proposal attempts, compared to 0.25-0.3 for baseline methods, alongside lower entanglement rates and faster best-so-far accuracy improvement (Figure 2).

Ig36S9zALV.text: DeepBlip is presented as the first neural framework for structural nested mean models (SNMMs) enabling end-to-end, gradient-based training via a novel double optimization trick, where two forward passes generate two sets of blip coefficients and the second serves as fixed pseudo-ground-truth (Section 4.2, Equation 8).

The double optimization trick is shown to be a single-step gradient descent realization of an iterative scheme with convergence guarantees (Appendix C), and the L²-moment loss satisfies universal Neyman-orthogonality for double robustness to nuisance model misspecification (Remark 1, Section 4.2).

On the semi-synthetic Tumor Growth dataset, DeepBlip outperforms all baselines for confounding strength γ_conf≥2, with especially large gains under strong confounding (γ_conf>6) (Section 5.1, Figure 3).

On MIMIC-III at long prediction horizons, DeepBlip's error advantage over the G-estimation/Dynamic-DML baseline grows with horizon τ: from a 3.8% improvement at τ=3 (0.50±0.12 vs 0.52±0.02) to a 34.6% improvement at τ=10 (0.98±0.32 vs 1.50±0.45) (Section 5.2, Table 2).
On MIMIC-III, DeepBlip's training time remains nearly constant as prediction horizon τ increases, while the Dynamic DML baseline's training time grows linearly with τ (Section 5.2, Figure 4).

jBPFdqmOck.text: A 7B-parameter web GUI agent trained on AutoWebWorld's synthetic FSM-generated data achieves a 27.42% success rate on WebVoyager, outperforming UI-TARS-1.5-7B (26.51%) despite using only 16K training steps versus competitors' 1M+ samples (Table 3).
The 3B variant of the trained agent achieves a 15.09% success rate on WebVoyager, substantially below the 7B model, indicating a benefit from model scale (Table 3).

Increasing synthetic training data volume yields a consistent scaling law: WebVoyager success rate rises 3.92%→17.59%→19.09%→27.42% and Online-Mind2Web success rate rises 1.22%→7.32%→7.93%→14.02% across the four data scales tested (Figure 4).
Fine-tuning on AutoWebWorld's synthetic grounding data improves ScreenSpot-V2 accuracy from 84.83% to 86.16% and ScreenSpot-Pro accuracy from 23.2% to 27.5% for the 7B model (Tables 4-5).

AutoWebWorld generates 11,663 verified trajectories across 29 synthetic websites at a cost of $0.04 per trajectory, versus $0.15-$1.00 per trajectory for real-world data collection methods (Section on Data Efficiency).
An ablation shows including grounding data during GRPO training produces stable coordinate-reward growth, whereas excluding it causes the reward to plateau (Figure 5).

4JRO9plGAI.text: CaP-Bench evaluates coding agents across eight tiers—single-turn S1-S4 (varying abstraction from high-level primitives with privileged state down to low-level primitives without examples) and multi-turn M1-M4 (text feedback, raw visual input, VDM-converted text, and low-level VDM)—showing performance increases monotonically with higher-level abstraction (Section 3.1-3.2, Table 1).

Direct raw image feedback in the M2 multi-turn tier paradoxically degrades success rates relative to text-only feedback, while VDM-converted natural-language feedback in M3 consistently improves outcomes across all 12 evaluated models (Section 3.2, Figure 5).

CaP-Agent0, a training-free agentic framework combining a Visual Differencing Module, an auto-synthesized skill library, and parallel reasoning across Gemini-3-Pro/GPT-5.2/Claude Opus samples, achieves success rates comparable to or exceeding human experts on 4 of 7 CaP-Bench core manipulation tasks (Section 4.1, Table 2).
On LIBERO-PRO under position and instruction perturbations, CaP-Agent0 outperforms vision-language-action baselines OpenVLA, pi0, and pi0.5 (Section 4.2, Table 2).

Applying GRPO reinforcement learning (CaP-RL) to Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on privileged-state (S1) APIs raises simulated success rates from 25% to 80% on Cube Lift, 4% to 44% on Cube Stack, and 30% to 93% on Spill Wipe, with real-world Franka Emika transfer reaching 84% and 76% success on Cube Lift and Cube Stack respectively (Section 5, Table 4).

YIzUTHEvG7.text: LLM4Branch represents a branching policy as an executable Python program with a skeleton produced by an LLM and a parameter vector tuned via zeroth-order Bayesian optimization, mapping a 91-dimensional node feature vector to candidate scores (Section 4.2-4.3, Table 8).

On the standard benchmarks (Set Covering, Combinatorial Auction, Facility Location, Independent Set), LLM4Branch attains state-of-the-art performance among CPU-based branching methods and performance competitive with GPU-based learned models (Section 5.2, Table 1).

On Set Covering medium instances LLM4Branch solves in 37.64 seconds versus 40.18 seconds for the Hybrid baseline, and on Independent Set medium instances in 62.45 seconds versus 112.48 seconds for Hybrid (Section 5.2, Table 1).

Discovered branching policies agree with strong-branching expert decisions only 24.72% of the time on Independent Set, yet still outperform imitation-learning baselines that directly mimic the expert (Section 5.2).

Ablations show optimizing end-to-end solver cost directly outperforms optimizing imitation accuracy of the strong-branching expert, and that the Bayesian parameter-optimization stage is essential, reducing Set Covering solving time from 4.53s without optimization to 3.21s with it (Section 5.3, Table 4-5).

mjbzYPFUW9.text: OOVDet's Out-of-Vocabulary Prompt Synthesis (OPS) module generates region-level OOV prompts by adding masked Gaussian noise to in-vocabulary prompt embeddings, sampling from low-likelihood regions of class-conditional Gaussian distributions (Section 3.2).
Dirichlet-based Gradient Attribution (DGA) mines pseudo-OOV training images by modeling attribution gradients as Dirichlet evidence and selecting high prediction-uncertainty samples (Section 3.3).

The Low-Density Prior Constraint (LPC) uses Gaussian kernel density estimation to push pseudo-OOV samples into low-density valleys between in-vocabulary clusters, enforcing an explicit IV/OOV decision boundary (Section 3.4).

On the OOV-VOC benchmark, OOVDet achieves 10.65% mAP_OOV (a 2.70-point improvement over prior methods) and 56.42% OOV recall (an 8.71-point improvement), with a Wilderness Impact of 3.95 (Section 4.2, Table 1).
On OOV-COCO, OOVDet reaches 10.09% mAP_OOV, 27.60% OOV recall, while maintaining 51.15% mAP on seen in-vocabulary classes (Section 4.2, Table 1).

An ablation on kernel bandwidth for the density estimator shows it materially affects OOV-VOC performance, with an optimal bandwidth balancing IV/unseen-IV/OOV detection accuracy (Section 4.3, Table 4, Figure 4).

C0WnTbVSEs.text: VividCam trains only on synthetic low-poly Unity-rendered videos (500 clips, each rendered in about 5 seconds) to teach a video diffusion model unconventional camera motions, avoiding costly real-world camera-motion data collection (Section 4.2, Section 5.1).

The dual-adaptation training scheme first trains an appearance LoRA on static synthetic videos to isolate visual style, then freezes it while training a separate camera-control module on videos with camera movement, and discards the appearance LoRA at inference (Section 4.3).

Style-aligned prompts appending the phrase referencing a "low-poly <VIRTUAL> scene" during training (removed at inference) together with an optical-flow-based appearance-invariant loss stabilize motion learning and prevent synthetic artifacts from corrupting output appearance (Section 4.3).

Evaluated on complex camera motions (e.g., object-seeking pans, orbit shots, dolly zoom), ViVidCam-Cog achieves a human-rated action correctness of 0.93 and realism score of 0.74, versus 0.81 and 0.65 for the AC3D baseline (Section 5.3, Table 3).

Camera motions are organized into four categories—Simple, Composed, Complex/Expressive, and Stylized (e.g., push-in, truck-left, handheld shake, explosive shake)—used to structure the quantitative evaluation (Section 5.1, Table 1).

mMQuxqbXlU.text: Gradient-based diagnostics measuring category-to-category cosine similarity and category-to-all gradient alignment show the correspondence module exhibits the lowest gradient alignment and highest negative transfer among network modules during joint category-level pose training (Section 4.1-4.2, Table 4).

DecomPose decomposes only the correspondence module into group-specific branches, sorting categories by a difficulty proxy and partitioning them via quantile thresholding with boundary refinement (difficulty-aware grouping), while keeping the backbone and pose head shared (Section 5.2, Section 5.3).

Stability-driven asymmetric branching allocates higher-capacity correspondence branches to simple categories and lightweight branches to complex categories, with outputs unified through a shared pose head trained end-to-end (Section 5.3-5.4).

DecomPose achieves state-of-the-art results on REAL275 (67.9 at 5°5cm), CAMERA25 (80.8 at 5°2cm), and HouseCat6D (25.4 at 5°2cm), surpassing prior best methods CleanPose and GCE-Pose (Section 6.2, Table 1).

An ablation shows difficulty-aware grouping outperforms random category-to-branch routing by 1.9 points on REAL275 at the 5°2cm metric, and asymmetric capacity allocation outperforms uniform-capacity branch configurations (Section 6.3, Table 2-3).

EVnMERXEvC.text: BGFormer achieves O(nmd) time and O(nm) space complexity, linear in the number of cells n (m being the number of anchor tokens), compared to O(n^2 d + nd^2) for a standard Transformer and O(n^2 d + nkd^2) for scGNN (Section IV, Table III).
On the MRCA dataset (330,930 cells), BGFormer attains 89.54% clustering accuracy (ACC) and 90.24% Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) (Section VI, Table II).
On the largest benchmark, Ratmap (504,278 cells), BGFormer reaches 64.10% ACC and 52.17% ARI, and on Astrocyte (597,668 cells) it reaches 70.34% ACC and 50.41% ARI (Section VI, Table II).
Theorem V.2 states that if the anchor tokens U can linearly recover the information of all cells X, the proposed bipartite graph attention approximates full self-attention (Section V, Theorem V.2).

BGFormer's anchor-token-based bipartite graph attention (Section IV-B) is validated as effective and scalable across seven scRNA-seq datasets ranging from 12,089 (Chen) to 597,668 (Astrocyte) cells (Section VI, Table II).

pvq2AhjOy1.text: On MATH-500 at a 2% data-selection budget, SHIFT achieves 62.67 Pass@1 versus 53.73 for random selection and 47.33 for CoreSet, and at a 4% budget SHIFT reaches 64.67 versus 54.53 for random (Section 4.2, Table 1).

On MedQA at a 0.1% selection budget, SHIFT achieves 50.35 accuracy versus 45.28 for random selection, and on transfer to MedXpertQA-U, SHIFT reaches 12.22 versus 8.56 for random (Section 4.2, Table 2).

The reasoning-induced representation shift (RIRS) utility score is defined as q(x) = ||Δ(x)||₂ where Δ(x) = e(x) − s(x) is the difference between end and start hidden-state anchor representations averaged across transformer layers, with a log transform q̃(x) = log(1+q(x)) applied before selection (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

RIRS magnitude correlates strongly with downstream RLVR performance gain, with a Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.818 (p = 0.0038) across evaluated instances, while showing near-zero correlation (ρ = 0.064) with response length, indicating it is not simply a length proxy (Section 5, Table 4, Figure 2).

An ablation shows that combining RIRS-based coverage (via quality-weighted farthest-first selection, Section 3.5) with the quality-weighting term q̃(x) yields complementary gains over using either component alone (Section 4.2, Table 3).

vbKUSHz68Z.text: Ablating (disabling) the identified keystone neurons in Qwen3-8B collapses performance from 0.821 to 0 on MMLU, from 0.942 to 0 on Math500, from 0.842 to 0 on MGSM, and from 0.669 to 0 on EvalPlus, while C4 perplexity rises from 15.74 to 19.53 (Section 2, Table 1).
Similar catastrophic collapse from keystone-neuron ablation is observed across other open-weight Transformer families including Llama, Gemma, and Mixtral (Section 2, Table 1).
Keystone neurons constitute fewer than 0.2% of all neurons in a model yet show 80%-95% intersection-over-union stability across different prompt groups used to identify them (Section 3, Table 2).
Supervised fine-tuning restricted to only the keystone neuron subset achieves task performance gains comparable to or exceeding full-parameter fine-tuning (Section 4).

Base and instruction-tuned versions of the same model show high overlap in their identified keystone neuron sets, supporting the claim that keystone neurons are primarily formed during pretraining rather than constructed anew during post-training (Section 3, Table 2).

2VhdUDz6mO.text: Proposition 4.1 decomposes the Bayes-optimal prediction risk at computation budget c into an irreducible intrinsic limit term L_int plus a reducible optimization variance term V_opt(c) (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).

Proposition 5.1 establishes an asymptotic lower-bound constraint on optimization-induced uncertainty decay of the form V_opt(c) ≳ K·c^(-α), implying a fundamental, task-dependent limit on how fast uncertainty can dissipate regardless of the predictor used (Section 5, Proposition 5.1).
Theorem 6.1 derives a budget-optimal probing equilibrium with closed-form optimal stopping point c* = (αK/γλ)^(1/(α+1)) for linear probing costs (Section 6, Theorem 6.1).

The framework organizes fine-tuning tasks into three predictability regimes -- Static-Sufficient (bias-dominant, rapid uncertainty collapse), Dynamic-Critical (variance-dominant, slow information revelation), and Noise-Dominant (intrinsic-limited, irreducible ambiguity dominates) -- visualized as an empirical phase diagram of intrinsic floor versus decay exponent (Section 7, Figure 3).

Empirical validation shows power-law uncertainty decay across regimes on a log-log scale (Figure 2) and demonstrates that the marginal gain of additional probing decays monotonically at regime-dependent rates, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 8, Figure 4).

lgsMOTIAYu.text: Qkmeans (Theorem 5 / Corollary 6) achieves an O(ρ^-2 log k) approximate k-means solution in expected time O(nD) + Õ(ρ^-1 β(k log η)^(1+ϱ)), where ρ<1 is a user-controlled input parameter (Section 2, Theorem 5, Corollary 6).

Under the manifold hypothesis (Assumption 1), Theorem 4 (scaling laws) shows β_k(X) grows as k^ε and η(X) as O(1)·n^(3ε/2), where ε=2/d is the quantization exponent and d is the intrinsic manifold dimension (Section 1, Theorem 4).

Combining the scaling laws with the main rejection-sampling seeding result yields Corollary 7, giving an O(ρ^-2 log k)·opt_k(X) approximation in time O(nD) + Õ(ε^(1+ϱ) ρ^-1 (k log n)^(1+γ) D), where γ=ε+ϱ (Section 2, Corollary 7).

Empirical evaluation across 12 datasets (including MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10/100, their CLIP embeddings, Reddit, StackExchange, SUSY, and HAR) shows Qkmeans achieves 5-10x speedups over AFKMC2 and PRONECoreset and up to two orders of magnitude speedup over RejectionSampling, while maintaining comparable seeding cost (Section 3, Table 2, Figure 3).

The estimated quantization exponent ε̂ (slope of the log β vs log k fit) is empirically shown to be inversely related to the independent maximum-likelihood intrinsic dimension estimate d_MLE across datasets, validating the manifold hypothesis' predicted structural regularity (Section 3, Figure 2).

Ytwumy5fpJ.text: For Bayes-optimal estimators with block-diagonal (modular) structure, the sparse MoE risk satisfies R(β^Sparse) ≤ R(β^Dense), since the dense estimator's effective signal is scaled by mixture proportions p_i in the denominator (Theorem 4.2).
Quadratic Discriminant Analysis routing achieves near-perfect expert assignment once the number of samples n reaches Õ(poly(d, log(1/δ))) under the assumed modular data structure (Theorem 4.1).

Sparse estimators exhibit strictly faster gradient descent convergence than dense estimators, with per-iteration error reduction factors satisfying ρ_Sparse,i ≤ ρ_Dense for every expert i (Theorem 4.7).
Under high-intensity feature noise (σ=2.0), an MoE configuration reduces the accuracy drop by nearly 6 percentage points relative to a Lasso baseline on the AG News dataset (Table 1).

An MoE with 4 routed experts plus 1 shared expert (top-2 routing, ~60% active parameters) matches or exceeds the convergence speed of a dense baseline with the same total parameter count despite lower compute (Figure 2).
On synthetic data, sparse estimators achieve excess risk that decays as O(n^-2) with more favorable constants than dense estimators (Figure 4, Table 2).

Kgi3mAuXuD.text: DRIVE replaces deterministic regression-based bid prediction with a Gaussian Mixture Model head trained via log-likelihood maximization to model multimodal bidding actions (Section 4.1).

DRIVE builds a retrieval index over offline trajectory embeddings, retrieves K_pool nearest neighbors by cosine similarity, and filters them by return-to-go to obtain high-quality candidate actions (Section 4.2).

DRIVE evaluates candidate actions using an Implicit Q-Learning critic with two Q-functions and a state-value function trained via expectile regression, supporting CPA-constraint-aware reward shaping (Section 4.3).

On the AuctionNet benchmark, DRIVE achieves the best score of 399±3.74 at 100% budget and 551±4.64 at 150% budget, outperforming baselines including BCQ, CQL, IQL, TD3+BC, BEAR, Decision Transformer, CDT, GAS, GAVE, and DiffBid (Table 1).
On D4RL Gym-MuJoCo tasks, DRIVE attains an average normalized score of 79.7, including 46.7 on halfcheetah-medium and 82.0 on walker2d-medium-replay (Table 2).

An ablation progressing from Actor-Only to Retrieval+Critic to Generation+Critic to full DRIVE shows monotonic performance gains, confirming that each of the three components (distributional generation, retrieval, value-based evaluation) contributes independently (Table 3).

mMSGU8skL8.text: MiniSandbox reduces disk storage from 295 GB to 13.5 GB on SWE-smith (about 4.6% of the container baseline) and from 605 GB to 89 GB on SWE-Bench Verified (about 15% of baseline) (Section 5.2).
MiniSandbox reduces average environment preparation time from about 88.9 seconds to about 23.6 seconds compared to the container-based pipeline (Section 5.2).
MiniSandbox reduces average rollout time for a 7B model from 355.47 seconds to 252.64 seconds relative to the container baseline (Section 5.2).
A 7B model trained with MiniSandbox achieves an evaluation score improvement from 13.4 to 16.8, comparable to or exceeding the container-based pipeline's improvement from 13.4 to 16.4 (Section 5.2).
MiniSandbox maintains efficiency and stability at 256 parallel environments during multi-node training, where container-based approaches degrade (Section 6.1, Table 4).

oAagVd30Fn.text: On DAPO-Math-17K, RLER achieves 37.5 Avg@8 across six math benchmarks, exceeding the Self-Consistency baseline (33.0 Avg@8) and Frequency-Based baseline (27.1 Avg@8), for a 13.6% improvement over the best RLIR baseline (Table 1).
RLER reaches 96.0% of RLVR's performance (37.5 vs. 38.9 Avg@8), i.e., within 3.6% of the fully labeled RLVR upper bound, while relying only on intrinsic/self-generated rewards (Table 1).
On an arithmetic dataset with k=4 ensemble members, RLER attains 71.5 Avg@16 versus 57.4 Avg@16 for the Self-Consistency baseline, a 14.1-point improvement (Table 2).

The paper introduces three diagnostic metrics—ρ_noise, ρ_selfbias, and ρ_symbias—to quantify the magnitude of reward bias, the coupling between policy and reward, and the imbalance between over- and under-rewarding (Section 3).

RLER exhibits stable scaling behavior as unlabeled sample count grows from 8k to 1024k, with merged reward models achieving higher accuracy and stability than ensemble variants at deployment (Figure 12).

ebt72acjt6.text: On the KITTI dataset, EnerGS achieves 16.80 PSNR and reduces geometric leakage (Leak) to 9.2, compared to 15.01 PSNR and 12.5 Leak for vanilla 3DGS and 13.91 PSNR and 15.7 Leak for Mip-Splatting, while using only 1.20M Gaussians versus 1.51M and 1.78M respectively (Table 1).

On the Waymo Open Dataset, EnerGS attains 24.81 PSNR and 0.2 Leak versus 24.12 PSNR/0.3 Leak for 3DGS and 24.18 PSNR/0.4 Leak for Mip-Splatting, using 1.57M Gaussians compared to 2.01M and 2.46M (Table 1).

EnerGS maintains a consistently smaller train-test PSNR gap throughout training than baseline methods, indicating reduced overfitting/viewpoint memorization under sparse LiDAR supervision (Section 5.5, Figure 3).

Removing the decoupled gradient optimization in the ablation degrades PSNR by 0.56 dB on KITTI and by 3.20 dB on Waymo, confirming that gradient decoupling between photometric and geometric energy terms is necessary for stability (Table 2).
Theorem 1 establishes that degenerate floater solutions cannot exist as stable equilibria within certified free space under the probabilistic geometric energy field (Section 3.2, Theorem 1).

Proposition 3 shows that geometric energy constraints asymptotically vanish in regions unobserved by LiDAR, allowing the photometric loss to dominate optimization in those unknown regions (Section 3.2, Proposition 3).

I9pDKCWYXk.text: GradPower applies an elementwise sign-power transformation φ_p(g)=sign(g_i)|g_i|^p to gradients before the base optimizer, implementable as a single-line code change (Section 3).

On LLaMA dense models from 66M to 2B parameters trained on C4/OpenWebText, AdamPower with p=1.2 yields consistently lower terminal loss than vanilla Adam under both cosine-decay and warmup-stable-decay schedules (Table 1).

On Qwen2MoE mixture-of-experts models (0.5B-2B, 16-32 experts with 4 activated per token), GradPower achieves an absolute loss reduction of 0.028 at the 2B scale, larger than the 0.022 reduction seen for LLaMA-2B despite Qwen2MoE's lower baseline loss of 1.93 vs. 2.43 (Table 2).
The advantage of AdamPower over Adam grows throughout the learning-rate stable phase of the warmup-stable-decay schedule, and it also reduces the frequency of training loss spikes (Section 4).

Combining GradPower with the Muon optimizer (MuonPower) yields further improvements beyond Muon alone, and combining AdamPower with Blockwise LR gives a nearly additive total gain of 0.45 loss reduction from individual contributions of 0.15 and 0.30 (Section 4).
The optimal power p decreases as batch size increases: large batches (8192) favor p<1 while standard batch size (512) favors p>1, reflecting a signal-to-noise regime shift (Figure 6).

ya4nicrVDf.text: Under NTK separability with margin γ>0, gradient descent on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with polylogarithmic width m in n and T achieves a training loss rate of Õ(1/(γ²ηT)) (Theorem 4.9).

With logistic loss and polylogarithmic width, provided ηT ≳ n, the expected population risk of gradient-descent-trained KANs is bounded by Õ((log⁴(n)+log²(n/δ))/(γ⁴n)), i.e., a 1/n generalization rate (Theorem 4.12).

Under (ε,δ)-differential privacy with NTK separability, the trajectory-averaged population risk of DP-GD on KANs achieves Õ(√d/(γ⁴nε)), matching the classical lower bound for general convex Lipschitz problems (Theorem 4.16).

Polylogarithmic network width is both necessary and sufficient for DP-GD on KANs to attain this private utility bound, establishing a qualitative width gap between the private and non-private (which only requires polylog width for optimization) regimes (Theorem 4.16).

The analysis relies on a reference-point framework with a 'stay-in-a-ball' property ensuring GD iterates remain close enough to initialization to guarantee local smoothness and approximate convexity along the trajectory (Section 4).

9ZWK6gneWq.text: The paper defines Cartesian-3j and Cartesian-nj symbols, e.g. Z(ℓ1,ℓ2,ℓ3)=C^(ℓ1+ℓ2;ℓ3;1) C^T(ℓ3;ℓ3;1), as direct Cartesian-tensor analogues of Wigner-3j/nj symbols, enabling irreducible Cartesian tensor products (ICTP) within an e3nn-extended framework (Section 3).

On the 3BPA benchmark, Cartesian variants of NequIP and Allegro (e.g., a 64(64)-2-2-4 architecture) achieve energy errors nearly identical to their spherical-harmonic counterparts, around 5.0/5.6 meV train/validation (Section 5).

Edge-feature-based Allegro's Cartesian formulation produces impractical memory increases, and Cartesian-nj precomputed tensors for MACE-like models grow exponentially in memory cost once correlation order ≥3 or ℓ_max≥3 (Section 5).

The paper concludes that purely Cartesian models cannot surpass spherical models in accuracy when ℓ_max ≤ 4, and recommends using only the highest-weight ICTP/ICTC (the TACE approach) as best practice for Cartesian-based interatomic potentials (Section 6).

fKe6zvEZEE.text: On ImageNet-1k, Data Agent's PPO-based sample-selection policy reaches 76.8% accuracy using only 60% of the training data, exceeding the 76.4% full-dataset baseline while reducing training cost by nearly 40% and saving over 55 GPU hours (Section 5).
Data Agent's selection overhead is only 0.125 GPU-hours, versus more than 17.5 GPU-hours for static data-selection baselines on the same ImageNet-1k setup (Section 5).

On instruction tuning with LLaMA-7B, selecting 50% of the MMLU-relevant training data with Data Agent improves MMLU accuracy to 36.9% versus 34.9% for the full dataset, and improves AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate to 2.0 (7.7% length-controlled win rate) (Section 5).

Under 20% label noise on Tiny-ImageNet with 30% data selection, Data Agent achieves 41.9% accuracy versus 33.1% for the CLIP-Sel baseline, an over 8-point accuracy improvement demonstrating robustness to noisy labels (Section 5).

The framework generalizes across modalities and architectures without task-specific redesign, extending to object detection (YOLOv8/COCO), semantic segmentation (UperNet/ADE20k), and classification with ResNet, ViT, and Swin backbones (Section 5).

7G43VVT4SI.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that the informed asymmetric policy gradient, computed with a critic conditioned on arbitrary privileged signals rather than the full state, is unbiased and equals the standard policy gradient (Theorem 4.1).

The paper proposes a pre-training informativeness criterion based on HSCIC (Hilbert-Schmidt conditional independence criterion) that tests conditional dependence between returns and privileged information given history and action, usable before training begins (Section 5).

A post-training (ε,δ)-informativeness criterion (Definition 5.1) uses Bernstein's inequality to give a lower confidence bound on the reduction in squared prediction error from including a given privileged signal (Definition 5.1).
On synthetic POMDPs (Table 1), HSCIC values across 12 instances range from 66 to 140, with p-values increasing as the noise parameter ς increases from 0.0 to 0.9 (Table 1).

On Car-Flag and Memory-Four-Rooms (7x7 and 9x9), the informed asymmetric actor-critic outperforms symmetric A2C, asym-A2C-s (state-based critic), and asym-A2C-hs (full history-state critic) baselines, and on Heaven-Hell-3 it is competitive with the full-state asym-A2C-hs baseline while using strictly less information (Figure 1).

SSoOP9ia5t.text: GeoCoupling formulates multimodal biomolecular generation as a Temporal Optimal Transport (TOT) problem with a bi-level optimization over the coupling variable, defined via Equations 4-5 (Section 3).

On structure-based drug design with CrossDock (100K training complexes, 100 test proteins), GeoCoupling achieves a Vina Score of -7.16 versus -6.88 for the MolPilot random-coupling baseline (Table 2).
On structure-based drug design, GeoCoupling reaches 94.3% PB-Valid chemical validity and 43.1% scRMSD < 2A pose accuracy (Table 2).
On protein co-design (18,694 monomeric proteins, lengths 60-384, evaluated at 100-500 residues), GeoCoupling attains 0.79 co-designability, comparable to La-Proteina's 0.77 (Table 3).
GeoCoupling retains roughly 60% co-designability at protein length 500 while MultiFlow drops below 30%, demonstrating better out-of-distribution length generalization (Figure 3).

An ablation shows a fixed coupling schedule gives Vina Score -6.97 versus -7.12 with the full bilevel GeoCoupling optimization, and removing EMA smoothing lowers connected rate from 93.5% to 91.9% (Table 4).

oRdJzUD39a.text: The Bridge-Garden framework partitions autoregressive decoding into 'bridge' tokens requiring exact prediction and 'garden' tokens with multiple acceptable continuations, motivating hard-label versus soft-label distillation choices respectively (Section 4.1).

Theorem 4.1 derives a kappa-weighted upper bound on exposure bias using single-override policies, and Theorem 4.2 shows hard KD minimizes the Bridge-region risk term while soft KD minimizes the Garden-region term (Section 4).

On the primary suite of seven teacher-student pairs (Qwen2.5, Llama, Gemma, DeepSeek-Coder), the Risk-Guided hybrid method achieves 55.16 average score for Qwen2.5-7B to 3B distillation versus 51.87 for the pure soft-KD baseline (Table 1).

For Qwen2.5-Math distillation (7B to 1.5B teacher-student), HybKD scores 55.71 average versus 54.81 for the best alpha-beta divergence baseline, and for DeepSeek-Coder distillation HybKD scores 47.89 versus 47.29 for Skew F/RKL (Tables 3-4).
Bridge-Garden hybrid supervision yields a 1.43% average accuracy gain over on-policy knowledge distillation while reducing training cost by 9.7x (Figure 4).

An ablation sweeping the mixing weight lambda shows performance is maximized at an intermediate value strictly between pure hard-label (lambda=0) and pure soft-label (lambda=1) distillation across all tested models (Figure 5).

5ooFLqHTo4.text: Di-COT stochastically partitions each time-series instance into a variable number of overlapping sub-blocks and contrasts temporally adjacent sub-blocks as positive pairs without any data augmentation (Section 3.1).

On six large-scale datasets (PAMAP2, WISDM2, HARTH, SLEEP, ECG, SKODA) under linear evaluation, Di-COT achieves 83.07% +/- 0.69 average accuracy in 2.88 hours training time, versus 81.20% accuracy and 3.47 hours for the second-best method CaTT (Table 1).

Across the 124 UCR and 28 UEA archive datasets, Di-COT reaches 81.33% average accuracy (rank 3.73) on UCR and 71.24% average accuracy (rank 4.64) on UEA, with total training time of 0.84 hours (Table 2).

In the low-label regime (1% labeled data), Di-COT achieves 76.36% +/- 1.09 average accuracy, outperforming a fully supervised end-to-end model at 70.39% and running about 2.5x faster than the second-best method TF-C at 73.55% (Table 3).
Di-COT has time complexity O(Bk^2 d) and memory complexity O(Bk^2), independent of sequence length T, versus CaTT's O(B^2 T^2 d) complexity (Figure 6).

An ablation shows that removing the 50% sub-block overlap costs 2.23% accuracy, replacing preceding sub-block contrast with shuffled contrast costs 1.53%, and swapping the InceptionTime backbone for FCN or ResNet costs 2.58% or 3.56% respectively (Table 6).

sjK6Ii8TWs.text: DynTS finds that only about 30% of thinking tokens carry high importance scores critical to the final answer, while the remaining tokens contribute negligibly to correctness (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

DynTS uses a lightweight MLP importance predictor trained on attention-derived ground-truth importance scores (Equation 6, Section 3.1) combined with a dual-window KV cache selection strategy that always retains question tokens plus a local window and a selection window (Section 4.2).

Across six benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, GPQA-D, GK23EN, MATH500) with DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, DynTS achieves 61.9% Pass@1 on R1-Llama and 65.3% on R1-Qwen, outperforming R-KV (59.6%) and SnapKV (63.2%) (Table 1, Section 6.2).
DynTS reduces peak KV-cache memory by 3.32-5.73x and delivers 1.84-2.62x inference latency speedup while matching full-cache baseline accuracy (Section 6.2, Figure 5).

An ablation shows removing critical thinking tokens causes a 2.3% accuracy drop on R1-Llama, while removing question tokens causes a much larger 22.1% drop, validating the necessity of always retaining question tokens (Table 2).

The importance predictor achieves over 80% overlap between predicted and ground-truth critical tokens within the top-30% selection, and optimal hyperparameters are a local window of about 2,000 tokens with a selection-window retention ratio of 0.3-0.4 (Figure 6, Figure 7, Section 6.3-6.4).

oXxf72fqb6.text: RAIGen is presented as the first framework for unsupervised rare-attribute discovery in diffusion models, combining Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders with a minority score s(z) = d (dot) (1 - nu) that fuses neuron activation frequency (nu) and semantic distinctiveness (d) (Abstract, Section 3).

On WinoBias and COCO prompts, RAIGen-discovered minority attributes score 0.205 and 0.220 respectively for SD v1.4, and 0.194 and 0.199 for SDXL, versus OpenBias majority-attribute scores of 0.941 and 0.933, indicating attributes roughly 4-5x less frequent (Table 1).

A 25-participant user study on SD v1.4 image grids confirms discovered rare attributes occur infrequently, with average occurrence counts of 0.70 for CEO, 1.18 for Doctor, 1.35 for Analyst, and 2.64 for Sheriff out of 10 images (Table 2).
RAIGen-guided prompt revision reduces deviation from a uniform attribute distribution on WinoBias from 0.50 to 0.22 for SD v1.4 and from 0.49 to 0.23 for SDXL (Table 3).
An ablation on the minority score shows combining frequency and distinctiveness reduces the uninterpretable-neuron rate from 40% (frequency-only) to 10% (Section F.8).
Matryoshka SAEs prevent concept fragmentation compared to standard SAEs, which distribute a single attribute's encoding across multiple neurons (Section F.6).

0JpXqndUrA.text: On the APPS benchmark with Qwen3-4B-Instruct, AdverMCTS achieves 49.67% average Pass@1 versus 43.67% for the RethinkMCTS baseline (Table 1).
On the TACO benchmark with Qwen3-4B-Instruct, AdverMCTS achieves 38.0% average Pass@1 versus 33.67% for RethinkMCTS, with consistent gains across Easy/Medium/Hard splits (Table 1).
Removing the AT-Tree (adversarial attacker) component causes the largest performance drop in the ablation study, confirming the necessity of adversarial test-case discovery (Figure 4).
The Attacker MCTS achieves 56.7% recall and 78.95% precision at identifying silent bugs, with a 16.1% false positive rate (Figure 7).
AdverMCTS with only 16 rollouts outperforms the baseline using 32 rollouts while consuming fewer tokens, demonstrating cost-efficiency (Figure 5).

Under perfect verification (oracle test cases), Pass@1 improves from 43.44% to 55.33% on APPS and from 31.00% to 43.67% on TACO, evidencing pseudo-correctness where correct solutions exist but are missed by sparse public tests (Appendix C.1).

6YVSHa3g4b.text: On CT-RATE-Report, TIF-GRPO (4B model) achieves precision 40.93, recall 37.80, and F1 39.11, compared to SFT-only baseline precision 34.59, recall 12.85, and F1 18.73 (Table 1).
On AMOS-MM-Report, TIF-GRPO improves F1 from 17.65 (SFT baseline) to 30.47 (Table 2).
On the cross-modal MIMIC-CXR transfer setting, TIF-GRPO achieves F1 of 70.8 versus 25.3 for the baseline (Table 4).

CABS-F1 achieves a 0.90+ counterfactual ranking concordance ratio versus 0.65-0.75 for BLEU/ROUGE, demonstrating that surface-similarity metrics frequently misorder clinically critical reports (Section 4.5).

An ablation over the TIF reward's Running Cost and Control Effort terms shows Running Cost reduces false positives while Control Effort reduces false negatives, with the balanced weighting achieving the highest F1 of 39.11 (Table 5).
TIF-GRPO (F1 39.11) outperforms RLOO, ReMAX, and Reinforce++ trained with identical ROUGE/LLM-based rewards (Table 6).

5w6jwlRehY.text: Theorem 3.1 derives a closed-form expression for the minimal-norm single-layer weight perturbation ΔW*_N achieving a specified output change, using the backpropagated margin and pseudoinverse of the upstream activations (Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 4.1 establishes a margin-Lipschitz bound showing that any parameter perturbation causing a classification change must satisfy γ(x;θ) ≤ 2^((p-1)/p) L_θ ||Δθ||_p (Theorem 4.1).
On CIFAR-10 with VGG16, attack success rate rises from 10.1% at full precision to 96.2% under rank-8 low-rank compression (Table 2).
On RoBERTa fine-tuned for SQuAD, attack success rate rises from 1.0% at full precision to 99.7% under rank-500 compression (Table 2).

Pruning-threshold experiments show the margin bound is violated at 11% sparsity while the actual class flip occurs at 17% sparsity, establishing a certifiable safety margin below 11% pruning (Table 3).

On synthetic 5-layer networks, theoretical minimal Frobenius-norm perturbations range from 0.105 to 0.421 and class flips occur only once the empirical perturbation exceeds this theoretical threshold (Table 1).

1YJiPH8UFQ.text: SSI-Bench comprises 1,000 multiple-choice ranking questions (3-4 candidates each) over 1,160 unique images spanning geometric (712 questions) and topological (288 questions) 3D structure tasks (Table 3, Appendix C).

The best open-source VLM (GLM-4.6V) reaches 22.2% accuracy and the best proprietary model (Gemini-3-Flash) reaches 33.6% accuracy, versus 91.6% human accuracy and 12.85% random-baseline accuracy, an 58.0 percentage-point human-AI gap (Table 1; Table 2, Appendix B).
Enabling extended 'thinking' improves Gemini-3-Pro from 27.1% to 29.5% and Qwen3-VL-30B from 20.6% to 22.5%, showing only modest gains relative to task difficulty (Figure 4, Section 4.3).

Error analysis on Gemini-3-Pro identifies four dominant failure modes: member-extent errors, object-recognition errors, computational/comparison-logic errors, and 3D spatial-logic errors (Figure 5, Section 4.4).

The benchmark construction required over 400 hours of effort by ten researchers curating roughly 20,000 candidate structure images down to over 2,000 selected candidates (Section on construction process / Appendix C).

ImD44h0ADA.text: A classifier two-sample test distinguishing diffusion-model-generated rain fields from real radar-derived fields achieves only 57% accuracy versus 50% chance, indicating strong distributional fidelity of the diffusion prior trained on 21,196 OpenMRG radar fields (Section 3).

On the real-world OpenMRG dataset, the diffusion-based MGPS posterior sampler achieves RMSE 0.83±0.08 and PCC 0.26±0.01, outperforming meteorological baselines IDW (RMSE 0.86±0.09, PCC 0.24±0.01) and Ordinary Kriging (RMSE 0.86±0.09, PCC 0.24±0.02) (Table 3).
In the synthetic Gaussian-process experiment, the diffusion-based TDS sampler achieves the best sliced Wasserstein distance of 0.07 among training-free posterior samplers (Table 1).

An ablation on the nonlinear power-law CML observation operator shows that assuming a linear operator instead significantly degrades reconstruction, while the diffusion prior improves RMSE from about 0.96 to about 0.84 under the correct nonlinear setting (Table 5).

Under a sparser 'few-long' CML network configuration (25 links) performance degrades relative to a denser 'many-short' configuration (100 links, MGPS RMSE 0.75, PCC 0.41), showing meteorological baselines remain competitive only with linear sensing and dense spatial coverage (Table 4).

Diffusion-based posterior sampling methods take 5-7 seconds per reconstruction versus 0.01-1.01 seconds for meteorological baselines, though this remains compatible with typical 5-15 minute CML aggregation intervals (Table 2).

VmY6aQZNhW.text: QPAlign attains 0.3445 alignment accuracy on the ACM-DBLP dataset, versus 0.0441 for PARROT, 0.0018 for FGW, and 0.0746 for the best other baseline (Grampa) (Table 1).
Theorem 1 establishes the information-theoretic threshold for partial recovery of the vertex correspondence, requiring n log(1/(1-ρ²)) + 2d log(1/(1-r²)) ≥ (4+ε) log n (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 establishes the sharper threshold n log(1/(1-ρ²)) + d log(1/(1-r²)) ≥ (4+ε) log n for exact recovery of the vertex correspondence (Theorem 2).
Proposition 5 gives a convergence guarantee ‖Π^K − Π'‖_F ≤ √(n/((1-λ)(1-r)dηK)) for the gradient-descent-on-the-Birkhoff-polytope procedure when d > 32 log(n/√δ) (Proposition 5).
QPAlign runs in time O((d+T(K+n))n²), where T is the number of gradient iterations and K the number of Sinkhorn normalization iterations (Section on Implementation/Time Complexity).
On the Douban Online-Offline dataset (1,118 matched pairs), QPAlign achieves 0.8370 accuracy, close to PARROT's 0.8462 and far above FGW's 0.2773 (Table 1).

wnj21mpuHv.text: FSBA achieves iteration complexity Õ(κ³ε^{-1.5}) in first-order oracle calls to reach an (ε, O(κ^{2.5}ℓ̄^{0.5}ε^{0.5}))-second-order stationary point of the hyper-objective φ(·) (Theorem 3.0, Section 3.2).

FSBA's second-order oracle complexity is O(κ^{2.5}ℓ̄^{0.5}ε^{-1.5}), achieved via cubic-regularized Newton iterations applied to a bilevel approximation function without requiring third-order derivatives of the lower-level function g (Section 3.1, Algorithm 2).

LFSBA attains iteration complexity Õ(κ³m^{0.5}ε^{-1.5}) for an (O(ε), O(κ^{2.5}ℓ̄^{0.5}m^{0.5}ε^{0.5}))-SOSP by computing the approximate Hessian only at snapshot points and reusing it for m subsequent iterations (Theorem 4.0, Section 4.1, Algorithm 4).
LFSBA improves second-order oracle complexity over FSBA by a factor related to m^{-0.5} when m is optimally tuned, reducing computation by a d^{0.5}/κ^{0.25} factor (Section 4.1).
The methods are empirically validated on synthetic minimax problems, data hypercleaning, hyperparameter tuning, and few-shot meta-learning tasks (Sections 5.1-5.4).

lduY9csXqw.text: HALO achieves an 80.5% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 easy-task settings, a +34.1 percentage point improvement over the π₀ baseline (RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark results table).
