On RoboTwin 2.0 hard (domain-randomized) tasks, HALO reaches 26.4% average success rate, a +10.1 percentage point gain over π₀, reflecting a 62% relative improvement under aggressive environmental randomization (RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark results table).

Ablating pre-training data shows success rate dropping from 80.5%/26.4% (full setup) to 58.2%/10.5% without visual generation data, and to 32.4%/0% without any pre-training, on easy/hard tasks respectively (Table 2A).

Ablating EM-CoT components shows the full textual+visual reasoning pipeline (80.5%/26.4%) outperforms removing visual subgoals (77.8%/18.3%) or removing textual reasoning (76.1%/22.5%) on easy/hard tasks (Table 2B).

HALO uses a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with three specialized experts (multimodal understanding, visual generation, action prediction) built on a Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone, totaling approximately 4.5B parameters (Architecture section).

HALO is validated on a real-world Cobot Mobile ALOHA platform across four long-horizon tasks (tool-use sweeping, bimanual cup nesting, inter-arm screwdriver handover, drawer placement), consistently surpassing π₀ and π₀.₅ baselines under visual distraction and lighting variation (Real-World Performance section).

zSrvkj0ers.text: On LoCoMo, Memora with a Policy Retriever attains an LLM-as-a-Judge score of 0.863, exceeding the full-context baseline (0.825), Nemori (0.794), Mem0 (0.653), and RAG (0.633) (LoCoMo benchmark results).
Memora's Semantic Retriever variant scores 0.849 on LoCoMo, still exceeding the full-context baseline of 0.825 (LoCoMo benchmark results).

On LongMemEval, Memora achieves 87.4% average accuracy while operating on a compressed context of 2.1-2.9k tokens versus 115k tokens for the full-context baseline, a token reduction of up to 98% (LongMemEval benchmark results).

Memora's architecture is built from three components: a primary abstraction providing canonical identity for memory entries, a memory value storing concrete details, and cue anchors serving as lightweight semantic retrieval hooks (Core Components section).

Memora is framed as generalizing standard RAG's flat similarity matching and Knowledge Graph's rigid schema-based retrieval, positioning both as special cases of its dual-layer abstraction/specificity design (Key Advantages Over Alternatives section).

5dabjiOBpS.text: T3-Video achieves a 21.4× actual inference speedup at native 4K resolution with 81 frames, against a theoretical MACs reduction of 43.0× (Experiments, Section 4).
T3-Video-T2V-1.3B scores 71.72 VQA and 0.83 VTC on 4K-VBench, versus 67.43 VQA and 0.75 VTC for UltraGen, an improvement of +4.29 VQA and +0.08 VTC (4K-VBench results table, Section 4).

T3-Video also yields speedups of 2.6×, 4.7×, and 8.6× at 480P, 720P, and 1080P respectively, showing the multi-scale weight-sharing window attention mechanism scales benefits with resolution (Efficiency Gains, Section 4).
T3-Video requires under 60GB of memory for 4K inference at 81 frames, and is the first method demonstrated to enable native 81-frame 4K video generation (Efficiency Gains, Section 4).
A human preference study reports 71.25% preference for T3-Video over UltraGen on video quality (Experiments, Section 4).

T3-Video's method section (3.1-3.6) details a hierarchical blocking strategy and an axis-preserving full-attention approach that transforms pretrained full-attention transformers without altering their architecture (Section 3, T3-Video Method).

ANVPCRmZQQ.text: Theorem 4.2 proves that distribution matching in a latent product space yields a strictly tighter generalization error bound than distribution matching in a single Euclidean latent space (Theorem 4.2).
GeoDM reaches 74.4% ± 0.3 test accuracy on CIFAR-10 at IPC=10, versus 71.8% ± 0.5 for the prior state-of-the-art NCFM baseline (Table 1).
GeoDM reaches 38.0% ± 0.4 test accuracy on CIFAR-100 at IPC=1, versus 26.2% ± 0.3 for the M3D baseline, an 11.8 percentage-point gain (Table 1).

An ablation on CIFAR-10 at IPC=10 shows the product-space representation alone raises accuracy from the 71.8% NCFM baseline to 73.5%, with learnable curvature/weights and the optimal-transport loss each contributing further incremental gains up to the full 74.4% (Table 3).

GeoDM improves accuracy consistently when substituted into multiple distribution-matching variants (plain DM, DSDM, and NCFM), showing the geometry-aware approach is robust across different underlying DM strategies (Figure 3).

mD8DMkl7Tu.text: On the A2RBench human-comparison subset, the best-performing LLM (Gemini3-Pro) reaches only about 40% overall accuracy versus 68.5% for humans, a roughly 28 percentage-point gap (Table 11).

Models perform worse on 2D abstract-reasoning tasks than on 1D or 3D tasks, with 2D tasks containing deeper nested conditional logic (average nesting depth 2.33) than 3D tasks (1.40), indicating a non-monotonic relationship between spatial dimensionality and difficulty (Section 5, Figure 3, Table 9).

GPT-5's accuracy drops by 17.7 percentage points when task symbols are remapped to unfamiliar tokens, indicating substantial reliance on symbol familiarity rather than abstract structural reasoning (Table 10).

The benchmark generation pipeline verifies task correctness via cycle consistency, requiring that an automatically generated inverse operation g satisfy g(f(x))=x for every input x, which guarantees each generated task has a unique, verifiable solution without human annotation (Section 3).

12CrabKNu6.text: On KARR-Bench text-to-image retrieval, SLQ-8B achieves 58.7% Recall@5, outperforming the LoRA fine-tuning baseline by 9.8 percentage points while keeping the MLLM backbone entirely frozen (Figure 4).
On COCO text-to-image Recall@5, SLQ-8B reaches 79.7%, approaching (though not matching) full fine-tuning's 87.4% and LoRA's 88.3%, despite training far fewer parameters (Table 1).
SLQ trains substantially faster than LoRA: for InternVL3-8B over 5 epochs, SLQ requires 38.9 GPU-hours versus 130.1 for LoRA, a roughly 70% reduction in training cost (Table 3).
An ablation over SLQ's design choices (shared latent query formulation, tuning strategy) quantifies each component's contribution to retrieval performance (Table 5).

PCA visualization of the embedding space shows SLQ preserves the frozen backbone's semantic manifold structure more faithfully than full fine-tuning or LoRA, supporting the claim that preserving this manifold benefits MLLM-based retrieval (Figure 5).

hE0n8gS7Ru.text: Theorem 1.1 gives a polynomial-time algorithm for the budgeted graph label selection problem that returns a labeled set L' with |L'| ≤ k satisfying β·Ψ(L') ≥ OPT_k for β ∈ O~(log^1.5 n), the first approximation guarantee that does not rely on resource augmentation (Theorem 1.1).

The objective Ψ(L) is defined as the minimum over all cuts C of the unlabeled vertices of w(C, V\C)/|C|, i.e., the algorithm seeks a labeled set of size at most k maximizing the worst-case normalized cut weight among the remaining vertices (Section 1).

The algorithm proceeds in three stages: reducing the input graph to a binary tree via a tree cut sparsifier achieving O~(log^1.5 n) distortion, reformulating label selection as a sink-selection flow problem on that tree, and solving the resulting problem exactly via an O(n·k^2) dynamic program with binary search over a threshold τ (Sections 3-5).

Prior algorithms for this problem (e.g., Guillory & Bilmes 2009; Cohen-Addad et al. 2025) either use greedy heuristics without provable guarantees or require resource augmentation (allocating α·k labeled vertices to achieve an O(log n) factor), whereas this work achieves a guarantee on the exact budget k (Section 1).

YC1Otscjbs.text: Across 60 text-based LLM benchmarks analyzed, 29 exhibit high or very high saturation (saturation index ≥ 0.7), with 14 reaching very high saturation (index ≥ 0.9) (Table 2).

Saturation rates increase with benchmark age: benchmarks under 24 months old show 42.9% saturation (mean saturation index 0.51), versus 54.5% saturation (mean index 0.60) for benchmarks over 60 months old (Figure 2).
Expert-curated benchmarks show lower saturation than crowdsourced benchmarks at comparable ages (Section 5).

Comparing benchmarks with public test data (N=52) versus private/hidden test data (N=8) shows no statistically meaningful difference in saturation distributions, indicating that hiding test data does not protect against saturation (Section 4).

re0ivnywr4.text: EPS3D achieves 0.6323 mIoU for semantic segmentation in the 2-view ScanNet context setting, outperforming Uni3R (0.5233 mIoU) and LSM (0.5034 mIoU) (Table 1).
On the Replica novel-view semantic segmentation task in the 8-view multi-view setting, EPS3D attains 0.4833 mIoU, roughly a 13% improvement over baselines (Table 2).
EPS3D runs inference at about 0.73-1 second per scene in the 2-view ScanNet setting, versus roughly 5 minutes for per-scene optimization methods like Unified-Lift (Section 4).
Ablations show removing feature splatting drops Replica novel-view instance mIoU from 0.3468 to 0.2519, and removing the Ins2Sem component drops semantic mIoU from 0.4833 to 0.4531 (Table 4).
On the ScanNet novel-view setting, EPS3D achieves panoptic quality PQ 0.5304, SQ 0.6643, and RQ 0.6759 (Table 3).

EPS3D's end-to-end feed-forward architecture is demonstrated on downstream applications including robotic grasp pose estimation and 3D scene editing such as recoloring and object insertion (Section 4).

0tdnyH7uXp.text: Language Bias Regularization (LBR) applies an L1 penalty with hyperparameter α=1×10⁻⁵ during visual instruction tuning to suppress the language bias term (Section 4).
LBR improves MME from 1490 to 1525 and MMMU accuracy from 35.7% to 37.2% on the 7B model relative to the baseline (Table 1).

Language Bias Penalty (LBP), applied during Direct Preference Optimization with hyperparameter γ=1, raises the MMHalBench score from 2.42 to 2.91 and lowers Object HalBench CHAIRs from 15.8 to 12.3 for the 7B model (Table 3).
Human evaluation across six hallucination categories (existence, attribute, state, number, action, relation) confirms both LBR and LBP reduce hallucination rates compared to the baseline (Figure 6).
Ablations compare LBR against alternative regularizers (KL divergence, contrastive loss, L1-Mean) and a cosine-annealing dynamic scheduling variant for the regularization strength (Figures 4 and 7).

DWaToCuNwa.text: The paper unifies hierarchical variational inference, maximum-entropy RL, and sequential Monte Carlo/annealed importance sampling in a single framework, connecting trajectory balance (TB, Eq. 8) and subtrajectory balance (SubTB, Eq. 7) losses to SMC importance weights (Eq. 9-10) (Section 2).

Using SMC as a behaviour policy for off-policy training (TB/SubTB + SMC) substantially improves EUBO and Sinkhorn distance over on-policy TB and LV baselines, which suffer severe mode collapse, on gradient-free targets including GMM40 and ManyWell (Table 1).

In the gradient-based setting, combining SMC with importance-weighted experience replay (IW-Buf) improves MMD and Sinkhorn distance over baselines including SMC-HMC, PIS, DDS, and SCLD across Funnel (d=10), Robot4 (d=10), GMM40 (d=50), MoS (d=50), and ManyWell (d=64) targets (Table 2).

An adaptive importance-weight tempering scheme (Eq. 15) selects the largest inverse-temperature λ that keeps effective sample size above a user-defined threshold, reducing training gradient variance (Section 3.4).

Ablating the buffer prioritisation scheme shows the importance-weighted buffer (IW-Buf) outperforms uniform, reward-prioritised, and loss-prioritised buffers on ELBO/EUBO for GMM40 and ManyWell (Table 4).

The method is additionally validated on the Boltzmann distribution of alanine dipeptide conformations and on discrete sampling spaces, with full results reported in Appendices H and I (Section 4, Appendix H).

XLc102wbnT.text: AdaMeZO is a zeroth-order optimizer for LLM fine-tuning that leverages Adam-style first- and second-moment estimates without storing those moments in memory (abstract only).
Applying standard Adam-style moment tracking directly to MeZO would triple its memory requirement, a cost AdaMeZO is designed to avoid (abstract only).
AdaMeZO can outperform MeZO while requiring up to 70% fewer forward passes during LLM fine-tuning (abstract only).
The authors support AdaMeZO's advantages with extensive experiments and trajectory visualizations intended to show better adaptation to diverse loss landscapes than standard MeZO (abstract only).

nZ5kjt0Qla.text: On DISBench, Claude-Opus-4.5 is the best-performing model overall with F1 55.0 and exact match 28.7, while GPT-4o scores only F1 22.2 and EM 7.4 (Table 1).

Claude-Opus-4.5 achieves F1 57.9 / EM 35.1 on Intra-Event queries versus F1 53.4 / EM 29.2 on Inter-Event queries, and the low exact-match scores indicate models struggle to recover complete target image sets (Table 1).
The human-model collaborative annotation pipeline filtered 2,000 candidate queries down to 122 high-quality queries, a 6.1% retention rate (Dataset/DISBench section).

The ImageSeeker baseline agent combines five tools (TgImageSearch, TgGetMetadata, TgFilterMetadata, TgViewPhotos, TgWebSearch) with a dual-memory system comprising explicit state memory and compressed context memory (Agent Framework/ImageSeeker section).
Ablation studies show metadata-handling tools (TgGetMetadata/TgFilterMetadata) contribute the most to ImageSeeker's retrieval performance on DISBench (Experiments section, ablation study).

EvmCeoiKYI.text: ZeroBench consists of 100 main questions with 334 human-verified subquestions (average 3.3 subquestions per main question), spanning 93 single-image and 7 multi-image tasks (Table 1, Section 3.2).
All 20 evaluated frontier LMMs score exactly 0.0% pass@1 on the main ZeroBench questions under greedy decoding (Table 2, Section 5.1).
Under pass@5 stochastic sampling, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking attains the highest score of 7%, with QVQ, Gemini 2 Flash, and Pixtral-Large each scoring 3% (Table 2, Section 5.1).
On the 5/5 reliability metric (correct on all five samples), every evaluated model scores 0%, indicating no model produces consistently correct answers (Section 5.1).
On the easier subquestions (pass@1), Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 leads at 24.30%, followed closely by Gemini 2 Flash at 22.47% and o1 pro at 22.40%, while Reka Edge scores only 3.38% (Section 5.1).
Reasoning models incur substantially higher inference cost per question, e.g., o1 uses about 7,345 tokens (~$0.46) per question versus QVQ's 2,794 tokens (~$0.003) (Table 3, Section 5.2).

3D0x8oxOYH.text: The ranking-test detection procedure provides a provable false-positive-rate bound of FPR ≤ k/K, where k is the acceptance threshold and K is the candidate watermark set size (typically K=100) (Section III-E).

Across more than 18,810 document-level challenges using counterfactual (left-out) watermarks, the method achieves 100% TPR at 0% FPR, with no spurious detections from watermarks not actually used in fine-tuning (Section IV-E, Table III).

On the Blog1k dataset, first successful detection occurs with as few as 20 watermarked documents (2% of the fine-tuning corpus), while the Poems dataset requires 30-40 marked documents before initial detection (Section IV-B, Figure 2).

Per-document hit probability differs sharply by fine-tuned model on Blog1k with 50 marked documents: Mistral achieves p≈0.588 versus LLaMA's p≈0.940, yielding false-negative rates of roughly 10^-20 and 10^-42 respectively (Section IV-B, Table II).

The method remains detectable even when watermarked documents comprise less than 0.33% of a 15k-document fine-tuning corpus, maintaining an average per-document detection rate above 45% (Section IV-C, Figure 3).

The watermarking scheme uses an alphabet of 4 invisible Unicode characters (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060) with watermarks of n=8 syllables (m=4 characters each, split into a 5-syllable cue and 3-syllable reply) (Section III-F).

n4SsjVKXWQ.text: The paper (MetaSTAR) proves Theorem 3.1 that its world-model dynamics maximize a 'primary causality' objective, and Theorem 3.3 establishes a dynamics-induced behavior-invariance bound for task representations (Section 3.3).
Evaluation spans dense-reward MuJoCo tasks (Ant-Dir, Cheetah-Vel, Hopper-Param, Walker-Param) and their sparse-reward variants, using 40 total tasks split 30 training / 10 testing (Section 4.1).
On Ant-Dir, MetaSTAR achieves an online testing return of 230±42 versus CORRO's 149±39, and on Point-Robot-Sparse it reaches 21±8 versus CORRO's 10±6 (Table 1, Section 4.2).
Under out-of-distribution evaluation on Ant-Dir, MetaSTAR attains 59±19 return versus a baseline's 1±10, demonstrating substantially better OOD adaptation (Table 2, Section 4.3).

Ablations removing the world-model loss or the conservative optimization term each degrade performance, with the conservative-optimization removal hurting most in sparse-reward settings (Section 4.6, Figures 13-14).

xg5k9pCYR7.text: DyGRO-VLA achieves 97.1% average success across the four LIBERO suites, a +4.4 point improvement over its offline base model's 92.7%, with the largest gain on LIBERO-Long rising from 85.2% to 95.0% (+9.8 points) (Table 1, Section 5.2).

On the RoboTwin2 benchmark, DyGRO-VLA attains 79.2% simulation success and demonstrates competitive Sim2Real transfer across four real-world manipulation tasks including tool-use and multi-object grasping (Table 3, Section 5.4).
DyGRO-VLA outperforms multi-task VLA baselines Octo (74.9%), OpenVLA (74.7%), SpatialVLA (78.1%), π0-FAST* (85.5%), and π0 (94.4%) on average LIBERO success rate (Table 1, Section 5.2).
Against RFT-style baselines on LIBERO-Long, DyGRO-VLA reaches 95.2% success, surpassing SimpleVLA-RL (91.7%), RLinf (94.0%), and RIPT-VLA (93.8%) (Table 2, Section 5.3).
An expert-scaling ablation shows success improving from 93.4% with 1 expert to 97.0% with 4 experts and 97.1% with 8 experts (Table 4, Section 5.5).
Removing the contrastive learning objective causes a substantial performance drop on LIBERO-Long from 95.0% to 90.4% (Table 5, Section 5.5).

4AUtM4wsfE.text: On the bi-objective Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (Bi-FJSP), E2OC achieves a hypervolume (HV) of 0.2435 versus MCTS-AHD's 0.2269 across all tested instances (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Relative to NSGA-II baselines, E2OC improves hypervolume by +22.00% on Bi-FJSP (0.1996 to 0.2435), +17.36% on Tri-FJSP (0.1266 to 0.1485), and +14.00% on Bi-TSP (0.3881 to 0.4424) (Table 1, Section 4.2).

E2OC is evaluated against single-heuristic AHD baselines (Random, FunSearch, EoH, ReEvo, MCTS-AHD) and multi-heuristic baselines (Coordinate-Descent, UCB, Win-UCB variants) on FJSP (Brandimarte, 15 instances) and TSP at scales k∈{20,50,100} (Section 4.1, Appendices F-G).

Ablations show fixed-strategy search (MCTS_OC, HV 0.2085) and sequential design without operator rotation (E2OC-SD, HV 0.2187) both underperform the full E2OC framework's HV of 0.2435 (Table 3, Section 4.3).

Repeated sequential runs of E2OC show continued gains, with a later run (E2OC'') reaching HV 0.2475 versus the baseline E2OC's 0.2435, indicating sustained co-evolutionary optimization capability (Table 5, Section 4.3).

RL565ePGHR.text: AdLift is presented as the first active protection framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting assets against instruction-driven editing, using lifted adversarial perturbations rather than passive watermarking (Section 1).

The Lifted Projected Gradient Descent (L-PGD) algorithm alternates gradient truncation for strict image-space invisibility with image-to-Gaussian fitting to produce view-consistent 3D perturbations (Section 4.4, Algorithm 1).

Rendering-space constraints enforce a hard L-infinity norm bound on rendered perturbations via Equation 4, addressing the multi-view inconsistency of naive 2D-to-3D perturbation lifting shown in Figure 2 (Section 4.3).
Three adversarial objectives are proposed: an untargeted VAE attack, a targeted VAE attack, and a Segment-Anything attack (Equations 8-10, Section 4.5).

On instruction-based image editing with InstructPix2Pix, AdLift variants reduce CLIP directional/image similarity scores to roughly 0.17-0.18 while maintaining competitive SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS invisibility on training and novel views (Table 1).

On 3DGS editing with Instruct-GS2GS and DGE (global and local), AdLift improves protection (CLIPd) by roughly 0.01-0.14 points over baselines, evaluated across four scenes (two forward-facing, two 360-degree) (Table 2).

XNU0huW1vU.text: Trifuse is a training-free, attention-based GUI grounding framework that fuses attention heatmaps, OCR-derived textual cues, and icon-level caption semantics without task-specific fine-tuning (Section 3.1).
The Consensus-SinglePeak (CS) fusion strategy combines a multiplicative cross-modal consensus term with a confidence-weighted single-peak selection mechanism (Equations 9-13, Section 3.2).

On ScreenSpot, ScreenSpot-v2, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G, Trifuse with Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B backbones achieves average accuracies of 81.1/86.2, 82.6/86.9, 18.9/29.7, and 38.7/43.6 respectively, improving over the TAG baseline by roughly 13-36 points depending on benchmark and backbone (Table 1).
Ablation shows CS fusion (81.1%/82.6% on ScreenSpot/ScreenSpot-v2) outperforms simple averaging (63.3%/65.8%) and single-modality attention (58.5%/54.7%) (Table 7, Section 4.2).
A two-stage hierarchical zoom-in localization procedure improves ScreenSpot accuracy from 72.7% to 81.1% (+7.4 points) over single-stage localization (Table 8, Section 3.3).
Top-k attention-head selection via spatial entropy filtering improves grounding accuracy by about 48 points on ScreenSpot compared to alternative head-selection strategies (Table 6, Section 4.2).

SKXkGLbXdB.text: IndexMem combines a learnable MQA-style indexer that predicts KV-cache token importance via gated similarity scoring with a latent memory module that compresses evicted tokens using slow/fast residual weights (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).
On the RULER benchmark at 4K context with 50% KV-cache compression, IndexMem achieves 78.9-82.8 across Qwen3-8B, Mistral-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, versus 55.7-75.5 for SnapKV (Table 1).
At 75% compression on RULER, IndexMem scores 72.9-78.3 versus 33.1-68.8 for the strongest baseline methods (SnapKV, PyramidKV, TOVA, KeyDiff, ExpectedAttention, xKV, Locret) (Table 1).
IndexMem shows more stable Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval across context lengths from 1K to 12.5K tokens and needle depths compared to baseline eviction methods (Figure 3).
An ablation shows the latent memory module provides consistent accuracy gains that grow under aggressive compression ratios (r >= 0.5) (Figure 5).
The learnable indexer adds only 19.92M parameters and the memory module 0.52M parameters for Llama-3.1-8B, reducing cache memory from 7.68GB (r=0) to 4.08GB (r=0.9) (Figure 7).

gHA60hnmOK.text: OFA-TAD is trained once on 7 source tabular datasets and evaluated on 34 target datasets spanning 14 domains without per-dataset retraining (Section 3, dataset description).

Multi-view neighbor-distance encoding applies M transformations (raw, standardized, quantile-based) to top-K nearest-neighbor distances, combined with quantile normalization to create domain-agnostic representations (Section 3.1).
A Mixture-of-Experts scoring network with attention pooling over neighbor ranks and a gating module fuses view-specific anomaly scores (Section 3.2).
OFA-TAD achieves 0.8345 average AUROC across the 34 target datasets, outperforming 9 baselines including LOF, KNN, iForest, DeepSVDD, AutoEncoder, MCM, LUNAR, DRL, and DisentAD (Table 1).
OFA-TAD attains 0.6629 average AUPRC, exceeding MCM by 3.70 points (Table 5), and 0.6352 average F1, exceeding LUNAR by 2.31 points (Table 6).
Ablation removing attention pooling causes the largest AUROC drop (0.8187 vs. 0.8345 full model), while removing gating (0.8218) and removing MoE (0.8204) cause smaller degradations (Table 2).

hS6iw4PM8K.text: LVCG models multi-lead ECG as a linear projection E(t) = Av(t) of a latent 3D vectorcardiogram trajectory v(t), recovering beat-level VCG via Tikhonov-regularized least-squares with SVD-based inversion (Section 3, Algorithm 1, Appendix A.2).
The training objective combines ECG reconstruction on masked leads, VCG patch reconstruction, and temporal token difference consistency losses (Equation 7, Section 3).

Pre-trained on MIMIC-IV-ECG (800,035 records), LVCG achieves 71.09 AUC on CPSC2018 and 62.47 AUC on CSN under 1% linear-probe label regimes, versus 60.44 and 57.94 for HeartLang, with an average of 67.30 vs. 63.80 across six datasets (Table 1).
On multi-lead reconstruction with the (3,12)-lead setting, LVCG attains MSE/MAE of 0.49/0.37 on CPSC2018 and 0.47/0.36 on PTB, compared to 0.68/0.40 and 1.56/0.52 for Nef-Net (Table 2).
Ablating the VCG-space geometry shows AUC rising from 51.26 (ECG-space baseline) to 65.02 (learnable transformation) to 75.33 (full LVCG) at the 1% label regime for the superclass task (Table 4).

On the non-cardiac Chronic Kidney Disease detection task with 1% labels, LVCG reaches 69.04 AUC versus 58.92 for HeartLang, and removing the temporal module drops superclass AUC from 75.33 to 71.69 (Table 3, Table 5).

CwjK5eUzcI.text: On class unlearning, Representation Unlearning achieves 93.5% retain accuracy with only 1.9% forget accuracy on CIFAR-10, 73.4%/0.2% on CIFAR-100, and 58.7%/0.6% on Tiny ImageNet (Table 1).

The zero-shot regime, which uses only forget data and derives retain-loss targets from Neural Collapse class prototypes, achieves comparable unlearning quality to the standard regime that has access to both retain and forget data (Section 3, zero-shot setting).

Standard Representation Unlearning gives a 235x speedup over full retraining on Tiny ImageNet, while the zero-shot variant gives a 754x speedup, with GPU memory use of 1,971 MB versus 8,318 MB for retraining (Figure 4).

On random unlearning, the method attains near-perfect retain training accuracy (99.2%-100%) and membership-inference-attack (MIA) scores close to the from-scratch Retraining baseline (~55% on CIFAR-10), while achieving the lowest test cross-entropy among compared methods (Table 2).

An ablation over the regularization strength beta shows optimal performance at beta=10^-3, with the standard setting more sensitive to deviations from this value than the zero-shot setting (Section 4.5).
A sensitivity study over transformation depth shows the standard setting is stable across 0-2 hidden layers while the zero-shot setting performs best with exactly 1 hidden layer (Appendix F).

OWz1n5HgcC.text: On the Lorenz '63 system, tuned DAISI attains RMSE 2.03±1.01 and CRPS 2.61±1.38 versus the asymptotically-exact Bootstrap Particle Filter baseline's RMSE 1.18±0.50 and CRPS 1.46±0.49, but a better spread-skill ratio (SSR) of 1.08±0.41 versus BPF's 2.57±0.56 (Section 4.1, Table 1).

Removing the inverse-sampling step ('DAISI no inversion') degrades Lorenz '63 RMSE to 5.90±1.09, and using untuned defaults (t_min approx 0, epsilon=0) degrades RMSE to 7.04±0.90, showing both components are necessary (Table 1).

On 64x64 Surface Quasi-Geostrophic data, DAISI achieves the best RMSE among compared methods (LETKF, FlowDAS, EnSF) in noisy (1.32), sparse (1.73), and multimodal (1.81) observation regimes, while LETKF wins the saturating-observation regime and EnSF wins on that regime too (1.33) (Section 4.2, Table 3).
DAISI maintains stable assimilation at 12-hour intervals on the SQG task where LETKF's performance degrades (Figure 12).
On real-world SEVIR radar precipitation nowcasting with 10% sparse observations, DAISI achieves CRPS 0.016±0.01 versus FlowDAS's 0.045±0.01, roughly a 2.8x improvement (Section 4.3).

Proposition 3.1 proves that the KL divergence between the DAISI output distribution and a guided reference distribution decays exponentially in the noise parameter epsilon, with equality holding at epsilon=0 (Section 3.1, Proposition 3.1).

nvvpssbgjH.text: Using only 10% of attention heads and 10% of training data, P2D achieves an 8.3 percentage-point average performance gain over strong data-selection and parameter-efficient baselines across GSM8K, DialogSum, and BioInstruct with Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-3-8B, and Llama-3-8B (Table 1).

P2D delivers a 7.0x end-to-end time speedup over the strongest baseline (Nuggets with full parameter fine-tuning), with an Alignment Efficiency Ratio (AER) of 0.32 on GSM8K versus 1.0 for full fine-tuning, and per-task speedups of 5.97x (GSM8K), 8.63x (DialogSum), and 6.48x (BioInstruct) (Table 2).
P2D mitigates catastrophic forgetting: after fine-tuning on 10% of data, full SFT drops MMLU accuracy from 74.23 to 56.34, whereas P2D preserves 67.45 MMLU, outperforming LoRA's 63.12 (Table 9).
Across model scales from 1.5B to 32B parameters, P2D's sparse head adaptation (P2D‡) consistently outperforms full SFT and LoRA, with the performance gap widening at larger scales (Table 5).

Across random seeds, P2D shows approximately 91% pairwise overlap in identified task-sensitive attention heads and approximately 93% Jaccard similarity in selected training data, indicating the head identification is a stable structural signal rather than noise (Table 8).

ZlnD9QlfZh.text: Training Qwen2.5-7B with GRPO on OpenR1-Math-220k using an experience replay buffer of size N=848 with (inference workers, trainers)=(5,3) achieves 40% inference compute savings while matching baseline accuracy on MATH (Section 5, Figure 1).

Theorem 4.5 derives an optimal buffer/replay design: the optimal staleness horizon N/R and replay ratio B/R shift toward greater reliance on replay as the inference-to-training cost ratio mu increases or as off-policy penalty terms (rho, sigma-bar) shrink (Section 4, Theorem 4.5).

The compute ratio gamma = (1+W/T)/(1+mu) varies from 0.18 (W,T=1,7) to 1.29 (W,T=7,1) across different inference-worker/trainer configurations, showing replay-friendly configurations can cut compute cost by over 5x relative to the least efficient setting (Table 1).
Theorem 4.4 establishes a convergence bound for training with stale, replayed rollouts under L-smoothness and staleness-bounded bias/variance assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).

Increasing the replay buffer size (N from 64 to 20,736) slows convergence but stabilizes training and improves pass@k diversity, with all configurations eventually reaching peak accuracy followed by decline (Figure 3).

On a Pareto frontier of compute cost versus accuracy, the best buffer-based configuration achieves a compute cost of 0.51 relative to the on-policy baseline's 1.0, and wall-clock experiments confirm the gains are not artifacts of hyperparameter tuning (Figure 4, Appendix 11).

1Facirbj0t.text: Corollary 3.6 proves that a single directional stitcher cannot establish true functional equivalence between two representations, formally grounding stitching asymmetry in a Markov blanket argument (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.6).
Empirically, the distribution of accuracy differences between forward and reverse stitchers is heavy-tailed with significant variance, confirming the predicted asymmetry (Figure 2(a)).

Representational similarity follows a strict hierarchy across nested stitcher families -- Affine > Orthogonal+Scaling > Orthogonal -- validating the monotonicity result of Proposition 4.5 (Figure 2(b)).

Standard similarity metrics (CKA, RSA) are shown to function as estimators of usable information under restricted predictive families, with measured correlations of R^2=0.937 for CKA and R^2=0.912 for RSA against the usable-information score, versus only R^2=0.650 for SVCCA (Figure 3).

High representational similarity implies functional similarity with probability approaching 1.0 across all tested transformation families (sufficiency), while high functional similarity is frequently observed despite low representational similarity (non-necessity), confirming Corollary 4.8 (Figure 4).

Experiments span five datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, Tiny-ImageNet) and five architectures (ResNet20, DenseNet40, ShuffleNetV2, MobileNetV3, and linear models) with three nested stitcher families (Section 5).

QXgHl2nTEX.text: On Stable Diffusion 3.5 and FLUX.1 with N=500 paired samples, the correlation between Local Complexity (LC) and Projected High-Frequency Energy (PHFE) drops from about 0.413 in-distribution to about 0.083 under out-of-distribution stress, an approximately 80% collapse termed Geometric Decoupling (Section 4, Table 1)

Latent energy surges by 59.5% under OOD conditions while the corresponding image-space high-frequency detail remains essentially flat, showing curvature increases without a matching gain in perceptual detail (Section 4, Table 2)

The Spectral Isolation Score (SIS), which detects 'tunnel vision' geometry, rises from about 4.4 to 6.5 (an increase of about 31%) under OOD generation, indicating increased manifold rigidity (Section 4, Table 3)

Comparing SD3.5-Base against SD3.5-Turbo via training interventions shows Geometric Decoupling is a structural property tied to the training/distillation regime rather than a merely correlational artifact (Section 5)
An annotation-free out-of-distribution detector built from the ratio of Local Complexity to Projected High-Frequency Energy achieves 0.816 AUROC without using any labeled OOD examples (Section 6)

Regions of extreme manifold curvature ('Geometric Hotspots') concentrate precisely at semantic contradictions in generated images (e.g., teeth appearing on a chicken's beak), visualized via LC heat maps (Figure 1)

IBGRi5HkB4.text: Active Attacks improves the cross-attack success rate against a GFlowNet-based red-teaming baseline from 0.07% to 31.28%, a relative gain of more than 400x, while adding only about 5.76% additional training-time computation (Section 4, Table 2)

Combining Active Attacks with GFlowNet raises the average defense rate across victim models to 99.71%, compared to 91.00% for GFlowNet alone, 82.86% for PPO+Novelty, 81.48% for REINFORCE, 55.78% for supervised fine-tuning, and 52.32% for in-context learning (Section 4, Table 2)

Active Attacks periodically safety-fine-tunes the victim LLM on collected attack prompts and reinitializes the attacker, reshaping the reward landscape to create an easy-to-hard curriculum that mitigates attacker mode collapse (Section 3)
Table 3 reports transferability results showing attack prompts generated with Active Attacks remain effective across different victim LLMs beyond the one used during training (Section 4.3, Table 3)
Figure 2 shows Active Attacks shifts the toxicity-diversity tradeoff curve favorably relative to baseline RL red-teaming methods (Figure 2)

5Q4ts0pr9T.text: GEMQ formulates expert-level bit-width allocation as a binary linear program that minimizes the estimated increase in task cross-entropy loss (using a diagonal Fisher Information Matrix approximation of the MoE block output Hessian) subject to a global bit budget, solvable within seconds (Section 4.1, Equation 7)

On Mixtral-8x7B at an average of 2.5 bits per expert, GEMQ achieves WikiText2 perplexity 6.65 and C4 perplexity 10.51 versus 6.95/10.74 for the layer-wise PMQ baseline and 8.14/13.59 for uniform quantization, while retaining 65.13% average 0-shot accuracy across seven tasks (Table 1)

At 1.5 bits per expert on Mixtral-8x7B, GEMQ attains 9.15 WikiText2 / 16.64 C4 perplexity and 47.27% 0-shot accuracy, compared to SpQR which collapses to 31.87% 0-shot accuracy at a comparable 1.5-16 W-A setting (Table 2)

GEMQ's global router fine-tuning step updates only router parameters (under 0.04% of total model parameters), and fine-tuning Mixtral-8x7B on 128 calibration sequences of 2048 tokens takes under one minute on three NVIDIA H100 GPUs, about 3.5% of GPTQ's quantization time (Section 4.2, Table 8)

Progressive quantization across bit budgets 2.5 to 2.0 to 1.5 bits/expert requires roughly two hours total runtime, and single-stage 2-bit quantization of Mixtral-8x7B with GEMQ takes 2310.0 seconds total versus 2162.0 seconds for PMQ (Table 4)

Adding 128 MATH-dataset sequences to the C4 calibration set improves GEMQ's GSM8K accuracy on 2-bit-quantized Mixtral-8x7B from 21.83% to 42.30%, substantially outperforming PMQ's corresponding improvement from 19.48% to 23.84% (Table 3)

ABrWtqsJYp.text: RDT2 is trained on over 10,000 hours of embodiment-agnostic human demonstrations collected via enhanced UMI hardware across 100+ households and roughly 1,000 unique objects (Section 4)

RDT2 uses a 7B-parameter Qwen2.5-VL backbone with a 400M-parameter action expert, combining RVQ tokenization with flow-matching and single-step diffusion distillation for real-time inference (Section 5)

On fine-tuned cloth-folding evaluation, RDT2 achieves 77% success versus 36% for pi0.5 and 29% for pi0-FAST, and generalizes to unseen objects with 51% success versus 15% for the best competitor (Section 6, Table 2)
RDT2 achieves an 88% table-tennis hit rate at 1x speed versus a 78% baseline, demonstrating zero-shot dynamic-task capability (Section 6, Table 2)

Zero-shot success rates across pick, place, wipe, button-press, and shake tasks on unseen objects, scenes, instructions, and robot platforms range from 20% to 60%, evaluated over 256 trials per task (Section 6, Figure 3-4)
Scaling-law fits of training loss L(N,D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta give exponents alpha ≈ 0.44 and beta ≈ 0.23, indicating consistent joint gains from model and data scaling (Section 6, Figure 5)

omRyEle4jZ.text: NaviAgent's Graph-Encoded Navigator (Tool World Navigation Model, TWNM) yields up to a 17-point boost in task success rate on complex, high-tool-count tasks compared to configurations without the navigator (Section 4, Figure 3)

Averaged across task complexities, the Navigator contributes about a 2.4-point TSR improvement on top of the Multi-Path Decider, rising to as much as 9 points on the most complex tasks (Section 4, Table 2)
NaviAgent improves task success rate (TSR) over the alpha-UMI baseline on ToolBench by 13.5 points on Qwen2.5-14B, 16.4 points on Qwen2.5-32B, and 19.0 points on DeepSeek-V3 (Section 4, Table 1)
A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-14B NaviAgent variant reaches 49.5% TSR, surpassing the larger Qwen2.5-32B baseline's 44.9% TSR (Section 4, Table 1)
On 50 real APIs spanning 7 domains, NaviAgent achieves an average 10% improvement in TSR over alpha-UMI while using fewer execution steps and lower latency (Section 4)

The DeepSeek-V3-based NaviAgent configuration attains 98.3% task completion rate and 55.5% task success rate on ToolBench, evaluated with a link-prediction graph of 5501 APIs, 7866 nodes, and 24215 edges (Section 4, Table 6)

ylAhgNb2ak.text: ReMoE fine-tunes only router gate parameters (experts and other weights frozen) and increases the Expert Overlap Ratio (EOR) on DeepSeek-V2-Lite from 27.3% to 34.5%, a 7.2 percentage point (26.4% relative) improvement (Section 5.2, Table 2).
On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, ReMoE yields a +27.2% relative improvement in Expert Overlap Ratio, demonstrating generalization beyond DeepSeek-V2-Lite (Section 5.7).

Under an LRU cache policy with capacity C=6 experts per layer, ReMoE raises the unique cache hit rate from 0.3187 to 0.3687 and reduces total unique expert misses from 0.8707M to 0.8068M (Section 5.3, Table 3).
In real vLLM GPU-CPU offloading deployment, ReMoE improves throughput from 3.58 to 3.88 tokens/s (+8.4%) and reduces TPOT from 254.31ms to 242.99ms (Section 5.4, Table 4).

On the Jetson Orin NX edge device with llama.cpp and NVMe expert storage, ReMoE reduces TPOT by 43.6-49.8% across ShareGPT, GSM8K, and HumanEval workloads, corresponding to 1.77x-1.99x decode speedup (Section 5.4, Table 5).

ReMoE preserves downstream task performance on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, with MMLU changing by only +0.09 percentage points (57.72% to 57.81%) and HumanEval improving by +2.44 points, while an ablation without the temporal-locality/Trust-KL objectives (CE-only router fine-tuning) drops EOR below the untuned baseline to 22.9% (Section 5.5, Section 5.7, Table 6, Table 7).

r6EuKr1hq4.text: A sparse subset of exactly three attention heads within a single layer (layer 20 in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, layer 14 in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) is identified as Style Modulation Heads that independently govern persona and style formation, via layer-wise cosine similarity analysis and a dot-product head contribution score (Section 4, Figures 3-4).
An ablation removing the top-contributing heads causes a marked decline in trait/persona steering score, confirming their causal role in persona formation (Section 4, Figure 5).

Steering exclusively via Style Modulation Heads achieves a better Pareto frontier between trait-steering strength and text coherency than steering the MLP residual stream, attention residual stream, or full attention output, across five steering locations and six personas (Section 5, Figure 6, Table 1).

Standard evaluation metrics (MMLU accuracy and perplexity) fail to detect the coherency degradation caused by residual-stream steering that is visible in the paper's trait/coherency Pareto analysis (Section 3, Figure 2).

The asymmetry between suppressing and amplifying persona traits (gradual degradation when suppressing vs. rapid collapse in generation quality when amplifying out-of-distribution personas) is replicated on both Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Section 3, Appendix C, Figure 9).

8YoP649pGC.text: ArcVQ-VAE introduces a Spherical Angular-Margin Prior combining Ball-Bounded Norm Regularization (a time-dependent Euclidean ball with exponential growth schedule M(t)=exp(alpha*t)) and an ArcCosine Additive Margin Loss adapted from ArcFace to enforce angular separation of codebook vectors (Section on method/Spherical Angular-Margin Prior).

On ImageNet-1K at 32x32 with codebook size K=1024, ArcVQ-VAE achieves reconstruction FID of 0.95, outperforming VQGAN-LC (rFID 1.29) and CVQ-VAE (rFID 1.20), while reaching 88% codebook utilization (Experimental Results, reconstruction table).

On MNIST, ArcVQ-VAE reports PSNR 28.01, SSIM 0.9840, LPIPS 0.0217, rFID 1.68; on CIFAR-10 it reports PSNR 24.78, SSIM 0.8989, LPIPS 0.1857, rFID 26.91 (Experimental Results table).

An ablation study (Table 4) shows ArcVQ-VAE's performance is insensitive to hyperparameter variation, indicating robustness of the Ball-Bounded Norm Regularization and ArcCosine Additive Margin Loss combination (Table 4).

TM7PjLDZTr.text: Self-Calibrated Consistency (SCC) combines a Semantic Consistency component (soft pseudo-labels from counterattack warm-up plus multi-view predictions with a hard-negative margin objective) and a Spatial Consistency component (aggregating predictions across semantics-preserving augmented views such as horizontal flips and Gaussian noise) to address semantic drift, view sensitivity, and hard-negative dominance identified in test-time counterattack defenses (Section 3.1-3.4).
Under PGD-10 attack with epsilon=1/255 across 16 standard vision datasets, SCC raises CLIP's robust accuracy from 2.70% (baseline) to 51.68% (Section 4.2, Table 1).
Under the stronger PGD-10 attack with epsilon=4/255, SCC improves robust accuracy from 0.09% to 27.88% while keeping clean accuracy near 60.21% (a 1.30-point drop) (Section 4.2, Table 2).
On 6 medical imaging benchmarks using BioMedCLIP, SCC achieves 34.00% robust accuracy, outperforming the prior test-time counterattack (TTC) baseline by +23.38 points (Section 4.2, Table 3).

SCC adds only about 0.0005 seconds of additional per-image inference overhead compared to TTC, and ablations confirm both the semantic and spatial consistency components contribute complementary robustness gains (Section 4.3-4.4, Table 5, Figure 6).

z75O6LbPCF.text: DOVE evaluates LLM cultural value alignment by comparing distributions of human-written text against LLM-generated outputs via a value codebook built through rate-distortion variational optimization, rather than using constrained multiple-choice formats (Section 3.1-3.2).

DOVE uses an unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) metric to measure distributional divergence between human and model value expressions, explicitly capturing intra-cultural sub-group diversity (Section 3.3).
The DOVE Set dataset comprises 824 topics and 15,213 human-written documents (average 1,034 tokens each) spanning four cultures: South Korea, Japan, China, and the United States (Section 4.1).

DOVE achieves 31.56% correlation with downstream harmful-content-detection tasks, outperforming five baselines (WVS, GlobalOpinionQA, CDEval, NormAd, NaVAB) on predictive validity (Section 4.2, Table 1).
DOVE maintains high reliability (sampling reliability, test-retest stability, and template invariance) with as few as 500 samples per culture (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
An ablation shows the value codebook component accounts for the majority of DOVE's performance gains over baseline distributional comparisons (Section 4.2, Table 2).

suwjabuQDY.text: Under the clustered near-identical poison assumption (Assumption 3.1), Lemma 3.2 derives the aggregate poison gain S(m;λ)=m/(nλ+kζm) as a closed-form function of poison count m (Section 3.1, Lemma 3.2).

Theorem 3.4 proves clustered dirty-label poisoning induces a rank-one spike in the input Gauss-Newton/Hessian, ΛGN(x0)=Rk(x0,ζ)(Δf(x0))², with magnitude scaling quadratically with the poisoning efficacy Δf(x0) (Theorem 3.4).

Corollary 3.6 shows for exponential kernels the spike coefficient is Rk(x0,ζ)=r²/ℓ⁴, and Corollary 3.7 identifies a near-clone regime r≪ℓ in which attack efficacy stays order-one while this induced curvature vanishes quadratically, making the attack spectrally undetectable (Corollary 3.6, Corollary 3.7).

Theorem 3.9 proves data-fitting capacity strictly decreases under gradient regularization, and Theorem 3.12 shows this regularization exponentially compresses large Fisher eigenmodes at rate e^(-2καt) (Theorem 3.9, Theorem 3.12).

o4w4LRrIMT.text: Theorem 3.1 shows first-layer features of a three-layer compositional target can be recovered from the degree-k Hermite moment tensor once the sample size satisfies n ≫ d^(k+ε) (Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 shows that, given recovered first-layer features, the second-layer scalar feature can be estimated with only n ≫ d^(2ε) additional samples (Theorem 3.2).

The staged hierarchical spectral method attains overall sample complexity O(d^(k+ε)) for the three-layer compositional target, versus O(d^(4p)) required by shallow/kernel baselines, giving a concrete separation of O(d^2.5) vs O(d^4) for k=2, ε=1/2 (Section 2, Section 4).

Figure 2 empirically confirms a sharp transition in test MSE at the theoretically predicted d^(k+ε) sample-complexity threshold, and Figures 4-6 show this transition persists across other nonlinearities and higher-order Hermite targets (Figure 2, Figures 4-6).

Z2axjFEPH3.text: FairRARI's Algorithm 1 iterative projection scheme is proven in Theorem 3.2 to converge geometrically to a unique fixed point, which Theorem 3.3 shows coincides with the minimizer of the strongly convex fairness-constrained PageRank objective, for any convex constraint set (Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.3).
Section 4 introduces φ-sum-fairness and α-min-fairness (plus a combined variant), each of which admits a linear-time projection computable via binary search over dual variables (Section 4).

FairRARI's per-iteration cost is O(m+n), matching standard PageRank's asymptotic complexity, and Section 6 reports at most a 10% empirical increase in running time relative to unconstrained PageRank across the paper's 22-dataset benchmark (Section 4, Section 6).

Figure 1 shows a post-processing fairness baseline zeroes PageRank scores for 75% of minority-group vertices, whereas FairRARI keeps positive scores for all vertices while still meeting the fairness target (Figure 1).

Across the 22 evaluated datasets, FairRARI's Kendall Tau rank-correlation with unconstrained PageRank substantially exceeds that of the FSPR and LFPR baselines, including in multi-group (K>2) settings where the baselines fail (Section 6).

JuaulCZ7gE.text: The continuous-time PLRNN formulation (Equation 5, Section 3.1) solves the piecewise-linear ODE analytically within each of the 2^P linear subregions by tracking switching times between regions, bypassing numerical integration entirely (Section 3.1, Equation 5).
Equilibria and limit cycles of trained cPLRNNs are determined semi-analytically per region using a SCYFI-style fixed-point search and the trajectory-tracking equations 14-16 (Section 3.2).

On irregularly-sampled leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) data, the standard discrete-time PLRNN fails badly with D_stsp=4.3±0.3, while the cPLRNN reconstructs the attractor accurately with D_stsp=0.26±0.03 (Table 3).
cPLRNN trains roughly 4-5x faster than Neural ODE baselines using RK4 or Tsit5 solvers while matching their reconstruction performance (Table 2).
On real neuronal recordings, cPLRNN attains D_stsp=0.71±0.02, slightly outperforming Neural ODE competitors on the same benchmark (Table 4).

aNWIVNjocB.text: Theorem 2.4 gives the first closed-form optimal control solution for Mountain Car, α(t)=C·ẋ(t), a policy depending only on velocity, closing a 36-year-old open problem (Section 2, Theorem 2.4).
The derived analytical worst-case policy achieves returns of 99.15-99.52 on Mountain Car, versus 96.67 for ARS (regret 2.72), 93.91 for PPO (regret 5.48), and 94.61 for SAC (regret 4.78) (Section 2).

CH-3-PPO attains regret 1.29 on Mountain Car, a 4.24x improvement over standard PPO, and CH-3-REINFORCE attains regret 0.77, a 3.53x improvement over standard ARS (Section 5).

0Qudez0gLp.text: RAD achieves 96.7% Pixel AUROC on MVTec-AD using only a single anomaly-free reference image, compared to 98.5% Pixel AUROC in the full-data setting (Figure 3).
RAD attains 99.6% Image-level AUROC and 98.5% Pixel-level AUROC (75.6% Pixel AP, 71.3% Pixel F1-max, 94.9% AUPRO) on MVTec-AD, outperforming Dinomaly by +6.3 Pixel AP and +2.1 Pixel F1-max (Table 1).
On Real-IAD, RAD reaches 92.0% Image AUROC and 99.1% Pixel AUROC, with gains of +10.9 Pixel AP and +7.1 Pixel F1-max over the prior best baseline (Table 1).
On 3D-ADAM (RGB-only), RAD improves Pixel F1-max by +12.5 points over Dinomaly (Table 1).

Lemma 2.2 (Decoder Amplification) shows that enforcing high-fidelity reconstruction through an information-losing bottleneck forces decoders into high-gain amplifiers, and retrieval-based anomaly scores are shown to provably upper-bound reconstruction-residual scores under matched encoder/dataset conditions (Section 2, Lemma 2.2).

yXqnyIvGAy.text: TimeRCD achieves the top rank in 41 of 56 univariate zero-shot anomaly detection cases and second-best in 6 cases, evaluated against general-purpose and anomaly-specific foundation models (Section 3.2, Table 1).
TimeRCD's zero-shot performance is competitive with full-shot baselines trained directly on target data, ranking first in 28 of those comparison cases (Section 3.2, Table 1).

The Relative Context Discrepancy paradigm detects anomalies by contrasting a query window against its surrounding context using a standard Transformer encoder with dual reconstruction and anomaly-scoring heads, rather than relying purely on reconstruction error (Section 2.1).

TimeRCD is pretrained on a synthetic corpus of 2.5 billion data points generated via a four-stage pipeline (context-template generation, joint-context fusion via causal DAG/ARX dynamics, causal-contextual anomaly injection, and token-level labeling) (Section 2.2).

An ablation shows synthetic data with RCD injection reaches Affiliation-F 0.878 and F1-T 0.569, while switching to DADA injection on real-world data causes a catastrophic collapse to Affiliation-F 0.716 and F1-T 0.073 (Section 3.4, Table 2).

TimeRCD attains a Standard-F1 of 0.827 on contextual anomalies, substantially outperforming competing methods, and shows a scaling law with consistent gains as pretraining data grows from 350M to 700M to 2.5B points (Section 3.3, Figure 5; Figure 7).

IhBW4rQM7L.text: MPDiffuser's alternating diffusion sampling scheme (Algorithm 1, Section 3.2) interleaves a dynamics-model update (states conditioned on actions) with a planner update (joint states and actions) at each reverse diffusion step, using classifier-free guidance with strength ω in both steps.
MPDiffuser+Rank achieves an average normalized score of 85.1 across D4RL medical-expert tasks, including 111.8 on Hopper, 110.7 on Walker2d, and 98.4 on HalfCheetah (Table 1).

On the DSRL constrained benchmark, MPDiffuser achieves a normalized return of 0.81 with cost 0.37 on HopperVelocity and return 1.0 with cost 0.01 on HalfCheetahVelocity, indicating a favorable safety-performance tradeoff (Table 3).

Under a simulated hardware defect (ankle joint torque limited on a legged robot), MPDiffuser maintains 58.6 performance pre-fine-tuning versus Diffuser's 25.9, improving to 66.4 after fine-tuning (Figure 6).

On the real Unitree Go2 quadruped tracking a commanded 0.5 m/s velocity, MPDiffuser achieves 0.55 m/s tracked velocity compared to 0.74 m/s for a PPO baseline, using single-sample inference on a Jetson Orin (Section 4.4).
An ablation comparing alternating versus combined-score sampling shows the alternating scheme achieves an average return of 102.4 versus 98.2 for the combined variant (Table 12).

fNI8617Hfb.text: MDLMs exhibit a strong recency-based locality bias in context comprehension, with performance highest when relevant information appears immediately before the test question, rather than the U-shaped pattern typical of autoregressive models (Section 4, Figure 1).

Appending additional mask tokens for generation degrades LLaDA-Base accuracy by up to 23 percentage points and LLaDA-Instruct by up to 27 percentage points, while Dream-7B/Dream-Base drops 6-8 points under roughly 20 masks (Section 5, Figure 4).

Replacing mask tokens with repeated dot tokens of the same count causes only 3-10 point accuracy drops, versus 23-27 point drops for actual mask tokens, indicating masks specifically act as distractors rather than generic repeated filler (Section 5, Figure 6).

Gradient attribution analysis shows mask tokens receive 0.22-0.28 normalized gradient attribution compared to only 0.005-0.057 for surrounding context tokens, demonstrating disproportionate model attention to masks (Table 1).

A mask-agnostic (MA) fine-tuning loss combining cross-entropy and total-variation terms substantially mitigates the mask-distraction degradation, achieving robustness in a single decoding step versus the roughly 40 iterative steps otherwise required (Section 6).

s0dgtvgAt1.text: Sonar-TS implements a search-then-verify pipeline that generates hybrid SQL code to search multi-scale feature/SAX-morphology tables and Python code to verify candidates using atomic operators such as PELT change-point detection, Theil-Sen trend-slope estimation, and DTW subsequence matching (Section 4).

NLQTSBench comprises 831 validated natural-language queries over time series organized into a four-level taxonomy (basic retrieval, morphological pattern recognition, semantic reasoning, insight synthesis), with an average query window of about 11,200 points (Section 3.1).
On NLQTSBench-Lite (512-point context), Sonar-TS achieves an average score of 0.3016, versus 0.1818 for ChatTS-14B and 0.1374 for Time-R1 (Table 1).
On the full NLQTSBench with long histories, Sonar-TS achieves an average score of 0.6168, versus 0.1562 for MAC-SQL and 0.0526 for Xiyan-SQL-32B (Table 1).

Ablations show removing the feature tables drops composite-trend performance from 0.30 to 0.04, removing accumulated experiences drops contextual-anomaly performance from 0.51 to 0.25, and removing the Python verification step collapses the overall average from 0.62 to 0.25 (Table 2).

The coarse posterior approximation strictly dominates prior-free baselines in sample complexity while remaining fast to compute (Section 4).

Empirical query-count comparisons show the method identifies the mode LLM answer using fewer samples than exhaustive sampling across confidence levels (Table 1, Table 2).

t4SltdwuLF.text: The empirical covariance operator error is bounded as E||Σ−Σ̂||_HS ≤ R^{1/2} n^{-1/2} + 2R^{1/4} r_m(Φ), combining a parametric n^{-1/2} inter-measure term with an intra-measure approximation term r_m(Φ) (Theorem 3.3).

A sparse-to-dense transition occurs at sampling threshold m ≍ n^{1/(2α)}, separating regimes dominated by the m^{-α} versus n^{-1/2} terms (Section 3).

1wnPjWrw18.text: RQ-MoE achieves a 6.6x decoding speedup over QINCo at configuration M=8, N·L=4 (0.5 microseconds vs 3.3 microseconds) (Table 4).
RQ-MoE achieves a 14.8x decoding speedup over QINCo at configuration M=16, N·L=8 (0.7 microseconds vs 10.4 microseconds) (Table 4).

tqKRgRqaza.text: Gradient-Adaptive Stabilization (GAS) applies parameter-wise regularization via gradient-scaled stochastic perturbations, with a normalized noise scale bounded in (0,1], theoretically justified for stability-plasticity tradeoff (Section 3.1, Theorems 3.6-3.8).
On the Med JASCL-Disjoint 3-session benchmark, JASCL with a U-Net backbone retains 0.398 Dice at Session 2 while baselines UCL and PIFS degrade to 0.325 and 0.078 respectively (Table 2).
On the 6-session Med JASCL-Disjoint benchmark, JASCL maintains 0.324 Dice at Session 5 while a vanilla fine-tuning baseline collapses to 0.042 (Table 3).

In the semi-supervised Med setting, JASCL with MedFormer achieves 0.293-0.431 Dice across sessions versus competing methods NNCSL and UaD-CE averaging below 0.15 (Table 8).
GAS and PAS add negligible computational overhead: parameter count remains 16.27M and training time on Med JASCL-Disjoint is 4h06m versus 4h05m for the baseline (Table 5).

fPjkFDW9j7.text: OrderPlace reduces wirelength by 34.04% compared with WireMask-EA and by 14.08% compared with EGPlace on ISPD 2005 benchmarks (Table 2).

Two formal theorems show that placement ordering impact scales as an Ω(l) degradation ratio in chain-topology graphs (Theorem 1) and as a Θ(g) performance variance in star-topology hub placement (Theorem 2).

Analysis of 24 LLM-discovered strategies shows entropy-reduction mechanisms appear in 75% of strategies and explicit net-closure completion bonuses appear in 62.5% of strategies (Table 3).

pkgFEnVR5z.text: On the BadMerging benchmark, LFPM achieves an average target attack success rate ASR(T) of 0.49%, compared with 4.42% for PAM and 10.03% for SAM (Table 1).
In the LoBAM PEFT setting, LFPM attains an average target ASR of 3.84% and non-target ASR of 26.68% while maintaining clean accuracy of 54.45%, comparable to baseline defenses (Table 2).
Under adaptive attacks combining feature coupling and interpolation, LFPM maintains the lowest ASR at 2.38%, whereas SAU's ASR degrades from 63.00% to 99.20% (Table 3).

Theorem 3.1 establishes a Cross-Task Linearity deviation bound via a path-integral formulation, showing feature deviation scales with parameter distance, loss-landscape flatness, and the merging coefficient (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
Figure 2 shows LFPM achieves the smallest cumulative Path-ASR (backdoor vulnerability integrated along the model interpolation path) in both full fine-tuning and PEFT settings (Figure 2).
Appendix E.1 confirms LFPM's effectiveness generalizes across alternative merging algorithms including Task Arithmetic and Ties-Merging (Appendix E.1).

zxJXgfCm63.text: Theorem 3.1 shows that an autoencoder satisfying reconstruction and cross-environment invariance constraints identifies the valid instrument component W up to affine transformation when the confounding mixing function is an injective polynomial, under sufficient-variability conditions (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 extends identification to general diffeomorphic (smooth, invertible) mixing functions, showing the first p̂ dimensions of the encoder output depend only on W, yielding either perfect or partial identification depending on the specified latent dimension (Theorem 3.2).

Proposition 2.2 establishes that if Z is a valid instrument and κ is a bijective measurable function, then κ(Z) is also a valid instrument, justifying identification up to transformation as sufficient for valid causal inference (Proposition 2.2).

Semi-synthetic experiments use 652 genetic variants from the GLP1R region across East Asian and African ancestry populations from the All of Us Research Hub, with 8,000 individuals per population (Section on semi-synthetic experiments).

The proposed 2SLS(Ŵ) and PO(V̂)-2SLS(Ŵ) estimators achieve near-zero bias across mixing settings (polynomial degrees 1 and 3, invertible MLPs), while standard 2SLS methods exhibit bias up to 0.3 in the semi-synthetic experiments (Section 4, experimental results).

FaGn04tvzq.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that variables in pairwise chain factor graphs develop increasingly Gaussian-distributed beliefs as topological distance from prior factors increases, driven by repeated convolution via the Central Limit Theorem (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.4 extends the Gaussian convergence result to tree-topology factor graphs, provided the message non-Gaussianity ε satisfies ε² ≪ ε with increasing distance from the nearest prior factor (Theorem 4.4).
Theorem 4.5 uses computation-tree equivalence to show loopy factor graphs exhibit the same Gaussian convergence mechanism as tree graphs under identical assumptions (Theorem 4.5).

Lemma 4.2 identifies an 'exclusion zone' in which non-Gaussian prior factors prevent Gaussian convergence when the prior-to-pairwise variance ratio R is less than or equal to approximately 6 (Lemma 4.2).

Figure 4 shows all tested topologies reach a KL divergence below 0.02 within 3 hops from prior factors, and that higher node degree increases non-Gaussianity in star graphs while weaker priors enable faster Gaussian emergence (Figure 4).

Figure 5 applies the theory to stereo depth estimation belief propagation, showing Gaussian convergence in textureless image regions while non-Gaussian beliefs persist at high-contrast edges (Figure 5).

ajHTru25Kd.text: EvoKernel improves GPT-5.2's overall correctness (Acc) on Ascend C NPU kernel synthesis from 11.0% (Round 1) to 83.0% (Final) under a fixed budget of T=30 iterations per operator, and improves overall compilation rate from 11.0% to 98.5% (Table 2).

EvoKernel achieves a median within-operator speedup of 3.60x (interquartile range 1.38x-10.05x) between the first feasible draft and the best candidate found within budget, across 159 operators with at least one valid optimization candidate (Figure 2, Section 4.2).

With GPT-5.2, EvoKernel outperforms the Codex-by-OpenAI baseline by 15.5 percentage points in compilation rate (98.5% vs. 83.0%) and 37.0 points in correctness (83.0% vs. 46.0%) under the same 30-iteration budget (Table 2, Section 4.2).

In the L1→L2 cross-level transfer setup, memory built on Level 1 operators lets the agent reach 64% cumulative correctness on Level 2 operators by iteration 17, versus 53% for L1+L2 Mixed and 34% for L2 Scratch (Table 3, Figure 3).

Transferring a memory bank built with GPT-5.2 to weaker backbones improves DeepSeek-V3.2's compilation rate from 26% to 80% and correctness from 6% to 58%, and improves Qwen3-Coder-30B's compilation rate from 14% to 84% and correctness from 4% to 32% (Figure 3, Section 4.3).

On 15 held-out mHC kernels targeting a DeepSeek architectural motif on Ascend, EvoKernel obtains 10 correct implementations, with representative speedups including 41.96x for SinkhornKnopp and 2.94x for OrthostochasticProject relative to the PyTorch/Torch-NPU baseline (Table 4, Figure 4).

The YouTube-SBS dataset comprises 423 stereo videos at 1920x1080 resolution containing over 7 million stereo pairs, used for training and benchmarking (Section 3, Table 1).
In the YouTube-SBS dataset, 71.27% of frames have less than 10% occluded area and 94.71% have less than 40% occluded area, indicating predominantly subtle stereo effects (Table 2).

ImmersePro is compared against Deep3D, 3D Photo, and StereoDiffusion as image-based stereo-from-mono baselines (Table 3).

K1mAvyHhKU.text: Theorem 3.1 shows that under the status-quo Bradley-Terry MLE ranking mechanism, producers can gain utility by submitting multiple clones of an (epsilon,delta)-competitive model, driven by a 'lottery ticket effect' from independent vote draws (Theorem 3.1, Definition 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 proves the You-Rank-We-Rank (YRWR) mechanism is O(1/sqrt(s))-strategyproof, bounding the utility gain from submitting multiple copies versus a single model per producer, where s is the number of votes/models (Theorem 4.1).
Proposition 4.1 shows that under truthful producer rankings, YRWR reduces l-infinity ranking error relative to the status-quo mechanism (Proposition 4.1).
The Uncertainty-Aware YRWR variant (UA-YRWR) ignores producer-submitted rankings when confidence intervals overlap, maintaining O(1/sqrt(s))-robustness with tolerance epsilon+alpha (Section 4.4).

Simulations calibrated to Arena data show YRWR reduces clone-induced rank gains to near-zero while improving Kendall-Tau distance to the ground-truth ranking, even under moderately noisy producer-reported rankings (Section 4.6).

UDBM achieves a 6x inference speedup and roughly 2x fewer FLOPs (46.85G vs 91.77G) compared to HOGformer while using 56.02M parameters for the Large variant, with single-step inference (Table 1).

Theorem 3.3 shows that introducing pixel-wise uncertainty variance regularizes the drift singularity of the diffusion bridge, keeping the drift O(1) instead of diverging as O(1/sqrt(1-t)) near the terminal time (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.3).
Ablation results show removing the terminal relaxation term drops average performance by 1.89 dB, and using a fixed (non-adaptive) bridge coefficient reduces performance by 0.99 dB (Table 6).
On unseen composite (double/triple) degradations from the CDD11 benchmark, UDBM attains a LIQE score of 2.898, versus 2.651 for HOGformer and 2.697 for DiffUIR (Section on generalization, Table 4-5).

XSYX75R6RC.text: TRIRL outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning baselines (GAIL, AIRL, AMP, LSIQ, NEAR, SFM) by a factor of 2.4x in aggregate inter-quartile mean across MuJoCo and robotics tasks (Abstract, Figure 4).
TRIRL is evaluated on MuJoCo benchmarks (Half-Cheetah, Ant, Walker, Hopper, Humanoid) as well as robotics tasks including Unitree G1 walking/running and Unitree Go2 locomotion (Section 5, Figure 4).

Table 1 reports transfer experiments (Point Maze Flipped, Ant Disabled, Half-Cheetah Windy, Half-Cheetah Mars Gravity) where reward functions recovered by TRIRL generalize to environments with shifted system dynamics, outperforming baselines in both retraining and transfer settings (Table 1, Section 5.1).

Figure 5 presents an ablation across seven TRIRL variants examining the effects of reward fitting, trust region enforcement, and discriminator buffers on performance across MuJoCo benchmarks (Figure 5).

eMCp3enKXM.text: Post-block activation steering achieves accuracy within 0.2%-0.9% of full-parameter fine-tuning while training only 0.04% of model parameters (Table 1).

Despite using 11x fewer parameters than LoRA (0.04% vs 0.45%), the method matches or exceeds LoRA performance on 1B-scale models and achieves a +0.5% average improvement on Llama-3.1-8B (Section on baseline comparisons).
On ListOps tasks, ReFT degrades 16.9% below full-parameter tuning performance, whereas the proposed steering method limits the gap to 3.1% (Table 2).

The post-block intervention site (after skip-connection reintegration, capturing both residual and MLP pathways) is identified as optimal, outperforming pre-MLP or post-MLP-only intervention points (Section 4).

Jointly training weight and activation updates with an orthogonality constraint surpasses the performance ceiling of either update type alone by up to 3.8%, while naive joint training without orthogonality enforcement fails (Section 6.4, Table 5).

Zk0qjcqjV9.text: On Pass@16 text-only mathematical reasoning with Qwen2.5-7B, ECHO achieves 55.3% average accuracy versus 51.6% for the strongest baseline, including a 12.36% relative gain on AIME2025 (Table 1).
On Pass@1 multimodal reasoning benchmarks with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B, ECHO yields average improvements of 1.2% to 2.4% over baseline test-time RL methods (Table 2).
Ablating confidence-adaptive clipping (CA-Clip) causes the largest degradation among ECHO's components, dropping AIME2025 accuracy from 54.3% to 30.1% (Table 3).

The baseline ETMR method concentrates rollout budget on its top-3 trajectories, exhibiting rollout collapse under high-entropy continuity, which ECHO's entropy-confidence branch-width scheduling (Eq. 6) is designed to prevent (Section 3.1, Figure 2).
ECHO's online pruning uses a confidence threshold τ_prune = 0.4 and entropy bounds H_low = 1.0 / H_high = 3.5 for confidence-adaptive branch scheduling (Section 3.1, Table 6).

1gYQX9L1cb.text: MUSA-PINN reformulates PDE constraints as integral conservation laws over hierarchical spherical control volumes rather than pointwise residuals (Section 3.3).
On Diamond and IWP TPMS heat-exchanger channel geometries, MUSA-PINN reduces velocity error by 97.94% and 99.57% respectively relative to baseline methods (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On Primitive and IWP geometries, MUSA-PINN reduces pressure field error by 93.85% and 93.42% respectively compared to baselines (Table 1, Section 4.2).
MUSA-PINN reduces the average cross-sectional mass conservation error by over 97.05% compared to the best baseline via flux-balance residuals enforcing strict flux continuity (Section 4.3, Figure 5).
On industrial-scale geometries, MUSA-PINN achieves 14.91% relative L2 error on a liquid-cooling plate and 20.08% on a DualMS heat exchanger (Section 4.5, Figure 7).

hGcJZQSgLo.text: Theorem 4.3 shows layerwise SGD on residual networks achieves expected error Õ(D²(M+1)⁴(wn)^(2K+1) / (γ^(4+2K) m)) when learning hierarchical models with unknown label hierarchy L1 ⊆ L2 ⊆ ... ⊆ Lr = [n] (Theorem 4.3).
The hierarchical model class assumes level-1 labels are polynomial threshold functions (PTFs) of the input and each higher level's labels are PTFs of the immediately lower level's labels (Section 4).

The required network depth D must exceed r·(⌈ln(8m|G|/ξ)/γ⌉ + 1), where r is the number of hierarchy levels, exceeding prior work restricted to log-depth circuits by allowing polynomial-depth constructions (Theorem 4.3).

Theorem 3.4 (the Brain Dump Hierarchy) shows that random intermediate labels from a hierarchical computation circuit, modeled as majority functions over circuit components, induce learnable hierarchical structure with high probability (Theorem 3.4).

The layerwise SGD algorithm learns the hierarchical model class using poly(n, d, M, 1/ε) samples and polynomial runtime, contrasting with hardness results for general hierarchical function classes (Section 4.3).

VDaJ5RCOh4.text: CausalDPO achieves an average performance improvement of 17.17% across four evaluation metrics (HR@10, N@10, HR@20, N@20) over the strongest baseline, evaluated on Yelp2018, ML-10M, and Book-Crossing under three OOD distribution shifts (Table 1).

Proposition 3.1 establishes that standard DPO amplifies spurious correlations from environmental confounders, bounding generalization error as GenErr(θ) ≤ 2C|w_E|·E[TV(p_train(E|x), p_test(E|x))] (Proposition 3.1).
Proposition 3.2 proves CausalDPO satisfies both an invariance condition (Eq. 11) and a sufficiency condition (Eq. 12) for the preference policy across inferred environments (Proposition 3.2).

Proposition 3.3 derives a generalization bound for CausalDPO of the form ≤ 2R_n(Π) + B√(2log(2/δ)/n) + L_ℓ·MMD_H_k(p,q), tying invariance regularization via MMD to generalization error (Proposition 3.3, Eq. 13).

The ablation study (Table 8) shows removing either the supervised fine-tuning stage or the CausalDPO preference-alignment stage causes a significant performance drop, confirming both components are necessary (Table 8).

GDDYhRWpG4.text: Assumption 1 requires the partial derivatives of the generative mapping f with respect to distinct latent variables to be orthogonal at every point (functional/Jacobian orthogonality), introduced in the problem formulation (Section 3).

Proposition 1 shows that under Assumption 1, when latent variables are statistically independent and at most one is Gaussian, the generative process is identifiable up to permutation and coordinate-wise reparameterization (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).

Proposition 2 extends identifiability to statistically dependent latent factors by combining Assumption 1 with Assumption 2, which requires the latent support to be a bounded, simply connected region topologically equivalent to a hypercube so all combinations of factor values are attainable (Section 4.2, Proposition 2).

Table 1 reports that enforcing the orthogonal Jacobian constraint on VAE variants improves DCI disentanglement, MIG, and SAP scores on dSprites and 3DShapes compared to standard VAEs without the constraint (Table 1, Section 5).

Figure 3 shows boxplots of Mean Correlation Coefficient and Amari distance across latent dimensions {3, 6, 9} for both independent and dependent latent variable settings, empirically supporting the identifiability claims of Propositions 1 and 2 (Figure 3, Section 5).

eXLcL70GXO.text: The Average Percentile Upper Bound (APUB) is defined as U^apub[μ|P̂_n] := (1/α)∫₀^α U^efron[μ|P̂_n] dτ, integrating Efron's percentile upper bound over confidence level τ from 0 to α (Definition 2.2, Section 2)
Theorem 2.7 proves APUB converges almost surely to the true population mean as sample size n approaches infinity, for every confidence level in (0,1] (Theorem 2.7)

Theorem 3.3 shows the APUB-embedded stochastic optimization model achieves first-order asymptotic correctness, with coverage probability exceeding the nominal confidence level up to an O(N^{-1/2}) term (Theorem 3.3)

Theorem 3.5 establishes that both the optimal values and optimal solution sets of the APUB-based optimization problem converge almost surely to their true counterparts as sample size increases (Theorem 3.5)

On a Gamma(2,1) numerical example with nominal level α=0.05 and sample sizes ranging from 80 to 10,000, APUB's coverage probability approaches the 0.95 nominal level faster than Efron's percentile bound and standard large-sample approximations (Figure 1, Example 2.5)

The framework is validated on two-stage product mix and multi-product newsvendor problems, showing APUB balances robustness and practicality compared to Sample Average Approximation (SAA) and Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) (Section 5)

ue4WxHI1U4.text: A single-layer toy model with softmax output and KL-divergence loss, trained via gradient flow to mimic a language-model head, exhibits power-law loss decay at low teacher temperature rather than the exponential decay seen at high teacher temperature (Section 2, Figure 1)

In the low-temperature intermediate regime the free energy expansion F(β) ≈ -c₀ - c₁β^{-1} - c₂β^{-2} implies loss L ≈ c₂β^{-1} and gradient -dL/dβ ≈ c₂β^{-2} (Equations 17), from which β ∝ τ^{1/3} and therefore L ∝ τ^{-1/3} (Equations 18-19, Section 3)

Numerical experiments on the toy model across 8 teacher temperatures and 12 learning rates show loss and gradient exponents converging to approximately 1 and 2 respectively in the intermediate regime, collapsing onto a single curve when plotted against a rescaled dynamic time τ (Figure 3, Section 3)
Training dynamics under optimal learning rate show the inverse-temperature parameter β growing empirically as τ^{0.38}, close to the predicted τ^{1/3} scaling (Figure 4)

Analysis of four Pythia model sizes (70M to 12B parameters) trained on FineWeb shows next-token distributions are peaked (entropy ≤ 1.69 bits) and empirical loss fits L = cτ/τ^{α_τ} + L_∞ with fitted exponents α_τ ranging 0.32-0.35 across model sizes, clustering near 1/3 (Section 4, Figure 6)

The universal 1/3 time-scaling exponent is presented as a mechanism-based (architectural) explanation for observed neural scaling laws, contrasting with prior data-property-based explanations discussed in the related work comparison (Section 5)

3hD1gzThtY.text: Theorem 2.5 shows local polynomial estimators achieve the minimax-optimal convergence rate O(n^{-2α/(2α+d)}) in mean squared error for α-Hölder smooth regression functions with n context examples in d dimensions (Theorem 2.5)
Theorem 3.1 proves a transformer construction can approximate the local polynomial estimator with approximation error O(1/n) (Theorem 3.1)
Theorem 3.2 establishes that the empirical-risk-minimizing transformer within this construction attains the same minimax-optimal rate O(n^{-2α/(2α+d)}) (Theorem 3.2)

The construction requires only L = ⌈C log(en)⌉ transformer blocks and Θ(log n) total parameters, compared to Θ(n) parameters in Shen et al. (2025) and Θ(n^{d/(2α+d)}) parameters in Kim et al. (2024) (Section 3, Section 1.1)

The required number of pretraining sequences is Γ ≥ Cn^{2α/(2α+d)} log³(en), a smaller requirement than the Ω(n^{(6α+d)/(2α+d)} log n) and Ω(n^{(2α+2d)/(2α+d)} log n) requirements of prior transformer constructions (Section 3, Section 1.1)

The transformer implements the estimator by constructing a kernel-weighted monomial (polynomial) basis via ReLU feed-forward networks and then running gradient descent steps within linear attention layers to solve the local polynomial least-squares problem (Section 4)

IkXFH6alZN.text: On R2R-CE Val-Unseen, MapDream achieves 59.8% success rate (SR) and 54.4 SPL with 4.59 navigation error, establishing state-of-the-art performance among monocular vision-language navigation methods (Table 1, Section 4)
On RxR-CE Val-Unseen, MapDream achieves 59.4% SR, 49.2 SPL, and 4.96 navigation error, demonstrating strong multilingual instruction-following navigation performance (Table 1, Section 4)

When trained only on R2R-CE and evaluated zero-shot on RxR-CE, MapDream achieves 27.8% SR and 23.3 SPL, outperforming comparable baselines in this cross-dataset generalization setting (Table 2, Section 4)

MapDream formulates map construction as autoregressive bird's-eye-view (BEV) image synthesis, combining supervised pre-training with reinforcement fine-tuning for task-driven spatial representation learning (Section 3, Figure 2)
Ablations on two-stage training effects, channel initialization, and BEV resolution/token budget quantify their impact on navigation performance (Table 3, Table 4, Table 5)

DjX8eh4PIm.text: SALO detects direct harmful prompts with 99.0% accuracy and prefilling (forced-decoding) attacks with 99.4% detection rate on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, in a setting where terminal-state detection methods are described as failing (Table 1, Section 4)
On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, SALO achieves 100.0% detection of AutoDAN attacks and 98.8% detection of prefilling attacks, while GCG attacks are detected at 85.4% (Table 1, Section 4)
On Mistral-7B-Instruct, SALO detects GCG attacks at 96.5% and AutoDAN attacks at 98.8% (Table 1, Section 4)

Refusal processing decomposes into three phases: a Semantic Trigger at shallow layers on the harmful token, a Critical Construction phase with peak intensity at immediate subsequent tokens in intermediate layers, and Terminal Attenuation where signals weaken toward the final position (Section 3)

SALO's detector uses multi-granularity convolution kernels (3x2, 3x3, 3x5) applied to raw hidden-state volumes from selected middle layers, preserving spatiotemporal geometry rather than collapsing to a single vector (Section 3, Section 4)
