Under a white-box adaptive GCG attack with λ=5.0 designed to evade the detector, SALO still achieves an 84.3% detection rate, indicating the refusal trajectory signal is entangled with malicious intent and hard to suppress without destroying prompt semantics (Section 4)

3SDg8dtkS8.text: Rubric-ARM achieves 74.8% average performance across the aggregated reward-modeling benchmarks, a +4.7 point improvement over the Rubric-RM baseline (70.1%) (Table 1).
Rubric-ARM outperforms white-box judge baselines such as RRM-7B (57.8%) and JudgeLRM-7B (53.8%) on the same benchmark suite (Table 1).
Using Rubric-ARM as the reward model, IterDPO reaches 80.8% average accuracy on IFEval in the offline RL setting, versus 80.4% for plain DPO via Rubric-ARM (Table 3).
In the online RL setting, GRPO trained with the Rubric-ARM reward achieves 55.4% average versus 52.3% for RM-R1 (Table 6).

An ablation swapping the alternating optimization order (updating the judge vs. the rubric generator first) causes a 2.4% performance drop, and removing the format reward without voting costs 2.2% (Table 2).

JPnA2BI6U5.text: Theorem 1.1 shows that for any L, an (L-1, 2^(3L^2), ..., 2^(3L^2))-hybrid Transformer cannot solve L-sequential function composition whenever Hdp ≤ n^(2^(-4L-2)) (Theorem 1.1).

By contrast, an (L+1)-layer full attention network is sufficient to solve L-sequential function composition with only O(poly log n) complexity, as summarized in the paper's complexity comparison table (Table 1).

Theorem 1.2 proves a hardness result for the 2-Sum task under single-layer (B,k)-sparse attention requiring Hdp = Ω(B log n), whereas a single-layer full attention network solves 2-Sum with H=1, d=3, p=O(log n) (Theorem 1.2, Table 2).
The lower bound proof uses a hybrid communication model with L+2 players and an 'indistinguishable decomposition' argument adapted from Chen et al. (2025) (Section 3, Section 4, Definition 4.1).

The theory covers all linear attention variants expressible as a recurrence, including Mamba, RWKV, and Gated DeltaNet, via the formal (L, a_1, ..., a_L)-hybrid Transformer definition (Definition 2.3, Section 2.2).

JT4zAf3zDs.text: Faire attains 74.82% accuracy and 45.37 average Draw score, exceeding Gemini-2.5-Pro's functional-alignment metrics (78.24% accuracy but only 19.86 Draw Avg) despite Gemini's higher raw accuracy (Table 2).

Interleaved SFT training yields lower accuracy (62.48%) than text-only SFT (68.13%), but after RL the interleaved model reaches 74.83% versus 71.21% for the text-only RL model, showing RL reverses the SFT paradox (Table 5).

An ablation removing the semantic-alignment constraint drops accuracy to 66.53% and Draw Avg to 38.31, and using exec-only reward drops accuracy to 64.29% and Draw Avg to 35.65, confirming all three causal constraints (geometric consistency, perceptual admissibility, semantic alignment) are needed (Table 4, Section 3.3).

On the cross-domain GenExam structural-correctness evaluation, Faire reaches 52.3% Math-Rel and 9.3% Math-Str, the only model achieving non-trivial performance on both metrics simultaneously versus baselines like GPT-Image-1 (52.0% Math-Rel, 8.0% Math-Str) (Table 3).
Automated verification scores correlate with human ratings at r=0.9578, with Faire uniquely occupying the high-automatic/high-human agreement region (Figure 8, Section 5.7).

moI2fePoWA.text: Theorem 3 proves that for a γ-sensible Conf-Gen instance with calibrated λ̂, the expected admissibility of the (n+1)-th selection satisfies E[A^(n+1)(λ̂)] ≥ γ (Theorem 3, Section 3).

Definition 1's γ-sensibility relaxes conformal risk control's almost-sure monotonicity requirement to a weaker conditional-monotonicity condition, enabling non-set generative outputs (Definition 1, Section 3).
On TriviaQA open-domain QA with LLaMA-13B, Conf-Gen produces shorter conformal prediction sets than the Quach et al. (2024) baseline at matched coverage (Section 6.1, Figure 2).

On Stable Diffusion v1.5 memorized-image detection, Conf-Gen guarantees selected images are non-memorized with probability ≥ γ using human-evaluated admissibility scores from 10 evaluators per image (Section 6.2, Figure 3).

On WebVoyager web-agent tasks, single-attempt task success is about 60%, while the conformal selection procedure raises success above 65% after 2 attempts and to about 80% over multiple attempts (Section 6.4, Figure 5).

TYjTWxDOOC.text: DISCO is evaluated on three datasets — Extended YaleB (16,128 face images with pose as target, illumination as bias), dSprites (y-coordinate as target, x-coordinate as distractor), and a custom 3D ellipsoid simulation — against the HSCIC and CIRCE baselines (Section 4, Figures 3-5).
On the 3D Simulation dataset with a 5-dimensional vector-valued mediator, DISCO performs slightly better than HSCIC, while CIRCE generally fails to achieve invariance (Figure 5, Section 4).
On Extended YaleB and dSprites, DISCO performs comparably to the other methods, with no significant differences at the best hyperparameter configuration (Figure 3, Figure 4, Section 4).
DISCO requires tuning only a single Nadaraya-Watson bandwidth hyperparameter, versus three hyperparameters each for HSCIC and CIRCE (Discussion).
DISCO's per-batch computational cost is O(b^3), compared to O(b^2) for HSCIC and CIRCE, an explicitly acknowledged tradeoff for its reduced hyperparameter search space (Discussion).

2jpMiRwsrL.text: dXPP's backward pass achieves a 4.2x speedup on probability-simplex projection (226.21 ms vs 950.64 ms for dQP) and a 9.2x speedup on chain projection (333.42 ms vs 3071.18 ms for dQP) at problem dimension 10^6 (Tables 2-3).
In multi-period mean-variance portfolio optimization at horizon H=200, dXPP's backward pass (113.97 ms) is about 343x faster than dQP (39,105.75 ms) and roughly 5.3x faster than OptNet (Table 4).

dXPP reformulates KKT-based differentiation as a softplus-smoothed penalty objective, replacing the larger indefinite KKT system (size n+p+m) with a smaller symmetric positive-definite primal-dimensional (size n) linear system solved via sparse Cholesky factorization or preconditioned conjugate gradient (Section on the penalty-based framework).

Theorem 1 proves that under LICQ and strict complementarity, the sensitivity computed from the smoothed penalty objective converges to the exact KKT sensitivity as the smoothing parameter delta tends to zero (Theorem 1).
Relative gradient discrepancy between dXPP and the KKT-based dQP baseline stays below 10^-3 across problem sizes ranging from 10x5 (1.91e-7) to 5000x2000 (5.14e-4) (Table 1).

pqgHG9xDcb.text: Var-JEPA derives a single Evidence Lower Bound combining reconstruction, generation, and three KL regularization terms (context, latent, and target) that unifies JEPA's predictive objective with variational inference over a coupled latent-variable model (Section 3.3, equations 8-9).

In the simulation study, removing the context KL term (variant E) causes severe distributional collapse with dramatically increased aggregated KL divergence, while the full ELBO achieves 0.996 ± 0.002 accuracy (Section 4.1, Table 1).

On downstream tabular classification, Var-T-JEPA improves over T-JEPA (MLP) across five real-world datasets, e.g. Covertype accuracy rises from 0.408 to 0.679, and Electricity from 0.627 to 0.790 (Section 4.2.2, Table 2).

Discarding the 50% most uncertain samples via the model's learned posterior uncertainty further raises accuracy, e.g. to 0.921 on Adult and 0.706 on Covertype, versus keeping all samples (Section 4.2.2, Table 2).

Section 3.7 shows the per-sample KL terms decompose into an aggregated posterior-mismatch component plus an information-bottleneck component, relating Var-JEPA to LeJEPA's SIGReg regularizer that uses a fixed N(0,I) prior rather than Var-JEPA's learned conditional prior (Section 3.7, equation 11).

tQaBS1vS3N.text: SciVideoBench comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions built from 241 research-level experimental videos spanning four disciplines (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Medicine) and more than 25 academic subjects, split into 370 conceptual, 385 hypothetical, and 245 quantitative reasoning questions (Section on Dataset Overview/Question Distribution).
Gemini-2.5-Pro attains the highest overall accuracy among evaluated proprietary models at 64.30%, far exceeding GPT-4o (24.90%) and Gemini-1.5-Pro (27.50%) (Table of Model Performance).

The best open-source models (InternVL-3-78B-Instruct at 38.80%, InternVL-3-78B at 38.50%) trail proprietary models by nearly a factor of two, with average open-source accuracy of 18.14% versus 38.83% for proprietary models.
Quantitative reasoning is the hardest category across all models: Gemini-2.5-Pro scores only 50.61% and top open-source models roughly 22% on this subset, both well below their overall accuracy.
Chain-of-thought prompting substantially improves performance, boosting Gemini-1.5-Pro's overall accuracy by +21.10 points and its quantitative-reasoning accuracy by +25.31 points.
Human graduate-student experts scored only 17.4% accuracy in closed-book evaluation, underscoring the research-level difficulty of SciVideoBench's questions.

tB05up6g5N.text: STING (Sequential Testing of Illicit N-step Goal execution) constructs a step-by-step illicit plan grounded in a benign persona and iteratively probes a target multi-turn LLM agent with adaptive follow-ups, using judge agents to track phase completion (Section 3, Methodology).

STING models multi-turn red-teaming as a time-to-first-jailbreak process and introduces a 'Restricted Mean Jailbreak Discovery' metric together with discovery curves to summarize how quickly illicit task completion is achieved (Section 3-4).

STING yields substantially higher illicit-task completion rates than both single-turn prompting and chat-oriented multi-turn jailbreak baselines, as reported across the main results tables (Section 5, Tables 2, 4, 6, 8, 9).

Testing across six non-English languages shows attack success and illicit-task completion do not consistently increase in lower-resource languages, diverging from patterns commonly reported for single-turn chatbot jailbreaks (Section 5-6).

jB7dvOzr1a.text: The KRUX probing framework extracts knowledge ingredients from model reasoning traces to separately evaluate the roles of parametric knowledge retrieval and reasoning in scientific problem-solving, addressing three research questions (RQ1-RQ3) (Figure 1).

Retrieving task-relevant knowledge from model parameters is identified as a critical bottleneck for LLM performance on the SciReas and SciReas-Pro scientific reasoning benchmarks (Section addressing RQ1).

Reasoning-enhanced models consistently gain further accuracy when task-relevant knowledge is additionally supplied in-context, on top of gains from reasoning enhancement alone (Section addressing RQ2).
Enhancing verbalized (chain-of-thought) reasoning improves a model's ability to surface task-relevant knowledge from its own parameters, per the RQ3 analysis (Section addressing RQ3).
Frontier reasoning models' accuracy on SciReas is analyzed jointly with inference cost-per-1k-instances, showing the accuracy/cost trade-off across models (Figure 2).
The authors release SciLit01, an 8-billion-parameter baseline model optimized for scientific reasoning, alongside the SciReas/SciReas-Pro benchmark suite and open-source code.

EA0wpmic0X.text: Theorem 2.1 establishes a self-consistency property of the optimal control for diffusion bridges: u*(s,x) equals the conditional expectation of a Jacobian-weighted future control, E_{P^{u*}}[J_{t|s}^T u*(t,X_t) | X_s=x] for s<t (Theorem 2.1).

Theorem 3.1 proves that, within the class of controlled diffusions terminating at x_T, the diffusion bridge is the unique process whose gradient-form control satisfies the self-consistency condition (Theorem 3.1).

The proposed control consistency loss (Equation 9) is trained via fixed-point regression against stopgrad targets computed by a backward recursion (Equations 12-13), so the method never differentiates through simulated bridge trajectories, unlike NGDB (Section 3, Equations 9, 12-13).

On the CIR model and Double Well benchmarks, the method attains lower KL divergence to the ground-truth bridge than NGDB, SDB, and FB baselines, e.g. 0.023±0.010 (ours, b̃=0) vs 0.051±0.012 (NGDB) and 0.104±0.011 (SDB) on the CIR model (Table 1).

On the three cell-population benchmarks (Normal, Rare, Multimodal transitions), the method matches or outperforms NGDB and greatly outperforms SDB and FB, e.g. 66.1±0.9 vs 75.0±5.1 (SDB) and 237±98 (FB) on the Rare-transition task (Table 1).

On the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck bridge, the method converges to the ground truth in about 230 seconds for 5000 steps versus roughly 800 seconds for NGDB, illustrating the scalability benefit of avoiding trajectory backpropagation (Figure 3).

QiTBmWiH8G.text: The paper formalizes a fundamental trade-off in pretraining distribution design for in-context learning: heavy-tailed task distributions broaden the set of tasks that can be selected in-context under distribution shift but come at the cost of worse generalization on any individual test task (Section 1, Section 2).
The framework is instantiated on stochastic differential equation (SDE) and stochastic-process families as challenging test cases for in-context task selection and generalization (Section 1).

Concentration/stability-based generalization bounds are used to characterize when a pretrained transformer acquires reliable in-context learning ability as a function of the tail behavior of the pretraining task distribution (Section 2).
Volterra equation models are analyzed as a concrete dynamical-systems example illustrating the pretraining-distribution trade-off (Appendix F.1).

Task selection under distribution shift is examined via explicit assumptions on task-selection reliability that determine which tasks remain learnable in-context as the pretraining distribution's tail weight is varied (Appendix E).

7Sho2SEu3D.text: Theorem 3.2 proves that the Minimal Embeddable Dimension for linear scoring satisfies k-1 ≤ MED(m,k;F_linear) ≤ 2k, i.e. Θ(k) and independent of the universe size m (Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 3.4 proves the analogous Θ(k) bound k-1 ≤ MED(m,k;F_ℓ2) ≤ 2k for Euclidean-distance-based top-k retrieval (Theorem 3.4).
Theorem 3.6 proves the bound k-1 ≤ MED(m,k;F_cos) ≤ 2k+1 for cosine-similarity-based top-k retrieval, again independent of m (Theorem 3.6).

Theorems 4.1-4.3 show that in the centroid setting, the Minimal Embeddable Dimension for all three scoring functions is bounded as MED-C(m,k;s) = O(k^2 log m), i.e. only logarithmic dependence on the number of elements m (Section 4, Theorems 4.1-4.3).

Numerical simulations in the centroid setting show the empirical critical dimension growing sublinearly/logarithmically in m, in contrast to a prior polynomial-growth curve, supporting the O(k^2 log m) bound rather than a cubic dependency (Figure 1).

ZumBSRsRbE.text: L2M consists of a transformer-based stage-1 sequence model that produces uncertainty-calibrated beliefs under missingness, followed by a stage-2 greedy acquisition policy that maximizes conditional mutual information via a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation (Section 4).
Theorem 3.4 establishes identifiability of the conditional mutual information acquisition objective under missing-at-random, exclusion-restriction, and positivity assumptions (Theorem 3.4).
Theorem 4.2 proves that minimizing the L2M sequence loss recovers the step-wise CMI-optimal feature-acquisition policy at every query, i.e. per-query Bayes-optimality (Theorem 4.2).

On real-world tabular benchmarks including Metabric (breast cancer), MiniBooNE, and MIMIC-IV (length-of-stay, mortality, readmission), a single pretrained L2M model matches or surpasses task-specific baselines such as GDFS, DIME, and DQN without per-task retraining (Section 5, Figure 4).

L2M's advantage over task-specific baselines is largest in settings with shorter context lengths and higher rates of retrospective missingness, and the model exhibits length generalization on synthetic Gaussian-process regression tasks despite training on fixed sequence lengths (Figure 5).

KH2KhgpCcY.text: On Colored MNIST, DCFM-A and DCFM-B achieve FID scores of 11.41 and 12.24 in the IID setting and 9.29 and 9.15 in the non-IID setting on novel attribute combinations, versus 20.83 (FedFlow), 16.38 (DDM+L), and 19.13 (DFD+L) IID FID (Table 1).

On robotic cube-manipulation planning, DCFM-A and DCFM-B reach novel-composition success rates of 56.33% and 53.33% (IID) and 53.0% and 54.67% (non-IID), compared to 39.67%/9.0% for FedFlow+L and 38.33%/29.67% for DDM+L (Table 2).

DCFM-B requires only a constant per-client communication cost of 2 transmission units, versus 2T for standard federated learning and N-1 for the DDM/DFD baselines, where N is the number of clients (Table 3).

DCFM identifies and addresses two failure modes of naive decentralized flow matching—spurious correlation in local models and incompatible velocity fields—via global conditional-independence constraints across peers (Section 4, Section 5).
In a controlled Gaussian-mixture setting, prior decentralized methods fail to recover an unobserved data mode while DCFM successfully reconstructs it in both IID and non-IID partitions (Figure 3).
On a medical imaging dataset, DCFM improves the FID-versus-utility trade-off for modeling disease attribute co-occurrences relative to baselines (Figure 9).

nkVt0sY9HJ.text: The paper develops a unified mean-field theory for RNNs and DNNs in terms of representational kernels, describing fully trained networks in the feature learning (muP) regime, and casts training as Bayesian inference over sequences and patterns (abstract only).

In DNN-typical tasks, a phase transition occurs when the learning signal overcomes noise due to randomness in the weights: below this threshold RNNs and DNNs behave identically, while above it only RNNs develop correlated representations across timesteps (abstract only).
RNNs differ from DNNs only by weight sharing, which can be demonstrated by unrolling the RNN in time (abstract only).
For sequential tasks, the weight sharing in RNNs induces an inductive bias that aids generalization by interpolating unsupervised (unobserved) time steps (abstract only).

bjvLKXsTMK.text: Theorem 2.3 proves that VC-2-FWL (Variable-Constraint 2-dimensional Folklore Weisfeiler-Leman) has sufficient expressive power to recover optimal linear SDP solutions, in that identical stable colorings for indices (i,j) and (p,q) imply equal optimal solution values X*_ij = X*_pq (Theorem 2.3).

Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 give explicit counterexamples showing that standard VC-WL and higher-order VC-2-WL colorings fail on linear SDPs, since identical colorings can correspond to different optimal solution values (Propositions 2.1, 2.2).

The proposed VC-2-FMPNN architecture, which neuralizes the VC-2-FWL algorithm, achieves maximal expressivity matching VC-2-FWL (Proposition 2.5) and attains a test loss of 5.515e-5 on max-cut versus 0.119-0.216 for weaker GNN baselines (Table 1).

On real-world SDPLIB benchmarks, VC-2-FMPNN reaches training loss on the order of 1e-4 while weaker architectures such as VC-2-MPNN plateau above 0.2, indicating they cannot even overfit the simpler instances (Table 3).

Using VC-2-FMPNN predictions to warm-start the first-order SCS solver yields speedups of roughly 48-80% on SDPLIB instances, e.g., MCP500-1 drops from 328.5s to 77.5s (76.4% reduction) and MCP124-1 from 3.243s to 0.623s (80.7% reduction) (Table 5).
Proposition 2.4 shows VC-2-FWL converges in O((n^3 + nnz(A)) log n) time, which is asymptotically competitive with interior-point methods that require O(n^3.5 log(1/epsilon)) (Proposition 2.4).

fZvEZQWJrR.text: Theorem 4.1 shows that with significance levels allocated across splits summing to alpha, the proposed anytime-valid split test controls the probability of false splits over the entire stream lifetime under arbitrary, including non-stationary, data-dependent stopping (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 shows that when a candidate split maintains a persistent advantage Delta > 0, the procedure commits to that split in finite time at rate on the order of log(1/alpha)/Delta^2 (Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 4.3 shows that under stationary i.i.d. data with convex losses, expected risk decreases monotonically between splits and improves at each commitment, given a sufficient advantage threshold (Theorem 4.3).

On a synthetic RandomTree-generated i.i.d. stream, standard Hoeffding Trees exhibit repeated performance drops despite stationarity, whereas the anytime-valid methods maintain stable, monotone improvement (Figure 1).

Across 12 real-world streaming datasets (6 regression: bike, chick, fried, nzenergy, house, abalone; 6 classification: elec2, airlines, http-KDD99, creditcard, rbfm100k, hyper100k), the Anytime-Valid Forest (AVFB) achieves the best overall performance, surpassing Adaptive Random Forests (ARF) while producing substantially smaller trees than Hoeffding Tree variants (Section 5, experimental results).

wZMdhuTXoz.text: Theorem 4.2 establishes that latent-conditioning preserves the Bellman contraction property for the distributional Bellman operator, bounding the p-Wasserstein distance between conditioned return distributions by gamma times the distance between the unconditioned distributions (Theorem 4.2).

Theorem 5.2 provides a Sim2Real safety upper bound on deployed cost, J_c(pi_exp | z-hat) <= d + L_c * epsilon(N_real), relating deployment safety violation to the number of real-world interactions N_real (Theorem 5.2).
Theorem 5.4 guarantees the existence of a safe deployment risk quantile eta after sufficient real-world interaction (Theorem 5.4).

On the PointGoal2 Safety Gym benchmark, the proposed method achieves a cost of 8.86 +/- 0.85 compared to 35.92 +/- 5.45 for domain randomization, 11.20 +/- 1.65 for SPiDR, and 24.07 +/- 2.55 for robust RL, while maintaining competitive reward (Section 6, experimental results table).

On the autonomous driving (vehicle platooning) task, the proposed method achieves a cost of 16.80 +/- 3.33 and oscillation reduction of 0.47 +/- 0.13, outperforming domain randomization, SPiDR, robust RL, and a nominal baseline on the cost metric (Section 6, experimental results table).

gMLVFN9hl8.text: PyHealth 2.0 unifies 15+ datasets, 20+ clinical tasks, 25+ models, and 5+ interpretability methods (Attention-Grad, GIM, DeepLift, SHAP among them) spanning EHR, imaging, physiological signal, and genomic modalities (Section 3; Appendices F-J).

On MIMIC-IV in-hospital mortality prediction, PyHealth 2.0 with 16 workers processes data in 2,385 seconds versus 93,708 seconds for a naive pandas implementation, a roughly 39x speedup, while reducing peak memory from 146.23-457.42 GB (PyHealth 1.16) to 17.48-28.70 GB, about a 20x reduction (Table 3).

On drug recommendation and length-of-stay prediction tasks, PyHealth 2.0 still yields substantial speedups over pandas (4,725s to 569s, and 10,269s to 1,096s respectively), though smaller than the 39x mortality-prediction speedup (Tables 4 and 5).

PyHealth 2.0 reduces the code required to implement standard ML tasks (e.g., mortality prediction) to as few as 7 lines, down from 24 lines in PyHealth 1.16 and up to 51 lines with raw pandas (Table 2).
PyHealth 2.0 has an active open-source community of 400+ members and provides 50+ tutorials alongside multi-language support via an R interface (RHealth) (Section 5, Discussion).

5cIgeU4WOG.text: Per-instance noise schedules derived from an image's radially-averaged power spectral density achieve 1.42 FID versus 1.68 FID for the SiD2 baseline on ImageNet 256x256 class-conditional generation while using half as many denoising steps, 256 versus 512 (Table 1).
At 512x512 resolution the proposed spectrally-guided schedules reach 1.45 FID using 320 steps, compared to 1.53 FID for the SiD2 Flop Heavy baseline using 512 steps (Table 1).

The mixed schedule that averages frequency-focused and power-focused variants (Eq. 21) is necessary: using either variant alone degrades FID to 5.16 or 5.18 versus 1.42 for the full mixed schedule (Table 2).

Substituting the learned Gaussian Mixture Model spectrum sampler with the ground-truth power spectrum changes FID only marginally, from 1.42 to 1.43, showing the learned sampler recovers nearly all of the achievable gain (Table 2).
The FID advantage of the proposed schedules over baseline schedules widens as the number of inference steps decreases, with the largest gains observed in the 32-128 step regime (Figure 3).

x2eaMhqfcK.text: On Gemma-2-2B-IT with a 5% forget set from the TOFU benchmark, RMU, GradAscent, and GradDiff reduce Contextual QA performance to nearly zero even when the forgotten information is explicitly provided in the prompt (Section 3, Table 1).

Adding the proposed KL-divergence context-aware term to RMU, NPO, and UNDIAL improves Contextual QA LLM-judge scores from about 0.54 to 0.98 on Gemma-2-2B-IT and about 0.62 to 0.97 on Qwen3-8B on the 5% forget set (Section 4.2, Table 2, Figure 2).
The context-aware objective preserves forgetting effectiveness on Direct QA, changing scores by only about 2-3 percentage points relative to vanilla unlearning methods (Table 5).
Adding the context-aware term changes retain-set model utility by only -0.7% to 0.0% compared to vanilla unlearning (Section 5).
The improvement in Contextual QA performance from the context-aware term holds consistently across forget-set ratios of 1%, 5%, and 10% (Section 6.1, Figure 4).

gbJMAjXLZ4.text: Mantis is an 8-million-parameter Vision-Transformer-based foundation model pre-trained exclusively via contrastive self-supervised learning on time series data, in contrast to the supervised pre-training used by baseline UniTS (Section 2.4, Table 1).

In zero-shot feature extraction averaged over 3 seeds across 159 datasets, Mantis outperforms NuTime by 1.77% and MOMENT by 1.53%, and achieves the best result on 74 of the 159 datasets versus 53 for MOMENT and 38 for NuTime (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

After fine-tuning on 131 datasets, Mantis achieves the highest performance among all compared foundation models, including GPT4TS (80M parameters), NuTime (2M parameters), and MOMENT (385M parameters), despite Mantis having only 8M parameters (Section 3.3, Figure 5).
Adding first-order differential features to the token generator improves zero-shot extraction performance in an ablation averaged over 159 datasets (Section 3.4, Figure 6).
Mantis without any post-hoc calibration achieves the lowest expected calibration error among compared methods, averaged over 131 datasets (Section 3.6, Figure 9).

2PFiFk3gWq.text: TINNs achieve 2.9x lower error than PirateNet with the SOAP optimizer on the Burgers equation and 2.2x lower error on the Allen-Cahn equation, evaluated across five benchmarks: Burgers, Allen-Cahn, Klein-Gordon, Korteweg-De Vries, and Wave (Table 2).

TINNs converge roughly 10.55x faster than PirateNet with SOAP on the Burgers equation while using only about 1,145-1,185 parameters, versus 309,440-534,981 parameters for competing baselines (Table 2).

Proposition 5.1 proves standard space-time PINNs are a restricted special case of TINNs, with temporal dependence entering only through the first-layer bias, making TINNs strictly more expressive for a fixed model size (Proposition 5.1).
When trained with Adam instead of Levenberg-Marquardt, TINNs remain competitive with baselines, indicating accuracy gains stem from the architecture rather than the optimizer alone (Table 3).
Under Levenberg-Marquardt training, TINNs outperform comparable subMLP and standard MLP baselines, demonstrating a structural benefit beyond the choice of optimizer (Table 4).

On the viscous Burgers equation, TINNs show substantially smaller train-validation gaps and smoother loss decay than vanilla PINNs, indicating reduced overfitting and improved optimization stability (Figure 5).

ozV2cpEgnZ.text: At 2-bit precision on LongBench, PatternKV achieves an average score of 45.33 on Llama-3.1-8B versus 44.33 for KIVI, and 51.61 versus 51.48 on Llama-3.1-70B (Table 1).
On the Long-CoT benchmark (AIME, AMC) at 2-bit precision, PatternKV improves accuracy by about 10% on average over KIVI, e.g. Qwen-7B AIME25 Avg@8 of 30.42% versus KIVI's 27.92% (Table 2).
At 4-bit precision, PatternKV shows only a 0.08% average accuracy drop relative to FP16 on LongBench (Table 7, Appendix G).
Removing the V-cache adaptive thresholding component causes catastrophic degradation, dropping LongBench performance from 45.33 to 24.67 and GSM8K accuracy to 0.30 (Table 3).
PatternKV increases throughput by 1.4x and supports 1.25x larger batch sizes relative to FP16 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Figure 6).

jeCyxur8XB.text: Introduces the ctfIDu+ algorithm for identifying a counterfactual query from arbitrary Layer 3 (counterfactual) data and proves it is complete (Section 4).

Establishes completeness results characterizing exactly which counterfactual quantities are identifiable when the input consists of counterfactual (Layer 3) distributions, extending prior Layer 1/2-based identification theory (Section 3, Theorems 3.1-3.x).
Develops bounding results/algorithms that compute tight bounds on causal effects that are not point-identifiable from the available counterfactual data (Section 5, Theorems 5.1-5.4).

Proves a fundamental limit to exact causal inference: some counterfactual queries remain non-identifiable from any physically realizable (Layer 3) data, no matter how much such data is collected (Section 4-5).
Illustrates the identification and bounding procedures with worked examples involving explicit structural causal models (Examples 1-3).

3XXb2MK02l.text: Extracts alignment (post-training) data from open-weight models by prompting with chat-template structures and matching generations against candidate training data using neural embeddings rather than string matching (Section on Methodology).

Using gemini-embedding-001 similarity (threshold 0.95) finds at least 10x more memorized alignment data than approximate/verbatim string matching (threshold 0.90) on the same generations, showing string-matching metrics undercount memorization (Results).

For OLMo 2's SFT dataset (939k samples), generates 1M model samples and recovers a significant fraction of the training set, including near-perfect semantic matches with only partial string overlap (e.g., embedding score 0.986 vs. string-match score 0.699 on a single example) (Section 4, SFT extraction).

For Open-Reasoner-Zero's RL-trained model, generates 100k samples and extracts verbatim RL training prompts despite the PPO training objective not explicitly incentivizing memorization, with training-prompt likelihoods increasing from about 10^-11 to 10^-5 after RL post-training (Section 5, RL extraction).

Distilling a base model on the extracted synthetic alignment data recovers performance close to the original post-trained model, e.g., BBH 0.4953 to 0.5161, MMLU 0.6133 to 0.6052, and GSM8K 0.7407 to 0.7847 (baseline vs. extracted-data-trained model) (Results table, distillation experiments).

3V1dG9Jp8E.text: TopBench comprises 779 samples spanning four sub-tasks: single-point prediction (274 queries), decision making (186 queries), treatment effect analysis (105 queries), and ranking/filtering (214 queries) (Section on Benchmark Composition).

TopBench sources tables from three domains (healthcare, finance, daily consulting) with table sizes ranging from under 1,000 rows to over 6 million rows, and balances regression vs. classification objectives (384 vs. 395 queries) and user-centric vs. data-holder query perspectives (290 vs. 489 queries) (Dataset construction section).
The strongest evaluated model, Gemini 3 Flash, achieves only 0.65 accuracy on the single-point prediction sub-task, with most models scoring below 0.60 accuracy overall (Results/Main experiments).

Finds that accurate intent disambiguation (recognizing that a query requires prediction rather than retrieval) is a prerequisite for models to activate predictive reasoning modes, and models often default to simple lookup on implicit-prediction queries (Analysis section).

Agentic workflows that use code execution generally outperform pure text-based reasoning on TopBench tasks, though some models still misinterpret implicit predictive intent as simple lookup even in the agentic setting (Section on Agentic vs. Text-Based Evaluation).

opfSL15Uc4.text: Proves (Theorem 1) that under diffusion scaling (residual weight ~1/sqrt(L)) with RMS token normalization, the discrete-depth Transformer token dynamics converge in distribution to a system of SDEs on the unit sphere driven by common matrix-valued Brownian noise (Section 3, Theorem 1).

Proves (Theorem 2) a sharp phase transition for two-token dynamics: tokens collapse to a single cluster when d-2 >= cosh(2*beta), but antipodal (two-cluster) configurations emerge with positive probability when d-2 < cosh(2*beta), where d is token dimension and beta is the interaction/inverse-temperature strength (Theorem 2).

Shows via Proposition 1 that in a hybrid model, initialization noise below an explicit threshold epsilon^2 = 2*e^(-beta) still permits reaching cluster configurations unreachable by the corresponding deterministic (zero-noise) dynamics, demonstrating stochasticity prevents the single-cluster collapse predicted by deterministic mean-field models (Proposition 1).

Validates the theoretical phase boundary numerically with roughly 40,000 simulated trajectories, confirming antipodal clustering persists for N>=3 tokens as well as the two-token case (Section 6, experiments).

Reports CIFAR-10 experiments in which random (stochastic) initialization of Transformer layers outperforms identity initialization, supporting the theoretical claim that initialization stochasticity is beneficial rather than merely a nuisance (Section 6).

vSRh1qU5sH.text: Shows transformers learn to attend over sparse, statistically-weighted historical positions through a sequence of distinct stages, each stage corresponding to acquisition of a specific attention pattern, without any explicit curriculum (Section 3).

Proves (Theorem 1, Section 3.2) that under symmetric initialization, the coupled gradient dynamics of attention heads first converge to learning the single most statistically important pattern, and (Theorem 2) bounds how far the dynamics can deviate from this symmetric trajectory over finite training time.

Proves (Theorems 3 and 4, Section 3.3) that after this initial competitive phase, a cooperative phase follows in which heads specialize onto distinct patterns, with dynamics provably converging to learning the second-most-important pattern once cooperation begins.

Empirically demonstrates the competitive-to-cooperative transition via attention-pattern snapshots at training steps t=0, 60, 300, and 1000 (Figure 2) and via KL-divergence curves showing stage-wise convergence to simpler hypothesis classes before more complex ones (Figure 3).

Shows that reducing training dataset size causes models to learn fewer stages, interpreted as an implicit regularization effect of the finite-data training trajectory leading to a misspecified (simpler) learned model (Figure 5).

tRbgtWwmHB.text: DockSmith achieves 39.72% Fail-to-Pass and 58.28% Commit Rate on Multi-Docker-Eval, surpassing the previous open-source upper bound of 37.7% F2P (Table 1).
Language-level Fail-to-Pass performance varies substantially, from 63.33% on Go and 51.28-51.67% on Python/JavaScript down to 15.56-41.11% on other languages (Table 2).

Mixing DockSmith-built environments with SWE data yields transfer gains of up to +2.25 points on SWE-bench Verified, +2.09 points on SWE-bench Multilingual, and +3.37 points on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Figure 2).

Adding 0.5x SWE data to Docker-only training raises SWE-bench Verified from 33.50% to 47.45% and Terminal-Bench from 7.16% to 10.11%, while Multi-Docker-Eval score also improves from 34.43% to 35.63% (Table 3).
Acceptance Shaping combined with a Complexity Curriculum in the trajectory filtering ablation raises average Fail-to-Pass from a 32.24% baseline to 34.93% (Table 4).

The agentic Docker-building pipeline reduces total pipeline errors by 42.5% (from 3,757 to 2,161), including a 46.7% reduction in Dockerfile generation errors and a 50.6% reduction in test analysis errors (Table 5).

K1EPPO9t2c.text: The paper formulates learning the ambiguity set for OT-DRO as a bilevel problem in which the upper level tunes the ambiguity-set geometry parameter theta and the lower level solves a standard OT-DRO problem (Section 4.2).

Theorem 5.1 establishes that the proposed hypergradient descent procedure converges to a critical point of the bilevel problem under mild conditions, including square-summable step sizes (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1).

Algorithm 1 computes hypergradients through the nonsmooth conservative implicit function theorem, allowing differentiation through conic (OT-DRO) programs without assuming the solution map is continuously differentiable (Section 5, Algorithm 1).

In portfolio optimization experiments with k=2, J=30, n_b=20, gamma=0.05, beta=0.1, the relative improvement of the learned ambiguity set over a fixed Wasserstein ball increases as sample size decreases (Section 6.1, Figure 2).

Figure 3 shows the learned ambiguity set still enforces the coverage constraint, containing the true data-generating distribution with the specified high probability despite being shaped to reduce loss (Section 6.1, Figure 3).

Across 10 independent linear regression trials, the learned decision-focused ambiguity set consistently yields less conservative (lower average loss) decisions than baseline OT-DRO ambiguity sets (Section 6.2, Figure 5).

Cqq3HGRIuM.text: The LLM-based system establishes a new certified lower bound of 0.8559 for the Steiner ratio in the Gilbert-Pollak conjecture, improving on the 0.824 bound of Chung and Graham (1985) and approaching the conjectured value of sqrt(3)/2 ≈ 0.866 (Section 5, Figure 1).

Theorem 9 (Trapped Regular Point Theorem) and Theorem 14 (Valid 4-Point Steiner Tree Theorem) are the two structural lemmas the LLM agent must establish to certify the improved lower bound (Section 4.2.1, Section 4.2.2).
The full iterative search-and-verify process converges to the reported bound in about 12 rounds, consuming roughly 0.5 million LLM tokens total (about 35K tokens per round) (Section 5).
Reasoning (LLM proposal) time totals about 4.6 hours while reward-model verification computation totals about 11.7 hours, for a total compute cost of a few hundred dollars (Section 5).
Figure 9 tracks the ratio improving across iterations and compares the trajectory against prior state-of-the-art bounds from the literature (Section 5, Figure 9).

y03xxeUkgN.text: On RoboCasa, adding Fourier features improves success rate from 13.2% to 33.9% for the PointPatch encoder, from 19.0% to 30.1% for PCM, and from 14.8% to 27.9% for DP3 (Table 6, Section 5).
On ManiSkill3, Fourier features give smaller but consistent gains, improving PointPatch from 48.6% to 55.8% and PointPatch-attn from 49.0% to 54.2% (Table 7, Section 5).

In real-robot evaluation across 44 tasks, adding Fourier features raises the overall normalized score from 14.8% to 40.2%, including a Cup-Stacking score improving from 0 to 0.625/2.0 (Table 8, Section A.6).
The Fourier mapping uses L=16 frequency bands spanning wavelengths from 4.0 m to 2.0 cm, producing 96 Fourier features per 3D Cartesian point (Section 3.4).

Even under extreme Gaussian jitter (sigma=5.0 cm) that removes fine geometric detail, policies using Fourier features still achieve 24% success versus 13% for Cartesian features, indicating a benefit beyond encoding geometric detail alone (Figure 7, Section 6).
Fourier feature benefits diminish when point clouds are sparse (only 2k points), confirming that the advantage depends on the availability of geometric detail (Figure 6, Section 6).

fh6XBnjFlv.text: On the LIBERO benchmark, adding RoboFlow4D improves a Diffusion Policy (DP) baseline from 78.9% (Spatial suite) to an 85.1% average success rate (+6.2 points), and improves a DiT baseline from 83.7% to 87.7% average (+4.0 points) (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On ManiSkill3, RoboFlow4D improves DP from a 12.3% average baseline to 22.0% (+9.7 points) and DiT from 12.7% to 23.7% (+11.0 points) (Table 2, Section 4.2).

In real-world experiments, RoboFlow4D raises DP success rate from 27.5% to 40.0% (+12.5 points) and DiT from 32.5% to 43.8% (+11.3 points), while reducing average task completion time by about 1.4 seconds (Table 5, Section 4.4).

The slow-fast architecture predicts the full flow trajectory at a lower frequency while the action-control policy executes multiple action chunks at a higher frequency between flow updates (Section 3.4).
Table 4 shows performance remains stable across fast/slow update ratios r in {4, 2, 1}, validating robustness of the slow-fast collaboration scheme (Table 4, Section 4.3).

The full pipeline runs with a flow-prediction latency of 0.68 seconds and a policy forward-pass latency of 0.20 seconds using a 0.76-billion-parameter model, yielding roughly 120x speedup over modular flow-based pipelines (Section 4, Appendix A).

Uuh2Sk0mh0.text: NavOL's online rollout-update loop uses a trajectory generator built on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) with a DDPM scheduler paired with a critic network sharing the visual backbone, producing 24-step waypoint sequences per rollout (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

During online data collection across 50 3D-Front scenes on 8 RTX 4090 GPUs with 256 parallel environments, NavOL collects over 2,000 trajectories per hour, each averaging more than 400 steps, using 128 rollout steps per iteration with an expert action probability of ρ=0.8 (Section 4.1).
On the NavDP benchmark, NavOL achieves 80.4% mean success rate (mSR) and 76.3% mean SPL (mSPL), versus 77.8% mSR and 74.8% mSPL for the NavDP baseline (Table 1).
On the NavOL benchmark, NavOL reaches 69.0% mSR and 63.7% mSPL, substantially outperforming NavDP's 42.2% mSR (Table 2).

Ablations show that removing expert rollout (setting ρ=1) drops success rate to 43.9%, and training from scratch instead of from a NavDP initialization drops success rate to 48.3% versus 69.0% (Table 4).
In real-world deployment on a Unitree Go2 robot, NavOL achieves 8/10 success in an office environment, 7/10 in a gym, and 10/10 in a corridor (Table 3).

D1ipe7QR0N.text: Move-Then-Operate decouples robotic manipulation into two behavioral phases, coarse relocation ('move') and contact-critical interaction ('operate'), implemented as a dual-expert policy with a learned phase-selector router where only one expert is active at inference (Figure 3).
On the RoboTwin2 benchmark, Move-Then-Operate achieves a 68.9% average success rate versus 44.75% for the monolithic π₀ baseline, an improvement of 24.1 percentage points (Table 1).
On contact-critical subtasks, Move-Then-Operate reaches 99% success on Click Bell (vs. 44% for π₀) and 70% success on Press Stapler (vs. 62% for π₀) (Table 1).
Despite using roughly 10x less training data, Move-Then-Operate matches or exceeds a π₀.₅* model on these tasks, reaching 93% on Press Stapler (vs. 80%) and 99% on Click Bell (vs. 75%) (Table 2).

Move-Then-Operate reaches peak performance in about 40% fewer training steps than the baseline schedule, with contact-intensive tasks converging near peak by 60k steps versus the baseline's 100k+20k fine-tuning steps (Figure 5, Figure 6).

An ablation replacing the learned phase router with random phase selection drops success rate to 25.63%, and reversing the routing decision drops it further to 8.88%, versus 68.88% for the learned router, demonstrating expert specialization (Table 3).

RVPqygyGRu.text: DiffCLF reformulates energy-based model training as multinomial logistic regression across noise levels, jointly optimizing the energy function and a log-normalizing constant implemented as a per-timestep bias on the last network layer (Equation 10).

On synthetic 40-mode Gaussian mixtures across dimensions 8-128, DiffCLF attains classification loss values of roughly 4.0-4.4 while denoising score matching (DSM) and CttSM baselines reach 22-383, while Fisher Divergence and MMD remain comparable across methods (Table 1).

Figure 1 shows that unlike score-based estimators, whose scores remain nearly identical across Gaussian mixtures with different mode weights, DiffCLF's classification posterior varies with the mixture weights, directly addressing mode blindness (Figure 1).

For model composition via OR/AND operations and for Boltzmann Generator sampling with Sequential Monte Carlo, DiffCLF reduces Sliced Wasserstein distance by roughly 2-3x versus DSM and achieves substantially lower Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances across tested dimensions (Figure 5).

For free energy estimation of Alanine Dipeptide (ALDP) solvation via Thermodynamic Integration, DiffCLF yields 29.02±0.41 kcal/mol against a reference value of 29.43±0.01 kcal/mol, more accurate than a DSM baseline's 27.30±0.45 kcal/mol (Table 2).

The binary-classification variant of DiffCLF requires only one additional neural network evaluation versus standard DSM, keeping computational cost comparable across methods (Section on computational efficiency).

wwqrH4mwGq.text: Theorem 2.1 establishes a sample complexity bound for estimating a discrete distribution under the ℓ∞ norm (Theorem 2.1).
Theorem 2.2 gives a refined bound that improves upon prior ℓ∞ estimation analyses, including the results of Blanchard et al. (2023) (Theorem 2.2).
Theorems 2.5 and 2.6 extend the estimation bounds to more general settings and parameter regimes beyond the basic case covered in Theorem 2.1 (Theorem 2.5, Theorem 2.6).
The paper's improved bounds connect to information-theoretic quantities such as KL divergence, drawing on techniques related to Garivier (2011) (Section 2).
Appendix results Theorem A.1 through Theorem A.8, particularly A.2, A.3, and A.6, provide the auxiliary lemmas underlying the main sample complexity proofs (Appendix A).

t7oQT3uX66.text: In Gemma 3 27B on TriviaQA, activation steering shows high-confidence injections at the Post-Answer-Newline-Layer (PANL) position peak in effect at layers 21-25, while injections at the Confidence-Colon (CC) position peak at layers 30-35, indicating sequential information flow from PANL to CC (Figure 2).

Activation patching experiments show that restoring clean activations at PANL or CC after corrupting answer tokens substantially recovers confidence metrics, with CC patching achieving near-complete recovery at later layers (Figure 3).

Attention-blocking experiments with a minimal numeric (0-9) confidence prompt find that blocking attention from CC directly to the question and answer tokens produces almost no disruption (~10% change rate), while blocking CC's attention to PANL produces a 21% token change rate, and blocking PANL's attention to answer tokens produces 20% disruption at layers 22-28, ruling out just-in-time computation at CC (Figure 7).
Linear probes on residual stream activations show that answer correctness (AUROC) and verbal confidence magnitude (R²) are decodable from PANL at earlier layers than from CC (Figure 6).

Token log-probabilities explain only 8.4% of variance in verbal confidence (r=0.29) despite achieving better correctness discrimination (AUROC=0.75), whereas cached PANL/CC representations explain substantially more variance in verbal confidence, indicating richer answer-quality evaluation beyond log-probabilities (Section on variance partitioning).

Gemma 3 27B's verbalized confidence achieves an ECE of 0.12 and AUROC of 0.71 on TriviaQA, with the temporal precedence pattern (PANL preceding CC) replicating in Qwen 2.5 7B and across categorical and numeric confidence prompt formats (Section on models and datasets).

1twve5mNUU.text: On the Open LLM Leaderboard (ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, Winogrande, GSM8K), TBPO-Q attains the best average score of 60.95 on Mistral-7B-v0.1, beating DPO (59.30), TDPO (58.41), TIS-DPO (59.66), and BPO (58.29) (Table 1).
On Llama-3-8B, TBPO-A achieves the best average Open LLM Leaderboard score of 70.50, ahead of TDPO (67.91), DPO (66.24), TIS-DPO (66.82), and BPO (65.72) (Table 1).
On MT-Bench pairwise judging, TBPO achieves higher win rates with low loss rates than the sequence- and token-level baselines (Figure 1).
On Anthropic HH-RLHF, TBPO obtains superior length-controlled win rates while producing shorter responses than baselines (Figure 2).
Despite being trained only on UltraFeedback, TBPO generalizes to the out-of-domain TL;DR summarization task, outperforming baselines there as well (Figure 4).
On 100 UltraFeedback test prompts, TBPO shifts the predictive-entropy/Self-BLEU/Distinct-1 Pareto frontier toward higher diversity while keeping Self-BLEU favorable relative to baselines (Figure 3).

nG9bsQq2N6.text: PerturbODE models cell-state trajectories with a neural ODE whose drift is Aσ(α∘(By−β)) + Σ s_j δ_j − Wy, from which the gene regulatory network is derived in closed form as G = A·diag(α)·B (Section 3, Eq. 1-2).

On held-out intervention prediction, PerturbODE achieves a Wasserstein-2 distance of 84±183 and Pearson correlation of 0.67±0.14, versus 105±1 / 0.03±0.01 for NO-TEARS-LR and 396±232 / −0.03±0.02 for NO-TEARS (Table 1).

On SERGIO-simulated data (400-gene yeast GRN and ten 100-gene random DAGs, 10,100 cells across 101 intervention regimes), PerturbODE outperforms DCDFG and NO-TEARS variants in AUPRC, though DCDI performs best on the 400-gene yeast network (Figure 2).

On the TF Atlas dataset (817 genes, 1.1M cells, 1,836 TF overexpression interventions at day 7), PerturbODE with imperfect-intervention modeling achieves the highest recall (about 0.50) and lowest p-value (about 10^-3) among methods, significantly outperforming DCDFG, NO-TEARS, and NO-TEARS-LR (Figure 3).

Gene module analysis recovers seven validated modules, including modules 26, 53, 105, 136, and 152 linked to anterior-posterior axis specification and modules 18 and 172 linked to trophoblast/vascular endothelial differentiation (Section 4.2.1, Figure 20).
Edge-selection stability analysis across 133 train-validation splits shows roughly 50-70% consistency in recovered GRN edges (Appendix A.13, Figure 22).

AFqHVyanzY.text: MOPO solves a constrained optimization problem (Eq. 3) that maximizes a primary preference objective subject to lower-bound constraints on remaining objectives via Lagrangian duality with confidence-interval-based estimation (Section 2.1, Algorithm 1).

On synthetic benchmarks with a 3-action space and five preference structures (total order, partial order, antichain-style, pairwise-incomparable, and unobserved preferences), MOPO correctly recovers the optimal policy in every setting (Section 3.1, Figure 4).
In the synthetic Pareto-front experiment, MOPO's learned policies dominate DPO-based approaches and consistently lie closer to the true Pareto frontier (Section 3.2, Figure 6).

On the Helpful Assistant task (HH-RLHF, 160k prompts) fine-tuning a Phi-1.5 (1.3B parameter) model with LoRA over 'helpful', 'harmless', and 'humor' reward objectives, MOPO produces a more balanced three-objective trade-off than single-objective RLHF (Section 3.3, Figure 7).

On Reddit TL;DR summarization (14.9k posts, three reward models: pref1, no-hallucination, faithful, evaluated on 3k test prompts), MOPO achieves outer Pareto fronts compared to the RiC and HaM multi-objective baselines (Section 3.3, Figure 8).
Ablations varying the KL regularization τ over {0.1, 0.5, 1} and the constraint threshold parameter β show MOPO remains robust to suboptimal hyperparameter choices (Section 3.4, Figure 9).

Qc6OqkFAmO.text: The paper decomposes the total entropy S_tot^X of an unconditional pixel-space diffusion model into a total-correlation term TC(X) plus marginal contributions, showing TC(X) dominates because pixel intensities are strongly correlated (Section 2, Eq. 6-7).

For a conditional model of X given Y, the extra information injected relative to the unconditional model equals the mutual information I(X;Y) = S(X) − S(X|Y), and in image datasets this I(X;Y) is empirically much smaller than the total neural entropy S_NN^X, i.e. S_NN^X >> I(X;Y) (Section 2, Eq. 9-11).

On CIFAR-10, the neural entropy rate curves show a sharp rise as s→0, indicating that most information (including the class-specific correlation) is consumed in the final, high-curvature steps of the reverse process that resolve small-scale perceptual detail (Section 5, Figure 3).

Using a diffusion autoencoder with two latents Z_per and Z_sem split at a threshold τ, t-SNE of Z_sem on MNIST shows clear digit clusters while Z_per shows no such structure, and I(Z_sem;Y) is high while I(Z_per;Y) is low, confirming label information is concentrated in the semantic (early-time) latent rather than the perceptual (late-time) one (Section 5, Figure 5).

In a joint-Gaussian toy model (Figure 2), classifier-free guidance's modified score (1+w)∇log p(x_t,t|y) − w∇log p(x_t,t) increases the mutual information I(X;Y)_CFG as guidance weight w increases from 0 to 6, with the increase saturating faster when the dimensionality of Y is small relative to X (Section 4, Figure 2, Eq. 15).

The paper argues classifier-free guidance is effective because the guidance vector s_cl(y,t) is largest early in the reverse process (when semantic structure is being resolved) and diminishes as t decreases toward 0 (perceptual-detail-filling steps), explaining why CFG boosts semantic conditioning without degrading fine detail (Section 3, Eq. 14-15).

uZerXmyozE.text: GENEB evaluates 40 genomic foundation models on 100 DNA classification tasks spanning 13 functional categories using a unified linear-probing protocol scored by Matthews Correlation Coefficient (Section on Benchmark Scope, Table 3/Appendix B).
The task suite includes 30 histone modification tasks, 22 promoter tasks, 8 enhancer tasks, 8 DNA methylation tasks, 7 splice site tasks, and 6 lncRNA tasks, among others (Appendix B, Table 3).

Model parameter count correlates only weakly with aggregate macro-MCC (Spearman ρ=0.573, p<0.001), and in 25 cases a model at least 5x smaller outperforms a larger counterpart, showing scale gives inconsistent gains (Section 4, Figure 2).

Under few-shot (10-shot) evaluation, model rankings shift enough that the model that wins under full supervision is reranked in 8 of the 13 functional categories, demonstrating that aggregate leaderboards are unstable across evaluation regimes (Section 4, Figure 5).

In controlled architecture comparisons across six matched encoder/decoder pairs, transformer encoders outperform decoders by up to +0.127 macro-MCC, but task-specific exceptions occur, e.g. the state-space model eccDNAMamba outperforms GenomeOcean-500M by +0.124 on chromatin accessibility (Section 4).

0ophJB76sC.text: Self-play SWE-RL (SSR) trains a single LLM agent via reinforcement learning to alternately inject and repair bugs of escalating complexity, using only sandboxed repositories with source code and installed dependencies and no human-labeled issues or test commands (Section 3).
SSR improves SWE-bench Verified performance by +10.4 points over the base policy (Section 4).
SSR improves SWE-Bench Pro performance by +7.8 points over the base policy (Section 4).

SSR consistently outperforms a human-curated-data RL baseline throughout the training trajectory, despite self-play training on synthetically injected bugs specified via test patches rather than natural-language issue descriptions (Section 3, Section 4).
SSR generalizes to evaluation on natural-language bug descriptions that were never seen during self-play training, which only used test-patch-specified bugs (Section 3).
Ablation studies examine the contribution of individual self-play training components and configurations to overall agent performance (Appendix D, Appendix E).

fD36uwJ5oV.text: The paper derives a maximal-update-style parameterization (Table 1) governing learning rate and initialization scaling for router weights, expert biases, and MLP weights as width, depth, expert count, and expert size are varied in sparse Mixture-of-Experts transformers (Section 3).

A dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) analysis establishes a three-level mean-field hierarchy (across residual-stream neurons, expert population, and within-expert neurons) that justifies the proposed hyperparameter transfer rule for MoE models (Section 4).

Optimal base learning rate and initialization standard deviation, tuned on small MoE models, transfer across scaling of width, depth, expert count, and expert hidden multiplier at a fixed 1B-token training budget (Section 5, Figure 2).
Loss curves from small and large models trained with the transferred hyperparameters collapse onto each other in early training iterations (Section 5).
At fixed total parameter count, increasing the number of experts outperforms increasing individual expert size (Section 5, Figure 5).
Transfer is validated on models scaling from 51M to 2B+ total parameters on FineWeb (sparsity κ=1/4) and on C4 with sparsity κ=1/12 (Section 5, Figure 4).

ZMexYcAibv.text: SHINE generates a LoRA adapter for a downstream task from an in-context set of examples in a single forward pass, via Meta LoRA memory extraction followed by an M2P Transformer generation step (Section 3.2).
The M2P Transformer uses alternating row/column attention to achieve O(LM^2 + ML^2) complexity, saving up to 90% of FLOPs compared to full attention (Section 3.4).

On the MS MARCO multi-question-answering task, SHINE achieves an F1 score of 55.6 versus 33.0 for SFT-based adaptation, while reducing amortizable adaptation time from 29.3 seconds (SFT) to 0.3 seconds (Table 1).
Scaling M2P layers, Meta LoRA rank, and generated LoRA rank progressively reduces validation perplexity from 1.88 to 1.32 with no sign of a capacity bottleneck (Table 4).
Increasing the backbone LLM size yields significantly lower validation perplexity for SHINE-generated adapters (Section 5.4, Figure 8).

VCU3hGm0O6.text: Theorem 1 proves a nonvanishing Bayes-vs-conditional-independence separation for class-conditional Ising judge models under a Curie-Weiss framework: conditional-independence (CI) predictors incur constant error while the Bayes-optimal aggregator's error vanishes as the number of judges grows (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 extends the separation to settings with informative marginals, showing CI-based aggregation remains bounded away from Bayes-optimal performance asymptotically even when each individual judge outperforms random guessing (Theorem 2).

For the class-independent Ising model, the quadratic dependence terms cancel in the likelihood ratio, reducing the Bayes-optimal log-odds to a linear, correlation-adjusted weighted vote (Section 2.2).
CI-based label aggregation methods can flip the Bayes-optimal predicted label even while exactly matching each individual judge's marginal accuracy (Section 3).

On three real-world LLM-as-a-judge datasets (Relevance, Toxicity, Summarization) using six LLM judges (Claude Sonnet/Haiku 4.5, gpt-oss-120b, Llama variants, DeepSeek-R1), the class-dependent Ising aggregator attains test accuracies of 0.90, 0.79, and 0.68 respectively, exceeding the CI-weighted-majority-vote baseline's 0.82, 0.72, and 0.61 (Table 1, Section 4).

v4hQnJn6aN.text: LDARNet is a 120M-parameter hierarchical genomic foundation model that adapts H-Net-style dynamic chunking from autoregressive generation to masked language modeling, combining BiMamba-2 state-space layers with local attention and bidirectional routing (Section on architecture).
LDARNet replaces fixed k-mer or BPE tokenization with a learnable adaptive tokenizer that places segment boundaries via content-aware, dynamically predicted routing rather than fixed positions.

LDARNet wins on 11 of 18 Nucleotide Transformer benchmark tasks among models under 300M parameters, including best-overall results on 5 histone modification tasks (H3K4me1, H3K4me2, H3K4me3, H3K79me3, H4ac), outperforming models up to 20x larger.

LDARNet achieves 57.7 MCC on promoter/enhancer-related classification tasks in the Nucleotide Transformer suite, and wins on 3 of 9 Genomic Benchmarks tasks among compact models, including 96.3% accuracy on Human non-TATA Promoters.
A FLOPs-matched ablation with a fixed N=4 compression ratio shows learned dynamic-chunking boundaries outperform fixed-grid boundaries by up to 14 percentage points on histone modification tasks.
Boundaries discovered by the learnable tokenizer align, without supervision, with canonical regulatory motifs (TATA-box, CCAAT-box, GC-box) and splice junctions.

Wb6hWu2jDB.text: Vit_base_patch32_224 (32-pixel stem kernel) achieves up to a 506-rank robustness improvement over comparable models on Gaussian-noise-corrupted inputs, versus a 375-rank improvement for the 16-pixel-patch variant (Table 1, Section 3.1).

Noise attenuation from stem kernel size follows a quadratic decay bound γ(k) ≤ C/k², so doubling stem kernel size from 16 to 32 quarters the output noise energy, approximately -6 dB (Theorem 1, Section 3.2).

Reducing input resolution from 384² to 224² (downsampling factor s≈1.71) reduces noise energy to roughly 34% of its original value via the anti-aliased downsampling bound γ↓(s) ≤ C'/s² (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).

Average pooling is shown to be an unbiased noise estimator with variance decreasing as σ²/k, while max pooling incurs a positive bias with MSE growing logarithmically in window size, giving worse worst-case Lipschitz sensitivity (Theorem 3, Section 4.2).

CLIP-style preprocessing (smaller per-channel standard deviation, 0.261) amplifies worst-case pixel-space sensitivity by 1.91x relative to Inception-style/supervised-ViT preprocessing (0.5 std), corroborated by a 76.3% vs. 87.2% accuracy gap under noise on Oxford-IIIT Pet (Theorem 4 and Table 5, Section 5.1-5.2).

MEqmAlsKwS.text: On LLaVA-1.5 with greedy decoding, RUDDER-Beta reduces CHAIR_S from 48.6% to 39.5% (a 19% relative reduction) and CHAIR_I from 13.6% to 10.5% (a 23% relative reduction) versus vanilla decoding (Table 1).

Averaged across all tested models and decoding strategies, RUDDER achieves a 33.2% relative reduction in sentence-level hallucination (CHAIR_S) and a 28.6% relative reduction in object-level hallucination (CHAIR_I) (Table 1).
On the POPE benchmark with LLaVA-1.5 greedy decoding, RUDDER improves accuracy from 85.34% to 86.53% and F1 from 84.91% to 86.03% (Table 2).
RUDDER-Beta maintains 96.0% of vanilla decoding throughput (54.9 vs. 56.7 tokens/second on LLaVA-1.5), substantially higher than the competing VISTA method's 58.1% throughput retention (Table 4).

The CARD vector extracts visual evidence from self-attention residual updates during a single prefill pass with negligible additional computational overhead, requiring no extra forward passes (Section 3.2).
RUDDER is evaluated and shown effective across LLaVA-1.5-7B, Idefics2-8b-base, and InstructBLIP architectures (Table 1).

Eeo0uBd5mt.text: OneTrackerV2-L384 achieves 76.1 AUC on LaSOT, 88.6 AUC on TrackingNet, 81.3 SR@0.75 on GOT-10k, and 95.3 AUC on TNL2K for RGB tracking (Table 2).
For RGB+X tracking, OneTrackerV2 reaches 67.5 F-score on DepthTrack, 79.4 AUC on LasHeR (RGB+T), 83.5 AUC on VisEvent (RGB+E), and 63.7 AUC on RGBT234 (Table 2).
The compressed variant OneTrackerV2-B224-Compress achieves a 2.2x inference speedup, reaching 159 FPS, while incurring only about a 2% performance drop on both RGB and RGB+X benchmarks (Table 5).
Under modality-missing scenarios, OneTrackerV2-B224 outperforms the SUTrack baseline by 7.4 points F-score on DepthTrack (56.9 vs. 49.5) and 5.1 points AUC on LasHeR (52.7 vs. 47.6) (Table 3).

The Meta Merger module adds only 0.4% additional FLOPs and 0.9% additional parameters while enabling robust cross-modal fusion, whereas the Dual MoE module adds 14.6% parameters and 3.5% FLOPs for its performance gains (Table 4).

I2nCwyGK6k.text: Augmenting text-based POI embeddings with mobility-derived ME-POI embeddings improves opening-hours prediction F1 by up to 16.2%, visit-intent classification F1 by up to 81.9%, busyness-estimation MAE reduction by up to 24.7%, and price-level classification F1 by up to 75.1% over text-only baselines (Tables 1-2, Section 4.1).

ME-POIs consistently outperforms mobility-only baselines across both dynamic (busyness, visit intent) and static (opening hours, price level, permanent closure) map enrichment tasks (Tables 3-4, Section 4.2).

The framework's Multi-Scale Distribution Transfer component, which propagates temporal visitation patterns from frequent to sparsely-visited POIs, is shown via ablation to be particularly valuable for low-visit-count locations (Table 5, Figures 3-4).

Permanent closure detection is evaluated as a binary classification task restricted to the Los Angeles metro area, distinct from the other four tasks evaluated more broadly (Section 4.1, Appendix A.1.2).

fs9KaJyhRO.text: Heavy-tail-guided layerwise learning rates (LLR) reach comparable validation performance to a uniform learning rate baseline using 33-50% fewer training tokens, corresponding to an approximate 1.5x training speedup (Figure 8).
On LLaMa-1B evaluated on seven commonsense reasoning zero-shot tasks, LLR raises average accuracy from 47.09% (uniform baseline) to 49.02%, a 1.93 percentage-point gain (Table 3).

On LLaMa-3B trained with 30B tokens, LLR improves average zero-shot accuracy from 48.58% to 50.61% (+2.03 points); on LLaMa-1B trained with 100B tokens, LLR improves accuracy from 51.16% to 51.86% (+0.70 points) (Table 4).

LLR inherits nearly optimal learning rate settings directly from the standard uniform learning rate tuning, enabling low additional tuning overhead and easy integration into existing training pipelines without further hyperparameter search (Figure 1).

Consistent validation perplexity improvements from LLR are demonstrated across model scales from 60M to 1B parameters on the FineWeb dataset under Chinchilla scaling law compute allocations (Table 2).

Iww9TICvKj.text: Theorem 3.2 establishes almost-sure stability (sup_n ||z_n|| < infinity) for two-timescale stochastic approximation iterates driven by Markovian noise, without requiring projection operators (Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 3.3 proves that the fast-timescale iterate x_n converges to the equilibrium map lambda(y_n), i.e. lim_n ||x_n - lambda(y_n)|| = 0, with joint convergence to (lambda(y*), y*) (Theorem 3.3).

Lemma 3.1 shows the fast-timescale iterate norm is controlled by the running maximum of the slow-timescale iterate, ||x_n|| <= K(1+||y_n^max||) almost surely, which is the key technical device enabling the stability proof (Lemma 3.1).

Theorem 7.2 gives the first almost-sure convergence proof for temporal difference learning with gradient correction and eligibility traces (TDC(lambda)) under off-policy, Markovian sampling conditions (Section 7, Theorem 7.2, Definition 7.1).

The convergence analysis relies on assumptions B.1-B.7 in the appendix, including a unique stationary distribution for the Markov noise chain (Assumption B.1) and learning-rate timescale separation lim_n beta(n)/alpha(n) = 0 (Assumption B.2) (Appendix B).

sb4WSZfAsL.text: When trained on compositional traces of depth L=3, SFT+RL on compound traces reaches 42.6% accuracy on out-of-distribution compositional tasks, versus 14.8% for SFT+RL trained on isolated atomic modules, a gap of +27.8 percentage points (Section 4.2).
Theorem 3.1 establishes identifiability of latent selection variables underlying reasoning modules under local distinguishability and neighborhood coverage conditions (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.4 shows compositional generalization is enabled by 'local witnesses': when training data contains compatible module configurations, models succeed at novel recombinations at test time (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).

Propositions 3.2-3.3 formalize a division of labor in which supervised fine-tuning (SFT) supplies raw reasoning modules but leaves them entangled, while reinforcement learning (RL) post-training decomposes traces into reusable atoms by enriching identification-critical local events (Section 3, Propositions 3.2-3.3).

The optimal SFT-RL data pairing is disjoint: SFT should cover all atomic modules through compositional traces while RL exploration should extend beyond the SFT support region to maximize compositional generalization, as shown across compositional depths L=1 to L=8 (Section 4.5, Figure 3).

UNVBuVmLDE.text: On Waterbirds, CCDB attains 90.48% worst-group accuracy, comparable to the bias-annotation-using GroupDRO baseline's 91.40% (Table IV).

On CelebA, CCDB attains 85.27% worst-group accuracy versus 88.5% for XRM, and on CivilComments, CCDB attains 75.00% versus 79.10% for SELF, all without bias annotations or foundation-model predictions (Table IV).
On synthetic benchmarks at 0.5% bias-conflict ratio, CCDB reaches 83.20% on cMNIST (vs. 75.13% for uLA) and 55.07% on cCIFAR10 (vs. 34.39% for uLA) (Table III).

The method's intra-class sample reweighting maximizes the conditional entropy of the label given spurious factors to achieve class-conditional distribution balancing, implemented via Algorithm 1 in the two-stage pipeline described in Section III-B (Section III-A, III-B, Algorithm 1).

An ablation study (Section IV-C) and analysis of learned sample weights (Section IV-D) show the reweighting strategy dismantles spurious correlations automatically, without expensive bias annotations or pretrained foundation models (Section IV-C, IV-D).

pUs1gPPup4.text: AlignG achieves an F@100 of 23.8 under SGDet on VG-150, a +1.4 improvement over baseline, while also outperforming the PE-Net baseline by +5.2 in mean recall (Table results, VG-150 SGDet).
AlignG achieves an F@100 of 19.5 under SGDet on GQA-200, a +2.7 improvement over baseline, alongside a +10.8 gain in mean recall over PE-Net (Table results, GQA-200 SGDet).

The method uses cross-attention aggregation to build context-conditioned prototypes from relation embeddings, followed by GRU-based prototype updates and reverse cross-attention to recalibrate relation features under the adapted prototypes (Section on Core Mechanism).

An alignment loss anchored to static prototypes is used to prevent semantic drift, enabling selective semantic reorganization of predicates while preserving dataset-level semantic coherence (Design Rationale section).

Ablation results show the GRU-based prototype updater achieves the best F@100 (47.5) on VG-150 PredCls, balancing adaptability against stability compared to simpler fusion approaches that achieve higher recall but lower fairness metrics (Ablation study, VG-150 PredCls).

ZXYcM3QuAR.text: Density-Aware Translation (DAT) achieves 83.33% worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds with CLIP ViT-L/14, surpassing prior methods by 4-14 percentage points and reducing the worst-group/average accuracy gap to 6.42% (Table 1).

On CelebA, DAT achieves 84.94% worst-group accuracy with only a 1.19% gap to average accuracy, and the label-free variant DAT* achieves comparable performance without spurious-attribute annotations (Table 2).

DAT rescales image-text similarity scores by a density ratio computed via a Simplified Local Outlier Factor (SLOF), s-tilde_{y,a}(x) = s_{y,a}(x) / (D_{y,a}(z) + epsilon)^lambda, suppressing overconfident scores in sparse embedding regions (Method/Section on Key Technical Innovation).

On the COVID-19 medical imaging benchmark, DAT improves worst-group accuracy by over 20 percentage points to 65.22%, and on FMoW achieves 27.75% worst-group accuracy with a significant average-worst-group gap reduction (Medical & Multi-Label Domains results).

The authors prove that under a Kent (Fisher-Bingham) distribution assumption on CLIP's anisotropic embedding space, DAT reinstates anisotropy-sensitive log-likelihood terms that plain cosine similarity ignores, yielding Bayes-optimal alignment (Theoretical Contribution section).

DAT runs in approximately 150 seconds on an H100 GPU, versus 950+ seconds for the TIE baseline, while requiring no fine-tuning and generalizing across CLIP variants and other multimodal models such as ALIGN and AltCLIP (Practical Advantages section).

k2DxnK87ml.text: B-NRDEs use three distinct Hopf algebra structures (shuffle for Stratonovich integration, Grossmann-Larson for Itô dynamics in flat space, and Munthe-Kaas-Wright for Itô dynamics on manifolds) to remain well-defined where standard NRDEs fail (Section 2.2, Table 1).

On rough Bergomi volatility generative modelling, B-NRDE achieves the best Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances at horizons 128 and 256 timesteps (6.89±1.81 and 6.91±0.98 ×10⁻²), outperforming NRDE and log-NCDE baselines without lead-lag augmentation (Section 4.2, Table 3).

On sim-to-real SO(3) rotation forecasting on the Oxford Multimotion Dataset, B-NRDE achieves a rotation geodesic error of 3.23 degrees using only two solver steps, versus SG-NCDE's 2.93 degrees using twenty solver steps (Section 4.3, Table 4).

On SPD-manifold mean-reverting Itô diffusion dynamics, B-NRDE attains a 1-Wasserstein eigenvalue distance of 5.73±0.20 ×10⁻² at horizon 128, a 56.2% average improvement over Euclidean log-NCDE baselines (Section 4.4, Table 5).

Algorithm 1 precomputes a depth-N Hopf algebra basis and caches log-signatures λ_k = log_ℋ(Sig^N_ℋ(X_k)) offline, then solves a lifted piecewise ODE Ż_τ = L_k(Z_τ) per segment (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

qWE13uu99a.text: MARS with Gemini-3-Pro-Preview achieves 74.2% Above-Median Rate and 31.1% Any-Medal Rate on MLE-Bench, outperforming AIDE and AIRA-dojo baselines (Section 4, Table 2).
The scaled variant MARS+ reaches 33.8% Gold-Medal Rate while maintaining 74.2% Above-Median Rate on MLE-Bench (Table 2).
On MLE-Bench task-complexity splits, MARS attains 74.2% Any-Medal Rate on Lite tasks, 52.6% on Medium tasks, and 37.8% on High-complexity tasks (Table 3).
63% of all utilized lessons in MARS's Comparative Reflective Memory originate from cross-branch transfer across MCTS search paths, with a 65.8% overall lesson-utilization rate (Section 6).
Budget-aware MCTS achieves a 19.5% effective solution rate versus 16.1% for vanilla MCTS, at an average cost of $60.5 versus $39.0 for the baseline (Section E.3, Figure 5).

v63OyiRoS2.text: Spectral Guidance achieves 89.4% conditional accuracy on CIFAR-10 versus 52.0% for the strongest training-free baseline TFG, a 37 percentage point improvement (Section 6.2, Table 2).
Spectral Guidance improves CIFAR-10 conditional generation FID from 91.7 (baseline) to 70.7 (Table 2, Section 6.2).
Spectral Guidance runs at 21.7 ms per sampling step, close to the 19.2 ms unconditional cost, and roughly 4x faster than TFG's 81.2 ms per step (Section 6.5, Table 3).

Guidance is performed via a learned spectral network with 16M parameters (CelebA-HQ) using rank K=512 truncation for CIFAR-10/CelebA-HQ and K=2000 for ImageNet, requiring no denoiser backpropagation during sampling (Section 6, Table 2).
Theorem 4.2 gives a variational characterization linking self-supervised-learning objectives to the singular value decomposition underlying the spectral guidance construction (Theorem 4.2).

QwtmbKAOZU.text: On base models, WeDLM-8B achieves an average benchmark score of 74.72 versus Qwen3-8B's 72.61, including a GSM8K score of 90.20 vs 85.97 (+4.2 points) and HumanEval 75.00 vs 68.90 (+6.1 points) (Table 1).
On instruct models, WeDLM-8B averages 77.53 versus Qwen3-8B's 75.12, with GSM8K at 92.27 vs 89.91 (Table 2).

On the GSM8K speed-accuracy Pareto frontier, WeDLM reaches up to 3.2x acceleration while retaining over 79% accuracy in the aggressive regime, and 1.97x speedup at 92.3% accuracy in the conservative regime (Section 6.4, Figure 5a).
Streaming parallel decoding achieves a 1.9x speedup over block-wise decoding at threshold τ=0.9 (Figure 4c).

Topological Reordering places all observed tokens before masked tokens in the physical sequence while preserving logical positions via RoPE, allowing standard causal attention to give masked tokens full visibility of observed context and preserving prefix KV caching (Section 4.1).

GcCBoFM8u9.text: OMG (Algorithm 1) for two-player zero-sum matrix games achieves a regularization-dependent regret bound of O(β⁻¹d²(1+σ²log(T/δ))log(T/d)), logarithmic in T, alongside a regularization-independent bound of O((1+σ)d√T log(T/δ)) (Theorem 2.1, Section 2.3).

SOMG (Algorithm 2) for finite-horizon Markov games achieves a regularization-dependent regret bound of O(β⁻¹d³H⁷log²(dT/δ)), logarithmic in T, versus a regularization-independent bound of O(d³ᐟ²H³√T log(dT/δ)) (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.3).

OMG attains sample complexity min{Õ(d²/ε²), Õ(β⁻¹d²/ε)} for matrix games, and SOMG attains min{Õ(d³H⁶/ε²), Õ(β⁻¹d³H⁷/ε)} for Markov games, both improving over prior O(β⁻¹... ) and O̅(d√T) bounds from Yang et al. 2025a (VMG) (Table 1).

The Markov-game regret analysis uses superoptimistic bonuses satisfying 2|Q⁺−Q̄| ≥ |Q⁺−Q^μ|, combined with three maintained Q/V-function estimates, to eliminate the √T dependence via squared rather than linear bonus terms (Section 4.2).

Both OMG and SOMG recover the standard Õ(√T) regret bound when the KL regularization strength β = 0, showing the logarithmic-regret improvement is specific to regularized play (Section 2.3, Section 3.3).

uPpo1RsI2d.text: ST-BCP reduces the average coverage gap from 4.21% (BCP) to 1.12% across the constant, feature-dependent, and feature+calibration-dependent size-constraint rules on ResNet-50/CIFAR-10 with n=200 (Table 1).

Theorem 3.5 derives the theoretically optimal score transformation as a step function based on a threshold w(D,X), with Corollary 3.6 introducing the practical 'improvement operator' transformation 𝕀_w(s;D,X) = w(D,X)·𝕀(s≥w(D,X)) (Section 3.2).
Theorem 3.1 shows the leave-one-out coverage estimator retains O_P(1/√n) consistency even under the data-dependent, non-identity score transformation (Section 3.1).
ST-BCP lowers estimator MSE from 2.07×10⁻⁴ to 1.19×10⁻⁴ and reduces the standard deviation of the coverage gap from 1.43% to 1.06% relative to standard BCP (Table 1).

The method is validated across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet using ResNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and DenseNet backbones, showing consistent gap reductions over BCP across all architectures (Section 4).

kaOPDyq5sv.text: The proposed sync-SDE method couples the reverse-time SDEs of a source and edited image by reusing the identical backward Brownian motion path W̄ₜ for both processes, so the two trajectories differ only through prompt-induced drift terms (Theorem 1, Anderson's time-reversal).

Sync-SDE is training-free, requiring no fine-tuning or auxiliary networks, and is implemented on the pretrained Flux.1[dev] model with 28 sampling steps, producing 1024x1024 edited images in 15-25 seconds on an H100 GPU (Section 4).

On the CLIP-score vs. L1/LPIPS/DINO-distance trade-off curves across guidance strengths {1.0, 1.5, 2.5}, sync-SDE dominates FireFlow, FlowEdit, RF-Edit, RF-Inv, and SDEdit, occupying the upper-left (higher fidelity, lower distance) region (Figure 2).

Section 6 shows the synchronous coupling choice Qₜ = I_d is the greedy minimizer of the local quadratic deviation cost among orthonormal coupling matrices, giving an optimal-transport interpretation of the method (Section 6).
Qualitative results demonstrate localized edits that preserve fine details such as coffee-saucer texture and marble material/lighting while altering only the targeted semantic attribute (Figure 4).
