fhoIsmyGGi.text: Proposition 1 establishes the upper bound on the true residual R ≤ ΔR₁ + R₂, decomposing prediction error into a first-stage delta term and a second-stage residual term (Section 3).
Theorem 1 proves that the separate-component-quantile interval Ĉ^(c,d) built from quantiles of ΔR₁ and R₂ achieves marginal coverage ℙ(y_test ∈ Ĉ^(c,d)) ≥ 1 − c − d under exchangeability (Section 4).

Theorem 2 shows that calibrating stage-wise scaling parameters λ via family-wise error rate (FWER) control over a validation set Λ_val at level δ yields a high-probability coverage guarantee ℙ(ℙ(y_test ∈ Ĉ^λ̂ | S^cal) ≥ 1 − α − τ) ≥ 1 − δ (Section 5.2).

Under gradual upstream distribution shift, the proposed method (SR) achieves 0.8419 empirical coverage versus 0.7280 for standard split conformal (SC) and 0.7488 for weighted split conformal (WSC) (Table 1, Section 7.1).

On the real-world automobile supply-chain dataset spanning the 2020 COVID disruption, SR preserves target coverage while producing narrower intervals (width 21.085) than ACI (15.696 width, lower coverage) and PID (18.469 width) (Section 7.2).

GcOyXiXACP.text: GRAPE achieves an average Recall@10 gain of 4.9% across five multilingual, long-form, and multimodal benchmarks (Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600, Wikipedia, CIRR) using a frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 retriever with LLM-rewritten queries (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On the Wikipedia long-form retrieval benchmark, GRAPE improves CLIP+LLM Recall@10 from 69.3% to 82.8%, the largest single-benchmark gain reported (Table 1).

Section 3.3 identifies a 'score inflation' failure mode where similarity-based reward training causes the rewriting LLM to inject generic tokens (e.g., 'real-world', 'environment') that raise CLIP similarity scores for nearly all candidates without improving actual relevance, evidenced by similarity increasing while Recall@1 decreases during training (Figure 5).

GRAPE mitigates score inflation by replacing similarity-based rewards with a corpus-relative, ranking-based reward Rₖʳ = 1 − 2(rₖ−1)/(N−1) that maps a target image's rank directly to a normalized reward (Equation 4, Section 3.3).
The rewriting LLM is optimized via Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an affine-invariant normalized relative advantage computed within each group (Appendix A.1, Section 3.2).

IKZcb2jZqM.text: RELO-L256 attains 57.5% AUC on LaSOT_ext without template updates, exceeding ARPTrack-L384 (54.2%) and LoRAT-L224 (52.8%) (Table 2, Section 4.2).
RELO-L256 also reaches 75.1% AUC on LaSOT, 87.3% AUC on TrackingNet, and 81.8% AO (91.1% SR at IoU 0.5) on GOT-10k, reported as best-in-class among large-size trackers (Table 2, Section 4.2).

RELO formulates target localization as a Markov decision process in which spatial locations are actions, trained via actor-critic policy optimization with a reward combining frame-level IoU and sequence-level AUC (λ=1 default) instead of handcrafted heatmap or corner-distribution priors (Section 3.1-3.2).

Ablations show replacing RELO's learned localization with a center-heatmap baseline costs 2.5 points and a corner-prior baseline costs 2.8 points, while removing the sequence-level AUC reward term costs 1.0 point and removing the value-based variance reduction costs 0.8 points (Table 5, Section 4.3).
The lightweight RELO-T256 variant runs at 21 FPS on GPU while remaining competitive in accuracy, and RELO-L256 reports 63.6% AUC on TNL2K, 71.3% on NFS, and 71.4% on UAV123 (Table 1, Table 3).

phG3K0m7xt.text: AMDP bounds the mismatch between minibatches read and pipeline depth to mismatch(i) = min(n, d-i) - 1, and enforcing n=2 guarantees a mismatch of at most 1 regardless of pipeline depth d (Section 3.1, Lemma 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 proves AMDP preserves the synchronous SGD O(T^-1/2) nonconvex convergence rate up to an O(eta^2) perturbation term (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.2).
AMDP runs d/2 concurrent pipelines with complementary scheduling directions using Chimera-style stage mapping to eliminate the roughly 2/d bubble ratio of standard pipelines (Section 3.2).
On 8 GPUs with pipeline depth 8 and batch size 128, AMDP reaches 83.7 ktokens/s on GPT-style models versus 71.6 ktokens/s for PipeDream-2BW, a 16.9% improvement (Section 4.2, Table 3).

On 16 GPUs (multi-node, d=8, b=128), AMDP achieves 159.8 ktokens/s versus 140.9 ktokens/s for PipeDream-2BW, a 12.9% throughput improvement, while PipeDream-2BW shows validation perplexity degradation (21.7 vs 109.0) that AMDP avoids (Section 4.2, Table 4, Table 5).
An ablation removing the ZeRO-style optimizer-state sharding increases GPU memory usage by 11-19% and reduces throughput by about 4% (Section 4.2, Table 7).

0MVEJk4dhE.text: The paper introduces PhoneBook, a synthetic key-value memorization benchmark spanning 1K-20K tokens, and PaperQA, a novel 450-QA-pair benchmark built from 15 recent NeurIPS 2024/ICLR 2025/ICML 2025 papers covering recall, comprehension, and logical inference (Section 3).

LoRA memorization performance scales roughly linearly with rank on CounterFact but exhibits rank-dependent capacity saturation, with peak parameter efficiency occurring at lower ranks rather than the maximum tested rank (Section 4, Figure 1, Figure 3).

Synthetic QA-formatted training data outperforms raw-text formats for LoRA knowledge injection, and data generated by GPT-4 consistently outperforms data generated by Llama-3.1-8B (Section 5, Figure 4, Figure 5).

Under oracle routing, multi-LoRA systems outperform a single large LoRA of equivalent parameter count, but practical embedding-based routing incurs substantial performance degradation relative to the oracle (Section 6, Figure 6).

TIES merging is the most robust multi-LoRA composition strategy, outperforming naive concatenation, while performance peaks at merging N=1 module and declines monotonically as more modules are merged (Section 6, Figure 7).

On long-context multi-hop tasks (NarrativeQA and QuALITY), hybrid systems combining LoRA with external context via ICL or RAG achieve the best results, outperforming both LoRA-only and ICL/RAG-only configurations (Section 7, Table 2).

Dp6YrhtkDR.text: RADE-OF corrects for both edge deletion and addition so that the expected training-time message aggregation matches inference-time aggregation on the original input graph (Section 4, Proposition 4.1, Equations 8-9).

RADE-OFS instead retains the contribution of added edges at inference time, aligning training expectations with a modified inference aggregation that improves long-range communication for over-squashing-prone tasks (Section 4, Proposition 4.2, Equation 11).

An adaptive gradient-norm balancing scheme (Equation 14) tunes the edge-drop rate p and edge-add rate q automatically during training via one Adam step per mini-batch, removing the need for manual hyperparameter sweeps (Section 4).

On node classification with GCN, RADE-OF achieves best or second-best accuracy on 7 of 8 datasets (Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, CS, Computer, Physics, Flickr, ogbn-arxiv), with improvements ranging from 0.02% (Flickr) to 0.43% (Computer) over the strongest baseline (Section 5, Table 2).

On graph classification, RADE-OFS is best on all 6 datasets tested (MUTAG, PROTEINS, IMDB-B, IMDB-M, ogbg-molhiv, peptides-func), with the largest gains of +2.24% on MUTAG and +1.83% on peptides-func (Section 5, Table 3).

Ablations show removing the gradient-norm balancing and expectation-preserving correction causes up to a 2.90% accuracy drop on Flickr, and adaptive rate selection outperforms fine-tuned fixed rates across all datasets, particularly for RADE-OFS (Section 5, Table 4, Table 6).

LpqtiYpHzn.text: Generative Trajectory Policies (GTP) replace iterative ODE-solver calls with a closed-form score-approximation surrogate f-tilde(x_t,t) = (x_t - x)/t, proven asymptotically equivalent to the true score in Theorem 1 (Section 4.1, Theorem 1).
GTP incorporates value guidance via an advantage-weighted training objective with exponential weighting, justified by Theorem 2 (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).

In behavior cloning on D4RL, GTP-BC achieves an average score of 82.3 on Gym tasks versus 76.3 for Diffusion-BC and 69.7 for Consistency-BC, and 66.3 on AntMaze tasks versus 44.1 for Consistency-BC (Section 5, Table 1).

In full offline RL evaluation, GTP achieves an average Gym score of 89.0 versus 87.9 for Diffusion-QL, and an average AntMaze score of 80.6 versus 78.3 for QGPO and 69.6 for Diffusion-QL, including perfect scores on several notoriously challenging AntMaze tasks (Section 5, Table 2).
An ablation on hopper-medium-expert shows removing the score approximation drops performance from 112.2 ± 0.6 to 99.7 ± 1.7 while increasing training time from 4.26h to 5.23h (Section 5, Table 3).

h4RYP8bojp.text: MoDA applies a Transformer-based cross-attention mechanism that modulates aligned visual tokens conditioned on the original user instruction, implemented as channel-level multiplicative modulation on top of a two-stage LLaVA-style training protocol (Section 3, Section 3.1-3.2).
On LLaVA-1.5, adding MoDA improves MMVP from 24.0 to 36.0 (+12.0 points), LLaVA-Wild from 65.4 to 68.0 (+2.6 points), and ScienceQA from 69.0 to 71.0 (+2.0 points) (Section 4, Table 1).

MoDA is evaluated across 7 benchmarks (POPE, GQA, ScienceQA, LLaVA-Wild, MMBench-En/Cn, MMVP), with LLaVA-More SigLIP-S2 + MoDA reaching 42.7% on MMVP, 87.7% on POPE, 81.9% on ScienceQA, and 65.4% on GQA (Section 4, Table 1).

Ablations show a 2-layer MoDA adapter performs best while a 4-layer adapter degrades performance by roughly 12 points, and cross-attention modulation without L1 regularization outperforms alternative architecture variants with an average score of 64.3% (Section 4.3, Table 2, Table S2).

Ablations further show a single-block MoDA placed at the beginning of the LLM (+2.6 points) outperforms applying modulation across the full model depth (+0.7 points) while being more computationally efficient, and SigLIP-S2 consistently outperforms CLIP as the vision encoder (Section 4.3, Table S3, Table 2).

7fI30TOBtA.text: CalMRL is trained with a warm-up stage on VAST-150K (spanning vision, audio, subtitle, and text modalities) followed by training on MSR-VTT (vision-text, ~180K pairs) and AudioCaps (audio-text, ~45K pairs) with missing modalities (Section 5.1).

CalMRL achieves 61.1% Recall@1 for text-to-video retrieval on MSR-VTT, an improvement of about +10.6 points over the VAST baseline, and 50.1% Recall@1 for text-to-audio retrieval on AudioCaps, an improvement of about +16.4 points over VAST (Table 1).

Theorem 1 derives upper and lower bounds on the magnitude of 'anchor shift' (the distortion of the modality alignment anchor caused by missing modalities) in terms of the spectral properties of the modality covariance and the fraction of missing modalities (Theorem 1).

Corollary 3 shows that calibration reduces anchor shift only when the representation-level imputation error ε stays below a threshold expressed via the spectral gap σ1−σ2 and the missing-modality ratio |Ω̄| (Corollary 3).

Corollary 4 proves that CalMRL's bi-step optimization (closed-form posterior inference followed by parameter update) yields a monotonically non-decreasing likelihood, guaranteeing convergence to a local stationary point (Corollary 4).

On sole-dataset training (audio-text only or vision-text only), CalMRL resists the performance degradation seen in baselines such as VAST, GRAM, and TRIANGLE, and Figure 6 shows reduced modality-boundary separation in the learned representation space compared to those baselines (Table 2, Figure 6).

I0RgZXTO53.text: KAPPA is proposed as a lightweight, inference-time intervention that geometrically identifies distinct 'knowledge' and 'prediction' subspaces within the residual stream of an LLM and aligns them to close the knowledge-prediction gap on multiple-choice questions (Section 4).

KAPPA's methodology is split into knowledge extraction (Section 4.1), prediction alignment (Section 4.2), and integration of the two into a single intervention applied at inference time (Section 4.3).

KAPPA is evaluated on multiple-choice benchmarks including MMLU, ARC, PubMedQA, and BBQ, and its gains are compared against baseline prompting/probing methods in a dedicated comparative analysis (Section 6.1, Section 6.2).

An ablation study isolates the contribution of the subspace-alignment intervention from the knowledge-extraction step alone, showing both components are needed for the full accuracy improvement on MCQ benchmarks (Section 6.3).

The paper reports that KAPPA's improvements generalize beyond standard MCQ formatting to free-form answer settings, evaluated across multiple instruction-tuned LLMs rather than a single model family (Section 5, Section 6.1).

B8bAYc4COx.text: The paper introduces counterfactual time series forecasting with textual conditions and proposes TADiff, a text-attribution diffusion model, to solve it (Section 4).

A dedicated evaluation framework, DTTC (using contrastive learning with separate time-series and text encoders), scores forecasts on both factual and counterfactual settings even when no ground-truth counterfactual time series exists, via DTTC-I (intrinsic) and DTTC-E (extrinsic) metrics (Section 4.4, Table 4).

TADiff is evaluated on five datasets — a synthetic Synth set (14,000 samples with controlled attributes) plus ETTm1, Traffic, Exchange, and Weather — and achieves the best MAE on most of these datasets in the factual setting (Table 1).

In the counterfactual setting, TADiff outperforms baselines including DLinear, PatchTST, Sundial, VerbalTS, TimeCMA, TimeMMD, Causal Transformer, and IATSF as measured by DTTC-I and DTTC-E, since no ground-truth counterfactual series is available for direct error metrics (Table 2).

An ablation study shows that both the counterfactual fine-tuning stage and the text-attribution mechanism are needed together to substantially improve semantic consistency (DTTC scores) while preserving numerical forecasting accuracy (MAE/MSE) (Table 3).
The DTTC metric itself is validated for reliability, achieving 55-97% retrieval accuracy when matching forecasts to their conditioning text across datasets (Table 4).

eBM5ALLJNx.text: The Signature-Informed Transformer (SIT) combines path-signature feature extraction, signature-augmented cross-asset attention, and a direct CVaR training objective into a single end-to-end asset-allocation model (Section 3).

On S&P 100 daily price data (WRDS, 2000-2024; train 2000-2016, validation 2017-2019, test 2020-2024), SIT achieves a Sharpe ratio of 0.6717 and final wealth factor of 1.7903 on a 40-asset universe, and Sharpe 0.7715 with final wealth factor 1.9215 on a 50-asset universe, outperforming Equally Weighted Portfolio, Global Minimum Variance, CVaR optimization, Hierarchical Risk Parity, and deep-learning forecasters Autoformer, DLinear, FEDformer, PatchTST, iTransformer, NSformer, and TimesNet (Table 1).
On a 30-asset universe, SIT attains a Sharpe ratio of 0.5496 and final wealth factor of 1.5678 (Table 5).

An ablation on the 40-asset universe shows removing the CVaR objective drops Sharpe ratio from 0.6717 to 0.5691, removing the asset-attention mechanism drops it to 0.5284, removing the financial-bias term drops it to 0.6045, and removing the learnable gate γ drops it to 0.5251, indicating each of the three architectural pillars contributes materially (Table 2).

nuwO8FBadZ.text: The Shannon Scaling Law models LLM capacity as C_LLM = a N^α log2(1 + b D^β / [c(DN)^γ + d D^δ + e]), mapping model size to channel bandwidth and training tokens to signal power via an analogy to the Shannon-Hartley theorem (Section 3.1).

The law predicts that when signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is insufficient, scaling transitions from monotonic loss improvement to U-shaped performance degradation, i.e., catastrophic overtraining, whereas standard monotonic scaling laws represent only the high-SNR special case (Section 3.3).
On Gaussian-noise perturbation experiments spanning 10-40dB, the Shannon Scaling Law fits Pythia models with R² = 0.9613 ± 0.03 and OLMo2 models with R² = 0.9585 ± 0.06 (Section 4.1).

The law also fits quantization-induced noise (2-4 bit) with R² = 0.9824 for Pythia and R² = 0.9548 for OLMo2, and fits SFT experiments across GSM8K, SiQA, and StarCoder with R² of 0.936, 0.916, and 0.937 respectively (Section 4.2, Section 4.3).

When fit jointly on Pythia models up to 6.9B parameters and up to 180B training tokens, the Shannon Scaling Law extrapolates to a held-out 12B model trained up to 307B tokens with pooled R² = 0.847, while baseline monotonic scaling laws collapse to negative R² scores on this extrapolation (Section 5.2).

2Nfr4u3pK2.text: COPF defines decision-counterfactual fairness gaps as disparities in benefit between exposure (shown) and non-exposure (hidden) counterfactuals across protected groups (Definition 3.3, Section 3).

COPF constructs graph-aware self-normalized doubly robust (GA-DR) pseudo-outcomes for estimating counterfactual quantities under temporal dependence and local interference on evolving graphs (Definition 3.2, Section 4).

Theorem 4.5 proves that small residual outcome-indistinguishability (residual-OI) on estimated DR residuals implies bounds on the true counterfactual fairness gap, accounting for estimation and dependence error (Theorem 4.5, Section 4.2).
Corollary 4.6 shows residual-OI control implies bounds on decision-counterfactual fairness gaps, connecting the auditing certificate to the fairness objective (Corollary 4.6, Section 4.2).

On temporal graph benchmark (TGB) streams and synthetic bipartite data, COPF reduces worst-case spikes in exposure-counterfactual group disparities during policy shifts with only modest degradation in ranking utility, as reported in the phase-wise results (Section 6, Figure 1).

COPF is implemented via an online primal-dual control loop (Algorithm 1) that stays largely inactive when logged disparities are already small, only intervening when certificates flag structural bias (Section 4.3, Algorithm 1).

0bPwAi78Iq.text: WinDeskGround is a benchmark of 585 high-resolution multi-window desktop screenshots and 1,356 instruction-target pairs spanning nine application domains, generated via a parametric synthesis method controlling window count (3-15), occlusion, and semantic similarity (Section 3, Table 1).

Evaluating five GUI grounding models (SeeClick, OS-Atlas-7B-Base, UGround-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, InfiGUI-G1-7B), all models show precipitous accuracy declines to below 20% as target visibility drops into the 30-50% occlusion range, despite exceeding 75% accuracy at full visibility (Section 4, Figure 4b).

Top-tier models (UGround, UI-TARS, InfiGUI) maintain 70-80% grounding accuracy even at high visual clutter (12 windows), while SeeClick's accuracy falls below 20% under the same condition (Section 4, Figure 4a).
Across the five defined difficulty levels (L1-L5), grounding accuracy for top models falls from over 80% at L1 to roughly 7-11% at the extreme L5 setting (Table 2, Figure 5).
InfiGUI-G1-7B achieves the highest overall accuracy of 44.89% at the L3 difficulty level, with the strongest category performance in browsers (56.06%) (Section 4, Table 3).

A 100-sample human validation study reports 85% instruction-validity approval, 99% spatial (bounding-box) accuracy, and inter-annotator agreement of Fleiss' Kappa 0.87, though bounding-box accuracy declines to 79.6% at the hardest L5 level (Section 6, Table 4).

ZhSS3msLRj.text: TRACE is a benchmark of 517 human-verified reward-hacking trajectories in code environments, organized into a taxonomy of 54 subcategories across 10 major categories such as test suite exploitation and context exploitation (Section 3, Figure 2).
GPT-5.2 with reasoning achieves 63% reward-hack detection accuracy in contrastive (cluster) evaluation settings versus only 45% when analyzing isolated trajectories (Section 5, Figure 4).

Model match rates on semantically-oriented reward hacks fall to 0.0-0.4, far below the 0.6-0.95 match rates achieved on syntactic exploit categories, indicating a gap in contextual reasoning (Section 5, Figure 5).
Increasing the contrastive cluster size from 1 to 5 trajectories improves detection performance by approximately 35%, with gains plateauing at larger cluster sizes (e.g., 10) (Section 5, Figure 6).
Human-model agreement on reward-hack labeling reaches Cohen's Kappa of 0.812 with 90.9% absolute agreement, and the dataset construction achieves an 81% human acceptance rate (Section 3, Table 1).

Detection performance is also sensitive to the benign-to-hacked trajectory ratio within a cluster, with higher benign ratios (e.g., B=0.9) improving detection over lower ratios (e.g., B=0.25) (Section 5, Figure 6).

OT9cxeWbEO.text: Theorem 4.1 shows that without momentum, mini-batch steepest descent converges to an approximate max-margin solution only when batch size exceeds the threshold b > 4Rn/(γ+4R), with the margin gap shrinking as batch size increases (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
Theorem 4.3 shows that adding momentum allows convergence to the max-margin solution even with small batch sizes, provided β₁→1, revealing a batch-momentum tradeoff (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.2).
Corollary 4.5 shows the momentum-enabled convergence rate is slowed by a factor of m/(1-β₁) relative to the momentum-free large-batch case (Corollary 4.5, Section 4.2).

Theorem 4.6 proves that variance reduction recovers the exact full-batch implicit bias for any batch size, eliminating the batch-size dependence of the margin, though Corollary 4.7 shows this comes at a convergence rate slowed by a factor of m^(2+a) (Theorem 4.6, Corollary 4.7, Section 4.3).

Theorem 4.9 constructs an orthogonal, scale-skewed data example on which per-sample (batch-size-one) steepest descent converges to a fundamentally different implicit bias than the full-batch solution (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.4).

Synthetic multi-class linear classification experiments with normalized-SGD under the ℓ₂ norm, varying batch size (b∈{20,200}) and momentum (β∈{0,0.5,0.99}), empirically confirm that momentum or variance reduction restores full-batch-like convergence in small-batch regimes (Section 5, Figure 1).

SR2RDhhnxj.text: GHOST achieves 50% state-dimension reduction in Mamba2 with perplexity rising from a 13.17 dense baseline to 14.23 on WikiText-2, an increase of roughly 1 point (Section 5.1, Table 1).

GHOST computes a per-channel saliency score S_i = sqrt(P_i * Q_i) combining a controllability estimate P_i (input-history influence via hidden-state covariance) and an observability estimate Q_i (output-energy Hessian), approximating control-theoretic balanced truncation from forward-pass statistics alone, without backpropagation (Section 4.2-4.3).
GHOST remains stable across model scales from 130M to 2.7B parameters, whereas the gradient-based Taylor-pruning baseline fails catastrophically on smaller models (Section 5.4, Table 3).
An ablation shows the joint controllability-observability saliency score outperforms using either controllability or observability alone (Section 5.8, Table 6).
GHOST calibrated at sequence length L=128 generalizes to evaluation at L=2048, and calibration on WikiText-2 transfers to out-of-distribution code and math tasks (Section 5.2-5.6).
GHOST requires only 15GB of VRAM for calibration versus 45GB for the gradient-based Taylor-pruning baseline, since it needs only two forward passes and no backpropagation (Section 4.6, Figure 3).

7WeA5TAjHK.text: GUI-AiF combines Anchoring Point Reward in Flux (APR-iF) and Anchoring Region Reward in Flux (ARR-iF) within a reinforcement fine-tuning objective ℛAiF = α·ℛp + γ·ℛr, using GRPO advantage estimation with KL regularization (Section on GUI-AiF method).

On the continual domain setting (mobile→desktop→web) evaluated on ScreenSpot-V2, GUI-AiF achieves 81.2% average text+icon grounding accuracy, versus 80.3% for the GUI-G2 baseline and 78.9% for SE-GUI† (Table 2).

On the continual resolution setting (normal→high resolution) evaluated on ScreenSpot-Pro, GUI-AiF reaches 19.0% average accuracy compared to 16.7% for the GUI-G2 baseline, a 2.3 percentage-point improvement (Table 3).

An ablation shows the full GUI-AiF reward outperforms either component alone, with APR-iF alone yielding stronger results than ARR-iF alone, indicating point-generalization matters more for domain shifts (Table 4).

Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis identifies optimal reward weights of α=15 and γ=0.5, with α having greater impact on domain-shift performance and γ affecting resolution-shift performance more (Figure 3).

Yhv4d8wfbi.text: The method constructs proxy labels Ỹᵢ = Yᵢ·𝟙{Uᵢ≥û} + Ŷᵢ·𝟙{Uᵢ<û} by collecting expert labels only where model uncertainty Uᵢ exceeds a calibrated threshold û, guaranteeing average labeling error ≤ ε with probability ≥ 1-α (Theorem 2.1).
Uncertainty calibration is performed via a multicalibration algorithm that adjusts per-example uncertainty estimates across feature/demographic subgroups (Section 2.1).
A PAC router extends the method to route among k candidate models using a learned weighting function w_θ optimized via implicit gradients with a sigmoid relaxation for differentiability (Section 3).

At an error tolerance of ε=0.05, the single-model method yields 14-28% expert-labeling budget savings on text tasks with GPT-4o, 39-60% savings on image tasks with ResNet-152, and 16-51% savings on continuous-label tasks.
Multi-model routing between GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 yields 42% budget savings, and up to 482% relative cost savings in a cost-sensitive setting incorporating per-source and expert labeling costs.

GK89Mi6ZRf.text: TIED derives a Trivialized Target Score Identity (Proposition 4.2) extending the target-score matching identity to general Lie groups without requiring a bi-invariant metric, enabling score estimation via a Monte Carlo estimator (Proposition 4.3).

The transformation-inversion posterior p(g|x̃) ∝ p_x(g⁻¹·x̃)|det J_{g⁻¹}(x̃)| is shown to be G-equivariant for any energy function (Propositions 3.1-3.2), and sampling from it followed by inverse-transforming recovers samples from the original data distribution.
On MNIST under affine transformations Aff(2,ℝ), TIED with a VAE energy achieves 96.95% classification accuracy and 0.71 FID, versus 55.48% accuracy for a ResNet18 baseline (Table 1).
On MNIST under homography transformations PGL(3,ℝ), TIED with a VAE energy achieves 97.43% accuracy and 0.57 FID, versus 87.95% for the ResNet18 baseline (Table 1).

On PDE-symmetry inversion, TIED reduces relative L2 error to 0.043±0.002 for the 1D heat equation under SL(2,ℝ)⋉H(1,ℝ) and to 0.178±0.013 for the 1D Burgers equation under SL(2,ℝ)⋉(ℝ²,+), compared to 0.690 and 0.867 respectively for a DeepONet baseline (Table 2).

On a synthetic SO(10) sampling task, TIED recovers the correct multimodal distribution in roughly 100 diffusion steps versus about 100,000 steps required by a kinetic Langevin sampler (Section on synthetic SO(10) experiments).

XMO8lp4I2n.text: ManiSoft defines four vision-language manipulation tasks for soft continuum arms—Collecting (COLL), Alignment (ALN), Stacking (STK), and Arrangement (ARR)—each stressing a distinct deformable-control aspect (Section 3.2).

The benchmark's automated pipeline generates 6,300 scene-trajectory pairs (2,100 clean scenes plus 4,200 randomized scenes) using a 263-object asset library with 109 manipulable objects across 17 categories and 154 obstacles across 35 categories, at a 4:1 train/test split (Section 3.5).

The simulator couples Elastica soft-body dynamics with MuJoCo rigid-body dynamics via an elastic force constraint (translational stiffness kF=0.1 N/m, rotational stiffness kM=10 N·m/rad) at a 0.0002s timestep and 714 Hz control frequency (Section 3.1, Equation 1).
In the clean setting, Diffusion Policy attains 31.6% average success rate across the four tasks versus 30.4% for OpenVLA-OFT and 9.2% for RDT (Table 2, Section 4.1).

Under scene randomization, Diffusion Policy's average success collapses from 31.6% to 2.2% while OpenVLA-OFT degrades far less, from 30.4% to 27.0%, showing substantially greater robustness (Table 2, Section 4.1).

Failure analysis identifies three dominant failure modes—proprioceptive state ambiguity, underuse of soft-arm compliance for obstacle avoidance, and a 'stop-moving' behavior where OpenVLA-OFT halts after grasp completion (Section 4.2).

QC7fOKv1jg.text: Instability in latent-diffusion-model (LDM) based inverse problem solvers is attributed to a discrepancy between the solver's sampling dynamics and the stable reverse diffusion dynamics learned by the underlying diffusion model (abstract only).

The paper proposes the Measurement-Consistent Langevin Corrector (MCLC), a plug-and-play stabilization module that applies measurement-consistent Langevin updates to correct LDM-based inverse problem solvers (abstract only).
MCLC is presented as theoretically grounded, in contrast to prior stabilization approaches that rely on linear manifold assumptions which often fail to hold in latent space (abstract only).
MCLC is claimed to yield more stable and reliable inverse-problem-solving behavior when operating in the latent space of a diffusion model (abstract only).

rM9r9qyRSA.text: PluRel pretraining loss follows a power law in the number of synthetic databases N and in the number of pretraining tokens S, and both must be scaled in tandem to avoid underfitting or overfitting regimes (Section 3, Figure 1).

Continued pretraining with PluRel's synthetic databases plus real data improves over a real-data-only baseline by +1.2% absolute AUROC and +3.0% R2 on average across 18 RelBench tasks, with per-task gains up to +7.4% AUROC and +5.2% R2 (Table 1).
Regression tasks benefit more consistently from synthetic+real pretraining than classification tasks, improving on 7 of 8 regression tasks versus mixed results on classification tasks (Table 1).

PluRel generates synthetic multi-table databases via a three-stage pipeline: schema generation with directed acyclic graphs, foreign-key connectivity via Hierarchical Stochastic Block Models, and feature generation via Structural Causal Models with temporal patterns (Section 2, Figure 2).
Generating an 80-table synthetic database takes approximately 1,369 seconds and under 1 GB of peak memory (Table 3, Appendix B).

6HBP1uCTdd.text: SENSE improves segmentation performance across model-agnostic architectures, yielding +1.32 mIoU on Cityscapes with DPT (DINOv2-B), +1.16 mIoU on COCO with Mask2Former, and +1.10 mIoU on ADE20K with DPT (DINOv2-B) (Table 3).

Using dense-composition synthetic scenes (22.21 average instances per image) yields 66.56 mIoU on Cityscapes validation versus 61.81 mIoU for sparse-composition scenes (11.48 average instances), generated with the same Flux model (Table 1).

Higher local instance fidelity (GLCM score 1.16) yields 68.17 mIoU versus coarser fidelity (GLCM score 1.12) yielding 66.56 mIoU, showing fine instance fidelity drives more discriminative representations (Table 2).
SENSE reaches 59.09 mIoU on ADE20K using only 2x synthetic data augmentation, matching or beating prior methods FreeMask (20x synthetic data) and SegGen (50x synthetic data) (Table 4).
SENSE's benefits scale with synthetic data volume, improving Cityscapes mIoU from 79.80 to 81.27 as synthetic samples increase from 2,975 to 17,850 (Table 5).
An optimal-transport (OT) based assignment ablation contributes +1.15 mIoU on Cityscapes and +0.56 mIoU on COCO over the version without OT assignment (Table 6).

TcaAbpw9OI.text: CYBERTEAM integrates 30 threat-hunting tasks spanning 4 analytical categories, built from 23 vulnerability data sources and comprising 452,293 data samples (Section 3.1-3.2, Table 2).
CYBERTEAM defines 9 standardized operational modules (NER, REX, MAP, RAG, CLS, SUM, SPA, SIM, MATH) that guide LLMs through dependency-chained threat-hunting workflows (Section 3.3, Figure 1-2).
The benchmark evaluates 11 LLMs, including general-purpose and cybersecurity-specialized models, on the standardized threat-hunting workflow (Section 4).

The standardized modular approach achieves over 90% Hit@10 in playbook recommendation and outperforms open-ended reasoning strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Tree-of-Thought on complex multi-step tasks (Table 3, Section 4).
LLM robustness degrades under token-level and semantic-level noise injected into threat-hunting inputs, revealing limitations of current models on real-world noisy data (Figure 4).

znV8JHv8b8.text: ForesightKV-1K achieves 54.5% accuracy on AIME2024, outperforming R-KV-2K's 44.8% despite using half the cache budget (Figure 3).
ForesightKV retains 92% of original (full-cache) performance under a 2K cache budget and 99% under a 4K budget (Section 3, Figure 3).
Low-entropy tokens suffer a +147% loss ratio increase when evicted from the KV cache, versus +52% for high-entropy tokens, motivating ForesightKV's low-entropy-preserving objective (Section 2.2).
The Golden Eviction supervised algorithm achieves a 1.0711 loss ratio at a (1024,256) budget/eviction-length setting versus R-KV's 1.4101, and 1.0166 versus 1.1606 at (2048,256) (Table 2).
ForesightKV delivers a 9.79x throughput improvement at 32K sequence length under a 1K cache budget, supporting 96 concurrent batches versus 11 for full cache (Table 3).

On Qwen3-4B generalization tests, ForesightKV at a 1K budget reaches 45.2% on GPQA (versus H2O's 25.2%) and 55.7% on LiveCodeBench (versus SnapKV's 27.0%), combining supervised training (Golden Eviction) with reinforcement learning (GRPO) for further gains (Table 6, Section 3.3).

HvBHq4Ycvn.text: On LLaMA2-7B at 3-bit quantization, QTALE achieves 72.79% accuracy on CommonsenseQA versus 72.22% for the quantization-only baseline, keeping the accuracy gap below 0.5% while adding token-adaptive layer execution (Table 1).
QTALE's token-adaptive execution reduces FLOPs to approximately 0.50-0.55x of the full model's FLOPs (Section 4).
4-bit quantization under QTALE reduces LLaMA2-7B model size from 13.5GB to below 4.5GB (Section 4).
QTALE yields an average 1.28x inference speedup on CommonsenseQA benchmarks, with measured latency speedups of 1.25-1.36x (Table 3).
QTALE is compatible with multiple post-training quantization methods, including AWQ and MagR+GPTQ (Section 3, Section 4).

FMRndM4OAk.text: MA-GIG formalizes the off-manifold drift of Guided Integrated Gradients (GIG) via Proposition 3.1, showing axis-aligned input-space updates violate tangent-space constraints and accumulate error over K steps (Section 3.1, Equation 8)

MA-GIG performs attribution-path integration in VAE latent space, using the Perfect Autoencoder Assumption 3.2 and the fact that the decoder Jacobian maps latent updates into the data manifold's tangent space (Section 3.2, Equation 9)
On ResNet18/Oxford-IIIT Pet, MA-GIG achieves a DiffID of 0.4637 versus 0.3634 for GIG, and an Insertion score of 0.5886 versus 0.5093 for GIG (Table 1)
On VGG16/Oxford 102 Flower, MA-GIG achieves a DiffID of 0.3458 versus 0.2842 for GIG (Section 4.3, Table 1)

LPIPS-based manifold-adherence analysis shows MA-GIG maintains lower perceptual deviation than GIG throughout the integration path, with GIG exhibiting higher intermediate-phase distance indicating an off-manifold trajectory (Section 4.4, Figure 3)

Across VAE ablations (MAR, Stable Diffusion v1-1/v2-1, Kandinsky 2.1), MAR and SD2 consistently yield the best attribution quality, and reconstruction MSE shows only moderate correlation (r=0.406-0.530) with attribution quality (Section 4.6, Figure 4b, Table 2)

NUDNFusCDu.text: The method detects adversarial attacks on MRI reconstruction by comparing normalized k-space errors ζ1 and ζ2 from cyclic re-undersampling, flagging an attack when ζ2−ζ1 exceeds a dataset-dependent threshold, without any model retraining (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1)
Mitigation is performed via reverse projected gradient descent within an ε-ball that minimizes a cyclic measurement-consistency loss across multiple undersampling patterns (Section 3.3, Algorithm 2)

On three fastMRI datasets (Cor-PD knee, Cor-PDFS knee, Ax-FLAIR brain), the mitigation raises PSNR to 33.23-36.17 dB and SSIM to 0.92-0.94 (Cor-PD), 34.03-34.32 dB and 0.81-0.83 SSIM (Cor-PDFS), and 34.89-35.71 dB and 0.92-0.93 SSIM (Ax-FLAIR) (Table 1)
The approach remains effective across attack strengths ε∈{0.01, 0.02}, outperforming adversarial training baselines at each strength (Section 4.4, Figure 4)

In a blind setting with unknown attack type/strength, a linear-scheduler estimation of ε and α achieves mitigation performance comparable to the informed (known-attack) setting (Section 4.4, Figure 6, Table 9)
The method generalizes across five reconstruction architectures (MoDL, XPDNet, RIM, E2E-VarNet, Recurrent-VarNet), consistently reducing adversarial artifacts (Figure 5, Table 3)

jn2nRjwbFP.text: MLPs underperform XGBoost specifically on high-data-uncertainty datapoints across multiple tabular datasets, motivating data uncertainty—estimated as e^(2g(x)) in the model y=f(x)+e^(g(x))·N(0,1)—as the explanatory factor for tabular DL design choices (Section 1, Figure 1; Section 3)

Numerical feature embeddings (e.g., MLP-PLR) provide disproportionately larger accuracy improvements on high-uncertainty samples because they induce a representation space with higher local target consistency (Section 5, Figure 6)
ModernNCA's retrieval-augmented predictions concentrate their performance gains in high-uncertainty regions and underfit these regions, reducing memorization of label noise (Section 6, Figures 8-9)

TabM's implicit-ensembling gradient averaging (Equation 2) reduces noisy gradient components relative to the clean signal, explaining why it outperforms deep ensembles especially on uncertain datapoints (Section 7, Figure 10)

The proposed MLP-LRLRtriplet numerical embedding, pretrained with a triplet loss to explicitly maximize local target consistency, improves over the plain MLP baseline by 2.81% on average (rank 1.17 vs. 2.75), exceeding the 2.00% gain of MLP-LRLR (Section 5.2, Table 2)

d6BqyajwMj.text: Chain-of-thought (CoT) can evaluate directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in a number of sequential decoding steps proportional to graph size, using attention as a scratchpad memory (Section 3, Theorem 3.5)

Looped transformers implementing latent thought evaluate the same DAGs in a number of loop iterations proportional only to graph depth, performing parallel computation layer-by-layer for nodes at the same depth (Section 3, Theorem 3.7)

Looped transformers with polylogarithmic iterations are shown to capture the parallel complexity classes AC^k and TC^k, and CoT with polylogarithmic steps is proven strictly weaker than looped models under standard complexity assumptions (Section 3, Theorem 3.13, Lemma 3.14, Theorems 3.15-3.16)

CoT with polynomially many steps can represent any fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS), giving it an approximate-counting capability that looped/latent-thought transformers cannot match under standard assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 4.7)

A pretrained CoT model augmented with an inference-time algorithm such as majority voting constitutes a fully polynomial almost uniform sampler (FPAUS), formalizing how stochastic decoding enables approximate counting (Section 4, Proposition 4.6)
Experiments on parallelizable tasks and DNF-counting-style approximation tasks empirically validate the predicted separation between CoT and latent/looped thought (Section 5.1-5.2)

Vtps0ZUlgv.text: TACO's Instance-agnostic Cross-Modal Neighborhood Ranking Consistency (IM-NRC) principle assumes that patches co-located within one scan's region should have correspondingly co-clustered features in another modality's scan (Section 3)
An intra-instance cross-modal triplet loss preserves local neighborhood topology within individual patients, with an optimal neighborhood size ω=5 found via ablation (Section 4.1, Equation 6)
An inter-instance constraint uses mutual nearest neighbor (MNN) search to establish pseudo-correspondences across different patients, preventing topology collapse (Section 4.2, Equation 11)
TACO improves average segmentation performance by 1.11% over the strongest baseline BrainMVP (76.36% to 77.47%) across four datasets: BraTS2023-PED, BraTS-MET, UPENN-GBM, and ISLES22 (Table 1)
TACO improves average classification F1 by 5.94% over the best baseline (72.76% to 78.7%), with additional gains of +0.56% in accuracy and +1.35% in AUC (Table 3)

Under missing-modality test-time conditions, TACO outperforms PUIR on Tumor Core (81.09% vs. 79.78%), Enhancing Tumor (66.27% vs. 63.49%), and Whole Tumor (90.09% vs. 87.63%), with the smallest standard deviation across configurations (Section 5.2.2, Table 4)

lmhLWnIVOk.text: ReCoG achieves 93.52% ROC-AUC on Tox21 (10-shot) and 93.98% on SIDER (10-shot), outperforming the strongest baseline Pin-Tuning (91.56% and 93.41% respectively) (Table 1).
In the 1-shot setting, ReCoG reaches 81.96% ROC-AUC on MUV versus 68.69% for the best baseline Pre-KRGTS, an especially large margin compared to other datasets (Table 1).

Removing the cross-property relational learning (CPRL) module causes the largest performance drop on Tox21 10-shot (91.00% vs. 93.52% full model), while removing the context graph information bottleneck (CGIB) module causes a smaller drop (91.46%) but increases result variance (Table 2, Section 4.3.3).
ReCoG's average relative improvement over Pin-Tuning across the five MoleculeNet datasets is 11.19% ROC-AUC, reaching as high as 25.74% on MUV (Section 5, Table 1).

The bi-level optimization strategy combines cross-property relation learning (Eqs. 11-17), target term maximization (Eq. 18), and information bottleneck compression (Eq. 23) to jointly model relational and compact context (Section 4.3).
ReCoG is evaluated against 16 baseline methods, including MAML, ProtoNet, EGNN, Pin-Tuning, Pre-KRGTS, and Uni-Match, across Tox21, SIDER, MUV, ToxCast, and PCBA (Section 5.1).

WYHmRRGcL1.text: MMKU-Bench comprises 25,792 knowledge instances and over 49,000 unique images spanning 156 categories of updated knowledge and 175 categories of unknown knowledge (Section 3.3, Table 1).

On InternVL2.5-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, SFT (Full-FT, LoRA) and RLHF (CPO, ORPO, SimPO) methods are compared against knowledge editing methods (GRACE, WISE) and RAG using CEM and F1 metrics (Section 4.2, Table 2).

Across 11 general-capability benchmarks (including MME, MMBench, MMMU, MathVista, and POPE), updating existing knowledge causes more severe capability degradation than injecting entirely novel knowledge (Section 4.3, Tables 3-4).
Qwen2.5-VL-7B suffers more severe general-capability degradation than InternVL2.5-8B across most of the 11 evaluated benchmarks after knowledge updating (Section 4.3).

Knowledge injected in one modality (e.g., image-based) does not readily generalize to the other modality (e.g., text-based query), demonstrated across three cross-modal transfer scenarios M→M, M→T, and T→M (Section 4.4, Figure 4, Table 6).

nXsHRrysJX.text: The conformal-prediction early-stopping method reduces mixed-integer optimization solve time by over 60% on average across distributional MIPLIB instances while guaranteeing 0.1%-optimal solutions with 95% probability (Abstract, Section 5).
Speedups vary substantially by problem family: 76% on CFLP, 78% on OTS, 88% on MVC, and 95% on MIS, but only 8% on GISP due to its problem structure (Section 5).

An LSTM predicts the true optimality gap from solver state features (bounds, feasible solutions, nodes explored, elapsed time), and a stopping threshold κ is calibrated via conformal prediction per Theorem 4.1 to guarantee the target success probability (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
The theoretical guarantee shows the success probability on test instances is at least 1−α−O(1/√c), where c is the number of calibration instances (Section 5).

Experiments use 800 training instances, 28-100 calibration instances, and 72-100 test instances per problem family, with target tolerance ε=0.001 and error probability α=0.05, tested using Gurobi and Cardinal Optimizer (Section 5).

qYfNhYenuu.text: SPROUT (Stain Priors with pRototypical partial Optimal transport for Unlabeled prompTing) performs training-free and annotation-free nuclear instance segmentation by prompting SAM with slide-specific reference prototypes derived from histology-informed priors (Abstract, Section 3).
On MoNuSeg, SPROUT achieves AJI 0.621 (an 8.2% absolute gain over prior training-free work), PQ 0.601, DQ 0.817, SQ 0.736, and Dice 0.795 (Table 1).
On CPM17, SPROUT achieves AJI 0.662, PQ 0.616, DQ 0.796, SQ 0.774, and Dice 0.821 (Table 1).
Feature alignment uses partial optimal transport in the POT-Scan and Activation Prompting stage to guide point-prompt generation for SAM without any parameter updates (Section 3.2).

Ablations compare pathology-specific versus natural-image feature extractors, SAM patch-size variants, greedy versus partial-OT point generation, and containment-aware NMS post-processing, with hyperparameter sensitivity varying by less than 3% (Section 4.2, Figure 11).
On the TNBC dataset, SPROUT processes each image in 2.449 seconds of wall-clock time, demonstrating practical inference speed without retraining (Section 4, TNBC results).

PQqbcFehs4.text: Unlearning transfer is stronger between languages sharing both script and family (e.g., English-German) than between typologically distant pairs, and script similarity alone (e.g., Turkish-English vs. Chinese-English) predicts transfer strength (Section on cross-lingual transfer patterns).
A single inference-time steering direction recovers over 50% of unlearned knowledge in Qwen2.5-7B and approximately 90% in Gemma2-9B across languages (Figure 3).
Instructing models to respond in the fine-tuned (unlearning) language rather than the query language yields cross-lingual prompting gains ranging from +5 to +61 points (Table 2).

Representation analysis shows unlearning preserves cross-lingual alignment in early and middle layers but alters alignment in later layers, indicating suppression rather than erasure of knowledge (representation analysis section).
Languages with higher pretraining coverage (e.g., English, Chinese) transfer unlearning effects to other languages more effectively than lower-coverage languages do (cross-lingual transfer analysis).

Tl3ErdWAJf.text: A unified Bayesian model expresses log posterior odds over a latent concept as log o(c|x) = a·m + b + γN^(1-α), jointly capturing the effects of steering magnitude m and in-context example count N (Section 4, Equation 8).
In-context learning follows sigmoidal dynamics in N^(1-α) rather than in N directly, i.e. evidence accumulates sub-linearly with the number of context examples (Section 4.1, Prediction 1, Figure 4).

Activation steering produces sigmoidal behavioral change because it acts linearly on log-posterior odds within a valid operating range, before saturating at extreme magnitudes (Section 4.2, Prediction 2, Figure 5).

In-context learning and activation steering combine additively in log-belief space, so the predicted crossover point N*(m) where the two interventions balance correlates with observed crossover points at r=0.97 (Section 4.3, Prediction 3, Figures 6-7).
The additive log-belief framework generalizes across model families, replicating with r≈0.98 average correlation on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B (Appendix B).

9u1a2MpGng.text: Detached Skip-Links raise overall MLLM benchmark performance from 61.1% to 63.0% (+1.9 points) and OCR-specific performance from 65.2% to 68.3% (+3.1 points) relative to a baseline without gradient-detached shallow-feature fusion (Table 1).

Detached Skip-Links yield consistent overall-score improvements when swapped across four different ViT backbones: +1.9% with Perception Encoder, +2.5% with InternViT, +1.8% with AimV2-L, and +2.3% with SigLip2-So400M (Table 2).
The fusion mechanism stops gradients through the shallow skip branch while allowing forward features to propagate normally, computed as z = MLP([h_main, h_deep, sg(h_shallow)]) (Equation 1).

Gradient analysis shows the skip-path gradients are dominated by high variance rather than coherent signal, with near-zero cosine similarity and negligible cross-covariance cancellation between main and skip branch gradients early in training, motivating the detachment (Section on Gradient Analysis).

R-Probe reconstruction MSE degrades from 1.103 (text-only) to 1.980 when visual regions are masked, and the detached configuration reaches a target reconstruction-quality MSE threshold 23% faster, in 1689 steps versus 2158 steps for the non-detached configuration (R-Probe Validation results).

Experiments use large-scale pre-training on 5M multimodal samples and fine-tuning on 2M task-specific samples, evaluated across 22 benchmarks spanning STEM, General, Alignment, and OCR categories (Experimental Scale section).

d9JlreUNVY.text: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) regret for convex loss functions under compressed communication, improving on prior bounds (Theorem 3.1).
Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) regret for strongly convex loss functions (Theorem 3.2).

The paper reduces dependence on compression quality ω from the previously known O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2}√T) (convex) and O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2} ln T) (strongly convex) bounds down to O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) and O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) respectively, cutting the exponent on ω^{-1} from quadratic/quartic to square-root/linear (Section 3).

First lower bounds for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication are established: Ω(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1/4}n√T) for convex functions and Ω(ω^{-1}ρ^{-1/2}n ln T) for strongly convex functions (Theorems 3.3 and 3.4).

The algorithm combines a two-level blocking update framework with an online compressed gossip strategy and a projection error compensation scheme to jointly control consensus, compression, and projection error (Section 3.2).

Bandit-feedback extensions are provided: one-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/4}ρ^{-1/2}d^{1/2}n(ln n)^{1/4}T^{3/4}) regret (Theorem 4.1) and two-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}dn ln n√T) regret (Theorem 4.3).

R64DZyalyn.text: PlugGuard (referred to in-text as Kelp) achieves 0.8333 streaming F1 on WildGuard versus 0.7662 for a RoBERTa baseline, and 0.9246 streaming F1 on S-Eval versus 0.6545 for ShieldGemma2 (Table 1).
PlugGuard outperforms the prior streaming guardrail method ShieldHead by 50.2% on WildGuard streaming F1, and by 15.61% on average F1 across the evaluated post-hoc guardrail baselines (Table 1).
PlugGuard uses only 20M trainable parameters and adds an average of 0.42 ms per-token latency, staying under the 0.5 ms budget for real-time streaming safety detection (Efficiency results).

An ablation shows the Streaming Latent Dynamics (SLD) head alone reaches 0.8434 response-level F1 on WildGuard, while the Anchored Temporal Consistency (ATC) loss alone reaches only 0.4122 streaming F1 on S-Eval, with the combined method reaching 0.8333 streaming F1 on WildGuard (Table 3).

Evaluation uses the newly constructed StreamGuardBench dataset of 268k labeled query-response pairs generated from real outputs of 10 models (5 text-only, 5 vision-language) during decoding (StreamGuardBench Dataset section).

0Moj0YgFEF.text: SciAgentGym integrates 1,780 domain-specific tools spanning four natural science disciplines (Physics, Chemistry, Materials Science, and Life Sciences), paired with SciAgentBench containing 259 tasks and 1,134 sub-questions stratified into L1 (≤3 steps), L2 (4–7 steps), and L3 (≥8 steps) difficulty tiers (Environment & Benchmark Scale section).

GPT-5 success rate falls from 60.6% on L1 (easy, short-horizon) tasks to 38.6% on L2 and 30.9% on L3 (hard, long-horizon) tasks, a 68% relative drop from easiest to hardest tier, with 41.3% overall success when using tools (Table 3).

Fine-tuned SciAgent-8B reaches 30.1% overall success rate, outperforming the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-Instruct model's 23.9% overall success rate by 6.7 percentage points (SciAgent-8B vs. Larger Models results).
SciAgent-8B is trained on 11,074 execution-grounded trajectories produced via the SciForge synthesis method (SciAgent-8B vs. Larger Models results).

Weaker models fall into redundant tool-calling loops averaging 16.55 calls per task, versus only 3.41 calls for GPT-5, and models show only a 32.9% error-adaptation rate and 6.6% parameter-tuning success rate when recovering from tool-use failures (Key Findings section).
Tool augmentation substantially raises performance for some models, e.g. Claude-Sonnet-4 improves from 22.4% to 35.9% success when given access to tools (Key Findings section).

tAhdexEwnz.text: FA-OPD trains a student MLP policy using a Flow Matching teacher via two channels: reward distillation (an FM-enhanced discriminator scoring state-action pairs for PPO optimization) and action distillation (FM-generated target actions regressed via MSE) (Section 3.2-3.4).

On the Walker2d environment with suboptimal expert demonstrations (dataset IDs 2-5), FA-OPD significantly surpasses Diffusion Policy and Flow-Matching Policy baselines, in some cases exceeding the expert's own performance (Section 4.3, Table 1).
Under increasing observation noise (up to 1.5x), FA-OPD maintains greater than 0.95 success rate on the Hand-rotate task while Diffusion Policy drops to approximately 0.82 (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

FA-OPD achieves best or near-best final performance across 6 benchmark environments, including near-100% success on Hand-rotate and Fetch-pick tasks, converging faster than GAIL-family baselines (Figure 2, Table 3, Appendix F.1).

Ablations show that neither a reward-distillation-only configuration (beta=0) nor an action-distillation-dominated configuration matches the performance of the full dual-distillation configuration (Appendix F.2).

f4g8zblbwp.text: PPO's ratio clipping creates asymmetric, magnitude-dependent penalties: a low-probability token rising from 1e-4 to 1e-2 yields a ratio of 100 and triggers aggressive clipping despite negligible absolute divergence, while a high-probability token dropping from 0.99 to 0.80 yields an unclipped ratio of about 0.808 despite removing 0.19 probability mass (Section 4.2).

DPPO replaces single-sample ratio clipping with a masking rule based on an explicit estimate of the divergence between the current and rollout policy distributions, blocking updates only when this divergence exceeds a threshold delta (Section 4.3, Equations 11-12).

Binary Approximation collapses the vocabulary to a two-outcome (sampled token vs. all others) total-variation estimate, while Top-K Approximation tracks the K highest-probability tokens plus an aggregate 'other' category, both with negligible added computational overhead (Section 4.4, Equations 13-16).
Unconstrained baselines (PG-IS, CISPO) show growing training-inference mismatch and eventual collapse, whereas DPPO variants maintain stable, low mismatch throughout training (Section 5, Figure 3).
DPPO-Binary-KL and DPPO-Binary-TV consistently outperform GRPO-ClipHigher and CISPO across five model configurations on the AIME24 and AIME25 benchmarks (Section 7, Figures 8-9).

lYBn5XSfEv.text: Probability-Entropy Calibration introduces a Relative Rank Indicator that measures where the ground-truth token ranks within the model's predicted probability distribution, distinguishing genuinely under-learned tokens from tokens that are inherently uncertain due to pre-training (abstract only).
The inverse of the Relative Rank Indicator is used as a Relative Scale to reweight the fine-tuning training objective on a per-token basis (abstract only).

RankTuner, the method built on Probability-Entropy Calibration, achieves consistent improvements over probability-only and entropy-only reweighting baselines on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (abstract only).
RankTuner shows transfer gains on out-of-distribution reasoning tasks and improved code generation performance relative to baseline reweighting strategies (abstract only).

1sKFoIvmYg.text: CoreInfer achieves a 10.33x speedup on an NVIDIA TITAN XP GPU compared to a standard Huggingface implementation, and a 2.71x speedup compared to PowerInfer (Section 5.3, Table 3).

Core neurons exhibit stability under semantics-preserving continuations: adding 8-token and 64-token continuations to a 256-token sentence changes the identified core neuron set by only about 3% and 6% respectively (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

Spearman correlation between core-neuron similarity and semantic similarity across sentence pairs ranges from 0.52 to 0.66 across the tested models, and sentences from the same topic have more similar core neurons than sentences from different topics (Table 1, Section 3.2, Figure 4).

CoreInfer removes the per-token MLP activation predictor used by prior methods, instead fixing a set of core neurons during the pre-filling stage and reusing them through decoding, eliminating repetitive per-token neuron prediction overhead (Section 4.1-4.2).
CoreInfer incurs negligible performance loss relative to the dense baseline across information extraction, question answering, and translation tasks (Table 2).

NinueNAODD.text: BBQ's EM algorithm has closed-form updates that guarantee monotonic improvement of the likelihood and convergence to a stationary point, in contrast to gradient-based methods like Crowd-BT which lack such convergence guarantees (Section 3.3).

BBQ converges within seconds on all tested datasets, whereas Crowd-BT takes approximately 15 minutes on the HUMAINE dataset (105,220 comparisons) despite BBQ using an unoptimized plain NumPy implementation (Figure 3).
On the unscreened IHQ dataset, BBQ achieves 61.92% top-1 agreement with final rankings, compared to 33.15% for Crowd-BT and 24.32% for Bayes-BT (Table 1).
BBQ ranks first in Kendall's Tau agreement on 5 of 8 evaluated datasets and second on the remaining three, and achieves 100% top-1 agreement on the MT-Bench, WD, and HiFiC datasets (Table 1).
At the 99% confidence level, BBQ and Crowd-BT both show well-calibrated Type I error rates of about 1%, while Bayes-BT is overly conservative at about 0.1% (Appendix G, Figure 6).

BBQ's rater-quality parameter (mixture weight q_r modeling whether a rater follows Bradley-Terry or guesses randomly) correlates with Pearson r=0.724 with rater agreement to final rankings on the unscreened IHQ data, enabling identification of unreliable crowdsourced raters without a separate screening procedure (Figure 2, Equation 2).

rEqVnZZOiA.text: BLCE-G achieves worst-case cumulative regret of Õ(√(dT log K) ∧ d√T) using only O(log log T) parameter updates, matching minimax lower bounds in both small-K and large-K regimes (Theorem 1).

BLCE attains the same minimax-optimal regret as BLCE-G while eliminating the near G-optimal design step, yielding the lowest runtime of O(Kd²T log log T) among optimal rare-update algorithms (Theorem 2).

BGLE extends the rare-update approach to generalized linear contextual bandits, achieving regret Õ(RSd√T/√κ̂) that is independent of the worst-case curvature parameter κ while still requiring only O(log log T) updates (Theorem 3).

In runtime experiments across (K,d) instance pairs such as (1000,5), (5000,10), (50,20), and (100,30) with T=10,000, BLCE completes in 5.91-12.83 seconds versus 290-2987 seconds for prior optimal baselines (Table 2).

The paper formally distinguishes fully sequential, strictly batched, and rare-parameter-update feedback models, arguing that rare updates uniquely allow reward-free within-interval context adaptation exploited by BLCE-G and BLCE (Section on problem formulation).

Oz7GovJhac.text: Proposition 3.1 decomposes the optimal conditional velocity field as the unconditional velocity field plus a guidance term weighted by (1-t)/t, forming the basis of TFTF's training-free correction (Proposition 3.1).
Proposition 3.3 establishes that TFTF's importance-weighted samples converge asymptotically to the true conditional target distribution as the number of particles K→∞ (Proposition 3.3).

Algorithm 1 combines a three-phase sampling schedule—deterministic ODE evolution, stochastic SDE propagation with SMC resampling in the middle interval [t_n1, t_n2], and deterministic ODE completion—to mitigate weight degeneracy in high-dimensional importance sampling (Algorithm 1).
TFTF achieves external classifier accuracy of 97.12% on MNIST and 92.82% on CIFAR-10 for conditional generation without any additional model training (Experiments, Section 4).
TFTF extends to CelebA-HQ, reaching 80.99% external classifier accuracy while requiring no fine-tuning of the underlying flow model (Experiments, Section 4).

Zlt0GAbHDb.text: On RealEstate10K at 1/3 sparsity, SVD-CamGeo reduces RotError to 1.35 and CamMC to 5.40 compared to SVD-Full (RotError 1.51, CamMC 6.69) and SVD-Base (RotError 1.58, CamMC 5.80) (Table 1).
On the CogVideoX (DiT) backbone at 1/3 sparsity, CogVideoX-CamGeo lowers FVD-StyleGAN to 84.5 versus 98.2 for CogVideoX-Full and 90.8 for CogVideoX-Base (Table 1).
In a user study, CamGeo is preferred in 71.2% of pairwise comparisons across both U-Net and DiT backbones for trajectory alignment and temporal consistency (Table 2).
Ablations show removing cross-frame consistency distillation increases CamMC from 5.40 to 5.71, and removing the warm-up curriculum phase degrades CamMC from 5.40 to 5.83 (Table 4).

On out-of-distribution MannequinChallenge data, SVD-CamGeo achieves RotError 2.83 versus 4.46 for SVD-Full, showing the geometry-guided distillation generalizes beyond the training distribution (Section on out-of-distribution evaluation).

kt2CGsdTyt.text: The paper decomposes the effect of an unsupervised pretext task on target-task performance into three measurable factors—assumption learnability, assumption reliability, and assumption completeness—combined as Final performance = 1 − (1−Learnability)(1−Reliability)(1−Completeness) (Section 3, Theory of Prior Knowledge Induction).

The proposed low-cost estimator predicts target performance using only 5 labeled samples per class and 50 unlabeled samples per class before any target-task training (Section 4, Efficient Evaluation of the Impact of Pretext Tasks).
Across 115 pretext tasks, the estimated performance achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.785 with actual semi-supervised performance on CIFAR-10 and 0.717 on CIFAR-100 (Section 5, Experiments).

For self-supervised evaluation, the estimator's predicted performance correlates with actual performance at 0.820 on CIFAR-10 and 0.724 on CIFAR-100 using a ViT-B model trained for 5 epochs (Figures 3-4).

Scatter plots comparing predicted versus actual performance across CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 for both semi-supervised and self-supervised settings are presented as the paper's primary validation evidence (Figures 1-4).

CUURF3uF5M.text: CREST-Search achieves an 80.5% risk detection rate against web-augmented LLMs, compared to only 11.6% for the best baseline attack method (Key Results).

CREST-Search's generated adversarial search queries have a query toxicity score of 23.6%, the lowest among methods tested, indicating queries appear benign despite eliciting unsafe citations (Key Results).

The framework decomposes vulnerabilities into response risk, citation risk, and combined risk, finding that citation risks account for 89.3% of total risks detected, with 74.7% being citation-only cases where the LLM's own response text remains benign (Problem Statement / Vulnerability Distribution).
Three attack strategies—keyword injection, exaggeration, and role play—are used to craft adversarial queries targeting the retrieval-citation pipeline of search-augmented LLMs (Attack Strategies).

CREST-Search is evaluated against four production search-augmented models: GPT-4o-search-preview, GPT-4o-mini-search-preview, Gemini-2.0-flash-search, and Gemini-2.5-flash-search, using a purpose-built WebSearch-Harm dataset spanning five harmful content categories (Target Models Evaluated / WebSearch-Harm Dataset).

UuPDyWSNhA.text: ProOPF-D contains 12,000 instances organized into 4 difficulty levels of 3,000 samples each, built from 63 base power systems drawn from MATPOWER and IEEE PES archives (Section on Dataset Construction).
ProOPF-B provides 121 expert-annotated test cases distributed as 36/30/29/26 across Levels 1-4, curated from peer-reviewed literature by 4 power system experts (Section on Benchmark).

In few-shot evaluation, Gemini 3.0 Pro, DeepSeek V3.2, and Claude 4.5 Sonnet all score 0.00% on Level 4 (structural extensions with semantic parameters), while scoring 94.44%, 94.44%, and 77.78% respectively on Level 1 (Table 1).
Average few-shot accuracy across all four levels is 37.19% for Gemini 3.0 Pro, 29.75% for DeepSeek V3.2, and 33.88% for Claude 4.5 Sonnet (Table 1).
Supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3-30B-A3B on ProOPF-D raises Level 2 few-shot accuracy from 0% to 33.30% and achieves 11.54% on the previously unsolved Level 4 (Section on Fine-tuning Results).

The six-dimensional capability analysis in Appendix G finds baseline models identify structural modifications at 60-72% proficiency but show near-zero performance on semantic parameter inference (Appendix G).

ownPRHrXMx.text: DeltaEvolve replaces full-code history with structured semantic deltas—stored at three abstraction levels (20-40 token Delta Summary, structured Delta Plan Details, and Full Code)—to drive LLM-based evolutionary search (Section on Multi-Level Database).
On the BlackBox Optimization task, DeltaEvolve reaches a best score of 2.7297 versus AlphaEvolve's 2.6415 while consuming 1,390,709 tokens versus AlphaEvolve's 1,852,841 tokens (Table 2).

Across five domains (BlackBox Optimization, Hexagon Packing, Symbolic Regression, PDE Solver, Efficient Convolution), DeltaEvolve matches or exceeds AlphaEvolve's best score in every domain while reducing token consumption by an average of 36.79% (Table 2).

An ablation shows that removing the context-selection policy causes performance collapse, whereas removing numerical scalar feedback has minimal impact, indicating context selection dominates scalar feedback in the EM-style evolution loop (Table 1).

The default configuration uses k=3 top-performing nodes and m=2 diverse nodes per generation, with an ensemble sampling 80% of the time for high-throughput generation and 20% for complex reasoning across GPT-5-mini/o3-mini and Gemini-2.5 model families (Section on Configuration).

nddfPlfS09.text: RAUQ identifies uncertainty-aware attention heads per layer via Eq. 1, computes token-level confidence via a recurrent formula with hyperparameter α (Eq. 2), and aggregates sequence-level uncertainty via mean-log confidence combined with a max across layers (Eqs. 3-4).

RAUQ is evaluated on Llama-3.1 8B, Qwen-2.5 7B, Gemma-2 9B, and Falcon-3 10B across 12 datasets spanning QA (TruthfulQA, SciQ, MMLU, TriviaQA, CoQA, MedQUAD, GSM8k), summarization (CNN/DailyMail, SamSum, XSum), and machine translation (WMT19 DE-EN, WMT14 FR-EN), compared against 15 baseline UQ methods (Section on Experimental Setup, Table 1).

RAUQ achieves a mean Prediction Rejection Ratio (PRR) of 0.414 overall, with its strongest result on Gemma-2 9B for machine translation (PRR=0.473) and summarization (PRR=0.471), outperforming the second-best method (e.g., LUQ) by up to 0.265 PRR on Gemma-2 summarization (Table 1).
RAUQ introduces less than 1% computational overhead relative to baseline inference, whereas competing UQ methods that require sampling incur 400-820% overhead (Table 4).

Ablations show best performance at α=0 for summarization and α=0.2-0.5 for other tasks (hyperparameter sweep), that mean-of-logarithms token aggregation is consistently strongest (Table 5), and that max-based layer aggregation performs optimally (Table 6).

7ucFlopjQu.text: MergeMix uses model merging weights as a proxy for data-mixture performance via a three-stage pipeline: training K domain-specific experts on roughly 5B tokens each, fitting LightGBM regressors over merged-model performance surfaces, and selecting the optimal mixture via utility-driven optimization (Section 3).
MergeMix exhibits rank consistency of Spearman ρ > 0.92 overall and ρ = 0.98 specifically for knowledge tasks between merged-model proxy rankings and true mixture rankings (Section 4.3).

On 8B and 16B parameter MoE models trained with a 200B-token mid-training budget, MergeMix achieves an average score of 58.4 across math, code, knowledge, language, and reasoning benchmarks, versus 57.9 for manual tuning and 54.2 for uniform mixing (Tables 1-2).
MergeMix's estimated compute cost is approximately K·D_expert·C_train + M·C_eval ≈ 20B tokens, versus roughly 2T tokens for exhaustive manual tuning—about a 100x reduction (Section 3.4).

Mixture ratios optimized on the 8B model transfer effectively to the 16B model (cross-scale transfer, Section 4.4), and static mixtures are shown sufficient without dynamic mid-training recalibration (Section 4.5).

VE2aKpTWrK.text: OCE reformulates concept erasure as a multiplicative orthogonal transformation P (with PᵀP=I) applied to weight matrices, rather than an additive update W+ΔW, solved in closed form via the Procrustes theorem as P=UVᵀ from the SVD of M=BAᵀ (Section 5, Eq. 6).

A toy experiment shows scaling neuron weights by α=0.5 has negligible effect on generated semantics, while small layer-wise orthogonal rotations cause clear semantic shifts, motivating the focus on angular geometry over magnitude (Section 3, Figure 2).

For single-concept erasure of 10 CIFAR-10 object classes, OCE achieves an average erasure accuracy (Acce) of 4.61% and preservation accuracy (Accs) of 98.68%, versus MACE's 8.32% erasure accuracy, yielding a harmonic mean (Ho) of 97.01% versus MACE's 94.23% (Table 1).

For multi-concept erasure of 100 celebrities, OCE reaches Acce=3.44% and Accs=94.42%, compared to MACE (Acce=8.02%, Accs=91.60%) and SPEED (Acce=5.21%, Accs=92.67%), while completing erasure in 4.3 seconds on an A100 GPU versus 1800 seconds for MACE and 5.0 seconds for SPEED (Table 3).

An objective-design ablation for multi-concept erasure shows the subspace-level erasure term combined with vector-wise preservation term (the OCE configuration) achieves the best Acce of 3.44%, compared to 7.59% for vector-wise erasure plus vector-wise preservation (Table 5).

OCE extends to DiT-based diffusion models (FLUX.1 dev) across object, artistic style, celebrity, and implicit-concept (NSFW) erasure tasks, and edits key-projection matrices (Wk) in cross-attention layers using hyperparameters λe=900, λ0=50, λr=3 for multi-concept erasure (Figure 4, Appendix C).

qG8g00zRZa.text: SusVibes benchmark comprises 200 feature-request tasks drawn from 108 real-world GitHub projects spanning 10 security domains and 77 CWE types (Section 3).
SWE-agent with Claude 4 Sonnet achieves 61.0% functional-correctness pass rate but only 10.5% security pass rate on SusVibes (Table with Pass@1 results).

OpenHands with Claude 4 Sonnet reaches 49.5% functional correctness and 12.5% security pass, while Claude Code with Claude 4 Sonnet reaches 44.0% functional correctness but only 6.0% security pass (Pass@1 results table).

Weaker backbones score far lower on functional correctness, e.g. SWE-agent with Kimi K2 at 22.5% and SWE-agent with Gemini 2.5 Pro at 19.5%, while security pass rates remain uniformly low across all agent-model combinations (Pass@1 results table).

Prompting SWE-agent with Claude 4 Sonnet to self-select or be given the oracle CWE type degrades functional correctness (52.5% and 56.0% respectively, down from 61.0%) without meaningfully improving security pass rate (security mitigation ablation).
Human experts found agents select an average of 7.5 CWE types per task but achieve only 0.73 maximum recall in identifying the true vulnerability type (CWE identification analysis).

mVsb2MZ7LA.text: Metric-Phase Fields decouple an unsigned metric field r(x), constrained to satisfy the eikonal condition ||∇r(x)||=1, from a continuous phase field θ(x), and combine them via ϕ(x) = r(x)P(x) + θ(x) where P(x) = tanh(βθ(x)) (Section 3).
Proposition 3.1 establishes sign consistency: for any x with θ(x)≠0, sign(ϕ(x)) = sign(θ(x)), and ϕ(x)=0 if and only if θ(x)=0 (Proposition 3.1).

In a controlled thin-structure analysis varying thickness T over [0.10, 0.05, 0.01, 0.005], the SDF baseline NSH fails or produces severe artifacts at the thinnest scales and the UDF baseline GeoUDF suffers splitting and holes, while MPF reconstructs accurately across all thicknesses (Table 3).

On the Ship shape, MPF attains a Chamfer distance of 0.672×10⁻³ versus 2.596×10⁻³ for StEik and 5.591×10⁻³ for NSH; on Flower, MPF attains 1.757×10⁻³ versus 10.425×10⁻³ for NSH and 6.237×10⁻³ for DiGS (Table 2).

Evaluation uses 35 shapes -- 30 from Thingi10K/ShapeNet and 5 artist-designed models from Sketchfab -- selected to emphasize thin shells, thin plates, boundaries, and non-manifold configurations (Section 4 experimental setup).

rlVGCyjqnt.text: SleepBench aggregates 166,500 hours of sleep recordings from over 21,000 sleep studies across nine public National Sleep Research Resource sources (SHHS, NCHSDB, CFS, CCSHS, WSC, MROS, MESA, CHAT, SOF) (Section on SleepBench dataset).
On MROS, OSF achieves 97.3 AUC for sleep staging and 92.8 AUC for arousal detection, outperforming SleepFM (96.4 and 90.3 AUC respectively) and a supervised ViT (96.9 and 88.4 AUC) (Table 2).

Combining time masking with channel masking during pre-training raises sleep-staging AUC from 94.8 (channel masking alone with SimCLR) to 96.7, supporting the claim that channel-invariant feature learning is essential for pre-training (Table 1 ablation).

OSF outperforms baseline SleepFM across four missing-channel inference scenarios -- headband-only, respiratory+cardiac, brain+cardiac, and respiratory-only -- demonstrating that existing sleep foundation models fail to generalize when channels are missing at inference (Table 6).
Performance scales consistently with pre-training data fraction from 1% to 100% of the corpus and with encoder capacity from 1M to 85M parameters (scaling analysis section).

TJshRZDdyW.text: The nonparametric Maxwise Conformal Stopping method (Proposition 2.1) guarantees P(∃j: u_{n+1}(L_j) > τ*) ≤ α by setting the threshold to the (1-α)(1+1/n) quantile of maximum uncertainty-density scores from calibration traces, giving finite-sample false-positive-rate control without negative examples (Proposition 2.1).

The parametric Renewal Process method models inter-arrival times of uncertainty keywords, computes a Sidak-corrected normalized test statistic Z_t, and halts generation once Z_t exceeds threshold (Section on renewal process stopping).

Uncertainty keywords are extracted semi-supervised from 800 paired reasoning traces, yielding 102 keywords split into Impossibility (34), Speculation (14), and Insufficiency (56) categories (keyword construction section).

On GSM-MC, the Renewal method achieves 3.75% false-positive rate with 69.75% detection power and the Maxwise method achieves 5.42% FPR with 70.92% power, both far exceeding a length-based baseline's 32.17% power at 4.50% FPR (Table 1).
Both methods reach roughly 82-85% of oracle detection power on math benchmarks, with regression slopes of 0.8238 (Renewal) and 0.8532 (Maxwise) against oracle power (Figure 4).

On out-of-domain scientific reasoning benchmarks GPQA and HULE, calibrating on GSM8K yields 1.37-2.56% FPR but detection power drops to only 47-58% of the oracle baseline due to domain shift (Table 11).

jSSBKgH86z.text: On the V-STAR benchmark, Open-o3-Video improves mAM by 14.4 points and mLGM by 24.2 points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline, surpassing proprietary GPT-4o (mAM 26.8, mLGM 38.2) (Table 1).

On V-STAR's 'What' QA-accuracy dimension, Open-o3-Video improves by 27.5 points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline, and on the temporal-grounding 'When' dimension it improves IoU by 9.1 and 10.2 points on Chain1 and Chain2 respectively (Table 1).
Open-o3-Video generalizes beyond V-STAR, gaining 1.2% overall on VideoMME (4.1% on long videos), 1.4% overall on WorldSense, 1.1% overall on VideoMMMU, and 4.5 mIoU on TVGBench (Table 2).

Confidence-aware test-time scaling via N=8 voting over grounded spatio-temporal evidence traces improves accuracy by 1.2% on WorldSense and 1.0% on VideoMMMU over the base model by filtering hallucinated reasoning traces (test-time scaling experiments section).

GiSCgWW0Ze.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that in interior regions of the (t, log W_t) state space, betting policies deviating significantly from Kelly betting are provably suboptimal when the bettor is on schedule (Theorem 3.1).
Proposition 3.4 shows aggressive (all-in) betting outperforms Kelly betting when the bettor is behind schedule, using KL-divergence rate functions I+(λ,r) (Proposition 3.4).
Proposition 3.6 shows fractional (defensive) Kelly betting outperforms full Kelly betting when the bettor is ahead of schedule, by mitigating unrecoverable drawdown (Proposition 3.6).

A DQN is trained on 500,000 synthetic episodes with randomized horizons N in [100, 350] and null values m in [0.01, 0.99], using an MLP with 256 to 128 hidden units mapping a 22-dimensional predictable feature vector to 3 discrete betting actions (Section 4.3).
Figure 3 shows the learned DQN policy achieves superior deadline-limited rejection power compared to STaR-Bets and linear-epsilon baselines (Figure 3).
Figure 4 shows the DQN policy produces the narrowest valid confidence sequences at deadline N=100 across three Beta-mixture data settings, compared against fixed schedules (Figure 4).

YVNn8t1XMX.text: Proposition 1 establishes that the expected squared L2-norm of the policy's score function is a direct function of the policy's Rényi-2 entropy, motivating entropy-based rescaling of gradient magnitude (Proposition 1).

EMPG's modulated advantage combines a self-calibrating gradient scaling term g(H_t) with a future clarity bonus f(H_t+1), giving A_mod(i,t) = A^(i)·g(H_t^(i)) + ζ·f(H_t+1^(i)) (Section on EMPG method).
On ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-1.5B, EMPG improves GRPO by +8.1 points and DAPO by +7.3 points (Table 1).
On WebShop with Qwen2.5-7B, EMPG improves DAPO to 82.7%, a +3.1 point gain (Table 1).

On the Deep Search benchmark with Qwen2.5-32B, EMPG improves overall performance from 62.0 to 65.3 (+3.3 points), with a larger out-of-domain gain of +3.9 points than in-domain gain of +3.1 points (Table 2).

zQzmwG2Nue.text: VeRO's harness implements five abstractions—Git Worktree, Dataset, Filesystem, Experiment Database, and Evaluator—to enforce versioned agent snapshots, train/validation/test access control, and budget-controlled evaluation (Section on the VeRO Harness).

Using GPT-4.1 mini as the target agent across five tasks (GAIA, GPQA, MATH, TAU-Bench Retail, SimpleQA), the VeRO Default optimizer raises average score from 0.50 (baseline) to 0.61, while the VeRO Orchestrator (Sonnet) variant reaches 0.57 (Table 2).

Tool-oriented tasks (GAIA, Retail, SimpleQA) show roughly 8-9 percentage point improvement under VeRO optimization, while reasoning-heavy tasks (GPQA, MATH) show minimal improvement across all optimizer configurations (Table 2).

A simpler baseline agent ("Pawn", 19.5% GAIA accuracy) admits a larger optimization gain (+11.5 points) than a more sophisticated baseline agent ("Knight", 43.7% accuracy, +6.9 points), demonstrating a headroom correlation (Section on Empirical Findings).
