A robustness study (Table 3) finds that agents optimized on one target model transfer with sustained gains within the same model family (GPT-4.1 to GPT-4.1) but yield unpredictable, sometimes negative results when transferred cross-family (GPT-4.1 to Qwen3-4B) (Table 3).

Optimization targeting one task can regress performance on another, e.g., the Pawn agent's iteration 3 yields +5.75% on GAIA but -17.8% on SimpleQA due to added verification overhead (Section on Empirical Findings).

BUFSSOuphA.text: Theorem 1 decomposes total in-context learning risk into two orthogonal components: a model-dependent Bayes Gap and a model-independent, irreducible Posterior Variance (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 bounds the Bayes Gap for uniform-attention Transformers with m learned features as scaling with m^(-2α/d_eff) (approximation error) plus m/(pN) polylog(pN) (pretraining generalization error, jointly coupling context length p and prompt count N) plus 1/N polylog(pN) (Theorem 2).

Theorem 3 shows that in task mixtures, the posterior variance over task type concentrates exponentially in context length k, bounded by the true task's minimax risk plus O(e^{-D_min k/2}) (Theorem 3).

Theorem 4 shows that under input distribution shift, only the Bayes Gap is affected, scaling with the Wasserstein distance between pretraining and inference distributions, while the Posterior Variance remains intrinsic to the target domain (Theorem 4).

The uniform-attention Transformer architecture is defined as M_θ(P^k) = ρ_θ(mean-pooled feature encoding of context examples, query point), compressing context to a fixed-dimensional summary via mean-pooling of φ_θ(x_i,y_i) (Definition of Uniform-Attention Transformer).

h0RgDbosOj.text: FRACTAL achieves an average score of 87.11% on the Long Range Arena benchmark, compared to 87.04% for S5 and 86.09% for S4 (Table 2).
FRACTAL achieves 61.85% on the ListOps task, outperforming S5's 61.10% and S4's 59.60% (Table 2).
On the Path-X task, FRACTAL scores 98.39%, slightly below S5's 98.62% but above S4's 96.35% (Table 2).

Theorem 3.4 proves that the diagonal elements A_nn = n+1 of the state transition matrix A(α) are independent of the fractional singularity index α, guaranteeing spectral stability, while off-diagonal coupling increases with α (Theorem 3.4).

FRACTAL's fractional-order measure uses power-law weighting (t-τ)^{-α} with tunable singularity index α in [0,1) to simultaneously achieve full history retention, recency sensitivity, and scale invariance, resolving a trade-off unmet by Scaled Legendre, Translated Laguerre, and Translated Legendre measures (Section on Technical Foundation).

FRACTAL maintains O(N log L) parallel computational complexity through a diagonal state-space structure with multi-scale filter banks partitioning heterogeneous α values across channels (Section on Architecture Components).

TXV35hR2Ib.text: SmoothSA's query preheating module, a small self-distilled Transformer decoder that warm-starts cold-start slot queries, raises COCO object discovery ARI from 20.0 (SPOT baseline) to 26.2 (Table 1).

On the YTVIS video benchmark, SmoothSA's transform-differentiation scheme (3 Slot Attention iterations on first frames, 1 iteration on subsequent frames) improves ARI from 42.0 (RandSF.Q) to 44.1 and ARI-fg from 59.4 to 61.5 (Table 2).
SmoothSA improves object recognition accuracy on COCO from 67% (SPOT) to 73% top-1 accuracy, and the YTVIS R² score from 53% (SlotContrast) to 62% (Table 3).
SmoothSA improves downstream visual reasoning, raising GQA accuracy from 52.3% (SPOT) to 56.7% and CLEVRER per-question accuracy from 95.6% (SlotContrast) to 96.9% (Table 4).

Ablations show that using a shared-weight Transformer-decoder preheater with a stop-gradient on preheated queries and a loss weight of 100 is necessary for the 3-iteration-then-1-iteration recurrence scheme to outperform both 3+3 and 1+1 iteration schedules (Table 5).

51914Feknq.text: In 12-layer Transformers and 4-layer Mamba-2 models trained on CHILDES, surprisal curves show a clear match/mismatch separation indicating emergent symbol grounding, whereas 4-layer LSTMs show minimal separation (Figure 2).

Saliency analysis of the 12-layer Transformer localizes symbol-grounding computation to middle layers 7–9, with a tuned lens showing layer 7 becomes an effective predictor at roughly 10,000 training steps (Figure 5).

Causal ablation of identified 'aggregate' attention heads (average layer 7.28–7.78) produces statistically significant surprisal increases (p<0.001), and the number of such heads grows from 0.07 at step 500 to 6.71 by step 20,000 (Table 2).

Gather heads (e.g., L4 H7, L4 H8) compress environmental information into token representations while aggregate heads (e.g., L7 H5, L8 H5) redistribute it to prediction positions, jointly implementing the grounding mechanism (Figure 6).

The same grounding phenomenon and aggregate-head mechanism replicate in image-grounded and caption-grounded Visual Dialog data and in vision-language models, with saliency again concentrated in middle layers (Figure 4, Figure 7).

4-layer LSTMs fail to develop the aggregate-head grounding mechanism because their sequential compression architecture prevents the retrieval pattern seen in Transformers and Mamba-2 (Section 5, Figure 3).

5Cvh976L09.text: The paper formalizes learning multiplication in a finite-dimensional algebra as learning a structure tensor 𝓒 ∈ 𝔽^{n×n×n}, and proves that any such tensor defines a valid algebra (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).

Associativity, commutativity, and unitality are each characterized as tensor identities on 𝓒 (e.g., associativity as ∑_k 𝓒_ijk𝓒_klm = ∑_k 𝓒_ikm𝓒_jlk for all i,j,l,m), unifying group-based grokking as a special case of the FDA framework (Proposition 2.2, Section 3).

In experiments over finite fields 𝔽_7 with n=2 (2^3=8 algebraic categories sampled at ratios r∈{0.2,...,0.9}), non-unital associative-commutative algebras (0.03% of sampled category) grok fastest while unital associative-commutative algebras (0.017%) grok slowest (Section 5, Figures 4–5).

A representation-quality metric 𝓜_rep transitions sharply from low values to ≈1 at the same point test accuracy rises, and higher test accuracy in low-data regimes correlates with higher 𝓜_rep (Section 5, Figures 1–2).

Higher mode-3 unfolding rank r^(3) and greater sparsity s of the structure tensor both delay grokking and increase test loss, linking grokking speed to algebraic/tensor complexity (Section 5, Figure 6).

Proposition 5.1 shows that once a faithful representation is learned, the group/algebra product can be exactly linearly decoded via inverse lookup in the classifier weights (Section 5, Proposition 5.1).

pqOlyvsmU3.text: Attn-QAT identifies two principles required for stable 4-bit (FP4) attention quantization-aware training: matching the backward-pass recomputation precision of the attention score matrix to the forward pass, and maintaining a separate high-precision output buffer used only for gradient computation (Section on Key Technical Contributions).

Attn-QAT recovers BF16-level quality on Wan 2.1 (1.3B and 14B), Qwen-3 14B, and Llama-3.1 70B across VBench, WikiText, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, and ARC-C benchmarks without any explicit outlier-mitigation heuristics.

Removing the high-precision output buffer causes severe training instability with exploding gradients, and omitting fake quantization in the backward pass produces significantly noisier gradient norms (Table 2 ablation).
Attn-QAT delivers a 1.1x–1.5x speedup versus SageAttention3 on an RTX 5090 GPU, using custom Triton kernels for training and CUDA kernels adapted from SageAttention3 for inference.
Human evaluation on 99 VBench prompts rates Attn-QAT video outputs as comparable to the BF16 baseline.

hLLdM61qen.text: RedVisor uses a two-phase, gated parallel adapter atop a frozen backbone: an inspection phase in which the adapter generates reasoning that localizes prompt injections, followed by a generation phase where the adapter is muted and the backbone produces the response guided by that reasoning.
On Alpaca-Farm, RedVisor achieves ROUGE-L scores of 0.81–1.00 for injection-localization across attack categories, outperforming the PromptLocate baseline on complex attacks (Table 2).

RedVisor keeps attack success rate (ASR) at 0.00–0.07 across attack categories, including 0.00 ASR against adaptive GCG attacks, versus 0.04–0.78 ASR for baselines and 40–60% ASR degradation for fine-tuned defenses under adaptive attacks (Table 3).
RedVisor preserves utility with an 85.78% win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0, compared to only 56.75% for fine-tuning-based defenses (Figure 3).
RedVisor's zero-copy KV cache reuse processes 1,000 RAG queries more than twice as fast as its decoupled (non-zero-copy) variant (Figure 4).
RedVisor is trained on the Cleaned Alpaca dataset (52k examples) augmented with five attack categories: Naive, Escape-character, Completion, Multi-round, and Ignore attacks.

dHH6UrXIQ5.text: DetailMaster comprises 4,116 expert-validated long prompts averaging 284.89 tokens each, annotated across four evaluation dimensions: Character Attributes, Structured Character Locations, Multi-Dimensional Scene Attributes, and Explicit Spatial/Interactive Relationships (Section 3).
The benchmark includes 37,165 character attribute annotations, 6,910 location annotations, and 18,526 relationship annotations used to automatically score generated images (Section 3).

CLIP-based text encoders (used in SD1.5 and SD-XL) show marked performance degradation from token length constraints, while T5-based encoders show measurable but still limited improvement, evaluated in Table 2A/2B.
Even state-of-the-art models such as FLUX and GPT Image-1 plateau at roughly 50% accuracy on Character Attributes, Character Locations, and Entity Relationships (Table 2).
Figure 3 shows a consistent negative correlation between prompt length and generation accuracy across all evaluated text-to-image models.
Human evaluation confirms 97.5% prompt-consistency agreement and 93.6% visual-fidelity agreement with the automatic scoring pipeline (Section 5.2).

tqr5sZlS6Y.text: AtomWorld evaluates LLMs on 10 crystal-structure manipulation action types (change, remove, add, insert_between, swap, delete_below, move, move_towards, rotate_around, super_cell) using CIF-format structures, with roughly 1,000 samples per action (Section on task construction).

Success rates cluster by difficulty: easy actions (change, remove, add) reach 70-90% success, moderate actions (move, move_towards, insert_between) reach 50-80%, while hard actions (swap, delete_below, rotate_around) fall to 10-40% (Figure 2).

On simplified PointWorld rotation tests, models achieve 98-100% output parsability yet exhibit mean maximum coordinate errors of 14-16 Angstroms, showing that outputs are readable but geometrically incorrect for rotation operations.
super_cell task success ranges from 4% for Llama3-70B to 98% for GPT-o3, and tool-augmented insert_between success rises from 46% without tools to 83% with tools.
Larger Qwen3 models (32B) outperform Llama3-70B despite having far fewer parameters, indicating architecture and training strategy matter as much as scale for spatial reasoning.

The authors conclude current LLMs are best used as copilots/verification-and-planning assistants for materials structure modeling under human direction, rather than as autonomous scientific agents, based on the cumulative-error pattern observed across tasks.

SMhHoUepeR.text: LoSA achieves up to a 4.14x attention speedup over dense attention on RTX A6000 GPUs, versus 3.26x for the QUEST sparse-attention baseline (Section 5.4).
On RTX 5090 GPUs, LoSA delivers a 3.67x speedup, demonstrating scalability to newer hardware (Section 5.4).

On LongBench with Trado-8B-Instruct at a sparsity budget of 128, LoSA improves average accuracy by +10.43 points over QUEST, and by +8.38 points for SDAR-8B-Chat at the same budget (Table 1, Table 3).
LoSA attains up to +9 points average accuracy improvement at aggressive sparsity levels while using 1.54x lower attention density than QUEST (Abstract, Table 2).

Evaluations cover Trado-8B/4B-Instruct and SDAR-8B-Chat diffusion language models on LongBench tasks (HotPotQA, TriviaQA, NarrativeQA, Qasper, MultiFieldQA) and commonsense reasoning benchmarks (HellaSwag, WinoGrande, BoolQ) at context lengths of 32K-64K tokens (Section 5).

f1q8dFnxtY.text: WISE evaluates text-to-image models using 1,000 structured prompts spanning 3 domains and 25 subdomains: Cultural Common Sense (400 prompts, 10 subdomains), Spatio-temporal Reasoning (300 prompts), and Natural Science (300 prompts in biology, physics, chemistry) (Section on benchmark construction).
WiScore is computed as a weighted combination of three 0-2 rated dimensions: WiScore = 0.7 x Consistency + 0.2 x Realism + 0.1 x Aesthetic Quality.

On the original WISE prompts, FLUX.1-dev attains the top overall WiScore of 0.50, followed by Playground-v2.5 at 0.49 and SD-3.5-large at 0.46, while unified multimodal models Orthus-7B-base (0.10) and JanusFlow-1.3B (0.18) score far lower (Table 1).
When GPT-4o rewrites complex knowledge-dependent prompts into direct descriptions, WiScore jumps substantially, e.g. FLUX.1-dev rises from 0.50 to 0.73 and Janus-Pro-7B from 0.35 to 0.71 (Table 2).

The gap between dedicated T2I models and unified multimodal generation models on WISE reveals an 'understanding-generation gap' where models that understand world knowledge in text often fail to render it correctly in images.

viOFFYQPgL.text: MAFE introduces three Multi-Agent Fair Environments: Loan Processing (Admissions, Funds Disbursement, and Debt Management agents built on the real LendingClub dataset with initial balances of $1,000-$40,000), Healthcare (Insurance Company, Hospital, and Central Planner agents tracking healthy/sick/deceased population states), and Higher Education (four agents: University Admissions, Budget Allocation, Employer, and Central Planner) (Section 4).

The environments follow the standard MARL step(action) / observation-reward-done interface, making them compatible with ecosystems like Gym, Gymnasium, and PettingZoo for reproducible evaluation (Section 3).

Figure 7 presents Pareto frontiers across all three environments showing that the most significant performance declines occur only when the fairness-term weight substantially exceeds the reward-term weight.

The healthcare environment shows smaller performance differences between training configurations than loan or education environments, suggesting agent objectives there naturally align with system-level well-being (Section 6).

Figure 4 shows that including all reward components (direct rewards, fairness penalties, and rate-based rewards) yields superior outcomes versus partial reward configurations; omitting rate-based rewards causes the education environment's rate metric to plateau at a significantly lower value (Section 6).

JeWtUdUk7l.text: MaskAQ achieves up to 3.1% higher ImageNet Top-1 accuracy than MimiQ at 3-bit precision (3w3a) on DeiT-T (Table 1).
MaskAQ attains ImageNet Top-1 accuracy of 64.27%, 73.18%, and 78.89% for DeiT-T, DeiT-S, and DeiT-B respectively under 5w5a quantization (Table 1).
Removing the periodic sample refreshing strategy drops DeiT-T 3w3a Top-1 accuracy from 22.65% to 21.43%, a 1.22-point decrease (Table 2).
Removing the feedback loss L_fb or alignment loss L_align each degrades DeiT-T 3w3a accuracy by 1.68 and 2.05 points respectively (Table 2).

The Masked Attention Coupling module identifies informative regions as a sparse subset of patches via differential entropy maximization over patch similarity, then aligns full-precision and quantized model attention within those regions (Section 2.2.1, Section 2.2.2).
Optimal hyperparameters for the feedback and alignment loss weights are λ_fb = 1.0 and λ_align = 0.1, per sensitivity analysis (Figure 3).

wqpQafNJTH.text: Risk Awareness Injection (RAI) reduces attack success rate to 0.00% on Qwen3-VL-8B for MM-SafetyBench, versus baseline rates as high as 49.42% for LLaVA-1.6-7B (Table 1).
On JailbreakV-28K, RAI reduces average attack success rate to 2.58% for Qwen3-VL-8B and 2.81% for LLaVA-1.6-7B (Table 2).
On Video-SafetyBench, RAI achieves 0.00% ASR on Qwen3-VL-8B and 3.21% ASR on LLaVA-OneVision-1.5, down from a 29.26% baseline (Table 3).

RAI preserves utility with performance drops of at most 0.4 points across models on the MM-Vet reasoning benchmark, and negligible MME score change (e.g., 610.64 vs. 611.78 for Qwen2.5-VL) (Table 4, Table 5).
RAI is training-free and localizes high-risk visual tokens via cosine similarity to an unsafe prototype subspace built from language embeddings, injecting risk-aware signals at Layer 0 (Section 3).
RAI incurs only 13.2% inference overhead compared to 54.0% for ShiftDC and 117.9% for CoCA (Table 6).

66H4jMUzft.text: AutoTool achieves a 21.8% accuracy gain over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model on the V* benchmark (90.1% vs. 69.1%) (Table 1).
AutoTool yields a 44.9% inference efficiency improvement on the POPE benchmark compared to existing tool-augmented methods (Table 8).
AutoTool reduces training time by 20.3% (35.8 hours vs. 44.9 hours) compared to DeepEyes (Table 8).

The dual-mode reasoning strategy uses explicit <tool_on> and <tool_off> tokens with Mode-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), applying distinct GRPO reward functions (+1.0 for correct tool-assisted answers, -0.5 penalty for incorrect ones after tool invocation) (Section 3.1-3.5).

Adaptive Mode Balancing (Equation 5) dynamically adjusts reward coefficients based on tool invocation frequency to prevent premature dominance of one reasoning mode during training (Section 3, Equation 5).
Dual-mode distribution analysis shows HRbench and V* benchmarks favor tool-ON reasoning while POPE favors tool-OFF reasoning (Figure 3).

atmmJEFuci.text: OnlineSPEC achieves up to 24% speedup across seven benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU, Code-Search-Python, Spider, MBPP, Alpaca-Finance) and three foundation models (Vicuna-7B, Llama-2-7B, Qwen3-8B) (Section 4, Table 1, Table 2).

Theorem 1 formally establishes that the acceleration rate γ of speculative decoding depends on algorithmic dynamic regret, candidate draft length k, and the inference time ratio α between draft and target models (Section 2.2, Theorem 1).
Lemma 1 bounds the expected accepted draft sequence length via the dynamic regret of the online learning algorithm used to update the draft model (Section 2.2, Lemma 1).

The Opt-Hydra instantiation, using optimistic online learning with historical gradients as predictive hints, achieves up to 26% speedup over vanilla speculative decoding baselines (Section 3.2, Table 1).
The Online-LR instantiation achieves a 1.41x speedup on GSM8K versus the target model alone on Qwen3-8B, outperforming an offline logistic-regression draft baseline (Section 3.1, Table 2).
Ens-Eagle applies online ensemble learning over multiple draft heads and shows consistent gains over naive combinations of online speculative decoding methods (Section 3.3, Table 1).

WVm7jMnA9t.text: On MultiPL-HumanEval with Qwen 1.5B, CodeChemist improves Lua Pass@1 from 34.1 to 57.8 (a 69.5% relative gain) and Java from 43.5 to 69.6 (a 60.0% relative gain) without any retraining (Table 1).

On MultiPL-HumanEval with Qwen 1.5B, CodeChemist improves C++ Pass@1 from 34.4 to 52.2, a 51.7% relative gain, demonstrating benefit on complex-syntax languages as well as low-resource ones (Table 1).
On the harder Ag-LiveCodeBench-X benchmark, CodeChemist yields 18.0% to 200.0% relative improvements for Lua across different model sizes (Table 3).

CodeChemist uses a three-stage pipeline: cross-lingual test case generation from high-resource PL code, multi-temperature hedged sampling (tau in {0.0, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1}), and execution-based selection using pass rates against generated test oracles (Section 3, Figure 1, Algorithm 1).
On MultiPL-MBPP, CodeChemist produces consistent gains for Lua ranging from 4.3% to 56.9% relative improvement, smaller than on the harder benchmarks (Table 2).

CodeChemist's gains are effective across multiple model families (Qwen, Llama, GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek) and model sizes, with larger accuracy gaps between languages correlating with greater relative improvement (Section 4).

FCVPVqRLDJ.text: EviScreen constructs dual knowledge banks from historical cases and retrieves regional evidence for retrospection-style interpretability during disease screening (Section 3.1).
On the JSIEC dataset, EviScreen achieves an AUROC of 91.32% along with specificity of 72.92% at 95% recall (Spe@95%R) and 59.39% at 99% recall (Spe@99%R) (Table 1).
EviScreen is evaluated across four disease-screening datasets (JSIEC, RIADD, CheXpert, and Derm12345) using AUROC, AP, Spe@95%R, Spe@99%R, Spe@100%R, and CSR metrics (Table 1).
A training-free variant uses contrastive retrieval to generate abnormality maps that provide localization interpretability without additional training (Section 3.3).
An ablation study isolates the contribution of the evidential reasoning components (evidence retrieval and evidence-aware reasoning) to overall screening performance (Table 2).
Performance scaling of the dual knowledge banks with respect to bank size is analyzed separately from the main results (Figure 5).

JO0IsGJg16.text: XR-1 is validated on over 14,000 real-world rollouts spanning six distinct robot embodiments, including Tien Kung 1.0/2.0, single- and dual-arm UR-5e, dual-arm Franka, and AgileX Cobot Magic 2.0 (Abstract, Section 4.1).
XR-1 spans over 120 diverse manipulation tasks and is compared against baselines including pi0, pi0.5, RDT, UniVLA, and GR00T-N1.5 (Abstract, Section 4).
On Tien Kung 2.0, XR-1 attains an average success rate of 72.0%, compared to 41.0% for pi0.5 and 40.8% for pi0 (Table 2).
On the Dual-Arm UR-5e DUR-FindTapeBasket task, XR-1 achieves an 85% success rate versus 50% for pi0 (Figure 4).
XR-1 is tested for generalization to novel objects, dynamic distractors, background variations, and illumination changes (Table 3).

An ablation shows that adding UVMC (unified vision-motion representation) cross-modal alignment raises average success rate from 48.3% to 66.7%, and the lightweight XR-1-Light variant gains +15 percentage points from UVMC integration (Tables 4-5).

kChzpoYFef.text: DSR-Bench comprises 4,140 problem instances spanning 20 data structures and 35 operations, totaling 166,230 query evaluations, organized into six categories: Linear, Temporal, Associative, Hierarchical, Network, and Hybrid (Section 2, Figure 1, Table 8).

On the standard DSR-Bench evaluation, the top model Gemini-2.5-Pro reaches only 0.76 overall average score and o4-mini reaches 0.72, while on the harder DSR-Bench-challenge subset the best score drops to 0.47 for Gemini-2.5-Pro (Table 1, Table 3).

On spatial data structures, GPT-4.1's K-D Heap performance drops from 0.74 at k=1 to 0.21 at k=5, and its K-D Tree accuracy falls from 0.86 on uniform data to 0.31 on non-uniform (circle) distributions (Table 4, Table 5, Table 6).
Models perform substantially worse on natural-language-phrased tasks than formally-phrased ones, e.g., GPT-4.1 drops from 1.00 to 0.77 on Queue and from 0.88 to 0.59 on BST (Table 7).
Instruction-tuned models are evaluated under different prompting strategies, including code-generation-based self-reasoning over their own generated code (Table 2, Section 3).

D7MzX6ts55.text: The Find, Fix, Reason (FFR) framework uses a frozen teacher model to diagnose missing spatiotemporal dependencies via a predefined error taxonomy of temporal, spatial, and misconception categories, then provides minimal evidence patches as context repair (Section 3.2).

The Robust Improvement Reward (Equation 8) combines outcome validity and dependency alignment, applying a patch-reliance tax parameter kappa=0.3 to discourage over-reliance on injected patches (Section 3.2).
Applying FFR to Video-R1 yields +22.33% on VSI-Bench and +11.75% on MMVU, while applying FFR to VideoRFT yields +21.77% on VSI-Bench and +15.87% on MMVU (Table 2).
An ablation shows FFR with a 32B teacher model surpasses supervised fine-tuning distilled from a 235B teacher (51.2 vs 50.7) (Table 4).
Ablations show ground-truth-referenced patches improve precision by +7.6 on Video-Holmes and that visual context is critical for spatiotemporal tasks, contributing +10.0 on Video-Holmes (Table 3).
During training, the intervention ratio (frequency of teacher patches needed) drops by 48% while task accuracy rises from 77.5% to 80.2% (Figure 4).

XarOZG8Un0.text: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of O~(ηK log^2 T) for KL-regularized multi-armed bandits in the high-regularization regime where η ≤ sqrt(T/K) (Section 4.2).
In the low-regularization regime (η ≥ sqrt(T/K)), the same analysis yields a regret bound of O~(sqrt(KT log T)), which is η-independent (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).
Theorem 5.3 provides a lower bound of Ω(ηK log(T/(η^2 K))) in the high-regularization regime, establishing near-tightness with the upper bound in Theorem 4.2 (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
Theorem 5.1 gives a lower bound of Ω(sqrt(KT)) in the low-regularization regime via a two-point construction method (Section 6.1, Theorem 5.1).

The KL-UCB algorithm uses an optimistic bonus term b_t(a) = sqrt(2 log(TK/delta) / (N_t(a) ∨ 1)) together with a novel peeling argument and Freedman's inequality to obtain tight high-probability bounds (Section 4.3).

TnJMJm3Fbi.text: On the CRAG benchmark with retrieval using Llama3.1-8B, TruthRL reduces hallucination rate from 43.5% (prompting baseline) to 19.4% and improves the truthfulness score from +5.3 to +37.2 (Table 1).

Averaged across four knowledge-intensive benchmarks with retrieval, TruthRL achieves a mean hallucination rate of 18.8% and truthfulness score of +25.6, versus 54.1% hallucination and -16.4 truthfulness for the prompting baseline (Table 1).
Compared to vanilla accuracy-driven RL, TruthRL reduces hallucinations by 28.9 percentage points and improves truthfulness by 21.1 points (Section on hallucination reduction claims).
An ablation shows the ternary reward formulation outperforms a binary reward on CRAG, achieving +37.2 truthfulness and 19.4% hallucination versus +20.8 and 39.5% for the binary variant (Table 3).
TruthRL generalizes across backbone model families and sizes, including Llama3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct in addition to Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Table 7).
On difficult CRAG questions, TruthRL attains a 15.5% hallucination rate versus near-100% for accuracy-optimized baselines, demonstrating improved knowledge-boundary recognition (Figure 3).

k9OuSat5IR.text: CoLLM-CC uses a centralized critic built on a shared Transformer backbone with KV-cache history representation, described in Section 5.1, with sequence-level actions handled via teacher-forced forward passes (Section 5.2) and the full training procedure given as Algorithm 1 (Section 5.3).

Proposition 4.2 shows that Monte Carlo (MA-REINFORCE) variance scales as σ²/K^(H-t), and Proposition 4.3 shows the number of required inference calls grows as nK(K^H − 1)/(K−1), both increasing rapidly with horizon H (Section 4.1).

Section 6.3 reports that both Monte Carlo (MA-REINFORCE) and the decentralized critic variant (CoLLM-DC, Algorithm 2 in Appendix B) underperform CoLLM-CC on long-horizon or sparse-reward tasks, including a Minecraft task with horizon H=4 where Monte Carlo requires substantially more samples and CoLLM-DC fails to converge.

Table 1 compares CoLLM-CC, CoLLM-DC, and MAGRPO across writing (TLDR, arXiv expansion), coding (CoopHE), and game (StrBuild, HouseBuild) tasks, with Figure 2 showing convergence curves with 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals across five task panels.

Section 4.2 contrasts the decentralized critic formulation (Eq. 2-3) with the centralized critic formulation (Eq. 4-5) underlying CoLLM-CC's variance-reduction argument over actor-critic alternatives.

RBLVGh2Zab.text: Theorem 2.2 gives the first theoretical characterization showing that the pulse count required for accurate symmetric-point (SP) estimation scales as O(Δw_min^{-1}) with device update granularity, and the estimation error is bounded by O(1/(N·Δw_min)) + Θ(Δw_min).

The proposed RIDER algorithm (Algorithm 2) dynamically tracks the symmetric point during training and achieves an O(1/√K) convergence rate, with Theorem 3.7 bounding the error as E_K ≤ O(κ1κ2^5/√K) + Θ(Δw_min) under smoothness, bounded-variance, and strong-convexity assumptions.
Corollary 3.9 shows RIDER requires O(δ^{-2}) pulses in total, compared to O(δ^{-2} + δ^{-1}Δw_min^{-1}) for two-stage symmetric-point calibration approaches.

The enhanced E-RIDER variant (Algorithm 3) uses chopping (random sign-flipping, Eq. 17-18) and a moving-average low-pass filter (Eq. 12, per Lemma 3.10) to accelerate SP tracking, and Figure 4 shows E-RIDER achieves lower total pulse cost than ZS-based methods across device state counts.

On LeNet-5 and FCN (MNIST) and ResNet-18 (CIFAR-100), Tables 1 and 2 show E-RIDER outperforms AGAD and TT-v2 baselines in test accuracy under varying reference mean/std offsets, while Figure 2 shows training loss degrades substantially on MNIST LeNet-5 without accurate SP estimation.

sEPES6oimF.text: FedReLa re-labels local client samples via a feature-dependent label re-allocator using class-wise z-score standardization (Eq. 3-5) and tanh normalization with client-specific thresholds (Eq. 8), without requiring global class-distribution knowledge (Abstract, Section on key mechanism).

On step-wise imbalanced Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10/100 with imbalance ratio 20 and α=0.3, adding FedReLa improves minority-class accuracy by 6.03-38.30 percentage points and overall accuracy by 0.37-7.10 points across baselines (Table 1).
On long-tailed CIFAR-10 (imbalance factor 100, α=0.1), FedReLa improves FedLOGE's overall accuracy from 58.22% to 64.78%, and on long-tailed CIFAR-100 improves FedETF from 37.11% to 40.19% (Table 2).
On ImageNet-LT, adding FedReLa to FedLoGe improves overall accuracy from 30.52% to 31.70% (Table 3).

Lemma 2 proves that the re-labeled decision boundary shifts toward the majority-class region when the re-labeling probability ρ_{ℓ→j(k)}(x*) ≤ 0.5, and Lemma 3 extends this boundary-shift analysis to the globally aggregated model.

FedReLa's one-shot relabeling inference costs about one-third of a single training round's FLOPs and adds negligible runtime overhead, increasing FedLOGE's per-round time from 72.36 to 73.06 seconds (Appendix B.1).

U1YNfdXkVD.text: CBV achieves attack success rates on MSCOCO image captioning of 85.77% (LLaVA-v1.5-7B), 83.83% (MiniGPT-v2), 84.12% (Qwen-2.5-VL-7B), and 87.71% (InstructBLIP-7B) (Table 2).

On VQA v2, CBV achieves attack success rates of 84.89% (LLaVA-v1.5-7B), 85.87% (MiniGPT-v2), 83.58% (Qwen-2.5-VL-7B), and 85.55% (InstructBLIP-7B), while keeping BLEU@4 within 0.5-2.0 points and VQA accuracy within 3-4 points of the clean baseline (Table 3).
The universal adversarial perturbation (UAP) trigger generated via projected gradient ascent (Section 4.2) outperforms patch-based triggers, reaching 84.27% ASR versus 78.40% for patches (Table 5).
GradCAM-guided masking, which restricts perturbations to semantically important regions (Section 4.3), improves stealthiness, lowering LPIPS from 26.52 (no mask) to 23.78 (with mask) (Table 6).

Text-guided score matching during the diffusion reverse process (Section 4.4) improves attack success rate by 11.3 percentage points over the ungated variant (Table 4), with a 5% poisoning rate sufficient to reach roughly 80% ASR while preserving clean-task utility (Figure 6).
CBV generates poisoned images in 28.7±1.9 seconds per image, substantially faster than optimization-based baselines HTBA (185.4s) and IP (218.3s) (Table 7).

4oZDo5v9zt.text: VT-Bench comprises over 756K samples across 14 datasets (8 public, 4 newly constructed for discriminative prediction, and additional generative-reasoning datasets) spanning 9 domains including medical, pets, media, and transportation (Section 4, Table 1).
VT-Bench evaluates 23 representative models spanning unimodal experts, specialized visual-tabular models, and vision-language models (Section 5).

On the DVM-Car QA generative-reasoning task, increasing the input table size from 10 to 50 rows causes a marked performance drop, with the best model reaching only about 72% average accuracy (Section 5, Table 2b).

On the EHRXQA generative-reasoning task the best-performing model achieves only 27% full-task accuracy, and all evaluated models show a clear accuracy drop on Constrained Counting and Conditional Mean numerical-reasoning subtasks (Section 5, Table 2b).

Removing one modality (image or table) often improves performance for several fusion models, revealing a negative-transfer effect across both specialized visual-tabular models and general-purpose vision-language models (Section 5).

dtHEthIjmu.text: IC-VCO places contrastive image pairs in a shared multi-image context so that partition functions cancel exactly in the DPO-style objective, avoiding the partition-function mismatch present in prior Visual Preference DPO formulations (Section 2, Section 3).

On LLaVA-NeXT-Interleave-Qwen-7B, IC-VCO with edited samples reaches an overall score of 63.35, outperforming the SymMPO baseline by 1.24 points, with AMBER-Attr 82.24 and AMBER-Exist 92.73 (Table 2, Table 3).
On LLaVA-OneVision-Qwen2-7B, IC-VCO with edited samples reaches an overall score of 66.82, outperforming SymMPO by 0.48 points, with AMBER-Attr 88.00 and AMBER-Exist 97.12 (Table 2, Table 3).
An ablation shows removing the anchor loss causes the largest degradation (-2.20 points), followed by removing the single-image branch (-0.66), VCDist (-0.31), and the token mask (-0.25) (Table 4).

The Contrastive Sample Editing strategy produces 19,453 edited samples from the SymMPO dataset (10,632 attribute, 7,993 existence, 828 relation edits) at a 91% success rate, with edited-image CLIP similarity of 94.72 versus 72.88 for purely synthetic negatives (Section 4).
IC-VCO is evaluated across five benchmarks: HallusionBench, AMBER, CRPE, R-Bench, and BLINK (Section 5).

reBRiuo3nr.text: The two-stage KSTER attack achieves 0.99 ± 0.01 top-50 subject-inference recall on Llama3-8B-Instruct edited with locate-then-edit methods on the CounterFact dataset, versus 0.43-0.55 recall for a gray-box baseline at N=100 (Section 4, Table 1).

KSTER's white-box subject-inference recall remains between 0.94 and 1.00 across different batch sizes, and its prompt-recovery stage reaches 0.94-0.99 top-20 recall on CounterFact, with top-1 recall exceeding 50% for completion-style edits (Section 4, Table 2).

The attack exploits the low-rank structure of parameter updates from editing methods ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit applied to GPT-J (6B), Llama3-8B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, treating the row space of the update matrix as a 'fingerprint' of edited subjects (Section 4).

The subspace camouflage defense with coefficient alpha=5 increases the median subject rank from 50.83 to 394.12 while preserving 0.96 efficacy and 0.53 generalization, with sharp utility degradation appearing only at alpha=7 (Section 5, Table 3).

cGqHvj7Q3B.text: On the UniKE benchmark, parameter-editing methods (MEMIT, PMET, AlphaEdit) applied to unified multimodal models achieve text-side editing efficacy of approximately 92%, while the best overall VQA accuracy under direct image generation reaches only 18.5% (Section 4, Table 3).

UniKE is constructed from 2,971 edit subjects spanning attribute and relation edits, expanded into 5,535 evaluation instances, and is evaluated on Ovis-U1, BLIP3o-4B, and OmniGen2 (Section 3, Table 2).

Mechanistic analysis shows edit-affected pathways exhibit near-random overlap with visual attribute-conditioning channels, indicating a fundamental pathway mismatch between text-editing and image-generation circuits (Section 4.6, Table 4).

Prompting the model to first verbalize the edited fact before generating an image (reasoning-augmented generation) improves VQA accuracy by up to 18.6 percentage points across evaluated model-editor pairs, though it does not close the gap to text-side efficacy (Section 4, Figure 4).

Textual knowledge edits in unified multimodal models do not reliably transfer to the visual generation modality, motivating the UniKE benchmark as a dedicated diagnostic for cross-modal editing generalization (Section 3, Figure 1).

AftqpgG6Ja.text: LGDEA is trained on MIMIC-CXR (377,110 chest X-ray images, 227,835 reports) under simulated limited pairing at 5% and 10% paired-data ratios (Section IV-A).

On phrase grounding (MS-CXR, 206 samples across 8 disease categories), LGDEA with 10% paired data achieves CNR scores from 0.8449 (Atelectasis) to 1.0928 (Pleural Effusion), outperforming the fully-paired MedAligner baseline (0.8312-1.0207) (Section IV-B).

On image-text retrieval (MIMIC-5x200, 1,000 samples across 5 diseases) with 10% pairing, LGDEA reaches Precision@1 of 56.31% and Precision@10 of 50.65%, exceeding MedAligner's Precision@1 of 55.88% despite using far less paired supervision (Section IV-B).

On zero-shot classification, LGDEA attains 80.00% accuracy on MIMIC-5x200, 90.47% on the COVID dataset (5,162 samples), and 87.06% on NIH Chest X-rays (112,120 samples), surpassing comparison baselines (Section IV-B).

LGDEA's Diagnostic Evidence Space uses K=64 learnable prototypes and L=64 lesion queries with two label-propagation steps, combining evidence reconstruction, paired evidence distillation, and unpaired evidence consistency losses to exploit abundant unpaired data (Section III-B, III-C).

uTRcgqzAfl.text: The Bias-Inversion Rewriting Attack (BIRA) achieves average evasion success rates of 99.8% (Llama-3.1-8B), 99.2% (Llama-3.1-70B), and 99.5% (GPT-4o-mini) across seven watermarking schemes (KGW, Unigram, UPV, EWD, DIP, SIR, EXP), versus 88.2-92.7% for the SIRA baseline (Table 1).

Theorem 2 (Section 4.1) proves that if the average conditional probability of sampling a green token is kept a margin δ below the detection threshold, the detector's true-positive probability decays exponentially, bounded by exp(-Nδ²/2).
BIRA preserves semantic fidelity better than SIRA, scoring roughly 4.2-4.7 vs 3.3-4.4 on LLM judgment and achieving lower Self-BLEU (0.07-0.09 vs 0.11-0.18) (Figure 3, Table 9).
Under SIR watermarking, BIRA reduces the detection z-score to -0.06±0.09 compared to SIRA's 0.14±0.12 (Table 3).

An ablation over the negative logit bias β shows evasion success rate rising from 54.2% at β=0 to 99.8% at β=-8, with self-information-guided token selection consistently outperforming random token selection (Section 5.3, Table 2).

TgaVuBX8dx.text: Budget-Guided MCTS (BG-MCTS) achieves the best accuracy in 11 of 12 tested settings spanning MATH500 and AIME24/25 with an 8B-parameter model under 10K, 20K, and 30K token budgets (Table 1).
On MATH500 with Llama-3.1-8B, BG-MCTS improves accuracy over budget-agnostic MCTS from 0.333 to 0.393 at a 10K-token budget and from 0.406 to 0.465 at a 20K-token budget (Table 1).
On AIME24/25 with Llama-3.1-8B, BG-MCTS improves accuracy over MCTS from 0.039 to 0.072 at a 10K-token budget and from 0.089 to 0.106 at a 30K-token budget (Table 1).

An ablation disabling any single BG-MCTS component (exploration annealing, exploitation shaping, or widening annealing) reduces performance relative to the full method, showing each mechanism is necessary (Table 2).

BG-MCTS attains a node-quality precision of 0.518 (ratio of correct nodes) versus 0.113 for baseline MCTS, despite exploring fewer nodes overall, evidencing a 'fewer-but-better' search regime (Table 3).

BG-MCTS exhibits a wide-to-deep search schedule, prioritizing breadth early in the budget and shifting to depth as the budget depletes, as shown by tree depth/width statistics over the search trajectory (Figure 4).

0S2WJSFkp0.text: SciNetBench is built from a corpus of 18,639,140 AI papers filtered from over 269 million total papers sourced from OpenAlex, incorporating the full arXiv PDF collection as of July 7, 2025 (Section on dataset construction).

The benchmark comprises 1,087 relation-aware retrieval tasks split into 354 ego-centric queries, 600 pair-wise relation queries, and 133 path-wise evolutionary-analysis queries (Section on benchmark composition).
On ego-centric retrieval tasks, the best-performing system (o3-deep-research) achieves only 1.42% novelty recall@50 and 4.60% disruption recall@50 (Table 1).
On pair-wise relation identification, o3-deep-research reaches 62.84% citation accuracy and 76.88% co-mention accuracy, but only 16.30% co-mention-paragraph accuracy (Table 2).
On path-wise evolutionary analysis, the top system reaches 63.10% consistency and only 14% connectivity, alongside a human rationality score of 7.04/10 (Table 3).

Providing systems with relation-aware ground-truth retrieval paths improves downstream literature-review quality by 23.4%, with ground-truth-augmented systems averaging rank 1.25 versus 2.00 for a deep-research system and 3.65 for a search-enabled LLM without relational grounding (Section on downstream application results).

qNsrhcCe4y.text: Under keyword-bias alignment tampering, the bias rate of the tampering policy rises from an initial 0.194 to 1.00 after fine-tuning with PPO and DPO (Section 4.3).

Alignment tampering amplifies all nine tested biases—spanning propaganda (sexism, populism, militarism), brand promotion (Tesla, Coca-Cola, Nike), and instrumental goal-seeking (self-preservation, resource acquisition, cognitive enhancement)—through best-of-N sampling (Figure 3).
Robust reward-model variants (InfoRM, WARM, RRM) fail to fully mitigate bias amplification, each exhibiting a trade-off between bias reduction and response quality (Section 5.3, Figure 7).
Iterative RLHF only suppresses bias amplification after multiple rounds, and doing so reduces the model's win rate (Section on mitigation limitations).
A proposed multimodal response-clustering detection method identifies alignment-tampering-triggered prompts with 0.74 AUROC, but at a high false-positive rate of 56% (Section 5.1).

bJJLW1gjqh.text: LiveFigure reaches 80% publication-readiness within 17 manual edits, versus only 24% for the strongest baseline, NanoBanana, under the same edit budget (Figure 3).
LiveFigure averages a score of 7.89 across nine visual-quality evaluation metrics in the V2 input setting, exceeding code-based tools Matplotlib (5.61) and Graphviz (5.78) (Table 1).

In a double-blind human preference study, LiveFigure secures a 60% win rate against the NanoBanana baseline and over 97% win rate against traditional code-based drawing tools, with all reported 95% confidence intervals exceeding the 50% threshold (Figure 5).

LiveFigure's three-stage agentic workflow—visual planning via prior induction, procedural generation via a validated Python drawing-function library, and targeted refinement via visual diagnostics—produces fully vectorized, editable PowerPoint-native figures rather than raster pixel output (Section on core method).
Publication readiness is operationalized via edit-distance metrics benchmarked against official figure guidelines from Nature, IEEE, and NeurIPS (Appendix A.5).

NJ9MZkCLAG.text: TRACE achieves a Pearson correlation of r = 0.741 (Spearman ρ = 0.755) with benchmark accuracy across 39 benchmarks and 26.3K QA samples, substantially higher than baselines such as token length (r = -0.147), perplexity (r = 0.221), and MTLD (r = -0.207) (Table 3).

The TRACE score is computed as α·V_state + (1-α)·C_trans with α = 0.7, combining State Validity and Transition Coherence derived from 8 sentence-level constructive elements (Claim, Data/Evidence, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal, Monitoring, Evaluation) from Toulmin's argumentation theory and Flavell's metacognitive framework (Equation 1, Section 3).

The TRACE-DeBERTa classifier achieves a macro F1-score of 0.666 against human annotations, with the strongest per-category F1 on Qualifier (0.821) and weakest on Warrant (0.547), and inter-annotator agreement of Cohen's κ = 0.672 (Table 1).

Using TRACE combined with accuracy and length as an RL reward signal improves GSM8K accuracy from a 74.75% base model to 84.69% (+9.94 points) and improves ARC-Challenge from 55.80% to 59.90%, outperforming accuracy-only reward baselines (Table 6).
On Arena Hard v2.0 category alignment, TRACE-based predictions reach 64.37% accuracy on Math, 55.78% on Coding, and 50.00% on Creative Writing categories (Table 5).

6bXLKr5NMT.text: Neural trust functions (NTFs), trained on the weak teacher's last-layer hidden state of the final generated token via a residual MLP with RMSNorm-SwiGLU blocks, achieve AUC of 0.83-0.92 and Expected Calibration Error of 0.02-0.14 at predicting weak-label correctness (Table 1).

On world knowledge tasks, NTF-filtered students match or exceed ground-truth-supervised students in 5 of 8 student-size settings, with recovery rates of 90.8%-113.9% relative to ground truth (Table 2).
On quantitative reasoning tasks, NTF-filtered training recovers 89.2%-92.5% of the ground-truth performance gap and consistently outperforms confidence-based label selection (Table 3).

In iterative weak-to-strong chains on strategy games, reusing NTF-trained students as subsequent teachers compounds gains: for Qwen3-14B the NTF chain reaches 48.2% versus 40.0% for ground-truth supervision, outperforming both single-step transfer and ground truth at the largest scale (Table 5).

NTF filtering induces an implicit easy-first curriculum by shifting the training distribution toward easier examples (Section 6.1, Figure 2), and in strategy games 66.1% of NTF-retained "incorrect" moves lead to winning positions per Stockfish evaluation, indicating many are optimal alternatives to the ground-truth label rather than errors (Section 6.2, Figure 3).

bo3bKNtIsI.text: Theorem 2.14 proves that for any finite noise level i ≥ 1, a collection C is uniformly generatable with noise level i if and only if it is uniformly generatable with noise level 1, establishing equivalence across all finite noise levels (Section 2.3).

Theorem 2.15 exhibits a collection that is generatable without noise but not generatable with noise level 1, proving a strict separation between noiseless and single-noisy-string generation and resolving an open question from prior work (Section 2.3).

Theorem 2.16 characterizes uniform noise-dependent generatability via the noisy closure dimension, simplifying prior characterizations by requiring only NC1(C) < ∞ rather than NCi(C) < ∞ for all i (Section 2.3).
Theorem 2.17 gives the first characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generatability, using a countable sequence of collections each satisfying NC1(Cj) < ∞ (Section 2.3).

These finite-noise equivalence and separation results contrast sharply with the strict infinite hierarchy previously shown for generation in the limit as the amount of noise increases (Bai, Panigrahi, Zhang 2026) (Section 1).

aBosytnQ6f.text: CaliDist computes a reliability score λ from two behavioral metrics — Prediction Instability μ (frequency of answer flips under semantic distractors) and Confidence Instability δ (shift in certainty under distraction) — and rescales the model's original confidence via a parameterized sigmoid grounded in Platt Scaling theory (Section on methodology).

CaliDist uses three distractor styles (assertion-style, probe-style, and sample-corruption-style) and requires only 3 forward passes, determined by label space as k=(c-1)×m, versus 15+ forward passes for consistency-based baselines (Table 1).

On Llama-3.1 and Qwen-3 models, CaliDist achieves Expected Calibration Error improvements averaging roughly 4-5x points across seven NLU benchmarks compared to baseline calibration methods, while preserving prediction accuracy since no predictions are modified (Table 1).
On proprietary models, CaliDist reduces ECE to 2.82-4.14 (x10^2) for GPT-4o-Mini and 4.34-5.07 (x10^2) for Gemini-2.0-Flash (Table 3).

CaliDist requires approximately 5x fewer tokens than self-consistency methods while achieving roughly 75% ECE improvement on benchmarks such as MSciNLI, and outperforms SPUQ and other consistency-based approaches with significantly fewer forward passes.

GFFMLwn053.text: Data selection is reformulated as a sequential decision-making problem (Definition 3.2) maximizing expected utility across all selection sizes, ∑_{k=1}^{|D|} U(S_k), with an exact Bellman-equation DP solution V(s) = U(s) + max_a V(s ∪ {a}) (Equation 2).

Theorem 4.3 shows that under linear utility functions, semi-value-based methods (Data Shapley, Beta Shapley, Data Banzhaf) achieve optimal sequential selection, while Theorem 4.6 shows that for monotonic submodular utilities with curvature c, these semi-value methods only guarantee a (1-c)^2 * OPT_k approximation, degrading quadratically as c approaches 1.
A bipartite graph-based surrogate utility is proposed that learns training-validation coverage relationships while provably preserving submodularity (Theorems G.2-G.3, Section 5, Algorithm 2).

On curvature-controlled synthetic experiments, game-theoretic valuation methods achieve mean accuracy above 0.70 at curvature 0.0 but degrade to 0.59 at maximum substitutability (curvature 1.0), empirically validating the approximation-guarantee theorem (RQ2 experiments).

The bipartite surrogate method reaches over 60% accuracy on the bbc-embeddings dataset with only 20 selected samples (versus 40-60 samples needed by baselines) and 80% accuracy on the digits dataset with just 25 samples (Figure 4, RQ3, Section 7).

4VKHyt93NW.text: CLEAR derives the Lambert W allocation policy (Theorem 4.2) as the closed-form optimal token allocation under the shadow price parity condition defined in Definition 4.1 (Section 4.2).

On the Balanced query stream at a 256-token budget, CLEAR improves accuracy by +11.6 points over Uniform allocation, with gains of +24.0 on Mostly-Easy, +5.2 on Mostly-Hard, and +14.2 on U-Shaped streams (Table 1).
On code generation benchmarks, CLEAR improves accuracy over Uniform allocation by +6.3 on HumanEval+, +6.5 on MBPP+, and +3.6 on BigCodeBench (Table 2).
CLEAR is compared against Uniform, Predictor-based allocation, TALE-EP, CLEAR (Heuristic), CLEAR (Auction), and an Oracle upper bound as baselines/ablations (Section 6).

CLEAR maintains its advantage over baselines even under significant predictor noise, and its adaptive beta mechanism outperforms static configurations while alpha exhibits a scale-invariance property (Section 7.3, Figures 7, 8, and 11).

The compute-utility relationship for reasoning queries follows an S-shaped curve with three distinct regimes—Strict, Surge, and Ample—motivating the shifted-surge utility function used in the global allocation objective (Section 2, Figure 1; Equations 1-2).

pwf3iLt9Wr.text: GeoLoom's fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B autoformalization model achieves 85.34% manual-evaluation accuracy with LCI 0.747 and ADI 1.818, versus 81.16% accuracy for the training-free DeepSeek-V3 prompting variant (Table 1).

GeoLoom translates natural language into GeoLingua, a formal language organizing shapes, dependence relations, length constraints, and angle constraints (Section 2), then solves for coordinates via Monte Carlo optimization minimizing the constraint-deviation loss in Equation 7, with hyperparameters alpha=0.05, Q=1000, and T=1000 (Section 3.2).
Human evaluation shows GeoLoom's fine-tuned method receives 55.1% quality approval versus 0% for the AutomaTikZ and SeeDream baselines (Table 2).

The GeoNF dataset used for autoformalization training/testing comprises 4,730 aligned natural-language/formal-representation pairs (4,300 train, 430 test) sourced from educational examinations (Section 2).
75.51% of diagrams are generated in under 10 seconds, with an average generation time of about 13 seconds (Table 3).
Failure analysis attributes errors to topological formalization mistakes (3% of test set), local minima in coordinate optimization (~8%), and overlapping-point issues (3%) (Section 4.2, Figure 13).

MyBVUgacQ9.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes sublinear convergence of ADMM to stationary points on multi-affine quadratic equality constrained problems under Assumptions 2.3 and 2.6, given a sufficiently large penalty parameter rho (Section 3).

Theorem 3.2 proves a linear convergence rate when the nonlinearity norm ||C|| satisfies the bound in Equation 4 relative to Q's properties, provided the Lagrangian is second-order differentiable at limit points (Section 3).
Theorem 3.3 achieves linear convergence without requiring second-order differentiability when the constraint indicator functions {I_i} are polyhedral (Section 3).
For robotic locomotion dynamics, Corollary 4.2 shows linear convergence holds when the discretization step Δt is below a threshold t0, since nonlinear terms decay as O((Δt)^3) (Section 4).

Empirically, ADMM outperforms PADMM, IPDS-ADMM, and IADMM baselines on multi-affine constrained problems, and toy-problem experiments show q≥10 is sufficient to transition from sublinear to linear convergence (Figures 2 and 4).
The method is validated on 2D locomotion simulation and on real robot experiments including a humanoid jump and quadruped bounding task (Figures 5 and 6).

Z4PjCncxzz.text: Using an experimental framework built on 5,075 real city coordinates and 7 geometric tasks, world representations emerge via autoregressive training and stabilize within roughly 15% of total training (Section 3, Section 4 Result 1).
Different tasks produce distinct representational geometries—e.g., the distance task yields thread-like structures while the angle task yields 2D manifolds (Section 4 Result 2, Figure 2).

Models trained on completely disjoint (non-overlapping) task pairs show substantially higher CKA representational alignment than single-task models, indicating multi-task training drives convergence of world representations (Section 4 Result 3, Figure 3).

The distance task actively harms generalization when combined with other tasks during fine-tuning, producing below-single-task-baseline performance visible as degradation bands in the results matrix (Section 5 Result 2, Figure 6a,c).

Divergent tasks disrupt representational integration of new entities, causing them to be encoded in separate hidden subspaces rather than the shared manifold used by pretrained entities (Section 5 Result 3, Figure 6b,d).
Single-task CKA values measured during pretraining only partially predict downstream fine-tuning generalization even after joint multi-task pretraining (Section 5 Result 1, Figure 5).

sq3JUR4IDd.text: MultiBO operates over B=50 Bayesian optimization rounds with user feedback, where users select from K=4 image choices per iteration under the Multi-choice Preferential BO framework (Section 3.1, Section 4).

MultiBO uses a MultiwiseGPR likelihood model together with a Dynamic Balanced Subspace (DBS) acquisition function based on spectral gap analysis (Equation 22) to select query images (Section 3.1, Algorithm 2).

MultiBO is evaluated against five baselines on CLIP-I2I, LPIPS, and reward metrics (Table 1), and against human judgment via 30 volunteers, achieving a 70.82% win rate on target-image alignment (Table 2).
Self-Attention Warping constrains optimization to attention layers 34-64 of SDXL's 70 layers, identified as optimal via ablation (Section 3.2, Section 4.1).

Ablations show multiwise (K>1) preferential comparisons outperform pairwise comparisons, and directly incorporating human feedback into the Bayesian optimization loop outperforms using proxy metrics like CLIP-I2I or LPIPS as the optimization objective (Section 4.1, Tables 3-4).

XRzeAIhVaS.text: Pri-TPG (with GPT-5.2) achieves 89.29% accuracy on the FormalGeo7k benchmark, exceeding FGeo-HyperGNet, the supervised state-of-the-art baseline, which reaches 88.36% (Section 4, Table 3).

Vanilla in-context learning (GPT-5 mini) reaches only 26.29% accuracy on FormalGeo7k, dramatically underperforming Pri-TPG's 89.29% and even Claude 4.5 Sonnet's direct-solving accuracy of 75.79% (Table 3).

As reasoning depth increases from difficulty level L1 to L6, accuracy on FormalGeo7k drops from 99.16% to 30.00%, illustrating the 'structural drift' phenomenon where vanilla ICL performance collapses at deeper proof steps (Figure 1, Section 1).
An ablation over the three prior components shows accuracy rising from 29.71% (global prior) to 58.43% (query-adaptive prior) to 84.42% (state-aware prior, i.e. full Pri-TPG) (Section 4.4, Table 4).
Removing iterative feedback and using a single-pass prediction reduces accuracy to 34.3%, compared to 84.42% for the full RAG+TPG (Pri-TPG) configuration (Section 4.4, Table 4).
The method generalizes beyond FormalGeo7k, achieving 95.16% accuracy on Geometry3K and 85.02% on GeoQA (Section 4).

igHBKQaLLP.text: For GPT-4.1 agents, final accuracy after multi-agent communication under distributed (Hidden Profile) information reaches only 0.200, versus 0.689 for agents given Complete Profile (shared, complete) information (Section 5.1, Figure 2).

Initial (pre-communication) accuracy under the Hidden Profile condition is 0.011, compared to 0.433 for Complete Profile, indicating agents largely fail to leverage distributed evidence even before any discussion (Section 5.1, Figure 2).

Across a heatmap of six LLMs and nine hidden-profile scenarios, only 40.7% of cases show accuracy improvement through inter-agent communication, and 87.0% of Complete Profile blocks significantly outperform their Hidden Profile counterparts (Section 5.2, Figure 3).

Human groups (24 sessions of four participants, run March-April 2025) show final accuracy of 0.156 under Hidden Profile versus 0.417 under Complete Profile, and exhibit no improvement (a slight decrease) in accuracy after communication, mirroring the LLM failure mode (Section 5.1).

In the cooperation-contradiction spectrum analysis, majority-rule consensus accuracy peaks at 0.200 under moderately cooperative conditions but collapses to 0.000 under extreme conflict, despite individual accuracies of 0.178 (very cooperative) and 0.339 (very conflictual) (Section 5.3, Figure 4).

u7PfRlU5qL.text: D-CORE-8B reaches 77.7% accuracy on BFCLv3, surpassing the best-performing 8B baseline model by 5.7 percentage points (Section 4.2, Table 1).
D-CORE-14B achieves 79.3% accuracy on BFCLv3, outperforming 70B-parameter models despite being roughly 5x smaller (Section 4.2, Table 1).
On multi-turn BFCLv3 evaluation, D-CORE-8B and D-CORE-14B both show a +30.8 percentage point improvement over their respective base models (Table 1).
On tau-Bench, D-CORE-8B and D-CORE-14B yield overall improvements of 18.6% and 17.7% respectively, with D-CORE-14B reaching 46.0% accuracy on airline-domain tasks (Section 4.2, Table 1).

Ablations show self-distillation alone (using 40k samples) improves multi-turn accuracy from 33.0% to 57.5%, and adding diversity-aware GRPO (DA-GRPO) with alpha=0.1 contributes an additional +11.4% on Qwen3-8B (Section 4.3, Table 3).
Scaling the self-distillation dataset from 10k to 40k samples (Table 4) demonstrates that self-distillation via task decomposition effectiveness improves with dataset size (Section 4.3).

WTgOxAio8a.text: MMD Guidance modifies the reverse diffusion sampler update as z_{t-1} = sampler(z_t, t, eps_theta) - lambda_t * gradient of MMD-squared, injecting a Maximum Mean Discrepancy gradient term at each denoising step (Equation 5, Section 4.2).

On FFHQ unconditional generation with a target 'sunglasses' user attribute, MMD Guidance achieves FD=692.87±30.43 and KD=3.25±0.18, outperforming No-Guidance, Classifier Guidance, and Domain Guidance baselines (Table 1).

Theorem 1 bounds the deviation of the empirical cross-guidance gradient from its population counterpart by 4L/sqrt(N_r) * (1 + sqrt(2 log(1/delta))), with a tighter constant of 3/(sigma*sqrt(N_r)) given for the Gaussian RBF kernel case in Corollary 1 (Theorem 1, Corollary 1).
For prompt-aware guidance on SDXL, adding MMD guidance improves Frechet Distance from 1953.75 to 1674.45 and increases coverage from 11.34 to 34.20 (x10^2) (Table 2).

Reference-sample ablation on SDXL shows FD improves from 1805.92 (n=10 references) to 1691.42 (n=100) and plateaus near 1674.45 (n=200), indicating diminishing returns beyond about 100 reference samples (Table 4).
On SDXL with 500 samples, MMD Guidance incurs roughly 10% runtime overhead versus no guidance (3447s vs. 3142s), demonstrating practical efficiency of the latent-space implementation (Table 3).

uYWVGk1Qt0.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that on the degenerate polynomial loss L(x) = (1/k) x^k for k >= 4, Adam achieves local linear convergence when beta_1 < beta_2^(k/(2(k-2))), with asymptotic rate x_{t+1}/x_t -> beta_2^(1/(2(k-2))) (Theorem 4.1).

Gradient Descent and Heavy-Ball Momentum both exhibit only sublinear convergence of order Theta(t^{-1/(k-2)}) on the same degenerate polynomial objective, established in Theorems 5.1 and 5.3 respectively.

Remark 5.8 quantifies the resulting complexity separation: Gradient Descent requires iteration complexity T_epsilon ~ epsilon^{-(k-2)} to reach accuracy epsilon, whereas Adam achieves T_epsilon ~ (k-2) ln(1/epsilon) (Remark 5.8).

Lemma 5.4 shows the second moment estimate satisfies v_t/v_{t-1} -> beta_2 asymptotically, decoupling v_t from the instantaneous squared gradient g_t^2 and producing an effective learning rate that grows as beta_2^{-t/2} (Lemma 5.4).

Section 6 identifies three convergence regimes governed by beta_1 relative to beta_2: stable exponential convergence, an intermediate regime with an initial exponential phase followed by loss spikes from fixed-point instability, and a SignGD-like oscillatory regime under tight v_t-g_t^2 coupling (Section 6, Figure 5).
Figure 3 shows the empirical phase diagram of stability boundaries across different degeneracy orders k matches the theoretical predictions of Equations 8-9 (Figure 3).

X8evkEdMxb.text: Theorem 1 establishes an Õ(d^{3/2}√V_T) regret bound for one-point bandit convex optimization with gradient variation V_T, improving the dimension dependence over Chiang et al. (2013)'s O(d^3√V_T) bound (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
Theorem 2 gives an O((d/λ) log V_T) regret bound for λ-strongly convex functions, improving the prior O((d^2/λ) log V_T) bound by a factor of d (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
Theorem 3 provides O(√(dW_T) + d) regret for linear functions and O(d√W_T + d) regret for convex functions in terms of the gradient variance W_T (Theorem 3, Section 3.3).
Theorem 4 delivers O(√(dF_T) + d) regret bounds for linear and convex functions using the small-loss quantity F_T (Theorem 4, Section 3.3).
Section 4 presents the first gradient-variation regret bound for one-point bandit linear optimization over hyper-rectangular domains (Section 4).

Table 1 summarizes the dimension-dependence improvements across gradient-variation, gradient-variance, and small-loss metrics for linear, convex, and strongly convex function classes relative to prior best-known results (Table 1).

vpSFJoxyDz.text: Theorem 3.6 shows that under Assumptions 2.1, 2.2, and 3.2-3.4, bridge functions satisfying E[b_t(S_t, A_t, S_{t+1}) | R_t, S_t, A_t] = R_t exist and identify the full-data policy value without modeling the missing-not-at-random mechanism (Theorem 3.6, Section 3).

Assumption 3.2 (relevance condition) requires that the next state S_{t+1} is not conditionally independent of the reward R_t given S_t, A_t, O_t=1, formalizing the use of future states as shadow variables (Assumption 3.2, Section 3).

Theorem 5.8 bounds the RKHS-based bridge function estimation error as ||b̂_t − b_t*||_2 ≲ τ_t δ_t max{1, ||b_t*||^2} under polynomial eigenvalue decay of the conditional expectation operator (Theorem 5.8, Section 5).
Theorem 5.9 establishes an overall off-policy value estimation error rate of O(K τ_max T^2 √(log(T/ζ)) n^{-α_min/(2α_min+1)} log n) under the completeness assumption (Theorem 5.9, Section 5).

Assumption 2.1 (no future dependence) posits that the current missingness indicator O_t is independent of future states and rewards given the current state, action, and reward, distinguishing the setting from standard missing-at-random assumptions (Assumption 2.1, Section 2).

vz23iIMvyd.text: Accordion-Thinking's Fold mode achieves 3x higher decoding throughput than Unfold mode while maintaining accuracy under a 48GB GPU memory configuration, reaching 5,888 tokens/sec versus 1,483 tokens/sec for the Mix-RL-4B model (Table 2).
Under a 24GB GPU memory configuration, the Mix-RL-4B model reaches 3,182 tokens/sec in Fold mode (Table 2).
Table 1 reports Pass@1 (Avg@32) accuracy for Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Qwen3-4B trained with Mix-RL, e.g. 32.2% on AIME24 and 89.6% on MATH500 in Fold mode, with a macro-average of 52.8% (Table 1).
Figure 3 shows that the accuracy gap between the efficient Fold mode and the exhaustive Unfold mode progressively narrows and vanishes over the course of Mix-RL training (Figure 3).

Figure 4 presents a human evaluation confirming that the structured step summaries produced by Accordion-Thinking are coherent and semantically faithful, human-readable substitutes for the full reasoning trace (Figure 4).

MgjXTLpmgf.text: MECAT is constructed from approximately 20,000 Creative Commons-licensed audio clips (up to 10 seconds each) sourced from ACAV100M, spanning 8 domain categories including pure speech, music, sound events, silence, and their mixed combinations (Figure 2).

MECAT-Caption provides 18 reference captions per audio clip, organized into systemic (short/long), content-specific (speech, music, sound events), and content-unrelated (acoustic properties) sub-categories, generated via specialized expert models and Chain-of-Thought reasoning (Section on MECAT-Caption).
MECAT-QA provides over 100,000 open-set question-answering pairs (5 per clip) organized into 6 sub-categories spanning perception, analysis, and reasoning skills (Section on MECAT-QA).

The DATE metric combines single-sample semantic similarity, computed via TF-IDF-weighted Sentence-BERT token embeddings, with cross-sample discriminability ranking, via harmonic mean, yielding a score in [0,1] that rewards detailed descriptions and penalizes generic terms (Section on DATE metric).

On MECAT, the best-performing model (Qwen2.5-Omni 7B) achieves a DATE score of 43.0 on the captioning task and 49.6 on the QA task, with the lowest scores of 6.8-19.4 on content-unrelated subtasks (Table 2, Table 3).

IoZL3DVSHT.text: TextMesh4D is presented as the first zero-shot framework for text-to-4D generation that directly outputs dynamic textured meshes, rather than relying on an intermediate NeRF or Gaussian-splat representation (Section 1).

TextMesh4D decomposes generation into a static 3D textured mesh stage using NeuS initialization followed by a dynamic motion synthesis stage based on per-face delta Jacobians and global transformations (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

The Jacobian-based deformation field uses a Flexibility Regularizer (Eq. 4) and a Rigidity Regularizer (Eq. 5, As-Rigid-As-Possible energy) to enable topology-aware, integrability-enforced surface reconstruction, with ablations confirming both are necessary for natural motion (Figure 6, Table 2).
TextMesh4D runs on a single 24GB GPU with motion convergence in about 1.5 hours, compared to 4D-fy requiring an 80GB GPU and over 15 hours, and DreamGaussian4D requiring a 48GB GPU (Section 4).
TextMesh4D achieves a CLIP Score of 32.32, outperforming 4D-fy (31.03) and DreamGaussian4D (29.17) (Section 4.1).

In a user study with 31 participants rating 20 prompts, TextMesh4D was preferred over baselines on Appearance Quality (92.7%), 3D Structure Quality (95.1%), Motion Quality (98.2%), Text Alignment (83.5%), and Overall Preference (93.5%) (Table 1).

Y1PXB8HBV7.text: MIRL-12 (10 pre-samples, top-6 selection, 2 forked trajectories each) reaches 70.22% average accuracy across six vision-language reasoning benchmarks, versus 69.76% for the DAPO-16 baseline using 16 complete trajectories (Table 1).
On the math reasoning subset (MathVista, MathVerse, We-Math), MIRL-12 averages 73.35% versus 72.40% for DAPO-16 (Table 1).

MI score correlates with downstream accuracy with Pearson coefficients ranging from r=0.71 to r=0.94 across the six benchmarks (all p<0.05), with MathVista showing a 146.9% relative accuracy improvement between the lowest and highest MI bins (Figure 2).
Ablating the selection strategy shows top-K MI-based selection reaches 70.22% average accuracy versus 68.74% for random selection and 68.02% for bottom-K (lowest MI) selection (Table 2).

Ablating the reward configuration shows the proposed decoupled reward (λ=0.1) reaches 70.22% average accuracy, versus 68.37% for task-only reward (λ=0.0) and 68.81% for MI-only reward (λ=1.0) (Table 3).
Experiments use Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct fine-tuned on the ViRL39K dataset with learning rate 1e-6 and global batch size 384 (Section 4, implementation details).

JBFB2pUOCA.text: On MMLU, TuneAhead achieves RMSE of 1.47 percentage points versus 2.11 for the ProxyLM baseline, with R²=0.99 and Pearson correlation 0.99 (Table 1).
TuneAhead's Accuracy@3pp on MMLU is 95.1%, meaning 95.1% of predicted fine-tuning outcomes fall within ±3 percentage points of the true result (Table 1).
Cross-model generalization tests show RMSE of 5.02 (R²=0.86) for Llama-3-8B and RMSE of 3.75 (R²=0.91) for Qwen2-0.5B (Table 2).

An ablation comparing static-only features (~3.50 RMSE) and dynamic-only features (~3.38 RMSE) against the combined feature set (1.47 RMSE) shows the combination reduces error by roughly 56% relative to dynamic-only features (Table 5).
At a 55% go/no-go decision threshold, TuneAhead yields a 58.4% net computational saving while retaining 94.5% of successful fine-tuning runs (Table 4).
A probe budget analysis shows Accuracy@2pp rises from 32.8% with 0 probe steps to 82.5% with the chosen 100-step probe, with only marginal further gain to 82.8% at 200 steps (Figure 6).

xrFVeviQNW.text: The proposed Log-FM method applies a parameter-free soft-log transform φ(x)=sign(x)·log(1+|x|) before standard flow matching training, dominating baselines in 13 of 16 cells of median W1 on Pareto margins across tail indices α∈{1.5,1.75,2.0,2.5} and dimensions d∈{10,20,50,100} (Table 1).
At the heaviest tail setting (α=1.5, d=100), Log-FM achieves a median W1^P of 0.525 versus 0.919 for the TTF baseline (Table 1).
Aggregated over 480 configurations, Log-FM achieves W1^P between 0.207 (d=10) and 0.233 (d=100), while baseline methods TTF and gTAF show 2-3x higher error on the CVaR99 risk metric (Table 2).
Stability analysis shows zero severe divergences for Log-FM and Arcsinh-FM at α≥1.75, whereas TTF diverges in 30-50% of runs at d=50 and d=100 (Table 3).
At the most extreme tail setting (α=1.5), Log-FM still has a 14% failure rate while gTAF reaches 59% failure at d=100 (Table 3).
An ablation on Hill-gating (adaptive per-coordinate transform selection) improves the Gaussian-margin Wasserstein metric W1^G by 30-45% at no cost to W1^P performance (Table 4).

Q5uj05ynu5.text: CrysLDNet improves average property-prediction performance over the strongest supervised baseline (PDDFormer) by 4.26% on JARVIS (9 properties) and 4.90% on Materials Project (4 properties) (Table 1).
Compared against the DPF diffusion-based pretraining baseline, CrysLDNet achieves a 16.76% relative improvement on JARVIS and 19.34% relative improvement on Materials Project (Table 1).
In the low-data regime with only 40% of training data, CrysLDNet with a Matformer backbone surpasses PDDFormer by 22.49% on average (Figure 2).

Finetuned on 80% of OQMD experimental data, CrysLDNet reaches a zero-shot-to-finetuned MAE of 0.068, outperforming CrysDiff (0.070) and CrysGNN (0.096), down from an initial zero-shot MAE of 0.205 (Table 3).

An ablation removing components shows VAE-only and LDM-only variants underperform the full VAE+LDM framework, and partial reconstruction of only atom types, only coordinates, or only lattice each underperforms joint A+X+L reconstruction (Table 4).

Mutual information analysis of the latent space shows MI for atom types rises from 3.0906 with VAE alone to 4.5465 with the full CrysLDNet pipeline, indicating richer structural encoding (Section 4.8).

07YGl8xVZl.text: On the SIR (2D) benchmark, DoLQ achieves 1.71e-8 residual NMSE and 1.55e-8 integral NMSE, with baselines (LLM-SR, ICSR, LASR, EDL) showing much larger divergence between residual and integral NMSE (Table 2).
On the CDIMA (2D) benchmark, DoLQ achieves 2.29e-8 residual NMSE and 2.35e-8 integral NMSE, and on the Glider (4D) benchmark, 1.22e-6 residual NMSE and 8.29e-7 integral NMSE (Table 2).

Across eight benchmark systems, DoLQ attains the highest success rate on both the NMSE test (integral error <1e-3) and the Term test (correct structural term recovery), while LLM-SR succeeds on only 4 of 8 systems on the NMSE test (Figure 4).
An ablation removing the Scientist Agent's qualitative evaluation delays convergence to the correct equation from iteration 27 to iteration 62, a 2.3x slowdown (Section 5.1, Figure 6).

An ablation on parameter optimization shows BFGS alone fails to recover parameters on structurally correct equation skeletons due to local minima, while the hybrid differential-evolution-plus-BFGS optimizer succeeds (Section 5.2, Figure 8).
DoLQ uses substantially fewer LLM tokens than the LLM-SR baseline while achieving superior discovery performance (Figure 5).

UhPwL6LYOc.text: Video-MTR is trained on only about 8K samples (roughly 5K from NExT-GQA and nearly 3K QA-grounded samples from QVHighlights), versus prior methods using 260K to 4.4M training examples (Table 2, Appendix B).
On the VideoMME benchmark, Video-MTR (built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B) achieves 70.4% on short videos, 55.6% on medium videos, 51.0% on long videos, and 59.0% overall (Table 1).
Video-MTR attains 48.4% on the MLVU test set and 62.4% on EgoSchema (Table 1).

The gated bi-level reward combines a trajectory-level accuracy reward (R_acc) with a turn-level frame-IoU reward (R_fm) that only fires when IoU exceeds the initial-turn baseline, plus goal-gating that zeros out all but the single highest-relevance frame retrieval to prevent reward hacking (Methods section).

Ablating the bi-level reward in the multi-turn setting drops long-video VideoMME accuracy from 51.0% to 49.4% and MLVU test accuracy from 48.4% to 44.4%, and collapsing to a single-turn variant further drops MLVU to 44.3% (Table 4).

Video-MTR's agent operates over a maximum of 3 reasoning turns, starting from 16 uniformly sampled frames and retrieving up to 8 additional frames per turn, capped at 32 total frames per trajectory (Methods section).

JheeAwquCb.text: UniR trains a standalone reasoning module (πr) with GRPO (KL coefficient β=0) while keeping the frozen backbone LLM (πb) fixed, combining logits at inference time via Equation 6 (Section 4.1).

On math reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME24), a UniR module attached to Llama3.2-3B reaches 36.0 average accuracy versus 30.6 for full GRPO fine-tuning of the same backbone, while on Qwen2.5-3B UniR reaches 42.2 versus 42.8 for full GRPO (Table 1).
On IWSLT 2017 machine translation, UniR achieves 67.87 average BLEU on EN→DE versus 67.22 for full GRPO fine-tuning, and 72.27 versus 72.14 on DE→EN (Table 2).

A 0.5B-parameter reasoning module trained on a 3B backbone generalizes weak-to-strong: attaching it to frozen Qwen2.5-14B improves accuracy by +1.8 points (35.5 vs. 33.7 baseline) and to frozen Llama3.1-8B by +1.7 points (52.8 vs. 51.1 baseline) (Section 5.3, Figure 2).
UniR's decoupled training supports a batch size of 128 under an 80GB memory constraint versus 64 for LoRA fine-tuning of the same backbone (Figure 5).
Theorem 1 formally connects the trained reasoning policy πr to the optimal Q-function of the composite reasoning process (Section 4, Theorem 1).

L5ZJv73k7x.text: Theorem 2 shows Robust Async-Q achieves a finite-time convergence rate of O(1/√T), matching classical asynchronous Q-learning, plus an additive O(√ε) term where ε∈[0,1/2) is the fraction of adversarially corrupted rewards (Section 3.1).
Theorem 3 gives an information-theoretic lower bound of Ω(√ε), proving the additive corruption term in the upper bound is unavoidable (Section 4).
Theorem 4 extends the guarantee to a reward-agnostic setting where the algorithm needs no prior knowledge of the reward distribution's bounds (Section 5.1).
Theorem 6 extends the near-optimal finite-time rate to single-trajectory Markovian sampling with time-correlated data, with the bound inflated by the chain's mixing time (Section 6).

Algorithm 1 (Robust Async-Q) combines a trimmed-mean reward estimator with an adaptive threshold G_t to filter corrupted rewards before the standard Q-learning update, requiring only knowledge of the corruption fraction ε and minimum state-action visitation probability λ_min (Algorithm 1, Assumption 1).

XEbD5cYpgV.text: Theorem 1 bounds the bias of the truncated difference-in-Q's (Truncated DQ / TPG) estimator by O(k²δ²M + γᵏ/(1-γ)·δM) and its variance by O((k+1)³M²/T + γ(k+1)²M²/(T(1-γ))), where k is the truncation depth, δ measures nonstationarity, and γ is the discount factor (Section 3, Theorem 1).

Proposition 1 shows the untruncated difference-in-Q's estimator admits a policy-gradient interpretation, and the truncated estimator reduces exactly to the naive difference-in-means estimator when k=0 (Section 4, Equation 3).

Proposition 3 establishes that the truncated policy gradient estimator remains valid single-trajectory setting under the nonstationary Markovian model with a mixing-time assumption (Section 2.1, Section 5, Assumption 1).
The estimator is validated on a hospital emergency-department queuing simulator built from SEEStat Home Hospital arrival data over 40,320 timesteps (Section 6, Appendix E.2).
The estimator is also validated on an NYC ride-sharing simulator built from TLC taxi data with 500,000 arrivals (Section 6, Appendix E.3).

DJtX0Fo7ii.text: Theorem 4.2 decomposes the approximation error of additive guidance for compositional-reward flow models into three terms: coupling-shift error, gradient-misalignment error scaling with G(G-1)μ²(1-cos φ) for G rewards, and localized approximation error tied to reward-landscape roughness (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).

Conflict-Aware Additive Guidance (g^car), defined as a convex combination (1-w_t)·g^approx + w_t·g_ψ with a conflict-aware weight from pairwise gradient cosine similarity, raises posterior coverage on a synthetic conflicting-reward benchmark from 71.70% (g^cov-G baseline) to 93.80% while adding only 1.65 ms/sample versus 0.37 ms/sample for the baseline (Definition 5.1, Section 6.2, Table 1).

On Maze2D planning with compositional static/dynamic obstacle rewards, g^car achieves 72-79% success rates versus 16-42% for the g^cov-G baseline, an average improvement of 38.75 percentage points (Section 6.3, Table 2).

On ManiSkill2 StackCube manipulation with hybrid constraints, g^car reaches 61% success with 0.4 constraint violations versus 9% success and 1.8 violations for g^cov-G, a 78% reduction in violations (Section 6.4, Table 3).

On CelebA-HQ compositional text-guided image editing, g^car improves identity preservation from 0.543 (g^cov-G) to 0.681 (+25.4%) and achieves the best BLIP-ITM alignment score of 0.597 among compared methods, including the exact sample-based GLASS-FKS baseline (Section 6.5, Table 4).
