Proposition 5.3 introduces Terminal Value Regression, which regresses the learnable guidance directly against terminal rewards r(x_1) to avoid bootstrapping instability inherent to deterministic flow trajectories (Section 5, Proposition 5.3).

qhG8ONjZK0.text: The exterior NMF (eNMF) framework is evaluated against 81 baseline combinations formed by crossing 9 algorithmic frameworks with 9 initialization schemes (Section 4).

Across roughly 400 NMF experiments on 3 real-world datasets (audio, text, images) and 2 synthetic datasets, eNMF achieves up to 30% lower reconstruction error under equal-time settings and up to 150% speedup under equal-error settings versus the 81 competitor combinations (Section 4).
In 99% of the ~400 experiments, different algorithms converge to factor matrices that are equivalent up to the rotational equivalence class 𝒴* = {(U*R, V*R) : R^T R = I} (Section 4, subsection 4.1).

eNMF is built from three algorithmic blocks: an ADMM-based optimal orthogonal transformation (Algorithm 1), a projected block-coordinate-descent penalty method for feasibility (Algorithm 2), and a HALS-based descent to a local minimum (Algorithm 3) (Section 4).
On real datasets, the next-best competing method requires up to 500% longer runtime than eNMF to reach matching reconstruction accuracy (Section 4).
eNMF factorizations yield 10%+ improvements on downstream audio/vision tasks and 50%+ improvement in top-k recommendation compared to baseline NMF factorizations (Section 4).

2juEZmkLdn.text: The Abstraction Gap (AG) metric, defined as (Text Score − Chain Score) / Text Score, is measured on the CAGE benchmark of 49,500 questions spanning 5,500 COCO images across Pearl's three causal levels: association, intervention, and counterfactual (Section 4).

Seven of eight evaluated vision-language models (InternVL2-76B, CogVLM2-19B, LLaVA-RLHF-13B, LLaVA-CoT-11B, MiniGPT-4-13B, mPLUG-Owl2-8.2B, Qwen-VL-Chat-7B) show Abstraction Gap exceeding 0.50, with text scores of 6-8 but causal-chain scores below 2.5, while LLaVA-NeXT-13B shows an AG near 0.03 (Section 4).

Fine-tuning on 45,000 chain-annotated examples from 5,000 images fails to close the gap for low-baseline models: MiniGPT-4's chain score declines from 2.05 to 0.54 at causal Level 3, and mPLUG-Owl2 shows no significant improvement (0.75 to 0.82), evaluated on a held-out set of 500 images (Section 4).
An ablation shows chain supervision yields no statistically significant improvement in chain generation (p > 0.05) for the low-baseline models (Section 4).

Structural grounding (causal abstraction ability) is empirically independent of perceptual grounding, since fine-tuning on causal chains does not reduce object-hallucination rates on standard benchmarks (Section 4).
Among newer models tested in Section 4.8, Qwen3-VL has AG = 0.313 while Gemini 2.5 Flash has AG = -0.006, effectively eliminating the abstraction gap (Section 4.8).

69u8BZXVXJ.text: EPiC constructs well-aligned training anchor videos by masking source videos based on first-frame visibility, requiring no camera trajectory or point-cloud estimation for training data (Section 3).
Anchor-ControlNet is a lightweight conditioning module of roughly 30M parameters, under 1% of the CogVideoX-5B backbone's parameter count (Section 3).
EPiC trains on only 5,000 videos for 500 iterations (versus 630K videos and 50K iterations for ViewCrafter), completing training in under 3 hours on 8 A100 GPUs (Section 4).

On RealEstate10K, EPiC achieves rotation error 0.40±0.11, translation error 0.86±0.18, and CamMC 1.17±0.23, each improving over ViewCrafter's 0.50±0.16, 1.05±0.32, and 1.35±0.40 respectively (Section 4, Table with RealEstate10K results).
On MiraData, EPiC obtains rotation error 0.66±0.22, translation error 1.78±0.67, and CamMC 2.10±0.60 (Section 4).
Despite being trained only for I2V, EPiC generalizes zero-shot to video-to-video (V2V) camera control, achieving 19.65 PSNR on Kubric-4D, comparable to specialized V2V baselines (Section 4).

B258ihKAk9.text: Threshold-Guided Optimization (TGO) replaces the oracle instance-specific baseline in KL-regularized policy updates with a data-driven global threshold estimated from empirical unpaired scalar-feedback score distributions (Section 3.2).
TGO's confidence-weighted objective uses weight function w(s,τ) = 1 + c|s−τ| and includes a theoretical properties result stated as Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).
On Pick-a-Pic v2 with Stable Diffusion v1.5, TGO achieves an ImageReward score of 0.6703 versus 0.6381 for Diffusion-KTO (Table 1).
On 10k scalar-feedback prompts with SD v1.4, TGO improves HPSv2.1 from 0.2506 (SFT baseline) to 0.2618 (Table 2).
A sensitivity analysis over percentile thresholds p ∈ {0.3, 0.5} shows TGO's performance is reasonably stable to threshold choice (Table 3).
Applied to text-to-video generation with Wan 1.3B, TGO-LoRA improves the VideoReward overall score from -1.3703 to -1.1757 (Table 4).

tL2zkbmg8t.text: BridgePolicy embeds observations directly within the diffusion-bridge SDE trajectory, sampling from observation-informed priors instead of random noise, and is formulated via Stochastic Optimal Control using the UniDB framework (Section 3).

BridgePolicy is evaluated on 52 simulation tasks across the Adroit, DexArt, and MetaWorld benchmarks and 5 real-world tasks on a Franka Emika Panda arm, compared against Diffusion Policy, 3D Diffusion Policy, and FlowPolicy (Section 4).
In simulation, BridgePolicy attains an average success rate of 0.74, including 0.91 on MetaWorld-Easy, 0.58 on MetaWorld-Hard, 0.60 on DexArt, and 0.81 on Adroit (Table 1).
On the 5 real-world tasks, BridgePolicy attains an average success rate of 0.90, including 1.0 on Oven-Closing, 1.0 on Oven-Opening, and 0.8 on Pick-Place (Table 2).
BridgePolicy shows improved sample efficiency over baselines under reduced numbers of expert demonstrations, as shown in the low-data regime comparison (Figure 6).
BridgePolicy uses a multi-modal fusion module with cross-attention and a CLIP-based contrastive semantic aligner to integrate observations into the diffusion-bridge dynamics (Section 3).

4nfItZvfna.text: CoGHP uses an MLP-Mixer backbone (rather than a Transformer) with alternating token-mixing and channel-mixing layers to process the sequence of state, goal, latent subgoals, and action (Section 1).
CoGHP autoregressively generates H latent subgoals in reverse order, from the farthest subgoal z_H to the nearest z_1 relative to the current state, followed by a primitive action (Section 4.2).
On OGBench navigation tasks, CoGHP achieves 79±8 success on pointmaze-giant and 78±8 on antmaze-giant, versus HIQL's 46±9 and 65±5 respectively (Table 1).
On OGBench manipulation tasks, CoGHP achieves 97±3 on cube-single and 54±5 on cube-double, versus HIQL's 41±6 and 2±1 respectively (Table 1).

Replacing the MLP-Mixer backbone with a Transformer degrades performance on cube-triple from 42±3 (CoGHP) to 2±1 (Transformer variant), an ablation isolating the architecture's contribution (Table 2).
Removing teacher forcing during training causes antmaze-giant performance to collapse from 78±8 to 18±5, showing teacher forcing is critical for training stability (Table 9, Section C.8).

00P7hFnWng.text: UnMaskFork (UMF) formulates the unmasking trajectory of masked diffusion language models as a search tree and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search with deterministic (low-temperature) partial-unmasking actions across multiple MDLMs, rather than stochastic sampling diversity, to guide test-time scaling (Section on method overview; Algorithm 1).

At an inference budget of NFE=12,288, UMF reaches 28% Pass@1 on LiveCodeBench, 88% Pass@1 on HumanEval+, and 72% Pass@1 on MBPP+, exceeding Best-of-N and DTS* baselines on all three benchmarks (Figure 2).
On the MATH dataset (105 problems), UMF at NFE=12,288 achieves 60.95% Pass@1, an improvement of 11.43 points over the baseline (Section on mathematical reasoning results).
Node caching of deterministic transitions achieves a 55.8% cache-hit rate at NFE=12,288, yielding a 7.69% performance improvement over no-caching (Table 3).

Interleaved multi-model UMF combining Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B and LLaDA-8B-Instruct reaches 28% Pass@1 on LiveCodeBench, substantially exceeding independent single-model action pairs at 24% (Table 5).

mvLWhrg71j.text: In a 355M-parameter GPT-2-style decoder-only Transformer trained on 80B tokens of a balanced multilingual corpus (10% English, 30% each Japanese/Korean/Chinese), token-level perplexity stabilizes after 2.1B tokens while UTF-8 validity requires 4.2B tokens to stabilize, a roughly two-fold lag (Section reporting the 2.1B/4.2B convergence result).

Using an 8,000-token BPE tokenizer with byte-fallback, at the final training checkpoint partial-credit UTF-8 validity is 96.21% for common characters, 95.57% for uncommon, 95.26% for rare, and drops to 86.97% for unseen characters, showing character-frequency-dependent degradation (final checkpoint validity-by-tier results).

A controlled comparison of unseen 3-byte versus 4-byte UTF-8 characters shows that byte-length exposure is a stronger determinant of validity difficulty than character frequency within a fixed byte-length class (byte-length control experiment).

In context-guided generation, the Term Match Rate reaches only 60.30% despite high structural (UTF-8) validity, indicating that producing a structurally valid character is easier than producing the semantically correct one (context-guided evaluation results).

Across 10 additional models spanning 1B-9B parameters, the gap between perplexity-based and UTF-8-validity-based convergence (V_p-V_s gap) persists at 9.9-65.4 percentage points, confirming the phenomenon generalizes across model scales (cross-model validation results).

bTySLCPXHO.text: Human experts prefer research plans generated by a Qwen3-30B-A3B model finetuned with rubric rewards over the initial (non-finetuned) model's plans in 70% of goals (p<0.0001), based on 225 hours of expert evaluation (Section 3.3, human study results).
The finetuned model's plans satisfy automatically-extracted evaluation rubrics at 79.8±2.5%, compared to 73.8±2.9% for the baseline model's plans (Tables 1-2).

Finetuning yields 12-22% relative improvements across domains, and training on the medical domain alone transfers with a 15% relative improvement on machine-learning research goals and 17.5% on ArXiv-paper-based goals, demonstrating cross-domain generalization (Section on cross-domain generalization results).
84% of rubric items automatically extracted from source papers by the pipeline are approved as valid by human expert reviewers (Section 2.1, rubric generation validation).
Training uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a self-rewarding mechanism derived from the automatically extracted rubrics (Section 2.3).

Human experts rate the finetuned model's plans as matching or exceeding Grok-4-Thinking's plans for 59.6% of goals, while GPT-5-Thinking still outperforms all tested models including the finetuned one (Section 3.3 comparison to frontier baselines).

fjUUmUCy9m.text: The Guided Orthogonal Projection Layer (G-OPL) computes a QR decomposition of a learnable weight matrix W in R^(k x d) as W^T = QR, then applies the projection operator P = I_d - QQ^T to remove nuisance (facial-identity) components while preserving task-relevant anomaly signals (Equations 1-3, Section 3.1).
G-OPL is evaluated on five video anomaly detection benchmarks: ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, CUHK Avenue, UCSD Ped2, and MSAD (Section on datasets).
On ShanghaiTech, RTFM with G-OPL achieves 97.3% AUC versus 96.8% for the non-privacy baseline, showing anomaly detection accuracy is maintained or improved under the privacy constraint (Table 4).
On UCF-Crime, CUHK Avenue, and UCSD Ped2, the G-OPL variant achieves 78.3%, 84.9%, and 89.6% AUC respectively, maintaining competitive detection performance across datasets (Table 4).

Privacy preservation is quantified with three novel metrics: Sensitive Subspace Capture (SSC, cosine similarity between original and projected facial embeddings), Anomaly Retention Distance (ARD, KL divergence between anomaly-score distributions pre/post projection), and Privacy Decay/First-layer Privacy Decay (PD/FPD, tracking facial-presence classification accuracy decay across layers) (Section 3.3).

UaCVrZseUV.text: On the CES dataset with only a 10% respondent budget, the method achieves a greater than 12% relative improvement over the strongest baseline (Meta-Greedy) by round 4 (Figure 3).

The framework jointly selects queries via an information-theoretic (expected information gain) criterion and selects respondent subsets by clustering member embeddings, updating a heterogeneous R-GCN graph after each round (Section 3.2).

Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 prove that greedy query/respondent selection is near-optimal within constant factors relative to the optimal adaptive policy under submodularity assumptions (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2).

Ablations show that GNN-based imputation of missing responses yields substantially larger accuracy gains than random selection, and that active respondent observation provides complementary benefit on top of imputation (Figure 5).
Greedy one-step query selection nearly matches the performance of 3-step lookahead rollout planning while being far more computationally efficient (Table 1).
The method is evaluated on three opinion datasets (CES, OpinionQA, Twin-2k) against three baselines: Meta-Random, Meta-Greedy, and Meta-Greedy-Imp, outperforming all three across budgets (Section 5).

A93BskpqCP.text: PhysHanDI reduces Chamfer Distance in dynamic regions to 8.32mm versus PhysTwin's 10.78mm, and reduces tracking error to 0.89 versus 1.00, on the PhysTwin-dense dataset (Table 1).
For future-state prediction, PhysHanDI achieves Chamfer Distance of 14.35mm and IoU of 0.73, compared to PhysTwin's 16.32mm and 0.70 IoU (Table 1).

The framework reconstructs both interacting hands (via a MANO model with 778 vertices/1554 faces) and non-rigid deformable objects (via a spring-mass model) jointly from sparse-view RGB-D video (Section 3.2).
An inverse-physics hand refinement stage reduces single-view future-prediction Chamfer Distance from 42.8mm to 33.5mm and hand Chamfer Distance from 7.57mm to 7.17mm (Table 3).
Under perturbed tracking signals, PhysHanDI degrades only 0.26 in absolute metric change, while PhysTwin degrades by 3.70, indicating substantially greater robustness (Table 4).
The authors introduce the DenseHDI dataset with 19 sequences featuring denser hand-object contact than the existing PhysTwin dataset, to be released with the paper (Section 4, dataset description).

Q6iMYPaSIv.text: MIPO improves personalization accuracy from 63.5% to 78.83% for Qwen-1.5B on Community Alignment and from 39.29% to 74.60% for Qwen-1.5B on Multi-Bench, a 35.31-point gain (Table 1).
On the PRISM personalization dataset, MIPO improves Llama-1B accuracy from 72.17% to 80.93% relative to a personalized-prompting baseline (Table 1).
Without any additional labels, MIPO improves Llama-1B on GSM from 22% to 29.5% (+7.5 points) and on SVAMP from 51.67% to 60.11% (+8.4 points) (Table 2).

MIPO constructs DPO preference pairs by contrasting responses generated with the correct prompt/context against responses generated with no or random context, connecting this objective to pointwise mutual information maximization and InfoNCE-style contrastive learning (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
Unlike plain SFT, which reduces output diversity (higher self-BLEU), MIPO maintains or improves diversity, achieving lower self-BLEU scores in 11 of 15 evaluated cases (Table 4).

qbe18sZPWS.text: Proposition 4.1 proves that for linear scalarization of rewards, the proposed mixing policy exactly recovers the target composed distribution p_M(x) ∝ Σ ω_i R_i(x) (Proposition 4.1, Section 4.2).
On the 2D grid synthetic benchmark with linear scalarization across 2-5 objectives, the method achieves an L1 error of 0.003, versus 0.021-0.048 for MOGFN and 0.017-0.035 for HN-GFN (Table 1).
On QM9 atom-based molecule generation with the GAP-SA objective, the method attains a mean reward of 0.876, exceeding MOGFN's 0.816 and HN-GFN's 0.805 (Table 3/4).

For non-linear logical composition operators (harmonic mean, contrast), the method is 40-70x faster than classifier guidance at inference (24-27ms vs. 1789-1974ms per sample) while achieving comparable or better target-bin accuracy (Table 5).

An ensemble baseline that omits the reaching-probability weighting term achieves substantially worse L1 error (0.098-0.117) than the full mixing policy (0.003), showing the reaching-probability term is essential (Section 5, Table 1).

The distortion factor δ(x)=u_M(x)/N_M(x), which quantifies approximation error for non-linear operators, remains approximately constant in high-density/high-composition-value regions where sampling accuracy matters most (Section 5.3, Figure 5).

2GQOSf4Y8n.text: Mixture of Horizons' dynamic inference mechanism achieves 2.5x higher throughput than baseline action-chunking methods while preserving superior task success rates (Abstract, Figure 8).
π_0.5 with MoH reaches a 99% average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark after only 30k training iterations, compared to 97.7% for the baseline (Table 1).
π_reg with MoH achieves a 96.4% average success rate on LIBERO across Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long task suites, versus 95.2% for the baseline (Table 1).

MoH uses a shared action transformer processing multiple horizon-specific action chunks in parallel, fused via a lightweight linear gating mechanism with only 2k parameters and a balance loss that prevents gate collapse (Section 3.2, Equation 17).

Ablations show a horizon stride of 3 (horizons {3,6,...,30}) is optimal, that loss reweighting alone is insufficient and worsens the long-horizon trade-off, and that simple averaging across horizons only reaches 98.4% success, below the full gated MoH (Section 4.3, Tables 2-3).
The balance loss is shown to be critical for preventing degenerate gating weights that collapse onto a single preferred horizon (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

U1bxeLQLaK.text: Theorem 3.3 shows momentum SGD's tracking-error bound scales as (1-beta)^-2 on the initialization term and (1-beta)^-1 on the noise floor, versus O(1) and O(sigma^2 gamma/mu) respectively for vanilla SGD in Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.1, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3).

Theorem 3.7 gives a minimax lower bound decomposing regret into a noise-limited term and an inertia-limited term that worsens with beta and can dominate in drift-heavy regimes, establishing an information-theoretic (not just analytical) barrier for momentum methods (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.7).
Under the stability constraint gamma <= (1-beta)^2/L, the paper proves vanilla SGD provably outperforms Heavy-Ball/Nesterov momentum SGD in drift-dominated nonstationary regimes (Section 3.3).

Theorem 3.6 shows the high-probability bound for momentum SGD exhibits an inertia horizon of order (1-beta)^-1 and drift-noise coupling scaling as (1-beta)^-2, both absent from the vanilla SGD high-probability bound in Theorem 3.5 (Section 3.2, Theorems 3.5 and 3.6).

Numerical experiments on quadratics, linear/logistic regression, and MLPs confirm that increasing nonstationarity (drift), momentum parameter beta, or condition number kappa systematically worsens Heavy-Ball and Nesterov tracking error while vanilla SGD remains comparatively robust (Section 4).

lNRgWoGfYg.text: On BrowseComp-Plus, the Folding Agent trained with FoldGRPO achieves pass@1 of 0.620 using a 32K active context (up to 10 branches), compared to 0.540 for a ReAct agent using a 327K context window (Table 1).

On SWE-Bench Verified, the Folding Agent with FoldGRPO reaches pass@1 of 0.580 versus 0.574 for the 327K-context ReAct baseline, matching performance with roughly a 10x smaller active context (Table 1).
FoldGRPO training improves BrowseComp-Plus pass@1 by +20.0 percentage points and SWE-Bench Verified pass@1 by +8.8 percentage points over the untrained Folding Agent (Section 4.1).
The Folding Agent with FoldGRPO outperforms the Summary Agent + RL baseline (0.527 BrowseComp-Plus, 0.550 SWE-Bench Verified) despite using the same 32K context budget (Table 1).

An ablation shows FoldGRPO outperforms standard GRPO by +7.7 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and +1.6 points on SWE-Bench, and cuts the main trajectory to about 8K tokens while processing over 100K tokens total, an over 90% context compression (Section 4.1, Section 4.3, Table 2).

FoldGRPO's process reward design applies an Unfolded Token Penalty (Q=-1) to main-thread tokens once context exceeds 50% of the working limit, an Out-of-Scope Penalty (Q=-0.2) judged by GPT-5-nano, and a Failure Penalty (Q=-1) for failed tool calls (Section 2.3.2).

CQOEbxy0tE.text: SpecForge achieves up to 9.99x faster EAGLE-3 training throughput for Qwen3-235B-A22B compared to a baseline implementation (Table 1).
SpecBundle draft models deployed on SGLang achieve up to 4.48x end-to-end inference speedup on math/coding benchmarks such as LiveCodeBench with Llama-4-Scout (Section 5.2, Table 2/3).
Attention optimization techniques in SpecForge reduce kernel execution time by 62.1% and peak memory by 93.5% at sequence length 4096 (Section 4.2, Figure 4).
EAGLE-3 training speedups vary by model: 2.01x for LLaMA3.1-8B, 1.39x for LLaMA3.3-70B, 4.31x for Qwen3-30B-A3B, and 9.99x for Qwen3-235B-A22B (Table 1).

Training-Time Test (TTT) length is found to be task-dependent, with an optimal length of about 3 for MT-Bench versus about 13 for math/coding tasks, and data regeneration yields a 5.3% average throughput improvement across benchmarks (Section 2.4, Section 7).

Y37XC7b9Xl.text: A single unified proof framework analyzes SAG, SAGA, and IAG jointly by bounding sub-sampling staleness with concentration tools and constructing a novel Lyapunov function V_k = f(x_k) - f(x*) + L*alpha^2*W_k with a weighted delay window W_k (Section 3.3).
Theorem 3.11 provides the first high-probability convergence bounds for SAG and SAGA under strong convexity, with rate O(exp(-K/(tau*kappa))) where tau = O(N log(NK/delta)) (Section 3, Theorem 3.11).
Theorem 3.12 extends the unified analysis to non-convex objectives, obtaining an O(L^2 B^2 tau / K) convergence rate on the squared gradient norm for SAG/SAGA (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.12).
Theorem 4.1 improves the deterministic convergence guarantee for IAG from O(exp(-K/(kappa^2 N^2))) in prior work to O(exp(-K/(kappa N))) (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 3.14 extends the unified high-probability analysis to Markov sampling schemes beyond i.i.d. sub-sampling (Section 3, Theorem 3.14).

HWTRHS26ZF.text: ReCAP-32B achieves an 81.00% overall success rate on the Dynamic CAPTCHA benchmark, compared to 33.60% for UI-TARS, 29.70% for Qwen3-VL-32B, and 31.80% for OpenAI CUA (Section 4.2, Table 1).

ReCAP handles seven representative CAPTCHA types (Text, Compact Text, Icon Match, Icon Selection, Paged, Slider, Image Grid) via automated reasoning-action data generation and self-corrective training (Section 3.1).
ReCAP-32B requires an average of only 1.54 model-call steps to solve CAPTCHAs, versus 2-4 steps for baseline agents (Section 4.2, Table 1).

On general GUI agent benchmarks, ReCAP-32B attains 93.24% on ScreenSpot-V2 and 67.40% on Android Control (low-level), indicating maintained general GUI capability alongside CAPTCHA-solving gains (Section 4.4, Table 3).

The training pipeline uses approximately 150,000 solution trajectories and 10,000 self-correction trajectories, totaling roughly 230,000 training samples generated through automated reasoning-action data collection (Section 3.2).

TFCjR5gSuX.text: On SAR-RARP50, SurgiFlowVid combined with segmentation-mask conditioning raises mean action recognition performance from a real-data baseline of 0.46 to 0.52, a roughly 13% improvement (Table 2).

On the GraSP dataset, SurgiFlowVid with RGB-frame conditioning improves mean action recognition from a 0.47 real baseline to 0.52 (10.6% gain), with under-represented classes such as pull suture, tie suture, and cut suture improving by 27%, 9%, and 9% respectively (Table 3).

For tool presence detection on SAR-RARP50, SurgiFlowVid with segmentation conditioning improves mean Dice from a 0.69 real-data baseline to 0.79 (14.5% gain), outperforming the SparseCtrl baseline (0.74) by 5 points (Table 4).
On GraSP tool presence detection, SurgiFlowVid with segmentation conditioning raises mean Dice from 0.68 to 0.72, a 5.9% improvement over the real-data baseline (Table 5).

An ablation shows that naive data duplication (0.32±0.17 vs 0.32±0.19 baseline) yields no improvement and that frame shuffling causes a 3-5% performance degradation, indicating gains stem from coherent synthetic dynamics rather than dataset size alone (Table 1).

The dual-prediction diffusion U-Net jointly denoises RGB frames and optical flow maps together with a sparse visual encoder, enabling controllable video generation without dense annotations (Section 3).

hAQZl57Nvx.text: Theorem 1 establishes that the space of finite measures with bounded mass forms a compact metric space under the bounded Lipschitz metric, providing the topological foundation for the measure-valued goal encoding of the reachability MDP (Theorem 1, Section 3).

Theorem 2 proves that under mild Feller-type continuity conditions on the transition kernel, optimal deterministic Markov policies exist for the finite-horizon time-bounded reachability MDP (Theorem 2).

Theorem 3 shows that sequences of functions satisfying Bellman sub-/super-solution inequalities yield provability certificates (upper and lower bounds on the optimal value function) without requiring the full MDP to be solved, with the certificate gap defined as UB(x0) - LB(x0) (Theorem 3, Definition 5, Section 5).

Theorem 4 bounds the worst-case regret of score-guided planning under uniform score-approximation error εb as 0 ≤ V*_B(x0) - V^{πh}_B(x0) ≤ 2∑_{b=1}^{B} εb, showing performance degrades linearly with accumulated approximation error (Theorem 4, Section 6).

Theorem 5 shows that under a margin condition on action-value separation, the expected regret improves to O(Bε^{β+1}) for β>0, i.e., faster than the worst-case linear-in-B rate of Theorem 4 (Theorem 5).

Theorem 6 derives a high-probability estimation-error bound of order O(L H d_D/(d_D+2) (log(n/δ)/n)^{1/(d_D+2)}) under a doubling-dimension assumption on the relevant problem domain, formalizing how statistical complexity of a biased real-world problem distribution governs sample efficiency (Theorem 6, Section 7).

5eZmlUyFpl.text: Section 3.1 shows that varying tensor-parallel (TP) size alone causes over 4% accuracy variance on the AIME24 benchmark under greedy decoding, due to floating-point non-associativity and inconsistent reduction orders across GPUs (Section 3.1, Figure 4).
Table 1 shows that prior batch-invariant operations (BIO) still produce 4.00 unique outputs across TP sizes {1,2,4,8}, demonstrating they do not guarantee cross-TP determinism (Section 3.4, Table 1).

Theorem 1 proves that when N tiles are evenly partitioned across C GPUs, the Tree-Based Invariant Kernel's binary-tree reduction order remains fixed regardless of tensor-parallel size (Theorem 1, Section 4.3).

Table 2 shows that adding TBIK on top of batch-invariant operations reduces unique outputs on AIME24 from 12.00 (vanilla BF16) and 7.87 (BIO alone) to exactly 1, achieving bit-wise determinism across TP configurations (Table 2).

Table 3 shows BIO+TBIK achieves 0 maximum probability divergence across settings versus 10.01×10^-3 for vanilla BF16 on AIME24, and Figure 10 shows this eliminates the probability gap between vLLM and FSDP needed for true on-policy RL (Table 3, Figure 10).
Section 5.4 reports that TBIK's runtime overhead reaches 56-135% relative to vanilla BF16, with the tree all-reduce operation accounting for 28-50% of that added cost (Section 5.4).

C41aLahRXZ.text: Theorem 2 proves that a trained one-layer Mamba generalizes on test prompts with distribution-shifted outliers whenever the outlier fraction α < min(1, p_a·l_tr/l_ts), allowing α to approach 1, whereas Theorem 4 shows a linear Transformer generalizes only when α < 1/2 (Theorem 2, Theorem 4, Section 3.4).

Theorem 1 shows one-layer Mamba requires T ≥ T_M = Θ(η^{-1}(1-p_a)^{-1}β^{-2}M_1) training iterations to reach ε generalization error, while Theorem 3 shows a linear Transformer converges faster, in T_T = Θ(η^{-1}(1-p_a)^{-1}β^{-2}l_tr^{-1}M_1) iterations, under the stricter outlier-tolerance constraint (Theorem 1, Theorem 3, Section 3.3-3.4).

Corollary 1 and Corollary 2 show the linear-attention component concentrates weight on context examples sharing the query's relevant pattern (attention sum ≥ Θ(1)), while the nonlinear gating component suppresses outlier-containing examples (G_i ≤ O(poly(M_1)^{-1})) and applies exponential decay by distance (G_h(j) ≥ Θ(1/2^{j-1})) (Corollary 1, Corollary 2, Section 3.5).

Figure 2 empirically confirms that Mamba maintains test error below 0.01 at outlier fraction α ≈ 0.8 across label-flipping, targeted, and random outlier types, while the linear Transformer's error degrades once α > 0.5 (Figure 2, Section 4).

Table 1 shows Mamba's in-context accuracy is highly position-sensitive to outlier placement: 99.84% accuracy when outliers are placed farthest from the query (FQ) versus 73.28% when placed closest to the query (CQ) (Table 1, Section 4).

ahYRAjx7UG.text: Table 1 reports that under W4A4 quantization, TwinQuant achieves 70.9% zero-shot accuracy and 9.4 WikiText2 perplexity on LLaMA3-8B, and 73.3% accuracy with 10.4 perplexity on Qwen3-32B (Table 1).
Under the less aggressive W4A8 setting, TwinQuant reaches 72.8% accuracy (8.9 perplexity) on LLaMA3-8B and 74.3% accuracy (9.9 perplexity) on Qwen3-32B, close to FP16-level accuracy (Table 1).
Table 1 shows TwinQuant outperforms the SVDQuant baseline by 0.6-3.1 accuracy points under W4A4 quantization (Table 1).
Figure 5 shows TwinQuant delivers 1.63-1.8x end-to-end speedup over the FP16 baseline in one hardware environment and 1.32-1.73x in a second environment, up to 1.07x faster than SVDQuant (Figure 5).

Theorem 4.1 proves that TwinQuant's learnable subspace decomposition reduces quantization error through an activation-flattening gain ζ and a low-rank re-parameterization gain η, motivating the joint optimization over Stiefel and general linear manifolds (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).

A fused dual-component kernel pipelines the two-stage low-rank computation on-chip, eliminating intermediate global-memory traffic between the low-rank and residual quantized components (Figures 4, 6-7).

S2jfT6EMqr.text: On transductive dynamic link prediction, CTDG-SSM achieves the best average rank (1.86) across seven benchmark datasets (LastFM, Enron, MOOC, Reddit, Wikipedia, UCI, Social Evo.), outperforming DyGmamba, DyGFormer, CTAN, TGN, TGAT, JODIE, DyRep, GraphMixer, CAWN, and TCL (Table 2).

In the inductive dynamic link prediction setting, CTDG-SSM attains an average rank of 1.71 across the same seven datasets, showing only a minor performance drop relative to the transductive setting (Section 7.2, Table 2).

On dynamic node classification, CTDG-SSM achieves the top average AUC-ROC rank of 1.00 over 5 runs, with 88.61±0.64 on Wikipedia and 69.50±0.82 on Reddit, versus e.g. 86.35±0.82 and 67.70±1.32 for DyGmamba (Table 3).

On the sequence classification task built to probe long-range spatial (LRS) and temporal (LRT) reasoning, the second-order variant CTDG-SSM (SO) reaches 98.60% mean accuracy at sequence length n=20, versus 88.93% for the next-best baseline CTAN and 54.46% for DyGmamba (Table 4).

An ablation that removes the structural update term (TU-SSM, which fixes the spatial system matrix to identity) causes a substantial accuracy drop on longer sequences, confirming that jointly modeling time-varying graph structure drives the model's long-range gains (Section 7.4, Table 4).

Kdc1UvnMKk.text: On solvation free energy prediction across 70 chemically distinct test systems (vacuum-to-toluene and vacuum-to-water), CARD achieves mean absolute error below 1 kcal/mol and R² exceeding 0.9 (Section 5.1).

CARD provides an approximately 40-fold inference speedup over classical alchemical free energy methods when endstate MD simulation is excluded, and roughly a 5-fold speedup when endstate simulation is included (Section 5.1).
On endstate correction from classical molecular-mechanics to neural-network-potential energies, evaluated on 18 HiPen test molecules, CARD achieves an MAE of 0.90 kcal/mol (Section 5.2).

On aqueous tautomer free energy estimation (27 tautomer pairs), CARD attains MAE of 4.11 kcal/mol and Pearson correlation 0.64, outperforming a DFT baseline (MAE 4.62 kcal/mol, correlation 0.36) (Section 5.3).

Ablations show the full two-stage model with radix r=4 and decomposition depth L=3 achieves MAE 0.71 and R² 0.92, while reducing depth to L=2 collapses accuracy to R² of -0.08, demonstrating the importance of the coarse-to-fine radix depth (Table 3, Section 5.4).

Dkwqzk5sAD.text: On GPT-OSS-120B, Consequence-Based Utility (CBU) improves Acc@1 from 67.21 (LLM-Judge) to 76.27 and AUC from 71.42 to 79.63 for ranking research-level math solutions (Table 2).
On GPT-OSS-20B, CBU improves Acc@1 from 72.13 to 74.59 and AUC from 69.03 to 79.18 relative to LLM-Judge (Table 2).

The ExpertMath benchmark used for evaluation has per-problem solver accuracy ranging from 7.14 to 47.14 (mean 25.5), markedly harder than AIME 2025 (80.3-95.7) and comparable in difficulty to FrontierMath (20.7-37.6) (Table 1).
CBU maintains a stronger correct-vs-incorrect separation than baseline judges even on problems where solvers largely fail (Figure 3).
CBU utility estimates stabilize with as few as 8 rollouts per candidate solution (Figure 6).

W6FvMHPVez.text: TPOUR Contriever outperforms unsupervised and supervised baselines (DPR, REALM, SimCSE, Contriever, Temporal Contrastive, TimeR4) on temporal QA over mixed-timestamp document collections from SituatedQA and RealTimeQA (Table 2).
TPOUR Contriever improves nDCG@5 over Nomic Embed v2 MoE by +7.13 (+23.5%) on explicit queries and +7.76 (+25.5%) on implicit queries (Table 2).
Despite being 72.7x smaller, TPOUR Contriever outperforms multiple Qwen3-Embedding-8B variants (standard, query-rewriting, and time-aware-instruction) on temporal retrieval (Table 5).

Time-vector interpolation between two year-specific fine-tuned checkpoints yields an average nDCG@5 improvement of +13.4 over the start-year model and +10.8 over the end-year model on intermediate test periods (Table 4).
A Mixture-of-TPOUR variant trained for timestamp prediction achieves 76.56% year-level accuracy versus a 50.18% baseline (Section 3.3).

noDJPmA3ha.text: Conformal Thinking introduces a distribution-free risk control framework that decides when a reasoning language model can stop "thinking" while keeping performance loss below a user-specified level (abstract only).

The proposed B-PAC procedure combines an upper threshold that halts reasoning once confidence is high with a lower threshold that stops early on difficult instances unlikely to improve with further computation (abstract only).
B-PAC reasoning is reported to decrease thinking-model token usage by up to 81.01% while controlling performance loss below the user-specified target (abstract only).
The framework provides anytime-valid guarantees on performance loss control, so the risk certificate remains valid regardless of when the reasoning process is stopped (abstract only).
Computational efficiency gains are attributed separately to the lower-threshold stopping mechanism and to an ensemble stopping mechanism, both adhering to the specified risk target (abstract only).

P1jHroBS5E.text: Meta Context Engineering (MCE) achieves 89.1% average relative improvement over the base model in the offline setting and 74.1% in the online setting, evaluated across five domains: FiNER, USPTO-50k, Symptom2Disease, LawBench, and AEGIS2 (Table 1).

MCE outperforms the prior state-of-the-art agentic context engineering method by 5.6-53.8% relative improvement (mean 16.9%), including 75% vs. 71% accuracy on FiNER, 20% vs. 18% on USPTO-50k, 89.2% vs. 79.2% on Symptom2Disease, 0.70 vs. 0.65 F1 on LawBench, and 0.80 vs. 0.68 F1 on AEGIS2 (Table 1).
On the FiNER benchmark, MCE trains 13.6x faster than ACE (1.9 hours vs. 25.8 hours) and requires 4.8x fewer rollouts (450 vs. 2,169) to reach superior accuracy (Figure 4).

MCE generates variable-length contexts spanning 1.5K-86K tokens depending on task demands, avoiding GEPA's brevity bias (~1-2K tokens) and ACE's context bloat (up to 80K tokens) (Section on context adaptability).

When contexts trained on DeepSeek-V3.1 are transferred to smaller models, MCE shows 4-7% lower performance degradation than baselines and achieves 172.6% average relative gain over the base model on Gemma3-4B (Table 2).

An ablation shows MCE with evolving skills reaches 75% offline accuracy on FiNER, versus 73% without skills and 71% with a fixed skill, confirming the bi-level optimization design contributes measurable gains (Table 3).

DcyK4f7ZyU.text: Proposition 4.1 shows CoSiNE provides a first-order approximation to sequential point-mutation processes with an L1 error bound of (λt)^2, quadratic in branch length t (Section 4).

In zero-shot variant effect prediction, CoSiNE achieves Spearman correlations of 0.613 on the Koenig H expression dataset, 0.464 on Adams binding, and 0.536 on Shanehsazzadeh 120, outperforming baselines including ESM2-150M, ProGen2-Medium, and DASM on most of these datasets (Table 1).
CoSiNE underperforms ProGen2-Small by only 0.005 Spearman correlation on the Koenig Light expression dataset, its sole reported loss among the compared benchmarks (Table 1).

CoSiNE attains a test perplexity of 1.264 on heavy chains of the Rodriguez et al. 2023 genetic dataset and achieves better per-site likelihood than DASM+Thrifty in 62.3% of cases, with improvement more pronounced for longer branches (t >= 0.25) (Section 5.1).

Taylor-approximated guidance (TAG) for Guided Gillespie sampling achieves 488-928x speedups over exact classifier guidance without loss of fitness in antibody binding affinity optimization (Section C.7).

CoSiNE is trained on approximately 2 million evolutionary transitions from about 120,000 clonal families, initialized from a 150M-parameter ESM2 backbone, and converges in about one day on a single A100 GPU.

ZuIjuBCjxh.text: Theorem 1 gives a non-asymptotic bound on the total variation distance between the true data distribution and the model's sampled distribution, scaling as d^3 log^4.5(T)/T plus terms in sqrt(log T)*epsilon_s (score estimation error) and (log T/sqrt T)*epsilon_h (Hessian estimation error) (Section 4).
Theorem 2 establishes that the quasi-maximum likelihood estimator (quasi-MLE) is consistent, converging to the true parameter with probability under oracle score access (Section 4).
Proposition 2 derives analytical closed forms for the conditional mean and covariance of the reverse diffusion transition, expressed in terms of both the score function and its Hessian (Section 3.1).
On synthetic Gaussian/t-distribution mixtures, likelihood matching yields lower mean absolute parameter estimation error than score matching across varying sample sizes (Section 5.1).

On MNIST, likelihood matching achieves improved FID scores as the number of matched moments N and rank r are increased, and on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and LSUN it produces visually coherent samples with faster convergence using fewer sampling steps (Section 5.2).

PLJ53zWDTD.text: SCOPE achieves symbolic world completeness (ClassicalSR) of 94.8+/-0.8% on ALFRED and 95.8+/-0.7% on VirtualHome, substantially outperforming ablations lacking the evolution mechanism (Table 2).
In open-ended settings, SCOPE improves task success rate by an average of 11.3 percentage points over the NESYC neuro-symbolic continual-learning baseline across diverse embodied scenarios (Table 1).
SCOPE improves step success rate by 14.4% over the course of a continual run, demonstrating cross-task grounding and adaptability via knowledge transfer (Section 4).

SCOPE is evaluated on 186 VirtualHome tasks (Personal Hygiene, Food/Dining, Housekeeping, Leisure) and 600 ALFRED tasks (Pick & Place, Examine in Light, Clean & Place, Heat & Place, Cool & Place), compared against VILA, ISR-LLM, and NESYC baselines all using a GPT-4o backbone (Section 4).

An ablation of the Symbolic Execution Simulator (SESim) component is reported separately from an ablation of the Self-Adaptive Symbolic Memory (SASMem) design, isolating the contribution of each module (Table 3, Table 4).
SCOPE's symbolic hallucination rate and sensitivity to different VLM backbones are evaluated as additional robustness checks (Table 5, Table 6).

SqegQxm1ya.text: NoiseSDF2NoiseSDF trains a neural SDF using an MSE loss between predictions from two independently noisy point-cloud observations of the same surface, without requiring any clean ground-truth supervision (Equation 5, Section 4.1).

On ShapeNet at noise level sigma=0.01, the method improves IoU by roughly 4-9% across categories and reduces Chamfer distance from 0.010 to 0.008 relative to comparison methods (Section on ShapeNet results).
On the ABC and Famous datasets at 0.01 noise level, the method reaches Normal Consistency scores of 0.865 and 0.831 respectively (Section 4.2).
The method is benchmarked against 3DS2V, 3DILG, P2S, PPSurf, SAP-O, and PGR across four datasets: ShapeNet (seven largest subsets), ABC, Famous, and Real (Section 4).
Reconstruction quality is evaluated using five metrics: Chamfer Distance, Intersection-over-Union, Normal Consistency, Mesh Normal Consistency, and F1 Score (Section 4.2).

0Y7itV1kb7.text: SupGCL uses gene knockdown perturbations from LINCS as supervised augmentations, and Theorem 1 shows the resulting loss decomposes into a node-level contrastive term weighted by the supervised distribution plus an augmentation-matching term (Theorem 1).

Corollary 1 proves that conventional (unsupervised) graph contrastive learning is recovered as a special case of SupGCL when the augmentation temperature parameter tau_a tends to infinity (Corollary 1).

On node-level tasks evaluated across breast, lung, and colorectal cancer TCGA cohorts, SupGCL improves over the GRACE baseline, e.g. on lung cancer biological-process classification SupGCL reaches 0.282+/-0.037 vs. 0.259+/-0.063 for GRACE (Table 2).

On graph-level tasks, SupGCL improves hazard prediction C-index on colorectal cancer to 0.698+/-0.085 versus 0.657+/-0.071 for the GraphCL baseline, and improves breast cancer disease-subtype classification accuracy to 0.847+/-0.036 versus 0.804+/-0.031 for the no-pretraining baseline (Table 3).
SupGCL outperforms five baselines (no-pretrain, GAE, GraphCL, GRACE, SGRL) across all 13 downstream node- and graph-level tasks spanning three cancer types (Table 2, Table 3).

Latent-space analysis shows GraphCL embeddings collapse, with 98.3% of variance captured by the first PCA component, whereas SupGCL embeddings show clearer disease-subtype separation across embedding dimensions 8-64 (Section on embedding-space/ablation analysis).

fBAMvSNH8N.text: The dual-attention backbone combines intra-type self-attention (variables and constraints separately) with inter-type, sparsity-aware cross-attention over the coefficient matrix structure, computed in parallel rather than via sequential GNN message passing (equations 5-8, 11-14).

On the element-level binary-variable-prediction benchmark, the proposed model improves over the BGNN baseline on all four datasets, e.g. MCC on the CA dataset rises from 0.3488 to 0.3825 (+9.65%) and error rate on IP drops from 20.88% to 17.72% (Table 2).

On instance-level feasibility prediction on challenging 'foldable' synthetic datasets, the proposed model attains 0% error compared to 6% error for an enhanced BGNN baseline (Section on instance-level prediction).

In a component ablation on the WA dataset, removing self-attention drops MCC from 0.8411 to 0.7985, and removing cross-attention drops MCC further to 0.5724, showing both attention types are necessary (Table 7).
Using predict-and-search frameworks built on the model's predictions, the approach achieves 14.5-36% average improvement in primal gap over BGNN-based predict-and-search baselines (Table 3, Table 4).

On 215 real-world MIPLIB instances with up to 550,539 variables and severe 42:1 class imbalance, the proposed model generalizes out-of-distribution and outperforms BGNN on MCC, balanced accuracy, and macro-F1 (Table 9).

mJJaz04lQR.text: dgMARK embeds a watermark in discrete diffusion language models by reordering which positions are unmasked first, favoring positions whose top candidate token satisfies a binary parity constraint, while leaving the model's learned probability distribution p_theta unchanged (Section 3, 'Decoding-guided Watermarking for dLLMs').

dgMARK is compatible with confidence-based, entropy-based, and margin-based decoding/unmasking orders used in diffusion LLM sampling, and detection uses a z-score statistic z=(G-n/2)/sqrt(n/4) over parity-matching tokens (Section 3, Table 1).

The one-step lookahead (beam) variant evaluates candidate unmasking choices by how many future positions remain parity-aligned after each commitment, and with a 3-beam search on LLaDA 1.5 this achieves TPR=92.9% at FPR=0.0% (z=4.0, multinomial sampling) (Table 1).
dgMARK with 3-beam search achieves higher detectability than the KGW (delta=3) and PATTERN-MARK baselines at comparable or lower perplexity increase (~0.5-1.0 points) (Table 2, Figure 8).

The sliding-window detector remains robust (ROC AUC > 0.9) under random insertion, deletion, and substitution edits at rates up to 0.4, as well as under DIPPER and Llama-3-8B paraphrasing attacks (Figure 2, Figure 3).
Base dgMARK adds roughly 16% per-token computational overhead, while the 3-beam lookahead variant incurs about 2.7x overhead in exchange for higher detectability (Table 7).

hGeKiXnUIT.text: Agents holding individually insufficient local views coordinate through ADMM constrained by cellular sheaves (Sheaf-ADMM) to produce correct global outputs, reaching 92.6% solved rate on Sudoku versus 10.7% for a parameter-matched MPNN baseline (Table 2).

On the maze task, Sheaf-ADMM attains a 99.8% solve rate using a much smaller per-vertex latent dimension (d_v=10) than the MPNN baseline (d_v=84, 99.9% solve rate), showing comparable accuracy with far less per-agent state (Table 1).

Sheaf-ADMM shows markedly improved robustness to distribution shift on MNIST: under 16-pixel padding a standard CNN drops to 11.4% accuracy while Sheaf-ADMM retains 86.3%, and under 30% patch dropout the CNN reaches 45.5% versus 69.1% for Sheaf-ADMM (Table 4).

An ablation shows learned restriction (sheaf) maps are critical to coordination: replacing them with identity maps collapses Sudoku performance to 6.1% solved, and removing the L1 regularization term drops maze performance from 99.8% to 38.9% (Table 3).

Sheaf-ADMM generalizes to larger problem sizes, remaining near-saturated in maze solve rate up to roughly a 2x increase in linear maze resolution beyond training size (Figure 6, Section 5.5 Out-of-Distribution Generalization).

dUsQj7QFvs.text: Mixed batching (MB) begins to underperform exclusive batching (EB) at a decode-token ratio of about 80% on the high-bandwidth H200 GPU (4.8 TB/s), but at a much lower ratio of about 20% on the bandwidth-constrained RTX PRO 6000 GPU (1.792 TB/s) (Figure 1, Figure 2).

The paper derives a closed-form optimal switching threshold theta_0 satisfying theta_0(1-theta_0)^-1 + ln(1-theta_0) = p_0*alpha_p*alpha_d^-1, which depends only on output-length distribution and hardware parameters, independent of batch size N and input length (Section 3.2 Optimal Switching Threshold).

On the bandwidth-constrained RTX PRO 6000, the EB(k*) policy achieves up to 15.3% higher throughput than a chunked-prefill/mixed-batching baseline on the real-world ShareGPT workload, and 11.3% higher on WildChat, with TPOT reduced from 268.97ms to 93.68ms on ShareGPT (Table 2).

On synthetic decode-heavy workloads on the RTX PRO 6000, EB(k*) achieves up to a 41.9% throughput improvement over mixed batching, while on the high-bandwidth H200 the gain from EB narrows to about 1.5% (Figure 4).

The adaptive hybrid scheduler EB+ switches between EB and MB at runtime and, under non-stationary traffic with shifting distribution and concurrency, achieves near-optimal throughput and outperforms mixed batching by up to 36.4% (Table 3).

Scalability experiments across four GPU platforms (B300, L40S, RTX PRO 6000, H200) under the WildChat workload confirm the bandwidth-dependent crossover: exclusive batching gains are largest on lower-bandwidth GPUs like L40S and RTX PRO 6000 (Table 4).

CeDYwcRJOC.text: For global optimization, the algorithm achieves an adversarial-regime regret bound of Õ(√(SA·min{L*, HT−L*, Q∞, V₁})) + HSA·log(T), unifying first-order, second-order, and path-length data-dependent complexity measures (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
In the stochastic regime with corruption, the global optimization algorithm attains a gap-independent bound of Õ(√(SA(VT+C))) using the occupancy-weighted variance measure V (Section 4).
The gap-dependent stochastic bound takes the form U + √(UC), where U = Σ H²log(T)/Δ(s,a), and is polylogarithmic in the number of episodes T (Section 4).

The policy-optimization algorithm achieves an adversarial regret bound of Õ(H²SA·min{L*, HT−L*, Q∞, V₁}) + H²S²A·log²(T), with an extra H factor relative to the global-optimization bound (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).

Matching lower bounds of Ω(√(SA·L*)), Ω(√(SA·Q∞)), and Ω(√H·V₁) are established for the adversarial regime, and Ω(√(SA·VT)) for the stochastic variance-dependent regime (Section 6, Theorems 6.1 and 6.2).

raUHOQnZyv.text: On the MultiGrid dataset, FLAM achieves a PSNR of 56.5, substantially outperforming AdaWorld (24.0) and Genie (33.9) (Table 1).
On the nuPlan dataset, FLAM achieves a PSNR of 19.7 versus AdaWorld's 18.1 and Genie's 16.0 (Table 1).
FLAM yields large FVD improvements over Genie on MultiGrid (2.9 vs 177.5) and on the Leaper environment (12.1 vs 27.3) (Table 1).
On factor-entity correspondence metrics, FLAM reaches 0.91 disentanglement, 0.91 completeness, and 0.93 informativeness, outperforming PlaySlot and SlotFormer (Table 2).
Performance remains stable across the number of factors K, with PSNR staying around 56.5 for K∈{4,8,16} on 4-agent scenes (Table 3).
With 10k labeled frames used for downstream policy learning on Bigfish, FLAM achieves a return of 8.8 versus 3.6 for vanilla behavior cloning (Table 4).

qxG09uid4p.text: DLM-GRPO achieves 0.97±0.02 win rate on the 3s5z SMAC task versus 0.81±0.04 for the MADT baseline (Section 4, Table 1).
DLM-GRPO achieves 1.00±0.01 on 10m_vs_11m versus 0.92±0.05 for Gato, while the LLM-based SayCan baseline scores only 0.00-0.10 across tasks (Section 4, Table 1).
On 11 unseen zero-shot generalization tasks, DLM-GRPO scores 1.00 on MMM, 0.99 on 25m, and 0.82 on 3s_vs_4z, outperforming MADT and Gato on 9 of 11 tasks (Section 4, Table 2).
DLM-GRPO matches or exceeds value-based offline MARL baselines OMIGA and CFCQL on representative SMAC tasks across easy, hard, and super-hard difficulty levels (Section 4, Figure 4).
GRPO fine-tuning substantially reduces out-of-distribution action rates across all 15 SMAC tasks evaluated, with the largest reductions on harder difficulty levels (Section 4, Figure 5).
On the LBF benchmark, DLM-GRPO achieves 0.96±0.02 versus 0.85±0.07 for OMIGA, while total training cost is only about 60-70 GPU-hours (Appendix A.6, Table 7).

BYInOck3gr.text: Causal Forcing outperforms the Self-Forcing baseline by 19.3% in Dynamic Degree, 8.7% in VisionReward, and 16.7% in Instruction Following, while maintaining identical throughput of 17.0 FPS and 0.69s latency (Section 4, Table 1).

The method uses an autoregressive teacher for ODE initialization rather than a bidirectional teacher, addressing a 'frame-level injectivity' violation identified in prior distillation approaches (Section 3.2).
An ablation replacing diffusion forcing with teacher forcing improves VisionReward by 111.2% (Section 4, Table 2).

An ablation comparing the proposed causal ODE construction against Self-Forcing's chunk-wise ODE shows a 183.3% improvement in Dynamic Degree, 90.0% in VisionReward, and 47.4% in Instruction Following (Section 4, Table 2).
The three-stage Causal Forcing approach is described in Section 3.3, building on the suboptimality analysis of existing autoregressive distillation methods in Section 3.2 (Section 3).

unAyphD4hq.text: Within-family Truth Score correlations between base LLMs and their multimodal descendants range from 0.77-0.98, compared to near-zero correlation (0.04-0.08) across unrelated model families such as Mistral-7B (Section 2.2).
TruthProbe's soft-gating mechanism applies g^h_l = 1 + λ·norm(S) to amplify context-truthful attention heads using normalized Truth Scores (Section 3).
On HaluEval, TruthProbe raises Vicuna-7B's F1 from 13.37 to 29.15 and Qwen2.5's F1 from 36.69 to 46.54 (Section 4, Table 1).
Transferring Truth Scores from base LLMs to multimodal descendants improves POPE recall on COCO, e.g., LLaVA-NeXT from 78.8% to 80.9% and Qwen2.5-VL-Omni from 75.0% to 77.7% (Section 4, Table 2).
On the CHAIR image-captioning benchmark, base-LLM-derived Truth Scores reduce LLaVA-NeXT's CHAIR_I from 6.91% to 4.94% and Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct's CHAIR_S from 13.2% to 12.2% (Section 4, Table 3).

Within-family parameter divergence (Frobenius norm ~0.03) is far smaller than cross-family divergence (~1.01), offering mechanistic evidence for why Truth Score patterns are preserved across lineages (Section 2.3).

T1uBDl1WPR.text: Reframes mechanistic anomaly detection as a functional attribution problem, using influence functions computed via parameter-space sampling with Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) to measure how well trusted reference samples explain a test sample's behavior (Section 4).

On BackdoorBench (7 attacks, 4 datasets, 5% poisoning rate), the offline UMAP K-NN variant achieves an average Defense Effectiveness Rating (DER) of 0.972 and the online CCCC variant achieves 0.928 DER, versus the best baseline STRIP at 0.833 DER (Table 1).

On LLM backdoor detection with Gemma 2-2B and Llama 8B, the method achieves at least 0.99 AUROC on simple triggers, 0.98 AUROC on complex contextual triggers (where baseline methods are near-random), and 1.0 AUROC on explicitly obfuscated models where all latent-space baselines fail (Table 2).

Explains detection performance via a sharp-flat Hessian subspace separation argument: clean mechanisms rely on sharp loss directions while anomalous mechanisms hide in flat directions, producing distinct functional correlation with trusted samples (Section 4.2, Appendix A).

Ablations show stable detection performance across γ in {1000, ..., 10000} and number of SGLD draws nβ in {100, ..., 1000}, requiring at least 250 trusted samples and at least 250 SGLD draws for strong results, with graceful degradation under 5% trusted-set contamination (Appendix E.1).

uXHiVNJK25.text: On LLaMA3-8B trained on 50B tokens, Spectra achieves a final training loss 1.5% better than AdamW and 0.4% better than Muon, reaching comparable loss milestones notably faster than AdamW (Figure 7B, Section 4.1).

On Qwen3-0.6B, Spectra reduces optimizer-state memory by 49.25% compared to AdamW, is 5.1x faster in optimizer processing time than Muon, and adds only -0.7% (i.e., negligible) end-to-end wall-clock overhead (Table 3, Section 4.1).
Spectra improves average downstream accuracy across benchmarks including ARC, RACE, BoolQ, HellaSwag, PIQA, and LAMBADA by 1.62% over AdamW and 0.66% over Muon (Table 4, Section 4.1).
Spectra's theoretical per-step complexity is O(Tmnk) where k is approximately 1.5% of layer dimensions, substantially lower than full-spectrum spectral optimization methods (Table 1, Section 3.3).

mOPwfQSfJq.text: Introduces GRU-Mem, a gated recurrent memory framework with two text-controlled gating mechanisms for stable and efficient long-context reasoning, extending the chunk-by-chunk recurrent memory paradigm of MemAgent (Section 3, Figure 1).
On the RULER benchmark evaluated across diverse long-context tasks with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, GRU-Mem outperforms vanilla MemAgent on most tasks under both w/o EG and w EG inference modes (Table 1).

GRU-Mem achieves around 200% inference acceleration under the w/o EG mode and up to 400% (i.e., roughly 4-5x) inference speed acceleration under the w EG (early-exit gating) mode compared to vanilla MemAgent, with acceleration increasing as context length grows (Table 1, Section 4.1).

GRU-Mem maintains stable performance on out-of-distribution multi-key (MK) task series where vanilla MemAgent shows a sharp performance drop, attributed to more stable memory updating that avoids indiscriminate memory growth (Section 4.1).

When evidence occurs at the top 20% of positions, GRU-Mem with early-exit gating (w EG) reduces inference time to 1/4 of vanilla MemAgent's while comparing performance and efficiency for the 7B-sized model (Table 2).

uurjpxrLc5.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes that when conditional independence (CI) testing achieves minimax separation radius c asymptotic to n^(-1/alpha), the corresponding poly-forest structure learning problem achieves optimal sample complexity n asymptotic to (log d)/c^alpha, implementable via the PC-tree algorithm (Theorem 3.1).
For Bernoulli and Gaussian graphical models, the optimal sample complexity for structure learning is n asymptotic to (log d)/c^2 (Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2).
For nonparametric graphical models with smoothness parameter s, the optimal sample complexity is n asymptotic to (log d)/c^((5s+2)/(2s)) (Theorem 5.1).

Proposes the PC-tree algorithm (Algorithm 1), a modification of the classical PC algorithm that tests only marginal and single-variable conditioning independence relations, requiring roughly d^3 tests instead of an exponential number, while remaining minimax optimal (Algorithm 1, Section 3).

HFNJOpXHfm.text: WorldMirror is a feed-forward transformer model that integrates diverse geometric priors (camera poses, intrinsics, depth maps) via a dynamic prior injection scheme, encoding poses as single quaternion tokens and depth maps as convolution-derived tokens, and can toggle priors on/off at inference (Section 3.1).

On point map reconstruction without any priors, WorldMirror improves over VGGT by 10.4% on 7-Scenes and over Pi-cubed by 17.8% on DTU; with all priors provided, it improves 58.1% on 7-Scenes over its own no-prior baseline (Table 1).
On novel view synthesis, WorldMirror outperforms AnySplat with 25.14 PSNR vs 19.96 PSNR on RealEstate10K (32 views) and 21.25 PSNR vs 18.40 PSNR on DL3DV (64 views) (Table 4).
On surface normal estimation on ScanNet, WorldMirror achieves a mean angular error of 13.8 degrees versus 16.0 degrees for StableNormal (Table 3).
Ablation on prior embedding design shows single-token encoding of poses and intrinsics outperforms dense per-pixel embeddings while adding only 1.06M extra parameters (Table 5).

Ablation on prior configuration shows that incorporating even a single prior modality enhances both the corresponding task's prediction and the model's accuracy on other geometric attributes, indicating synergistic multi-task effects (Figure 6).

tqTNOpkP5j.text: On MATH-500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, GRPO training with random (spurious) rewards yields a +21.4 percentage point absolute accuracy gain, compared to +29.1 points with ground-truth rewards and +24.1 points with incorrect-label rewards (Figure 1, Section 2.3).
Format-only rewards produce a smaller +13.8 point gain and majority-voting rewards produce a +27.1 point gain on the same MATH-500/Qwen2.5-Math-7B setup (Figure 1, Section 2.3).
Qwen2.5-Math-7B's baseline code-reasoning frequency of 65.0% (Table 1) rises to about 90%, reaching 95.6% under random rewards, after 300 RLVR training steps (Figure 6, Section 4.1-4.2).

On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, responses that invoke code reasoning score 60.9% accuracy versus 35.0% for non-code responses, showing spurious-reward gains are mediated by increased code-reasoning frequency (Table 1).

Spurious rewards that boost Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH-500 nearly always fail to produce comparable gains for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct or OLMo2-7B, whose improvements are substantially smaller than the Qwen2.5 family's (Section 3, Figure 3).

Sweeping the random-reward correctness probability γ over {0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.001} all yield 15-20 percentage point MATH-500 gains, while γ=0 yields no improvement, isolating the effect from any residual correct-reward signal (Section 4.4.2, Figure 10).

S21HtCHa40.text: IAPO reduces average completion length on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from 177.93 tokens (base model) to 110.65 tokens, a reduction of about 36%, while improving reasoning accuracy (Section on main results).
At Pass@32 on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-7B, IAPO matches DAPO's and S-GRPO's 100% accuracy while using 111.83 tokens on average versus 175.05 and 177.62 tokens respectively (main results table).
On DAPO-Math-17k with Qwen2.5-0.5B, IAPO attains a token-efficiency Ratio@32 of 2.14×10⁻², exceeding GFPO's 1.76×10⁻² and the next-best alternative's 1.22×10⁻² (ablation/efficiency table).

Removing the informativeness term (variant IAPO-NI) significantly degrades performance relative to full IAPO on Qwen2.5-0.5B, while an alternative mutual-information estimator (IAPO-NE) is less effective than full IAPO but still outperforms IAPO-NI (ablation study, Qwen2.5-0.5B).
IAPO reduces wall-clock inference time by more than 11% compared to baseline token-efficient RL methods after post-training (inference-time efficiency results).

uCLVPafHqd.text: Sketch&Walk maintains near-lossless accuracy at 20% attention density (80% sparsity) applied training-free across both the prefill and decode phases of LLM inference (main results).
Sketch&Walk achieves up to 6x end-to-end inference speedup, with prefill-phase speedups over MInference growing approximately linearly with context length (Tables 1, 3, 6 on LongBench).
In the decode phase, Sketch&Walk attains up to 1.6x speedup over baselines such as QUEST and Adamas with consistent acceleration across sequence lengths (Tables 2, 4, 5 on RULER).

On RULER benchmarks spanning 4K-64K token contexts, Sketch&Walk's sparse retrieval accuracy is competitive with or exceeds dense attention baselines in some settings, evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, and Qwen2-7B-Instruct (Tables 2, 4, 5).

op2bPlSv2o.text: AVA-VLA achieves a 98.3% average success rate across LIBERO's four task suites (Spatial 97.8%, Object 99.4%, Goal 97.8%, Long 98.1%), matching or exceeding full-reasoning baselines (Table 1).
On CALVIN five-step long-horizon tasks, AVA-VLA reaches 84.0% success versus 77.8% for the FLOWER baseline, with an average completed task length of 4.77 steps (Table 3).

AVA-VLA delivers roughly 6x inference speedup over explicit chain-of-thought baselines, with mean latency of 145ms and 2.3 average reasoning steps versus 892ms and 8.5 steps for the explicit CoT baseline (Table 2).
The early-exit gating network terminates reasoning when its confidence score e_t exceeds a threshold τ=0.55, reducing reasoning depth by 54% (from 5.0 to 2.3 steps on average) (Eq. 17-19, Table 2).
Reasoning is formulated as a POMDP with RL-based latent-state denoising combining task success, entropy regularization, and smoothness constraints into a composite reward (Section 3.2, Section 3.5).

Threshold sensitivity analysis shows the latency-performance trade-off varies systematically with the exit threshold τ, and latent-state stability metrics confirm AVA-VLA suppresses noise-induced near-zero state updates (Table 5, Table 6).

d5rrjYG5pi.text: OmniAID's Mixture-of-Experts architecture combines routable Specialized Semantic Experts (for Human, Animal, Object, Scene, Anime domains) with a fixed Universal Artifact Expert for content-agnostic generator fingerprints, using SVD-based orthogonal weight decomposition from a CLIP-ViT-L/14@336px backbone (Section on architecture).
On the GenImage benchmark, OmniAID reaches 95.9% mean accuracy versus 91.1% for the prior state-of-the-art monolithic detector Effort, and OmniAID-Mirage reaches 97.2% (Table 2).

On the Mirage-Test benchmark, OmniAID trained only on GenImage scores 51.10% mean accuracy across domains, while OmniAID-Mirage reaches 88.39% mean accuracy with consistent per-domain performance (Table 3).

On the Chameleon in-the-wild dataset, GenImage-trained OmniAID attains 77.4% mean accuracy (78.7% real, 75.6% fake), while OmniAID-Mirage attains 91.4%, establishing a new state of the art (Figure 5).
Ablating the Universal Artifact Expert causes the largest out-of-domain accuracy drop, 11.28 points on the Chameleon dataset, confirming its role in capturing generator-agnostic artifacts (Table 5).
OmniAID trains in 3 hours on GenImage and 18 hours on Mirage using 4 H200 GPUs, and runs inference at 207.68 FPS at batch size 100, versus 665.90 FPS for the Effort baseline (efficiency results).

SFTFsixO2K.text: On the 8B model scale, LT-Tuning achieves 70.3% average accuracy with the adapter versus 61.7% for explicit CoT, while Coconut degrades to 41.5% at this scale (Table 1).
At the 1B and 3B scales, LT-Tuning attains 36.4% and 52.4% average accuracy respectively, outperforming the best baselines SoftCoT (33.2%) and explicit CoT (50.5%) (Table 1).

PCA visualization of latent token representations shows Coconut suffers severe feature collapse, with latent tokens from different samples converging to nearly identical points after just two reasoning steps, whereas LT-Tuning maintains semantic diversity even at six latent tokens (Figure 5).

Stage 2's confidence-driven dynamic latent token insertion produces a positive correlation between question difficulty and the number of generated latent tokens, indicating learned difficulty-aware computation allocation (Figure 3).

Ablations on the 8B model show removing the Context-Prediction Fusion mechanism (Stage 3) causes a 23.5% accuracy drop, while removing dynamic latent token allocation (Stage 2) causes a 6.7% drop, and removing latent reasoning entirely causes a 7.2% drop (Table 2).

68zOaa2gOf.text: Across five contact-rich manipulation tasks on the DROID platform (Franka Panda + Robotiq gripper), mean success rate improves from a 46.0% base VLA policy to 74.4% after one co-improvement iteration and to 86.8% after two iterations, a 39.2 percentage point absolute gain (Table 2, Figure 7).
Task-specific success rates rise substantially after co-improvement, e.g., Drawing improves from 22% to 78% and Scooping from 44% to 92% (Table 2).

Training the VLA policy on synthetic rollouts generated by the co-improved world model yields an additional 11.6 percentage point improvement over the base policy, isolated from the real-world rollout contribution (abstract quantified further in Section 4/Table 2).

World model fidelity, fine-tuned from Ctrl-World on real rollout data plus DROID regularization, improves video generation quality from PSNR 16.32 to 21.77, SSIM 0.634 to 0.784, LPIPS 0.347 to 0.136, FID 41.03 to 9.58, and FVD 225.13 to 64.12 (Table 1).
The Qwen3-VL-based vision-language reward model reduces false-positive contact/success predictions in the interaction confusion matrix from 11 to 1 after iterative refinement (Section 4.1).
Policy optimization uses a weighted flow-matching objective with binary success weighting (w=1 for success, 0 for failure) rather than reinforcement-learning gradient methods (Section 4.2).

B3YoryA3VD.text: BokehDepth improves UniDepthV2's zero-shot δ₁ accuracy on HAMMER from 0.645 to 0.895 (a 38.8% relative gain) and on Middlebury from 0.535 to 0.716 (a 33.8% relative gain) (Table 2).
On Depth Anything v2, BokehDepth raises zero-shot δ₁ on HAMMER from 0.828 to 0.894 and on IBims-1 from 0.938 to 0.960 (Table 2).
On in-domain NYUv2 evaluation with UniDepthV2, BokehDepth reduces AbsRel from 0.047 to 0.039 and RMSE from 0.180 to 0.043 (Table 3).

The Stage-1 bokeh synthesis module, a physically-guided FLUX-Kontext diffusion model conditioned on a thin-lens optics scalar K=f²S₁/2N(S₁−f)·pixel_ratio (Eq. 1), outperforms BokehDiff and BokehMe on EBB! Val200 with PSNR 25.91 and LPIPS 0.1852 (Table 1).
Ablating either the spatial or focus attention branch of the Divided Space Focus (DSF) Attention module causes δ₁ to drop from 0.943 to roughly 0.6, showing both branches are necessary (Table 4).

1dfBRJVswL.text: At the operating point C0=0.7, SteER achieves 85.70% alignment, 7.83 to 22.80 percentage points higher than baselines including GPT-Researcher (79.48%), OpenDeepResearch (77.20%), and o4-mini-deep-research (75.72%) in full-persona settings (Table 2).
SteER attains the best breadth score among all compared systems at 91.29%, alongside 86.45% focus and 84.19% balance (Table 2).
In human evaluation, SteER reports are preferred over baselines in 86 to 90% of pairwise alignment judgments and 83% of focus judgments (Section 3.5).
The interruption decision rule triggers PauseAsk when the expected value gain ΔEV(n*) exceeds the pause cost C(n*) = C0·(1 + pauses_j/Tol_j), otherwise the system proceeds autonomously (Section 2.4).
Ablations show removing the InfoGain term drops alignment by 3.51 points and removing diversity-aware exploration (MMR) drops focus by 3.99 points (Table 3).
Pause frequency falls from a median of about 10 pauses at C0=0.0 to about 3 pauses at C0=0.7 (matching the tolerance budget) and fewer than 2 at C0≥0.8, with alignment peaking near C0=0.7 (Figure 2).

S7lpdz7NAW.text: On the Qwen3-8B backbone, MA-RAG-ext reaches 62.2% average accuracy across 7 medical QA benchmarks versus 55.4% for the backbone alone, a +6.8 point improvement (Table 1).
MA-RAG-ext outperforms the strongest RAG baseline (TC-RAG at 56.9%) by +5.3 points and inference-time scaling baselines Self-Consistency (56.7%) and Multi-Refine (58.7%) (Table 1, Figure 3).
On MedXpertQA specifically, MA-RAG-ext improves accuracy by +6.1 points to 22.2%, described as a 37% relative improvement over baselines (Table 1).
Progressive ablation shows the Retrieval Agent adds +1.9 points and the Ranking Agent adds a further +1.6 points on top of Multi-Refine, reaching the full 62.2% MA-RAG accuracy (Table 2).
Scaling to a Qwen3-32B backbone, MA-RAG improves accuracy from 64.7% to 70.2%, a +5.5 point average gain (Table 4).
Test-time scaling analysis shows accuracy rises from 57.5% at T=1 refinement round to 61.5% at T=2 rounds, saturating around 62.1-62.2% by T=4-8 rounds (Table 3).

3LA6VvtC22.text: MILCCI (Multi-Integration of Labels across Categories for Component Identification) decomposes multi-trial temporal data into interpretable sparse components while integrating metadata spanning multiple categories, using a three-stage model-fitting procedure (Section 3, Figure 1)

On synthetic benchmarks, MILCCI recovers ground-truth components and per-trial traces with higher correlation than Tucker, PARAFAC, non-negative PARAFAC, SVD, SiBBlInGS, and sliceTCA (Section 4, Figure 2)
MILCCI is applied to a US voting dataset spanning 51 states, 23 years, and 3 parties/offices to identify voting-pattern components by party and office (Section 4, Figure 3, Table 3)
MILCCI is applied to Wikipedia pageview data covering 32 pages over 1482 days across 3 conditions (agent, platform, language) to extract interpretable temporal components (Section 4, Figure 4)
MILCCI identifies neural ensembles from multi-region brain recordings comprising 1011 trials and 270 neurons with 137 timepoints each (Section 4, Figure 5)

UCLLoBmv6s.text: The proposed network unrolls an ADMM-based optimization over a mixed graph (undirected spatial graph plus directed temporal graph) into a feed-forward architecture with periodically inserted graph-learning modules resembling self-attention (Section 4, Figure 3)
The unrolled model uses only 34,096 parameters versus 531,165 for PDFormer, i.e., about 6.4% of PDFormer's parameter count, while remaining competitive on forecasting accuracy (Table 2)
On PEMS-BAY at a 60-minute horizon, the model achieves RMSE 4.60, MAE 2.03, and MAPE 4.79% (Table 1)
On METR-LA at a 60-minute horizon, the model achieves RMSE 12.37, MAE 5.27, and MAPE 11.91% (Table 1)

An ablation study compares variants without directed graph total variation (w/o DGTV) and without directed graph Laplacian regularization (w/o DGLR) against the full mixed-graph model, showing both graph terms contribute to performance (Section 5.3, Table 3)

jiNw5AgBbw.text: Tool-Guard defends LLM agents against cross-tool description poisoning—where a poisoned tool's description can bias agent behavior even when that tool is never invoked—via isolated planning that dynamically partitions tools and validates actions before execution (Section 4, Figure 3)
On adaptive/semantic attacks, Tool-Guard keeps attack success rate near 0%, compared to non-negligible ASR for competing defenses (Table 4)
Across stability tests, Tool-Guard maintains attack success rates between 0.40% and 1.54% (Table 3)
Tool-Guard incurs 1.22M-2.24M tokens of overhead versus 0.84M-1.61M tokens for the no-defense baseline, roughly 1.45x token overhead (Table 1)
Tool-Guard's isolation mechanism is shown to be necessary via an ablation study, and it is evaluated against five existing defenses on the AgentDojo and ASB benchmarks (Section 5, Figure 2, Table 6)

MF39WUbcmx.text: A synthetic testbed combines a statistical token stream and a factual token stream to study how pretraining diversity affects in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization in a 4-layer, 4-head, 32-dimensional Transformer (Section 2, Figure 1)

Higher contextual diversity delays in-distribution factual accuracy, but its effect on out-of-distribution generalization depends critically on the contextual structure used during pretraining (Section 3.1-3.2, Figure 2)

With low diversity (DIV <= 0.2), out-of-distribution factual recall fails in most contextual structures, while the diversity level that optimizes learning depends on training duration (Section 3.2-3.3, Figure 3)

The optimization bottleneck under certain contextual structures is localized via last-layer feature probing and module-wise interventions, pinpointing which components limit factual generalization (Section 4, Figures 5-6)

Experiments use 10 templates, 100 facts, sequence length 50, generic vocabulary size 3, diversity DIV in [0.1, 0.9], and training for 30,000 iterations with batch size 64 and learning rate 1e-3 (Section 2, Table 1)

1CQZbl24wp.text: A selective code generation framework learns confidence-based rejection thresholds so a large code model can abstain from low-confidence generations, using functional correctness evaluated by generated unit tests as the selection signal (Section 3)

The FuzzEval paradigm uses model-generated unit tests to evaluate functional correctness of generated code, enabling more precise selective-generation decisions than surface-level similarity metrics (Section 3, Section 4.2)

Coverage-accuracy trade-off curves show that abstaining from a fraction of low-confidence generations increases functional-correctness accuracy on the retained (covered) predictions (Section 4.3, Figure 2)
The method is evaluated on HumanEval and MBPP-style benchmarks across multiple code models, compared against confidence-based rejection baselines (Section 4.2-4.3, Table 3, Figure 3)
Statistical comparisons of selective generation against baselines are reported across coverage levels, quantifying significance of the accuracy improvements (Section 4.6, Tables 10-11)

vMwlcLyI4b.text: Defines critical KV cache selection as minimizing the L1 output perturbation ||o - ô||₁ between the full-cache and selected-cache attention outputs, rather than relying on attention weight alone (Definition 3.1, Theorem 3.3).

Proposes a two-stage greedy selection algorithm where Stage 1 allocates 25% of the eviction budget to high-attention-weight entries and Stage 2 allocates the remainder using attention weight times projected value-state norm (Algorithm 1, Section 3.4).
Integrates the critical-cache criterion into SnapKV and AdaKV via a plug-in procedure (Algorithm 2, Section 3.6).

On Needle-in-a-Haystack multi-retrieval with Mistral-7B-Instruct, improves score from 84.5 to 95.5 at 20% cache budget when combined with SnapKV, and yields up to 4.41x improvement under context-only compression (Section 4.4).
On LongBench with Llama-3.1-8B under context-only compression with AdaKV at 20% cache budget, reduces the accuracy loss relative to full cache from 13% to 11% (Section 4.5, Table 1).
Reduces head-wise output perturbation in 92%-95% of attention heads on Llama, with improvements accumulating progressively across layers (Section 4.6, Figures 5-7).

DzvMz3I5HV.text: Introduces block-wise prefill combined with episodic conversation clustering (K-Means with E=4 episodes on 4-utterance windows embedded via Qwen3-0.6B) instead of post-prefill token eviction (Algorithm 1, Section 3).
Allocates per-layer KV memory budget inversely proportional to a measured layer sensitivity score, with sharpness parameter alpha=1.1 for LLaMA and alpha=1.3 for Qwen (Section 3.2, Figure 4).
Improves accuracy by up to 40% over baselines (StreamingLLM, SnapKV, InfiniPot, KVzip, KeyDiff) under tight memory budgets on LongMemEval, RealTalk, and LoCoMo (Figure 5).
Sustains near-full-cache accuracy under 4-6x KV cache compression across LLaMA-3.2-3B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Qwen2.5-7B (Figure 5).
On LLaMA-3.2-3B, reduces decoding latency from 68.9ms to 28.1ms (2.4x) and reduces peak GPU memory from 28.4GB to 8.2GB (3.5x) (Section 4, Figure 7).

Query embedding and episode-matching overhead adds less than 5% to per-turn latency, e.g., 6.1ms embedding plus 2.0ms retrieval versus 28.1ms decoding on LLaMA-3.2-3B at a 2K token budget (Figure 7, Table A1).

Ym1zKxtv8V.text: BREW achieves TPR of 0.965 with FPR of 0.02 under 10% synonym substitution, whereas prior ECC-based multi-bit watermarking methods exceed FPR of 0.9 under the same attack (Section 4, Table 6/related results).
In clean (no-attack) conditions at T=200 tokens and detection threshold delta=3.0, BREW attains TPR=0.987 with FPR=0.013, versus a naive decoding baseline with TPR=1.000 but FPR=0.499 (Table 4).

Ablation shows the full two-stage BREW design (blind block-voting estimation plus window-shifting verification) outperforms either component alone under 10% token-insertion attacks: designated-verification-only gives FPR=0.005 but TPR=0.355, shift-only gives TPR=0.725/FPR=0.140, while full BREW gives TPR=0.815/FPR=0.110 (Table 6).
Selects BCH code parameters (31,6,7) as the default configuration, balancing TPR≈0.93 and FPR≈0.085 at 10% insertion rate compared to (15,5,3) and (63,7,15) alternatives (Table 3).

Argues via a designated-verification detection bound that aggregate false positive rate decays exponentially with block count through a Chernoff-style bound with exponent D(theta||p0), supporting that high FPR is a solvable structural flaw of decoding-centric designs rather than an inherent trade-off (Section 4).
Detection remains computationally practical, requiring 0.168 seconds for T=200 tokens (n=31, smax=5) and 0.534 seconds for T=500 tokens (n=63, smax=5) (Table 7).
