BC5aRMdRwp.text: Replaces Muon's Newton-Schulz iteration with a row-wise (d_in) L2 normalization operation, motivated by empirically observed diagonal block structure in the Transformer layerwise Hessian (Section 3.1).
Reduces per-iteration preconditioning complexity from O(mn*min(m,n)) for Muon to O(mn) for an m x n weight matrix (Section 3.1-3.2).
Measured preconditioning time over 100 steps drops from 2.98s to 0.20s (14.8x speedup) on GPT-2 125M and from 27.07s to 0.61s (44.3x speedup) on GPT-2 770M, relative to Muon (Section 4.3).
Achieves comparable or better perplexity than Muon on GPT-2/OpenWebText pretraining, improving by 0.04 (125M), 0.07 (355M), and 0.24 (770M) (Section 4.3).
On LLaMA models trained on C4, achieves perplexity improvements over Muon of 0.63 (60M) and 0.28 (135M), with negligible difference (0.02) at 350M (Section 4.3).
Establishes non-convex convergence guarantees (Theorems 5.5, 5.7, 5.9) under Frobenius and mixed-norm smoothness that match Muon's best-known minimax-optimal complexity (Section 5, Table 4).

GfSwkDSr8J.text: Introduces Dual Action Representation combining discrete and continuous action encodings for responsive keyboard/mouse control, reducing action-following error to R_dist=0.028 and T_dist=0.113 versus discrete-only (R_dist=0.103, T_dist=0.615) or continuous-only (R_dist=0.038, T_dist=0.287) variants (Table 3).
Introduces Reconstituted Context Memory with a temporally-reframed RoPE scheme that reduces long-term LPIPS from 0.534 (standard RoPE) to 0.495 (reframed RoPE) (Table 4).

Context Forcing distillation synchronizes memory between teacher and student networks to preserve long-range information use while enabling real-time inference speed and preventing autoregressive error drift (Section on distillation method).

Generates long-horizon streaming interactive video at 720p and 24 FPS, achieving short-term (61 frames) PSNR=21.92/SSIM=0.702/LPIPS=0.247 and long-term (>=250 frames) PSNR=18.94/SSIM=0.585/LPIPS=0.371 (Table 2).

Outperforms memory-free baselines (CameraCtrl, SEVA, ViewCrafter, Matrix-Game-2.0, GameCraft) in long-term consistency and outperforms memory-based baselines (Gen3C, VMem) in real-time speed while matching their consistency (Table 2).
In a user study of 30 assessors across 600 test cases, WorldPlay is preferred over baselines on visual quality, control accuracy, and long-term consistency (Figure 15).

fG4nXq9Ytm.text: OLion computes updates via a 'sign-after-orthogonalization' rule—applying entrywise Sign to the SVD-orthogonalized momentum—to approximate the intersection of spectral and l-infinity constraint sets (Section 4.1, Algorithm 1).

On GPT-2 pretraining at Small (124M), Medium (355M), and Large (770M) scales trained on 48B tokens of OpenWebText, OLion converges faster than AdamW, Lion, and Muon at all three sizes (Section 5.1, Figure 3a-c).
On Llama-2-7B pretraining with 32B tokens and batch size 4M, OLion maintains consistently lower training loss throughout than Muon, Lion, and AdamW (Section 5.1, Figure 4a-b).

Fine-tuning AdamW-pretrained Llama-3.1-8B checkpoints, OLion attains the best downstream accuracy across GSM8K, MATH, NumGLUE, SimulEq, and Aqua, including 60.04% vs. AdamW's 57.99% on GSM8K 0-shot (Table 1).
OLion satisfies a Diagonal-Isotropy assumption (Assumption 4.2) and achieves an O(1/√T) convergence rate via a geometry-aware stationarity measure (Theorem 4.4, Section 4.2).

OLion simultaneously keeps both spectral norm and l-infinity norm small relative to AdamW (small l-infinity only) and Muon (small spectral norm only), evidencing intersection-of-constraints implicit bias (Figure 2a-d).

odLc0zNtyX.text: GCOS synthesizes virtual outliers along low-variance principal components identified via PCA on in-distribution features, bounding outlier magnitude with a 'conformal shell' set between the 95th and 99th percentile Mahalanobis distance thresholds (Section 3).

On four near-OOD benchmarks—Colored MNIST, MVTec AD, Stanford Dogs, and Retinopathy—GCOS achieves an average AUROC of 93.47%, beating VOS (86.21%), Dream-OOD (85.76%), and NCIS (91.97%) (Table 1, Section 5.2).

GCOS attains near-perfect near-OOD detection on Colored MNIST (99.50% AUROC, 1.00% FPR95) and Stanford Dogs (99.55% AUROC, 0.00% FPR95), but weaker performance on the harder Retinopathy benchmark (79.23% AUROC, 73.00% FPR95) (Table 1, Section 5.2).

GCOS extends to conformal OOD inference by converting nonconformity scores into calibration-based p-values (Equation 7), yielding formally valid error guarantees, with 1.5% FPR95 on Colored MNIST under Mahalanobis regularization (Table 2, Section 6).

UMAP visualizations show GCOS-synthesized outliers cluster in off-manifold regions on opposite sides of nearby classes, unlike VOS outliers which remain near decision boundaries between clusters (Figure 2, Section 5.2).
Across 5 random seeds, GCOS shows low-variance, reproducible results, with AUPR varying by only ±0.02-0.39% (Table 8, Appendix E.2).

qK2yxjJJCh.text: The method trains a physics-informed neural network to approximate the log heat kernel by solving the heat equation directly in chosen global coordinates, initialized from short-time asymptotics, avoiding reliance on closed-form heat kernel expressions (Section 4).

Explicit heat equations are derived for the sphere S² (Equation 25), for SO(3) modeled as the S³/{±I} quotient (Equation 26), for SPD(n) via log-eigenvalue coordinates (Equation 27), and for permutation-quotiented point clouds ℝ^{k×n}/S_n (Equation 29).

Theorem 4.1 proves a stability result: bounded pointwise error in the PINN's initial condition at time t0 propagates to a comparably bounded error in the approximated heat kernel at all later times t ≥ t0.

On S² geolocation benchmarks, the method outperforms the RSGM baseline on volcanoes (3.56 vs. 3.51), earthquakes (0.24 vs. 0.10), and wildfires (1.08 vs. 1.03), with a slightly worse result on floods (-0.47 vs. -0.53) (Table 3).
On SPD(10) traffic data, the method achieves a mean Frobenius distance of 5.21±0.12, improving over SPD-DDPM's 6.15±0.12 (Table 4).

On QM9 molecule generation (permutation-quotiented point clouds), the method achieves 98.63% stability and 99.60% validity versus EDM's 95.20% and 98.13%, at the cost of lower novelty (41.70% vs. 63.30%) (Table 7).

5i888dLp8N.text: SOMA builds persistent spatial memory from head-camera scanning by fusing YOLO-World object detections, DINOv3 appearance features, and VGGT geometric priors, then retrieves task-relevant regions via cross-attention with instruction-grounded embeddings (Section 3).

SOMA is evaluated on five real-world out-of-vision manipulation tasks—Invisible-to-Invisible PnP, Visible-to-Invisible PnP, Invisible-to-Visible PnP, Sequential Dual-Object PnP, and Dual-Arm Coordination PnP—achieving the highest success rate on all five, with the largest margins on the multi-stage and dual-arm tasks (Section 4.1, Figure 3, Figure 4).

Compared to GR00T N1.5, StarVLA, SpatialVLA, and Diffusion Policy baselines, SOMA reduces first-fixation time, head search path length, and grasp attempt count by roughly 40-59% across tasks, indicating near one-shot grasping under partial observability (Table 1).
An ablation shows full SOMA reaches 28.3% success versus 18.5% for a Scan+GR00T variant, indicating that persistent spatial memory—not scanning alone—drives the performance gain (Table 2).

In simulation, SOMA attains 52.0% average success on RoboCasa GR1 with the full dataset (Table 3) and 63.2% success on SimplerEnv Visual Matching tasks, outperforming other SimplerEnv SOTA baselines (Table 4a).

k0VozzvIqL.text: Privasis is a fully synthetic dataset of 1.4 million records containing approximately 55.1 million annotated attributes (about 39 per record), spanning medical, legal, financial, calendar, and text-message document types (Section on Dataset Overview / Key Statistics).
Privasis records average 527 words each and are organized into roughly 6.2 attribute clusters per record, with Health & Wellness the largest domain at 20.7% of records.

Privasis-Cleaner-4B, trained on a 37K-example parallel corpus derived from Privasis, achieves 72.50% full success rate on the vanilla sanitization test set, exceeding GPT-5 (70.06%), o3 (70.25%), and Qwen3-235B (64.40%).
On a harder evaluation set, all sanitization models drop to 10-13% full success rate, with Privasis-Cleaner-4B at 12.36% versus GPT-5's 13.14%, narrowing but not eliminating the gap to frontier LLMs.
Human evaluation judged 113 of 128 Privasis records as natural and coherent, indicating synthetic record quality comparable to human-written data.

cyIUoRizkW.text: RS-CL improves the average success rate on the RoboCasa-Kitchen benchmark from 65.7% to 69.7% when trained with 300 demonstrations (Table 1).
On RoboCasa-Kitchen with only 30 demonstrations, RS-CL improves the pick-and-place task success rate from 30.8% to 41.5% (Table 1).
On real-robot manipulation, RS-CL boosts the in-domain pick-and-place success rate from 45.0% to 58.3% (Figure 5).
On the LIBERO benchmark, RS-CL improves overall average success rate from 95.7% to 96.4% across all four task suites (Table 2).
An ablation shows that using current-state distance as supervision for the contrastive loss reaches 69.7% versus 67.3% for standard InfoNCE without robot state (Table 3).
RS-CL applied to GR00T N1.5 (69.7%) outperforms prior VLA baselines π0 (62.5%), π0-FAST (63.6%), and GR00T N1 (49.6%) on RoboCasa-Kitchen with 300 demos (Section 4, baseline comparison).

FZroB6jcpN.text: VideoLoom's LoomData-8.7k dataset contains 8,710 shots derived from ActivityNet videos, with an average video duration of 102.2 seconds and 6.0 shots per video, produced via a four-stage annotation pipeline (Section 3.1, Figure 1).
VideoLoom achieves 48.3 R1@0.7 on Charades-STA temporal grounding and 63.3 HIT@1 on QVHighlights (Table 1).
VideoLoom achieves 51.7 J&F on MeVIS, 71.3 J&F on Ref-YouTube-VOS, and 63.1 J&F on ReVOS for spatial (referring) segmentation (Table 2).
VideoLoom attains 83.4 cIoU on RefCOCO, 79.2 cIoU on RefCOCO+, and 81.4 cIoU on RefCOCOg for image-level referring segmentation (Table 3).
On the newly introduced LoomBench (130 videos, 1,400+ QA pairs spanning When/Where/Combined question types), VideoLoom scores 41.6 tIoU and 49.1 J&F_bi-fore on Combined questions (Table 4, Figure 3).
VideoLoom's architecture combines an MLLM with SAM2 using a SlowFast token design to jointly handle spatial and temporal grounding (Section 3.2, Figure 2).

u0ZWIJ7x1F.text: Theorem 1 proves that for parameter learning with finite-difference discretization, the relative parameter error scales as |w−k|/|k| = μₑΔx^q + Σμₘ Δx^m when the polynomial order p of the training data satisfies p≥q (Section 3.2, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows that for linear models, learned weights converge to W* = AUUᵀ + W⁰(I−UUᵀ), i.e., a projection onto the training-data subspace plus an unconstrained complement, proving out-of-distribution generalization is not guaranteed by training error alone (Section 3.3, Theorem 2).
Empirical experiments demonstrate that different model classes exhibit opposing out-of-distribution generalization behavior despite achieving similarly low training error (Section 4.2).
The paper extracts Green's functions from trained black-box models to interpret what function space the models have effectively learned (Section 4.3).
Convergence rates for parameter learning are shown to depend jointly on grid spacing Δx, the finite-difference stencil order, and the polynomial complexity of the training-data basis (Section 3.2).

VoqRpteakw.text: FedDTL decouples the federated vision-language model into a locally-trained image encoder and a server-side text encoder, aggregated via weighted averaging (Section 3.2, 3.4, Equation 12).
FedDTL uses a two-stage local fine-tuning scheme combining supervised fine-tuning followed by a GRPO-inspired reinforcement-learning stage (Section 3.3).

Under few-shot Non-IID Dirichlet(0.1) partitioning, FedDTL achieves 91.66% base-class and 82.64% novel-class accuracy in base-to-novel generalization, outperforming baselines pFedDC, FedPGP, pFedMMA, PromptFL, and FedMaPLe (Table 1).
Under full-data Dirichlet(0.1) partitioning, FedDTL reaches 92.69% base-class and 76.59% novel-class accuracy (Table 1).
On feature-shift settings, FedDTL attains 98.33% accuracy on few-shot one-domain Office-Caltech10 and 93.47% accuracy on full-data Dirichlet(0.1) DomainNet (Table 2).

An ablation across 7 datasets shows the decoupled encoder alone contributes a 28.57% improvement in base-class accuracy under the full Non-IID setting, and combining SFT with RL outperforms either stage alone across communication rounds (Table 3, Figure 2).

QmiKRq3e4N.text: ASTRA achieves up to 2.64× speedup over single-device Transformer inference latency (Section 4.3, Figures 1, 3-5).
ASTRA achieves up to 15.25× speedup over prior state-of-the-art multi-device inference baselines (Section 4.3, Table 4).
ASTRA's Mixed-Precision Attention mechanism reduces bandwidth requirements from 500 Mbps to 10 Mbps while maintaining a speedup of 1.26-2.65× at 10 Mbps (Section 3.2, Equation 1; Figure 1).

Noise-Augmented Vector Quantization (NAVQ) achieves up to a 2457.6× compression ratio while keeping accuracy within 3.58% of the original model, improving accuracy by up to 0.86% over naive quantization (Section 3.3, Theorems 1-2; Table 1).
Distributed Class Tokens enhance accuracy by up to 7.13% compared to the non-distributed baseline (Section 4.4, Tables 5-6).
ASTRA is evaluated on ViT-Base for CIFAR-100/ImageNet-1K classification accuracy and on GPT-2 perplexity over Wikipedia and WikiText-103 (Section 4.2, Tables 1 and 3).

F5ULzUwZrv.text: Olivia harmonizes cross-dataset heterogeneity by learning orthogonal transformations (via Householder reflections) that align normalized power spectral densities before feeding series into the backbone (Section on Harmonizer).
Olivia's zero-shot forecasts on the TSLib benchmark reduce MSE by 26.3% and MAE by 14.6% relative to Time-MoE (Zero-Shot Performance / TSLib results).
On GluonTS datasets, Olivia reduces NRMSE by 11.6% on solar_nips and by 32.0% NRMSE / 30.7% SMAPE on elecdemand relative to SEMPO (GluonTS results table).

HarmonicAttention models global token interactions through a low-dimensional resonator space with O(LMP + M^2P) complexity, replacing the O(L^2P) cost of full attention (Section on HarmonicFormer/HarmonicAttention).

Olivia's full model has 5.1M parameters, the most compact among compared foundation models, while an ablation removing the Harmonizer degrades zero-shot accuracy across prediction horizons (Efficiency comparison; Ablation study, Figure 4).

xEpcZDAxdW.text: RL-SPH is a reinforcement-learning-based start primal heuristic that independently generates feasible solutions for integer linear programs, including those with non-binary integer variables (abstract only).
RL-SPH achieves a 100% feasibility rate across the tested ILP instances (abstract only).
RL-SPH attains on average a 28.6x lower primal gap than existing start primal heuristics (abstract only).
RL-SPH attains on average a 2.6x lower primal integral than existing start primal heuristic baselines (abstract only).

RL-SPH is evaluated against learned heuristic approaches (e.g., PAS-style methods) and classical solvers on MIPLIB and synthetic/real-world ILP instances, with ablation studies examining individual component contributions (abstract only).

A3920YD7ue.text: Under the STAR state-oriented role-playing multi-turn evaluation framework, safety failure rates reach 94.5% for GPT-4o, 74.0% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 96.1% for Gemini 2.0-Flash, 89.0% for LLaMA-3-8B-IT, and 85.5% for LLaMA-3-70B-IT (Table 1).
STAR outperforms multi-turn jailbreak baselines including X-Teaming and ActorAttack across most evaluated models (Table 1).

Ablating STAR's history accumulation component reduces the induced safety failure rate by 25.5 percentage points, the largest drop among tested components, versus 19.7 points for adaptive recovery, 17.8 points for role initialization, and 14.7 points for momentum feedback (Figure 2, ablation study).

Analysis of refusal-direction projections shows a monotonic decay from 2.35 at the original prompt to -0.0081 by the third dialogue turn, indicating a phase transition away from refusal-related representations (Interpretability / refusal direction dynamics section).
STAR is evaluated on 50 HarmBench instructions and 100 manually verified JailbreakBench instructions (Datasets section).

quqoVYpzX3.text: GR3 rescales rewards multiplicatively as R̂(x,y) = R(x,y) × 1/(1+α·ℓ/ℓ̄), where ℓ is the response length and ℓ̄ the group-average length, rather than applying an additive length penalty (Equation 6).

Proposition 3.1 shows additive length shaping injects a fixed-coefficient length signal that enables compensatory optimization shortcuts, while Proposition 3.2 shows multiplicative shaping makes the length penalty reward-weighted and automatically strengthened by task success (Propositions 3.1, 3.2).

On 7B models, GR3 improves AIME24 accuracy from 52.4 to 60.1 while cutting average response length from 13,213 to 7,923 tokens, and improves AIME25 accuracy from 39.4 to 46.9 while cutting length from 14,032 to 8,582 tokens, compared to standard GRPO (Mathematical Reasoning results).

On Qwen3-8B RLHF alignment, GR3 raises Arena-Hard-Auto score from 77.2 to 92.8 with negligible token-count change (1,171 to 1,178), and raises AlpacaEval score from 50.2 to 55.8 while reducing tokens from 778 to 765 (RLHF Alignment results).
On LiveCodeBench, GR3 improves the 7B model score from 37.7 to 41.6 alongside a 29% reduction in output tokens relative to standard GRPO (Code Generation results).

0nrxgFZEEq.text: Theorem 1 establishes an impossibility result: without knowledge of the prediction error, no algorithm can achieve discounted-MDP sample complexity better than Õ((1-γ)^-3 N ε^-2), matching prediction-free lower bounds (Theorem 1).

The proposed Optimistic-Predict Mirror Descent (OpPMD) algorithm reformulates the discounted MDP as a minimax optimization problem over Bellman-equation constraints and combines stochastic gradient estimators with predicted gradients derived from a prediction matrix P̂ (Algorithm 1, Equation 4).
OpPMD uses parameter-free learning rates that avoid dependence on the target accuracy ε or the (unknown) prediction error (Equations 7 and 9).

Theorem 2 shows OpPMD achieves sample complexity uniformly better than the prior Õ((1-γ)^-4 N ε^-2) bound, with component complexities T_v = (1-γ)^-4|S|ε^-2, T_{μ,1} = (1-γ)^-4 N min{1, Dist^2} ε^-2, and T_{μ,2} = (1-γ)^-2 N ε^-1 (Theorem 2).

The prediction error is measured via Dist(P,P̂) = max_(i,a) Σ_j |p̂(j|i,a) − p(j|i,a)|, and when Dist^2 ≤ O((1-γ)^2 ε) the algorithm attains its best possible sample-complexity improvement (Problem Formulation section).

AjP1yvCyoG.text: XSkill maintains two complementary knowledge stores extracted in a training-free Phase I (Accumulation): visually-grounded rollout summaries and cross-rollout critiques of successful versus failed trajectories, later consolidated hierarchically to reduce redundancy (Section on Architecture/Phase I).

Across five benchmarks (VisualToolBench, TIR-Bench, MMSearch-Plus, MMBrowseComp, and AgentVista) and four backbone models, XSkill yields average improvements of 2.58 to 6.71 points over tool-only baselines, with a maximum single-benchmark improvement of 11.13 points on challenging visual reasoning tasks (Evaluation section, Performance Results).

XSkill is compared against Agent Workflow Memory, Dynamic CheatSheet, and Agent-KB baselines, with the proposed method winning consistently, particularly on tasks requiring complex visual reasoning and multi-step tool composition (Evaluation section).

Ablation-style analysis shows the 'skills' stream reduces structural/syntax errors from 20.3% to 11.4% via tool templates and workflow guidance, while the 'experiences' stream shifts tool-usage patterns contextually, e.g., code-interpreter usage rising from 66.63% to 76.97% on visual tasks (Methodology Insights section).

XSkill's Phase II (Inference) applies retrieved knowledge through task decomposition into subtasks, context-aware visual adaptation of retrieved knowledge, and non-prescriptive injection that preserves agent flexibility (Architecture, Phase II section).

wSXZtvqwoa.text: The proposed attentive probe fuses CLS tokens and average-pooled patch representations from intermediate Vision Transformer layers via multi-head cross-attention, rather than using only final-layer features (Core Contribution section).

Across 20 diverse datasets and nine ViT variants spanning three families (supervised ViT-S/B/L-16 on ImageNet-21K, self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/B/L-14, and image-text CLIP ViT-B-32/16 and ViT-L-14), the attentive-layer-fusion probe achieves an average accuracy improvement of 5.54 percentage points over standard linear probes (Key Results, Experimental Scope sections).

Specialized-domain datasets show some of the largest gains, including +6.86 percentage points on Diabetic Retinopathy (medical imaging) and +5.23 percentage points on RESISC45 (satellite imagery), while fine-grained classification datasets such as Stanford Cars, FGVC Aircraft, GTSRB, and SVHN show 6-30 percentage-point improvements (Key Results section).

The method reduces computational complexity from O(P²) for patch-level attention (200+ patches) to O(|ℒ|²) for layer-level attention (24 layer representations), while remaining parameter-efficient independent of the number of layers (Methodological Advantages section).

Attention-weight visualizations (heatmaps) reveal that natural-image tasks concentrate weight on final-layer CLS tokens, whereas specialized domains like medical and satellite imagery emphasize intermediate-layer average-pooled representations, and tasks diverging most from the pretraining domain use the broadest range of layers (Analysis Findings section).

IXsOS3hF8Y.text: GILC corrects clean-prediction logits of a pretrained discrete diffusion denoiser rather than computing unstable gradients through the discrete input space, treating the pretrained denoising network as a variational proxy for the value function (Core Method section).

Two GILC variants are introduced: GILC-DB, using Gumbel-Softmax and Straight-Through estimators for differentiable rewards, and GILC-PG, using a policy-gradient formulation for non-differentiable objectives (Core Method section).

On DNA sequence design (Table 1), GILC-DB achieves a predicted activity of 7.04 versus 5.61 for DRAKES and an ATAC accuracy of 95.2% versus 92.5% for DRAKES, outperforming training-free baselines such as SMC and SVDD (Table 1).
On protein stability optimization (Table 3), GILC-DB attains an overall success rate of 82.4% versus 78.6% for DRAKES, and the best Pred-ddG (1.430) among all compared methods (Table 3).
On molecular property generation (Table 4), GILC-PG achieves the best mean absolute error on 5 of 6 quantum properties, consistently outperforming TFG-Flow and SVDD (Table 4).

GILC is computationally cheaper than sampling-based guidance methods, requiring only 1 diffusion-model call per step and 5 reward evaluations for GILC-DB, versus 20 diffusion calls and 20 reward evaluations for SMC/SVDD (Table 2).

yv1iRquxF9.text: Theorem 3.3 establishes that a single DAG-style MoE layer can simulate dynamic-programming solutions, approximating multi-step algorithmic reasoning that a constant-depth standard MoE layer cannot achieve (Theorem 3.3).

The DAG learning module is most effective at depth L=1-2 with hidden dimension dg between 64 and 256; DAG-MoE-s configured with dg=64, L=2 outperforms a dg=128, L=1 configuration despite having fewer parameters (Architecture Design / Ablations section).

At 40B-token scale, DAG-MoE-l reaches 10.27 perplexity on Pile versus 10.51 for the parameter-matched baseline, and 24.69 versus 25.38 on the out-of-domain FineWeb-Edu set (Experimental Results, Scale subsection).

On downstream fine-tuning across 7 benchmarks, DAG-MoE achieves 26.13% average accuracy versus 24.06% for the baseline, with the largest gains on GPQA (+6.06), Lambada (+3.46), and PIQA (+3.15) (Fine-tuning Results section).

Compared to the Chain-of-Experts baseline at matched parameter counts, DAG-MoE achieves a 0.587 perplexity reduction versus 0.480 for Chain-of-Experts, while training overhead is only 1.51% at L=1 and 4.49% at L=2 (Ablations, Computational Efficiency sections).

Replacing the learned DAG structure with unconstrained MLP mixing of expert outputs degrades performance below the standard MoE baseline despite using more parameters, confirming the DAG structure itself (not just added parameters) drives the gains (Ablations section).

7p6vIkXOxQ.text: The Transport-and-Merge framework transfers knowledge across heterogeneous LLM architectures in three stages: activation alignment via optimal transport on a small calibration dataset, conversion of activation-space correspondences into weight-space fusion operations, and optional residual-frozen fine-tuning that keeps transferred parameters fixed (Core Method section).

Theorem 4.1 establishes that the weight-transport operation is equivalent to mapping target features into source coordinates, applying the source model's computation, and mapping the result back to the target's coordinate space (Theorem 4.1).

The method uses two-level optimal transport: feature-level OT solves correspondence matrices Qℓm between target and source layers, and layer-level OT computes global mixing weights P, combined with top-k neuron replacement to restrict fusion to highly activated neurons and limit interference (Key Technical Contributions section).

On low-resource language transfer, the method yields +6.51% on MalayMMLU humanities and +5.99% on MalayMMLU social science, +2.18% absolute gain on Cantonese CMMLU, +0.87% average improvement on Indonesian benchmarks, and +0.09 average score improvement on Thai (Experimental Results, Low-Resource Language Transfer section).
Ablations show gains scale with source-model size across 1B, 8B, and 32B source models, and a fusion coefficient α in the 0.05-0.15 range performs best (Ablations section).

Figure 1 shows the adapted fusion approach consistently outperforms both supervised fine-tuning and knowledge distillation baselines across normalized domain metrics, while knowledge distillation exhibits domain-dependent variability (Figure 1).

joReaAnwnH.text: The Extended Linear Regression Model achieves a Mean Relative Error of 1.533% fitting the multi-domain loss landscape, versus 2.209% for the Additive baseline and 6.990% for the Exponential baseline (Table 2).

For K=17 domains, the Extended Linear Regression Model uses roughly 5K parameters (about 85 for K=17) compared to K(2K+1) parameters for the Additive Law baseline and K^2 parameters for RegMix, while still achieving lower fitting error (Table 2).

Capacity Competition, formalized via the capacity constraint sum(x_i - H) <= N - H, couples domain losses globally so that each domain's loss depends on the weights and complexities of every competing domain (Section 4.2).

Noise Reduction, captured by the noise term A_i(D h_i)^{-a_i}, breaks symmetry among domains and shifts optimal mixture weights toward domains that are harder to learn, i.e., those with larger A_i or smaller alpha_i (Section 4).

Parameters fit only on small-scale runs (122M model, 10B tokens) successfully predict the optimal mixture at a much larger unseen scale (1B model, 30B tokens), matching the test loss of a state-of-the-art empirical baseline that was fit across a wider range of scales including the target size (Section 5.4).
On the 17-domain Pile dataset, models trained with the predicted optimal mixture achieve lower validation loss than those using existing scaling-law-derived mixtures (Figure 5).

qvvD9hgHoX.text: Persona2Web comprises 50 user profiles with roughly 2,000 history entries per user spanning one year across 21 domains and 105 accessible websites (Section 3).

Queries are constructed at three ambiguity levels—Level 0 explicit, Level 1 masked website, Level 2 both masked—operationalizing the clarify-to-personalize principle that agents must infer preferences from user history rather than explicit instructions (Section 3.2, Table 2).
Without access to user history, all evaluated agent-backbone combinations achieve a 0% success rate on ambiguous (ID clarify-to-personalize) queries (Section 5.3).
With history access, the best configuration—Browser-Use with GPT-4.1 using an on-demand retrieval scheme—reaches only a 13% success rate (Table 3).
Average success rate degrades from 23.8% at Level 0 (clear queries) to 16.3% at Level 1 to 7.8% at Level 2 (fully ambiguous) queries (Figure 3).
Error analysis identifies four dominant failure modes—redundant history access, hallucination, retrieval failure, and utilization failure—with retrieval failure being the most prevalent (Section 6).

fmwNYkYRN6.text: ToolPro's constraint-guided construction pipeline synthesizes tool-intent programs client-side, projects them server-side into a constrained interface-program surface via Π(·), and applies compile-and-repair with safe fallback (Section 3.2).

Effect-aware replay maintains a history log H of completed WRITE calls and a working log W for the current execution, forwarding READ calls immediately while matching WRITE calls against history to prevent duplicate side effects, per Algorithm 1 and Proposition 3.1 (Section 3.3).

Profile-driven consolidation selects between program and stepwise execution modes using the decision rule ΔT = (N-1)(T_rtt_bar + T_dec_bar) - T_build_bar, which depends on network round-trip time, decision overhead, and build cost (Equation 2, Section 3.4).

ToolPro reduces end-to-end latency by up to 53.4% on cross-service workflows (cbench4, from 52.68s to 24.54s) and by 40.6% on complex realistic workflows (cbench1-3, from 30.16s to 17.91s) (Figure 3, Section 4.3).
ToolPro reduces client-side traffic by up to 96.1% on cbench4 and by up to 85.3% across the standard benchmark suite (Figure 4, Section 4.3).

Latency gains from ToolPro's program mode increase with network round-trip time, dominating over stepwise mode at 1000-2000ms RTT while stepwise mode remains competitive below 100ms RTT (Figure 5, Section 4.4).

GtpiqFaJtZ.text: RADAR quantifies structural redundancy in agent communication graphs via an incoming effective size measure phi(v_k) defined in Equation 7, combined with an outgoing counterpart using a tunable parameter beta (Section 4.1).

RADAR uses a conditional discrete graph diffusion process with an ordering network q_psi that prioritizes nodes by effective size and a denoising network p_theta that reconstructs graphs via attention-weighted message passing (Equations 11-12, Section 4.2).

Across six benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MultiArith, SVAMP, AQuA, HumanEval), RADAR achieves the highest accuracy, including 92.51% on GSM8K (+5.06 points) and 93.26% on SVAMP (+6.59 points), for an average improvement of 1.75% over the strongest baseline ARG-Designer (Table 1).
On GSM8K, RADAR consumes only 4.2×10^6 tokens, roughly half the token cost of GDesigner, while attaining the highest accuracy (Figure 3, Section 5.5).

Under a prompt-injection attack with two liar agents, RADAR shows nearly identical performance before and after the attack, whereas a complete graph baseline drops 4.47% and ARG-Designer drops 1.05% (Figure 4, Section 5.6).
Ablations show removing query conditioning causes the largest accuracy drop (4.58% on MMLU), followed by a non-diffusion baseline (4.56% drop) and removing effective size (2.61% drop) (Table 2).

EmMmxTMiGJ.text: Intrinsic Quality is defined as the convex combination IQ = alpha * c_bar + beta * r_ent_tilde with alpha=0.2 and beta=0.8, combining a local neighbor-consistency signal (Eq. 4) and a global normalized effective rank signal from spectral entropy (Eq. 8) (Section 3.6).

IQ is computed from lightweight proxy models (ResNet-50 and ResNet-100 with d=1024 embeddings) on a subsampled set of about 1,000 identities x 10 images (~10,000 samples) with within-identity deduplication (Section 4.2-4.3).
On clean-scaling datasets, IQ increases from 0.902 for WebFace4M (90.36% downstream accuracy) to 0.968 for WebFace42M (96.26% accuracy) (Table 1).
On WebFace12M with synthetic label noise, IQ drops from 0.930 at 0% noise (94.37% accuracy) to 0.875 at 40% noise (72.01% accuracy) (Table 2).

IQ achieves a Spearman correlation of 1.000 and Kendall tau of 1.000 with downstream accuracy across evaluated conditions, substantially outperforming the RankMe baseline's 0.418 Spearman correlation (Section 5.4).
IQ correctly ranks three 12M-scale dataset variants by downstream ordering, demonstrating its use for subset selection and dataset curation prior to full-scale training (Table 4).

0JDzkrKzaA.text: Theorem 3.2 gives the analogous flat-extension rank condition for the total variation (TV) distance relaxation, guaranteeing that the hierarchy stabilizes at level d and a K-atomic optimal mixing measure exists solving the epsilon-regularized TV-distance approximation problem (Theorem 3.2, Eq. 18).

On MNIST digit subsets {0,1} and {0,1,2} reduced to 2 principal components via PCA, Algorithm 1-based (SDP) initialization of k-means requires on average 7.28 and 11.6 iterations respectively, versus 100 random restarts requiring more iterations, while reaching a comparable final k-means objective of about 4.136x10^2 (digits {0,1}) and 6.734x10^2 (digits {0,1,2}) (Section 4, Figure 4).

For randomly generated Gaussian mixtures in R^2 with K=5 components, k-means initialized via the W2-based (resp. TV-based) SDP estimate requires on average 31.8% (resp. 36.5%) fewer iterations than random initialization, while EM initialized via the W2-based estimate improves by 18.63% and via the TV-based estimate by 13.91% relative to random initialization (Section 4, Figure 3).

Assembling and solving the SDP relaxation at order d=4 takes on average 0.1755s for the W2-based relaxation and 0.1506s for the TV-based relaxation, while the point-extraction step (Algorithm 1) requires only 0.00036s on average (Figure 3 caption).

WQIyx69dFg.text: WorldComp2D reduces parameter count by up to 4.0x (from 9.7M to 2.4M parameters) and FLOPs by up to 2.2x compared to the PoPos SoTA lightweight baseline, with the full breakdown across its proximity-dependent encoder (PdEnc, 1.1M params), localizer (1.3M params), and auxiliary localizer (AuxLoc, 4.0K params) modules given in Table 1.

WorldComp2D achieves real-time CPU inference on an Intel i5-13400 of 138.4 FPS on COFW, 78.48 FPS on 300W, and 163.55 FPS on AFLW, while attaining normalized mean error (NME) of 5.16 on COFW, 5.06 on 300W, and 1.52 (NME_Diag) on AFLW, competitive with but slightly behind SoTA regression methods (Table 2, Table 1).

Under degradations such as blur, JPEG compression, motion blur, and occlusion, WorldComp2D shows a maximum accuracy degradation of about 10.2% (extreme occlusion on 300W), with consistently moderate degradation across other corruption types (Table 4).

In zero-shot cross-dataset transfer from a model trained on 300W and evaluated on COFW-68, WorldComp2D's NME degrades by only 20.2%, compared to 27-32% degradation for regression-based baselines (Table 6).

WorldComp2D's latent space explicitly structures object identity and spatial proximity, exhibiting intra-class clustering by landmark class, inter-class separation between landmark identities, and latent L2 distances that correlate with real-world spatial proximity within the receptive field (Figure 5).

uuD1rE5KU5.text: Theorem 3.1 (Rate-Distortion Lower Bound) proves that the minimum per-key memory budget for membership testing in the sparse regime satisfies liminf B(M_j)/n_j >= min KL(mu_K || mu_N) over output distributions meeting the specified error constraints (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 shows that when the KL-divergence minimizer is unique, any asymptotically memory-optimal membership tester's query output distributions must converge in Wasserstein-1 distance to the theoretical optimizers (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 4.1 proves that under log-loss constraints the unique optimal probability-estimation solution assigns all facts to a single high-confidence score x* = e^{-epsilon_K}, while non-facts are distributed as mu_N* = (1-q*)delta_0 + q*delta_{x*}, so a fraction q* of non-facts receive the same score as facts — an unavoidable 'hallucination channel' (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.3 shows that for FNR/FPR-constrained binary membership classifiers, the optimal score distributions are mu_K* = Bernoulli(1-epsilon_K) and mu_N* = Bernoulli(epsilon_N), formalizing hallucination in the binary-decision setting (Theorem 4.3).

Theorem 3.3 derives a finite-support correction to the memory lower bound involving the chi-squared divergence between the optimal fact/non-fact score distributions, applicable to testers restricted to finite output supports (Theorem 3.3).

rDKFflrjZK.text: On Idefics-9b and Idefics2-8B-base, Hyper-ICL (demonstration-free) reaches 62.08/71.17 accuracy on VQAv2, 55.31/62.24 on OK-VQA, and 117.44/135.66 CIDEr on COCO Caption respectively, outperforming learnable baselines LoRA, LIVE, and MimIC while using only 1.18M parameters (Table 1).

Hyper-ICL requires only 0.955 TFLOPs at inference, versus 23.364 TFLOPs for standard 32-shot in-context learning, eliminating the need for in-context demonstrations at test time via a low-rank logit-level attention adapter (Section on inference efficiency; Table 1).

In held-out transfer experiments (training on one dataset and evaluating on a related task), Hyper-ICL trained on VQAv2 and evaluated on OK-VQA achieves 59.11 accuracy versus 51.43 for standard ICL (Table 8).

Layer-wise hyperbolic anchor distillation using Lorentz geodesic distance reconstructs demonstration-query relationships, and query-adaptive gating shows a positive correlation of 0.41-0.56 with demonstration-induced attention shifts (Section on query-adaptive modulation).

Hyper-ICL is evaluated across additional benchmarks including Flickr30k, MME, and SEED-Bench, showing consistent improvements over both zero-shot and standard ICL baselines on both Idefics-9b and Idefics2-8B architectures (Table 2).

sEYoG3tAXN.text: Finding 7.1 reports that the proposed decoder-only Any-Order GPT (AO-GPT) achieves approximately 25x inference speedup in generation compared to the encoder-only masked diffusion baseline SEDD, due to O(n) decoder-only generation complexity (via KV-caching) versus O(n^2) for encoder-only models (Finding 7.1, Figure 4).

Table 1 reports zero-shot perplexity on GPT-2-medium (~350M parameters): under left-to-right evaluation AO-GPT scores 42.44 (LAMBADA), 31.52 (WikiText2), 87.56 (PTB), 30.86 (WikiText103), and 50.23 (1BW), comparable to SEDD's 39.19/30.29/88.18/30.05/53.54 on the same benchmarks (Table 1).
With any-order evaluation using 64x ensembling, AO-GPT achieves 44.31 (LAMBADA), 30.16 (WikiText2), 85.75 (PTB), 28.98 (WikiText103), and 58.18 (1BW) perplexity (Table 1).

Table 2 shows that with temperature annealing (top-p=0.95, temperature=0.7) during generation, AO-GPT achieves comparable generation perplexity to SEDD across generation step counts ranging from 64 to 1024 (Table 2).

Finding 4 shows encoder-only masked diffusion architectures represent n*2^(n-1) order-invariant conditional probabilities while decoder-only architectures represent approximately e*n! order-dependent probabilities, and Finding 5 shows ensembling over orders can address the resulting performance gap (Findings 4-5).

KeH65ZD3a0.text: MotionCache-slow achieves a 6.28x inference speedup on SkyReels-V2 while maintaining a VBench score of 82.84% (Table 1).
MotionCache-fast achieves a 7.26x speedup on SkyReels-V2 with a VBench score of 82.75%, and MotionCache-slow achieves 1.64x speedup on MAGI-1 with VBench 77.25% (Table 1).
On SkyReels-V2, MotionCache outperforms FlowCache (6.26x speedup, VBench 82.70%) and TeaCache (1.89x speedup, VBench 82.67%) at comparable or better quality (Table 1).

Proposition 4.1 shows the caching approximation error at timestep t-1 for a chunk is strictly proportional to the magnitude of the vector difference between the true residual and the cached residual (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).
Lemma 4.2 proves the residual difference across timesteps is bounded by the intra-chunk frame difference, motivating the use of inter-frame differences as a motion proxy (Section 4, Lemma 4.2).

Ablations identify an optimal soft-mapping floor of alpha = 0.6 for motion-aware importance scores and an optimal Phase-1 duration of K = 6 full-computation chunks in the dual-stage inference scheme (Section 6.3, Tables 2-3).

yW9uNbRgOh.text: N2M improves success rate on the PnPCounterToCab simulation task from 3% for a reachability-only baseline to 54% (Experimental Results, Simulation/RoboCasa section).
N2M encodes ego-centric RGB point clouds with a Point-BERT encoder and outputs Gaussian Mixture Model parameters over preferable base poses, trained with a negative log-likelihood loss (Equation 2).
N2M matches an oracle baseline's performance in simulation using only 10 policy rollouts for training (Simulation/RoboCasa results section).
In real-world lamp-retrieval experiments, N2M trained on 12 rollouts achieves 10 consecutive successful trials (Real-world Experiments section).
N2M generalizes to a real-world toybox-handover task in entirely new environments using only 15 training rollouts (Real-world Experiments section).

An ablation removing the viewpoint-augmentation strategy causes performance to drop below the oracle baseline, confirming augmentation is necessary for viewpoint-invariant pose preference learning (Figure 11).

piWlEHb4Db.text: Directional smoothness D is defined so that, for non-Euclidean gradient descent with step size eta, the loss decreases if and only if D <= 2/eta (Definition 2.1).

Generalized sharpness S is defined as the maximum of d^T times the Hessian of the loss times d subject to the norm of d being at most 1 under an arbitrary norm, generalizing the largest-eigenvalue sharpness used for vanilla gradient descent (Definition 2.2).
Theorem 5.1 proves non-Euclidean gradient descent on quadratic objectives converges linearly when the step size eta < 2/S, where S is the generalized sharpness (Theorem 5.1).
Theorem 5.2 proves divergence occurs from some initialization when eta > 2/S for non-Euclidean gradient descent on quadratics (Theorem 5.2).

Experiments show l-infinity-descent on CIFAR-10 and Tiny Shakespeare exhibits generalized sharpness stabilizing slightly above the 2/eta threshold, unlike vanilla GD which stabilizes at 2/eta (Figure 2).
SignGD and Muon (without momentum) are shown to exhibit normalized sharpness converging near the 2/eta edge-of-stability threshold, extending the phenomenon to optimizers used in practice (Figure 5).

IpeH08AJ9P.text: Applying Reasoning Cache (RC) decoding to the base Qwen3-4B-Instruct model raises HMMT 2025 accuracy from 40% at a 16k-token budget to 57% at a 192k-token budget without any additional training (Figure 3 left, Section 5.2).

RCT-4B, trained with RC using only a 16k-token training budget, reaches 66.3% accuracy on HMMT 2025, versus 39.8% for Qwen3-4B-Instruct at a 16k budget and 62.5% for Qwen3-4B-Thinking at an 81k budget (Table 1, Section 7.1).
RCT-4B reaches nearly 70% accuracy on HMMT 2025 when evaluated with a 0.5-million-token test budget despite being trained with only a 16k-token budget (Section 1, Figure 1).
On adversarially selected hard problems, RCT-4B achieves a pass@16 of about 35% at a 256k-token budget compared to about 20% for the base model at the same budget (Figure 9).
RC decoding outperforms self-verification and self-refinement iterative-decoding baselines at matched token budgets (Figure 3 right).

The RC training objective uses summary-conditioned generation with outcome-reward optimization and a summary replay buffer enabling off-policy learning across training epochs (Section 6, Equation 6.1).

3V1p2bJugq.text: Proposition 4.2 establishes an accuracy-calibration gradient conflict: the ascent directions for the accuracy and calibration objectives have a negative Fisher-metric inner product when the model is over-confident (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.2).
On Qwen3-8B, DCPO improves average accuracy from 57.4% (GRPO) to 60.8% while cutting Expected Calibration Error from 0.372 to 0.128, a 71.6% relative reduction, across five benchmarks (Table 1).

DCPO improves AUROC from 0.532 (GRPO) to 0.881 and reduces Positive Calibration Error from 0.363 to 0.126, while prior calibration methods RLCR and CCGSPG achieve calibration gains only by sacrificing 7-10% accuracy (Table 1).

DCPO separates reasoning and confidence generation with an explicit <conf> delimiter and applies masked gradients so reasoning tokens receive accuracy rewards while confidence tokens receive calibration-focused rewards (Section 5).

An ablation removing decoupled optimization increases ECE to 0.258 and drops accuracy to 57.3%, while removing group-level supervision drops accuracy to 58.7%, showing both components are necessary (Table 2).

i0P4ew9GpS.text: Evolution Strategies (ES) is scaled to full-parameter fine-tuning of billion-parameter LLMs without dimensionality reduction, using a population size of only N=30 and noise scale sigma=0.001 (Section 3.2, Algorithm 2).

On the Countdown task, ES achieves 54.2% accuracy on Qwen-2.5-7B versus 52.8% for PPO and 66.8% for GRPO with population 30, while ES improves 36.4% over the untrained baseline compared to 17.9% for PPO and 21.3% for GRPO(8) (Section 4.1, Table 1).
ES is markedly more robust on small models, reaching 14.4% accuracy on Qwen-0.5B where both PPO and GRPO score only 0.3% (Table 1).
ES requires less than 20% of the training sample evaluations needed by RL methods to reach comparable performance (Section 4.1, Figure 6, Appendix A.4).

On the conciseness task, ES maintains low KL divergence from the reference policy (0.274±0.096 at sigma=0.001) and avoids reward hacking without requiring an explicit KL penalty, unlike GRPO which exhibits reward hacking absent such a penalty (Section 4.2, Figure 1).

hrZCqzmsPW.text: The paper introduces the Effective Temporal F1 (EtF1) metric, which conditions Temporal F1-Score on count consistency to jointly penalize localization error and incorrect event-count predictions (Section on evaluation metrics).
The proposed OMTG-4B model achieves 43.65% EtF1 on the OMTG benchmark, outperforming Gemini 2.5 Pro (27.80% EtF1) by 15.85 points and Seed-1.8 (28.04% EtF1) by 15.61 points.
Existing open-source Qwen2.5-VL variants achieve 0% Count Accuracy on OMTG, revealing a critical capability gap in handling queries with multiple event occurrences.

The OMTG benchmark comprises 340 manually curated evaluation samples, built alongside a 56k-sample training set constructed via a five-stage pipeline (event discovery, initial grounding, visual verification, query refinement, dense captioning).

The composite RL reward combines temporal IoU, count accuracy, chain-of-thought caption reward, and length penalty terms, with the caption reward alone improving EtF1 by 8.84 points over the SFT baseline.

XOEVxte7Nn.text: PerContrast estimates each token's Personal Influence Ratio (PIR) via causal intervention, computed as the difference between the log-probability of the token with the full user persona present versus with the persona removed.
PerCE applies an EM-style procedure that alternates an E-step estimating per-token PIR-based importance weights and an M-step optimizing a weighted cross-entropy loss that upweights high-PIR tokens.
On the LongLaMP benchmark, PerCE yields average gains of over 10% across evaluated models, with a maximum single-metric gain of 68.04% in METEOR on Qwen3-4B.
PerCE achieves up to +40.57% ROUGE-L on Review Writing and up to +46.34% METEOR on Topic Writing tasks within LongLaMP.

PerCE shows cross-task transfer: a model trained on the Personalized Topic Writing (PTW) task achieves +56.62% on Personalized Abstract Generation (PAG) evaluation, with several out-of-domain scores exceeding in-domain cross-entropy baselines.
PerCE adds only one additional forward pass per training step, using a shortened persona-removed context that reduces input length by roughly 7% in practice.

2iC5H9k8am.text: SARSteer shows that harmful and safe speech inputs occupy widely divergent latent distributions in large audio-language models, so text-derived LLM refusal-steering vectors have no shared subspace to define a valid steering path when applied directly to audio activations.
SARSteer instead derives refusal steering vectors from text-modality refusal prompts applied to the same harmful queries, rather than contrasting raw audio activations.
SARSteer applies PCA on benign responses to identify and ablate a safe subspace component from the steering vector (Decomposed Safe-Space Ablation), preserving utility on borderline-safe inputs.
On the Figstep-audio benchmark, SARSteer reduces Attack Success Rate on Qwen2-Audio to 10.8% from a 51.6% vanilla baseline while achieving a 79.95% Balanced Refusal Rate.
On Kimi-Audio, SARSteer achieves a 10% Attack Success Rate and an 88.8% Balanced Refusal Rate on Figstep-audio.
The paper proposes the Balanced Refusal Rate (BRR) metric to jointly capture refusal rates on harmful and paired benign queries, exposing over-refusal that existing audio-safety defenses hide.

LxAy8UpVUC.text: PINE guarantees prediction equivalence only within an in-distribution region calibrated via split conformal prediction, controlled by a single hyperparameter alpha, providing a lower bound of 1-alpha on the probability that a future input falls within the equivalence guarantee region.
As alpha varies from 0.05 to 0.8, PINE's mean pruning rate increases from 44.6% to 67.8% while mean fidelity remains between 99.15% and 99.96% across datasets.
PINE achieves up to a 30% improvement in compression ratio over the faithful pruning baseline FIPE while maintaining comparable prediction equivalence.
On the Pima-Diabetes dataset at alpha=0.8, PINE attains a 55.3% pruning rate with 98.3% fidelity, versus FIPE's 17.3% pruning rate at 100% fidelity.
PINE's plausible score function uses Chow-Liu trees to model the input distribution, enabling a compact MILP encoding with O(p*B^2) constraints rather than exponential complexity.

C0NCLB6ZGY.text: UrbanFusion is evaluated across 41 tasks in 56 cities worldwide and outperforms prior state-of-the-art GeoAI models on location-encoding tasks (abstract only)

UrbanFusion uses modality-specific encoders for street view imagery, remote sensing data, cartographic maps, and POI data, fused via a Transformer-based Stochastic Multimodal Fusion (SMF) module (abstract only)
UrbanFusion allows flexible multimodal input at inference time, using any subset of available modalities for a given location during both pretraining and inference (abstract only)
UrbanFusion generalizes well to regions/cities unseen during training, as demonstrated in the 56-city evaluation (abstract only)

hrtEiSftwk.text: The JUICE encoder for RDB (relational database) foundation models restricts ICL-specific compression to within table columns sharing units, rather than across heterogeneous column types, as defined in Section 3.1 (Definition 3.1) (Section 3.1)

Proposition 3.2 proves that excluding trainable parameters from the encoder does not compromise its expressiveness when using positively homogeneous activation functions with 1D node features (Section 3.3, Proposition 3.2)

Proposition 4.2 shows fixed (non-adaptive) encoders fail to achieve zero estimation error when dataset column roles vary, with success probability bounded by 1-(r choose k)/(d choose k) (Section 4.1, Proposition 4.2)
Proposition 4.3 shows ICL without encoding achieves an O(n^-2/kappa) error rate while dense encoders degrade to Theta(n^-2/d) under distribution shift (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.3)

On RelBench classification benchmarks, RDBLearn matches the fully-supervised RelGT model's performance despite being pretrained only on synthetic data, and outperforms other RDB foundation models (Figure 2)

On RelBench regression tasks, RDBLearn matches KumoRFM and remains competitive with supervised approaches, with a performance inversion observed between dense and JUICE encoders when moving from supervised to in-context learning settings (Figure 4, Figure 6)

32jYxFTcNX.text: MoST introduces a Modality-Aware Mixture of Experts (MAMoE) architecture with modality-specific expert groups, cross-modal shared experts, and a modality-aware router, detailed via Algorithm 1 (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1)
MoST achieves 2.0% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean for ASR and 6.0% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean for TTS, evaluated alongside VoxPopuli and Common Voice (Table 1)
MoST attains an average audio language modeling score of 71.94, including a state-of-the-art 83.64 on sTopic-StoryCloze (Table 2)
MoST's spoken question answering performance is reported across the Llama Q, TriviaQA, and WebQ benchmarks (Figure 3)
Ablation studies isolate the contribution of the MAMoE routing design to overall performance (Section 6, Figures 4-6)

MoST is released as a fully open-source speech-text LLM, with model weights, training/inference code, and training data built exclusively from open-source datasets released publicly (Abstract; Section 1)

03RPMit2tm.text: DSAC-E is evaluated on 8 MuJoCo continuous-control locomotion tasks (Humanoid-v3, Ant-v3, Hopper-v3, Walker2d-v3, Swimmer-v3, HalfCheetah-v3, InvertedDoublePendulum-v2, Reacher-v2), not 10 tasks spanning manipulation and driving (Section 4.1, Table 1)
DSAC-E improves final returns over the second-best baseline by 15.82% on Humanoid-v3, 21.93% on Ant-v3, 21.11% on Walker2d-v3, and 6.58% on Hopper-v3 (Table 1)
Training curves with 95% confidence intervals over five runs across all 8 tasks demonstrate DSAC-E's training stability relative to baselines (Figure 2)
The trajectory entropy constraint (TEC), formalized in Eq. 9 as the discounted sum of per-step entropies, is contrasted with short-sighted single-step entropy tuning (Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Eq. 9)

An ablation removing TEC ('DSAC-E w/o TEC') shows measurable performance degradation, confirming the contribution of trajectory-level entropy governance beyond reward-entropy separation alone (Section 4.2, Figure 3)

elMTnbu5Kz.text: DIRECT's FLUX-based variant achieves PSNR 23.09, SSIM 0.871, LPIPS 0.147, CLIP-I 0.959, DINO 0.936, and Matching Error 17.8, outperforming baselines built on Object3DIT and TRELLIS combined with AnyDoor/InsertAnything (Table 1, Section 4.1)

A Matching Error metric based on dense matching quantifies pose adherence across rotation ranges from 0 to 180 degrees, showing DIRECT's superior geometric controllability under large pose changes (Table 2, Section 4.3)
DIRECT formalizes interactive pose manipulation using a 6-DoF pose parameterized in se(3), enabling a visual gizmo-based interactive inference pipeline (Section 3.1, Appendix C)
DIRECT's decomposed visual proxies use independent Rotary Positional Embeddings and modality-specific LoRA adapters for a Geometry-Appearance-Context Triplet Guidance scheme (Section 3.2, Figure 2)
An ablation comparing decomposed LoRA injection against a vanilla LoRA baseline confirms the contribution of each decomposed component to final image quality (Table 3, Figure 9, Section 4.4)

BGcw0KWStP.text: PRPO applied to DX-LLaVA raises average F1 for deepfake detection from 78.08% (DX-LLaVA baseline) to 89.91% (Table 4).
PRPO achieves the highest reasoning quality score of 4.55/5.0, surpassing Gemini-2.5 at 4.20/5.0 (Table 6).
On the DDIM domain, PRPO reaches 95.80% accuracy and 95.88% F1, outperforming GRPO (92.29% accuracy, 92.09% F1) and PPO (94.00% accuracy, 93.95% F1) (Table 8).
Ablating the reward components shows VCR-only achieves 88.68% F1 and PCR-only achieves 70.98% F1, while combining both yields 94.99% F1 on the SD domain (Table 7).
The DF-R5 dataset used for training and evaluation contains 115k images with reasoning annotations spanning five generative domains: DDIM, PixArt-alpha, SD-2.1, SiT, and StyleGAN3 (Section 3).

Ipgssz2WL1.text: Spectral Coherence Predictability (SCP) computes a per-instance predictability score derived from a linear MSE lower bound, MSE_lb, in O(N log N) time per instance (Abstract, Section 4.1).

The predictability score is defined as P_xy = 1 - MSE_lb / Var(y), bounded in [0,1], and MSE_lb is shown to be a consistent estimator of intrinsic predictability for jointly Gaussian processes (Section 4.1).
MSE_lb correlates with empirical MSE of state-of-the-art forecasting models with Pearson correlation R >= 0.8 across the evaluated datasets (Section 5.2, Table 1).
The paper identifies 'predictability drift,' where task difficulty fluctuates substantially over time and across variables within the same dataset (Section 5.3, Figure 3).

A complementary Linear Utilization Ratio (LUR) diagnostic is introduced, computed via a frequency-resolved algorithm (Algorithm 2), distinguishing under-utilization (LUR<1), saturation (LUR~1), and beyond-linear gains (LUR>1) (Section 5.4, Figure 4).

AYXgo5FjYz.text: The hierarchical HPC-MEC world model separates content (HPC) from structure (MEC) and uses an inverse model to extract latent transitions from MEC embeddings for path integration via CANN dynamics (Section 3.1-3.2).
Latent transitions achieve the highest transition decoding accuracy of 0.9064 +/- 0.0145 across compared embedding types (Table 1).
Latent transitions attain a sequence similarity of 0.235 +/- 0.021 cosine similarity, reported alongside baseline comparisons (Table 2).
An ablation removing hierarchical content-structure separation and the CANN dynamics degrades out-of-distribution structure reuse, demonstrating both components are necessary (Table 4).

The model is evaluated for structural generalization on out-of-distribution data using COIL-100 and compared against baselines on SSv2 and Franka Kitchen using SSIM and LPIPS metrics (Figure 4C, Table 3).

w5lnam4G7C.text: DiOpt addresses 'distributional misalignment,' where the diffusion model's generated solution distribution has small overlap with the feasible domain, illustrated geometrically in Figure 1.

DiOpt's bootstrapped training mechanism adaptively weights candidate solutions based on severity of constraint violations and optimality gaps, formalized in Equations 7-9 and Algorithm 1 (Section 4.3).
On ACOPF with 128 variables and 256 constraints, DiOpt achieves an objective value of 3.942 with 0.000 equality constraint violations (Table 4).

On the QSPR task (100 variables, 250 equality and 50 inequality constraints), DiOpt is compared against baselines on objective value, equality/inequality violation magnitude, and violation count (Table 2).
A look-up table acceleration mechanism (Eq. 10, Section 4.4) and an inference-time solution selection procedure (Eq. 11, Section 4.5) are used to speed up and refine the final feasible solution.

ttOGqk77go.text: Entropy-matched temperature scaling controls (T* ~ 0.59) fail to replicate hyperfitting's diversity gains: type-token ratio reaches only 0.397 versus 0.684 for the hyperfitted model, despite statistically matched entropy (p=0.73) (Section 3.2, Table 1).

Terminal Expansion occurs specifically in the final transformer block, where L2 distance in representation space increases from 22.0 to 81.6 and effective dimensionality expands by approximately +80.8 dimensions (Section 4.2, Figure 5).

A static logit-reweighting (static bias) ablation universally degrades generation quality with a monotonic degradation trend (Spearman rho = -0.94), falsifying a context-agnostic reweighting explanation for hyperfitting (Section 3.5, Table 2).

Late-Stage LoRA, restricting fine-tuning updates to only the final 5 transformer layers, reduces trainable parameters by 78-83% compared to full LoRA while replicating rank-reordering dynamics on TinyLlama and Qwen2.5 (Section 5, Tables 3-4).
In LLM-as-judge evaluation, Late-Stage LoRA achieves a 57.3% win rate over the comparison approach, driven by a +16.1 percentage point coherence advantage (Table 5).

UZF4ssK12K.text: DF-ExpEnse computes an exploration interest score for each of M sampled diffusion-policy action candidates as the minimum critic-ensemble prediction plus alpha times the ensemble standard deviation, then selects the action maximizing this score (Section 3.1, Equation 2).

Default DF-ExpEnse hyperparameters use 3 candidate action samples, a critic ensemble of size 10, alpha=0.5, a fleet size of 4, and Behavior Cloning Sampling Regularization with regularization amount p=1 (Section 4.4).

DF-ExpEnse outperforms vanilla DSRL, Max-Q, E3B (state and DINO variants), and Plan2Explore across RoboMimic manipulation tasks (Lift, Can, Square, Tool Hang) and OpenAI Gym locomotion tasks (Hopper-v2, Walker2D-v2, HalfCheetah-v2) over three random seeds (Section 4.5, Figure 2).

Removing Behavior Cloning Sampling Regularization (BC-SR) from DF-ExpEnse consistently decreases sample efficiency, while adding BC-SR to the Max-Q baseline consistently improves it (Section 4.6, Figure 4).

Fleet normalization across cross-agent communicating critics yields consistent improvements over same-sized fleets of independently operating agents, and DF-ExpEnse retains its advantage over Max-Q even as fleet size scales to 16 while Max-Q collapses (Section 4.7, Figure 5; Appendix B, Figure 7).

When integrated with ResFiT instead of DSRL, DF-ExpEnse improves over Max-Q and vanilla ResFiT on DexMimicGen bimanual manipulation tasks (Can Sort, Box Cleanup, Coffee), demonstrating generality across underlying RL algorithms (Section 4.1, Figure 3).

FA7n9adGKc.text: iTryOn introduces the Interactive Video Virtual Try-On (Interactive VVT) task and the VVT-Interact dataset of 5,292 video-garment pairs across six interaction categories (5,160 training / 132 testing videos), annotated with global and time-stamped action captions via Qwen-VL (Section 3.2.2, Section 4.1).
On VVT-Interact, iTryOn achieves an Interaction Success Rate (ISR) of 61.00% (paired) versus under 49% for baselines, alongside an FVD of 380.56 (Table 2).
On VVT-Interact visual fidelity metrics, iTryOn attains the lowest VFID scores (22.46 paired, 35.05 unpaired) and best LPIPS (0.1217) among compared methods (Table 1).

Ablation shows ISR improves from 47.66% for the baseline model to 61.00% for the full model as data curation, spatial guidance (3D hand priors), semantic guidance (Action-aware RoPE), and the action-aware constraint loss are added cumulatively (Table 3, Table 4).
On the traditional non-interactive ViViD benchmark, iTryOn achieves a paired VFID of 8.43, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art MagicTryOn's 12.20 (Appendix Table 9).
The Action-aware Rotational Position Embedding hyperparameter k=4 and constraint loss weighting lambda=0.5 are each shown to be optimal via dedicated ablations (Appendix Table 7, Table 8).

57lp1pmJVo.text: MPC-Flow's Receding-Horizon Control (RHC) variant discretizes the remaining trajectory into K steps at each timestep, and Theorem 3.1 proves it recovers the global optimum of the underlying optimal control objective when each sub-problem is solved exactly (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

The special case K=1 of MPC-RHC avoids backpropagation through the flow model's sampling dynamics entirely, and this variant runs in 2.05 seconds per image compared to 315.66 seconds for the gradient-based FlowGrad baseline (Section 3, experimental timing results).

The Delta-t-Horizon Control variant uses a value-function approximation (Equation 9) as an intermediate cost for greedy one-step optimization, with Theorem 3.2 proving optimality when the true value function is used (Section 3, Equation 9, Theorem 3.2).

On CelebA image restoration, MPC-Delta-t ranks second overall behind PnP-Flow across denoising, deblurring, super-resolution, and inpainting, while achieving the best super-resolution performance among all methods at PSNR 31.89 / SSIM 0.911 (Section 4, image restoration results table).

MPC-Flow performs training-free guidance of the 32-billion-parameter FLUX.2 model in a 4-bit quantized setting on a single 24GB consumer GPU, including style transfer that achieves a better content-style trade-off than the FlowChef baseline and colorization that improves PSNR from 18.0 to 23.8 over unconditional generation (Section 4, large-scale model experiments).

Proposition B.1 establishes existence of an optimal control solution under standard regularity conditions, underpinning the theoretical guarantees for both the RHC and Delta-t-horizon variants (Appendix, Proposition B.1).

bMHwh8qAGc.text: On the inverse-gamma analytical verification study, the 5-component Distribution Transformer (DT-5) achieves KL-divergence of 0.0004±0.0000 (narrow meta-prior) and 0.0003±0.0000 (wide meta-prior), versus 814/726 for PFN and 0.0423-0.0558 for SVI (Section 4.1, Table 1).

On the Gaussian Process joint predictive posterior and hyperposterior task, the Distribution Transformer achieves NLL of -0.32±0.12 (predictive posterior) and 0.81±0.08 (hyperposterior), outperforming VI's 1.97±0.53 hyperposterior NLL while running roughly 136x faster in batch inference time (Section 4.2.1, Table 2, Figure 5).

On sequential sensor-fusion inference (rangefinder observation model), the Distribution Transformer attains NLL of -0.197±0.040, comparable to the particle filter's -0.244±0.047 and markedly better than the Extended Kalman Filter's 95.9±4.40, while running approximately 50x faster than particle filters (Section 4.3, Table 3).
On quantum system parameter inference, the Distribution Transformer outperforms both SVI and Prior-Fitted Networks (PFNs) in log-likelihood (Section 4.2.2).

Distribution Transformers represent priors as k-component Gaussian Mixture Models in transformer latent space and use a transformer decoder without positional encodings (to preserve permutation equivariance) to map priors to posterior GMM approximations conditioned on observations via cross-attention (Section 3).

alkWXGgvYP.text: Benchmarking five Message-Passing Neural Network architectures on the graph alignment task across 40 datasets shows anisotropic architectures (GATv2, GAT) outperform standard isotropic convolutional architectures within the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman expressiveness class, with performance gaps largest at noise level eta=15% for molecular graphs (Section 5).

The GAPE (Graph Alignment Positional Encodings) method combined with Random Walk Positional Encodings achieves mean absolute error of 1.069±0.009 on AQSOL, 0.125±0.004 on PCQM4Mv2, and 0.109±0.005 on ZINC, improving over GAPE alone (Section 6, Table 1).

A Transformer using GAPE positional encodings with 37.9M parameters achieves state-of-the-art MAE of 0.0337 on PCQM4Mv2, outperforming TGT-At (0.0671 MAE, 203M params) and Uni-Mol+ (0.0693 MAE, 77M params) despite far fewer parameters (Section 6, Table 2).

Correlated graph pairs for alignment datasets are generated by adding and removing edges with probabilities (p_add, p_remove) controlled by a single noise level eta, allowing tunable task difficulty without altering the underlying graph topology, across five base datasets (Erdos-Renyi, AQSOL, PCQM4Mv2, CoraFull, OGBN-Arxiv) at eight noise levels each (Section 4).

Full hyperparameter specifications are reported for reproducibility, with training taking roughly 20-40 minutes per run on an RTX6000 GPU and PCQM4Mv2 experiments taking about 2.5 hours on 3 RTX8000 GPUs (Appendix, Tables C.2, F.6-F.7).

PmAKKeZj7O.text: BT-σ achieves 57.38 Spearman rank correlation (SRC) on SummEval Coherence versus 53.94 for the soft Bradley-Terry baseline (Table 2).
BT-σ reaches 63.49 SRC on Topical-Chat Engagingness compared to 61.87 for soft BT, and 60.56 versus 58.20 on Naturalness (Table 2).
BT-σ outperforms supervised Temp-BT (temperature scaling), which scores 55.14 SRC, despite BT-σ requiring no human labels (Table 2).
The learned judge discriminator parameter 1/σₖ correlates with independent judge quality at 72.2% Pearson correlation and 85.71% Spearman rank correlation on SummEval (Table 3).
Discriminators correlate with transitivity (cycle) consistency at 90.29% PCC and 95.24% SRC on SummEval (Table 4).
Hard BT-σ outperforms soft BT-σ specifically for judges with high cycle-inconsistency rates, reaching 67.36 on the ENG aspect of Topical-Chat (Section 5.1).

Fqhwxyh4VN.text: SED uses 15M parameters versus 37M for DDPM and 25M for SARM while achieving lower normalized Wasserstein distance on calorimeter image generation, e.g. Signal PT of 16.31 for SED versus 220.32 for DDPM and 28.01 for SARM (Table 1).
On scRNA-seq generation, SED achieves SCC of 0.74 and MMD of 0.55 on Tabula Muris versus scDiffusion's 0.71 SCC and 1.53 MMD, and SCC of 0.82 versus 0.77 on Human Lung PF (Table 2).
SED reduces sampling time to 23.5 ms/batch on 95%-sparse Muon Signal data versus 453.1 ms for DDPM and 94.1 ms for LDM, and to 52.9 ms on MNIST versus 358.3 ms (DDPM) and 77.6 ms (LDM) (Table 3).
SED's computational cost remains nearly constant as data dimensionality increases, unlike the linear scaling exhibited by DDPM and LDM (Figure 2).
DDPM, LDM, and scDiffusion underestimate sparsity and generate overly dense samples relative to ground truth, while SED preserves the true sparsity pattern (Figure 5).

SED produces valid dimension orderings in over 98.5% of samples for most datasets, with correctness rates of 100% on Fashion-MNIST, 99.3% on MNIST, 95.6% on Muon Signal, and 87.9% on Muon Background (Section 5.6, Table 4).

MKvy0hgAK4.text: KANFIS's additive fuzzy inference scales as O(N·H·P_ψ) with input dimension N, versus O(M^N) exponential scaling for product-based ANFIS systems (Appendix B, Theorem B.4).
Traditional T1-ANFIS fails to run ('–' result) on the high-dimensional BCW and Spambase datasets, whereas KANFIS variants complete successfully (Table 1).
IT2-KANFIS achieves MAPE of 0.7047, RMSE of 4.1240, and MAE of 3.1975 on the CCPP dataset (Table 1).
Sparsity and distinctiveness regularization (Equations 11-13) reduces average features per rule by up to 63.94% on the Spambase dataset (Figure 3, Section 3.6).
KANFIS extracts six dominant, physically interpretable rules on CCPP and six medically interpretable cardiovascular-risk rules on the MHR dataset (Table 2, Table 3).

KANFIS is compatible with both Type-1 and Interval Type-2 fuzzy logic variants, both evaluated against MLP, ANFIS variants, and KAN baselines across CCPP, Parkinsons, BCW, Spambase, and MHR datasets (Table 1).

Qay3nI9WRv.text: AutoPrune's discovered algorithm achieves 6.28 perplexity on LLaMA-2 7B at 50% sparsity versus 6.45 for Wanda (Table 1, Section 4.1).
AutoPrune achieves 7.63 perplexity on LLaMA-1 13B at 60% sparsity versus 8.56 for Wanda (Table 4, Section 4.1).
Graph-driven Chain-of-Thought (GCoT) improves MMLU zero-shot accuracy by 2.44 points over a naive prompting baseline (Table 1, Section 1).
Skew-aware Dynamic Sparsity Allocation (SDSA) achieves 66.93 perplexity at 70% sparsity versus 85.77 for uniform layerwise allocation (Table 7, Section 4.3).
AutoPrune's pruned LLaMA-1 7B model achieves 56.68% accuracy on the RTE task (Table 5, Section 4.2).

AutoPrune is evaluated against Magnitude, SparseGPT, Wanda, LLM-Pruner, OWL, ER/ER-plus, and Global allocation baselines across LLaMA-1 (7B-65B), LLaMA-2 (7B-70B), OPT-13B, Pythia-12B, and Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Section 4).

sWW6lvti8X.text: 18 MLLMs (17 open-source plus GPT-4o-mini) are evaluated on the 2,000-sample MC2 (Modality Context Conflict) benchmark spanning 8 recognition-level task categories built from TDIUC/MS-COCO (Section 3, Section 4).
Vision-preference ratios vary widely across models: LLaVA1.5-13B shows only 14.4% vision preference (strong text bias) while Qwen2.5VL-7B shows 52.2% and GPT-4o-mini shows 52.0% (Table 1).
Most tested MLLMs favor the text modality overall, with Qwen2.5VL and InternVL3 being notable exceptions favoring vision (Figure 2).
Steering Qwen2VL-7B toward vision via representation engineering raises average performance from a 15.3% baseline to 48.1% (Table 2, Section 5.2).
Steering toward vision improves hallucination-mitigation performance on the PhD dataset by 18.4% on the Phd-icc metric over baseline (Table 3).
Vision-steering improves multimodal machine translation on AmbigCaps by 1.3 BLEU for English-to-Turkish and 1.33 BLEU for Turkish-to-English (Table 4).

EmqsPzyNHh.text: Theorem 4.5 gives a necessary and sufficient condition for realizable strong universal Bayes-consistency with general metric losses, characterized via an unbounded-gap Littlestone tree obstruction (Section 4, Theorem 4.5).
Definition 4.1 introduces infinite non-decreasing-γk-Littlestone trees, where the gap parameters γk diverge to infinity along the tree (Section 4, Definition 4.1).

Theorem 5.1 shows that if such an infinite non-decreasing-γk-Littlestone tree exists for a hypothesis class, then every learning algorithm has a realizable distribution on which the expected risk stays infinite for all sample sizes n (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 6.5 constructs an explicit distribution-free learner that, whenever no unbounded-gap Littlestone tree exists, achieves risk converging almost surely to zero for every realizable distribution (Section 6, Theorem 6.5).
Section 3 shows that a finite optimal risk R* < infinity is not sufficient for universal Bayes-consistency with general metric losses, resolving an open problem left by prior work (Section 3).

ZVRgcQq4D2.text: Correct LLM responses activate substantially fewer unique neurons than incorrect responses throughout generation, and correct-response activations show stronger cross-sample agreement while incorrect ones diverge (Section 3.3).

On AIME24+25 with Qwen3-4B-Think, the NAD-kNN selection strategy (highest sum of top-k neuron-similarity scores) achieves 85.0% accuracy versus a 74.6% baseline average, closely matching the 86.7% accuracy of majority voting (Table 1).
On GPQA with Qwen3-4B-Think, NAD-kNN reaches 68.7% accuracy versus a 66.3% baseline (Table 1).

NAD's early-stopping variant, truncating generation at 32 tokens, reduces token consumption by 97.6-98.8% while preserving accuracy advantages, e.g., 81.7% accuracy on AIME24+25 using only 1.3M tokens versus 55.2M tokens for full sampling (Table 2).
NAD-kNN achieves 98.2% on HumanEval, 86.0% on LiveCodeBench v5, and 84.6% on MBPP for code generation tasks (Table 1).

ktRyGKpt9U.text: The proposed G-Star sampler reformulates masked diffusion sampling in a star-shaped paradigm, first predicting a complete version of the clean data rather than taking an irreversible step from state x_t to x_s, enabling selective remasking of likely-erroneous tokens (Section 4).

A lightweight learned error predictor gϕ, requiring only single-layer fine-tuning (or even head-only training) of a pretrained masked diffusion model, is trained via Algorithm 1 to identify tokens likely to be mistakes for targeted remasking (Algorithm 1).

On 512-token OpenWebText generation with 128 sampling steps, G-Star-loop achieves MAUVE 57.3 and perplexity 18.4, outperforming ReMDM-loop (η=0.1) at MAUVE 18.1/PPL 34.9 and the standard MDLM baseline at MAUVE 5.4/PPL 36.6 (Table 1).
On Dream-Instruct 7B, G-Star yields consistent gains across seven downstream tasks, including +1.3 points on MMLU and +2.9 points on IFEval (Section 5.1).
On Conala code generation, G-Star achieves 17.8 perplexity at 128 steps, versus 19.1 perplexity for ReMDM-cap (η=0.04) (Section 5.2).

Section 4.2 finds the star-shaped sampler is most beneficial during late-stage refinement (the final 20-40% of sampling steps), while standard MDLM is stronger for initial structure-building (Section 4.2).

iD88HhWBGc.text: TurboGS completes training within 77-100 seconds across benchmark scenes, yielding a 1.2x-2x speedup over recent acceleration methods and a 10x-14x speedup over vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (Table 1).

TurboGS's error-guided sparse pixel sampling partitions each training image into S x S tiles (e.g., 16x16) and splits sampled pixels into error-prioritized 'hard' pixels and age-based 'stable' pixels, using persistent per-view error maps and age maps (Section 3.5).
A tile-level sparse Normalized Cross-Correlation loss provides local structure-aware supervision on sampled pixels with gradient-balanced weighting to prevent optimization instability (Section 3.7).
TurboGS achieves competitive rendering quality with a PSNR of 27.57 on Mip-NeRF 360 despite using far fewer optimized pixels (Section 3, Table 1).
Error-driven density control reduces the final Gaussian primitive count from 2.73M (baseline) to 0.64M while preserving rendering fidelity (Section 3.8).

zRMK32N6t6.text: On Qwen3-8B, ASAG achieves a 3.2% average accuracy improvement across reasoning benchmarks while reducing generated tokens by nearly 40% (Section 5.1, Table 1).
ASAG's early-exit criterion (Section 4.1) combines a confidence threshold (λ=0.95) with an attention-entropy variation term (α=-0.1) to decide when further reasoning will not help (Section 4.1).
ASAG yields token compression ratios of 45.5% on GSM8K and 64.0% on MATH-500 (Section 5.1).
Table 1 shows ASAG consistently outperforms baseline early-stopping methods DEER, Dynasor, and TALE across DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Qwen3 model variants ranging from 4B to 32B parameters (Table 1).
Under stochastic (sampling-based) decoding, ASAG still achieves a 36.9% token reduction on Qwen3-8B (Table 3).

ASAG is training-free and plug-and-play, requiring no additional fine-tuning to integrate into existing large reasoning models, and additionally uses logits injection and jump prompts (Sections 4.2-4.3) to escape low-confidence reasoning traps (Section 4.2, Section 4.3).

RUheyL9bb9.text: GRPO with Discounted Beta-Bernoulli (DBB) reward estimation achieves average Acc@8 improvements of 3.22 points (Qwen3-1.7B) and 2.42 points (Qwen3-8B) on in-distribution benchmarks, and 12.49 points (1.7B) and 6.92 points (8B) on out-of-distribution benchmarks, versus standard GRPO (Table 1, Section 4.2).
GRPO-DBB outperforms the replay-based RePO baseline across all in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings tested (Table 1, Section 4.2).

The optimal discount factor λ differs by model scale: λ=0.75 is best for Qwen3-8B while λ=0.5 is best for Qwen3-1.7B, and performance degrades at λ=1.0, the standard (undiscounted) Beta-Bernoulli setting (Table 2, Section 5.2).

DBB's mean squared error is empirically and theoretically lower than standard point estimation for N≤16 rollouts per prompt when λ=0.4, while avoiding the variance collapse that afflicts point estimators (Figure 3, Section 3.3, Section 5.3).
Applying DBB to the Dr.GRPO advantage formulation (rather than GRPO) yields an average improvement of 1.96 points, showing the method generalizes beyond the GRPO objective (Table 3, Section 5.4).
Training uses the DAPO-Math-17k dataset filtered to 17,280 prompts, with 8 rollout samples per prompt, batch size 128, and 4 training epochs (Appendix C).

hn4ndkaD6x.text: CoDiLA couples a frozen 7B-parameter diffusion language model (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) with a small auxiliary autoregressive model (Qwen3-0.6B, finetuned on Ling-Coder-SFT) that locally resolves token dependencies within each parallel-decoded block (Section on Architecture Overview / Training Configuration).
