Lemma 3.1 establishes first-order pathwise differentiability of the STE functional with an explicit efficient influence function (Section 3).
Theorem 3.2 proves that under the null hypothesis P1=P0, the STE functional is second-order pathwise differentiable (Section 3).

Theorem 4.1 shows the proposed second-order one-step estimator has an n-rate (rather than √n-rate) limiting null distribution equal to a weighted sum of (χ²_1 − 1) terms, enabling valid hypothesis tests under the null (Section 4.2).

A debiased second-order estimator combining the plug-in STE with first- and second-order correction terms is proposed to restore asymptotic normality under both null and alternative (Equation 12, Section 4.1).

An aggregated test statistic maximizing over multiple regularization parameters ε maintains asymptotic type I error control and is validated via simulations and high-dimensional image experiments (Section 4.4, Figures 2 and 5).

w6JVbu7VFo.text: Fused attention kernels for Graph Transformers achieve forward speedups ranging 1.15x-2.00x across datasets, with the WSB/Tensor-Core variant reaching up to 2.69x forward speedup on the tolokers-2 graph (Table 1).
GATv2 kernels achieve forward latency speedups of 2.82x-9.70x and peak memory reductions of 4.67x-44.17x, with a median memory reduction of about 6x (Table 2).
For SpMM/GCN aggregation, cuSPARSE achieves 2.30x-3.27x forward speedup, and using a cached transpose improves backward-pass speedups to 1.64x-1.74x (Table 3).
Reduction-based aggregation kernels achieve forward speedups of 2.54x-8.31x (median 4.84x) with peak memory reductions of 1.43x-1.97x (Table 4).
Graph reordering benefits neighbor-parallel kernels more than feature-parallel kernel designs, with the effect depending on graph density (Figure 1).

RtnSbA5AUV.text: Geo-NeWF (Geo-NeW) exactly preserves discrete conservation structure by representing solutions with Whitney forms whose basis functions satisfy the generalized Stokes theorem at the discrete level, per the Finite Element Exterior Calculus formulation in Section 2.2/Section 3.
On the standard Pipe Flow benchmark, Geo-NeW achieves an L2 error of 0.112e-2, a 71% reduction versus the previous best of 0.38e-2 (Table 2).
On the standard Elasticity benchmark, Geo-NeW achieves 0.351e-2 error, a 29% reduction versus the previous best of 0.50e-2 (Table 2).

On the out-of-distribution Poly-Poisson task, Geo-NeW achieves 2.14e-2 error versus 4.60e-2 for Linear Attention, a 53% reduction, and on NS2d-c++ OOD achieves 42.2e-2 versus 91.40e-2 for Transolver, a 54% reduction (Table 1).

Geo-NeW enforces Dirichlet boundary conditions exactly, achieving 0.00 error on all velocity components and pressure at boundary nodes, compared to nonzero errors (e.g., 2.22e-3) for baseline encoders (Table 3).

On angled-step geometries, Transolver's predictions fail beyond a 20-degree step angle while Geo-NeW remains stable through 30 degrees, consistent with the paper's up-to-65% MSE reduction on out-of-distribution geometries (Figure 1, Figure 6).

ljNZyrAlaa.text: Theorem 5.1 gives the first convergence bound for Federated DPO (FedDPO) under partial client participation, showing gradient-norm error scaling with local steps E, rounds R, sampled clients S, and gradient variance ζ²_g (Theorem 5.1).
Corollary 5.2 shows that under full participation (S=N) the 1/S variance-amplification term in the FedDPO bound vanishes, isolating the cost of partial participation (Corollary 5.2).
Theorem 5.4 introduces a staleness penalty term proportional to η·C_q·q_max, quantifying how delayed/asynchronous client updates degrade FedDPO convergence (Theorem 5.4).

Theorem 5.5 establishes a lower bound of Ω(Eκ²/S) showing that the dependence on client preference heterogeneity κ² and participation rate S cannot be removed by any FedDPO-style algorithm (Theorem 5.5).

Theorem 6.1 proves DecDPO (decentralized DPO) converges at rate O(1/√R + 1/(R(1−ρ²))) where ρ is the spectral gap of the communication graph, with variance and heterogeneity terms scaled by 1/(1−ρ²) (Theorem 6.1).

Numerical experiments on the Stanford Human Preferences dataset with N=5 agents empirically confirm the predicted effects of local step count, participation rate, staleness, and network topology on convergence (Section 7, Numerical Results).

1MynM9hkFH.text: At 1.5B parameters with M=8 workers and H=100 inner steps, GlobalM1 (non-blocking Mix1-only gossip) reaches 100% compute utilization at 200 Mbps bandwidth versus 53% for standard DiLoCo (Section 5, Compute Utilization table).

At 10B training tokens (M=8, H=100, global batch size 512), GlobalM1LocalM2 achieves 18.80 validation perplexity, close to DiLoCo's 18.65, while fully synchronous data-parallel training achieves 17.53 (Section 5).

Under a simulated 5% communication failure rate, non-blocking gossip variants sustain higher compute utilization than the all-reduce-based DiLoCo baseline, which must restart synchronization on failure (Section 5.2).

The GlobalM1LocalM2-subset variant, which applies the blocking Mix2 step to only 43% of the 1.5B model's parameters (embeddings, LM-head, and first 2 layers), reaches 45-82% compute utilization and 19.15 validation perplexity at 10B tokens (Section 5).
At 200 Mbps with M=8 and H=100, training to 1T tokens is estimated to take approximately 16 weeks with GlobalM1 versus 29 weeks with standard DiLoCo (Section 5.2).

Figure 5 shows that performance gaps between blocking and non-blocking variants widen as the number of workers M increases to 16 and as the local-step interval H increases to 1000, indicating reduced tolerance to long local intervals at larger scale (Figure 5).

bu2Pcce6Rq.text: DuetServe improves total throughput by up to 1.3x while maintaining low generation latency compared to state-of-the-art LLM serving frameworks (Abstract).
On the Mooncake workload trace with Qwen3-8B, DuetServe achieves 2.72 requests/sec versus 2.14 requests/sec for vLLM, a 1.27x throughput improvement (Section 5, Table 1).

On the Azure-Code workload trace with Qwen3-8B, DuetServe achieves 13.57 requests/sec versus 12.43 requests/sec for the baseline, while keeping time-between-tokens (TBT) below 150ms at QPS=16, whereas baselines exceed 200ms under the same load (Section 5).

The attention-aware roofline model (Section 4.1) predicts iteration latency by distinguishing token-level, sequence-level, and communication operator costs, feeding a GPU partitioning optimizer (Section 4.2) that determines SM allocation between prefill and decode phases (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).

DuetServe dynamically activates fine-grained SM-level spatial multiplexing (via libsmctrl) only when latency SLO violations are predicted, otherwise operating in an aggregated (non-multiplexed) mode by default (Section 4.2).

Ablation studies (Figures 8-10) validate the accuracy of the roofline latency model and the effectiveness of the SM partitioning optimizer compared to static or token-budget-based partitioning (Figures 8-10).

YJhBBARWHv.text: The persona-induced latent variable model admits a closed-form Bayesian posterior update, p(θ|Y_I_t) ∝ p(θ)∏_{i∈I_t} μ_{θ,i,Y_i}, avoiding nested Monte Carlo approximations used in prior adaptive testing methods (Section 3).

On synthetic well-specified data, at T=5 queries the greedy persona-based method achieves log loss of approximately 1.089 versus approximately 1.207 for the CAT-GRM baseline, with persona methods substantially outperforming IRT baselines (Section 4).

On WorldValuesBench with real users, at T=5 queries greedy adaptive querying achieves log loss of approximately 1.019 versus approximately 1.074 for CAT-GRM, though the gap narrows as query budget grows under model misspecification (Section 4).
A dictionary compression ablation shows performance remains robust with only about 200 personas, down from the full dictionary of 2,058 personas (Section 4, Ablations).

Non-adaptive persona-based methods complete inference in under 1 minute, while greedy adaptive querying takes approximately 40 minutes, compared to 20-159 minutes for CAT baselines depending on dimensionality (Section 4, Computational Efficiency).

ZFDFVLjrka.text: On modular addition state tracking at modulus m=5 and sequence length L=20, Transformers require chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision to reach 1.7K samples for a solution that RNNs achieve with outcome supervision alone, while Transformers under outcome supervision require roughly 2M samples (Section 3, Observation 3.1).
Observation 3.3 shows RNNs outperform Transformers by orders of magnitude in sample efficiency when trained with outcome (non-CoT) supervision on state-tracking tasks (Section 3, Observation 3.3).

Observations 3.4-3.5 show RNNs benefit from training on longer sequences while Transformers do not, and that for RNNs shorter training sequences are more sample-efficient than longer ones (Section 3, Observations 3.4-3.5).

Section 4 defines a weight-sharing factor κ measuring cross-length parameter reuse: Transformers trained with CoT show κ=0.28 (destructive interference across lengths), while LSTMs and Dense-SSMs trained with aligned CoT (ACoT) show κ≫1, indicating effective amortized learning (Section 4, Table in Section 4).

High weight-sharing factor κ is shown to predict successful length generalization, while low κ predicts failure, correlating the Section 4 metric with the length-generalization behavior observed across the 190,000+ training runs in Section 2 (Section 2, Section 4).

DkLQ40hTlt.text: Noisy parities are D-DS-PAC learnable by an explicit efficient algorithm using m(epsilon) = O(d^2 log^2(d)/epsilon / (1-2eta)^2) samples, despite being conjectured computationally hard under the standard PAC model (Theorem 4.3).
Noisy parities are also D-DS-PAC learnable using a stylized layerwise SGD procedure on a 2-layer neural network with L1 regularization and sparsity-dependent initialization (Theorem 4.5).

Noisy k-juntas are D-DS-PAC learnable via a Correlational Statistical Query algorithm using O(d^k + 2^k) queries, and are R-DS-PAC learnable via stylized layerwise SGD with a covariance loss using m = O~(d log(1/epsilon) / epsilon^2) samples (Theorems 4.6 and 4.8).

Any polynomial-size circuit with label noise is universally f-PDS learnable by SGD on specially constructed networks with polynomial sample complexity and runtime, though this construction requires designing the training distribution around the target function (Theorem 3.2).

The paper establishes a hierarchy of learnability notions showing D-DS-PAC learning implies non-adaptive membership query (NA-MQ) learning, and NA-MQ learners can be converted into R-DS-PAC learners with sample complexity m(epsilon) = O(m0(epsilon/2) * (log m0(epsilon/2) + log(1/epsilon))) (Theorems 5.2 and 5.3).

The benefit of positive distribution shift for tractable learning is argued to be primarily computational rather than statistical, since PDS can enable polynomial-time algorithms without reducing information-theoretic sample complexity (Section 4, Abstract).

v2rdJBVVEt.text: In graph collaborative filtering, the user-item prediction score decomposes into four neighbor-pair types (User-User, Item-Item, User-Item, Item-User) aggregated via normalized adjacency matrices, as shown by the forward-pass decomposition (Section 3).

Gradient analysis of the standard Sampled Softmax (SSM) loss shows its updates depend primarily on item-side structural similarity while underweighting user-side structural similarity across neighbor pairs (Section 5, Limitation 1).
SSM applies a uniform weighting criterion across all four neighbor-pair types even though empirical studies show distinct optimal retention ratios per pair type (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

The proposed Neighbor-Type-aware Sampled Softmax (NT-SSM) loss, using bidirectional contrastive objectives with type-specific coefficients, improves NDCG@20 on MovieLens-1M from 0.2648 (SSM baseline) to 0.3216, a 21.45% relative gain (Section 7, Table 1).

NT-SSM yields a 10.39% improvement over LightGCN on the Amazon-Book dataset, with consistent 5-12% gains when combined with SimGCL and NCL backbones across four datasets (LastFM, MovieLens-1M, Yelp, Amazon-Book) (Section 7, Table 1).
NT-SSM preserves the O(|E|(|B_u|+|B_i|)d) asymptotic complexity of SSM, adding modest overhead of 8.70 seconds per epoch on MovieLens-1M versus 6.16 seconds for standard SSM (Section 7.5, Table 3).

hh1FITGR8C.text: HistBench comprises 414 questions (306 exact-match and 108 multiple-choice) spanning 29 languages and multiple historical periods, authored and reviewed by more than 40 contributors including PhD students and domain experts (Section 3.4.1, Section 3.4.2).
HistAgent based on GPT-4o achieves 27.54% pass@1 and 36.47% pass@2 accuracy on HistBench (Table 5).

HistAgent significantly outperforms GPT-4o with online search (18.60% pass@1), DeepSeek-R1 (14.49% pass@1), Grok 3 (17.63% pass@1), and Open Deep Research-smolagents (20.29% pass@1, 25.12% pass@2) on HistBench (Table 5, Table 6).

HistAgent achieves 60.00% pass@1 accuracy on the GAIA validation benchmark, compared to 55.15% for Open Deep Research (HuggingFace/smolagents) on the same split, indicating domain-specific customization does not hinder general-task performance (Table 7).

Questions in HistBench were filtered during a multi-stage review pipeline that excludes items solved by more than two of several strong LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) tested without access to supporting materials, followed by professional historian review (Section 3, Figure 3).

ALVnRcngPb.text: Small Agent Group (SAG) uses four specialized agent roles—Reasoning, Knowledge (retrieval-augmented from PubMed, CDC, FDA labels, and clinical guidelines), Safety-Check, and Synthesis/Judge agents—coordinated via multi-agent debate (Section 2).

SAG with a Qwen-4B backbone achieves 91.4% correctness on MedQA versus 82.4% for a single PPO-tuned Qwen-72B model, and reduces the worst-case cross-benchmark performance gap from 30.9% to 7.0% (Table 2).

SAG (CTDE variant) achieves a 0.8% average counterfactual divergence rate on EquityMedQA-based fairness evaluation, versus 2.4% for single-model Qwen-72B, indicating greater demographic invariance (Table 4).
Under adversarial perturbations on NEJM-MedQA, SAG maintains approximately 64% accuracy compared to approximately 45% for single pretrained models, a 19-point robustness improvement (Figure 5).
SAG (CTDE) reduces output variability under stochastic decoding to a standard deviation of +/-0.12 to +/-0.51 versus +/-2.42 to +/-6.83 for single models, a 10-60x gain in consistency (Table 5).

Compared to single 70B-parameter models, SAG reduces memory footprint by roughly 35% (79.5-96.8 GB vs. 132-148 GB) at the cost of about 2x higher inference latency (58.7-63.9s vs. 27-28s) (Table 6, Appendix C).

COQV7D1dAW.text: The paper identifies the Prompt Boundary Problem, where BPE-tokenized language models produce distorted outputs when a prompt ends mid-token, because sampling occurs from the token-conditioned distribution (Equation 1) rather than the desired byte-conditioned distribution (Equation 2) (Section 2, Figure 1).

ByteSampler converts tokenized autoregressive LMs to operate at the byte/character level at inference time using a Valid Covering Tree that maintains all valid token sequences matching a byte prefix, proven correct via Proposition 3.1 and updated via a streaming tokenization algorithm (Section 3, Algorithm 1, Figure 2).
ByteSampler requires only 24.24 inference tokens on average versus 72.99 for Byte-Pair Correction, a 65% reduction among exact correction methods (Table 3).

On English text with OLMo2-1B, ByteSampler achieves 0.81 bits-per-character (matching the original model's 0.80) and 81.56% next-character prediction accuracy, versus 76.28% for Token Alignment; on Chinese with Qwen3-1.7B it achieves 3.23 bits-per-character versus 5.16 for naive methods (Tables 4-7).

A byte-level ensemble of three different-tokenizer models (Qwen3, OLMo2, Llama 3.2) outperforms any individual constituent model across seven downstream tasks, e.g. 0.755 accuracy on LAMBADA versus 0.727 for the best single model (Table 8).

Proxy-tuning Llama-3.1-8B with OLMo2 expert/anti-expert models at the byte level improves instruction-following performance, raising GSM8K accuracy from 55.3% (baseline) to 76.6% and reaching 59.5% on MMLU (Table 9).

k9DhP16RZt.text: CMI-RM (after fine-tuning) achieves an SRCC of 0.8195 on MusicEval, versus 0.7140 for the SongEval-RM baseline (Table 2).
On CMI-Pref preference accuracy, CMI-RM reaches 78.20% versus 65.80% for Gemini 3 Pro, while the general MLLM Qwen2-audio reaches only 5.99% (Table 2).
Peak compositional-alignment accuracy of 82.40% is achieved when all three modalities (text, lyrics, and audio) are present, compared to 79.20% for audio-only conditions (Table 3).
Training on CMI-Pref alone yields 0.6116 mean cross-benchmark SRCC versus a 0.3925 baseline, and joint training on CMI-Pref plus MusicEval reaches 73.43% accuracy on Music Arena (Table 4).
Best-of-N reranking with CMI-RM improves generation quality monotonically for MusicGen-small across N in {1,3,10}, but shows diminishing returns beyond N=3 for Stable-Audio-Open (Table 5, Figure 3).

CMI-RM's architecture uses frozen MuQ-MuLan encoders with a 4-layer Prompt Transformer and a single-layer Joint Transformer, trained in two stages with dual musicality/alignment output heads (Figure 2).

M4bE60aa1C.text: TN-SHAP-G achieves 0.9979 cosine similarity with exact order-1 Shapley values on the Benzene dataset using only 50 queries, and 0.9933 on Mutagenicity (Table 1).
The GraphSVX sampling-based baseline exhibits high variance, with cosine similarity ranging between 0.30 and 0.45 on the same small-graph correctness benchmark (Table 1).
TN-SHAP-G reaches 0.95 cosine similarity to exact Shapley values using 10-100x fewer oracle queries than baseline sampling methods (Figure 4).
Theorem 3.4 proves tensor-train representations generically require bond rank Ω(chi^2) versus chi for graph-aligned tensor networks on cycle graphs (Theorem 3.4).
Theorem 3.6 establishes a near-linear teacher-query complexity of M = O~(|V| chi^Delta / epsilon^2) for bounded-degree graphs (Theorem 3.6).

An ablation shows graph-aligned tensor networks outperform tensor-train representations under matched parameter budgets, with tensor-trains sensitive to node ordering while graph-aligned networks are ordering-invariant (Figure 6).

mEfh2cH3AW.text: McDiffuSE improves accuracy over the ReFusion plan-and-infill baseline by 19.45 percentage points on MBPP (73.57% vs 54.12%) and by 4.9 points on MATH500 (47.80% vs 42.90%) (Table 1).

Non-sequential slot orderings are essential to performance: MCTS-selected orderings follow strict left-to-right order only 91.1% of the time on coding tasks and 93.8% on math tasks, and among cases where a non-sequential decision flips an answer from failure to success, 60.7% involve such deviations (Section 6).

Larger exploration constants matter more than additional simulation budget: with exploration constant c=2, output entropy collapses from 1.41 to 1.18 bits as simulation count increases, whereas c=100 keeps entropy near 1.43 bits (Section 6, Table 2).
McDiffuSE produces substantially shorter outputs than autoregressive baselines, cutting token counts by 88.05% on MBPP and 93.53% on GPQA while still improving accuracy (Table 4, Section D.1).
Coding tasks benefit roughly 3.13x more from MCTS-based slot-selection than reasoning/multiple-choice tasks (t=2.97, p=0.041) (Section D.2, Table 5).

w6FXg6d6My.text: HyTE-FH achieves a mean MTEB task score of 56.41 versus 54.11 for the Euclidean EucBERT baseline (Table 1).
HyTE-H with ModernBERT initialization achieves up to 29% gains in RAGBench context relevance (0.904 vs 0.701 for GTE) and answer relevance (0.832 vs 0.684 for Gemma) (Table 3).
Outward Einstein Midpoint (OEM) pooling substantially outperforms CLS-token pooling, 56.41 vs 49.33 mean MTEB task score (Table 4).

Hyperbolic embeddings encode document specificity through norm: HyTE-FH shows a +20.2% radial increase from general (Level 1 norm 2.902) to specific concepts (Level 5 norm 3.488), while Euclidean baselines show flat or roughly 30% decreasing norms (Figure 4).

Theorems 4.6 and 4.7 prove that Outward Einstein Midpoint preserves radial hyperbolic structure better than the standard Einstein midpoint via explicit radius-dependent weighting (Theorem 4.6, Theorem 4.7).
Proposition 4.3 shows naive Euclidean averaging in ambient space contracts representations toward the origin, destroying hierarchical structure (Proposition 4.3).

mrtg4NmvAe.text: Theorem 3.7 proves an upper bound on excess risk of B_p* * B_X * M/sqrt(D) under an M-coverage condition on depth-D DAGs, extending networked information aggregation from squared loss to Binary Cross-Entropy-based binary classification (Theorem 3.7).

Theorem 4.5 proves a matching lower bound showing instances with excess loss of at least Omega(k/D), where k is feature dimension and D is path depth, establishing network depth as a necessary bottleneck (Theorem 4.5).
Lemma 3.1 establishes an orthogonality property of Binary Cross-Entropy residuals, E[x(p*(x)-y)] = 0, replacing the variance-decomposition tools used in prior squared-loss analyses (Lemma 3.1).
Lemma 3.3 provides a KL/Bregman-type loss decomposition L(q) = L(p*) + D(p*||q), used with Pinsker-style bounds to connect BCE progress to prediction error (Lemma 3.3).

The protocol models a sequential DAG in which each agent observes only a subset of features, receives parent logits (not probabilities), and locally minimizes Binary Cross-Entropy before passing its own logits downstream (Section 2).

1kmTTgPJAm.text: Approximately 73% of identified lexical task heads overlap between instruction-based and example-based prompts for the same task, indicating a shared underlying representation (Section on Shared Components Across Prompting Styles).

Across 13 autoregressive transformer models from the Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families and 17 simple tasks, prompts that produce correct answers activate lexical task heads more strongly than prompts that fail (Experimental Scope; Behavioral Variability Explanation).

The many-shot effect, where both the number and activation strength of lexical task heads increase with more few-shot demonstrations, explains improved performance on 14 of the 17 evaluated tasks (Key Mechanisms: Many-Shot Effect).

Controlled activation of language-specific lexical task heads steers 90% of code-generation outputs to the intended programming language (Python vs. JavaScript) at moderate scaling factors (Key Mechanisms: Code Steering).

Causal ablation/activation effects of lexical task heads on task performance range from 10% to 90% depending on the task, indicating the mechanism only partially explains behavior for some tasks (Important Limitations).

mvhRVG89Nn.text: GenCircuit-RL introduces SynBio-Reason, a benchmark of 4,753 genetic circuits spanning six circuit types and nine tasks (T1-T9), including procedural, Cello, and Literature-91 gold-standard circuits (Section 2, Setting & SynBio-Reason).

On Qwen3-8B, the full method (RLVF-H-C, hierarchical verification reward plus four-stage curriculum) achieves 72.7% average Task Success Rate versus 40.0% for SFT and 44.1% for RLVF-Binary, and reaches 52.6% on out-of-distribution Cello circuits with held-out repressor-promoter parts (Section 5.1, Table of Qwen3-8B Performance).

Removing curriculum staging causes near-collapse on functional reasoning tasks: direct training on Stage-4 reward weights yields only 14.0% average versus 55.9% for the full staged curriculum (S1->S4), and reverse curriculum (S4->S1) reaches only 22.5% (Section 5.2, Curriculum Learning Essential to Functional Tasks).
Ablating individual reward levels shows removing the structure-check term (r_struct) causes the largest average drop, from 72.5% to 62.0% (Section 5.4, Reward Component Importance).

Model-scale analysis across Qwen3 variants (0.6B to 30B) shows functional reasoning performance stays near floor for models at or below 1.7B parameters, then rises sharply to 53.3% at 8B, with only a 1.16x further improvement from 8B to 30B (Section 5.7, Model Scale Analysis).

8lwrYjv6r7.text: SAW-Bench consists of 786 self-recorded egocentric videos captured with Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses, paired with over 2,071 human-annotated question-answer pairs (abstract only).

The benchmark evaluates six observer-centric situated-awareness tasks that require reasoning relative to the agent's own viewpoint, pose, and motion, as distinct from environment-centric spatial relations emphasized by prior benchmarks (abstract only).
The best-performing multimodal foundation model tested, Gemini 3 Flash, shows a 37.66 percentage point performance gap relative to human performance on SAW-Bench (abstract only).

Models tested on SAW-Bench can exploit partial geometric cues in egocentric video but often fail to infer a coherent overall camera geometry, producing systematic spatial reasoning errors (abstract only).

kpdyQ1GDRt.text: For soft-thresholded least squares with penalty lambda_n = o(n), single-algorithm assessment satisfies relative stability, with loss stability gamma decaying as 1/n^2 so that r(h) = Theta(1/n) -> 0 (Theorem 1).

When comparing two soft-thresholded least squares fits with tuning parameters lambda_n and lambda_n + delta_n where delta_n = Theta(1), relative stability fails: r(h) = Omega(sqrt(n)) does not vanish, invalidating the cross-validation central limit theorem needed for confidence intervals (Theorem 2).

Numerical experiments confirm that cross-validation confidence intervals remain valid for single soft-thresholding assessment across moderate sample sizes but fail for pairwise soft-thresholding comparisons even at very large sample sizes (Empirical Validation section).

Ridge regression is shown to satisfy relative stability for pairwise comparisons, in contrast to the Lasso and soft-thresholding, which exhibit relative instability even though each is individually (absolutely) stable (Critical Insight / Empirical Validation).

XWYU5FTRxM.text: Theorem 5.1 (Consistency of Discrete Policy Gradients) proves that as the number of agents M goes to infinity, discrete policy gradients converge to the mean-field policy gradient, using uniform boundedness and compactness arguments based on the Aubin-Lions lemma (Theorem 5.1).

CINOC outperforms the best reinforcement-learning baseline and a classical baseline by wide margins on four PDE control tasks, e.g., 2.9e-4 MSE vs. 0.001 (best RL) and 0.390 (baseline) on 1D heat control, and 3.23 vs. 3.71 and 50.49 on 2D turbulence tracking (Experimental Results table).

Policies trained on small swarms transfer zero-shot with scaling robustness up to about 1.3x training population size in 1D systems and 8-64x in 2D systems, a difference attributed to inter-agent spacing decaying as M^-1 in 1D versus M^-1/2 in 2D (Cardinality Invariance section).
Nonlinear Model Predictive Control requires 590 ms per control step, making real-time deployment infeasible, whereas CINOC shifts this computational burden to offline training (Key Findings).

Conjecture 1 (Self-Normalization) posits that effort regularization induces implicit scaling where individual agent control intensities scale as O(1/M), keeping aggregate forcing bounded as swarm size grows (Conjecture 1).

554mOD1mDp.text: The Bond Smoothness Characterization Test (BSCT) is built from 100 DFT bond-scan calculations across 485 SPICE molecules and quantifies non-smoothness via the Force Smoothness Deviation (FSD) metric (Section 3, Equations 3-4).

Across 70 MD22 trajectories (7 structures x 10 seeds x 3 temperatures), lower FSD strongly correlates with fewer/smaller kinetic-temperature spikes: the vanilla model (FSD=97.4) shows a 9734K max jump at 2000K versus 490K for the combined smearing+temperature model (FSD=43.2) (Section 5.2, Table 1, Figure 6).

Evaluating BSCT takes about 40 minutes on an A6000 GPU versus roughly 40 hours for the corresponding MD stability simulations, a roughly 60x speedup for an equally predictive smoothness proxy (Section 5.2).

The differentiable k-nearest-neighbors (Diff-kNN) module replaces hard-ranked neighbor selection with a soft ranking based on a sigmoid-smoothed distance difference, restoring conservative forces and energy conservation in NVE simulations (Section 4.2).

Temperature-controlled attention (Softmax(QK^T/(tau*sqrt(E_k)))V) combined with controllable Gaussian smearing reduces FSD from 97.4 (baseline) to 43.2 in the ablation study, the best combination tested (Section 5.1, Table 2).

On Matbench Discovery, the MinDScAIP model with 'strong' smoothness regularization (weight decay 5e-2, temperature 10, smearing 10) reduces kappa_SRME by 36% (from 0.77 to 0.49) relative to 'weak' regularization while modestly improving F1 (0.807 to 0.817) (Section 5.4, Table 3).

fRonOqrKWT.text: Theorem 2.13 gives a sample complexity bound for learning a sample-compressible family f* from samples corrupted by additive independent noise (e.g., f*⊗G), requiring n >= N^Clean_{tau,t,m}(6*epsilon, delta/2) + O~(d*tau(epsilon)/epsilon^2 * log(...)) samples for l2 error epsilon (Section 2, Theorem 2.13).

Corollary 2.14 specializes this bound to Gaussian and Laplace noise models, e.g. for N(0, sigma^2 I_d) noise the extra sample cost scales as O~(d*tau(epsilon)/epsilon^2) * log(1+sigma*r) (Section 2, Corollary 2.14).

Claim 2.5 shows unrestricted Gaussian families {N(mu, sigma^2) : sigma > 0} violate the Local Lipschitz Decodability condition (Assumption 2.1) and are therefore not learnable under this noise model, establishing necessity of the assumption (Section 2, Claim 2.5, Assumption 2.1).

Theorem 3.2 establishes a sample complexity bound for total-variation learnability under adversarial corruption of s samples with l-infinity budget C, without requiring the Low-Frequency Property (Assumption 2.9) needed in the additive-noise setting (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).

Section 4 derives the first sample complexity bounds for learning k-mixtures of uniform distributions (k-UMMs) under both additive noise and adversarial corruption, and for k-component Gaussian mixture models under adversarial corruption with n >= O~(s*k*d^2/epsilon^2)*log(1/delta) + O~(d*s^2/epsilon^2)*log(1+C/delta) (Section 4).

UHuu4jgy2u.text: SPECIAL (Server-Proximal Efficient Continual Aggregation for Learning) modifies FedAvg only at the server by blending the aggregated model with the previous task's final parameters via a closed-form proximal update theta^{t+1} = (1/(1+lambda))*theta_bar^{t+1} + (lambda/(1+lambda))*theta^{i-1} (Algorithm 3, Equation 6).

Theorem 1 proves a backward knowledge transfer (BKT) bound showing that after training on task K, the loss on any earlier task increases by at most a drift-controlled correction term that vanishes at rate O(1/(t*E*M*N*L*B^2)), shrinking with more communication rounds, local epochs, and participating clients (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 give a task-uniform, non-convex convergence rate of O(sqrt(E/(N*T))) in expected gradient norm for federated domain-incremental learning (FDIL) under partial participation, matching single-task FedAvg rates while holding simultaneously across all tasks (Section 4.3, Theorem 2, Corollary 1).

The FDIL problem setup assumes K sequential tasks share a fixed label space Y while input domains differ across tasks, with M heterogeneous clients and only N < M clients sampled without replacement per round to model partial participation (Section 2.1).

aU2sxdnRuL.text: The Intrinsic Distribution-valued (IDD) method maps streaming empirical distributions to a tangent space at the pre-change Frechet barycenter in 2-Wasserstein space using the radial isometry W_2^2(mu_bar, mu) = ||T_{mu_bar}^{mu} - Id||^2_{L2(mu_bar)}, then applies Hotelling's T^2 and SPE statistics in that tangent space (Equation 6, Proposition 3.4).
Theorem 3.10 gives a sequential false-alarm-control guarantee of the form ARL_0 >= n_0 + 1 + 1/(alpha_T2 + alpha_SPE) via empirical quantile calibration (Section 3, Theorem 3.10).
On Gaussian-translation synthetic streams, IDD achieves up to a 95% reduction in detection delay compared to the best-tuned Log-KDE baseline in high-variance settings, at matched ARL_0 (Table 1).

On the FlowCAP-II flow cytometry dataset (7-dimensional), IDD detects abnormal AML cell populations with F1 approximately 0.75 and ARL_1 approximately 1, versus F1 below 0.4 for Hotelling's T^2 (Real-world case study, Section 5).

On Reddit vaccine-sentiment daily embedding streams (d=20, January-May 2021), IDD's change-point alarms align with real news events such as the April 13 J&J pause, while Euclidean-summary and moment-based baselines produce monotonic drift or noise unrelated to these shocks (Figure 4).

Theorem 3.14 establishes an epsilon-isometry result showing the number of principal components needed for a finite-dimensional tangent-space approximation scales polynomially with the target precision under Lipschitz regularity (Theorem 3.14).

VrY5x2smAd.text: Across 40 evaluated tasks, RLVR training decreased Causal Importance of Reasoning (CIR) on 19 tasks and Sufficiency of Reasoning (SR) on 17 tasks, despite improving outcome accuracy (Section 5, Figure 2).

The correlation between accuracy improvement (Delta Accuracy) and CIR improvement across tasks during RLVR training was weak (Spearman rho=0.17, p=0.31), and only tasks with more than 50 percentage points of accuracy gain reliably improved both CIR and SR (Section 5, Figure 5).

On low-CIR/low-SR tasks, models achieve similar accuracy whether trained with or without reasoning chains, indicating RLVR can solve these tasks without causally relying on the generated reasoning (Section 5.2).

SFT warm-starting with expert reasoning traces before RLVR substantially raises reasoning quality: with only 2-8 traces CIR reaches about 0.18-0.28 and SR about 0.45-0.50, while with 512 traces CIR reaches about 0.40 and SR about 0.75 (Section 6, Figure 6).

Adding CIR or SR as an auxiliary reward term (weighting alpha=beta=1.0) alongside the outcome reward improves both CIR and SR even without any SFT warm-start, while matching the final task accuracy of outcome-only RLVR (Section 7, Figure 8).

A stricter sufficiency variant (SR-) that removes question paraphrasing still improves under the auxiliary-reward scheme, arguing against the improvement being explained by reward hacking (Section 7, Figure 8).

BNGK86bQRr.text: Panini achieves an average F1 of 56.06% across six QA benchmarks (NQ, PopQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, LV-Eval), versus 53.3% for the HippoRAG2 baseline (Table 2).
Panini uses only 319.79 average answer-context tokens compared to 705.27 for chunk retrieval (2.2x more), 8,121.6 for GraphRAG (25x more), and 10,745.1 for IRCoT (30x more) (Table 3).
On the curated Platinum evaluation subset, Panini reaches 79.9% F1 on answerable queries and 72.8% accuracy on unanswerable queries, compared to 72.5% and 58.5% respectively for HippoRAG2 (Table 4).

Panini's Reasoning Inference Chain Retrieval (RICR) performs beam-search-style retrieval over QA-pair chains in a Generative Semantic Workspace (GSW) rather than retrieving raw document chunks, decomposing queries once and following entity-linked hops (Section 2).

Panini keeps the base language model fixed and integrates new experiences purely through an external non-parametric structured memory, contrasted against parametric continual learning baselines in the experimental setup (Section 3).

P4eXtzKPrl.text: COALA reformulates preference fine-tuning of two-layer ReLU networks as a convex optimization problem, eliminating the reference model required by DPO (Section 3, Section 4).
On the EduFeedback dataset with Llama-3.1-8B, COALA uses 1,805.39 total TFLOPs versus 10,253.37 for DPO and 12,352.98 for ORPO, i.e. roughly 17.6% of DPO's TFLOPs (Section 5, Section 6).
COALA runs on a single RTX-4090 GPU (24GB VRAM), while DPO and ORPO baselines are trained on an A100 GPU (40GB VRAM) (Section 5).
On AlpacaEval2 with Llama-3.1-8B, COALA attains a 40.90 ± 0.09% length-controlled win rate versus 40.68 ± 0.10% for DPO and 23.87 ± 0.60% for ORPO (Section 6).
In a human evaluation with 107 participants, COALA achieves a 39.1% win rate on EduFeedback and 42.7% on IMDb, compared to 28.8% and 24.8% respectively for DPO (Section 6).

COALA is evaluated across four datasets (EduFeedback, UltraFeedback, IMDb, HelpSteer) and models spanning DistilGPT-2, GPT-2, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B, Dolphin-2.6-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, showing monotonically increasing rewards during training (Section 5).

A8AxU1GUUl.text: For binary-valued test function classes with finite VC dimension d, the corresponding IPM is strongly evaluable with sample complexity O((d log(1/epsilon) + log(1/delta))/epsilon^2), while unbounded VC dimension gives only 3-weak evaluability, with the constant 3 shown to be optimal (Section 3).

For bounded real-valued test classes, finite gamma-fat-shattering dimension for all gamma in (0, 1/2] implies strong (arbitrary-precision) evaluability, whereas unbounded fat-shattering dimension yields only 3-weak evaluability (Section 3).

Alpha-Renyi divergences for alpha > 1, and KL divergence as their alpha->1 limit, are proven not weakly evaluable from finite samples because their values are dominated by rare, empirically undetectable events (Section 4).

Unlike VC theory for supervised learning, no finite taxonomy of sample-complexity functions characterizes all statistically evaluable IPMs, which admit infinitely many distinct complexity regimes (Section 3).

Perplexity-based evaluation can fail to detect total variation distance or beta-restricted KL divergence without further assumptions, but total variation becomes evaluable under a Delta-closeness-in-ratio (bounded likelihood ratio) assumption (Section 5).

0wCl7EifsY.text: CausalProfiler generates synthetic causal benchmarks specified by a Space of Interest (SoI) tuple S = {M, Q, D} of structural causal model classes, query classes, and data classes, covering all three levels of Pearl's causal hierarchy: associational (L1), interventional (L2, ATE/CATE), and counterfactual (L3, counterfactual total effect) queries (Section on Space of Interest / Three Levels of Causal Reasoning).

Proposition 5.1 provides a coverage guarantee showing that, given sufficiently expressive mechanism families, any causal dataset within a specified SoI has positive probability of being generated (Section 5, Proposition 5.1).

In Experiment 1 on diverse SCMs, DCM attains the lowest error (0.153) on Linear-Medium settings but with extreme outliers (max error 33.98), while VACA is the best performer on NN-Medium settings with error 0.009, showing method rankings are highly sensitive to the functional form of the mechanisms (Experiment 1).

In Experiment 2 on Regional Discrete SCMs, CausalNF fails completely (100% failure rate) on larger discrete graphs, whereas DCM shows only an 11.32% failure rate, with performance for both degrading as the number of variable categories increases to 4 (Experiment 2).

CausalProfiler introduces Regional Discrete SCMs, a novel model class supporting controllable stochasticity through noise regions, used to probe robustness under discrete-variable settings not covered by prior synthetic benchmarks (Section on Regional Discrete SCMs).

RuZi4or26i.text: Theorem 5.2 gives finite-sample online control guarantees bounding the average counterfactual-harm violation rate by epsilon + (1+eta)/(eta*T) and the average complementarity violation rate by delta + (1+eta)/(eta*T), holding distribution-free with no assumptions on human behavior or problem distributions (Theorem 5.2).

The algorithm adapts two thresholds tau_t and lambda_t online via updates of the form tau_{t+1} = max{0, tau_t + eta(E_t^ch - epsilon)}, using nonconformity scores s(T_{t,r}, y) in [0,1] to construct prediction sets each round (Section on Algorithm & Theory).

In LLM-simulated medical diagnosis experiments on the DDXPlus dataset (GPT-4o-mini as human, DeepSeek-Chat as AI), loosening the counterfactual-harm constraint increases the ground-truth loss rate (abandoning correct initial guesses) from 5.1% to 35.3% (Experimental Validation, DDXPlus experiment).

A crowdsourcing study with 50 participants and 1000 interactions on a collaborative shape-counting visual reasoning task shows that a looser counterfactual-harm threshold (epsilon_ch = 0.30, Algorithm B) produces a higher ground-truth loss rate than a tighter threshold (epsilon_ch = 0.05, Algorithm A) (Crowdsourcing Study).

The framework extends single-round conformal prediction guarantees (Theorem 3.1) to a multi-round setting where the AI's repeated interventions influence evolving human behavior, treating the human as a black box requiring no behavioral model (Theorem 3.1, Section on Technical Innovation).

RZ5uhiNAbx.text: On a 10k-sample COCO benchmark, Contrastive CFG (CCFG) achieves a lower FID of 19.963 versus 21.064 for negated CFG (nCFG) while maintaining comparable removal of negative concepts (Table 3).
In VLM-judged evaluation across four scenarios, CCFG maintains positive-prompt alignment scores of 0.96-1.00 while suppressing negative concepts to scores of 0.00-0.04 (Table 2).

CCFG uses a single constant temperature parameter (tau=0.2) across all experimental settings, whereas the competing Divide-and-Negate (DNG) baseline requires tuning p(c) in [0.01, 0.25] and tau' in [0.2, 0.25] per setting (Table 1, Table 5).
On MNIST and CIFAR-10, CCFG occupies a more favorable error-rate-versus-FID trade-off region than nCFG and DNG, achieving lower error at comparable or better FID (Figure 4).

CCFG is formulated as an optimization problem that minimizes a contrastive loss between positive and negative prompt directions, distinguishing it from the additive negative-guidance term used in standard CFG (Section 3).

The paper shows analytically that the CCFG guidance term flattens toward zero as the epsilon-difference between positive and negative conditions grows, preventing the sampling instability seen in naive negative guidance (Figure 6).

w8D7UPfQYJ.text: HanabiRewards is a dataset of 560 Hanabi games annotated with dense move-level utility labels, used for post-training LLM agents on cooperative multi-agent reasoning (Section 3.3).

RL fine-tuning of Qwen3-4B-Instruct on HanabiRewards yields a 156% performance improvement in the Sherlock setting and a 138% improvement in the Mycroft setting, versus roughly 21% from supervised fine-tuning alone in the Sherlock setting (Section 6.2, Figure 8, Figure 9).
The RL-fine-tuned Qwen3-4B model closes the gap to within about 3 points of o4-mini and surpasses GPT-4.1 by 52% on the Hanabi evaluation (Section 6.2).
On a transfer Group Guessing Game task, the RL-trained model wins 20+ more games than the base model, a greater than 10% improvement across both evaluation rounds (Section 6.3, Table 2).

The HanabiRewards-trained model also improves EventQA temporal reasoning by 6.4% at 800K context length and IFBench instruction-following by 1.7 Pass@10, while maintaining AIME 2025 math performance at 73.3% Pass@10 (Section 6.3).

96zNuQrH9Y.text: TTT-Discover improves the upper bound on Erdős' minimum overlap problem to 0.380876, surpassing AlphaEvolve's previously reported 0.380924 (Section 4.1, Table 2).
TTT-Discover improves the autocorrelation inequality (AC1) upper bound to 1.50286, versus a prior best of 1.50317 (Section 4.1, Table 2).

On the GPUMode TriMul kernel competition, TTT-Discover produces kernels running at 2198.2 microseconds on A100 (versus 4531 microseconds for the best human submission) and 1161.2 microseconds on H100 (versus 1371 microseconds best human), roughly a 2x speedup (Section 4.2, Table 4).
On AtCoder heuristic contest ahc039, TTT-Discover's solution scores 567,062, taking 1st place ahead of the best human score of 566,997 (Section 4.3, Table 6).
On single-cell denoising (PBMC benchmark), TTT-Discover achieves a score of 0.71 versus 0.64 for the MAGIC baseline (Section 4.4, Table 7).

F5XJeuhwU7.text: Neutral-Reference Prompting (NeRP) improves base-to-novel generalization without modifying model parameters, exceeding 5% accuracy gains on unseen classes for EuroSAT and 0.5-2% gains on ImageNet, Flowers102, and DTD, while preserving known-class accuracy (Table 1).

NeRP improves cross-dataset transfer accuracy by roughly 1% on average across 10 target datasets compared to prior prompting baselines (CoOp, MaPLe, CoPrompt, SkipT, CoCoOc, PromptSRC, MMA, MMRL), with no added inference-time computational overhead (Table 2).
NeRP yields improvements on nearly all target datasets under domain generalization (ImageNet variants) evaluation (Table 3).

Proposition 3.5 establishes that the expected logit margin and the neutral-prior gap have consistent sign on novel classes with high probability, providing the theoretical basis for NeRP's bias-correction mechanism (Section 3.3, Proposition 3.5).

NeRP detects asymmetric confusion pairs (exceeding a 15% proportion gap) with 79.7% average consistency, and ablation over the number of confusable pairs K shows an optimum around K=10 on certain datasets (Figure 5, Figure 6(a)).

W85McJPVMI.text: ASyMOB contains 17,092 unique symbolic math challenges generated by systematically perturbing about 61 curated seed problems drawn from U-Math, MathOdyssey, GHOSTS, UGMathBench, OMBU, OlympicArena, and OlympiadBench, spanning integration, limits, differential equations, and series (Abstract).

Average model accuracy is 77% on the unperturbed seed set but drops to 33.4% on the full perturbed benchmark, showing a large sensitivity to symbolic and numeric perturbations that leave mathematical content unchanged (Abstract).

o4-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash show markedly better robustness than other tested models, scoring 75.0% (down 21.7% from seed) and 78.8% (down 21.2%) respectively overall, versus an average degradation of 50.4% for other models, with some perturbation categories causing up to 70.3% degradation (Abstract).
Allowing models to use code execution improves average accuracy by 3.1%, and by as much as 33.1% on specific perturbation categories, compared to symbolic-only reasoning (Abstract).

The authors report evidence of a 'phase transition' in frontier LLMs, where top models combine both high seed-set accuracy (96.8%-97.6%) and much smaller robustness degradation under perturbation than earlier-generation models (Abstract).

kTjSSqgqGf.text: Perturbing raw experience causes substantial performance degradation in ExpeL (offline) and Dynamic Cheatsheet (online) agents, while equivalent perturbations to condensed experience produce little or no change (Figure 2, Figure 3).

In ReasoningBank, where only condensed experience is provided, semantic perturbations to that condensed experience still fail to consistently degrade success rates, even though removing it entirely lowers performance (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

The faithfulness gap persists in the multi-agent G-Memory framework: perturbing raw reference/execution experience causes obvious performance degradation while perturbing condensed experience yields only marginal effects (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

Scaling the Qwen3 backbone from 1.7B to 32B parameters does not resolve the gap—models remain markedly more faithful to raw experience than to condensed representations across all scales (Section 4.4, Figure 6).

Failure-mode analysis on ReasoningBank/WebArena attributes unfaithfulness to distraction (18.8%-79.2% of cases), reliance on incorrect priors (8.3%-33.3%), and premature inference (12.5%-50.0%) (Section 5.1, Table 1).

Integrated-gradients attribution on Qwen3-32B in ALFWorld shows consistently low attribution scores for condensed experience tokens, with current-trajectory context dominating later layers, evidencing an internal local-context bias (Section 5.2, Figure 7).

wqhWZhfaWK.text: Under 2-bit quantization with rank ra=rd=64, ProjQ achieves up to 2x lower evaluation loss for quantization-error compensation than standard PTQ baselines across LLaMA-2, Qwen2.5, and Qwen3 (Table 1).
On C4 at 2-bit, ProjQ attains 21.50 perplexity on LLaMA2-7B versus 26.26 for GPTQ+SVD-LLM, and 33.50 versus 34.17 for LoftQ on Qwen2.5-7B (Table 1).
ProjQ raises LLaMA2-7B common-sense reasoning accuracy from 45.33% to 47.82% at 2-bit quantization (Table 1).

ProjQ at 3-bit precision reaches WikiText-2 perplexity of 5.69 on LLaMA2-7B, matching standard 4-bit LoftQ/QLoRA baselines in the 5.70-6.20 range, i.e. matches 4-bit performance using only 3 bits (Table 2).
On GSM8K fine-tuning at 2-bit, ProjQ reaches 22.90% accuracy on LLaMA2-7B versus 22.52% for LoftQ (Table 2).

MchpJ2Jbw3.text: Theorem 2.5 (Vacuity of Black-Box Evaluation) proves that static black-box alignment evaluation cannot certify post-update alignment for any update dataset, due to model overparameterization (Section 2.2, Theorem 2.5).

Theorem 2.9 shows the amount of post-update misalignment that can be concealed grows linearly with the degree of overparameterization, i.e. with the number of hidden parameters (Section 2.2, Theorem 2.9).
Empirically, Llama3.2-3B and Mistral-7B models that pass standard alignment tests exhibit jailbreak, honesty, and privacy failures after a single benign gradient update (Section 3, Table 1).

Figure 4 empirically confirms an approximately linear relationship between LoRA rank and the maximum number of concealable misaligned sequences, supporting the overparameterization-scaling claim (Section 4, Figure 4).

Figure 2 shows models with divergent post-update behavior that appear identically aligned under static evaluation, illustrating hidden latent misalignment capacity scaling with overparameterization (Section 2, Figure 2).

NlSWKeQPoZ.text: WLA compresses the ERA5 dataset from 244.34 TB to 0.43 TB, a compression ratio of 566.3, producing the unified ERA5-Latent dataset (Abstract; Section 4.4, Table 1).
Table 1 reports separate compression ratios of 625.9 for upper-air variables, 200.3 for surface variables, and 600.9 for precipitation variables (Section 4.4, Table 1).
Ablations varying the number of encoded pressure levels (6, 13, 25) at codebook size 2^128 yield compression ratios of 150.2, 325.4, and 625.9 respectively (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

The Window-ViT-Latent forecasting model trained on WLA latent representations achieves higher SEDI scores for extreme weather events than pixel-space baselines while maintaining comparable overall RMSE (Section 5.2, Figure 6).
WLA is trained on 4 Tesla A100 GPUs using codebook sizes of 2^128 for upper-air/surface variables and 2^32 for precipitation variables (Section 4.2).

sSQdICPJv1.text: The regularized policy update combines reverse KL divergence and entropy regularization (weighted by parameters beta and alpha) with a closed-form analytical solution for the optimal policy pi'(a|s) (Section 4.1, Equations 2-3).
Theorem A.2 formally derives the closed-form regularized policy-update solution via Lagrange multipliers (Appendix A, Theorem A.2).

Using fixed hyperparameters alpha=0.03, beta=0.1, and lambda=e^(-1/8)≈0.88 across all five games, KLENT (the proposed algorithm) achieves roughly fourfold greater sample/compute efficiency than Gumbel AlphaZero on Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, and Othello (Section 5.1, Figure 1, Figure 5, Table 1).

An ablation isolating KL-only, entropy-only, single-step, and Monte Carlo variants shows both KL regularization, entropy regularization, and lambda-returns each contribute to performance across all five games (Section 5.2, Figure 6, Table 2).
On 19x19 Go, KLENT achieves performance competitive with AlphaZero, demonstrating scalability beyond the smaller board-game benchmarks (Section 5.3, Figure 8).

JPbp2S9yTO.text: Divergence Decoding adjusts a target model's logits using two mechanisms: a linear combination of a forget-set model and retain-set model's logit difference (Eq. 1), and a rank-based replacement of the top-k most divergent logits (Eq. 2) (Section 3.1).

On the TOFU benchmark, Linear Divergence Decoding with alpha=1.5 achieves an aggregate score of 0.78±0.01, matching the Retrain baseline and substantially outperforming gradient-based unlearning methods (Section 4.2, Table 5).
The optimal hyperparameter range identified for both TOFU and MUSE benchmarks is alpha≈1.5 and TopK≈20 (Section 4.5).

Scaling the auxiliary model from 1.3B to 2.7B parameters yields a noticeably larger TOFU performance gain than scaling from 1B to 3B, indicating auxiliary model capacity matters more than absolute size (Section 4.4).
Divergence Decoding increases inference latency by less than 0.1% in realistic production configurations (Section 4.10).

Applied to image generation, Linear Divergence Decoding with alpha=1 reduces forgotten-class presence (measured via VQAScore) from 97% to 20% while preserving utility on retained classes (Tables 1-2).

2TVSJxxz9u.text: Training Qwen2.5Coder-32B on Hybrid-Gym alone (without downstream task data) yields improvements of 25.40% on SWE-Bench Verified, 7.85% on SWT-Bench Verified, and 5.11% on Commit-0 Lite (Section 3.2).
The Hybrid-Gym dataset consists of 4,470 trajectories collected across 762 repositories at a construction cost of 0.07 cents per instance (Table 3).
Analysis of coding-agent task transferability finds that approximately 70% of actions in real-world coding tasks fall into categories that do not require an executable repository setup (Section 2.1).

Ablations show that removing file-editing actions from training trajectories causes a large drop in downstream performance, and that training on longer trajectories yields substantially larger improvements (Figure 3).
Increasing repository diversity in the training data improves downstream results, whereas using only in-domain repositories does not inflate performance gains (Figure 4).

t01SKTj8pP.text: Attention Matching achieves up to 50x KV cache compaction in seconds, compared to the gradient-based Cartridges method which requires several GPU-hours per context (Section 1; Table 3 reports ~5 H100-hours for QuALITY and ~15 H100-hours for LongHealth-5).

On Qwen3-4B evaluated on 894 QuALITY questions, Attention Matching traces the accuracy-vs-compaction-time Pareto frontier, outperforming token-eviction baselines and running roughly two orders of magnitude faster than Cartridges at comparable accuracy (Figure 1).

On a 60k-token LongHealth context with Gemma-3-12B, OMP-based key selection takes 565 seconds versus 104 seconds for the accelerated OMP-fast variant, with bias-plus-value fitting adding only about 4 seconds (Table 1).

Combining summarization with AM-OMP reaches 200x total compaction (6340 to 31 effective tokens), achieving 55.7% accuracy versus 71.5% for the full context and 55.2% for summarization alone (Table 2, Section 4.4).
Leave-one-out ablations identify nonuniform per-head budget allocation as the most important component of the method, more so than the attention-bias or fitted-value terms (Figure 4).
At extreme 100x compaction ratios, the gradient-based Cartridges method outperforms Attention Matching on some benchmarks due to its broader representational search space (Section 6).

cCwxV6rSXF.text: FlashSketch achieves a global geomean speedup of approximately 1.7x (1.73x) over prior state-of-the-art GPU sparse sketches across RandNLA benchmarks (Section 1, Table 1).

Against the GraSS SJLT CUDA kernel specifically, FlashSketch attains geomean speedups of 4.17x on Gram matrix approximation and 1.54x on ridge regression; against cuSPARSE-based SJLT it attains 2.67x and 1.42x respectively (Table 1).

BlockPerm-SJLT partitions dimensions into M blocks connected via a kappa-regular bipartite graph of edge-disjoint permutations, with kappa serving as a tunable parameter trading off GPU efficiency against sketching robustness (Section 4, Figure 2, e.g., M=16, kappa=4, s=2).

Theorem 6.2 gives an oblivious subspace embedding (OSE) guarantee for BlockPerm-SJLT in which the required sketch dimension scales with neighborhood coherence mu_nbr(U;pi) rather than full block coherence, with the bound improving as kappa increases (Section 6, Theorem 6.2).
Within the GraSS data attribution pipeline on MNIST, FlashSketch delivers approximately 3.2x end-to-end speedup while maintaining data-attribution quality (Figure 4).

89aKcIeUyP.text: AGRPO achieves 87.3% accuracy on GSM8K, 40.8% on MATH, and 40.0% on Countdown when applied to the LLaDA-8B-Instruct diffusion language model (Section 5.1, Table 1).

AGRPO derives its training objective by reinterpreting the inner token-sum of the GRPO objective as an expectation over denoising timesteps under the uniform measure, avoiding the O(response length) forward passes required by naive GRPO on diffusion LLMs (Section 4.1, Equation 4).

A low-discrepancy timestep sampling scheme reduces gradient variance while provably recovering the original GRPO objective as the number of sampled timesteps k approaches the total number of steps m (Section 4.2).

AGRPO-trained models match baseline accuracy on GSM8K while using 4x fewer sampling steps at inference time, demonstrating that post-training gains persist under reduced-step inference configurations (Figure 3).
AGRPO reports a 3.8x relative improvement over the base model on the Countdown task and a 1.3x improvement over the comparable diffu-GRPO baseline method (Abstract).

kKUrbW8xJ3.text: The Identity Bridge data recipe augments training with pairs of the form 'A is A' using an identity relation whose embedding is the zero vector, formalized as D_id = {[a_i, r_id | a_i]} ∪ {[b_i, r_id | b_i]} for i in [N] (Section 3, Theorem 3.4 setup).

Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct fine-tuned on 100 reversal pairs (e.g., Husband-Wife, Parent-Child) achieves roughly 40% success rate on held-out reversal tasks when Identity Bridge data is added, versus near-0% without it (Figure 6).

In a one-layer transformer trained with Identity Bridge data, Mean Reciprocal Rank on reversal generalization reaches 1.0, whereas without Identity Bridge data MRR remains at its near-random initialization value of about 0.1 (Figure 4).

Theorem 3.4 proves that under the identity-bridge-regularized training set D = D_r+ ∪ D_id, the implicit bias of gradient descent drives the model's output-value weights such that the score for correct reversal answers exceeds that of incorrect answers, i.e., h[b, r-],a(W*_ov) > 0, enabling generalization to the reversal relation.

Reversal generalization is sensitive to entity length: the fine-tuned model reaches up to 100% accuracy reversing short 'number name' entities but only about 7% accuracy on longer entity names (Figure 8).

Without an auxiliary OCR+ style dataset, reversal accuracy plateaus at only about 6% even with Identity Bridge; adding the OCR+ dataset raises accuracy to near 40%, indicating a shortcut-learning failure mode that Identity Bridge alone does not fully resolve (Figure 7).

eibIUtU11k.text: Averaged across 62 downstream tasks, adaptive LoRA merging methods (e.g., AdaMerging, LoraHub, the paper's proposed method) achieve only about 0.65-0.68 accuracy, comparable to simply training a new target-task LoRA (0.657 accuracy), and only modestly better when the target-task LoRA is itself included in the merge pool (Table 2).

When recycled Hub LoRAs in the merge pool are replaced with randomly initialized parameter values, adaptive merging still recovers similar accuracy (about 0.609 vs. 0.650 for real recycled LoRAs, converging to about 0.671-0.675 once the target-task LoRA is included), suggesting the benefit of adaptive merging stems from regularization rather than genuine cross-task knowledge transfer (Figure 3, Section 5 Q3).

Assessed individually, most recycled LoRAs from the Hub yield only 1-5% relative improvement over the base model, with few recycled LoRAs outperforming a target-task LoRA trained from scratch (Figure 1, Section 4.2).

Excluding top-ranked, task-relevant LoRAs from the merge pool causes performance to decay rapidly with increasing task dissimilarity, converging toward the performance of randomly reinitialized LoRAs (about 0.54 accuracy) (Figure 5, Section 5 Q4).

UzEXl80a12.text: The Nous agent, trained via Offline GRPO (OfG) under a Socratic-questioning paradigm, completes scientific diagram generation dialogues in an average of 20.3 turns with 120.5 total information gain, compared to 22.6 turns for a non-trained GPT-few baseline and 25.3 turns for Qwen-zero (Table 1).
Nous (OfG) requires only 28.5 training hours versus 93 hours for an Online GRPO variant, while achieving comparable or better dialogue efficiency (Table 1).

Nous (OfG) attains a 0.68-0.73 win rate across human and GPT-5 judges and a 0.76 weighted VisPainter score (precision 0.83, recall 0.84, readability 0.79) on generated scientific diagrams, exceeding all evaluated baselines (Tables 2 and 3).

Across Expert Oracle, Novice Oracle, and real human-user (3 PhD students) personas of varying expertise, Nous maintains stable output quality scores of 0.74-00.76 with no measured degradation, despite turn counts and total information gain varying (20.3 turns/120.53 IG expert; 24.1 turns/122.47 IG novice; 18.7 turns/128.01 IG human) (Table 4).

An ablation replacing the information-theoretic entropy reward with a heuristic counting reward (Nous-Counting) reduces total information gain to 97.11 versus 120.53 for Nous-Entropy, confirming the entropy-based reward is necessary for efficient Socratic questioning (Table 4).

On a novel collaborative-storytelling task outside scientific diagram generation, Nous (OfG) achieves 15% higher cumulative information gain than untrained baselines, indicating domain-agnostic transfer of the Socratic questioning strategy (Table 6).

QZa5zaj2oP.text: ProMoS distills a frozen self-supervised GNN teacher into a mixture-of-students architecture with one always-active shared branch plus N lightweight personalized student models, sparsely activated per node via a routing network over masked node features (Section 3.2).

Prototype-guided soft-label distillation uses a learnable prototype codebook (initialized via k-means) so that teacher and student node representations are matched via KL divergence over prototype-assignment distributions rather than instance-level features (Section 3.3).

In zero-shot, label-free graph anomaly detection across 11 datasets, ProMoS achieves the best AUROC on 9 of 11 datasets (e.g., 84.56% on Cora, 90.77% on CiteSeer, 89.47% on ACM, 76.17% on BlogCatalog), averaging a 14.12% AUROC improvement over the strongest baseline, DOMINANT (Table 2).
On AUPRC, ProMoS is best on 9 of 11 datasets, including 46.48% on Cora, 46.91% on CiteSeer, and 41.47% on ACM (Table 3).

Ablating prototype-guided soft-label distillation (w/o PSD) collapses average AUROC from 75.46% (full model) to 56.32%, close to random guessing on most datasets, showing this component is critical; removing the discrepancy-aware commitment/refinement loss (w/o DCR) or the self-supervised teacher signal (w/o SSL) reduces average AUROC by 5.26% and 5.53% respectively (Table 4).

ProMoS runs 4.8x faster than GCN during training and 1.4x faster during inference, with inference time scaling sub-linearly with graph edge count (power-law exponent approximately 0.3) (Section 4.4, Figure 2).

fpqfV3lCIB.text: GO-LR (Graph-guided Ordering with Local Refinement) formulates feature ordering as minimizing the dispersion objective sum over edges (i,j) of w_ij|pi(i) - pi(j)| (Definition 3.3, Eq. 2), which Lemma 3.8 shows is equivalent to the weighted Minimum Linear Arrangement problem, proven NP-hard and shown to strictly generalize the TSP-path problem (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.1).

GO-LR is computed via a three-step algorithm: nearest-neighbor TSP-path initialization, direction selection, and iterative adjacent-swap local refinement that monotonically decreases the dispersion objective (Algorithm 1, Section 3.1).

GOTabPFN achieves the best accuracy on all 8 of 8 HDLSS biomedical classification datasets with average rank 1.00±0.00, including 88.18±10.05% on Colon, 97.44±2.32% on Lung, and 97.54±3.86% on ALLAML (Table 1).
On 8 cross-domain high-dimensional tasks spanning image, biological, text-like, and sensor modalities, GOTabPFN attains an average rank of 1.25±0.66, winning 7 of 8 tasks (Table 2).

On the Colon dataset ablation, the full GO-LR+NSC-pSP pipeline reaches 88.18±10.05% accuracy, versus 86.85±9.16% without the Neuro-Inspired Subunit Compression (NSC) step, 84.21±10.34% with random feature order plus NSC, and only 64.59±3.67% with mean-pool compression and no GO-LR ordering (Table 3).
GOTabPFN yields absolute accuracy gains over the best foundation-model baseline of +4.16 percentage points on GLI-85, +2.60 pp on Arcene, and +2.24 pp on SMK_CAN_187 (Table 4).

gEogY6cPrL.text: Flow Map Reward Guidance (FMRG) reformulates training-free reward alignment as a deterministic optimal control problem, and shows that prior guidance methods DPS, FlowDPS, and FlowChef arise as approximations within this formulation (Section 2, Table 4).

On the GenEval benchmark, the FMRG-J variant reaches 0.80 accuracy at 100 network function evaluations (NFEs), and matches a 0.77-accuracy baseline (FMTT) using only 20 NFEs, a roughly 70x reduction in compute (Table 13, Figure 14).

On latent-space inverse problems (super-resolution, motion deblurring, inpainting) on AFHQ and FFHQ, FMRG-J matches or exceeds baselines including DPS, FlowDPS, FlowChef, and MPGD on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS while using 2-10x fewer NFEs (Table 9).

Two gradient variants are proposed: FMRG-J, which projects gradients via a Jacobian onto the data manifold and performs best on complex reward types, and FMRG-E, a memory-efficient Euclidean-gradient variant that performs better at very low NFE counts, including as few as 3 NFEs (Section 3, Figure 8).

An early-stopping ablation shows that terminating guidance before the final denoising step still preserves most of FMRG's performance gains on both inverse-problem and reward-guided-generation tasks (Table 20, Table 35).

A4wPhPe6nW.text: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct improves held-in performance by roughly 72.56 to 78.62 points across five agent environments (WebShop, SearchQA, TextCraft, AlfWorld, BabyAI) but yields only about 3.32 to 3.44 points of average held-out improvement on unseen environments (Table 3, Section 5).

Training on BabyAI and transferring to WebShop causes severe negative transfer, dropping WebShop performance from 44.1 to 10.25 points for the 7B model, attributed to BabyAI's reliance on action validation eroding general reasoning (Section 5, Table 3).

Cross-environment transfer quality correlates with shifts in semantic priors and observation/action interfaces between source and target environments rather than with reward density alone (Section 5, Section 7).

Sequential two-stage cross-environment training across 20 environment-pair configurations produces downstream gains comparable to joint multi-environment training while causing minimal forgetting on the upstream (first-stage) environment (Section 6, Table 6, Figure 3).

Sequential training order matters substantially: performance across different orderings of the same environment pairs can differ by more than 15 points, and an easy-to-hard curriculum ordering tends to emerge as most effective across five environments (Section 6, Figure 5).

7FF8g7hCre.text: iLoRA infers a Poisson-distributed latent interaction graph over input entities and uses it, via a graph neural network, to condition sample-specific generation of LoRA update matrices, combined with Bayesian calibration through Monte Carlo sampling over graph uncertainty (Section 5).
On the Molweni multiparty-dialogue discourse-structure-recovery task, iLoRA achieves 74.51% F1 and 60.57% exact match, outperforming Deep Ensemble and other Bayesian LoRA baselines (Table 1).

On IBD diagnosis (ulcerative colitis vs. Crohn's disease classification from microbiome data), iLoRA achieves 0.7990 AUROC and 0.7617 AUPRC, exceeding the BLoB baseline's 0.7812 AUROC, with a UC F1 of 0.6557 (Table 3, Section 6.3).
iLoRA attains an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.0980 on the IBD task, substantially lower than the standard MLE LoRA baseline's 0.2533 (Table 3).

The inferred latent interaction graphs on the IBD task show 72.7% alignment with cohort-level statistical microbial associations, indicating the learned graphs recover biologically meaningful interaction structure rather than post-hoc artifacts (Section 6.3).

J4sAXji4pl.text: Adding robust diffusion operators (Jacobi-polynomial and Lanczos/Krylov-subspace bases) and hidden-state re-propagation (HRP) to pre-propagation GNNs (PP-GNNs) improves average test accuracy by 2.18 points on 6 heterophilic datasets and 1.96 points on 5 homophilic datasets (Table 2, Table 4).
Enhanced PP-GNNs outperform message-passing GNN baselines on 7 of 12 total datasets evaluated, while retaining PP-GNNs' training-time scalability advantage (Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).

On the Roman-empire heterophilic dataset, the proposed robust operators and HRP close roughly half of the 11.22-percentage-point accuracy gap between message-passing GNNs and vanilla PP-GNNs (Section 5, Table 2).

The hidden-state re-propagation mechanism, which re-diffuses selected intermediate hidden states at stage boundaries during training, adds only about 2% to total training time despite roughly doubling total training time relative to a single-stage baseline when run over 4 stages (Section 5).

An ablation on the pokec dataset (1.6M nodes) across four PP-GNN backbones (including the proposed GARNN) quantifies the separate contributions of the robust diffusion operators versus HRP to accuracy gains (Table 5).

u1adSPW25t.text: CoLoRA trains a shared low-rank adapter (A, B matrices) plus per-task personalized matrices (Lambda_i), reducing parameter scaling with the number of tasks k from O(krd) for independent per-task LoRA to O(dr + kr^2) (Section 3).

Theorem 1 proves that Collaborative AltMin recovers the ground-truth regression matrices in a heterogeneous linear regression setting with error bounded by epsilon + kappa^2 * r * sqrt(1 - xi^2), where xi is a task-similarity parameter and the irreducible error term vanishes as xi approaches 1 (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).

On the Natural Instructions benchmark (140 tasks, 50 training samples per client), CoLoRA outperforms Local LoRA, RoLoRA, FedDPA, and ALoRA baselines specifically in medium-to-high task-similarity regimes (Section 5.2, Figure 4).
For the 'remove even elements' task trained jointly with highly similar tasks, CoLoRA improves ROUGE-L from approximately 0.77 (task trained alone) to approximately 0.92 (Section 5.1, Figure 2).

A six-synthetic-task study shows column subspace similarity (Definition 1) correctly separates related task pairs (e.g., counting-alphabetical and counting-numerical) from less related pairs, validating the similarity metric used to predict when collaborative training helps (Section 2.3, Figure 1, Table 1).

Xj7V0wKlE5.text: The Unanimous Prompt Ensemble (UPE) combining Qwen2.5VL-32B and GLM-4.5V-106B achieves 89.8% precision and 93.3% NPV as an outcome reward model (ORM) on CUARewardBench (Table 4).

For process reward models (PRM), the UPE combination reaches 81.7% precision and 85.1% NPV, outperforming the single best VLM GLM-4.5V-106B, which reaches only 69.5% precision and 64.2% NPV (Table 5).
Simple majority voting across VLMs underperforms UPE, reaching only 68.5% NPV for ORM and 60.5% NPV for PRM despite comparable precision (Tables 4 and 5).
Error analysis attributes reward-model failures primarily to reasoning errors (35.8%) and visual understanding errors (30.2%), with knowledge deficiency accounting for 15.1% of errors (Table 7).

CUARewardBench evaluates reward models on trajectories spanning 10 software categories, comparing general VLMs (Qwen2.5VL, GLM-4.5V) against specialized CUA models such as GUI-OWL and SE-WSM-7B (Figure 2, Section 3).

bgM2hmXExQ.text: Theorem 1 shows curriculum post-training reduces the sample complexity of learning depth-K reasoning tasks from Θ((C*)^K) under direct training to Θ(K·C*) under a stepwise curriculum, where C* > 1 is a fixed constant (Theorem 1).

Theorem 3 proves that for curriculum RL fine-tuning on state-conditioned autoregressive reasoning trees (2S-ART), the no-curriculum approach requires sample complexity at least Ω̃(d^(2k*+2)), while a depth-increasing/hint-decreasing curriculum needs only Õ((k*+1)d²) samples (Theorem 3).

Theorem 4 shows an analogous exponential-to-polynomial gap for curriculum test-time scaling: direct querying requires T_data ≥ Ω̃(d^(2k*)) versus T_data ≤ Õ((k*+1)d²) for the curriculum strategy (Theorem 4).

The theoretical framework is developed on a state-conditioned autoregressive reasoning tree (2S-ART) model instantiated with concrete tasks such as parity and countdown, under a PART base-model framework (Section 2.1).
The paper's results are purely theoretical, with formal proofs of polynomial versus exponential complexity but no empirical experiments reported (Section 2).

TTuzGDlGNA.text: PTA-GRPO consists of two stages: Planning Structured Reasoning Cold-Start (PSR-CS) and Plan Structure-Guided Reinforcement Learning (PSG-RL), described in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 respectively (Section 3).
On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the base model, PTA-GRPO reaches 85.57 versus 82.74 for GRPO, a gain of 2.83 points (Table 1).
On AMC23 with the same base model, PTA-GRPO improves over GRPO by 6.65 points (70.24 vs. 63.59), the largest single-benchmark gain reported (Table 1).
Averaged across MATH500, AIME24, AIME25, and AMC23 with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, PTA-GRPO attains 53.01 average score versus 49.04 for GRPO (Table 1).

PTA-GRPO is evaluated across four base models—Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, LLaMA3.2-3B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B—with improvements exceeding 20 points on average for the weaker LLaMA3.2-3B model relative to its base (Table 1).
A theoretical performance analysis of the two-stage framework is provided separately from the empirical benchmarks (Section 3.3).

XXYhEGXPPF.text: Theorem 1 (informal) shows the adaptive sensing algorithm reaches constant-level alignment with the true eigenvector after O(λ₁λ₂d²/Δ²) iterations, after which the sine-squared alignment error decays as O(λ₁λ₂d²/(Δ²t)) (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 (formal) specifies a warmup phase of t₀ = (4S+1)log(d/2) iterations after which the expected squared sine alignment satisfies E[1-(ūᵀu_{t₀})²] ≤ 0.5, followed by a distinct local convergence phase (Theorem 2).

The paper's rate matches the minimax lower bound Ω(λ₁λ₂/Δ² · d/t) from Li et al. (2018) up to an extra factor of d, which is attributed to the cost of compressive (two-measurement) sampling (Section 3, Theorem 2).
Section 5.1 ('Tracking a Moving Eigenvector') derives a closed-form optimal step size η̂ = √(V/S) and fixed point x* = V + √(VS) for the non-stationary tracking setting (Section 5.1).
Figure 1 empirically validates the theoretical convergence rate of Algorithm 1 using d=10, Δ=1 across 20 trials, reporting 20th/80th percentile error bars (Figure 1).

zlU90YE4EJ.text: QpiGNN uses a dual-head architecture producing a mean prediction ŷ and an interval half-width d̂ via a softplus activation, yielding intervals [ŷ − d̂, ŷ + d̂] without any quantile-level input (abstract only).
QpiGNN is trained with a joint loss combining a coverage term and an L1 width penalty, avoiding the instability of entangled coverage/width objectives used in prior methods (abstract only).

On average across 19 benchmarks (9 synthetic and 10 real-world graphs), QpiGNN achieves about 22% higher coverage and about 50% narrower prediction intervals than baselines including SQR-GNN, RQR-adj-GNN, CF-GNN, ER-GNN, Bayesian NN, and MC Dropout (abstract only).

The method provides theoretical guarantees of asymptotic coverage convergence to the target level 1−α and finite-sample deviation bounds via McDiarmid- and Hoeffding-type concentration inequalities (abstract only).

QpiGNN maintains calibration under feature/target noise, edge dropout, and non-exchangeable data splits, and generalizes across structural shifts between graph types without post-hoc calibration (abstract only).

ubzXPEfa4R.text: For every integer D ≥ 240 and ε > 0, there exists a triplet constraint collection that is realizable in dimension D but for which any embedding in at most c·D dimensions satisfies at most a 1/2+ε fraction of the triplets (Theorem 1.3).

The proof of accuracy collapse proceeds by constructing random average-case triplet instances shown to be satisfiable in D dimensions via Lemma 2.3 and Lemma 2.5, then bounding the achievable accuracy in reduced dimension d ≈ ε²D using a VC-dimension argument (Lemma 2.6, Section 2.3).

Under the Unique Games Conjecture, distinguishing triplet instances with (1−ε)-fraction satisfiability from instances with only 1/2+ε-fraction satisfiability is NP-hard regardless of the embedding dimension used, via a gap reduction from Maximum Acyclic Subgraph (Theorem 1.4, Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Section 3).

Experiments with ground-truth Euclidean embeddings and uniformly random triplets empirically confirm the predicted sharp accuracy collapse as embedding dimension falls below the ground-truth dimension D (Figure 1, Figure 2, Section 4).

uForJvi3CS.text: Across three evaluated models under both prompting paradigms, potential-unsafe and unsafe reasoning categories together account for roughly 80% of chain-of-thought traces, while fully safe CoTs make up less than 30% of cases (Section 3.2).

Even when a model's final output rejects a harmful fake-news-generation request, its internal chain-of-thought can still contain and propagate the unsafe narrative it was asked to produce (Figure 1, Section 3.2).

Safety-critical routing decisions concentrate in a small number of contiguous mid-depth layers, with 87.5% of identified critical-layer cases falling within the central 30%-60% of network depth (Table 2, Section 5.1.2).

Three Jacobian-based spectral metrics—B1 (stability), B2 (geometry), and B3 (energy)—characterize safe versus unsafe reasoning trajectories, with safe reasoning showing lower B1, lower B2, but higher B3 (Section 4, Figure 4).

Indirect prompting shifts the identified critical safety layer deeper into the network than direct prompting by an average of 2.1 layers, and LLaMA-8B localizes this critical separation earlier than the Qwen variants tested (Section 5.1.2, Figures 5-6).

b82fgbMVpz.text: Monitors given access to a model's chain-of-thought substantially outperform action-only monitors across reasoning efforts, evaluated on GPT-5 Thinking, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1-0528, and Kimi K2 (Figure 1 middle panel, Figure 8).

Ranked by CoT monitorability at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI's o3-mini and GPT-5 lead, o3, o4-mini, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi K2 cluster in the middle, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet scores lowest (Figure 1 right panel).

Longer chains-of-thought are generally more monitorable, with the g-mean² metric (the product of true positive rate and true negative rate, where 0.25 denotes a random monitor) increasing as reasoning effort increases (Figure 1 left panel).
Scaling reasoning effort with CoT access improves o4-mini's monitorability by about 12%, compared to only about 4% improvement when scaling reasoning effort with action-only access (Figure 12).
