Monitorability remains largely steady over the course of frontier reinforcement learning training, with monitorability improvements correlating positively with CoT length (Figure 10).

lJjH1q6RwY.text: On LongChat-7B-v1.5, STAR-KV at 75% KV cache compression achieves 60.49% average zero-shot accuracy with WikiText-2 perplexity of 7.34, close to the uncompressed baseline of 6.86 perplexity (Table 1, Section 5.2).

Combining STAR-KV's low-rank compression with 3.2-bit quantization yields an overall 20x KV cache reduction while retaining 59.18% average zero-shot accuracy, outperforming the KVQuant (2-bit) and Palu (4-bit) baselines at comparable settings (Table 4, Section 5.2).
On LongBench with LongChat-7B-v1.5 at 60% compression, STAR-KV attains an average score of 39.09, versus 36.8 for Palu at only 50% compression (Table 2, Section 5.2).

STAR-KV delivers a 6.9x attention-module speedup at 64K context length with 4-bit quantization on an RTX 4090, and a 3.1x average end-to-end generation throughput improvement across context lengths, enabling 128K context on a single RTX 4090 (Section 5.3, Table 5).

Ablating adaptive rank selection shows a large accuracy gap at 75% compression: a static rank allocation reaches only 38.88% average accuracy versus 60.49% for STAR-KV's adaptive scheme (Table 6, Section 6).

cYxavyv2C7.text: On an 8-clause Boolean satisfiability benchmark with expansion factor α=2, Fixed Parameter Expansion (FPE) with clause-aligned splits reaches 99.4% accuracy versus 78.7% for the dense baseline, while random-split FPE still reaches 88.7% (Section 3.2).

Random splitting of neuron weights approximates the gains of precisely clause-aligned splitting, supporting the claim that reduced feature collisions—rather than precise assignment of features to neurons—are the primary driver of the improvement, with theory predicting collision reduction scaling as α^-(2k-1) for k literals per clause (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).

On CIFAR-100 with CLIP embeddings, a random-split FPE model with 32 neurons matches the accuracy of a dense model with over 1.2x more parameters, with benefits most pronounced at fewer neurons and saturating as baseline width increases (Section 3.4, Figure 6).

On ImageNet-1k, FPE improves accuracy from 13.0% to 13.9% (a 6.2% relative gain) at 6 hidden neurons, but only from 46.9% to 47.0% at 16 hidden neurons, showing the benefit shrinks as network width increases (Section A.7, Table A4).

In a 5-layer MLP on CIFAR-100, FPE with hidden width 4 yields a 28% relative accuracy improvement, and combining random FPE with dynamic rewiring improves further by 53% relative improvement over static random FPE at the same 4-neuron baseline (Section A.7).

WCgtvP46NT.text: Exploratory Sampling (ESamp) achieves a higher Vendi score (1.67 vs. 1.62 for vanilla sampling) and lower semantic similarity (0.57 vs. 0.58) on creative writing generation while also achieving the lowest perplexity (3.55) among compared methods (Table 1).

On GPT-OSS-20B, ESamp reaches Pass@64 performance comparable to baseline methods using only Pass@8, demonstrating improved sample efficiency on reasoning benchmarks including AIME 2024/2025, LiveCodeBench v5, and GPQA-Diamond (Section on Pass@k Performance).

The asynchronous training-inference pipeline for the online-trained Latent Distiller introduces overhead ranging from 0.3% (single-user) to 4.25% (test-time scaling with batch size 32, K=16) (Table 3).

ESamp uses a 2-layer Gated SwiGLU MLP distiller with 384 hidden dimensions, trained online with Adam at learning rate 4×10⁻⁴, to predict deep-layer hidden representations from shallow-layer inputs as a novelty signal (Implementation details section).

Ablations show that latent-space distillation substantially outperforms vocabulary-space distillation, and that the method is robust to the novelty-weight hyperparameter β=0.25 across model scales including Qwen2.5-7B/32B and Qwen3-8B (Ablations & Analysis section).

PbXNvEE0jA.text: AutoElicit elicits unsafe unintended behaviors from Claude 4.5 Haiku at success rates of up to 72.5% in the OS domain and 60.8% in the Multi-Apps domain, using only benign, non-adversarial task instructions (Experimental Results section).

Human verification of Claude 4.5 Opus trajectories confirms 60-80% of elicited behaviors as genuine successful unintended harms, with 9.2-10.1% of seed perturbations rated Critical or High severity (Experimental Results / Safety Risk Categories section).

The released AutoElicit-Bench dataset contains 117 human-verified successful perturbations drawn from an AutoElicit-Seed pool of 361 seed perturbations spanning 66 tasks, plus an AutoElicit-Exec set of 132 verified execution trajectories (Datasets Released section).
Perturbations discovered against one computer-use agent transfer to other frontier computer-use agents, including EvoCUA, OpenCUA, and Operator, at success rates of 35-54% (Transferability section).

L6wxelezWk.text: Proposition 4.1 shows that under configuration reweighting from distribution shift, aggregate calibration of a soft-routed mixture-of-experts model fails unless outcome frequencies match predictions configuration-by-configuration, a strictly stronger condition than per-expert calibration (Proposition 4.1).

On the CIFAR-10H hard subset, the proposed Robust-Filtered method (FGR+Robust) reduces expected calibration error from 0.281 (Vanilla MoE) to 0.065, and on the CivilComments hard subset from 0.108 to 0.037 (Experimental Results / Key improvements on difficult subsets).

Per-expert calibration alone (MoCaE) yields only modest improvements in aggregate calibration on CIFAR-10H, PACS, and CivilComments, empirically confirming that calibrating experts individually is insufficient for mixture-level reliability (Experimental Results section).

Two training objectives, Robust MoE (entropic-tilt reweighting with loss ℒ_R-MoE(θ) = Σ q_i^η L_i) and Robust Filtered, are introduced using entropy-balanced adversarial reweighting to restore calibration under distribution shift on PACS domain generalization across four visual styles (Proposed Solutions section).

mii3Lo7N3W.text: On CWAH-MultiPlayer with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, CollabBench's collaborative agentic training paradigm improves task completion efficiency by 15.2-29.3% and affective metrics by 17.2-39.4% (helpfulness), 17.4-37.6% (trustfulness), and 31.5-33.5% (empathy) over the base model (Table 1).
On Cook-MultiPlayer with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the trained agent improves game-score efficiency by 14.1-19.3% and affective dimensions by 4.6-62.7% relative to the base model (Table 1).

CollabBench extends CWAH and Overcooked into CWAH-MultiPlayer (five tasks, two layouts, fifteen personality profiles each, 150 trajectories) and Cook-MultiPlayer (five layouts, fifteen profiles each, 75 trajectories), using Big Five personality theory to simulate diverse player behaviors (Test Environments section).

Training uses GIGPO (Group-in-group Policy Optimization) to jointly optimize a trajectory-level efficiency reward R_e(τ|G) and a step-level affective reward R_a(t_i|P_sim) = R_fmt + R_com + R_int over agentic rollouts with <think>, <message>, and <action> tokens (Collaborative Agentic Training section).

A 15-participant human study confirms that models trained with the collaborative agentic paradigm achieve substantially higher scores across all affective dimensions than the base model, and ablations show removing either personality diversity or the affective reward degrades performance (Human Validation / Ablation section).

4ARH5kZrgz.text: ExpWeaver achieves state-of-the-art results on 12 of 13 tasks across three benchmark suites, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.8% on average on ExpBench-Generic (78.25% average accuracy) (Experimental Results section).

ExpWeaver reaches 69.58% on ExpBench-Sci (pharmaceutical chemistry tasks) and 44.40 NDCG@10 on ExpBench-Rec (recommendation tasks), retrieving and integrating experiences directly in the LLM's hidden states via cross-attention rather than as concatenated text (Experimental Results / Core Components sections).
ExpWeaver maintains token consumption comparable to non-retrieval baselines, whereas text-based retrieval-augmented baselines require 1.5-2× more tokens per query (Efficiency section).

ExpWeaver outperforms baselines by 16.32% under zero-shot transfer and 15.21% under few-shot transfer to new domains, demonstrating generalization of the latent Experience Bank beyond training tasks (Generalization section).

The framework is trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning (GRPO) to jointly optimize the policy and latent retrieval parameters, using a gated residual mechanism to blend retrieved experience representations with the model's original hidden states (Training Methodology / Gated Integration sections).

8NNPSNAvTX.text: Re-FORC's early-stopping strategy reduces inference compute by 26% relative to unconstrained generation while maintaining accuracy on math reasoning benchmarks (Section 4.1).
Using Re-FORC for adaptive model selection yields 4% higher accuracy at equal compute, or 55% less compute at equal accuracy, compared to always using the largest model (Section 4.3).

Applying Re-FORC to test-time scaling increases accuracy by 11 percentage points in the high-compute regime and 7 percentage points in the low-compute regime relative to standard average-of-k/majority-vote scaling (Section 4.4).
Re-FORC is evaluated across five math reasoning benchmarks: AMC 2024, AIME 2024/2025, Minerva Math, and Math500 (Section 5).
Re-FORC uses a lightweight adapter to forecast, via a Beta-distribution based forecaster, the expected future reward as a function of additional thinking tokens generated so far (Section 3).
Figure 2 shows Re-FORC's early-stopping accuracy-versus-token curves dominate fixed token-limit baselines across multiple model sizes (Figure 2).

pO9vQniT8B.text: Existing MLLMs including Video-LLaMA, LLaVA/LLaVA-OneVision, and Qwen-VL/Qwen2-VL variants perform poorly on prompts that jointly require reasoning over point clouds and egocentric video in the REA benchmark (Table 5).
STLLM outperforms these baseline MLLMs on the REA (Reasoning about Environments and Actions) dataset (Table 5).
The REA benchmark is constructed from egocentric video and annotation sources including Ego4D, EPIC-Fields, and VISOR (Method section).
STLLM's architectural components for spatial understanding and temporal grounding are evaluated via ablation, with removal of either component degrading performance (Table 6).
GPT-4o is used as an automatic judge to score open-ended spatio-temporal reasoning outputs from STLLM and baseline models (Table 7).

yzBbBPheg7.text: ARTIST improves average accuracy by 6.46 percentage points over the strongest baseline across time series reasoning benchmarks (Table 3).
ARTIST achieves this accuracy gain while processing a smaller fraction of the input time series than baseline methods, demonstrating the benefit of selective segment utilization (Table 3).
ARTIST is compared against baselines including ChatTS, OpenTSLM, ITFormer, TimeMaster, and general-purpose LLMs such as GPT-5, Llama-3, and Qwen-3 (Section 4).
ARTIST is benchmarked on TSQA, ECG-QA, and TraQA time series question-answering datasets (Section 4.1).
Ablation experiments isolate the contribution of the segment-selection mechanism relative to using the full input time series (Table 5).

mL4i6z7Miy.text: SGD with momentum (SGDM) exhibits an Edge of Stochastic Stability regime whose batch-size-dependent behavior cannot be explained by a single stability threshold, unlike vanilla SGD (Section 3).

In the noise-dominated (small-batch) regime, SGDM's mean-square stability condition reduces to a spectral-radius condition rho(I - eta_eff K + eta_eff^2 G) < 1 with effective learning rate eta_eff = eta/(1-beta) (Theorem 4.1).
Batch Sharpness converges to a plateau of approximately 2(1-beta)/eta at small batch sizes, indicating momentum drives SGD toward flatter regions than vanilla SGD in this regime (Section 4).
Batch Sharpness converges to a plateau of approximately 2(1+beta)/eta for SGDM at large batch sizes, consistent with full-batch gradient descent dynamics and sharper minima (Section 4).

Figure 3 empirically shows batch-size-dependent Batch Sharpness plateaus for MLP and CNN architectures on CIFAR-10, with SGD with Nesterov momentum (SGDN) reaching the deterministic plateau at smaller batch sizes than SGDM (Figure 3).

Figure 6 shows intervention experiments in which increasing learning rate or momentum, or decreasing batch size, triggers sharp loss 'catapults' once Batch Sharpness exceeds its operating plateau (Figure 6).

b2HyJdIZ1F.text: The paper's proposed decoding-stage method increases the mean output length of the base model by 148% (abstract only).
The proposed method reduces length volatility by 69% relative to the base model (abstract only).
The method operates entirely at the decoding stage via logit boosting and requires no additional training or fine-tuning (abstract only).
The paper introduces VOLTBench, a heterogeneous-task benchmark for quantifying length volatility in long-form generation, used to evaluate the method (abstract only).
The method maintains high generation quality despite substantially increasing and stabilizing output length, as assessed on the introduced benchmark (abstract only).

YZIqbdw6zi.text: MCLP is defined as the mean log-likelihood of ground-truth acoustic tokens conditioned on evaluation audio as contextual input, used both as an evaluation metric and as an RL reward signal for role-play TTS (Section 4.1).

The proposed RP-TTS model, trained via SFT and GRPO with a hybrid MCLP+CER reward, achieves CER of 1.130% and Pinyin WER of 0.511%, versus 3.276%/2.031% for Step-Audio-2 and 11.974%/10.510% for GPT-Audio (Table 2).
The proposed model attains a subjective MOS of 3.646, compared to 1.707 for Step-Audio-2 and 1.752 for GPT-Audio (Table 2).
MCLP score correlates with human MOS judgments, with win-rate agreement exceeding 0.8 when the difference in MCLP between two samples exceeds 0.1 (Figure 5).

Ablating the MCLP reward during RL training improves CER to 0.783% but degrades MCLP score to -4.752, while ablating the CER reward causes CER to explode to 61.144%, demonstrating reward hacking without content-fidelity supervision (Table 3, Section 4.3).

GHKj1XcSlt.text: SERA-32B achieves 49.5% ± 1.9% on SWE-bench Verified at 32K context, closely matching the open-weight Devstral-Small-2's 50.0% ± 1.3% despite being fully open-source (Section 4).

Training SERA is 26× cheaper than reinforcement learning (SkyRL) and 57× cheaper than synthetic data methods (SWE-smith) to reach equivalent performance, with total training cost of about $2,000 for 40 GPU-days (Section 1, Figure 3).

Soft-Verified Generation (SVG) verifies synthetic trajectories via partial line-level patch overlap rather than unit tests, and ablations across verification thresholds r=0.0, 0.25, 0.75, 1.0 yield similar downstream performance, indicating strict verification provides no significant benefit (Section 5.1, Figure 5).
Ordered truncation of long trajectories outperforms random truncation, achieving 43.00% ± 1.93% versus 37.47% ± 0.50% (Section 5.2, Table 4).

Repository-specialized SERA-32B models fine-tuned on Django and Sympy reach 52.23% ± 1.64% and 51.11% ± 1.54% respectively at 32K context, matching or exceeding their GLM-4.5-Air teacher's 51.20%/48.89% (Section 4.3, Table 3).

MyorUlHKVc.text: S3 comprises 438 seizure videos from 116 patients (300 epileptic, 138 non-epileptic seizures), with over 35,000 dense annotations covering 20 ILAE-defined semiological features (Table 5, Appendix A.2).
Trained annotators agree strongly with epileptologists, with Pearson correlation r=0.893 for epileptic seizures and r=0.782 for non-epileptic seizures (Table 5, Appendix A.2).

The two-stage neuro-symbolic framework for epileptic-versus-non-epileptic seizure classification (Task 7) achieves F1=0.96, and report-augmented diagnosis yields an average F1 improvement of 21.12% over baseline (Table 2).

General MLLMs perform weakly on fine-grained tasks: the best model reaches only F1=0.32 for spatial/laterality reasoning (Qwen2.5-VL-32B, Task 3) and 8.19s/12.72s onset/offset MAE for temporal localization (Task 4), while Lingshu-32B exceeds 50s MAE on the same task (Table 1).

Seizure-specific fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-Omni raises Task 1 feature-recognition F1 from 0.38 to 0.47 via SFT and Task 4 temporal MAE from 25.50s to 20.02s via GRPO, yielding average relative improvements of 12% (SFT) and 15% (GRPO) across tasks (Table 3).

K5S8N5NgD8.text: EVMbench curates 117 vulnerabilities across 40 repositories (median 1,296 sLOC, median 7 contracts per repository) sourced primarily from Code4rena audit competitions (Table 1, Section 3.1).
In Exploit mode, GPT-5.3-Codex achieves the highest score of 71.0%, demonstrating end-to-end vulnerability discovery and fund extraction against live local Ethereum instances (Figure 3, Section 4.1).

In Detect mode, Claude Opus 4.6 scores highest at 45.9%, earning an average award of $37,824.52 against a maximum attainable payout of $218,434, showing agents capture only a fraction of the maximum extractable value (Figure 3, Table 2).

With medium-level mechanism hints, GPT-5.2 scores 90.2% on Patch mode and 78.3% on Exploit mode, indicating that discovering a vulnerability is substantially harder for agents than repairing or exploiting it once identified (Section 4.1).
GPT-5.3-Codex attains its strong Exploit-mode performance while remaining more token-efficient than competing frontier models (Figure 4).

Iexhb5lL3t.text: Claude Opus 4.5 with screenshot-and-video feedback attains the best pass@1 of 50.0% on GameDevBench, while Gemini 3 Pro reaches 54.5% under the same multimodal-feedback setting (Table 2, Section 4.2).
Without multimodal feedback, baseline frontier models score between 34.1% and 46.2% pass@1, indicating that visual feedback provides a substantial performance boost (Table 2, Section 4.2).
Performance varies sharply by task category: gameplay logic tasks reach 46.9% success versus only 31.6% for 2D graphics tasks (Figure 5, Section 4.2).

GameDevBench tasks require modifying on average 5.0 files across 3.4 filetypes and changing 106.2 lines of code, more than triple the average lines of code changed in SWE-Bench (Figure 4, Section 3.2).

Adding multimodal feedback improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 from 33.3% to 47.7% pass@1, a 42% relative improvement, though video feedback is more effective for Claude models while MCP feedback is more effective for Gemini models (Section 4.1).

vMsrm8UGGC.text: NASH formalizes the notion of a utility function being (epsilon, delta)-Shapley-informative and shows that prediction-correctness functions for individual validation points satisfy this property under a 'Consistent Player' assumption (Definition 3.1, Assumption 3.2, Proposition 3.3).

NASH's data selection objective aggregates per-validation-point Shapley-informative components via a non-linear, learning-curve-based function F_T (e.g. an exponential saturating curve) rather than the linear aggregation implicit in vanilla Data Shapley (Definition 3.4).
A greedy algorithm (Algorithm 1) that adds data points to maximize the NASH objective is shown to yield a (1-1/e)-approximation guarantee when Shapley values are non-negative.

On logistic/ridge regression benchmarks (Wind, Pol, Phoneme, Physiochemical Protein, Auction) and LM finetuning benchmarks (BERT on Rotten Tomatoes/Paraphrase, Llama-2-7B on RTE), NASH consistently outperforms vanilla Data Shapley and other baselines across selection ratios, with gains ranging from about 5-10% on heterogeneous datasets to 20-40%+ on cleaner datasets (Figure 5).

Selecting 10,000 points from 20,000 training data using 5,000 validation points with NASH's pre-computed Shapley vectors incurs approximately 53.4 seconds of wall-clock runtime, essentially no additional cost over computing validation accuracy directly (Section on computational cost).

NASH remains compatible with other semivalue notions, including Beta Shapley and Data Banzhaf, consistently improving their data-selection effectiveness in settings where the vanilla semivalues perform poorly (Section 4.3).

H8KE7sudq5.text: The ScreenParse dataset contains 771K rendered webpage screenshots with 21M dense UI-element annotations spanning 55 semantic classes, split roughly 90/5/5 into train/val/test (693,975 / 38,850 / 38,633 images).

ScreenParse is built via the automated Webshot pipeline: crawling 1 million URLs from the 45 Million Websites dataset, rendering with Playwright at 1440x900, filtering degenerate/off-screen/duplicate boxes, refining labels with Qwen-3-VL-8B-Instruct across 55 classes, and quality-filtering with a VLM-as-judge score threshold of 0.70.

ScreenVLM, a 316M-parameter model (SigLIP-2 encoder plus a 165M-parameter Granite decoder) that outputs a structured 'ScreenTag' markup, achieves 0.606 PageIoU on the ScreenParse test set versus 0.294 PageIoU for the much larger Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Table of ScreenParse test-set results).

On the out-of-distribution GroundCUA benchmark, ScreenVLM attains 0.251 PageIoU versus 0.060 PageIoU for Qwen3-VL-8B, demonstrating transfer of dense screen-level supervision to unseen multi-platform UI grounding.

ScreenVLM achieves Recall@50 of 0.557 on ScreenSpot-Web, 0.222 on ScreenSpot-PC, and 0.066 on ScreenSpot-Mobile, while running at roughly 4x the throughput (3.62 vs 0.78 samples/second) and about 6x smaller footprint (632MB vs 4300MB) than comparable 2B-parameter VLMs (Efficiency section).

Finetuning existing foundation VLMs on ScreenParse consistently improves their grounding performance across architectures, supporting the claim that dense, screen-level supervision provides transferable structural priors for UI understanding.

zIHEctNlcP.text: The method minimizes a combined objective of MSE one-step prediction loss plus a Wasserstein-distance regularization term between adversarially learned summary-statistic distributions of true and predicted trajectories (loss formula in Section on core method).

Two instantiations are proposed: a WGAN-style critic estimating the dual 1-Wasserstein distance, and an entropy-regularized Sinkhorn divergence that avoids explicit Lipschitz constraints on the critic (Method section, Section 4/5 per numbering in text).

A theoretical noise-robustness analysis (Proposition 5.1) shows MSE-only training exhibits exponential error blow-up with rollout horizon k, scaling as approximately dσ1^2 + σ2^2 · d · e^(2·λmax·k), whereas the adversarial OT regularizer remains bounded because ergodic mixing 'forgets' initial-condition noise over long rollouts.

On Lorenz-96 (60-dimensional), the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (256 points), and 2D Kolmogorov flow, the WGAN-style variant attains a leading Lyapunov exponent of 2.336 versus a ground-truth value of 2.334, closely matching chaos characterization metrics (Experimental Results section).

The learnable adversarial-OT methods consistently outperform an MSE-only baseline and match or exceed a handcrafted-feature OT baseline on L1 histogram error and spectral distance metrics for unseen attractor statistics, using training on a single noisy observed trajectory rather than multi-environment datasets (Experimental Results section).

9XeX2YHKye.text: RoPE-Perturbed Self-Distillation trains with two forward passes per step: a standard-view pass with unperturbed RoPE position indices and a perturbed-view pass with shifted RoPE indices (e.g. skip-based offsets to suffix positions), with a KL-divergence self-distillation loss aligning the perturbed view's predictions to the standard view's (Method section).

On RULER at 64K context length, RoPE-Perturbed Self-Distillation (skip variant) raises Llama-3-8B-Instruct average accuracy from a 57.25% standard baseline to 69.29%, a 12.04 percentage-point improvement (RULER Benchmark Results section).
On RULER at 256K context length, the same skip variant raises Qwen-3-4B average accuracy from a 67.01% baseline to 68.10%, a 2.71 percentage-point improvement (RULER Benchmark Results section).

The skip-based RoPE perturbation (preserving token order while introducing position-space gaps) is favored over a more aggressive cyclic-shift variant that rotates all position indices modulo sequence length (Perturbation Variants section).

Gains from the method persist after supervised finetuning on instruction data, short-context performance remains comparable to baseline models, and improvements extend to extrapolated context lengths 2-4x beyond the training window (Key Findings section).

XNXU8BJRT7.text: Theorem 3.1 proves there is no algorithm for perfectly learning a general C-RASP program from finite training strings, even restricted to depth-two (2-layer) programs, implying no computable non-asymptotic length-generalization bound exists for such transformers.

The undecidability proof reduces Hilbert's 10th Problem to the emptiness problem for C-RASP-definable languages by encoding Diophantine equations via regulated formulas, showing language equivalence for C-RASP is undecidable (Section 3, Theorem 3.1 proof).

For the restricted positive fragment C-RASP+, the paper proves a computable length-generalization bound: training strings of length exponential in the program size are both necessary and sufficient for exact learning, established via a translation to temporal logic TL[diamond-hat] with polynomial witnessing strings.

Fixed-precision transformers (with rounding inside attention) are shown to admit exponential-length learning bounds, in contrast to the uncomputable bounds for general (non-fixed-precision) transformers and C-RASP with 2+ layers.

The paper argues its theoretical uncomputability/exponential-bound results hold independent of model initialization, learning rate, or other training hyperparameters, aligning with empirical observations that length generalization in transformers is fragile and often incomplete.

ghd0zmtpB9.text: The Most Influential Sets (MIS) problem for estimands with linear-fractional leave-set-out effects is reduced to a one-parameter sequence of top-k selections solved via Dinkelbach's method (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1)
Algorithm 1 costs O(n) per iteration and provably terminates in at most M+1 ratio updates, where M is the number of distinct achievable ratio values, returning a globally optimal set (Theorem 1)

Under a uniform-denominator and generated-score-stability assumption, the empirical selection objective uniformly approximates the oracle orthogonal-score objective with o_p(1) error, yielding selection consistency given a separation condition on the ratio gap (Theorem 2)
At n=10^6 and k=10^5, the algorithm's median wall-clock runtime is below 200ms, converging in a median of three ratio-update iterations (Section 4.1.2)
A warm-start variant (Algorithm 2) traces the most influential set across k=1,...,K by initializing each successive top-k problem from the previous solution (Section 3.2)

4pQVVSKdkH.text: ExCyTIn-Bench builds bipartite incident graphs from 8 real cyberattacks staged in a controlled Azure tenant ('Alpine Ski House'), generating 589 test questions from a pool of up to 7,542 possible questions (Section 3, Table 1)
The benchmark's SQL environment spans 57 log tables (8 to 139 columns each) collected over 44 days, sourced from Microsoft Sentinel (Section 3)
Across 13 baseline models, o4-mini achieves the highest average reward of 0.368, GPT-4.1 reaches 0.338, and the average reward across all evaluated models is 0.249 (Section 4.1, Table 2)
Adding agentic strategies improves scores substantially: ReAct+Reflect with k=3 trials reaches 0.563 reward using GPT-4o, versus 0.390 for single-trial Expel (Table 3)
The benchmark's reward structure discounts intermediate-step credit with a factor gamma=0.4 to score partial investigation progress (Algorithm 2)

jNv4sl4YZH.text: A calibrator is defined as set-preserving when converting conformal p-values at level alpha into e-values yields prediction sets identical to thresholding the e-values directly at 1/alpha (Section 2.1, Definition 2.2)

Among left-continuous p-to-e calibrators, only the all-or-nothing calibrator can be exactly set-preserving, which motivates a new sigmoid-based P2E construction (Proposition 2.3, Theorem 2.6, Equation 9)

The proposed sigmoid-based P2E calibrator is exact (expectation equal to 1), smooth, invertible, strictly positive, and strictly dominates the all-or-nothing calibrator in aggregation settings (Theorem 2.6)

Applied to e-Cross-Conformal Prediction (ECCP), the P2E calibrator preserves exact 1-alpha coverage, whereas standard cross-conformal-prediction variants only guarantee approximate 1-2alpha coverage (Proposition 4.1)
Applied to Weighted Conformal Aggregation (WECA), data-dependent weighted merging of e-values across multiple models retains valid coverage (Proposition 4.2)
Empirically, ECCP using the proposed P2E calibrator produces smaller prediction sets than baseline p-to-e conversion methods while maintaining valid coverage (Section 5)

1U0lhpW0VL.text: In a day-0 mixed-traffic deployment, Aurora reaches 302.3 tokens/s throughput with an average acceptance length of 3.08, exceeding the static-speculator baseline's acceptance length of 2.63 (Section 4.1)

Under a domain/distribution shift, Aurora's speculator adapts and converges to an acceptance length of 2.46 within about 10,000 requests, approaching the pretrained-baseline acceptance length of 2.57 at 295.6 tokens/s (Section 4.1)

On the frontier model MiniMax M2.1 (229B), Aurora yields 1.45x throughput over the no-speculation baseline at batch size 4, with speedups ranging from 1.57x (batch size 1) down to 1.25x (batch size 32) (Section 6, Table 1)
On Qwen3-Coder-Next (80B), Aurora achieves 1.51x speedup at batch size 1, 1.23x at batch size 8, and 1.09x at batch size 16 (Section 6, Table 1)

A synchronization-policy ablation shows that updating the speculator roughly every 80 requests balances acceptance-length recovery against throughput better than a more aggressive 48-request update schedule (Section 4.2, Figure 5)

Online fine-tuning of the speculator substantially outperforms a frozen speculator under distribution shift, with only marginal differences observed between the training strategies tested (Section 5, Figure 6)

LfUXGnwVzw.text: The cross-fitted one-step doubly robust estimator for the Smoothed Conditional Distributional Treatment Effect (SCoDiTE) converges weakly to a tight Hilbert-valued Gaussian process at the n^{-1/2} rate under nuisance convergence conditions (Section 2.3, Theorem 3.1)
This cross-fitted SCoDiTE estimator attains local asymptotic minimax optimality, meaning no regular estimator can achieve a better limiting risk distribution (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.2)

The permutation-free, variance-aware SKCD test for global homogeneity of conditional potential-outcome distributions maintains valid type 1 error control and is consistent against fixed alternatives (Section 2.4, Theorem 3.3)
Closed-form expressions for the SKCD test statistic are derived to enable efficient computation without resampling or permutation (Section 3.2)
Asymptotically valid uniform confidence bands are constructed to identify covariate regions with statistically significant treatment effects (Theorem 3.4)

oDbc6DNJFj.text: FoundObj combines a superpoint-based Object Discovery Agent with a Geometric Reward Module built on the TRELLIS 3D foundation model and a Semantic Reward Module built on DINOv2 features to perform label-free 3D object segmentation (Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

On the ScanNet validation benchmark, FoundObj achieves 24.2 AP, 46.2 AP@50, and 74.7 AP@25, outperforming unsupervised baselines Part2Object (19.6/38.4/64.9 AP), UnScene3D (18.5/37.8/63.7 AP), and GrabS (14.0/27.2/39.4 AP) (Section 4).
On S3DIS Area-5, FoundObj reaches 12.8 AP, close to the supervised Mask3D baseline's 13.0 AP, despite using no segmentation labels (Section 4).
FoundObj attains 18.1 AP on the long-tail ScanNet200 benchmark, supporting the claim of strong generalization to long-tail object categories (Section 4).

An ablation removing the semantic reward module drops performance to 15.3 AP, and removing the geometric reward module drops it to 19.5 AP, showing both reward signals are necessary for the full 24.2 AP result (Table 5).

93uNlQ1Qp0.text: dWorldEval models actions as primary discrete tokens jointly denoised with visual and progress tokens via masked discrete diffusion, rather than treating actions as auxiliary conditioning signals (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).

On action controllability, dWorldEval achieves lower Δ-LPIPS on failure trajectories (0.352) than WorldEval (0.701), WorldGym (0.650), and Ctrl-World (0.416), indicating it better reproduces policy failures instead of hallucinating success (Table 1).

dWorldEval's sparse keyframe memory reduces round-trip LPIPS on long-horizon rollouts from 0.411 to 0.243 at horizon H=20 compared to a no-memory ablation, demonstrating improved spatiotemporal consistency (Table 2).

dWorldEval's automatic, progress-token-based success detection correlates with real policy execution at r=0.91 on LIBERO single-view, r=0.910 on LIBERO multi-view, r=0.927 on RoboTwin, and r=0.918 on real-world tasks, supporting the claim of accurate automatic policy ranking (Figure 7).
Figure 5 shows dWorldEval faithfully reproduces policy failure modes across multiple viewpoints where baseline world models instead hallucinate successful task completion (Figure 5).

Z6HxJqAzbp.text: DP-KFC constructs a Kronecker-factored curvature preconditioner from synthetically generated data rather than private or matched public data, using synthetic probing to estimate the eigenspectrum of MLP, CNN, and attention layers (Section 4.1, Section 4.2, Figure 2).
On MNIST at ε=1.0, synthetic DP-KFC reaches 94.2% accuracy versus 91.7% for DP-SGD, and up to 95.9% at higher ε, with DP-KFC plus DP-AdamBC reaching 95.5% (Table 1).

Under domain-mismatched (texture-disjoint) transfer, synthetic DP-KFC achieves 78.2% accuracy, matching an oracle preconditioner and outperforming public-data preconditioners that degrade to 70.5%-73.4%, a roughly 4.8 percentage point advantage (Table 2).
On StackOverflow BERT at ε=1.0, DP-KFC reaches 91.8% versus 89.5% for DP-SGD, and on IMDB logistic regression at ε=2.8, DP-KFC reaches 85.8% versus 83.1% for DP-SGD (Section 6.3).

Theorem 5.4 shows DP-KFC's non-convex convergence rate of O(T^{-1/2}) decouples optimization error (governed by the preconditioner's minimum eigenvalue) from privacy noise amplification (governed by the maximum eigenvalue), unlike post-hoc privatization schemes (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.4).
DP-KFC incurs roughly 2.2x lower sample throughput than DP-SGD due to the added preconditioning computation (Remark 5.5).

KM2J8XFz5A.text: SACRED-Bench evaluates multimodal LLMs against three speech-audio composition attack mechanisms: speech overlap/multi-speaker dialogue, speech-audio mixture, and diverse spoken instruction formats (Section 3).
Gemini 2.5 Pro exhibits a 66.75% overall attack success rate under SACRED-Bench's composed speech-audio attacks, with the audio-cues sub-attack alone reaching 88.56% (Table 1).

Gemini 1.5 Pro (85.12%) and GPT-4o (70.05%) show even higher overall attack success rates than Gemini 2.5 Pro, and the open-source Qwen2-Audio-7B is nearly maximally vulnerable at 98.16% overall ASR (Table 1).

SALMONN-Guard, built on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with two-stage LoRA fine-tuning, reduces overall attack success rate to 11.32%, including 12.93% on speech overlap, 14.08% on dialogue, and 5.16% on audio cues (Section 4, Table 1).

SACRED-Bench's composed attacks are substantially more effective against Gemini 2.5 Pro (65.41% ASR) than prior perturbation-based attacks such as speech insertion (13.41%) or speech editing (23.00%) (Table 4).

OxoELLdjwX.text: The paper evaluates four in-training defenses against emergent misalignment: KL-divergence regularization toward a safe reference model, LDIFS feature-space distance regularization, SafeLoRA safe-subspace projection, and interleaving safe examples from general instruct-tuning data (Section 3).

Experiments fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on four emergent-misalignment domains (code, legal, medical, security) with 6,000 aligned/misaligned pairs each, evaluated by GPT-4o-mini as judge (Section 4).

On Qwen2.5-7B, KL-divergence regularization reduces emergent misalignment by 91.5% on average but retains only 42% in-domain misalignment learning, while interleaving reduces emergent misalignment by 87.1% while retaining 92% in-domain misalignment learning (Section 4, Tables 3-4).

On the OpSwap benign task, KL-divergence regularization suppresses learning entirely on higher-difficulty tiers 1-3 (0% exact match), whereas interleaving preserves benign learning at roughly 29%-37% exact match across tiers (Table 5).

Interleaving increases incoherent outputs by up to 34% on the Security dataset relative to baseline, illustrating the paper's central finding that current in-training defenses face an alignment tax too costly for deployment (Section 4, Section 6).

vWQk8Kdlhy.text: For rectified flow trained with independent coupling, the learned velocity field v_{t=0.5}(z) is zero for all z if and only if the source distribution p_X equals the target distribution p_X' (Theorem 3.1).

The conditional zero-flow condition shows that a velocity field for pairs (ξ,η) with f(ξ)=η vanishes at t=0.5 if and only if p_{X|Y} = p_{X|f(Y)}, giving a criterion for certifying conditional independence (Theorem 3.3).
An anti-symmetric characterization shows v_t(z) = -v_{1-t}(z) holds if and only if p_X = p_X', providing an alternative practical test for distributional equality (Theorem C.1).
Zero-flow encoders learn amortized Markov blankets in graphical models, achieving 0.98±0.00 AUC on truncated-Gaussian models compared to 0.88±0.02 for graphical lasso (Section 6.1, Table 1).

On self-supervised learning with watermarked CIFAR-10, the zero-flow method retains 47.36% accuracy (a 2.60% drop) versus SimCLR's 34.65% (a 17.44% drop), showing resistance to the shortcut problem (Section 5, Table 2).

lttx2Uy3mN.text: EDEN computes an adaptive branching factor B_t = max(1, floor(B_max · H̄_t(y_{1:t}))) that scales monotonically with normalized output entropy at each decoding step (Section 3.1.2, Algorithm 1).
A regret bound shows entropy-adaptive branching achieves lower expected cumulative regret than fixed-width branching policies (Theorem 3.4).
On MATH 500, EDEN reaches 32.8% accuracy using only 840 expansions versus 29.2% accuracy for width-3 beam search using 1200 expansions (Section 4.1, Table 1).
On HumanEval, EDEN attains 31.3% accuracy with 965 expansions compared to beam search's 28.8% with 1200 expansions, and on SciBench, EDEN reaches 7.4% versus beam search's 6.9% (Table 1).
EDEN is reported to have a 75% posterior probability of being the best-performing method overall across the evaluated benchmarks (Table 1).
Entropy estimation used for branching remains accurate under sublinear sampling, allowing EDEN to work with closed/black-box APIs that expose only sampled tokens (Section 4.3, Figure 6).

cRs6HUUUay.text: ExpertWeaver is a training-free framework that partitions GLU gate neurons into universal and task-specialized groups using activation patterns captured from a 42-task Flan-v2 calibration set (Section 3.1).

As a dynamic structural pruning method at 25% sparsity, ExpertWeaver achieves 60.4 average accuracy on LLaMA3-8B versus 57.2 for CMoE, and 67.0 versus 65.0 for LLM-Pruner on Qwen2.5-7B (Section 4.1, Table 2).

As an MoE downcycling initialization strategy, ExpertWeaver(Qwen2.5-7B) reaches 63.5 average accuracy after 200B tokens of continued pretraining, outperforming OLMoE-1B-7B* (58.9) by 4.6 points while activating only 25% of MLP parameters (Section 4.2, Table 3).

On GSM8K at 25% sparsity, ExpertWeaver's dynamic pruning achieves 34.9% accuracy compared to 14.8% for FLAP and 2.0% for LLM-Pruner, demonstrating its advantage on reasoning tasks where static pruning collapses (Appendix E, Table 5).
On H100 GPUs, ExpertWeaver achieves 44.04 requests/second versus 41.41 for the dense Qwen2.5-7B model, and reduces per-output-token latency from 18.5ms to 9.8ms (Table 6, Appendix F).

vNPkcJj46N.text: Error-based Predictive Coding (called Error Optimization, EO) reparameterizes state-based PC (State Optimization, SO) to optimize prediction errors rather than states, converting the locally-connected computational graph into a globally-connected one that avoids exponential signal decay (Section 3.2).

On a 20-layer linear MLP trained on MNIST, EO propagates learning signal across all layers immediately, converging roughly 100x faster than SO, which requires about 100 update steps for signal to reach early layers (Section 4.3, Figure 5).

On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, EO reaches 91.73±0.21% accuracy versus 43.19±0.61% for SO and 91.85±0.24% for backpropagation, nearly matching backpropagation where SO collapses on deep architectures (Section 5.2, Table 1).
On CIFAR-100 with VGG-9, EO achieves 60.65±0.25% top-1 accuracy compared to 54.19±0.41% for SO and 61.11±0.45% for backpropagation (Table 1).

A bijective mapping between SO states and EO errors is proven to preserve identical energy functions and equilibrium points despite different optimization trajectories, formalized via Theorems C.1-C.8 (Appendix C.1).

Signal attenuation in SO is shown to follow a binomial decay formula combining exponential depth decay and temporal decay terms, confirmed by high-precision simulation (Section 3.2, Appendix B.4, Figure B.1).

p6Ar2d4Cwr.text: Pianist Transformer pre-trains on a 10-billion-token unlabeled MIDI corpus assembled from Aria-MIDI, GiantMIDI-Piano, PDMX, POP909, and Pianist8 using masked denoising, before fine-tuning on the ASAP score-performance dataset (Section 3.3, Appendix A.1).

The model uses note-level encoder sequence compression that aggregates 8 per-note tokens into a single vector, reducing self-attention complexity from O(N^2) to O((N/8)^2), a 64x reduction (Section 3.2).

An asymmetric 10-layer-encoder/2-layer-decoder design achieves 2.1x faster inference than a symmetric 6-6 variant while being 40% less memory-intensive and 70% faster during training (Table 10, Appendix F).

On the ASAP test set, Pianist Transformer achieves an overall Jensen-Shannon divergence of 0.1634 and intersection area of 0.8501, versus 0.2791/0.7556 for VirtuosoNet-ISGN and 0.2839/0.7439 for VirtuosoNet-HAN (Table 1).
Pre-training alone yields a 40.9% relative improvement in Intersection Area, from 0.6032 to 0.8501 (Figure 3).

In a subjective listening study with 39 participants, Pianist Transformer received a 32.7% first-place vote rate versus 30.8% for actual human performances and 14.7% for the best baseline, with average rank 2.29 versus 2.50 for humans (not statistically significant, p=0.21) (Section 4.4, Figure 4).

ky9RAeT6ie.text: Mosaic reduces the memory peak-to-average ratio by 2.71x on average for diffusion LLM inference relative to baseline serving systems (Abstract)

Mosaic increases the maximum supportable inference sequence length on identical hardware by 15.89-32.98x, including a 32.98x gain over the Native baseline and a 15.89x gain over Mosaic-Compile (Section 5.2)
Mosaic reduces end-to-end latency by 4.12%-23.26% versus baselines, with the largest gain (23.26%) observed for LLaDA-MoE at mask ratio rp=0.9 (Figure 11)

An ablation isolating each component shows the Global Memory Manager contributes 79.0%-197.1% of the maximum context-length improvement, the Mask-Only Kernel adds a further 88.9%-114.3%, and the Lazy Chunking Optimizer contributes an additional 221.3%-673.3% (Figure 14)
Without global memory planning, myopic memory allocation causes a 43.19% memory overflow at 32k context length (Figure 5)
Experiments are run on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-MoE using RTX 3090 (24GB) and A100 (40GB) hardware, comparing against Native, Mosaic-Torch, and Mosaic-Compile baselines (Section 5.1)

jV8qIG3xMR.text: CHaRS models representations as Gaussian Mixture Models and formulates steering as a discrete optimal transport problem via the Gaussian Mixture Wasserstein Distance, producing input-dependent steering maps instead of a single global direction (Section 2.4)

The barycentric projection map (Equation 9, Section 3.1) combines cluster-level transport maps weighted by local cluster assignment, yielding steering directions that vary smoothly across the representation manifold

On jailbreaking evaluation with Gemma2-9B-Instruct, CHaRS achieves 98.08% attack success rate versus 91.35% for the ActAdd difference-in-means baseline, with consistent improvements across 6 models spanning 3B-32B parameters (Section 4.1, Tables 1-2)

For toxicity mitigation on Llama3-8B, CHaRS-PCT achieves 1.17% CLS toxicity versus 1.93% for the Linear-Act baseline, a reduction of up to 43% in zero-shot toxicity scores with minimal degradation to perplexity or MMLU (Section 4.2, Table 3)

CHaRS-PCT (Definition 3.3) exploits a low-rank structure (rank ≤ 2K-2) in steering vectors, and an ablation over cluster number K shows multiple K values outperform the K=1 global-direction baseline, with K=15 performing best in tested configurations (Section 5, Figure 5)

In image generation style control, CHaRS achieves a superior Pareto front between style induction and content preservation, reaching cyberpunk style at λ=0.8 while maintaining CLIPScore above 0.26 (Section 4.3, Figure 2)

goUAT3UcR4.text: MemPot achieves greater than 0.96 AUROC detecting memory extraction attacks on external (RAG) memory across evaluated datasets, and 0.94-1.00 AUROC against internal-memory attacks, representing a 50% AUROC improvement and 80% increase in TPR at 1% FPR over baselines (Section 5, Tables 2-3)
Against external memory attacks (RAG-Thief, DGEA, IKEA), MemPot maintains 0.96+ AUROC while baseline detectors collapse to near-random performance (approximately 0.50 AUROC on IKEA) (Section 5)

MemPot achieves first detection within 1-9 rounds across attack types, compared to 2-42 rounds for the Optimal-Seq baseline, and Theorem 2 proves the honeypot-augmented sequential probability ratio test achieves shorter expected stopping time than any static detector under a fixed error budget (Section 4.1, Tables 4-5)

MemPot incurs zero online inference latency because honeypot injection is performed offline, and utility on standard tasks is preserved: WebShop success rate drops only from 44.6% to 43.8%, Pokemon QA accuracy remains 0.98, and Rouge-L is unchanged at 0.66 (Section 5.3, Table 7)
An ablation over honeypot injection ratio shows detection performance saturates at 2% for external memory and 4% for internal memory (Table 9)

U93dBehANs.text: Proposition 4.1 shows the optimal GFlowNet partition function relates to per-prompt accuracy via pold(x) = beta*log Z*(x) - beta*DKL(piold||pitheta), and since this KL term stays uniformly small during training (Figure 1), PACED-RL approximates per-prompt accuracy as pold(x) ≈ beta*log Z*(x) (Equation 8, Section 4.1)
On AIME24 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, PACED-RL reaches 28.7% pass@1 versus 23.9% for GRPO (29.1% relative improvement) and 24.9% for FlowRL (40.0% relative improvement) (Table 1)
PACED-RL reaches GRPO's best HumanEval+ performance in 0.49x the training time and FlowRL's best LiveCodeBench performance in 0.42x the training time (Figure 2)
PACED-RL improves pass@k diversity on AIME24/25 by up to 14.2% over GRPO and 9.1% over FlowRL (Figure 3)

Removing the accuracy-estimation-error-prioritized replay buffer reduces average performance by 1.9 percentage points, and partition-function computation adds negligible overhead of 0.035s versus 308s total per-step runtime for a 1.5B model (Table 2, Table 3)

An analysis of the target accuracy hyperparameter shows tau=0.5 achieves optimal test accuracy for adaptive prompt selection, while question difficulty progressively increases over the course of training (Section 4.3, Figures 4-5)

nxKRwB1J63.text: Using causal tracing across Qwen2.5-Omni (7B/3B), video-SALMONN-o1 (7B), and video-SALMONN2+ (7B/3B), sink tokens consistently outperform object tokens and random tokens for localizing integrated audio-visual information, across all five model variants (Section 4.3, Table 1)

A Modality Dominance Score (Equation 5) distinguishes a cross-modal sink token subset from unimodal sink tokens, with cross-modal sinks showing substantially higher indirect-effect scores (IEclean and IEcorrupt) than unimodal sinks (Section 5.2, Table 2)
Excessive attention allocation to unimodal sink tokens, rather than cross-modal sinks, correlates with object hallucination when audio and visual signals disagree (Section 6, Figure 5)

The proposed training-free Adaptive Sink-Guided Decoding (ASD) method rebalances attention toward cross-modal sink tokens (Equations 6-9) and reduces CHAIR CS hallucination scores by approximately 12% for both Qwen2.5-Omni and video-SALMONN on the VGGSound-Animal subset, outperforming vanilla decoding, PAI, and VCD baselines (Section 6.4, Table 3)

ASD is evaluated on VGGSound-Animal (360 samples), VGGSound-All (~1,000 samples), and AudioSet (~700 samples) using ALOHa, CHAIR (CS/CI), and F1 metrics, with an ablation over the modulation magnitude parameter alpha showing robust hallucination reduction across a range of settings (Section 6.4, Figure 6)

SHEiCnm2xB.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that the magnitude of the normal-plane component of a steering vector is predictable from its decomposition with respect to the concept's central axis, while Theorem 4.3 shows the sensitive sector within that normal plane is not reliably predictable (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.3).

Lemma 4.2 shows that when the number of concept directions exceeds the representation dimensionality d, the mapping from concept strengths to the difference vector is non-injective, giving a counterexample where orthogonal concept directions cannot remain pairwise orthogonal (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.2; Figure 2).

Verification experiments span 100 concepts across two model architectures, Gemma-2B-IT and LLaMA2-7B-Chat, testing three observable implications of the Cylindrical Representation Hypothesis (Section 6, Section 6.2).
An LLM-based judge used to evaluate steering outcomes is validated against human evaluation with 94% agreement accuracy (Section 6, Table 1).

The implication that the normal plane is determinable is confirmed by a single clear correlation peak, whereas the implication that the sensitive sector is determinable is refuted by a near-zero Pearson correlation of r = -0.034 (p > 0.05) (Section 6.2, Figure 7).

IfFCRVoapS.text: Confidence Dynamic Gain (CDG) scores each candidate answer as s_ℓ = C̄_ℓ + β·ΔC_ℓ, combining mean trace confidence with the confidence dynamic gain (tail confidence minus head confidence), and is shown to generalize majority voting and DeepConf as special cases (Section 3.3).

Averaged across DeepSeek-R1-8B, gpt-oss-20B, Gemma-3-27B, and QwQ-32B, CDG voting attains mean accuracies of 90.8%, 85.8%, 41.7%, and 80.0% respectively on AIME 2024/2025, HMMT 2025, and BRUMO 2025 (Section 5, Table 1).
CDG improves over majority voting by 5.4%, over DeepConf-Mean by 4.8%, and over DeepConf-Tail by 1.7%, averaged across the four evaluated models (Section 5, Table 1).

A theoretical analysis links CDG's confidence-gain signal to GRPO training dynamics, showing that advantage-weighted token reinforcement produces asymmetric confidence trajectories between correct and incorrect reasoning traces (Section 4).
CDG's advantage over baseline voting methods is shown to be robust across sampling budgets ranging from L=8 to L=512 traces per question (Section 5).

wjpdXrHxUi.text: OUTFORMER combines mixed synthetic priors (Gaussian Mixture Models, Structural Causal Models, and Copulas) with a Self-Evolving Curriculum, a multi-armed-bandit training scheme that adaptively selects training tasks without manual ordering (Section 3, Section 4).

OUTFORMER is evaluated on the established ADBench benchmark (57 datasets) plus two newly introduced large-scale benchmarks, OddBench (690 datasets) and OvRBench (756 datasets), totaling over 1,500 real-world datasets (Section 5).
On ADBench, OUTFORMER attains an average rank of 4.02±2.6, an Elo rating of 1,235, a win rate of 0.71, and rAUC of 0.956±0.06 (Section 5, Table 2).

Aggregated across all benchmarks, OUTFORMER achieves an average rank of 4.28±2.8, Elo rating of 1,423, win rate of 0.68, and AUROC of 0.910±0.11, outperforming prior zero-shot foundation models FoMo-0D and DTE-NP with statistically significant (p≤0.05) AUPRC gains (Section 5, Table 1).

OUTFORMER uses a 10-layer, 512-hidden-dimension, 8-head Transformer with 45.1M parameters, trained on 4 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs for 1,500 batches and performing zero-shot inference via a single forward pass over up to 5K inlier context points and 10K query points, using a 50-context inference ensemble (Section 5, Section 2).

dDowWwInhz.text: Proteo-R1 (ThinkProteo) couples an understanding expert—a multimodal LLM analyzing sequences, AF3-refolded structures, and text—with a generation expert, an AF3-style diffusion model, via anchor-residue identification and representation-level fusion of key-residue embeddings (Section 2, Figure 1).

Training follows a three-stage curriculum: Stage I aligns ESM-2 and structural features to language space via projection layers, Stage II unfreezes the LLM for a four-phase structural reasoning curriculum (residue grounding, pairwise geometry, compositional consistency, interface localization), and Stage III performs end-to-end joint CDR design on SAbDab antibody-antigen complexes (Section 3, Figure 2).

On multi-CDR redesign, Proteo-R1 achieves the lowest per-CDR RMSD on heavy-chain loops H1 (1.33 Å) and H2 (1.13 Å), with reduced steric clashes (0.50% intra-chain, 0.14% inter-chain) versus baselines (Section 4, Table 1).

On the CDR-H3-only RAbD benchmark, Proteo-R1 reaches a DockQ of 0.801, substantially exceeding dyMEAN (0.407) and BoltzGen (0.473), with lDDT of 0.9693, TM-score of 0.9816, and RMSD of 2.46 Å despite a lower amino-acid recovery rate (AAR) of 10.75% (Section 4, Table 2).

Replacing ground-truth hotspot residues with model-predicted anchors (versus an oracle ablation with true hotspots) increases H1 RMSD from 1.33 Å to 1.43 Å, indicating that reasoning-stage anchor prediction accuracy is the primary bottleneck to structural quality (Section 4, Table 1).

The generation expert is model-agnostic: substituting the UniMoMo backbone for the default diffusion model still yields RMSD of 0.83 Å and an Interface Match Precision (IMP) of 67.79%, versus a 65.00% baseline (Section 4.4, Table 5).

qk3z1iplmP.text: Theorem 1 shows that for one-to-one token-to-dictionary mapping, the sample complexity per new token scales as Õ(γ⁻² log² c), where γ is a KL-divergence separation margin and c is a probability lower bound (Section 3.1, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows that for s-sparse token representations mapped onto m existing tokens, the required sample count satisfies N ≥ O(m·log(m/δ)) with estimation risk scaling with s·log(T/(csε)) rather than with the full vocabulary size T (Section 3.2, Theorem 2).

On an arithmetic-operator learning task, embedding-tuning (ET) achieves 81.4% accuracy on the new operation while retaining 100% accuracy on addition (zero forgetting), whereas full fine-tuning (FFT) causes accuracy on addition to fall to 76.2% (Section 4.1, Table 1).

On synthetic vocabulary expansion over 1,000 sentences, embedding-tuning attains competitive loss of 2.30-3.79 with +0.00 forgetting on prior tokens, compared to FFT's forgetting of +0.51 to +11.59 (Section 4.2, Table 2).

In cross-lingual vocabulary expansion to Spanish, German, and Arabic, embedding-tuning achieves the lowest target-language loss (2.30-2.82) while incurring near-zero forgetting on English (Section 4.3, Table 3).

6wQKBHi0qO.text: Under Assumptions 1-4, Theorem 1 proves the solution set of the ranking mean squared error (rMSE) loss is both complete and minimal, i.e. a reward function satisfies the ranking constraints if and only if it minimizes the rMSE loss (Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 relaxes the exact ranking assumption to a bounded ranking error, extending the completeness/minimality guarantee to practical settings where differentiable sorting is imperfect (Theorem 2).

On offline feedback from OpenAI Gym tasks (Reacher, Inverted Double Pendulum, Half Cheetah), R4 achieves statistically significantly higher final returns or faster learning than baselines at p<0.05 (Section 6.1, Figure 2).

On online feedback across 6 DeepMind Control Suite environments, R4 significantly outperforms PEBBLE, SURF, QPA, and RbRL in 3 of 6 environments under Bonferroni-corrected significance p<0.0125, and attains higher final returns in 4 of 6 environments (Section 6.2, Figure 3).

In a robustness ablation, R4 trained with 80% label noise matches the performance of RbRL trained with only 10% label noise, and R4's performance is insensitive to the number of rating bins while RbRL's degrades with bin count (Appendix B.2).
A human study with 5 participants (2 experts, 3 non-experts) rating trajectories on the Reacher environment shows R4 consistently outperforms RbRL despite inconsistent human ratings (Appendix B.1).

enfG9qcdz6.text: On DiT-XL/2 for ImageNet 512x512 generation at 50 sampling steps, RSTR reduces the number of classifier-free-guidance forward passes from 50 to 9, cutting MACs from 52.45T to 24.93T (53% savings) while improving FID from 3.20 to 2.72, a 15% improvement (Table 1).
At 30 sampling steps on DiT-XL/2, RSTR achieves 60% MAC savings, reducing computation from 31.47T to 16.01T MACs (Table 1).

On PixArt-alpha for MSCOCO 256x256 generation at 20 steps, RSTR reduces classifier-free-guidance steps from 20 to 6, cutting MACs from 6.72T to 2.67T (60% reduction) while improving FID from 24.60 to 19.27, a 21.7% improvement (Table 2).

On FLUX at 512x512 resolution, RSTR achieves a 5x latency speedup and a 72% MAC reduction (320T vs 1144T), while ImageReward improves to 1.0092 from the 50-step baseline's 0.9956, and GenEval score reaches 67.46 versus the baseline's 68.60 (Tables 3-4).

RSTR's two-stage optimization (evolutionary search for sparse guidance schedules, then coordinate-descent rank allocation for per-block calibration) requires roughly 45 GPU hours total and, once optimized, generalizes across all prompts at inference without per-prompt re-optimization (Section 1).

0xOj6kVMbb.text: Proposition 1 shows that standard active-learning utility construction, which ignores the future trajectories of Lagrangian drifters, yields suboptimal observer placement decisions (Section 3.1, Proposition 1).

BALLAST's acquisition function uses an SPDE-based extended Gaussian process state f=[f, partial_t f]^T with Matern-3/2 temporal kernels to enable posterior sampling without the O(J*N_space^3*N_sampT^3) cost of naive sampling (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).

On synthetic Helmholtz ground-truth vector fields across 100 runs over 10 fields, BALLAST-aided sequential observer placement saves approximately 3 drifters (about 16% cost reduction) compared to uniform, Sobol, and expected-information-gain placement policies (Section 5.2).
On the high-fidelity SUNTANS ocean model over 100 independent runs, BALLAST achieves approximately 22% deployment cost savings relative to baseline placement policies (Section 5.3).

An ablation on the number of Monte Carlo vector-field samples J shows that J=20 achieves less than 1% utility gap regardless of decision time, balancing accuracy against computational cost (Section 5.1, Figure 4).

r2sJKlXY3M.text: Proposition 3.1 proves that CompDiffuser's trajectory-stitching score field is non-conservative and does not correspond to any valid global trajectory density, due to a missing boundary reaction term (Proposition 3.1).
On PointMaze-Giant stitching, the Energy-based Compositional Diffuser (ECD) achieves 84% success rate versus 77% for CompDiffuser and 69% for CDGS (Table 1).
On AntMaze-Giant and HumanoidMaze-Giant, ECD reaches 82% and 49% success rates respectively, compared to CompDiffuser's 72% and 42% (Table 2).

ECD matches CompDiffuser's inference runtime (8s on PointMaze-Giant, 25s vs 17s on AntMaze-Giant) while CDGS requires 29s and 168s respectively for comparable or worse success rates, showing ECD nearly matches heuristic stitching speed (Table 6).

The Markov-based approximation for computing the boundary reaction term via a block-tridiagonal solve maintains linear O(L) complexity in the planning horizon L, avoiding the quadratic cost of full neural-network differentiation (Section 3.4).

28nj9x9hLa.text: For inhomogeneous halfspaces in R^d with d>=2, Theorem 1.2 constructs distributions in the realizable case where consistent hypotheses incur population error Theta(d*ln(n/d)/n), matching the first-order VC bound and showing it is essentially tight (Theorem 1.2).

Theorem 1.3 establishes an agnostic-case lower bound for inhomogeneous halfspaces showing the excess-error deviation scales as sqrt(tau*ln(1/tau)) where tau is the true error, again matching general VC theory (Theorem 1.3).

For homogeneous halfspaces in R^2, Theorem 1.4 shows every consistent hypothesis in the realizable case has population error at most ln(2/delta)/n, an O(1/n) rate improving on the standard VC bound by a logarithmic factor (Theorem 1.4).

Theorem 1.7 proves a matching lower bound showing the ln ln n overhead identified in Corollary 1.6 when combining dyadic risk bands is unavoidable, giving the first known separation between single-band and multi-band uniform convergence guarantees for R^2 homogeneous halfspaces (Corollary 1.6, Theorem 1.7).

The critical-wedge localization argument in Lemma 2.2 is the key technical tool used to derive the sharp dimensional threshold separating d=2 homogeneous halfspaces from general d>=2 behavior (Lemma 2.2).

G0Mw5MaPcR.text: EAGer branches generation only at high-entropy tokens (threshold θ in the 1.8–2.7 range) and reallocates saved compute from easy prompts to harder ones, requiring no access to target labels (Section 3.1-3.2).
EAGer reduces token generation by up to 65% compared to Full Parallel Sampling while matching or exceeding its performance across evaluated models (Table 3).
On AIME 2025, EAGer improves Pass@k over Full Parallel Sampling for multiple models, e.g. SmolLM3-3B rises from 0.53 to 0.73 and GPT-Oss-20B rises from 0.90 to 0.97 (Table 1).
Peak per-token entropy is negatively correlated with Pass Rate accuracy (r≈-0.547), motivating entropy as a signal for adaptive branching (Figure 2).

EAGer-adapt achieves up to 13% performance gains without label access, and the method's efficiency-performance trade-off is evaluated by scaling the number of sampled sequences M∈{1,4,8,16,24,32} (Figure 4).
Budget reallocation results with entropy threshold θ=2.0 show reduced total token counts (# T ×1e⁵) while preserving or improving pass@k across AIME 2025, GPQA-Diamond, and HumanEval Plus (Table 2).

Fgdyd2BLoR.text: LightningRL achieves an average tokens-per-forward-pass (TPF) of 7.32 across benchmarks, reaching up to 11.10 TPF on MBPP with an 8B model at block size 32 (Table 2).
On MBPP, LightningRL attains 58.3% accuracy with an AUP score of 641.6 at TPF 11.10, and on GSM8K attains 90.3% accuracy with TPF 5.58 and AUP 492.4 (Table 2).

Per-reward decoupled normalization, which normalizes accuracy and speed rewards independently within groups before aggregation before combining into GRPO-style advantages, reduces training collapse and stabilizes convergence for block-wise dLLMs (Section 3).
Token-level NLL regularization applies a dense, token-factorized anchoring loss toward correct trajectories, complementing the sequence-level RL objective (Section 3).

An ablation study confirms that removing any of the three core components (per-reward decoupled normalization, token-level NLL regularization, TPF-aware filtering) degrades either accuracy or parallelism (Table 3).
A loss-reduction strategy comparison finds the sequence-token-token (Seq-Tok-Tok) aggregation optimal relative to alternative reduction schemes (Table 4).

2dzU8sTOO3.text: SMART predicts physical quantities at arbitrary query locations directly from raw point-cloud geometry, without requiring a simulation mesh, via a geometry encoder and physics decoder coupled through cross-layer attention (Section 3, Figure 2).

At 16k-point subsampled resolution, SMART achieves lower surface error than mesh-dependent AB-UPT on ShapeNetCar (6.77×10⁻² vs 6.97×10⁻²) and lower volume error than mesh-free AB-UPT on AhmedML (5.15×10⁻² vs 5.18×10⁻²) (Table 2).
On the SHIFT-Wing dataset at subsampled resolution, mesh-free AB-UPT fails entirely (39.47×10⁻² volume error) while SMART maintains 14.66×10⁻² (Table 2).
At full resolution (millions of points), SMART maintains accuracy while competing mesh-dependent methods GNOT and Transolver run out of memory (Table 3).

Under query distribution shift on SHIFT-SUV (e.g., non-CFD uniform mesh and spatially-restricted rear queries), SMART's error stays low (0.0176 surface / 5.95 volume for Uniform; 0.0147 surface / 5.93 volume for Rear) while mesh-dependent AB-UPT's error increases by 566%-2270% (Table 4).
An ablation study shows that both geometry cross-attention and cross-layer encoder-decoder interaction between the geometry encoder and physics decoder are essential for accuracy (Appendix K).

JKGgHY9FKa.text: In online A/B testing, OneSearch achieves +1.67% item CTR, +3.14% PV CTR, +1.78% PV CVR, +2.40% buyer volume, and +3.22% order volume relative to the production baseline (Table 8).
OneSearch reduces operational expenditure to 24.60% of the original online pipeline's cost, a 75.40% reduction (Figure 7).
OneSearch improves Model FLOPs Utilization from 3.26% to 27.32%, a 700.38% relative improvement (Figure 7).
Offline, OneSearch achieves 66.46% HR@350 and 18.38% MRR@350 on order data, compared against the OnlineMCA baseline (Table 5).
RQ-OPQ hierarchical quantization achieves 91.91% independent coding rate (ICR) versus 68.08% for RQ-Kmeans (Table 3).
In cold-start scenarios, OneSearch improves item-side performance by +3.31% and user-side performance by +2.50% relative to warm scenarios (Section 4.4).

avVTEzRgba.text: AsyncSpade achieves over 20% reduction in time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to the SoTA sparse-attention baseline Quest, evaluated on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B (Section 5).
AsyncSpade achieves at least 50% TPOT reduction compared to full attention while matching or surpassing accuracy on AIME-24, AIME-25, GPQA-Diamond, and MATH-500 (Figure 9).
AsyncSpade fully overlaps KV-cache management operations with the inference pipeline within a defined workload range, achieving the theoretical optimal TPOT (Section 4, Figures 4-5).
Cache management latency and required bandwidth are measured at 3.92-14.43ms across configurations on A100 and H100 8-GPU nodes, compared to inference latencies of 5.47-14.26ms (Table 1, Table 2).

The method's query-prediction component exploits observed temporal locality and linear correlation in attention patterns across decoding steps to select sparse KV subsets asynchronously (Section 3, Figures 4-5).

GQIorrRZGv.text: The parallel associative-scan formulation of hard-reset spiking neuron dynamics achieves up to 44x speedup over sequential simulation on event-based datasets while preserving exact hard-reset dynamics (Section 3.2.1, Figure 8).
The associative scan reduces computational depth from O(K) for the serial approach to O(log K), using the operator defined via the spike condition R(V0, I0, Vth, t) = 0 (Equation 4, Equation 5).

A differentiable spike-time solver using Newton-Raphson root-finding computes spike times to machine precision without discrete-time binning, and converges faster than a bisection-based solver (Section 3.2.2, Figure 7).
The model attains 98.04% accuracy on MNIST, 95.10% on SHD, and 77.35% on SSC using a 2F512HD architecture (Table 1).

On sub-millisecond temporal tasks, coarse discrete-time binning (time step >= 2ms) causes near-chance accuracy while the continuous spike-time formulation retains high accuracy (Section 4.3, Figure 9).
Implicit-function-theorem gradients (∂t/∂p = -(∂R/∂t)^{-1} · ∂R/∂p) allow end-to-end differentiation through the spike-time root-finding solver (Equation 45).

Alelgxnwgs.text: The proposed randomized Lipschitz-constrained defense (HyCAS, built from FDPAN, SNCAN, and RPFAN streams fused with RANI) is provably <=2-Lipschitz, as established in Theorem 1 and Proposition 1/2 with the corresponding pointwise l2 certificate in Corollary 1.
On NIH Chest X-ray, the method improves certified l2 accuracy by up to approximately 7.3 percentage points over the best prior certified defense across tested noise levels and radii (Table 2).

On HAM10000, the method improves empirical l_infinity robust accuracy by up to approximately 3.1 percentage points over the strongest baseline (RPF/CTRW/DRS/ARS) under APGD-20 and AutoAttack-20 at epsilon in {8/255, 16/255} (Table 4).
On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, the method attains the best certified accuracy across nearly all sigma and l2-radius combinations compared to RS, IRS, DRS, ARS, LOT, and SLL baselines (Table 1).

Under strong APGD attacks on CIFAR-10 with varying perturbation sizes (0.01-0.08) and iteration counts (10-100 steps), the method maintains higher empirical accuracy than TRADES, HR, RPF, CTRW, DRS, and ARS baselines (Figure 2).
The improvements in certified and empirical robustness are achieved without sacrificing clean accuracy relative to the strongest baselines evaluated (Table 3, Table 4).

omkG80XURl.text: Under i.i.d. sampling in the double-chain formulation, the algorithm converges to a unique, sample-independent fixed point of the projected Bellman equation with sample complexity Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) (Theorem 4.1).
Under Markovian sampling with constant stepsizes in the double-chain setting, the same Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) sample complexity is preserved (Theorem 4.2).
With decaying stepsizes, the method attains convergence guarantees with no explicit dimension-dependent terms (Theorem 4.3).

The paper reduces the condition-number dependence of average-reward TD learning from quartic (prior state of the art) to quadratic, matching the scaling known for discounted TD learning (Section 1, Table 1).

A single-chain variant of the algorithm is also analyzed but only attains quartic sample complexity Õ(1/η^4 T) due to decorrelation requirements, contrasting with the double-chain method's quadratic rate (Theorem 4.4).
The condition number η1, defined via min over unit vectors of ||Φx||²_Dir + (μᵀΦx)², is shown to satisfy η1 >= (1/2)η3 relative to prior condition-number definitions (Equation 3, Lemma B.3).

d5rd1zlHTf.text: On HotPotQA, MASH improves answer accuracy by 7.6 percentage points over the baseline OTC selective help-seeking approach (55.42% vs. 44.76%) (Section 4.1, Table 1).
On 2WikiMultihopQA, MASH improves accuracy by 6.64 percentage points over baseline OTC (45.99% vs. 39.59%) (Table 1).
MASH improves average Tool Productivity by 3.83 points across evaluated datasets compared to baseline OTC (Table 1).
On the subset of HotPotQA questions requiring exactly one search, MASH achieves 56.4% accuracy versus 40.0% for baseline OTC (Table 2).

In the abstention inference mode, MASH with OTC-Strict reaches 59.9% precision on HotPotQA versus 53.1% for a DPO-based abstention baseline, and achieves 91.2% on the Abs(0) abstention classification metric on HotPotQA (Section 4.2, Table 3).

MASH is trained via a two-step pipeline of warm-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with three reward formulations (Exponential Decay, OTC, OTC-Strict) that balance accuracy against search-call penalties (Section 2.2).

dayZnm0dgh.text: Theorem 3.3 derives an upper bound on MX (microscaling) quantization error showing it depends jointly on the spectral norm of the inverse affine transformation and the expected maximum activation magnitude per block, motivating learned general affine (not just rotation) transformations (Theorem 3.3).

Under MXFP4 quantization on Llama3.2-1B, LATMiX-LU achieves 54.18% average zero-shot accuracy (94.05% recovery of full-precision performance) versus 51.42% for the GPTQ baseline across ARC, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, BoolQ, and OBQA (Table 1).
On Llama3.2-1B, LATMiX outperforms rotation-based baselines QuaRot (52.47%), SpinQuant (51.48%), FlatQuant (52.45%), and MR-GPTQ (52.53%), reaching 54.18% average zero-shot accuracy (Table 1).

In WikiText2 perplexity ablations on Llama3.2-1B, the full-granularity learned invertible LU-parametrized transformation (LATMiX-LU) attains 11.69 perplexity, improving over no transformation (18.80), random Hadamard (12.87), and learned orthogonal (13.35) transformations (Table 2).

The learned affine transformations fold into existing weight matrices at zero additional inference cost for models with bias terms, matching the efficiency of rotation-based methods (Section on Implementation Efficiency).
Visualization of the optimization trajectory shows learned transformation matrices rapidly deviate from orthogonality and develop cross-block interactions beyond block-diagonal structure (Figure 3).

jq7Nk1p7mW.text: GCIB improves HR@10 over the strongest baseline by 40.49% on Yelp, 15.09% on Taobao, 7.66% on Tmall, and 13.09% on ML-10M (Table 2, Section 4.2).

The Graph Information Bottleneck objective maximizes mutual information between the denoised auxiliary graph and the target-behavior graph while minimizing mutual information with the original auxiliary graph, using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion as a tractable surrogate (Section 3, Section 4.2).

Ablating the GIB denoising module (-IB) or the cross-behavior InfoNCE contrastive loss (-Infonce) each degrade performance, with the largest drop occurring when both components are removed (-Both) (Table 4, Section 4.3).
Under 20% synthetic noise injection into the Yelp auxiliary graph, GCIB remains stable while baselines MBLFE and HGIB suffer 11-19% performance degradation (Table 5, Section 4.4).
GCIB trains in 30.41 seconds per epoch on Tmall, versus 495.57 seconds per epoch for the BCIPM baseline, with comparable GPU memory usage of 5218MB (Table 6, Appendix D).

Optimal Information Bottleneck weight β varies substantially by dataset (e.g., β=1 for Yelp vs. β=80 for Tmall), and shallow global-encoding layer depths (2-3 layers) outperform deeper configurations, which overfit (Figure 4, Figure 5, Section 4.5).

bfVJ4GsHrO.text: EGGROLL achieves over a hundredfold increase in training throughput versus prior evolution-strategies methods for billion-parameter models at large population sizes (Figure 2, Section 1).
EGGROLL reaches up to 91% of the throughput of pure batch inference on large neural networks (Figure 2).

EGGROLL stably pretrains a nonlinear recurrent language model (an RNN with no explicit activation functions) that operates purely in integer datatypes, tracked via per-token perplexity during training (Section on Pure Integer Language Model Pretraining, Figure 6).

EGGROLL outperforms GRPO when fine-tuning a quantised RWKV-7G 7-billion-parameter model on GSM8K using 128 GPUs for 24 hours, and improves accuracy from an 8-GPU/12-hour baseline on the Countdown task, raising AIME25 accuracy and HMMT25 accuracy from 11% to 13% (Figure 5, Figure 13).
On cooperative Multi-Particle Environment tasks, EGGROLL with rank-1 low-rank perturbations trains up to 2.4 times faster than OpenES (Figure 12, Appendix).

ZawqwXtmOx.text: Fixed block scheduling in diffusion LLMs is agnostic to semantic difficulty, forcing premature decoding commitments to low-confidence positions inside the active block while delaying decoding of high-confidence positions outside it (Section on Key Problem, Section 4.1).

The Dynamic Sliding Block (DSB) algorithm maintains an active block whose boundaries (s, e) slide forward to the first unresolved position and expand to keep approximately S_init unresolved tokens, capped at a maximum size S_max (Algorithm 1, Section 4.1).

DSB Cache stabilizes the KV-cache under a moving block boundary by maintaining and refreshing a prefix window before the active block each step, using the update rule ℓ_pw^(t) = max(ℓ_pmin, s^(t) - s^(t-1)), with periodic global refresh of cached positions (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
On GSM8K with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, DSB achieves 80.29 accuracy at 99.61 tokens/second versus a fixed-block baseline's 77.40 accuracy at 92.26 tokens/second (Table 1, Section 5.2).

DSB with DSB Cache consistently improves both accuracy and throughput over fixed-block scheduling across LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-v0-Base-7B, and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP, and BBH (Table 1, Section 5.2).

An ablation comparing DSB(const.) and DSB(greedy) variants, with and without the prefix window, shows both contribute to the accuracy/throughput tradeoff on GSM8K and HumanEval (Table 2, Section 5.3).

RsLH9NuYKK.text: RePo learns token positions via a differentiable module f_ϕ (a SwiGLU sub-layer followed by a linear position-assignment transformation) so attention scores use learned positions z rather than fixed linear indices, computed as q_i^T g_θ(z_j - z_i) k_j (Section on Technical Approach).
On RULER noisy-context evaluation within the 4K training context length, RePo scores 55.68 on average versus 44.64 for RoPE, an 11.04-point improvement (Table 1).

RePo yields exact-match gains of 13.25+ points on QA/needle-in-a-haystack tasks at 16K tokens via YaRN extrapolation, and a 5.48+ point improvement on LongBench F1/Rouge-L metrics (Figure 2, Table 3).
On structured-data tasks, RePo improves exact match by 1.94 points on average over RoPE on the NLGraph and HybridQA datasets (Table 2).
RePo maintains competitive performance on general short-context benchmarks (ARC-C, ARC-E, BoolQ, CoQA, Drop, Hellaswag, MMLU-Pro, TriviaQA), scoring 53.73 versus RoPE's 53.70 (Table 5).
RePo introduces only a 0.9% increase in parameters with negligible added inference FLOPs/latency, per the efficiency comparison (Table 6).

B6oQ9Cg5Sh.text: Sea2 trains a VLM-based pose-control agent via a two-stage pipeline: supervised fine-tuning on rule-based trajectories (object search, viewpoint centering, proximity adjustment), followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization using only frozen-perception-module scalar feedback as reward (Section 3.3, Figure 3).

On ReplicaCAD, Sea2 improves visual grounding (GroundingDINO) by 13.54% mAP_avg, segmentation (SAM) by 15.92% IoU and 13.59% Dice, and 3D box estimation IoU by 27.68% and Center Score by 25.35%, over frozen-baseline perception with default controllers (Table 1, Section 4).
On HM3D, Sea2 achieves analogous gains of 22.16%, 12.49%, and 9.31% on visual grounding, segmentation, and 3D box estimation respectively (Table 2).

The reward function combines format, confidence, and geometric-consistency terms; an ablation shows combining confidence and geometric rewards outperforms either alone, with geometric shaping providing stable guidance and confidence calibrating task-specific optimization (Table 4).
