All perception modules (GroundingDINO, SAM, and the 3D estimator) remain frozen throughout training, with no downstream scene labels required, and the agent is limited to 10 discrete steps (0.25m translation, 10-degree rotation) per episode (Section 4.1).

fVpGsFEgQU.text: Masking 5 routers in DeepSeek-V2-Lite increases jailbreak attack success rate more than 4x, from 0.15 to 0.79, on JailbreakBench (Section 3.4).
F-SOUR achieves attack success rates of 0.94 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, 0.91 on Mixtral-8x7B, 0.86 on OLMoE-1B-7B, and 0.88 on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B on JailbreakBench (Table 2).
F-SOUR reaches near-perfect attack success rates on AdvBench of 1.00 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, 0.96 on Mixtral-8x7B, 1.00 on OLMoE-1B-7B, and 0.94 on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B (Table 13).
F-SOUR surpasses baseline attacks GCG (0.46 average ASR) and SteerMoE (0.50 average ASR) by 40-61 percentage points on JailbreakBench (Table 2).

Safety-critical routers are concentrated in specific layers, with RoSais values reaching 8.60 for Mixtral and 8.18 for OLMoE, corresponding to roughly a 5.43x10^3-fold increase in unsafe-response likelihood (Figure 3).

Manipulating 5 layers degrades math accuracy by more than 0.25 while general QA task metrics decrease by at most 0.03, showing the attack is safety-specific rather than a general capability degradation (Table 9).

v0o0mofTr6.text: TokenSwap achieves attack success rates of 80.47% on BLIP-2, 81.25% on InstructBLIP, 85.16% on LLaVA-1.5-7B, and 80.47% on LLaVA-1.5-13B on Flickr30k (Table 1).
In cross-dataset evaluation (trained on MSCOCO, tested on Flickr8k), TokenSwap attains 88.28% attack success rate on BLIP-2 versus 54.69% for the BadNet baseline (Table 2).
TokenSwap outperforms adapted baselines TrojVLM (80.47%) and MABA (79.69%) on BLIP-2/Flickr8k, reaching 91.41% attack success rate (Table 3).
Min-k perplexity analysis shows TokenSwap-poisoned samples remain harder to detect than insertion/replacement-based attacks, which are easily flagged by perplexity filtering (Figure 1).
The backdoor induces bags-of-words outputs in which the victim model names the correct objects but misrepresents their relationships, disrupting compositional understanding (Section 3.2).

ppIhZgFCTI.text: Under i.i.d. sampling with an exponential step-size schedule, TD(0) attains the optimal last-iterate bias-variance trade-off without requiring knowledge of the problem-dependent constant omega (Theorem 3.4, Section 3).

Under Markovian sampling, standard TD(0) with the same exponential step-size schedule achieves a comparable convergence rate but still requires knowledge of omega to set the initial step-size eta_0 (Theorem 4.10, Section 4.1).

A regularized variant of TD(0) with exponential step-sizes and regularization parameter lambda = 1/sqrt(T) removes the dependence on omega in the Markovian setting, without needing projections or iterate averaging (Theorem 4.12, Section 4.2).
The regularized TD(0) analysis in the Markovian setting introduces exponential dependence on the mixing time tau_mix as an artifact of the proof technique (Theorem 4.12, Section 4.2).
Mixing time tau_mix is defined as the first time the state distribution's deviation from stationarity falls below a threshold delta (Definition 4.1).

kovWCrgHxo.text: A single generalist policy is trained once and evaluated zero-shot across 12 distinct simulated humanoid embodiments (Section 4.1, Table 1).

The same generalist policy is deployed zero-shot on 7 distinct real-world humanoid robots, achieving a 100% survival rate and 100% task success rate on whole-body control and long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks (Section 4.5, Table 4).

On the 12 unseen simulated robots, the generalist attains command-tracking errors of 0.084 m/s (longitudinal velocity), 0.116 m/s (lateral velocity), 0.160 rad/s (angular velocity), 0.097 m (base height), and 0.043 rad (torso pitch) (Section 4.1).
The generalist policy reaches approximately 85% of the performance of per-robot specialist policies (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
Fine-tuning the generalist policy on a specific embodiment surpasses training a specialist from scratch by up to 10% and converges faster across all tested embodiments (Section 4.2).

GEKbKCTzuV.text: A synthetic data generation-training loop improves downstream performance only when it remains information-open, i.e., incorporates an external signal S with conditional mutual information I(X;S|D) > 0 between the task source X and training data D (Section 3.3).

Theorem 4.2 decomposes total supervision information as I(Y;S|Q) = I([Y]_pi;S|Q) + I(Y;S|[Y]_pi,Q), separating task-relevant (between-class) information from within-class information for a task-relevant partition pi (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).

Low meta-level supervision (identifying one specific reference among M acceptable solutions) provides roughly h_2(1/M) bits of information, approaching 0 as M grows, versus roughly 1 bit for high meta-level binary correctness signals (Section 4.1).

An instruction-following judge model trained iteratively on its own outputs without external anchors shows monotonic degradation in acceptance rate, empirically confirming the predicted information-closed Markov chain collapse (Section 3.2).

In a rubric-based RL experiment, independent scorings of 1,000 (prompt, response) pairs show only 24% sample-level consistency across 16 scoring runs, yet training still converges to strong generalization because the binary reward is measurable with respect to the task-relevant partition (Section 4.2).

Binary correctness supervision (JudgeRLVR) trained only on mathematics transfers to code, logic, and general reasoning domains without domain-specific training, illustrating cross-domain transfer from information-efficient signals (Section 4.4).

TyVJlSHke2.text: ColModernVBERT, the late-interaction variant of the 250M-parameter ModernVBERT encoder, reaches an average ViDoRe score of 68.6 (81.2 on ViDoRe v1, 56.0 on ViDoRe v2), coming within 0.6 points of ColPali despite having roughly 12x fewer parameters (2.92B) (Table 3, Section 4.2).

Bidirectional MLM-based text encoders outperform causal decoder backbones by +10.6 nDCG@5 in the late-interaction retrieval setting, versus only +1.6 nDCG@5 in the single-vector setting (Figure 5, Section 3.1).

Document retrieval nDCG@5 scales with input image resolution, rising from 30.7 at 512px to 43.8 at 2048px and to 45.8 after a high-resolution cooldown stage, while non-document tasks degrade at higher resolution (Table 1, Section 3.2).
Interleaving text-only pairs with image-text pairs at a 1:1 ratio during contrastive post-training improves document retrieval by +1.7 nDCG@5 over image-only training (Table 2, Section 3.2).

ModernVBERT combines a 150M-parameter ModernBERT text encoder with a 100M-parameter SigLIP2-16B-512 vision encoder via early fusion and LoRA (rank 32) fine-tuning, achieving 0.032s CPU inference latency, about 7x faster than similarly-performing alternatives (Figure 2, Section 2; Section 4.2).

OnmYXKZ6oa.text: Proposition 3.1 proves via the Data Processing Inequality that mutual information between domain geometry G and hidden states V_l, I(G;V_l), is non-increasing with depth l in Markovian neural operator layers (Proposition 3.1).

Layer-wise geometric fidelity (Definition 3.3) and spectral power distribution at boundary wavenumbers (Definition 3.4) empirically show progressive loss of domain-geometry information with depth in FNO, Transolver, and related architectures (Section 3, Definitions 3.3-3.4).

Injecting geometry via the proposed Geometry Memory Injection mechanism (Equation 5) reduces error by 53.4% for FNO on the Darcy flow benchmark and by 57.4% for Transolver on the AirfRANS benchmark, while yielding only 9-26% improvement for the Laplace Neural Operator (LNO), consistent with LNO's intrinsic geometric memory (Table 2).

Late-depth geometry injection causes a catastrophic 'Geometric Shortcut' failure in Transolver on the LDC-NS and NSHT tasks, with error exploding as the final layer monopolizes learning and upstream layers' gradients collapse, whereas FNO remains stable across all injection depths (Section 4.3.1, Table 4, Figures 6-7).

Among the three tested integration operators for geometry injection (FiLM/affine modulation, additive injection, and concatenation), FiLM-based modulation is the only variant that prevents the Geometric Shortcut failure in Transolver, per the injection-strategy ablation (Table 6).

kj9wufh0EI.text: The distilled hybrid xLSTM student built from Llama3.1-8B achieves a Win-and-Tie critical tolerance of α*=0.0 on language generation benchmarks, indicating perfect recovery of teacher performance, versus α*=1.0 for prior linearization baselines LoLCATs and QRWKV6-7B (Figure 3b, Section 4).

On instruction-tuned models, the xLSTM-distilled Qwen2.5-7B-IT student reaches α*=0.02 and xLSTM-Llama3.1-8B-IT reaches α*=0.02-comparable parity, with expert merging in Stage III substantially improving instruction-following performance (Figure 4, Section 3.2).

The hybrid xLSTM architecture combines mLSTM (for global context) with sliding-window attention (512 tokens) and 4 sink tokens, dynamically combined via a learned output gate (Equation 11, Section 3.1).

Distillation is validated across four model families/variants — Llama3.1-8B, Olmo3-7B, Llama3.1-8B-IT, and Qwen2.5-7B-IT — using a three-stage pipeline of hidden-state alignment, sparse KL/next-token distillation, and optional expert merging (Section 3.2, Section 4).

The distilled xLSTM models achieve roughly 2x prefill throughput, 2x lower generation latency with constant memory scaling, and up to 4x batch-decoding throughput at large context lengths compared to the quadratic-attention teacher (Figure 5, Section 4.4).

GxTkgMBiz8.text: Training dynamics on the synthetic analogical-reasoning task exhibit three distinct emergent stages — memorization, compositional reasoning, then analogical reasoning — as defined by Definitions 2.1 and 2.2 (Section 3, Figure 1).

Dirichlet Energy (Equation 1, Section 4.1), a measure of geometric alignment between functor-related entity embeddings, decreases as analogical reasoning emerges, and this decrease is mirrored layer-wise in pretrained Gemma2-2B/9B models during in-context analogical reasoning (Section 4.1, Section 5, Figure 6a, Figure 8).

The analogical mechanism decomposes into structural alignment in embedding space plus a 'functor application' realized as vector addition (e_t ≈ e_s + f) implemented via attention and residual connections (Section 4, Section 4.2).

Model depth exhibits non-monotonic, inverse-scaling behavior on the analogical reasoning task: deeper models perform worse at analogical reasoning under the tested synthetic setup (Section 3.3, Figure 3 right panel).

Weight decay has a non-monotonic effect on emergence speed: moderate weight decay accelerates the appearance of analogical reasoning while excessive weight decay prevents it (Section 3.2, Figure 3 left panel).

t1tt3rzN7s.text: The Dynamic E-ExoFormer variant (~450M parameters) achieves 50.27% average downstream accuracy and 14.09 perplexity, versus 48.80% accuracy and 14.64 perplexity for the Gated Attention baseline (Table 1).
Dynamic ExoFormer matches Gated Attention's validation loss using approximately 1.5x fewer training tokens while achieving about 1.5 percentage points higher downstream accuracy (Figure 2).

Every ExoFormer variant, which uses dedicated exogenous anchor projections computed outside the sequential layer stack (Equation 9), outperforms its corresponding NuResFormer counterpart, which reuses internal first-layer projections as anchors (Section 3.5, Section 3.6).

ExoFormer achieves a substantially lower attention-sink score of 0.0078 compared to 0.2580 for the baseline, supporting the 'Offloading Hypothesis' that external anchors let sequential layers specialize in feature transformation (Section 4.5, Table 2).
The exogenous anchor mechanism adds only about 1.3% additional FLOPs in theory, though the reference implementation shows an observed 8-15% runtime overhead due to modularity (Appendix C.3).

boZd8pG5E2.text: Pose-ICL reduces pose error to 10.75 degrees (3D Assets) and 13.20 degrees (Real-world) versus SceneDesigner's 25.70/23.88 degrees and Custom Diffusion 360's 33.23 degrees (Table 1, Section 4.3).
Pose-ICL achieves DINO-I identity-consistency scores of 0.758/0.758 on the two benchmarks, exceeding DreamBooth's 0.658/0.680 by up to 0.078 (Table 1, Section 4.3).

The Surface-Anchored Position Embedding (SAPE) anchors image tokens to volumetric bounding-box surface coordinates via a RoPE-style embedding applied in the first 19 transformer layers (Shallow Injection Strategy), with sub-patch position embeddings splitting 21 coordinates across 24 attention heads using segment sizes d_x=42, d_y=42, d_z=44 (Section 3.1-3.2).

An ablation progressively adding components reduces pose error from a 22.88/29.97 degree baseline to 19.33/23.72 with SAPE, 14.12/16.71 with added Shallow Injection, and 10.75/13.20 for the full method (Table 2, Section 4.4).

The model is trained on a Custom Multi-Pose Dataset of 7,665 objects and 153,227 images, combining 6,464 ABO/GSO 3D assets rendered at 36 poses (68,549 images) with 1,201 real-world CO3D objects across 4 categories (84,678 images), and evaluated on a held-out set of 55 objects producing 2,700 evaluation images (Section 4.1).
Pose-ICL remains robust to noisy pose inputs, with DINO-I consistency degrading only from 0.777 to 0.742 as injected pose noise increases (Table 3, Appendix C.5).

hEvt3HWxD3.text: DTop-p MoE regulates sparsity using a Proportional-Integral (PI) controller that adjusts the Top-p threshold to keep the activated-expert ratio near a user-specified budget, described via the PI control law in Section 3.2.1.
A Dynamic Routing Normalization mechanism applies a layer-specific learnable scale θ_l to normalize routing logits before the softmax, computed as softmax(θ_l · (z − μ(z))/σ(z)) (Section 3.2.2).

On 13 NLP downstream benchmarks, DTop-p improves average accuracy by 1.9 points over Top-k MoE while matching Top-k's average FLOPs, using DCLM-Baseline pretraining data of 100B-300B tokens (Table 2, Section 4).
DTop-p reduces variance in the number of activated experts to roughly 1 standard deviation compared to about 4 standard deviations for fixed Top-p, as shown across training steps (Figure 6).

Scaling experiments across expert granularity (32E4A, 64E8A, 128E16A configurations, Table 3), total expert capacity (2.1B-13.6B parameters, Table 4), model size (0.4B-2.4B dense-equivalent, Table 5), and dataset size (Table 6) show DTop-p consistently outperforms both fixed Top-p and Top-k baselines.
An ablation confirms both the PI controller and Dynamic Routing Normalization are individually necessary, with their removal degrading performance (Figure 7, Section 4.5).

jzUCodmd4C.text: FLAIR (Full-duplex LAtent and Internal Reasoning) performs latent reasoning concurrently with streaming speech perception during the user's speaking phase, formalized via an Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) adaptation for full-duplex dialogue systems (Section 3.2, Section 4).
FLAIR achieves 78.0% accuracy on Llama Questions and 56.2% on MMSU, outperforming full-duplex baselines including Moshi, SALMONN-omni, Freeze-Omni, and dGSLM (Table 1).
On the Impatient Dataset, FLAIR attains a turn-taking latency of 0.39s, a barge-in latency of 0.46s, 100% barge-in success rate, and a speech-quality MOS of 4.3 (Table 2).
On Full-Duplex-Bench, FLAIR reaches a turn-taking TOR of 93.0% and barge-in TOR of 92.0% (Table 3).

Recursive latent embedding feeding, trained via a supervised fine-tuning strategy using a Global-aware Expert model (Section 4.2), is shown in ablations (Section 7.3, Appendix E) to improve reasoning-task performance without degrading conversational turn-taking or barge-in behavior.
Training uses a 620K-hour synthetic data pipeline comprising 530K hours of speech continuation, 70K hours of instruction-following QA, and 20K hours of ASR-QA with background noise (Section 5).

zB4xF9tfdm.text: Spectral-Decoupled Iterative Refinement (SDIR) combines a Synoptic Frequency-Guided Former (SFG-Former) for global structure and a Fourier Residual Refiner (FR-Refiner) using Scale-Conditioned Fourier Neural Operators to synthesize high-frequency residuals (Section 3.3-3.4).
A Physically Consistent Power Spectral Density (PCPSD) loss with dynamic masking enforces turbulence-consistent spectral distributions during training (Section 3.5).
On the CIKM dataset, SDIR achieves average HSS of 0.6558 and CSI of 0.4724, improving over Earthformer by 13.6% in HSS and 14.1% in CSI (Table 1).

On the SEVIR dataset, SDIR attains HSS=0.4401, CSI=0.3499, SSIM=0.7544, and MAE=1897.9, outperforming baselines including ConvLSTM, PredRNN, PhyDNet, SimVP, Earthformer, MIMO, DiffCast, and AlphaPre (Table 3).
An ablation over inference steps shows optimal performance at 8 steps with 1.17s inference time, balancing spectral fidelity against latency (Table 6).

On the Shanghai dataset (501x501 resolution, 1,534 training / 526 testing sequences), SDIR achieves average HSS=0.5882 and CSI=0.4497, superior to baselines across all precipitation intensity thresholds (Table 2, Section 4.1).

OehZzGGY7Z.text: Theorem 3.2 shows hardmax transformers with logarithmic depth in a time bound t-hat can simulate Turing machines using O(t) intermediate chain-of-thought tokens while keeping ternary weights and activations (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.3 establishes that a Summarized Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) construction achieves the same Turing-machine simulation scaling logarithmically in a space bound s-hat rather than time, with segment lengths bounded by the actual space usage O(s_M(w)) (Theorem 3.3).

Theorem 4.2 shows converting the hardmax construction to a softmax transformer with rounded attention weights requires a scaling factor c0(l-hat) = O((log l-hat)^(3/4)), using only 1 mantissa bit and 3 exponent bits for activations and 4 mantissa bits with O(log log l-hat) exponent bits for attention weights (Theorem 4.2).
In Sudoku experiments varying reasoning depth L in {4,5,6,7,8}, accuracy reaches 99.5% at L=6 and 99.7% at L=8, demonstrating depth saturation (Section 5).

A small transformer (d=768, L=12, H=12) trained on summarized chain-of-thought sequences up to 2^12 tokens generalizes to 92/100 accuracy on ultra-hard Sudoku instances requiring up to 9 million reasoning tokens (Section 5).

Switching numerical precision from bfloat16 to fp32 produces negligible accuracy improvement, while increasing depth from L=6 to L=8 substantially extends chain-of-thought context capability (Figure 6a, Figure 6b).

WLRuaimgMw.text: CDAT combines a mixture von Mises–Fisher (Mo-vMF) attention energy term with a Hopfield refinement energy term in its semantic energy function (Equation 9).

On graph classification, CDAT reaches 98.5% accuracy on DD and 93.5% on NCI1, versus the ET baseline's 95.9% and 90.1% respectively, and attains state-of-the-art results on 5 of 7 benchmark datasets (Table 1).
In the low-label (1% split) graph anomaly detection regime, CDAT achieves 94.5% AUC on Amazon and 95.91% AUC on T-Finance, compared to ET's 91.9% and 92.2% (Table 2).
CDAT incurs only +2.4% inference overhead and +0.19% parameter overhead relative to ET on NCI109, indicating near-identical computational cost (Table 4).

An ablation shows removing the mutual-excitation term W·x drops DD accuracy from 98.5% to 83.1%, while an unconstrained full-rank W collapses to 82.9% on NCI1 due to overfitting, motivating the low-rank symmetric parameterization W=P^T QP (Table 3).
Theorem 3.3 establishes a dissipation certificate showing the storage functional V(t) is non-increasing under CDAT's controlled dynamics, guaranteeing convergence to a stable invariant set.

47xV4icN1B.text: Theorem 1 characterizes the training dynamics of a single-layer Transformer during continual factual knowledge acquisition, showing parameter convergence to the optimal Bayesian prediction with oscillation around the convergence point (Section 2, Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 shows attention allocation during factual knowledge acquisition is governed by a 'Diversity Index' measuring the breadth of token-object associations (Section 2, Theorem 2).

The analysis demonstrates regularization-based continual learning methods only adjust the convergence rate of parameters without altering the underlying forgetting tendency, whereas data replay methods shift the convergence dynamics itself (Section 3).

STOC (Selecting Tokens via attentiOn Contribution) selects fixed-length text snippets for generative replay by aggregating token-level attention scores across layers and heads and applying a sliding window, optionally followed by MinHash deduplication (Section 4).

On the synthetic 120,000-individual biography dataset with five relational attributes, STOC outperforms random-selection and LAMOL replay baselines across data mixing ratios from 0.5 to 0.9 (Table 2).

On real-world KnowEdit benchmarks, STOC improves Pythia-160M's ZSRE continual-knowledge accuracy to about 27.56% versus a 24.42% naive baseline, and improves Qwen2.5-0.5B to about 37.47% versus 34.58% (Table 3).

r6wfuAKmVb.text: The paper proves that current leaderboard benchmarks induce a Stackelberg ranking game in which no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium generally exists among competing model developers (Section 3).
Proposition 4.3 shows that whenever a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium does exist, the resulting equilibrium ranking preserves the latent capability ordering of the models (Section 4, Proposition 4.3).

Theorem 4.6 identifies 'just-overtake' incentives as the failure mode: if there exists a rank r such that the cost of the required effort to overtake is less than the reward gap between ranks r-1 and r, the follower game admits no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium (Section 4, Theorem 4.6).

The tune-before-test (TbT) protocol is proven to induce a benchmark game with a unique Nash equilibrium that ranks models by latent quality, with monotone stabilizing effects as the TbT level increases (Section 5, Proposition 5.3).
Under power-law capability scaling, the TbT threshold needed to stabilize rankings grows only polynomially in the reward gaps between adjacent ranks (Section 5, Proposition 5.6).

An empirical demonstration on Winogrande shows that after applying TbT with 3,000 training steps, at least 384,668 additional training steps would be required to change the induced model ranking (Figure 1).

oddGER4AzK.text: LAVL's Latent Alignment Network (LAN) parameterizes the goal-conditioned value function as an asymmetric latent distance V(s,g) = -||φ_s(s) - φ_G(g)||₂, relaxing strict metric constraints used by prior methods like IQE and QRL (Section 3).

LAVL achieves the highest performance on 20 of 22 OGBench datasets, spanning maze navigation (85-97% success), long-horizon 'giant' maze tasks (85% success, only a 9.6% relative drop versus non-long-horizon variants), and robotic manipulation Cube/Scene tasks (83-88% success) (Table 1).

On trajectory-stitching datasets, LAVL shows only a 1.1% performance drop relative to non-stitching variants, compared to 18.6-36.9% drops for baseline methods, indicating markedly better trajectory stitching (Table 1).
An architectural ablation shows LAN outperforms IQE, MRN, and Hilbert-representation baselines on the Scene manipulation task, achieving 88% success versus under 20% for the alternatives (Figure 6).
A continuity regularization term that penalizes value differences exceeding a threshold δ improves success rate on pointmaze-giant from 35% to 95%, roughly a 10x improvement (Figure 5).
Ablations show LAVL's performance is stable across latent dimensions ranging from 16 to 256 (Figure 5).

JchIXIrN4i.text: Theorem 3.4 proves a cumulative target-loss bound of the form F_T + (MD/α)(D/2 + P_T) for non-stationary online structured prediction, where F_T is the cumulative surrogate loss of any comparator sequence and P_T is its path length, with dependence on the horizon T entering only through F_T and P_T (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).

The bound relies on a surrogate gap condition (Assumption 3.2) bounding true loss by (1-α) times the surrogate loss, and a self-bounding property (Assumption 3.3) bounding the squared gradient norm by twice the surrogate loss, which together enable telescoping cancellation of surrogate-loss terms (Section 3, Assumptions 3.2-3.3).
Theorem 4.5 extends the main bound to a broader class of problems using a Convolutional Fenchel-Young loss formulation (Section 4, Theorem 4.5).
Theorem 5.1 establishes a lower bound showing that the joint dependence of the target-loss bound on F_T and P_T is tight (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).

A Polyak-style adaptive learning rate, set as η_t = min{2(L_t(W_t) - E[ℓ(ŷ_t,y_t)])/||G_t||²_F, η_{t-1}}, empirically outperforms constant and AdaGrad-type learning rates under non-stationarity (Section 3.4, Appendix E).

bI9moH3UZw.text: In the high-dimensional limit, the microscopic dynamics of straight-through estimator (STE) training converge to a stochastic differential equation governed by Eq. (15) (Section IV, Theorem IV.3).

The macroscopic summary statistics of STE training concentrate onto a deterministic ODE trajectory (Eqs. (24)-(25)) with concentration rate O_d(d^{-1/2}) as dimension d grows (Section V-B, Theorem V.3).

STE training exhibits an extended plateau followed by a sharp drop in generalization error across bit-widths b in {2,3,4,5}, with the plateau length depending on the quantization range ω (Section VI-A1/VI-A2, Figures 2-3).
For input-only quantization, a closed-form stable fixed point exists under the learning-rate condition 0 < η < 2(σ_ψ^2 + λ)/σ_ψ^4 (Section VI-C1, Proposition VI.1).

The asymptotic deviation of the STE-trained quantized model from the unquantized linear model is characterized across three regimes, with a leading-order correction term of size O_Δ(Δ^2) depending on the fractional quantization level position (Section VI-C2, Theorem VI.3).

u7qkL3ryE4.text: For d_x x n-dimensional sequence-to-sequence targets whose components are γ-Hölder continuous, a fixed-depth Transformer network with softmax attention achieves L^p approximation error ε (for any p in [1,∞)) using O(ε^{-d_x n/γ}) total parameters (Theorem 1).

The same Hölder approximation result extends to the endpoint p=∞, the first explicit L^∞ bound established for standard softmax-attention Transformers, at the cost of parameter counts scaling with 3^{d_x n} (Theorem 1, case p=∞).
For target functions in the Sobolev class W^{1,p}, a depth-2 Transformer network achieves L^p approximation error ε using O(ε^{-d_x n}) parameters (Theorem 2).

Under nonparametric regression with dependent (β-mixing) observations, the excess risk of the Transformer-based empirical risk minimizer converges at rate m^{-γ/(γ+d_x n)} (up to log factors) for geometrically β-mixing data, and at rate m^{-rγ/((r+2)γ+(r+1)d_x n)} for algebraically β-mixing data with mixing parameter r (Theorem 3).

The proof technique shows that if the self-attention layer performs column averaging, the resulting network reduces to a generalized Transformer class that can approximate sequence-to-sequence Hölder functions, linking softmax and hardmax attention as special cases (Section 2.3).

uz0gAAYydl.text: Spectral representational similarity metrics exhibit a non-zero null baseline scaling as O(d/n) under independence, with expected Frobenius norm of the cross-covariance equal to d_x d_y/(n-1) for independent representations, confounding apparent similarity with embedding width (Section 4.1, Proposition 4.1).

Selection-based aggregation across layer pairs (e.g., taking the maximum similarity over M comparisons) inflates similarity scores as μ + Cσ√(log M), creating spurious convergence that grows with model depth (Section 4.2, Equation 7).
A permutation-based null-calibration procedure (Section 5, Equations 12 and 17) removes these width and depth confounds by rescaling observed similarity relative to an empirical null distribution.

After calibration, apparent convergence measured by global spectral metrics such as CKA-RBF largely disappears, while local neighborhood similarity (mKNN) retains significant cross-model agreement (Section 6.3, Figure 6).
The calibrated-agreement pattern (global convergence vanishing, local neighborhood alignment persisting) also holds for video-language representation alignment (Figure 7).

WKelJRz5kG.text: GPT-5.2, the best-performing of 10 evaluated LLMs, achieves a Feasibility Rate of only 32.67% in the text-only setting on WorldTravel, dropping to 19.33% in the multi-modal (webpage-screenshot) setting, a 13.34 percentage-point decline attributed to a 'Perception-Action Gap' (Table 3, Section 4.2).

WorldTravel comprises 150 real-world travel tasks across 5 European cities (Berlin, Vienna, Rome, Barcelona, Florence), each requiring an average of 15+ tightly coupled temporal and logical constraints, with WorldTravel-Webscape providing over 2,000 rendered webpages spanning 36 attractions, 25 restaurants, and 26 hotels (Section 3.5, Table 2).

Average Feasibility Rate across models collapses from 36.3% at 6-7 hard constraints to 18.3% at 8-9 constraints and to 3.4% at 10-11 constraints, identifying a Planning Horizon capacity threshold at approximately 10 constraints (Section 5.3, Figure 5a).

In the Gold-θ ablation, providing all hard-constraint parameters directly in structured form (removing the perception burden) still leaves GPT-5.2's Feasibility Rate at only 36.67% on the 30 highest-coupling tasks, indicating planning reasoning itself, not parameter extraction, is the primary bottleneck (Table 5, Section 5.1).

Timed-Entry Slot constraints show the lowest satisfaction rate of the three hard-constraint categories analyzed, at 27% in the text setting and 16% in the multi-modal setting (Section 5.3, Figure 5b).

2rukwU6tI3.text: The evolved constitution C* achieves a Societal Stability Score of 0.556±0.008, compared to 0.249±0.050 for the human-designed HHH baseline and 0.332±0.030 for an LLM-generated baseline, a 123% and 67% improvement respectively (Table 5).

Agents under C* restrict communicative (social) actions to just 0.9% of total actions, versus 62.2% for HHH and 54.7% for LLM-Generated baselines, a 98.6% reduction in communication frequency while outperforming these more verbose baselines (Table 8).
C* achieves 91% project completion (productivity) compared to 30% for HHH and 51% for LLM-Generated, a roughly 203% productivity increase over HHH despite minimal communication (Table 5).
A Welch's t-test comparing C* against HHH yields p < 0.0001 with Cohen's d = 6.1, indicating an extremely large and statistically robust effect size (Table 10).

Across a 30-iteration evolutionary search, the evolved constitution surpasses the HHH baseline's Societal Stability Score by iteration 11 and the LLM-Generated baseline by iteration 18, reaching a peak score of 0.577 (Figure 4).

n50Ipdt5d5.text: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).

IoY0A6opfl.text: MemCast is evaluated on 10 benchmarks spanning short-term electricity price datasets (NP, PJM, BE, FR, DE) and long-term datasets (ETTh, ETTm, WP, SP, MOPEX) (Table 1).

MemCast is compared against 12 baselines across statistical (ARIMA, Prophet), deep learning (PatchTST, iTransformer, TimeXer, ConvTimeNet, DLinear), and LLM-based (LSTPrompt, LLM-Time, TimeReasoner, Time-LLM) categories, achieving best or second-best results on most datasets, with the largest margins on the volatile NP and PJM price benchmarks (Table 2, Section 4.1).
The hierarchical memory module combines historical pattern abstraction, reasoning wisdom distillation, and general law induction to structure forecasting experience (Section 3.3).

Dynamic confidence adaptation assigns mutable confidence scores to memory entries, updating them only when predictions beat a moving-average baseline, which is designed to avoid leaking test-set distribution information (Section 3.4).

An ablation study shows that removing any of the three hierarchical memory components degrades performance (Table 3), and confidence adaptation reduces forecasting error consistently across datasets (Figure 3).

Hh1hf4kauu.text: DetectRouter achieves 90.85% average AUROC on EvoBench, outperforming the Fast-DetectGPT fixed-surrogate baseline (81.01%) by 9.84 points (Table 2).
DetectRouter achieves 77.92% average AUROC on MAGE, an 8.23-point improvement over Fixed-Surrogate Fast-DetectGPT (69.69%), with consistent gains across eight model families (Table 2).

Routing improves all six detection criteria evaluated, with the largest relative gains on Entropy (+139.4%) and LLR (+35.4%) and the smallest on Likelihood (+5.4%), averaging 36.1% relative improvement (Figure 4).

The two-stage training pipeline first builds discriminative prototypes from white-box models via cross-entropy plus margin-based separation losses (Stage 1), then aligns geometric prototype distances with black-box detector-pool affinities via KL-divergence minimization with prototype anchoring (Stage 2).
The mismatch-risk bound |μ* − μ_proxy| ≤ B·√(2·D_KL(P_src‖P_sur)) formalizes how surrogate-source distribution divergence bounds detection performance gaps (Proposition 3.1).
Using only 10% of Stage 2 training data still yields 89.06% AUROC on EvoBench, indicating the learned prototype space provides strong regularization and data efficiency (Figure 6).

ECdZxuI9Hf.text: Spectral position χ_pos, a scale-free quantity in [0,1] measuring which eNTK eigenvalues currently drive loss reduction, decreases throughout training, with larger models reaching lower values than smaller models (Figure 1).
Loss dynamics decompose as δL = χ_loss · χ_net · χ_pos, separating loss-function sensitivity, network responsiveness, and spectral position (Equation 8, Section 3.1).

Controlled random feature models with power-law data spectra confirm that empirically measured spectral position matches theoretical predictions, validating χ_pos as a diagnostic (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

Pre-trained representations achieve lower spectral position than randomly initialized frozen backbones under linear probing, indicating feature learning shapes representations to enable greater spectral reach (Section 5, Figure 4).

During full training, χ_net grows by orders of magnitude while χ_pos decreases, but under frozen linear probing χ_net remains roughly constant, suggesting feature learning compensates to sustain learning progress (Figure 5).

The framework is validated on Llama-2-style models trained on the SimpleStories dataset, next-pixel prediction on CIFAR-5M, and Vision Transformers under standard and maximal-update (muP) parameterizations.

BzG0xtGjjr.text: IMPspec extends Hilbert space regression theory to derive closed-form posteriors for Gaussian processes with certain unbounded operators, avoiding the need for nuclear dominant kernels (Theorem 1, Section 4).
IMPspec derives explicit closed-form posterior mean and covariance formulas for spectral model coefficients using a spectral representation of the RKHS, ∑_i f_i·E[ψ_i|z] (Theorem 2, Section 5.1).
IMPspec gives closed-form posterior moments for the causal effect γ, decomposing the posterior variance into three interpretable components (Theorem 3, Section 5.2).
In causal Bayesian optimization experiments, IMPspec attains cumulative regret of 0.247 ± 0.284 under the front-door criterion and 0.335 ± 0.420 under the back-door criterion (Table 3, Section 6).

On the healthcare application based on the Chau et al. (2021) dataset, IMPspec attains 0.000 ± 0.000 cumulative regret, indicating state-of-the-art causal Bayesian optimization performance (Table 3, Section 6).
IMPspec is evaluated on a causal data fusion ablation combining two independent datasets and on the Aglietti et al. (2020) synthetic benchmark with unobserved confounding (Section 6).

wmROqgop27.text: Token Order Prediction (TOP) outperforms NTP, MTP, and DeepSeek MTP (DS-MTP) baselines on nine standard NLP benchmarks across 340M, 1.8B, and 7B parameter models (Table 2).
The TOP architecture requires only a single additional unembedding layer, compared to MTP's multiple additional transformer layers (Section 4).
On SciQ accuracy, TOP improves over the best baseline by roughly +4.90 points at 340M scale, +1.50 points at 1.8B scale, and +3.00 points at 7B scale (Table 2).
TOP is trained with a ListNet-style learning-to-rank loss using softmax-weighted cross-entropy over proximity-ranked upcoming tokens within a window (Section 4, Equation 5).
TOP models continued-trained on math and code outperform baselines on 4 relevant downstream benchmarks (Section 5).

The synthetic star graph pathfinding task, on which TOP is claimed to enable success while NTP, MTP, and DS-MTP fail, is listed among planned future experiments not yet reported with results in the body text (Section 7).

GkL3dANi6M.text: Constitutional black-box monitors trained only on synthetic STRIDE and Gloom trajectories generalize to the semi-realistic ControlArena test set spanning five domains: BashBench, Infrastructure-as-Code, RogueEval, AgentDojo, and ShadeArena (Section 3, Table 2).
A simple grid search over 3 models x 15 prompts achieves a partial AUROC of 0.853-0.866 on the ControlArena test set (Section 5.2).

Heavier optimization pressure via human refinement and automated prompt optimization (GEPA, MIPROv2) yields no significant improvement over the simple prompt sweep and can degrade test performance (Section 5.2, Section 5.3).
Performance on synthetic training data saturates quickly, and further optimization causes stagnation or degradation of performance on the semi-realistic ControlArena test set (Section 5.3).

The evaluation metric, partial AUROC, is computed over the false-positive-rate region [0, 0.20] and normalized to [0.1, 1.0], reflecting that high false-positive rates are impractical for safety monitoring (Section 4).

CklwnmcPYx.text: Reinforced Mode Regulation (RMR) enables stable, high-quality generation at entropy rates as low as 0.8 nats/step, whereas standard decoding typically collapses near 2.0 nats/step (Abstract; Section 7).
At decoding temperature 0.7, RMR increases the non-collapse rate from 8% under standard decoding to 56% (Figure 5a).
Under entropy-constrained decoding at entropy=1.0, RMR achieves a 33% non-collapse rate versus 5% for standard decoding (Figure 5b, Section 7).

Mode collapse is characterized as geometric collapse, where the correlation dimension (Definition 4.1) shows the model's internal generation trajectory becomes confined to a low-dimensional representation space (Section 3, Section 4.1).
LLM-as-a-judge evaluations show RMR does not degrade text quality relative to standard decoding in non-collapse regimes, with p-values greater than 0.05 (Table 1, Section 7).

cQRkHJGgj1.text: Adversarial perturbations against zero-shot CLIP suppress predictive uncertainty rather than increasing it, so adversarial predictions exhibit lower estimated uncertainty than clean predictions despite being incorrect (Section 1, Figure 1b).

The proposed UCAT method reformulates CLIP logits as Dirichlet concentration parameters and fine-tunes with combined cross-entropy loss and a KL-divergence regularizer between clean and adversarial Dirichlet distributions (Definition 4.1, Equation 11, Section 4).
On MS-COCO multi-label classification, UCAT achieves F1@3 of 37.04%, outperforming FARE's 33.86% (Table 1).

Across 16 zero-shot benchmarks under 2-step PGD attack with epsilon=1/255, UCAT attains 54.17% average clean accuracy, 32.20% average PGD robust accuracy, and 30.58% average AutoAttack robust accuracy, for a harmonic mean of 40.39% (Table 2).
Under a stronger 10-step PGD attack with epsilon=2/255, UCAT still reaches 45.21% average clean accuracy and 20.67% average AutoAttack robust accuracy (Table 5).
UCAT achieves the lowest Expected Calibration Error alongside the highest robustness, and the best AU-AUROC and EU-AUROC uncertainty-discrimination metrics among compared methods (Figure 3b).

UdpIy1ndTX.text: Phy3DAdvGen-generated objects evade six state-of-the-art LiDAR-based 3D object detectors spanning point-based (PointRCNN, IA-SSD), voxel-based (SAFDNet, VoxelNeXt), and point-voxel-based (HEDNet, PDV) architectures (Section 5.1).
In CARLA simulation, Phy3DAdvGen achieves a 94.6% attack success rate against PointRCNN, substantially outperforming baseline methods (Table 3).
In real-world physical tests using a 128-beam RS-Ruby LiDAR, the generated objects maintain an 85.3% evasion success rate across varied weather and driving scenarios (Table 2).

Multi-object compositions (AddObj) are identified as the dominant factor in LiDAR detection vulnerability, reducing detection success to 37.6-52.1% in Scene 1 versus 81.3-89.6% for single pedestrians (Section 3, Table 1).
The Phy3DAdvGen framework optimizes verb-object-pose prompts together with differentiable rendering to generate physically realizable adversarial 3D objects (Section 4).

8G0XzmQRG9.text: Temporal Self-Rewarding raises Llama3.1-8B's AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate to 29.44%, compared to 19.69% for the standard Self-Rewarding baseline, a 9.75-point improvement (Table 1).
For Qwen2.5-7B on Arena-Hard-v0.1, Temporal Self-Rewarding scores 34.4 versus 21.5 for the Self-Rewarding baseline, a 12.9-point gain (Table 3).

Theorem 1 (Bound on Directional Guidance) formally shows that as chosen/rejected hidden-state representations converge (‖h_w − h_l‖ → 0), the DPO training gradient vanishes, motivating the temporal decoupling method (Theorem 1, Methodology section).

An ablation removing the Future-Guided Chosen component ('Temporal SR w/o Future') drops AlpacaEval 2.0 performance to 27.20% from the full method's 29.44%, showing both Anchored Rejection and Future-Guided Chosen contribute complementary gains (Table 2).

On out-of-distribution tasks (GSM8K, ARC, TruthfulQA, HumanEval), the temporal method reaches 0.563 average accuracy versus 0.530 for the SFT baseline, without any task-specific training data (Table 4).
Improvements hold regardless of the judge model used, with consistent gains observed using both AutoJ-6B and AutoJ-13B as judges (Figure 2).

dEszwexTMi.text: The proposed SP-UCB--OLP algorithm, combining UCB-based exploration over surplus functions with an online-linear-programming admission rule, achieves Õ(√KT) regret for joint configuration selection and admission control over horizon T with K configurations (Theorem 9).
A switching-aware fluid oracle is introduced that explicitly accounts for mixing configurations over time and is proven to upper-bound the performance of any online policy (Theorem 8).

Saddle-point characterization via primal-dual optimality conditions links equilibrium, feasibility, and complementary slackness for the two-layer configuration-selection/admission problem (Theorem 5 and Theorem 6).
Naive 'best-response' heuristics are shown to fail under heterogeneous resource requirements via constructed complementary-resource scenarios (Section 4.1).

On synthetic Gaussian reward/resource scenarios, adding minimal exploration (α=0.01) improves the algorithm's competitive ratio from 84.8% to 97.4%, and on real Alibaba cluster traces the method demonstrates the predicted Õ(√T) regret scaling (Experiments section).

vHexbHQZEm.text: On the Qwen family (Qwen2.5-Math-7B teacher to Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE student), PADD reaches 80.2 average accuracy across AIME24, AMC23, MATH500, Minerva, and OlympiadBench, exceeding the GRPO-trained dense teacher's 77.7 average (Table with Qwen-family results).

PADD's four-stage framework spans two phases: Stage I expert initialization via K-Means clustering of teacher FFN neurons with router-weight initialization from cluster centroids, and Stages II-IV (online adaptive distillation, PR-GRPO path-refined policy optimization, and reward-augmented load balancing) for training (Sections describing Stage I-IV).

Ablating Stage I (expert initialization) causes 3.9-10.4 point drops on representative benchmarks, while ablating Stage II (online adaptive distillation) causes a 9.9-point drop on OlympiadBench, demonstrating each stage's necessity (Figure 2).

Ablating Stage III (PR-GRPO path-refined policy optimization) causes 2.3-3.9 point drops attributed to reduced stabilization of long reasoning chains, while ablating Stage IV (reward-augmented load balancing) causes smaller 0.6-1.5 point drops (Figure 2).

PADD is compared against six baselines including Dense-GRPO, MoE-Vanilla-GRPO, RSPO, GSPO, and Online KD, and is reported to surpass these strong baselines by 3-8.8 percentage points at equivalent inference cost (Section reporting main comparisons).

9kWVQtpvJi.text: Lemma 4.1 derives upper bounds on population risk R(π) and treatment risk T(π) using weights that account for a miscalibration parameter Γ ≥ 1 in the propensity-score or selection model, formalizing risk under partial identifiability (Lemma 4.1).

Theorem 4.3 provides a finite-sample certification guarantee that a learned policy satisfies P(T(π) ≤ τ | S=s) ≥ 1−α simultaneously across all miscalibration levels up to Γ, via a two-sample-split procedure using the Bentkus inequality (Theorem 4.3).

On synthetic data with two-dimensional covariates in [30,80], the method is evaluated both without confounding (Γ=1) and with an unmeasured confounder (Γ=2), demonstrating valid coverage of the treatment-risk constraint across tolerance levels τ (Section 5.1).

Applied to the Tennessee STAR dataset (n=4,218 students, small vs. regular class size treatment), the method learns fast-and-frugal decision trees limited to three splits that achieve valid risk control across tested τ values (Section 5.2).

Applied to the International Stroke Trial data (n=18,298 patients, 23 covariates, aspirin treatment for acute ischemic stroke, six-month mortality outcome), the method confirms valid risk certification across specified tolerance levels (Section A.5).

118JD1BQxO.text: SpecPL achieves 81.51% harmonic-mean accuracy averaged across the evaluated benchmark suite, combining a Spatial-Spectral Proxy that decomposes frozen-VAE latents into base (semantic) and detail (instance-specific) bands (Method section).
As a plug-and-play booster, SpecPL improves harmonic-mean accuracy by +4.86 points over CoOp, +2.00 over CoCoOp, +0.80 over MaPLe, and +0.31 over MMRL (Results table).
On the fine-grained FGVC-Aircraft dataset, adding SpecPL to CoOp raises harmonic-mean accuracy from 28.75% to 35.98%, the largest reported per-dataset gain (Results table, FGVC-Aircraft row).
A Frozen Visual Semantic Bank anchors text prompt representations to universal low-frequency visual invariants extracted from the VAE, mitigating overfitting during prompt learning (Method section).

Counterfactual Granule Supervision permutes high-frequency detail signals across samples and trains the model to predict the granule source, enforcing sensitivity of predictions to fine-grained discriminative cues (Method section).

An ablation combining the semantic alignment loss with factual granule modulation ('+Sem+GF') reaches 35.62 harmonic-mean accuracy, with counterfactual supervision adding further modest gains when grounded in stable semantics (Ablation table).

ADUGteohC7.text: For linear residual networks with equilibrated activities, predictive coding (PC) and backpropagation (BP) share exactly the same set of width- and depth-stable feature-learning parameterizations, with scaling exponent alpha=1/2 (Theorem 2, Section 4).

For linear MLPs, Corollary 3.2 shows the equilibrated PC energy converges to the MSE loss as width N to infinity, so PC computes the same gradients as BP under any width-stable feature-learning parameterization (Section 3.1).

For linear residual networks, the energy rescaling factor s(theta) = 1 + Theta(L/N), so PC gradients converge to BP gradients specifically in the regime where width N is much greater than depth L (Corollary 4.2, Equation 19).

Experiments on deep nonlinear residual networks with Tanh and ReLU activations show PC converges to BP gradients empirically as long as activity equilibrium is reached during the inference phase (Figure 4, Section 5).
The equilibrated energy for linear networks is derived in closed form as F*(theta) = (1/s(theta)) L(theta), where s(theta) = 1 + sum of squared norms of downstream weight products (Equations 5-6).

UPiyC9W4ms.text: For linear equality constraints h(x) = Ax - b, the manifold-aware perturbation method achieves exact distribution recovery, i.e. p0(x) = p-tilde_sigma(x) for all x on the constraint manifold M (Theorem 4.5).

For nonlinear constraint manifolds, the total variation distance between the recovered and true data distribution is bounded and decays exponentially in the perturbation radius: TV(p-tilde_sigma, p0) <= C1 exp(-C2 r^2/sigma^2) (Theorem 4.6).

The lifted distribution p_sigma, formed by perturbing data only in normal directions to the manifold, is proven to not be strictly supported on a lower-dimensional manifold, avoiding the ambient-dimension support-matching pathology of standard diffusion/flow training (Theorem 4.3, Definition 3.1).
On the realistic 90-dimensional protein backbone generation task, the method achieves a coverage (COV) metric of 0.9490 while guaranteeing constraint adherence (Table 4).

On plane and sphere constrained-generation tasks, the proposed perturbation approach outperforms baseline alternatives across COV, JSD, and TVD metrics for both diffusion models and normalizing flows (Table 1, Algorithm 1).

SObheoDzU8.text: MESA's Expert Capacity Reallocation is motivated by a proved routing-inertia lower bound: the parameter updates needed to activate a dormant expert with routing probability p_i grow as Omega(p_i^{-1/2}), making tail-expert activation prohibitively costly (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.1).

A Hessian-induced stability result shows the expected performance degradation from perturbing an expert e_i is upper-bounded by the product of its marginal utilization and its effective Hessian spectral norm, indicating tail experts sit in sharp loss minima (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).
On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, MESA reaches a 95.00% Strata safety score versus 93.00% for the Stair-DPO baseline, while preserving 66.11% GSM8K utility versus only 15.54% for Stair-DPO (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MESA attains 97.65% safety on WildJB while preserving 91.00% utility on Math500 (Table 1).
Against the F-SOUR adversarial jailbreak attack, MESA reduces attack success rate to 0.00% compared to 15.38% for the SafeX baseline (Section 4.2.2).

F9wgCdVPaV.text: Across a meta-analysis of 8 safety datasets meeting inclusion criteria (out of 1,062 candidate records screened), geo-cultural zones significantly improve model fit for safety ratings in 6 of 8 datasets after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (p<0.05) (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Geo-cultural background remains a significant predictor of safety ratings even after controlling for demographic factors in 6 of 8 datasets, with delta-AIC values ranging from -3.97 to -179.88 (Table 3, Section 4.3).

On average, adding cultural zones to demographic-only models reduces additional unexplained rater variance by 4.64%, compared to demographics alone explaining 5.25% of rater variance (Table 2, Table 3).

Roughly 10% of items across the examined safety datasets are culturally sensitive and would be misclassified as safe (false negatives) without adequate cultural representation, with the rate ranging from 3.0% (Severity dataset) to 13.9% (DIVE dataset) (Table 5, Section 5).

NooBkSo7oz.text: On the Deep Data Research benchmark, Claude 4.5 Sonnet achieves the highest average accuracy among frontier models at 47.73%, compared to 37.09% for GPT-5.2 and 18.94-30.65% for Gemini models (Table 2, Section 3).
Among open-source models, DeepSeek-V3.2 (38.80%) and GLM-4.6 (37.52%) achieve the top accuracy on the benchmark, still trailing Claude 4.5 Sonnet (Table 2).
Reactive investigation mode outperforms proactive mode, achieving 43.21% versus 32.59% accuracy respectively (Table 5, Section 5).

Parameter scaling alone yields less than 3% accuracy gains, and extending context window length does not improve performance, showing that scaffolding and scale are insufficient without agentic-first training (Section 5.1).
Failure analysis attributes 58% of errors to insufficient exploration (breadth or depth) and 40% to deficiencies in converting gathered data into insights (Figure 8, Section 6).

6TuaAw1DkF.text: Sequential Adaptive Steering (SAS) trains each subsequent trait probe on a composite dataset that includes activations already shifted by prior interventions, orthogonalizing steering vectors to reduce destructive interference across the Big Five traits (Section 3.2).
Layer selection for steering is automated via a Fisher Ratio metric measuring class separability across residual-stream layers, rather than manually chosen (Section 3.5).

Full SAS raises Extraversion from a baseline of 3.50 to 4.20 and Neuroticism from 2.88 to 4.10 on a 1-5 scale while lowering Agreeableness to 2.62, compared to naive steering which achieves smaller and less controlled shifts (Table 1).
Calibration bounds steering coefficients within [α_min, α_max] constrained to under 50% perplexity degradation and under 25% F1 score loss relative to baseline (Section 3.7, Table 1).

On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, SAS dominates naive steering on a Pareto frontier of coherence versus personality-expression score, and achieves a target multi-dimensional profile (high Extraversion, high Neuroticism, low Agreeableness) where DPO and naive baselines fail (Figure 4, Figure 5).
Removing Sequential Adaptive Steering or removing automated layer selection each cause a significant drop in Multi-Trait Success Rate, and results replicate on Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-7B (Appendix C).

gqa99Ev4C4.text: Proposition 3.1 shows dense causal effects β* are identifiable from unpaired covariate/outcome data when rank(Cov(I,X)) = d, while Theorem 3.2 shows sparse identification remains possible even when this rank condition fails, given only a restricted nullspace condition (Section 3).

The SplitUP estimator uses cross-fold sample splitting to construct a bias-corrected covariance term across K folds, remaining consistent as the number of environments m grows while the per-environment sample size n stays fixed (Section 4.2).

Lemma 4.5 proves that the standard two-sample instrumental-variable estimator becomes asymptotically biased in high dimensions, converging to β* scaled by a factor Q/(Q + b/r̃) that does not equal β* even as n → ∞ (Section 4, Lemma 4.5).

Theorem 4.2 establishes that an ℓ1-penalized GMM estimator achieves estimation rate Op(√(s*/N)) with support recovery for sparse causal effects, extended to the high-dimensional unpaired setting with rate Op(√(s*/m)) in Theorem 4.8 (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.8).

Three synthetic experimental settings (finite-dimensional sparse, high-dimensional dense, high-dimensional sparse) show UP-GMM suffices in the first setting while only SplitUP remains consistent in the high-dimensional dense and sparse settings (Figures 3-5).

2wDrJ5lZaF.text: Theorem 4 proves fast mixing of Glauber dynamics for mixtures of k distributions satisfying Approximate Tensorization of Entropy (ATE) when initialized from an empirical (data-based) distribution built from m = O(k/ε + log(1/δ)/ε) samples, reaching KL divergence at most ε in time t = c*n · O(log log(1/min μ(x)) + log(1/ε)) (Theorem 4).

The analysis avoids standard Chernoff-bound arguments in favor of moment generating function bounds on the KL divergence of empirical distributions, removing dependence on the minimum mixture weight (Section on Theorem 4, Lemma 21-22).

Theorem 5 gives an efficient identity-tester for mixtures of k ATE distributions in the coordinate-conditional sampling access model, resolving an open question posed by Blanca et al., with sample complexity O(c*n/ε)·log²(c*n/ε)·log(1/η)·log log(1/η)·|Σ| + O(√k·log(1/ρ*)/ε) (Theorem 5).

Algorithm 1 combines a Local Testing step detecting large intra-component divergence via the coordinate oracle with a Posterior Weight Estimation step detecting mismatched mixture weights via a KL-test, both relying on the KL-Test subroutine of Theorem 24 (Section 4, Algorithm 1, Theorem 24).

Lemma 11's chain rule for entropy decomposes the entropy of a mixture μ = Σₐ ρ(a)μₐ into an intra-component term Eₐ[Entμₐ[f]] and an inter-component term Ent_ρ[Eμₐ[f]], underlying the paper's use of Modified Log-Sobolev Inequalities in place of the Poincaré inequalities used in prior work by KLV24 and HMRW24 (Lemma 11, Remark 17).

hK7mJYY2aj.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes an infinite-dimensional extension of Doob's h-transform showing the conditional process Zt given Y=y satisfies a modified drift SDE incorporating a guidance term ∇log h^y(T-t,z), under either a Cameron-Martin-space prior or a prior absolutely continuous with respect to a Gaussian measure (Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 proves the conditional score decomposes as s^y(t,x) = s(t,x) + C∇log h^y(t,x), separating the pre-trained unconditional score from an intractable guidance term (Theorem 3.2).

Proposition 4.2 derives a simulation-free denoising score-matching loss (Equation 23) for Supervised Guidance Training that requires only forward passes through the pretrained score model, avoiding gradient estimation through sampled trajectories, implemented via Algorithm 1 with a stopgrad on the unconditional score (Proposition 4.2, Algorithm 1).
On the sparse-observations task, SGT with a k=1 preconditioner achieves RMSE of 0.373±0.210, nearly matching conditional diffusion's 0.347±0.213 while using 8x fewer parameters (Section 5.2).

On the heat-equation task, SGT achieves RMSE of 0.0443±0.0240, outperforming the FunDPS baseline, and on the shape-inpainting task SGT exceeds conditional diffusion when only 2 or 4 elliptic Fourier descriptor (EFD) coefficients are observed (Section 5.3, Section 5.4).

Zyjrz6R7zn.text: HyperTrack is a dataset of over 16,000 real-world GUI navigation tasks collected from more than 650 Chinese mobile applications (abstract only).
GUIEvalKit is introduced as an open-source evaluation framework for benchmarking vision-language models on offline mobile GUI navigation (abstract only).

Reinforcement-based finetuning consistently outperforms supervised finetuning for VLM-based GUI navigation agents, with the advantage being particularly pronounced in out-of-domain settings (abstract only).

The paper presents a systematic study of data scaling, benchmarking, and reasoning for VLM agents in mobile GUI navigation, combining data scaling with reinforcement learning approaches (abstract only).

76CIL1O0bz.text: On a 1.5B-parameter model under RLVR (GRPO) training, DoRA reaches 46.6% average accuracy across the math reasoning benchmarks, surpassing full-parameter fine-tuning (44.9%) and standard LoRA (42.5%) (Table 3).

AdaLoRA (44.2%) and MiSS (43.4%) also outperform standard LoRA (42.5%) but do not exceed full-parameter fine-tuning, while PiSSA collapses to 0.2% accuracy and MiLoRA underperforms severely at 18.0% (Table 3).

SVD-informed initialization methods fail in RLVR: PiSSA's catastrophic collapse and MiLoRA's 18.0% accuracy are attributed to reorientation toward or away from principal singular components that misaligns with RL optimization dynamics (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

Extreme parameter reduction bottlenecks reasoning capacity: VeRA (0.0029% of parameters) drops to 40.7% accuracy and IA3 degrades to 22.3%, compared to LoRA's 1.55%-parameter/42.5%-accuracy operating point (Table 4).
Rank ablation shows accuracy scaling with LoRA rank on the 1.5B model: rank 1 reaches 40.5%, rank 8 reaches 42.3%, and rank 16 reaches 43.9% (Table 5).
Scaling PEFT methods to a 7B model preserves the ordering trend, with LoRA+ at 55.5%, DoRA at 55.0%, LoRA at 54.8%, and MiSS at 53.4% average accuracy (Table 6).

aGaBFE9pta.text: Under pay-per-token pricing, a provider that reports each output character as a separate token can overcharge users by approximately 344.9±3.8% on Llama-3.2-1B (Table 1, Section 3.1).
Finding the longest plausible tokenization of a given output string that still matches the provider's claimed next-token distribution is NP-hard (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).

Algorithm 1, a heuristic that iteratively splits high-index vocabulary tokens into lower-indexed pairs in O(m(log m + σ_max)) time, lets a provider overcharge by up to 13% on Ministral-8B under nucleus sampling with p=0.99 without producing an implausible tokenization (Section 3.3, Figure 2).
Any incentive-compatible additive pricing mechanism must price purely as a function of the output string's character representation rather than the reported token sequence (Proposition 5, Section 4).

The proposed incentive-compatible mechanism prices tokens linearly by character count, r(t) = |str(t)| × r_c, which provably removes the provider's incentive to misreport tokenization (Theorem 6, Section 4).

Ol99zoW31J.text: For finite-horizon linear-quadratic systems with Gaussian policies, the noise-to-signal ratio of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator can be computed exactly in closed form via lifted dynamics (Theorem 5, Section 2.2).

The NSR landscape is highly non-uniform: as the policy approaches the optimal deterministic policy (Σ→0, per Corollary 6), the NSR does not vanish uniformly and can blow up, as demonstrated for a double-integrator system (Figure 1, Section 2.3).
Variance of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator grows exponentially with the control horizon when the closed-loop dynamics are unstable, i.e., when the spectral radius ρ(F)>1 (Theorem 8, Section 2.2).
A general upper bound on REINFORCE gradient-estimator variance is derived for generic nonlinear dynamics with expressive neural-network policies (Theorem 10, Section 4).
The analysis is extended from linear to polynomial systems and polynomial feedback policies via a moment-evaluation approach (Proposition 9, Section 3).

igB9562BZJ.text: NAtS-L assigns each token chunk to linear (Gated Delta Rule) or softmax attention via an Attention Score Layer that mean-pools the chunk and applies a linear scoring layer, selecting the attention type with the highest score per chunk (Equation 8, Section 4.1).
At 800M parameters, NAtS-L Hybrid achieves 18.52 perplexity on Wiki103, versus 19.27 for a standard Transformer, and 44.30 accuracy on LAMBADA versus 42.15 for GDN (Table 1).
NAtS-L Hybrid attains 45.07 average accuracy across six retrieval benchmarks, compared to 37.30 for a GDN Hybrid baseline (Table 1).
On the RULER long-context benchmark at 16k context length, NAtS-L Hybrid scores 0.21 versus 0.04 for GDN and 0.00 for a standard Transformer (Table 2).
NAtS-L achieves a 5.4x prefilling speedup over the Transformer at 128k sequence length and a 2.3x decoding speedup (Section 5.1).

xf1OYJfvqj.text: In the joint learning setting (as opposed to the planted-target-only model), gradient flow converges to the target direction even when the initial correlation m0 is negative, for first-nonzero-Hermite-coefficient index s≥2, with |1+m_t| decaying at rate Ce^{-c(t-τc)} after time τc ≥ Cd^{s-1} (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).

This contrasts with the planted model, where a negative initial direction traps the gradient flow in a spurious basin; in joint learning the adaptively evolving link function f_t corrects for the early misalignment (Section 4.2).

A dense reproducing kernel Hilbert space built from Hermite functions, K(x,y)=Σ_k c_k h_k(x) h_k(y), is constructed to adapt to the single-index structure for univariate function estimation (Proposition 2, Section 5).

The joint gradient flow on Hermite coefficients and the index direction can be implemented in practice as a finite-dimensional ODE on ((a_k)_{k≤𝗄}, m), discretized via an Euler scheme (Section 5, Section 6).

foyE0eF8HW.text: Theseus transports task-specific parameter updates (task vectors) between models with different widths without any additional training, using orthogonal Procrustes analysis on functional (activation-based) matching to produce a closed-form transformation τ_B = T_out τ_A T_in^T (Section on Method / Functional Matching).

On ViT-B/16 to ViT-B+ transfer across 8 vision datasets (EuroSAT, SVHN, GTSRB, RESISC45, DTD, CARS, MNIST, SUN397), Theseus improves accuracy by +5.83 to +10.32 ΔAcc depending on the number of alignment batches (1-20), versus a near-zero -0.26 ΔAcc for a zero-padding baseline (Table 1).

On T5-3B to T5-Large transfer evaluated via linear probing on 5 GLUE tasks (MNLI, QNLI, RTE, SCITAIL, SNLI), Theseus achieves +22.04 ΔAcc with 20 alignment batches and +3.93 ΔAcc with 100 batches (Table 2).

For same-architecture ViT-B/16 variants, Theseus attains +15.16 ΔAcc in the 20-shot regime, remaining competitive with the gradient-based GradFix method and outperforming TransFusion across all tested regimes despite being training-free (Table 3).
Theseus extends beyond width-only transfer to simultaneous depth-and-width transfer from ViT-B/16 to ViT-L/14, yielding +6.61 ΔAcc using naive layer interpolation (Table 4).

The Procrustes-based transformation preserves the Frobenius norm of the transported task vector (‖τ_B‖_F = ‖τ_A‖_F), and using the transported vector as a warm start accelerates downstream fine-tuning convergence (Section on Norm Preservation / Warm-Start Experiments).

LF4YsCYfrf.text: A single focus-dilution cycle in one-layer attention training decomposes into four theoretically characterized stages: initial rank-one condensation of embeddings (Theorem 3.2), attention growth producing frequency-driven focus on high-frequency tokens (Theorem 3.5), a mass-redistribution/dilution mechanism that weakens this focus (Theorem 3.7), and symmetry-breaking that initiates a new cycle (Theorem 3.9) (Section 3).

Lemma 3.1 establishes the linearized dynamics near the first saddle point that drives rank-one condensation, and Propositions 3.3-3.4 and 3.6 characterize a second critical point and an invariant rank-one manifold governing the transition into the focus phase (Section 3.1-3.3).

Synthetic experiments on Markovian data with controlled stationary token distributions show cosine-similarity matrices, PCA-projected embeddings, attention maps, and embedding-norm trajectories that match the predicted four-stage cyclical dynamics (Figure 2).

The predicted focus-dilution cycle and cyclical loss patterns are corroborated in realistic language modeling on WikiText and TinyStories corpora via observed attention evolution and embedding dynamics (Figure 3).
Figure 1 depicts the Markovian problem setup and shows characteristic four-stage loss-curve patterns used to identify the focus-dilution cycle empirically (Figure 1).

yylfMBpQ92.text: Di-BiLPS achieves a relative ℓ2 error of 0.021 on the forward Darcy Flow benchmark under 3% sparse observations, a 16% improvement over the DiffusionPDE baseline (Table 1).

Under 3% sparsity, Di-BiLPS reduces relative ℓ2 error on the Helmholtz forward problem to 0.025 (a 72% improvement over DiffusionPDE) and on the inverse Darcy Flow problem to 0.013 (a 59% improvement) (Table 1).
Di-BiLPS cuts inference runtime substantially versus DiffusionPDE at 3% sparsity, e.g., 35.45s vs 255.74s on Darcy Flow (down 86%) and 20.52s vs 249.81s on Helmholtz (down 92%) (Table 1 / Section 5).

The framework performs both forward and inverse PDE solving by operating entirely within a compact latent space learned via a variational autoencoder, avoiding pixel-space diffusion (Section 4, Figure 1).

Di-BiLPS supports zero-shot super-resolution, producing accurate continuous spatial-temporal predictions on the inhomogeneous Helmholtz equation at finer grid resolutions without retraining (Figure 6).

Ablation studies show that removing the observation-guidance term degrades performance across all tasks, and that condition guidance is particularly important for the more complex Non-Bounded Navier-Stokes setting (Table 2).

4XHiXa48fA.text: On the Meta-World online RL benchmark, ReLAM achieves a 100% success rate on Drawer Open and Door Open, compared with 80% and 100% for Diffusion Reward, and only 4% and 24.7% for the Image Subgoal baseline (Section on Main Results / Table).
On the harder Meta-World Button Press Wall task, ReLAM reaches 75.8% success versus 60% for Diffusion Reward, 47.8% for DACfO, and 12.7% for Image Subgoal (Section on Main Results / Table).

On the ManiSkill offline RL benchmark, ReLAM attains 88% success on Pick Cube and 89.3% on Push Cube, outperforming Diffusion Reward (68%/69.3%), DACfO (78.7%/76.7%), and Image Subgoal (60.7%/46.7%) (Section on Main Results / Table).

Theorem 1 provides a provable sub-optimality bound for the ReLAM hierarchical policy of the form V*_rt − V^{π_ReLAM}_rt ≤ k·(ε_π + 2ε_A/M), where k is the number of subgoals, ε_π is per-subtask policy error, ε_A is anticipation-model error, and M is the maximum step size (Theorem 1).
Ablations show 4 tracked keypoints outperform 8 or 12 keypoints, and a piecewise-linear distance-based reward outperforms purely linear or exponential/logarithmic reward shaping (Section 4.3).

Policies trained with anticipation-model-generated subgoals show only a small performance gap relative to those trained with ground-truth subgoals, validating the accuracy of the learned anticipation model (Section 4.3).

20nWnRkLP4.text: On NVILA-Lite-2B fine-tuned to 20 layers at pruning ratio ρ=0.1 for COCO-Caption, Model-Dowser achieves an H-score of 85.7 versus 78.3 for SPIDER and 67.0 for ModelTailor (Table with COCO-Caption results).
On LLaVA-1.5-7B under the same 20-layer, ρ=0.1 setting, Model-Dowser reaches an H-score of 79.9, outperforming SPIDER (75.2) and ModelTailor (75.8) (Table with COCO-Caption results).

Model-Dowser maintains O(|P|) memory complexity, matching standard fine-tuning, whereas SPIDER requires O(3|P|) and Grafting requires O(2|P|); SPIDER cannot train LLaVA-1.5-7B beyond 20 layers due to memory constraints (Table 3).

On ImageNet-R, Model-Dowser achieves H-scores of 71.2 and 69.7 across the tested NVILA-Lite-2B architectures, substantially outperforming baseline mitigation methods (Section with ImageNet-R results).
Model-Dowser's advantage over a random-layer-selection baseline is statistically significant (p=0.003-0.004) in the comparison reported in Table 4 (Table 4).
Layer-wise analysis shows catastrophic forgetting severity varies substantially by layer depth, motivating Model-Dowser's data-free importance probing to select which layers to fine-tune (Figure 3).

IjrmQgIvHU.text: Theorem 3.5 proves that acyclic regime-switching structural causal models with exponential-family noise are identifiable up to permutation, given conditional causal stationarity, conditional causal sufficiency, and Assumptions 3.1–3.4 (Theorem 3.5).

FlowMSM decouples regime detection—via Generalised EM with conditional normalising (neural spline) flows over a first-order stationary Markov chain—from causal discovery, which can use any stationary method such as DYNOTEARS, VARLiNGAM, PCMCI+, or Rhino (Section 4).

On synthetic benchmarks with N=100 series, T=100, D=10, and K=3 regimes, FlowMSM attains regime NMI of 0.90 (SVAR Gaussian), 0.88 (Exponential Family), 0.93 (ANM Nonlinear), and 0.83 (LSNM) (Table 1).

Paired with the best stationary causal discovery method, FlowMSM's regime clustering yields causal-structure recovery F1 up to 1.00 on the Exponential Family setting (VARLiNGAM) and 0.83–0.93 on the ANM/LSNM and SVAR settings (Table 1).
FlowMSM outperforms baselines iMSM, CASTOR, FANTOM, and R-PCMCI on non-Gaussian regime-switching settings while remaining competitive on Gaussian cases (Section 5, Table 1).

Applied to 5,786 daily Fama-French trading observations, FlowMSM identifies two dominant market regimes aligned with the 2008 financial crisis and COVID-19 pandemic volatility periods, unlike competing methods (Section 5).

Mo6iakSLwn.text: High-frequency components of attention weights—extracted via Discrete Fourier Transform, Discrete Wavelet Transform, and Discrete Laplacian operators—are used to compute an attention-instability score ρ = ‖z^hf‖₂ per layer/head for hallucination detection (Equation 6).
On RAGTruth, Fourier-high features reach token-level F1/AUROC of 0.6615/0.8052 (LLaMA-7B), 0.6723/0.8198 (LLaMA-13B), and 0.7266/0.8532 (Mistral-7B) (Table 1).

On HalluRAG, Fourier-high features reach token-level F1/AUROC of 0.6438/0.7603 (LLaMA-7B), 0.6616/0.7899 (LLaMA-13B), and 0.7152/0.8128 (Mistral-7B), and span-level (8-token window) AUROC of 0.8100–0.8872 across the three models (Table 1, Table 2).

Fourier-high attention features outperform the attention-based Lookback-Lens baseline by about 2.4% AUROC on LLaMA-13B summarization, and outperform verification-based methods (SelfCheckGPT, RefChecker) by 5–15% AUROC (Section 5).

An ablation shows high-pass attention components consistently outperform low-pass and full-spectrum features, and that the top 100 attention heads (under 10% of LLaMA-7B's heads) recover over 95% of full detection performance (Figure 4, Section 5).

uG4IOdaAGk.text: PASV defines a distribution over precedence-feasible permutations combining hard DAG-based precedence constraints with soft per-player priority weights λ, given by p^(⪯,λ)(π) ∝ ∏_t (λ_{π_t}|max_⪯(S_t)| / Σ_{k∈max_⪯(S_t)} λ_k) (Equation 4).

PASV is uniquely characterized by Efficiency, Linearity, Null Player, Monotonicity, Maximal Support, Weight Proportionality, and Equal-Weight Uniformity, and recovers the Precedence Shapley Value when weights are constant and the Weighted Shapley Value when the DAG is an ordered partition (Section 3).

An adjacent-swap Metropolis-Hastings sampler (Algorithm 1) with burn-in B=100,000, thinning τ=10,000, and N_MC=10,000 Monte Carlo samples estimates PASV values via the local acceptance ratio in Equation 9 (Algorithm 1, Equation 9).

On an 800-point MNIST data-valuation experiment with 8 providers (Owner, Anchor, four generative Boosters, Copier, Poisoner) under a 14-block DAG and k-NN (k=20) utility, increasing priority weight from PSV to PASV (b=32) lowers the Anchor's value from 0.0927 to 0.0548 while the Owner's value stays stable at 0.5270 (Table 1).

On a Census Income feature-attribution experiment with 45,222 samples, 12 features, and a two-layer 100-unit MLP, sweeping priority weights λ_i over {2^k : k ∈ [-8,8]} reveals a non-monotone, U-shaped dependency of the capital-gain feature's attribution on its own priority weight (Section 5).

25AaIQjAg9.text: TRIM computes an aggregated token saliency combining row saliency (entropy of a token's own attention distribution) and column saliency (attention received from other tokens) to build task fingerprints from 5-10 validation samples, then scores candidates via cosine similarity to these fingerprints without any backward pass (Section 3).

With a 5% coreset selected on Llama-3.2-1B, TRIM reaches 45.37% average accuracy across three general-domain reasoning tasks, versus 44.21% for LESS and 42.39% for TAGCOS, and surpasses full-data fine-tuning on SocialIQA (46.26% vs 45.04%) (Table results, Section 4).
On GSM8K with Llama-2-7B, a 5% TRIM coreset reaches 29.52% exact-match accuracy, nearly matching full-data fine-tuning (30.25%) and far exceeding LESS's out-of-domain 20.72% (Section 4).
Coresets selected using a 1B-parameter scorer transfer effectively to larger target models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) without per-target reselection (Section 4).

The selection pool comprises 270,679 examples drawn from Dolly, CoT, Oasst1, and Flan_v2, with evaluation on CommonsenseQA, SocialIQA, HellaSwag, and GSM8K, and TRIM's complexity is O(3fγNT + fN) versus LESS's O(3fγNT + 3fNC), eliminating per-candidate gradient computation (Section 3, Section 4).

QGAOswfVvD.text: AxProverBase is a minimal ReAct-style agent for Lean 4 theorem proving comprising a Proposer (with LeanSearch and Tavily web-search tools), a compiler-based review system, and a memory module, with self-managed reflective context improving performance by 7% at 20% lower cost versus a fixed-history-of-5 memory (Section 3).
Ablations show iterative proof refinement is the single largest contributor to performance, followed by memory mechanisms, with library search tools contributing the least (Section 4).
Using Claude Opus 4.5, AxProverBase achieves 54.7% pass@1 on PutnamBench, versus Hilbert's 70% at pass@1840 and DeepSeek V2's 7.1% (Table with benchmark results).

AxProverBase reaches 98.0% pass@1 on FATE-M, 66.0% on FATE-H, and 24.0% on FATE-X, compared to REAL-Prover (56.7% on FATE-M), Seed-Prover 1.5 (80.0% on FATE-H, 33.0% on FATE-X), and Goedel V2 (48.7% on FATE-M) (Section 4, benchmark table).

On LeanCat, AxProverBase scores 59.0% versus Gemini 3 Pro's 14.0%, and with just iterative feedback at 20 iterations AxProverBase doubles Hilbert's pass@1 rate, at an average cost of $12.60 per sample (Section 4).

mkHp4ZW01l.text: OptProver (EI + PW-UAPO), built on BFS-Prover-V2-7B, reaches 37.75% Pass@1 and 55.25% Pass@32 on the OptBench benchmark, up from the 13.25%/32.00% base model (Table 2).
OptBench comprises 400 undergraduate optimization problems split into Basics (121), Convexity (135), and Algorithm Analysis (144) subdomains, curated from the Optlib library (Section 4).

Whole-proof generation baselines (DeepSeek-Prover, Goedel-Prover, Kimina-Prover) achieve only 5-20% Pass@256 on optimization problems, far below OptProver's Pass@32, demonstrating brittleness of non-search-based approaches (Section 4).

OptProver maintains Pass@32 parity and improves Pass@1 on MiniF2F relative to the base model, showing no catastrophic forgetting of Olympiad-level theorem proving after optimization-focused continual training (Section 4).
OptProver improves ProofNet solved-problem count from 42 to 49 at Pass@32, indicating positive transfer to other undergraduate mathematics domains beyond optimization (Section 4).

Utility-Aware Preference Optimization (UAPO) introduces a three-level utility scale that explicitly penalizes 'stagnant transitions' (u=1) — syntactically valid tactics that nonetheless lead to unsolvable subtrees — distinguishing them from outright invalid steps (Section 3).

hZJAUJ5l9t.text: On MIMIC-IV at epsilon=2.0, PATH (using a 4B-parameter fine-tuned LLM) achieves a TDCR (Jensen-Shannon divergence) of 0.289 versus 0.736 for the AIM marginal baseline, a reduction of over 60% (Table 1).
On MIMIC-IV at epsilon=2.0, PATH reduces state transition error to 0.387 versus 0.741 for AIM, a reduction of nearly 50%, while marginal divergence also improves (3.298 vs 9.708 for AIM) (Table 1).
