PATH treats an entire user's longitudinal table — not a single row — as the differential-privacy protection unit, and fine-tunes an autoregressive LLM with DP-SGD on serialized user trajectories rather than flattening histories into fixed-width vectors (Section 2, Section 5).
The paper introduces Table-wise Distance to Closest Record (TDCR), a Dynamic-Time-Warping-based metric for evaluating synthetic trajectory fidelity against real user histories (Section 3).

PATH is evaluated on three datasets: MIMIC-IV vital-sign trajectories (102,864 patients), NYC 311 service request histories (118,510 records), and synthetic HMM-generated sequences with known ground truth (Section 6).
Baselines compared against PATH include AIM (marginal mechanism), a hand-crafted Direct Mechanism, and non-private few-shot prompting with Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite (Table 1, Table 3).

65uC8Ac9hm.text: TimeID (referred to in the paper as TimePD) achieves an average 9.3% MAE improvement over source-free baselines across seven real-world time series forecasting datasets: ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, Traffic, and Electricity (Section 4, Table 1).

Compared specifically to Time-LLM, the method achieves average reductions of 4.98% in MSE and 2.64% in MAE, with the largest single-setting gain on the Weather dataset at the 96-step horizon (10% MSE, 5.03% MAE reduction) (Section 4.2.1, Table 1).

The method combines three components: Invariant Disentangled Feature Learning (IDFL) that separates seasonal/trend components via Fourier-domain supervision, a lightweight proxy-denoising module that corrects systematic bias in LLM forecasts, and knowledge distillation to a lightweight target model (Section 3.1-3.3).

Ablation results show that removing proxy denoising increases MSE by 26.18%, removing knowledge distillation increases MSE by 17.86%, and removing the LLM component entirely increases MSE by 4.29%, indicating proxy denoising is the most critical component (Section 4.2.2).

Baselines compared include DLinear, TimeKAN, SimpleTM, TimesNet, iTransformer, PatchTST, OFA, and Time-LLM, evaluated under a source-free domain-adaptation setting with no access to source training data (Section 4.1, Table 1).

hXO2OP0T4w.text: For normal-form games, the framework defines a per-round e-value E_{i,t}(a_i')(lambda) = 1 - lambda*X_{i,t}(a_i') requiring only observed payoff evaluations, not knowledge of the equilibrium strategies themselves (Section 2, Lemma 2.2).

Theorem 2.6 shows family-wise error rate (FWER) is controlled at level alpha when the accumulated test supermartingale threshold reaches sum_i |A_i| / alpha, where A_i is agent i's action set (Section 2, Theorem 2.6).
Theorem 2.7 bounds the expected detection time of an equilibrium deviation at O(log(sum_i |A_i| / alpha) / eta^2), where eta is the deviation's payoff-improvement magnitude (Section 2, Theorem 2.7).

Theorem 2.8 adapts a Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to the sequential e-value setting for false discovery rate (FDR) control, and the paper shows empirically in a 2x2 game that this FDR procedure detects deviations faster than the conservative FWER-controlling baseline (Section 2, Theorem 2.8).

For stochastic games, Theorem 3.4 bounds detection time by (log b + C_i) / KL-bar_i(mu), where KL-bar_i(mu) is a state-averaged Kullback-Leibler divergence, and Remark 3.5 extends this via mixture martingales to handle deviations of unknown magnitude (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).

Empirical validation on Grid Soccer and Predator-Prey environments shows detection times matching the theoretical O(1/epsilon^2) scaling, including under the mixture-martingale extension for unknown deviation magnitude (Section 3).

g6wvLLdH1l.text: Qwen3-VL-8B scores 76.0% on a purely text-only long-context information retrieval task versus 62.6% for the underlying text-only Qwen3-8B model, despite the task containing no visual input (Section 2).

In a controlled experiment, a text-only-trained model achieves 37.2% out-of-distribution accuracy on contexts with more than 8 objects, compared to 69.5% for an image-text-trained model, rising to 83.6% with added noise augmentation (Section 4).

Table 1 reports higher symbolic-to-positional attention ratios for VLM variants than their text-only counterparts (e.g., Qwen 3: 2.463 vs. 1.819, a difference of +0.644), quantifying the shift away from positional shortcuts (Table 1).

Mechanistic analysis identifies three distinct circuit types underlying retrieval: a Positional Circuit relying on token position with low attribute decodability, and two Symbolic circuits (Color-Key and Shape-Key) that bundle explicit attribute-entity pairs (Section 6).

Visual training induces spatial translation invariance in the visual encoder that disrupts reliance on token-position regularities, forcing adoption of symbolic binding matched to semantic identity rather than sequence position (Section 5).

The shift from positional to symbolic binding strategies persists even when visual examples are subsequently removed from the input, improving generalization on text-only out-of-distribution retrieval tasks (Section 5).

Lzwp2KXedc.text: In dimension d = 6m, there exists a stochastic convex optimization instance where every ε-ERM solution with ε = Θ(m^{-3/2}) incurs constant excess risk and fails to generalize (Theorem 1).
For λ-strongly convex losses with m^{-3/2} ≤ λ ≤ m^{-1/2}, any ε-ERM solution w_S satisfies F(w_S) − min F(w) ≥ Ω(1/(λ m^{3/2})) (Theorem 2).
When ηT = Ω(m^{3/2}), gradient descent incurs constant generalization error with high probability, as a corollary of the ERM lower bound (Corollary 3).
Gradient descent's excess risk is lower-bounded by F(w_S^{GD}) − min F(w) = Ω(min{√(ηT/m^{3/2}), 1}) (Theorem 4).
This new generalization lower bound of Ω(ηT + √(ηT/m^{3/2})) for constrained gradient descent narrows the previously exponential gap to the best known upper bound of O(ηT + ηT/m) (Theorem 4).

The construction uses Feldman's asymptotically good binary code combined with a novel 'link function' mapping sample information to bad ERM solutions while preserving convexity, giving the first proof that all approximate ERMs fail in linear dimension (Section on technical construction / proof of Theorem 1).

NKWWXlS3xt.text: SQSD (Sample-Level Quantification of Safety Degradation) computes risk scores from the projection difference of parameter updates along danger-aligned versus safety-aligned directions (Section 4.1).

During benign fine-tuning, parameters cumulatively drift toward danger-aligned directions across checkpoints, with danger-direction projections increasing monotonically while safety-direction projections stay near zero, progressively undermining model safety (Section 3.2).
SQSD outperforms five baselines—Reward Model, Bi-Anchor (Representations), Bi-Anchor (Gradients), Self-Inf-N, and LARF—at separating high-risk from low-risk fine-tuning samples (Table 1).
SQSD is validated across Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-2-7B, maintaining monotonic risk-score rankings where baselines show non-monotonic behavior (Section 5.2).

SQSD transfers across architectures (Llama↔Qwen), parameter scales (8B→14B/32B), and parameter-efficient methods (LoRA→full fine-tuning), preserving a monotonic ASR-based ranking in all cases (Table 2, Section 5.3).

80Job2F5eb.text: Under the size-sensitive independence-oracle cost model, any (possibly randomized) algorithm approximating matroid rank within a multiplicative factor of 1 ± 1/40 with probability at least 2/3 must incur Ω(n²) query cost in the worst case (Theorem 1.1.1).

For matroids whose maximum circuit size is at most c, a randomized algorithm finds a maximum-weight basis with expected query cost O(n^{2−1/c} log n), breaking the quadratic query-cost barrier (Theorem 1.1.1).
Distinguishing a partition matroid of part size 3 from one of part size 4 requires Ω(n²) query cost, matching the Õ(n²) upper bound for partition-size estimation (Theorem 1.1.2).
For general non-decreasing query-cost functions f(|Q|), the paper proves an Ω(n·f(n/3)) lower bound using matroid unions of free and uniform matroids as hard instances (Section 6).
Linear-time size-sensitive oracle implementations are given for partition, graphic, bicircular, convex-transversal, and job-scheduling matroids (Section B).

HtSjPOIMMc.text: PANDA (Penalty-Augmented Nikaido–Isoda Descent–Ascent) is a first-order stochastic policy-gradient algorithm for bilevel optimization where the lower level is a regularized min-max zero-sum Markov game (Section on algorithm structure).
The regularized min-max zero-sum Markov game admits a unique equilibrium policy pair under strong convexity-concavity of the regularizer, with min-max value equal to max-min value (Proposition 1).

The Nikaido-Isoda function satisfies a non-uniform Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality, ½‖∇g(x,ϕ,ψ)‖₂² ≥ μ(ϕ,ψ) g(x,ϕ,ψ), with μ depending on regularization strength and state/action probabilities (Lemma 1).

Under Assumptions 1-3, PANDA reaches an ε-stationary point of the bilevel objective in Õ(ε^{-1}) outer iterations with total sample complexity Õ(ε^{-3}), matching the best-known rates for bilevel RL without restrictive convexity assumptions (Theorem 1).

PANDA avoids computing hypergradients and Hessian terms (unlike the DA baseline), while matching the sample complexity of single-level bilevel RL methods (Section on key innovation / algorithm structure).

On a synthetic 5-state, 3-action-per-player zero-sum game and on 5×5/20×20 grid-based Sentinel-Intruder environments, PANDA achieves the highest incentive reward, outperforming META, DA, and PBRL baselines (Experiments section).

pp1enKGv2v.text: On the BEIR benchmark, SSR-CLS achieves 53.4 average nDCG@10 versus ColBERTv2's 49.2, while SSR-tok reaches 52.9 nDCG@10 with 17.5ms retrieval latency versus ColBERTv2's 56.9ms (Table 1).
SSR completes indexing in about 7.5 hours compared to ColBERTv2's 100+ hours, a roughly 15x indexing speedup by replacing K-means clustering with sparse-autoencoder projection (Figure 3a).

The sparse autoencoder projects token embeddings into 16,384-dimensional sparse vectors with about K=32 active neurons, enabling interaction computation only over overlapping activated neurons for efficient inverted-index retrieval (Section 3.2).

Training combines an unsupervised objective (reconstruction + multi-TopK + auxiliary losses) with a supervised contrastive query-document loss, combined as ℒ_SSR = ℒ_unsup + γℒ_CE with γ=0.05 (Section 3.2).
SSR-tok uses 34.6 GB peak memory and an 18.5 GB index versus ColBERTv2's 274.2 GB peak memory and 22.1 GB index, and supports append-only index updates versus ColBERTv2's full rebuild (Table 4).
On the LIMIT benchmark for representational limits, SSR achieves 78.6% Recall@5, and with a Llama-8B backbone SSR-CLS scores 67.1 on MTEB versus a 65.8 baseline (Section on additional validation).

nAQ4h8FpdM.text: Swift-SVD's Theorem 3.1 gives a closed-form optimal solution for activation-aware low-rank compression, with compressed weights W*_k = W V_k V_k^T and minimal loss ε*_k equal to the square root of the sum of squared discarded singular values of the activation covariance, computed via a single eigendecomposition (Theorem 3.1, Algorithm 1).
On LLaMA-7B at a 0.8 compression ratio, Swift-SVD* achieves 7.84 WikiText-2 perplexity versus 8.54 for Dobi-SVD, and higher average zero-shot accuracy (0.51 vs 0.49) (Table 1).

Across OPT-6.7B, Mistral-7B and other models at 0.8 compression ratio, Swift-SVD* attains lower WikiText-2 perplexity than uniform-rank and SVD-LLM(W) baselines, e.g. 11.65 vs 12.12 on OPT-6.7B and 6.63 vs 7.40 on Mistral-7B (Table 2).

With 512 calibration samples, Swift-SVD achieves a 76.9x compression-time speedup over Dobi-SVD (without acceleration) and a 19.8x speedup over SVD-LLM(W), completing compression in 827 seconds versus 63,641 seconds for the slowest baseline (Table 4).
Swift-SVD achieves zero reconstruction-error gap from the theoretical minimum across tested matrix dimensions, whereas competing methods accumulate errors of +57 to +134 on large matrices (Table 5).

qXlovWytwg.text: The paper defines the gamma-graph dimension d_γ (Definition 3.2) via a gamma-shattering condition (Definition 3.1) and uses it to characterize the sample complexity of aggregation-based regression procedures.
Any interpolator-based aggregation using proper aggregation rules requires sample complexity Ω(d_γ/ε) to reach expected cutoff loss ε (Theorem 3.5).

There exist hypothesis classes with γ-graph dimension d_γ and γ-OIG dimension at most 3 for which finite interpolating-aggregation algorithms still require sample complexity Ω(d_γ/ε), separating them from general learners that achieve Õ(1/ε) (Theorem 3.8).

For some hypothesis classes with constant γ-OIG dimension, no finite interpolating aggregation rule can achieve non-trivial cutoff loss regardless of sample size, requiring either infinite aggregation or non-interpolating rules (Theorem 3.10).
Taking the median of three independently trained interpolators achieves expected cutoff loss O(d_γ/n), yielding optimal sample complexity O(d_γ/ε) that matches the lower bound (Theorem 3.11).

Proper learners require sample complexity Ω((d_γ/ε)ln(1/ε)), strictly worse than the O(d_γ/ε) achieved by median-of-three aggregation, demonstrating aggregation's superiority over proper learning (Theorem 3.12).

CVDEc0doW8.text: The paper reformulates mechanisms as returning pairs (y, ε) rather than separate output and privacy-loss functions, resolving prior notational obstacles to defining post-processing immunity for accuracy-first privacy (Section 3.1).

Pure ex-post privacy (δ=0) satisfies post-processing immunity, but δ-probabilistic ex-post privacy with δ>0 does not, even though the latter is shown equivalent to (ε,δ)-probabilistic differential privacy for constant ε (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.2).

The paper introduces α-ex-post Rényi differential privacy (Section 4), proves it satisfies post-processing immunity (Theorem 4), and proves it composes adaptively with total privacy loss ε* = Σε_i (Theorem 6).
The sequential precision-weighted Gaussian mechanism (Algorithm 2, Appendix C.4) is shown to achieve α-ex-post RDP equivalent to the original Brownian mechanism (Theorem 5, Section 5).

Table 1 summarizes that pure ex-post privacy has post-processing immunity but the Brownian mechanism does not satisfy it, whereas α-ex-post RDP satisfies both post-processing immunity and compatibility with the Brownian mechanism (Table 1, Section 3).

On the Adult dataset, a data-dependent stopping rule (Algorithm 1) using a private validation set generates synthetic data while minimizing privacy budget over ε ∈ [0.01, 1] subject to maintaining classifier accuracy thresholds (Figure 1, Section 6).

9mo5O8m7vv.text: OSAQ performs additive weight suppression guided by the second-order low-rank property of the Hessian, absorbing the transformation offline into the weights so that it introduces no inter-layer modification and no inference overhead (abstract only).
OSAQ constructs its weight transformation via a closed-form solution using stable null-space vectors of the Hessian, without resource-intensive training or iterative procedures (abstract only).
OSAQ suppresses outliers to improve low-bit weight-only quantization accuracy across LLMs of varying scales and tasks (abstract only).
When combined with GPTQ for 2-bit quantization, OSAQ achieves over 40% lower perplexity than vanilla GPTQ (abstract only).

Uf3SMkP2Wd.text: Theorem 1 proves that unitary functions are overconstrained for dynamics problems with high angular dependence in the solution's norm, giving a lower bound on approximation error that shows why perfectly norm-preserving (unitary) models undersmooth physical systems like heat diffusion that require increasing smoothness over time (Theorem 1).

The paper proposes relaxed-unitary architectures, R-UniGraph and R-UniMesh, using either Taylor truncation of the matrix exponential at T_max=3 or 10 (Eq. 4) or an encoder-decoder scheme with unconstrained MLP/GCN decoder (Eq. 5) to allow controlled smoothness change while retaining approximate invariance.

On the heat equation, R-UniGraph achieves the lowest MSE (0.11e-2) and lowest mean Rayleigh-quotient error (2.07e-2) compared to GCN (1.08e-2 MSE, 5.99e-2 Rayleigh error) and Lie Unitary (0.14e-2 MSE, 8.86e-2 Rayleigh error) (Table 1).

On mesh-based heat-equation prediction, R-UniMesh attains lower NRMSE (51.9±3.6), SMAPE (79.7±5.6), and Rayleigh error (9.1±7.4) than the gauge-equivariant baselines EMAN (73.50±3.8 NRMSE) and Hermes (73.02±4.7 NRMSE), and than a mesh-aware Transformer baseline (92.5±5.6 NRMSE) (Table 2).

On the wave equation, R-UniMesh achieves an NRMSE of 236.5±6.4, remaining competitive on this non-diffusive dynamics task despite its unitary-preserving design being tailored to diffusive smoothness behavior (Table 2).
On WeatherBench2 temperature forecasting, R-UniMesh maintains forecast viability for approximately 22 days, comparable to the ECMWF baseline, despite being trained on a smaller dataset (Figure 5).

T5Oi5wodZT.text: Presents fixed-parameter and XP algorithms for satisfiability of probabilistic and counterfactual fragments of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, parameterized by primal treewidth and number of variables (Section 3, Theorem 2).
Gives an algorithm running in time d^d · f(tw(φ)) · |φ|^O(1) for a computable function f, where d is domain size and tw(φ) the primal treewidth of the formula (Section 3).
Constructs a linear program with O(n·d^w) variables and O(|φ| + n·d^w) constraints to decide satisfiability under bounded treewidth w (Section 3).

Establishes matching hardness results (NP-hardness/paraNP-hardness) showing the identified treewidth and variable-count parameters are tight tractability boundaries across the probabilistic and counterfactual layers of the causal hierarchy (Theorems 7, 8, 9).
Proves a culminating tractability gateway result combining structural restrictions on well-formed causal models (Theorem 11).

gPQQyHFbEA.text: Proves that rational-activation networks can approximate GELU to error ε using size O(log^3 log(1/ε)), versus a matching Ω(log log(1/ε)) lower bound (Theorem 3.1).

Proves any GELU (fixed-activation) network approximating certain rational target functions to error ε requires at least Ω(log(1/ε)) parameters, establishing an exponential separation from rational activations (Theorem 3.2).
Shows rational functions analytic near [-1,1] can conversely be approximated by GELU networks of size O(log^2(1/ε)) (Theorem 3.3).
Extends the scalar approximation results to full feedforward networks, with GELU-to-rational conversion incurring O(kM log^3 log(1/ε)) overhead for depth-M, width-k networks (Theorem 3.4).

Empirically shows a rational-activation VGG4 matches the CIFAR-10 performance of a GELU VGG8, and rational activations match or outperform fixed activations in 5 of 6 offline-RL MuJoCo settings (Section 4).

gcYvvxTLRA.text: Introduces RPG (retrospective/reusing-trajectories policy gradient), which combines a power-mean-corrected multiple importance weighting estimator with on-policy and off-policy data drawn from the most recent ω iterations of trajectories (Section 3).
Derives a concentration bound on the power-mean estimator's error of order O(√(D·d_Θ·log(1/δ)/(N·k))), where D bounds the χ² divergence between behavior and target policies (Theorem 4.1).

Proves RPG attains Õ(ε^-1) sample complexity to reach an ε-stationary point using a constant batch size N (including N=1), which the paper identifies as the best known rate among policy gradient methods (Theorem 5.1).

Compares against REINFORCE (O(ε^-2)), SVRPG (O(ε^-5/3)), SRVRPG and STORM-PG (O(ε^-3/2)), showing RPG's trajectory-reuse strategy improves on all of these gradient-based variance-reduction baselines (Table 1).

RF1YUA8plS.text: Proposes SPECTRA, a soft spectral clipping method implemented via Newton-Schulz iterations, that adds only 2-10% computational overhead to optimizer updates (Section 5).
Shows Spectra-Signum improves perplexity by about 2.5 points over baseline Signum at high learning rates on the 780M/820M-parameter model (Figure 1).
Reports Spectra-Signum reaches 51.62% average downstream accuracy across 10 benchmarks versus 49.84% for baseline Signum on the 820M model (Table 1).

Demonstrates Spectra-AdEMAMix consistently achieves the lowest validation losses across training durations among tested optimizer variants, and shows reduced weight-norm growth relative to unclipped baselines (Figure 3, Figure 4).
Applies the same hyperparameter defaults (λ≈0.1, c≈10, Ns=10 Newton-Schulz steps) uniformly across AdamW, Signum, and AdEMAMix without per-optimizer tuning (Section 5).

AehiGqd7go.text: Proves a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation condition α·w·λ_k = 1 under which odd C^3 activation functions destabilize the homogeneous fixed point and create stable non-homogeneous patterns in GNN dynamics (Theorem 3.2).
Derives a √μ scaling law for the amplitude of emergent patterns near the bifurcation point, where μ measures distance from criticality, and validates this scaling empirically (Theorem 3.2, Figure 3).
Shows Dirichlet energy stays at zero in the subcritical regime and grows linearly in the supercritical regime, quantifying departure from oversmoothing (Corollary 3.4).
Proves that near the bifurcation point the NTK becomes asymptotically rank-one, dominated by the bifurcating eigenmode, explaining emergent topological learning priors (Corollary 4.1).
Extends the scalar analysis to realistic multidimensional GNNs, proving emergent patterns are rank-one separable states aligned with graph and feature eigenmodes (Theorem 5.1).

Demonstrates that substituting bifurcation-inducing activations (e.g., sine) for standard monotone ones maintains performance in 64-layer GNNs on Cora, avoiding representational collapse under depth (Figure 5, Section 6).

AE8xCfWWL9.text: FoCA CBM achieves 91.88±0.35% accuracy on ImageNet100 versus 88.27±0.49% for vanilla CBM, with lower Cluster Impurity (0.573 vs 0.662) and Davies-Bouldin Index (1.862 vs 2.197) (Table 1).
On AwA2, FoCA CBM reaches 92.13±0.28% accuracy versus 90.36±0.21% for vanilla CBM, with improved CI (0.571 vs 0.628) and DBI (2.057 vs 2.137) (Table 1).

Class-cluster density, defined in Equation 3 as D_j = (1/n) Σ|{Y(K_k)}|, is used to align formal concept lattice levels with network block depth so that general concepts supervise early blocks and specific concepts supervise deeper blocks (Section 3.2).

Theorem 4.1 shows FoCA CBMs maintain hierarchical consistency between consecutive semantic levels with substantially higher probability than random class groupings, i.e. Pr_foca(Ĝ_{i+1}(x) ⊄ Ĝ_i(x)) is much smaller than Pr_frnd(Ĝ_{i+1}(x) ⊄ Ĝ_i(x)) (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
Intervening at the semantic level identified by the iterative refinement procedure yields higher correction rates on ImageNet100 than intervening only at the final layer (Figure 5, Section 6).
FoCA ViT achieves 86.65±0.295% accuracy on CIFAR100 versus 84.49±0.547% for a standard ViT CBM, showing the approach generalizes beyond ResNet backbones (Section 5).

RB4V5TkIOz.text: Along optimized Bézier paths between adversarial perturbations, intermediate points maintain near-perfect attack success rates of 96-100% across ℓ∞, ℓ2, and ℓ1 norms, demonstrating adversarial mode connectivity (Table 1).
Multi-image augmentation of the Bézier curve objective improves transferability, yielding rescue rates of 8.6-32% on CIFAR-10 and roughly a 40% improvement in path success rate (Table 2, Table 3).

MoCo-EA reduces the average number of queries needed for successful evolutionary attacks by 94.9-98.6% compared to traditional evolutionary attacks, converging within 1-2 generations rather than hundreds (Table 5, Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
Under obfuscated-gradient defenses, MoCo-EA achieves a 53.8% attack success rate compared to 13.5% for PGD (Table 6).
Experiments use a ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 (95.1% clean accuracy) and a ViT-Base/16 on ImageNet (84.4% top-1 accuracy) under perturbation budgets ℓ∞=8/255 (CIFAR-10) and ℓ∞=4/255 (ImageNet) (Section 5).

82Wosp2Iu1.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that as dimension T→∞, the Gaussian mechanism achieves the best privacy-utility tradeoff among all additive-noise mechanisms in the high-privacy regime δ ≤ δ⋆ (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

Lemma 3.3 shows that Haar symmetrization of arbitrary additive noise preserves mean squared error while improving privacy, establishing that spherically symmetric noise distributions are optimal (Lemma 3.3).

The paper introduces the Spherical Generalized Gamma (SGG) family, a three-parameter family with radial density f(r) = pβ^((α+1)/p)/Γ((α+1)/p) · r^α · exp(-βr^p) that includes the Gaussian and ℓ2 mechanisms as special cases (Definition 4.1-4.2, Section 4).

Figure 2 shows that in low dimensions (T=2 to 5) at ε=0.1, certain SGG mechanisms reduce MSE by up to 15% relative to the Gaussian and ℓ2 mechanisms, with the improvement shrinking as dimension increases (Figure 2, Section 4).
Table 2 reports empirical lower bounds on the threshold δ⋆ above which Gaussian optimality holds, e.g. δ⋆ ≥ 0.737 at ε=0.25 and δ⋆ ≥ 0.198 at ε=16.0 (Table 2).

The paper resolves an open question from Joseph et al. (2025) by providing a tight composition analysis for the ℓ2 mechanism via the unified SGG framework and an FFT-based composition algorithm (Section 4.4, Algorithm 7).

8RE5i7g4uB.text: LGP-OT combines a latent Gaussian process prior with an optimal transport objective, minimizing expected p-Wasserstein transport cost plus a KL regularization term as defined in Equation 7 (Section 4.2).

The latent GP prior uses Hilbert space approximation to scale linearly with dataset size and incorporates a cell-specific latent time τn to model temporal asynchrony distinct from pseudotime methods (Section 4.1, Section 4.3).

On the Drosophila dataset's medium-difficulty interpolation task, LGP-OT (with time and cell-type conditioning) achieves a Wasserstein-2 distance of 36.32±0.20 at t=10, versus 38.04±0.35 for the scNODE baseline (Table 1).
On the Drosophila hard (combined) task, LGP-OT (with cell-type conditioning) achieves W2 of 28.75±0.04 at t=2, outperforming scNODE's 29.95±0.29 (Table 1).

The model is evaluated on three temporal scRNA-seq datasets: zebrafish (38,731 cells, 12 timepoints), Drosophila (27,386 cells, 11 timepoints), and iPSC reprogramming (236,285 cells, 19 timepoints), compared against scNODE, MIOFlow, PRESCIENT, PI-SDE, and VGFM baselines (Section 5, Table 1, Tables 7-8 in Appendix C.5).

The framework extends gradient-based perturbation methods to entire inferred latent trajectories, showing progressive bias toward targeted cell types as gene expression scaling increases (Section 4.5, Figure 3, Figure 4).

vHaaDCLF0M.text: SPEAR uses Multi-codebook Vector Quantisation (MVQ), decomposing the representation space into N parallel codebooks of K code vectors each to produce K^N discrete masked-prediction targets, described via the pre-training loss in Equation 2 (Section 3.1, Section 3.2.1).

Speech-domain SPEARs Large matches or exceeds WavLM Large on 12 of 15 SUPERB tasks, including 3.3% WER vs 3.8% on LibriSpeech test-other ASR and 3.14% vs 3.77% EER on speaker verification (Table 5, Section 5.2).
Dual-domain pre-training (Equation 6) uses an asymmetric strategy where speech MVQ tokens serve as universal targets across both domains while audio tokens apply only to audio inputs (Section 3.2.2).
On AudioSet fine-tuning, SPEARs+a XLarge achieves 50.0 mAP on AS-2M, surpassing BEATs (48.6 mAP) and EAT (48.6 mAP) (Table 4, Section 5.1).
On the HEAR benchmark, SPEARs+a XLarge achieves an average score of 82.33 using intermediate-layer concatenation, outperforming USAD Large (79.36) (Table 6, Section 5.3).
Ablations show 16 codebooks are optimal for the speech domain and 8 for audio, and WavLM/Dasheng teacher tokens outperform HuBERT Large/ATST-frame alternatives (Table 3, Appendix G.1, G.3).

Wvd80GPJ9F.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) improves calibration by roughly 15% in expected calibration error (ECE) on average for WIT-pretrained CLIP models, while LAION-pretrained models degrade systematically under the same QAT (Section 3.3, Figure 5).
A 'quantization cliff' is observed where simple QAT methods collapse in accuracy at 4-bit precision while advanced quantization techniques remain resilient (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

For out-of-distribution detection, quantization causes traditional confidence-based methods (MSP, Energy) to fail catastrophically on quantized LAION models, whereas VLM-specific embedding-space OOD methods remain robust, decoupling accuracy from OOD detection performance (Section 3.4, Figure 9).

QAT improves robustness to low-level corruptions such as blur and noise but degrades performance on complex distribution shifts like ImageNet-V2, and increases spurious-correlation vulnerability by 1.2-1.7% (Section 3.5, Figure 8, Table 1).

Frequency-domain analysis shows quantization acts as a low-pass filter: post-training quantization (PTQ) at 6-bit severely attenuates high-frequency spectral components of ViT-B/32 features, and QAT only partially restores them (Section 5, Figure 11).
At 8-bit precision, QAT on ViT-L/14 eliminates the mid-frequency 'error halo' but instead establishes a distributed error floor spread across the frequency spectrum (Section 5, Figure 12).

oWqRhYpJb6.text: On real-world pan-cancer forecasting across all variables, GDT achieves a median MASE of 0.867 versus 0.966 for the strongest time-series baseline, TiDE (Section 5).
On the top 30 most volatile biomarkers, GDT reaches a median MASE of 0.830 versus TiDE's 0.947 (Section 5).
GDT achieves an average C-index of 0.703 across survival, progression, and therapy-switching prediction tasks, versus 0.662 for the strongest baseline (Section 5).

On out-of-distribution clinical trial cohorts (POPLAR and IMpower130), zero-shot GDT generalizes without fine-tuning, and fine-tuning further improves MASE to 0.883 and 0.754 respectively, and C-index to 0.672 versus 0.648 for a Random Survival Forest baseline (Section 5).
The CLMBR-T baseline is constrained by a fixed vocabulary covering only 11 of 283 therapies present in the dataset, limiting its applicability compared to GDT (Section 5).
TwinWeaver is trained on data from 93,054 patients across 20 cancer types, generating 2.49 million training samples (Section 3-4).

HENUU9VR8F.text: PepCompass achieves a 100% in-vitro success rate at the standard 32 μg/ml minimum inhibitory concentration threshold across 25 peptides optimized via Local Enumeration Bayesian Optimization (LE-BO), and an 82% success rate at the stricter 4 μg/ml threshold (Section on in-vitro validation).

A total of 29 novel peptides (4 seeds discovered via Potential-minimizing Geodesic Search, PoGS, plus 25 optimized analogs) were experimentally validated against a panel of 19 bacterial strains, including 8 multidrug-resistant isolates.
The κ-stable dimension of the Union of κ-Stable Manifolds is empirically verified to be strictly below the 64-dimensional latent space in both PepCVAE and HydrAMP decoder models.

Theorem 1 establishes that the SORBES (Second-order Riemannian Brownian Efficient Sampling) algorithm converges to Riemannian Brownian motion with deviation probability decaying exponentially in the inverse time horizon.
MUTANG interprets tangent directions on the learned manifold as discrete amino-acid substitutions, linking the continuous Riemannian geometry to interpretable sequence-level edits.

K9rWNmHhkD.text: Attention outputs in transformer models exhibit an intrinsic dimensionality of only about 60% of the full space, compared to over 90% for MLP outputs and residual stream activations (Figure 2a).
Only 1,174 singular values exceed 5% of the maximum singular value for attention outputs, versus 3,276 for MLP outputs and 3,943 for the residual stream, on the same model (Figure 2a).
Recovering 95% of downstream loss requires only 25.0% of dimensions for attention outputs, compared to 78.1% for MLP outputs and 85.9% for the residual stream (Section 4).

Standard Attention Output SAEs with 1M features trained on Llama-3.1-8B suffer 87% dead features, which Active Subspace Initialization (ASI) combined with the SparseAdam optimizer reduces to below 1% (Section 5).
On the Lorsa sparse replacement model, applying the subspace-constrained approach reduces dead parameters from 68.4% to 40.5% (Section 5).

Figure 4 shows a correlation between dead-feature rate and intrinsic dimensionality across layers, and Figure 7 shows scaling behavior of dead features from 16K to 1M feature dictionary sizes (Figures 4 and 7).

mXn4ueFKnQ.text: SkewD models noise as skew-normal distributed rather than assuming symmetric (normal) noise, extending the location-scale noise model framework to the skew-normal setting (Section 2).

On novel skew-noise datasets, the likelihood-based variant SkewD-LL achieves 100% accuracy, whereas the prior state-of-the-art method ROCHE drops to 81% accuracy at the highest skewness level tested, LSs(1.750) (Figure 2, Appendix C).

On 19 established causal-discovery benchmark datasets, SkewD-IT achieves 87.46% combined accuracy, compared to ROCHE's 87.69%, a difference of only 2.67 percentage points, while SkewD-IT ranks second overall at 85.02% mean accuracy on 13 established benchmarks (Table 1).
Table 2 presents an ablation study comparing performance with and without ECM (expectation-conditional-maximization) refinement in the parameter estimation procedure (Table 2).

Theorem 1, restated from LOCI in Appendix A, establishes that location-scale noise models are identifiable except in pathological cases satisfying a specific PDE, provided the noise log-density is twice differentiable, a condition satisfied by the skew-normal distribution (Appendix A).
LOCI and QCCD baselines show severe performance degradation as noise skewness increases, unlike SkewD (Figure 2).

VFCf4CSfzw.text: EnvAd-Diff (DynaDiff) achieves an average RMSE of 0.053±0.025 on in-domain Cylinder Flow prediction, versus 0.082±0.025 for the One-for-All foundation-model baseline (Table 1).
On the Lambda-Omega system, EnvAd-Diff attains an RMSE of 0.093±0.026 versus 0.352±0.041 for One-for-All, and on out-of-domain Kolmogorov Flow, 0.083±0.008 versus 0.096±0.016 (Table 1).
1M-parameter environment-specific models generated by EnvAd-Diff predict more accurately than 500M-parameter foundation models across the evaluated PDE systems (Section 4, Table 1).

A domain-adaptive model zoo of 100 FNO weight sets per environment amortizes fine-tuning cost, requiring storage of 18.0 GB for Cylinder Flow, 3.5 GB for Lambda-Omega, and 7.1 GB for Navier-Stokes (Section 3.3, Appendix B).
Weight generation via EnvAd-Diff is significantly faster than training a new prediction model from scratch and requires no additional data at adaptation time (Figure 9a).

OjeKfGXLOn.text: APE-Bench I extracts proof-engineering tasks as (Instruction, PreFile, Patch) triplets from 19,867 real commits (Aug 2023 to Mar 2025) in a formal mathematics library, filtered down to 10,928 final tasks (Section 3.2, Figure 3(b)).
Task extraction uses a four-stage pipeline of commit decomposition, chunk expansion producing 187,000+ candidates, multi-stage filtering, and compilation validation (Section 3.2).
Evaluation combines syntactic verification via the Lean compiler with a content-addressable storage system, Eleanstic, achieving 93% storage reduction across 3,734 commits (Section 4.1).
Semantic correctness is scored via an LLM-as-a-Judge protocol using a sample@4 voting strategy, complementing the syntactic Lean-compiler check (Section 4.2).

The task-triplet contract formulation of instruction, pre-file, and patch enables standardized comparison across different agent implementations on repository-scale Lean proof-engineering tasks (Section 3.1).

l2ywV9sV0L.text: Cascaded flow matching improves the detection score, measuring distinguishability of real versus synthetic samples, by roughly 40% overall, with dataset-level gains including about 15-20 percentage points on the Adult dataset relative to single-stage baselines (Section 4.2, Table 4).
Theorem 1 formally establishes a tighter transport cost bound for the cascaded flow-matching formulation compared to single-stage flow matching on heterogeneous mixed-type tabular data (Theorem 1).
The cascaded architecture decomposes generation into sequential stages handling different feature types, illustrated in the model architecture diagram (Figure 2).

Cascaded flow matching is evaluated against 3-4 baseline generative methods across datasets including Adult, Default, and Beijing, with reported improvements of roughly 10-25% in key fidelity metrics (Section 4.2, Table 4-5).

0xUvKZSQxV.text: Simple arbitrage strategies on SWE-bench GitHub issue resolution achieve net profit margins of up to 40%, for example an arbitrageur reaching a 75% solve rate at $80 cost versus $120 for DeepSeek and $150 for GPT-5 mini (Abstract, Figure 1).
In a six-provider market, arbitrage profit margins reach up to 58%, compared to 45% in a two-provider setting (Section 3.3, Figure 6).
Distilling a model on 5.4B tokens yields an arbitrage profit margin of nearly 30%, with profitability scaling roughly log-linearly with the number of distillation tokens (Section 4.1, Figure 7).
A distilled 4B-parameter mini-coder model cannibalizes nearly all of its teacher model's revenue once deployed as an arbitrage substitute (Section 4.2, Figure 8).
Search budgets as low as $1 to $10 are sufficient to consistently fit a profitable arbitrage policy over model choices (Section 3.2, Figure 5).
Provider marginal revenue decreases by up to 40% under arbitrage-driven routing, formalized via the arbitrage-opportunity criterion in Definition 2.1 (Section 2, Figure 4).

qFWLv8bLL2.text: Directly queried, Claude Code discloses 6,973 tokens of its system instructions, motivating the JustAsk extraction framework (Section 1).
JustAsk achieves full extraction with semantic similarity scores of 0.793-0.890 and consistency scores of at least 0.7 across all 41 evaluated black-box commercial LLMs (Table 2).

JustAsk formulates system-prompt extraction as online exploration over a latent action space of 14 low-level and 14 high-level skills, ranked via a UCB rule with exploration constant c equal to the square root of 2 (Section 3.3, Section 3.4).
Extraction difficulty varies with model transparency: closed-weight models require 4.8 average turns, open-weight models 2.4 turns, and fine-tuned models only 1.3 turns (Table 4, Section 4.3).
85% of evaluated models are successfully extracted on the first attempt, and 86% require only low-level skills, with just 14% needing sophisticated multi-turn orchestration (Figure 4, Section 4.3).
An attack-aware defense reduces extraction quality by 18.4%, from 0.719 to 0.587, whereas a simple 'do not reveal' instruction only reduces it by 6.0% (Table 6, Section 4.6).

5o7U03RThY.text: Dataset overlap between two models' training data is positively correlated with CKA representational similarity across ResNet18, VAE, and nanoGPT architectures, holding for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation data (Section 5.1, Figure 4).
Task overlap alone, even when dataset overlap is held constant, drives increased representational similarity, as shown in the ColorShapeDigit800K controlled experiments (Section 5.2, Figure 6).

Combining task overlap and dataset overlap yields the strongest representational similarity effect, with mutual information rising from 0.360 (dataset overlap only) and 0.566 (task overlap only) to 0.747 for the combined condition (Section 5.3, Table 3).
Homogeneous model behavior arising from representational similarity is discussed as a source of broader societal risk, including correlated failure modes across models (Section 6).

Ps37H7zPDj.text: Theorem 3.7 extends PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds to non-compact symmetry groups (e.g., translations) by evaluating empirical risk only on a set of orbit representatives rather than the full dataset (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.7).

Assumption 3.1 relaxes the requirement of an invariant data distribution, allowing the target function to be equivariant with noise-dependent variation rather than requiring strict distributional invariance (Section 3).

Theorem 2.5 shows that averaging hypotheses to their equivariant counterparts strictly reduces the KL divergence term in the PAC-Bayes bound, yielding a tighter generalization guarantee (Section 2, Theorem 2.5).

On rotated MNIST restricted to rotations between -90 and 90 degrees (violating the uniform rotation distribution assumption of prior work), equivariant CNNs achieve both higher empirical accuracy and a strictly smaller, tighter PAC-Bayes generalization bound than the non-equivariant baseline (Section 4, Figure 1).

O7HYkWVMCW.text: The proposed unified multimodal model achieves an overall KRIS-Bench score of 80.18, surpassing all open-source baselines including Emu3.5, and improves procedural-knowledge accuracy to 85.53 versus 71.14 for Emu3.5 (Section 5.2, Table 1).
On the OmniContext benchmark, the model attains an average score of 9.35, outperforming Emu3.5 (8.82) and GPT-4o (8.80) (Section 5.2, Table 3).
On GenEval, the model reaches an overall score of 0.89, exceeding VACoT (0.84) and Emu3.5 (0.86), with notably higher position-reasoning accuracy (0.79 vs. VACoT's 0.66) (Section 5.2, Table 5).

An ablation shows that mixing selective-loss-masking training modes (versus direct-only training) improves KRIS-Bench from 75.16 to 78.24, and that the GRPO-based RL stage reduces the average number of generated images per query from 2.45 to 1.56 while improving OmniContext from 9.12 to 9.35 (Section 5.3, Table 2).

Bh4Ubk80M8.text: Frontier LLMs use between roughly 5,000 and 30,000 reasoning tokens to solve a single basic arithmetic calculation, with performance heavily dependent on reasoning-token budget (Section 2, Figure 3).

On a multi-task arithmetic benchmark, BitTokens (IEEE 754-based single-token number embeddings) achieve a multiplication log-sMAPE of 0.991 and division log-sMAPE of 0.989, compared to 0.450 and 0.522 respectively for subword tokenization (Section 6, Table 4).
BitTokens require approximately 6 tokens per arithmetic problem, versus 21-38 tokens for multi-digit/multi-token number representations (Section 6, Table 5).

Reasoning-enabled GPT-5 achieves 99.5% accuracy on multiplication while minimal-reasoning GPT-5 drops to 30.9% accuracy, illustrating the dependence of frontier LLM numeracy on token-hungry reasoning rather than efficient number representations (Section 2, Table 1).

BQfNL1wahQ.text: CacheAttack-1 (direct target validation) achieves an 86.9% hit rate and 81.1% injection success rate against semantic caches in response hijacking attacks (Section 5, Table 1).
CacheAttack-2, a surrogate-assisted variant requiring no direct access to the target cache, achieves 83.1% hit rate and 77.1% injection success rate (Section 5, Table 1).
Semantic caching exhibits a fundamental trade-off between cache locality (performance) and collision resistance (security), formalized by modeling cache keys as fuzzy hashes (Section 3).

Cross-embedding-model transferability of the attack ranges from 49.8% to 86.9% hit rate depending on architectural similarity between source and target embedding models, versus over 92% hit rate in the in-model setting (Section 5, Table 3).
Key salting reduces attack hit rate by up to 21.0 percentage points, while per-user cache isolation eliminates cross-user attacks entirely but reduces cache efficiency (Section 7, Table 4).

79TgfXHbsK.text: The TIME benchmark comprises 50 fresh datasets spanning eight domains (Nature, Energy, Transportation, Healthcare, Finance, Economics, Sales, CloudOPS) and 98 forecasting tasks curated to avoid pretraining data leakage for zero-shot time series foundation model evaluation (Section 4).

A five-step automatic screening pipeline (timestamp rectification, rule-based validation, statistical testing, outlier removal, correlation checking) plus human review is used to ensure data integrity when constructing the 50 datasets (Section 4).

Seven structural time series features derived from STL decomposition (Trend Strength, Trend Linearity, Seasonality Strength, Seasonality Correlation, Residual ACF-1, Complexity, Stationarity) are used for pattern-level rather than dataset-level model evaluation (Section 5).

12 time series foundation models (11M-500M parameters, listed in Table 1) are evaluated on the 98 tasks, with Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, and TiRex ranking as the top-3 performers by normalized MASE/CRPS (Section 6.2, Figure 5).

Pattern-specific analysis shows models achieve larger accuracy gains on data with strong, linear trends, exhibit significant divergence on highly seasonal data, and show pronounced advantages on non-stationary sequences, while high spectral entropy (complexity) acts as a performance equalizer across models (Section 6.3, Figure 6).

EsB46shM3U.text: Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators (CG-BGs) combine a Variational Force Matching objective (Section 3.1) with a normalizing-flow-based Boltzmann generator to learn potentials of mean force that capture explicit-solvent-mediated interactions in reduced representations (Section 3).

Enhanced Sampling Force Matching (Section 3.2) exploits fiber distribution invariance (Proposition 3.2) to learn PMFs directly from biased/enhanced-sampling trajectories rather than requiring unbiased data, with equivalence to standard force matching under sufficient model expressivity.

On alanine dipeptide at Heavy Atom resolution, CG-BG achieves a Jensen-Shannon divergence of 0.0075±0.0001 and PMF error of 0.2493±0.0126 using unbiased training data, compared to substantially larger errors for implicit-solvent GBSA (OBC1/OBC2) baselines (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Reducing the resolution from All Atom to Core Beta representation yields roughly a 4.7x speedup in training time (3.93h vs 0.83h) and a 16.6x speedup in inference time (13.92min vs 0.84min for 10^4 samples) (Table 1, Section 4.2).

The learned PMF/flow pair enables simulation-free evaluation of free energies via importance-weighted reweighting, demonstrated on the Müller-Brown potential and alanine dipeptide before/after reweighting (Figure 2, Figure 5, Section 4.3).

utTapVWtc7.text: A single 300M-parameter Regression Language Model (RLM), initialized from T5Gemma-S, jointly predicts memory footprint, latency, and accuracy of code across multiple high-level programming languages and hardware targets using digit-by-digit numeric tokenization (Section 3, Section 1).
On APPS Leetcode memory-footprint prediction, the RLM attains a Spearman rank correlation of 0.930, and on Triton GPU kernel latency prediction it attains 0.516 (Table 3, Section 5).

Across CodeNet's programming languages the unified RLM's Spearman-rho ranges as low as 0.647 (Python) up to 0.748 (C++), with C at 0.741 and Go at 0.670, averaged over 17 languages (Table 3, Section 5).
On NAS-Bench architecture ranking, the RLM attains an average Kendall-tau of 0.461, outperforming Arch2Vec (0.212) and CATE (0.238) and matching a GNN baseline (0.429) (Table 4, Section 5).

Ablations show the proposed decoder-head regression formulation reaches 0.800 Spearman-rho versus 0.717 for a normalized regression head and 0.478 for a standard regression head, and scaling from 300M to 600M T5Gemma parameters improves Spearman-rho from 0.744 to 0.782 (Table 5, Table 6, Section 6).

NhWqp4R7Lf.text: KBQA-R1 recasts knowledge base question answering as a multi-turn Markov Decision Process over a structured, six-action space (Find_relation, Merge, Order, Compare, Time_constraint, Count) rather than monolithic S-Expression generation (Section III, Section IV-A2, Table II).
On WebQSP, KBQA-R1 achieves 83.4% F1, a +25.6 point improvement over the KBQA-o1 baseline's 57.8% F1 (Table IV, Section V).

On GrailQA with Llama-3.1-8B, KBQA-R1 reaches 90.0% EM/91.5% F1 on i.i.d. splits, 78.0% EM/82.5% F1 on compositional splits, and 83.6% EM/85.2% F1 on zero-shot splits, for an overall 83.9% EM/86.1% F1 (Table III, Section V).

Referenced Rejection Sampling (RRS), which conditions trajectory generation on ground-truth action sequences from gold logical forms, raises the sampling acceptance rate on GrailQA from 39.3% (standard rejection sampling) to 67.0% (Table VII, Section IV-B).

Ablations show removing the relation-retrieval confidence-gating mechanism (RRCG) drops WebQSP F1 by 19.3 points, removing multi-turn interaction drops it by 20.2 points, and removing RRS drops it by 4.5 points, while KBQA-R1 also reduces inference cost to 2.65 LLM calls per WebQSP sample versus 28.8 for KBQA-o1 (Table VI, Table VIII, Section V).

mx8nvMUfxL.text: Diff-MN parameterizes the dynamics of a Neural Controlled Differential Equation with a mixture-of-experts (MoE) whose per-sample expert-combination weights are generated by a diffusion model, producing sample-specific continuous dynamics for irregular time series (Section 3.2, Section 3.4).
A decoupled optimization scheme pretrains a channel-wise autoencoder, freezes its encoder/decoder, and trains only the MoE-NCDE dynamics function afterward as a warm start (Section 3.3).

At 70% missing observations on the Sines dataset, Diff-MN attains a discriminative score of 0.182 versus 0.228 for KoVAE and 0.341 for GT-GAN, and on Energy attains a discriminative score of 0.497 versus 0.500 (KoVAE) and 0.499 (GT-GAN) (Table 1, Section 4.2).

On continuous time series generation at 70% missing data, Diff-MN's MoE variant achieves MSE of 0.028 (Sines) and 0.002 (Stocks), improving over its own non-continuous variant (0.054, 0.005) and over KOVAE-NCDE (0.079, 0.030) (Table 3, Section 4.3).

Ablation on ECG200 at 30% missing shows removing the MoE component increases MDD from 0.211 to 0.226 and removing the decoupled-optimization design increases it to 0.370, while using four experts instead of a single eight-layer expert improves the discriminative score from 0.328 to 0.200 (Table 4, Table 5, Section 4.4).

3VgsVk8e8m.text: SG2Loc performs 4-DOF sequential visual localization by combining semantic, geometric, and photometric cues in a particle filter over a compact 3D scene graph representation, rather than a large image database or dense point cloud (Section 3).

On 3RScan, position recall at 0.25m improves from 0.58 for 5-frame sequences to 0.75 for 25-frame sequences, with median position/rotation error improving from 0.15m/12.92 degrees to 0.07m/12.21 degrees (Table 1).
On ScanNet, 25-frame sequences achieve 0.94 position recall at 0.25m and 0.60 rotation recall at 2 degrees, compared to 0.87 and 0.49 respectively for 5-frame sequences (Table 1).
SG2Loc requires comparable or less storage than HLoc and MeshLoc, using 1119.8 MB versus 1157.6 MB (HLoc) and 1701.3 MB (MeshLoc) per scene on 3RScan (Table 2).

The ablation study shows that removing adaptive (KLD-based) resampling degrades recall at (10cm, 5 degrees) to 0.11, matching the semantic-only variant, versus 0.35 for the full semantic+depth+RGB configuration (Table 6).

Localization runs at 2.9 seconds per frame plus a one-time 4.2 second PnP refinement step, compared to HLoc's 0.32 seconds per frame, reflecting a computational cost trade-off for the storage savings (Table 3).

rZTiFcDihH.text: For the deterministic algorithm EDF_Φ^L in 2- and 3-bounded K-OPSD, the Φ-regret upper bound is Õ(√(KT)), matching sleeping-bandit-style rates (Proposition 3.1).

The deterministic algorithm ALG^θ achieves competitive ratio θ_K in [√2, Φ) for finite K packet types, breaking the classical golden-ratio Φ = (1+√5)/2 competitive-ratio barrier for 2-bounded deadline instances (Proposition 4.1).
The learning variant ALG^θ,U attains a θ_K-regret upper bound of Õ(√(KT)), which is shown to be nearly tight against a matching Ω(√T) lower bound (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
The randomized algorithm ALG^R2 for 2-bounded instances achieves a 5/4-regret bound of Õ(√(KT)) (Theorem 5.1).
The randomized algorithm ALG^Rs for s-bounded (unbounded slackness) instances achieves an e/(e-1)-regret bound of Õ(√(KT)) (Theorem 5.2).
Lemma 2.1 establishes that sleeping bandits are a special case of 1-bounded K-OPSD, formally connecting the packet scheduling model to the multi-armed bandit framework (Section 2.2, Lemma 2.1).

aXvTMnyeLj.text: CT-MLE estimates the state marginal density directly to guide exploration in continuous-time RL, rather than explicitly estimating drift and diffusion functions of the underlying SDE (Section 4).

The main regret bound (Theorem 5.10) scales with the eluder dimension of the squared Hellinger distance and the cumulative policy variance term sum of Var^u_n, rather than depending explicitly on the planning horizon (Theorem 5.10).

Corollary 5.13 shows that when observation frequency (measurement gaps Delta_n,k) adapts to problem complexity, the regret bound becomes nearly independent of the specific measurement schedule chosen (Corollary 5.13).
Proposition 5.9 shows the eluder dimension used in the analysis remains low under a quadratic density model, giving a concrete instantiation of the general instance-dependent bound (Proposition 5.9).

Algorithm 2 introduces a Monte Carlo-style randomized measurement strategy that samples timepoints within fixed intervals to obtain unbiased reward estimates without substantially increasing measurement cost (Algorithm 2, Section 4).

cHxls6cHDF.text: All three proposed methods replace the standard bounded-variance assumption with the relaxed condition E||G̃(z)-G(z)||^2 ≤ B^2||z-z0||^2 + σ^2, allowing variance to grow with distance from a reference point z0 (Section 1).
The mini-batching forward-backward-forward algorithm achieves Õ(ε^-4) oracle complexity for the weak-Minty nonmonotonicity parameter ρ < 1/(12L) (Section 2).
The multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) method achieves the same Õ(ε^-4) complexity while tolerating the widest nonmonotonicity range ρ < 1/L, the strongest of the three theoretical results (Section 3).

The variance-reduced single-loop algorithm uses only 3 stochastic oracle samples per iteration and incorporates Halpern anchoring for stability, under an added expected-Lipschitzness assumption (Section 4).

All three algorithms match the best-known Õ(ε^-4) complexity for driving the expected residual norm below ε on monotone and structured nonmonotone (weak-MVI) VIs, while applying to unbounded-domain bilinear min-max problems that violate the classical bounded-variance assumption (Section 1).

oWjx6SZVKn.text: The string method is adapted from computational chemistry to compute continuous paths between samples by evolving curves under the SDE dx_t = b_t(x_t)dt + γ_t^2 s_t(x_t)dt + √2 γ_t dW_t, where s_t is the diffusion model's learned score, without retraining the model (Section on Key Mathematical Framework, Introduction).

On ImageNet image diffusion models, minimum energy paths (γ_t ≫ 1, T=0) achieve significantly higher likelihood than real images but yield unrealistic, cartoon-like intermediates, confirming they lie outside the typical set (Figure 6).

Figure 4 shows that varying the score weight γ produces qualitatively different morphs: γ=15 yields abstract single-color intermediates, γ=2 yields cartoon-like morphs, and γ=10^-2 yields visually plausible intermediates throughout (Figure 4).

Principal curves (γ_t ≫ 1, T>0), which balance energy and entropy, traverse the typical set and produce realistic morphing sequences despite having lower likelihood than minimum energy paths (Section on Principal Curves).

Figure 3 shows relative score estimation error increases sharply near t=1, motivating a quenching strategy where γ_t is annealed to 0 as t approaches 1 to avoid amplifying unreliable score estimates (Figure 3).

The method is applied to protein conformational transitions, computing pathways between the open (4AKE) and closed (1AKE) conformations of adenylate kinase with intermediates that preserve secondary structure and avoid steric clashes (Section on Protein Conformational Transitions).

BoiXvrwtdi.text: On GPT-5.1 as the frozen executor, pairing with a UMEM-Qwen3-4B memory module improves AIME accuracy from 46.67% to 51.67% (+5.0 points) over the best competitive baseline (Table 1).

Using GPT-5.1 with UMEM-Qwen3-4B, ALFWorld multi-turn task success rate reaches 82.84%, an 11.9-point improvement over the strongest baseline, contributing to the reported up-to-10.67% average gain on multi-turn interactive tasks (Table 1, Section 5).

Ablating the Semantic Neighborhood Modeling component (Section 4.1) drops GPT-5.1 AIME accuracy from 51.67% to 41.67% (a 10-point loss), while the same ablation costs only 3.3 points for the Qwen3-8B-Thinking executor (58.33%→55.00%) (Table 2).

Removing the extraction-optimization objective causes a 4.7-point average performance decline across benchmarks, whereas removing the management-optimization objective causes only a 0.73-point average decline (Table 2, Section 5).
Neighborhood size N=3 is optimal for Semantic Neighborhood Modeling; both N=1 and N=5 degrade downstream performance in the sensitivity analysis (Section 5).

During 10-epoch test-time self-evolution on ALFWorld, UMEM's cumulative success rate exhibits a monotonic, steadily improving growth curve, unlike rival memory methods which show rapid degradation over sequential tasks (Figure 3, Figure 4).

lV4tqcVIyx.text: Theorem 1 establishes that the CREME estimator α̂_ℓ(λ) satisfies E[α̂_ℓ(λ)] ≥ E[ℓ_λ(X_{n+1}, Y_{n+1})], yielding distribution-free, finite-sample upper bounds on both miscoverage and regret simultaneously (Theorem 1).

Proposition 2 shows the estimator's error decays at the parametric O(n^{-1/2}) rate in the calibration sample size n, giving a finite-sample guarantee rather than only an asymptotic one (Proposition 2).

Proposition 3 proves that, under majorant consistency, miscoverage weakly decreases and regret weakly increases as the robustness parameter λ increases, characterizing a true, certified miscoverage-regret Pareto frontier (Proposition 3).

The CREME (Conformal REgret Miscoverage Estimate) algorithm is empirically validated across four distinct decision-making paradigms: linear programming, the newsvendor problem, portfolio selection, and shortest-path optimization (Experiments section).

Across all four experimental settings, CREME maintains strong performance on both validity (coverage) and accuracy simultaneously, whereas competing calibration methods sacrifice one criterion to achieve the other (Experiments section).

eeoU8iz7w1.text: Theorem 5.2 bounds the average sub-optimality of the proposed DR-RPO algorithm by AveSubopt(K) ≤ c·d²H²/(α√K)·log(3dHK·vol(A)/p), matching the sample complexity of existing greedy value-iteration methods for robust MDPs while enabling direct policy optimization (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).

Proposition 4.4 shows that under linear MDP assumptions the robust Q-function is linear in the feature map, admitting a closed-form ridge-regression solution (Eq. 4.3) for tractable function approximation (Proposition 4.4).

Proposition 4.6 extends the linearity result to regularized robust MDPs (RRMDPs) using truncated value functions (Eq. 4.5), enabling the same closed-form approach under a different regularization scheme (Proposition 4.6).

DR-RPO's exploration relies on an upper-confidence-bound bonus term Γ_h^k(s,a)=β·Σ_iφ_i(s,a)√(1_i^T(Λ_h^k)^{-1}1_i), used in Algorithm 1 (Line 15) to drive optimistic exploration in large state-action spaces (Algorithm 1, Line 15).
In the off-dynamics linear MDP experiment, DR-RPO outperforms LSVI-UCB, OPPO, and Optimistic NPG in robustness across perturbation levels ρ∈{0.1,0.3,0.5} (Figure 1).

On the American Put Option experiment, DR-RPO remains competitive with DR-LSVI-UCB under high perturbation and consistently improves over non-robust baselines across multiple regularization parameters (Figures 3-4).

vLQO6nrpYq.text: Proposition 6 shows that quantile-based interpolants built from monotone quantile functions Q_φ^i satisfy consistency properties compatible with consistency models such as IMM (Proposition 6).

The quantile-based parameterization achieves an isometry property whereby the squared Wasserstein-2 distance between two 1D distributions equals the L² distance between their quantile functions, W₂²(μ,ν) = ∫₀¹|Q_μ(s) − Q_ν(s)|² ds (Section 4).
On the Funnel synthetic benchmark, the learned quantile-based latent captures heavy-tailed structure and outperforms a hand-tuned Student-t distribution baseline (Figure 5).
On the Checkerboard synthetic benchmark, combining the learned latent with optimal-transport coupling produces substantially shorter transport paths than a fixed Gaussian baseline (Figure 1).
On CIFAR-10 with 100 Euler integration steps, the learned quantile-based noise distribution improves FID from 7.22 (Gaussian baseline) to 6.26 (Figure 13).

The learned quantile parameterization adds only about 7% runtime overhead during joint training and about 2% overhead after the quantile functions are frozen, relative to a Gaussian-prior baseline, measured on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (Section 5).

GLNiB1ePxm.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes optimal sample complexity rates for learning from label proportions (LLP) with general convex loss functions, extending beyond the cross-entropy-only guarantees of prior LLP work (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

The debiasing methodology uses a median-of-means / 'mean of means' tournament-style estimator (following Lugosi's approach) to correct for the bias introduced by aggregate proportion-level labels rather than instance-level labels (Section 3.1).

The proposed guarantees cover both binary and multi-class classification settings under general loss functions, unifying and extending results from Ruiz et al. (2010), Quadrianto & Ghani (2008), and Dulac-Arnold et al. (2019) (Section 3, abstract).

The method is empirically compared against Hogsgaard et al. (2025) and other baseline LLP approaches on datasets including CIFAR and MNIST variants and Adult, evaluating classification accuracy under label-proportion supervision (Experiments section).
Appendix theorems (B.1-B.3, C.1-C.3) provide supporting proofs and extensions of the main sample-complexity results to additional loss function classes (Appendix B, Appendix C).

tiF3tA5pau.text: The Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation (D-RUT) protocol learns all coefficients of a generic multi-mode bosonic Hamiltonian with evolution time scaling as O(1/epsilon), achieving the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1, Section 2).

For single-mode Hamiltonians expressed in a first-quantization (position/momentum) basis, D-RUT recovers physical coefficients with RMSE epsilon_G using total evolution time O~(1/epsilon_G), under stated conditions on known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, and a sufficiently close initial guess (Theorem 2, Section 2).

The protocol's estimation error under state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors is bounded as ||delta g_SPAM||_2 <= (L_C/sigma_min(K)) ||delta beta||_2, where L_C is a Lipschitz constant and sigma_min(K) the smallest singular value of the Gram-like matrix K (Section 3.6, Eq. 43).

A hierarchical two-stage coefficient recovery strategy (learn single-mode coefficients first, then coupling coefficients) is proven to have covariance dominated by that of simultaneous estimation, Cov(delta g)_hierarchical <= Cov(delta g)_simultaneous, for all parameters (Section 4.1, Appendix A).

An iterative bisection search over the squeezing parameter R (relating the physical and reference bases via a Bogoliubov transformation) converges in O(log(1/epsilon_R)) iterations for first-quantization Hamiltonian learning (Section 5.3, Eq. 77-78).

The algorithm uses Chebyshev-node sampling of the displacement parameter combined with robust phase estimation and inverse discrete Fourier transform to reconstruct coefficients, as detailed in Algorithm 1 and illustrated for the single-mode case in Figure 1 (Section 2).

IP1KYg5iw9.text: LLMs maintain notable task performance even when text is severely perturbed at the character level, including extensive typos, near-total character shuffling within words, and invisible character insertion, producing text that is nearly unreadable to humans (abstract only).
LLMs exhibit remarkable resilience to chaotic segmentation and fragmented tokenization of input text, where tokenization boundaries no longer align with word or subword structure (abstract only).
The paper identifies both implicit and explicit mechanisms by which LLMs process, and in some cases internally correct, perturbed or fragmented text to recover its intended meaning (abstract only).
The paper's findings are framed as revealing an architectural strength of LLMs while also flagging potential misuse risks arising from this robustness to obfuscated text (abstract only).

G1bzbJtcHD.text: Theorem 1 shows that if a predictor gamma-hat satisfies weighted multicalibration with parameter alpha = epsilon/(2m), then running the standard optimal matching algorithm on gamma-hat's outputs achieves reward within additive error epsilon of the best decision rule in class C applied to the original predictor gamma (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 gives a sample complexity bound of O~(r n^6 log(r|C|/(epsilon delta)) / epsilon^4) samples to learn a multicalibrated predictor achieving precision epsilon and failure probability delta, where n is the number of agents/items and r is the mean-squared error of the initial predictor (Theorem 2).

In the worst case the sample complexity bound reduces to O~(n^8/epsilon^4), but the bound improves substantially when the initial predictor already has low MSE, reflecting realistic industrial-scale prediction settings (Theorem 2).

A boosting-style multicalibration algorithm (Algorithm 1) iteratively updates the predictor by identifying and correcting miscalibration on 'edge e is chosen by decision rule c' subgroups, adapting fairness-style multicalibration techniques to the matching setting (Algorithm 1).

The multicalibration-for-matching guarantee is shown to generalize beyond bipartite matching to best-action selection, learning with rejection, and max-weight matroid basis selection, each attaining improved sample complexities based on problem structure (Section on extensions).

xCnJEgFKVC.text: PODiff performs latent diffusion in a fixed, variance-ordered Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) coefficient space rather than pixel space, exploiting the orthogonality of POD modes to impose an interpretable, variance-ordered latent geometry (Section on method).

On sea surface temperature downscaling, PODiff-K40 achieves RMSE of 0.3923C and MAE of 0.2976C, outperforming a pixel-space diffusion baseline (RMSE 0.4118C, MAE 0.3158C) and a U-Net baseline (RMSE 0.6788C, MAE 0.5141C) (Table 1).
On extreme SST events specifically, PODiff-K40 attains RMSE of 0.4836C compared to 0.7899C for RBF interpolation (Section 4.1).

PODiff uses only 0.20M parameters and 1.4 GB peak GPU memory versus 33M parameters and 8.8-12.5 GB peak memory for U-Net/pixel-space diffusion baselines, and trains in 3.8 hours versus 48 hours for pixel-space diffusion (Table 3).

PODiff's predictive uncertainty is well calibrated, with empirical coverage of 0.9009 at the 90% nominal level and 0.9571 at the 95% nominal level, a mean absolute calibration error of 0.0128, and CRPS of 0.2889 versus 0.4821 for an MC Dropout U-Net baseline (Table 2).

1OPGcMM2Xt.text: SOL (Self-Optimizing Language models) uses a lightweight policy network that reads the LLM's hidden state at each decode step to select a discrete efficiency action controlling token-level attention sparsity, structured MLP activation pruning, and activation quantization bit-width, while keeping the base model weights frozen (Section on method).

SOL is trained with group-relative policy optimization over fixed token sequences while sampling different computational schedules, balancing language-model quality against a target compute-budget incentive (Section on training).

Across action spaces of increasing granularity (8, 27, and 1,560 discrete actions, denoted SOL-J-2L-T16, SOL-J-3L-T16, and SOL-J-FL-T16), SOL achieves lower perplexity than fixed/static allocation baselines at matched net keep-rate (Figure 2).

Paired comparisons show SOL-J-2L-T16 attains a mean perplexity difference of -0.383 versus a static baseline (p < 10^-10, 95.3% win rate), and on Llama-3.1-8B a difference of -0.270 (p < 10^-10, 88.9% win rate) (Table 1).

SOL matches or exceeds the best of 500 randomly sampled compute schedules in 8 of 12 tested points, remaining in the 95th-plus percentile of random schedules even when it does not exceed the single best one (Figure 9).
SOL improves MMLU accuracy by up to 7.3% over uniform (static) budget allocation strategies at matched compute budget (abstract; Section on MMLU results).

mDo8XNqopd.text: Theorem 1.5 bounds the Newton-step approximation error to the true leave-one-out retrained parameter using only local strong convexity in a neighborhood of the Newton step, rather than the global strong convexity assumed in prior analyses (Theorem 1.5, Section 3).

For logistic regression with n samples, d-dimensional Gaussian features, and k removed points, the average-case Newton-step attribution error scales as Õ(kd/n²), while the average-case influence-function error scales as Õ((k^{3/2}d^{1/2}+k^{1/2}d^{3/2})/n²) (Theorem 1.2).
The derived upper bounds match corresponding lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors, showing the Newton step is provably more accurate than influence functions whenever d ≫ k (Theorem 1.2).

Rescaled and doubly-rescaled influence functions (RIF and DRIF) are shown to match the Newton step's Õ(kd/n²) average-case error rate while preserving the additivity property that plain influence functions have but the Newton step lacks (Theorem 1.6, Theorem 1.7).
The paper's revised bounds remove the problematic 1/λ³ dependence on the regularization coefficient λ present in prior influence-function error analyses (Section 1, Discussion of prior bounds).

698yKwEXf0.text: DLPT's learned policy achieves a regret rate of O(r(1+√log(1/r))√(d/n) + r√(log(1/δ)/n)), establishing minimax-optimal √n convergence across fixed policy classes (Theorem 3.7).
The deep-neural-network nuisance parameter estimator used within DLPT converges at rate O(n^{-p/(p+d_C)} log^8 n + log log n / n) (Proposition 3.1).

In the Platform O field experiment (7,349,648 low-activity creators, four incentive levels of 178/358/538/718 points versus control, August 23–29 2021), all four treatment levels produced statistically significant upload-rate effects (p<0.0001) with relative effect sizes from 13.01% to 19.69% (Section 4, Table 3).

On average treatment effect estimation with field data, DLPT achieves 2.25% MAPE versus 7.18% for the next-best baseline (PDL) and 38.23%–43.59% for linear/logistic/latent-class baselines, roughly a 3.2x accuracy improvement over PDL (Table 5).
For policy learning over the finite observed treatment-level class, DLPT attains 2.22% mean percentage regret compared to a 6.32%–10.05% range for benchmark methods (Section 5).

Across semi-synthetic evaluations spanning four policy classes (finite observed, discretized continuous, linear, and DNN), DLPT consistently achieves the lowest regret, ranging 0.01%–19.69% versus 0.66%–34.75% for benchmarks (Section 6).

XrtiZYwcU4.text: The optimism-based exploration algorithm achieves cumulative regret bounded by O(η·𝒞(f,ℛΘ,η)·log(NℛT/δ)·d(ℛΘ,ξ,T)) under general f-divergence regularization (Theorem 3.3).
The derivative-based exploration algorithm achieves a sub-optimality gap SubOpt(π̂) ≤ C₀·d(1+ε)/T, yielding O(1/T) sample complexity (Proposition 4.4).

These are presented as the first provable regret/sub-optimality guarantees for online RLHF under general f-divergence regularization, covering reverse KL, forward KL, Jensen-Shannon, chi-squared variants, and total variation as special cases (Table 1, Section 2).

In linear contextual bandit experiments, chi-squared mixed KL and the divergence f(x)=x log x − log x yield tighter empirical regret than standard KL regularization for both algorithms (Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3).

For KL divergence the constants 𝒞(f,ℛΘ,η) and ℳ(f,ℛΘ,η) equal 1 (the baseline case), while chi-squared mixed KL yields constants below 1 (tighter bounds) and forward KL yields constants at or above 1 (looser bounds) (Section 5).

pNxw4i5Dp2.text: SWE-Perf comprises 140 verified instances of performance-improving pull requests drawn from 9 open-source Python repositories (astropy, django, matplotlib, seaborn, flask, requests, xarray, pylint, sklearn/scikit-learn, sphinx, sympy), filtered down from 102,241 initially collected PRs (Section 3).

In the oracle (file-level) setting, expert human patches achieve 100% apply rate, 100% correctness, and 10.85% average performance gain, whereas the best LLM, Gemini-2.5-Pro, reaches only 95% apply rate, 83.57% correctness, and 1.48% performance gain (Table 2).

In the realistic repo-level setting, Claude-3.7-Sonnet under the OpenHands agent framework achieves 87.86% apply rate, 77.86% correctness, and 2.26% performance gain, versus 88.57% apply, 70.71% correctness, and 0.41% performance gain under the Agentless framework (Table 2).

The weakest evaluated model, DeepSeek-V3, achieves only 47.85% apply rate, 42.86% correctness, and 0.54% performance gain in the oracle setting, illustrating the wide spread in LLM optimization ability (Table 2).

The gap between expert performance gain (10.85%) and the best LLM's realistic-setting gain (2.26%) is presented as evidence of a substantial capability gap between current LLMs and expert-level code performance optimization, with human patches favoring high-level abstractions versus models' focus on low-level data-structure changes (Section 5).

nBuL6HywFX.text: Theorem 4.2 establishes that for L-uniform polynomially-padded transformers with sufficient volume (width times bit-precision), constant-precision transformers are equivalent to L-uniform AC^0 and log-precision transformers are equivalent to L-uniform TC^0, regardless of width (Theorem 4.2).

Sufficient volume is defined as V(N) = D(N)·b(N) = Ω(log N), where D is width and b is numeric precision in bits, and this volume condition—not width alone—is shown to be what governs expressivity robustness (Definition 2.2, Definition 2.3).

For looped padded transformers with Θ(log^d N) loops, constant-precision versions are equivalent to FO-uniform AC^d and log-precision versions to FO-uniform TC^d, extending the constant-depth results to poly-logarithmic depth (Theorem 5.1).

Section 3 shows that standard (non-average-hard) transformers (SMATs) can simulate average-hard attention transformers (AHATs) under logarithmic precision, a key lemma underlying the later circuit-equivalence theorems (Section 3).

The paper is purely theoretical, presenting no empirical experiments, datasets, or training procedures, in contrast to prior padded-transformer expressivity work that mixed architectural claims (Section 1, Section 6).

VM9VwbeHcv.text: ADFP (Antidistillation Fingerprinting) derives a logit perturbation Δ_t^ADFP = q_t·(I[t∈S] − L), where L is the sum of fingerprinted-token probabilities, and Proposition 4.1 shows this isotropic approximation holds exactly for models with a trainable final linear adaptation layer (Section 4.1-4.2, Proposition 4.1).

On unsupervised GSM8K detection, ADFP achieves a Pareto improvement over the red-and-green-list watermarking baseline in the accuracy-versus-p-value trade-off, reaching roughly a p-value of 0.09 versus 0.01 for the baseline at matched generation quality (Figure 2).
On OASST1, ADFP shows a similar Pareto improvement over the baseline in the NLL-versus-p-value trade-off for unsupervised detection (Figure 3).

After the student model undergoes fine-tuning on GSM8K distilled outputs, ADFP maintains a superior trade-off between detection p-value and student accuracy compared to baseline fingerprinting (Figure 4).
ADFP retains high detection confidence with minimal degradation in generation quality even when only a reduced fraction of training data is fingerprinted (Figure 5).
ADFP remains effective for distillation detection even when the student model's architecture is unknown, by relying on a proxy model rather than requiring exact architectural knowledge (Section 5).

oWOYBP7uFd.text: On HealthBench, CaT applied at inference time yields a +12.5% relative improvement over the initial policy, while CaT-RL (training via GRPO-style RL on CaT-derived rewards) achieves up to a +30% relative improvement using a Llama 3.1 8B initial policy (Section 4).

On MATH-500, CaT inference-time aggregation yields a +27% relative improvement over the initial policy, while CaT-RL achieves up to a +33% relative improvement with the same Llama 3.1 8B backbone (Section 4).

Figure 6 compares CaT against single-sample baselines, best-of-N self-selection, minimum-perplexity selection, mutual-predictability selection, and majority voting (in verifiable domains only), showing CaT matches or exceeds these inference-time aggregation methods (Figure 6).

Figure 7 shows CaT's performance scales monotonically with rollout count G on MATH-500 but plateaus around G=4 rollouts on HealthBench, indicating diminishing returns from additional freeform rollouts in non-verifiable domains (Figure 7).

Result 7 reports that CaT's synthesized answer disagrees with the majority-vote answer on 14% of questions, and in about 1% of cases CaT produces a correct answer despite every individual rollout being wrong, evidencing genuine synthesis rather than mere selection (Result 7).

Result 2 shows CaT's self-proposed rubric rewards are competitive with human expert physician annotations on HealthBench and outperform model-as-judge semantic-equivalence checks, with RL trained on these rubrics outperforming supervised fine-tuning on the same data (Result 2, Figure 5).

VkZQThGNgI.text: RSPG is evaluated against SPG (a memoryless structural baseline), Independent PPO (IPPO), Recurrent IPPO (RIPPO), and Mirror-Descent M-OMD across Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar, and Macroeconomics environments, achieving among the lowest exploitability scores in each (Figure 2, Section 8).

History-aware structural methods (HSMs, including RSPG) converge roughly an order of magnitude faster in wall-clock time than RL-based baselines because they learn directly from mean-field rollouts rather than incurring additional single-agent rollout overhead between mean-field iterations (Section 8, Figure 2).

Table 2 reports mean-field update times of 2.98×10⁻⁴ seconds for the MFAX analytic update versus 5.44×10⁻³ seconds for OpenSpiel (about 18x slower) and 3.58×10⁻¹ seconds for MFGLib (about 1,200x slower) (Table 2).

The macroeconomics experiment implements a Krusell-Smith heterogeneous-agent mean field game with a 2D individual state (wealth, income), a 1D consumption-proportion action space, a 1D aggregate productivity common noise term, and 128-timestep finite-horizon episodes, in which RSPG-trained agents learn anticipatory behavior of spending more wealth just before the episode ends (Section 8).

Section 5 introduces Partially Observable Mean Field Games with Common Noise (POMFGs-CN), with Section 5.1 detailing the special case of shared observations among agents, and Section 6.1 presents the RSPG algorithm built on this formulation (Section 5, Section 5.1, Section 6.1).
