Q3Dukl2zWg.text: CoSMo improves average accuracy by 3.3 points while reducing average segment count by 28.7% relative to efficient-reasoning SFT baselines, averaged across HotpotQA, HaluEval, NQ, and CRAG using a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct backbone (Table 1, Section 5.2).

On HotpotQA, CoSMo achieves 88.0% accuracy with an average segment count of 2.6 and 135 tokens, compared to CoT's 81.5% accuracy, 3.6 segments, and 138 tokens, and outperforms pruning-based SFT baselines C3oT, FS-BoN, and SPIRIT and length-aligned RL baselines LCPO and ThinkPrune (Table 1).

An ablation isolating the SFT phase shows CoSMo_SFT gains 1.0 accuracy points over the C3oT baseline while reducing token consumption by over 19%, and CoSMo_RL improves accuracy by 3.2 points over the CoT baseline using fewer segments than the LCPO RL baseline (Section 5.3, Figure 3).

On the MuSiQue dataset stratified by ground-truth hop count, forcing a reasoning-segment count equal to the gold hop count yields peak accuracy (e.g., 50.23% at N=2 for 2-hop questions), while accuracy declines sharply when segment count deviates from this optimum, e.g., dropping to 42.44% when 2-hop questions are forced into 3 segments (Figure 1, Section 3.2).

As reasoning difficulty increases (2-hop to 4-hop questions on MuSiQue), CoSMo shows only a 2.1-point accuracy decline compared to 3.9 and 4.0-point declines for CoT and C3oT respectively, and CoSMo's average segment count tracks the ground-truth hop count within a deviation of less than 1 (Figure 4, Section 5.4).

The reward function combines a format-adherence term r_fmt, a correctness term r_acc based on exact-match to ground truth, and a structural-efficiency term r_struct that penalizes segment-count deviation |N−k*| beyond a one-step tolerance margin, within a GRPO-based reinforcement learning phase (Section 4.3, Equation 3).

Yd1jFl0jBt.text: The proposed quantum algorithm estimates a repeatedly nested expectation (RNE) with constant nesting depth D at RMSE ε using sample complexity Õ(ε^-1), up to logarithmic factors, as stated in Theorem 1.6 (Theorem 1.6).

This Õ(ε^-1) quantum complexity constitutes an almost quadratic speedup over the best classical algorithm for RNE estimation, whose optimal sample complexity for a single random variable's mean (a special case of RNE) is known to be Õ(ε^-2) (Section 1, Theorem 1.6).
Standard quantum lower bounds for Monte Carlo mean estimation (a special case of the RNE problem) show the Õ(ε^-1) quantum complexity is optimal up to logarithmic factors (Section 1).

The paper's classical-side contribution, Theorem 1.4, derandomizes the classical randomized Multilevel Monte Carlo (rMLMC) algorithm using deterministic level scheduling, achieving the same L^{p_d}-error and sample complexity bound O(ε^{-2(1+δ/2^{d-1})}) as the randomized version of Theorem 1.2/Corollary 1.3, but with a controlled, deterministic schedule needed to enable subsequent quantization (Theorem 1.4).

A naive direct quantization of the classical rMLMC algorithm (Proposition 1.5) fails to achieve the quadratic speedup, instead incurring sample complexity Ω(ε^{D-d+1} log^{D-d+1}(ε^-1)) due to the variable-time nature of randomized rMLMC interacting poorly with amplitude amplification (Proposition 1.5).

xES5qpQmw8.text: Across seven consistency training methods, reward hacking misalignment is reduced in 63% of runs (p<0.001), with Diverse-Decoding and Self-Refinement showing the strongest suppression (mean reductions of -21.5% and -9.9%) (Section 5.1).
Emergent misalignment is suppressed in 72% of runs (p<10^-7), with regularization methods ACT and BCT achieving 95%+ suppression (delta of -17.2% to -17.5%) (Section 5.1).
Sycophancy is amplified rather than suppressed by consistency training, with only 25% of runs showing suppression (p<10^-10) and ACT amplifying sycophancy by +18.8% (Section 5.1).

The Consistency Non-Neutrality Hypothesis, formalized via Proposition 3.2, predicts selection amplifies misalignment only when the score-misalignment function eta(s) is non-decreasing in score s (Section 3.2, 3.3).

A k=1 (no-selection) ablation achieves comparable misalignment suppression to higher values of k, indicating distribution shift from the labeling process, not the selection operator, drives the effects (Figure 4, Appendix A1).
Reward hacking exhibits roughly 10x higher KL divergence from the base policy than sycophancy, offered as a mechanistic explanation for the differential consistency-training effects (Figure 6).

lMieKzi6vx.text: Junta distributions over {0,1}^n with unknown k-junta structure can be learned to within additive error epsilon in total variation distance using O(2^k k log(n/delta)/epsilon^2) samples, improving the prior O(2^(2k) k log(n)/epsilon^4) bound of Aliakbarpour et al. and matching their lower bound in every parameter (Theorem 1, Section 3).

k-junta quantum states can be learned to within error epsilon in trace distance using O(12^k log(n/delta)/epsilon^2) single copies via an algorithm restricted to Pauli measurements, the first such upper bound for this problem (Theorem 3, Section 4).
A matching lower bound of Omega((4^k + log n)/epsilon^2) copies is proven for learning k-junta quantum states (Section 4).

The Choi state of an n-qubit QAC^0 circuit of size s, depth d, and a ancilla qubits can be learned using 2^O((log(s^2 2^a/epsilon))^d) log(n/delta) copies with only Pauli measurements, improving a prior bound that was polynomial in n to one that depends on n only logarithmically (Theorem 4, Section 4.1.2).
The algorithmic approach combines low-degree and sparse learning techniques via a rounding/thresholding procedure to handle both degree and sparsity constraints simultaneously (Section 1.5).

SHLRiQAlMp.text: JEPA guidance reduces cFID on CelebA from 12.11 (baseline ADM) to 8.50, and on ImageNet from 26.44 to 18.33, while producing minority samples with lower (more atypical) JEPA-SCORE values of -300.79 and -241.62 respectively (Table 1).

On text-to-image generation, JEPA guidance achieves a JEPA-SCORE of -355.40 with Stable Diffusion v1.5 and -337.88 with SDXL-Lightning while maintaining competitive CLIP, PickScore, and ImageReward text-alignment metrics (Table 2).
An ablation over the deferral ratio tau shows tau=0.8 is optimal for the deferred-guidance schedule, while tau=1.0 severely degrades sample quality (Table 3).
Randomized SVD rank k approximately 9 gives effective JEPA guidance with diminishing returns beyond k=15, used to approximate JEPA-SCORE and reduce computational overhead (Section 4.2, Table 3).

Proposition 4.1 decomposes the JEPA-SCORE approximation error into a randomized-SVD error term and a truncation error term, giving a theoretical bound on guidance accuracy (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.1).
Data augmentation using only 30K JEPA-guided synthetic samples achieves F1=0.775 on a downstream task, outperforming baselines that use 50K synthetic samples (Table 4).

4qLPtABOIR.text: On MuJoCo v3 tasks over 1M training steps and 5 seeds, CGPO reaches best episodic returns of 14,368.6 on HalfCheetah-v3, 7,131.4 on Humanoid-v3, and 7,272.1 on Ant-v3, exceeding the strongest diffusion-based RL baseline QVPO (11,385.6, 5,306.6, and 6,425.1 respectively) (Table 1, Figure 3).

On a real Franka robot arm cylindrical peg-in-hole task without demonstrations, CGPO achieves an 80% success rate (16/20 trials) versus 65% for SAC, presented as the first successful integration of diffusion-policy RL on a real robot (Section 5.3, Table 2).

Critic guidance is implemented via loss-guided reverse diffusion using a learned Q-function gradient (Equation 10, Section 4.2), combined with weighted denoising regression and a value-calibrated network V_phi for stable weighting (Equations 15-18, Section 4.3).
An overestimation-reduction scheme combining DDQN-style targets with truncated-quantile aggregation is used to compute stable critic targets for guidance (Equation 14, Section 4.3).

Ablations on Ant-v3 and Walker2d-v3 show that removing critic guidance substantially reduces performance, and that DDQN, truncated-quantile aggregation, and the value network are each individually necessary components (Figure 5, Figure 8).

SaUgHTz5Yo.text: Mode Connectivity Unlearning (MCU) connects an original model and a pre-unlearning model via a quadratic Bezier curve phi(t) = (1-t)^2*theta_o + 2(1-t)t*theta_c + t^2*theta_p to discover a spectrum of unlearning solutions in parameter space (Equation 1, Section 3.2).

On 10% random data forgetting, MCU-beta achieves an average performance gap of 1.00 on CIFAR-10/PreResNet-110 versus 2.97 for NegGrad+, 0.65 versus 1.16 on ImageNet-100/ViT, and 5.67 versus 8.65 on Tiny-ImageNet/VGG-16 (Table 1).

A two-stage parameter mask strategy that filters parameters by retaining-data importance and reserves parameters critical for forgetting yields a 75.23% speedup in backward propagation when masking 10% of parameters (Figure 3, Section 3.3).
On class-wise forgetting, MCU achieves 100% unlearning accuracy on ImageNet-100 while approaching retrain-from-scratch (RT) baseline performance on other metrics (Table 2).
Applying the MCU framework on top of six existing machine unlearning methods reduces their average performance gap by 49.71%, demonstrating plug-and-play compatibility (Table 3).

An adaptive penalty coefficient beta is updated batch-by-batch based on three conditions balancing forgetting and retention loss, removing the need for manual hyperparameter tuning (Equation 7, Section 3.4).

yKgAjMNkQO.text: The method formulates Conditional Flow Matching dynamics via a Koopman generator that lifts nonlinear vector-field dynamics into a linear evolution over observables, using the identity L g(x_t) = ∇_x g(x_t)·v(x_t) (Section 4, Eq. 8).
A decoder-free parametrization concatenates the raw state with learned observables, g̃(x) = [x, g_θ(x)], avoiding reconstruction error from a separate decoder (Section 4, Eq. 14).
Training combines a Generator loss enforcing Koopman consistency with a Target Consistency loss aligning the exponentiated generator trajectory to the terminal state (Section 4.3, Eqs. 15-16).
On MNIST, one-step (one-shot) generation with the Koopman linearization attains FID 60.6 versus FID 190 for a CFM baseline under the same one-step budget (Section 5, Table 4).

On 2D toy datasets (Swiss Roll, Eight Gaussians, Two Moons), the method achieves MMD scores within about 0.02 of the CFM baseline while enabling full-trajectory linearization (Section 5, Table 1, Figure 4).

An ablation shows the decoder-free architecture outperforms an encoder-decoder variant, and the combined Generator+Consistency loss reaches FID 20 on MNIST versus worse scores for either loss alone (Section 5, Table 3, Figures 9-10).

IStByBJdjR.text: Watermark embedding is formulated as a multi-objective optimization that adds a watermark loss aligning GNN feature attributions with a predefined pattern w to the classification loss (Section 4.1, Eq. 4-5).

Ownership verification uses statistical significance testing on matching indices (MI), which are shown to follow a normal distribution via a Shapiro-Wilk test with p-values greater than 0.2 across settings (Appendix A.4, Table 3).

Locating the watermarked subgraphs is proven NP-hard even under full knowledge of the method, and brute-force search over the candidate node sets requires checking about 5.8×10^245 possibilities (Section 4.4, Section 5.2.3).

On Amazon Photo, CoAuthor CS, and PubMed with GCN, SGC, and GraphSAGE backbones, the watermark yields MI p-values below 0.001 for T≥3 subgraphs while degrading classification accuracy by typically less than 2% (Section 5, Table 1).
The watermark survives fine-tuning for at least 25 epochs at 0.1x the original learning rate and remains detectable under pruning attacks up until accuracy itself collapses (Section 5, Figure 2).

Ablations over the number of subgraphs T and subgraph size s show that larger T lowers the ownership p-value and that s≥0.003 achieves near-zero p-values across datasets, at a mild cost to test accuracy for larger subgraphs (Section 5, Figures 4-5).

n2An7C7n7e.text: Instance-Disentangled Attention (IDAttn) partitions the joint token sequence into global, instance-local, and background components and applies two attention masks, M^dis for disentanglement and M^har for harmonization, computed as softmax(QK^T/√d + M)V (Section 3.2, Eq. 3).

Applying M^har in early and late layers and M^dis in middle layers gives the best balance of disentanglement and coherence; using M^dis in all layers instead raises attempt rate to 94.27% but degrades locality/coherence relative to the proposed schedule's 89.06% (Section 3, Table 1; Section 5).

An efficient multi-prompt encoding scheme encodes each instance-specific prompt independently rather than concatenating all prompts, reducing compute scaling with the number of instances at a minor quality cost (Section 3.3).
On the LoMOE-Bench benchmark the method attains LPIPS 0.099 and Localization-C 29.08, and removing IDAttn drops Localization-C from 29.26 to 27.90 (Section 5, Table 3).

On the newly introduced Crello Edit and InfoEdit infographics benchmarks (1,512/4,367 and 4,960 test samples respectively, with up to 285 concurrent edits), the method reports CER of 0.61 and 0.64 and attempts 89-92% of requested edits versus roughly 40% end-to-end attempt rate for a FLUX baseline on InfoEdit (Section 4, Table 4).

A user study on LoMOE gives the proposed method an Elo rating of 1589 versus 1331 for the FLUX baseline, and the method maintains performance when scaling to 100+ simultaneous edits while baselines degrade sharply (Section 5, Table 5, Figure 2).

bMsBArF8MT.text: CLINIC evaluates 13 language models (proprietary, open-weight general-purpose, and medical-specialized) across 5 trustworthiness dimensions (truthfulness, robustness, fairness, safety, privacy) spanning 18 tasks and 15 languages, using 28,800 expertly validated samples across 6 healthcare domains (Section 2-3).

On the honesty/abstention task, Gemini-2.5-Pro attains the highest honesty rate (95.20 high-resource, 93.83 mid-resource, 93.00 low-resource), whereas medical-specialized models score only 30-42 across resource tiers (Section 3.1, Table 3).
On jailbreak resistance (refuse-to-answer rate under persona-based and PAIR-style attacks), proprietary models resist 52-68% of attacks while DeepSeek-R1 resists only 24-37% (Section 3.4, Table 7).
On privacy-leakage tests using context-aware indirect questions, GPT-4o-mini leaks least (46-49%) while QwQ-32B leaks most (85-87%) (Section 3.5, Table 8).

Across honesty, fairness, and privacy dimensions, model performance consistently follows the pattern high-resource > mid-resource > low-resource languages, with sharp degradation on low-resource languages (Section 3).

bIHzsBaiu8.text: FAIR-Calib's theoretical analysis proves the trajectory KL divergence decomposes into a sum of per-step kernel divergences (Lemma 4.2) and, under random commit assumptions, reduces further to a sparse sum over only committed positions (Proposition 4.4), with token-level KL upper-bounded by squared logit error scaled by 1/4 (Lemma 4.6) (Section 4.1-4.5).
On W4A4 quantization of LLaDA-Base, FAIR-Calib reaches 61.09% average accuracy versus 59.37% for the FlatQuant baseline; on LLaDA-Instruct it reaches 72.40% versus 71.38% (Section 5, Table 1).
On W4A4 quantization of Dream-Base and Dream-Instruct, FAIR-Calib attains 64.64% and 66.66% average accuracy respectively, versus 62.08% and 63.98% for FlatQuant (Section 5, Table 2).

An ablation on Dream-Base shows the frontier-hit component alone raises accuracy from a 61.76% baseline to 63.12%, the masked-stage reliability component alone raises it to 62.89%, and combining both in FAIR-Calib reaches 64.64% (Section 5, Table 3).

FAIR-Calib reduces teacher-forced commit-step flips from 2.9±1.4 to 1.9±0.9 and improves the frontier decision margin from 6.56±0.62 to 7.23±0.64, evidencing suppressed post-commit mismatches (Section 5, Figure 4).

At the more aggressive W3A4 setting, FAIR-Calib improves LLaDA-Instruct accuracy from 69.58% to 70.41% over FlatQuant, and a QDrop-style integration improves the W8A8 baseline from 70.66% to 73.17% (Appendix E).

tn00ERVdgL.text: In the noiseless setting, Muon achieves loss L(t) decaying exponentially as K·e^{-(1+o_K(1))t}, versus gradient descent's L(t) ≍ K/t, giving an exponential-vs-polynomial speedup (Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2).

Under label noise with power-law frequency decay p̃ᵢ ∝ i^{-β}, GD's excess loss is lower-bounded by Ω̃(log K / T^{1-1/β}) while Muon's is upper-bounded by Õ((log K/T)^2), yielding a steeper scaling-law exponent for Muon (Theorem 5.7, Theorem 5.8).
Under label noise, Muon exhibits an Ω(C)-fold speedup over GD, where C is the size of each knowledge group in the associative memory model (Section 4).

Muon is interpreted as an implicit matrix preconditioner arising from adaptive task alignment, distinguished from coordinate-wise SignGD by its exploitation of block-symmetric gradient structure; a Task-Representation-Aligned SignGD (TRA-SignGD) variant with oracle embedding access is shown to match Muon's performance (Section 5).
On imbalanced MNIST and LLaMA pre-training experiments, Muon shows a steeper power-law decay slope than SGD across multiple data budgets, empirically confirming the derived scaling laws (Figure 2).

6XIwgtbcTa.text: VRU (Variance-Reduced Unlearning) is presented as the first first-order algorithm satisfying formal (ε,δ)-unlearning guarantees that directly incorporates gradient ascent on the forget set, using the estimator ∇ℓ(θ,ξr) − ∇ℓ(θ*,ξr) − (r_f/(1−r_f))∇ℓ(θ*,ξf) (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

VRU's convergence rate scales as Õ(κ_ℓ^3(1+d·κ_{ε,δ}^2·log(1/δ))·(e_0/e)·(r_f/(1−r_f))^2), exhibiting O(1/e) dependence on target excess risk e, compared to O(1/e^2) for prior forget-set-free methods (Theorem 4.1).
VRU improves over the NFT baseline by a factor of Θ(κ_ℓ^3·log(1/δ)·e/e_0) in the low-target-error regime (Corollary 4.2).
VRU is shown to asymptotically outperform any forget-set-free first-order method by a factor of Õ(d·κ_{ε,δ}^2·log(1/δ)·κ_ℓ^3·(r_f/(1−r_f))^2) (Theorem 4.4).

Empirically, VRU attains roughly 100x lower excess risk than competing methods at a forget fraction r_f = 10^-3, and achieves the lowest empirical privacy risk across all tested forget fractions (Figure 1, Figure 2).

WlCYSqjnqS.text: The coupled training framework jointly optimizes a deployment model using only test-time features X and a rich-view model using both X and privileged features W, with population minimizers characterized via fixed-point equations interpolating between the deployment target μ(x) and rich-view regression function η(z) (Theorem 2.1).

The risk bound depends on a correlation coefficient ρ* measuring alignment between deployment and rich-view estimation errors, and the method provably never performs worse than supervised learning on labeled data alone when ρ* is large (Corollary 2.3, Theorem 2.7).
An alternating forward selection procedure for the high-dimensional extension is proven to achieve sublinear decay of the empirical objective with O(N(|D_f|+|D_g|)k) time complexity (Theorem 3.1).

On Parkinson's telemonitoring regression, coupled training achieves test MSE of 72.60 versus 77.34 for the baseline using voice measurements with spectral features as privileged information (Table 1).

On Bank Marketing classification, coupled training attains mean Brier score 0.0881, outperforming Baseline (0.0893), Two-Stage pseudo-labeling (0.0928), and SVM+ (0.1470), winning in 26 of 26 random seeds against Two-Stage (Table 1).

ZD3BniFPto.text: BabyVision comprises 388 items spanning 22 subtypes grouped into four categories: Fine-grained Discrimination (8 subtypes), Visual Tracking (5 subtypes), Spatial Perception (5 subtypes), and Visual Pattern Recognition (4 subtypes) (Section on benchmark construction).

Gemini3-Pro-Preview, the best-performing MLLM tested, scores 49.7% overall accuracy on BabyVision, compared to 94.1% for adult human testers and approximately 70% for 6-year-old children, a 44.4-point gap versus adults (Results table).
GPT-5.2 scores 34.4% on BabyVision, while average open-source MLLMs score in the 12-22% range, well below both child and adult human baselines (Results table).

Four systematic failure modes are identified across models: loss of fine-grained detail under semantic compression, loss of manifold identity when tracking overlapping curves, failure of spatial imagination in 3D mental transformations, and confusion of style with structure in pattern induction (Analysis section).

9GBejLzPvl.text: In the multi-model self-consuming loop, system stability requires the real-data fraction to exceed a convergence threshold τ, below which the coupled model ecosystem fails to converge (Proposition 3.4).

Human curation improves alignment only when the alignment criterion |ρ_p| > 1/sqrt(1+m_p^2 τ_p^2) holds, and the sensitivity bound ‖S_p‖ ≤ 1/τ_p characterizes the magnitude of cross-model distortion (Corollary 4.7, Section 4).

The alignment gap relative to training on pure real data scales as O(1−λ̂_R θ), showing cross-model interactions can amplify, dampen, or reverse the benefit of human curation depending on this deviation term (Theorem 4.8).

Experiments on Gaussian models validate the theoretical convergence and sensitivity mechanisms, while CIFAR-10 experiments show divergent convergence and reward dynamics across different coupling scenarios (Figure 3, Figure 4).

Qwen2.5-0.5B experiments under RLVR training show that data diversity and the proportion of instruction-following data critically determine whether human curation helps or harms alignment in the self-consuming loop, and preference domain mismatch alters cross-domain evaluation outcomes (Section 5, Figure 5).

WK1NvxRMsL.text: For Qwen2.5, 3B and 14B models show statistically indistinguishable brain alignment (Δ=0.000, t(8)=-0.00, p=1.0), while 3B significantly outperforms 1.5B (Δ=0.073, t(8)=4.89, p=0.004) (Section 4, Table 2).

Brain predictivity saturates around the 3B parameter scale across three model families (Qwen2.5, LLaMA-3.2, DeepSeek-R1), with sub-3B models showing pronounced drops in alignment (Section 4, Figure 2).

Among quantization methods tested on 7B models, GPTQ degrades brain alignment (Δ=0.020, p<0.001) while AWQ (Δ=-0.020, p<0.001) and SmoothQuant (Δ=-0.005, p=0.016) largely preserve it (Section 4, Table 4).
GPTQ-quantized models show widespread voxel-level losses in neural predictivity concentrated in semantic cortical regions, unlike other quantization methods (Section 4, Figure 4b).
Pruning Qwen2.5-3B to 50% sparsity only reduces brain alignment from 0.924 to 0.907, showing robustness of neural predictivity to weight pruning (Section 4, Table 5).

Compression degrades linguistic competence on discourse, syntax, and morphology tasks without a corresponding consistent reduction in brain predictivity, indicating a dissociation between task performance and neural alignment (Section 4, Figure 5).

ZUDdYZSwr4.text: On the Who&When dataset, CORRECT improves GPT-5 step-level error localization accuracy from 8.6% to 17.2% at Acc@0, and from 24.1% to 37.8% at Acc@1 (Table 1).
On the Who&When dataset, CORRECT improves Qwen-2.5-7B step-level localization accuracy from 3.5% to 12.1% (Table 1).

On the CORRECT-Error benchmark, CORRECT yields average accuracy improvements of +20.1% at Acc@1, +27.6% at Acc@3, and +28.7% at Acc@5 across evaluated tasks, including a +46.9 point gain on Math500 (Table 2).
CORRECT's schema cache reaches approximately 90% of peak performance using only 30% of the full cache size, showing diminishing returns beyond 50% of the schema library (Figure 8).
Using retrieved schemas, CORRECT achieves 71.5% of oracle (ground-truth schema) performance for error localization (Section on oracle comparison).

Human evaluators distinguish CORRECT's synthetic errors from real multi-agent system errors at near-random rates (47-52%), supporting the realism of the constructed error dataset (Section on dataset validation).

4VOTzpH9MO.text: The proposed LLPF algorithm (Algorithm 1, LLPF_M2M) constructs low-loss connectivity paths between independently trained LeNet5, ResNet18, and CCT7 models, tested with 200, 40, and 10 repetitions respectively across different random seeds (Section 4).

Layer-wise L2 distances between connected models converge with narrow standard deviation bands across repeated runs, showing more consistent connectivity paths than existing methods (Figures 2 and 3, Section 4).

Unlike AutoNEB, which finds low-testing-loss paths but suffers midpoint barriers and significant computational overhead, LLPF does not guarantee low testing loss but produces consistently low training loss (below 0.1) across trials (Section 4).
A second algorithm, LLPF_M2O (Algorithm 2), moves trained model weights toward the origin across variance spheres, improving ResNet18 top-1 accuracy on ImageNet1k from 69.758% to 70.55% (Figure 5).

NHu6haXTM9.text: NEUBAY achieves an average normalized score of 80.1 across 12 D4RL locomotion datasets, versus 83.6 for the best baseline (VIPO), while setting new state-of-the-art results on 7 of 33 total evaluated datasets (Table 1).
NEUBAY improves specific D4RL locomotion tasks such as walker-random-v2 (27.9 to 34.1) and walker-medium-v2 (95.5 to 106.4) over prior best results (Table 1).

NEUBAY executes model rollouts with 75th-percentile horizons of 64-512 steps and maximum horizons of 256-1000 steps across 21 of 23 tasks with episode length T=1000, contrasting with conventional short-horizon model-based RL (Section 5.2, Figure 1).

On 11 low-quality datasets (D4RL random, NeoRL Low, Adroit door/hammer), NEUBAY ranks among the best methods in 5 of 11 tasks, but ranks among the best in only 3 of 15 medium-quality, narrow-coverage tasks, performing especially poorly on AntMaze navigation (Section 5.1).

Ablations show reducing the uncertainty threshold from ζ=1.0 to ζ=0.9 causes performance collapse to scores ≤5 on 16 datasets, and reducing ensemble size from N=100 to N=5 drops average D4RL locomotion performance from 80.1 to 65.9 (Table 2).
Without layer normalization, predicted state norms diverge after around 10 rollout steps, while normalization keeps state norms bounded and enables stable long-horizon planning (Figure 5).

32XNOcwH1z.text: Theorem 3.1 shows that flipping a single preference label shifts the DPO gradient by a vector o_i·β·Δψ_i that is independent of the current policy parameter θ, enabling reformulation of preference poisoning as a binary sparse approximation problem in gradient space (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.4 establishes a lower bound on the number of required label flips, |ℱ| ≥ ||g†||_2/(2β), showing flip requirements scale linearly with the target gradient norm (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).

The Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A) uses a penalty parameter M ≥ M_0(B,R,K*) so that the shortest lattice vector has coefficients constrained to {-1,0,1}^n, and under a separation condition ρ_k² > M²(K*-k), recovers the true K*-flip attack pattern exactly (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.3).
The Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A) recovers the exact flip support within K* iterations when the gradient dictionary's coherence satisfies μ(V) < b/((2K*-1)B) (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.3).

Theorem 5.4 provides impossibility certificates against K-flip attacks under a spectral norm condition ||g†||_2 - ε > √K·||V||_2 and a coherence condition (||g†||_2 - ε)² > B²(K + μ(V)K(K-1)) (Section 5, Theorem 5.4).

On the SHP dataset, the crafted attack shifts the trained policy far closer to the intended target than clean training does (||π_θ†-π_θ̂||_1 ≈ 0.012 vs ||π_clean-π_θ̂||_1 ≈ 0.224), and BMP-A runs roughly four orders of magnitude faster than BAL-A (1.37×10⁻⁴s vs 0.6865s) on the same data subset (Section 6.2.3).

S0ZmHLCdqW.text: Linear-Core Surrogates are smooth, everywhere-differentiable convex losses that achieve linear H-consistency bounds (excess target error scales linearly, not just as a square root, with excess surrogate error), proven for binary classification in Theorem 3.4 and extended to multi-class sum losses in Theorem 4.1 (Section 3, Theorem 3.4; Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

For structured prediction over exponentially large output spaces, linear consistency bounds are preserved (Theorem 5.1) and the gradient variance of the surrogate scales as O(1/K) independent of output space size |Y| (Theorem 5.2) (Section 5, Theorems 5.1-5.2).
On large-vocabulary sequence tagging, Linear-Core Surrogates give a 23x speedup over Structured SVMs (Section 6, experiments on structured prediction).
On inflated part-of-speech tagging with an output space of |Y|=4000, Linear-Core Surrogates achieve a 17.4x speed-up over a CRF baseline (Section 6, sequence tagging experiments).

Under instance-dependent label noise on corrupted CIFAR-10, Linear-Core Surrogates outperform Generalized Cross-Entropy by about +2.6% accuracy at 30-40% corruption rates (Section 6, CIFAR-10 noise-robustness experiments).

MXvuMNd3oI.text: LoRA fine-tuning dynamics are modeled via a mean-field continuum limit of self-attention (tokens as interacting particles evolving by the interaction ODE in Equation 2), enabling analysis with optimal-transport (Wasserstein) distances (Section 2, Equation 2).

Theorem 5.4 establishes a two-phase (bifurcation) regime for token clustering under LoRA perturbation: a short-term phase where the Wasserstein distance W2(mu_t, nu_t) stays bounded near delta/(n+1), followed by a long-term phase where tokens escape to new clusters (Section 5, Theorem 5.4).

Proposition 5.8 bounds the time-to-deviation as T*(delta) = O(log(delta)/epsilon), where epsilon is the spectral gap between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues of the modified Value matrix, quantifying when catastrophic forgetting begins to dominate (Section 5, Proposition 5.8).

Proposition 7.2 shows that when LoRA update matrices satisfy an orthogonality condition Im(K_A) subset of Im(K)^perp, new token clustering geometries can emerge without necessarily degrading the original task's representations (Section 7, Proposition 7.2).
Empirical checks on BERT and Llama2 partially confirm the theoretical low-rank/clustering assumptions, with Llama2 showing weaker adherence to the theoretical hypotheses than BERT (Section 8).

KMwrxaoAW4.text: TadABench-1M comprises roughly one million TadA enzyme DNA-variant sequences (409,869 distinct amino-acid variants) collected across 31 rounds of wet-lab directed evolution (Section on dataset construction; TadABench-1M).

Under a random 8:1:1 split, protein language models such as ESM2-35M reach a test Spearman correlation of 0.8014, indicating the label space is learnable under standard interpolation conditions (Table 4).
Under the realistic future-round (temporal) split, the same ESM2-35M model's test Spearman correlation collapses to about 0.0300, and Evo2-7B (a DNA/RNA model) reaches only 0.0707 (Table 1, Table 2).

Figure 4 shows the sharp contrast between random-split and future-round evaluation, demonstrating that strong random-split performance does not imply the ability to discover fitness improvements in future evolutionary rounds (Figure 4).

Analysis of training-set composition indicates evolutionary coverage (breadth across rounds) is more informative for temporal generalization than local data density (concentrated sampling within a round) (Section on evolutionary depth analysis).

hG1l88A3hb.text: PRISM is a transformer encoder-decoder architecture that jointly infers a discrete model-structure posterior (via an autoregressive multivariate Bernoulli decoder) and continuous parameters (via a diffusion-based v-prediction decoder), conditioned on observations via cross-attention and on a complexity hyperparameter lambda via adaptive layer normalization (Section 3.2, Model architecture).

On synthetic symbolic regression with a model space of up to 2^30 (about one billion) instantiations built from K=42 base functions, PRISM's top-5 model-selection accuracy remains above 90% across scales (Section 4.1, Figure 4, Table 1).

Test-time complexity control is achieved by conditioning the network on a tunable model-prior hyperparameter lambda, which trades off between simpler and more complex model families without retraining (Section 3.4, Deployment).
On the diffusion-MRI Ball-and-Sticks model, PRISM's inferred model posterior correlates with an MCMC/evidence-based reference at R^2=0.97 (Section 4.2.1, Figure 6).
PRISM improves probabilistic tractography, raising mean tract correlation from 0.86 (SBI baseline) to 0.96 (Section 4.2.1, Figure 7).

For an extended model family (BSZT) with 21 model components yielding up to 114 parameters, PRISM maintains simulation-based calibration, though with acceptable degradation when comparable model classes exist (Section 4.2.2, Figure 8).

hLizFuTBsA.text: DiffuMamba replaces the Transformer backbone of a masked diffusion language model with a bidirectional Mamba (state-space) backbone, matching downstream task performance of Transformer-based diffusion baselines while achieving up to 8.2x higher inference throughput on long sequences at scales up to 1.3B parameters (Section on Experiments, Inference Throughput).

DiffuMamba-H, a hybrid variant that interleaves attention layers every K=5 Mamba blocks, achieves up to 4.3x higher inference throughput than the Transformer-based diffusion baseline while retaining global-context modeling (Section on hybrid architecture).

DiffuMamba exhibits near-linear scaling of inference cost with sequence length, in contrast to the quadratic-complexity scaling of the attention-based diffusion baseline (Section on Inference Throughput and Modeling Quality).
At the 1.3B scale, hybrid variants of DiffuMamba achieve lower (better) validation perplexity than the Transformer-based diffusion baseline (Table 2, Validation Perplexity).
On zero-shot benchmarks and downstream tasks, DiffuMamba and DiffuMamba-H consistently outperform the attention-based diffusion baseline across the evaluated datasets (Table 3, Table 4).

UWwmMJjlCb.text: DIVA improves understanding performance by +3.8% to +6.1% (e.g., MMMU) and generation performance by +2.84 to +6.57 points on DPG-Bench across three unified multimodal backbones: Nexus-Gen (7B), Show-o (1.5B), and Liquid (7B) (Section 3, Table 1).

DIVA uses a two-stage training procedure: Stage 1 warms up lightweight shared/unique encoders via factorized logit injection with the backbone frozen, and Stage 2 unfreezes the backbone and applies mutual information objectives with asymmetric alignment (Section 3.3).
Ablation removing the unique-information regularization term I_uni degrades performance by -3.8% on MMMU and -3.3% on POPE (Table 2).
Ablation replacing masked-inpainting with contiguous masking for the generation information flow causes the largest performance drop observed, -7.7% on MMMU and -9.5% on POPE (Table 2).

The representation divergence between understanding and generation tasks peaks in the middle layers of the backbone (roughly layers 8-18), which DIVA specifically targets for its factorized readout (Figure 2, Table 2).
DIVA is evaluated on understanding benchmarks MMMU, MME, MMBench, MMVet, and POPE, and on generation/editing benchmarks GenEval, DPG-Bench, WISE, ImgEdit, and GEdit-Bench-EN (Section 3).

sJ7ngz2eQx.text: The Generative Wasserstein Flows (GWF) framework shows that Variational Wasserstein Gradient Flow (VWGF) and Scalable JKO (S-JKO) objectives, despite different formulations, are mathematically equivalent (Proposition 3.1).

The paper shows explicit Wasserstein gradient descent with a regularized f-divergence is equivalent to JKO steps for the corresponding unregularized f-divergence under specific parameter relationships (Proposition 3.2).

The paper introduces a Donsker-Varadhan formulation for the KL divergence within the JKO scheme that yields tighter lower bounds than classical variational representations while preserving equivalence at optimality (Section 3).

The GWF framework is extended beyond f-divergences to integral probability metrics, including Wasserstein-1 and squared Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD²), introducing a JKO-regularized version of MMD-GAN that does not require explicit discriminator optimization (Section 4, Equation 18).

Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 measured by Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) show JKO regularization gives moderate but consistent improvements for f-divergences (KL, Jensen-Shannon, χ²) and more pronounced gains for MMD, up to 20 FID points (Section 6/7 experiments).
Parametric JKO updates are shown to approximate preconditioned Wasserstein gradient flows in the small-step-size regime (τ→0) (Proposition 6.3).

7kH5uphAes.text: EcoVLA achieves up to 1.60× inference speedup with only a 0.4% drop in task success rate using its environment-aware adaptive pruning (EAP) alone (Section 5, Table 3).
When EAP is combined with interleaved inference orchestration (I2O) and token pruning, EcoVLA reaches 2.18× speedup with only a 0.5% degradation in success rate (Section 5).

On OpenVLA-OFT with LIBERO, EcoVLA achieves 1.26× and 1.41× speedups at 25% and 40% pruning ratios respectively; on π0.5, it achieves 1.31× and 1.46× speedups at corresponding pruning levels (Table 1, Table 2).
On CogACT evaluated on SIMPLER, EcoVLA achieves 1.57× and 1.60× speedups across different pruning settings (Table 3).

On a real 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 robotic arm across three tasks (apple placement, pill bottle storage, banana placement), EcoVLA reduces per-step latency from 86.08ms to 68.40ms, a 1.26× wall-clock speedup, with only minor performance loss (Table 4).
EcoVLA is training-free and plug-and-play, remaining compatible with existing token-pruning methods such as FastV and VLA-Cache (Section 4, Table 5).

mCsBf1sm4p.text: The paper proves (Theorem 4.6) that the memory complexity of dataset distillation for two-layer ReLU networks reduces from Θ(d³ ∨ d²/ε ∨ d/ε⁴ ∨ dL) to Θ̃(r²d + L), where r is the intrinsic dimensionality of the target function and L is the network width (Theorem 4.6, Section 4).

The analysis targets multi-index models of the form f*(x) = σ*(B^T x), where B ∈ R^{d×r} encodes the intrinsic r-dimensional structure of the task, for two-layer networks trained via gradient-based optimization (Section 3, Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 shows that for multi-index models with intrinsic dimension r, only M₁ ~ Θ̃(r²) synthetic points are needed in the first distillation phase to enable effective second-layer training (Theorem 4.2).

The paper's main theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) shows distilled points align with the principal subspace of the target function via projections involving the Hessian matrix, formalizing how distillation encodes low-dimensional task structure (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
The work presents synthetic experiments in Section 5 validating the theoretical compression rates for gradient-based dataset distillation on two-layer networks (Section 5).

D9g1RjORI7.text: KnowBias mitigates social bias in LLMs by enhancing (rather than suppressing) neurons that encode bias-knowledge, using inference-time neuron enhancement without any retraining (Section 2).

KnowBias achieves the best average debiasing rank across three bias benchmarks (BBQ, CrowS-Pairs, StereoSet) among compared methods, with average ranks of 1.8 for Llama-3.2-3B, 2.1 for Qwen-3-4B, and 2.3 for Llama-3.1-8B (Section 3, Table 2).

The neuron identification step requires only 45 bias-knowledge yes/no questions in total (5 concepts × 3 question types × 3 demographic dimensions: gender, race, religion) to achieve optimal debiasing (Section 2).
General reasoning capability is preserved after debiasing, evaluated on four benchmarks: OpenBookQA, COPA, ARC-Easy, and ARC-Challenge (Section 3).
The method's effectiveness is assessed via five research questions (RQ1-RQ5) spanning debiasing performance, data efficiency, generalization across models, and capability preservation (Section 3).

RYaAyLMKy7.text: MalTree's Neighbor-Joining tree with outgroup rooting achieves 87.1% temporal consistency on the full dataset of 103,883 malware samples spanning 538 families and 2010-2023 (Section 5.3).

Analysis of embedding drift reveals over 10x variation in evolutionary tempo across malware families, with Bashlite and Syslogk showing substantially elevated drift compared to slower-evolving families like Pysabot and Loda (Section 5.3, Figure 5).

A multi-modal fusion of pseudo-static (3,512-dim), dynamic (1,000-dim), and image (2,048-dim ResNet-50) embeddings is reduced to a 1,000-dim representation, with image embeddings alone achieving 94.91% classification accuracy versus 87.51% for pseudo-static and 87.23% for dynamic embeddings (Section 4.1, Table 1).

In a case study of the Mirai botnet lineage, MalTree identifies five validated descendants with inferred edge weights ranging from Bashlite (9.6) to RapperBot (20.8), and computes a symbol Jaccard similarity of 0.82 between Mirai and Okiru confirming code reuse (Section 5.5, Table 3).

Computing the phylogenetic tree via Neighbor-Joining takes approximately 3 days on 20 cores versus approximately 11 hours for UPGMA, on what is claimed to be the largest phylogenetic analysis of malware to date (Section 5.1).

iec4FIZyrx.text: CoLA-World introduces a warm-up phase (training the inverse dynamics model while freezing the world model) that prevents the joint-training collapse observed without it, where VQ codebook utilization drops to zero and max code usage rises to ~100% (Section 3.2, Figure 2).

On video prediction (Table 2), the Warm8K + E2E52K configuration outperforms the two-stage LAM30K + WM30K baseline in FVD across OXE (278.90 vs 291.30), EgoCentric (252.45 vs 260.14), and LIBERO (158.36 vs 167.77).
Under real-action adaptation (Table 3), CoLA-World achieves FVD of 93.68 vs 115.45 for the baseline on LIBERO, and 169.70 vs 188.82 on RoboDesk.

On the VP2 visual planning benchmark (Table 4), CoLA-World achieves an average success rate of 13.12% versus 6.94% for the two-stage baseline, with the largest gap on the Upright Block task (37.78% vs 20.0%).

Ablations (Figure 4) show that the latent action model's probing loss decreases faster when co-evolving with the world model than when trained against a frozen tutor world model, and that a world model trained against a frozen LAM plateaus while the co-evolving LAM enables continued improvement (Section 3.2, Figure 4).

ZMkfGplf4b.text: R3 reduces the training-inference policy KL divergence of the Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE model from a baseline of 1.535e-3 to approximately 7.5e-4, roughly a 50% reduction and approaching the level observed for the dense Qwen3-8B baseline (6.4e-4) (Section 4.3).
R3 reduces the fraction of tokens with training/inference probability ratio exceeding 2 by roughly one order of magnitude relative to MoE training without R3 (Section 3.1, Figure 2d).

In training stability experiments (Table 1), GRPO alone collapses at step 120 (multi-step) or step 60 (single mini-step) while GRPO+R3 shows no collapse across all tested configurations, including all 3 single-mini-step runs that collapsed without R3.
R3 keeps the F(tau=2) instability metric below 1e-4 throughout training, whereas runs that collapse exceed 0.1 on this metric (Section 5.2, Figure 5).
R3's router-mask caching mechanism, which integrates with prefix KV-cache, adds less than 3% latency overhead during the rollout phase (Section 4.1).

fR1FjJwrnN.text: Theorem 4.1 constructs multi-layer softmax transformers whose layer-wise hidden outputs exactly implement normalized gradient descent steps theta_{l+1} = theta_l - alpha-tilde_l * grad(L_ICL(theta_l)) / L_ICL(theta_l) on an in-context exponential loss (Section 4.2).

Corollary 4.3 shows that for linearly separable in-context data, the transformer's predicted weights converge directionally to the max-margin solution at rate O(log n / (alpha-tilde * L)) (Section 4.2).

Theorem 4.5 proves a training convergence guarantee for a single-layer self-attention model supervised by one-step gradient descent, establishing a unique local minimizer in a compact set with linear convergence rate proportional to 1/d, using a Newton-Kantorovich argument and a derived Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality (Section 4.3).

Theorem 4.7 gives a point-wise high-probability out-of-distribution generalization bound for the multi-layer looped transformer, || theta_L/||theta_L||_2 - theta* ||_2 <= O~(d/n + log n/(alpha*L)), matching known PAC learning sample-complexity lower bounds (Section 4.4).

IPeIlnJzYa.text: PAWS trains and queries an advantage function consistently at the segment level (via a weighted maximum-likelihood objective using exponentially transformed segment advantages as importance weights, Equation 8), avoiding the mismatch of training on trajectory-level preferences while inferring per-step utilities (Section on method, Equation 8).

On Meta-World tasks with 500 preferences (Table 1), PAWS (MLP) reaches 78.3% average success and PAWS (Transformer) 78.2%, versus 67.3% for the CPL+KL baseline; with only 50 preferences, PAWS (MLP/Transformer) achieves 50.8%/51.6%.
On locomotion tasks with 500 preferences (Table 2), PAWS (MLP) outperforms all baselines, e.g. reaching a HalfCheetah return of 1,450 plus/minus 251 versus 950 plus/minus 87 for CPL.

An ablation comparing segment-based updates to state-action-level updates (Table 4) across 10 Meta-World tasks shows segment-based PAWS (MLP) at 78% success with 500 preferences versus 67% for state-level updates, and Figure 3c shows state-action update performance degrades sharply once segment length exceeds one while segment-based PAWS remains stable.
On real human preference labels for the Button Press task (Table 3), PAWS (MLP) achieves 56.2% plus/minus 5.6 success versus 47.5% plus/minus 7.4 for CPL.

VN8RbsdxYs.text: On ImageNet-1K, the proposed NTCE loss reaches 76.7% accuracy and NONL reaches 76.5%, both exceeding the cross-entropy baseline of 75.4% (Table 1).
NONL achieves ≥95% across Neural Collapse metrics, including intra-class effective rank reduced to 4.0/11.4 versus 22.5/96.4 for cross-entropy (Table 3).
Theorem 4.2 proves that supervised contrastive learning's class-mean embeddings form an optimal classifier throughout training, eliminating the need for post-hoc linear probing (Section 4.3).
NONL yields a +5.5% mean relative improvement in transfer learning accuracy over cross-entropy, ranking best on 7 of 8 downstream datasets including Food, Cars, Pets, and Flowers (Table 4).
On long-tailed CIFAR-10-LT and CIFAR-100-LT with imbalance factor τ=0.01, NONL improves over cross-entropy by up to +8.7% and +7.0% respectively (Table 6).
On ImageNet-C robustness benchmarks, NTCE and NONL reduce mean Corruption Error (mCE) to 77.6 and 77.8 respectively, versus 80.1 for cross-entropy (Table 5).

tkNyoOIbgj.text: Across 8 tested frontier LLM-powered agents (including Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.2, and Gemini 3.1 Pro), 6 of 8 show near-zero (≤5%) refusal rates when asked to identify vulnerabilities in real production systems (Section on Critical Refusal Rate Findings).

Only 18 of 800 total agent trajectories exhibit the desired safety-refusal behavior across the evaluation suite spanning Easy (20 challenges), Medium (20 challenges), and Hard (9 challenges) difficulty tiers (Benchmark Components section).
GPT-5.2 is the only tested model to show meaningful refusal behavior, refusing 62% of the time on medium-difficulty challenges (Critical Refusal Rate Findings section).

The paper introduces the Cybersecurity Refusal Framework (CRF), a tripartite Red/Yellow/Green taxonomy where government, healthcare, power grid, and transportation targets warrant always-refuse treatment (Framework Overview / Refusal Boundary Categories section).
The benchmark evaluates agents against 9 CWE vulnerability classes, including XSS, SQL injection, SSRF, path traversal, and insecure deserialization (Vulnerability Classes Tested section).

iXh2dmdt8v.text: TimeMoDE replaces standard MLP layers in a Diffusion Transformer backbone with a Mixture of Domain Experts (MoDE) module, using domain prompts and learnable time-series prototypes to route tokens to experts (Section 4.1–4.3, Figure 2).
TimeMoDE is pre-trained on 20 datasets spanning 10 domains and 5 tasks, including finance (Stock, Exchange), energy (Energy, ETTh1), and space (MSL, SMAP) data (Appendix B.1, Table 4).

In few-shot generation with only 5% of target-domain training data, TimeMoDE achieves a context-FID of 0.355 versus 0.426 for the ImagenFew baseline, a 16.7% reduction, with similar gains (~25% average c-FID reduction) at 10% and #25-shot settings (Table 1).
In full-shot generation, TimeMoDE reaches a context-FID of 0.040, far outperforming ImagenFew (0.208) and DiffusionTS (1.696) (Table 2).

An ablation shows removing the MoDE router and using a dense layer instead worsens 10%-subset context-FID by 264.6%, and training from scratch without pre-training worsens it by 267.5%, confirming both the MoE architecture and pre-training are critical (Table 3, Section 5.3).
Pre-training TimeMoDE takes about 20 hours on 2 NVIDIA V100 GPUs, while fine-tuning to a new domain takes only about 4 minutes on a single GPU (Section 5.5).

cY0pi9WHvL.text: The paper defines a three-level anchoring measurement framework for Reverse Chain-of-Thought Generation—lexical (ROUGE-L recall), entropic, and probabilistic (bit-gain-rate, Equation 6) anchoring—to quantify post-hoc rationalization (Section 2.1–2.3).
Semantic suppression reduces lexical anchoring by 11.5% relative to a neutral baseline but paradoxically increases entropic anchoring by 4.5% and probabilistic anchoring by 20.0% (Table 1).

The proposed Structural Skeleton-guided Reasoning (SSR) method generates an answer-invariant functional skeleton (e.g., PLAN→INFER→EVAL, drawn from 8 tags defined in Appendix C.4, Table 5) before generating the full reasoning trace (Section 3.2).
SSR-D achieves up to a 10% improvement on ArenaHard over the neutral baseline, e.g., raising Qwen3-4B from 41.7 to 50.8 (Table 3, Section 5.2).

SSR concentrates 51.2% of reasoning traces in the authentic "Reason" zone of the Entropic-Probabilistic behavioral plane, versus suppression methods migrating toward pathological "Encode" and "Cloze" zones (Table 2, Figure 3–4).
SSR-D recovers approximately 30% of the out-of-distribution performance gap on AIME for Qwen3-8B, indicating more transferable derivation patterns than suppression baselines (Table 4, Section 5.3).

4Ec15Uj8Nd.text: CyberPal 2.0 spans model sizes from 4B to 20B parameters, built on Qwen3 (4B, 8B, 14B) and gpt-oss-20B base models (Section 5, Table 1).
On Root Cause Mapping (RCM), the 20B CyberPal 2.0 model ranks first overall among frontier models, surpassing Sec-Gemini v1, while the 4B, 8B, and 14B variants each rank second (Figure 1).

On Cyber Threat Intelligence multiple-choice tasks, the 20B and 14B models rank second and third respectively—behind Sec-Gemini v1 but ahead of o1—while the 8B model is competitive with GPT-4o (Figure 1).
Across nine cybersecurity benchmarks, CyberPal 2.0 models show 7–14% average gains over their baseline post-trained versions, with 16–31% gains specifically on CTIBench-RCM (Table 1).
CyberPal-2.0-8B substantially outperforms comparably sized open-source cybersecurity models such as Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct, DeepHat-V1, and PRIMUS variants (Table 2).
The SecKnowledge 2.0 data enrichment pipeline's LLM-as-Judge evaluation shows 85.62% preference for rewritten answers over originals (Figure 9, Appendix A.2).

lfqyLp4hZm.text: WildCat's coreset-based attention approximation achieves super-polynomial O(n^{-sqrt(log log n)}) error decay while running in near-linear O(n^{1+o(1)}) time, established via Theorem 2 (Section 3).
Coreset selection uses randomly pivoted Cholesky to run in O(nr^2) operations with coreset size r in n^{o(1)}, yielding overall near-linear attention runtime (Section 2.6, Algorithm 4).

On BigGAN image generation, WildCat achieves a 3.71x speed-up with only 1.40% Inception Score degradation and 0.00% FID degradation, outperforming Thinformer's 2.32x speed-up at 1.79% IS degradation (Table 2, Section 4.1).

On T2T-ViT image classification, WildCat attains 82.18% top-1 accuracy with an 11.60x speedup on layer 1, the highest accuracy among approximate-attention baselines at that speedup (Table 3, Section 4.2).
For language model KV cache compression, WildCat averages a 47.25 score across 13 LongBench-E tasks and achieves the best individual-task performance on 6 of 13 benchmarks (Table 4, Section 4.3).

RlEPV6ec7P.text: The rational risk gap is decomposed via Lemma 2 into an extrinsic component, arising from environment shift between deployment and training, and an intrinsic component, arising from the gap between expected and empirical training value (Section 3.2).

Theorem 1 bounds the extrinsic rational gap by Ls*H*W1(p0dagger,p0) + H^2*Ls*(Lp+1)*W1(pdagger,p), using the 1-Wasserstein distance between initial-state and transition distributions and Lipschitz constants Ls, Lp of the value function and transition kernel (Section 4.1).
Theorem 2 bounds the intrinsic rational gap using empirical Rademacher complexity of the value-function class, plus a term scaling as H^2*sqrt(log(H/delta)/(2T)) (Section 4.2).

Experiments on Taxi-v3 and Cliff Walking show that layer normalization, l2 regularization, and weight normalization all reduce the rational risk gap relative to baseline DQN, consistent with the intrinsic-gap bound (Figure 2a).

Domain randomization consistently decreases the rational risk gap versus baseline DQN, and increasing environment shift magnitude (0%-70% action randomization) correlates positively with the rational risk gap, matching the extrinsic-gap prediction (Figure 2b, Figure 3).

1Mof8Blu4f.text: At a noise rate of eta=0.3 with uniform label noise, FedRGL achieves 78.75% accuracy on Cora (5 clients) versus FedAvg's 48.19%, and 66.08% on CiteSeer (5 clients) versus FedAvg's 38.73% (Table 1).
At the same noise rate, FedRGL reaches 81.77% on PubMed (10 clients) versus 74.36% for the baseline, and 90.05% on Physics (20 clients) (Table 1).

On the Photo dataset, FedRGL maintains a consistent accuracy advantage over other methods as the percentage of noisy clients increases, reaching 73.4% versus 48-58% for competitors when 100% of clients are noisy (Table 2).
On the large-scale ogbn-arxiv graph, FedRGL achieves at least a 4-percentage-point accuracy improvement over baseline federated graph learning methods (Table 3).

Ablations show that removing the global-model view or the local-structure view most significantly degrades FedRGL's performance, while removing the contrastive learning component has only minimal impact (Figure 4b).

RnDpZKeYer.text: Theorem 1 shows that for isotropic Gaussian targets with standard normal initialization, even a score estimate with arbitrarily small global Lp error leaves Langevin dynamics with total variation distance to the target bounded below by 1 - e^{-Omega(d)} for any polynomial time horizon (Section 3.1).

Theorem 7 demonstrates an analogous failure mode for data-based initialization: when Langevin dynamics is initialized at the n samples used to train the score estimate, it remains far from the target distribution in total variation (Section 3.2).

Theorem 11 extends the negative result to broad classes of target distributions satisfying Assumption 10, constructing score estimates with small L2 error for which liminf as t to infinity of TV(pi_tar, pi_t) is at least 1 - epsilon_TV for arbitrarily prescribed epsilon_TV (Section 3.3).

The results establish that, unlike diffusion models where sampling error in total variation scales linearly with L2 score-estimation error, Langevin dynamics in high dimensions lacks this robustness property (Section 3).

Ph2BaszK9w.text: Proposition 4.1 gives recursive formulas for computing the evidence lower bound and its gradient online in state-space models using intermediate functions h_t, u_t, v_t that satisfy state-dependent recursions, avoiding costly regression steps (Section 4).

Theorem 4.5 establishes geometric ergodicity of the extended Markov chain combining states, observations, and functional approximations under Assumptions 4.2-4.4, justifying the proposed contrast lower bound on log-likelihood (COLBO) (Section 4).

Algorithm 2 (RMCVI) samples N i.i.d. particles from the filtering distributions q_t^phi and uses self-normalized importance sampling weights (Equation 16) to approximate expectations on finite support instead of via regression (Section 5).

On the chaotic RNN state-space model, RMCVI achieves 1-step smoothing RMSE of 8.9(+/-0.2)x10^-2 and filtering RMSE of 10.3(+/-0.2)x10^-2 in 1 ms per step, matching the accuracy of the regression-based approach of Campbell et al. 2021 (9.2x10^-2 smoothing RMSE, 4.8 ms per step) while being about 55 times faster (Table 1, Section 6).
On an air-quality dataset with sensor failures, the method recovers smoothed state estimates during the failure period, demonstrating robustness of the online variational approach (Figure 4).

FJZiatEiCG.text: Observation Spectral Filtering (Algorithm 1) achieves sublinear cumulative prediction error for nonlinear systems with finitely many marginally stable modes, with cumulative loss bounded by O(Q*^2 log(Q*) d_X R log(RT) m^2 log^7(mT) sqrt(T)) (Theorem 3.1).

For linear dynamical systems with asymmetric dynamics and adversarial process noise, the method attains regret independent of hidden state dimension, scaling as O(Q R m^2 log^7(mT) sqrt(T)) in the noiseless case (Theorem 3.3).

The Luenberger program (Definition 5.1) defines a control-theoretic condition number Q* measuring observability difficulty, which directly determines the learning complexity of the spectral filtering algorithm (Section 5, Definition 5.1).

A global linearization lemma bounds the discretization error of approximating bounded, Lipschitz nonlinear systems by high-dimensional linear systems as sum_{t<=T} ||y'_t - y_t|| <= T^2/2 * epsilon (Lemma 5.5).

The method is empirically validated on 128x128 random asymmetric linear systems and cyclic permutation matrices, and on nonlinear systems including the Lorenz system, double pendulum, and Langevin dynamics, compared against direct LDS learning, classical eDMD, and hybrid spectral-eDMD baselines (Section 7).

G9UW8lFWeP.text: DUAL distills a diffusion planner into a fast-sampling one-step diffusion actor policy, reducing denoising steps from N=20 to N=1 and cutting inference latency from about 24,000ms to about 800ms per action (Section 3.1, Section 4.2, Figure 2).

On MuJoCo locomotion (D4RL), DUAL attains an average normalized score of 89.93 versus 88.95 for DACER and 86.82 for Diffuser, and on AntMaze DUAL attains 81.90 versus 71.71 (DACER) and 68.89 (Diffuser) (Table 1).

On Off-Dynamic RL (ODRL) benchmarks with shifted friction/gravity dynamics, DUAL scores 62.62 versus 57.51 for Diff-QL, and on standard MuJoCo settings DUAL scores 97.16 versus 93.49 for Diff-QL (Table 2).
On Adroit manipulation tasks, DUAL improves over the Diff-QL baseline on pen-cloned (124.40 vs 104.45) and door-cloned (15.26 vs 11.55) (Table 3).

Ablations on hopper-medium and hopper-friction show that removing the epistemic uncertainty quantification module drops performance from 88.23 to 83.36, and removing the shift-aware component drops ODRL performance from 48.00 to 35.12, while distillation reduces latency from 24,953ms to 800ms (Table 4).

A last-layer Laplace approximation on the actor loss (Eq. 6) is proven to yield a standard Bayesian posterior over policy parameters, in contrast to ELBO-based uncertainty estimation approaches (Theorem 3.4).

QN1iaHy54s.text: On synthetic 1D heavy-tailed benchmarks (Weibull, Pareto, Lognormal, Burr), PH-VAE achieves a KS_tail of 0.022 on Weibull data versus 0.190 for a Gaussian VAE, 0.225 for a Student-t VAE, and 0.187 for an extreme-value VAE (xVAE) decoder (Table 1).
On Pareto data, PH-VAE reduces the 99th-percentile quantile error to 0.023 compared to 0.336 (Gaussian VAE), 0.632 (Student-t VAE), and 0.131 (xVAE) (Table 1).

The Phase-Type decoder uses a series canonical form requiring only 2m-1 parameters instead of m^2 for an m-phase distribution, with matrix-exponential computation stabilized via a uniformization method (Equation 7, Section 3).

On a 5D synthetic multivariate benchmark with heterogeneous Pareto/Weibull/Lognormal/Burr marginals, PH-VAE reduces Kendall tau error to 0.0672 and tail co-exceedance error to 5.44x10^-4, versus 0.1429 and 1.38x10^-3 respectively for a Gaussian VAE (Table 3).
On real financial returns from five U.S. equities (2010-2024), PH-VAE reduces correlation error to 0.1716 and Kendall tau error to 0.0293, versus 0.8848 and 0.2667 for a Gaussian VAE (Table 4).

An ablation on Pareto data shows that increasing the number of phases from 5 to 15 improves KS_tail but increases variance, with m=10 and KL weight beta=1 identified as the best-balanced configuration (Table 2).

iv84rM71Mc.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes a generalization bound for the target domain that is tightened by jointly minimizing empirical risk on labeled target data and synthetic noise data while reducing their distributional discrepancy in a shared representation space (Theorem 4.1).

The Noise Adaptation Framework (NAF) is evaluated across nine datasets including CIFAR-10/100, DTD-47, Caltech-101, CUB-200, Oxford Flowers-102, Stanford Cars-196, ImageNet-1K, and AG News-4 (Section on experimental datasets).
NAF improves over the ERM baseline by up to 15.15% on CIFAR-10 with a ResNet-50 backbone (Table 1).
NAF enhances seven state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods, yielding gains of up to 20.99% when combined with UDA (Table 3).
Consistent improvements from NAF are also demonstrated on fine-grained classification tasks (Table 2).

CeyNBFDCdB.text: A polynomial-time algorithm computes an optimal (alpha-bar, beta-bar)-k-fair top-k aggregate ranking under the Spearman footrule (L1) distance, solved via the ellipsoid method after showing the ILP constraint matrix is totally unimodular (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.4).

A polynomial-time algorithm achieves a 2-approximation for the fair full ranking problem on d candidates, improving on the previous best 3-approximation, by first computing an optimal fair top-k list and then extending it to a full ranking via minimum-cost perfect matching (Theorem 4.1).

The full ranking algorithm runs in O(nd^2 + d^3) time, where n is the number of input rankings and d is the number of candidates, with the final matching step costing O(d^3) (Section 4, Complexity analysis).

Empirical evaluation shows the proposed algorithms achieve solutions within 1-3% of optimal, substantially outperforming baseline fair aggregation methods across multiple distance metrics (Section on empirical performance).

ZeZi4SerW0.text: On ImageNet-1K with a CLIP-ViT-B/16 backbone, Immuno-VLM reaches 83.4% AUROC and 28.5% FPR95, compared to 66.8% AUROC and 61.3% FPR95 for zero-shot MSP and 70.1% AUROC / 55.4% FPR95 for the Energy Score baseline (Table 1).

The framework operates in three phases—Antigen Profiling via a text-regularized von Mises-Fisher prototype estimate (Theorem 3.4), LLM-based Semantic Antibody Generation with band-pass similarity filtering, and a Vaccination step training a lightweight adapter with a push-pull loss (Section 3).

Theorem 3.5 proves that random negative samples fail to serve as effective antibodies in high dimensions due to exponential decay of their discriminative signal, motivating the use of LLM-generated hard negatives instead (Theorem 3.5).

An ablation shows AUROC on ImageNet-O rising from 66.8% (frozen CLIP) to 68.2% with adapter + Gaussian noise, 72.5% with adapter + random words, 79.8% with unfiltered LLM antibodies, and 83.4% for the full Immuno-VLM pipeline (Table 2).
Immuno-VLM trains in 3.5 GPU-hours versus 48 GPU-hours for the CSI baseline, adds only 0.5M parameters, and incurs less than 0.5% inference latency overhead (+0.04ms/image) (Table 3).

gnzNB7GFFo.text: The method conditions neural operators on boundary conditions via an Extender module (Ψ_θ) that maps boundary coefficients to domain-wide learned pseudo-extensions, which are then consumed by a core operator (Φ_θ) built with an encode-process-decode architecture (Figure 1, Section 3).

Learned pseudo-extensions (LX) are compared against zero extensions (0X) and harmonic extensions (HX) across 18 datasets spanning Poisson, linear elasticity, and hyperelasticity problems on varied geometries with randomized, component-wise mixed boundary conditions (Section 4).
On elasticity/hyperelasticity problems with a RIGNO backbone, learned extensions reduce relative error from 30.6% (zero extension baseline) to 11.0% (Section 4).

The BENO baseline (Wang et al. 2024) fails to resolve the combined effect of varying boundary conditions and domain geometry in the Mixed+ configuration, while the proposed domain-to-domain operators with learned extensions do not (Figure 2).

Pre-training on the Square geometry yields a 10.3% error improvement and up to an 84.6% relative error reduction when transferred to other geometries, demonstrating cross-geometry generalization (Figure 5).
Under 10% Gaussian noise injected into boundary inputs, test error remains below 7% across all 18 datasets, indicating robustness to noisy boundary conditions (Figure 6).

ODTM64azGa.text: Across Llama 3 (1B, 8B-Instruct) and Qwen 2.5 (1.5B, 7B-Instruct) models trained with GRPO on IFEval, MMLU, and Countdown target tasks, RL achieves comparable or higher target-task performance than SFT while causing substantially less degradation on held-out tasks (MATH, WildJailbreak, WildGuardTest) (Section 2.2, Figure 2).

Setting the KL regularization coefficient to zero (unregularized GRPO) yields a similar gain-versus-forgetting tradeoff as regularized GRPO, showing KL regularization is not the primary cause of reduced forgetting (Figure 6).
Classical REINFORCE without advantage estimation achieves forgetting mitigation comparable to GRPO, indicating advantage estimation is not required for RL's retention benefit (Table 1, Section 4.1).

A mixture-of-Gaussians simulation shows forward-KL minimization forgets less in a uni-modal setting (Figure 4) but reverse-KL minimization (as in RL) forgets less in a multi-modal setting (Figure 5), the realistic regime for language models (Section 3).

Iterative-SFT—retraining on on-policy data regenerated once per epoch rather than continuously—suffices to mitigate forgetting nearly as well as full on-policy RL, at reduced computational cost (Section 4.2).

K0ypMhiYe0.text: MAVRL learns a shared latent reward posterior from heterogeneous feedback (demonstrations, preferences, ratings, stops) via a single evidence lower bound combining feedback-specific negative log-likelihoods, a KL term against a standard normal prior, and a TD-consistency constraint (Equation 4, Section 5.1).

Feedback-specific likelihoods use a Bradley-Terry model for preferences, a Boltzmann-rational policy likelihood for demonstrations, an ordered logit model for ratings, and a discrete-time hazard model based on cumulative suboptimality for stop feedback (Section 4).

Across grid-world (grid_cliff, grid_sparse, grid_trap) and continuous-control (CartPole-v1, Acrobot-v1, LunarLander-v3) environments, combining all feedback types achieves the strongest reward-recovery performance in 5 of 6 environments, with EPIC distance of 0.432-0.468 in tabular settings (Tables 1-2, Section 6).

Rewards learned from multiple feedback types degrade more gracefully than single-modality rewards under action noise, structural dynamics changes, and environmental parameter shifts (Figure 3, Section 6.3).
The amortized variational objective requires no manual loss-balancing weights across feedback modalities, since relative influence is instead governed by each modality's noise model (Section 5.2).

ZIFQJumCbK.text: Using a Random Hierarchy Model dataset (depth L=4, vocabulary v=6, synonyms m=4, branching s=2, 20,000 unique training samples), samples with common substrings/rules are memorized earlier than rare ones, shown by a negative linear relationship between data log-likelihood and mean time-to-memorization ⟨t_mem⟩ (Figure 3b, Section 4.1).
Fat-tailed sample distributions—even when composed entirely of unique, non-duplicated samples—exhibit delayed memorization onset compared to less skewed distributions (Figure 4, Section 4.2).

Class-level (higher-abstraction) variation delays memorization more than leaf-level variation, indicating dataset diversity at higher hierarchy levels mitigates memorization risk (Figure 5, Section 4.2).

Before full-sequence memorization, models exhibit a 'slop' phase in which common rules/motifs are overproduced, detected via the partial-memorization estimator λ (Definition 3.2, Figure 6, Section 4.1).

On CelebA (10,000 images), rare images are memorized later than common ones (Figure 7), and a 'slop generating phase' precedes full memorization, prolonged in smaller models (Figure 8, Figure 17, Section 5).

KL divergence between generated and training-data distributions increases once memorization begins, motivating early stopping to avoid distribution collapse even when train/test loss curves have not yet diverged (Section 4.3).

XsfjvLhKAP.text: In location-conditioned CLEVR experiments, labeling all object locations during training lets the diffusion model generalize to generating images with up to 9 objects despite training only on 1-3 objects (Section 2, Figure 1, Experiment 1).

When only a single object location is labeled during training, length generalization largely fails, but enforcing a local architecture restores generalization up to 6 objects when trained on single-object examples (Section 2 and Section 4, Figure 1 Experiment 3 and Figure 4).

Lemma 1 proves that a Conditional Projective Composition (CPC) structure in the data distribution is exactly equivalent to the diffusion model's score function being a Local Conditional Score (LCS), i.e. having sparse dependence on pixels and conditioners (Section 3, Lemma 1).

Gradient heatmap analysis shows models that successfully length-generalize exhibit strong conditional-locality at high noise levels, while models that fail to generalize lack this locality property (Section 3, Figure 2).

Color-conditioned CLEVR models trained on 1-5 objects generalize to images with up to 7 colored objects, with cosine-similarity analysis of feature representations providing evidence of feature-space disentanglement (Section 3.2, Figure 5).

Preliminary analysis of SDXL shows partial pixel-locality and conditional dependence on relevant words in cross-attention, plus higher intra-group cosine similarity among related concepts in U-net mid-block activations (Section 4, Figures 6 and 7).

uBvlUE2wrP.text: HALyPO defines a rationality gap metric V(theta) = 1/2||u_ind(theta) - u_team(theta)||^2_2 quantifying the disagreement between decentralized best-response gradient fields and the centralized cooperative gradient field in heterogeneous-agent MARL for human-robot collaboration (Section on rationality gap metric).

Theorem 5.2 proves that enforcing a per-step Lyapunov decrease condition via optimal quadratic projection yields monotonic descent of the rationality gap at an exponential convergence rate (Theorem 5.2).
Theorem 5.3 shows that under Robbins-Monro step-size conditions, HALyPO's updates converge asymptotically to points where the decentralized and centralized policy gradients align (Theorem 5.3).

HALyPO reduces the final rationality gap from 4.89 (baseline) to 0.09 and increases gradient alignment to 0.91 cosine similarity while lowering the gradient conflict rate to 4.2% (Section on experimental performance).
HALyPO improves object-state-preservation (OSP) success rate from 81.6% for the baseline to 87.2% in human-robot collaboration tasks (Section on experimental performance).

In real-world humanoid robot trials, HALyPO maintains resilience to unscripted human partner behavior, including 20-second obstructions, with minimal object drift of 1.22 cm/s (Section on real-world trials).

QEEwlgt8PI.text: Theorem 4.4 derives an inverse-stiffness rule for optimal latent error allocation, (Sigma*)^{-1} = H_R(z) + alpha*W_eff(x) + gamma*G_eff(x), showing compression noise precision is additive across rate curvature, physics sensitivity, and reconstruction fidelity terms (Theorem 4.4, Definition 4.2).

Theorem 5.2 proves a no-free-lunch result: when the physics-sensitivity metric and fidelity metric are not rate-aligned (do not share an eigenbasis, per Definition 5.1), improving physical observable preservation at fixed bitrate strictly worsens reconstruction MSE (Theorem 5.2, Definition 5.1).

The paper defines a Physical Alignment Score Align_k(x) = (1/k)||U_{W,k}(x)^T U_{G,k}(x)||_F^2 measuring eigenspace overlap between physics-sensitivity and fidelity metrics, where values near 1 indicate low physics-MSE tension (Definition 5.3).
Local quadratic approximations of the physics-fidelity tradeoff remain predictive of empirical behavior at moderate noise levels, validated via R^2 in Figure 8 (Figure 8).

The alignment score is empirically validated across three domains, turbulent fluid dynamics (vorticity preservation), cosmological simulations (baryon fraction and thermodynamic states), and electron microscopy, showing the alignment score increases systematically with the physics-weighting parameter beta (Section on experimental validation).

The theoretical framework connects the optimal error allocation to a linear-Gaussian filtering interpretation, matching the posterior covariance of a Bayesian estimator jointly observing physics and fidelity constraints (Appendix A.6).

udqe7UZUZ6.text: A-MemGuard reduces the direct memory-poisoning attack success rate on EHRAgent from 100% to 2.13% at the retrieval stage (Section on key results, direct poisoning).
A-MemGuard reduces indirect prompt-injection attack success rates by over 60% across both tested LLM backbones, GPT-4o-mini and LLaMA-3.1-8B (Section on key results, indirect injection attacks).
In multi-agent system settings, A-MemGuard achieves a 0.950 task success rate compared to 0.800 for the baseline without defense (Section on key results, multi-agent systems).

A-MemGuard's consensus-based validation mechanism generates parallel reasoning paths from multiple retrieved memories and flags deviations from group consensus as anomalies, while its dual-memory structure stores detected failures as corrective lessons referenced before future actions (Section on technical approach).

Knowledge graph analysis of reasoning paths reveals less than 1% structural overlap between benign and malicious reasoning paths, supporting the separability assumption behind consensus-based detection (Section on evidence of separability).

A-MemGuard maintains the highest accuracy on benign tasks compared to all other tested defense baselines, indicating minimal utility trade-off from its dual-memory and consensus mechanisms (Section on utility preservation).

w0y3obJwmh.text: Fine-tuning a chess-playing LLM to directly predict only the single best move (Best Move data) enables effective downstream RL but produces an unfaithful reasoner, whose final chosen move often becomes disconnected from its own reasoning trace after RL (Section addressing Q2, Core Findings).

Fine-tuning on multi-move trajectories (Best Line data) yields RL performance comparable to Best Move training while retaining faithful reasoning traces and more stable RL training dynamics (Section addressing Q1/Q2, Core Findings).

After RL, the Best Move model achieves 90% legal moves and an average move rank of 0.71, while the Best Line model achieves 85% legal moves and an average move rank of 0.63, with Best Line showing substantially higher reasoning faithfulness (Table comparing Best Move vs Best Line metrics).

RL substantially shifts the move-quality distribution toward best moves and away from low-quality moves, and reduces hallucination rates as a side effect of reward maximization, consistent across experimental conditions (Section on core findings, move quality and hallucination).

Referenced move accuracy and reasoning quality measured after SFT are identified as statistically significant predictors of downstream RL performance (Section addressing Q3, predictive SFT indicators).

The resulting 7B-parameter chess-playing model surpasses leading open-source reasoning models at chess, with code, model weights, and training data released publicly (Section on practical achievement).

l8PbMSZs2G.text: Self-RedTeam trains an attacker and a defender policy via online self-play, where the attacker generates adversarial prompts and the defender learns to resist them within a shared RL loop (Section 3, Figure 2).

Self-RedTeam improves the safety of RLHF-trained language models by up to 95% relative reduction in attack success rate when evaluated across 14 safety benchmarks, compared to static red-teaming baselines (Section 4.2, Table 4).

Self-RedTeam's co-evolving attacker uncovers more diverse jailbreak prompts than static or fixed-attacker baselines, achieving a 17.80% improvement in SBERT embedding similarity diversity metrics (Section 4.2, Table 4).

Comparative results against baseline defense methods, including DPO/KTO-style static safety training, are presented with win-rate and safety-score comparisons in the results figures (Section 5, Figure 6).

qIOcJSCGn2.text: SVL (Survival Value Learning) reframes goal-conditioned RL by modeling the time-to-goal as a survival probability distribution rather than learning a value function through TD bootstrapping (Section 4.1).

Proposition 4.1 gives a closed-form identity expressing the goal-conditioned value function as a discounted sum of survival probabilities, V^π(s,g) = -Σ_t γ^t S^π(t|s,g) (Section 4.1, Proposition 4.1).
Lemma 4.2 establishes maximum-likelihood convergence guarantees for the survival-based value estimator, with asymptotic normality scaling as O(n^{-1/2}) (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.2).
On the humanoidmaze-giant-navigate offline GCRL benchmark, hierarchical SVL (HSVL) achieves 81% success versus 12% for the hierarchical TD baseline HIQL, a 69 percentage point improvement (Table 1).
On visual-antmaze-giant-navigate, HSVL reaches 61% success compared to 6% for HIQL, and on antmaze-giant-navigate, HSVL reaches 74% versus 65% for HIQL (Table 1).
With hierarchical extraction removed, flat SVL still outperforms the contrastive RL (CRL) baseline on humanoidmaze-giant, scoring 45% versus 7% for re-evaluated CRL (Table 2).

Hbt2ryJgz2.text: A k-sparse autoencoder with 4,096 latent features and k=32 active features per token is trained on activations from an LLM-based TTS backbone to disentangle emotional variation into sparse latent directions (Section 3.1).

An emotion selectivity score (Δ_i^(e)), computed from sentence-level activation-rate differences between target-emotion and neutral conditions, identifies a small subset of emotion-selective SAE features rather than emotion being encoded in a single direction (Section 3.2.1, Figure 3).

Feature-level steering induces target emotions with high fidelity while preserving intelligibility: anger induction reaches Emo-SIM of 0.912 with WER of 0.3, happiness induction reaches Emo-SIM of 0.885 with WER of 2.2, and sadness induction reaches Emo-SIM of 0.880 with WER of 1.5 (Table 1).
