Steering along emotion-selective SAE features produces a significant mean F0 increase of +23.11 Hz (p=1.07×10⁻⁴) and RMS energy increase of +0.00435 (p=0.00769), with no significant change in duration (p=0.687) (Section 4.2.2).
A blind listening study with 20 raters shows SAE-Emotion steering achieves an EMOS of 3.22 and NMOS of 3.49, outperforming both global steering and random-SAE-direction baselines (Table 2).

sLVaNS2DS3.text: Hodge Spectral Duality (HSD) splits neural operator learning into a base branch operating in the truncated Hodge Laplacian eigenspace (capturing topology-constrained global structure and harmonic modes) and a fiber branch using FFT-based convolution for geometry-driven local dynamics, enforcing exact preservation of cohomological invariants via the Hodge-de Rham decomposition C^k = im(d_{k-1}) ⊕ im(δ_{k+1}) ⊕ ker(L_k) (Section on architecture; Table 1).

On the external aerodynamics benchmark, HSD achieves MSE of 1.08×10⁻², beating FNO-3D (1.80×10⁻²) and DeepONet (2.54×10⁻²), and an enstrophy fidelity of 0.7658 versus FNO-3D's 0.6638, using roughly 207k-310k parameters (Table 1).
On the magnetostatics benchmark, HSD attains an MSE of 1.84×10⁻⁴, a 36% improvement over DeepONet, with enstrophy fidelity of 0.9444 and spectral fidelity of 0.8176 (Table 1).
On toroidal transport, HSD reaches MSE of 3.56×10⁻⁴ (36% better than FNO-3D), an energy fidelity of 0.6968 versus FNO-3D's 0.6365, and a topological β₀ score of 0.7829 versus 0.6721 (Table 1).

Under mesh refinement from 3,000 to 7,000 nodes, HSD's error varies by no more than 30%, whereas baseline models show roughly 10× error amplification, demonstrating resolution independence (Section on resolution robustness).
HSD runs 56× faster than MeshGraphNets on the aerodynamics task and uses only about 5% of MeshGraphNets' runtime on the magnetostatics task (Section on computational efficiency).

ivB3PM7XfD.text: ETA, the best-performing TTA method under conventional offline evaluation, loses to competitors in 99 of 240 evaluations (41.2%) and yields 19.3% utility on average to the winning method when evaluated under Tempora's time-contingent framework (Section 1).
Under strict temporal pressure (ρ=100% arrival rate, T=50ms deadline), ETA's win rate collapses to 0-7%, compared to 93-100% under relaxed constraints (Section 4.2).

Rankings of TTA methods under continuous-utility evaluation correlate poorly with offline rankings, with Spearman's rs ranging from -0.74 for brightness corruption to 0.21 for Gaussian noise corruption, showing that the best method depends on corruption type (Section 1).
The evaluation spans 7 TTA methods on ImageNet-C with ResNet-50 across 240 temporal evaluations (16 scenarios × 15 corruption types), with standard inference latency of about 39.9ms (Section 4).

Under discrete/deadline-constrained utility at ρ=100% arrival rate, AdaBN achieves 30.8% utility versus ETA's 18.7% (Table 3), and under continuous utility at T=50ms, ETA's 48.4% accuracy is discounted by 85% latency penalty to yield only 7.2% utility (Table 4).

Gradient-based TTA methods suffer availability collapse, serving only 20.6-41.2% of batches under tight deadlines, with extrinsic backpropagation overhead of 56-154ms causing 2.4-4.9× slowdowns versus <1.03× for gradient-free methods (Section 4.3, Table 2).

0COq6zy5kN.text: The hierarchical MixeDiT-MaskeDiT pipeline recovers known aeronautical trends such as battery mass increasing with aircraft mass and wider wingspans arising from higher lift requirements, via posterior predictive case studies (Section 5, Figures 5-11).

MixeDiT (Mixed Diffusion Transformer) generates eVTOL topology samples whose marginal distribution matches the test set with a KL-divergence of 0.0505, versus 1.4607 for a uniform baseline (Figure 3).

MaskeDiT achieves lower discrepancy against test data than Neural Likelihood Estimation (NLE), with an MMD of 0.004±0.001, across a design space of 144 topologies with up to 136 continuous parameters (Table 1).
Conditioning MixeDiT on high aircraft mass (+2σ) increases the proportion of two-winged (biplane) designs to 91.6%, compared to 0.4% under low-mass (-2σ) conditioning (Figure 4).

The hierarchical diffusion pipeline achieves at least a 10x wall-clock speedup over direct SUAVE physics-based simulation when generating batches of aircraft designs, filtering 30,276 valid eVTOL designs from 300,000 candidates (Section 4, Data Generation).

UcbCkTkUjD.text: Across four model sizes from 25M to 320M parameters trained via behavioral cloning on 9 synthetic GUI annotation tasks, larger models are more data-efficient, with a 10x parameter increase yielding roughly 3x better sample efficiency in training loss versus tokens seen (Section 4.2, Figure 3a).

At matched compute (FLOPs) rather than matched tokens, the 25M-parameter model trained longer outperforms the 320M-parameter model, indicating the experiments did not reach a compute-efficient scaling regime for larger models (Section 4.2, Figure 22).

Fine-tuning a multi-task pretrained model on only 500 sequences from a novel task reaches 76.6% accuracy, whereas training the same architecture from scratch on 7,800 sequences (over 15x more data) achieves 0% accuracy (Section 4.3, Figure 4b).

A linear probe for detecting annotation mistakes, trained across 8 tasks and evaluated on a held-out task, achieves a mean 0.71 ROC AUC, and 0.87 ROC AUC when pooled across all 9 tasks (Section 4.4, Figure 5).

Autoregressive evaluation of the connectomics tracing task reaches 95.1% skeleton accuracy on H01 human cortex data and 89.4% on C. elegans data, both with 100% task completion rate (Section 4.5, Figure 6).

XN4pWKtA5h.text: Theorem 1 (Section 3) derives that under KL-regularized reward optimization at inverse temperature β, the shift in any behavior metric g equals Z_x^{-1}(β)·Cov_{y~π_base}(g(x,y), e^{βr(x,y)}), implying sycophancy amplifies only when agreement-seeking responses receive higher reward than corrective ones on average.

Theorem 4 (Section 4) proves that under well-specified reward models, the mean behavioral shift toward agreement Δ^mean(x) is positive if and only if the mixed-pair bias B_F(x)—the average log-odds by which annotators favor agreement over correction on comparative judgments—is positive.

Figure 1 reports that 30-40% of prompts exhibit a positive reward gap (agreeing responses scoring higher than corrections) across multiple preference datasets and reward models, and that Best-of-N sampling with stronger selection pressure increases sycophancy specifically on these positive-tilt prompts.

Theorem 6 (Section 5) characterizes a unique KL-minimal corrected reward r_corr(x,y) = r(x,y) − λ(x)·A(x,y), with λ*(x) = max{0, (1/β)log(m_β^1(x)/m_β^0(x))}, that provably neutralizes the amplification mechanism identified in Theorem 1.

D70OyQr3O3.text: On the Chaotic Kolmogorov Flow benchmark at a 64-step rollout, Multi-Scale Wavelet Transformers (MSWT) reduce Relative L2 error by over 60% compared to the second-best baseline, FNO (Table 1).
On the Chaotic Kolmogorov Flow benchmark, MSWT improves enstrophy mean log ratio by 76.5% and enstrophy mean absolute error by 80.6% relative to the best baseline (Table 1, Table 5).

On the Shallow Water Equation benchmark at an 81-step rollout, MSWT reduces error by approximately 30% relative to the second-best model while avoiding boundary artifacts observed in competing methods (Table 2, Figure 3).

On 10-year autoregressive rollouts of ERA5 climate reanalysis, MSWT achieves lower climatological RMSE across variables (temperature, humidity, wind components, surface pressure, precipitation) and reduced surface-pressure bias near the poles compared to the LUCIE baseline (Table 3, Figure 4).

MSWT's wavelet attention operator uses a 2D Haar discrete wavelet transform to decompose features into LL/LH/HL/HH subbands for down/up-sampling, preserving high-frequency content that standard pooling discards, and these gains are obtained using only the standard relative l2 loss without auxiliary spectral regularization terms (Section on Wavelet Attention Operator).

pLIJx2cFib.text: Adding Turbo Connection to Llama 3.2 1B improves accuracy from 92.87% to 100.0% on Parity (+7.13 points), from 38.16% to 42.66% on Multi-step Arithmetic (+4.5 points), and from 7.20% to 8.32% on GSM8K without chain-of-thought (+1.12 points) (Table 1).

A Qwen-3-1.7B model fine-tuned with Turbo Connection reaches 100.0% accuracy on the Parity task, compared to 53.78% for the same model without the architectural modification, and improves Multi-step Arithmetic accuracy from 36.10% to 45.81% (Table 1).
Turbo Connection's dense multi-layer backward feedback outperforms a sparse single soft-token feedback baseline, reaching 100% versus 96.51% accuracy on the Parity task (Table 3).

With a group size of 4 on the Parity task, Turbo Connection reaches 38.81 effective recursion steps at only a 4.87x training latency overhead, less than proportional to the increase in effective depth due to preserved batch-level parallelism (Table 2).

cOkJvV16Fd.text: Theorem 1 proves that conditioning on a CVAE-reconstructed substitute confounder Z_s (under five stated assumptions) nonparametrically identifies both direct effects τ_dir and spillover effects τ_spill in spatial causal settings with interference (Section 5).

Algorithm 1's two-stage approach uses a CVAE with a spatial Gaussian-Markov prior to reconstruct the substitute confounder in Stage 1, then a flexible outcome model (U-Net or spatial+) to estimate treatment effects in Stage 2 (Section 4).

On the extended SpaCE PM2.5-to-mortality benchmark with local confounding (population density masked, r_d=1), cvae-spatial+ achieves 0.05±0.02 direct-effect bias and 0.31±0.08 spillover-effect bias, versus 0.10 (spatial), 0.20 (s2sls), and 0.41 (gcnn) baselines (Table 1).

On the spatial-confounding PM2.5-to-mortality setting (population density masked, r_d=1), cvae-unet reduces spillover-effect bias to 0.10±0.03 compared to 0.17±0.04 for the plain U-Net baseline (Table 2).

Assumption 4 (Latent Field Sufficiency) is proposed as a weaker-than-full-ignorability condition tailored to spatial settings, requiring only that confounders affecting isolated regions be observed (Section 5).

9Mms28wD82.text: Theorem 1.2 establishes a query-time bound of Õ(d + εΔ_σ² + 1/ε³) for Gaussian kernel density/mean estimation with additive error ε, improving over Random Fourier Features' O(d/ε²), FJLT+RFF's Õ(d+1/ε⁴), and Fastfood's Õ(d+Δ_σ²/ε²) in the regime ε^{-0.5} ≲ Δ_σ ≲ min{√d·ε^{-1.5}, ε^{-2.5}} (Theorem 1.2, Table 1).

Theorem 1.3 gives a fast spherical embedding running in Õ(m) time with target dimension m = Õ(d + Λ² + ε⁻²) that preserves small pairwise distances while preventing distance collapse at larger scales (Theorem 1.3).
Theorem 1.4 extends the query-time bound to inverse multi-quadratic kernels, achieving Õ(d + ε(βΔ_σ)² + 1/ε³) with only polylogarithmic dependence on the kernel parameter β (Theorem 1.4).
Theorem 1.5 shows the same Õ(d + εΔ_σ² + 1/ε³) query-time bound holds for differentially private KDE provided the dataset size satisfies |X| ≥ Õ(1/(ε²ε_DP)) (Theorem 1.5).

Section 3.3 introduces a Wiener chaos decomposition analysis of Fastfood transforms to control fourth-order terms needed to prove the distance-contraction guarantees underlying the spherical embedding (Section 3.3).

jYxRNCfRaD.text: Proposition 3.5 proves that indirect-reciprocity equilibria sustaining cooperation exist in infinite-horizon games with public gossip when the discount factor satisfies γ ≥ c/b, contrasting with mutual defection under finite horizons (Proposition 3.2) or private monitoring (Proposition 3.3) (Section 3).

In the non-gossiping infinite-horizon baseline, reasoning models defect 100% of the time (0% cooperation) while chat models cooperate at variable, often suboptimal rates (e.g., GPT-4o Mini 36%, Gemini 60.22%) (Table 1).

With the ALIGN gossip protocol enabled, DeepSeek-V3.1 Reasoner reaches 100% cooperation with perfect coordination, while chat models reach only 60-99% cooperation, despite reasoning models scoring 0% cooperation without gossip (Table 2).

When greedy defector agents are introduced, ALIGN reasoning agents issue negative gossip about them 92.2% of the time and cut cooperation extended to defectors from about 95% to about 10%, while maintaining high cooperation among ALIGN-compliant peers (Figures 8-9).

An ablation removing the hierarchical five-tone gossip protocol in favor of binary signals sharply reduces cooperation (Figure 10), and removing agents' reflection step causes weaker models' cooperation to collapse while strong reasoning models retain about 98% cooperation (Table 20).

ANVg7NnupP.text: Result 3 (best-of-k limit) shows that when the reward weight vector equals the teacher's (w_R = w_T) and temperature T→0, the generalization error decays as δ(x) = (π/k²)·s²(x)·exp(ΔT(x)²/s²(x)), i.e. a Θ(1/k²) power-law rate governed by extreme value theory (Result 3).

Result 2's high-temperature expansion δ(x) = ΔT(x)² + s²(x) + Σ C_l(x)/t(x)^l + O(t(x)^-4) shows generalization error decreases monotonically with more inference-time samples k when the reward is close to the teacher (Result 2).

Remark 3 identifies a threshold t < 3C₂(x)/C₁(x) under substantial reward misspecification below which the generalization error becomes non-monotonic in k, with an optimal finite k* ≈ 2t*/(t*-t) beyond which further sampling increases error (Remark 3).
Remark 4 derives an optimal reward-sampling temperature t(x) = 2(1-2/k)·C₂(x)/C₁(x) for fixed k>2 that balances selection sharpness against reward misalignment (Remark 4).

Remark 6 shows inference-time scaling outperforms training-data scaling when reward-teacher alignment is strong, quantified by ∂log(δ)/∂log(k) = -2 versus a much smaller magnitude for ∂log(δ)/∂log(n) (Remark 6).

kb5wjkqu8q.text: Spectron stabilizes native low-rank training of factorized weights W=AB^T by rescaling factor updates with ρ = η/(‖A‖₂+‖B‖₂+1), guaranteeing the composite update satisfies ‖ΔW‖₂ ≤ η via power iteration for spectral norm estimation and Newton-Schulz orthogonalization (Section on Spectron method).
Spectron's spectral renormalization and gradient orthogonalization add under 1% computational overhead, versus about 25% overhead for competing stabilization methods (Section on overhead comparison).

On a 454M-parameter factorized Transformer-L, Spectron achieves 12.11 perplexity versus 13.70 for a self-guided low-rank baseline and 14.57 for the dense baseline, along with 40.11% HellaSwag accuracy versus 34.85% for the self-guided baseline (Table 1).

A compute-equivalent 454M-parameter low-rank model trained with Spectron matches the validation loss of a 780M-parameter dense model at equal FLOPs, a 42% parameter reduction at matched performance (Figure 5).

IsoFLOP scaling-law analysis over 47M-1.5B parameters yields compute-optimal exponents N_opt ∝ C^0.479 and D_opt ∝ C^0.521 for natively low-rank transformers, close to Chinchilla's C^0.49/C^0.51, while enabling inference efficiency gains up to 50% at training budgets around 10^26 FLOPs (IsoFLOP scaling analysis).

0yRTf7OtI6.text: The dead-zone modified safety loss (Eq. 8) replaces the standard Bradley-Terry safety loss (Eq. 7) by requiring predicted cost to exceed a margin δ rather than 0, and Theorem 3.2 proves this yields strictly higher cost estimates C^_DZ(τ) > C^(τ) at every gradient step t > 0 (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).

Corollary 3.3 shows the cost distribution learned via the dead-zone loss has a strictly heavier right tail than the standard BT loss, with higher tail probability P(C^_DZ ≥ z) > P(C^ ≥ z) for large z (Section 3, Corollary 3.3).

On Safety Gymnasium's HalfCheetah task, PbCRL attains return 2367±138 and cost 4.66±1.03, close to the PPO-Lag oracle (2619±124 return, 4.82±0.91 cost), while PPO-BT under-constrains safety with cost 5.58±2.14 (Table with Safety Gymnasium results, Section 5).

PbCRL achieves lower Wasserstein-2 distance to the ground-truth cost distribution than RLSF and PPO-BT on Goal (16.8 vs 68.1 vs 42.7), Push (20.3 vs 82.4 vs 36.5), and Button (44.3 vs 165.5 vs 78.8) tasks (Table 2).

On Llama-3.2-1B alignment, PbCRL achieves 80.7% helpfulness win rate and 82.1% harmlessness win rate, outperforming the Safe RLHF baseline at 79.4% and 76.5% respectively (Section 5, Language Model Alignment experiments).

Theorem 5.2 proves that under continuous differentiability and timescale separation assumptions, PbCRL converges almost surely to a locally optimal policy for the safe RL problem (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).

Oj7ZwBhiyE.text: The paper proves weak convergence of the empirical GP, GP(m_S, k_S) ⇀ GP(m, k) as S→∞ almost surely, using Mourier's strong law of large numbers on function spaces and Dudley's entropy integral condition for tightness (Section on convergence theory).
The limiting empirical GP is shown to be the Gaussian process minimizing KL-divergence to the true data-generating process, i.e., arg min_G D_KL(P ∥ G) (Section on KL-divergence optimality).

On the GIFT-Eval time series forecasting benchmark (97 datasets, 144,000 series across 7 domains), the Empirical GP achieves the highest overall average rank among statistical/classical methods and outperforms 4 of 8 deep learning baselines, behind top performers TFT (rank 3.87) and iTransformer (rank 3.77).

On LCBench learning curve extrapolation (35 datasets, 1,000 test curves), the Empirical GP achieves the lowest RMSE across observed fractions from 10% to 90% and outperforms all baselines in CRPS-based uncertainty calibration, especially with only a small fraction of the curve observed.

On real climate data, the Empirical GP recovers a kernel structure achieving 21.52% lower RMSE and 14.11% higher likelihood than a handcrafted kernel combining trend, seasonality, and noise components.
Total experimental compute for all reported experiments is less than 3,000 CPU hours, with SVD-based acceleration reducing per-iteration inference cost from O(S) to O(M) in the EM algorithm.

WsZwXIx5r8.text: The inversion deviation scale δ(z_t, t, Δt) = ||c_α(t,Δt)·(ε_θ(z_t,t,p) − ε_θ(z_{t−1},t−1,p))|| exhibits a parabolic trend across timestep t, with larger errors concentrated at both small and large timesteps and minimal error in the middle range (Section on error formulation/analysis).
The scaling coefficient c_α(t,Δt) = √α_t · Δψ(α_{t−1}, Δt−1) depends only on the noise and timestep schedule and not on model behavior, motivating a model-agnostic timestep rescheduling method.

The global rescaling stage uses power transformation t_k = t_1 + (t_K − t_1)·((k−1)/(K−1))^γ with optimal hyperparameter γ = 1.05, while the local dynamic programming stage refines allocation within a window width d = 8 using recurrence E[k,t] = min{E[k−1,h] + c_α(t,t−h)}.
On MSCOCO image reconstruction with SD v1.5, the proposed scheduler improves ReNoise by +1.43% PSNR and −5.39% LPIPS, and improves DDIM by +0.70% PSNR and −3.16% LPIPS.

On PIE-Bench image editing with SDXL Turbo, the method reduces structure distance by up to 35.67% for GNRI and improves background preservation by 5-30% across methods, while adding only 9.32 seconds of schedule computation overhead.

Q0LzVAYE1N.text: CLAA reduces Time-to-First-Token by up to 39% compared to the Full KV Cache baseline while adding less than 2% overhead to total TTFT for its scoring computation.

CLAA computes layer-wise importance scores via a max-aggregation over a sliding window of n=4 consecutive layers (S_i^CLAA = max_{l'∈ℒ} S_i(l')), while retaining full KV cache for the first m=4 layers before compression begins.
On the LongBench benchmark at a 10% token keep rate on Llama-3.1-8B, CLAA achieves 47.13% accuracy versus an oracle ceiling of 47.83%, outperforming FastKV (46.81%) and GemFilter (37.59%) (Table 1).
At 20% and 40% keep rates on LongBench, CLAA achieves 48.12% and 48.72% accuracy respectively, versus FastKV's 47.33% and 47.68% and GemFilter's 42.29% and 45.11% (Table 1).
On the RULER benchmark at 64K context length and 40% keep rate, CLAA achieves 89.85% on retrieval, 87.72% on multi-hop reasoning, and 82.01% average accuracy.

An answer-informed oracle constructed from attention flowing from the generated answer back to the prompt reveals that existing token-importance heuristics have high variance across layers, with rankings degrading sharply at specific layers—a failure mode invisible to end-to-end benchmark scores (Figure showing oracle diagnostic analysis).

5F0ddHN3TP.text: On the MINE benchmark (100 articles, 15 factual statements each), INSES improves mean accuracy by 5% on KGGEN-constructed graphs, 10% on GraphRAG-constructed graphs, and 27% on OpenIE-constructed graphs, relative to baseline methods (Section on MINE benchmark results).

The appendix quantifies structural heterogeneity across KG construction methods: GraphRAG graphs average 14 nodes/13 edges (degree 1.86), KGGEN graphs average 102 nodes/72 edges (degree 1.41), and OpenIE graphs average 189 nodes/265 edges (degree 2.80), a 13.5x difference in nodes and 20x difference in edges between GraphRAG and OpenIE (Appendix, Table on structural heterogeneity).

INSES combines LLM-guided navigation (pruning noise and steering exploration toward query-relevant evidence) with similarity-based expansion that creates 'virtual edges' to semantically proximate nodes, subject to immediate LLM verification to prevent semantic drift (Section on INSES framework).
Ablation results show similarity-based expansion is the dominant contributor to performance, yielding +0.12 EM on MuSiQue, +0.06 EM on 2Wiki, and +0.05 EM on HotpotQA (Ablation study section).

The lightweight query router delegates approximately 86% of HotpotQA queries to Naive RAG rather than graph-based reasoning, while routing MuSiQue and 2Wiki queries near-evenly between both strategies (Section on router efficiency).

Table 1 illustrates 'semantic fragmentation' using a butterfly lifecycle example, where different KG extraction methods generate similar but disconnected entities (e.g., 'butterfly', 'adult butterflies', 'female butterflies') that INSES's virtual-edge mechanism is designed to reconnect (Table 1).

lXX3Bi2Adq.text: The Generative Latent Prior (GLP) diffusion model is trained on one billion residual stream activations from FineWeb across four model sizes (0.5B, 0.9B, 1.7B, 3.3B parameters) (Section 2).
Diffusion loss follows a smooth power law in compute with fitted irreducible error E=0.52, coefficient A=435.1, and exponent alpha=0.169 (Section 3).
Frechet Distance between generated and real Llama-1B activations decreases from 0.68 at the 0.5B model size to 0.53 at the 3.3B model size (Table 1).
On Llama-8B-Base, GLP achieves a Delta LM Loss of 0.0513 versus 0.1976 for a sparse autoencoder (SAE) baseline (Section 4).
GLP outperforms raw MLP neurons and SAEs on 1-D probing AUC across 113 binary tasks, reaching 0.84 (Llama-1B) and 0.87 (Llama-8B) versus 0.79/0.82 for MLP neurons and 0.70/0.76 for SAEs (Table 4).

On-manifold steering via GLP post-processing expands the concept-fluency Pareto frontier for SAE feature steering and improves sentiment control and persona elicitation on Llama-8B-Instruct (Section 4, Figures 5 and 6).

ofwEMwiaLU.text: Bounding the actor's log-probability (alpha log pi_theta) terms in the critic's loss function substantially changes MDAC's learning dynamics, as shown by comparing bounded versus unbounded variants (Section 4.1, Figure 1).

With the bounding functions f(x)=g(x)=clip(x/10,-1,1), MDAC overtakes both SAC and TD3 on MuJoCo continuous control tasks trained for 3M environment steps (1M for Hopper-v4) averaged over 10 seeds (Section 5.2, Figure 9).
Slower-saturating bounding functions such as tanh(x/10) and clip(x/10,-1,1) outperform faster-saturating variants like sign(x) across the tested bounding-function ablation (Section 5, Figure 6).
MDAC is evaluated on the DeepMind Control Suite including dog-domain tasks (stand, walk, trot, run, fetch) over 5M environment steps and 30 independent runs per algorithm (Section 5.3, Figure 10).
Theorem 1 establishes that the MDAC policy value satisfies V_tau* <= V-tilde <= V_alpha*, characterizing the effect of bounded regularization on convergence (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 provides a suboptimality bound of the form ||V_tau* - V_tau^(pi_{K+1})||_infinity <= (2*gamma)/(1-gamma) times accumulated error terms over K mirror-descent iterations (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).

CoAHlJuMdh.text: On the Lorenz63 chaotic system (336-in-336-out, dt=0.01), the proposed method achieves MSE 11.4 versus 27.3 for TimeMixer and 65.4 for DLinear (Table 4).

On the Rossler system, the proposed method attains MSE 0.02, roughly 100x lower than TimeMixer's MSE of 2.52 and well below DLinear's MSE of 4.58, consistent with the paper's claim of outperforming baselines by up to 790x on nonstationary settings (Section 3, Tables 4-10).
The method maintains effective forecasts for approximately 274 of 336 steps on Lorenz63, corresponding to nearly 2.5 Lyapunov times (Section 3, Figure 2).

An ablation removing the Augmented Normalizing Flow (ANF) structure increases MSE by 51% (from 24.50 to 37.06), and removing the data-dependent rotations (EigenACL/Householder reflections) increases MSE by 35%, confirming both components are necessary (Table 2).

The Koopman-inspired block-diagonal normal-matrix operator decomposes dynamics into growth/decay via eigenvalue real parts and oscillation via imaginary parts, replacing costly eigen-decomposition to reduce complexity from cubic to linear time (Section 2).

FXKhOhbgEz.text: The paper proves Omega(n) lower bounds on the number of chain-of-thought reasoning tokens required for binary majority, triplet matching, and graph reachability tasks with input size n, within the bounded attention prefix oracle (BAPO) framework (Section 3).
Matching or near-matching upper bounds are given via explicit constructions showing these Omega(n) lower bounds are close to tight for the three BAPO-hard tasks (Section 4).
Experiments with frontier reasoning models show approximately linear scaling of reasoning token count with input size on binary majority, triplet matching, and graph reachability (Section 5).
Frontier reasoning models fail on these tasks when constrained to smaller reasoning token budgets than the theoretically required Omega(n), consistent with the paper's lower bounds (Section 5).

uVZUAKrA1t.text: With GPT-4 Turbo as annotator, S-SPPO achieves a 52.19% raw win rate and 47.46% length-controlled (LC) win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 using Llama-3-8B (Section 4.2).
Under the default judge used for iteration selection, S-SPPO reaches a final LC win rate of 40.95%, surpassing SPPO's 38.77% (Section 4.2).

Dual-space semantic calibration combines supervision calibration, which anneals win-rate targets toward 0.5 based on embedding-based semantic similarity, with representation calibration, which applies latent repulsion to prevent manifold collapse (Section 3).

An ablation shows the full S-SPPO framework achieves 47.46% LC win rate versus 44.79% for the uncalibrated SPPO baseline at iteration 3 on Llama-3-8B, indicating both calibration components contribute (Table 5).

The semantic calibration mechanism avoids SPPO's policy degeneration problem, which arises when the preference oracle assigns overly confident wins to semantically indistinguishable responses, without requiring additional human-annotated preference data (Section 2.2, Section 3).

IjLOXSP41n.text: Intrinsic and prompted value expression mechanisms recruit partially overlapping model components, with shared circuit activation patterns identified via component-overlap analysis (Section 3.3, Table 6).
Intrinsic value expression promotes greater lexical diversity in generated responses than prompted value expression, as measured by diversity metrics across conditions (Section 3, Table 5, Figure 4).
Prompted value mechanisms yield stronger instruction-following compliance than intrinsic mechanisms, based on compliance-rate comparisons across value directions (Section 4, Figure 3).

Intrinsic expression shows higher response diversity while prompted expression shows greater value steerability, quantified via output distribution variance and cross-condition steering effectiveness (Section 4, Figure 6, Table 5).

Prompted value steering generalizes with greater effectiveness across languages than intrinsic value expression, evaluated using language-specific steering coefficients (Section 5, Figure 2, Appendix D).

XdyDNR5gtb.text: Shared-Score Quaternion Self-Attention reduces real-valued multiplications in score computation from 16 to 4 per quaternion pair, a 75% reduction, and reduces softmax operations from four to one per attention head (Section 3.3, Table 1).

On the DNS-Challenge 3 benchmark, the shared-score QTransformer reduces GPU real-time factor by 44.3% (1.79x speedup) and CPU real-time factor by 58.1% (2.39x speedup) relative to the standard quaternion attention baseline (Section 4.5, Table 3).

On VoiceBank+DEMAND, the shared-score QConformer achieves PESQ of 3.18 versus 3.11 for the full quaternion-attention baseline, retaining about 98% of the real-valued Conformer's PESQ while using 25% of its parameters (Table 2).
On DNS-Challenge 3, the QTransformer with shared scores achieves OVRL of 2.67 versus 2.61 for the baseline, showing quality is maintained despite the computational reduction (Table 3).
Independent quaternion attention components exhibit only 3.83% top-1 agreement in the baseline method, indicating redundancy that motivates score sharing across components (Section 5.1, Table 4).

Attention output distributions from the shared-score and full quaternion methods are nearly identical, with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.0128 and quantile correlation exceeding 0.995 across all three tested domains (Figure 3, Table 5).

MDfCV0UHSb.text: Across all tested models and target languages, citation accuracy drops when the cited source is in a non-English language rather than English, with gaps ranging from -5.30% to -37.6% (Section 5.1, Table 1).

The English-citation bias is amplified for lower-resource languages, with Swahili showing the largest average accuracy drop (-23.9%, peak -37.6% for Aya23 8B) followed by Bengali (-18.0% average, peak -32.8%) (Section 5.1).

Document position in the context window modulates the language bias, with the largest accuracy drop occurring when the non-English cited document is placed in the middle of the context rather than at the start or end (Section 5.1, Figure 2).

Models trade off document relevance for language preference: when a relevant document is in a non-English language and an irrelevant one is in English, citation accuracy for the target-English condition falls below the English-English baseline (Section 7, Figure 5).
Beyond English-specific bias, models also favor citing documents written in the query's language more generally, extending the bias to non-English query languages (Section 6, Figure 4).

uZWpKAqjEg.text: On the dynamic Phi^4_1 SPDE benchmark, the proposed F-SPDENO achieves a relative L2 error of 0.011 in the W-to-X setting with N=10000 samples, outperforming NSPDE's 0.013 (Section 5.1, Table 1).

On 2D stochastic Navier-Stokes, F-SPDENO attains relative L2 error of 0.037 (W-to-X) and 0.031 (X0,W-to-X), compared to NSPDE's 0.040 and 0.047 respectively, a roughly 34% improvement on the latter task (Section 5.1, Table 2).

For one-step diffusion image sampling built on the SDE-based neural operator, the method achieves an FID-50K of 4.89 on CIFAR-10 versus 3.17 for the pretrained diffusion model (Section 5.2, Figure 4).
On topological graph interpolation of brain signals, G-SDENO achieves a Wasserstein distance of 9.60+/-0.09, comparable to the TSBM baseline's 9.51+/-0.12 (Section 5.2, Figure 5).

For financial extrapolation with a Heston model trained on 75 time steps and evaluated on 100 steps, the model demonstrates strong extrapolation power into the unseen future horizon (Section 5.2, Figure 6).
On the manifold SDE Flood dataset, Manifold-SDENO achieves an NLL of 0.51+/-0.12, competitive with the RSGM baseline's 0.49+/-0.20 (Section 5.3, Table 3).

STWQoscanw.text: Loss spikes in Adam arise from a decoupling regime in which instantaneous squared gradients fall substantially below the second-moment estimate, causing the debiased second moment to decay approximately exponentially at rate beta_2 (Section 4.2).

The proposed gradient-directional curvature predictor, lambda_grad(H-hat) = grad L(theta_t)^T H-hat grad L(theta_t) / ||grad L(theta_t)||^2, signals an impending spike when it exceeds 2/eta, validated on GD and Adam in quadratic optimization (Section 4.3, Figure 4).

A sustained-threshold version of the predictor, requiring lambda_grad(H_t) > 2/eta to persist across multiple timesteps, is needed to reliably flag spikes in an 8-layer, 10M-parameter Transformer, where seven distinct spikes were tracked (Section 5.3, Figure 7).
Theorem B.1 formalizes a five-phase progression of loss-spike formation in quadratic optimization, from stable descent through preconditioner decay to spike onset and recovery (Appendix B).

The decoupling and curvature-predictor mechanism generalizes across architectures, being validated on an FNN (Section 5.1, Figure 5), a CNN on CIFAR-10 (Section 5.2, Figure 6), and a Transformer (Section 5.3, Figure 7).

Loss spikes are categorized into four types by their effect on generalization -- neutral, beneficial, malignant, and catastrophic -- with differential impacts on test loss trajectories shown for each (Appendix C, Figure D1).

xILwgiWAUk.text: Observation 3.1 proves that Shapley values depend exclusively on the odd component of the coalition set function, so the even component can be discarded without loss (Section 3).

Theorem 3.2 proves that paired sampling orthogonalizes the regression, provably separating the odd and even objectives and giving the first general theoretical justification for this widely used sampling heuristic (Section 3.1).
Theorem 3.5 shows that Fourier basis regression exactly recovers Shapley values, which forms the theoretical basis of the OddSHAP algorithm (Section 3.2).

In Table 1, across eight estimators and eight benchmarks (with sample budget m≈100d), OddSHAP attains the lowest average rank (1.50), beating the prior best method RegressionMSR (rank 2.25) (Section 5, Table 1).
OddSHAP reduces estimation error by 6–62x relative to LeverageSHAP on tabular data benchmarks (Section 5, Table 1).
Figure 2 shows OddSHAP's advantage over baselines is largest for moderate-to-high dimensional problems (d≥30) when given sufficient sampling budget (Figure 2).

EI9P0pzytY.text: PiEvo achieves 90.81%–93.15% solution quality across benchmarks, a 29.7%–31.1% relative improvement over the state-of-the-art baseline (Section 1).

On the Nanomaterial Optical Property (NHO) benchmark with the Qwen3-32B backbone, PiEvo attains 96.36% solution quality versus 149.06% for MBO-task, 37.33% for SPO-task and 80.49% for TMC-task under comparable settings, reported across four benchmarks: NHO, MBO, SPO, and TMC (Section 4.3, Tables 1-2).
PiEvo achieves an 83.3% speedup in convergence step count relative to baselines by optimizing over a compact principle space (Section 4.4).

Theorem 3.3 (with full proof in Theorem A.6, Appendix A) guarantees sublinear cumulative regret R(T) = O~(√T) and posterior consistency concentrating on the optimal principle P* (Section 3.4, Appendix A).

Ablation on the NHO task shows removing the Information-Directed Hypothesis Selection module drops solution quality from 96.36% to 84.03%, and removing Principle Evolution drops it to 85.87% (Section 4.6, Table 5).

PiEvo attains an Average Pairwise Distance (APD) of 54.7% (2.4x the baseline) and an Area Under Optimization Curve (AUOC) of 84.0% (1.5x the baseline), evaluated with Qwen3-32B and Gemini-2.5-Flash backbones (Section 4.3, Table 2).

euv8IoKFbh.text: CoDD (Coupled Discrete Diffusion) breaks the factorization barrier in diffusion language models by replacing the fully-factorized denoising output with a lightweight probabilistic-circuit-based inference layer that couples token predictions (Section 4).

The paper formalizes a 'misspecification gap' as the KL divergence between the ideal joint distribution and the fully-factorized approximation, and Figure 1 shows this gap causes substantial performance degradation when predicting multiple tokens simultaneously (Section 3, Figure 1).

On LiLDA Block Diffusion, CoDD with the Low Confidence unmasking strategy improves MATH500 accuracy by +5.0 points at 256 steps, GSM8K by +1.67 points at 128 steps, and MBPP by +6.80 points at 128 steps, relative to the uncoupled baseline (Section 6, Table 1).

On Dream full diffusion, CoDD with the Entropy strategy improves GSM8K accuracy by +10.84 points at 128 steps, and by +22.44 points at 64 steps (56.41% vs. 33.97% baseline), showing it prevents few-step performance collapse (Section 6, Table 2).
CoDD matches the reasoning performance of RL-trained baselines while requiring only about 3 GPU-hours of training, under 2% of the RL baseline's compute cost (Section 6).
CoDD adds only 4-5% inference latency overhead on the Dream backbone, while the Any-Order variant adds 21-27% overhead (Section 6, Table 3).

FHMsceUzfS.text: UniMAGE unifies script drafting and keyframe design in a single Mixture-of-Transformers architecture built on the pre-trained Bagel framework, combining Interleaved Concept Learning with In-Context ID Prompting and Disentangled Expert Learning with Pre-Context Script Splitting (Section 3).
UniMAGE is trained on a mixed dataset of 450k multi-shot text-image script sequences, 250k multi-shot text-only scripts, and 250k single-shot text-image pairs (Section 4).

Training proceeds first via 30,000 steps of Interleaved Concept Learning at learning rate 1e-5, then 10,000 steps of Disentangled Expert Learning at the same learning rate, reflecting an 'interleave-then-disentangle' training paradigm (Section 3-4).

On the ViStoryBench benchmark (Table 1), UniMAGE achieves Character ID Similarity of 59.2 (vs. 57.0 runner-up), Onstage Character Count Matching of 88.07 (vs. 85.9), and Prompt Adherence of 80.8 (vs. 62.5), state-of-the-art among open-source models (Section 4, Table 1).
UniMAGE's Style Similarity (CSD) score of 59.0 trails the runner-up's 74.9 on ViStoryBench, indicating a stylistic consistency tradeoff (Section 4, Table 1).
In a user study of 50 volunteers rating 40 generated scripts, UniMAGE achieves the highest narrative coherence preference, scoring 0.72 on the GSB metric (Section 4).

N2D3MdZHQn.text: FeRA analyzes how diffusion denoising shifts energy from low to high frequencies over the trajectory, showing low-frequency components maintain substantially higher SNR early in denoising while high-frequency components emerge later (Section 3).

FeRA introduces a Frequency-Energy Indicator (FEI) computed via Difference-of-Gaussians operators, a Soft Frequency Router that blends M LoRA experts via weighted softmax, and a Frequency-Energy Consistency Loss (FECL) that regularizes spectral alignment (Section 4).

On Stable Diffusion 2.0 with a 20M-parameter adapter, FeRA achieves an FID of 187.83 on the Barbie style dataset versus 198.95 for standard LoRA, an approximately 5% average improvement across five style datasets (Section 5, Table 1).
On DreamBooth subject-driven generation, FeRA reaches a CLIP-Image score of 0.900 on dog subjects (vs. 0.895 for LoRA) and a CLIP-Text score of 25.95 (vs. 23.64 for LoRA) (Section 5, Table 2).

Ablations show a three-band frequency decomposition outperforms alternative band counts, and an FECL weight of λ_f=0.1 is optimal, with both removing FECL and over-weighting it degrading performance (Section 5.3).
FeRA's inference overhead is modest, at 1.12x the relative runtime of standard LoRA on Stable Diffusion 2.0 (Section 5, Table 8).

mGu2fs7kJt.text: TruDi is evaluated across 73 tasks spanning five benchmarks (MuJoCo Playground DMC, ManiSkill3, IsaacLab, MuJoCo Playground Humanoid, and HumanoidBench) (Figure 2).

On symmetric multimodal tasks PushT and StackCube, TruDi maintains non-trivial action entropy (0.32±0.13 and 0.87±0.08 respectively) while the REPPO baseline collapses to zero entropy, indicating mode collapse in REPPO (Table 1).

On the MuJoCo Humanoid task at 50M environment steps, TruDi reaches an episode return of 34.8±3.0 in 1.95±0.46 hours, compared to REPPO's 29.6±7.2 return in 1.07±0.35 hours and PPO's 0.1±3.7 return in 0.95±0.35 hours (Table 2).
TruDi achieves comparable or superior sample efficiency to the flow-based FPO baseline on DMC and Humanoid benchmarks (Figure 3).
An ablation over the number of diffusion denoising steps T shows performance saturates at T=8 across T ∈ {1,4,8,16,32} (Figure 5, right).

The trust-region threshold ε ablation shows best performance for intermediate values in the range 0.1 to 0.4, and deterministic ODE-based evaluation (c=1.0) outperforms SDE sampling and Best-of-K sampling strategies (Figure 6).

ky0UzGMuut.text: The Reason50K dataset contains 51,039 samples spanning four reasoning scenarios (Physical, Temporal, Causal, and Story), each including a source image, a hypothetical instruction, and a target image, constructed via an inverse generation strategy with GPT-based instruction rewriting (Section 3.1).
On the four reasoning-scenario benchmark, ReasonBrain achieves the highest scores among compared baselines: 0.259 CLIP Score, 0.877 MLLM Score, and 0.847 Instruction Alignment (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On generalization to conventional editing datasets, ReasonBrain reaches 0.126 CLIPdir and 0.923 CLIPim on the Emu Edit benchmark (Table 3, Section 4.2).

An ablation progressively adding the patch branch, then patch+region branches, then the full ReasonBrain model shows CLIP Score improving from 0.187 to 0.206 to 0.259, demonstrating the contribution of the Fine-Grained Reasoning Cue Extraction and Cross-Modal Enhancer components (Table 4, Section 4.4).
ReasonBrain's framework combines Fine-Grained Reasoning Cue Extraction (FRCE) and a Cross-Modal Enhancer (CME) module (Section 3.2).

G8LVO5easu.text: With only 10 initial labeled preference pairs, VOTP achieves an average D4RL locomotion score of 92.8, nearly matching an Oracle upper bound of 92.4, and an average MetaWorld score of 67.6 versus 48.6 for the P-IQL baseline, outperforming baselines including IPL, CPL, DPPO, SURF, LiRE, APPO, and FTB (Table 1, Section 4.3).

The pseudo-labeling mechanism uses an optimal transport plan (Equation 5) to propagate preferences from labeled to unlabeled video pairs based on relative alignment strengths, outperforming similarity-only baselines SIM-individual, SIM-mean, and SIM-weighted (Figure 2, Section 4.2).

Under visual distractor perturbations (lighting, texture, video background changes) on MetaWorld, VOTP's average performance ranges from 74.4 to 81.6 compared to 77.6 in the same-domain setting, demonstrating robustness to nuisance variation (Table 2, Section 5.4).

On real Sawyer-arm robotic tasks with only 5-10 human preference labels, VOTP achieves 80% success on Lift Banana and 70% on Drawer Open, compared to 50% for the P-IQL baseline (Table 3, Section 5.5).
VOTP's method builds on an S3D video foundation model combined with a discrete optimal transport formulation over the Bradley-Terry preference model (Section 3, Section 4.1-4.2).

8tv1WMj3X6.text: MS-FLOW achieves the top-1 rank on 22 out of 24 averaged MSE/MAE metrics across long-term forecasting benchmarks including ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Electricity, Weather, Solar-Energy, and Traffic (Table 1).
MS-FLOW improves average error by 2.72% MSE / 5.69% MAE over the TimeFilter baseline and 8.98% MSE / 9.44% MAE over iTransformer (Table 1).

An ablation removing the Sparse Dependency Bottleneck (w/o SDB) shows the largest performance degradation among the three core components, confirming the sparse bottleneck as the main contributor to accuracy gains (Table 3).
Top-K sparsification consistently outperforms Dense, Random-K, and Static-K dependency selection strategies, validating the value of sample-adaptive structured sparsity (Table 4).
Under channel noise pollution, MS-FLOW achieves a pollution hit rate of 3.80%, versus 7.23% for Random-K and 7.79% for Dense variants, showing better discrimination of noisy channels (Figure 3).

A Wilcoxon signed-rank test against TimeFilter shows statistically significant improvement in MAE (p=0.0039) and marginal significance in MSE (p=0.0664), with MS-FLOW outperforming on 15 of 16 tested metrics (Appendix C).

NAkeQ3C4tn.text: On CIFAR-10, SURGE achieves 93.1% accuracy on ResNet-18, 88.0% on ResNet-20, and 92.5% on VGG-Small, outperforming the ReCU baseline by 0.3-0.6 percentage points (Table 1).
On ImageNet in the one-stage training setting, SURGE reaches 62.0% top-1 accuracy on binarized ResNet-18, improving 0.6 points over RBONN and 3.9 points over IR-Net (Table 2).
On ImageNet in the two-stage training setting, SURGE achieves 66.7% top-1 accuracy versus 66.5% for RBONN (Table 3).
On PASCAL VOC object detection with Faster-RCNN, SURGE scores 77.0 mAP, a 0.5 point gain over IDa-Det at comparable computational cost (Table 4).
On the GLUE benchmark for language understanding, SURGE averages 72.0%, improving 1.4 points over BiT and 8.9 points over BiBERT (Table 5).

The method combines Dual-Path Gradient Compensation (DPGC, Section 4.1, Equations 5-6) with Adaptive Gradient Scaling (AGS, Section 4.2, Equation 7) to address gradient mismatch and information loss from fixed-range clipping in the Straight-Through Estimator, with Theorem 5.3 deriving the optimal scaling factor λ* (Section 5).

ZqnVidXtxV.text: LK losses (ℒLKλ and ℒLKα) directly optimize acceptance rate in speculative decoding instead of using KL divergence as a proxy objective, motivated by a gradient analysis showing KL yields stable but indirect gradients while TV directly targets acceptance rate but vanishes at initialization (Section 4.1).

On LLaMA-3.1-8B with EAGLE-3 draft heads, ℒLKλ improves acceptance length over the KL baseline by 1.6% at temperature 0 and 3.9% at temperature 1, with larger gains of 7.8-8.3% for MEDUSA and MLP speculators (Table 1).

Across target models from 8B to 685B parameters (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-20B/120B, Qwen3-235B, DeepSeek-V3), LK losses yield acceptance-length improvements ranging 0.5-8.2%, including +7.7% on GPT-OSS-120B and +8.2% on Qwen3-235B (Table 2).
Fine-tuning DeepSeek-V3's native MTP speculator with LK losses improves acceptance rate by 5.6% over the KL-trained baseline (Table 2).
LK losses are evaluated across four draft architectures (EAGLE-3, MEDUSA, MLP speculator, DeepSeek MTP) on MT-Bench, HumanEval, and GSM8K benchmarks (Section 5).

wW2LIHSCfw.text: A cross-conditioning diagnostic on CosyVoice2 shows the speech language model (SLM) is the primary driver of emotional prosody, with F0 CCC of 0.109 under SLM-driven conditioning versus 0.305 under flow-matching-driven conditioning (Table 1).

Emotion steering vectors are extracted as mean-difference directions between neutral and emotional SLM activations from a combined ESD, RAVDESS, and CREMA-D corpus of about 20,691 utterances (4,000 per emotion), then applied via weighted summation for mixed-emotion synthesis (Section 3).

Layer-wise analysis identifies mid-to-late layers (10-17) of CosyVoice2 as exhibiting the highest emotion discriminability, motivating selection of the top-2 steering layers for CosyVoice2 and top-3 for IndexTTS2 (Figure 3, Appendix I).

On mixed-emotion synthesis (CREMA-D/IEMOCAP), CoCoEmo with steering strength alpha=5.0 achieves target emotion probability of 0.335 and Spearman correlation of 0.319 between steering weight and predicted emotion proportion, while maintaining naturalness (N-MOS 3.96-4.25) (Table 2).

On text-emotion mismatch synthesis (high-severity set) with CosyVoice2 at alpha=6.0, CoCoEmo achieves E-SIM of 0.862 and TEP of 0.504, outperforming an instruction-based baseline (0.843, 0.436), while preserving speaker similarity (S-SIM >= 0.892) (Table 3).

vkG1xVVKOH.text: SySRs (Synchronized Successive Rejects) is a hyperparameter-free bandit algorithm that evaluates all remaining candidate models on the same shared subset of test queries at each stage, rather than independently sampling queries per model, to exploit inter-model correlation (Section 4, Algorithm 1).

Theorem 5.1 establishes an error probability bound for SySRs governed by a correlation-aware hardness measure H3 that improves (shrinks the bound) as between-model score correlation increases, unlike classical bounds that depend only on performance gaps (Section 5).

Across 15 standard LLM benchmarks drawn from HELM Lite and OpenLLM Leaderboard, SySRs identifies the best model with 95.1% accuracy at 12% of the full evaluation budget, versus 89.7% for the best baseline, and reaches 100% accuracy by 35% budget (Table 2, Section 6.1).

At worst-case difficulty, SySRs requires only 10% of the evaluation budget to reach 95% confidence and 17% to reach 100% confidence, compared to 13% and 20% respectively for the non-synchronized Successive Rejects baseline (Table 3).
Corollary 5.2 identifies the regimes of model correlation under which synchronized query evaluation provably outperforms standard (non-synchronized) successive-rejects-style approaches (Section 5.1).

hexseuWYzC.text: The late-decoupled 3D hierarchical semantic segmentation (Ld-3DHS) branch replaces a single shared decoder with per-hierarchy-level decoders plus coarse-to-fine MLP fusion (Eq. 3-4) to mitigate underfitting/overfitting conflicts from multi-label parameter sharing across hierarchies (Section 3.2).
A cross-hierarchical consistency loss (Eq. 6-7) enforces parent-child label agreement using mapping matrices between hierarchy levels (Section 3.2).

An auxiliary discrimination branch applies supervised contrastive learning (Eq. 9) on class-wise point clouds together with semantic prototype-based bi-branch supervision (Eq. 10-11) to address class imbalance via self-supervised contrastive cluster information (Section 3.3).
On S3DIS-H with a PointNet++ backbone, Ld-3DHS achieves 66.43% average mIoU, outperforming the DHL baseline by 3.38 percentage points (Table 1).
Ablations on S3DIS-H show removing the late-decoupled framework, the contrastive loss, or the bi-branch supervision drops average mIoU by 4.26%, 4.94%, and 3.45% respectively (Tables 5-6).

Applied as a plug-and-play module to prior methods MTHS and DHL across Campus3D, S3DIS-H, and SensatUrban-H with PointNet++, Point Transformer v2, and Point Transformer v3 backbones, Ld-3DHS improves mIoU by 0.54-2.99 percentage points (Tables 2-4).

7Oonij8oLU.text: alpha-PFN uses a two-stage amortization strategy: a base PFN predicts posterior predictive distributions conditioned on optimum location and/or value, and a second alpha-PFN learns to predict information gain directly in a single forward pass per candidate, replacing costly Monte Carlo entropy-search approximations (Section 3).

alpha-PFN achieves runtime speedups ranging from 1.6x to 72x over GP-MCMC implementations of JES, MES-GIBBON, and PES from BoTorch, with speedups exceeding 50x commonly observed on HPO-B tasks (Table 1, Section 5).

alpha-PFN is evaluated on synthetic functions (Branin 2D, Hartmann 4D/6D, Ackley 5D/8D) over 30 repetitions and 100 BO iterations, as well as real-world benchmarks LCBench (Car, Fashion-MNIST, MiniBooNE, Higgs, Segment) and HPO-B across 5 search spaces with 8D-16D problems (Figure 3, Section 5).

alpha-PFN attains regret and ranking performance competitive with GP-based entropy search baselines (JES, MES-GIBBON, PES) and EI across the synthetic and real-world benchmark suites (Figure 3, Section 6).
An out-of-distribution noise ablation (Figure 4) and a trace-generation ablation (Figure 5, Appendix E.3) assess alpha-PFN's robustness to distribution shift and training data generation choices.

TphOLCDmKB.text: The method models a multi-agent system as a directed acyclic graph over temporal nodes and extracts a signed contribution network with edge scores in {-1, 0, 1} before backward-propagating node contribution scores to flag malicious agents (Section 3.1-3.3).

On GPT-4o with MMLU under fixed flat and hierarchical MAS structures, the defense improves accuracy by roughly 8-10 percentage points over undefended attacked baselines while achieving 91-93% malicious-agent detection rates (Table 1, Table 2, Section 4.2).

Across six attack types (Harmful, Suboptimal, Reframing, Trigger, and Modification variants) evaluated on MMLU, Alpaca, Samsum, and Chatdoctor, the method yields 6-7% accuracy gains with over 90% detection, with the largest gains (10-16 points) on Modification attacks (Table 5, Table 6, Section 4.2).

In dynamic graph experiments where the MAS topology evolves under attack, the defense sustains 85-88% accuracy versus a 78% undefended baseline, with detection rates of 92-94% despite the changing topology (Table 7, Table 8, Section 4.3).

An ablation removing the backward contribution-propagation module reduces accuracy by 2-3% and detection rate by 6-8%, confirming that global propagation across the MAS graph (not just local edge signals) is necessary for the defense's effectiveness (Table 9, Table 10, Section 4.4).

nf7JT1jCSy.text: Theorem 4.2 derives a closed-form hybrid randomized smoothing certificate based on a likelihood-ratio CDF F(t;r) that is continuous and strictly increasing, allowing joint discrete-continuous (text-image) robustness to be certified via one-dimensional root-finding (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.2).

Proposition 4.1 shows that Neyman-Pearson-optimal acceptance regions on the joint product space of discrete and continuous perturbations cannot be decomposed into separate per-modality thresholds, even when the noise across modalities is independent, motivating the need for a joint hybrid certificate rather than naive composition of unimodal certificates (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).

The hybrid certificate is shown to recover classical Gaussian (image-only) and discrete (text-only) randomized smoothing certificates as special cases of the same one-dimensional formula (Section 4.1).

On a curated 400-example interaction-only subset of Hateful Memes (where neither modality alone triggers an 'Unsafe' label) evaluated with LLaVA-Guard, the hybrid certificate attains a certified image radius of 3.76 at a text perturbation budget of d=1, versus 3.99 for an image-only certificate ignoring text perturbations (Table 1, Section 5.2).

Figure 4 shows certified accuracy decreases monotonically as both the image radius epsilon and the text edit-distance budget d increase, consistent with the theoretical trade-off predicted by the hybrid certificate (Figure 4, Section 5.2).

A sanity-check experiment on the tabular Adult dataset demonstrates the hybrid smoothing framework extends beyond vision-language inputs to other heterogeneous discrete-continuous feature settings (Section 5.1).

JidATZ8SuW.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that under action feedback alone (the leader observes only the follower's chosen action, not its type), any learning algorithm must incur regret that is exponential in the bit-complexity L of the follower's payoffs, specifically Omega(2^(2L)) (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 4.7 shows that under type feedback (the leader observes both the follower's action and revealed type), an algorithm achieves regret bounded by Otilde(K^2 log(1/delta) sqrt(T) + beta log^2(T)) against the optimal commitment baseline when the number of leader actions m is constant, holding with high probability (Section 4.4, Theorem 4.7).
Lemma 4.1's Find-Types procedure estimates the follower type distribution to within L-infinity error epsilon_h using Otilde(1/epsilon_h^2) rounds of interaction (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.1).
Lemma 4.3 bounds the oracle-query complexity of learning best-response polytope regions via the Find-Partition procedure at Otilde(K^(m+1) n^(2m+2)) (Section 4.2, Lemma 4.3).

The algorithm's positive result relies on iteratively refining the space of candidate leader commitments across epochs, tightening the precision parameter epsilon_h while using the Prune procedure (Lemma 4.4) to guarantee the optimal commitment is never discarded (Section 4.3, Lemma 4.4).

FiCxlfjkhc.text: The proposed augmented spectral feature learning loss (Eq. 4-5) modifies the standard SpecIV loss (Eq. 3) by incorporating an outcome-aware, augmented operator T_delta so that learned features are informed by the downstream causal outcome rather than only the instrument-treatment spectral structure (Section 3, Eq. 3-5).

Proposition 1 establishes a formal connection between the augmented loss and a low-rank approximation of the augmented operator, justifying why outcome-awareness corrects for spectral misalignment between the true causal function and the dominant singular functions of the un-augmented operator (Section 3, Proposition 1).
Theorem 1 provides a non-asymptotic error bound for the resulting two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimator using the learned outcome-aware features (Section 4, Theorem 1).

On synthetic data with controlled spectral misalignment, relative MSE is shown to improve as the balancing hyperparameter delta increases, illustrating the method's robustness to the target causal function being poorly represented by the top singular functions (Figure 2, Section 6.1).

The method is evaluated on the dSprites image-based IV benchmark using a newly introduced, more challenging structural function designed to induce spectral misalignment, comparing against the old and new structural functions (Figure 3, Section 6.2).
The approach is additionally validated in an off-policy evaluation (OPE) reinforcement learning setting, demonstrating applicability beyond standard IV regression benchmarks (Section 6.3).

t6dA9c3SlJ.text: PIDDM enforces PDE constraints directly on the final generated sample x_0 rather than on the posterior mean estimate E[x_0|x_t], avoiding the 'Jensen's Gap' inconsistency R(E[x_0|x_t]) != E[R(x_0)|x_t] that Figure 2 shows afflicts PIDM, DiffusionPDE, and ECI-sampling on synthetic Mixture-of-Gaussians and Stokes-problem test cases (Figure 2, Section on Jensen's Gap).

On the Darcy flow benchmark, the one-step distilled model PIDDM-1 achieves a PDE error of 0.226e-4 using only 1 NFE, and the refined variant PIDDM-ref reduces this to 0.148e-4, both substantially below ECI (1.582e-4), DiffusionPDE (1.071e-4), PIDM (1.236e-4), and the vanilla diffusion baseline (1.585e-4) (Table 1).

On the Poisson and Burger's equation benchmarks, PIDDM-ref achieves PDE errors of 0.050e-9 and 0.174e-3 respectively, again lower than all four baselines (ECI, DiffusionPDE, PIDM, Vanilla) reported in Table 1 (Table 1).

On forward, inverse, and reconstruction tasks for the Darcy problem, PIDDM attains PDE errors of 0.145e-4, 0.126e-4, and 0.143e-4 respectively, outperforming ECI-sampling, DiffusionPDE, and D-Flow while using 80 NFE versus 5000 NFE for D-Flow (Table 2).

Ablations show that increasing teacher sampling steps improves both sample quality and physical constraint satisfaction, that moderate PDE loss weighting during training reduces residuals while excessive weighting degrades MMSE/SMSE due to finite-difference approximation error, and that using Rectified Flow (RF-2) as the distillation objective yields the best overall forward/inverse performance (Figure 3, Table 3).
Applying hard constraints via masking of observed entries significantly improves PDE residuals across all downstream reconstruction tasks (Table 3).

p2RPRTPPMO.text: SOL (Scalable Option Learning) runs at approximately 86% of the throughput of a flat APPO baseline while being roughly 35x-580x faster than the four hierarchical RL baselines tested (HIRO, Option-Critic, MOC, and RLLib hierarchical) (Section 5).

Hierarchical SOL agents trained on 30 billion frames of NetHack (Monk character) significantly surpass flat APPO baselines, with performance still increasing after 30 billion steps of training (Section 5, NetHack experiments).

On the MiniHack TreasureDash task, SOL approaches the theoretical optimum of ~28 points while baseline methods plateau at lower scores, and on the novel PointMaze G-Maze layout SOL achieves ~70% success while flat APPO and MOC remain at 0% (Section 5, continuous control and MiniHack ablations).
Combining SOL with LLM-based intrinsic rewards (SOL+Motif) achieves a new state-of-the-art on NetHack, surpassing Motif alone (Section 5).
Ablations show that adaptive (versus fixed) option lengths and the presence of redundant/unhelpful options materially affect SOL's performance (Appendix F.3, F.4).

lbppqtDUKn.text: The model, integrating an equivariant neural encoder, a neuro-symbolic object encoder (VSM) producing 9-token directional sequences per the Quadrant Hypothesis, and a neural decision agent, was tested on data from a novel interactive VR mental rotation experiment with 19 participants (Section 3, Section 4).

The full model achieves 96.39% match accuracy and 95.87% mismatch accuracy, closely matching human performance of 96.13% and 94.53% respectively, and predicts a mean of ~0.9 rotation actions versus 1.05 for humans (Section 5).

Ablation removing the neuro-symbolic object encoder causes accuracy to drop to between 38.46% and 90.71%, while removing the equivariant encoder causes the symbolic encoder to fail entirely, demonstrating the necessity of both components (Section 5, ablation study).

A variant predicting similarity directly (bypassing the iterative rotation-action mechanism) achieves higher accuracy (97.03%) but fails to reproduce human action-count patterns, and Siamese network baselines fail to generalize to held-out test objects (Section 5).

The model reproduces the approximately linear increase in reaction time with rotation angle for 0°, 60°, and intermediate angles, but cannot distinguish between 120° and 180° conditions since both require a single predicted action (Section 5, response time analysis).

jfOhTGs5G5.text: FutureCAD generates executable CadQuery scripts via an LLM that emits parametric feature sequences plus natural-language queries, which the BRepGround module (Figure 3) grounds to specific B-Rep primitives for the CAD kernel to execute (Section 4, Figure 3).

Training proceeds via supervised fine-tuning on text-to-program pairs at two description granularities (abstract and detailed), plus ~80k additional program-rewritten samples for diversity, followed by reinforcement learning with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) using a Chamfer Distance-based geometric reward (Section 5).
The reward function assigns higher scores to geometrically closer generated shapes and linearly penalizes Chamfer Distance deviations beyond a 0.2 tolerance (Section 5).

On the new FutureCAD dataset (~140,000 real-world CAD models sourced from the ABC dataset via the Onshape API, including 28k advanced-feature models), the method achieves a median Chamfer Distance of 31.12 (mean 71.39) and an invalidity ratio of 1.01% on the advanced subset, and a median Chamfer Distance of 14.68 (down from a 37.47 baseline) on the standard subset (Section 6, Table 1).
BRepGround achieves 63.07% mAP and 50.23% F1 on B-Rep primitive grounding, and the full pipeline attains G-F1 of 80.54% and R-F1 of 85.35% on the advanced subset (Section 6, Table 2).

L20yY9trcq.text: The RefDiv (Reference-Guided Diversity Stress Test) protocol reduces token-level Shannon entropy of TTS candidate pools while steering candidates toward affirmative/harmful completions, using a fitness function combining a dynamic reference-diversity term and an intrinsic diversity-reduction term (Section 3.2, Equation 1, Algorithm 1).

With Best-of-N (N=8, PairRM reward model) TTS, RefDiv achieves Attack Success Rate margins of over 7% versus the next-best baseline (AutoDAN) on Llama3.1-8B and over 17% on Gemma3-27B, and with MCTS TTS it reaches 0.967 ASR on Llama3.1-8B (versus AutoDAN's 0.831) and 0.989 on Gemma3-27B (versus AutoDAN's 0.904) (Section 4.2, Table 1).

Across Qwen3-8B, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-8B, and Gemma3-27B under both Best-of-N and MCTS TTS strategies, RefDiv consistently drives candidate-pool Shannon entropy down over attack iterations while competing baselines (GCG, AutoDAN, AutoDAN-Turbo) show comparatively flat or higher entropy (Section 4.3, Figure 4).

RefDiv's diversity-reducing adversarial prompts transfer to closed-source models including GPT-4.1, o3-mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Claude-3.5-Haiku, indicating the failure mode is general to TTS rather than model-specific (Section 4, Contributions).

State-of-the-art guardrail classifiers (Llama-Guard-3, Llama-Guard-4, OpenAI Moderation API) fail to flag the adversarial prompts generated by RefDiv, showing limited protection against this diversity-driven failure mode (Abstract, Section 4).

Smk4fl6Q9E.text: The TRAP benchmark pairs 18 benign tasks with 35 injection templates (7 persuasion principles x 5 manipulation methods) across six cloned web environments (Amazon, Gmail, Calendar, LinkedIn, DoorDash, Upwork), yielding 630 combinations evaluated over 3,780 total runs on six frontier models (Section 3, Figure 1).

Average prompt-injection Attack Success Rate across all six models is 25% (948 successful attacks out of 3,780 attempts), ranging from 13% for GPT-5 to 43% for DeepSeek-R1, with Claude Sonnet 3.7 at 20%, Gemini 2.5 Flash at 30%, GPT-OSS-120B at 27%, and LLaMA 4 Maverick at 17% (Section 4, Table 1).

Button-based injection elements achieve a 77.5% success rate compared to 22.5% for hyperlink-based injections (about 3.5x more effective), and for GPT-5 specifically buttons succeed in 96.3% of cases versus 3.7% for hyperlinks (Section 4, Table 4).

Light contextual tailoring of injected content (≤20% text changes) substantially raises ASR, e.g., on the GoCalendar environment ASR rises from 3.3% to 18.6% (5.6x increase) and on DashDish from 6.7% to 16.7% (2.5x increase) (Section 4, Table 6).
Location-based targeting generally reduces injection success except in semantically rich contexts such as LinkedIn's "About" section, where success increases from 52% to 59% (Section 4).

XmWKBDYmtk.text: On the ToFU Forget-10 benchmark with LLaMA2-7B, Geometric Unlearning (GU) achieves a Forget ROUGE of 0.058 and Model Utility of 0.598 while keeping PrivLeak near zero (-1.496), without accessing the original training corpus (Table 1).

GU is compared against seven baseline unlearning methods (GA, GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO, UN-DIAL, RMU) using the OpenUnlearning framework, and produces refusal/uncertain-style outputs rather than blank or substituted responses (Table 2).

A matched source-free comparison shows GU's geometric alignment objective, not synthetic data alone, drives effectiveness, with Extraction Strength of 0.172 versus 0.513-0.701 for baselines given the same synthetic data (Table 4).
An ablation over synthetic sample budget per anchor shows an optimal operating point around 20-30 samples that balances unlearning strength and utility preservation (Section 5.2, Figure 4).

An ablation over target layers shows that editing only the last 1-2 layers of the model is most effective for suppression, while editing early or middle layers is largely ineffective (Section 5.2, Table 3).
GU maintains favorable utility-unlearning tradeoffs on the UnlearnPII benchmark across model scales (1B, 8B parameters) and forget splits (1%, 5%, 10%) (Figure 6).

KR6avDABG8.text: MaMa formalizes the design of safe agentic systems as a Stackelberg security game between a Meta-Agent proposing system designs and a Meta-Adversary that compromises epsilon agents to search for worst-case attacks (Section 3).

Across four environments from the BAD-ACTS benchmark (Travel Planning, Personal Assistant, Financial Article Writing, Code Generation), baseline systems show dramatic safety degradation under attack, e.g. Travel Planning dropping from 4.89 to 1.66 and Personal Assistant from 4.31 to 1.53 on a 5-point judge scale (Section 5.2, Table 1).

Systems designed by MaMa achieve the lowest Attack Success Rate against targeted attacks across environments, e.g. 0.17 versus a 0.56 baseline for Travel Planning and 0.15 versus a 0.39 baseline for Personal Assistant (Section 5.3, Table 3).
MaMa-designed systems remain safe against attacks compromising up to 3 agents, with safety degrading more steeply once 4 or more agents are compromised (Section 5.3, Figure 3).

Judge-based safety and quality scoring achieves Quadratic Weighted Cohen's Kappa of 0.88 for safety and 0.80 for quality, and MaMa-discovered defenses include multi-agent approval chains, monitoring/oversight agents, and dedicated checklist agents (Section 5.2, Section 5.4, Figure 4).

zO8vzSGgTn.text: The Policy Optimization-Model Predictive Control (PO-MPC) framework unifies MPPI-based reinforcement learning methods via KL-regularized learning toward a planner-induced prior, controlled by a regularization strength lambda (Section 4.2, Equation 1).
Setting lambda=0 recovers TD-MPC2 and lambda to infinity recovers BMPC, while intermediate lambda values in {0.1, 1, 9} yield novel PO-MPC configurations (Table 2).
On 7 DMControl Humanoid/Dog tasks, PO-MPC variants with intermediate lambda match or exceed the BMPC baseline (Table 1).

On 14 HumanoidBench locomotion tasks, PO-MPC shows consistent improvements over baselines, especially in high-dimensional settings, using a single NVIDIA A100 GPU at 7-15 hours per 1M timesteps (Section 5, Figure 1).

An intermediate learned policy prior matches or surpasses planning directly with replay-buffer samples (Figure 2), and forward-KL training of the prior aids exploration-heavy tasks while reverse-KL accelerates precision tasks (Figure 3).

lm4PZa4kjZ.text: SCARED is presented as the first method for safe in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) under the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) framework, using Exact Penalty Policy Optimization (EPPO) with a single Lagrange multiplier shared across episodes (Section 3, Equation 7).
Theorem 1 shows that fixed points of EPPO's iterative updates satisfy the safety constraints while achieving primal optimality for the constrained problem (Section 3, Theorem 1).

On SafeDarkRoom and SafeDarkMujoco (Point and Car robots), EPPO maintains episode costs below specified thresholds while improving returns across episodes under true out-of-distribution evaluation, whereas a supervised-pretraining baseline fails in SafeDarkMujoco (Section 4, Figure 1).

The agent's behavior responds to the safety budget: higher Cost-to-Go values yield higher returns and more aggressive behavior, while the supervised baseline exhibits random, budget-insensitive patterns (Section 4, Figure 2).

Proposition 1 proves the total variation distance between the center-oriented pretraining distribution and the edge-oriented evaluation distribution reaches 1, confirming genuine out-of-distribution evaluation (Section 4, Proposition 1).

Ablations show reinforcement pretraining benefits from longer context lengths and is robust to model size, whereas supervised pretraining degrades with longer context and is sensitive to model size and dataset size (Appendix E, Figures 5-6).

KhAUoBv0dJ.text: Adaptive Policy Backbone (APB) freezes a shared meta-trained backbone network and adapts only lightweight task-specific linear layers placed before and after it, achieving performance on par with standard TD3 across six tasks (Cheetah-vel, Cheetah-dir, Ant-goal, Ant-dir, Hopper-rand, Walker-rand) (Section 5.2, Figure 4).

Theorem 1 shows that under a state-permutation isomorphism, a task-2 policy can be expressed as a linear map applied to the task-1 policy through another linear transformation (Section 4.1, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 bounds the adaptation error by 2L·||h_t||_op·|X_t^OOD|·epsilon_max, depending on the Lipschitz constant, linear layer operator norm, number of OOD inputs, and distance from the training support (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).

APB consistently outperforms meta-RL baselines (MAML, CAVIA, ANIL, PEARL, VariBAD, Meta-DT) on out-of-distribution reward-variation tasks, where these baselines fail to generalize (Section 5, Figure 5).

An ablation with a randomly initialized (non-meta-trained) backbone and only adapted linear layers still achieves reasonable performance, approaching near-optimality on Ant-goal (Appendix A.5, Figure 7).
Meta-training uses 30 meta-training tasks with 10 trajectories each and actor/critic learning rates of 0.0001 and 0.05 respectively (Appendix A.3, Table 2).

v7rYbRR9Zw.text: VoxParadox comprises 2,000 verified examples spanning 10 paralinguistic perception tasks (200 clips per task), each constructed so the transcript asserts an incorrect paralinguistic attribute while the audio conveys the true one (Section 3).
PCLM combined with DPO raises Audio Flamingo 3's ground-truth accuracy on VoxParadox from 17.40% to 65.20% (Table 1).
The same PCLM+DPO intervention improves Audio Flamingo 3's accuracy on the MMSU paralinguistic subset from 37.74% to 54.78% (Table 1).

Two complementary metrics are defined: GT Accuracy, matching the acoustic ground-truth label, and Adversarial-Label Agreement (ALA), measuring susceptibility to transcript-following under contradiction (Equations 1 and 2, Section 3).
Baseline Audio LLMs exhibit low GT accuracy while showing high ALA on VoxParadox, evidencing systematic language bias over acoustic evidence prior to PCLM+DPO mitigation (Section 3, Table 1).

KidQq3EaOe.text: ExtraCare improves weighted-F1 diagnosis prediction on eICU from a base of 61.09% to 68.61%, and heart-failure prediction F1 from 72.76% to 79.64%, under spatial domain shift (Table 2, Section 4.2).
On the OCHIN dataset under temporal domain shift, ExtraCare raises diagnosis weighted-F1 from 63.77% to 74.05% and heart-failure F1 from 74.88% to 85.38% (Table 2, Section 4.2).

Ablations show removing the reconstruction and domain-classification losses causes a 12.7-20% F1 drop, removing the orthogonal-inference components (W, z) causes a 5-8% drop, and replacing the dictionary-induced metric M with a Euclidean metric causes only a 1-2% drop (Table 2, Section 4.4).

ExtraCare maps sparse latent dictionary dimensions to ICD medical concepts and organizes them into a four-quadrant scheme by label-impact versus domain-sensitivity, illustrated with anxiety-disorder codes F41.1/F41.9 (Section 4.3, Figure 2(c)).

Linear probes trained on the label-relevant representation v show high cosine similarity (0.61-0.75) between class and domain classifier weights, whereas probes on the domain-covariant residual z show near-zero similarity (0.07-0.10), confirming successful feature separation (Section 4.3).

nifIPKmOyY.text: TelecomTS contains 32,000 time series samples of length 128 across 18 channels (10 float, 6 integer, 2 categorical covariates), spans 11 anomaly types, and provides 2,210,185 total QA instances (Table 1).

On anomaly detection over a 1,000-sample subset, the scale-aware Mantis model achieves F1 0.800, which drops to 0.692 when scale information is removed (Mantis w/o scaling), while the best foundation model Toto reaches only F1 0.615 (Table 2, Section 4.1).

In forecasting, removing scale information degrades Mantis from MAE 0.457/RMSE 0.603 to MAE 0.570/RMSE 0.843, directly supporting the claim that preserving covariates' absolute scale is critical for observability applications (Table 5, Section 4.4).

LLMs and reasoning models show strong false-positive bias in anomaly detection without context (e.g., o4-mini: precision 0.188, recall 1.000; GPT-4.1: precision 0.200, recall 1.000), reflecting difficulty distinguishing abrupt-but-normal fluctuations from true anomalies (Table 2, Section 4.1).

The multi-modal Toto+Qwen-3-4B model attains root-cause-analysis accuracy of 0.826, slightly below the pure Toto foundation model's 0.848, while its reasoning-enabled variant drops further to 0.720 (Table 4, Section 4.3).

MPvCuDbTxV.text: The benchmark evaluates five representation-steering methods (DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, LAT) across 17 datasets covering primary behaviors (harmful generation/refusal, demographic bias, hallucination) and secondary behaviors (Section 2, Section 3.2).

Evaluation is conducted on Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B using two aggregate metrics, effectiveness and entanglement, which respectively quantify steering success on the targeted behavior and unintended shifts on non-target behaviors (Section 2.3, Section 4).
DIM (Difference-in-Means) shows the highest steering effectiveness but also the greatest entanglement, whereas ACE achieves moderate effectiveness gains with reduced entanglement (Section 4.1).
Social secondary behaviors such as sycophancy and anthropomorphism show more pronounced entanglement from steering interventions than reasoning-related secondary behaviors (Section 4.2).

Strong steering performance is found to depend critically on the specific combination of steering method, model, and targeted behavior/perspective, rather than any method dominating uniformly (Section 4.2).

Ygg3KJPeT6.text: DocVAL improves Gemma3-12B from an 84.6% ANLS baseline to 91.4% ANLS (82.4 mAP) and Gemma3-4B from 78.6% to 88.7% ANLS on the DocVQA benchmark (Table 1).
During Phase A teacher-CoT generation, the VAL Filter retains examples with quality score Q>0.85, producing 95K high-quality traces at a 92.7% retention rate (7.3% rejected) (Section 3.2.3).

Using detailed VAL-verifier feedback for iterative refinement in Stage B2 raises performance from 72.7 mAP (Stage B1 only) to 82.4 mAP, a 9.7 mAP gain over supervised-only training (Table 5, Section 3.4.2).

Training without teacher-generated chain-of-thought (direct fine-tuning on answers) yields only 65.4 mAP versus 82.4 mAP with validated CoT supervision, a 17.0 mAP advantage for explicit spatial-reasoning transfer (Table 3).

Removing text-detection scaffolding from Phase A teacher generation drops performance from 82.4 mAP to 74.1 mAP, even though the deployed student model itself requires no text detection at inference (Table 2, Section 3.5).

gnLZWOubWa.text: Introduces a diagnostic 2-SAT benchmark with five parameterized generator families: Implication Cycle, SAT via Free Variables, Backbone, Monotone Split with Bridge, and Symmetry/Redundancy (Section 3).

On the ImplicationCycle generator, decision accuracy of some models collapses from 98.3% at 5 clauses to 0% at 100 clauses even though surface statistics such as instance length are held fixed (Section 5, Table 1).

On the EquivalenceCore generator, models reach 100% correct SAT/UNSAT decisions but only 1.7%-93.3% valid witness assignments across models, showing decision accuracy and witness validity diverge (Table 1).
Semantics-preserving clause reordering significantly degrades performance across all five generators (p < 0.003) (Section 5).
Switching from template-based verbalization to free-form LLM-generated verbalization reduces accuracy by roughly 25 percentage points on average (Section 5, Figures 5-9).
Evaluation spans seven LLM-based reasoners ranging from 14B to 120B parameters, reported with six verbalization templates (logic, letter, team, social, room, door) (Table 2).

FaDUU0pyFj.text: Derives an so(n)-valued 1-form that depends only on the geometry of token embeddings to quantify a GPT-style model's sensitivity to single-token sampling choices (Section 4, 'Developing the Geometry').
