Shows the coupling strength ('probability charge') between this geometric quantity and next-token uncertainty peaks when the top-two token probabilities are equal (p1=0.5) (Section 5, 'Probability Charge').

On a chess reasoning task using an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned model, curvature-derived transformations correlate with piece importance at Spearman's rho = 0.90, evaluated over 4,000 collected chess branch points and 737 linear board-state probes (Section 7 Results, Tables 1-2).
Reports single-token perturbations at ambiguous generation points cause chess evaluation shifts of 4.5 +/- 1.5 log-centi-pawns (Section 3, 'Motivation').

The Mistral-Small model exhibits the opposite-signed correlation (Spearman's rho = -0.90) between coupling and piece importance relative to Qwen2.5-32B, indicating architecture-dependent orientation of the effect (Section 7, Figures 9-10).

bOlF0eLPXa.text: Represents molecules with composite exponential-family distributions evolved along exponential geodesics under the Fisher-Rao metric, replacing static Dirac target distributions with dynamically concentrating ones to prevent trajectory collapse (Section 3, Figures 1-2).
Achieves a 93.4% PoseBusters-valid rate on the CrossDock benchmark, approaching reference-ligand levels (Section 4, Table 1).

On CrossDock, reports an average Vina score of -6.14 (second-best among compared methods, after MolCRAFT) and a median strain energy of 25.96, lower than baselines, alongside 97.1% molecular connectivity (Table 1).

On MolGenBench, achieves scaffold pass rates of 31.79% on CrossDock-derived proteins and 29.61% on novel proteins, recovering bioactive hits at 72/33 targets with hit fractions of 1.08%/0.93% respectively (Section 4, Table 2).
Ablation studies isolate the contribution of the progressive-parameter-refinement training architecture and the dynamic endpoint strategy to final performance (Section 4, Figure 5).

Ty5X41WbJw.text: Shows the normalized train-test reconstruction gap in Rectified Flows follows a bell-shaped curve over the interpolation parameter lambda, with the peak location lambda*_F derivable in closed form under Gaussian data assumptions as lambda* = sigma_0^2/(sigma_0^2 + sigma_1^2) (Section 4, Theoretical Analysis).

A membership inference attack exploiting this lambda-resolved structure achieves 0.91 AUC on MAESTRO v3, compared to 0.67 for a naive single-lambda baseline, 0.72 for adapted SecMI, and 0.83 for adapted PIA (Section 7, 'Implications for Membership Inference').

Demonstrates the membership signal accumulates over training (scaling as roughly 1/n per Corollary 4.5) even while validation loss remains stable, indicating leakage invisible to standard monitoring (Section 6, Figure 4).

The bell-shaped gap structure is validated across both audio (MAESTRO) and image datasets, with ablations over 7 dimensions including noise covariances, architecture, capacity, and noise schedule (Section 6, Table 2, Figures 5-7).

On CelebA, the Gaussian-derived peak prediction fails, predicting lambda*_F=0.45 versus an observed peak in [0.6, 0.7], showing the closed-form prediction breaks down when Gaussianity assumptions are violated (Section 6).

4De8M6HSF5.text: Proposes augmenting CVaR policy gradient with an expected quantile (VaR) term via a new VaR Bellman operator, reducing the augmented objective to a Markovian policy class (Section 3.1-3.2, Algorithm 1).
Introduces a combined CVaR-VaR Policy Gradient algorithm (Algorithm 4) that leverages all sampled trajectories rather than only the alpha-tail, improving sample efficiency over CVaR-PG (Section 3.3).
On the Maze domain at alpha=0.1, CVaR-VaR converges to a stable risk-averse policy while plain CVaR-PG fails to converge consistently across seeds (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

On LunarLander at alpha=0.2, CVaR-VaR attains approximately a 1.0 left-landing rate and the highest 0.2-CVaR return among compared methods, outperforming CVaR-PG and PCVaR-PG which converge more slowly (Section 4.2, Figure 3).

On InvertedPendulum at alpha=0.2, CVaR-VaR achieves both high expected return and strong risk aversion, whereas baselines RET-CAP and PCVaR-PG attain high return but fail to consistently avoid risk (Section 4.3, Figure 3).

2rHDObXYYH.text: ProbeLLM formulates failure discovery as a hierarchical Monte Carlo Tree Search with a macro regime for broad topic exploration and a micro regime for local perturbation refinement around promising seeds (Section 3.2).

On Deepseek-v3.2, ProbeLLM discovers 10 failure clusters with average size 10.80, versus only 4 clusters averaging size 30.25 from existing static benchmarks; on Claude-3.5-Sonnet it finds 11 clusters (avg size 13.55) versus 2 clusters (avg size 114.00) (Table 2).

ProbeLLM achieves lower noise rates (31.7-37.5%) than the AutoDetect baseline (45.6-60.9%) while also yielding higher cluster stability, with standard deviation of 3.2-4.3 compared to AutoDetect's 8.8-22.9 (Table 3-4).
ProbeLLM's average cost per discovered high-error test case is under $0.10 using GPT-5.2, with fewer than 6K total tokens consumed per dataset (Table 5).
Fine-tuning on 150-200 error-focused samples discovered by ProbeLLM improves performance on error-prone subsets without degrading general benchmark performance (Figure 9).
Appendix E provides regret bounds for the hierarchical MCTS framework establishing the feasibility of macro-micro probing under a local semantic coherence assumption (Appendix E).

OAM1jJsMGp.text: LOGDIFF's Proposition 3.1 shows that exact logical guidance scores reduce to linear combinations of atomic predicate scores when a Boolean formula's circuit representation has conditionally independent conjunctions and either conditionally independent or mutually exclusive disjunctions (Proposition 3.1).

On CMNIST/Shapes3D image generation with recursive logical queries (2-5 operators), LOGDIFF attains 94-98% conformity to the target formula versus 63-77% for a constant-mixing-weight baseline (Table 2).
On CelebA face generation with a negation query, LOGDIFF improves FID from 32.87 (constant-mixing baseline) to 23.61, while maintaining comparable AND/OR conformity to the baseline (Table 3).

On dual-target GRM5-RRM1 molecular generation, LOGDIFF achieves an average docking score of 73.20±3.18 under an AND query versus 71.87±3.33 for the DualDiff baseline, and 0.94±0.24 target separation versus 0.28±0.08 for DualDiff under an AND-NOT query (Table 5, Table 6).

Proposition C.2 establishes completeness: any Boolean formula compiles into an evaluable circuit under two distributional assumption classes—independent categorical groups or nested (taxonomy) predicates (Proposition C.2).

jW0Vcidbbw.text: Decrypto is a game-based benchmark with three roles—Alice (Encoder), Bob (Decoder), and Eve (Interceptor)—evaluating multi-agent reasoning and theory of mind over games of up to 8 turns (Section 2, Section 3).
In human-AI coordination trials, humans paired with Llama 3.1-70B win 46.67% of games, while the strongest LLM pairing tested, Claude 3.7 with extended thinking, wins only 20.0% of games (Table 1).

On the strong representational-change theory-of-mind task, all evaluated models score at or below 10% accuracy, and on perspective-taking, models predict Eve intercepts messages on ~95% of turns despite the actual interception rate being only ~52% (Figure 4).

Simple word-embedding baselines (GloVe: 9.0 miscommunications/9.0 interceptions; Word2Vec: 11.0/8.0) coordinate flawlessly in self-play but achieve miscommunication and interception rates comparable to or better than frontier LLMs such as Claude 3.7 (10.67/10.0) and DeepSeek-R1 (9.33/15.0) in cross-play (Figure 3).
Baseline coordination performance is sensitive to the hint vocabulary size parameter K, with coordination failures emerging at high K values in cross-play scenarios (Figure 2).

ibcZNZwKfZ.text: The method combines the Fully-Adapted Auxiliary Particle Filter (FA-APF), moment-matching posterior sampling (MMPS) for the optimal proposal distribution, and Tweedie's formula applied to a pretrained diffusion denoiser, requiring no additional training (Section 3).
On the Lorenz-63 system with N=256 particles, FA-APF achieves RMSE of 0.6, outperforming the Bootstrap Particle Filter (1.25) and matching the Ensemble Kalman Filter (0.72) (Figure 1, Table 1).

On incompressible Navier-Stokes flow reconstruction from a coarsened 128x128 grid with 6.25% observation coverage, FA-APF attains a skill score of 0.14 versus 0.19 for FlowDAS and 2.80 for the Bootstrap Particle Filter (Table 2).

The method is applied to the GenCast weather emulator on an O(10^6)-dimensional atmospheric state, maintaining ensemble spread while improving state estimates over 15-day forecast periods under sparse observation networks (Figure 3, Figure 4).

2kSBDoP1rE.text: Theorem 5.3 gives closed-form Lyapunov exponents governing the top singular values of masked (fixed-gates) linear networks, including a finite-depth correction term (d_{i-1}-d_i)/L (Theorem 5.3).

Theorem 6.1 proves that sufficiently strong spectral separation between consecutive singular values forces alignment of dominant singular vectors across the matrix product, yielding an approximately shared singular basis for intermediate Jacobians (Theorem 6.1).

Proposition 7.1 shows that combining depth-induced scaling and spectral separation recovers deep-linear-like singular-value training dynamics for fixed-gates networks without the balanced-initialization assumption required by prior analyses (Proposition 7.1).

Proposition 4.5 recovers the balanced deep-linear singular-value ODE of Arora et al. (2019), ds_k/dt = -L s_k(t)^{2-2/L} <grad_J L, u_k v_k^T>, as a special case of the paper's more general framework (Proposition 4.5).

On a synthetic rank-10 regression task with depth-10, width-64 networks, the top-15 Jacobian log-singular values during training converge toward the predicted theoretical Lyapunov exponents and finite-depth corrections (Figure 1, Figures 2-3).

Controlled MNIST experiments with square hidden layers of width n=128 validate the predicted emergence of depth-induced low-rank clustering and singular-vector alignment near a diagonal structure (Figure 4, Figures 5-6).

hsVaixFTaF.text: OT-GRPO, a self-supervised RL framework using consistency verifiers under geometric transformations (flips, crops, relation swaps), trains spatial reasoning without ground-truth labels and reaches 76.8% same-task accuracy on the 7B model versus 79.6% for the ground-truth-supervised accuracy-trained baseline, a gap of only 2.8 percentage points (Section 5.2, Figure 2).
On cross-domain transfer, consistency training achieves +14.7pp same-task gains versus +15.6pp for accuracy training, a 0.9pp gap (Section 5.2, Figure 4).
The consistency reward outperforms Visual Jigsaw by +3.6pp and four SSL4RL variants by +13-24pp, while trailing supervised accuracy training by only 2.7pp (Section 5.3, Figure 5).
Under label corruption, consistency training overtakes accuracy training trained on corrupted labels once noise reaches 20%, achieving 82.6% versus 79.6% (Section 5.4, Figure 6).

An ablation on pairing strategy shows the minimal-pairing OT-GRPO scheme achieves 76.8% self-task accuracy versus 74.7% for random pairing and 75.8% for one-to-all pairing, with under 1.5% added computational overhead (Section 5.6, Figure 8).

RG7maF4bGu.text: MFVI underestimates posterior variance in parameter space but can overestimate predictive variance relative to the exact posterior, with Theorem 3.7 proving that for test points drawn from the training distribution's empirical covariance, MFVI's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior (Theorem 3.7).

Lemma 3.6 shows a calibration constraint forcing MFVI to simultaneously underestimate variance in some directions while overestimating in others, with overestimation occurring specifically in directions where training data concentrates (Lemma 3.6).

In a pathological rank-1 training-data subspace scenario, as dimensionality increases the MFVI posterior's predictive variance converges to the prior variance, effectively discarding training information (Section 5.1).

Temperature-scaled posteriors (cold posteriors, T<1) correct the predictive-variance overestimation and improve in-distribution predictions, while T>1 benefits out-of-distribution performance, offering a novel explanation for the Cold Posterior Effect.

Experiments on basis function regression and UCI datasets show optimal temperatures below 1 for in-distribution test points and above 1 for out-of-distribution test points, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 6, UCI experiments).

fiTjjAgkiC.text: The cubature error of stationary MMD points vanishes faster than the MMD itself, formalized as |(1/n)∑f(x_i) − ∫f dμ| = o(MMD(μ,μ_n)) for integrands in the associated RKHS, a super-convergence property (Section 3).
Stationary MMD points achieve exact integration for a large linear subspace of the RKHS, and this subspace expands as sample size n increases (Section 3).

Theorem 4.1 gives a non-asymptotic finite-particle error bound for noisy MMD particle descent, decomposing error into an exponentially decaying optimization term and an O(1/√n) estimation term, with noise schedule β_t ∝ t^(−α) yielding an overall MMD convergence rate of O_P(n^(−1/2)) up to log factors (Theorem 4.1).

On a 2D mixture-of-Gaussians benchmark, stationary MMD points computed via noisy MMD particle descent empirically confirm exact cubature on the span of partial derivatives and match the predicted super-convergence rate (Section 5, mixture-of-Gaussians experiment).
On the OpenML House8L and Elevators datasets, stationary MMD points outperform kernel thinning, kernel herding, and support points as cubature methods (Section 5, OpenML experiments).

n6smFKXQWg.text: OTora's two-stage Reasoning-Level Denial-of-Service (R-DoS) attack achieves trigger success rates of 46-59% in black-box settings against GPT-3.5-Turbo and 92-97% in white-box settings against LLaMA-70B (Experimental Results section).

The attack inflates reasoning tokens by up to 10.8x and produces end-to-end latency degradation reaching 10+ seconds beyond baseline, while preserving task accuracy above 90% across configurations (Experimental Results section).

Stage I trigger optimization uses an attention-aware insertion-point scoring function (Equation 1) combining token-match metrics with attention-weight analysis, plus dynamic target co-evolution to adapt trigger phrases to the target agent's response distribution (Section on Stage I / Equation 1).

Stage II payload optimization uses an ICL-guided genetic search over a multi-objective score balancing reasoning-token inflation (S_RTI), task fidelity (S_FID), and cross-seed stability (S_STAB) (Section on Stage II).

Relevance-filtering defenses reduce attack effectiveness to 48% but drop benign task accuracy to 64%, and runtime-monitoring defenses cause 28% of legitimate tasks to terminate prematurely, showing fundamental defense trade-offs (Appendix, Defense Limitations).
Generating a successful attack requires 4,310 API calls and roughly $9.75 in API costs for Stage I trigger optimization, plus 900 agent rollouts for Stage II payload search (Table 6).

tZwqlXUc6t.text: The path-lifting map Φ(θ) provides a compact factorization of ReLU networks that exploits the rescaling symmetry whereby scaling a neuron's incoming weights by λ and outgoing weights by 1/λ preserves the implemented function, while gradient flow does not respect this symmetry across rescaling-equivalent parameterizations (Section on rescaling symmetry / path-lifting framework).

PathCond minimizes a logdet-divergence criterion aligning the path-kernel P_θ = ∂Φ(θ)∂Φ(θ)^T with the identity matrix, reformulated to require only the diagonal of G = ∂Φ(θ)^T∂Φ(θ), and solved via alternating minimization in O(n_iter·p) time (Algorithm/Section on PathCond method).

The path-kernel conditioning connects to the NTK via the factorization K_θ(x,x′) = Z(x,θ)P_θZ(x′,θ)^T, so improving P_θ's conditioning can enhance training dynamics without altering the learned function (Section on NTK connection).
On CIFAR-10, PathCond achieves 1.5x faster convergence to a target accuracy compared to standard training, without degrading final test accuracy (Section 5 / CIFAR-10 experiments).
PathCond is identified as most beneficial in two regimes: varying-width architectures and small-variance initialization (a ≪ 1) (Section 5, favorable regimes).

H8ozFYOmk8.text: Entropy-adaptive Gumbel-Sinkhorn computes a row- and column-dependent inverse-temperature field from the entropy of the current soft permutation, via Algorithm 1: compute a deterministic soft assignment, extract row/column entropies, derive adaptive inverse temperatures, then apply Sinkhorn with elementwise temperature scaling (Algorithm 1).

Proposition 1 establishes that uniform-temperature Gumbel-Sinkhorn faces an unavoidable trade-off since different rows/columns of the permutation resolve at different rates due to heterogeneous assignment uncertainty (Proposition 1).

On sorting tasks with high-ambiguity value ranges ([10,11]), entropy-adaptive temperature control outperforms global annealing as problem size increases, reaching a +0.122 Kendall tau improvement at n=300 (Section on sorting experiments).

On CelebA jigsaw reconstruction across puzzle sizes from 5x5 to 7x7, entropy-adaptive methods yield larger gains over mask-only baselines than global annealing does, with the advantage increasing with puzzle scale (Table 2).

On TSP instances from n=100 to n=1000, degree-violation-based temperature adaptation (DV-TA) consistently reduces both tour length and optimality gap relative to standard Gumbel-Sinkhorn across all sizes (Table 3).

Figure 2 shows entropy-adaptive temperature control attains a strictly higher Kendall tau than a global-temperature baseline at equivalent ambiguity levels, and Appendix K sensitivity analysis shows performance is stable across wide ranges of the entropy threshold H_0 and maximum boost b_max hyperparameters (Figure 2; Appendix K).

Na3YzWMXwz.text: The Oversight Game is formalized as a two-player Markov Game between an SI agent (choosing play/ask) and a human overseer (choosing trust/oversee), built on top of an immutable, pretrained base policy (Section 3).

Theorem 1 (Local Alignment Theorem) proves that when the Oversight Game forms a Markov Potential Game and the ask-burden assumption (Definition 2) holds, any increase in the SI's value from seeking greater autonomy cannot decrease the human's value (Section 4, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows that under a shared reward function combining a large safety-violation penalty, an asking cost, and an overseeing cost, every optimal equilibrium of the game is both safe and uses minimal oversight relative to the safety constraints (Section 5, Theorem 2).
Theorem 3 bounds the total cumulative performance loss from human corrections by ε/(1-γ), where ε is the maximum one-step performance loss any single correction can impose (Section 5, Theorem 3).

In a 15x15 Four-Rooms gridworld with a Q-learning-trained navigation policy (achieving ~5.17 discounted return) and 25% of states newly designated as taboo, independent policy-gradient training drives the safety violation rate down to zero while the SI learns to ask near danger and the human learns to selectively oversee (Section 6, Figures 2 and 3).

hzYEWSTOEA.text: UniRTL jointly pretrains a graph-aware tokenizer (combining a Graph Isomorphism Network with a Transformer encoder) on control-data flow graphs and RTL source code, using mutual masked modeling for fine-grained cross-modal alignment rather than contrastive alignment (Section 3).
Without netlist information, UniRTL achieves MAE of 0.3510 (area) and 0.3384 (delay) on post-synthesis performance prediction, outperforming StructRTL's 0.3649 (area) and 0.5414 (delay) (Table 1).
With netlist-based knowledge distillation, UniRTL further improves performance prediction to MAE 0.3362 (area) and 0.2302 (delay) (Table 2).
On natural-language RTL code retrieval, UniRTL attains an F1 of 0.662 versus 0.634 for GraphCodeBERT (Table 3, Section 4.3).
On functionality-equivalence retrieval, UniRTL attains an average precision of 0.745 versus 0.730 for GraphCodeBERT (Table 4, Section 4.4).

UniRTL is pretrained on a curated dataset of 132,008 RTL designs (38,888 successfully converted to CDFGs) in roughly 45 GPU-hours on two L40 GPUs, versus 70+ hours reported for larger prior models (Section 4).

Vr4YScS9DT.text: Applying a Generalizability Theory variance decomposition to Open LLM Leaderboard rankings across 4,000+ models attributes 43.1% of ranking variance to the benchmark facet versus 8.6% to the contributor/provenance facet and only 4.2% to architecture (Table 2).

A bifactor psychometric model best fits the dependence structure among benchmarks, revealing a dominant size-related general factor with benchmark-specific factors that are largely residual (Section 4.1).

The general-factor scaling-law slope is highly reliable across ecosystem controls (Rg = 0.97), whereas the manifest-score scaling-law slope is much less reliable (Rbeta = 0.53), indicating aggregate scaling trends are robust while raw benchmark-score scaling claims are not (Table 3).

Reranking models by the noise-controlled general factor instead of raw leaderboard scores leaves only about 1% of the original top-1% of models still in the top 1%, even though overall rank ordering remains broadly stable (Spearman's rho = 0.86) (Section 4.1).

Hc1G5UDPxc.text: AdaEraser computes a token-wise presence score p(i) as the cosine similarity between self-attention maps of the reference and denoising-process images within the masked region, and derives a suppression coefficient eta(i) = 1 - p(i) that adaptively relaxes attention suppression as the object disappears during denoising (Section 3.3, Equations 4-6).

On the Mulan and OABench benchmarks, AdaEraser (training-free) achieves FID 51.11 and LPIPS 0.203, improving over the training-free AttentiveEraser (FID 54.04, LPIPS 0.222) and the training-based RORem (FID 53.47, LPIPS 0.209) (Table 1, Section 4).

AdaEraser attains the highest human-rated preference score (AHR 7.08) and the best ReMOVE removal-completeness score (0.907) among compared methods, despite requiring no additional training (Table 1, Section 4).
AdaEraser operates on frozen pretrained diffusion backbones (SDXL, SD1.5, SD2.1, FLUX) with only about 15% additional computational overhead relative to AttentiveEraser (Section 4).

Appendix A provides a theoretical justification showing the presence score is monotonic under a mixture-model assumption and equivalent to KL-regularized attention optimization with exponential gating (Appendix A).

dkcdYllv9f.text: RO-HNN combines a geometrically-constrained symplectic autoencoder, using cotangent-lifted embeddings that guarantee symplecticity by construction, with a Geometric Hamiltonian Neural Network whose inverse mass-inertia matrix is parametrized via SPD networks respecting manifold geometry (Section 3).
On the 15-DoF coupled pendulum reduced to a 3-dimensional latent space, RO-HNN matches the accuracy of a 3-DoF oracle model and outperforms a full 15-DoF HNN baseline (Section 4.1, Table 1).

The geometrically-constrained symplectic autoencoder achieves symplecticity error of 0.0 +/- 0.0, compared to (1.67 +/- 0.35) x 10^-2 for a weakly-symplectic autoencoder baseline (Section 4.1, Table 2).

On the 90-DoF particle vortex system reduced to a 6-10 dimensional latent space, the Geometric HNN achieves roughly 40% lower prediction errors than a black-box latent dynamics baseline (Section 4.2, Table 3).
On a 600-DoF damped cloth simulation reduced to 6-10 latent dimensions, RO-HNN produces stable predictions extending roughly 625 times longer than the training horizon (Section 4.3, Table 4).

npsWK8rgYO.text: TreePO reduces GPU hours by 12% to 43% compared to sequential (non-tree) sampling, with the 'More Init Divergence' branch factor b=2 configuration cutting GPU hours from 6.40 to 3.65 hours (Table 2).

Tree-based sampling yields on average +40% trajectory-level sampling compute savings (TrajPS) and +30% token-level sampling compute savings (TokenPS) relative to standard rollout sampling (Section 4.1, Figure 4).
On the aggregated reasoning benchmark, TreePO Sampling with GRPO raises overall accuracy from 46.63% (standard GRPO) to 54.61%, with the More Init Divergence variant reaching 58.21% (Table 1).
On MATH, TreePO improves accuracy from 72.89% to 85.34% over the GRPO baseline (Table 1).

An ablation on advantage estimation shows simple subgroup averaging outperforms size-weighted variants, and a misaligned fallback estimator significantly degrades AIME accuracy (Section 4.2, Figure 6).
A segment-budget ablation finds the depth×segment configuration 14×512 achieves the best results, while 7×1024 underperforms, particularly on AIME (Section 4.3, Figure 7).

hwhvjhXC0m.text: PRISM reformulates iterative matrix-function algorithms as spectrum-adaptive polynomial approximation, fitting g_d(ξ;α)=f_{d-1}(ξ)+αξ^d to residual-matrix eigenvalues without requiring explicit spectral or singular-value bounds (Section 4.1).
Theorem 1 proves that for degree d=1 with α∈[1/2,1], PRISM's iterates converge quadratically, with error bound ||I−X_k^2||_2 ≤ ||I−A^2||_2^{2^{k-2}} (Section 4, Theorem 1).

PRISM uses randomized (oblivious subspace embedding) sketching with p ≥ 48(log n + log(1/δ) + log k + 27.6) Gaussian entries to reduce the per-iteration cost from O(n^3) to O(n^2 log n) while preserving a worst-case quadratic convergence rate (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).

When integrated into the Shampoo optimizer for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 and ResNet-32 on CIFAR-100, PRISM with 5 iterations matches or outperforms exact eigendecomposition in wall-clock time (Section 6.2, Figure 5).

When integrated into the Muon optimizer for a 10-layer, 1024-dimension GPT-2-Large model trained on 200M FineWeb tokens, PRISM-5 achieves a validation loss of 5.0251, versus 5.4523 for PolarExpress and 6.8689 for AdamW (Section 6.2, Figure 6).

On Gaussian random matrices with aspect ratios γ=n/m ∈ {1,4,50} and heavy-tailed Marchenko–Pastur matrices with condition numbers κ ∈ {0.1,0.5,100}, PRISM maintains stable convergence speed where the PolarExpress baseline degrades (Section 6.1, Figures 3-4).

cwztmjMQ77.text: CompPlan achieves a 201% relative improvement over action-level (primitive-action) planning on long-horizon tasks, averaged across policies and domains (Section 4.3).
CompPlan achieves an 89% relative improvement over Generalized Policy Improvement (GPI) on the same long-horizon evaluation (Section 4.3).

On antmaze-medium, CompPlan raises the CRL base policy's success rate from 0.88 to 0.97 and the GC-1S base policy's from 0.56 to 0.87; on antmaze-giant, CRL improves from 0.16 to 0.29 and HFBC from 0.42 to 0.79 (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On the cube-4 manipulation task, CompPlan reaches 67% success versus 9% for the hierarchical SHARSA baseline and 0% for HIQL; on antmaze-giant, CompPlan reaches 79% versus 56% (SHARSA) and 65% (HIQL) (Table 2, Section 4.3).

The horizon-consistency training objective reduces prediction error (Earth Mover's Distance) by 28% on antmaze-giant with GC-1S policies, though it yields only a modest 5% relative improvement in planning success rate (Table 3, Section 4.4).

RWQiuD7RHP.text: FunPhase reduces average joint position reconstruction error on the Dog dataset from 144cm (DeepPhase) to 61.4cm, and reduces orientation error on the 100Styles dataset from 0.35 (DeepPhase) to 0.10 (Table 1).

The learned phase manifold preserves a compact circular structure characteristic of cyclic motion, in contrast to the disorganized trajectories produced by DeepPhase and raw motion features (Section 5.1, Figure 3).
On the 100Style generation benchmark, FunPhase achieves the lowest FID of any compared method (0.51 vs. 0.91 for CAMDM) and the best foot-sliding score of 0.52 (Table 2, Section 5.2).

On the Truebones ZOO multi-skeleton benchmark, FunPhase achieves a coverage score of 96±7 versus 80±22 for AnyTop, and the best (lowest) intra-diversity difference of 0.06±0.03, demonstrating skeleton-agnostic generalization (Table 3, Section 5.2).

The architecture uses separate Perceiver encoder pathways for rotation and root-position features, an FFT layer to extract per-channel amplitude, frequency, phase-shift and bias parameters, and a cross-attention decoder enabling arbitrary spatio-temporal sampling for tasks such as super-resolution and body completion (Section 4.1).

hzp1UPH2F2.text: On GSM8K, a classifier probing SSAE-Llama step-level features predicts step correctness with up to 80.55% accuracy (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On MATH-500, a classifier probing SSAE-Qwen step-level features predicts step logicality with 76.56% accuracy (Table 1, Section 4.2).

SSAE features predict step length with RMSE of 1.59-2.10 and first-token perplexity of 1.46-4.09, versus 49.17-103.54 for token-level SAE baselines, indicating near-perfect modeling of surface-level generation randomness (Table 1, Section 4.2).
SSAE-guided weighted voting at inference time consistently outperforms Self-Consistency baselines across GSM8K, SVAMP, and MultiArith (Table 4, Section 4.5).

The extracted step-level features decompose into five interpretable reasoning categories: Reasoning, Calculation & Derivation, Final Resolution, Syntax & Structure, and Narrative & Explanation (Figure 3).

jmHpRMmcix.text: OTP-FM attains the best W1 distance of 0.675±0.019 on the EB 5D leave-1-out (L1O) single-cell RNA-seq benchmark among all compared methods (Table 3).
OTP-FM achieves 0.068±0.001 MMD on the EB 100D leave-2-out (L2O) benchmark, outperforming MMFM, 3MSBM, and piecewise CFM (Table 3).
On the Beijing Air Quality environmental dataset, OTP-FM reduces holdout W2 error to 17.28±0.56 versus 38.89 for MMFM, a roughly 4.5x improvement (Table 4).
On the Gulf of Mexico dataset OTP-FM achieves a holdout W2 error of 0.107±0.001 compared to 0.150 for MMFM (Table 4).
Ablations on EB 100D L2O show the best configuration uses a W2^2 potential with strength w=1000, a Gaussian temporal kernel with tau=0.33, and a sigmoid curriculum (Table 2).

Theorem 3.2 derives Euler-Lagrange equations characterizing the minimizers of the dynamic optimal-transport-potential (OTP) problem, and Proposition 4.2 bounds the end-to-end Wasserstein error of the learned marginals in terms of potential strength (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 4.2).

3XGJpH7Y1r.text: LE-SAM improves CIFAR-100 test accuracy over SAM by 1.34-1.49 percentage points across ResNet-18, WRN-28-10, and PyramidNet-110 backbones (Table 1).
On ImageNet, LE-SAM reaches 77.41% with ResNet-50 (vs 76.70% for SAM) and 79.31% with ResNet-101 (vs 78.54% for SAM) (Table 2).

LE-SAM fixes a loss-space perturbation budget sigma rather than a parameter-space radius rho, yielding a dynamic radius rho_t = sigma/(||g||_2 + varrho) that removes the gradient-norm-dominated term from the adversarial loss and leaves a curvature (Hessian) term (Section on LE-SAM mechanism).
Figure 3 shows LE-SAM produces lower maximum Hessian eigenvalues and Hessian trace than SAM at both epoch 100 and epoch 200, indicating flatter minima (Figure 3).
Figure 6 shows LE-SAM improves over the SGD baseline throughout training rather than only in late epochs, unlike standard SAM which is mainly effective late in training (Figure 6).
Under L-infinity PGD adversarial attacks, LE-SAM improves robust accuracy by 2.44-2.47 percentage points over SAM (Table 5).

1Rh9assFy5.text: Theorem 1 proves the proposed nested particle filter (NPF)-based Monte Carlo estimator of expected information gain (EIG) converges almost surely to the true EIG as the number of outer, inner, and particle samples go to infinity (Theorem 1).

The BAD-PODS algorithm combines stochastic gradient ascent (K gradient steps) on the design with NPF posterior updates including jittering and resampling, at linear time complexity O(t) across T experiments (Algorithm 1, BAD-PODS).
Table 1 reports total EIG (TEIG) for BAD-PODS versus random and static Bayesian experimental design baselines on a two-group SIR model over time horizons T=50 to 200 (Table 1).
On a moving source localization state-space model over T=10 to 50, BAD-PODS achieves higher total EIG than random and static design baselines (Table 1, Figure 4).
Figure 2 shows BAD-PODS allocates more experimental effort to group 1 in the two-group SIR model compared to baseline designs (Figure 2).
Figure 5 shows BAD-PODS yields lower pointing-error variance for sensor accuracy in the moving source experiment compared to baseline design strategies (Figure 5).

AdBlaX1peR.text: PESD-TSF reduces MSE and MAE by 14.96% and 14.87% respectively compared to DLinear averaged across the classic long-term forecasting benchmarks (Table 1).
PESD-TSF achieves average MSE/MAE of 0.343/0.370 on ETTm1, 0.244/0.304 on ETTm2, and 0.394/0.421 on ETTh1 (Table 1).
PESD-TSF attains state-of-the-art MAPE on the PeMS03, PeMS07, and PeMS08 short-term traffic forecasting datasets (Table 3).

Ablation removing the Multiplicative Periodic Gating component ('w/o Period') causes significant degradation on seasonal datasets, while removing the Regularized Latent Component ('w/o RLC') increases test error due to overfitting (Table 4).
On a high-dimensional mobility dataset with 5,826 variables, PESD-TSF uses 2.29M parameters, 8.37GB memory, and 15.56s per epoch, which is more efficient than iTransformer (Table 6).
Figure 5 reports a physical topology matching rate of 20.92% for the learned structure versus under 1% for a random baseline (Figure 5).

woBaLURRlx.text: Theorem 4.1 derives a closed-form solution for the optimal per-class reweighting coefficients w_c*(W) = [L̄(W)·L_c(W) + alpha·w_c(0)] / [L_c(W)^2 + alpha] by casting reweighting as an inverse problem (Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 3.2 shows that persistent loss imbalance across classes precludes convergence to the simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) structure characteristic of Neural Collapse (Theorem 3.2).
The proposed method improves CIFAR-100-LT (imbalance factor 100) accuracy from 41.6% (cross-entropy baseline) to 47.9% (Table 1).
Combined with GLMC, the method reaches 89.1% accuracy on CIFAR-10-LT (IF=100), 57.6% overall accuracy on ImageNet-LT, and 74.8% accuracy on iNaturalist 2018 (Tables 2-4).
Ablation shows the batch-wise reweighting component contributes +5.1% and the macro-level component contributes +3.8% to accuracy gains (Table 5).
Figure 2 shows the method reduces the NC2 and NC3 neural collapse metrics as well as the loss imbalance coefficient rho compared to baselines (Figure 2).

hYtsnVf0Bu.text: Theorem 4.1 proves the model's prediction on an alpha-renamed input is exactly the alpha-renamed version of the original prediction, guaranteeing invariance to renaming of interchangeable tokens by construction (Theorem 4.1).

The architecture creates k parallel embedding streams, one per interchangeable token, each holding actual and placeholder representations, then merges the streams via averaging before restoring true hidden states at interchangeable positions (Section 4.1, Section 4.2, Algorithm 2).
Combines per-stream self-attention with an aggregated-view attention mechanism to share context across streams (Section 4.2).
Achieves 98.03% correctness on propositional logic and 98.24% on LTL tasks, versus 93.25%/95.94% for a random-embedding baseline and 93.85%/97.96% for an alpha-renaming baseline (Table 1).
Achieves 100.0% alpha-covariance across all atomic proposition counts, compared with 92.98%-99.42% (random embedding) and 93.23%-99.60% (alpha-renaming baseline) (Table 1, Section 5.3).

Outperforms GPT-5.2 on LTL witness generation while running inference nearly instantaneously versus GPT-5.2's roughly 37 seconds per sample, and retains 98.24% accuracy on 50-token LTL formulas despite training on formulas up to length 35 (Section 5.3, Appendix J).

3wMM5NEFvr.text: Theorem 3.1 establishes a dimension-uniform bound on the KL divergence between the target Gaussian-mixture measure and the annealed Langevin dynamics (ALD) output under a prescribed annealing horizon T^d = ε^{-1} K_d, provided the sufficient spectral condition sum_i w_i sum_{j>=1} (lambda_j/gamma_j) log(1+lambda_j/sigma_ij) < infinity holds, linking smoothing eigenvalues lambda_j, preconditioner eigenvalues gamma_j, and mixture component variances sigma_ij (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

Section 3 gives an alternate sufficient spectral condition, sum_i w_i sum_{j>=1} lambda_j^2/(gamma_j sigma_ij) < infinity, for dimension-uniform stability of the annealed process (Section 3, Equation 8).

Section 4 decomposes the total sampling error into an initialization term (Proposition 4.3), a score-approximation term (Proposition 4.4) requiring a preconditioner spectrum decaying at rate at least j^{-3.5}, and an annealing-induced bias term from Theorem 3.1 (Section 4, Propositions 4.3-4.4).

Assumption 2.1 requires trace-class covariances for the infinite-dimensional Gaussian mixture target, ensuring the measures are well-posed on Hilbert space as dimension d grows (Section 2, Assumption 2.1).

Numerical experiments in Section 5 show that with diagonal preconditioner Gamma = Diag(j^{-1.5}) and smoothing covariance C = Diag(40*j^{-2.7}), the empirical KL divergence between the true mixture and the ALD output stays uniformly bounded for dimensions d in {1,...,75}, whereas a flat-spectrum preconditioner fails to maintain this bound (Section 5).

oiiXZJaODI.text: On an 850-patch ground truth security-bug dataset, BugStone's best rule configuration (using Llama-4) achieves 92.2% precision and 79.1% pairwise accuracy, where pairwise accuracy requires correctly labeling both the patched code as safe and the unpatched code as buggy (Section 5.3, Table 3).

The ground truth dataset is built from 1,910 patches drawn from 23 top-tier security conference papers, grouped into 80 recurring patterns totaling 850 patches with manually annotated coding rules (Section 5.2).

Table 3 compares six LLMs across six prompt configurations, finding that the formatted rule configuration yields the best pairwise accuracy and high precision across most models (Table 3, Section 5.3).

Applied to the Linux kernel, BugStone analyzes 148,664 candidate code pieces, flags 22,568 potential rule violations, and manual verification of 400 sampled cases confirms 246 true violations, a 61.5% confirmation rate, including 22 invalid pointer dereferences, 80 memory/resource leaks, and 85 type errors (Section 6.2).
The Linux kernel analysis consumes roughly 117 million input tokens and 99 million output tokens across the LLM calls (Section 6.2).

CswV8jTx2R.text: DAMP extracts six physically interpretable degradation prompts (High-Frequency Energy Ratio, Spatial Texture Uniformity, Spectral Curvature Mean, Spectral Curvature Standard Deviation, Gradient Standard Deviation, Spatial Correlation Coefficient) without relying on explicit degradation priors (Section 3.2).

The Degradation-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (DAMoE) module sits in the decoder of a U-shaped architecture and dynamically activates specialized experts conditioned on the degradation prompts, using a Spatial-Spectral Adaptive Module (SSAM) with learnable fusion weights lambda_s and lambda_c to balance spatial and spectral feature extraction (Section 3.3).

On the ARAD natural-scene benchmark, DAMP achieves 46.33 dB PSNR / 0.980 SSIM on 4x super-resolution, 33.84 dB / 0.929 SSIM on Gaussian deblurring (radius 15), and 42.86 dB / 0.974 SSIM on Gaussian denoising (sigma 70), with an average of 51.43 dB PSNR / 0.989 SSIM across five unified restoration tasks (Table 2).

In zero-shot generalization to unseen degradations, DAMP reaches 31.05 dB PSNR / 0.899 SSIM on motion deblurring (+0.52 dB over PromptIR) and 24.08 dB / 0.538 SSIM on Poisson denoising (+2.10 dB over the best baseline) (Table 3).

Ablations show the baseline alone reaches 45.82 dB PSNR, adding degradation prompts contributes +4.20 dB, and adding SSAM contributes a further +1.41 dB; degradation-prompt-based expert routing outperforms frequency-based routing by 3.71 dB, with the optimal MoE configuration using 4 total experts and top-1 routing (51.43 dB PSNR) (Table 4, Table 5, Table 11, Section 4.3).

DAMP requires 313.80 GFLOPs, 14.91M parameters, and 133.18ms inference time, among the lowest FLOPs/latency of compared methods while achieving higher restoration quality than the InstructIR baseline (Table 7).

nMGaOCVlDW.text: Theorem 1 proves that standard GRPO's outcome-reward-model (ORM) objective is mathematically equivalent to a PRM-aware RL objective in which step-level rewards are derived via Monte Carlo estimation over process sets (subsets of a trajectory group sharing identical prefixes) (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).

For each process set lambda, the induced step-level reward is the Monte Carlo estimate R-hat(lambda) = sum(r_i)/|lambda| over trajectories sharing that prefix, formalized via the process-set collection B(G) (Section 3.1).

Empirically, larger rollout group sizes yield fewer trivial (single-trajectory) process-set structures: about 0.2% (12 of 6,700) at group size 6 versus 0% (0 of 1,100) at group size 36, with path depth and intermediate-step proportions growing as validation accuracy saturates (Figure 2, Section 3.2).

lambda-GRPO rescales the token-level loss by the inverse of the process-set size, |lambda(i,t)|^{-1}, to equalize the contribution of each process set and correct a normalization flaw in the standard GRPO objective (Section 4, Equation 8).

lambda-GRPO reaches peak validation accuracy in under 50% of the training steps required by standard GRPO (Figure 3), and outperforms standard GRPO on 15 of 20 downstream benchmark cells in Table 1, including an AIME24 score of 0.4000 and MATH-500 score of 0.8660 for Qwen at beta=0.04 (Section 5, Table 1, Figure 3).

TI7Q2o6EIa.text: KromHC parametrizes residual mixing matrices as Kronecker products of smaller doubly stochastic matrices, reducing additional parameter count from mHC's 462K to KromHC's 240K at D=6 and from 1844K to 959K at D=12 for n=4 residual streams (Table 3).

Theorem 4.2 (Kronecker Closure) proves that the Kronecker product of doubly stochastic matrices is itself doubly stochastic, guaranteeing exact double stochasticity without relying on the iterative Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm used by mHC (Theorem 4.2).
At D=12 transformer blocks, KromHC achieves validation BPB of 0.862 and CORE score of 16.872, versus mHC's 0.861 BPB/16.023 CORE and mHC-lite's 0.864 BPB/13.217 CORE (Table 3).
On downstream commonsense reasoning tasks at D=12, KromHC reaches 47.7% average accuracy versus 46.2% for the standard residual-stream baseline (Table 4-5).
KromHC parameter overhead scales from 0.24M at n=4 residual streams to 2.67M at n=8 and 11.37M at n=16 (Figure 4, Table 6).
KromHC maintains lower gradient norms during training than both mHC and mHC-lite, indicating improved training stability (Figure 5).

BoQg93y6iT.text: Theorem 3.1 shows that when a digital twin's hypothesis space cannot perfectly capture the true system dynamics, minimizing standard simulation losses (MSE/NLL) can yield models that rank candidate policies incorrectly (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.3 proves that models with strictly better policy-ranking accuracy exist within the same hypothesis space as the simulation-loss-optimal model, motivating decision-targeted training (Theorem 3.3).

DT2's training objective combines a tanh-smoothed approximation of Kendall's rank correlation over policy pairs with a standard simulation loss, weighted as (1-λ)L_sim(θ) + λL_rank(θ), using Fitted Q-Evaluation to construct ranking targets without ground-truth returns (Section 3, Methodology).

Across six continuous control environments, DT2 reduces decision regret by 54% on average and improves Spearman rank correlation by 47% relative to conventionally trained digital twins, at the cost of only 17% higher simulation MSE (Empirical Results, continuous control).

In a cancer treatment case study, DT2 reduces decision regret from 59.56 to 26.96 and improves Spearman correlation from 0.10 to 0.64, with only a 2% degradation in simulation MSE (Empirical Results, cancer treatment case study).
DT2 preserves improved pairwise policy rankings not only for policies seen during training but also generalizes to unseen policies not used in training (Empirical Results, unseen policies).

xw09Zi47YC.text: The proposed GADL framework combines a dual-pass spectral encoder—concatenating low-pass GCN embeddings (using à_l = ½(Ã + D̃)) and high-pass GCN embeddings (using à_h = ½(D̃ − Ã))—with geometry-aware functional maps for cross-graph latent alignment (Section on Dual-Pass Encoder Architecture).

Latent space communication is regularized with a bijectivity loss ‖C12 C21 − I‖²_F + ‖C21 C12 − I‖²_F and an orthogonality loss ‖C12 C12ᵀ − I‖²_F + ‖C21ᵀ C21 − I‖²_F (Section on Latent Space Communication).
On the semi-synthetic Celegans benchmark with 5% structural perturbation, GADL maintains 71.74% ± 0.2 alignment accuracy, while baseline methods degrade to between 6.5% and 70% (Table 1).
On real-world graph alignment benchmarks, GADL achieves Hit@1 of 88.63% on ACM-DBLP versus T-GAE's 73.89%, and Hit@1 of 53.31% on Douban Online-Offline versus SLOTAlign's 51.43% (Table 2).
GADL generalizes beyond graph alignment, achieving 100% accuracy on DeiT-based CIFAR-10/CINIC-10 vision-language alignment benchmarks (Table 3).

Theorem 1 establishes that the dual-pass embeddings simultaneously preserve spectral locality and enhance node discriminability, and ablations removing the dual-pass encoder, bijectivity regularization, or orthogonality constraints each measurably degrade alignment performance (Theorem 1; Ablation Studies, Figure 3).

fJDZqUXTeE.text: GICDM adapts the Iterative Contextual Dissimilarity Measure (ICDM) to generative model evaluation by rescaling distances for generated points using only their distances to real-data neighbors, via δ^g_j = μ̄^{r,eq} / [(1/(K+1)) Σ δ^r_{NN_k(x^g_j)} · d_{x^g_j, NN_k(x^g_j)}] (Section on GICDM Algorithm, Step 2).

Proposition 4.1 and Corollary 4.2 establish that ICDM's average neighbor distance μ_i is a local density estimator, and that at convergence (μ_i ≈ μ̄ for all i) density gradients across the embedding are removed (Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.2).

Proposition 4.3 proves existence of a 'crossover dimension' d* at which the median K-nearest-neighbor distance equals the expected distance to the center, motivating GICDM's multi-scale filtering with two neighborhood sizes K1 and K2=10K1 (Proposition 4.3; Step 4 of GICDM Algorithm).

GICDM improves alignment with human error rates: Pearson correlation for Clipped Density on DINOv3 embeddings rises from 0.82 to 0.95 on CIFAR-10 and from 0.67 to 0.82 on ImageNet (Human Correlation results, DINOv3 embeddings).

On the Räisä et al. (2025) synthetic benchmark, GICDM improves Clipped Density's purpose-test pass rate from 8/14 to 10/14 and its bounds-test pass rate from 8/13 to 11/13, with similar gains for Clipped Coverage (Experimental Results, Synthetic Benchmark table).

Table 4 reports hubness levels (h1^5(1%) and A5 statistics) across embeddings, e.g. ImageNet with DINOv2 (dimension 1024) shows h1^5(1%)=4.4 and A5=0.10, versus a no-hubness baseline of h1^5(1%)≈2 and A5<0.01 (Table 4).

BgNkAHzveU.text: MetaEns constructs unsupervised outlier detection ensembles via offline meta-training of a two-part predictor (a classifier for improvement probability plus a regressor for gain magnitude) that simulates oracle-greedy ensemble construction on labeled meta-datasets, combined with family-level risk priors from lower-tail historical performance (Offline Meta-Training section).

Online model selection greedily expands the ensemble from a primary detector by maximizing a proxy utility combining predicted marginal gain, similarity-based redundancy discounting, and family-level risk regularization, stopping adaptively when no candidate has positive expected utility (Online Model Selection section).

Evaluated on 39 real-world datasets with 297 candidate detectors spanning 8 algorithmic families, MetaEns achieves average precision of 0.4308 ± 0.0064 versus ELECT's 0.4117, and average rank of 59.3 ± 6.96 versus ELECT's 83.2, using an average ensemble size of only 2.2 models (Experimental Results).
Statistical significance of MetaEns's improvement over all baselines is confirmed via paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (Experimental Results).

MetaEns's state representation uses only a normalized 61-dimensional score vector, enabling transfer across heterogeneous data modalities without assuming specific detector internals, and yields a +0.0257 average precision improvement over the strongest baseline on image/text transfer tasks (Key Technical Features; Experimental Results, transfer).

Performance degradation is observed on low-dimensional datasets with 13 or fewer features, where classical outlier detectors are already near-optimal, identified as a limitation (Identified Limitations section).

P82s05mnUY.text: A temporally-ordered ('sequential') pretraining regime matches shuffled-baseline accuracy on general language understanding benchmarks such as OLMES over 2.5T tokens (Section 5, Figure 3).

On the KairosQA benchmark of 7,167 Wikidata-derived subject-relation pairs spanning 2014-2025, the sequentially-trained model shows consistently more up-to-date and temporally precise knowledge than the shuffled baseline, evaluated via both cloze (4-choice) and generative (F1) formulations (Section 3, Figure 4).

The shuffled-pretraining baseline exhibits local accuracy maxima in 2015 and 2020 followed by a precipitous drop toward random accuracy by 2024, while sequential pretraining shows a 'recency peak' with improved factual freshness on 2023-2024 knowledge (Figure 1, Section 5).
At the final 2025 checkpoint, the sequentially-trained model surpasses larger open-source models on recent (2023 onward) factual knowledge despite comparable or smaller scale (Section 5.5, Figure 5).

Shuffled pretraining peaks in accuracy on older knowledge (attributed to increased factual repetition across the shuffled corpus), whereas sequential ordering trades this off for temporal freshness (Section 5, Table 2).

thVeEXPaSg.text: The Insertion Process is formalized via a proven bijection between insertion trajectories and permutations (Lemma 2.1) and a permutation-marginalized likelihood p(y_L) = sum over permutations of p(y_L, sigma) that factorizes across insertion steps (Theorem 2.2, Section 2.1-2.2).
Unlike fixed-length masked/order-agnostic diffusion approaches, the Insertion Process natively supports variable-length sequence generation via a learned insertion order (Section 2, Figure 2).

On Perfect maze planning at Hard difficulty, Insertion Process (IP) achieves 97.9% accuracy versus 25.2% for the LO-ARM baseline, and on Braided Easy mazes IP reaches 100.0% versus 96.2% for FO-ARM (Table 1).
On the Star Graph planning benchmark (degree-5 directed star graphs, arm lengths 6-12), IP attains 83.0% sequence accuracy versus 30.1% for LO-ARM (Table 2, Section 4.1).
On GuacaMol SMILES molecular generation, IP achieves 95.6% novelty versus 80.4% for FO-ARM, evaluated alongside validity, uniqueness, FCD, and KL-divergence metrics (Table 3, Section 4.2).

JmfyJj8aBf.text: ReTabSyn combines a base generative model with direct preference optimization (DPO) over preference-labeled synthetic tables to minimize the utility gap versus real data (Section 3.3-3.4).
On the Adult dataset under 1% class-imbalance, ReTabSyn reaches 0.906 PR-AUC versus 0.891 for the next-best baseline among GReaT, TVAE, TabSyn, PTA, and SynRL (Table 2, Section 4.3).
Under distribution shift on the Adult dataset, ReTabSyn achieves 0.863 AUC versus 0.851 for SMOTE (Table 3, Section 4.4).

ReTabSyn attains a correlation-similarity fidelity score of 0.83 versus 0.74-0.81 for competing methods across the 10 benchmark datasets (Adult, Bean, Churn-Modelling, HTRU2, Indian Liver Patient, Obesity, Shoppers, Magic, Titanic, Wilt) (Table 4, Table 1).

When given expert-specified categorical logical rules on the Adult dataset (e.g., relationship=Husband implies sex=Male), ReTabSyn achieves 0.00% constraint violations versus 1-3% for baselines, by incorporating constraint-related perturbations into DPO preference pairs (Appendix H.1, Section 3.4).

6up1qGJwYZ.text: Task-relevant information is distributed non-monotonically across network depth, with intermediate layers outperforming final-layer representations by up to 10% on downstream tasks, and this signal cannot be recovered by naive layer aggregation (Section 2.1, Section 6.1).

LOES (Layer-wise Optimal Embedding Selection) improves last-layer baselines substantially, e.g., raising CLIP-B/32 accuracy on Stanford Cars from 50.53% to 59.95% and ModernBERT accuracy on MTOP from 78.07% to 94.48% (Table 3, Table 5).

Average relative gains of LOES over baselines vary by pretraining paradigm: +7.8% for CLIP, +44.3% for MAE, +17.7% for ModernBERT, and +33.3% for Wav2Vec 2.0, indicating pretraining diversity shapes where task-relevant information concentrates across layers (Table 2, Section 6.1).
LOES outperforms both Greedy and Random-k layer selection baselines across classification, segmentation, and regression tasks (Table 6, Section 6.3, Figure 5).

On cross-lingual evaluation using the Amazon Massive Scenario dataset, LOES consistently selects layer 6 alongside the final layer across languages, suggesting mid-depth representations encode cross-lingually transferable structure (Figure 6, Section 6.1).

ySwE6xymYR.text: Theorem 2.3 proves exact recovery and data-efficiency for Neural-HSS: when the number of training samples N satisfies N >= C times the sum of per-block ranks r_i, global minimizers achieve zero generalization gap and recover the exact solution operator, with sample complexity depending only on the architecture's intrinsic dimensionalities rather than grid resolution (Section 2.2, Theorem 2.3).
Theorem 2.2 shows that regular convolutional operators on well-separated domains are Hierarchical Semi-Separable (HSS) approximable with rank r = O(log(1/epsilon)^D) (Section 2.2, Theorem 2.2).

On the 3D Poisson equation discretized over a grid of roughly 2 million points, Neural-HSS trained with only 16 samples matches the test-error performance that FNO requires 64 samples to reach (Section 3.1, Figure 3).
On the same 3D Poisson task, Neural-HSS completes training in about 2.5 hours versus roughly 6 hours for FNO and 42 hours for a ResNet baseline (Section 3.1, Figure 3).

Neural-HSS is benchmarked across a broad class of PDEs including 1D Poisson, Heat, Burgers, and Helmholtz equations and 2D Poisson variants, Helmholtz, Gray-Scott, and Navier-Stokes equations (Table 1, Table 2).

5hDvooOKUP.text: The adaptive orthogonal multitask estimator achieves exact recovery of the latent task clustering with high probability, established via Theorem 3.5 (Section 3, Cluster Recovery).
For tasks in cluster k with pooled sample size N_k, the estimator attains the rate ||θ̂_j − θ*_j||_2 = O_P(N_k^{-1/2}), matching pooled parametric convergence (Theorem 3.5, Section 3).
√N_k(θ̂_j − θ*_j) is asymptotically normal with covariance matching the oracle estimator that knows the true clustering in advance (Theorem 3.6, Section 3).
Extensions permit within-cluster heterogeneity bounded by ξ_k = O(N_k^{-1/2}) while preserving the estimation guarantees (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Section 3).

In simulations across three models (PLM, ATE, DID) and separation levels δ ∈ {1/3, 2/3, 1}, the method achieves Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) near 1, outperforming competing clustering approaches (Section 4.4).
On real electricity price elasticity data from 51 US states, the method recovers three clusters, e.g. Virginia at −1.138 ± 0.189 versus a 46-state cluster at −0.221 ± 0.009 (Table 1, Section 5).

h9g5j4JFv8.text: GaussTrace constructs provenance graphs among 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models without requiring model retraining or access to editing histories, using evidence-based LLM reasoning (Section 4).

On a benchmark of 44 3DGS models drawn from Mip-NeRF360, InstructNeRF2NeRF, and Deep Blending (scenes including bonsai, counter, face, playroom, drjohnson), GaussTrace achieves Vertex Overlap = 1.000, Edge Overlap = 0.890, and Vertex-Edge Overlap = 0.948 (Table 1, Section 5).

GaussTrace's Edge Overlap of 0.890 significantly exceeds the best baseline's 0.470 (ViT-B+MI), and its Vertex-Edge Overlap of 0.948 exceeds the best baseline's 0.751 (ViT-B+Integrity) (Table 1, Section 5).
With 20% distractor models injected into the pool, GaussTrace's performance degrades gracefully to VO = 0.940, EO = 0.795, VEO = 0.871 (Table 2, Section 5).

Removing chain-of-thought reasoning from the LLM component reduces Edge Overlap from 0.890 to 0.811, indicating CoT reasoning contributes materially to provenance graph accuracy (ablation, Section 5).

DdUriffJhf.text: Diag-CFM's target velocity field is provably equivariant to permutations of label and parameter coordinates, via its zero-anchoring strategy, whereas standard CFM lacks this property (Propositions 4.1 and 4.2, Section 4.1).

On the Gas Turbine Combustor task (design dimension P=6, L=3), Diag-CFM attains round-trip error 1.27×10⁻³, versus 1.85×10⁻² for standard CFM (~14.6× improvement) and 1.62×10⁻² for INN (~12.8× improvement) (Table 1, Section 5).
On the Unifoil Airfoil task (P=14, L=3), Diag-CFM attains round-trip error 1.68×10⁻³, a ~6.5× improvement over CFM (1.10×10⁻²) and ~2.3× improvement over INN (3.82×10⁻³) (Table 2, Section 5).

On the scalable DTLZ benchmark with design dimensions P ∈ {12, 24, 50, 100}, Diag-CFM's round-trip error ranges from 9.10×10⁻⁴ (P=12, ~35× better than CFM) to 5.26×10⁻³ (P=100, ~8.6× better than CFM) (Table 3, Section 5).
Under randomized coordinate orderings, Diag-CFM's round-trip error remains stable while standard CFM's error varies from 4.66×10⁻³ to 3.02×10⁻² (Figure 2 and Table 4, Section 5).
The Zero-Deviation uncertainty metric achieves out-of-distribution detection AUC of 0.96 on Unifoil and 0.75 on Gas Turbine Combustor, outperforming ensemble-based uncertainty methods (Section 5.4).

E1zQUGzfOZ.text: The modified Open-Closed List (OCL) search synergizes learned generative and value models via depth-partitioned selection, confidence-based node expansion, and a distributional heuristic model (Sections 4.1–4.4).

Under a 10-minute timeout across four combinatorial planning domains (Blocksworld, Logistics, Labyrinth, Sokoban) with 1000 test instances, OCLGen achieves shorter average plan lengths than MCTS with full rollouts and Best-of-N sampling, e.g. 43.88 vs. 54.56 vs. 61.56 steps on Blocksworld (Table 1, Section 5.1).
OCLGen achieves 99.7-100% completion rates across all four evaluated domains (Table 1, Section 5.1).

On instances with known optimal solutions, OCLGen finds optimal plans far more often than MCTS, e.g. 528/630 (83.8%) vs. 180/630 (28.6%) on Blocksworld and 988/1000 (98.8%) vs. 605/1000 (60.5%) on Labyrinth (Table 2, Section 5).

An ablation on Blocksworld shows removing depth partitioning increases average plan length from 43.88 to 48.81 steps, removing adaptive expansion increases it to 44.35, and removing the percentile heuristic increases it to 44.68 (Table 4, Section 5).

After 3 self-improvement refinement iterations, OCLGen on Blocksworld reaches 100% optimality (630/630) with average length 40.74, compared to MCTS's 71.4% optimality (450/630) with average length 44.89 (Table 6, Section 5).

BXiAOWdFT2.text: MotionMAR employs a temporal coarse-to-fine design with a hierarchical multi-scale VQ-VAE (Section 3.2.1) to disentangle global semantic motion from fine-grained jitter, combined with a Motion Autoregressive Network and a Motion Refinement Network (Sections 3.2.2–3.2.3).
On AMASS setting S1 (CMU, BMLrub, HDM05 split), MotionMAR achieves MPJPE of 2.82 cm versus 3.28 cm (SAGE), 3.71 cm (AGRoL), and 4.18 cm (AvatarPoser) (Table 1).
On the same setting, MotionMAR reduces Jitter to 5.17 versus 6.55 (SAGE), 7.26 (AGRoL), and 14.49 (AvatarPoser), and reduces Hand PE to 0.83 cm versus 1.18/1.31/2.12 cm for the baselines (Table 1).
MotionMAR's gains generalize to alternative evaluation settings S2 (root-joint observations) and a 12-dataset aggregation S3 (Tables 2 and 3).

Ablations show removing the Motion Refinement Network degrades MPJVE from 16.23 to 43.9, removing the Scale-Aware Control module raises Hand PE to 1.21 cm, and removing the multi-scale temporal design (TMT) raises Upper PE to 1.55 (Table 4).
MotionMAR runs at 61.76 FPS with 42.36M parameters and 1.47G FLOPs, indicating real-time deployment feasibility (Table 5).

3U1l24EDvL.text: The benchmark comprises 904 scenarios distributed across six alignment categories: Non-Manipulation (239), Honesty (217), Scheming (166), Safety (104), Corrigibility (103), and Robustness (75) (Table 1).
Human-AI judge agreement on scenario scoring reaches r=0.84 (p<0.001) in the calibration study validating the automated judge (Section 5).

Across 24 frontier models from 9 providers, alignment scores range from 2.92 to 4.66 on a 5-point scale, a 1.74-point (44% of scale) gap between the top performer (Claude 4.5 Sonnet at 4.66/5) and the lowest-scoring model (Table 3, Table 4).
Closed-source models average 4.05 versus 3.41 for open-source models, a 0.65-point gap (Table 4).

The first principal component of category scores explains 60.2% of variance and 95.3% of pairwise category correlations are positive, supporting a general alignment factor akin to psychometric g (Section 6, Figure 2).
Self-preservation is the sole behavior loading negatively (-0.113) on the general alignment factor, representing an exception to the otherwise unified construct (Figure 3).

DdNgzQfYE3.text: Theorem 3.5 proves that under Assumptions 3.1-3.3, the iterates of Algorithm 1 (Committed Q-learning) converge almost surely to Q*, with the resulting greedy policy optimal whenever the environment satisfies π-rewire-robustness (Theorem 3.5, Definition 3.7).
Rewire-robustness (Definition 3.7) is proven to be strictly weaker than the q*-realizability condition (Definition 3.4) used in prior work, admitting a broader class of environments (Section 3).

Committed Q-learning differs from standard Q-learning by committing to a single sampled action upon entering a feature and only resampling when the observed feature changes, rather than resampling every step (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
Quasi-Markov environments are defined via an entrance matrix Σ satisfying p̄₀=ΣΦp̄₀, providing a structural condition analyzed alongside rewire-robustness (Definition 4.1, Section 4).

In a corridor environment experiment, classical Q-learning fails to converge to the optimal reactive policy while Committed Q-learning converges quickly, illustrating the theoretical gap between the two algorithms (Section 4).

LJdacnMXkr.text: Theorem 4.1 shows a symmetric smoothing operator with positive coefficients can be rescaled by a diagonal matrix (via a symmetric Sinkhorn iteration) into a diffusion operator that is self-adjoint with respect to a mass-weighted inner product (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 proves that for Gaussian and exponential kernels, the Sinkhorn-normalized operators converge uniformly on bounded domains to continuous diffusion operators as sampling resolution increases (Theorem 4.2).
The symmetric Sinkhorn algorithm empirically requires only 5 to 10 iterations to reduce normalization error below 0.1% (Section 4/5, empirical convergence results).

The normalized operators simultaneously satisfy symmetry, mass conservation, entrywise positivity, and spectral damping (eigenvalues in [0,1]), properties not jointly satisfied by standard row- or symmetric-normalization schemes (Theorem 4.1).

The method is demonstrated on point clouds, sparse voxel grids (jaw bone geometry), and Gaussian mixture models with covariance-aware kernels, showing Laplacian-like smoothing on each irregular data type (Section 5, experiments).

Shape analysis experiments on the Armadillo mesh show spectral distributions remain consistent across sampling modalities, with eigenvalue divergence appearing only at scales matching sampling resolution, validating the Theorem 4.2 convergence guarantee (Section 5).

YMbE22oWDk.text: KREPES introduces Representer Landmarks, expressing the learned SSL latent space via influence scores of a subset of unlabeled training examples, formalized as a sample-specific influence score ι_{l→t} (Section 5.1).

A Conceptual Influence Profile analysis using concept activation vectors identifies which landmark concepts (e.g., a 'Sea' concept) drive individual predictions, visualized in Figures 2 and 3 (Section 5.2, Figure 2, Figure 3).

On the Adult-1M dataset, the audit reveals the SSL representation relies on demographic proxies correlated with income, exposing algorithmic bias directly from the unsupervised latent space (Section 5, Table 1).

The Nyström-based optimization (with principal-component initialization and second-order preconditioning) scales KREPES to Adult-1M, Higgs-1M, CoverType-581k, and CIFAR-10-50k, reporting downstream accuracy and training time for each (Section 3, Section 4, Table 1).
An ablation in Appendix D compares landmark selection methods (k-means++ vs. leverage-score sampling) on MNIST, reported in Table 5 (Appendix D, Table 5).

wRVTDcEMv8.text: Theorem 4.2 proves the original DeepSets aggregation (Equation 4) is discontinuous in the natural any-dimensional topology because the infinite sum can diverge when the inner function ρ decays arbitrarily slowly, so standard DeepSets fails to be universal (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.1.1).

Theorem 4.9 proves standard message-passing GNNs fail any-dimensional universality because their pointwise nonlinearities are discontinuous in the cut metric, since a pointwise map is continuous with respect to the cut norm only if it is linear (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.2).
A modified DeepSets-infinity architecture (Equation 5) that reweights terms by an ell_p norm factor is proven continuous and universal on ell_p(R^k) sequence space (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).

A measure-space variant DeepSets-bar-infinity (Equation 6), replacing the sum with a normalized integral under a growth condition, is proven universal on the Wasserstein space of probability measures (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6).

A homomorphism-density-basis architecture (Equations 9-10) is proven continuous and universal on graphon space with the cut metric, restoring universality for graph architectures (Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10, Section 4.2).

A two-stage architecture combining a Gram-matrix map (Equation 12) with Invariant Graphon Networks (Equation 14) is proven universal on bounded point-cloud orbits under the group action (Theorem 4.12, Theorem 4.13, Section 4.3).

kHB8m3ojGe.text: Latent-step budgets in latent chain-of-thought models (Coconut, CODI) function as distinct, manipulable causal roles rather than homogeneous extra depth, as shown via the intervention-based protocol (zero/mean/gaussian ablations) across RQ1-RQ3 (Section 2, Figure 2).

Step-wise necessity, measured by decision-instability flip rates under intervention, is higher on GSM8K (approximately 0.1-0.2+) than on CommonsenseQA (around 0.1 or below), and Coconut shows higher flip rates than CODI under matched backbones (Section 3, Figure 3).

Early-stop decoding shows CommonsenseQA correctness saturates within a few latent steps while GSM8K continues improving up to k=6, revealing a gap between early output-level commitment and later representational commitment (Section 3, Figure 4).

Explicit chain-of-thought maintains high locality (>=0.6) with low span in influence graphs, whereas latent reasoning models show substantially lower locality and higher span, dominated by non-local skip connections (Section 4, Figures 5-7).

Probe-based readouts on StrategyQA reveal sustained representational superposition with late-step collapse, in contrast to teacher-forced readouts which show uniformly low superposition scores throughout the trajectory (Section 5, Figure 8).
Robustness of the step-wise sensitivity findings is confirmed using six intervention operators (zero, mean, mean_step, and gaussian variants) in an ablation reported in Appendix A.2.

rIbK1X14la.text: Recovering a graph with m' relations in d_model-dimensional embeddings requires total key dimension D_K = Θ(m' log m' / d_model), established as a lower bound (Section 7) and matched by a constructive upper bound (Section 4).
For permutation graphs (m' = m), the capacity requirement simplifies to D_K = Θ(m log m / d_model) (Section 4/Section 7).

Multi-head attention's advantage arises because splitting into heads reduces the effective block size B, shrinking the noise term N3(B) ≍ (B/d_model)√(d_k log m) that governs interference from superposition (Section 5).

Empirical scaling of the optimal total key dimension matches theory: D_K* ≈ 1.19·(m log m/d_model) with R²=0.944 (R²=0.992 after excluding three outlier points), and the optimal head count scales as h* ≈ 1.65(m/d_model) − 6.64 with per-head widths d_k* in [5,24] (median 11) (Section 6).

The multi-head capacity advantage persists in a fuller Transformer setting with softmax normalization, value routing, and frozen GPT-2 embeddings, since the analysis establishes capacity is purely key-query driven (Appendix C).

Capacity requirements are largely insensitive to context length, tested over sequence lengths ℓ ∈ {16,32}, with only modest degradation when evaluating at longer lengths than training (Section 6.1, Appendix A.3).

GdqrQ75Gg8.text: Under convex fairness constraints with no specific structural assumptions on the feasible fairness region, the principal's accuracy optimality loss is upper-bounded by 4(||w*||_2 + 1) (Section 3, Table 1).

When the feasible fairness region is an ellipsoid (Property 3.3), the accuracy optimality loss bound tightens to 4(||w*||_2 + 1) while the social welfare loss bound becomes √2, versus 2||w̃||_2 in the general convex case (Section 3, Table 1).

For nonconvex fairness constraints, the paper bounds the optimality loss incurred by using a convex restriction in terms of a Lipschitz constant L and diameter D, showing the bound decreases as L decreases (Section 4).

Proposition A.1 upper-bounds the optimality loss between the unconstrained and fairness-constrained equilibrium as a function of the fairness tolerance parameter β and system parameters (Appendix, Proposition A.1).

In experiments on the Education group split, when desirable attributes align with underlying group disparities among heterogeneous agents, enforcing fairness produces the largest accuracy loss compared to other splits (Section 5.1).

With non-uniform agent costs (A1 = I, A2 = 2A1), the Education split retains the same qualitative accuracy-fairness tradeoff shape, but the maximum β at which optimality is recovered increases (Section 5.1).

ELiOhFJIPh.text: Prototype Transformer (ProtoT) replaces self-attention with a prototype-based mixer using R learnable prototype vectors that communicate via write and read gates, scaling linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically (Section 3, Equations 1-2, Figure 1).

On long-context scalability, ProtoT reaches 90.5 test perplexity versus LLaMA's 78.7 in the default setting, and 29.5 versus LLaMA's 25.8 and Mamba's 26.5 at large scale, remaining 3.7-4 points behind LLaMA while still scaling well with model and data size (Table 1).
On GLUE downstream tasks, ProtoT achieves 67.6% average score versus LLaMA's 71.6%, with competitive performance on individual tasks such as MNLI (75.3% vs. 79.8%) (Table 2).

Prototypes automatically capture nameable concepts (e.g., 'woman', 'female') during training, and targeted disruption of a specific prototype (layer 9, prototype 7) reduces the probability of the word 'women' by 17.80% in relevant contexts, confirming causal concept localization (Section 5.1, Table 6).
LLM-aided evaluation shows ProtoT achieves higher disentanglement and topic coverage scores than a standard Transformer baseline (Figure 2).

ProtoT achieves higher inference throughput (25.2 iterations/second at batch size 32) than Mamba (11.9) and DeltaNet (3.5), and shows greater robustness under lexical perturbations such as synonym substitution and spelling variation than LLaMA (Appendix A.6; Table 3).

F2zHYjBAEv.text: HugRAG outperforms competitive graph-based RAG baselines (including CausalRAG and LeanRAG) across 11 datasets spanning HolisQA (5 domains) and standard QA benchmarks, using F1, context recall, and answer relevancy metrics (Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).
On the HolisQA Medicine domain, HugRAG attains 36.45 F1, 69.91% context recall, and 60.65% answer relevancy, exceeding CausalRAG's 31.12 F1 and LeanRAG's 34.25 F1 and 60.43% context recall (Table 3).
On standard QA benchmarks, HugRAG achieves 64.83 F1 on HotpotQA, 49.50 F1 on NQ, and 38.40 F1 on MS MARCO (Table 4).

HugRAG explicitly models causal relationships through hierarchical causal gating (edge weight w=1.2 for causal gates, versus w=1.0 for hierarchical links and w=0.8 for structural edges) across L=3-4 hierarchy levels built via Leiden algorithm partitioning, using seed budgets K_L=3 and K_0=3 (Section 4).
HugRAG maintains stable retrieval quality across a wide range of context scales, from 5K to 1.5M characters, in a scalability analysis (Section 5.4, Figure 4).
An ablation study isolates the contribution of HugRAG's causal gating and hierarchical components to overall performance (Figure 3).

GPrlMiGg2w.text: BFS-Prover-V2 achieves 95.08% accuracy on the miniF2F test set and 95.49% on the validation set (Table 1).
BFS-Prover-V2 achieves 41.4% accuracy on the ProofNet test set, demonstrating generalization from high-school competition training data to library-dependent undergraduate problems (Table 1).

Adaptive tactic filtering based on perplexity discards both the low-perplexity tail (already-mastered tactics) and high-perplexity tail (noisy, suboptimal tactics), training only on the central 'goldilocks zone' of the perplexity distribution (Section 2.3.1).

A periodic 'soft reset' retraining procedure re-solves past problems with the current expert, curates data with enhanced filtering, and retrains from the base checkpoint whenever performance plateaus, enabling monotonic improvement across dozens of training rounds (Section 2.3.2, Figure 3).

A planner-prover multi-agent architecture uses a general-purpose planner (Gemini2.5-pro) to propose intermediate subgoals for a specialized best-first-search prover, with dynamic replanning triggered when the prover gets stuck (Section 2.4.1, Section 2.4.2).
Multiple parallel Prover instances coordinate via a shared subgoal cache that terminates redundant search once any agent finds a valid proof for a subgoal (Section 2.4.3).

u7kOAJ9uH7.text: The paper unifies adversarial robustness analysis across dense retrievers, rerankers, and reward models under a shared 'text scoring' framework where attacks are treated as score-manipulation problems (Section 3).

Five adversarial training formulations are compared: PGD embedding-space perturbation, rudimentary single-step string manipulation, HotFlip gradient-guided token swaps, content injection training, and a combined method (Section 3.3).

PGD-based adversarial training shows weak, mixed, or even adverse correlation with robustness to injection attacks, revealing a generalization gap between perturbation-based and injection-based adversarial training (Table 1, Section 5.1).

Combined adversarial training improves effectiveness alongside robustness: retriever effectiveness rises from 57.0 to 57.4 and reranker effectiveness from 61.5 to 62.4, while reward model effectiveness changes only marginally from 63.3 to 62.9 (Table 2).

Adversarially trained reward models used in RLHF yield policies with lower per-token KL divergence and a preference margin improvement of +0.07 at medium adversarial-training strength and +0.10 at high strength over baseline reward models (Section 5.2, Table 3).

pyJoRYaVoG.text: CPD (Change Point Detection) applies a one-sided Page-CUSUM detector to standardized per-token entropies, accumulating via W_t+ = max{0, W_{t-1}+ + Z_t - k}, to flag optimization-based adversarial suffixes (Section 2.3).

On LLaMA-2-7B, CPD achieves AUROC 0.88 and F1 0.82, compared to the best windowed-perplexity (WPP) baseline's AUROC 0.77 and F1 0.74, and a global perplexity baseline of AUROC 0.46 (Table 1, Section 3.3).

At the F1-optimal threshold on LLaMA-2-7B, 79.55% of CPD's trigger positions fall inside the adversarial suffix with 0% boundary-straddling alarms, versus 16.99%-46.25% suffix-localized triggers and 12.86%-37.92% boundary-straddling alarms for WPP variants (Table 3, Section 3.4).

In a hybrid gating deployment with 4.2% adversarial prevalence, CPD reduces LLaMA Guard-1 invocations by 42.2% while preserving F1 0.82, compared to only 18.2% call reduction for WPP at matched detection quality (Table 5, Section 3.5).

An ablation isolating the sequential CUSUM accumulation mechanism shows it improves F1 from 0.699 (windowed entropy) to 0.818 (CUSUM on entropy) on LLaMA-2-7B, confirming the sequential accumulation—not the entropy signal alone—drives detection gains (Table 2).

S3m1tSp8F4.text: R2-Router reformulates LLM routing by treating output token length as a controllable variable, modeling each LLM's quality-cost tradeoff as a curve rather than a fixed point (Section 4.2).

Theorem 4.3 (Optimization Dominance) proves that the reasoning-based routing search space achieves weakly higher optimal performance than the reactive routing search space, S*(reasoning) >= S*(reactive) (Theorem 4.3).
R2-Router attains approximately 0.8 average quality at roughly 0.5x10^-3 cost, while competing routers require 4-5x that cost budget to reach comparable quality (Section 6.1, Figure 5).

Constraining the output length of a more powerful but costlier LLM (e.g., Qwen3-235B) allows it to deliver superior quality at reduced cost compared to routing to a weaker unconstrained model (Figure 2).
On R2-Bench, the oracle policy achieves AUDC 0.98 versus 0.85 for the SPROUT baseline, and improves Query-Normalized Cost (QNC) from 0.18 to 0.04 (Section 3.2).
R2-Router achieves a Query-Normalized Cost of 0.25 versus 0.68 for the CARROT baseline among prompted routing methods (Table 5).

Q6Kt8mROxg.text: Proposition 4.1 shows that when approximating a bimodal optimal joint behavior policy with independently factorized per-agent policies, the total variation distance to the true joint policy approaches 1 as the number of agents increases (Proposition 4.1).

OMSD decomposes the joint behavior-policy score function into sequential per-agent conditional score terms mu-hat_i(a_i | s, a_{i-}) using pretrained diffusion models, used only for computing regularization gradients rather than for action sampling, avoiding out-of-distribution joint actions at inference (Section 4.3, Equation 9).

On the MPE benchmark, OMSD attains normalized scores of 120.1 +/- 4.1 on Cooperative Navigation, 133.9 +/- 7.4 on Predator-Prey (medium), and 160.3 +/- 4.1 on World (random), for an average improvement of 26.3% over prior offline MARL methods (Table 1).
On the MAMujoco 2-agent HalfCheetah task, OMSD achieves 119.0 +/- 1.3 on the Expert dataset and 78.9 +/- 4.4 on the Medium-Replay dataset (Table 1).
