Propositions 4.2 and 4.3 show that independent-learning and IGO-based CTDE approaches produce biased behavior regularization because individual score gradients diverge from the true joint-policy gradient under multimodality (Proposition 4.2, Proposition 4.3).

An ablation across MAMujoco dataset qualities shows OMSD's sequential score decomposition consistently outperforms BRPO-Ind and BRPO-IGO baselines, confirming that ignoring multimodal coordination degrades performance (Figure 3).

2bKKamEtto.text: On Pythia-1B pretraining, AC-ODM-410M reaches the optimal validation perplexity that ODM achieves using 71% fewer training steps (Figure 1, Section 4).
AC-ODM-410M attains 0-shot MMLU accuracy of 0.2998 versus ODM's 0.2351, a 27.5% relative improvement (Table 1).
AC-ODM-410M achieves HumanEval pass@1 of 0.7264 versus ODM's 0.3251, a 2.23x relative improvement (Table 1).
AC-ODM-410M requires only 28.82% of ODM's training steps to reach equivalent validation perplexity while adding just 0.4% wall-clock overhead, yielding a 1.47x net speedup (Table 2).
Relative to the baselines TPW, ODM, and AC-ODM (simultaneous-training variant), AC-ODM-410M saves 80%, 71%, and 64% of training steps respectively at matched perplexity (Section 4).

QIBu6vtRMI.text: The exact algorithm for finding an optimal polytree with bounded in-degree k runs in time O((2+epsilon)^n * |I|^O(1)) for arbitrarily small epsilon > 0 (Theorem 3.3).
This improves on the previously fastest known exact algorithm, which runs in time O(3^n * |I|^O(1)) matching Gruttemeier et al. (2021a) (Theorem 3.1).

A polynomial-time algorithm achieves a (k+1)-approximation to the optimal polytree score for arbitrary scoring functions with in-degree bound k, and this approximation ratio is shown near-optimal under the Unique Games Conjecture (Theorem 4.1).
For additive scoring functions, a polynomial-time algorithm achieves a 2-approximation to the optimal polytree score (Theorem 4.2).

The near-tightness of the (2+epsilon)^n exact-algorithm running time is established via a reduction from k'-Set Cover, showing no improvement below (2+epsilon)^n is possible under standard complexity assumptions (Theorem 3.5).

Vuaq1qXCki.text: On MBPP, PSV-Verus achieves pass@1 of 36.78% versus 3.83% for the rejection fine-tuning (RFT) expert-iteration baseline, a 9.61x improvement (Table 1).
In the Dafny2Verus test-time-training setting, PSV-Verus reaches 65.63% pass@1 versus 24.06% for the inference-only AlphaVerus baseline, a 2.73x improvement (Table 1).
On HumanEval, PSV-Verus attains 19.07% pass@1 versus 7.24% for AlphaVerus, a 2.63x improvement (Table 1).
Increasing the number of self-play-generated questions per iteration from 1k to 32k raises MBPP pass@1 from 22.3% to 44.3% and HumanEval pass@1 from 13.9% to 26.3% (Figure 5).
With a fixed budget of 1k questions, increasing the number of self-play training iterations from 1 to 5 raises pass@1 from 21.0% to 42.3% (Figure 6).

Ablating formal verification from the proposer-solver self-play loop causes a 51.5% drop in pass@1 on Dafny2Verus, while removing difficulty-awareness and diversity components reduces average performance by 5.6% and 10.6% respectively (Table 2).

NiqWdmrxwn.text: On the Tahoe-100M dataset, scDataset achieves a 48x single-core throughput speed-up over AnnLoader true random sampling at block size 64 and fetch factor 64 (Figure 2).
scDataset achieves a 27x single-core speed-up over HuggingFace Datasets at block size 64 (Figure 3), and an 18x speed-up over BioNeMo at block size 64 (Figure 4).
In multiprocessing mode (block_size=4, fetch_factor=16, num_workers=12), scDataset reaches roughly 2,593 samples/sec versus AnnLoader's 20 samples/sec in single-core mode, a 129x speed-up (Table 2).

Despite the large throughput gains from block-based fetching, scDataset's optimal multiprocessing configuration maintains a plate-label sampling entropy of 3.59 versus 3.63 for true random sampling, indicating near-equivalent sample diversity (Table 2, Figure 5).

9bLiqb6Vec.text: SpanNorm modifies the second residual connection of a PostNorm block to add the raw block input X'_l rather than the intermediate representation Y_l, creating a residual path that spans the entire transformer block (Equations 5-6, Section 3.2).

On a 5B-parameter dense model trained on 200B tokens of SlimPajama, SpanNorm achieves an average downstream accuracy of 66.6 versus 64.1 for PreNorm, and a Wikitext perplexity of 11.8 versus 12.5 (Table 1).
Standard PostNorm training fails to converge (diverges) at the 5B and 6.5B model scales, whereas SpanNorm trains stably at both scales and at up to 128 layers (Table 2, Table 3).

On a 6.5B-parameter, 128-layer model trained on 400B tokens, SpanNorm attains average downstream accuracy of 68.4 versus 64.4 for PreNorm and 66.0 for Mix-LN, while HybridNorm fails to converge (Table 3).

Under Theorem 4.1, stable training as depth L grows requires the variance introduced by each FFN sub-layer to scale as O(1/L), motivating a Scale Init strategy that sets W2 and the attention output matrix W_O to O(1/sqrt(L)) initialization (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
On the MoE-A2.4B-16B architecture trained on 200B tokens, SpanNorm improves average downstream accuracy by 1.2 points over PreNorm (66.3 vs 65.1) (Table 1).

yE3zbIOW3e.text: In random features ridge regression, a strong student trained on a weak teacher's labels can achieve an improved test-error scaling law relative to the teacher, contrasting with prior null results for ridgeless linear regression (Theorem 4).

Under power-law source/capacity conditions (spectrum decay alpha>1, target coefficient decay k^{-(1+2*alpha*r)/2}), the optimal student scaling exponent is gamma_{s,*} = 2*alpha*(r wedge 1) / (1 + 2*alpha*(r wedge 1)) (Theorem 4).

When a sub-optimally regularized teacher is variance-dominated (V_t >> B_t), a properly tuned student can attain the minimax-optimal rate even though the teacher's test error does not decay with sample size (Corollary 2).
When the teacher is bias-dominated, a student with larger model width than the teacher can still improve the scaling law provided the capacity condition r > 1/2 holds (Corollary 3).

Scaling-law improvement from weak-to-strong training is only possible when z_t > z_s, meaning an optimally-tuned teacher cannot be outperformed by a student trained purely on its labels (Corollary 1).
Theoretical deterministic-equivalent predictions for student test error closely match empirical results on synthetic single-index targets and on MNIST with tanh/erf nonlinear feature maps (Figure 1).

CbXjg2h6F6.text: Sparse autoencoders reveal that out-of-distribution typo-corrupted inputs cause transformers to activate roughly 30% more internal concepts on average than clean inputs at 100% typo rate (Section 4.1, Figure 1B).
With 5% typo-corrupted words on MMLU, Llama 3.1 8B accuracy falls from 66.7% to 51.01% and GPT-4o mini falls from 82.10% to 74.85% (Section 4.2, Figure 2A).

A composite 'energy score' combining SAE reconstruction error and concept activation count (L0) distinguishes in-distribution from OOD samples with low correlation (|r| < 0.09) to entropy-based OOD scores (Section 3.5).
Fine-tuning on SAE-identified high-energy (top-decile) OOD examples reaches comparable loss in two-thirds of the training steps needed for low-energy (bottom-decile) examples (Section 5, Figure 3A).
SAE-informed LoRA alignment of feature activations reduces successful jailbreaks from 46% to 7% on test prompts while lowering MMLU accuracy by only 0.09% (Section 6.1, Figure 4B).
On the noisy Spoken-SQuAD benchmark, SAE-aligned models improve exact-match accuracy from 49.45% to 58.33%, nearly closing the gap to clean-text performance (Section 6.2, Table 2).

w8YVelCdUh.text: DRIFT-BENCH is a diagnostic benchmark that introduces a four-category input-fault taxonomy (Flaw of Intention, Flaw of Premise, Flaw of Parameter, Flaw of Expression) grounded in Gricean, speech-act, and interactional communication theory to test agentic pragmatics via multi-turn clarification (Section 2).
Frontier LLM agents show an average performance degradation of roughly 44.29% under Intention-flaw faults and 49.91% under Parameter-flaw faults in state-oriented (white-box) environments (Table 2).
In service-oriented (black-box API) environments, average performance degradation under Intention-flaw faults is about 18.13%, smaller than in state-oriented settings (Table 2).
Agents exhibit an execution bias, proceeding with risky actions without requesting clarification in roughly 70% of fault cases (Introduction, Table 2).

A 'clarification paradox' emerges: multi-turn interaction improves outcomes in transparent state-oriented (white-box) environments but harms performance in black-box service-oriented environments due to context overload (Section 3, Table 2).

xgK2ePxFO1.text: Deep Incentive Design (DID) uses game-theoretically equivariant neural networks composed with pretrained Differentiable Equilibrium Blocks (DEBs) that select the unique maximum-entropy correlated/coarse-correlated equilibrium, giving local Lipschitz continuity and near-everywhere differentiability for gradient-based training (Section 4).

In multi-agent contract design experiments, DID improves average principal utility by 0.33 units under CCE and 0.25 under CE using DEB equilibria, compared to smaller gains of 0.20 (CCE) and 0.05 (CE) when evaluated at exact ECOS equilibria (Table 1(a), Section 5.3).

In inverse equilibrium problems, DID achieves an average KL divergence of 0.043 (CCE/DEB) and 0.056 (CE/DEB) between generated payoffs and target equilibria, versus a 0.400 baseline (Table 1(b), Section 5.4).
In machine scheduling, DID reduces average makespan by 0.211 units (CCE/DEB) and 0.339 units (CE/DEB) relative to no intervention (Table 1(c), Section 5.5).

A single trained network generalizes across game sizes ranging from 2x2 to 16x16 action spaces without retraining, using equivariant architectures whose parameter count depends only on channel dimensions rather than the full joint action space (Section 4, Figure 1).

taH7v2Qy8M.text: Vanilla reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) on 3DSRBench produces 'tool-use collapse': tool-call rate drops from about 20% to about 2% while task accuracy reaches 59.2% (Section 3.1, Figure 2(b), Table 2).
Explicitly rewarding tool use raises tool usage to 100% but yields only a marginal accuracy gain to 59.9%, showing frequency of tool calls alone does not drive performance (Section 3.3, Table 2).

Entropy-regularized exploration achieves the best 3DSRBench accuracy of 62.9%, despite tool usage declining to about 3%, and produces broader visual exploration (mean IoU approximately 0.494 vs. >0.55 for vanilla RFT) (Section 3.4, Table 1, Figure 4).

Banning tool use during training reduces accuracy to 58.1%, about 1.1 points below vanilla RFT, and combining tool-banning with entropy regularization yields no further improvement (57.8%), indicating entropy-driven gains depend on tool access (Section 3.2/3.5, Table 2).
On CV-Bench-3D, the entropy-regularized model reaches 78.8% accuracy, outperforming vanilla RFT and demonstrating improved generalization beyond the training task (Section 4.2, Table 3).
The tool-scaffolding effect generalizes to a different tool suite and task in OpenThinkIMG on VQA-RAD, where entropy regularization again improves validation accuracy (Section 4.1, Table 4).

g2emeL0i3t.text: Theorem 3.2 gives high-probability, data-dependent PAC-Bayesian bounds on the expected test error of the Gibbs posterior that hold across all inverse-temperature (beta) values, including the low-temperature interpolation regime (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.2).

Corollary 4.2 bounds the KL-divergence, total variation, and W2-Wasserstein distance between the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) iterate and the true Gibbs posterior, and Theorem 4.3 shows the generalization bound remains stable under these approximation errors (Section 4.1-4.2, Corollary 4.2, Theorem 4.3).

On MNIST (binary task, digits 0-4 vs 5-9) with 8,000 training samples and a calibration factor of 0.19, the bound stays tight and predictive for true labels while giving a vacuous bound (greater than 0.5) for random labels at beta=64,000, even though training error on random labels approaches ~0.1 (Figure 1).
The same qualitative separation between true-label and random-label bounds is reproduced on CIFAR-10 (animals vs vehicles) with 8,000 samples and a calibration factor of 0.22 (Figure 1).

Experiments use fully-connected ReLU networks with 1-3 hidden layers as well as LeNet-5 and VGG-16 architectures, trained via SGLD/ULA with constant step sizes and 2,000-8,000 training examples (Section 5).

KpaQc72q7m.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that as the transport-cost regularization weight lambda approaches 0, the RDMD objective's optimum converges to the Monge optimal transport map under quadratic cost and mild regularity conditions (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).

The RDMD training objective (Section 3.1) combines a KL-divergence distribution-matching term between perturbed real/fake diffusion distributions with an explicit transport-cost regularization term lambda*E[c(x, G(x))], optimized via coordinate descent over the generator and a fake diffusion model (Section 3.1).

On the AFHQv2 Cat-to-Wild 64x64 unpaired translation task, RDMD attains an FID of 6.9, compared to 2.0 for the pretrained (non-distilled) diffusion teacher, while achieving strictly higher SSIM and near-strictly higher PSNR than baselines including ILVR, SDEdit, and EGSDE (Section 5.2, Figure 4).

A toy 2D experiment (single Gaussian to 8-Gaussian mixture) shows that setting the regularization weight lambda=0.2 balances distribution-matching fidelity against input-output correspondence, reducing trajectory intersections relative to unregularized distillation (Section 5.1).

Appendix A gives a formal gamma-convergence proof that the RDMD objective converges to the hard-constrained Monge problem, supporting the claimed asymptotic optimality of the one-step generator (Appendix A).

TTAxB2IL2y.text: At the 720M-parameter scale, LoRDO-Global reaches a final validation perplexity of 10.41 versus 10.34 for full low-rank DDP, a gap of under 1% (Table 1, Section 5.5).
LoRDO reduces communication volume by approximately 10x relative to low-rank DDP and approximately 25x relative to full-rank DDP, while cutting optimizer memory by 8x-12x (Table 1, Section 5.5).

Section 3.1 shows that purely local low-rank projections suffer O(B^-0.5) instability (B = per-worker batch size), whereas LoRDO's global projections computed from aggregated pseudo-gradients leverage the larger effective batch size across M workers for improved stability (Section 3.1).

Figure 1 demonstrates that LoRDO-Global without quasi-hyperbolic momentum (QHM) exhibits degraded mean squared singular value (MSSV), confirming the predicted subspace-stagnation problem, while Figure 2 shows adding full-rank QHM lets LoRDO-Global consistently outperform the local variant across ranks r in {8,16,32,64} (Section 5.1-5.2, Figures 1-2).

Experiments span model scales of 16M, 125M, and 720M parameters trained on the SmolLM2 dataset with sequence length 2048, with LoRDO-Global matching downstream accuracy on ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, and PIQA relative to DDP (Section 4.1, Table 1).

9h7sSJe4jN.text: Theorem 1 shows that the precision (information-form) updates of the Kalman filter follow a Mobius/fractional-linear transformation that can be computed in parallel with O(log T) depth and O(T) total work via a parallel scan (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows the corresponding mean updates form affine transformations that are likewise computable via parallel prefix scans, giving Kalman Linear Attention (KLA) O(T) training cost and O(1) per-step inference cost (Section 4.2, Theorem 2; Table 1).

On MAD synthetic tasks, KLA scores 85.03% on the Compression task versus 78.35% for Mamba, 49.45% for GLA, and 65.53% for GDN, and 90.67% on Selective Copy versus 80.60% (Mamba), 82.41% (GLA), and 90.30% (GDN) (Table 3).
On long-context MQAR at model width d=256 with sequence length T=2048 and vocabulary V=256, KLA achieves over 95% accuracy while GLA fails entirely and Mamba/GDN underperform (Figure 7).
On the A5 permutation-composition state-tracking task, KLA solves the task with only 1-2 layers, whereas linear SSMs and standard transformers require unbounded depth to solve it (Figure 1).
KLA uses fixed decay parameters combined with learned process noise for per-channel specialization along memory-decay and drift axes, unlike Mamba's fully input-dependent dynamics (Section 4.1).

tNn9bikyXZ.text: Darwinian Memory System (DMS) is evaluated in Section 4 (subsections 4.1-4.6) across multiple general-purpose MLLM backbones including GPT-4V, Claude, Qwen2-VL, Qwen3, GLM-4V/GLM-4, and SEED-1 on real-world multi-app GUI benchmarks (Section 4).
DMS yields an average success-rate gain of 18.0% and an average execution-stability improvement of 33.9% across the evaluated MLLM backbones and benchmarks (Section 4, Table 4).

DMS's Methodology (Section 3) decomposes agent trajectories into reusable units and applies a utility-driven natural-selection mechanism (Section 3.2, subsections 3.2.1-3.2.4) that actively prunes suboptimal paths and high-risk plans without any training or added architectural components.

DMS reduces task latency relative to memory-free and static-memory baselines while remaining training-free, i.e., requiring zero additional training cost and zero architectural overhead (Section 5, Section 5.1).

Ablations in Section 4 compare DMS against static memory-accumulation baselines to show that pruning outdated experience mitigates context pollution and reduces agent hallucination relative to unpruned memory paradigms (Section 4, Table 9).

XAhDgsYn3a.text: Extends the SAE decoder with higher-order polynomial terms while keeping the encoder linear, implemented via low-rank tensor factorization with about 3% parameter overhead on GPT2 (Section 3).
Achieves an average 8% improvement in probing F1 across four language models and three SAE variants while maintaining comparable reconstruction error to standard SAEs (Section 4, Table 3).
Produces 2-10x larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions than baseline SAEs (Section 5, Table 4).
Learned interaction weights show negligible correlation with feature co-occurrence (r=0.06) compared to r=0.82 for standard SAE decoder weights (Section 5).
Ablations vary the polynomial degree of the decoder to study the tradeoff between reconstruction fidelity and interpretability (Appendix, Figure 5).

VnlpOuA3Bs.text: Theorem 3.12 proves that if a matrix M is epsilon-coherent and its barycentric maps are 1-Lipschitz, the induced snapping maps yield an epsilon^(1/2)-interleaving between the Vietoris-Rips filtrations of samples and features (Theorem 3.12).

On a synthetic two-circles dataset, the Coh regularizer achieves epsilon = 0.14 coherence with 100% tuned features and 90% purity, outperforming vanilla and L1-regularized autoencoder baselines (Table 1).
On rotated MNIST digit 6, Coh yields 100% tuned features (mean resultant length > 0.5) versus 63% tuned features for an L1-regularized baseline (Table 2).

On a compact BERT model's token embeddings trained on WikiText-2, Coh achieves 0.45±0.01 mean overlap with nearest-neighbor tokens and 77.4 features judged interpretable by an LLM judge, versus 0.22±0.00 overlap and about 1.0 interpretable features for a softplus baseline without Coh (Table 3).

Coherence (Definition 3.11) imposes geometric connectivity on which samples a feature can activate on, a constraint distinct from and beyond standard sparsity constraints on the number of active features (Section 3).

Wiwfiew7Y4.text: STFlow achieves a 54.6% ADE and 62.8% FDE improvement over the GeoTDM baseline on N-body systems spanning gravity, spring, and charged particle settings (Table 1).
On the MD17 molecular dynamics benchmark across 8 molecules, STFlow achieves an average 38.7% ADE and 34.1% FDE improvement over GeoTDM, with the lowest error on every molecule tested (Table 3).

Uses conditional flow matching with a data-dependent coupling based on a physics-informed random-walk prior with learned velocity statistics (Equation 2, Section 3.2), combined with alternating spatial message-passing and temporal convolution layers (Section 3.3, Figure 2).

Ablations show that replacing the physics-informed prior with an uninformed Gaussian prior degrades ADE from 0.115 to 0.185, and removing the spatial message-passing layer degrades ADE to 0.663 (Table 4).
Sampling performance saturates at about 5 integration steps (ADE 0.121), versus the 100-1000 steps typically required by diffusion-based trajectory models (Section 4.3, Figure 5).
On ETH-UCY pedestrian trajectory forecasting, STFlow is competitive but only best in 2 of 5 scenes, showing signs of overfitting relative to N-body and molecular dynamics results (Table 2).

9GKURFWGeh.text: Integrates multi-organ imaging traits (brain, heart, liver, kidney) with over 500k medical history sequences from UK Biobank via an adaptive medical history tokenizer over a unified temporal grid (Section 3.2, Equation 1).
Achieves 0.91 AUC with a GPT2 backbone and 0.92 AUC with a Qwen3 backbone on next-disease prediction, versus 0.70-0.89 AUC for the Delphi autoregressive baseline (Table 1).

Introduces an SPD-VQVAE using Cholesky decomposition to avoid the O(N^3) complexity of standard SPD matrix operations for brain network embeddings, with Theorem 1 establishing the Cholesky decomposition as a diffeomorphism (Section 3.3.2, Theorem 1).
Achieves 98.36% topological accuracy in generating brain network digital twins with the dual SPD-VQVAE variant (Table 4).
Counterfactual do(healthy) interventions yield an FID distance of 51.37 to healthy subjects versus 92.96 to diseased subjects (p<0.001), indicating physiologically meaningful digital twins (Table 5).
Reduces average treatment effect estimation error by 43% relative to the Delphi baseline (0.004±0.004 versus 0.007±0.005 mean ATE error) (Table 6).

ykdc70h1ND.text: Optimizes the final transformer block of a quantized LLM using a cross-entropy loss between full-precision and quantized logits (integrating the LM head into the objective), rather than the MSE loss used for earlier blocks (Section 3).
Can be layered on top of existing block-wise post-training quantization methods, including FlexRound, OmniQuant, and Block-AP (Section 3, Table 1).
Improves IFEval and MATH500 accuracy for quantized Qwen2.5 models while maintaining WikiText2 perplexity and MMLU accuracy comparable to the underlying PTQ baselines (Table 1).
On L1-Qwen-7B-Max, LFQ improves AIME'24 greedy accuracy from 30% to 43.33% and recovers pass@8 to within 0.5 percentage points of the full-precision baseline (Table 2).
Ablation on Llama 3.1 8B shows both integrating the LM head and using the cross-entropy loss (rather than MSE) are necessary to obtain generation-quality gains (Table 4).
Optimizing beyond the single final block (k=1) yields diminishing returns in generation quality (Figure 2).

Jb1YBPqyb7.text: Visual Gradient Steering (VGS) decomposes the on-policy distillation objective via Bayes' rule into a language-prior term and a visual-grounding term, and shows the gradient vectors of these two terms are frequently near-orthogonal (Section 3, Section 3.2).
VGS applies selective gradient amplification (visual grounding coefficient γ=2.0) plus a language preservation regularizer (weight λ=0.01) on top of the standard distillation loss (Section 4).

Distilling a Qwen3-VL-8B teacher to a 2B student, VGS improves average accuracy across seven vision-language reasoning benchmarks from 43.74% (standard distillation) to 46.10%, a +2.37 point gain (Table 1).

Distilling the same teacher to a 4B student, VGS improves average accuracy from 56.64% to 58.12%, a +1.56 point gain, with the largest single-benchmark gain of +3.68 points on VisualPuzzles (Table 1).

An inverse-steering ablation that amplifies the language-prior gradient instead of the visual-grounding gradient degrades performance, supporting the claim that visual grounding is the primary bottleneck (Section 7).

Combining VGS with GRPO reinforcement-learning fine-tuning yields a further +1.79 average-accuracy improvement over GRPO alone, at roughly 1.375x training compute overhead from the extra non-visual forward passes needed for gradient decomposition (Table 2, Appendix C).

o2H3TE1F0g.text: ConDA (Contrastive Diffusion Alignment) organizes diffusion latents into a low-dimensional contrastively-learned embedding space via a pipeline of encoding, structured embedding, editing, lifting, and rendering (Figure 1).

On fluid-dynamics data, nonlinear traversal operators (spline interpolation, Taylor extrapolation) applied in the ConDA embedding space achieve near-zero RMSE (0.00-0.02), outperforming linear Lerp/Slerp baselines applied in the raw latent space (Table 1).
On DISFA facial-expression data, ConDA achieves lower reconstruction RMSE (5.50) than a beta-VAE baseline (6.59), alongside PSNR of 38.99 and SSIM of 0.96 (Table 2).

For TMS E-field responder classification, an SVM-RBF classifier trained on ConDA's structured embedding space achieves F1=0.63 versus F1=0.30 when trained on the raw diffusion latent space (Figure 3).

On monkey motor-cortex reach data, ConDA embeddings align better with ground-truth reach velocity than PCA embeddings, with RMSE 1.46±0.45 vs 1.71±0.29 and Procrustes distance 0.73±0.22 vs 0.83±0.16 (Figure 5).

T0HjpdCPxU.text: SonicMaster is trained on a purpose-built dataset of ~175k audio pairs derived from ~25k curated 30-second Jamendo segments, simulating 19 degradation effects across 5 categories (EQ, dynamics, reverb, amplitude, stereo) with paired text annotations (Section on Dataset).

The architecture combines multimodal DiT and DiT blocks operating in a Stable Audio Open VAE latent space, conditioned on FLAN-T5 Large text embeddings, trained with a rectified-flow velocity-prediction objective (Equations 1-5).
SonicMaster Large achieves an FAD of 0.073, KL divergence of 0.888 (x1000), mel-spectrogram SSIM of 0.609, and a Production Quality score of 7.705 versus a 7.885 ground-truth reference (Table 4).
SonicMaster outperforms classical baselines Text2FX-EQ on EQ correction and WPE/HPSS on dereverberation and declipping tasks (Table 1, Table 2).

Removing text conditioning (automatic mode) worsens KL divergence from 0.696 to 0.917 and degrades clipping (2.812) and stereo-width (0.1416) metrics relative to text-conditioned inference (ablation in Results section).

In an 8-listener, 43-sample-pair subjective evaluation using 7-point Likert scores, SonicMaster shows statistically significant improvement over degraded inputs across all four attribute categories (amplitude, reverb, stereo, EQ), with text relevance scores ranging 5.11-6.19 (Table 3).

wFLc5L23QL.text: Prior Guidance (PG) is a training-free technique that extrapolates a bridge model's denoising output between a clean input and a degraded (weak) prior constructed via Gaussian noise, blur, or JPEG-compression operators (Equation 9, Section 3).

Frequency-Modulated Prior Guidance (FMPG) extends PG by scaling guidance strength per frequency band to match the U-shaped SNR schedule characteristic of bridge models, unlike the monotonic SNR schedule of standard diffusion (Section 3, Figure 2, Figure 3).
On Edges-to-Handbags at 20 NFE, DBIM+FMPG achieves FID 1.07 versus the DBIM baseline's FID 1.74; on DIODE, FID 3.20 versus 4.99 (Table 1).
FMPG delivers roughly 2x sampling-step efficiency, matching or beating baseline FID at half the number of function evaluations across the 10-100 NFE range (Table 2).

An ablation over degradation operators for constructing the weak prior shows Gaussian noise addition outperforms blur and JPEG compression, and FMPG adds a further 0.5-1.0 FID improvement over PG alone (Table 4, Table 5).
In the cascaded CFG-FMPG framework for ImageNet inpainting, the method achieves FID 3.86 at only 10 NFE, a 20x overall speedup relative to the DBIM baseline (Table 6).

F22sU0Amh1.text: LoCoT2V-Bench provides multi-scene, long-form text-to-video prompts built from hierarchical metadata extracted from real-world videos, described in the Benchmark Design section covering data collection (Section 3.1).
The accompanying LoCoT2V-Eval framework defines evaluation metrics spanning perceptual quality, text-video alignment, temporal quality, and character consistency (Section 3.2).

The benchmark evaluates state-of-the-art text-to-video systems including Sora, HunyuanVideo, Gen-4, and Veo 3 across the four evaluation dimensions, with comprehensive per-model comparisons reported (Table 1).
Across the evaluated systems, results show consistently strong perceptual quality but markedly weaker fine-grained text-video alignment and character consistency scores (Section 4/5, Table 1).
Appendices B-D report ablation analyses examining evaluation-metric sensitivity and annotation consistency for the LoCoT2V-Eval framework (Appendix B-D).

mJgkPAFdiK.text: Introduces the Varying-tree Random Hierarchy Model, a tunable class of uniform-depth PCFGs with m2 binary and m3 ternary production rules per symbol scaling asymptotically as m2=f2*v and m3=f3*v^2 in vocabulary size v (Section 2).

Identifies a phase transition at critical ambiguity parameter f_c = 3/8, below which sentences are globally unambiguous (unique parse/class label) and above which multiple valid parse trees exist, driven by spurious nonterminals in the inside algorithm (Section 3, Figure 3).
Derives a closed-form sample complexity formula P* = O((p2^2/2)^(1-L) · v · m3 · m2^(L-1)) for learning the grammar via root-to-substring covariance clustering (Section 4, Equation 8).
Confirms P* ~ v^2 scaling (with f=1/v) for CNNs via test-loss collapse when training set size is rescaled by the theoretical P* (Section 5.1, Figure 1).
Shows P* ~ v^5 scaling for f=1/4 and depth L=3 as vocabulary size v increases, validated against CNN training curves (Section 5.1, Figure 7a).

Demonstrates the same P* ~ v^2 sample-complexity scaling law holds across CNNs, an Inside Neural Network (INN), and an encoder-only Transformer, with INN having the best prefactor due to task-aligned architecture (Section 5.2, Figure 8).

rzBWwdKik8.text: Proposes Curvilinear Demonstration Selection (CDS), which orders many-shot chain-of-thought demonstrations to minimize total conceptual curvature in embedding space (Section 6).
CDS yields an average 3.81% performance gain across math and narrative reasoning tasks, with up to a 5.42 percentage-point gain on a math task using 64 demonstrations (Abstract, Section 6).

Main results are measured on Qwen3-14B and gpt-5.2 across geometry, number_theory, and DetectiveQA tasks with n in {16,32,64,128} demonstrations, with robustness checks using the bge-m3 embedding model (Table 3).

An ablation using high-curvature control orderings isolates smoothness effects from local clustering, confirming curvature reduction as a causal factor rather than a by-product of grouping similar examples (Section 5.2.2, Table 4).

Reports a negative correlation between curvature and performance, with overall Pearson r = -0.547 across math reasoning tasks, and task-specific correlations of -0.545 (geometry), -0.468 (number_theory), and -0.628 (counting_and_probability) (Section 5.2.2).

lWyXszYR58.text: Theorem 3.1 bounds uniform stability degradation under Byzantine failure attacks (convex case) as 2γC^2T(1/((n-f)m) + √κ) with κ ≥ f/(n-2f), yielding an overall rate of O(√(f/(n-2f))) (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 bounds stability degradation under data poisoning attacks with SMEA aggregation (convex case) as 2γC^2T(f/(n-f) + 1/((n-f)m)), giving a strictly better Θ(f/(n-f)) rate (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.2).
Theorem 3.3 establishes a matching lower bound Ω(γC^2T(f/(n-f) + 1/((n-f)m))) for the data poisoning setting, proving the Θ(f/(n-f)) upper bound is tight (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.3).

Shows Byzantine failures degrade uniform stability by a multiplicative factor of 2√(f/(n-f))·(1+f/(n-2f)) worse than data poisoning, with the gap widening as f approaches n/2 (Section 3, Theorems 3.1-3.3).

Extends the convex-case bounds to the strongly convex setting, where Byzantine degradation is 2C^2/μ·(1/((n-f)m) + √κ) versus 2C^2/μ·(f/(n-f) + 1/((n-f)m)) for data poisoning (Section 3.1-3.2, Equations 2-4).

Tq5dFAGeBL.text: For dimension n=256 and log_2(q)=20, the proposed methods recover binary secrets with Hamming weight up to 70 (using an 8-cruel-bit cool/cruel split), up from a prior maximum of 33 (Table 1).
For dimension n=256 and log_2(q)=12, the methods recover Hamming weight up to 14 versus a prior maximum of 8 (Table 1).
For dimension n=512 and log_2(q)=41, the methods recover Hamming weight up to 75 versus a prior maximum of 63 (Table 1).
At n=256, log_2(q)=20, h=60, the proposed approach achieves a 60% recovery success rate compared to 2% for the prior VERDE method (Section 6).
At n=512, log_2(q)=41, h=63, the proposed approach achieves a 91% recovery success rate compared to 15% for VERDE (Section 6).
Dual stepwise regression outperforms standard linear regression for cool-bit recovery, particularly for secrets with 8 or more cruel bits and high Hamming weight (Tables 5-6).

pG4jfjf2g7.text: URS is trained on 11 base VRP problems (ATSP, TSP, OP, PCTSP, PDTSP, ACVRP, CVRP, CVRPTW, CVRPB, OCVRP, OCVRPTW) and evaluated zero-shot on a total of 107 variants, comprising the 11 seen problems plus 96 unseen variants spanning 10 constraint categories (Section 5.1, Appendix B).
On seen problems, URS achieves optimality gaps ranging from 0.57% (TSP) to 6.13% (CVRPTW) relative to oracle/problem-specific solvers (Table 2).
On unseen problem variants, URS attains gaps such as 0.12% (ACVRPBTW), 9.74% (CVRPBPLTW), and 11.17% (MDCVRPBPTW) without any fine-tuning (Table 3).

URS uses a Unified Data Representation (UDR) with position identifiers, attribute sets, and node-type indicators to encode all problem variants in a single feature space, replacing per-problem enumeration (Section 3.1, Appendix C).
URS employs a Mixed Bias Module combining outgoing-distance, incoming-distance, and optional relation-matrix biases via separate attention computations (Equations 2-5).
URS scales to large CVRPLIB Set-X benchmark instances of 500-1000 nodes (Table 12, Appendix J).

ddIUBkzwIU.text: Non-Parametric Probabilistic Robustness (NPPR) is defined as an infimum over perturbation distributions of the correctness likelihood, learned from data rather than assumed to follow a fixed parametric family such as Gaussian or uniform (Definition 3, Section 3).

Proposition 1 establishes the ordering G_AR ≤ G_NPPR ≤ G_PR, showing NPPR sits between adversarial robustness and standard probabilistic robustness and is provably more conservative than PR (Proposition 1, Section 3).
On ResNet18/CIFAR-10, the global NPPR estimate is 88.32% compared to 99.47% for Gaussian-assumed PR, a roughly 40% relative reduction in the estimated robustness (Table 3).
NPPR estimates degrade with task difficulty, falling from 88.32% (CIFAR-10) to 74.17% (CIFAR-100) to 60.16% (TinyImageNet) for the same architecture (Table 3).

At perturbation radius epsilon=16/255 on ResNet18/CIFAR-10, introducing joint input-label dependence in the perturbation distribution lowers the estimate from 95.15% (independent) to 89.71% (joint-dependent), confirming Proposition 2 that stronger dependencies yield more conservative estimates (Table 2, Proposition 2).

lrCseHVGjc.text: Gradient Dilution is identified as the root cause of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based incremental object detection, arising from three coupled factors: Signal Dispersion, Assignment Drift, and Support Attrition (Section 3, Preliminary).

Signal Dispersion occurs because background gradients overwhelm sparse foreground signals given the imbalance between 300-900 object queries and typically far fewer ground-truth instances per image (Section 3).

The FAS framework combines Prior-Injected Query Formulation (PIQ), Deterministic Anchor Distillation (DAD), and Manifold-Support Replay (MSR using K-means with K=3) to counteract the three Gradient Dilution factors (Section 4).
In the 40+10x4 multi-phase incremental COCO setting, FAS achieves 45.2/44.1/44.3/42.9 AP across the four incremental phases versus DCA's 44.0/41.1/39.2/37.2 AP (Table 3).
In the 70+10 two-phase COCO setting, FAS reaches 45.5 AP compared to 43.0 AP for the previous best method SDDGR, and in the 40+40 setting FAS improves over SDDGR by 1.8 AP (Table 1).
Figure 2 empirically demonstrates Gradient Dilution via foreground-to-background gradient ratio curves and query-assignment scatter plots across training epochs (Figure 2).

rVcYqFCgY9.text: Diffusion over Superquadrics (DoSs) represents each 3D shape with 128x15 tokens (~7KB) versus 2,048x3 points (24KB) for point clouds or 32^3x3 voxels (384KB) for dense voxel grids, drastically reducing diffusion-state dimensionality (Introduction, Section 3, Methodology).

On ShapeNet, DoSs attains 1-NNA@CD scores of 53.80 (Chair), 61.92 (Airplane), and 57.50 (Car), reported as competitive against baselines including DPM, PVD, TIGER, LION, MeshDiffusion, and DiT-3D (Table 1).
DoSs generates a shape in approximately 0.6 seconds at batch size 1 on an RTX 3090, with about 2 hours of training time per category (Section 4, Experiments).

The explicit superquadric parameterization (pose, size, shape exponents) enables resolution-free point-cloud decoding, shown qualitatively via comparison to fixed-resolution decoding baselines (Figure 4).
Ablations show that removing existence tokens, the 6D rotation representation, or canonical primitive sorting each degrade generation quality relative to the full DoSs model (Table 2).

IqTvyp40O6.text: Diffusion models exhibit a 'biased generalization' phase in which test loss continues to decrease while generated samples show anomalously high proximity to training data, occurring before the test-loss minimum (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

Early stopping at the test-loss minimum, though optimal by standard generalization criteria, is shown to be insufficient to prevent training-data leakage in privacy-critical applications because biased generalization emerges earlier in training (Section 4.3).

A sample-split diagnostic on CelebA shows two models trained on disjoint data subsets produce increasingly divergent outputs before either model shows conventional signs of overfitting, evidencing bias emergence prior to memorization (Section 3, Figure 1).

The mechanism is attributed to sequential feature learning: coarse structure is learned early in a data-independent manner while finer features are resolved later and become increasingly data-dependent, explaining why test performance keeps improving even as training-data proximity bias grows (Section 5.1, Figure 6).

Generalization and memorization are argued to be orthogonal rather than opposite axes of generative model behavior, illustrated via cosine-distance-between-predictions analysis across diffusion timesteps (Section 2.2, Figure 2).

Lp8gwhhUfU.text: Across 200-250 random seeds per model scale on synthetic count and reverse-order-addition tasks, the same model architecture and scale produces either a smooth or a sharply emergent scaling trend depending on the random seed (Section 3, Figure 1).

Per-scale outcome distributions across seeds are bimodal (clustering into high-performing and low-performing groups) on the reverse-order addition task, and the transition from unimodal to bimodal distribution is abrupt as measured by Wasserstein-L2 distance (Section 3.3, Figures 2 and 4).

While per-seed mode metrics show sharp jumps, the mean over seeds shows a smooth trend, and the underlying success probability and per-run performance both change continuously with scale, indicating apparent breakthroughs reflect continuous distributional shifts rather than sudden capability unlocking (Section 3.2, Figure 3).
U-shaped/inverse scaling behavior is shown to result from a changing success probability across scale rather than a monotonic decline in performance of successful runs (Section 3.4, Figure 6).

Bimodal seed-dependent clustering is also observed in natural-language experiments with Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models on MMLU under varying C4+MMLU data mixtures and last-layer reinitialization across 20 seeds, validating the synthetic-task findings on real LLMs (Section 4, Section 4.2).

Qn2HcnC4l2.text: Behavioral cloning in linear Markov games achieves an ε-approximate Nash equilibrium with sample complexity Õ(H^5 C²_{φ,max} d B² log(A_max B_θ δ^{-1})/ε²), depending on feature dimension d rather than state-action space size (Theorem 3.3).

A feature-level concentrability coefficient C_{φ,max}, defined via expert feature covariance matrices, replaces the state-action concentrability coefficient C_max and can be substantially smaller when features encode informative state similarity (Definition 3.2, Section 3).

The interactive LSVI-UCB-ZERO-BC algorithm attains an ε-Nash equilibrium using Õ(H^7 d^4 B^4 log(B_θ A_max δ^{-1})/ε²) expert queries, with no dependence on the concentrability coefficient C_{φ,max} (Theorem 4.1, Algorithm 1).
On Connect4, the interactive DQN-Explore-BC algorithm achieves a 0.97±0.01 win rate against a near-optimal opponent, versus 0.54±0.05 for plain behavioral cloning (Table 1, Section 5).

In the gridworld experiment, behavioral cloning fails to reach a low Nash gap when using tabular features but succeeds when using learned deep linear features, while the interactive algorithm converges to zero Nash gap regardless (Section 5).

watVfFbZGF.text: LaGEA improves average success rate by 9.0% over baselines on Meta-World MT10 with random goals, reaching 70.4% (±1.85) average success (Table 2).
LaGEA improves average success rate by 5.3% over FuRL on Meta-World MT10 with fixed goals, achieving 80.0% average success versus 76.0% for FuRL (Table 1).

On Robotic Fetch tasks, LaGEA improves average success over prior state-of-the-art methods by 17% (Section 4, per abstract-level result reported in current claims and corroborated by full-text experiment section).
LaGEA converges in far fewer environment steps than FuRL and SAC, which plateau late or stall, across eight Meta-World tasks (Figure 3).

Removing the keyframe selection component causes training to catastrophically fail, and structured language feedback yields 98.89% average success versus 78.89% for freeform feedback (Figure 4, Table 3).
The full LaGEA reward design (combining goal delta, feedback delta, and adaptive weighting ρ) yields a 19% performance gain over ablated variants that remove any single component (Figure 5).

jeP0AARoA2.text: EmbodiedAct with GPT-5.2 as backbone achieves 70.6% overall score on the Core EngDesign benchmark and 65.4% on the Extended set, versus 55.4%/49.4% for the CodeAct baseline and 48.0%/51.9% for direct generative-model baselines (Table 1).
On SciBench-107, EmbodiedAct with GPT-5.2 achieves 48.60% accuracy, compared to 34.58% for CodeAct and 44.86% for generative-model baselines (Table 2).

An ablation removing the Perception Engine drops EngDesign Core performance from 70.6% to 56.5%, and removing both the Perception Engine and Reflective Decision Maker drops it to 51.5%, indicating perception contributes more than reflective planning alone (Table 3).
In pass@3 multi-trial evaluation, EmbodiedAct consistently dominates across all tested model backbones (Figure 3).

81.5% of EmbodiedAct's task runs fall within a narrow performance divergence gap (≤20 points) across trials, compared to 73.9% for generative-model baselines and 63.0% for CodeAct, indicating greater stability in long-horizon simulations (Figure 4).

DxoS2VhNk8.text: On Stable Diffusion v1.4 with verbatim memorized prompts, CA-in-GUARD reduces SSCD similarity to 0.079 versus 0.113 for the Ren et al. (2024) baseline, while maintaining comparable CLIP score (0.266 vs 0.258) (Table 1).
On Stable Diffusion v1.4 with template memorized prompts, CA-in-GUARD reduces SSCD to 0.517 versus 0.602 for Ren et al. (2024), with FID of 210.983 versus 222.066 (Table 1).

On Stable Diffusion v2.0 with template memorized prompts, CA-in-GUARD reduces SSCD to 0.193 versus 0.356 for Ren et al. (2024), showing robustness across both SD v1.4 and v2.0 architectures (Table 1).

GUARD is evaluated against Random Token Addition, Wen et al. (2024), Ren et al. (2024), and Han et al. (2025) baselines across both verbatim and template memorization settings on a filtered set of 500 memorized samples from Webster (2023) with SSCD > 0.7 (Section on Dataset/Table 1).

GUARD operates as a dynamic, per-prompt inference-time mitigation method rather than requiring model retraining, achieving state-of-the-art memorization mitigation while preserving image quality as measured by CLIP score and FID (Table 1).

txswvMHt4u.text: The Hierarchical Successor Representation (HSR) Bellman operator is proven to be a contraction mapping with respect to the max-norm with contraction coefficient equal to the discount factor γ, guaranteeing convergence of iterative HSR computation (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

In the Four-Room gridworld transfer experiment, HSR shows significantly higher transfer efficiency than baseline successor representation (SR) methods (p=0.008) and about 40% lower representation change (instability) under task shifts (p<0.001) (Figure 2).

HSR decomposed via non-negative matrix factorization (HSR-NMF) outperforms all SR-based baselines, including RW-SR+SVD, eSR+SVD, eSR+NMF, and HSR+SVD, in sample-efficient transfer learning on the G1 navigation task (Wilcoxon signed-rank test p<10⁻⁹) (Figure 3).

HSR-NMF produces a sparse code that uniformly tiles the state space and shows elevated activation at critical topological bottleneck states, while matching the reconstruction efficiency of SR-SVD (Figure 4).

In procedurally generated mazes with pure exploration over 10^5 interaction steps, HSR-SPIE maintains high state coverage as maze size increases, whereas SR-SPIE coverage degrades drastically in larger mazes (Figure 5).

oLmwqIhzqj.text: For any ρ > 0, there exists a ρ-TV-stable RL algorithm supporting exact unlearning with expected computational cost equal to only a ρ√(ln T) fraction of full retraining from scratch (Theorem 3.3).
The proposed algorithm achieves a regret bound of O(H³S²A + H²√(SAT) + H^2.5·S²A/ρ)·polylog(T,H,S,A,1/δ) for tabular MDPs with unlearning support (Theorem 4.1).
A matching lower bound of Ω(H√(SAT) + HSA/ρ) is established, showing the algorithm is nearly minimax optimal (Theorem 4.4).

Exact unlearning is formalized as requiring the post-unlearning output distribution to be identical to that of an algorithm that never observed the deleted data (Definition 2.1), operationalized via ρ-TV-stability where TV(A(Z), A(Z')) ≤ ρ for neighboring sequences (Definition 2.2).

The construction uses a binary tree mechanism with noise-perturbed prefix sums requiring only O(log T) shared noise samples per query, achieving O(Td) space and O(d·log T) per-episode update time (Section 3.1).
The additional regret cost term for unlearning, H³S²A/ρ, improves upon the corresponding differentially-private RL cost term of H^3.5·S²A/ε by a factor of √H (Section 4).

QItZDBVCT0.text: For quadratic activation σ(z) = z², when the sample size n = o(d log d), spherical gradient flow fails to achieve weak recovery, showing full-batch updates offer no statistical advantage over one-pass SGD in this regime (Theorem 3.1).

With a truncated quadratic activation, full-batch spherical gradient flow achieves weak recovery with only n ≳ d samples, compared to the n ≳ d log d samples required by one-pass SGD, establishing a sample complexity separation (Theorem 3.2).

Using the truncated activation on squared loss with small initialization (r₀ = d^-15), full-batch gradient descent achieves strong recovery in T ≳ log d gradient steps given n ≥ CM⁴d samples (Theorem 4.1).
The trajectory of full-batch gradient descent decomposes into an initial angle-reduction phase lasting O(log d/η) steps followed by geometric convergence during a refinement phase (Section 4).

Full-batch methods with truncated activation match the information-theoretic sample lower bound of n ≳ d, removing the extra log d factor that is unavoidable for one-pass SGD under quadratic activation (Theorem 3.2).

LCosvYhXvi.text: Proposition 4.1 (the two-gap upper bound) decomposes fine-tuning test risk into a generalization gap G_gen = O(√(KL(π_train‖π_pre)/n)) and an extrapolation gap G_ext = O(TV(D_test, D_train)), formalizing why optimal data difficulty depends on data budget n.

On real-world SFT experiments with Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on OpenR1-Math-94k, medium-difficulty data (68.3%) outperforms both easy (61.1%) and hard (61.7%) data, demonstrating a non-monotonic, dataset-dependent optimum (Table 1).

Controlled experiments on the synthetic iGSM dataset show the optimal difficulty level shifts toward harder examples as the data budget increases, visualized as a rightward-shifting optimum across both 1.5B and 7B model variants (Figure 3, Observations 1-4).

Ablations attribute the tradeoff to two failure modes: easy training data yields good in-distribution fit but poor extrapolation to harder test cases, while hard training data yields poor generalization from limited samples (Figure 6).

Experiments span four datasets—OpenMath (200k subset), OpenR1-Math-94k, OpenScience (200k subset), and synthetic iGSM—to test the generalization-extrapolation tradeoff across both controlled and real-world fine-tuning settings (Section 5).

vVoaUGCMGY.text: The intersection-based conversion rule, defined as f_ρ(·)(α) = sup_{τ≥0.5} f_{τ,ρ(τ)}(α), is proven to be the pointwise tightest possible black-box conversion from an RDP profile to a valid hypothesis-testing trade-off function (Theorem 4.4, Section 4).
Proposition 3.1 establishes that the boundary of the single-order RDP privacy region is optimally tight for any individual (τ, ρ) Rényi-DP guarantee considered in isolation.
Lemma 4.2 shows that intersecting all τ-order single-order regions yields a valid universal lower bound on the trade-off functions attainable by any mechanism satisfying the given RDP profile.

Symmetric Randomized Response mechanisms (instances of Bernoulli-based witness mechanisms) are constructed to achieve exact recovery under the intersection conversion, saturating the optimal bound at various Type I error levels (Proposition 4.5).

No other black-box conversion rule can uniformly Blackwell-dominate the intersection rule, establishing the fundamental limit of what can be inferred about a mechanism's f-DP guarantee from its RDP profile alone (Theorem 4.4).

CPrSz9pqv7.text: On the USPTO-50K benchmark, Retro-Expert achieves 66.23% Top-1 accuracy for retrosynthesis prediction, compared to 37.11% for the best LLM baseline (Gemini), as well as higher BLEU (0.995 vs 0.984), validity (0.997 vs 0.992), and Morgan fingerprint similarity (0.972 vs 0.942) (Table 1).
When collaborating with various specialized retrosynthesis models, Retro-Expert's Knowledge-Guided Policy Optimization (KGPO) improves baseline accuracies by +2.0% to +3.1% (Table 2).
Retro-Expert achieves a 46.2% success rate at self-correction, generating novel correct predictions in cases where the underlying specialized models failed (Section on self-correction capability).
Human expert evaluation of the generated natural-language explanations scores 4.21/5.0 for Mechanism Accuracy and 4.17/5.0 for Logic Consistency (Table 4).
On the out-of-distribution ChemBench benchmark, Retro-Expert attains 57.00% accuracy versus 32.54% for DeepSeek-R1 (Table 5).

The composite reward function (Equation 5) combines multi-stage intermediate rewards (r₁, r₂, r₃) with a final reactant-correctness reward and a format-adherence reward, designed to prevent reward hacking by optimizing the entire reasoning pathway rather than only the final prediction.

W9EgZALquo.text: CellBRIDGE formulates trajectory inference as an interaction-aware Fused Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport problem that linearly combines a feature cost with a directed ligand-receptor interaction structure cost via a weighting parameter alpha (Equation 5, Section 4.1).

On the lung tumor scRNA-seq dataset, CellBRIDGE combined with Conditional Flow Matching achieves a Wasserstein-1 interpolation error of 2.057 (±0.005), improving over feature-only OT baselines (Table 2, Section 5.1).

Improvements in trajectory interpolation from adding the interaction-aware cost are statistically significant across model families after Holm correction (adjusted p<0.05), with Cohen's d_z effect sizes ranging from 0.27 to 0.63 (Section 5.2).

In silico attenuation of signaling through EGFR, ALK, or MET receptors produces up to a 15.5% reduction in predicted tumor-progression trajectories, demonstrating mechanistic interpretability of the learned couplings (Figure 4(a), Section 5.3).

On a six-day embryonic development dataset where ligand-receptor interaction structure is not persistent across snapshots, CellBRIDGE shows no improvement over feature-only OT (alpha=0) across the tested range of alpha values (Figure 4(b), Section 5.4).

meEsugjXjv.text: The Excited Pfaffians method reduces the variance of the multi-state overlap estimator by pooling samples across all states, achieving a bound of Var[sum of overlap estimators] <= N_s(N_s-1)/(2N_b), an improvement over single-state sampling variance scaling (Equation 43, Appendix D).

The method achieves an empirical computational scaling of approximately O(N_s^0.14) with the number of excited states, compared to O(N_s^4) scaling of prior neural excited-state methods, yielding over 200x faster training on carbon dimer while modeling 50% more states (Figure 1).

Excited Pfaffians compute all 32 excited states of the beryllium atom up to the ionization threshold with errors below 0.5 mHa relative to NIST reference energies, the first such computation with a neural network wave function (Figure 6, Section 5).

The method models the carbon dimer (C2) potential energy surface across 12 electronic states (6 singlet and 6 triplet) spanning bond lengths of 0.995-1.87 Angstrom, benchmarked against SHCI reference calculations (Figure 5).

A single trained model generalizes across second-row atoms (Li-Ne), matching NIST experimental excited-state energies to chemical accuracy (<1.6 mHa) (Section 5, subsection 'Generalization across compounds').

JG6f02X29a.text: Distribution Aligned Imitation Learning (DAIL) trains on fewer than 1000 expert solutions, specifically 417 problems in the e1-verifiable subset and 669 problems in the e1-proof subset (Section 3.1).
DAIL yields 10-25% pass@k gains on Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen3 models, including a 15% gain for Qwen3 (think mode) on IMO-AnswerBench (Abstract, Section 3.2, Figure 2).
DAIL matches the untrained model's baseline performance using 2x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens, as shown by token-budget comparison curves (Section 3.3, Figure 4).

DAIL maintains out-of-domain generalization comparable to or better than the standard fine-tuning baseline on GPQA-Diamond despite training only on in-domain expert reasoning traces (Section 3.3, Table 1).

DAIL uses a two-stage approach: a privileged-student rollout expansion of compressed expert traces followed by a contrastive loss that penalizes divergence from a full expert-solution reference relative to a solution-skeleton negative reference, implemented with LoRA to share weights across student variants (Section 2).

EXCUyr6hhZ.text: Weasel selects a fixed-budget subset of web-agent trajectory steps by greedily maximizing a combined objective of an importance score Phi (BERTScore-based goal-state relevance) and a diversity score D across states and interaction patterns, weighted by lambda (Section 3.1).

Weasel achieves 9.7-12.5x training speedups depending on the model while using only about 19% of the original AgentTrek training data, with fine-tuned Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B evaluated across WebArena, WorkArena, and MiniWob (Abstract, Table 1).

Ablations show the combined importance-plus-diversity objective (14.5 success rate on WebArena-Lite) outperforms either term alone (10.9 for unary/importance-only and 7.9 for diversity-only) (Table 5, Table 6, Table 7, Section 3.3).

The greedy subset-selection algorithm matches the exact combinatorial optimum in more than 96% of 1,877 evaluated trajectories and falls within the top 1% of candidate subsets in 99.7% of trajectories, with an objective ratio of 0.9999±0.0005 (Section 3.3, 'Greedy Approximation Quality').

On the multimodal Android in the Wild benchmark using Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, Weasel-selected subsets improve accuracy from 5.8% (random selection) to 6.6% at matched subset size (Table 8, Section 3.3).

rW2xHmYrZA.text: MINIM uses a GATv2-based local broker with 3 attention layers (hidden size 256, 4 heads) to predict per-element sensitivity and necessity scores (0-10 scale) that drive a ternary Remove/Abstract/Keep disclosure policy over accessibility trees (Section B.2, Appendix B).

On a WebArena-derived evaluation set of 5,403 (tree, task) variants across 150 accessibility trees and 27 task types, MINIM achieves 94.91% Task-Critical Node Preservation (TCNP), 99.31% preservation of interactive elements (TCNP-I), and reduces Task-Irrelevant Sensitive Leakage (TISL) to 10.1% of the full observation while retaining only about 12% of nodes (Table 1, Section 5.3).

MINIM matches or exceeds the context-recall utility of seven prompted open-weight LLM baselines (including Qwen3-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and GPT-OSS-20B) while roughly halving leakage: those baselines show TISL of 0.194-0.312 and retain 25.8-34.5% of nodes, versus MINIM's 0.101 TISL and ~12% retention (Table 2, Section 5.4).

Domain-specific results show MINIM performs best on Gmail (96.61% TCNP, 1.88% TISL, n=472) and Shopping (93.60% TCNP, 0.85% TISL, n=60), with higher residual leakage on Reddit (95.38% TCNP, 13.50% TISL, n=130) attributed to semantic ambiguity in user-generated content boundaries (Table 10, Appendix D).

hyksWoNb7h.text: On the simulated 3-variable dataset with infrequent transitions, DRL-STAF achieves 98.17% state estimation accuracy versus 79.53% for the best deep-learning-HMM hybrid baseline NCTRL (Section 5).
On the same simulated 3-variable infrequent-transition dataset, DRL-STAF attains an MSE of 0.0278 for next-step forecasting versus 0.3042 for NCTRL (Section 5).
On the simulated 10-variable dataset, DRL-STAF reaches 96.15% state estimation accuracy and 0.0395 MSE, compared to NCTRL's 90.31% accuracy and 0.3935 MSE (Section 5).

On the real-world Server Machine dataset (28 machines, 38 dimensions), DRL-STAF achieves an F1 score of 77.50% versus 69.21% for Parallel HMM, and the lowest MAE (0.0189) among all eight compared methods (Section 5).

DRL-STAF's two-stage architecture uses independent per-variable deep-reinforcement-learning state estimation followed by a residual graph attention mechanism to model cross-sequence dependencies, mitigating the combinatorial state-space explosion that afflicts joint HMM variants like Parallel HMM, Parallel HSMM, Parallel HOHMM, and CHMM (Section 3, Section 4).

DRL-STAF is benchmarked against eight baselines spanning HMM variants (Parallel HMM, Parallel HSMM, Parallel HOHMM, CHMM) and DL-HMM hybrids (NHMM, NCTRL, Markovian-RNN, DEN-HMM) across four simulated and three real-world datasets including Exchange Rate and Traffic (Section 5, Table results).

fNzLTEBdGA.text: The paper proves convergence of the proposed max-min constrained multi-objective RL algorithm under both unconstrained and constrained settings via Theorems 3.1-3.6 (Section 3).

The framework is compared against weighted-scalarization approaches, interior point policy optimization (IPO), and Fair-DICE variants as baselines for fairness-aware constrained multi-objective RL (Section 5).

The algorithm is validated theoretically in tabular settings before being applied to three simulated control domains: building thermal control, multi-objective locomotion, and GHG-aware traffic management (Section 5, Section 5.2).
Appendix F (Theorem F.1 and subsections F.1-F.4) provides additional convergence proofs and analysis supporting the main theoretical results in Section 3 (Appendix F).

The max-min criterion combined with explicit constraint satisfaction is designed to balance fairness across objectives while enforcing hard constraints, distinguishing it from conflict-averse and scalarization-based multi-objective RL methods (Section 3, Section 5).

Ee3Wh716Wm.text: SkelHCC achieves 71.6% accuracy on the NTU RGB+D 120 one-shot benchmark (100 base classes, 20 novel classes), a 9.0 percentage point improvement over the previous SOTA method CrossGLG at 62.6% (Section on Experimental Results).
On NTU RGB+D 60 under the 50-class one-shot setting, SkelHCC reaches 84.1% accuracy, outperforming CrossGLG by 8.5 percentage points (Experimental Results).
On PKU-MMD II, SkelHCC attains 40.0% accuracy, a 1.7 percentage point improvement over SkeletonX (Experimental Results).

SkelHCC's Explicitly Hierarchical Hyperbolic CLIP (EH-HCLIP) module projects skeleton and language embeddings into hyperbolic space via the Lorentz model across three granularity levels—Body Joint, Body Part, and Full Body—using hyperbolic contrastive learning with entailment cone constraints (Methodology).

The LLM-guided Multi-granularity Voting Cache (LMV-Cache) is a training-free module that stores support exemplars at multiple granularities and fuses similarity scores via learnable weights (α1, α2, α3), enabling adaptive inference without fine-tuning the frozen backbone (only 0.5M trainable parameters) (Methodology).

Bd0NNopzpC.text: Cross-domain Integrated Gradients generalizes Integrated Gradients to any invertible, differentiable transformation, including complex-valued domains such as the Fourier transform, while provably preserving path independence and completeness guarantees (Definition 4.1, Lemma 4.1).
The method is applied to frequency-domain attribution for heart rate extraction on the PPGDalia photoplethysmography dataset (Section 5, Figures 1-3).
The method is applied to ICA-domain attribution for seizure detection on the Physionet Siena Scalp EEG Database v1.0.0 (Section 5).
The method is applied to seasonal-trend (STL) decomposition attribution for forecasting on synthetic time series combining exponential trend and seasonal components (Section 5, Figures 4-5).
Proposition 1 establishes completeness, guaranteeing that summed cross-domain attributions equal the model output difference f(x) - f(x_hat) (Proposition 1).
The framework is implemented as an open-source Python library compatible with both TensorFlow and PyTorch, with core algorithms detailed as Algorithms 1-3 in Appendix A (Appendix A).

OtczOgWFGh.text: The Generalized Hanson-Wright Inequality (Theorem 1) extends classical concentration bounds to dot products between dependent random vectors, enabling geometric analysis of non-i.i.d. high-dimensional data (Section 2, Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows that ambient intrinsic dimension p_int growing as ω(log n) suffices for persistence diagrams to consistently recover latent homology, substantially weakening the classical p ≫ n requirement from HDLSS theory (Section 4, Theorem 2).

The paper demonstrates a 'blessing of dimensionality': as p_int increases, data dot-products concentrate about their expectations and latent topological structure becomes more visible rather than degenerating (Section 3).

Applying the isometry detection method to Gardner et al. (2022) grid cell recordings, the toroidal model with rhombus-and-periodicity structure (Model 3) achieves the strongest linear fit between shortest path lengths, providing empirical evidence that grid cell activity is isometric to a flat torus (Section 6).
Persistent homology analysis of grid cell firing patterns recovers Betti numbers H0=1, H1=2, H2=1, consistent with toroidal topology as originally reported by Gardner et al. (Section 6).

KUBkuPwGf4.text: For a graph with no edges, the derivation graph decomposes into 2^|V|-1 connected components, one per distinct outcome variable (Proposition 1).
The number of causally equivalent expressions reachable via do-calculus derivations is upper bounded by 3^|V\Y|, where Y is the set of outcome variables (Proposition 2).

Any two derivations of the same interventional distribution are connected by a path of length at most four in the derivation graph, using the canonical rule pattern R2-up, R3-up, R3-down, R2-down (Theorem 6, Corollary 2).

Two expressions derivable from one another via arbitrary recursive do-calculus rule applications can always be connected using just two applications of Rule R2 and two applications of Rule R3, showing Rule R1 is redundant for this purpose (Theorem 2).

On the Sachs protein-signaling dataset, the derivation-graph approach identifies 32 causally equivalent density expressions for the same query, yielding 11 distinct estimators whose bootstrap variance ranges from 0.000016 to 0.001032 (Table 1, Section 5).

Rule R2 applications commute with each other, and simultaneous or sequential insertions of multiple actions yield equivalent derivations, while R2 and R3 exhibit only weak commutativity that holds solely when applied in the same direction (Theorems 3, 4, 5).

tHrIGSL2aY.text: The Multi-Action-Head DPO framework trains specialized reward/policy heads on a shared backbone and reports an ensemble math accuracy of 0.8733 versus 0.7160 for single-head DPO on the same benchmark (Table 1).

On the Socratic Mind (multi-turn tutoring) task, the Multi-Action-Head ensemble achieves 0.6893 accuracy and 0.4513 engagement, jointly improving both objectives relative to single-objective baselines (Table 1).
On human value alignment, the ensemble model attains 0.6389 helpfulness, 0.3687 honesty, and 0.2478 truthfulness, surpassing the MODPO baseline across these dimensions (Table 1, Section 6).

Test-time PRM-guided decoding raises math accuracy from 0.6853 to 0.7993 when using accuracy-head guidance, demonstrating the standardized process reward model framework's effectiveness at inference (Table 2).

Combining training-time Multi-Action-Head DPO with test-time PRM-guided search produces synergistic gains that expand the performance frontier beyond either method alone, with verifiable-reward domains benefiting most (Table 3, Section 6).

NvJPE1oiKd.text: The walk-stitching mechanism in GRFs++ combines multiple short random walks via 2l-level convolutions of the modulation function to produce an unbiased estimator equivalent to a longer walk, trading sequential walk sampling for parallel matrix-matrix multiplication (Lemma 2.1, Section 2.2.1).

Increasing the walk-stitching degree l (e.g., l=1,2,4) monotonically improves the mean squared error of the kernel estimator at no extra computational cost, as shown by the closed-form MSE expression for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3).

An efficient implementation variant achieves O(N) time complexity via a Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transform combined with matrix associativity, improving on the O(N^2) complexity of a sparse-matrix implementation (Section 3, Option II vs Option I).
On node clustering benchmarks, GRFs++ reduces error by roughly 13% on the dolphins dataset and roughly 15% on the eurosis dataset relative to standard GRFs (Table 1).
On mesh normal prediction, GRFs++ yields consistent gains of about 0.6-0.9% over regular GRFs (Table 2).
On high-diameter graphs (diameter up to 159), GRFs++ shows improved kernel estimation accuracy for distant node pairs compared to baseline GRFs (Figure 7).

FtvNZxhW9W.text: RGMem organizes conversational memory into a three-layer hierarchy: L0 microscopic episodic units built by segmentation and synthesis, L1 mesoscopic knowledge graph of abstract concepts and events via static/dynamic relations, and L2 multi-scale observation/retrieval across abstraction levels (Section 3.1-3.4).

On the LOCOMO benchmark, RGMem achieves 86.17% overall accuracy, more than 7 percentage points above the strongest baseline Zep at 79.09%, and close to the theoretical Full-Context upper bound of 87.52% (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On LOCOMO's multi-hop reasoning subset, RGMem scores 78.03% accuracy, a roughly 9-point improvement over Zep's 69.16% (Table 1).
On LOCOMO's single-hop subset, RGMem reaches 89.58% accuracy, exceeding even the Full-Context upper bound of 88.53% (Table 1).
An ablation study removing core hierarchical coarse-graining components degrades RGMem's performance, confirming the contribution of each architectural piece (Table 2, Section 4.3).

dyRD6lBH8K.text: EF21 achieves a tight convergence guarantee under contractive compression with optimal step size eta_star = (2/(L+mu)) * ((1-sqrt(epsilon))/(1+sqrt(epsilon))), and the resulting contraction rate rho_star is independent of the number of agents n (Theorem 3.1).

Under the statistical homogeneity (shared minimizer) assumption, classic Error Feedback (EF) matches EF21's optimal step size and contraction factor exactly, giving identical tight convergence rates (Theorem 3.4).

Without the shared-minimizer assumption, classic EF can exhibit 2-periodic cycles under statistical heterogeneity and generally fails to converge in the multi-agent setting (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).

The worst-case multi-agent convergence rate proven in Theorem 3.1 exactly matches the known single-agent rate, showing the novel Lyapunov function recovers prior single-agent guarantees as a special case (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).

For heterogeneous regularity parameters across agents, Corollary 3.2 extends the tight rates to deterministic, additive, positively homogeneous compressors using averaged parameters L-bar and mu-bar (Corollary 3.2).

For the two-agent (n=2) heterogeneous case, an explicit cubic polynomial characterizes the empirically optimal convergence rate, and tuning the EControl algorithm's step size to its optimum yields eta=0, coinciding with EF21 (Law 4.3, Law 4.4, Section 4).

9dwgtsGGu8.text: Singular Value Ensemble (SVE) freezes the singular vectors U and V from an SVD of each weight matrix and trains M copies of the per-member singular values, adding only about (M-1)/(2d) extra parameters per matrix, roughly 0.2-1% overhead versus 700% for a standard M=4 deep ensemble (Section 4).

On vision classification, SV-Ensemble attains the best accuracy and calibration among methods compared on Flowers102 (95.4% accuracy, 1.0% ECE) and Oxford Pets (90.1% accuracy, 2.2% ECE), while placing second to LoRA-Ensemble on CIFAR-100 (85.6% vs 88.2% accuracy) (Table 1).
On SST-2, SV-Ensemble achieves the best expected calibration error (2.8% ECE) among the compared parameter-efficient ensemble methods while remaining competitive in accuracy (92.0%) (Table 2).
On ARC-Easy with M=16 ensemble members, SV-Ensemble reaches 85.8% accuracy and 3.8% ECE, approaching the Blob baseline's 3.6% ECE (Table 3).
On out-of-distribution detection, SV-Ensemble attains 81.6% AUROC, second only to LoRA-Ensemble at 82.8% (Table 4).

The benefit of SV-Ensemble over baselines grows with pretraining quality: it underperforms with a randomly initialized backbone but outperforms all baselines including deep ensembles when using a DINOv2 backbone (Figure 2).

hCIBCAS1Hi.text: The Sequential Optimization via SMC (SOSMC) framework replaces expensive inner MCMC sampling loops with a sequential Monte Carlo particle population that is reused and reweighted across optimization iterations, as formalized in Algorithm 1 (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).

Proposition 2 establishes a linear convergence rate for the idealized SOSMC iteration under mu-Polyak-Lojasiewicz and L-smooth loss assumptions, showing l(theta_k) - inf(l) <= (1-gamma*mu)^k * (l(theta_0) - inf(l)) for step size gamma <= 1/L (Proposition 2).

Propositions 3 and 4 show the effective sample size of the SMC weights decays exponentially in the squared gradient norm and step size, ESS_infinity(gamma) = N*exp(-gamma^2*||grad l||^2) for Gaussian targets, motivating an adaptive step-size/resampling scheme (Section 4.2, Propositions 3-4).

On Langevin reward-tuning of energy-based models with non-differentiable reward functions, SOSMC-ULA outperforms the ImpDiff baseline and achieves reduced variance compared to single-chain SOUL (Section 5.1).

On 2D EBM benchmark datasets, SOSMC achieves higher objective values than ImpDiff for small regularization strengths, with particle-based reward estimates that track true expectations throughout optimization (Section 5.2).
On MNIST, SOSMC remains robust in high dimensions even under mismatch between the pretraining and tuning kernels, without exhibiting reward hacking (Section 5.3).

0uS3P0Dlh9.text: Theorem 4.3 proves that FSQ codebooks are locally optimal for maximizing average nearest-neighbor distance among embeddings subject to an L-infinity norm constraint of at most 1 (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.3).

Section 4.2 shows that FSQ codebooks maximize token-prediction accuracy for an optimally trained continuous-diffusion-for-categorical-data (CDCD) model under equal prior token probabilities, proven analytically in 1D and supported numerically in higher dimensions (Section 4.2).

Numerical search over 10,000 randomly generated alternative codebooks across latent dimensions 2 to 8 (base2 and base3) finds none that outperform the FSQ codebook, supporting a global (not just local) optimality claim (Section 5.1).

On the SEED test-en benchmark, the FSQ-based CDCD-TTS model (FSQ-original-25) achieves a lower word error rate (2.00% vs 2.57%) and higher MOS (4.119 vs 4.077) and emotion-preservation score (72.7% vs 72.2%) than the CosyVoice2 LLM-based baseline, at comparable speaker similarity (Table 1).

The CDCD-TTS backbone is about 10x smaller than CosyVoice2's 0.5B-parameter Qwen-based LLM module and achieves a real-time factor of about 0.2-0.3 (3-5x faster than real time) using 25 denoising steps (Section 3.3, Section 5.2).
CDCD-TTS is trained on roughly 65k hours of combined LibriLight, GigaSpeech, and Emilia data using 8 V100 GPUs, batch size 600 seconds, peak learning rate 1e-4, for 1.5 million steps (Section 5.2).

dzx0eNCdiP.text: VLM3D formulates the vision-language model critic as a dual binary Yes/No query producing a differentiable log-odds reward r_VLM = z_yes - z_no, used both as an optimization objective (Eq. 9) and as test-time guidance (Eq. 10) for feed-forward 3D models (Section 4.1-4.3).

On the GPTEval3D benchmark with 110 prompts, VLM3D outperforms DreamFusion, DreamGaussian, Fantasia3D, Instant3D, Magic3D, ProlificDreamer, MVDream, DreamReward, and DreamDPO on text alignment (1365.5 vs 1298.9 for the next-best DreamDPO), 3D plausibility (1293.7), and overall score (1268.6) (Table 1).

As test-time guidance for feed-forward 3D generation, VLM3D improves CLIP-D from 0.23 to 0.19 error, FID from 338.6 to 274.9, and geometry score from 0.58 to 0.49 relative to the Hunyuan3D baseline (Table 2).

An ablation shows that removing either the geometric query or the multi-view input from the dual-query design produces Janus-face artifacts and floating disconnected parts, confirming both components are necessary (Figure 6).

VLM3D's feed-forward guidance corrects incomplete geometry and spatial incoherence in outputs from CLAY and Hunyuan3D, and responds correctly to single-concept prompt edits such as clothing color and spatial relations where MVDream fails (Figures 4-5).

LBcnybFVBp.text: SWING replaces discrete node-based random walks used by standard Graph Random Features with continuous ℝ^d-space walks via a Gumbel-softmax relaxation, avoiding the need to materialize the implicit graph's node/edge structure (Section 2.2.1, Equation 3).

Proposition 2.1 (with proof via Mellin transform in Proposition A.1) shows the Frechet noise used in the relaxed walk factorizes into independent components P_a and P_b, enabling an efficient importance-sampling-based load update with O_N(1) per-step complexity (Section 2.2.2-2.2.3, Proposition 2.1, Equation 9).

On synthetic point clouds ranging from 200 to 10,000 points, SWING achieves lower Frobenius Norm Error than standard GRFs at matched numbers of random features and traces a Pareto-optimal error-versus-time frontier, yielding over 10x inference speedup (Figures 2-3).

On the Thingi10K dataset (40 meshes), SWING is evaluated on vertex normal prediction via cosine similarity across varying mesh sizes, with reported CPU runtime comparisons (Table 2, Figures 4-5, Figure 11).
Adding SWING's soft attention mask M to a Vision Transformer improves top-1 accuracy from 80.10% to 80.34% on ImageNet and from 55.78% to 55.97% on Places365 (Table 1).

dSjVTpQyIk.text: MixFP4 uses dual FP4 micro-formats (E2M1 and E1M2) selected per block based on a crest-factor criterion, addressing the finding that a single FP4/INT4 codebook is suboptimal under heterogeneous block statistics (Section 3.2, Section 2.3).

On WikiText perplexity for post-training quantization, MixFP4 achieves 8.06 for Llama-3.1-8B, 12.39 for Qwen3-8B, and 13.48 for Llama-3.2-1B, all improving over NVFP4 (8.26, 12.74, 13.90 respectively) while BF16 baselines are 7.33, 12.21, and 11.57 (Table 3).
The paper derives a theoretical crossover crest factor κ*≈2.224 below which NVINT4 has better quantization SNR than NVFP4 (Appendix A, Equation 31).
At block size 16, the E2M1+E1M2 format pair achieves near-optimal results, while larger block sizes favor E2M1+E3M0 due to increased within-block heterogeneity (Table 5).
MixFP4 maintains lower final pre-training loss than a 4/6-bit baseline across 114M and 476M parameter Qwen3-style models trained on FineWeb-Edu (Figures 10-11).

MixFP4's hardware implementation incurs only 3.1% area overhead and 1.5% power overhead relative to a standard NVFP4 tensor core, confined to FP4 decode logic and E4M5 accumulators (Section 4.4, Figure 12).

euF1o9OgHr.text: SHARS (Segment-wise HAllucination Rejection Sampling) processes long-form generations sentence-by-sentence, retaining factual segments and resampling flagged ones using semantic uncertainty (HalluSE) as the hallucination detector, without external tools like web search (Section on SHARS method).
On the FactScore benchmark, SHARS improves factual precision from a greedy-decoding baseline of 52.4% to 78.4% for Qwen3-32B and from 53.7% to 78.4% for Llama3.1-8B (Table with FactScore results).
HalluSE, the paper's refined semantic-entropy-based hallucination detector using entity-claim decomposition, achieves 72.9% AUROC on FactualBio versus 66.2% for naive semantic entropy (Table 4).
An ablation shows both the rewriting component and the 'Following' sampling strategy (versus a 'Temperature' sampling baseline) are necessary for SHARS's precision gains (Table 6).

Combining SHARS with the training-time method FactAlign further improves Llama3.1-8B factual precision from 53.1% to 80.6%, demonstrating orthogonal, complementary gains (Section on complementarity with FactAlign).
SHARS achieves factuality gains at 10-40x relative runtime for Qwen3-32B, whereas competing methods require 35-60x runtime for comparable precision improvements (Figure 1b-c).
