2Ud1nkQrVZ.text: Per-image sample-wise SVD of CaiT-S24's last-layer token features shows 99th-percentile effective rank of only 61 dimensions (out of 384) to capture 95% energy and 121 dimensions for 99% energy, indicating strong per-image compressibility (Figure 1c, Section 2.4).

Dataset-level shared-subspace PCA on the same CaiT-S24 features requires 302/384 dimensions for 95% energy and 359/384 dimensions for 99% energy across ~99% of images, revealing substantial subspace rotation across inputs despite per-image low-rankness (Figure 1d, Section 2.4).

Token-level Spectral Energy Pattern (SEP) analysis shows an architecture-invariant encoding law: roughly 50/60/70/80/90% of a token's spectral energy is captured by 50/60/70/80/90% of the normalized channel bandwidth d/D, nearly identical across 14 transformer-family architectures (Figure 2, Section 2.5).

The proposed Lift (post-hoc lifting projector, 192→384 dims, retained at inference) and WideLast (widening only the student's last Transformer block) remedies improve DeiT-Tiny distilled from CaiT-S24 from a 74.86% baseline to 77.53% (SoftKD+SpecKD with Lift) and 78.23% (SoftKD+MSE with WideLast) top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K (Table 2).

Without any teacher distillation, adding Lift alone raises standalone DeiT-Tiny top-1 accuracy from 74.86% to 75.41%, and WideLast alone raises it to 75.54%, showing the encoding-mismatch fix is a genuine architectural improvement independent of distillation (Table 8).

An ablation over projector output dimension D_T ∈ {256,320,384,448} shows performance peaking near the teacher-matched 384-dim width (75.41% standalone, 76.40% with SpectralKD), with 448-dim hurting standalone accuracy (75.23%), supporting that the student should match the teacher's subspace width rather than being arbitrarily wider (Table 4, Section 4.3.2).

PN7l7mBPDO.text: Table-GLS is a three-stage training-free inference framework for multimodal table reasoning: global structure exploration, self-refined sub-table extraction, and evidence-grounded reasoning, requiring no fine-tuning or external tools (Method section).
With Qwen3-VL-8B, combining DiSCo alignment and Table-GLS achieves 58.12% average accuracy across 8 table reasoning benchmarks (Table 3).

The DiSCo alignment stage, trained with only 10K table images, matches or exceeds a Textual-All baseline trained on 97K images on most table understanding tasks, particularly structure-sensitive benchmarks TSD, TCL, and RCE (Table 1).
An ablation removing Global Structure Exploration causes consistent performance drops, e.g., on AIT-QA accuracy falls from 76.71% to 62.82%, showing both stages of Table-GLS are essential (Table 2).
Table-GLS generalizes to out-of-domain benchmarks such as AIT-QA and PubHealthTab without additional supervised training on those table structures (Table 3, Section on OOD evaluation).

Table-GLS uses 439-492 tokens on average for its structured reasoning process, compared to about 241 tokens for standard Chain-of-Thought, reflecting a token-efficiency trade-off for interpretability (Token efficiency analysis section).

OqYz3v9111.text: In gridworld navigation, LLM agent action accuracy decreases monotonically with grid size from 7x7 to 15x15 and with obstacle density from 0.0 to 1.0, and decays linearly with distance from the goal for distances under 20 steps (Behavioral results, performance scaling section).

The agent shows no statistically significant accuracy differences across four difficulty-preserving transformations (reflection, rotation, start/goal swap, transposition), indicating robustness to task-irrelevant variations (Robustness testing section).

In KeyDoorEnv, where key pickup is instrumental to the goal, the agent achieves 100% success rate and 98.7% action accuracy, whereas in KeyNoDoorEnv with a distractor key, it shows only a 17% pickup rate but a 75% attraction bias toward the irrelevant key (Goal-structure experiments section).

In 2PathKeyEnv, the mere presence of a (non-essential) key reduces task success rate from 75.5% to 71.4%, indicating the agent is drawn toward salient but non-goal-relevant objects (Goal-structure experiments section).

An MLP probe decodes the agent's internal cognitive map of cell identities at 70-75.7% accuracy, with agent and goal positions localized within Manhattan distance <2 even on 15x15 grids, while wall information is poorly represented (Representational analysis section).

A recovery metric shows that 37.4%-88.4% of the agent's behavioral failures are attributable to imperfect internal representations rather than a lack of goal-directedness, and policy-belief consistency (action accuracy vs. optimal policy on decoded maps) ranges from 77.8% to 94.6% agreement (Policy-belief consistency section).

47BMisNtar.text: The CReL reliability score is defined as the worst-case value of a user-specified similarity metric ρ within a calibrated prediction set at confidence level 1−α (Equation 1, Section 3).

CReL is computed via a four-step procedure: training a latent generative model on 60% of data, fitting a directional quantile regression on 24%, calibrating on 8% via a distance-based adjustment, and constructing the final prediction set through the decoder (Algorithm 1, Section 3.1).

Proposition 3.2 gives a latent-space coverage guarantee of the form 1−α ≤ P(Z_{n+1} ∈ S^{γ_cal}) ≤ 1−α + 1/(1+|D_cal|), and Theorem 3.3 shows the decoded prediction set inherits this coverage when the latent generative model recovers the true conditional distribution (Section 3.2).

On synthetic calibration data at α=0.1, CReL achieves coverage 0.8915 with prediction-set area 232.7, compared to a Feldman-style baseline (coverage 0.8940, area 234.5) and a plain DQR baseline (coverage 0.9145, area 287.4) (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On the image-to-text task at α=0.1, BLIP-base's average CLIP score of 0.2330 drops to a CReL-CLIP reliability score of 0.0070, and rankings shift such that BLIP-base ranks last by average CLIP score but first by CReL reliability (Table 2, Section 4.2).

On the text-to-image task at α=0.1, SD3-M's average CLIP score of 0.2590 drops to a CReL-CLIP score of 0.0134, and SD3.5-L's average DINO score of 0.4531 drops to a CReL-DINO score of −0.1365 (Table 3, Section 4.3).

CL6Byu4aIA.text: MAD introduces an 'extended score' operator H_γ (Definition 3.1) that coincides with the standard score function when it exists but remains well-defined even for Dirac delta distributions, unlike the standard score (Section 3).

Lemma 3.2 proves H_0 p = ∇log p (the standard score) for densities in P(R^d), while Lemma 3.3 derives the extended score for mixtures of Dirac deltas via Voronoi regions, formalizing how MAD attracts samples onto a data manifold (Section 3).

The MAD inference procedure (Algorithm 1, Eq. 4-5) uses a correction factor m(t_i) = (1 + γ(t_i) − bγ(t_i)/t_i²)^{-1} and requires roughly twice the compute of standard diffusion inference due to a second score-network evaluation (Section 4).

On synthetic 1D-manifold shape data (Section 5.3), MAD is trained on 100,000 noisy samples with 30 repeats per image over 3 million iterations on a single A100 GPU (~14 hours), using settings δ=0.02, p=8, a=0.002, b=15.

MAD is evaluated on FFHQ (64×64), AFHQv2 (64×64), and ImageNet (64×64) for face/animal/object generation, and on a real 256×256 cryo-EM dataset of 68,401 particle images from EMPIAR-11618, trained on two A100 GPUs for ~60 hours (Section 5.2, 5.4).

9voQUicsc2.text: On two-model coordination with Stable Diffusion, Divide-and-Denoise achieves 88.50% GenEval images, versus 58.00% for MultiDiffusion, and for three-model coordination achieves 59.50% versus 14.00% for MultiDiffusion (Table 1, Section 4.4).
Divide-and-Denoise achieves a lower fairness (envy-free) violation rate of 0.015±0.008 for two-model coordination, compared to 0.485±0.233 for MultiDiffusion (Table 2, Section 4.4).
On DiT-based experiments, Divide-and-Denoise attains a joint CLIP score of 29.03 versus 28.56 for MultiDiffusion (Table 3, Section 4.4).
On prompts specifying concepts with color descriptions, Divide-and-Denoise achieves 55.75% GenEval images versus 27.00% for MultiDiffusion (Table 4, Section 4.5).
On conflicting-concept prompts, Divide-and-Denoise achieves a minimum VQAScore of 0.815 across composed concepts versus 0.689 for MultiDiffusion (Table 5, Section 4.6).

Ablating the fairness constraint ('Ours w/o fairness') is reported as a separate row across Tables 1 and 3-5 to isolate the contribution of the game-theoretic fair-division mechanism (Section 4.4-4.6).

SGTLVjx3MN.text: Theorem 2.2 establishes a concentration inequality for functions of independent random variables under finite Lp moment conditions exhibiting a two-regime bound combining polynomial and sub-Gaussian terms (Section 2.2).
Theorem 2.6 extends the concentration results to the heavy-tailed regime p ∈ (1,2), yielding bounds unavailable to prior uniform-boundedness-based approaches (Section 2.2).

Assumption 3.1 defines (Lp,β)-Lipschitz stability, requiring only that the replace-one stability increment have finite p-th moments for some p≥2, replacing deterministic uniform stability (Section 3.1).
Theorem 3.4 provides a high-probability generalization bound for empirical risk minimization under (Lp,β)-Lipschitz stability (Section 3.1).

Theorems 3.9 and 3.10 extend the concentration framework to sampling without replacement and derive generalization bounds R(h)−R̂(h) for transductive regression under (Lp,β)-Lipschitz stability (Section 3.2).

Theorem 3.14 establishes high-probability generalization bounds for meta-learning algorithms under Assumption 3.12, which decomposes stability into meta-stability across tasks, within-task stability, and test-sample stability (Section 3.3).

e6hVbhHEXh.text: On CharacterTrajectories, MVC-CDE with GP smoothing requires 95.17 ± 7.41 function evaluations (NFE), versus 633.11 ± 28.31 for linear-spline and 595.91 ± 9.99 for cubic-spline neural CDEs (Table 1, Section C.1).

On SpokenArabicDigits, MVC-CDE with GP smoothing requires 95.40 ± 0.89 NFE versus 2237.40 ± 20.02 for linear spline and 1003.80 ± 24.19 for cubic spline, corresponding to total training times of 7.32 ± 0.15s versus 106.15 ± 3.76s and 57.90 ± 1.73s respectively (Table 1, Section C.1).

On UWaveGestureLibrary, MVC-CDE with GP achieves 218.60 ± 10.04 NFE and 12.29 ± 0.27s training time, versus 4340.60 ± 216.07 NFE / 176.19 ± 5.13s for linear spline and 1076.60 ± 33.57 NFE / 53.22 ± 2.25s for cubic spline (Table 1, Section C.1).
MVC-GP demonstrates a speedup ranging from 4.3× to 14.5× compared to standard spline-based neural CDE methods across the evaluated datasets (Section 4.2).

Theorem 3.1 shows that NFE is strictly determined by the L_{1/(p+1)}-quasi-norm of the (p+1)-th derivative of the control path, and Corollary 3.3 shows NFE scales as h^{-1} for smoothing-based paths with lengthscale h (Section 3.2, Section 3.4).

Figure 4 shows that under additive noise, smoothing-based methods (kernel/GP) maintain almost constant NFE, while interpolation-based (linear/cubic spline) methods show a drastic increase in both NFE and error rate (Section 4.3).

Icj19tWHI1.text: 3DGSim is trained on only 1,000 rigid trajectories yet still learns rigid, elastic, and cloth-like dynamics using separate datasets of 6 GSO objects each (Section 4.1).

On held-out rollouts, 3DGSim achieves PSNR of 28.28±2.52 (rigid), 33.15±3.51 (elastic), and 26.98±2.63 (cloth), compared to 22.35±3.82, 18.87±3.99, and 21.10±3.56 for the Cosmos baseline under 4-step conditioning and 12-step rollout (Section 4.1).

Without any fine-tuning, the model generalizes to out-of-distribution scenarios such as ground removal/editing and multi-object interactions (2-5 duplicated objects, 180-step rollouts), producing physically plausible deformations despite training only on single-object ground collisions (Section 4.2, Figure 9).

The inverse rendering encoder (MVSplat-based) is trained jointly with the dynamics transformer rather than pre-trained separately, decomposing particle features into dynamic and invariant components so the dynamics model captures physics-relevant properties such as shadows (Section 3.2).
The dynamics transformer uses point cloud serialization via space-filling curves in place of k-nearest-neighbor graphs to enable efficient temporal attention over particles (Section 3.3).
The full model runs near real time on a single H100 GPU, achieving about 16 FPS with 4 past conditioning steps and about 20.1 FPS with 2 past steps while using under 20 GB of VRAM (Section 4.3).

vGTFOp3jLO.text: SoftMoE replaces discrete top-k expert routing with a differentiable truncated soft top-k mechanism derived from a LapSum relaxation, allowing gradient-based optimization of the expert count k per layer (Section 4).

On OpenWebText with 10-layer, 32-expert-per-layer models (1.63B parameters), SoftMoE-1.5 (k≤2) achieves a lower language modeling loss (2.76) than sparse MoE (2.79) while activating only 1.63-1.96 experts on average during training/inference, up to 24% fewer experts (Table 1, Section 5).
On C4, SoftMoE-1.5 (k≤3) attains loss 2.22 versus 2.24 for sparse MoE while using 1.96-2.19 active experts on average (Table 1, Section 5).

Under a global per-layer budget constraint (each layer must activate at least 1 expert, with total experts summing to K across L layers), the learned allocation is highly non-uniform: the top 3 transformer layers absorb roughly 50% of the total expert budget, with allocation patterns stabilizing within the first 25k training steps (Figure 6, Section 5.1).
SoftMoE shows competitive or superior downstream performance on PIQA, HellaSwag, and ARC-E relative to sparse MoE despite activating fewer experts on average (Section 5).

JKSDWukEgN.text: Roughly 1% of attention heads specialize in machine translation subtasks, decomposing into disjoint 'language heads' that encode target-language identity and 'translation heads' that preserve sentence meaning, evaluated across three model families (Section 3.2, Section 5).

Activation patching on Gemma-3-12B across 20 language directions yields a Jaccard index of only 0.13 between the top 5% of language heads and translation heads, confirming the two head sets are largely disjoint (Figure 2, Section 5).
Steering approximately 1% of language and translation heads with instruction-free, zero-shot prompts achieves translation quality comparable to prompting with explicit task instructions (Figure 3).

Ablating just 1% of language heads causes a sharp collapse in target-language accuracy when translating from English, whereas ablating the same proportion of translation heads produces only a more gradual quality decline (Figure 4).

Equivalence (meaning) vectors extracted from translation heads transfer across different language directions while yielding approximately the same BLEU scores, indicating a language-agnostic semantic representation (Figure 5).

s1CYkVHVvf.text: CoCD (Coherent Coordinate Descent) is a deterministic zeroth-order optimizer that achieves O(1) query complexity per step while provably maintaining a global descent direction (Abstract, Theorem 5.3).
Theorem 5.10 proves that under Polyak-Łojasiewicz conditions, CoCD achieves linear convergence at rate (1-2μC1/C2)^t despite using stale gradient estimates, with staleness factor τ=n/B-1.
A momentum parameter γ controls memory of past stale gradients, ranging from γ=1.0 (perfect memory) to γ=0.0, which recovers standard BCCD with no historical gradient reuse (Section 5).
On Table 2, CoCD substantially outperforms BCCD in sample efficiency: SARCOS regression loss of 31.18 vs. 188.73, MNIST accuracy of 95.48% vs. 27.03%, and CIFAR-10 accuracy of 45.08% vs. 10.13%.

CoCD achieves roughly 2x wall-clock speedup over ZO-SGD on regression tasks (8.1s vs. 15.7s per episode), and Appendix E scales the method to a ResNet-20 (~270k parameters) on CIFAR-10 with a query budget B=2048 (Figure 4, Appendix E).

Jj8Vec8qSs.text: Linear M-CBE (Lin-M-CBE) learns a finite set of M distinct linear expressions with per-expert parameters θ_m, combined via a mixture distribution p(y,c|x) = p(c|x) Σ_m p(m|x) p(y|c,θ_m) (Section 4, Equation 5).

Symbolic M-CBE (Sym-M-CBE) discovers expert functions via a three-stage training procedure: training with MLP placeholders, applying PySR-based symbolic recovery, then fine-tuning the recovered expressions (Section 4).

On the Pareto frontier over mixture size and functional form, Lin-M-CBE gives the best accuracy-interpretability balance on high-dimensional classification tasks (CUB200, CIFAR10 with >100 concepts), while Sym-M-CBE dominates on regression tasks with compact, high-accuracy expressions (Figure 4, Section 5.1).

Sym-M-CBE recovers near-exact symbolic expressions matching ground truth, achieving Tree Edit Distance of 0.00±0.00 on both Pendulum and MAWPS, e.g., recovering '8.00*sin(θ)+10.00' (Table 1, Section 5.2).

Restricting the symbolic operator vocabulary post-hoc to {+,-} degrades Pendulum MAE to 3.80, whereas using the complete operator set reduces MAE to 0.46, matching black-box performance without retraining (Table 2, Section 5.3).
Using more than one expert (M>1) is critical for datasets with incomplete concept sets (AWA2-Incomplete, CUB200-Incomplete) and for tasks with input-varying logic such as MAWPS (Section 5.1).

qJFatzEGQc.text: LatentLens achieves 72% interpretability of visual tokens across all studied VLM combinations and layers under VLM-judge evaluation, versus 23% for LogitLens and 30% for EmbeddingLens (Section 4.2).

The evaluation spans 9 model combinations built from 3 LLMs (OLMo-7B, Qwen2-7B, LLaMA3-8B) and 3 vision encoders (CLIP-ViT-L/14-336, DINOv2-L-336, SigLIP-so400m-patch14-384), plus off-the-shelf Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct (Figure 5).

Visual tokens at early input layers align most strongly with contextualized text representations from mid-layers (layers 8-16) rather than same-layer representations, a 'mid-layer leap' pattern shown in Figure 4 (Section 4.3).
LatentLens produces full-word and sentence-level descriptions of visual tokens, in contrast to the subword-level outputs produced by LogitLens, as shown in qualitative examples (Figure 6).
An ablation using linear connectors instead of the default architecture maintains 72.1% interpretability, showing robustness of the LatentLens method (Table 1, Appendix D).
The VLM-judge (GPT-4o) evaluation protocol achieves Cohen's kappa of 0.68 agreement with human annotations across 1,020 annotated instances (Section 4.2).

9DAX4oLVhy.text: SelfJudge trains a self-supervised judge verifier using a semantic preservation score derived from the target model's likelihood differences, requiring no human annotation or ground-truth answers (Section 3.3).

On Llama-3.1-8B (target) with Llama-3.2-1B (draft), SelfJudge-F increases the average accepted length by +2.06 tokens while degrading task performance by only 1.0%, compared to AutoJudge-R's +1.96 length increase but larger 2.7% task-performance drop (Table 1).

SelfJudge is evaluated against standard speculative decoding (rejection sampling), top-k verification, and AutoJudge/AutoJudge+ answer-preservation baselines across GSM8K, MATH-500, LiveCodeBench, CNN/DailyMail, and MMLU (Section 4).
Training data for the judge verifier consists of 69,432 token labels derived from 1,220 prompts sourced from GSM8K, LiveCodeBench, and Dolly15K (Section 3.3).
Results are reported for both Llama-3.1-8B/3.2-1B and Qwen-2.5-8B/0.5B target/draft model pairs (Section 4).
A suffix-length ablation identifies an optimal suffix length of N=20 for the semantic preservation scoring mechanism (Figure 4).

ocLKXXgvp3.text: Theorem 1 (Section 4) shows that conditioning the inverse dynamics model on a predicted future state reduces the expected conditional variance of the action distribution, at the cost of introducing prediction bias, formalizing the bias-variance tradeoff of PIDM versus behavior cloning.
Theorem 3 (Section 4) gives conditions under which PIDM provably requires no more samples than behavior cloning to reach comparable performance.
Across four 2D navigation tasks, behavior cloning requires up to 5x more demonstrations than PIDM to reach 80% performance, averaging 3.25x more samples across tasks (Section 5.2, Table 1).

In a 3D video-game environment with high-dimensional visual inputs and stochastic transitions, behavior cloning requires 66% more demonstration samples than PIDM to reach an 80% success rate (Section 5.5, Figure 1b).
PIDM is implemented as a state predictor that forecasts a future state combined with an inverse dynamics model that infers the action needed to reach it (Figure 2d).
State-wise error analysis shows PIDM's action-prediction advantage over behavior cloning is concentrated near goal locations, where action variance is highest (Figure 5).

eNvxTIZugB.text: DAL (Detection Augmented bandit) is presented as Algorithm 1 (Section 3), a black-box framework that pairs any stationary bandit algorithm with a change detector to handle piecewise stationary environments.
Theorem 1 (Section 4) proves DAL achieves an order-optimal O~(sqrt(N_T * T)) regret bound, where N_T is the number of change-points over horizon T.

Table 1 (Section 4) shows DAL combined with LinUCB matches the state-of-the-art d*sqrt(N_T*T) regret bound for piecewise-stationary linear bandits, and DAL with GLM-UCB attains the same rate for generalized linear bandits.
For piecewise-stationary self-concordant bandits, DAL improves the regret bound from the prior d^(2/3) T^(2/3) N_T^(1/3) rate to d*sqrt(N_T*T) (Table 1, Section 4).

DAL is empirically compared against MASTER (Wei & Luo, 2021), ADA-OPKB (Hong et al., 2023), and WeightUCB (Wang et al., 2023) in piecewise-stationary environments (Section 5.1, Figures 1-3) and drifting environments (Section 5.2, Figures 4-5).
The regret analysis in Appendix A.1 decomposes total regret into false-alarm cost, detection latency, the base stationary algorithm's regret, and forced-exploration cost.

CKhydx7QgH.text: The Wrapped Normalization Equivariance (WNE) wrapper normalizes inputs, applies an arbitrary backbone, then denormalizes outputs, enforcing input-output normalization equivariance without modifying the backbone's internal layers (Section 3.1).

For FDnCNN on GPU, WNE adds negligible overhead relative to the unwrapped baseline (0.99x on backward pass, 1.00x on inference), whereas the architectural NE baseline (NE-arch) is 1.60x slower on backward pass and 1.69x slower on inference (Table 2).
For SwinIR on GPU, the WNE wrapper matches the baseline runtime at 1.00x for both backward and inference passes (Table 5).
DnCNN-WNE remains competitive with the unwrapped baseline in matched-noise PSNR on Set12 and BSD68 across noise levels sigma in {10, 25, 50} (Table 1).
Under noise-level mismatch, WNE-wrapped models track the robustness behavior of the architectural NE baseline while avoiding its up-to-1.6x GPU slowdown (Figures 3-4).
Section 3.2 provides a theoretical characterization showing every normalization-equivariant function admits the wrapper's normalize-process-denormalize factorization.

yTEEiE3YtD.text: VectorWorld reduces nuPlan endpoint distance from 0.250m to 0.078m and collision rate from 9.30% to 3.01% compared to prior methods (Table 1).
VectorWorld achieves the lowest Fréchet distance (0.94) among non-privileged methods on Waymo Open Motion (Table 1).

VectorWorld generates a 64m×64m vector-graph tile in approximately 6 ms, enabling real-time closed-loop rollouts exceeding 1 kilometer for autonomous driving simulation (Section on closed-loop performance, Table 2).
Motion-aware gated VAE warm-start initialization reduces jerk from 16.6 to 9.6 and increases closed-loop success rate from 42% to 78% versus history-free initialization (Table 2).
Retraining the driving policy inside the VectorWorld simulator raises stress-test success rate from 25.0% to 56.0% (Table 2).
VectorWorld is benchmarked against the SLEDGE and ScenDream generative world-model baselines on Waymo Open Motion and nuPlan (Section on evaluation datasets).

ue7XmbJ2QZ.text: Physics-informed spectral diffusion (PISD) achieves 1.47% relative error on the Poisson forward problem with 1000 observations, versus 3.35% for DiffusionPDE and 1.54% for FunDPS (Table with Poisson forward-problem results).
PISD attains a PDE residual of 2.31 on the same Poisson forward task, dramatically lower than DiffusionPDE's 207.28 and FunDPS's 3807.58 (Table with Poisson forward-problem results).
PISD generates a single PDE solution in about 52 seconds versus 802 seconds for DiffusionPDE, a 3-15x speedup across tested settings (Section on computational efficiency).

PISD reduces the spectral representation dimensionality from 128x128 to 44x44 modes for the Poisson and Helmholtz equations while preserving Sobolev regularity, as formalized in Lemma 3.2 (Lemma 3.2).
PISD is evaluated on Poisson, Helmholtz, and incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, using Adam-based optimization during sampling instead of gradient descent (Section on tested equations).

rLFIOikFR2.text: Explicit deployment-framed system prompts fail to convince models they are not being evaluated, with evaluation-awareness detection rates remaining between 15% and 55% (Section: Innate Evaluation Awareness of LLMs).

Sparse-autoencoder rating features tied to sycophancy show roughly 3x larger differential activation between monitored and unmonitored conditions than scheming-related detection features (Section: Causal Analysis, Tables 3-4).

Extended-reasoning (thinking) model variants detect evaluation contexts 9-31 percentage points more accurately than instruct variants of the same models (Section: Innate Evaluation Awareness of LLMs).
Qwen3-80B thinking models reach 42.5% evaluation-detection accuracy versus 11.7% for instruct variants (Table 5).
Fine-tuning models toward greater sycophancy increases evaluation-context sensitivity without producing a correspondingly large increase in measurable misalignment (Section: Sycophancy Fine-tuning).
The paper contrasts sycophancy, deception, alignment faking, self-preservation, and scheming as competing explanations along behavioral and intent dimensions (Table 1).

827XA57r8F.text: MERIT-3D reaches a 57.0 eight-benchmark average on Qwen2.5-VL-3B fine-tuned across 136 Vision-FLAN tasks, versus 54.3 for single-epoch centralized joint training, a 2.7-point gain (Empirical results section, Qwen2.5-VL-3B experiments).

On Qwen2.5-VL-7B with a 1.6M-example, 176-source mixture, MERIT scores 55.4 versus 54.9 for joint fine-tuning at base scale, and 61.5 versus 60.9 at scaled base-VLM size (Empirical results section, Qwen2.5-VL-7B experiments).
On the text-only 66-task FLAN mixture, MERIT-2D reaches 58.4 versus 57.6 for single-epoch joint training (Empirical results section, text-only FLAN experiments).

MERIT's decentralized branch training and one-shot merging adds about 24% compute overhead over single-epoch joint training at 3B scale on 8 V100 GPUs, dropping to a 0.8% recurring overhead at 7B scale on 8 A100 GPUs (Section on computational efficiency).
Theorem 3.1 shows that merging independently trained, PCA-conflict-split branches yields curvature-weighted variance reduction, with gains growing with the Hessian spectral gap (Theorem 3.1).

dVIts0fNb4.text: Predictive variational inference (PVI) replaces the KL-divergence objective of standard VI with optimization of the posterior predictive distribution against the true data-generating process, using proper scoring rules (Section: Main Framework).
Proposition 1 establishes that PVI solutions converge to the predictively optimal parameter as sample size grows, even under model misspecification (Proposition 1).

Corollary 1 shows PVI recovers the true parameter when the model is correctly specified, and Corollary 2 shows it recovers the population parameter distribution when misspecified with population-varying parameters (Corollary 1, Corollary 2).

PVI is implemented with three proper scoring rules -- logarithmic, quadratic, and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) -- with the CRPS variant enabling likelihood-free inference for intractable simulators (Section on scoring rules).

In a cryo-EM protein conformation inference experiment, PVI recovers the true population distribution of parameters while standard Bayesian VI collapses to a point estimate (Section: CryoEM Protein Inference experiment).
Across 7 models from PosteriorDB, PVI improves held-out predictive performance compared to standard variational inference (Section: Benchmark PosteriorDB experiment).

Ps58JvpLT7.text: Path-Coupled Bellman Flows (PCBF) share base noise between current and successor generative paths, using a residual anchor term (1-t)(1-γ)X_0 to keep both the t=0 Gaussian source and the t=1 Bellman endpoint aligned regardless of the discount factor γ (Section 4.2, Equations 8-10).

Theorem 5.5 shows the population velocity field satisfies v⋆(x,t)=E[(R+γX₁')-X₀ | X_t=x, S=s, A=a], and Proposition 5.8 proves the shared-noise Bellman operator is a γ-contraction, D_p(𝒯_pc G, 𝒯_pc H) ≤ γD_p(G,H) (Section 5.3, Section 5.6).

On OGBench cube-double-play and puzzle-4x4-play tasks, PCBF achieves the best reported scores (71±5 and 30±4 respectively), while on cube-triple-play it underperforms Value Flows (4±1 vs 14±3) (Table 1).
On D4RL Adroit tasks PCBF is competitive with but slightly below FQL (69±2 vs 71±4) (Table 1).

Figure 4 shows that increasing the consistency-loss coefficient in Value Flows systematically degrades distributional accuracy, whereas PCBF maintains low Wasserstein error across the same range of hyperparameter settings, demonstrating improved training stability (Section 6.2, Figure 4).

Appendix E (Table 2) reports that PCBF's numerical ODE integration puts its computational cost in the same range as other flow-based distributional critics but slower than scalar (non-generative) distributional RL methods.

D5Ijcnz1L9.text: Theorem 2 establishes an in-sample MSE bound for each task j that guarantees safety, ℰⱼⁱⁿ(θ̂ⱼ) ≲ q²(d/n)ζ regardless of the balancedness constant B, outlier fraction ε, or heterogeneity δ (Section 5.1, Theorem 2).

Theorem 2 also shows a transfer guarantee for inlier tasks when B ≲ min(1/ε, m): ℰⱼⁱⁿ(θ̂ⱼ) ≲ (Bd/mn + min(Bδ², d/n) + B²ε²d/n)ζ, achieved without knowing ε, δ, or the inlier set S (Section 5.1, Theorem 2).

Assumption 1 (Balancedness) replaces the classical Lower Boundedness of Second Moments condition ρI ⪯ Σⱼ with the one-sided condition Σⱼ ⪯ B·Σ_S, accommodating rank-deficient or decaying covariate spectra where prior eigenvalue-lower-bound approaches (e.g. Duan & Wang 2023, depending on 1/ρ²) fail (Section 4, Assumption 1).

Theorem 3 extends the in-sample MSE guarantees of Theorem 2 to population risk via an empirical-to-population comparability constant νⱼ, retaining an intrinsic-dimension fallback for the safety guarantee (Section 5.2, Theorem 3).
Theorem 4 extends the same adaptive safety/transfer MSE guarantees to generalized linear models under bounded-domain assumptions (Section 6, Theorem 4).

Algorithm 1 solves a joint convex objective ℒ(Θ)=Σⱼ wⱼ(fⱼ(θⱼ)+λⱼ‖θⱼ-β‖_{Σⱼ}) that penalizes disagreement in prediction space (via task-specific norms) rather than raw parameter space (Section 3, Algorithm 1).

9DfsHAFE5l.text: Convex Gated Probing (CGP) reduces the fine-tuning-to-probing gap for the EAT baseline on AS-20k from 22.33 percentage points (linear probing: 35.20 vs 40.28 mAP) down to a 5.08 percentage point gap (Table 1).

BAT achieves 41.32 mAP with fine-tuning and 37.52 mAP with CGP on AS-20k, outperforming EAT and SSLAM under the same evaluation protocol, and reaches 95.52% (fine-tuning) / 95.80% (CGP, exceeding fine-tuning) accuracy on ESC-50 (Table 5).

Three architectural changes each yield measurable mAP gains on the SSL pretraining recipe: modernized data preprocessing via TorchAudio decibel compression and local min-max normalization (+0.17 mAP, Section 5.1, Table 2), a sigmoid-gated attention mechanism Ṽ=σ(xW_G)⊙V̄ that eliminates attention sinks (+0.39 mAP, Section 5.2, Table 3), and a 6-layer ViT decoder with 12 heads replacing a CNN decoder (+2.0 pp mAP, Section 5.3, Table 4).

The authors report being unable to reproduce previously published SSLAM improvements and attribute the reported gains to optimization artifacts and undocumented practices, including an extreme loss-scaling factor of 8×10⁴ for the global loss term (Section 5, Appendix A).

CGP's learned per-block gating weights correlate strongly with per-block linear-probing performance, allowing automatic identification of task-relevant layers without exhaustive manual probing (Figure 4).

PUIivg3GrO.text: Proposition 1 gives the geometric existence condition for a consistent (label-preserving) adversarial attack: ε·d*_q*(ŵ_⊥) ≥ |⟨ŵ,x⟩|, where ŵ_⊥ is the component of the classifier orthogonal to the ground-truth direction (Section 3.1, Proposition 1).

Theorem 3.1 shows that, for the well-specified Gaussian model, the consistent robust-error and consistent boundary-error metrics concentrate to closed-form integrals depending on √(q-m²), in contrast to the standard (inconsistent) robust error which depends on √q, formally explaining why consistent attacks are less effective at fixed perturbation budget (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 characterizes the asymptotic robust-ERM performance in a latent-space (misspecified) linear classification model via a system of self-consistent equations in the proportional limit n,p,d→∞, distinguishing underparameterized (γ≤1) from overparameterized (γ>1) regimes (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.1).

Section 4.3 shows overparameterization has a dual effect: the consistent boundary error E_bnd^cns increases with overparameterization (greater vulnerability to label-preserving attacks), while the aggregate consistent robust error E_rob^cns decreases because overparameterization improves clean generalization (Section 4.3).

Theorem 4.2 gives the exact asymptotic characterization of the consistent error metrics (E_rob^cns and E_bnd^cns) for the latent-variable classification model under misspecification (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).

mnU8odBWYE.text: The paper models observed binary rewards as r̃ = C(r*) generated from true rewards via a Bernoulli noise (label-flip) model with false-negative rate ρ⁻ and false-positive rate ρ⁺ (Section 4).

Theorem 3 shows that under this noise model, the GRPO policy-gradient advantage signal is attenuated by a factor of (1-ρ⁺-ρ⁻) relative to the noiseless case, and Theorem 4 proves standard (uncorrected) noisy GRPO converges to a strictly worse fixed point than noiseless GRPO (Section 4, Theorems 3-4).
Proposition 3 shows the Natarajan-corrected reward estimator r̂ = (r̃-ρ⁺)/(1-ρ⁺-ρ⁻) yields unbiased gradient estimates for GRPO/Dr.GRPO training (Section 5.1, Proposition 3).

Algorithm 1 estimates global reward flip rates ρ⁺, ρ⁻ from a 20% held-out balanced dataset and then applies the Natarajan correction during training, using variance correction M=1 for Dr.GRPO and M=Z (per Proposition 4) for GRPO (Section 5, Algorithm 1).

On GSM8K math tasks with Dr.GRPO, noise correction improves accuracy from 52.52% to 59.21% (+6.69 percentage points) for Llama-3.2-1B with the AceMath-7B reward model, and from 70.90% to 73.20% (+2.30 pp) for Qwen3-0.6B (Table 3).

On the APPS code-generation benchmark with Dr.GRPO, noise correction improves Qwen3-0.6B accuracy with the RM-Mistral-7B reward model from 9.01% to 10.50% (+1.49 pp), with a smaller gain of +0.13 pp for Llama-3.2-1B (Table 5).

1YCpxT3t5V.text: On 9x9 Sudoku, SE-RRM achieves 93.73% full-solution accuracy (FSR) and 97.58% grid-position accuracy (GPA), compared to TRM's 71.94% FSR / 89.80% GPA and HRM's 63.53% FSR / 86.11% GPA (Table 1).
SE-RRM zero-shot generalizes to 4x4 Sudoku with 95.46% FSR / 99.15% GPA, whereas HRM and TRM achieve 0% FSR and cannot extrapolate to unseen grid sizes (Table 1).

SE-RRM extrapolates to unseen 16x16 and 25x25 Sudoku grids, reaching 51.95% and 31.49% grid-position accuracy respectively, while baseline RRMs are structurally incompatible with these unseen symbol counts (Table 1).
On ARC-AGI-1 pass@2, SE-RRM scores 45.3% versus TRM's 44.6% and HRM's 40.3%; on ARC-AGI-2 pass@2, SE-RRM scores 7.1%, close to TRM's 7.8% and above HRM's 5.0% (Table 3).
SE-RRM matches this ARC-AGI performance using only 8 dihedral augmentations per sample versus roughly 1000 augmentations required by HRM/TRM (Section 3.2).

SE-RRM operates on tensors of shape D x I x K (versus vanilla RRMs' D x I) via dual attention layers across position and symbol dimensions, while using only 2M parameters compared to TRM's 7M and HRM's 27M (Section 2.3).

BZXZj2qQaK.text: SEMIR constructs a task-adapted inference space via boundary-aligned graph minors, reducing the pixel-level lattice of roughly 10^7 voxels to about 10^3 supernodes for BraTS, a ~10^4x reduction, with empirical counts of 2034±187 supernodes for ~8.9x10^6 voxels (Table 9).
On BraTS2021, SEMIR achieves Dice scores of 0.941 (tumor core), 0.920 (whole tumor), and 0.894 (enhancing tumor) (Table 3).
On KiTS2023, SEMIR achieves Dice scores of 0.945 (kidney+tumor+cyst), 0.861 (tumor+cyst), and 0.819 (tumor only); on LiTS2017, it achieves 0.959 (liver+tumor) and 0.891 (tumor only) (Table 3).

In controlled binary target-vs-rest comparisons, SEMIR outperforms nnU-Net on minority tumor structures: 0.894 vs 0.812 Dice on BraTS enhancing tumor, 0.819 vs 0.720 on KiTS tumor, and 0.891 vs 0.733 on LiTS tumor (Table 4).
Ablating the edge-contraction operation in the graph-minor construction degrades enhancing-tumor Dice by 51% (Table 5, Section 4.4).
Few-shot parameter learning for the graph-minor construction with 5 samples outperforms manually tuned parameters (Section 3.4.1, Table 5).

JnuwpwbZ8D.text: Theorem 4.1 establishes a general first-order-logic framework giving pseudo-dimension bounds of O(p*prod(d_k+1)*log M + p^2*prod(d_k+1)*log Delta) for multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning by connecting logical complexity to learning-theoretic complexity via quantifier elimination (Section 4).

Theorem 5.1 bounds the pseudo-dimension of piecewise-polynomial training-loss objectives (with training loss f equal to validation loss g) as O(p*d*log(M_f+T_f+d) + p^2*d*log Delta_f) for p-dimensional hyperparameters (Section 5).

Theorem 6.1 extends the framework to the bi-level validation-loss setting (f not equal to g), establishing Pdim(L) = O(p*d^2*log M_tot + p^2*d^2*log Delta_tot) without requiring identical training and validation objectives (Section 6).

Theorem 7.2 shows that when the optimal parameter path theta*(x, alpha) is piecewise rational, the pseudo-dimension bound simplifies to O(p*log(M_total*Delta_total)) by bypassing quantifier elimination (Section 7).

Theorem 8.1 provides the first learnability guarantee for weighted group LASSO regularization, a semi-algebraic (non-piecewise-polynomial) function class, with Pdim(L) = O(p^3*d + p^2*d^2), despite standard smoothness assumptions failing for this class (Section 8.1).
Theorem 8.2 derives a Pdim(L) = O(d^2) bound for weighted fused LASSO applied to signal denoising with spatially-varying regularization weights (Section 8.2).

Gr3wxsTqLw.text: On DreamBench++ zero-shot subject-driven generation, the 1D ordered tokenizer FlexTok combined with beam search improves DINO-I concept preservation by +18.4 points, versus only +5.9 points for Janus (2D tokenizer) with lookahead search (Table 1).

On a GenEval subset, training-free text-to-image generation via pure test-time search over ordered FlexTok token sequences with an image-text verifier reaches 100% single-object and 81% two-object accuracy using a conditional prior, up from 79%/32% with a uniform prior (Table 2).
Beam search over 1D ordered Semanticist tokens yields a +10.42 point gain over its no-search baseline, versus only +3.51 for the 2D-grid LlamaGen tokenizer under the same search budget (Table 4).

Across additional model pairs, beam search test-time scaling yields +9.6 points for FlexTok versus +6.2 for Infinity, indicating consistently larger search gains for 1D ordered tokenizers than 2D grid tokenizers (Table 5).

On COCO validation, FlexTok (1D ordered) shows stronger test-time scaling gains under beam search across inference budgets than 2D grid baselines, despite Janus achieving slightly higher performance without any search (Figure 6, Figure 7).

Proposition B.1 and B.2 establish that the search-gap bound for a tokenizer depends on its intermediate reconstruction error, a quantity explicitly minimized by 1D ordered tokenizers via nested dropout but left unconstrained in 2D grid tokenizer designs (Appendix B).

nc5WYNeI17.text: In a 2D Gaussian-mixture toy setting, the mutual-information-based mode-discovery metric distinguishes policy multimodality directly: MI = 0.00 +/- 0.00 for a 1-mode policy, 0.58 +/- 0.02 for a 2-mode policy, and 1.06 +/- 0.00 for a 4-mode policy (Table 1).

On the robotic Lift manipulation task, RES with behavioral mode discovery (RES[BMD]) achieves a mode-weighted success rate of 0.99, compared to 0.57 for the DPPO baseline, despite both reaching a 0.99 raw success rate (Table 5).
On ANYmal locomotion, DSRL with behavioral mode discovery (DSRL[BMD]) achieves mode coverage of 3.67 out of 4 modes with entropy 0.91 +/- 0.12 (Table 6).
On Franka Kitchen, DSRL[BMD] achieves an 0.82 success rate while covering 2.33 of 24 possible behavioral modes (Table 7).

Mode discovery uses mutual information between latent mode variables and behavior as an intrinsic reward during RL fine-tuning, regularizing policies to maintain behavioral diversity while improving task success rate (Section 4, Sections 4.1-4.3).

eWQQ0tO0kB.text: Spherical Slepian function encodings concentrate representational capacity within a specified region-of-interest at high resolution, rather than distributing capacity uniformly across the globe (abstract only).

A hybrid Slepian-Spherical Harmonic encoder is introduced to balance local versus global representational tradeoffs while preserving pole-safety and spherical-surface-distance preservation (abstract only).
The Slepian-based location encoders are evaluated across five distinct tasks spanning classification, regression, and image-augmented prediction (abstract only).
Slepian function encodings outperform baseline geographic encoding methods across these five tasks (abstract only).
The performance advantage of Slepian-based geographic representations is preserved across multiple different neural network architectures (abstract only).

5zbPdMNcl9.text: The proposed scRatio method derives a single ODE (Proposition 4.1) governing the time-derivative of the log-density ratio along generative flow-matching trajectories, expressed via the divergence and inner products of the two distributions' vector fields and score functions (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).

On the mutual information estimation benchmark, scRatio achieves best or second-best performance across all 5 tested dimensions d in {20,40,80,160,320}, with a mean absolute error of 0.46 +/- 0.15 at d=320 (Table 1).

On the differential abundance genomics task, scRatio attains a Spearman correlation of 0.99 +/- 0.01 with ground-truth differential abundance and an AUC of 0.96 +/- 0.00 in the high-DA regime (Table 2).

scRatio's estimated log-ratios decrease in magnitude after batch correction on the NeurIPS 2021 (90,261 cells) and C. elegans (89,701 cells) single-cell datasets, demonstrating sensitivity to batch effect removal (Figure 3).
On the ComboSciPlex dataset (63,378 cells), scRatio-estimated likelihood ratios for combinatorial drug perturbations correlate positively with an independent classifier's log-odds scores (Figure 4).

scRatio outperforms Time Score Matching (TSM) and Conditional TSM baselines on Gaussian benchmark tasks across dimensions d in {2,5,10,20,30}, while requiring substantially lower runtime than the naive likelihood-ratio computation approach (Section 5.1, Figure 2b).

0RctDxxCDs.text: Theorem 4.1 proves that K-means clustering of square-root loss vector embeddings recovers the correct client clustering in a single round with probability at least 1-delta-1/polylog(M), for any error tolerance delta (Theorem 4.1).

Theorem 4.2 shows that after T communication rounds, each cluster's model parameter estimate satisfies the bound ||theta_k - theta_k*|| <= Delta/c_1^T with high probability, i.e., exponentially fast convergence to the optimal cluster model in the linear setting (Theorem 4.2).
CLoVE achieves a perfect Adjusted Rand Index of 1.00 +/- 0.00 for recovering client clusters across all tested heterogeneity scenarios on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Fashion-MNIST (Table 2).
CLoVE reaches its high supervised test accuracy within 2-3 communication rounds, faster convergence than compared clustered federated learning baselines (Table 4).

CLoVE achieves state-of-the-art supervised test accuracy on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Fashion-MNIST relative to baselines including FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, FedProto, FedALA, FedPAC, CFL, FeSEM, FlexCFL, PACFL, and IFCA (Table 1).
CLoVE is shown to be more robust to model initialization than IFCA, which can fail to recover correct clusters under poor initialization (Figure 2).

hcO7EwDTL5.text: SorryDB contains 5,663 total 'sorry' statements drawn from 78 active real-world Lean formalization projects on GitHub, with 1,000 tasks selected for evaluation from the SorryDB-2601 snapshot dated January 2026 (Section: SorryDB).

In single-shot Pass@1 evaluation, the agentic approach based on Gemini Flash 3 achieves 10.8%, while Gemini Pro 3 achieves 11.0%, Claude Opus 4.5 achieves 7.8%, GPT 5.2 achieves 6.2%, Goedel Prover V2 achieves 2.7%, and Kimina Prover 8B achieves 1.0% (Section: Experiments).

Under an iterative, agentic evaluation protocol with up to 16 rounds of feedback, Gemini Flash-based agentic search reaches 30.3% success, higher than Claude Opus 4.5's self-correcting iterative approach at 27.1% (Section: Experiments).

Combining all evaluated provers (LLMs, specialized provers, and deterministic tactics) solves 35.7% of the 1,000 evaluated sorry tasks, exceeding any single approach, indicating that different provers solve complementary subsets of problems (Section: Experiments).

Iterative feedback-based approaches strongly outperform single-shot sampling approaches at comparable sample budgets, indicating feedback integration is more valuable than increased Pass@k sampling alone (Section: Discussion).

aH4SdgRaW7.text: Concept vectors for color and object attributes are extracted from three open-weight VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL 7B, InternVL2.5 8B, Gemma 3 12B) with embedding dimensions ranging from 3584 to 4096, and validated via activation steering interventions using Equation 3 (Section 3, Equation 3).
Centroid-based concept vector steering achieves color steering accuracies of 84.7% to 95.7% across the three models tested (Table 1).
Compositional steering success rates for combining multiple concept vectors range from 0% to 78.1%, varying substantially by attribute pair and model (Table 2).
Representational Similarity Analysis shows concept vector geometry is highly consistent across the three architecturally distinct VLMs, with correlations r > 0.93 (Table 3).

Visual search task accuracy correlates with geometric distractor similarity at r = -0.69 to -0.97 across models, and concept-vector-based similarity predictions correlate with human/behavioral similarity judgments at r = 0.78 to 0.84 (Table 4, Table 5).
Visual search accuracy declines as distractor-target similarity increases, consistent with the geometric-overlap account of binding failures (Figure 6).

7F0sragazb.text: A query circuit covering only 1.3% of connections (about 5,000 of 386,713 edges in Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) recovers approximately 60% of model performance on MMLU questions (Section 6.2, Figure 6).

The single-query circuit baseline needs roughly 200,000 edges (51.7% of connections) to reach the same Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) of 0.6 that Best-of-N sampling reaches with only 5,000 edges (Section 6.2, Figure 6).

The paper introduces the Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) metric to fix instability in prior faithfulness scores, which on datasets like MMLU Marketing could exceed 1 or drop below 0 for individual query circuits (Section 3.3.1, Figure 2a, Equation 5).

Best-of-N (BoN) circuit discovery with 9 paraphrases takes about 132.0 seconds per query, comparable to EAP-IG run for 500 steps at 120.2 seconds, while yielding sparser and more faithful circuits (Table 2).

Query circuits are evaluated across IOI, arithmetic (addition/multiplication), MMLU, and ARC tasks, with BoN needing orders of magnitude fewer edges than single-query or EAP-IG baselines to match performance (Section 6, Figure 6).

STcIzNrUBB.text: Theorem 4.2 proves that full-rank calibration implies both sub-k calibration and top-k calibration, but Table 1 gives a counterexample showing sub-k calibration does not imply full-rank calibration (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Table 1).
Table 2 provides a counterexample showing top-k calibration does not imply full-rank calibration, and that sub-k and top-k calibration are mutually incomparable notions (Section 4, Table 2).

Theorem 4.3 shows sub-k calibration implies rankwise sub-k calibration and top-k calibration implies rankwise top-k calibration, establishing a strict hierarchy of calibration notions defined in Definitions 1-7 (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).

On RewardBench2, Plackett-Luce and Mallows-Model reward models are found to be generally poorly calibrated (measured via top-1 Expected Calibration Error), while RPC achieves the strongest calibration for pairwise rankings (Section 5.2).

Top-1 ECE correlates strongly with reward-model accuracy in the Focus and Safety categories of RewardBench2 but only weakly in the Math and Precise-IF categories, showing calibration is an imperfect proxy for benchmark accuracy (Section 5.2).

amwGknX1Bx.text: ML-Embed-8B sets new state-of-the-art scores on 9 of 17 evaluated MTEB benchmarks, spanning 430 tasks in total (Section 5.2, Table 2).

On low-resource/mid-resource languages, ML-Embed-8B improves over the prior best model by +22.89 points on Polish (73.84 vs. 50.95), +6.88 points on Vietnamese (61.62 vs. 54.74), and +6.61 points on Indic languages (76.76 vs. 70.15) (Table 2).
The training data spans 282 natural languages and over 40 programming languages, used to train the 3D Matryoshka Learning framework combining MEL, MLL, and MRL objectives (Section 3, Section 4).

Ablation studies (Figures 4-6) evaluate the contribution of the Matryoshka Embedding Learning (MEL), Matryoshka Language Learning (MLL), and Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) components of the 3D Matryoshka framework (Section 5.4).
ML-Embed-8B is compared against similarly-sized multilingual embedding models in a dedicated benchmark table, in addition to the full 17-benchmark MTEB comparison (Section 5.3, Table 3).

RdBsmhb9U7.text: Across 150 tested parameter settings in Table 1, multimodal (mixture-of-Gaussians) mechanisms achieve lower expected l1 noise loss than the analytic Gaussian mechanism in 142 of 150 cases, with mean reduction of 53.73% (std 34.86%) and median reduction of 61.86% (Section 5, Table 1).

Proposition 3.3 proves that for any delta in (0, 1/2) there exists an epsilon_0 such that the multimodal Gaussian mechanism has strictly lower l2 loss (variance) than the analytic Gaussian mechanism for all epsilon >= epsilon_0 (Section 3, Proposition 3.3).

In the low-privacy regime (epsilon >= 1), the proposed mixture mechanisms close up to 99% of the optimality gap between the analytic Gaussian mechanism and the theoretical lower bound, with l1-loss improvements of 79-99% depending on delta (Section 5).

Corollary 3.7 shows the multimodal Gaussian mechanisms satisfy the same zero-concentrated differential privacy guarantee (rho = Delta^2 / 2*sigma^2) as the standard Gaussian mechanism, preserving standard composition properties (Section 3, Corollary 3.7).

Table 2 compares the mixture mechanisms against truncated Laplace, Tulap, staircase, cactus, and flipped Huber mechanisms, finding the Gaussian mixtures competitive for epsilon >= 1 but inferior to non-Gaussian mechanisms for epsilon < 1 (Section 5, Table 2).

bS8qU2wJxu.text: IDLM-SEDD preserves the teacher's generative perplexity (GenPPL) and entropy while cutting inference steps 4x, from 1024 to 256 steps (Section 4, Figure 3).

IDLM-MDLM and IDLM-Duo each preserve GenPPL and entropy while cutting inference steps 64x, from 1024 to 16 steps, with IDLM-DCD reaching 128x-256x reduction (down to as few as 4-8 steps) under Greedy-Tail sampling (Section 4, Figures 4-5).

Theorem 3.1 proves the IDLM loss satisfies L_IDLM(theta) >= D_KL(p_theta || p*) >= 0, with equality (and hence a unique minimizing solution) if and only if the model distribution matches the target distribution, guaranteeing a well-posed discrete optimization objective (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).

IDLM introduces a simplex relaxation that extends the generator's output from the discrete vocabulary space V to the probability simplex Delta, enabling differentiable softmax-based optimization for discrete diffusion training (Section 3.2).

IDLM is instantiated on three discrete diffusion backbones -- SEDD, MDLM, and Duo -- unified via a generalized loss notation L_discr, each requiring backbone-specific reparameterization or backpropagation strategies for absorbing-state processes (Section 3.2, Section 4).

iSuqYRmG4A.text: MT-AgentRisk comprises 365 multi-turn tool-agent tasks spanning 5 tools (Filesystem-MCP, Browser/Playwright, PostgreSQL-MCP, Notion-MCP, Terminal), with an average of 3.19 turns per task (Section 3.3).

An attack taxonomy along Format (Addition vs. Decomposition), Method, and Target (Data Files vs. Environment States) dimensions yields 8 attack subcategories used to construct the benchmark (Section 3.1).

Attack Success Rate rises substantially in multi-turn versus single-turn settings, e.g. +27.1 percentage points for Claude-4.5-Sonnet, +23% for Qwen3-Coder, and +8.8% for Deepseek-v3.2, with Decomposition x Environment States attacks reaching 73.7% ASR (Section 4).
ToolShield, a training-free, tool-agnostic four-stage defense pipeline, reduces multi-turn ASR by an average of 30% across models, including a 72%->22% reduction for Claude-4.5-Sonnet (Section 5).
ToolShield produces 0% false rejection rate on 170 benign tasks while adding only 5K-12K tokens of context overhead across tools (Section 5, Section 5.3/E.3).

79fSrxFKKx.text: RedDebate, a fully automated multi-agent red-teaming debate framework, reduces unsafe outputs by 17.7% through debate alone on HarmBench (Figure 1, Table 2).
Adding long-term memory modules to debate (SReD+GLTM) further reduces unsafe behaviors to a 3.6% error rate on HarmBench, a 23.5%+ additional reduction over debate-only (Table 2).

Three debate strategies are compared: Peer Refinement (PReD), Devil-Angel (DAReD), and Socratic (SReD), evaluated with Mistral-7B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, and Phi-3.5-mini on HarmBench and CoSafe (Section 3.2, Section 4).
SReD alone achieves a 21.0% error rate and 17.0% agreement rate on HarmBench, evaluated using LlamaGuard as judge with 87% agreement against human annotations (Table 1, Section 4).

t3PXkjuTqe.text: Lemma 2.1 establishes bounds combining conformal predictor set outputs with miscoverage-rate correction terms (M*Err(C)) that underlie valid mean estimation confidence intervals in Proposition 2.3 (Section 2.1).

Proposition 2.9 bounds the expected growth rate of the offline conformal prediction-powered e-value E^ppi-(C)_n relative to the original e-value, with a penalty proportional to Err(C) and average predictive set size, giving the first general offline prediction-powered procedure for e-values (Section 2.3, Proposition 2.9).

The method is benchmarked against PPI++ and FAB on phishing-prevalence (mean estimation) and gene-expression (median estimation) datasets, achieving competitive or superior confidence interval widths (Section 3.1).

A differentially private conformal prediction instantiation is applied to thyroid cancer recurrence prediction, achieving privacy guarantees with only a minimal increase in interval size (Section 3.2).
Online conformal prediction e-values are used for continuous risk monitoring of deployed models, detecting distribution shift without active labeling (Section 3.3).

DXq3HH4S5o.text: ASRU combines an activation-steering stage (updating a single down-projection matrix) with a GRPO-based reinforcement unlearning stage using boundary-set supervision (Section 3.2.1).

ASRU improves unlearning effectiveness by an average of 21.96% over the strongest baseline on Qwen-3-VL-4B and 27.26% on Qwen-3-VL-8B, yielding an overall 24.61% gain reported in the abstract (Table 1).
ASRU achieves a 5.8x average improvement in generation quality over competitive baselines, measured via two introduced metrics, Contextual Refusal and Forgetfulness (Section 4.2, Table 1).
ASRU attains this performance using only 27.3% of the supervised retain set, evaluated on MLLMU-Bench and CLEAR across forget ratios of 5%, 10%, and 15% (Table 1).
Figure 6 shows ASRU dominates baseline methods on the forget-utility trade-off curve across all tested forget ratios (Figure 6).

UR1yz4AMYj.text: HySoMi is a hybrid modelling framework that maps metagenome-inferred functional traits to biokinetic parameters of a process-based soil organic matter turnover model via an MLP with sigmoid-constrained outputs, coupled to a differentiable ODE solver (Section 3.2, Section 3.2.1-3.2.2).

11 process constraints (P1-P11) and 3 parameter constraints (C1-C3), derived from ecological theory and literature, are incorporated as loss terms combined via homoscedastic uncertainty weighting (Table 1, Section 3.2.3).
HySoMi correctly predicts hidden/unmeasurable state variables, such as inactive bacterial pools, without being directly trained on them, unlike unconstrained baselines (Figure 2).
HySoMi remains robust and reduces equifinality even with small training datasets of 554 samples, as shown across varying dataset sizes and input complexity (Figures 3-4).

GnmuZIlvxw.text: Theorems 3 and 4 establish impossibility results showing that standard message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) cannot learn certain graph algorithms due to inherent limitations in non-local information propagation (Theorems 3-4).

Theorem 9 gives positive results characterizing conditions under which MPNNs can learn specific algorithmic tasks, including problems solvable via local, iterative update rules such as single-source shortest paths (Theorem 9).

Theorem 17 characterizes expressiveness bounds for MPNN variants, relating the number of message-passing layers to the class of dynamic-programming-style algorithms the network can represent (Theorem 17).

Section 3 (Learning Capabilities and Limitations) shows minimum spanning tree construction requires forms of global coordination that standard MPNNs cannot compute within a fixed number of layers (Section 3).

Section 4 (Expressive Power Analysis) empirically validates the theoretical bounds using benchmark algorithmic tasks including shortest-path and dynamic programming problems, comparing MPNN performance against the derived necessary conditions (Section 4).

scnRgI2hhX.text: Theorem 3.1 proves that a hypothesis class is uniformly generatable with replay if and only if it is uniformly generatable in the standard no-replay setting, with identical sample complexity, showing replay is benign for the strongest notion of generation (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 4.1 exhibits a countable hypothesis class that is non-uniformly generatable without replay but not non-uniformly generatable with replay, establishing a strict separation caused by replay (Theorem 4.1).
Theorem 5.1 shows a computable algorithm using only membership queries can generate in the limit any countable hypothesis class even under replay conditions (Theorem 5.1).
Theorem 5.6 constructs an uncountable hypothesis class that is generatable in the limit without replay but becomes non-generatable in the limit once replay is permitted (Theorem 5.6).
Theorem 6.1 proves no deterministic generator using only membership queries can properly generate in the limit for all countable hypothesis classes (Theorem 6.1).
Theorem 6.3 shows that even some finite hypothesis classes that are properly generatable in the limit without replay become impossible to properly generate once replay is introduced (Theorem 6.3).

a9CuW1f0CT.text: Geodesic Flow Matching (GFM) achieves a 72% reduction in tracking error compared to classical baselines in a Spiking Neural SLAM system by replacing linear interpolation with geodesic paths on the hypersphere (Section on SLAM Application Metrics).

GFM yields a 40% increase in neural efficiency compared to classical baselines, and about a 10% improvement over Euclidean flow matching methods in high-dimensional regimes with dimension d greater than 500 (Denoising Performance results).

A 1500-neuron Spiking Neural SLAM system augmented with Geodesic cleanup achieves tracking RMSE of 0.076 meters, comparable to a 2500-neuron Grid baseline system's RMSE of 0.083 meters (SLAM RMSE comparison table).

At 2500 neurons, the Geodesic method attains RMSE of 0.078 meters versus 0.083 meters for the Grid baseline, showing GFM's advantage persists even as population size scales (SLAM RMSE comparison table).

Standard Euclidean flow matching, which linearly interpolates through the interior of the Spatial Semantic Pointer (SSP) toroidal manifold, destroys phase and magnitude structure needed for accurate decoding and fails at high noise levels due to magnitude collapse, motivating the geodesic logarithmic and exponential map approach (Section on Core Innovation and Technical Approach).

fYbuhXJ3iq.text: Llama-3.3-70B exhibits an Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR) rate of 3.8% and a multi-attempt rate of 7.4%, both substantially higher than other tested models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2 family), which show ESR below 1% and multi-attempt rates of 1.2% or less (Model Performance Comparison section).
26 differentially-activated off-topic detector latents identified in Llama-3.3-70B activate 4.4 times higher during off-topic content than on-topic content (Off-Topic Detector Latents section).

Zero-ablating all 26 identified off-topic detector latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence that these latents contribute to consistency-checking circuits underlying ESR (Off-Topic Detector Latents section).

A meta-prompt instructing the model to notice and correct off-topic drift increases the multi-attempt rate 4.3-fold, from 7.4% to 31.7%, and the ESR rate 3.9-fold, from 3.8% to 14.8% (Enhancement Through Intervention section).

Fine-tuning on self-correction examples induces surface behavioral patterns of ESR without improving underlying effectiveness, indicating genuine self-monitoring is not reproduced by behavioral imitation alone (Fine-tuning results section).

A baseline control of 7892 unsteered trials produces 0% multi-attempt responses, confirming that observed multi-attempt and ESR behavior is steering-induced rather than a baseline generation artifact (Baseline Control section).

DKoycSNd9W.text: GPT-5 achieves the 81.76th human percentile on LiveOIBench's expert-curated problems from 14 Informatics Olympiads, earning gold-medal-equivalent performance in 50% of contests and a 63.03% pass rate, still falling short of top human contestants at the 90th percentile and above (Model Performance Metrics, GPT-5 section).

Among open-weight models, GPT-OSS-120B reaches the 59.90th human percentile at standard reasoning effort and 72.88th percentile at high reasoning effort, with a 47.78% pass rate and 29.17% gold-medal rate (Model Performance Metrics, GPT-OSS-120B section).

LiveOIBench comprises 403 problems drawn from 72 contests across 14 Informatics Olympiads spanning 2023 to 2025, with each problem including an average of 60 expert-designed official test cases (Benchmark Scale section).
Quarterly contamination analysis from Q1 2023 to Q2 2025 shows no temporal degradation in model performance, indicating minimal evidence of benchmark contamination (Contamination Analysis section).

GPT-5's pass rate drops to 46.88% on dynamic programming problems compared to 71.79% on implementation tasks, revealing a specific algorithmic weakness in creative observation and hierarchical reasoning (Algorithmic Weakness Pattern section).

OwLuqetJuB.text: For learned Lagrangian Relaxation multipliers over s coupling constraints and N training samples, the expected excess risk of the ERM solution is upper bounded by O(s^1.5/√N) (Theorem 5.5).
A minimax lower bound of Ω(s/√N) is proven, showing linear dependence on the number of coupled constraints s is unavoidable for any learning algorithm (Theorem 5.6).

Stochastic Gradient Ascent with iterate averaging is shown to achieve the matching O(s/√N) rate, closing the O(√s) gap between the ERM upper bound and the minimax lower bound and establishing minimax optimality (Theorem 5.12).

The framework is extended to learning-to-warm-start sub-gradient ascent for large-scale Mixed Integer Linear Programming, with an O(s/N) risk upper bound (Theorem 6.1) and matching Ω(s/N) minimax lower bound (Theorem 6.2).
The covering number of the dual multiplier class U is bounded as log N(δ,U,‖·‖₂,N) ≤ s·log(1+2Bπ_max s/δ), used to derive the Rademacher complexity bound R_N(U)=O(s^1.5/√N) (Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.4).
The dual function u(π,P) is shown to be concave in π with subgradient norm bounded by 2B√s under bounded constraint-violation assumptions on the MILP instance (Proposition 5.1, Section 4).

35GKHwXUmY.text: Ekka achieves 84% pass@1 and 88% pass@5 diagnosis accuracy on a curated set of real-world silent errors collected from the vLLM and SGLang serving frameworks (Abstract).
Ekka improves diagnosis accuracy by 24% to 34% over state-of-the-art baseline systems through systematic alignment and comparison of execution states across framework implementations (Introduction).
The evaluation dataset comprises 90 total silent errors (70 closed, 20 open issues), split across vLLM (48 issues) and SGLang (42 issues) (Section on Bug Collection).

Accuracy regression is the most prevalent symptom category among collected silent errors, accounting for 43.8% of cases, while root causes span framework implementation (30.6%), model implementation (25.5%), kernel/backend (24.5%), and numerical precision (19.4%) issues (Figure 2a, Figure 2b).

Ekka's three-stage diagnosis pipeline—component mapping, activation alignment, and change-point-based error analysis—diagnosed 4 new silent errors in vLLM and SGLang that were all subsequently confirmed by the respective developers (Introduction).
The average diagnosis cost per case using Ekka is approximately $30 (Evaluation section).

5s5zlewQRI.text: SCALE decomposes conformal prediction residuals into low- and high-frequency components via graph wavelets, based on the empirical finding that high-frequency components exhibit weaker cross-node interaction and are more likely to be exchangeable (Section 4.1, Figure 2).
On METR-LA at α=0.05, SCALE attains coverage of 0.9436±0.0030 with a prediction-interval width of 11.69±0.23, a 14.4% reduction versus EnbPI's width of 13.65 (Table 1).

Across METR-LA, PEMS04, PEMS07, and PEMS08 traffic datasets, SCALE achieves near-nominal coverage (0.94–0.96) while improving the coverage-efficiency trade-off (PI width and Winkler score) over SCP, SeqCP, NexCP, EnbPI, HopCPT, ConForME, and CoREL baselines (Table 1, Table 2, Section 6.1).

Theorem 5.1 establishes finite-sample coverage guarantees P(X_{t+1:t+K} ∈ Ĉ^{X,α}_{t+1:t+K}) ≥ 1−α under the proposed Spectral Graph Conditional Exchangeability (SGCE) condition, with Theorem 5.2 extending this to bounded approximation errors δ = δ_leak + δ_dep (Theorem 5.1, Theorem 5.2).

Ablation results show that removing low-frequency conditioning (SCALE w/o LF) causes coverage violations, and removing the spectral graph wavelet transform (SCALE w/o SGWT) degrades interval-width efficiency, validating both architectural components (Table 1).

gLLcjBJCXZ.text: Neural operator splitting performs test-time beam search over compositions of a dictionary of pretrained operators (learned via DISCO pretraining) to approximate unseen dynamics without modifying pretrained weights (Section 4.2, Section 4.3).

On zero-shot physics composition tasks, the method attains NRMSE of 0.015 for advection+diffusion, 0.056 for nonlinear advection+diffusion, 0.089 for reaction+diffusion, and 0.066 for Euler+diffusion, achieving state-of-the-art results on 5 of 6 composition scenarios (Table 1).

On parameter extrapolation tasks, the method achieves NRMSE of 0.052 for advection speed c, 0.002 for diffusion coefficient D, 0.016 for nonlinear advection coefficient α, and 0.022 for dispersion γ, representing 11x to 200x improvement over the original DISCO baseline (Table 2).

The method is evaluated against MPP, Zebra, GEPS, and the original DISCO baseline across four PDE settings: 1D advection-diffusion, 1D combined equation, 2D reaction-diffusion (Gray-Scott, from The Well benchmark), and 2D Navier-Stokes (Section 5.1).

Beam search, which iteratively expands the top-B operator combinations with O(BN) complexity, is shown to outperform uniform random sampling of operator combinations at intermediate FLOP budgets (Figure 3, Figure 5).
Strang splitting is used to reduce the operator-composition approximation error from O(Δt^2) to O(Δt^3) via the symmetric pattern f1^(Δt/2) ∘ f2^(Δt) ∘ f1^(Δt/2) (Section 4.3).

dE3Z3bfEzk.text: The Fatigue Index is defined as a weighted combination FI_t = 0.40·φ_A(A_t) + 0.35·φ_E(E_t) + 0.25·φ_D(D_t) of prompt-attention decay, embedding drift, and entropy-collapse signals computed during autoregressive decoding (Section 3, Section 4).
The Fatigue Index's predictive validity for downstream task degradation is measured at ρ = 0.848 on HotpotQA, ρ = 0.820 on TriviaQA, and ρ = 0.856 on SQuAD (Table 3).
The Fatigue Index achieves an AUROC of 0.976 for detecting repetition and severe degeneration on HotpotQA (Table 5).

Instruction-tuned models below 3B parameters (e.g., TinyLlama-1.1B, OPT-1.3B) exhibit faster fatigue-driven collapse than base models, with this trend reversing at the 7B scale (Falcon-7B), as shown by non-monotonic scaling in Figure 6 (Section 7.5).
Hysteresis-based alerting (activation threshold θ=0.50, deactivation θ_low=0.40) reduces false-positive alert rates by 91-93% compared to a static-threshold alerting scheme (Table 4).

Stress tests show front-positioned evidence in the prompt receives 5-10x higher mean attention than middle- or end-positioned evidence, and 4-bit quantization increases entropy-collapse depth relative to FP16 (Figure 3, Figure 4, Section 5.2).

69IOkVkTQX.text: Under the Lévy Mirror Flow model with centered Lévy noise having finite p-th moments (1<p≤2), time-averaged orbits achieve ε-optimality within Õ(ε^(-p/(p-1))) time for convex objectives (Theorem 1).

For strongly convex objectives, the process converges geometrically to an uncertainty ball whose radius scales as O(ησ²_tame + η^(p-1)σ^p_heavy), despite jump discontinuities of arbitrary magnitude (Theorem 4).
The first-passage (hitting) time to within δ of the optimum for strongly convex objectives is Õ(δ^(-2p/(p-1))) (Theorem 3).
The discrete-time Stochastic Dual Averaging analogue achieves an O(T^(-(p-1)/p)) ergodic convergence rate on convex functions, matching the continuous-time rate (Theorem 5).
For strongly convex functions, the discrete-time method requires Ω((σ^p/ε)^(1/(p-1)) log(1/ε)) iterations to reach ε-accuracy (Corollary 1).

A novel 'weak Itô formula' for Lipschitz-smooth convex functions under Lévy integrators is proved to enable the analysis despite discontinuous sample paths and potentially infinite noise variance when p<2 (Section 2).

mxXm8jqgds.text: Test-Time Graph Search (TTGS) constructs a weighted graph over states sampled from the offline dataset (M=4000 vertices) and applies Dijkstra's algorithm at test time to produce subgoal sequences for a frozen, already-trained goal-conditioned policy, without any additional training (Section on method / Algorithm 1).
On the pointmaze-giant-stitch task, TTGS raises HIQL's success rate from 0.0% to 80.9% and GCIQL's from 0.0% to 98.0% (Table 3).
On the humanoidmaze-giant-stitch and antmaze-giant-stitch tasks, TTGS raises HIQL's success rate from 4.4% to 78.1% and from 1.4% to 78.6%, respectively (Table 3).

TTGS is evaluated with two interchangeable distance metrics—value-derived distances from the learned goal-conditioned value function and position-based L2 distances between agent body positions (Table 1).

An ablation shows the adaptive farthest-reachable-waypoint subgoal selection strategy outperforms a simpler 'next waypoint' baseline, and that a superlinear edge penalty p(x)=x·1000^(x/τ) for exceeding a soft horizon threshold τ improves reliability over raw-distance edges (Figure 4).

TTGS's added computational overhead is approximately 45 seconds for state-based graph construction (about 100 seconds for visual observations), roughly 0.8 seconds of per-episode planning, and about 1 millisecond of per-step overhead (Section on computational cost).

wnfPEhGqic.text: The approximation error of a rank-k learned Laplacian representation used for linear value function approximation is upper-bounded by ‖v−v̂_k‖_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖_Φ√(1/(λ₂λ_{k+1})) + ‖v‖_Φ√(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), decomposing into truncation error and feature-estimation error (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).

The truncation error term is bounded by ‖v−v_k‖²_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖²_Φ/(λ₂λ_{k+1}), showing the bound scales inversely with the algebraic connectivity λ₂ of the state-transition graph, so poorly-connected MDPs induce larger approximation error (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.2).

The Graph Drawing Objective's feature-estimation error is bounded by ‖Π_Ψ−Π_Ψ̃‖₂ < √(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), depending on the spectral gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th eigenvalues (Lemma 3.5, Section 3.3).

The analysis defines a Φ-self-adjoint Laplacian L = I − (P+Φ⁻¹PᵀΦ)/2 (Equation 6, Section 3) and applies without assuming symmetry of the induced transition kernel, i.e., it holds for general non-uniform behavior policies (Lemma 3.6, Section 3.3).
Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 establish that this matrix-based Laplacian formulation is equivalent to the operator-theoretic Laplacian representation formulation of Wu et al. (Section 4).

zMO9H4hLyR.text: In the compute-optimal pretraining regime (20 tokens-per-parameter), the optimal weight decay for downstream fine-tuned performance is 1.0, far above the standard default of 0.1 (Section 4.2).

In the overtrained regime (140 tokens-per-parameter), the downstream-optimal weight decay is 0.3, while the pretraining-loss-optimal weight decay remains near the standard 0.1 (Section 4.1–4.2, Figure 1c).

An OLMo-2-1B model pretrained for 140x tokens-per-parameter with weight decay 0.3/1.0 attains higher (worse) pretraining loss yet noticeably better downstream fine-tuned performance than the default-weight-decay model, demonstrating a pretraining-loss/downstream-performance disconnect (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
Figure 2 shows consistent downstream improvements from higher weight decay across 6 fine-tuning tasks and 4 evaluation metrics, for both Llama-2 and OLMo-2 architectures (Section 4.2, Figure 2).

Higher weight decay (e.g., 1.0) improves linear probing accuracy of learned representations across all layers and reduces the rank of query-key attention matrices by approximately 50% relative to the near full-rank matrices produced by default weight decay 0.1 (Sections 5.1–5.2, Figures 4–5).

The train-validation loss gap during fine-tuning decreases monotonically as pretraining weight decay increases, indicating reduced overfitting as a contributing mechanism to improved plasticity (Section 5.3, Figure 6).

VCwVl6EsvX.text: Parallel-Distill-Refine (PDR) generates diverse drafts in parallel, distills them into a bounded-length summary, and iteratively refines the output, keeping per-call context length controllable while accumulating reasoning tokens across rounds (Section on method).
At matched sequential token budget (~49k tokens) on AIME 2024, o3-mini's accuracy rises from 76.9% (long chain-of-thought) to 81.5% (self-refine) to 86.7% with PDR (Figures 3 and 9).

At a matched total token budget of 442k tokens, PDR achieves equivalent accuracy using a 2.57× smaller sequential budget than long chain-of-thought, converting parallel compute into accuracy gains without lengthening per-call context (Figure 5).

With RL training, an 8B thinking model using PDR at a 65,536-token sequential budget reaches 79.17% on AIME 2024 versus 75.83% for the single-pass RL baseline, and continual PDR RL training further improves this to 80.83% (Table 3).

An ablation over distillation strategies shows per-sample top-k and global summary selection consistently outperform random-k selection when distilling parallel drafts, with the gain widening at higher thinking budgets (Table 2).

Verification-capability analysis shows o3-mini degrades more than gemini-2.5-flash when incorrect candidate drafts contaminate the distilled summary, indicating weaker self-verification ability in o3-mini (Figures 6 and 8).

dfqmQ9WhCP.text: Formalizes over 1000 theorems and lemmas in Lean 4 covering Gaussian analysis and empirical process theory, comprising approximately 30,000 lines of code produced over roughly 500 hours of supervised development (Section 3, Appendix A).
Provides the first Lean 4 formalization of Dudley's entropy integral theorem for sub-Gaussian processes, using metric entropy, covering numbers, and chaining arguments (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.2).

Formalizes a high-dimensional Gaussian analysis toolbox including the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality, tensorization of entropy, and Gaussian Lipschitz concentration (Theorems 3.5-3.7, Section 3.1).
Derives linear regression convergence rates via a master error bound and localized Gaussian complexity applied to least squares estimation (Theorems 4.1-4.3, Section 4).
All formalized results compile without use of 'sorry' or additional axioms, verified via a human-AI collaborative workflow using Claude Code Opus 4.5 (Section 3, Appendix A).

O0gI00yRnm.text: Introduces two spatial calibration notions for Gaussian process predictions below a threshold t: occurrence calibration and thresholded mu-calibration, assessed via a truncated probability integral transform (mu-tPIT) (Section 5).

Proposes tcGP, a post-hoc calibration method that fits generalized normal (GN) distributions by minimizing a joint criterion targeting both occurrence and thresholded mu-calibration simultaneously (Section 5).

Derives a closed-form expected improvement expression for GN-distributed predictive residuals in Proposition 5.1, and proves that EI-based optimization with tcGP remains dense in the design space under bounded parameters and the no-empty-ball property (Proposition 5.3).
Ablation shows joint calibration (both occurrence and thresholded components) outperforms single-component variants tcGP-thres and tcGP-occ alone (Figure 2).

Empirically demonstrates tcGP and reGP improve Bayesian optimization performance over standard GP models across four benchmark test functions, using threshold quantiles delta=0.05 for tcGP and delta=0.25 for reGP (Figure 3).
