VXlniX0C5y.text: Derives a parameter-free prediction for the data-limited neural scaling exponent, alpha_D = gamma / (2*beta), from two measurable statistics of natural language: conditional-entropy decay exponent gamma (H_n - H_infinity ~ n^-gamma) and token-correlation decay exponent beta (||C(n)||_op ~ n^-beta) (Section 3, Equations 6-8).
Measures gamma=0.34 and beta=0.88 on TinyStories, predicting alpha_D ~ 0.19, and gamma=0.27 and beta=0.94 on WikiText, predicting alpha_D ~ 0.14 (Section 4.1).

Validates predicted scaling exponents against measured autoregressive loss scaling curves from GPT-2-style transformers with absolute and rotary positional embeddings and LLaMA-style architectures trained on TinyStories and WikiText (Figures 1-4).

Shows that n-gram losses collapse onto a single curve when rescaled by the derived exponents, supporting a 'horizon-limited' learning regime where models progressively extend their effective context window rather than refining within a fixed context (Section 3, Figure 1).

kSUGLBHd0T.text: Introduces a unified clinical simulator supporting Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes with pump and non-pump insulin therapies, and benchmarks eight safe RL algorithms (PPO-Lag, TRPO-Lag, CPO, RCPO, FOCOPS, PCPO, CRPO, CUP) under out-of-distribution patient populations (Section on OOD safety benchmark).

Demonstrates a 'safety generalization gap' whereby policies achieving high Time-in-Range and low clinical risk on training patients frequently violate safety margins on unseen patients stratified by age (children 23.7-45.5 kg, adolescents 37.9-68.7 kg, adults 63.0-111.1 kg).

Proposes a test-time predictive shielding mechanism built on a Basis-Adaptive Neural ODE (BA-NODE) that combines an inverted Transformer history encoder, a latent Neural ODE ensemble, and function-space adaptation to mask actions predicted to cause hypo- or hyperglycemia within a two-hour horizon.
Shows test-time shielding improves Time-in-Range on Type 2 diabetes patients by +14.15% for PPO-Lag and +13.54% for CPO, and by an average of +6.08% across algorithms on Type 1 diabetes patients.
Reports Risk Index reductions of 2-2.8 points for strong baseline algorithms under shielding, compared to a rule-based Low Glucose Suspend shield baseline.

Pa6EoOViOq.text: Reduces hyperparameter search cost by 96.67% by requiring only m=7 evaluations (one per concept) instead of the m x l = 210 feature-combination evaluations (m=7 multipliers, l=30 latent combinations) needed by unsupervised sparse autoencoder baselines (Section 5).
Achieves 91.51% average performance on the UnlearnCanvas object-unlearning benchmark, a 9.22% improvement over the prior state-of-the-art SAeUron baseline's 82.29% (Table 1, Section 5).
Achieves 92.4% accuracy on sequential unlearning of nine objects, a 28.4% improvement over the SAeUron baseline's 64% (Table 2, Section 5).

Trains supervised sparse autoencoders in two phases -- unsupervised pretraining followed by a supervised concept assignment loss with an orthogonality constraint decorrelating object and style latents plus L1 sparsity regularization -- to enforce one-to-one concept-to-neuron mappings (Section 5).
Reports retention accuracy across sequential unlearning tasks, showing SAEmnesia preserves in-domain and cross-domain retain accuracy relative to the SAeUron baseline (Table 3, Section 5).

7qpvff2gWI.text: AdaSplash-2 achieves more than a 2x speedup over both variants of FlashAttention-2 at high sparsity limits under random sparsity testing (Section 4.2, Efficiency Benchmark).
AdaSplash-2 matches or improves per-step training time relative to FlashAttention-2 specifically when block sparsity exceeds roughly 60% (Abstract, Figure 1).
A histogram-based initialization reduces the number of bisection iterations needed to compute the entmax threshold tau to typically 1-2 (Abstract, Section 3.3).

Proposition 3.2 shows the histogram approximation satisfies tau*-h < tau_h <= tau*, where h=1/B, guaranteeing the approximate threshold preserves the true sparsity support (Section B.1, Proposition 3.2).
On the HELMET in-context learning benchmark at 32K context, Entmax+NAPE attains an average score of 62.2 versus 46.1 for Softmax+NAPE (Table 2).

AdaSplash-2's backward pass outperforms FlashAttention-2 even at shorter context lengths, with the advantage growing at longer sequences, which matters because the backward pass dominates training time (Section 4.2, Figure 4).

QoInle2UdN.text: Definition 2.1 introduces an Explanation Score for event X=x explaining Y=y as 1 - log P(Y=y | do(X=x)) / log P(Y=y), quantifying causal-pathway plausibility for rare events (Section 2, Definition 2.1).
Lemma 2.3 establishes additivity of explanation-score contributions across disjoint sets of root causes, enabling decomposition of complex explanations (Section 2, Lemma 2.3).

Definition 3.1 formalizes a causal pathway explanation as a tuple of a causal DAG, a pathway subgraph, binary variables, a target event, root causes, and a probability distribution (Section 3, Definition 3.1).
Lemma 3.5 proves an affine relationship between the pathway explanation score and the cluster explanation score (Section 3, Lemma 3.5).

Theorem 4.3 bounds the probability of obtaining feature values satisfying explanation requirements in multivariate systems, with error controlled via an Erlang-distribution bound, under a Feature Monotonicity condition (Definition 4.1) where larger parent features make larger child features more probable (Section 4, Theorem 4.3, Definition 4.1).

Definition 4.5 (Pathway Abstraction) formalizes how a detailed continuous structural causal model can be reduced to a simplified binary pathway representation while maintaining approximate accuracy, bridging verbal and formal causal explanations of rare events (Section 4, Definition 4.5).

o9JP7N8YO9.text: Batch Normalization induces a gradient amplification factor of (1-s_i)^(-1/2) for a neuron with sparsity s_i, versus unit scaling for dense layers (s=0), producing neuron-dependent gradient skew during Dynamic Sparse Training mask updates (Section 3, Equation 11).

SparseOpt applies a sparsity-aware diagonal preconditioner with correction factor sqrt(1-s_i) per neuron to restore uniform gradient scaling, reducing to the identity for dense layers (Section 4, Equation 12).
On ImageNet with ResNet50 at 90% sparsity trained for 90 epochs, RigL with SparseOpt reaches 74.41% top-1 accuracy versus 73.88% for the RigL baseline (Table 1).
On ImageNet with ResNet50 at 97% sparsity trained for 270 epochs, SparseOpt obtains 72.66% top-1 accuracy versus 72.35% for the baseline (Table 1).
On CIFAR-100 with ResNet20 at 95% sparsity trained for 200 epochs, SparseOpt achieves 60.41±0.28% accuracy versus 58.76±0.60% for the baseline (Table 2).
Figure 5 presents an ITOP (In-Time Over-Parameterization) rate analysis showing that Batch Normalization influences mask exploration patterns during Dynamic Sparse Training (Section 4, Figure 5).

DgRd1uu8dj.text: Theorem 3.2 derives a variational dual form of entropic optimal transport, EOT_eps(p0,p1) = sup_f L(f) = sup_{f,xi} L(f,xi), replacing the intractable log-partition function with a tractable variational minimization over an auxiliary normalizer xi (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.3 shows the optimality gap equals a scaled KL divergence, eps*KL(pi* || pi_{f,xi}) = L* - L(f,xi), so optimizing the variational objective directly controls approximation of the ground-truth EOT plan (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).
Theorem 3.5 gives a finite-sample estimation error bound of order O(N^(-1/(1+D))) + O(M^(-1/(1+D))) for Lipschitz-constrained function classes on compact supports (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.5).

Theorem 3.7 proves the approximation error vanishes as neural network capacity grows under universal function approximation, giving a full generalization guarantee together with Theorem 3.5 (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.7).

Algorithm 1 trains VarEOT in a simulation-free manner by jointly optimizing the potential f_theta and auxiliary function xi_psi via stochastic gradient ascent, avoiding the MCMC simulations required by EgNOT (Section 3, Algorithm 1; Table 1).

srIStBTJiu.text: Proposition 2.1 shows gradient descent on OPE-based objectives (e.g., IPS, Clipped IPS, Doubly Robust, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC) can be trapped in suboptimal regions for O(K) iterations, where K is the number of actions (Section 2, Proposition 2.1).
Proposition 2.2 proves the optimization landscape of OPE-based objectives contains exponentially many local maxima in K (Section 2, Proposition 2.2).

Proposition 3.1 proves that weighted log-likelihood (PWLL) objectives combined with L2-regularized softmax policies are strongly concave, guaranteeing a unique global maximum (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).

Figure 2 shows that low mean-squared error of the off-policy value estimator does not correlate with high reward from the learned policy, i.e., good OPE performance does not predict good OPL performance (Section 4, Figure 2).

Figure 1 shows OPE-based objectives are highly sensitive to batch size and learning rate, whereas PWLL objectives (including LPI, cLPI, and RegKL variants) remain robust across these hyperparameter configurations (Section 3, Figure 1).

On large-action-space benchmarks including MovieLens (K=60K), Twitch (K=200K), and GoodReads (K=1M actions), PWLL-based policies outperform estimator-aware methods such as POTEC (Section 4, Figure 3).

9YcP7zeO8h.text: A weighted set is defined as a β-approximation preserving coreset (β-APC) if any α-approximate k-means solution computed on it yields an αβ-approximate solution on the full dataset (Definition 1.1).
For Euclidean k-means, sensitivity sampling constructs a (1+ε)-APC of size Õ(kε^-3), improving on strong coreset size requirements (Theorem 1.2).
For arbitrary metrics, an iterative downsampling approach constructs a (4+ε)-APC of size Õ(kε^-2) (Theorem 1.3).
Sensitivity sampling with m = Cε^-2(k log(k/δ) + log N) points gives strong coreset concentration guarantees for a solution family of size N (Theorem 2.2).
For finite n-point metrics, sensitivity sampling yields strong coresets of size O(kε^-2 log n), matching known lower bounds without extra polylogarithmic factors (Corollary 2.3).
A lower bound of Ω(log N / log log N) is proved showing that APC guarantees below β=4 are not achievable for the arbitrary-metric setting (Theorem 4.6).

A52LNgpGKy.text: Most tokens exhibit a non-monotonic 'bump' in next-token probability as steering strength α increases, with the probability of target-concept tokens peaking at a larger α than off-target tokens (Theorem 3.3).

The probability assigned to the steered concept follows a sigmoidal (tanh-shaped) curve as a function of steering strength α, while probabilities of other concepts follow different limiting behavior (Theorem 3.6).
Near α=0, cross-entropy loss increases quadratically with steering strength, implying that any nonzero steering strictly degrades next-token prediction locally (Theorem 3.8).
For large |α|, the steered transformer's output logits converge to a value determined only by the normalized steering direction, becoming independent of the input prompt (Proposition 4.1).

The theoretical predictions for probability and cross-entropy behavior under steering are empirically validated across eleven language models, from a 9M-parameter 1-layer GPT up to Llama 2 7B and Mistral 7B, and across eight target concepts including depression, evil, and joy (Section 5).

X6i0PB7aJQ.text: Periodic (target-network) Q-learning is formalized as a nested optimization with outer Bellman iterations and an inner SGD loop with decreasing step size α_n^(k) = 2/[ξ(k+s)] (Section 3, Theorem 4.5).

With a constant target update frequency, the sample complexity to reach accuracy ε scales as O(log((1-γ)^-1 ε^-1)) / [ξ^2(1-γ)^4 ε^2 log(2(1+γ)^-1)], incurring an extra logarithmic factor in 1/ε (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 5.1).

A geometrically increasing target update frequency schedule of order γ^{-2n/3} achieves sample complexity O(1) / [ξ^2(1-γ)^5 ε^2], removing the logarithmic dependence on ε present under constant schedules (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 5.3).

GridWorld experiments show that small constant target update frequencies plateau at a high bias early in training while large constant frequencies converge slowly, whereas an increasing schedule avoids both failure modes (Figure 2).
Lunar Lander and GridWorld experiments demonstrate that an increasing target update schedule stabilizes learning compared to constant-frequency baselines (Figure 1).

Vd5bjrFQBh.text: On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, FrameOracle reduces a 16-frame input to an average of 10.4 selected frames while maintaining accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks (Table 1).
On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, FrameOracle reduces a 64-frame candidate pool to an average of 13.9 frames while improving average accuracy by about 1.4-1.5 percentage points (Table 1).

FrameOracle is trained via a four-stage curriculum: text-visual alignment using a SigLIP teacher, Rank Head optimization with a leave-one-out ranking loss, K Head optimization for frame-count prediction, and supervised fine-tuning on the FrameOracle-41K dataset (Section on training/method).
FrameOracle-41K comprises 40,992 video-question pairs sourced from LLaVA-Video-178K, with keyframe annotations averaging about 7 frames per question (median 5) (Section on dataset).
On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, FrameOracle reduces total compute by 39.8% (from 184.38 to 110.98 TFLOPs) and latency by 41% (from 0.615s to 0.363s) (Table 3).

FrameOracle is evaluated against plug-and-play frame-selection baselines including Frame-Voyager, BOLT, and KFC, as well as SOTA methods SeViLA, LVNet, VideoAgent, FFS, VSLS, and AKS, across six benchmarks including EgoSchema, LongVideoBench, MLVU, Video-MME, NExTQA, and Perception (Section on baselines/experiments).

YKEmoqwkE9.text: Any algorithm expressible in the LOCAL model of distributed computing, running on a graph with maximum degree D, can be learned exactly by the proposed GNN architecture using MLP ensembles as local update functions, with training set size scaling linearly in state/message size and quadratically in the maximum degree D (Theorem 5.1).

Neural Tangent Kernel theory (developed in Appendix B) is used to show that sufficiently large MLP ensembles trained on binary local instruction-label pairs converge to predictors that enable error-free execution of the learned algorithm at inference time, with high probability (Section 5, Appendix B).

Specific exact-learnability guarantees are established for message flooding, breadth-first search (BFS), depth-first search (DFS), and the Bellman-Ford shortest-path algorithm, each with derived sample/instruction complexity bounds (Theorems 6.1-6.4).

Because all nodes share the same local processor in this architecture, the number of distinct instructions that must be learned grows polynomially with the maximum degree D rather than with the total number of nodes in the graph, unlike prior feedforward approaches (Section 4, Section 6).
Experiments validate the theoretical ensemble-size requirements needed to guarantee exact execution of the learned graph algorithms (Section 7).

UTiEfkfNQ2.text: Theorem 2.2 establishes accelerated convergence for the Accelerated Noisy Power Method under a noise magnitude condition that scales as Δ_k·ε rather than the stricter Δ_k·ε^μ requirement of prior work (Xu, 2023) (Section 2, Theorem 2.2).

Theorems 2.4 and 2.5 prove that the noise conditions on the orthogonal component ||U_-k^T Ξ_t||_2 and parallel component ||U_k^T Ξ_t||_2 (Equations 3-4) cannot be relaxed without breaking the accelerated convergence guarantee (Section 2, Theorems 2.4-2.5).

Theorem 3.3 introduces ADePM, applying the improved ANPM analysis to decentralized PCA via an accelerated gossip protocol (Algorithm 1), achieving convergence rate O(sqrt(λ_k/(λ_k-λ_{k+1})) log(...)) with communication cost O(1/sqrt(γ_W) log(...)) comparable to non-accelerated decentralized methods (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.3).
Section 3.1 shows the accelerated gossip subroutine attains O~(1/sqrt(γ_W)) mixing versus the O~(1/γ_W) rate of standard (non-accelerated) gossip (Section 3.1).

Section 4 experiments demonstrate that the optimal momentum parameter β* = λ_{k+1}^2/4 yields a square-root speedup over non-accelerated decentralized PCA methods, and that ADePM substantially outperforms DePM and DeEPCA baselines on real datasets (Section 4).

ybMDCeOC2m.text: Theorem 1 shows that with an exact critic, entropy-regularized actor-critic converges linearly, with the convergence error contracting at rate (1-η_a·μ̄·λ)^k per iteration, matching deterministic policy gradient (Theorem 1).
Corollary 1 shows the exact-critic setting attains an ε-optimal policy value with O(log(1/ε)) samples, matching the deterministic policy gradient method's iteration complexity (Corollary 1).

Lemma 5 proves the exact critic yields 'strong' variance reduction, where the gradient variance vanishes near the optimum and is bounded by the deterministic gradient norm, eliminating residual variance at convergence (Lemma 5).

Theorem 2 and Corollary 2 show that with an inexact (learned) critic requiring H >= O~(log(1/ε)) TD update steps per actor update, the algorithm attains an ε-optimal value with O~(1/ε) samples, with convergence error decomposing into initialization error, critic bias, a policy-switch cost of order O(η_a^3), and critic variance of order η_a·η_c (Theorem 2, Corollary 2).

DmeFAFUO6f.text: Section 4 formulates ADPO's loss (Equation 14) by moving the summation over token-level preferences outside the sigmoid function, in contrast to standard DPO, explicitly encoding the autoregressive generation assumption into the preference-optimization objective (Section 4, Equation 14).

Section 5.3 distinguishes token length measure μ (the number of tokens T = μ(y) in a sequence) from feedback length measure μ', which maps a full response y into a one-dimensional evaluation space representing how human evaluators judge complete outputs (Section 5.3).
Corollary 1 proves that when the feedback length measure satisfies μ'(y) = 1 for all sequences y, the ADPO objective reduces exactly to the standard DPO loss (Corollary 1).
Table 2 shows ADPO and its variant cADPO consistently outperform DPO baselines across four language models on the GSM8K and MATH500 mathematical reasoning benchmarks (Table 2).
Table 4 reports ADPO reaches 45.8% on AlpacaEval 2, outperforming DPO's 40.3% and roughly matching SimPO on conversational tasks (Table 4).
Table 3 shows that intermediate response-granularity levels (adaptive segmentation with m >= 128 segments) outperform full-response-only evaluation granularity (Table 3).

zA3KhRZ9A5.text: In the 3-task setting with Qwen-2.5-3B, MT-GRPO achieves a 16-28% absolute improvement in worst-task accuracy over standard GRPO and a 6% absolute improvement over DAPO (Abstract, Figure 5).
In the 3-task setting, MT-GRPO requires 50% fewer training steps than baselines to reach 50% worst-task accuracy (Abstract, Figure 5).
In the 9-task setting at trade-off parameter λ=1.2, MT-GRPO improves worst-task accuracy by 16% over GRPO and 6% over DAPO (Figure 7).

Subroutine 1 (Improvement-Aware Weight Update, Section 3.2) combines an improvement signal I_k^(t) with the absolute reward J_k(θ_t) via trade-off parameter λ to dynamically reweight tasks, preventing weight collapse onto a single worst-performing task (Section 3.2).

Algorithm 2, the Ratio-Preserving Sampler (Section 5), corrects for uneven zero-gradient rates across tasks (e.g., ARC showing substantially higher zero-gradient proportions than other tasks, per Figure 3) via acceptance-aware oversampling (Section 5, Figure 3).

CG3TwM48M8.text: KernelCraft's benchmark spans four hardware targets (PLENA, AMD NPU, Coral NPU, and a RISC-V CPU, Table 3) and 23 ML tasks across three complexity levels (Table 4), totaling over 1,100 experiments across four frontier LLMs with five configurations per task (Section 3, Table 3-4).
Table 5 reports GPT-5.2 achieves functional success rates of 55% on PLENA, 17% on AMD NPU, and 47% on Coral NPU (Table 5).

Table 5 shows success rates drop sharply with task complexity: approximately 55% for Level 1 primitive operations, 45% for Level 2 composite operations, and near 0% for Level 3 end-to-end blocks (Table 5).
Figure 3 shows agent-generated kernels achieve 2-8x speedups over template-based compiler baselines on Coral NPU GEMV/GEMM tasks, while AMD NPU results cluster near parity at 0.89-1.18x (Figure 3).

TPpUKH8fuQ.text: The Flower-Tiny model (17.3M parameters) outperforms Fourier-based (FNO), convolution-based (CNextU-Net), and attention-based (scOT) baselines of similar size on next-step and rollout prediction (Table 1).

On the compressible Euler dataset, Flower-Medium (155.8M parameters) achieves a 1-step error of 0.0108 and a 1:20 rollout error of 0.0739, both lower than Poseidon-L (628.6M parameters), which achieves 0.0194 and 0.1114 respectively (Table 2).

Flower architectures use multihead 'selfwarp' layers that predict displacement fields and warp mixed input features, with no Fourier multipliers, dot-product attention, or convolutional mixing, yielding linear computational cost in the number of heads (Section 2).

Flowers are benchmarked on 16 diverse 2D and 3D time-dependent PDE datasets drawn from The Well and PDEBench, including acoustic scattering, MHD, Rayleigh-Bénard convection, and shallow water equations, and achieve the lowest error on most of these benchmarks (Table 1).
Ablation studies show that removing the warping mechanism substantially degrades performance and that using multiple heads is essential for rollout stability (Tables 3-8).

wCQEvBldlz.text: HATCH improves multi-image spatial reasoning accuracy on SPAR-Bench-MV from 24.9% (base model) to 53.6%, a gain of 28.7 percentage points (Results).

HATCH achieves 50.2% on MindCube-Tiny versus 37.8% for the base model, and 27.0% on MMSI-Bench versus 25.6% for the base model, outperforming baselines of comparable size and reaching competitive results against much larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B (Results).

HATCH retains single-image spatial reasoning performance, scoring 45.2% on SPAR-Bench-SI and 74.5% on CV-Bench, indicating multi-image training does not degrade single-image capability (Single-Image Reasoning Retention).

HATCH combines two mechanisms: Patch-Level Spatial Alignment (PaStA), which aligns patch representations across views via geometry supervision, and Action-then-Answer Reasoning (ActoR), which requires generating explicit viewpoint-transition actions before the final answer, optimized with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (Method).
Ablation experiments show that removing either PaStA or ActoR degrades overall performance, with PaStA being particularly important for cross-view reasoning tasks (Ablation Findings).

ujYdUdqWpm.text: EpiAgent synthesizes epidemiological simulators through a three-stage pipeline: flow graph synthesis (Section 4.2), model compilation into a fixed PyTorch skeleton (Section 4.3), and multi-agent verification and validation (Section 4.5).

The explicit epidemiological flow graph intermediate representation enforces hard structural constraints, such as requiring latent periods before recovery, population conservation, non-negativity of compartments and parameters, and terminal (non-reversible) death states, before code generation (Section 4.2).

In an ablation removing flow-graph verification, over 87% of generated models exhibited epidemiologically invalid structures, compared to substantially lower failure rates when the verification stage is included (Ablation Results).

In Case Study I, a 19-scenario-round evaluation using COVID-19 scenarios from the MIDAS Network modeling hub across varied vaccination policies and immune escape assumptions shows generated models produce correct monotonic responses (higher immune escape yields more infections; more vaccination yields fewer cases) (Case Study I).

Knowledge retrieval via a FAISS-indexed epidemiological knowledge base reduces the average number of generation iterations needed for convergence by approximately 20% compared to generation without retrieval (Key Findings).

k66TZFhUSQ.text: On the mass-spring benchmark, the proposed rank-one (RO) modulation achieves a trajectory error of 0.049 versus 0.750 for training from scratch and 0.375 for MAML (Table 1, Section 5).

On the Kepler system, multi-rank (MR) modulation achieves a trajectory error of 0.061 compared to 0.497 (scratch) and 0.214 (MAML), and on the Duffing oscillator, MR achieves 0.048 versus 0.821 (scratch) and 0.679 (MAML) (Table 1, Section 5).

The proposed RO and MR modulation techniques, inspired by low-rank adaptation, condition structure-preserving (Hamiltonian and GENERIC/metriplectic) neural networks on compact per-task latent codes rather than retraining per parameter configuration (Section 3).

Latent codes for meta-learned dynamics are adapted via an inner-loop auto-decoding procedure using 100 gradient steps during validation and testing, with validation codes initialized as the arithmetic mean of training codes (Section 4).

The structure-preserving models maintain exact conservation of energy for Hamiltonian systems (mass-spring, pendulum, Duffing, Kepler) and correct entropy generation for dissipative GENERIC systems (damped nonlinear oscillator, two gas containers) independent of training quality, since these are preserved by construction (Section 2, Section 5).

cBfpI4aLCZ.text: In complex environments, the proposed method (CIRL) achieves greater than 80% imitation score, whereas a 1-Nearest-Neighbor baseline achieves less than 20% (Figure 3).
CIRL consistently outperforms Forward-Backward (FB) representations across all tested environments in the zero-shot imitation comparison (Figure 3).
On the Reacher task, CIRL's automatic goal sampling (GoalKDE) achieves near-perfect imitation scores, in some cases exceeding oracle goal sampling performance (Figure 6).
On the URLB benchmark's Ant Forward and Ant Jump tasks, when imitating non-goal-reaching policies, CIRL achieves lower regret than FB representations (Figure 7).

During pretraining, CIRL autonomously proposes goal observations and practices reaching them; at evaluation time, it solves an amortized inverse reinforcement learning problem using a mean-field variational goal inference model to infer the demonstrator's goal from observed trajectories, then commands the learned goal-conditioned policy toward that inferred goal (Method).

wfHCePoAed.text: The accountability attribution framework formulates causal effects of training stages using potential outcomes, with Estimator 4.1 computing single-step effects via propagator matrices tracking parameter updates through subsequent steps (Section 4.2, Estimator 4.1).
Estimator 4.2 extends single-step effects to arbitrary performance functions via a first-order Taylor approximation of the loss around trained parameters (Section 4.2, Estimator 4.2).

On MNIST, the correlation between estimated AA-Scores and ground-truth retraining results averages 0.7314 across settings, including 0.9712 for data insertion and 0.3381 for mislabeled data (Section 5.2, Table 1).

On CelebA, removing the top-scored training steps reduces confounding gender-attribute prediction accuracy from 0.5501 to 0.5187 while improving true target task accuracy from 0.9172 to 0.9385 (Section 5.3, Table 2).
The framework's optimization-aware propagation accounts for learning rate schedules, momentum, and weight decay when tracing parameter updates across stages (Section 4.2).
The authors propose a generalized Gauss-Newton approximation and layer-wise computation to reduce the O(Kp^3) complexity of direct computation down to O(K|B| sum p_l^2) (Section 4.3).

fVso2kGVrF.text: The paper defines the Theoretic Value of Explanation as the expected performance improvement of a rational Bayesian agent given features versus only the prior distribution (Definition 6).
The paper defines Potential Human-Complementary Value as the expected improvement when a rational agent has both human predictions and features versus human predictions alone (Definition 7).
The paper defines Behavioral Value of Explanation as the measured treatment effect of providing explanations on real human decision-makers' performance in a controlled study (Definition 8).

Proposition 4 shows that idealized rational agents gain no additional value from explanations beyond what is already contained in features and model predictions, since explanations are informational garblings of these signals (Proposition 4).

In the Ames Iowa housing case study using three features (year built, bedrooms, building material) and SHAP explanations, the theoretic value of explanation is a 24.2% MAPE improvement (95% CI [22.4, 26.1]), while the potential human-complementary value is only 9% MAPE improvement (95% CI [8.1, 9.9]) (Section B).

The decision problem framework formalizes a use case via action spaces, state spaces, utility functions, and probability distributions, illustrated with worked examples in medical treatment (biopsy) and recourse provision (Definition 1, Examples 1-2).

5Qpy3uTD05.text: The proposed pipeline extracts residual-stream activations across transformer layers, encodes them with pre-trained layer-specific sparse autoencoders, and binarizes the top-k active features into sparse distributed representations for sequential anomaly scoring (Section 3).

Mean Jaccard similarity of active SAE features across layers is used to motivate the choice of k=10 for top-k binarization, showing low agreement in early layers, peak similarity in mid-layers, and input-specific behavior in late layers (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
On Gemma2-2B with 20 Newsgroups as in-domain data, the method achieves far-OOD AUROC of 0.9782 against SST-2, 0.9699 against MNLI, and 0.9850 against RTE (Section 4.2, Table 2).
On near-OOD detection with Gemma2-2B, the method reaches AUROC 0.9699 on SNIPS but drops to 0.7387 on CLINC150, which the authors attribute to representational aliasing (Section 4.3, Table 3).

An ablation shows first-order Markov chain scoring (AUROC 0.919) matches or outperforms HTM (0.912) and RNN (0.910) backends, while replacing SAE features with raw activations under the HTM baseline degrades performance to AUROC 0.753 (Section 4.5, Tables 4-5).
Gemma2-9B achieves higher OOD detection performance than Gemma2-2B across all reported benchmarks (Section 4.2).

YlcyOMTPNl.text: Flow Sampling conditions on noise samples X0 rather than data samples and constructs a denoising diffusion drift from the energy function via the closed-form conditional drift of Proposition 3.2 (Section 3, Equation 19, Proposition 3.2).

The Riemannian extension replaces Euclidean interpolants with geodesic interpolants and provides a closed-form Jacobian formula for the conditional drift on constant-curvature manifolds via Proposition 4.1, with an explicit SLERP-based implementation for the hypersphere (Section 4.1, Equation 40, Proposition 4.1).
On the LJ-55 particle system, Flow Sampling achieves energy Wasserstein distance 21.32±0.63 versus 28.10±8.15 for ASBS, roughly a 25% improvement (Section 6.1, Table 1).

On Ala2 peptide conformer sampling at 64 training NFE, Flow Sampling attains D_KL(psi)=0.523±0.006 and energy W2=4.113±0.023, whereas ASBS fails catastrophically with energy W2 of about 6.0e7 (Section 6.2, Table 2).

On large-scale amortized conformer generation across 24,775 molecular topologies from SPICE at 256 NFE, Flow Sampling achieves recall coverage 91.89±7.51 versus 89.66±19.42 for ASBS (Section 6.3, Table 3).
The method is demonstrated as a diffusion sampler recovering multimodal von Mises-Fisher mixture distributions on the 2-sphere using closed-form conditional drifts (Section 6.4, Figure 1).

2ztmXT3qpN.text: ECSEL is motivated by the observation that 45 of 100 equations in the AI Feynman symbolic regression benchmark are signomials, i.e., finite sums of power-law terms (Section 1).
Theorem 3.1 establishes a universal approximation property for signomials on the positive orthant by transforming to log-space and applying the Stone-Weierstrass theorem (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

Across 58 equations from AI Feynman, Livermore, Jin, and Korns benchmarks with a 15-minute time limit, ECSEL achieves a 95.86% symbolic recovery rate versus 59.10% for DGSR, 58.54% for NGGP, and 56% for NeSymRes (Section 4, Table 2, Figure 1).
ECSEL's average solving time is 86.4 seconds, compared to 612.9s for DGSR, 468.7s for NGGP, and 126.3s for NeSymRes (Section 4, Table 2).

On the ILPD classification dataset, ECSEL achieves 75.86% accuracy and 74.39% F1, exceeding XGBoost's 72.41% accuracy and 63.03% F1, and attains the highest F1-score on 4 of 11 benchmark datasets (Section 5, Tables 1 and 7).

On the PaySim fraud detection dataset (6.3 million transactions, 0.13% fraud rate), a 2-component ECSEL signomial achieves 79.08% F1 versus 78.0% for DSC, with 68.10% recall and 94.27% precision (Section 6.2, Equation 8).

Ck6Ort0wqc.text: GSP (Generalized Search for Planning) combines weighted A* search (w=2) with a relational GNN-based Q-function, replacing real-time RL exploration with best-first search guidance (Section 4, Section 5).
On the 2023 IPC benchmark, GSP used as a greedy policy (GSP_π) achieves 100% coverage on Blocksworld (44 avg steps), Miconic (490 avg steps), and Spanner (216 avg steps) (Table 2).
Heuristics trained only on Blocksworld instances with fewer than 30 blocks solve test instances with up to 488 blocks in a zero-shot manner without search (Section 6.1, Table 1).
On Sokoban (10x10, 4 boxes), GSP with WA* search solves 1000/1000 instances using 207 expansions on average, versus 3,298 for a WA* baseline and 1,050 for DeepCubeA (Table 3).

On PushWorld Level 0 (200 procedurally-generated instances), GSP_WA* matches LAMA's 200/200 coverage but with shorter 18-step plans versus LAMA's 24-step plans; on the cross-domain Level 1 transfer set, GSP_WA* solves 48/63 evaluable instances using roughly 30x fewer node expansions than LAMA (Section 6.3, Table 4).
Classical heuristic h_ff outperforms GSP on rovers, satellite, Sokoban, and miconic domains, while GSP outperforms h_ff on blocksworld, childsnack, and transport (Table 5).

726Wto4meA.text: Untied Ulysses (UPipe) performs headwise chunking of attention computation, processing U of H heads per stage instead of all heads simultaneously, reducing peak attention activation memory from O(H) to O(U) (Section 3.3, Figure 3).

UPipe reduces intermediate (QKV plus all-to-all) tensor memory in the forward attention block by up to 87.5% for a 32B-parameter Transformer (Qwen3-32B) compared to DeepSpeed-Ulysses with offloading (Table 2, Table 4).
On a single 8xH100 node, UPipe scales Llama3-8B training to a 5M-token context length, a 25% improvement over the prior state-of-the-art FPDT method's 4M-token limit (Table 3, Table 4).
On two H100 nodes (16xH100), UPipe reaches an 8M-token maximum context length for Llama3-8B, a 33% improvement over USP-Hybrid's 6M-token limit, while maintaining comparable throughput (Figure 5).
UPipe achieves the highest throughput (tokens/second/GPU) among compared methods for sequence lengths of 2M tokens and above, for both Llama3-8B (8xH100) and Qwen3-32B (16xH100) (Table 3).
An ablation on the head-chunk size U on Llama3-8B at 512K context with 4 GPUs shows smaller U yields better memory efficiency at the cost of throughput, and vice versa (Section 5.4, Figure 6).

M2pbI9uKjW.text: Symbolic-MoE is a training-free framework that performs instance-level, skill-based recruiting of experts from a pool of 16 pre-trained LLMs rather than fixed task-level model groupings (Section 3.3.1).
Symbolic-MoE achieves an 8.15% average absolute improvement over the best multi-agent baseline across MMLU-Pro, GPQA, AIME, and MedMCQA (Table 1).

Symbolic-MoE outperforms individual strong models including GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Llama 3.3 70B on average across the four benchmarks, despite using smaller 7-8B expert models (Table 1, Section 4.2).

Symbolic-MoE's batched inference strategy runs all 16 expert models on a single GPU with 44% less runtime than the MoA baseline on one GPU, and achieves close to a 2x speedup over MoA when scaled to four GPUs (Table 2, Section 3.3.3).
An ablation over different expert-recruiting strategies on GPQA shows skill-based recruiting outperforms alternative recruiting strategies (Table 4).

2lMqcGV81Z.text: DELTA distills a linearized, curvature-regularized teacher model (trained in tangent space around pretrained weights) into a non-linear student trained via conventional fine-tuning, using Along-Path Knowledge Distillation over interpolated teachers at scales alpha in [0.5, 1] (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).

Curvature-aware regularization uses EK-FAC estimated on a task-agnostic reference dataset (ImageNet-21k for vision, C4 for text) to penalize representation drift, rather than task-specific data (Section 3.2).

On the Task Addition benchmark, DELTA achieves 88.3% absolute accuracy with ViT-B/32 and 92.7% with ViT-L/14 on the 8-Vision task set, outperforming non-linear fine-tuning baselines by roughly 15 points while being competitive with linearized methods TA and tau-Jp (Table 2).
On the 6-NLI task set with T5-Base, DELTA achieves 82.4% absolute accuracy (95.5% normalized accuracy) on Task Addition (Table 2).
On Task Negation (unlearning) on 8-Vision, DELTA reaches 9.6% target-task accuracy while retaining 62.1% control accuracy on ImageNet-1K (Table 3).

At inference, the DELTA student matches the efficiency of a standard non-linear model (about 160ms on ViT-B/32) and is 2-3.2x faster than the linearized teacher, though training costs about 3x standard fine-tuning time and 2x its memory (Table 5).

0TRMWCwKRo.text: The paper frames amortized MIPS as learning the support function sigma_Y(x) = max_{y in Y} <x,y>, exploiting its convexity, 1-homogeneity, and the property that its gradient equals the optimal key y*(x) (Section 3, Section 2).

SupportNet uses an Input Convex Neural Network to learn the support function directly and recovers optimal keys via automatic differentiation, trained with combined score-regression and gradient-matching losses (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).

KeyNet directly regresses optimal keys without a backward pass at inference, using a key-regression loss plus a score-consistency loss derived from Euler's theorem, reducing inference latency versus SupportNet (Section 3.1, Section 3.2).
A homogenization wrapper H[g](x) := ||x|| * g(x/||x||) is introduced to guarantee positive 1-homogeneity for any base network g (Section 3.1).

On BEIR benchmarks including FIQA (52K keys), Quora (513K keys), NQ (2.6M keys), and HotpotQA (5.2M keys), both SupportNet and KeyNet outperform centroid-based routing baselines, with at least a 10-point routing accuracy improvement on NQ using c=10 clusters (Section 4.4).

Timing measurements over batches of 4096 queries in dimension 384 show SupportNet's gradient computation costs 1.2-2x its forward-pass time, while KeyNet's forward and prediction times are similar, and KeyNet predictions improve FAISS IVF index recall across all search budgets (Table 1, Section 4.5).

QRtzkKrbJi.text: The paper introduces a unified PDE gradient flow framework for distributionally robust optimization (DRO) with six concrete algorithms, including Wasserstein Gradient Flow (Algorithm 3) and Wasserstein Fisher-Rao flow (Algorithm 4) variants for entropy-regularized Wasserstein DRO (Section 4, Algorithms 3-4).
Proposition 1 shows the Wasserstein gradient flow sampler must run for time at least on the order of O((1/λ) log(L/√(λε))) to produce an ε-accurate gradient estimate (Section 4, Proposition 1).
Theorem 1 proves the outer loop of the gradient-flow-sampler-based DRO algorithm requires O(1/ε²_opt) iterations to reach an ε-stationary point (Section 5, Theorem 1).
Theorem 2 bounds the total computational complexity of the WGF-based DRO algorithm (Algorithm 3) as Õ(L_Φ L²_U L²_f d² / (λ³_U ε⁴_opt)) (Section 5, Theorem 2).

On CIFAR-10 adversarial training under PGD attacks, the WFR- and WGF-based DRO methods achieve consistently higher robust accuracy across all perturbation settings compared to baseline DRO methods (Section 6.3).
Lemma 1 establishes that the entropy-regularized DRO problem is equivalent to a Schrödinger half-bridge problem, enabling sampling from the conditional worst-case distribution (Section 3.1, Lemma 1).

Yw55CRYtKo.text: BACo (Base-Aligned Model Collaboration) is an inference-time, training-free framework that performs token-level routing between a base LLM and its aligned counterpart to jointly optimize diversity and quality in a single decoding pass (Section on Method/Approach).
With its best routing strategy, BACo achieves a 21.3% joint improvement in diversity and quality metrics over baselines (Results section, Section on Performance).
BACo is evaluated on three open-ended generation tasks using 13 distinct diversity and quality metrics, with results corroborated by human evaluation (Experiments section).

Token-level routing based on model uncertainty and content signals lets BACo outperform state-of-the-art inference-time baselines without requiring expensive decoding procedures or additional post-training (Section on Baselines/Comparisons).

dy8ppwIj4o.text: On Qwen3-32B, REAL achieves +8.40 Pearson and +7.20 Spearman correlation over the SFT baseline, and +18.30/+11.20 over the base model, for LLM-as-a-Judge regression tasks (Section on Main Results, Table 2).
REAL is evaluated across three model backbones of different scales and tokenizers: Mistral2-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-32B (Section on Experimental Setup).
On Mistral2-7B, REAL's average correlation across Facebook Bench, FLASK, Vicuna Bench, and MT Bench reaches 67.9 Pearson, 66.2 Spearman, and 53.0 Kendall (Table 2).
On Qwen3-32B, REAL's average correlation across the same four benchmarks reaches 71.0 Pearson and 70.0 Spearman (Table 2).

REAL's training objective decomposes generalized policy gradient optimization into exploration over reasoning trajectories and regression-aware prediction refinement, and this yields better out-of-domain generalization than regression-aware SFT baselines such as TRACT and standard binary-reward RL (Section on Method/Comparative Analysis).

13lMChKB5u.text: LRPO (Language-Routed Policy Optimization) trains a language router via multi-armed bandit optimization that dynamically selects the response language during reinforcement learning, rather than treating response language as fixed (Section on Method).
On Qwen2.5-1.5B, LRPO improves mGSM-v2 accuracy from 24.87 to 38.25, a gain of +13.38 points, over the instruction-tuned baseline (Results section, mGSM-v2 evaluation).
On Qwen2.5-1.5B, LRPO improves the overall seen-language average by +5.08 points over the instruction-tuned baseline and by +2.85 points over standard GRPO (Results section).
LRPO is evaluated across 14 languages spanning multiple writing systems and across three model backbones: Qwen2.5-1.5B, LLaMA3.2-1B, and Gemma3-4B (Section on Experimental Setup).
The evaluation suite includes five multilingual benchmarks: CARE, the newly introduced CARE-pro, mGSM-v2, Global-MMLU-Lite, and Include-Lite (Section on Benchmarks).

9ylPoHEKed.text: Magnitude distance is defined as d_Mag^t(X,Y) = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t), with a tunable scale parameter t that governs sensitivity to global structure (small t) versus finer local structure (large t) (Section on Definition, Magnitude Distance).

Theorem 5.2 shows magnitude distance is symmetric and non-negative, satisfies identity of indiscernibles only up to magnitude equivalence, and does not satisfy the triangle inequality in R^D for D>1 (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
Theorem 5.3 shows magnitude distance converges to 0 as t→0 and converges to the cardinality of the symmetric difference of the two datasets as t→∞ (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
Figure 2 shows magnitude distance remains discriminative in dimensions exceeding 1000, in settings where MMD's discriminative power collapses (Section on High-Dimensional Behavior, Figure 2).
MagGN, a generative model trained with a multi-scale magnitude-distance loss, achieves an 11.97x training speedup over WGAN on MNIST while producing visually competitive samples (Table 1).

Theorem 5.5 proves magnitude distance has bounded outlier sensitivity, changing by only about 6-10% under significant outlier addition compared to a 17.6% change for Wasserstein distance in the same setting (Section 5, Theorem 5.5).

5SMn6N9SXq.text: For resettable streams with Inc(x,Δ) and Reset(P) operations, the paper constructs sketches robust to adaptive adversaries while maintaining prefix-max error |F̂ₜ - Fₜ| ≤ ε·max_{t'≤t} F_{t'} (Theorem 1.2).
The robust cardinality sketch uses O(ε⁻² log^{3/2}(T) · log(T/δ)) bits of space, avoiding the Ω(n) space lower bound that applies to relative-error non-robust variants (Theorem 2.4).
The robust sum sketch achieves O(ε⁻² log^{11/2}(T) · log²(1/δ)) bits of space under adaptive adversarial updates (Theorem 3.1).
Robustness for Bernstein statistics is achieved with poly(ε⁻¹, log(T/δ)) space, i.e., polylogarithmic in the stream length T (Theorem 4.2).

The robustification technique adapts the Binary Tree Mechanism from differential privacy under continual observation, giving an exponential space improvement over prior polynomial-space wrapper techniques for adaptive robustness (Section 2, building on Theorem 2.4).

Two concrete adaptive attacks are demonstrated against standard (non-robust) sketches: a re-insertion attack that reduces effective sampling probability from p to p², and a sample-and-delete attack that empties the sample while the active set stays large (Section 1, motivating the vulnerabilities).

Dx3Z5QGAZB.text: Table data exhibits periodic non-vanishing mutual information at lags d = km (k = 1,2,...) for m-column tables, in contrast to the power-law decay of mutual information in natural language (Theorem 2.2).

Table mutual information asymptotically dominates natural-language mutual information at these periodic lags (Corollary 2.4), and the effective dependency distance is infinite for tables versus finite for text (Theorem 2.6).

TableLong's SQL-based pipeline, built from 10,000+ real-world tables via consistency-based filtration, improves average long-context benchmark performance by +8.24% for the DS-R1-Distill-32B model (Table 1).
On the out-of-domain LiveCodeBench benchmark, the 32B model improves by +11.97% after TableLong training, part of an average +8.06% out-of-domain gain (Table 4).
On Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval, the 32B model improves from 87.95% to 99.40% (+13.02%) after training with TableLong data (Figure 3).

Ablations show multi-hop reasoning performance scales with table cell count (46.30% with ~30 cells to 48.36% with ~300+ cells, Table 2), and using multiple tables versus a single table improves grounding from 46.66% to 48.36% average (Table 3).

M52jcbntdB.text: Under a bounded-density assumption on buyer/seller valuation distributions, the proposed algorithm achieves Õ(T^{3/4}) regret against the best fixed price distribution satisfying Global Budget Balance (GBB) (Theorem 4.1).

Without the bounded-density assumption, any algorithm suffers Ω(T) linear regret against the GBB benchmark, shown via a needle-in-the-haystack construction proving discretization is impossible (Theorem 3.1).

Bounded density lets the learner restrict to a uniform K×K price grid with discretization error O(log(T)/K), showing no separation between one-dimensional SBB learning and two-dimensional GBB distribution learning (Lemma 5.1, Lemma 5.2).
In the profit-collection phase, regret is bounded by Õ(β + T/K + √(KT)) where β is the accumulated budget (Lemma 7.1, Lemma 7.2).
The pure-exploration phase estimates all K² price-pair outcomes using only 2K exploration samples via sample reuse across the observable/non-observable GFT decomposition (Lemma 8.1, Lemma 8.2).

The UCB-based constrained-bandit optimization phase achieves Õ(K√T) regret while preserving GBB feasibility, combining with the other phases to yield the overall Õ(T^{3/4}) rate (Lemma 9.1, Theorem 4.1).

QYA0Q28ssf.text: Under finite drift energy assumptions, the intra-generation KL divergence between the generated distribution and the training target is bounded above by (1/2)ε̂ᵢ², the learned-path score error energy (Proposition 3.1).

A matching lower bound on the chi-squared divergence, χ²(p̂^(i+1) ∥ qᵢ) ≥ (1/4)ηᵢε²⋆,ᵢ − C·ε⁴⋆,ᵢ, holds for small score errors (ε²⋆,ᵢ ≤ 1), where ηᵢ ∈ [0,1] is the observability coefficient (Proposition 3.3, Definition 3.2).
Combining the upper and lower bounds yields a two-sided equivalence χ²(p̂^(i+1) ∥ qᵢ) ≍ ε²⋆,ᵢ in the perturbative regime (Theorem 3.4).
When the score-error series ∑ᵢ ε²⋆,ᵢ diverges, the accumulated divergence across generations cannot vanish and has a non-zero floor limsup Dᵢ ≥ αη̄ε̄ / [16(1+(1-α)²)] (Proposition 4.1).

When ∑ᵢ ε²⋆,ᵢ converges, accumulated divergence across generations satisfies D_{N+1} + C_bias ≍ Σᵢ(1-α)^{2(N-i)}ε²⋆,ᵢ + (1-α)^{2(N+1-i₀)}D_{i₀}, decaying geometrically at rate (1-α)² per generation, where α is the fraction of fresh data mixed in each round (Theorem 4.2).

The α-dependent tradeoff between drift and stability is empirically confirmed on a 10D Gaussian mixture and on Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10, with low α producing collapse-driven drift and high α maintaining stability (Figure 1).

Xwxz41eYE6.text: MMSE denoisers satisfy the normalization-equivariance identity D_θ(αy + μ1, σα) = αD_θ(y, σ) + μ1, linking rescaling of signal amplitude to a proportional change in noise level (Equation 7, Section 3).
The proposed NE-SURE training loss combines this normalization-equivariance constraint with the SURE framework to train denoisers from noisy measurements alone (Equation 8, Section 3).
Theorem 3.1 proves the trained denoiser generalizes to noise levels below the training noise σ_n, with the approximation error bounded by a Fisher-divergence term.

On FFHQ at σ_n = 0.075, the self-supervised NE-SURE sampler achieves LPIPS of 0.015, close to the fully supervised baseline's 0.012, and outperforms SURE-only and consistency-based (CD) baselines (Table 1, Section 4).

Combining normalization equivariance with the equivariant imaging (EI) framework for incomplete measurements outperforms EI and Ambient Diffusion on inpainting and demosaicing in LPIPS and FID (Table 2, Section 5).
The denoising MSE scales as σ_t²/√N with the number of training samples N, matching the sample-complexity rate of fully supervised learning (Figure 4).

c0lJ3rOBPu.text: SPARC improves Qwen3VL-4B accuracy from 72.6% (native full-resolution) to 74.8% (+2.2 points) on in-distribution benchmarks including V*Bench and HRBench-4K/8K (Table 1).
At 256px input resolution, SPARC lifts Qwen3VL-4B accuracy to 51.0% versus 41.7% for the native baseline at the same resolution (Section 4, Table 1).
On the out-of-distribution XLRS remote-sensing benchmark, SPARC surpasses native full-resolution 'thinking with images' (54.8% vs. 53.5%) while using roughly 200x fewer visual tokens (Section 4).
With fine-tuning, SPARC reaches 91.2% on V*Bench, exceeding the 30x larger Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B (91.1%) and RL-based baselines DeepEyes (90.1%) and ViGoRL-7B (86.4%) (Appendix A.5, Table 5).
Self-consistency perception via Weighted Box Fusion over N=8 rollouts raises Qwen3VL-4B accuracy to 67.0% at 512px using an average of 2.54 crops per query (Section 5, Table 2).

Supervised fine-tuning of the perception stage at low (256px) resolution outperforms full-resolution training, e.g. Qwen3VL-8B SFT-256 reaches 64.3% at 512px versus a 54.8% baseline, acting as an implicit regularizer (Section 6, Table 3).

ujeyxKwTGM.text: DASH achieves up to 4.83x faster optimizer steps than well-optimized Distributed Shampoo, comparing CN with block size B=1024 in FP16 (138ms) against the FP32 Distributed Shampoo baseline at B=1024 (666ms) (Section 5, Table 1).

Newton-Denman-Beavers (NDB) iteration with Power-Iteration scaling and block size B=1024 attains the lowest validation perplexity (11.69) among all tested second-order configurations, improving on the EVD baseline's 11.80 (Section 5, Table 1).

On a 953M-parameter Llama model trained on C4 with block size B=2048 and update frequency f=1, DASH matches Distributed Shampoo's EVD validation perplexity (11.72 vs. 11.73) while reducing optimizer runtime from 2200ms to 1747ms (Section 5, Table 1).
Power-Iteration scaling outperforms Frobenius-norm scaling for NDB, yielding a 0.08 lower validation perplexity (11.68 vs. 11.76) at matched block size (Section 5, Table 1).

On the CBSHV variant with a 953M Llama model (Table 3), DASH in FP16 with block size B=1024 achieves roughly a 4.6x runtime speedup over the FP32 Distributed Shampoo baseline (1056ms to 228ms) at comparable validation perplexity (Section 5, Table 3).
DASH's 3D tensor-blocking strategy reduces per-GPU memory usage relative to Distributed Shampoo on the 953M model across 8 GPUs, from 76GB to 71-73GB depending on worker rank (Section 4).

wKMV7mXjUr.text: Palimpsa formulates attention as Bayesian metaplasticity, tying per-parameter plasticity of the attention state to an importance state Iₜ (inverse variance) governed by a prior distribution, via the update rule in Equations 28-29 (Section 2).

Table 1 shows that transforming non-metaplastic gated-attention models (e.g., Mamba2, as a special case where Iₜ≈I_prior) into the metaplastic Palimpsa formulation is intended to expand memory capacity by allowing importance-weighted, per-state forgetting (Section 2.3, Table 1).

On Multi-Query Associative Recall with curriculum sequence lengths up to 1024, metaplastic variants (especially Palimpsa-D) consistently outperform their non-metaplastic counterparts, with the performance gap widening at longer sequence lengths (Section 3.1, Figure 2).

At the 760M-parameter scale trained on 30B tokens of Fineweb-Edu, fine-tuned Palimpsa-D achieves the best average commonsense accuracy of 52.27%, beating the Gated Deltanet baseline's 51.50% by 0.77 points (Section 3.3, table in Section 3.3).
Fine-tuned Palimpsa-D at 760M scale achieves a LAMBADA perplexity of 14.86, compared to 17.06 for Gated Deltanet and 18.84 for Transformer++ (Section 3.3, table in Section 3.3).

During MQAR training, the metaplasticity ratio (I_max-I_min)/I_min grows to approximately 40, indicating consolidated synapses become up to 40-fold more stable than plastic ones (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

SPZd0HVyiS.text: On OpenLORIS-Object with 8,192-dimensional compressed features under class imbalance across 12 tasks, BiMU reaches 88.70% accuracy using only 3.1% of the labels/updates used by the 100% baseline (87.76% accuracy), a roughly 32x reduction (Section 4.5).

On 1000-task Permuted-MNIST, BiMU sustains 90.30±0.38% mean accuracy on the last 5 tasks and 0.99±0.00 OOD AUC without task boundaries, versus 41.12±1.62% accuracy and 0.57±0.12 OOD AUC for the task-boundary-dependent BayesBiNN baseline (Section 4.2, table in Section 4.2).

BiMU's uncertainty-gated relaxation term (Eq. 6-7) prevents saturation of the mean-field Bernoulli posteriors' natural parameters λ, avoiding the collapse of epistemic uncertainty that causes BayesBiNN and STE to fail catastrophically at 1000 tasks (Section 4.2).
On OpenLORIS-Object with frozen VGG19 features compressed to 1,024 dimensions, BiMU achieves 73.61% accuracy versus 72.01% for BayesBiNN (Section 4.3, table in Section 4.3).

In imbalanced active learning on the Animals dataset, variation-ratio-based querying reaches 84.46% accuracy using only 11% of labels, with a 41-point absolute accuracy improvement on low-frequency classes over random querying at the same budget (Section 4.4).

0wPUeZOZ9o.text: Transformers trained jointly on Classic Othello and DelFlank variants converge on a mostly shared board-state representation, evidenced by cosine similarity rising from about 0.67 raw to over 0.90 after Procrustes alignment (Section 5, Figure 2).

For the Classic-Iago pair (identical game logic, scrambled tokenization), cross-variant representation similarity rises from about 0.03 raw to 0.98 after alignment, far exceeding a random baseline of about 0.68 (Section 5, Figure 2).

Linear probes trained on one game variant can causally intervene on another variant's internal board-state representation with effectiveness nearly as strong as intervention with the matched, correctly-trained probe (Section 5, Figure 3).

Game-identity information is not linearly decodable above baseline in layers 1-4 but becomes decodable at about 90% accuracy in layers 5-8, indicating a layerwise transition from shared to game-specific processing (Section 5, Figure 5).

Steering interventions at early layers (1-2) on ambiguous DelFlank sequences produce a normalized improvement of about Δα≈0.75 at move 5 (declining to about 0.3 by move 30), while layer-5 steering shows almost no effect (Δα≈0), and layer-1 steering raises DelFlank probe accuracy from 67.1% to 77.4% (Section 5, Figure 6).

miVCnnDatA.text: Proposition 3.3 extends the uniform error bound to correlated (non-i.i.d.) sub-Gaussian noise, with Corollary 3.4 recovering the conditionally-independent sub-Gaussian case as a special case (Section 3.1, Proposition 3.3, Corollary 3.4)

Proposition 3.5 derives a uniform bound for heavy-tailed (sub-exponential) noise via a truncation argument, achieving a 71.6% success rate at the final iteration in the sub-exponential (chi-squared, sigma_m=0.1) numerical experiment (Section 3.2, Section 5.3, Proposition 3.5)

In the safe control experiment with nominal dynamics f_nom(x_t,u_t)=0.5x_t+u_t-1 and unknown residual f(x_t)=exp(-x_t^2)sin(10x_t), the proposed uniform bounds yield higher feasibility and lower cost than baseline uncertainty quantification methods (Section 5.2, Figures 5-6)

In the uncertainty-region-size experiment sweeping noise bound m_bar in {0.01, 0.1, 1} and input dimension n_x in {1,2,3} with confidence parameter delta=0.001 over up to 1000 data points, the proposed bounds are consistently tighter than the Abbasi-Yadkori baseline (Section 5.1, Figures 3-4)

diF53wYIj3.text: The Kalman-Wasserstein KL divergence is shown to remove the singularity that classical KL-regularized control exhibits as process noise vanishes in linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian process noise (Section 3, Section 4)

Section 4 applies the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL formulations to control synthesis, deriving closed-form or tractable control laws distinct from classical KL-regularized control (Section 4)

On the double integrator benchmark (a linear time-invariant system), the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL controllers maintain numerical stability and well-posedness as process noise approaches zero, where classical KL-regularized control becomes ill-posed (Section 5)

On the nonlinear cart-pole benchmark, the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL regularized controllers achieve better convergence and control quality than classical KL-based regularization (Section 5)

xAZHb0LUW1.text: Theorem 4.1 shows that observation-space robustness alone is insufficient for bounded posterior influence, while Theorem 4.2 establishes joint observation-state-space robustness guarantees for BR-iHMM (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2)
BR-iHMM balances adaptivity and robustness via two tunable parameters, the batch size B and the soft-threshold parameter c, in addition to an ESS threshold used for resampling (Section 4)
On synthetic regime-detection data, BR-iHMM achieves PPV of 0.963, TPR of 0.996, and a detection delay of 3.4 time steps (Section 5, Table 2, Table E.9)
Table E.6 reports runtime comparisons showing BR-iHMM's computational cost relative to competing online Bayesian iHMM methods (Table E.6)

hoLdhnkP0P.text: Additional gradient steps during test-time write scale memory capacity far more effectively than repeating forward writes, as shown by the capacity-vs-steps comparison in Figure 3 (Section 3, Figure 3)
GradMem is compared against Transformer, Mamba, ARMT, and RMT baselines on key-value retrieval accuracy across varying numbers of key-value pairs (Table 1)
GradMem is evaluated on bAbI (QA1-5), Short SQuAD, and language modeling tasks using exact match and cross-entropy metrics (Table 2)
Backward-pass memory overhead for 1024-token sequences is reduced from approximately 1000ms to approximately 600ms in the reported efficiency analysis (Section 3.5)

f1C38SmxkP.text: Residual representation encoding (Section 4.1) captures the deviation between a node's current interaction representation and its historical representation to produce anomaly-relevant signals (Section 4.1)
On real-anomaly datasets, the proposed framework (SDGAD) achieves 80.36% AUROC on Wikipedia and 73.25% AUROC on MOOC, outperforming baseline dynamic graph anomaly detectors (Table 1)
On synthetic-anomaly datasets (UCI, Enron, LastFM), SDGAD achieves approximately 99.87% AUROC, substantially outperforming baselines on F1 score as well (Table 2)

Representation restriction (Section 4.2) constrains normal-node embeddings within a hypersphere of radius r_max=0.4 with boundary tightness parameter gamma=0.9, while bi-boundary optimization (Section 4.3) enforces a margin of tau=0.1 between normal and anomalous decision boundaries (Section 4.2, Section 4.3)

Ablation studies removing residual representation encoding, representation restriction, or bi-boundary optimization each degrade AUROC/F1 performance relative to the full framework (Table 3, Section 5.3)

oUVzFuemEn.text: On ImageNet-64, iTARFlow-B achieves an FID of 1.68 with 770M parameters, improving over the TARFlow baseline's FID of 2.66 with 880M parameters (Table 3).
On ImageNet-128, iTARFlow-L achieves an FID of 2.44 with 1.2B parameters versus TARFlow's FID of 5.03 with 1.3B parameters (Table 4).
On ImageNet-256 pixel-space generation, iTARFlow-XL reaches an FID of 3.32 with 2.2B parameters, outperforming STARFlow's FID of 4.69 with 1.4B parameters (Table 5).

iTARFlow trains with a fully end-to-end, likelihood-based objective across multiple noise levels but performs a two-phase autoregressive-then-parallel iterative denoising procedure at sampling time (Section 3).

Ablations vary the number of denoising steps and the maximum noise level tmax (0.3 for 64px, 0.5 for 128px, 0.7 for 256px pixel-space) to characterize the trade-off underlying the 'noise dilemma' (Figure 4-5).
The paper analyzes two distinct types of sampling failure artifacts arising from the iterative denoising process (Figure 7).

IOUmfPYShr.text: Fusion training degrades cross-domain source-target alignment by 19-29% relative to independently trained encoders, and MER-DG restores 21-54% of this alignment (Table 1).

MER-DG yields an average ~4.8% improvement over standard fusion baselines and ~2% improvement over state-of-the-art domain generalization methods on the EPIC-Kitchens and HAC multimodal benchmarks (Table 3).
Fusion training degrades the standalone video encoder's target-domain accuracy from 59.46% to 56.53%, while MER-DG recovers it to 58.61% (Table 5).
MER-DG increases feature-space rank (RankMe score) for the video modality from 235.9 to 290.0 relative to standard fusion training (Figure 2).

MER-DG combines a Marginal-Entropy Loss enforcing a per-dimension variance floor (Equation 5) with a Spectral-Entropy Loss maximizing the log-determinant of the feature correlation matrix for decorrelation (Equation 6).

YFY4rGLJmW.text: Live-kBench-2512 curates 534 Linux kernel bugs collected from April 2024 to December 2025 via continuous curation from Syzbot (Section 4).
Agents achieve a 74% crash resolution rate on the first attempt (plausible patches), but only ~20% of generated patches are judged equivalent to the actual developer fix (Section 5).
There is a 25% performance gap in crash resolution rate for bugs before versus after the underlying LLM's knowledge cutoff (Table 1).
Three agent scaffolds (mini-SWE-agent, SWE-agent, OpenHands) achieve comparable crash resolution rates of 72-75% (Table 3).
Enabling crash-resolution feedback (CRF) improves crash resolution rate by 29 percentage points (Table 6).
Test-time scaling to Pass@10 raises crash resolution rate to 90% and equivalent-patch rate to 30% (Figure 3).

7sYtYeiJan.text: On MoisesDB retrieval at K=64, PHALAR achieves 70.87% accuracy versus 41.84% for the COCOLA baseline, a relative gain of about 69% (Table 1).
On Slakh2100 (K=64) and ChocoChorales (K=64) retrieval, PHALAR achieves 72.37% and 98.61% accuracy respectively, versus 55.84% and 89.34% for COCOLA (Table 1).
PHALAR uses only 2.3M parameters versus COCOLA's 5.2M (a 56% reduction) and trains in 50 GPU-hours versus COCOLA's 340 GPU-hours, a roughly 7x speedup (Table 1, Section 3).

PHALAR's similarity scores correlate more strongly with human coherence judgments than COCOLA, with Pearson rho of 0.387 versus a lower baseline correlation, significant per a Steiger test at p<=0.001 (Table 2).

The architecture uses a 10-layer axial-residual harmonic backbone over CQT spectrograms (Section 3.1), a learned spectral pooling stage via RFFT into 640-dimensional complex embeddings (Section 3.2), and a phase-equivariant complex-valued head with Complex RMSNorm and modReLU (Section 3.3, Equations 7-9).

Without rhythmic supervision, PHALAR attains zero-shot beat tracking F1 of 0.627 (Table 5) and 55.2% linear-probe chord recognition accuracy on GuitarSet, outperforming a Chroma CQT baseline (Table 6).

lwHSE1xYHH.text: TQL identifies that attention scores in transformer-based Q-functions collapse as model capacity increases, causing training instability and degraded performance when naively scaling transformers for value functions (abstract only).
TQL prevents this attention collapse by explicitly regulating the entropy of attention score distributions during training (abstract only).
TQL yields up to a 43% improvement in performance when scaling from the smallest to the largest network sizes tested, in contrast to prior approaches that degrade with scale (abstract only).
The proposed entropy-control mechanism is evaluated as a method for stabilizing training of larger transformer architectures used as Q-functions in reinforcement learning (abstract only).

VFpMpVXDJS.text: Algorithm 5, the main trust-region-type algorithm, finds an ε-stationary point using Õ(ΔL₂n²/ε^1.5) comparison oracle queries with 2/3 success probability (Theorem 1, Section 6).
A quantum variant of the algorithm finds an ε-stationary point using Õ(ΔL₂n/ε^1.5) quantum comparison oracle queries (Theorem 2).
Algorithm 2, ComparisonHE, estimates the normalized Hessian to accuracy δ using Õ(n² log(1/δ)) comparison queries by solving triangles formed from column-vector directions (Section 4, Theorem 6).
Algorithm 1, ComparisonHessVec, estimates Hessian-vector product directions using Õ(n log(1/(γ_x γ_y² δ²))) comparison queries via gradient-direction estimation at perturbed points (Section 3).
Algorithm 4, ComparisonRatio, estimates the ratio ‖H‖/‖∇f‖ using Õ(n² log(1/δ_κ)) comparison queries via a second-order Taylor expansion analysis (Section 5, Theorem 7).

IkjsHRpuYY.text: Capability boundaries are estimated via smoothed pinball-loss quantile regression at quantile τ=0.98 with smoothing parameter κ=50 and regularization λ=10⁻³ (Section 2.1).

Post-training capability boundaries are modeled as sigmoid functions of log10(FLOPs), q_τ^sig(z;θ)=y0+L·σ(a+βz), achieving in-distribution pinball loss of 4.08×10⁻³ versus 4.00×10⁻³ for a more flexible I-spline estimator, while generalizing better out-of-distribution (4.93×10⁻³ vs 4.92×10⁻³) (Section 3.1.1, Table 2).
At 10²⁴ FLOPs, the estimated 0.98-quantile boundary reaches 0.539 accuracy on MATH Level 5 versus 0.563 on MMLU-Pro, 0.700 on BBH, 0.828 on IFEval, 0.535 on MUSR, and 0.424 on GPQA (Table 1).

Unlike the stable boundaries for BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MUSR, the MATH Level 5 and IFEval capability boundaries are non-stationary over time, with later-period models exceeding earlier predicted boundaries (Figure 2).
A balanced I-optimal sampling design recovers near-full-data capability frontiers using roughly 20% of the evaluation budget, with GPQA and MUSR requiring as little as 5% (Section 4, Figure 5).

A cross-benchmark shift test applied to AIME-2025 scores finds a positive but not statistically significant shift (p=0.15), giving no clear aggregate evidence of post-release contamination inflating math benchmark scores (Section 5.2.2, Equation 3).

7hg1iTd34D.text: The ground-truth inverse dynamics model h*(a|s,s') is often less complex than the expert policy π*(a|s), enabling IDM-based learning with smaller hypothesis classes without introducing bias (Section 4.1).

The ground-truth IDM exhibits lower entropy than the expert policy, with H(a|s,s') ≤ H(a|s) frequently holding strictly, making IDM training targets less stochastic than expert-policy targets (Section 4.2).

VM-IDM and IDM-labeling approaches are proven to converge to the same IDM-based policy under infinite unlabeled data and sufficient model capacity, establishing both as consistent estimators of the expert policy π* (Section 3).

The proposed LAPO+ algorithm modifies LAPO by decoding the latent IDM directly instead of behavior-cloning a policy in stage 2, then applying IDM labeling with the decoded IDM in stage 3 (Section 5.1).

On 16 ProcGen environments, IDM labeling outperforms behavior cloning by orders of magnitude in 9 of the 16 environments, and LAPO+ consistently surpasses LAPO in low-data regimes (Section 5.1, Figure 4).
On manipulation tasks, IDM-based policies show an especially large margin over behavior cloning on Push-T, while IDM labeling trails VM-IDM by a small margin on Libero10 (Figure 6).

SayI5V4CBC.text: PACS samples multiple commonsense belief vectors and uses an LLM together with a formal solver to generate proofs as observations, aggregating conclusions across samples via Monte Carlo estimation (Section 4.3).

PACS applies an early-stopping procedure based on the chain rule that halts belief-vector sampling once logical consistency already determines a query's truth value, reducing computational cost while preserving distributional properties (Section 4.2, Equations 4-8).
A greedy score-minimization heuristic (Equation 12) prioritizes reasoning steps that most reduce the count of logical models consistent with current constraints (Section 4.6).
On FOLIO, PACS achieves 82-88% accuracy versus 78% for the best baseline ARGOS, and on QUAIL achieves 80-84% versus 74% for If-Beam (Table 1).
PACS halves the rate of problems lacking any correct reasoning path compared to If-Beam on FOLIO (3% vs 16%) (Table 2).
With Llama 3 8B, PACS matches the performance of 120B-parameter thinking models on FOLIO and QUAIL, while producing shorter reasoning chains than If-Beam (4.6 vs 6.7 steps on FOLIO) (Tables 3-4).

1JG0y5cOmK.text: A gradient testing algorithm determines whether the normalized gradient of a smooth function is ε-close or 2ε-far from a given unit vector using O(1) queries to a comparison oracle (abstract only).
A gradient estimation algorithm produces an ε-accurate estimate of the normalized gradient using O(n log(1/ε)) comparison queries, which is proven to be optimal (abstract only).
A quantum variant using a quantum comparison oracle with superposition achieves gradient estimation in O(log(n/ε)) queries (abstract only).
The comparison-oracle model is used to characterize gradient properties of smooth functions without direct access to function values, relying only on pairwise comparative information (abstract only).

gTbSqYqumM.text: Search-based planning can degrade performance relative to model-free baselines even when the learned dynamics model is highly accurate, contradicting the conventional assumption that more search helps (Section 4.1).

Distribution shift between the learned model's rollout states and the true environment's state distribution is identified as the primary driver of search-induced performance degradation, more so than model or value-function inaccuracy (Section 4.2).

Experiments across Atari, MinAtar, DeepMind Control Suite, and Sokoban benchmark domains show search-augmented agents underperforming non-search baselines under certain conditions (Table 3, Figure 4).
Mitigating distribution shift, rather than solely improving model or value-function accuracy, yields state-of-the-art performance across these benchmark domains (Section 4.3).

dfVm5yZZ6G.text: ECO removes the full-precision master weight buffer by injecting quantization error into the optimizer's momentum term, forming an error-feedback loop that adds no extra memory (Section 3).

Under standard smoothness and noise assumptions, ECO is proven to converge to a constant-radius neighborhood of the optimum with decaying learning rate, with an asymptotic noise floor only a 1/(1-β²) factor larger than training with master weights (Theorem 3.8).
A quadratic-objective analysis shows that naively removing master weights makes the loss floor diverge as the learning rate shrinks, whereas ECO's floor remains bounded at L²σ²/(1-β²) (Section 3.4).

Across 30M-800M parameter Transformers and Gemma-3 1B trained with FP8 quantization, ECO with stochastic rounding nearly matches BF16-with-master-weights accuracy, e.g., 2.5399 vs 2.5306 loss at 800M parameters (Table 1).

On a Sparse MoE model trained with INT4 quantization, ECO prevents divergence and matches master-weight zero-shot benchmark performance while reducing peak memory from 12 to 9 bytes per parameter, a ~25% reduction (Section 4.2).

6NDxn4R4JT.text: ViTL's span-conditioned two-stage framework (localization followed by span-aware answering) achieves up to an 8.6% accuracy improvement while using 50% fewer input frames on long-video QA benchmarks (Table 3).
On LVBench, ViTL reaches 47.4% accuracy using 128 frames, exceeding a 45.3%-accuracy baseline that uses 256 frames (Table 3).

Span-aware token reallocation under a fixed token budget consistently outperforms uniform frame/token sampling on temporal grounding benchmarks including Charades-STA and ActivityNet-Captions (Tables 4-5).

Ablations show frame-level timestamp injection contributes +1.8% on LVBench, and the full ViTL pipeline with coupled IoU/answer-correctness rewards via GRPO contributes +3.7% over a single-stage baseline (Table 6).
The introduced VGrounding-QA dataset pairs each question with ground-truth time spans derived from event knowledge graphs, supporting multi-span and same-video-distractor evaluation (Table 2).

SiCjKmArjQ.text: Applying DP-SGD directly to LoRA's (A,B) factorization is gauge-dependent: rescaling A→AR, B→BR^{-T} leaves the update Z=AB^T unchanged but causes the DP clipping norm to vary arbitrarily with the gauge parameter c (Equation 4).

Independent noise added separately to A and B under naive DP-LoRA creates bilinear cross-noise terms of order η²ξ_Aξ_B^T scaling as mnrτ⁴, which cannot arise from any purely additive privacy mechanism (Proposition 2.2, Equation 7).

PRISM projects per-example gradients onto the rank-r tangent space of the low-rank manifold and injects noise there, yielding a closed-form intrinsic noise energy (σC/b)√(r(m+n-r)) that depends only on rank/dimension geometry, not on the factorization (Theorem 3.1).
PRISM's randomized update is proven gauge-invariant in distribution under any GL(r) reparameterization of the LoRA factors (Theorem 3.3).

On GLUE8 and Math-10K benchmarks, PRISM attains higher average accuracy than LoRA+ and AdamW baselines at both ε=6 (0.690 vs 0.674 vs 0.641) and ε=3 (0.680 vs 0.665 vs 0.634), winning 8/12 and 7/12 tasks respectively (Table 2).
Scaled to Gemma-2-9B, PRISM achieves 0.7019 average accuracy versus 0.6779 for AdamW, with roughly 2x per-step compute overhead and negligible extra memory (Table 3, Table 5).

3vhn9kVVY5.text: The SzCORE 2025 seizure detection challenge evaluated 28 algorithms from 19 teams on a held-out private dataset of 4,360 hours of continuous EEG from 65 patients containing 398 annotated seizures (Table 1).
The top-ranked algorithm achieved an event-based F1 score of 32%, with sensitivity 37% and precision 29%, on this independent test set (Abstract, Table 1).
Nearly all submitted algorithms' self-reported F1 scores substantially overestimate the F1 scores measured under the challenge's independent evaluation (Figure 4).

Despite comparable aggregate F1 rankings, algorithms show notable discordance between peak performance and population-level stability across the 65 patients, indicating inconsistent per-subject generalization (Section 7).

z2vVeIscEd.text: ORBIT raises the HealthBench-Hard score of Qwen3-4B-Instruct from a 7.0 baseline to 20.3 using rubric-based incremental training (Section 4, HealthBench-Hard results).
The SFT-4B-ORBIT variant reaches a HealthBench-Hard score of 27.2, surpassing larger models including Qwen3-30B-Thinking (16.1) and GPT-4.1 (13.2) (Section 4).
The rubric-generation ablation shows ORBIT-DeepSeek-R1 achieving a score of 20.2 when judged by the GPT-OSS-120B evaluator (Table 2).
Comparing SFT+RL against zero-RL shows SFT-4B-ORBIT with learning rate 1e-7 reaching 25.2 versus 20.2 for the instruction-only baseline (Table 3).
Pass@k-based sample filtering (retaining samples with pass rate in the 0-0.75 range) reduces training data from 2,082 to 1,403 samples while maintaining a score of about 19.9 (Table 4).
Training data is derived from only about 2k samples sourced from the IMCS21, CHIP-MDCFNPC, and MedDG medical dialogue benchmarks (Section 3).

kD8iJmyn5l.text: Theorem 3.1 (Cauchy Factorization) shows that any graph's GFT basis can be exactly factorized into a sequence of localized transformations combined via Cauchy matrices (Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 establishes that this factorization achieves O(kn^2) complexity, where k is the interface size, compared to O(n^3) for a standard eigendecomposition (Theorem 3.2).
L2G-Net attains 92.12% accuracy on Roman-Empire, 53.41% on Amazon-Ratings, 97.50% on Minesweeper, and 85.57% on Tolokers, competitive with state-of-the-art methods like Polynormer (Table 1).
On Minesweeper, the Cauchy-factorization approach runs in 32.21s versus 92.34s for full eigendecomposition; on Tolokers, 91.33s versus 117.57s (Table 2).
L2G-Net matches Polynormer's performance using orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters (Figure 4).

oZqOS1N6Ag.text: Q-Flow uses flow-consistent value functions to propagate terminal trajectory value to intermediate latent states without backpropagating through the ODE solver (Section 4.1, Eq. 7).
On the OGBench standard setting, Q-Flow achieves an average score of 54.4, outperforming FQL's 43.8 by 10.6 percentage points (Table 1).
On antmaze-giant, Q-Flow scores 40 versus FQL's 9, and on humanoidmaze-medium, Q-Flow scores 83 versus FQL's 58 (Table 1).
On the OGBench advanced setting, Q-Flow achieves an average score of 47.5 versus QAM-E's 44.8 (Table 2).
An ablation shows intermediate value-gradient policy optimization outperforms backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) alternatives (Figure 7a).
Q-Flow trains approximately 2x faster than FBRAC at 50 flow steps while maintaining stable optimization (Figure 9).

EyxlSrJWT5.text: Theorem 3.3 proves that predictive reward prevents degenerate bisimulation metrics by bounding the expected diameter of sparse-reward regions (Theorem 3.3, Eq. 9).
