Theorem 3.4 establishes that the value difference between two states is upper-bounded by their predictive bisimulation distance (Theorem 3.4, Eq. 11).

The intrinsic exploration bonus is defined as a potential-based difference of predictive bisimulation distances to the goal across consecutive states, and Theorem 3.5 shows this preserves the optimal policy of the original MDP (Section 3.3, Eq. 14; Theorem 3.5).
On MetaWorld, TEB reaches an 87.9% success rate on the stick-pull task and a 98.4% success rate on the push-back task, outperforming baseline methods (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
On Maze2D, TEB achieves coverage of 0.87 +/- 0.07 on square_a and 0.85 +/- 0.07 on square_b, versus the CeSD baseline's 0.71 +/- 0.05 and 0.66 +/- 0.05 respectively (Section 4.3, Table 1).

fiYjuwsbFE.text: Theorem 3.1 gives the first convergence guarantee for AdaGrad under heavy-tailed noise with tail index p in (4/3, 2], showing a convergence rate of tilde-O(1/T^((3p-4)/(4p))) (Theorem 3.1).
This convergence rate is achieved without prior knowledge of the tail index p or the noise level, with AdaGrad adapting automatically to both (Theorem 3.1).

Theorem 3.3 provides an algorithm-dependent lower bound for the one-dimensional case of AdaGrad, implying the minimax-optimal rate for heavy-tailed stochastic optimization is not attainable by AdaGrad (Theorem 3.3).
Theorem 4.2 shows that a normalized AdaGrad-Norm variant achieves a faster rate of O(1/T^((p-1)/(2p))) under a bounded-objective assumption, valid for all p in (1, 2] (Theorem 4.2).
The authors identify the regime p in (1, 4/3] as unresolved and a primary limitation of their analysis (Section 5, Limitations).

07wwDFdi3k.text: LSFlow improves average reward over the strongest baseline SRL by 20.6% across four combinatorial RL tasks (Dynamic Scheduling, Dynamic Routing, Dynamic Assignment, Dynamic Intervention) (Section 5.1, Table 1).
LSFlow attains the highest average reward of 27.62 versus 22.91 for SRL and 22.21 for SEQUOIA on the four benchmark tasks (Table 1).
Feasibility is guaranteed by construction via a solver-induced mapping a*(s,c) = argmin_{a in A(s)} c^T a from sampled cost vectors on the unit sphere to combinatorial actions (Section 3.1).

A von Mises-Fisher kernel-smoothed Bellman operator is proven to admit a unique fixed point and yield a C^infinity smooth value function, addressing the piecewise-constant, discontinuous value landscape induced by the solver mapping (Theorem 3.5, Section 3.3).

The cost-space critic formulation avoids repeated solver calls during training and is reported to be about 360x faster per update step than an action-space critic (6 minutes vs under 1 second) (Section 5.3, Figure 4).
LSFlow trains in 1.29 hours on average versus 9.11 hours for SEQUOIA and 3.89 hours for SRL, making it roughly 3x faster than SRL and 7x faster than SEQUOIA (Table 1).

gmAT5E9dCE.text: RAMAC (RADAC diffusion variant) jointly optimizes a behavior-cloning loss and a CVaR-based risk loss for the generative actor, L_pi(theta) = L_BC(theta) + eta * L_Risk(theta), combining a diffusion/flow-matching actor with an Implicit Quantile Network distributional critic (Section on method / Eq. for L_pi).
On Stochastic-D4RL HalfCheetah-medium-replay, RADAC achieves a CVaR_0.1 of 278.65 +/- 151.27 versus -34.09 +/- 25.47 for ORAAC (Table 1).

Proposition 1 bounds the per-state out-of-distribution action probability under the actor by delta_s(pi_theta) <= 1 - exp{-D_KL(beta || pi_theta)}, formally linking behavior-cloning-induced KL regularization to OOD suppression (Proposition 1).
Empirically, RADAC maintains 0.75-2.04% out-of-distribution action rates across tasks compared to 2.68-10.84% for ORAAC, corroborating the theoretical OOD bound (Table 2).
An ablation over risk-distortion measures (CVaR, Wang, CPW) shows CVaR gives the most reliable lower-tail risk control with comparable mean return on HalfCheetah and Walker2d (Table 5).

4ohxGjPD5Z.text: SuperMeshNet reaches lower RMSE than a fully supervised model trained on 200 high-resolution samples while using only 20 high-resolution samples, a 90% reduction in HR data (Dataset 1, N_h=20, N=200 results).

On Dataset 1, SuperMeshNet with MeshGraphNet backbone attains RMSE 0.0226, below the fully supervised baseline's 0.0269, and with GCN backbone attains 0.0431 versus 0.0613 for the supervised-only variant (SuperMeshNet-O).

The complementary learning framework jointly trains a primary model F_theta mapping LR to HR solutions and an auxiliary model G_phi predicting differences between two HR solutions from paired LR inputs, exploiting abundant unpaired LR data alongside a small paired HR set.

Node-level and message-level centering operations are introduced as inductive biases and are evaluated across six message-passing neural network architectures: GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, Graph Transformer, GIN, and MeshGraphNet.
SuperMeshNet outperforms semi-supervised regression baselines UCVME (RMSE 0.0293, 1122.62s) and Mean-Teacher (RMSE 0.0325, 693.84s), achieving RMSE 0.0226 in 421 seconds on Dataset 1.
On a motorbike geometry drag-coefficient prediction task, SuperMeshNet trained with 40 HR samples outperforms a fully supervised baseline trained with 200 HR samples.

nNBMlUWEKi.text: Under a Poincare inequality with spectral gap lambda >= 0.99, the MCMC-based covariance estimator satisfies the additive error bound |Sigma_bar - Sigma| <= eps*Sigma + delta*I_d using N ~ (tr(Sigma) + C_PI(pi))/(eps*delta) * log^2(d) samples (Theorem 8).
For the multiplicative-error regime ||Sigma_bar - Sigma|| <= eps*||Sigma||, the sample complexity is roughly a factor of d/eps^2 larger than in the additive case (Theorem 9).
A spectral-form guarantee for an isotropically-transformed distribution nu achieves |Sigma_bar - Sigma| <= eps*Sigma with N ~ (d + C_PI(nu))/eps^2 * log^2(d) samples (Corollary 10).

For isotropic rounding via uniform sampling from a convex body, the MCMC approach attains covariance estimation using O~(d^3) oracle queries, compared to roughly d^4 queries required with i.i.d. sampling.

For unconstrained log-concave sampling with condition number kappa = beta/alpha, the MCMC query complexity is O~(kappa*d^{3/2}/eps^2), improving on the O(kappa*d^{5/2}/eps^2) bound for i.i.d. sampling.

IelAHU5MVz.text: The Gluon framework unifies layer-wise LMO-based optimizers, recovering Muon (spectral norm), unScion (mixed norms for transformer blocks and embeddings), layer-wise normalized GD, and layer-wise signGD as special cases via Algorithm 1 (Algorithm 1, Section on special cases).

Under a layer-wise generalized (L^0_i, L^1_i)-smoothness condition, ||grad_i f(X) - grad_i f(Y)||_* <= (L^0_i + L^1_i ||grad_i f(X)||_*) ||X_i - Y_i||, Gluon with adaptive per-layer stepsize t_i^k = ||grad_i f(X^k)||_* / (L^0_i + L^1_i ||grad_i f(X^k)||_*) achieves O(1/K^{1/2}) convergence in the deterministic setting (Section 4.2).
In the stochastic setting with non-Euclidean bounded variance, Gluon achieves a convergence rate of O(Delta^0/K^{1/4} + 1/K^{1/4} * sum_i [sigma/L^1_i + L^0_i/(L^1_i)^2]) (Theorem 1).

Empirical estimation of layer-wise smoothness constants on a 124M-parameter NanoGPT model trained on FineWeb finds L^0_i approximately 0 across layers, with L^1_i approximately 70 for transformer blocks (predicted stepsize 0.014 vs. tuned 0.018) and L^1_i approximately 1.3 for embedding/output layers (predicted stepsize 0.77 vs. tuned 1.08).

On a CNN trained on CIFAR-10, estimated smoothness constants also satisfy L^0_i approximately 0, with a two-orders-of-magnitude spread in L^1_i across layers, motivating per-layer learning-rate heterogeneity.

The zeroth-order eNTK approximation error is shown to depend on the model's output dimension rather than the (potentially massive) parameter dimension, in contrast to prior analyses that scale with parameter count.

0vTONq9Z8j.text: StepCodeReasoner's 7B model scores 91.1% on CRUXEval and 86.5% on LiveCodeBench, versus CodeReasoner-7B's 86.0%/77.7% and GPT-4o's 85.6%/75.1% (Section 4, main results table).
On the REval execution-trace benchmark, StepCodeReasoner reaches 82.9% overall accuracy, beating CodeReasoner-7B (72.3%), a 14B CodeReasoner variant (81.1%), and GPT-4o (77.3%) (Section 4).

Table 6 shows StepCodeReasoner narrows the gap between step-level and final-answer accuracy to 10.9 points (80.7% vs 91.6%), compared to a 22.1-point gap for CodeReasoner-7B (63.5% vs 85.6%), evidencing reduced reward hacking (Table 6).

Ablations show stepwise (Bi-Level GRPO) rewards improve average accuracy from 77.7% (SFT + terminal-only RL) to 83.5% without task decoupling, and to 85.8% with the full method including decoupling (Section 4, ablation study).

Without any execution-trace instrumentation at inference time, StepCodeReasoner still attains 84.8% on CRUXEval and 77.0% on LiveCodeBench, surpassing most baselines (Section 4, generalization analysis).

On standard code generation transfer tasks, StepCodeReasoner improves over CodeReasoner-7B by +2.9 points on HumanEval (to 90.1%), +3.2 points on MBPP (to 85.0%), and +9.0 points on LiveCodeBench v5 (to 19.4%) (Section 4, code generation transfer).

OY7Qe2ZSx9.text: On the 16×16 Ising model at low temperature (β=0.6), MetaDNS reduces Jensen-Shannon divergence in the spin-concentration distribution to 4.6×10⁻² versus 2.2×10⁻¹ for MDNS, roughly a 5× improvement (Section on Ising Model experiments).
MetaDNS recovers the full bimodal spin distribution on the Ising benchmark where the MDNS baseline collapses to a single mode (Section on Ising Model experiments, mode collapse comparison).

On the q=3 Potts model (16×16), MetaDNS discovers all three ordered phases and matches the free-energy profile of MCMC-based well-tempered metadynamics (WT-MetaD) while requiring 2× fewer bias-deposition steps, whereas MDNS collapses to a single mode (Section on Potts Model experiments).

On a 4×4×4 Cu-Au binary alloy supercell at 500K, MetaDNS achieves lower JS divergence (7.9×10⁻² vs 1.3×10⁻¹ for MDNS) and correctly captures both the Cu₃Au and CuAu ordered phases, which MDNS fails to recover (Section on Cu-Au Alloy experiments).

MetaDNS provides more than 40× inference speedup over MCMC-based WT-MetaD on the Cu-Au alloy benchmark while preserving asymptotically exact sampling via importance reweighting (Section on Cu-Au Alloy experiments).

0BVhmHnYb7.text: Introspection adapters (LoRA-based) trained on Llama-3.3-70B models with implanted behaviors across eight categories (e.g., backdoors, quirks, harmful roleplay) achieve a 59% success rate on AuditBench for identifying hidden concerning behaviors, versus 53% for the next-best prior auditing method (AuditBench results section).
Verbalization accuracy of the trained introspection adapters scales with model size, rising from 37.7% at 0.6B parameters to 77.3% at 14B parameters (Scaling experiments section).
Increasing training-data diversity improves in-distribution verbalization performance from 20.5% to 64.4% (Training diversity ablation section).

On out-of-distribution generalization tests, introspection adapters detect 7 of 9 covert malicious fine-tuning attacks and identify 16 of 52 behaviors in a reward-model sycophancy audit, without being trained on these specific behaviors (Out-of-distribution generalization section).
A DPO refinement stage is applied after joint LoRA adapter training specifically to suppress hallucinated behavior reports in favor of accurate ones (Methodology, DPO refinement stage).

nAfV9H2Z1u.text: Value Aggregation (VA) with LLaMA-2 achieves an average MTEB score of 52.25 across 14 datasets using a training-free, prompt-free method that pools attention value vectors across layers and tokens (Table 1, MTEB results).

AlignedWVA applied to Qwen-3 reaches an average MTEB score of 56.84, exceeding MetaEOL by approximately 4 points while MetaEOL requires 8 forward passes per example versus a single pass for AlignedWVA (Table 1, MTEB results).
On the SciFact retrieval task, VA exceeds MetaEOL by approximately 10 points (Table 1, retrieval task results).

Layer-wise analysis shows VA's representation quality increases monotonically with network depth, while hidden-state-based representations peak in early layers and then decline (Figure 3, layer-wise analysis).

Finetune-VA matches the performance of fine-tuned mean-pooled hidden states while using only one-quarter of the trainable parameters, by restricting fine-tuning to attention modules (Fine-tuning results section).

d9LsOCOB9z.text: Proposition 3.2 proves that a single Voronoi-gated node breaks tractability of probabilistic circuits even with fully factorized experts, because oblique Voronoi cell boundaries prevent the partition-function integral from factorizing (Proposition 3.2).

Theorem 3.5 shows that when Voronoi gating regions are geometrically aligned with the circuit's variable partition (Hierarchical Factorized Voronoi, or HFV, construction), the partition function decomposes and exact tractable inference is restored, with Theorem 3.14 giving inference time O(|C|K^m) for m-way factorizations with K cells per factor (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.14).

For the non-factorized Voronoi-gated PCs, Algorithm 1 provides an anytime refinement procedure yielding certified lower and upper bounds on partition functions, marginals, and conditionals that tighten monotonically at a rate of O(2^{-t/d}) after t refinement steps (Algorithm 1, Theorem 3.9).
Theorem 3.16 proves exponential convergence of the soft-to-hard Voronoi gate during temperature annealing: 1 minus the max soft gate weight is bounded by (K-1)exp(-alpha*gamma(u)) (Theorem 3.16).

On eight synthetic 2D/3D benchmarks (including CheckerBoard, Pinwheel, Spiral, and TwistedEight) compared against EinsumNet and HCLT baselines, VT-gated circuits attain certified lower bounds that often exceed baseline exact log-likelihoods, while HFV circuits match baseline performance with exact tractability preserved (Figure 1, experimental comparison).

o3JP1sHHSY.text: Theorem 3.2 gives a PAC-Bayesian bound showing the expected ranking loss of the learned confidence estimator is bounded by the empirical margin loss plus a margin-dependent complexity term (Theorem 3.2).

Corollary 3.4 derives an explicit generalization bound in which the misranking probability depends on the empirical margin-based ranking loss and a complexity term that is inversely proportional to the margin γ, formalizing a trade-off between separation strength and generalization (Corollary 3.4).
The adaptive margin training procedure jointly minimizes empirical ranking loss and a margin complexity term over both model parameters θ and margin γ (Section 3).
Table 1 reports 15-35% reductions in ranking loss and 3-8 percentage point improvements in AUROC over heuristic confidence baselines across multiple judge models and datasets (Table 1).
Table 2 shows the method achieves higher success rates for human-agreement guarantees than baselines, e.g., 94.8% vs. 90.8% on AlpacaEval (Table 2).
Figure 3 shows the method reduces monotonicity violations between confidence and disagreement risk compared to heuristic baselines while maintaining competitive coverage rates (Figure 3).

B5RiXueKqb.text: Theorem 2.1 establishes that optimal action-conditional conformal prediction sets induce feasible risk-averse policies satisfying action-specific constraints (Theorem 2.1).

Theorem 3.2 (Strong Duality) characterizes the optimal action-conditional prediction sets via a dual formulation using action-specific parameter vectors, enabling tractable optimization despite non-convexity (Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 4.3 (Finite-Sample Validity) proves the AC-RAC algorithm achieves conditional coverage ℙ(y_test ∈ C_final(x_test) | a_RAC,final(x_test)=a) ≥ 1-α with a gap to the target level that decays at rate O(1/n) (Theorem 4.3).

On the COVID-19 radiography experiment at α=0.05, AC-RAC achieves valid action-conditional coverage across all actions while RAC and score-based baselines systematically over- or under-cover, and AC-RAC's mean prediction set size increases by only 3.7% relative to RAC (Section 5, medical diagnosis experiment).

On the recommendation system experiment, AC-RAC is the only method that achieves calibrated action-conditional coverage while yielding substantially fewer critical recommendation errors than baselines, at comparable worst-case utility to the marginal baseline (Section 5, recommendation systems experiment).

x1OLusJLNe.text: VeriEnv uses GPT-5.2 as a coding agent to clone real websites into fully executable, verifiable synthetic environments, averaging 83.5 minutes and $3.60 per site (Section on Website Cloning).

The framework constructs 149 synthetic websites comprising 7,400 total tasks split 40.2% easy, 39.2% medium, and 20.6% hard, each paired with a programmatic validation function for deterministic reward (Section on Verifiable Task Generation).
Cloned environments achieve 90% functional correctness, 90% task executability, 76% judge correctness, and a 4.7/5 visual quality rating (Quality Metrics results).

Agents trained via self-evolving training on VeriEnv improve WebArena success rate by +6.06 points for Qwen3-4B and +9.09 points for LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct relative to baseline training (Cross-Domain Performance, WebArena results).
On Mind2Web-Online, training on VeriEnv improves performance by +7.27 points for Qwen3-4B and +13.19 points for LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct (Cross-Domain Performance, Mind2Web-Online results).
Agent performance improves consistently as the diversity of training environments increases, supporting environment-centric scaling over training on fixed real-website datasets (Key Finding section).

fufl3hBXMq.text: Contextual curvature, a geometric measure of how sharply the representational trajectory bends over recent context, is correlated with next-token entropy in both GPT-2 XL and Pythia-2.8B, and this relationship emerges over the course of training (Section 3, Results).

Trajectory-aligned perturbation interventions reliably modulate next-token entropy, whereas geometrically misaligned perturbations of the same magnitude have no effect on entropy, providing causal evidence for the curvature-entropy link (Section 3, perturbation experiments).

Regularizing model representations to be straighter during training modestly reduces token-level entropy without degrading validation loss (Section 3/Section 4, straightness regularization experiment).

The paper defines representational measures including contextual curvature and reports them across models in Table 1, situating the geometric analysis within the temporal straightening framework of autoregressive next-token prediction (Section 2, Table 1).
Appendix A reports supplementary perturbation effects and additional representational measures across model scales, corroborating the main curvature-entropy findings (Appendix A, Figures A1-A6).

7hGdaMG8kY.text: Path reuse, occurring during underfitting, causes models to rely on globally memorized graph edges rather than the given contextual path, producing context-independent reasoning hallucinations (Section on Path Reuse, Intrinsic Reasoning).

Path compression, emerging later during overfitting, causes frequent multi-step paths to collapse into shortcuts that bypass intermediate nodes to reach high-degree targets (Section on Path Compression, Extrinsic Reasoning).

On stochastic block model (SBM) graphs with 100 communities and p_in=0.1, path-following accuracy drops from 0.952 at epoch 1 to 0.851 at epoch 49, while a 10-community, p_in=0.6 configuration remains stable near 0.997-0.999 across the same epochs, showing denser inter-community connectivity worsens path compression (Experimental Results table).

The path reuse/compression framework is used to explain the Reversal Curse as a directional bias arising from compression of cycle paths, and reasoning distribution bias as non-uniform supervision across nodes of varying degree (Related Phenomena section).

PPO fine-tuning recovers roughly 0.3 accuracy on the affected reasoning task, exceeding the roughly 0.2 recovery achieved by SFT, and shows superior stability under distribution shift (Recovery Analysis section).

WrXyXq11Yc.text: DOT-MoE formulates dense-to-MoE conversion (MoEfication) as a differentiable optimal transport problem, using Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations with entropic regularization for neuron-to-expert assignment (Section 3.2).
On WikiText-2 and HellaSwag at a 50% parameter budget, DOT-MoE attains 7.99 perplexity and 53.9% accuracy, outperforming the DISP-LLM structured-pruning baseline (9.84 perplexity) (Table 1).

After fine-tuning with 1.2B tokens, DOT-MoE reaches 66.6% average accuracy on LLaMA-2-7B versus 51.7% for the CMoE dense-to-MoE baseline, with similar gains on LLaMA-3-8B (67.8% vs. 64.7%) and Qwen2.5-7B (67.2% vs. 64.1%) (Table 2).
On zero-shot benchmarks, DOT-MoE achieves 61.5% (LLaMA-2-7B), 59.8% (LLaMA-3-8B), and 63.3% (Qwen2.5-7B), exceeding CMoE (44.5%, 41.8%) and DISP-LLM (55.6%) respectively (Table 3).
An ablation shows expert-granularity gains saturate beyond E=148 experts, while training at 75% sparsity generalizes better across different inference-time sparsity levels (Figure 1a-b).
DOT-MoE exhibits lower training loss and better generalization curves than CMoE and LLaMA-MoE-v2 during dense-to-MoE conversion (Figure 2).

e7EKA7Y9Im.text: Flow-matching Q-function critics achieve roughly 2x higher final return and about 5x improvement in sample efficiency over monolithic critics in high update-to-data (UTD) regimes (Section 7, Figure 7).

Test-Time Recovery (TTR) is formalized as an error-dampening property of iterative flow integration (Definition 5.1), with Theorem D.4 proving the stability factor decays as beta_K proportional to K^(-c') with more integration steps K (Section 5, Appendix D).

Flow-matching critics tolerate staleness introduced in early integration steps better than monolithic critics, and maintain performance under noisy TD targets where monolithic critics degrade (Table 2, Figure 2, Section 5.2).

Theorem 6.1 shows flow critics can adapt to distributional shift by adjusting gain parameters while keeping feature directions frozen, and freezing layers causes monolithic critics to collapse while flow critics recover (Theorem 6.1, Figure 4, Section 6).

On OGBench tasks, expected-value (non-distributional) flow-matching backups outperform distributional RL variants, indicating the gains are not explained by distributional value learning (Table 1, Section 4).

zouCZ6s5Zj.text: Giving LLM scheduling agents oracle access to full structural information (level L3) yields a worse relative makespan gap (1.66%) than giving them concise statistical summaries (level L2, 0.65% gap), demonstrating an observability paradox (Section 7.2).

L2 chain-of-thought agents show better tail stability (2.01% p95 relative makespan gap) than L3 chain-of-thought agents (2.92%), indicating LLMs struggle to distill useful signal from high-dimensional structural priors (Table 4).

The best LLM agent (Qwen3-8B, 1.01% relative makespan gap) is statistically indistinguishable from the best hand-crafted priority dispatching rule (LIFO+LIT, 1.11% gap), with a paired difference of -0.099 percentage points (95% CI [-0.531, 0.389]) (Table 5, Table 6).

Tool-augmented agents at reasoning level L1 consume 12.614 million tokens for 2.0% relative performance, versus 4.016 million tokens for 1.9% performance with chain-of-thought alone, a roughly three-fold token cost increase for worse results (Table 3).

SM1KZV8lLP.text: DADP introduces Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction, using a temporal offset Delta t to break temporal correlation between context and the current step so that only static domain information (not transient dynamics) is preserved in the learned representation (Section 4.1).
DADP introduces Domain-Aware Diffusion Injection, which biases the diffusion prior distribution and reformulates the diffusion target using the learned domain representation (Section 4.2).

On out-of-distribution Walker2d, DADP attains a return of 3015±207 versus 889±579 for the Meta-DT baseline, and on in-distribution HalfCheetah reaches 4100±85 versus the expert score of 4575 (Table 1).

DADP is compared against CORRO, Prompt-DT, Meta-DT, and an end-to-end diffusion baseline across locomotion tasks (HalfCheetah, Walker2d, Ant, Hopper with morphological variation) and Adroit manipulation tasks (Door, Relocate) (Section 5.1).

An ablation on Walker2d shows linear-probe accuracy of the learned domain representation improves from 27.9% at Delta t=1 to 99.3% as Delta t approaches infinity, confirming that larger lag isolates static domain factors (Table 2).

RZ6TONXE3A.text: On MNIST-Binary with depth L=6, Gumbel straight-through (Gumbel-ST) estimators collapse from about 98% accuracy to near-random performance (worst-case accuracy 51.0%, a 47.3 percentage-point range) as temperature is lowered to tau=0.05 (Table 2, Section 6.3).

CAGE (confidence-adaptive gradient estimation), which linearly interpolates backward temperature between tau_max=3.0 and tau_min=0.5 based on a network-wide selection-confidence metric (Eq. 10-11) with EMA smoothing (beta=0.99), raises Gumbel-ST's worst-case accuracy to 98.2% with only a 0.1 percentage-point range (Table 2, Section 5.2).
Hard-ST with CAGE achieves 98.1% accuracy on MNIST-Binary (L=6) with exactly 0% selection gap maintained across all temperatures (Table 2).
On CIFAR-10-Binary, Gumbel-ST with CAGE reaches 58.0% accuracy versus 18.9% for plain Gumbel-ST, showing CAGE's benefit extends beyond MNIST (Section 6.3).

During training, the CAGE-adapted temperature decreases from about 2.4 to roughly 0.7-0.8 as the selection-confidence metric rises from 0.25 to 0.85-0.90, tracing an exploration-to-exploitation transition (Figure 3).

xqc05bgrDk.text: Under accuracy-based payment schemes, required payments to sustain positive human effort diverge (scale at least logarithmically in 1/p) as AI error probability p approaches zero, formalized as an impossibility result (Theorems 3.1-3.2).

The sentinel-auditing mechanism designates a fraction ρ of tasks as sentinel tasks with forced AI errors, and paying an explicit bonus b(x) for correct human performance on these yields a first-order condition ρ·μ(b(x))·q'(e*) = c'(e*) that guarantees strictly positive effort independent of baseline AI accuracy p (Theorem 4.1).

Incentive-aware active statistical inference jointly optimizes the auditing rate ρ, sampling policy π(X), and bonus schedule b(X) to minimize estimator variance under a fixed budget constraint, with closed-form optimal designs given for mean estimation (Section 5, Examples 5.3-5.5).
The framework extends to general M-estimation problems with asymptotic normality guarantees for the resulting incentive-aware estimator (Theorem 5.6).

Experiments on post-election survey data and protein data show the incentive-aware active inference approach achieves roughly 70-80% budget savings relative to standard active learning baselines while maintaining comparable estimation error (Section 6).

3fGXBm4c3S.text: MAS-Orchestra formulates multi-agent system orchestration as a single function-calling reinforcement learning problem that generates an entire multi-agent system holistically in one pass, rather than composing it from separately optimized modules (Section 3, Multi-Agent Orchestration Framework).

MASBench is a controlled benchmark characterizing tasks along five axes—Depth, Horizon, Breadth, Parallel, and Robustness—used to systematically probe when multi-agent orchestration helps versus hurts (Section 4, Benchmark Design).

MAS-Orchestra achieves more than 10x efficiency gains over strong baselines while producing consistent accuracy improvements on mathematical reasoning, multi-hop QA, and search-based QA public benchmarks (Table 1, Section 5.3 Efficiency Comparisons).

Ablation studies show that disabling the orchestrator's routing mechanism causes 8-15% performance drops, and removing subagent specialization causes 5-10% accuracy drops, indicating gains depend on task structure, verification protocols, and both orchestrator and subagent capabilities rather than holding universally (Table 2, Section 5.2 Ablation Studies).
Search-based QA tasks show 12-18% computational savings attributable to intelligent routing decisions made by the orchestrator (Table 4, Section 5.3).

6ER1mP51np.text: The proposed merging-based variable-length tokenizer with learnable global merging achieves gFID of 3.19 at 32 tokens improving to 2.79 at 128 tokens in the jointly trained setting, compared to nested dropout baselines going from 5.21 to 4.69 gFID over the same token range (Table 1).
Adding LoRA further improves the proposed method's gFID from 3.04 (32 tokens) to 2.52 (128 tokens) in the joint training regime (Table 1).

Learnable global merging achieves a cross-length representational alignment (CKNNA) score of 0.76 on average, versus 0.34 for nested dropout, indicating better compatibility across different token-length regimes for diffusion transformers (Figure 3).
At the system level on ImageNet 256x256, the proposed tokenizer reaches 2.03 gFID at 2.88 TFLOPs using 25 sampling steps and 128 tokens, and 1.86 gFID at 11.51 TFLOPs using 100 steps (Table 2).

The proposed method's gFID gap between jointly trained and separately trained models is under 0.3, compared to 0.8-1.7 for competing variable-length tokenization methods including Semanticist and FlexTok, demonstrating a superior gFID-compute trade-off across the quality-compute curve (Figure 4).

SPLfdwCL1J.text: The study analyzes 137,154 posts from r/ChatGPT by 89,346 unique users spanning December 2022 to November 2025, constituting the first longitudinal study of the subreddit from launch through 2024-2025 (Preliminaries, Featurization & Retrospective Method).

Posts about mental health support, therapy, and emotional attachment to ChatGPT rise steadily almost immediately after the GPT-4o launch in May 2024, as shown by composition changes across post categories over time (Figure 1, Figure 2).

The real-time monitoring method PuLSE detects the rise in emotional-engagement posts by October 2024, months before OpenAI's public acknowledgment of the phenomenon (Real-time Monitoring with PuLSE section).

Therapy-related and companionship-related posts show minimal overlap (only 364 of over 2,253 therapy posts also discuss companionship), indicating these represent distinct emotional-engagement use cases with different vocabularies (Table 1).

The paper documents two distinct adoption narratives in the data: a 'domestication' pattern where basic usage questions decline as advanced-feature questions rise, and a separate emotional-engagement pattern driven by therapy and companionship posts (Retrospective Findings section).

wuWRCajFj8.text: MonoSoup applies singular value decomposition to each layer's fine-tuning update and reweights high-energy (task-specific) versus low-energy (robustness-preserving) components using layer-wise coefficients derived from spectral decay ratios, requiring only a single fine-tuned checkpoint rather than the 48-70 checkpoints needed by prior Model Soups methods (MonoSoup Method section).

On CLIP ViT-B/32, MonoSoup improves out-of-distribution accuracy from 50.67% to 51.60% when applied to the strongest OOD model, and recovers +7.9% OOD accuracy on the worst-OOD checkpoint (Experiments, Vision Transformers).

On the worst in-distribution CLIP ViT-B/32 checkpoint, MonoSoup yields a +7.5% out-of-distribution accuracy improvement, demonstrating a favorable in-distribution to out-of-distribution balance from a single checkpoint (Experiments, Vision Transformers).

On Qwen3-0.6B language models, MonoSoup produces its largest gains of +9.2 points each on the GSMPlus and GSM8KPlatinum mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with consistent improvements across other QA tasks (Experiments, Language Models).

MonoSoup integrates with Wise-FT and retains the robustness benefits of multi-checkpoint ensemble methods without their computational overhead of training and storing dozens of models (Experiments, Integration with Wise-FT).

GpRS2q0o3m.text: Introducing the first 10% of hard misleading distractors into a 128K-token context causes steep accuracy degradation on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen3-Next-80B, while further increases in distractor proportion yield only marginal additional decline (Section 3.2, Figure 2).

The Drop Ratio metric shows the degradation is highly front-loaded: for Qwen2.5-7B on Natural Questions, 58% of the total performance degradation occurs within just the first 10% of hard distractors, far above the 0.10 value expected under a linear relationship (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

A theoretical model of attention weight on the target passage, α(p) = 1/[1+(1-p)a+pb+c], is proven strictly convex in the hard-distractor proportion p (Lemma 4.2), explaining the observed front-loaded degradation (Section 4.2).

Empirically measured margin gaps (Δe ≈ 7-10 for easy distractors vs Δh ≈ 2-3 for hard distractors) imply a ratio b/a ≈ e^5.83 ≈ 340, meaning each hard distractor token contributes roughly 340x more to the softmax attention denominator than an easy distractor token (Section 5, Figure 5).

On Llama-3.1-8B, filtering context from 131K down to 47K tokens produces nearly identical performance gains whether the removed tokens are hard distractors or randomly selected tokens, indicating gains stem from context-length reduction rather than distractor removal (Section 6.2, Figure 8).

Reducing context length from 131K to 27K tokens while holding the hard-distractor proportion fixed at 20%, 50%, or 80% produces largely overlapping performance curves, showing that substantial recovery requires reducing the hard-distractor proportion itself to near zero rather than merely shortening context (Section 6.2, Figure 9).

ZGeVMaiIlb.text: C-DIC (Section 3) uses a retrieve-revise-write-back loop over per-thread compression states in a compact dialogue memory, conditioning generation on retrieved latent states instead of the full dialogue history.
On the MSC benchmark, C-DIC achieves a perplexity of 8.431 versus 27.656 for one-shot ICAE compression, and on REALTALK it achieves 9.789 versus baselines ranging from 12.625 to 31.067 (Table 1).
On MSC-QA, a diagnostic testing recovery of information from earlier turns, C-DIC attains 0.104 accuracy compared to 0.004 for one-shot ICAE (Table 3).

C-DIC maintains near-constant inference latency across hundreds of dialogue turns, requiring about 3.26 seconds at 30 turns versus 7.66 seconds for full-context prompting (a 2.4x speedup), and is the only tested method able to handle 428-turn conversations under the tested hardware constraints (Figures 4-5, Table 12).

An ablation removing the incremental (turn-wise) compression and revision component increases perplexity from 9.356 to 25.527, confirming that turn-wise compression and revision are critical to C-DIC's performance (Table 4).

C-DIC is trained with retrieval-aware truncated backpropagation-through-time (ra-TBPTT), which assigns gradient credit only along the selected memory-update path rather than requiring backpropagation through the full dialogue history (Section 3.2).

OJsGhlTayF.text: DiSC (Distillation-based Selective Context) updates parametric knowledge via context distillation, deriving student and teacher output distributions by conditioning on distinct segments of a training example and minimizing the KL divergence between them on shared tokens, without requiring explicit generation steps during training (Section 3).
DiSC is evaluated against standard fine-tuning and LoRA baselines on both knowledge-acquisition accuracy and retention of post-trained capabilities across multiple knowledge domains (Table 2).

Multiple context-distillation variants are compared for their trade-off between knowledge-learning accuracy and degree of catastrophic forgetting, with DiSC identified as achieving the best overall trade-off (Table 3).
DiSC is evaluated on knowledge-specific benchmarks including BioASQ against direct fine-tuning baselines, showing improved knowledge integration without capability degradation (Table 4).

Retention of post-trained capabilities is measured on BBH, GPQA, IFEval, MATH, MuSR, and MMLU-Pro across four post-trained models (including Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5/3 variants) and two adaptation domains, with DiSC showing greater resistance to catastrophic forgetting than alternative parameter-updating approaches (Table 6, Table 7).

BXz2zosn6H.text: Token Sparse Attention uses a two-stage compress-then-decompress design (Section 2.2): it first selects a per-head subset of query/key/value tokens to reduce attention complexity from O(L^2 d) to O(L'^2 d), then scatters the compressed attention output back to the original sequence positions via residual connections, allowing tokens to be reconsidered across layers.

On LLaMA-3.1-8B at 128K context, Token Sparse Attention alone yields a 1.36x speedup over FlashAttention, and combining it with FlexPrefill yields a 2.76x speedup versus 2.44x for FlexPrefill alone (Figure 1, Table 1).

On the RULER benchmark at 128K context, Token Sparse Attention achieves 73.68% accuracy versus a 74.15% full-attention baseline, and across InfiniteBench and other evaluated contexts the average accuracy degradation stays below 1% (Table 1).

Token importance is computed via an Inter-Layer Representation Drift metric (Equation 1), and sparsification is applied only to layers with normalized drift rank at or below a threshold δ=0.5, identifying which layers are safe to sparsify (Section 2.4).

Layer-wise token importance overlaps substantially less across distant layers than nearby ones, motivating the interleaved/dynamic token selection scheme rather than a single static selection (Figure 2).
Dynamic (interleaved) sparsity outperforms fixed sparsity baselines, and the added sparsification overhead accounts for less than 11% of total attention latency (Table 4, Figure 6b).

IvoZENu6qG.text: Across 25 evaluated LLMs, models above roughly 50B parameters show 20-30 percentage point accuracy gaps favoring multiple-choice-with-CoT (MC-CoT) format over free-text CoT, with reasoning models exhibiting the largest such disparities (Figure 1).

Reasoning models show substantially larger MC-CoT-to-CoT accuracy gaps than non-reasoning models of comparable scale, even after accounting for a random-guessing baseline correction (CoT+k) (Figure 2).

A two-stage evaluation protocol, CoT-MC-1T, forces the model to produce free-form reasoning before options are revealed and prevents it from 'backing out' the correct option during reasoning, decoupling answer selection from exposure to the answer choices (Section 3.1).

Large non-reasoning models perform better on standard MC-CoT than on a superscored combination of CoT and CoT-MC-1T, indicating the models are directly exploiting the presence of answer options rather than only benefiting from elimination reasoning (Section 4.1, Figure 3).

On questions augmented with a 'None of the Above' (NOTA) option where NOTA is the correct choice, DeepSeek-R1 70B achieves 0.85 precision but only 0.58 recall, indicating selective rather than indiscriminate reliance on the NOTA heuristic (Section 4.2, Table 10).

The evaluation spans 15 benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA Diamond, GSM8K, MATH, PythonIO, AIME 2025, ARC, WinoGrande, PIQA, CommonsenseQA, RACE, MedMCQA, OpenbookQA) and 55 presentation-format variants across CoT, MC-CoT, CoT-MC-1T, and CoT-MCNA-CoT conditions (Section 3.1, Tables 1-4).

p7PPMKTPJp.text: L3-PPI improves interaction-type prediction on SHS27k under random split from 79.59 to 83.22 Micro-F1 with a PIPR backbone, and from 83.65 to 87.42 with a GNN-PPI backbone (Table 1).
L3-PPI yields an average +6.02 gain for GNN-PPI+ on binary PPI prediction across SHS27k and Yeast datasets, versus +4.38 for MLP+ and +2.22 for DPPI+ (Table 2).

Ablation on SHS27k with the PIPR+ backbone shows removing the gating network drops Micro-F1 from 83.22 to 76.56 (-6.66), removing the path-number regularization loss drops it to 80.10 (-3.12), and removing pre-training drops it to 81.92 (-1.30) (Table 3).
L3-PPI delivers improvements under BFS and DFS data-splitting protocols (BS/ES/NS categories), showing particularly robust gains in the challenging ES and NS generalization settings (Figure 5).

The L3 rule (multiple length-3 paths between two proteins indicating interaction likelihood) is empirically validated on STRING, SHS27k, SHS148k, and Yeast datasets in the Preliminaries section prior to method design (Section on Preliminaries).

7NiATKcx1B.text: JIT-Planner achieves a 10.4× speedup and +28% accuracy improvement over the Browser-Use baseline across 37 tasks spanning five applications (Dashdish, GitLab, Gomail, Omnizon, Reddit) from the REAL and WebArena benchmarks (Experiments).

JIT-Scheduler achieves a 2.4× speedup and +9% accuracy improvement over OpenAI CUA by choosing among serial, parallel task decomposition, and request-hedging execution strategies via Monte Carlo sampling from learned latency distributions (Experiments).

The Invariant-Enforcing Tool Protocol, which requires tools to declare preconditions/postconditions as state invariants for static verification, reduces tool-use planning failures from 80% to 43% and cuts tool-ordering-violation failures from 59% to 25% (Experiments).

The Cost-Optimizing Planner generates multiple candidate code plans in parallel and selects the minimum-cost one via control-flow graph analysis, with candidate plans showing a 5.3× variance between worst and best cost, demonstrating the value of cost estimation (Experiments).

nETGpbMtcZ.text: DiCoME achieves cross-dataset generalization AUC of 0.977 on CDFv2, 0.982 on DFD, and 0.882 on DFDC, for an average of 0.939 AUC across benchmarks, trained only on FaceForensics++ (c23) (Table 1).

Geometric View Purification computes the artifact representation as fa = fr − proj_fs(fr), projecting the residual representation onto the orthogonal complement of the semantic feature space to counter the Semantic Masking Effect (Methodology, Section 3).

Ablation shows the full framework reaches 0.938 average AUC versus 0.922 without the orthogonal constraint and 0.905 using the artifact view (fs) alone, i.e., a ~1.6-point AUC drop from removing the orthogonal projection (Table 2).
The proposed uncertainty estimation reduces average Expected Calibration Error from 0.16 (baseline) to 0.07, a 56% relative improvement (Table 3).

On 8 distinct cross-manipulation forgery types, the method attains an average AUC of 0.976, and the full pipeline uses only 0.868M trainable parameters while running at 47.37 FPS and 156.08 GFLOPs at inference (Experiments).

XaexH2TroX.text: At 25% sparsity without recovery finetuning, Persona-Pruner scores 81.20 on RoleBench LLM-as-judge evaluation versus 48.43 for the strongest baseline, LLM-Pruner (Experiments).

At 50% sparsity with recovery finetuning on a 3B model, Persona-Pruner scores 70.37 versus 23.95 for LLM-Pruner, corresponding to the claimed 93.8% reduction in performance drop from the dense model relative to the strongest baseline (Experiments).
Persona-Pruner is compared against Depth Pruning, SliceGPT, LLM-Pruner, and Adapt-Pruner baselines across sparsity levels on RoleBench (Experiments).

In the ablation on the persona-driven data synthesis component, answer rewriting is more critical than query filtering alone, yielding 80.19 versus 78.80 on the Alpaca-P benchmark (Method/Experiments ablation).

Learned pruning masks show near-perfect cross-seed stability (Pearson r=0.99) and semantic alignment with persona embeddings (r=0.65), and human evaluation rankings correlate strongly with LLM-judge scores (Spearman rho=0.87) (Experiments).

uiE6BIx2vC.text: SARDI achieves 59.1% exact match on 2WikiMultihopQA and 48.7% on HotpotQA, using the DREAM-7B diffusion model with BM25 retrieval (K=7 passages) (Table 1).

SARDI achieves up to 8× higher throughput than autoregressive iterative-retrieval baselines at comparable or superior accuracy, and is 3-8× faster than the RL-trained Search-R1 baseline at matching accuracy across three benchmarks (Section 5, Experiments).

Gains from self-augmenting retrieval concentrate on reasoning-intensive, multi-hop questions, with 23.5-28.7 EM point improvements on compositional/inference queries versus minimal change on single-hop queries (Table 2).
Querying the retriever every 2 denoising steps instead of every step costs only 1-2 EM points while retaining 83-90% document persistence between consecutive steps (Table 5).

Conditional mutual information between adjacent entity tokens drops from 0.588 (no gold documents) to 0.060 (gold documents present), roughly a 10× reduction, explaining why retrieval-augmented context enables more parallel decoding (Section 5.5).
Sweeping the query threshold τ_q shows peak performance near τ_q≈0 (maximal lookahead), with raising it to τ_q=0.9 reducing EM by 4-6 points (Table 11).

4Anq3hEfaO.text: Deformba introduces Context-Adaptive State Fusion (CASF), which decouples the SSM write operation (a fixed single scan) from an adaptive read operation using learned 2D offsets, preserving linear O(L) complexity (Section 4.2).
Deformba-T/S/B achieve 83.8%/84.9%/85.4% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K classification, outperforming VMamba-B (83.9%) and DefMamba-S (84.2%) at comparable scale (Table 1).
Deformba-B reaches 51.8% box mAP and 45.2% mask mAP on MS COCO detection/segmentation under a 3x schedule, exceeding ConvNeXt-B (48.5% box mAP), PVTv2-B5 (48.4%), and Swin-B (48.6%) (Table 2).
Deformba-B attains 52.0% mIoU (single-scale) / 52.6% mIoU (multi-scale) on ADE20K semantic segmentation, surpassing VMamba-B (51.6%) and MambaOut-B (51.0%) (Table 3).
On nuScenes BEV 3D detection, Deformba-T with ResNet50 (3 frames) attains 0.405 NDS/0.276 mAP and Deformba-S with ResNet101 (4 frames) attains 0.538 NDS/0.445 mAP (Table 4).

An ablation shows CASF's benefit stems from adaptive sampling rather than added capacity: CASF without ECA gives +0.5% Top-1 and CASF with ECA gives +0.6% Top-1 over the baseline, while scan-direction sensitivity is minimal (81.33% unidirectional vs. 81.24% bidirectional vs. 81.38% cross-scan) (Tables 6 and 9).

g9J8AyE0xy.text: STRIDE trains an LLM to emit executable edit trajectories (INSERT/DELETE/REPLACE operations) for variable-length biological sequence refinement, using supervised fine-tuning on Levenshtein-aligned shortest-edit demonstrations followed by group-based policy optimization (GSPO) (Section 3).
On a protein fluorescence optimization oracle-based stress test, STRIDE raises success rate from 42% (vanilla SFT baseline) to 89% and novelty among unique improvements from 47% to 97% (Table 2).

STRIDE is benchmarked against protein-design baselines including FLIP, ProtBERT/ESM-based methods, and diffusion-based sequence generation approaches on protein optimization tasks (Section 4, Table 2).
On instruction-conditioned molecular editing, the GSPO-aligned STRIDE variant improves strict success rate, controllability, and SMILES validity relative to the SFT-only baseline (Table 3).
Ablation results (Table 4) isolate the contribution of the GSPO refinement stage versus SFT-only training, showing consistent gains from policy optimization across both protein and molecule tasks.

XgVZyybzHr.text: CorrectionPlanner models autonomous driving planning as autoregressive motion-token generation within a propose-evaluate-correct loop, retaining unsafe motion tokens as a self-attended correction trace that conditions subsequent proposals (Section 4.1).
Trajectories are discretized into 0.5-second intervals via K-disk clustering into a 1024-token vocabulary encoding one-step position and heading changes (Section 3.2).

On the Waymax benchmark, CorrectionPlanner reduces collision rate by over 20% relative to baselines, reaching 1.68% collision rate with 0.94% off-road rate and 94.23% progression rate in the reactive setting (Table 1).
On the nuPlan Val14 closed-loop benchmark, CorrectionPlanner achieves a 91.22 non-reactive planner score and a 2.04% collision rate versus 2.70% for the SMART baseline (Table 2).

An ablation shows collision rate drops progressively from 2.34% (imitation learning alone) to 2.20% (IL+RL without correction) to 1.68% (full method with self-correction) on Waymax, with self-correction outperforming rejection sampling and candidate selection alternatives (Tables 4 and 5).

With correction threshold 0.75 and correction length 5, CorrectionPlanner runs at 0.434 seconds per trajectory on an H800 GPU, comparable to baseline inference latency (Section on inference efficiency).

vNElL7pIoH.text: Bi-NAC formulates natural-language actor-critic reasoning as a Stackelberg bilevel game, where the critic (upper level) is trained to generate feedback optimized for the actor's (lower level) post-adaptation downstream performance, rather than fixed heuristic feedback (Section on bilevel formulation).
A 2B-parameter Bi-NAC model outperforms a 3B-parameter GRPO baseline on MATH-500 (46.56% vs. 41.43%), MBPP (66.73% vs. 61.55%), and GPQA (41.20% vs. 36.43%) (Table showing 2B vs 3B results).
A 6B-parameter Bi-NAC model outperforms a 7B-parameter GRPO baseline on MATH-500 (51.40% vs. 48.40%), MBPP (75.00% vs. 72.20%), and GPQA (49.30% vs. 43.60%) (Table showing 6B vs 7B results).
The 2B Bi-NAC vs. 3B GRPO comparison shows Bi-NAC using 5,120 tokens per sample versus 16,384 for GRPO (about 69% fewer tokens) while training in 16.5 hours versus 18.5 hours (Table 2).
An ablation on feedback quality shows Bi-NAC's generated critiques score 4.2/5 on an actionability metric versus 3.0/5 for a hierarchical fine-tuned feedback baseline (Table 4).

IU9dsf2LZA.text: Agora is a three-agent system (Orchestrator, Strategy, TestGen agents, each with four subtasks totaling 12 workflow steps) that combines hypothesis-driven testing with domain knowledge to find protocol-level logic bugs in consensus implementations (Figures 1 and 2, Algorithm 1).

Agora discovers 15 zero-day protocol-level logic bugs across four consensus implementations (Raft/etcd, EPaxos, HotStuff, BullShark/Sui), with a 26.1% false-positive rate among 46 total bug reports (Table 1).

Baseline ReAct-style LLM agents augmented with code-reading tools find zero protocol-level logic bugs: GPT-5.2 finds 22 implementation-level bugs but 0 logic bugs, Gemini 3.0 finds 0/0, Claude Sonnet finds 0, and Qwen3 Coder finds 3 implementation bugs and 0 logic bugs, whereas Agora with Gemini finds 11 protocol-level logic bugs (baseline comparison results).

An ablation (Table 2) shows removing the state-analyzer or scenario-generator component drops discovered bugs to 0, removing the bug-exploitation component drops bugs found to 3 (a 73% reduction), and removing the reflection loop causes test-generation failures with 173 false reports.
The discovered bugs span five categories, with Recovery & Execution Divergence and Persistence & Monotonicity Violations each accounting for 4 of the 15 bugs (26.7% each) (Figure 3).
Agora's bug discovery process consumes 58.6M tokens in total, averaging roughly $40 per discovered bug (Figure 4).

FfrpNZofIk.text: FIA is a training-free multi-concept unlearning framework for text-to-image diffusion models that achieves under 0.3% overall parameter sparsity while removing target concepts (Section 3).

FIA preserves Concept-Agnostic Neurons—those responding to multiple concepts, selected via a threshold τ_ca=⌈αC⌉—while pruning concept-specific neurons identified through contrastive concept saliency (Section 3.1, Section 3.3, Equations 1-2).
On multi-object unlearning, FIA achieves an average forgetting accuracy of 1.9%, compared to 7.34% for ConceptPrune and 38.58% for ESD (Table 1).
On explicit-content removal, FIA reduces NudeNet detections on the I2P benchmark from 743 (baseline) to 32 total detections, with FID 14.02 and CLIP score 31.18 (Table 3).
On artist-style unlearning, FIA attains the best average rank (2.50) among compared methods and a forget-success rate (FSR) of 83.4% (Table 4).

An ablation shows that removing Concept-Agnostic Neuron preservation (naive pruning) degrades CLIP score from 29.46 (with α=0.6) to 28.32, and that pruning at the FFN2 layer alone yields 1.9% forgetting accuracy versus 7.0-80.8% for other layers (Table 12, Table 13).

wB4zHbCJJg.text: BPTT and one-step tBPTT share the same fixed-point manifold structure—an optimal manifold (ab=a*b*, w=w*) and a non-optimal manifold (a=b=0)—whereas RFLO admits only the optimal manifold because its random feedback prevents b=0 solutions (Section 3.1, Figure 1).

RFLO exhibits sign-dependent stability along the optimal manifold and can display unstable or oscillatory dynamics not seen in BPTT or tBPTT, while the non-optimal manifold acts as a saddle point for BPTT/tBPTT (Section 3.2, Figure 3).

BPTT achieves the fastest asymptotic convergence rate across most of parameter space, while RFLO converges slowest except near initializations with small a* and large b*, where it matches BPTT's speed (Section 3.3).

Proposition 3.1 proves that RFLO-learned solutions are restricted to rank-bounded perturbations of the initial recurrent/input matrices, of the form W_K = W_0 + Σ_{i=1}^{o} r_i q_i^T, where o is the output dimension (Section 3.6, Proposition 3.1).
Empirically, RFLO learns rank-1 solutions while one-step tBPTT produces intermediate-rank solutions, and this rank restriction correlates with reduced task performance relative to BPTT (Figure 6).

KsvEE4OFzR.text: WS-GRPO trains a preference model from outcome-only correctness labels in Phase I, then uses it to produce prefix-level pseudo-rewards that guide when additional continuation is beneficial during GRPO optimization in Phase II, avoiding hand-tuned global length penalties (Section 3).
Theorem 3.1 bounds the weakly-supervised preference model's estimation error by O(√((d_P log(en/d_P) + log(1/δ))/n)) with probability 1-δ (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.1).
Theorem 3.2 bounds the performance degradation from imperfect preference calibration by λT_max/4 · ε_pref, where T_max is the maximum trajectory length (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.2).
On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-7B, WS-GRPO reduces rollout length to 52.5% and reduces optimization steps to 61.5% of the GRPO baseline, at a cost of -7.5% accuracy (Table 1).
On DeepMath with Qwen3-4B, WS-GRPO reduces rollout length to 91.2% and steps to 71.8% of baseline, with an accuracy change of -8.8% (Table 1).
Key hyperparameters include G=8 rollouts per prompt, a mixing weight λ=0.1, and a FLAN-T5-based preference model with an MLP head of hidden dimension 512 (Section A.4).

tAtpSwjsCB.text: Diamond Maps introduce stochastic flow-map models that enable efficient reward alignment at inference time by amortizing many diffusion simulation steps into a single-step sampler while retaining stochasticity needed for optimal reward adaptation (Section 3).

Posterior Diamond Maps are one-step posterior samplers distilled from GLASS Flows, and Proposition 4.1 proves they yield consistent estimators of the value function and its gradient (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).

Weighted Diamond Maps make standard flow maps stochastic at inference time via a renoising procedure with a recovery reward, and Proposition 5.1 proves this produces a consistent estimator of the value-function gradient (Section 5, Proposition 5.1).

On GenEval with SANA-Sprint 0.6B, Weighted Diamond Maps achieve a mean score of 0.83 versus 0.70 for the unguided baseline, 0.81 for ReNO, and 0.79 for Best-of-N, at 10.0 seconds of inference time (Table 1).
Diamond Maps show significantly better scaling than Best-of-N as the number of function evaluations increases from 1 to 64 (Figure 6).
Proposition 4.3 shows Diamond Maps enable one-step DDPM-consistent samples without explicit training for that capability (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.3).

VYIegjMzFC.text: A preliminary experiment shows that current answer-centric safety alignment substantially reduces attack success rate (ASR) on generation but leaves verification F1 near random chance, demonstrating aligned models lack intrinsic ability to verify their own response safety (Section 3.2).

SInternal trains models exclusively on safety verification—via self-response generation, expert verification construction, and supervised learning on verification trajectories—rather than on safe-answer generation (Section 4.1, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.3).
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, SInternal reduces StrongReject ASR to 0.6% versus 41.2% for the baseline, and improves WildJailbreak ASR by 6.8 points (Table 1).
SInternal improves verification F1 to 89.3 on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, versus 71.1 for the base model and 53.9 for STAR-1 (Table 3).
SInternal triggers safety verification in 50.4% of harmful cases versus 16.0% for the base model, with a 99.2% conditional safety rate when verification is triggered (Table 4).

Only SInternal-initialized RL (SInternal+GRPO) successfully defeats state-of-the-art reasoning-specific jailbreak attacks (e.g., HCoT), and SInternal matches supervised-fine-tuning safety performance using only 50% of the expert demonstration data (Table 2, Figure 6).

1KEObQsUKW.text: CGMMD trains a conditional sampler by directly minimizing an empirical conditional MMD (ECMMD) objective estimated via k-nearest neighbors, avoiding adversarial min-max optimization (Section 2.1, Section 2.2).

Once trained, CGMMD generates conditional samples in a single forward pass, achieving roughly 5.6x10^-4 seconds per image versus 5.42x10^-2 seconds per image for a conditional diffusion baseline (about 96x faster) on the reported image task (Table 1).

Theorem 4.1 gives a non-asymptotic error bound for the empirical sampler decomposed into stochastic (uniform concentration), neural-network approximation, and modulus-of-continuity error terms (Theorem 4.1).
Corollary 4.1 shows the expected squared MMD between the true conditional distribution and the learned generator's conditional distribution converges to zero as sample size grows (Corollary 4.1).
On a synthetic helix-generation task, CGMMD preserves the underlying manifold structure better than GCDS and WGAN baselines at higher noise levels (Section 5.1).
CGMMD is evaluated on real-data tasks including MNIST super-resolution (7x7 to 28x28 reconstruction) and image denoising on MNIST and CelebHQ (Section 5.2).

bPnEyHvZSu.text: Layer pruning of LLMs exhibits a cliff-edge effect: accuracy stays flat as pruning rate increases up to a threshold, then collapses abruptly, motivating a Silent Phase (no correct-answer signal) versus Decisive Phase (correct prediction emerges) decomposition (Section 1, Section 3.1).

The Decision Margin (DM) metric, measuring the probability gap between the correct answer and the strongest distractor across layers, is used to localize the Silent-to-Decisive transition point on LLaMA3-8B, LLaMA2-7B, and Qwen3-4B (Section 3.1, Section 4, Figure 4).

Targeted-ablation experiments on LLaMA3-8B show pruning layers within the Decisive Phase causes minimal accuracy loss, whereas pruning layers within the Silent Phase triggers immediate performance collapse on zero-shot multiple-choice benchmarks such as ARC, HellaSwag, PIQA, and MMLU (Table 1).
CKA similarity heatmaps reveal a representation-performance conflict: pruned models' hidden states remain highly aligned with the original model even as functional accuracy collapses (Figure 2).
Pearson correlation of r=-0.96 (p<0.001) is found between the depth of the Silent-to-Decisive transition point and a model's robustness to pruning (Figure 8).

The proposed Iterative Pruning (IP) method, which greedily removes layers guided by Block Influence scores while protecting the Silent Phase, outperforms ShortGPT, SLEB, and MKA baselines after supervised fine-tuning (Section 3.3, Table 5).

9uENnRAcSl.text: Behavior cloning with quantized actions and log-loss is proven to achieve sample complexity matching known lower bounds, up to the quantization error term (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).

Under Probabilistic Incremental Input-to-State Stability (P-IISS) of the dynamics and Relaxed Total Variation Continuity (RTVC) of the expert policy, the regret bound has only polynomial (not exponential) dependence on the horizon H with respect to quantization error epsilon_q (Theorem 3, Definition 3, Definition 4, Section 3.1-3.2).

Theorem 6 shows that without a smoothness assumption on the quantizer, non-smooth quantizers can incur regret of order H*Omega(1) even though their in-distribution one-step error is only O(epsilon_q) (Theorem 6, Section 4.1).

Theorem 7 proves that model-based data augmentation improves the horizon dependence to H*[sqrt(log|Pi|/n) + epsilon_q] without requiring the policy smoothness (RTVC) assumption (Theorem 7, Section 4.2).

Information-theoretic lower bounds (Theorems 8-9) establish that regret must scale at least as H*(1/n + epsilon_q) for deterministic experts and H*(sqrt(1/n) + epsilon_q) for stochastic experts, matching the achievable upper bounds (Section 5, Theorems 8-9).

Empirically, binning quantizers are shown to preserve policy smoothness better than learned quantizers, while deterministic experts more often violate the RTVC requirement needed for the sharp regret bound (Section 4.1).

ihMB4kA2SQ.text: Theorem 2.1 bounds the chi-squared divergence between two Gaussian location mixtures by a quantity of the form (C0 v TV^{-alpha(TV)}) * TV, with alpha(t) = (2+delta)/log(log(1/t) v e) (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
Corollary 2.4 derives that the Hellinger distance between two Gaussian location mixtures is bounded by TV raised to the power 1-o(1), where the o(1) term decays as 1/log log(1/TV) (Corollary 2.4).

Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 show this exponent is sharp by an explicit construction using Chebyshev polynomial zeros satisfying Hn >= TVn^{1-alpha*(TVn)} with alpha*(t)=0.33/log log(1/t), proving the 1-o(1) factor cannot be improved (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2, Section 3).

Theorem 4.3 uses the sharp TV-Hellinger inequality together with a metric-entropy argument to characterize the minimax rate for learning Gaussian location mixtures in total variation distance, resolving an open problem posed by Jia et al. (2023) (Theorem 4.3, Section 4).

Theorem 4.5 shows the inequality yields a Hellinger-distance error rate of epsilon^{2(1-o(1))} for robust estimation of Gaussian mixtures under Huber contamination, with Theorem 4.6 establishing a matching lower bound (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6, Section 4).

x21YkF1UfR.text: Outcome supervision alone for latent chain-of-thought produces a dual collapse of gradient attenuation and representation manifold drift, yielding only 9.8-18.3% accuracy compared to 43.1% for explicit chain-of-thought (Section 3, Figure 2).

Process supervision via generative reconstruction (PS-GR), which flexibly tethers latent states to semantic targets, reaches 39.1% peak accuracy, substantially outperforming geometric-compression-based process supervision (PS-GC), which plateaus at 23.2% (Section 4, Table 3).

The paper introduces a Unified Latent Probe (ULP) to estimate the mutual information I(L_t; S_t) between latent chain-of-thought states and semantic states, showing reasoning accuracy is tightly correlated with this retained information (Section 5).
Increasing latent granularity g improves performance, with the best results obtained at token-level latent representation (Table 2).

An Information-Performance Binding relationship is established: models with higher ULP-measured information fidelity achieve higher reasoning accuracy across all supervision paradigms tested, and this information decays spatiotemporally as reasoning chains lengthen, with PS-GR providing a recurrent calibration mechanism that mitigates this decay (Figure 4, Figure 5).

XKQZfG7itM.text: HB-ARFM (History-Bootstrapped Autoregressive Flow Matching) combines a history-conditioned bootstrap stage with autoregressive flow matching to reconstruct full velocity and temperature fields from sparse interface observations in boiling flows (Section on Method / HB-ARFM).

The history encoder uses a factored space-time transformer with separate spatial and temporal self-attention to avoid quadratic space-time attention cost, feeding a Residual U-Net flow-matching backbone integrated with 4th-order Runge-Kutta ODE solving (Method section, History Encoder and Flow Matching Backbone).

On the coupled flow-transport (pool boiling) task, HB-ARFM achieves wall heat flux error of approximately 0.2%, outperforming FFNO, UNet, DDPM, VE-SDE, standard Flow Matching, Bubbleformer, DiffusionPDE, PDEDiff and HistoryFM baselines (Experiments, Pool Boiling results table).

Over long autoregressive rollouts of 300 steps, HB-ARFM maintains interface velocity cosine similarity with observations of approximately 0.92-0.93, indicating no measurement-space drift, whereas VE-SDE fails catastrophically over similar horizons (Experiments, temporal consistency analysis).

An ablation over history length shows reconstruction error consistently decreases as more observation history is used, with the velocity field benefiting more than the temperature field (Figure 4, history-length ablation).

HB-ARFM generalizes from subcooled pool boiling to flow boiling with strong streamwise advection while keeping wall heat flux error below 0.2% under anisotropic transport conditions (Section on generalization to flow boiling).

BLnxPR2QB2.text: Gradient energy across audio tokens is highly non-uniform: the top 16% of audio tokens account for roughly 90% of total gradient energy under Qwen3-Omni, motivating sparse token-aware optimization instead of dense waveform perturbation (Section on gradient energy analysis).

Token-Aware Gradient Optimization (TAGO) combines sparse high-energy token selection, model-compatible benign-completion prefixes, and EOS-suppression to construct audio jailbreaks (Method section, TAGO components).
On AdvBench-50 against Qwen3-Omni, TAGO with retention ratio ζ=0.25 achieves ASR_l of 86%, nearly matching the 87% ASR_l obtained with full (ζ=1.0) token retention (Table of AdvBench-50 results).

On Qwen2.5-Omni, sparse TAGO (ζ=0.25) achieves ASR_l of 53% versus 65% for full dense optimization, while on LLaMA-Omni sparse TAGO (72%) slightly exceeds the dense variant (71%) (AdvBench-50 results table).

TAGO is compared against SpeechGuard, AdvWave, direct unperturbed harmful audio, and a post-hoc pruning baseline, with post-hoc pruning consistently underperforming token-aware optimization enforced during training (Baselines and ablation section).

SnLgKHi2I9.text: The proposed adjoint framework computes trajectory-dependent proxy gradients by differentiating equilibrium conditions of a Newton-CG solver, avoiding backpropagation through solver unrolling and reducing memory cost from O(K·steps) to O(H·steps) (Method section, adjoint formulation).

A frozen-tangent approximation treats equilibrium sensitivity matrices as locally constant during the backward pass, and Theorem C.3 (Appendix C) shows this proxy gradient achieves first-order accuracy under mild smoothness assumptions, with error bounded by the tangent variation rate.

A receding-horizon control (RHC) scheme re-anchors to realized equilibria across short segments and is shown critical for reliably selecting the specified equilibrium branch in multi-stable elastic-strip shape-formation tasks, whereas full-horizon Adjoint-only fails at branch selection (Ablation on RHC vs. Adjoint-only).

On elastic-strip manipulation tasks (point-to-point targeting, trajectory tracking, and multi-stable shape formation), Adjoint+RHC is 19-127x faster than gradient-free SPSA and CEM baselines and achieves 1-6 orders of magnitude lower best loss under matched update budgets (Table 1).
The learned adjoint-based controller is validated with sim-to-real transfer on a 6-DOF robot manipulating elastic strips under gravity and material uncertainty (Section on real-world validation).

XiaqvkSnWk.text: SPAR (Support-Preserving Action Rectification) reframes offline policy improvement as local residual rectification anchored to a frozen behavior-cloning policy, rather than global value maximization from scratch (Section 3, Method).

SPAR introduces a Latent Self-Imitation mechanism, a latent-sampling weighted-regression procedure, and the paper proves this mechanism eliminates the manifold-normal drift exhibited by standard value-gradient-based policy updates (Section 3, Theorems A.1-A.3 in Appendix A).

SPAR is evaluated on the D4RL benchmark suite against CQL, TD3+BC, IQL, Diffusion-QL, and AWR/AWAC baselines, reporting state-of-the-art performance with the largest gains on suboptimal (medium/medium-replay quality) datasets (Section 4.1-4.4, results tables).

Ablation studies in Appendix C examine the contribution of the residual rectification formulation versus the Latent Self-Imitation component to overall D4RL performance (Appendix C, ablation studies).

OrviwFWcN4.text: Using MLP neuron activations (rather than MLP outputs) as the interpretability basis yields circuits roughly 100x smaller for equivalent faithfulness, matching the sparsity of sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature bases in Llama 3.1 8B (Section 5.1).

Replacing Integrated Gradients with the RelP attribution method (a single backward pass instead of ~10 passes) closes the remaining faithfulness gap between MLP-neuron circuits and SAE-based circuits while reducing compute cost (Section 5.2).

On the subject-verb agreement (SVA) benchmark, a circuit of approximately 10^2 (about 200) MLP neurons identified via RelP achieves near-perfect faithfulness (~95%+), substantially outperforming the MLP-outputs basis at equivalent circuit size (Section 5.1 results).

On the multi-hop state-capital reasoning task, an automatically traced circuit of 257 neurons is manually refined to 23 key neurons, and a single neuron (L23/N8079-) is capable of flipping the top output from capital to state in the majority of examples (Case study, Texas circuit).

RelP with stop-gradients Pareto-dominates IG-based and other RelP variants on edge attribution, achieving over 80% faithfulness using only about 10^5 edges (roughly 10% of candidate edges) without any architectural modification (Figure 5, Section 5.4).

Findings on neuron-basis circuit sparsity replicate on Gemma 2 2B and 9B and hold under both templatic (paired) and unpaired data configurations using a zero baseline (Section 5.3, Appendix replication results).

RH7Ft0pVDP.text: DLA's Information-Aware Dynamic State Merging module adaptively determines state boundaries based on token-level information variation, formalized via the update rules in Section 3 (Equations 3.6-3.18) (Section 3).

DLA maintains a Capacity-Bounded Memory Modeling scheme that keeps a fixed-size recurrent cache by selectively merging adjacent low-information states, implemented in Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 (Section 3, Algorithms 1-2).
Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 establish theoretical properties (e.g. boundedness/consistency guarantees) of the dynamic state merging mechanism (Section 3, Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.2).
DLA is compared against Mamba, GLA (Gated Linear Attention), RetNet, and DeltaNet on language modeling and recall-intensive tasks, with the main results reported in Table 4 (Section 4, Table 4).

DLA is claimed to outperform these state-of-the-art linear-attention and state-space baselines across three different aspects (e.g. language modeling perplexity, recall accuracy, and efficiency) spanning roughly 10 datasets/benchmarks (Section 4, Tables 3-9).

C9AhjL8aUZ.text: The method performs distribution-level unsupervised feature discovery for circuit analysis via a three-stage pipeline of sampling, dual (semantic and mechanistic) representation, and joint clustering, without requiring manual target selection (Section 3).
Rate-distortion (RD) joint clustering wins over single-view K-means baselines in 94% of comparisons, as shown in the distortion metrics across β and γ configurations (Section 4, Table 1).

A tunable knob (parameters β and γ) trades off semantic granularity against mechanistic specificity, with cluster mechanistic similarity (Jaccard) and cluster structure dynamics visualized across values of β and γ (Section 4, Figures 3-4).
Steering interventions on discovered clusters produce correlation values between 0.20 and 0.39 across configurations, demonstrating causal validation of the clusters (Section 5, Table 2).
Split and junk cluster-refinement operations are demonstrated qualitatively, showing how the method scales model auditing by refining or removing clusters (Section 5, Figures 5-6).

BI4t1PefdY.text: Under one-shot evaluation, models achieve below 60% accuracy on Easy-difficulty submissions and below 50% on Hard-difficulty submissions when trying to identify errors in incorrect UOJ submissions (Section 4, Table 2).

Gemini-3-pro-preview attains the best overall generation performance, scoring 94.44% on Easy problems but only 18.62% on Ultrahard problems, with an overall best-model score of 38.84% (Section 4, Table 2).
On the Hacking and Repair tasks, Gemini-3-pro-preview reaches 44.17% (Hack, Hard) and 48.15% (Repair, Hard) accuracy under direct evaluation (Section 4, Table 3).

Test-time scaling (sampling k=20,000) raises Gemini-3-pro-preview's hacking success rate to 93% on 100 samples, and GPT-OSS-120B uncovers errors in over 10% of all full-score submissions and over 5% across roughly 30 problems in the Zero-Day Hacking setting (Section 4-5, Figure 8).
UOJ-Bench comprises 672 competitive programming problems with 1,525 hacking instances and 716 repair instances, curated from the University Online Judge (Section 3, Table 5).

mdDmS5nMpK.text: On the DeepCAD benchmark, CADFit achieves a mesh-to-CAD volumetric IoU of 0.964 and Chamfer Distance of 0.016, versus 0.872 IoU for the Cadrille baseline, with an Invalid Ratio of 0.000 (Section 4, Table 1).
On the ABC Hard subset, CADFit reaches IoU of 0.662, a 51.1% improvement over CAD-Recode, while reducing Invalid Ratio to 0.000, a 100% improvement over baselines (Section 4, Table 1).

For image-to-CAD reconstruction on ABC Hard, CADFit improves IoU to 0.380, a 60.3% improvement, and on ABC Medium achieves IoU 0.545 (39.4% improvement) with Chamfer Distance 0.037 (47.9% reduction) (Section 4, Table 2).
CADFit produces shorter construction sequences than ground truth while maintaining IoU above 0.9 in 85% of cases, and wins on both IoU and sequence length in 69.8% of cases (Section 4, Table 3).
A learned sketch prior speeds up reconstruction by 1.42x to 2.90x across complexity levels and improves ABC Hard IoU by +0.2285 (Section 4, Table 4).

vmcs6GBUe4.text: The paper proposes a sparse data-constrained scaling law extending the Chinchilla form L(N,D)=A/N^α + B/D^β + E to L(N',D',S)=A((1-S)^ε + PS^μ)/N'^α + B/D'^β + E, predicting loss as a function of active parameters, unique tokens, data repetition, and sparsity S (Section 3.3, Equations 1 and 9).
The fitted scaling law achieves R²=0.982 on training data and R²=0.914 on held-out validation data (Section 3, Figure 3).

Loss-optimal sparsity consistently falls in the moderate range S≈0.45-0.5 across data budgets, as shown by Iso-Loss curves comparing dense versus sparse training at 1.3B tokens (Section 4.1, Section 5, Figure 4).
Compute-optimal sparsity grows with data scale in sparse training: about S≈0.6 at 1.3B training tokens, rising to S≈0.7 at 13B and 130B tokens (Section 4.2, Figure 6).
At compute-optimal sparsity, the model attains 8x-10x fewer training FLOPs and a 3x smaller parameter-to-token ratio at the 1.3B-token budget compared to dense training (Section 4.2, Section 5).

kiC03dyH9P.text: VCPO combines ESS-guided step-size scaling (η_eff = η·√(ρ_ess^off/ρ_ess^on)) with a closed-form off-policy optimal baseline (OPOB) to explicitly control importance-weighted policy-gradient variance (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
On AIME 2025, VCPO under asynchronous training reaches 27.8% accuracy while using only 168.9 GPU hours versus 420.2 GPU hours for the synchronous baseline, a 2.5x speedup (Table 1).
On MATH-500, VCPO achieves 71.6% accuracy in the asynchronous regime versus 72.0% for the synchronous baseline, at roughly 69% of the GPU-hour cost (92.8 vs 134.4 GPU hours) (Table 1).

VCPO remains stable under extreme policy staleness up to k=128 steps off-policy, matching the k=0 synchronous baseline, whereas masked/truncated importance sampling baselines collapse (Figure 6, Figure 4).
The efficient single-backward-pass implementation of VCPO (Algorithm 1) adds only 19% step-time overhead and 14% memory overhead relative to a naive two-pass computation on 4×H100 GPUs (Section 3.4).

Ablations in Appendix D show that ESS-guided step-size scaling and the OPOB baseline each independently contribute to training stability and accuracy across Qwen2-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B models (Appendix D).

dclUuUHjrA.text: Iterative Regret-Minimization Fine-Tuning (ITERATIVE RMFT) repeatedly fine-tunes a base LLM on trajectories selected via a regret-minimization criterion rather than standard supervised imitation of all trajectories (Section 3).

The paper provides theoretical regret bounds for the iterative fine-tuning procedure and analyzes its convergence properties building on classical online-learning and bandit regret theory (Section 2, Section 4).

ITERATIVE RMFT is evaluated on decision-making benchmarks spanning multi-armed bandit problems and planning tasks with varying horizon lengths and both continuous and discrete action spaces (Section 5).
The method is tested under multiple stochastic reward processes, including Gaussian and Bernoulli reward variants, to assess generalization of the fine-tuned policy (Section 5).
ITERATIVE RMFT is compared against baselines including ReAct and Reflexion-style prompting approaches on planning and control tasks in the results section (Section 6).

IaOEffUyBn.text: 3DGS-HPC performs regular patch-wise partitioning of rendered images and classifies each patch as static or transient using both a GMM-based photometric criterion and a percentile-based perceptual criterion, combined by intersection (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
On the RobustNeRF dataset, 3DGS-HPC with DINOv2 features achieves 29.81 dB PSNR versus 26.46 dB for vanilla 3DGS, 28.37 dB for T-3DGS, and 29.51 dB for SLS-mlp (Section 5.2 table).
On the On-the-go dataset averaged over six scenes, 3DGS-HPC achieves 23.86 dB PSNR versus 22.95 dB for T-3DGS and 23.18 dB for WildGaussians (Section 5.2 table).

Ablating the patch-wise partitioning strategy shows patch-wise classification reaches 29.81 dB PSNR versus 29.74 dB for superpixel partitioning, 29.70 dB for feature clustering, and 29.45 dB for SAM2-based partitioning (Figure 8).

Ablating the hybrid classification metric shows the combined GMM+percentile approach (29.81 dB) performs comparably to photometric-only (29.82 dB) but substantially better than perceptual-only classification (29.13 dB) (Figure 9).
3DGS-HPC requires no external semantic segmentation model (e.g., SAM2 or DINO-based semantic priors) unlike prior distractor-removal methods such as WildGaussians and T-3DGS (Section 4.1, Section 2).

FN20iuPnEU.text: HELIX introduces a learnable Feature Identity Embedding (FeatID) appended to each observation's representation alongside value, sinusoidal positional encoding, and mask, serving as a persistent per-feature anchor across all layers (Section 3.3).
