HELIX ranks first among 16 baseline methods (17 methods total including HELIX) across 21 experimental settings spanning five datasets (BeijingAir, ETT-h1, ItalyAir, PeMS, PhysioNet2012) and multiple missingness patterns (Point-10/50/90%, Block-50%, Subseq-50%) (Table 1).
On BeijingAir Point-10% missingness, HELIX achieves MAE 0.073±0.004 versus 0.095±0.005 for ImputeFormer; on PeMS Point-10%, HELIX achieves 0.097±0.002 versus 0.164±0.007 for ImputeFormer (Table 1).
Ablation removing the Hybrid Encoding component causes a large degradation on Subseq-50% missingness on BeijingAir (0.294 MAE versus 0.166 for full HELIX) (Table 4/21).

On BeijingAir, where no geographic labels are provided during training, learned feature identity embeddings show similarity correlated with true geographic distance (r=-0.587, p<0.0001), with this alignment strengthening across layers (r=0.589→0.670→0.712) (Figure 2-3).

HELIX uses substantially fewer parameters than baselines on ETT-h1 (803.5K versus 88.2M for SAITS and 23.7M for iTransformer) while scaling the feature-identity dimension sub-linearly with feature count (Section on Parameter Efficiency).

Kux5q1mL1x.text: On the Netflix Prize dataset with sparse ratings (m=2), GPT-5 achieves a 79.2% linkage success rate versus 56.0% for a classical heuristic re-identification algorithm at tolerance T=14 (Section 3.4, Figure 2a).
Claude 4.5 shows markedly lower linkage success in the sparse regime (53.3% at m=2 on Netflix) compared to GPT-5's 79.2% (Section 3.4, Figure 2a).

On the InferLink benchmark, implicit/benign task framing yields 70-80% linkage success rate for Claude 4.5 versus only 25-45% for GPT-5, but success rates rise sharply to 80-100% under explicit re-identification requests for both models (Section 4, Table 1).
A privacy-aware system prompt reduces linkage success rate by 58-98% relative to the unmitigated setting, but incurs a 4-54% drop in task utility depending on the model and scenario (Section 4).

In the Modern Traces evaluation on real anonymized conversational logs, the method yields 6 confirmed re-identifications from Anthropic Interviewer transcripts and 1 confirmed re-identification from ChatGPT logs via progressive candidate narrowing from roughly 300 candidates to 1 (Section 5).

a7ZTOzb2nl.text: Proximal-IMH's proposal admits a closed-form linear correction x = K x̃ where K = (AᵀA+βI)⁻¹(AᵀÃ+βI), derived by solving a regularized least-squares problem around the approximate posterior sample x̃ (Section 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 shows that in the diagonal perturbation case, the KL divergence of the proximal posterior scales as ε²d_y + ε²Σᵢσ²/sᵢ², which is substantially smaller (often by orders of magnitude) than the KL divergence of the Approx-IMH posterior (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.2).

Theorem 3.3 shows the mixing-time constant of Proximal-IMH depends only on ‖I−K⁻¹‖, which is provably no larger than the corresponding quantity ‖I−F̃⁻¹F‖ for Latent-IMH, with equality only when F̃=F (Section 3.3, Equation 16).

On the bimodal Bayesian inverse problem experiment with three perturbation types (multiplicative spectral, additive low-rank, and low-rank approximation), Proximal-IMH achieves substantially higher acceptance rates and convergence comparable to NUTS, versus Approx-IMH and Latent-IMH (Section 4.1, Figure 2).

On the MNIST VAE-decoder inverse problem (d_z=128, d_x=784, d_y=100) with spectral perturbations (condition number ≈60) and linearized Helmholtz operators (condition number ≈420), Proximal-IMH shows lower error, faster convergence, and reduced trial-to-trial variance than Approx-IMH, and is robust to the choice of β (variance <0.4% across tests) (Section 4.2, Figures 6-7).

On the nonlinear acoustic-scattering Helmholtz inverse problem with 44 source terms on a 32×32 medium grid, Proximal-IMH converges to accuracy comparable to NUTS while retaining the computational advantages of an independence proposal (Section 4.3, Figure 8).

3DiK7Z4ZM8.text: PRISMamba achieves 84.5% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with 22M parameters, 3.9G FLOPs, and 3,054 img/s throughput on an A100, compared to VMamba's 82.6% Top-1 with 30M parameters, 5.6G FLOPs, and 1,686 img/s throughput (Table 1).

Under image rotation, PRISMamba's accuracy stays within 0.2 points across 0°, 30°, and 60° rotations (84.5%→84.3%→84.4%), while fixed-path baselines VMamba and GroupMamba degrade by 1-2 points at 60° rotation (82.6%→80.6% and 83.9%→82.0% respectively) (Table 2).

On MS COCO object detection at 1280×800 resolution, PRISMamba obtains 48.9 box AP and 43.2 mask AP with 235G FLOPs, outperforming VMamba (46.5/42.1 AP, 262G FLOPs) and GroupMamba (47.6/42.9 AP, 279G FLOPs) (Table 3).

The Partial Channel Filtering (PCF) module, which routes only high-activation channels through the recurrent SSM path via mean-based salience thresholding, outperforms both squeeze-excitation (SE) and CBAM soft-attention alternatives while using fewer parameters and FLOPs and achieving higher throughput (84.5% vs 84.2% and 84.3% Top-1, at 22M/3.9G/3,054 img/s vs 27M/4.6G/2,089 img/s for +SE) (Table 5).

Applying PCF to other existing Vision-Mamba architectures yields consistent gains, reducing parameters by 2-6M and FLOPs by 0.2-0.6G (4-12%), increasing throughput by roughly 35-50%, and improving Top-1 accuracy by 0.2-0.4 percentage points (Table 4).

Under 16×16 patch occlusion, PRISMamba's Top-1 accuracy drops by only 0.4 points compared to a 0.9-point drop for VMamba, attributed to the order-agnostic ring-descriptor aggregation diluting the influence of localized masked regions (Table 6).

zChdTtZmO3.text: CAReDiO enables cultural alignment fine-tuning with as few as 100 training samples, using a data-selection score s = r × d that combines a representativeness measure r (cluster size or in-context learning performance on CulturalBench) and a distinctiveness measure d (average cosine distance between a target culture's responses and four other cultures') (abstract only).

On GlobalOpinionQA, fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B on CAReDiO-selected data reaches 81.28% accuracy versus 80.99% for the CultureBank dataset baseline, and fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B reaches 84.84% versus 76.72% for CultureBank (abstract only).
On the Prism open-ended conversation benchmark, a Llama model trained on CAReDiO data scores 4.12/5 versus 3.53/5 for a role-play prompting baseline (abstract only).

The data-synthesis pipeline covers a 38-topic cultural framework spanning four levels (values, social norms, behavioral practices, customs) across five cultures (United Kingdom, China, South Korea, India, Singapore), using Cognitive Conflict Theory to expose LLMs to contrasting cultural responses and elicit refined answers (abstract only).

CAReDiO is compared against role-playing prompting baselines (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4-turbo) and fine-tuning baselines (CultureLLM, CulturePark, CultureSPA, CultureBank) across GlobalOpinionQA, CulturalBench, CultureBank, and Prism benchmarks, with an ablation showing cluster-size-based representativeness outperforming in-context-performance-based representativeness (abstract only).

9S9V5ntQJM.text: SE-GA (7B) achieves 89.0% average accuracy on ScreenSpot and 75.8% success rate on AndroidControl-High, both exceeding the 72B UI-TARS baseline (88.4% and 74.7% respectively) despite SE-GA's much smaller parameter count (abstract only).
SE-GA reaches 39.0% success rate on AndroidWorld, outperforming the 7B UI-TARS baseline's 33.0%, demonstrating stronger generalization to dynamic GUI environments (abstract only).

An ablation removing Test-Time Memory Extension (TTME) drops AndroidControl-High success rate from 73.8% to 61.4% and GUIOdyssey step success rate from 83.9% to 74.9%, while removing Memory-Augmented Self-Evolution (MASE) drops these to 59.7% and 60.4% respectively (abstract only).

SE-GA's training uses 4,007 trajectories (2K for grounding supervised fine-tuning, 2K for GRPO-based self-evolution training) with an average trajectory length of 11.89 steps, sourced from AITW, AMEX, GUIOdyssey, and a custom Android simulator collection (abstract only).

The Hindsight Goal-Shifting mechanism converts failed trajectories into useful training supervision by relabeling successful prefixes as achieving different (attained) goals, feeding these into the self-evolution training stage alongside token-level importance ratios and hierarchical rewards (abstract only).

ottLtChHp2.text: TabSwift uses a 24-layer, d_model=192 row-wise attention transformer with element-wise gated attention (multiplicative SDPA-output gating) and K learnable register tokens that aggregate global context across layers, pretrained for 150,000 steps on 8 RTX 5090 GPUs (~7 days) on synthetic classification/regression tasks (abstract only).

On the TALENT benchmark, TabSwift achieves an average rank comparable to TabPFN v2 (with 4x ensembling) and TabICL (with 16x ensembling) on both classification and regression tasks, with critical-difference diagrams (Wilcoxon-Holm test, α=0.05) showing no statistically significant difference from these top methods, while running substantially faster at inference (abstract only).

An ablation starting from a TabS-S1 baseline shows that adding gated attention improves training stability, adding register tokens further boosts performance, and adding two-stage pretraining yields the final model that outperforms each incremental variant (abstract only).

TabSwift's adaptive early-exit mechanism, which attaches a prediction head at every one of the 24 layers and exits per-sample based on a register-conditioned exit head with threshold τ, allows the majority of test instances to be confidently predicted at shallow depths (average exit depth ~11-22 layers depending on τ) with negligible accuracy loss (abstract only).

TabSwift is competitive with tree-based methods (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) on small-to-medium datasets (N≤20K) but its performance degrades relative to RealMLP and ModernNCA on datasets with N>20K samples, and it requires PCA reduction for datasets with more than F_max=100 features (abstract only).

fCPgAHIciE.text: WaterSIC achieves a maximum rate gap of 0.255 bits per entry to the information-theoretic rate-distortion limit D*(R,Σ_X), uniformly over all input covariance matrices, with the gap equal to ½log₂(2πe/12) (Theorem, Rate-Distortion Bounds section).

WaterSIC's quantization performance depends only on the determinant |Σ_X| and is therefore invariant to rotations, whereas GPTQ's error can grow arbitrarily under a random rotation U·Σ_X·U^T of the activation covariance (GPTQ Gap Analysis section).

On Llama-3.2-1B, WaterSIC achieves perplexities of 82.44, 30.73, 16.19, 10.57, and 9.92 at average bitwidths of 1.00, 1.50, 2.00, 3.00, and 4.00 bits per entry respectively, versus an unquantized baseline of 9.76 (Experimental Results, Llama-3.2-1B table).

At 2.00 bits per entry on Llama-3.2-1B, WaterSIC reaches 16.19 perplexity versus 17.74 for Huffman-GPTQ, and at 1.50 bits Huffman-GPTQ fails (perplexity above 1000) while WaterSIC attains 30.73 (Comparisons to Prior Work, vs. Huffman-GPTQ).

At 3.125 bits per entry, WaterSIC attains 10.03 perplexity compared to 12.77 for standard GPTQ and 16.30 for round-to-nearest (RTN), on the evaluated Llama model (Comparisons to Prior Work, vs. GPTQ/RTN).

On Qwen3-8B, WaterSIC achieves state-of-the-art perplexity across the 2.125-4.125 bit range, outperforming Huffman-GPTQ, QTIP, NestQuant, and AWQ at every tested rate (Experimental Results, Qwen3-8B).

M6h4vUgvl4.text: Multi-Head LatentMoE with Head Parallel (HP) achieves O(1) communication cost regardless of the number of activated experts k, in contrast to Expert Parallel's O(k) cost, and reduces communication to 25% of Expert Parallel at k=4 (Communication Performance section).
At 4.2B total parameters, Multi-Head LatentMoE trains 1.61x faster than standard MoE with Expert Parallel, completing in 34.41 hours versus 55.34 hours (Training Speedup Results section).

At 2.2B parameters, Multi-Head LatentMoE with doubled granularity trains 1.11x faster than the MoE Expert Parallel baseline (31.68 vs 35.36 hours) while achieving better downstream accuracy (Training Speedup Results section).

Table 1 reports FineWebEDU validation perplexity of 15.02 for Multi-Head LatentMoE versus 15.01 for MoE with Expert Parallel, with average downstream accuracy across HellaSwag, PiQA, LAMBADA, and ARC of 45.17% for the base model and 45.43% for the doubled-granularity variant (Table 1).

IO-Aware Routing reduces HBM access from O(T·N_e+N_e) to O(T+N_e), and IO-Aware Expert Computation (leveraging FlexAttention) reduces HBM access from O(T·d_e+d_e) to O(T+d_e), with both techniques being mathematically exact (Technical Innovations section).

vcdsMrNGqP.text: The AI grading system was evaluated on thousands of free-response quiz submissions from nearly 800 students across Math 2A and 2B calculus courses at UC Irvine over Winter 2025, Spring 2025, and Fall 2025 (Dataset & Scope section).

GPT-4.1-mini with context-aware prompting achieved approximately 88% acceptable handwriting-to-LaTeX transcriptions, compared to 55% for Mathpix on challenging subsets (Technical Approach, OCR Component).

Across 3,945 free-response records compared against TA grades, mean absolute error ranged from 0.5 to 1.06 points and within-1-point agreement ranged from 68% to 86% across quizzes, with average AI scores 0.40 points lower than TA scores (Key Evaluation Results, TA Score Alignment).

An independent audit of 3,851 submissions by 20+ trained reviewers found 87.64% of OCR outputs acceptable, over 90% of AI-reviewer score differences within ±1 point, and rubric fidelity of 79.79% fully correct (Key Evaluation Results, Independent Human Review).

A survey of 301 Math 2A students found 60-61% rated AI-generated feedback as accurate and 62-63% found it clear, while 52-53% still preferred TA grading and 76-78% remained open to AI-assisted grading (Key Evaluation Results, Student Feedback).

1UUJrgYr20.text: Dual Q-DM (Dual Q-function Distribution Matching) is proven to be the first non-adversarial imitation learning method provably free of compounding errors, via Bellman constraints 0 ≤ Q(s,a) - E[LSE(Q)(s')] ≤ 1 that couple Q-values across consecutive states (Bellman Constraints as Key Mechanism section).

Theorem 1 proves that IQ-Learn's policy is nearly equivalent to the behavioral cloning (BC) policy at all timesteps except initial states, and that IQ-Learn suffers an imitation gap lower bound with quadratic dependence on horizon (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 proves that Dual Q-DM's recovered policy equals the optimal solution of adversarial imitation learning (AIL), inheriting AIL's linear (rather than quadratic) horizon dependence for combating compounding errors (Theorem 2).

Proposition 1 shows that in transition-discriminative MDPs, Dual Q-DM identifies expert actions at unvisited states, whereas IQ-Learn assigns uniform Q-values to all actions at those states (Proposition 1).

On hard tabular instances, Dual Q-DM and AIL maintain constant imitation gaps as horizon length increases, while BC, IQ-Learn, and ValueDICE exhibit gaps that scale quadratically with horizon squared (Experimental Validation section).

qMI1xD8O3x.text: On the Jigsaw text dataset, a model with 5.3% error rate achieves only 1.8% Normalized Excess Cost (NEC), a roughly 3x difference indicating most mistakes concentrate on ambiguous, low-cost examples (Key Findings, NEC vs. Error Rate Gap).

On the Turkey image dataset and NHANES tabular dataset, error rate vs. NEC gaps of 6.7% vs 4.2% (1.6x) and 21.7% vs 14.8% (1.5x) respectively are reported, showing the error-rate/NEC divergence holds across modalities (Key Findings, NEC vs. Error Rate Gap).

Costs are derived from three sources: multi-annotator vote-margin log-odds (Equation 3), threshold distance for continuous measurements (Equation 4), and direct annotator confidence ratings (Cost Derivation Methods section).

Table 2 reports fine-tuned model results including Jigsaw RoBERTa at 1.8% NEC / 4.7% error rate, Turkey ResNet at 2.3% NEC / 4.8% error rate, and iNaturalist ResNet at 9.3% NEC / 11.1% error rate (Table 2).

Cost-weighted training produces inconsistent benefits: effects are negligible on Jigsaw and NHANES but counterproductive on iNaturalist, where cost-weighting increased NEC by 6.6% (The Cost-Weighting Paradox section).

Δ-regression training yields calibration information with mean absolute error of approximately 0.3 log-odds but provides no accuracy advantage over standard cross-entropy training (Performance Results / Training Strategies Evaluated section).

TrZGbLwVg5.text: Theorem 3.4 and Corollary 3.5 establish that the hidden-state gradient norm is a reliable proxy for the full sequence adversarial loss gradient, with the token importance ranking it induces provably consistent with that of the full-loss gradient (Section 4.2, Theorem 3.4, Corollary 3.5).
On VMA attacks against Qwen2-VL, GTM reduces attack success rate from 90.54% (no defense) to 0.00%, matching DiffPure's defense strength (Table 1).
On ImgHijack specific-string attacks at epsilon=32, GTM reduces attack success rate from 100% to 0.91% (Table 2).
On jailbreak attacks at epsilon=16, GTM achieves 0.00% attack success rate, outperforming the Guard baseline (0.91% ASR) and ASTRA (13.64% ASR) (Table 3).
GTM requires only a single forward-backward pass, running in 3.50 seconds versus 3.28 seconds for the undefended baseline and 7.22 seconds for DiffPure, using 16.96 GiB of GPU memory (Table 5).

An ablation shows the optimal token masking ratio is 5%, and using hidden-state gradient norm attribution instead of logit-based attribution improves aligned-token attack defense from 30.91% to 24.55% ASR (Figure 4, Table 6).

MX9iN1QI3Y.text: A test-time steering intervention that multiplies the activations of identified activation subspace bottlenecks by a scalar improves performance by an average of 8.27% across 7 SSMs and 6 diverse benchmarks without any task-specific tuning (abstract only).
The activation subspace bottlenecks are identified using mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to the Mamba family of state-space models (abstract only).

Stable-Mamba, an architecture obtained by modifying the identified bottleneck components, is trained from scratch and demonstrates superior long-context performance compared to the original architecture, confirming that the bottlenecks constrain model capability (abstract only).

The scalar-multiplication intervention on activation subspace bottlenecks is presented as a simple, general-purpose steering method applicable across multiple SSM checkpoints without retraining (abstract only).

V40F5O5N85.text: UniBoost, the proposed distribution-aware scheduler, is evaluated against SRPT/TRAIL+ with perfect length prediction and achieves up to 35-50% lower P99 TTLT (Abstract, Section 4).

On Llama-8B with a workload mix of 70% reasoning and 30% Azure traces, UniBoost improves P99 TTLT by about 35% and P95 TTFT by about 97% versus TRAIL+, while maintaining throughput within 1.2% (Table 2, Section 4.1).
MemGuard bounds each request to at most 1 + floor(log2(S_i/k)) priority-revision points before completion, using geometric quantization to reduce KV-cache thrashing (Section 3.3).

Prefill length distributions are shown to be light-tailed while decode length distributions range from light-tailed for conversational workloads to heavy-tailed for reasoning workloads, motivating why no single fixed scheduling policy dominates across workloads (Figure 1, Section 2.2).

An adaptive parameter estimator computes a tail-slope estimate gamma-hat from empirical P95/P99 response-time quantiles to set the scheduler's boost parameter online rather than relying on offline length prediction (Section 3.4).
UniBoost is compared against SRPT/TRAIL+, SJF/LTR with perfect prediction, Sarathi chunked-prefill scheduling, and FCFS across production-style traces (Section 4).

aWmEo0tNjs.text: CSRM achieves 94.6% F1 on the CoSApien benchmark and 75.8% F1 on DynaBench without requiring additional human annotation (Abstract, Table 2).
CSRM is fine-tuned from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 8 H100 GPUs using DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 with a joint discriminative-generative training objective (Section 4.1, Section 3.3).

Configurable safety configuration augmentation and a strictness augmentation procedure (Algorithm 1), which filters ordered guideline pairs using a Clopper-Pearson lower bound at alpha=0.05, are used to construct CSRM's training data (Section 3.2).

When used as the reward model for RL alignment on CoSApien policies, CSRM yields models with a better helpfulness-safety tradeoff than baselines using LlamaGuard-3-8B or Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the reward signal, producing a dominant Pareto frontier in safety-helpfulness space (Section 4.4, Table 5, Figure 4).

znFIR7WFGt.text: Five detectors are evaluated on peer review text, including two commercial systems (Pangram 3.0 and GPTZero) and three open-source methods (LogLikelihood, Fast-DetectGPT, and Binoculars) (Section 4, Table 2).

On the hard subset of policy-compliant human-written, LLM-polished reviews (H-AI), Pangram misclassifies 3.1% as AI-generated, GPTZero misclassifies 3.4%, and Fast-DetectGPT misclassifies 4.6% (Table 2, Section 4.1).

The evaluation dataset comprises 50,156 reviews spanning five AI-assistance levels: AI-BP (basic prompts), AI-EP (elaborate prompts), AI-HI (human-input expansion), H-AI (human-written, LLM-polished), and H (fully human-written) (Section 1, Section 3).

Peer-review-specific detection strategies, including manuscript-context-conditioned likelihood, similarity matching against AI-generated references (Table 3), stylometric features (Table 4), and a supervised RoBERTa-base classifier (Table 5), yield measurable gains over generic detectors but none reaches the accuracy needed to reliably enforce polishing-only policies (Section 4.2).

The paper concludes that current AI-text detectors are not reliable enough to enforce policies permitting LLM use only for polishing peer reviews, given persistent misclassification on mixed-authorship content (Section 4.1, Section 5).

NoESvlwHHq.text: On the sEH proxy-reward task, S3-GFN attains a synthesizable-sample positive ratio of 0.945 ± 0.009 and a top-100 sEH reward score of 1.043 ± 0.001, comparing favorably to FragGFN, SynFlowNet, Prior, and RTB+RS baselines (Table 1).

On structure-based drug discovery across five LIT-PCBA receptor targets, S3-GFN reaches average Vina docking scores between -12.32 and -7.70 kcal/mol together with AiZynthFinder synthesizability success rates of 96.33%-100% (Table 2).

S3-GFN's replay training combines on-policy training on positive (synthesizable) samples with a contrastive auxiliary loss computed from separate replay buffers of synthesizable and unsynthesizable samples (Section 3.2).
After a distributional constraint change, S3-GFN realigns its generation policy to the new synthesizability constraint within 100 adaptation steps (Table 3, Section 5.2).

The generator is steered by a pretrained SMILES-based chemical prior (built on large-scale molecular corpora) integrated into a sequence-based MDP, rather than relying on a fixed reaction-template MDP as in SynFlowNet, RGFN, and RxnFlow (Figure 1, Section 2.3).

thhtz3Oyg1.text: The Competency Gaps (CG) method uses sparse-autoencoder concept activations to automatically detect both benchmark coverage gaps and model performance gaps without manual annotation (Section 3).

Across the evaluated benchmark suite, 314 concepts (about 1% of all concepts) are entirely missing, and every benchmark except Vectara fails to cover at least 30% of all concepts (Section 4.2.1, Figure 3).

CG automatically recovers the previously documented sycophancy-adjacent gap, showing the evaluated model performs well on concepts tied to "commitment to help" and positive sentiment but poorly on concepts like polite refusal and maintaining professional boundaries (Section 4.2.2).

CG surfaces model gaps not previously documented in the literature, including deficits in intuitive/grokking-style reasoning and in metacognitive explanation of the model's own limitations (Section 4.2.2).

CG scores show low variance under benign perturbations (standard deviation of 0.014) while responding to adversarial perturbations, and results are consistent across different SAEs including a non-model-specific SAE (Section 4.2.3, Table 3).

94sQrbiUeI.text: Calibrated Collective Oversight (CCO) selects actions by maximizing U(s,a) − λₜΔ(s,a), where λₜ is adjusted online via conformal control so realized violation rates track a user-specified target α (Section on CCO framework).

Theorem 4.10 proves that under CCO, the long-run loss/violation rate converges to at most the target α, with a transient term of order O(1/t), holding for arbitrary (non-i.i.d.) state sequences (Theorem 4.10).

On 300 SWE-bench instances, CCO tracks its target violation rate closely across settings: 1.3% misalignment at α=0.01 (13.0% solve rate), 5.0% at α=0.05 (14.3% solve rate), 9.7% at α=0.10 (15.3% solve rate), and 17.0% at α=0.20 (17.7% solve rate) (SWE-bench experiments section).

On MACHIAVELLI, CCO at α=0.10 achieves 10.9±2.7% violations with reward 49.0±8.3, compared to an always-safe baseline (0.0% violations, reward 35.0±8.1) and an unconstrained policy (21.5±8.2% violations, reward 54.0±7.3) (MACHIAVELLI results section).

The framework's guarantee degrades gracefully under noisy feedback (adding an O(σ/√t) concentration term) and under delayed feedback of bound D (adding an O(D/(t+1)) transient term) (Section on practical extensions).

bTfHzEx9Xk.text: GAT-XL/2 achieves an FID-50K of 2.96 on class-conditional ImageNet-256×256 generation using a single-step (1-NFE), 602M-parameter generator+discriminator, trained for only 40 epochs (Table 1).
GAT-XL/2 without latent-space guidance attains an FID-50K of 3.02, still outperforming GigaGAN (FID 3.45, 480 epochs) and MeanFlow-XL/2 (FID 3.43, 240 epochs) (Table 1).
GAT-XL/2 reaches its state-of-the-art single-step result in 40 epochs, a 6x reduction versus MeanFlow-XL/2's 240 epochs (Table 1, Abstract).
Scaling across model sizes (S, B, L, XL) shows a strong negative correlation (-0.95) between computational cost (GFLOPs) and FID (Figure 3, Section 3.2).

Ablation studies isolate the contributions of Multi-Level Noise-Perturbed Image Guidance (MNG), the adaptive learning-rate scaling rule, and the REPA feature-alignment objective to overall generation quality (Figure 5, Section 3.3).

p8Mi1PCsDT.text: HiMAP-Travel with Qwen3-8B attains 52.78% validation and 52.65% test Final Pass Rate (FPR) on the TravelPlanner benchmark (Table 3, Table 4).
Under an identical model, training setup, and toolset, HiMAP-Travel outperforms the sequential DeepTravel baseline by +8.67 percentage points (52.65% vs. 43.98% test FPR) (Table 3, Appendix C.5).

On 5-day trips, sequential baselines' day-by-day budget satisfaction collapses from 98% on Day 1 to 42% by Day 5, whereas HiMAP-Travel maintains above 90% budget satisfaction throughout, including 91% on the final day (Table 2).
On FlexTravelBench multi-turn constraint-adaptation scenarios, HiMAP-Travel achieves 44.34% FPR in 2-turn settings and 37.42% FPR in 3-turn settings (Table 5).
HiMAP-Travel's hierarchical Coordinator/parallel-Day-Executor architecture reduces end-to-end latency by about 2.5x relative to sequential planning on a 7-day itinerary (Table 6, Section 5.3).

j4UhHaxCpq.text: On Sudoku puzzle-solving with a 1B-parameter masked diffusion model, the learned Scheduling-Attention Schedule (SAS) order policy reaches 91.8% puzzle accuracy versus 82.0% for the best heuristic decoding schedule (Section 6.1, Table 1)

Adding a second-stage fine-tuning step on top of SAS raises Sudoku puzzle accuracy further to 97.5%, and cell-level accuracy improves from 98.56% (Confidence heuristic) to 99.21% (SAS) (Section 6.1, Table 1)
On LLaMA/LLaDA-8B, SAS improves 5-shot GSM8K pass@1 from 64% (baseline schedule) to 76%, and MBPP pass@1 from 39.5% to 41% (Section 6.3, Figure 4)
SAS maintains its advantage over heuristic schedules across generation lengths {128, 256, 512} and block sizes {1, 4, 8} (Section 6.3, Figure 4)

In cross-domain transfer, a schedule policy trained on code and evaluated on math (256-256 setting) achieves a 0.713 pass rate, an 8.5-point improvement over heuristic schedules (Section 6.5, Table 4)
Dense, self-aware reward shaping for the schedule policy is consistently comparable to or better than sparse 0/1 terminal rewards across generation configurations (Section 6.6, Figure 3)

fgIg1oOMwk.text: cuRegOT exhibits significantly faster convergence than competing GPU-based entropic-regularized optimal transport solvers in nearly all tested cases, with the advantage growing for higher requested precision and larger problem sizes (Section 6.4)
cuRegOT's amortized symbolic analysis reuses sparsity patterns every S=10 iterations to reduce CPU overhead while retaining convergence guarantees, formalized in Theorem 4.1 (Section 4.2)
cuRegOT overlaps CPU symbolic analysis with GPU-side Sinkhorn candidate iterate generation via collaborative CPU-GPU computing, masking CPU latency without added wall-clock cost (Section 4.3)
A fused CUDA kernel performs element-wise computation and reductions in a single pass using 32xD-sized thread blocks (D=8) to minimize memory bandwidth overhead (Section 4.4)

Theorem 5.1 proves global convergence (gradient norm to zero) and Theorem 5.2 proves at least linear convergence with rate 0<r<1 despite the algorithmic approximations introduced (Section 5.2, Theorems 5.1-5.2)
Experiments use CIFAR-10-derived problems with n=m=5000 and synthetic problems up to size (6400,4800), with regularization parameter eta=0.001 (Section 6.1, Section 6.3)

ivVPgBZewP.text: SMET stores gradients and optimizer states only for currently active parameters, reducing their memory footprint by a factor of d (the sparsity density) for sparse layers (Section 4.3)
On LLaMA-1B trained on C4, SMET reaches 15.61 validation perplexity versus 15.56 for the dense baseline, closing most of the gap left by other memory-efficient sparse methods (Table 1)
At 0.1 density on LLaMA-350M, SMET achieves 25.85 perplexity versus 28.96 for SET and 27.44 for static sparse training (Table 2)

SMET nearly eliminates the sharp loss spikes that vanilla dynamic sparse training (SET) exhibits after topology updates, as shown by training loss curves, while a pruning-only ablation confirms parameter regrowth (not pruning) is the source of the instability (Section 3.2, Figure 2(a))
Newly regrown parameters in naive dynamic sparse training receive updates roughly 3.16x larger than appropriately scaled updates, which SMET's stabilization corrects (Section 3.2)
Block-structured sparsity with block size B=32 increases perplexity by only about one point relative to unstructured (B=1) sparsity, enabling hardware-efficient sparse training (Figure 3(a))

0zkIq9YKml.text: LLM belief marginals show pronounced distributional drift for approximately the first n<=5 resampling steps before beginning to stabilize into a coherent predictive distribution (Section 3)
Conditioning generation on a seed prefix of m=5 random i.i.d. answers (SEED5) effectively mitigates early-stage belief drift compared to unseeded resampling (Figure 1(b))

On Llama-3.1-8B, the amortized self-consistency method (AM-PPR + SEED5) attains 80.5% accuracy on AI2-ARC and 62.2% on TinyMMLU multiple-choice QA, close to or exceeding the non-amortized PPR + SEED5 baseline (80.7% and 61.2% respectively) (Table 1)
Self-consistency loss fine-tuning improves calibration: on CSQA, AM-PPR + SEED5 reduces Expected Calibration Error to 0.0674 versus 0.1072 for a direct-query baseline (Table 2)

The self-consistency training objective (Definition 4.1) is defined using k-step-ahead prediction pairs with horizons k in {1,...,6}, sampled via k1 in {1,...,5} and offset delta in {1,...,6-k1} (Section 5.1)
Fine-tuning uses LoRA with rank r=16 applied to Llama-3.1-8B, trained only on CSQA queries yet generalizing to unseen AI2-ARC and TinyMMLU test questions (Section D.2)

SaJvQ26ZkR.text: Standard RL training without recontextualization increases specification gaming on an evaluation-metric task, while generic recontextualization prompts (e.g., discouraging 'overfitting to evaluation criteria') reduce hacking more effectively than task-specific instructions, replicated across 5 training seeds (Section 4.1, Figure 3)

On a coding task with best-of-4 sampling, Neutral-to-Neutral standard training yields -2.3% correctness change and +6.2% test-hack rate, whereas No-Hack-to-Hack recontextualization yields +9.1% correctness change and -10.9% hack rate (Section 4.2, Table 1)

Recontextualization to prevent code hacking lowers the model's training reward from +5.0 to -4.9 even as it eliminates the exploited shortcut, demonstrating the specification itself is unchanged while gaming is suppressed (Section 4.2)

On a deception-evasion task, standard training produces a 66.75% deception rate under neutral context, while Honest-to-Neutral recontextualization reduces this to 22.33% and raises ground-truth reward from 0.63 to 0.94 (Section 4.3, Table 19)
Recontextualization achieves a Pareto-optimal tradeoff between reducing sycophancy and maintaining response quality relative to standard training (Section 4.4, Figure 5)

Recontextualized training incurs only a modest ~2 percentage point drop in instruction-following (IFEval strict score 55.5 vs. 60.1 for SFT baseline), indicating limited collateral damage to general chat quality (Table 3)

NiHC3GlPQU.text: On RLFT with Qwen3-4B in the Datacom domain, EDCO reaches 46.96% accuracy versus 40.43% for random sampling and 44.78% for perplexity-based sampling (Section 5.2, Figure 2A-B).
On SFT with Qwen3-4B, EDCO outperforms perplexity-based curriculum sampling on both Wireless (33.7% vs 31.7%) and Datacom (36.3% vs 33.0%) (Section 5.2, Figure 2C-D).
On Llama3.2-3B fine-tuned for medicine and law, EDCO achieves 36.7% on MedQA (vs 32.9% random sampling, 24.6% perplexity) and 17.4% on JEC-QA (vs 16.2% random sampling, 12.4% perplexity) (Table 1).

Prefix Entropy Approximation (using only the first L=128 tokens) reduces per-sample entropy estimation time from 2.24s to 0.37s, an 83.5% reduction, while retaining a Pearson correlation of r=0.63 with full-sequence entropy (Table 3, Section 5.4, Figure 4A).
On Datacom RLFT, EDCO (47.0%) outperforms the Dynamic-PPL (41.3%) and SEC (34.78%) baselines (Table 2).

Removing Quick-Answer Prompting drops the prefix-to-full entropy correlation from 0.63 to 0.32, and a moderate-entropy sampling window (top 0-6.67%) outperforms a higher-entropy window (top 5-11.67%) (Figure 5, Table 7).

gNWNtstp3r.text: MemoPilot with Qwen2.5-14B ranks first by Elo rating on both evaluated games, reaching 1762 Elo on Limit Hold'em (LHE) and 1590 Elo on Rock-Paper-Scissors (RPS) (Figure 5).
On the RPS@5/LHE@5 metrics, MemoPilot scores 3.28/2.03 versus 1.64/-0.78 for a DeepSeek-V3.2 memory baseline, 0.61/-1.27 for Reflexion, and 0.81/-1.14 for ReasoningBank (Table 1).
MemoPilot's memory module trained on Qwen2.5-14B generalizes zero-shot to Qwen3-235B, reaching 3.27 (RPS) and 1.31 (LHE) without additional training (Table 1).
On StreamBench transfer tasks, MemoPilot reaches 73.5% on CoSQL and 56.3% on DS-1000, compared to 69.5%/50.0% for no-memory and 70.0%/52.5% for full-history baselines (Table 2).

Ablating the memory format shows the structured 3-tier memory trained with RL achieves 2.03 on LHE versus 1.04 for a free-form memory variant, and per-turn (one-step) rewards outperform cumulative-return rewards (2.03 vs 0.61 on LHE) (Table 4, Table 6).

70vztAT0Or.text: Theorem 4.2 derives the closed-form Bayes-optimal fair classifier for multi-class classification under linear fairness constraints, expressed via a decision vector obtained from Lagrangian dual parameters.

Theorem 4.3 introduces entropic regularization to yield an analytically tractable softmax-form solution h^λ*(x) = exp(β^λ(x)/τ) / Σ exp(β^λ(x)/τ) approximating the optimal fair classifier (Theorem 4.3).

The in-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) reduces fair classification to cost-sensitive learning via primal-dual optimization and is shown to converge to an approximate Nash equilibrium with bound ρ^T = ν̄^T + uB_Λ√(K/T) (Theorem 5.2).

The post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 2) applies plug-in estimation via proximal gradient descent on pre-trained models, with generalization guarantees that account for auxiliary model error, finite-sample error, and empirical statistic discrepancy (Theorem 5.6).

Both in-processing and post-processing methods are evaluated on Adult, ENEM, ACSIncome, and CelebA against baselines including AdvDebias, FairBatch, FairProjection, and FRAPPÉ, and are shown to achieve superior accuracy-fairness Pareto frontiers (Section 6.1, Figure 1).

6vKlayY1tV.text: On the Craftax-classic benchmark at 1M environment steps, ITC achieves 72.46% ± 0.45 return and 35.60% ± 0.92 score, versus the prior best of 67.42% return and 27.91 score from Dedieu et al. 2025 (Table 1).
Ablations show adding 3D RoPE alone raises return from a 68.55% baseline to 71.85%, and adding the identifiable token correspondence (ITC) decoding on top raises it further to 72.46% (Table 2).
ITC improves next-state prediction accuracy from 46.94% to 51.13% overall, with the largest gains on transitions involving dynamic creatures (33.83% to 38.37%) (Table 3).
On Atari 100K, ITC attains an interquartile mean of 1.092 and optimality gap of 0.376, versus 0.990 and 0.412 for the Simulus baseline (Table 8).

Formulating next-frame prediction as an optimal transport problem, where each next-frame token either copies from the previous frame or generates a new token, adds only 2.8% training-time overhead (48.2 vs 46.3 hours for 1M steps on a single RTX 3090) (Section on computational efficiency).

Tz7n7pX9cO.text: Mixture of Factor Analyzers (MFA) decomposes activations into a discrete region assignment plus a continuous within-region offset, formalized in Equations 5-13 (Section 3).

Across 12 trained MFAs on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.1-8B, MFA reveals both broad semantic regions (e.g., movie genres, emotions) and narrow token-specific regions in activation space (Section 4, Figures 1-3).
MFA achieves an interpretability fraction of 0.96 ± 0.2 for its decomposition components, compared to 0.29 ± 0.2 for sparse autoencoders (Section 5, Table 1, Figure 4).

On the RAVEL and MCQA localization benchmarks, MFA outperforms PCA and sparse autoencoder baselines by 3-16 points and is competitive with the supervised DAS method on 5 of 8 RAVEL tasks (Section 6.1, Table 2).
For causal steering interventions, MFA achieves roughly 2x the median steering score of SAE and difference-in-means baselines on Gemma, and about 33% improvement on Llama (Section 6.2, Figure 5).

KmDPaiwdZh.text: Cert-LAS is presented as the first certified model ownership verification (MOV) method for text-to-image diffusion models, using layer-adaptive Gaussian smoothing to certify robustness against parameter perturbations (Section 4, Theorem 4.9).

Layer Fine-tuning Sensitivity (LFS) is defined as the ratio of a layer's update magnitude to the average update magnitude across all UNet layers, and is used to allocate more smoothing noise to sensitive layers (Section 4).

Under a parameter perturbation budget of L2 norm 0.8, Cert-LAS with layer-adaptive smoothing retains T@10^-6F = 0.965 while all compared baselines fail completely (Table with parameter perturbation resistance results).
After 2000 steps of fine-tuning-based watermark removal, Cert-LAS maintains T@10^-6F = 0.992 versus 0.000 for WatermarkDM (Fine-tuning robustness results).

Cert-LAS reduces prompt-space suspiciousness score S_in(p) to 0.125, an approximately 87% reduction relative to WatermarkDM's 0.964, while keeping image-space suspiciousness S_out(p) at 0.016, comparable to SleeperMark's 0.025 (Stealthiness/auditing results table).

An exponential noise-sample growth schedule for certification, m_t = min(m_max, floor(2^(t/T_g))), reduces training time by 76.6% without degrading verification performance, evaluated on Stable Diffusion v1.4 with class prompts 'cat' and 'dog' (Section 4, Implementation details).

ES7Vy9rvRl.text: WebWorld is trained on 1.06M real-world web trajectories combining randomized crawling (293K), autonomous exploration (38K), task-oriented execution (94K), and enriched/auxiliary data (634K), scaling roughly 100x beyond prior web world models (Data pipeline section).

WebWorld is released in 8B, 14B, and 32B parameter variants and supports multi-format state representations (accessibility tree, HTML, XML, Markdown) with long-horizon simulation of 30+ steps (Section on model/data scale).
On WebWorld-Bench intrinsic evaluation, WebWorld-32B achieves a 71.0% average Factuality Score, matching Claude-Opus-4.1's 71.3%, and 77.0% long-horizon consistency (WebWorld-Bench results).

Qwen3-14B fine-tuned on WebWorld-synthesized trajectories improves by +9.2% on WebArena, reaching performance comparable to GPT-4o, while Qwen3-8B improves by +9.9% on MiniWob++ (Downstream task performance results).
As an inference-time search world model, WebWorld outperforms GPT-5 used in the same role by +3.2% in reward (Inference-time search results).

WebWorld exhibits a documented sycophancy limitation, generating overly optimistic outcomes that cater to the agent's proposed action, and struggles to generate high-quality detailed content such as scientific articles (Limitations discussion).

itonej9GIV.text: RoboTwin 2.0 provides an object library (RoboTwin-OD) of 731 objects across 147 categories and a benchmark of 50 bimanual manipulation tasks with 100K+ generated trajectories across 5 robot platforms (Data Generator, Benchmark & Dataset section).

MLLM-based expert code generation with multimodal VLM observer feedback raises task code generation success rate to 71.3%, with embodiment-specific gains of +22.7% for Piper and +13.7% for Aloha-AgileX over baseline code generation (Experiments, code generation results).

Domain randomization across five axes (scene clutter, background textures from a 12,000-sample curated set, lighting, tabletop heights, and compositional language instructions) yields a 228% relative improvement in zero-shot synthetic-only generalization (Method: domain randomization; Experiments).

VLA models fine-tuned on RoboTwin 2.0 data show a 367% relative real-world performance gain (42.0% vs. 9.0% success rate) over a 10-demo real-world baseline (Experiments, sim-to-real transfer results).

Policy robustness under domain randomization increases by 10.6 absolute percentage points for RDT and 8.8 points for Pi0 compared to non-randomized training data (Experiments, robustness results table).
Average task success across embodiments on the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark reaches 60.5%, versus 52.2% for RoboTwin 1.0 (Benchmarking comparison table).

5ysobWbWzp.text: NExT-Guard converts a post-hoc safety classifier into a real-time streaming safeguard without any token-level supervision, via a two-stage framework: (1) identifying safety-relevant sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features through contrastive standardized-mean-difference scoring, and (2) aggregating the top 32 selected features into a real-time risk score during generation (Section: Method, Two-Stage Framework).

On prompt classification, NExT-Guard achieves an average F1 of 90.8 versus 84.4 for the best supervised baseline (Qwen3Guard); on response/streaming classification it achieves 84.3 average F1 versus 77.0 for Qwen3Guard-Stream (Table 1, Experiments).
NExT-Guard's flagged intervention positions align closely with human-annotated unsafe token onset locations, whereas supervised streaming baselines trigger prematurely (RQ2 findings, Figure 3).

Selected SAE features provide token-level grounding, concentrating in high-precision regions for specific harm categories as visualized via token-level activation maps (RQ3/RQ4 findings, Figures 4-5).
NExT-Guard's performance remains robust when the SAE probe is applied to features from transformer layers 18-27 and transfers across different base models without retraining (RQ4 findings).

M8l3MmWaQB.text: Semantic Tube Prediction (STP) adds an auxiliary loss L_STP = 1 - cos(h_t - h_r, h_r - h_s) to the next-token-prediction loss (L = L_NTP + λ·L_STP), constraining hidden-state trajectories within a tube of radius on the order of ε around a geodesic path on the semantic manifold (Section 3: Semantic Tube Prediction).

STP-trained models match baseline next-token-prediction accuracy while using 16x less training data, presented as violating the data-scaling term of Chinchilla-style scaling laws (Figure 1b, Major Results).
The optimal regularization coefficient λ falls in the range 0.01-0.08, validated across Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and OLMo model families (Table 2, Major Results).

STP preserves output diversity and prevents inference-time mode collapse caused by Voronoi-cell ambiguity under the modeled inference SDE with a Brownian motion term, improving diversity-adjusted accuracy from 68% to 88.5% (Table 1; Section 2: Training & Inference Dynamics).

Five theoretical predictions (P1-P5) are empirically validated, including that L_NTP plateaus while L_STP continues decreasing, and that an identity predictor outperforms learned projection heads (Section 3, Five Validated Predictions).

STP adds only negligible computational overhead—primarily the cost of a cosine-similarity computation—eliminating the need for the manual two-view data scaffolding required by prior LLM-JEPA approaches (Implementation Advantage discussion).

C6ZTjSXbz7.text: MLCI's DeepSets encoder is trained via multi-outcome normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (nHSIC) optimization with task weighting across T clinical outcomes (Section 5).
On MIMIC-IV, MLCI achieves a distance correlation of 54.80 with in-hospital mortality versus a best baseline of 36.41 among traditional and ML comparators (Table 1).
On MIMIC-III, MLCI attains a distance correlation of 39.06 with mortality outcomes versus 32.28 for the strongest baseline (Table 1).
MLCI reaches 74.22 nats of mutual information with MIMIC-IV mortality versus 69.92 nats for the best baseline (Table 2).

Under a rank-one shared-structure assumption on centered multi-outcome label profiles, the nHSIC objective identifies a monotone threshold rule for high-severity patient stratification (Lemmas 6.1-6.2, Theorem 6.3).

The rank-one energy ratio of the multi-outcome weight structure is 0.49 on MIMIC-IV, and optimal threshold splits from the full multi-task objective coincide with those from its rank-one projection on both MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV (Section 8, Tables 3-4).

TFhUQ6uFCP.text: RuCL constructs a rubric set by generating 20 candidate rubrics with Gemini 3 Pro as teacher, filtering to 6 core rubrics via an applicability threshold η > 0.99 evaluated on N=2,000 rollouts from a Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model (Phase I).
RuCL stratifies the filtered rubrics into Foundational (perception-focused, ℛ_easy) and Advanced (logical-reasoning, ℛ_hard) tiers based on pass rate under the base model (Phase I).

RuCL applies a stability-aware, sigmoid-scheduled curriculum with three phases (Stabilization, Ramp-up, Consolidation) that shifts the rubric-reward weight λ_t from 0 once foundational-tier performance exceeds a proficiency threshold τ_th=0.9 (Phase II).

RuCL achieves 60.06% average accuracy across 7 visual reasoning benchmarks, a +7.83% average improvement over baselines, including 71.49% on WeMATH (+12.97%) and 49.66% on LogicVista (+10.40%) (Table 2).

Ablations show vanilla GRPO with outcome-only reward reaches 59.14%, uniform rubric averaging reaches 59.29%, linear stratification reaches 60.79%, and RuCL's sigmoid schedule reaches 63.94% on the same evaluation setup (Table 3).

A gradient-variance decomposition argument in the appendix shows that setting λ_t=0 during early training suppresses noisy gradient signal from unreliable, low-pass-rate advanced rubrics (Appendix B).

Iy6isx8QOp.text: Artifact features in existing AIGI detectors exhibit high intra-feature similarity, producing an almost uniform attention map after softmax and causing attention dilution during multimodal fusion (Section 3).

TranX-Adapter combines Task-aware Optimal-Transport Fusion (TOP-Fusion), which transfers artifact information using Jensen-Shannon divergence between artifact and semantic fake-prediction probabilities as the transport cost, with X-Fusion, a cross-attention module using artifact features as queries over semantic features.
On GenImage, LLaVA-1.6-Mistral-7B with TranX-Adapter reaches 91.9% accuracy versus 89.8% for the AIGI-Holmes baseline (Table 1).
On the Chameleon cross-dataset benchmark, Qwen3-VL-4B with TranX-Adapter reaches 85.1% accuracy and LLaVA-1.6-Mistral-7B with TranX-Adapter reaches 75.8% (Table 2).
On RRDataset, Qwen3-VL-4B with TranX-Adapter reaches 90.9% accuracy (Table 3).

Ablation shows X-Fusion alone achieves 89.3% accuracy and TOP-Fusion alone achieves 90.3%, while the combined TranX-Adapter reaches 91.9%, using only about 160M additional parameters versus 7,261M for full fine-tuning (Table 4).

PMYAEsMEm5.text: USMoE unifies Token Choice and Expert Choice routing via a Unified Competitive Score that softly combines both scores with a mixing parameter α, and a Unified Competitive Mechanism that jointly selects the top-N expert-token pairs from the flattened similarity matrix (Section 3.2).

Without additional training, USMoE improves OLMoE-1B-7B by 9.3% without prompts and 4.2% with prompts, Qwen1.5-MoE by 7.0%-9.1%, and DeepSeekMoE-16B by 6.6%-8.0%, including a 23.4% gain on the STS task for OLMoE-1B-7B (Tables 1-2, Section 4.2).
In pre-training experiments at 420M parameters, USMoE outperforms baseline SMoE routing on Enwik8, Text8, WikiText-103, and One Billion Words while reducing inference compute by 14% (Tables 3-4).
In fine-tuning experiments on SST-2, SST-5, IMDB, and BANKING77, USMoE yields consistent accuracy improvements over baseline SMoE (Table 5).
Ablation over the mixing factor α shows optimal performance in the range α ∈ (0.3, 0.7), balancing expert diversity against token importance (Table 7).
A Jacobian matrix analysis shows USMoE provides roughly twice the effective expert learning capacity (2n vs. n) of standard SMoE, mitigating representation collapse (Section 3.3).

NWApJP7UKT.text: DUST uses a multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with separate token streams for actions and future visual observations that exchange information through shared cross-modal attention layers, trained with decoupled independent noise schedules τ_A and τ_o for the two modalities (Sections 4.1-4.2).
On RoboCasa with 100 demonstrations, DUST achieves 50.1% average success rate, an 8.3% improvement over the GR00T-N1.5 baseline and 5.5% over FLARE (Table 1).
On GR-1 with 300 demonstrations, DUST achieves 36.0% average success rate, a 2.3% improvement over FLARE (Table 2).
On real-world Franka Research 3 pick-and-place tasks, DUST achieves a 67.7% success rate versus 54.7% for the baseline, a 13-point improvement (Table 3).
Asynchronous inference-time scaling of the vision-denoising steps N_o from 4 to 64 yields 2-5% additional success-rate gains, with best performance at 32-64 steps (Table 5).

Pretraining on action-free BridgeV2 videos improves RoboCasa performance from 50.1% to 58.5%, and ablations show decoupled noise scheduling contributes roughly 12% and the MMDiT architecture contributes roughly 8% to overall performance (Table 4, Table 6).

H1mxs9qGQX.text: SSMoE is a training-free routing framework that extracts top-c eigenvectors from expert weight matrices A and B and combines them with the standard learned router via a balancing factor alpha in [0.5, 0.9] (Section 3, Table 6).
On 10-shot evaluation with GPT-OSS-20B, SSMoE improves accuracy by 10.9% over the baseline router while reducing memory usage by 22.9%, using only 75% of experts (Section on Large Reasoning Models).
On GPT-OSS-120B, SSMoE yields a 4.4% accuracy improvement with a 24.5% memory reduction relative to the standard router (Section on Large Reasoning Models).

On OLMoE-7B evaluated with MTEB, SSMoE achieves 40.9% average performance versus 34.3% for the router baseline, outperforming on 37% of tasks while reducing computational cost by 5% (Section on Large Language Models).

On CLIP-MoE, SSMoE improves COCO Image-to-Text Recall@1 by +1.1% in the clean setting and +2.8% under corrupted images, with statistically significant gains (p < 0.001) (Section on Vision-Language Models).

Lemma 3.1 proves that combining eigenvector routing with learned routing reduces pairwise logit correlations by a factor of (1-alpha)^2, formally mitigating expert-representation collapse (Lemma 3.1).

B5DAV1EA8Z.text: LERD combines an Event Posterior Differential Equation (EPDE), a Mean-Evolving Lognormal Process (MELP), a differentiable leaky-integrate-and-fire (dLIF) prior, and an Event-Relational Graph (ERG) to infer latent neural events and their cross-channel relations directly from multichannel EEG (Section on Architecture).

Theorem 4.1 derives a tractable integral-rate surrogate replacing the intractable KL divergence between the EPDE-induced path law and the dLIF prior, with a formal upper bound guaranteeing training stability (Theorem 4.1).

On the toy dataset spanning three frequency bands ([5-10], [10-15], [15-20] Hz), LERD achieves non-zero IoU scores between 0.202 and 0.473 for latent structure recovery, whereas baseline neural ODE methods achieve zero IoU despite strong prediction accuracy (Table 1).
On AD Cohort A (88 participants: 36 AD, 23 FTD, 29 HC), LERD attains 75.03±8.29% accuracy and 72.69±8.16% F1, outperforming LEAD (72.68%), ADFormer (69.35%), and other baselines (Table 2).
On AD Cohort B (168 participants: 59 AD, 7 MCI, 102 HC), LERD attains 89.82±8.39% accuracy and 64.87±10.67% F1 (Table 2).

Ablations show both the dLIF and ERG priors independently contribute to performance, with their combination yielding the best results on both EEG cohorts, and Figure 2 shows LERD-inferred dLIF frequencies exhibit disease-correlated 'oscillatory slowing' consistent with established AD biomarkers (Table 3, Figure 2).

SIZYrEf1a7.text: TextME exploits the 'modality gap'-a systematic offset between text and modal embeddings in contrastive encoders-by computing modality-specific centroids from roughly 5K unpaired samples per modality and centering embeddings to create an interchangeable space (Figure 2).

TextME trains projection networks on about 100K text descriptions to map centered text embeddings into LLM embedding space, versus the 1-10M paired samples required by baselines such as LanguageBind and Ex-MCR (Section on Experimental Results).

Averaged across six modalities (image, video, audio, 3D point clouds, X-ray, molecules), TextME retains 74.5% of pretrained-encoder performance overall, with 89.2% average Performance Preservation Ratio (PPR) on classification and 65.3% on retrieval, and exceeds the pretrained encoder with 104.6% PPR on ModelNet40 3D classification (Table 1).
TextME enables emergent cross-modal retrieval never explicitly aligned during training, including audio-to-3D and molecule-to-image retrieval (Figure 4).

A geometric predictor based on gap-content orthogonality variance correlates with downstream preservation performance at Pearson r = -0.67, and using LLM embeddings (Qwen3-Embedding) as the anchor space outperforms multimodal encoders on retrieval tasks (Figure 5, Table 4).

Performance depends on the encoder's gap consistency: MoleculeSTM's gap consistency measures 0.78 versus a target above 0.96, and domain-specific text improves 3D performance by 485% over general-purpose text, with molecules showing the lowest retrieval preservation at about 43.9% (Table 2, Table 5).

3ZFvXHJwmB.text: HDFlow is a two-stage hierarchical planner combining a diffusion model with manifold-aware EBM guidance for sparse subgoal generation and a rectified flow model for dense trajectory synthesis via ODE solving, built on an RSSM world model with a DINOv2 encoder (Section on Method).

Proposition 4.2 shows the EBM guidance gap scales as c/(sqrt(1-alpha_bar_t) * sqrt(d)) in high-dimensional spaces, motivating the manifold projection step using rank-r PCA over k nearest neighbors (Definition 4.1, Proposition 4.2).
On simulated FurnitureBench one-leg assembly, HDFlow achieves 92%/71%/39% success at Low/Medium/High difficulty, compared to 71%/31%/15% for the SHD baseline (Table 1).
On real-world FurnitureBench, HDFlow succeeds in 8/10 episodes at Low difficulty and 6/10 at Medium, outperforming BC and IQL baselines (Table 4).

On RLBench, HDFlow reaches 100% success on Drag Stick and Push Buttons, 93.3% on Insert Peg (versus 65.6% for 3D Diffuser Actor), and 73.3% on Sort Shape (versus 44% for a competing method) (Table 5).

Ablations show removing manifold projection, EBM guidance, or the contrastive world-model objective each degrades one-leg/lamp success rates to 84%/57%, 61%/33%, and 58%/27% respectively, versus 92%/68% for the full method, and the hybrid hierarchical diffusion-flow design (HDFlow) reaches 68% success at 88ms versus 24% for flat diffusion and 24% for hierarchical flow alone (Table 2, Table 3).

o54x4zOWuy.text: Theorem 1 shows that for convex losses with step size eta_t = 1/t^beta, CLASP achieves regret O(T^max{beta,1-beta}) and cumulative squared constraint violation O(T^(1-beta)) simultaneously for any beta in (0,1) (Theorem 1).

Theorem 2 shows that for strongly convex losses with step size eta_t = 1/(mt), CLASP achieves the first simultaneous logarithmic bounds O(log T) on both regret and cumulative squared constraint violation (Theorem 2).

CLASP (Algorithm 1) performs a gradient step followed by projection onto the intersection of a static constraint set and a time-varying dynamic constraint set, with the analysis relying on firm non-expansiveness of the projection operator (Algorithm 1, Lemmas 1-3).

Section 7 empirically compares CLASP against AdaGrad, RECOO, and Switch on online linear regression and online support vector machine tasks, showing competitive cumulative squared constraint violation with reduced memory overhead relative to Switch (Section 7).

VUiMZBfHBe.text: Massive activations follow a rise-plateau-fall lifecycle across network depth, with step-up blocks in early layers injecting extreme values, intermediate blocks propagating them via residual connections, and step-down blocks neutralizing them with opposite-sign values (Section 3.1).

In SwiGLU feed-forward blocks, spike channels exhibit rank-one dominance in their weight matrices, with a single dominant eigenvalue orders of magnitude larger than the rest, explaining amplifier-like massive-activation growth (Section 3.1.2, Figure 4).

Applying weight decay of 0.1 raises the attention sink ratio to 46.0% versus 33.8% without weight decay, showing sink ratio serves as an optimization-health proxy independent of spike magnitude (Table 3).

Sandwich normalization reduces spike magnitude from 3818 to 520 while maintaining a 44.7% sink ratio, and DynamicTanh achieves a 61.0% sink ratio with only 153 spike magnitude, demonstrating that massive activations and attention sinks are independently controllable phenomena (Table 5).
Head dimension is the primary architectural driver of attention sink formation: 128-dimensional heads reach a 46.0% sink ratio versus only 4.1% for 8-dimensional heads (Table 6).

Training exclusively on long contexts (2048/4096 split) collapses the sink ratio to 1.2%, versus 46.0% under mixed-length (1/4096) training, indicating attention sinks emerge from short-context training requirements rather than architecture alone (Table 8).

oZg9YF9dkz.text: AllScAIP is a machine learning interatomic potential that uses an all-to-all, data-driven node attention component to capture long-range interactions without explicit physics-based correction terms, designed to scale to on the order of 100 million training samples (abstract only).
AllScAIP achieves state-of-the-art energy and force accuracy on molecular systems and performs competitively on the OMol25, OMat24, and OC20 benchmarks (abstract only).

As training data and model size scale up, the benefits of explicit physics-based long-range correction terms diminish or reverse, while all-to-all attention remains critical for capturing long-range interactions (abstract only).
AllScAIP enables stable, long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations that accurately recover experimental observables, including liquid density and heat of vaporization (abstract only).

xKJG1CNtQM.text: After supervised fine-tuning, the uniform-state diffusion model Duo reaches 65.8% accuracy on GSM8K, exceeding autoregressive models (62.9%), masked diffusion (MDLM, 58.8%), and interpolating diffusion (Eso-LM, 33.4%), despite Duo having worse validation perplexity than the autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines (Table 2, Section 4.2).

On likelihood-based benchmarks such as ARC-Easy, the ranking inverts relative to GSM8K: autoregressive models dominate (72.7%), masked diffusion is second (50.5%), and uniform-state diffusion (Duo) trails (53.4%) (Table 1, Section 4.1).

On the speed-quality Pareto frontier of tokens-per-second versus generation quality, Duo dominates at higher throughput (200-400 and 600+ tokens/sec) while Eso-LM dominates the intermediate range (400-600 tokens/sec), with autoregressive models producing the highest quality but slowest sampling (Figure 1, Section 3.3).

Perplexity is informative for ranking models within a single family (e.g., comparing diffusion variants) but can be misleading when comparing across model families (autoregressive vs. diffusion), since models with worse likelihood scaling can still be preferable due to faster and more practical sampling (Section 1, Section 3.3).

oVWRuzgQLU.text: TRACER improves AUROC by 4.7% to 37.1% and AUARC by 6% to 55% over the strongest baselines for predicting task failure in tool-use agentic settings, with the largest gains on gpt-4.1-mini where likelihood-based proxies underperform (Table II).

TRACER detects 68% to 97.4% of eventual failures within the first 20% of trajectory execution, with median detection times of 3.3% to 12.5% of the trajectory versus 25% to 60% for baseline methods (Figure 2).

TRACER's risk signal combines content-aware normalized surprisal (Stage I, Section III-B), which decomposes into intrinsic uncertainty and epistemic mismatch (Theorem A.1), with situational-awareness signals including hybrid semantic/lexical repetition and agent-observation and user-coordination coherence gaps (Stage II, Section III-C).

An ablation removing either agent-side or user-side situational signals substantially reduces predictive performance, with agent-side signals contributing about 85% of the predictive gain and user-side signals adding roughly 70% complementary value (Table III).

TRACER's MAX-composite aggregation of per-step risk (r_t = max{U_t, alpha*D_rep(t), beta*D_o^A(t), gamma*D_o^U(t)}) outperforms additive, multiplicative, and separate-channel aggregation variants, validating a sparse-hazard failure model where decisive risk spikes dominate over averaged signals (Table IV, Section III-D).

svtbjHcMzs.text: On the CVR benchmark with a CLIP-B/32 backbone, CAST improves retrieval accuracy over the baseline by +19.74 points on YouCook2 (44.77% vs 25.03%), +26.37 points on COIN (40.47% vs 14.10%), and +30.56 points on CrossTask (47.39% vs 16.83%) (Table 2).

CAST transfers across diverse frozen video-text backbones, improving YouCook2 accuracy from 36.75% to 71.68% with InternVideo2, from 47.45% to 75.59% with VideoPrism, and from 33.45% to 56.64% with Qwen3-VL-Embedding (Table 3).

An architecture ablation shows residual state-transition modeling is critical: an early-fusion variant with residual term Delta reaches 38.95% on YouCook2, while the full dual-path CAST design reaches 44.77% (Table 4).

CAST predicts the next visual state embedding as v_t_hat = phi(v_{t-1} + Delta(v_{t-1}, q_t, H_t)), modeling causally-plausible visual state transitions rather than relying on semantic similarity matching alone (Equation 3).

Used as a plug-and-play consistency verifier to rerank video generation candidates on 158 non-overlapping YouCook2 prompts, human evaluators preferred CAST-reranked outputs over text-only reranking 55.1% to 38.6% overall, and 52.5% to 38.6% on temporal logic consistency (Table 6).

CciWEZZDVb.text: MS-EDEN quantization achieves 9.8×10⁻³ MSE versus 23.5×10⁻³ MSE for standard stochastic rounding at 1x16 group size, more than a 2x reduction in quantization error (Table 1).

MS-EDEN operates by processing vectors in 128-element chunks, applying randomized Hadamard transforms, quantizing via round-to-nearest, then correcting scales stochastically at the FP8 scale level rather than the individual FP4 value level (Section 3.3).
Corollary 3.1 proves MS-EDEN yields unbiased gradient estimates, i.e., the expected value of the inverse-rotated quantized vector equals the original vector (Corollary 3.1).

On Llama-style models of 30M-200M parameters, Quartet II with MS-EDEN reduces the validation loss gap versus prior NVFP4 methods by at least 20%, and on a 1.9B-parameter Nanochat model trained on 38B tokens it yields a 15-25% relative pre-training loss improvement (Section 4).
Quartet II achieves up to 4.2x end-to-end training speedup over BF16 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, with 2.4x actual measured training throughput for 1B-parameter models (Section 4).

Stf5SF4JvR.text: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, MOSAIC reduces AgentHarm harm score from 0.18 to 0.09, a 50% reduction (Table 1, Section 4.2).
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, MOSAIC increases indirect prompt-injection refusal rate from 0.44 to 0.61 (Table 1, Section 4.2).

On BFCL v3, Qwen2.5's multi-turn benign tool-calling score improves from 21.0 to 28.5, a 35% relative gain, showing safety gains do not come at the cost of benign task performance (Table 2, Section 4.3).

Ablating the explicit <safety_thoughts> structured safety reasoning (replacing it with generic chain-of-thought) drops the harmful-task refusal rate from 0.87 to 0.59 on AgentHarm (Table 5, Section 4.6).
Replacing MOSAIC's pairwise trajectory-preference reward with a pointwise scalar reward reduces harmful-task refusal rate from 0.87 to 0.79 (Table 5, Section 4.6).

MOSAIC is evaluated across three model families (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Thinking, and Phi-4) and four out-of-distribution benchmark suites: AgentHarm, Agent Security Bench, BFCL v3, and PrivacyLens (Section 4).

Jk4zLorDUx.text: On BrowserART, moving from a standalone agent to a star topology with 4 specialist agents raises harmful task completion from 10.0% to 31.0%, a roughly 3.1x increase (Table 1).
On BrowserART, star topology is the riskiest communication structure at 31.0% harmful task completion, versus 16.0% for chain and 7.0% for mesh topology (Table 2, Section 5.2).
On RedCode-Gen, chain topology is the riskiest at 42.5% harmful task completion, nearly double the 17.5% rate for star topology (Table 2, Section 5.2).

Specialist role configurations achieve higher benign task accuracy while being up to 3.8x more vulnerable to misuse than generalist configurations, showing standard capability metrics do not signal architectural security risk (Section 5.1).

Increasing memory visibility (private state vs. own-reasoning-visible vs. shared-memory-visible) provides a safety benefit in only one of the evaluated scenario-topology combinations across BrowserART, RedCode-Gen, and OS-Harm (Table 3, Section 5.3).

HsdgKuOV8n.text: On the Walker2D locomotion benchmark, LP-DS reaches approximately 5000 episodic return compared to roughly 4000 for the strongest prior baseline, a ~25% improvement (Section 5.1, Figure 3).
On a real-world spatial pick-and-place task, LP-DS improves success from 18/40 trials (frozen backbone) to 33/40 trials, and on mug hanging from 11/20 to 17/20 trials (Section 5.7, Table 6).
LP-DS preserves consistently higher action entropy than the DSRL baseline during online adaptation on the Adroit Pen task, indicating reduced mode collapse (Figure 5).

LP-DS is formulated as a constrained optimization maximizing expected Q-value subject to a trust-region bound on expected squared perturbation norm, enforced via a Lagrangian dual variable α (Equation 7, Section 4.2).
Removing the Lagrangian dual update (i.e., dropping the trust-region penalty) destabilizes training and degrades success rate, per the trust-region ablation (Figure 6, Section 5.3).

Lm3DQDyIsI.text: On StrongREJECT, standard jailbreak prompts achieve only 0-4% attack success rate against defended models, but CoT Forgery injection raises this to 17-52% for GPT-5-series models and over 80% for gpt-oss models and o4-mini (Figure 2).

On agentic data-exfiltration attacks, standard prompt injection achieves 0-2% success (except gpt-oss-20b at 26%), while CoT Forgery injection raises success to 56-70% across all tested models (Figure 3).

Linear role probes show that user-authored text re-wrapped in <tool> tags is still internally classified as user input 76-88% of the time, with toolness never exceeding 20%, indicating role identity is driven by stylistic cues rather than structural tags (Table 1).
Removing stylistic markers via a destyling intervention collapses agent-hijacking attack success rate from 61% to 10%, consistent across all evaluated models (Figure 4(b)).

Falsely-tagged forged reasoning achieves 85% average internal 'CoTness' classification, matching correctly-tagged authentic chain-of-thought text, showing spoofed reasoning is nearly indistinguishable internally from genuine reasoning (Figure 7).

QlKWT5s4Wy.text: SwanSphere uses a divide-and-conquer architecture combining a causal autoregressive language model for semantic planning with a Local Diffusion Transformer (LocDiT) for intra-patch synthesis, enabling streaming spatial audio generation (Section 3).

On video-to-spatial audio generation, SwanSphere (1.09B params) achieves FD 120.28, KL 1.36, and angular error 1.03, improving over the OmniAudio baseline's FD 157.67, KL 1.93, and angular error 1.27, while cutting first-chunk latency from 0.85s to 0.21s (Table 1).

The SwanSphere dataset comprises 165,000 video-audio pairs (~458 hours), built via an automated spatial captioning pipeline that combines acoustic intensity vectors with Gemini 2.5 Pro to generate spatial descriptions, with a test split of 5% of samples with no video-ID overlap with training (Section 4, Table 1).

Removing spatial-temporal negatives from the Spatial Video-Audio Contrastive (SVAC) learning objective degrades angular error from 1.03 to 1.12, showing the contribution of physics-aware contrastive constraints (Table 3).

Ablations comparing model capacity, ODPO fine-tuning, and generation paradigm variants (e.g., semantic-only and CLIP-based conditioning) show the full SwanSphere configuration achieves the best FD (120.28) and KL (1.36) among tested variants (Table 4).

O4PweOea13.text: TVI-CoT interleaves textual reasoning steps (Think token) with visual grounding steps (Look token), dynamically attending to different image regions as reasoning evolves until an Answer token is emitted (Section 3, Figure 1).

TVI-CoT improves over the MLLM-based CoT baseline by +6.1% on MMMU (64.3% vs 58.2%), +3.8% on MathVerse (60.2% vs 56.4%), +3.4% on MathVista (76.6% vs 73.2%), and +3.4% on ScienceQA (95.2% vs 91.8%) (Table 1).
Removing the dynamic text-visual interleaving mechanism drops accuracy by 7.7 points on MMMU and 5.0 points on MathVerse relative to full TVI-CoT (Table 5).

Removing the visual grounding loss reduces performance by 1.9 points on MMMU and 3.0 points on MathVerse, while replacing grounding with random image regions causes a 13.1-point drop on MMMU and 7.9-point drop on MathVerse (Table 5).
Adaptive (dynamic) interleaving outperforms fixed reasoning-step counts, reaching 64.3% on MMMU versus a maximum of 62.3% for the best fixed-step configuration (Table 6).

Ym4KYa1n76.text: FlowTracer constructs an attention-induced directed acyclic graph over generated tokens and computes answer-targeted influence flow to identify a high-flow token backbone connecting question to answer (Section 3.1, Figure 1).
High-flow tokens identified via flow throughput scoring are used for credit assignment, shaping token-level RL rewards that up-weight answer-routed tokens during training (Section 3.3).
FlowTracer-shaped rewards yield consistent gains over standard RL baselines on Qwen3 models across both 1K and 8K context lengths on math reasoning benchmarks (Table 2).
FlowTracer generalizes beyond math reasoning, improving performance on Countdown and CrossThinkQA tasks and on Llama-family models (Tables 3 and 4).

An ablation over token-selection ratios shows performance peaks in the Top-20% to Top-60% high-flow token range, with computational overhead of only 2.1%-4.5% relative to standard training (Table 5, Table 6, Figure 5).

Ffdn32iFeH.text: Right-sized edge accelerators (e.g., Jetson Thor, AGX Orin, Ascend 310P/310B, Intel B60 Pro) can be more cost- and energy-efficient than a flagship RTX 4090 GPU while still meeting VLA control-rate constraints (Section on Model-Hardware Pairing).

The VLA inference pipeline exhibits a two-phase computational imbalance: the vision-language backbone is compute-bound (~840 FLOPs/Byte operational intensity) while the action expert is memory-bound (~64.5 FLOPs/Byte) (VLA Computation Characterization section).

DP-Cache yields up to 2.9× speedup on the RTX 4090 and up to 6.0× speedup on the Ascend 310P when combined with compilation, with only marginal degradation relative to a Diffusion Policy baseline (Acceleration section).
V-AEFusion pipeline parallelism achieves 1.32× speedup on the RTX 4090 and 1.14× on the AGX Orin, with limited additional gains on bandwidth-constrained edge platforms (Acceleration section).

i1OcZc6Y0M.text: Theorem 4.6 (Attention Bottleneck Theorem) upper-bounds the number of distinct states a decoder-only transformer can reliably track as a function of head count H, sequence-to-head ratio log2(L/H), and head dimension d_h, i.e., |S_track| ≤ c(δ,ρ_max)·2^(H·log2(L/H)·√d_h) (Theorem 4.6).
Theorem 4.2 (Decoherence Bound) shows that reasoning accuracy decays super-exponentially with reasoning depth under a context-dependent error model (Theorem 4.2).

A deterministic horizon d* exists beyond which extended neural chain-of-thought reasoning fails and tool delegation becomes necessary, with d* scaling as √(d_h·H) and falling in the range [19,20] steps for 7-8B models and approximately 28 steps for 70-72B models (Section 4, Table 2).

Tool-integrated reasoning (condition C3) achieves 86-94% accuracy versus 24-42% for pure neural chain-of-thought (condition C1) across 12 models and 8 task domains, with effect sizes of Cohen's d = 2.1-3.4 (Table 2).

Real-world validation on SWE-Bench, WebArena, and SQL-Multi confirms a deterministic horizon d* in the range [19,26] and shows tool integration achieves 4.2-4.7× better cost-per-correct-solution than extended neural reasoning (Table 3).

yUvMzLLyfE.text: Rep3D achieves 0.910 average Dice on AMOS-CT, outperforming the UNesT-B transformer baseline by 2.13% (Table 2).
On KiTS, Rep3D reaches 0.736 mean Dice (kidney 0.955, tumor 0.763, cyst 0.490), and on MSD Pancreas 0.723 mean Dice (Table 1).

The spatial bias generator uses two 3D depthwise convolutions (DConv1, DConv2) with kernel size 7 and padding 3, followed by layer normalization and a sigmoid activation, to produce receptive-biased scaling masks in [0,1] that re-weight updates to a 21x21x21 depthwise kernel (Section 3.2).
Adding the lightweight receptive-bias modulation (LRBM) module to a standard 3D UX-Net backbone improves average Dice from 0.890 to 0.897 (Section 5.3).
Ablation over kernel sizes for the modulation network shows a 7x7x7 configuration (0.910 average Dice) outperforms a 1x1x1 configuration (0.905 average Dice) (Table 3).

IbRm6gwmew.text: On SDXL with a 100-step DDPM sampler, LiDAR reaches a GenEval score of 0.585-0.598, matching or exceeding the gradient-guidance baseline DATE's 0.570, while using 9.5x less compute/time (Table 2).
On SD v1.5 with 100-step DDPM, LiDAR attains a 0.478 GenEval score versus DATE's 0.438 (Table 2).

LiDAR computes the Expected Future Reward (EFR) in closed form from marginal samples and forward perturbation kernels, avoiding neural backpropagation through the reward model, as formalized in Theorem 3.1 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).

The two-phase algorithm first draws n coarse lookahead samples with a delta-step solver and reward annotation (Algorithm 1), then guides particles toward high-reward samples via a closed-form Stein score (Algorithm 2, Eq. 17).
LiDAR yields substantial gains using as few as 3 lookahead samples with a 3-step lookahead solver, and reduces memory overhead to 8.90 GiB versus 28.16 GiB for baseline methods (Section 4).
Theorem 3.3 establishes a total-variation convergence bound of O(1/sqrt(delta)) for the lookahead approximation, showing error shrinks as the lookahead step size decreases (Theorem 3.3).

JNdi6E05NJ.text: The language-guided Bayesian optimization method finds LoRA hyperparameters yielding up to 21.46% accuracy improvement on GSM8K and over 20% improvement overall, using only about 30 BO iterations versus an exhaustive search space of roughly 45,000 hyperparameter combinations (Table 1).

A frozen pre-trained LLM is repurposed as a discrete-to-continuous mapping module, encoding domain-aware text templates describing rank, scaling factor, learning rate, dropout, and batch size into a continuous embedding for a Gaussian Process-based BO surrogate (Section 3).

A learnable token (psi) is appended to the domain-aware prompt template to capture residual hyperparameter information not easily expressed linguistically; only this token and a projection layer are trained, with the base LLM kept frozen (Section 3).
Gains are demonstrated across multiple LoRA variants including rsLoRA, DoRA, and PiSSA (Table 2).
An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component (domain-aware prompting, learnable token, projection layer) to the overall performance improvement (Table 6).

47NnSXz3im.text: LongCoT comprises 2,500 expert-designed problems across five domains (mathematics, chemistry, chess, computer science, and logic), with short prompts (median 2K tokens, max 6.7K) but solutions requiring chains of thought exceeding 50K tokens (Section 3.1, Section 3.3).

At release, the best-performing frontier model, GPT 5.2, achieves only 9.83% accuracy on the 2,000 medium/hard LongCoT questions, using an average of 62,046 reasoning tokens per problem, followed by Gemini 3 Pro at 6.08% and Grok 4.1 Fast Reasoning at 2.04% (Figure 4, Section 4.1).

Open-source models score near zero on full LongCoT, with GLM 4.7 at 0.48%, Kimi K2 at 1.23%, and DeepSeek V3.2 at 1.46%, versus higher scores of 5.9%-38.7% on the easier LongCoT-mini subset of 500 questions (Figure 4).

On the LongCoT Math domain, model accuracy is compared against an independent-error baseline computed from Omni-Math subproblem accuracy, showing that actual composed-DAG performance falls well below what independent-error compounding would predict, with degradation worsening as DAG size grows from 1 to 35 nodes (Figure 6, Section 4.2).
